# COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY

OR THE UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL LIBRARY OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, COMPARED WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED THROUGHOUT THE TEXT, AND ALSO WITH HEADINGS AT THE TOP MARGIN OF EACH PAGE DISTINGUISHING AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, YET POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER any one of the Fathers wrote upon any theme may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHAT PLACES OF THEIR WORKS, COMMENTED UPON EACH TEXT OF EACH BOOK OF SCRIPTURE. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one weighs: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time united in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

# THIRTY-ONE BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE TWELVE MINOR PROPHETS BY THE RIGHT REVEREND LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF TUITZ

## PROLOGUE OF LORD RUPERT TO HIS EXPOSITION OF THE TWELVE PROPHETS

[Col. 0009A] 1–3 We do not vainly hope, most illustrious Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, that our discourse is pleasing to the Holy Spirit and to all the holy prophets through whose mouth he himself spoke, when, in proclaiming the mysteries of Christ the Son of God, we use their testimonies fittingly and appropriately. For by one and the same act, while we offer our faith to God, we are also witnesses for them and bear testimony to their faith. We do not doubt that this is pleasing and delightful to them.

For one of them, Isaiah, exceedingly rich in the treasure of faith and in the word of the Lord, says: “And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a large scroll, and write upon it with a man’s stylus: Swiftly strip off the spoils; quickly seize the prey. And I brought to myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah [Col. 0009B] son of Barachiah; and I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: Call his name, Hasten to strip off the spoils; Hurry to seize the prey; because before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8).

What is that large scroll which he says he was commanded to take, if not the entirety of the Holy Scriptures, in which are the faithful testimonies of Christ—the holy One whom God first promised to Abraham? And what was it for him to write in such a book, with a man’s stylus, the name of the child concerning whom he had foretold, “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son” (Isa. 7), if not to receive prophetic grace, becoming one of those who wrote down the testimonies concerning that same coming Christ [Col. 0010A] and who testify that he was God before he came into this world through birth in the flesh?

This is elegantly proclaimed through such a name: “Hasten to strip off the spoils; Hurry to seize the prey,” and through the explanation of the name: “before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians.” For what manner or measure of hastening to strip spoils, or of swift seizure of prey, is it to strip spoils first, to seize prey first, before having a mother or calling a father—who was Joseph, according to the adoption of this child? Thus it is as though he said that this child, whom the Virgin conceived and bore, was God before becoming man, and that he saved Jerusalem and Judah [Col. 0010B] from Rezin king of Damascus and Pekah king of Samaria, son of Remaliah, who were then attacking him together, and likewise from the other enemies from whom that people was delivered by heavenly aid.

Certainly, to write prophecies of this kind was to approach the prophetess of whom he says, “I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.” Who is that prophetess, if not she of whom he had spoken beforehand, the mother of Emmanuel—the Virgin Mary, full of grace—in whom every prophecy was to be fulfilled? This approach to the prophetess is like the entrance of an honoured man into the sanctuary of the Lord with a solemn offering, with a talent of proved and most pure gold to offer.

As witnesses that he thus approached [Col. 0011A] that prophetess, and that he wrote his own portion of the prophecies to be fulfilled in her, he rejoices that he has both apostles from among the Jews and holy teachers from among the Gentiles, in these words: “And I brought to myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah, son of Barachiah.” Uriah, the priest, whose name means “the Lord is my light,” signifies the apostolic dignity. Zechariah, whose name means “mindful of the Lord,” son of Barachiah—that is, “of the blessed of the Lord”—signifies the assembly or congregation of the Church from the Gentiles, adorned with holy teachers. If one considers the writings of all these, namely the apostles and teachers, it is plain that they are witnesses of Isaiah the prophet: that he thought and believed most rightly concerning this child, the son of such a prophetess, since they steadfastly employ his words in the preaching of this faith.

What we have said of Isaiah alone we say also of the other [Col. 0011B] prophets: that in truth it was granted them by the Holy Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills, to take a great scroll—that is, Holy Scripture, of which Moses wrote the first and great portion—and to write upon it with a human stylus; that is, with the same authority by which Moses first wrote, to write something according to their human measure, or something that might be read by a human being; and in this manner to approach that prophetess, and thereby to have two witnesses, that is, believers both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, that they had thought very rightly concerning Christ the Son of God and had spoken in the Holy Spirit. This grace is truly great. For to read that great book has indeed been granted to many, but to write in it, and to be foremost within the canon of Holy Scripture, has been granted to very few.

Therefore, as we said at the outset, we do not vainly hope that our discourse is pleasing to the holy prophets together with Christ, when, in preaching the mysteries of Christ, we honour that same Christ by their confession and the words which they wrote. [Col. 0011C] And to whom would it not be desirable to give delight and exultation in this matter to such and so great heralds of the eternal King, so that they may rejoice that we are witnesses to so great a reality? For in due season they will be able to repay a good return.

Know, my Father, that in this hope or expectation I have devoted labour, as to the other Scriptures, so also to the volume of the Twelve Prophets: seeking Christ, whose truth possessed their hearts, filled their mouths, and guided their pen, so that in all they wrote they might tend toward his glory and honour. I now say something with which you yourself do not disagree: just as we read of a certain land that gold is born there and that the gold of that land is excellent, so one may rightly say of holy prophetic Scripture that in it [Col. 0012A] is found the testimony of Christ the Son of God, and that the testimony of this Scripture is excellent.

You, together with you Cuno, the abbot of the monastery of Siegburg—a small yet faithful peg, fixed in a secure place, a member of the household of faith and knowledge—have urged me on, as in certain other matters, so also in this part, that, though I was sluggish, I might not be able altogether to sleep, but might touch upon this volume as well. This I have now done through the end of Micah, who is sixth in this order. Nahum followed as seventh; but because he says almost nothing about the coming of Christ that properly proclaims him in the literal sound itself, my zeal grew cold, because the delight which had made the difficulty bearable in the others was greatly diminished.

Behold: upon this occasion I sat down with the work unfinished—I, the sluggish one—perhaps intending to undertake nothing concerning the six latter prophets. Why am I now more sluggish than usual in this work? You have given me an empty name, and not without labour.

# RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE PROPHET HOSEA

[Col. 0011C] 5 Hosea is placed first in the order of the Twelve Prophets. How much light of wisdom is required for understanding him, he himself indicates not lightly when at the end of his book he says: “Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them?” [Col. 0011D] (Hos. 14). For by asking in wonder and wondering in his question, he strongly affirms that he has hidden, with diligent and manifold effort, the pearls of spiritual understanding most deeply in a narrow letter, so that whoever among those who meditate upon the law of the Lord finds them after applying all the powers of holy study must truly be counted wise and discerning.

Someone therefore says: To what end was such diligence directed? Did the holy spirit of prophecy, which spoke in this prophet and in the others, wish the treasure of its meaning to remain hidden from us? Is the prophetic spirit of wisdom not benevolent, and for that reason did it conceal itself in such a manner that we might scarcely, or never, find it? On the contrary: this wisdom is hidden and this treasure concealed precisely in order that it might be found. For unless it had hidden itself, it certainly could not today be found.

You will rightly perceive this if you carefully consider the condition of that time. Did the prophets, each in his own [Col. 0012C] age, speak as freely as they are read openly today? Did they not prophesy amid great fear? For one of them says: “If priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord” (Lam. 2), “prophecy and destruction have become terror and a snare” (Lam. 3). Those who prophesied were slain, and prophecy itself became a snare to them, so that they seemed to be slain as though justly and reasonably.

For example, Isaiah, though holy and noble—as one whose son-in-law was King Manasseh—was ensnared by what he had prophesied when he said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. 6). For in the Law the Lord says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Therefore, before unjust judges [Col. 0012D] he was as though ensnared by his own speech and prophecy, because he had dared to utter things contrary to the holy Law and to the Lord himself by writing that he had seen the Lord, although the Lord had said that he could not be seen by a human being. Thus, after a sort of trial, he was condemned. Finally, the Hebrews report that he was sawn asunder by Manasseh, his aforementioned son-in-law.

What do you suppose would have happened to him if, just as he said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up,” he had also stated in plain speech how, or in what order, that same Lord would be crucified by the Jews themselves and only then, by rising from the dead, be lifted up to that high throne at the Father’s right hand? Surely they would not have waited even to condemn him by a trial. Rather, as they did when the blessed proto-martyr Stephen said, “Behold, I see [Col. 0013A] the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7)—he who had indeed been crucified by them—they did not wait for trial to take place, but, crying out, stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord (ibid.). In the same madness, shouting loudly as though zealously for the Lord, they would all have rushed upon Isaiah.

Nor did they fear death merely out of concern for themselves, lest they should be killed, so much as they feared that the sacred writings might be endangered and erased from human memory. For at that time, while prophets were being slain by some, prophetic writings were preserved by others. But if they had openly proclaimed to the Jews so great a crime and the punishment for so great a crime that would befall them, those writings would by no means have been preserved.

For example, when the king burned the words of the Lord which Baruch the scribe had written from Jeremiah’s mouth, cutting the scroll with the scribe’s knife and casting it into the fire, Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah opposed the king, though he did not heed them [Col. 0013B] (Jer. 36). Certainly, had that same Jeremiah written in explicit terms and names what he understood about the passion of the Lord and the coming destruction of the city and of the whole nation which would follow because of it, they would not merely have failed to prevent that scroll from being cut up or burned; they would even have hastened to destroy the entire prophetic Scripture which the Church of Christ now enjoys. Nor would they merely have sent Jeremiah into the pit, as they had already done, but would either have committed him alive to the fire or cruelly killed him by some other means.

At that time, therefore, the age had to be accommodated, so that the Holy Spirit might compose the Scriptures of truth, while truth might not altogether generate for itself a harmful hatred in future ages. For if Christ, the Son of God, speaks in the Psalm: “God showed me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people ever forget. Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 58), why would it not also suit the prophets of Christ to say: “God showed us concerning these harlots, Oholah and Oholibah, one of whom is Samaria and the other Jerusalem [Col. 0013C] (Ezek. 23): do not provoke them too greatly, lest they ever forget me, or lest peoples yet to come always remain ignorant of God. If these women are willing to receive or preserve the Scriptures, exercise prudent discernment; conceal under figures and riddles the mysteries of the Godhead that is to descend to the earth.”

Therefore, when this one prophet—first, as was said, in the order of the Twelve—says, “Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them?” (Hos. 14), and in saying this confirms that he has marked hidden meanings, difficult to understand, within enigmatic language, he is rightly judged not envious but provident. For he stored a good treasure safely for the future co-heirs of grace, leaving its key to him to whom David left it, he who likewise wrote the Psalms in a closed form, so that he himself might open them in the fullness of time to whomsoever he would.

Thus in the Apocalypse he is called “the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts; who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3); and he says to the angel of Philadelphia: “Behold, I have given before you [Col. 0013D] an open door, which no one can shut” (ibid.). May he deign to open for us the door of understanding, through which he deigned to introduce those before us and our Fathers, the teachers of the Church, so that we too, with them, may see what God did, when, and how: he who was represented in the action of this prophet approaching a harlot woman once, twice, and a third time, begetting by her two sons and a daughter, and afterwards still approaching an adulterous woman.

For that the prophet was commanded to do these things in likeness of God himself is attested by the One who speaks in the same book: “I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied vision, and in the hand of the prophets I was represented” (Hos. 12). It is also not irrelevant to ask what cause defended these holy prophets, so hated in their own times that many of them were cruelly killed, and so commended them to that nation, sinful though it was, that it received their writings with the same summit of canonical authority as the Law of Moses itself.

If you ask, the fitting answer is that the authority and judgment of the holy and provident law of the Lord truly came to the aid of their dignity. For the Lord said, as you find in the book of Deuteronomy: “But the prophet who, corrupted by presumption, wishes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him to say, or in the name of other gods, shall be put to death. And if you answer in silent thought, ‘How can I understand the word which the Lord has not spoken?’ [Col. 0014A] you shall have this sign: what that prophet foretold in the name of the Lord has not happened—this the Lord has not spoken, but the prophet invented it through the swelling of his own spirit; and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18).

Since this just and incontrovertible Law says this, then conversely, whatever a prophet has foretold in the name of the Lord and has happened, the Lord has spoken; therefore you shall fear him. Now these holy prophets, when they were sent to foretell from afar the coming of Christ, were also at the same time given or commanded to prophesy things near at hand, by which they might more swiftly be proved truthful: namely, the approaching Assyrian captivity of Israel, likewise the impending Babylonian deportation of Judah, and, in addition, certain lesser matters which we read inserted in their writings.

When, therefore, that captivity or deportation soon happened as prophetic truth had foretold through them, it publicly established that they had spoken truthfully in the name of the Lord and that the Lord had sent them. Thus the fulfilled part of prophecy demonstrated that the remaining and greater matter concerning the promise or coming of the Messiah would also be true.

Having noticed this, I think the reader who seeks in the holy prophets the mystery of the kingdom of God, or the coming of Christ the Son of God, may be helped somewhat not to wonder or take offence when he hears in their sacred writings now the threat of the aforementioned captivity or deportation, now suddenly the promise signifying eternal freedom and the Lord’s coming: perceiving the former prophecy as concerning what is near at hand, the latter as concerning what is far off, and yet seeing things so distant in time conjoined so closely in the letter.

For example, when this same prophet had said: [Col. 0014B] “Blow the trumpet in Gibeah, the horn in Rome (Roma); howl at Beth-aven, behind you, Benjamin. Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of correction; among the tribes of Israel I have made known what is certain” (Hos. 5)—words by which he clearly proclaims the imminent captivity of the ten tribes—he immediately afterwards adds what undoubtedly concerns the release from the invisible captivity of our souls, speaking thus in the person of our Saviour: “In their affliction they shall rise early to me: ‘Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and cure us. He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence. We shall know and follow on, that we may know the Lord,’” and so forth (Hos. 6).

But postponing to their proper place the many things that might be said about this, let us now enter upon the sequence of the prophecy.

# COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET HOSEA

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0015]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0015C]

“The word of the Lord which came to Hosea son of Beeri.” In order that we may be attentive, this Scripture at its beginning is called the Word of the Lord. “The Word of the Lord,” says the blessed Jerome, “which was in the beginning with God, and was God, came to Hosea son of Beeri.”

Nor does this truly conflict with the rule of faith firmly maintained by the Church: that the Word which was in the beginning with God was not made but born, not created but begotten. For this Word came to human beings, but it did not come to God; rather, it was in the beginning with God. Indeed, it came to human beings incidentally and in time, but with God it never did not exist.

Nevertheless, wherever in the sacred Scriptures we read that the Word of the Lord came to this or that person, it signifies great human blessedness. Truth itself commends this blessedness in David when he says: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law” (Ps. 93). For the person to whom the Word of the Lord comes swiftly learns supreme wisdom sweetly and amid great abundance of delight, because this Word is “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1). When it shines upon the human mind, it suddenly enlightens and suddenly teaches. It does not lead the ear of the hearing heart into uncertainty, but makes it so certain, and causes it to hold what it sees so firmly, that it does not hesitate to say that the Word came—came, I say—because that which it announces as future shall most certainly occur and shall be immutably fulfilled; it is impossible that what it declares shall happen should not happen.

[Col. 0015D] Blessed, therefore, is that person, and he may glory greatly in the Lord concerning his blessedness, because he received it not from a human being nor through a human being, but through the revelation of the Holy Spirit (Gal. 1). Only apostles and prophets may glory in the Lord on account of this prerogative of instruction, because they were instructed in this manner: not by a human being, as has been said, nor through a human being, but through the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, whatever they wrote is so authoritative and has so firm a foundation of truth that it is wicked to doubt any saying of any of them. Certainly, no one has ever adequately known the manner in which they were instructed, or the force or speed of their teacher, except one who has deserved to experience it.

Furthermore, it must be known that everywhere among the holy prophets this expression, “the Word of the Lord came,” looks toward the promises, now fulfilled, of the incarnate Word. On account of the excellence of this intention they deserve to be called not merely seers or sons of prophets, but prophets; for seers or sons of prophets could also have been so called because of lesser matters which they foresaw. But Holy Scripture calls prophets only those who foretold the coming of Christ or to whom a word concerning his coming was given.

Nor should it be ignored that Abraham was the first father among them, and John, the forerunner and baptizer of Christ himself, was the last. For first to Abraham was given the promise—indeed, the reiterated promise—of the blessed seed, in these words: “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). Between the two, that is, after the promise and before the reiterated promise, the word of the Lord came to Abraham. This statement was written concerning him once and again because of the aforementioned seed:

“After these things had taken place, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: ‘Do not fear, Abram; I am your protector,’” and so forth. When he said in reply, “But you have not given me seed, and behold, one born in my household shall be my heir,” immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “This man shall not be your heir, but he who shall come forth from your womb, him you shall have as heir.” And he brought him outside and said to him: “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can.” And he said to him: “So shall your seed be.” “He believed the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15).

[Col. 0016C] That Abraham was a prophet because the word of the Lord came to him is attested by the Lord himself, who, reproving Abimelech on Abraham’s behalf in a dream by night, says: “Therefore now return the man’s wife, because he is a prophet, and he shall pray for you, and you shall live” (Gen. 20).

Finally, a statement of this kind is written concerning John the Baptist. Luke writes in these words: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, the Word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness” (Luke 3). That he is or was a prophet is attested by the same Lord when he says concerning him to the crowds: “But what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. 11).

Therefore, whenever we hear in the sacred Scriptures that the speech or Word of the Lord came to holy persons, it is delightful and most beautiful to reflect that this is said in such a way that one should understand: concerning the reality that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). And for this reason John was more than a prophet, while the others were prophets: because he preceded the Word made flesh in birth by six months, a great and prophetic office indeed; yet by no lesser privilege of grace, when already a young man, he pointed to him with his finger, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and deserved to baptize him—the One taking away the sins of the world—in the flowing Jordan (John 1).

But it was too little that those to whom the Word of God came should be called prophets. The Holy Spirit spoke something greater concerning them in David: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81). For what reason, except because the Word of God came to them? (John 10.) For the Lord himself declares this to be the reason when, speaking to the calumniating Jews, after first saying, “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High”’?” he immediately adds: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken” (ibid.), and so forth.

[Col. 0016D] Therefore prophets are gods, because they are those to whom the word of God came. And if they are rightly called gods, are they not also rightly called saviours? If Scripture called “saviours” those through whom God worked temporal deliverance for Israel, for example: “And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, who raised up for them a saviour and delivered them, namely Othniel son of Kenaz” (Judg. 3); and likewise: “And they cried out to the Lord, who raised up for them a saviour, Ehud” [Col. 0017A] (ibid.)—if, then, it called them saviours through whom God delivered Israel temporally, how much more rightly are those called saviours whose labour cooperated with our Saviour God toward our eternal salvation?

Beautifully, therefore, and not without a certain divine foretokening, this one of them, and the first of the twelve, is called Hosea, which is interpreted “saviour.” For he is called the son of Beeri, which is interpreted “of my well.” And who is he of whom God the Father may rightly say, “the son of my well,” except Christ, the only-begotten Son and Word of God, born from the secret place—or the height or depth—of the paternal heart? Therefore this man bears the type of Christ our Saviour not only by office, but also by name, both his own and his father’s.

It follows: “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, king Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of [Col. 0018B] Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.” Uzziah, who was also Azariah, reigned over Judah fifty-two years (2 Chron. 26); and after him his son Jotham sixteen years (2 Chron. 27). Likewise after him Ahaz sixteen years (2 Chron. 28), and after him Hezekiah twenty-nine years (2 Chron. 29): together making about one hundred and thirteen years. Since this is a long period for one man to be thought to have prophesied continuously, at least this must be established: that this prophet touched both the final years of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel—who had already begun to reign while Uzziah was reigning in Judah, as has been said, and reigned forty-one years—and the first years of Hezekiah’s reign. For his prophecy begins thus: “Call his name Jezreel, because yet a little while, and I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.” This occurred almost immediately [Col. 0018C] after the death of that same Jeroboam: his son Zechariah succeeded him, reigned only six months, and Shallum struck and killed him and reigned in his place.

Here one may properly ask what the purpose of this passage is: why it relates that this prophecy continued from the days of Uzziah, during which Jeroboam also reigned, down to the days of Hezekiah king of Judah. To this we must first say that, while Hezekiah was reigning, in the sixth year of his reign—which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel—Samaria was captured, and the king of the Assyrians carried Israel away into Assyria and placed them in Halah and Habor, beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes, because they had not obeyed the voice of the Lord their God (4 Kings 17). Thus the intention of the Spirit of sacred Scripture is to testify that the [Col. 0018D] kings and people of Israel were without excuse, because the Lord never ceased to send prophets among them. In the days of none of their kings was the prophetic voice absent: it threatened the coming wrath of the Lord and foretold the future captivity, until it came, lest Israel might excuse itself on grounds of ignorance while worshipping the calves made by Jeroboam, and indeed Baal, whom Jezebel introduced.

Before Hosea there was Elisha, who also died while Joash, the father of this Jeroboam, was reigning; and before Elisha, Elijah; likewise others, such as Micaiah son of Imlah (3 Kings 22), many sons of the prophets, and so forth. Thus, if we rightly recall from the first Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, and to whom Ahijah the Shilonite foretold the evil to come upon him according to his deserts, the prophetic testimony, as has already been said, [Col. 0019A] was not absent against them until the fulfilment of the foretold captivity. In every respect God the judge is therefore praiseworthy, whereas the people with their kings are without excuse. The title of Isaiah’s book also indicates that he prophesied under the same kings of Judah.

Observe carefully, in the Spirit of God, the preservation of each dignity. Having said, “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah,” he only then adds, “and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.” Yet that Jeroboam was earlier in time than them all; for in the twenty-seventh year of his reign Uzziah, also called Azariah, began to reign in Judah (4 Kings 15). Why, then, is he placed in the sequence after rulers so much younger? Was this done by chance? Certainly not. Rather, the kingdom of Judah was legitimately the kingdom of David; but the kingdom of Israel, torn away from [Col. 0019B] David’s house, was a usurpation and a cult of idolatry: it served not the Lord’s Temple but golden calves. Therefore Jeroboam ought not even to have been mentioned in the order of kings or placed at the head of the title of the holy Scriptures, except for the reason already stated: this prophecy was also directed against those idolatrous kings of Israel whom Elijah, Elisha, and the other prophets opposed, so that unrepentant Israel might be without excuse together with its kings.

Accordingly, although several other kings of Israel reigned at Samaria in the times of these kings of Judah, none is named here but this one alone; and although he was earlier in time, he is placed later in position, as was fitting. For it is enough to show that prophetic admonition was continually given to the kings of Israel: namely, that [Col. 0019C] Hosea began to prophesy in the days of Jeroboam, after Elisha had died, Elisha having prophesied even in the days of his father Joash.

“The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea. And the Lord said to Hosea: Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications, and have children of fornications; for the land, committing fornication, shall commit fornication away from the Lord. And he went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel; because yet a little while, and I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu; and I will cause the kingdom of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

We cannot maintain that “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea” was said because he was the first [Col. 0019D] of those to whom, or in whom, the Lord spoke by the mode of prophetic speech, or to whom the coming captivity of that people was shown beforehand. It may indeed be certain that he was the earliest in time among the other prophets whose prophetic books survive, and that he preceded Isaiah by some years—Isaiah is read to have died near the beginning of Hosea’s book. Nevertheless, there were other prophets in whom the Lord undoubtedly spoke, most notably Samuel and David, Elijah and Elisha, who preceded Hosea by no few days.

If, then, one chooses to understand the phrase, “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea,” as meaning, “The Lord first spoke in Hosea,” nothing contradictory is found, provided that you understand [Col. 0020A] “among those who prophesied under the aforesaid kings.” For Isaiah, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah also prophesied under the same kings.

Nor do we consider it superfluous to give here the interpretations of their names. Uzziah means “strength of the Lord”; Jotham, “the Lord’s completion”; Ahaz, “strength”; Hezekiah, “the Lord’s dominion.” These reigned in Judah, whose name means “confession.” But in Israel—which had made idols for itself and had been separated from God’s Temple and the house of David—Jeroboam reigned. His name means “temporality” or “delay,” because he loved the world and believed that a long stay in it was eternal life, delighting not in future things but in present ones.

Although this is rightly understood as just stated, nevertheless “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea” is also understood in this way: the Lord first spoke in him these things that immediately follow, “Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications,” and so forth. Finally, this point also must not be passed over: the Lord’s speaking *to* Hosea and the Lord’s speaking *in* Hosea are not altogether the same. The Lord speaks to Hosea, or to anyone else, when he sends his words through an angelic appearance or some other manifestation; he speaks in someone when, without any outwardly appearing form, he speaks in that person’s heart through the hidden inspiration of his power.

“Take,” he says, “for yourself a wife of fornications, and have for yourself children of fornications.” To follow for the moment the simple literal sense, the prophet is not blameworthy if he converted a prostitute to chastity; rather, he is to be praised because [Col. 0020C] he made a bad woman good. For a person who remains good is not himself defiled by association with one who is bad; rather, the bad person is changed into good if that person follows the example of the good. These and many similar things have been said, and may be said, in defence of the holy man, who served not his own desire but the heavenly command: by that command, even things that appear shameful or dishonourable are neither shameful nor dishonourable when done.

Moreover, those who are lovers of truth and gladly embrace the spirit everywhere rather than the letter are readily persuaded—or can be persuaded—that none of the things here written concerning an act of fornication happened bodily, but all happened spiritually: that is, by a vision or ecstasy. For it is neither unheard-of nor unusual for someone, taken outside bodily sensation—that is, in ecstasy or in a nocturnal vision—to seem to himself to have taken a wife and begotten children [Col. 0020D] by her. How much more, when a heavenly visitation establishes prophecy, could imaginings of such matters be presented notably through a vision! Does not the Apocalypse of John contain matters much more numerous and extensive than these, all of which, as he himself testifies, he saw and performed in the Spirit?

Here one may properly ask what need there was for these figurative representations, or how the Lord who speaks in the prophet is likened through them in the hand of that prophet, as he himself testifies, saying in the same prophet: “And in the hand of the prophets I was made like” (Hos. 12). Therefore, before we proceed through the sequence of the text, it is pleasing first to set forth what the wondrous God has done according to these analogies with human beings, so that afterwards, when we discuss each action or saying of the analogy according to the time of prophecy, [Col. 0021A] we may at the same time unfold mysteries that are not unknown.

Who does not know that the whole human race withdrew from fellowship with its Creator and, by withdrawing, committed fornication? For to withdraw from the Creator and serve the creature is to commit fornication. Thus the Psalmist says of this sort of fornication: “You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you” (Ps. 72 [73]). Therefore God took a fornicating woman to himself when he approached a people turned away from him, the Chaldean people from which he brought Abraham out: “For I,” he says, “am the God who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. 15). He made a covenant with him and had from his flesh Israel—that is, the seed of God, the children of God, the children of promise. Yet children of fornication were born alongside them: that is, children of the flesh, who are not children of God or children of promise. Of this very distinction the Apostle says: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children; but, ‘In Isaac shall seed be called for you’; that is, not the children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. 9).

These people, in Egypt, where they worshipped the Egyptian gods—as is reproached to them in many places of Scripture, especially in Ezekiel (Ezek. 16)—openly showed that they were children of fornications, and from that time did not cease to commit fornication. Yet Jezreel, that is, the seed of God, was never absent from that people: namely, many who had faith in that blessed [Col. 0021C] seed which God promised Abraham. Conversely, the children of fornication, that is, the children of the flesh, always persecuted the seed of God or the children of promise, not only until Naboth was killed—he is here called Jezreel, for he was a Jezreelite—but forever. Hence also the Apostle: “But just as he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. 4).

Then again, after no small interval of time—that is, after four hundred and thirty years—God approached that fornicating woman and begot a daughter, who should be called “Not having obtained mercy.” For he gave the law on Mount Sinai, which did not give life and did not bring to perfection; and he established the Synagogue, of which, with reference to the portion of the reprobate—which was the greater part—you may rightly say that that daughter did not obtain mercy. “For,” says the Apostle, “the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law but through the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4), and so forth. Since that daughter did not receive this righteousness of faith, she therefore did not obtain mercy; indeed, she obtained wrath. “For the law works wrath.”

A third time God approached the fornicating woman and again begot a son, that is, the prophetic word. For he sent prophets and added their Scriptures for profitable reading. But that fornicating woman not only did not return from her fornications: she was even divided against herself. Behold, two fornicating women have now been made from one: one of them is called Oholah, the other Oholibah in the same prophets. This division of one [Col. 0022A] into two occurred when Samaria, withdrawing with the ten tribes from the house of David, appointed a king for itself; worshipping golden calves in place of God, it prostituted itself also to Baal and the other monstrous deities. This is Oholah. For Jerusalem, with the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin—which itself too worshipped Baal—is Oholibah.

God approached this woman for the fourth time when the Son of God was born from her flesh, from a virgin’s womb. To her, in a manner of speaking, he said: “For many days you shall wait for me; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man; and I also will wait for you, because for many days the children of Israel shall sit without king, without ruler, without sacrifice, without altar, without ephod, and without teraphim” (Hos. 3).

Therefore, in order that the Lord might be likened in the hand of this prophet, he said: “Take for yourself [Col. 0022B] a fornicating wife, and have children of fornications.” Why? “Because,” he says, “the land, committing fornication, shall commit fornication away from the Lord.” “Therefore,” he says, “have children of fornications, that they may be a sign and portent of the things done and yet to be done between this people and me, the Lord of their fathers.” It must be noted that he said not merely, “Because she shall commit fornication,” but, “Because, committing fornication, she shall commit fornication.” He placed first “committing fornication” and then “shall commit fornication,” so that the sense is: because this people has committed fornication away from its God, commits fornication now, and shall commit fornication still more in the future.

“And he went,” he says, “and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore a son.” Gomer means “completed” and “perfect” in our language; Diblaim means “cakes.” It is a mass of fat figs, which people shape in the manner of bricks, pressing and compacting them so that [Col. 0022C] they may remain unharmed for a long time, and which afford a pleasant sweetness in eating. “Therefore I took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim,” he says: that is, I prophesied among a people completed or perfected in the completion and perfection of pleasurable fornication after the golden calves and after the Baals.

“Call the son born from her Jezreel,” he says. Jezreel is a city, the metropolis of the ten tribes, from which Naboth came and in which he was killed. Thus the name Jezreel is used for Naboth himself. The meaning is: Naboth the Jezreelite, though stoned (3 Kings 21) and dead to human beings, lives to me; his blood cries to me, and he will soon receive vengeance, not only from his murderers but even from the man who appeared to have been the avenger of his blood. For this is what he says: “I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.”

For Jehu, at the Lord’s command, killed the house of Ahab because of the sin of Naboth’s blood, as had been foretold to Ahab: “You have killed and also taken possession” (ibid.). And afterwards: “In the place where dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall also lick your blood” (ibid.). Likewise: “Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel” (ibid.). Since, therefore, Jehu did not shed the blood of Jezreel, or Naboth, but rather killed Naboth’s murderers, why ought that blood of Jezreel to be visited upon his house? Plainly because he did not truly obey out of zeal for God, but served his own ambition to reign, once the royal house had been destroyed. He is quite clearly convicted of this because [Col. 0023A] he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, and himself worshipped golden calves—something he would not have done if he had been zealous with true zeal for the Lord’s cause (3 Kings 19).

Therefore he too, or his house, is rightly counted among the killers of Jezreel, that is, the persecutors of the seed of God; and vengeance for such sin is judged due from him and from the rest of the people of Jezreel. And so it happened. After his great-grandson Jeroboam died, under whom this Hosea began to prophesy, Shallum killed Zechariah, Jeroboam’s succeeding son, in the sixth month of his reign and reigned in his place (4 Kings 15), being born from another lineage. Nor is it surprising that the house of Jehu was overthrown, when the kingdom of the house of Israel itself—that is, of the ten tribes—was likewise destroyed. For when Zechariah, the last of Jehu’s line, had been killed, the kings of Assyria immediately captured Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh beyond the Jordan. Then, after a few years—namely forty-nine—from Zechariah, whom Shallum killed, as has been said, the ten tribes were led into captivity in the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign.

This is what he says: “And I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” For near the city of Jezreel, the metropolis of Samaria, there are very broad plains and a valley of immense extent, in which Israel, after battle with the Assyrians, was struck down and carried away captive.

The passage now prompts us to ask why, passing over Naboth’s proper name, when he could have said, “I will visit the blood of Naboth the Jezreelite,” he preferred to say, “I will visit the blood of Jezreel,” which is not the name of a man but of a city, according to its interpretation. For, as has already been said, it means “seed of God” and suits not only one man but all alike who are God’s seed, God’s people, God’s elect. We reply that Naboth alone was not to be visited. Jezebel, Ahab, and the frenzied multitude of the people with them did not persecute him alone; they persecuted and killed all whom they could find who were the Lord’s seed, who prophesied in the Lord’s name, who spoke God’s Word. Hence Elijah’s complaint as he fled: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19).

And who does not know that the bloody madness of that Jezebel, in her own time, extended also into envy? Athaliah, Jezebel’s daughter, after the death of her son Azariah—for she had married Joram, king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, and Jehu had killed her already-mentioned son Azariah—was enraged and raged against the Lord himself. She rose up and killed all the royal seed, certainly not without the favour or consent of the princes. They too, held by her flattering favours and ensnared, killed at her command the outstanding prophet Zechariah during the reign of Joash, who had remained alive, as it is written: “They assembled against him and cast stones at him, by the king’s command, in the court of the house of the Lord” (4 Kings 11). King Joash did not remember the mercy which Jehoiada, Zechariah’s father, had shown him, but killed his son. [Col. 0024A] When he was dying, he said: “May the Lord see and require it” (2 Chron. 24).

Thus Elijah, already mentioned, when he was fleeing and hiding in a cave, answered mournfully when the Lord said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”: “Lord, they have torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” The Lord said: “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord. And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind overturning mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19), and there was the Lord.

Surely, to the prophet who desired the coming of the Saviour, who would take away sins and bring in everlasting righteousness—and whom this Hosea also desires and prophesies—such an oracle was prefiguring the coming captivities both of Israel and of Judah. This prophet too does not pass them over in silence: he pronounces the future evils of both Israel and Judah, and foretells the mysteries of the Saviour’s coming, necessary to our salvation, as the following passages will show in their places.

Finally, in his speaking there to Elijah, the Lord signifies by the great and strong wind, overturning mountains and shattering rocks, the coming captivity of the ten tribes of Israel, which took place under Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, while Hoshea was reigning. “The Lord is not in the wind,” he says: that is, it is not yet the end; the Lord Messiah, who was awaited, has not yet come. By the earthquake he signifies the first deportation [Col. 0024C] of the tribe of Judah, when Jehoiakim king of Judah was to be carried over to Babylon with forty thousand, none being left except the poor (4 Kings 24). “The Lord is not in the earthquake,” he says: that is, it is not yet the end; the Lord has not yet come.

By the fire he wishes the second captivity of Judah and Jerusalem to be understood, when, after Zedekiah rebelled, the king of Babylon came again, and Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house, burned every house with fire, and destroyed the walls of Jerusalem round about (4 Kings 25). “The Lord is not in the fire,” he says: that is, after the Temple has been burned and the city destroyed, the time of the Lord’s coming will not yet be.

“And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze, and there was the Lord.” The sound of a gentle breeze was the hidden and secret coming of the Lord, whom the Virgin Mary conceived as if from a gentle breath—that is, from the Holy Spirit. From the aforesaid wind to the earthquake—that is, from the captivity of the ten tribes to the first deportation of the children of Judah—there were about one hundred and twenty-seven years. They are calculated as follows. In Hezekiah’s sixth year the king of Assyria carried Israel away into Assyria. Hezekiah himself reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem; thus twenty-four years of his reign remained. Added to these are the fifty-five years of his son Manasseh, the two years of his son Amon, the thirty-one of Josiah, then the eleven years of Eliakim, called Jehoiakim, and finally the three years of his son Jehoiachin: the result is 126 years [the printed “XII” is evidently corrupt; read “CXXVI”]. From that earthquake to the fire—that is, from the first deportation to the burning of the Temple and city—were the eleven years of King Zedekiah.

From that fire or captivity to the sound of the gentle breeze, that is, to Christ’s coming, the intervening number of years was revealed to Daniel in these words: “Seventy weeks are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be removed, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed,” and so forth (Dan. 9). Certainly Elijah’s desire was that iniquity should be removed by Christ’s coming and everlasting righteousness brought in, he who at that time, when iniquity abounded, thought himself left alone.

Therefore, because during those same times not Naboth alone but the blood of many prophets and righteous persons was being shed, which heavenly justice ought to require, the proper name Naboth is rightly not used; rather, the name Jezreel, common according to its interpretation, is employed. And in a remarkable way the vengeance to be exacted is foretold as beginning with the most righteous persons of that homicidal people, with the head of the bloody kingdom, such as the house of Jehu then was. That house appeared to have rendered great service by killing Ahab’s house, yet it nevertheless continued the idolatry which caused the shedding of the blood of the saints.

But one may still ask what was so great among prophets or righteous persons about Naboth the Jezreelite that, on his account, all the righteous persons or prophets who were killed should be signified by this name, Jezreel. We answer that his killing truly was great, and ought to have been remembered among the deaths of all prophets and righteous persons, because he was killed in such a manner that before or after him, down to the Passion of Christ our Lord, scarcely anyone besides our Lord himself is reported to have been killed in such a way or in such an order.

For what happened? When Ahab said to him, “Give me your vineyard, that I may make it a garden of olive trees,” and so forth, Naboth merely answered: “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (3 Kings 21). Because of this, Jezebel, indignant and fiercely enraged, promised the vengeance of her authority and wrote letters: “Proclaim a fast,” she said, “and make Naboth sit among the leading men of the people. Send two men, sons of Belial, against him, and let them bear false witness, saying: ‘He blessed [i.e. cursed] God and the king.’ Bring him out, stone him, and so let him die” (ibid.).

In this way hypocrisy, hateful to God, advanced splendidly cloaked in the attractive appearance of legal procedure. Thus Naboth would be killed not merely as a righteous man by unjust persons opposed to God, but as though a guilty man and blasphemer by righteous judges zealously acting for God, keeping the holy law, fasting, humbling their souls in fasting, and proclaiming: “Let us fast, because we have heard such great wickedness in our days, lest perhaps we be swallowed up from the earth together with the blasphemer.” In full knowledge, under a pretence of justice, they contrived such things with workers of iniquity, so that a woman’s madness or frenzied greed might be satisfied. How great, do you suppose, must God’s concern have been when he saw this? What a spectacle it was in heaven when crafty dissemblers, thirsting for such cruel blood [Col. 0026A], proclaimed or celebrated a fast! His death is therefore rightly memorable among the deaths of all prophets and righteous persons, where such an apparatus of hypocrites and such a face of murderers is seen.

Add that in such a killing there is a most splendid type of the Lord’s Passion. For what is different here? But since we have treated this mystery more fully in another work, we prefer now to pass it over.

This one point, however, must not be passed over: what he says, “And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel,” was fulfilled spiritually, as all evangelical and apostolic teaching bears witness. For the bow of Israel—that is, every carnal confidence of Judaism, confidence in circumcision and ceremonies, confidence in proud spirit and blood, [Col. 0026B] by which they gloried against the Lord himself, saying, “Our father is Abraham; we were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8)—as is seen today, was broken. They are not permitted to glory, because not only has their carnal law been despised, but they themselves have been led captive among all nations.

All this happened in the valley of Jezreel, that is, in the humility of the seed of God, which is Christ. For through the humility of Christ’s Passion, just as the nations were exalted by receiving faith in him, so conversely the Jews, despising him, were cast down and broken, according to that prophetic song of the Blessed Virgin: “He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1).

It follows: “And she conceived again [Col. 0026C] and bore a daughter, and he said: Call her name ‘Without Mercy,’ because I will no longer continue to have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will forget them with forgetfulness; and I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God; and I will not save them by bow, sword, war, horses, or horsemen.”

This daughter is a great increase of the preceding sentence. For the prior sentence was: “I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” All of this was fulfilled when the king of Assyria, as has already been said, defeated the ten tribes of Israel in battle and carried them away captive. A calamity equal to that befell Judah when the king of Babylon came, captured the city of Jerusalem, and carried that people off captive into Babylon.

God the judge made a great distinction between the two captivities: Judah’s captivity was to be released after seventy years, whereas the captivity of the ten tribes was never afterwards to be released. This is what he says: “Because I will no longer continue to have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will forget them with forgetfulness; and I will have mercy upon the house of Judah.” That is, “I will not release the captivity of the ten tribes, but I will call Judah’s exiles back from Babylon.”

Yet at the same time when the ten [Col. 0026D] tribes were carried into captivity, the Lord had mercy on the house of Judah (4 Kings 8). For when, in the sixth year of King Hezekiah, Shalmaneser king of Assyria had carried Israel away, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah Sennacherib the Assyrian marched against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them, coming as far as Jerusalem. But the angel of the Lord came [Col. 0027A] and struck 185,000 in his camp; Sennacherib returned and remained in Nineveh. While he was worshipping his god Nisroch in that god’s temple, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword (4 Kings 19).

Thus, if you consider both occasions of mercy, you will see that it was truly said: “I will save them in the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow, sword, war, horses, or horsemen.” For the children of Judah neither drew the bow nor brandished the sword nor mounted horses against their enemies or captors, either on the night when the Assyrian camp was struck or at the time when they were released from Babylonian captivity. Rather, while the Assyrians slept, the angel of the Lord struck their camp. And while the prophets prayed, or other righteous people did so, indeed even angels interceded, in accordance with Zechariah’s words, “And the angel of the Lord answered and said: ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year’” (Zech. 1)—the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians to issue an edict and grant freedom to go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the Lord God in Israel.

“I will save them,” therefore, he says, “in the Lord their God, and not by bow or sword.” If you ask the reason, or the justice of the judgment, why the Lord ought to have mercy not on Israel but on the house of Judah, you must know that there was a great difference in sin between the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah. Some kings of Judah were righteous, namely David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, who committed no sin of idolatry; also Jehoshaphat, except that he formed friendships with Ahaziah king of Israel, whose works were wicked, and with his father Ahab. Therefore Jehu son of Hanani rebuked him when he saw him and said: “You give help to the wicked and join in friendship with those who hate the Lord” (2 Chron. 19). Some of the others also repented and did what was pleasing before the Lord.

But among the kings of Israel there was none who did what was right or pleasing before the Lord, none at all who departed from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. All remained unrepentant; all defended their sins and rejected the Lord’s word. [Col. 0027D] Hence in this prophet the Lord says: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me. For now Ephraim has committed fornication; Israel is defiled. Their thoughts will not allow them to return to their God” (Hos. 5).

Therefore, since there was so great a difference in sin between the one group and the other, judgment rightly had to be pronounced differently upon each. Thus this daughter is rightly called “Without Mercy,” because Israel was not merely taken captive, but was taken captive without the mercy of release.

According to the mystical interpretation likewise, the prophetic Spirit speaks truly. For now that the Synagogue has been rejected, the truth became clear that that daughter did not obtain mercy. She was born when, as was said above, God approached the woman a second time in order to unite her to himself: when, four hundred and thirty years after the covenant had been confirmed, he gave the law on Sinai and the Synagogue was born, a Synagogue destined not to obtain mercy. She was a slave-daughter in name: a daughter in name indeed, but by merits a slave to be cast out.

“For Sinai,” says the Apostle, “is a mountain in Arabia” (Gal. 4). In ancient times Arabia was only that region now unnamed, a wilderness and no small part of Egypt, where Mount Sinai is, on which the law was given and from which Hagar came, Hagar who signifies the Old Testament. Therefore, after saying, “For these are the two Testaments, one indeed from Mount Sinai,” he added: “Bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar” (ibid.), which is joined in signification, of course, to the Jerusalem that now is and is in slavery with her children.

And shortly afterwards, after saying, “But just as he who had been born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now,” he immediately says: “But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman’” (ibid.; Gen. 21). Thus that daughter and slave woman did not obtain mercy, as was already signified in no small matter when the bodies of her children fell in the wilderness and did not enter that land of promise (Num. 14).

No one fails to know, or ought to fail to know, that all the faithful and elect from that same people did not belong to this daughter, but to the earlier son—namely Israel, that is, the seed of God.

It follows: “And she weaned her who was without mercy; and she conceived and bore a son, and he said: Call his name [Col. 0028C] ‘Not My People,’ because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.”

Two increases of misery had now been born, namely a son and a daughter. The son, namely, in order that Israel might be carried captive; the daughter, in order that this same captivity might not be released. Israel, indeed, considered in himself, is not a good son; but in respect to the fact that his blood was to be required, he became an evil for that people. But the daughter truly...

Weaning is the permanence of captivity, to which no nourishment of milk is supplied, no consolation that captivity will be released. What, finally, does this third son mean? What are we to understand by him, except that which his name proclaims—“Not my people”? For this is the greatest increase of miseries: that a captive people, [Col. 0028D] having no appointed time for the ending of its captivity, should be called—and should be—that which God says of it: “Not my people.” For if the people were indeed captive, and its bodily captivity were never to be ended, yet it were not also cast away by God in respect of the soul, this would be an endurable evil, and the condition—or misfortune—of captives groaning for a time would in great part be well ordered. But now the evil is beyond remedy, because the visible Assyrian has seized and holds their bodies, while the invisible Assyrian deceives and possesses their souls.

Let someone now say: “What then will become of God’s purpose?” For God had proposed and promised Abraham that he would bring to himself from his seed an innumerable people, like the stars of heaven; and, having entered into a covenant, he had confirmed that he would be Abraham’s God and the God of his seed: [Col. 0029A] “Look up,” he says, “at the heaven, and count the stars, if you can.” And he said to him: “So shall your seed be.” And immediately it follows: “Abraham believed the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15). Likewise, elsewhere the same God says to him: “And I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you” (Gen. 17).

What then will happen, when there he said, “That I may be your God and the God of your seed after you,” but here says, “For you are not my people, and I will not be your God”? Or how will the splendid number of the elect from his seed be fulfilled according to the number of the stars of heaven, when there he said, “So shall your seed be numerous, like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 15), but here [Col. 0029B] compares them rather with the sand of the sea than with the stars of heaven? For it follows, and he said: “And the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which is without measure and cannot be numbered.” Indeed, the watery sand of the sea is very unlike the shining stars of heaven; and by the very fact that it is here said to be without measure and incapable of being numbered, it conveys Israel’s emphatic rejection: that it possesses neither the measure of any gift nor a place in God’s reckoning.

What then, as we have begun to ask, will become of God’s purpose? Has the Word of God failed? Certainly not. Rather, taking account of the Word of God promising Abraham, let us hold to the definition or determination of the seed of that same Abraham. For, says the Apostle, “Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed [Col. 0029C] children; but, ‘In Isaac shall seed be called for you’; that is, not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but those who are children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. 9).

Therefore, whencesoever they come, wherever they are, and whoever they may be, if they possess faith in the promise—which, as has already been said, was reckoned to Abraham himself as righteousness (Gen. 15)—they are without doubt counted as seed. Accordingly, since the fleshly Israelites have apostasized, other persons are rightly sought, in whom God’s purpose may be fulfilled. It follows, therefore: “And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Sons of the living God’; and the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and shall appoint for themselves one head, and shall rise up from the earth, because great is the day of Israel.”

The apostolic authority has made this passage, sufficiently clear in itself, still clearer [Col. 0029D]. For after the foregoing determination of Abraham’s seed, with a few words intervening, it says: “God, wishing to show wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might show the riches of the glory of his grace upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared in glory. These he also called: us, not from the Jews only, but also from the Gentiles, as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call that which was not my people, my people; and her who was not beloved, beloved; and her who had not obtained mercy, having obtained mercy. And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they shall be called sons of the living God’” (Rom. 9).

By these words he strongly and carefully establishes that this prophecy concerns the Gentiles, who are to be received in the place of those [Col. 0030A] who, being from Israel according to the flesh, or Abraham’s seed, have fallen away through hardness and unbelief. But concerning those who are saved or will be saved from that nation, he immediately adds: “But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved’” (ibid.).

By such a sequence or progression of words, he plainly joins together in Christ the elect from the Gentiles and those saved or to be saved from Israel, teaching that both alike, on account of faith in Abraham’s seed—which is Christ—are all Abraham’s seed; and that this is what the prophet here says: “And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and shall appoint for themselves one head, and shall rise up from the earth, because great is the day of Israel.”

This, finally, began to be accomplished in this way: the children [Col. 0030B] of Israel, namely the Apostles, who are children of Israel both according to the flesh and according to faith, were gathered together with the children of Judah—that is, with the elect from the Gentiles, whom, by bringing them to faith in and confession of Christ, they made children of Judah. They were gathered together in the unity of faith, so that, as the Apostle says, “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. 3). And they appointed for themselves one head: namely, that One of whom the Apostle says, “Therefore, as through the offence of one man came condemnation upon all people, so also through the righteousness of one came justification of life upon all people. For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous” (Rom. 5).

Having appointed this head, “they shall rise up,” he says, “from the earth,” so that they may no longer think upon or seek [Col. 0030C] earthly things, “because great is the day of Israel.” Great is the day and great the illumination of God’s seed, which is Christ—the seed, I say, risen from the dead. Those who rise with him surely rise up from the earth, doing what the same Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

If, therefore, the first ascent having taken place—which is the first resurrection—the bodies too will at last rise from the earth, which will be the second resurrection; and they will follow their head, as members joined to the head. Christ himself also expressed this meaning very beautifully and succinctly when he said: “Wherever the body may be, there [Col. 0030D] the eagles also shall be gathered” (Matt. 24).

By speaking in this way in the prophet, the Holy Spirit wonderfully made the prophecy of the salvation of the Gentiles largely manifest, yet at the same time rendered the writings pleasing to the Jews themselves, or to fleshly Israel, who have always hated the salvation of the Gentiles. For what would they hear more gladly than what is said here: “And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and shall appoint for themselves one head, and shall rise up from the earth”?

For that great evil of discord had long ago befallen Israel and Judah: the kingdom was divided, ten tribes departed from the house of David, and, split into two kingdoms, Israel and Judah at times even fought hostile battles against one another (3 Kings 12). This text [Col. 0031A], however, appears to prophesy to them that at some time Israel and Judah are to be gathered together again into one, and, united under one king, ought to rise up from the earth in order to fight and subdue to themselves the kingdoms of the whole world, far more strongly and warlike than did those kingdoms to which they themselves have hitherto been subject—namely, the Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman kingdoms.

Thus even now they gladly preserve the prophetic text and, unaware of it, serve the benefit of the Gentiles by continually carrying our testimonies with them. Now the prophetic discourse turns in apostrophe to the ministers of that calling, through whom the sons of the living God were to be called from the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” and says:

## Chapter II

“Say to your brothers, ‘My people’; and to your sister, ‘She who has obtained mercy.’” [Col. 0031B] “To your brothers,” he says. To which brothers? Where are they living, and whence do they come? Surely, to brothers who possess Abraham’s faith—wherever they come from, wherever they may be, from whatever nation they derive their origin, whether Jews or Greeks. “To your brothers and your sister”: that is, recognize as brothers only those who are true Israelites, those who have not passed over into the rites of the Gentiles, or who have abandoned the rites of the Gentiles and the worship of idols; recognize their Church as your sister. Call those brothers “my people,” and call that sister “she who has obtained mercy.”

But do not entertain inconsolable grief concerning your brothers, who are your kinsmen according to the flesh, and concerning your sister, the fleshly Synagogue [Col. 0031C], because I have said to those brothers, “You are not my people,” and to that sister, “She has not obtained mercy.” Rather, console yourselves for the grief which you say is so great, and for the pain that is continual in your heart, by the goodness of the recompense: for if your brothers according to the flesh are no longer my people, and if your fleshly sister has not obtained mercy, then, conversely, she who was not my people is now called—and is—my people; and she who had not obtained mercy is now called “she who has obtained mercy” (Rom. 9).

Indeed, the Apostle indicates that this verse also—“Say to your brothers, ‘My people’; and to your sister, ‘She who has obtained mercy’”—belongs to the calling of the Gentiles [Col. 0031D]. He not only took the preceding verse as testimony—“And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called children of the living God”—but also prefaced the sense of this one by saying: “I shall call not-my-people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy” (ibid.).

It follows: “Judge your mother, judge her; for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. Let her remove her fornications from before her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts, lest perhaps I strip her naked and set her as on the day of her birth.”

We have already said above that, in the action of this prophet, the Lord—that is, the prophet—was represented as approaching a prostitute once, twice, and a third time, as has already been stated; and afterwards as still being commanded [Col. 0032A] to love a woman loved by a friend and an adulteress, a point not yet reached. For this passage still represents the likeness of the Lord, who approached that nation once, twice, and a third time: first by confirming his covenant with Abraham; then by giving the Law on Mount Sinai; then by sending the prophets; and finally by assuming flesh from that very people.

It has also been said that, whereas previously there had been as it were one woman—that is, one nation—after the division, when the ten tribes withdrew from the house of David, there were now reckoned two women. Both are accused by the prophets of the crime of fornication: one is called Oholah, which is Samaria; the other Oholibah, which is Jerusalem (Ezek. 23). This prophet prophesied among Oholah, and was from the tribe of Issachar. [Col. 0032B] Therefore Oholah was his mother according to the flesh, as she was also the mother of Amos, Obadiah, and many others who prophesied in the same period.

Yet while they were prophesying, that mother nevertheless committed fornication and did not cease from her fornications; for absolutely none of her kings departed from the sins of Jeroboam. Therefore, now that the symbolic action performed in the person of the prophet has been completed, Oholah—that is, the entire nation of the ten tribes, or its capital Samaria—is openly accused: “Judge your mother, judge her.”

“O prophets,” he says, “O all Israel—that is, the seed of God—what do you find fault with in this my decree? Why do you waver at this my judgment? Is it because your mother is the house of Israel, concerning which I spoke, saying that I would no longer have mercy upon her, but [Col. 0032C] would utterly forget them, whereas upon the house of Judah I would have mercy, that you take offense and wish this judgment to be reversed? Behold: weigh the grounds yourselves; judge for yourselves whether it ought to be otherwise.

“Do you wish, and does she herself wish, that I should again have mercy upon her? Behold, I am ready, provided that she does one thing. What is that? Let her remove her fornications—that is, let her cease to commit fornication. But she does not listen to this; she does not cease to commit fornication. Produce, if you have anything; advance something on her behalf by which she can be justified or defended. Since, through Jeroboam’s agency, she despised me, her lawful husband, and submitted herself to golden calves, has she ever ceased to commit fornication? At what time, or under what king, did she rest?

“Certainly her sister Oholibah did not persist so continuously in fornication; her sister, the house of Judah, did not, I say, persist so continually in madness, although for a time she was greatly mad. In the days of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah, and sometimes under other kings also, she removed her fornications. Judge, therefore, whether I ought to have mercy upon this one as I have upon her sister, the already-mentioned house of Judah, and whether I ought thus to deliver her from the Assyrians, just as I have decreed to bring back that sister’s captivity from Babylon. [Col. 0032D]

“Consider this very ground of judgment in relation both to your mother and to that place of which I said: ‘And it shall be in the place where it is said to them, “You are not my people,” that it shall be said to them, “Children of the living God.”’ For that place is the Gentile world, and it will remove its fornications; but your mother has not removed them, nor does she wish to remove her fornications. Therefore judge her also in this matter, and judge justly: because she ought not to remain in my house with her fornications. [Col. 0033A] Conversely, there is no reason why she who abandons her fornications should be rejected by me, since I am equally the Creator not only of Israel and Judah, but also of the other nations.”

It should be observed with how much circumspection he commanded that the fornications be removed, according to the person and gestures of the prostituted woman, when he said: “Let her remove her fornications from before her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts.” He used “face” for “eyes,” and “between the breasts” for “heart”; for the heart lies between the breasts. Hence in the Song of Songs the chaste bride says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall lodge between my breasts” (Song 1).

It is, of course, through these two—the heart and the eyes—that the flood of fornication is drawn in; afterwards the incontinent body is driven to the act of lust as if by the mighty force of a torrent.
