[Col. 0033B] First, through the windows of the eyes or sight, and of the other senses, all of which are in the face, death enters (Jer. 9); and once the mind has been captured, fornication or adultery is subsequently carried out in deed.

Yet by “fornication” on the face one may properly understand bodily fornication; and by “adultery,” said to be between her breasts, spiritual corruption. For that nation is reproved in the Scriptures as having sinned in both ways. For example, in the one and same sin of Baal-peor, Israel committed fornication spiritually against God and was joined bodily with the daughters of the Midianites. “For they called them to their sacrifices; and they were initiated into Baal-peor, and ate sacrifices of the dead” (Ps. 105).

[Col. 0033C] “Lest perhaps,” he says, “I strip her naked, and set her as on the day of her birth, and make her like a wilderness, and set her as a land without a way, and kill her with thirst.” This is plainly the same as if he were saying: “Lest I do what I have spoken; lest I fulfill the prophetic foreshadowing concerning the sons and daughter whom the prostituted woman Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, bore in the previously described vision.”

“But is what I have spoken not fixed and irrevocable?—when I said: ‘I shall make the kingdom of the house of Israel cease; and I shall no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel; and you are my people, and I shall not be your God.’ What, then, is the point of its being recalled again, when he says, ‘Let her remove her fornications,’ and adds, ‘Lest perhaps I do to her these things or those things which I have spoken’?

“A similar case is this: [Col. 0033D] when judgment had already been pronounced upon King Nebuchadnezzar, so that Daniel said, ‘This is the interpretation of the decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king: they shall drive you away from men, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals’ (Dan. 4), and so forth, Daniel himself says: ‘Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by alms, and your iniquities by mercies to the poor; perhaps God may forgive your offences’” (ibid.).

What ought we to observe from this except that it lies within our choice whether God ought or ought not suspend his judgment? For we ought neither to impute our evils to God nor to suppose that fate rules us—which would be utterly foolish and impious. That is: it is not because God foresaw or foretold something that this or that evil therefore came about; rather, [Col. 0034A] because the evil was going to occur or be done, God therefore foresaw it and fixed beforehand a judgment upon it.

If, therefore, you ask why God fixed an irrevocable judgment, the answer is that God foresaw incorrigible wickedness. Again, if you ask why, after giving judgment, God counsels correction, the answer is that God does so in order that we may know by experience that they are incorrigible: thus, although he expects that they will not return, God nevertheless invites them to repentance through great patience.

Therefore the prophetic discourse, circumspect on every side and full of the eyes of providence, speaks thus: “Let her remove her fornications from before her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts, lest perhaps I strip her naked.”

Why, then, did he not say, “Lest I strip and make her naked” [Col. 0034B], but rather, “Lest I strip her while naked”? Or how can she be stripped if she is already naked? It may indeed be understood in this way: “lest I strip her naked,” that is, lest by stripping her I make her naked. Yet it seems better to understand it thus: that she is already naked and still has something of which she may be stripped. For nakedness is twofold, or double: one visible, the other invisible. Invisible nakedness occurs when the soul is stripped inwardly of the glory or grace of God, in accordance with which Holy Scripture says of that same people: “Moses saw that the people were naked—for Aaron had stripped them for the disgrace of their filth and had made them naked among their enemies” (Exod. XXXII).

For this was said because they had made and worshipped the calf. And, as the psalm says: “They changed [Col. 0034C] their glory into the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Ps. CV). For this reason they had been stripped of God’s help; indeed, for this reason God said that he would destroy them, had not Moses himself stood before him on their behalf, with a broken and contrite heart. Visible nakedness occurs when outward adornment and outward prosperity are also removed—such as, among other things, the distinctive glory formerly possessed by that people in the city of Jerusalem and in the Temple which Solomon built there.

Certainly, when the prophet here uttered these words, Samaria—or the ten tribes—was already naked with that nakedness of which Scripture, as has been said, declares: “Moses saw that the people were naked,” and so forth. For that took place and was said on account of the crime of one molten calf. Here, however, the sin of Jeroboam [Col. 0034D] reigned over them in two golden calves. And because that adulterous people had thus stripped itself of the help or grace of God, it surely deserved also to be stripped of visible and temporal goods: that is, of all the resources of that land which God, her former and lawful husband, had bestowed upon her.

He therefore says: “Lest perhaps I strip her naked.” As though he said: Lest I take from her the adornment of temporal and visible glory, so that she may be stripped in the eyes of human beings—whose eyes alone she knows how to fear—because she is already naked in my eyes and is not ashamed of that nakedness.

And immediately he adds: “And I will set her as on the day of her birth; I will make her like a wilderness; I will set her like an impassable land; and I will kill her with thirst.” What was the day of birth [Col. 0035A] of that adulteress? Surely it was the day or time when her fathers went down into Egypt and the sons of Jacob became sojourners in a land not their own, far from the land that had been promised to them, because of their crime against their brother Joseph, whom they sold. For this reason God called a famine upon the land: Joseph had been sold by them as a slave; and for this reason, when they went down into Egypt, they became strangers and were justly subjected to bondage by the permission of God the Judge.

There that adulterous woman was born, because, as the children of Israel grew and multiplied there, a people was made from very few persons. And what was she like there, she of whom we are now speaking, when she was born? Certainly naked with both kinds of nakedness already described. For scarcely anyone does not know that, in that first beginning [Col. 0035B], she was naked of external goods and of every earthly prosperity. She then possessed neither kingdom nor any sovereignty; nor could she glory in any honour of this world when she served under whips and blows, in mud and brick, while so many such masters mocked her.

Moreover, who does not know that in those same beginnings she was also naked of the glory of the God of her fathers? For she also served the monstrous gods of her masters, the Egyptians, in accordance with the prophetic testimony of Ezekiel: “Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother; and they committed fornication in Egypt; in their youth they committed fornication there; there their breasts were pressed down, and the breasts of their virginity were crushed. Their names were Oholah, the elder, and Oholibah, her younger sister. And I possessed them, and they bore [Col. 0035C] sons and daughters” (Ezek. XXIII), and the rest.

Therefore, when he says that he will set her “as on the day of her birth,” what else must be understood but that, as he had already said, she will be naked and stripped: naked of the glory of the one God, stripped of possessions or of the honour of kingship and every temporal power, just as she was when she served in Egypt? Note also how aptly he adds: “And I will make her like a wilderness, and I will set her like an impassable land, and I will kill her with thirst.” He did not say, “I will lead her through the wilderness and through an impassable land,” as he did after the day of her birth, when he led her out of Egypt. Rather, he says, “I will make her herself like a wilderness, and I will make her herself like an impassable land,” so that she herself may be a wilderness and a deserted [Col. 0035D] or impassable land: deserted by God; impassable and solitary, that is, destitute of every throng of holy angels and of the vigilant protection of Michael, once her prince.

Again, he did not say, “I will weary her with thirst,” as likewise happened when he led her from Egypt after that same day of birth; rather, he says, “I will kill her with thirst,” so that she may no longer drink from the rock that was struck with the rod of the cross, and of which the lifeless rock then poured forth most abundant waters for them as a figure.

He further added: “And I will not have mercy on her children, because they are children of fornications.” Children differ from their mother in the same way that an imitator of wickedness evidently differs from its inventor. For just as, in a favourable sense, the mother is a soul that has conceived the Word of truth from the Spirit of God, while a son or daughter [Col. 0036A] is one who, by hearing the Word of teaching from her mouth, makes progress: so, in the unfavourable sense, any soul that invents evils is a mother, and whoever is deceived by her is a son.

Thus, in that people the adulterous mother is the Synagogue, and the children are the members of the people whom she deceives. Although such a mother bears greater condemnation than her children, nevertheless, because there is little difference in fault between deceiving and being able to be deceived, maternal condemnation is rightly poured out also upon the children when he says: “And I will not have mercy on her children.” Why? “Because,” he says, “they are children of fornications.” This is the same as saying that they too are incorrigible or unchangeable.

For Wisdom, speaking of such persons, after it had said, “But, judging them in parts, you gave them room for repentance,” immediately adds: “Not being ignorant how wicked [Col. 0036B] their nature is, and their innate malice, and that their thought cannot be changed forever. For they were an accursed seed from the beginning” (Wis. XII). All this is expressed here briefly by the phrase, “because they are children of fornications”: namely, that their nature is wicked, their malice innate, their thought incapable of change forever, and that they too, like the Amorites and Hittites, are an accursed seed.

Yet statements of this sort do not blame the nature God created; rather, they most forcefully rebuke the abuse of nature, because accidental wickedness, through habit, has been transformed into nature. He therefore justly defends the judgment in which he said, “I will not have mercy on her children,” by saying, “because they are children of fornications.” Nevertheless, [Col. 0036C] the invincible disputant, the Word of God, further confirms the same reason by adding: “Because their mother has committed fornication.”

For we must remember that the present passage is a judgment between the adulteress and God, once her lover, beginning from the words: “Judge your mother; judge.” For he had given her a choice, or free will, by saying: “Let her remove her fornications”—understand: if she wishes the judgment to be changed which I uttered, namely, “she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.” But she stubbornly persists in her fornications and loves adulteries. It follows, therefore: “And she who conceived them has been put to shame, because she said: ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my waters, my wool and [Col. 0036D] my flax, my oil and my drink.’”

“She who conceived them,” he says, “has been put to shame”: that is, she is ashamed as one is usually ashamed when convicted and defeated in a lawsuit, having nothing to mutter against judges or accusers, convicted by manifest and inexcusable guilt. For when I sent my prophets, I said to her—as I still say now—“Let her remove her fornications from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts”: that is, let her cease to worship golden calves and to make Baals for herself. But she said—and even now obstinately continues to say—“By no means; rather, I will go after my lovers.” Nor did she say this only in words: she also defended her words by deeds, killing those same prophets. Hence Elijah, fleeing, complained: “Lord, they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets [Col. 0037A] with the sword; and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (III Kings XIX).

Thus she said: “I will go after my lovers,” the demons whom she worships in idols, calling them, in the most foolish error, her lovers, though they are enemies of the human race; and she despises me, the true God and true friend, just as a woman might despise her lover. But how, or when, did she say—or begin to say—“who give me my bread and my waters, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink”? Surely when, coming up out of Egypt, she so quickly departed from the way of the Lord, made herself a molten calf, worshipped it, and, while sacrificing, said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII). Then she began to say of her false lovers that they gave her her bread and [Col. 0037B] waters; and she lied.

For it was not they, but the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, who rained bread from heaven upon them and poured water from the rock by the hand of Moses. Again, when she appointed golden calves for herself, she lied when she spoke under the prompting of Jeroboam, whom, having abandoned the house of David, she followed in adultery: “Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (III Kings XII). Certainly, when she said, “who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” she was at the same time asserting that she had received from them everything that she was able to possess or obtain from the time she came up from Egypt.

All these things the prophetic discourse here aptly expresses, maintaining the metaphor of the woman already begun, depicting her as applauding herself: “They give me my bread and my waters, my wool [Col. 0037C] and my flax, my oil and my drink.” Wool and flax are the material instruments of every woman’s work. Oil and drink, moreover, are both the things and the names of pleasure. Bread and water are necessities, because the weakness of human nature cannot subsist without them.

In all these things the adulteress is shown to be a liar: not those calves, nor Baal, whom Jezebel introduced, but God, one and true, bestowed these things upon her, in order that, moved by his benefits, she might love him, abandoning all the abominations of foreign gods, as it is written: “And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

It follows: “Therefore, behold, I will hedge [Col. 0037D] your way with thorns; I will enclose it with a wall, and she shall not find her paths. She shall pursue her lovers and shall not overtake them; she shall seek them and not find them. And she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now.’”

The interruption of this true and just denunciation should be carefully observed. For he had not yet completed the harsh denunciation of her guilt, when he suddenly inserts, so quickly, a certain sweetness of promise—especially in saying, “And she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now.’” Although the kings and rulers of that people were so impatient of such statements as these now being made—“because they are children of fornications,” “because their mother has committed fornication,” and so forth—that they killed many of the prophets, [Col. 0038A] they could nevertheless bear more patiently words of this kind, in which the children of Israel are foretold to return to their God.

Accordingly, after this brief insertion of a mitigating sweetness, he at once resumes the accusation he had begun and says: “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her and gold, which they made into Baal. Therefore I will turn back and take away my grain in its season, and my wine in its season; and I will free my wool and my flax, which covered her shame. And now I will uncover her folly in the sight of her lovers, and no man shall deliver her from my hand. I will make all her joy cease: her festival, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her festal times. And I will destroy her vine [Col. 0038B] and her fig tree, of which she said: ‘These are my wages, which my lovers gave me.’ I will turn her into a forest, and the beasts of the field, birds of the sky, and creeping things of the earth shall devour her. And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals, on which she burned incense and adorned herself with her earring and necklace, and went after her lovers and forgot me, says the Lord.”

We have set down all this here in continuous course so that we may likewise connect what follows with its proper sense. For just as the words, “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine,” and so forth, must in construction be joined to the preceding words, because she said, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my waters, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink,” so likewise to the words, “And she shall say: ‘I will go [Col. 0038C] and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now,’” must be joined in construction the following words: “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and lead her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart; and I will give her her vine-growers from that same place, and the valley of Achor for the opening of hope. There she shall sing as in the days of her youth and as in the days when she came up out of Egypt. And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: she shall call me ‘my husband,’ and shall no longer call me ‘Baalim,’” and so forth.

For she was not to be rewarded because she burned incense to Baal and adorned herself with her earring and necklace, went after her lovers, and forgot the Lord—so that the Lord should say, “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and lead [Col. 0038D] her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart,” and so forth. Rather, it was because, in seeking her lovers and not finding them, she would say what was said above: “I will go and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now.”

She was to be allured by the Spirit of grace and the outpouring of mercy. Thus the divine discourse, most experienced and supremely powerful in medicine, dispenses its carefully weighed and proportioned utterances, mixing bitter things with sweet and sweet things with bitter. It avoids and escapes offending childish lips and an impatient throat, in order somehow to pour in the remedy, however tempered, completely, and for it to be held inwardly under the highest authority, so that Holy Scripture may possess the Holy Spirit.

Nor does it accomplish this as though by flattery, nor does it promise to the same generation which it had called children of fornications the boast of secret address and the dispensation of faith. Rather, the prophetic discourse proceeds with true discernment and discerning truth, recognizing within one and the same people those to whom bitter things and those to whom sweet things are rightly offered. For one and the same people, or Synagogue—indeed, also the Church—contains within itself both good and bad: those who are truly called and are the body of Christ, and those who are called his body because of pretence, though they are not.

Hence comes Tyconius’ judgment among the seven rules, concerning the mixed body of the Lord, or the feigned and true body of the Lord; and it has great force in this place, so that you may discern and understand distinctly that in one and the same people or Church there are both those to whom the most sweet consolation of grace is gently offered and those to whom, because of an unrepentant heart, wrath and tribulation are promised.

And who could worthily admire prophetic wisdom in this: that just as the good and the reprobate are mixed and cannot now be distinguished, so it mixes and moderates its utterances, and one cannot determine or discover which human persons it justifies and condemns? Let secular persons, then, admire the artful compositions of secular rhetoricians, contrived to win human favour. Let ecclesiastical and spiritual persons admire the true and discerning eloquence of the saints through whom God spoke.

Having said this briefly, let us now, for the continuation of the text, repeat those same prophetic words and examine each point more carefully. “Therefore,” he says, “behold, I will hedge her way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a wall, and she shall not find her paths.” The way or path of one who says, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my waters,” leads down to hell. If such paths are smooth and without obstacles, so that the soul which turns away from its Creator prospers in temporal prosperity, it can scarcely, or never, be recalled or hear the warning voice behind it. But if adversities arise and temporal tribulation or distress overtakes one who is running, then, as has often happened, that person remembers the Lord his God.

Thus it is written of the children of Israel themselves, against whom this prophetic discourse is chiefly directed: first in Egypt, “because they groaned because of their works, they cried out, and their cry because of their works went up to the Lord; and he heard their groaning” (Exod. III). Then, in the book of Judges, it is repeatedly written that, when they had forsaken the Lord and he therefore handed them over to the nations, they cried to the Lord, and he often delivered them (Judg. III).

Therefore, when he now says, “Behold, I will hedge your way with thorns and enclose it with a wall,” this is great mercy. For if he did not do this, God would then rather be angry and have forgotten his mercies; as the Psalmist, having said, “The sinner has provoked the Lord,” immediately adds, “according to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek” (Ps. IX). The thorns of adversity usefully prick and wound the foot of one running toward evils [Col. 0040A] and craving destructive delights, so that, at least warned by the prick of such thorns and hindered by such a wall, the rational soul may say: “I will go and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now”; that is, “I will serve the living and true God and not the pride of human beings or evil spirits, because even in this present life it is much sweeter to bear the Lord’s yoke than to become the servant or slave-girl of human beings.”

Some from that people did this; they reflected in this way and, returning thus to their heart, fled the gates of eternal death which they had approached.

Next, it should be noted how wisely the divine discourse rebukes that falsehood which says of its lovers, “who give me my bread, my waters, my wool, my flax, my oil, and my drink.” For it says: “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil [Col. 0040B] (Ps. IV), and multiplied silver for her and gold, which they made into Baal.” She did not know what she ought not to have failed to know: namely, that the Israelite people did not become wealthy as other nations did. Other nations acquired or possessed lands by hereditary right from their powerful ancestors in this world. But this people sprang from fathers who were strangers and newcomers.

Abraham was a stranger, Isaac a stranger, Jacob a stranger, “passing from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people” (Ps. CIV), and they possessed no land of their own. For, as the Apostle says, they awaited a city having foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb. XI). Their faith indeed earned this, that God promised also to them and their seed what they did not seek, namely the lands or regions of nations. But those who immediately sprang from them—the children of Jacob—made themselves unworthy of the same promise by selling their brother Joseph (Gen. XXXVII). For this reason they became strangers and served in Egypt.

Moreover, in the wilderness through which he led them, though by the grace of their Deliverer they had been freed undeservedly, they nevertheless made themselves unworthy of that same promise, so that the Lord said to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Let me alone, that my anger may rage against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII). Thus, those who inherited no land from paternal possession [Col. 0040D] would not have deserved to obtain even the land which divine generosity had promised them because of the faith of their fathers, unless God, in order to establish his glory and truth, had suspended from them the wrath deserved together with their fathers and shown mercy, Moses pleading with him in contrition—that is, in the deepest humility of heart: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and I will give all this land of which I have spoken to your seed, and you shall possess it forever’” (ibid.).

She did not know this; but the seven women understood it very well, who say in Isaiah: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called [Col. 0041A] upon us; take away our reproach” (Isa. IV). For all the Churches of the nations say this as a rebuke to this harlot, who possessed neither bread to eat nor clothes to cover herself, but received them on the condition that she should call upon the name of the Lord, as the Psalmist says: “And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. CIV).

“We,” say these women, “ask nothing of you as wages of this kind: that, in order that we may receive your Gospel or faith, you should grant us foreign lands or regions. Rather, we shall eat our own bread and cover ourselves with our own garments, which we have before knowledge of your name. Indeed, we shall gladly share our bread and clothing with you and with those who preach your name; only deign to be called and to be [Col. 0041B] our God, and take away from us the reproach of our former life or conduct, so that we may not be without a husband and may not, as hitherto, be without God in this world.”

Let him therefore say: “And she did not know”—that is, she was unwilling to know or remember—“that I gave her grain, wine, and oil,” by giving her a land fertile in grain, wine, and oil; “and I multiplied silver and gold for her,” especially in the days of Solomon, of whom Scripture relates: “There was no silver, nor was it counted of any value in the days of Solomon, because the king’s fleet went by sea with Hiram’s fleet once every three years to Tarshish, bringing from there gold and silver, elephant tusks, apes, and peacocks” (III Kings X).

From that abundance of gold Samaria, separating itself from the house of David and the house of Solomon, first made two golden calves and then Baal. Therefore, after saying, “I multiplied silver and gold for her,” he fittingly immediately adds: “which they made into Baal.” O dreadful ingratitude! From my gold and my silver they made things contrary to me: calves, Baal, and other monstrous deities. “Therefore I will turn back and take away my grain in its season, my wine in its season, and free my wool and my flax, which covered her shame.”

“I will turn back,” he says, “and, having turned back, I shall go away; I shall withdraw and abandon her, so that, as I have already said, she may not be my wife and I may not be her husband.” He says this rightly with respect to those whom he foresaw would not repent. For what was said before—“She shall pursue her lovers and shall not overtake them; she shall seek them and not find them; and she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband’”—was said with respect to those who have returned or will return to the Lord, at least after experiencing evils, when the soul, brought to understanding through affliction, has found that those whom it followed and sought as lovers were not lovers but, as they truly are, most cruel enemies.

“I will turn back,” therefore, he says—that is, I will withdraw—and this woman will no longer be my wife. Nor content with this, I will also remove temporal goods which I did not bestow upon her as a first dowry. This is what he immediately adds: “And I will take away [Col. 0042A] my grain in its season, and free my wool and my flax, which covered her shame.” The meaning is: I gave her excellent land, producing grain in its season and wine in its season. Such grain and wine are mine because the land itself, as I said through Moses, is mine: “you are my tenants” (Lev. XXII).

Here, certainly, by grain and wine he intends all things that that land could produce for sustenance. By wool and flax, moreover, let us understand all clothing. “I will take away,” therefore, he says, “my grain and my wine, and free my wool and flax”: that is, I will reduce her to poverty and to complete want of food and clothing, so that, as was said above, she may be as on the day of her birth; that is, possess nothing in her own right, as when she was born and served in Egypt, where she is known to have possessed nothing except the punishment of miserable servitude.

And the sharpness of the expression deserves careful notice when he says: “I will free my wool and my flax.” This is as though he said: Her perversity is so great that even inanimate things ought to be pitied because they serve her, and wool and flax are in great captivity because they minister to the uses of one who is a slave of sin.

But how or when did these cover her shame? Leaving aside for the moment the common use by which the bodies of men and women everywhere were covered—although even this was most unworthy, that, clothed in garments which God had given, they defiled themselves with lusts and prostrated themselves before images—leaving that aside, how magnificently did the Lord’s wool and flax cover her shame in this: that the sanctuary of the Lord and all the worship of his tabernacle or priesthood were wonderfully fashioned from wool and flax, according to the pattern which he himself prescribed to Moses, and were then found in that people alone.

For of the vestments which Moses made for his brother Aaron, according to the order or command of the Lord saying, “These shall be the vestments in which Aaron is sanctified to minister to me: the breastpiece and ephod, the tunic and close-fitting linen garment, the turban and the belt. You shall make them for him and his sons, that they may exercise the priesthood for me; and you shall take gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen” (Exod. XXVIII)—of the beauty and sacramental meaning of these things no discourse of ours suffices to give an explanation.

What shame of that woman—that is, of the Israelite people—did that wool and flax cover? Surely both her actual sins and original sin, after whose commission our first parents covered their shame, that is, their private parts, with fig leaves (Gen. III). The ornaments of wool and linen used in priestly worship covered that shame in that people. It should be noted that they covered it indeed, but did not erase it. For only by the blood of Christ Jesus is such shame not merely covered but also erased and washed away.

Accordingly, when he says, “I will free my wool and my flax, which covered her shame,” this must be understood as though he said: I will also take away from her the shadowy priesthood, by which the common nakedness of humankind was in some measure covered in this people. For later he says to her: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, that you may not exercise priesthood for me.”

It is therefore a great reproach to priests of this kind when wool and flax are said to be freed as though from ignoble servitude—things for which it is certainly as great a nobility as can belong to inanimate objects to be employed in the worship of the Lord’s priesthood or altar (III Kings XII).

It continues: “And now I will uncover her folly in the sight of her lovers, and no man shall deliver her from my hand. And I will make all her joy to cease—her feast, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her temporal festivals.” Once, as has been said, the Lord’s wool and flax which covered her shame have been freed, her folly is uncovered in the sight of her lovers, so that she appears contemptible in the eyes of those whom she perversely desired to please. For when captivity came upon that people, she was so deprived of temporal goods that she had nothing with which to rejoice by celebrating her festivals. Certainly she appeared base among the nations, and those nations—whose masters she had prostituted herself to as lovers—mocked her.

Likewise, what follows was certainly fulfilled: “And I will destroy her vine and her fig tree, of which she said: ‘These are my wages, which my lovers gave me’; and I will turn her into a forest, and the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the creeping things of earth shall devour her.” For from the time she said, after the golden calves were formed, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt”—which was to say, “These are my wages, which my lovers gave me”—she did not cease to commit fornication with them. For this reason the coming army of Assyrians and Chaldeans devastated everything that grew in that land, especially its most delicate figs and vines; and, when the inhabitants failed, the beasts of the field, birds of heaven, and creeping things of the earth freely devoured what grew.

Yet this was not the end. The punishment of the unrepentant was not to be completed or ended by that hostile devastation alone; eternal vengeance accompanies temporal vengeance, as Moses declared in the song of Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath and shall burn even to the uttermost parts of hell” (Deut. XXXII).

It follows, therefore: “And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals [Col. 0043D], on which she burned incense and adorned herself with her earring and necklace, and went after her lovers and forgot me, says the Lord.” When he says, “I will visit the days of the Baals,” that is, the days or festivals of idols—*Baalim* being a plural form derived from the singular *Baal*—the words “I will visit” must be understood to mean “on the day of vengeance.” For this is what he said to Moses when, in the wilderness, the people first made an idol for themselves, namely the molten calf: “But on the day of vengeance I will visit upon them this sin also” (Exod. XXXII).

Whatever idols that people worshipped from that time onward are all signified here together under the one plural name *Baalim*, because Israel was at that time defiled by the worship of Baal, when this prophet prophesied; and Baal was almost the chief ground of the prophets’ accusation, because on his account Jezebel killed the prophets of the Lord.

But what is that day of vengeance except the same day which must be believed to be the day of salvation? For the time or day of which the Apostle says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI), is a day of salvation or propitiation for believers, but conversely a day of vengeance for unbelievers. On it he avenges Jewish unbelief—he of whom the Psalmist says: “God of vengeances, Lord; God of vengeances has acted freely. Rise up, judge of the earth; render recompense to the proud” (Ps. XCIII).

On this day of vengeance the days of the Baals are visited upon that people, in a visitation known to the whole world: for they were made captives in body and cast into outer darkness in soul because of the days of the Baals, on which their fathers burned incense, and whose iniquity they imitated in such a manner that they deservedly undergo judgment of condemnation on its account.

Now the first idol they worshipped after the exodus from Egypt was made from the ornament of women’s earrings, as it is written: “And Aaron said to them: ‘Take the golden earrings from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.’ The people did as he commanded, bringing their earrings to Aaron. When he had received them, he shaped them by a founder’s craft and made from them a molten calf. And they said: ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt’” (Exod. XXXII).

Rightly, therefore, after saying, “I will visit upon her the days of the Baals, on which they burned incense,” he immediately adds: “And she adorned herself with her earrings and necklace.” For, because she first made an idol for herself from her earrings, as has been said, she is rightly blamed for adorning herself with her earrings and necklaces in honour or worship of the Baals. Thus, in every idol she subsequently worshipped, the form of the first idol, made from earrings, is justly brought to remembrance by God the Judge, who speaks in jealousy: “And she went after her lovers and forgot me.”

It follows: “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and lead her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart; and I will give her her vine-growers from that same place, and the valley of Achor for the opening of hope. There she shall sing as in the days of her youth and as in the days when she came up from Egypt.”

“Therefore,” he says, “behold, I will allure her.” But he had said before: “And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals,” and so forth. Does the discourse refer in both cases to one and the same group, when there it speaks of wrath but here plainly sounds grace? Therefore, as has already been said above, the discourse returns to the better part: that is, to the part which, at least warned by evils, finally recognizes herself and her God, and says the words which this same prophet had previously set forth above: “I will go and return to my former husband, because I was better off then than I am now.” For
that this may become clearer, the whole chapter must be set down here.

Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and lead her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart; and I will give her her vine-dressers from that very place, and the valley of Achor, for the opening of hope. And there she shall sing as in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt. And [Col. 0045A] it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that she will call me “My Husband,” and will no longer call me “Baalim.” And I will remove the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their names. And on that day I will make a covenant for them with the beast of the field, with the bird of heaven, and with the creeping thing of the earth; and I will break bow, sword, and war from the land, and make them lie down in safety. And I will betroth you to myself for ever; I will betroth you to myself in judgment and righteousness, in mercy and compassions; and I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And it shall be on that day: I will answer, says the Lord, I will answer the heavens, and they shall answer the earth; and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these shall answer Israel. And I will sow her for myself in the land; and I will have mercy on her who had been without mercy; and I will say to my [Col. 0045B] people, “You are my people,” and he shall say, “You are my God.”

The slow-moving yet distinct conclusion of this lengthy chapter, or abundant promise, must indeed be carefully noted. After he said, “I will allure her, I will lead her, I will speak to her heart, I will give her vine-dressers, and there she shall sing, and she shall call me ‘My Husband’”; and then, by apostrophe, “I will betroth you to myself”; and again, “I will sow her for myself, and I will have mercy on her”—as though you were to ask and say: “Whom will you allure? Whom will you lead? To whose heart will you speak? To whom will you give vine-dressers? Who is she that will sing, or that will call you her husband? Whom will you betroth to yourself, or whom will you sow for yourself? And on whom will you have mercy?”—he immediately answered with a deliberate response and expression, saying: “Her who had been without mercy; and I will say to not-my-people: ‘You are my people.’”

That this is so, as we have said, [Col. 0045C]—namely, that these words refer to her who said above, “I will go and return to my former husband”—and that she is every soul whatsoever that turns to the Lord, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles, the Apostle too testifies. For, after he had said, “God, wishing to display wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory,” he immediately added: “Even us, whom he called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles; as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call not-my-people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy’” (Rom. 9).

Meanwhile, this too must be noted: he did not say, “I will have mercy on her who is without mercy,” but, “on her who had been without [Col. 0045D] mercy.” The Israelite nation is now without mercy, and this is so, as was said above, from the time when the ten tribes were carried into captivity by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians. Therefore it was said above: “And she conceived again and bore a daughter; and he said to her: ‘Call her name Without-Mercy, because I will no longer continue to have mercy upon the house of Israel,’” etc.

Accordingly, the remaining tribe of Judah too is now without mercy, because the Jews were cut down by Roman swords and carried captive among all nations; it is plain that they are without mercy. But the Gentile world had been without mercy; now, however, it is not without mercy, God saying in this prophecy: “I will have mercy on her who had been without mercy.” Hence the same Apostle, who says above, also says [Col. 0046A]: “For just as you too once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these too have now not believed because of your mercy, in order that they too may obtain mercy” (Rom. 11).

Therefore, as has already been said above, what he says—“Behold, I will allure [her],” etc.—must not be referred to the immediately adjoining words of Scripture, in which the meaning is plainly otherwise, but to the earlier passage, where the good part, the chosen part, returning to her heart, says: “I will go and return to my former husband, for then it was better with me than now.”

Let us therefore say—or rather inquire—what it means for her to be nursed, led into the wilderness, spoken to her heart, given her vinedressers from that same place, and what follows. “For this reason,” he says, “behold, I will nurse her.” [Col. 0046B] To be nursed is to be tenderly cherished and, because of weakness, brought back to infantile delights. This is altogether blameworthy in those converted from Judaism. For, speaking to them, the Apostle says: “For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary beginnings of the words of God; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5). “For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the perfect, to those who by practice have their senses trained to discern good and evil.”

The faith of the Gentiles, however, is for this reason of greater praise and merit: although it was necessary that she should be nursed, this nursing nevertheless more quickly became capable of receiving solid food—that is, the word of righteousness, namely spiritual teaching. [Col. 0046C] This is the nursing by which, at Christ’s coming, the whole Church, coming both from Jews and Gentiles, was nursed.

It resembles that nursing by which the generation of the children of Israel that went up out of the land of Egypt was nursed. Therefore, having said, “Behold, I will nurse her,” he added, “And I will lead her into the wilderness”; and, after a few intervening words: “And there,” he says, “she shall sing as in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.” For who does not know that that nation, or generation, had its path hedged with thorns in Egypt, and accordingly was nursed and led into the wilderness for forty years, and sang as it ascended? For because the Egyptians hated the children of Israel, mocked and afflicted them, and embittered their life with the hard works of mud and brick, [Col. 0046D] and with every servitude by which they were oppressed in labors upon the land (Exod. 1)—these were the real thorns of misery—they groaned and cried out to the Lord. He had truly been the former husband in whom their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had faith; yet they would never have remembered him, while serving the gods of the Egyptians, unless violent affliction had forced forth groaning and awakened a perception lulled into neglect by an abundance of fish and by pots of meat.

Then for this reason God nursed that same nation by many miracles, with which he scourged Pharaoh and Egypt. This was doubtless sweet to that people, when it saw heaven fighting so wondrously on its behalf. In short: it crossed the Red Sea; Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and [Col. 0047A] horsemen; and, ascending, it sang: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15).

Thus it was led into the wilderness, while the Lord’s nursing continued: so that the Lord rained bread upon it and, when the rock was struck, gave abundant water to the thirsty, both beasts and human beings. There he spoke to its heart by leading it about and teaching it—indeed, also testing it—as Moses says in one place: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deut. 3). He promises to do something like that nursing, as has already been said, when he declares: “For this reason, behold, I will nurse her and lead her into the wilderness,” and so forth.

And this he did at the coming of his Son, through the mystery of the passion and resurrection of our same Lord Jesus Christ. For [Col. 0047B] all who, abandoning their former errors, turned to the living and true God—which is to return to the former husband—were, precisely because they had so returned, nursed by that same Lord in his Church, not only through the word of most sweet preaching, but also through the most sweet gifts of the Holy Spirit and delightful miracles, which at that time he graciously deigned to work abundantly and joyfully through the apostles and apostolic men.

He therefore says: “For this reason, behold, I will nurse her.” He immediately adds: “And I will lead her into the wilderness.” For we know that believers were so delighted by the wonders worked by the grace of the Holy Spirit which came upon the apostles that they also sought the solitary life, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles; nor did anyone [Col. 0047C] who possessed anything call it his own, but all things were common among them (Acts 2; 4).

He adds further: “And I will speak to her heart.” And this was done by him who promises it: he himself, who speaks these things in the prophets, promised it with his own mouth and fulfilled it when he became man. For he said: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14). Again: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth and will announce to you the things to come” (John 16).

Having said these things at the time of his passion, he afterward rose again and, according to his promise, spoke to their hearts—or taught them all truth through the Holy Spirit—as it is written: “Then he opened their [Col. 0047D] understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24). Still more, on the fiftieth day, by giving them the Holy Spirit, he spoke to their hearts; and from that time the Church has not lacked those into whose minds he may instill truth and knowledge of the Scriptures, so that the truth of his saying may be fulfilled: “And I will speak to her heart.”

He adds further: “And I will give her vinedressers from that same place.” Her vinedressers are the apostles and all who become their apostolic successors—that is, preachers of truth. For she of whom, or into whom, these things are said is the Lord’s Church: it is a vineyard, or is called a vineyard, as we read in many places in Scripture. Thus in Isaiah: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5). Again, in David: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt” (Ps. 9 [LXX numbering]).

Therefore her caretakers are rightly called vinedressers here; and he says that he will give them to her not from elsewhere, but “from that same place”—that is, from her own stock, from that people itself, wherever it is worthy to be called, or to be, the Lord’s vineyard. For wherever the Lord’s vineyard is, wherever the holy Church is spread throughout the world, among her or among the faithful inhabitants themselves there live and move persons whom the Church may choose as its prelates. This occurs through the action and ordering of him who speaks here, saying, “And I will give her her vinedressers from that same place,” so that the gifts of his Spirit may not be lacking in every place of his dominion.

Thus formerly, at the beginning of this planting, when it was being pressed among the thorns of Egypt, he gave Moses and Aaron as vinedressers from that same place. Thus likewise, when she was carried away captive into Babylon, he gave Zerubbabel, [Col. 0048B] Jeshua, Nehemiah, and Ezra as vinedressers from that same place. Thus at his coming, when he sought fruit from the vineyard and was rejected by evil cultivators, he gave it the best vinedressers (Matt. 21), namely apostles from that same place. Thus, wherever among all nations he extended that same vineyard—that is, his Church—he gave it vinedressers and illustrious protectors, martyrs and confessors and virgins, from those same places; and even now he does not cease to give it prelates and those whom it needs.

There follows: “And the valley of Achor for the opening of hope.” 21 The words “I will give her” are understood. By a very brief recollection he illuminates for us a great and extensive passage of the Old Scripture, which is as follows. Achor, son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah, took something from the accursed thing of Jericho, concerning which Joshua had said to all Israel: [Col. 0048C] “Cry aloud, for the Lord has given you the city; and let this city and all that is in it be anathema” (Josh. 6). For this reason the Lord was angry, and Israel could not stand before its enemies, but turned its back, fled, and was struck down by the men of the city of Ai. The Lord said to Joshua: “I will no longer be with you until you destroy the one guilty of this crime” (Josh. 7).

And it came to pass that Achor was discovered by lot; they led him to the valley of Achor, and all Israel stoned him. The name of that place was called the Valley of Achor to this day. Only then did the Lord say to Joshua: “Do not fear or be dismayed” (Josh. 8), and so forth. What was thus done historically, the Lord promises to do again spiritually. For he said concerning the future: “And I will give her vinedressers from that same place, to the valley of Achor.” For what purpose? “For the opening of hope,” he says: that she herself may not be doubtful or uncertain concerning her hope.

He therefore discloses the beautiful mystery of that historical event: namely, that just as, after Achor was put to death, the children of Israel took hope of conquering their enemies and were not disappointed, so, after the synagogue of the Jews together with the city of Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, the Temple burned, and the Jews themselves killed and taken captive throughout the whole world, hope of victory was opened to the apostles and the other believers—a hope by which they subjected the whole world to faith in Christ.

Thus here in the Gospel Achor of the tribe of Judah was Judas Iscariot, a disciple of Christ, who is the prince of our confession, from the tribe of Judah; and with him [Col. 0049A] that whole assembly of wicked scribes and Pharisees, with whom he held secret and stealthy counsel concerning the betrayal of the Savior. For Achor truly stole from the accursed thing of the city of Jericho when that thief, Judas, keeper of the Lord’s money-bags, accepted thirty pieces of silver as the price of blood. For that city, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, ought to be called not so much Jerusalem as Jericho.

The walls of that city fell already visibly before the eyes of the Lord when, by denying and delivering the Lord to be crucified, it drove every heavenly defense away from itself; but they fell visibly also when it was surrounded and overthrown by the Roman army. And just as that Achor, discovered by lot, confessed with his own mouth and said, “Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and thus and thus I did; desiring this and this, I took them away” (Josh. 7), so this Judas Iscariot, marked out by the Lord’s mouth as the betrayer, afterward confessed, throwing the thirty pieces of silver into the Temple and saying to the elders and chief priests: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27).

And Achor was stoned, insofar as, with that Judas the betrayer, the whole assembly that had jointly purchased the betrayal was destroyed: “not one stone remained upon another” (Matt. 24). And all this occurred “for the opening of hope.” For if that Temple and that city had remained in their glory, they would have greatly obstructed Christ’s Gospel, gravely hindered the faith and hope of the Gentiles, and made many doubt.

I shall say more: even if all had believed and received faith in Christ, and it had therefore happened that the Romans did not come to take away the place and [Col. 0049C] nation (John 11), they would nevertheless have disturbed evangelical truth and the rule of Christian faith. This is readily demonstrated from the few who believed. For few were converted to the faith in comparison with the whole Jewish multitude. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that certain persons from among them came down from Judea to Antioch and taught the brethren who had believed from among the Gentiles, saying: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15). A considerable dissension arose between Paul and Barnabas and them; and when the apostles and elders assembled to consider this matter, and much disputation took place, they were scarcely quieted for a time by testimonies from the Scriptures (ibid.).

What, then, might have happened—or what a multitude of disturbances do you suppose the Jews would have caused—if they had been converted to faith in Christ? Certainly they would more obstinately have mixed the Gospel with circumcision, and from both would have made neither, or nothing. “For if you are circumcised,” says the Apostle, “Christ profits you nothing” (Gal. 5).

Accordingly, the providence of God is to be praised and revered, which blinded them, as he says in Isaiah: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn and I heal them” (Isa. 6). For it is far better that Christ should not be known or the sacrament of baptism received by them—through which those who turn are healed by receiving remission of sins—than that Christ should be known [Col. 0050A] and baptism received in such a way that circumcision of the flesh and carnal Judaism are nevertheless practiced. For by this arrangement they would have contributed nothing to themselves and would have harmed the Gentiles greatly.

After all this he says: “And there she shall sing as in the days of her youth, and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.” “She shall sing there,” he says. Where? In that nursing, in that leading forth, in that speaking to the heart, in that opening of hope. There she shall sing; there she shall offer praises and thanksgivings. How? “As in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt”—that is, as she sang in the days when she was young, in the days when she went up from the land of Egypt.

For then the Church of God was young and, as though following the youthful heat of blood, did not possess the mature and secure judgment of old age in preferring spiritual things to bodily things, heavenly things to earthly. How did she sing in those days? When her doorposts had been marked with the blood of the lamb, when Egypt’s firstborn had been struck down, when she crossed the Red Sea, and when Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen, she sang this song: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exod. 15), and so forth.

In accordance with those days—that is, according to what was prefigured in them—behold, the holy Church now, her foreheads marked with the sign of the cross and with the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, the firstborn of death having thereby been destroyed—that is, original sin—crosses the Red Sea, namely the sacrament of holy baptism made red by Christ’s blood. All having been buried, she sings the glorious song of which that song of Moses was a prefiguration, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “And I saw as it were a glassy sea [Col. 0050C] mingled with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing upon the glassy sea, having harps of God; and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages” (Rev. 15), and so forth.

There follows: “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: she shall call me, ‘My husband,’ and shall no longer call me Baalim; and I will take away the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their name.” This has happened and is happening exactly as it is said. For, taught by our master and Lord Jesus Christ and by the Holy Spirit, the blessed Church has now learned to call God her husband. This is especially so because a good and great part of the Church—the blessed Virgin Mary—was so wondrously joined to God most high that she conceived his seed, that is, his Word, his only Son, in her own womb, and happily bore God and man for the salvation of all believers.

After her, every soul whatsoever which conceives in its mind unto righteousness the faith of that incarnate Word and brings it forth unto salvation by confession of the mouth (Rom. 10)—and the universal Church consists of many such believers—rightly says to God: “My husband,” because she deserves to be called God’s wife. “And she shall no longer call me Baalim,” he says; understand, “as she has done until now.” 22 For when calves had been fashioned and Baal adopted, together with the other monstrous forms of gods signified by this plural term *Baalim*, each time Israel said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt” (Exod. [Col. 0051A] 32), it called *Baalim*—a thing even to hear is wicked—the one who had brought it up from Egypt.

“And I will take away,” he says, “the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their name,” in accordance, namely, with the apostolic saying: “Let neither obscenity nor foolish talk even be named among you, as is fitting for saints” (Eph. 5). For *Baalim* may indeed have a tolerable interpretation, namely “having me,” which a faithful soul may rightly say concerning the true God; but this name *Baalim*, introduced by Jezebel in connection with the Sidonian idol which they call Baal, is excessively polluted and defiled. Therefore no interpretation of that name, however attractive, ought to please.

“She shall no longer remember their name,” he says, “and I, in return, shall no longer remember its name,” or their names, as it is written in the Psalm: “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods, nor will I remember their names with my lips” (Ps. 3 [LXX numbering])—that is, I shall not remember all the impious acts for which they have been named robbers, adulterers, and the like, nor punish them on their account.

“And I will make for them a covenant on that day with the beast of the field, with the bird of heaven, and with the creeping thing of the earth; and I will break bow and sword and war from the earth, and make them sleep securely.” “I will make for them,” he says. For whom? He had used the singular number, saying: “She shall call me, ‘My husband’; and I will take away the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their name.” But now he speaks in the plural, saying: “And I will make for them.” For whom, then? Surely for her aforesaid vinedressers—that is, [Col. 0051C] her preachers.

For the Lord made a covenant for them with the beast of the field, with the bird of heaven, and with the creeping thing of the earth. This may first be properly understood according to the letter. For the apostles and holy Fathers, having the grace of working miracles, are recorded to have commanded beasts, birds, and creeping creatures or serpents; and these obeyed them so readily that they became a marvel to peoples, to the glory of Christ, as though they had made a covenant with them. Thus, according to this sense, it is now said both beautifully and truly: “I will make for them a covenant with brute animals.”

But according to the anagogical sense, the Lord made a covenant for his vinedressers with beasts, birds, and creeping things because he joined Gentiles to the holy apostles and other believers from the circumcision in the unity of faith and the grace of the Gospel. Their former life or conduct deserved to be likened to beasts, birds, and creeping things, in accordance with that vision of the Apostle Peter recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “And I saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending, like a great sheet lowered by its four corners from heaven to earth; in it were all quadrupeds, creeping things of the earth, and birds of heaven. And a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat’” (Acts 10).

Understanding that the Gentiles were signified by these creatures, he later said: “You know how abominable it is for a Jewish man to join himself or approach a foreigner; but God has shown me that I should call no human being common or unclean” (ibid.). The Lord made a covenant for them with such persons, [Col. 0052A] saying to him: “What God has purified, do not call common,” or unclean (ibid.).

And whenever a worldly or powerful person, proud, harsh, or deceitful, changes his character for the better, adopts a stricter purpose of holy religion, and joins himself to the humble, gentle, and simple, the Lord makes a covenant for the saints with beasts and creeping creatures of this kind. The prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; calf and sheep and lion shall remain together, and a little child shall lead them. Calf and bear shall feed; their young shall rest together; and the lion shall eat straw like an ox. The nursing child shall delight himself over the holes of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (Isa. 11).

For what Isaiah elsewhere says concerning the last days—that is, concerning the Lord’s coming—“He shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples, and they shall forge their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles; nation shall not lift sword against nation, nor shall they any longer be trained for war” (Isa. 2)—this same thing this prophet immediately adds, or rather God in this prophet, when he says: “And I will break bow and sword and war from the earth.”

For this happens whenever a warrior, long devoted to secular military service, casts away weapons of war by which people are killed and, changed into monastic or clerical dress, sings the tokens of peace; or when one who has become a hermit, who formerly wielded sword and spear, cleaves the earth with a plough and cuts a modest crop and grass with a sickle, sustaining the body with what is necessary.

And in individual persons the Lord spiritually breaks bow and sword and war when, after the battle of vices by which the lawful soldier was wearied, saying, “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind,” he is at last delivered from this body of death, and this through the grace of God by Jesus Christ (Rom. 7). For the Psalm especially speaks of this peace: “His place has been made in peace”—understand, God’s place—“and his dwelling in Zion.” It immediately continues: “There he broke the powers of the bows, shield and sword and war” (Ps. 57 [LXX numbering]), that is, every assault of the vices.

There follows: “And I will make them sleep securely.” Understand: in that peace. For there one sleeps securely, namely with that sleep of which the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: [Col. 0052D] “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5). For with the heart awake one sleeps securely when, worldly cares having been removed and the motions of vices restrained, the soul, free through God’s grace, delights sweetly in contemplating God alone.

Or certainly, “I will make them sleep securely” means: I will make them confidently undergo the sleep of death, namely because of a good conscience, in reliance on which the Apostle desired “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 2).

Having said these things concerning the vinedressers, he immediately turns in apostrophe to that same vineyard, that is, to the universal Church, and says to her: “And I will espouse you to myself forever; and I will espouse you to myself in judgment and righteousness, in mercy and compassion; and I will espouse you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

Wonderful intimacy! Wonderful grace! This woman to whom he speaks had been a harlot; she had gone after her lovers, but, checked by thorns and by a hedge so that she could not find her paths, she finally said: “I will go and return to my former husband, for then it was better for me than now.” Yet behold: she is brought to betrothal, and God becomes her lover; amid ineffable endearments she is promised that she shall be a bride, as though a virgin—indeed, truly a virgin.

For the Apostle says to the Corinthians, who had certainly been Gentiles and whose soul had gone after many lovers, that is, after many gods: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). God is such a lover of souls that, however much a soul may have committed fornication, as soon as it is joined to the true God by faith, it is a virgin. A human being cannot do this, for such is neither the nature nor the law of the flesh. According to the flesh, she who has once been corrupted cannot be a virgin; indeed, not even a lawful wife, once repudiated by her husband.

Therefore through another prophet he says to this same woman: “It is commonly said: ‘If a man dismisses his wife and, departing from him, she takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled?’ But you have committed fornication with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you” (Jer. 3). When he says, “And I will receive you,” we must understand from the previously cited testimonies: I will make you both [Col. 0053C] bride and virgin.

We must now carefully consider the threefold repetition of this intimacy and grace: “I will espouse you to myself forever; I will espouse you to myself in judgment and righteousness, and in mercy and compassion; I will espouse you to myself in faith.”

What is the first thing he promises when he says: “I will espouse you to myself forever”? What else but that he promises those nuptials, with the delight of which all holy Scripture sweetens the soul that reads and understands it? In a certain place in his Gospel this Bridegroom says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. 22). What these nuptials are has now become known to us: God the Father and King made nuptials for his Son when he willed him to become incarnate, and the bridal chamber of these nuptials was the Virgin’s womb.

For in that womb the nature of this woman—our nature, human nature—was joined to the nature of God. From it Christ, who was God, came forth as God and man, having a bride and therefore being a bridegroom, as it is written in the Psalm: “And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18 [LXX numbering]). These betrothals are eternal. Therefore, when he had said, “I will espouse you to myself,” he added, “forever”: that is, once I have assumed the nature of your flesh, I shall never put it away, nor shall it vanish, as certain heretics suppose; rather, both Word and flesh—that is, both God and man—I shall be forever.

What, further, is the second thing he promises when he says: “I will espouse you to myself in judgment and righteousness, and mercy and compassion”? What else but that he promises that judgment which God himself, having become man, carried out against the ruler of this world by dying for our offenses, in order to cast him out? For when that hour was imminent he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12).

Accordingly, his resurrection is our righteousness. “For he was crucified,” says the Apostle, “for our offenses, and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4). His mercy is the remission of sins, which is the first gift of the Holy Spirit. On the very day of his resurrection, as he breathed upon his disciples standing in their midst, he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). His compassions are distributions of gifts, which are the second gift of the same Holy Spirit, concerning which it is written that [Col. 0054B] on the day of Pentecost divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to the apostles and rested upon each of them (Acts 2).

“In these, therefore, I will espouse you to myself,” he says: “in judgment and righteousness, and mercy and compassion.” That is: I shall pour out my blood and die for you, so that, the ruler of this world having been judged, he may be cast out; I shall rise for your justification; I shall have mercy upon you by giving the Holy Spirit for remission of sins; and I shall have compassion upon you by giving and distributing to you divisions of gifts—namely gifts of healing, workings of miracles, kinds of tongues (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

What then is the third thing he promises when he says: “I will espouse you to myself in faith”? What else but what the Apostle, writing to the Romans, argues with the greatest vigor: that a human being is justified by faith, not by works? (Rom. 4.) “What,” he says, “shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh found? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Gen. 15). “To the one who works, wages are not reckoned according to grace but according to debt. But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is reckoned as righteousness; as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: ‘Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered’” (Ps. 13 [LXX numbering]), and so forth, down to the words: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through [Col. 0054D] our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 3).

Therefore, when he says: “I will espouse you to myself in faith,” we must understand: and not by works, since no flesh shall be justified before him by works of the law. But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ upon all who believe.

Certainly, when we say or read these things, we do not reject the works of the Ten Commandments, inscribed upon tablets of stone by the finger of God; rather, we reject the works of fleshly ceremonies, in which the Jew boasts, though God hates them, as he says in Isaiah: “New moon and Sabbath and other feasts I will not endure. Your new moons and your solemnities my soul has hated” (Isa. 1).

Finally, this blessed dispensation having been promised and, as it were, secured indissolubly by the threefold cord of threefold repetition, he briefly appraises the sum of the betrothal and of the whole dowry, saying: “And you shall know that I am the Lord.” What then? Is it a small thing to know that he is the Lord? Surely those wise masters and learned scribes and Pharisees, who had taken—or seemed to themselves to have taken—the key of knowledge, did not know (Luke 11).

For when they tested this Lord in order, as though wise, to catch him in speech (Matt. 22), he, seeming ignorant but mindful of the Scripture saying, “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Prov. 26), repaid them in kind by putting to them this question: “What do you think concerning the Christ? Whose son is he?” When they answered, “David’s,” he said: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as the footstool [Col. 0055B] of your feet’” (Ps. 109). “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” And no one could answer him a word (Matt. 22).

They did not know—indeed, they refused to know—how or from where the Son of David is David’s son. But you, he says, shall know; you shall know, I say, that I am the Lord not only of David, whose son according to the flesh I am, but also of angels and human beings, heaven and earth, sea and all things in them: for I am their Creator, and therefore their Lord.

Lest anyone judge this a small matter: this knowledge is eternal life. For he himself said in one place to the Father: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). This knowledge proceeds not from human teaching but from the revelation of God the Father; and in this revelation is true blessedness. Therefore, when Peter began to know that this one is the Lord, he spoke to him thus: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

There follows: “And it shall be in that day: I will hear, says the Lord, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth; and the earth shall hear the grain and wine and oil, and these shall hear Israel.”

If in these sayings also you consider only the letter, it is very slight, and what that letter says does not appear worthy of the majesty of the Lord God who speaks these things. For the letter is indeed adorned by a metonymic transference, when heavens, earth, grain, [Col. 0055D] wine, and oil are said to hear or to be heard; but on the surface it seems to promise nothing other than temporal things, by which the soul is not refreshed but only the belly, which is destined for destruction, is filled.

Therefore, that we may attain a meaning in this letter also worthy of God, 24 let us raise the eyes of our mind to him to whom the Psalmist says: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall contemplate wonders from your law” (Ps. 18 [LXX numbering]). First we must enumerate these hearings: the Lord hears the heavens; the heavens hear the earth; the earth hears the grain, wine, and oil; and these hear Israel. There are surely four hearings and a hidden progression, but the Apostle makes it plainer and clearer when, writing to the Romans, he first says, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord [Col. 0056A] shall be saved,” and immediately adds: “How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? But how shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10).

The progression differs in words but is the same in meaning, except that here it is arranged descending, whereas the Apostle arranges the same steps as though ascending. Thus the heavens, whom the Lord here promises that he will hear, are the very preachers of whom the Apostle speaks at the fourth step: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” If you seek testimony, that of the Psalmist is familiar and ready at hand: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18 [LXX numbering]); that is, the apostles and other preachers proclaim the Gospel of Christ, the Son of God.

Therefore, when the Lord says here, [Col. 0056B] “I will hear the heavens,” it must be understood thus: I shall fill the apostles with the Holy Spirit, so that they may have authority to preach as sent by God. “For how shall they preach unless they are sent?” Again, when he says, “And they shall hear the earth,” it must be understood thus: and, as they preach, the inhabitants of earth shall hear them, according to the words, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18 [LXX numbering]). “For how shall they hear without a preacher?” Therefore the heavens hear the earth—that is, through abundant love the apostles will not endure refraining from descending to instruct the ignorance of earthly persons.

Again, when he says, “And the earth shall hear the grain and wine and oil,” it must be understood thus: earthly human beings, by believing, shall receive the good word of God, just as this inanimate earth receives seed or plants destined to produce grain, wine, and oil. Thus indeed—and no otherwise—only by hearing will they be able to believe. “For how shall they believe him whom they have not heard?”

Again, when he says, “And these shall hear Israel,” it must be understood thus: their belief shall call upon the seed of God, that is, Christ, whom, unless they believe, they will not be able to call upon. “For how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” Therefore all that we have—the fact that we have been granted to know and call upon the Lord Jesus Christ—must be ascribed to the grace of the merciful God, since indeed the Lord would not first have heard the
nor would the heavens heed the earth, nor would the earth heed the wheat and the wine and the oil, nor would these heed Israel, [Col. 0056D] unless God, or the Holy Spirit, had sent preachers; nor would they preach, and through them people would neither hear nor believe nor call upon Christ.
