It is pleasing briefly to run through the particular meanings of these “heedings.” The Lord heeded the heavens when he visited the apostles who longed for him, first and second after his resurrection. First, on the very day on which he rose, when—as Luke relates—they were speaking of him and saying, “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon,” he stood in their midst and said to them, “Peace be with you” (Luke 24); and, as John reports, “He breathed upon them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them’” (John 20). For this is the first gift of the Holy Spirit which he gave them, [Col. 0057A] for the forgiveness of sins.

Second, when they were all persevering unanimously in prayer with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers (Acts 1), he sent them the Holy Spirit in a distribution of graces, signified by the divided tongues which appeared. For this is the second gift of the Holy Spirit, by which he gave or distributed to them gifts of various charisms. Because of these two visitations, in which the Holy Spirit was given to them, he was fittingly not content to say only once, “I will heed,” but repeated it and used the same word twice. “And it shall be,” he says, “on that day: I will heed, says the Lord, and I will heed the heavens.”

The heavens heeded the earth when the apostles obeyed the utterances of Holy Scripture which speak on behalf of the earth, that is, of the Gentiles. For example, [Col. 0057B] when they had said, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles,” they immediately added: “For thus the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth’” (Isa. 49; Acts 13).

Likewise: “When they had passed through Mysia, they went down to Troas, and a vision appeared to Paul by night. A certain Macedonian man was standing and beseeching him, saying, ‘Cross over into Macedonia and help us’” (Acts 16). Having seen this, they became certain that God had called them to evangelize them.

The earth heeded the wheat and wine and oil when the Gentile world obeyed Christ’s Gospel, so as to live according to his command, to establish itself according to God’s word—which is good and [Col. 0057C] spiritual wheat—and according to the good pleasure of the Holy Spirit, whose two gifts just mentioned are rightly understood by the wine and oil.

These, moreover, heeded Israel and do not cease to heed it, while they fill the mouths of the dumb and, in filling them, open them; while they make the tongues of infants eloquent and restore ears for hearing and obedience. This accords with what the Spirit, foreseeing that they would be filled with this same wheat, wine, and oil, foretold in the Psalm: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 21). For “they shall praise” means nothing other than “they shall call upon [him],” which is here signified by the word “heeding.”

It follows: “And I will sow her for myself in the earth, and I will have mercy upon her who was without mercy; and I will say to that which was not my people, ‘You are my people,’ [Col. 0058A] and he shall say, ‘You are my God.’”

“I will sow her for myself in the earth”—understand, throughout the whole earth; that is, by scattering the word of preaching, I will spread the Catholic Church throughout the whole world, so that it may exist not only among one Jewish people, but among every people and nation. This agrees with what the Son testifies in the Psalm was said to him by the Father: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2).

“And I will have mercy,” he says, “upon her.” Upon which “her”? Upon her “who was without mercy.” By doing all these things which I have promised thus far—nursing her and leading her into the wilderness, speaking to her heart, and accomplishing the rest—I will have mercy upon her. And this is the mercy which I shall show to her who was without mercy.

We have already said above [Col. 0058B] that all the things contained in this chapter of the extended promise under relative pronouns, beginning with the words, “Behold, I will nurse her,” are brought to completion by this clause, “who was without mercy”; and that here at last it is indicated for whom promises of this kind are made. This is done with remarkable truth and even with the art of expression, so that she may not be wholly enraged against the Scripture that had to be preserved—the Scripture against which it was said above concerning her, “Call her name, Without Mercy” (Hos. 1).

For she who is called “Without Mercy” thinks that these good things are promised to herself, and that she herself is the one of whom it is now said, “And I will have mercy upon her who was without mercy.” Yet it is quite another thing to be called, or to be, without mercy, and another to have been [Col. 0058C] without mercy. 25. For the carnal house of Israel is called and is without mercy, to which he says, “I will no longer continue to have mercy” (ibid.). But the Gentile world was without mercy, and God now has mercy upon it.

This becomes clearer from what he immediately adds: “And I will say to that which was not my people, ‘You are my people’; and he shall say, ‘You are my God.’” For this is the Gentile people, to whom Paul says: “At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in this world. But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off have been made near by the blood of Christ” (Eph. 2).

## Book II

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057D] In the preceding passage, where it was said: “And the Lord said to Hosea: Go, take for yourself a wife of fornication, and beget children of fornication,” we recalled—and must still recall—the verse written much further on in this prophet, where the Lord says: “And I have spoken to the prophets, and I have multiplied vision, and have been likened in the hand of the prophets” (Hos. 12). We said that the Lord was likened in the hand of this prophet, namely in that he approached the prostitute once, twice, and a third time, and begot children of fornication.

[Col. 0058D] For this is analogous to the fact that the Lord approached the Hebrew nation a third time: first, when he made a covenant, or confirmed the testament, with Abraham (Gen. 15); second, when he gave the Law on Mount Sinai, after four hundred and thirty years (Exod. 20); third, when he sent forth the prophetic word to be written down—such as David was the first both to write and to sing. But after Solomon’s death the ten tribes were separated from the house of that same David; and only the tribe of Judah followed his house, together with the tribe of Benjamin adjoining it. Thus, from the one house of Jacob two houses were made: one, the house of Israel; the other, the house of Judah. Of these, after saying in this passage, “Call her name Without Mercy,” he immediately added: “For I will no longer continue to have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy upon the house of Judah.” These are, as we have already said elsewhere, the women of whom one is called Oholah in Ezekiel, the other Oholibah (Ezek. 23). Let us therefore consider what follows.

## Chapter III

“And the Lord said to me: Go again, love a woman beloved by her friend and adulterous, as the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look to foreign gods and love grape-husks.”

This woman is Oholibah herself, that is, Jerusalem or the house of Judah. And why is she called beloved by her friend? Plainly because of what he said above: “And I will have mercy upon the house of Judah.” In distinction from the house of Israel, concerning which he said, “For I will no longer continue to have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them,” this woman is called beloved by her friend.

In what respect did he have mercy upon the house of Judah? Certainly in this: when Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians had deported the house of Israel, while the king of Babylon had taken the house of Judah captive, the Lord freed the house of Judah from captivity after seventy years; but he did not free the house of Israel. Rather, they are held captive in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes (4 Kings 17). “Israel,” Scripture says, “was deported from its land into Assyria unto this day.” This woman, therefore, is rightly called beloved by her friend, because he struck this Oholibah more sparingly than her sister Oholah, mindful of their former friendship—or rather, of his own purpose, of which something must presently be said in this passage.

But observe how, after calling her “a woman beloved by her friend,” he immediately adds, “and adulterous”—understood to mean, “as is her sister also.” For it follows: “As the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look to foreign gods and love grape-husks.” It is as though he said: Because the house of Judah is as adulterous as the house of Israel. For although both were loved by the Lord, they often looked to foreign gods and loved grape-husks—that is, the same gods, indeed demons, who truly are like grape-husks.

For just as, at vintage-time, once the grapes have been pressed and the wine stored in cellars, the grape-skins are thrown out, so, after judgment had taken place in the heavens and a division had been made between the good and evil angels, the good were established in blessed dwelling-places, while the evil were cast out. Oholibah loved these beings, who falsely claimed to be gods, and looked to them no less than Oholah; that is, the house of Judah no less than the house of Israel, Jerusalem no less than Samaria.

Hence in Ezekiel, after the Lord had said of Oholah, that is, Samaria: “They uncovered her shame; they took her sons and daughters, and slew her herself with the sword,” he immediately added: “When her sister Oholibah saw this, she raged in lust more than she, and gave herself shamelessly in her fornication beyond her sister’s fornications to the sons of Assyria—governors and magistrates coming to her, clothed in varied garments, horsemen riding horses, all of them young men most excellent in appearance” (Ezek. 23).

Moreover, in another sense, Jews even now, while rejecting wine, love grape-husks: for in all things they flee the life-giving Spirit and follow the cheap, dry letter that kills.

But let us return to the order of the text. “Go again,” he says, “love a woman beloved by her friend and adulterous.” After you, Hosea, approached that Gomer daughter of Diblaim once, twice, and a third time, and she conceived and bore children so many times, go again and love her sister, an adulteress like her.

The mystical meaning is this: after those three things already spoken or performed—the testament confirmed with Abraham, the Law given through Moses on Mount Sinai, and the prophetic word administered and written down by many prophets—at last, O Savior, Son of God, Word of the Father, enter the world to save the human race, and, I say, from the house of Judah, from the seed of David, from the Virgin Mary, be born as a man. For this was to love that woman—indeed, to give her a kiss. In accordance with this, the good part, the chosen part of the same woman, said through<sup>26</sup> Solomon: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 2). That is to say: He who formerly, speaking or appearing through figures, made a testament or covenant with Abraham; who afterward gave the Law upon Mount Sinai; and who afterward sent the prophets—let that same one now come and unite himself to me through the most holy mystery of his Incarnation.

It follows: “And I dug her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, and for a homer of barley and a half-homer of barley. And I said to her: You shall wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, nor shall you belong to a man. Yet I also will wait for you; for the children of Israel shall sit many days without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without ephod, and without teraphim.”

Just as a little earlier, when speaking according to the figure of a woman—“and she went after her lovers,” and so forth—he suddenly passed to the figure of a vineyard and said: “And I will give her her vinedressers from that place”; so here also, from the figure of the woman of whom he had said, “Go again; love a woman beloved by her friend,” he suddenly passes to the figure of the vineyard, saying: “And I dug her for myself.” For “I dug” pertains properly to a vineyard; in another translation, in place of this word, it is written: “And I hired,” because this seemed more applicable to the figure or proper character of a woman.

But what is meant by this amount of fifteen silver pieces, likewise a homer of barley and half a homer of barley? Many things could indeed be said concerning this: namely, that the number fifteen of silver pieces may be referred to the fifteenth day of the moon, on which the children of Israel departed, liberated from the Egyptians; while the homer of barley and the half-homer of barley, amounting together to forty-five measures, may fittingly be referred to the forty-five days in which, after leaving Egypt, they reached Mount Sinai on the forty-fifth day. For those who came in forty-five days to the place where they received the Law are aptly said to have been hired for forty-five measures of barley.

We do not consider this interpretation, handed down by the ancients, insignificant; but because, as already stated, the present passage looks to the Savior’s coming, we endeavor to unfold the mystery of this letter according to those same times. For from that time onward the Jews sit without king and prince.

[Col. 0061A] As we seek to find, in accordance with the promise of him who says, “Seek, and you shall find” (Matt. 7), this at last occurs to us: neither in the silver nor in the barley does the quantity reach the number two, nor yet does it remain at one. It would be one if he had said: “And I dug her for myself for ten pieces of silver.” For ten is the second unity. Likewise, if he had said, “And for a homer of barley,” and had not added, “and half a homer of barley,” there would likewise be unity in the stipulated quantity.

He exceeded unity, yet did not reach two: for there are not twenty silver pieces, a number constituted by twice ten; nor are there two homers of barley, which is the simple number two. At each limit—that is, both in tens and in units—there is one half; and, as has been said, in neither does it reach two.

Now without the number two, or with less than two, there is no marriage—neither the bodily marriage which God joined in the beginning, nor the spiritual marriage of which this mystical discourse is here addressed to the prophet. Of it the Apostle, after first saying, “And the two shall be one flesh,” immediately added: “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5).

What then does it mean that he spoke not of twenty silver pieces, nor of two homers of barley—the marital number—but in both cases rose above unity and yet did not reach two, except that this woman, though beloved, from whose flesh Christ God deigned to become man and to come forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, did not attain to marriage with that same Christ? For it follows: “And he said to her: You shall wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, nor shall you belong to a man; yet I also will wait for you.”

Thus this deficiency in the number two, both in the tens and in the units, signifies a deficiency of marriage. Therefore neither unity alone nor the complete number two is present, because that nation from which Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, was born is not a virgin—since she is called an adulteress in the present passage—nor does she deserve to be wife or spouse, because she is without a husband; because, not confessing the Son, she does not have the Father either.

Conversely, she who has this husband, who deserves and truly is called bride, is both virgin and spouse; and therefore the amount of her silver is reckoned by unity and by two. Thus in the Song of Songs you read: “A vineyard belonged to the Peaceful One, in that which has peoples; he handed it over to keepers: a man brings a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit” (Song 8). And immediately that man himself, namely Christ, says: “My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit” (ibid.).

For the thousand, as reckoners know better, is the fourth unity. The same character by which one is marked in the units place, when transferred to the thousands place, signifies a thousand. But two hundred, in the hundreds place, are signified by the same character as two in the units place. Therefore, just as that woman is neither a virgin nor joined to a husband, and consequently her silver is neither ten nor twenty, nor is her barley one homer nor two homers; so, conversely, this woman is both virgin and spouse, and consequently her silver pieces are both a thousand and two hundred.

Furthermore, this also must be noted: the former receives both silver and barley, whereas the latter receives silver only. For the former indeed has something of silver—that is, of holy speech—in the Law and the prophets, but she rests upon the barley alone of the killing letter. The latter, however, possesses only silver in all that she has: she does not attend to the barley of the letter, but delights solely in the silver of the life-giving Spirit. And she says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings: silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11).

Thus it is said to her who does not possess the grace of marriage: “You shall wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, nor shall you belong to a man.” What this means is immediately explained in these words: “For the children of Israel shall sit many days without king, without prince, without ephod, and without teraphim.”

[Col. 0062B] Behold, today we see the truth of this prophecy fulfilled: the Jews, led captive among all nations, are without king and prince. This was not so before Christ came; rather, as the patriarch Jacob foretold: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 46)—until his coming, even if they did not always have a king, they nevertheless always had a prince. Thus they had leaders and judges from among themselves even while captives in Babylon. For there too they exercised their judicial affairs among themselves. For example, having condemned Susanna to be led to death, they returned to judgment and judged and put to death the two elders who had given false testimony against her (Dan. 13).

But when Christ came, whom they did not receive, they had foreign judges and governors; nor were they permitted to judge or to conclude a judicial matter by themselves. Hence, when Pilate said to them concerning the Lord Jesus, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law,” they answered: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18).

From that time they sit without king and prince, and the days are many. For because they do not seek Christ as their king, they are not worthy to have either king or prince from among themselves. They sit also without sacrifice and altar, because having lost the place where they had Temple and altar, concerning which it was commanded them in the Law: “In the place which the Lord<sup>27</sup> shall choose, you shall sacrifice to him, and not in every place” (Deut. 12), they offer no legal victims at all.

They sit also without ephod and teraphim. *Ephod* properly denotes the shoulder-garment, but here it is understood to mean every priestly vestment. *Teraphim* properly denotes figures and images, but here it is used for every priestly ornament. The Jews have lost all these things.

But how do they await Christ, or how does Christ await them? For he says: “You shall wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication; nor shall you belong to a man; yet I also will wait for you.” Clearly, they await wrongly, because, rejecting him who has already come, they promise themselves another Messiah. Hence he himself, after saying, “I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me,” added: “If another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5).

Christ, however, awaits them rightly: namely, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters. “Blindness,” says the Apostle, “has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11). This is exactly what he immediately adds here: “And afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall be in awe toward the Lord and toward his goodness in the last days.”

Meanwhile, he says, “You shall not commit fornication, nor shall you belong to a man.” That is: you shall neither prostitute yourself shamefully to lovers nor be joined to me, your lawful husband, by whom you were hired. For in these days Israel, or the Synagogue, neither publicly commits fornication with Baal or with golden calves, as it then did, nor belongs to Christ her husband; and consequently she does not have God, Christ’s Father, either.

After these days—or after these things—they will return, as has already been said; for when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, they will seek the Lord their God and David their king: that is, they will confess God the Father and his Son, Jesus Christ. “And they shall be in awe,” he says, “toward the Lord and toward his goodness in the last days.”

Having named two persons, namely the Father and the Son, he adds a third, the Holy Spirit, when, after saying, “They shall seek the Lord their God and David their king,” he adds, “And they shall be in awe toward the Lord.” They shall indeed be in awe—that is, they shall marvel beyond expression, astonished by the greatness of the event or of their joy—just as Thomas was in awe when the Lord said to him: “Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful.” He answered and said to him: “My Lord and my God” (John 20).

For just as Thomas was not with the other disciples on the day when Jesus came, and did not believe when they said, “We have seen the Lord,” but after eight days was with them, saw Jesus coming again, and believed: so today the Jews are not with us and do not believe when we tell them that he whom they crucified has risen. But afterward they will be with us; they will know him, and they will be in awe toward his goodness in the last days. It follows.

## Chapter IV

“Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land. For there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.”

After writing at the beginning of the book, as was fitting, concerning Christ, and employing a remarkable likeness or parable of the woman whom he was commanded to approach once, twice, and a third time, and likewise concerning the beloved and adulterous woman whom he was commanded still to love, he now at last treats what is not indeed first, but nevertheless the good secondary duty in the order of prophetic office: namely, rebuking the sins in which the people then stood, and for which they would finally deserve to be cast out and scattered.

Ezekiel likewise, at the beginning of his book—that is, in the earlier visions—set forth, far in advance, the mysteries of the Son of God through four faces: of a man, a calf, a lion, and a flying eagle. Then at last he prophesied or wrote concerning matters of lesser or secondary importance, namely the imminent captivity of the people who were to migrate to Babylon: “Therefore, son of man, prepare for yourself vessels for migration, and you shall migrate by day before them” (Ezek. 12), and so forth.

He therefore says: “Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land.” Children of Israel, about to be led into captivity, toward whom the Lord will no longer continue mercy, to whom the Lord says, “You are not my people,” hear the word of the Lord; hear and know that judgment is being undertaken with you, because you do not suffer, or shall not suffer, without cause, but because of many preceding causes.

Hear and know, you yourselves; let the entire world and all generations, both present and future, hear and know that the reasons are grave for which you are to be left without mercy, for which the Lord has a judgment with you without mercy. What are those reasons? He says: “For there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land,” and so forth.

Before we discuss causes of this kind, it must be understood that he censures the sins of that people as no less than the sins of the Gentiles, and that this prophetic truth establishes and promises justification in faith in Christ alone—the faith through which Abraham too was justified before he was circumcised.

And, so that the whole body of the prophecy may shine forth, we now say that from here to the end of the volume he mentions and repeats sins seven times, and on each occasion his discourse returns to Christ, who alone is the righteousness of all believers and penitents. These occasions must now be counted or indicated beforehand.

First, among other statements, he speaks thus: “According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; they committed fornication and did not cease. For a spirit of fornications deceived them, and they committed fornication away from their God, because they associated with harlots and sacrificed with effeminate persons; Ephraim is a partner of idols: leave him.” By these words he certainly charges and convicts them of being under sin no less than the Gentiles; then at last he introduces Christ, who alone justifies, as speaking thus to both: “In their tribulation they shall rise early to me, saying: Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike and cure us” (Hos. 6), and so forth.

Second, beginning thus: “But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly against me. Gilead is a city of those working an idol, supplanted by blood, and like the jaws of men who are robbers” (ibid.), and so forth, down to: “From the days of Gibeah Israel has sinned; there they stood. Battle against the sons of iniquity shall not overtake them in Gibeah; according to my desire I shall correct them; peoples shall be gathered against them when they are corrected for their two iniquities” (Hos. 10). At last he introduces Christ, righteous and making righteous, thus: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck. I shall mount Ephraim; Judah shall plough; Jacob shall break up his furrows for himself. Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap according to the command of mercy; renew fallow ground for yourselves; for it is time to seek the Lord, until he comes and teaches you righteousness” (Hos. 10).

[Col. 0065A] Third, immediately repeating the sins: “You have ploughed,” he says, “impiety; you have reaped iniquity; you have eaten the fruit of falsehood” (ibid.), and so forth. Having said these things, he immediately promises the coming of that same Savior, speaking in the person of God the Father: “As morning passes away, the king of Israel passes away; for Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos. 11).

Fourth, again repeating the sins and saying: “They sacrificed to the Baals and offered sacrifice to images<sup>28</sup>; yet I, like a foster-father of Ephraim, carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I healed them. I shall draw them in the cords of Adam, in the bonds of charity; and I shall be to them as one lifting the yoke from their jaws, and I bent down to him that he might eat. He shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Asshur himself shall be his king, because they refused to return” (ibid.), and so forth. Suddenly the discourse returns to that same Savior and promises him: “They shall follow the Lord,” he says, “as a lion he shall roar; for he himself shall roar, and the children of the sea shall be afraid; and they shall fly like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I shall settle them in their houses, says the Lord” (ibid.).

Finally, the Lord of whom he says, “As a lion he shall roar,” is our Savior, of whom the patriarch Jacob also foretold: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up; resting, you have lain down as a lion and as a lioness” (Gen. 49). He roared, and the children of the sea were afraid, because he rose again and sent out his apostolic preachers; and the nations of the world were afraid and converted to repentance. They flew away, and even now do not cease flying away, like a bird from the Egypt of this world; and he settles them in his houses, namely in those heavenly dwelling-places of which he said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places. If it were not so, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14), and so forth.

Fifth, immediately striking at sins by saying: “Ephraim has surrounded me with commerce, and the house of Israel with deceit,” and so forth, down to: “Therefore they shall be like a morning cloud, and like dew passing away in the morning, like dust carried from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney” (Hos. 13). Immediately the Savior himself promises his coming: “But I,” he says, “am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God apart from me, and there is no Savior besides me” (ibid.), and so forth.

Sixth, the Lord immediately mentions sins, saying: “According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their heart and forgot me,” and so forth. Then at last he again promises his coming: “From the hand of death,” he says, “I shall deliver them, and from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell,” and so forth, down to: “And he himself shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.” He himself, I say—namely Christ—who said in his own person, “I shall be your death, O death,” because through his death he overcame the strong armed man and plundered his vessels.

Seventh, the prophet sharply condemns the same sins, saying: “Let Samaria perish, because she has provoked her God to bitterness; let them perish by the sword; let their little children be dashed to pieces and their pregnant women be ripped open.” Immediately he looks toward Christ, or Christ’s coming: “Return,” he says, “O Israel, to your God” (Hos. 14), and so forth, to the end. By these words he mystically signifies beforehand both the conversion of true Israel, remission of sins through that same Christ, and the abundant and gratuitous outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, as often as he strikes at or enumerates the sins of the nation, so often his prophetic discourse concludes its course in the coming or mystery of the Son of God, clearly indicating that no one can be justified and saved from sins except through his grace or faith. Hence the Apostle, having fittingly recalled both Jewish and Gentile sins, finally says: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5).

Let us now enter upon the order of exposition of the text itself. Having prefaced, as has been said: “Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land”—a statement which could have rendered them not merely attentive but astonished, had they possessed ears to hear—he immediately begins to state the cause as follows: “For there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing and lying, murder and theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood. Because of this the land shall mourn, and everyone dwelling in it shall languish, together with the beast of the field and the bird of heaven; even the fish of the sea shall be gathered together. Yet let no one judge, and let no man be reproved; for your people are like those who contradict the priest,” and so forth.

A method of exposition would require that nearly this entire part of the prophetic discourse be set out here, down to the words, “In their tribulation they shall rise early to me,” unless we wished to avoid offending the reader who hastens toward the exposition.

Finally, we suppose that nowhere did the Apostle more certainly have in view—or could have had in view—the point at which, writing to the Romans, after most vigorously rebuking the sins of the Gentiles, he at once turns to the Jew and says: “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every man who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the very things which you judge” (Rom. 2), and so forth. [Col. 0066D] Indeed, if you wish to know how truly he said to the Jew judging the Gentile, “You do the very evils which you judge,” compare the evils here set down concerning the Jews with those which the Apostle there recounts concerning the Gentiles, and it will be clearer than daylight that their evils and these men’s evils are not merely similar but identical. The words are different, certainly, but the realities are the same.

This point must first be briefly noted: just as the Apostle there says, “Therefore God gave them up”—that is, the Gentiles—“to the desires of their hearts and to impurity” (Rom. 1), and repeats this very word “gave up” a third time, saying, “For this reason God gave them up to dishonourable passions” (ibid.); and again, “And since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind, to do things which are unfitting” [Col. 0067A] (Rom. 1): so here the same God gives up, or commands to be given up, the fornicating Jew three times, when he abandons him and forbids him to be rebuked.

For first he says: “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked; for your people are like those who contradict the priest.” Secondly: “I will not punish your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery, because they themselves kept company with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men.” Then, thirdly: “Ephraim is a companion of idols; leave him alone. Their drinking-party is set apart; they have committed fornication incessantly.” For sound understanding recognizes no difference between the Apostle’s statement that God gave up the Gentiles and this prophet’s statement that the Jewish man was forbidden to be rebuked, that God said he would not punish, and commanded that he be left alone—namely, according to [Col. 0067B] the desires of his own heart.

Again, what the Apostle says of the Gentiles—“filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, greed, malice, full of envy, murder” (ibid.), and so forth—the prophet here also declares concerning the Jews, though more briefly, when he says: “Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.” Hence the admirable and praiseworthy ordering of the truly wise Apostle: in the dispute between Jews and Gentiles, which was the reason for writing the Epistle to the Romans, in order to restrain both parties, he touched upon the Gentiles before the Jews.

For what reason? Plainly because the whole controversy arose from the Jews, who despised all nations; and their guilt was greater, because, possessing the Law, they were transgressors of the Law and therefore [Col. 0067C] ought themselves to have been struck first and shown what they were. But the Gentiles were more patient in listening. Praiseworthy, therefore, as has been said, is the Apostle’s administration or discrimination in rebuking: deferring the rebuke of those who deserved more and earlier to be rebuked, but were less patient, he first rebuked those who were indeed less blameworthy but more patient.

Therefore, as we said above, the argument required that the lengthy chapter of this prophetic discourse be set down here and compared with the apostolic passage. But, content to have touched upon the sum of both, let us henceforth run through the individual points selectively and consider gradually how each agrees with individual sayings of the Apostle.

He says: “There is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land.” Therefore, he says, the Lord has a judgment against the inhabitants of the land: judgment, I say, and not mercy. “For I will no longer add mercy to the house of Israel,” because in the land—that is, in those same inhabitants of the land—there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God. These three things, if rightly considered, are such that wherever they are found, judgment should give way and the mercy of God should come near; but wherever they are absent, mercy should have no place and judgment should take place.

For where there is no truth, there is no confession of sins; and conversely, where there is no confession of sins, there is no truth. “If we say,” says the Apostle, “that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” [Col. 0068A] (1 John 1). But here, after a few intervening words, it is said: “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked; for your people are like those who contradict the priest.” Certainly, to contradict the priest is to defend one’s sin, because it is the priest’s office to rebuke the people for sin. Therefore, just as truth was not in the Gentiles, so truth was not—or is not—in the Jews, that is, in that carnal Israel.

Yet the Apostle rebukes the absence of truth among the Gentiles more sharply when he says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness; because what is known of God is manifest to them” (Rom. 1), and so forth. Therefore, that the Jews’ guilt against truth may truly be equated with the Gentiles’ guilt, let us inquire; and it will immediately appear how they too held down the truth of God in unrighteousness.

For after they had made golden calves, they said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12). In this unrighteousness both Jeroboam and the people held down and suppressed the truth of God. For they were not ignorant, but pretended ignorance, because what was known of God was manifest among them—not only, as among the Gentiles, from the creation of the world, but more than among the Gentiles from the Scripture of the Law which they had received. Above all, because they had torn themselves away from the house of David, that truth was not in them of which the same writer says: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not turn from it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” [Col. 0068B] (Ps. 131).

“There is also no mercy in them,” he says; and this corresponds to what the Apostle likewise says of the Gentiles: “Without natural affection, without covenant, without mercy” (Rom. 1). Indeed, these men were so without mercy that they did not even know how to show mercy while fasting, as Isaiah said and wrote of them in those same times: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you exact payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and you strike wickedly with the fist” (Isa. 58).

To sum up briefly many things that might be said here: when he says, “There is no mercy,” it follows that there is no love or charity either, not only toward one’s neighbour but also toward God. For whoever does not love his neighbour and does not show mercy to his neighbour plainly does not love God either. Hence John says: “Whoever possesses the goods of this world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” [Col. 0068D] (1 John 3). Thus the Lord’s judgment is just also on this account: since they do not love, neither should they themselves be loved; since they do not show mercy, neither should they obtain mercy. Thus, above, when he had said, “Call his name ‘Without Mercy,’” he immediately said: “For I will no longer add mercy to the house of Israel, but I will forget them with utter forgetfulness.”

“And there is no knowledge of God in the land.” If here you look to the verse which follows later—“Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not perform priestly office for me”—then surely what he says here of the Jews or Israelites corresponds to what the Apostle likewise says of the Gentiles: “Because they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge” [Col. 0069A] (Rom. 1). He said this about those for whom it was not readily available from the Law to possess knowledge of God, but to whom it could nevertheless be known; indeed, they could not fail to possess even knowledge of him itself. “For God,” he says, “made it manifest to them. For his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made, are clearly seen from the creation of the world; likewise his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (ibid.).

How much more fittingly may the same be said of the Jews, to whom knowledge, or acquaintance, with God was made available not only from the creation of the world but from the written Law? Moreover, concerning the saying, already partly mentioned, “Because you have rejected knowledge,” more must be said in its proper place later.

It follows: “Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.” Without doubt this corresponds to what the Apostle says there concerning the Gentiles: “Filled,” he says, “with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, greed, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, hateful to God, abusive, proud, arrogant, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly.” For what follows—“without natural affection, without covenant, without mercy”—is the same, as we have already said, as what was stated here before: “There is no truth; there is no mercy.”

What the Apostle says, that the Gentiles were filled with such things, this prophet sufficiently expresses of the Jews by the word “overflowed,” saying, “They have overflowed”; for this is plainly a word not of moderation but of fullness [Col. 0069C]. We say these things, and we make—and shall make—this comparison between the prophetic and apostolic passages, so that it may not escape our memory that, as we have already said, the Apostle most rightly, after listing the vices of the Gentiles, turns to the Jewish man: “You are inexcusable,” he says, “who judge, for you do the very things which you judge” (Rom. 2).

Since the rest is sufficiently clear in itself, there is a question concerning this one phrase, “and blood has touched blood”: what does it mean? It is rightly understood as though it said, “Sin has been added or joined to sin,” since sin is customarily signified by the name “blood,” as there: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50). But in this sense it seems to say nothing other than what preceded. For when it says, “Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have overflowed,” what else does it mean but that sin has been added to sin? Therefore, when it says, “And blood has touched blood,” consanguineous intercourse seems to be condemned, because it is contrary to God’s Law, which says: “No man shall approach a near relative of his own blood” [Col. 0069D] (Lev. 18).

After such and so great evils have been set forth: “Therefore,” he says, “the land shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak, together with the beast of the field and the bird of heaven; even the fish of the sea shall be gathered together.” The sense is this: because the evils which I have predicted have overflowed, the land itself—which did not sin and could not sin, being an inanimate thing—will undergo a share in the punishment; and it will mourn, that is, its pleasant appearance will cease, as the natures of the elements are turned to their opposite or to disorder, and, together with human beings, the things created for human use fail: namely, the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea.

“The fish of the sea shall be gathered together,” he says; that is, they too shall be brought together so as to bear a share of punishment for human sin, and the abundance of all goods may be diminished not only in the fields but also in the waters.

It follows: “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked.” In a remarkable way, he who punishes sins thus forbids sinners to be judged and prohibits them from being rebuked. Why he wishes this, he immediately adds as the reason: “For your people are like those who contradict the priest.” Here one must remember the verse: “The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the multitude [Col. 0070B] of his wrath, he will not seek” (Ps. 9). What sinner, or when did he provoke the Lord? Plainly, that sinner who, “when he has come into the depth of evils, despises” (Prov. 18). Then he provokes the Lord when he adds rebellion to his sins and defends his deeds; and thus, as is written elsewhere, “he runs against the Lord with outstretched neck and armed with fat neck” (Job 15).

“He will not seek this man,” or this man’s sins, “according to the multitude of his wrath”; that is, he will by no means visit his iniquities with the rod nor his sins with blows, but will now keep silence, to speak at another time. For he will say: “You did these things, and I kept silence” (Ps. 49). Therefore, when he says, “Let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked, for your people are like those who contradict the priest,” he threatens an exceedingly great wrath; because, according to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek, judge, or rebuke, in order to remove his mercy from them, as he said at the beginning: “For I will no longer add mercy to the house of Israel.” Again: “Because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.”

For what does he mean by “For your people are like those who contradict the priest,” unless it is as though he said: Because they are rebellious and lifted up in pride, they defend their sins? For it is the priest’s office, as we already noted, to rebuke the people for sins in God’s stead. Therefore those who contradict the priest, following the example of Adam, who contradicted God while defending his sin, are consequently expelled—as Adam was from paradise—from God’s kingdom and from the present Church: just as this people was expelled into Assyria [Col. 0070D].

Having said this, he immediately addresses the people themselves and says: “And you shall fall today, and the prophet also shall fall with you.” Since I do not judge and do not rebuke, because you are, O people, like those who contradict the priest, you shall fall today—understand, by iniquity. This fall happens today, or is a present-day fall, to distinguish it from the subsequent fall by which, after these things, you will fall into the punishment of Gehenna: you who today fall into the pit of guilt.

“The prophet also shall fall with you”—understand, the blind prophet who offers guidance to you, blind as you are, because he is a false prophet. Such indeed were the prophets of Baal, four hundred and fifty men, who suffered the first fruits of their fall when Elijah, zealous for the Lord, killed them (3 Kings 18). Thus, while you fall today, because he is blind, the prophet too will fall with you, blind nonetheless. “Can the blind lead the blind? Will not both fall into the pit?” (Matt. 11).

For concerning this very blindness it immediately follows: “By night I have made your mother keep silence.” What does he say by “night” except the darkness of ignorance? Accordingly, he immediately adds, explaining that night: “My people have kept silence because they did not have knowledge.” That this night of ignorance was voluntary, that they willingly admitted those darknesses of ignorance by refusing “to understand, that they might do good” (Ps. 35), the following verse testifies: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not perform priestly office for me.”

But if it is still asked where or when, by what they said or did, that people rejected the knowledge of God: behold, it is written in the Book of Kings that, in answer to Jeroboam, the whole multitude of Israel, after saying to Rehoboam son of Solomon, “Your father imposed a very harsh yoke upon us,” and so forth, suddenly cried out: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse? Return to your tents, O Israel. Now look to your own house, David.” And Israel departed from the house of David [Col. 0071B] (3 Kings 12).

Plainly, by departing thus, it rejected knowledge, unwilling to know and scorning to consider that knowledge and salvation were from the house of David, to whom the Lord had sworn, saying: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). Therefore, in rejecting David, did it not reject him who is the fruit of David’s womb, in whom true knowledge is? For, having devised a plan, Jeroboam made two golden calves and said to them: “Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

Thus this night, this rejection of knowledge for which the people are here blamed, corresponds to what the Apostle says in the often-mentioned place about the Gentiles: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools and changed their glory into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed creatures, and serpents” [Col. 0071C] (Rom. 1).

Did not Jeroboam and all Israel, by making calves and worshipping them, change their glory into such likenesses, especially since the Psalmist also said of another time against the same people—not Gentiles, certainly, but Jews—“They changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass” (Ps. 105)? Truly, then, their foolish heart too was darkened no less than that of the Gentiles, and this very darkening of heart is the night of which he now says: “By night I have made your mother keep silence.”

By “mother of the people” he means their teacher, the synagogue. She is compelled to keep silence by night when, because of the dark ignorance of the foolish and darkened heart, the authority or place for teaching is taken away. When the mother who taught keeps silence, it necessarily follows that the children who were taught kept silence too—that is, they kept silence together.

Accordingly, he immediately turns to those who wondered, with both ears ringing, and said: “Why has the Lord done this to this land and to this people?” (3 Kings [Col. 0072A] 9). “Therefore,” he says, “my people kept silence because they did not have—indeed, because they did not wish to have—knowledge.” In what did they keep silence? Namely, in that they ceased to celebrate or be celebrated, because “their festivals, their Sabbaths, their new moons or Kalends, and all their temporal feasts I have cast away.” For it is better for me that, led into captivity, they should keep silence than that under my name they should dance before their calves and leap while singing.

And I say to this people: “Take away from me the noise of your songs” (Amos 5); go down and keep silence in the land of captivity, in the land of the Assyrians. But if it still murmurs and says, “Why has this been done to me?” I say to it: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not perform priestly office for me.” Therefore, not to perform priestly office and to keep silence are equivalent; for just as freedom of speech prevails in the exercise of priestly office, so conversely the authority to speak falls away in the cessation or deposition of priesthood.

It follows: “And because you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children.” Forgetting here stands for contempt, as also there, when the Psalmist had said, “They changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass” (Ps. 105), he immediately added: “They forgot God who saved them” (ibid.). [31] For a similar cause—indeed the same or a greater cause—had preceded, so that he should say here, “You have forgotten the law of your God”: for then they had made one calf in the wilderness, but now they made two, and placed one in Dan and the other in Bethel (3 Kings 12).

He speaks, however, turned toward her of whom he had said, “By night I have made your mother keep silence”: namely, the synagogue, mother of the people, or the assembly of priests or elders, on whose governance or teaching the common people depended. “Therefore you have forgotten the Law”—that is, you have despised the Law of your God. I return like for like: “I too will forget your children,” that is, I too will despise your children, just as he said above, “For I will no longer add mercy to the house of Israel, but I will forget them with utter forgetfulness.”

Having said these things to that mother—that is, to the company or multitude of priests and teachers—he turns again to the hearers and speaks thus, complaining concerning the same men: “According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into disgrace. They shall eat the sins of my people, and they shall lift up their souls to their iniquity” [Col. 0072D]. “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest; and I will punish his ways upon him, and render to him his devices.”

“According to their multitude,” he says. Whatever overflows or increases beyond reason, number, or lawful order ought rightly to be called multitude or multiplicity. It is certain that in those days the company of priests had grown beyond the order and limit established by the holy Law. For it is written: “And Jeroboam made shrines on high places, and priests from the lowest of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi” (3 Kings 12). And elsewhere it is written: “For whoever wished, filled his own hand, and became a priest of the high places” (3 Kings 13).

The priests had thus been multiplied, being chosen indiscriminately from all tribes. That king, as he thought, had provided wisely for himself: in order to have a multitude of priests, he made priests for himself from the lowest of the people [Col. 0073A]. For such men, the more worthless they were in the populace, the readier they were for that honour. They rejoiced to rise by office above the people, though by their low condition they had remained hidden among, or beneath, the people.

He says therefore: “According to their multitude, so they sinned against me”; that is, the more numerous they were or became, the more they deceived the people into sinning against me. What, conversely, shall I do? “I will change,” he says, “their glory into disgrace.” And the sense is: since they changed their glory both formerly into the likeness of a calf eating grass (Ps. 105), and now into the likenesses of calves eating grass, it will come about that they will be such men as those of whom it may rightly be said: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3).

In what are these men judged to have their belly as their god? Clearly in what follows: “They shall eat the sins of my people.” The priests chosen from the lowest of the people, as has already been said, strove to rise above their former condition or poverty; and Jeroboam, who had appointed them, pretended that he had himself made a true imitation of the holy Law. For because the Law had commanded that the sons of Levi, having no possessions of their own, should receive tithes and offerings from the people and derive their maintenance from them, he had made priests from the lowest of the people so that, about to receive so many tithes and offerings, they might be the more eager to cultivate falsehood and deceive the people, the lower they had been [Col. 0073B] (Num. 18).

“They shall eat the sins of my people,” therefore, he says; that is, having begun, they will not cease to eat as long as they can. For those ate the sins of the people who, solely in order to obtain tithes and offerings for themselves, kept the people in sins and falsehood—fully worthy, in every respect, of that saying of the Apostle concerning the Gentiles, which he states in the often-mentioned passage as follows: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest among them” (Rom. 1).

For priests of this sort were not ignorant that there was nothing true in those golden calves. Yet they held down the truth; they hid the truth in their hearts and preached falsehood with their lips, saying: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” [Col. 0073D] (3 Kings 12). These scoundrels, slaves of their own gluttony, acted thus in order that they might eat the sins of the people. Since they were of the lowest of the people, they would not have so much to eat unless the people sinned: unless, worshipping calves as God, the people honoured them as priests of Levitical stock, by giving and offering what would suffice for their bellies.

Receiving these things, they pronounced the giver blessed; and in truth they made those who were dying—that is, sinning unto death—as though secure of life. Therefore, after saying, “They shall eat the sins of my people,” he immediately added: “And they shall lift up their souls to their iniquity.” For their iniquity was their departure from the house of David and from the temple of the Lord, and their worship of golden calves. To this iniquity [Col. 0074A] they lifted up their souls, strengthening them with lying words so that they might trust in those calves as in God and fear nothing, as though they possessed a lesser divinity in that gold, because the calves were beautifully fashioned and they often celebrated lavish festivals before them.

Concerning the disgrace of which he says, “I will change their glory into disgrace,” he explains more fully afterward. For after inserting, “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest; and I will punish his ways upon him, and render to him his devices,” he immediately adds: “They shall eat and not be satisfied; they committed fornication and did not cease, because they forsook the Lord by not keeping themselves. Fornication and wine and drunkenness take away the heart. My people consulted his piece of wood, and his staff announced to him; for a spirit of fornications deceived them, and they committed fornication away from their God. They sacrificed upon mountain-tops, and burned incense upon hills, beneath oak and poplar and terebinth, because its shade was good. Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication and your brides shall be adulteresses. I will not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery, because they themselves kept company with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men; and a people without understanding shall be beaten. If you commit fornication, O Israel, let Judah at least not forsake [variant: ‘not sin’]. Do not enter Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven, and do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’ For Israel has turned aside like a wanton heifer. Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place. Ephraim is a companion of idols; leave him alone. Their drinking-party is set apart; they have committed fornication incessantly. Their protectors loved to bring disgrace. A spirit has bound him in its wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices” [Col. 0074B–C].

This entire passage is similar in sense and order to that passage of the Apostle beginning, “Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts in impurity, to dishonour their bodies among themselves,” and ending, “Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. 1).

And this especially must be noted: just as the Apostle, when he says for the third time concerning the Gentiles, “God gave them up,” expresses their disgrace most strongly in the second or middle position, saying: “For their women changed the natural use into that use which is contrary to [Col. 0074D] nature. Likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned [32] in their desires for one another, men working shamefulness with men” (ibid.); so here you have the same concerning the Jews.

For after he first said, “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked,” and now says a second time, “I will change their glory into disgrace,” and a third time, “Ephraim is a companion of idols; leave him alone; they have committed fornication incessantly”—which is as though he said, “I shall give him up,” or “I give him up,” using the word employed by the Apostle, namely, “to dishonourable passions”—in the middle of this judgment or pronouncement he expresses more strongly the shameful cause involving both women and men.

For he says first concerning the women: “Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication and your brides shall be adulteresses. I will not punish your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery” [Col. 0075A]. Then he immediately adds concerning the men: “Because they themselves kept company with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men.”

Now let us return to the order. He had said: “They shall eat the sins of my people”; he had threatened a judgment common to people and priests, saying: “It shall be as with the people, so with the priest.” Then immediately, condemning the excess of their eating—indeed, their voracity—he says: “They shall eat and shall not be satisfied.” He immediately adds: “They committed fornication and did not cease.” He briefly expresses the two principal evils, namely greed and lust, and how insatiable they are.

For once greed has occupied the mind, nothing is enough. Therefore he says: “They shall eat and not be satisfied”; that is, the priests who were appointed from the lowest of the people shall receive from the people, and having received, however much it may be, they will not be content. Likewise, when lust has infected a person, it never says, “Enough” (Prov. 30); and although its thirst is quenched for an hour, it immediately burns again. Therefore he says: “They committed fornication and did not cease”; for even into decrepit old age they rotted in the mire of lust, according to the saying: “The beasts rotted in their dung” [Col. 0075B] (Joel 1), that is, brutal and unclean people ended their lives in their sin.

Why was this so? Why did they not cease, or why could they not cease, to commit fornication? He says: “Because they forsook the Lord.” In what way? “By not keeping themselves,” that is, by failing to guard themselves. For they could have guarded themselves, possessing free choice and at the same time seeking God’s help. They did not do this; rather, they forsook the lawful Lord and voluntarily subjected themselves to the tyrant of death, that is, to sin.

It is just, moreover, that every slave be handed over to his own master. Therefore they ought also to have been handed over to sin, as to their master, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Thus, just as the often-mentioned Apostle says of the Gentiles: “Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts in impurity, to dishonour their bodies among themselves, because they changed the truth of God into a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator”; so it must be said of these men that they were handed over to their master, the spirit of fornication, in order to commit fornication and not cease, because they forsook the Lord [Col. 0075C].

“Fornication,” he says, “and wine and drunkenness take away the heart. My people consulted his piece of wood, and his staff announced to him; for the spirit of fornications deceived them.” See to what the blind impulse of fornication brought them! The Gentiles, with whom we compare these men in every respect as to sin, “changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed creatures, and serpents.” But my people set up their piece of wood, their staff, as God for themselves. In what respect, then, is this man better than the Gentile whom he judges?

And see how reasonably, about to state the excess of so great madness, he first said: “Fornication and wine and drunkenness take away the heart,” so that he may be inexcusable in having lost his heart so completely that he set up his staff as God for himself. For he did not lose his heart by chance or by a fated necessity, so as to fall into such madness; rather, by committing fornication, drinking wine, and becoming drunk, he overwhelmed the power of reason, so that he did not recognize the difference between the true God and his staff.

And the aggravation of the sin is truly fitting and just when he says, “Their piece of wood, and their staff announced to them,” because from the same wood they made for themselves both a god and a staff. Thus the sense is like that in which Isaiah denounces the folly of idolatry in these words: “He took from them—that is, from the trees of the forest—and warmed himself; he kindled a fire and baked bread. But of the remainder he made a god and worshipped it; he made a graven image and bowed down before it. He burned the middle of it in the fire, and from its middle ate meat; he cooked food, was filled, warmed himself, and said: ‘Ah! I am warmed; I have seen the fire.’ But of the remainder he made a god and a graven image for himself: a foolish heart worshipped it” [Col. 0076B] (Isa. 44).

Furthermore, a kind of divination is to be understood here, of which it is properly said: “His staff announced to him.” The Greeks, as blessed Jerome says, call it *rhabdomancy* (*rhabdomanteia*), divination by rods. Hence we also read in Ezekiel that Nebuchadnezzar mingled his rods against Ammon and Jerusalem, and the rod came forth against Jerusalem.

And whence came such madness upon my people of old? “For,” he says, “the spirit of fornication deceived them, and they committed fornication away from their God.” In this one brief verse both kinds of fornication, bodily and spiritual, are included: spiritually, because they committed fornication by following idolatry; bodily, because they dishonoured their bodies among themselves.

Of spiritual fornication he immediately says: “They sacrificed upon mountain-tops and burned incense upon hills, beneath oak and poplar and terebinth, because its shade was good.” This was the spiritual fornication of which he said: “They committed fornication away from their God.” And according to these words, one should observe the wandering license, or licentious wandering, of this fornication. He did not say, “They sacrificed in corners or chambers,” but: “Upon mountain-tops,” he says, “upon hills, outside under the open sky, publicly beneath oak, beneath poplar”—not because any necessity of bad weather required them to be sheltered, at least by branches and foliage, but because its shade was good [Col. 0076D].

The punishment for this fornication is bodily fornication, just as the Apostle says concerning the Gentiles: “Therefore God gave them up to dishonourable passions. For their women changed the natural use into that use which is contrary to nature” (Rom. 1). And immediately after this it follows: “Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication and your brides shall be adulteresses. I will not punish your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery.”

Just as the Apostle says, “Therefore God gave them up, and their women changed the natural use,” so here too, though using a different conjunction of equivalent force, he says: “Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication” [Col. 0077A]. The former by saying “gave them up,” and the latter by saying, “I will not punish them when they have committed fornication,” both indicate God’s just judgment: he abandons to bodily fornication and permits to be defiled, outside all dignity of reason, those who committed fornication away from God by spiritual fornication.

Again, just as there the Apostle immediately adds: “Likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their desires for one another, men working shamefulness with men” (Rom. 1), so here he immediately says: “Because”
and they themselves consorted with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men (ibid.). This is the same as if he said: “And males, committing with females and with males the passive depravity of lust, sacrificed themselves to the devil; they dedicated to the devil temples consisting of their own bodies.” For “effeminate men” are so called because they are males enslaved to sin in a womanly manner, in accordance with that saying: “Whoever lies with a male in womanly intercourse shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 20).

Likewise, as the Apostle says there concerning the Gentiles: “Although they had known the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. 1). So here he immediately adds concerning these people: “And a people without understanding shall be beaten.” What he says here—that the people, though it had received the Law, was without understanding—and what the Apostle says of the Gentiles—that they did not understand, though he had first stated that they knew God’s righteousness—is not an excuse for the ignorance and error of the simple, but an accusation of contempt: they refuse to know and are unwilling to understand. Thus the Psalm says of such a person: “He would not understand, so as to do good” (Ps. 35).

Meanwhile, the caution of the expression must not be passed over: how the prophet, as far as possible, avoids offending the impatient by avoiding the present tense and using other tenses—now the future, now the past. For he does not say in the present tense, “Therefore they commit fornication,” but, “Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication.” Likewise, he does not say, “Because they themselves consort with prostitutes and sacrifice with effeminate men,” but, “They consorted,” he says, “and sacrificed”: not addressing them to their face, but, as though speaking about others, suddenly turning toward them in apostrophe. Thus his manner of speech somewhat softens the attack upon a most bitter and harsh matter, yet nevertheless sets forth the whole truth.

Moreover, why is it that amid the words he speaks concerning Israel, that is, the ten tribes, he suddenly turns and says: “If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not sin”? What else does he imply except that the crimes of the same fornication—indeed, of the same fornications—had flooded into Judah, as both prophetic and evangelical Scripture plainly testifies? For Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had walked; for the daughter of Ahab was his wife, and he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord” (4 Kings 8). Thereafter the history of the kings of Judah unfolds full of evils. Thus Isaiah also, proclaiming his vision under the same kings, cries out concerning Judah and Jerusalem and says: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1).

[Col. 0078A] And lest you suppose that Judah committed fornication less than Israel, God speaks in Ezekiel: “Oholah committed fornication against me and raved after her lovers, the approaching Assyrians” (Ezek. 23), etc. Immediately after this he adds: “When her sister Oholibah saw this, she raved in lust more than she, and shamelessly offered fornication beyond her sister’s fornication to the sons of Assyria” (ibid.). It is well known that this Oholibah is Judah, or Jerusalem. For, he says, “Samaria is called Oholah, and Jerusalem Oholibah.”

When therefore he says, “If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend,” the prophet’s great astonishment should be understood: Israel, having once begun its fornications with the golden calves, not only did not return to chastity with the Temple of the Lord and the house of David, from which it had cut itself off, but, persevering in those fornications, made Judah or Jerusalem like itself. Thus, as the Apostle also recalls, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one” (Rom. 3), etc.

And lest you think too lightly of the fornications of Judah’s daughters or women, this especially bears witness: the history in the Book of Kings relates, “Asa did what was right before the Lord, as David his father had done; and he removed the effeminate men from the land and cleansed away all the filth of idols which his fathers had made. Moreover, he removed even his mother Maacah, lest she should be chief in the rites of Priapus; and in the place which she had consecrated he destroyed her grotto, shattered the utterly shameful image, and burned it in the brook Kidron” (3 Kings 15). Where the queen was such a woman, what do you suppose the rest to have been?

Immediately he says to both—namely Jerusalem and Judah: “Do not enter Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven, and do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives’; for Israel has wandered aside like a wanton heifer; now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place.” As though forgetting what he had said—“Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked; for your people are like those who contradict the priest”—he now again judges and rebukes by saying, “Do not enter Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven.”

For Beth-aven is the very place formerly called Bethel; it was named Beth-aven, that is, “house of an idol,” because one of the golden calves had been placed there by Jeroboam. Gilgal also had been an older site of idolatry, as Scripture testifies in its account of the valiant man: “When Ehud had presented gifts to King Eglon, he sent away the companions who had come with him, and, returning from Gilgal, where the idols were, said to the king: ‘I have a secret word for you, O king’” (Judg. 3). Likewise, a little later: “But Ehud, while they were disturbed, escaped and passed beyond the place of idols from which he had returned” (ibid.).

Surely, in saying once and again that he returned from the place of idols, or from Gilgal where the idols were, Scripture fittingly signifies his return to God; and therefore he was worthy for the Lord to raise him up as saviour when the children of Israel cried to Him, because he had already withdrawn from their sins (ibid.). Nor should this be ignored: Saul, requested as king against the Lord’s will, was anointed at Gilgal (1 Kings 11).

When therefore he says, “Do not enter Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven, and do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’” he rebukes in this passage the sins alike of pride, idolatry, and perjury. As we have already said, he seems almost to have forgotten that shortly before he forbade this same people, as one that contradicted, to be judged and rebuked. Therefore it must be carefully noted that, after he had made a turning address almost in renunciation, saying, “For Israel has wandered aside like a wanton heifer; now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place,” he immediately—the same one who had said above, “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked”—confirms the verdict, namely the judgment of abandonment, when he says: “Ephraim is a partner of idols; leave him alone.”

[Col. 0079B] This is the same as if he said: “Did I not tell you, O prophet: ‘Let no one judge and let no one rebuke, for your people are like those who contradict the priest’? Why then do you again rebuke or seek to establish your case by saying, ‘Do not enter Gilgal,’ etc., and pour forth speech where there is no hearing? Leave him alone; do not judge him; do not rebuke him, because he is a partner of idols and a partner of demons, sinning not through ignorance but through pride and contempt. Therefore leave him alone: hand him over, or leave him as one already handed over, to a reprobate mind, so that Ephraim may do what is unfitting, may have passions of dishonour, and may dishonour their bodies among themselves, because they love and defend their fornications” (Rom. 1).

For this is what follows: “Their feast is set apart; they have committed fornication utterly; her protectors have loved to bring disgrace.” By “their feast set apart” he means sacrifices to demons, with which the confusion of lusts is consequently mingled, according to that saying: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32).

Therefore leave him alone, because in acting thus—as you too testify—“Israel has wandered aside like a wanton heifer,” that is, casting off the yoke of the Law and contradicting the priest. Certainly, what the Prophet says, “Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place,” signifies the present vengeance which Israel was soon to receive even in this world. It is the same as if he said: “In the present time, while the spirit governs these limbs—that is, while I am alive—the Lord will pasture them in a broad place like a lamb”; that is, the Assyrians will lead them into captivity, and there they will be scattered in the captivity of a broad land and remain there for a long time. For “lamb” here does not commend simplicity, but indicates usefulness, as in: “They are set as sheep in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48).

Thus for the third time he has judged that the contradictory people are to be abandoned: first by saying, “Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked”; then, “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery”; and now by saying, “Ephraim is a partner of idols; leave him alone.” We have already said that the Apostle, speaking of the Gentiles in the same sense, likewise said three times: “God handed them over”—namely, “to the desires of their hearts unto impurity,” “to passions of dishonour,” and “to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. 1). Accordingly, to be handed over is to be abandoned or not rebuked, because they are contradictory.
