[Col. 0080A] Furthermore, this too must be considered carefully: the pride among the Gentiles which the Apostle denounced—and whose punishment was the passive shamefulness of lust—when he said, “They became vain in their reasonings; professing themselves to be wise, they became foolish” (ibid.), he likewise denounces here among the Jews or Israelites when he says: “The spirit has bound him in its wings.” For by wings is signified pride or the exaltation of the mind; because of this, demons too are sometimes understood in Scripture under the figure of birds, as in: “And some fell beside the way, and it was trampled down, and the birds of heaven ate it” (Mark 4).

Therefore the spirit of fornication—of which he said above, “For a spirit of fornication has deceived them”—has bound him in its wings; that is, it has seized him and subjected him to passions of dishonour because through pride he exalted himself and became vain in his reasonings. While that spirit binds him, “he shall be ashamed,” he says: namely, with the shame of dishonourable passions and shameful conduct, and this because of their sacrifices; that is, because they forsook the living and true God and sacrificed to demons in the golden calves, Baal, and the other monstrous forms of gods.

Death follows this shame, concerning which the same Apostle says in the passage often cited: “Although they had known the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1).

[Col. 0080C] Therefore, once the Apostle had recalled the impurities, dishonours, and passions of dishonour which the Gentiles committed, it is especially clear and convincing from this Prophet how truthfully and consistently he turned to the Jew, who judged and despised the Gentiles, and said—as we have already mentioned above—“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2). Immediately thereafter he continues: “For we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things” (ibid.). What else does the prophet add here in this passage? For he says:

[Col. 0080D]

### Chapter V

“Hear this, priests; pay attention, house of Israel; and listen, house of the king: for the judgment concerns you.” “The judgment concerns you,” he says—understand, as the Apostle says, *according to truth*, that is, without distinction of persons. For this reason he summoned both the priests and the house of Israel—that is, the people—and the house of the king—that is, the rulers—to hear, attend, and listen: because the truth of judgment is directed toward all alike, so that the severity of the Judge spares neither priestly grey hairs, nor the common people or their youthful age, nor the thrones of rulers, nor does it show them reverence.

With this same truth of judgment in view, the Apostle will allow no distinction between Jew and Greek. “For all,” he says, “have sinned and stand in need of the grace of God” [Col. 0081A] (Rom. III). Yet, as the priests’ sin is greater, so greater judgment falls upon them; therefore the strictness of the prophetic utterance attacks them above all others, when it immediately adds: “For you have become a snare for the watchtower, and a net spread over Tabor, and you have turned sacrifices aside into the deep.”

By these words he describes the magnitude of their sin. For just as wild beasts and birds are caught by snares and nets in woods and mountains, so the priests ensnared the folly of the people with fables and cunning devices resembling doctrine, so that they might not remember the house of David and the temple of the Lord, which was in Jerusalem, but might serve the king’s golden calves and the other images together with them. They did this not only by persuading them verbally not to wish to go there, but also by watching and laying traps, lest [Col. 0081B] some who wished to go might prevail. This is what he says: “For you have become a snare for the watchtower.”

Now Tabor is a round and lofty mountain situated on the plains of Galilee, and here it stands for any mountain. For, plainly, just as snares or nets are stretched and spread on a wooded mountain for catching prey, so their deceitful schemes were laid out and succeeded in deceiving.

But when he says, “And you have turned sacrifices aside into the deep,” he sharply rebukes the utterly senseless deceitfulness of such priests. They ought to have lifted sacrifices up to heaven by serving and sacrificing to the Creator; instead, they let them sink into the depths of hell by serving and sacrificing to the creature of gold and silver. Its glitter deceived the eyes of its beholders, because greed seized their hearts.

Further, lest they excuse themselves on grounds of ignorance, [Col. 0081C] he pronounces a most weighty and powerful sentence: “And I,” he says, “am the instructor of them all.” For he had instructed all of them; in his law he had foretold to all: “You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on earth below, or of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not worship or serve them” (Exod. XX).

Therefore, when he says, “I am the instructor of them all,” it is as though he said: They have no excuse for their sins, because I gave a public law to all, that they should not make images for themselves of calves—indeed, not of anything at all among everything that is in heaven, on earth, or in the sea.

Having said all this, he immediately, as though the prophet were asking [Col. 0081D] why he had said, “Ephraim is a companion of idols; leave him alone,” gives the reason for this abandonment and says: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me, because Ephraim has now committed fornication; Israel has been defiled. They will not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord their God, because a spirit of fornication is in their midst, and they have not known the Lord.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I say, ‘Leave him alone’: I who know their thoughts—that they will not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord.”

This must be understood, and we must hold a good opinion of the Lord: he abandons or hands over no one—the word which, as has often already been said, the Apostle uses—unless he sees that person to be incorrigible. For, as the same Apostle says, he “wills all [Col. 0082A] people to be saved” (I Tim. II), if they themselves are willing.

But perhaps someone may object here: He knew that the Sodomites, Tyrians, and Sidonians could repent, and nevertheless he abandoned them. For he himself says: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. And you, Capernaum,” he says, “will you perhaps be lifted up to heaven? You shall descend to hell. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained to this day” (Matt. XI).

What, then, is to be said to this? Why did he abandon the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Sodomites and not perform his mighty works among them, if, through such works, they could have been recalled and could set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord? [Col. 0082B] Was it because he did not wish them to be saved—he who, as the Apostle says, “wills all people to be saved” (I Tim. II)? Or is it rather true that they could have repented in sackcloth and ashes, yet still not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord?

For it must be carefully observed that repentance and returning to the Lord are not equal or equivalent things. Otherwise we must confess that Ahab, the impious king of Israel, returned to the Lord because he repented for the blood of Naboth whom he killed. When Elijah said to him in the word of the Lord, “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they shall lick your blood also,” he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, and slept in sackcloth (III Kings XXI).

Did this man set his thoughts [Col. 0082C] upon returning to the Lord? Certainly not. Although he repented for Naboth’s blood, he nevertheless did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam—that is, from the golden calves; indeed, neither did he cease to worship Baal, whom Jezebel had introduced. He repented, not in order to attain God’s eternal kingdom, but lest he be deprived of Samaria’s temporal kingdom. He received his reward, the reward for repentance of the sort he sought: that, while living, he should not lose his kingdom. For the Lord said to Elijah: “Because, therefore, he has humbled himself on my account, I shall not bring evil in his days; but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house” (ibid.).

Thus likewise the Sodomites, the Tyrians, and the Sidonians, if mighty works had been done among them, would indeed have repented (Luke X); nevertheless, [Col. 0082D] not with the intention or faith by which they might attain the invisible kingdom of God, but in order that, in this visible age, they might remain like other cities and flourish in their own peace.

Thus the Lord certainly knew that they would repent if mighty works had been performed among them; but he also knew that they would not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord. Therefore, when he says of them, “They would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (ibid.), it does not follow that he did not wish them to be saved, but that he had no regard for such repentance of theirs—a repentance undertaken not for God and the kingdom to come, but for their present condition.

Therefore, what he says concerning this people—“I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me, because Ephraim has now committed fornication; Israel has been defiled. They will not set [Col. 0083A] their thoughts upon returning to the Lord”—is the reason why he also said, “Leave him alone,” or, “Let no one judge or rebuke a man.”

The same must be thought concerning every person, Jew or Greek alike, whom God abandons: namely, that he knows not only what each person is now, but also how that person will persist in evil, and that he will not set his thoughts upon returning to the Lord; and therefore he abandons or leaves him. “For Ephraim,” he says, “has now committed fornication; Israel has been defiled.” This I know concerning the present or the past; and, no less, I know—and it is not hidden from me—concerning the future that they will not set their thoughts upon returning, but will remain incorrigible.

Ephraim means Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim. Israel, [Col. 0083B] however, means the ten tribes which withdrew with him from the house of David. He says that Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam—committed fornication and that Israel was defiled, because Jeroboam made golden calves and the people worshipped them in accordance with his favor.

Why will they not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord? “Because,” he says, “a spirit of fornication is in their midst, and they have not known the Lord.” This is a great and powerful cause, sufficient to ensure that they never change their thoughts for the better. He did not merely say, “Because a spirit of fornication is in their midst,” but added, “And they have not known the Lord”—especially concerning those who received the written law and therefore cannot excuse themselves through ignorance.

What, [Col. 0083C] I ask, does it mean to say of such people, “They have not known the Lord,” except the same thing the Apostle says of the Gentiles: that “they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge” (Rom. I)? Thus they did not know—that is, they were unwilling to know, or, knowing him, they despised him. Therefore the spirit of fornication was in their midst; therefore they were handed over to a reprobate mind, just like the Gentiles, to do what is unfitting. And, handed over in this way, they will not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord, bearing the just judgment of their own condemnation.

And so that it may become clearer that “they have not known the Lord” means, “They were unwilling to know him or despised him,” and that for this reason they were handed over so that a spirit of fornication might be in their midst, it immediately follows: [Col. 0083D] “And the arrogance of Israel shall answer him to his face, and Israel and Ephraim shall fall in their iniquity.”

For arrogance is the exaltation of mind or spirit by which one is raised even to contempt for God, so that he does not know him—that is, he despises knowing or venerating him. This arrogance answers in the face of a person of this kind when he is paid what he deserves. What is that? The Apostle says of the Gentiles: “And since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.” This repayment or recompense is a wondrous and terrible answer to arrogance, which this prophet also briefly indicates when, after saying, “And the arrogance of Israel shall answer him to his face,” he at once adds: “And Israel and Ephraim [Col. 0084A] shall fall in their iniquity; Judah also shall fall with them.”

Having reviewed these matters in order, we must now recall and repeat what we have said more than once: namely, that the Apostle, after recounting the sins of the Gentiles, most truly cried out against the Jew as subject to a similar or equal guilt, saying: “Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the very same things that you judge” (Rom. II). And that this apostolic truth can be confirmed more fully or readily by no testimony of Scripture than by that of this prophecy.

It follows: “With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the Lord, and they shall not find him; he has been taken away from them.” What he says here, “With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the Lord,” concerns Israel and Judah, [Col. 0084B] who fell in their iniquity. This is what the often-mentioned Apostle says of the same people, who, as we have seen today, were broken off and fell like branches from the root of the good olive tree—that is, from the faith of the fathers (Rom. XI). “Israel, pursuing righteousness, did not attain to a law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not by faith, but as though by works: they stumbled upon the stumbling-stone” (Rom. IX). And immediately afterward: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X).

Their righteousness, which they seek also to establish, is to seek the Lord with their flocks and herds—that is, to vie in sacrificing flocks and herds—while pretending not to hear him cry out in opposition through David: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from [Col. 0084C] your flocks” (Ps. XLIX). And in Isaiah: “‘What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?’ says the Lord. ‘I am full. I have not desired the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. Who required these things from your hands?’” (Isa. I).

Finally, if we consider rightly, for the people coming up from Egypt, where they had been accustomed to sacrifice flesh, sacrifices of this sort were not so much commanded as permitted. He himself testifies to this when he says in Jeremiah (ch. VII): “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For I did not speak to your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but this command I gave them, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; walk in every way that I command you, that it may go well with you.’”

Since this is so, then, as he says here, they will indeed go with their flocks and herds to seek the Lord; but what follows will occur: “And they shall not find him,” because they stumbled upon the stumbling-stone and the rock of offense [Col. 0084D] (Rom. IX), and, striving to establish such a righteousness of sacrifices, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness, which is Christ. Therefore they shall not find him.

“He has been taken away from them.” How has he been taken away from them? Did he move from place to place? Certainly not. Rather, they themselves have been blinded; judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, they have been disinherited from such a good, and it has been bestowed upon others. For in the place of those who, though natural branches, were broken off and fell through unbelief, those who were like a wild olive tree have been grafted into the good olive tree and stand by faith. That is, while they did not believe, the Gentiles believed; the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained the righteousness which is by faith. Thus the Lord—or Christ, the righteousness of God—has been taken away from them.

Someone may say: Where, then, did he go, or how was the truth of God fulfilled, he who made a covenant with Abraham and with his seed, as Scripture testifies, saying: “On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham” (Gen. XV); and again: “And I will establish my covenant,” he says, “between me and you, and your seed in its generations, as an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you” [Col. 0085A] (Gen. XVII)?

To this the prudent wisdom of the prophetic Spirit replies: “They have transgressed against the Lord, because they have begotten foreign children.” Its meaning is this: If the question concerns the covenant which God made with their fathers and whether he who made it has been faithful, God is easily and truthfully vindicated. God indeed made that covenant, but they transgressed it—that is, they rendered it void—as was said of them to the prophet Jeremiah: “They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers, who refused to hear my words. These too have gone after foreign gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have rendered void my covenant, which I made with their fathers” (Jer. XI).

He briefly states every mode of transgression in saying that “they have begotten foreign children.” They begot them, I say, not so much through carnal procreation as through spiritual seduction. Nor did they merely beget foreign children: the parents themselves proved to be foreign children—that is, children of the flesh, indeed, but not to be reckoned or counted as seed. For the Apostle says: “Not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor are all children of God because they are Abraham’s seed; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’ That is, not the children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of promise are counted as seed” [Col. 0085C] (Rom. IX).

Therefore they begot foreign children: that is, they became such people themselves, or so trained their own children, that that seed of which it was said to Abraham, “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII)—namely Christ—may truthfully say: “Foreign children lied to me; foreign children rose up against me and became lame, departing from their paths” (Ps. XVII).

For those hard in heart and uncircumcised in ears, all this evil is too little: that, as the prophetic utterance threatens, they should not find the Lord and that he should be taken away from them by passing over to the faith of the Gentiles. They must also be struck by present evils, since they love present goods alone. Therefore it follows: “Now a month shall devour them with their portions.”

It is as though he said: Not only is that eternal evil prepared for them in the future—that they will be unable to find the Lord—but even now, in the present, the transitory goods that they alone love shall be taken from them, and the temporal evils that they alone fear shall be brought upon them. These are their portions, the portions of the ungodly; whereas, by contrast, the holy and righteous man says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. CXLI).

Therefore, “with their portions”—that is, with the temporal goods which alone they love—“a month shall devour them” [Col. 0086A]. A month is a short period, a brief number of days, and is always in movement or change, especially the lunar month, the only kind they knew from the Law and observed, they against whom this prophetic discourse is directed. Thus whenever in Holy Scripture we read that something occurred or was to occur on the tenth or fifteenth day of the month, we undoubtedly understand nothing other than the tenth or fifteenth lunar day.

The moon itself never remains in the same state, but is always changing: now it advances by increase until it is full; now it undergoes a decrease of light until it is wholly extinguished. Thus in this place “a month” is rightly understood as the temporality and mutability of the world or of this present life. This, he says, “shall now devour them,” because not only eternal evils in the future, but present evils also, are about to be received in the present age by both Israel and Judah.

We see that this was fulfilled long ago. For Israel has, since that time, been held captive in the land of the Assyrians. The Jews, indeed, were released from Babylonian captivity after seventy years; but later, at the hands of the Romans, they fell by the edge of the sword, were led captive among all nations, and lost their portions—that is, the earthly goods which alone they sought—because they would not have the Lord as their portion.

Having said this, the prophet’s Spirit immediately, with remarkable sharpness, cries out as follows, signifying that the destruction which he predicted is now imminent: “Sound the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl at Beth-aven.” A horn is made from the curved horn of an animal; but the trumpet is commanded by the Law to be made of bronze or silver, and it gives its sound in war and at solemn observances [Col. 0086C] (Num. X).

Gibeah and Ramah are neighboring cities in the tribe of Benjamin. This is the Gibeah in which Saul was born. Ramah is the very place which the king of Israel attempted to occupy, as is read in the Book of Kings, in order to block exit and entry for the tribe of Judah and Benjamin (III Kings II). Beth-aven, moreover, is in the tribe of Ephraim and was previously called Bethel.

Since he had earlier foretold the captivity of the ten tribes and the two, saying, “Now a month shall devour them with their portions,” he urges them, as though the nearby captivity were already impending, to sound horns and trumpets, exhorting one another to a common mourning. The sense is: Do not bewail your captivity in a subdued voice, but sound horns and trumpets so that all around may hear. This sense is well suited by the fact that Gibeah means “hill” and Ramah “height.” Thus they are told: “Sound the horn [Col. 0086D] in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah”—that is, go up to the mountains and hills and bewail aloud your impending captivity. Howl also at Beth-aven, where one of the golden calves stands, for whose worship its inhabitants will now be handed over into captivity.

And it is fittingly added: “Behind you, Benjamin.” For where the tribe of Benjamin ends, this city was built not far away in the tribe of Ephraim, namely beyond Benjamin, at its rear. Thus, when he leaps from the third person to the second and says, “Sound the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl at Beth-aven; behind you, Benjamin,” he both adorns the matter appropriately with remarkable rhetorical art and sharply expresses the imminent tumult of captivity.

Without delay, the Spirit returns with the same force to the third person and says: “Ephraim shall be desolate on the day of rebuke.” Above he had said, “Judah also shall fall with them,” namely with Israel and Ephraim; but now he says nothing of Judah and says of Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes—“Ephraim shall be desolate,” that is, it shall be without consolation amid the miseries of captivity.

And rightly so. Judah too was not then to be held captive in Babylon without consolation. It would have many consolations, especially through the glorious holiness of Daniel and his companions, by whom God displayed his mighty acts on behalf of the Jews, so that they could glory in their God before the king of Babylon. Then, after seventy years, they were to be consoled by release from captivity. Israel or Ephraim, captive in the land of the Assyrians, lacked consolations of this kind [Col. 0087B].

Therefore, as has already been said, Judah is rightly passed over here when it is said, “Ephraim shall be desolate on the day of rebuke”: that is, the people of the ten tribes shall have no consolation from God on the day or at the time when, because of their iniquities, they are handed over to their enemies. The chief author of these iniquities was Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam and the other kings who came from the tribe of Ephraim.

Why they had to be distinguished in this way, so that Israel or Ephraim should be desolate, we have already said elsewhere: some kings of Judah were righteous, such as David, Hezekiah, and Josiah; others, although they sinned by worshipping foreign gods, returned and repented, such as Manasseh; and under other kings too, the people of Judah returned to the worship of God. But no king at all of the kingdom of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes, for all of whom Ephraim is here used, since those kings descended from him—departed from the sins of Jeroboam, namely from the golden calves which he made.

For this reason, a little earlier the Lord had said: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; they will not set their thoughts upon returning to the Lord.” Then, lest anyone should have leisure to doubt the truth of the one who threatens, it follows: “In the tribes of Israel I have shown faithfulness.” It is as though he said: Whatever I have hitherto promised [Col. 0087D] or threatened to Israel has taken effect, and in all things I have shown myself true. Therefore let no one flatter himself concerning this utterance as though it were uncertain, because in this matter too, as in the others, I shall certainly be proved a faithful and truthful God.

It follows: “The princes of Judah have become like those who move a boundary-marker; upon them I shall pour out my wrath like water. Ephraim suffers oppression, crushed in judgment, because he began to go after filth.”

What we were now saying—that Judah sometimes placed an end to its iniquities, while Ephraim perpetuated the crime of idolatry, and therefore Judah’s captivity ought to have an end while Israel’s or Ephraim’s ought not to be ended—may suitably be understood from these present words. It is as though Truth or God’s Justice said: For this reason, as I said at the beginning of this prophecy, “I shall have mercy on the house of Judah” (Hos. I), because “the princes of Judah have become like those who set a boundary”; and for this reason I shall no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel (ibid.), because “he began to go after filth,” and, as I have already said, he will not set his thoughts upon establishing a boundary, ceasing to go after it, and bringing that very filth to an end.

According to this sense, what he says, “Upon them I shall pour out my wrath like water,” surely resounds with a great remembrance of mercy within that wrath itself. Judah’s captivity was indeed wrath due to its sins; but just as visible water is accustomed to wash away bodily filth, so that captivity also washed away the people’s sins, so that in some of them—namely in the three youths—there remained no sin for which their bodies ought to have been harmed in the Babylonian furnace [Col. 0088B] (Dan. I).

Thus, “The princes of Judah have become like those who set a boundary” may be understood as though he said: They placed an end to their evil ways, which the kings of Israel did not do; and therefore my wrath—that is, the present captivity—shall be like water to them, that is, it shall contribute to the cleansing of their sins.

By contrast, Ephraim, suffering oppression—that is, being led captive by Assyria which oppresses it—was crushed in judgment: that is, because its cause deserved it, God judged otherwise, that its captivity should not be released but perpetuated in the land of the Assyrians. Why? “Because he began to go after filth.” It is said with utmost severity, “Because he began to go after filth”; and one must understand: he will not cease to grow filthy, according to that saying, “Let him who is filthy become still more filthy” (Rev. XXII).

For when he says, “he began,” he implies that the completion of their filthiness had not yet come, although the golden calves which Jeroboam made and the Baal whom impious Jezebel additionally introduced were already very great filth. Israel had already become filthy in them, and the filth was great; yet he did not say, “because he went,” but “because he began to go after filth,” plainly wishing us to understand that, as he had begun, so he would persist in filth, would not set his thoughts upon returning, and would not seek cleansing from that same filth [Col. 0088C].

To this he adds: “And I am like a moth to Ephraim and like decay to the house of Judah.” A remarkable mercy: Ephraim went after filth, which is true filth; but I, who could have been its glory, seemed to it like filth—indeed, like a moth and decay. For it was ashamed to confess me before the Gentiles, as though my laws were contemptible.

For example, circumcision is a sign of faith looking toward that seed which was promised to Abraham. Ephraim was ashamed to observe this and the other observances of the holy Law, which the babbling of neighboring Gentiles ridiculed, ignorant of the hidden mysteries, just as swine are accustomed to trample pearls. Accordingly, I was counted by it as a moth and decay, so that it was ashamed to confess the glory of my name, just as a person who is excessively ashamed commonly covers and conceals a moth of the head.

“And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond; and Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king; but he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able [Col. 0089A] to free you from the bond. For I am like a lioness to Ephraim, and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah. I, I will seize and go; I will take away, and there is none to rescue. Going, I will return to my place, until you fail and seek my face.”

This is a remarkable rebuke of defective sight. Ephraim saw its sickness and Judah saw its bond; yet the former judged its sickness so great and the latter its bond so strong that they could in no way be healed or released by the God of their fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Therefore Ephraim fled to Assyria as though it were stronger than God, sending it gifts.

For I read in the Book of Kings that, under King Menahem, who ruled the ten tribes, Israel sent gifts to the Assyrians so that he might free it from its Damascene enemies. Judah also, under King Ahaz, sent gifts to Tiglath-pileser so that he might free it from oppression by the king of Damascus (IV Kings XV).

Plainly, both saw wrongly: the one its sickness and the other its bond. For, if they had seen rightly, they would know what follows: “He himself will not be able to heal you, nor free you from your bond.” Indeed, they will become adversaries to you and, as deserters of God, will exact vengeance from you. Therefore, when he had said, “And he sent to the king,” he significantly added, “the avenging king,” sharply rebuking the folly of that people. Seeking, while God is angry, to obtain a human helper, it encounters the same man as God’s avenger, who leads God’s deserters into captivity as though he had sworn to God to execute vengeance.

Therefore he says: “For I am like a lioness to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah.” [Col. 0089C] The sense is this: Although they have gone to Assyria and sent gifts to it so that it might deliver them, it will not be able to heal them or release them from the bond of their captivity. For I shall show that, when I oppose it, every human plan is vain; indeed, that when I am angry, hope placed in a human being turns to the contrary, since they will be led captive by those whom they prepared for themselves as a refuge.

And because God as avenger did this, God, I say, is accustomed to do this: the person who flees to someone, fleeing and departing from God, is especially captured and crushed by that very person, whether he flees to a human being or seeks the assistance of demons in images.

Nevertheless, what he immediately says—“I, I will seize and go; I will take away, and there is none to rescue”—is most beautiful and reasonable when understood in a good sense. For afterward those who are seized by the Lord, whose seizure is certainly good and health-giving, say in this way: “Come, let us return to the Lord, because he has seized and will heal us” (Hos. VI).

Therefore let us expound the present place according to the good captivity of which the Psalm also speaks: “You ascended on high; you took captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII), or, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.” Having recounted their sins so far and shown that, with God angry because of the same sins, no one can save or heal them, he finally promises in this way that he himself, the Savior, will come to heal those who flee to him: “I, I will seize.”

“I,” he says, “who am like a lioness to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah, shall at last seize and go.” He says, “I will seize,” but does not state what he will seize. Yet, as has already been said, those who return to the Lord make clear, by their return, what he seizes when they say: “Because he has seized and will heal us.” Therefore, when he says, “I, I will seize,” he promises that he will seize us, seize our nature, so as to become man.

Accordingly, let us consider the course of him who seized us, and then we shall clearly perceive the course of this utterance, which runs as follows: “I, I will seize and go; I will take away, and there is none to rescue. Going, I will return to my place, until you fail and seek my face. In tribulation they shall rise early to me, saying: ‘Come, let us return to the Lord, because he has seized and will heal us; he will strike and heal us. He will make us alive after two days; on the [Col. 0090B] third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence. We shall know and follow on, that we may know the Lord.’”

Christ our Savior, who speaks these things, did so. He seized us and went, as he says: “I, I will seize and go.” For in seizing our nature—that is, in becoming man—he passed from this world through the passion of death. Thus his Evangelist says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII). Again: “Knowing that he came from God and goes to God” (ibid.).

Then, when he had gone in this manner, he took the spoil of hell, as he had said: “When a strong man, armed, guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke XI).

Therefore, when he had said, “I, I will seize and go,” he fittingly at once added: “I will take away, and there is none to rescue.” It is as though he said: I shall assume human nature and go to the passion of death; and, with none able to resist, I shall rescue my elect from the enclosures of hell—I, that lioness, I, that lion’s cub, whom the patriarch Jacob, looking far ahead, said: “Judah is a lion’s cub. You have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness” (Gen. IV).

After accomplishing these things, rising from the dead, he went into heaven, whence he had come, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Therefore, after he had said, “I, I will seize and go; I will take away, and there is none to rescue,” he fittingly at once added: “Going, I will return to my place.” For his place is that seat of majesty, that shared session with God the Father [Col. 0090D], where he led captivity captive (Ps. LXVII), whom he seized when he placed there the human nature which had been a stranger: a nature whose origin is not heaven but earth, whose native country or original place is not the height of the heavens but the lowliness of dust.

Having returned to that place, he hid his face from that people to whom this Scripture speaks, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in and thus all Israel should be saved. Therefore, when he said, “I shall go and return to my place,” he fittingly at once added: “Until you fail and seek my face.” “Until you fail,” he says: plainly, with that failure from which, grieving, the Apostle says they had not yet failed: “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness [Col. 0091A] of God. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to every believer” (Rom. X).

Thus, when he says, “Until you fail and seek my face,” it is as though he said: Until you cease to desire to establish your own righteousness and to glory in the works of the Law, and believe in me, seeking only the righteousness of God, the righteousness of faith.

Having said this, he immediately says of all—both Jews and Gentiles—who would repent, believe in Christ, and be justified through his faith: “In their tribulation they shall rise early to me,” understanding them to say:

### Chapter VI
“Come, and let us return to the Lord; for he himself has seized us, and he will heal us; he will strike, and he will cure us. He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up.”

That first the Jews, [Col. 0091B] and then the Gentiles, said this and did this after Christ had gone and returned to his place—that is, after he ascended into heaven—is plain. For when the Holy Spirit had been given to the apostles and Peter was speaking to the people, they were pierced in heart and said to him and to the other apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” But Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts II). In that tribulation—that is, in that compunction and act of repentance—they rose up to the Lord; and they rise even now “in the morning,” that is, when the night of unbelief has passed and been driven away, together with the deeds of ignorance’s darkness.

Thus rising, they say: “Come, and let us return to the Lord.” For those who have known Christ preach him to others; not content with their own salvation alone, they strive also to preach to others the word of salvation, that they too may [Col. 0091C] be saved. What is that word? “For he himself,” they say, “has seized us, and he will heal us; he will strike, and he will cure us.” This word of salvation cannot be expressed more magnificently or more concisely. The entire fruit of conversion to Christ and of Christian faith is contained here in a few words: namely, the two resurrections by which we rise through Christ—the first, that of souls; the second, that of bodies.

For when he says, “For he himself has seized us, and he will heal us,” the meaning is this: because he took up our nature and will save us from our sins, according to his name, Jesus—that is, “Saviour.” Yet although he has already healed you who believe and have been baptized in his name, he will nevertheless still strike and afterwards [Col. 0091D] cure us. That is, he has left upon us the sentence of death for this body, of which he said: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III); and so it shall happen. But afterwards he will cure us—that is, on the last day he will cause us to rise in the resurrection of the flesh, since he has already healed and made us live by the resurrection of the soul, that is, by the remission of sins.

Hence the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead” (Rom. VIII)—that is, certainly destined to die—“because of sin; but the spirit lives because of justification.” Concerning that second resurrection of the flesh he immediately says: “He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up.” The meaning is: he will give us life on the last day, by the life or resurrection of the flesh; and we ascribe this to his own person, who died for us, because he will raise us up by virtue of his resurrection, which took place on the third day [Col. 0092A].

Thus healed and cured—that is, made alive and raised in soul and body—“we shall live,” he says, “in his sight”; that is, we shall be immortal. For we shall no longer be able to die because of beholding him, since we shall see him as he is, and thereby shall be like him (I John III). Then we shall know, and shall follow, so that we may know the Lord. We shall know, I say, and know him—not as now, in part, but perfectly. For the Apostle says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (I Cor. XIII). Again: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (ibid.). “Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known.”

“We shall follow,” he says. Whither shall we follow? Certainly to the fountains of the waters of life, as another prophet says: “For he who has mercy on them shall rule them, and shall give them drink at fountains of the waters of life” (Isa. XLIX). And in the Apocalypse we read: “For the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne shall rule them and lead them to fountains of the waters of life” (Apoc. VII). This is as though he said: they become immortal by seeing or beholding God.

They will say this while exhorting one another; the apostles or apostolic men will say it while preaching to the peoples; and they will add: “His coming forth is prepared like the dawn.” As though saying: What we say—“he himself has seized us, and he will heal us”—was not done in a corner. Rather, as dawn is seen by all, cannot remain hidden, and comes in order to be seen—indeed, in order to give light—so his coming forth, by which he came forth from his invisible things [Col. 0092C] to our visible things, became known to all. The whole world heard; no one can excuse himself on grounds of ignorance.

This is what the Psalmist likewise says: “He placed his tent in the sun” (Ps. VIII), that is, he set forth his humanity openly. And then: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat” (ibid.), because the report of his coming was heard by all, both Jews and Gentiles, and the preaching of his Gospel was heard.

They add further: “And he will come to us like the early and latter rain upon the earth.” In the literal sense, the early rain is that rain which, after the seeds have been cast, God gives to the land of Palestine, so that the moistened seeds may become warm. The latter rain is called that which brings those same fruits to maturity. For that land does not receive rain from heaven as frequently as ours does, but only twice a year.

Spiritually, both kinds of rain or shower—namely, early and latter—must be understood as holy prophetic and apostolic Scripture. For prophetic Scripture is itself the early rain; because, just as seeds moistened by the early rain sprout, so this Scripture, by frequent proclamation, made the promise of the coming Christ, made to Abraham, an object of expectation. But evangelical or apostolic Scripture is the latter rain; because, just as fruits are brought to maturity by the latter rain, so this Scripture confirms that Christ, of whom the prophets foretold, has now come.

Therefore, they say, “he will come to us like the early and [Col. 0093A] latter rain”: that is, he will come to us in such a manner, or deal with us in such a manner, as the Scriptures of both the New and the Old Testament bear witness.

Having said this concerning those who were going to believe and receive faith in his coming, he immediately turns to those whom he foresaw would not believe, and says: “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away in the morning.”

Thus indeed, when the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob, and then his brother Esau wept with a great cry, saying, “Have you not reserved a blessing for me also?” Isaac answered and said: “I have made him your lord, and have subjected all his brothers to his service; I have established him with grain and wine. And after these things, what shall I do for you, my son?” And afterwards: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above” (Gen. XXVII).

Certainly that Isaac bore the type of Christ; and the two sons, as has already been said, represented mystically the two peoples: the one Abraham’s seed by bodily descent alone, the other his seed by imitation of faith. There Isaac, in the type of Christ, says to the rustic son: “And after these things, my son, what more shall I do for you?” Yet he immediately finds what to do and says: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.” Here likewise Christ in prophecy says to carnal Israelites or carnal Jews—whoever are children of the flesh and not children of promise—“What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?” Yet he immediately finds, or knows, what he shall do when he says: “Your mercy is like a [Col. 0093C] morning cloud and like dew that passes away in the morning.”

This mercy is that small mercy which Isaac had in view when he said: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.” For the abundance of temporal or bodily things is a small mercy; and the sum of all such things is there comprehended in the richness of the earth and the dew of heaven.

But the great mercy is that blessing bestowed or poured out upon the simple Jacob, dwelling at home, according to these words: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field full of blessing, which the Lord has blessed.” And afterwards: “Let peoples serve you and tribes adore you. Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you. Let him who curses you be cursed; and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings” [Gen. XXVII]. For in blessing thus, Isaac invoked the great mercy: namely, that Christ should be born from Jacob’s seed.

Accordingly, because there is so great a difference between mercies, David—who had certainly received the lesser mercy, in the richness of the earth and in dew from heaven above, as a wealthy and renowned king—when he said, “Have mercy on me, O God,” immediately added, “according to your great mercy” (Ps. L). In what respect? Surely in this: that he might not be deprived, because of the matter of Uriah the Hittite, of the promise that Christ would be born from his seed. Hence later he says, “that you may be justified in your words”—understand: “have mercy on me,” by preserving for me the great mercy you promised. For God had already promised him Christ when he said: [Col. 0094A] “I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever” (II Kings VII).

Therefore here also, after the great mercy has been spoken of in relation to the children of promise through their faith—“In their tribulation they shall rise early to me, saying: Come and let us return to the Lord, for he himself has seized us and will heal us; he will strike and cure us,” etc.—he immediately turns to the children of the flesh as to Esau: “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away in the morning.”

It is as though he said: To the chosen people, whose type was Jacob, receiving great mercy and great blessing by holding the faith of Abraham’s seed—which is Christ—what more shall I do after these things for you children of the flesh, who, like Esau, delay and wander outside? Until now your blessing or mercy has been in the richness of the earth and in dew from heaven above; but now, as captivity hastens, let that same blessing pass away, just as a morning cloud passes away and is no longer there at noon or evening; and just as dew passes away, which covered the grass in the morning but quickly vanishes when the sun rises, and is no more.

So it will happen to you who were drenched in the morning and moistened with morning dew—that is, who sought present gladness and only the perishable goods of this present age. Your cloud passes away and your dew dries up when the sun rises: that is, your joy will be turned into sorrow, and your delights will not be found hereafter, where the true Sun, Christ, shining in his power, will be seen at noon [Col. 0094C].

“Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets, and slain them by the words of my mouth.” “Therefore,” he says, namely because you seek only the morning cloud of temporal things and transient dew, and pay no attention to the glory of God and the kingdom to come, “I have hewn”—that is, I have inflicted many blows—upon the prophets who, according to your own inclination, flattered and applauded you, seeing vanities and speaking lies. Such certainly were the prophets of Baal. As we read in the books of Kings, Elijah the Tishbite killed four hundred and fifty men in one day (III Kings XVIII); likewise Jehu, who overthrew the house of Ahab, struck down a great multitude of them (IV Kings X).

All this was done at the Lord’s command; therefore, after saying, “I have hewn them by the prophets,” he immediately added, “and slain them by the words of my mouth.” This was rightly done: those who, for temporal profit and, as another prophet says, “for a handful of flour” (Ezek. XIII), had not only abandoned the great mercy of God but had also drawn the popular multitude away with them, were first to be hewn down and slain in their own persons; then the people were to be led into captivity, deprived of the morning mercy already mentioned and of the dew that passes away.

How justly these things were done or are done is now known throughout the whole world, wherever the light of truth is. It follows: “And my judgments shall come forth like light.” The meaning is: just as light kindled illuminates eyes darkened in the night, so these announced judgments will be clear to those who until now had been in the night of ignorance, so that they may say: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. XVIII). Therefore “my judgments shall come forth like light”: that is, what I have willed, or what I have judged useful, will be known more plainly.

What is this? He says: “For I have desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offering.” The Lord is found recalling this pronouncement of his once and again in Matthew. For when, as he reclined in the house of Matthew himself, the Pharisees murmured, saying to his disciples, “Why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners?” he said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do” (Matt. IX). He immediately adds: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ [Col. 0095B] For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX).

Again, when his disciples were hungry and were plucking and eating ears of grain on the Sabbath, they said: “Behold, your disciples are doing what it is not lawful for them to do on Sabbaths.” After other matters he said: “But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned these innocent men.”

Therefore, when he says in this prophet, “For I have desired mercy and not sacrifice,” he gives an adequate reason for his judgments, and explains why above, among other things, he said: “They shall go with their flocks and their herds to seek the Lord, and shall not find him.” For they knew how to show mercy to their neighbours neither in body nor in soul, though they were ready sacrificers of flocks and slaughterers of herds. For the Gospel saying which we have recalled bears witness that he desired both [Col. 0095C; 0096A] forms of mercy: mercy toward body and mercy toward soul.

When, in receiving Matthew, a sinner or tax collector, he says, “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’” he plainly signifies that he required the mercy bestowed in the care of souls. But when he defends his hungry disciples, plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath, against the charge of Sabbath-breaking, saying, “But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned these innocent men,” there he certainly testifies that he desired the mercy bestowed on neighbours in their bodily needs.

Therefore the judgments of the Lord are true and manifest like light, and the case of carnal Israel or Ephraim and carnal Judah fails. For they eagerly offer sacrifice, which the Lord does not desire, and lack the bowels of mercy, which the Lord does desire; they multiply burnt offerings, which the Lord does not require, and neglect the knowledge of God, in which the Lord always desired and desires a rational creature to be exercised. They did not assent to his will; they did not carry out what he desired—namely, mercy and knowledge of God.

This is what he immediately adds: “But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they dealt treacherously against me.” The meaning is: they sinned, and, by defending their sin through pride and contradicting me, became merciless and cruel against themselves and against their descendants. But now, as we bring this second book to an end, let us take the beginning of the following book from this same chapter.

# THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0095]

[Col. 0095C] 41 In the Song of Songs the beloved speaks to his friend: “Show me your face, my friend, my beautiful one, my dove; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (Song II). We suitably recall a voice or address of this kind now, because, while preserving the higher level of heavenly grace or love, in which the beloved Christ and his friend, the holy Church, are recognized, the mind of every wise person is the beloved, and holy Scripture is his friend or beloved, if he is such a person that his conscience may truthfully bear him witness that he loves the true beauty and beautiful truth of holy Scripture.

For these are that person’s words: “I said to wisdom, ‘You are my sister’; and I called prudence my friend” (Prov. VII). Therefore the studious mind now says—and the difficulty of the present Scripture itself urges it to say—“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.” The face of this holy Scripture has never been shown except to the wise, and its voice has never sounded except in the ears of one who loves it; nor does anyone else deserve to know how sweet its voice is and how beautiful its face.

For he who wrote says: “Who is wise and shall understand these things? Who is intelligent and shall know them?” (Hos. XIV). Therefore, striving to have the Spirit—the gracious author of the seed of this sweetness and beauty—favourable to us, let us diligently follow this beloved or friend along the path begun, that we may deserve to see her face and hear her voice—[Col. 0096D] that is, to perceive her intention and behold her true meaning.

When the Lord had said in this prophet: “For I have desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offering,” he immediately added: “But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they dealt treacherously against me.” From this chapter he begins again to denounce the sins of the people. Thus it must again be recalled that, as we have already said above, this prophet seven times strikes at the sins of his sinful nation, and just as many times his discourse returns to the coming or sacrament of the Son of God; he ends each course there, indicating to the wise and intelligent person—who deserves to know these things—that no one can be justified and freed from sins except through the grace or faith of Christ.

The first course, which we have treated thus far, began in this way: “For there is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land.” At last, in the person of the Christ to come, he said: “In their tribulation they shall rise early to me,” etc.; and only then returned to the beginning of the rebuke, saying: “For I have desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offering; but they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they dealt treacherously against me.”

For when he says, “For I have desired mercy and the knowledge of God,” it must be understood or recalled that at the beginning of the chapter he had said, “There is no mercy and there is no knowledge of God in the land.” Now, therefore, proceeding in the order undertaken, we should not pass carelessly over the fact that he says two things in the present verse: “They transgressed like Adam; there they dealt treacherously against me.” In this brief verse he touches both their original sin and their actual sins.

For by saying, “They transgressed like Adam,” he strongly accuses their actual sins. In worshipping idols and committing their other crimes, they did not sin merely in some incidental way; they did not offend through ignorance or weakness. Rather, in the worst manner of sinning, they sinned knowingly, knowing that they did evil. In abandoning the house of David and the temple of the Lord, which was in Jerusalem, and worshipping golden calves, they defended their sin by contradicting all the holy prophets whom the Lord sent [Col. 0097C]. Hence the Lord also says above: “For your people are like those who contradict the priest.” This indeed was to transgress the covenant as Adam transgressed it. For he both transgressed and proudly defended his transgression, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III).

But in adding, “There they dealt treacherously against me,” he refers to original sin. For when he says “there,” it is to be understood “in Adam”; for he had said first, “They transgressed the covenant like Adam.” And they truly dealt treacherously in Adam, because, as the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all men, in whom all sinned” [Col. 0097D] (Rom. V). Therefore, when he says, “There they dealt treacherously against me,” the frequently mentioned Apostle agrees with the prophet also in this statement, proving that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin, and adding these words: “For there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

Having said this, he immediately treats more fully of actual sin—namely, the sin of idolatry and worship of golden calves—by which, as Adam did, they transgressed the covenant, as has already been said. For it follows: “Gilead is a city of those who work an idol, supplanted by blood; and like the jaws of men who are robbers, a band of priests killing on the way as they go from Shechem, because they have committed wickedness.”

Gilead is a city situated beyond the Jordan in the tribe of Gad, in which an idol was first consecrated. It was also a city of fugitives. But the more famous it was, the more it became the source of idolatry and every evil. And because these men first consecrated idols or especially assisted in evil, as the present passage testifies, they were the first to be captured by the Assyrians and carried into captivity.

Moreover, Shechem was a city on the boundary between the ten tribes [Col. 0098A] and the two; it was later called Neapolis. Through it lay the route for Israelites going to Jerusalem, where alone it was lawful to offer sacrifices. Therefore at the three times when, according to the commandment of the Law, the people had to ascend to the temple of the Lord, their priests placed robbers on the road to lie in wait for those travelling there. Their purpose was that the people should worship golden calves at Dan and Bethel rather than worship the Lord at Jerusalem; and they killed on that very road those whom they could not turn back.

Gilead is now called an accomplice of those priests because the Gileadites joined themselves to them in an iniquitous alliance and cooperated with the priests in killing. The meaning, therefore, is this: if you ask why he said, “But they transgressed the covenant like Adam,” who certainly sinned not through ignorance but knowingly and arrogantly, and boldly defended his sin against God who reproved him—behold the obvious result or work of that evil defence. For there is no clearer proof of defence than killing those who refuse to share in the common acceptance of one’s committed sin.

Gilead was a place of killing, by a marvellous perversion, [Col. 0098C] a marvellous supplanting. For it ought to have been a city not of killers but of those who released a fugitive from killing, according to the Law of the Lord, which says: “And when the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not deliver him into his hands, because he struck his neighbour unknowingly, and he was not proved to have been his enemy two or three days before; and he shall dwell in that city until he stands before judgment, giving an account of his deed, and the high priest who is in office at that time dies” (Josh. XX).

It is rightly called “supplanted by blood,” because, having destroyed or abandoned its appointed peace, it accepted bloodshed in exchange for it. It is also called “like the jaws of men who are robbers,” because, just as robbers, hidden in jaws—that is, in caves and secret places—strip and kill passers-by, so in that city, which ought to have been an asylum for fugitives, bloodthirsty priests lying in wait for the people’s simplicity stripped them of faith, killed them in mind, and deprived of clothing and killed in body those whom they could not deceive.

The prophet, grieving over so great a crime, cries out: “In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing. There Ephraim committed fornication; Israel was defiled.” For what could be more horrible, what more deserving of an outcry, than that this should occur not in any ordinary people or nation but in the house of Israel, in God’s nation, in the Lord’s portion, as Moses says: “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the measure of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII)? The sin of another nation in idols is error. But the sin of Israel, which had knowledge of the true and one God and had received the Law, is horror.

Therefore he so often calls that people’s sin fornication, and now too says: “There Ephraim committed fornication; Israel was defiled.” Ephraim, as has often been said, is Jeroboam himself, of the tribe of Ephraim; Israel is the ten tribes, which were defiled by following him when he sinned—that is, when he made golden calves for himself as gods. For just as a woman is defiled by adultery, so that people, having abandoned God, was defiled by idolatrous worship.

These things were said against Israel, that is, the ten tribes. But was he angry only with them? Was not great wrath also to come upon Judah, as we now see, according to its deserts? It follows: “But you also, Judah, set a harvest for yourself [Col. 0099B] when I turn back the captivity of my people.”

It is as though he said: At the beginning of this prophetic discourse, I said, “I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy on the house of Judah and save them in the Lord their God.” And this is true. For the captivity of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes, will not be recalled from the land of the Assyrians. But your migration, O Judah, is to be brought back from Babylon after seventy years.

Nevertheless, when I turn back that captivity of my people—when I bring back to their land those among you who remain, worthy to be saved as a remnant through their own faith and merits, until the fullness of time in which the universal captivity of all my people is to be turned back through the coming of Christ the Saviour—you, Judah, “set a harvest for yourself” that must be cut down. That is, know that the multitude of ill-born children in which you will multiply is to be mown down by Roman swords, just as the ten tribes are now, or rather even more than now, being mown down and carried away by the Assyrians.

For what reason? For what deserts or sins? He says:

## CHAPTER VII

“When I wished to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim was revealed, and the wickedness of Samaria; for they worked falsehood, and a thief entered, plundering, a robber outside.”

The meaning is: when I came to save Israel, that iniquity was revealed and that wickedness of the Jews manifested itself, of which the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria had been a type [Col. 0099D] or foreshadowing—when, having abandoned the house of David, it preferred Jeroboam; and, having abandoned the Lord God, chose rather to worship golden calves.

Let us endeavour carefully to expound the passage of this prophecy which we now enter, remembering the saying at the end of the book which we have often recalled: “Who is wise and shall understand these things? Who is intelligent and shall know them?” Let us understand and know that the things which the prophetic eye here foresees and prescribes are so great, or of such a kind, that if he had uttered them in plain words, they would have been far too intolerable for people of that time to hear, as we have already said in the prologue to this present work.

Indeed, he here mystically describes Judah’s sin against the Saviour, whose blood it shed, because of which such things occurred, or had to occur, in the destruction of that nation. Foreseeing these things, he rightly says: “But you also, Judah, set a harvest for yourself.” “When,” he says, “I wished to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria were revealed.”

Whoever is not yet wise or intelligent in the manner required by the holy spirit of prophecy in the passage already mentioned supposes that nothing else is signified here than as though it were said: When through David, my chosen one, I wished to instruct Israel to know the true God and to hold firmly to the lawful worship of my name alone, the iniquity of the children of Israel burned more fiercely and their wickedness raged more stubbornly. Nor did they cease until, when the governance of the kingdom had passed to their descendants, they cast off the yoke, withdrew from the house of that same David, and made gods for themselves according to the prompting of their iniquity, according to the malicious desires [Col. 0100B] of their heart.

But that David was not only the father of our Savior according to the flesh; in his wondrous deeds he also bore the figure of that same Savior. His kingdom was a preparation for Christ’s kingdom—or rather, Christ’s kingdom and David’s are one kingdom—according to which the angel also says to Mary concerning him: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1).

Conversely, Jeroboam and those who followed him in abandoning David bore the type of the Jews and Pharisees, who denied Christ before Pilate and said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). That fury by which, condemning Christ, they demanded that Barabbas, a murderer and author of sedition, be released to them was like the wickedness [Col. 0100C] by which those who followed Jeroboam “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” (Rom. 1). Or, as it is written here, they “worked falsehood,” because, despising truth, they made and worshipped falsehood in the golden calves.

Therefore, in these words let us contemplate both the likeness and the reality. The likeness lies in the condition of that time, namely, in the way Ephraim—or those ten tribes—thus withdrew from the house of David. The reality lies in the Savior’s coming, when the Jews, rebelling against truth, denied him and refused to be the people of this king. Thus, when he says, “When I wished to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim was revealed,” let us set before the mind’s eyes both David, Christ’s father according to the flesh, [Col. 0100D] and this his son, the true David; for each in his own way wished to heal Israel: the former by composing the psaltery, the latter by assuming flesh.

For David himself testifies that the man-made psaltery was a type of Christ’s flesh or body, when in a psalm he introduces the Father, while Christ’s body rests in the tomb, speaking to the same Son: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). And the latter answers: “I shall arise at dawn” (ibid.). David wished to heal Israel by means of his man-made psaltery, because he sang heavenly words with the psaltery precisely in order to lead a people devoted only to earthly things into love and hope of the future kingdom, which is the true health of the heart. Before him no one did this: no one announced heavenly promises in [Col. 0101A] explicit words, or the punishments of eternal fire.

This is so true that in Moses you will find almost nowhere promises of paradise or of God’s kingdom, nor threats of hell, under explicit names, apart from one place in the Song of Deuteronomy, where he says: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn to the uttermost depths of hell” (Deut. 32). All things are enclosed under figures: eternal goods are signified under the name of the land of Canaan, a land as though flowing with milk and honey; while everlasting evils are signified, as recompense according to deserts, under the names of famine, pestilence, the sword, and harmful beasts.

For such, and in a sense childish, was the understanding of the carnal people in the condition of that time: they knew how to love only present prosperity and to fear only present adversity. Hence David was the first, as has already been [Col. 0101B] said, openly to express in words the glory of the heavenly kingdom, adding the power of musical sweetness and the ordered form of divine worship, while the Lord wished to heal Israel: that is, so that, with a sound heart, it might make little of earthly things and desire heavenly things more.

Yet this psaltery, or this harp, to which the Father said, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp,” did this much more fully when he opened his mouth, as Matthew writes: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), and so forth. Certainly these words sounded utterly contrary to carnal Israel’s expectation, since they call blessed the poor, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those enduring persecution for righteousness’ sake.

For carnal Israel thought otherwise: [Col. 0101C] it held blessed only those prospering in this world’s course—those who were truly proud, harsh, or tyrannical, laughing and exulting even amid the worst things; strangers to miseries and therefore unable to feel compassion for the wretched; luxuriating in every pleasure of heart and body; waging war and, puffed up by military triumphs, able by their power to kill and persecute whom they wished. Such a disposition was indeed a great infirmity. But he wished to heal Israel, so that it might think soundly.

Against both of them the iniquity of Ephraim was revealed: that is, all those who refused to be healed persecuted them. First, who does not know how many adversities David, that psalmist of God’s kingdom, endured, and how many evils he suffered from them? They hated him without cause to such an extent that [Col. 0101D] they even made his son Absalom king for themselves, since they had no other leader under whom, rising up, they might drive him from the kingdom. After Absalom’s death they followed Sheba son of Bichri. When he too had died, they kept quiet, conquered and unwilling, through the wisdom of David himself and of his son Solomon. But afterward, as soon as an opportunity was given through Rehoboam’s imprudence, they threw off the yoke from their necks and made for themselves another king and foreign gods—that is, golden calves (4 Kings 17).

This was the iniquity of Ephraim and this the wickedness of Samaria: Jeroboam, of the tribe of Ephraim, wickedly committed this wrong, and Samaria—by which his entire kingdom is understood, for it was the metropolis of the ten tribes—maliciously embraced the same thing, namely, envying the house [Col. 0102A] of David and envying and begrudging the tribe of Judah because kings were to be appointed for it alone from that tribe.

For at one point the men of Israel said to King David: “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan?” And every man of Judah answered: “Because the king is nearer to me.” The man of Israel replied: “I have ten parts; I am greater” (2 Kings 19). Thus, when sedition had been stirred up, a certain man of Belial, Sheba son of Bichri, blew the trumpet and said: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Kings 20).

Finally, from sayings and deeds of this kind it is plainly understood what was the wickedness of Samaria of which he now speaks here: its cause was envy, which can truly be called wickedness because it produces every malicious contrivance of thought. Iniquity especially deserves to be called wickedness when it conducts itself so that it can appear to proceed with wisdom or reason. Samaria could seem to have acted wisely or reasonably in following and making Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim king, because when the patriarch Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons Manasseh and Ephraim, he said: “He indeed”—that is, Manasseh—“shall become a people and shall be multiplied; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall grow into nations” (Gen. 48).

And in Chronicles we read: “Reuben was Israel’s firstborn; but when he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, son of Israel” (1 Chron. 5). [Col. 0102B] He did indeed say “to the sons of Joseph” in the plural; but since, as has been said, he preferred Ephraim, the younger, to the elder, the tribe of Ephraim rightly seemed to itself able to glory in the birthright.

Thus Samaria’s sin, in departing from the house of David and envying the tribe of Judah because kings or rulers were to spring from it, ought rightly to be called wickedness: although it acted against truth and reason, it seemed not to lack the support of reason and divine authority. Observe also how he says: “The iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria was revealed.” He does not say that iniquity arose or began to arise when “I wished to heal Israel,” but that it was revealed. It lay concealed so long as Israel had leaders or rulers who compelled it to worship God, of whom David had been the best or greatest.

But it was revealed when those men died and departed, just as Scripture says in one place: “When the Lord raised up judges, in their days he was moved to mercy, heard the groaning of the afflicted, and delivered them from the slaughter of ravagers. But after the judge had died, they turned back and did much worse than their fathers had done, following foreign gods and worshipping them. They did not abandon their inventions or the very hard way in which they had been accustomed to walk” (Judg. 2). In the same way that iniquity and wickedness were revealed when David had died, for while he reigned they had not dared to reveal themselves. Indeed, they were revealed then far more greatly than ever before.

Previously, when some calamity pressed upon them and, amid tribulation, they cried to the Lord, [Col. 0103A] they turned to the Lord and abandoned foreign gods when some deliverer—that is, a good judge—had been raised up. But from the time when their iniquity was thus revealed, so that they made the calves, they never departed from those calves, as Scripture plainly says of each individual king: that they did not depart from Jeroboam’s sins.

Still pursuing this iniquity or wickedness, the prophetic utterance immediately adds: “For they have worked falsehood; a thief entered in, plundering, a robber outside.” They worked falsehood by saying of the calves, which certainly were not gods: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12). Both the devil invisibly and Jeroboam visibly worked to bring that deed about. Therefore it is beautifully and truly said: “A thief entered in, plundering”—namely, the devil secretly devouring souls by the wickedness covertly instilled—and “a robber outside,” namely, Jeroboam, the visible robber, who outside—that is, outwardly—fashioned idols outside the Lord’s house or portion, caused Israel to sin, and thus committed a great and cruel robbery.

We have explained how, in that time when David reigned or had now departed, the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria had been revealed when the Lord wished to heal Israel. Let us now explain how, at the last time, when in his coming the Savior likewise wished to heal Israel, a similar wickedness or iniquity—indeed, according to the likeness, a much greater one—was revealed.

“When I wished to heal Israel,” says the healer and savior of Israel, the author of that healing. A little before, after saying: “In their tribulation they will rise early to me,” he immediately introduced the words of those rising to him: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has wounded and he will heal us” (Hos. 6). Of this healing or health—that is, remission of sins and the first resurrection, which is the resurrection of the soul—something has already been said in the same place.

When God, made man, wished to heal Israel with that health, beginning to preach visibly and in person, and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 4), then the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria were revealed: that is, the iniquity of the Jews and the wickedness of the scribes and Pharisees, of which the iniquity of Ephraim and wickedness of Samaria previously discussed according to the letter [Col. 0103D] or history were types.

For an evil spirit stirred them up (1 Kings 16), so that they mocked, persecuted, and blasphemed the teacher of repentance, who taught by his word of preaching and performed works that no one else had done; for example, saying: “You have a demon” (John 8), and again: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. 12).

Christ did not please them as such a preacher: a teacher of repentance, persuader to poverty and example of humility, master of meekness, exhorter to mourn for sins, proclaimer of righteousness and seeker of mercy, commender of purity of heart, rewarder of peace, and comforter of those suffering persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. 5). Why? For what reason did they reject, hate, and assail one preaching such things?
