Clearly because they thought and loved all things contrary to these, and desired a Messiah to come who would exalt them in this world, disturb the peace of the nations until he had subjected all the ends of the earth to their dominion through wars and military triumphs, construct for them a golden and jewelled Jerusalem upon the earth, and in all such matters literally fulfil their desire, as the prophetic letter seems in many places to sound.

Yet he himself briefly expresses their purpose and disposition in one place: “How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?” [Col. 0104B] (John 5). Therefore they persecuted the one wishing to heal them, like madmen striking a physician who offers an antidote. Nor did they cease until, handing him over, they denied him before Pilate, chose Barabbas the robber and author of sedition, and demanded that their own king be crucified (Matt. 27).

In this way the iniquity of Ephraim and wickedness of Samaria were revealed in them—indeed, fulfilled by them. Thus they filled up the measure of their fathers; thus they revealed and testified that they consented to their fathers. For what those earlier people began—departing from David’s house and killing the Lord’s prophets—these completed by crucifying the son of David, the Son of God, and then killing, crucifying, scourging, and persecuting from city to city the prophets, [Col. 0104C] wise men, and scribes whom he sent.

In all these matters they worked falsehood, lying against that same king whom they denied and accused as evil and a deceiver. The following too is clear in them: “A thief entered in, plundering, a robber outside.” Judas the traitor was the thief, and the Pharisaic party the robber. Judas was a thief of the Lord’s money-boxes, as the evangelist testifies: “He was a thief and, having the money-boxes, carried what was put into them” (John 12). The Pharisees and priests, moreover, practised robbery in the temple, making prey of the people through buying and selling. Therefore, when he drove them out (Matt. 21), he cited the testimony from Isaiah: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’” (Isa. 56); and immediately added the words from Jeremiah: “But you have made it a den of robbers” (Jer. 7).

That thief within, among the disciples of the Lord Jesus—a false disciple and pretended friend—and that robber outside, that is, an open enemy, formed a common plan and, as has already been said, worked falsehood. The chief craftsman of this falsehood was Caiaphas, who lied thus, while that whole council of evildoers conspired to deceive the wretched people: “It is expedient for you that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish, lest perhaps the Romans come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11).

So completely, when the Lord wished to heal Israel, did Israel in its own manner refuse healing, as he declared in other words: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, [Col. 0105A] you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you: how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!” (Matt. 23).

It follows: “And lest they say in their hearts, ‘I have remembered all their wickedness’: now their inventions have surrounded them; they have been before my face.” This is a strong and true confirmation of the just judgment or vengeance of God which he had previously announced in saying: “And you also, Judah, appoint a harvest for yourself” (Hos. 6), calling “harvest,” as has already been said, the vastness of the destruction by which they were to be ruined by the Romans.

“Lest,” he says, “they say in their hearts, ‘I have remembered all their wickedness.’” As though he said: Lest they murmur and rebuke as unjust the sentence which says, “That upon you may come all the righteous blood [Col. 0105B] shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (Matt. 23); lest, because what was punished in the fathers is punished again in the sons, any ground of just complaint remain to them, it is removed.

For Jews answering us on such matters customarily say: “Why do you think that at this time vengeance is exacted upon us for something that was punished long ago?” For example, when we tell them that the sin which their fathers formerly committed in the wilderness by making and worshipping the calf is visited upon them now, when they have been so blinded, they reply that the Lord then remembered that wickedness, since on that day twenty-three thousand of them fell. In saying this, they do not observe that after this was done through the hands of the sons of Levi, to whom Moses also said: “Today each of you has consecrated your hands to the Lord, against his son and his brother” (Exod. 32), Moses afterward prayed: “Forgive them this sin.” God answered: “My angel shall go before you; but in the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs also” (ibid.).

Therefore, “lest they say in their hearts, ‘I have remembered all their wickedness’”—that is, that I punished every individual sin in its own time, and therefore that all things ought not now come upon this generation—I say to them: “Now their inventions have encircled them,” as with a long cord, because they imitated all the sins of previous generations. And those inventions “have been before my face,” because they took no care to blot them out by any satisfaction of repentance.

Such are their inventions [Col. 0105D] that encircled them: they contrived causes of death against one man in such a way that it was deservedly said, and deservedly ought to be fulfilled: “All these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. 23). For all who, from the blood of righteous Abel onward, killed righteous men or prophets made themselves like Cain, who killed Abel (Gen. 4); like Saul, who persecuted David and on his account slaughtered eighty-five men, priests of the Lord, and struck their city with the edge of the sword (1 Kings 21); like Jezebel and Ahab, who killed righteous Naboth and the Lord’s other prophets (3 Kings 2). Therefore these people bore in their generation the iniquities of those persons and of all who had been like them.

[Col. 0106A] What are those inventions that encircled them and by which they made themselves like all of those people? He says:

> “In their wickedness they made the king glad,  
> and the princes in their lies.  
> All are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.  
> The city rested a little from the mixing of the leaven,  
> until the whole was leavened.  
> The day of our king!  
> The princes began to rage from wine.  
> He stretched out his hand with mockers,  
> because they applied their heart like an oven,  
> while he lay in wait for them.  
> All night he slept, baking them;  
> in the morning he himself burned like a flaming fire.”

Who was this king, and who were these princes, whom the adulterers made glad both by their wickedness and their lies, being heated as an oven is heated by the baker? The following interpretation is useful; although it is not found openly stated, it may nevertheless be inferred from the events that it occurred in this manner.

King Jeroboam and his princes, who favoured him and obediently lent themselves to every crime, were made glad in this way. We shall defer for a little the prophetic mystery concerning the Savior’s death, of which we were speaking, lest we seem to have neglected an interpretation that is at least reasonable and plausible.

“All are adulterers,” that is, departing from their own husband, God, “like an oven heated by the baker”; for as an oven is heated to bake bread, so they were heated by Jeroboam’s wickedness and the fire of idolatry. “The city rested a little from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.” After fabricating the idols, Jeroboam did not compel the people to worship them, lest perhaps, if some resisted from zeal for God’s religion, the worship of idols should come to nothing. [Col. 0106C] Therefore the city rested for a little while, until the people should consent to the king of their own will: first the princes, then their followers, who favoured the king and princes, and finally the entire people, should be corrupted. This is what he means by “until the whole was leavened.”

For things done willingly endure for a long time, whereas those done under compulsion are quickly undone. Jeroboam considered this and preferred that the people should submit to a new worship of idols voluntarily rather than under coercion. Thus, when the whole mass of the people had been heated in veneration of the calves, they began to say at Jeroboam’s doors: “The day of our king”—that is understood—“this is the day which our sovereign has established for us as a festival. We celebrate it; in it we rejoice; in it we worship the golden calves.”

As the people thus cried out, “the princes began,” he says, “to rage from wine”: that is, not only were those who ought to have been rulers of the people not angry, but, further, losing the understanding of their minds, they began to rage from wine, suffering madness both from luxury and idolatry.

What did the king do in response? “He stretched out his hand,” he says, “with mockers, because they applied their heart like an oven, while he lay in wait for them.” The princes were mockers, because they wickedly mocked the people and led them far from their God. They agreed with its error and rejoiced that they had applied their heart like an oven, so that the king might heat them and make them burn in idolatry’s flames. With these mockers, with such princes, he stretched out his hand, as though blessing them and giving thanks for their ready consent, [Col. 0107A] “while he lay in wait for them”: that is, while he held within himself the wicked plan of wholly turning them away from the Lord’s temple, lest by going to Jerusalem to worship and sacrifice they gradually return to their senses and again accept one and the same king with Judah.

While he was contriving such things, “all night he slept, baking them; in the morning he himself burned like a flaming fire.” The sense is this: after he had introduced the fire of wickedness into their hearts, saw them raging, and saw that no one resisted his will, he slept all night—that is, he lay secure, cunning amid darkness, baking them with the fire of impiety. But in the morning he himself, burning with the flames of his crimes, came to sacrifice.

Let these things, recounted concerning former times according to conjecture rather than history, suffice in whatever measure they can. Let us attend to the fact that he is a prophet, conscious of such depth that at the end of the book he says what has often already been recalled: “Who is wise and shall understand these things, intelligent and shall know them?” (Hos. 14). Let us return to the mystery of the Savior which we began above, and endeavour to follow the prophet, who looks toward the future, with the eye of understanding.

These are their inventions—the inventions of the Jews—which encircled them and which they could not escape, on account of which they were judged and condemned to be cut down like a dry harvest by the Romans’ sickle of war:

> “In their wickedness they made the king glad,  
> and the princes in their lies;  
> all are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.”

These adulterers are those whose crime another prophet foresaw: “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). [Col. 0107C] For he foresaw the sacrilege of the Jews and that night in which they raged against the Lord and against his Christ, not without a certain resemblance to the Sodomites.

The ancient history is well known: when the Lord lodged with Lot, the men of the city surrounded his house that very night, from boy to old man, all the people together; they called Lot and said to him: “Where are the men who entered in to you by night?” (Gen. 19), etc. In likeness to them, these men, heated like an oven by the baker-devil, after eating their paschal lamb that night, drunk and filled with food, surrounded the Lord and seized him in order to hand him over to the Gentiles for mockery, scourging, and crucifixion (Matt. 20).

“In their wickedness they made the king glad.” Which king? Clearly Pontius Pilate, or even Caesar himself, whom they thought to please by flattery when they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). For the passage in Acts of the Apostles confirms that Pilate is rightly called king here. When the believers at prayer said: “Lord, you who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them, who by the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of our father David your servant, said: ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ’” (Ps. 2), they immediately added: “For truly there assembled in this city against your holy [Col. 0108A] servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and peoples of Israel” (Acts 4).

That passage of Scripture testifies that Pontius Pilate and Herod were those kings of whom it had been written: “The kings of the earth stood forth.” And rightly so: they were tetrarchs, that is, these rulers each held a fourth part of the Jewish kingdom—Pontius Pilate, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias. The Jews made their king glad in their wickedness when they seized the Lord Jesus and handed him over to be crucified.

Pilate indeed spoke words which appeared sorrowful, saying: “I find no case against him,” and other such things; he even washed his hands and said: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man; see to it yourselves” (Matt. 27). But he lied, being a man without truth and a possession of falsehood itself. For when the Lord said to him: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” he immediately said insolently: “What is truth?” and, without waiting for an answer, went out again (John 18).

How far, do you suppose, was he from truth, and how false was he? Indeed, he was not merely false, but also a hypocrite and a crafty man: he feigned justice as though pious, while impiously rejoicing. Someone may ask: What reason or necessity had he, while rejoicing, to pretend sadness? Clearly, he feared the secular justice of the Roman Empire, then in force, lest he be called to account for killing an innocent man and incur the penalty for homicide. This nevertheless happened to him later.

This was his fear, which the evangelist also mentions where, after the Jews said, “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God,” he immediately adds: “When Pilate therefore heard this saying, he was more afraid” (John 19). Yet the Lord himself still seems to excuse him when he says: “Therefore he who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (ibid.). He does not excuse the murderer, but condemns the Jewish crime more severely in comparison with his.

For Pilate, who had received neither the Law nor the Prophets, is accused in the Lord’s killing as guilty of homicide because he could know him to be nothing other than a man. But the Jew is convicted by the Law and Prophets because he handed over not merely a man but his King and God; and therefore he has the greater sin, for which he has no excuse.

Thus in their wickedness they made glad Pilate, king or tetrarch or governor—indeed, not merely one king, but the kings Pilate and Herod. For, when Pilate learned, says the evangelist, that he was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem in those days. “Herod, seeing Jesus, rejoiced greatly” (Luke 23), hoping by the sight of his miracles to feed or satisfy the royal and proud curiosity of his eyes. For it follows: “For he had desired for a long time to see him, because he had heard many things of him and hoped to see some sign done by him.” When he answered nothing, Herod, with his soldiers, despised and mocked him; and, dressing him in a white garment, sent him back to Pilate. [Col. 0109A] “Herod and Pilate became friends with each other on that very day; for previously they had been enemies” (Luke 23).

This was their joy: to enter into friendship and agreement in order to mock and destroy the Lord. The princes whom they likewise made glad in their falsehoods were chiefly the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. They wickedly rejoiced when, according to their own will, the crowds lied, calling him a great deceiver and evildoer and saying: “We found this man subverting our nation and forbidding tribute to be paid to Caesar” (ibid.), and similar things.

“The city rested a little from the mixing of leaven until the whole was leavened.” It is well known that the Jewish feast, at whose approach the Lord was sought in order to be killed, was the feast of unleavened bread. From the evening when he was handed over until the eighth day, leavened matter was not found in their houses, according to the Law’s command (Deut. 16). Yet they themselves were leavened with the old leaven, the leaven of wickedness and malice (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore the city is aptly said to have had an admixture of leaven then, when it most vainly avoided leaven outwardly in its bread but did not fear being leavened inwardly by malicious and bloody designs. The city rested a little from the mixing of such leaven because, after they had been leavened by that counsel of evildoers as they plotted to kill him, the Jews of Jerusalem restrained themselves and rested a little because of the crowds who had come up from other cities or [Col. 0109C] regions and had welcomed him with palm branches, crying: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21).

Hence, when they had held council to seize and kill him by deceit, the evangelist says that they said: “Not on the feast day”; and he adds the reason: “Lest there be a disturbance among the people” (Matt. 26). They did not say this from religious purpose, as though the feast should retain the adornment of peace, but lest he should be taken from their hands by the aid of the people gathered for the feast. For when the traitor came who would hand him over without crowds, they went out to seize him on the very night of the feast, against religious custom and against the Law’s ordinance.

For when the Law had said, “Dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood that is on the threshold and sprinkle from it the lintel [Col. 0109D] and both doorposts,” it also added: “None of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning” (Exod. 12). Thus the city that ought to have feasted on unleavened bread rested with an evil and malicious purpose from the time when it began to be leavened by the mixing of that leaven, mixed together by the evil assembly of the council. The elders, scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests did this, so that it might rest until the whole was leavened—that is, until all should be confirmed more and more in the same consent to wickedness.

Having said this, the prophet suddenly cries aloud the terrible voices of those who had seized the Lord: “The day of our king!” Imagine them saying: “Honour to our king, honour and loyalty to Caesar! For we have no king [Col. 0110A] but Caesar, and on this day we have done him honour by seizing this man who forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar. Let this day be memorial to him, for whose honour and loyalty we mock, spit upon, crown with thorns, scourge, and crucify this man who calls himself king.”

While saying these and similar things, “the princes began,” he says, “to rage from wine.” They truly began to rage in mind, because they seized him not in the morning while fasting and sober, but gorged and drunk in the evening, once the day was already closed, during that feast and that paschal night, when, undoubtedly, it was customary and pleasant for them to dine richly and drink abundantly. Drunk and loosened by a full stomach, they could set no limit to their fury as they persecuted “a poor and needy man, and one stricken in heart, to put him to death” [Col. 0110B] (Ps. 108).

Hence among other things it is said in his person: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me,” or “exercised themselves against me,” “and those who drank wine sang of me” (ibid.). For they had drunk wine that night, as has been said, and thus, as drunkenness increased their fury, they sang against him. They sang, I say, not as David sang God’s praise, but made a dreadful clamour of voices, chanting reproaches and blasphemy against God’s name, as he himself says: “The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me” (Ps. 68).

It follows: “He stretched out his hand with mockers, who applied their heart like an oven, while he lay in wait for them. All night he slept, baking them; in the morning he himself burned like a flaming fire.” Who stretched out his hand with [Col. 0110C] those mockers? Clearly the Pilate already mentioned. How did he stretch out his hand? Certainly by sending the cohort to seize the Lord, as the evangelist testifies: “Judas therefore, having received the cohort and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons” (John 18).

For in distinguishing “having received the cohort” from “officers from the chief priests and Pharisees,” he plainly indicates that Judas received the officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, but the cohort from the governor, in whose power were the cohorts and the other military ranks of the Roman Empire. Thus he stretched out his hand with the mockers: he sent a military hand, that is, a cohort, while the Pharisees and chief priests likewise sent their own officers.

And they are rightly called mockers, because on that night, after seizing the Lord, they mocked him by spitting in his face, striking him with fists, slapping his face, and the rest.
doing the things which we read in the Gospel. In reliance on what confidence did he thus stretch out his hand? “Because,” he says, “they applied their heart like an oven”; that is, because he well knew that they had delivered him up out of envy. Trusting in that blaze of envy, he stretched out his hand by sending the cohort to seize him, “while he lay in wait for them”; that is, so as to lay snares for them, so as to make the flame of envy grow more and more within them. For he said: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” (Matt. 27). Again, when he had brought him out and sat upon the judgment-seat: [Col. 0111A] “Behold,” he said, “your king.” When they cried, “Away, away, crucify him!”—“Shall I crucify your king?” he said (John 19). By saying such things he plainly lay in wait for them; that is, he acted so that the flame of envy might increase more and more in them.

And see the wickedness of this most deceitful, crafty, and treacherous man. “All night,” he says, “he slept while cooking them; in the morning he himself was kindled like a flaming fire.” Throughout which night did he sleep? Plainly, throughout that same night in which he stretched out his hand, that is, sent the cohort. For his person was nowhere present, nor did he take part, during that whole night in which they, kindled like an oven and raging madly in their burning against him, cried out, spat upon him, struck him with fists, and slapped his face. Meanwhile he kept himself within until morning; and then he appeared, [Col. 0111B] himself kindled like a flaming fire. For, “when morning had come,” says the Evangelist, “they led him bound and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor,” namely, after taking counsel in order to hand him over to death (Matt. 27). In that council Pilate—he who had slept all night—kindled like a flaming fire, burst out into words: himself burning, setting others aflame, and by the words mentioned above urging on those who burned, lest they cool from that fire of envy with which they burned.

Why say more? “They were all heated like an oven, and they devoured their judges.” “They were all heated,” he says: the sedition gained strength; and Pilate himself saw—or rather, rejoiced with malignant joy to see—that the sedition was gaining strength, while he accomplished nothing by considering how he might find some charge against him, and by pretending to wonder that they pressed him to crucify [Col. 0111C] their king. Thus all were heated by the flame of zeal and envy, like an oven: all, I say—the chief priests and Pilate himself, the scribes and Pharisees, persuading the crowds of Jews, shouting aloud, the governor’s soldiers mocking him, and carrying out all that is written.

But what is this? “And they devoured,” he says, “their judges.” It is wonderfully said that they devoured their judges. Woe to those devourers, because they devoured—that is, condemned—those by whom they are to be judged. The first of the judges is the Lord Jesus Christ himself, the coming judge of the living and the dead; the other judges are the apostles, to whom he himself said: “You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). These men, [Col. 0111D] so far as lay in their power, devoured, because they thought they were killing the Lord himself in such a way that he would altogether die and his name perish. They put the apostles to flight, moreover, and compelled Peter, the greatest among them, to deny him. Therefore these wretches, to be shut out from the gates of mercy, with remarkable misfortune devoured those whom they will have as judges; they will have as judges those whom they devoured, insofar as and in whatever way they were able.

It follows: “All their kings have fallen; there is none among them who cries to me.” This is rightly to be understood both of the state of that time, when they worshipped the golden calves, and of the time of the aforesaid Passion of the Lord. For then too all the kings of the ten tribes fell in such a manner that not even one withdrew from the sins of Jeroboam. Likewise, when they condemned Christ, [Col. 0112A] their kings so fell, their rulers or princes were so blinded and collapsed like broken branches, that there is none among them who cries to the Lord. They do indeed cry out, but not to the Lord—rather, against the Lord—blaspheming Christ as God and Lord. And although from that time onward they strive to cry out and sacrifice, that prophetic saying resounds against them: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

What, then, did they become by falling in this way? He says: “Ephraim himself was mingled among the peoples.” Everyone who departed from the house of David is called Ephraim; but especially that people which crucified Christ, the son of David, because by so doing it truly departed from the house of David. And concerning both this and that [Col. 0112B] departure we have already spoken above: this one resembles that one; indeed, the departure begun there was consummated here. Therefore Ephraim—that is, all carnal Israel and carnal Judaism, among whom David and his seed, Christ, are not found—was mingled and is mingled among the peoples; that is, it is reckoned among the Gentiles. By contrast, true Israel is reckoned among the Gentiles yet dwells alone, according to the saying: “A people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the Gentiles” (Num. 23). Moses likewise speaks in blessing: “Israel shall dwell securely and alone” (Deut. 33). This Israel is holy and clean. But he who is denoted in the present passage by the name Ephraim is unclean and defiled, mingled among the peoples.

This is what follows: [Col. 0112C] “Ephraim has become a hearth-cake which is not turned.” This is as though he said: Baked by the flames of envy as in an oven, he is pressed beneath the ashes of his sins and does not turn to repentance. For just as a hearth-cake is not cleansed of ashes unless it is turned over, so the Jewish people—which, as has often already been said, truly departed from the house of David and is therefore denoted by the prophetic Spirit under the name Ephraim—is not freed from its sins, 48 because it does not turn to faith in Christ. Thus it is mingled among the peoples and is rightly designated by the names of the peoples with whom it has mingled and to whom it has made itself like, according to the saying: “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). Nor indeed is it merely mingled among the peoples; it is even surpassed by them in evil deserts.

For example, when the Lord says: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, one greater than Jonah is here” (Matt. 12), and similar passages. Let us carefully follow the words of prophetic truth by which this Ephraim is severely reproved: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it; moreover, grey hairs have been scattered upon him, and he himself did not know.” It is plainly evident that strangers devoured his strength; that is, they took away every royal or princely dignity by which he had formerly been strengthened, as it were in his youth. For behold, today he has neither king nor prince nor leader, and “he did not know,” he says. What did he fail to know? Plainly, what he ought not to have failed to know but to have known most fully: that his strength would not first be consumed, [Col. 0113A] would not altogether be devoured, before the true Strength and Prince of might, Christ, should come. For thus the patriarch Jacob had foretold: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49). At the time when he came—the one whom we believe to have come, born from a virgin’s womb, whom this Ephraim denied—this took place. Strangers, namely the Gentile Romans, devoured his strength; that is, they took away his kingdom and gave it to their own retainers, namely Herod and his descendants; and later they came and moreover took away his place and nation. This he did not know—or rather, refused to know—in order that he might say, or may say, that Christ has now come, if the word spoken by so great a patriarch is true.

Nor did strangers devour that strength in such a way that [Col. 0113B] it can be recovered, but so that it is irrecoverable. This is what he says: “And grey hairs have been scattered upon him, and he himself did not know.” It is as though he said: Just as a man turning grey from old age no longer has hope that the strength of youth will be restored in him, so that people, since it has lost its kingdom in this way, has no hope of recovery except the hope that is vain, will prove false, and will deceive it—namely, when it receives Antichrist in place of Christ. This he did not know: he did not observe these grey hairs upon himself. But every man who was, or now is, a true Israelite does not fail to know that Ephraim has so aged and grown grey that it is no longer as it was yesterday or the day before yesterday, when, although often defeated or captured by enemies, it could recover its kingdom—the strength, as it were, of youth—after the exhaustion of captivity.

An instructed person understands these grey hairs [Col. 0113C] by looking to the likeness of aged Abraham and Sarah, a mother now exceedingly old. For just as they then begot Isaac when grey hairs had been scattered upon them, although Sarah had formerly been barren (Gen. 21), so Christ ought at last to have been born of that people when it had been weakened by the loss of its kingdom. How did he not know this, or how was he ignorant? In the evil—and indeed worst—fashion of ignorance: by refusing to understand, refusing to know, rejecting this knowledge, as the Lord says above: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me” (Hos. 4). Therefore, when it is said, “and he did not know,” and “he himself was ignorant,” it is as though it were said: He was blinded through the fault of pride because he scorned to know.

[Col. 0113D] Hence it immediately adds: “And the pride of Israel shall be humbled before his face.” For it is now manifest that the pride of Israel has been humbled before his face, because “blindness has happened to Israel” on account of pride (Rom. 11), as the Apostle says; the veil placed over their heart (2 Cor. 3), prefigured by Moses’ face veiled outwardly, is the humiliation of Israel’s pride. Before the sight of all who, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord, this humiliation that befell him because of pride is recognized in his face—that is, in his heart and understanding. Moreover, that same pride was humbled before his face also in this way: first, that he was oppressed by the yoke of captivity under the Assyrians and Babylonians because he killed the prophets; and afterward, more miserably, that he was scattered by the Romans because he crucified Christ, the Lord [Col. 0114A] of the prophets.

Although in that same humiliation he raised his neck against the Lord, saying: “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been slaves to anyone” (John 8), nevertheless, being slaves of sin, they also bore a slavish yoke under men: they served the Romans as they had served other kingdoms, and they still had to undergo the grievous experience of that same servitude, falling by the edge of the sword and being led captive into all nations. In all these things he is indeed humbled, but pride nevertheless persists, while in their synagogues they blaspheme Christ, whom they have experienced as conqueror. This is what follows: “They did not return to the Lord their God, nor did they seek him in all these things.” Truly a stiff-necked people (Exod. 32), which, restrained by so many scourges, [Col. 0114B] does not return to the Lord.

Astonished at this, the Lord himself speaks in Isaiah: “Why should I strike you any more, while you add transgression?” (Isa. 1). Plainly, like a strict master, when in chastising he has exhausted every rod and every scourge, he marvels at a slave who is incorrigible and obstinate. Whence comes this? Namely, because they have a veiled and hardened heart—or rather, because they do not even have a heart. For it follows: “Ephraim has become like a deceived dove, having no heart.” In that he does not simply say, “he has become like a dove,” but adds, “deceived,” he wholly removes in the present passage the good significance of the dove. Moreover, when he further adds “having no heart,” he wonderfully expresses the same deception and the emptiness of every good [Col. 0114C] thing. For in contrast to what is customarily said or written of a dove as a favorable comparison—“having no gall”—here it is said, “having no heart.” How great, do you suppose, is the difference between having no gall and having no heart? How great, I say, is the difference between a dove having gall and no heart, and a dove having no gall and having a heart? Great indeed, and wholly contrary.

So clearly, and with so great a dissimilarity, carnal Israel is separated from spiritual Israel: such then was that Ephraim who was deceived so as to depart from the house of David, and such now is this Jew who denied Christ, the Son of God. He ought to have been a dove by remaining in the simplicity and unity of his fathers’ faith; but both then and now, deceived by the devil, he departed into the gall of bitterness and the poverty of heart. Where did he depart? Where did he go? “They called upon Egypt, [Col. 0114D] and went to the Assyrians.”

How did they call upon Egypt? They worshipped Egyptian gods, since they came out of Egypt in body and not in mind. For when they had scarcely come out, they made and worshipped a calf in the wilderness (Exod. 32), according to the custom of the Egyptians, as they had been accustomed to do among them. Their words too, when calling upon Egypt, were these: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full” (Exod. 16). Again: “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt” (Num. 14), and similar words. But after they had obtained a land so good that they had no need of Egyptian meat or bread, they nevertheless called upon Egypt. For they made two calves [Col. 0115A] with the same—indeed, greater—madness than that with which they had once made and worshipped one in the wilderness. In this manner, calling upon Egypt on account of their gluttony, 49 and luxury, they also went to the Assyrians and became like them, namely through pride; and so, mingled among the peoples, they deserved to be called not so much Israelites as Egyptians or Assyrians.

Moreover, when, as has often already been said, they denied Christ and professed that Caesar, and no other, was their king, they called upon Egypt and went to the Assyrians; that is, they made themselves companions in damnation of men without God, who love this world alone, and of malignant spirits. But what follows? “And when they shall have departed, I will spread my net over them; I will draw them down like the birds of heaven” [Col. 0115B]. In keeping with the metaphor of the deceived dove having no heart, this aptly signifies that those who dared in pride to raise themselves up as though flying will be caught in their pride; yet they are feeble and weak, like a dove.

“When they shall have departed,” he says—namely, of old, by saying, “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (3 Kings 12), and now by crying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 16)—“then I will spread my net, and I will draw them down like the birds of heaven,” so that they may neither be able to fly with the glorious and free whom they emulate by the wing of liberty, nor be free in my sight, but may pay the penalty for vain hope and presumption: first as captives among the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and [Col. 0115C] afterward, under the Romans, scattered and fettered throughout the whole world by the bonds and nets of captivity.

Having said this, he immediately adds an equitable and just sentence, saying: “I will chastise them according to the report of their assembly.” For the report of their assembly was that which we still hear and read today: for they imagined a vain fear for themselves and said, “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). The chief priests and Pharisees invented this fear when they had assembled a council; and the whole gathered assembly heard the entire counsel and willingly gave it ear, so that they might seem, as though out of necessity, to kill Christ. But what contrary outcome befell them! It was not that, after killing him, they reigned with the Romans; rather, [Col. 0115D] as this itself required, they suffered punishment under the Romans, and the Romans came and took away their place and nation. Therefore, he says, “I will chastise them according to the report of their assembly”; that is, I will bring upon them the dread which they feared, which they fabricated for themselves—not truly fearing it, but wishing such a fear to appear real.

“Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they shall be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me. And I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me.” I will chastise them so that woe may be theirs in respect of the soul because they departed from me, and that they may be laid waste in respect of the body because they transgressed against me. For they did not merely transgress against my law: they laid hands upon me myself; they themselves delivered me up to be crucified. And see how ungrateful [Col. 0116A] they are. “I redeemed them”—both formerly from Egypt and now from sins by my blood, even forgiving them the crime of my death, so that I said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23)—“and they stubbornly spoke lies against me.”

For they also gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep; and if this should be heard by the governor, we will persuade him and make you safe.” But they, having received the money, did as they had been instructed. “And that saying has been spread abroad among the Jews unto this day” (Matt. 28). These and similar lies they spoke against me, and they do not cease to speak them.

And they did not cry out to me in their heart, but they howled [Col. 0116B] upon their couches. Over grain and wine they ruminated, and they withdrew from me. Let us carefully consider the divine justice in these words, for here is the reason why carnal Israel is judged or reckoned to be Edom or Esau, and not Israel. “And they did not cry out,” he says, “to me, but they howled.” What is it to cry out to the Lord, except to desire the Lord? If, however, someone multiplies prayers, however much he may cry and weep, yet has no intention of deserving to possess God himself, but seeks to obtain some other earthly or transitory thing, he cannot truly be said to cry out to the Lord—that is, to cry in such a way that his cry reaches the hearing of the Lord God. One who cries in this manner is plainly like Esau, of whom it is written: “When Esau heard [Col. 0116C] his father’s words, he roared with a great cry, and, stunned, said: ‘Bless me also, my father’” (Gen. 27).

Certainly he sought no other fruit of the blessing than this: that he might be rich and powerful in this world. Therefore it follows afterward: “And when he wept with a loud lamentation, Isaac, moved, said to him: ‘In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be.’” For Isaac knew what he was seeking, and therefore defined his blessing accordingly. He says, then: “And they did not cry out to me in their heart, but they howled upon their couches”; that is, they were not devoted to me, their heart was not right with me; they did not seek myself, but the things that are mine, and for these they howled upon their couches—that is, in their synagogues, which indeed are not my Church but their own chambers. They truly howled because, he says, “they ruminated over grain and wine”: they sought only things of the belly, and withdrew from me, namely by not seeking to possess me.

In this way they truly do not belong to the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob (Ps. 23), but to the generation of Esau. The Apostle, understanding this, says to the Hebrews: “Let no root of bitterness springing up again hinder you, and through it many be defiled; let there be no fornicator or profane person like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal. For know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12). To this day the unhappy Jews [Col. 0117A] howl thus in their chambers, nor do they find a place for repentance so that they may be able to inherit the blessing, although they seek it with tears. Why? Because they do not cry out to the Lord in their heart, but ruminate over grain and wine: that is, they do not seek heavenly grace, do not desire remission of sins, do not long for the glory of the future kingdom; but they howl and ruminate because of their anger over that land, in which they remember having had an abundance of grain and wine, as it is written in the Psalm: “Speaking in the anger of the land, they devised deceits” (Ps. 34).

For since they do not fail to know that, from the coming of our Savior onward, they lost that land because of his blood, they are angry and, inflamed with malicious zeal, blaspheme him. “And they withdrew from me,” he says. [Col. 0117B] They truly withdrew—indeed, they even sent an embassy after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 1). “And I instructed them, and strengthened their arms; yet they devised evil against me.” This sentence conveys a great sense of astonishment. It is as though he said: I, against whom they devised wickedness—I am he who instructed them; I am he who strengthened their arms. I instructed them, certainly, by giving the Law and teaching that a person’s life does not consist solely in grain and wine, over which they now ruminate, but in the word of God, as Moses says: “He afflicted you with want and gave you manna for food, which neither you nor your fathers knew, in order to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds [Col. 0117C] from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8).

After I had instructed him, after I had given them the Law, led them about, and taught them—guarding them as the pupil of my eye—I then strengthened their arms, establishing them upon an exalted land so that they might eat the fruits of the fields (Ps. 104). Thus they were strengthened so as to kill mighty kings, leaders, princes, and their kings, and for a long time to possess the labors of the nations. He who did these things for them is I myself, against whom they devised evil—namely, that they might crucify me. For they said: “Let us hang him on the tree; and accordingly he will be accursed, nor will he be reckoned the son of the Blessed One,” of whom the Psalmist sang: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117). For Moses wrote that “he who hangs on a tree is accursed by God” (Deut. 21).

[Col. 0117D] They devised this evil against me; but this very evil blinded them, so that they neither saw nor knew that, on the contrary, through his cross blessing would be given to all nations—that is, remission of sins—and that through it he would draw all things to himself (John 12). “They turned back so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow.” Wonderful is the rebellion of the perverse, to whom that which is sweet and light for the upright in heart appears unbearable, and which they cannot endure. For the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. 11), but their stiff necks and ill-strengthened shoulders could not bear it. Therefore they turned back so as to be without a yoke, so that they might have neither law nor king opposing their evil wills. Yet in turning back thus they became like a deceitful bow: that is, they killed [Col. 0118A] and ruined themselves in the manner of a deceitful bow which, as the arrow recoils, strikes the one who bends it.

For in fleeing the yoke of God, or Christ’s rule, they submitted themselves to the ruinous yoke of men; they made for themselves the deadly yoke of the Roman empire. Indeed, while bending the bow for a bitter purpose, “that they might shoot the blameless man in secret” (Ps. 93), they perished by that same bow when its very arrows recoiled upon themselves; they struck themselves with eternal condemnation, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). This is what immediately follows:

“They shall fall by the sword, their princes because of the fury of their tongue.” For the fury of their tongue proved to be like a sharp sword, as the Psalmist sang: “They sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Ps. 63). [Col. 0118B] Again: “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). That fury of the tongue was the evil utterance which they made firm for themselves by crying: “Away, away; crucify, crucify!” (John 19). And this sword of the tongue, so sharp, also passed through Mary’s soul, according to Simeon’s saying (Luke 2). “Because of that fury”—that is, on account of that fury of their tongue—“their princes shall fall by the sword,” he says; and so it happened.

We read and marvel at Josephus’s account of that wretched destruction of Jerusalem, in which they fell in such a manner that they can never recover their former condition: cut down outside by Roman swords, within by the swords of their own fellow citizens and fellow tribesmen. Thus they fell very differently from how they had fallen by the swords of the Assyrians or Babylonians—and deservedly, [Col. 0118C] because they had drawn out the cord of their sins too long. For he says: “This is their mockery in the land of Egypt.” The sense is: this madness of sinners is not new, but long-standing, from the time when this nation was born in the land of Egypt.

For there their fathers, who mocked Christ, Lord of the Law and the Prophets, mocked Moses, sent to them by God to deliver them from the hand of the Egyptians. Although they cried out to the Lord because of affliction and harsh slavery, yet in astonishing madness they mocked the deliverer sent to them, disdaining to understand that they were being visited and were to be saved through him. Thus Stephen, the first martyr, after having said: “He supposed that his brothers would understand that [Col. 0118D] God was giving them salvation through his hand,” adds: “But they did not understand” (Acts 7). And a little later: “This Moses, whom they disowned, saying” (Exod. 2), “‘Who appointed you ruler and judge?’—this man God sent as ruler and redeemer, who received words of life to give us. Our fathers would not obey him, but rejected him; and in their hearts they turned back to Egypt, saying to Aaron” (Exod. 32), “‘Make us gods to go before us. For we do not know what has become of this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt.’ And they made a calf in those days” (Acts 7).

Therefore it is plain that their mockery was already raging in Egypt, and this may also be inferred from their own attesting words. For when Pharaoh pursued them, and they saw his army, [Col. 0119A] they said: “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, and so you brought us out to die in the wilderness. What did you intend by doing this, by leading us out of Egypt? Is this not the word that we spoke to you in Egypt, saying: ‘Depart from us, that we may serve the Egyptians’?” (Exod. 14). There indeed they testify that they rejected him with astonishing cruel envy: though they cried to the Lord for their deliverance, they hated the person effecting their deliverance; and though they desired salvation for themselves, they envied the glory of the saving ministry of the person whom they knew.

Corrupted by the same disease, when they had demanded a king with excessive importunity, they hated the person given them according to the Lord’s heart as he reigned, and envied the glory of the conqueror whose victories over hostile nations they themselves gloried in. So much was this the case that they set up against him [Col. 0119B] his son Absalom, then Sheba son of Bichri, then Jeroboam son of Naboth, once and again saying: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Kings 20). As the same wickedness, or mockery, persisted, when they awaited the Messiah—the great king foretold through the prophets, coming for the great glory of their race—they hated his person, and with excessive cruelty envied the glory of Christ which they could perceive from reading, in the person standing in their midst.

Thus “this is their mockery in the land of Egypt”: that is, as they mocked Moses in the land of Egypt, so they mocked Christ the Son of God; as they mocked David, so by mocking they rejected Moses, [Col. 0119C] rejected David, and rejected Christ before Pilate. Therefore they shall fall by the edge of the sword, as has already been said, because of this fury of their tongue, because of this mockery of theirs. What then will you do, O prophet?

## Chapter III
“In your throat let there be a trumpet, like an eagle over the house of the Lord, because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law. They will call upon me: ‘My God, we have known you.’ Israel has cast away the good; the enemy shall pursue him.”

Announce these things; and in announcing them, let there be a trumpet in your throat, because for this people there is war, not peace. For an eagle shall come over the house of the Lord—that is, the Roman Empire, whose military standard was the eagle—and shall come over the city in which the house of the Lord stands. In Ezekiel, where the prophecy is directed against Judah, after the ten tribes had already been carried away to the [Col. 0119D] Assyrians, Nebuchadnezzar is signified by the eagle in these words:

> “A great eagle, with great wings, long-limbed in its flight, full of feathers and swiftness, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar; it plucked off its topmost branch,” etc.

“Do you not know what these things signify? Say: ‘Behold, the king of Babylon comes to Jerusalem, and he shall take its kings and princes and bring them to himself in Babylon’” (Ezek. 17).

But here, where the prophecy is woven not only against Judah but against all Israel, and where it is commanded, as it were, to cry aloud like a trumpet, the eagle is rightly understood, according to what was said above, as the eminence of the Roman Empire. Its military standard, as has already been said, was the eagle before it adopted the standard of the cross, because the eagle is said to be king of birds. In its honor Herod too fixed a golden eagle above the temple of the Lord, as Josephus relates [Col. 0120A].

“This eagle,” he says, “shall come over the house of the Lord”—that is, the Roman Empire shall come to destroy beyond recovery the glory of the Jewish priesthood. For what reason? “Because,” he says, “they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law.”

For someone might object and say that God either did this, or allowed it to be done, contrary to his own ordinance, contrary to the covenant or pact which he made with their fathers. To pass over other passages, he said to Solomon, who first built that house of the Lord:

> “I have heard your prayer and supplication which you made before me. I have sanctified this house which you built, to put my name there forever” (3 Kings 9).

But see what follows afterward [Col. 0120B]:

> “But if you and your children turn away, not following me or keeping my commandments and ordinances which I have set before you, but go and worship foreign gods and adore them, I shall remove Israel from the surface of the land which I gave them; and the temple which I sanctified for my name I shall cast away from before my face. It shall become a proverb and a byword among all peoples, and this house shall become an example.”

Therefore that house stood under a covenant—that is, under the condition that righteousness be kept; and God certainly foreknew that they would not keep it. For if he had foreknown that they would keep it, he would by no means have made his benefits conditional upon them, repeatedly saying, “If you keep my commandments,” “if you walk in my ways”—a frequent formula in the Law. But when he spoke to Abraham in the promise concerning the seed, which is Christ, he spoke absolutely, in the indicative or promissory mode [Col. 0120C]. For he did not say, “If you depart from your land,” but rather, “Depart from your land,” he says, “and so forth, and I shall bless you” (Gen. 12); and, “In you all kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

Likewise, in the promise he did not say, “If you do this thing and do not spare your only son, all nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed.” The things promised universally to the people on account of the worship of the tabernacle or house of the Lord, and the keeping of ceremonies, divine providence placed under a condition, foreknowing that they would not keep the condition or covenant of the promise and would make this covenant void. Jeremiah too cries this out in plain words [Col. 0120D]. For after first saying, “Hear the words of this covenant and do them,” he afterward adds:

> “And they went after foreign gods to serve them; the house of Israel and the house of Judah made void my covenant which I made with their fathers” (Jer. 11).

Again, elsewhere he says:

> “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is here’; for if you truly amend your ways and your pursuits, I shall dwell with you in this place” (Jer. 7).

Therefore, when he had said, “Let there be a trumpet in your throat, like an eagle over the house of the Lord,” lest he be accused of changeableness, as though rejecting the house which he had previously chosen or received into covenant, he at once gave the reason, saying, “Because they have transgressed [Col. 0121A] my covenant and violated my law”—which is as though he said: because they have made my covenant void.

This reason is sufficient against Jewish boastings; nor do they deserve to be heard otherwise, so long as, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God. Among other things by which they defend themselves against faith in Christ, they also mockingly claim that God is mutable if he has rejected the house sanctified to his name and seeks another among Christians.

But one already deserving by faith well earned to enter the sanctuary of God and understand their latter end hears and gives other reasons; he understands and declares why the eagle had to come once and again over that house of the Lord. For Nebuchadnezzar came over it once [Col. 0121B] (4 Kings 25)—he who, as already stated, must be understood in Ezekiel through the eagle—and he burned that same house with fire. A second time the Roman Empire came with its victorious eagles (2 Macc. 5), and it carried away beyond recovery not only that house, but also the place and the nation.

The first occurrence took place by God’s permission in order that the old priesthood might be corrected. The second took place in order that it might be removed altogether. For the people and priests of that time had to be corrected and instructed, so that they and their descendants might know that the Lord chose not the nation for the sake of the place, but the place for the sake of the nation; and that he delights no more in gold and stones, with which that house shone splendidly, than in smoke or ashes, unless temples of hearts and bodies are prepared for him as a dwelling [Col. 0121C].

But the priesthood of that house or temple had to be removed altogether at Christ’s coming, because the sacrifice of that time had not been commanded but permitted, until the necessary priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek should come with Christ’s command and presence. That sacrifice was not commanded, as has already been said, but permitted, is testified by the Lord himself in Jeremiah:

> “Add your burnt offerings to your victims, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and victims. But I commanded them this word, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way which I command you, that it may go well with you’” (Jer. 7).

Therefore that sacrifice was not commanded but permitted. But for what purpose was it permitted? Above all, so that its order might restrain the carnal people, lest they too quickly fall away to the sacrifices of the Egyptians and other nations; so that at least under the name of the true God they might sacrifice rich flesh-offerings, from which they could not possibly be wholly torn away [Col. 0121D].

Meanwhile the Holy Spirit began to testify to this through the mouth of David, although David himself was most zealous in that same religion of sacrifice. For he says:

> “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49).

Surely these utterances would have achieved little in bringing down the pride of that priesthood if, after Christ’s coming, both place and nation had remained standing and such an eagle had not come over that house of the Lord [Col. 0122A]. Indeed, even now, after not one stone has been left upon another, they blaspheme Christ throughout the earth in captivity; and by blaspheming they endeavor to hinder the chariots of Christ’s Gospel as they race onward. What would they do if, strengthened while standing in their own land and possessing that splendid house still surviving, they could point to such a support for their faith with the finger?

Therefore, when such an eagle came, the house of the Lord had to be destroyed, as the angel foretold Daniel:

> “And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and the people who are to deny him shall not be his. And the people with the leader who is to come shall destroy the city and sanctuary; its end shall be devastation, and after the end of war desolation is decreed. Sacrifice and offering shall fail, and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation; and desolation shall continue unto consummation and the end” (Dan. 9).

Now let us return to the text of the letter. After giving the reason why the eagle was permitted to come over the house of the Lord, saying, “Because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law,” he immediately adds [Col. 0122B]: “They will call upon me: ‘My God, we have known you.’”

The sense is: With astonishing shamelessness, though they are transgressors and violators, they call upon me, saying, “My God, my God, we have known you.” This resembles the passage in Isaiah:

> “For day after day they seek me and desire to know my ways, as though they were a nation that had done righteousness and had not forsaken the judgment of their God” (Isa. 58).

Thus they lie when they say, “My God, we have known you.” The Son of God himself refutes them in this saying: “My Father,” he says, “is the one who glorifies me, whom you say is your God; and you have not known him” (John 8) [Col. 0122C]. Why? Surely because of what Isaiah also prophesied:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29).

Thus in every respect their deeds are contrary to their words. Therefore this prophet immediately adds: “Israel has cast away the good; the enemy shall pursue him.”

What good, or whom who is good, has Israel cast away, except God, who is the highest good, who alone is good and supremely good, to whom it says merely with its mouth, “My God, we have known you”? For it cast him away not only because it once said, “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (3 Kings 12), and set up calves for itself as a god; but also because, what is greater, it cast the Son of God outside the city, denied him before Pilate, and crucified him when cast outside among criminals [Col. 0122D].

Therefore “the enemy shall pursue him,” he says, in accordance, surely, with the curses which Moses, foreknowing, laid down in the Law:

> “May the Lord give you over to fall before your enemies. You shall go out against them by one way and flee before them by seven; and you shall be scattered throughout all kingdoms of the earth. Your corpse shall become food for all birds of heaven and beasts of the earth, and none shall drive them away” (Deut. 28).

That this happened so needs no assertion from us.

It follows: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them. They made their silver and their gold into idols for themselves, that they might perish” [Col. 0123A].

Who are those who reigned not from me? Surely those who cast away the good: first, those who withdrew with Jeroboam from the house of David; then those who crucified or denied the Son of God, the son of David.

First, we must consider whether those kings who reigned over the ten tribes after the kingdom was torn away from the house of David truly reigned from God or not. For the following passage, written concerning that division of the kingdom, seems to conflict with these words:

> “Ahijah took hold of the new cloak with which he was clothed, tore it into twelve parts, and said to Jeroboam: ‘Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes’” (3 Kings 11).

Likewise, when Rehoboam had gathered a great army to restore the kingdom to himself [Col. 0123B], the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, the man of God, saying:

> “Speak to Rehoboam and to all the house of Judah, saying: ‘You shall not go up or fight against your brothers, the children of Israel. Let every man return to his house, for this thing has come from me’” (2 Chron. 11).

These passages, as has been said, seem to conflict with these words: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them.” But far be it that the words of holy Scripture should conflict with or contradict one another. We therefore seek how both the historical truth may stand and this prophetic declaration may nevertheless be true.

Attending to this, we consider the origin of that evil or schism; for plainly it preceded the event which history relates as carried out through the hands of Ahijah the Shilonite and confirmed through Shemaiah, the man of God [Col. 0123C]. What was the origin of that evil except the hatred by which Israel always hated David its king? For that people, intent upon evil pursuits and the worship of idolatry—which it could not serve while David reigned—never willingly endured wisdom, courage, and humility, the three chief endowments of David.

The consummate judgment in this matter was that, since they had no other person whom they could set up to overthrow him, they accepted his son Absalom. Yet while David lived, and while his son Solomon advanced in wisdom, their sins could not be consummated so that the judgment of God might be allowed to come into effect (3 Kings 11) [Col. 0123D]. But when the merits of David’s house, which had outweighed their sins, were so weakened that Solomon, corrupted by fornications, served foreign gods, then at last God withdrew his hand. Israel prevailed against the house of David and, like an unbroken horse throwing itself about, broke the bridle and went away; it accepted Jeroboam as a rider suited to its own pursuits.

This certainly was not from God; and therefore he now says: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them.” But that Rehoboam could not restrain or recall them came about by divine judgment; and therefore there he says, “For this thing has come from me.”

The decisive proof of the statement, “They have reigned, and not from me,” is at hand: they reigned without the lawful anointing of God [Col. 0124A]. For royal anointing remained in David’s house and in the tribe of Judah, whereas the kings of the ten tribes reigned without anointing. Only Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, was made king by some kind of anointing, and this was from the Lord; yet God did not thereby approve Jehu himself, but exacted fitting vengeance upon the house of Ahab.

One of the sons of the prophets merely poured a small flask of oil over his head and said:

> “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘I have anointed you king over the people of the Lord, Israel; and you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master. I shall avenge from the hand of Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the Lord. I shall destroy the entire house of Ahab’” (4 Kings 9), etc.

This one man reigned from the Lord, and God in some measure deigned to acknowledge that prince [Col. 0124B]; yet this was only for vengeance, because he destroyed the house of Ahab and exterminated Baal, not for grace, because he did not abandon the sins of Jeroboam—that is, the golden calves.

Therefore the statement is in every respect true: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them.” Apart from this one anointed man, whose anointing was imperfect, all the rest, just as they reigned without anointing, reigned without the calling of divine grace.

Now we must also consider those who withdrew so far from the house of David that they crucified the son of David, the Son of God, and how truly it was said of them: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them.” For this was rightly prophesied in condemnation of those who wished to be exalted temporally in this world without the help of God’s visiting grace, as the Lord himself indicates in the Gospel parable:

> “But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves: ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours.’ And they seized him, cast him out of the vineyard, and killed him” (Matt. 21).

What does this parable indicate except that the scribes and Pharisees, seeing Jesus, did not fail to know him but hated him, as he himself says: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15) [Col. 0124C]. Since the tenants said, “This is the heir,” none among them may excuse himself by ignorance. Therefore, when they say, “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours,” the one who is killed rightly and truly says: “They have reigned, and not from me”—that is, they wished to reign without me and to be rich without me, sitting upon Moses’ seat and making prey of the people; so that they even tithed mint and dill, while neglecting justice and faith and all the weightier matters of the Law (Matt. 23).

But when, judging themselves with their own mouth, they had said, “He will miserably destroy those wicked men and lease his vineyard to other tenants” (Matt. 23), what did he add? “Therefore I say to you,” he says, “that the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (ibid.).

Therefore, his saying, “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not acknowledge them,” means the same as: They indeed wished to reign, but the kingdom of God shall be taken from them, because they did not wish to reign [Col. 0125A] from me and refused to acknowledge me in their authority, pursuing their greed in every way.

For this is what follows: “They made their silver and their gold into idols for themselves, that they might perish.” The sense is: they loved silver and gold more than God; indeed, lest they suffer any loss of gold and silver, they hated Christ and his Father God; they hated and crucified Christ, the Son of God. For they committed robbery in that temple of God and gathered gold and silver for themselves, making prey of the people.

Does not Christ’s apostle testify that avarice is the service of idols? (Col. 5.) Therefore he rightly says that they made their silver and gold into idols for themselves, because avarice is the service of idols—especially in those who, though they had present among them Christ, the Son of God, disputing against their avarice, favored silver and gold more and killed Christ, the enemy of mammon—that is, the despiser of silver and gold.

With what fruit? With what reward? “That they might perish,” he says [Col. 0125B]. For the fruit of such idols, the fruit of mammon, the fruit of silver and gold, is the destruction of both their soul and their body. They perished spiritually through the invisible apparitions of evil spirits; they perished bodily through the visible swords of the Romans.

Thus the house of David conquered; all who withdrew from the house of David were conquered.

It follows: “Your calf, Samaria, has been cast away; my wrathful anger is kindled against them.”

There was indeed a long contest between the house of David and the golden calves made by Jeroboam, but in the end the house of David conquered—conquered, I say, when Christ, son of David, ascended the cross [Col. 0125C]. There the horn of David, the horn of salvation brought forth and raised up for us in David’s house, broke, cast away, and crushed the calf of Samaria: that is, every impiety separating itself from the house of David, in which now the prince sits—David’s own son. The beginning of this separation was that oft-mentioned material calf of Samaria.

And it is well said that, though there were two calves, he now says in the singular, “Your calf has been cast away.” For it signifies more than if he had said, “the two calves,” just as we sometimes mean more by “the soldier” in the singular than by “soldiers” in the plural. For we commonly say “the soldier,” while meaning an army. “Your calf, Samaria, has therefore been cast away”—that is, all idolatry has fallen; and from that prince of David’s house, Christ, God and man, they received the sentence: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95), and “the prince of this world has been cast out” (John 12) [Col. 0125D].

It is also noteworthy that in this place he addresses Samaria, because when error or idolatry began to be destroyed through the sacrament of Christ’s passion, this destruction began in Samaria. For when Jerusalem did not receive Christ’s faith but rather persecuted it—as it is written, “A great persecution arose in the Church that was at Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (Acts 8)—Samaria received the word of God with great joy, as the sequence of the reading in the Acts of the Apostles plainly shows.

“My wrathful anger is kindled,” he says [Col. 0126A]. Against whom, or in whom, is he angry except against those who made the calf, who stubbornly followed idolatry, who withdrew from David’s house because of the service of idols—indeed, who denied Christ, born from David’s house? Surely the scribes and Pharisees are included among these, and especially are or were such persons. Therefore from that time onward their temple or altar deserves to be called not God’s altar but Samaria’s calf: behold, the wrath of the Lord is kindled against them, their calf has been cast away, and David’s house has been magnified. Their temple and sacrifice have been removed, but Christ and his Church remain forever.

And why is my wrathful anger kindled against them? Clearly because they cannot be cleansed. For this is what he immediately adds with astonishment and interrogation: “How long will they be unable to be cleansed? For it too is from Israel; a craftsman made it, and it is not God.”

When he asks, “How long will they be unable to be cleansed?” he intends us to understand: forever. And he gives the reason why they cannot be cleansed forever: “For it too is from Israel,” he says; “a craftsman made it.” This reason must be carefully considered [Col. 0126B].

First, it must be known that a person is incorrigible when he falls into falsehood not through ignorance but through malice, inventing falsehood from his own heart. For the person who speaks a word against the Holy Spirit is the one who, knowing God’s truth, devises falsehood against it and holds the truth in falsehood, as the Apostle says. Whoever is such a person is guilty of an eternal offense and shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come, because what he does or says comes from himself: he is not deceived by another, but devises deception from his own heart and is condemned by his own judgment (Matt. 12; Titus 3).

Certainly Jeroboam was such a person; and the Holy Spirit, author of sacred Scripture, wished this to be made known to us, setting forth his sin in words such as these:

> “Jeroboam said in his heart: ‘Now the kingdom will return to the house of David if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem; the heart of this people will turn back to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to him.’” (3 Kings 12)

“And, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves and said to them: ‘Do not go up to Jerusalem any longer. Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt’” (ibid.) [Col. 0126C].

Therefore the true reason for the impossibility of cleansing, stated as “For it too is from Israel; a craftsman made it,” is this: Israel and its king Jeroboam did not think the golden calf to be God because they were induced from elsewhere or deceived by another. Rather, knowingly aware that it was not God, they maliciously fabricated it by artifice, intending solely that the people subject to them, bewitched by such deception, should by no means seek the true God.

Therefore they cannot be cleansed, and all the kings of Israel had impenitent hearts in that sin. Baal, however, was not adopted in such a way that it could be said, “It too is from Israel.” For neither Israel nor Israel’s king invented Baal from his own heart by a contrived device; rather, Jezebel came from Sidon bringing him with her, and Israel accepted him out of favor toward the queen and King Ahab, seduced and excessively disposed to serve a woman’s cruelty. Therefore they could at some time be cleansed and cease worshiping him, as we have in those same sacred writings [Col. 0127A]. For Jehu zealously did what was right and pleasing in the Lord’s eyes in this matter, and destroyed Baal from Israel (4 Kings 10).

Judah’s sin was not of the same kind, although it worshiped both Baal and the other monstrous idols. None of these was from Judah itself; it received them from elsewhere, and therefore it could be cleansed and was cleansed on several occasions, as we read: this king and that one broke the statues or images, overthrew the sacred groves, and did what was right in the eyes of the Lord.

But after the Jews arrived at the point of committing a sin of which one may truly say, “It is from themselves,” and of which they themselves were the makers, they can no longer be cleansed. What sin is that? Certainly that gilded falsehood which they fabricated, saying: “He blasphemed, because he said himself to be the Son of the blessed God”; and, “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (Matt. 27; John 1) [Col. 0127B].

It is the falsehood, I say, which they fabricated when they gave abundant money to the soldiers so that they might say, “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep” (Matt. 28). Just as it was truly said there concerning the calf, “It too is from Israel; a craftsman made it, and it is not God,” so here one may truly say concerning this falsehood: it is from Israel, or from the Jews; a craftsman made it—that is, a malicious mind devised and fabricated it—and it is not true.

Scripture relates that each act was done after a plan had been devised or adopted. And just as there, while the tongue outwardly displayed the calf and said, “These are your gods, Israel,” the inward conscience, a resisting witness, knew and declared that it was not God; so here, while they deliberated and by money obtained the spreading abroad of the report, “They stole him while we were asleep,” they knew and heard their resisting conscience within: “It is not true” [Col. 0127C].

Having thus sinned—not through ignorance of truth but by devising falsehood—they could no longer be cleansed. It is no longer forgiven them, either in this age or in the age to come, because such a sin is accompanied by an impenitent heart resisting the Holy Spirit.

Both have been cast away: that calf toward which they formerly turned when they withdrew from David’s house, and that idol of avarice, serving which they crucified Christ, David’s son. The wrath of the Lord is kindled against them. Truly the calf has been cast away. For it follows: “For the calf of Samaria shall become spiders’ webs.”

Likewise, his anger was truly kindled against them. Therefore he immediately adds: “For they shall sow wind and reap a whirlwind. The standing stalk has no bud in them; it shall not produce flour; and if it does produce it, strangers shall eat it” [Col. 0127D].
