Both matters are demonstrated by these experiences: both that the calf was cast away and that the wrath of the Lord was kindled against them. For this is a great casting away, or rejection: the calf formerly worshiped, made golden and polished because of the frequency of festivals, is left among spiders’ webs—that is, it is so neglected that spiders are free to cover and soil the whole calf with the weaving of their webs.

This happened as stated through the triumph of Christ’s passion, not only with the calf of Samaria but with all the idols of the nations. Likewise, the calf of Jewish falsehood, of which we have already spoken, has become spiders’ webs—that is, it is as weak and powerless against the truth as spiders’ webs are. Hence Isaiah says:

> “They have hatched the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Their webs shall not become clothing, nor shall they cover themselves with their works” (Isa. 59).

For example, to show how easily their falsehood may be refuted, we say to them: O watchful soldiers [Col. 0128A], who say—as you were instructed—that his disciples came by night and stole him while you slept: if you slept, as you say, how can you know that they came and stole him? Therefore you and your counselors have woven spiders’ webs, because just as a spider’s web is easily broken, so too is the construction of your falsehood dissipated.

Again, the statement, “They shall sow wind and reap a whirlwind; the standing stalk has no bud in them; it shall not produce flour; and if it does produce it, strangers shall eat it,” indicates great wrath. In its literal sound these words signify the whirlwind of war and a famine of bread; but the things understood in their spiritual sense are far more grievous: namely, the whirlwind of eternal judgment and a famine of hearing the word of God.

But that people was such that it did not fear these spiritual or invisible evils, desiring only present and bodily goods and fearing bodily evils [Col. 0128B]. Therefore, in accordance with its childish understanding, he framed the letter in such a way that it outwardly sounds a famine of bread while inwardly signifying a famine of hearing the word of God—a famine by which that people has now perished.

“They shall sow wind”: that is, they shall perform useless works; and just as a stormy whirlwind ordinarily follows wind, so a powerful tempest of God’s judgment shall undoubtedly follow their works. The standing stalk among them is the letter of the Law and Prophets; and this stalk “has no bud,” or has no bud in them.

It must be carefully observed that, when he said “the standing stalk,” he did not say, “There is no bud in it,” but “There is no bud in them.” For in the stalk of sacred Scripture is the bud or grain of spiritual understanding [Col. 0128C], but not in them, because they do not understand the life-giving Spirit and merely chew over the killing letter.

He repeats the same point in other words, saying, “It shall not produce flour; and if it does produce it, strangers shall eat it.” For “it shall not produce flour” is to be understood as “in them,” just as he had already said, “There is no bud in them.”

But in whom is there a bud, or for whom does that stalk produce flour? Surely in strangers—that is, in the nations or peoples who believe in Christ and eat from the stalk of that letter the flour of spiritual understanding. For this is what he means by, “And if it does produce it, strangers shall eat it.”

It would be a minor matter for those unbelievers to suffer such famine or barrenness, unless they also now endured present bodily evils. It follows, therefore:

[Col. 0129A] Israel has been devoured; now among the nations he has become like an unclean vessel, because they themselves went up to Assyria. The sense is: the enemies devoured Israel so thoroughly that it is no longer a people, as had been foretold: “And I will provoke them by that which is not a people,” or, “I will move you to jealousy by a non-nation” (Ps. 77; Rom. 10). When they have fallen by the edge of the sword, those remaining of them will be carried captive among all nations, and wherever they are, they will be regarded as unclean—as indeed they are.

For they are those who, while blaspheming the Lord, said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of the demons” (Matt. 12). Of them this was spoken: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it wanders through waterless places seeking rest; and, finding none, it says: ‘I shall return to my house whence I came.’” [Col. 0129B] “And when it comes, it finds it swept clean with brooms; then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, entering, they dwell there. And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11).

The unclean spirit went out of the man and wandered through waterless places when it departed from the people of Israel, who under Moses and Aaron had received the worship of God, and took possession of the nations. Seeking rest there, it did not find it, because Christ came, the expectation of the nations, troubled it mightily, and cast it out. It therefore returned to its house—that is, to the synagogue of that people. Finding it swept clean with brooms and adorned, that is, made outwardly beautiful through hypocrisy, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, it now dwells there with seven [perhaps “seven,” as printed] other spirits more wicked than itself—that is, [Col. 0129C] with every spirit of impiety and blasphemy.

Thus it was rightly said: “Now among the nations he has become like an unclean vessel,” for he has an unclean spirit dwelling within him. The nations themselves, however, are unclean vessels, plundered from that strong, armed man, as Christ himself says, signifying himself: “How can anyone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his vessels unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house” (Luke 11; Matt. 12).

Why, then, did Israel become unclean? “Because they themselves,” he says, “went up to Assyria.” Assyria, which is interpreted “directing,” signifies the proud devil in many passages of Scripture; as there: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my wrath and the staff: my indignation is in his hand” (Isa. 10). And shortly afterward: “When the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I shall visit the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of the loftiness of his eyes” (ibid.). Therefore, because they themselves went up to Assyria—that is, because they exalted themselves into pride, so that they became sons of Assyria, as the Lord says, “You are of the devil’s party” [or “from the devil,” John 8]—they consequently became like an unclean vessel among the nations.

Thus that prophecy of blessed Mary was also fulfilled: “He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent away the rich empty” (Luke 2). For because of their pride they were scattered and became contemptible throughout all lands; and the standing stalk, as has already been said, does not [Col. 0130A] make flour in them. And even if it does, strangers will devour it.

He still reproves the ascent by which they went up to Assyria, adding: “Ephraim is a solitary wild ass for himself; they gave gifts to lovers, and even hired nations for a payment.” A wild ass—that is, a savage ass—signifies a foolish and proud man, as is written in Job: “The empty man is raised up into pride and thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild ass” (Job 11). Thus carnal Israel, or the Jew, is rightly understood here by the wild ass: he despised being bound by the Lord’s tether and led to his manger, as the Lord himself says in Isaiah: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me” (Isa. 1).

[Col. 0130B] For just as the ox which knows its owner and the ass which knows its master’s manger signify every believer and faithful person—the former from the Jews, the latter from the nations—so Israel, which did not know that same Lord, or the people which did not understand him—indeed, which refused to know or understand him—is rightly called a wild ass: an ass indeed, but proud; an ass through folly, yet unbridled and contemptuous of the Lord’s manger, or ignorant through pride.

What did this solitary wild ass—that is, this people fleeing from God its ruler and alone, as one which had deserted God and was deserted by God—do, or where did it turn? “They gave gifts,” he says, “to lovers, and even hired nations for a payment.” To what kind of lovers did it give gifts? Certainly to faithless lovers, lovers [Col. 0130C] who love deceptively, who love in such a way as to make others appear loved, who feign love in order to deceive: namely, so that after they have called souls away from God their true Creator, they may immediately attack them, stripped naked and without help, possess them, and exercise their tyranny over them.

“Lovers,” therefore, is said ironically; in truth he could have called them enemies. Such were the Assyrians and the other nations to whom, Sacred History reports, Israel sent gifts, placing no hope in divine help. But, that you may understand this as said prophetically concerning future events: then they gave gifts to lovers when, crucifying Christ the Son of God, they reserved Barabbas as though he were a gift for a feast-day—not, certainly, for God, but for the devil and all evil spirits, those utterly false lovers and most certain deceivers. And in order to destroy the truth of the Lord’s resurrection, they purchased the aforesaid lie by giving abundant money to the soldiers.

What will the Lord do to this wild ass, this people which fled in such a manner? He says: “Now I shall gather them; they shall rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes.” The meaning is: since they fled from me, I shall gather them for siege and sword: first those of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, then those of the Romans; and afterward, as I have already said above, “for many days they shall sit without king and without prince” (Hos. 3).

Observe that he said, “they shall rest for a little while,” since it was labor and a great burden to them to have kings and princes whose severity might bind that wild ass to the Lord’s manger—[Col. 0131A] such as the judges were until Samuel, through whom Israel was saved; such as the kings David, Hezekiah, and Josiah were; then again such rulers as the leaders of the Maccabees; and finally Christ himself, King of kings and Prince of princes. All these were a burden to them; and, impatient, they could not bear them, as though bent and panting beneath an excessive weight, loving their own will—just as unruly boys and insolent youths generally hate sterner masters and tutors.

They shall rest for a little while from such a burden, with a rest exceedingly ruinous; for now, “I shall let them go according to the desires of their heart, that they may walk in their own devices” (Ps. 80). They shall indeed rest, but only for a little while. For when, by killing their greatest King and Prince, Christ, they had cast him off and supposed that through this deed they would long rest from a seemingly unbearable burden, then they would be pressed by another burden and, subjected to most grievous enemies, would have no rest.

“Because Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning, altars were made for him unto transgression. I shall write for him my many laws, which have been reckoned as alien.” This is the cause of the evils that follow. How did he multiply altars for sinning? Namely, by worshipping something other than the one God, and by sacrificing outside the sanctuary or outside the lawful order. For there was one God and one altar of his, wherever and in however many places his name is invoked in one faith. But he made another altar for his calf, which, as has been said above, is not God. This, indeed, [Col. 0131B] was to multiply altars for sinning. And altars thus constructed became for him a transgression when, receiving Baal also and the other monstrosities of gods, he had as many altars as demons to whom he sacrificed.

“I shall repay him for his multiplicity.” For because he multiplied altars, I too shall multiply my laws, rejecting by the new law the sacrifices established for them by the old law. Hence what follows: “They shall offer sacrifices; they shall immolate flesh and eat it; but the Lord will not accept them.” These laws concerning flesh and sacrifices are counted by him as alien, yet they are mine.

Does not David also testify to this same thing when he says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109)? They rejected my altar and multiplied their own altars; I too shall reject their flesh-sacrifices and multiply my laws, which through blindness of mind they will be unable to understand and will reckon as alien, though they are mine. They will sacrifice flesh and the Lord will not accept it; a new sacrifice will be offered and the Lord will accept it. The laws of the old and the new sacrifice will not be contrary, but manifold. They, however, call them contrary because they are blind.

Nevertheless, the Lord writes, and does not cease writing, his laws—Gospel laws—to that same people. This must be noted: he did not merely say, “I shall write laws,” but, “I shall write for him,” for those same manifold laws which they count as alien are contained in their own books, having been borne witness to by the Law [Col. 0132A] and the Prophets. Great is the punishment for their preceding sins: that they have been so blinded as to count these laws alien—whatever laws God writes through teachers or scribes of Gospel truth, through ministers of the New Testament, not with the letter but with the Spirit (2 Cor. 3). Great, I say, is their condemnation: from such brightness they are hidden beneath the veil of the heart.

This is what immediately follows: “Now he will remember their iniquity and visit their sins.” For “now”—that is, in this very fact that they count these laws alien, do not accept them, do not understand them, or refuse to understand them—the Lord remembered their iniquity. This blindness is the visitation of their sins, which they committed from the day when they first fashioned the calf in the wilderness until [Col. 0132B] the day when they shed Christ’s blood, as God the avenger foretold to Moses: “But on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs also” (Exod. 32).

This is the vengeance which, demanding retribution for Christ’s blood in the Psalm, after saying, “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68), immediately added: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back always” (ibid.). The prophet, more secretly indicating the same thing in the present passage, immediately adds:

“They shall turn back into Egypt.” Egypt is interpreted as “darkness.” The sense, therefore, is: they will be blinded and harden their heart, just as Pharaoh and Egypt hardened theirs. Thus the Apostle, when speaking of them with profound grief, suddenly brought forward Pharaoh as an example in this way: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth’” (Rom. 9).

For this resembles that case: just as Pharaoh and the Egyptians, seeing the mighty works of God, were more and more hardened and blinded through envy, so these men, who ought to have been Israel, the greater the glory of Christ they hear from the laws already mentioned, the more they harden themselves, take offence, stumble into blasphemies, and fall with blind eyes. Thus it was truly said: “They shall turn back into Egypt,” that is, [Col. 0132C] they shall become Egypt; like Egypt, through pride and envy, they shall be blinded and hardened.

Hence it further follows: “Israel forgot his maker and built shrines.” This is the same as saying: blindness befell Israel; being thereby greatly darkened, he forgot his maker and did not place his hope in God. And what did he who forgot the Lord do? “He built,” it says, “shrines.” Therefore he truly turned into Egypt, because he built dwellings for the spiritual Pharaoh—that is, the devil—with a misery of servitude greater than that under which they had once built the cities Pithom and Rameses for that Pharaoh (Exod. 1).

“And Judah multiplied fortified cities.” The meaning is: he did not trust in the Lord, but in fortified cities, as though such fortifications could protect him when God opposed him. [Col. 0133A] But see what God says against this: “I shall send fire into his city, and it shall devour his houses.” According to the history of the past, these events occurred as they are said to have occurred. For, as the history of Kings relates, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah Sennacherib came up, took all the fortified cities, destroyed them, and burned them with fire (4 Kings 18). Then, still more fully, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon burned Jerusalem and also the Temple (4 Kings 25). Finally the Roman army fulfilled this prophecy most completely, because [Col. 0134A] then fire irrecoverably devoured the houses of that people.

Spiritually, the shrines and fortified cities which that Israel or Judah built and multiplied were superstitions and devices of impiety, by which they defend themselves since Christ, truth and champion of truth, came; even now they shelter themselves in them as if fortified against the preaching of Gospel faith. On this account they have been delivered to fire in a twofold manner, according to that saying from the Song of Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 22).

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133B] 57 In the present passage the prophetic Spirit, by a lengthy invective, denounces the sins of Judah or Israel, or Ephraim, and foretells for them evils exceedingly bitter and long-lasting—evils not to end before the Roman army came and filled up in them, in vengeance for Christ’s blood, the accumulated measure of their miseries.

Christ himself, who long ago spoke in the prophets, testifies to this. Drawing testimony from this present prophetic denunciation and speaking as he was being led away to be crucified, he says: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills: ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23).

[Col. 0133C] For this prophet had foretold it beforehand, and below it is written: “Burdock and thistle shall grow over their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us’” (Hos. 10). The Lord spoke of the tribulation and wrath that would come by the hands of the Romans upon that people in vengeance for his blood. Therefore, by whatever name this prophet calls them—whether Judah, Israel, or Ephraim—they are the Jews of that time, whom the prophet foresees as he directs his gaze toward Christ’s coming. These evils are especially proclaimed against those who, in crucifying the great and true David, were to fill up the measure of their fathers who had departed from David’s house. Let us now, following the course begun, pursue the order of the prophecy.

## CHAPTER IX

“Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the peoples, because you have committed fornication away from your God. You loved payment above all threshing-floors of wheat. Threshing-floor and winepress shall not feed them, and wine shall deceive them. They shall not dwell in the land of the Lord.”

It is well known that Israel wished to rejoice and exult like the peoples. This sin of his is manifest, as this prophet says below: “From the days of Gibeah,” etc. (ch. 10)—that is, from the days of Saul, who was from Gibeah. For then Israel made manifest this very desire to rejoice and exult like the peoples, when Samuel spoke these words: “Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint for us a king to judge us, as all the nations also have” (1 Kings 8).

And when [Col. 0134B] the Lord said: “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you but me, that I should not reign over them. According to all the works which they have done from the day I brought them out of Egypt until this day, just as they have forsaken me and served foreign gods, so they are doing to you also” (ibid.)—when, I say, the Lord said these and other things and Samuel solemnly testified to all of them, Israel once again made its wish to rejoice and exult like the peoples still more firmly clear, saying to him: “By no means; for a king shall be over us, and we also shall be like all the nations. Our king shall judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles for us” (ibid.).

Indeed, this is the joy of the peoples and the exultation of the nations: to have a king other than God. Israel wished to rejoice with this joy and exult with this sort of exultation when it demanded King Saul; when it followed Jeroboam, abandoning David’s house; and when, before Pilate, it denied Christ and said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

But such rejoicing and exulting are not permitted to that people which received the Law and professed God’s worship, as they are permitted to other peoples that never possessed knowledge of God. Those peoples may, like the other nations, forsake God and prosper in temporal goods. Thus he says: “Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the peoples”—understood: because it is not permitted to you. Why? “Because you have committed fornication away from your God.” It is as though he said: An adulteress who has departed from her husband by fornication is judged differently from a prostitute who has pledged fidelity to no one and has never been bound by the marriage bond.

[Col. 0134C] You had God as your husband; despising such a husband, you slept with another man—indeed, with many men: long ago in the wilderness and in Samaria, and also in Jerusalem, with golden calves, with Baal, and with the other monstrosities; and finally with Barabbas the robber, whom, after denying Christ, you chose in his place. Your husband discovered these adulteries.

The Law itself, which you professed, commanded: “If a spirit of jealousy stirs up a husband against his wife, he shall bring her to the priest. And when the woman stands in the presence of the Lord, he shall uncover her head and put upon her hands the sacrifice of remembrance and the offering of jealousy. He himself shall hold the most bitter waters, into which he has put cursed things with an imprecation. He shall adjure her and say: ‘If you have turned aside from your husband, have been defiled, and lain with another, you shall be subject to these curses. May the Lord make you a curse and an example to all among his people. May he cause your thigh to rot and your swollen womb to burst. May the cursed waters enter into your belly; and when the womb has swollen, may the thigh rot.’ And all the people shall answer: ‘Amen, amen’” (Num. 5).

[Col. 0135A] A prostitute who has no husband, against whom a spirit of jealousy can rightly be stirred, is not examined or judged in this way, even in this present age. Therefore do not rejoice, do not exult like the peoples, because you have committed fornication away from your God; for the curses of the Law written against you do not permit you the joy or exultation of the peoples: “You shall be cursed in the city and cursed in the field; cursed shall be your storehouse and cursed your remnant; cursed the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land, the herds of your cattle and the flocks of your sheep” (Deut. 28), and so forth.

[Col. 0135B] 58 To the peoples, however, these temporal goods are at least granted: for example, that their storehouses may be full, overflowing from one thing into another; that their sheep may be fruitful and abundant in their offspring, and their cattle fat (Ps. 143). Why is this so? On what grounds has God so judged? Surely because the peoples possess the fruits of their own labors, whereas you received the labors of others as a payment for keeping God’s Law, as is written in the Psalm: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, that they might keep his ordinances” (Ps. 104).

Having received this payment, you ought to have loved God the giver and kept his Law. But what is the case? “You loved payment,” he says, “above all threshing-floors of wheat.” Your love was perverse. You ought to have loved God and made use of the payment; but you, on the contrary, loved the payment and despised God. Thus you committed fornication away from your God because you diverted to loving payment the love by which you ought to have loved God. And you did this not sparingly, nor in any ordinary manner, but “above all threshing-floors of wheat”—that is, with such boundless desire and such profound greed that all the threshing-floors of wheat cannot satisfy you.

[Col. 0135C] For your greed is a fire that never says, “Enough.” The Lord himself, detesting such a perverse order of love, says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left aside the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matt. 23). Again: “They love the chief places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (ibid.). He reproves you for loving payment both in honor and in money, since in both cases the love of the soul committing fornication away from God is perverse: loving God’s thing and neglecting God.

What then? What does the prophetic word declare should happen? “The threshing-floor and winepress,” it says, “shall not feed them, and wine shall deceive them.” Turning to his hearers, and wholly turning away from the fornicating people, the Spirit who says these things announces to others what will justly happen because of this. It is as though he said: Since he loved my payment and despised me myself, that payment—namely, wheat and wine—will be taken from him; and because he hoped in them, they will deceive him, as is contained in the curses of the Law: “You shall sow much seed in the ground and gather little, because locusts will devour everything. You shall plant and cultivate a vineyard, but you shall not drink wine nor gather anything from it, because it will be ravaged by worms” (Deut. 28).

[Col. 0135D] It would have been too little that the wheat threshing-floor should not feed them and the wine should likewise deceive them, unless, both in the former devastation by Assyria and afterward in the defeat by the Roman army, they were also led away captive. Therefore, suddenly completing the sentence, he says: “They shall not dwell in the land of the Lord”—understood: but shall be led captive among all nations, and shall have rest nowhere, as Moses likewise foretold: “The Lord shall scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to its other end. Among those nations also you shall have no rest, nor shall there be rest for the sole of your foot” (ibid.), and so forth.

Observe that he did not say, “They shall not dwell in their own land,” but, “They shall not dwell in the land of the Lord.” He refuses to profess that the land into which the children of Israel entered in order to possess it either was or ought to have been their land; it was the Lord’s land. And rightly so, for this is confirmed by the authority of the Lord himself, who said among the other legal ordinances concerning the land which he commanded to be observed: “The land also shall not be yours in perpetuity, because it is mine; but you are my strangers and tenants” (Lev. 25).

[Col. 0136A] For the land was not that people’s from the beginning, nor did it acquire that land through its merits, being a people of exceedingly stiff neck. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed them before you: ‘The Lord has brought me in to possess this land because of my righteousness,’ when those nations have been destroyed because of their impieties. For it is not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart that you enter to possess their lands; but because they acted impiously, they were destroyed when you entered, and so that the Lord might fulfill his word, which he promised on oath to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Know therefore that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God has given you this excellent land as a possession, since you are a people of most stiff neck” (Deut. 9).

Thus it was rightly said: “They shall not dwell in the land of the Lord”—meaning, “They shall not remain in the land that the Lord gave them.” It was by no means theirs, but the Lord’s land, since it was neither theirs from the beginning nor gained by any merits of their own.

Moreover, there is another land more worthily called the Lord’s land: namely, the land of the living (Ps. 141), in which the Psalmist says that his portion lies and that he believes he shall see the Lord’s good things (Ps. 26). Will these tenants at least be able to dwell in that land? Will that land of the living receive those whom this land of Canaan spewed out? By no means. For it follows:

[Col. 0137A] “Ephraim has returned to Egypt, and in Assyria he eats what is defiled. They shall not pour out wine-offerings to God, nor shall they please him. Their sacrifices are like mourners’ bread; all who eat it shall be defiled, because their bread for their own soul shall not enter into the house of the Lord.”

Thus he rightly did not say specifically, “They shall not dwell in this land of the Lord,” but generally, “They shall not dwell in the land of the Lord.” For just as they were bodily cast out of that land of the Lord, so spiritually and invisibly they were condemned, so that their souls should not enter that heavenly house of the Lord. Why? “Because Ephraim,” he says, “has returned to Egypt”—that is, those who ought to have been children of Abraham became Egyptians: proud in their sins and, through their pride, blinded [Col. 0137B] and hardened.

Observe that he has now said this same thing for the third time in this invective, though with words or syllables slightly changed. Above he had said: “They called upon Egypt and went to Assyria” (Hos. 7). Then: “They shall turn back into Egypt, and Israel forgot his maker” (Hos. 8). Now, for the third time, he says: “Israel has returned to Egypt, and in Assyria he eats what is defiled.”

The increasing degrees of evil according to each expression should also be observed. What he says second—“They shall turn back into Egypt”—is more than what he first said, “They called upon Egypt”; and what he says third—“Ephraim has returned to Egypt”—is more than what he says second, “They shall turn back into Egypt.” For by using the past tense, “he has returned to Egypt,” he expresses a completed departure; and by adding, “and in Assyria he eats what is defiled,” he strongly rebukes the delight of its sin or apostasy.

According to these words, that people unquestionably declined from bad to worse and then to worst. When they first came out of Egypt, by making the calf they called upon Egypt, saying: “Let us make ourselves a leader and return to Egypt” (Num. 14); but they were not permitted to follow their own will. But when they increased that sin, departed from David’s house, and made not merely one but two calves (3 Kings 12), they were permitted to follow their own will. It was therefore fitting for the prophetic Spirit, according to that event, to say: “They shall turn back into Egypt.”

[Col. 0137C] But that turning was not yet complete. For the Lord was still sending them his prophets, and David’s lamp was still preserved in the tribe of Judah, where at last they crucified Christ. Directing his sight to that final point, the prophet now uses the past tense, saying: “Ephraim has returned to Egypt”—that is, the Jews have been blinded; darkness has come; their eyes have been darkened; and, like Pharaoh and Egypt, they have hardened their heart. Adding, “and in Assyria he eats what is defiled; they shall not pour out wine-offerings to God, nor shall they please him,” he plainly asserts that whatever the Jews thereafter eat as something sacred, they eat it defiled with the Assyrians—that is, with evil spirits. Whatever they thereafter pour out as an offering, whatever they sacrifice, is not pleasing to God but opposed to him.

Accordingly, the same God says through Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? I have not desired holocausts of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain” (Isa. 1 [printed “Isa. III”]). When he says these and the other things, he surely confirms the present passage of prophecy: “They shall not pour out wine-offerings to God, nor shall they please him.”

[Col. 0138A] And in order to express how defiled is what he eats in Assyria—that is, with evil spirits, which are customarily signified by the Assyrians—he immediately says: “Their sacrifices are like mourners’ bread; all who eat it shall be defiled.” Among the Jews, when a sacrifice was offered for a dead person, the sacrifice itself was called “mourners’ bread,” because it was offered for the dead person, over whose death the relatives mourned. Whoever ate or touched anything in the house of the dead was considered unclean. Therefore they ate elsewhere until the seventh day.

The sense, then, is this: just as the things in the house of a dead person became unclean, and whoever ate or drank them was considered unclean, so the sacrifices of these people—sacrifices which the Lord testifies in Isaiah that he hates—are unclean, and whoever eats from them is defiled. Why? “Because their bread,” he says, “for their own soul”—understood, laid up for them, according to the saying, “Whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap” (Gal. 6)—“shall not enter into the house of the Lord,” since it is sacrificed or offered outside the Lord’s grace and outside faith in Christ.

The prophet had said these things as though looking toward those standing around him. Now he again turns upon those to whom he had previously spoken his eyes, terrible in their strong zeal, [Col. 0138B] and says: “What will you do on the solemn day, and on the day of the Lord’s festival?” He cried out these words as a question in order to awaken them. Having aroused all who heard to attention, he turns again and explains why he questioned them so severely. For he says:

For behold, they have departed from devastation; Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them; the nettle has inherited their precious things of silver; burdock is in their tents. The days of visitation have come; the days of recompense have come.

It is as though he were saying: These people mock me as though I were promising a distant day, when I say, “What will you do on the solemn day, and on the day of the Lord’s festival?”—as is their custom, to deride the prophets. For example, as they say in Isaiah: “Command upon command, command upon command; wait upon wait, wait upon wait; a little here, a little there” (Isa. 28). Since, therefore, they do not believe in that day, or at least despise it as though it were to come not soon but far off, behold, a troubling proof is given them from close at hand, so that they may have no leisure to dissemble concerning that day which will someday come, which I call solemn, which I call the Lord’s festival. “For behold, they have departed,” that is, without doubt the ten tribes will shortly depart into Assyria, and the remaining two into Babylonia, “from devastation.” They will depart into exile, leaving here only the devastation of the land; for it will remain laid waste by sword and fire. “Egypt will gather those who survive among them; Memphis will bury them.” This happened thus. The remnant of the Jews, after the murder of Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had set over the land, fled from the Chaldeans against the Lord’s command and entered Egypt (4 Kings 23); and afterwards, as the book of Jeremiah testifies, they were there slain by Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. 41). Memphis, whose inhabitants buried them, was the metropolis of Egypt before Alexandria was founded.

Why, when he had said, “Behold, they have departed,” did he add, “from devastation”? He makes this quite clear in the words: “The nettle has inherited their precious things of silver; burdock is in their tents.” By these words he indicates a long and great desolation: where once there had been most beautiful dwellings, desirable and comparable to precious silver, there burdocks and nettles sprang up. From this evidence of present or more swiftly impending evils, they could receive faith concerning greater evils from afar, so that it might not please them to laugh or sneer at the question: “What will you do on the solemn day, and on the day of the Lord’s festival?”

Indeed, he explains more clearly who that solemn day, the day of the Lord’s festival, is when he repeats and says: “The days of devastation have come. The days of recompense have come”—that is, they will most certainly come. Whether he says “day” in the singular or “days” in the plural, he means the same thing. For what is here called a day is elsewhere also called a year. Thus in Isaiah Christ himself says: “For the day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come” (Isa. 63). It is also called a time, as it truly was when our Lord came into this world; and, weeping over the city which refused to recognize him when he came, he said: “They will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke 19). What there is called “the time of visitation,” and in Isaiah “the year of recompense,” is here called “the days of visitation,” “the days of recompense.” This time of visitation, this day or year of recompense, is for the visiting Lord the solemn day of festival, because from that time the Son of Man was crowned with glory and honor; and, as we read in the Song of Songs, it became “the day of his espousals, the day of the joy of his heart” (Song 3). But for those frenzied men, who did not recognize—indeed, rejected—the grace of the visiting physician, it is a day of recompense, a day of slaughter, as Isaiah says concerning such a day: “For it is a day of slaughter and trampling and weeping from the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision” (Isa. 22).

It follows: “Know yourself, Israel, to be foolish; the prophet to be mad; the spiritual man [*vir spiritualis*]—that is, possessed—because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness.” Again turning to him concerning whom the preceding words had been spoken, as though to listeners, he endeavors to offer him counsel and instill sound thoughts. For this is sound counsel: “Know yourself to be foolish; know yourself to be mad; know yourself to be spiritual,” that is, deranged, pursuing the spiritual things of wickedness and following the spirit of error. For such knowledge is the way, or beginning, of wisdom. This is known of himself by the man upon whom the spirit of the fear of the Lord has looked, whom it has judged worthy of its instruction. Hence Solomon says: “The vision which the man spoke, with whom the Lord is, and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said: ‘I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me. I have not learned wisdom, and I have not known the knowledge of the holy ones’” (Prov. 30).

Therefore he intends to awaken him to the great vision by exhorting him to know that he is foolish; for this is the vision spoken by the man with whom God is. The Apostle also intends this when he says: “If anyone among you thinks himself wise, let him become foolish, that he may become wise” (1 Cor. 3). Nor does he admonish that people in this way without cause, but because of a great matter: for scarcely are the people of any nation so delighted to appear wise, learned, and teachers as are the people of Israel. Therefore, deceived by the spirit of pride, they became teachers of error, unwilling to be disciples of truth. Hence comes that woe which the Lord pronounces against them: “Woe to you, lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11).

The sense, therefore, is this: O Israel, who seem wise to yourself, who have prophesied with great exaltation of mind and have laughed at your prophets saying, “Peace, peace” (Jer. 6), and, “Evils will not come upon them”: know and confess yourself foolish; know and confess yourself a mad prophet, following false madness; know yourself to be a spiritual man, that is, deceived by the spirit of error; and know that these things have happened to you because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness. For if you know this, if you confess it, then, speaking with God, you may become wise and your iniquities will be forgiven you. But if you are unwilling now to know, you will someday know; and without the fruit of repentance you will repent that you were foolish, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Therefore we have wandered from the way of truth; the light of righteousness has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. We have been wearied in the way of iniquity and have walked difficult paths, but the way of the Lord we have not known” (Wis. 8).

He cried out to Israel, urging—indeed, impressing upon it—that it should know and confess that it was foolish. But it stubbornly defended its folly, saying that it was wise. Therefore he turns again to the listeners and says in complaint: “The watchman of Ephraim with my God—the prophet—has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways; madness is in his house. They have sinned deeply, as in the days of Gibeah. He will remember their iniquity and visit their sins.”

It is a most great marvel of wickedness or presumption when he says, “the watchman of Ephraim with my God.” For what is it to be a watchman “with God,” except to contend with God by the subtlety of one’s watchfulness? Just as to fight “with an enemy” is the same as to fight against an enemy, so here to watch “with God” is the same as to watch against God. For he did not say “the watchman of God,” which would have been good. Such ought to be anyone whom God has appointed in his own stead to keep watch for the guarding of souls. But he said “the watchman with God,” which is evil. Thus is rightly denoted anyone who, by some contrivance, endeavors to oppose the counsels of God. This Ephraim did; this Jeroboam did. For he said in his heart: “Now the kingdom will return to the house of David, if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem; and the heart of this people will turn to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to him.” And, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves and said to them: “Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” And he placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan (3 Kings 12).

Such was Ephraim’s watchman, and thus cunningly, as he thought, did he keep watch; and he compared this watchfulness with God’s watchfulness, preferring it to the counsel or watchfulness of the one who had said to him: “If, therefore, you hear all that I command you and walk in my ways and do what is right before me, keeping my commandments and my precepts, as David my servant did, I will be with you and build you a faithful house, as I built for David; and I will give Israel to you and afflict the seed of David because of this, yet not all days” (3 Kings 11). Did he not think that he could provide better for himself by devising another plan for himself?

He says, therefore: “The watchman of Ephraim with my God.” This expression conveys the feeling of one both astonished and grieving. For he did not merely say, “a watchman with God,” but “a watchman with my God.” Ephraim too had prophets—such as those four hundred and fifty men whom Elijah killed in one day (3 Kings 18), and such as those whom Jehu later slaughtered, all that there were, by means of a pretended sacrifice to Baal (4 Kings 10). Indeed, from the beginning, when he had made the golden calves, Jeroboam established prophets for himself as well as priests. One of these was he who deceived the man of God coming from Judah with the word of the Lord against Jeroboam, and brought him back with him to eat and drink in his house; for which cause, after he departed, a lion found him on the road and killed him (3 Kings 13).

Therefore, when he had said, “The watchman of Ephraim with my God,” he added: “The prophet has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways.” By “prophet” he means Ephraim, that is, Ephraim as having prophets. And because those prophets were truly mad and prophesied nothing conducive to salvation, but merely uttered certain useless things in a frenzied mind, he added: “Madness is in the house of his god.” And who was his god? Certainly the golden calf. Such was the house of his god—that which had been called Bethel, that is, “house of God.” That madness, namely mad prophecy, already existed there at that time is plain. For it is written thus: “Now a certain old prophet dwelt in Bethel; and his son came to him and related all the works which the man of God had done that day in Bethel, and the words which he had spoken to the king” (3 Kings 13), and so forth.

The sort of prophecy which they uttered is rightly called madness here. For what could be more mad—if we bring forward something concerning the very man whom we have just mentioned—what, I say, could be more mad than that he deceived that man of God and caused him to fall into disobedience, knowing and intending the very outcome that occurred? For he cried out and said: “Because you have been disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and have not kept the commandment which he commanded you, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (ibid.). Again, when the lion had killed him and he had buried him, he said to his sons: “When I have died, bury me in the tomb in which the man of God is buried; place my bones beside his bones” (ibid.). “For the word which he foretold in the word of the Lord will certainly come.”

Truly this man was mad: wicked in such a manner toward another, and still more wicked toward himself. For what did he do, except through madness kill himself and perpetrate the death of his own soul, with eyes open, together with another’s death? For, O madman, if that man’s corpse is not brought into the tomb of his fathers because he was disobedient to the mouth of the Lord, what will happen to you, who knowingly did that by which you became disobedient to the mouth of the Lord? Such prophecy, such a mad prophet, he says, “has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways”—understood of Ephraim. Those prophets were all intent upon ensnaring and prevailed by deceiving under the name of prophets, divining something or other. For what did they say except what that aforesaid man said: “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me in the word of the Lord” (ibid.)? If by saying this he became a snare to the man of God, so that he deceived him and brought him back with him, how much more did they deceive the people and spread a snare of deception over all its ways? For they did not allow any prophet of the Lord to possess authority, when that false prophet dared to compare himself with him and say, “I too am a prophet like you.”

Indeed, at times even by a blow of the fist a hostile prophet did not hesitate to claim authority for himself against a prophet of the Lord. As it is written elsewhere: “Now therefore,” Micaiah said to King Ahab, “behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all your prophets who are here, and the Lord has spoken evil against you.” But Zedekiah son of Chanaana came forward, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said: “Has the spirit of the Lord then departed from me and spoken to you?” (3 Kings 22).

But now, to return to the chief point—that is, to the time of the Lord’s Passion, toward which the whole course of the prophecy is directed—then truly “the prophet became a snare of ruin,” when Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation. His purpose, of course, was to impress upon the people that, unless they killed him, the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation. By prophesying in this way, he ensnared everyone and drew them into consent to sin; and that sin, like an inextricable snare, became, as is now apparent, the cause of great ruin both to place and nation.

There the Jewish people might rightly be called Ephraim, because, as has already been said above, Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes which departed from the house of David—there brought its sins to completion by crucifying Christ, the Son and Lord of David. Let it therefore be said: “The watchman of Ephraim with my God; the prophet has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways; madness is in the house of his god.” For he watched, and, as though watching, contended with God, supposing that he could destroy God’s counsel by his own counsel. For he said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.” But God, on the contrary, watched to the effect that, if they did not let him go on thus, all would believe in him.

Moreover, in everything that the Lord did or said, that Ephraim was present as a watchman—the fabricator of falsehood, Pharisaic envy—in order either to deny his wondrous works or to corrupt them by a malicious interpretation, and in order, if only at some point, to catch him in speech. Hence the Psalmist, after saying, “My enemies have spoken evil against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’” (Ps. 40), immediately adds concerning any one of them: “And if he entered in to see, he spoke vain things; his heart gathered iniquity to itself. He went out abroad and spoke the same thing.” The sense is: if any of them approached my teaching or my table fellowship, he approached only to lay snares for me; and, going out to his companions, he spoke “the same thing,” that is, in accordance with the very iniquity which his heart had gathered to itself.

Certainly, because that Ephraim acted so maliciously: behold, “madness is in the house of his god”—madness, I say, which the whole world heard. For from that time the seditious raged horribly, and the sedition which they preferred to inherit in Barabbas the robber, after condemning Jesus, the Prince of Peace, they so stirred up while shut within that, as Josephus testifies, they caused both amazement and grief to the besieging Romans. This occurred especially in the Temple, whose very strong defenses the seditious men abused. Therefore it is rightly said: “Madness is in the house of his god.” And who was his god but Mammon? In serving him they had made that house a den of robbers, and in it had long carried on robbery.

O their inexcusable wickedness! “They have sinned deeply,” he says, “as in the days of Gibeah”: that is, as they began to do in the days of Saul, who was from Gibeah, when the Lord, not unaware how far down into the depth of sin they had begun to descend and would proceed, said to Samuel: “Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, lest I reign over them” (1 Kings 8). It did not immediately come about that the Lord no longer reigned over them, especially since afterwards, when Saul was removed, he gave them David as king according to his own heart. Yet it was most certainly going to happen that they would bring to completion what they had begun when they said: “Appoint for us a king, as all the nations have”; and again, “We will by no means listen to you; for a king will be over us, and we also will be like all the nations.” They fulfilled this very thing by denying Christ the King and saying: “We have no king but Caesar.”

Between these, indeed, came the departure of the ten tribes from the house of David, following Jeroboam and the golden calves. Yet throughout the whole sequence of times and generations there was one and the same cord of sin, by which they deserved, when the Lord scourged them, to be cast out from his Temple and kingdom. This is what he immediately says: “He will remember their iniquity and visit their sins” (Matt. 23), so that, just as he said, “All these things will come upon this generation,” they may receive a twofold vengeance of remembrance and visitation: temporal and eternal alike.

And so that it may be clear that the prophetic Spirit means the same thing that the Lord means by saying, as has already been noted, “All these things will come upon this generation”—namely, that sons who imitate their fathers ought to bear their fathers’ former sins—he repeats the matter more deeply and says: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruits of a fig tree at its top I saw their fathers. But they went in to Baal-peor, and were estranged unto shame, and became abominable like the things which they loved. Ephraim has flown away like a bird; their glory is from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception.”

Here God himself, speaking in the prophet and recalling the very sins that were to be visited, first briefly yet wonderfully brings his own benefits back to the listeners’ memory, so that anyone considering the ingratitude of those against whom the discourse is directed may marvel with Moses and say: “A crooked and perverse generation—is this what you repay to the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” (Deut. 32). “Like grapes,” he says, “in the wilderness I found Israel.” Israel must here be understood as the whole good, the whole elect people. Conversely, by Ephraim, “who has flown away like a bird,” are to be understood all those who are only children of the flesh and not children of promise. Therefore their glory is said to be “from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception,” because they glory in Abraham according to the flesh alone and are therefore not reckoned in the seed.

“I found Israel like grapes”: that is, I rejoiced over the children of Israel who believed in me as someone rejoices when, while passing through or travelling, he finds sweet grapes to eat. This finding was an act of grace. Where did I find them? “In the wilderness”: that is, in such a place that it was remarkable for grapes to grow, where it was a great thing for Israel—that is, souls seeing God, or upright souls—to be found. That wilderness was the land of Egypt, because every land or nation which abandons, or does not have, the true God is itself justly abandoned by him and is a wilderness.

It was not only a wilderness but also a place of terror, according to that saying of Deuteronomy: “He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude.” Certainly, that wilderness too through which he led them around for forty years may be understood here; but Egypt itself was a more horrible wilderness for them, where, serving in works of mud and brick, they suffered precisely this: that, as though abandoned, they groaned and cried aloud to the Lord. That he found Israel there like grapes—that is, that he heard their groaning—he did for love of their fathers, as Scripture testifies. For after it had first said that their cry ascended to the Lord because of their labors and that he heard their groaning, it immediately adds: “And God remembered the covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and the Lord looked upon the children of Israel and delivered them.”

Rightly, therefore, after saying, “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel,” he immediately adds: “Like the first fruits of a fig tree at its top I saw their fathers.” And the sense is: when I heard their groaning, I remembered the covenant which I had made with their fathers.

62. But how those fathers are said to be, as it were, the first fruits of the fig tree, and in what sense, Scripture itself instructs us in that passage where Adam and Eve, after committing sin, knew that they were naked, sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves loin-coverings. The human race is therefore rightly called a fig tree for this very reason: the first parents of the human race, having become transgressors, are known to have covered their shameful parts with fig leaves. The fathers of Israel were, as it were, the first fruits of this fig tree, because in the earliest ages of the world they, from among the human race, pleased God. “I found their fathers,” he says, “not like the first leaves, but like the first fruits.” As fruits are better than leaves, so I found their fathers more useful than the rest of the multitude of humankind. For—something not to be recalled without groaning—this fig tree luxuriated greatly in leaves: it quickly put forth many leaves, but produced fewer fruits more slowly.

Those whom nature brought forth in its usual way, apart from the blessing or grace of the Creator who said, “Increase and multiply,” and who belong to that wrath by which he said to the woman after sin had been committed, “I will multiply your pains and your conceptions”—these are not fruits but leaves of this fig tree. But the children of blessing are fruits of the same tree; and the fathers of Israel, of whom mention has already been made, were like the first fruits at the summit of the tree, because by the merit of their first faith they hold pre-eminence and are highest in the whole human race.

[Col. 0145C] “But they themselves,” he says, “went in to Baal-peor.” Not only did they do this, but among all that they did, this was most disgraceful: seduced through the women of Midian by a spirit of fornication (Num. XXV), they were initiated into Baal-peor, whom the Latins call Priapus. “And in doing this,” he says, “they became estranged unto shame”: that is, they became aliens, no longer sons of such fathers as I saw, knew, and chose, that I might be their God. They were led away from that glory into shame: into the dishonour of their God, of their belly, and of those things below the belly, by eating sacrifices of the dead and fornicating with the women who invited them to their sacrifices.

Would you know into how great a shame they became estranged? “And they became,” he says, “abominable like the things they loved.” Therefore they became like Baal-peor, to whom they went in. And indeed they became so, as another prophet testifies when he says of such idols: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII). It should be observed that this prophet did not say, “They became abominable like the things they made,” but “like the things they loved”; nor did the other merely say, “Like those who make them,” but added, “and all who trust in them.” Each person is such as that which he loves or in which he trusts. This is so true that those who love God or trust in God are, on the authority of Holy Scripture, called even gods or sons of God.

But if someone commits iniquity without also loving it, he is not yet rightly called abominable like the things which he has done. For it may happen that he recovers honour and blessedness, God covering his evil deeds, according to the Psalmist: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. LXXXI). He immediately identifies by name those who loved the evils they did, saying: “Ephraim has flown away like a bird.” For the sins of Ephraim—that is, of Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim—at that time were the golden calves; and they loved those sins so much that not one of the kings of the ten tribes departed from them. Therefore all of them, whether earlier or later, who loved their own iniquity are rightly denoted here by the name Ephraim.

And see how he has set the two in opposition: “I found Israel like grapes,” he says, “and I saw their fathers like the first fruits at the top of the fig tree; but Ephraim flew away like a bird.” In accordance with this comparison, it often happens that, on the same vine from which a grape hangs, or on the same fig tree in which sweet fruits are found, a bird commonly perches—but very differently from what is desired or useful to the farmer who approaches. The grape and the fruit await his hand, that he may pluck them and put them into his mouth; but the bird springs up and flies away.

[Col. 0146B] Thus Ephraim—whoever he is, a son of the flesh and not of promise—did not await the Lord’s hand and did not obey his will; but, untamed and fleeing, he abandoned David his king and denied Christ, the son of David. But Israel—whoever proved to be a son of promise—clung to the good root and drew from it the richness of love; and, like a grape or the fruit of a fig tree, delighted the Lord who gathered and chose him. What this grape or fruit glories in—the root that bears it, the root of paternal faith—that bird, that winged and fugitive Ephraim, cannot glory in.

“But their glory,” he says, “from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception.” The sense is: they glory in being Abraham’s seed according to the flesh; in producing physical offspring in Israel; in their wives bearing abundantly; in the wombs of their married women not being barren; and in their conceptions being numerous. In such things they glory and say, “We are Abraham’s seed; Abraham is our father” (John VIII). “Even if they rear children, I will make them childless among men.” It is as if he said: They glory as though benefiting Israelite flesh and contributing greatly through their offspring; but I shall make it plain that I do not delight in a multitude of children who are children not of promise or faith, but merely of flesh. For even if they rear and bring them up, even if they bring the glory of their childbirth, womb, and conception as far as adolescence and youthful strength, I shall make them childless: their children shall fall by the sword before their parents’ eyes, and it shall seem preferable to them that they had begotten no children.

Nor shall I be content with this: “Woe also to them when I depart from them.” That is: Not only will this evil befall them, that they become childless and that the children whom they have reared fall into the mouth of the material sword; but after I have departed from them in this way, after I have delivered them thus into the enemy’s hand, there follows yet a woe—namely, the judgment of eternal condemnation. So too, after the Psalmist had said, “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword,” he immediately added, “They shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII). That is, their bodies will be delivered to swords, but their souls to evil spirits.

For what reason? He says: “Ephraim, as I saw, was Tyre, founded in beauty.” The sense is: they will endure so terrible a judgment, condemned in body and soul, because their sin does not arise from ignorance or weakness but from pride, which is known to be signified by Tyre. For example, when the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart was lifted up and you said, ‘I am a god; I sit in the seat of God in the heart of the sea,’ though you are a human being and not God, and have set your heart as the heart of God” (Ezek. XXVIII). And shortly afterward: “Thus says the Lord God: You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.”

[Col. 0147B] Therefore, after first declaring, “I shall make them childless among men; woe also to them when I depart from them,” he immediately adds, “Ephraim was Tyre, founded in beauty.” In a remarkable manner he gives a sufficient reason for the just condemnation: namely, the greatness of their pride. And pride is rightly indicated through Tyre as the vice of the sinner who is arrogant and defends his sins. For, just as Tyre, surrounded by the sea, could not be attacked without danger to those fighting against it, so one of this kind is not usually reproved without danger to the reprovers—like this very people, who killed the prophets who reproved them, and the Lord of the prophets himself.

Observe also the force of the distinction when he says, “Ephraim, as I saw, was Tyre.” It is as though he said: Ephraim appeared proud in my eyes. To call someone proud in the Lord’s eyes is a most serious indictment; conversely, to be or to be called humble in the Lord’s eyes is a great commendation. The beauty of which he says, “founded in beauty,” is false and vain: all the proud see themselves as beautiful, because they disdain to recognize their own filth. Indeed, they are accustomed to become angry when one who rebukes them somehow points out that they are filthy. Thus Tyre is founded; thus one who is proud and arrogant seems to stand firm in himself.

[Col. 0147D] Therefore it is just that Ephraim suffer what has already been stated. This very point is repeated when he immediately adds: “Ephraim brings forth his sons for slaughter.” That is: Therefore, as I have already said, “I shall make them childless,” so now I repeat: Ephraim brings forth his sons to be killed. He begets children destined for death; indeed, he himself kills them by his evil example, so that they are likewise slain by the sword.

It follows: “Give them, O Lord.” What will you give them? “Give them a childless womb and dry breasts.” A remarkable cry, a remarkable petition. The prophet had heard the great severity of a just sentence, the just killing of children; and, wonderfully pitying the distress of the unhappy parents, he cried out and said, “Give them, O Lord.” Then, before he had finished speaking, reflecting sorrowfully within himself upon what he had requested, he asks: “What will you give them? What do I desire that you should give them? That they be safe? That woe should not be theirs, or that they should live with their children?” Certainly I have not dared to ask for anything such as that; rather, “Give them a childless womb and dry breasts.”

Why? Because those days will be such that they will say, “Blessed are the barren and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse” (Luke XXIII). Knowing this, the Lord himself, as he was being led away to be crucified, said to the women who wept and lamented for him: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children; for behold, days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse.’”

[Col. 0148B] Therefore, Lord, give them a childless womb, because blessed are the wombs that did not bear; and give them dry breasts, because blessed are the breasts that did not nurse. O unhappy fertility and fertile unhappiness! In comparison with it, barrenness—which among that people was considered a curse—is blessedness.

After this intervention by the prophet, the divine Majesty continues his reasoning in his own person and says: “All their wickedness is at Gilgal, because there I hated them.” Above he had said, “Woe to them when I depart from them,” and so forth; now he says, “All their wickedness is at Gilgal.” The sense is: Do not wonder, O prophet, nor consider the sentence more severe than just, or the vengeance too hasty. The wickednesses for which they are punished, and on account of which the sentence is pronounced, are not new; they have grown old and from ancient days have always advanced from bad to worse.

For at Gilgal they worshipped idols worse than at Bethel. They worshipped the calf-idol at Bethel in the time of the kings; but already in the time of the judges they acted wickedly at Gilgal, having idols there. Thus it is written in the Book of Judges: “When Ehud had offered gifts to King Eglon, he sent away the companions who had come with him, and, returning from Gilgal, where the idols were, he said, ‘I have a secret word for you, O king.’” And shortly afterward: “But Ehud, while they were in confusion, escaped and passed through the places of idols from which he had returned” (Judg. III).

It is fittingly said that he had returned from the place of idols, that is, from Gilgal, for in mind he had abandoned the idolatry which Israel followed. And remarkably it is written earlier in the same book: “The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping and said, ‘Why have you done this?’” (Judg. II). Finally, the angel of the Lord is said to have gone up to them from Gilgal, where the idols were, as has been said, so that you may understand that he went down there to see their wickednesses—by the same kind of descent by which it is said elsewhere: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied; I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII).

Moreover, they made Saul king for themselves against the Lord’s will. And when the Lord did not rejoice in them, indeed said to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but me, lest I reign over them; according to all their works which they have done from the day when I brought them out of Egypt until this day—just as they forsook me and served foreign gods, so they do also to you” (1 Sam. VIII)—they nevertheless, despising the Lord’s offence or complaint, rejoiced. For it is clearly written there: “They offered peace-offerings there before the Lord, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced there exceedingly” (1 Sam. XI).

[Col. 0149A] Truly, exceedingly: for it is excessive for people to rejoice when they have acted wickedly, and to exult in utterly evil things (Prov. II), as these rejoiced when they had acted so wickedly as to reject the Lord from reigning over them. This too should be especially observed: the joy of those who rejoiced in this manner was there turned into shame. For Saul, presumptuously and against the law—though he was not of the tribe of Levi—offered a burnt offering there; and for this he deserved to hear: “Your kingdom shall no longer endure. The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his own heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded” (1 Sam. XIII).

Their wickednesses, then, are not new, because of which I now prophesy woe to them: these wickednesses of theirs were long ago at Gilgal, and there they rejoiced in most evil things. Therefore the sentence of the judge is not now more hasty than just, because as they rejoiced in evils, so they will not cease to rejoice until they speak against me with their lips and shake their heads, saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVII), and so forth.

“There,” he says, “I hated them.” Where? In those very wickednesses, because they acted—and act—so wickedly that they even exult in the worst things. “Because of the wickedness of their devices I will drive them from my house; I will no longer continue to love them.” This has now happened three times. First, the Lord drove the ten tribes into the Assyrians out of his house—that is, out of Bethel, which is interpreted “house of God,” the name Jacob gave the city. But Jeroboam made it a house of an idol by placing there one of the golden calves.

Then he drove the tribe of Judah out of his house—that is, out of the Temple at Jerusalem—and caused it to be carried away into Babylon. Yet then he continued to love them, for after seventy years he brought them back when their captivity was ended. But now, for the third time, he drove them from his house in such a manner that he considered it worthy to signify this very thing by the fearful sign of driving buyers and sellers from the Temple with a whip, saying to them: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. XXI).

[Col. 0149D] Thus, after they had been driven out—as was signified there—they were to fall by the sword and be led captive into all nations (Luke XXI). “I will not continue to love them,” he says, because, although they are punished in the present, remission will not come to them even in the age to come. But it should be known that God drives no one from his house unless that person first departs voluntarily, with a heart turned away.

He therefore continues and states the reason why he foretold that he would drive them from his house: “All their princes are apostates.” This is as if he said: Therefore I will drive them from my house because all their princes are apostates. All have departed in mind; and although they honour me with their lips, their heart is far from me (Isa. XXIX). Scripture openly reports of the kings of the ten tribes that all departed from God. Not one of them departed from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin.

But concerning the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests—that they truly were apostates—God himself was both judge and witness, when the Saviour said: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (Luke XVI), and other such things. Therefore, if you ask why God drove them out of his house, why they were not received in the Church or house of God, he tells you: Because all are apostates; that is, before they were visibly driven out in body, they departed in mind, were far away in heart, and therefore were driven out bodily as well. They lost the earthly gains or advantages of God’s house—the only things they loved.

After saying these things and giving such a reason, he immediately confirms the sentence he had set forth, repeating it thus: “Ephraim has been struck; their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit. Even if they beget children, I will kill the dearly beloved offspring of their womb. My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him; and they shall be wanderers among the nations.” For what had he said above? “Even if they rear children, I will make them childless among men.” He now repeats the same thing by saying, “Even if they beget children, I will kill the dearly beloved offspring of their womb.”

[Col. 0150B] Moreover, when he says, “Ephraim has been struck; their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit,” it was much in accordance with their own understanding that, as he had said above, “Their glory is from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception.” For while they glory in the fruit of the flesh and, by many births and conceptions, contend that what he now says is not fulfilled in them—“Their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit”—he rightly and suitably, as though correcting their words and completing the sentence in full, immediately adds: “Even if they beget children, I will kill the dearly beloved offspring of their womb.”

It is as if he said: As long as they beget children and multiply the fruit of the womb, they think they bear fruit. They do not think that their root has dried up, that they have been struck by the sword of severance and uprooted from the land of the living. But, tormented by the slaughter of their most beloved children, they will cry out and say that it would have been better for them not to have begotten children.

As God says this, the prophet immediately, as witness to the true and just sentence, concurs in his own person and says: “My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations.” By these words he expresses both condemnations already mentioned: that, in soul, they are deprived of God’s kingdom, since God has rejected them; and, in body, they are captives and expelled from their own place, since they are wanderers among the nations. This is because they did not listen to him—that is, because they did not understand, but because they were unwilling to understand.

It follows:

## Chapter X

“Israel is a leafy vine; its fruit is proportionate to it. According to the abundance of its fruit it multiplied altars for itself; according to the fertility of its land it abounded in idols.”

Above he had said, “Their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit.” But now he says, “Israel is a leafy vine; its fruit is proportionate to it.” Explaining what he meant by “its fruit is proportionate to it,” he immediately adds: “According to the abundance of its fruit it multiplied altars; according to the fertility of its land it abounded in idols.” Therefore, where he says, “They shall bear no fruit,” one must understand: no good fruit; and where he says, “Their root is dried up,” one must understand: dried up from all richness of faith or love of God. But here, where he now says, “Israel is a leafy vine; its fruit is proportionate to it,” one must understand: evil fruit.

For the evil fruit is their many altars and abundant idols: that fruit according to whose abundance it multiplied altars, adding, “According to the fertility of its land it abounded in idols.” This fruit—that is, the fertility of the land in the ordering of divine providence—is neither good nor evil, but intermediate between the two. It ought to have been a temporal reward for good fruit, that is, for good merits; but through the perversity of those who use it badly, it has become an instrument of evil works. Therefore, by its own nature, this fruit deserves to be judged neither evil nor good in the judgment of God, but, as has been said, intermediate between good and evil.

[Col. 0151B] But the fruit of which he said, “They shall bear no fruit,” is without doubt good; whereas the fruit of which he added, “Its fruit is proportionate to it; according to the abundance of its fruit it multiplied altars,” is without doubt evil. Good fruit and evil fruit are distinguished by a striking denunciation in Isaiah, where God says of this leafy vine: “I expected it to produce judgment, and behold iniquity; righteousness, and behold a cry” (Isa. V).

At the time when this leafy vine, Israel, had departed from the house of David, it is not related that it made for itself very many altars or idols of gods—except for the two calves, one of which it placed at Bethel and the other at Dan. Yet even this is rightly charged with multiplicity, since it is much to have, outside the altar of the one God, even one other altar. Likewise, at the time when it departed so completely from the house of David as to crucify the son of David himself, it is not recorded that it had other gods. Indeed, it gloried greatly, with proud religion, in the worship of the one true God. Yet it is rightly condemned for a multiplicity of altars and idols in this: rejecting the altar or sacrifice of Christ, the true and highest priest according to the order of Melchizedek, it established for itself another altar—its own altar—and the sacrifice of the blood of goats and calves, giving itself over excessively to avarice, which is the service of idols (Col. III).

Moreover, this vine made its fruit evil and proportionate to itself in that, according to the bitterness of its root or heart, it gave to the one thirsting on the cross vinegar or wine mixed with myrrh.
