“Their heart is divided; now they shall perish.” By a right and most just judgment, the heart of those who divided themselves from God is divided. From the sequence of the history in the Books of Kings, it is openly known how truly and how repeatedly their heart was divided after they divided themselves from the house of David. For they were divided against themselves almost ten times, set up different kings for themselves after striking down others, and at last, according to this prophetic declaration, were carried away into irrevocable captivity and perished.

[Col. 0152A] But at the time when they divided themselves from the true David—that is, from the Son of God—it is astonishing to say how cruelly the multitude of Jews was divided against itself by discord, as the tragedy of their miserable destruction, written by Josephus and published throughout the whole world, bears witness. For through implacable internal factions they proved far more cruel to themselves than the Roman army besieging them outside could have been. And justly so, because in condemning Jesus, the Prince of Peace, they had chosen for themselves Barabbas, the author of sedition.

Foreseeing them, therefore, with prophetic eye, he pronounces God’s just sentence against them in a brief but different declaration: “Their heart is divided; now they shall perish.” For destruction follows division, according to the saying: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Matt. XII). In the following words he describes the destruction and ruin of their divided kingdom or heart: “He himself shall break their idols and lay waste their altars.” This occurred in the near term, when they were devastated in a deserved desolation as the Assyrians carried them captive; and it was to occur in the distant future, when the Romans came and took away both their place and their nation (John XI). Then their idols were broken with a most severe breaking.

It should be observed that he did not say, “Hostile armies shall break them,” but “He himself”—that is, my God, who, as said above, “will reject them”—“shall break their idols and lay waste their altars.”

God does not wish it to be ascribed to a human being when, through a human being, the vengeance of divinity is carried out according to the deserts of sinners. But if anyone attributes to himself the fact that, with God permitting, he has prevailed in doing anything against the people of God, he thereby draws down upon himself all the more the heavenly indignation, and it sometimes happens for this very reason that he is able to do less harm. Hence, in the Song of Deuteronomy, after saying, “I shall make their memory cease from among men,” he immediately adds: “But because of the wrath of their enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their adversaries should grow proud and say: ‘Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord, has done all these things’” (Deut. 32). [Col. 0152D]

That Assyrian, through whom at that time God shattered their images and ravaged their altars, arrogated to himself that he had done this by his own strength; and therefore God speaks against him in indignation: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my wrath; the staff itself—in his hand—is my indignation” (Isa. 10). He gloried in this, as though he did everything by his own powers; and therefore it is afterwards said against him: “Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?” For, as the same prophet had previously declared, he said: “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood; and I have removed the boundaries of peoples, and plundered their princes” (ibid.). [Col. 0153A]

Surely, by glorying thus and exalting himself in this way, he brought upon himself the heavenly indignation already mentioned, which is immediately threatened against him in these words: “Therefore the Lord, the God of hosts, will send leanness among his fat ones, and beneath his glory a burning will be kindled like the burning of fire” (ibid.). Therefore, when prophetic speech so forcefully declares, “He himself will shatter their images and ravage their altars,” let us understand it as though it said: “Not the exalted hand of enemies, but the Lord, has done all these things.” He himself then shattered and ravaged through the Assyrians; and later he was to shatter their images and ravage their altars through the Romans, [Col. 0153B] because they departed from the house of David, because they crucified Christ, the Son of David.

For what reason? He says: “Because now they will say, ‘We have no king; for we do not fear the Lord; and what will a king do for us?’” Surely a great and grave ground of condemnation is that they say, “We have no king,” and that the conscience of sinners says this: “For we do not fear the Lord”—that is, “We have resolved not to fear the Lord”—and accordingly, with swelling of heart, declares: “What will a king do for us?” Just as they had formerly said: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings 12). For as they said this, so their followers were to say against the true David: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19).

Indeed, they cried this aloud, so that when [Col. 0153C] Pilate said, “Shall I crucify your king?” they replied: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). Certainly, while saying these things they were also saying, “For we do not fear the Lord”: that is, they had resolved not to fear the Lord, not to bear the yoke of his fear, but stubbornly to break and cast away every bond of his holy commandments. Surely, where a rebellious conscience clothes itself in such great presumption, it follows that they should even say, “And what will a king do for us?” It followed that those whose purpose was not to fear God should despise the King, the Son of God. For they were not ignorant of him; rather, they despised and hated him.

Therefore the King himself, rejected by them as they said, “And what will a king do [Col. 0153D] for us?” after saying, “If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done, they would not have sin,” immediately added: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15). For this reason, behold, he himself destroyed the images of their avarice and ravaged their temple and altar.

Having said these things, he who was speaking about them turns again to them and says: “Speak words of useless vision; make a covenant; and judgment shall spring up like bitterness upon the furrows of the field.” It is plain that here, when he says “Speak,” it is not the command of one who wishes it, but the permission of one who is indignant and the turning-away of one who abandons them. The sense is: You are no longer to be taught what is useful, nor admonished to speak useful things. For you do not speak useless things because you err in ignorance; rather, knowingly [Col. 0154A] and with deep counsel of malice, you construct lies, and, corrupted by arrogance, prophesy from your own hearts. Yet you refuse to understand true and useful prophecy.

Therefore speak such things as you yourselves choose; speak words of useless vision. For you neither seek to speak useful words or perform signs that benefit people, nor has this been given or permitted to you. We must understand concerning false prophets that, even if they sometimes foretell future events, they nevertheless prophesy nothing useful. And although they are reported to have performed, or to be destined to perform, certain signs and wonders, no one of their signs is shown to have any benefit.

Thus John in the Apocalypse, after saying, “And he performed great signs, and deceives those dwelling on the earth because of the signs which were given to him to perform in the sight of the beast” [Col. 0154B] (Rev. 13), indicates that this very greatness of the signs will be vain and entirely useless, by specifying: “So that he even makes fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of men” (ibid.). For what benefit is there in fire falling from the air, in the sight of men or upon men, by demonic agency? Such signs are not of the kind of those which the Lord showed us in himself: “Go,” he says, “announce to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the gospel” (Matt. 11).

These are useful things, as are the words themselves by which, because of these very signs, it is right to believe. But you, O prophets of the calves—those which Jeroboam made and [Col. 0154C] Ephraim worshipped—speak words of useless vision, because this is what you wish; and you will make a covenant, understood as certainly not with God but with falsehood. So Isaiah says to such mockers: “For you have said, ‘We have struck a covenant with death, and made a pact with hell. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and have been protected by falsehood’” (Isa. 28).

You will make such a covenant, and on account of it judgment shall spring up like bitterness: namely, so that your covenant may be destroyed and turned into implacable enmities, and it may become for you as the Lord says there through the same Isaiah: “Hail will overturn the hope of falsehood, and waters will overwhelm the protection. Your covenant with death shall be annulled, and [Col. 0154D] your pact with hell shall not stand. When the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trampled by it” (ibid.), and so forth.

“This judgment,” he says, “shall spring up from your covenant like bitterness”: that is, as true bitterness, as a truly bitter root, according to the words of Moses: “Lest perhaps there be among you a man or woman, family or tribe, whose heart has turned away to go and serve the gods of the nations, and there be among you a root producing gall and the bitterness of serving foreign gods.” Moses called it a root producing gall and bitterness (Deut. 29). And this prophet, after saying, “Judgment shall spring up like bitterness upon the furrows of the field”—that is, so that they may remain uncultivated when their cultivators have been led into captivity—immediately added: “The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the cows of Beth-aven. Its people mourned over it, because it departed from them. Indeed it too was carried to Assyria, a gift to the avenging king; shame shall seize Israel, and Israel shall be ashamed of its own will.” [Col. 0155A]

For this is the bitterness that produces judgment. This is the root which, as Moses says, produces gall and bitterness. Prophetic speech again turns to its hearers, wonderfully proclaiming the reason why Israel is judged: “The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the cows of Beth-aven.” In mockery he calls them not male calves but cows—that is, females—so that Israel may be understood to have worshipped not only calf-gods but cow-goddesses. Nor did he merely say, “They worshipped cows,” but “They worshipped the cows of Beth-aven.”

For there is a great distinction between cows which could be set up in Beth-aven—that is, “the house of an idol”—and cows which walk in herds and range in pastures. The latter live and feel; the former, formed of gold or of whatever other metal, are not only senseless but inanimate images. It is evident that a living, animate body, capable of sensation, is far superior to an inanimate body. He therefore rebukes very aptly and forcefully the utterly debased folly of human beings by saying: “the cows of Beth-aven”—that is, they worshipped cows that did not even live and provide nourishment of milk, but lifeless likenesses of cows. [Col. 0155B]

It should also be noted that he did not say, “The kings of Samaria worshipped,” but “The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped.” For one is properly said to worship who, by his own will and earnestness of soul, performs worship and adoration or veneration. Therefore this prophetic utterance does not permit the people to appear excusable when it says, “The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the cows of Beth-aven.” For this would not properly have been said, nor could it be said, if, while the kings worshipped calves, the people had obeyed only from fear and not by their own will; if they had submitted unwillingly rather than consented voluntarily.

And from what is it evident that the inhabitants of Samaria worshipped those cows? He says: “Because its people mourned over it.” To show that by “the cows of Beth-aven” one golden calf at Bethel is intended, he did not say, “The people mourned over them,” but “over it”—that is, over the golden calf. When, or for what cause, did the people mourn over it? Clearly because, in a time of need and distress, golden calves also, among other gifts, [Col. 0155C] were sent to the Assyrian kings.

We read in the Book of Kings that Menahem, king of Israel, sent a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of Assyria, that he might give him help (4 Kings 15); and some suppose that golden calves were also sent among these gifts. “And,” they say, “that we may know this to be what we are saying, the following verse plainly shows it: ‘Indeed, it too was carried to Assyria, a gift to the avenging king.’” Therefore the people mourned—people who would assuredly not have mourned unless they had willingly served such idolatry, with affection rather than merely from fear of the kings.

Thus, after saying, “The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the cows of Beth-aven,” in order to confirm that they really worshipped the calf and voluntarily served it, he gave an unconvincing reason when he said, “Because its people mourned over it.” For it follows that those who mourned when it was taken from them possessed or held it with affection. “Its people”—understood to mean the calf’s people—is said with great reproach, since they ought to have been the people of the one true God. [Col. 0156A]

Moreover, the Hebrews also relate that the golden calf was secretly taken away by its priests and that, in its place, gilded bronze calves were set up. Therefore, while the people mourned, in the time of need and distress, as has already been said, that golden calves had been sent to the Assyrian kings, the temple-servants rejoiced because their fraud could not be accused or discovered. This is what he immediately adds:

“And its temple-servants rejoiced over it in its glory, because it migrated from it.” While the people mourned, the temple-servants rejoiced in its glory—understood as the people’s glory—that is, in the calf which they had as their glory. For they had exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of a corruptible being—not of a man, but of a calf.

And which way of life is held more detestable: that of the people, who mourned over the calf as though their God had been taken away, or that of the temple-servants or priests, who rejoiced because the theft they had committed in relation to that kind of god had not been discovered? We judge that a deeper abyss of condemnation is deservedly appointed for those mockers: the common people perhaps mourned in error, but they rejoiced mockingly in utterly wicked things, because it migrated from it—that is, from the people. The sense is: They rejoiced that it had migrated, that it had thus been given to the Assyrian kings, as though it could no longer be discovered whether it was gold or bronze. [Col. 0156B]

But what happened next? “Shame,” he says, “shall seize Ephraim, and Israel shall be ashamed of its own will.” For after the calf, as though golden, had been carried to Assyria as a gift, the fraud was discovered and reported by letter to the king of Israel. Thus they were especially ashamed through the very thing by which they thought to please him, and they offended those to whom they had sent gifts, who judged this to have been accomplished not through the priests’ theft but through the kings’ fraud and contrivance. From this Ephraim’s shame began; from this Israel was put to shame.

It follows: “Samaria caused its king to pass away like foam upon the surface of water, and the high places of the idol—the sin of Israel—shall be destroyed.” Indeed, as the due reward of persistent wickedness, Samaria, or the ten tribes, earned this: that its king should pass away and its kingdom be dissolved [Col. 0156C] like foam upon the surface of water. This is certainly a true comparison.

For as, when a pot boils, the upper waters rise into foam and bubbles; and the leaping bubbles collide, and as some emerge, others burst and break apart—so Samaria, or the ten tribes, continually boiling with the fire of discord, created one king after another. As is readily gathered from reading the Book of Kings, as many as ten times, when kings were struck down, other kings succeeded them, according to the number of the ten pieces of the garment, which, when torn, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite told Jeroboam to take: “Take for yourself ten pieces. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes’” (3 Kings 11).

For, as has already been said, ten times that kingdom of the ten tribes was torn apart through discord; ten times it caused its king to pass away like foam or a bubble upon the surface of water, accepting another after one had been struck down. First, it was torn away to Jeroboam. Second, Baasha struck Nadab, son of Jeroboam, and reigned in his place. Third, Zimri, commander of half the cavalry, struck Elah, son of Baasha, and reigned in his place. Fourth, Omri, commander of the army over Israel, was made king by the army; and after he died in his sins, his son Ahab reigned in his place. Fifth, Jehu killed Joram, son of Ahab, and reigned in his place. Sixth, Shallum struck Zechariah, the great-grandson of Jehu, and reigned in his place. Seventh, Menahem struck that same Shallum and reigned in his place. Eighth, Pekah, son [Col. 0157A] of Remaliah, struck Pekahiah, son of Menahem, and reigned in his place. Ninth, Hoshea, son of Elah, struck Pekah, son of Remaliah, and reigned in his place. Tenth, at last the kingdom was torn apart in the Assyrian king, who besieged the aforementioned Hoshea, sent him bound to prison, and transferred Israel to the Assyrians (4 Kings 17).

Thus and thus Samaria, by its evils, caused its king to pass away. “And,” he says, “the high places of the idol shall be destroyed”—those of which Scripture so often reports: “Nevertheless the people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.” This was the sin of Israel.

That all these matters, like the preceding ones, should be understood more deeply, as befits prophetic dignity, is urged upon us by what is immediately added: “Burdock and thistle shall grow up over their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’” [Col. 0157B] For this was predicted not at all concerning the distress of that captivity in which they were then transferred to Assyria, but rather concerning the almost indescribable destruction by which the Jews, because of the crime of the Lord’s death, were overthrown and led captive among all nations. The Lord himself confirms this by his own authority. When women followed and lamented him as he was being led to death, he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23).

It should be noted that he did not say simply, “Then they will say to the mountains,” but “They will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’” This is the same as saying: Then, in that tribulation or distress, what was foretold through Hosea will begin to be fulfilled. And if it then began to be fulfilled, and they then began to say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” when those days came which our Lord said would come, he was certainly not directing these words, when he spoke or wrote them, to his own times or to the calamities which the prophet himself then saw. [Col. 0157C]

And indeed, if you rightly consider what Israel then suffered—when, in the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, transferred Israel to the Assyrians, and placed them in Halah and in Habor, beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes (4 Kings 17)—it was not an evil of such a kind or so great that the prophetic Spirit would deem it fitting to cry out thus: “And they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’”

Indeed, even if the Assyrian king had preferred to sell them into slavery as male and female servants rather than settle them in his own cities, it would have been a tolerable—indeed, desirable—evil in comparison with the so miserable destruction of Jerusalem. So Esther also, after saying to the king, “For I and my people have been handed over to be crushed, slaughtered, and destroyed,” immediately added: “Would that we had been sold as male and female slaves; the evil would in some way have been tolerable, and I would have remained silent in grief” (Esther 7).

Therefore, since the things which we have discussed from these prophetic words have partly [Col. 0158A] been drawn not from the known history of events but from Hebrew tradition, as we have mentioned above, and since the prophet himself suggests that these things will be intelligible not to unbelieving Jews but to the wise, when he says, “Who is wise and will understand these things, discerning and will know them?” (Hos. 14), it is pleasing to repeat the same matters and to compare or set forth the prophecy, according to the times that were then future, with known events or meanings, in the same sequence and course until we reach the present passage—without doubting that Christ and his times are the sum or chief subject of this, or indeed of all holy prophecy.

“The inhabitants of Samaria worshipped the cows of Beth-aven.” The inhabitants of Samaria were truly the Jews, who appeared to inhabit the holy city Jerusalem and the temple in it—the temple of the divine name—not in heart, certainly, but only in body. For if they did not hesitate to call our Lord a Samaritan (John 8), who according to the flesh was certainly a Jew from Jews, and dared to say this because he had remained for two days in the city of the Samaritans after speaking with the Samaritan woman (John 4), how much more should Scripture itself call “inhabitants of Samaria” those who cruelly imitated and fulfilled the sin of Samaria? [Col. 0158B]

For Samaria departed from the house of David and made for itself another king and other gods. But the Jews denied and crucified the Son of David, the Son of God, and professed Caesar to be their king (John 19); at that time they asked that Barabbas be released to them (Matt. 27), and they will receive Antichrist in place of Christ. They are therefore truly inhabitants of Samaria: that is, aliens from David, from his city Jerusalem, from the temple in it, and from the temple of the Lord’s body, in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2).

These worshipped the cows of Beth-aven, namely those to whom another prophet speaks: “Hear this word, fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your masters, ‘Bring, and we shall drink.’ The Lord has sworn by his holiness: behold, days shall come upon you when they shall lift you with hooks, and your remnants with boiling pots; and you shall go out through breaches, each one straight ahead, and you shall be cast out into Harmon, says the Lord” (Amos 4). [Col. 0158C]

The cows of that time, one against another, were the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas. They devoured the people as green grass, just as cows customarily devour it; and this occurred in Beth-aven, which means “house of an idol”—that is, in that temple which was called the temple of the Lord and ought to have been a house of prayer, but was a house of Mammon, since they themselves had made it a den of robbers (Matt. 21).

The Jews worshipped these cows: for with voluntary cruelty they submitted themselves to those chief priests and consented to kill the Lord in that Beth-aven—that is, for the sake of that house of their idol, namely their Mammon or their money. And they believed those cows as though in a divine oracle, when they said to them: “Let us kill him, lest perhaps the Romans come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11). They worshipped such fat cows bellowing these things to them: that is, they willingly listened.

How is this proved? “Because,” he says, “its people mourned over it.” This is clear. For the people voluntarily took mourning upon themselves over it—understood as their god, namely unrighteous Mammon—whom, by serving, they certainly did not serve God. And in a sense they mourned that there was among them such a man as was called Christ, acclaimed king of Israel, whom, unless they killed him, the Romans would come and take away their place, so beautiful [Col. 0159A] and so rich.

This was like the case when, at wicked Jezebel’s command, the chief men of the people feigned mourning and proclaimed a fast, in order that, under the appearance of a necessary judgment of justice, they might kill Naboth, setting two men, sons of Belial, against him to give false testimony (3 Kings 21). The whole people, intent upon cruelty, accepted with feigned sorrow the voluntary necessity of killing the Lord; but the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees rejoiced in the secret of their hearts because their malicious plot had prevailed.

He therefore says: “And its temple-servants rejoiced over it in its glory, because it migrated from it. Indeed, it too was carried to Assyria, a gift to the avenging king.” For those men were then temple-servants, not of truth but of error and malice, according to the Lord’s saying: “You have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11). “They rejoiced,” he says, [Col. 0159B] “in its glory, because it migrated from it”—that is, they rejoiced in the people’s money, because they made prey of the people, hoping that, once Christ had been killed—the one who rebuked their avarice—their own profits would henceforth increase.

That they killed Christ with such hope or intention is proved by the parable in which the tenants, seeing the son of the householder, said: “This is the heir; let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21). And to whom could it be doubtful, or who could fail to know, how their god Mammon, whom they served, migrated from them, so that their silver, gold, place, and nation deservedly came into the hands of the Romans?

Indeed, they themselves earned this when, having gathered with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we slept” (Matt. 28). In this way, certainly, their god—who is no other than unrighteous Mammon—was carried as a gift to the avenging king in the Assyrians, because their money was dedicated to evil spirits and to the devil, father of lies, when they purchased such a lie. Thus, by a very just judgment, it came about that they were handed over to that avenging king, so that the king and father of lies might reign over them and execute vengeance upon them through Roman hands. [Col. 0159C]

They indeed rejoiced for a very brief hour, thinking that thereafter abundant money would pass more freely from the people into their purses. But that rejoicing was changed into genuine mourning, because they endured a great and miserable vengeance, at which the whole world marvelled. Therefore it is added: “Shame shall seize Israel [otherwise: Ephraim], and Israel shall be ashamed,” as has now openly happened when they fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations (Luke 21). And in their remnant, the whole world beholds not only the dispersion by which they have been scattered (Judith 5), but also the blindness of mind that has happened to Israel (Rom. 11).

And fittingly, after saying, “Israel shall be ashamed,” he added, “of its own will,” because the Jews so willed it, so by their own choice they determined and prescribed it for themselves: denying Christ as king and professing Caesar; killing Christ and releasing Barabbas; and crying before Pilate, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). [Col. 0160A]

It follows: “Samaria caused its king to pass away like foam upon the surface of water, and the high places of the idol—the sin of Israel—shall be destroyed.” As has already been said, Samaria is rightly understood in this passage also as Judaea, because Judaea truly made itself like, and worse than, Samaria, which had been severed from David’s house, when it refused to have the true David, Christ, as king. It therefore caused its king to pass away: that is, it preferred to have a passing, temporary king rather than its own king. Yet it is not granted even to have a temporary king; its kingdom was wholly taken away, and both leader and king passed from it.

For no Caesar deigned even to reign over them or to have them as citizens in his kingdom, but only as captives, though they had flattered him by saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). As foam swiftly passes over the surface of water, so the kingdom of Judaea was in a short time scattered and reduced to nothing; and the high places of the idol—the sin of Israel—were destroyed. For not one stone was left upon another (Luke 21), and that which ought to have been the temple of the Lord was destroyed by the Romans. [Col. 0160B]

But it was a high place of an idol and the sin of Israel from the time they were polluted by Christ’s blood—murderers and slaves of sin, slaves of Mammon, their god or idol. And what wonder is it if, after Christ’s murder, that temple is called a high place of an idol, when even before then the same house had been called a den of robbers? (Matt. 21).

Therefore the high places of the idol shall be destroyed: that is, the pinnacle of Jewish pride and the foundation of Pharisaic avarice—the beauty of the temple from which salvation departed—shall be annihilated, as is signified in the Gospel when it says: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8). In the following words he expresses with what great destruction and tribulation of the nation this was to happen: “Burdock and thistle shall grow up over their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’” [Col. 0161A]

When he says, “Burdock and thistle shall grow up over their altars,” it is a sign of utter desolation, so that not even walls and the outermost traces of buildings may remain. But when he adds, “And they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us,’” he strives forcefully to declare that wrath and tribulation, which was so great that it cannot adequately be described. For it belonged to them to say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall upon us,” since they would rather die than see the things that bring death.

And indeed this text expresses very aptly and elegantly how greatly they wished to hide, if it had been possible. For throughout the time of the siege, as Josephus reports, the number of those killed or dead from famine and other calamities amounted to one million; those who survived fled into valleys and underground caves, and even tried in vain to conceal themselves in sewers. To have hidden, or wished to hide, in this way was surely to say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall upon us.” [Col. 0161B]

Why, then, did our Lord, drawing this testimony from the prophet, prefer to say, “Then they will begin to say”? Why did he not say, “They will say,” but “They will begin to say”? Clearly because, when they thus fell by the edge of the sword (Luke 21), it was not the end but the beginning of sorrows (Mark 13). Another time will come, another day will arrive—the day of judgment—when, with greater distress, they will say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall upon us.” They will say to the holy fathers and patriarchs, “Protect us”; they will say to Moses and the prophets, “Excuse us.”

But they will say this in vain. For, on the contrary, “There is one who accuses you,” says the Lord, “Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5). The expressions proclaimed concerning mountains and hills are indeed different: “to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’” Yet their meaning is the same. For the prophet says, “They shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall’;” but the Lord says, “Then they shall begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’” [Col. 0161C]

It follows: “From the days of Gibeah Israel has sinned. There they stood. The battle at Gibeah against the sons of iniquity shall not overtake them. According to my desire I will chastise them. Peoples shall gather against them when they are chastised for their two iniquities.”

Once, twice, and a third time—indeed, a fourth—the prophet recalls the antiquity, or long-standing nature, of their sin, so that no one may judge the sentence of the punisher too hasty or harsher than just. First, above, he said: “Their mockery in the land of Egypt”; then, after some intervening words, he said again: “They have sinned deeply, as in the days of Gibeah.” Again: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal, because there I hated them.” Now for the fourth time, with the same purpose, he says: “From the days of Gibeah Israel has sinned”—that is, from the very time when Israel did not cease to sin at Gibeah.

Israel there sinned once and twice with sins of which Scripture preserves a savage and horrifying memorial. A Levite came to that city with his wife and lodged there. And behold, during the night men of that city surrounded the house in which he stayed, wishing to kill him and tormenting his wife with an incredible frenzy of lust. Finally, she died (Judges 19). [Col. 0161D]

Where such bodily wickedness of fornication reigned, spiritual wickedness had also already grown strong; and the same Scripture nevertheless recounts this, reporting in the preceding passage the idol made in Micah’s house. With what insistence and violence the sons of the tribe of Dan seized it for themselves together with the priest, saying to him: “Come with us, that we may have you as father and priest” (Judges 18), and so forth.

But the children of Israel treated that fornication of idolatry as nothing—indeed, they also committed it themselves—yet because of that bodily fornication they went up to attack Gibeah against the sons of Benjamin. Defeated once and twice in battle, they finally became victors and almost destroyed one tribe of Israel. Afterwards Saul was chosen king from that same city, with such great offence to God that he said to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but me, lest I should reign over them” (1 Kings 8).

Surely, as Israel thus sinned and sinned, the children subsequently born also sinned together with them. In true and just judgment, God thus declares and rebukes them when he says, “There they stood.” This is the same as saying: “My children, though born much later, sinned there; they transgressed in those their fathers, because they did not depart from their fathers’ sins, but, by doing worse things, filled up their measure.” [Col. 0162A]

For this reason a harsher and stronger judgment had to be inflicted upon them. Intending this, he immediately says: “The battle at Gibeah against the sons of iniquity shall not overtake them.” The sense is: The evil which they are to suffer will not be like that battle at Gibeah which they had against the sons of iniquity, whose incredible frenzy of lust killed a woman by tormenting her. It will be far more violent, incomparably greater. This is what he immediately says: “According to my desire I will chastise them.”

This is a great and grave threat, which according to the literal sense signifies that God, who is indeed incapable of suffering, desires the magnitude of the vengeance he will inflict. It resembles what he says in Isaiah: “Ah, I will be comforted over my enemies” (Isa. 1). This is said in the likeness of a person greatly exasperated and so desirous of seeing vengeance that, before it occurs, he cannot in any way be comforted.

And he immediately indicates briefly what he will do: “Peoples,” he says, “shall gather against them when they are chastised for their two iniquities.”

Because of its two iniquities, Israel is said to deserve correction, in accordance with what the same God says in Jeremiah: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns which cannot hold water” [Col. 0163A] (Jer. 2). This could not be said of another nation, of any people ignorant of God. For any nation ignorant of the true God that worshipped false gods is rightly said to have committed only one iniquity. But this nation, in which God was known, is truly charged with having two iniquities when it turned aside to idolatry: namely, abandoning the true God and, in his place—or against him—worshipping foreign gods. For one is guilty in a double sense when, knowing the good, one chooses evil instead; whereas one is simply guilty when, not knowing the good, one receives evil as good.

Thus, both when that people made and worshipped one calf in the wilderness, after seeing many great works of the true God, and when, abandoning the house of David and the Temple of the Lord, it set up for itself two calves—and indeed whenever [Col. 0163B] it worshipped either those or the gods of the nations—it did so. But especially when it asked that Barabbas be released to it and Christ crucified, it committed two iniquities; it sinned doubly, rejecting the good and choosing evil, making sweet bitter and bitter sweet, calling darkness light and light darkness.

“Therefore, when they are corrected for their two iniquities,” he says, “nations shall be gathered against them”: that is, because of the author of sedition whom they chose for themselves, they may be handed over to the sword; and because they denied Christ, they may become the portion of foxes—that is, of evil spirits.

It follows: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck. I will mount upon Ephraim; Judah shall plough; Jacob shall break up his furrows” [Col. 0163C].

Perhaps you were wondering in amazement what cause or what bond had held that people, so firmly bound to idolatry, for so long—from the days of Gibeah, indeed from the days of Egypt, as he said above: “their mockery in the land of Egypt” (Hos. 7). As though you were asking this, he fittingly expresses the true cause by an apt and elegant comparison. “Ephraim,” he says, “is a heifer trained to love threshing.”

Here the custom of the promised land is touched upon, where heifers, together with other animals, were accustomed to tread out grain. When they are wearied by very heavy labor, they normally leave the threshing-floor. Yet, loving the threshing-floor because they eat the grain upon it—hence the saying, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out grain” (1 Cor. 9)—they return to it of their own accord. Ephraim, therefore, is like a young cow, [Col. 0163D] because it has learned to tread out the threshing-floor. Nor has it merely learned this; through excessive habituation it has even begun to love what it has been trained to do, although threshing brings labor.

So too the Israelite people: although it was frequently afflicted and suffered many adversities because of idolatry, nevertheless, desiring to follow its own wishes and the greediness of its belly, it willingly returned to idols. This could have been represented by any other comparison than that of such a heifer; yet the insight of the prophetic Spirit displayed wonderful appropriateness in choosing this comparison. For because Ephraim—or Israel, divided from the house of David—worshipped calves, and indeed worshipped a calf from the beginning, when it came out from the land of Egypt, this same nation is most aptly here called a heifer, while it is reproved for having prostituted itself away from the true God and submitted [Col. 0164A] to the worship of calves.

Then, in saying, “And I passed over the beauty of her neck; I will mount upon Ephraim,” he speaks of great wrath. The beauty of the neck signifies the pride of those sinners, who take pleasure in themselves in their sins. But the passing over or mounting of which he says, “I passed over,” or “I will mount upon Ephraim,” while signifying as certain—both in the future and past tense—what he intends to do, is the same vengeance which we read prescribed in Exodus in these words: “You are a stiff-necked people; once I will go up in your midst, and I will destroy you” (Exod. 33).

Nor was that threat empty. For he went up once: once he was born as man, once he suffered, died, and rose again, and ascended into heaven; and then at last he destroyed that stiff-necked people, exceedingly unable to endure his ascent. What is here called “the beauty of the neck” is there called “ornament,” when the Lord says: “Now put off your ornament, that I may know what I shall do to you” (ibid.). Therefore the children of Israel put off their ornament from Mount Horeb.

As long as the sinner proceeds adorned—that is, proud in sins—as long as he lifts his handsome neck, pleasing himself, rejoicing that he has done evil and exulting in most wicked things (Prov. 2), God in a sense does not know what he shall do to him: mercy does not know by what entrance it may come to him when the severity of judgment has been set aside. Therefore, after pronouncing the judicial sentence, “You are a stiff-necked people; once I will go up in your midst and destroy you,” he immediately offers counsel: “Now,” he says, “put off your ornament, that I may know what I shall do to you” [Col. 0164C]—that is, humble yourself in repentance, so that I may have mercy on you.

Therefore, when he says here, “And I went up,” or “I will go up, over the beauty of her neck”—namely, the heifer that loves threshing, that is, the people returning so often and so obstinately to idolatry—he signifies that wrath which the same people then drank to the dregs of the cup, when God made man went up in its midst. From that time the beauty of its neck was broken, because those proud sinners fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive into all nations (Luke 21).

But that same ascent was appointed both for the ruin of proud blasphemers and for the resurrection of humble believers and confessors. It follows, therefore: “Judah shall plough; Jacob shall break up his furrows.” Behold, we see—and the whole world knows—that, Ephraim’s neck having been crushed, Judah ploughed and Jacob broke up furrows for himself. For when the unbelieving Jews, who denied the Son of David, had been scattered—as Ephraim had once departed from the house of David—the ploughshare of Gospel preaching ploughed the hearts of the nations; and Jacob, that is, “the supplanter,” namely the Gentile people, broke up furrows for itself, practicing cultivation in order to sow or receive the seed, the word of God [Col. 0164D].

Judah ploughed, since the apostles were Jews according to this very name, Judah, that is, “confession”: as the first to confess Christ, the Son of the living God, they preached him to the nations. The nations themselves, however, became Jacob, because they supplanted Esau when they received the birthright of salvation that had belonged to the Jews. Furrows are made by ploughing; by breaking up [Col. 0165A] the furrows, what has been ploughed is made fit to cover and cherish the seed.

At once the spirit of prophetic grace congratulates these farmers or ploughmen and says: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap at the mouth of mercy; renew for yourselves fallow ground.” Preachers sow when they proclaim the word; they reap when they rejoice at believers’ confession. Thus it is beautifully distinguished: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap at the mouth of mercy,” because, as the Apostle says, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

And because no one ought to be content with his own righteousness or salvation, but should make an effort to save others also, he adds and says: “Renew for yourselves fallow ground.” To renew fallow ground is to cultivate places formerly uncultivated, as by clearing woodland. Now the nations had previously been like forests, plainly occupied by wild beasts, that is, evil spirits. Conversely, in comparison with the nations, the Jews were beautiful houses, cultivated land, and prosperous cities. Hence, after the Psalmist had said, “Behold, we heard of it” (Ps. 131)—namely, the Church, or the ark of the Lord’s Incarnation and sanctification—in Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem, intending that the Jews be understood by Ephrathah, [Col. 0166A] he immediately added, because that same ark of sanctification passed from the Jews to the nations: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (ibid.), that is, among the nations, who from forest became fields, from barren wilderness became cultivated and fruitful.

Therefore, “renew for yourselves fallow ground”: that is, by preaching Christ’s Gospel to the nations, prepare for yourselves a new Church, a new people of acquisition; acquire them for God, for your salvation and glory. And because, when “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered” (Rom. 11), it will come to pass that he will look with mercy upon the heifer—that is, that Synagogue—over whose beautiful neck he has now passed so severely, it follows and says: “It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.”

For the time for the remnant of Israel to seek the Lord will be when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered [Col. 0166B]. Then the Lord will come and teach them righteousness, having turned away iniquity, just as the Apostle, after saying that “blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and so all Israel might be saved,” adds the prophetic testimony: “As it is written, ‘There shall come from Zion one who delivers and turns impiety away from Jacob’” (Isa. 59).

## Book Five

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0165C] 71 For the order of the present prophecy to be remembered more clearly, it has already been said—and must be said again and again—that from the words, “There is no truth and no knowledge in the land” (Hos. 4), seven times until the end of the volume it recounts and repeats sins; and at each recurrence the discourse returns to Christ, who alone is the righteousness of all believers and penitents.

Now, for the second time, beginning from the words, “But they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant” (Hos. 6), it has proclaimed the abundance of sins in a long and vehement discourse, concluding thus: “It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.” Now, repeating the same sins for the third time, it says: “You have ploughed impiety, you have reaped iniquity, you have eaten the fruit of falsehood, because you have trusted in your ways” [Col. 0165D].

Most aptly, through the comparison of those who plough, reap, and eat their fruits, it denotes the obstinacy of incorrigible sinners, who, beginning badly, advance to worse things and, ending most wickedly, perish. For just as ploughing, reaping, and eating the fruit differ by successive stages, so divine judgment recognizes in sinners a distinction according to the successive growth of sin.

Accordingly, when a corrupted mind labors under an intended sinful act and turns over in its inmost thought how it may bring an impious will to the effect of action, it is like one ploughing or sowing. But when, after the work of iniquity has been completed, it springs up rejoicing that it has done evil and exulting in most wicked things [Col. 0166C] (Prov. 2), it is like one reaping. And when it has gone so far as to defend, in a proud spirit, its sins against the law of God that rebukes it, and to proceed secure with an unrepentant heart, it is like one who eats fruits stored away after the harvest.

Therefore, after saying, “You have eaten the fruit of falsehood,” he immediately adds—as though one of those to whom he speaks were asking him, “How or why do you say that I have eaten the fruit of falsehood?”—“Because you have trusted in your ways.” This is the same as saying: Because you defend your sins with a proud neck.

Original sin—that is, Adam’s sin—was committed through the same stages. First, indeed, he ploughed impiety when he desired likeness to God. For unless he had first swelled inwardly, unless he had desired divinity or likeness to divine majesty, he would not have yielded so readily when tempted outwardly. Then he reaped iniquity when he transgressed the command set before him concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 3), disobeying the voice of the Lord. Then he ate the fruit of falsehood when he took pleasure in that very sin and defended himself against God’s rebuke.

From that point the entire corrupt offspring of the corrupted parent contracted the same stages—for example, Ephraim or Jeroboam, whose sin is so often commemorated in holy and prophetic writings. For he ploughed impiety when he devised a plan and said: “Now the kingdom will return to the house of David if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem” [Col. 0167A] (3 Kings 12), etc. He reaped iniquity when, having devised the plan, he made two golden calves and said: “Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt” (ibid.). He ate the fruit of falsehood when, while reigning in this way without God, he stubbornly despised the prophets sent to him with God’s word, as Scripture relates, and trusted in his own ways, in his calves.

Finally, that Jewish assembly, which not merely departed from the house of David but even crucified the Son of David, ploughed impiety when the chief priests and scribes sought how they might kill him (Luke 22). It reaped iniquity when they asked and obtained from Pilate that he be killed (Acts 13). To this day they eat the fruit of falsehood, since they purchased falsehood—or the fruit of falsehood—with a large sum of money given to the soldiers, so that they would say: “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.” “And that saying has been spread among the Jews to this day” (Matt. 28) [Col. 0167B]. And they trust in their ways while, wishing to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God.

Where sin has thus been accumulated and strengthened by such ploughing, such reaping, and likewise such eating or confessing, plainly the time and place have now come for judgment or for a punishing sentence. It follows, therefore: “In the multitude of your mighty men tumult shall arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be laid waste.”

Whoever completes his sins in the ways stated above is rightly said to have mighty men—mighty men who are evil, of course, opposed to the good mighty men. Such were David’s first mighty men, to whom none of the other mighty men attained. Those three mighty men of his were virtues: wisdom, humility, and strength, which Scripture thus designates and briefly comprises: “These are the names of David’s mighty men: David, sitting in the chair, wisest among the three.” “Sitting in the chair, wisest”: this is wisdom. “He himself was like the tenderest worm of wood”: this is humility. “He killed eight hundred in one assault”: this is strength.

In opposition to those mighty men, these people have mighty men: folly, pride, and rashness, which they suppose to be true strength. Accordingly they deserve no mercy and quickly experience vengeance. This is what he says: “In the multitude of your mighty men tumult shall arise among the people, and all your fortresses shall be laid waste” [Col. 0167D].

This happened both when the ten tribes were carried captive into Assyria and when the Jews, conquered by the Romans, fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive into all nations. For tumult arose among that people through a threefold discord, divided against itself, as histories relate; and all its fortresses were laid waste, so that not one stone was left upon another. This happened “in the multitude of your mighty men,” that is, because of the multitude of its mighty men of the sort already described: for the Jews were mighty in evil in that manner, as the Savior himself testifies in the Psalm: “For behold, they have hunted for my life, and mighty men have rushed upon me” (Ps. 58) [Col. 0168A].

Now, addressing those to be devastated, the prophetic discourse says: “As Salmana was devastated by the house of him who judged Baal on the day of battle, when a mother was dashed down upon her children, so Bethel has done to you because of the wickedness of your evils.”

The historical event is well known, and he announces that their devastation will be like it. For in the Book of Judges it is written that an angel appeared to Gideon and said to him: “Go in this your strength, and you shall deliver Israel from the hand of Midian.” And afterwards: “Take your father’s bull, and the other bull seven years old; you shall destroy the altar of Baal which belongs to your father, and cut down the grove around the altar” (Judg. 6). After doing this, at the Lord’s command he went forth with three hundred men and conquered Midian by a remarkable kind of battle.

He divided the three hundred men and gave them trumpets in their hands, empty jars, and lamps in the midst of the jars. When he himself and the three hundred men who were with him entered one part of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch of the night, with the guards awakened, they began to sound the trumpets and strike the jars together. As they sounded in three places around the camp and broke the jars, they held lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right, and cried: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Therefore the entire camp was thrown into confusion, and the fugitives cut one another down in mutual slaughter, while the men of Israel shouted and pursued them [Col. 0168B] (Judg. 7).

Two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, were captured and killed; and afterwards Zebah and Salmana, kings of Midian. The prophet here calls that day “the day of battle,” when he says: “As Salmana was devastated by the house of him who judged Baal on the day of battle.” For the one who judged Baal was Gideon himself. Hence he was called Jerubbaal, because his father had said: “Let Baal take vengeance upon him who has undermined his altar.”

Isaiah, however, calls the same day “the day of Midian”: “You have broken the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9). Each prophet, both this one and Isaiah, likened Christ’s triumph over both his invisible and visible enemies to that triumph by which Gideon thus triumphed over Midian with those three hundred men. Indeed, the Psalmist also prays that God’s enemies and Christ’s adversaries may be made like those princes of Midian, one of whom was Salmana, in their ruin: “O God, make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, Zebah and Salmana” [Col. 0168D] (Ps. 80).

A great and memorable battle: according to its likeness, the spiritual warfare of the Lord was confirmed and foretold by the testimony of three prophets—Isaiah, David, and this Hosea. For, as Catholic and orthodox interpreters have drawn out in exposition, Gideon prefigured Christ, while the three hundred men with him prefigured preachers of the Holy Trinity; Midian, however, prefigured all Christ’s enemies. The fact that those men carried not swords but lamps in jars in their left hands, while in their right hands they held sounding trumpets, was a type of this: holy preachers held the salvation of their bodies as the lesser concern and the word of preaching as the greater concern [Col. 0169A]. When the pots or jars were broken, the lamps shone out amid the clatter of trumpets, and the enemies fled and perished, because when bodies were laid low in death, the greatness of the graces hidden more obscurely within them shone forth more clearly through miraculous signs; and thus the hostile designs of evil spirits or impious human beings against Christ were scattered.

Now let us continue the interpretation we have begun, according to the order or tenor of the present text. “As Salmana,” he says, “was devastated by the house of him who judged Baal on the day of battle, when a mother was dashed down upon her children, so Bethel has done to you because of the wickedness of your evils.” He did not say, “As Midian was devastated,” but “As Salmana was devastated,” who was king of Midian. For it is written there: “And Gideon said to the men of Succoth, ‘Give, I pray you, loaves to the people who are with me, for they are very weak, so that we may pursue Zebah and Salmana, the kings of Midian’” [Col. 0169B] (Judg. 8).

How was that Salmana devastated? When Gideon had captured them, namely Zebah and Salmana, he said to them: “What sort of men were those whom you killed at Tabor?” They answered: “They were like you, and each one of them like a king’s son.” He said to them: “They were my brothers, sons of my mother. As the Lord lives, if you had spared them, I would not kill you”; and the subsequent words conclude thus: “Then Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Salmana” (ibid.).

Therefore, after saying, “As Salmana was devastated by the house of him who judged Baal on the day of battle,” the prophet added, “when a mother was dashed down upon her children,” because they had violently dashed down Gideon’s mother upon her sons. Their death could not but be a crushing blow to their mother’s womb; for that reason too Gideon refused to spare Salmana and killed him.

“So Bethel,” he says, “has done to you because of the wickedness of your evils.” Whether you consider the condition of the time when the ten tribes were carried into Assyria, or that when the Jews were slain by Roman swords, the comparison is true in both cases. For they suffered these things because the earlier ones killed the prophets, and these later ones killed Christ and the apostles; and by doing so they dashed down the mother upon her children—that is, they grievously saddened the Church of God.

For the former, Bethel was a city of that name, [Col. 0169D] in which they had set one of the calves that they worshipped. For the latter, Bethel was the very house of the Lord in Jerusalem, according to the interpretation of the name—for Bethel means “house of God”—in which they served not God but Mammon. That house brought this upon them because of the wickedness of their evils: that, as Salmana was devastated, so they too might be devastated and suffer final extermination.

Why? Because they were no longer like Abraham or Israel, but like Salmana, who ruled the Midianites. That name is interpreted “consummation,” signifying that they were consummate in every kind of wickedness, in all the ways stated above: ploughing impiety, reaping iniquity, eating the fruit of falsehood, and trusting in their ways.

Therefore let Gideon, whose name is interpreted “one who enters the womb”—namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who was not conceived from male seed but, coming from heaven through himself, entered and filled the Virgin’s womb—say to them: “What sort of men were those whom you killed at Tabor?” The sense is: What does your conscience answer you? What kind of men were those whom I sent to you, some of whom you killed and crucified, some of whom you scourged in your synagogues and persecuted from city to city? [Col. 0170A] (Matt. 23).

For truth does not cease to confront their guilty conscience; rather, they continually bear about with themselves accusing thoughts. They are said, moreover, to have done this at Tabor—and rightly, because Tabor is interpreted “coming light,” and they did this at the coming of, and because of the coming of, the true light, which is Christ, unwilling that anyone should see or be shown so great a light.

They reply: “They were like you, and each one of them like a king’s son.” For they cannot fail to answer this, since they sinned not ignorantly but knowingly; and they clearly knew that they were like Christ—namely prophets, sages, and scribes—and that one among them was like a king’s son, indeed the true King’s Son: the one who asks this, convicts their consciences, and orders them brought forth for the judgment of death [Col. 0170B].

“They were my brothers,” he says, “sons of my mother. If you had spared them, I would not kill you.” Christ truly calls the blessed apostles his brothers, because even before they had glorified him by their sufferings or deaths, he said to Mary after he rose from the dead: “Go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father’” (John 20). They are also sons of his mother, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, “which is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4), of whom Christ too, according to the flesh, was made a son—the unique son, the firstborn from the dead.

“If you had spared them,” he says, “I would not kill you,” because the guilt even of Christ’s death would have been forgiven the Jews if, after his resurrection, they had believed his apostles, in accordance with the prayer he made when they crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23).

Having set these matters forth, the person of God the Father immediately speaks thus of the grace of the same Savior, by which believing elect persons are justified.

## Chapter XI

[Col. 0170D]

As the morning passes, so the king of Israel has passed away; for Israel is a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. The meaning is this: the king of Israel ought to have been none other than God, and Christ the Son of God, whom the faith of the patriarchs had awaited. Hence, when the children of Israel asked for a king, the matter displeased Samuel; and the Lord said to him: “They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them” (1 Sam. 8). Yet whoever was able to reign in Israel did not wait for the lawful time of God’s kingdom; rather, rising eagerly against one another and striking down other kings, they reigned in succession until Herod reigned, who was not of Israelite stock. With him there ceased to reign in Israel a mortal man who would pass away, although certain descendants of that same Herod afterward rent apart, rather than governed, some portions of that kingdom [Col. 0171A]; for then Christ the King was born, whose kingdom does not pass away but remains for ever (Luke 1).

Therefore the king of Israel had to pass away and cease, especially at the time when Herod was such a king as belonged neither to Judah nor to any tribe of Israel, at the time when Christ, the true King, was born. And indeed so it happened. For, as the morning passes, the king of Israel passed away, and the earthly kingdom of Israel came to an end. Morning does indeed pass quickly, yet it returns again. But such a king, or the kingdom of Israel, will not return again. Thus, after saying, “As the morning passes,” he was not content to say, “The king of Israel passes,” but, expressing an absolute and irrevocable passing away, he says: “The king of Israel has passed away” [Col. 0171B]—one who will now return no more; whereas morning passes indeed, but will return once the night has passed. Why? “For Israel,” he says, “is a child”—that is, he has been born who alone ought to reign in Israel with heavenly sovereignty, whom that foreign king Herod sought to destroy (Matt. 2). “And I loved him,” he says, namely according to the other prophet through whom this same God the Father spoke: “Behold my servant; I will uphold him; my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased” (Isa. 42). “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17).

And this child is most rightly called Israel in the present passage because of what follows: “And out of Egypt I called my son.” For this child underwent the trials or afflictions of Israel, beginning with the fact that he fled from Israel [Col. 0171C] into Egypt, where Israel of old had lived as a stranger. Knowing this, the divine Evangelist, after saying, “He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt, and remained there until Herod’s death,” immediately added this testimony: “that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Matt. 2). There the house of Israel served because of its sins, because they had sold their brother Joseph (Gen. 37); there this king of Israel became an exile. Called out of Egypt, he was tested in the wilderness for forty days (Matt. 4). There Israel of old, having come out of Egypt, was tested, because it tested God in the wilderness for forty years: it sinned by maligning [Col. 0171D] the land of promise, which it had explored for forty days; and therefore, God the Judge reckoning a day for a year, it remained there, as was said, for forty years. But he, who did not test God but was tested, immediately after forty days began to enter the true land of promise and to bring his hearers into it, by preaching, casting out demons, performing other miracles, suffering death, rising from the dead, and ascending into heaven.

Thus this Son is rightly called Israel here; and this testimony taken by the Evangelist fittingly concerns his flight into Egypt and return from it: “Out of Egypt I called my son.” The people Israel also, when called out of Egypt, was called a son, as it is written: “You shall say [Col. 0172A] to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me,” and you refused to let him go. Behold, I will slay your firstborn son’” (Exod. 4). Therefore the people Israel too was called a son in respect of the elect portion; but this was only by the grace of him who is the only Son—not adopted but begotten—who was to be born according to the flesh from that people, in order through his passion to bring many sons into glory, not disdaining to have them as brothers and co-heirs. Otherwise, unless this beloved Son of God, who was to come, had come, Israel too, like the other nations, could never have been called the son of so great a Father. The Apostle testifies to this: though he himself was of that people, he nevertheless says, “For we too were once [Col. 0172B] by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2).

But if you ask what happened of old when Israel came up out of Egypt—since, as the Evangelist says, that saying spoken by the Lord through this prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my Son,” was fulfilled when the child Jesus fled into Egypt and returned from there—hear what follows: “They called them, and so they went away from before them; they sacrificed to the Baals and made offerings to images.” Here, now for a fourth time recounting the sins of that same people, the prophetic discourse returns to earlier times. The meaning is: I indeed called the children of Israel out of Egypt at that time; but they did not then leave Egypt, except for a very few. They left in body, but [Col. 0172C] did not leave in mind. Others called them, and, despising me, they followed those others instead. Indeed, though they went bodily out of Egypt, they remained so completely in Egypt in their minds that they sacrificed to Egyptian images and, moreover, offered sacrifice to the Baals. Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, destroyed Baal’s idol (Judg. 8); but afterward they turned back to sacrifice to it, especially at the summons of their kings and of the impious Jezebel. By thus departing from before them, they showed that they had by no means gone out of Egypt, since they had not abandoned Egyptian sins.

“And I was like a foster-father to Ephraim; I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I healed them.” The present passage, though briefly, gives a lofty enough indication of the wonderful patience of God, of which Paul also speaks in the Acts of the Apostles: “For forty years [Col. 0172D] he bore with their ways in the wilderness” (Acts 13). “And I,” he says, “was like a foster-father to Ephraim; I carried them in my arms.” For just as a foster-father patiently bears with a little child who has not yet reached an age capable of understanding and cannot yet distinguish good from evil, enduring its childish foolishness—though at times, stirred to anger, he may strike it, yet more often applying comforting caresses—and carries it in his arms however ungrateful it may be: so the Lord God who speaks these things patiently bore with a people untaught and ignorant of the spiritual mysteries of God’s heavenly kingdom. Although he struck down the bodies of many of them in the wilderness, he nevertheless dealt tenderly with many who remained, by great miracles, leading them about and teaching them, as [Col. 0173A] Moses says, and guarding them “as the pupil of his eye” (Deut. 32).

This is what he means when he says, “I carried them in my arms”; for by “arms” he means the strength of the miracles performed for them. Hence, after Scripture said, “The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel,” it immediately adds: “But they had gone forth with a high hand” (Exod. 14). And the Psalmist says: “He brought Israel out from their midst with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm” (Ps. 135). Nor is Ephraim named here without reason, though it was only one tribe of that people. Since the ingratitude of that tribe was greater, because Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim made the golden calves, that tribe is fittingly singled out more severely wherever the greater benefits of God toward the ungrateful nation are recalled [Col. 0173B].

“And they did not know that I healed them.” Truly they did not know it—so much so that, when he gave them certain healing bonds, that is, legal commandments, they stood at a distance, terrified and shaken with fear, saying to Moses: “Speak to us, and we will listen; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” Moses, on the contrary, so that they might know that the Lord wished not to kill but to heal them, said: “Do not fear. For God has come to test you, and that his terror and dread may be in you, and that you may not sin” (Exod. 20).

In accordance with the sense of those same words which the Lord then spoke, the prophet continues and says: “I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the cords of love.” For when Moses said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from among your brothers, like me; him you shall hear,” he immediately added: “As you requested,” he says, “from the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said: ‘I will no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire any more, lest I die.’ And the Lord said: ‘They have spoken well in all that they have said. I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers like you, and I will put my words in his mouth; he shall speak to them everything that I command him. But whoever will not listen to his words which he speaks in my name, I myself will exact punishment’” (Deut. 18) [Col. 0173C].

Accordingly, as there in words of this kind, so here in saying, “I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the cords of love,” God the Father promises human beings the incarnation of his only-begotten Son [Col. 0173D]. For when this came to pass, God truly raised up for human beings, from among their brothers, a prophet like Moses: that is, God made such that people could speak with him as they spoke with Moses, to whom they had said: “Speak to us, and we will listen; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” And now he drew us with the cords of Adam, being made a son of Adam, or Son of Man; these are cords of love. For in becoming the Son of Man from Adam’s flesh, he bound us to himself in a wondrous manner and drew us to himself with cords of love. From this we know that he heals us, for he says, “They did not know that I healed them.”

At last he directs the wearing of these same cords especially toward this end: that, coming into this world, he might correct in his elect the sin of gluttony through which the first human being perished, and through which the aforesaid children of Israel tested God by craving a craving in the wilderness (Ps. 108), training them to work for food that does not perish and to eat and drink the sacrament of his body and blood (John 6). It follows: “And I shall be to them as one lifting the yoke from upon their jaws, and I bent down to him that he might eat.” Teeth are set in the jaws, and food, first ground by them, is sent inward. Thus the jaws rightly signify gluttony, through which, as has been said, the first human being perished, and through which the children of Israel, testing God, said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” [Col. 0174B] (Ps. 82), and other such things.

And when he himself was present and said to them: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent,” they said to him: “What sign then do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness” (John 6). They clearly meant that he should feed them either in the same way in which their fathers ate that bread without work of their own, or as he himself had shortly before satisfied five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (Luke 9). Thus, as it were with jaws gaping, they gave expression to the craving for food that they had.

Therefore, when he says, “And I shall be to them as one lifting the yoke from upon their jaws, and I bent down [Col. 0174C] to him that he might eat,” the meaning is: I, drawing them with the cords of Adam, with the cords of love, as has been said, shall restrain and check in them the immoderate appetite for eating through which the first human being perished and to which, following his example, they are excessively devoted—saying to them, “Work not for the food that perishes,” and other such things. For “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6). By that descent I bent down to him that he might eat; and whoever, working rightly in faith and obedience, ate this bread would live, desiring to escape within himself the unbelief and disobedience through which he had died in the first parent’s evil eating.

It follows: “He shall not return to the land of Egypt, and Assyria itself shall be his king, because [Col. 0174D] they refused to turn back. The sword has begun in his cities; it shall consume his chosen men and devour their heads; and my people shall hang in suspense for my return. But a yoke shall be laid upon them together, which shall not be removed.” When, as said above, he carried that people through the wilderness in his arms and gave them bread—that is, manna, a figure of the living and life-giving bread—they repeatedly quarrelled by murmuring (Exod. 16), saying: “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt” (Num. 14). But when he himself bent down to them, that they might eat—when he testified that he was the living bread who had come down from heaven, so that whoever ate of him should not die (John 6)—there was no such uproar among the people that it might appoint itself a leader and return to Egypt. On the contrary, it gloried greatly in that city and temple; yet Assyria itself—that is, the devil—is nevertheless its king.

Why? “Because,” he says, “they refused to turn back”—understood: so that they might eat that bread which, as has been said, bent down, that is, descended from heaven, in order that whoever works the work of God might eat. That Assyria—that is, the devil—has from that time truly been its king, because it denied and blasphemed its own king, the king of righteousness and prince of peace, and would not turn to him, was made clear by what followed. “For,” he says, “the sword has begun in his cities”: namely, when that people was surrounded by the Roman army. In a remarkable way, before [Col. 0175B] the walls were assaulted from without by siege engines, innumerable bodies of citizens were more miserably slain within by the swords of factions, as Josephus’s account of the dreadful and universally famous tragedy of Jerusalem’s destruction attests. Thus it was rightly and truly said: “The sword has begun in his cities,” because the sword devastated them within before fear from the enemy’s presence outside struck those shut in.

What follows, “It shall consume his chosen men and devour their heads,” means, as though he said, that it will destroy not merely their leaders or princes but all their rule, in accordance also with Daniel’s prophecy. After saying, “After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and there shall not be a people for him who is to deny him,” Daniel continues: “And the people with the leader who is to come shall destroy the city [Col. 0175C] and the sanctuary; its end shall be desolation, and after the end of the war desolation is decreed. Sacrifice and offering shall fail, and in the temple there shall be an abomination of desolation; and desolation shall endure until the consummation and the end” (Dan. 9).

But, as he says, “There shall not be a people for him who is to deny him,” the Jews have nothing to do with Christ, though they maintain that they await Christ. This is what he now says in the present passage: “My people shall hang in suspense for my return.” For now they hang between the two: they have neither the God of their fathers nor do they worship idols, as they once worshipped Baal and the calves. Christ will indeed return to them, so that a remnant may be saved (Rom. 9); but meanwhile there has been laid upon those who do not believe a yoke which shall not be removed: the yoke of sin and the yoke of captivity, by which they were led captive into all nations.

Intending and foreseeing this, namely that a remnant might be saved, he immediately says: “How shall I give you up, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel? How shall I give you up? Shall I make you like Admah, like Zeboiim? My heart has been turned within me; my repentance has been stirred together. I will not execute the fury of my wrath; I will not turn back to destroy Ephraim, because I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst.” Admah and Zeboiim are known to have been cities of the Sodomites. There were five cities: Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, and Bela, which is Zoar (Gen. 14). Hence that region itself was called the Pentapolis. Those cities were so overthrown by fire and sulphur that no remnant of them survived [Col. 0176A].

Therefore, when he says, “How shall I give you up, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel?”—understood, *you who do not deserve protection*—he immediately adds the deserved judgment, saying: “I shall make you like Admah, like Zeboiim.” He threatens that people with so utter a rejection that not even a remnant of it ought to be saved.
