Having said this, he immediately, as if touched inwardly by grief of heart, judges his own judgment to be excessively severe and says: “My heart has been turned within me; my repentance has been stirred together.” The meaning is: as soon as I spoke evil against you and pronounced a harsh sentence, compassion touched me, mercy prevailing—as though the compassion of a father softens the severity of a judge. “I will not,” he says, “execute the fury of my wrath; I will not turn back to destroy Ephraim”—understood, in the manner in which I destroyed Admah and Zeboiim [Col. 0176B], leaving no remnant of them. I shall not so turn back; I shall not so depart from my inherent mercy as thus to fulfil my wrath, “because I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst.”

When a man is angry and deeply wounded by an injury received, he sets his whole purpose upon exacting vengeance and satisfying himself with the penalties of the one who injured him; he seeks not repentance but, as has been said, vengeance alone. But I am God, the Holy One in your midst, desiring not vengeance or punishment from wrath but the repentance of sinners from mercy. “Therefore I shall not enter the city.” That is, I shall not strike indiscriminately like a human being who, angry and, as has often been said, breaking into a city because of an offence, burns with rage, makes no distinction of ages, ranks, or conditions, but involves all alike, strikes everyone without distinction, pursues those who flee, and slaughters those who meet him [Col. 0176C].

In this sense the Apostle also says: “Has God rejected his people? By no means. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And shortly afterward: “What does the divine answer say to Elijah? ‘I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’ So then, at this time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11). God, then, is angry not with the nation but with unbelief; for he is not so angry as to be unwilling to receive any remnant from that people of his if they turn back. No Jew, I say, is rejected merely because the Jewish nation killed Christ; rather, whoever denies Christ, whether Jew or Gentile, makes himself rejected in his own person.

Hence, in the passage mentioned above, after Daniel said, “After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain,” he adds: “And there shall not be a people for him who is to deny him.” He did not say, “There shall not be his people who is to kill him,” but “who is to deny him.” For Christ’s killing is without doubt forgiven to his killers, according to his own prayer: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 13); but the obstinacy of denial is condemned and merits no pardon. Therefore God did not make that people of his like Admah and Zeboiim, from whose bodily conflagration none of the inhabitants escaped, because many survived the bodily destruction [Col. 0177A]; and the remnant from them would have been overthrown when the fullness of the Gentiles entered, unless by his own will—unless through gratuitous mercy—he had restrained the fury of his wrath. By a wholly just judgment he would have destroyed them like Admah and Zeboiim, with no remnant preserved. Hence Isaiah too says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we should have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1).

It follows: “They shall walk after the Lord; he shall roar like a lion, because he himself shall roar, and the children of the sea shall fear; and they shall fly away like a bird from Egypt, like a dove from the land of the Assyrians. And I will place them in their houses, says the Lord.” “Therefore,” he says, “I shall not destroy them utterly, because the remnant shall walk after the Lord,” that is, they shall believe in Christ. For Christ will be known and feared by them at the acceptable time [Col. 0177B], as a lion is known and feared by its roar. “For he himself,” he says, “shall roar like a lion.” Not content to say this once, he repeats it: “For he himself shall roar, and the children of the sea shall fear.” Our Lord Jesus Christ roared like a lion when he shattered hell and conquered death, in accordance with Jacob’s prophecy: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49). Therefore they shall walk after the Lord roaring as a lion, and shall fear: that is, they shall believe in Christ glorified after death had been conquered and hell despoiled, shall follow his footsteps, and shall be subject to him in fear.

But who are those who will thus walk after the Lord and thus fear? “The children of the sea,” he says. He does not say, “The children [Col. 0177C] of Ephraim” or “the children of Israel,” to whom above he had said: “How shall I give you up, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel?” Rather, “the children of the sea”: that is, whoever believe and are baptized. For Jesus was to die not only for the nation, or for the remnant of the nation, but “to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11). He therefore uses a broader and more universal expression: “children of the sea,” that is, children of baptism, children of regenerating grace, from whatever people or nation they may be. The remnant of the children will walk after the Lord and fear along with these; and thus the scattered children of God will be gathered into one.

The prophet adorns this gathering of their unity most beautifully when he says: “And they shall fly away like a bird from Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will place them in their houses [Col. 0177D], says the Lord.” Egypt, or the land of the Assyrians, is this world for all who wander and follow the ruler of this world, who is signified by Assur. He who, abandoning earthly desires, follows heavenly grace is fittingly said to fly away like a bird; thus they escape so that the pursuing devil finds no traces of fault in them, just as no tracks remain from birds’ flight when they are borne freely through the air on their wings. Nor was he content with the general expression, “they shall fly away like a bird,” but immediately specifies the likeness of that bird to which heavenly grace is suitably compared: “and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians.” For the dove especially signifies the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit appeared in this form [Col. 0178A] over our Lord when he was baptized (Matt. 3). Made alive by the sacraments of that same Holy Spirit, we have flown away from Egypt and the land of the Assyrians—that is, from the darkness of ignorance and from the desires of earthly affections.

“And, flying away thus, I will place them in their houses, says the Lord”: in their houses, that is, in dwellings prepared for them. For from the beginning of the world, when he blessed the first created human beings and said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1), he prepared for them eternal houses or dwellings, of which, when about to die, he immediately said: “In my Father’s house are many dwellings” (John 14); and on the last day he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you [Col. 0178B] from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XII
Ephraim has surrounded me with denial, and the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah comes down as a witness with his God, faithful with the holy ones. Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the scorching wind. All day long he multiplies falsehood and devastation; he has made a covenant with the Assyrians, and carried oil into Egypt.

For the fifth time, the prophetic discourse accuses the sins of the people who wish to justify themselves; and Majesty consigns the accused before its tribunal, from whose hand no one can escape if it enters into judgment with human beings. “Ephraim,” he says, “has surrounded me with denial, and the house of Israel with deceit.” According to the plain sense of the letter, he directs the reader to the times when, as has often already been said, Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim, made golden calves (3 Kings 12). For then both he in denial and the house of Israel in deceit surrounded God, when he and the house of Israel devised such a plan in order to drive away from themselves the house of David. There indeed was deceit: Israel sinned not through ignorance but through malice; there he openly denied God, who had brought Israel out of the land of Egypt, when he attributed both that name and that deed to those calves, saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (ibid.).

But does he who says these things have in view only those calves in this prophet, which Ephraim made at that time, and not rather those many calves and bulls of which he had already spoken in another prophet: “Many calves have surrounded me; fat bulls have besieged me” (Ps. 21)? Let us therefore follow the prophetic Spirit as it looks rather toward those times when the deserters of the Son of God, the Son of David, so imitated the sin of that Ephraim which then denied David—or rather the Lord himself in David, to whom the promise had been made—saying, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings 12), that they surrounded him, saying: “How long do you take away our life? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10). For then they surrounded him in denial, and said these things to him because their intention was assuredly such that, if he confessed himself to be Christ, they might accuse and deny him—which they did before Pilate [Col. 0179A].

Likewise, when they sent to him certain Pharisees with Herodians, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth; tell us therefore: Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 22), then the house of Israel surrounded him with deceit, since they had devised a plan to trap him in speech. He now truly says that the heirs of the sin of that Ephraim or Israel which departed from the house of David would do and say these and similar things: “Ephraim has surrounded me with denial, and the house of Israel with deceit.”

But for those who received and confessed him, in accordance with the present confession of Peter and the Apostle, saying, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16), what he immediately says is appropriate: “But Judah comes down as a witness with his God, faithful with the holy ones” [Col. 0179B]. For *Judah* is interpreted “confession”; and therefore all confessors of power are rightly signified by this name. This opposition must be carefully observed: Ephraim surrounded the Lord in denial; but Judah—this very name *Judah*, that is, confession—comes down as a witness with his God in confession. Clearly, denial and Judah, that is, confession, are opposites; likewise, surrounding the Lord and descending with the Lord are opposites.

Nothing is truer than this prophetic proclamation. Whoever surrounds the Lord in denial is proud against the Lord, and through pride falls into the judgment of the devil. Conversely, whoever confesses the Lord, confessing the Son of God in the humility of the Son of Man, comes down and thereby deserves to be exalted. This Judah is rightly called a witness—not any sort of witness, but a faithful one—opposite to the house of Israel, which surrounded the Lord with deceit [Col. 0179C]. Deceit and faithfulness are opposites. Therefore the confessor and faithful witness comes down with his God and with the holy ones.

For example, when one of those who came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, “confessed and did not deny, and confessed, ‘I am not the Christ’” (John 1). Likewise: “He who is to come after me,” he says, “has been made before me, because he was before me; and from his fullness we all have received” (ibid.). In this manner, surely, all the saints come down; and with them every confessor and faithful witness comes down, confessing that he existed before all things and that they themselves all received from his fullness [Col. 0179D]. Conversely all the proud, such as the scribes and Pharisees were at that time, are lifted on high; hence they became like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth (Ps. 1).

He says, therefore: “Ephraim feeds on wind and follows the scorching wind.” To feed on wind is to be puffed up by the spirit of pride; to follow the scorching wind is to be corrupted by lust. These are consequent sins or vices: when pride has lifted up the spirit, the spirit of fornication corrupts the flesh as well. What follows—“All day long he multiplies falsehood and devastation”—is plainly suited to the same persons, who all day long, that is, obstinately, invented a lie and an empty fear, saying: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11)—and thus multiplied devastation [Col. 0180A], that is, prepared a manifold overthrow for their cities.

How else did such an Ephraim—that is, the people deserting the true David—make a covenant with the Assyrians and carry oil into Egypt, except by doing the will of evil spirits and wickedly flattering the power of this world, so as to say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19)? Oil sometimes signifies the sweetness of flattery, as there: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140), that is, “Let no one’s flattery delight my mind.” Indeed, by saying, “We have no king but Caesar,” and “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend,” and other such things, he carried oil into Egypt; yet he was not even accepted for a time by those Egyptians, that is, the Roman rulers among the Gentiles [Col. 0180B]. For in return for the sweetness of such oil they obtained no favor of alliance, but rather the great punishment of their own overthrow.

It follows: “For the Lord has a judgment with Judah, and a visitation upon Jacob. According to his ways and according to his devices he will repay him. In the womb he supplanted his brother; and in his strength he was directed with the angel, prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him.”

The Lord had said: “Ephraim has surrounded me with denial, and the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah comes down as a witness with his God, faithful with the holy ones.” Now, as though someone were asking what cause Ephraim had for denial, what cause the house of Israel had for devising an idol, while Judah, by contrast, descended as a faithful witness with his God, the prophet himself adds, speaking in his own person: “For the Lord has a judgment with Judah, and a visitation upon Jacob” [Col. 0180C].

The sense is this: they surrounded the Lord, denying him and speaking deceitfully, because the Lord himself established a judgment with Judah and exercised a visitation upon Jacob, discerning—and teaching that it must be discerned—who are truly Jews and who, on the contrary, call themselves Jews when they are not, but are in the synagogue of Satan (Rev. 3); who, I say, are truly Jacob, and who, conversely, call themselves Jacob or Israel when they are not, but are Esau.

In exercising such judgment with Judah and such visitation upon Jacob, our coming Lord did not wish them to be reckoned Jews or sons of Jacob merely because they were children of the flesh, unless they were also children of promise or faith [Col. 0180D]. Hence the Apostle says: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are the seed of Abraham, are all children of God; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called,’ that is, not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but those who are children of promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. 9).

Finally, that being children of the flesh is of no benefit when they are not children of promise is confirmed by the most just sentence when he says: “According to his ways and according to his devices he will repay him.” Whom does “him” mean? Surely the one who, though he ought to have been Jacob or Judah, a faithful witness, became Ephraim, who faithlessly departed from the house of David, and indeed deserves to be called Canaan, as we have in what follows. Thus, when he says, “According to his ways and according to his devices he will repay him” [Col. 0181A], it must be understood: equally as to a Gentile. For the Apostle says: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of a human being who works evil—of the Jew first, and also of the Greek. For there is no respect of persons with God” (Rom. 2).

In these words he briefly defines the truth of the Judge, or the true sentence of the Judge discerning who is truly called and is Jacob: “In the womb he supplanted his brother; and in his strength he was directed with the angel, prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him.” In saying these things, he most subtly requires anyone wishing to maintain that he is from Jacob to act in the same way. He declares that the people which truly is and is called Jacob is the people which acts similarly.

“In the womb,” he says, “he supplanted his brother,” whence he was called Jacob [Col. 0181B] (Gen. 25), that is, “supplanter.” Therefore, whoever wishes truly to be called or to be Jacob amid the hardships of this life, let him contend in the understanding of truth against this people, which, though red with cruelty, earthly in greed, and hairy in manners, arrogates God to itself while it does not possess the Son of God; and by fighting unto victory let him take away its birthright.

Again: “And in his strength,” he says, “he was directed with the angel, prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; and he wept and entreated him.” He refers to the familiar history: when Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia, and after everything belonging to him had been taken across, Jacob remained alone beyond the ford. “Behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. And when he saw that he could not overcome him, he said to him: ‘Let me go, for dawn has now risen.’ He answered: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ And he blessed him in that same place” (Gen. 32) [Col. 0181C].

Therefore, whoever wishes not only truly to be called or to be Jacob, but also Israel, should likewise in his strength—that is, in his faith—be directed with Christ, the Angel of great counsel, and prevail over this angel, specifically by doing penance and producing fruit worthy of penance. For in saying, “And he was strengthened,” then adding, “He wept and entreated him,” he may rightly be understood to speak of the strength of penitents. For they are truly strong in weeping urgently and perseveringly begging remission of sins, according to: “From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

Whoever thus imitates the father Jacob, who wrestled with the angel and as a victor obtained a blessing from him [Col. 0181D], is assuredly now truly Jacob, whatever people or nation he may belong to, and deserves to be called Israel. He adds further: “In Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us; and the Lord God of hosts—the Lord is his memorial.”

Here he plainly maintains that the angel with whom that patriarch Jacob was directed, or wrestled, was the Lord himself, saying: “In Bethel he found him, and the Lord God of hosts—the Lord is his memorial.” For Scripture bears witness that the one whom he had formerly found in Bethel was the Lord himself. For it is written: “He saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, its top reaching heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending upon it; and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: ‘I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac’” (Gen. 28) [Col. 0182A].

Therefore in Bethel he found him, namely the angel with whom he afterward wrestled, who also said to him: “Since you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?” (Gen. 32). Bethel is interpreted “house of God.” Therefore whoever desires to prevail over such an angel, so as to obtain the remission of sins through tears as a victor, should seek him in Bethel in order to find him—that is, in the house of God, which is the Church. For outside this house of God there is no place in which anyone may find him, or in which he imparts his speech to anyone. Hence he now says: “And there he spoke with us.”

Who or how great is he whom Jacob then found in Bethel, and whom anyone deserving now to be called the seed of that same Jacob or Israel must find in the house of God, he expresses more plainly when he immediately says: “And the Lord God of hosts—the Lord is his memorial” [Col. 0182B]. For this Angel of great counsel is truly Lord and God: the Lord God of hosts, that is, the Creator and King of all angels and all elect human beings. And this name, “Lord,” is his memorial just as it is that of God his Father. For no one speaking in the Spirit of God disavows or forgets it, but keeps it in remembrance and says, “Lord God.”

The prophet now turns to the hearer and says: “And you shall return to the Lord your God; keep mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always.” When he says “and you,” it must be understood, “as that man did,” or “according to his example.” And how did that Jacob return to the Lord his God, keep mercy and judgment, and always hope in his God? Surely when, living as an exile and fleeing his brother Esau, who was no longer an exile but had become very powerful by taking wives from the daughters of Canaan, among whom his father Isaac lived, he was then deprived of every human consolation; weeping, as has already been said, and praying, he turned to the Lord his God and prevailed over the angel [Col. 0182C], strengthened by this tearful prayer:

> “God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Lord, you said to me: ‘Return to your land and to the place of your birth, and I will do you good.’ I am less than all your mercies and the truth which you have fulfilled toward your servant. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies. Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I greatly fear him” (Gen. 32).

Thus also you, whenever Esau persecutes you—that is, any false brother of whom Esau was an example—or whenever your flesh persecutes your spirit, return to the Lord your God and pray to him. And so that you may deserve to be heard, be strong in earnest prayer, as he was directed with the angel in his strength; be persistently strong, as he was when he said: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

He kept mercy and judgment, namely by walking in the ways of the Lord. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and judgment” (Ps. 24) [Col. 0183A], or mercy and truth. Consequently, and rightly, he always hoped in the Lord his God: that is, amid all the adversities which he suffered in great number, he was not disappointed in his hope. For the Lord delivered him from the hand of Esau, whom he feared; and at last, after the many days of his sojourn, after one hundred and thirty years of life, having again seen the face of his son Joseph, he consoled himself, saying that he would now die gladly (Gen. 45).

Such is the judgment with Judah and this visitation upon Jacob: whoever lives according to these examples of that father is alone to be called and to be a Jew, Jacob, and indeed truly Israel. What, then, of one who is contrary in faith or merits to that same father, yet glories only in the flesh of Jacob or in merely carnal Judaism? Hear what follows: “Canaan is in his hand, a deceitful balance; he loved oppression” [Col. 0183B].

A remarkable and merited placement—or rather opposition—of names and titles according to each person’s merits: to the one who, according to the example of the father already mentioned, is directed with the angel in his strength and prevails over the angel, it is rightly said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?” (Gen. 32). But to the one who does not act similarly, and indeed envies one who does so act, it is said according to the sense of this prophetic utterance: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Canaan.” The same God confirms this in another prophet when he says: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). For the Amorite and the Hittite were descendants of Canaan [Col. 0183C].

For this reason especially, anyone called a Jew or Israelite according to the flesh, but who degenerates in conduct from so great a father, deserves to be called Canaan: namely, because of the malicious duplicity of earthly greed, aptly expressed in these words: “A deceitful balance is in his hand; he loved oppression.” This is contrary to what Scripture says concerning that father: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. 25). Simplicity raised him so that he deserved to be called Israel; deceitfulness cast down his children according to the flesh so that they are called Canaan.

If, by holding a deceitful balance in their hand contrary to the justice of God’s law, which says, “You shall have a fair measure and a just sextary” (Lev. 19) [Col. 0183D], they deserve to be called Canaan, how much more ought they to be called not Jews but Canaanites because, plotting to seize and kill Jesus (Matt. 26), they accomplished this with a balance, weighing out thirty silver pieces, the price of his blood? Surely the prophetic word truly says of the Jews of that time: “Canaan loved oppression,” because with greater diligence and urgency they oppressed Christ the King, the true David, to crucify him, than that Ephraim of old, of whom this prophet immediately says, separated itself from the house of David.

“And Ephraim said: ‘Yet I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself. All my labors shall not find in me the iniquity which I have sinned’” [Col. 0184A]. By adding, “And Ephraim said,” he expresses more plainly whom he designated by the name Canaan in the preceding verse. For he who by birth was Ephraim and, because of his separation from the house of David, not merely an Ephraim but a notable Ephraim, deserved rightly to be called Canaan through holding a deceitful balance in his hand and finding an idol for himself.

See how remarkable is the consolation of folly. Although this Canaan had a deceitful balance in his hand, and a conscience accusing him of sin which he could nowhere escape, he consoled himself and said: “Yet I have become rich.” “However or wherever I may have acquired wealth,” he says, “whether the balance in my hand was just or deceitful, I have become rich; I have attained what I sought; I have found an idol for myself.” Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim might have said this, since he was able to compel the worship of a calf in place of God [Col. 0184B].

But the Jews of that time, principally contemplated by the prophet—that is, when the true David came to reign—when they had heard him dispute against their greed, and especially the scribes and Pharisees, rejoiced when they crucified him, as though, once he had been killed, they would henceforth be free to serve their idol, namely Mammon, that is, to attend to their profits. Thus, although such a Canaan or Ephraim was tortured by a cruel conscience, he consoled himself, saying: “Yet I have become rich.”

By contrast, he said: “Yet woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6) [Col. 0184C]. The Apostle James likewise says against those same rich persons: “Come now, you rich; weep, howling at the miseries which shall come upon you” (Jas. 5).

But that rich Canaan—that is, the Jewish or Pharisaic assembly—said to itself, as this prophet sets forth: “All my labors shall not find my iniquity which I have sinned.” The sense is: none of my sins could be punished, nor can the iniquity which I committed be punished by the destruction of the city and temple. Could he believe or hear that that place, so profitable, would be destroyed because of the blood of Jesus Christ? Indeed, it was charged as a crime against Stephen, the first martyr, that he preached thus, as Scripture relates: “They set up false witnesses, who said: ‘This man does not cease to speak words against the holy place and the law. For we heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place’” (Acts 6) [Col. 0184D].

“Come now, you rich,” says the Apostle already mentioned, “weep, howling at the miseries which shall come upon you. Your riches are rotten, and your garments are eaten by moths” (Jas. 5). And shortly afterward he says: “You have feasted on earth and nourished your hearts in luxury. On the day of slaughter you have led forth, killed, and he did not resist you” (ibid.). Therefore this man who held a deceitful balance and loved oppression vainly consoled himself by saying, “Yet I have become rich,” for neither will his riches profit him nor will he lack the inheritance of the name Canaan, wickedly exchanged.

It follows: “And I, the Lord your God from the land of Egypt, will still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast” [Col. 0185A]. This is connected with what was said above. For he does not promise this favor to that Canaan whose hand holds a deceitful balance, or to Ephraim who found an idol for himself and gloried in having become rich; rather, he promises it to the one to whom he had said: “And you shall return to the Lord your God; keep mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always.”

This is the person who, when judgment was held with Judah and visitation made upon Jacob, was found to be truly a Jew and a true Israelite, imitating him who supplanted his brother in the womb and was directed with the angel in his strength, as has already been said. Therefore what he said, “Hope in your God always,” is joined to what he says: “And I, the Lord your God from the land of Egypt”—that is, from the time when, having come out of the darkness of ignorance, you offered me the true sacrifice of faith [Col. 0185B].

The tents which he promises in saying, “I will still make you dwell in tents,” are those of which the Psalmist says: “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts!” adding, “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83). For the tents—that is, the shelters of those who are pilgrims or labor in adversity—are the distinct orders of those serving God in the Church. When the soul is placed among them, it longs and fails for the courts of the Lord, desiring to migrate from these confinements into the breadth of the heavenly Jerusalem, where the expanse is so great that one person’s possession cannot be constrained by another’s possession, and what each possesses is sufficient to each, so that no one desires more.

The order of the statements must therefore be observed. Having said, “I, the Lord your God from the land of Egypt,” he adds, “I will still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast” [Col. 0185C]. It is well known that the children of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt, lived in tents. Therefore they celebrated each year the very famous feast of Tabernacles, *cenophegia* (Exod. 23). The sense, then, is this: long ago I made your fathers, ascending from the land of Egypt, dwell in tents until I brought them into the land of promise. But just as there is another Egypt than that which Egypt signified, and another promised land of which that land bore a type, so there are still other tents of which those tents were signs; and I will make you dwell in them “as in the days of the feast,” that is, as was signified by those feasts of Tabernacles, because “all these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10) [Col. 0185D].

And indeed whoever has come out from spiritual Egypt by believing in Christ sits in other, that is, spiritual tents, and says while seated: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord.” Having said these things, he immediately adds: “And I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied vision, and in the hand of the prophets I was made like.”

This is connected as follows with the preceding sense. “I,” he says, “the Lord your God from the land of Egypt, have made myself known from that time onward by such deeds and words that no one can excuse himself on grounds of ignorance of my name. For, in order to make myself known, I multiplied vision from the time when I appeared to Moses from the midst of the bush in a flame of fire, and he said: ‘I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not burned’” (Exod. 3) [Col. 0186A].

Then I spoke through that prophet and through other prophets, and multiplied vision: that is, I appeared in many ways to be seen and known by the prophets; and in the hand of the prophets I was made like, namely by performing many deeds that bore certain likenesses of myself. For example: hostile Egypt and Pharaoh were indeed scourged by the ten plagues in the hand of Moses, but victory could not be brought to completion except through the blood of the slain lamb.

There, surely, I was made like in the hand of Moses. For what was then represented or prefigured was this: by the ten legal commandments of righteousness, holy people who observed them before my coming would indeed harass the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil, by resisting, opposing him, and striving to leave the kingdom of death; yet they would not prevail [Col. 0186B]. For the law was to bring nothing to perfection, as the Apostle says (Heb. 7), until at last I entered the world to be sacrificed and to become the sacrifice of righteousness, the true Lamb of God, who alone by my blood would accomplish what could not be accomplished by human righteousness, however vigorously people might fulfill the commandments of the law.

By many such deeds and many likenesses I was made like in the hand of Moses and of the prophets. The tribe of Judah especially, in whose possession were the temple and the cult of religion or priesthood, could not be excused through ignorance of such things, since they were written. It follows, therefore: “If Gilead is an idol, yet those sacrificing calves in Gilgal were in vain.”

The sense is: if the ten tribes worship idols, being without the temple of God, priests, and the religion of God, yet you, O Judah, have vainly forsaken God and worship idols in Gilgal, though you possess the temple, priesthood, and all else belonging to the rite of divine worship [Col. 0186C]. Gilead is both a mountain and a city situated near that same mountain beyond the Jordan in the tribe of Gad; concerning it we previously read: “Gilead, city of those working an idol, supplanted by blood.” Gilgal, however, is in the tribe of Judah near Bethel, concerning which it was said above: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal.” Thus the ten tribes are rightly indicated by Gilead, and the tribe of Judah by Gilgal, according to the trope called synecdoche, that is, “comprehension,” when the whole is understood from a part or the part from a whole.

It may also be understood otherwise: even if Gilead is an idol, or although the Gileadites abound in idols, nevertheless there was remarkable madness of superstition at Gilgal [Col. 0186D]. They were not content to venerate fixed monstrosities in one place, but continually ran from place to place and visited various sites of idols, as though invited to splendid festivals. For he immediately adds: “For their altars are like heaps upon the furrows of a field.” That is to say: whereas they ought to have offered sacrifices or firstfruits in one place, namely Jerusalem, to the one God, they so multiplied altars, as has already been said above, and so abounded in images, and so many altars stood in the villages, that they were like heaps of gathered sheaves.

Is this the inherited faith of the fathers, that, when the Lord has held judgment with Judah and visitation upon Jacob, the sons of Judah or sons of Jacob should deserve to be called by those names? Certainly not. For it follows: “Jacob fled to the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he served. But through a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved” [Col. 0187A].

This consideration has no small bearing upon that judgment, or operation of the Lord upon Jacob, in distinguishing who is truly and who falsely called the seed of Jacob. Why did he flee to the region of Syria and serve for a wife? Clearly, lest he should ever be brought by the women of Canaan to such altars. For Rebekah said to Isaac: “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the stock of this land, I do not wish to live” (Gen. 27). Therefore Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and gave him this command: “Do not take a wife from the land of Canaan; but go, travel to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, the father of your mother, and take for yourself from there a wife from the daughters of your uncle Laban” (Gen. 28) [Col. 0187B].

Thus he fled the women of that land, who could be a stumbling block and cause of sin to him; and Moses wrote that his example ought to be followed for the same reason: “You shall not make a covenant with them, nor spare them, nor contract marriages with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son; for she will seduce your son so that he does not follow me, and serves foreign gods more; then the wrath of the Lord will be angry and swiftly destroy you” (Deut. 7).

But these men, on the contrary, ran from Gilead to Gilgal and from Gilgal to Gilead, seeking and pursuing idols from which Jacob fled by passing from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people [Col. 0187C]. Therefore they falsely call themselves his sons, since they are rather Canaan, as was said above, whose works they followed.

It is indeed a great commendation of the fugitive that it is said, “and he served for a wife.” He preferred to obtain a wife according to the good pleasure of God, father, and mother by his own servitude, rather than to take daughters of Canaan to the offense of his parents, as Esau did. Of Esau it is written: “Esau, when forty years old, took wives: Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon of the same place; and both offended the mind of Isaac and Rebekah” (Gen. 26). That wife for whom he served was Rachel. He did not serve or make the agreement for Leah, but for Rachel alone, whom he loved and asked from her father [Col. 0187D].

He repeats this, saying, “and he served for a wife, and for a wife he served,” because twice he underwent seven years’ service for one and the same Rachel. He served seven years before taking a wife; he was cheated of the marriage due to him; but when he had made his complaint, immediately after union with Leah, whom he had not sought, he again served another seven years for the desired marriage with Rachel.

Observe that the name is so suddenly changed: “Jacob fled to the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife.” When he fled he was called Jacob, but when he served he deserved to be called Israel, his merits having increased, as the narrative of his return from servitude relates. To this same distinction between so great a father and those who, though children of his flesh, nevertheless do not deserve to be reckoned as his seed, belongs what is immediately added: “But through a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved” [Col. 0188A].

For the contrary must be understood: “But these have by no means gone out of Egypt in mind; rather, they themselves are Egypt, making and worshiping for themselves gods—namely Egyptian calves, whose worship they learned in the land of Egypt.” Therefore God immediately complains in his own person, saying:

## Chapter XIII.

Ephraim provoked me to anger by his bitter offences, and his blood shall come upon him. And immediately the prophet continues: “And the Lord his God will repay his reproach.” “When Ephraim spoke, terror seized Israel; and he sinned in Baal, and died.” And now they have added to sin: they made for themselves a molten image from their silver, in the likeness of idols. It is wholly the work of craftsmen. Of these they say: ‘Sacrifice human beings, you who worship calves.’”

All that has here been said, in the prophet’s vehement denunciation, strongly proves—while justifying the Lord’s judgment and visitation upon Jacob—that they neither are nor deserve to be called Israel, such as the Lord truly brought out of Egypt through the prophet. For they were others, far different—indeed contrary—to the true and faithful Israel whom the Lord brought out of Egypt through the prophet Moses, speaking with a true heart: “Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exod. 5). They were those who, by their bitter offences, provoked that same Lord to anger, testing him, speaking wickedly of him, and always murmuring against him.

That Israel, such as Joshua or Caleb, was preserved in that same prophet, crossing through the Red Sea; but the bodies of those others were laid low in the wilderness. The worst and most conspicuous of them all was Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim—who, by dividing the people from the house of David, established golden calves to be worshipped as God. Therefore the discourse immediately returns to him, the Lord saying: “Ephraim provoked me to anger by his bitter offences, and his blood”—that is, his sin—“shall come upon him”: namely, that he may perish and lose the kingdom in his descendants, which he thought he would maintain in such a manner.

And because a present punishment alone is not rendered to the impenitent, the prophet adds:

> “And his reproach,” he says, “the Lord his God will repay to him.”

That is, even in the age to come the memory of so great a reproach will not be blotted out: he cast himself down so far as to forsake God the Creator and worship, not so much a calf as an inanimate and senseless likeness of a calf. Nor will the destruction of himself alone, but also of all whom he led into so great a reproach, recoil upon him.

Therefore, further denouncing his sin: “When Ephraim spoke,” he says, “terror seized Israel; and he sinned through Baal, and died.” The meaning is this. When Jeroboam said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12), a dreadful and delusive terror seized Israel, so that it either believed the statement true or did not dare to contradict it; and it worshipped not only those calves, but also Baal, through the agency of Ahab and Jezebel, and thus died.

From that time the practice of idolatry grew so greatly that almost everywhere individuals made idols for themselves according to their means, in their fields and houses. This is what he says: “And now they have added to sin: they made for themselves a molten image from their silver, in the likeness of idols”—namely, that they too might have their own calves. For since the king had gods of gold, they made themselves gods of silver according to their ability. “All this,” he says, “is the work of craftsmen,” as it is written elsewhere: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands” (Ps. 113 [114–115]).

Since this is so, he rightly marvels and says: “Of these they say: ‘Sacrifice human beings, you who worship calves.’” For it is truly astonishing and utterly wretched folly to command that human beings, who are God’s work, be sacrificed to such works of craftsmen. This immense evil was by no means unfamiliar to them. For it is written: “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan” (Ps. 105 [106]).

But who are those who say these things? Undoubtedly the priests or the craftsmen whose work this is. “You,” they say, “worshippers of idols, who lack sacrificial victims: sacrifice to these same calves your sons and daughters, worshipping the idols or calves with us.” Having given such and so many reasons by which, in the Lord’s judgment upon Judah or visitation upon Jacob, they may be convicted of deserving to be called rather the seed of Canaan than the seed of Jacob, it now remains to pronounce the fitting sentences of judgment and to determine what punishment these false sons, and what grace the true sons of that father Jacob—whose God is said, or is to be called, Lord—rightly receive.

It follows:

> “Therefore they shall be like a morning cloud, and like the dew that passes away in the morning; like dust snatched from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney. But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no saviour apart from me. I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude.”

The former sentence is pronounced upon those sons of Jacob according to the flesh and not faith: their memory shall perish. The following words concern these sons not only of the flesh but also of faith: at the advent of Christ the Saviour, they are to be saved in the Lord with eternal salvation.

In the sentence concerning those who are rejected, these four things are used as comparisons: cloud, dew, dust, and smoke. It should be noted that none of them is given without a qualifying addition signifying evil; for each, when used simply, is commonly taken in a good sense. For it is written: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60). Again: “May my teaching condense as rain, my speech flow as dew” (Deut. 32). Or, as Abraham says to God: “I will speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). And the Psalmist says: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. 103 [104]).

Thus all these four, when stated simply in Scripture, may be understood in a good sense. Therefore each is here used with appropriate qualifications distinguishing them from the signification of everlasting good: a morning cloud; likewise morning dew passing away in the morning; dust snatched from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind; and likewise smoke snatched from a chimney by a whirlwind. Thus all these appropriately signify the perishing memory of those who, though they ought to have been the seed of Jacob, through their own fault degenerated into that Canaan whom the holy father cursed.

Although these four together signify that their memory is to be blotted out, they differ in their proper meanings. The last two—dust snatched from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind and smoke from a chimney—express manifest wrath; but the preceding two, a morning cloud and morning dew passing away, express a certain mercy, though temporary and soon passing, according to what was said above in this same prophet: “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning.”

Accordingly, both here and there the morning cloud and the passing morning dew signify the temporal blessings bestowed upon that nation: good in themselves, but soon to pass away because of the people’s evil. The following two plainly signify eternal evils, as has already been said. For the wicked perish in retribution as dust carried off from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind and as smoke vanishes when swept from a chimney by a whirlwind; as the Psalmist also says: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1). Again: “But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, shall vanish; they shall vanish like smoke” (Ps. 36 [37]).

Thus that morning cloud or passing morning dew is the portion of such sons as Esau, to whom his father Isaac said: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be” (Gen. 27). But the portion of those who are the seed of Jacob, or are reckoned in the seed, and are Israelites, is the Lord, as the immediately following words declare:

> “But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no saviour apart from me. Behold, I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude.”

For the Lord God who speaks these words, saying, “There is no saviour apart from me,” is Christ, the Son of God: the fruit of that blessing which Esau did not deserve but Jacob obtained, according to these words: “Let peoples serve you and tribes worship you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down before you. Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings” (ibid.).

This, undoubtedly, was being accomplished in the Holy Spirit: when Jacob and Esau were to be divided, according to the divine oracle, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb” (Gen. 25), the seed of Abraham—which is Christ—was to be born not from Esau but from Jacob.

Therefore, when he says, “But I am the Lord your God,” it should be noted that he adds, “from the land of Egypt.” In this he briefly establishes that he is not a recent God, although in the last days he was born of the Virgin. He could have said, “But I am the Lord your God from Abraham,” just as, when the Jews said, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”, he answered: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8).

Why, then, did he prefer to say, “from the land of Egypt”? Clearly because he became better known then and showed his power in signs and wonders such as he had not shown to Abraham. Hence at that time he said to Moses: “I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 6). For then he made a covenant with them on Mount Sinai, that he might be their God. They said to Moses: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do and obey.” But he sprinkled the blood he had taken upon the people and said: “This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words” (Exod. 24).

The beginning of those words was: “You shall have no strange gods before me.” Therefore he rightly says here too: “You shall know no God besides me.” And immediately he adds: “And there is no saviour apart from me.” This God and Saviour, Christ, is God because he created; Saviour because, having become human, he saved. Hence he willed to be called Jesus, which is interpreted “Saviour” [or “Salvation”]. Truly, apart from him there is no saviour, “for there is salvation in no one else, nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

It is a most gracious remembrance when he finally says: “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude.” For it is no small matter for one who knows all things and knows all through knowledge, to be known by grace with that knowledge according to which he says to one of them, the true Israelite Moses: “You have found grace before me, and I have known you by name” (Exod. 33). We read that this was then spoken to him; but what he says to one he says to all whom he chooses, foreknown and predestined at that time, indeed before and after that time, because he has written the names of all in the book of life.

Accordingly, this too should be understood: the elect are known in the wilderness, especially in the land of solitude—in the wilderness of this age, where no one has ever seen God (1 John 4), in the solitude of the heart and the hidden place of the concealed conscience. There God alone, looking upon the soul surrounded by temptations, exercises it, tests it, and, judging one who runs lawfully worthy of his knowledge, declares that he knows it. To such persons, thus known or named, he himself says in the Gospel: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

## Book Six

[Col. 0191]

[Col. 0191C] For the sixth time now, the Lord sets forth the sins of this same nation and turns to the hearer, saying:

> “According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied. And they lifted up their heart and forgot me.”

This saying commends the goodness of God who does good, but nevertheless most vehemently condemns the ingratitude of those to whom good was done. It is like what the Psalmist says of the same people: “They ate and were exceedingly satisfied, and he brought them their desire; they were not disappointed in their desires” (Ps. 77 [78]). And immediately afterward: “In all these things they still sinned” (ibid.), and, “My enemies shall not turn back” (Ps. 55 [56]).

Let us now consider the particular force of the words. “According to their pastures,” he says, “they were filled.” By this qualification—“they were filled and satisfied according to their pastures”—he indicates a manner of filling and satisfaction that is not good or praiseworthy. What, or of what kind, were their pastures? Certainly the things they desired, on account of which they murmured and spoke wickedly of God (Ps. 77 [78]). For example, when they said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt for nothing. Cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to mind. Our soul is parched; our eyes look upon nothing but manna” (Num. 11).

Because they desired such things in such a manner and, in their desire, were filled with them even to nausea, these are rightly called their pastures. For they followed God not for his own sake but for the sake of these things. On the other hand, those who follow God for his own sake do not call such things their pastures; rather, the word of God is their food or pasture, according to that saying in Deuteronomy: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8).

Therefore, when he says, “According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied,” he rebukes them sharply. It is as though he said: “By eating and drinking they received their whole reward for having come out of the land of Egypt and for having accepted the law of God for a time.” It is altogether a fault to follow God for the sake of such pastures. Accordingly, rebuking such people in the Gospel, he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Work not for food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6).

Likewise, all who stand at Christ’s altar should regard themselves as rebuked if they do so not for love of the sacraments they jointly celebrate, but solely in order to live from the altar’s revenues. Therefore, the words, “According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied,” are like what the Psalmist says, as we have already noted: “The Lord brought them their desire” (Ps. 77 [78]). Such fullness of belly undoubtedly produces exaltation of mind; such satisfaction produces forgetfulness of God.

It is well known and evident that this happened to them. Hence he immediately says: “And they lifted up their heart and forgot me.” For those who received the best land as a possession, and who were filled by its fruits and became rich, were lifted up in pride. They asked for a king, refusing to hear the voice of the Lord and Samuel, and saying: “Not so! Rather, a king shall be over us, and we also shall be like all the nations, and our king shall judge us” (1 Kings 8 [1 Samuel 8]).

With the same exaltation of mind they rejected the house of David and made Jeroboam their king; he made calves for them in place of God. This was indeed a great forgetfulness of God (3 Kings 12 [1 Kings 12]). Therefore he now says: “And they forgot me.” Yet it must be understood: they were not permitted, nor will they be permitted, wholly to forget. For it follows:

> “And I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians. I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs; I will tear open the inward parts of their liver, and consume them there like a lion; the beast of the field shall tear them.”

The meaning is this: I shall hand them over to four kingdoms, represented by the lioness, leopard, bear, and beast of the field, unnamed here, so that when they have been oppressed and torn apart they may, through the magnitude of their miseries, be compelled to remember me whom they forgot. For these four beasts signify the four kingdoms—Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman—as is especially made clear by Daniel’s vision, where he says: “I was looking in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were contending upon the great sea; and four great beasts, diverse from one another, came up from the sea. The first was like a lioness and had wings like an eagle’s. Another was like a bear. Another like a leopard. The fourth was terrible, marvellous, and exceedingly strong” (Dan. 7).

As Daniel did, so here he also left the fourth beast unnamed, saying: “The beast of the field shall tear them.” “I will therefore be to them like a lioness and like a leopard”—that is, I shall hand them over to the Babylonians and Macedonians—“on the way of the Assyrians”: that is, because they advanced proudly in opposition to me; for “Assyrians” is interpreted “those who direct.” “I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs.”

Those who wrote about the natures of beasts say that among all wild animals none is fiercer than a bear when she has lost her cubs or is in need of food. Therefore, since in Daniel the kingdom of the Persians and Medes is signified by a bear, the utter cruelty of Haman the Agagite is not unfittingly understood through the ferocity of such a bear. Indignant that Mordecai would neither worship him nor bend the knee to him, Haman “counted it as nothing to lay hands upon Mordecai alone”; for he had learned that Mordecai belonged to the Jewish nation, and he preferred to destroy all the Jewish people who were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus (Esther 3).

And because they were to suffer these evils under the kingdoms already mentioned because of their sins, he says: “And I will tear open the inward parts of their liver.” According to natural philosophers, the power of pleasure and desire resides in the liver. Thus, by the inward parts of the liver he briefly signifies every desire that gives birth to sin. These inward parts were, as it were, torn apart by beasts of this kind, because their sins were punished by the oppressing kingdoms.

And because, when they confessed their sins in tribulation, he was eventually to spare them, he adds: “And I will consume them there like a lion.” Natural philosophers report that a lion spares a human being who has fallen down. Therefore, “there”—that is, under those kingdoms—“I will consume them,” he says, not indiscriminately or without any distinction, but “like a lion”: for though my wrath will be terrible against them, I shall spare those who fall prostrate and confess their sins in tribulation.

What will happen at last? “The beast of the field shall tear them”: the fourth beast, terrible, as Daniel says, marvellous and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest beneath its feet, altogether unlike the other beasts (Dan. 7). How will it tear them? Certainly by cutting them off in a wretched destruction and carrying them captive among all nations.

He now turns to the people itself, which is thus to be torn apart, and says: “Your destruction, O Israel; only in me is your help.” It is as though he said: You yourself are the cause of your destruction; you stored up destruction for yourself by departing from me, who alone could and was accustomed to help you. Nowhere is help for you except with me, if you repent.

And to confirm by rebuke that help is truly in him alone, he adds:

> “Where is your king? Let him now save you in all your cities; and your judges, of whom you said: ‘Give me a king and a prince.’ I will give you a king in my fury, and take him away in my indignation.”

He sharply strikes at the people’s vain estimation, for they asked for a king when they had God as king. He asks this in order to arouse them to reflection and teach them that help is only in God. It is like that question: “Where are their gods in whom they had confidence, whose sacrifices’ fat they ate and whose libations’ wine they drank?” (Deut. 32). For, just as there, when no answer is forthcoming, he fittingly adds: “See that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me” (ibid.), so here, after saying, “Where is your king, and your judges, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and a prince’?”, he adds: “I will give you a king in my fury, and take him away in my indignation.”

This had happened in the first king, Saul, whom he gave to the people when it asked. Indeed, he gave that king in his fury, as his own words show when he says: “This shall be the right of the king who shall rule over you: he shall take your sons and place them in his chariots; he shall make for himself horsemen and runners before his chariots,” and the rest, which he concludes thus: “He shall tithe your flocks, and you shall be his slaves; and you shall cry out in that day because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, and the Lord shall not hear you in that day, because you asked for yourselves a king” (1 Kings 8 [1 Samuel 8]).

Given in his fury, he took him away in his indignation, saying to Samuel: “I regret that I have made Saul king” (1 Kings 15 [1 Samuel 15]). And soon afterward Scripture says: “But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him” (1 Kings 16 [1 Samuel 16]). The same must be understood of Jeroboam and the other kings of the ten tribes: because they desired it and separated themselves from the house of David, he gave them in his fury and took them away in his indignation—some in their lifetime, others by striking them down in their descendants.

David, however, was neither requested by the earlier people nor given by the Lord in his fury; rather, the Lord first chose him in mercy, gave him in grace, established and preserved him in highest condescension. Therefore, when he says, “Of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and a prince,’” it must be understood: and I answered you in hidden judgment, saying, “I will give you a king in my fury, and take him away in my indignation.”

It follows:

> “The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hidden. The pains of a woman in labour shall come upon him. He is an unwise son; for now he shall not stand in the breaking of the children.”

It has often already been said that Ephraim—that is, the kings of the ten tribes—followed together the way of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, so completely that, as Scripture testifies, none of them departed from his sins. Therefore, as though you were asking what cause there was for fury or indignation, he says: “The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up”: that is, the iniquity of those kings was not loosed and could not be loosed, because they were incorrigible and impenitent, and every one of them always defended his own wickedness.

This is what follows: “His sin is hidden.” He calls sin hidden where it is not exposed by any voice of confession, but is instead covered by the shield of a proud defence. There iniquity is bound so that it cannot be loosed or forgiven. In contrast, the holy man says: “I made my offence known to you; I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31 [32]). Such a man is a wise son; but of this one it is said: “He is an unwise son.”

For how can he be a wise son who has departed from the Father by whom he had been adopted, when God said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4)? At present he hides his sin before human beings; before God, though he cannot hide it, he defends it with an impenitent heart. But, he says, “the pains of a woman in labour shall come upon him.” For as a woman may conceal her conception for a time, but at last, in giving birth, reveals the hidden thing as the pains bear witness, so anyone of this kind may, somehow, dissemble and conceal his sin for a time; but in its due time all the hidden things of his heart will be made manifest with pain, according to the saying: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be known” (Matt. 10).

Then he will plainly see for himself that he is an unwise son. And how is it proved that he is an unwise son? He says: “For now he shall not stand in the breaking of the children.” The meaning is: those who are truly children possess breaking, and they stand in tribulation—that is, they repent, having a contrite and humbled heart. Indeed, to be so broken or crushed is truly to stand, as it is written of one of these children: “He said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him” (Ps. 105 [106]).

By “breach” he means an extreme and vehement humility, in which Moses stood so as to hold God, though God said: “Let me go” (Exod. 32). Those who stand in such contrition are wise children. For by breaking themselves in repentance they become wise children. But the one who, as has been said, bound up his iniquity with an impenitent heart may indeed be called a son while he boasts and says, “We have one Father, God” (John 8); but he is neither called nor is a wise son.

It remains, therefore, that just as he assigned due fury and indignation to those others, so conversely he should promise a fitting and gracious consolation to these children whose portion is contrition—that is, a contrite and humbled heart. Let us hear it set forth in a truly great and resonant declaration:

> “I will deliver them from the hand of death; I will redeem them from death. I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell.”

Christ, the Son of God, conqueror of death and author of life, speaks this in his own person with a great voice and the great authority of truth: “I will deliver them,” he says, “from the hand of death; I will redeem them from death.” Whom does “them” mean, if not the children whose hearts are engaged in a contrite pursuit of repentance? First in their catalogue is Abel, whose very name signifies the lament of repentance, for it is translated “mourning.” From him to the last elect person, all who repent and confess themselves sinners—for “all sinned in Adam” (Rom. 3)—receive this consolation: delivered from the hand of death and redeemed from death.

Nor is this gracious condescension of mercy set forth once and again without reason—“I will deliver them from the hand of death; I will redeem them from death”—but because of the twofold death in which we all died in Adam: one of the body, the other of the soul. Thus, from the hand of death—namely, that death by which Adam died on the day he transgressed the commandment, which is death of the soul—I will deliver them. From the death which God imposed in these words, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), which is death of the body, I will redeem them.

How will I deliver them? At what price will I redeem them? He says: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell.” Not with gold or silver, but by killing their death with my death. I shall die so that they may live, and I shall descend into hell. This is what he says, addressing death itself and hell itself: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell”—he who is the mighty conqueror of death and hell, the lord of life and death.

How death was, or could be, the death of death, he briefly indicates by saying: “I will be your bite, O hell.” The sense is: You will bite me in deception, as is suggested by what is said of you in Job: “With a hook he shall catch him in his eyes” (Job 40 [41]). Again: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” (ibid.). I, having become human, will be a hook to you, because as in a hook the softness of flesh is displayed while the sharp point of iron is concealed, so the weakness of humanity will invite you, enemy of the human race, to bite; but the inward strength of divinity will pierce you, so that you hang captive.

Because I shall become such a bite to you, I shall be the death of death: for the inward parts of death, your interior in hell, will not contain me when you have bitten life. Your belly will be torn open and you will send life forth again; death having died, all who are worthy of this life will escape alive. Christ bit hell in another way when he delivered one part—namely, his own elect—but left another part, namely the reprobate. For from what we bite we consume one part and leave another.

It follows:

> “Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he divides among brothers.”

When the prophet heard of the grace of the Deliverer and Redeemer, he saw also what he had cause to grieve over: namely, that in his flesh, from his nation or his Israelite brothers, there would be division. This is the very matter over which the Apostle groans almost inconsolably in these words: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh: Israelites, whose are the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9).

The division among brothers, over which the Apostle there groans with continual pain, the prophet here mourns in advance, saying: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes.” Who divided so among brothers except hell, whose bite the Deliverer and Redeemer said he would become? For the devil, designated by the name of hell, blinded the Jews and divided them from their brothers and from his apostles, so that they expelled them and the apostles had to preach rather to the foreign Gentiles.

“Therefore,” he says, “consolation is hidden from my eyes.” He does not say that consolation has perished, but that it is hidden: that is, it cannot quickly be found; I cannot easily be comforted. Yet it is found in that hope by which the Apostle also comforted himself when, having said, “Blindness has happened in part to Israel,” he added: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11).

To this meaning belongs what the prophet immediately adds here:

> “The Lord shall bring a burning wind rising from the wilderness, and it shall dry up his veins and lay waste his fountain; and he himself shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.”

Here he calls the Holy Spirit a “burning wind,” just as there, in the mystical sense, the wind signifies the grace that saved us in Christ’s baptism. When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, “the Lord removed it by a strong and burning wind blowing all night, and turned it into dry land” (Exod. 14). Therefore the Lord shall bring a burning wind—that is, the Holy Spirit burning intensely—when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in; and it shall dry up his veins, namely those of hell, and lay waste his fountain, by taking away all causes and abundance of unbelief, so that the remnant of Israel may be saved (Rom. 9).

Meanwhile, “he himself,” he says, “shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.” For he himself is that stronger one who came upon the strong man armed while he guarded his court, and distributed all his weapons. Every elect person is indeed a desirable vessel and a precious treasure. Since he leaves no one behind—whether Jew or otherwise—whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, it is rightly said in universal language: “He himself shall plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.”

This happens and does not cease to happen through the wind rising from the wilderness: namely, through the Holy Spirit proceeding from Christ’s humility, Christ who had been deserted by his own people; the burning wind, that is, drying by its heat the wantonness of the flesh and the humours of vices. Finally, this sixth repetition ends by returning to Christ, who is our righteousness; and the commemoration of sins and of that same righteousness begins thus for the seventh and last time:

## Chapter XIV
“Let Samaria perish, for she provoked her God to bitterness. Let her perish by the sword; let their little ones be dashed to pieces, and their pregnant women be ripped open.”

This beginning is unlike all the others, because those passages rehearse sins and set them before the eyes, whereas here, as though correction were despaired of, in the very first utterance he immediately brings forth a judgment—less a rehearsal of sins than a sentence avenging idolatry. “Let Samaria perish,” he says. Why? “For she provoked her God to bitterness.” This is a great and terrible [Col. 0198B] cause or accusation: for God is sweet by nature, and the cause by which He appears to have been provoked to bitterness cannot be slight. An unrepentant heart brought this about, and Samaria was guilty of this crime; among her kings not one at all departed from the sins of Jeroboam, who made Israel sin.

“Let her perish,” therefore, he says, because justice must be allowed its course; for an unrepentant heart obtains no pardon. Nor, indeed, must she be allowed to perish only in respect of the soul, but also in respect of the body. Therefore, when he had said, “Let Samaria perish,” he also granted bodily destruction, saying, “Let them perish by the sword,” and so forth.

Here the Synagogue is not excepted from the name or condemnation of Samaria—a Synagogue which surpassed Samaria’s sin, since it not only, like Samaria, tore [Col. 0198C] itself away from the house of David, but also, as has often already been said, crucified Christ, the son of David, the Son of God. And therefore it perished, because it provoked its God to bitterness, so greatly that, when He thirsted on the cross, it gave Him vinegar to drink (John 19), or, as another Evangelist writes, gave Him wine mixed with gall to drink (Matt. 27).

Accordingly, that she might perish, the Lord Himself granted it and foretold it with His own mouth. And because the principle of justice required that she perish, He indeed wept over her with human affection (Luke 19), and by weeping foretold it; but by the impassible power of His divinity He maintained over the very one whom He wept for a fixed and unchangeable sentence.

Having said that Samaria is to perish, he now says what Israel is to do: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, 85 for you have fallen through your iniquity.” He who speaks these things [Col. 0198D] at the end of the book is Christ Himself, the end of every consummation. Sent to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel (Matt. 10), He began His preaching thus: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4). In the same sense He says here: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God” (ibid.).

He immediately adds the reason why they must return, or why repentance must be undertaken: “for you have fallen through your iniquity.” When He says, “through your iniquity,” He briefly indicates that every sinner must cut off from himself the iniquity which he has committed, whatever it may be, so that he may by no means excuse or defend himself, as Adam did, in whom we all sinned and fell, both Gentiles and Jews. As [Col. 0199A] the Apostle says: “For we too were once children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2).

By joining actual sins to that original sin, Israel fell no less than any Gentile nation, as the prophetic discourse has hitherto demonstrated by so often recounting its sins. Therefore return, O Israel—you first; for conversion is necessary because you have fallen. Confess this very thing also: that you have fallen through your iniquity. For this confession is the beginning of confession.

Perhaps some will say, as those who were pierced in heart said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). To these, or to whatever similar things terrified and contrite persons may say, once they recognize their iniquity, He immediately comes to meet them and says: “Take words with you, and [Col. 0199B] return to the Lord, and say to Him: Take away all iniquity, receive what is good, and we will render the calves of our lips.”

“You who return to the Lord,” He says, “take words with you.” Why words rather than gifts? Clearly, so that you may know that there is no difficulty with God: He does not require from you things which perhaps you could not obtain for the redemption of your souls. I do not therefore say, Take gold with you, take silver with you, or a multitude of goats or calves, and other such things which are not available to everyone. Rather, take with you words, which you can obtain without loss of property—the words of confession and prayer. These can be ready at hand for you; and they suffice for God for your salvation and make satisfaction for your iniquities.

With these [Col. 0199C] resources return to the Lord God, who has no need of your goods. And, as I have already said, do not be troubled as though you lacked great gifts of precious gold and silver with which to honor the face of so great and mighty a Lord whom you would appease. Rather say to Him: “Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good.” Do not say, “We have no iniquity,” for then you lie and deceive yourselves (1 John 1). But say to Him: “Take away all iniquity,” because our iniquities are many.

Say confidently, “and receive what is good,” knowing what good He requires; and, knowing this, add: “and we will render calves—not of herds, but of our lips.” For You are sufficient; You are full. Therefore You have no need to eat the flesh [Col. 0199D] of bulls or drink the blood of goats, but only that calves of lips should be offered to You—that is, a sacrifice of praise. And this will please You better, because it is a testimony of good will.

Accordingly, after the Psalmist had said, “I will praise the name of God with a song, and magnify Him with praise” (Ps. 68), which is indeed to render calves of the lips, he immediately added: “And it will please God more than a young bullock bringing forth horns and hooves.” Meanwhile, care must be taken lest, after the calves of lips have been rendered—that is, after words of confession and praise—the works of iniquity be repeated.

Accordingly, it follows, and on this point He instructs them what they should say and promise, introducing words of this kind in their person: “Assyria will not save us; we will not mount horses; nor will we say any longer: [Col. 0200A] ‘The works of our hands are our gods,’ for You will have mercy upon the people that is in You.” For it must be understood: “And say this to Him also.”

And what is it to say to Him, “Assyria will not save us,” except as if they said: “We shall not, as we have done hitherto, put our trust in man, nor make flesh our arm”? For Israel often, as the sacred histories attest, trusted in princes and in the sons of men, and sought their help—above all that of the Assyrians, who were most powerful.
