Likewise, what is it to say to Him, “We will not mount horses,” except as if they said: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19)? Finally, Israel sinned in this too: it greatly desired to mount horses, wrongly emulating Pharaoh’s chariots and cavalry, although [Col. 0200B] the children of Israel departed Egypt on foot and were gloriously saved, while Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen perished, drowned in the sea. Therefore Scripture rebukes them elsewhere, saying: “Egypt is man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit” (Isa. 31).

For this reason the king of Israel, when He came blessed in the name of the Lord, did not mount a horse or a chariot, but the colt of an ass, the foal of a beast under the yoke—despising the pride of the world, which chiefly glories in chariots and horses.

As to the third thing they say, “Nor will we say any longer, ‘The works of our hands are our gods,’” it is known from when they began to say, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12), when they fashioned a calf at the very departure from Egypt, how from [Col. 0200C] that time onward they sinned in idols, as it is written: “They mingled among the nations, and learned their works; and they served their graven images” (Ps. 105).

Therefore promise amendment, he says, with respect to the three crimes on which all sins depend: one is trusting in the sons of men; another, glorying in a multitude of horses and chariots; the third, defiling oneself in the filth of idols. From these arise all the sins which Scripture, both historical and prophetic, recounts or rebukes as having been committed by the Israelite people no less than by other nations.

But with what confidence, with what awareness of power or ability, ought you to promise amendment for so many and such great crimes? Can you [Col. 0200D] trust that by your own strength you can shake off the yoke of whatever sin you have once given yourselves over to? Certainly not, because “it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. 9).

Therefore, when you have said, “Assyria will not save us; we will not mount horses; nor will we say any longer, ‘The works of our hands are our gods,’”—which is to promise a complete amendment of sins—say also to Him: “For You will have mercy upon the people that is in You.” The sense is: trusting in the assistance of Your mercy, we promise these things, because it is Yours, and it befits Your honor, to have mercy upon that people which is in You, which believes in You, and to stretch out Your hand, so that they may be able to abandon their customary evils and change their former way of life for the better.

Whoever you are who take these words with you, [Col. 0201A] whoever you are who render such calves of the lips, devoted to the labor of repentance, hear what He Himself, who invites you to repentance, has long ago declared as the counsel of your salvation:

“I will heal their wounds; I will love them freely, because My wrath has turned away from them. I will be like dew; Israel will blossom like a lily. Its root will burst forth like Lebanon. Its branches will spread abroad, and its glory will be like the olive tree, and its fragrance like Lebanon. Those sitting in its shade will return; they will live by grain and blossom like a vine. Its memorial will be like the wine of Lebanon.”

Here the person of the Savior Himself speaks more plainly, promising His 86 coming for the salvation of penitents in a sweet-sounding promise, gracious in its sweetness. “I will heal,” He says, “their wounds”; that is, I will turn their sorrow into joy—those who are sorrowful unto repentance and have a contrite and humbled heart. Such wounds are worthy of healing; such woundedness deserves to have the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter.

Not because of gifts which they first gave Me. “For who has first given to Me, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11). Rather, I will heal them freely; I will cure them by a gratuitous remission of sins. This is what He means when He says, “I will love them freely.” Of My own accord I shall come, and, having become man, of My own accord I shall undertake the office of healing.

“For My wrath has turned away from them,” He says, according to what is written elsewhere on this same matter: “You have blessed Your land, O Lord; You have turned away Jacob’s captivity. You have forgiven the iniquity of Your people; You have covered all their sins. You have softened all [Col. 0201D] Your anger; You have turned away from the wrath of Your indignation” (Ps. 89). For God had been angry with the human race in Adam, and we all bore that wrath. Hence He says elsewhere: “For we have failed in Your anger, and in Your fury we have been troubled” (Ps. 84).

That wrath of Mine has turned away from them in the fullness of time, when what had been foretold was fulfilled: “You have blessed Your land, O Lord”—namely, so that I, the new Adam, might be born from the holy Virgin. For with this same blessing in view He says, “I will be like dew; Israel will blossom like a lily.” For He was like dew when, overshadowing the Virgin through the grace of the Holy Spirit, He descended into her womb.

Then Israel truly blossomed like a lily, because the true Israelites—the apostles, that is—[Col. 0201D] bore fruit not in the flesh but in the spirit, imitating by a new way of life the lily, that is, their master and teacher Christ, the son of virginal beauty. In that beauty strength will likewise be present, so that they may be most steadfast in faith. Therefore He immediately says: “Its root will burst forth like Lebanon.”

Lebanon is a mountain whose most excellent trees, as high as they stretch their crowns into the winds, sink their roots as deep into the lower regions, so that they stand with stable mass and are shaken by no storm. Moreover, by its name Lebanon signifies the same beauty of purity as the lily, for it is interpreted “whiteness.” Therefore, “Its root will burst forth like Lebanon”: that is, the apostles and the other preachers will arise from the root of Israel, which is Christ, such that they will be strong in faith [Col. 0202A] and pure in life.

“Its branches will spread abroad”: that is, His hearers will advance from strength to strength. “Its glory will be like the olive tree”: that is, He will speak peace to the nations, as is written elsewhere (Zech. 9). For the olive signifies peace and, even among the Gentiles amid the madness of wars, has customarily been an emblem of peace. Therefore, “Its glory will be like the olive tree,” He says: that is, He will proclaim peace and establish peace between God and men, as He also wished this to be signified when, coming to His Passion, through which He reconciled us to God, He was received by the crowds with branches of palm and olive.

“And its fragrance [will be] like Lebanon”: that is, it will have a good reputation everywhere, as the Apostle says: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2). This fragrance, this glory of peace and mercy, will invite the nations [Col. 0202B] to believe.

It follows, therefore: “Those sitting in its shade will return.” “They will return sitting,” that is, having been converted, they will sit in its shade, and for that very reason, because they will be sitting, they will be protected beneath its shade. For sitting signifies humility, according to the Psalmist’s saying: after he had said, “It is vain for you to rise before dawn,” he immediately added, “Rise after you have sat down” (Ps. 126): that is, only then hope to be exalted, after you have humbled yourselves.

To those who sit in this manner life-giving nourishment is supplied from heaven, and they always progress from good to better. Accordingly He immediately says: “They will live by grain, and blossom like a vine.” The grain by which the inner person lives is the word of God, whose understanding is customarily given not to those who stand erect, but to those who sit—that is, not to the proud but to the humble.

Certainly, the vine after whose likeness they are said to blossom must be distinguished from the evil vine. For there is an evil vine, of which it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah” (Deut. 32).

He says: “Its memorial will be like the wine of Lebanon.” For this vine is very greatly distinguished, by the very words, “Its memorial will be like the wine of Lebanon,” from that vine of Sodom, whose grape is called—and is—a grape of gall, and whose cluster is called—and is—most bitter. Finally, serpents are said to flee the wine of Lebanon—or rather Lebanon itself—especially because of the scent of cedar, which they cannot bear. But there it was said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” [Col. 0202D] (ibid.).

Yet the wine of Lebanon may be called mixed wine, seasoned with various spices so as to have a most pleasing fragrance; among these spices frankincense is especially fragrant. For among Greeks and Hebrews *Libanus* means both a mountain and frankincense.

It follows: “Ephraim, what have idols any longer to do with Me? I will hear him and direct him; I will be to him like a green fir tree; from Me his fruit is found.”

At the end He strikes down the adversary triumphantly, foreseeing in God’s grace the completed victory according to His purpose. For this Ephraim is every adversary of truth, whoever anywhere has placed, or does not cease to place, a scandal or stumbling block before souls, so that they may not attain the knowledge of truth—following the example of that Ephraim, namely Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim, who [Col. 0203A] made golden calves, intending thereby that the children of Israel, by frequently going up to Jerusalem to pray, should not someday return to the house of David.

At that time he indeed prevailed according to his intention and held the people fast in the sin of idolatry. But when I have become, in the manner described above, like dew, and Israel has blossomed like a lily, what then, O Ephraim, can idols do to Me any longer? Will they be able to show themselves to Me in the path of Gospel preaching? Will the images or lying fabrications of yours be able to turn away spiritual Israel, coming from East and West to the faith of the Gospel in order to believe in Me, the son of David, just as golden calves turned away carnal Israel, lest it go up to Jerusalem and return to David its king? No.

But what then? “I will hear him and [Col. 0203B] direct him; I will direct him like a green fir tree.” That spiritual Israel will ascend the straight way into the heavenly Jerusalem, after the likeness of the green fir tree, whose upright stature reaches upward, so that it may come to its king David—to Me, its God and Savior, the son of David. As it strives toward Him, I will hear and direct it; and this is its fruit, namely that it arrives where it strives to go: this fruit is found from Me, because without Me it can do nothing (John 15). Confessing this, it is very unlike carnal Israel, which, seeking to establish its own righteousness, is not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10).

“Who is wise, and understands these things? Who is discerning, and will know them?” From the beginning of the book we have always had this verse before our eyes, and therefore have always recognized that we could say nothing worthy concerning [Col. 0203C] this Scripture, reverencing it as a casket closed upon a truly heavenly treasure—nor could anyone else, whoever he may be, unless the Holy and True One who has the key of David should deign to open it for him: He who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3).

For if He who wrote it confesses that it is either difficult or impossible 87 to understand and know these things, what can we do, whose eyes are bleared and darkened by the filth of sins, unable to gaze upon the brilliant radiance of the sun? Nevertheless, whatever those things may be which still lie hidden from us as closed, and however slight those things may be which we have been able to understand or know from it, let us say with Him in conclusion what is true: “For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous shall walk in them; but transgressors shall fall in them.”

The ways of the Lord chiefly treated in this prophet are those judgments of the Lord that are truly incomprehensible (Rom. 11), by which He withdrew from the Jews and passed over to the Gentiles. In these ways the righteous walk. For example, the Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, although he suffers continual sorrow for these same brethren of his, nonetheless confesses that the ways of the Lord are straight and [Col. 0204B] says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways!” (ibid.).

But transgressors, especially the Jews, fall in these ways when they justify themselves and resist the truth, envying the salvation of the Gentiles. We have observed, indeed, especially from this prophet, as we have said in its proper place, that they are convicted of having sinned and needed the grace of God no less than the Gentiles—a point which the Apostle strongly affirms when writing to the Romans: “For you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2).

Finally, concerning this matter they are convicted seven times, as we have distinguished, in this prophet: namely, because he repeats that people’s sins seven times and on each occasion has recourse to the grace or coming of Christ, who alone justifies every human being, both Jew [Col. 0204C] and Gentile. Accordingly, what Moses invokes against the transgressing people when he says, “May the Lord give you over, falling before your enemies; by one way you shall go out against them, and by seven you shall flee” (Deut. 28), may also be fittingly and delightfully seen in this Scripture: the transgressing men already mentioned, justifying themselves, are convicted by a sevenfold repetition, and thus they fall seven times.

## RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE PROPHET JOEL

[Col. 0203]

88 “Those who work in me,” says Wisdom, “shall not sin; and those who elucidate me shall have eternal life” (Ecclus. 24).

The Wisdom that speaks these words is Christ, whom the Apostle also proclaims as “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1), and who elsewhere declares: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24). This Wisdom lies hidden especially in the prophets and therefore asks to be elucidated, promising a great reward to those who elucidate her—that is, eternal life.

In hope of so great a reward, we who are insignificant join our study to the studies of the holy Fathers, who labored exceedingly both in the prophetic writings and in the other sacred Scriptures. Their aim was that Christ, the Wisdom of God hidden in them, might be recognized, and that a clear exposition might strikingly reveal His face to readers—the face which the providence of the Holy Spirit willed to remain hidden from the unworthy beneath the thick veil of the letter.

This hope of eternal life is strengthened and gladdened by its first, preparatory reward, if what He promised us comes to pass: “Those who work in me shall not sin.” For, just as “idleness has taught much evil” (Ecclus. 33), so, conversely, good occupation and meditation upon the Scriptures often exclude wicked thoughts and grave sins which might otherwise enter.

Of almost everything that we venture to write, or have ventured to write thus far, this reply of ours can truthfully be made to everyone: let them by no means ascribe it to presumption or vain rashness that we, the last of men, undertake any work in the Scriptures of Wisdom after the great works of the holy Fathers. For we exercise ourselves in this way so that, according to His promises, we may not altogether continue in sin in the present life, and may possess eternal life in the future.

Therefore, seeking You with a single eye—that is, a faithful intention—and desiring to elucidate You, go before us by inspiring us and accompany us by helping us, O Wisdom of God, who promise so great a reward to those who work in You and elucidate You. After Hosea, grant that we may behold with unveiled face Joel, who follows him in the order of the twelve prophets.

# BOOK ONE OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET JOEL

[Col. 0205]

89 CHAPTER I

[Col. 0205A]

“The word of the Lord which came to Joel son of Phatuel.”

Concerning the expression used or written of the prophets, “The word of the Lord came,” we spoke at the beginning of the preceding prophet, Hosea, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers and the rule of the Catholic faith: it came to the prophets—that is, it acceded in time, or temporally—but with respect to God it was by no means made. For it is not a created thing, as the Arians prate; rather, in the beginning it was with Him.

This Word is Christ the Son of God, whom Joel son of Phatuel signifies by both his own name and his father’s name, no less than his predecessor Hosea son of Beeri. For Joel means “God,” while Phatuel is interpreted “the breadth of God.”

Moreover, concerning the Word of the Lord, Christ the Son of God, the faith has long ago prevailed by a long victorious contest and proclaims that He is God. And what is the breadth of God, except God’s love or charity? For after the Psalmist had said, “I have seen an end of every perfection” (Ps. 118), wishing charity to be understood—the charity of which the Apostle also says, “The end of the commandment is charity” (1 Tim. 1)—he immediately added: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

The same Apostle confirms by these words that Christ is the Son of this breadth of God: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love” (Col. 1). Thus both Joel’s own name and his father’s name indicate this: those to whom the word of God came are by grace gods and sons of God’s love, just as the only Son of Love Himself recalled that it was written, saying to the Jews: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said: You are gods, and all are sons of the Most High’?” (John 10).

The things which a prophet of so great a name is about to say must not be considered few or slight, though his discourse is brief, especially because he begins thus:

“Hear these things, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the earth. Has this happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation. What the caterpillar left, the locust consumed; what the locust left, the *bruchus* consumed; and what the *bruchus* left, the blight consumed. Awake, you drunkards, and weep; wail, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”

These words and all that follows are truly many and great; and the very manner in which they are uttered—indeed, forcefully dashed against our ears—is such that whoever is not awakened by these most terrifying cries must be considered not merely asleep but overwhelmed and buried in drunkenness.

For he foretells both the first and the second [Col. 0206A] coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the great and terrible day, earnestly intending that people should prepare themselves for His coming through repentance. This is the prophet’s chief purpose. For whatever other events he predicts as coming first or sooner, it was necessary that they both be brought about by God and announced beforehand through the prophets, so that, when they were quickly fulfilled, they might establish for mortals faith in the far greater events to come much later.

Accordingly, observe the prophet’s wonderful discernment—or rather, that of the Holy Spirit speaking through the prophet. Foreseeing that he would address a multitude not all of one disposition, he divides and distinguishes them in two ways at the beginning, where he seeks to make all his hearers attentive: “Hear these things, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the earth.”

Elders and inhabitants of the earth differ as heaven and earth differ in Isaiah’s words: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth” (Isa. 1). For the old age of such elders is so venerable that they are deservedly called heavens: elders, namely, on account of the grayness of their minds or the maturity of their understanding, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Venerable old age is not long-lived, nor is it counted by number of years; for the gray hair of man is understanding, and the age of old age is an unstained life” (Wis. 4). They are heavens because they can say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

By contrast, “inhabitants of the earth” here is said reproachfully of all those who bear hearts so earthly and think so earthly that they deserve to be called earth as well; such were those to whom it was said concerning the serpent: “You shall eat earth all your days” (Gen. 3).

All humankind is divided into these two parts, and each part finds or hears in this prophet something by which it may be awakened or frightened. For some have faith so gray with age, after the example of the elder Abraham their father, that they do not doubt that God cares about human actions; and, hearing the promise of Christ’s coming and the threats of the coming judgment, although they abound in temporal prosperity, they nevertheless believe and fear what is to come.

Others, very unlike these, have no regard for future good or evil, provided that they abound in present goods. Such people must be awakened by temporal adversities, so that at least affliction alone may give understanding to hearing.

Therefore, having demanded attention at the outset, so that all may have ears to hear, he immediately says: “Has this happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.” As if to say: No age remembers the things I am about to say; they did not happen in your time, nor in that of your fathers and ancestors.

What are these things? “What the caterpillar left,” he says, “the locust consumed; what the locust left, the *bruchus* consumed; and what the *bruchus* left, the blight consumed.” He first set before the inhabitants of the earth evils soon to come; afterward he would speak of Christ and the future judgment, and of what they ought to expect, so that they might not doubt the greater events that were to come from afar when this prophetic portion concerning lesser events had swiftly been fulfilled.

By the caterpillar we understand the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Chaldeans, who, proceeding from one region of the world, devastated everything belonging both to the ten tribes which Jeroboam separated from the house of David and to the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin. By the locust, the Medes and Persians, who, after overthrowing the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. By the *bruchus*, the Macedonians and all Alexander’s successors, especially King Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who sat in Judaea like a *bruchus* and devoured all the remnants left by the former kings; under him the wars of the Maccabees are narrated. By the blight, the Roman Empire, which as the fourth and last so oppressed the Jews that, driving them from their own borders, it led or sent them into captivity. Josephus writes more fully, in seven books, the astonishing and pitiable tragedy of this event, recounting the triumphs of Vespasian and Titus. These four kingdoms overthrew Judaea.

It is no wonder that these same kingdoms are here foretold under the names of such worms, whereas in Daniel they are signified by terrible beasts: a lioness, a bear, a leopard, [Col. 0207C] and another, unnamed, said to be marvelous and very strong, having great iron teeth (Dan. 7). For, against the weakness of human beings—especially of the Jews—those kingdoms indeed appeared like strong and ferocious beasts. Yet before the omnipotence of the Godhead they were judged weak and fragile, even small: like a locust, like a caterpillar, like a grub, and like mildew; and all their splendor was vain.

At least, “hear this with your ears, all inhabitants of the earth.” If I were now to tell you what, after a while, I shall tell the elders—concerning the coming of the Lord and his great and terrible day that is to come—and if no evil or adversity happened in your days, you would lie drowsing indulgently upon your beds; turning onto the other side, you would tell me that this would happen only after a long time [Col. 0207D] (Ezek. 12), and you would not put faith in my words.

The elders listen differently. They are not roused by afflictions, but for love alone they keep wakeful guard over God’s commandments. Abraham, old and of a good old age and full of days, as Scripture testifies, had not yet heard any trumpet concerning the judgment to come by fire; yet, solely for love of the Creator, obeying the command, he departed from his land and kindred (Gen. 12). Likewise, all other elders who, according to his example, served in a good old age have no need of present evils to awaken them; rather, they willingly believe beforehand whatever good God promises to the upright and whatever evil he threatens against the reprobate.

But you, inhabitants of the earth, because you do not listen willingly, must be girded about by the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew already mentioned, so that you may not sleep. “Wake up, drunkards, and weep; and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, for it has perished from your mouth.”

One should note in what sense he says, “you who drink wine,” adding, “in sweetness.” He does not condemn the creature wine, but the luxury of those who drink it: they draw it immoderately, not merely to meet necessity, but to excite pleasure because it is sweet. Yet what is possessed or drunk with sweetness is never lost without the bitterness of grief. Therefore, “because it has perished from your mouth, wake up,” he says, “you drunkards,” who, as another prophet says, “are mighty to drink wine and strong men at mixing [Col. 0208A] drunkenness” (Isa. 5).

“Wake up”: that is, allow yourselves to be taught by this evidence that God cares about human deeds, and that on his final day, great and terrible, as we have foretold to you, he will bring all things into judgment. For already he partly judges and partly punishes, while sweet wine perishes from your mouth. Thus awakened, then at last “weep and howl”: that is, repent, so that you may escape the evils to come—evils much greater than these.

How did the wine perish? He says: “For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and innumerable. Its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of lion cubs. It has made my vine a wilderness and stripped the bark from my fig tree. Stripping it bare, it plundered and cast it down; its branches have become white.”

Under the metaphor of locusts, the coming of enemies is described—here more especially that of the Assyrians and Babylonians, who then threatened. For he seems later to treat in sequence of the empire of the Medes and Persians, who were to come afterward, of the Macedonians, whom we know arose much later, and also of the Romans, who last of all destroyed everything; and by distinct proclamations he foretells the evils impending upon the Jews under each kingdom.

For just as he first set forth four things—the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew—signifying those four kingdoms, so he also cries out four evils, considering what was to happen under those same kingdoms. First he says: “Wake up, drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.” Then, second: “Mourn like a virgin girded with sackcloth [Col. 0208D] for the husband of your youth. Sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord,” and so forth. Then, third: “Gird yourselves and mourn, priests; howl, ministers of the altar; enter in, lie in sackcloth, ministers of God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God,” and so forth. Then, fourth: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the earth be troubled,” and so forth.

We judge that these four proclamations are made according to the oppression of the four kingdoms already mentioned, concerning which we must still speak more fully in sequence. For what follows next—“Now therefore says the Lord: ‘Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning’”—foretells and sounds forth the Gospel preaching of repentance, which began first at Jerusalem and was afterward preached among all nations.

Now let us return to the sequence. “For a nation,” he says, “was coming up upon my land, strong and innumerable.” How is it “strong,” when it is compared to caterpillars or locusts? Yet truly, as has already been said, the nation or kingdom of the Assyrians or Babylonians is rightly compared, in comparison with God’s strength, to tiny and sluggish worms; nevertheless, against the weakness of the Jews it is truthfully proclaimed a strong and innumerable nation.

Accordingly, in this same prophet the Lord calls the locust, the grub, the mildew, and the caterpillar his strength, in these words: “And I will restore to you the years which the locust, the grub, the mildew, and the caterpillar have eaten—my great strength, which I sent against you.” There is therefore in them a certain strength of God, but not that strength which cannot be made weak. It is a weak strength, yet sufficient against the weakness of man, who is unable to resist even a flea so as to be able to sleep.

Thus you may call not only the multitude of locusts or caterpillars, but also the very Chaldean army figured by them, strong and innumerable. For what is more innumerable or stronger than locusts, against which human skill cannot resist? Immediately, according to the metaphor begun from the multitude of locusts, he expresses the strength of this same nation: “Its teeth,” he says, “are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of lion cubs.” Since a locust customarily harms with a tiny tooth, he fittingly attributes not iron weapons but harmful teeth to the nation which he figured by a locust.

In a remarkable manner the locust’s teeth are here said to be “like the teeth of a lion.” So also in Revelation, “the appearances of the locusts are said to be like horses prepared for battle, and their teeth like lions’ teeth” (Rev. 9). How small the bodies; how great and powerful the teeth said to be in their mouths! Or rather, how weak and short-lived the human agents are, yet how great a power they are permitted to wield against a sinful people when God is angry.

The wickedness of the enemies is described under the figure of locusts; and then the locusts themselves are spoken of as though they were compared with enemies. When you read “locusts,” think of enemies; when you have thought of enemies, return to locusts. Therefore, “its teeth”—that is, the teeth of the nation of locusts, [Col. 0209D] all of which must be understood figuratively—are “like lions’ teeth, and its molars like those of lion cubs,” so that those equated with locusts in multitude and in the youthful leap of their brief life may be compared with lions in ferocity and cruelty.

This nation, he says, “has made my vine a wilderness”: namely, that vine concerning which the Psalmist says, “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it” (Ps. 77 [78]). “And it stripped the bark from my fig tree”: namely, the same Jewish people, to whom I eventually came that I might eat fruit from it; but I found none, cursed it, and it withered (Mark 11), because of the same persistent barrenness, on account of which it also happened that, long ago, a multitude of such locusts stripped that same fig tree of its bark.

“Stripping it bare,” he says, “it plundered [Col. 0210A] and cast it down; its branches became white.” Let us recognize that all this is said under the locust metaphor: they ravage everything so completely that they gnaw away the bark of trees, cast them down stripped bare, and, after consuming every trace of green, leave their branches white and dry. So it happened, and so wine perished from your mouth, O inhabitants of the earth, you who drink wine in sweetness: that you may awaken, you drunkards buried in long drunkenness; that is, that each of you may reflect and say, “What have I done?” and be strengthened for repentance, weeping, and howling.

It follows: “Mourn like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of your youth [variant: *her* youth]; sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord; the priests, ministers of the Lord, have mourned.”

After the kingdom of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, or Babylonians, the kingdom of the Medes and Persians held the Jews captive. Under that kingdom Nehemiah mourned and wept, as he himself relates among other things in these words: “For I,” he says, “was the king’s cupbearer. And it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, that wine was before him. And I lifted the wine and gave it to the king; and I was as one languishing before his face.”

When we read these words and what follows, we plainly see that they fit the time and event which this prophet proclaims: “Mourn,” he says, “like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of your youth.” For what reason? “Sacrifice and libation,” he says, “have perished from the house of the Lord; the priests, ministers of the Lord, have mourned.” Indeed, Nehemiah had previously stated this very cause of his grief, saying: “And Hanani, one of my brothers, came—he and men of Judah; and I asked them about the Jews who had remained and survived the captivity, and about Jerusalem. And they said to me: ‘Those who remain and have been left from the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach; the wall of Jerusalem has been destroyed, and its gates have been burned with fire.’ And when I heard words of this kind, I sat down and wept, and mourned for many days, and fasted and prayed before the face of the God of heaven.”

Rightly, therefore, both here and all who mourned for such a cause are commanded to be likened to a virgin mourning for the husband of her youth. For they mourned not like those mentioned above, because wine had perished from their mouths and they no longer drank it sweetly, [Col. 0210D] but because both sacrifice and libation had perished from the house of the Lord at Jerusalem.

Further, God—who in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob betrothed to himself a virgin bride unstained by any filth of idolatry—is compared to the husband of youth when he says, “for the husband of your youth.” For any man who has taken a virgin as his betrothed or wife is customarily called the husband of youth or the husband of a virgin. In accordance with this comparison, God also speaks reprovingly through Jeremiah: “Did you not call me Lord, father, and prince of your virginity?” (Jer. 3).

Nor should it be passed over that, when he had said, “Mourn like a virgin,” he added, “clothed in sackcloth.” Indeed, under the same kingdom of the Persians, namely also of the Medes, when Haman wished to destroy the whole Jewish people who were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus because Mordecai would neither bend the knee to him nor worship him, “Mordecai, hearing this, tore his garments, clothed himself in sackcloth, scattered ashes upon his head, and cried with a loud voice in the middle of the city street, showing the bitterness of his soul” (Esther 4).

Likewise the other Jews wept and fasted, Queen Esther especially undertaking this; she also sent these words to Mordecai: “Go and gather together all the Jews whom you find at Susa, and pray for me. Do not eat or drink for three days and nights, and I, together with my maidservants, will fast likewise; and then I shall enter before the king” (ibid.).

At that time, indeed, the people to whom it is now said, “Mourn like a virgin,” was clothed in sackcloth and mourned for the husband of its youth—that is, for the God of its fathers—because it had offended him. Esther herself confesses and says, among other things: “For we have sinned in your sight, and therefore you handed us over into the hands of our enemies; for we served their gods. You are righteous, O Lord” (Esther 14).

As they said these and similar things, they no doubt also remembered the excellent land which God had given them and grieved for themselves because, while they were led into captivity, that land endured prolonged desolation. Thus it is rightly added: “The region has been laid waste; the ground has mourned, because the grain has been devastated, the wine has failed, the oil has languished. The farmers are ashamed; the vinedressers howl over wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has failed, and the fig tree has languished. Pomegranate, palm, [Col. 0211C] apple, and all the trees of the field have dried up, because joy has been confounded by the children of men.”

That all these things happened in accordance with this prophecy under the already mentioned kingdom of the Babylonians, and continued until the empire of the Persians and Medes, is shown by the lament of the aforesaid Nehemiah when he says: “And I feared greatly and exceedingly, and said to the king: ‘May the king live forever. Why should my face not be sad, since the city, the house of my fathers’ tombs, lies deserted, and its gates have been burned with fire?’” (Neh. 2).

Therefore, where there has been mention, as to a virgin, of the husband of her youth whom she offended, and for that reason she is commanded to mourn, it fittingly recalls that all these useful things, produced by the excellent soil, have been plundered or devastated, failed, languished, and perished, so that by these too her cause for mourning may be fittingly increased. For these things also belong to the dowry which she received from such a husband when she departed from Egypt, followed him, and received the lawful tablets of marriage on Mount Sinai.

For this very reason that husband gave her the land of Canaan: that she might preserve the fidelity of marriage, as the Psalmist testifies in these words: “And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 105).

And see how forceful, though brief, is the rebuke in this recollection. For if you asked why “the region has been laid waste and the ground has mourned,” why “the grain has been devastated, [Col. 0212A] the wine has failed, the oil has languished,” and the rest have perished or dried up, he immediately gives the reason: because, he says, “joy has been confounded by the children of men”—that is, because the children of men have confounded joy, or have not kept the order of joy.

For first and chiefly they ought to have rejoiced in the Lord; secondarily, not in material goods, but in the Lord’s goods—over grain, wine, oil, and the other things given by the Lord. This was the right order of joy. The children of men so disordered this order that they neglected to rejoice in the Lord but desired to rejoice in the Lord’s goods. The children of men did this; and therefore, “Mourn like a virgin,” because such people were with you or among you, who made the husband of your youth offended with you and made his house a stranger to him.

It follows: “Gird [Col. 0212B] yourselves and mourn, priests; howl, ministers of the altar; enter in, lie in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God. Sanctify a fast; call an assembly; gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the earth, into the house of your God, and cry to the Lord: ‘Ah, ah, ah, for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One.’”

After the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, already discussed, such things certainly happened to the Jews under the kingdom of the Greeks, for which reason the prophetic Spirit ought thus to have cried out—not less, but indeed more—than he had cried out for the evils which were to occur under the two preceding kingdoms.

For then, according to Daniel’s prophecy, “from one of the four horns of the great goat, which struck the ram to the ground and trampled it, there came forth one little horn, and it became great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the strength; it was magnified even to the strength of heaven, and it cast down some of the host and of the stars and trampled them; and it was magnified even to the prince of the host, and took from him the continual sacrifice, and cast down the place of his sanctification” (Dan. 8).

This was the illustrious Antiochus, son of King Antiochus, as the book of Maccabees testifies: the root of sin. He built the abominable idol of desolation upon the altar of God and did such deeds as horrify us when we read them in both the first and second books of Maccabees (1 Macc. 1).

Then indeed “sacrifice and libation perished from the house of God,” and for this reason the priests girded themselves and mourned; the ministers of the altar howled; and the ministers of the Lord entered in and lay in sackcloth. For example: “They assembled,” it says, “and came to Mizpah, and fasted, and clothed themselves in haircloth with ashes upon their heads, and laid aside their garments; and they spread out the books of the Law, and brought the priestly ornaments, the firstfruits, and tithes; and they summoned the Nazirites who had completed their days; and they cried out in a loud voice to heaven, saying: ‘What shall we do with these, and where shall we take them?’” (1 Macc. 3), and the rest.

Foreseeing them fasting and having need to fast, the prophet says, “Sanctify a fast; call an assembly.” What he says, “sanctify a fast,” is plainly like that passage in Isaiah: “Do not fast as you do to this day” (Isa. 58). And immediately afterward: “Is not this rather the fast which I have chosen? Loosen the bonds of wickedness; untie the bundles that oppress. Let those who are broken go free, and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring needy wanderers into your house” (ibid.).

Thus sanctifying—that is, making holy—the fast, “call,” he says, “an assembly; gather the elders, all inhabitants of the earth.” He divides the summoned assembly into two unequal flocks, namely elders and inhabitants of the earth, saying, “Gather the elders, all inhabitants of the earth,” concerning whose difference we spoke above where he says: “Hear these things, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the earth.”

When they have therefore been gathered, “cry,” he says, “to the Lord, and say: ‘Ah, ah, ah, for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One.’” Warned by present evils and assured by the testimony of the elders, let all the inhabitants of the earth believe and cry out that “the day of the Lord is near,” that the day of judgment will come, that the great and terrible day of the Lord will come.

For, as the prophet testifies much later, all these things will take place “before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2); and for this reason they will know before it comes, so that its coming may be believed without doubt when those things foretold by the same prophets have been accomplished. If anyone should wish to doubt that part of the prophecy, namely the great and terrible day of the Lord, let the fulfilled part of this prophecy be shown him as evidence—namely the caterpillar, locust, and grub, of which we have already spoken—so that he may be compelled to know that that day also “will come like devastation from the Mighty One”: “like devastation,” I say, in order that, as Isaiah says, it may make the whole world a wilderness [Col. 0213C] (Isa. 14) and destroy sinners from it (Isa. 13).

And let it be said to people of this kind: “Have not foodstuffs perished before your eyes, and joy and gladness from the house of your God?” The sense is: Why do you still remain unbelieving? Why do you still wish the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord to be uncertain? Have you not seen, or do you not see with your own eyes, that the portion of prophecy which we prophesied to you has been fulfilled? Have not the caterpillar, locust, and grub already come, and, while they devastated, did not foodstuffs perish and “joy and gladness from the house of your God”?

While some still remained in impenitence, the same prophetic Spirit turns to his own people: “The beasts of burden have rotted in their dung.” For beasts of burden rotting in their dung means that carnal and luxurious persons end their lives in the stench of luxury. Such indeed were those of the time of the aforementioned Antiochus, as the same book of Maccabees testifies. For example, it says: “Jason dared, under the citadel itself, to establish a gymnasium and to place the finest youths in brothels” (2 Macc. 4). Again: “But the worst and most grievous invasion of evils for all was this: the temple was full of luxury and feasting, of men consorting with prostitutes; women even intruded themselves into the sacred precincts, bringing in things that were forbidden” (2 Macc. 6).

Accordingly, in keeping with that time, he cries out: “The beasts of burden have rotted in [Col. 0214A] their dung,” for those people indulged in luxury with a remarkable impenitence of heart, while foodstuffs and joy and gladness from the house of God had perished before their eyes. Indeed Antiochus had already captured the city by arms, and for three whole days there were eighty thousand slain and forty thousand bound (2 Macc. 5).

Still proclaiming such desolation, he continues and says: “The granaries have been demolished, the storehouses scattered, because the grain has failed. Why has the animal groaned? The herds of cattle [variant: rams] have lowed, because there is no pasture [Col. 0214B] for them; even the flocks of sheep have perished. To you, Lord, I shall cry, because fire has consumed the beauties of the wilderness, and flame has set ablaze all the trees of the land. Even the beasts of the field have looked up to you like a threshing floor thirsty for rain, because the springs of waters have dried up, and fire has consumed the beauties of the wilderness.”

“Because the grain has failed,” he says, “therefore the granaries have been demolished”; and because the wine has perished, “the storehouses have been scattered,” since granaries and winepresses are prepared in vain if there are no grains and wines. But what does he mean by asking and saying, “Why has the animal groaned? The herds of cattle have lowed,” and immediately giving their reason, saying, “Because there is no pasture for them”?

Certainly he wishes those who, though human, do not know how to groan except over scarcity of food, who have no grief over their sins, and who consider only this to be misery or cause for sorrow—that something be lacking to their belly—to be regarded as brute animals and herds of cattle. Such animals or herds not only groan when they have no pasture; “even the flocks,” he says, “of sheep have perished.” That is, people of this kind, numerous as flocks of sheep, fall away in time of temptation, murmuring if they are not filled and blaspheming God.

But if anyone asks, “What do you do, prophet, so that a rational person whom you do not wish, or judge, to be a brute animal may follow your example?” “To you, Lord,” he says, “I shall cry, because fire has consumed the beauties of the wilderness [Col. 0214D] and flame has set ablaze all the trees of the land.” The sense is: To you, Lord, I shall confess my sins—I, or every rational and discerning person—because on account of our sins we have been handed over into the enemy’s hand, and they have devastated our land and set it ablaze.

Nor is this all: “Even the beasts of the field,” he says, “have looked up to you like a threshing floor thirsty for rain, because the springs of waters have dried up.” That is, there is such drought and lack of rain that, with the springs dried up, even the beasts of the field perish of thirst, suffering punishment because of human sins. “And fire,” he says, “has devoured the beauties of the wilderness”: that is, it reduced places formerly beautiful to a wilderness by burning them.

He was not content to have said this only once, but repeated it a second time. For earlier he had already said: “Because fire has consumed [Col. 0215A] the beauties of the wilderness, and flame has set ablaze all the trees of the land.” Later he will say the same thing a third time in these words: “A numerous and strong people, like it there has not been from the beginning, nor shall there be after it through the years of generation and generation. Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame. The land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a wilderness of desolation” (Joel 2).

For that city Jerusalem was consumed by fire once, twice, and three times: first, when the Babylonians came after it; second, under King Antiochus, as it is written concerning him: “And he suddenly rushed upon the city, struck it with a great blow, destroyed many of the people of Israel, took the spoils of the city, and burned it with fire”; third, it was burned when the Romans pressed upon it. Foreseeing that exceedingly dreadful destruction, he now cries out most vehemently for the fourth time and says:

## CHAPTER II.

“Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land be troubled, for the day of the Lord comes, for it is near: a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind; like a sea spread out over the mountains, a numerous and mighty people. None like it has existed from the beginning, nor shall there be after it unto the years of generation upon generation. Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a consuming flame. The land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desert wilderness”—“and there is none who escapes it.”

This “numerous and mighty people” is not inappropriately understood as the Roman people. Of what other people, indeed, can it more fittingly be said that none like it “has existed from the beginning”? For neither the Babylonian people, nor the Assyrian, nor the Persian or Median people of the second kingdom, nor the Macedonian or Greek people of the third kingdom, was like it, as Daniel too declares concerning the fourth beast, which signified this fourth kingdom, in these words: “And behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest beneath its feet. But it was unlike the other beasts which I had seen” (Dan. VII).

“Therefore,” he says, “blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain,” and so forth as above. Of the three preceding cries, this fourth is sharper and far more vehement, plainly in accordance with the dissimilarity of the fourth beast of which Daniel bears witness, as has already been said [Col. 0215C–D]. For terrible indeed was what he had said, “Awake and weep,” foreseeing the Assyrians or Babylonians; and what he had said, “Mourn like a virgin clothed in sackcloth,” beholding the Persians and Medes; and what he had cried, “Gird yourselves and mourn, priests,” foreseeing the Greek kingdom under which Antiochus Epiphanes crushed the Jews. But far more terrible is what he now says, foretelling the coming of the Romans: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land be troubled, for the day of the Lord will come, for it is near: a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind.”

Hence it must also be observed that the prophets foretold three devastations, which were the three kingdoms; but the destruction wrought by the fourth kingdom of the Romans was foretold both by the prophets and by the Gospel [Col. 0216A]. For example: “When they were leading the Lord Jesus to be crucified, and a great multitude of people and of women followed him, who were weeping and lamenting him, he turned to them and said: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, days will come in which they shall say: Blessed are the barren wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed. Then they shall begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us” (Matt. XXIV).

Likewise, when some spoke of the temple, saying that it was adorned with fine stones and offerings, he said: “These things which you see—days will come in which there shall not be left one stone upon another which shall not be destroyed” (Mark XIII) [Col. 0216B].

It is fitting, therefore, that the prophet himself does not now proclaim in his own person—as he had proclaimed concerning the other evils which were to come under the three earlier kingdoms—“Awake and weep; mourn like a virgin; gird yourselves and mourn, priests”; rather, he entrusts this announcement to others, namely Christ and his apostles, saying: “Blow the trumpet in Zion.” Stephen the first martyr, while sounding the evangelical trumpet, was accused on account of this song or announcement by those who said: “This man does not cease to speak words against the holy place and the law. For we heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and alter the traditions which Moses delivered to us” (Acts VI). There likewise it is written: “Then they suborned men to say that they had heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God” (ibid.) [Col. 0216C].

In the following discourse he notably cleared himself of the charge of blasphemy against Moses and God, or the Law; but concerning the statement, “This Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place,” he offered no defense, but said only: “Solomon indeed built him a house; yet the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands” (Acts VII). For it was true that that place was to be destroyed; and this evangelical trumpet might be sounded in Zion, truthfully proclaiming a great howling upon that holy mountain of God.

That times of this kind are called the Lord’s—as here, when it says, “for the day of the Lord comes”—is most fittingly said against sleepers and drunkards, of whom he had said above, “Awake, drunkards” [Col. 0216D]. For those who sleep, sleep by night; and those who are drunk, are drunk by night: that is, forgetful of themselves and unmindful of God, and thus surrounded in their sins by an evil security, so that with closed eyes they do not see that God cares about human deeds. Certainly, when by the punishment of adversity they are compelled to remember their evil deeds and to see what they have done, then day comes upon them; yet not simply day, nor a day of sun, brightness, and clarity, but “a day,” he says, “of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind”—such, indeed, as that day or time was to be for the Jews when they were surrounded by Roman enemies.

“Then,” he says, “let all the inhabitants of the land be troubled.” He says this, of course, by concession, because thus it must happen. And rightly he calls those who killed Christ “inhabitants of the land,” as though because of an earthly dwelling, just as he himself had said through the Psalmist: “Speaking deceit in wrath of the earth, they devised plots” (Ps. XXXIV), namely when they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John XI) [Col. 0217A].

That time, as has already been said, is called the day of the Lord, though not yet “great,” which is commonly said only of the final day of judgment. Thus this prophet later says: “Before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” He compares the darkness and gloom, cloud and whirlwind of that day—whose greatness is loudly proclaimed in every manner of speech—with the great impending calamity, saying, “like a sea spread out over the mountains.” For what greater or more dreadful thing can happen in this world before its end than for the sea to be spread over the mountains, as happened in the flood? The sense, therefore, is this: just as in the flood the mountains were no more able than the valleys to remove themselves from the waves, so in that inundation of Roman multitude and strength the proud chief priests were no more able to provide for themselves than were the insignificant and common people.

See, moreover, how fitting this comparison or likeness is. For it follows: “A numerous and mighty people; none like it has existed from the beginning, nor shall there be after it unto the years of generation upon generation.” The likeness of the sea and the Roman people is fitting indeed: so numerous and so mighty a people covered almost all the nations of the world with its multitude, shook them with its strength, advanced and retreated like waves, swelled up against all mountains and covered them—that is, crushed all the kings or kingdoms of the nations by its power [Col. 0217B–C]. Certainly no people like it “has existed from the beginning, nor shall there be after it unto the years of generation upon generation”; and Daniel too, as was said above, testifies concerning the fourth beast by which the Roman Empire was represented, that it “was unlike the other beasts” (Dan. VII), namely the lioness, the bear, and the leopard, by which the preceding kingdoms were signified.

“Before its face,” he says, “is a devouring fire, and behind it a consuming flame.” That this happened precisely as it is said is clearer than daylight to those who read Josephus’s account of that destruction of Jerusalem. Before the Roman army surrounded the city, those who had been introduced as if for its defense, raging within in a threefold factional conflict, consumed with many fires both the buildings of the city and abundant stores that could have sustained a long war. After the enemies had entered victorious, the defeated rebels, continuing obstinate unto the end, persisted in an incredible fury until both the Temple and whatever remained within the walls of the wretched city were burned, although their enemies pitied them and wished to spare them [Col. 0217D].

He briefly describes what the face of the country was before the arrival of so mighty a people and what it became through its arrival, when he adds: “The land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desert wilderness; and none escapes it.” The sense is: when the hostile army came, the region before it—that land of promise—was “like a garden of delight,” planted with vineyards, palms, olives, and other trees of diverse kinds, and moreover distinguished by the most august Temple, than which nothing more beautiful or glorious could have existed in the world. But when the victor departed, the land left behind by such an army was “like a desert wilderness,” according to the words of the Lord weeping over Jerusalem and saying: “For if you had known, even you, indeed in this your day, the things belonging to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and they will surround you and hem you in on every side; they will cast you and your children who are in you to the ground, and they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX) [Col. 0218A–B].

“And they will cast to the ground your children who are in you,” he says—so that none may escape, just as here, after saying, “behind it a desert wilderness,” he adds, “and none escapes it.” For it is recorded that none escaped from that innumerable multitude without perishing by famine and sword, outside and inside; and those who could remain were carried away into captivity.

He still speaks, with the greatest admiration for it, of the strength of that very numerous people: “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and they run like horsemen. Like the sound of chariots they leap upon the tops of the mountains; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble; like a mighty people prepared for battle. At its presence peoples shall be tortured; every face shall be turned into a pot. They shall run like mighty men, and like warriors they shall climb the wall. Each man shall walk in his own ways and shall not turn aside from his paths. No one shall press upon his brother; each shall walk in his own track. They shall even fall through the windows and shall not be broken. They shall enter the city, fall upon the wall, climb into the houses, and enter through the windows like a thief” [Col. 0218B–C].

In short, swiftly running sentences he has proclaimed the strength and speed of so numerous a people. Therefore, O elders and inhabitants of the land, to whom he said at the beginning, “Hear these things, and receive with your ears, all of you,” although he has named the caterpillar, the locust, the bruchus, and the rust, do not mock as though this speaker had ineptly called your attention to mean and petty things. For these caterpillars or locusts, this bruchus or rust, are not for you petty matters or contemptible little worms, even though all human beings of all kingdoms, because of their vanity, are contemptible before heavenly power. For the persons under discussion are human beings to you—or rather, men mighty and swift against you. He has indeed named locusts and things of that sort, yet they are nonetheless mighty and swift.

This is what he says: “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and they run like horsemen.” In horses and horsemen, strength and swiftness are jointly sought in practice [Col. 0218D–0219A]. Here, when it is said, “their appearance is like the appearance of horses,” the little word *quasi* (“as if,” “like”) indicates likeness; but here, “they run as horsemen,” it indicates truth or the proper reality of the thing. For *quasi* or *sicut* (“as,” “like”) does not always signify likeness only, but sometimes also the reality of the thing. For example: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I), that is, truly of the Only-Begotten from the Father. Likewise in the psalm: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those comforted” (Ps. XXV), that is, truly comforted.

Accordingly, “they run as horsemen”: that is, they will not be like ordinary caterpillars or locusts, sluggish or briefly deceiving, but will be warriors and will proceed on running horses. When they are declared like horses by the words, “their appearance is like the appearance of horses,” this indicates that they possess pride, strength, and eagerness for battle, according to the bearing of that naturally fierce and proud animal. The Lord says to blessed Job: “The glory of his nostrils is terror. He digs the ground with his hoof; he exults boldly; he goes forth to meet armed men; he despises fear and does not yield to the sword. Above him the quiver will sound, the spear and shield will flash; boiling and raging, he swallows the ground and does not reckon that the sound of the trumpet is a blast. When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Aha!’ [variant: *Vah*]. From afar he scents battle, the exhortation of commanders, and the howling of the army” (Job XXXIX) [Col. 0219B].

Let these words be said of every horse of the Lord, of such as are spoken of in the text: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. III). They are understood mystically, yet there is no doubt that they may also fittingly and truthfully be said literally of a four-footed horse. But if these things are rightly understood spiritually of every holy and mighty preacher whose rider is the Lord, and who for that reason does not fear the dangers of the world, why should not the pride of the above-mentioned kingdoms—especially Roman power—also be said to be carnally similar to it?

Thus their appearance is like the appearance of horses, because, as the same Lord says: “Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?” (Job XXXIX). He alone could give strength to the kingdoms already mentioned, especially to the Roman Empire, and clothe its neck with neighing, so that, from pride or covetousness alone, it might rise up as though neighing against every kingdom until it made it subject to itself: so that “the glory of its nostrils might be terror,” that is, it might glory whenever an opportunity for dreadful war was given it; so that it might dig the earth with its hoof by most greedily seeking the treasures of the kings of the world; so that, exulting boldly, it might advance to meet armed men; so that it might despise fear and not yield to the sword [Col. 0219C–D].

What follows—“like the sound of chariots they leap upon the tops of the mountains”—indicates their assured triumphal glory: that they would without doubt accomplish victory and, with victorious chariots, according to their custom, lead the noble pageant of triumph. It also, in a manner, mocks Jewish pride or rashness by saying, “they leap upon the tops of the mountains,” because, when God was angry with them, they dared to summon against themselves to war those victorious over all nations, as if they themselves were impassable mountains [Col. 0220A].

Then, in saying, “like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble,” it declares that this same victory was surely to be completed by fire. The final clause of the proclamation admirably removes the character of caterpillars or locusts: “like a mighty people prepared for battle,” insisting and repeating that they are not to be thought real locusts, but a multitude of human beings under that name.

Observe also what beauty of eloquence exists upon the very surface of the prophetic speech. Five comparisons are set forth, and each succeeding one resounds more vehemently than the preceding and presents greater terror: “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses.” This is already terrible; but what follows is greater: “and they run like horsemen.” For a horseman is evidently more than a horse. What follows is far greater: “Like the sound of chariots they leap upon the tops of the mountains.” Again, far greater and more terrible: “Like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble.” Then what follows is clearer and more abundant: “Like a mighty people prepared for battle.” Thus, as if ascending and increasing in magnitude through individual stages, its force and great-sounding sharpness produce something greater than a rhetorical declamation. And after this excursion, as though recovering its breath, it continues in briefer movement and says: “At its presence peoples shall be tortured; every face shall be turned into a pot” [Col. 0220B–C].

How, or nearly how, this happened is clear to readers from the already mentioned historian’s account. Tormented by a dreadful siege, blackened and swollen by unbelievable famine, faces that had been lively and beautiful were turned into a pot. These things and those which follow are clear to the understanding: namely, because the Romans “ran like mighty men and, like warriors, climbed the wall; and walking in their ways”—that is, not abandoning what they had begun—“they did not turn aside from their paths.” They did not abandon hope of victory because of any difficulty; and “no one shall press upon his brother,” as fleeing men do when they break out wherever they can, disordered and confused. Rather, each walked in his own track—a thing especially praiseworthy in that people—keeping their ranks and always advancing with military discipline [Col. 0220C–D].

Only this requires a small question: he then says, “They shall fall through the windows and shall not be broken,” and afterward, “They shall enter the city, run upon the wall, climb into the houses,” and finally adds, “They shall enter through the windows like a thief.” How does it suit the horsemen or chariots of the Roman Empire to be said to fall through windows, enter through windows, and act in the manner of a thief? For the likeness of a thief, or climbing through windows, seems incongruously ascribed to so mighty an empire.

But it must be known that the Roman Empire deserved not only praise for strength but, conversely, reproach for profound greed; and this vice is marked in it when it is said, “They shall climb or enter through the windows like a thief.” Indeed, Josephus does not altogether pass over windows of this sort in that destruction. Among other things he relates and says: “Then one of the soldiers, without waiting for any command and without fearing so great a deed, but impelled by a certain divine force, was lifted up by one of his comrades, and carried fire snatched from burning material into the golden window through which there was access, from the northern side, to the structures built around the Temple.” And shortly afterward: “The hope of plunder urged very many on, supposing that everything inside was full of money, because they saw that the doors were made of gold” [Col. 0221A].

For such a reason, I should not doubt that they are deservedly marked in this way, as said to climb through windows in the manner of a thief. And, if it seems little to pass over this instance, what wickedness or greed of a thief does not that surpass which the same writer records? “For,” he says, “among the Syrians, one of the deserters was discovered collecting gold coins from the excrement of his belly; for they came after swallowing them, because the insurgents searched them all, and there was a great quantity of gold in the city. But when this device was discovered in one man, the report spread through the whole camp that deserters came full of gold. Therefore a multitude of Arabs and Syrians searched the torn-open bellies of the suppliants. And I think that no calamity more savage than this befell the Jews. In one night the entrails of two thousand were exposed.”

Considering these things, one may not inaptly say that those enemies were warriors for their strength, but comparable to most cruel thieves for their excessive greed [Col. 0221B–C].

It follows: “At its presence the earth trembled; the heavens were shaken; sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness. And the Lord gave his voice before his army, because his camps are exceedingly numerous, because they are strong and execute his word. For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who shall endure it?” “At its presence,” he says. At whose presence? Certainly that of the numerous and mighty people, the Roman people, like which none had existed from the beginning. At the presence of such a people—that is, as a sign that it would come and do all the things already mentioned—the earth trembled; and by its trembling it signified that great wrath would come upon the Jews, namely when the Lord, hanging upon the cross because of their crime, gave up the spirit.

Nor indeed did the earth alone tremble: “the heavens,” he says, “were shaken; sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness.” For then “from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour” (Matt. XXVII); and, as has already been said, when “crying with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit,” the earth was shaken and the rocks were split [Col. 0221C–D]. This occurred at its presence—that is, as a sign of the coming of that same people to avenge the blood of the Lord—as he himself also said there: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep also for yourselves and for your children. For behold, days will come in which they shall say: Blessed are the barren and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed. Then they shall begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us” (Luke XXIII).

It should therefore be noted that after he said here, “The earth trembled; sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness,” he immediately adds by a most rapid conjunction: “And the Lord gave his voice before his army.” From this one may perceive that in that earthquake and those darknesses our Lord, when he gave up the spirit and cried out with a loud voice, signified that his justice called that army—the army of the Roman Empire—his army, for the vengeance of his blood; and that his blood would not cease crying from the earth until that army came [Col. 0222A].

See how magnificently it is said, and how fittingly it may be said, of the man crucified and seemingly forsaken, who said, “My God, why have you forsaken me?”, that he had an army before whose face he would give such a voice. If you wonder that such a thing is said of one poor, he adds more fully and abundantly in words of this kind: “because his camps are exceedingly numerous, because they are strong and execute his word.” For truly even in that hour, when he appeared so forsaken, his camps were exceedingly numerous and strong: not only the camps of angels, concerning whom he said to Peter, “Put your sword back into its place. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. XXVI). Yet they were also the camps of the Romans, which would come and execute his word by surrounding the city, encircling it with a rampart, hemming it in on every side, casting it and its children in it to the ground, and leaving not one stone upon another, according to his word [Col. 0222B–C].

Do not wonder, for you shall see greater things. “For,” he says, “the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who shall endure it?” Certainly he himself bore witness to this in the same place. For he said: “Nevertheless I say to you: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming in the clouds of heaven”—understood: with great power and majesty, as elsewhere he said: “For the powers of heaven shall be shaken; and then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (ibid. XXV). Therefore it is not strange that it is said, “because his camps are exceedingly numerous, because they are strong and execute his word”; I say, it is not strange in comparison with greater things. “For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who shall endure it?” This is the same as saying: “He is the one appointed by God judge of the living and the dead” (Acts X); and great shall be the day of that same Lord when he comes in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead [Col. 0222C–D].

After these cries concerning impending evils, which had to occur on account of sins under those four principal kingdoms, he turns to the remainder and says: “Now therefore, says the Lord: Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts, and not your garments; and turn to the Lord your God, because he is gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and ready to relent concerning evil. Who knows whether he may turn and forgive and leave behind him a blessing? Sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God.”

Therefore, he says, since “wine has perished from the mouth of those who drink it with sweetness”; since “sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord”; since likewise sacrifice and libation have vanished from the house of our God; since again a numerous and mighty people has come up, like which none existed from the beginning; and since, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke through our mouth, the Babylonian, Persian or Median, Macedonian, and Roman kingdoms have crushed you—now you who see these things happening, turn yourselves, not doubting that that day of judgment, or the great and terrible day of the Lord, will come, according to the testimony of the same prophetic truth, a great part of which is fulfilled under those kingdoms before your own eyes [Col. 0223A–B].

“Turn, I say, to me,” says the Lord, “with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning.” For this is true conversion: first to change the heart inwardly through repentance. But to fast, weep, and mourn, and to go about outwardly in this garb while retaining inwardly in one’s heart the former purpose of sinning, is not truly to turn to me. First, therefore, “turn to me with all your heart”; then at last show the repentance of your soul by fasting, weeping, and mourning, so that, fasting now, you may later be satisfied; weeping now, you may later laugh; mourning now, you may later be comforted.

And because it is customary in grief and adversity to rend garments—as the high priest is remembered to have done in the Gospel to aggravate the charge against the Lord the Savior (Matt. XXXI), and as Paul and Barnabas are recorded to have done when they heard blasphemous words (Acts XIV)—I therefore command you not at all to rend garments, but hearts, which are full of sins and which, like wineskins, burst of themselves unless they are rent. When you have done this, return to the Lord your God, whom your former sins had made alien to you. Do not despair because of the magnitude of your crimes: great mercy will blot out great sins. For he is “gracious and merciful,” preferring the repentance of sinners to death; “patient and abundant in mercy,” not imitating human impatience but awaiting our repentance for a long time; and “ready to relent,” or repent, concerning evils, so that, if we repent concerning sins, he too may repent of his threat and not bring upon us the evils he has threatened, and, through our change of purpose, may himself be changed [Col. 0223C–D].

It should be noted how carefully he desires them to be cautious even in repentance, and removes their confidence, when he says: “Who knows whether he may turn and forgive and leave behind him a blessing?” It is as if he said: I indeed exhort you, as far as lies with me, to repentance, and I know God to be unspeakably merciful, as David says: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity” (Ps. L). But because we cannot know the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Isa. XL), let him temper his pronouncement; and I rather hope than presume [Col. 0224A].

Meanwhile, only let “sacrifice and libation to our God” be offered—understand, the sacrifice of a contrite heart and the libation of devout confession and good work—and let us leave to his judgment what we do not know, namely whether he may turn and forgive and leave behind him a blessing, while we hang upon the hope of mercy.

An example of how God is said or hoped now to turn and leave a blessing behind him is what he himself says in Exodus: “The blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses in which you are; and I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall not be among you a destroying plague when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. XII). Indeed, by these words he declares that he will turn to the sign of the blood, see the blood, pass over, and leave blessing and life behind him [Col. 0224A–B].
