According to this likeness, after the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, all who mark their doorposts—that is, their foreheads—with his blood, and who have received the repentance preached in his name, have a hope that is not vain that God will turn to this sign and leave blessing behind him, passing over them while striking the Egyptians—that is, all the proud and unrepentant—with the sentence of eternal judgment. This repentance and remission of sins had to be preached among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, as he himself testified after he had risen, speaking to his apostles: “For, as it is written, thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and remission of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV) [Col. 0224B–C].

It follows, therefore: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; call an assembly; gather the people; sanctify the Church; assemble the elders; gather the little children and those who suck the breast. Let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room.” He prophesies that all this will happen, while at the same time exhorting that it be done diligently and earnestly.

For this Zion is Jerusalem, from which, as has been said, the preaching of repentance had to begin. To preach it is indeed to sound a trumpet, because evangelical preaching proclaims a very great matter: the wrath to come, from which each person may escape by repenting. The apostle Peter first sounded this trumpet in that Zion, beginning from the testimony of this prophet which follows later, and finally saying: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized for the remission of sins,” also testifying with many other words, exhorting them, and saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts II). What else was he doing but sounding a trumpet when he said, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation?” For he signified the coming Romans and the impending destruction of that crooked generation, so that by repentance they might obtain for themselves not only remission of sins and future life, but also present salvation, deserving likewise to escape the present evils about to come upon that generation [Col. 0224D–0225A].

And this occurred. When the destruction was imminent, the faithful were divinely warned to leave, and thus were saved from that generation, just as Lot was saved from the burning of Sodom (Gen. XIX); and no Christian was shut in or besieged with them.

Notice that, as they sound the trumpet in Zion, he says: “Sanctify a fast.” For it is much more to sanctify than to preach a fast, since even impious persons can fast or preach fasting, persons who seek by fasting not remission of sins but only a remedy for present evils. Such was Ahab’s fast, after he had killed Naboth in order to possess his vineyard. For when he heard Elijah’s words, “he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed down” (III Kings XXI) [Col. 0225A–B].

For what reason? Was it that he might receive remission of sins and obtain eternal salvation? Certainly not, but lest he be deprived, while living, of his temporal kingdom. Therefore he did fast, but he did not sanctify the fast; and for that reason he received not the reward of the saints, but his own reward, a transitory reward. For the Lord said to Elijah: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Therefore, because he has humbled himself on my account, I shall not bring evil in his days, but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house” (ibid.).

Therefore, “sanctify a fast”: that is, observe the fast in order that you may be holy. And for it, “call an assembly; gather the people; sanctify the Church”—that is, by sanctifying through baptism establish the new Church of Christianity; and within its bosom together “assemble the elders and gather the little children and those who suck the breast,” so that the maturity of the elders—that is, of the wise—may instruct little children who still need milk and lead them on even to solid food [Col. 0225B–C].

What he then adds, “Let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room,” is the same as what the Apostle says: “But this I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (I Cor. VII). Likewise: “I want you to be without anxiety. He who is without a wife thinks of the things of the Lord, how he may please God. The unmarried woman and the virgin think of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit” (ibid.). Certainly, to live according to preaching of this evangelical or apostolic sort is for the bridegroom to come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room [Col. 0225C–D].

It follows: “Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, ministers of the Lord, shall weep and say: Spare, Lord, spare your people; and do not give your inheritance to reproach, that nations may not rule over them. Why should they say among the peoples: Where is their God?”

This admonition to repentance and conversion is more copious, after those great wars or conflagrations of the numerous and mighty people “like which none existed from the beginning”—the people whom we understand to be the Romans—than in the foregoing passages, where the earlier kingdoms,
Babylonian, Persian, and Macedonian [kingdoms] are, we observe, signified. And rightly so: for where this fourth kingdom—“this fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth” (Dan. 7)—devoured and crushed the other nations, and especially the Jews, and trampled what remained beneath its feet, a much greater and more widely renowned preaching of repentance, or penitential devotion, was heard and received throughout the whole world. That same beast, which had punished the impious Jews, did not cease to persecute and crush the devout martyrs; and the more it afflicted them, the more it stirred all the faithful to prayer and the weeping of repentance.

Foreseeing, then, that this would happen: “Between the porch,” [Col. 0226B] he says, “and the altar the priests, the ministers of God, shall weep and shall say: Spare, O Lord, spare thy people, and do not give thy inheritance over to reproach, so that the nations may rule over them.” What he says, “between the porch”—which we may call the portico before the doors—and the altar, signifies the priests’, Levites’, and other ministers of the Lord’s continual devotion and continence. In order always to be ready for prayers and sacrifices continually to be offered to God, they dwell, even today, near the temple or churches dedicated to God, in sacred and chaste houses under regular discipline—just as this prophet, when he spoke these things, foresaw would come to pass. Those who are such men, and do not forget their own purpose—the purpose for which they undertook to be priests or ministers of the Lord—weep and pray day and night, with frequent nightly vigils and daily fasts, for the sins of the Christian people. And it is beyond doubt that they did this especially then, when the Roman Empire already mentioned was raging and the excessive heat of persecution pressed hard upon them.

“Spare,” he says, “O Lord, spare thy people.” In what respect? Namely, in this: “Do not give thy inheritance over to reproach.” If you ask what reproach they fear: “So that the nations,” he says, “may rule over them”—that is, so that impious heathen may conquer them and rule their souls, while blaspheming you, the living and true God, and Christ your Son. The same men fear this in the Psalm, saying: “Help us, O God our Saviour; and for the glory of thy name, O Lord, deliver us, and [Col. 0226D] be gracious to our sins for thy holy name’s sake” (Ps. 78). Finally, they go on and say, “lest perhaps they say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’” (ibid.). Here they speak the very same complaint and question: “Why do they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” (ibid.).

The meaning is: Why are we thus put to death all day long for your sake and counted as sheep for slaughter (Ps. 42), so that enemies and persecutors of Christians may have occasion to insult us and say, “Where is their God?” They point their finger at the sun or moon, at some golden or silver image, or indeed at one of stone, and say: “Behold, these are our gods. But where is their God? He appears nowhere: they can neither see him nor show him, and, having no help from him, they are put to death and perish all day in our hands.” While enduring such reproaches amid innumerable tortures of death, and the saints, humbled by their sins, say: “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people.” The sense understood is: do not, as it is written elsewhere, leave—that is, do not permit to remain too long—“the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity” (Ps. 124).

To understand such groanings of the imprisoned more truly, let us recall the sufferings of the devout martyrs. In some accounts it is written that faithful persons, hiding in crypts and caves, buried the bodies, weeping and deeply sorrowful, and for many days did not cease to utter the lowing of tears.

As they thus lament, a consoling oracle immediately answers: “The Lord was zealous for his land and spared his people. And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I shall send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them; and I shall no longer make you a reproach among the nations. And him who is from the north I shall remove far from you, and I shall drive him into a pathless and desolate land: his face against the eastern sea, and his end toward the final sea. And his stench shall rise, and his rottenness shall rise, because he acted proudly.”

It was foolish, O priests and ministers of the Lord—it was foolish—to say among the peoples, “Where is their God?”, because they saw the rod of sinners allowed “over the lot of the righteous,” and their bodies visibly slaughtered, while God did not appear to defend them, and then supposed either that they had no God or that their God could not help them. It is not so. Rather, “the Lord was zealous for his land,” with a good zeal, a fatherly zeal; and as a father who strikes his sons nevertheless has pity on them and spares them, so he struck his people and, in striking, spared them as sons.

It should be noted that when he said, “The Lord was zealous for the land,” he added, “his own.” For he calls his own land, literally, the land of Canaan, given by himself to the children of Israel. Thus he says elsewhere: “For the land is mine, and you are my tenants” (Lev. 25). Spiritually, however, it is the Church, which, by purchasing it with his own blood, he made his own. Just as the Lord was zealous for that land on account of the children of Israel, because when they entered it they defiled [Col. 0227D] it, and he handed them over into the hands of the nations, yet nevertheless spared his people by giving them over to mercies in the sight of all who had taken them captive; so he has often been zealous for his Church, lest the unworthy handle its sacraments unworthily. He permitted persecutions so that the elect might be sifted like wheat, with the chaff departing (Luke 22). Such at the beginning was the traitor Judas. It is necessary, he judges, that heresies also exist, in order that those who are approved may become manifest; yet amid those very tribulations they become more illustrious, glorified by powers and signs (1 Cor. 11).

Those ignorant of this discipline of the Father, seeing the bodies of martyrs tortured, said among the peoples: “Where is their God?” Those outside, not knowing the true God, indeed said, “Where is their God?” But those who seemed to be within, while ostensibly professing the same God, said: Where is the holiness or perfection of their ways? There is a great and evident judgment upon this evil inference in the friends of blessed Job. For, inferring wrongly from his being struck that he must have been impious in the sight of the Lord—though he had possessed among men the reputation of a devout or righteous person—they said: “Where is your fear, your strength, and the perfection of your ways? Remember, I beg you: who ever innocent perished? Or when were the upright destroyed? Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity and sow sorrows reap them: by the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his wrath they are consumed” (Job 4)—that is, as you are now consumed.

Thus foolish men argued at length, striving to compel him to yield to their conclusion: that no good judgment at all ought to be formed concerning the life of anyone whom adversity oppresses or divine scourges encompass; and that no one is bodily consumed except in recompense for his own wickedness. But he understood something more than what is said here, “The Lord was zealous for his land and spared his people”: namely, that those whom God afflicts are not always to be regarded as sinners or impious men, as such people suppose; nor are all whom God strikes, or permits to be struck, struck with the zeal of correction for purification. Some are struck for testing, that their crowns may be multiplied. Therefore he says among other things: “At least now understand that God has afflicted me, and encompassed me with his scourges, not by an equal judgment.”

For when he says, “not by an equal judgment,” it is as though he said: Not, as you suppose, in repayment for my wickedness or impiety. Where an impious man is struck for his impiety, there is an equitable judgment. But where the Father is zealous for a sinning son and spares him, judgment does not attain to equality, because “mercy exalts itself over judgment” (Isa. 2 [cf. Jas. 2:13]). Where, however, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil, is tested by blows in order to be crowned, there is no longer either equitable judgment or judgment exalted by mercy, but grace and glory. Therefore it must be understood that in the words, “God has afflicted me not by an equal judgment,” *equal* is not used for justice, as for rectitude, but for equality. For whether God punishes a proud impious man, corrects an erring son, or intends to test by patience a holy and perfect man, he is always just and upright.

But let us now return to the words of prophecy which we began. When he had said, “The Lord was zealous for his land and spared his people,” to show how he spared them, he added: “And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I shall send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them, [Col. 0228D] and I shall no longer give you over as a reproach to the nations.” As in the other matters, so also in hearing this utterance, the elders and inhabitants of the land, invited at the beginning to hear, are distinguished and hear differently.

For the inhabitants of the land understand here only the grain by which the belly is filled, the wine by which the fleshly heart is made glad, and the oil by which the fleshly face is brightened. But the elders, considering the majesty of him who promises these things as something great, perceive things worthier of him: namely, that grain, wine, and oil by which those who eat and drink and are anointed attain the eternity of glory—especially because later, in the promise of these goods, it says: “My people shall not be put to shame for ever.” This bodily grain, wine, and oil are indeed gifts of God, and sometimes are given, and have been given, as a certain consolation to those who fear God. Yet they are given in vain and received in vain unless, while using them, we work for or seek that grain which is the Word of God—namely Christ, who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit” (John 12)—and that wine and oil which the Samaritan pours into the wounds of the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10). For of such gifts the majesty of the one promising may truly say: “You shall be filled with them.” These alone can fill, unto sufficiency, the emptiness of our mortality.

With this interpretation leading the way, the following words too are worthily understood: “And I shall no longer give you as a reproach among the nations; and him who is from the north I shall remove far from you, and I shall drive him into a pathless and desolate land: his face against the eastern sea, [Col. 0229C] and his end toward the final sea. His stench shall rise, and his rottenness shall rise, because he acted proudly. Do not fear, O land; exult and rejoice, for the Lord has magnified himself in acting. Do not fear, beasts of the region, for the beauties of the wilderness have sprouted; for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and vine have yielded their strength. And you, children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, because he has given you the teacher of righteousness, and will make the early and latter rain descend upon you as in the beginning. And the threshing-floors shall be filled with grain, and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil; and I shall restore to you the years which the locust, the beetle, rust, and caterpillar have eaten—my great strength which I sent against you. And you shall eat, eating, and be filled, and shall praise the name of the Lord [Col. 0229D] your God, who has done wonders for you. And my people shall not be put to shame for ever; and you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people shall not be put to shame for ever.”

No one ought to doubt that the teacher of righteousness whom this prophetic rejoicing mentions, saying, “Rejoice in the Lord your God, because he has given you the teacher of righteousness,” is Christ, the Son of God. Because he was given in the Lord God his Father, who gave him, it is surely right to exult and rejoice. Let us now retrace the prophetic sequence of the letter, and desire, so far as we can, to follow the Spirit wherever he leads us.

On account of those who say among the peoples, “Where is [Col. 0230A] their God?”, the prophet corrects their perverse understanding: “The Lord,” he says, “was zealous for his land and spared his people.” That is, it is not as they wish to suppose: their God does not exist or has abandoned them. Rather, like a master of a household, he chastened his sons with fatherly zeal, and afterward spared them, not handing them over to death, but indeed giving them promises of life. For this is what follows: “And the Lord answered and said to his people.” It had not been stated beforehand that his people consulted the Lord; nevertheless it says, “And the Lord answered.” In that very answer we have the promise of the teacher of righteousness, who is Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, as is clearer than light from what follows.

Therefore, when we read this sequence of the letter, “The Lord was zealous for his land and spared his people, and the Lord answered,” we rightly understand that, stirred by the Lord’s zeal and warned by the fatherly blow, the people cried to the Lord. Then at last he both spared them and “answered,” promising Christ, their deliverer and author of eternal salvation, at the proper time to ears that were watchful; and in the meantime he also gave certain temporal saviours to save them as types of him whom he was to send.

For example, when the children of Israel were serving alien gods in Egypt, forgetful of the God of their fathers, the Lord was zealous by stirring up Pharaoh, so that he might be the king who did not know Joseph and might oppress them with hard labours. As he himself testifies when he says: “For this reason I have raised you up, that I may show in you my power and that my name may be declared in all the earth” (Exod. 9; Rom. 9). Thus, stirred by the Lord’s zeal, “groaning because of their labours, they cried aloud; and their cry rose to the Lord, and he heard their groaning” (Exod. 2). And he answered them, namely through Moses, according to these same words of this prophet: “And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I shall send you grain, wine, and oil”—for example, by saying: “Hear, Israel, my commandments; write them in your heart as though in a book, and I shall give you a land flowing with milk and honey.”

He more clearly promised them this teacher of righteousness when Moses said: “A prophet from your nation and from your brothers” (Deut. 18), “like me”; and the rest, as the Lord himself had said to Moses: “I shall raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I shall put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he speaks in my name, I shall be avenger” (ibid.).

Again, when the Lord was zealous and handed them into the hand of the king of Babylon, stirred by that same zeal they cried to the Lord, especially Daniel and his companions; and the Lord answered him with many plain things concerning this same teacher of righteousness, especially what Daniel himself relates thus: “While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, Gabriel, flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice; and he taught me and spoke to me and said: Daniel, I have now come out to teach you.” And shortly afterward: “Seventy [Col. 0231A] weeks are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may receive an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. 9). After a few intervening words: “And after sixty-two weeks,” he says, “Christ shall be killed, and his people, who will deny him, shall not be his” (ibid.).

Many examples are unnecessary. But this must be noted without doubt: whenever, whether before or after his advent, the Lord has been zealous for his land or his Church, by his zeal he stirred his elect to greater earnestness in invoking him. Remembering mercy in wrath, he so answered and dealt with them that there was no occasion to say among the peoples: “Where is their God?” “Therefore you shall be filled,” he says, “and I shall no longer give you over as a reproach among the nations.” When he says this, it is to be understood: indeed, I shall make the prince of your reproach cease. For it follows: “And him who is from the north I shall drive away from you.”

For who is from the north except the devil, the prince of reproach, who said in his heart: “I shall sit upon the mount of the [Col. 0231B] covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14)? Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the prince of the kingdoms mentioned above; Haman of the race of Agag, who wished to destroy the entire Jewish people; Antiochus Epiphanes; and Nero, the stain of the Roman Empire—each in his own time was a prince of reproach. God made him cease when, through the Passion of Jesus Christ his Son, his teacher, whose clear commemoration is made here, he cast him out, as Christ said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12). As types of him, Nebuchadnezzar too was driven out of his kingdom and ate grass like an ox (Dan. 4); Haman was hanged on the gibbet which he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7); and Antiochus was broken without hand (1 Macc. 6). They were from the north in such a manner as to exhibit plainly in themselves the type of the north—that is, of the devil.

Therefore, when he says, “And him who is from the north I shall remove far from you,” it should be understood: just as I removed far away, each in his own time, those who bore his likeness. Of this northern one—that is, the devil frozen by treacherous and cold malice—Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon bore the type especially because he was also northern in location: according to the geographical position of the land of Judaea, he came from the northern side.

Moreover, after he had said, “And I shall drive him into a pathless and desolate land,” he immediately added: “His face toward the eastern sea, and his end toward the western sea.” According to the literal sense, this cannot be understood of any of the four kingdoms so often mentioned. For nowhere do the sacred writings report that the Lord repelled the enemies of Judaea or Israel in such a way that he enclosed their army between two seas. One, the eastern or first sea—as it is called in another translation—is the sea beside the wilderness, stretching eastward, in which Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim formerly stood, and which is now called the Dead Sea because no living creatures live there. The other, the final sea, lies to the west and leads toward Egypt; on its shore lie Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, Joppa, Caesarea, and the other maritime cities. No Scripture reports that, when the Lord drove them back, Israel’s enemies were enclosed between these seas.

Had this ever happened, it would be pleasing to set the structure of an allegorical meaning upon the foundation of the letter or history, as is customary in other, or at least in most, passages of Scripture. But now these things are spoken spiritually and ought to be understood or explained spiritually: not concerning the bodily slaughter or blood of enemies, but solely concerning the spiritual captivity of the stripped enemy’s head—that is, the devil. The Lord Jesus cast him out and sent him forth into a pathless and desolate land, so that he might remain or exercise power only among those who, deserters and abandoned, did not receive the faith of him who cast him out and sent him forth, nor the grace of evangelical preaching; abandoned precisely because they deserted God.

“His face,” he says—that is, the face of this expelled or cast-out one—“is toward the eastern sea, and his end toward the western sea.” The first or eastern sea and the final sea are the first and second regeneration, or resurrection, of the dead. The first regeneration is the grace of baptism, by which we are reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. The second or final regeneration of the dead is the bodily resurrection, as the Lord testifies: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit [Col. 0232C] upon the seat of his majesty” (Matt. 19).

The first regeneration, which is baptismal grace, flowing or taking its origin from the opened side of Christ, is called a sea because, in the likeness of the sea through which the children of Israel passed after Pharaoh had been drowned with his chariots and horsemen, it conveys all the children of God regenerated from death to life—after the devil and all his peoples have been drowned—to the harbour of salvation. It restores the blessed hope of attaining life and opens the kingdom of immortality, which will without doubt be received after the end of this temporal life. The second regeneration, the resurrection of the dead, is called a sea, and the final sea, because without doubt for him and his angels, and for all who shall be on the left, it will be a deep sea; indeed, as we read in the Apocalypse (ch. 19), “a lake [Col. 0232D] of burning fire and sulphur,” into which this northern one—that is, the devil—shall be “cast down before the sight of all,” as the Lord says to blessed Job (ch. 40).

Thus, “the face of this expelled or cast-out one [is] toward the eastern, or first, sea, and his end toward the final sea.” The exact wording should be observed: his face is not *toward* but *against* the first sea; his end is not *against* but *toward* the final sea. For his face—that is, his most wicked purpose—tends not toward but against that sea, by which we mean the grace of saving baptism, lying in wait for all baptized in Christ Jesus so that he may defile them again. And concerning them he presumes, as it is said to blessed Job: “He has confidence that Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40). But his end or conclusion shall be brought by judgment to that final sea, to that sulphurous lake of burning fire; and into it, as has already been said, he shall be “cast down before the sight of all” (ibid.).

“And his stench,” he says, “shall rise, because he acted proudly.” To what place, or in what manner, shall his stench and rottenness rise? Surely to the sight or knowledge of all the saints and elect, as Isaiah writes of both him and all his followers, angels and men: “And they shall go forth”—that is, the saints and elect—“and shall see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be a satiety of sight to all flesh” (Isa. 66). [Col. 0233B] This is so “because he acted proudly”—that is, because he puffed himself up against the Creator.

Concerning both matters—the guilt of his pride and the punishment of his stench or rottenness—Isaiah again says against this one under the name of the king of Babylon: “Your pride has been dragged down to hell; your corpse has fallen; the moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering. How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning? You have fallen to earth, you who wounded the nations; you who said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne; I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14), and so forth.

And rightly it is said that his corpse has fallen because of pride, and that he is stench—indeed, that he himself is a corpse and rottenness. For he lost life, that is, God, and is dead through malice, though alive in essence. For just as a body abandoned by the soul is dead, so a rational creature separated from God is truly dead. Hence, because graves are called receptacles of corpses, while the devil, dead to God as has been said, lies in the minds of the impious, the prophet rightly says: “There is Assur and all his multitude, and around him his graves” (Ezek. 32). This is as if it said openly: There is the devil, of whom Assur bore the type through pride, and all his angels; and there all the reprobate who followed him shall be joined to him, as the Judge says to those on his left: “Depart, you cursed, into [Col. 0233D] the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

These things are great, and therefore great faith is plainly needed to believe them. Therefore it follows and says: “Do not fear, O land; exult and rejoice, for [Col. 0233D] the Lord has magnified himself in acting.” What it says, “Do not fear,” is as though it said: Do not distrust. For fearfulness is used for unbelief, as in the Apocalypse, where, after first saying: “He who conquers shall possess these things, and I shall be his God, and he shall be my son,” it immediately adds: “But the fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars shall have their part in the lake of burning fire and sulphur” (Rev. 21).

Since the fearful are joined with the unbelieving, fearfulness is unquestionably understood as evil and contrary to faith; it may rightly also be called hesitation or doubt, in accordance with the words of the apostle James: “Let him ask in faith, hesitating in nothing. For he who hesitates is like a wave of the sea, moved and carried about by the wind. Let not that man suppose that he shall receive anything from God. A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. 1). Conversely, exultation or joy is used for the cheerfulness of faith, in accordance with the Lord’s words to the Jews: “Abraham your father exulted that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8). For he exulted—that is, he believed exultantly and possessed cheerful faith.

Therefore, when he says, “Do not fear, O land; exult and rejoice,” it is as though he said: Concerning all that is told you, O human being, do not hesitate or distrust; do not be earth with a heavy [Col. 0234B] heart, but believe eagerly and possess the joy of hope. “For the Lord has magnified himself in acting”—that is, he is magnificent, having proposed such great things and able to accomplish them. So too the Psalmist testifies, exulting and rejoicing over the future as though it were already done: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Then they shall say among the nations: ‘The Lord has magnified his action with them.’ The Lord has magnified his action with us: we have become joyful” (Ps. 125).

But perhaps those of little faith still seem to have something to fear, asking, “What shall we eat, or what shall we drink?” while we remain in this body, before we come to those goods of the age to come, since “the caterpillar and locust, beetle and rust” consume everything and “fire has consumed the beauties of the wilderness.” Therefore it follows: “Do not fear, beasts of the region, for the beauties of the wilderness have sprouted; for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and vine have yielded their strength.” It is as if he said: This portion about which you beasts are anxious—and on this very account are rightly called beasts rather than human beings, because such desolation distresses you—this portion, I say, can be restored. For after they have been burned, the beauties of the wilderness will sprout again, and the fig tree, vine, and other trees will once again yield their fruit and strength. “Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added [Col. 0234D] to you” (Matt. 6). Rejoice in this alone: that you first seek the kingdom of God and hope to find it, not in all these things which are added to you.

This is what he immediately says: “And you, children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, because he has given you the teacher of righteousness, and will make the early and latter rain descend upon you from the beginning.” It is as if he said: To the beasts I said that they should not fear, showing them this consolation, that the beauties of the wilderness have sprouted and the tree has borne its fruit. I judged them to be beasts, though they ought to be human beings, as long as they are excessively anxious for their bellies. But to you, children of Zion—that is, rational human beings intent upon winning heavenly things—I say this: exult and rejoice, not in the fig tree or vine or any shoots of the wilderness, however beautiful, but in the Lord your God. Let this be the chief reason for exultation and joy: that he has given you the teacher of righteousness, namely Christ, whom he caused to be born for you from a virgin, so that he might justify you and teach you to be justified not by works of the law but by faith (Rom. 2). He “will make the grace of this teaching descend upon you” in the beginning like “the early and latter rain.”

“In the beginning,” I say: first to the Jew, then to the Greek. For the children of Zion are rightly understood as the Jews, the children of the primitive Church who received the word of salvation, because it was necessary that the word of God first be preached to them. Therefore he called that preaching or teaching the early rain. And because, when the fullness of the nations has entered in, it will then again be preached to them and a remnant from them will be saved, he rightly called that rain both early and latter.

“And the threshing-floors,” he says, “shall be filled with grain, and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil.” Grain is sought in the threshing-floor; in the presses, wine is separated from the grape and oil from the lees by pressing. Both, then—the threshing-floor and the press—signify the pressures or tribulations which the saints, following the example of Christ, the teacher of righteousness already mentioned, were to endure because of the preaching of his teaching. “Therefore,” he says, “the threshing-floors shall be filled with grain and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil”: that is, the more they are afflicted and the heavier pressures they endure, the greater abundance of the Word and the more plentiful grace of the Holy Spirit they shall receive from above and pour out, without ceasing from preaching.

“And I shall restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, rust, and caterpillar have eaten—my great strength which I sent among you.” According to the letter, because these things were promised by the Lord, they are believed to have happened in such a way that the previous barrenness was compensated by new harvests, and whatever “the locust, beetle, rust, and caterpillar” had consumed was made up in following years. But it is difficult, or even impossible, to understand this restoration as referring to the four kingdoms often mentioned, which are represented under these names. For how could a temporal restoration of years—that is, of annual harvests or fruits—be made to those who died in Babylonian captivity or under the yoke of the other kingdoms, after fire or the hand of the enemy had taken such things away while they still lived?

Therefore we must understand a spiritual and eternal restoration, bestowed at the advent of the Saviour, here called the teacher of righteousness, upon all who, while awaiting the kingdom of God, had been unjustly oppressed under those same kingdoms. For in his Passion the Saviour liberated all of them, descending into hell and bringing them forth into those eternal delights of paradise. There were Daniel and his companions, and the other elect of that time, whose years Babylonian captivity had taken away. There were Esther and the others whom the pride of the Persian or Median kingdom could not separate from the worship of God. There were the Maccabees, whom Antiochus, the reproach of the Macedonian kingdom, could not turn aside. There were the apostles and holy martyrs [Col. 0236A], whom the bestial savagery of the Roman Empire could not conquer.

“I shall restore to you the years,” he says, “which the locust, beetle, rust, and caterpillar have eaten”: that is, I shall console you for all the evils which those kingdoms opposed to God’s kingdom brought upon you. Meanwhile, it should be particularly noted that he both magnifies and diminishes those kingdoms—so strong, so mighty—in a marvelous way: he compares them to the tiniest worms, locust, beetle, caterpillar, and rust, and yet calls them his strength, saying: “My great strength which I sent against you.” Nor will this seem so strange if, as we briefly noted far above, we make the distinction that, compared with eternal majesty, these kingdoms of the world, however strong, are undoubtedly exceedingly slight.

But in relation to human weakness, whenever the vanity of human beings must be scourged, the tiniest locusts can suffice as God’s hand and can be most powerful scourges, no less than the kingdoms themselves which are here signified by them. Was not the power [Col. 0236B] of God shown against Egyptian pride through plagues of flies and locusts, and especially through gnats (*cyniphes*), mosquitoes so small that they can scarcely be seen by the eyes? Was not the multitude of such creatures so great a strength of God that Pharaoh’s army could not resist it? If the locusts themselves could be of such strength, what wonder that the kingdoms signified by them should be called God’s strength?

Yet Christ, the power and wisdom of God, is called and is another, different power of God. The Arian heretics, understanding this wrongly—or rather labouring to understand it perversely—when they were asked by the Catholic bishops at the Council of Nicaea, as ecclesiastical history relates, whether they affirmed that the Son of God was not a creature but the power and wisdom of God, according to the Apostle’s words (1 Cor. 1), signalled to one another, saying: “For these things also come to us.” For the caterpillar and locust are called the great power of God. But we, detesting their corrupted mind, [Col. 0236C] [understand] the locust indeed, and the other things of this kind, by which especially—
…Egypt has been crushed; we confess it to be a great strength of God. Great, I say, and powerful enough indeed to overcome the pride of the fleshly Pharaoh; but Christ is the power or strength of God, alone sufficient to destroy the tyranny of Pharaoh—that is, of the devil. For it was not the locust [Col. 0236D] or the caterpillar, but this power of God alone, Christ, that could cast him out.

This too should be noted: when he had said, “My great strength,” he added, “which I sent upon you.” For truly the Lord both sent the kingdoms already mentioned and the other enemies against His people, and permitted them to come, because of their many transgressions of His commandments. Yet woe to those whom, for such reasons, He permitted for a time to prevail against His elect. As an example, He Himself testifies somewhere, when it is said of one such: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in his hand is my indignation” (Isa. 10).

In this manner, when the years “which the locust, the beetle, the blight, and the caterpillar” consumed have been restored, “you shall eat,” He says, “eating and being filled, [Col. 0237A] and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you; and my people shall never be put to shame.” Here the fullness of eternal glory is plainly promised, concerning which David also says: “I shall be filled when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; and those who seek Him shall praise the Lord; their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. 21).

For where else is, or can be, the satisfaction of God’s elect, to whom He says, “You shall eat, eating and being filled,” except in the delights of paradise? There, since Christ by His passion dissolved the wall of enmity (Eph. 2), the blessed shall be filled as they enjoy the vision of God. There they praise the Lord’s name, for their food is the very praise of God, who shall wondrously [Col. 0237B] renew them; and they shall not be put to shame for ever, because they have been delivered from the shame of sin and glorified with eternal glory:

“And you shall know,” He says, “that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people shall never be put to shame.”

That is: what here you knew in part and saw through a mirror and in an enigma, walking by faith, then you shall know and see face to face, walking by sight. It was, and is, delightful to the holy Fathers and to the other elect of that people to know how the Lord God was in their midst. For how is He in their midst, or what does it mean that He is in their midst? Surely, to be in their midst is to have assumed, in the truth of human nature, flesh from their flesh.

To know and see that He is their Lord God, [Col. 0237C] and that there is no other—for apart from Him there is no God, since Father and Son are not two gods, but the Son is one God in the Father—to know and see this, I say: the Son of God, equal to God the Father according to divinity and like unto them according to true humanity, is a matter of ineffable blessedness and glory.

Therefore He repeated what He had said shortly before: “My people shall never be put to shame.” Repetition is confirmation: they shall not be put to shame; indeed, glorious, magnificent, and honoured shall be the people to whom such a Son was promised, and from whose flesh He was born. And that saying of the Apostle shall be glorious to them: “For surely he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2); and this glory shall be eternal, once every shame that came upon the human race through Adam’s sin has been removed.

These glorious things have thus far been said to the children of Zion, whom Christ, this Teacher of righteousness, visited at His coming and led forth from darkness by His passion, in accordance with the faith of the Fathers who had awaited Him. As the Apostle Paul testifies (Heb. 11), all died without receiving the promises. For, descending to hell and rising from the dead, He brought them all into the true land of promise.

It is evident, moreover, that after completing the dispensation of His glorification, He gave a greater and more abundant outpouring of grace, or of the Holy Spirit: not, as formerly, to one nation, but to all nations, in accordance with the truth of the promise made to Abraham: “And in your seed [Col. 0238A] all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

It follows, therefore:

> “And it shall come to pass after these things: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. And even upon my male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit.”

For in saying “upon all flesh,” He permits no exception of nation or persons. Before Jesus was glorified, He had poured out His Spirit only upon the children of Zion, and prophets and wise men came only from that nation. But after He was glorified by rising again and ascending into heaven, with the abundant fruit of preceding ages, He made no distinction between Jews and Gentiles, but willed that remission of sins should be preached to all alike. [Col. 0238B]

This is what He now says: “And it shall come to pass after these things: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.” Yet here it is pleasing to recall that, after the Apostle had said, “Glory, honour, and peace to everyone who does good” (Rom. 2), he immediately qualified this by saying, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1): namely, granting to the believing Jew, or to the Jew who does good, the first rank in glory, honour, and peace, since his are the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; his are the fathers, and from them Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen (Rom. 9). But to the Greek—that is, the Gentile—he grants a rank almost second, although there is no distinction in the abundance of the remission [Col. 0238C] of sins.

The prophet appears to intimate this ordering here also. Having first said, “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” he immediately adds: “And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions; and even upon my male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit.” For he was speaking to the children of Zion, whose sons were certainly the apostles and whose daughters were the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ and the other women who at that time remained and prayed with the same apostles, as Luke records:

> “All these,” he says, “were persevering with one accord in prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” [Col. 0238D] (Acts 1).

These sons and daughters of the children of Zion, having received the Holy Spirit, prophesied—that is, they spoke in diverse tongues concerning heavenly mysteries. These old men, such as Peter, who was foremost among them, and later Paul, dreamed dreams; and the young men, such as John, saw visions.

Nor shall I be content, He says, to have given this grace to your children alone; “but upon my servants also,” from whatever nation they may be, “I will pour out my Spirit.” This designation of male and female servants of God is plainly broader than that of children of Zion. For the children of Zion belong to one nation, namely the Jewish nation; but the male and female servants of God are the elect from every nation. They are called not only servants but also sons of God, as John, after saying that [Col. 0239A] Jesus was to die for the nation, added: “And not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11).

Surely this reason for the outpouring of the Holy Spirit—that they are God’s male and female servants—is worthier and richer than the reason that they are children of Zion, that is, Jews. For the good Lord owes grace not to the Jew alone, but to all His male and female servants. Yet, as has already been said, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.

Further, it should be noted that, when He said, “But even upon my male and female servants I will pour out my Spirit,” He did not add, “and they shall prophesy”; nor did He say, “their old men shall dream dreams, and their young men shall see visions,” as He had said concerning the sons of the children of Zion. For it must be understood that although many in the Church of the Gentiles [Col. 0239B] have possessed the spirit of prophecy, dreamed memorable dreams, and seen visions worthy of remembrance, nevertheless the children of Zion and the children of her children alone—namely, the earlier prophets and the apostles who succeeded them—these alone, I say, possess prophecies, dreams, or visions that hold the highest rank of canonical authority and are of truth and certainty as fully established as the Law and the Gospel.

It was therefore rightly said: “But even upon my male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit”; and it was not added, “and they shall prophesy,” or “shall dream,” or “shall see visions.” For with holy teachers, and with all who in Christ’s Church after the prophets and apostles have merited to receive the holy spirit of understanding, it was sufficiently well provided that they should be able knowingly and faithfully to interpret or explain prophetic and apostolic dreams [Col. 0239C] and visions.

There is no doubt that both the reality of this outpouring and its sign occurred on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ’s disciples. Its reality, indeed, consisted in this: then prophetic—indeed, more than prophetic—grace was bestowed upon the apostles, who were the sons of the sons of Zion, as has already been said, and who until then had been unlettered and unlearned men; and from that time they began to dream dreams (of which we read some instances in the Acts of the Apostles) and to see visions, such as those which we especially marvel at in the Apocalypse of John. Its sign, however, lay in their speaking the languages of all nations (Acts 2). For by this it was signified that the same outpouring of the Holy Spirit must be bestowed upon all flesh, or upon the Lord’s male and female servants, in every people and nation [Col. 0239D].

Knowing this already at that time, the apostle Peter said: “Men of Judaea, and all who dwell in Jerusalem: let this be known to you, and receive my words with your ears. For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; but this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh,’” etc. (Acts 2).

It follows: “And I will give wonders in heaven and on earth: blood, and fire, and a vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.”

What he seems here to have said concerning the wonders alone—namely, that these would be given in heaven and on earth before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, which is the day of universal judgment—must likewise be understood and supplied concerning all the other things which this same prophet has hitherto foretold here. For the caterpillar, the locust, the cankerworm, and the blight—that is, the four kingdoms—were to come; then the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; and these have now come before that great and terrible day arrives [Col. 0240A].

Therefore, as has already been said above, both those to whom the apostle Peter, while present, applied the testimony of this prophet, and all who from that time until us have heard, and shall hear hereafter, must certainly know that that day of the Lord is great and terrible; indeed, they are not permitted to doubt that it is so, because it will come, because so great a part of those things which this prophet uttered with one and the same mouth has already been fulfilled [Col. 0240B].

Finally, God and his Word, Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, are engaged in a great contest concerning this matter. A great and sharp contest, I say, in demanding that he be believed: namely, that such a day, so great a day of dreadful judgment, will come, after which there will no longer be any time for repentance. John likewise says this in the Apocalypse:

> “And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth lifted up his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ages of ages that time shall be no more; but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be completed” (Rev. 10).

He contends concerning this matter so that he may be believed, because it is indeed an exceedingly great concern, and it is supremely beneficial for wretched people to know it, so that they may be able to escape such wrath [Col. 0240C].

Now he says: “And I will give wonders in heaven and on earth: blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.”

It is as though he said: People will not believe that God is concerned with their actions, or that that great and terrible day has been appointed for judging them. No, I say: they will not believe, they will not listen, they will not take heed, unless they see great and numerous wonders occur. Therefore I shall pour out my Spirit, as I have already said, and through his power I shall give wonders in heaven and on earth, so that the preaching of judgment may everywhere be confirmed by accompanying signs.

I shall give blood; I shall give fire—understand, as a testimony to them—so that, moved not only by the marvels of miracles but also by the greatness of perseverance, when they see so many thousands of witnesses persevere even unto blood, and see that the fire of God’s love cannot be extinguished in them by any waters of persecutions or by any floods, however numerous they may be, they may believe their testimony, or else be without excuse [Col. 0240D].

I shall also give a vapour of smoke, likewise as a testimony to them. Smoke here may be understood either as the blindness that befell Israel or, certainly, since smoke commonly provokes tears, as the compunction of penitents. For each of these possesses the force of a wonder and plainly confirms that judgment is to come. These wonders are given on earth.

But the words which follow—“The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood”—are wonders given in heaven [Col. 0241A]. By these verses he also reminds us of what the Lord said: “And there shall be,” he says, “signs in sun and moon and stars,” etc., up to the words, “and then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke 21). For what is now said here is the same: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” Just as it is said there, “and then they shall see the Son of Man coming,” so here it could likewise have been said, “and then the great and terrible day of the Lord shall come.”

Whoever, stirred by such wonders, performs repentance or is converted will be saved. For the wonders themselves, as has already been said, will occur precisely so that people may be converted and saved. This is what follows: “And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” [Col. 0241B].

When he says “everyone,” it must be understood without distinction between Jew and Greek. For when the Apostle intended this point and said, “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. 10), he employed the present testimony: “‘Everyone,’” he says, “‘who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’”

This prophet likewise removes that distinction between Jew and Greek and at the same time confirms that he rightly said “everyone” universally, in the very same verse which he immediately adds: “For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.” For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem—that is, among the Jews—and among the remnant—that is, among the Greeks—there shall be salvation, for whomever the Lord finds, that is, whom calling grace has first enabled to call upon the name of the Lord [Col. 0241C].

Meanwhile, it must be known that there is a definite order or course in calling upon the Lord’s name: first, that one calls upon him so that he may grant the spirit of thinking and doing what is right; then, so that on his great and terrible day God may not enter into judgment with a human being, but mercy may triumph over judgment.

It must further be considered carefully and faithfully how, after saying, “And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, because on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant,” he concluded by saying: “Whom the Lord shall call” [Col. 0241D]. Clearly, he attributes this very calling upon the Lord’s name, as is fitting, not to those who call, but to the grace that calls.

Confirming this, after using the example, “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,” the Apostle immediately made a most beautiful ascending sequence: “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how, indeed, shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10).

Thus, ascending step by step, he has recourse to God, proving that the calling upon the Lord’s name must wholly be ascribed to calling grace. For unless he had sent them, they would not have come or preached; if preaching had not taken place, they would not have heard; if they had not heard, they would not have believed; if they had not believed, they would not have called upon him [Col. 0242A].

Moreover, where did the Lord say this: that salvation should be on Mount Zion or in Jerusalem, and among the remnant—that is, among Jews and Greeks to be called by the Lord? Certainly, in his foreknowledge, in his predestination before the ages of the world. For those whom he called in time, he foreknew and predestined before all times, as the same Apostle says, “to be made conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8).

It remains now to explain why, or in what respect, that day of the Lord is great and terrible. Therefore it follows:

## Chapter III
“**For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will contend with them concerning my people [Col. 0242B] and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations; and they divided my land, cast lots over my people, placed a boy in a brothel, and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.**”

These things are indeed great and terrible, so that on their account that Day of the Lord is rightly called great and terrible. That day, because of its greatness, and “days” in the plural—the time of many days or years—is said to be a time to which no succession or alternation of light and darkness will follow. And he says “behold,” testifying that it is near at hand, although it may seem far off to any fool who says that this will happen in distant times. He deceives himself; for, as another prophet says, “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and hastens exceedingly” (Zeph. 1:14). And indeed he perceives that day to be near and swiftly coming who considers eternity, in comparison with which all the time of the passing age—whose end that day will be—is reckoned as a moment and as nothing.

“When I restore,” he says, “the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem.” Here Judah and Jerusalem are one: the single race of the elect, or confessors of God; the one city, the heavenly Jerusalem. Its captivity began when the first human beings, deceived through the devil’s envy, were expelled from the delights of paradise (Gen. 3), dead in soul and destined to die in body. Their captivity will then be restored, because they will rise incorruptible, freed both from the yoke of sin and from the debt of death, alive in soul and body and no longer subject to death in either.

“Then,” he says, “I will gather [Col. 0242D] all nations.” This is the very thing which the Lord says in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 15 [cf. Matt. 25:31–32]). But what does he mean when he says, “I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat”? Certainly he recalls this place both because of the interpretation of its name and because of an event which had occurred recently when this prophet prophesied.

For we ought to understand the times in which this man prophesied as the same times which we read of in Hosea, who says: “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel” (Hos. 1). Now, about eighty years earlier, while Jehoshaphat was reigning, the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon, together with Moabites, gathered against Jehoshaphat to fight against him, from the regions beyond the sea and from Mount Seir, as Jehoshaphat himself says in his prayer:

“Now therefore, behold, the sons of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, through whose land you did not permit the children of Israel to pass when they came out of Egypt, but they turned aside from them and did not destroy them—see, they act in the contrary manner and endeavour to drive us out from the possession which you gave us, O Lord our God. Will you not therefore judge them?” (2 Chron. 20).

As he spoke these and other things, and all Judah stood before the Lord with their little children, wives, and children, the word of the Lord came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah “in the midst of the assembly, and he said: Hearken, all Judah, you inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you, King Jehoshaphat. Thus says the Lord to you: Do not fear; for this battle is not yours, but God’s. Tomorrow go up against them; only stand confidently, and you shall see the help of the Lord upon you. O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear or be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the Lord will be with you” (ibid.).

And it happened as the Lord had spoken. “For the sons of Ammon and Moab rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to kill and destroy them. And when they had completed this work, they turned even against themselves and struck one another down with mutual wounds; nor did anyone remain who could escape death” (ibid.). Therefore that valley is called the Valley of Jehoshaphat, or, according to the interpretation of the name Jehoshaphat, the Valley of the Lord’s Judgment [Col. 0243C]; for Jehoshaphat himself had, in a wonderful accordance with his name, which means “Judgment of the Lord,” said: “Will you not therefore judge them, O Lord God?” And the Lord judged them in such a way that, turned against themselves, they struck one another down with mutual wounds, and no one remained, as has already been said, who could escape death.

It is also called the Valley of Blessing, because the liberated sons of Judah blessed the Lord there, as is written in the same place: “For three days,” he says, “they could not carry away the spoils because of the abundance of the plunder. But on the fourth day [105] they gathered in the Valley of Blessing” (2 Chron. 20). Since they blessed the Lord there, they called that place the Valley of Blessing to the present day.

Therefore, when he says, “I will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat,” he recalls for us an event of great miracle and fittingly indicates that something similar will happen on the Day of Judgment: no one who inflicts evils upon God’s servants precisely because they are God’s servants will be able to escape the sentence of condemnation—just as none of those who had gathered there against Judah and Jerusalem could escape death. They will be judged from their own consciences, just as those men were struck down by their own weapons and mutual wounds.

Nor should this be passed over: just as one and the same place, for the reasons mentioned, is called both the Valley of Jehoshaphat, that is, of the Lord’s judgment, and the Valley of Blessing, so too that session of the Lord’s majesty, when the nations are gathered for judgment, will be for those on the left a condemnation, when he says, “Depart, you cursed” (Matt. 25), but for those on the right a blessing, when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father” (ibid.).

Let us continue with the rest. “And I will contend,” he says, “with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel.” It is a remarkable expression, full of the gravest meaning, when the most mighty God says, “I will contend.” Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear and understand that this is terrible; for this reason that Day of the Lord is called great and terrible. For what could be more terrible than God’s contention with human beings at such a time? He speaks pointedly, as though he had never otherwise contended with human beings, although after that judgment by water—that is, the Flood—he did many terrible things with or against humanity.

For afterward “he rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Gen. 19); he drowned Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen in the Red Sea (Exod. 14); and he overthrew in the wilderness all the Israelites aged twenty and above who had come out of Egypt, except for a very few. This was done so terribly that the earth swallowed some of them alive. And he delivered the Israelites themselves, whom he had brought into the promised land, five times into slavery because of their transgressions: first into the hands of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia; then into the hands of Eglon, king of Moab; third into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan; fourth into the hands of Midian; fifth into the hands of the Philistines. After these things he delivered them into the hands of four kingdoms: Babylonian, Persian or Median, Macedonian, and Roman (Num. [Col. 0244C] 14, 16; Judg. 13, 4).

It will also come to pass that, in his own time, he will permit Antichrist to prosper, and that such tribulation will occur “as has not been from the beginning of the world” (Matt. 24). Certainly all these things are small in comparison with that great and terrible day. Therefore he speaks pointedly now of that day: “There I will contend,” as though those former acts had not yet been contention.

Concerning what, then, will that contention be? “Concerning my people,” he says, “and my inheritance Israel.” The true Israel is indeed that people for whom God has such concern that he contends concerning it; and therefore he was not content to say, “concerning my people,” but added, “and my inheritance Israel.” Certainly the whole multitude of the elect—all who have been predestined to eternal life—is the people of God and his inheritance, and the one true Israel. But for the moment let us consider that particular people from whom Christ came according to the flesh, so that we may show from definite passages of Scripture that the nations inflicted upon it the evils here recounted.

First, after saying, “I will contend with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel,” he added: “Whom they scattered among the nations, and they divided my land.” We read that the Assyrians and Chaldeans did this, because, after transferring the children of Israel and Judah, they settled foreign peoples in their cities in their place. Indeed, they left scarcely any remnant of that people, except that Nebuzaradan, commander of the army of the king of Babylon, left in the land of Judah some of the poor common people who had absolutely nothing, and gave them vineyards and cisterns (Jer. 39).

What follows—“and they cast lots over my people”—is recorded as having been done by the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. For thus it is written: “In the first month, which is called Nisan, in the twelfth year of the reign of Ahasuerus, a lot was cast into an urn, which in Hebrew is called *Phur*, before Haman, to determine on what day and in what month the Jewish people should be killed; and the twelfth month came forth, which is called Adar” (Esth. 3).

What is then added—“and they gave a boy for a prostitute”—refers to the third kingdom, namely that of the Greeks. Under it the Jews too were so corrupted through imitation of them that they placed a boy in a brothel. Thus we read in the book of Maccabees: “Besides this, Jason, the brother of Onias, promised another one hundred and fifty talents, if authority should be granted him to establish there a gymnasium and an ephebate” (2 Macc. 4). And shortly afterward: “For he even dared to establish a gymnasium beneath the citadel itself, and to place the best of the young men in brothels” (ibid.).

To state this more plainly, it is what the Apostle, detesting it horrifically among the Gentiles, says: “Their males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires toward one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense which was fitting for their error” (Rom. 1).

What follows still further—“and they sold a girl for wine, that they might drink”—is what procurers do: forcing girls into prostitution, they purchase debauchery from debauchery itself. From the shameful and infamous trafficking of those bodies, they make for themselves foul—indeed, so to speak, dog-like—banquets; drinking wine from it, they turn the price of another’s lust into fuel for their own passion. This too is not entirely passed over as having occurred there under the same Greek kingdom. For it is written: “The temple was full of debauchery and revelry, of men consorting with prostitutes; and women thrust themselves into the sacred precincts, bringing in things which were unlawful” (2 Macc. 6).

The fourth kingdom, that of the Romans, indeed oppressed the Jewish people more severely and scattered it more widely among the nations. But God rightly makes no mention, in his contention, of the affliction which that people then suffered [Col. 0245D], because that calamity enveloped none of God’s elect who belonged to his grace or had been predestined to life. For before the Roman army arrived, the faithful were warned by an angel to leave that place, as Hegesippus reports.

Having said these things against all nations universally, he directs the threat of the same judgment particularly against them and says:

“**What are Tyre and Sidon to me, and every border of the Philistines? Are you rendering vengeance to me? And if you take vengeance against me, swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense upon your own head. For you have taken my silver and gold, and carried my precious and most beautiful things into your shrines; and you have sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so that you might remove them far from their borders. Behold, I will raise them from the place where you sold them, and I will turn your recompense upon your own head. I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken.**”

Unless the divine utterance had named, after Tyre and Sidon, also every border of the Philistines, we would not find where or when, according to the letter, [106] that was done which he now says: “For you have taken my silver and gold, and carried my precious and most beautiful things into your shrines.” For we read not that Tyre and Sidon did this, but only the Philistines, in the first book of Kings: “The Philistines fought, Israel was defeated, and the ark of God was captured” (1 Sam. 4). And shortly afterward: “But the Philistines took the ark of God and carried it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon” (1 Sam. 5).

The ark itself, the tablets of the covenant within it, the golden jar containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, the mercy seat, and the two cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat were silver and gold (Heb. 9), and could in a certain way be called his “precious things.” The Philistines then carried these “into their shrines” when, as has just been said, they brought “the ark into the temple of Dagon and set it beside Dagon” (ibid.).

Here, moreover, it must not be passed over that the Jews derive a vain—indeed, a pitiable—consolation for themselves from this utterance addressed to these people: “Behold, I will raise them,” namely the sons of Judah and Jerusalem, “whom you sold to the sons of the Greeks, from the place where you sold them; and I will turn your recompense upon your own head, and I will sell your sons into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken.”

From this utterance, I say, they wish these words to be understood of the Romans under the names Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines, because Vespasian and Titus, after the Temple of Peace was built at Rome, consecrated the vessels of the Temple and all its offerings in that sanctuary. They therefore promise themselves—or rather dream—that in the end time they will be gathered by the Lord to be restored to Jerusalem. Not content with this happiness, they assert that God himself will hand the sons and daughters of the Romans over into their hands, so that the Jews may sell them not to Persians, Ethiopians, and other nearby nations, but to the Sabaeans, a most distant people, because the Lord has spoken, in order to avenge the injury done to his people.

We, on the contrary, say that not the Romans, but those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, are designated and struck under the names Tyre and Sidon; and that they are included within every border of the Philistines, for the same reason that God, considering this in another prophet, says when reproving that same people: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). For just as the Amorites and Hittites, so also the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Philistines were born not from the line of Shem or Japheth but from the descendants of Ham, who proved reprobate.

And because God considers not the lineage of the flesh but the character of the mind, Jews also—even though according to the flesh they descended from Shem through Abraham—are nevertheless counted among Ham’s descendants, at least those who despise the human weakness assumed for their sake by the true Father Noah, whose name means “rest,” namely Christ, who is rest for all the saints, just as Ham mocked and announced abroad his father’s nakedness.

We have stated why, in the present passage, Jews who remain in the synagogue of Satan are rightly understood under the names Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon, like the other regions of Canaan, may have been allotted or assigned to the people of Israel; but because they were situated in the heart of the sea, they could not easily be besieged by enemies and could by no means be captured or possessed by Israel. In the same way, the Jews ought to have been captured by the weapons of evangelical preaching; indeed, the word of God had first to be preached to them. But because, surrounding themselves with the depths of malice and hiding themselves, as it were, in an abyss of wicked knowledge, they rejected it and could not be conquered by the weapons of truth and justice, the apostles left them and turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13).

We likewise state why these same Jews are included within the border of the Philistines. The Philistines—that is, the *Philisthiim*—were the first to envy the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt and crossed the Red Sea, and then the others did so too. Moses says in his song: “You have led in your mercy the people whom you redeemed; in your strength you have carried them to your holy dwelling-place. The peoples rose up and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of the Philistines” (Deut. 32). Then concerning the others: “Then,” he says, “the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew stiff with fear” (Exod. 15).

So indeed, when people believe in Christ and pass through the sea of baptism, the Jews first envy them, as we read in Acts (Acts 14), and then the other nations, which have also been stirred up to this by the Jews’ example and frequent seditions. Those Philistines, or *Philisthiim*—a name interpreted as “those falling through drink”—carried the Lord’s silver and gold into their shrines, that is, into the temple of Dagon: namely, the ark covered all around with gold, and the other precious or beautiful things, such as the mercy seat and the two cherubim.

But these men hold, insofar as lies in them, the golden or silver truth of the Lord’s Incarnation in a lie. By doing this, they place the Lord’s precious things in the temple of Dagon, interpreted as “fish of sorrow”: that fish is Leviathan, the serpent, the twisting bar, and he lies in his temple, dwelling in the unbelieving hearts of these people.

Therefore, when he says here to Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines, “You sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so that you might remove them far from their borders,” let the Jews know that this too is spoken against themselves. For the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem were the apostles and the other disciples. They sold them to the sons of the Greeks—that is, by rejecting the word of God and judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, they drove them out to the Gentiles, all of whom are to be understood under the one name “Greeks,” as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. 10). And again: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of a human being who does evil: of the Jew first and also of the Greek. But glory and honour and peace to everyone who does good: to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2). By “Greek,” certainly, he means every Gentile.

That expulsion of the apostles to the Gentiles is rightly called a sale, because they drove them out for the same hope of temporal advantage for which they had also killed their Lord. What was that hope? Certainly the very hope suggested in the Gospel parable, when the tenants of the vineyard said to one another upon seeing the householder’s son: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21). This was their hope: that if they killed Christ the Son of God and expelled his disciples, they might obtain more freely the advantages of that land and Temple.

Thus, “You sold them,” he says, “to the sons of the Greeks, so that you might remove them far from their borders”: that is, hoping for and loving only earthly things, you drove the preachers of heavenly things far away among the nations, lest they should preach to their own people—that is, to you, to whom the word of God ought first to have been preached.
