Yet in doing this they said, and do not cease to say, that God belongs to them, is their God, and that they carry out all this persecution in his service. Therefore he began in this way: “What are you to me? Are you rendering vengeance to me?” As though he said: Why do you say that I am your God, when it is plain that you have not known me? “Why do you honour me with your lips, when your heart is far from me?” (Matt. 15). You say, “We have one Father, God”; but what are you to me? (John 8). Do you suppose that you render service and “repay vengeance” (John 16) when you persecute the preachers [107] of evangelical truth?

One of you, Saul, once did this in simple error, being a more abundant zealot for the traditions of his fathers; but he received mercy because he acted ignorantly in unbelief. You, however, do this maliciously, having no excuse for your sin, because you saw and hated the Son and me, his Father. Do you then “render vengeance to me,” as you wish to suppose? Certainly not: rather, you exercise cruel hatred, and take vengeance against yourselves in opposition to me.

Therefore I say: “And if you take vengeance against me, I will swiftly and speedily return recompense upon your own head,” taking vengeance against you because you take vengeance against me. For you do not sin through ignorance, but you took “my silver and gold,” such as those of which it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11). And elsewhere: “More desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Ps. 18), or “than gold and topaz” (Ps. 118). These, I say, “my precious and most beautiful things,” you took by violence and “carried into your shrines”: that is, you corrupted them by perverse teaching in your hearts, which are now no longer temples of God but shrines of demons. And those who taught no otherwise than as they had been taught by me, since you could not overcome them by argument, you persecuted with fury and removed far from their borders.

But what then? As I have already said, “I will return recompense to you.” For “behold, I will raise them from the place where you sold them.” How or when will I raise them? On the last day, already spoken of above, I will raise them, so that the dead may rise; and the apostles and preachers will come one by one from the places to which you drove them and sold them by the aforesaid sale. They will come, I say, not alone or in a few numbers, but bringing a multitude of Gentiles and commanding abundant armies equipped with the weapons of salvation (Eph. 6), whom they acquired through “the word of God which you rejected, judging yourselves unworthy of eternal life” (Acts 13).

Then “I will turn your recompense upon your own head, and I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah.” This is a worthy and just turning of recompense upon your head. For just as you exchanged Christ for Barabbas and sold his blood, and surrendered the true apostles in exchange for false apostles and drove them out to the Gentiles, so it will happen to you on that day of resurrection. For according to what is written, “The righteous is delivered from distress, and the wicked shall be given in his place” (Prov. 11), you will be handed over to the sentence of condemnation; and when they have been received into the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, you will be cast outside.

Such a sale and exchange will be made concerning you into the hands of the sons of Judah—that is, into the hands of the apostles—for they will be your judges, “sitting upon twelve thrones and judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 12:16 [cf. Matt. 19:28]). Nor indeed will you be sold to a nearby nation, but by them to a most distant nation: namely, wicked spirits, a nation most distant from you in community of nature and from every bond of the human condition.

For by the Sabaeans, whose name means “captors,” wicked spirits may be understood, just as in the book of Job this is to be taken in a mystical sense: “The oxen were ploughing and the asses grazing nearby, and the Sabaeans rushed upon them, took everything away, and struck the servants with the sword” (Job 1). Morally, wicked spirits are understood through the Sabaeans: when power over them is divinely granted to those spirits, they take away all the labours of the soul and all useful faculties, and strike with invisible swords. Thus, he says, they will sell them to the Sabaeans—that is, they will join them to wicked spirits for torment—because the Lord has spoken, whose utterance is true and whose word is truth.

“**Proclaim this among the nations: sanctify war; rouse the mighty; let all men of war come up. Beat your ploughshares into swords and your hoes into spears. Let the weak say: ‘I am strong.’ Break forth and come, all nations from every side, and gather yourselves together. There the Lord will cause your mighty ones to fall. Let the nations rise up and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about.**”

There is here a grand and powerful rush of rhetorical—indeed, more than rhetorical—declamation, because the matter is great and must by no means be spoken of feebly. “What I have foretold,” he says, “that I shall gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and the rest which follows down to, ‘They will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken’—proclaim it,” that is, preach among the nations, according to the words: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark, final chapter). Again: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew, final chapter).

“And sanctify war,” he says: namely, by baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that they may be armed and prepared with the weapons of holiness and justice for that war, the universal judgment. Since baptismal sanctification alone is not sufficient for participation in that battle, “Rouse the mighty; let all men of war come up”: that is, “teach them to observe all that I have commanded you” (ibid.), so that they may then have confidence on the Day of Judgment as mighty ones and come up as men of war, as terrible judges, “having two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles, to execute upon them the written judgment” (Ps. 149).

And because the king of this war is exceedingly great, and it is most harmful to neglect him: “Beat,” he says, “your ploughshares into swords and your hoes into spears.” That is, set aside for the Gospel of Christ and the word of God the labours of the age and the use of this world, “whose form has passed away” (1 Cor. 7), so that by devoting yourselves to it you may put on the best weapons, which you will need in that war.

“Let the weak say: ‘I am strong’”: that is, whoever desires to be prepared for that battle should then hope to be found strong in the Lord when he humbly recognizes how weak he is in himself. For strength is perfected in weakness—that is, in the recognition of one’s own weakness. Thus, “Break forth,” he says, “and come, all nations from every side”: that is, from east and west, north and south—all nations, I say—for with God there is no respect of persons or distinction; but distinguishing all according to their merits, he will reward the good and punish the wicked. Therefore “come and gather yourselves together,” some to be separated to the right and others to the left.

While uttering these words, the prophetic Spirit, who until now has spoken in the plural concerning many or to many, suddenly and remarkably turns in apostrophe to someone in the singular, saying: “There the Lord will cause your mighty ones to fall.” Who is this possessor of the mighty ones whom the Lord will cause to fall there, if not he who in blessed Job is said to be king over all the children of pride? (Job 41). Certainly there the Lord will cause all his mighty ones—that is, the proud—to fall, together with their king or prince, saying, as we read in the Gospel: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

And, not deigning to speak further with that mighty one of mighty ones, he resumes the preceding discourse; the same Lord says: “Let the nations rise up and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all nations round about.” The Valley of Jehoshaphat has already been discussed above. But it should be observed that, whereas he had said, “I will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will contend with them there,” [108] he now puts it differently: “Let all rise up and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat.” When the Lord summons unbelievers or hostile powers to judgment and contends with them on behalf of his people, he says: “I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat.” But when he exhorts believers to battle, he says: “Let all men of war come up; let the nations rise up and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat.”

For he who is judged is situated in the valley; but he who obtains there the title of man of war, standing on the right, and even more whoever sits in the order of the twelve thrones, will certainly be on high. What he adds—“For there I will sit to judge all nations round about”—is made sufficiently clear by the Gospel words: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:31), and the rest.

It follows: “**Put in the sickles, for the harvest is ripe. Come and go up, for the winepress is full and the vats overflow, because their wickedness is multiplied.**” Who says this, to whom it is said, and what is signified by “Put in the sickles” and “the harvest is ripe,” is sufficiently indicated by the Gospel parable of the sower, or of the field containing good seed and tares. When the servants of the householder said concerning them, “Do you wish us to go and gather them?” he replied: “Let both grow together until the harvest; and at the time of harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather first the tares and bind them into bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn. The harvest,” says the Lord, “is the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13).

Therefore, he who says, “Put in the sickles, for the harvest is ripe,” is the Son of Man, who before he became the Son of Man was, as he is now, the Son of God, and who spoke these things and the rest through the prophets. Those to whom he says this are his angels, the reapers; and the ripeness of the harvest itself is the end of the age, when, in accordance with the foregoing contention of judgment, the wheat and tares of the field must be separated.

What follows—“Come and go down, for the winepress is full and the vats overflow”—likewise fittingly signifies the same matter by another comparison. For then universally what now occurs sometimes in individual cases will take place: the elect will be wholly separated from the reprobate, just as in winepresses the wine to be stored in cellars is separated from the grapes to be cast outside. Therefore what he says, “because their wickedness is multiplied,” must be understood as though he said: Because wickedness has so abounded that the charity of many has grown cold (Matt. 24), the execution of judgment ought no longer to be delayed, so that the elect may be separated from the reprobate, and the simple from the malicious.

Having said these things, he cries out terribly and says: “**Peoples in the valley of slaughter, for the Day of the Lord is near in the valley of slaughter. The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness.**” Therefore the peoples or nations mentioned above are gathered in the valley of judgment, or slaughter, so that, apportioned to right and left, they may be judged by the Lord. Neither sun nor moon nor the other stars will be able to behold the sorrow of that day and the torments of the perishing. Instead, they will withdraw their light and will not dare to look upon the severity of the Judge, who repays each person’s deed upon his own head—not because God’s judgments are more merciful, but because every creature trembles at the torments of others.

In the same sense in which he says here, “The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their light,” another prophet says: “That Day of the Lord is darkness and not light. Is not the Day of the Lord darkness and not light? And gloom, with no brightness in it?” (Amos 5). And another says: “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind” (Zeph. 1).

Moreover, when he says once and again, “in the valley of slaughter,” he intends the same meaning as above, where he said, “in the valley of Jehoshaphat.” He reminds us of the history mentioned above: in the valley of Jehoshaphat the children of Ammon and Moab and of Mount Seir gathered [Col. 0252C] to fight against Judah, but turned against one another and cut each other down with mutual wounds. Hence, precisely because they were cut down by their own swords, it is rightly called the valley of slaughter; just as, conversely, because there the children of Judah blessed the Lord, it was called the valley of blessing. As those men cut themselves down by mutual wounds, so on that day all the reprobate are to be condemned from their own consciences.

It follows: “And the Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem shall give forth his voice. And heaven and earth shall be shaken; and the Lord shall be the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Israel.” Since the discourse thus far concerns that great and terrible day of the Lord, this roaring and this voice of the Lord are rightly understood as that of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming [Col. 0252D] in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil unto the resurrection of judgment” (John 5).

For that voice of which he had earlier spoken, saying, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (ibid.)—that is the roar and the voice by which, through dying and rising again, he terrified and conquered hell, and carried spoil away from it, according to Jacob’s prophecy: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up” (Gen. 49), etc. With that roar the prophet Amos begins, saying: “The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem shall give forth his voice” (Amos 1). [Col. 0253A] This is as though he said: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

For what follows there, “the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel was dried up,” Carmel being interpreted “knowledge of circumcision,” is understood of the pride of the Scribes and Pharisees, who professed themselves shepherds of the people, and who, because of their own traditions, had abandoned God’s traditions: that is, their supposedly beautiful doctrine ought to mourn and wither when Christ’s Gospel shines forth.

Therefore “the Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem shall give forth his voice,” namely, when, from the midst of the saints with whose thousands he shall come, and from the midst of the angels who shall come with him—whose single fellowship is rightly called Zion and Jerusalem—sitting on [Col. 0253B] the throne of his majesty, “he shall say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom.’ But to those at his left: ‘Depart, accursed, into eternal fire’” (Matt. 25).

Then indeed heaven and earth shall be shaken, as the Lord himself says: “The powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Matt. 24). Nor will the earthquake at his coming be slight, but so great that all the dead, struck as though asleep, shall be awakened. Even the elect themselves will fear and tremble; yet in that very fear and trembling they shall retain a strong and firm hope. This is what he immediately says: “and the Lord, the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Israel.” For the entire people of God’s elect is rightly called, and is, his people; all of whom his majesty shall then in a wondrous manner both terrify and strengthen, [Col. 0253C] because they never hoped in themselves but in the Lord, never presumed upon their own strength but upon the Lord’s strength. In contrast, false Israelites hope in themselves and wish to seem strong by themselves, while “seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10).

All these things were preached to the nations according to the command given above: “Proclaim this among the nations”; and whatever [109] has been said from that place onward, the prophet spoke in the person of God. Now at last God himself speaks in his own person and says: “And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, on my holy mountain; and Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through her. And it shall come to pass on that day that the mountains shall drip sweetness, [Col. 0253D] and the hills shall flow with milk, and waters shall run through all the streams of Judah. And a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord and shall water the torrent of thorns. Egypt shall become desolate, and Idumea a wilderness of destruction, because they acted wickedly against the children of Judah and shed innocent blood in their land. But Judea shall be inhabited for ever, and Jerusalem unto generation after generation; and I shall cleanse their blood which I had not cleansed, and the Lord shall dwell in Zion.”

In a wondrous way the Lord joins words spoken in his own person to the prophet’s words by the conjunction “and,” as though saying: All these things which I commanded to be proclaimed among the nations shall come to pass; and then you who are my people, who are called and truly are the children of Israel, shall know that I am the Lord your God—shall know, I say, because you shall see. You shall see, [Col. 0254A] no longer “through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

“I, that Lord your God, shall then be known by you as dwelling in Zion, on my holy mountain”; and, as another prophet testifies: “Then shall I speak to my enemies in my land, and in my wrath shall trouble them: I, he says, have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2). And then Jerusalem shall be holy: namely, she whom, as the Apostle says, “I presented to myself as a glorious bride, having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5); and concerning whom John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw the new city Jerusalem coming down from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 21).

“And strangers,” he says, “shall no longer pass through her.” “Strangers,” I say—that is, [Col. 0254B] the fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars—who formerly passed through her and wearied her, shall no longer be able to pass through her, because they shall be cast outside; and, as it is written there, “their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (ibid.). Again, it is written there: “Outside are dogs and sorcerers, the unchaste and murderers, idol-worshippers, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood” (Rev. 22).

Therefore “strangers shall no longer pass through her”; “and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21). “And it shall come to pass on that day,” he says, “that the mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk, and waters shall run through all the streams of Judah.”

[Col. 0254C] The mountains of that city are the prophets and apostles, while the hills are the other saints. Because the peoples subject to them received their teaching here, they shall therefore share there also in their glory; and, beholding them, they shall drink the sweetness of divine charity implanted in them, and by fellowship shall draw it in, because they shall behold more fully in them the glory of God, through whose teaching they came to know God’s glory. The Psalmist signifies this in a brief verse: “They shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your countenance, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light they shall see light” (Ps. 35).

Indeed, sweetness shall drip from the mountains and milk shall flow from the hills; and through all the streams of Judah—that is, through all the hearts of believers or confessors—waters shall run, springing up into eternal life. Yet the fountain of this same sweetness, this same milk, [Col. 0254D] and these same waters shall go forth, he says, from the house of the Lord into the mountains, the hills, and all those streams. This house is rightly understood as the structure of Christ’s body; for it is “the house which Wisdom built for herself” (Prov. 9).

He says therefore: “And a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord and shall water the torrent of thorns”: the fountain of life and torrent of delight proceeding from that house of the Lord shall water the torrent of thorns—that is, the whole body of the elect—so that it may no longer be what it was, running from east to west amid the thorns of tribulations and sins, but may be a torrent of delights, abounding in the richness of everlasting goods. Of this likewise we read in the Apocalypse: “And he showed me a river of living water, clear as [Col. 0255A] crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the middle of the street of the city; and on either side of the river, the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, rendering its fruit each month” (Rev. 22).

It must briefly be said here that this fountain or river is the Holy Spirit, who also says in the prophet: “Behold, I turn toward them as a river of peace and as an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66). This river of peace, this torrent of glory, this river of joy, this torrent of delight, this abundance of God’s house, is the Holy Spirit. For he is the love of bridegroom and bride. Flooded and healed by him, what was a torrent of thorns shall become a torrent of delights: that is, our condition, which was mortal and miserable, shall become immortal and blessed.

Egypt and Idumea are spiritually contrary to this city according to the new interpretation and according to the reality itself; accordingly, they shall receive contrary things. Egypt is interpreted “darkness,” Idumea “earthliness”; and they signify all those “whom their own wickedness has blinded” (Wis. 2), and who through desire bear earthly hearts. He says therefore: “Egypt shall become desolate, [Col. 0255B] and Idumea a wilderness of destruction.” Why? “Because,” he says, “they acted wickedly against the children of Judah and shed innocent blood in their land”—the children of Judah.

Just as we understand Jerusalem and Zion not carnally but spiritually, so too we understand as the children of Judah all who confess the one true God, in accordance with the name Judah, which means “confession,” and who suffer wicked treatment on account of that same confession from Egypt and the children of Edom: “They say, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” (Ps. 136)—Jerusalem being understood. For they would lay bare the city, that is, the Church of God, and would have no voice of Judah—that is, of confession—heard from her at all. Therefore, while the Lord dwells in her amid abundance of sweetness, a river of milk, and waters running through all the streams of Judah, they, conversely, shall become desolation and a wilderness of destruction.

Hence there follows: “And Judea shall be inhabited for ever, and Jerusalem unto generation after generation; and I shall cleanse their blood which I had not cleansed, and the Lord shall dwell in Zion.” All these things, spoken spiritually, wonderfully flatter carnal Judea, or Israel glorying in the flesh. For although they are said especially against them, [Col. 0255D] since they are earthly and love earthly things, shed the blood of the holy prophets in their land, and consequently have deservedly been blinded and reduced to [Col. 0256A] Egypt, they boast that these things have been said on their own behalf.

For these words seem strongly to support their opinion that a kingdom of a thousand years is promised to them within the borders of Judea: a golden Jerusalem, the blood of sacrifices, sons and grandsons, unbelievable delights, and gates distinguished by a variety of gems. According to this prophecy, they suppose that in that lovely length of years they shall dwell amid drops of carnal sweetness from the mountains, white streams of milk from the hills, and most pure, springing waters through all the streams of Judah, in such abundance that even torrents of thorns shall be changed so that, all around, not thorns but most beautiful and fruitful trees may grow, as in a paradise of delights.

According to the letter they dream these things and err; yet this error has always benefited, and still benefits, the prophetic [Col. 0256B] [110] writings, by causing them to be preserved by their enemies. For so many things are said against them that they would undoubtedly provoke them to a hatred too impatient to endure, if they had been expressed in plain words. Therefore, as the Lord says in Isaiah, “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8), so here too we should believe that it was necessarily done: this mystical testimony was bound up, laid aside for Christ’s disciples, and to be preserved by Christ’s enemies, because of the beauty of its binding, because of the letter’s surface which flatters them.

The final closure of that same binding is this: “And I shall cleanse their blood which they have not cleansed. And the Lord shall dwell in Zion.” Whose blood shall I cleanse? Clearly that of the Egyptians and [Col. 0256C] Idumeans, whom the Jews do not perceive to be themselves, although they are the greatest of murderers, who “shed innocent blood.” “Their blood,” he says, “which they have not cleansed, I shall cleanse”: that is, I shall punish their murders and their other sins, for which they have not repented. For if they themselves had cleansed them by temporal repentance, I would not cleanse—or punish—them by the sentence of eternal judgment.

The prophet echoes the person of the Lord who speaks, turning to us and saying: “And the Lord shall dwell in Zion,” namely in that Zion “whose foundations are in the holy mountains, whose gates the Lord loves above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86), concerning which the Holy Spirit speaks both wonderfully and truly: “And man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded [Col. 0256D] her” (ibid.). There he shall dwell; there he shall make his everlasting abode; there God, the God of gods, shall always be seen, and shall always be desirable to behold.

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Amos

[Col. 0255]

111 Third in the order of the twelve prophets, holy Amos commends the great grace of his teacher and instructor, the Holy Spirit, referring it to that Spirit’s glory by declaring who he was and from where he was taken up to become a prophet. For he himself says in the heading of his prophecy: “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (Amos 1). And elsewhere: “I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but a herdsman plucking sycomore figs; and the Lord took me as I followed the flock and said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel” (Amos 7).

For it is a great proclamation of the Lord’s grace and glory that he graciously willed and effectively could make a man carrying out a shepherd’s work a prophet. Yet we fear being accused of presumption, as we endeavour to treat words not of a man but of God, words not uttered from the soil but drawn forth from heavenly teaching; before their majesty, great and ancient men, far greater than we, confess that the powers of their own understanding fail.

For who, they say, can worthily set forth the three and four crimes [Col. 0257] of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the children of Ammon, and Moab, and, in the seventh and eighth degree, of Judah and Israel? What then? Shall we relax our slack hands and make the dignity and difficulty of these words an occasion for slumber and sleep, like the lazy? If we do this, the saying of the Wise Man stands against us, so that we cannot excuse ourselves:

> “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom. Though she has no guide, instructor, or ruler, she prepares food for herself in summer and gathers at harvest what she may eat. How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, doze a little, fold your hands a little to sleep; and poverty shall come upon you like a traveller, and want like an armed man. But if you are diligent, your harvest shall come to you, and want shall flee far from you” (Prov. 6).

To what end are these words directed except to inspire hope in the needy soul, so that, trusting in God’s help, it may hasten, after the example of the ant, to bear burdens greater than its shoulders and prepare food for itself? For famine is coming upon the lazy and sleepy who sleep during this present time; it shall meet them like an armed man. Foreseeing it, the Psalmist, after saying, “The Lord knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance shall be for ever” (Ps. 36), added: “They shall not be confounded in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied” (ibid.).

By “the evil time” and “the days of famine” he plainly means the day of judgment, when the wicked and lazy, who here neglected every word proceeding from the mouth of God—in which man lives, and without which he does not live (Deut. 8)—shall hunger and thirst for ever. Let us therefore rise also to this part of God’s discourse; and whoever reads these little works of ours should know that he is entreated to say of us with kindly, smiling eyes the words of the same Wise Man: “The ants are a feeble people, who prepare their food in harvest” (Prov. 30).

## Commentary on the Prophet Amos

### Book One

[Col. 0257]

111 Chapter I

[Col. 0257A]

“Words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.”

Amos, whose name means “a people torn away,” by the very interpretation of his name presents a harsh omen to Israel, to whom he is sent: namely, that it was soon to be torn away from its own land into captivity, since, by worshipping the golden calves, it had already been torn away from the house and stock of David whom the Lord had chosen. These are his words, uttered from the living fountain—that is, the one Word of God—and therefore necessarily to be fulfilled in all the truth of the events that follow; for Amos “was among the shepherds of Tekoa.”

Now Tekoa is the name of a town six miles south of Bethlehem; and beyond it there is no village, not even rustic huts of the kind Africans call *mapalia*, resembling ovens rather than houses. So great is the desolation of the wilderness, stretching as far as the Red Sea and the borders of the Persians, Ethiopians, and Medes. Since the dry and sandy ground produces no crops at all, everything is full of shepherds, who compensate for the barrenness of the land by the multitude of their flocks. From this number of shepherds Amos the prophet also came: unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge. For the same Holy Spirit who spoke through all the prophets spoke through this man also.

Moreover, Tekoa means “trumpet.” Thus the very name of the village greatly suits the subject—namely, this prophecy—which, if it is rightly heard, if we have ears to hear, is so great and powerful that it is rightly called the trumpet of God.

These words, “which he saw concerning Israel,” imply: things coming upon Israel like a great weight. Otherwise, if Israel had not transgressed, and if he were therefore announcing not adversity but prosperity, it would more properly have been said, “to Israel” or “for Israel.” He saw, moreover, with that vision by which words can be seen: that is, the vision of the mind, which is true vision, on account of whose excellence prophets are also called Seers.

Uzziah, in whose days he saw these things, was also called Azariah, king of Judah. When he attempted to claim for himself the priesthood which was not due to him, he was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chron. 26); and at that time the Lord’s wrath was shown not only by his punishment but also by the earthquake, which the Hebrews report to have occurred then. He testifies that he saw these things “two years before that earthquake.” Why he has now mentioned that same earthquake will be more suitably discussed shortly, when, in the necessity of discovering the mystical sense, we examine the summit of Carmel: why, after first saying, “The Lord will roar from Zion and give forth his voice from Jerusalem, and the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned,” he added, “and the summit of Carmel was dried up.”

This Jeroboam, moreover, is not the son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, but the son of Joash, son of Joathan, son of Jehu, the great-grandson of that same Jehu; under him Hosea, Joel, and Amos prophesied.

Let us now take up the words themselves: “The Lord will roar from Zion and give forth his voice from Jerusalem; and the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel was dried up.” He begins his utterance from that to which the chief intention of the holy prophets tends: namely, from the advent then awaited and from the Gospel of Christ, the Son of God; and, concerning what was to befall the Jews in their misery because of their rejection and repulse of him, this prophet taken from among shepherds speaks wonderfully and terribly.

For “the Lord will roar from Zion”: that is, Christ the Son of God, God and Lord, having become man and suffered death, will shatter hell and conquer death, like a most mighty lion, like a lion’s whelp—that is, the most mighty Son of the most mighty God—according to the prophecy of Jacob, who says: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness: who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49).

Having sent forth so great a roar from Zion, then from Jerusalem—which is one and the same city—he “will give forth his voice”; that is, he will send out the preaching of the Gospel. He himself testified, according to the Scriptures, that this had to happen: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24).

What then was to befall the wretched Jews? Clearly a twofold evil, a double destruction: one temporal, the other eternal; or one bodily, the other spiritual. Of the temporal or bodily destruction he says: “And the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned.” Of the eternal or spiritual: “And the summit of Carmel was dried up.”

What beautiful things, or whose beautiful things, belonging to the shepherds mourned—and how did they mourn? Certainly that beautiful city Jerusalem, which killed both the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself; and the august temple within it, than which nothing in the world was more august; and whatever beautiful or pleasant things those false shepherds—the Scribes and Pharisees, who professed themselves shepherds though they were ravening wolves—could possess. They mourned with inconsolable grief when the Romans surrounded and devastated everything; after their victory, all Jews who could survive sword, famine, and fire were led captive among all nations. This was, and is, temporal destruction, bodily destruction.

But what was Carmel, what its summit, and how was it dried up? The interpretation of the name Carmel quickly reveals the matter; for Carmel means “knowledge of circumcision.” Thus Carmel, according to its name, signifies circumcision—that is, Judaism, which greatly glories carnally in its knowledge. The summit of that Carmel was the generation which crucified the Savior: “the generation whose eyes, as Wisdom says, were lofty, and whose eyelids were raised on high” (Prov. 30).

For that generation of circumcision judged itself to be, or to possess, the highest summit of knowledge, so that the Lord said that it had taken away even the keys of knowledge: “Woe to you,” he says, “because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11). Such also was the summit of Carmel, dried up after the Lord’s roar from Zion and his voice from Jerusalem, because from then on every dew of heavenly grace departed from them. The Lord commanded his clouds not to rain upon them, because they rejected the Word of God and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.

Upon that summit—that is, upon that generation—all the sins of all the other nations came, according to the declaration of the Lord himself. Having said, “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify,” and so forth, he added: “So that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen I say to you: all these things will come upon this generation” (Matt. 23).

It follows, therefore: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he threshed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges.” This is eternal destruction, spiritual destruction, in that he says, “I will not turn him back.” For whom does he call “him,” if not the summit of Carmel—that is, as we have already said, the pride of the knowledge of circumcision, of which that generation was in some sense the summit?

For when he says, “I will not turn him back,” Damascus cannot be supplied, since Damascus is feminine in gender. Likewise, when it is said, “For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back,” it cannot refer to Gaza, since Gaza is the name of a city and feminine in gender. And when it is said, “For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn him back,” “him” cannot suitably be referred in the singular to the plurality of the sons of Ammon.

Therefore, when he says, “I will not turn him back,” Carmel, or the summit of Carmel, must be understood: that is, the circumcised Jewish people, and especially that generation of the same people which crucified the Lord. Its condemnable character is indicated by the interpretation, already given, of the name Carmel.

For that generation is not lightly, nor without the weight of great indignation, called here the summit of Carmel; but in the same spirit and with the same anger in which the devil, under the name of the prince of Tyre, is called in the Prophet a Cherub because of his presumption in knowledge—Cherub meaning “fullness of knowledge”: “You,” he says, “were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were an outspread and protecting Cherub, and I set you on the holy mountain of God” (Ezek. 28). Again: “I cast you out from the mountain of God and destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones” (ibid.).

Likewise, the man to whom full knowledge was proposed as the price of transgression—when it was said, “And you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 36)—is marked by the same fault in the tree of transgression, since, because of what happened, a name was written for it ironically, so that it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Thus, through the summit of Carmel, according to the interpretation already given, we judge that the pride of that generation—or of circumcision excessively presumptuous in its knowledge—is here terribly denoted. Its presumption was so great that it hoped to entrap Christ, the power and wisdom of God, by deceit, and so make void God’s counsel: so that him who came blessed in the name of the Lord it might cause to be considered accursed under the hand of the law of the Lord, because the law had said: “He who hangs on a tree is accursed by God” (Deut. 21).

Accordingly, it is said terribly, and must be considered with fear and reverence, that because of the crimes of Damascus, of Gaza, of Tyre, of Edom, of the sons of Ammon, of Moab, of Judah, and of Israel, the Lord here judges and condemns that summit of Carmel, so that he does not turn it back—that is, he utterly rejects it and hands it over to blindness—according to the testimony of another prophecy, in which the same Lord says: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

Who could have perceived this unless the Lord himself had said more plainly and in harmony with it in the light of the Gospel what we have already cited: “So that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (Matt. 23). And again: “Amen I say to you: all these things will come upon this generation” (ibid.). Finally, if all things, then the crimes of Damascus and Gaza, of the Philistines and Tyre, of Edom and Moab, and of their fathers Judah and Jerusalem, had to come upon that generation according to this prophecy.

Yet, although they are said to come upon the summit of that generation, they are not said to be removed from those whose earlier crimes they were, or by whom they were begun. For each of those men had to bear his own burden; but that most unhappy generation had to bear both the burdens of all of them and its own proper burden. Truly an unhappy generation, set apart for an evil day, as this same prophet elsewhere says when, after crying, “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion,” he adds among other things: “You who are set apart for an evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity” (Amos 6).

For just as our Lord, blessing his apostles and saying, “I have sent you to reap that for which you have not labored; others have labored, and you have entered into their labors” (John 4), does not exclude the reward of those who labored and did not reap—namely, the holy patriarchs, who waited and “all died without receiving the promises” (Heb. 11)—but gives precedence to those who, without the labor of waiting, deserved to see him present with blessed eyes; so likewise, when he says, “All these things will come upon this generation,” he does not remove the punishment of Damascus and the rest, but judges that the punishment of that generation, which filled up their measure, will be greater.

Let us now continue the order of the text: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back.” He rightly places the crimes of Damascus first, because from Damascus came the beginning of the blood of which the Lord says: “So that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (1 John 3). For that is said to be the place where Cain killed Abel, and to have derived the origin of its name from that event. Damascus indeed means “drinking blood.”

Here the three and four crimes must be reckoned and identified by their proper qualities. The first crime is perverse will. Though it cannot be completed in deed, it is nevertheless a crime. Hence, because hatred is already the will to kill, every such person is called and is a murderer: “For everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (Matt. 9). Thus he who hates is already dead; but his death lies hidden within, and he can again be turned to life, just as the Lord raised that girl who had not yet been carried out but lay in the house (Luke 7).

The second crime is to have fulfilled one’s will in deed. By this act the sinner is dead and carried outside; yet he can still be raised, as the Lord raised the young man who was being carried out dead through the city gate.

The third crime is to have turned an evil deed into a habit; then the sinner is dead and buried. Yet he can still be raised to life, as the Lord raised Lazarus, already buried for four days and stinking (John 11).

The fourth crime is to take pleasure in one’s own sin and, in a spirit of pride, to resist God calling one back to repentance and his law rebuking one. This is a diabolical crime, marked in the Psalm by a brief verse: “They have said: We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11). To commit this crime and to speak in this way is to utter a word against the Holy Spirit, and it “will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12). It does not please the Holy Spirit to turn back one who has raised himself into this crime.

Now let us carefully consider the distinction or tenor of this text. “For three crimes,” he says, “of Damascus, and for four.” He does not say, “For three crimes and for four crimes of Damascus,” but places the name Damascus between “three” and “four,” and then adds the crimes. This construction must be watchfully considered throughout. Thus he says, “For three crimes of Gaza,” and then adds, “and for four.” “For three crimes of Edom,” he says, and then, “and for four.” It is precisely so in all the rest. Nowhere does he join three and four crimes.

If he did so, three and four would seem to be crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, Judah, and Israel. But now it is worth considering that each of these—Damascus and the rest—has only three crimes, while the summit of Carmel, that is, the often-mentioned generation in whose time the Lord came, has four. Indeed, it would not have had that fourth crime unless the Lord had come to it, as he himself testifies: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15). Again: “If I had not done among them works which no other has done, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (ibid.).

Therefore, because the Lord did not come to Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, or Moab—and neither had he come to Judah or Israel in earlier times as he came in the time of that generation—there are only three crimes of Damascus and the rest, but four of the summit of Carmel: that is, of that evil and adulterous generation of Jews, or Scribes and Pharisees, because they saw the Son of God and his works and hated both him and his Father.

Finally, Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, and Moab had these three crimes: evil will, evil deed, and the habit of evil deed. But regarding the fourth—that is, the proud defense of their crimes—they may seem to possess some defense, since they neither saw Christ nor knew his good Father, nor heard his law rebuking them.

Judah and Israel, indeed, before this generation had the law, transgressed it, and killed the prophets in defense of their transgression. Yet they are not so culpable; in comparison with that often-mentioned generation, they are far more excusable. For there are examples, both from Judah and Israel, of persons who would have repented had the miracles been performed among them which were performed in that generation.

For King Ahab of Israel, when he heard through Elijah the Tishbite the words of the Lord concerning the blood of Naboth whom he had killed, repented; he fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head. Therefore the Lord said: “I will not bring evil upon his house in his days” (3 Kings 21). And Manasseh king of Judah, after acting impiously and shedding much innocent blood, when he was afflicted, prayed to the Lord and did great repentance before the God of his fathers.

But that generation of which we are now speaking neither believed the Lord foretelling future evils, as Ahab king of Israel did, nor repented because of its great afflictions after the evils themselves had come, as Manasseh king of Judah did—although they perished by famine, sword, and fire, and although those who remained were led captive among all nations.

The Lord himself bears witness that the rest named in this place—Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Idumea, and the sons of Ammon—would have repented had this been announced to them. For when he reproached the cities in which very many miracles had been performed and which had not repented, saying, “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida,” he added: “For if the miracles performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth” (Matt. 15). What he testified concerning Tyre may be understood likewise of the other cities or nations, among which Tyre is here named in third place.

But if you ask, Why then was it not announced to them? Why were miracles not performed among them, since they would have believed and repented? For the present it must be answered briefly that God did not care, nor ought to have cared, for such repentance as theirs, which would not have been undertaken for the eternal salvation of the age to come, but in order to avoid adversity and retain the prosperity of the present life.

In this respect alone the often-mentioned generation proved more inexcusable and more criminal than all the rest: it believed neither the threats of temporal misery which the Romans were to bring, nor the Lord announcing the judgment to come or the fire of Gehenna; always unbelieving, always stiff-necked and rebellious.

Therefore Damascus and the rest have only three crimes, while the summit of Carmel has four, because the fourth is an unrepentant heart, or rebellion and defense of crimes. Three and four make seven, because an odd number is indivisible: it cannot be divided into equal parts. Just as it often signifies totality, so in Cain, who was a type of that generation, it signifies an indivisible or unending vengeance, when it is said concerning Lamech: “Vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech” (Gen. 4).

Indeed, vengeance seems to be extended when it is said of Lamech, “seventy-sevenfold,” because the number is longer; but, on the contrary, it signifies a divisible vengeance for Lamech, since that number is divisible, while “sevenfold” signifies an indivisible vengeance for Cain, since the number is indivisible. For no number other than one measures seven; but other numbers also measure seventy-seven, namely seven and eleven. For seven times eleven, or eleven times seven, is seventy-seven.

Thus, when it is said, “Vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain,” an indivisible and therefore greater vengeance is announced; but when it says, “For Lamech, however, seventy-sevenfold,” a divisible and therefore lesser measure of vengeance is assigned. Accordingly, when the Lord says, “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (ibid.), it must be understood: unless he repents. And in the law, whenever it is said that whoever does this or that shall surely die; and in the Gospel, “For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26), it must necessarily be understood: unless they repent.

The latter showed that he had no heart, since, though no one called him to judgment, he confessed himself guilty: “For,” he says, “I killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise” (Gen. 4). But the former, even when questioned by the Lord, impudently denied it, saying: “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (ibid.); and, when convicted, he despaired: “My iniquity,” he said, “is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (ibid.).

Thus this number seven also signifies the unending vengeance of that generation when it is said, “For three crimes” of these nations, “and for four, I will not turn him back.” This is the same as saying: Because of all righteous blood shed upon the earth, I shall cast away that generation; for, adding its own four crimes to the three crimes of others, it filled up the measure both of its fathers and of all nations.

He includes the crimes of Damascus in this one act: because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges. Damascus is known to have done this when Hazael reigned, according to Elisha’s prophecy. For it is written: “And he stood with him and was troubled until his face was flushed, and the man of God wept. Hazael said to him: Why does my lord weep? And he answered: Because I know the evils you will do to the children of Israel. You will set fire to their fortified cities, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little ones, and rip open pregnant women. And Hazael said: What is your servant, a dog, that I should do such a great thing? And Elisha said: The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria” (4 Kings 8).

What the prophet foretold came to pass, and in Hazael’s act the three crimes spoken of above are distinguished as follows. The first crime was his unsolicited hatred, by which he hardened his heart against God’s people, though he had suffered no injury from them; indeed, he was ungrateful both to God and to his prophets, Elijah and Elisha, through whom he had been marked out as king. For the Lord said to Elijah: “Go, return by your way through the wilderness to Damascus; and when you arrive there, anoint Hazael king over Syria” (3 Kings 19). The same had been revealed to Elisha when he said to him, as has already been quoted: “The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria” (4 Kings 8).

The second crime was that he fulfilled that hatred in deed, when he went up against Ahab king of Israel to fight at Ramoth-gilead, repaying evil for good, just as his predecessor Benhadad had done. For what good had the king of Israel done for him? When the defeated Syrians said, “Behold, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful. Let us therefore put sacks around our waists and ropes upon our heads, and go in to the king of Israel; perhaps he will save our lives,” Benhadad came out to him, and the king lifted him into his chariot. Benhadad said to him: “The cities which my father took from your father I will restore; and make streets for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria, and I will depart from you under a covenant.” So he made a covenant and dismissed him (3 Kings 20).

Both broke this covenant, because over Ramoth in Gilead, which was an Israelite city, each in his own time—Benhadad and Hazael alike—went up to fight against Israel.

The third crime of that same Hazael, king of Syria or Damascus, was that, not content with one victory at Ramoth-gilead, as often and as extensively as he could, he struck Israel and cut it down throughout all its borders, as the same sacred History later testifies: “And Hazael struck them throughout all the borders of Israel, from the Jordan toward the eastern region: all the land of Gilead, and Gad, and Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer which is above the torrent Arnon, and Gilead, and Bashan” (4 Kings 10).

Gilead, moreover, means “heap of witness,” and this name signifies the martyrs, that is, Christ’s witnesses. In persecuting them, that often-mentioned summit of Carmel exceeded the cruelty of this Damascus, or king of Damascus, and filled up its three crimes more abundantly with its own four crimes. Accordingly, just as all righteous blood, so also the blood which Damascus then shed, had to come upon that summit.

Yet here one may ask how the blood which Damascus then shed can be counted among righteous blood. For it is certain that at that time wretched Israel was defiled with the worship of idols; and for this reason it was handed over into the hands of enemies, enduring the just wrath of the Lord. To this it must briefly be answered that even then there was some righteous blood in Israel. The Lord testifies to this when he says to Elijah: “And I will leave for myself in Israel seven thousand men whose knees have not bowed to Baal” (3 Kings 19).

By the number seven thousand was signified the whole body of those who, even in that evil time, while Ahab and Jezebel reigned, did not consent to impiety, but remained hidden among themselves and worshipped the true God of their fathers. The bestial fury of Damascus threshed some of them. Moreover, even in all whom it dismembered while ranging about, those enemies persecuted not their merits of life but the confession of the true God—envying them above all because they were said to possess the true God, after the envy of Cain, who hated his brother for no other reason than that he seemed to him a worthier worshipper of God (Gen. 4).

Therefore reason does not exclude their blood either from all righteous blood shed upon the earth; and it judges, according to the Lord’s judgment, that it came upon that summit of Carmel, so that it was dried up and the Lord did not crush it—that is, upon the Jewish people of that time, under whom and by whom the blood of the Lord, and of the prophets, wise men, and scribes whom he himself sent, was shed by killing, crucifying, scourging, and persecuting from city to city.

It follows: “And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the houses of Benhadad; and I will break the bar of Damascus, and destroy the inhabitant from the house of the idol, and him who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure; and the people of Syria shall be transported to Cyrene, says the Lord.”

As has already been said above, when the Lord says that all things shall come upon that generation from the blood of righteous Abel—which generation we understand through the dried-up summit of Carmel—those who shed righteous blood are nevertheless by no means free or immune from punishment. Rather, they received punishment in their own persons also, and transmitted some inheritance of that punishment, as of their guilt, to that generation.

Thus, when he now says, “And I will send fire into the house of Hazael,” and so forth, we should understand it as done to that Damascus and that Syria for their three crimes—that is, because of their three crimes which we have already mentioned—while at the same time we regard that fire and dispersion, by which that generation perished, as coming upon the three crimes of Damascus and the four crimes which it added in its own time.

For we read that Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, after killing Rezin king of Damascus, transported all the people of Syria to Cyrene. Hence he now says: “And I will break the bar of Damascus, and destroy the inhabitant from the house of the idol”: that is, all the strength of the Syrians, by which, as by some bar, it repelled the assaults of enemies. And to show the futility of help from idols, when the people of Damascus were being taken captive at the Assyrian’s coming, he significantly says: “And I will destroy the inhabitant from the field of the idol.”

At the same time he accuses the people of luxury in saying: “And him who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure,” by whom we understand Rezin. The preceding words, “And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the houses of Benhadad,” indicate that Hazael, during the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, was already dead in Syria, and that his son Benhadad had succeeded him in the kingdom. From him all later kings of Syria and Damascus acquired the name Benhadad.

For this reason he did not say, “I will send fire into Hazael,” but “into the house of Hazael”: that is, into his royal house, over which his son Benhadad then presided. Yet Scripture does not explicitly say that material fire consumed his house, whether when Joash son of Joahaz struck Syria during the reign of Benhadad, Hazael’s son, or when the king of Assyria killed Rezin. For it is written: “Now Hazael king of Syria died, and Benhadad his son reigned in his place. And Joash son of Joahaz recovered from the hand of Benhadad son of Hazael the cities which he had taken from the hand of Joahaz his father in war; Joash struck him three times and restored the cities to Israel” (4 Kings 13).—“For the king of Assyria went up to Damascus, devastated it, and transported its inhabitants to Cyrene; and he killed Rezin” (4 Kings 16).

Nowhere here or there is fire mentioned, so that we could demonstrate the magnitude of a material conflagration corresponding to the grandeur of the prophetic proclamation. At the same time it should be noted that against all these denunciations of crimes—except in the eighth place, where it says, “For three crimes of Israel”—the same punishment by fire is appended in the same manner:

“And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the houses of Benhadad; and I will send fire into the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its buildings; and I will send fire into Teman, and it shall devour the buildings of Bozrah; and I will kindle fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its buildings; and I will send fire into Moab, and it shall devour the buildings of Kerioth; and I will send fire into Judah, and it shall devour the buildings of Jerusalem.”

These are the seven avengings by fire, corresponding to the three and four crimes by which Judah—or Jerusalem in that often-mentioned generation—filled up the measure of all righteous blood, whose material fire or conflagration the whole world heard about. Therefore, if history fails us by which material fire, sent against those particular buildings and walls according to this prophecy, can be demonstrated, nevertheless—and indeed much more—we should marvel at and revere the truth of the prophecy as fulfilled according to the subtlety of its intention. For that unhappy generation brought upon itself the fiery punishments of those nations whose crimes it filled up, and deserved a fire which, beginning here, would have no end, according to that declaration of the Lord in Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32).

It follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back, because it transported an entire captivity, to shut it up in Idumea; and I will send fire into the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its buildings; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; and I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord God.”

The five cities of the Philistines are named in many places. For example: “These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned to the Lord as an offering for their offense: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron” (1 Kings 6). The prophetic discourse here names all of them except Gath. Yet it does not wholly pass over that same Gath, when, having named the others, it finally says: “And the remnant of the Philistines shall perish.”

Concerning this nation—the Philistines—it must be known that when the children of Israel came up from Egypt through the Red Sea, it was the first to envy them. For among the other nations named at that time, we hear this one mentioned first in the pain of envy in the Song of Moses: “The peoples went up,” he says, “and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of the Philistines. Then the princes of Edom were troubled,” and so forth (Deut. 32). Among those suffering the pains of envy, he placed the inhabitants of the Philistines first.

Therefore, in the order of criminal nations, he might seem to have placed the crimes of the Philistines before those of Damascus or Syria. But it must be understood that even before the departure from Egypt—indeed, before Israel went down into Egypt—envy more directly stirred Syria to persecute the saints. The same Moses testifies to this when he says in Deuteronomy: “And the priest, receiving the basket, shall set it before the altar of the Lord your God, and you shall speak in the presence of the Lord your God: A Syrian persecuted my father, who went down into Egypt and lived there as a stranger with a very small number; and he grew into a great and strong nation,” and so forth (Deut. 26).

“The Syrian,” he says—that is, Laban from Mesopotamian Syria—having taken his brothers with him, pursued my father Jacob, whom he also overtook on Mount Gilead; but he saw in a dream one saying—
God: “Take care not to speak harshly against Jacob” (Gen. XXXI). That persecution by the Syrian [Col. 0268C] was already then both dangerous and a sign of the great persecution by which the proud were beginning to persecute the humble, according to the interpretation of the very name “Syrian.” For “Syrian” is interpreted as “exalted.” Rightly, therefore, the Philistines are placed here not before but after Syria, or Damascus—not only for this reason, but also because, as has already been said above, there was the beginning of the shedding of righteous blood, when the deadly Cain slew his righteous brother Abel.

Likewise, it is rightly asked why, at the head of the condemnation of the Philistines, Gaza rather than Ashdod, or Ashkelon, or indeed Ekron, is named, in the words: “For three crimes of Gaza?” To this it must be said that Gaza more fittingly bore the sad foretoken both of Jewish crime and of condemnation [Col. 0268D], namely because there Samson, the strongest man, both died and, in dying, killed more than he had killed while alive (Judg. XVI). What, then, is indicated in this deed of Gaza, or of the Philistines, by the crimes of which number has already been given? “Because,” he says, “it carried away a complete captivity, in order to shut it up in Idumea.” This appears to mean that Gaza carried off captives from the people of the Idumeans, and that it sold to the Idumeans those whom it had captured from the Jews. But even if this happened, it was neither so plainly accomplished nor with such a multitude of captives or persons sold that it should have been handed down in the sacred Histories; and therefore the matter seems too slight to deserve prophetic denunciation or complaint.

Accordingly, one must inquire more deeply [Col. 0269A] what Gaza, or the Philistines, acting in conspiracy with the Idumeans, did against the people of God. It has already been said that, when the children of Israel came up from Egypt through the Red Sea, the nation of the Philistines was the first to envy them. But it must be known, and there is no doubt, that if the Idumeans—the sons, that is, of Esau—had been willing to bring aid, as they ought by right, to the children of Israel as to their brothers, then both the Philistines and the Canaanites, of whom there will be discussion later, would not so easily have attempted to oppose them. Therefore it is likewise beyond doubt that their first concern was to revive among the people of that same Esau—that is, among the Idumeans—the ancient flame of envy which Esau had borne against his brother Jacob; indeed, by the evil winds of persuasion, to increase it, so that the Idumeans might agree with the other nations rather than with the Israelites, and, along with them, undertake common hostilities against [Col. 0269B] Israel.

That the Philistines were the first to do this is proved, for those who attend closely, by the testimony of Scripture. For it is written: “Therefore, when Pharaoh had sent forth the people, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near, thinking that perhaps the people might repent if they saw wars rising up against them, and return into Egypt” (Exod. XIII). “If they saw,” he says, “wars rising up against them”—which certainly would have happened, since already then, as stated above, “pangs seized the inhabitants of Philistia” (Exod. XV). Nor would they lightly have dared to do this without the agreement of Israel’s brothers, that is, the Idumeans; rather, they had prepared with them a common conspiracy and the same purpose.

This is sufficiently evident from the fact that, when the children of Israel turned aside from the Philistines [Col. 0269C], their own brothers, the Idumeans, were the first of all nations to meet them armed, as it is written: “Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, to say: ‘Thus says your brother Israel: We beseech you, let us pass through your land.’ Edom answered: ‘You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will meet you armed’” (Num. XX). Again, when they pleaded, he answered: “You shall not pass through.” And immediately he went out to meet them with an immense multitude and a strong hand, and would not yield to the petitioner by granting passage through his borders. “Therefore Israel turned aside from him” (ibid.).

Thus there is no need to doubt that the prophet looked to this when he said: “Because it carried away a complete captivity [Col. 0269D], in order to shut it up in Idumea.” For it carried away the complete captivity—that is, the children of Israel—when their captivity or sojourn in Egypt had been completed and passed, as they were coming up: that is, it caused them to turn aside and make a circuit by the way of the wilderness. Had the Lord not foreseen this, and had he led Israel through the land of the Philistines, the Philistines would certainly have shut them up in Idumea: that is, as the Idumeans came armed to meet them, as has already been said, the Philistines themselves would have pursued them from behind; and thus they would have crushed them when enclosed, and Israel would have repented of having left Egypt, when it saw wars rising up against it on every side.

The generation of the Jewish people, of which frequent mention has been made, fulfilled in this manner the measure of the crimes enumerated in this deed. When very many believed in Christ [Col. 0270A] and, at the preaching of the Gospel, crossed the Red Sea of baptism, pangs seized the Jews with the scribes and Pharisees; and they attempted to carry them away, in order to shut them up in Idumea—namely, when they pressed the matter by sending false apostles to induce them into their earthly and fleshly ceremonies, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And certain men, coming down from Judea, taught the brethren: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the law of Moses, you cannot be saved’” (Acts XV). Likewise: “But some who had risen from the sect of the Pharisees, who had believed, said that it was necessary to circumcise them and to command them also to keep the law of Moses” (ibid.). By saying and doing these and similar things, they stirred up no small disturbances against the Gospel of Christ.

Therefore, “For three crimes of Gaza, and for four I will not turn him back,” he says—understand: the summit of Carmel, that is, that generation of the Jewish people, upon which, just as all the other things, so also these three crimes of Gaza with its four crimes justly came. For just as Gaza, or the Philistines, envied with evil intent, persecuted in deed, and, as far as they could, did not cease to oppose; so they likewise envied the Gospel of Christ with evil intent, opposed it in deed, and even now do not cease to blaspheme—having a fourth crime in that they despise to hear the Law and the Prophets testifying against them.

“And I will send,” he says, “fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him who holds the sceptre from Ashkelon; and I will turn [Col. 0270C] my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord.” Sacred History does not relate where or when these things were notably accomplished according to the letter. But in that generation they happened thus. For the Lord sent fire upon its wall through the hands of the Romans, and devoured its houses; he scattered the inhabitants from Jerusalem and the holder of the sceptre, so that they should no longer have king or kingdom, since they denied Christ their King. And he turned his hand against all who survived the fire already mentioned, so that they were scattered and led captive among all nations.

The names themselves—Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Philistines—are suited to such a generation. Gaza, indeed, sounds like “strength,” and signifies the Jews’ rebellion against truth. Ashdod is interpreted as “the fire of the breast or of a paternal uncle,” and signifies the burning envy in them of their father the devil, which overflows in them. Ashkelon is interpreted as “murderous fire,” and denotes their homicidal fury. Ekron means “barrenness,” and signifies their destitution, because they flee the fruit of the Spirit and pursue the chaff of the letter. “Philistines” means “falling through drink”; and by this name we understand their truly drunken stumbling, according to what is written in the Psalm: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back always” (Ps. LXIII).

It follows: “Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Tyre, and for four I will not turn him back, because it shut up a complete captivity in Idumea, and did not remember the covenant of brothers; and I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its houses.’”

The same impiety which he had charged against Gaza he also charges against Tyre, saying: “because it shut up the captivity in Idumea.” That it may become clear from the authority of Scripture when or how this happened, let us look back at the sequel of the history mentioned above. After it had first been stated that the king of Edom denied passage through his land to Israel when it asked, and immediately came out to meet them with an innumerable multitude and a strong hand, there follows at once: “When the Canaanite king of Arad, who dwelt in the south, heard that Israel had come by the way of the spies, he fought against [Col. 0271B] him, and, gaining the victory, carried off spoil from him” (Num. 21). Here we judge that Tyre is put in place of the Canaanite, and that “for three crimes of Tyre” is said where it might have said “for three crimes of the Canaanite.” For the Tyrians and Sidonians are Canaanites.

But if it is asked why he chose here to write the name of Tyre rather than the designation of the Canaanites, we should know that the prophetic Spirit proposed to condemn in this sequence only those nations which had suffered no injury from Israel and had undertaken gratuitous hostilities against it, although Israel was not seeking their lands. Now Israel was seeking to possess the land of Canaan and had come up from Egypt in order to possess it; therefore the whole Canaanite people did not exercise such gratuitous [Col. 0271C] hostilities against Israel. Yet Tyre and Sidon, although they too, as has already been said, were Canaanite, are not recorded to have been objects of Israel’s design for possession or of Israelite warfare. Thus, the universal name “Canaanite” being suppressed, the name Tyre is used, because it hated Israel without cause, like Syria and the Philistines, and Edom, the sons of Ammon, and Moab—lands which the Lord had neither promised nor wished to give to Israel.

Now let us consider a certain difference, within the same crime, between the two passages. Of Gaza he had said, “because it transported a complete captivity, to shut it up in Idumea”; of the Canaanite, that is, Tyre, he now says, “because it shut up a complete captivity in Idumea.” Indeed, to have transported it with the intention of shutting it up is less than to have shut it up. It is evident that this is what happened in the events mentioned. There the Philistines did not shut up in Idumea that complete captivity coming up from Egypt, but were only prepared to shut it up; therefore the Lord led Israel around by the way of the wilderness. Hence the Philistines are charged with having transported the captivity, and then Idumea came out armed against it. But concerning the Canaanite, in whose place we understand the name Tyre to be used here, it is written that he attacked Israel when it was enclosed between himself and Idumea. For Israel had then come to Mount Hor, which is on the borders of the land of Edom. After it had been stated why Israel turned aside from Edom—“when they had moved the camp from Kadesh, they came to Mount Hor, which is on the borders of the land [Col. 0272A] of Edom”—there follows: “When the Canaanite king of Arad, who dwelt in the south, heard that Israel had come by the way of the spies, he fought against him” (Num. 21). This, indeed, was to shut it up. The other thing, however, was only in the will of the Philistines; and therefore it was said of Gaza that it transported the captivity in order to shut it up. But here it is said of Tyre that it shut it up.

It should also be noted how appropriately, in such a place, at such a time, and in such an event, he makes mention of captivity. By this word he strikes hard at the cruelty of their hearts: they begrudged the release of a complete or consummated captivity, prolonged for a long time, though they had suffered no injury from those captives—a captivity of such a kind that all people ought at least out of common humanity to have sympathized and said something like Jethro the Midianite, Moses’ kinsman, that is, father-in-law: “Blessed is the Lord, who delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh. Now I know that the Lord is great above all gods, because they dealt proudly against them” (Exod. 18).

It should likewise be noted that, after saying, “because it shut up a complete captivity in Idumea,” he added in the plural, “and they did not remember the covenant of brothers.” Who were those who did not remember the covenant of brothers? Clearly Tyre, or the Canaanite, and Idumea. For both entered into a plan and had one and the same intention: Idumea, or Edom, to go out armed against its brother returning from captivity; the Canaanite, to approve Idumea’s malice against its brother and, by hastening together with weapons, to show that fraternal hatred pleased him. Thus one of them attacked the covenant of brothers, the natural covenant; the other helped that it might be attacked.

Moreover, the Tyrians were in a sense brothers of the Jews, because Hiram, ruler of Tyre, had friendships with David and Solomon (3 Kings 5:6), so much so that he conveyed cedar timbers by rafts as far as Joppa for the building of the Temple and palace, while they supplied grain and oil to the Tyrians and gave him twenty cities in Bashan as a gift—cities which he refused to accept because they were full of grass. But what Tyre did against Israel or [Col. 0272D] Judah after that alliance and before the time of this prophecy, and how or when it shut up a complete captivity, sacred History does not relate. Likewise, what follows—“I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its houses”—is not found expressly handed down in the sacred writings.
