Nebuchadnezzar indeed, king of the Chaldeans, besieged and captured Tyre, according to the prophecy of Ezekiel: “He shall surround you with fortifications and carry an embankment into Egypt” (Ezek. 26); and again: “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army perform a great service against Tyre” (Ezek. 29), and the rest. Yet all this could have happened or been completed without a conflagration of fire. Therefore, however vengeance was exacted upon that Tyre, there is no doubt that the crimes of that same Tyre, like all the others, came upon that oft-mentioned generation; because what Tyre is accused of having done, that generation fulfilled spiritually by persecuting, as was already said above, the faith of Christ’s Gospel.

Accordingly, when he says, “For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back,” one must understand, as in the other cases, “the summit of Carmel.” For “him” cannot refer to Tyre, since Tyre is feminine. Why the summit of Carmel signifies that generation of the Jewish people which crucified the Lord has often been stated and must be kept in mind throughout this sequence of reading.

There follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his compassion, held fast to his fury beyond measure, and preserved his indignation to the end. And I will send fire into Teman, and it shall devour the houses of Bozrah.”

Behold, Edom is now blamed for the third time: first, when Gaza or the Philistines were charged; then, when Tyre’s crimes were reproved; now it is said in its own person what it did and what it deserves to receive. And rightly so: though the individual nations are rebuked on individual occasions, this impious brother of Israel is brought a third time before the judgment of the divine word, “because he pursued his brother with the sword and violated his compassion.”

Let us lift our eyes upward and consider the condition of that time, when Edom, as has already been said, denied its brother Israel passage through its land and even came out armed against it with an innumerable multitude and a strong hand; then we shall understand how great a violation of compassion this was. Israel was coming out, released from captivity, while Edom lived on its mountain, rich and strong. And although he was Israel’s full brother, born of the same father and, as the Apostle says, begotten together from one intercourse, he so closed every natural affection of brotherhood that among all nations none was more cruel against Israel; he strengthened the hands of the other nations and was the first author and forerunner of persecution and hatred.

Nor was his hatred directed against a human brother, but against God. For what cause was he borne along in such great hatred against Israel? Surely because of the blessing by which, through the Lord’s appointment, his brother had been preferred before him. Therefore, after the prophet said, “because he pursued his brother with the sword and violated his compassion,” he added, “he held fast to his fury beyond measure and preserved his indignation to the end.” He speaks of that fury and indignation because Edom—that is, Esau—raging and indignant, always hating Jacob, said in his heart: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I will kill Jacob my brother” (Gen. XVII). This inherited purpose of hatred the posterity now under discussion preserved to the end, doing to the extent of its power whatever fury and indignation suggested.

Indeed, while the children of Israel served in Egypt and paid Pharaoh and the mocking Egyptians the due of a most harsh servitude in mud and brick, Edom wickedly consoled itself over that unfortunate brother, and the spirit of hatred rested a little, judging that the blessing by which younger Jacob had been preferred before elder Esau must always prove vain: Edom was already reigning, while Jacob wandered miserably. But when God’s mighty works were done in Egypt for that brother; when Edom heard that he had gone out with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm—there can be no doubt that envy was renewed, fury blazed up, and indignation boiled over. For Edom was first with the sword, constant in hatred, and frequent in warfare against Israel, until, David prevailing, it perceived itself weaker in the Lord’s blessings, Jacob stronger, Israel more worthy: “All Idumea became subject to David under tribute; and he placed guards in Idumea and established a garrison” (2 Kings 8).

Therefore Edom has everywhere a bad and exceedingly bitter memory in the holy Scriptures. All murderers, all persecutors of the godly, have inherited its name so as to be called Edom, because it was the example of them all. For example: “Remember, O Lord,” says the Psalmist, “the sons of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” (Ps. 136). This is as if he said: All citizens of God’s kingdom, rejoicing above the rivers of Babylon—that is, above the course of the confusion of this age—say, “Remember, Lord, the afflictions inflicted upon us by the sons of Edom,” that is, the imitators of Esau, who was called Edom because of the greatness of his savagery. *Edom* means “earthly” or “bloodthirsty,” because they desire Jerusalem to be laid bare even to its foundation, so that the entire building of faith and truth may be utterly destroyed.

The greatest and best-known of all such murderers are the carnal Jews, sons of Abraham or Israel. They too, following the example of the elder Esau, lost their birthright—namely, “the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the promises,” which, as the Apostle says, ought to have been theirs (Rom. 9); while the nations, following the example of younger Jacob, inherited these same things. And just as Edom, the nearer in flesh to Israel coming up from Egypt, was the more wicked than the other nations in hatred, so the Jews, the nearer in flesh to Christ, were the more pernicious to the Christian people from the beginning of the preaching of evangelical faith—first before all nations, and the greatest among all nations as enemies and persecutors.

Thus what is now said—“For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back”—must indeed be referred to both, but especially to the Edom which is not according to flesh but according to spirit: namely, the Jewish people, signified by the summit of Carmel, as has often been said and must yet be said.

The punishment of this Edom is fire, of which we have often spoken: fire sent upon that generation which crucified the Savior in such a manner that, set ablaze by the Romans, it burns in the Lord’s fury “to the lowest depths of hell” [Col. 0275A] (Deut. 32), as he himself foretold through Moses: “Therefore I will send fire into Teman.” Teman is a region of Idumea; its name means “the south,” and it signifies the once-bright glory of the Temple of the city of Jerusalem. And when he says, “It shall devour the houses of Bozrah,” he signifies not another city but Idumea itself in the literal sense; in the mystical sense, however, he signifies the same Jerusalem, once fortified by the protection of God and the angels. For *Bozrah* means “fortified”; hence in Isaiah is that voice of astonishment: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength” (Isa. 63). For the astonishment is that, after suffering such things from the Idumeans—that is, the Jews—and from the city of Jerusalem which he had fortified by his protection, he comes sprinkled with his own blood.

There follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge his border. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its houses amid wailing, on the day of war, and in a whirlwind on the day of battle’s tumult; and Melchon shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord.”

This Ammon and Moab, whose crimes he is about immediately to state, were related to Abraham, being the sons of Lot, who was the son of Abraham’s brother. Therefore they too ought to have been more merciful toward the children of Israel than the other nations, especially since Israel had done them no injury and had not sought their lands. For these are those whose lands the Lord expressly forbade Israel: the Edom just mentioned, this Ammon, and the Moab following. Thus Moses recalls in Deuteronomy:

“The Lord said to me: ‘You shall pass through the borders of your brothers, the sons of Esau. Therefore take great care not to provoke them. For I will not give you any of their land, as much as the tread of one foot can occupy, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.’”

And again: “We came,” he says, “to the road that leads into the wilderness of Moab; and the Lord said to me: ‘Do not fight against the Moabites, nor enter into battle against them. For I will give you nothing of their land, because I gave it as a possession to the sons of Lot.’” [Col. 0275D] And afterward: “The Lord spoke to me, saying: ‘Today you shall cross the borders of Moab, the city named Ar, and you shall approach the territory of the sons of Ammon. Beware lest you fight against them or move to battle. For I will not give you anything of the land of the sons of Ammon, because I gave it as a possession to the sons of Lot’” (Deut. 2).

Since, then, Ammon and Moab were related to Israel, as has been said, and had suffered no injury either from Israel or from Israel’s God, they should have borne toward Israel a more merciful disposition than the other nations. Yet, like Edom, they proved instead more merciless and leaders in impiety. The Psalmist testifies to this. After saying, “The tents of the Idumeans and Ishmaelites have together plotted against your covenant: Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre; Assyria also came with them” (Ps. 82), he added: “They became a help to the sons of Lot.”

Among the other nations he had already named the sons of Lot by saying “Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon”; but he had not said which peoples were more vehement in that conspiracy. Therefore, lest this too should escape us, he says, “They became a help to the sons of Lot.” It should indeed be observed that he did not say that the sons of Lot became a help to the others, but that the others became a help to the sons of Lot. Thus it was not so much the others who drew the sons of Lot into hostilities against Israel as the sons of Lot who drew the others.

Ammon is therefore rightly charged in this deed, “because he ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge his border.” He does not say, in order to avenge his own injury or recover his own loss, but “in order to enlarge his border”—an indication of greed, an excess of wrongdoing, and proof of cruelty. For what could be more greedy, more unjust, or more cruel than to rip open pregnant women for such an object alone? Accordingly David ought not to be accused of cruelty but praised for justice and strength in doing similar or greater things to them, as it is written: “David therefore gathered all the people and went against Rabbath. And when he had fought, he captured it; and bringing forth its people, he sawed them, passed iron carts over them, divided them with knives, [Col. 0276C] and made them pass through brick-moulds” (2 Kings 12). Thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon. This, I say, was not cruel but just, because he rendered to them as they had done.

Now the sons of Ammon seem to have done this during Saul’s reign, when Nahash the Ammonite came up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead. When its inhabitants begged and said, “Make us your allies and we will serve you,” he said: “On this condition I will make a covenant with you: that I gouge out all your right eyes” (1 Kings 11). But Saul struck them and they were scattered, so that not two of them were left together; and the sons of Ammon are not recorded to have done anything of this kind then which would deserve so great a lament of the prophetic Spirit.

We therefore judge that the prophet had rather looked to the earlier history, namely to the time of the Judges, when Jephthah was sought out to judge the children of Israel because he was “a very mighty and warlike man, born of Gilead” (Judg. 11). For then the Lord, angry against the children of Israel, had delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and the sons of Ammon; they were afflicted and grievously oppressed for eighteen years. “The sons of Ammon fought against Israel,” Scripture says (ibid.), and Israel was greatly afflicted. “As they pressed them hard, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah as a helper” (ibid.). For those who read the rest and consider Jephthah’s vigorous dispute with the sons of Ammon, it is clear that the sons of Ammon inflicted that oppression, particularly in Gilead; and, among other things, they also ripped open pregnant women, although this precise expression is not written there, and they did it “in order to enlarge their border.”

For when Jephthah gave orders to the king of the sons of Ammon and said, “What is there between me and you, that you have come against me?” he replied falsely: “Because Israel took my land when it came up from Egypt, from the borders of Arnon as far as Jabbok and Jordan.” Therefore the Lord threatens that he will kindle fire in the walls of Rabbah, the metropolis of the Ammonites, so that “its houses may be devoured amid the shouting and wailing of the victorious army, on the day of tumult and whirlwind,” when its captives are led away after Nebuchadnezzar’s victory; and the Ammonites’ idol called Melchon, that is, “their king,” shall be carried to the Assyrians, and its princes shall likewise be taken away.

In the same manner as the other things had to come upon that oft-mentioned generation, these things too, which the sons of Ammon did, had to come upon it. Therefore the Lord’s words, “For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn him back,” must be referred to the summit of Carmel, of which we have already spoken; and, to avoid tediousness, it would not be necessary to repeat this so often, if it did not seem advantageous for the reader’s memory. There follows:

## Chapter II

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea to ashes. And I will send fire into Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth; Moab shall die amid tumult and the blast of the trumpet; and I will destroy the judge from its midst, and all its princes with him, says the Lord.”

Concerning Moab and Ammon, and especially Edom, it has already been stated how rightly they are charged with so great a crime, because they exercised hostilities against Israel coming up from Egypt, although they were related in flesh. Those who inquire what is meant by “because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea”—a king already buried, who had gone up against Moab with King Joram of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah (4 Kings 3)—say that, in revenge for grief, his bones were afterward torn up and burned by the Moabites. This is the Hebrew tradition. On this account, they say, God declares that he will send fire into Moab—a name signifying either the metropolis of the Moabites or the whole province—so that it may devour the houses of Kerioth, which is the name of a city.

But this seems too slight for the grandeur of prophetic authority: that what the Holy Spirit speaks in them should be established merely from Jewish opinion and not from the holy Scriptures. We therefore seek another burning which Moab committed, according to sacred Scripture. We read in the book of Numbers that Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent for and summoned Balaam son of Beor, a diviner, to come and curse Israel. Since he could not do this because God forbade him, he finally said: “Yet, returning to my people, I will give counsel concerning what your people shall do to this people” (Num. 24). Afterwards it is written: “The people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who called them to their sacrifices. And they ate and worshiped their gods, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor” (Num. 25).

That was a great burning, a great flame of lust, which consumed the people. And what were those men or those daughters of Moab, if not the bones of the king of Idumea? For who is the king of Idumea but the spirit of pride, which is said to be over all the earthly—that is, those devoted to earthly desire, according to the meaning of the name Idumea? That they came to that burning of their flesh through the spirit of pride is shown by the single example Scripture recounts: “And behold, one of the children of Israel went in before his brothers to a Midianite prostitute, while Moses and the whole assembly of the children of Israel looked on and wept before the entrance of the Tabernacle” (ibid.). It was surely great impudence and pride, at such a time—when the Lord had already said to Moses, “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them up before the sun on the gallows,” and Moses had likewise said to the judges of Israel, “Let every one kill his neighbors who were initiated into Baal-peor” (ibid.), and for this reason the children of Israel wept before the entrance of the Tabernacle—for a man to go in to a prostitute in contempt of heavenly wrath, before all their eyes.

By what name, then, could the dignity of the prophetic Spirit more fittingly call such fornicators than “the bones of the king of Idumea”? Should it have called them children of Israel? Balaam and Balak indeed had a common plan and one intention: to set the children of Israel aflame. This is recalled in the Apocalypse: “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumbling-block before the children of Israel: to eat and to commit fornication” (Rev. 2). But he could not so much cause the children of Israel themselves to stumble as cast a stumbling-block before them. For it is one thing to see a stumbling-block before oneself, another to be made to stumble and be inflamed by the scandal of burning lust.

Thus, as those who do not make use of such a stumbling-block are rightly called and are members of Christ, the King of glory, so conversely those who have been made to stumble or set aflame in this way are called and are members of the ruler of this world, the king of Idumea. They are more suitably called bones than members, although members are or have bones, because the native fire is planted in bones and marrow: when straw was added from without—that is, the daughters of Moab and Midian—it flamed there in unlawful burning. To have caused such an astonishing burning was a crime [Col. 0278D], especially with the intention that God, offended, might depart from Israel; and for this Moab is rightly rebuked as wicked.

But if, according to the Hebrew opinion stated above, it burned the bones of a dead man with material fire to ashes, I do not know whether that could be regarded as a great crime, since among almost all nations it has been customary to burn dead bodies to ashes and bury the ashes themselves. Hence tombs are called *busta*, that is, from burning, because they contain the remains of burned corpses.

Again, there is no doubt that this crime of burning also pertains to that generation which crucified the Lord, and upon which all the evils of former generations had to come. For they too are rightly called and are Moab and Idumeans. *Moab* means “from the father”; and the Lord shows whose children from the father they are or were, saying: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). They burned the bones of the king of Idumea; indeed, they themselves were the bones of the king of Idumea, king of all the children of earthliness and pride, bones set aflame by the fire of lust. Isaiah bears witness, looking ahead to that generation: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1).

Therefore, as the fullness of Moab’s sin, so the fulfillment of its punishment came upon that generation. For when he says, “I will send fire into Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth”—the name of a city in Moab—“and Moab shall die amid tumult and the blast of the trumpet, and I will destroy the judge from its midst and kill all its princes with him,” who does not know that this was all accomplished by the Roman destruction? Concerning the three crimes and the four, and the words “I will not turn him back,” this has often been said and it is tedious always to repeat it.

There follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. For their idols deceived them, after which their fathers went. And I will send fire into Judah, and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem.”

Behold, in this also there is no distinction between gentile and Jew. The divine word, an impartial judge, spares no person: when it has weighed the sentence of judgment, it treats Judah equally with the Syrian, the foreigner, the Tyrian, the Idumean, the Ammonite, and the Moabite; nor does it separate in punishment those whom guilt has joined. If a subtle rationale is sought, who should be punished more deservedly than one who received not only the natural law, as the other nations did, but also the written law?

It should therefore be noted that he does not reproach the foregoing nations with rejecting God’s law and despising his commandments, but with violating their own natural feelings, and with doing all cruel things without affection and without mercy, having no regard for common humanity and giving no attention even to the affection of recognized kinship. But he reproaches Judah because it rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. Because it rejected and despised the order and way of that law, its idols deceived it. Although he says, “its idols deceived it,” it is nevertheless certain that Judah could not first have been deceived by idols unless it had rejected the law of the Lord and failed to keep his commandments.

These are the idols after which their fathers went in Egypt: following the images of the Egyptian calf, worshiping Baal-peor, and serving Astaroth and the Baals (Judg. 3). Nor were they lightly deceived; they raved so much for their idols that their kings killed the prophets and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood up to the brim. Therefore the Lord threatens that he will send fire into Judah, to devour the houses and foundations of Jerusalem; and this was done.

But if all things had to come upon that generation from the blood of righteous Abel, as we have often said, how much more must these things come upon it, for which Judah is here blamed? Certainly we have said, and say, that all the things suffered by the saints from the blood of righteous Abel had to come upon that generation, through whatever nations or persons righteous blood was shed; so that we must not fail to recognize that especially the blood which Judah shed returned upon it.

For the Lord said both things: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.’ Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets. And you, fill up the measure of your fathers—serpents, offspring of vipers” (Matt. 23). He said this, indeed, to that generation concerning those fathers whose descendants or inheritors in murder the Jews were, both according to the flesh and according to iniquity; and they afterward killed Christ himself, who was speaking these things.

Again: “That upon you,” he says, “may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (ibid.), and the rest.

Indeed, the blood of righteous Abel was shed before the fathers came into being, from whose flesh the Jews boast themselves to have been born. Therefore the crimes or evils both of the other nations, discussed above, and of Judah, of whom the present discourse treats, were bound to come upon that generation. Thus, “For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke him”; that is: I shall abandon the wicked assembly of children, designated by the summit of Carmel, because of the crimes of their fathers, whose measure they themselves have filled up. Both what the Lord here says through the prophet, “I will send fire into Judah, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem,” and what the same Lord says of himself, “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23), came to pass; and there is scarcely anyone who does not know that it happened.

It follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke him: because he sold the righteous man for silver, and the poor man for sandals; they crush the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; a son and his father have gone in to the same girl, in order to profane my holy name; they have reclined beside every altar upon garments taken in pledge; and they were drinking the wine of those who have been condemned in the house of their god.”

Around Mount Carmel we tread, as it were, a steep path of ascent, going and returning there as often as the Lord says, “I will not revoke him for three and four crimes.” Finally, wherever or however often, in this sequence of crimes or criminals, we hear or read “I will not revoke him,” we understand Mount Carmel, set down at the beginning, to be implied. By it we said that the pride of carnal Judaism is signified, according to the very name Carmel, interpreted “knowledge of circumcision”; and especially that generation which crucified the Saviour.

We suppose that the reader who follows us—if there is anyone who wishes, by reading, to follow, or by following to read these things—has grown weary as he is repeatedly turned back to the same summit of Carmel, as though he were obliged, short of breath, to climb again and again to a fortress raised high and overhanging the clouds on a mountain peak. Yet whoever he may be, we ask that he be patient: the end is now at hand, and he will no longer be wearied by this circuit or return.

“For three crimes of Israel,” he says, “and for four, I will not revoke him.” We must now remember our purpose: at the beginning of this prophet we promised that we would explain why he mentioned the earthquake, 122 when, from the necessity of finding the mystical sense, we were investigating Carmel’s summit; namely, where, after the words, “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Thecua, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel,” he added: “two years before the earthquake.”

The Hebrews recall that the earthquake occurred when Uzziah king of Judah, claiming for himself an unlawful priesthood, was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chron. 26). In mentioning the earthquake, then, he also mentioned that leprosy. Why? Because the forehead of King Uzziah—the highest and most upright part of the body—signifies the same thing as this summit of Carmel; and the leprosy of the forehead, that is, the drying-up of Carmel’s summit, signifies the rejection of the proud and exalted generation which crucified the Lord.

So too with Miriam, Moses’ sister: when she murmured against Moses in pride, she was struck for that reason with the plague of leprosy (Num. 12). Likewise King Uzziah, who arrogantly usurped the priesthood and was therefore struck with leprosy on the forehead, bears one and the same signification: the pride of that generation. Yet the meaning of this same affliction differs in the two cases. Miriam, because of the uncleanness of leprosy, was separated outside the camp for seven days and afterward recalled; she signifies the Synagogue, which at last is to be regarded as healed of the leprosy of unbelief, when “the fullness of the nations has entered,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 11). Uzziah, however, remaining leprous until the day of his death, signifies the incurable sin of that same Synagogue, as regards that aforesaid generation and all Jews who meanwhile now depart this life, bearing a perpetual leprosy, to be healed “neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

Uzziah is interpreted “strength of the Lord”; but this name suits that generation only by antiphrasis, or irony, because it is deceived as though acting strongly when, by blaspheming Christ, it professes that it is rendering service to God. His son Jotham, whose name is interpreted “the Lord’s completion” or “perfection,” governing the household of the leprous king, signifies the younger people from among the nations, of completed and perfect faith, to whom the kingdom of God was given, as the Lord foretold: “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21).

Nor is it devoid of mystery that this plague of leprosy occurred on the summit of the royal forehead together with an earthquake. For when the unhappy generation condemned itself to such leprosy by saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27), and afterward the Lord gave up the spirit, the earth was shaken; and then the Roman world was stirred for the destruction of that nation. Meanwhile, it is clear that the prophet indicates one and the same rejection of the Synagogue for pride in a few words, both by the leprosy of the royal forehead and by the dryness of Carmel’s summit.

There are two mountains called by this name: one, in the southern region, where Nabal the Carmelite, husband of Abigail, was (1 Sam. 25); the other, overlooking the sea near Ptolemais, where the prophet Elijah, bending his knees, obtained rain (1 Kings 18). Here Carmel is to be understood as the one where, after a drought of three and a half years, rain was given. For there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit speaking in the prophet had regard to the event of that miracle, which had happened to the children of Israel not very many years before—indeed, as a figure, like almost all the rest.

For what was it that Elijah shut up the heavens, except that Christ closed the mouths of the apostles to the sinful Synagogue and to the people who rejected and abandoned him, leaving them dryness and hunger for hearing or understanding the Word of God? Again, what does it mean that, when Elijah prayed once more on Carmel’s summit, heavy rain came, except that Israel will again receive the dew of faith and the rain of salvation when “the fullness of the nations has come in” (Rom. 11)?

So great meanwhile is the dryness of unbelief as the three and four crimes, so often repeated here, deserve. Since these amount to seven, we judge them to be the spirits of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel. After saying, “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a man” (Matt. 12), he concludes: “Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in they dwell there” (ibid.). Likewise, the punishment for the same dryness of unbelief is as great as must be understood through the seven fiery acts of vengeance arranged in this reading: a universal and unending punishment, according to the meaning of the number seven, the indivisible number. For just as that generation bore the crimes of all nations, so also the punishments for all nations that shed righteous blood came upon it.

It should be noted that only here, in the eighth place, when it is said, “For three crimes of Israel,” is the vengeance of fire not repeated, so that, as has already been said, there may be only seven; by this number universality is customarily signified. At the same time, one must know that only seven nations are named here, because Judah and Israel are one people by nature, though divided by schism, from the time when Jeroboam tore ten tribes away from the house of David and from the royal tribe of Judah. This prophet was sent to the greater part of the division, that is, to the ten tribes called Israel; and therefore he placed Israel last, because he was going to speak more concerning it or against it.

Thus far, as best we could, we have dealt with the seven nations, the crimes of seven nations, and the seven fiery acts of vengeance for those crimes. Now at last let us hear Israel’s case in the judgment of the Lord.

After prefacing, as with the others, “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke him,” he immediately says: “Because he sold the righteous man for silver, and the poor man for sandals; they crushed the heads of the nations into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; a son and his father went in to the girl, in order to profane my holy name; they reclined beside every altar upon garments taken in pledge, and were drinking the wine of those who had been condemned in the house of their god.”

Perhaps it may seem strange to anyone that, at the beginning of Israel’s crimes, he preferred to set down something other than the worship of idolatry by which Israel was then stained—especially since, among other matters, the scandal of the calves made by Jeroboam, from whose sin none of Israel’s kings after him departed, was exceedingly grave and beyond remedy. Yet it is fitting and very orderly that the first thing mentioned is that Israel sold the righteous man for silver, because the first sin committed in that house was that the sons of Jacob—who is also Israel—sold their brother Joseph (Gen. 37). Then indeed they “sold the righteous man for silver.”

In that sale there was a twofold fault: he was both their brother and righteous. They sold him for twenty pieces of silver. What was this price for a righteous brother among so many brothers? Since the sellers were ten of the eleven brothers—Benjamin, the twelfth, being still little, was not there—only two silver pieces could fall to each one. Rightly, then, after saying that they sold “the righteous man for silver,” he added, “and the poor man for sandals,” because each of them could scarcely purchase sandals worth anything from the price of so great a sale.

This crime, begun in that nation, advanced so far that the Jews both persuaded others to sell Christ, supremely righteous and the Holy of Holies, and themselves bought him for thirty pieces of silver. When Judas returned that price to them, Caiaphas, the high priest of that year, could not even have shod himself very splendidly with it. Yet all of them could thenceforth have been unshod, 123 by losing their place, their nation, and the glory of the Temple in which they walked so proudly shod.

The prophet continues: “They crush the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble.” This is surely the work of the proud, especially since the Law expressly forbids oppression of the poor—the Law, I say, first given to those who themselves had been especially poor and had, through God’s mercy, come out of Egypt, the furnace of poverty (Exod. 1). The Egyptians had done this to them, subjecting them to the hard labour of clay and brick and crushing their heads into the dust of the earth—that is, lower than the dust of the earth.

It had been the Egyptians’ practice to turn aside the way of the humble, as Scripture elegantly and briefly intimates when Joseph says: “When Pharaoh calls you and asks, ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall answer, ‘Your servants are shepherds from our childhood until now, both we and our fathers.’ You shall say this so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, because all shepherds of sheep are detestable to the Egyptians” (Gen. 46). Did they not, then, become Egyptians themselves, crushing the heads of the poor and turning aside the way of the humble?

Indeed that crime advanced among them so far that they struck and crushed with a most insulting and excessively contemptuous tongue the head and forehead of poor Christ, who was uniquely humble. For example, when they said: “Whence has this man this wisdom and these powers? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not his sisters all with us?”—and similar things (Matt. 13).

“And a son and his father,” he says, “went in to the girl, in order to profane my holy name.” This too is surely a crime and a detestable abomination, condemned by the just sentence of the Law: “Whoever sleeps with his stepmother and uncovers his father’s shame—both shall surely die; their blood shall be upon them” (Lev. 20). Reuben is recorded as the first in that nation to do this: he went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine (Gen. 35).

But this cannot also be imputed to the father, though it is said, “A son and his father went in to the girl, in order to profane my holy name,” because the son alone committed the crime; the father suffered the injury and himself pronounced the penalty: “You have been poured out like water; do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. 49). Moreover, there is no doubt that this very crime grew among his descendants, since Isaiah, foreseeing it, called their rulers rulers of Sodom and their people the people of Gomorrah.

Certainly the Jews omitted none of the things done by the Canaanites; otherwise that land would not have vomited them out, as it had vomited out the Canaanites, by God’s judgment. For after forbidding this crime, among others, God finally says: “Keep my laws and judgments and do them, lest the land into which you are entering to dwell vomit you out. Do not walk in the statutes of the nations whom I am about to expel before you. For they did all these things, and I abhorred them” (Lev. 18).

In this crime he declares there to be a profanation of his holy name, because to defile one’s father with such foulness—as Absalom also defiled his father David (2 Sam. 16)—is to violate his holy name, from whom “every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3).

“And they reclined,” he says, “upon garments taken in pledge beside every altar.” Surely even retaining the poor man’s pledge is against the Law. For in the Law the Lord says: “But if he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight; you shall return it to him before sunset, that, sleeping in his garment, he may bless you, and you may have righteousness before the Lord your God” (Deut. 24). How much greater, then, is the crime “to recline upon garments taken in pledge,” and to do so “beside every altar”?

For a double crime is indicated here: the foulness of lust and the service of idolatry. The meaning is that, having altars everywhere, fashioning images of calves, worshipping Baal-peor, serving Astaroth and Baalim, and the other monstrosities of gods and goddesses, they stretched garments taken in pledge on cords beside all those altars and made *parapetasmata*, that is, curtains or veils, so that no one could see them committing fornication in the temple. Drunken and enslaved to lust, they even bought the wine they drank not from their own labour but from extortions. Therefore he immediately adds: “And they drank the wine of those who had been condemned in the house of their god.”

They did this in the shrine of their god, so that they polluted by filth and debauchery those whom they regarded as gods. The Jews also filled up the measure of this crime in retaining poor persons’ garments so completely that, when they handed over the Saviour, they simultaneously fulfilled the Scripture saying: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (Ps. 21 [22]).

Then they also drank the wine of his condemnation, as he himself complains in the Psalm: “Those who drank wine sang songs against me” (Ps. 68 [69]). For there is no doubt that those elders and priests were drunk—especially drunk on that Paschal night—when they seized our Lord; rejoicing as though over a victory, they drank more copious cups to one another and offered wine to each man the more eagerly according as he seemed more swift and ready in their service: to seize him, hold him, urge on his companions that they might lead him carefully, insult him, and congratulate the rulers on this, as though they were great victors.

It follows: “But I destroyed the Amorite before their face, whose height was like the height of cedars, and who was strong as an oak; and I crushed his fruit above and his roots beneath. I am he who made you come up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorite; and I raised up from your sons prophets, and from your young men Nazirites. Is it not so, children of Israel? says the Lord. And you will give wine to the Nazirites to drink, and will command the prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’”

A remarkable and terrible contrast. For to what end is this remembrance, set in contrast, of the destruction of the Amorite and of his height, except to show that God stands opposed and hostile to those who turn aside the way of the humble and, in pride, crush the heads of the poor—the crime for which he rebukes Israel, made proud from having been poor?

“But I,” he says, “destroyed the Amorite.” He could surely have said: “But I cast the devil down from heaven because of pride.” For *Amorite* is interpreted “one who makes bitter,” and signifies the devil, who is wholly bitter with the gall of hatred and every kind of wickedness, always and incurably bitter, and utterly opposed to every sweetness of divinity.

God surely destroyed this sort of Amorite, drove him from his boundaries, and maintains the unalterable sentence of his destruction, saying in the Psalm: “He who works pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100 [101]). And lest you doubt whom he calls that Amorite, he says, “whose height was like the height of cedars.” Another prophet testifies that this is the devil, saying to Pharaoh in the Lord’s discourse: “To whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and thick with foliage, lofty in height; its top was raised among dense boughs. The cedars in the paradise of God were not taller than it; the fir-trees did not equal its summit, and the plane-trees were not equal to its foliage. No tree in paradise was like it” (Ezek. 31).

Therefore this 124 Amorite is the devil, of whom the Amorite whom Israel killed while Moses was still living was a type. The Psalmist also recalls him, saying: “And he struck mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan” (Ps. 134 [135]). These were two kings of the Amorites. Recalling them in Deuteronomy, Moses says: “Og king of Bashan alone remained from the stock of the giants. His iron bed is shown in Rabbah of the Ammonites, nine cubits long and four cubits broad according to the measure of a man’s cubit” (Deut. 3).

Here, under the one name “Amorite,” we should remember both: the proud human king and the devil, king and prince of all. His height was like that of cedars—indeed, he himself was a cedar and wished to be higher than all in the paradise of God, that is, than all angelic powers. And he was strong as an oak because he scorned to bend beneath God and to be subject to his Creator.

Thus the contrast is remarkable and terrible, as has been said. After first setting forth Israel’s sin of pride in turning aside the way of the humble, he says, “I destroyed the Amorite,” and so forth. By this he dreadfully intimates that the unhappy Jews, lifted up in pride, would fall under the judgment of the devil, just as the human Amorite—who, as has been said, was a type of the devil—did: that is, the kingdom of God, from which the Amorite devil fell, would be taken away from them; and their place or land, from which the human Amorite perished when God destroyed him, would be removed from them.

Therefore, when he says, “I destroyed the Amorite,” this must be understood: “And I am not changeable; I shall not rebuild what I have destroyed, so that I who customarily destroy the proud should begin to favour you in your pride and your turning aside the way of the humble, because you are sons of Abraham according to the flesh.” It shall not be so. Rather, just as I reserved “many dwelling places in my Father’s house” for the humble to be raised from the earth after the proud Amorite—that is, the bitter devil—had been cast down because of pride, and just as I gave your fathers the land when the human Amorite and proud giant had been struck down, because your fathers were poor and humble, so, because you turn aside the way of the humble, “the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a humble nation producing its fruits; and your earthly place and nation together shall also be taken away” (Matt. 21).

Does not the name Amorite—that is, “one who makes bitter”—also suit the Jew, who is wholly set in the gall of bitterness and hates both Christ, whose works he saw and heard, and Christ’s Father, God himself? (John 15).

By the comparison with the height of a cedar or an oak, he signifies that he threatens both judgments already mentioned in brief words when he adds: “And I crushed his fruit above and his roots beneath.” The fruit above of the Jewish people was the heavenly gifts of God, while its roots beneath were the earthly goods in which it fixed the root of its heart—something it ought not to have done. The Lord crushed both these fruits, because, as has already been said, Israel lost both kinds of goods in that Amorite whose land it possessed for a time. Thus both the fruit and the root were crushed, so that not only his land was taken away, but he himself was cut down by the sword and all his posterity commanded to be destroyed.

Moreover, the fruit above of the Amorite devil was crushed when he was cast from heaven into this air. But his roots beneath will be crushed when he is wholly uprooted also from this air or world, where he bears evil fruit in the hearts of the faithless, and is cast down into hell.

He reminds the ungrateful Israelites in this manner of the two kinds of goods he had bestowed on them, which he was about to take away because of their pride: “I am he,” he says, “who made you come up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorite.” This is an earthly benefit. “And I raised up prophets from your sons, and Nazirites from your young men.” This is a heavenly benefit. How many Nazirites—that is, holy persons—and prophets did the Lord raise up from that nation, who bore fruit for the kingdom of God? Who can deny it? Certainly no one. Therefore he confidently asks: “Is it not so, children of Israel? says the Lord,” knowing that they can give no answer but that it is so.

They lost both, as has already been said: both the heavenly kingdom of God, in which there is a multitude of prophets and Nazirites—that is, holy persons—and the earthly place that had been the Amorite’s. Yet the gifts of God’s kingdom are lost by no one unwillingly, but only willingly; and so by them as well. They lost them willingly; they rejected them willingly. This is what immediately follows: “You gave wine to the Nazirites to drink and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’”

To give wine to Nazirites, who had the vow of continence upon them, and make them guilty of violating that vow, is sufficient evidence that they wished to have no holy person at all. To command the prophets not to prophesy was surely not merely to speak but even to act against the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets.

Although they thus despised the heavenly kingdom of God, they nevertheless always wished to retain the earthly place of the Amorite. Certainly this did not please heavenly justice. But what follows? Immediately: “Behold, I will creak beneath you, as a cart laden with hay creaks; flight shall perish from the swift, the strong shall not retain his strength, the mighty shall not save his life, he who holds the bow shall not stand, the swift of foot shall not save himself, the horseman shall not save his life, and the stout-hearted among the strong shall mourn naked on that day, says the Lord.”

When he briefly says, “Behold, I will creak beneath you, as a cart laden with hay creaks,” he indicates that they will be unable to retain the often-mentioned place of the Amorite, but must migrate to another, because they despised that which is better, God’s kingdom. Like hay cut down and put on a cart to be burned, it is dry and can no longer receive the dew of heaven or produce flower or fruit.

Further, a creaking cart, by its very creaking and loud groaning from afar, declares itself weighed down by its burden. By this comparison, therefore, he seems to signify that whenever Israel is cut down and removed from its land, it will happen in such a way that the surrounding nations far and wide may know that its iniquity has deserved this. Hence the Lord, speaking to Solomon of such matters, says: “Everyone who passes by shall be astonished and hiss, and say: ‘Why has the Lord done thus to this land and to this house?’ And they shall answer: ‘Because they forsook the Lord their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and followed foreign gods, worshipped them, and served them; therefore the Lord brought upon them all this evil’” (2 Chron. 7).

This surely is the Lord’s creaking like a cart laden with hay: not allowing the causes of their ruin or captivity to remain hidden. And because a cart moves more slowly and therefore can be overtaken more quickly by those pursuing it, while captured hay is easily scattered or even set on fire, he says: “Flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not retain his strength.”

If we refer these words and the rest individually to the impending captivity of the ten tribes, they are handed down as to be understood individually as follows. “Flight shall perish from the swift”: the Hebrews understand this as Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had formerly fled into Egypt. Here, however, let us take not the rulers themselves, 125 but their houses and offspring. “The strong shall not retain his strength”: they interpret “the strong” as Baasha, who was most ready for war. “The mighty shall not save his life”: they understand this of Omri. “He who holds the bow shall not stand”: they think this is said of Jehu son of Nimshi, who struck Joram king of Israel with an arrow. “The swift of foot shall not save himself”: they understand Menahem, who hurried in vain to send gifts to the king of Assyria. “The horseman shall not save his life”: they interpret this as Pekah son of Remaliah, who, allied with the Syrian, ravaged much territory during the reign of Ahaz king of Judah (2 Kings 17). “The stout-hearted among the strong shall flee naked on that day, says the Lord”: only Hoshea, who was the last king of the ten tribes and attempted to recall the erring people to the worship of God, shall come out of the conflagration as though naked. He calls him naked because the ten tribes were captured under him. This, says blessed Jerome, is what the Hebrews maintain.

But if we also wish to refer these things to that time which the prophet foresaw when he said at the beginning, “The Lord will roar from Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem” (Hos. 1)—namely, to the time of Gospel preaching, followed by the final captivity of that people—then that Pharisaic or Jewish assembly is properly denoted by all these names. For it truly and by a true likeness deserved, because of its sins, to be called hay; but falsely, in its vain self-estimation, it could for a time seem “swift, strong, mighty, holding the bow, swift of foot, a horseman, and stout-hearted.”

It is therefore noteworthy and worthy of reflection that as often as he threatens them here with evil in these declarative words—“I will creak beneath you; flight shall perish; the strong shall not retain his strength; the mighty shall not save himself; he who holds the bow shall not stand; the swift shall not save himself; the horseman shall not save himself; the stout-hearted shall flee”—that is, eight times, our Lord likewise cries out, “Woe,” eight times against that generation: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses while making long prayers. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who travel sea and land to make one proselyte. Woe to you, blind guides, who say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’ Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but inwardly are full of robbery and uncleanness. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones and every uncleanness. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous” (Matt. 23).

Conversely, one should observe that the same Lord pronounces his saints blessed the same number of times, that is, eight times: “Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are those who mourn. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. Blessed are the merciful. Blessed are the pure in heart. Blessed are the peacemakers. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5).

Likewise, as many words as were set out above for the condemnation of the unhappy—“I will creak beneath you,” and the rest—so many, that is, eight, are the proclamations of blessedness for the saints: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven; for they shall possess the earth; for they shall be comforted; for they shall be filled; for they shall obtain mercy; for they shall see God; for they shall be called children of God; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

Nor without reason is the number eight considered here in the reward of the godly and there in the condemnation of the same [read: of the ungodly], because both portions will be brought to completion in the eighth age of the world. Then it will be plainly known that “the judgments of the Lord are just and true” (Ps. 18 [19]). Not partially, as now, but wholly, it will be known how truly it is done—or has been done—by judgment that he has likewise said eight times: “I will not revoke him.” This is the supreme vengeance for the three and four crimes.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0289]

[Col. 0289C] The very great and nevertheless just judgments of the Lord concerning the Israelite people are most astonishing: for that people, as it is more distinguished than all others in the portion of the elect, so also in the portion of the reprobate it has become more contemptible than all before God and men, condemned both in the present age and in the age to come. These judgments are indeed worthy of admiration, but should not be investigated with excessive presumption.

For it is written: “He who is an excessive searcher into majesty shall be overwhelmed by it” (Prov. 25). Who, then, should be judged an excessive investigator of majesty except one who investigates majesty beyond what he ought? There is certainly a definite place in which alone we are permitted to investigate it: namely, Holy Scripture. The Psalmist testifies that we may investigate the judgments of the Lord only in it and through it when he says: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth” (Ps. 118 [119]). By adding “of your mouth,” he shows that he is content with the authority or testimony of sacred Scripture, which indeed the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

And who investigates the judgments of the Lord apart from it except one who bears witness to the conjecture of his own heart? Such an investigator of majesty is surely excessive; therefore, overwhelmed by it, he falls into diverse and contrary heresies. Let us therefore, content with the proper place, apply a well-disposed mind and an attentive ear to the utterances of divine authority.

[Col. 0290C] These utterances, indeed, proceed from the oracle of the Holy Spirit with wonderful subtlety as follows.

## Chapter III
> “Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, children of Israel, concerning the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying: You alone have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities. Shall two walk together unless they have agreed? Shall a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Shall a lion’s cub utter its cry from its den unless it has seized something? Shall a bird fall into a snare on the ground without a fowler? Shall a snare be taken up from the ground before it has caught something? If a trumpet sounds in a city, will not the people be afraid? Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done? For the Lord God will not do a thing unless the Lord has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion roars: who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?”

These sayings are truly most clear and exceedingly splendid; yet their brightness and clarity shine less upon us because we endure our own darkness, and our bleary eyes are dazzled by excessive brightness. But if, through the inspiration of him whose sayings these are, we have deserved in some measure to grasp their meaning, we shall certainly be able to praise the Lord’s judgments not merely humbly but also knowingly. “Hear,” he says, “the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, children of Israel.”

This man, shortly before a shepherd from Tekoa and immediately a heavenly rhetorician, being about to say great things, appropriately demands an attentive hearer. He does so by recalling a great and well-known benefit: after first saying, “Hear the word which the Lord has spoken,” he adds, “concerning the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt.” For the recollection of this benefit ought especially to bring it about that hearers who could already be attentive may also become well disposed.

“But the Lord spoke, saying: ‘You alone have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities.’” At this utterance of the Lord, Israel, unrepentant yet not unpunished, exalts itself in its punishment; and from that punishment, which it cannot conceal or disguise, it still defends its guilt, proudly saying: “For this reason we alone, above the other nations, are chastised by God and led captive among all nations: because he loves us more than the other nations, as he himself says through the prophet: ‘You alone have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities.’ For the Lord does not determine concerning us, as he patiently waits in the case of other nations so that, when the day of judgment comes, he may punish them in the fullness of their sins, that after our sins have run to their end he should then at last exact vengeance upon us.”

Thus, captives in body and soul still console themselves—but truly in vain—so long as they remain unrepentant and do not renounce the sin for which they are punished. For what does God intend by correcting, what does the Lord intend by visiting iniquities, except that the sinner, admonished by blows, may acknowledge sin, seek pardon, and turn toward better things? He wholly intends that the sinner who displeased God may also displease himself. But if he is so rebellious and stiff-necked that this cannot be accomplished by chastisement, then at last God no longer acts as a merciful father, but as an angry judge: he casts the obstinate person out and rejects him, as in no way suited or consenting to himself.

God, wishing this intention of his to be known, says later in the same prophet: “Therefore I gave you cleanness of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places, and you did not return to me” (Amos 4, and what follows). Thus the people, oppressed by such great evils, have no basis for consolation, since they are in no way schooled by punishment into correction. And because they flatter themselves in this matter through the Lord’s words, “You alone have I known among all the families,” these same words must be turned back upon them in a sterner sense.

“I have known you,” says the Lord, “among all families, in such a way as to make you possess knowledge of me, by giving you the written Law, which I had not given to the other nations.” Now it is fitting that the servant who knows his master’s will and does not perform it should deservedly be beaten with many stripes, whereas the one who does not know should be beaten with few (Luke 12). Therefore, “I will visit upon you all your iniquities” [Col. 0292A], when judgment comes and mercy is removed, with such severity that I shall not even wish to confer with you a word of warning.

And if you still inquire, behold how reasonable this is through a comparison intelligible to every hearer: “Shall two walk together unless they have agreed?” You will surely answer me: No. To this I say: We are two—God, who rebukes or corrects, and Israel, which is corrected. Clearly we do not agree, because corrected Israel does not heed God when he corrects. We disagree exceedingly in this: I rebuke; it defends itself. Behold, so many years have passed, and there have been so many kings, since Jeroboam made the golden calves. I sent prophets, and none agreed; for none of the kings departed from Jeroboam’s sins.

Likewise, I myself came, rebuking and correcting, God made man. Yet you justify yourselves before men; and though you are sick, you say to the physician: “You are not necessary to us.” Therefore we shall not walk together; rather, Israel shall be led captive to the Assyrians and Judah among all nations. Israel will be judged unworthy of any further converse with me through prophets or preachers, because it is written: “Do not pour out a word where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32).

But if a further comparison or example is sought, behold another: “Shall a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey?” It is the lion’s nature to remain silent so long as it has not found prey; but once prey is found, it roars, so that whatever animal it may be, terrified and stunned by the roar, falls and yields itself as prey to the stronger—not so much patiently as impatiently.

Now the lion, by comparison, is God most mighty, whose wrath no one can resist. His prey is every elect person who, wherever he may be, because he has been predestined to life, is sought by God himself, so that, upon hearing his voice—whether through an angel, prophet, or the Scriptures—he may tremble; and, fearing the day of judgment or the punishment of Gehenna, may humbly submit himself altogether, embrace repentance, and thus yield into God’s portion and become one spirit with him, being well devoured, according to the saying: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10).

Therefore, when he says, “Shall a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey?” it is as though he said: Is it fitting for God to speak words there, or to send a prophet there, where he knows that there is no one worthy of eternal life? When reason requires you to answer this, “No,” you must consequently, as is just, grant that God’s judgment was just in closing to Israel the mouths of the prophets and uttering over it no roar of his preaching.

The Son of God observed this same principle in his advent. Hence follows: “Shall a lion’s cub utter its cry from its den unless it has seized something?” The lion’s cub is Christ, the mighty Son of the most mighty God, according to the patriarch Jacob’s saying: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up.” His den was his tomb, concerning which Jacob immediately adds: “Resting, you lay down as a lion and as a lioness; who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49).

The voice which this lion’s cub gave from that den is the preaching of the Gospel, which he caused to be heard among all nations after he leapt from that den—that is, from the tomb—by rising from the dead. He says, then: “Shall a lion’s cub utter its cry from its den unless it has seized something?” As if to say: Will he preach his Gospel, or command it to be preached, among nations or in places where he knows there is no one who belongs to him and ought to receive the grace of preaching? Certainly not. Rather, he will remain silent and forbid his preachers to utter their voice there.

For concerning these very preachers it is written: “Having passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they came to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16). Therefore this lion’s cub gives his voice there, or at that time, where or when he knows that he will find what he may seize—that is, someone who will be saved by believing. Hence again it is written in the same place: “When they had passed through Mysia, they went down to Troas. And a vision appeared to Paul by night: a certain Macedonian man stood and begged him, saying, ‘Cross over into Macedonia and help us.’ When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to depart for Macedonia, being assured that God had called us to evangelize them” (ibid.).

Meanwhile, it should be noted that in the preceding verse, when he says, “Shall a lion roar,” he significantly adds, “in the forest,” and only then adds, “unless he has prey.” The same phrase must likewise be understood in the following verse when he says: “Shall a lion’s cub utter its cry”—namely, *in the forest*? For what should be understood by “the forest” except the multiplicity of humankind, which has increased beyond the number [of the elect], and whose abundance is wholly wild and barren?

For the lion, or the lion’s cub, does not seek to seize the forest, but something *in* the forest. That is, God, or Christ the Son of God, did not seek those whose birth was caused by sin, but sought and seeks only the children of blessing through his Law or Gospel. He himself knows where or when he ought to seek them, and who they are.

Whom, then, do we call the children of blessing? Surely those whom, when the first human beings had been created, he commanded to be born by blessing them, as it is written: “And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it’” (Gen. 1). He commanded only his elect to be born then; and unless sin had intervened, only the elect would have been born, or would be born.

Whoever are born beyond the number of the elect are born because of sin, and sin is the cause of their multiplicity or multitude. For because of sin the Lord said to the woman: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3). This multiplicity, before this lion or lion’s cub, is indeed a forest, into which all God’s elect have been cast down and scattered, wandering so that they could not be found or distinguished unless God, or the Son of God, sought them with great vigilance, like a hungry lion or a famished lion’s cub.

Therefore, by these three verses—“Shall two walk together unless they have agreed? Shall a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Shall a lion’s cub utter its cry from its den unless it has seized something?”—by these three verses, I say, if they are rightly understood, we consider God sufficiently excused for having said so often above, “I will not turn him,” and for the fact that his silence is not the cause of some persons’ destruction.

For some did not perish because he was silent; rather, because they could not be converted, he withheld his voice from them, “not being ignorant,” as Wisdom says, “that their nation was wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could not be changed forever; for their seed was cursed from the beginning” (Wisdom 12).

But perhaps someone will say: This same lion’s cub said with his own mouth, “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done repentance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11). Likewise: “For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained to this day” (ibid.). Why, then, did the lion not at least roar there, since there was something he could have seized?

But we have already spoken elsewhere on this matter. Therefore it need not detain us long; nevertheless, we repeat briefly that God neither cared, nor ought to have cared, for such repentance on their part as would not have been undertaken for the eternal salvation of the age to come, but to avoid adversity and retain the prosperity of the present life.

To continue the prophetic words, we must first know that, just as it belonged to the prophetic Spirit to justify God and defend him concerning those who perish, so it likewise belonged to that same Spirit to commend God’s grace in those who are saved. Having observed this, let us see what follows: “Shall a bird fall into a snare on the ground without a fowler?”

Oh, how the comparisons of worthless things proclaim a precious mystery! This prophet, taken from pastoral life, is content to commend divine mysteries by comparisons drawn from things he was accustomed to see or do in the pastures. Thus he begins: “And the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned” (Amos 1); then says: “The Lord will roar from Zion” (ibid.); and, “Shall a lion roar in the forest, and shall a bird fall into a snare?” and other similar sayings, almost all of which are pastoral.

Things or instruments belonging not only to fishermen but also to shepherds suffice for heavenly teaching, so that, taught through their comparisons, they may fittingly teach the glory of heavenly things. “Shall a bird,” he says, “fall into a snare on the ground without a fowler?” You will plainly answer: No. Unless the fowler skilfully stretches his snare with care and strives with every effort to catch the bird, the bird, always fleeing and wandering—whether it be dove or turtledove, or indeed a fat thrush—will sooner run into the jaws of a hawk, sooner yield as prey to the hawk, than of its own accord fly to the table of the renowned king.

What grace, then, does the provident fowler owe the bird when he has caught it with his snare? Certainly none; rather, the whole matter must be attributed to his own skill. So indeed, when God’s truth has caught in its snare a wandering soul flying through empty things and false madness, so that it consents to the truth, being beneficially ensnared by the word of salvation—which it cannot contradict and therefore does not even wish to contradict—the whole must be attributed to God’s grace, which stretches the snare of its good word, so that the wandering little bird, namely the soul, may come into the hand of the Lord God before it runs into the jaws of the devil.

Thus, through this comparison this verse commends God’s grace; the following verse commends the effective force of God’s power, his efficacious power. For he says: “Shall a snare be taken up from the ground before it has caught something?” This is the same as saying: God intends a good work, a perfect work. “Shall my word return to me empty?” Certainly not. For he himself says in another prophet: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth and soak it and cause it to sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55).

Let us understand this saying in the same sense, as though the prophet said: Just as a snare shall not be taken up from the ground before it catches something, so my word shall not go forth in vain, but shall prosper in this: that it may bring back to me the entire number of the elect.

But in the gathering of the elect, rightly understood through the catching of the snare—as likewise through the casting of fishermen’s nets—does the wisdom of reason alone operate, or also the most mighty terror of judgment, heard throughout the world? Therefore follows: “If a trumpet sounds in a city, will not the people be afraid?”

For the trumpet, a signal of war, signifies the revelation of God’s wrath to come upon every ungodly person. At that time it was announced by the voices of the Law and the prophets, but at last it is revealed through Christ’s Gospel. “For the righteousness of God,” says the Apostle, “is revealed in it” (Rom. 1). Again: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (ibid.).

Therefore, when he says, “If a trumpet sounds in a city, will not the people be afraid?” it seems to be the same as saying: Although the word or wisdom of God, catching the simple in their simplicity and the wise in their cunning, has been signified by the comparison of a snare, nevertheless do not suppose that God’s word must always sound in a subdued voice, whisper in corners, and be heard from the ground. It shall be heard terribly throughout the whole world, like a trumpet sounding in a city; and when the people hear it, they will undoubtedly be afraid.

But the city of the devil, opposed to the city of God, is not converted either by the subtlety of the snare or by the terror of the sounding trumpet, so as to come to its senses and escape God’s wrath. Therefore evil does not fail it, neither in this age nor in the future one, by the working of God’s judgment.

Thus follows: “Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” Indeed, no one can deny that evil exists in that city—that is, in this world, “which lies in the evil one” (John 5)—but citizens of that city, rebellious and unbelieving toward God, strive to deny that the Lord himself causes that evil.

For example: evil came upon the city of Samaria because of the golden calves which Jeroboam made, from whose sins none of the kings of Israel departed; namely, the evil by which Israel was led captive by the Assyrians. Likewise evil came upon the city of Jerusalem, when it was first destroyed by the Babylonians and afterward by the Romans. Did not the Lord cause such evil? For the evil which is iniquity the Lord did not cause; but the evil which is suffering on account of iniquity, the Lord brought in.

How can this be proved? He says: “For the Lord God will not do a thing unless the Lord has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.” Surely, a great and evident argument proving that the Lord caused this kind of evil is that, before he does it, before the evil itself comes, while the secret still lies hidden in the Lord’s plan, he reveals it to his servants the prophets, that they may proclaim what is to come, so that some who hear may fear, guard themselves, and flee, according to the saying: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59).

Thus the Lord God did not make the flood (Gen. 6) without first revealing his secret to Noah his servant. Thus he did not rain fire and sulphur upon Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 18) without first revealing his secret to Abraham his friend. Thus he did not strike Egypt, nor drown Pharaoh and his whole army in the Red Sea (Exod. 34), without first revealing his secret to Moses his servant.

The same should be understood concerning everything else which has been done or will be done until the last trumpet, at whose sound the final judgment will be held: nothing has been done or will be done without having first been revealed. Therefore there shall be no evil in the city which the Lord has not caused; and this can be proved from the fact that the Lord God does nothing unless he first reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.

While saying these things—the man who was a shepherd—he must be understood as if saying: The Lord will cause evil in Israel, and before he causes it he has revealed his secret to me, his servant and prophet. Also, it must be remembered that rebellious and contemptuous Israel, together with its kings, imposed silence on the prophets, as the Lord himself said above in his own person: “You gave wine to the Nazirites, and commanded the prophets, saying: ‘Do not prophesy.’”

And to which of all prophets would they give this command more insolently than to this one who had been a shepherd? Therefore, a shepherd indeed of livestock, but an imperial commander in authority, he girds himself with strong authority and says: “The lion roars: who will not fear?” He immediately explains why he has taken up this comparison by the question which follows: “The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?”

For this is its meaning: You kings and princes and proud rich men are accustomed to command prophets and say, “Do not prophesy.” Who am I? Yet I say to you: when the Lord speaks and says, “Go and prophesy,” I fear as at the roar of a lion; I dare not be silent, and I am under the necessity of prophesying, although you are kings and I am a shepherd. And what do you want? “If it is just before God to obey you rather than God, judge for yourselves” (Acts 5).

But was he to await the decision or judgment of those whose custom was to command and tell prophets, “Do not prophesy”? Would they not, according to their own will, judge that obedience should be rendered not to God rather than men, but to men rather than God? Indeed, they would reckon preferring God to a human king to be rebellion. Hence it is written much later: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: “Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear all his words” (Amos 7).

Rightly, then, without waiting for an answer, after saying, “The lion roars: who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?” he immediately and steadfastly added the Lord’s own roar, the Lord God’s own utterance:

> “Make it heard in the palaces of Ashdod and in the palaces of the land of Egypt, and say: Assemble upon every mountain of Samaria, and see the many madnesses in its midst, and those suffering oppression in its inner chambers. They have not known how to do what is right, says the Lord, storing up iniquity and plunder in their houses. Therefore thus says the Lord God: The land shall be afflicted and encircled; your strength shall be taken from you, and your houses shall be plundered.”

This is the lion’s roar; this is the Lord’s utterance, terrifying the prophet lest he dare to be silent or delay to prophesy. He is commanded to announce to Ashdod and the land of Egypt what follows: “Tell those nearby,” he says, “to assemble and behold Israel’s crimes, lest they judge the sentence unjust.” It is as if he said: First see what they do, and then approve my judgment.
