Moses showed that he possessed this concern when the Lord was angry because of the calf which Aaron had made and said, “Let me alone, that my fury may be angry against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32). Standing “in the breach”—that is, in profound humility of heart before him—Moses prayed, saying: “Do not, I beseech you, let the Egyptians say: ‘He brought them out craftily, in order to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth.’ Let your anger cease, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people” (ibid.).

Therefore, since then, as it seemed to my friend Moses, it did not serve my honor to destroy them lest the Egyptians say such a thing, because the causes for which I could justly be angry against my people were not yet known to them, now let the madnesses which they commit become known both to the Egyptians and to Ashdod—that is, to the Philistines, Israel’s perpetual enemies. Let them see the magnitude of the madness—or rather, the many madnesses—in the midst of Samaria: that in place of God they worship calves, sacrifice their sons, and further commit oppression in their inner chambers; so oppressive, so unjust, that they do not know how to do what is right—that is, they do not approve uprightness or justice in any way.

For in this case not to know is to despise. In the same manner Pharaoh, not understanding, said: “I do not know God, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5). The Jews also, seeing the Lord and works such as no one else had done, said: “We know that the Lord spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9).

Now in this passage their “not knowing” is chiefly indicated to have been caused by covetousness, which blinds even the eyes of the wise, when it immediately adds: “Storing up iniquity and plunder in their houses.” How great a condemnation it is to heap up treasures from iniquity and plunder cannot be adequately expressed—especially among that people which was poor in Egypt (Exod. 23) and which the mercy of the liberating God brought out from that furnace of poverty. This pride is especially detestable in servants redeemed from poverty and slavery.

Therefore he appropriately says, “Assemble upon every mountain of Samaria and see,” intending by the name “mountains” to indicate the greatness of their pride. The province of Samaria is indeed situated in mountainous country; but for recognizing the justice of God’s judgment on the day of judgment, it is more valuable to consider the height of Samaritan pride than the earthly or local mountains of Samaria.

“Therefore,” he says, “the land shall be afflicted and encircled; your strength shall be taken from you, and your houses shall be plundered.” It would have been too little to say, “The land shall be afflicted and encircled,” unless he had added, “and your strength shall be taken from you.” For the land had been afflicted even before those times: when, as we read in the book of Judges, “the Lord gave Israel into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him eight years” (Judg. 3); when he strengthened Eglon, king of Moab, against them and they served him eighteen years; when he gave them into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, who oppressed them grievously for twenty years; when he gave them into the hands of Midian for seven years and they were greatly oppressed by them; and when he gave them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, who afflicted and grievously oppressed them for eighteen years.

So many times—that is, five times—the land had been afflicted; but your strength, O Israel, had not yet been taken from you, for you had not yet departed captive from your own land. Now, however, “your strength shall be taken from you, and your houses shall be plundered,” because you will depart captive, all your possessions becoming spoil to the Assyrians who take you captive.

For if someone asks: “Will no remnant remain?” he immediately adds:

> “Thus says the Lord: As a shepherd rescues from the lion’s mouth two legs or the tip of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued, who dwell in Samaria in the wound of a bed and on the couch of Damascus.”

These remnants—namely, two legs and the tip of the ear of any small animal—are small indeed, but being rescued from the lion’s mouth they have this use: from them one may recognize what kind of animal the lion devoured, whether sheep or calf, donkey or foal. Although animals passing under the shepherd’s rod have four legs, two legs suffice for judgment, one from the front and one from the rear.

“So,” he says, “shall the children of Israel be rescued”: that is, some will survive the great devouring and many deaths, whose calamity will cause people to remember what they once were and what grace they lost because of their sins. We now recall that verse in the Psalm: “God has shown me over my enemies; do not kill them, lest my people ever forget; scatter them in your strength” (Ps. 58).

We do not think that saying concerns only the dispersion of the Jews carried out under the command of Vespasian and Titus, but also the captivity of the ten tribes which was then impending and came about through the Assyrians who took them captive. The Spirit of prophecy foresaw both captivities, which took place so that they might confirm the faith of the nations not merely in one place but throughout the whole earth. For that reason, part of them was drawn out “like two legs or the tip of an ear from the lion’s mouth”—that is, from the slaughter of the ravagers—and permitted to live, so that by their testimony or memorial also God’s justice might be proclaimed and the truth of the Scriptures might be everywhere, as they carried them about; through those Scriptures Christ, the Son of God, is known, having testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

Miserable remnants, therefore, thus rescued, useful to others and not to themselves. He immediately adds the cause of such great devouring:

> “Those who dwell in Samaria in the wound of a bed and on the couch of Damascus.”

It is a great cause and the guilt of a great crime which he signifies by words of this sort. For at the time when the captivity of the ten tribes was impending under this prophet’s ministry, Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, and Rezin king of Syria were allied; and together they went up to wage war against Jerusalem. When they besieged Ahaz, they could not overcome him (4 Kings 16).

Therefore the children of Israel, or inhabitants of Samaria, are reproved because they rested “in the wound of a bed and on the couch of Damascus”: that is, because they trusted in man, having abandoned God’s help. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17).

Who can adequately follow the force of the meaning when it is said, “in the corner of a bed and on the couch of Damascus”? Damascus is intended to be a couch—or rather, a sick man lying on a couch—as it truly was, since its king was a mortal man subject to sin and corruption. This is remarkably signified through the “wound of a bed.”

For what seems to be the strength of a human being without God is such weakness that it is like a wound of a bed: that is, like an extremely severe wound on account of which the wounded person necessarily lies upon a bed and can help neither himself nor another. Even if Damascus—that is, Rezin, king of Damascus—had suffered no bodily wound, nevertheless, in order to rebuke Israel’s folly in making flesh its arm and turning its heart from the Lord, that aid could fittingly and truly have been called a couch, which is a sick man’s bed. It could, I say, have been called the wound of a bed, or the bed of a wounded person.

But Rezin was also bodily wounded. For Ahaz sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians, saying: “Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen up against me.” The king of the Assyrians went up against Damascus, devastated it, transferred its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin (4 Kings 16).

Thus by “the corner of a bed” we understand Rezin as wounded—indeed, as killed. By “the couch of Damascus,” however, we understand the devastation and removal of the inhabitants of Damascus itself: certainly a great sickness, as though Damascus lay upon a couch.

Therefore Israel is reproved for its folly in placing confidence in such great weakness. As was fitting, it was disappointed and afterward itself departed captive, as into the lion’s devouring, so that whatever of it survived thereafter was all reckoned, compared with its former wholeness, as two legs and the tip of an ear.

It follows:

> “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob, says the Lord God of hosts: for on the day when I begin to visit Israel’s transgressions, I will visit also its altars at Bethel; the horns of the altar shall be cut off and shall fall to the ground; and I will strike the winter house together with the summer house; the ivory houses shall perish, and many houses shall be destroyed, says the Lord.”

Wonderful and just are the words of the Lord, and mighty is the authority of the Holy Spirit: how it thunders from a shepherd’s mouth no less than from an emperor’s. Above he had said: “Make it heard in the palaces of Ashdod and in the palaces of the land of Egypt”; now he says, “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob, says the Lord God of hosts”; and for a third time he will say, “Hear this word, fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria.”

If he had already been raised from shepherd to king, like David, what could we wish to add to such majesty of expression? Observe how beautifully and aptly he now interposes, “says the Lord God of hosts,” when he announces visitation upon the altars of Bethel, where Israel worshipped the image of a calf eating grass. Does he not aptly proclaim his own patron, the Lord God of hosts, against Israel’s patron of that time—not the Lord or God of hosts, but a horned calf, not only dumb but also without understanding, and not only without understanding but inanimate?

“Hear,” therefore, he says, “and testify against the house of Jacob,” lest anyone excuse himself through ignorance—and this not because I, a herdsman or shepherd of calves, say it, but because “the Lord God of hosts” says it, against your god: not even a calf full of sap or blood, but the empty image of a calf.

And what does he say? “For on the day when I begin to visit Israel’s transgressions”—on the day, I say, that is, openly, so that the causes of the visitation, namely Israel’s transgressions, may be clearer than light or day, even in the palaces of Ashdod and in the palaces of the land of Egypt, so that no one need ask why the Lord did this to this land and this people—then “I will visit” also “the altars of Bethel,” so that the memory of the calves may perish. One of them is at Bethel, which, according to its very name, ought to be the house of God.

Observe how magnificently he strikes such a god, how elegantly he strikes the horned calf, when he says: “The horns of the altar shall be cut off”—that is, because of the horned form of the grass-eating calf which Israel worshipped. When the horns of the altar have been cut off—that is, when the worshippers of the horned image have been laid waste—“they shall fall,” he says, “to the ground,” understood as not their own ground, because they shall be led captive into a foreign land.

What he then adds, “And I will strike the winter house together with the summer house,” we can understand simply according to the literal sense.

…that is, they possessed such great wealth that they had two sets of houses, winter and summer residences, some facing north and others south, to make provision, according to the changing conditions of cold and heat, for the temperateness of the climate. Likewise, what he says—“and the ivory houses shall perish”—may stand according to the historical sense. For we read that Ahab, king of Israel, so overflowed with luxuries that he built himself an ivory house (3 Kings 22).

Rightly, then, does the severity of heavenly wrath rise against such people: since the Lord had given them the regions of the nations and the labours of peoples as a possession [Col. 0301C] so that they might keep His ordinances and seek His law, they, on the contrary, proceeded in every way against His ordinances and His law, and even applauded golden calves with impious worship, according to the saying: “The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, became corpulent, became bloated, and forsook God his Maker” (Deut. 32).

On account of such fatness—or growing fat, becoming corpulent, becoming bloated, and kicking back—the divine discourse, rising in a wondrous invective as beautifully as it is truthfully, as justly as it is forcefully, cries out and says:

## Chapter IV

“Hear this word, you fat cows, who are on Mount Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your masters, ‘Bring, and let us drink.’” This very word—“Hear”—he now strikes for the third time upon the ears of the wretched with a crashing sound. For first he had said, “Make it heard in the houses of Ashdod.” Then, as though coming nearer, he said, “Hear, and bear witness in the house of Jacob”; now, as though arriving at the summit, that is, at the priests themselves: “Hear this word,” he says, “you fat cows.”

Certainly such priests of demons, devourers of possessions and human souls, deserved to be struck more sharply and boldly—men taken from the lowest ranks of the people, who held the truth in falsehood, as though hired for this very purpose. For Jeroboam made priests from the lowest of the people, acting cleverly indeed, and knowing how gladly low-born men would welcome sudden riches with his favor. Behold, such priests are rightly called fat cows. They might have been called fat calves; it would have suited them well to be called calves, since they were worshipers of calves, trusting in images of calves and made fat by their commerce with them. Why then, though they were male, did he prefer to call them female cows rather than male calves? Clearly for an increase of shame: because, enslaved to calves by a remarkable sort of fornication, they ought to be called cows, since, just as visibly they prostrated themselves in worship before such calves, so invisibly their souls were prostituted to bulls—that is, to evil spirits.

Thus the words, “Hear this word, you fat cows,” carry no slight weight. For at once they forcefully assert these three things: likeness, of which the Psalmist says, “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 134); fornication, by which, abandoning the Creator, they committed fornication with images of calves; and the shameful indulgence of the belly which they cherished in idleness, while wealth flowed in from the whole people—truly grown fat, made sleek, swollen, and thus kicking back, like fat cows, not merely fat but also horn-goring.

For the pride of the rich is indicated in the words, “who are on Mount Samaria”; and the savagery of horn-goring cows in what immediately follows: “who oppress the needy and crush the poor.” Then, who can sufficiently admire the words, “who say to your masters, ‘Bring, and let us drink’”? Who but the Holy Spirit could speak thus through the mouth of a shepherd? Fat and excessively pampered cows do not allow themselves to be led far from their stalls, even merely to drink; instead, they command that clear waters from a pure spring be brought to the stalls themselves. And whom do they command? Their masters. By what words or comparison could the indignity of the matter have been expressed more magnificently?

Those priests, taken from the lowest ranks of the people, as has already been said, became supreme and wealthy by that appointment; and, like fat cows, swollen with an idle belly, they reclined at tables full of delicacies and exercised sufficient authority by saying to their masters, their kings: “Bring, that we may drink, and thereafter we will make you secure. For so long as regular provisions and cups do not fail us by royal decrees, it will be our concern and our foresight to keep the minds of this people preoccupied, lest they wish to go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem; for if that happened, they would kill their king and the kingdom would return to the house of David. We shall make you secure from this danger; only see to it that there is no lack of drink for us. Cups will make us eloquent, so that, with golden calves set up, we may speak beautifully and elegantly in the ears of the people: ‘Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt’; and there will be no one able to know otherwise against us who assert this.”

Therefore, he says, “Hear: ‘The Lord God has sworn by his Holy One: behold, days shall come upon you when they shall lift you up with poles, and your remnant in boiling pots; and you shall go out through breaches, one after another, and you shall be cast into Harmon,’ says the Lord.”

Who is this Holy One by whom the Lord God swore? Certainly he ought not to be less than or inferior to the Lord God himself. “For men,” says the Apostle, “swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath for confirmation is for them the end of every dispute” (Heb. 6). When God promised Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself. Therefore this Holy One of his, by whom God swears, is his Son—whom even the evil spirit, to its own torment, as the Evangelist testifies, confesses to be the Holy One of God: “There was,” he says, “in the synagogue a man having an unclean demon; and he cried out with a loud voice, saying: Leave us; what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God” (Luke 4).

Therefore the Lord God swore by his Holy One—not by one lesser or greater, but by one equal to himself. But what was the point of the Lord’s swearing by that Holy One in such a matter? Clearly because the Lord God had a controversy against Israel concerning that Holy One from the house of David, to whom the promise regarding that Holy One had been made. Yet those fat cows were able to hold back the truth of that promise in the falsehood which they worshiped; nor did they share in the promise of God with those who said: “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (3 Kings 12).

What did the Lord God swear by that Holy One? “Behold,” he says, “days shall come upon you, and they shall lift you up with poles, and your remnant in boiling pots; and you shall go out through breaches, one after another, and you shall be cast into Harmon.” The meaning is: a day of captivity and distress is coming—not far off and after many ages, but already imminent—when you shall be taken in battle, carried away, and removed by right of victory. Already the paths of captivity stand open before you; you shall go out, one against another, so that in turn and face to face you may behold one another’s misery; and you shall be cast into the regions of Armenia, called Harmon, and into the cities of the Medes.

We may admire more than we can express how much beauty there is in his preserving the metaphor of cows which he had begun: those whom he had called fat cows, he says have their flesh carried on poles and in boiling pots. We ourselves have sometimes seen this done: after the meat had been thoroughly cooked, a boiling, steaming cauldron was lifted on poles and carried from place to place—that is, from the kitchen some distance away to the house of those dining. Thus the prophetic speech wonderfully proclaims that, boiled by the burning distress of captivity, they shall be carried to the place where, captive under human masters, they shall also be devoured by evil spirits because they are unrepentant.

It follows: “Come to Bethel and act impiously; at Gilgal multiply transgression; bring your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes every three days; sacrifice praise from leaven; call out voluntary offerings and proclaim them. For thus you have desired, children of Israel.” This is a very grave mode of speech, by which he now says, “Come and do this and that,” although he who says it hates these very deeds of theirs. It is not the speech of one willing, but of one abandoning; not of one inviting, but of one expelling; not of one exhorting, but of one indignant (Judg. 3). Therefore he rightly added—and had to add—“For thus you have desired, children of Israel.”

It is as though he said: Therefore I say, “Come to Bethel,” where your god is, your calf, because “thus you have desired” and have come thus far. Therefore I say, “Act impiously,” because you act impiously and desire to act impiously. I say, “Come to Gilgal,” where there were idols even long before Jeroboam’s calves (3 Kings 12), because you come and wish to come. I say, “Multiply transgression,” because you multiply it and wish to multiply it. I say, “Bring your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes every three days,” because you offer—and desire to offer—to those to whom you ought not.

For you have adulterated the solemnities of three days, concerning which the law says—or rather, concerning which I said in the law: “Three times each year you shall celebrate feasts for me: namely, the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of the month of firstfruits, and the feast at the year’s end” (Exod. 23). You have adulterated these feasts so that you celebrate them not for me but for your calves, lest the common people should seem deprived of any divine joy. Indeed, in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, your king Jeroboam established a solemn day for his shrines and calves on the high places, in imitation of the feast celebrated in Judah (3 Kings 12).

Again I say: “Sacrifice praise from leaven,” because this is what you do and desire to do—leavened with “the old leaven, the leaven of malice and wickedness,” contrary to every authority of the holy and spiritual law, which forbids offering anything leavened in sacrifice. Your gods so desire it: that you should be leavened and without “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Therefore sacrifice praise from leaven to them, because, being sinners, you cannot sacrifice to me a praise pleasing from your mouth.

While doing all these things, “call out voluntary offerings and proclaim them,” because you do this and desire to do it: you honor the sacrifices which you offer to your calves by the very names by which the authority of the law designates those offered to me: “burnt offering and sin offering” (Ps. 39), and peace offerings. Proclaim these “with the sound of trumpet, harp, tambourine and choir, strings and organ, and loudly sounding cymbals, with cymbals of jubilation” (Ps. 150), so that you may be judged to have sung more powerfully and more loudly than the tribe of Judah or the house of David in the temple of the Lord, because you are more numerous.

All this, as has already been said, was spoken not with the intention of one willing, but with the indignation of one abandoning, as were many other sayings found in Scripture. For example, the Lord himself said to his betrayer: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13). Likewise: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26). And in the Apocalypse we read: “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Apoc. 12). Finally, these and other such words are not the words of one commanding or voluntarily permitting, but of one allowing and abandoning, because he does not fail to know—as Wisdom says—“that their nation is wicked, their malice is natural, and their thought cannot be changed forever” (Wis. 12).

Why do you seek farther for explanations that excuse God’s justice? In this passage he himself excuses it more carefully in what follows. For he says: “Therefore I gave you numbness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” Clearly, when he says, “yet you did not return to me,” he proves that they were incorrigible, while he himself had applied the fitting remedy of famine’s scourge in order to correct them.

He wonderfully expresses the greatness of the scourge, the greatness of the famine with which he rebuked them, by saying, “I gave you numbness of teeth in all your cities,” and adding, “lack of bread in all your places.” This is as though he said: The famine lasted so long, and food was so scarce, that whenever some food of whatever kind was found, their teeth were numbed as though struck by something unfamiliar. For we read that, during the reign of Joram son of Ahab over Israel, such a great famine arose in Samaria that “a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver” (4 Kings 6).

There followed immediately a famine lasting seven years, which Elisha also foretold when he spoke to the woman whose son he had restored to life: “Arise, go—you and your household—and live as a resident alien wherever you can find a place. For the Lord will call for a famine, and it shall come upon the land for seven years” (4 Kings 8). Although the severity of this corrective discipline was so great, it is astonishing that none of the kings of Israel departed from Jeroboam’s sins—that is, from the golden calves—and that Israel proved so stubbornly rebellious and so stiff-necked that it did not return at all to the Lord its God. Therefore, fittingly reproving them, he says: “Yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

It follows: “I also withheld rain from you, when three months still remained until harvest; I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. One part was rained upon, and the part upon which I did not rain dried up; two and three cities came to one city to drink water, and were not satisfied; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Not only did I give you “numbness of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places,” but I also withheld rain from you when three months remained until harvest—the rain called the latter rain, exceedingly necessary for the thirsty fields and lands of Palestine—so that, when the grass was swelling toward harvest and the wheat was coming to maturity, it should wither in excessive drought; and thus, as the grain perished and famine pressed them, they should also endure the burning of thirst and lack of drink.

For in those regions, apart from small springs, all waters are cistern waters. If divine wrath holds back the rains, the danger from thirst is greater than that from famine. And lest perhaps they should think that this had happened to cities and peoples by a law of nature, by the course of the stars, or by changing seasons, he says that he rained upon one city and its fields, while withholding rain from another, so that two and three cities should go to another city and yet not be satisfied by drinking water. Such a distribution of rain could sufficiently demonstrate that this drought had arisen not by chance but by the reason of heavenly judgment.

Yet they had a more certain prophetic word, to which they paid no attention. For this reason they are all the more inexcusable. Indeed, Elisha the prophet foretold that famine—or “numbness of teeth”—of which mention was made above, speaking to the woman whose son he had restored to life: “Arise, go—you and your household—and live as a resident alien wherever you can find a place. For the Lord will call for a famine, and it shall come upon the land for seven years.”

Elijah also foretold—and in a sense brought about—the drought, or withholding of rain, saying to Ahab: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except according to the word of my mouth” (3 Kings 1). Who had leisure, meanwhile, even to suppose that these evils had happened by chance, or to doubt whether they had come by heavenly judgment?

Add that those same prophets, so great in name and in miracles, together with the prophetic word gave heavenly signs by which wretched Israel—unless it had entirely lost reason—could have been taught that neither Jeroboam’s calves, nor Baal, nor the monstrosities worshiped as gods, were anything or had any power; rather, that the one God who had brought them out of Egypt through Moses and Aaron alone was God. For Elijah, who prayed in prayer that it might not rain, performed, if you count them, eight remarkable signs; but Elisha performed sixteen, namely twice as many, according to the request which he made when Elijah said: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.” And he said: “I beg that a double portion of your spirit may come upon me” (4 Kings 2).

To what was Elisha directing this request, except that by the efficacy of miracles he might reveal to the erring people the glory of the true God? “Yet you did not return to me, says the Lord,” because through all these things it could not be brought about that the wretched worship of those calves should be abandoned even during the reign of a single king.

It follows: “I struck you with scorching wind and blight; the multitude of your gardens and vineyards, your olive groves and fig trees, the caterpillar devoured; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” It belonged to intemperate luxury to multiply gardens, especially through sin or injustice, as Ahab did when he spoke to Naboth and said: “Give me your vineyard, that I may make it a vegetable garden”; and because he refused to give it, Ahab killed him and took possession of it (3 Kings 21). Therefore he rightly struck such persons “with scorching wind and blight and consuming caterpillar,” because they would see with no small grief whatever they had multiplied for themselves by such or so great injustice perish. Yet the correction applied to them did them no good: “For you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

“I sent death among you by the way of Egypt; I struck your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses; I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” Israel is instructed by every scourge and torment. Therefore, at the very time when they sought help from the Egyptians, death was sent among them; their young men were struck with the sword; and cruel captivity enclosed the horses which they had multiplied for themselves contrary to God’s command, so that the stench of the camps of the living filled their nostrils.

Yet this “way of Egypt” can also be understood more deeply: not as a journey of the body but of the mind, according to what the Lord says in another prophet: “And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you may drink troubled water?” (Jer. 2). The Lord forbade this kind of way of Egypt—which, as has been said, belongs not to the body but to the mind—through Moses in these words: “You may not make a man of another nation king, who is not your brother. When he has been established, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back into Egypt, exalted by the number of his cavalry; especially since the Lord has commanded you that you shall by no means return again by the same way” (Deut. 17).

Clearly, as soon as they established over themselves as king Jeroboam son of Naboth, he—exalted by the number of his cavalry, for he reigned over more tribes than the house of David, that is, over ten tribes—led the people back into Egypt, not by going to Egypt on foot, but by making golden calves according to Egyptian custom.

Therefore, both where he first said, “I gave you cleanness of teeth,” and afterward where he said, “I also withheld rain from you,” and when he says, “I struck you with scorching wind,” it is not unfitting to understand, “by the way of Egypt,” which he finally expresses here when he says, “I sent death among you by the way of Egypt”: that is, because of the way of Egypt, because of the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, making it like the Egyptians in worshiping calves, as has already been said, according to Egyptian custom.

For because of that cause all the evils came upon them which the Lord here recalls that he had inflicted with the intention of correction. “Yet you did not return to me,” he says; for they never abandoned those same calves, however great the evil or affliction by which they were oppressed.

It follows: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord. Therefore I will do this to you, Israel.” Before the times of this prophet, nothing of that sort had happened to that people; therefore the event is that in which “God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” Thus, although he speaks in the past tense—“I overthrew you”—it must be understood of the future, as though he said: “I shall overthrow you.” For it is not unusual for prophets to announce future events by words in the past tense.

Nor is there any doubt that, foreseeing the captivity of the ten tribes, he also foresaw the overthrow of Judah or Jerusalem, especially since he himself later says: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria” (Hosea 6). Therefore, when he says, “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” he foretells both the captivity of the ten tribes and the overthrow of the Jews. The latter was more like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah than the captivity of the ten tribes, since the city of Jerusalem was burned both by the Babylonians and by the Romans.

And because he adds, “You became like a brand snatched from the fire, and you did not return to me,” it seems preferable to understand the final overthrow wrought by the Romans rather than the first wrought through the Babylonians. For in that Babylonian overthrow they were not so hard of heart; rather, they returned in mind to the Lord, so that after seventy years they deserved to return bodily to their own place. But after the destruction wrought by the Romans, they persist in unbelief and hardness of heart.

And who would not marvel at the aptness of the comparison applied to those who were devoured? “You became,” he says, “like a brand snatched from the fire.” For just as a brand snatched from a fire visibly shows what it is—namely, that it has been snatched from a fire—and it cannot be doubted or concealed that it has burned, so the Jews, led captive among all nations, are not allowed to forget how or for what reason God overthrew them. Nor is it astonishing or unjust that they were overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, since their iniquity was greater than the sin of Sodom and Gomorrah, as Jeremiah testifies: “The iniquity of the daughter of my people became greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment” (Lam. 4).

That the iniquity of the Jews truly became greater than Sodom’s sin he proves by adding: “and hands did not seize her” (ibid.). What does he mean by saying, “and hands did not seize her”? We read that, when the Lord lodged with righteous Lot in Sodom, “all the people together surrounded the house, from boy to old man, and said: Bring out the men to us, that we may know them” (Gen. 19). Great was their iniquity; yet “hands did not seize her”—that is, it did not advance to the accomplishment of the deed.

But how far did the iniquity of the Jews advance? When the Lord was lodging in Jerusalem and had celebrated the Passover, they surrounded him as he went out with swords and clubs, and “laid hands on him”: namely, on him on whom hands were not laid in Sodom. They seized him, I say; they apprehended him, mocked him, scourged him, and killed him. Therefore they were justly overwhelmed like Sodom, except that a part of them survived “like a brand snatched from the fire.” This has the effect that the memory of Christ is more celebrated throughout the whole world, especially through the monument of such a conflagration, made known to all peoples, according to the verse of the psalm already mentioned above: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people ever forget. Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 58).

What he next adds—“therefore I will do this to you, Israel”—we judge to be a threat of that same great overthrow. Thus it is announced in both tenses, past and future: it was already then indeed done or fixed in the purpose of God, but had not yet been done in fact and was to occur much later, because they persevered in evils, as he had reproached them so often already, saying five times in succession, “yet you did not return to me.”

It follows: “But after I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel. For behold, he who forms mountains and creates wind, and declares his word to man, who makes the morning mist and walks upon the high places of the earth—the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

First, it must be observed and carefully considered that, whereas until now the discourse has been addressed in the plural—“I gave you cleanness of teeth, and you did not return to me; I also withheld rain from you, and you did not return to me; I sent death among you by the way of Egypt, and you did not return to me; I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you did not return to me”—now, where he promises the great consolation of great grace, he somehow changes his voice. Leaving the plural number, he speaks in the singular: “Therefore I will do these things to you; after I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel.”

With him who “has the key of David” (Apoc. 3) opening the door for us, we first understand this: in the present passage, Israel in the singular differs from those children of his in the plural—repeatedly struck, overthrown in this manner, and not returned to the Lord—as much as the root of the good olive tree differs from its branches: rejected branches, branches broken off through unbelief, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11). Yet, after the natural branches had been broken off, a branch of the wild olive had to be grafted into the holy and good root of that same olive tree, until the full number of the elect—that is, of those predestined to life—should be complete. This has been done and is being done.

Therefore the same Apostle says to each of us who have come from the Gentiles: “If some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive, have been grafted among them and made a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you” (ibid.), and so forth.

Thus, when he says, “Therefore I will do these things to you, Israel,” it is the severity of God foretelling that he must break off the natural branches because of unbelief. But when he adds, “After I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel,” it is the goodness of that same God promising the good olive tree—namely Israel, which by faith deserved to be heir of the world—that he will graft the wild olive into its root, with so great an increase of the branches being grafted in that it shall suffer no loss from its natural branches that were broken off.

“Prepare,” therefore, he says, “to meet your God”: that is, receive in your faith the coming of Christ, the Son of God—your God, your Savior. And as though Israel asked why it was told, “to meet your God,” he adds: “For behold, he who forms mountains and creates wind, and declares his word to man, who makes the morning mist and walks upon the high places of the earth—the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

Therefore I said, “Prepare to meet your God,” because, behold—this is to be understood—he comes; for such a one, so great as this wondrous description requires us to understand, is near at hand. When you receive him, prepared in a few persons, meeting him in the apostles, he will open your root with the blade or hoe of the Gospel word; and, because so many natural branches have been broken off, he will restore your losses according to the wonderful utterance of prophetic truth which must be understood from these present words.

First, it must clearly be seen, lovingly received, and firmly held that, when one person speaks of another, and the speaker himself is the Lord, while he commends the one of whom he speaks by saying, “The Lord of hosts is his name,” what else should we desire than that the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of the prophets, should testify that God’s Son Jesus Christ is God, Lord God of hosts, equally with his Father? The things proclaimed certainly suit so great a name; for no one but the Lord God can do them.

“He forms mountains,” he says. He could have said, “forming light and stretching out the heavens,” or “founding the earth and pouring out the seas”; for it is true that these things are proclaimed of the Son just as of the Father. But it was more relevant to the present matter that he should say, “forming mountains.” Why? Clearly because the discourse began with Sodom: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.”

We read that where Sodom was overthrown, the Lord said to Lot: “Save your life; do not look back, and do not stand anywhere in the surrounding region; but save yourself on the mountain, lest you too perish.” Lot also said: “I beg you, my lord, because your servant has found favor before you and you have magnified the mercy which you have shown me in saving my life: I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me and I die. This city is near, to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it” (Gen. 19).

Therefore we judge that we are sent back to that Scripture when, in this passage, after saying, “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” it adds: “Prepare to meet your God, Israel; for behold, he forms mountains.” Clearly he who there said, “Save yourself on the mountain,” is here said to be “forming mountains,” when the Father says concerning him: “Behold, he forms mountains.”

For, overthrowing that Jewish people “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” he formed the mountains of evangelical perfection and said to Lot—that is, to the man turning away from evil, for *Lot* is interpreted “turning aside”—to the man desiring to turn away from the evil of Sodom and Gomorrah: “Save yourself on the mountain”; that is, enjoy evangelical perfection, so as not even to seek a wife. Lot, indeed, in the person of those who are weak, fashioned mystical words for us when he said, “I cannot be saved on the mountain.” This is our saying: “We cannot enjoy evangelical perfection, lest perhaps we burn; and it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7).

Nevertheless, many have ascended those mountains which this Lord formed: that is, they have embraced the purpose of evangelical and apostolic perfection, neither marrying nor burning, but living in a virginal purpose like the angels of God. The first and greatest of all the mountains which this Lord God of hosts formed at his coming is the blessed Virgin Mary, from whose flesh Christ the Son of God took flesh without marital intercourse, according to the prophetic vision in which “a stone was cut from the mountain without hands and crushed every kingdom of the world” (Dan. 2).

It is indeed wonderful that he formed a mountain from which he himself, like a stone, should be cut; yet no less marvelous is what another Scripture says of that holy heavenly city Zion: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86). After this mountain, the same Lord God of hosts formed other mountains at his coming: namely his apostles. Whoever effectively strives toward their perfection magnificently escapes the danger of the overthrow by which that Sodom—that is, Jewish unbelief—is known to have been overthrown. He is also safe from the tribulation of the flesh, possessing great refreshment, signified in the present passage when, after “behold, he forms mountains,” it adds, “and creates wind.”

For what can more pleasantly be understood here by “wind” than the good tempering of the continent flesh, like a sweet breeze breathing upon those holy mountains? Heretics argued from this passage that the Holy Spirit is a creature, because the Hebrew word translates into Latin as *spiritus*, “spirit.” But, blessed Jerome says, both “wind” and “spirit” are denoted by the same word. Since they were perversely disposed, they wished to understand not wind, nor even the human spirit, but the Holy Spirit, seeking to support with so small and fragile an instrument so great an impiety: that the Holy Spirit is a creature.

Therefore a rendering of the aforesaid word, “and creating a word,” is more agreeable to chaste faith than “and creating a spirit.” Yet, if we read “spirit,” we could and ought by no means to understand the Holy Spirit, but the spirit either of a human being or of any living creature, or likewise wind, according to: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind” (Ps. 148).

Thus, after the overthrow and burning of the Sodomites, one who desires to escape is beautifully told: “Save yourself on the mountain.” “And creating wind”—that is, instructing men supreme in evangelical preaching, and granting sweet refreshment to their chaste purpose, so that they may not even at any time be painfully inflamed by the heat of the flesh to the point of intolerable temptation. These mountains are certainly holy and beautiful, and by their merits can assist those who are tempted. Therefore the Psalmist says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me” (Ps. 120). And because they do not possess this power from themselves but from the Lord, he immediately adds: “My help is from the Lord” (ibid.).

To these mountains—that is, to the holy apostles and to every person who, following their example, strives toward perfection—it is fitting to receive “a wind blowing with dew” (Dan. 3). Whether against the Babylonian furnace or against burning Sodomite sulphur, what is hidden in the holy Scriptures is more familiarly revealed to them, as the Evangelist tells concerning those disciples: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

Accordingly, after he had said, “forming mountains and creating winds,” he added: “and declaring his word to man.” It is as though he said: “He is also the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3), and who opens the understanding of whomever he wills, so that he may comprehend the mysteries of the Scriptures.

For to which angel or human being—to whom, I say, besides the one true God—could this proclamation apply: “declaring his word to man”? For indeed a holy angel and a holy human being have often declared the word, but never *their own* word; rather, they have declared, or ought to have declared, only God’s word. For all who have come declaring their own word are thieves and robbers. Therefore the sheep did not hear them (John 10), nor ought they to have heard them, since they spoke from themselves and prophesied out of their own hearts. Sacred law commands that one of this kind be despised and not feared—indeed, even put to death. “The prophet,” it says, “who, corrupted by presumption, shall wish to speak in my name things which I did not command him to say, or in the name of foreign gods, shall be put to death” (Deut. 18). [Col. 0312D]

Likewise: “Whatever that prophet shall have predicted in the name of the Lord, and it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has fabricated it through the swelling pride of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (ibid.). Concerning this manner of declaring his own word, or uttering his own discourse, the Lord himself defends himself before his detractors when he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7). For what does “my teaching is not mine” mean, unless it is as though he said: It is not, as you wish to suppose, invented by myself and unsupported by any truth of things? For he adds and says: “If anyone wills to do his will, he shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself” (ibid.). Likewise, he says to his disciples: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, [Col. 0313A] but the Father’s who sent me” (John 14).

Therefore, when he said, “and declaring his word to man,” he asserted in a few syllables the great authority of his divinity, because God alone is truthful in declaring his own word. But when he is about to declare it, he commonly allows great ignorance to come beforehand, so that after he has declared it, whoever it is to whom he has declared it may know that he has nothing which he has not received. Hence, after he had said, “and declaring his word to man,” he fittingly added, “making the morning mist.”

For example: before declaring his word to Amos, he had made morning mist for him; that is, he first made a rustic shepherd into an illustrious prophet. Likewise, he first allowed the apostles to have hearts blinded, so that he said to them: “Are you also still without understanding? How do you not yet understand?” (Matt. 15), before [read perhaps: *before he*] opening their understanding so that they might comprehend the Scriptures. [Col. 0313B]

This is truly great, and it was fitting here to mention it in praise of his wisdom: that for those to whom, by declaring his word, he proposed to show the clear sun of knowledge, he first brings on—or permits there to come on—the dullness of heart or ignorance, as it were a morning mist, so that, when the mist has been driven away and they see the sun, they may not boast as though they had not received it.

What he next adds, “and walking upon the high places of the earth,” may indeed be understood in a favorable sense: namely, that these high places are the mountains which he himself, as has already been said, formed. Yet because he did not say, “dwelling in the heights,” but “walking upon the high places of the earth,” [Col. 0313C] and because “high places” are more often understood in an evil sense (for God alone is truly called, and is, Most High), we may here understand the wrath that overtook the earthly, exalted generation of Jerusalem, because it did not receive but rejected the aforesaid word of the Lord which had been announced to it.

For another prophet also says: “What is Jacob’s wickedness? Is it not Samaria? And what are Judah’s high places? Is it not Jerusalem?” (Mic. 1). The Lord is said to walk, or ascend, upon these high places—that is, in order to destroy them—as he said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel: You are a stiff-necked people; once I shall go up into your midst, and I shall destroy you” (Exod. 33).

This indeed took place when the desolation of that people came, the Romans having surrounded them; and the Lord himself, foreseeing it, said: “For there shall be great distress upon the earth, and wrath against this people” (Luke 21). [Col. 0313D] Therefore, after he had said, “and walking upon the high places of the earth,” he added in a remarkable way: “the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

For he truly is the Lord God of hosts: not only do legions of angels knowingly serve him in heaven, but on earth the Roman armies also served him unknowingly, avenging his blood, the blood of his prophets, and every righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel, as the Lord himself foretold (Luke 11).

It follows:

## Chapter V.

[Col. 0314A]

> “Hear this word which I raise over you as a lament, O house of Israel: ‘She has fallen; she shall rise no more; the virgin Israel has been cast down upon her own land, and there is none to raise her up.’”

In a striking way, where he had said before, “and he treads upon the high places of the earth; the Lord God of hosts is his name,” he now solemnly proclaims, with a great cry, the words of him who declares his word to man: “Hear,” he says, “that word which I raise over you as a lament, O house of Israel.” Do we not have the same in the Gospel: that this Lord, declaring his word and not being heard, raised up a lament, foretelling what was to come—namely, that he would send the Roman army for their overthrow? He raised, I say, a lament over Jerusalem: “Jerusalem,” he says, “you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Matt. 23), adding, “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (ibid.).

[Col. 0314B] Was not a lament raised loudly over them when he repeatedly said there: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men; woe to you, who devour widows’ houses; woe to you, who traverse sea and land in order to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves; woe to you, who say: Whoever swears by the Temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the Temple is bound; woe to you, who tithe mint and dill and cumin; woe to you, who cleanse the outside of cup and dish; woe to you, who are like whitewashed tombs; woe to you, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the memorials of the righteous” (ibid.)? Truly the lament is great—and, what is greater still, [Col. 0314C] it is not without tears. For, as another Evangelist relates: “Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If only you too had known …’” (Luke 19).

Therefore, when he now says, “Hear this word which I raise over you as a lament, O house of Israel,” we rightly understand these to be the words of the Lord who “forms the mountains,” as was said above, creates “the wind,” declares “his word to man,” makes “the morning mist,” and treads “upon the high places of the earth.” For he himself, lamenting in the Gospel, declares the reason why he raises a lament over the house of Israel: “Behold,” he says, “your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

Indeed, the words, “She has fallen; the virgin Israel shall rise no more. She has been cast down [Col. 0314D] upon her own land, and there is none to raise her,” must be understood of the natural branches of the olive tree. As we recalled above from the Apostle, they were broken off because of unbelief (Luke 11), nor can they be grafted in. For there is none who can raise up those cast down upon the earth, as the apostles discovered. Here, however, we must understand what we discussed above as said to the good root: “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel,” so that the text which immediately follows may remain continuous in sense:

> “For thus says the Lord God: The city from which a thousand used to go out shall have a hundred left in it; and the city from which a hundred used to go out shall have ten left in the house of Israel.”

This is a great consolation for the faithful good root, which suffered great [Col. 0315A] loss in the breaking off or cutting away of the natural branches, lest because of these things there be great sorrow and continual anguish in its heart. For others shall be brought in, the Lord saying: “Thus the city from which a thousand used to go out shall have a hundred left in it, and that from which a hundred went out shall have ten left in the house of Israel.”

To understand this usefully, one must remember what he said above: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah”; and one must recognize that, just as the carnal house of Israel became like Sodom in condemnation, so conversely the fullness of the Gentiles—which was Sodom—became spiritually the house of Israel. At the same time, it must be recalled that not even ten righteous persons were left in Sodom, for whose sake the Lord would have spared the whole place and not destroyed them. For thus Abraham spoke to the Lord, [Col. 0315B] beginning with fifty and gradually reducing and diminishing the number, until at last he concluded: “I beg you, Lord, do not be angry if I speak only once more. What if ten are found?” He said: “I will not destroy it for the sake of ten” (Gen. 18).

Having observed this, when he has now said, “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” let us not doubt that he also intended to say: “I shall not overthrow that which had been Sodom”—namely, the Church drawn from the Gentiles. Why? Clearly because of the ancient decision: I must be faithful to my faithful friend Abraham, so that wherever I find ten righteous persons, I do not destroy the city because of them. But behold: in the Church of the Gentiles I shall find not only ten righteous persons, but even a hundred, where formerly [Col. 0315C] a thousand went out—that is, where previously no one was left, but all went their own ways, without God, strangers to salvation; and all these are signified by “a thousand.” For universality is customarily signified by the number one thousand, as in: “He has remembered his covenant forever, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. 104).

Further, perfection is customarily signified by the number one hundred and by the number ten, as in: “He shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19). And we read in the book of Maccabees: “But Judas Maccabaeus, who had been the tenth, withdrew to a desert place” (1 Macc. 5). “The tenth,” that is, one made perfect in the paternal law of the ten commandments. Such persons, then—the hundredth and the tenth, that is, the perfect—shall remain in the city, or Church, [Col. 0315D] of the Gentiles, from which a thousand formerly went out; that is, all were condemned. And for the sake of those who are perfect, the rest—sinners indeed, but repentant on the day of judgment—shall be saved and shall remain in the house of Israel, like wild olive shoots grafted into the good olive tree in place of the natural branches which were broken off (Luke 11).

In quantity, a hundred out of a thousand is greater than ten left out of a hundred; but in proportion there is equality in both, because, just as a hundred is a tenth of a thousand, so ten is a tenth of a hundred. Appropriately, moreover, sanctification of righteousness or of the righteous is understood by the tenth, because by the ordinance of the Law the tithe of all things is the Lord’s portion (Lev. 27).

What we say or understand here is confirmed by the reading of another prophet, namely Isaiah. For after he had said: “Make the heart of this people blind, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn and I heal them. How long, O Lord? Until the cities are laid waste without inhabitant, the houses without a human being, and the land is left desolate” (Isa. 6)—words which signified that the natural branches of which we have spoken were to be broken off—he immediately added: [Col. 0316A] “And that which had been left in the midst of the land shall be multiplied; and there shall yet be in it a tenth, and it shall return and shall be for a display, like a terebinth and like an oak which extends its branches. The holy seed shall be that which remains in it” (ibid.).

Clearly, in both this prophet and that one, the sanctification or multiplication of the righteous is rightly understood under the mystery of the tithe, which is the lawful portion of the Lord or of his altar. And the multitude of branches to be grafted into Israel, the good root, from all nations, as though from the wild olive, is beautifully promised under the name of a tithe, because Israel is recorded as the first to have vowed to God tithes of his possessions:

> “If the Lord is with me,” he says, “and keeps me on the way by which I walk, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and if I return safely to my father’s house, the Lord shall be my God; and this stone which I have erected as a memorial shall be called the house of God; and of all things which you give me, I shall offer you tithes” (Gen. 28).

A beautiful exchange, a beautiful recompense. Israel promises that in the house of God he will leave tithes from the Gentiles. For after saying, “The city from which a thousand went out shall have ten left in it,” he added, “in the house of Israel.” Surely, he who destined for Israel such abundant multitudes of salvation, or of those to be saved, did not vainly preface and say beforehand: “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel.”

It follows:

> “For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me and live. Do not seek Bethel; do not enter Gilgal; do not cross over to Beersheba. For Gilgal shall go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nothing. Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph be consumed like fire, and it devour, with none to quench Bethel.”

This passage, by the connecting phrase with which it begins—“for thus says the Lord to the house of Israel”—refers us back [Col. 0316D] to what was said above in the Lord’s person: “Come to Bethel and act wickedly; go to Gilgal and multiply transgression” (Hos. 4), and so forth, ending: “for thus you have desired, children of Israel.” Its sense is this: Above I said to you, in words resembling an exhortation, “Come to Bethel and act wickedly”; but this was not the language of one exhorting or willing, but rather of one indignant and hating. For if the Lord’s will is sought, this is rather what he wills and declares as his will: “Do not seek at Bethel, and do not enter Gilgal.”

In seeking there, you certainly shall not live, but shall rather die. For I, the living and life-giving God, am not there; the golden calf is there. I do not call it dead, for it was never alive or animate; [Col. 0317A] but I say that where your calf is—your god—there is one neither dead nor alive, yet still death-dealing, because those who seek it die. Therefore, “do not seek at Bethel, nor enter Gilgal,” which is a place of idolatry; “and do not cross over to Beersheba,” where in stubborn error you have been accustomed to worship idols.

Next, it should be noted that when he says, “Gilgal shall go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nothing,” he is silent about Beersheba. For when the ten tribes were conquered, the city called Beersheba, which was in the tribe of Judah, was at that time neither captured nor destroyed. When the Lord had said these things, the prophet immediately adds in his own person an exhortation prompted by good will: “Seek,” he says, “the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph be kindled like fire.” By “the house of Joseph,” because of Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim and the house of Joseph, we must understand the ten tribes. They were called Israel and retained the ancient name because they comprised the greater part of the people. But the two tribes ruled by the line of David, who was from the tribe of Judah, were called Judah and possessed Jerusalem, where the Temple of God was.

When the house of Joseph has been set ablaze, it shall devour and consume Bethel, and there shall be none to quench it, when it has been kindled by its kings. All these things are spoken so that, although on the surface of the letter or of prophetic utterance they announce the imminent captivity of that time, by which the ten tribes were afterwards to be transported among the Assyrians, they may nevertheless, when carefully examined, also apply to the captivity of the Jews, which remains dispersed even now.

To make this clearer, it must first be said that Bethel means “house of God,” Gilgal “rolling-place,” and Beersheba “well of the oath.” Who does not know that that was once the house of God in which the Jews vainly gloried, trusting in lying words and saying: “The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord is here” (Jer. 7)? Their carnal ceremonies, moreover, were—and have been since they crucified Christ—their rolling-place: a rolling-place, I say, such that the Apostle counts them as loss “and considers them as dung” (Phil. 3), and not without prophetic warrant. For in Malachi the Lord says: “Behold, I shall cast back upon you the arm, and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities” (Mal. 2).

[Col. 0317D] Their well of the oath was their deep desire for gold and silver—and so much a well of the oath that they greatly preferred an oath by gold to an oath sworn by the altar or in the Temple. Hence the Lord says: “Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the Temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the house that is upon it is bound” (Matt. 23).

Therefore Christ, who truly is life, says: “Seek me and you shall live; do not seek at Bethel”—that is, in that house of God which, though it ought to have been “a house of prayer, has become a den of robbers” (Matt. 21). For as I foretold through the prophet: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like [Col. 0318A] a hyena’s den” (Jer. 12). Do not seek me there, because, when they wished to stone me, I hid myself and went out of the Temple (John 8).

“And do not enter Gilgal”: that is, despise the rolling-place of the old ceremonies and now regard it as dung, so that you may not even be circumcised with that bodily circumcision with which Joshua circumcised the people at Gilgal. “For if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5).—“And do not cross over to Beersheba”: that is, do not pursue the depth of Pharisaic avarice, which is accompanied by perjuries.

When Christ’s apostles preached these things after his passion, and the Jews refused to hear them, what follows was to occur: “For Gilgal shall go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nothing”; together with what is added: “Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph be consumed like fire, and it devour, with none to quench Bethel.” For that Bethel which ought to have been the house of God, or of Christ—of whom Joseph bore a type—not only became useless, but was also burned with fire because of its uselessness. Fire devoured it, and there was none to quench it. Indeed, even now it “burns invisibly unto the lowest depths of hell, the fire kindled in the Lord’s wrath” (Deut. 32); and that place, now no longer truly Judaea but to be called Gilgal in the manner stated above, has been led captive among all nations.

It follows:

> “You who turn judgment into wormwood and cast righteousness down upon the earth—the maker of Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning and changes day into night; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name. He smiles upon devastation against the strong man, and brings destruction upon the mighty.”

Here we must understand: I speak to you, “you who turn judgment into wormwood.” It is a great fault and a great cause of condemnation to turn the sweetness of judgment into the wormwood, or bitterness, of iniquity, and the beauty or sweetness of righteousness into the horror of outcry. Isaiah laments this very thing in other words, under the figure of a vineyard: “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5); and explaining what he meant, he says: “I expected it to produce judgment, and behold iniquity; righteousness, and behold [Col. 0318D] outcry” (ibid.).

Truly unhappy are those who drew out so long a cord of iniquity and outcry that they reached Christ himself, to be condemned by an unjust judgment and by clamour: crying, “He is guilty of death”; crying, “Crucify, crucify”; crying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” We must indeed view those times which were then present or imminent in such a way that we do not doubt that the prophetic Spirit looked rather to the future time, when the worst of sons, by killing Christ, were to fill up the measure of their fathers.

And if the principal part of prophecy in this prophet and the other prophets was hidden or veiled, it was hidden precisely because those cruel and rebellious fathers would not merely kill those who prophesied or wrote—which they did—but would also burn and destroy the Scriptures, if such a mystery had not been concealed beneath an obscure letter.

Accordingly, what follows—“the maker of Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning and changes day into night; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name”—we should not doubt to be fitting testimony concerning Christ himself. This person, rather than the person of the Father, needed for our sake to be defended by the testimony of the Scriptures as the maker of the stars, of night and day—indeed, of all things made—because “without him nothing was made” (John 1).

But why, though he is maker of all things, is he here called only the maker of Arcturus and [Col. 0319B] Orion, of day and night, and of rain poured upon the earth? Clearly so that, together with the Creator’s power, the grace of that same Savior might also be commended mystically. Arcturus, placed at the pole of heaven and shining with the rays of seven stars, continually revolves and never sets; indeed, as it revolves, it rises. Orion, however, rises in the very weight of the winter season; and by his rising he stirs storms and disturbs seas and lands. Thus in blessed Job, where it says: “He makes Arcturus and Orion and the Hyades and the inner regions of the south” (Job 9).

By Arcturus, which, as has been said, ever revolves and never sets, we understand—following the exposition of blessed Gregory—the holy Church, established by the sevenfold Spirit, which unceasingly endures the persecutions of the wicked and yet persists without failure to the end [Col. 0319C] of the world. By Orion, on the other hand, we understand the holy martyrs, who came forth before the face of heaven as in winter, destined to bear the burden and distress of persecutors.

Yet because we wish to establish—and to show established—the ancient divinity of Christ, the new man, by such or similar testimonies, we judge it sweeter and more delightful, within the whole body of that same holy Church, to point out almost with the finger those persons for whose likeness he is aptly said here to have made Arcturus and Orion, although in relation to those persons he was a man born later.

Therefore, by Arcturus, which, as has been said, shines with seven stars, let us understand the ancient patriarchs from whom Christ came according to the flesh: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and their wives Sarah and Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. These seven persons, like Arcturus bright with seven stars, continually revolved and never set: that is, throughout their lives, travelling from place to place because of faith in God, they journeyed as pilgrims and never, through distrust, returned to the land of their former birth.

Abraham never returned to Chaldea, although he travelled in so many places and at times under the pressure of famine. Indeed, he said even to his servant: “Take care never to bring my son back there” (Gen. 24), when he was speaking of Mesopotamia, where his kindred dwelt after Terah, his father, had departed from Chaldea. How much more would he have forbidden his son to be taken back to Chaldea! Therefore, when it says, “the maker of Arcturus,” it is most fittingly understood of Christ, God and man: before he was born, he was in heaven the maker of the stars, and on earth the maker of his fathers and mothers, as of seven shining stars—Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Rachel and Leah.

[Col. 0320A] By Orion, however, we understand Moses. Just as Orion at his rising, as stated above, stirs storms and disturbs seas and lands, so Moses at his coming shook Egypt with the storms of the ten plagues, divided the sea, and drowned Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen. This greatly commends the majesty of the divinity of the man Jesus Christ: that he made such an Orion, whom his adversaries so greatly preferred to him, saying: “We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from” (John 9).

He himself beautifully and wisely indicated that he had made that Orion when, after they said, “In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such women,” “he bent down and wrote with his finger upon the ground” (John 8), signifying that he was the one by whose finger the tablets received by Moses had been written—the authority of whom was maliciously alleged against him.

After making that Arcturus and Orion, he also did what is wonderfully signified by the words, “turning darkness into morning and changing day into night.” For when he made such an Arcturus and such an Orion—that is, when he created the above-mentioned patriarchs and gave the Law to Moses—the Gentiles were darkness because they had no knowledge of God. But when he became man, he turned that darkness into morning because he enlightened the Gentiles by evangelical preaching. Conversely, he changed day into night, because he left Judaea—where God had previously been known, and whose knowledge is God—in blindness because of its unbelief.

After these things he also wrought that marvel: he chose teachers from among the Gentiles, whose teaching filled the whole world. This is signified when it adds: “who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth.” In the literal sense, this occurs almost every day. He raises the exceedingly bitter waters of the sea by heavenly heat and refines and strains them into the sweet taste of rain, like a medicinal cupping vessel, which [Col. 0320D] draws moisture and blood upward by the heat of its upper circuit. From this we learn the source of rains.

Plainly, according to this likeness, heavenly grace called many people from the depth of the age, overflowing from the false and bitter floods of pagan literary and philosophical studies; it turned their watery knowledge into the sweetness of heavenly wisdom, and, as they spoke with their mouths and wrote with their pens, abundantly watered and sufficiently drenched the face of the earth—that is, the faith of the Church—with many books and copious treatises. Hence the Psalmist says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. 64); and again: “You shall set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. 67). By “voluntary” he means given freely, with no preceding merits.

[Col. 0321A] “The Lord,” he says, “is his name.” Steadfastly, truly, and confidently it must be confessed before men, before kings and rulers or judges, before all nations, and against the Jews who are his enemies, that he who is such and so great, doing such and so great things, is “the Lord,” and that “this is his name”—although for a time he was despised, although for an hour he was crucified, and lay dead in the tomb.

But his enemies persisted in denying him, saying: “We do not want this man to be Lord; we do not want him to reign over us” (Luke 19). What then follows? “He smiles upon devastation against the strong man and brings destruction upon the mighty.” Who has not heard of the devastation and desolation of that strong and mighty people? They are strikingly called strong and mighty here because the unhappy people rose against him—whose name, as has been said, is the Lord—with the strength of pride and the power of audacity: not as one truly strong against one weak, but as one truly frenzied against a physician. In wicked strength they cast him out; in wicked power they killed him. In wicked strength and power, after his resurrection, they persecuted and expelled his apostles, and rejected the word of God which they wished to speak to them.

Therefore he brought “devastation upon such a strong man and desolation upon such a mighty man,” using the Romans as his servants—far more than he had previously used the Assyrians as attendants and the Babylonians as executors of his judgment. Thus the ten tribes were transported irrevocably among the Assyrians, while Judah was transferred to Babylon, to be recalled at the appointed time.

What that strong and mighty people suffered, as though at the hands of the Romans, this Lord did chiefly by not sparing or pitying them, but, as it were, smiling upon them because they had said in their apparent caution and foresight: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11). He smiled, I say, in the sense in which Wisdom says in his person: “I too shall laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1).

We may properly call it a smile when someone is angry and, parting his lips slightly, pretends to smile in order to display the magnitude of his anger. Scripture uses such words concerning the Lord, who suffers no passions, so that it may affirm as strongly as it can that, though the Lord is merciful by nature, he by no means has mercy upon the strong and mighty—that is, upon one proud in sin. But, as Scripture again says: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, but mercy shall be granted to the lowly” (Wis. 6).

“You turn him who is such and so great, who can do such and so great things, into wormwood,” he says: so that, though he is sweetest by nature and contains within himself all the sweetness of his nature, he pours out upon you, as though smiling, all the bitterness of his wrath. Now, as though someone were asking how or by what conduct they could have turned so sweet a being into wormwood for themselves, he turns to the questioner and says:

> “They hate him who rebukes in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks perfectly.”

[Col. 0322A] Here we must carefully observe, lest we determine by uncertainty or conjecture who that strong and mighty man is, upon whose devastation or desolation the sweet Lord, turned into wormwood, rightly smiles. He does not say that they sinned or committed something deserving reproof in the gate—that is, in the courts, which were customarily held at the city gate. Nor does he say that they spoke imperfectly. Rather: “They hated,” he says, “the one who rebukes; they abhorred the one who speaks perfectly.”

This is the unforgivable sin; this is the sin of the stronger and mightier: not to sin through ignorance or weakness, but to defend the sin of pride with an unrepentant heart, even to hate the one who rebukes and to abhor the one who dares speak perfectly—that is, not what pleases them, but what opposes their evil deeds.

But who rebuked in the gate, or who spoke perfectly? David did rebuke them, and spoke many things perfectly; and for this they hated and abhorred him, saying: “What portion have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kgs. 12). They also hated and abhorred this one who speaks these words, and the other prophets. Nevertheless, as with the other matters, so this also was truly and without doubt fulfilled in Christ alone, who rebuked justly and spoke perfectly.

For he himself speaks in the Psalm: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me” (Ps. 118); and again: “With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119). Therefore, remembering this when they abhorred him, and because of this saying, “He who hates me hates my Father also” (John 15), he then said: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.” Immediately he added: “But this happened in order that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (ibid.).

Therefore, above all we understand Christ here: him whom “they hate as one rebuking in the gate,” that is, openly and publicly, as he himself said: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have said nothing in secret” (John 18).
