And he fittingly rebuked thus “in the gate,” that is, not in secret, because he called himself the gate or door, and convicted of injustice those who had taken away the keys of the gates of knowledge.

We should truly call him alone one who speaks perfectly: “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). In this respect and according to this kind of perfection—because “deceit was not found in his mouth”—he is rightly called one speaking perfectly. Yet, no less in wisdom and teaching, he alone spoke perfectly: perfectly, I say, and so wonderfully that the servants of the chief priests and Pharisees, who had been sent to arrest him, said: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 7).

It follows:

> “Therefore, because you plundered the poor man and took from him a choice spoil, you shall build houses of squared stone and shall not inhabit them. You shall plant most desirable vineyards and shall not drink their wine, for I have known your many crimes and your strong sins—you who are enemies of the righteous, accepting a bribe and oppressing the poor in the gate. Therefore the prudent person shall be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

[Col. 0323A] Here he indicates more plainly that, although he uses words in the past tense, saying: “They hated the reprover in the gate and abhorred one speaking perfectly; you plundered the poor man and took a choice spoil from him,” he nevertheless weaves a prophecy about the future and directs it toward Christ, the true poor man, when he adds: “The prudent person shall be silent at that time.”

But that poor man possessed nothing in this world. How, then, did they plunder him, or what choice spoil did they take from him? Clearly, when they crucified him, “they divided his garments among themselves and cast lots over his clothing” (Ps. [Col. 0323B] 21). This was indeed great spoil in the magnitude of its sacrilege, though not in the quantity of its possessions.

But for those who look more deeply, there appears that spoil which he himself indicated in the Gospel parable, in which the tenants, seeing the householder’s son, said among themselves: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21). Thus they plundered that poor man—of whom we read in the Psalm, “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man” (Ps. 40), and again, “He persecuted the needy and destitute man, and the contrite in heart, in order to put him to death” (Ps. 108)—that poor man, I say, the humble Christ; and they “took a choice spoil from him” when they turned the people away from him, filling up the measure of their fathers, the kings of Israel, whom they imitated.

For just as those kings tore the ten tribes away from the house of David and from the Temple of the Lord, and made them worship the images of a calf—something already done when this prophecy was composed—so these men turned the people away from the Son of David, the Son of God, and made them believe their lies rather than God’s truth.

“Therefore,” he says, “you shall build houses of squared stone and shall not inhabit them; you shall plant most desirable vineyards and shall not drink their wine.” See what an example he now supplies of that turning of which he said, “You who turn judgment into wormwood.” For in the Law the merciful Lord ordained that, when the army was going out to battle, this proclamation should be made for all to hear:

> “Who is the man who has built [Col. 0323D] a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another dedicate it. Who is the man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that all may be permitted to eat from it? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another enjoy its use” (Deut. 20).

This he ordained then in his sweetness; but now, judgment having been turned into wormwood, he determines the opposite. “You shall build houses of squared stone,” he says, “and shall not inhabit them.” For the captor granted no such privilege; instead, demolishing and burning houses, cutting down vineyards, and forcing into swift captivity those builders and planters whom he did not kill with the sword, he ensured that they would neither dedicate the beautiful houses they made [Col. 0324A] nor drink the wine of the most desirable vineyards which they had carefully cultivated in ordered planting.

Why? Because, he says, “I have known your many crimes”—not merely many, but also, what is worse and unworthy of pardon—“I have known your strong sins.” For your sins do not proceed from weakness or ignorance, but from proud strength; they spring from strong pride, according to the Psalm: “Therefore pride possessed them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity comes forth as though from fatness” (Ps. 72).

Your iniquity toward your neighbour and your impiety toward God come forth not from weakness but from fatness. O you who are wickedly strong in sins, behold: I set it out for you briefly—“enemies of the righteous, accepting a bribe and oppressing the poor in the gate.”

[Col. 0324B] Since an enemy is so called from *standing against* (*obsistere*), by adding, “enemies of the righteous, accepting a bribe and oppressing the poor in the gate,” he gives fitting reasons for having said: “I have known your strong sins.” Truly they are “enemies of the righteous,” especially those who fulfilled the measure of their fathers in this: that they not only accepted a bribe in order to oppress the poor in the gate—that is, in judgment—which both they and their fathers often did, but also bargained for and gave a bribe—thirty pieces of silver—so that the Righteous One might be handed over.

Therefore, he says, because they are so strong and are “enemies of the righteous, the prudent person shall be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.” Truly, in this saying too, the Righteous and Prudent One made this prophet very truthful when, before unjust judges, because it was an evil time, he kept silent, as the Gospel narrative relates. For when the Evangelist said that the high priest arose and said to him, “Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” he added: “But Jesus was silent” (Matt. 26). And indeed, he kept silent as one prudent, knowing that whatever he answered to those plotting against him would be turned into an accusation against him.

Hence, according to another Evangelist, he said: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I ask, you will not answer me or release me” (Luke 22). That silence, moreover, signified another silence by which he now remains silent toward them, “commanding his clouds not to rain upon the vineyard…”

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]
that rain” (Isa. 5), that is, by forbidding [Col. 0324D] his own people to refrain from preaching the Gospel among them, because the time is evil, as Wisdom says: “Do not pour out speech where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32).

For the time is evil there because there is no hearing. Having said these things concerning the certain condemnation of the enemies of the righteous man, since there may be among them some—however very few—who sin through error and not through hatred of the righteous man, the prophetic discourse turns to them and says: “Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and the Lord, the God of hosts, will be with you, as you have said: Hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate; perhaps the Lord God may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.”

The fruit of this exhortation certainly did not wholly perish; for even at that time some sought good, so that the Lord said to Elijah: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (3 Kings 19). The same likewise occurred in the time of evangelical grace; for thus the Apostle says: “Even in this time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 6).

He fittingly now recalls Joseph, saying: “Perhaps the Lord God may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.” For Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, was of the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. Joseph’s life, commendable in itself, and likewise his deeds and sufferings, bore a type of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom the remnant was saved. But that part which says, “establish judgment in the gate,” did not take effect. Never, from the time when Jeroboam made the calves, did they hold a public judgment in order to abandon the calves and return to David their king. Nor, in the time when they crucified Christ, did they so establish judgment in the gate as to allow any testimony to Christ’s truth from the Scriptures to be publicly demonstrated to them by preaching.

It follows: “Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Ruler: In all the streets there shall be lamentation, and in all places outside they shall say, ‘Woe, woe!’ They shall call the farmer to mourning, and to lamentation those who know how to lament; and in all the ways there shall be lamentation, because I shall pass through your midst, says the Lord.”

This needs no exposition, because the matter is known and plain. For, to say nothing of the captivity of the ten tribes among the Assyrians and of Judah’s removal among the Babylonians: in what streets was there not lamentation, in what ways was there not mourning, and where was it not said, “Woe, woe!” when those “enemies of the Just One,” namely of Christ, were surrounded by the Roman siege? This also was remarkable, and seems not to be passed over here: before everyone said, because of the event, “Woe, woe,” one man, by a marvelous portent, as Josephus relates in *The Jewish War*, cried in every street and throughout every way, “Woe, woe.”

Jesus, he says, son of Ananus, a common man and a rustic, four years before the war began, while the city was in deepest peace and prosperity, when he had come for a festival day, suddenly began to cry out: “A voice from the East, a voice from the West, a voice from the four winds; a voice against Jerusalem and the Temple, a voice against husbands and newly married brides, a voice against all the people.” Crying these words day and night, he went about through all the city’s lanes. On this account, though scourged and torn with lashes to the very bones, he answered every blow: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem.” When Albinus, then governor, asked who he was, whence he came, or why he said these things, he gave no other reply, but, as though rehearsing a fixed speech, continued to cry, “Woe, woe to Jerusalem.” He did this continuously for seven years and five months, until, at the time of the siege, resting a little and then walking around upon the wall, he again cried in a loud voice: “Woe, woe to the city.” But when he finally added, “Woe also to me,” a stone hurled from an engine immediately killed him.

The words added at last—“because I shall pass through your midst, says the Lord”—signify great wrath and that abandonment which we observe to have been signified in the Gospel. For when they had led him to the brow of the hill upon which their city was built, to throw him down, “he himself,” says the Evangelist, “passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4). By passing through and going away in this manner he signified in deed that what he had shortly before threatened them in mystery would without doubt come to pass. For he said to them: “Truly I say to you, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months, when a great famine came upon the whole land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow woman at Zarephath of Sidon. And many lepers were in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (ibid.).

For, almost with the force of an oath, by saying “truly,” he terribly indicated that they would suffer an excessive famine of God’s word. In passing through, he would leave them, while the jar of meal and the flask of oil—that is, evangelical teaching and the grace of the Holy Spirit—would not fail among a certain Gentile widow, Elijah, that is, God the Lord, namely Jesus Christ, being present. He further indicated that they would be dead in the leprosy of their sin, while Naaman the Syrian—that is, the Gentile people—was healed through the washing of Elisha, that is, Jesus Christ. For *Elisha* is interpreted “the salvation of my God”; and that salvation for us is the Lord Jesus Christ.

One further point must not be passed over: in such a passing-through of the Lord they are said to call the farmer to mourning. We judge this to have been said with wonderful reproach. For what? Do farmers truly know how to mourn as they ought? Or whom ought we to understand as “the farmer,” except one so rustic that he lacks the knowledge of mourning? For knowledge truly makes mourners. Accordingly, just as in the order of the spirits, the spirit of knowledge is third upward from the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11), so in the order of the Beatitudes the Lord places the blessedness of mourners in third place: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

Foolish, therefore, are those who, when the Lord is passing through, call the farmer to mourning rather than the cultured or ecclesiastical person well trained in holy knowledge: that is, those who mourn only the loss of temporal goods, not spiritual ones; only bodily funerals, rather than the deaths of souls. Finally, when he had said, “they shall call the farmer to mourning,” he added, “and to lamentation those who know how to lament,” not as his own judgment, but according to their vain estimation.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327A] 141 “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved” (Song 4), says the bridegroom in the Song of Songs; and it is known that this bridegroom is Christ, and his beloved is the holy prophetic and apostolic Church. What greater beauty can that beloved possess than the understanding of truth and the knowledge of God hidden in the sacred writings?

For just as Moses’ outward face was made radiant by converse with God (Exod. 34), so too the faithful souls of Moses, the prophets, and the apostles shone with their inward countenance illuminated by the holy spirit of knowledge, possessing a beautiful and radiant understanding of truth. Again, just as Moses had to veil his face when he spoke to the people—for Aaron and his sons, seeing the brightness of his face, were afraid to come near—so Moses and the prophets had to cover the brightness of their inward meaning with a coarser veil. For the Jews or children of Israel of that age could by no means have endured it if they had preached in plain and open words the mysteries of Christ and the Church which they knew.

For how then would they have endured it? How would rebels and unbelievers have wished the Scriptures to remain safe, when even now they are exceedingly impatient to see or hear anything spiritual? We say this lest it seem surprising that Amos here and the other prophets spoke so obscurely, according to that saying of the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17), that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets. Yet the very fact that they spoke, as it were, darkly, they did with a single eye having no portion of darkness: that is, not from envy, but from caution; not begrudging understanding to readers, but guarding against the malice of readers, to whom not everything ought to be entrusted, just as pearls are not to be cast before swine (Matt. 7).

Therefore, since we have heard the Beloved saying, “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you,” and afterwards, “Arise, make haste, my beloved; come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (Song 4), let us understand Christ to desire the beauty of Holy Scripture to appear: the beauty of prophetic truth, the beauty of the dove, whose, as the Psalmist says, “feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67).

And because it is not fitting that she be brought or come through any others than those who love purity of heart, “Come,” he says, “from Lebanon, come.” This is as though he said: Let those handle you who, according to the name of Lebanon, which is interpreted “whiteness,” are pure. He briefly expresses the primary reward of this labor, if it is worthily performed, when he says, “you shall be crowned.” This should suffice for the lover of wisdom—which is the beauty of the holy Church—that she herself be crowned in wisdom. For in whom will wisdom be crowned except in one who is wise?

Accordingly, just as in the Psalm the Lord says, “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113), so now, crying, “Not to us, Lord, not to us,” but to your Word, your wisdom, the Scriptures of your truth, prepare a crown, let us carry through the course of study that we have begun.

After the prophet, or the Lord speaking in the prophet, has so often said, “Seek me and live; seek the Lord and live; seek good and not evil, that you may live,” and so forth, he suddenly cries out terribly and says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? That day of the Lord is darkness and not light: as when a man flees from before a lion and a bear meets him, or enters a house and leans his hand on the wall and a serpent bites him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and no brightness in it?”

A great outcry, a remarkable denunciation: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord!” It would not seem so strange if it were said: Woe to those who do not fear the day of the Lord. For not to fear belongs entirely to wicked or ungodly men (Prov. 20); but to desire it may belong to the good, so much so that the Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). Indeed, even such persons’ desire is not without a certain fear. For who will glory that he has a pure heart? Yet that fear is not servile but filial; it has no punishment, because it has great consolation in hope.

When, therefore, he says, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord,” what does he do except strike at the boldness of those who trust in themselves as righteous? There is no doubt that, greatly wearied by the madness of those who were such, he cried out in this way. What they habitually said in resisting and contradicting the prophets, how they customarily mocked and ridiculed them and displayed their own confidence, we gather from other passages of Scripture.

For example, after Isaiah had said, “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with a cart-rope,” he added: “Who say, ‘Let his work hasten; let it quickly come, that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may know it.’” Surely these are the words of those who desire wrongly and insolently, and hear wrongly and foolishly. And who could sufficiently wonder at the disposition of one who is wrongly self-confident and bold in such matters? One such was Zedekiah, who struck Micaiah on the cheek and said: “Has the Spirit of the Lord then left me and spoken to you?” (3 Kings, final chapter).

It is also relevant to recall that they insulted the prophets, according to the words which they utter in song and mockery in Isaiah: “Command upon command, command upon command; wait upon wait, wait upon wait; a little here, a little here” (Isa. 28). Thus they sang as though desirous and impatient of delay, as though refusing to grant that a prophet should be considered true because they did not more swiftly obtain the words of the prophesying prophet, or of the commanding Lord, after far too much waiting.

We can therefore understand how and by whom this man was wearied or provoked when he cried out: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? That day of the Lord is darkness and not light.” He labors as he cries; crying, he labors, so that before it comes we may perceive and escape the distress of that day of the Lord. For there will be distress for sinners on every side: “as when,” he says, “a man flees from before a lion and a bear meets him; he enters a house and leans his hand on the wall, and a serpent bites him.”

Many things may be inferred from these comparisons. According to the historical sense and the opinion of the Jews, the meaning seems to be this: those fleeing from Nebuchadnezzar the lion will encounter Ahasuerus, under whom Esther’s history is narrated; or, after the Assyrian and Chaldean empire is destroyed, the Medes and Persians will arise. And when, under the reign of Cyrus, you have returned, and under Darius’s command have begun to build the house of the Lord, and have placed all your confidence in the Temple, so that you rest in it and lean your weary hands upon its walls, then Alexander king of the Macedonians, or Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, will come, linger in the Temple, and bite you like a serpent—not outside, in Babylon and Susa, but within the borders of the holy land.

This opinion of the Hebrews is far too narrow and slight. It does not attain the profundity of the day of the Lord, nor does it reach to the times of the Roman Empire, under which their woe was much greater than under the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Persians, Medes, and Macedonians. Let us therefore refer all these things to the day of the Lord, to the coming of the Lord. For the terror of his majesty may not unfittingly be compared to a lion and a bear, especially since Jeremiah, in Lamentations, after first saying, “Even when I cry and plead, he has shut out my prayer; he has blocked my ways with squared stones; he has overthrown my path,” immediately added: “He has become a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding” (Lam. 3).

Thus when he says, “as when a man flees from before a lion and a bear meets him,” we understand in the two comparisons the day of the Lord: his first and second coming. For at his first coming he came upon them like a lion. Indeed, he was slain as a lamb and “did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53); but he rose like a lion and sent forth his roar through all the earth. Hence this same prophet said at the beginning: “The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he shall utter his voice.”

They fled then from the face of this lion, but they did not escape. For a bear met, or will meet, those who wished to flee: that is, the unavoidable terror of the second coming. And it is fitting that such a bear should meet them, because they fled from the lion’s face. They ought rather to have fallen prostrate before that lion—that is, done penance in response to the preaching of Christ’s Gospel. For just as a lion is said to spare a prostrate man, so Christ spares a sinner doing penance.

They fled from him as rebels and unbelievers; and in fleeing they went out from the house of the Lord, from the Church of God’s saints, while he pursued them and exacted vengeance for all the righteous blood shed upon the earth (Matt. 23). He signified this to them when, with a whip made of cords, he drove all who were selling and buying from the Temple (Luke 12). Thus the lion pursued them as they fled, and the bear met them. For, as he had foretold, saying, “There shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath upon this people” (Luke 21), when the Romans came they fell by the edge of the sword (Isa. 8; Zech. 12), were led captive into all nations, and—as shall happen—“they shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19); nor could they flee away from their distress.

Meanwhile, thus hemmed in between lion and bear—that is, between the wrath of the first and the wrath of the second coming, or day, of the Lord—they enter the house and lean their hand upon the wall, trusting in carnal ceremonies and thinking that Moses is their patron. For they lean their hand upon him as upon a wall, when they glory in Moses by circumcising and observing the Sabbath, as we often hear them boasting in our own hearing. “The one who accuses you,” says the Lord, “is Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5). Surely that hope is not true hope, but the devil’s deception. Therefore, after saying, “he enters the house and leans his hand upon the wall,” he added, “and a serpent bites him.” Thus the Antichrist will deceive those who presume in this way in this age, and in the age to come the devil will not cease to torment them.

Having said these things, he immediately cries out in inquiry: “Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and no brightness in it?” He questions sharply and strictly, knowing that what he foretold cannot be denied: that this day of the Lord is darkness and not light. He knows, I say, that where the lion is fled, the bear meets one, and when both are avoided, the biting serpent is present, there is dark confusion, confused gloom, and no light of illuminating counsel. And he rightly doubled the sharpness and force of his question with somewhat different words: “Darkness and not light; gloom and no brightness.”

Now, as we have already said, the day of the Lord is not one but two; likewise, the comings of the Lord are not only one but two: one in which he has already come, the other in which he will undoubtedly come. Both befall unbelieving Jews as a judgment of condemnation, as condemnation to blindness. For of the first he says: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9). And the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened to Israel, and he gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear” (Rom. 11). And in Isaiah: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes” (Isa. 6). Again: “The Lord has mingled for you a spirit of drowsiness, and he shall close your eyes; he shall cover your prophets and princes who see visions” (Isa. 29). And there are many similar sayings.

Concerning the second coming, after much else, he says: “He shall look upward and gaze upon the earth, and behold distress and darkness, dissolution, anguish, and pursuing gloom; and he shall not be able to fly from his distress” (Isa. 8). Rightly, therefore, he was not content to say once, “Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light?” but repeated, “and gloom and no brightness in it,” because in each day, or coming, of the Lord, together with the outward distress of tribulation, they have within themselves the darkness of confusion; in each their eyes are darkened so that they do not see; in each their way is darkness and slipperiness.

It follows: “I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not receive the odor of your assemblies. Even if you bring me your burnt offerings and gifts, I will not accept them; nor will I regard the vows of your fattened beasts. Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not hear the music of your lyre. And judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent.”

According to the sense which we took a little earlier from the wall—where he said that the serpent bites the one who leans his hand upon it—these words are very suitably added. For, as we said there, the wall upon which they lean is carnal ceremony. But how could the wall of festivals stand, or bear upon itself the one who leaned upon it, when God hated those festivals? “I hate,” he says, and not only do I hate, but I also “reject your festivals.” Therefore Paul rightly, and not without great mystery, when he stood in the council of the Jews to give account for himself, and Ananias the high priest commanded those standing by to strike him on the mouth, said to him: “God shall strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23).

And when those standing by said, “Do you revile God’s high priest?” he replied, “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest.” Truly he did not know, nor did he wish or ought to have known, that that man was high priest whose priesthood, according to this prophecy, God hated and rejected; for it was a wall upon which the serpent bit anyone who leaned his hand. It had not yet been struck down, and the wall of that priesthood still stood whitewashed: the exceedingly beautiful Temple still stood, and the customary worship continued, crowds frequenting and celebrating in that place. But afterwards God would strike and destroy it through Roman arms. Thus, after it was struck down, that wall was neither whitewashed nor overlaid again so as to recover its former glory.

Hence this same prophet afterwards says: “He showed me this, and behold the Lord stood upon a plastered wall, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said, ‘A mason’s trowel.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘Behold, I shall place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer overlay it’” (Amos 7).

All the things which he now condemns by saying, “I hate and reject your festivals; I will not receive the odor of your assemblies; I will not accept your burnt offerings and gifts; I will not regard the vows of your fattened beasts; take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not hear the music of your lyre”—all these things, I say, while they still stood and were celebrated, constituted a wall overlaid and whitewashed. But now it is manifest that God has rejected them. To hate, reject, and refuse odor are spoken by a human analogy, so that we may understand God’s effect through our own language.

Meanwhile, we should note how he said: “Even if you offer me your burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them.” He said, “to me,” not “to the calves” to which they sacrificed at Bethel and Dan. We say this against the Jewish defense. For they say that God spoke and said, “I hate and reject your festivals,” and the rest, because at that time they sacrificed to the calves which Jeroboam had made. He also fittingly says: “Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not hear the music of your lyre”—namely, the songs of the Levites, by which they praised the Lord—calling them noise and a confused sound, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

Having said these things, by which he plainly announces the rejection of that people, or of carnal Judaism, he immediately and pertinently adds: “Judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent” (Ecclus. 15). For this judgment truly needs revelation, and the depth of this judgment—by which it was thus judged and done that, as we said above, the natural branches being broken, others should be grafted into the good root—cannot be understood by anyone except him to whom God has deigned to reveal it by his Spirit.

Hence, after the Apostle had discussed this matter at length, he finally cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). It is therefore pertinent, as has been said, that he says: “Judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent.” For just as water has a hidden source but a manifest and visible course, so the depth of God’s judgments is indeed incomprehensible, but from many visible things it is known that all his judgment is just.

And fittingly, after saying, “Judgment shall be revealed like water,” he added, “and righteousness like a mighty torrent,” thereby indicating that no one can resist, or even answer, the righteousness or just judgment of God. Thus the same Apostle, arguing on this very matter, after first setting forth: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?’” suddenly cried out with just indignation: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9).

He rightly said both: “Judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent,” because the authority of Holy Scripture, which everywhere defends God’s righteousness, firmly repels the insolent inquirer who answers presumptuously, while gently instructing the humble hearer with some small measure of revelation. So the same Apostle, after repelling the presumptuous man by saying, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” turns to the humble hearer and speaks more gently: “But if God, willing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,” and so forth.

Surely the following passage in this prophet belongs to the same revelation of judgment or righteousness, when God himself asks and says: “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel?” And immediately he adds: “And you carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I shall cause you to migrate beyond Damascus, says the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

This, I say, belongs to the revelation of God’s judgment or righteousness. For by these things God is greatly vindicated: that he did not unjustly reject that people (Exod. 9), nor act from changeableness of mind or adopt a new plan in thus abandoning the nation which he had once chosen as his own because of its deserving merits. “Their heart was never right with him,” says the Psalm (Ps. 77), “nor were they found faithful in his covenant.” Hence he convicted them by asking: “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years?” and so forth.

Therefore, in order to understand God’s judgment and righteousness in this severity, by which, as said above, he did not spare the natural branches, let us likewise turn with open eyes to those times to which the present words refer us. Having gone out of Egypt and crossed the Red Sea, they immediately made the head of a molten calf. They first made an altar for it; they offered it burnt offerings and peace offerings before they did so to the Lord. Moses was still on the mountain speaking with God and receiving instruction about the construction of the tabernacle and the establishment of sacrificial rites; during that delay they committed this crime.

Moses then carried out a kind of vengeance, saying, “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh” (Exod. 31), and on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell. But this was not the Lord’s vengeance or sentence; for the Lord had not commanded it, but Moses had. Strictly pious with a good zeal, and piously stern, he hastened to forestall God’s wrath and strove utterly to turn away God’s vengeance. But God, knowing that they would not cease from sins of this kind, was unwilling to be content with the vengeance Moses had carried out. He said: “But on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs.” Again: “You are a stiff-necked people; if I go up once into your midst, I shall destroy you” (Exod. 33).

Therefore, when after saying, “Judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent,” he adds, “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years?” he wishes sufficiently to vindicate himself from having sought or issued a new sentence in rejecting that people through a change of mind arising from new causes.

And so that the following words may be suitably joined—“Did you offer me victims and sacrifices?”—one must understand: “No, but to the calf which you made.” Perhaps it should be read: “But you carried the tabernacle of your Moloch, and the image of your idols, the star of your god, whom you made for yourselves.” The meaning is this: Moses indeed seized the calf which you made, burned it, and ground it to powder; but you persevered in idolatrous worship and set before yourselves figures which one could not shatter or deny to be heavenly—namely, the stars of heaven.

Stephen the first martyr had this in view when, after saying, “They made a calf in those days, offered sacrifice to the image, and rejoiced in the works of their hands,” he immediately added: “But God turned and gave them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you offer me victims and sacrifices?’” (Acts 7), and the rest.

But what was that turning by which God thus turned them? Was the whole purpose of God or Moses in breaking the calf that they should worship not the form of a calf but rather the host, or stars, of heaven? For after he had said here, “You carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols,” he showed in the next phrase what that image or idol was, saying, “the star of your god”—that is, Lucifer—which the Saracens venerate even to this day.

What then was that turning? Surely it was grievous and far different from what God intended. It is as though he says: God—or Moses—in breaking the calf intended that they should instead turn to worship the stars of heaven; that they should carry not the tabernacle of God, which Moses made at God’s command, but “the tabernacle of Moloch,” that is, of their king, namely Lucifer, whom they honored as God, calling him their king.

From that time on, all that they did is shown to have been done not for God but for idols. For though we read that, after making the calf, they offered certain things to the Lord, they did so not willingly but through fear of punishments and of the slaughter of those who fell because of idols.

Thus judgment is revealed to those who attend in the Scriptures to the merits of preceding events. Therefore, he says, “I shall cause you to migrate beyond Damascus”: that is, you shall be led into Babylon, which indeed lies beyond Damascus in relation to the position of your land. The Lord says this; the Lord has purposed and determined to do these things. What Lord, or what kind of Lord? Do you wish to know his name? “The God of hosts is his name.” Why was it fitting that he should be called by such a name in the present passage? Because he has many armies serving his judgment or righteousness, so that his word against you may be fulfilled. He has the armies of the Assyrians and Chaldeans; he has the armies of the Medes and Persians; he will have the armies of the Macedonians and Greeks; he will have the armies of the Romans. Through them judgment concerning you will plainly be carried out before the whole world, and then woe to you. For it follows:

## CHAPTER VI
“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and who put your trust in Mount Samaria; chief men, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel in pomp. Pass over to Calneh and see; go thence to great Hamath; descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to whatever are the best kingdoms among them, to see whether their border is broader than your border. You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity; [Col. 0335A] who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery—as David, they thought, had instruments of song—drinking wine from bowls, anointed with the finest ointment, and suffering nothing over the breaking of Joseph.”

This woe is plainly proclaimed against impious priests. The preceding woe, however—“Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord”—was proclaimed generally against all who despise God’s judgment, of whatever rank they may be.

At this point one should not pass over the great miracle of surpassing eloquence in the Holy Scriptures. For although, in their inward sense, the mysteries of heaven possess great majesty, nevertheless on the surface their expression shines with the utmost beauty—just as if one found a precious casket which, silver on the outside, held costly gold within—according to that Psalm: “The wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII). This is as though it said: the letter of Holy Scripture is beautiful and bright outwardly, but inwardly it contains mysteries of spiritual understanding far more beautiful and far more precious.

But does this point need our assertion? The holy Fathers have splendidly perceived and observed that even this prophet, taken from being a shepherd, did not lack—and does not lack—that eloquence of which secular men are so greatly proud, the companion of heavenly wisdom. Blessed Father Augustine, the most trustworthy appraiser of divine discourse, takes up this passage among others for treatment as an example (On Christian Doctrine, book IV, ch. 7):

> “I see that I must say something also about the eloquence of the prophets, where much is concealed through figurative expression; and the more those things seem to be covered by transferred words, the sweeter they become when opened.

And I shall do this especially from the book of that prophet who says that he was a shepherd or herdsman, and was thence taken by divine command and sent to prophesy to God’s people. Therefore, when he rebuked the impious—proud and luxurious, and consequently most devoid of brotherly love—the prophet himself, rustic or sprung from rustic stock, cried out, saying: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and put your trust in Mount Samaria,” and so forth.

Would those men, who, as learned and eloquent persons, despise our prophets as though uneducated and ignorant of speech, have wished to speak differently, if something of this kind had to be said to such people—provided, at least, that they did not wish to speak madly? What is there that sober ears could desire more in this expression?

First, with what force is the invective hurled, as it were, against slumbering ears in order to awaken them? “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and who put your trust in Mount Samaria; chief men, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel in pomp.” Then, to show them ungrateful for God’s benefits, who had given them broad expanses of kingdom—although they placed their trust in Mount Samaria, where idols were everywhere worshipped—he says: “Pass over to Calneh and see; go to great Hamath; descend to Gath of the Philistines, [Col. 0336A] and to whatever are the best kingdoms among them, to see whether their border is broader than your border.”

At the same time, as these things are said, the speech is adorned by the names of places as though by lights: Zion, Samaria, Calneh, great Hamath, and Gath of the Philistines. Then the words joined to these places are varied most fittingly: “You are wealthy; you put your trust; pass over; go; descend.”

Next, the captivity that is to come under an iniquitous king is announced as drawing near, when the words are added: “You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity.” Then the grounds of their luxury are set forth: “You who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.” These seven clauses form three paired periods.

For he does not say: “You who are set apart for the evil day; you who draw near to the throne of iniquity; you who sleep on ivory beds; you who luxuriate upon your couches; you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.” Had he said this, it would indeed have been beautiful for all six clauses to proceed from one repeated pronoun and each to be concluded by the speaker’s voice. But it is more beautifully done when two clauses are attached to the same pronoun, unfolding three statements: one concerning the prediction of captivity—“you who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity”; another concerning sensual indulgence—“you who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon your couches”; and a third concerning gluttony—“you who eat lambs from the flock and calves [Col. 0336C] from the midst of the herd.” Thus the speaker may either finish each separately, making six clauses, or suspend the first, third, and fifth in his voice, then connect the second with the first, the fourth with the third, and the sixth with the fifth, thereby making three paired periods most fittingly: one showing impending calamity; another, an impure bed; and the third, a lavish table.

Then he rebukes the luxurious pleasure of the ears. Having said, “who sing to the sound of the psaltery”—for music can be practised wisely by wise persons—with a remarkable elegance of expression he relaxes the force of the invective and speaks not to them but about them, to remind us to distinguish the music of the wise man from that of the man given to luxury. He does not say: “You who sing to the sound of the psaltery, and think that you possess instruments of song like David”; rather, after saying to them what the luxurious ought to hear—“You who sing to the sound of the psaltery”—he also in a sense revealed their ignorance to others, adding: “Like David, they thought that they possessed instruments of song, drinking wine from bowls and anointed with the finest ointment.”

These three clauses are better delivered if the first two members of the period are held in suspension and the third brought to a close. Now the addition to all these: “and they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph,” is said with marvellous beauty. He did not say, “they suffered nothing over the breaking of their brother”; Joseph is put in place of “brother,” so that any brother might be signified by the particular name of one of the brothers whose fame is renowned both in the evils he endured and in the goods he rendered in return.

[Col. 0337A] Let these observations on the beauty of the letter suffice here, with a fitting recollection of so great a teacher. Knowing the gracefulness of Holy Scripture and wishing it to be known, he adopted this chapter as the nearest example and, as it were, wiped bleary eyes with his fingers, so that we may clearly see how splendid expressions accompany the wisdom of God speaking in the prophets: wisdom not directed toward eloquence, yet eloquence not departing from wisdom.

Let us now return to the mysteries of meaning. “Woe,” he says, “to you who are wealthy in Zion and put your trust in Mount Samaria.” He announces both destructions, or both captivities: that of the two tribes, whose royal city was Zion, and that of the ten, whose capital was Samaria.

When he says, “Woe to you who are wealthy [Col. 0337B] in Zion,” we should not suppose that only the captivity is announced in which the two tribes were carried away to Babylon, to return after seventy years. Far more does he announce that captivity in which they are now scattered throughout the whole world, their city and temple destroyed. While that temple stood, impious priests were exceedingly wealthy in Zion; proud of their wealth, they crucified the poor Christ for this one reason: that he disputed against their wealthy avarice.

The “chief men and heads of the people” of that time—Annas and Caiaphas, the other rulers and elders—were truly “set apart for the evil day” and drew near “to the throne of iniquity.” Born evil in an evil time—for it would have been better for them had they not been born—they sentenced the Son of God to death. This truly was to draw near to the throne of iniquity.

From that throne of iniquity fury cast down the high priest headlong, when, after saying, “I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou art the Son of God,” Jesus answered, “Thou hast said it”; and he tore his garments, saying, “He has blasphemed” (Matt. XXVI). From that time onward, neither could that throne of iniquity stand, nor could the high priest sit upon it.

We do not doubt that these men were already present to the prophetic spirit, so that the prophet saw them in a marvellous way drawing near—indeed rushing and making the assault of an unrestrained outcry—upon the throne of iniquity, when Pilate sat upon the judgment-seat and said, “Behold your king.” “Away, away,” they cried, “crucify him. We have no king but Caesar. If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar’s friend” (John XVI).

Therefore the chief men of that time, as has already been said, were indeed “set apart for the evil day” and drew near “to the throne of iniquity.” The following words are equally plainly applicable to them: “You who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.” For the apostle James too, in precisely this sense, after first saying, “Come now, you rich: weep and howl for the miseries which shall come upon you” (Jas. V), afterwards added: “You have feasted upon earth and nourished your hearts in luxuries. On the day of slaughter you have led [him] away; you have killed the righteous one, and he did not resist you” (ibid.).

The remaining words—“who sing to the sound of the psaltery; like David, they thought that they possessed instruments of song; drinking wine from bowls, anointed with the finest ointment, and suffering nothing over the breaking of Joseph”—apply to the same persons as gravely as they do truly. Concerning them, as the Lord himself testified (Matt. XV), Isaiah prophesied well: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

And therefore they falsely thought that they possessed instruments of song as David had them, however clearly or loudly they might sing to the sound of the psaltery with their lips. Who can doubt that, on the night when they seized the Lord, they drank wine to vomiting, since it was their Passover evening? Therefore they are rightly rebuked here as “drinking wine from bowls.” And in the Psalm, speaking in the person of the Prophet himself: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine made songs about me” (Ps. LXVIII).

How especially true, moreover, is the final statement, “and they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph,” if one carefully considers that he is most fittingly designated by the name Joseph, whose type he bore: “Joseph was sold as a slave and was humbled in fetters and afflicted, so that iron passed through his soul” (Ps. CIV), and afterwards was made prince of Egypt. For while the Lord hung broken upon the cross, they suffered nothing over his breaking.

Finally, not to mention that they mocked him as he hung there, that passers-by blasphemed him, taunting and shaking their heads, and saying: [Col. 0338C] “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself” (Matt. XXVII)—not to mention these things, this alone sufficiently shows how truly they suffered nothing over his breaking: when he said, “I thirst,” they put a sponge full of vinegar upon hyssop and offered it to his mouth (John XIX). For who would not marvel how far removed they were from compassion for him, when, at such an hour, in such distress, with such thirst, they gave vinegar to one who said, “I thirst”?

What he says—“and they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph”—must therefore be weighed on a great and subtle balance. Let him then say to these impious persons, sleeping [Col. 0338D] and luxuriating, eating and drinking, singing while eating and drinking, and suffering nothing over the breaking of Joseph: “Pass over to Calneh and see; go to great Hamath; descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to whatever are the best kingdoms among them, to see whether their border is broader than your border.”

You indeed know well enough that the whole extent of all kingdoms is broader than your border, that is, the land of promise; but you must know it in another manner: unwillingly, and detained through a long captivity, you shall see it with your own eyes. This mockery is like saying to someone cast into a fiery furnace, “Go and see whether it is hot,” or to one who is about to be cast into the sea, “Go and see whether it is deep.”

“Calneh,” a city of Persia; “great Hamath,” which is now called Antioch, “great” to distinguish it from lesser Hamath, called Epiphania; “Gath of the Philistines, [Col. 0339A] and whatever are the best kingdoms among them”—it is enough to have named these for all the nations to which they were to be led captive. Of this captivity he immediately adds: “Therefore now they shall go into exile at the head of those who go into exile, and the faction of the luxurious shall be taken away.”

For what does it mean to say, “At the head of those who go into exile they shall now go into exile,” except, as if he said: more remarkably—indeed, more miserably—and with a greater spectacle before the whole world, they shall go into exile than any other persons or peoples who have ever gone, or ever shall go, into exile? Many peoples, conquered by others, have left their homes and been led captive; but these were and are so pre-eminent among all exiles that no migration has ever displayed, or could display, such a marvel.

Josephus himself, observing this, when he described their miserable destruction and the miseries they deserved, says that he cannot recount their iniquities one by one; but, to speak briefly, he thinks that no other city ever suffered such things, and that no nation since human memory has been more savage in wickedness. Thus, he says, “they shall now go into exile at the head of those who go into exile”: that is, in the quality and extent of their exile they shall be the most eminent and most noted of all exiles or captives.

Although he says, “they shall now go into exile,” this is rightly understood of the impending captivity of the ten tribes at that time; nevertheless, indeed far more, it must be understood of this final captivity in which the Jews were captured and scattered under Roman leadership. For this was not hidden from the prophetic Spirit, since the whole intent of prophetic contemplation undoubtedly looked especially toward Christ’s coming.

“And the faction of the luxurious,” he says, “shall be taken away.” A “faction” is a conspiracy or agreement of evil men. It is well known that they conspired or agreed to Christ’s death at the instigation of the chief priests and elders, who persuaded the crowds; and they did this with excessive and most cruel wantonness—or wanton cruelty—when, on that night, they mocked him, struck him with fists, beat him with slaps, spat upon him, plucked his cheeks, crowned him with thorns, and finally crucified him.

Therefore when he says, “the faction of the luxurious shall be taken away,” he foretells great future weakness for those who did the deeds just mentioned: namely, that, as we now see, they cannot form factions, conspire, or unite in conspiracy to kill any of those who call upon Christ.

Indeed, when they killed Christ, they had already been so diminished in authority that they had no judges from among themselves. Hence, when Pilate said, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law,” they replied, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John XVIII). Yet they were still sufficiently factious, and able to be so, as to gather a council, dare to raise a tumult before the governor of Roman authority by demanding that he be crucified, and afterwards dare to kill and crucify certain wise men and prophets whom Christ sent to them after his resurrection, scourging them in their synagogues and persecuting them from city to city (Matt. XXIII).

But after forty-two years they went into exile, as has already been said, “at the head of those who go into exile”; and from that time their faction was so taken away that they no longer dare to rage or openly stand against the Lord and against his Christ, seeing Christ publicly worshipped against them and around them, and reigning as Lord, according to the saying: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. CIX).

It follows: “The Lord God has sworn by his own soul, says the Lord God of hosts: I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his house, and I will hand over the city with its inhabitants.” It is wonderful to say that “the Lord has sworn,” and this “by his own soul”—not because God has a soul, but because he speaks in human affections. What has “the Lord God sworn by his own soul”? Namely, that he abhors the pride of Jacob and hates his house, as he also says in Isaiah: “Your new moons, Sabbaths, and feast days my soul has hated” (Isa. I)—and that he will hand over the city with its inhabitants.

What he had said, “I abhor the pride of Jacob,” he repeats and explains what Jacob’s pride was by saying, “and I hate his house.” “His house”—that is, the temple, then unique—he says was his pride. That this is so is proved by other words of the same Lord God in Ezekiel: “Behold,” he says, “I will defile my sanctuary, the pride of your power” (Ezek. XXIV).

Surely the Lord God would not say this or that unless he had found them to possess an intolerable pride because of that temple. For they gloried in God’s temple with a perverse glory, since they did not seek or care that God should be glorified in his temple; and their spirit was lifted up in contempt of all nations because of that temple, because of that name—that the true God was named among them, though not honoured.

The Lord God “swore by his own soul,” that is, by himself, that he abhorred and hated this pride, “because,” as the Apostle says, “he had no one greater by whom to swear. For men swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of all their disputes for confirmation” (Heb. VI). His word could indeed have been believed even had he not sworn. “But he more abundantly willed [Col. 0340D] to show the immutability of his counsel, and therefore interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation” (ibid.).

Let us therefore hold most firmly the conviction concerning the rejection, as the Apostle says, of the former commandment (Heb. VII), or of the old priesthood or temple, and concerning the introduction of a better hope: namely, that God rejected the former with hatred, but approved the faith of the Gospel with love.

Under the same oath, what follows is confirmed: “And I will hand over the city with its inhabitants.” Certainly that surrender ought not to have been light or small, when he so threatened it with an oath interposed. The following words too are announced under the same oath:

[Col. 0341A] “And if ten men remain in one house, they too shall die. And his kinsman shall take him and burn him, in order to carry the bones out of the house; and he shall say to him who is in the inner rooms of the house, ‘Is there still anyone with you?’ And he shall answer, ‘It is finished.’ And he shall say to him, ‘Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord.’ For behold, the Lord has commanded, and he will strike the greater house with ruins and the smaller house with breaches.”

It must be remembered that above he said: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you did not return to me” (Amos IV). Behold, here in the overthrow there is something more severe than there. For when the discourse concerned the overthrow to be made upon the Sodomites, Abraham said at the end: “What if ten righteous persons are found?” The Lord replied: “I will not destroy it for the sake of ten” (Gen. XVIII).

But now he says here: “If ten men remain in one house, they too shall die.” We understand “those remaining” here to be righteous persons, as also above where it was said: “The city from which a thousand went out, a hundred shall remain in it; and that from which a hundred went out, ten shall remain” (Amos V).

Clearly, when he says, “If ten men remain in one house, they too shall die,” he announces that in his wrath he will make no distinction between righteous and unrighteous persons, but will condemn righteous and unrighteous Jews alike under one sentence of death. This is confirmed in Ezekiel in clearer words, where the Lord God says: “Behold, I am against you; I will draw my sword from its sheath and kill in you the righteous and the wicked” (Ezek. XXI).

What then? Has God forgotten his justice? Wishing him to remember it, Abraham stood before the Lord and, drawing near, said: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked?” And again he said: “If there are fifty righteous persons in the city, will they perish together? Will you not spare that place for the fifty righteous persons if they are in it? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should become like the wicked. This is not yours, you who judge the whole earth.”

The Lord consented, and said: “I will spare the whole place for the sake of fifty; I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there; I will not strike for the sake of forty; I will not do it if I find thirty there; I will not kill for the sake of twenty; I will not destroy for the sake of ten” (ibid.).

Has he, I ask, forgotten so great a mercy when he says, “If ten men remain, they too shall die,” not in a city but “in one house”? Certainly not. Rather, those righteous persons are exceedingly unrighteous. They are rightly left behind as the remnant, because they are righteous in such a way that, wishing to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to God’s righteousness, as the Apostle says: “For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness” (Rom. X).

What that righteousness of God is, he immediately adds: “For Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes” [Col. 0342A] (ibid.). He wonderfully indicates this righteousness, against whom they would conceive a rebellious and obstinate hatred—namely Christ, by faith in whom all holy and righteous persons have been justified—when he says: “And his kinsman shall take him and burn him, in order to carry the bones out of the house; and he shall say to him who is in the inner rooms of the house, ‘Is there still anyone with you?’ And he shall answer, ‘It is finished.’ And he shall say to him, ‘Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord.’”

Let whoever wishes read the History of Josephus, where he describes the destruction of Jerusalem, and he will know how truly that calamity was foretold in words such as these: “His kinsman will take him away and burn him, and will say: ‘Is anyone still with you?’ And he will answer: ‘It is finished.’” For there was no measure or number [Col. 0342B] of those dying within and perishing by famine, nor could the living suffice to carry out the dead.

And although they can know this and are unable to conceal it—that this befell them because of the blood of Jesus Christ—it is very remarkable that, with unconquerable heart, they said then and even now say, each to another: “Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord”—the name of that same Jesus Christ, whom Christians confess in public confession to be God and Lord. They prefer to be condemned and to await eternal condemnation rather than confess or hear the name of this Lord, wonderfully steeped in the gall of bitterness, breathing implacable hatred against the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and envying the salvation of the Gentiles.

Yet some among them appear righteous to themselves [Col. 0342C] by observing the righteousnesses of the flesh and professing the commandments of the Decalogue: to have no strange gods; not to make a graven image; not to take the name of the Lord in vain; to keep the Sabbaths; to honour father and mother; not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to steal; not to bear false witness; not to covet (Deut. V). But what sort of righteousness is theirs when they hate him through whom alone all who are truly righteous are justified? God seeks that one person—where he may be, or among whom he may dwell—in order to spare them; and because he is not among them, he has poured out his indignation upon them, as he himself says in Ezekiel:

> “And I sought among them for a man [Col. 0342D] who would set a hedge in place and stand in opposition before me, so that I should not destroy them; and I found none. And I poured out my indignation upon them; in the fire of my wrath I consumed them” (Ezek. XXII).

Therefore, he says, “they shall die,” even the righteous; or, as in the same Ezekiel, “I will slay in you,” he says, “the righteous and the wicked” (Ezek. XXI), even if “ten men are left in one house.” “They shall die,” I say, “because, behold, the Lord has commanded”—that is, he has spoken through the prophets—and, fulfilling his word, “he will strike the greater house with ruins and the lesser house with breaches.”

By “the greater house” he means the ten tribes, called the tribes of Israel; by “the lesser house” [Col. 0343A] he means the two tribes ruled by David’s line. In the striking of each house, this must be noted: he says that the greater will be struck with ruins, but the lesser with breaches. For Israel, because it had sinned more grievously, is struck with ruins. But the house of Judah, in which the Temple stood and which had sinned less grievously, is not struck with ruins but with breaches, while it is held in captivity for seventy years.

But conversely it may be said that the house of Judah sinned more grievously. For in Ezekiel, after the Lord had first said, “Son of man, make Jerusalem know her abominations” (Ezek. XVI), he says among other things: “And Samaria did not commit half your sins, but you surpassed her in your crimes and justified your sisters”—namely [Col. 0343B] Sodom and Samaria—“in all your abominations which you have committed” (ibid.). Therefore, the breaches of the house of Judah must also be understood as greater than the ruins of the house of Israel.

To make this entirely clear, let us consider not merely that captivity of seventy years, but rather that in which the Jews are now dispersed among all nations after the Roman destruction. For then the house of Judah was struck not merely with breaches, nor merely with ruins, but with both breaches and ruins; for Jerusalem, before the city fell, was first struck by divisions within itself. For while Titus, as Josephus relates, was still arranging imperial affairs at Alexandria, the sedition at Jerusalem grew and was divided into three factions under Eleazar, John, and [Col. 0343C] Simon. Eleazar held the upper parts of the city, Simon the lower, and John the middle. Whoever wishes to know more fully by what pitiable divisions the house of Judah was struck, while these leaders never rested from faction, should read the narrative of the historian just mentioned.

Moreover, anyone desiring to understand the justice of God’s judgment which struck that house with such divisions must first observe in what respect this lesser house—that is, the house of Judah—surpassed the greater house, namely the house of Israel, in sin, as we said above on the testimony of the prophet speaking to Jerusalem: “And Samaria did not commit half your sins, but you surpassed her [Col. 0343D] in your crimes.” The sins, 148—or crimes—of both must be confessed and compared, so that it may appear how truly it was said: “Samaria did not commit half your sins.”

Certainly Samaria’s sins were these: that the ten tribes, of which Samaria was the metropolis, separated themselves from the house of David and rejected him, saying, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (III Kings XII). And as they rejected David, so also, abandoning God, they worshipped golden calves in God’s place.

But Jerusalem’s sins were these: that concerning Christ, the Son of God—the true David, David’s son according to the flesh and David’s Lord according to his divinity, Christ, I say, God and man, king [Col. 0344A] and saviour—they not only said, “We have no share in this Son of God, son of David,” or, “We have no king but Caesar”; but also asked that Barabbas, the author of sedition, be released to them in his place (Matt. XXVII).

If these matters are duly considered, truly “Samaria did not sin half as much,” since, in proportion as this God-and-man, the son of David, is greater than David himself, so the sin committed against him must be judged greater—especially since Jerusalem not only rejected him, as Samaria rejected David, but also killed him and asked, as has already been said, that Barabbas, the author of sedition, be released in his place. Therefore, because it thus severed itself from the kingdom of Jesus Christ, son of David, it was surely, by a most just judgment, [Col. 0344B] struck with divisions: by severing itself from Roman rule to its own harm, it stirred up against itself the conquerors of the world; and, most remarkably, though besieged from without, it perished within through threefold faction, as already said, more through seditions than through the siege.

It follows:

> “Can horses run upon rocks, or can one plough with buffaloes? For you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood—you who rejoice in a thing of nothing, who say: ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’”

Why he introduced these comparisons of horses and buffaloes he almost explained himself when he said: “You who rejoice in a thing of nothing, who say: ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’” [Col. 0344C] Here he strikes at vanity and pride in a wonderful manner by questioning them about horses and buffaloes. The wisdom of God mocks those who trust in chariots and horses, as Ephraim did at that time, and those who stood with the horns of pride raised against the strength of heaven, as this Christ testifies in the Psalm through the Prophet’s mouth:

> “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me” (Ps. XXI).

A most severe mockery resounds in words of this kind. It is as though the wisdom of the prophetic Spirit said: “Although I foretell that the greater house will be struck with ruins and the lesser with breaches, you nevertheless strive in riding to be like the Egyptians and Assyrians; but you [Col. 0344D] well know that horses cannot run upon rocks.” This is enough to say; for what he said much earlier may be understood: “Flight shall perish from the swift” (Amos II). You will not be able to escape, hindered by many stumbling-blocks of adversities, just as your horses cannot run upon rocks.

Such speech also contains jest mingled with severity when it is said to those rejoicing in horses: you truly “rejoice in a thing of nothing,” because your horses cannot “run upon rocks”; that is, they will prove deceitful for your deliverance in the time of distress, when you are struck with ruins and divisions.

Likewise, when he says, “Or can one plough with buffaloes?” if you consider what follows—“you who say, ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’”—the words likewise contain bitter jest, belonging to that laughter of which Wisdom says: “I too,” she says, “will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. I). It is as though he said: Since you are proud—and therefore, as stated above, I swore by my own soul, saying, “I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his house”—since, I say, you declare that you have acquired horns through your own strength, [Col. 0345A] you will be to me like buffaloes: so untamed that they do not receive the yoke upon their necks; and, though they are wild oxen, they refuse because of their ferocity to break the ground with the ploughshare. Thus you will certainly be useless to me for the work or kingdom of God; and when you have wandered and been scattered, I shall employ other oxen, tamed oxen, and shall say to them: “Take my yoke upon yourselves” (Matt. XI); and they will produce fruit for the kingdom [Col. 0345B] of God, according to the saying: “Amen, I say to you: the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

These buffaloes truly say, “Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?” when, “seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X); and because of this fierceness they turn “judgment into bitterness and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood,” an extremely bitter herb. For since, as already said, desiring to establish their own righteousness, they cast Christ’s yoke from themselves, they deservedly experience bitter judgment—that is, judgment without mercy. And because they do not seek the sweetness of God’s righteousness, they dread the wormwood of their own righteousness, so that they may not even have rest in this age or be able [Col. 0345C] to remain in their own land.

Thus it follows:

> “Behold, I will raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation; and it will crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the wilderness.”

This is the bitterness of judgment which they drank: that even in this age they were crushed and overthrown, from beginning to end, from head to tail, from the borders of their land facing the rising sun to the torrent of the wilderness facing the west—that is, from Hamath (also called Epiphania, having received its name from Antiochus’s epithet Epiphanes) to Rhinocorura, between which and Pelusium a branch of the Nile, or a stream coming from the desert, enters the sea. As it was said, so it came to pass: [Col. 0345D] Israel was crushed and overthrown from all its borders—first the ten tribes by the Assyrians, and afterward Judah and Benjamin by the Chaldeans and Romans.

The prophet’s following words indicate how the crushing or overthrow of those horned buffaloes—that is, of those refusing to bear the yoke—was to come about, and by what or how great successive developments it would reach its consummation. For he says:

## Chapter VII
> “The Lord God showed me this: and behold, a maker of locusts at the beginning of the growth produced by the latter rain; and behold, the latter growth after the shearing of the flock. And it came to pass, when it had finished devouring the grass of the land, that I said: ‘Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you. Who will raise up Jacob, since he is small?’ But the Lord relented concerning this: ‘Even this shall not be,’ says the Lord God.  
>   
> “The Lord God showed me this: and behold, the Lord God called judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and consumed, as it were, a portion. And I said: ‘Lord God, cease, I beseech you. Who will raise up Jacob, since he is small?’ The Lord relented concerning this: ‘Even this shall not be,’ says the Lord God.  
>   
> “He showed me this: and behold, the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, with a mason’s trowel in his hand. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A mason’s trowel.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘Behold, I shall place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer coat it over, and the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste.’”

These three manifestations or visions [Col. 0346B] must be recognized. For this reason we have set out the whole of the present chapter, so that the meaning may be more immediately at hand concerning the things that were being foreshown as future: namely, the three stages of the evil—or of the crushing and overthrow already mentioned—which are known from the sacred histories. Those stages must first be recalled, and only then must we follow the tracks of the present text.

The first was when the king of the Assyrians came up and carried Israel away into Assyria (Jer. LII). Not long afterward he came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and advanced as far as Jerusalem; but he did not prevail, for the Lord said to Isaiah: “I shall put a ring in your nostrils and a hook in your lips, and I shall lead you back by the way through which you came. For the angel of the Lord came in that night and struck [Col. 0346C] one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp” (Isa. XXXVII).

The second was when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, himself came, together with his entire army, against Jerusalem, captured it, and Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house; and the entire army of the Chaldeans destroyed the wall round about.

The third was when the Romans came and took away both place and nation (John XLVIII), temple and city, so that no stone was left upon another (Luke XIX).

Marvellous images of these future events were foreshown to this prophet in these three manifestations. For when he says, “The Lord God showed me this: and behold, a maker of locusts,” he understands—and wishes us to understand—the army of the Assyrians, comparable to locusts because of both their multitude and the vanity of their brief, leaping life; likewise because of the devastation of everything growing which they were to effect after the manner of locusts.

The maker of this locust, certainly, is the Lord: “maker,” I say, that is, creator—the same one who is the maker and God of great men, that is, holy or elect men. Nor is “maker” improperly used in the present place. For the smallness of such men, who, seeking not eternal glory, pass through the vanity of this age in a brief leap—for the littleness and insignificance of such men merits that God should be called not their maker in the fuller sense, but their fabricator.

Thus we read in Isaiah: “He who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts” (Isa. XL). And why, or how rightly, he said this he briefly explains a little later, saying to Israel, to whom he had previously spoken: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, offspring of Abraham my friend, whom I took hold of from the ends of the earth. You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them” (Isa. XLI).

For the multitude of men pursuing vanity is swept away by a light occurrence, and their memory perishes in a short time; just as we sometimes read that a locust, caught by the wind and cast into the sea at the Lord’s command, is carried off. Thus both the Assyrians and any men of this kind are rightly designated by the name of locusts.

When, moreover, he had said, “Behold, a maker of locusts, at the beginning of the latter-rain growth,” he indicates the time at which that locust would come: when everything is green, every field is fertile, the blossoms of diverse trees burst forth into fruits of their own kind, and the flowers of trees and the grasses of grain-fields promise an abundance of all things. Certainly, to be devastated at that time is, as it were, to be shorn: when the beauty of things has been removed, naked want appears plainly like baldness upon the brow.

But because after that same devastation sufficient fruitfulness was restored, the Lord then spoke to Hezekiah through Isaiah: “And this shall be the sign for you: eat this year what grows of itself, and in the second year eat fruits; but in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit” (Isa. XXXVII). Therefore, I say, after saying, “at the beginning of the latter-rain growth,” he added: “and behold, the latter growth [Col. 0347C] after the shearer of the flock”—Sennacherib being understood.

For what was said, “in the third year sow and reap,” was indeed a restoration, but a later one; and this was after the shearing of the flock, that is, after Sennacherib’s devastation.
