Isaiah calls this shearer, or shearing, a sharp razor which shaved all the hair and locks of the Israelite body: “On that day,” he says, “the Lord shall shave with a hired razor, with those beyond the river, with the king of the Assyrians, the head and the hair of the feet and the whole beard” (Isa. VII).

He had already laid everything waste; he had already taken all the fortified cities of Judah; and that shearer was besieging Jerusalem, the only city left, so that after shearing or shaving it might also cut off the head. Yet, as Scripture reports, King Hezekiah [Col. 0347D] and Isaiah son of Amos the prophet prayed against his blasphemies and cried out to heaven (IV Kings XIX).

This is what he immediately says: “And it came to pass, when it had finished devouring the grass of the land, that I said, ‘Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you.’” In keeping with the metaphor of the locust, he said, “when it had finished devouring the grass of the land”: that is, when it had already devastated everything, its army covering the land by its multitude.

What he relates that he said—“Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you”—was to be said by King Hezekiah and Isaiah the prophet’s son, praying, as has been said, and crying out to heaven. Likewise, what he says here—“The Lord relented concerning this: ‘Even this shall not be,’ says the Lord”—was to happen: namely, that the Lord would relent and speak thus.

For there it is written: “Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it; no shield shall occupy it, nor shall a rampart surround it. By the way by which he came he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord. And I shall protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (Isa. XXXVII).

Therefore, when he says, “Even this shall not be,” the sense is this: it shall indeed happen that that shearer—or the shearing of the flock, that is, Sennacherib’s army—will take the other cities of Judah and devastate everything around Jerusalem; “but this also shall not happen: that he shall enter this city.”

Further, when the prophet, after saying, “Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you,” adds, “Who [Col. 0348B] will raise up Jacob, since he is small?”—who can adequately express how searchingly he rouses and strikes the Lord, that He may remember His mercy? For when he says, “Who will raise [him] up?” he seems in some sense to rise and strike God, asking Him who it was that so often delivered Jacob from distress and from the slaughter wrought by devastators; and whether He has changed from Himself and forgotten His own nature, whose proper characteristic was mercy.

He adds also the reason why God had so often raised Jacob and ought still to raise him from danger: “because he is small.” “Small,” I say, means humble. If humility and contrition of heart were the reason for which God so often raised him, then certainly He was worthy to raise him then also, because King Hezekiah humbled both himself and his people before the Lord, as it is written: “And it came to pass, when Hezekiah heard the words of Rabshakeh, that he tore his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord; and he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests clothed in sackcloth, to Isaiah” (ibid.).

Nor did Jacob show himself small at that time merely in outward attire; he also testified to it in words, according to the words of the same king speaking to Isaiah: “Lift up prayer, therefore, for the remnant that has been found” (ibid.). For the ten tribes had already been carried away into Assyria; and thus Jacob, being small, remembered himself to be not so much a nation as the remnant of a nation.

Then, when he says: “The Lord God showed me this: [Col. 0348D] and behold, the Lord God called judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and consumed at once a portion,” he understands—or wishes us to understand—that the Lord would call Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to come against Judah and Jerusalem and to set the temple and Jerusalem on fire. This was to “call judgment by fire”: that is, to judge even to the point of fire.

For Nebuchadnezzar was not to be spoken of as Sennacherib had been: “He shall not enter this city.” Rather, by a just judgment the city was to be handed over into the hands of the king of Babylon and his servants, to be burned with fire.

“The great deep” means the whole of Judaea, or the city itself. Because of its profound avarice it deserved to be called a great deep, so much so that they had made even the house of the Lord into a den of robbers, as the Lord God complains in Jeremiah (Jer. VII). When he adds, “and it consumed at once a portion,” “of God” must be understood; for the temple itself ought to have been God’s portion, though, because of the depth of avarice, it could become a great deep or a den of robbers.

What follows—“And I said, ‘Lord God, cease, I beseech you. Who will raise up Jacob, since he is small?’”—was to be said by Daniel and his companions, captives in Babylon after that judgment of fire. For example: “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, I, Daniel,” he says, “understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet: that seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation should be fulfilled; [Col. 0349B] and I set my face toward the Lord my God, to seek him in prayer and supplication, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes” (Dan. IX), and so forth.

To pray that the captivity might be ended after the prophesied seventy years was to say, “Lord God, cease, I beseech you.” Here it is not said, as above, “Lord God, be gracious”; rather, “Lord God, cease, I beseech you.” For it was not to happen that Nebuchadnezzar should be driven back by a gracious Lord, as Sennacherib had been, but that at least after vengeance the agitation of heavenly wrath should cease.

The same must be understood concerning the repeated words, “Who will raise up Jacob, since he is small?” As we said above, He who had been accustomed to cast Jacob down and deliver him from distress because of his humility—by which he is called small—ought in consequence to raise him from the Babylonian captivity, because the captives humbly entreated Him. For example, Daniel says in the prayer mentioned above: “For because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people are a reproach to all those round about us” (ibid.).

Likewise: “Because we are diminished more than all nations, and today are lowly in all the earth because of our sins; and at this time there is no ruler, prophet, or leader, no burnt offering, sacrifice, oblation, incense, or place of first-fruits before you, that we may obtain mercy; but may we be received with a contrite heart [Col. 0349D] and a humble spirit” (Dan. III).

Thus Jacob, small, having often been raised up, still had to be raised. Therefore he now says, “Who will raise up Jacob because he is small?” so that, when the Lord answers, “I am he who have often raised him up” (Isa. XLV), the speaker may in some sense draw this conclusion from such a reason: Therefore now raise him from the Babylonian captivity, “because he is small,” that is, still humble. So long as he remains small and unrepentant, so long you must raise him up.

Then, when he says, “He showed me this: and behold, the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, with a mason’s trowel in his hand,” it must be carefully noted that he introduces the Lord’s question: “What do you see, Amos?” This was neither said nor done in the preceding manifestations.

For where he said, “The Lord God showed me this: and behold, a maker of locusts,” it was not said: “And the Lord said to me, ‘What do you see, Amos?’” Likewise, where he said, “The Lord God showed me this: and behold, He will call judgment by fire,” it was not said: “And the Lord said to me, ‘What do you see, Amos?’”

A most grave matter is announced through the mason’s trowel to be placed in the midst of the people. Therefore, in order that the prophet may attend carefully to what he sees, he is asked: “What do you see, Amos?” It must likewise be attentively observed that, when the Lord had said, “Behold, I shall place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer coat it over; and the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste,” the prophet had no further spirit to say either what he had first said—[Col. 0350B] “Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you”—or what he had said the second time—“Lord God, cease, I beseech you.”

This, I say, must be carefully noted and diligently considered, because such a vision and such a silence were by no means without significance. For in this third manifestation the prophet was shown the final and irrecoverable destruction which occurred in vengeance for the blood of Jesus Christ and was carried out by Roman hands. From that time there is no prophet to intercede for that nation, that God may be gracious and cease, as Isaiah laments: “There is none,” he says, “who calls upon your name, who rises and holds fast to you” (Isa. LXIV).

Indeed, when Sennacherib king of Assyria came as far as Jerusalem, King Hezekiah and Isaiah the prophet said, “Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you.” When the children of Judah had migrated to Babylon, Daniel and his companions said, “Lord God, cease, I beseech you.” But now there is no one who should intercede for that temple to be restored or for those sacrifices to be celebrated again.

Having observed this distinction in both the letter and its meaning, let us now at last examine more closely the tracks of the Scripture already begun.

“And behold,” he says, “the Lord upon a plastered wall, and a mason’s trowel in his hand.” He said “plastered wall” as though he had said “whitewashed wall.” What a whitewashed wall, or plastered wall, should be understood to signify, the apostle Paul wonderfully suggests. Standing before the council, when the high priest Ananias commanded those standing by to strike him on the mouth, he said: “God shall strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII).

Therefore that wall or whitewashed partition was that priesthood. The Lord coated or whitewashed that wall, holding the mason’s trowel in His hand, as long as He allowed carnal Judaism to appear glorious: while the temple stood and religion flourished in carnal ceremonies.

But: “Behold,” he says, “I shall place the trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer coat it over.” Israel was naked—naked, uncomely, and weak—though it had formerly been coated over and strengthened by me, just as a wall is coated and reinforced by a mason’s trowel; thus it received not only beauty but also strength against the injury of rains and frequent storms.

Indeed, they imagine themselves to be masons, and desire to coat their own wall by their own ingenuity. But neither is the coating beautiful if it is not from God, nor can the wall stand. Therefore, in Ezekiel, speaking of this same matter, the same Lord says: “Say to those who plaster the wall without mortar that it shall fall. For a flooding rain shall come, and I shall cause very great stones to rush down from above, and a storm-wind to scatter it. For behold, the wall has fallen. Will it not be said to you, ‘Where is the plaster with which you plastered it?’” (Ezek. XIII), and so forth.

Truly, as He says there, “Behold, the wall has fallen” (ibid.), the Lord will not again “coat it over.” What there says, “Behold, the wall has fallen,” He says here in the same sense: “The high places of the idol shall be demolished, [Col. 0351B] and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste.”

Indeed, when He spoke in Ezekiel, the wall had already fallen not only among the ten tribes, but the portion of Judah also had migrated to Babylon, and Ezekiel himself was one of the captives. Yet it still remained that the wall should fall again in Judah irrecoverably—which occurred after the Lord’s Passion.

Therefore, after having there said in the past tense, “For behold, the wall has fallen,” He immediately added words in the future tense: “Therefore I shall cause a storm-wind to burst forth in my indignation, and there shall be a flooding rain in my fury, and great stones of wrath for utter destruction; and I shall destroy the wall which you plastered without mortar, and level it to the earth, and its foundation shall be uncovered.”

Gabriel the angel, speaking to Daniel, expresses this ruin or destruction of the wall and desolation of the Jewish sanctuaries more clearly than light in these words: “And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and his people who will deny him shall not be; and the people with their coming leader shall destroy the city and sanctuary, and its end shall be devastation; and after the end of the war desolation is decreed. And sacrifice and offering shall fail, and in the temple there shall be an abomination of desolation, and desolation shall persist unto completion and the end” (Dan. IX).

After these words, by which the common calamities of the whole nation were certainly foretold, he immediately adds, terribly, the personal calamities of certain individuals: namely, King Jeroboam and Amaziah, the priest of that time. It follows:

> “And I shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. And Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: ‘Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the whole land cannot bear all his words. For Amos says this: “Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall migrate captive from its land.”’  
>   
> “And Amaziah said to Amos: ‘You seer, go away; flee into the land of Judah; eat bread there, and prophesy there. But you shall no longer prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.’  
>   
> “And Amos answered and said to Amaziah: ‘I am not a prophet, nor am I a prophet’s son; but I am a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore trees. And the Lord God took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said to me: “Go and prophesy to my people Israel.” And now hear the word of the Lord. You say: “You shall not prophesy against Israel, and you shall not drip forth words against the house of the idol.” Therefore thus says the Lord: “Your wife shall commit fornication in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured by a line; you shall die in an unclean land; and Israel shall migrate captive from its land.”’”

As has already been said, this part of the prophecy foretells the personal evils of the king of that time, Jeroboam, and of the priest Amaziah. This must be considered to the praise of God’s judgment: whoever of them is greater in guilt is struck more severely by the strictness of the avenging sentence.

“I shall rise,” He says, “against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.” Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, son of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, is included as one to be struck with the sword—and this occurred. Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against Zechariah, struck him openly, killed him, and reigned in his place, in accordance with the word which the Lord had spoken to Jehu: “Because you have zealously done everything which was in my heart against the house of Ahab, your sons to the fourth generation shall sit upon the throne of Israel” (IV Kings X).

Thus it must be noted that He did not say, “I shall rise against Jeroboam,” but “against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”

Amaziah, however, when he attempted to charge the prophet with the crime of rebellion, did not wish to report his words exactly, but added something of his own so that the charge might appear greater. It seemed insufficient to him, for inflaming the king’s wrath, that Amos had said from the Lord’s mouth, “I shall rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.” For this could be understood not as saying that Jeroboam himself would be struck with the sword, but his descendants after his death—and that in fact occurred.

Therefore, that lying witness and false accuser distorted the saying when he declared, “Amos has rebelled against you,” and added: “Jeroboam shall die by the sword.” In doing so, he sufficiently reveals with what wicked intent he had long lain in wait for the prophet’s speech, so that the priest of the golden calf—and therefore a rich man, indeed a fat cow, as this same prophet said above: “Hear this word, you fat cows who are on Mount Samaria” (Amos IV)—might find grounds to accuse him. They wish “fat cows” to be understood as priests, among whom this man was one of the chief.

At last he found a ground of accusation when the prophet mentioned the king; and, as already said, lest the charge seem small because the prophet had spoken of the king’s house, he redirected it to the king’s own person, corrupting the purity of the saying.

Therefore God’s return of severity or justice is marvellous: to the fornicating priest, committing fornication with golden calves and holding the people in that same fornication, it is said, because of his corruption of the divine or prophetic saying: “Your wife shall commit fornication in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured by a line; and you shall die in an unclean land.”

Certainly, because he was greater in crime than the king himself, he ought also to be greater in punishment. King Jeroboam was to receive bodily vengeance not in himself but in [Col. 0353A] his house—that is, in the son who succeeded him, so that he should be struck with the sword. But this man was to receive in his own person death; in his own wife, the disaster of fornication; and in his sons and daughters, vengeance by the sword.

These things were near at hand and soon to be fulfilled, so that, being presently fulfilled, they might establish the credibility of the other things which were to be deferred longer; and so that the prophet, whom Amaziah was seeking to prove false, might be shown faithful and true by the evils of his adversary which he had quickly prophesied, making it evident that he had spoken all things not from his own heart but from the mouth of the Lord.

But how does he say—or dare to say—“You seer, go away; flee into the land of Judah; eat bread there, and prophesy there; but you shall no longer prophesy at Bethel, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom”? The horned buffalo does not speak mildly or rise gently against God; it brandishes the horn of pride and refuses the Lord’s yoke, in accordance with the truth of the same prophet’s earlier saying: “Can one plow with buffaloes?”

He calls him “seer,” that is, prophet, saying “you who see”; yet he commands that himself and his king be heard rather than God, whose will the prophet sees and by whom he has been commanded to prophesy.

What does Amos say in return? “I am not,” he says, “a prophet, nor a prophet’s son; but I am a herdsman, a dresser of sycamore trees. And the Lord God took me as I followed the flock, and said to me: ‘Go and prophesy to my people Israel.’” What else does he say but precisely what the apostles said: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V)?

How great, do you suppose, was the sternness which this man of prophetic authority, rightly indignant and ennobled by the Holy Spirit, bore in his heart, when heaven thundered and commanded him to prophesy, while he heard, in opposition, a frog croaking in the mud and saying, “You shall no longer prophesy”?

Therefore the Holy Spirit pronounced from the oracle of His breast a punishment worthy of the pride of this most contemptible man, [Col. 0353C] saying to him: “And now hear the word of the Lord. You say: ‘You shall not prophesy against Israel, and you shall not drip forth words against the house of the idol.’ But I shall not merely continue to prophesy against Israel and to drip forth words against the house of the idol: I shall also prophesy against you. Hear now your own share of prophecy: ‘Your wife shall commit fornication in the city,’” and the rest as above.

That, when about to say these things in a spirit of strength, he first says, “I am not a prophet, nor a prophet’s son; but I am a herdsman, a dresser of sycamore trees, and the Lord God took me as I followed the flock and said to me, ‘Go and prophesy to my people Israel,’” is a great testimony to holy humility and a well-ordered mind. For though he is about to say, “Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, and your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword,” and so forth, he first humbly states what he had been and what he had become through grace, not merits: namely, that he had not undertaken the prophetic ministry by hereditary right, nor begun to prophesy out of his own heart, but had acted under a necessity to obey the grace that breathed upon him and the command of the Lord who sent him.

Truly, anyone who looks upon this prophet and the others with kindly eyes understands how free from presumption, and with how great fear, they prophesied. As one of them says: “If prophet and priest are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord” (Lam. II)—“prophecy and crushing have become terror and a snare to us” (Lam. III).

This is as though he said: Because prophets and priests correcting the people’s sins are killed, and cannot be safe even in the Lord’s sanctuary, we prophesy or speak prophecy not without fear. Yet the terror of death or crushing, the Lord’s command, and pressure from every side overcome even that fear: for if we prophesy, we are killed; if we do not prophesy, woe to us, because a stewardship has been entrusted to us by God.

Therefore, when he answers the idolatrous priest who says to him, “You shall no longer prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom,” saying: “And now hear the word of the Lord. Therefore your wife shall commit fornication in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured by a line; you shall die in an unclean land; and Israel shall migrate captive from its land”—we must yield to truth and sympathize with necessity. For it is not the impulse of an impatient mind but the word of the Judge; its authority imposes necessity upon the prophet, though willingness to obey is not lacking.

To weigh rightly how much justice there is in this severity, consider who first said these words: “Israel shall migrate captive from its land.” If you look through all that precedes, you will nowhere find the prophet to have said this in those very words, although his words had the same sense. This priest, his slanderer, hastened to bring an accusation framed with total deliberation, in order to increase hostility against him: “Amos says this: ‘Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall migrate captive from its land.’”

We have already spoken above of the falsehood in the first part, where he said, “Jeroboam shall die by the sword.” But concerning this part, “and Israel shall migrate captive from its land,” it must be said that it was true, although the prophet had not used the same words. It could indeed be inferred from his words; but precisely in this statement the accuser’s slander is very conspicuous and blameworthy.

For what then? Could he not also have inferred from Amos’s words that he foretold the same captivity with grief, and in foretelling it grieved over it? Had he not shortly before heard the prophet say: “And it came to pass, when it had finished devouring the grass of the land, I said: ‘Lord God, be gracious, I beseech you’”? And again: “Lord God, cease, I beseech you”?

He was therefore truly a slanderous accuser and witness, reporting and bitterly expressing only those points from which hostility could be fashioned, while wholly suppressing those which could rightly have won favor. Accordingly, the justice of God is praiseworthy in the sentence passed upon the condemned priest, and the prophet’s strength in truth must be proclaimed. Strengthened by God speaking within him, he confessed what he had felt and did not deny it; and he added what he had not yet said, declaring the deserved wrath to the impious priest.

Scripture does not report when or how the judgments written above were fulfilled upon him; their fulfillment lies concealed amid the mass of evils. For Holy Scripture has not undertaken to recount every event that befell individual persons who were more insignificant and obscure. Thus also, when Micaiah answered Zedekiah, who had struck him on the cheek and said, “Has the Spirit of the Lord then departed from me and spoken to you?”: “You shall see on that day when you enter chamber within chamber to hide yourself” (III Kings XXII)—it was not deemed worthy of individual narration how this was fulfilled, because, as has already been said, the majesty of Holy Scripture does not so debase itself as to recount everything while lingering over insignificant persons without purpose.

## Book Four

[Col. 0355]

[Col. 0355B] It must be held in memory what manifestations, and of what kind, the prophet has already recounted as shown to him.

The first is this: “The Lord God showed me, and behold, a maker of locusts at the beginning of the latter-rain growth; and behold, the latter growth after the shearing of the flock,” and the rest. By this we understand the Assyrians, who, after carrying away the ten tribes, were to come against Judah as far as Jerusalem and devastate everything in the manner of a shearer, or razor, shaving head, hair of the feet, and the whole beard, as Isaiah also foretold (Isa. VII).

The second is this: “The Lord showed me, and behold, the Lord God called judgment by fire,” and the rest. By this we understand the Babylonians, who were to come and burn the city of Jerusalem and likewise the house of the Lord with fire.

The third is this: “The Lord showed me, and behold, the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, and a mason’s trowel in his hand,” and the rest. By this we understand the final desolation wrought by the Romans, which is never to be restored, according to the words of the Lord: “Behold, I shall place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer coat it over.”

After these manifestations of their evils, it was fitting that the principal cause of those same evils should also be shown by its own manifestation or image. That cause is avarice, the root of all evils. The Jews, especially infected by it, advanced into every crime and finally came to crucify the Lord of glory—chiefly because he disputed against their avarice, proving them to be men of that generation who had made the house of his Father, which ought to have been a house of prayer, into a den of robbers, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy (Jer. VII).

It follows, therefore:

“This the Lord showed me: and behold, a hook for fruit. And he said: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A hook for fruit. And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer pass them by. And the hinges of the temple shall creak on that day, says the Lord God; many shall die, and silence shall be cast forth in every place.”

Clearly, when the Lord, after showing the hook for fruit, says, “the end has come upon my people Israel,” it must be understood: because of this hook, or because of what “this hook for fruit” signifies. [Col. 0356B] That this is avarice, as has already been said, is declared by what follows. For it continues: “Hear this, you who crush the poor and cause the needy of the land to fail, saying: When will the harvest pass, so that we may sell our wares, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain, diminishing the measure, increasing the shekel, and introducing deceitful balances, so that we may acquire the needy for silver and the poor for sandals, and sell even the refuse of the grain?” And again, a little later: “I saw,” he says, “the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: Strike the hinge, and let the lintels be shaken. For avarice is at the head of them all” (Amos 9). Therefore, when he declares that the crime of avarice is the cause of the evils that were to come, he marks it by a remarkable and wonderfully fitting comparison, [Col. 0356C] showing beforehand “a hook for fruit”: a hook by which the branches of a tree are customarily drawn down in order to pluck fruit that cannot be reached by hand.

Avarice is indeed a hooked hand, and it is never stretched out except to receive. Men who possess something are like branches bearing fruit—white or red, lovely in appearance and pleasant to eat. Avarice cunningly lies in wait for such people, fashioning the hook of every sort of device and repeatedly winding it about in silence, because it fears being heard; thus the fruit, once pulled off, causes loss, yet the owner does not notice, until, when the thief has had his fill, he discovers his loss too late and groans. In this vision there is a true and fitting comparison: the deceit of avarice is likened to a hook, and temporal goods, around which [Col. 0356D] avarice labours, to fruit.

For fruit is a trivial thing, and especially delights children; but to men, and particularly healthy men, it is of little account. Thus the goods of the present age are trivial, and greatly delight those who are childish in understanding; but to the wise, whose minds are upon heavenly things, they are contemptible. Whenever earthly men have sought to make an ecclesiastical man’s soul conform to themselves, you may rightly say, lamenting over him, in David’s words: “They made Jerusalem a keeper of fruit” (Ps. 78 [Vulgate]). Elsewhere, the holy man, reviewing and counting his empty months, says: “My days were swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good; they passed by like ships carrying fruit” (Job 9). Finally, if you consider that all temporal goods, which the hook of avarice greedily draws to itself, are rightly designated by the useful name of fruit, you should know that the first man committed the sin of covetousness, by which he perished, not through gold or silver, but through a small fruit (Gen. 3).

[Col. 0357A] Let us now continue the text begun. “What,” he says, “do you see, Amos? A hook for fruit.” You see, certainly, a small thing, but a sign of a great evil. For, as has already been said, it signifies the evil of avarice, because of which an end was to come upon that people. For he immediately says: “The end has come upon my people Israel.” What end, or what kind of end? Certainly an evil end; and how evil it was, and by what name it ought to be called, we find in Daniel in these words: “And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and the people that are to deny him shall not be his. And the people with the ruler who is to come shall destroy [Col. 0357B] the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be devastation; and after the end of the war desolation is decreed, and sacrifice and offering shall fail, and in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall persist unto consummation and the end” (Dan. 9).

Therefore, after he had said, “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer pass them by,” he immediately added: “And the hinges of the temple shall creak on that day, says the Lord God.” For who has not heard of the creaking of the hinges of that temple—that is, the overthrow of the city and sanctuary accomplished when the Romans conquered? And in using the creaking of the temple’s hinges to signify the report or fame of so great a ruin, how much beauty and solemn weight there is! [Col. 0357C] As for the addition, “many shall die,” Josephus bears witness to its truth, reporting an almost unbelievable multitude of the dead while describing that tragedy. Then, when he says, “silence shall be cast forth in every place,” it is as though he said: Those who survive shall be carried captive among all nations, cast down and silent; they shall have no authority to speak. The Christ whom they refuse to confess, they will not dare openly to blaspheme.

[Col. 0357D] But by inserting, “I will no longer pass them by”—that is, my people—he briefly indicates that the rite of their Passover, or the slaughter of their paschal lamb, by whose blood they customarily marked their doorposts, would now do them no good. Formerly the same Lord said: “The blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses in which you are; and I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall be no destructive plague among you when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. 12). But now he says concerning the same people: “I will no longer pass them by.” For since they shed the blood of the Lamb of God, the blood of Christ the Son of God, the blood of their dumb animal, their lamb, is no longer received by God. Rather, those marked with the sign of Christ’s blood, the seal of the cross of the Son of God, are the houses of Israel. But that people, formerly called Israel, is reckoned among the Egyptians, because it does not possess this sign; and therefore, he says, “I will no longer pass them by”—and it must be understood: but I shall strike them, as formerly I struck the land of Egypt, so now I shall strike every soul of an unbelieving and evil-working person, both Jew and Greek—indeed, first and more severely the Jew than the Greek (Rom. 2). [Col. 0358A]

Understanding these things in the hook for fruit which he had seen, and in the words he had heard—“The end has come upon my people”—the prophet immediately announces and says: “Hear this, you who crush the poor and cause the needy of the land to fail, saying: When will the harvest pass, so that we may sell our wares, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain, diminishing the measure, increasing the shekel, and introducing deceitful balances, so that we may acquire the needy for silver and the poor for sandals, and sell the refuse of the grain?” “Hear,” he says, “what the Lord spoke to me, showing me a hook for fruit. For the speech concerns you who are [Col. 0358B] avaricious, who do such things, who plunder the poor by deceit, as a hook draws down small branches in order to pluck fruit.

“For while you greedily desire that, once the harvest has passed—that is, been consumed, though it is small for the poor—you may sell your goods at a higher price; while you desire the Sabbath to arrive—that is, the seventh year, in which, according to the Law, the land rests and it is unlawful to sow or reap—so that then, opening your stored grain, you may sell it at your pleasure; while you diminish the measure and increase the shekel—that is, the price—forcing the poor man by want to buy even the refuse of your grain; and while in such wretched commerce you also employ deceitful balances; while, I say, you thus bring it about that you acquire your needy brethren for silver—for compelled by necessity, they sell themselves to you—and possess impoverished people for sandals, that is, for a small and trifling price, scarcely enough to purchase sandals: then indeed you pluck fruit with a deceitful hook. Therefore the end called devastation comes upon you, as Daniel says. For by doing these things you will not cease until you kill Christ because of your avarice, since he himself will dispute against it; and from that time the end shall be upon you; from that time, I say, desolation shall persist unto consummation and the end” (Dan. 9).

“You, I say, who are such and do such things, hear this.” What shall we hear? Certainly both what I have already said, “because the Lord showed me a hook for fruit,” in which the speech concerns you, and what I shall immediately say. What is that? “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: If I forget all their works unto the end! Shall not the earth be shaken over this, and every inhabitant of it mourn? And all of it shall rise like a river, and shall be cast out and flow down like the stream of Egypt. And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: the sun shall set at noon, and I shall make the earth dark on a day of light; and I shall turn [Col. 0358D] your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I shall bring sackcloth upon every back of yours and baldness upon every head; and I shall make it like mourning for an only son, and its latter end like a bitter day. Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall send famine upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord. And they shall be shaken from sea to sea, and shall roam from north to east, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it.”

[Col. 0359A] Hear all this, you avaricious and rapacious people, not delighting yourselves in drawing down fruit of the sort already described. “The Lord has sworn.” I have now said for the third time that “the Lord has sworn.” First I said, “The Lord God has sworn by his Holy One.” Second, I said, “The Lord God has sworn by his soul.” And now, for the third time, I say, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob.” The threefold repetition of the oath is a strong confirmation of your condemnation.

[Col. 0359B] But what sort of oath is this: “the Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob”? When it says, “The Lord has sworn by his Holy One,” this is as though it said, “He has sworn by his soul,” that is, by himself. But when it now says, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob,” it should not properly be understood as though it said, “He has sworn by the pride of Jacob.” For what would it be for God to swear by anyone’s pride? Indeed, it is not fitting—rather, it is not even lawful—for a human being to swear by a cause or thing unworthy and contrary to holiness. It must therefore be understood thus: “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob,” as though he said, “The Lord has sworn because of the pride of Jacob.”

So too, in the Psalm, when he says: “For forty years I was offended by that generation, and I said: These always err in heart, and they have not known my ways; to whom I swore in my wrath” (Ps. 94 [Vulgate]). It must be understood as though he said: I swore because of my wrath, because they provoked me to anger, “They shall not enter into my rest.” Thus, I say, in the present passage, when he says, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: If I forget all their works unto the end,” it must be understood as though he said: “The Lord has sworn because of the pride of Jacob: I shall never forget all their works.”

[Col. 0359C] For pride is truly the reason why the Lord swears, why he confirms by an oath his sentence against the sinner, though his simple word is truth. For by being proud the sinner provokes the Lord to swear, according to that saying in the Psalm: “The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the multitude of his wrath he will not seek” (Ps. 9 [Vulgate]). So long as someone sins through ignorance, so long as someone transgresses through youth or infirmity, groaning because “he sees another law in his members, opposing the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin which is in his members” (Rom. 7), he has not yet provoked the Lord; [Col. 0359D] the Lord has not yet confirmed his sentence against him by an oath. Therefore the Psalmist, having hope, says: “Remember not, O Lord, the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24 [Vulgate]).

Pride alone is that whose sins the Lord does not wish to forget; provoked by it, [Col. 0360A] he does not seek “according to the multitude of his wrath,” that is, “he will not require” the sinner (Ps. 10 [Vulgate]), because he is greatly angered with him. It should also be noted how he says: “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob.” We know that the patriarch Jacob, whose sons according to the flesh these men were, or are, possessed great humility and had no pride. Otherwise, how could we suppose that he was able to wrestle with God and prevail with the angel (Gen. 32; Hos. 12), except by the power of great humility, which is true strength? How also could Moses have held God when he said, “Let me go” (Exod. 32), unless he was strengthened by the virtue of humility, standing, as the Psalmist says, “in the breach,” that is, in extreme humility of mind, “before him” (Ps. 105 [Vulgate])?

Jacob, then, was not proud but humble, and for that reason he could wrestle mightily with God. The manner of expression, therefore, must be noted, as has already been said. For he does not say, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of the people,” concerning whom he had said, “The end has come upon my people,” but he says, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob.” He briefly indicates [Col. 0360B] that pride in the sons of a poor man, who was humble throughout his whole life, is utterly unfitting and deserving of great punishment.

Jacob was wholly unlike his brother Esau: while Esau hunted abroad, Jacob, a simple man, remained at home. At his father’s and mother’s command, in order to take a wife, he went abroad; with his staff he crossed the Jordan. He did not recline on an ivory bed, but lay on bare ground with a stone placed beneath his head; and he saw a great vision, namely a ladder reaching to heaven and the Lord leaning upon the ladder. For a wife he served seven years once and then again; and for the wages he was to take from the sheep, he tended his father-in-law’s flock for six years. Later he returned with two companies, having no abiding city here but seeking the future one; a stranger and sojourner [Col. 0360C] upon the earth, he went from place to place, pitching and striking his tents. Finally, coming into Egypt with all his household and standing before Pharaoh, he was not ashamed to confess his pilgrimage: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years, few and evil; and we, your servants, both we and our fathers, are shepherds of sheep” (Gen. 47).

In the sons, I say, of such a father, who lived so humbly, pride is most blameworthy—indeed, detestable. Accordingly, “The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob” aptly indicates in brief how grievously the Lord bore it that the sons had so proudly degenerated from a father so humble. And what did he swear? “If I forget,” he says—that is, I shall by no means forget—[Col. 0360D] “all their works.” It is understood: whatever they did after they came out of Egypt and fashioned and worshipped the calf. For although Moses then held the Lord and he was appeased, so that he did not do the evil he had spoken against his people, yet afterward he said: “But in the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs also” (Exod. 32). From that time onward, I shall not forget all their works; indeed, from the blood of righteous Abel onward, all things shall come upon their wicked generation (Matt. 23).

After prefacing this oath, as though you were asking how he would remember the works which he had sworn he must not forget, he asks while still in the very fervour in which he swore, and says: “Shall not the earth [Col. 0361A] be shaken over this, and every inhabitant of it mourn?” As though he said: Must no penalty be imposed in remembrance of those works? Is only slight wrath due to this people doing such things? Shall not the heavens rightly reveal its iniquity, and the earth rise up against it? Certainly it shall happen, because it is just that it should happen. I have sworn, and the sentence is unchangeable: because of this, or for this reason—that Jacob has become proud—the earth shall be shaken; the head of the earth, the Roman Empire, shall be shaken and rise against it. And when the earth is shaken—when the earthly power of so great an empire is set in motion against it—“every inhabitant of it” shall mourn, namely because it entertained the fear that it could not inhabit the land unless one man died. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11). [Col. 0361B] Therefore “every inhabitant of it,” that is, of the land, shall mourn. This indeed happened in that siege, when unbelievers had gathered together in a multitude, drawn to punishment by God’s judgment.

Accordingly he suitably adds at once: “And all of it shall rise like a river, and shall be cast out and flow down like the stream of Egypt.” It was indeed remarkable that, when the Romans were coming to besiege Jerusalem and the Passover solemnity was already at hand, so great a multitude gathered there, trusting in the great strength of the spacious city, that he rightly says, “And all of it shall rise like a river”—that is, its inhabitant. For it came abundantly like a river and, by its gathering, filled the city’s walls. [Col. 0361C] But since, after an innumerable heap of corpses, the walls were broken and laid open, the survivors were to be captured and carried captive among all nations, he rightly adds: “And it shall be added and flow down like the stream of Egypt.” For the survivors were cast out, as has already been said, and flowed away throughout the whole world—those who had flowed together like a river, thinking they could remain safe within.

And how did they flow away? “Like the stream of Egypt,” he says. The expression is remarkable and indicates a remarkable mystery. He did not wish to say, “like the Jordan,” which was the river of that people’s land and much nearer to those besieged and then led into captivity than any stream of Egypt. Why? Because that people did not wish to be like the Jordan; it did not wish to receive the sacrament of Christ’s baptism, [Col. 0361D] Christ having been baptized in the flowing Jordan. Therefore it flowed away like the stream of Egypt. For behold: in truth the Jews are reckoned, both with God and with men, and are, like Egyptians—indeed truly Egyptians, that is, people of darkness—because they are blinded in heart.

Accordingly he immediately adds: “And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: the sun shall set at noon, and I shall make the earth dark on a day of light.” For who is this sun but Christ, the sun of righteousness, the true and eternal sun, who illumined the whole world on this day, in this time? And when did this day of light begin, except when this sun, the Dayspring from on high, visited us? In a wondrous manner Mary, that is, “star of the sea,” bore him. It was night; and the star, arising from the Spirit of her Creator, conceived when she was little, bore the great sun, and from then on it has been a day of light. Noon, moreover, was when the same sun, raised from the earth, rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

[Col. 0362A] At this noon, or day of light, the Lord made the earth—that is, Judaea—dark, so that they are no longer called or are Jews, but Egyptians, that is, dark and blind people, because Christ the sun set for them, since they do not believe that he who died rose again. The sign of this darkening and blindness of their hearts was that at noon, that is, at the sixth hour, when they crucified him, this daily or visible sun was darkened and darkness came over the land. They committed so great a crime during their feast called *Phase*, that is, Passover. He continues, therefore, and declares firmly, under the same decree and according to just judgment: “And I shall turn your feasts [Col. 0362B] into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I shall bring sackcloth upon every back of yours and baldness upon every head.”

This is so plain and well known that it needs no exposition. Their feasts were turned into mourning because, by killing Christ during their Passover feast, they caused Christ’s disciples and his mother to mourn, according to Simeon’s prophecy: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2). Therefore, when the Passover feast was approaching, as has already been said, those under siege began to mourn; all their annual feasts became mournful, and all their songs were changed into lamentation. So great, indeed, was the misery then that they never had a better reason to put sackcloth upon their backs and shave their heads, as was customary in mourning, as a sign of great sorrow.

[Col. 0362C] What he adds next—“And I shall make it like mourning for an only son, and its latter end like a bitter day”—announces an incurable sorrow and an irrecoverable desolation. For what kind of mourning is mourning for an only son? Certainly inconsolable, because another child offers no consolation to one whose only son has died. Christ is the only-begotten, not only of God the Father, but also of the Synagogue, from whose flesh he assumed flesh. He died for her; for this cruel mother killed him, and she does not wish to hear that he rose again—indeed, she does not wish even to know that he is the only-begotten Son of God. [Col. 0362D] Yet God has no other only-begotten Son, nor will he send another, because he is the only-begotten. Therefore the mourning of the Synagogue, which killed the only-begotten, shall be inconsolable for ever, as he himself said in Zechariah: “They shall look upon me whom they pierced, and shall mourn for him as for an only son, and grieve as men grieve at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12).

Now they refuse to mourn for him, but at the last they shall mourn. Therefore, after saying, “And I shall make it like mourning for an only son,” he immediately added, “and its latter end like a bitter day.” The latter things are those which follow the present age. In those last things he promises them mourning and says that they shall be like a bitter day—that is, truly a bitter day—as, conversely, when the saints say, “We have become as those who are comforted” (Ps. 125 [Vulgate]), it is clearly as though they said, “We have truly been comforted.” [Col. 0363A] For that day on which, as has already been said, they shall see him whom they pierced, or look upon him whom they pierced, will truly be bitter to them, as another prophet says: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be troubled there” (Zeph. 1). Then they shall be unable to conceal the mourning for the only son which they now conceal, saying to one another in their miseries: “Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord” (Amos 6).

Meanwhile they are miserable throughout the world and deserve to find no word of consolation, whereas formerly in Egypt and Babylon, or whenever they were afflicted, they found consolation by crying to the Lord. This is what he immediately says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall send famine [Col. 0363B] upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord. And they shall be shaken from sea to sea, and shall roam from north to east, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it.”

It is remarkable and pitiable that they, from whose land we strangers have harvested and eaten the bread of the Scriptures, suffer hunger and perish from thirst: they hunger and do not eat; they thirst and do not drink. More remarkable still, they themselves bring and carry this bread about for us, and yet do not find it, as is mystically signified in the Gospel. When a very great multitude came to the Lord and he wished to give them food, “there was one boy there, who had five barley loaves and two fish” (John 6). He had them and did not eat; [Col. 0363C] he carried them and did not hunger; but Jesus took them from him, broke them, and gave them to those whom he wished to refresh (ibid.).

Thus the Jews, because they are childish in understanding and do not know what they carry, carry the bread which is the word of God, yet are fasting in mind and dry in soul, because the Lord has sent upon them a famine for hearing the word of the Lord. It is, I say, remarkable and pitiable that, loaded with the word of the Lord, they roam from the Atlantic Sea to the British Sea—that is, from south to west—and from north to east, the four quarters of the world, “seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it.” They do not find it because they are blind; therefore they cannot see the very thing they carry. Their own wickedness has blinded [Col. 0363D] them.

But how does it happen that they seek and do not find, when the Lord says, “Seek, and you shall find” (Matt. 7), and likewise, “He who seeks finds” (ibid.)? How can this agree, except because they do not seek as they ought, because they do not seek in him in whom they ought to seek? Whoever seeks in Christ finds what he may eat so as not to hunger; he finds what he may drink so as not to thirst. Therefore he says: “He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6). And again: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). But they hate Christ and wish to have no fellowship with Christ. How, then, could they find, when in a remarkable fashion they seek the word of God without the Word of God, who is Christ?

[Col. 0364A] A remarkable madness in those who seek: they seek the word of the Lord in such a way that they want some prophet to arise for them, grieving because they possess no human glory—someone who might perform signs and foretell future events to satisfy their desire, so that they may gather again and return to that earthly Jerusalem, no longer made of stone but golden and jewelled, according to their vain and excessively avaricious hope. Hungering thus, they shall never eat; thirsting thus, they shall never drink; seeking the word of the Lord thus, they shall never find it. Instead of the word of the Lord, they receive the spirit of error; instead of Christ, they shall receive Antichrist.

It continues: “On that day beautiful virgins and young men shall fail from thirst, those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say: Your god, O Dan, lives; and the way of Beersheba lives; and they shall fall and rise no more.” [Col. 0364B] Although a little earlier, after saying, “I shall send famine upon the land,” he immediately added, “not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord,” yet when he says, “On that day beautiful virgins and young men shall fail from thirst,” both meanings are rightly understood: both the famine of bread and thirst for water, and the famine and thirst for hearing the word of the Lord. For although the Jews now, even though captive, have bread and water, certainly they did not have them then, when, as has already been said, they were surrounded by enemies in vengeance for Christ’s blood. Then, I say, virgins and young people also failed physically from thirst, with so great and astonishing a collapse that it is remarkable if anyone can read of that calamity without horror of mind.

[Col. 0364C] But since bodily hunger and thirst ought to be reckoned trivial by comparison with the hunger and thirst for hearing the word of the Lord, which are hunger and thirst of the soul, he said, “I shall send famine upon the land,” and then, lest it be thought that he was repaying their avarice with the slight vengeance of bodily famine, “not a famine,” he says, “of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord.” The sense is: I do not first send upon them a famine of bread and a thirst for water; rather, the first vengeance shall be a famine for hearing the word of the Lord, and famine of bread and thirst for water shall be added to it.

Ancient history, Latin and Greek alike, and that of all barbarian nations, relates that nothing is harsher than famine, [Col. 0364D] which often compels the besieged to eat human flesh and rage against their own nature, so that even parents do not spare their little children; as that unhappy Mary did not spare hers, who during that siege cooked and ate her little child. What, then, should be said of the hunger of souls, which is undoubtedly felt after the present life, if bodily hunger produces this? Both oppressed the Jewish people at that time; and even now the worse famine and thirst, that of the word of the Lord, continues to oppress it.

What or what sort are the virgins and young men who thus fail? He says: “Those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say: Your god, O Dan, lives; and the way of Beersheba lives.” At the time when these things were prophesied, a golden calf was worshipped in Dan, which is at the boundary of the land of Judaea. [Col. 0365A] They went there by the way of Beersheba, namely by a long journey, avoiding the kings of Judah. Indeed Jeroboam had made those calves for this very reason: so that the ten tribes would not go up to pray in Jerusalem (3 Kings 12 [1 Kings 12]), judging that the people’s heart might return to its lord, the king of Judah.

Such an object—a calf’s face—had come into such veneration among them that, as people had customarily sworn, “The Lord God lives,” for example when Jonathan said, “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, O king, if I know” (1 Kings 17 [Vulgate]; cf. 1 Sam. 20), or Elijah, “As the Lord God lives, in whose presence I stand” (3 Kings 17 [Vulgate]; cf. 1 Kings 17), so now, swearing commonly, they would say: “The god of Dan lives, and the way of Beersheba lives,” by which one goes to Dan. That calf was golden; and consequently the people could easily be persuaded that it was a god. [Col. 0365B] Why? Clearly because the spirit of avarice had taken possession of their minds; therefore gold was no small thing in their thoughts, and such metal pleased their eyes far more than their God pleased their minds.

Thus their god was gold; their god was Mammon. Can the scribes and Pharisees of the time in which our Lord suffered—the one to whom the whole purpose of the holy prophets tends—be considered free from such wickedness? Did not Mammon especially possess their minds? And did they not swear by the same god by whom those people swore when they said, “Your god, O Dan, lives”? “Woe to you,” the Lord himself says, “blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound” (Matt. 23). [Col. 0365C] Did they not prefer gold to God? “For he who swears by the temple,” he says, “swears by it and by him who dwells in it” (ibid.). Therefore, just as they preferred gold to the temple, so they preferred it to him who dwells in the temple, saying: “Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.”

Therefore, when he says, “those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say: Your god, O Dan, lives,” let us not omit those who taught that one should swear by gold, since they worshipped gold far more greedily than their fathers did. Their fathers worshipped gold so that, by going up to worship in Jerusalem, they might not learn to return to David their king. But these men, in order that they might possess gold more freely—gold by which they taught that one ought to swear rather than by God or by the temple of God—[Col. 0365D] killed the true David, the son of David, the Son of God, their king.

Such is their god: the god of Dan, which is interpreted “judgment,” for it drew them to eternal judgment. Likewise, such is their way: Beersheba, which is interpreted “well of the oath” or “well of satiety,” because they swore by the gold with which they wished, indeed, but could not, be satisfied. Therefore “they shall fall,” he says, “and shall rise no more,” consumed by the famine already described, the famine for hearing the word of God, as we learn from those who remain of them.

[Col. 0366A] Finally, the words of holy Job apply especially to them: “Sterile through need and hunger, they gnawed in the wilderness, foul with calamity and misery; they ate herbs and the bark of trees, and the roots of junipers were their food. Snatching these from the valleys, when they found individual things, they ran to them with shouting” (Job 30). We may certainly compare their fables and genealogies to herbs, trees, and juniper roots. Whenever we engage them in discussion, if some occasion concerning fables and genealogies arises, there they are noisy and desolate; like persons snatching some herb, bark, or juniper root from the valleys, they run shouting to every particular, declaiming as they unravel some trifles, and in their own judgment acting as teachers. But in expounding the meaning of Scripture, they are so sterile through want and hunger, so foul and miserable, that we may not only grieve but even marvel at the weakness of their childish understanding.

## Chapter IX
“I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, [Col. 0366B] and he said: ‘Strike the hinge, and let the thresholds be shaken. For greed is at the head of them all, and I will slay their last one with the sword. There shall be no escape for him. He shall flee, and none of those who flee shall be saved.’”

The avenging sentence against the aforesaid pride of Jacob is still being brought forth and declared more and more clearly when he says: “For greed is at the head of them all.” For that greed is also to be treated as arising from pride is attested by the wise man, who, after saying, “Nothing is more wicked than a greedy man” (Ecclus. X), immediately added: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (ibid.). For pride is the companion of riches. Therefore the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to think proudly” (1 Tim. VI).

But now, entering into the mystery of this wondrous vision, let us follow the sequence of the text. “I saw,” he says, “the Lord standing upon the altar.” Truly it was a great vision and the signification of a great matter. He saw it by the prophetic Spirit, and what such a vision foreshowed to him was indeed to come to pass. We ask, therefore, where or when anything of this kind occurred, as a sign of which the Lord ought to have been seen standing upon an altar. But, searching through the whole Gospel of Christ and through every mystery of evangelical grace, nothing so great and so evident, corresponding to the particular character of this vision, presents itself to us as the form or posture of our Lord Jesus Christ crucified.

For when crucified and made a sacrifice for us, he stood upon the altar of the cross—an arduous station, a laborious station for himself. It must be carefully observed, [Col. 0366C] and the spectacle of that standing must never depart from the eyes of our mind. He hung and stood, with his hands fastened to the horns of the cross, and his feet joined to the foot-resting wood by the fastening of nails, in the posture of one standing. Thus he himself stood as the victim, while the cross was the altar.

Because of such standing of his, that temple of Jewish pride was destined to be destroyed—most justly, certainly—because cruel men, mocking him as he stood thus, said: “Aha! You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days!” (Matt. XXVII). Therefore, standing thus, he said: “Strike the hinge, and let the thresholds be shaken.” To whomever he said it—whether to the prophet who saw these things or to an angel—that striking of the hinge and shaking of the thresholds in the vision most certainly signified the coming destruction of the temple [Col. 0366D] by so great a blow and so great a shaking that the whole world still marvels at it today.

For what reason? “For greed,” he says, “is at the head of them all”: namely, that most cruel greed, whose fruit was this crime of greedy and impious men, who made the Lord stand thus upon the altar of the cross. For, since he daily disputed against their greed, he especially provoked them by no longer enduring the stubbornness of their greed, through which they had made his Father’s house—a house of prayer—a den of thieves (Matt. XXI). He fulfilled the Scripture that says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII), turning over the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, and, having made something like a whip from cords, driving them all out (Matt. XXI).

Therefore greed was at the head—that is, in the supreme purpose—of them all; and so, when the hinge had been struck and the thresholds shaken, that is, when the chief priesthood and the highest ranks of the scribes and Pharisees had been destroyed, “I will also slay their last one,” that is, the common people, “with the sword. There shall be no escape for them.” For they shall be surrounded and hemmed in on every side. And even if someone flees, “none of those who flee shall be saved. If they descend even to hell, my hand shall bring them out from there; and if they ascend even to heaven, I shall drag them down from there; and if they hide upon the summit of Carmel, searching there I shall take them away; and if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them. And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I shall command the sword, and it shall kill them; and I shall set [Col. 0367A] my eyes upon them for evil.”

Wonderfully, the Lord who, as has already been said, was to stand upon the altar of the cross, at the same time as he foreshows that standing declares his omnipotence. In a striking utterance he affirms that none of his enemies can escape his hands. Now, that we may weigh these words better, let us at the same time remember what he, having become man and now about to suffer—or to stand upon the altar of the cross—said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII). He said this to those who had already resolved to lift him up upon the cross.

If indeed you consider only the drawing of grace, when he says, “I will draw all things to myself,” you must surely understand: all the elect. But if you observe that through that lifting-up of the Son of Man upon the cross he received judicial authority over the living and the dead—he received it according to his humanity, though according to his divinity nothing was lacking to him—then, when he says, “I will draw all things to myself,” it must be understood as an act of power: none of you shall be able to escape my hands. For, possessing authority to exercise judgment, I shall sit upon the throne of my majesty; all nations shall be gathered before me; and I shall place all the elect at my right hand, but the reprobate at my left.

Clearly, the same thing is to be understood there and here: namely, that no one can escape the hands of this Lord, who upon the altar of the cross, in such a painful posture, stood while hanging and hung while standing. “If they descend,” he says, “even to hell,” [Col. 0367B] and so forth.

He spoke of five things, three of which were impossible to occur, one impossible not to occur, and one possible to occur. For it is impossible that a living man, fleeing distress, should descend to hell and live there in unimpaired life. Yet he says: “If they descend even to hell, my hand shall bring them out from there.” Again, it is impossible for a man to take on birds’ wings and fly into heaven; yet he says: “And if they ascend even to heaven, I shall drag them down from there.” Again, it is impossible for a man to be changed into a fish and enter the depths of the sea; yet he says: “And if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them.”

What, then, does he maintain by means of these impossibilities, except that a man can nowhere escape his hands, since he could drag him down even from there, or pursue him even to that place to which no living person can flee? One of the things he said, as we have stated, is possible: namely, to ascend to the summit of Carmel. But see with what mockery he says, “if they hide upon the summit of Carmel.” For one who wishes to hide is accustomed to seek valleys and hollows in the ground rather than mountain summits; moreover, a city or anything else situated upon a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt. V).

Yet there is a certain way of descending into hell by which a person may descend while fleeing the Lord’s face: namely, when, in despair, he hands himself over to the devil in an evil compact, turning away from God. Isaiah indicates that some such persons were among the people when he says: “For you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and we have made a pact with hell. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and have been drawn along by falsehood” (Isa. XXVIII).

Likewise, in a certain way one ascends to heaven when someone is lifted above himself on the wings of pride. And in a certain way one enters into the depths of the sea: namely, by pursuing curiosities and taking upon oneself the excessive cares of this age. Whichever way you understand either that descent to the lower regions, or that ascent to heaven, or that immersion in the depths of the sea, this saying of David must always be sung: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend to hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me and your right hand shall hold me” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

There is also a certain way of hiding upon the summit of Carmel, according to the very name Carmel, which is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision.” For when the enemies of Christ dispute and contend, as if knowingly, about circumcision of the flesh, so as to seem reasonably to reject the faith of the Gospel, behold, they are hidden upon Carmel’s summit. But Christ, searching there, takes them away, when we Christians, by searching the Scriptures, prove them false.

The last of the things said—“And if they go into captivity before their enemies”—was impossible not to occur. For they themselves could not avoid being led captive among all nations. [Col. 0369A] “There,” he says, “I shall command the sword, and it shall kill them.” This has often occurred: there has been very great slaughter among the scattered Jews, the Lord, of course, commanding the sword, in whose power every sword is; for “there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII).

What he then adds—“and I shall set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good”—he accomplishes in the two ways just mentioned: when he commands the serpent and it bites them invisibly with an evil bite, which is the eternal death of the soul; and when he commands the sword and it kills them with visible killing, which is bodily death. This, we understand, is also meant in the Psalm when it says: “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword” of the Romans; and, with respect to the soul, they are portions of foxes, that is, of evil spirits (Ps. LXII).

With respect to the soul, indeed, all of them—because they are unrepentant—die by the serpent’s bite and are portions of foxes. But with respect to the body, the sword was not commanded to kill all of them; for, apart from the fact that a remnant is to be saved (Rom. XI), their life and dispersion also serve the memory and honor of Christ. Thus he himself says in the Psalm: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people ever forget. Scatter them in your power” (Ps. LVIII).

For it greatly benefits those who worship Christ that Christ’s Jewish enemies live among them. For they carry with them the books in which are found all the things by which we confirm the Christian faith; and no one can say that it is a new teaching when we produce ancient authority from the books which they possess.

It follows:

“And the Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth and it melts, and all who dwell in it shall mourn. And all shall rise like a stream and sink like the river of Egypt. He who builds his ascent in heaven and has founded his bundle upon the earth; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.”

Because he had said, “I shall command the sword, and it shall kill them,” the prophet very fittingly adds: “And the Lord God of hosts”—that is, he himself is the one who says that he will do this. For he can surely command the sword who is the Lord of hosts, who has not merely one army but many armies: the armies of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and especially of the Medes, Greeks, Romans, and all nations have served and do serve him, though unknowingly, so that one kingdom may be destroyed when another succeeds it, by his just judgment. As he will say afterward: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I shall destroy it from the face of the earth.”

When, therefore, he says, “And the Lord God of hosts,” it is understood: he himself is the one. He does not wish you to marvel that he said he would command the sword, he who, when he stood, as has been said, upon the altar—that is, the instrument of the cross—displayed no sword, nor even wished to ask the Father to furnish him with what he could have supplied to himself: more than twelve legions of angels (Matt. XXVI).

What he immediately adds, “who touches the earth and it melts,” [Col. 0370A] can be understood in both senses, good and evil. For after he was lifted up from the earth, some who touched him were saved and others perished. Certainly those few from among the Jews and many from among the Gentiles who touched him melted and were pierced in heart, and did penance. Likewise, many Jews and Gentiles who melted wrongly and in envy, when the Gospel of Christ touched them—that is, struck them—perished and are perishing both in soul and body.

For there is no doubt that “to melt away” is used in both a good and an evil sense. In a good sense, as there: “My zeal has made me melt away, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. CXVIII). In an evil sense, as elsewhere: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and melt away” (Ps. CXI).

Likewise, what follows, “and all who dwell in it shall mourn,” is rightly understood in both senses. For those who were pierced in heart and did penance had good mourning, according to: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). But those who did not repent, especially the Jews, had evil mourning, namely that of which it was said above: “I shall turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation” (Amos VIII).

Likewise, what follows—“and all shall rise like a stream and sink like the river of Egypt”—must be divided between the two senses. For rising is good, sinking is evil. In those who repented, faith in the Gospel and the grace of the Holy Spirit, flowing forth from Christ the fountain, rises like a stream. In those who were or are unrepentant, especially among the Jews, all the vanity and uselessness of carnal ceremonies sinks away and is everywhere contemptible; no true worshipper of God now embraces them.

“It sinks,” I say, “like the river of Egypt,” because the ceremonies of carnal Judaism are not merely despised in any ordinary way, but so that whoever performs them is regarded and is as an Egyptian—that is, dark and altogether unworthy to pass through the Red Sea, which is Christ’s baptism.

This verse of prophecy is also fulfilled in those Gentiles who have believed, in such a manner that the greatly fearsome saying applies: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII). For because few are chosen, it is rightly said, “and all shall rise like a stream,” since a stream is smaller than a river. And because many are called who do not attain the ascent of election, it is rightly added, “and it shall sink like the river of Egypt.”

From those very persons who rise like a stream is fulfilled, as has been said, God’s purpose in the building up of the Church of Christ, “which is his body, his fullness” (Eph. I), of which “he himself is the head,” as the Apostle says (Col. I). Rightly, therefore, it is added: “He who builds his ascent in heaven.” For the ascent of every stream—that is, of every elect person possessing spiritual grace from him—is his own ascent. For when “the tribes, the tribes of the Lord, went up there” (Ps. CXXI), it is not the capacity of those ascending but the grace of the one calling that accomplishes it. “And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

And the Apostle, after saying: “He who descended is the same also who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things; and he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers,” completes the sentence thus: “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. IV).

Beautifully, then, it is said: “He who builds his ascent in heaven,” because the ascent of the saints is the building up of Christ’s body, and the fact that the members follow by ascending [Col. 0371B] is due to the grace of the head that goes before, which alone ascended by its own power.

“And he has founded his bundle,” he says, “upon the earth.” Clearly, when Christ ascended into heaven, he left a small number of apostles upon the earth. Sending upon them the Holy Spirit of love, he bound them as it were into a bundle by the bond of charity and unity of faith; and he “founded the bundle,” that is, set it as a foundation, and upon it built his Church. Then he also filled some from among the Gentiles with such abundance of heavenly grace and the word of teaching that, in imitation of the apostles, they could instruct Christ’s Church.

Hence he immediately adds: “He who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth.” By the name “sea,” Gentile nations are sometimes signified, as in: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV). For this is its meaning: We shall not fear the tribulations to come when the Jews, to whom the Gospel had first to be preached, are troubled and reject the Word of the Lord, and the apostles are transferred into the midst of the Gentiles.

Thus, “he who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth” means the same as saying: He calls upward Gentile people who possess the false and tasteless waters of worldly knowledge, makes them savor heavenly things, and appoints them as teachers, so that by speaking and writing alike they may shower the earth of the Church. Who does such great and such wonderful things? “The Lord,” he says, “is his name,” for truly he could not do such things, nor could he, rising from the dead, build his ascent in heaven, unless he were Lord.

Therefore David too, after saying, “Make a way for him who ascends above the west” (Ps. LXVII), immediately added, “The Lord is his name” (ibid.). The Jews bore very grievously the calling and reception of the Gentiles, envying their salvation—for example, when they said to Peter: “Why did you enter in to men who have the foreskin?” (Acts XI), and many similar things. Rightly, therefore, it follows:

“Are you not to me, sons of Israel, like the children of the Ethiopians? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene? [Col. 0372A] Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I shall destroy it from the face of the earth.”

It is as if he said: Why do you Jews glory in being God’s special possession and disparage the Gentiles? “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also” (Rom. III). Like Ethiopians, so you are mine; you are neither more nor less closely related to me, because I created Ethiopians just as I created Jews. But if you glory in this and boast that, for this reason, you belong to me rather than other nations—because I made you come up from the land of Egypt—are you therefore of a different nature or condition from other human beings?
