Surely I also made the Philistines come up from Cappadocia and the Syrians from Cyrene.

Therefore, do not raise yourselves in pride because I brought you out of Egypt and did not permit you, as my special people, to serve Pharaoh; nor suppose that for this reason the kingdom of God is owed to you alone. For in this world I have joined Ethiopians, Philistines, Syrians, and Jews, though separated by places and bodies, under the law of mortality; and according to my own will I assign my servants here and there and transfer them through all provinces. In that heavenly Zion, whose foundations are in the holy mountains, I similarly place in fitting dwellings all persons from every nation whom faith has commended, as he says through the Psalmist: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me. Behold, foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia—these were there” (Ps. LXXXVI).

On the contrary, as all have been made in an equal condition, so whoever sins shall be punished by the equal sentence of my judgment, and I shall overthrow every impious kingdom without distinction of persons. For “behold,” he says, “the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom, and I shall destroy it from the face of the earth.” What kingdom, or the kingdom of what nation, sinned as greatly as that one which killed the prophets and crucified the Lord of the prophets himself?

Therefore, do not, lifted up in pride, judge that sinners coming to faith from among the Gentiles ought to be rejected. For Jews no less than Greeks—indeed, first, or more than Greeks—shall receive wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, if they do not obey the truth (Rom. II), so that even their temporal kingdom shall be destroyed; for “I shall destroy it from the face of the earth.”

“Nevertheless, in destroying I shall not destroy the house of Jacob, says the Lord. For behold, I shall command, and I shall shake the house of Israel among all nations as grain is shaken in a sieve, and not one little stone shall fall upon the earth. All the sinners of my people who say, ‘Evil shall not draw near or come upon us,’ shall die by the sword.”

God commends his certain and unfailing providence when, after stating, “Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I shall destroy it from the face of the earth,” he adds: “Yet, in destroying, I shall not destroy the house of Jacob.” It is the same as saying: I shall indeed destroy the house of Jacob in the reprobate, but I shall not destroy it in the elect. For while the Jewish kingdom is being crushed by Roman power, while people are killed and scattered captive among all nations, it is impossible that any of those whom God foreknew and predestined should perish to God (Rom. VIII).

He did not crush that kingdom or nation in such a way as to will that none from it should be saved. Hence the Apostle says: “Has God cast away his people? Far be it. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not cast away his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. XI), and so forth.

By a very beautiful comparison he indicates the very mystery of which the Apostle says: “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in” (ibid.). By a beautiful comparison, I say, the same thing is prophesied here in the words: “For behold, I shall command, and I shall shake the house of Israel among all nations as grain is shaken in a sieve, and not one little stone shall fall upon the earth.”

Every tribulation and distress by which the Jews were hemmed in, afflicted, scattered, and dispersed among all nations was like the shaking of a sieve: as if the dusty ruins of collapsed walls were placed in a sieve and shaken, so that, when the dust falls to the ground, only the little stones remain, to be used in the work of restoration. Therefore, after saying, “All the sinners of my people who say, ‘Evil shall not draw near or come upon them,’ shall die by the sword,” he immediately adds: “In that day I shall raise up the fallen tabernacle of David, [Col. 0373C] and rebuild the openings of its walls; I shall restore the things that had fallen, and rebuild it as in ancient days, so that they may possess the remnant of Idumea and all nations, because my name has been invoked upon them, says the Lord, who does these things.”

The apostles prove the meaning of these words when the question was raised why Paul and Barnabas had received Gentiles without circumcision and Sabbath observance. Peter answered as he ought. Approving his judgment, James said: “Brothers, listen to me. Simon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name; and the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: ‘After these things I shall return and rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen; and I shall rebuild its ruins and raise it up, so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the nations upon whom my name has been invoked, says the Lord, who does these things. His work is known to the Lord from eternity’” (Acts XIII).

Therefore the house of Israel shaken in the sieve is the ruined house and fallen tabernacle, because the Lord, standing upon the altar—that is, hanging upon the altar of the cross through their act, as has already been said above—commanded the hinge to be struck, so that the thresholds might be shaken. And the remaining little stones, not one of which fell upon the earth, are the remnant of which the Apostle, after first stating what the divine answer said to Elijah, says: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal. So then,” he says, “at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI).

Moreover, all the sinners of the same people are sinners precisely in that “they say: ‘Evil shall not draw near or come upon us,’ and therefore they shall die by the sword,” he says. Thus it is no slight crime to say, “Evil shall not draw near or come upon us,” when God, or the Holy Spirit, says through the mouths of the prophets, “Evil shall draw near and come upon you.” That this crime is truly great has been proved by an ancient and deeply grievous example. For God said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. III). On the contrary, the serpent said: “By no means shall you die” (ibid.).

Thus the same evil spirit who spoke through the serpent—“By no means shall you die”—when God had said, “You shall die,” spoke through the mouths of false prophets: “It shall not draw near or come,” when the Holy Spirit through his prophets said: “Evil shall draw near and come upon you.” Accordingly, the false prophets themselves are like the serpent and worthy of a curse; while the sinners who believe false prophets more than the Lord’s prophets die by the sword as justly as Adam, or his wife, received the sentence of expulsion from Paradise because they believed the serpent more than God.

But here we understand the sword not only as that of the Romans, since not all sinners of that people died by it, but rather as the invisible sword which strikes the inward parts of every unrepentant soul, and of which the Psalmist, in fear, says: “Deliver me from the evil sword” (Ps. CXLIII).

Behold, on this day, which “is the day of salvation and the acceptable time” (2 Cor. VI), that fallen tabernacle of Jacob is raised up. For in place of unbelieving Jews, believing Gentiles are set as living stones upon the foundation of the living apostles and prophets (Eph. II); and in this way the true David, the cornerstone, is rebuilt as in ancient days—not from works of the law or ceremonies of the flesh, but from faith, through which Abraham was justified, through which Noah pleased God, and through which Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice to God (Hebr. XI).

And now the descendants of this David possess the remnant of Idumea and all [Col. 0374D] nations, without respect of persons, because the name of the Lord is invoked over them. For where the name of the Lord is invoked, there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. And so that you may know that everything you have heard is stable and fixed and cannot remain undone, it is not another, but he himself, who “says the Lord, who does these things.”

What are these things? What do you show us by saying, “who does these things”? Clearly: standing upon the altar; striking the hinge and shaking the thresholds; killing by the sword all whose chief principle is greed; touching the earth so that it melts; causing all who dwell in it to mourn; building his ascent in heaven and founding his bundle upon the earth; calling the waters of the sea and pouring them out upon the face of the earth; destroying the sinful kingdom and shaking the house of Israel among all nations; raising the tabernacle of David—that is, his Church, for he himself is the true David; and possessing the remnant of Idumea—that is, making heavenly those who are earthly and who think in an earthly way. For with him, to have spoken is to have done.

It follows: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when the ploughman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the sower of seed. And the mountains shall drip sweetness, and all hills shall be cultivated. And I shall restore the captivity of my people Israel; and they shall build deserted cities and dwell in them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine. They shall make gardens and eat their fruit. And I shall plant them upon their own soil, and I shall no longer uproot them from their land which I gave them, [Col. 0375B] says the Lord your God.”

See what the end of speaking in this prophet is like. If you look only at the outer bark of the letter, what is promised by the glorious and great God is cheap and slight, because it is common to good and evil alike. The good need not care greatly for it or seek it with great concern; but it is desirable to the wicked, whose god is the belly, of whom the Apostle says: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI).

But if you strip away the bark, as this prophet himself was stripping sycamore trees, and seek beneath the usefulness of the letter the precious—that is, spiritual—meaning, then what the God of glory promises at the conclusion of this discourse to those hoping in him is glorious and splendid: “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II).

Someone may say: What necessity was there that, especially at the end of the discourse, such a letter should be put forward as most flatters the carnal? Clearly, it was expedient that it should deceive those childish people among whom the Holy Scripture had to be preserved, with a good deception, for the sake of those for whom the mysteries contained in the prophets were to be useful when revealed in their own time.

For there is a good deception, by which not only a reprobate person but even a good person, without knowing it, renders obedience to the divine counsels—so much so that Jeremiah says: “You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived; you were stronger than I and prevailed” (Jerem. XX). It is the same as saying: I had resolved to be silent about such matters, but you stirred within me, so that I could not be silent, something like the movement of an impatient spirit—that is, a good and strong zeal.

For he continues afterward and says: “And I said: I shall not remember him, nor speak in his name. And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I grew weary, unable to endure it” (ibid.).

Conversely, we shall say to these childish and carnal persons, who would never have preserved the Holy Scriptures if they had understood their force: The Lord deceived you, and you have been deceived; he was stronger than you and prevailed. For if he had spoken in the prophets so that the letter seemed to promise no good thing to you, wicked as you are, you would have been angry against the prophetic Spirit, just as your king Ahab was angry with the prophet Micaiah, saying to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: “Did I not tell you that he prophesies no good to me, but always evil?” (3 Kings, final chapter).

Angry in this way, you would have burned the Holy Scripture, just as King Zedekiah did. When the words of Jeremiah were read to him (Jerem. XXXVI), after three or four pages had been read, he cut the scroll with the scribe’s knife and threw it into the fire that was upon the brazier, until the entire scroll was consumed by the fire in the brazier.

Therefore it was good for you to be deceived like children, and for spiritual things to be promised to spiritual persons in such a way that you carnal persons thought carnal things were being promised to you: such as these—that the ploughman should overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes the sower of seed. This occurs through favorable weather, when, immediately after the harvest has filled the barns sufficiently for the current year, the ploughman who follows casts seed in hope of the next, and, with no intervening delay, the time of vintage arrives, which the ripeness of the grapes does not permit to be postponed further.

Understanding these things carnally, you flatter yourselves, telling yourselves that after adversities prosperity is again promised to you, although you are unrepentant. And indeed, through this occasion the Holy Scripture has been preserved among you until now and is preserved. But meanwhile you are captive and dispersed, and you shall die in your sin.

Now, at last stripping away this letter, let us seek the meaning hidden within. “Behold,” he says, “days are coming, says the Lord, when the ploughman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes the sower of seed.” These days have already come, as the Lord himself testified when he spoke to his disciples, saying: “Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest. He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. For in this saying is the true word: one is he who sows and another who reaps. I sent you to reap what you did not sow. Others labored, and you have entered into their labors” (John IV).

Briefly, those who labored and sowed were the patriarchs and prophets; but those who entered into their labors were the apostles. For the patriarchs, laboring—that is, journeying—and passing “from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people” (Ps. CIV), sowed: that is, they deserved to receive the promises of the blessed seed to come, which is Christ. Yet they did not see him with their own eyes; they only longed for him in hope and thereby served in the manner of ploughmen and sowers.

But the apostles saw Christ present, the same Christ, with blessed eyes and received him in the manner of reapers. Therefore he said to them: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X).

Therefore, when he now says, “the ploughman shall overtake the reaper,” it is the same as saying: the patriarchs and apostles shall rejoice together in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, in whom they receive together the promised blessing, “so that,” as he says, “he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.” For the apostles did not enter into their labors in such a way as to exclude them; rather, behold, they rejoice together: those who sowed before his coming and these who reaped at his coming.

Moreover, the treader of grapes who overtakes the sower of seed is the same as the reaper, and the sower of seed is the same as the ploughman. For, as has been said, the earlier holy fathers were both ploughmen and sowers, while the apostles were both reapers and [the supplied source ends here].

They are winepress-treaders, being reapers because Christ, present among them, was ripe grain for them; winepress-treaders, because they received from him the new wine of the Holy Spirit, or because, sharing directly in his Passion, they drank his cup. “And the mountains,” he says, “shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall be cultivated.” The mountains are likewise the apostles, because of the loftiness of their merits [Col. 0377B]; throughout the whole world they dripped the sweetness of peace and the remission of sins, preaching repentance and the remission of sins in the name of Jesus Christ. Those who heard them and were justified by hearing, like well-cultivated hills, yielded good fruit.

“And I will restore,” he says, “the captivity of my people Israel”; that is, I will loosen the bonds of sins and tear down the prison of error and ignorance—the true captivity in which we were held, we who are now called, and are, Israel. What he then adds—“And they shall build deserted cities and dwell in them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine” [Col. 0378A]—now requires no exposition, since we see everywhere on earth, throughout the wilderness of paganism, which had formerly been abandoned by God, Christ’s Churches rising up. These are rightly called cities because of the firmness of faith; vineyards because of the gladness of hope, which does not disappoint (Rom. V); and gardens because of the delights of charity. In them dwell those who built them by the word; from them those drink the wine of joy who formed them by commandments; from them those eat fruit who advanced them by counsels. For just as one who reaps, so also one who builds cities of this kind, plants vineyards of this kind, or makes gardens of this kind, receives a reward and gathers fruit unto eternal life.

Hence it follows: “And I will plant them upon their own soil, and I will no longer uproot them from their land [Col. 0378B] which I gave them.” For the soil which he gave to his saints is the paradise of delights, in which he placed the first human being. Therefore, because all lost that soil or land in Adam and became deprived of the kingdom of heaven, but through Christ’s coming recovered it in such a way as not to lose it again, he rightly added immediately after saying, “And I will plant them upon their own soil”: “I will no longer uproot them from their land which I gave them.” Then, rejoicing, he turns to the ear of each one of us, saying: “The Lord your God says.”

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Obadiah

[Col. 0377]

**163** Obadiah is fourth in the order of the twelve prophets. He is said to be the one who speaks to Elijah in the Book of Kings:

> “And now you say to me, ‘Go, tell your lord: Elijah is here.’ But when I have departed from you, the Spirit of the Lord will carry you away to a place that I do not know; and when I go in and report it to Ahab, if he does not find you, he will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the Lord from his childhood. Has it not been reported to you, my lord, what I did when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord: that I hid one hundred men of the prophets of the Lord, fifty and fifty in caves, and fed them with bread and water?” (3 Kings 18).

He is also said to have been that third captain of fifty whom Elijah spared when he said:

> “Man of God, do not despise my life, and the lives of your servants who are with me. Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the first two captains of fifty, and the fifties who were with them; but now I beseech you, have mercy on my life.” (4 Kings 1)

Afterwards, having left the service of King Ahaziah, he became Elijah’s disciple and prophesied. He also died a natural death and was buried with his fathers in the city of Sebaste, where the prophet Elisha and John the Baptist likewise rest in veneration.

Therefore, because he had supported one hundred prophets, he received prophetic grace; and from being a commander of an army he became a leader of the Church. Hence our Lord rightly and plausibly says in his Gospel: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. 10). For the truth of this saying is proved by the preceding example: because he had then fed a little flock of prophets in Samaria, having himself become a prophet, he now feeds the Churches of Christ throughout the whole world.

And this should be noted: just as, in the Acts of the Apostles, the first man to be crowned with martyrdom was, by a certain divine foreknowledge, called Stephen, which means “crowned,” so this man, who was destined to serve the Lord in such a way and to receive such a reward for his service, was called Obadiah, which means “servant of the Lord.”

Let us approach this servant of the Lord and hear what he says through him who spoke through the holy prophets—the Spirit of the Lord—without doubting that, although this prophet is small in the count of his verses, he is nevertheless great in meaning: that is, wholly spiritual.

## Commentary on the Prophet Obadiah

### Book One

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377C] **164** “The vision of Obadiah.” The vision said to belong to Obadiah is God’s vision, that is, the vision which God showed to Obadiah. Thus Ezekiel too says: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions” [Col. 0378C] (Ezek. 1). For this reason those now called prophets were formerly called seers, because they saw God’s visions. For in the Book of Kings we read:

> Formerly in [Col. 0379A] Israel, anyone going to consult God would speak thus: “Come, let us go to the seer.” For he who is called a prophet today was formerly called a seer. (1 Kings 9)

These kinds of visions differ in this respect: in one case, with God showing them, symbolic images are seen—such as those especially seen by the already-mentioned Ezekiel and Daniel; in another, divine utterances are seen and perceived in their own manner without images, as Obadiah here says of himself, “The vision of Obadiah,” yet relates that he saw no likeness or image.

Regarding this latter kind of vision, there is no doubt that the holy prophets possessed certain sight or understanding, while the Holy Spirit spoke within them. But concerning that kind of seeing in which images were displayed beforehand, this must be understood: understanding did not immediately follow the sight. Daniel testifies to this concerning himself. When he had seen four great beasts coming up from the sea, he says: “I approached one of those standing by, and I asked him the truth concerning all these things” (Dan. 7).

Likewise, when he had seen a ram thrusting with its horns toward the west, north, and south, and a running he-goat opposing it, having a conspicuous horn between its eyes, he afterwards added: “When I, Daniel, saw the vision and sought understanding, behold, there stood before me something like the appearance of a man; and I heard a man’s voice between the banks of Ulai, and he cried out and said: ‘Gabriel, make this vision understood’” (Dan. 8).

“Thus says the Lord God concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy among the nations: ‘Rise up, and let us rise against him for battle.’” [Col. 0379C]

Edom is Esau himself, who is also called by another name, Seir. But why he was called Edom, the history tells, saying: “Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came to him from the field exhausted, he said, ‘Give me some of this red cooking’; for which reason his name was called Edom” (Gen. 25).

For *Edom* means “red,” and this name is a memorial of his gluttony, because he sold his birthright for red stew. Yet he was also red in complexion, as it is written: “The first who came out was red, and altogether hairy like a skin” (ibid.). Hence it should be noted that the accidental colour of his nature was not judged blameworthy, so that he should be marked and called Edom on that account—especially [Col. 0379D] since holy David too was ruddy (1 Kings 16). Rather, it was the vice of his mind and his immoderate desire for the red stew which deserved that he should inherit such a name.

But what was the people of that Edom doing at that time, or what did it deserve, that so harsh a prophetic vision—or word of the Lord—should be displayed against it? For it is indeed very harsh, as is evident from the whole course of this reading. If we review the events of those times, it is clear that Edom was allied with Israel, so much so that it went with Jehoram son of Ahab—under whom this Obadiah had fed the prophets of the Lord—to battle against Moab (3 Kings 22).

What, then, must be observed here, except that the words of this vision, since they are not the words of a human being but of the Holy Spirit, must be weighed spiritually? For Edom, interpreted “red” or “bloody,” was not merely that one man, the son of Isaac and Rebekah, but every person who imitates his vice, pursuing gluttony and bearing hatred toward a brother, as he is known to have done.

If this were not so, the Apostle would certainly not say to those who were indeed descended according to the flesh—not from Esau, not from Edom, but from Jacob:

> “Watching lest anyone fall short of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up again hinder you, and through it many be defiled; lest anyone be sexually immoral or profane like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal.” (Heb. 12)

Therefore, if you properly weigh the words of the vision—which no history testifies were fulfilled worthily in that Edom—and likewise recall the condition of affairs in Israel when this Obadiah prophesied, you should not doubt that under the name of Edom the vision is directed against carnal Israel.

For then, while Ahab and the impious Jezebel reigned, the prophets of the Lord began to be killed, so that Elijah said: “Lord, the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant. They have destroyed your altars [Col. 0380A] **165** and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone remain, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19).

Certainly, those who were being killed, Elijah himself who was fleeing, and the rest of whom the Lord said, “I have left for myself seven thousand men whose knees have not bowed before Baal” (ibid.)—these are Jacob and the Israelites. But those who killed them were Edom, since they carried out in deed the hatred which that man conceived in his mind, whose children they are by imitation, when he said in his heart: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I shall kill my brother Jacob” (Gen. 27).

Otherwise, how will this stand which, in this prophet, after the words “that a man may perish from the mountain of Esau,” adds: “Because of slaughter and because of iniquity against your brother Jacob”? For that Esau or Edom, whom Rebekah bore, certainly always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which their father had blessed him, but he did not kill him. These, however, who were born from Jacob according to the flesh and imitated Esau’s hatred, killed their brothers; nor did they cease killing until they killed Christ himself.

And if you ask why they were signified by the name Edom when they could have been expressed more plainly by other names that would seem proper to the Jewish or Israelite people, we answer this: it would have been the act of a very incautious and undiscerning person to proclaim in plain language and with proper terms the destruction of the people among whom, for the time being, prophetic visions and all the holy Scriptures alone had to be preserved—until, after Jesus was glorified and the Spirit given, they should be spread throughout the whole world in the languages of all nations and become clear to the open understanding of believers.

Let us now enter upon the text of this vision. After stating, “Thus says the Lord concerning Edom,” he immediately adds: “We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy among the nations.” He speaks this in the person of himself and the other prophets, before beginning to relate what the Lord says to Edom.

Thus Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, after writing, “Peter rose up in the midst of the brothers and said” (Acts 1), before beginning to relate what Peter said, inserted from his own person: “Now there was a crowd of about one hundred and twenty persons together.”

Thus, as though someone were asking, “Who are you, and how or from where do you know what the Lord says to Edom?”—“We prophets,” he says, “who almost all speak against Edom, have heard the report from the Lord. And he has sent,” that is, he will most certainly send, “an envoy among the nations, who will say: ‘Rise up, and let us rise against him for battle.’”

This envoy is Christ, sent to the nations and desired by the nations, as it is written in Haggai: “I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2). This envoy is not said to have been sent to the nations in the sense that he himself in person came, or was bound to come, to the nations. For he was brought to completion in Judaea, and he assigned to his apostles the duty of carrying out his embassy among the nations, as Paul, one of them, says: “Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We entreat you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

These are the envoy’s words: “O nations, rise up, and let us rise against Edom for battle.” Certainly this has also happened bodily, when nations rose up from the Roman Empire for the destruction of the Jews; and from that time it continues to happen, while believers from the nations fight against them with the word of truth, taking weapons from the armoury of the holy Scriptures.

We have heard this report from the Lord, we who await and receive that envoy. But Edom—who does not receive him, indeed who kills him, just as it killed before and after him the prophets, wise men, and scribes whom he sent—must hear the other things which the Lord says to it. What are they?

“Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly contemptible.” What an opening for those who say to this Edom: “I have made you small among the nations.” *Small* can sometimes be understood in a good sense, but not here. For it follows: “You are exceedingly contemptible.” Therefore, “I have made you small” means: I have shown you to be envious—of whom another Scripture rightly says, “Envy kills the little one” (Job 5).

For you envy the nations because, in comparison with you, the nations have become great by receiving Christ and consequently rightly glorying in the faith of their father Abraham. Hence comes the saying: “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger” (Rom. 10). For you are jealous of and envy the nations, seeing fulfilled in them that prophetic saying: “I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me” (ibid.).

Since you are thus small, you are consequently and rightly exceedingly contemptible—understand: because of the slaughter and because of the iniquity against your brother Jacob, which I shall state later. For you envied as one small; you killed as one envious. Therefore you are so contemptible that you are like Cain, “a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Gen. 4), cast out from the face of the Lord, because, as he killed his brother Abel through envy, so you killed Christ and his prophets through envy.

Therefore, I say, you are exceedingly contemptible, not only to God but also to human beings, among whom you are held captive and dispersed, your captivity and dispersion themselves bearing the mark of your crime and not allowing your iniquity to remain concealed.

Certainly, the preceding fault of pride was the cause of your becoming so contemptible. I say, therefore:

> “The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who exalt your throne, who say in your heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the earth?’ Though you rise like an eagle and place your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord.”

That other Edom, whose hatred you imitate—you who are called Jacob according to the flesh—dwells in rocks, as the letter sounds. For the whole southern region of the Idumaeans, from Eleutheropolis as far as Petra and Zaila—for this is Esau’s possession—dwells in caves. But you, who imitate for the worse everything said of Esau, glory in that rock and dwell in the clefts of another rock.

What is that rock? Abraham, your father according to the flesh. Thus Isaiah says: “Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn” (Isa. 51), meaning Abraham and Sarah. For he immediately adds: “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you” (ibid.).

You dwell in the clefts of that rock, and from there pride has lifted you up. For example, when you say, “We are Abraham’s seed; Abraham is our father” (John 8). You say these and similar things, pride lifting you up—namely, by behaving proudly against that rock which, laid in the foundation, supports Abraham and all the other saints who deserve to be called rocks or living stones because of faith.

Nor have I said, or do I say, that you are lifted up *in* the rock, but that you dwell in the clefts of the rock and are lifted up. For you have split that rock—that is, Abraham’s flesh—by irreparable clefts: first, when the ten tribes, through Jeroboam’s division, were cut off from the house of David, who possessed the inheritance of blessing, with which, after Abraham and Isaac, upright Jacob deserved to be blessed, so that Christ might be born from his seed (Gen. 25); and again, when you denied that the Son of David was the Son of God, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

Thus, dwelling in the clefts of the rock, you exalted your throne, choosing rather that the Roman kingdom [Col. 0382D] **166**, or the name of Caesar, should be named over you than the kingdom or name of poor Christ, whose kingdom is not of this world but from heaven.

Certainly, you are deceived in vain when you say in your heart, “Who will bring me down to the earth?” For finally: “Though you rise like an eagle and place your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord.”

Rise now like an eagle and set your nest among the stars: for example, by saying, “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8). This is a flight of a mind exceedingly high in pride. Yet I shall bring you down from there, proving and convicting you of the falsehood that God is not your father, but that you are from your father the devil, whose desires you wished to do.

It follows:

> “If thieves had entered you, if robbers by night, how would you have been silent? Would they not have stolen what was sufficient for themselves? If grape-gatherers had entered you, would they not at least have left you clusters of grapes? How Esau has been searched out! His hidden things have been investigated!” [Col. 0383A]

It is a most severe mockery to say to one whose possessions have all been searched by thieves and whose hidden things also have been investigated: “If thieves had entered you, how would you have been silent?” Who deserves such mockery except one who is exceedingly contemptible—so vain that, though he was entirely stripped by thieves while asleep, still unaware that he slept, he boasts that he is prudent and can scent a thief’s arrival a whole month beforehand?

To make the manner of this mockery more evident, let us take an example from somewhere else. In Terence’s comedy, the moralizing brother, angry with his brother because he is ruining his son by allowing him to devote himself to love affairs, is mocked by a servant as follows (*Adelphoe*, Act III, scene IV, 31):

> You, altogether as you are, are nothing but wisdom;  
>   
> That utterly frivolous fellow—would you really have allowed  
> Your son to do these things?

He replies:

> “[lacuna] Would I have allowed him? Would I not, for a full six months,  
> Have scented it beforehand whenever he began anything?”

And the servant, persistently making sport of him, says:

> “You tell me about your vigilance?”

As though he were saying: “You need not tell me; for I know that your son has until now been watchfully guarded by you, lest he should fall in love.” Yet that son, whom his foolish father boasted that he had guarded so carefully, was wholly devoted to the love of a certain harp-girl, though another had taken the reputation for that love upon himself. But, setting aside these trivial examples, let us come to the matter and show [Col. 0383C] what thieves and what robbers entered into this Edom.

In the Psalm where all nations are commanded to clap their hands and rejoice to God with the voice of exultation, they say: “He has chosen for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. LXVI). In saying this the Holy Spirit refers us to history. For just as Esau or Edom, who was born first, was rejected by God and Jacob was loved, so the Israelite people, who had first been accepted by God with a certain familiarity, was afterwards rejected; while the nations, which had previously possessed no knowledge of him, received his blessing. Thus there Jacob, and here the nations, are rightly called thieves—not because of their own fault, but as a reproach to him or to those who, sleeping in deadly negligence, had the birthright taken away from them.

For who, if we speak meanwhile according to the history, [Col. 0383D] would hesitate to call Rebekah and Jacob thieves in that deed, especially since Isaac himself, their father, says: “Your brother came deceitfully and received your blessing” (Gen. XXVII)? Jacob is called a thief for the same reason for which he is called deceitful. Moreover, we say that the Lord himself likens himself to a thief, saying: “If therefore you do not keep watch, I shall come upon you swiftly like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I shall come upon you” (Rev. III). It is certainly clear that he says this not to rebuke the one coming, but to mock the one sleeping.

Therefore, when, as has already been said, the brother came deceitfully and received the blessing, Rebekah the mother knowing and cooperating, then thieves entered into Edom. And when, [Col. 0384A] blindness having befallen Israel, “the fullness of the Gentiles” entered in (Rom. XI) and took the blessing neglected by the Jews—that is, Christ—they likewise, indeed even more fully, entered into Edom; rather, they do not cease to enter.

We have spoken of thieves; what shall we say of robbers? For he said both, “If thieves had entered into you,” and, “if robbers by night.” Nowhere in the Scriptures do we recall that the name “robber” serves as an image of anything good. For, as has been said, the Lord likened himself to a thief; but neither he nor any godly person ought ever to be likened to a robber, since it is a name denoting cruelty. Therefore the nations believing in Christ, and by believing supplanting unbelieving and cruel Edom—that is, the Jewish people—were thieves, like Jacob, who came deceitfully in order to receive the blessing. But the robbers were [Col. 0384B] the scribes and Pharisees, who, practising their greed by robbery, slaughtered the souls of that same people.

For indeed, if they had not been robbers, the Lord would never, after first saying, “It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer,” have said against them, “But you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. XII). Was it not there, by robbing in the Temple and making plunder of the people, that they came to the point of slaughtering their souls by urging that Christ should be killed? In urging this, did not robbers enter by night? For they spread over those wretches a dense darkness of deception, so that, though they were robbers, they appeared to be counsellors. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” To this one among [Col. 0384C] them, Caiaphas, high priest of that year, replied: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die, and that the whole [Col. 0386C] nation should not perish” (John XI).

O most pleasant counsellor, most cruel robber! At this Edom was silent—that is, it assented, following the cruel advice. “For from that day they planned to kill the Lord Jesus” (ibid.). Rightly, then, it is said against him in mockery and with most bitter irony: “If thieves had entered into you, if robbers by night, how would you have been silent?” For this is said more bitterly and sounds harsher than if it were said in wonder: “While thieves entered into you, while robbers by night, how were you silent?” Likewise, what follows—“Would they not have stolen what was sufficient for themselves?”—strikes this same [Col. 0384D] Edom much more forcefully than if it were said, “They stole what was sufficient for themselves.”

This concerns, according to the type which appeared beforehand in Jacob, the aforementioned nations supplanting the Jews. The prophetic Spirit rightly says that they “stole what was sufficient for themselves”: that is, they took from the Jews only those things sufficient for their salvation. For these thieves did not deign to steal burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats (Heb. IX), nor the new moon, the Sabbath, other festivals, the Kalends, and the remaining carnal ceremonies. Rather, they rejected them and accounted them as dung, believing faith and righteousness sufficient for themselves, according as the holy Apostles wrote to them:

> [Col. 0385A] “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; and that you do not do to others what you do not wish done to yourselves. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well” (Acts XV).

This is plainly like entering a vineyard and, carefully gathering the clusters of grapes, leaving behind only the leaves. Hence he continues fittingly: “If grape-gatherers,” he says, “had entered into you, would they not at least have left you a cluster of grapes?” Finally, Scripture repeatedly declares that the Israelite people was the Lord’s vineyard. 167 For example, that passage in Isaiah: “I shall sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard. A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil; and he fenced it, removed the stones from it, and planted it with choice vines,” and so forth, down to: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V).

[Col. 0385B] Never has the insensible vineyard of any man been so stripped by grape-gatherers as this living and sentient vineyard of the Lord has been despoiled by these thieves. For grape-gatherers, however diligent, sometimes leave at least a cluster hidden among the leaves. But these aforementioned thieves—that is, the Gentiles called to faith—entered the vineyard of the Law and the Prophets, seized everything, and leave for that silent and sleeping Edom nothing but the leaves of the letter that kills. It has no remaining cluster at all of the life-giving Spirit.

Therefore, asking in wonder and wondering in his question, he says: “[Col. 0385C] How have they searched out Esau, investigated his hidden things?” It is understood: those thieves who entered into him. But what were the hidden things of that Jewish people, which, as has often been said, was prefigured in name and deeds by Edom or Esau? What, I say, were its hidden things except the spiritual mysteries of the Law and the Prophets? These could fittingly be signified by Esau’s very fine garments, which Rebekah had at home with her.

These thieves searched deeply; in a marvellous way they investigated Esau’s hidden things when, understanding the Law and Prophets spiritually, they also covered the bare hands and neck with goatskins—that is, by making open confession of their former deeds and their old pride, they performed repentance. These are Esau’s hidden things; these are his very fine garments, which the Apostle recalls: “Whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and [Col. 0385D] the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. IX). They searched out and investigated all these things and transferred them to themselves.

It follows: “All the men of your covenant have sent you away as far as the border; they have mocked you; the men of your peace have prevailed against you; those who eat with you will set snares over you.” It was a grave guilt of this Edom that it had many confederates; it was a grave offence in carnal Israel that it so often made a covenant with profane nations, despite the Lord’s prohibition in the Law: “You shall not make a covenant with them” (Exod. XXIII), “nor join your children to theirs in marriage” (Deut. VII), “for they will seduce your son so that he does not follow me and serves foreign gods more readily; [Col. 0386A] then my wrath will be kindled and will swiftly destroy you” (Exod. XXXII). And so it happened: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and these became a stumbling-block to them” (Ps. CV).

By doing this and persisting in it, they came at length to such a point that, most willingly submitting themselves to the rule of the Roman people and saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX), they crucified Christ, the Son of God, their king. Through the succession of many ages, many peoples were thus allied with this Edom, and in striving to be like them it killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself.

But the mockers—truly mockers, though falsely called men of peace—of whom he now says, “They have mocked you; the men of your peace have prevailed against you; those who eat with you will set snares [Col. 0386B] over you,” were the priests, and above all Annas and Caiaphas. They mocked that people far more ruinously by persuading it that Barabbas should be released to them and Christ crucified than Jeroboam and his priests had formerly mocked it by making golden calves for them to worship and causing them to abandon David their king, displaying the handsome images of the calves and saying: “These are your gods, O Israel” (III Kings XII).

For they ate with that unhappy Edom and satisfied their own greed from it; and, so that they might be permitted to eat and make plunder from the people, they therefore mocked it thus and therefore laid snares over it. The greatest of the mockers was the aforementioned mocker Caiaphas, saying: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI).

Meanwhile, the precise force of this expression must be carefully observed. He did not say, “They will lay snares under you” or “against you,” but, “They will lay snares over you.” For it cannot adequately be expressed how wicked the mockery and how persistent the traps of deception are when one who urges another to be deceived possesses, along with the craft of persuasion, greatness of power—as did Caiaphas and the other leaders who persuaded the crowds. For, being socially above the common people in pride, they were more wicked than the wicked people: clever in persuasion and factious in provocation. Therefore the prophetic Spirit says against them through Isaiah:

> “Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men, who rule over my people who are in Jerusalem. For you have said: We have struck a covenant with [Col. 0386D] death, and made a pact with hell” (Isa. XXVIII), etc.

Men allied in this way, or men of peace, sent you away as far as the border. To what boundary did they send him away? Plainly, to the boundary of blessing: beyond the bounds of the promise made to Abraham in these words, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed, and in Isaac your seed shall be called” (Gen. XXVIII). The men of covenant, the mocking men, sent him beyond the bounds of that great inheritance because their wicked alliance was the cause of his being cast outside so great a good and not reckoned among the seed, since he was not of faith.

Did not the earlier Edom, or Esau, for this reason send himself away as far as the boundary, so as not to follow the blessing and not to remain within the bounds of the inheritance [Col. 0387A] which his father Isaac intended to assign to him as firstborn? For because he wished to have as his allies the people of this world, he was expelled beyond the limits of the heavenly blessing. For it is written: “Esau, when he was forty years old, took wives: Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon of the same place; both of whom offended the mind of Rebekah” (Gen. XXVI).

Did not Rebekah’s offended mind judge unworthy of blessing the son who, as he had first sold his birthright for food, so later, in taking foreign wives, became a servant of lust because he despised the blessing of Abraham’s seed? For, wishing to become renowned and powerful on earth, he immersed himself in kinships of sin. [Col. 0387B] Against these Abraham, taking precaution, had bound his faithful servant by oath, saying: “You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites” (Gen. XXVIII), among whom I dwell.

Nor should this be passed over: when the same Esau saw that his father had blessed Jacob, and also perceived that his father did not willingly look upon the daughters of Canaan, he went to Ishmael and took as wife, besides those whom he had previously had, Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham and sister of Nebaioth (ibid.). This plainly caused him to be sent yet further to the boundary and cast out, because he thus associated himself with rejected Ishmael. For Sarah had said: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI), and so it had happened.

[Col. 0387C] According to this likeness, as we have said, the Apostle testifies that this happened to carnal Israel because of its allies, writing to the Galatians: “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman’” (Gal. IV). 168

Plainly both Ishmael and Esau, who, born according to the flesh, persecuted Isaac and Jacob, born according to the Spirit, prefigured the carnal Jews, who did not cease to persecute and kill the spiritual Ishmael, until they themselves were sent away, as has been said, as far as the boundary.

It follows: “There is no wisdom in him. Shall I not on that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau? And your mighty [Col. 0387D] men from the south shall be afraid, so that a man may perish from Mount Esau, because of slaughter and because of violence against your brother Jacob. Shame shall cover you, and you shall perish for ever.”

Up to this point, “Those who eat with you will set snares over you,” the prophetic discourse was addressed to Edom itself. Then, wishing to make the attentive hearer marvel at what was being said, it suddenly turns and says concerning that same Edom: “There is no wisdom in him.” Truly, there is no wisdom in him who did not beware of the snares laid over him, but, foolish and improvident, favoured those lying in wait for him. Therefore good wisdom is not in him.

On the other hand, his aforementioned ambushers possessed evil wisdom, as was said of the same persons through another prophet: [Col. 0388A] “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent before yourselves” (Isa. V). Again: “Wise to do evil, but unable to do good” (Jer. VI). Therefore, after saying, “There is no wisdom in him,” because there is a kind of wisdom or prudence that is not good and is more properly called wickedness, he immediately adds: “Shall I not on that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise from Idumea, from Mount Esau?”

For wisdom or prudence rightly judged worthy of destruction is wickedness, or folly. For it is written: “I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the prudence of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX). This is written in blessed Job; and when the Apostle recalled that Scripture, he immediately said: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (I Cor. I). [Col. 0388B] Elsewhere he says: “For the prudence of the flesh is death” (Rom. VIII). Again: “For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (ibid.).

This has been said because the prudence which he laments as absent from that Edom is one thing—namely, good prudence—and the prudence which he says he will destroy from its mountain, that is, from its pride, is another—namely, evil prudence, which is properly called wickedness. It should likewise be observed that, in saying, “Shall I not on that day destroy the wise from Idumea?”, he clearly indicates that he prophesies of the future, although until this point he has used verbs in the past tense.

Behold, we see; behold, we read in amazement and, reading, marvel in histories more than tragic, how terribly those wise and prudent men—that is, the wicked—destroyed themselves by the judgment of the Lord. Following Esau’s example in hating his simple brother Jacob, [Col. 0388C] they persecuted and killed those who were truly wise, the prophets; and finally, after long testing the Lord himself, their brother according to the flesh, “that they might ensnare him in his speech” (Matt. XXII), they eventually devised such a counsel of their wisdom that they hanged him upon a tree, wishing on that account to have him considered accursed.

For, wickedly wise and perversely prudent, they knew that it was written in the Law that “he who hangs on a tree is accursed by God” (Gal. III). Yet, if they had been truly wise and prudent, they would also have understood from the place where this is written that punishment does not make one accursed, but guilt. Therefore let us not hesitate to set forth the very wording of the Law:

> “When a man has sinned a crime deserving death and has been condemned to death and hanged on a gibbet, [Col. 0388D] his corpse shall not remain upon the tree, but you shall bury him on that same day, because he who hangs on a tree is accursed by God; and you shall by no means defile the land which the Lord your God has given you as a possession” (Deut. XXI).

It does not merely say, “when a man has been hanged on a gibbet,” which is punishment; it first states the guilt: “when a man has sinned a crime deserving death.” Those wise and prudent men did not see—or did not wish to see—this, because their wisdom was not that which gives light, but wickedness which blinds, as it is written: “They thought these things and erred; for their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. II).

“Therefore I shall destroy,” he says, “on that day the wise and prudence from Mount [Col. 0389A] Esau”; that is, I shall condemn, like Esau, the Jews who think earthly things and in Esau’s likeness are proud, so that they may be proved foolish—not merely in any fashion, but so that they cannot bear the light of wisdom. For this is what the prophetic discourse, once again turning to him, means: “And your mighty men from the south shall be afraid, so that a man may perish from Mount Esau.”

The south is this time of grace, from which the Sun of righteousness, Christ, rose on high and, shedding forth the rays of his divinity—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—has illuminated and warmed the world. Hence the Psalmist says: “In the sun he has placed his tabernacle, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. He has rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his circuit to its summit; and there is none who can hide from [Col. 0389B] his heat” (Ps. XVIII).

From this south the mighty men of this Esau are afraid, as was prefigured when Moses’ face had become radiant from communion with the word of God, and Aaron and his sons, seeing it, were afraid to come near (Exod. XXXIV). Thus, I say, these mighty men are afraid—that is, rebels against the light, of whom it is written in the Psalm: “Mighty men rushed upon me” (Ps. LVIII). Their fear is malign, because it proceeds from envy. For they envy the brightness of this eternal sun, and whatever they hear concerning his glory they think is spoken against themselves, since they wished to extinguish one such as he.

Hence it comes about that the man from the mountain of this Esau perishes: while they flee the light, the men who trust in their own strength go to destruction, lifting up their heads upon the mountain of pride. Nor do they now deserve to be called men, but rather women, in accordance with what the same Lord says in [Col. 0389C] Isaiah: “The exactors have despoiled my people, and women have ruled over them” (Isa. III).

The prophetic discourse states the sin of this Esau more plainly when it immediately says: “Because of slaughter and violence against your brother Jacob, you shall perish for ever.” If we look only to the two persons formerly designated by these proper names, Jacob and Esau, the letter will not stand; for Esau did hate his brother Jacob, but did not kill him. But concerning the carnal sons of Israel, or the Jews, it is only too well known that they killed their brothers, the prophets of the Lord, and the Lord himself, their brother according to the flesh; and for this reason shame covered them and destroyed them for ever.

Not merely because they killed him, [Col. 0389D] but because they refused to believe in him when he rose again. It must especially be observed that he did not say only “because of slaughter,” but added, “and because of violence against your brother.” For the crime of slaughter would have harmed no one had the wickedness of unbelief not also persisted. Therefore, as has often been said, the name Esau or Edom signifies all imitators of that first Esau, and the name Jacob all followers of him whom Esau hated.

The Psalmist grants that all the future things which this prophecy cries out against this cruel Edom may occur, and rightly so, when he speaks in the voice of one invoking judgment: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Make it empty, make it empty, even to its foundation’” (Ps. CXXXVI)—[Col. 0390A] that is, who, mutually exhorting and inflaming themselves to hatred of those who think heavenly things, say: “Empty out and remove the things contrary to us or to our way of life, even to the foundation,” that is, to the end, so that all may yield to our manner.

This is what the present discourse reproaches them for when it immediately adds: “In the day when you stood against him, when strangers were taking his army captive and foreigners were entering his gates and casting lots over Jerusalem, you too were as one of them.” When Ahab ruled in Samaria and Jehoshaphat in Jerusalem, at the time when this Obadiah had hidden and fed the prophets of the Lord, we read that this Edom did such a thing. For the sons of Edom gathered with the sons of Moab and Ammon to fight [Col. 0390B] against Jehoshaphat.

Yet at that time they neither captured his army as they wished nor entered the gates of Jerusalem. For when Jehoshaphat prayed and said, “Now therefore, O Lord, behold, the sons of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir are striving to cast us out from the possession which you gave us” (II Chron. XX), and the word of the Lord came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah the Levite, saying, “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not be afraid; tomorrow go forth, and the Lord will be with you” (ibid.), the sons of Ammon and Moab rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to kill and destroy them. And when they had carried out this deed, they turned even against one another and fell by mutual wounds.

Thus it is indeed true that, when foreigners were taking—or intended to take—the army of Jerusalem captive, the foreigners and strangers were the sons of Moab and Ammon. Edom, who was also Seir, was as one of them; but, as has been said, they neither captured it nor entered the gates of Jerusalem.

Accordingly, since this whole prophetic vision is spiritual, let us pursue it spiritually, as we have begun. For, as has often already been said, carnal Israel, persecuting his spiritual brother Israel and killing the prophets of the Lord, is himself Edom. And indeed, whenever foreigners captured the host of those who truly were or are Israelites, whenever strangers entered the gate and cast lots over Jerusalem, carnal Israel himself was as one of them—indeed worse and more hostile than any one of them.

First, around the very times in which this prophet prophesied, foreigners—that is, the Syrians—were waging war against Israel under the kings Ben-hadad and Hazael; but within Israel itself those who deserved spiritually to be called sons of Edom acted far more wickedly: “Lord,” says Elijah, “they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19). Then, down to Gospel times, whenever foreigners or strangers captured or entered the gates of Jerusalem—that is, when the Babylonians came, and after them Antiochus, and entered its gates not merely but also killed many who persevered for God’s covenant—there arose wicked men from Israel itself, more destructive to their brethren than the Gentiles were. Witness is the suffering of Jeremiah (Jer. 38), whom the Babylonians preserved while men of his own nation afflicted him (1 Macc. 7; 2 Macc. 14); witness is the distress of the Maccabees, whom wicked men from Israel, and especially the impious Alcimus, injured more than any Greek.

After these things, both the holy Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles testify how truly it was said against this Edom—that is, the carnal Jew—“you also were as one of them,” namely, of the alien or foreign nations to whom he delivered Christ for mockery, scourging, and crucifixion (Matt. 20), and among whom he strove to make Christ’s disciples hated everywhere, stirring up seditions and inflaming crowds wherever they went preaching Christ’s Gospel. For the Jews did this as long as they were permitted—as long as their nation and their place endured. But provident divinity, as is written elsewhere, foreseeing the future, destroyed and exterminated them through the Roman devastation; their cities were laid waste without inhabitant, their houses without a person, and their land was left a desert, so that the power to call out and rage might be taken from those whose will was obstinate and insatiable.

Holding this as most certain, the Spirit of truth immediately says with the greatest firmness in this prophet: “And you shall not look down on the day of your brother, on the day of his exile; and you shall not rejoice over the children of Judah on the day of their destruction; and you shall not magnify your mouth on the day of distress; neither shall you enter the gate of my people on the day of their ruin, nor shall you too look down upon his evils on the day of his desolation; nor shall you send forth against his army on the day of his desolation; neither shall you stand at the outlets to kill those who flee, nor shut up his survivors on the day of tribulation.”

To what he had said shortly before—“Because of slaughter and because of violence against your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall perish for ever”—is joined: “And you shall not look down on the day of your brother.” Yet in a remarkable way all these utterly wicked acts are affirmed to have been done by this Edom, while he is forbidden as though he were about to do them. For what is more wicked than to despise, on the day of his exile, not merely any exile but one’s exiled brother; to rejoice in his destruction; to magnify one’s mouth in all his distress; to enter his gates, leaping upon his ruins; to look down on him in his evils; to stand at the outlets to kill the fugitive or shut up his survivors? Since Wisdom decrees that one must not rejoice at the ruin of even a hated enemy (Prov. 24), who does not see how truly it was said above: “There is no prudence in him” who bears such a mind toward his brother?

Therefore, in a reversal, let the Holy Spirit who speaks in the prophets taunt him; let the Lord who dwells in heaven laugh and deride him, saying: “You shall not look down; you shall not rejoice; you shall not magnify your mouth,” and so forth. For whom can this Edom—that is, the earthly man, namely the Jew—despise, he who is so despised throughout the whole world, as was said to him above: “Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly contemptible” (Jer. 49)? He lost his place and his nation. Had he not lost them, he would not cease to despise, magnify his mouth, and even kill; but he is, in truth, captive.

[Col. 0392A] We must now carefully observe by how many, and how great, names, after saying “on the day of your brother,” he described and illuminated this same day. He subordinated seven days to one day: after first saying, “You shall not look down on the day of your brother,” he adds, “on the day of his exile; on the day of destruction; on the day of distress; on the day of ruin; on the day of desolation”; again, “on the day of desolation”; “on the day of tribulation.” Clearly, by the number seven he signifies the multitude of all miseries or tribulations endured by that brother who is simple and gentle, meek and humble in heart: whoever lives according to Christ’s example; whoever lives as an exile in this present age or time, which revolves through seven days.

We read the same number of tribulations in blessed Job: “In six tribulations,” he says, “he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will touch you” (Job 5). By the number seven, as already said, is signified the totality of the tribulations which the saints suffer in this age. Their seventh—that is, the final tribulation of each elect person—has sure consolation, just as in the ordering of the world the seventh day has no evening.

Therefore, when we read the brother’s day, whom Edom persecutes, as distinguished sevenfold, we should not suppose it was done without purpose. He has no abiding city here (Heb. 13), but is a pilgrim; he has lost his life for God, or for Christ, in order to find it (John 12); he is distressed, having hope, “because he shall stand with great steadfastness against those who distressed him” (Wisdom 5); suffering the ruin of present goods, he endures patiently for hope of future goods; he appears contemptible in his desolation, wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth, so that he may be found approved by the testimony of faith; again, he appears deserted by a kind of desolation when he is killed and looks to the right or left and finds no one to defend him; he flees and finds none to meet him or with whom he may safely hide.

He could have said: “But even such a day of your brother—his day of exile, his day of destruction, which appears to you as true destruction when he loses his life in order to find it—will not last long.” This, I say, he could have said; and although he did not say it, it must nevertheless be understood. For it follows: “For the day of the Lord is near upon all nations.” Here also, when he says “upon all nations,” one must understand: “and first upon you.” For he immediately continues: “As you have done, so shall it be done to you; he turns your recompense upon your head.”

As though he said: Meanwhile, before your brother’s day of exile is ended, before that great day of the Lord comes upon all nations—the day of judgment—you will receive public vengeance here in this age, with all nations hearing, seeing, and marveling; so that you can no longer despise, but are yourself despised, and are far more contemptible than every Christian people wandering and suffering distress, though it be shut up and killed. After this private and proper portion, you will receive common vengeance with the other nations on that near day of the Lord: the day of judgment, the bitter day, the day of tribulation and distress, the day of calamity and misery, the day of darkness and gloom, the day of cloud and storm, the day of trumpet and alarm, as the prophet Zephaniah says (Zeph. 1).

Join to those terrifying descriptions of that day the preceding statement: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be distressed there.” Behold, you have the day of the avenging Lord proclaimed just as many times—that is, seven times—for the consolation of this brother, whose day of tribulation Edom had proclaimed seven times. Therefore, since this Edom of whom we speak was to suffer first an individual or private punishment from the Roman nations, and then universal punishment with the other nations on the day of judgment, it is fittingly said: “As you have done, so shall it be done to you,” and then repeated: “He will turn your recompense upon your head.”

For what does “As you have done, so shall it be done to you” mean except that you will be recompensed according to your merits? Yet he added, “He will turn your recompense upon your head,” because this earthly and bloodthirsty Edom, who killed Christ and Christ’s prophets, has a double recompense, a double crushing, according to another prophet. After saying, “Bring terror upon them” (Jer. 17)—understand, the terror which they experienced when they said, “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11)—so that it might happen to them as they feared, he was not satisfied with this recompense alone, but still threatened the same unbelieving and impenitent persons with eternal punishment: “Crush them, O Lord my God, with a double crushing” (Jer. 17).

Having said this to Edom, he turns to those of whom and for whom he had spoken, who are afflicted first by Edom and then by the other nations, and says to them, confirming what he had said for their consolation: “For the day of the Lord is near upon all nations. For as you drank upon my holy mountain, all nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow down, and shall be as though they had not been.”

If these words are still addressed to Edom himself, they have this meaning: Just as you drank upon my holy mountain Zion and rejoiced in the destruction or ruin of the children of Judah, so all nations, turned against you, shall drink and be filled with your evils. But if we prefer to understand them as spoken for the consolation of those who, as stated above, are afflicted by the wicked in this age, then the passage from Isaiah assists our interpretation: “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath; you have drunk to the bottom the cup of stupor, and have drained it to the dregs” (Isa. 51). And shortly afterward: “Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation. You shall not add to drink it any longer; and I will not put it in the hand of those who humbled you” (ibid.).

Therefore, just as all of you drank—whose destruction your enemies rejoiced in—or you, brother, who are despised and are also called Jerusalem, “This is the whole generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. 23)—just as, I say, you drank, God permitting you to be afflicted, so all persecuting nations shall drink, receiving an equal, indeed a double, return in the reckoning; as the Apocalypse foretells against Babylon, which is the totality of these nations: “Render to her as she herself rendered to you, and repay her double according to her works; in the cup in which she mixed for you, mix her a double portion” (Rev. 18).

Thus, after saying, “As you drank upon my holy mountain,” that is, “you suffered persecution for my name,” he rightly added, “all nations shall drink continually,” because the discourse concerns not so much temporal as eternal recompense. This is further repeated and amplified by saying: “They shall drink and swallow down, and shall be as though they had not been.” For a double portion will be mixed for them, as has been said, because they mixed a hard and bitter cup for the saints; yet they killed only the body. But for themselves it shall be mixed so that both body and soul are cast into Gehenna. Thus they shall not drink in any ordinary way, but with open and wide mouth shall swallow to the bottom the whole judgment of condemnation contained in the cup of the Lord’s wrath. When this occurs, then they shall be as though they had not been. They shall indeed exist in substance, but shall not exist in any capacity: they will no longer be able to persecute or cause any stumbling-block in the kingdom of God.

Conversely, the saints’ being will be true and blessed. Hence it immediately follows: “And on Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and there shall be a Holy One.” That Mount Zion is the glorious city, the heavenly Jerusalem, of which David says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86). In that Zion there shall be salvation, and there shall be a Holy One: namely Christ himself, because he is its salvation and Savior. How will this Holy One be in it? Exceedingly well, exceedingly blessedly: he will remain for ever a participant in its nature, he who is its maker or founder, as is written in the psalm just mentioned: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (ibid.). This is the permanence of Zion’s Savior, because of the city Zion itself, or Jerusalem, it is written elsewhere: “Its participation is in the same” (Ps. 121), and the Holy One himself says: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3).

[Col. 0394D] This opposition is indeed the contrary one: the nations shall be as though they had not been; but the Holy One shall be, and his city shall be salvation, with such a being as will be subject to no disasters and have no end: “And the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed them. And the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall be kindled among them and devour them, and there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.”

With marvelous invective the prophetic speech pursues the name Esau, who is also Edom. It had first spoken against him, and after briefly pronouncing condemnation also upon the other nations, it now returns to inveigh against him. In the holy Scriptures this name Edom has an exceedingly evil reputation, more so than that of any other nation. For example, when David says in the psalm, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136), intending Babylon to mean all nations, among whom all the holy citizens of God’s kingdom are held captive while they live in the body, what seems harsher to you: what they complain of universally concerning Babylon, or what they complain of particularly concerning Edom?

Indeed, concerning Babylon—or to Babylon itself—the language is milder: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept.” Likewise: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who repays you the recompense you rendered to us” (ibid.). But regarding this Edom the lament is not expressed so sparingly or gently. The wounded soul, unable to bear its most acute pain, raises its spirit from the deep and lifts its voice higher toward heaven, to him alone who considers labor and pain: “Remember, O Lord,” it says, “the sons of Edom in the day of Jerusalem” (ibid.). For a wound inflicted by a brother is endured more bitterly—by one from whom consolation against others ought to have been expected.

Thus Jacob, when his own brother Edom persecuted him in his own person (Gen. 27); thus Joseph, when he was sold by his brothers (Gen. 37); thus the holy prophets and apostles, when they suffered persecution and death from their fellow-countrymen, the Jews; thus Catholic Christians, when they are afflicted by heretics, who are false brothers, suffer more bitterly and sharply than when hostile foreign nations, with whom they share neither kinship nor profession, attack them. Hence: “For if an enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me” (Ps. 54), and so forth.

Let us now follow the order. “And the house of Jacob,” he says, “shall possess those who had possessed them.” Such possession is not understood for the good of those possessed. For it follows: “And the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall be kindled among them and devour them.” Therefore they shall be possessed to their harm, just as fire and flame possess stubble. Such preeminence of those who possess is judicial authority.

Finally, in judgment all the saints shall consume their false-brother persecutors. Their first exemplars were the patriarch Jacob and his son Joseph: the former suffered persecution from the very brother who was Esau both in name and in fact; the latter from his brothers, who were not Esau in name but were Esau in fact and imitation. How did these possess Jacob, that is, God’s servants—these persecutors, these false brothers, whose first exemplars, as has been said, were Esau, Rebekah’s firstborn, and Joseph’s brothers? They possessed them by cruel assault: in their own time the Jews, and in their own time the heretics, having the power to kill them and to persecute them from city to city.

Therefore the house of Jacob—that is, the whole company of God’s servants—shall possess them with a fitting possession, not to make use of them, but that they may be confounded and handed over to perpetual fire at the judgment of their mouths. This is what he says: “And the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau stubble.” This is surely a very fitting confirmation. Because fire produces flame, Jacob, who begot, is called fire, and Joseph, who was begotten by him, flame. But Esau himself, rooted in the earth according to the lower part of the blessing—his father saying, “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be” (Gen. 27)—is compared to stubble, all whose greenness has passed away, whose appearance has withered, and which is useful for nothing but to be given to fire.

Just as all saints of the Old Testament may rightly be called fire, and all saints of the New Testament, from the coming of Christ—whose figure Joseph bore—may rightly be called flame, so their persecutors, like Esau, shall be stubble: “they shall be kindled among them and devour them, and there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.” For the great confirmation of the sentence he thus concludes, “because the Lord has spoken,” so that you may understand: his speech and word are truth, and what he says cannot remain unfulfilled. As he himself says, foretelling the future judgment: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24).
