It follows: “And those who are toward the south shall inherit Mount Esau; and those in the plains, the Philistines; and they shall possess the territory of Ephraim and the territory of Samaria; and Benjamin shall possess Gilead; and the captivity of this host of the children of Israel [shall possess] all the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Bosporus, shall possess the cities of the south. And saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall belong to the Lord.”

No history testifies that all these things were fulfilled according to the letter—namely, that carnal Israel, or the Jew, after this prophecy possessed Mount Esau. Nor could this, or the other things that follow, have been so great, even if they ever happened, that the Holy Spirit would have deigned, by foretelling them, to fill the prophetic trumpet that was to be heard throughout the whole world. This is especially clear from the statement, “the captivity of this host of the children of Israel shall possess all the Canaanites as far as Zarephath.” If we follow the plain letter, it cannot stand, since it is certain that it never happened, nor should happen, that the captivity of the ten tribes which then threatened, by which they were carried away into Assyria, should be recalled and possess all the Canaanites.

For the prophetic Spirit could not be contrary to himself: promising in this prophet what he denied in another, namely in Hosea when he said, “Call her name ‘Without mercy,’ because I will no longer add to show mercy to the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; yet I will have mercy on the house of Judah” (Hos. 1)—that is, I will recall the children of Judah from Babylonian captivity after seventy years. Nor do we read anywhere that the captivity of Jerusalem was in Bosporus, a region of the northern sea, so that, according to the letter, “the captivity of Jerusalem which is in Bosporus shall possess the cities of the south.”

Therefore, since all these things are spiritual, examining them spiritually, let us first consider the number of these promises, for they are seven. The first is: “Those who are toward the south shall inherit Mount Esau.” The second: “Those in the plains [shall inherit] the Philistines.” The third: “They shall possess the territory of Ephraim and the territory of Samaria.” The fourth: “Benjamin shall possess Gilead.” The fifth: “The captivity of this host of the children of Israel [shall possess] all the Canaanites as far as Zarephath.” The sixth: “The captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Bosporus, shall possess the cities of the south.” The seventh: “Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau.”

These seven saving and consolatory promises complete the praise of the Lord in saying: “And the kingdom shall belong to the Lord.” Above there had likewise been written seven days of miseries against Edom, the oft-mentioned persecutor of his brother. After the opening words, “You shall not look down on the day of your brother,” there followed a sevenfold description of his day: “On the day of his exile; on the day of destruction; on the day of distress; on the day of ruin; on the day of desolation; on the day of his tribulation.” For the description of that day was thus completed because “the day of the Lord is near.”

Therefore, just as there, in the sevenfold repetition of “day,” that is, the time in which the saints are pilgrims in this world, we understand the totality of evils which they suffer, so here in these seven promises we discern the totality of the consolations by which they are consoled by the Lord amid, or after, all pressures. These promises are against the same Edom—that is, the Jewish people, the killer of his brother, namely the Lord and the holy prophets.

For this people, because of multiple though similar reasons, is called here Esau, Philistines, Ephraim or Samaria, Gilead, and Canaan. But the saints, likewise for multiple reasons—that is, the various distributions of graces—are said to dwell toward the south and to be in the plains; they are named Benjamin, the host of the children of Israel, Jerusalem whose captivity is in Bosporus, and saviors, to whom Jesus Christ, the supreme and only Savior, communicates his own name in accordance with their office.

Let us therefore say: “He who is toward the south,” he says, “shall inherit Mount Esau”—the true Jacob, that is, the supplanter of the Jewish people, who is called Edom or Esau, dwells toward the south, which we understand as the grace of the Holy Spirit. But Esau lifts himself up upon a mountain when, wishing to establish his own righteousness, he is not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10), in the likeness of those brothers. One of them, Jacob, dwelt at home with his mother Rebekah, who signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit; the other, Esau, exercised himself in the mountains and woods, a skilled hunter and a man of the field (Gen. 25).

Just as Jacob, dwelling with his mother, inherited the blessing and his brother’s birthright, so Christ’s disciples, secure in the grace of the Holy Spirit, inherited the kingdom of God taken away from the Jews, in order that they might bear its fruits (Matt. 21), as the Lord himself foretold to them in the Gospel. They are accordingly said to dwell toward the south, that is, toward the midday region, by which the bright light of wisdom is understood.

It follows: “And those in the plains [shall inherit] the Philistines.” Those who are denoted by the name Esau—just as they are on the mountain of pride, wishing to establish their own righteousness (Rom. 10), as we have said—are rightly also called Philistines because they have fallen from grace, considering themselves justified by works of the Law and without faith in Christ. For “Philistines” is interpreted “falling by a drink.” The Lord mixed for them—that is, for the Jews—a spirit of dizziness (Isa. 19), giving them, as the Apostle recalls, “a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear” (Rom. 11); “and their table became before them a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68).

[Col. 0398B] Those who dwell in the plains are the humble, to whom, by the grace of humility, understanding has been given so that they understand the Scriptures and, understanding spiritually, trust not in their own righteousness but in God’s. Justified by faith, these obtain the Philistines according to the mystical victory of David, who struck the Philistine by casting one of five stones into his forehead (1 Kings 17). By that one stone is figured the one faith of Jesus Christ, by which alone we are justified, and which is also mystically and figuratively preached in the five books of Moses.

“And they shall possess,” he says, “the territory of Ephraim and the territory of Samaria.” Ephraim was the tribe from which Jeroboam tore Israel away from the house of David and instituted golden calves to be worshipped as God. In this place it rightly signifies also the assembly of scribes and Pharisees, who stirred up the people against the true David, Christ the Son of God, and never ceased to devise their falsehood against the truth of Gospel faith. Likewise Samaria, because, seduced by that same Jeroboam into that sin, it had a kingdom divided against the Davidic kingdom, signifies the Jewish people divided from Christ and seduced by elders and chief priests, just as Jeroboam, king of the tribe of Ephraim, seduced Samaria.

Therefore they shall possess the territory of Ephraim and the territory of Samaria: that is, having the holy Spirit of counsel, they shall overcome the malice of both rulers and people, destroy the counsels they devised against the Lord, and condemn them on the day of judgment.

“And Benjamin shall possess Gilead.” Gilead is the mountain to which Jacob came as a fugitive from Haran on the seventh day of his journey; from that mountain the city founded there also received its name. Idolatry especially reigned there. Hence it is written in Hosea: “Gilead is a city of those working an idol, undermined with blood, and like the throat of men who are robbers” (Hos. 6). Benjamin, moreover, is interpreted “son of the right hand.” Therefore Benjamin shall possess Gilead: that is, those possessing the Spirit of strength shall justly judge not only Jewish unbelief but all idolaters, against whom they fought courageously unto death.

“And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel [shall possess] all the Canaanites as far as Zarephath.” The children of Israel, the children of promise, are all the elect of that former people, whose patriarch Israel—also Jacob—was their father according to the flesh, and of whom the apostles were the best members. The Canaanites, however, by that very name Canaan, which is interpreted “their movement,” are those who fell through pride with moved foot, even if they were born from the same flesh; as the Lord testifies when he says through the prophet: “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). For the Amorite and the Hittite were sons of Canaan; yet the Jew is a son of Israel according to the flesh, and nevertheless this reproach is addressed to the Jew through the prophet.

Zarephath, moreover, is a Sidonian town—Sidonians too are Canaanites—situated on the public road, where a widow once fed Elijah. The mystery of that widow is known in the school of Christ’s Church, in what she says: “Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and make bread for myself and my son” (3 Kings 17). Thus, he says, the captivity of this host of the children of Israel—that is, the apostles of Christ, truly sons of Israel—leaving their own Jewish people who rejected them and passing over to the nations, shall condemn the Canaanites who call themselves Jews and shall be their judges; but they shall administer salvation to the nations, so that through them what was prefigured in that widow of Zarephath may be fulfilled.

Thus the Lord himself, solemnly intimating this, said with his own mouth: “Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow woman” (Luke 6). Behold, now also, and until the end of the age, Elijah—whose name means “My God,” namely the Lord Jesus Christ—is fed by that widow and feeds her jar of flour: that is, he multiplies through the Spirit of spiritual knowledge the small amount of knowledge which Gentile peoples could possess by nature; and, baking through the mystery of the cross, whose sacrament he meditates, he certainly gathers two sticks and makes from the Scriptures bread of life.

“And the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Bosporus, shall possess the cities of the south.” In Scripture Jerusalem is not unknown to signify the Church, which is the heavenly city. A very great part of it was removed from the true sun in the error of Gentilism before the Savior’s coming, and is therefore rightly understood through the captivity that is in Bosporus. For Bosporus, as was said above, is a region of the northern sea, and no Scripture records that the captivity of earthly Jerusalem was carried away there.

Therefore it shall possess the cities of the south, that is, of the midday region. This we now see taking place, when those who formerly lacked knowledge of God, being dark and cold, possess the fullness of true light and warmth. It is as though people were transferred from the north to the south to inhabit shining cities, through the favor of God, who visited the nations by his grace and mercy alone.

“And saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau.” Those are rightly called saviors through whose ministry converted sinners are saved, as the apostle James says: “He who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way shall save his soul from death” (James 5). This the apostles especially did after Christ, through whose preaching the nations were converted from the error of their way. Therefore they are saviors, and they shall go up to Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau: that is, they shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 29). Carnal Israel, as we have often said, is called and is Esau precisely because he is unbelieving and a persecutor of his brother.

Their mountain, to which they shall ascend, is called Zion, and is the height of virtues; but Esau’s mountain is the swelling of pride. Their expectation of judgment is full of fear. “And the kingdom shall belong to the Lord”—to the Lord, I say, whose gifts all these things are: that the saints shall thus inherit, thus possess, and thus judge; and afterwards shall judge, and after the judgment shall share in the kingdom at his eternal table, according to his faithful promise: “And I appoint to you, as my Father appointed to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Jonah

[Col. 0399]

174 The soul that seeks Christ declares by these words the purpose for which it seeks him: “Who will give you to me as a brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me?” (Song of Songs VIII). Conscious of being greatly despised, and in its own judgment very contemptible, it trusts that through him alone it will become noble and renowned, if it deserves to find, embrace, and kiss such a beloved—not only within, in the secret chamber of conscience, but also outside; that is, so that it may also come to the attention of that beloved’s friends that it has seen him, recognized him, believed in him, and loved him. For then it can no longer be contemptible in the eyes of God the Father, or in the sight of its friends, namely the holy angels and holy human beings.

But where does it seek, or where ought it to seek, where he is found or can be found, except in Scripture, and especially in the prophetic Scriptures, which are indeed the word of the Lord? There he is sought and found, because the prophets testify what that beloved is like. In some prophets he is found more readily, in others with greater difficulty. But in Jonah, whom we now desire to enter, it shines forth most clearly that the miracle performed in him was a proclamation of Christ. For Christ himself spoke with his own mouth, and the whole world heard: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. XII).

Therefore let us enter this prophet with all the greater eagerness, the more clearly and beautifully we recognize in him Christ’s testimony—Christ whom we have undertaken to seek in the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets. Let us pray that he who is a type of the Savior, and who, remaining three days and nights in the belly of the whale, prefigured the Lord’s resurrection, may also obtain for us fervor and the grace of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with his very name, Jonah; for it means “dove.” And who does not know that in the Scriptures the grace of the Holy Spirit is often signified by a dove? Especially because that same Holy Spirit appeared over our Lord in the form of a dove [Col. 0401] (Luke III).

Moreover, to refer this whole prophet to the understanding of the Savior—his flight, his boarding a ship and paying the fare, his sleeping—is laborious and, as was said before us, requires the greatest exertion. Yet the more difficult it is, the more beautiful we hope it may be, with the finger of God cooperating according to his good pleasure. Attentive labor will attempt to bring forth the splendid mysteries of Christ from what is obscure.

# COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET JONAH

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0401]

### 175. CHAPTER I

[Col. 0401A]

“And the word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it, because the cry of its wickedness has ascended before me.”

Grammarians may perhaps be surprised that it begins in this way with a conjunction—“And the word of the Lord came”—when nothing has preceded in the letter. But if we attend to the reason why Jonah was sent to preach to the Gentiles, we are not surprised. For such an opening sounds not merely well, but wonderfully and with great force, in our ears.

What was the reason? Plainly this: the children of Israel did not heed the prophets of the Lord. So many prophets were sent, so many miracles were done, captivity was so often foretold to them because of the multitude of their sins, and yet they never repented. For not even in the time of a single king did they cease worshipping the golden calves; and not one of all the kings of the ten tribes departed from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin (III Kings XII).

To pass over the rest: Elijah, sent in the word and Spirit of the Lord, did many wonderful things; yet he did not bring it about that those calves should be abandoned, although through signs he finally obtained this much—that the people should know Baal was not God and should cry: “The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God” (III Kings XVIII). His disciple Elisha succeeded him. Seeking, with the same purpose of recalling the people, to perform more signs than Elijah had done, he said: “I pray that your spirit may be doubled in me” (IV Kings II); and what he asked came to pass. For if you count correctly, Elijah performed eight signs and Elisha sixteen; this was the double portion. After these things Elisha died; and, as before his death, so after it, the worship of the calves persisted in Israel.

The Lord marvelled at Israel and was weary of it, knowing that if he sent to the Gentiles he would find them much more ready to believe. Hence he spoke thus to one of the prophets: “Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak my words to them. For you are not being sent to a people of profound speech and difficult language—to the house of Israel—nor to many peoples of profound speech and unknown language, whose speech you cannot understand; and if I sent you to them, they would listen to you. But the house of Israel will not listen to you, because they will not listen to me” (Ezek. III [Col. 0401D]).

What the Lord thus said, preferring the Gentiles to Israel in reproach of Israel because of their readiness to hear and believe, ought to have been proved by experience. Jonah was chosen for the service of this proof. After Elisha’s death, Scripture makes this mention of him in the book of Kings: Jeroboam, son of Joash, son of Jehu, king of Israel, restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the wilderness, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which he spoke through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet.

Therefore, when it begins with the conjunction, saying, “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah,” it sends us back to the things already stated, so that the sense is this: The children of Israel did not heed what the Lord commanded when he sent to them through the hand of his servants the prophets; but they hardened their necks, gave themselves over to doing evil before the Lord [Col. 0402B], and provoking him. Therefore the word of the Lord came to Jonah: “Arise,” he says, “and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it,” so that, by comparison with the Gentiles, Israel might be shown still more deserving of condemnation. Thus the Lord’s judgment, by which he was handing them over or would hand them over to captivity, might be demonstrated beyond reproach: the Ninevites repenting, while the children of Israel persisted in impenitence.

This Jonah is called the son of Amittai, that is, “of truth.” The Hebrews hand down that he was the son of the widow of Zarephath, whom Elijah the prophet raised from the dead; and afterward his mother said to Elijah: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true” (III Kings XVII). For this reason the boy himself is said to have been called son of Amittai. For *Amittai* means “truth” in our language. Since Elijah spoke what was true, he who was raised is called the son of truth.

Further, when the Lord says, “Because the cry of its wickedness has ascended before me,” this is the same as what is said in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Gen. XVIII); and to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV).

176 Now, since this Jonah, sent to Nineveh, is a type of the Savior sent to the Gentiles, it must be said when, where, and how the word of the Lord came to him who, according to his divinity, is himself called and is the Word of the Lord. If you ask where: surely at the streams of the Jordan. If you ask when: plainly when John was preaching and baptizing with the baptism of repentance. If you ask how: certainly when the heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit descended upon him [Col. 0402D] in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father sounded at the same time: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke III).

Then, I say, and in this manner, the word of the Lord came to him, as he himself confirmed with his own mouth. For when he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day according to his custom, and stood up to read. The book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him; and when he unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me, sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” And he said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke IV).

Hence, because the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, Jonah fittingly signified him also by his very name [Col. 0403B]. For, as has already been said, it means “dove”; it also means “sorrowful.” This interpretation likewise pertains to the mystery, because he is the one whom Isaiah foretold as “a man of sorrows” and “acquainted with infirmity,” adding: “Surely he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. LIII). From the baptism of repentance which he received, entering upon fasting (Matt. IV), then continuing repentance by preaching and enduring persecutions, sorrowing for us and carrying our sorrows even to the gibbet of the cross.

Did he not know to which poor persons he was sent to preach good news, to which captives to proclaim release? Could he fail to know that the ministry of his preaching belonged to the Gentiles, when prophets could know and foretell it? So too did that last Simeon, who called him the salvation of the Lord, “prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for the revelation of the Gentiles” (Luke II). Yet he did not then wish to go to the Gentiles; indeed, he forbade his disciples to go, saying: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X). To the Canaanite woman crying after him he did not answer at once (Matt. XV), but preached only to the Jews, except that he remained two days in Samaria (John IV).

It follows, therefore: “And Jonah arose to flee to Tarshish from the face of the Lord.” It sounds harsh, indeed, and what is said—that Jonah fled from the face of the Lord—does not seem fitting for the Savior. But if you consider the intention of the fugitive, the flight is not very blameworthy even in the prophet, because it was not unbelief but compassion that caused it. For with devout affection he grieved for his own people, that is, the Hebrew people, because he was being sent to preach to the Ninevites for the condemnation of his own people, so that the Assyrians might be justified in comparison with Israel, and Israel, condemned in comparison with the Assyrians, might be handed over to perpetual captivity. He did not hate the salvation of the Gentiles, but feared the condemnation of his own nation; and therefore, in fleeing, he was not greatly displeasing to God. Indeed, because of the greatness of his compassion, he was very pleasing to him.

He might have been more displeasing had he not grieved, just as Moses was not displeasing when he said: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if you do not, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. XXXII); nor was the Apostle displeasing when he wished himself to be anathema from Christ for his brothers (Rom. IX). Thus this man too was not displeasing in fleeing in such a manner, as the outcome of events especially proved. For which of all the prophets was glorified by so great a miracle, or foreshadowed Christ’s death and resurrection by so marvelous an example?

Therefore, what Jonah did in fleeing from the face of the Lord, not very blameworthily, the manifest reality in some fashion indicates that Christ the Lord did praiseworthily. For Christ did not flee through disobedience at any time, but for a time recoiled, in compassionate feeling, from the condemnation of his own people. Those tears which he shed, when he saw the city and wept over it, saying, “If you too had known” (Luke XIX), and the rest, are witnesses. That weeping, I say, testifies how truly he would have wished, in the affection of his humanity, to avert the judgment of his divinity which hung over his people [Col. 0404B].

For Christian faith knows, and ought to know, that in the one and same Christ, just as there are two natures, one of divinity and the other of humanity, so there were two wills or operations. The will of divinity was to abandon Judaea and hand Jerusalem over into the hands of its enemies. The will of humanity was that his nation, or the city of Jerusalem, should be delivered and should not suffer so miserable a destruction. The former will was just; the latter was compassionate. It was fitting for the will of divinity to take precedence, and for that of humanity to follow.

Thus, yielding obediently, when he had said, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVII), unwilling that his people should perish because of the crime of his death, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). And again: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (ibid.).

Jonah, then, commanded to preach in Nineveh, fled to Tarshish, that is, into the sea. For Tarshish is generally called “sea,” as in the passage: “In a violent spirit you will break the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. XLVII). But Christ was born, and, though God, became human, in order that he himself might be the expectation and Savior of the Gentiles. He delivered himself to the waves of the Jews, who, because of the repeated tempests of their seditions, might more than any nation be considered like the sea. Neither of them—neither Jonah nor Christ—begrudged salvation to the Gentiles; but each grieved that condemnation was impending over his own nation.

“And he went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish; and he paid its fare and went down into it, that he might go with them to Tarshish from the face of the Lord.” We read in the books of Kings (III Kings II) and Chronicles (II Chron. II) that Joppa is a port of Judaea, to which Hiram, king of Tyre, transported rafts of timber from Lebanon, to be conveyed to Jerusalem by land. In accordance with the character of the region, coming from mountains and heights to Joppa and the plain, he is rightly said to have gone down. The haste of the fugitive and fearful man should be observed: he did not idly choose a place of flight; for he did not desire to flee to a fixed destination, but seized the first opportunity of sailing, hastening to go anywhere whatever.

According to this likeness, our Lord, entering the synagogue once beautiful—for the name Joppa means “beautiful”—established for himself a ship, that is, the school of evangelical preaching [Col. 0405A]. The twelve apostles were the rowers of that little ship. To them he gave the fare, that is, the gifts of graces: namely, power and authority over all demons and to heal infirmities (Luke IX); and he promised the kingdom of heaven, so that, entering the sea—that is, the restless people of the Jews—they might row vigorously by going about through cities and villages and preaching the Gospel.

The fact also beautifully alludes to this mystery that he called most of those to whom he gave such fare from their boats. For they were fishermen, and he called them so that, changing their oarage, he might make fishers of human beings out of fishers of fish.

Therefore, while the passible and weak flesh had not yet obediently become strong, because it delayed to carry out the will of divinity concerning the rejection of Judaea and the reception of the Gentiles, and, as has been said, wept over the city about to fall (Luke XIX), “he learned obedience,” says the Apostle, “from the things which he suffered” (Heb. V). For, perfected through suffering, he became such that he would obey strongly, and thereafter could extend sorrow or compassion only to those who repent; since, though before his passion he wept over the impenitent, he now sees the wicked burning in hell with dry eyes.

The present history mystically prefigured what he would suffer, and how he would learn obedience from the things that he suffered. “But the Lord sent a great wind upon the sea, and a great tempest arose in the sea, and the ship was in danger of being broken apart [Col. 0405C]. And the sailors were afraid and cried out to God; and they threw the articles that were in the ship into the sea, that it might be lightened of them. And Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship and slept a heavy sleep.”

As regards the historical account, both the omnipotence of the Lord, against whom nothing is secure, and the sailors’ fearfulness and the prophet’s greatness of soul are described. He is troubled neither by the storm nor by danger, retaining the same disposition in calm weather and in impending shipwreck. In short, the others cry to their gods, throw out their goods, and each strives to do what he can; but Jonah is so quiet, secure, and tranquil in mind that he goes down into the inner part of the ship and enjoys peaceful sleep.

Yet his sleep was not due to security but to sorrow. For we also read that the apostles, in the Lord’s passion, were overcome by sleep because of the greatness of their grief (Matt. XXVI). According to the mystery undertaken, however, the disturbance of the sea, or the greatness of the storm and the ship’s danger, are the Jewish seditions and persecutions, and all the Lord’s sufferings. The sailors’ fear is the fear of the apostles; Jonah’s sleep is the great tranquillity of divine patience in Christ, by which the strength of majesty, restraining itself, delayed to rescue his humanity and his disciples from dangers.

To consider this more fully, it is pleasant to recall at the same time that our Lord God himself once boarded a little ship in his own person, his disciples followed him, a great commotion arose in the sea, the disciples were afraid, and he himself slept (Matt. VIII). Both here and there, the movement of the sea signified the force of persecution and the sleep the silence of his patience. Unable to bear it, in our tribulation we say: “Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII). Elsewhere too, when a little ship was likewise being tossed by waves, we read that he came to the disciples walking upon the sea (Matt. XIV), signifying by that miracle that he would powerfully overcome those same sufferings. Now let us proceed with the matter according to the order of the letter.

“The Lord,” he says, “sent a great wind upon the sea, and a great tempest arose in the sea.” What was that wind which stirred up the crowds of the Jews as though they were a sea, except the spirit of deception which incited them to hatred of our Lord? It blew upon them inwardly, so that they raged against him and disturbed themselves with seditions [Col. 0406B].

But how did the Lord send such a wind? By just judgment, certainly, because he knew that they had always resisted his Holy Spirit. Did he not for the same reason send a lying spirit to deceive Ahab, king of Israel? For he said: “Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up to Ramoth-gilead?” One said words of this kind, and another said differently. Then a spirit came forth and stood before the Lord, and said: “I will deceive him.” The Lord said to him: “How?” And he said: “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said: “You will deceive him and prevail. Go forth and do so” (III Kings XXII).

As he then sent a lying spirit to deceive Ahab, who with his wife Jezebel had killed the prophets of the Lord, so he sent an evil spirit by which the Jews were stirred up, as the sea is accustomed to be moved by the wind, so that they might rage against the Lord and fill up the measure of their fathers.

Someone may say: Did the Lord, then, make the Jews so evil, or did he will them to be so evil that they should kill Christ, the Son of God? Certainly he did not make them evil or will them to be evil; but since they were evil, he permitted them the opportunity to complete their wickedness. The same must be understood concerning Pharaoh. God did not make him evil; but, since he was evil, he raised him up as king, in order to show his power in him (Exod. IX): that is, to give through a known person an example of how well he could cast down human pride.

Thus, to one who asks why God raised Pharaoh, although he was evil, to be king, the right answer is: “In order to show his power in him.” So likewise, to one who asks why he permitted the Jews, though evil, to have power to kill Christ, the right answer is: In their crime he might bring his wrath to its end, taking vengeance upon the human race in Christ, upon whom he had placed the iniquities of us all (Isa. LIII).

Therefore the great wind which the Lord sent into that sea—that bitter people of deep wickedness—was the unclean spirit of whom Christ spoke in the very passage where, replying to those who tested him and asked for a sign, he said that no sign would be given them except the sign of this Jonah, and added these words: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it wanders through waterless places, seeking rest and finding none; then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came’” (Luke XI [Col. 0407A]).

For the spirit had gone out of that people when it received the Law on Mount Sinai (Exod. XX); it returned when, seeing the Son of God cast out demons, that people blasphemed, saying: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. XII). Therefore he then said: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a person,” and so forth. That return in which it said, “I will return to my house from which I came,” was a sending by the Lord like the sending mentioned above, at the place and time when the lying spirit said, “I will deceive Ahab in this way” (III Kings XXII), and the Lord answered: “You will deceive him and prevail. Go forth and do so” (ibid.).

In the same way, I say, when it said, “I will return to my house from which I came, and I will make its last state worse than the first” (Matt. XII [Col. 0407B]), the Lord, the just judge, said: “You shall return and prevail,” or, “Return, and do so.” For because they did not receive the truth of the flesh so as to be saved, he sent that kind of wind into that sea; therefore God sent, and will send, them an operation of error, as the Apostle says, so that they may believe a lie, and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity (II Thess. II).

“And,” he says, “a great tempest arose in the sea, and the ship was in danger of being broken apart.” A great tempest arose in the sea because of Jonah’s voyage. A great disturbance arose among the Jewish people because of Christ’s preaching. Hence comes that accusation by those who made a tumult and said: “He has stirred up the people, teaching throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee even to this place” (Luke XXIII [Col. 0407C]). The ship was in danger of being broken apart, and the sailors were afraid. Evangelical teaching was often assailed by opponents and blasphemers, and the apostles were afraid.

Those sailors, not yet knowing the true God, cried out to their god; but the apostles, in that very danger, confessed Christ the Son of God amid Jewish blasphemies. Meanwhile the same sailors threw into the sea the goods that were in the ship, in order that it might be lightened of them; that is, they neglected, despised, and cast away all things that can be possessed or desired in this world, so as to be freer and more unencumbered, according to the counsel which says: “Do not carry a purse, nor a bag, nor sandals; nor have two tunics” (Luke X [Col. 0407D]).

But he himself slept, because, though omnipotent, he restrained his omnipotence and did not avenge the injuries of the Jewish tempest. It follows: “And Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship and slept a heavy sleep.” How could he have slept peacefully amid such great disturbance unless this happened to him figuratively, and he was made to sleep by God’s ordering? For, as has already been said, it was to come to pass that, amid Jewish tempests, our Lord, though the most mighty God, would bear himself with great patience—which is, in a sense, to sleep.

That sleep is rightly called heavy, because it was heavy to the apostles, and is heavy to us, that he who is the guardian of Israel (Ps. XII) should sleep amid adversities, while he does not more quickly restrain both the blasphemies brought against his name and the afflictions which his disciples endure in this world [Col. 0408A].

“And the captain came to him and said: ‘Why are you oppressed by sleep? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps God will take thought for us and we shall not perish.’” Since it is natural for each person, in his own danger, to hope more from another, the captain, who ought to have consoled the frightened passengers, saw the magnitude of the danger, woke the sleeper, reproached him for careless security, and urged him also to entreat his God according to the share of strength allotted to him.

Here he is a type of the apostle Peter. For when the Lord said: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI), and again: “But whom do you say that I am?” (ibid.), Peter answered before the others, or first among them: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.). By this merit he stands out among the other apostles in the Church as the captain, or helmsman, stands out among the other sailors in the little ship.

But when the Lord had designated him thus, saying, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah” (ibid.), and immediately began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise on the third day, Peter took him and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; be gracious to yourself; this shall not happen to you” (ibid.). In saying this, he was indeed rebuking the Lord, as a captain rebukes Jonah for sleeping, because he forbade the Lord to suffer; he urged him to turn matters by his own power, as though awake, as the powerful and most mighty Son of God [Col. 0408C].

It follows: “And each man said to his companion: ‘Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us.’ And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.” They knew the nature of the sea, and having sailed for so long, they knew the character of storms and winds. Certainly, if they had seen the ordinary waves rise—the waves which they had sometimes experienced—they would not seek through a lot the author of the shipwreck, nor desire by an uncertain means to avoid a certain danger.

We ought not immediately, under this example, to put faith in lots, or join to this testimony that passage from the Acts of the Apostles in which Matthias is chosen to the apostolate by lot (Acts I), since the privileges of individuals cannot make a universal law. But according to the moral interpretation undertaken, whenever a storm of worldly waves rises against Christ’s little ship and Christ’s disciples, such a lot must be cast in such a manner that each person may know on whose account that evil has come, or what is the cause for which he suffers.

For it can happen, in persecution for the Christian name, that not Christ himself but something else, stored up in one’s intention or conscience, is the reason why someone called a Christian suffers and is tossed amid surging adversities. If this were not so, Paul would never say: “Even if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII). It can also happen that one who believes in Christ suffers something at the hands of an unbeliever because of his own evil deed. Hence Peter says: “It is better to suffer while doing good, if the will of God so wills, than while doing evil” (I Pet. III [Col. 0409A]). Again: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer, or coveter of others’ property” (I Pet. IV).

Blessed is that conscience in which a person has the testimony that he suffers as a Christian, and that Christ is for him the cause of suffering or passion. Then the lot truly falls upon Christ, as it fell upon Jonah: he himself is the cause of the raging waves. The holy apostles have such a conscience among stormy Jews. For example, when Thomas said to his fellow disciples: “Let us also go and die with him” (John XI).

“And they said to him: ‘Tell us, on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your work? What is your land? Where are you going? Or from what people are you?’” The brevity of these words should be noted, such as is admired in the distinguished poet: “Young men, what cause compelled you to attempt unknown ways? Where are you bound? What is your race? From what home? Do you bring peace here, or arms?” The person, region, journey, and city are asked about, that from these the cause of the danger might be known. “Tell us,” they say, “on whose account this evil has come upon us: what work do you do? From what land, from what people do you come, and where do you hasten to go?”

Our Lord was questioned about these matters not only by his own sailors, that is, his apostles, in private inquiries, that they might know; his adversaries also questioned him about them in public tumults, that they might see who he was, what work he did, where he came from, and where he was tending. For when he said to them, “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sin,” they said to him: “Who are you?” (John VIII [Col. 0409C]). Again, when he said, “I am with you a little while longer, and I go to him who sent me. You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come,” they said among themselves: “Where is this man about to go, that we shall not find him? Is he about to go into the Dispersion among the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?” (John VII).

They also insolently asked about his origin, when he said, “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me,” and they said: “Where is your father?” (John VIII). Likewise they asked what his work was. When he said, “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent,” they said: “What sign, then, do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?” (John VI). Pilate too, having heard them say, “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God,” entered the praetorium again and said to him: “Where are you from?” (John XIX [Col. 0409D]). Yet he had previously asked and heard that, under Herod’s jurisdiction, he was a Galilean—that is, a man [Luke XXIII].

If, therefore, those whom we mystically understand by the swelling waves of the sea questioned him as to who he was, what his work was, what his land was, where he was going or was about to go, how much more surely did his familiar apostles ask these things—those who labored with him in the rowing or voyage of the Gospel, and to whom, as the Gospel relates, he spoke privately concerning the kingdom of God (Luke XI).

It follows: “And he said to them: ‘I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord God, who made sea and dry land.’” It belongs greatly to the mystery that he did not say, “I am a Jew” or “an Israelite”—names, namely “Jews” and “Israelites,” which discord had divided, after Jeroboam severed the ten tribes from the house of David (III Kings XII)—but said: “I am a Hebrew.”

*Hebrew* means “one who passes over.” This name is very fitting for Christ, who did not come into this world to remain or to reign, but to pass through as a traveler, having here no abiding city or kingdom; so that he might pass through and, in passing, perform the work of salvation. Of himself, as though of another, he says: “And, passing through, he will minister to them” (Luke XII). And the Evangelist says: “Knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII).

Then he says: “And I fear the Lord God of heaven.” This too accords with his humanity, because he is the one concerning whom the prophet foretold: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI). Truly he was filled with holy fear and most reverent, with that fear which ought rightly to be called and regarded as humility. He himself professes to be the teacher of this fear, that is, of humility, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

It should also be noted in the prophet that he did not say, “I flee the Lord God of heaven,” but, “I fear him.” For although he had fled from the face of the Lord, he had by no means fled from God, nor wished to flee from him. For it is one thing to flee the Lord, and another to flee from the face of the Lord. To wish to flee the Lord is always evil, and especially belongs to those who hate him, though they cannot escape him, as it is written: “May your right hand find all who hate you” [Col. 0410C] (Ps. 20). But one who loves God may sometimes flee from the face of the Lord—that is, shrink from the judgment or fearful purpose of God—as did this man, who shrank from exercising the prophetic office to the condemnation of his own people. But why, at such a moment, did he say, “who made the sea and the dry land,” especially he who, fleeing from the face of the Lord, had gone into the sea, leaving the dry land, unless to show that in reason he held a sure faith or knowledge of the Creator’s omnipotence, although in the affection of the flesh, fleeing from it, he had attempted to avoid the wrath impending over his people because of their deserts?

So also our Lord, undoubtedly possessing a rational soul, knew according to that reason that the judgment of the divinity inherent in him was just—the judgment [Col. 0410D] which decreed that the Gentiles should be saved and Judaea abandoned—although, in the affection of his humanity, he delayed the Gentiles and was zealous for Judaea, so that he wept over her (Luke 19). And Jonah indeed, surrounded by waves and overtaken by that storm, says: “I fear the Lord God.” But Christ himself, “learning obedience through the things which he suffered” (Heb. 5), says: “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14); and immediately adds, “Arise, let us go” (ibid.), which was the same as if he had said—for he was always intent upon heavenly mysteries—“Since such is the Father’s will, leaving Judaea, let us pass over to the Gentiles.”

“And the men feared with a great fear, and said to him: ‘What have you done?’ For they knew that he fled from the face of the Lord, because Jonah had told them” [Col. 0411A]. The order of the narrative is inverted. For since it might have been said that there was no cause for fear in his confession, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land,” it immediately gives the reason why they feared: because he had told them that he was fleeing the Lord’s presence and had not done his commands. Thus they say, “What have you done?” that is: “If you fear the Lord, why do you flee? If you proclaim such power in him whom you worship, how do you think that you can escape him?”

Likewise Christ’s apostles did not have cause to fear merely because he said who he was, but because he also told them that he had come to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt. 20)—as though he had fled from the face of the Lord. He himself, in his own person, never did this disobediently, as has already been said [Col. 0411B] above; but those did it whose sins he bore upon himself, for whom he had to suffer or die. For when Adam and his wife heard the voice of the Lord God walking in Paradise in the afternoon breeze, “they hid themselves from the face of the Lord God amid the trees of Paradise” (Gen. 3). “In Adam,” says the Apostle, “all sinned” (Rom. 5); and therefore you rightly say that all hid themselves from the face of the Lord in him. Christ, however, did not sin in his soul or hide himself; but, as has been said, he bore upon himself the sins of those who sinned in him and hid themselves in him from the face of the Lord.

He told his apostles that he himself had to die and give his life as a ransom for them; and therefore [Col. 0411C] they feared, both for themselves and for him, because, being still weak, they were not prepared to die for him.

It follows, therefore: “And they said to him: ‘What shall we do to you, so that the sea may cease from us?’ For the sea went on and swelled. And he said to them: ‘Take me and cast me into the sea, and the sea will cease from you. For I know that this great storm is upon you because of me.’ And the men rowed, that they might return to the dry land, but they could not, because the sea went on and swelled over them.”

According to this likeness of the sailors, fearing thus and speaking such words, who does not see that the apostles acted and spoke devoutly when “the sea went on and swelled over them”—that is, when the implacably seditious crowd, seeking the Lord, surrounded them? [Col. 0411D] “Seeing what was about to happen,” Luke says, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” And one of them struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear (Luke 22), namely Peter, whose likeness we understand in the helmsman. But Jesus answered and said, “Allow this far” (ibid.). And in another Evangelist: “Put your sword back into its place. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled?” (Matt. 26). But a little earlier he had said: “Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you will be scattered, each to his own, and will leave me alone” (John 16).

Certainly these and other like sayings resemble the saying which Jonah here uttered with wonderful grandeur: “Take [Col. 0412A] me and cast me into the sea, and the sea will cease from you.” But they rowed in order to return to dry land; for they had also begun to strike with the sword, as has already been said, that together with the Lord himself they might escape that crowd. Yet they could not, because the sea went on and swelled over them. For those pursuing them were stronger than the few, especially since he for whose sake the great storm had arisen was voluntarily offering himself to suffering, because his passion or death was necessary for the world.

“And they cried to the Lord and said: ‘We beseech you, Lord, let us not perish for the life of this man; and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for you, O Lord, have done as you pleased.’ And they took Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the sea stood still from its raging. And the men feared with a great fear, and offered sacrifices [Col. 0412B] to the Lord, and made vows.”

This cry of the sailors is the grief, mourning, and weeping of the disciples when they were obliged to take Jonah and cast him into the sea. Then they cried out, because, when all things had been accomplished and they received his body by permission and buried it, they uttered the voices of their sorrow: first the centurion, as the Gospel relates, saying, “Truly this man was righteous,” and, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27; Luke 23); and all his sailors, who stood afar off, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, and all their crowd, who returned beating their breasts (Luke 23), said in some manner: “We beseech you, Lord, let us not perish for the life of this man,” and so forth.

Moreover, in that all the disciples fled after leaving him (Matt. 26), [Col. 0412C] they cast the Lord into the sea: they dismissed him, they left him alone. Their thus abandoning him belonged to weakness; their burying him belonged to duty. Whichever way you understand the fulfillment, the sailors who laboured as much as they could and rowed with all their strength had already provided a fitting likeness of these men, namely the apostles. And because they achieved nothing, at last, sorrowing and groaning, they cast the prophet into the sea.

The sea indeed ceased from its raging; but the men “feared with a great fear”: that is, the Jews, sated with their crime, ceased persecuting the disciples. But the apostles were in the greatest grief for their teacher and Lord. “And they offered sacrifices to the Lord,” it says, “and made a vow.” [Col. 0412D] The apostles offered sacrifices: sacrifices of penitence and confession with mourning and tears; and they themselves became living sacrifices, especially Peter, who offered a sacrifice by weeping over his denial of him. James, the Lord’s own brother, offered a sacrifice in that Gospel which is written “According to the Hebrews,” when he is reported to have vowed that he would not eat bread until he had first seen him risen from the dead.

## Chapter II

“And the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights.”

This fish, or the belly of this fish, signifies, according to the Lord’s own authority, the heart of the earth—that is, the tomb. For he said: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three [Col. 0413A] nights” (Matt. 12). Therefore, although Jonah himself says in his prayer, “Out of the belly of hell I cried, and you heard my voice,” we understand from this, and must understand, that the fish’s belly signifies not hell, into which the soul descends, but the tomb, in which the body was laid.

But if someone insists that “the heart of the earth” should be understood as hell, because the depths or lower parts of the earth are believed to lie below—as is written of Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed: “They went down alive into hell” (Num. 16), covered by earth—let him answer how the Lord’s soul is to be believed to have been in hell for three days and three nights, when immediately, on that very day on which it departed from the body, having shattered hell, it entered Paradise, according to what he said to the confessing thief: [Col. 0413B] “Amen, I say to you: Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23).

Therefore the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah: that is, he provided that the Lord’s body should have a burial prepared in the earth, which, with its great belly, receives all dying human beings. How or when did he prepare it? Certainly, he prepared it by inspiring righteous Joseph to bury him. But there is another, more splendid preparation in which one may admire the preparation of this matter: namely, the decree or authority of the holy and mystical Law.

“When a man has committed a sin worthy of death and, having been condemned to death, is hanged upon a gibbet, his corpse shall not remain upon the wood, but you shall bury it on that same day, because he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God; and you shall not defile your land [Col. 0413C] which the Lord your God has given you as a possession” (Deut. 21).

[Col. 0413D] We cannot sufficiently admire the providence of God in making such a decree. For by this decree of the Law the scribes and Pharisees were wonderfully deceived in their malice: they thought that our Lord, truly and uniquely blessed, was made accursed by this kind of death; and they were caught, so that, willing or unwilling, he whom they had pursued with insatiable hatred could not lack burial. They were deceived, I say, because when they read, “He who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God,” they did not attend to what preceded: “When a man has committed a sin worthy of death.” For by placing this first, the sacred and just Law establishes that the accursedness arises not from the punishment but from the cause or guilt. They, however, wished it to be thought that such a punishment made one accursed.

But what cause or purpose required God to provide burial in this manner for his Son Jesus Christ? Surely this: that, just as his soul, descending to the lower regions, might deliver the souls of all the elect, so his body, buried in the earth and joined to bodies through burial, might bring them the grace of resurrection, rising first so that the other bodies might follow, as will come to pass. Therefore, by a great and venerable design, the law concerning the burial of all who had been crucified was given in the words stated above, so that, while all were buried, one crucified man should not lack burial.

“But you shall bury him on the same day.” For what reason? “Because,” it says, “he who hangs upon the wood is accursed [Col. 0414A] by God.” The declaration of accursedness indeed sounds harsh: that he who came “blessed in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21) should be called accursed by the prescription of the Law. But if you rightly consider what has been added—“by God”—a great sweetness lies hidden in the harsh expression. For it is very different to be accursed by God and to be accursed by one’s own sin. For all who are accursed in condemnation are not accursed by God, though God himself has sometimes foretold them to be accursed, as with Cain, to whom he said: “Now therefore you shall be accursed upon the earth” (Gen. 4); but he did not say, “You are accursed by me, as I accursed you.” The accursedness of such persons is their own sin; and sin is not from God.

Our one and only Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, was accursed by God, because he bore upon himself the accursed things—that is, the sins—of us all, and this from God. For Isaiah says: “The Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all” (Isa. 53). Why then, it may be asked, do we have this in the Apostle’s reading? “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon the wood’” (Gal. 3). Where he recalls this as written, the word “everyone” does not occur; and conversely, where the former text has “by God,” you do not find it in the Apostle.

But it should be known that he cited the testimony not according to the Hebrew truth, but according to the then current Greek translation of the Seventy Interpreters, the Vulgate; and this necessarily, because it would have been altogether inopportune, when he was beginning from the Scriptures to commend God’s truth to Greeks [Col. 0414C], to demonstrate that something in the Scriptures then required correction—and likewise to commend the grace of Christ, who, in order to give blessing among the Gentiles, endured the repute of accursedness among Jews who misunderstood the decrees of the good and holy Law.

“Therefore,” it says, “you shall bury him on the same day, and you shall not defile your land which the Lord your God gave you as a possession.” What is that land which the Lord God gave us as a possession, if not Christ’s flesh, which, as has already been said, the authoring Spirit of the holy Law ensured should be buried? For how could the earth which we tread be defiled more by one who had been buried and received into its bosom than by the crucified corpse in its tomb? Rather, that body is defiled—that is, because of its own defilement and uncleanness it is cast away—which deservedly comes to be denied burial, as it was said of a certain man, in part as a punishment: “He shall be buried with the burial of an ass” (Jer. 22).

[Col. 0414D] These matters have been said at greater length in order that we might show the burial prepared for our Lord by the authority of the Law, according to that mystical or figurative preparation of which it is said: “And the Lord prepared a great fish to devour Jonah.” That preparation, namely the decree of the Law, made way for the other preparation, of which Joseph, a righteous man, deserved to be the minister. Of this preparation the Gospels thus report: “Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid” (John 19).

“And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.” The question is how, according to this type, the Lord was in the heart of the earth three days and three nights, when, having yielded up his spirit at the ninth hour on the day of Preparation, he was buried and rose at midnight at the beginning of the first day of the week. To this the same answer must be given that has already been given by the holy Fathers: we understand the whole from the part, so that from his death on the Preparation we count one day [Col. 0415A] and night, the second day as the Sabbath, and the third night, assigned to the Lord’s Day, as belonging to the beginning of the other day. Nor is it unfitting, according to the trope called synecdoche, to understand the whole from the part in such a matter.

For while still mortal and living among mortals, he said: “And now I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world, and I come to you. While I was with them, I kept them in your name” (John 17). Whatever reason you give or understand for which he truthfully said that he was no longer in the world, for that same reason you consequently understand that he was already in the belly of the whale.

Now the evening or night preceding the day on which he was crucified, died, and was buried had already come. Therefore the whole day of the Preparation, together with the night that went before, is rightly reckoned as belonging to the burial. For from that evening or hour in which, being in agony or struggling with death, he was betrayed and seized, whatever was done to him or around him, whatever he suffered, was a descent into the fish’s belly, a going into the heart of the earth—especially since those who had set their minds not on heaven but on earth were acting upon him according to their own heart, and would not cease until he had been killed and delivered to the earth.

Concerning the Sabbath and the night before it [Col. 0415C], there is no question that he rested in the tomb throughout that entire day. He rose at midnight of the third day, but it was not believed that he had risen until the evening of that same third day, when, standing in the midst of his disciples, he said to them: “Peace be with you” (John 20). Therefore that day too is counted with the other two, so that there are three days; and what Truth himself said of himself is true: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12).

Here it is also pleasing not to pass over this point: if you calculate from the hour when he gave up the spirit to the hour when he rose, that is, to midnight, you will find that the sacred and venerable number three shines out both in the quantity of hours and in the number of days [Col. 0415D]. For he gave up the spirit at the ninth hour, and three hours of that day remained. These, joined to the twenty-four hours of the following night and day and to the six hours until midnight of the night on which he rose, make thirty-three hours: a number containing two threes, one in the tens place and the other in the units.

Likewise in years the same number must be considered, for the year in which he suffered was his thirty-third year: he was baptized in the thirtieth year of his age and suffered in the third year of his preaching. What does such, or so great, an observance of the number three mean in the dispensation of his holy humanity? For thirty years—which number, as has been said, is three tens—[Col. 0416A] he lived in concealment, and in the third year of his preaching he suffered; for thirty-three hours he lay lifeless, and on the third day he rose.

We venerate this observance of times, not doubting that a worthy mystery lies within it. Although we cannot comprehend it all as it is, this at least occurs to us, in which we take no small delight: namely, that this second Adam offered himself to make satisfaction for us to the Holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—whom the first Adam had offended. For the first Adam, made with the cooperation and, in some manner, the reverently bestowed care of the omnipotence of the whole Trinity for its own glory, according to the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1; the citation reads “Gen. III”), offended in such a way as to despise the likeness set before him by God [Col. 0416B], losing faith, forfeiting hope, and lacking charity.

For he lost faith who believed the serpent rather than God: he gave more heed to the serpent saying, “You shall not die by death,” than to God saying, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (ibid.). He lost hope who, conscious of sin, fled into hiding in order to conceal himself from the face of the Lord. He did not possess charity, for he repelled by proud self-defence the God who sought and reproved him. Thus the former offended the Holy Trinity and lost God’s likeness; but the latter had come for this purpose, and had been born human for this purpose: that the humanity assumed by God might appease the Holy Trinity for humankind and restore the likeness in human beings. It is therefore pleasing that, in making satisfaction to the divinity, he observed the number three in all the matters stated above.

[Col. 0416C] Add also this most beautiful point: our same Lord was brought to completion by three sufferings—scourged, crucified, pierced with a lance—and, between two thieves, he himself was the third, exchanged for the thief Barabbas. Rightly, therefore, the appeased Trinity at once began to reveal its face to the human race, bringing out of the region of darkness all who, having faith in the One who was to come, had departed this life; and it willed that we who remained should be preached to, so that we might be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Now let us proceed with the remaining matters. “And Jonah prayed from the belly of the fish to the Lord his God, and said: ‘I cried to the Lord out of my tribulation, and he heard me.’” The statement, “And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly [Col. 0416D] of the fish, and said,” means that, after he perceived himself safe in the fish’s belly, he did not despair of the Lord’s mercy, but turned wholly to supplication. For God, who said of the righteous, “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90), and, “When he calls upon me, I shall say to him: ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58), was present with him. And he may say, because he was heard: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4).

“And Jonah prayed.” If Jonah is a type of the Lord, and by being in the whale’s belly three days and three nights signifies his passion, then Jonah’s prayer also ought to be a type of the Lord’s prayer. Therefore let us consider this prayer first according to Jonah himself, and then according to the person of the Saviour.

[Col. 0417A] “I cried to the Lord out of my tribulation, and he heard me. Out of the belly of hell I cried, and you heard my voice.” He did not say, “I cry,” but, “I cried”; nor does he pray about the future, but gives thanks for the past, indicating that when he had been cast into the sea and saw the whale, the huge bulk of its body, and its enormous jaws swallowing him with open mouth, he remembered the Lord and cried out—whether as the waters gave way and his cry found room, or with the whole affection of his heart, which is assuredly a great cry in God’s ears. He cried to him who alone knows human hearts, who says to Moses, “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14), although Scripture recalls that before this utterance Moses had cried out nothing. The Apostle also speaks of this cry of the heart: “Crying in your hearts, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8).

By “the belly of hell” he means the whale’s belly because of its vastness. “And you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the sea, and a flood surrounded me.” The sense of the conjunction by which he says, “and you cast me,” is this: “When I cried, you heard my voice; and though you heard, you nevertheless cast me into the deep”—understand: “in order that you might deliver me [Col. 0417B] for the greater glory of your power, because I shall again see your holy temple.”

“You cast me into the deep,” and not merely into the deep, which might have been near the shores or not far from dry land, but “into the heart of the sea,” that is, into the midst of the sea. For an animal’s heart is in the middle; accordingly, by metaphor, “the heart of the sea” means the middle of the sea. “And a flood,” he says, “surrounded me”: that is, the inundation of the sea, flowing and ebbing, enclosed me on every side. Repeating the same thought, he says: “All your whirlpools and your waves passed over me.”

[Col. 0417C] And I call them your whirlpools and your waves not merely because you made them, as I said above, “I fear the Lord God who made the sea and the dry land,” but also because you set them in motion because of me and commanded them to swell over me. “And I said: ‘I am cast away from the sight of your eyes; nevertheless, I shall again see your holy temple.’” It should be noted that he asserts not that he then first speaks, but that he had said: “I am cast away from the sight of your eyes; nevertheless, I shall again see your holy temple.” It is clear, therefore, that when he was being cast into the sea, amid that tribulation, according to the multitude of his sorrows, the Lord’s consolations made his soul glad; prophetic grace was poured into him more abundantly and mercifully, so that he might know that from such profound rejection he would yet be wonderfully raised, [Col. 0417D] and, still living among the living, would come to the Lord’s temple with sacrifices and offerings, returning fitting thanks to the wondrous God.

That he asserts himself to have said this then, he confirms in the whale’s belly in these words: “The waters surrounded me even to my soul; the abyss enclosed me; the sea covered my head. I descended to the extremities of the mountains; the bars of the earth shut me in for ever. And you will raise my life from corruption, O Lord my God.” By all these declarations, in which he truthfully affirms a most true matter—“The waters surrounded me even to my soul; the abyss enclosed me; the sea covered my head. I descended to the extremities of the mountains; [Col. 0418A] the bars of the earth shut me in”—by adding to all these declarations, “And you will raise my life from corruption,” he fittingly gives glory to the most high God, fully knowing and faithfully asserting that he is able to do whatever he wills (Rom. 4), and that with him what was eternally impossible for human beings is possible (Luke 18).

For, because of human impossibility, when he had said, “The bars of the earth surrounded me,” he added, “for ever”; and because of God’s possibility, he added: “And you will raise my life from corruption,” adding at the same time, with the affection of one who lovingly entreats: “O Lord my God.” By the corruption from which he hopes his soul will be raised, he means the whale’s belly, in which shipwrecks were driven; and that a human being could be preserved among them is a great glory of divine omnipotence. [Col. 0418B]

Such also is the case of the three children cast into the furnace of blazing fire, who remained so unharmed that not even the smell of fire touched their garments, and many other things done above nature by the Lord of nature (Dan. 3). How sweet and salutary it is for one who, after the tranquillity of a continent life, falls into the waves of temptations and perhaps suffers shipwreck of chastity, falling into the work of sin as into the jaws or belly of a whale, to remember this prophetic prayer. With the same faith, similar contrition of heart, and such humble affection of piety, let that person lovingly entreat the Lord his God, who alone sees the waters surrounding and penetrating even to the soul: the waters of carnal passions and the abyss of the human heart, the sea of desire, the force of raging and [Col. 0418C] boiling nature, and the straits of the soul or conscience. Being weak, it cannot of itself escape in order to breathe and recover the health-giving air of chastity and purity, shut in by desires or perverse loves as by certain bars of earth.

It follows: “When my soul was distressed within me, I remembered the Lord, that my prayer might come to you, to your holy temple.”

This, which we have already said above, is here plainly confirmed: namely, that at the very hour or moment when he was cast into the sea, inspired by the grace of the prophetic Spirit, he said: “I am cast away from before your eyes; yet I shall again behold your holy temple.” For this is what he now says: “When my soul was distressed within me, I remembered the Lord, that my prayer might come to you, to your holy temple” [Col. 0418D]. We should observe that, in an unusual manner, a prayer is made for a prayer, while he prays that his prayer may ascend to God’s temple. And in this the steadfastness of great faith is to be noticed. Surrounded by waters, hemmed in by the deep, covered by the sea, shut in by the bars of the earth, he neither doubts nor asks whether God can hear his prayer, whether His ear can be present there, and hear from the belly of the whale what is said to Him; but, holding it certain within himself that nothing can be hidden anywhere, he faithfully prays that God Himself may make a way for the prayer striving to break forth to Him through such great and profound straits, and Himself receive it as it comes.

This great faith possesses great merit; it is honourable before God, because it is taught, or instructed, and possesses holy knowledge [Col. 0419A]. For what is this? Does not faithful prayer proceed from the root of the good Word? But where is the Word rooted, or from where is it born, except from the heart of God the Father, who, as the Catholic faith firmly maintains, is the begetter of the good Word, the eternal Word, which is itself God? Wherever, therefore, a man may be confined, or wherever the spirit of a man may be straitened—whether by the bars of hell or of earth—if he has within himself the word of faith, then while he prays it cannot be unknown; indeed, by that very word of faith he powerfully touches the bowels of God, the heart of the most high Father, whence the good Word has its origin.

Let us therefore take from the words, “When my soul was distressed within me, I remembered the Lord,” this instruction: that we may know that at the time when our soul fails and is torn away from the frame of the body, we ought to turn our thought nowhere else except to Him who is our Lord both in the body and beside the body. Thus our prayer will reach His holy temple, the very height of heaven, whose immensity is His great house and holy temple [Col. 0419B]. Those can do this—those can have or retain this faith at that moment of death—who, while living in the body, have loved the truth. Conversely, those who love falsehood, choked in that hour by the greatness of terror, cannot find the good Word.

Hence there immediately follows: “Those who keep vanity vainly forsake their mercy.” He did not say, “those who practise vanities.” For “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1), lest he seem to condemn everyone and deny mercy to the whole human race; but rather, those who keep vanities or falsehood—those “who have passed into the affection of the heart” (Ps. 72)—who not only practise vanities but keep them as though they loved them and thought they had found a treasure. “They forsake,” he says, “their mercy.” Although mercy may be offended—by which we may understand God Himself: for the Psalmist says, “My God is my mercy” (Ps. 58)—yet He does not forsake or reject those who keep vanities, but waits for them to return. They, however, of their own accord forsake mercy that stands ready and freely offers itself.

“But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of praise; whatever I have vowed, I will render to the Lord for my salvation.” The sense is this: But I, although I have committed vanity, do not keep it. Rather, I make a vow to You: a vow of amendment, a vow of obedience, and of going wherever You command [Col. 0419C–D]; and, by sacrificing this obedience to You with a voice of praise, I shall render these vows to the Lord for my salvation. For it was vanity that, when You commanded me to go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach there, I took the initiative to flee from Your presence to Tarshish. I feared that unrepentant Israel might be condemned if Nineveh repented; I preferred affection for my own nation to Your will. But I shall not keep this vanity—that is, I shall not persist in this purpose—having been warned by this present affliction that Your will must be followed more than the affections of the flesh.

Unhappy Israel, scourged by so many and such frequent evils, still keeps vanities by stubbornly worshipping the golden calves which Jeroboam, a craftsman of vanity, made [Col. 0420A]. At no time under any of its kings did it depart from its sins; and by doing this it forsook its mercy. But I, still pitying it, entertained the vain plan of fleeing from Your presence. Yet now, in this tribulation, I do not keep that vanity; I reject such an intention. If I did not do so, I would vainly forsake my mercy—vainly, I say, because I would gain no fruit from it, neither for Israel, a fugitive from its God, on whose account I fled from Your presence. Therefore may my mercy in turn not forsake me, since I do not forsake mercy—a mercy accustomed to forsake only those who forsake it, and to hide itself only from the impenitent.

“And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.” This is a great work and manifest testimony to the goodness and omnipotence of God, who inclined His ear even that far, heard and weighed what was occurring in the whale’s belly, what faith was saying, what prayer was undertaking, and spoke—and was able to speak—to the fish so that it vomited Jonah forth: and certainly not into the water, where he would be endangered, but onto dry land, where he would be saved [Col. 0420B]. He plainly spoke this not by moving lips, which He did not have, nor by an elemental voice, but by that Word through whom He made both the whale and the sea itself. Pressed by the power of that Word, the belly of the beast restored the prophet, in whatever manner and wherever that Word willed.
