Now, returning according to our purpose to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us reconsider this same prayer in relation to Him; for, as we have already said, this prayer of the prophet is a type of His prayer.

“I cried to the Lord from my tribulation, and He heard me” [Col. 0420C]. Let us first hear the Apostle speaking: “Who, in the days of His flesh, offered prayers and supplications with loud crying and tears to Him who was able to save Him from death, and was heard because of His reverence” (Heb. 5). Let Christ therefore say, “I cried,” because He truly cried with loud crying and tears. From where did He cry? “From my tribulation,” He says, “from the belly of hell.” He spoke of two things: tribulation and the belly of hell. His tribulation was the anguish of His Passion, from which He cried, as the Evangelist reports: having fallen upon His knees, being in agony, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood running down onto the ground (Luke 22). From that hour until, crying with a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit, He cried with a loud cry.

“The belly of hell” was His descent to the lower world, and the whole concealment or depression of His body while it lay in the tomb [Col. 0420D]. Certainly, what He cried from tribulation was heard at that time by human beings. For among the things heard from the mouth of Him crying, He said: “Heli, Heli, lama sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). And at the end of His tribulation, crying out, He said: “Father, into Your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23).

But what He cried from the belly of hell could not be heard by any mortal. Yet before He Himself came into this world, His Holy Spirit foretold in Holy Scripture what He would cry, just as He foretold the words which, as we have said, were heard while He cried: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Ps. 86), and “Father, into Your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30). Finally, that psalm, “Lord God of my salvation, by day I cried and at night before You. Let my prayer enter into Your presence” (Ps. 15), and so on to the end of that same psalm, consists of the words of His cry from the belly of hell, asking for the renowned glorification of the Resurrection, as the discerning reader undoubtedly perceives [Col. 0421A].

Therefore, He says: “From my tribulation I cried to the Lord”—understand, interceding for transgressors that they might not perish—“and He heard me”: namely, so that through my Passion the sin of Adam’s transgression might be loosed and all the sins of those who believe in me might be blotted out. “From the belly of hell I cried, and You heard my voice”—understand, so that You would not leave my soul in hell, nor give Your Holy One to see corruption (Ps. 88).

“And You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the sea, and the flood surrounded me. All Your whirlpools and Your waves passed over me.” The sense is this: In accordance with the truth of the matter, You heard me; but according to human estimation, You cast me away, in keeping with the psalm mentioned earlier: “I was reckoned with those who go down into the pit” (Ps. 87), and with the verse of another psalm: “But You have rejected and despised; You have delayed Your Christ” (Ps. 88) [Col. 0421B]. For this is how it appeared to those who, mocking and shaking their heads, said: “He trusted in God; let Him now deliver Him if He wishes” (Matt. 27).

Thus, according to their estimation, You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the sea—that is, into everything that the seditious Jews, like the sea, wished to do to me—and the flood surrounded me: namely, the overflowing tribulation with which they relentlessly afflicted me. All those whirlpools of Yours, all those waves which I endured, passed over me—that is, without doubt, they will pass away. For they will not remain but will quickly come to an end. Your whirlpools and Your waves fled, because it lay not in the power of those who afflicted me, but in Yours, how long their raging madness should flood over me [Col. 0421C].

“And I said: I am cast away from before Your eyes; yet I shall again behold Your holy temple.” As I have already said, “You cast me into the deep”; so now, repeating himself, He says: “And I said, I am cast away from before Your eyes”—understand, according to their estimation or according to the truth of the matter—“yet I shall again behold Your holy temple”: that is, I, the soul which descended to hell, shall again enter and resume my body, which is Your holy temple, according to the saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But, the Evangelist says, He spoke this “of the temple of His body” (John 2).

We see it fulfilled, we believe it, and therefore we speak it: Your whirlpools, O God—the whirlpools of mortality and the waves of every misery which You brought upon us on account of Adam’s transgression—passed over Him and came to an end. And He again beheld Your holy temple: that is, He resumed the body which is in the primary sense Your holy temple [Col. 0421D–0422A]. He is now in the midst of the Church, which is also called, in a secondary sense, Your holy temple; and now He sees that holy temple in joy, as He had said: “And I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 16).

But where, or in what place, did He say what He now recalls Himself as having said in the words, “And I said: I am cast away from before Your eyes”? The Psalmist, before this Jonah, in whom the same Christ speaks, foretold in His person: “But I said, in the excess of my mind: I am cast away from before Your eyes” (Ps. 30). For when He says, “I said in the excess of my mind,” it is the same as saying, “I foresaw in the depth of understanding which surpasses the intelligence of every creature”; and he adds: “Therefore You heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to You” (ibid.). This also was stated previously here: “From the belly of hell I cried, and You heard my voice,” or, “I cried to the Lord from my tribulation, and He heard me” [Col. 0422B].

Meanwhile it is very beautiful to consider how He likewise says elsewhere: “In the day of my tribulation I cried to You, for You heard me” (Ps. 85). Such a statement, “I cried to You because You heard me,” has greater force in meaning than if it had been said, “You heard me because I cried to You.” For all the saints were heard because they cried. But this Holy One of holy ones alone can truly say, “I cried because You heard me.” For He is the one chosen from among thousands, who alone came into this world to cry for all because He knew that He would be heard for His reverence.

Indicating this in the psalm, He speaks through the prophet’s mouth: “You did not require burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39) [Col. 0422C]. The sense is: When, therefore, I understood that You did not desire those sacrifices of brute animals, and that none of all the righteous could make full satisfaction for sin, then I said: “Behold, I come,” knowing without doubt that, when making satisfaction for all and crying out, You would hear me.

This is why, crying with a loud voice at Lazarus’s tomb, He does not pray that He may be heard; rather, He says: “Father, I thank You because You have heard me; and I knew that You always loved me, that You hear me” (John 11). In short, we must conclude that He alone is the one who says, “I cried to You because You heard me”; whereas any saint says, “Because I cried to You, You heard me.”

It follows [Col. 0422D]: “The waters surrounded me even to my soul; the deep enclosed me, and the sea covered my head; I went down to the extremities of the mountains; the bars of the earth shut me in for ever; and You will raise up my life from corruption, O Lord my God.” Since in the type of Christ His prophet both suffered and poured out prayer, it is most fitting to show each of these expressions as uttered according to the sequence of Christ’s Passion, as the course of the events of that Passion unfolded. “The waters,” he says, “surrounded me even to my soul.”

Undoubtedly, when the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council, saying, “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs,” and the rest; and from that day they planned to kill Him (John 11), then the waters surrounded Him even to His soul, because they had, as it were judicially, determined the sentence of His death [Col. 0423A].

“The deep,” He says, “enclosed me.” For Judas, who betrayed Him, having received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, came with lanterns, torches, and weapons. Then indeed the deep enclosed our Lord: the deep, namely, of iniquity, plotting its dark secret, as He Himself says in judgment: “But this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke 22).

“And the sea covered my head.” Certainly, when the high priest said: “I adjure You by the living God, tell us whether You are the Christ, the Son of God,” and He answered, “You have said it”; and because of this they cried aloud, saying, “He is guilty of death”; and they spat in His face, struck Him with fists, and slapped His face (Matt. 26), then the sea covered His head [Col. 0423B].

“I went down to the extremities of the mountains.” Truly, when, at the demand of those saying, “Away, away, crucify Him” (John 19), and, “Do not release this man to us, but Barabbas”; when He was reckoned among criminals and crucified between two thieves, then He went down to the extremities, or lowest ends, of the mountains. Thus the prophet truly foretold of Him: “He has neither form nor comeliness; and we saw Him, and there was no appearance, and we desired Him—despised and the lowest of men” (Isa. 53).

“The bars of the earth shut me in for ever.” Truly, when the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said: “Command, therefore, that His tomb be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps His disciples come and steal Him”; and he said, “You have a guard; go, guard it as you know how”; and they departed and fortified the tomb, sealing the stone with the guards (Matt. 27), then the bars of the earth shut Him in for ever according to their estimation. They rejoiced over Him, thinking not that He would rise, but that His name would perish for ever [Col. 0423C]. This was their false joy and vain hope. Yet according to the truth of the matter, it was to come about that His flesh would not see corruption.

Therefore He says: “And You will raise up my life from corruption, O Lord my God”: that is, You will cause me—shut in by the bars of the earth and pressed down by the sealed stone—to rise again, You who are my Lord and my God, of whom I am servant and creature according to the form of a servant, according to that humanity whose lifeless body could be shut in by the bars of the earth [Col. 0423D].

It follows: “When my soul was distressed within me, I remembered the Lord, that my prayer might come to You, to Your holy temple.” He Himself plainly disclosed the distress of His soul when He said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26). Moreover, His sweat made the distress of His soul more apparent; according to another Evangelist, being in agony and praying more earnestly, He gave forth sweat, and His sweat became like drops of blood running down onto the ground (Luke 22). “Then,” He says, “I remembered the Lord”: namely, in that I subordinated the inclination, or effect, of the flesh to the counsel or purpose of divinity, saying: “Nevertheless, not my will but Yours be done” (ibid.).

What was that will? “That my prayer,” He says, “might come to You, to Your holy temple” [Col. 0424A]. This was Your will: that through my Passion I should save the nations, just as the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand in my person through the mouth of David, saying: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; this day I have begotten You. Ask of me, and I will give You the nations as Your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as Your possession” (Ps. 2). This was what pleased You: that I should ask in this way—or rather, that I myself, in dying, should become both sacrifice and prayer for the nations. But I should not prefer the Jews, although my kindred and tribesmen, to them because of human affection; indeed, I should leave them.

Why? Surely because, while the nations repent, these remain unrepentant. This is what immediately follows: “Those who keep vanities vainly forsake their mercy.” How did the Jews keep vanities? Truly, with much effort and remarkable obstinacy. Although there are many evidences of this, it pertains to the present place to recall only these two as testimony.

After they killed Him, they took care to fortify the tomb, sealing the stone with guards, inventing this pretext: “Lest perhaps His disciples come and steal Him” (Matt. 27). But in truth they intended that even if He came to life after three days, as they remembered that He had foretold, He should not be able to come forth, pressed down by the stone and, as we have here, shut in by the bars of the earth [Col. 0424B]. Then, when some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened, they assembled with the elders; having taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: “Say that His disciples came by night and stole Him while we were asleep” (Matt. 28).

Thus they laboured to keep their vanity so much that they even gave a large sum of money to preserve it, so that they might hold the truth of God captive in a lie [Col. 0424C]. This vanity is great—greater than anyone can adequately express in words. By doing this, therefore, they forsook their mercy: that is, they abandoned the grace of the remission of sins. Hence it should be noted that He did not say, “Those who practise vanities will vainly forsake their mercy.” For they would not have lost access to mercy merely because, in killing Christ, they committed vanity, unless they had also kept vanities by remaining in unbelief and setting their own faithlessness against the faith of the Gospel.

Accordingly, it was much better said, “They forsook their mercy,” than if one were to say, “Their mercy forsook them.” For mercy forsakes no one; rather, all keepers of vanity, all defenders of iniquity once committed, forsake it. Nor should this be passed over: in saying, “They will forsake mercy,” He adds “their,” because, as we have already explained, the prophetic discourse concerns the Jews, whose mercy Christ is first of all. For, as the Apostle says: “The adoption as sons is theirs, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9) [Col. 0424D–0425A].

Therefore the Jews, by keeping vanities, rejecting the same Word of God, and judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, forsook their mercy; and they rejected mercy which did not forsake them but rather visited them, unwilling to recognize the time of their visitation (Luke 19), seeking not eternal mercy but temporal glory.

But observe further that, when He is about to say, “They will forsake their mercy,” He first adds, “vainly.” For they could not even preserve what they thought to reserve for themselves by killing Christ: namely, their place and nation, and even the profitable privilege of their temple or priesthood. On its account, excessively puffed up with a spirit of pride against all nations, as the peculiar people of one God, they drew from the whole world a great name and great profit [Col. 0425B]. It did not turn out according to their hope. Rather, just as, by rejecting the Word of God, they judged themselves, as has been said, unworthy of eternal life, so too they were judged unworthy of the prosperity of this present life: they fell by the edge of the sword and, having lost their place, were led captive among all nations.

“But I will sacrifice to You with the voice of praise; whatever I have vowed, I will render to the Lord for my salvation.” But they forsake their mercy; yet because of them the praise and glory of mercy will not be diminished. For I will sacrifice to You with a voice of praise: I will acquire other tongues in place of their tongues, that they may sing to You, as it is written elsewhere: “Therefore I will confess You among the peoples, and sing a psalm to You among the nations” (Ps. 56) [Col. 0425B–0426A]. “Whatever I have vowed, I will render to the Lord for my salvation”: that is, I shall so instruct the nations in knowledge of Your name, and so kindle them with the fire of Your love, that they may make and fulfil for their salvation vows far more numerous than the Jews ever made.

He says these things as one obedient; for, as the Apostle says, “He learned obedience through the things which He suffered” (Heb. 5). Indeed, through sufferings and death itself He was instructed unto impassibility—He who until then, being passible through the affection of the flesh, had wept over His own nation. Thus changed, with every affection of this kind laid aside, He came to have a ready will to leave their house to them desolate and turn to the nations. The voice of one thus instructed is that uttered through the Psalmist: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory” (Ps. 107) [Col. 0426B].

For what immediately follows—“Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (ibid.)—is the voice of the Father, or of divinity, raising the flesh from the tomb. Therefore in this prophet, as a type of Him, it is immediately added: “And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.” For the Lord spoke to earth and death, and restored this our Lord Jesus Christ, who had been dead, to life, loosing the pains of hell, since it was impossible for Him to be held by it (Acts 2).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0425]

[Col. 0425C] 186 Jonah too, now as a type of our Lord Jesus Christ—who, as we have recalled above, according to the Apostle learned obedience through the things which He suffered (Heb. 5)—had been taught by the greatness of tribulation that the heavenly command must be obeyed. He bore a will ready for this, being bound by the vow made in the belly of the whale, as he himself indicates when he says: “Whatever I have vowed, I will render to the Lord for my salvation.” Foreseeing this vow, the Lord had said to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land. These things having been set forth, Scripture continues and says:

## CHAPTER III.

And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: “Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it the proclamation which I shall speak to you.” With great earnestness the merciful God sought the repentance of the Ninevites [Col. 0425D], which indeed, as God who knows all things, he knew would not fail to follow when the preaching had been heard. But someone will say: Why did the Lord, God not only of the Ninevites but of all nations, care more for the Ninevites than for the other nations? For other nations also might have turned to repentance if God had sent them preachers, as the Son of God himself testifies concerning himself: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the mighty works which were done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” [Col. 0426C] (Matt. 11). Likewise: “For if the mighty works which were done in Capernaum had been done in Sodom, it would perhaps have remained to this day” (ibid.). Why, then, did he send no preacher or prophet to Tyre and Sidon, or to Sodom, while he so urgently compels this Jonah to go to the Ninevites, although he foresaw that those nations too, like the Ninevites, could turn to repentance? Did he not wish them to be saved, and for that reason send no one to them? For this seems to follow: that he did not wish them to be saved, since he bears them witness that they would have repented had he sent them preachers—which he did not do. But, on the contrary, the Apostle says that he “wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2). It is a fine question, one which has troubled very many people even in our own times [Col. 0426D]; therefore we must pause a little at this point.

First, it must be said that when the Lord says of them that, if mighty works had been done among them, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth—though he did not provide that such works should be done—it does not follow that you should say that he did not wish them to be saved. Rather, it follows only that he did not concern himself with their repentance. This indeed would follow if every repentance were sufficient for salvation; but it is not so. For only that manner of repentance leads to salvation in which a person repents because he believes that the universal judgment and the kingdom of heaven are to come, from which sinners will be excluded and cast into Gehenna [Col. 0427A]. When, therefore, someone repents in order to escape eternal evils and attain everlasting goods, he is judged faithful; and by repenting through faith, he is saved. God has never neglected to send preachers or to reveal knowledge of the truth to any of all those whom he foresaw could be converted to such repentance.

There is another repentance, or intention of repenting, when someone repents in order only to escape present evils, or the evils of the present age, and to retain present goods, having neither faith in nor concern for future and eternal goods or evils. If you seek examples, such was the repentance of Ahab, who repented only over the blood of Naboth, whom he and his wife Jezebel had killed, because the Lord had threatened him through Elijah, saying: “Behold, I shall bring evil upon you, and I shall cut off your posterity; and I shall make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Naboth, son of Ahijah.” Therefore he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with lowered head [Col. 0427B] (3 Kings 21): he acted thus lest he be deprived of his temporal kingdom. If repentance of this intention is very earnest, it deserves to obtain what it intends, as did the aforesaid Ahab, of whom the Lord then said to Elijah: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Therefore, because he has humbled himself on my account, I shall not bring the evil in his days, but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house” [Col. 0427C] (ibid.).

But if it is more sluggish and is uttered, so to speak, only from the lips’ outermost edge—“I have sinned”—it profits nothing, as Saul indeed said to Samuel: “I have sinned, because I have transgressed the word of the Lord; but now, I beg you, bear my sin, and return with me, that I may worship the Lord”; yet he did not obtain it. For Samuel said: “I shall not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you, that you should not be king over Israel” (1 Kings 15). The former and better mode of repentance, however—whereby a person is pricked with remorse for sin not because of temporal goods but because of God himself and faith in the age to come—is sometimes received at the first confession without great work or toil. An example is David [Col. 0427D], who, when he said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the Lord,” immediately heard: “The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Kings 12).

Therefore, when the Lord says of Tyre and Sidon, and likewise of Sodom, that if mighty works had been done among them, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes, or perhaps would have remained until today, no one should be disturbed by the suspicion that he did not wish them to be saved and therefore did not perform mighty works among them. It must be understood that there is a twofold manner, 187 or intention, of repentance: it is one thing to repent through fear of temporal or present evil, another to repent through faith in the kingdom of God. Those, indeed, are or were unrighteous who would have repented only for temporal advantage, as, the Lord says, the Tyrians and Sidonians would have done. Yet most unrighteous [Col. 0428A] are those who repented neither to avoid temporal nor eternal evils—such as the Jews, to whom the Lord threatened both the Gehenna of eternal fire and the destruction which the Romans would bring about, yet for neither reason did they turn to repentance. Therefore the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Sodomites, though truly unrighteous, are justified in comparison with them—only in the sense that they are not saved, but that their punishment is more lenient.

What, then, shall we say concerning these men, that is, the Ninevites, to whom the Lord so earnestly took care to send this prophet for preaching? Were they going to repent through faith in the kingdom of God? Certainly not, but through fear of temporal destruction. Thus at the first time, in response to this preaching, they repented and obtained pardon [Col. 0428B]. But afterward, once they had recovered a harmful security and persisted in their former vices, they provoked God’s sentence against themselves; and under Astyages, king of the Medes, while Josiah was king among the Jews, they were overthrown. Knowing this, Tobit said to his son: “The destruction of Nineveh will be near, for the word of the Lord shall not fail” (Tob. 14), which Jonah the prophet had spoken. And soon afterward: “For I see that its iniquity will bring its end” (ibid.).

Therefore, apart from the mystery—by which we rightly take very great delight in the Ninevites’ repentance, since it was a sign of the repentance of the Gentiles according to God, able to attain the kingdom of heaven—apart, I say, from this mystery, there is nothing in which we should prefer, or ought to prefer, the repentant Ninevites to other nations. For other nations also could similarly have repented [Col. 0428C], that is, with temporal concerns in view, as the Lord testifies when he utters the aforesaid judgment about Tyre and Sidon. But if it is further asked why God was pleased to provide this sort of demonstration, against unrepentant Israel, in the case of the Ninevites rather than other nations, and to show that they were justified in comparison with Israel—who repented neither through fear of temporal nor of eternal evils, nor abandoned the golden calves—it must briefly be said: Nineveh, a great city, was the metropolis of the Assyrians. But God’s justice intended to hand Israel over into the hands of the Assyrians, as indeed happened in the ninth year of Hoshea. For Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured Samaria [Col. 0428D] and carried Israel away into Assyria. “And Israel was carried away,” says Scripture, “from its own land into Assyria, unto this day” (4 Kings 17). It was therefore shown beforehand that the Assyrians were justified in comparison with Israel, lest God should seem to subvert justice by handing Israel—who professed itself to be God’s peculiar people—into their hands. For it appears unjust to accusers that Israel, God’s people, should be removed from its own land while the Assyrians remained powerful in their land, and should be held in the cities of the Assyrians in perpetual captivity. A reasonable cause was given: namely, that the Assyrians could at least turn to repentance out of love for their land, whereas this had long been attempted vainly with Israel; and the proof of this reason was sought [Col. 0429A] through Jonah’s ministry and found. But both these people and those were far too unprepared to receive faith in God’s future kingdom; and therefore at that time it was fitting that this should be preached neither openly to Israel or the Jews, nor in any fashion to the Assyrians or other nations.

Let us now return to the sequence of the prophecy, keeping before our eyes in what follows the sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, whose mystery of suffering we beheld in what went before. “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it the preaching which I shall speak to you.” The prophet is not told, “Why did you not do what had been commanded you?” Rather, the rebuke of shipwreck and devouring alone suffices him, so that he who had not recognized God commanding might understand God delivering.

Concerning our Lord Jesus Christ as man—in whom, though he is God, his humanity suffered—it should be known that, when after the travail of death he rested in the tomb, the word of the Lord came to him a second time, that he should rise to preach. For the first time, as we discussed above, the word of the Lord came to him when he was baptized by John, when the Holy Spirit was seen over him in the form of a dove [Col. 0429B] (Matt. 3), and Isaiah’s saying was fulfilled: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Isa. 61), etc. He himself bore witness that this was spoken of himself, saying: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4).

But the word which came or was spoken to him as he rested in the tomb he did not himself recite in the same manner; nevertheless it is known from the Psalm already mentioned above, where the voice of the Father says thus: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” [Col. 0429C] (Ps. 107), with the sense understood: “to confess me among the peoples, to sing praise to me among the nations.” For immediately the person of the Son, lying in the tomb according to the body, answers: “I shall arise at dawn”; and he adds, “I shall confess you among the peoples and sing praise to you among the nations” (ibid.). This, assuredly, is to preach in Nineveh, the great city. Holy Scripture bears witness to the proclamation which the Godhead speaks, holding an ancient purpose concerning the salvation of peoples or nations.

[Col. 0429D] “And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, the great city, according to the word of the Lord. And Nineveh was a great city, a journey of three days. And Jonah began to enter into the city, a journey of one day; and he cried out and said: ‘Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.’” According to the letter, Nineveh was a great city, of such extent that it could scarcely be encircled in a three-day journey. But he, mindful of the command and of his former shipwreck, completed the journey of three days in the haste of one day. Yet it may also be understood that he preached only in a third part of the city and that the word of the preaching swiftly reached the rest. This can especially be inferred from what is immediately added: “And the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord, proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least; and the word reached [Col. 0430A] the king of Nineveh.” It does not say, “And Jonah reached” him, but “the word reached the king of Nineveh.” Who could doubt that the report of so great a matter moved more swiftly than the prophet’s feet, especially since he entered throughout the whole day crying aloud, and in crying would surely have become known to only a few in that first entrance? The Ninevites’ readiness for repentance, then, seems to be commended in this: before Jonah reached the king of Nineveh, he believed, the report of the word of the Lord having preceded him.

This interpretation will be still more pleasing in the mystery. Nineveh also, the great city of a three-day journey, is this world, or the globe consisting of the last three parts: Asia, Europe, and Africa. After his passion and resurrection, Christ Jesus entered this threefold world in the journey of one day; that is, he illuminated it with the illumination of the one God [Col. 0430B], so that the nations, which followed many false marvels of gods, might be freed from their error by knowing the one God. He did not indeed go forth to the nations in his own person, but in his apostles, in whom he himself assuredly speaks. When he sent them, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), he also said: “And behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (ibid.). Thus he himself came to Nineveh, that is, to the nations, because he is truly with those whom he sent and speaks in them.

[Col. 0430C] “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” The meaning is: “There is still given to you nations a time for repentance,” and God has placed this time in his own power; when it is fulfilled, the world will be consummated and judged by fire. For the number forty belongs to repentance. Moses fasted forty days on Mount Sinai (Exod. 24, 34); Elijah, fleeing Jezebel, fasted forty days (4 Kings 19); and the Lord himself, the true Jonah, sent to preach to the world, fasted forty days (Matt. 5), leaving us the inheritance of the forty-day fast, so that every year, when about to celebrate his Paschal mystery, we may for so many days prepare ourselves to eat his body and drink his blood.

Thus, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown”: that is, there is still given to the nations a short time of repentance, after which there will no longer be time [Col. 0430D], just as John in his Apocalypse testifies that the mighty angel descending from heaven—who is Christ, the Son of God—confirmed with an oath: “And the angel,” he says, “whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth, raised his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ages of ages that there shall be time no longer; but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be consummated, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets” (Rev. 10). The mystery of God will be consummated; Nineveh will be overthrown; the world will be judged by fire; ungodly persons will be cast with the devil and his angels into eternal fire; and there will no longer be a time of repentance.

The preaching of such a great matter is indeed a cry, a crash terrible to every ear that hears it; so that nothing is more terrible to hear, as was perceived by him who speaks thus: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those human beings who hold the truth of God in injustice” [Col. 0431A] (Rom. 1). It therefore pertains well to the mystery that Jonah, entering the city, is said to have cried aloud that Nineveh would be overthrown.

“And the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord, proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. And the word reached the king of Nineveh. And he rose from his throne, cast off his garment from himself, clothed himself in sackcloth, sat in ashes, and cried aloud and said: ‘In Nineveh, by decree of the king and his princes: Let men and beasts, oxen and flocks, taste nothing; let them neither feed nor drink water; let men be covered with sackcloth [Col. 0431B] and cry mightily to the Lord; and let each person turn from his evil way and from the iniquity which is in their hands. Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn away from the fury of his wrath, that we may not perish?’”

This event, most memorable, needs no exposition. Yet this must always be held in memory: it happened for Israel’s condemnation that the Ninevites so quickly and earnestly repented through fear of temporal evils, whereas Israel, so often rebuked and warned through the prophets, repented neither through fear of temporal nor eternal evils, so as to depart from the sins of Jeroboam and abandon the worship of the golden calves.

But in the mystery it is far more delightful that the men of Nineveh believed in [Col. 0431C] the Lord: that is, while the Jews contradicted and blasphemed, the nations received Christ’s Gospel, rejoiced, and glorified God. For they proclaimed a fast and clothed themselves in sackcloth; that is, they prepared themselves for so great a grace by every disposition of humility. Yet they did this with joy, keeping before their eyes the pleasant fruit of their present sorrow: namely, forgiveness and the kingdom of heaven opened to them.

“And the word reached the king of Nineveh.” If Nineveh is the whole world, what can we understand by the king of Nineveh except the Roman Empire? Indeed, the Roman Empire so surpassed all kingdoms in terror and power as royal authority surpasses leaders or satraps in any kingdom. The word reached such a king of Nineveh before Jonah himself did, because Rome, the head of the world, heard Christ’s Gospel before it saw Christ’s apostles; and, weighing it wisely, judged the message faithful and worthy of acceptance, becoming a great example of belief to other nations. For they would not have thought contemptible what Roman wisdom had approved as reasonable by its own belief. Hence the Apostle, rejoicing, says: “First indeed, I always give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in the whole world, praying that somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, in the will of God, to come to you” [Col. 0431D] (Rom. 1). For he had not yet come to them, as he makes still clearer immediately afterward: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, that I have often purposed to come to you and have been hindered until now” [Col. 0432A] (ibid.), etc.

Therefore, with the word preceding it to such a king of Nineveh, he “rose from his throne,” and so forth, as above. The hearing of the word advanced and gradually prevailed so greatly that the summit of so great an empire descended from the height of secular glory, bent beneath itself, and inclined knee and head, when Emperor Constantine was baptized by blessed Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See. Although it is sufficiently well known how greatly earthly power then rose up for Christ’s Gospel in him, it should nevertheless be recalled briefly from the privilege of the holy Roman Church which the same Emperor Constantine established. In it he says, among other things [Col. 0432B]:

“We have also decreed that our same venerable father, Sylvester, supreme pontiff, and all his successors in the pontificate, should use the diadem—that is, the crown which we have granted him from our own head, of the purest gold and precious gems—and should bear it on their head to the praise of God and our Lord, for the honor of blessed Peter the Apostle. Yet the most blessed pope himself did not at all permit himself to use that golden crown over the clerical crown which he wears for the glory of blessed Peter the Apostle. But we placed with our own hands upon his most sacred head a Phrygian cap of shining whiteness, signifying the splendid resurrection of the Lord; and, holding the bridle of his horse out of reverence for blessed Peter the Apostle, we performed for him the office of groom, establishing that all his successors should uniquely use the same Phrygian cap in processions, in imitation of our imperial dignity [Col. 0432C]. Thus the pontifical summit might not be diminished in honor, but might be adorned even more highly than the dignity and glory of earthly imperial power.

“Behold, we hand over and leave to the aforesaid most blessed pontiff, our father Sylvester, universal pope, both our palace, as stated above, and the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and of the western regions, to him and to his successors in the pontificate, to be administered by their authority and jurisdiction through this our sacred and imperial pragmatic constitution; and we grant that they remain subject to the right of the holy Roman Church. Therefore we have judged it fitting that our empire and royal power be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium, in an excellent place, a city be built bearing our name [Col. 0432D], and that our empire be established there. For where the primacy of priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the Emperor of heaven, it is not just that an earthly emperor should have power there.”

Surely, when the aforesaid Constantine said and did these things, then the king of Nineveh rose from his throne; then the Roman Empire rose up at the word of the Lord and cast off its garment—that is, it abandoned the frenzied religious cults in which it had been entangled, received the Christian religion, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes, so that after the austerity of repentance it might fittingly be clothed in the delight of righteousness, saying with the Psalmist: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Ps. 29).

For it is a religious custom and an ordered tradition of evangelical profession that, after repentance has been undertaken for former errors, each person first be instructed as a catechumen in the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, and then rise with Christ in holy baptism, rejoicing in the first resurrection—that is, in the forgiveness of sins. The law and order of this sacrament, and of the whole religion of the Church, are fortified and strengthened in many ways by the decrees of the Rome already mentioned [Col. 0433A], because it became the seat of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of his fellow-participant Paul; illuminated by their preaching and crowned by their martyrdom, it raised itself above all churches as their head, and the sacred tongue of its bishops is more widely renowned among all nations than the purple of the Caesars or Augusti ever ruled.

It also accords well with this mystery that the king of Nineveh cried aloud and said: “In Nineveh, by decree of the king and his princes: Let men and beasts, oxen and flocks taste nothing,” etc. For as at that time it was fitting for this to be done according to the edict of the king of Nineveh, so the ecclesiastical order ought to be observed according to the faith and tradition of blessed Peter and Paul, who are, or ought to be, the mouth and tongue of the Roman See.

Certainly, by men and beasts covered in sackcloth and crying to God, we must understand rational and irrational persons—or wise and simple persons—doing repentance at the preaching of the Gospel, according to what is said elsewhere: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord” [Col. 0433B] (Ps. 35). But by saying, “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” uncertainty and doubt are introduced, so that, while people are uncertain of salvation, they may nevertheless not despair, but rather repent more earnestly and move God more strongly to mercy.

“And God saw their works, because they had turned from their evil way; and God had mercy concerning the evil which he had said he would do to them, and did not do it.” He did not first see when they were thus covered; he did not, I say, first see their sackcloth when they put it on. Rather, he had seen long before he sent the prophet there, when Israel was killing prophets who preached its impending captivity; and he foreknew without uncertainty that, if he sent prophets far away to the nations announcing such a thing, they would listen and repent. Therefore he saw—that is, he caused it to be seen by this demonstration—how blameworthy Israel was in [Col. 0433C] comparison with the nations, so that not only the prophets but the whole world too, on hearing it, might acknowledge the judgment to be just: God showed mercy to the nations and not to Israel, because they turned from their evil way, while Israel persisted without repentance [Col. 0433D].

Here we understand “evil” as affliction, that is, the overthrow of Nineveh which he had spoken of and had threatened through the prophet. It is not an indication of changeableness that God, as though repenting, often remits what he had threatened. Rather, it is especially a mark of constancy and an unchangeable mind, because he is accustomed to threaten sinners with that intention: that they may repent. Thus here he says: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” [Col. 0434A] And in the Law he says: “Whoever does this or that shall surely die.” Likewise in the Gospel, when he says: “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26), the discerning reader should understand: “unless he is converted, unless he repents,” in accordance with the saying: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. 17). That is, he has already prescribed what punishment or sentence follows sin, which he will certainly fulfill unless you are converted.

## CHAPTER IV.

And Jonah was afflicted with great affliction, and he was angry; and he prayed to the Lord and said: “I beseech you, Lord, was not this my word when I was still in my own land? For this reason I forestalled it by fleeing to Tarshish. For I know that you are my God, gracious and merciful, patient and of great compassion, forgiving evil.” [Col. 0434B] “And now, Lord, I beg you, take my life from me, for death is better for me than life.”

In order properly to weigh the prophet’s affliction and anger, and also his words, “And now, Lord, I beg you, take my life from me,” etc., we must likewise keep before our eyes Moses’ affliction and anger, and his words. For he too was afflicted with great affliction, was angry, and spoke sorrowfully when the people sinned. Indeed, describing his affliction, he says: “When I saw that we had sinned against the Lord our God and had made for you a molten calf, I fell down before the Lord as before, for forty days and forty nights, eating no bread and drinking no water” (Deut. IX), etc.

He showed his anger openly in the same matter when, standing at the gate of the camp, [Col. 0434C] he said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, join himself to me.” And when all the sons of Levi had gathered to him, he said: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” They did so, and on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell (Exod. XXXII).

Moreover, these are his words of exceeding grief and affliction: “But I beseech you, forgive them this sin; or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (ibid.). Thus let us weigh this man’s affliction and anger, and his words, “I beg you, take my life,” in the same sense. He was afflicted with great affliction because Israel was falling under divine judgment, while Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, was being justified by comparison with it through believing and doing penance; nor could he deny that the sentence was right and that a just captivity was impending over his own nation.

Moses afflicted himself for the people in order that he might be heard; this man was afflicted with great affliction because he was not heard. Moses was angry with righteous anger and good zeal, saying, “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh,” and twenty-three thousand fell. This man too was angry, but he could not fulfill his anger in deed by turning away the Lord’s anger through the punishment of the people—that is, the authors or priests of the calves—as Elijah too had killed the priests of Baal, four hundred and fifty men (III Kings XVIII).

Therefore, weary of his life, he did not speak conditionally, as Moses did: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if [Col. 0435A] you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.” Rather, absolutely, he says: “I beg you, take my life, because death is better for me than life.” The meaning implied is: because the fear which I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened. This I feared and dreaded: that you, a gracious and merciful God, patient and of great compassion, would be ready to forgive and grant pardon to the penitent Ninevites, and in their repentance would show how condemnable impenitent Israel was; and that [190] its condemnation would be caused not by your harshness, but by its own impenitence.

“For this reason I forestalled it by fleeing to Tarshish”: namely, not because I begrudged pardon or repentance to the Ninevites, but because I feared that my own nation, once chosen above the other nations, would now be found worse than the rest and more stiff-necked.

[Col. 0435B] But since Jonah is a type of Christ, how does it suit Christ to be afflicted and angry after he rose from the dead, just as Jonah, when so afflicted and angry, had come out from the belly of the whale? For before his resurrection he is indeed recorded to have been afflicted and angry over the destruction of his nation, when, seeing the city, he wept over it, and, entering the Temple, terribly drove out those buying and selling there (Luke XIX). But after he rose from the dead, just as he no longer dies, so neither is he afflicted.

Therefore, just as he did not come to the Gentiles in his own person and yet is rightly said to have come—namely, through his apostles, in whom he himself speaks—so he is likewise rightly said to be afflicted in those same persons, because they were afflicted and grieved, although in his own person he is no longer afflicted. One of those afflicted, in whom Christ undoubtedly speaks, Paul the apostle says thus: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that there is great sorrow for me and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren” (Rom. IX), etc.

And the Lord said to Jonah: “Do you think that you are right to be angry?” What the Lord says to one Jonah, he says to all who, in the discharge of their office, are angered while caring for people. In the very midst of their anger they must be called back within themselves, so that they may examine their cause or intention and, with attentive discernment, weigh whether they are rightly angry or not. For if they are angry not with people but with people’s sins, if they hate and persecute not people but people’s vices, [Col. 0435C] they are rightly angry and their zeal is good. But if they are angry not with sins but with people, if they hate and persecute not vices but people, they are wrongly angry and their zeal is evil. Therefore all must watchfully attend to and decide this, when it is said to one: “Do you think that you are right to be angry?”

And Jonah went out of the city and sat opposite the east of the city, and made himself a shelter there; and he sat beneath it in the shade until he should see what would happen to the city. And the Lord God prepared an ivy plant, and it grew over Jonah’s head, that it might be a shade over his head and protect him, for he had labored. And Jonah rejoiced greatly over the ivy plant. And God prepared a worm at the rising of dawn on the next day, and [Col. 0436A] it struck the ivy plant, and it withered. And when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot, scorching wind; and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he was overcome by the heat, and he asked that he might die and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

To the afflicted and angry prophet there is further given a reason for him to be more and more afflicted and angry. For through this likeness of the ivy plant, so quickly sprung up and so quickly withered, he could by the prophetic Spirit understand before it happened what we understand to have happened: namely, that salvation would at some time pass to the Gentiles, not only then, at that immediate time, when the ten impenitent tribes were given over to the Assyrians as more righteous, being inclined to repentance, but also when Jerusalem itself and the whole nation had been abandoned.

According to the historical sense, indeed, the things now said—“And Jonah went out of the city,” and what follows—come after the preceding events; but according to the mystery they come before them. For Jonah’s going out of the city and sitting opposite the east of the city mystically intimates to us that the Lord, or the Word of the Lord, at the beginning left the nations of the whole world, as the apostle says: “He permitted them to walk in their own ways” (Acts XIV).

And he made himself a shelter: namely, by taking Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as the fathers, and choosing their race, because he found rest for himself in their faith. For this is what is meant by the words: “And he sat beneath it in the shade until he should see what would happen to the city.” Thus he confined himself within their generations until the time of the reconciliation of the Gentiles, which he himself foreknew, should come.

What is then added, [Col. 0436C] “And the Lord God prepared an ivy plant, and it grew over Jonah’s head, that it might be a shade over his head and protect him—for he had labored,” we understand mystically to mean that, after the pleasant shelter of the fathers’ faith, he gave the Law and instituted the priestly religion through Moses, so that beneath it the Word of the Lord, or Spirit of truth, might be covered, veiled by figures and by the usefulness of the letter. This is aptly signified by the greenness of the light ivy plant, or, as some would have it, of the gourd.

For the gourd and the ivy are of such a nature that they creep along the ground, having broad leaves like a vine-leaf; and, without forks or supports on which to lean, they do not seek higher things. Thus indeed the letter of the Law and of all the ceremonies is broad and a very dense shadow; it obscures itself. [Col. 0436D] Unless it is raised by the supports of spiritual understanding, it is neither lofty nor precious.

“And Jonah,” he says, “rejoiced greatly over the ivy plant,” because the Word of the Lord, which is Christ, dwelling in the prophets and holy people before he was incarnate, was meanwhile preserved beneath it, and was honored even by those ignorant persons from whom, according to the condition of the time, what was contained beneath the shelter of the letter was concealed and ought to have been concealed.

Nor is it unfitting that he is said to have rejoiced with great joy in such a thing after labor. For, on account of those among them who were pleasing amid those ceremonies, he rejoiced; they made him glad through their faith—or rather, his joy was their joy when they rejoiced in him. For example, David, when bringing back the ark of the Lord, danced before the Lord with all kinds of wrought wood, with citharas, lyres, timbrels, sistrums, and cymbals; and he leapt and danced, saying: “I will play, and I will become more lowly than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (II Kings VI).

[Col. 0437A] In such things our Jonah—that is, Christ, or the Word of the Lord not yet incarnate—was then truly rejoicing with great joy and resting, for he had labored: namely, by enduring the manners of that people in the wilderness. Nor did he cease to rejoice until he took flesh from there and God became man.

But when Christ suffered and rose again, repentance and remission of all sins in his name began to be preached to the Ninevites, that is, to all the Gentiles. Then that whole shelter of the Law and ceremonies was dissipated, so that the city of Jerusalem and the Temple itself were wholly destroyed, as is known to the whole world.

Therefore the ivy plant withered, struck by the worm at the ascent of dawn: that is, at the revelation of the resurrection of our Lord, who rose at dawn. The worm here is rightly understood as the Roman Empire, just as in Joel, by the caterpillar, locust, beetle, and blight, the four principal kingdoms are understood, of which the last was the Roman. For the first was Babylonian, the second Persian, and the third Macedonian. By these, that place and nation were torn apart at different times; finally it was irrecoverably destroyed by the Roman Empire, which the Lord had of course prepared for this very purpose, as is said here: that the Lord prepared the worm.

Thus, just as the conversion of the Gentiles was signified by the repentance of the Ninevites, so the abandonment of the Jews was signified by the drying of the ivy plant. What follows—“And when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot and scorching wind, and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he was overcome by heat”—signifies the tribulation which Christ endured in his disciples from the Jews, [Col. 0437C] [191] while the worm was being prepared to strike the ivy plant; that is, while the arrival of the Romans to overthrow Judaea was delayed. Even before it was overthrown by men, it had already been overthrown before God; and from the time it shed Christ’s blood, it was wholly withered.

Hence came that great affliction and anger of Jonah mentioned above, who was afflicted with great affliction and angry. For the apostles and other disciples from that nation had great sorrow, both from the spirit of charity and from the affection of kinship, so that with afflicted hearts they grieved for them as brethren and rebuked them as with a severe mouth. For example, the proto-martyr Stephen, compassionating them with great charity, cried out, saying: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge” (Acts VI); and, rebuking them with great severity: “Stiff-necked,” he says, “and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did” (ibid.), etc.

And the Lord said to Jonah: “Do you think that you are right to be angry over the ivy plant?” And he said: “I am right to be angry, even unto death.” And the Lord said: “You grieve over the ivy plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow; it was born in one night and perished in [Col. 0438A] one night. And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know the difference between their right hand and their left, and many cattle?”

Plainly, here an argument from the greater is made in order to constrain the prophet to agree, and to judge that mercy toward the repentance of the Ninevites ought to be granted. For, without any contradiction, one human being—indeed, even one living, sentient beast—is greater than one hundred and twenty thousand ivy plants or gourds, which, even if they possess some sort of life, nevertheless perform no office of sense. Yet he was more angry over the withering of one ivy plant or gourd than he would have grieved over the destruction—had it occurred according to his prophecy—of one hundred and twenty thousand people and many beasts. And he who was angry that an ivy plant for which he had not labored was not preserved for him would have borne it calmly if God had overthrown so many people and beasts whom he had created.

But it may be objected that, as a prophet with foreknowing Spirit, he foresaw what the drying of the gourd signified: namely, that his own Israelite nation, in comparison with the Gentiles, was far more condemnable than a beast; and for this reason he was angry, grieving with human affection for his own kindred. To this it must knowingly be answered that all that kindred, all that Israelite multitude which did not receive the Word of the Lord, but rather killed the prophets who proclaimed the Word of the Lord, and was therefore to be led into captivity, was justly reckoned in the Lord’s sight as ivy or gourd.

For in another prophet we have heard the voice saying: “Cry.” And when he said, “What shall I cry?”: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the Word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. XL). [Col. 0438C] Therefore Israel too, because it did not receive the Word of the Lord which remains for ever, was grass; and thus, by an apt comparison, Jonah was shown how highly he ought to value that carnal kindred for which he was jealous against the Ninevites—as if the Lord were saying to him: “Israel is to me like ivy or grass, because the Word of the Lord does not remain in it.”

But the Ninevites, who heard and believed, are people and are beasts: that is, they surpass unbelieving Israel by as much as living and sentient beasts surpass senseless ivy, or as people who live, sense, and discern surpass it. Add also this: so many living people do not know the difference between their right and left; but Israel, possessing the Law and the prophets, cannot have an excuse from ignorance. If, therefore, sorrow admits reason, the reproved prophet undoubtedly confesses that God’s mercy is more just than the zeal of a human being.

Finally, that we may refer this also in mystery to the person of Christ, let us first recall that, struggling in his passion, he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). Then he added: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (ibid.). For he was sorrowful over the future destruction of Jerusalem in vengeance for his blood; therefore, seeing the city earlier, he had wept over it. That sorrow or weeping arose from weak flesh; for the spirit was willing, knowing that concern was not to be given to carnality but only to divine justice.

Therefore let the willing spirit say to the weak flesh: “You grieve over the ivy plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow,” etc. Indeed, all the beauty of the city and the worship of the splendid Temple ought to have been reckoned as a small thing, like ivy, in the sight of the Godhead. For our Jonah—that is, the dove, or sorrowing Christ—had not labored for it. God did not become man and undergo the labor of the passion in order to glory or rest in such a Temple or in those carnal ceremonies of the Temple, but in order to save Nineveh, to redeem the world by his passion, according to that prophetic voice of God the Father: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II).

[Col. 0439B] “Nor did you make the plant grow,” he says: that is, you did not require that sacrifices and burnt offerings of this kind should be offered to you, according to Jeremiah: “I did not speak,” he says, “to your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but this I commanded them, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God” (Jer. VII), etc.

This kind of ivy plant was born in one night and perished in one night, because that people quickly received the Law, saying: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exod. XXIV). It quickly abandoned it: first by following Jeroboam and saying, [Col. 0440A] “We have no part in David” (III Kings XII), and serving golden calves; and then, at the persuasion of the chief priests, by denying and crucifying Christ, the Son of God.

Therefore, as we have already said, let the willing spirit say to weak flesh: “You grieve over the ivy plant”—that is, over your kindred Jewish nation—“and shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city? Shall I not provide for the salvation of the Gentiles throughout the whole world, who are ignorant and wandering?” For there are many thousands of persons among the Gentiles who go, as they are led, to dumb idols—not through malice, but through ignorance. Without doubt they would correct their ways if they possessed knowledge of the truth, if it were shown them what is the difference between right and left: that is, between God’s truth and human falsehood.

Because they do not yet know this, they are like little children who, through the weakness of infancy, do not know the difference between right and left: that is, which hand, right or left, is stronger and more suited to every use, because they have not yet experienced it. For as they have only recently come forth from the womb, both little arms and both hands are still equally weak for the time being. There were more than one hundred and twenty thousand such persons in that Nineveh, being a great city. For, since it extended over a journey of three days, it is not incredible that there should have been in it such a multitude merely of little children and infants at the breast, who, as has already been said, had acquired no experience of which of their right and left hands was stronger.

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Micah

[Col. 0439]

192 Micah, sixth in the order of the twelve prophets, is to be believed, in accordance with his name, which is interpreted “humility,” to have been humble in his own eyes. For the mystery of the coming Christ, the Son of God, which from the beginning was revealed not to the proud but to the humble, as he himself declared in his own words—“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI)—was so revealed to Micah that he knew and foretold not only that Christ would come or be born, but even the place of his birth. For he says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V).

Even proud persons could not doubt that this was said through this humble man concerning Christ the ruler and the place of his birth. For when Herod asked them where Christ was to be born, they answered that he ought to be born in Bethlehem of Judah, using this present testimony. Micah seems to have received beyond the other prophets the grace also of designating the place of his birth—apart from holy David, who recalls that with great affliction, vigils, and prayers he sought and found this very thing, when he says: “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, made a vow to the God of Jacob: ‘If I enter the tent of my house, if I ascend the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob’” (Ps. CXXXI).

For by these words, according to the literal sense, he declares that, after receiving the promises concerning Christ’s birth from his seed, he also wished to know where he would be born; and for this desire he vowed that he would grant no rest to his body until he had first gained knowledge of the thing he desired. Then, when he immediately adds, “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah” (ibid.), he plainly declares that it was revealed to him while he prayed that Christ’s birth would take place in Bethlehem, his city, because Ephrathah itself is Bethlehem.

What was revealed to David while he prayed with such earnestness, this man too received by no small grace—humble according to his name, born in Moresheth, which is interpreted “inheritance,” and which was a village of no great size. The mystery of that name likewise suits him, as it does all those whose inheritance is the Word of the Lord and who can say with David: “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart” (Ps. CXVIII).

This man, as has been said, is sixth in the order of the twelve prophets; placed, as it were, in the heart of the volume, he contains profound mysteries and is difficult to investigate. Therefore, since it is difficult and may be judged rash to search into such depths after the studies of the great Fathers, we who follow as the last might now think that we ought to desist from the intention of writing. Yet meanwhile such weakness of mind reveals itself in us that, admonished by its consideration, we remember the verse: “My soul has slumbered through weariness; strengthen me in your words” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

For we suffer weariness in the leisure of the present life and, as if sleeping, make way for the vain phantasms of thoughts. Nor is there anything besides a study of this kind that can strengthen the state of our mind, poor and sluggish as it is, after the likeness of the servant who received neither five talents nor two, but only one (Matt. XXV). The one talent is understanding, with which our perversity knows itself to have been endowed. Therefore we must flee the example of the wicked servant, who hid his talent by digging it into the ground and brought back not even the interest of some good discourse.

[Col. 0441] Whatever judgment others may make of our intention, we profess that our purpose is, by meditating and writing, to disclose the weariness of this present life, console our exile, and acquire as an inheritance the testimonies of Christ, the Son of God, for ever. Therefore, attending to him who says to all his servants, “Trade until I come” (Luke XIX), let us seek profit—profit also from this prophet.

193 COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET MICAH

BOOK ONE

[Col. 0441]

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0441A]

“The word of the Lord which came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.”

The Word of the Lord, which is accustomed to descend to the prophets, descended also to Micah, whose name, as has been said, means “humility.” He came from Moresheth, a humble place and a village of no great size; its name signifies “heir” in our language, as was also said above.

The principal purpose of this Word of the Lord, this prophetic word, is, as in the other prophets, to proclaim the impending ruin of the Israelite people, whose restoration from the multitude of the Gentiles must take place through Christ’s coming. The fall of Israel is twofold: inwardly, they fall away from the grace of God or eternal life; outwardly, they are led captive by the hands of enemies from the land which the Lord gave them to possess. Both evils, both this prophet and the other prophets foretell with groaning, and they receive consolation in the coming Christ whom they announce.

It is therefore pleasing first to distinguish this prophecy according to its divisions. For, if we observe rightly, the things we have mentioned are repeated three times in this prophet: namely, the complaint or lamentation over the falling Israelites, who, like natural branches produced from a good root, were broken off through unbelief; and consolation concerning Christ’s coming, through whose grace unnatural branches from the wild olive were grafted in from among the Gentiles (Rom. XI).

First, in the opening, after stirring attention to hear, it runs thus: [Col. 0441C] “Hear, all peoples; and let the earth and its fullness attend.” He begins the rejection of that nation and the causes of its rejection thus: “All this is in Jacob’s wickedness and in the sins of the house of Israel. What is Jacob’s wickedness? Is it not Jerusalem?” Beginning and proclaiming in this way as far as: “Would that I were a man without the Spirit, and would rather speak falsehood: ‘I will pour out for you wine and drunkenness’; and this people will have one upon whom it is poured out” (Mic. II), he immediately consoles the faith of the fathers over the loss of their carnal children in Christ, through whom their losses are restored from among the Gentiles. For he says: “Gathering I will gather Jacob; I will bring together the remnant of Israel wholly into one; I will set him as a flock in a fold, like sheep in the midst of pens; they will make a tumult because of the multitude of people. For the one opening the way will go up before them; he will divide, and they will pass through the gate and go out by it; their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head” (ibid.).

Then, repeating it a second time, he says: “Hear, princes of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel: is it not yours to know judgment—you who hate the Lord and love evil?” etc., as far as: “Therefore because of you Zion shall be ploughed as a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the Temple the high places of forests” (Mic. III). [Col. 0442A] Immediately, promising the consolation already mentioned in Christ, he says: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains and shall be exalted above the hills; peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall prophesy” (Mic. IV), etc.

Among these things he also foretells the place of the birth of that same Christ in these words: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel” (Mic. V).

Then, repeating for the third time, he says: “Hear what the Lord says: Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice,” etc., as far as: “For the son dishonors his father, the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are those of his household” (Mic. VI, 7). By these words, of course, the condemnation of the Jewish or Israelite nation for unbelief is proclaimed. Immediately the election of the Gentiles consoles itself in Christ through the mouth of the same prophet in this way: “But I will look to the Lord and wait for God my Savior,” etc., to this conclusion: “He will return and have mercy upon us. He will cast down our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. You will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from ancient days” (Mic. VII).

Having observed these things, we judge that the darkness of which it is written in the Psalm, [Col. 0442C] “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII)—that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets—has been illumined. For the prophet is illumined by this lampstand, which is Christ, while he both predicts and laments the falls of Abraham’s seed or the Israelite nation, which occurred at different times and through various events, and, foreseeing the restoration to come from the Gentiles through Christ, rejoices spiritually.

Therefore the Word of the Lord is this Scripture: that is, a prophetic testimony concerning the coming of Christ, who is the Word of the Lord. This Word came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah: namely, in the same times, or under the same kings, in which Hosea and Isaiah prophesied, except for Uzziah, under whom Micah did not prophesy.

[Col. 0442D] “Which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem”: this title contains more than that of any of the others. For of none of them is it written both “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem,” but either “concerning Judah and Jerusalem,” or “concerning Israel”—that is, concerning the ten [Col. 0443A] tribes which from the days of Jeroboam had been divided from the house of David and from Judah, whose capital was Jerusalem.

This Micah the Morasthite alone—humble according to his name, born in a small village, heir of that Word which was to be placed not in a royal city nor on the golden bed of princes, but in little Bethlehem and in a manger, incarnate from a poor Virgin—received great authority from the Spirit’s strength, so that he might see and thunder judgments upon both kingdoms, indeed upon the two divisions of one kingdom or nation: that is, upon Samaria and Jerusalem.

This is clear from what follows. For example, when he says: “I will make Samaria like a heap of stones in a field when a vineyard is planted,” etc. Again: “Therefore because of you Zion shall be ploughed as a field and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones” (Mic. III).

We shall now enter upon the sequence of the prophetic discourse.

“Hear, all peoples; let the earth and its fullness give heed; and let the Lord God be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. For behold, the Lord will go forth from his holy place; he will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth. The mountains beneath him shall be consumed, and the hills shall be split like wax before fire, like waters rushing down a steep descent.”

What does such an opening mean? Why does he summon all peoples to listen? Of what matter does he desire the Lord God to be their witness? We inquire and desire to know the prophet’s concern: for what cause is he concerned, and what is the source of his great anxiety? We think indeed that we already perceive [Col. 0443C] the cause for which the soul of a faithful, devout lover of the divine name is distressed. For he knows the fickleness of peoples who have no knowledge of God, and he fears that what he foresaw God would do to the Israelite nation—the nation with which he had made a covenant, whose God he was, among whom he had been known—may redound among them to the reproach of the divine name. This, I say, he fears: lest the nations should at some time say, “Where is their God?” (Ps. 113), or at least, “Where are the faithfulness and power of their God?”

Such concern truly proves a person faithful to God—the character which we read that holy Moses first possessed, he who was faithful in all God’s house. For when the Lord, angered because of the calf which they had made, said, [Col. 0443D] “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Let me alone, that my wrath may burn against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32), Moses prayed to the Lord his God: “I beseech you,” he said, “let not the Egyptians say: ‘He brought them out deceitfully, in order to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth.’ Let your anger cease, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people” (ibid.).

Likewise, elsewhere, when they had disparaged the land which the scouts had examined, and the Lord said, “Therefore I shall strike them with pestilence and consume them” (Num. 14), Moses replied: “Then the Egyptians, from whose midst you brought this people out, will hear that you have killed so great a multitude as though one person, and will say: ‘He was unable to bring this people into the land concerning which he had sworn; therefore he killed them in the wilderness’” (ibid.).

Joshua too, when he immediately fell before the ark of the Lord and cried out, “Ah, Lord God, what shall I say when I see Israel turning its back before its enemies?” (Josh. 7), added this also, as the greatest consideration after the rest: “And what will you do for your great name?” (ibid.).

Thus we perceive this prophet too crying out from the same concern: since the sentence can no longer be recalled and the Lord’s anger cannot be appeased, and Israel must migrate from its land and be led into captivity, let the peoples at least know the causes and not blaspheme the name of the Lord. For Israel’s abandonment is not due to God’s changeableness but to his truth; not to unfaithfulness but to judgment; not to lack of power but to justice. Let all recognize that, although he has abandoned that people to whom—or for whose sake—he swore to their fathers, nevertheless [Col. 0444B] “the Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144).

He was especially concerned, however, about the Philistines, a nation which had been Israel’s enemy above all others from the very departure from Egypt and which was more troublesome to Israel once it had settled in the land of promise. Among the Philistine nation, moreover, the Gittites were bitterer enemies because of Goliath and the other sons of Rapha, or Orpah, who fell by the hand of David and his servants, as we read in the Book of Kings (1 Sam. 17). Therefore he later says: “Do not report it in Gath; do not weep with tears”—that is understood to mean, because they undoubtedly will not sympathize with you, but will exult over you and mock the name of the Lord.

Therefore, he says, “Hear, all peoples, and let the earth [Col. 0444C] and its fullness give heed”: namely, so that you may know the Lord’s judgment, and the reasons for which he has turned into an enemy against those over whom his name was invoked, whose fathers he received into friendship, and to whom he swore to give the land from which he now makes their children depart.
