Hear the causes of these evils; and let the Lord God be a witness against you—bearing witness for himself and defending himself, that the covenant which he made with them was broken not on his side but on the people’s side.

For if, before bringing this evil upon them, he had not foretold it himself through his prophets and specified its causes, it would not be surprising, O peoples, if God seemed blameworthy to you; indeed, there would be no basis on which his judgment or justice could be defended adequately before you. And if at some time you were told, [Col. 0444D] “Turn to this living and true God, who is called the God of the Hebrews, and concerning whom the psalm speaks: ‘God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel’” (Ps. 75), perhaps he would seem suspect to you as a God who is not faithful: he who had been known and now hid his face and became unknown, abandoning without cause, through a random change of mind, those whom he had once received. You therefore would not set your heart upon him or entrust yourselves to him.

Let the Lord God himself therefore be a witness against you, “the Lord from his holy temple”: that is, from the dwelling-place of the hearts of his faithful prophets, who are his temple, whom he inhabits through faith. Through our mouth let him speak on his own behalf and bear witness concerning himself: that Jerusalem’s abandonment is not his will; that he would not abandon her unless he himself had first been abandoned by her; and that he may declare what the people did against him, how they withdrew, and how they despised hearing him when he called them back. Thus God was necessarily obliged to do what immediately follows.

What is that? “For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth; the mountains beneath him shall be consumed, and the hills shall be split like wax before fire, like waters rushing down a steep descent.”

The meaning is this: behold, the Lord will withdraw and remove all help [Col. 0445A] from his former people, where, or in whom, he was known as anyone is known in his own place. He will go forth from there; and by the very event of their disasters and perpetual captivity it will become manifest that he has truly gone forth and withdrawn from that place which was his own.

When it is said, “and he will come down,” it must be understood as in this passage: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have carried out in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18). He will come down, then—understand, not for their good, but as he came down to visit or avenge the sins of the Sodomites. For these people too, as another prophet testifies, “proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not hide it” (Isa. 3).

“And he will tread upon the high places of the earth,” precisely because they are high: that is, because they sin by being proud and are proud by sinning, and—what is most condemnable—exalt themselves in their own estimation despite being creatures of earth. “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10). Therefore he will tread and trample them down because of their pride. “And the mountains shall be consumed”: that is, the sinners themselves, lofty in their own eyes, whose pride first became manifest in this, that, preferring Jeroboam for themselves, they despised humble David, saying, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (1 Kgs. 12).

These mountains—that is, the highest rulers—and the hills—that is, those of intermediate rank—will be consumed and split like wax before the fire beneath him, whose wrath cannot be endured. And just as waters running down a steep descent do not return upward, so they, once fallen into captivity among the Assyrians, will not be recalled. For Judah’s migration into Babylon [Col. 0445D] was indeed to be recalled for a time, but afterwards, under the Romans, it was to be dispersed utterly. The captivity of the ten tribes among the Assyrians, however, was never to be, nor is it, restored.

When the Lord God has thus gone forth from that place which was his own, do not suppose, O peoples, that he has acted from changeableness or that the fault lies with him. What, then? “All this is because of Jacob’s transgression and the sins of the house of Israel.” All guilt comes from Jacob; all cause comes from Israel. Jacob has transgressed in every wickedness; Israel has violated the Lord’s covenant by many sins. But “God,” Moses says, “is faithful, without any iniquity, just and upright” (Deut. 32); as the Psalmist says, “For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91).

“What is Jacob’s transgression? Is it not Samaria? What are Judah’s high places? Is it not Jerusalem?” As though he said: Jacob’s transgression—that is, that of the ten tribes—needs no demonstration, because it is plainly known and public. Samaria itself is transgression, because throughout the kingdom whose capital is Samaria golden calves are publicly worshipped as God, along with Baal and the other monstrous gods. There the prophets of the Lord were killed, and Jezebel killed very many of them (1 Kgs. 18).

Likewise Jerusalem, Judah’s capital, and that temple once belonging to the Lord, has become a kind of lofty idol, especially since Athaliah, Jezebel’s daughter, reigned there and introduced or increased there a flood of idolatry.

“And I will make Samaria like a heap of stones in a field when a vineyard is planted; I will cast her stones down into the valley and uncover her foundations. All her carved images shall fall; all her wages shall be burned with fire; and I will make all her idols into destruction. For they were gathered from a harlot’s wages, and they shall return to a harlot’s wages.”

The phrase “and I will make Samaria” is connected with what was written a little earlier, where he said: “And the valleys shall be split like wax before fire, like waters rushing down a steep descent.” The comparison is quite fitting: Samaria is made like a heap of stones in a field when a vineyard is planted. Such a pile of stones is a very weak structure, because it lacks mortar and one stone does not adhere to another.

For Samaria always had dissensions, especially among its kings, so frequently replaced—some killed and others succeeding them, or rather invading in their place. Thus it happened that until the day of the final [Col. 0446C] captivity they never cohered among themselves: divided against one another, they who had divided themselves both from God and from David’s house.

Now the vineyard mentioned here was planted at the time when, with as many shoots as there were chosen people of that nation, it was transplanted from Egypt and planted after the nations had been expelled. Its shoots were those belonging to him who says, “I am the vine” (John 15): namely, those having faith in him who was still to come, just as we, by believing that he has come and by abiding in him, are shoots of the same vine. But Samaria—and all the multitude of fleshly Israel, divided and not remaining in that faith or promise—differed in a certain way from that already mentioned election as much as a heap of stones differs from a planted vineyard. That heap is not a vineyard, though it is gathered on account of the vineyard that has been planted.

The comparison is therefore fitting when he says: “And I will make Samaria like a heap of stones in a field when a vineyard is planted,” adding, “and I will cast her stones down into the valley and uncover her foundations.” This is as though he said: I shall deliver the ten tribes into captivity and reveal the causes of that captivity.

What he subsequently adds—“All her carved images shall fall; all her wages shall be burned with fire; and I will make all her idols into destruction”—belongs to the same uncovering of her foundations. For having carved images or idols in one’s possession is like a house’s resting upon corrupt foundations and therefore being unable to stand.

“For,” he says, [Col. 0447A] “they were gathered from a harlot’s wages, and they shall return to a harlot’s wages.” The meaning is this: Samaria, like a prostitute who gathers very much from the shameful trade of her body, likewise gathered gold and silver for herself. The Lord testifies to this when he says in another prophet: “Their mother has committed fornication; she who conceived them has been put to shame. For she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my waters, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’ And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver and gold for her, which they made into Baal” (Hos. 2), and the rest, which he concludes thus:

“These wages are mine, which my lovers gave me” (ibid.).

Although the Lord himself multiplied for her the gold and silver from which she made idols for herself, yet because she did not know this but attributed them instead to her lovers and called them their wages, he now rightly says, “They were gathered from a harlot’s wages,” and immediately adds, “and they shall return to a harlot’s wages.”

“To a harlot’s wages” is as though he said, “to nothing,” because a harlot’s wages are reckoned as nothing. Scripture testifies to this when it says, “The price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread” (Prov. 6). She falsely called the things which God had given her the wages of her lovers; but she was truly a harlot, because, as the history in the Book of Kings testifies, that same capital, Samaria, was born—that is, founded—as though by fornication, [Col. 0447C] and as soon as it was founded it prostituted itself to Baal.

For it is written thus: “Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver; he built upon it and named the city which he had built Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill” (1 Kgs. 16). When, six years later, he had died, it is again written: “Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord beyond all who were before him. Nor was it enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; he also took as wife Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, went and served Baal, and worshipped him. He set up an altar in the temple of Baal which he had built in Samaria, and planted a grove” (ibid.).

Certainly the soul of Omri, Samaria’s founder, was a harlot, as were those of the other kings who committed fornication with the golden calves; Jezebel was a harlot of demons; and with her the soul of her husband Ahab, together with the entire people of the new city, immediately began to commit fornication with Baal. Samaria, therefore, was truly a harlot.

The prophet prophesies all these things in such a manner that he grieves that what he says is true and cannot remain unfulfilled. Hence there immediately follows: “Because of this I shall lament and howl; I shall go stripped and naked; I shall make lamentation like that of dragons, and mourning like that of ostriches, because her wound is hopeless; because it has come as far as Judah and touched the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem.”

This is rightly understood according to the literal sense: namely, that while lamenting and howling for the impending captivity of his people, [Col. 0448A] he went stripped of clothing and naked, displaying the inward grief of his soul by the outward state of his body, or displaying the misery of those who were to be taken captive. We read that Isaiah too did this by the Lord’s command: “Go and loose the sackcloth from your loins and remove your sandal from your feet” (Isa. 20); and subsequently: “As my servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot, this shall be a sign and portent of three years over Egypt and Ethiopia; so the king of the Assyrians shall threaten the captivity of Egypt and the deportation of Ethiopia” (ibid.).

When he then adds, “I shall make lamentation like that of dragons and mourning like that of ostriches,” he declares very sorrowfully that his mourning and lamentation for that people will by no means be beneficial or heard. Who sympathizes with dragons as they sound their fearful hissing when they are overcome? Who pities ostriches that leave their eggs in the dust, when the creature itself does not pity itself or its own nature?

Other Scriptures too testify that this people deserved such a comparison. Jeremiah says in the Lamentations: “The daughter of my people is cruel like an ostrich in the wilderness” (Lam. 4). And John the Baptist says: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3).

Therefore, “I shall make lamentation like that of dragons and mourning like that of ostriches”: that is, lamentation deserving no compassion and mourning to be soothed by no consolation. For even if dragons grieve, they have no pious groan capable of evoking sympathy, but the tumult of burning anger, against which one must guard. Likewise, even if ostriches mourn, their innate cruelty remains; their empty folly cannot be bent to the natural care or concern for their offspring.

Why do you say this? “Because,” he says, “her wound is hopeless; because it has come as far as Judah and touched the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem.” I speak thus because there is no hope of mercy from the Lord, or of release from captivity, for the ten tribes; as he himself says through another prophet: “I shall no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel” (Hos. 1).

“It has come as far as Judah and touched the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem.” The books of Kings and of Isaiah testify that this happened. For after devastating Samaria, the Assyrian came even to Jerusalem, at the time when Rabshakeh was sent to taunt them (2 Kgs. 18; Isa. [Col. 0448D] 36). At that time, however, Judah’s or Jerusalem’s wound was not hopeless as Israel’s or Samaria’s was. For the angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in Sennacherib’s camp; but later Jerusalem was overthrown by the Chaldeans, and its people were led to Babylon (2 Kgs. 19).

Later still, Jerusalem’s wound became hopeless at the hands of the Romans, and the Jews were more grievously struck, led captive among all nations, than the ten tribes had been when the Assyrian carried them away.

It follows: “Do not report it in Gath; do not weep with tears. In the house of dust, sprinkle yourselves with dust.” As though he said: This has befallen you as an addition to your miseries: when you suffer, no one sympathizes, because, having offended God, you are hateful also to all the nations.

Therefore I said, “I shall make lamentation like that of dragons,” because when dragons are overcome, whether by elephants or by people, and consequently sound a great hissing, no person comes running in order to grieve over their death. Dragons and human beings have natural enmities toward one another. So too, while you are captured by enemies, none of the neighboring nations will sympathize; none will fail to rejoice at your evils.

Gath, a city of Palestine, will rejoice still more: Goliath and his brothers, who fell by the hand of David and his servants, came from there (2 Sam. 21). It will therefore console itself more than the rest by rejoicing in your misery. Do not then report it in Gath—indeed, wish for what is impossible, that it may not hear of your disasters. Do not weep with tears, for your weeping will become its joy and laughter. Conceal your weeping; do not let grief burst forth in sobs, lest your adversaries rejoice.

Do not go outside; instead, in the house of dust sprinkle yourselves with dust. In the collapsing house, let only you yourselves see yourselves sprinkled with the ash of its ruins. He says these things as though giving counsel; yet these words are not words of reason but of grief, which often admits no reason. For however much the captives conceal themselves and hold back their tears, it is impossible for their calamity to be unknown to their enemies, especially to their neighboring enemies, as the Philistines were.

Nor does the Judge—namely, the Divinity—delay to give a definite sentence from the prophet’s heart and mouth, which he pronounces thus: “Pass on, you fair dwelling, disgraced with shame.”

He calls Samaria “the fair dwelling,” since it was situated in the most beautiful and fertile region of Judah. Therefore he says to it: O you who dwell in a most fruitful region, you who are disgraced with shame, pass on and be led into captivity, bearing the judgment of your disgrace. Then he immediately turns to us and says: “She who dwells at the outlet has not gone forth.”

Whether he says this of the same fair dwelling, that is, Samaria, or rather of Jerusalem, of which he speaks openly in the following verse, is uncertain. But if it is said of Samaria, the meaning is: “She who dwells at the outlet has not gone forth,” that is, she stands at the very gates of Assyrian captivity. As soon as she is moved from her own borders, she enters enemy territory. Yet, however near it may be, it is not sufficiently clear how she who is commanded to pass on and does pass on can suitably be said not to have gone forth.

But if one prefers to understand this as said of Jerusalem, the meaning is: You inhabitants of the fair dwelling, namely Samaria, pass on now; but Jerusalem on this occasion does not go forth, though she dwells at the outlet—that is, although her departure or migration has long been prepared, it is delayed for a little while, because Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah together supplicated God and held it back by their prayers (2 Kgs. 19; Isa. 37). This is said according to the comparison of someone about to depart and already standing in the doorway, whose departure is certain indeed but is delayed for certain reasons.

It is clear to anyone who considers the matter that Jerusalem [Col. 0450A] was then delivered from the hand of the Assyrians who had carried the ten tribes captive, but was later handed over to the Chaldeans and led to Babylon. Of this Jerusalem the following immediately speaks:

“The neighboring house shall receive lamentation from you, she who stood by herself, because she was weakened for good, she who dwells in bitterness; because evil has come down from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem: the tumult of chariots, an astonishment to the inhabitant of Lachish.”

For Jerusalem, which meanwhile stood by herself and which, as we have said, did not then go forth, had as her neighboring—indeed, kindred—house Israel, namely the ten tribes. Jerusalem received its lamentation from you, O fair dwelling, to whom it was said, “Pass on,” that is, go away captive. She received that lamentation and applied it to her own correction, so that she might be weakened—that is, humbled before God. Thus she stood, because she who dwells in bitterness “was weakened for good.”

The narrative in the Book of Kings and the prophet Isaiah plainly testifies that this weakness was for her good and that these were her bitternesses. For after the ten tribes had been transported, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. He sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to blaspheme the living God and reproach him with loud cries (2 Kgs. 18). When Hezekiah heard through the messengers who came to him with torn garments, he too tore his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord. He sent Eliakim, who was over the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered in sackcloth, [Col. 0450C] to Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet; and they said to him: “Thus says Hezekiah: ‘This day is a day of tribulation, rebuke, and blasphemy, because children have come to birth, but there is no strength to give birth’” (Isa. 37; 2 Kgs. 19), and so forth.

Thus she was weakened and dwelt so deeply in bitterness that she was compared to a woman in labor who has no strength for childbirth, because evil had gone up from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem. And there was “the tumult of a chariot for the astonished inhabitant of Lachish,” a city in the tribe of Judah which Sennacherib had captured, and from which he sent his servants to Hezekiah. His chariots were so numerous that they were rightly called “chariots of astonishment.”

He says that this evil came down from the Lord because Sennacherib would not have come except by the Lord’s judgment or permission. Sennacherib himself, eager to claim this knowledge and grossly abusing it, added no small falsehood of his own. For he said: “Did I come up against this place to destroy it without the Lord’s will? The Lord said to me: ‘Go up against this land and destroy it’” (Isa. 36).

He aptly says that the evil came down to Jerusalem’s gate, because Sennacherib’s messengers, through whom he had sent these messages, came to Jerusalem and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field; and they called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward of the household, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went out to them (ibid.).

But this prophet says, “She who dwells at the outlet has not gone forth”—understand, although Rabshakeh cried: “Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: Make with me that which is useful to you; make with me a blessing, and come out to me” (Isa. 36), and so forth. She does indeed dwell at the outlet, as has already been said, because the Babylonian captivity was near; but she did not then go forth, nor was he himself permitted to enter. For the Lord said through Isaiah: “He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it, nor occupy it with a shield, nor surround it with a siege-work” (Isa. 37), and so forth.

It follows: “The beginning of sin is in the daughter of Zion, because in you have been found the transgressions of Israel. Therefore he shall send messengers over the inheritance of Gath; the house of falsehood shall be a deception to the kings of Israel. I shall yet bring an heir to you, O inhabitant of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come as far as Adullam.”

These are names of cities in the tribe of Judah: Lachish, Mareshah, and Adullam. Gath, however, as has already been said, is the name of a city of Palestine. Nevertheless this entire passage is obscure, because Scripture records no events involving these places in that Assyrian invasion, except what they shared with the other cities: the king of Assyria went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. The only exception is that Rabshakeh is recorded as having been sent from Lachish to Jerusalem to King Hezekiah with a great force.

Since, then, nothing from the Scriptures supports an interpretation that might make this passage clearer, a reader can demand nothing further than the words of blessed Jerome himself, who discusses it uncertainly [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Commentary on Micah*, Book I, chapter 1, cols. 1060–1061, vol. XXV.] and, as he himself admits, steers his little boat as best he can among rocks and most jagged crags.

[Col. 0451C] “The chariots and horsemen of the Assyrians,” he says, “will therefore come to you, O city of Lachish, devoted to idols, because the transgressions of Israel have also been found in you, and you were the beginning of idolatry in Judah. For through you, as through a gate, the impiety of the ten tribes migrated to Jerusalem. Nor will the tumult of the chariot come only through Lachish, but also upon Gath, the capital of Palestine, of which I said above, ‘Do not report it in Gath.’ For he will send his Assyrian marauders, whom he calls messengers, and will possess the house of idolatry and city of falsehood, which was a source of deception to the kings of Israel.

“What follows, ‘I shall yet bring an heir to you, O inhabitant of Mareshah,’ makes a fine play upon the name. Since Mareshah means ‘inheritance,’ he calls the coming of enemies into it ‘heirs.’ And Mareshah—that is, the inheritance which is glorious among the cities of Israel—will come as far as Adullam, a city of Judah. Thus where it says ‘of glory,’ the genitive singular of *this glory* is intended, not the nominative plural, *these glories*.

“Or we may understand it this way: the captivity of Israel which comes upon Lachish, Gath, and Mareshah will also come as far as Adullam. ‘The glory of Israel’ should be read more emphatically, so that by antiphrasis disgrace or devastation is meant.”

He now repeats in other words what he said a little earlier, “Pass on, you fair dwelling, disgraced with shame”: “Make yourself bald and cut off your hair for the children of your delight; widen your baldness like the eagle, because they have been led captive from you.”

There, when he says “pass on,” the meaning is undoubtedly “you will pass on”; and here, “make yourself bald and cut off your hair, and widen your baldness,” means, “You will be made bald and shorn, and you will widen your baldness.” Yet when he says, “like the eagle,” he briefly indicates that other children will be restored in place of the former ones, so that either the prophet himself or anyone else who understands spiritually may not lack consolation in Israel’s very baldness and shearing, for which he could grieve.

For how, or for what purpose, does the eagle become bald or enlarge its baldness? Clearly, when it has grown old, at a fixed time it loses its old feathers and remains bare of plumage; but when new ones grow, it itself becomes young again. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102).

Therefore the prophetic Spirit mystically intimates that in place of the children of delight—that is, the children of fleshly Israel, who had fallen from faith and were soon to be carried captive from their land—others would be substituted: not children of flesh but children of promise and faith. Thus Israel, becoming young again like an eagle renewed with bright feathers and wings, would fly into heaven. This is now taking place and does not cease to take place until the end of the age: believers from all nations are reborn like new feathers, while the fleshly children, like old feathers, are dispersed in perpetual captivity among all nations.

It follows.

## Chapter II
Woe to you who devise what is useless and work evil upon your beds. In the light of morning they do it, because their hand is against the Lord. [Col. 0452C] They coveted fields and took them by violence; they seized houses and oppressed a man and his household, a man and his inheritance. Therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, I am devising evil against this family, from which you shall not remove your necks; nor shall you walk proudly, because it is a most evil time.”

Thus far he had said that, because of the wickedness of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel, Samaria was to be delivered up, and evil was to come down from the Lord upon the gate of Jerusalem. He had wished all peoples, and the earth with its fullness, to know the justice of the Lord, thus taking vengeance upon His former people; but he had not stated the manner of their wickedness or sins—that is, whether they had sinned in such a way as to deserve to endure so great a wrath. Therefore, that God’s justice may be made more manifest, [Col. 0452D] and that they themselves may be known to be without excuse: “Woe,” he says, “to those who devise what is useless and work evil upon their beds”; and immediately, turning to his hearers, he says: “In the light of morning they do it, because their hand is against the Lord,” and so forth.

He expresses the character of their sin especially in what he says: “In the light of morning they do it, because their hand is against the Lord.” For what is “in the light of morning” except, as though he said, “not in ignorance”? And what is “because their hand is against the Lord” except, as though he said, “not through weakness, but through pride”—or, as the Psalmist says, “their iniquity has proceeded as from fatness” (Ps. [Col. 0453A] 72)? For this is the worst kind of sin: when someone is known to sin not through ignorance, not through weakness, but knowingly through pride.

Indeed, if someone sins through ignorance or transgresses through weakness, pardon is still near to him. Hence the Psalmist, firmly holding the anchor of hope, says: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24). He used “youth” for weakness, because youth itself is a great weakness of the flesh. But the proud sinner provokes the Lord, and the Lord, as the same Psalmist says, “according to the multitude of His wrath, will not seek” (Ps. 10); that is, He will not seek again one who is perishing, nor offer him pardon, because He is greatly angered.

Woe, then, to you, O Jeroboam, whose sins are now chiefly at issue, where it was said above [Col. 0453B]: “All this is in the wickedness of Jacob and in the sins of the house of Israel” (Mic. 1). For you caused Israel to sin (3 Kings 21); and therefore you alone suffice, by way of example, to be brought forward in the midst of all those against whom woe is pronounced, because they devise what is useless and work evil upon their beds. In the light of morning—that is, knowingly, or with deliberation and, as it were, wisely—they do it, because their hand is against the Lord.

For Scripture plainly testifies concerning you thus: “And Jeroboam said in his heart: ‘Now the kingdom will return to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, the heart of this people will turn to their lord Rehoboam king of Judah; they will kill me and return to him.’ And, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves, [Col. 0453C] and said to them: ‘Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt’” (3 Kings 12).

This is what you devised that was useless. Useless, I say, because it did not profit you—indeed, it was ruinous, because it harmed you exceedingly. For if you had not devised this, you could have reigned better and longer; because the Lord had spoken to you through the prophet thus: “If, therefore, you hear all that I command you, and walk in my ways, then I will be with you, and I will build you a faithful house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you” (3 Kings 11).

But because you devised this, you not only failed, by devising and doing it, to secure the kingdom for yourself; you also most unhappily cast down yourself and your throne, according to the words of the same Lord speaking through the same prophet [Col. 0453D]: “Because you have done thus, behold, I will bring evils upon the house of Jeroboam; and I will strike off from Jeroboam everyone who urinates against a wall, both the confined and the last in Israel. I will sweep away the remnant of the house of Jeroboam, as dung is usually swept away until it is clean. Those of Jeroboam who die in the city shall the dogs eat; but those who die in the field shall the birds of heaven devour, because the Lord has spoken” (3 Kings 14).

Therefore, what you devised was exceedingly useless; and thus you deservedly ought to have become an example to all who similarly devise what is useless and work evil upon their beds. Who are they? Clearly, all such as are not led into it by another, but fashion and invent evil out of their own hearts, being malicious; [Col. 0454A] and Scripture plainly reproves you for having done this when it says, “And Jeroboam said in his heart” (3 Kings 12), and so forth.

Hence another prophet, speaking of your calf, says: “It too is from Israel; a craftsman made it” (Hos. 8). You are that craftsman, most notorious among all craftsmen who work, or have worked, evil upon their beds—that is, who have invented it out of their own hearts; who do it in the light of morning, that is, with deliberation, not ignorantly but knowingly, as has already been said. This is proved most particularly by the fact that their hand is against the Lord—that is, because, when reproved, they vigorously defend their sin. You did this: reproved by the prophet, you stretched out your hand against the Lord, as it is written: “When the king heard the word of the man [Col. 0454B] of God, who had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, ‘Seize him!’ And the hand which he had stretched out against him withered, and he could not draw it back to himself” (3 Kings 13).

Such men, as they are wickedly strong against the Lord, are also strongly wicked against their brothers and neighbours over whom they prevail. Therefore he immediately adds: “They coveted fields and took them by violence; they seized houses and oppressed a man and his household, a man and his inheritance.”

One example is enough to show that woe belongs to such men—namely, Ahab king of Israel, who coveted Naboth’s vineyard; and because Naboth would not give it, Ahab, together with his wife, falsely accused that man and his inheritance. The accusation was as follows: “Take,” she said, “two men, sons of Belial, [Col. 0454C] against him, and let them bear false witness: ‘Naboth has cursed God and the king.’ Then lead him out and stone him, that he may die” (3 Kings 21). And so it was done.

Such were the wicked deeds of Jacob, and such the sins of the house of Israel. Among its kings these two, Jeroboam and Ahab together with his wife Jezebel, are most notorious for their crimes. Neither kings nor common people departed from their sins; indeed, in the end they advanced so far into worse things that they devised what was useless and worked evil against the Lord Christ himself, so that they falsely accused such a man and his inheritance when, on seeing Him, they said: “This is the heir; let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours” (Mark 12).

Woe, therefore, to them. For thus says the Lord: “Behold, I devise evil against this family, from which you shall not remove [Col. 0454D] your necks; nor shall you walk proudly, because their time is most evil.”

We see that this happened. The ten tribes submitted to the yoke of Assyrian power, from which they neither could nor can remove their necks. The tribe of Judah, carried into Babylon, did indeed again remove its neck from that captivity; but, with the Romans again taking them captive, they can no longer raise their necks or walk proudly. For they are contemptible in the sight of all people, and theirs is a time of sufferings, especially because of the city by which they were blinded.

It follows: “In that day a parable shall be taken up against you, and a song shall be sung with sweetness by those who say: ‘By devastation we have been laid waste; the portion of my people has been changed. How does he withdraw [Col. 0455A] from me, when he returns, who divides our regions?’ Therefore there shall be none for you casting the measuring-line of the lot in the assembly of the Lord.”

Those who desire to seek out and investigate the true meaning of the Scriptures recall the hunting of wild beasts, in which practice the question of which dogs are truly hunting-dogs is tested. For those that do not possess such a nature or keenness as to be drawn by an unwearied love of the chase, as soon as they are hindered by thickets, marshes, boulders, or crags, sluggishly forget the fleeing roe-deer or fawn of the stag and return empty to their domestic sleeping-places.

But dogs of good breed, or naturally suited to hunting, are overcome by no obstacle of difficulty. Rather, they go swiftly through rough and trackless places, wherever the delightful scent of the quarry once seen draws them, as though [Col. 0455B] they would die unless they caught it, groaning miserably unless they seized it.

If we are the Lord’s dogs, the meaning of truth is for us the quarry in the densest forest of the holy Scriptures. We run in order that we may seize it; and then we are glad, then we desire to rejoice before Him, if, persistently intent amid all the difficulties of the letter, we bring back a good and useful meaning that builds up the reader and delights him as though he were a guest at a feast.

The present chapter, according to the already mentioned comparison with hunts, is so difficult that because of its difficulty blessed Jerome—an earnest interpreter of meanings and a faithful expositor of the letter—says:

> [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Commentary on Micah*, book I, chapter 2, col. 1168, vol. XXV.]  
> “But if anyone, meditating upon the law of the Lord day and night, has greater diligence, greater ability, leisure, and grace, and can say something more plausible concerning the present [Col. 0455C] chapter, I do not disdain it, I do not envy him; rather, I desire to learn from him what I do not know, and I shall gladly profess myself his disciple—provided that he teaches and does not disparage. For nothing is so easy as to dispute, while idle and asleep, concerning the labour and watchfulness of others.”

He said this because of the difficulty of the present chapter, in which it was thus spoken through this prophet: “In that day a parable shall be taken up against you, and a song shall be sung with sweetness by those who say, ‘By devastation we have been laid waste,’” and so forth, as above.

Jerome, however, gave this interpretation: “As they worked evil against the Lord, so they will endure the evils of perpetual captivity, and they will come into such distress that all their songs and psalms will be turned into mourning, and the people will know how to say nothing else but this: ‘By devastation we have been laid waste,’ or, ‘By misery we have been made miserable.’ For the land of promise, which had first perhaps been divided beyond the Jordan among the two and a half tribes by Moses casting the line (Num. 32), and afterwards apportioned by Joshua among the remaining tribes (Josh. 13), [Col. 0455D] has been divided among the nations by the Roman surveyor. And there was no one to prevent it; rather, since all nations possess it, there is no one among the Jews who possesses the former condition of ancient liberty.”

When Jerome says these things, and many similar things in different places, he makes the hearer into a gaping and barking dog, so that, as in many other cases, in the present passage too, feeling himself still to be beneath the fleeing quarry, he does not cease to pursue it, however much it may flee, [Col. 0456A] like a roe-deer or a fawn of stags.

We say, therefore, that that day—or most evil time—in which he foretold that a parable would be taken up against them and a song sung with sweetness, is the present time. For now we have taken up a parable concerning them, since the Apostle wrote in this way: “Now all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10).

Certainly, the fact that the bodies of those who had crossed the Red Sea and had been baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea were overthrown in the wilderness; the fact that the ten tribes were divided from the house of David and went away captive into Assyria; and the fact that the holy city Jerusalem was consumed by Chaldean fire and Judah migrated into Babylon—all this is a great parable, a parable taken up against all of them for us.

[Col. 0456B] Finally, in accordance with these events, Mother Church considers the losses that have often occurred among the multitude of believers, or among Christians in name only; and, for the correction or consolation of her children, she often recounts parables of this kind. Thus, when false brethren, who appear to profess the same faith, are judged unworthy of the land of eternal promise because of evil conduct, they are, as it were, overthrown in the wilderness. Or, when manifest heretics, renouncing the truth of the faith, truly separate themselves from the house of David and make calves of impious doctrines, shining, as it were, with the golden brilliance of eloquent speech, always intent on deceiving the simple.

What shall I say of the Babylonian captivity? Is it only a parable for us, and not also a sweet song? For whenever we sing, [Col. 0456C] “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, O Zion” (Ps. 136), and so forth, a song is sung which has been taken up against them and is fitting for us. For, having our eyes unveiled in Christ, we understand in that captivity—which then happened through Nebuchadnezzar to one people—the universal captivity of the human race that came about through the devil in the transgression of the first man.

To sing in this way is to say: “By devastation we have been laid waste.” This is true, so that we may also truly say: “By death we have died.” For “in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15).

But what follows, “the portion of my people has been changed,” pertains more specifically to some elect and holy person from that nation—for example, to the Apostle—whose people according to the flesh is the Jewish people. For he describes what portion of his people it was in these words: “Whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9).

Let, therefore, either that same Apostle or any other holy and true person from that people say: “The portion of my people has been changed”; that is, all dignity has been taken from the Jews and given to the Gentiles. When this is said and done, a parable concerning the two brothers Jacob and Esau is also taken up against them (Gen. 25), because, according to the bodily event that happened to them, [Col. 0457A] this spiritual mystery takes place: the spiritual birthright of the Jews is changed—that is, given to the supplanting people of the Gentiles.

Certainly, such a taking up of a parable or song is worthy of the present proclamation of the prophetic Spirit, because it is great and pertains to that reception of which the Apostle spoke when he said: “What shall their reception be, but life from the dead?” (Rom. 11).

Such a parable is said “with the sweetness of those who say it.” For such a song is truly sweet—but only to those who say it and know how to say it. Conversely, to those against whom it is spoken according to such a parable, the torment is exceedingly bitter.

Where it says, “the portion of my people has been changed,” in order that the following little verse may cohere, one must understand the voice of one lamenting and saying: “How does he withdraw [Col. 0457B] from me, when he returns, who divides our regions?”

For just as the aforementioned Esau, crying out with a loud cry and weeping with great lamentation, said: “Justly is his name called Jacob, for he has supplanted me now a second time: he first took away my birthright, and now for the second time he has stolen my blessing” (Gen. 27), so the Jewish people, seeing the people believing from among the Gentiles return against it now for a second time and not cease, grieves and is tormented, and says: “How does he withdraw from me, when he returns, who divides our regions?”

For we, returning, divide the regions of the Jews in this: having tasted the sweetness of the birthright which we formerly took—that is, the preaching of the Gospel which we received—we gird ourselves again and enter upon all their Scriptures: the Law, the Prophets, and [Col. 0457C] the Psalms. Christ measures and divides these regions—that is, He opens their meaning for us, so that we may understand. The Jew would wish us to withdraw, at least content with the birthright—that is, with the word of the Gospel, which it was necessary to speak to him first. But we do not desist until, as has been said, by taking hold of all the Scriptures, we show that they have been despoiled and stripped bare of every truth.

Therefore, since according to such a parable this people is Esau, who first lost the birthright and then all the regions of eternal blessing, it is rightly said to it immediately: “Therefore there shall be none for you casting the measuring-line of the lot in the assembly of the Lord.”

And the sense is this: Because you, O carnal people, who consider yourselves the seed of Jacob, have become such that such a parable is rightly taken up concerning you, and the song in which you are sung declares that you are Esau; that you are the unbelieving multitude which, although it crossed the sea, was overthrown in the wilderness and did not enter the land of promise; that you are the crowd which divided itself from the house of David and made golden calves—for this reason no one from your assembly shall be counted among those whom the Lord has called to receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.

It follows: “Do not speak, speaking; it shall not drip upon these; shame shall not overtake them,” says the Lord of the house of Jacob. “Has the Spirit of the Lord been shortened, or are these His thoughts?”

The order of the words is: “O house of Jacob, the Lord says: Do not speak, saying, ‘He will not pour down upon these men; shame will not overtake them.’ Do not speak, saying, ‘Has the Spirit of the Lord been shortened, or are such his thoughts?’”

Now the meaning of this can almost be learned by daily experience. For whenever we speak to them, saying that every person who does not believe in Christ is condemned, and that an unbelieving Jew has no share in salvation through Christ, according to the saying, “He who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3), then, all the more, when we strive to prove this from the more ancient Scriptures, they seize their shield more combatively against us. They make the greatness of their fathers a shield for their hearts, saying that it is impossible for their race to be condemned; and they also say this: “Is God a liar, or is God changeable?” (Num. 23). “Does he change, like a human being, through differing wills, so that formerly we had to undergo circumcision, but now baptism; so that formerly he confirmed a covenant with us and with our fathers, but has now turned to hostility?”

Certainly, just as they now speak concerning the future judgment, so also then, when the prophets foretold the coming of the Assyrians or Chaldeans and that this people would go into captivity because of its sins, they rejected everything said, wished it to be unbelievable, and argued that it was impossible for the holy people, the holy offspring of holy fathers, the holy place, and the beautiful and glorious Temple to be so abandoned. Therefore they said, in accordance with these words: “He will not pour down upon these men, and shame will not overtake them. Has the Spirit of the Lord been shortened, or are such his thoughts?” They said, I mean, that the prophets were liars and blasphemers—or rather, that they ought not to be called prophets at all, but audacious impostors—because they dared to say that wrath ought to pour down from heaven upon Abraham’s children, upon Isaac’s race and Jacob’s stock; that shame would overtake a nation so exalted and honored; that the Spirit of the Lord was said to be so brief that he so quickly repented of the good things he had promised them; and that God, who is unchangeable, was said to have such—that is, such changeable—thoughts.

For they said: “These men have sought not this people’s peace, but its harm.” Therefore, seeing this, the prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—says: “Do not speak, uttering words of this kind. For what? Are not my words good to him who walks uprightly? But, on the contrary, my people has risen up as an adversary.”

It is as though he said: “Why do you say such things, and zealously contend as though on my behalf, declaring that I am a faithful God, a patient and long-suffering God—which, you claim, I would not be if evil poured down from me upon you and shame overtook you? Even when I do this to you, are not my words nevertheless good and prosperous to the one with whom they ought to be so? And who is that, except the one who walks uprightly? Conversely, they must be harsh and adverse to one who does not walk uprightly, who has risen up in opposition—as my people has done. Consult the Law that you received, and it itself will answer what conditions have existed between me and you.”

For example: “Keep therefore the commandments, ceremonies, and judgments which I command you this day to do. If you keep and do them, the Lord your God will keep for you the covenant and mercy which he swore to your fathers” (Deut. 6). “Behold,” he says, “I set before you today blessing and curse: blessing, if you obey the commandments of the Lord your God; curse, if you do not hear the commandments of the Lord your God” (Deut. 11). But behold, my people has not kept my commandments; rather, it has risen up in opposition. Can it now demand, or ought it to demand, that my words should be good to it, as they ought to be to one who walks uprightly, rather than undergo the curse contained in the decree of the conditional Law?

Then, as though the people were asking in what way it had not obeyed the Lord’s commandments but had rather risen up as an adversary, he immediately continues and says: “You have taken the cloak from above the tunic, and you have turned into war those who passed by in simplicity. You have cast the women of my people out from the house of their delights; from their little children you have taken away my praise forever. Arise and go, for you have no rest here. Because of its uncleanness, it shall be destroyed with a most grievous corruption.”

He has supplied the reasons by which the people is convicted of having risen up as an adversary. But the reasons had to be universal—that is, relevant to the whole people—because it was not said of one individual that he had risen up as an adversary, but of the whole people. The address is directed to the whole people: “You have taken the cloak from above the tunic,” and all the rest is expressed in verbs of past time. This would not seem so fitting if he were speaking merely of daily injuries or robberies.

Therefore, from the evidences of Holy Scripture, we must show where, when, and how the people of the Lord so rose up as an adversary that it took the cloak from above the tunic and did these other things; and likewise who he was from whom they took the cloak from above the tunic. Wishing to do this, we first ask why Ahijah the prophet, when speaking with Jeroboam in the word of the Lord concerning the kingdom, signified the matter itself [201] by the new cloak in which he was clothed, tearing it into twelve pieces and saying: “Take ten torn pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom of Solomon from his hand and give you ten tribes” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 11).

He plainly signified the kingdom of Israel by his cloak. Therefore, when the present passage says, “You have taken the cloak from above the tunic,” it leads us to observe that heavenly grace had given Israel and Judah to David, its servant, like a cloak over a tunic, so that he might reign over both. Previously, it had clothed him as with a tunic when it first gave him the kingdom over Judah alone. For he reigned seven years in Hebron over the house of Judah before reigning over all Israel. But when all the tribes came to David in Hebron and anointed him king over themselves—after, as we have said, he had already reigned seven years over the house of Judah—then the Lord added to that same David a cloak as well as a tunic (2 Kings 5).

And appropriately, just as Israel is understood through the cloak, so the house of Judah is understood through the tunic. For just as a tunic clings more closely to the body than a cloak, so the tribe of Judah was nearer to David himself than the other tribes; for he himself came from that tribe.

Therefore, O my people, if you ask why I said, “On the contrary, my people has risen up as an adversary,” behold, I tell you: because you took the cloak from above the tunic—that is, you removed yourselves from David’s seed; you yourselves, the ten tribes, departed from him, in order that you might also depart from me, as indeed you did. For, abandoning my altar and Temple, despising the promises made to David concerning the Seed, which is Christ, you worshiped and did not cease to worship the golden calves which Jeroboam made.

In doing this—or in having long intended to do it—you turned into war those who passed by in simplicity. Who were they? Certainly David himself and his men: mighty men, indeed exceedingly mighty, and as strong as they were, so simple—that is, walking with God and men in good faith and with a single heart. You turned them into war by setting Absalom over yourselves as king against his father (4 Kings [2 Kings] 23), and, after his death, by again following Sheba son of Bichri (2 Kings 20).

Already at that time you nearly took the cloak from above the tunic in the sense explained, because, when Sheba sounded the trumpet and said, “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 12), all Israel separated from David. Thus he remained for a little while without the cloak, clothed only with the tunic, because only his fellow tribesmen, the men of Judah, adhered to him. For he had sinned in the matter of Uriah, and therefore suffered: the Lord withdrew your peace for a short time, though not the grace of his help. For, the Lord being soon merciful to him, he recovered the cloak as well as the tunic—that is, Israel as well as Judah.

But when his son Solomon sinned, not against one man, as David himself had sinned against Uriah, but against God himself, worshiping foreign gods because of his desire for women, then the house of David was weakened and you prevailed in taking the cloak from it; for it could not resist you. Why? “For before this,” says the Lord, “this word”—that is, this judgment—“had come to pass”: namely, that the house of David could not resist because sins demanded it, and that I should abandon you according to the desires of your hearts.

The particular force of the expression should be noted: “You turned into war those who passed by in simplicity.” For “passing over” belongs to the holy elect, who “have no abiding city here, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13), according to the name of the Hebrews, from whom David sprang both in faith and in flesh. For the Hebrew name is rendered in Latin as “passers-over” (*transitores*). Such were David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and the rest of the faithful house of David, between which house and the house of Jeroboam there was always war, as Scripture relates (3 Kings [1 Kings] 14).

In accordance with that likeness, there is now always war, and will be until the end of the age, between those who fix their minds upon the present age and those who strive to pass over to the eternal goods of the age to come. Therefore, he says, “You turned into war those who passed by in simplicity”; and in that war you gained an evil triumph. How? “You have cast the women of my people out from the house of their delights, and from their little children you have taken away my praise forever.”

Who were the women of my people, except the weaker persons among you, who ought to have been my people? And what was the house of delight of such women, except my house in Jerusalem, the house of prayer in which my name was invoked? You cast those women out of that house—that is, the weak and poor, over whom you prevailed, as men are accustomed to prevail over women. You cast them out, I say, by maintaining and compelling observance of that decree of Jeroboam: “Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem; but go and worship the calf, even to Dan” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 12).

Thus, in casting out the women, you took away my praise forever from their little children; that is, you caused the ignorant and wandering multitude to persist in evil, so that they might never depart from the sins of Jeroboam.

Here we should note the threefold distinction among sinners which we are accustomed to observe in Holy Scripture: those who sin through ignorance, those who sin through weakness, and those who sin through pride. For those who sin through pride are precisely those against whom he most vehemently inveighs when he begins, “On the contrary, my people has risen up as an adversary.” Those who consent to sins through weakness are denoted in the next passage: “You have cast the women of my people out from the house of their delights.” But those who sin through ignorance are those of whom he says: “From their little children you have taken away my praise forever.”

All alike are without excuse: both those strong men, destroyers of the simple, who violently despoiled them; and those women who, though they ought to have been men, had womanish courage in such danger, fearing human beings more than God; and those little ones in understanding who lacked the knowledge of God. All alike are struck by one sentence, which he at once pronounces: “Arise and go, for you have no rest here.”

When he says this, that which is well known and ought to be understood must be supplied: “because of the sins of Jeroboam,” or, “because you have not departed from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 10). Thus in the following verse—“Because of its uncleanness, it shall be destroyed with a most grievous corruption”—the present nominative case required by the third-person verb *corrumpetur* (“it shall be destroyed”) is not expressed.

This did not happen through the ignorance or carelessness of an eloquent writer, but through the nature and stern indignation of the prophetic Spirit, which detests the infamous name and judges it superfluous to write in its book the name which the whole Sacred History has denounced in speaking of every king of Israel: “He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin” (ibid.). Therefore, in “because of its uncleanness,” Jeroboam is understood—he whom you, O reader, cannot fail to know. Because of the uncleanness, I say, of him who caused Israel to sin, shall Israel, which embraced his uncleanness, be destroyed with a most grievous corruption.

See, therefore, that you become familiar and at home with Holy Scripture; then you will observe how familiarly the prophetic Spirit, after saying, “Arise and go, for you have no rest here,” turns to you and says: “Because of the uncleanness of Jeroboam, Israel shall be destroyed with a most grievous corruption.” Because of what uncleanness? Surely because of the worship of the calves, which was the great uncleanness of him who made them. For if it was truthfully said [202] of the one calf which they made in the wilderness: “Moses therefore saw that the people had been stripped naked; for Aaron had stripped them for the shame of their filth” (Exod. 32), how much more rightly is it said concerning the two calves, “because of its uncleanness,” namely, the uncleanness of the one who made them?

Therefore, because of his uncleanness, because of his calves—not lords but calves—because Israel became unclean, it shall be destroyed, not by any ordinary corruption, but by a most grievous corruption: not merely by the captivity of bodies now impending, but also by the rejection of souls and irrecoverable condemnation, because they refused to repent.

Having said these things by the Lord’s command, he immediately adds from his own feeling: “Would that I were not a man having the Spirit, and that I might rather speak falsehood.” For a man of God could not be without grief, without mercy, without compassion toward his own race, though he inveighed against them in the word of the Lord with so vehement a zeal. So too the Apostle, while vehemently inveighing against the same race and declaring its blindness, first said: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart” (Rom. 9).

For with what force he immediately adds there: “For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (ibid.). In the same way this prophet says: “Would that I were not a man having the Spirit, and that I might rather speak falsehood.” Surely, whoever does this is accursed by God, as a false prophet speaking from his own heart—not what God inspires, but what the devil, father of lies and ancient serpent, whispers.

To this the Lord replies: “I will pour out for you wine unto drunkenness, and this people will be the one upon whom it is poured.” It is as though he said: “It shall not be as you now wished; but I will pour out for you as I have poured out until now: not the water of falsehood, as for false prophets, but the wine of truth, as for holy seers; and this unto drunkenness, until you are made drunk and cannot keep silent, but speak from the abundance of your heart. And the one upon whom the rain of true prophecy is poured is this people for whom you grieve. However much you grieve, it is this people—this very people, I say—which, as you prophesied, is to be destroyed with a most grievous corruption.”

Such grief is worthy of the Lord’s consolation. Therefore he continues, and the Lord, consoler both of him and through him of his other humble servants, says: “Gathering, I will gather you wholly, O Jacob; I will bring together into one the remnant of Israel; I will place him together like a flock in a sheepfold, like cattle in the midst of folds; they shall make a tumult because of the multitude of men. For the one opening the way shall go up before them; they shall divide and pass through the gate, and go out through it; their king shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.”

Clearly these are consolatory words, so that Jacob or Israel may not grieve—that is, whoever, born according to the flesh from that holy patriarch, is also his son according to faith—as this prophet had said in grief, “Would that I might speak falsehood”; that is, “Would that so great a loss of the Israelite multitude might not occur according to my prophecy. Would that blindness might not happen to Israel.”

The Spirit consoles him in the same way as the Apostle, who, after saying in the passage mentioned above that “blindness in part has happened to Israel” (Rom. 11), added, “until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (ibid.). That fullness of the Gentiles is here called Jacob—that is, “supplanter”—in the words, “Gathering, I will gather Jacob wholly.” For the remnant of Israel, which, as the same Apostle says, “has been saved according to the election of grace” (ibid.), is plainly expressed in the following words: “I will bring together into one the remnant of Israel.”

The meaning is: by gathering Jacob—that is, the Gentile people, the supplanter—and bringing together the remnant of Israel, I will make one assembly, so that they may be one in having one faith and one Spirit; so that there may be no distinction based upon carnal origin, but all, both Jews and Greeks, may be sons of Israel and sons of Abraham and may be reckoned without distinction in the Seed.

He repeats this and adorns it with a beautiful comparison: “I will place him together like a flock in a sheepfold, like cattle in the midst of folds.” “Like a flock in a sheepfold” and “like cattle in the midst of folds” seem to say the same thing; but he did not repeat them without reason. For there is now indeed one flock and one fold, but the flock of Jewish people comes from one place and the flock of Gentile people from another. For that Shepherd of all said: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10).

Therefore I will place together the remnant of Israel as a flock in the sheepfold and the fullness of the Gentiles as cattle in the midst of folds; and “together,” I say, means having one faith and one Spirit, simply obeying the one rule of truth, as gentle sheep are subject to their shepherd. Nor will the multitude be small: “They shall make a tumult because of the multitude of men,” because these sheep are human beings, and these people will be so numerous that throughout the world they will make a great and public tumult of divine praise, filling heaven and the verdant paradise as they feed, with a great rejoicing.

When this has happened, neither you, Micah, nor any of the prophets or apostles will have grief or sorrow over the loss of Israel’s carnal children. Explaining how or by whom such a gathering was to be made, he says: “For the one opening the way went up before them; they shall divide, pass through the gate, and go out through it; their king shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.”

This one who opens the way, this king and Lord who passes before them, is the one who says in the Gospel passage already cited: “I am the good shepherd” (ibid.). How did he go up, opening the way before them? “When he has sent out his own sheep,” he says, “he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice” (ibid.). How does he go before them, unless by suffering for them, leaving an example of suffering and opening the entrance to Paradise?

Therefore, he shall go up—understand, upon the cross—and the good shepherd shall be lifted up from the earth by laying down his life for his sheep. He shall go up above the setting—that is, above death—by rising again; for he shall trample death. He shall go up above the heavens of heavens and sit at the right hand of the Father, opening the way before them, so that the lowliness of the flock may reach where the exaltation of the Shepherd has gone before.

Thus, when he has opened the way, from that time onward they shall divide and pass through the gate and go out through it: namely, that gate of which the Psalmist says, “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous entered through it” (Ps. 117 [118]). What is this gate, except that very passion of Christ, apart from which there is no gate and no way by which anyone can enter into life?

“They shall divide,” he says, “and pass through and go out through” that gate which the soldier’s lance made in the side of the crucified one—the outpouring of blood and water which flowed from it—just as the Red Sea was divided, through which the children of Israel passed, while Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen was drowned (Exod. 14). It must be divided in such a way that we firmly confess and hold that the one and same Christ, into whose death we were baptized, is God and man; and that, discerning the two natures with assured distinction, we confess him impassible in his divinity but once suffering in his humanity.

As they thus divide and pass through, “their king,” he says, “shall pass before [203] them,” which has already occurred: for he passed from this world to the Father. And “the Lord [shall be] at their head,” because “Lord” is his name, and he himself is the head while they are the members; he is king and they are the people; he is shepherd and they are the sheep of his pasture.

Of this passing and going out through this gate he himself speaks in the passage already cited: “If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; and he shall go in and go out and find pasture” (ibid.). For one enters when, by receiving faith, one becomes a sheep of this shepherd; and one goes out when one ends this present life, and then finds the unfading pasture of eternal life. But there too he says: “All who came are thieves and robbers” (ibid.). Again: “The thief does not come except to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (ibid.). This is what the prophet, perceiving that he would most certainly say it, as though he had already said it, immediately declares:

## CHAPTER III

“And he said: Hear, princes of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel: Is it not yours to know judgment—you who hate good and love evil? You who violently took their skins from them, and their flesh from their bones; who ate the flesh of my people, flayed their skin from them, broke their bones, and cut them up as in a cauldron, like flesh in the midst of a pot.”

After he has denounced the sins of the ten tribes and the loss of Jacob’s flesh which befell them—those souls being lost and their bodies carried into irrevocable captivity—he consoles them by the promise of our King and Lord, of whom we have now spoken. Then, beginning again from another starting point, he sets forth the sins of Judah and Jerusalem and foretells the punishment, which he concludes with a similar end, as the following sequence of Scripture shows.

For after prefacing, “Therefore because of you, Zion shall be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones” (Jer. 26), he immediately adds concerning Christ: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Mic. 4), and so forth.

Therefore, since he has said, “I will place him together like a flock in a sheepfold and like cattle in the midst of folds,” concerning the Lord who goes up and opens the way, and then adds, “Hear, princes of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel,” “false princes” and “false leaders” must be understood; for in truth they are thieves and robbers.

And the words which follow—“Is it not yours to know judgment, you who hate good and love evil?”—would better show how great and grave their force is if we look at the beginning of the same discourse, which is this: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). The reason for this opening statement was that the Pharisees—whom he elsewhere called blind guides (Matt. 15)—had cast out of the synagogue the man blind from birth whom he had enlightened, because of his testimony to the truth.

When therefore he had begun in this way, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind,” and they objected, “Are we also blind?” (John 9), he showed by his following words that they deserved blindness. They did not yet appear blind to themselves, but it would soon happen that their eyes, as those of thieves and robbers, would be torn out. For he continues: “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10), and so forth.

Therefore, O false princes and false leaders of the house of Israel—true thieves and true robbers—you who did not enter through the door into the sheepfold but climbed up another way: for you did not enter through the true word of God, but through your own falsehood, pursuing shameful gain; you who hate good and love evil; you who cast out the seeing and enlightened man and wish every sheep to be blind—hear this: “Is it not yours to know judgment?” Understand: and not mercy. For mercy has gone far from you; but you shall know judgment and experience the severity of the Judge, so that you may become as I said: “For judgment I came, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” This is yours; this is your portion and what is laid up for you.

Why? Because you do what belongs to the thief, who comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. You, I say, do what belongs to the thief, and came for no other purpose than to steal, slaughter, and destroy, since “you violently took their skins from them and their flesh from their bones.” In saying this, he maintains the metaphor of sheep begun earlier, which the thief steals in order to slaughter and devour their flesh after their skins have been removed.

For these thieves and robbers, who seemed to themselves princes and leaders, made prey of the people and devoured their property. Yet it was too little merely to gnaw away or swallow their possessions with a deep and insatiable avarice, unless they also delivered their deceived souls to everlasting Gehenna. Therefore he supplies in the following verse what he had said less fully. Turning to the hearers, so that the force of his denunciation and lament may sound more keenly, he says: “Who ate the flesh of my people, flayed their skin from them, broke their bones, and cut them up in a cauldron and like flesh in the midst of a pot.”

Truly, therefore, thieves; truly robbers. Truly, I say, thieves who both stole, slaughtered, and destroyed. For they slaughtered bodily those who did not consent and refused to hear the voice of strangers; and they destroyed those who consented to them, while killing the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls. In both respects they were thieves; in both respects robbers.

“They ate,” he says, “the flesh”—that is, the sins—“of my people,” as it is said through another prophet: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4). For flesh and blood commonly signify sins, as there: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). They consumed the possessions of those whom they encouraged to sin, not only possessions voluntarily offered, but also those extracted by deceit and violence.

Heavenly eloquence has fittingly represented this in the ordered course of the same metaphor: “They flayed their skin from them and broke their bones,” as usually occurs in slaughtering and devouring sheep. First, the skins are skillfully flayed off; then the bones, because, through their hardness, they resist the teeth and knife, are broken so that one may reach the fatness of the marrow through what lies in the middle—that is, through the flesh, for it lies between the skin and bones. Finally he says: “They cut them up as in a cauldron,” or only this, “like flesh in the midst of a pot.”

But because we should not suppose that he said both phrases without purpose, we inquire into both kinds of cutting-up and both instruments of the penal workshop: the cauldron and the pot.

First, it should be observed that a cauldron and a pot differ in this: a cauldron has a wide mouth above, whereas a pot, having a narrow opening, broadens in its belly. From a boiling cauldron, something can be removed by hand only with difficulty; from a pot, with still greater difficulty. Therefore we understand here two confinements of the unfortunate, for which those men—that is, the princes and leaders—were responsible: namely, the suffering they were to endure from the Romans in their most burning siege, and that which they were to suffer from evil spirits in the fire of Gehenna.

For according to prophecy they were to be crushed by a double crushing (Jer. 17), which the Psalmist distinguishes more clearly: “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62 [63]). From the Roman siege, as from a cauldron, some survived, though with difficulty; but from the narrow confinements of Gehenna [204], as from the inner part of a pot, escape is more difficult—indeed altogether impossible. These are very unlike, or rather altogether and utterly contrary.

[Col. 0467A] I shall set these words alongside those written above, which were spoken by the good shepherd, that is, Christ: “I will gather them together like a flock in the fold, like sheep in the midst of their pens.” He who spoke those words is himself the shepherd; those who do these things are themselves the killers. Concerning them it is further added: “Then they will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear them; and he will hide his face from them at that time, as they have acted wickedly in their contrivances.” Then, he says, when I shall set them like a flock in the fold and like sheep in the midst of their pens; when I shall bring in the other sheep which I have, which are not of this fold, because they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd, with no distinction made between Jew and Greek—then both those thieves and robbers, and these foolish sheep, or rather goats more than sheep, or wandering sheep, which have heard the voice [Col. 0467B] of strangers, will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear them. And not only will he not hear them, but he will also hide his face from them at that time, as they have acted wickedly in their contrivances: that is, as they have deserved, having done evil not in ignorance but wickedly; not having fallen into sin by chance or imprudence, but bent upon evil, devoted and zealously intent with their whole heart not on avoiding but on proclaiming everything wicked. Thus, when the Psalmist had said, “They have become corrupt and abominable,” he added, “in their pursuits” (Ps. XIII).

And these things certainly correspond in contrast to the foregoing passage, where, after saying, “I will set them like a flock in the fold, like sheep in the midst of their pens,” he continued and said: “They will make a tumult because of the multitude of men; for the one opening the way [Col. 0467C] has gone up before them, and their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head.” Those people will make a tumult because of the multitude of men, and the Lord will go up, opening the way before them; these will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear them. Before those, their king will pass, and the Lord at their head; before these, not only will the Lord not pass, and not only will he not be at their head, but he will even hide his face from them. This, beyond doubt, has now happened and is happening, with a veil moreover placed upon their heart so that they cannot see.

It follows: “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and preach peace; but if anyone does not put something into their mouths, they consecrate war against him. Therefore night shall be to you instead of vision, and darkness to you instead of divination. The sun shall set upon the prophets, and day shall grow dark over them. Those who see visions shall be ashamed, and the diviners shall be ashamed, and they shall cover their faces, because there is no answer from God.”

Among all the rulers and leaders of the kind discussed thus far, the prophets of that time were not to be passed over: biting prophets and deceivers of the people—namely Annas and Caiaphas. One of them, who was high priest that year, prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order to gather into one the scattered children of God. For he said: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI). Indeed, [Col. 0468A] when he said this, what he thought in his mind was false, but what his voice uttered was true. For he thought—or wished others to think—that unless Jesus, who was called king and Christ, should die, he would give the Romans, to whose rule they were subject, cause to come and take away both their place and nation (ibid.). And this was false: Christ had not come to take away the kingdoms of the Romans or of other nations, nor to furnish an occasion for hostilities by claiming for himself any earthly power. But his words meant that Jesus was to die for the redemption of all God’s children; and this was true, and was truly so fulfilled.
