Therefore those prophets—that is, the chief priests, one of whom prophesied in this way—were not to be passed over without hearing something more than the other rulers and leaders. “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and preach peace.” There is no doubt that those prophets led the people astray more than the prophets of Baal had ever led them astray, such as existed in the times of Ahab and Jezebel. For those led the people astray so far that they forsook the Lord and worshipped Baal. These led them astray so far that they crucified the Lord and chose Barabbas. What follows, “who bite with their teeth,” is wholly true, and accords with the Psalmist: “Their teeth were weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). Thus these murderers were as venomous as the peace they preached was counterfeit. Since there are many indications of this, it is remarkable that [Col. 0468C] our Lord was handed over to them by a kiss of peace.

“And if anyone,” he says, “does not put something into their mouths, they consecrate war against him.” This is a brief but exceedingly profound and vehement denunciation of their greed. It may indeed be understood of the multitude, since it is true of many that they regarded as enemies those who did not give to them, and as friends those who put something into their mouths. Yet it must be understood above all of our Lord: they consecrated war against him precisely because he did not put anything into their mouths; indeed, he disputed against their greed. In short, had this Messiah—that is, the Christ promised through the prophets—come in such a way as, supported by an earthly kingdom, to enlarge their houses and increase [Col. 0468D] their riches, then he would have pleased them, and then they would have offered him their peace. But because he came poor and despising riches; because he preached that not the rich but the poor would be blessed; and because, as has already been said, he disputed against their greed, they consecrated war against him. That is, so far as they could, they exerted themselves to make it appear holy and fitting to the service of blessed God if they killed him.

This is so true concerning prophets of this sort that it has also been established by certain experience in the case of many people. For when he put something into their mouths, when from five barley loaves and two fish he satisfied five thousand men, then they wanted to seize him and make him king, as it is written: “Jesus therefore, knowing that they would come to seize him and [Col. 0469A] make him king, fled again to the mountain, himself alone” (John VI). But when they perceived that he no longer wished to put anything into their mouths, or in whatever manner they wished, when he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (ibid.), and so forth, they began to consecrate war against him, murmuring and saying: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I came down from heaven’?” (ibid.).

If this was so among the common people, what do you suppose was the case among those greedy prophets and deep lovers of riches, when he who was preached as Christ not only did not promise them, as they wished, the treasures of the whole world, [Col. 0469B] but even disputed against their greed? Doubtless they despaired of him, saying that he would not put anything into their mouths; and therefore they consecrated war against him, judging it holy if they crucified him as a deceiver and magician.

What does the Lord say concerning prophets of this kind? “Therefore night shall be to you instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination. The sun shall set upon the prophets, and day shall grow dark over them.” Vision and divination differ in this respect: divination is never taken in Scripture in a good sense. “There shall be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel” (Num. XXIII). And when this is in any way taken away, or is declared to have no effect, in the words, “Night shall be to you instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination,” [Col. 0469C] it must be understood thus: You, not knowing or refusing to know that prophecy is one thing and divination another, think yourselves to be prophets as you wish to be, so that you may be thought to see visions of God, though you are rather like soothsayers, diviners, or fortune-tellers. For where you receive something to bite upon, there you preach peace; and if anyone does not put something into your mouths, you consecrate war against him. But whether you wish to call what you speak vision, your vision will be night; or whether you call it divination, there is not light there, but darkness—the darkness of falsehood and the night of lying—because, indeed, the sun has set over us and the day has grown dark.

Who is that sun, if not he of whom it is written: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise” [Col. 0469D] (Mal. IV)? And who is that day, if not he himself who says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII)?

We see that it has happened thus: since the aforementioned Caiaphas uttered his bloody prophecy—a cruel prophet bent upon blood—there has been no vision or truth among them. And just as royal dignity perished and priestly authority fell, so also every prophetic grace departed from them. At times they have practised divination, and unhappy men still strive to practise it, promising themselves prosperity after the end of the evils which they now suffer, scattered abroad and bearing the yoke of captivity, as though they in turn were to possess the Romans themselves as slaves, according to that saying: “And the house of Jacob shall possess those who possessed them” (Obad. I). But such [Col. 0470A] divinations are darkness and not light, night and not the day of true vision. For what was said through the Psalmist by way of concession has befallen them: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling-block; let their eyes be darkened that they may not see” (Ps. LXVIII).

For that sun has set over them and grown dark; and in its very setting it signified the night and darkness of which the present discourse speaks by means of the darkness which then came over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth hour (Matt. XXVII). And truly, although he rose again, it is rightly said that he set over them: for they do not believe that he rose from the dead, and accordingly they remain continually in night and darkness. All who believe glory in him as enlightened; [Col. 0470B] but those who do not believe are confounded, unable to endure the brightness of this sun shining upon them, just as once they could not endure the brightness of Moses’ face, but fled with faces and hearts turned away (Exod. XXXIV; II Cor. III). Indicating this, he says here: “Those who see visions shall be ashamed, and the diviners shall be ashamed; and all shall cover their faces, because there is no answer from God.” For, convicted by evident realities, those liars who “saw”—that is, who pretended that they saw—visions are ashamed, since whatever they say or have said was not an answer from God; rather, they prophesied from their own hearts. And even now they cover their faces, having the veil of wickedness placed over their heart.

Having said these things concerning the deceiving and biting prophets, the worst of whom, as has already been said, were Annas and Caiaphas, he immediately speaks of himself: “But I am filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and truth, to declare to Jacob its wickedness, and to Israel its sin.”

[Col. 0470C] He set this in opposition quite deliberately and not without weight of reason. For those whose custom it was to despise or even mock the prophets of the Lord could have objected to him, and perhaps had already snatched the word from his mouth, saying: Since, as you say, night is instead of vision and darkness instead of divination for prophets, we now care nothing for your vision either, since it is no answer from God but divination which you have invented. Thus they said to Jeremiah: “You speak falsely. The Lord our God has not sent you saying, ‘Do not go into Egypt to dwell there’; but Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us” (Jer. XLIII).

Moreover, prophets of the kind concerning whom he said, “Therefore night shall be to you instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination,” undoubtedly raged against this man, just as they raged against another prophet of the same name, namely Micaiah son of Imlah. For when he said to Ahab: “Now therefore, behold, the Lord has given a lying spirit into the mouth of all these your prophets, and the Lord has spoken evil against you,” Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came forward, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said: “Has the Spirit of the Lord then left me and spoken to you?” (III Kings XXII). Therefore, after saying the foregoing things concerning the prophets, he quite fittingly [Col. 0471A] declared this of himself: “But I am filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and truth,” and so forth—as though he were saying: The prophets who preach peace and say, “Peace, peace” (Jer. VI), will themselves be ashamed, because their answer is not an answer from God. But I am filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, because I announce what is true and do what belongs to one who judges, in declaring to Jacob its wickedness and to Israel its sin.

And after God, I have no witness more certain than the conscience of Jacob or Israel itself as to whether I speak truly or not. For it is its own wickedness and its own sin, and its conscience does not fail to know it; and thereby it recognizes whether I speak from my own heart, or whether the strength of judgment and truth resides in that utterance.

“Hear these things, rulers of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert all that is right; who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Her rulers judged for gifts, and her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money; and they rested upon the Lord, saying: ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils will not come upon you.’ Therefore, because of you Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall become the high places of forests.”

This man indeed proclaimed this as one strong, as a judge, as a truthful witness, filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, against rulers and judges, priests and prophets. For he declared to each its own wickedness and sin: to the rulers, that [Col. 0471C] they judged for gifts; to the priests, that they taught for payment; to the prophets, that they practised divination for money; and that, fattened by gifts, grown sleek by payments, swollen with money, they rested upon the Lord like fat cattle over their manger, saying that the Lord was plainly in their midst because nothing was lacking to their bellies—as though they strengthened themselves against the prophets of the Lord by saying: “Evils will not come upon you; the Lord is good” (Lam. III); “the prophets speak falsehoods.”

Above he had already said concerning the rulers and leaders: “Then they will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear.” He had said concerning the prophets: “Therefore night shall be to you instead of vision.” Although there is great vengeance in both sentences, this final crash had not yet reached their ears—a crash which [Col. 0471D] they cannot ignore: “Therefore, because of you Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall become the high places of forests.”

This happened exactly so, as the whole world has heard: after the sons of such rulers and judges, such priests and prophets had filled up the measure of their fathers by crucifying Christ the Son of God (Matt. XXVI), Zion, or Jerusalem, was made desolate; and no stone of city or temple was left upon another that was not destroyed (Luke XIX). This prophecy is mentioned in Jeremiah as follows:

[Col. 0472A] “Then men from the elders of the land arose and spoke to the whole assembly of the people: ‘Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house shall become the high places of forests.” Did Hezekiah king of Judah, and all Judah, condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord, and did the Lord not relent concerning the evil which he had spoken against them?’” (Jer. XXVI).

I have recalled these words because it seemed to them that the Lord had relented, since what had been prophesied did not occur quickly in their days. But that prophet, or the Spirit of the Lord in whose strength he prophesied, whose judgment and truth he knew himself [Col. 0472B] to be filled with, was not looking to the present times of King Hezekiah, nor even to the Babylonian captivity. For Zion, or Jerusalem, was indeed captured, but not so utterly overthrown that no stone was left upon another. He looked to that time when the Lord of the prophets would be crucified by rulers judging for gifts, by priests teaching for payment, and by prophets divining for money—men who abhorred judgment and perverted all that was right, so much so that they said, “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. XII), and, “This man said: ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days’” (Matt. XXVI). They built Zion with blood and Jerusalem with [Col. 0472C] iniquity, so that deservedly there should come upon them all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel onward (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore, contrary to their supposition, the Lord did not relent concerning the evil which he had spoken against them, since the avenging word of the Lord is established in truth without repentance, as it is written elsewhere: “Moreover, the Victor in Israel will not spare and will not be turned by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent” (I Kings XV). He did not spare, nor was he turned by repentance, because the rulers did not cease to judge for gifts, the priests to teach for payment, and the prophets to divine for money, so that they made the house of the Father, which was—or ought to have been—a house of prayer, a den of robbers (Luke XIX).

Hence it should be observed that he who foretold through this prophet, “Therefore, because of you [Col. 0472D] Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall become the high places of forests,” himself, when he had wept over that same city, saying, “Days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and cast you to the ground, and will not leave in you one stone upon another,” immediately entered the temple and began to cast out those who sold and bought in it (ibid.). By this he pronounced judgment upon the future overthrow of the city and temple, chiefly on account of the fault of the priests, who in that temple had become chief robbers.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0473]

[Col. 0473A] It must be kept firmly in mind what we have already said: the principal aim of the prophets is to proclaim the loss suffered by the Israelite people through unbelief in such a manner as to announce the completion of the election from the fullness of the Gentiles, which was to come through faith in Christ. Pursuing this point now in this second book, after he had prefaced, “Hear, rulers of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel, who hate good and love evil,” and the rest—which he concluded thus: “Therefore, because of you Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall become the high places of forests”—he immediately added as follows:

## CHAPTER IV
And it shall come to pass: in the last of days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the summit of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall go [Col. 0473B] and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” And he shall judge among many peoples and rebuke strong nations even afar off. And they shall cut their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into hoes; nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn warfare any more. And every man shall sit beneath his own vine and beneath his fig tree, and there shall be none to frighten him, because the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken. For all peoples shall walk, each in the name of his own god; but we shall walk in the name of our God for ever and beyond.

This is a plain prophecy concerning the fullness of the nations, which now comes in while blindness has happened to Israel [Col. 0473C] (Rom. XI); while, as it is written above in this prophet, “night is to them instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination. And the sun has set upon the prophets, and the day has been darkened over them” (Mic. III); and furthermore Jerusalem has been reduced to a heap of stones, and those of them who survived the sword have been led captive among all nations (Luke XXI). The very nations whose salvation is foretold are expressly named in the words: “Peoples shall flow to him, and many nations shall hasten,” etc.

But Christ, to whom the peoples flow and the nations hasten, is signified not by an explicit or proper name, but by a mystical designation, when it is said: “The mountain of the house of the Lord is established on the summit of the mountains.” For that Christ ought rightly to be understood by the name of mountain is clear both from many passages of Scripture and especially from that vision in Daniel, where it is written: “But the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. II).

Wonderful, therefore, and venerable is the carefulness of the prophetic Spirit, which in such a place called Christ “the mountain of the house of the Lord,” where it had said, “the mountain of the temple shall be in the heights of the forests.” For what? Had it not sufficiently offended, or could it not offend, the rebellious ears of the people, [Col. 0474A] when it said, “the mountain of the temple shall be in the heights of the forests”? Let, then, the sweet oracle concerning the mountain of the house of the Lord soften those whom the grievous announcement concerning the mountain of the temple had exasperated—those beneficially mistaken by the ambiguity of “mountain,” so that they might suppose both utterances to concern one and the same mountain. Their error greatly benefited them in this: that they did not hasten to strike him as violent madmen might strike a harsh physician; and in this: that they preserved the prophetic Scripture and did not commit it to the fire, though it would profit many ages thereafter.

Let us now carefully consider these promises of the Holy Spirit concerning us Gentiles, which we gladly hear. “And it shall be,” he says, “in the last of days.” What does he mean here by “in the last of days”? Isaiah says, “in the last days” (Isa. II). By “the last days” or “the last times” of that people against whom the discourse has hitherto been directed, we rightly understand those of which the Saviour says in the Gospel, after saying, “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a man” (Matt. XII), and so concludes: “And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (ibid.).

Therefore, the very time in which those things were to be fulfilled that he had said before—namely, “and Jerusalem shall be a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple the heights of forests”—is the last of days: the last days and last times of that people are worse than the former. But for those who receive Christ there is the fullness of time, as the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” [Col. 0474C] (Gal. IV).

Thus in the last of days—that is, in the same time when Jerusalem shall be a heap of stones and the mountain of the temple shall be in the heights of the forests—there shall be the mountain of the house of the Lord, established on the summit of the mountains and exalted above the hills. This is as though he said: Christ, who is the height and dignity of all the saints, shall then become known throughout the whole world. For the house of the Lord is the Church of the Lord, and the mountain of that same house is Christ.

The Psalmist, foreseeing both—the house and the mountain—after first saying, “The King of powers, of the beloved, of the beloved” (Ps. LXVII), immediately says: “to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house; when the heavenly one discerns kings over her, they shall be whitened as snow in Zalmon: the mountain of God, a rich mountain, a curdled mountain” (ibid.). For he is a lofty and exalted person, since he is God and man, king and priest: King of kings and priest remaining for ever.

Therefore the mountain is established on the summit of the mountains and exalted above the hills, because he is higher than patriarchs and prophets, all kings and priests, and every saint; and above that house of the Lord he distinguishes and orders kings—kings, I say—and prophets, as was said in the verse of the Psalm (ibid.). They themselves confess this, saying: [Col. 0475A] “From his fullness we have all received” (John I).

But how far does his exaltation reach? Surely to the right hand of the Father, which no mountain—that is, no angel—nor any hill—that is, no holy human being—attains. “For to which of the angels,” says the Apostle, “did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’?” (Heb. I). Truly, then, he is established above the summit of the mountains and exalted above the hills, as he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they, God saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

He is also called, as we have already mentioned, “the King of powers, of the beloved, of the beloved” (Ps. LVII), that is, king of his own powers, who is uniquely the beloved of God the Father, who says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III); and “king to divide,” that is, to distribute spoils for the beauty of the house, in order to give gifts to men from that seat of majesty. These gifts may rightly be called spoils, just as those good garments of Esau, with which Rebekah clothed her younger son Jacob [Col. 0475B] (Gen. XXVII).

For, according to that type, those who were first—the Jews—were despoiled of the heavenly gifts bestowed by the divine grace of the Holy Spirit upon the beauty of the house of the Lord, that is, upon the beauty of the Church from the nations. From this point, as has already been said, by sitting at the Father’s right hand, he became established on the summit of the mountains and exalted above the hills—this mountain of the house of the Lord, the rich mountain, the curdled mountain: that is, God made man, man assumed into God. In him all are made white as snow when we receive forgiveness of sins, because he himself is white with every kind of holiness; this is understood there through the name of the mountain, Zalmon.

He is said to have been established for this glory, for this exaltation—that is, prepared before all ages. He himself intimates this when he says: “If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before” (John VI). For although Christ, according to his humanity, is younger than all angels and than many men, or even than the ages of the world, yet according to his divinity he is unquestionably far more ancient than all angels and men, heaven and earth.

Since, therefore, this mountain of the house of the Lord is of such height that nothing is above it, how is he the foundation of the house of the Lord? For in the Prophet: “Behold, says the Lord, I shall send into the foundations of Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious corner-stone, founded in the foundation” (Isa. XXVIII). That stone is without doubt Christ. And in the Apostle: “No one,” he says, “can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Col. 0475D] (I Cor. III).

If we look at an ordinary, earthly building, it is clear that the foundation is the lowest and bottommost part of the entire building. Here, then, the comparison especially fails: the foundation of an earthly building is set below and raises the structure above itself; but the foundation of this spiritual house of the Lord is above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God (Heb. XII). The structure is suspended, adhering to that same foundation, so that those still dwelling in this world, or in their mortal body, may say: [Col. 0476A] “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

What follows, “and peoples shall flow to him, and many nations shall hasten and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us of his ways, and we shall walk in his paths,’” has been accomplished from that time onward, is being accomplished, and does not cease to be accomplished until the end of the age. For nations and peoples flowed to that mountain, Christ, and do not cease to flow with the sacred stream of baptism, ever since he gave the rule for baptizing: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

Those to whom he spoke this directly, namely the apostles, and those invited and instructed through them, or who after them increased in evangelical faith, do not cease to preach and exhort one another. The sum of all their preaching and exhortation is this: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob”—with the implication, that we may hold the one faith of himself and of his one Church—and “he will teach us of his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.” For it plainly does not suffice to believe unless we also act according to his commands and strive to enter by his paths, that is, by the narrow and confined way that leads to life [Col. 0476B] (Luke XXIV). Therefore, when he had said, “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” he added: “teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII).

And what he adds here, “for from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,” he himself likewise confirms in the Gospel, saying: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” [Col. 0476C] (Luke XXIV).

“And he shall judge among many peoples and correct strong nations even afar off.” He shall judge—that is, the word of the Lord shall judge—for even in this present age the word of God is the true judge. Hence the Apostle says: “For the word of God is living and effectual, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. IV). Wondrous is the power, wondrous the vitality, of the word of the Lord that judges peoples and rebukes nations, permitting neither the thoughts nor the intentions of the heart to remain hidden.

Wherever it comes and wherever it is preached, such judgment takes place, and such a separation of peoples or nations, that even members of one household—that is, those who dwell in one house—are divided against one another; and those who are approved and those who are reprobate become manifest, that is, those who belong and those who do not belong to God. The incarnate Word himself, seeing this, said: “Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace on earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). He immediately adds testimony perhaps taken from this prophet: “For I have come [Col. 0477A] to separate a man against his father, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X).

In this manner the Word of the Lord has already judged, and judges, among many peoples; and in this manner he rebukes strong nations: while father rebukes son and son father, mother daughter and daughter mother, mother-in-law daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law her mother-in-law, in the faith or Gospel of Christ, and does not allow them to remain excused or excusable—lest perhaps anyone in the future universal judgment should say: “I did not know; I did not hear; it was not announced to me.” And he rebukes not merely any nations, but strong ones—Greeks and Romans as well—adding “even afar off,” that is, from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. XLIX), as it is written of such persons in the Psalm: “Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). Again: “His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his course reaches to its height; and there is none who can hide from his heat” (ibid.). This is plainly as if he said that no one will have sufficient excuse on the ground of ignorance.

Having said these things, he immediately adds concerning those whom he foresees will not contradict the judging and rebuking Word of the Lord, but will do penance by yielding to the truth: “And they shall cut their swords into ploughshares and their spears into hoes. Nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn [Col. 0477B] warfare any more.” Do we not read that this has everywhere happened among peoples and nations as Christ’s Gospel has shone forth, and see that it is happening, while men formerly restless and warlike, laying aside the weapons of war and changing even their outward form or dress, bear the signs of evangelical peace, some being converted to the cenobitic and others to the eremitic life?

Yet, however matters may stand with others, does not the entire priestly order and every ministerial rank of the sacred altar so beat swords and spears into pieces that it is not even permitted them to touch them with their hands? It was not so before this mountain of the house of the Lord became known. Indeed, before Christ’s coming priests, no less than the rest of the people, were permitted to gird themselves with arms and train for battle. Moreover, the tribe of Levi especially earned the priesthood for this reason: because, using swords, it did not spare even its own brothers. As it is written: “Whoever is for the Lord, let him join me,” said Moses. And all the sons of Levi gathered to him [Col. 0477C]. To them he said: “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbour.” And they did so, and about twenty-three thousand men fell. And Moses said: “You have consecrated your hands to the Lord today, each one upon his son and his brother, that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. XXXII).

Likewise Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, because he went in after the Israelite man into the brothel and pierced both together—the man, namely, and the woman—the Lord therefore spoke concerning him thus: “Behold, I give him the peace of my covenant, and it shall be to him and to his seed after him a covenant of everlasting priesthood” (Num. XXV).

It is not so now. Priests are not permitted to kill, nor may priests be made from those who have killed, ever since Christ himself, the head of the evangelical priesthood, said to Peter when he drew his sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear: [Col. 0478A] “Put your sword back into its sheath, for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI). Therefore, whatever others may do—although they are laymen, they lay down arms by voluntary resolve—priests and all ministers of Christ’s altar are under an ordinance necessarily to be observed: they must cut their swords into ploughshares and their spears into hoes, and learn warfare no more. As has been said, this had formerly been permitted.

What follows, “And every man shall sit beneath his vine, and there shall be none to frighten him,” is fulfilled as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, be content with these” (I Tim. IX). He is rightly said to sit beneath his own vine and beneath his own fig tree who, content with what is his own or granted to him, does not covet or seize another’s property. Certainly that ancient people cannot be justified in this respect either, since unless the Lord had promised and given them other people’s vineyards and fig trees, they would never have accepted his law so readily.

But the seven women who take hold of one man say: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called over us: take away our reproach” [Col. 0478B] (Isa. IV). That is, all the nations of whom the present discourse speaks, converted to Christ by the sevenfold Spirit, do not seek, as the reward of their received faith, that he give them other people’s lands and possessions gained by others’ labour; rather, they are content with what they possessed before Christ’s Gospel. They ask only that his name be called over them and that, having received forgiveness, they may be free from the reproach of sins.

And because what he said—“Every man shall sit beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree”—is not sufficient for perfection, he adds what is perfect: “and there shall be none to frighten him.” How true this is is proved by the countless thousands of martyrs whom persecutors could not frighten, even by taking away not only fig trees and vines but their very lives, as they surrendered their bodies to punishments for God’s sake.

This prophecy is true, because “the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken”: “for all peoples shall walk, each one in the name of his own god; but we shall walk [Col. 0478D] in the name of the Lord our God for ever and beyond.” This is a good and firm reason confirming that there is none to frighten such persons: for all peoples—that is, only those who have not flowed to that mountain of the Lord, whose God is not Christ—shall walk in the name of their own god, that is, in care for their belly, which belly is their god; and for this reason they could be frightened. But we are not so. For we have another God, as it is written: “For our God is not as their god” (I Cor. VI), because their transient god is the belly (Phil. III), according to which they walk temporally; but our God is this mountain of the house of the Lord, Christ, in whose name we shall walk for ever and beyond, because he is with us and shall be until the consummation of the age and beyond.

It follows: “In that day, says the Lord, [Col. 0479A] I will gather her who limps, and I will collect her whom I had cast out, and her whom I had afflicted; and I will make her who limps a remnant, and her who had laboured a strong nation; and the Lord shall reign over them on Mount Zion from now until eternity.” What has been said thus far, from “Peoples shall flow to him, and many nations shall hasten,” up to the present verse, is solely a promise concerning the election of the nations. But the present verse proclaims the election and fellowship of both, namely Jews and Gentiles.

For “I will gather her who limps,” he says—meaning the Israelite nation; “and I will collect her whom I had cast out and afflicted”—namely the other nation, or rather the Gentile world. The Israelite nation is rightly called limping, and the Gentile world cast out and afflicted. Israel had not been utterly cast out by God, nor did it altogether walk with God; rather, it limped between two parts, worshipping partly the Lord God and partly Baal and the other monstrous gods. The Gentile world, however, had been altogether cast out and afflicted by error continuously through every generation.

Moreover, and more grievously, the Jewish nation appeared limping on that day now under discussion, according to the type or figure that had gone before in its father Jacob, when he wrestled with the angel, prevailed, and the latter touched the sinew of his thigh [Col. 0479B] (Gen. XXXII). It is pleasing now briefly to touch upon the mystery of this matter.

Jacob wrestled with God and, as victor, wrung a blessing from him, as though from one unwilling and reluctant, who said: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen” (ibid.). For so it was to be: God would threaten to depart from Jacob’s seed because of the sins of that rebellious and unbelieving nation. When he first spoke thus to Moses, because of the calf they had made—“Let me alone, that my wrath may grow hot against them and I may destroy them, and make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII)—Moses rose up in brokenness, that is, in great humility of mind. Standing in God’s presence, the man wrestled with God as he resisted and held him back from doing this.

By this prolonged wrestling God was restrained whenever he turned away from that nation because of its sins, for at no time were there lacking faithful persons among that people, in whom Jacob was father both according to faith and according to the flesh. By their merits and most earnest prayers God was strongly bound and not released until he blessed Jacob, until the lawgiver fulfilled his blessings by giving that blessing in which all nations would be blessed [Col. 0479D] (Gen. XXII), as he had spoken to Abraham. That blessing, in his seed, is the grace of the Holy Spirit poured out through Christ’s passion upon all nations.

For then God truly blessed Jacob, in the holy apostles, with every spiritual blessing; but the sinew of his thigh withered, because whatever they had been accustomed to do or sacrifice carnally was rejected. All genealogies also came thereafter to be regarded as fables, since it was, as it were, the element that alone had served for weaving genealogies [reading uncertain]. Faith alone is proclaimed, and nothing is said of his flesh. And because faith has been proved in the apostles and others, however few, as though in a sound foot, while in many there is only boasting in the flesh, like a weak foot, Jacob is rightly now said to limp in his posterity.

Therefore, “In that day,” says the Lord, “I will gather her who limps, and I will collect her whom I had cast out and afflicted”: that is, I shall receive both in such a way as to make no distinction between Jew and Greek.

And as though you were asking how he says that he will gather her who limps and collect her who has been cast out or afflicted, he says: “I will make her who limps a remnant, and her who had laboured a strong nation.” As was said, so it was done. For evangelical grace did not gather limping Israel in its entirety, but made it into a remnant—that is, it took a remnant from it [Col. 0480B]—among whom the Apostle testifies that he himself is, in these words: “Has God cast away his people? By no means. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. XI).

And immediately afterward: “What does the divine answer say to Elijah? ‘I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’ So therefore at this time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (ibid.). Again: “But Isaiah,” he says, “cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved’” (Isa. X).

Therefore, although the limping one has stumbled by limping for the most part, “I will make her a remnant,” he says; but her who had laboured I will not merely revive, but “I will make [Col. 0480C] her into a strong nation,” that is, I will clothe the Church gathered from the nations with such a spirit of strength that, as she is fruitful in multitude, so she may be glorious in victories. It will become a thing worthy of wonder, so that it may be said of her: “Who is this that rises like the dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” (Song VI). Truly strong, truly arrayed like an army for battle. For, not to mention the rest, whose entire warfare is spiritual, against invisible enemies and against the vices of the flesh: who could count her soldiers—at least those whom she calls her martyrs, or Christ’s martyrs? We know those remnants; we know this strong nation; and we know that all that they are is of grace, not of debt. Hence, giving thanks, they say in the Apocalypse: “For you were slain [Col. 0480D] and redeemed us to God by your blood from every tribe and tongue and people and nation; and you made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign upon the earth” (Rev. V).

Therefore the Lord of whom it is finally said here, “And the Lord shall reign over them on Mount Zion, from now and for ever,” is truly called King of kings and Lord of lords, because those of whom he is king are themselves all kings and priests, and shall reign for ever. That the Lord who reigns over them here on Mount Zion is the proper person of the Son is attested by the Son himself in the Psalm, saying: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his ordinance. The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. II).

Now there can be no doubt that Mount Zion is the heavenly Church, according to [Col. 0481A] the Apostle’s words: “You have come,” he says, “to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Heb. XII). Nor is there any need to repeat how fittingly, in the present prophecy, Christ is now signified by the designation of the heavenly Mount Zion or mountain of the Lord’s house, and now Christ’s Church; plainly because of what had been stated previously: “For your sake Zion shall be ploughed as a field, and the temple-mount shall become the height of forests” (Mic. III). Thus the offence or hatred which, on hearing these words, might have flared up the more fiercely against the prophets is wisely softened, while glorious things are said of other realities under the same names.

If such great and glorious things are deservedly said of the nations flowing together to this mountain [Col. 0481B] of the Lord, and of the remnants of the limping one—that is, of the Jewish people—which were foreseen as to be gathered together into one, what ought to have been said of the firstfruits of that same people? That is, what ought to have been said of the primitive Church, or of the primordial Church, of the patriarchs and prophets and all the elect who preceded and awaited Christ’s coming, and all died without receiving the promises, from whom Christ himself came according to the flesh? For concerning that part, or in reference to that part so excellent, the text of the present prophecy has so far said nothing properly suitable. Yet surely to it are addressed the words immediately following:

“And you, misty tower of the flock, daughter of Zion, to you it shall come; and the first power shall come, the kingdom to the daughter of Jerusalem. Why now are you drawn tight with grief? [Col. 0481C] Is there no king for you, or has your counsellor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman in labour?”

For the daughter of Zion, or daughter of Jerusalem, in the present passage is the primitive Church itself of the patriarchs and prophets and other saints. She was drawn tight with grief while she awaited Christ, as though she had no king or counsellor, although she held him in promise and hope. She is now called the daughter of Zion or daughter of Jerusalem because, while she was a pilgrim in this world, her mind was fixed upon that Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels (Heb. XII), as the Apostle says. Enjoying their ministry, she, a sweet daughter, was as it were suckled with maternal milk by heavenly visions and frequent promises; [Col. 0481D] she was nourished, strengthened, and comforted with blessed hope.

To such a daughter it is then said: “And you, misty tower of the flock”—understand: be comforted and possess the brightness of joy, for the first power shall come to you. She is called a tower at this point because God had strengthened her, both visibly and invisibly, like a mighty fortress: visibly, by the temple and altar, concerning which Isaiah says, “He built a tower in its midst” (Isa. V); invisibly, by ranks of angels. Likewise, in the Song of Songs it is said to her: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of mighty men” (Song IV).

For, if we consider rightly, this is said as beautifully as it is truly concerning her [Col. 0482A] from whom we have received all armour, that is, all canonical Scripture, by which we are armed. Without it we should all be unarmed—every one of us from the nations who, called to Christ’s soldiery, speaks or does anything bravely. For the whole Old Testament and the whole New Testament come from her. Rightly, therefore, is she called a tower, and a tower of the flock; for we, who are “the flock of the Lord, his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIX), are protected and defended in her.

This tower is called misty, undoubtedly because of frequent adversities, because of the grief by which she was drawn tight because her king, who was to rule in that tower, had not yet come, and because of the contempt with which she has often been despised by mocking enemies. Yet she was and is nevertheless radiant. For elsewhere she says: “When I sit in darkness, the Lord [Col. 0482B] is my light. I will bear the Lord’s wrath, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment. He will bring me forth into the light; I shall see his righteousness” (Mic. VII).

Or she is called misty also because a multitude of unbelievers has always been found in her, as was prefigured both in the temple built by Solomon (III Kings VIII) and on Mount Sinai when the law was given (Exod. XX). For there a very dense cloud covered the mountain, and here a mist filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the mist.

What shall I say to you, O such daughter of Zion? “To you it shall come, and the first power shall come, the kingdom to the daughter of Jerusalem.” Because what he had said—“to you it shall come”—seemed too little, understanding the one who is to reign as Lord, he heightened the good news by repeating it and saying: “And the first power shall come; the kingdom shall come first to you, daughter of Jerusalem.” For so it was to be, and so it came to pass. Power came in the advent of the King and Lord: namely, that great and wondrous power which the Evangelist beautifully expresses in so few words, saying: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I). And it was that kingdom of which he says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV).

This kingdom shall come first to you, daughter of Jerusalem; this power, O daughter of Zion, shall come as the first to you—that is, it is to be given first to you. For although the Apostle says that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, and that there is no respect of persons with God, yet the same Apostle says, “First to the Jew and then to the Greek” (Rom. II). Again: “What advantage, then, has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them. For what if some of them did not believe? Has their unbelief nullified the faithfulness of God? By no means. But God is true” (Rom. III), and so forth.

Therefore the first power and the first kingdom came to you, O daughter of Zion, because you, holy patriarchs and prophets, you holy apostles and the other saints from that people, rightly possess the first place in the kingdom and power of the children of God. Since this is so, O daughter of Zion or daughter of Jerusalem, why now are you drawn tight with grief? “Is there no king for you, or has your counsellor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman in labour?”

Indeed, at that time, and from the time when the promise concerning Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, was made, Zion or Jerusalem—that is, the souls of many holy patriarchs and prophets, kings and all the righteous—were thus drawn tight with grief, desiring to see the fulfilment of the promise. Pain seized them like women in labour, as is signified by the wondrous sign in the Apocalypse, where it says: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars; and being with child, she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth” (Rev. XII).

That Zion was this same Jerusalem; that woman clothed with the sun and with the moon beneath her feet was she who had Christ in promise, and who abounded in and surpassed others in temporal goods; and the crown of twelve stars on her head was, at the beginning of the nation, the sons of Jacob, fathers of the twelve tribes. Being with child—that is, keeping the faith and hope of the promise in her heart—she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth, because with great longing she desired to see the thing for which she had hope, just as a woman desires to see born the child whom she carries conceived.

The Holy Spirit, the wondrous comforter of all the saints, both reproves and stirs up this pain. He reproves it by saying: “Why now are you drawn tight with grief? Is there no king for you, or has your counsellor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman in labour?” He immediately stirs her up by adding: [Col. 0483C] “Grieve and strive, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labour.”

We must therefore know that there is a great difference among those who suffer in childbirth. For one woman’s soul departs because of her pain in labour; and if it is said to her, “Do not fear, for you have borne a son” (I Kings IV), or, as we read elsewhere, “Do not fear, for you shall have this son also” (Gen. XXXV), she does not answer or take notice. In accordance with this kind of comparison, the Holy Spirit did not will the Church, mother of the coming Christ, to grieve. For although the saints died before they saw the Christ of the Lord, they nevertheless ought to have had—and did have—faith in the resurrection and the age to come: namely, that although they died while awaiting him, nevertheless they would see him both apart from the flesh and afterward [Col. 0483D] in their flesh.

Therefore, when he says, “Is there no king for you, or has your counsellor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman in labour?” he exhorts all the saints by this very saying not to grieve “as do the rest who have no hope” (I Thess. IV). But when he immediately adds, “Grieve and strive like a woman in labour,” he urges them to grieve according to God—that is, not to lose in sorrow or pain the confidence of hope and the principle of faith. Hence it should be observed that he does not merely say here, “like a woman in labour,” but says, “Grieve and strive”: that is, hold firmly to hope in pain. And he adds “like a woman in labour,” because just as a woman in labour at length sees the fruit of her pain and no longer remembers her anguish because of joy, since a human being has been born into the world (John XVI), so you [Col. 0484A] shall see the Lord who delivers and redeems you, and your pain shall be turned into joy.

This is to be understood from what follows: “For now you shall go out of the city, and dwell in the country, and come as far as Babylon; there you shall be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.” With respect to the outward sense of the letter, we understand this as the well-known captivity of the Jews, by which they were to be led to Babylon and brought back after seventy years. Spiritually, however, we know another Babylon, just as we know that this Zion or Jerusalem, of which he now speaks, is the city of the living God—that is, the universal fellowship of all saints and elect, whose king and counsellor is Christ, who is foretold by the prophet in the present passage.

Keeping before our eyes, therefore, the universal captivity of this Zion, which befell it in Adam, we understand these words more worthily and fully when, after first saying, “Grieve and strive, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labour,” he adds: “You who now shall go out from the city, dwell in the country, and come as far as Babylon—there you shall be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.”

“Now,” he says—that is, before that last time in which those things I foretold take place, when the mountain of the Lord’s house, which is Christ, has been manifested—meanwhile, while he delays and he who is to come has not yet come, you shall go out of the city and dwell in the country and come as far as Babylon. That is, having been sentenced in Adam, you shall be born outside Paradise, from which he was expelled, and you together with him, in whose loins you were; you shall remain in the captivity of the present age; and after dwelling in this country you shall come as far as Babylon, namely by dying and through death descending to the confusion of infernal darkness. There your holy fathers also descended, as one of the greatest of them says: “I shall go down mourning to my son in the underworld” (Gen. XXXVII).

“There you shall be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.” For God and Lord, the Son of God, your deliverer and redeemer, shall descend there: for your sake made human, suffering, crucified, dead, buried, and afterward raised from the dead, “the pains of the underworld having been loosed,” since “it was impossible” for him to be held by it (Acts II). In this way he shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies, namely malignant [Col. 0484D] spirits, giving his own blood as the price for you, so that they may have no claim upon you on account of original sin.

The Lord said this concerning that spiritual Babylon and your invisible enemies. Now, finally, hear what this same Lord says concerning your visible enemies: “And now many nations have assembled, which say: ‘Let her be stoned, and let our eye look upon Zion.’ But they have not known the thoughts of the Lord, nor understood his counsel, because he has gathered them like hay on a threshing-floor. Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion; for I will make your horn iron, and your hoofs bronze, and you shall crush many peoples, and you shall devote their plunder to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.”

Who does not know that many nations have assembled against this Zion from the beginning of the age, from the time when deadly Cain killed his brother Abel, the first citizen of this city? (Gen. IV.) Sacred books are full of tearful histories, and almost everywhere throughout the divine page are heard the groans of this Zion, as the nations come and “set the corpses of your servants, O God, as food for the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints for the beasts of the earth”; as they “pour out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there is none to bury them” (Ps. LXXVIII).

Yet they feel no compassion for groaning Zion; rather, with obstinate cruelty they urge one another on, saying: “Let this Zion be stoned”—that is, let no one spare her. And in their desire they say: “Let our eye look upon Zion.” By this saying a violent hatred and envy is indicated, which cannot be lightly sated unless it sees many miseries. When they have attained this, they burst into malicious laughter and dance in cruel applause, opening their mouth wide, as it is written, and saying: “Aha, aha, our eyes have seen” (Ps. XXXIV)—understand: the evils of this woman which we desired, and this has turned out well for us.

“But they,” he says, “have not known the thoughts of the Lord, nor understood his counsel, because he has gathered them like hay on a threshing-floor.” The sense is this: the nations have assembled against you, and boasting in their multitude, they could see only things present and manifest—your calamity and their prosperity in this world. But they neither knew nor understood what the Lord had purposed for the future, and what counsel he had formed concerning you and them.

But behold, I tell you his counsel and thoughts: “He has gathered them like hay on a threshing-floor,” so that, when they are gathered, he may say to you: “Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion; for I will make your horn iron, and your hoofs bronze, and you shall crush many peoples, and you shall devote their plunder to the Lord and their strength to the Lord God of all the earth.” Although they suppose themselves strong and robust, yet, since they are flesh, they are like hay, because “all flesh is like hay, and all its glory like the flower of the field” (Isa. XL). And the people truly are hay.

Therefore, just as hay in the field is green for a time and, in its season when dry, is carried to the threshing-floor, where it is threshed by toothed saws or iron wagons—while the wheat is stored away and the straw and chaff cast out are committed to fire—so you, O Zion, shall thresh and crush in the Lord’s judgment all the nations who have gathered together, proudly and wantonly exulting over you, like green hay. Yet this will be so that whoever among them lays himself low in humility, you may consecrate him like wheat to the Lord of all the earth, by killing whatever in him was vicious; but whoever lifts himself up on the wind of stubborn pride, you shall deliver him like straw and chaff to everlasting fire.

For they shall not be able to withstand you, who have an iron horn and bronze hoofs. Your horn is Christ, the unconquerable king and magnificent victor; your hoofs are the apostles, born from your flesh, firm in faith, ringing in speech like bronze, a very resonant metal. For “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world; there are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard” (Ps. XVIII).

Thus far the discourse has been addressed to her who is the true Zion and true Jerusalem, beginning in this way: “And you, misty tower of the flock, daughter of Zion.” But concerning that earthly Jerusalem which killed the prophets and stoned those sent to her (Matt. XXIII), hear what is said:

## Chapter V

“Now you shall be devastated, daughter of a robber. They have laid siege against us; with a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.”

What judge, or how great a judge? Surely he who is both great God and appeared humble—a fact preached with much caution, as was necessary at that time, in the words which follow: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from days of eternity. Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labour gives birth; and the remnant of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel.”

As has already been said, the discourse is addressed to and concerns that Jerusalem which killed the prophets: “Now,” he says, “you shall be devastated, you who are not truly a daughter of Zion but truly a daughter of a robber: you who asked that Barabbas, a murderous man and robber, be released to you, but killed the author of life” (Matt. XXVIII). “Now,” I say, “you shall be devastated; now your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, encompass you and hem you in on every side, and cast you and your children who are within you to the ground” (Luke XIX).

For what reason shall you be so devastated, and why shall your children be cast down? “They have laid siege against us; with a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.” “They laid siege against us”—against us prophets and wise men and scribes—that is, some of us they killed and crucified, some of us they scourged in their synagogues and persecuted from city to city (Matt. XXIII). For their laying siege against us consisted wholly in this: they wished to shut our mouths, lest we should teach in the name of the judge of Israel, whose cheek they struck with a rod—indeed, with a reed, with which they struck him after crowning him with thorns, authority having been granted to them, as he said: “But this is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke XXIII).

By a part he signified the whole—that is, by the striking of his cheek, his entire passion. Beautifully, indeed, for this was the beginning of his passion: one of the attendants gave him a blow, saying: “Is this how you answer the high priest?” (John XVIII). Insolent cruelty; cruel insolence of the officer and buffoon, who, flattering his master the high priest and wishing to please him, rushed forward and struck the judge of Israel on the cheek before him. Nor is he judge of Israel alone, but of all human beings, because he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead (Acts X).

And, that you may be still more horrified at the audacity of the scoundrel who struck him, that judge is not merely human but also God. This is attested by the following words: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from days of eternity.” For what does it mean that he “shall come forth from you,” O Bethlehem, and nevertheless that “his going forth is from the beginning, from days of eternity,” except that there are two goings forth, that is, births? One according to the flesh, by which he shall come forth from you, O Bethlehem, from David’s seed; the other according to divinity, by which he shall not come forth, but “his going forth,” he says, “was completed long ago”—not from the world but from the beginning, not in days of temporality but from days of eternity. For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this one was in the beginning with God” (John I).

Thus he testifies here that the judge of Israel is both God and human; but it was not expedient at that time for this to be declared in such a way that the common people would understand it. For how could they endure to hear that he who was the God of Israel would become human and be struck on the cheek? Therefore the prophetic discourse is dispensed cautiously and prudently: turning suddenly away from the daughter of the robber, to whom it had been speaking, saying, “Now you shall be devastated, daughter of a robber,” and so forth, it turns to another, namely Bethlehem. It speaks to her in such a way as both to attest the truth of the two natures, divine and human, in Christ, and to state that same testimony in words which those who were deaf, or had no ears to hear, would not then easily perceive.

That Bethlehem and Ephrathah are names of one and the same city of David—or village in which David was—is established from Scripture, which says: “Rachel died and was buried on the way that leads to Ephrathah; this is Bethlehem” (Gen. XXXV). Moreover, when it says, “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah,” we must understand, in the estimation of human beings, in whose eyes you are scarcely a small village; for they regard not heavenly but earthly magnitude. Yet certainly before God you are not least.

Otherwise, unless the opposite negation is understood in the prophet’s meaning along with the same affirmation by which he says, “You are little”—“but before God you are not least”—as if he said, “You seem little or least, but you are not least,” the Gospel’s citation of this testimony will seem discordant. There the chief priests and scribes are said to have answered Herod’s inquiry thus: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah” (Matt. II). Since here it says, “You are little,” while there it is written, “You are by no means least,” the lyre plainly sounds discordantly; but in meaning there is clear harmony. When the prophet says, “You are little,” understand, in the eyes of all human beings; and when the Gospel says, “You are by no means least,” understand, before God.

What follows—“Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labour gives birth, and the remnant of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel”—has plainly been fulfilled and is yet to be fulfilled. Because they struck the cheek of so great a judge of Israel, who came forth according to the flesh from Bethlehem, from David’s seed, and whose going forth according to divinity is from days of eternity, that same judge therefore gave them up—understand: into the hands of the sword, into captivity among all nations, and into the portions of foxes (Ps. LXII), that is, of malignant spirits.

How long shall he give them up in this manner? “Until the time,” he says, “when she who is in labour gives birth.” She who is in labour is not this daughter of the robber—that is, earthly Jerusalem, barren before God—but that spiritual Jerusalem or Zion, to whom he said above: “Grieve and strive, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labour.” That mother shall give birth—understand: to the remnants of the Jews, or Israel—according to the words: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return from them” (Isa. X). For this is what he immediately adds here: “The remnant of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel.”

Whose brothers? Surely the brothers of the judge of Israel himself, because the Jews who struck his cheek are his brothers according to the flesh. The time when this shall happen will be when the fullness of the nations has entered.

It follows: “And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God; and they shall return, because now he shall be magnified to the ends of the earth.” The judge of Israel, as has already been said, shall give them up because they struck his cheek; and, rising from the dead, he shall stand—understand: at the right hand of God, mighty and exalted—according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazing into heaven, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God; and he said: Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts VII).

He shall stand, therefore—that is, the conqueror of death shall himself fight for those dying for his sake—and shall feed his people as a rich and most mighty king, “in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God”: that is, as mighty God, possessing the exalted name which is above every name (Phil. II), namely the same kind of name as the Father has, who, because of his assumed humanity, is called and is his Lord God. For he himself says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John XX).

“And they shall return,” he says, “because now he shall be magnified to the ends of the earth.” What he says here—“he shall feed,” “they shall return,” and the rest—we find expressed more plainly in the Psalm: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord; their hearts shall live for ever and ever. All the ends of the earth shall remember and return to the Lord” (Ps. XXI).

He shall feed, therefore—that is, [his people] unto the ends of the earth, as far as he shall be magnified—not with any ordinary food but with the sacrament of his body and blood. The poor who eat and drink it shall be satisfied; for their hearts—that is, their souls—shall live for ever and ever, as he himself says: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI).

It follows:

“And this one shall be peace to the Assyrian when he comes into our land and when he treads in our houses.”

In some manuscripts it is read “to the Assyrians,” and the construction seems more orderly. For if “the Assyrian” is to be read, why did he choose the inverted wording, “the Assyrian when he comes,” rather than saying, “when the Assyrian comes”? Therefore both readings must be expounded: first, according to this wording, “And this one shall be peace, when the Assyrian comes into our land.”

When the devil, says blessed Jerome, who is called Assur, comes upon the land and territory of believers—those whom the Lord feeds in strength and in the majesty of the name of the Lord their God—and treads them down with various tribulations, and arrogantly ascends and crushes the houses of our souls, that is, our bodies; if nevertheless he separates us in no way from Christ’s love, then Christ’s peace, or Christ himself, shall be in us, and it shall be said of the saint: “The enemy shall achieve nothing against him” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Now, to speak according to the other construction of the text, reading thus: “And this one shall be peace to the Assyrians, when he comes into our land,” we must first know that the phrases “when he comes into our land,” “when he treads in our houses,” and, as we have again a little later, “when he treads on our mountain,” are rightly understood of the Lord himself. This is especially so since, at the beginning of his discourse, this same prophet said: “For behold, the Lord shall go forth from his place, and descend and tread upon the high places of the earth” (Mic. I), and so forth, up to the words, “What are the high places of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?” (ibid.).

The sense will be: “And this one,” namely the Lord, magnificent to the ends of the earth, “shall be peace to the Assyrians”—that is, to all nations, among whom the Assyrians were at that time the most powerful; hence they may rightly be understood here as representing all nations. This one, I say, shall be peace to the Assyrians: he shall speak peace to the nations; he shall proclaim peace to those who had previously been enemies, when he comes into our land, that is, when he visits us, and when he treads in our houses—understand: because “you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX), O aforementioned daughter of the robber.

For this reason he shall tread in our houses; for this reason he shall trample temple and city, so that not one stone remains upon another. That the Lord treads and tramples is attested by himself when he says in another prophet: “I trod them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath” (Isa. LXIII). Woe, therefore, to you who asked that Barabbas the robber be granted to you! You are consequently rightly called daughter of a robber, whose seditions you inherited. Woe to you: you who are called Israel shall be trampled down, but your peace shall be for the Assyrians, that is, for the nations who repent, as was signified when the great Assyrian city Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jon. V).

It follows: “And we shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight leading men; and they shall feed the land of Assur with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with its spears; and he shall deliver [us] from Assur when he comes into our land and when he treads upon our mountain.”

This is the voice of those in whose person he said above, “They have laid siege against us”: “And we shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight leading men.” It is, namely, the voice of the prophets, wise men, and scribes, whom that judge of Israel said to those who struck his cheek: “Behold, I send [them] to you.” They likewise speak these words: “And we shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight leading men.”

Against whom do they say, “We shall raise them up”? Surely against that same, often-mentioned judge of Israel. Certainly they promise no mean service, no small portion of honour from their labour, for glorifying that great judge whom the children of that daughter of the robber dishonoured so grievously as to strike his cheek.

We must diligently inquire who the seven shepherds and eight leading men are, then what it means for them to be raised up over this judge of Israel; and then it will become clear that this promise is neither slight nor uncertain. We know from Holy Scripture seven persons illustrious in faith and distinguished in merits, and likewise eight leading men. Although we have known them until now, our mind had not yet so carefully weighed their number and their particular grounds, until the close attention demanded by the present passage stirred us up.

Let us therefore recall first the seven shepherds, and then, in order, the eight leading men.

The first shepherd was Abel, of whom it is written: “Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and he offered to the Lord gifts from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat; and the Lord looked with favor upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4). The second shepherd was Abraham; the third, Isaac; the fourth, Jacob, who, standing before Pharaoh with his sons, when Pharaoh asked, “What is your occupation?” replied: “We, your servants, are shepherds of sheep, both we and our fathers” (Gen. 47). His fathers were Abraham and Isaac, who indeed tended flocks, [Col. 0490C] so that the land could not contain them because of the multitude of their flocks. Hence there was a quarrel between the shepherds of Abraham’s flocks and Lot’s (Gen. 13), and a dispute between the shepherds of Gerar and the shepherds of Isaac (Gen. 26).

Yet we count these seven as most eminent shepherds not because of the number of their flocks or their care of them, but because divine authority has commended itself in what concerned their pastoral affairs. Therefore, as we have begun to say, the first of these was Abel, who offered the Lord gifts from the firstborn of his flock, gifts which the Lord deemed worthy of his regard. The second was Abraham, who took from his herd a very tender and excellent calf and made a memorable feast for his illustrious guests—namely, the three angels who came [Col. 0490D] in the figure of the Holy Trinity (Gen. 18). The third was Isaac, who was led like a ram to be sacrificed, and in whose place Abraham offered as a burnt offering a ram caught by its horns among the thorns (Gen. 22). The fourth was Jacob, who brought two kids from the flock as food for his father and received the blessing; then, while tending his father-in-law’s flocks, he was increased by the Lord’s blessing (Gen. 27).

The fifth was Joseph, who, when he was sixteen years old, was tending the flock with his brothers; thereafter he was sold and became ruler of Egypt (Gen. 37). He was not ashamed of this occupation, although the Egyptians abhorred all shepherds of sheep, saying to his father and brothers: “When Pharaoh summons you and asks, ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall answer: [Col. 0491A] ‘We, your servants, have been shepherds from our childhood until the present, both we and our fathers’” (Gen. 46). The sixth was Moses, who tended the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, priest of Midian; and while tending them, when he had driven the flock into the inner part of the wilderness, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God, and the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush (Exod. 3). The seventh was David, who said of himself to Saul: “Your servant was tending his father’s flock, and a lion or a bear would come and take a ram from the midst of it. I pursued them, struck them, and snatched it from their mouth. They rose against me, and I seized their jaws, choked them, and killed them. For I, your servant, have killed both lion and bear. Therefore this uncircumcised Philistine also shall be like one of them, [Col. 0491B] because he has dared to curse the army of the living God” (1 Sam. 17).

Behold, these are the seven illustrious shepherds whom, as Scripture testifies, divine authority has commended. The eight principal men, moreover, are these: first, Joshua son of Nun; second, Caleb son of Jephunneh; third, Othniel son of Kenaz; fourth, Ehud son of Gera, son of the Benjamite; fifth, Barak son of Abinoam, of Kedesh in Naphtali; sixth, Gideon; seventh, Jephthah the Gileadite; eighth, Samson. These eight deserve to be called principal men because, under the leading authority of God and clothed with the Spirit of the Lord, they were appointed judges and delivered their people; hence they deserved to be called saviors of Israel.

The first of them, Joshua, and the second, Caleb, brought the people into the land of promise. The Lord said [Col. 0491C] to Moses: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of the Lord, and lay your hand upon him” (Num. 27), etc. But of Caleb he says: “My servant Caleb, who, being filled with another spirit, has followed me, I shall bring into this land which he has traversed, and his seed shall possess it” (Num. 14). This divine testimony commends his preeminence, besides other matters too lengthy to insert here.

The third, Othniel son of Kenaz, delivered Israel from the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, whom they had served for eight years. Scripture says: “And they cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a savior and delivered them: Othniel, namely the son of Kenaz; and the Spirit of the Lord was in him, and he judged Israel” (Judg. 3). [Col. 0491D] The fourth, Ehud, delivered Israel from the hand of Eglon king of Moab, whom they had served for eighteen years. Scripture says: “And the children of Israel cried to the Lord, and he raised up for them a savior, Ehud son of Gera” (ibid.), etc. The fifth, Barak son of Abinoam, delivered Israel from the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who had grievously oppressed them for twenty years; and he himself was raised up by divine authority through Deborah the prophetess, wife of Lapidoth (Judg. 4; the printed “Num. VI” is evidently erroneous). The sixth, Gideon, delivered Israel from the hand of Midian, whom they had served for seven years, at the command of the angel who appeared to him (Judg. 6; printed “Num. VI”). The seventh, Jephthah the Gileadite, delivered Israel from the hand of the children of Ammon, who, together with the Philistines, had grievously oppressed them for eighteen years. It is written of him: “The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he went over [Col. 0492A] against the children of Ammon to fight them. The Lord delivered them into his hands, and he struck them with an exceedingly great slaughter; and the children of Ammon were humbled before the children of Israel” (Judg. 11; printed “Num. XI”).
