The eighth, Samson, was [^c0066-215] foretold by an angel of the Lord to his barren mother: “This one,” he said, “shall be a Nazirite from his infancy and from his mother’s womb, and he shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines” (Judg. 13).

These are the eight principal men, who are joined to the seven shepherds in a remarkable way and arose between the sixth shepherd, Moses, and the seventh, David. Thus Joshua, the first of the principal men, together with Caleb, brought into the promised land the children of Israel whom Moses, the sixth shepherd, as has been said, brought out of Egypt; and David, the seventh shepherd, completed the deliverance from the hand of the Philistines which Samson, the eighth principal man, [Col. 0492B] had begun.

We have, then, the seven shepherds and the eight principal men, known and distinguished for their proper deeds. “We shall raise them up,” says the prophet, “over him”—that is, over the often-mentioned judge of Israel whose jaw was struck. How shall we raise them over him? By teaching that what was bodily accomplished through them is spiritually done or fulfilled through him. We shall teach, I say, that in him the truth succeeded the figure of those things which preceded in them. In doing this, we prophets, sages, and scribes—among whom I am—shall raise them up over him. For although, in time, I am absent from them in body, I am present with them in spirit; through their spiritual study it comes about that, in the reading of such shepherds and principal men, nothing dead [Col. 0492C] or idle remains, while all things are referred to Christ. Thus these men also live with him, and those who shall then exist will profit through these men.

Therefore, after saying, “We shall raise up over him seven shepherds and eight principal men,” he immediately added: “And they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with its spears.” This means: all the nations now without God, possessing no food of the Word of God, will then advance by reading the mystical examples of these men—nations of whom Assyria and Nimrod, that is, the Assyrians and Babylonians, were then the greatest and most hostile to God. For the beginning of Nimrod’s kingdom was Babylon in the land of Shinar; and Assyria departed from that land and built Nineveh. Nor is it doubtful or unknown that the Assyrians later carried away the ten tribes, while the Babylonians—represented here by Nimrod—carried away the two remaining tribes, Judah and Benjamin.

The reconciliation of the nations is therefore magnificently promised when such prophecy is framed concerning those who were then most hostile: “They shall shepherd the land of Assyria and the land of Nimrod,” and this not without weapons, but “with his sword and with his spears”—that is, with the Word of God, which is living, effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4), and with the declarations of truth, which are his spears or arrows. With his sword and those spears he will defeat the devil, who formerly held the land, and will set humankind free. This is what he says: “And he shall deliver from Assyria when he comes into our land and when he treads upon our mountain.” That is as though [Col. 0493A] he said: At the same time when, according to the present prophecy, he comes into the land and tramples the Jews by overthrowing the city and temple, he will deliver from the devil the nations which until then were the land of Assyria and the land of Nimrod. Nimrod is interpreted “temptation,” and, by the statement written of him—“He was a mighty hunter before the Lord” (Gen. 10)—he signifies the devil, who possessed the nations like a strong armed man guarding his courtyard (Luke 11).

It follows: “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among many peoples like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass, which do not wait for a man or await the sons of men.” The remnant of Jacob are believers from the Jews. One of their finest number, the Apostle, after asking, “Has God cast off his people?” immediately added: [Col. 0493B] “By no means. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11; printed “Rom. XII”). For although those who will believe in the future, when the fullness of the nations has entered, are called a remnant, these too are rightly called a remnant: those few who then believed while the multitude remained in unbelief. The same Apostle testifies to this when, after citing the example of Elijah, to whom the divine response said, “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 18), he says: “Thus then, even in this time, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11).

“The remnant of Jacob,” therefore, he says, “shall be among many peoples like dew from the Lord, like drops upon the grass”: that is, the apostles of Christ, or the ministers of this same judge of whom the discourse has until now spoken, will distill or rain upon the nations holy and divine knowledge drawn from their heavenly way of life. Dew falling gently and drops descending gradually upon the grass signify evangelical or apostolic teaching given by the Lord, proclaimed with discernment according to the capacity of the hearers, and of twofold benefit to us: cooling and sanctifying us. For our earth had been parched by the heat of vices and struck, as it were, by a scorching wind from the evil spirit, so that the human heart could not inappropriately be compared to the Babylonian furnace. But then the Lord began to send, as it were, a breeze of dew (Dan. 3), when through apostolic preaching he stirred us to love heavenly things. Likewise, [Col. 0493D] our hands, empty of good works, were like thin and barren grass; but now drops from the Lord have fallen upon the grass, when this same teaching made us bloom again in love of neighbor and brightened our faces in giving alms.

And he rightly says of this dew and such drops: “Which do not wait for a man or await the sons of men.” Having expressly said “like dew,” he added “from the Lord,” because the Gospel or teaching administered through the apostles did not at any time come through human instruction or teaching, but was given from heaven. The Holy Spirit taught them invisibly, without delay or interval, so that those who had been unlettered and ordinary men [Col. 0494A] (Acts 4) suddenly became skilled in letters and mighty in all speech (Luke 24).

The same must be understood of the prophets, and first of Moses. He indeed learned human knowledge from human beings and was, as Stephen the first martyr says, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words; but he learned divine knowledge, so as to compose his Pentateuch, not through a human being but through God alone, who appeared to him in that bush. This must likewise be understood altogether of David and the other prophets, and of Christ’s apostles, whom all and only the Church of Christ receives at the summit of the canon. Hence Peter says in his Epistle: “Understanding this first, that prophetic Scripture does not arise from private interpretation. For prophecy was not at any time brought by human will, [Col. 0494B] but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1). And of the other apostles who were there when the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues and rested upon each of them (Acts 2), it is certain that they learned not from a human being nor through a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.

Concerning Paul, however, who was not there then but was called later, certain adversaries of his—the false apostles—wished to create doubt. Seeking to corrupt the truth of the Gospel which many peoples received from his mouth, they disparaged him and sought to diminish his authority because he had not been a disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ while the Lord was still living among human beings. For this reason, in many places, he defended his apostleship [^c0066-216], especially in the Epistle to the Galatians, where he says: “For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel preached by me is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from a human being nor learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

Thus, after saying of the remnant of Jacob, “They shall be among many peoples like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass,” he fittingly added, “which do not wait for a man or await the sons of men.” It is as though he said: The apostles of Jesus Christ will be wise and eloquent, filling the whole world with saving teaching; but they will receive that teaching not from human masters, nor acquire it by the labor of their own study or intellect, but perceive it through the hidden inspiration of heavenly grace. This is true of the remnant of Jacob, I say—that is, of the apostles—just as it is of the prophets, who are sons of Jacob both in flesh and in faith. [Col. 0494D] But the conclusion is not, and cannot be, the same concerning other teachers of the churches who arose from the Gentiles. They too are indeed like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass, sweetly handling and profitably expounding prophetic and apostolic Scriptures; yet each of them, in order to do this, waited for a man and looked for the sons of men. For after God they submitted themselves to many guides or teachers. Hence the Church of Christ does not hold valid whatever they said merely because they said or thought it, but because they were able to confirm their statements or opinions by prophetic and apostolic testimonies or by some plausible reasoning.

It follows: “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forests and like a roaring lion’s cub among flocks of sheep; when it passes through, tramples down, and seizes, there is none to rescue.” How different, how utterly dissimilar, are the comparisons here ascribed to the same remnant of Jacob! He had said, “The remnant of Jacob shall be like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass,” and immediately now says, “The remnant of Jacob shall be like a lion among the beasts of the forests and like a roaring lion’s cub among flocks of sheep.” What is more unlike than the sweetness of dew and the fierceness of a lion? What more different than the gentleness of drops falling upon grass and the savagery or onrush of a lion’s cub roaring among flocks of sheep? Yet the sweetness of dew or gentleness of drops, and equally the fierceness of a lion or onrush of a lion’s cub, are here ascribed by comparison to that same remnant of Jacob. Why? Because the apostles of Christ, the teachers of peoples or nations, are both gentle and stern: gentle in teaching and exhorting, stern in rebuking and punishing.

For example, Paul, while teaching among other things, says: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5). What could be sweeter than this dew of love, what gentler than this drop of true and genuine devotion? [Col. 0495C] The rest as well, down to “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6), is such a gentle rain and such dew that no one can doubt that it comes from the Lord, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation.

But later the same Apostle says, after much else: “Behold, this is the third time that I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. I have foretold, and I foretell, as though present with you and now absent, to those who formerly sinned and to all the rest, that if I come again I shall not spare. Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Behold the sternness of a teacher, like the roar of a lion over the beasts of the forests and like that of a lion’s cub over a flock of sheep. For we rightly take as beasts of the forests those whom he rebuked for the uncleanness, fornication, [Col. 0495D] and indecency which they had committed. Was he not like a lion over such people? For he says: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be removed from among you”—that is, the man who had his father’s wife. “For I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, him who has acted thus: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5).

Those who, like flocks of sheep, were as it were terrified by the roar of the lion’s cub were the people to whom he rejoicingly says: “For though I made you sorrowful by my Epistle, I do not regret it. And though I made you sorrowful for a time, now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance; for you were made sorrowful according to God” (2 Cor. 7), etc. Let us suppose, however, that these examples have been drawn from the rather stern Paul, as though we were saying that he displayed the lion’s ferocity more than the other apostles. Yet, to pass over much, did not Peter too roar like a lion or lion’s cub among flocks of sheep when, in the assembly of the disciples, he rebuked first Ananias and then his wife Sapphira, and they fell and died because they had lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5)?

Truly, then, the remnant of Jacob is “like a lion’s cub, which, when it passes through”—understand, fearing no one’s encounter—“and tramples down,” namely the rebellious, “and seizes,” understand, the liars, just as the aforesaid Ananias and Sapphira were caught [Col. 0496B] and exposed while lying to the Holy Spirit—“there is none to rescue.” Having spoken these things of the remnant of Jacob, the prophetic discourse immediately turns to that judge of Israel of whom it had said above, “They shall strike the jaw of the judge of Israel with a rod,” and says:

“Your hand shall be exalted over your enemies, and all your foes shall perish.” Those are reckoned public adversaries or enemies of the Lord’s majesty who are not merely sinners but also impious in hating his name—especially those of whom he himself speaks in the Gospel: “Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father. But this is to fulfill the word written in their law: ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15). “Your hand shall be exalted,” he says, over such enemies—understand, so that they may not see your glory; indeed, so that they may see and be confounded. Another prophet, after asking, “The wicked shall not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26), immediately gave this twofold answer: “Lord, let your hand be exalted so that they may not see; let the jealous peoples see and be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies” (ibid.). Thus, in a just rebuke he says, “Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see your glory”—understand, so as to have any share in your glory; and in a severe and exceedingly harsh concession he immediately says, “Let them see and be confounded.”

And what is here said, “All your foes shall perish,” is likewise granted there in the words, “Let fire devour your enemies.” For when your hand shall be exalted, O Lord—when you appear seated upon the throne of your majesty as King and Judge of Israel, with the sheep set at your right hand and the goats at your left—then all your enemies shall perish: that is, the devil and his angels. Then fire will devour your enemies, both the devil and his angels and the impious people who follow him, as you say: [^c0066-217] [Col. 0496D] “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Nonetheless, this may be referred to the whole Church, whose head is that judge: “Your hand shall be exalted over your enemies, and all your foes shall perish,” because those who are enemies or foes of the head are enemies or foes of the body, which is his Church; and where the head is exalted, there unquestionably the body will be exalted as well. Therefore this is rightly understood as said also to the Church herself, especially since above it was said to her: “Arise and thresh, daughter Zion” (Mic. 4), etc.; and immediately the same Church is told: “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: I shall take away your horses from your midst and scatter your chariots; I shall destroy the cities of your land and destroy all your fortifications; I shall take away sorceries from your hand, and there shall be no divinations in you. I shall cause your carved images and statues to perish from your midst; I shall uproot your groves from your midst and crush your cities; and I shall take vengeance in wrath and indignation upon all the nations that have not obeyed.”

In these words the Church of God may greatly console herself by considering the state of eternal life—what it will be from that day when all her enemies perish. For these words promise that not only every evil, but even the things which in this world appear to be, and are in a certain sense, good—though neither true nor sufficient goods—will be entirely absent there. Who does not know that sorceries, divinations, carved images, statues, worship of works of human hands, and groves chosen or consecrated for sacrifice to demons are genuine evils? Who likewise denies that horses, chariots, cities, and fortifications are false goods? “The horse is deceptive for salvation,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 33); and, “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 20).

Horses and chariots may indeed be useful—indeed necessary—to carry slow and infirm bodies, or even saints fleeing from city to city when persecution presses and they must flee quickly. Yet such use is less a true good than a consolation for genuine infirmity, and it often proves excessively deceptive; for, as has already been said, “the horse is deceptive for salvation”—to which one might add, but not deceptive for weariness. How much better it is for our bodies, now heavy, to be changed and to enjoy the swiftness of angels than falsely to console bodily heaviness by riding in horses or chariots! Therefore it is a promise of great blessedness when he says, “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: I shall take away your horses from your midst and scatter your chariots,” etc. For he had prefaced this by saying, “And all your enemies shall perish.” It is thus as if he said: On that day I shall do what you now cry out to me to do, saying, [Col. 0497D] “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 25). First, I shall take away your horses and scatter your chariots—that is, I shall make the earthly body so swift that it will be wherever it wishes, which could not be accomplished through horses and chariots. “For then,” the Lord himself says, “people shall be equal to angels, and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection” (Luke 20). If equal, then undoubtedly they shall be equally swift as angels, needing neither horses nor chariots.

What then shall I say about cities and fortifications, when he says, “I shall destroy the cities of your land and destroy all your fortifications”? It is known that Cain killed his brother Abel out of envy, and that he first built a city and named it after his son Enoch (Gen. 4). But Abel and all the other saints have no abiding city here, but seek the city to come (Heb. 13). “Therefore,” he says, “I shall destroy the cities of your land and overthrow all your fortifications”—not only spiritual ones but also those made by hands and material ones; and undoubtedly it must also be understood: all the seditions and desires of cities and fortifications, and all the disasters and evil anxieties which Cain brought upon mortal human beings. Their aggregate is called, and is, Babylon, with which, as we hear the voice from heaven say in the Apocalypse, “the kings of the earth committed fornication and lived in luxury” (Rev. 17). And there it is written: “And a mighty angel took up a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such violence shall Babylon, that great city, be thrown down, and shall be found no more’” (Rev. [Col. 0498B] 18).

Great rest, therefore, is promised to holy Zion, that is, the Church, in the destruction of the cities and fortifications of the earth. For with their destruction there is consequently understood the destruction of all desirable things in cities—things whose sight has tempted and wearied the holy citizens of God’s kingdom while pilgrims in this world: namely gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, marble, cinnamon, amomum, perfumes, ointment, incense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, beasts of burden, sheep, horses, carriages, slaves, and all the rest, of which the wise man rightly says, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1). Their covetous merchants, now made rich, insult your poor children, O holy Zion. But then, while they weep and mourn and say, “Woe, woe” (Rev. 18), these people will rejoice and gladly see even their own fortifications perish—the fortifications which they had here out of necessity, not in order to attack others, but in order to gain some relief when others attacked them.

“And I shall take away sorceries from your hand.” Here too it must be understood: so that you may no longer do any evil. For from that day onward it will be impossible for the holy society of the elect to commit or permit anything evil; innocence will be firm and incorruptible. The ancient serpent will no longer have power or permission to hiss anything or to persuade any of the saints to evil, as he did [Col. 0498D] when he persuaded the woman to eat what was forbidden and give it to her husband (Gen. 3), by which sorcery the whole human race has since been poisoned. In brief: the Lord will so remove sorceries from the hand of his elect that, having now given them the will not to do evil, he will then grant what is greater and more perfect—namely, the inability to do evil.

“And there shall be no divinations in you.” Divination is false prophecy. It will undoubtedly be happily absent then, when the presence or full knowledge of God, and the present face of truth, enlighten all, and nothing is uncertain or unknown. The saints cannot attain this perfection in the present life; rather, they say, “We know in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, [Col. 0499A] but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

“And I shall cause your carved images and statues to perish from your midst, and you shall no longer worship the works of your hands.” Before that day, every soul that worships the true God or calls upon his name must also provide against worshiping the works of its hands—namely, carved images and statues. Yet a great part of God’s people, the chosen people who worship the one God, does not attain this matter’s perfection while it lives in the body. For even if the hand outwardly remains idle and does not make itself a visible statue, is not the mind—an exceedingly swift artist—very often fashioning some image for itself when it remembers its Creator and wishes to contemplate him, to whom it says in prayer, “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6; printed “Matt. IV”)? For it quickly sets before itself, or gladly receives when it quickly arises, the image of a handsome and great old man of venerable appearance, seated in great [^c0066-218] counsel; perhaps it thinks that the reality is as it reads or hears in Daniel’s vision: “Thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat; his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool” (Dan. 7), etc. Such words speak of God as if he were localized, though he is not localized.

To err simply in this manner is pardonable; but to defend the same error stubbornly is damnable, because it is heretical. Hence the Anthropomorphites are called heretics: they have attempted to assert that God has a human form and is distinguished by bodily members. Therefore the present words, “I shall cause your carved images and statues to perish from your midst, and you shall no longer worship the works of your hands,” must be believed to be fulfilled on that day in such a way that no one will err in this manner concerning the divine substance, when all see what he is like. Thus John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

What follows, “And I shall uproot your groves from your midst and crush your cities,” will likewise [Col. 0500A] be perfectly fulfilled on that day, though it has now been fulfilled or is to be fulfilled only in part. It is not already perfection that those who worship the true God do not frequent groves or seek hiding places and darkness in order to sacrifice to the princes of darkness; nor that they do not shut their cities—that is, conceal their consciences—but appropriately open them by confessing their sins. This, I say, is not yet perfection but the beginning of blessedness. For there are still many things, not only evils of which they are ashamed, but also good things to be disclosed, which they hide and wish to hide: in shame for what is blameworthy, and in flight from vain glory for what is praiseworthy.

But then there shall be nothing that they wish to remain hidden, nor shall there occur against their will what the Apostle says: “The Lord shall come and bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4). [Col. 0500B] For concerning evils, where remission will be certain, they will have no reason to be ashamed; indeed, they will have much cause for joy: the great grace and glory of the forgiver, to be magnified without end. Concerning good things, moreover, there will be no need to hide them in flight from vain glory, because such a wind cannot blow where the true and stable glory of God, abounding over all, surpasses all things and holds all orders of angels and human beings in the foundation of its vision with sweet trembling.

Therefore the uprooting of groves and the destruction of cities will then be wholly complete, since there will be no one who wishes to do anything secretly or who wishes his conscience to be in any way enclosed lest it be seen. By contrast, the wicked shall then go into everlasting punishment and reproach. This is what he announces at the end of the discourse: “And I shall take vengeance in wrath and indignation upon all the nations that have not obeyed.”

## Book Three

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499D] [^c0066-219] Of the matters hitherto spoken in this prophet, or on account of this prophet, two openings have struck our ears forcefully: the first, namely: “Hear, all peoples, and let the earth and its fullness attend” (Mic. 1); the second: “Hear, rulers of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel” (Mic. 3). In the first prophetic denunciation, Samaria—that is, the ten tribes—is condemned, and the restoration from the nations through Christ of what they had lost is promised in these words: “For one who opens the way shall go up before them; they shall divide and pass through the gate and go out by it, and their king shall pass before them” (Mic. 2).

In the second denunciation Jerusalem, or the tribe of Judah, is more severely rebuked. The prophet says to its rulers, its priests, and its prophets: “Therefore because of you Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones” (Mic. 3). By these words the desolation is plainly foretold which the Romans wrought while they laid that same daughter waste with robbers, because she had struck the jaw of the judge of Israel, as the sequel of the same discourse plainly prophesies. Likewise, the restoration of the Jews’ loss through the salvation of the nations is promised in these words: “Peoples shall flow to the mountain of the Lord, and many nations shall hasten” (Mic. 4). And again: “The remnant of Jacob shall be among many peoples like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass” (Mic. 5), etc.

Behold, now for the third time the prophetic discourse, raising its voice like a trumpet, summons neither Samaria alone, as in the first denunciation, nor Jerusalem alone, as in the second, but addresses both parties together and begins thus:

## Chapter VI
Hear what the Lord says: “Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Let the mountains hear the judgment of the Lord, and the strong foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a case against his people, and he will enter into judgment with Israel.” [Col. 0501A] “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I been burdensome to you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and freed you from the house of bondage, and sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim unto Gilgal, that you might know the righteous acts of the Lord.”

With words of this kind the judgment of the Lord begins to be conducted concerning great matters; and, as has already been said, both parties—namely Samaria and Jerusalem—are summoned together and in some sense stand present, like two defendants who are to receive differing sentences of judgment and mercy according to their merits. For they are unlike one another: one remains rebellious even under judgment; the other lies prostrate before the judge and seeks pardon.

[Col. 0501B] Samaria, indeed, which maintained itself in perpetual schism from the house of David and the temple of the Lord, and whose kings never departed from the sins of Jeroboam—that is, from worshipping the calves which he made—nor even repented when God the judge threatened the captivity close at hand: this is the defendant who, even in judgment, through obstinacy provokes the judge’s anger more and more. Jerusalem, however, which at that time sometimes repented, and some of whose kings turned to repentance, such as Manasseh (2 Chronicles 33), while others were righteous and holy, such as David, Hezekiah, and Josiah—for apart from these all sinned in idols—is the defendant who, prostrate before the judge, confesses guilt, asks for, and merits pardon.

[Col. 0501C] For we do not read that any among the ten tribes carried off into Assyria repented and made satisfaction to God; but concerning the sons of Judah led into Babylon there is much at which we may marvel and with which we may sympathize: while Daniel in the lions’ den, and his companions cast down in the Babylonian furnace, entreat God, the merciful judge (Daniel 6).

Therefore, when judgment has been set forth in the person of the Lord saying, “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I been burdensome to you? Answer me,” another person suddenly presents himself, saying: “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend my knees to God Most High?” We should understand this to be Jerusalem, which, as has been said, was then about to repent. But the words which follow in the repeated outcry—including the judge’s declaration, “You have kept the ordinances of Omri and every work of Ahab”—we should not doubt were spoken against Samaria, [Col. 0501D] which, like a rebellious defendant, neither asks nor merits pardon from the judge.

Now let us follow the words in their order. “Hear,” he says, “what the Lord speaks.” The prophet cries this in his own person, plainly as a herald obeying the judge seated in court, so that silence may be secured and the crowd made attentive to hear. This having been prefaced, the words which the Lord speaks follow: “Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and the hills shall hear your voice.”

Concerning these mountains and hills against which he is commanded to contend in judgment, different interpreters have held different opinions. Some understand angels, to whom the administration of human affairs has been entrusted, and who, as the Apostle says, are ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who receive the inheritance (Hebrews 1); and they wish judgment to be contended against them if they have not done all that belonged to their duty. Others interpret them as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the remaining patriarchs, before whom, as auditors summoned to judgment, the case of the people Israel is to be examined.

[Col. 0502A] But neither interpretation proceeds freely or is confirmed by the plain words of Scripture—especially since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are saints and friends of God, while the holy angels, already separated from evil angels by the past judgment, are secure of their salvation and established in blessedness. How then could I confidently affirm either concerning these or concerning those mountains and hills that a contention of divine judgment is conducted against them?

Therefore, that the meaning may be more straightforward, let us follow that to which the present text plainly leads us, since at the beginning of the contention it is immediately said, “My people, what have I done to you?” Thus the people Israel, both of whose parts—Samaria and Jerusalem—we said shortly before were summoned to judgment, are rebuked under the names of mountains and hills in these words. Nor are they inappropriately represented by mountains, because each part ruled and exalted itself upon mountains: the ten tribes on Mount Samaria, and the two remaining tribes, Judah and Benjamin, on Mount Zion. Thus the same Lord says through another prophet: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria” (Amos 6).

[Col. 0502B] Therefore, “against the mountains”—that is, against Samaria and Jerusalem, dwelling on mountains and trusting in mountains—“arise,” he says, “and contend in judgment”; and let “the hills,” that is, their lesser dependent cities, hear your voice. At this decree of the Lord proposing judgment, the same herald—that is, the prophet who had spoken first, saying, “Hear what the Lord speaks”—again, in accordance with his office, desiring to make the multitude of the people, or the mountainous height of the rulers, yet more attentive, cries and says: “Let the mountains hear the judgment, and the strong foundations of the earth, because the Lord has a case with his people, and he will enter into judgment with Israel.”

The mountains, as has been said, are called Samaria and Jerusalem, each of which is a metropolis situated on a mountain. By “the strong foundations of the earth” we may suitably understand the kings of both parts. Royal power is in some sense the foundation of the earth—that is, of the people. Hence in Greek a king is called *basileus*, that is, “the base of the people,” because peoples and other ranks rest upon their kings as columns rest upon bases.

[Col. 0502C] Therefore, you strong foundations of the swelling, mountainous earth—that is, evil-strong kings, kings trusting in your own powers and riches, who support Samaria and Jerusalem situated on mountains and, what is worse, trusting in mountains—hear the judgment of the Lord; for, what is greatly to be feared, the Lord has a case with his people and will enter into judgment with Israel.

For a sensible person ought greatly to fear lest God enter into judgment with him; for he knows that he cannot answer him one thing out of a thousand. Therefore he lies prostrate and asks, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142).

After this interjection by the prophet, it is not the prophet—though he seemed to have been addressed in the words, “Arise and contend in judgment”—but the Lord himself, in his own person, who begins to contend in judgment in this way: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt, freed you from the house of slaves, and sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.”

[Col. 0503A] Who speaks these words while contending in judgment but the Lord? And who had said, “Arise and contend in judgment,” but the Lord? Does one and the same person then both command and obey, so that he who speaks and he to whom it is spoken are one and the same? We inquire and investigate this carefully because we greatly desire that here also he may appear who so often in the Scriptures speaks as God to God, Lord to Lord, Father to Son. Many words are found spoken between these persons; among them the sweetest and clearest is that which David heard in the Spirit and reported to us: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109).

Let the person of the Father, then, be the one who says, “Arise, contend in judgment”; let the person of the Son be the one who, obeying the word, contends in judgment and says: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome to you? Answer me.” For what? Because he had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary, did he therefore not know how to contend in judgment? On the contrary, he was already able to plunder and take spoil. Hence it is said of him to another prophet: “Call his name, Hasten to take the spoil; hurry to plunder” (Isaiah 8).

[Col. 0503B] For what reason? “Before,” he says, “the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away” (ibid.). Damascus and Samaria, of course, were then attacking Judah with all their might. This is to say: Therefore call the name of the child whom he had earlier foretold should be called Emmanuel (Isaiah 7), “Hasten to take the spoil; hurry to plunder,” since before he is born into the world and has a father and mother—a putative father, namely Joseph, and a natural mother, namely Mary—he delivers, and has hitherto delivered, Judah and Jerusalem from their enemies.

A marvelous hastening, an unheard-of speed! No one has ever been so swift as to do anything before being born or conceived, except this one alone, who was first God, begotten from God the Father, before he became man, himself born of a woman. Therefore, just as he was commanded to be called “Hasten to take the spoil; hurry to plunder,” so, in accordance with the present subject, he could be called “Hasten to judgment; hurry to contend and to enter into judgment with Israel.” For he in whom Israel has so often been judged, so as to be handed over to enemies, and so often delivered from enemies, is one and the same Word of the Lord, one and the same Son of God: true God, judging justly before he became man to be judged unjustly.

[Col. 0503C] Now then let us hear the questions and arguments of the one contending in judgment: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome? Answer me.” Having prefaced this question, lest the people should have occasion to recount the troubles it suffered when he so often handed it over into the hands of the nations and those who hated it ruled over it, he also sets forth this case of his, by which he shows that he was first in benefits and received evils in return for good things, when he says: “For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slaves; and I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam” (Numbers 2 [citation as printed]).

Nor did I send before you only those who were your brothers, but also the foreigner, namely Balaam son of Beor, who was not of your people, to bless you. This is what he immediately adds: “My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim unto Gilgal, that you might know the righteous acts of the Lord.” And the sense is: Was I burdensome to you in that I bestowed these benefits upon you?

[Col. 0504A] The phrase “from Shittim unto Gilgal” is to be understood as though he said: “Going from place to place and changing places, so that they might survey the whole army of Israel with their eyes—as though I could not go with one who goes, and pass with one who passes.” And I did this so that my mercies and righteous acts might be known to you.

Therefore, when, after prefacing “What have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome?” he immediately adds, “For I brought you up from Egypt through Moses and Aaron,” and then asks them to remember how he restrained Balaam son of Beor from cursing them—were not both these things pleasant to the people rather than burdensome? At the same time it is necessary to remember what the people, conversely, did, so that, when the cases are compared in the opposing judgment, it may appear how just God is and how unjust Israel is.

For what did the people do to God? Was it not rather they who were burdensome to him? When God brought them out of Egypt, they made a molten calf and offered sacrifices to it. God sent Moses and Aaron before the people; the people, bitterly afflicting them, nearly stoned them (Exodus 32). When God restrained Balaam from cursing the people (Numbers 22), the people immediately committed fornication with the daughters of Midian and were initiated into Baal-peor (Numbers 25).

[Col. 0504B] Let us pass over the rest. Although in the present judgment the Lord did not recount them, being content to mention a few, in every instance, I say, we shall find recompense from the people. When God brought the people into the land he had promised, the people committed worse acts than the very nations of that land, among whom they mingled and whose gods they worshipped (Judges 2). God gave the people David, a king after his own heart; the people, separating themselves from the house of David and from the temple of God, worshipped golden calves (3 Kings 12).

Finally—and this is greatest of all—God, made man from the seed of Abraham, fulfilled the promises he had made to him and presented himself to the people; the people denied him, prepared a cross for him, and pierced his side with a spear (John 19). Therefore it is not without cause that the judgment of the Lord is to be adjudicated with his people and with Israel, because great and numerous matters are brought into question from the unjust side of the people: some had preceded this prophecy, others were still to follow.

[Col. 0504C] Nor should any of us suppose himself free from such an adjudication, since we too are Israel, whom the Lord brought out of the Egypt of this age—that is, from the darkness of ignorance—and sent before us Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, causing us with unveiled face to contemplate the things done through them, because they happened figuratively. Each person’s conscience knows what recompense he has rendered to God.

Therefore, when we hear God saying to a human being, “What have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome to you?” let there not be in us a hard and unyielding heart or an iron neck. For the most high God stoops and speaks in this manner to miserable man so that, at least pierced by compunction because of God’s humility, the human being may say, “I have sinned against the Lord” (1 Kings 7), after the example of David, with whom God deigned thus to enter into judgment after he had sinned with Bathsheba.

“I,” he says, “anointed you king over Israel, [Col. 0504D] and I rescued you from the hand of Saul and gave you the house of Israel and Judah; and if these things are small, I shall add to you far greater things” (3 Kings 12). By speaking first in this manner, he endeavored to soften and by loving-kindness make the heart tender, so that he might better and more deeply wound it by immediately adding: “Why then did you despise the word of the Lord, to do evil in my sight?” and so forth (ibid.).

Whoever similarly pierced by compunction and beneficially bound in judgment speaks the words which immediately follow here in the prophet: “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend my knees to God Most High? Shall I offer him burnt offerings and yearling calves? Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams or with many thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?”

In each of these questions, except “Shall I bend my knees to God Most High?” one must understand “No.” For God does not delight in burnt offerings, yearling calves, rams, and fat goats; and even if he did delight in such things, it would not be a worthy price or an equal redemption to offer a brute animal to so great a judge for the sin of a rational soul.

[Col. 0505A] Still more, to offer one’s firstborn or the fruit of one’s womb for one’s crime is utterly contrary to reason, especially since doing this is itself a crime of the most cruel paganism—although Jephthah, a mighty man, fulfilled his rash vow by sacrificing his daughter (Judges 11).

Indeed, in every person whom repentance has pierced before us, the one and same Spirit considers such matters—“What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?” and the rest—according to the Apostle’s words: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Romans 8).

Nevertheless, that we may maintain a fixed order and not depart from what has preceded, where we distinguished Samaria and Jerusalem as two defendants, one of whom persists in guilt even under judgment while the other strives for pardon: clearly this person who, on hearing the judgment, says, “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?” and the rest, is Jerusalem. For by thus confessing its sins it deserved that its captivity should be ended after seventy years, while the ten tribes remained in perpetual captivity. God the judge had also spoken beforehand through another prophet: “For I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, but will utterly forget them; yet I will have mercy on the house of Judah and save them in the Lord their God” (Hosea 1).

[Col. 0505B] Where do we read that captive Judah, or Jerusalem under affliction, had pious concern for its crime, according to the words, “Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams or with many thousands of fat goats?” Certainly in that prayer in Daniel: “We have sinned, O Lord; we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously, we have departed and turned aside from your commandments and judgments” (Daniel 6). And elsewhere: “At this time there is no ruler, prophet, or leader, no burnt offering, sacrifice, oblation, incense, or place of firstfruits before you, that we may find mercy; but may we be received in a contrite soul and a spirit of humility, as in a burnt offering of rams and bulls, and as in thousands of fat lambs” (Daniel 3).

What, then, does the divine answer say to this? “I shall tell you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk watchfully with your God.” Therefore do not be anxious about burnt offerings and yearling calves, about thousands of lambs and fat goats, nor about any things at all outside yourself. For God does not seek what is yours, but yourself; not your possession, but your spirit; not your ram or goat, but your heart. Offer that, for this is good. Offer it, I say, by doing justice, loving mercy, and walking watchfully with your God.

[Col. 0505C] What is it to do justice except to anticipate God’s judgment? But you anticipate God’s judgment if you judge yourself beforehand in God’s sight, lest you be judged by God. “For if we judged ourselves,” says the Apostle, “we should certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11).

This, then, is already the difference between these two defendants, one called Samaria and the other Jerusalem: Samaria resists judgment, never abandoning its calves, and therefore the Lord says, “I will no longer have mercy upon her.” Jerusalem, however, yields to judgment and asks pardon; therefore he says, “But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah and save them in the Lord their God” (Hosea 1).

It is good, then, to follow judgment; but it is best to do justice, namely by judging oneself beforehand. And then to choose—or rather, diligently seek—mercy, which is to be merciful, so that one may oneself obtain mercy. Examples at that time were especially Daniel and Nehemiah. Daniel, when the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation had been completed, greatly sympathizing with his desolate nation, said: “I set my face toward the Lord my God, to seek him in prayer and supplications, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes” (Daniel 9).

[Col. 0505D] Nehemiah, when he heard the report, “The wall of Jerusalem has been broken down and its gates burned with fire,” said: “I sat down and wept and mourned for many days; and I fasted and prayed before the face of the God of heaven” (2 Esdras 1), and so forth.

What is then said here in the prophet—“to walk watchfully with your God”—is the same as saying: “Henceforth beware of sin.” Such watchfulness existed in Daniel and his companions during that same captivity to such an extent [Col. 0506A] that they would not permit themselves even to be defiled by the king’s table or by the wine he drank.

Having said these things to the person who had asked, “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?” and so forth, he immediately adds, as though that person asked, “If then I do these things as you have shown me, what will follow?” He says: “The voice of the Lord cries to the city: there shall be salvation for those who fear my name.”

He makes more explicit the person whom we said above was Jerusalem, like a defendant under judgment who confesses and repents, while the other—Samaria, that is, the ten tribes—persists in evil. Against them he immediately launches this invective, with no slackening of his cry: “Hear, tribe. And who will approve it? There is still fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of iniquity, and a scant measure full of wrath. Shall I justify wicked scales and deceitful weights in the bag, by which her rich have been filled with iniquity, and her inhabitants spoke falsehood, and their tongue was deceitful in their mouth? And I therefore began to strike you with destruction because of your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied, and your humiliation shall be in your midst. You shall seize, and not save; and those whom you save I shall give to the sword. You shall sow and not reap; you shall tread olives and not anoint yourself with oil; and new wine, and not drink wine. And you have kept the ordinances of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab, and you have walked in their counsels, that I might give you over to destruction, and its inhabitants to hissing; and you shall bear the reproach of the peoples.”

[Col. 0506B] The cry of the Lord is plainly divided: it announces consoling words to the city, namely Jerusalem, that salvation belongs to those fearing the Lord’s name—his children who are to return from captivity. But what does it say to the ten tribes, according to their deserts? “Hear,” he says, “O tribe”—understand, “your work,” which is now rebuked in the judgment of the Lord. “And who will approve it?” Certainly no upright person; no one but a wicked person, whose greed may approve it, though reason disapproves it. Yet in judgment, when the matter is exposed naked, it is remarkable if even a wicked person dares approve it with stubborn shamelessness.

What is it? “There is still fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of iniquity, and a scant measure full of wrath.” He brings one crime of the ten tribes into judgment, but through that one embraces all the rest together. And rightly so, for greed is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6). He suitably denotes greed by the name of fire. For the two are alike. “Fire never says, ‘Enough,’” says Wisdom (Proverbs 30), and “the greedy person shall not be filled with money” (Ecclesiastes 5).

[Col. 0506C] Therefore “there is still fire in the house of the wicked”: that is, greed, which is also the service of idols (Colossians 3), reigns so completely in Samaria that it worships gold as God, for it worships golden images of calves. The word “still” indicates the duration and persistence of sin. For from the time Jeroboam made those calves, through so many years or periods, with so many kings succeeding or changing, and with so many signs and wonders displayed through Elisha and Elijah, the worship of the same calves persisted; and none of the kings at all had departed from the sins of Jeroboam, [Col. 0506D] down to the last, Hoshea son of Elah, who began to reign in Samaria in the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah (4 Kings 15), under whom this prophet prophesied.

Therefore “there is still fire in the house of the wicked”: insatiable greed has persisted among you far too long, O ten tribes, who are the house of the wicked one, namely Jeroboam who caused you to sin. You devoted yourselves to him as to the lord of the house for evil, though you ought to have been the house of the Lord God.

That greed must be understood by the name of fire, as has been said, is sufficiently suggested by the following text. For after saying, “There is still fire in the house of the wicked,” he immediately adds, “Treasures of iniquity and a scant measure full of wrath. Shall I justify wicked scales and deceitful weights in the bag, by which her rich have been filled with iniquity, and her inhabitants spoke falsehood, and their tongue was deceitful in their mouth?”

A scant measure, forbidden by the law of the Lord, and deceitful—that is, unequal weights, when goods are sold by one weight and bought by another—are surely instruments of greed. This truly is the fire that destroys all good things and never says, “Enough” (Proverbs 30). “Shall I,” he says, “justify these things?” Certainly not; rather, I shall condemn them. The smaller measure, which takes in less merchandise for sale, takes in a greater wrath to be poured back into your bosom.

[Col. 0507A] If poor people did this, poverty might defend the crime by necessity. But now, he says, “her rich have been filled with iniquity”: that is, with wicked riches, which are amassed through wrongdoing. “And those dwelling in it”—understand, in the house of the wicked—“speak falsehood, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth,” because the accumulation of riches is followed by falsehood, and the hand accustomed to laying up treasures possesses a fraudulent tongue. Truth produces poverty.

“And I therefore began to strike you with destruction because of your sins”—understand: and I shall not cease striking until destruction is complete, because you persist in sins. As though he said: “For this reason I have already often sent the king of Assyria against you; and because you persist in sin, I shall send him again.”

For since this prophet prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, the sequence of the history now fittingly comes to mind because of his saying: “And I therefore began to strike you with destruction because of your sins.” Thus, in the twelfth year of Ahaz Hoshea began to reign in Samaria over Israel; and Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him, and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute (4 Kings 17). This was the beginning of the striking of which he now says: “And I therefore began to strike you with destruction.”

[Col. 0507B] It continues: “But when the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea, attempting rebellion, had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, in order that he might not pay tribute to the king of Assyria as he had been accustomed to do each year, he besieged him and sent him bound into prison; and he ranged through the whole land. Going up to Samaria, he besieged it for three years. In Hoshea’s ninth year the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried them away into Assyria, placing them in Halah and Habor, beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes” (ibid.).

This was Hezekiah’s sixth year and Hoshea’s ninth, Hoshea having begun to reign in Ahaz’s twelfth year. For as is again written below in that passage: after three years, in Hezekiah’s sixth year—that is, Hoshea king of Israel’s ninth year—Samaria was captured, and the king of Assyria carried Israel away into Assyria.

Therefore, when he says, “And I therefore began to strike you with destruction because of your sins,” and immediately adds, “You shall eat and not be satisfied, and your humiliation shall be in your midst; you shall seize and not save, and those whom you save I shall give to the sword; you shall sow and not reap; you shall tread olives and not anoint yourself with oil, and new wine and not drink wine”—when, I say, he speaks both those things concerning the past and these concerning the future, this is understood: that he prophesied this discourse, which begins, “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I been burdensome to you?” between the two Assyrian invasions.

[Col. 0507C] The Lord said concerning the first invasion, “And I began to strike you,” namely when you became tributary to enemies; but concerning the second, “You shall eat and not be satisfied, and your humiliation shall be in your midst,” and the rest: namely, because you, Israel, shall go away captive and your king Hoshea shall be sent bound into prison.

The phrase “your humiliation shall be in your midst”—the humiliation being understood as both the imprisonment of King Hoshea and the captivity of the whole people—is an expression like “Your blood shall be upon your own head” (3 Kings 2): that is, your destruction shall come from yourself and shall more rightly be charged to no one but you, as you receive what you deserve and cannot fail to know that it is just.

What follows—“You shall seize and not save, and what you save I shall give to the sword”—seems to reproach King Hoshea because he did not turn rather to God, but, as has been said above, sent messengers to the king of Egypt (4 Kings 17), so as to seize him as a peg or staff on which he could lean. By doing this, he shall save neither his own people nor himself—understand, from paying tribute to the king of Assyria. Indeed, those whom he thought to save in this way the Lord gave to the sword, because it was especially on this account that the king of Assyria angrily came up and captured them, not without the will and judgment of the Lord.

[Col. 0507D] Finally, when he says, “You shall sow and not reap; you shall tread olives and not anoint yourself with oil; and new wine, and not drink wine,” he inflicts upon him a great torment in every phrase, since his heart was wholly devoted to such possessions with the greed and avarice that the preceding words have indicated. For the more greatly anyone suffers from the disease of greed, the more he is tormented by hearing or seeing another reap what he himself sowed, anoint himself with oil, and drink the wine for which he himself labored up to the winepress and stored in the cellar.

The connective word in “And you have kept the ordinances of Omri” joins this statement to the earlier verse: “There is still fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of iniquity, and a scant measure full of wrath.” Omri was Ahab’s father, and he built Samaria, as it is written: “Omri reigned over Israel twelve years. He reigned six years in Tirzah; and he bought the mountain of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built upon it, and called the city which he had built Samaria after Shemer, the owner of the mountain of Samaria.”

[Col. 0508A] “But Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord and acted more wickedly than all who had been before him” (3 Kings 16). In this his ordinances, which “you have kept,” are indicated. For he confirmed the ordinances of Jeroboam, who had given them when he formed the calves, saying: “Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12). Omri confirmed them by building another metropolis, namely Samaria, against the ancient and lawful metropolis, Jerusalem, the city of David. By thus confirming Jeroboam’s ordinances, he made them his own ordinances; and Ahab his son enlarged them. Therefore, after saying, “You have kept the ordinances of Omri,” he adds, “and every work of the house of Ahab.”

What was the work of Ahab’s house? He reigned in Samaria twenty-two years and “did evil in the sight of the Lord more than all who had been before him. Nor was it enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam: in addition he took as wife Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians; and he went and served Baal in the temple which he had built in Samaria, and planted a sacred grove” (3 Kings 16).

[Col. 0508B] Then this was the work of his house—that is, of himself and of his wife Jezebel—that they killed the prophets of the Lord, so that Elijah, thinking himself to be the sole survivor, said: “Lord, they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone remain, and they seek my life to take it away” (3 Kings 19).

You have kept such ordinances and works of theirs. For you, Israel—or you, Hoshea king of Israel, in whose days Israel is punished with you—never departed from their sins, and “walked in their vanities,” provoking me so greatly that I might give you over to destruction, as is just, and “its inhabitants”—understand, those of Ahab’s house, which is Samaria—“to hissing,” that is, derision; and “you shall bear the reproach of the peoples,” namely you wicked kings, since whatever Israel suffers is the result of your crime and your madness. Or the statement may be taken conversely: Israel as a whole suffers whatever madness you committed.

It follows:

## CHAPTER VII
Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering clusters of the vintage in autumn. There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired early figs [Col. 0510D]. The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright man among men. All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother to death. They call the evil of their hands good. The prince demands, and the judge is ready to render it. And the great man has spoken the desire of his soul, and they have troubled him. He who is best among them is like a paliurus [a thorny shrub], and he who is upright like a thorn from a hedge.

These sayings flow from the fountain of compassion; for in a perfect person the good zeal by which saints seem to rage is never without compassion. They are angry with sins; they pity sinners. Thus Moses, raging against sins and girded with strong zeal, said: “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh”; and on that day about twenty-three thousand fell (Exod. XXXII). Yet, pitying sinners, he said to the Lord: “Either forgive them this offence, or, if You do not, blot me out from Your book which You have written” (ibid.) [Col. 0511A]. Many other saints are known to have acted thus; it would take far too long to run through their examples.

Not to pass over this prophet: what could be more forceful, what more vehement, than the denunciation with which he had concluded a little earlier: “I will make all the idols of Samaria perish, because they were gathered from a harlot’s wages, and they shall return to a harlot’s wages” (Mic. I)? Yet what could be said more gently than what he immediately adds: “Because of this I will lament and howl; I will go stripped and naked” (ibid.)? Thus also in the present passage, after he had vigorously rebuked the treasures of iniquity, the scant measure, the wicked balance, and deceitful weights, and, like an adversary, had pronounced a sentence of vengeance from the Lord’s judgment, he is immediately [Col. 0511B] wounded by genuine compassion: “Woe is me,” he says, “for I have become like one gathering clusters of the vintage in autumn,” and so forth.

Certainly, what he desired he expressed more aptly by a true and fitting comparison than if he had stated the matter itself in bare words. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts,” the Lord Himself says in Isaiah, “is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). And the Psalmist says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; You drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. LXXIX). But when it was expected to produce grapes, it produced wild grapes (Isa. V). This prophet experienced that: for during his prophecy, or that of the other men whom the Lord sent, none of Israel’s kings repented.

Using, therefore, a fitting comparison, he says: “I have become like one gathering clusters of the vintage in autumn.” And he immediately adds: “There is no cluster to eat” [Col. 0511C], that is, none who produces the fruit of repentance. For all who are unrepentant offend God, like sour grapes that cannot be eaten. But penitents are like ripe grapes or figs, sweet and pleasant: “My soul desired them,” he says, “but I did not find them.” For this is what follows: “The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright man among men.”

From the land—that is, from Samaria—the holy man has perished who might have been to me like a cluster fit to eat; and among men—that is, among the ten tribes—there is no upright man who might have been to me like an early fig. For which of all the kings of Samaria or of the ten tribes is not written of as having “done evil in the sight of the Lord”? But it is not so with the kings of Jerusalem. She both said above (Mic. IV), “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?” [Col. 0511D] and will later say, “But I will look to the Lord and wait for God my Saviour.” For David, Hezekiah, and Josiah were good clusters fit to eat—that is, holy men; and some of the others, though at first sour, were afterwards changed through repentance and became sweet and upright.

Now hear, kings of Samaria or of the ten tribes, how sour and unpleasant they were. “All,” he says, “lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother to death.” Surely, the dreadful and long tragedy of the kings of Israel is indicated in few words. For almost all, after—or beginning with—Jeroboam, who was first, lay in wait for blood and hunted one another to death.

After the aforementioned Jeroboam, his son Nadab succeeded him; Baasha plotted against him, struck him down, reigned in his place, and struck down the entire house of Jeroboam (III Kings XV) [Col. 0512A]. Baasha was succeeded by his son Elah. His servant Zimri rebelled against him, killed him, reigned in his place, and struck down the entire house of Baasha. Zimri himself reigned seven days. Omri marched against him, and, seeing that the city was being captured, Zimri set fire to the royal house over himself and died. Then one half of the people followed Tibni, and the other half Omri. But Omri prevailed and reigned, and Tibni died.

After him—that is, after Omri—his son Ahab reigned. Jehu son of Nimshi killed Ahab’s son Joram and reigned in his place; he struck down all who belonged to Ahab’s house, all his acquaintances, Ahaziah king of Judah [Col. 0512B], and his brothers, for they were of Ahab’s stock (III Kings XVI). And Jehu reigned, as did his sons, to the fourth generation (IV Kings IX).

After this, Shallum son of Jabesh struck down Zechariah son of Jeroboam, son of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, and reigned in his place for one month. Menahem of Tirzah then struck him down and killed him, and reigned in his place (IV Kings XV). Pekah son of Remaliah then struck down Menahem’s son Pekahiah and reigned in his place (IV Kings XVI). Hoshea son of Elah conspired against this man, laid snares for him, struck and killed him, and reigned in his place. In Hoshea’s ninth year Israel was carried captive.

Where there was so great and bloody a division among kings, how great could the desolation of the kingdom and the turmoil among those supporting rival factions have been? Thus he did not speak without cause: “All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother to death” [Col. 0512C].

Moreover, though all the kings of Israel were so reprobate that he rightly said here, “The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright man among men,” Scripture marks out three of them as especially infamous: the first Jeroboam, who made the calves; Omri, who founded Samaria; and Ahab, who worshipped Baal and, together with his wife Jezebel, killed the prophets of the Lord. This prophet also mentioned them a little earlier when he said: “You have kept the ordinances of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab” (Mic. VI).

He seems here again to touch upon the evil memory of these three in the three statements which he adds in this order: “They call the evil of their hands good; the prince demands, and the judge is ready to render it; and the great man has spoken the desire of his soul, and they have troubled him.” For the one who called the evil of his hands good was Jeroboam, together with the priests whom he himself appointed from the lowest of the people: after making calves, they said, “Behold your gods, O Israel” (III Kings XII). By “the prince who demanded, and the judge who was ready to render,” we understand Omri. In opposition to Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, where the temple of the Lord stood, he wished to make a capital of his own; he bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer, who owned the hill, for whatever price he chose—namely, two talents of silver—and judged concerning the price according to his own will, because he was prince (III Kings XVI) [Col. 0512D].

“The great man who spoke the desire of his soul” may be understood as Ahab. Throwing himself upon his bed and turning his face toward the wall, when Jezebel asked him, “Why do you not eat bread?” he said: “I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, ‘Give me your vineyard for money; or, if it pleases you, I will give you another vineyard for it.’ But he said, ‘I will not give you my vineyard’” (III Kings XXI). Thus that great man spoke the desire of his soul, the excess of his covetousness.

That he is called “great” in such a matter is made a remarkable and angry mockery by his wife, who responded to this with irony: “You possess great authority, and you govern the kingdom of Israel well! Rise and eat; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite” (ibid.) [Col. 0513A]. “And they troubled him,” he says. Who troubled him, and whom did they trouble? Surely Ahab and his wife Jezebel troubled Naboth, by bringing against him false witnesses who said: “He cursed God and the king”; and they stoned him, and so he died (ibid.).

Thus, after rightly saying, “The great man has spoken the desire of his soul,” he added, “and they have troubled him,” using the relative pronoun of the man whose proper name he had not given. He intended, surely, that the righteous Naboth should be very well known: so well that it is, in a sense, unnecessary to name expressly one who ought always to remain in everyone’s memory, since his blood always cries out and always accuses the sacrilege of the ungodly.

Do you still wish to hear how reprobate all those kings were? He says: “He who is best among them is like a paliurus, and he who is upright like a thorn from a hedge.” The best among the kings of Israel was Jehu, for he alone of them all is recorded to have been anointed king by the hand of Elisha [Col. 0513C], who poured oil over his head and said: “I have anointed you king over the people of the Lord, Israel, and you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master” (IV Kings IX), together with the other things which he vigorously carried out.

For he destroyed Ahab’s house; he cast down Jezebel, whom dogs also ate; he struck down with the sword all the priests of Baal; he destroyed Baal’s temple and made it into latrines; and thus he destroyed Baal from Israel (IV Kings X). Jehu, therefore, was the best among them, namely in the respect we have stated. Yet he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, as is also written of him: “Nevertheless, he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin; nor did he abandon the golden calves which were in Bethel and Dan” (ibid.) [Col. 0513D].

Thus this “best” man was truly like a paliurus: that is, a plant armed with thorns, pricking, holding fast, and wounding the one who approaches, and seizing with its hooked tooth. For even in the very act in which, by the Lord’s command, he destroyed the house of Ahab and Jezebel in vengeance for the blood of the prophets and the blood of all His servants, he took care to satisfy not so much love for God as his own ambition, drawing the kingdom to himself by a single covetous desire; and for this reason he pricked with arrows and wounded with the sword.

Further, by “the upright one among them” is understood Hoshea, the last king, of whom it is written: “He did evil before the Lord, but not as the kings who had been before him” (IV Kings XVII). For he is said to have granted permission to those wishing to go up and offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem [Col. 0514A], something the earlier kings had not done, as they persisted in the sins of Jeroboam, who had forbidden it, saying: “Do not go up to Jerusalem” (III Kings XII).

Perhaps, in granting this permission, Hoshea was mollified by some favour from the king of Judah; for it could hardly have been unwelcome to him that this same Hoshea had killed Pekah son of Remaliah and reigned in his place. For Pekah son of Remaliah had been Judah’s enemy, since he went up with Rezin king of Syria to wage war against Jerusalem. Therefore Ahaz, constrained by necessity, sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, saying: “Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen against me” (IV Kings XVI).

Nevertheless, in whatever way and for whatever reason he did less evil than the kings before him, it is certain that he did evil before the Lord, because Scripture bears witness. Therefore even he who is upright—Hoshea is understood—is like a thorn from a hedge [Col. 0514B]. For just as, in a thorny hedge, where help is expected, pain is inflicted, so Hoshea, while he sends to the king of Egypt and seeks by his aid to suppress Jerusalem, by that very act prepares an occasion of captivity for Israel.

Therefore it is no wonder that He sought clusters of the vintage and found no cluster to eat; that His soul desired early figs and did not find them. “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they harvest grapes from a bramble or from a paliurus” (Matt. VII).

It follows: “The day of your watchmen, your visitation, has come; now their desolation shall be.” “Do not believe a friend; do not trust in a leader. From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the barriers of your mouth [Col. 0514C]; for son dishonours father, daughter rises against her mother, daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; the enemies of a man are those of his own household. But I will look to the Lord and wait for God my Saviour. The Lord my God will hear me.”

Whether you understand these words as addressed to Samaria, to whom He had said above, “You have kept the ordinances of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab, and have walked in their counsels,” or to Jerusalem, the matter is evident under either interpretation. For the captivity of both Samaria and Jerusalem—which is here called “visitation” or “the day of watchmen”—was then coming and near. Yet it is preferable to understand the words as addressed to Jerusalem, because she is the one who answers, and to whom it is fitting to answer: “But I will look to the Lord and wait for God my Saviour.” This is indeed the same city which, with humility, said above: “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord?” and so forth (Mic. VI).

That the speech is addressed to Jerusalem concerning those against whom He had said, “He who is best among them is like a paliurus, and he who is upright like a thorn from a hedge”—namely, the kings or princes of Samaria—is especially shown by the fact that, after saying, “The day of your watchmen, your visitation, has come,” He immediately adds: “And now their desolation shall be” [Col. 0514D]. Whose “their,” if not the people among whom, as He had complained above, there was no upright man, so that he who was best among them was like a paliurus, and he who was upright like a thorn from a hedge?

Their desolation was then at hand: that is, the irreversible captivity of the ten tribes. But it was not so with Judah or Jerusalem. The king of Assyria would indeed come as far as Jerusalem itself—hence later it is said to her, “Assyria shall not come as far as you”—but he would not devastate it; for the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “He shall not enter this city nor take it” (Isa. XXXVII). Likewise, that city was indeed to be delivered to the Babylonians, but restored after its appointed time, that is, after seventy years (IV Kings XVI). Hence He later says to her: “The day when your walls shall be built is appointed.”

Therefore what follows—“Do not believe a friend, and do not trust in a leader; from her who sleeps in your bosom guard the barriers of your mouth; for son dishonours father, daughter rises against her mother, daughter-in-law [Col. 0515B] against her mother-in-law; the enemies of a man are those of his own household”—expresses the magnitude of the calamity of those of whom He had said, “And now their desolation shall be.” The hearer should consider and weigh how great the disorder of affairs and confusion among common or middling people was, or could have been, where the kingdom of the ten tribes, severed from David’s house, was divided against itself by so many and such frequent divisions, as we have briefly set forth above: kings being killed and succeeded by their killers.

There, one must believe, no false friend was lacking, made manifest by an opportune moment and an occasion for wrongdoing—such as Ahithophel was before those times in David’s kingdom. Since the fraudulent friend especially employs treachery, Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, and Hoshea son of Elah, the last of the kings of Israel, are rightly counted among such persons. One of them plotted against Nadab son of Jeroboam, struck him down, and reigned in his place (III Kings XV) [Col. 0515C].

Likewise, among those whose examples occasion the words, “Do not trust in a leader,” Zimri is rightly counted. Though commander of half the cavalry and servant of Elah son of Baasha, he rebelled against him, struck and killed him, and reigned in his place (III Kings XVI). These men therefore serve as an example to the whole world that one should not believe every friend or trust every leader. The prophet says: “Do not believe a friend; do not trust in a leader”—that is, do not place your hope in men on the ground that they are leaders or are called friends. For many leaders are unfaithful, and many friends treacherous, as experience made clear in those times.

“From her who sleeps in your bosom,” he says, “guard the barriers of your mouth.” Before those times, a great warning example in this sort of matter had occurred in Delilah, who deceived Samson (Judg. XVI); but much more so in Jezebel in those same times. She destroyed her husband Ahab by saying to him as he lay upon his bed: “Rise and eat bread, and be of good cheer; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite” (III Kings XXI) [Col. 0515D]. For he had opened to her the barriers of his mouth by telling her why he was sad, and in that matter and all others had altogether entrusted her with every key of his soul.
