Scripture testifies to this when it later says: “There was no other like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord; for Jezebel his wife stirred him up, and he became abominable, to such a degree that he followed the idols which the Amorites had made, whom the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel” (ibid.) [Col. 0516A].

Although only a few examples of such conduct by identifiable persons are recorded, no one can doubt that many such things happened then. Likewise concerning what immediately follows, “for son dishonours father”: although only two examples are recorded—one in which Reuben went up to his father’s bed (Gen. XLIX), and another in which Absalom defiled his father David (II Kings XVI)—and these occurred before those times, it must nevertheless not be doubted that many similar acts were committed in those same times. Another prophet bears witness when, among the other crimes of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes—he says: “Son and father went in to the girl, in order to profane my holy name” (Amos II) [Col. 0516B].

The deeds of women are not written down in the sacred books, except those of women who did such great things that memorable deeds of men could not be recorded without remembering them. Thus the evil deeds which Jezebel and her daughter Athaliah did in Israel and Judah are recorded because those women were especially causes of storms in which men suffered shipwreck.

Accordingly, concerning what follows, “daughter rises against her mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,” it is superfluous to seek the history of those times, since it is established that in every age women are or have been more prone and more ardent than men toward every disgraceful act. And who can doubt that, in that tempest, daughter rose against mother and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law [Col. 0516C], when even now the examples of daily life are so numerous that we ought rather to mourn that they are so numerous than seek them out?

Similarly, his saying, “The enemies of a man are those of his own household,” is so certain that even in those same times some kings of Judah are recorded to have been killed by conspiring servants; and now there are more examples than require proofs. This final statement, “The enemies of a man are those of his own household,” includes all other, more distant family relations, and for that reason there is less that is surprising, though no less dangerous, in their enmities—for example, nephews or cousins.

But why did he omit the son-in-law, though he did not pass over the daughter-in-law, saying, “And daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,” when son-in-law and daughter-in-law stand in the same degree of affinity? Likewise our Lord in the Gospel, when He foretold that the same relationships would be divided against one another for the sake of the Gospel, and also gave them reciprocally in this manner: “For from this time there shall be five divided in one house, three against two and two against three: father against son and son against his father, mother against daughter and daughter against her mother, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matt. XI; Luke XII) [Col. 0516D].

It should be noted that He was silent about the son-in-law. If He had said, “father-in-law against son-in-law and son-in-law against his father-in-law,” He would no longer have separated only three against two and two against three, but four against two and two against four, and would nonetheless have spoken truly. For it has indeed often happened that three were divided against two—namely, the son, daughter, and daughter-in-law against the father and mother. Yet it happens more often [Col. 0517A], and is almost customary, that son-in-law is divided against father-in-law and father-in-law against son-in-law.

Therefore, if He was silent about the son-in-law because such division is not so remarkable or rare, why was He not silent about the daughter-in-law, when it is also almost customary for a daughter-in-law to be disliked by her father-in-law, to such a degree that the Comic Poet says: “What is this?”

… “All mothers-in-law hate their daughters-in-law” (Terence, *Hecyra*, Act II, scene I, 5).

Moreover, it should be understood that a son-in-law’s pride or quarrelsomeness does not produce, or involve, as much disorder. For a daughter-in-law, lest she rise up against her mother-in-law, ought to be restrained by fear and reverence for her husband, to whom she is subject according to the law [Col. 0517B] (Eph. V). A son-in-law, however, though he owes affection to his wife, does not owe her subjection; and therefore, if he sets himself against his father-in-law and mother-in-law, the parents of his wife, it is not so remarkable or shameful.

In Matthew the Lord states the sense more fully, in the very words of this prophet: “Do not suppose,” he says, “that I came to bring peace upon the earth. I came not to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matt. X).—“And a man’s enemies are those of his own household.”

What then? Did the Savior come to cause in human beings that which, before his coming, he rebuked in them through the prophet? Far be it. It is one thing for people to be separated through hatred of sin, another through hatred of human beings. That hatred by which we hate the sins of people is good—indeed, perfect; it is proclaimed in that verse of the psalm: “Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred” (Ps. 138 [139]). The Savior came to send or effect the sword and separation of that hatred, so that whoever desires to be his disciple may take no account of anyone, however closely related, who opposes him in the way of God.

But that hatred through which human blood is sought, or good people are envied, belongs to murderers. The same Lord rebukes the separation produced by that hatred through this prophet; for because they had separated themselves from the house of David, they were handed over to a spirit of discord and sedition. This also happened in earlier times, when they appointed over themselves as leader Abimelech, son of Jeroboal, who killed all his seventy brothers. Hence it is written: “And the Lord sent [Col. 0517D] an evil spirit between Abimelech and the inhabitants of Shechem, and they began to hate him” (Judg. IX).

It follows: “But I will look to the Lord, and wait for God my Savior. My God will hear me. Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen: I shall rise. When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment. He will bring me out into the light; I shall see his righteous acts. My enemy will see, and she who says to me, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’ will be covered with shame. My eyes shall look upon her; now she shall be trampled like the mud of the streets.”

These are plainly the words of one confessing and hoping; they are uttered through the prophet in the person of the tribe of Judah, or Jerusalem, which was to be led captive to Babylon, after the ten tribes had first been carried away to Assyria—the tribes against whom the preceding pronouncement was directed. For we must remember that the judgment is the Lord’s, and that Samaria and Jerusalem are judged from the point where he says: “Let the mountains hear the judgment of the Lord, and the strong foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a judgment with his people, and he will enter into judgment with Israel. My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I wearied you? Answer me” (Mic. VI), and so forth.

Under this judgment, we have said, Israel and Judah were brought forward as two defendants: Samaria, unrepentant, and Jerusalem, giving voice to repentance—above, where it began: “What worthy offering shall I make?” (ibid.); and here again: “But I,” he says, “will look to the Lord,” and so forth. This was altogether to happen, and it happened precisely as these prophetic words foretold it would. For when judgments had been given—when the ten tribes had been led away to Assyria and the children of Judah to Babylon—that captivity did not look to the Lord in repentance; but this one looked to the Lord and waited for the Lord its Savior, and its God heard it. Thus it was able to say against Babylon, which had taken it captive: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen: I shall rise.”

And what is truer than the statement: “When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light”? When the children of Judah underwent the darkness of captivity and mourning, made humble and contemptible in the sight of the Babylonians, behold, the Lord was their light: a light illuminating a lamp through prophetic grace, which he set [Col. 0518C] upon a lampstand so that it might shine for King Nebuchadnezzar and all those in his kingdom. For their adversaries it was confusion and reproach; for them, consolation and joy.

We mean Daniel and his companions. The beginning of their illumination was that, while they were praying, the king’s dream and its interpretation were revealed to Daniel. This was their first cause of consolation and honor, so much so that King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshiped Daniel; he ordered offerings and incense to be offered, that sacrifice might be made to him. Then he raised him on high, gave him many great gifts, appointed him ruler over all the provinces of Babylon, and chief of magistrates over all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel [Col. 0518D] then asked the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon (Dan. II).

Later they were cast into the furnace of blazing fire; yet they walked unharmed in the midst of the fire, while Nebuchadnezzar said: “Behold, I see four men, unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no injury in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. III). Certainly they shed forth another light of divine splendor, for the consolation of themselves and of their fellow-captive Jewish brethren. The other miracles thereafter celebrated in connection with them, especially through Daniel, were so many and so illustrious, and the visions which he saw so great and splendid, that there should be no doubt that the saying applies to them: “When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light” [Col. 0519A].

What follows—“I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment”—is confession and great praise of God’s justice. For Jerusalem itself, in whose person these words are spoken, truly sinned greatly and deserved the Lord’s wrath for many sins, no less than Samaria, except that among Jerusalem’s kings there were also some righteous men, and some penitents. It therefore ought to bear the wrath of the Lord, especially because of the sins of Manasseh, although he at last repented. For Scripture says of his sins—and that wrath came principally because of him:

“This came about [227] by the word of the Lord against Judah, to remove it from before him because of all the sins of Manasseh which he committed, and because of the innocent blood which he shed and with which he filled Jerusalem—the blood of innocents; and for this reason the Lord would not be appeased” (IV Kings XXIV).

“I will therefore bear,” she says, “the wrath of the Lord,” assenting to justice, “because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment.” How? “He will bring me,” she says, “out into the light; I shall see his righteous acts. My enemy will see, and she who says to me, ‘Where is your God?’ will be covered with shame.” This had already begun to happen when the three youths were brought out of the fiery furnace and Daniel from the lions’ den, while the Babylonians who accused them saw their glory—or rather, God’s glory through them—and were covered with shame (Dan. VI).

It was completed when Babylon, overthrown by the Persians and Medes, saw others release the captivity and rebuild Jerusalem, which it had burned with fire (II Chron. XXXVI). For foreseeing the overthrow of that enemy, Babylon, he continues in the prophet, in the person of Jerusalem: “My eyes shall look upon her; now she shall be trampled like the mud of the streets.” For it was trampled by the Medes and Persians before the eyes of Daniel, who was one of those captives brought from Jerusalem and had not yet closed his eyes, overtaken by death. Daniel himself also saw with his own eyes the writing which he interpreted for King Belshazzar: *Mane, Tezel, Phares*—that is, “he has numbered and completed and divided your kingdom, and given it to the Medes and Persians.” That same night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was killed, and Darius the Mede succeeded him as king (Dan. V).

After these words there immediately follows: “The day for your walls to be built.” Clearly, what the prophet, in the person of Jerusalem hoping in the Lord, had said, is confirmed by the Lord himself through the prophet, when he says to Jerusalem: “The day for your walls to be built”—understood: the days have been fixed by God. Through another prophet, Jeremiah, these are prescribed in this manner: “And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. And when the seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, says the Lord, for all their iniquity” (Jer. XXV), and the rest.

For after the end of those years, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians and caused a proclamation to go throughout his whole kingdom, even in writing: “Who is there among you of all the people of the Lord God of heaven? May his God be with him. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judaea, and build the house of the God of Israel. He is the God who is in Jerusalem” (I Ezra I).

Then, after the night of adversity, day shone forth, because the rebuilding of the city walls or of the temple which had been destroyed could be counted as a day—a day, I say, of such long duration as the light of that restoration endured. But the Jews who arose later began to misuse their day, abandoning the law of the Lord, until desolation again came, an irreparable desolation.

It follows, therefore: “On that day the law shall be removed far away; on that day Assyria shall come even to you, even to fortified cities, and from fortified cities even to the river; and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. The land shall be a desolation because of its inhabitants and because of the fruit of their thoughts” (I Macc. I).

The histories of those times, especially the books of Maccabees, testify that the law was removed far away on that day—that is, in the time now under discussion: “For lawless sons went out from Israel and persuaded many, saying: ‘Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us.’ And they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to the customs of the nations; they made themselves foreskins; they departed from the holy covenant; and they joined themselves to the nations” (I Macc. I).

This indeed was the removal of the law far away, while the Maccabean brothers—Judas, Jonathan, and Simon, sons of Mattathias—and after them John, son of Simon, surnamed Hyrcanus, struggled and wished to retain it. All died, sometimes prospering in retaining the law; nevertheless, day by day the law was removed farther and farther away, and there was no king. The descendants of the aforesaid John contended most bloodily and wickedly for kingship and priesthood, until Roman power intervened and imposed as king one not of that people: Herod, born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother.

Thus the law was made remote, a foreign king was set up contrary to the law, and then came the desolation of that people which continues even now. Of this he adds: “On that day Assyria shall come even to you,” using the name Assyria to signify all the nations through whom that people and the metropolis of the same people, Jerusalem, were destroyed.

Assyria was indeed the first to come up against Jerusalem before the Babylonians, in the reign of Hezekiah, under whom this prophet prophesied; but it was repelled, after one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in its camp had been struck down by the angel of the Lord (IV Kings XIX). Assyria is therefore rightly used for all the Assyrians, Babylonians, Greeks, and Romans, because it was the first of all to come against Jerusalem.

When it is said, “On that day Assyria shall come even to you,” what does “shall come even to you” mean except: Assyria, or Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, will indeed now be repelled from you, but your enemies will not always be repelled in this manner? What follows—“and shall come to fortified cities, and from fortified cities even to the river; and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain”—powerfully expresses a complete and universal upheaval of the whole world for the destruction and desolation [Col. 0521A] of one land, of which he immediately says: “And the land shall be a desolation because of its inhabitants and because of the fruit of their thoughts.”

Nor is it strange that a just prophet should prophesy so great a desolation of the same land so suddenly after the consolation in which it was said, “The day for your walls to be built.” For Daniel likewise, when he prayed, understanding from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to Jeremiah the prophet, that Jerusalem’s desolations should be completed in seventy years (Jer. XXV), concludes the vision in this way: “The people with a coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; its end shall be devastation; after the end of war, desolation is decreed; sacrifice and offering shall fail; and desolation shall endure unto completion and the end” (Dan. IX).

What has happened and has continued since then, the prophet declares in the following words, praying as he prophesies and prophesying as he prays: “Feed your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest. They shall feed in the midst of Carmel, Bashan, and Gilead, as in days of old, as in the days of your departure from the land of Egypt.”

To whom is this said—“Feed your people, the flock of your inheritance”—except to him who testifies that he himself does this and is the minister of this office, saying: “I am the good shepherd; I am the door of the sheep. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out, and find pasture” (John X). “For you were once,” Peter says, “like sheep going astray” (I Pet. II).

And “dwelling alone in the forest” means wandering, lacking a shepherd, and exposed to the jaws of wolves, because there was no one to seek them. For, as was said above, the law had been removed far away, and there were corrupt shepherds, feeding themselves and not keeping the law. Therefore, through another prophet, he speaks against them—he himself to whom it is said here, “Feed your people [228] with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest”:

“Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd; they became food for all the beasts of the field and were scattered; and there was no one to seek them, no one,” he says, “to seek them” (Ezek. XXXIV). “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock when he is among his scattered sheep. I will feed my sheep, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord” (ibid.).

Therefore to him whom the prophetic Spirit knew to have such a purpose it is rightly and confidently said that he should feed with his rod—that is, with his justice. He answers and says: “Bashan and Gilead shall pasture in the midst of Carmel, as in days of old, as in the days of your departure from Egypt. I will show him wonders.”

Great is what the good shepherd promises in these words: “Bashan and Gilead shall pasture in the midst of Carmel.” This is plainly in the same sense as the passage already cited from another prophet: “I will feed them,” he says, “on the mountains of Israel, beside streams, and in all the inhabited places of the land. I will feed them in very rich pastures, and their pastures shall be on high mountains. There they shall rest in green grass, and in fat pastures they shall feed” (ibid.).

For Scripture testifies that Carmel, Bashan, and Gilead were regions suitable for feeding flocks. That Nabal was from Carmel is evident from the fact that David, the distinguished shepherd who bore the type of Christ the good shepherd, fed sheep there. For it is written: “When David heard that Nabal was shearing his flock, he said to his servants: ‘Go up to Carmel, and you shall come to Nabal’” (I Kings XXV). And shortly afterward: “We were never burdensome to them, nor did anything of the flock ever go missing all the time they were with us in Carmel” (ibid.).

Moreover, how rich in pasture Bashan and Gilead were is sufficiently indicated by the fact that the sons of Reuben and Gad urgently petitioned Moses for them, because they possessed much livestock and had immense wealth (Num. XXXII). Carmel is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision”; Bashan, “confusion”; Gilead, “the migration of testimony.”

Thus Carmel, Bashan, and Gilead, both by their realities and by their names, signify those most fertile pastures of Christ’s sheep, where they are fed and made fat: now feasting on the holy Scriptures, and afterward on the delights of paradise. First they possess knowledge of true and spiritual circumcision; then they make a salutary confession of former sins; and then they attain the consequent perfection of faith, so that they may confirm and defend that same faith by the testimonies of the law and prophets.

What follows—“as in days of old, as in the days of your departure from Egypt, I will show him wonders”—we rightly understand at last if we do not forget that the Apostle looks back upon and recalls those days of old, those days of your departure, O ancient Church, from Egypt, and the wonders which the Lord showed in those days. “All these things,” he says, “happened to them as a figure of us.”

Does not every ecclesiastical order, by reading and writing, preach and sing together that we are the people of the Lord and the sheep of his pasture, or the flock of his inheritance? In likeness to those days, we were freed from the spiritual Pharaoh—that is, the devil—and from the sins in which we served him; we came out from the Egypt of this world, that is, from the darkness of ignorance; our foreheads were marked with the sign of Christ’s passion, he who is both the true lamb and the good shepherd; we passed through the sea of baptism; and behold, we ate spiritual food [Col. 0522D] and drank spiritual drink, namely the body and blood of that same shepherd and lamb (I Cor. X).

“I will show him these and the other wonders,” he says—understood: to every believer, or to my people, the flock of my inheritance, whom I have purposed to feed with my rod, that is, with my justice or with my power, which was then signified by that rod of Moses with which he performed signs.

It follows: “The nations shall see and be confounded at all their strength. They shall put their hand over their mouth; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick dust like a serpent. Like creeping things of the earth, they shall be disturbed from their dwellings; they shall fear the Lord our God and be afraid of you.”

This too was to happen, and did happen, as in the days of old, according to the days of the departure from Egypt. For as in those days the nations saw and were confounded and troubled—“the peoples went up and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia; then the princes of Edom were troubled, trembling seized the mighty men of Moab, and all the inhabitants of Canaan were frozen with fear” (Exod. XV)—so, when this shepherd fed his people, the flock of his inheritance, for whom he deigned to die and whom he purchased with his blood, he showed innumerable wonders wrought through his apostles and martyrs. The nations and their rulers saw; Jews and gentiles saw; and they were confounded at all their strength. For their strength, deemed great and supported by laws and arms, could not overcome the miracles which the good shepherd, with his rod—that is, in his power—performed among his people or flock through weak and despised human beings, not only through persons of advanced age, but often through boys and girls.

They were therefore confounded at all their strength, which could only strike earthen vessels and could not take away the treasure within them. And what shall I say of the wisdom of those same nations? They were no less confounded by this also. This is what he immediately says: “They shall put their hand over their mouth.” In comparison with the heavenly wisdom which spoke through them and made their tongues eloquent, all secular eloquence was and is mute; and, convicted and confounded, it puts its hand over its mouth, bearing witness through its very silence that it is overcome.

This clearly took place according to those days of old, the days of the departure from Egypt. For then Moses said: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent; from yesterday and the day before I am slow and impeded in speech.” “Who,” says the Lord, “made a human mouth? Or who fashioned the deaf and mute mouth? Was it not I?” (Exod. IV). And again, when he said: “Behold, I am uncircumcised in lips; how will Pharaoh hear me?” (Exod. VI), the Lord said: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet” (Exod. VII).

What follows—“their ears shall be deaf”—is understood both of the Jews and of unbelieving gentiles, but especially of the Jews, whose ears are said to be, and are, more abominably deaf, because the message was first announced to them and they received the law and the prophets. For they despoiled their ears of good hearing. This too was according to those same ancient days, the days of the departure from Egypt, when they took golden earrings from the ears of their wives, sons, and daughters [Col. 0523D], brought them to Aaron, made a molten calf from them, and worshiped it (Exod. XXXII). Because of their other sins, and especially because of that one, their ears are now deaf, as the Lord says: “But on the day of vengeance I shall visit upon them this sin also” (ibid.). Then they despoiled their ears of gold to dishonor God; now their ears are despoiled of obedience to the Son of God.

Then, he says, “they shall lick dust like a serpent”: that is, they shall desire only earthly things, in accordance with the likeness of the serpent to whom it was said: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III). By the word “shall lick” he fittingly expresses their excessive and utterly prone desire for earthly things, according also to the Psalmist’s words: “His enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. LXXI [72]). Yet they were unable even to do that securely. For it follows: “Like creeping things of the earth they shall be disturbed from their dwellings”—understood: both gentiles and Jews.

For the Jews were disturbed from the city and temple which were in Jerusalem and scattered through all lands; the gentiles, from their shrines and temples where they sacrificed to demons. This too plainly happened in accordance with those ancient days, when, at the entry of the children of Israel, the nations of the Canaanites—unclean nations, like creeping things—were driven from that land.

The final statement—“They shall fear the Lord our God and be afraid of you”—is understood: O Christ. For suddenly, with thanksgiving, he brings about that conversion among both unbelieving and believing Jews and gentiles; this may rightly be understood according to the great difference between dread (*formido*) and fear (*timor*). Unbelievers indeed dread him through an accusing conscience, but uselessly, as demons do; for it is written: “The demons also believe and tremble” (Jas. II). Believers and the devout, however, fear with the useful fear which is the beginning of wisdom.

It follows: “Who is a God like you, who takes away iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance?” This is said, and ought to be said, in praise and wonder at inexhaustible grace, which never grows weary of receiving those who turn to it, however greatly they have sinned or however long they have persisted in sins. For all Israel, in whom blindness has now occurred, will be saved when the fullness of the gentiles has entered (Rom. XI).

Rejoicing in this, he says: “Who is a God like you?” For he did not add, “who made heaven and earth and sea and all that is in them” (Ps. CXLV [146]), or, “who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XII)—things already done—but “who takes away iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance,” something still to come.

Nor, having said this, was he content as though you might ask why he said it. He continues: “He will not send forth his wrath again, because he delights in mercy. He will return and have mercy on us. He will cast down our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea.” These too, like the preceding words, are spoken and take place as in the days of old, according to the days of the departure from Egypt.

For in those ancient days, at that departure from Egypt, he said: “I will see the blood and pass over you; and there shall not be among you a plague to destroy, when I strike the land of Egypt” (ibid.). In accordance with that likeness, the Lord, when he is to judge this world, sends forth his signs beforehand, so that the remnant of Israel may be saved; he will pass over their sin, lest they be condemned together with the world. For he delights in mercy, and therefore never ceases to preach repentance. When they have embraced it, “he will not send forth his wrath again,” he says—understood: as he has done hitherto, blinding the heart of this people, making their ears heavy, and closing their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted (Isa. VI).

Again, in those days of departure from Egypt, he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt (Exod. XII) and drowned Pharaoh’s whole army, with its chariots and horsemen, in the Red Sea (Exod. XV). In accordance with that likeness, he says, “He will cast down our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea”: that is, he will blot out all our sins in Christ’s baptism.

Now bringing his discourse to an end, he again turns familiarly to him and says: “You will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from days of old.” These are all the ways of the Lord: mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV [25]). In these he reverently completed his discourse, speaking to him in whom mercy and truth met together, and justice and peace kissed one another (Ps. LXXXIV [85]).

Justice itself is the truth which, he says, “you will give to Jacob,” by rendering to each according to his works (Ps. LXI [62]). Peace itself is mercy, which, he says, “you will give to Abraham,” by blessing all nations in his seed (Gen. XXII), so that they may receive forgiveness of sins through you—the same Christ, Son of God, who are Truth itself, whose gift is mercy. “Which you swore,” he says, “to our fathers from days of old,” so that it would be impious for anyone to doubt that mercy and truth will be fulfilled.

It is pleasing, moreover, to observe that mercy is declared to be given to more people, truth to fewer. For he does not say, “You will give mercy to Jacob, truth to Abraham,” but “truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham.” Jacob, indeed, is proclaimed the father of only one people, the Israelite nation; Abraham, however, is the father of many nations. God says: “I am, and my covenant is with you; and you shall be the father of many nations. Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have made you father of many nations” (Gen. XVII).

Nor should we omit that Abraham pleased God before he was circumcised. Hence the Apostle says: “How was Abraham’s faith reckoned to him as righteousness? In circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which is in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, and might be the father of circumcision” (Rom. IV).

Thus, when it is said, “You will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham,” truth overflows to many, but mercy to far more; and the prophetic Spirit rightly perceived that this is beneficial for us. For, in order to be saved, we seek not so much the truth of the Judge as the mercy of the Creator. Finally, even if among the circumcised there were holy and perfect persons for whom God’s truth abounded unto a crown, yet for us gentiles it is mercy which the same God bestows. Hence the same [Col. 0526A] Apostle says: “For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers; but that the gentiles should glorify God for mercy” (Rom. XV).

We ought to know to which fathers the Lord swore these things, as this writer recalls when he says, “which you swore to our fathers from days of old.” They are especially the father Abraham and the patriarch David. For the Lord swore truth to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI [132]). He swore mercy to Abraham concerning the wretched nations, saying: “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son: I will bless you, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

And indeed he has already given truth and mercy, but this gift will be openly manifest to all in the future judgment. For we must end this prophetic discourse in such a way as to remember its beginning: “Let the mountains hear the judgment of the Lord, and the strong foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a judgment with his people, and he will enter into judgment with Israel” (Mic. VI).

Certainly, what we have said concerning the one Israelite people, then divided into two parts—Samaria and Jerusalem—we think and say also concerning the whole human race. For just as then the Lord, setting forth judgment, presented himself between the two parties, adjudging Samaria, as an unrepentant defendant, to perpetual captivity, but decreeing that Jerusalem, as a repentant defendant, should be released from Babylonian captivity, so he has done from the beginning of the world, does now, and will do at the end of the world.

To speak briefly [230] of judgment: between Cain and Abel, both of whom, like all of us, had sinned in Adam, he presented himself in such a manner that he wholly rejected Cain, who was unrepentant, but accepted Abel, who was penitent and bore fruits worthy of repentance (Gen. IV). Moreover, the Gospel has not been silent about the end of the world: dividing all nations into two divisions, as though into two defendants, he will hand over the one part, set at his left like an unrepentant defendant, to everlasting fire, declaring that it has borne no fruit of repentance; but he will call the other part, set at his right like a defendant who has borne fruits worthy of repentance, into the kingdom (Matt. XXV).

And that we may know how constant this Judge is in such discrimination: at the very moment of his death, while he hung between two thieves, he left one unrepentant and blaspheming, opened the gate of paradise to the other, penitent and confessing; and immediately, abandoning the unrepentant Jewish people, he received the repentance of the gentiles (Luke XXIII).

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Six Later Prophets

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525D] The fervor of that praiseworthy pursuit—the labor of attending to the prophets—had grown cold within me, as Jesus son of Sirach says: “The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients, and will devote himself to the prophets” (Ecclus. XXXIX).

I had begun to do this with fervent zeal. Two years before this, I had entered upon the volume of the Twelve Prophets and, examining as far as I could the first six in their order—as far as their wisdom admitted one who sought it, that wisdom which is Christ—I had done so because Christ, the wisdom of God, is truly their wisdom; all their prophecy and every divinely inspired Scripture tend toward him.

When I came to Nahum, who is seventh in order, I stopped; and, as though struck by an obstacle, with my whole zeal grown cold, I no longer wished to proceed. I shall now tell you, O Ekkenbert, venerable abbot, what cause thwarted my eager mind. You preside over the monastery of Corbie and diligently seek by study and reading that same wisdom of the ancients which I have mentioned.

For you deigned to write to me and, by your letter, urge me that I should treat the later six prophets with the same zeal with which, as it seemed to you, I had treated the first six. By this you showed, certainly, that you possess a single eye, having no share of darkness—unlike some people, who, because they envy others for attaining what they themselves have not attained, are unable to see any lamp, however brightly it shines.

The reason why I interrupted that work is this: namely, the difficulty, as though rebuking presumption, made my spirit weary. Meanwhile the venerable Father Cuno of the monastery of Siegburg, thinking that I had carried that work through to the end and was therefore at leisure, seized the occasion of mutual conversation: “Write for me,” he said, “a book on the victory of the Word of God.” Saying this, and repeating it often, he did not desist until he had directed my mind where he wished; and behold, with God’s help I completed thirteen little books. I had scarcely drawn that little work on the victory of the Word of God from its sheath, scarcely reached the harbour of completion, when, mindful of your admonition, my eager mind turned again to the six latter prophets whom I had omitted, grew warm with love for them, and knew—or hoped—that meditation upon their wisdom would not lack its reward.

For they laid the foundation, and whoever “builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, shall receive his own reward,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3). Someone may say: “Then are your thoughts golden, and your words, in your own estimation, silver?” I do not say so; but this is your judgment, and that of many others who, like you, are well disposed. Yet I can scarcely believe even them when they say that our thoughts and words resemble those thoughts and words of which the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of her back are in the paleness of gold” (Ps. 67).

Its sense is this: If you are diligent in the books of the Old and New Testaments—those middle books which are chosen in common by the faithful from both Testaments and held in authority—and if, I say, you are diligent in them, if you persevere in them until the sleep of death, then it will become apparent to you, and through you will become known to others, that “the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of her back are in the paleness of gold”; that is, that the outward expression of Holy Scripture, which appears cheap to the ignorant, is itself more illustrious than all worldly eloquence, “like silver tried in the fire” (Ps. 11); and that the mystical sense hidden beneath the words is, like the back beneath the wings, itself more splendid like gold.

Therefore, since you too exhort me, and since hope of reward is in God, let this one also of the sons of the captivity build, as he has begun, what he can upon this foundation. Long ago, while the sons of the migration were building the walls of Jerusalem, it was said in mockery: “Let them build: if a fox should climb up, it would leap over their stone wall” (2 Esdras 4). But they, in return, said: “Hear, O our God, for we have become an object of contempt. Turn their reproach upon their own head” (ibid.).

Did a fox, in accordance with their reproach, climb up and leap over the wall—and over what those hoping in the Lord had built? On the contrary, their reproach was turned upon their own heads, and “great shall be the latter glory of this city or house, more than the former, says the Lord of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. 1). Whence we shall have to speak more fully in its proper place.

Nearly similar things befell all who, with faithful diligence, built what they could upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets: for while they lived, while they built, they endured reproaches from no one [the printed reading is difficult: de nullis]; but, when those who reproached them had departed, their building remained.

What has been said thus far, the writer’s pen had already copied out almost to the final little word, when behold, two brothers named Helmuvard, arriving from the monastery of Büsens, handed me a short letter. That letter alone may support my case, lest anyone reading my writings accuse in me an excessively presumptuous boldness rather than recognize a diligent goodwill toward the Word of God, through which we were made and restored.

For among other things the writer of the letter says—their prior, a learned scribe and faithful disciple of the Holy Scriptures, named Reginhard, of whom I do not doubt that he had obtained from you the copy of the first six prophets which I had sent you:

“But you still owe it to love; you owe it to the honour and service of the Beloved, and through him and for his sake to our desire, that, as you have begun, you should unfold the words of his mouth to the end; lest, if because of their difficulty we perhaps follow too sluggishly and do not vigorously ‘run after the fragrance of his ointments’ (Song 1), it be imputed to you, who, having been brought into the king’s storehouses, concealed the riches of the bridegroom which you beheld there.

“I mean the exposition of the twelve prophets, of which I copied out a portion long ago with such eagerness that I seemed only now to have devoted myself to such study. But the more I delight in the part, the more violently do I burn with expectation for the whole.”

Thus spoke the man whom I have mentioned. I say nothing of that monitor—and almost commander—of mine at Siegburg, who, when he made little progress by his usual admonition, pressed me more sharply, as if in jest, while I hesitated. “I command you,” he said, “by the authority of the Holy Spirit.”

And therefore, since the Beloved himself says, “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen to you: make me hear your voice” (Song 8), obeying you and my other admonishers as friends of the Beloved who are listening, I shall enter upon this task and commit the course of navigation through this portion of the whole deep to the Holy Spirit.

## 232. COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET NAHUM

### BOOK ONE

[Col. 0527]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0527A]

The burden of Nineveh: the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. The “burden” imposed by the supreme Majesty upon Nineveh proclaims the wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, which the Apostle likewise declares to fall “upon every soul of man that does evil” (Rom. 2). For what reason? By what preceding offences did Nineveh deserve that the prophetic Spirit should proclaim wrath against her without any compassion? For if you weigh the whole burden properly, if you consider carefully the entire course of the prophecy, he speaks almost throughout neither compassionately nor with counsel toward repentance, but rather as one deliberating—and almost exulting—over vengeance most certain; except for a few things which he inserts for the consolation of God’s people, in accordance with his own name, Nahum. For it means “Comforter.”

For example: “The sound of the whip and the sound of the rushing wheel, of the snorting horse, the racing chariot, and the horseman mounting; of the flashing sword and glittering spear; of a multitude slain, a heavy ruin, and corpses without end” (Nah. 3). Again: “Your guards are like locusts, and your little ones like swarms of locusts, which settle in hedges on a cold day. The sun rises, and they fly away; and the place where they were is not known” (ibid.). These few examples have been given because almost the entire text of the prophecy is of this kind: the Holy Spirit, speaking in the prophets—though merciful by nature—seems to mock without mercy.

What then is the reason, or what were their deserts, for which he inveighs against them so fiercely? The cause must be recognized, so that God’s justice may also be recognized, and consequently the very beauty of the present prophecy may shine forth more brightly. For what seems obscure [Col. 0529B] and closed is made so chiefly because its cause has not yet been understood.

Let us therefore say: Nineveh, a great city, was the metropolis of the Assyrians. The Assyrians then ruled above the other nations and oppressed them by their dominion. Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first to begin doing this; from him the city Nineveh was either founded or named. Therefore the Lord speaks thus through Isaiah: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury; the staff in his hand is my indignation” (Isa. 10). For as the rod of fury, as the staff of the Lord’s indignation, it struck down nations, shattered kingdoms, and pressed them beneath its yoke for nearly thirteen hundred years.

Over and above its other evils, the supreme sacrilege of its pride and lofty heart was this: after taking the ten tribes captive, it overflowed even against Judah and Jerusalem (4 Kings 17), [Col. 0529C] where the word of promise was, from which salvation had to come—that is, Christ had to be born, according to God’s truth, from David’s seed. Hence the prophet’s grief, hence his sorrowful cry: “The spread of his wings shall fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel” (Isa. 8).

And the sense is: His pride will aim at this, and this will be the purpose of the devil, whom his pride serves: that what God swore in promising us your coming may not come to pass—“Hear, O house of David: behold, a virgin shall conceive, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7). Is this a small cause?

Let that great and memorable sign of the Apocalypse be recalled, which appeared in heaven: “A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and a crown of twelve stars upon her head; and,” he says, “being with child, she cried out in labour and was tormented to give birth. And a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had borne her son, he might devour him” (Rev. 12).

This mystery, rightly understood, plainly shows that Nineveh—that is, the Assyrian empire—took upon itself a truly great burden, a great judgment; and likewise the individual kingdoms which in their own times attacked the place and nation. That nation is figured by the woman with child, because Christ was to be born from it; whereas the kingdoms themselves are rightly understood through the dragon’s seven heads. For from the time when the woman began to be with child—that is, from the time when the word of promise was made to Abraham [Col. 0530A] concerning his seed, which is Christ, in whom all nations would be blessed—seven kingdoms are counted, through which the devil continually tried to ensure that this promise would not be fulfilled, that salvation would not come, that Christ would not be born:

the kingdom of the Egyptians, which ordered the male children of the Hebrews to be killed (Gen. 34; Exod. 1);

the kingdom of the ten tribes and of the carnal Jews, which, under Ahab and Jezebel, began to kill the prophets of the Lord (3 Kings 20);

the kingdom of the Assyrians and Babylonians, reckoned as one head because they came from the same region—the former took the ten tribes captive, the latter Judah (4 Kings 17);

then the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, under which Haman wished to destroy the whole race of the Jews (Esth. 3);

then [Col. 0530B] the kingdom of the Macedonians or Greeks, under which the Maccabees suffered;

then the kingdom of the Romans, under which Christ himself and his martyrs suffered.

The seventh head will be the kingdom of Antichrist. Just as all the wicked are called, and are, members of the devil, so these kingdoms were the heads of the dragon just described. Each in its own time, driven by a diabolical spirit, stood against the woman with child—that is, against the Church hoping in the word of promise—and shed very much blood.

This is the subject of that little work of ours, mentioned above in the prologue, entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Now, therefore, as though the doorway of the discourse has been opened, we must enter into the profound sequence of this prophecy.

“The burden of Nineveh: the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.” [Col. 0530C] Nahum, as has already been said, means “Comforter.” Here, moreover, Nineveh is the whole world: the condemned world, that is, the whole body of the reprobate; and the world which persecutes God’s elect. This is so not only because of the interpretation of the name—since Nineveh means “beautiful,” and the world in Greek is called *kosmos* (κόσμος), that is, “beautiful” or “ordered”—but also because Nineveh was then the head of the world, and the Assyrian empire, holding primacy over the other kingdoms, boasted against the Lord, as we read in Isaiah (Isa. 10).

Does not this man, therefore—whose name, Nahum, is translated from Hebrew as “Comforter,” just as *Paraclete* is translated from Greek—does not this Comforter, I say, now rebuking the world under the name of Nineveh, both bear the name and perform the office of him of whom the Saviour says in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, he will rebuke the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 10)?

And concerning what sin did he then rebuke the world, unless it was that the Assyrians—whose metropolis, as has been said, was Nineveh—not only did not hope in you, but even attacked you; and “the spread of their wings filled the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel” (Isa. 8)? Concerning what righteousness did he rebuke the world, unless it was that righteousness of God which David desired when he said: “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 56)?

The Holy Spirit then rebuked the world concerning precisely that righteousness, both in this prophet and in the other prophets: the several heads of the dragon gaped cruelly [Col. 0531A] for the destruction of the aforesaid woman with child, so that she might not give birth to the male child who would come to God and to his throne—as he himself says: “Because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer” (John 16). For God’s righteousness consists in this; in this God was justified in his words: as he promised, so he swore to David, and so he set one from the fruit of David’s womb upon his throne (Ps. 131). The world was rebuked concerning this righteousness in the prophets, and he rebukes it concerning it in the Gospel, because it strove to prevent God from being thus justified in his words; and, when the Gospel shone forth, it strove still more to prevent God from being proclaimed as justified in his words.

But how was the world then rebuked concerning judgment? For the prince of this world had not yet been judged; that judgment of the world had not yet occurred, of which the Saviour said: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12). How, then, did he rebuke the world concerning judgment, unless because, while the world watched and marvelled at the successive heads of the dragon, he condemned them in such a way that Pharaoh was drowned in the sea as a kind of likeness of the judgment of the prince of this world; Jezebel was eaten by dogs; Nebuchadnezzar became like an ox; Haman himself hung upon the gallows which he had prepared for another; and Antiochus Epiphanes perished, crushed without human hand?

Thus indeed the world was already rebuked concerning judgment, because, though seeing the miraculous punishments of the ungodly, it nevertheless did not depart from ungodliness, but after their example did not cease to assail the place and nation from which salvation was to come.

Finally, this too must not be passed over: just as there are some in whom the Spirit of truth rebukes the world, and others for whom he himself is the Paraclete, so this title is divided in one direction and another: “The burden of Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum.” For certainly there are some for whom this prophecy is a burden of condemnation, and others for whom it is a book of consoling vision. Nor is it without reason that, in so great a business or office, he calls himself an Elkoshite, from the very small village of Elkosh, humbly acknowledging his own littleness, so that humility of mind might persevere amid great grace; because “our Lord God, who dwells on high, himself looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 112).

The weight or pressure of the burden can be felt from the very beginning of the book when he says: [Col. 0531D] “God is jealous, and the Lord takes vengeance; the Lord takes vengeance and possesses wrath. The Lord takes vengeance upon his adversaries, and he is angry with his enemies.”

That God is jealous, and that his jealousy ought to be imitated by the saints, was known to him who says: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). Although there are many examples and testimonies of God’s jealousy in Scripture, I have preferred to use this testimony because it comes closer to our purpose, as we seek, so far as possible, to show in what matter, concerning what, and against whom God’s jealousy is or has been directed.

We understand that God’s jealousy has always been, or is, directed toward the Church; especially from the time when the Church was made pregnant by him through the word of promise, when Abraham believed him who promised, and left this faith to his people: that in his seed, which is Christ, all nations would be blessed. In what did God’s jealousy toward his beloved thereafter consist? Namely, in presenting her to himself as a chaste virgin, lest she commit fornication with foreign gods—she who would bear a son to him and bear to the world the author of salvation.

Against whom was such jealousy of God directed? Certainly against this aforesaid dragon, which, having seven heads, stood before that woman who had the Word of promise in her womb, in order either to corrupt or kill her. That is, having the seven kingdoms already mentioned, it stood and acted against the Jewish people, against David’s line, in order either to defile her in soul through idolatrous worship or to kill and destroy her utterly in body.

Therefore God is jealous—that is, a vehement lover—and the Lord takes vengeance, because in that very jealousy he frequently avenged the sins of that people. For example: when he was jealous for that people, serving foreign gods in Egyptian slavery, and came down to deliver it with a mighty hand and uplifted arm, he immediately punished their murmuring so that he struck down in the wilderness all who had been numbered from twenty years old and upward (Num. 14). Thereafter, through succeeding times, as often as they sinned, “he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Ps. 105).

Yet with some of them he was not content with bodily or temporal punishment, but took vengeance also upon the soul. Hence he repeats, “The Lord takes vengeance,” and adds, [Col. 0532C] “and possesses wrath.” Of such persons another prophet, conceding divine justice, says: “Bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God” (Jer. 17). And in Deuteronomy the Lord says: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32).

What has been said thus far plainly concerns that people which professed itself the friend and people of God. He next speaks of those who are openly his enemies or foes: those for whom he is not jealous, knowing that they are against him, so that they do not even confess him with their mouths, but indeed persecute his name in his confessors. “The Lord takes vengeance upon his enemies, and he himself is angry with his foes.”

This verse differs from the preceding one in this respect: there God is called both jealous and vengeful Lord; and with regard to those who were or are reprobate from his own people, he is declared both to take vengeance and to possess wrath—the wrath feared by the Psalmist when he says, “O Lord, rebuke me not in your wrath” (Ps. 6). But in this verse the name of jealousy or of a jealous one is wholly omitted: the Lord is said only to take vengeance and to be angry, and those upon whom he takes vengeance and with whom he is angry are openly declared to be enemies and foes. Such was Pharaoh; such was Jezebel; such was Nebuchadnezzar when he said, “Who is the God who will deliver you from my hand?” (Dan. 3); and such are or were all who stretched out their hand against God, who were strengthened against the Almighty, who ran against him with uplifted neck and armed themselves with stout neck.

God, jealous for Abraham’s seed which he was to take hold of, was not jealous of them, but rather jealous against them. The jealous God was jealous, and the vengeful Lord took vengeance: jealous in defending and delivering, and vengeful in visiting their iniquities with the rod and their sins with stripes. Nor did he cease to be jealous for that people and mercifully to punish its sins until he took flesh from it. When this had been done, he ceased to be jealous, because that same nation rose up in opposition. In Ezekiel he declared as though past what was then future: “My jealousy has departed from you, and I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. 16).

Nevertheless, no passion belongs to God. He is neither angry nor wrathful in the human manner, nor is he in any way capable of suffering; but whatever is signified by these expressions he does impassibly. [Col. 0533B] Therefore, after saying, “The Lord possesses wrath, and he himself is angry with his enemies,” he immediately adds: “The Lord is patient and great in strength, and in cleansing he will not make innocent.”

When he says, “The Lord is patient,” he declares the Lord to be such that he never experiences any passion arising from impatience at his own fury or anger. Similarly, when he says, “great in strength,” he proclaims him as one who is broken by no weakness of pain. But someone may say: How then is he merciful? Or how is the spirit of piety—which is in him or from him—the second in the order of the seven spirits, after the spirit of the fear of the Lord?

To this I say: we do not call that piety a passion, but rather a virtue, as true charity is. We commonly read of four passions of the human mind: joy and grief, fear and hope. But certainly in the divine Scriptures there are four things bearing these same names which are not passions but great virtues; and we distinguish or define them by brief differences.

The joy of the world is a passion; joy in the Holy Spirit, or rejoicing in the Lord, is a virtue. The grief or sorrow of the world is a passion; sorrow according to God, which works salvation, is a virtue. The fear of the world—the fear which has punishment, according to which someone is called cowardly—is a passion. “The holy fear of the Lord, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18), according to which someone is called God-fearing, reverent, or religious, is a virtue. Likewise worldly hope, when someone hopes in the world or in the princes of the world, is a passion. Hope which is in God, just like faith and charity, [Col. 0533D] is a virtue.

These things have been said so that, while we deny the four passions in God, we do not deny in him the four virtues of the same names, which no one can possess except from God, except from the Spirit of God.

“The Lord is patient,” he says: that is, he judges with tranquillity; “and great in strength, and in cleansing he will not make innocent.” “Great in strength and patient” has the same order of meaning as in that verse of the Psalm: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient” (Ps. 7). For “in cleansing not making innocent” means being a righteous judge; and “great in strength and patient” means the same as “strong and patient.”

These three attributes belong to him who sits upon the throne and judges equity: that he be righteous, strong, and patient. He is righteous in that, while removing whatever things are evil or harmful, he accepts no person but considers only the cause; and he does not, out of private favour, leave unpunished as though innocent the man whom guilt makes culpable—even if he is one “who took sweet food together with him,” his like-minded companion, his guide, and his acquaintance (Ps. 54).

This may be observed, as in many similar cases, in the fact that the Lord, seeing the city Jerusalem, wept over it (Luke 19), and yet did not prevent its enemies from surrounding it with a rampart, hemming it in on every side, and casting down to the ground it and its children within it, leaving not one stone upon another (ibid.). For it is impossible for him to do anything unjustly, or to show mercy or spare unjustly, unless the humility of repentance has first gone before. “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5), he says—that is, I cannot act as unjust judges do, who call good evil and evil good, following their own will rather than the merits of things; “but as I hear, I judge, and therefore my judgment is true.”

Moreover, he is strong in this: when anyone is guilty and, as his case requires, condemned to punishment, he cannot escape or resist God’s hand. Thus this same prophet says below: “Who shall stand before the face of his indignation, and who shall resist in the wrath of his fury?” The implied answer is: no one—not man, angel, devil, nor Antichrist, whom, says the Apostle, the Lord Jesus Christ “will kill with the spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2): that is, as easily as you scatter a little dust by blowing with your mouth.

He is patient in that he waits for the sinner’s repentance and calls him to mercy before pronouncing judgment. Sometimes he does so even for one whom he does not fail to know will remain impenitent, so that every penitent person may know that whatever is saved is owed to the patience which waits; and so that no impenitent person, in his condemnation, may complain as though God’s impatience had been hasty.

It follows: “The Lord’s way is in storm and whirlwind, and clouds are the dust of his feet.” The Lord’s ways are his aforementioned jealousies and acts of vengeance: acts of vengeance as though possessing wrath, for removing or punishing his adversaries and enemies. A storm and whirlwind of sea or air conceal the sun and threaten immediate death; clouds covering the earth obstruct the sight of the eyes, [Col. 0534D] so that for those travelling by land or sea, even in daytime, as though at night, danger is often uncertain. In accordance with their likeness, these aforesaid ways of the Lord have been or are uncertain to human eyes or understanding, because those acts of vengeance of the Lord encompass righteous as well as unrighteous persons.

This is immediately expressed in figurative speech through metaphor: “Rebuking the sea, and drying it up; and bringing all rivers into a desert. Bashan and Carmel are weakened, and the flower of Lebanon has withered. Mountains are shaken by him, and hills are laid waste; and the earth trembled before his face, the world and those who inhabit it.”

By the widely differing things—sea and rivers, Bashan and Carmel, Lebanon, mountains and hills, earth and world—we understand the differing conditions of the inhabitants of the world, because for their differing causes he has taken vengeance upon them with nearly similar punishments, as the jealous God and vengeful Lord takes vengeance.

For example: Lebanon is a name by which the one temple of the Lord in Jerusalem is sometimes understood, as there: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11). [Col. 0535A] Lebanon, I say—the place and nation where God was known and his name was great—did it at that time suffer less adversity, or was it less shaken or laid waste, than the other nations to whom he was not known and by whom the living and true God was not worshipped? On the contrary, the jealous and vengeful God took vengeance upon that place more severely. Crushed by many evils, not only Israel, that is the ten tribes, was carried into Assyria, but Judah also into Babylon, after city and temple had been given to the flames.

There, beyond doubt, were the Lord’s ways in storm and whirlwind, and clouds were the dust of his feet. There, just as the other nations bore their burdens, so too that holy place bore its burden—and was punished more severely; and righteous persons were carried captive together with sinners, among whom Daniel and his companions were especially famous. Many sinners and godless people had peace, while they were scourged.

As in cloud, storm, and whirlwind the sun is concealed and the day darkened, so the beauty of God’s justice was not seen; weak persons thought that God’s providence did not exist. The Psalmist speaks in the person of such people: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72). And afterward: “Therefore in vain I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent, and I was scourged all day long” (ibid.), and so forth.

Finally, at the Lord’s rebuke, the sea is dried up together: that is, according to the Lord’s judgment, because of Adam’s sin the whole human race is held under the same condition of death; all, righteous and unrighteous, die. These too are many cloudy ways of the Lord, and many are almost scandalized, as it were, by the dust of his feet rushing into their eyes. “The learned man dies,” says Ecclesiastes, “just like the unlearned; and therefore I grew weary of my life” (Eccles. 2).

Meanwhile, it should be noted that by seven expressions—a number which frequently signifies universality—all the acts of vengeance of the jealous God or vengeful Lord are proclaimed in this passage. At his rebuke the sea is dried up; rivers are brought into a desert; Bashan and Carmel are weakened; Lebanon’s flower has withered; mountains are shaken by him; hills are laid waste; and the earth or world trembles.

And indeed, if you weigh the matter properly: just as there were seven heads of the dragon mentioned above—that is, seven chief kingdoms of the world set upon the wood, which stood against the woman with child from the time that the word of promise was made to Abraham—so there were seven acts of vengeance, one upon each head of the same dragon.

The first act of vengeance occurred when, at the Lord’s rebuke, the middle of the sea was dried up: it was passable for the children of Israel, but it covered Pharaoh and the chariots of his army (Exod. 14).

The second occurred when, because of the worship of calves and the murder of prophets, the ten tribes were, like flowing rivers, irreversibly carried into the desert of captivity (4 Kings 17); and in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians, who had taken them captive and wished to take Judah captive, were slain (4 Kings 19).

The third occurred when, after the city and temple of the Lord were burned, Nebuchadnezzar was changed, as it were, into an ox, and Babylon was overthrown by the Medes and Persians (Dan. 4).

The fourth occurred when the exceedingly proud enemy Haman and the other enemies of the Jews were so weakened in the kingdom of Ahasuerus that Haman himself was hanged on the gallows, and the number of the slain reached seventy-five thousand (Esth. 4).

The fifth occurred when, after the Maccabees had already suffered much, the proud Antiochus Epiphanes and the other mountains—that is, the kings of Syria—were, as we read, greatly shaken to their own harm by the Lord’s help (1 Macc. 6).

The sixth occurred when, after the Lord’s passion, the malignant hills—that is, the murderous Jews—were utterly laid waste, so that they fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations (Luke 21).

The seventh will occur when Antichrist has been killed and the Lord comes for judgment: then the world will truly tremble, and its inhabitants will tremble, so that the dead rise in terror.

Since, then, the Lord is so great in strength, what remains except that we humble ourselves under his mighty hand? Intending this, he immediately asks: “Who shall stand before the face of his indignation, and who shall resist in the wrath of his fury? His indignation is poured out like fire, and rocks are dissolved by him.”

To stand before the face of the Lord’s indignation is to be able to trust in one’s own righteousness and, because of an abundance of works or consciousness of virtues, to have no need of mercy. But who is sufficient for this? “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” says the Psalmist, “for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142). And in Job it is truly said: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity. How much more shall those who dwell in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation, be consumed as by a moth?” (Job 4).

Moses also, invoking the Lord’s name, says: “Ruler, Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and abounding in mercy, and true, who keep mercy unto thousands, who remove iniquity, wicked deeds, and sins; and no one is innocent before you by himself” (Exod. 34).

It is superfluous now to establish that no one’s own merits are sufficient, and that we are saved only by God’s grace; for this has long since been demonstrated from the holy Scriptures, and the Apostle’s judgment is true: “All have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. 3). And it is right, in such a matter, that God’s indignation is named when he says: “Who shall stand before the face of his indignation?” For he deserves indignation who trusts in his own works, and it is just that he fall when he thinks himself to stand (1 Cor. 10).

Moreover, to resist God is to defend one’s own iniquity and take pride in one’s sin. Such are those of whom the Psalmist says: “We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?” (Ps. 11). [Col. 0537A] Pharaoh was such when he said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5). To him the Lord said, among other things through Moses: “How long will you refuse to submit to me? Let my people go to me. But if you resist and refuse to let him go” (Exod. 10), and so forth.

These are two contrary forms of pride. One presumes upon his own righteousness and trusts that he will stand with God in judgment and be justified; the other defends his very unrighteousness and refuses to submit in order to make satisfaction to God. The presumptuous man regarding righteousness may sometimes seem to stand before men, but before God he has fallen. The defender of unrighteousness, even if he is permitted for a time to resist, cannot long possess peace; rather, as soon as the wrath of the Lord’s fury reveals itself, he experiences in his own desolation how powerless he is to resist.

“For his indignation is poured out like fire,” he says—understand, upon the person who presumes that he can stand before God’s face as righteous—“and rocks,” that is, minds resistant with hard neck and rebellious against God, “are dissolved by him.” Thus Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened like a rock, melted like wax before the fire of the Lord’s wrath.

It remains, therefore, that the person who desires to experience the Lord not so much as strong as good should exalt himself in neither direction: that is, just as he does not rebel by defending his iniquity, so he should not presume upon his righteousness. Instead, let him place his hope in God; and if he is in tribulation, confessing his sins, let him never despair of God’s mercy.

For it follows: “The Lord is good and strengthens in the day of tribulation, and knows those who hope [Col. 0337C] in him; and in the passing flood he will make an end of its place, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.”

Thus far, according to the proposition which he first set forth in saying, “The burden of Nineveh,” he has said many grave things concerning the great strength of the jealous God. Now, in accordance with his name, Nahum, he consoles those who in this world are under oppression and suffer tribulation from godless people. Such were some in those days under King Hezekiah, while the king of Assyria besieged Jerusalem (4 Kings 19); such were Daniel and his companions in Babylon, who had not forgotten the Lord of their fathers (Dan. 3).

For even from the experience of others it is plain how truly this good Lord says that he strengthens in the day of tribulation and knows those who hope in him. For the Lord was truly good to them and strengthened them well in the day of tribulation, proving by manifest and glorious judgments that he knew those who hoped in him. He sent his angel, and by his dew cooled the blaze of the Babylonian furnace; he sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths so that they did not touch Daniel, whom he knew to hope in him.

What follows—“And in the passing flood he will make an end of its place”—is confirmed by the experience of the same period. For he will punish them in a flood that does not remain but passes away, and afterward he made an end of its place—namely, the place of the flood. What was the flood of that time? What was the place of the flood? And how did the Lord make an end of its place?

The flood of that time was the multitude of Assyrians and Babylonians, as Isaiah says of them: “Behold, the Lord shall bring upon them the strong and abundant waters of the river, the king of Assyria and all his glory; he shall rise above all his channels and overflow all his banks; and there, passing through Judah, cleansing and leaping over, he shall come as far as the neck” (Isa. 8). Therefore a kind of flood overflowed when peoples had assembled in such great multitude; but that flood passed away because that multitude perished.

Moreover, the place of the flood was Nineveh, the metropolis of the Assyrians; Babylon was the place of the flood, from which the Chaldeans overflowed over that same land. The Lord made an end of both places, because, by the Lord’s will, the Chaldeans overthrew Nineveh and the Persians and Medes overthrew Babylon.

And it should be noted that, although he said “in the passing flood,” he did not likewise say “a passing end of its place.” For adversity which God brings upon his elect for their discipline is temporal and passes away. But the final punishment by which the same jealous God avenges himself upon his enemies does not pass away; it remains established and rests upon them: it begins here and does not end for eternity.

For Isaiah says: “At the voice of the Lord Assyria shall be terrified, struck with the rod; and the passage of the rod shall be established, which the Lord shall cause to rest upon him” (Isa. 30). Conversely the Psalmist says of the righteous: “The Lord shall not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Ps. 124). That is, he will not permit the power which he allows sinners over the righteous, for their correction or testing, to last longer than they can bear, lest excessive force of affliction compel them to consent to what sinners will.

The full establishment of the rod by which Assyria is struck consists in this brief statement immediately added here: “Darkness shall pursue his enemies.” This is undoubtedly true of all God’s enemies: when they have ended their present life wickedly, the acts of vengeance by which the Lord avenges himself upon them do not end with their fleshly death. Rather, darkness pursues their souls, and evil spirits, who are darkness and not light, seize them.

Conversely, concerning the elect whom they afflicted for a time, or on behalf of those elect, hear what the consoling Spirit immediately says: “What do you devise against the Lord? He himself will make an end; a second tribulation shall not arise.”

Turning toward those of whom he had been speaking, he strikes their malicious intention with a sharp invective, saying: “What do you devise against the Lord? He himself will make an end.” Let us consider the condition of that time and investigate from the Scriptures how maliciously the Lord’s enemies devised against the Lord.

Nor should we suppose that only the Assyrians or Chaldeans, before or about the time of this prophecy, were enemies of the Lord and conceived the thought for which the Spirit of the Lord inveighs against them thus. Syria and other nations were also involved, but especially the ten tribes which had been divided from the house of David.

To prove this with suitable testimonies, Isaiah speaks, by the Lord’s command, to Ahaz: “Do not fear, and let not your heart be faint because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the burning wrath of Rezin, Syria, and the son of Remaliah; because Syria has devised evil counsel against you, and Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, saying: ‘Let us go up against Judah, trouble it, tear it away to ourselves, and set in its midst as king the son of Tabeel’” (Isa. 7).

Meanwhile, by these prophetic words the house of David was confirmed in what God had promised and sworn to David: that Christ would be born from his seed. Thus in the same place, among other things, he says: “Hear therefore, O house of David: the Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (ibid.).

There should be no doubt that, among the other enemies, the ten tribes especially envied the tribe of Judah and the house of David, because they had hope in the word of promise that was to be fulfilled from that house or tribe, [Col. 0539B] and were accustomed sometimes to boast, saying such things to the kings—
of Samaria and all Israel, as Abijah king of Judah once said: “Do you not know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?” (2 Chron. 13). And afterwards: “Now therefore you say that you are able to resist the kingdom of the Lord, which he possesses through the sons of David?” (ibid.).

These things have been said so that it may not be unknown how great—and from what source great—the envy was which the dragon, the devil, had instilled into the other nations against Judah and the house of David: so that even their kindred, the ten tribes, were especially envious and, having shared counsel with the Syrians, wished to tear Judah away and transfer it to themselves, and to set a foreign king in their midst.
