Against counsels or designs of this sort, instilled into the nations by the devil, who intended that the nation from which Christ was to be born should not survive, this saying must be understood as a most severe denunciation: “What are you devising against the Lord? He himself will bring about an end.” What an evil consummation it would have been, if Judah had been removed, if the house of David had been torn away, so that there would have been no source from which the promise concerning the blessed seed might be fulfilled! Then indeed a double tribulation would have risen up against the sons of David.

But he who faithfully makes promises had promised and sworn thus: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes”—namely, those of David’s sons—“but I will not scatter my mercy from him” (Ps. 88 [89]). As was said, so it was done. They could raise a rod against Jerusalem and at times strike the sons of David, even to the point of burning the city and the Temple and carrying them into captivity: this was one single and purely temporal tribulation. But the other tribulation intended by the devil did not arise—the one which would make the affliction double and utterly exterminate the nation, leaving no source from which that promise might be fulfilled.

237 The Holy Spirit hates all who desired such a consummation—those who, before Christ came and after he came, still laboured that there should be no remembrance of his name and that his Church should nowhere endure. The Spirit speaks in the Psalm: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” (Ps. 136 [137]).

Jerusalem [Col. 0540A] is the whole body of those who awaited the Christ who was to come, and who received and receive him when he came. The sons of Edom—that is, the sons of earthliness—are all those who persecute or have persecuted them; and the laying bare of which they say, “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation,” is that consummation which, as this prophet adds, the Lord did not bring about and will not bring about. Is the consolation contained in the words, “A double tribulation shall not rise,” a small one? All who have wished and wish to live devoutly in Christ, or in God, suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3), and have suffered it: Hezekiah in his time, when the Assyrians overflowed Judah and Jerusalem; Daniel and his companions in their time; the Maccabees in theirs; and all Christians or Catholics in theirs, whose tribulations in this life have been or are many. Yet this is one single tribulation: however long or varied, it is the affliction of one present life.

But he says here: “A double tribulation shall not rise.” Therefore they will not be afflicted in the age to come; and it must be supplied: there, without doubt, those who afflicted or afflict them will be afflicted. Suppose, then, that those who afflicted the righteous did not suffer, or do not suffer, tribulation in the present age. We nevertheless know that many—indeed innumerable persons—after committing cruel crimes against the saints, ended their present life amid bitter affliction and passed into eternal tribulation: Antiochus Epiphanes, the impious Herod, and the Jews who killed Christ, and who for that reason, surrounded by the Romans, were crushed with a double destruction, according to the prophet [Col. 0540C] (Jer. 17); because, as the Psalmist had foretold, they were delivered to the sword according to the body (Ps. 62 [63]) and became the portion of foxes according to the soul (ibid.), that is, of malignant spirits.

Compare any impious person of this kind who ended his present life in peace with any devout person who ended life in tribulation, even though he were a sinner—of the sins of such persons it is written: “In tribulation thou dost forgive all the sins of men” (Tob. 3). Behold: this man’s tribulation is single, and that man’s likewise single; but they differ in this: the one is temporal or momentary, the other everlasting. Is this consolation, then, drawn forth through Nahum—that is, “the Comforter”—a small one? Rather, it is great and full of joy, so that whoever are well-disposed toward them, hearing them say or sing, “We have become as those comforted” (Ps. 125 [126]), may answer and join the refrain: “The Lord has magnified his dealings with them” (ibid.).

Add that the single tribulation of the godly might be compared with the double tribulation of many wicked persons, such as the aforesaid Herod and all who, while enduring punishment without possessing the spirit of repentance, “went to their own place” (Acts 1), from temporal torment to eternal torment. What sort of comparison is this? The things are wholly incomparable. Let them therefore speak of their consolation; admiring it, they will never cease to say: “The Lord has magnified his dealings with us; we have become joyful” (Ps. 125 [126]).

It follows: “For as thorns entwine one another, [Col. 0541A] so is their banquet when they drink together. They shall be consumed like stubble full of dryness.”

A little earlier, speaking of the Lord’s enemies, he had said, “Darkness shall pursue his enemies”; and, in the middle of his discourse, not content to speak about them, he suddenly turned toward them and, with a righteous and vehement movement of spirit, cried out in denunciation: “What are you devising against the Lord? He himself will bring about an end. A double tribulation shall not rise”—namely, against his elect, although it will rise against very many of you. Now, as though the movement of his spirit had been calmed, he turns again toward us and speaks more tranquilly about those of whom he had begun to speak. He gives the reason why darkness pursues the Lord’s enemies, and why a triple tribulation, denied to the saints, is to be understood as having arisen or as about to arise against certain leaders of the wicked.

“This,” he says, “is the reason: ‘For as thorns entwine one another, so is their banquet when they drink together.’” What is a place where thorns entwine one another like? Surely, it is unpleasant and unmanageable: if they are handled, they prick, tear, and rend; and if seed is cast among them, when it begins to sprout it is choked, as the Lord himself mentions. Such were and are the Lord’s enemies. They are unpleasant and unmanageable. If anyone wishes to handle them—if anyone rebukes their incestuous deeds or robberies by the word of the Lord—they do not merely prick, nor merely tear or rend; at times armed with iron barbs, they shed blood and kill bodies. They cannot kill souls, but [Col. 0541C] they do not allow the seed of God’s word, by which souls ought to live, to grow.

Such were the Lord’s enemies, entwining one another—that is, taking mutual pleasure in evil. Notice that he did not say, “As thorns entwine one another, so are they”; he said something stronger: “So is their banquet when they drink together.” For at banquets and amid drinking they customarily arm one another, with more abundant talk, and incite one another to the slaughter of the saints. Examples sufficient for this purpose are ready at hand.

At a banquet and amid drinking, Herod and Herodias were truly thorns entwined with one another; through their wickedly associated dancing-girl, they pricked John—they beheaded John (Matt. 14). At a banquet and amid drinking, the Jewish chief priests, already drunk, as being on the paschal night, sent a cohort and attendants to seize our Lord. Thus his foreknowing Spirit complains in the Psalm, among other things: “Those who drank wine sang against me” (Ps. 68 [69]).

And lest the discourse entirely pass over the earlier times of the prophets: in the Babylonian captivity, which was a tribulation for the people of God, the already drunken Belshazzar ordered the gold and silver vessels of the Lord’s Temple to be brought; “and the king and his nobles drank from them; his wives and his concubines drank wine and praised their gods of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone” (Dan. 5). In the tribulation under Antiochus, in which the Maccabees suffered, the Temple was full of debauchery and revelry and of men fornicating with prostitutes; and women thrust themselves of their own accord into the sacred buildings, [Col. 0542A] bringing in things that were not permitted (2 Macc. 6).

Rightly, therefore, and as it ought to be, it was said: “So is their banquet when they drink together.” How, then, was a fitting tribulation, appropriate to them, to arise? “They shall be consumed,” he says, “like stubble full of dryness.” A truly fitting tribulation: because, like thorns, they choked the good seed so far as lay in their power and hated the grain of wheat, they themselves will be found like stubble bereft of every grain; they shall be consumed by fire like stubble full of dryness.

“Full of dryness” is wonderfully said. For what is dryness but emptiness? Therefore the stubble is here said to be full of dryness. Not without reason, not without great weight of meaning, did he speak thus. The Spirit who convicts the world knew that the false fullness of the rich of this world is true leanness, [Col. 0542B] and that the greenness of such grass—for “all flesh is grass”—is true dryness.

It follows: “From you came forth 238 one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression.”

Here he accommodates himself familiarly and speaks to the heart of Jerusalem, which is not unmanageable as such thorns were or are: it does not reject rebuke, nor make an excuse for itself in sins. He makes known to it from what source, or in what respect, God’s severity toward it is just, when he permits it to be afflicted by Assyrians, Chaldeans, or any enemies and foes of God. “From you,” he says, “came forth one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression”—not merely any one individual, but a multitude of transgressing persons. Thus we have it written in one place:

“In those days lawless men came forth from Israel and persuaded many, saying: ‘Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us; for since we withdrew from them, many evils have found us.’ And the proposal seemed good in their eyes” (1 Macc. 1), etc.

This was the beginning of sorrows. Nor should we suppose that the beginning of sorrows happened in this way only at the time concerning which these things are written. In every tribulation which befell that nation or the Church of God, it can plainly be demonstrated that this was the beginning: that from her came forth one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression.

Consider the first tribulation: their harsh and miserable slavery in Egypt. Did not such a cause precede it? Did there not come forth from you, O Jacob [Col. 0542D] or Israel, a hostile brotherhood, transgressing and violating moral law and natural law, and devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting that what the Lord had decreed and signified should not happen—namely, that his dreams should benefit their brother Joseph in no respect? (Gen. 37).

Likewise, concerning every tribulation with which the house of Jacob or the house of Israel was afflicted from that time until Christ’s coming, it must be understood that this was the beginning of the tribulation: that from it came forth one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression. We could adduce sure testimonies for each instance, were excessive prolixity—notorious for producing weariness—not to be avoided.

Concerning the tribulation with which Jerusalem or Judah was afflicted about the period of this prophecy—namely, when first the king of Assyria overflowed the land, then besieged Jerusalem, and then the king of Babylon besieged the city and carried Judah captive—we must not pass over how, in order that this might happen, there came forth from her one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression.

Was it not a going forth from the holy nation or root when the kings of Judah received Baal and worshipped him in the Temple of the Lord (4 Kings 21)? And after the death of the high priest Jehoiada, the princes of Judah entered and did homage to King Joash; softened by their attentions, he consented to them. “They forsook,” it says, “the Temple of the Lord God of their fathers and served groves and carved images; and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem because of this sin.” They also killed Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada; and “King Joash did not remember the mercy which Jehoiada, that man’s father, had shown him, but killed his son” (2 Chron. 24).

After this came Amaziah, who set up for himself as gods the gods brought from the children of Seir and worshipped them. When the prophet said to him, “Why do you worship them?” he replied, “Are you the king’s counsellor? Be silent, lest I kill you” (2 Chron. 25). After him came Uzziah, who, while usurping the priestly office, was struck with leprosy on the forehead; then Jotham (2 Chron. 27); then Ahaz, who walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and furthermore cast images for the Baals (2 Chron. 28); then Hezekiah, during whose reign the Assyrians came into Judah and besieged the city, and Rabshakeh came out to them (4 Kings 18).

The Hebrews, wishing Rabshakeh to have been Isaiah the prophet’s son, think the words, “One came forth devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression,” were spoken of him. But it seems slight to understand this of one person, since it is not plainly proved from the Scriptures; whereas the evil or transgression of almost all the kings or princes is known. For, apart from David, this Hezekiah, and Josiah, all sinned.

Therefore he speaks to Jerusalem’s heart and appeals to its conscience, lest it fail to know or attribute to itself the cause of whatever tribulation arose against it—as when the Assyrians overflowed it. But the Comforter immediately adds: “Thus says the Lord: Though they are complete, and so numerous, even so they shall be shorn, and he shall pass away.”

This was undoubtedly spoken of the Assyrians and their king Sennacherib, as something that would happen; and so it happened. For as easily as hairs are cut by scissors, so easily, in one night, when the angel of the Lord struck, one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were cut down. Sennacherib, rising in the morning and seeing so great a multitude overthrown, went forth shorn and shaved and returned as he had come. For he had himself, by the permission of God the just judge, shaved Judah—that is, he had gone up against all the fortified cities of Judah and taken them (4 Kings 19).

Accordingly, this was said against Ahaz: “In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor, with those beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head and the hair of the feet, and the whole beard” (Isa. 7). As long as Jerusalem and the Temple stood, however much the Assyrians devastated the surrounding country, it was like a kind of shaving. But when the city itself was burnt and the Temple set aflame with Chaldean fire, it was more than shaving; fittingly it was foretold through Ezekiel under the name of the harlot Oholibah: “They shall cut off your nose and ears, and those who remain shall fall by the sword” (Ezek. 23).

But what does it mean that he first said, “Though they are complete, and so numerous,” and only then added, “Even so they shall be shorn, and he shall pass away”? What is this completeness which, even if it could be present in the Assyrians or other persons, could not benefit them? It may indeed be understood thus, as though he said: Even if the Assyrians are perfectly strong, or complete in strength, and their strength is increased by the number of all nations—nevertheless, since he had said to Jerusalem, “From you came forth one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting [Col. 0544B] transgression,” by which a great imperfection in Jerusalem’s righteousness is shown, we may not unreasonably understand, in the words “Though they are complete,” a certain completeness of the Assyrians’ supposed righteousness.

Lest this seem strange or novel, we should know that whenever the Assyrians or other nations, envious of the Jews for saying that they possessed the good God and a holy law, heard of any evil among them, they attacked them most hostilely, magnificently justified themselves in comparison with them, and moreover blasphemed their God. Hence we read in Isaiah: “Their rulers”—that is, those of Jerusalem or of my people—“act unjustly, says the Lord, and my name is continually blasphemed among the nations” (Isa. 52). And when David had said, “I have sinned against the Lord,” because he had sinned against Uriah the Hittite, Nathan said: “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, by this deed you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme” (2 Kings 12), etc.

We have said this in order that it may be clear that the Church of God was then, as it is now, a spectacle to men of the world; and that the nations have always seen their own impiety with closed—or rather blind—eyes, but the transgressions of God’s worshippers with open eyes. Do we not see even today that if any person of holy profession is defamed by the charge of some transgression, secular people at once disparage not merely that person but the entire profession? Yet they do not wish us, if any one of their wives [Col. 0544D] is caught in adultery, to say that all the others are such as the one woman is proved to be.

But let us return to our subject. “From you,” the Lord says, “has come forth—and has long been accustomed to come forth—one devising evil against the Lord, inwardly plotting transgression.” Such evil will be defamed, such transgression will very often be publicly proclaimed, that people will say that nothing like it has ever been heard or seen among the nations, and that even Sodom and Gomorrah were more righteous. The Assyrians will appear righteous in comparison with you, just as many pagans are or seem to be more righteous, according to a certain worldly justice, than many who have professed the worship of the one God and were reared in his house under his law: by honouring parents, not killing, not committing adultery, not stealing, not bearing false witness against a neighbour, [Col. 0545A] and doing many things which among believers are true marks of that righteousness which comes from God.

But the Lord says this: even if some Assyrians were perfect in these works, and if among them not a few but many were perfect, “even so they shall be shorn”—that is, they shall be struck together in one night. When one hundred and eighty-five thousand have been struck, Sennacherib, shorn and shaved, shall pass away. “He shall pass away,” he says: slain by his sons in the house of his god—such a passing away that his place is not found. Nor will they die merely shorn by the death of the body; they will die also by a double destruction—that is, by the death of both body and soul—however perfect and however justified they may be in comparison with my saints, who are sinners.

Why? Clearly because “the sparrow has not found herself a house, nor the turtle-dove a nest in which to place her young” (Ps. 83 [84]). That is: neither is their heart subject to God by thinking many things wisely, nor does their flesh, by doing any good works, hope for a reward from God in the future; rather, it gathers vanity for itself in the present age. Therefore, as the Wise Man has said: “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman who does good” (Sir. 42). According to the sense hidden in this saying, it is much better and more useful to have faith with few works than to perform many works and lack faith. For it is written concerning faith that without it it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11); but concerning works, although they too are necessary, nowhere is it written that without them it is impossible to please God.

[Col. 0545C] It follows: “I have afflicted you, and I will afflict you no longer.” It is as though he said: You, O Jerusalem, from whom came forth one devising evil against the Lord and inwardly plotting transgression, I did not leave unpunished, but afflicted. And as it was said above, “A double tribulation shall not rise,” so now I say: “I will afflict you no longer.” I afflicted you in the present life; I will not afflict you in the future.

There is a great difference between you and the nations without God in this matter of affliction: many of them too are afflicted in the present age, but all will be afflicted in the future; and there the affliction will not be temporal but eternal. What does it avail that some of them received their good things in their lifetime and were permitted to fulfil their pleasures to the end of the present life? They will then be tormented when you are comforted—you who likewise received evil things in your lifetime.

Thus, without any difficulty, the saying “I have afflicted you, and I will afflict you no longer” is rightly understood as though it said: I afflicted you in the present life, and I will not afflict you in the life to come. Yet there is still too little consolation in this saying because of the weaknesses of those who are still imperfect and still need to be nourished. If this very affliction of the present life continues unceasingly, they quickly fail and nearly fall into despair.

Therefore the Comforter adds and supplies what was lacking in both the earlier and the present saying—where he had said, “A double tribulation shall not rise,” and where he says, “I have afflicted you, and I will afflict you no longer.” What does he add, and how does the Comforter supply what was lacking? “And now I will break his rod from your back and tear apart his bonds.” “And now,” he says—that is, even in the present life, [Col. 0546A] before you end this life—this tribulation will end, so that while living in the body you may see vengeance upon the enemy Sennacherib; for “I will put a ring in his nostrils and a bridle on his lips, and I will bring him back by the way by which he came” (4 Kings 19), and he shall return here no more.

It should be noted that the words, “I will break his rod from your back and tear apart his bonds,” sound both the release or liberation of Jerusalem and, in words especially fitting, wrath against the nation, against the enemy. For he was not content to say, “I will break the rod and loosen the bonds,” but: “I will crush the rod and tear apart the bonds.” It is greater indignation to crush underfoot than to break with the hands; likewise, it is a greater punitive act to tear a bond apart suddenly than gradually to loosen it with some delay.

Therefore this very mode of speech indicates the magnitude of indignation against those who, by a power permitted them, feed upon the sufferings of God’s servants at their own will or by the design of a hidden judgment, and who moreover dare to boast against God—as Assur or Sennacherib said: “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood” (Isa. 10), and similar things.

What, then, has been accomplished by these words of the Comforter except that, when you hear from the rebuking speaker the aforesaid words, “What are you devising against the Lord? He himself will bring about an end. A double tribulation shall not rise,” you may now know that he is loudly proclaiming and saying to them: indeed, a double consolation shall rise. And truly, just as it was and is true that a double tribulation shall rise against none of God’s elect, so it was true to say of many that a double consolation shall rise. The best-known among us is blessed Job, whose latter end the Lord blessed more than his beginning after his trial, and to whom he added double all that he had in the present life; without doubt he was to receive far more and far better things in the future life (Job 42).

Yet persons of this kind refuse to be comforted by such things; and even if consolations of this sort abound, they are unwilling to set their heart upon them. So said one who was rich, powerful, and glorious on earth: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76 [77]). And if someone should ask where or in what “my soul refused to be comforted,” and in what it consented to be comforted, he replies: earthly things are not a consolation to me; “but I remembered God and was delighted” (ibid.).

Concerning Hezekiah, the king of that time, it must not be passed over that he ought rightly to have received as a double consolation what was said to him by the Lord through Isaiah the prophet: “I have heard your prayer and seen your tear. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days, and I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king, and I will protect it” (Isa. 38). Besides the common consolation laid up for him with all the elect in the future age, this too was a great consolation in the present life: the Lord added fifteen years to his days, because through this it came about that he had a place and a name in the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0547A] son of David. For he had not yet had a son, and he was preserved for this purpose, that he might beget one and, as is said in the genealogy of Christ, sit among the fathers as a father.

Conversely, it was said above that there were or are some of the worst wicked persons upon whom a double tribulation rightly rose; and here Sennacherib may suffice as an example. The prophetic discourse immediately turns upon him in this denunciation, a harsh message indeed of double tribulation: “And the Lord will command concerning you: no seed shall be sown from your name any longer; from the house of your god I will destroy the carved image and the molten image; I will make your grave, because you are dishonoured.”

For what, or to whom, will the Lord command against you, except to the striking angel, that he may go forth and strike one hundred and eighty-five thousand in your camp in one night, and then that your sons Adrammelech and Sharezer may strike you with the sword while you worship your god Nesrath in his temple (4 Kings 19)? Thus comes about what is said: “No seed shall be sown from your name any longer.” From the tribulation which was great for you in the present age, you have been transferred to be afflicted in another age, buried in hell. Hence it is also said here: “I will make your grave, because you are dishonoured.”

What God establishes stands immovably; it cannot be changed or removed. He establishes your grave, to be understood as in hell, where not only the rich man of the Gospel possesses a grave (Luke 10), but also all who are or were like him; and especially you, Assur, concerning whom it is written in Ezekiel: “There is Assur and all his multitude round about him, his graves, and all the slain, those fallen by the sword, whose graves were given in the depths of the pit; and his multitude was set around his grave—all slain and fallen by the sword, who once gave terror in the land of the living” (Ezek. 32).

For what reason will I establish your grave there? “Because you are dishonoured.” Dishonoured, that is, proud. For pride is dishonour: insofar as anyone is proud, he is dishonoured. Thus the same Lord, when he said to Edom, “You are exceedingly contemptible” (Obad. 1), immediately added this reason: “The pride of your heart has lifted you up” (ibid.). Therefore this man is among those against whom a double tribulation rightly rose, just as Hezekiah, on the contrary, belongs among those whose consolation, as we have said, is double.

The inserted words, “From the house of your god I will destroy the carved image and the molten image,” announce the devastation to follow: the whole of Nineveh was to be overthrown by the Chaldeans. For where carved and molten things—that is, images of gods, such as both Chaldeans and Assyrians revered and worshipped—are not spared, what will become of ordinary houses, the marketplace, and the whole city? Nineveh was devastated. This same prophet will later say mockingly: “And I,” says the Lord of hosts, “will uncover your shame before your face and show the nations your nakedness” (Nah. 3).

He here briefly foreshadows that nakedness when, directing judgment against that great pride, he says: “From the house of your god I will destroy the carved image and the molten image.” It is clear that names will not be spared when enemies do not spare even reverence for the gods, crying in mutual exhortation: “Plunder the gold, plunder the silver” (Nah. 2). Pride is rightly mocked, for it was so great that in holy and prophetic Scriptures it is repeatedly compared to the pride of the devil.

Indeed, in the prophets Nineveh itself is understood as the world and its king as the devil, because of the loftiness of his magnificent heart and his eyes. For example, the Lord speaks in Ezekiel: “Behold, Assur was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches and thick in foliage, lofty in height. No cedars in the paradise of God were higher than it; no tree of the paradise of God was comparable to it” (Ezek. 31), etc.

Why, then, did Assur deserve this memorial, that his name should be so often mentioned in the argument or judgment concerning the devil’s condemnation? Namely, because, among other presumptuous enterprises of tyranny by which he afflicted the nations, he added this: he attempted to destroy Jerusalem, where the word of promise had been deposited, and the house of David, from which Christ had to be born according to the Lord’s promise and oath to David himself (2 Kings 7).

Accordingly, we wish to extend our discourse more fully concerning the distresses of Judaea, and thereafter to pursue the prophecy in such a way that we give attention rather to those things of which there can be no doubt that they were likenesses or types, throughout all that the prophet foretells against Nineveh on behalf of Judah and Jerusalem.

241. BOOK II.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547D] “Let the Midianites perceive you as enemies,” the Lord says to Moses, “and strike them, because they too acted as enemies against you and deceived you by their snares through the idol of Phoge and through Cozbi, the daughter of a Midianite prince, their sister” (Num. XXV). Since it is written concerning the Midianites alone that the Lord spoke against them and gave such a command, should it be thought that the servants of the Lord, such as Moses was, ought rightly to have been perceived as enemies by the Midianites alone? On the contrary, it must unquestionably be understood of all nations whatsoever that acted as enemies against Israel in the manner of Midian: God willed both Moses and all who possess the spirit of Moses to be their enemies, and to desire against such peoples the vengeance which He Himself, granting it to Moses, commanded: “First avenge the children of Israel upon the Midianites, and then you shall be gathered to your people” (Num. XXXI).

For what reason? Are not all holy or perfected persons, who have no spirit other than that which those men had, commanded with Peter to put the sword back into its sheath? (Matt. XXVI.) Why, then, did swords thus commanded rage then, or why ought they to have raged? Doubtless, they then ought to have raged for Christ—for the same Christ for whose sake, now that Christ’s enemies rage against us, we ought to maintain unarmed patience. At that time the matter was in danger, because it was possible for that nation, from which Christ was awaited to be born, to be destroyed unless it were defended by every means against the nations whom the devil persistently employed to remove the hope of the world, which is Christ.

But now the matter itself is secure, [Col. 0549B] because Christ has been born; and even if the entire good tree of the line of rulers should be bodily cut down, there is no loss to human salvation, because the whole fruit of the good tree has already been taken up into heaven. These things have been said for this reason, and must often be said again and always retained in memory: so that the wholly just hostile vehemence of the saints may be better understood. So far as they were able, with God’s help, they both sought vengeance from God against their enemies—God’s enemies, impious nations—and inflicted it by their own hand; and, when vengeance had been obtained or witnessed, they still assailed them as enemies. Thus this writer, who composed so joyous a prophecy against Assyria—or rather, against every person acting as an enemy, as was said above—seems in some sense to leap in a triumphant song, proceeding as follows:

## Chapter II

[Col. 0549C]

Behold, upon the mountains, the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace. Keep your feasts, O Judah, and fulfil your vows, for Belial shall no longer pass through you; he has utterly perished. The one who scatters has come up before your face, maintaining the siege. Watch the way; strengthen your loins; reinforce your strength mightily. For as the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Jacob, so he will repay the pride directed against Israel, because devastators have scattered them and corrupted their shoots.

These words, and all that follows to the end, resound with great joy, great and triumphant exultation; and the reason for all this rejoicing is this: “For as the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Jacob, so he will repay the pride directed against Israel.” [Col. 0549D] Thus the matter concealed beneath these words is no small one—“as the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Jacob”—since the whole ground or substance of consolation and joy is contained in them.

What, then, is meant by: “As the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Jacob, so he will repay the pride directed against Israel”? Jacob and Israel had one and the same father, and Jacob and Israel were one and the same people. If it had said, “As the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Judah, so he will repay the pride directed against Israel,” the meaning would present itself without difficulty or hesitation: just as the Lord avenged Judah and Jerusalem upon King Sennacherib and his army, so he will avenge the ten tribes called Israel upon Nineveh or the Assyrians, by whom, under the reign of Shalmaneser, those same ten tribes had been taken captive. [Col. 0550A]

Yet, although this interpretation too is reasonable, and Jacob may fittingly be understood as Judah, I am inclined to extend the mind’s view more broadly, so that under the names Jacob and Israel may be understood all the elect, both ancient and new: both those who preceded and those who follow Christ’s coming. For we willingly understand Jacob, the father according to the flesh of the twelve sons and consequently of the twelve tribes of Israel, as prefiguring Christ, the father according to the Spirit of the twelve apostles and of all who have believed or believe in him through them.

Accordingly, these words have the broadest and wholly plain sense found in the Apostle’s statement concerning the former people: “All these things happened to them in figure.” For just as those things of which the Apostle expressly made mention—the benefits of God—happened to them figuratively (1 Cor. 10) and are truly fulfilled in Christ’s Gospel, so that vengeance upon the Assyrians happened figuratively to those in whose time it occurred and is truly fulfilled in Christ’s Gospel. [Col. 0550B]

This is indeed a great and worthy reason for which the Holy Spirit should cry out through the prophet: “Behold upon the mountains the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace”; for which he should rejoice with them and say, “Keep your feasts, O Judah, and fulfil your vows”; and for which he should stir them to joy and confidence, saying, “Watch the way; strengthen your loins; reinforce your strength mightily,” and so forth. “So that,” he says, “you may do this also, and may not attend only to the fact that the Lord thus repaid the pride of the Assyrians which they exercised against Jacob: Sennacherib did not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it, nor occupy it with a shield; but when one hundred and eighty-five thousand had been slain by the angel of the Lord, he returned by the way [page 242] through which he had come, was killed, and Nineveh was overthrown” (4 Kings 19). [Col. 0550C]

Do not, I say, attend only to this; but consider also that, as the Lord repaid pride directed against Jacob so that the Assyrians were cut off; as he repaid pride directed against Jacob so that Pharaoh, with his chariots and horsemen, was submerged in the sea; as he repaid pride directed against Jacob so that Babylon was overthrown by the Persians and Medes; as he repaid pride directed against Jacob so that Haman, the enemy of the Jews, was hanged upon the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai; as he repaid pride directed against Jacob so that Antiochus Epiphanes was crushed without human hand—so he will repay pride directed against Israel: the new people reborn through evangelical faith, whose generation according to the Spirit is from Christ, the father of the twelve apostles, of whom Jacob, the father according to the flesh of twelve sons, went before as a type. [Col. 0550D]

How will he repay the pride directed against this Israel, in a manner corresponding to what he repaid for pride directed against that Jacob? Surely in this way: the devil, prince of this world, who dared to come against this Israel, in whom he has nothing, shall be slain by the blood and water flowing from his side, just as that fleshly Pharaoh with all his people was drowned in violent waters. Thus he shall be pierced by the wood of the cross, as Haman was pierced; and as Antiochus was crushed, so finally the devil himself, and the whole world agreeing with him, shall be condemned at the final judgment—just as Assyria, which came against Judah and Jerusalem and seemed invincible to itself, was overcome, and Nineveh, the head of its pride, was overthrown. [Col. 0551A]

Behold, O Judah, upon the mountains—behold the feet, that is, the preachers, passing beyond every height of the age: the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace, preachers of repentance and forgiveness of sins, sin having been destroyed, righteousness accomplished, and the prince of this world already judged. According to the likeness of the blow inflicted in part, the same thing has happened among the Assyrians and without doubt will happen in the whole, namely this world and its prince.

Therefore keep your feasts, O Judah—that is, you who confess the prophetic and evangelical faith. Keep your feasts and fulfil your vows: abstain from evil works and persevere in good works. Celebrate now in truth the feasts once celebrated in figure. For example, know that the lamb which you formerly ate in shadow, by eating which you celebrated the crossing of the sea and the drowning of the fleshly Pharaoh, was a sign of Christ the Lamb; and recognize that the other feasts of the Law were patterns of evangelical glory. [Col. 0551B]

But what benefit is there in outwardly celebrating feasts of whatever kind, unless the feast of contemplation is in the mind? Therefore, when he says, “Keep your feasts, O Judah, and fulfil your vows,” ask the Psalmist, and he will tell you how you ought to do it: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for you. Make vows and fulfil them to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” (Ps. 73 [Vulgate numbering]).

These are your feasts, O Judah: that your thought may confess to God; and if not every thought can be festive and bright, at least let the remnant of thought keep festival—that is, after the assaults of evil thoughts, let good thoughts at least sometimes occupy the place of the mind, according to the saying: “You have sinned; be at rest” (Wisdom 21 [citation uncertain]). [Col. 0551C]

On such a feast-day fulfil your vows. The highest or best of these vows, according to the Psalmist, is to receive “the cup of salvation” (Ps. 113 [Vulgate numbering]): that is, to imitate the death of the Saviour, who by dying made peace between God and humankind, and preached and proclaimed that peace through feet, as already stated—that is, through preachers or apostles sent throughout the world, walking upon the mountains, that is, above every height of the age.

Certainly it is no vain feast to celebrate thus and to have this reason for the feast: “Belial shall no longer pass through you; he has utterly perished”—namely, in the likeness of Assyria or Sennacherib, who returned by the way through which he came and shall no longer be able to pass through you. For Belial, which is interpreted “without yoke,” namely the devil, rebellious against God from the beginning, shall no longer be able to pass through you after Christ, by dying and rising again, has dedicated your feasts to you, O Judah. From that time onward he has utterly perished. [Col. 0551D]

Not that his substance has ceased to exist, but that the death of the human race—which entered this world through his envy (Rom. 5)—has utterly perished: I mean universal death, the double death of both soul and body. [Col. 0552A]

Where or when did this Belial perish? Where did the death he inflicted die—the death from which he himself is called Death? Surely, where Christ died, there the death of our souls died; and where Christ rose again, there the death of our bodies perished. Therefore, in keeping your feasts, O Judah, remember that he is your very feast, of whom you say: “By dying he conquered our death, and by rising again he restored life.” Hence it is said: “Belial shall no longer pass through you; he has utterly perished.”

For if you consider only that Sennacherib departed and did not return, and perished, then it is not true to say, “Belial has utterly perished,” since after him a great deal of Belial, like him, passed through you and did you far greater harm. Perhaps you say, O Judah: “So long as Nineveh stands, how can you tell me that Belial has utterly perished? So long as the world stands, how can I be consoled over the destruction of death? For behold, Nero rages, Decius is mad, Maximian, armed with death, raves; and besides these there are many sons of Belial, of whom Antichrist will be the worst. How then do you now say that Belial has utterly perished?” [Col. 0552B]

To this I say: “The one who scatters has come up before your face, maintaining the siege.” Who is he who has come up? Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against that Nineveh and, before your face, O Judah—you who at that time were in the world, that is, in your presence or with your knowledge—scattered that Nineveh, maintaining the siege around it until he captured it. But in this there is little, indeed almost no consolation for you. For Nebuchadnezzar afterward proved worse for you than Sennacherib had been.

Who, then, is he who has come up and who shall thus scatter this world, the great Nineveh, before your face, so that you may have perfect consolation? Surely, Christ who descended is the one who ascended; and as he ascended, so he shall come (Acts 1), to scatter Nineveh—that is, to judge the world before his face. [Col. 0552C]

Whatever Nero or Diocletian, or rather the devil or Antichrist, does in the meantime, diminishes the truth in no respect: you may truly say, “Belial has utterly perished; the prince of this world has been cast out.” Here it is neither disputed nor can it be disputed that death—both deaths, of soul and body—has been swallowed up in the victory of this ascender to heaven.

What if the enemy still kills the body in the members? In the end, he cannot kill the soul made alive by the death of the head, that is, Christ. And concerning the death of the body itself, it is so certain that it shall perish in the members that you may now truthfully and securely say that it has perished—especially because Christ the head has risen, and some members, that is, many saints, have risen with him. [Col. 0552D]

Formerly the dragon, the devil, aimed at and hoped for this: that he might bring it about that from that woman—the people which according to the flesh is also called Judah or Judaea—there should not be born the male child who was to rule the nations with an iron rod (Rev. 12). Therefore, armed with seven heads, he tried to destroy her. [Col. 0553A] But he can no longer hope for this, because that Son has now been born and has now been caught up to God and to his throne.

Henceforth he aims only, through Nero and all those like him, that he should not be expected to return. But hold firmly that, as he ascended, so he shall return, to scatter Nineveh before your face; that, with you looking on, he may judge the world that does not believe and persecutes you; maintaining the siege in such a way that no place of escape shall be open to anyone, whether from east or west or from the desert mountains (Ps. 74 [Vulgate numbering]), because God himself is judge: he encloses all things, and none can snatch anything from his hand.

Knowing that this is to come, believing that he will return for this purpose, do what I now say: “Watch the way; strengthen your loins; reinforce your strength mightily.” [Col. 0553B] Do these things; live thus. For this is nothing other than what he himself said in the Gospel before ascending: “Let your loins be girded, your lamps burning, and be yourselves like people awaiting their lord when he returns from the wedding” (Luke 12).

What else is it to keep watch, after the likeness of people awaiting their lord, than to watch the way: to await with concern him who is to come and who is himself the Way? And what else is it to strengthen the loins than to have the loins girded: that is, to keep the body chastened and the heart chaste against lust or sensuality, which is in the loins? Moreover, to reinforce strength mightily is undoubtedly to keep lamps burning: that is, with the honour of chastity to perform good works and persevere in them. [Col. 0553C]

But how and from where is strength of this kind reinforced mightily? What is the strong reinforcement of this virtue? Truly, humility: not a false but an altogether true awareness of weakness. For every virtue is strengthened in it; as the Apostle says, “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

We do not say that weakness itself is the humility necessary for us, but that an awareness of weakness—whether one’s own fragility or the common condition—advances one toward humility as a kind of instrument. Of one’s own fragility, as in the Apostle’s words: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan” (ibid.). Of the common condition, as in Job’s words: “Remember, I pray, that you have made me like clay, and will reduce me to dust” (Job 10), and so forth. [Col. 0553D]

If experience is sought that every virtue is strongly reinforced by humility, behold: Jacob was able to wrestle with the angel and not be overcome (Gen. 38 [citation as printed]); and Moses was able to hold God when he said, “Let me go” (Exod. 3 [citation as printed]). That the great strength of both was reinforced by humility is proven by clear testimonies. For concerning Jacob, in Hosea, after it has been said, “In his strength he was directed with the angel, and prevailed over the angel, and was strengthened” (Hos. 12), it is immediately added: “He wept and besought him” (ibid.). Concerning Moses, when the Psalmist said, “And he said”—God being understood—“that he would destroy them,” he immediately added: “Had not Moses his chosen stood in the breach before him” (Ps. 103 [Vulgate numbering]). [Col. 0554A] For what is “in the breach,” except in the utmost humility of mind?

Once it has thus been understood what is meant by “reinforce your strength mightily,” the following words can bear a reasonable sense, as they stand in most manuscripts and do not differ from the Septuagint translators: “For as the Lord has repaid Jacob’s pride, so he will repay Israel’s pride.” We understand Jacob and Israel as the old and the new, that is, both those who were under the Law and those who believe in the Gospel, as has already been stated above.

What was Jacob’s pride, and how did the Lord repay Jacob’s pride? Without doubt, Jacob’s pride was displayed when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram contended concerning the priesthood and, with their whole company, stood against the Lord. The Lord repaid that pride so that the earth was split beneath their feet and, opening its mouth, swallowed Dathan and Abiram with their tents and all their pride; they went down alive into hell, covered by the earth, and perished from the midst of the multitude. [Col. 0554B] Fire also went out from the Lord and killed two hundred and fifty men who offered incense (Num. 16).

Likewise Saul, although he was the Lord’s anointed, grew proud; and the Lord repaid his pride by delivering him to an evil spirit (1 Kings 16). There are more examples of this kind than can now be set down briefly.

Therefore, when he has first said, “Reinforce your strength mightily”—that is, possess humility in all things—he immediately adds, “For as the Lord has repaid the pride directed against Jacob, so he will repay the pride directed against Israel.” This wording, as already noted, does not differ from that of the Septuagint translators, and it instils great fear into all Israel who, by believing in Christ, has deserved to be called Israel. [Col. 0554C]

For God is terrible in his counsels concerning the children of men (Ps. 65 [Vulgate numbering]). Therefore each person must be more cautious and devote himself more diligently to humility when he has received greater gifts of heavenly grace. This is required not only by the Apostle’s warning: “Do not boast against the branches that were broken off; do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you” (Rom. 11); but in every way, so that one person may never be puffed up against another, and that no one while alive may suppose that he has already attained.

The pride of Israel—that is, of believers—has among its other evils produced heresies, and it has done no less harm through those who seemed to be within than through those Gentiles who were or are outside. But what follows—“Because devastators have scattered them and corrupted their shoots”—refers to devastators of the Lord’s vineyards, against whom the Beloved himself says in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy our vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed” (Song 2). [Col. 0554D]

These devastators have acted worse than those devastators: the latter openly scattered, that is, persecuted; but the former corrupted deceitfully and sometimes ravaged the shoots by open violence. Therefore the Lord will repay the pride of this Israel as he repaid the pride of that Jacob. To use the Apostle’s example: he repaid that Jacob in this way—that all indeed crossed the sea; all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; all ate the same spiritual food; [Col. 0555A] all drank the same spiritual drink; but God was not pleased with many of them (1 Cor. 10)—with the implied meaning that they did not at least enter the land which was a shadow of that land of the living for which we hope in the future, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. “Now these things happened as figures for us,” and the rest. Let us now pursue what follows.

“The shield of his mighty men is fiery; the men of his army are in scarlet. The reins of the chariots are fiery on the day of his preparation, and the agitators are asleep. They are disturbed in the ways; the chariots have collided in the streets; their appearance is like lamps, like lightning flashing to and fro.”

“The shield,” he says, “of his mighty men is fiery.” Whose mighty men? Do you suppose they belong to that Nebuchadnezzar who came up to scatter that local, though great, Nineveh? His mighty men’s shield may indeed have been fiery or shining in some fashion, and the men of his army may have worn scarlet leggings and greaves, or garments of any other beautiful colour. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, would by no means have lowered himself so far as, without reference to mystery, to proclaim at such length trifles or vanities of this sort—shields and chariots, chariot reins and racing teams, scarlet clothing and bright appearances of men—and to deign to make them known to the ages to come, for which he intended the prophetic Scripture to endure. [Col. 0555B]

Let us therefore follow the Spirit wherever he goes, so far as we are able; and because these are words of the Holy Spirit, let us seek spiritual mysteries rather in the words.

The shield of the mighty men of him who, as stated above, ascended into heaven in order to scatter Nineveh—that is, to judge the world—is fiery; the men of his army are in scarlet; and the reins of his chariots are fiery on the day of his preparation. First we must ask what this preparation, or day of preparation, is and what is being prepared; then the remaining matters will become clearer, since they contain great majesty of spiritual meanings. [Col. 0555C]

What is being prepared except that the world may be judged? And what is the preparation for this except the preaching of the Gospel? And what is the day of his preparation except the entire period up to the consummation of the age? Indeed, however long its duration and however great its number of years, just as it is rightly called a time, so it is rightly called a day, as the Lord himself testifies when he says in the prophet: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49). The Apostle echoes: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). [Col. 0555D]

Thus the one and same day which is a day of salvation to the believing world is a day of preparation to the unbelieving world. Within this day of preparation we must find the fiery shields of his mighty men, the scarlet garments of his men, the fiery reins of the chariots, the chariots colliding in the streets, flashing appearances, and the other insignia of military equipment which he repeatedly presses upon us in his proclamation, so that it is clear, or ought to be clear, that he is dealing with serious and great matters.

Here we understand his mighty men to be those of whose multitude two stood beside the apostles at the beginning of this preparation, when he ascended and the apostles watched him going into heaven. They stood beside them in white garments and said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). [Col. 0556A] Thus, I say, he will come to scatter Nineveh—that is, to judge this world.

One of these mighty men, among the princes, is Michael. Concerning him, in the Apocalypse, where the Son of the blessed woman ascends and is caught up to God and to his throne, it is written: “And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon” (Rev. 12), and so forth. The shield of these mighty men is the Word of God—the Word is God—and this shield is certainly fiery, because it is written: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire” (Ps. 118 [Vulgate numbering]); and again, Solomon was told: “Every word of God is a fiery shield” (Prov. 30).

Against whom is such a fiery shield kindled except against the dragon and his angels? The fire of these fiery shields is intolerable to them. Hence Ezekiel reproaches him, where under the names of nine stones he speaks against him concerning the nine orders of angels: “I cast you out from the mountain of God and destroyed you, O protecting cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones” (Ezek. 28). [Col. 0556B]

The men of whom he says, “the men of his army are in scarlet,” are understood to be those who, aided or cooperating with those mighty beings, have always conquered the dragon invisibly and sometimes visibly as well. As it is written in the same place: “They overcame him because of the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 12), and “they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7).

Next, by the fiery reins of the chariots we understand the prelates or rulers of the Churches. Just as reins guide a chariot, so their rules or admonitions guide that chariot of which it is written in the Psalm: “The chariots of God are many thousands, a multitude of those rejoicing” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate numbering]). The reins are fiery because their words or deeds, indeed their whole rule, are not, or ought not to be, without the great ardour of good zeal. [Col. 0556C]

Those mighty men with fiery shields, those men of his army in scarlet, and those fiery reins of the chariots do not fail on the day of his preparation; and all their action is preparation from that time to the end of the age—the preparation for the scattering by which Nineveh, that is, the world, is to be scattered; the preparation for the judgment by which this world is to be judged.

For in the meantime, through them the Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16). While he convicts it, those who believe flee from the world that is to perish, and the world that refuses to believe becomes inexcusable. This is his preparation.

“And the agitators,” he says, “are asleep.” The agitators are plainly not his: the other things are his. The mighty men whose shield is fiery are called, and are, his; the men of his army in scarlet are called, and are, his; the chariots with fiery reins and the entire preparation are called, and are, his. But the charioteers are neither called nor are his. [Col. 0556D]

For who are the agitators except the restless, hostile, violent, insulting, or proud? Such persons he does not have; such persons are not from God but from the evil one, from the condemned world, from the world lying in evil.

What did that aforesaid Assyria first do in its time that it should be marked in this way, so that it itself, and all agitators like it, might rightly be called agitators? In Isaiah, where its coming is announced by the prophetic voice, it is said among other things: “They have passed through the course” (Isa. 10), namely the Assyrians hastening against Jerusalem, exceedingly certain and confident that its destruction was already accomplished; and, he says, “he shall shake his hand over the mountain of the daughter of Zion and the hill of Jerusalem” (ibid.). [Col. 0557A]

Since that Assyria or Sennacherib shook his hand in hostility, flattering himself, mocking the holy place, swelling with pride in himself, rashly playing against God, the Holy Spirit rightly marked him, so that he himself and all agitators like him might be called agitators.

Like him, in this day of preparation of which we speak according to this prophet—while preparation is being made for Nineveh, that is, the world, to be judged—were Nero, Diocletian, Maximian, and all others who stirred themselves up against the Gospel of this preparation, filled with a diabolical spirit; and behold, they are asleep. What does “asleep” mean? They are dead.

Were not those beautiful men, the men of the army of the ascender to heaven, who overcame the dragon, as stated above, through the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 12) and through the word of their testimony, and are therefore in scarlet—were they not also dead? They are indeed dead, but they are not asleep. [Col. 0557B] For though they are dead to the world, they live to God; and they still serve in the camp of their king, the king of the living, no less than they served while living in the flesh.

Indeed, undoubtedly, in a wondrous manner, though they have laid aside the flesh and are in another age, they are present with us and, by their merits, govern and by their virtues strengthen the remaining army still sojourning in this age. But those agitators are dead to God and no longer live to this age. They neither can nor will be able to harm or benefit the living. Therefore it is true to say that they are asleep: they are buried in the deep sleep of death, from which they shall not awake until heaven is worn away; nor will they thereafter create any obstacle or impediment for those mighty men, the aforesaid men, the chariot, or the Lord’s reins. [Col. 0557C]

They are asleep, I say, amid their activity, or while what follows is occurring: “They are disturbed in the ways; the chariots have collided in the streets; their appearance is like lamps, like lightning flashing to and fro.”

As already said, that Chaldean army may have been so swift, so hurried, and so splendid, with so many chariots racing together against Nineveh, that because of their multitude they could not find room in the road and collided with one another in the streets. The appearance of the Babylonians may have been so flashing, or bright with some unknown light, that they terrified their opponents by sight before striking them down with the sword. Yet we have dwelt sufficiently on this literal meaning. Let us rather follow the Spirit and run after him. [Col. 0557D]

In this day of preparation for the judgment by which the world is to be judged—a world of which that Nineveh was both a part and a type—the men of Nineveh are disturbed, with diverse disturbance in the ways and streets, and with chariots colliding. In what ways or streets? Surely in those in which Wisdom cried aloud with the evangelical voice, as we have in Proverbs: “Wisdom preaches outside; in the streets she gives her voice; at the head of the crowds she cries aloud; at the gates of the city she utters her words” (Prov. 1). Again: “Does not Wisdom cry aloud, and Prudence give her voice? Standing at the highest and loftiest heights above the way, in the midst of the paths, beside the city gates, at the very entrances, she speaks, saying: ‘O men, I cry to you’” (Prov. 8), and so forth. [Col. 0558A]

Therefore they were disturbed not in secret but in the ways; not in corners but in the streets, when they heard the voice of Wisdom, when they heard the Gospel in which, as the Apostle says, “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of those who hold the truth of God in injustice” (Rom. 1). They were disturbed and shaken; trembling seized them (Ps. 47 [Vulgate numbering]) as they heard that there is another and better city than their Nineveh, another age than the present age, and that this age is to be judged by fire.

“There were pains as of a woman in labour” (ibid.). There, I say—that is, in that disturbance and trembling—there is pain not without fruit, just as the pain of a woman in labour is not without fruit. For many, hearing what is being prepared for Nineveh, that is, for this world, were so disturbed that they were made sorrowful unto repentance, and so trembled that they quickly sought how they might flee from the wrath to come and escape that judgment. [Col. 0558B]

But others, who were unbelieving, were so disturbed and shaken that in anger they directed and agitated themselves against the Gospel of this great preparation; hence shortly before they were called charioteers.

But whose chariots collided in the streets? Surely the chariots of Aminadab, whose name is interpreted “the willing one of my people.” This Aminadab is Christ, and his chariots collided in the streets, meeting the oncoming chariots of the proud one of this age. Of such chariots Zechariah says: “He is poor, and riding upon an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass; and I shall scatter the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be destroyed” (Zech. 9). [Col. 0558C]

The chariots of Aminadab are the four Gospels, by which four great mysteries are preached to us against Nineveh: the incarnation of Aminadab himself, whose face is the face of a human being; his passion, which is the face of a calf; his resurrection, which is the face of a lion; and his ascension, which is the face of a flying eagle.

There is great disturbance there because there is a great collision of chariots. Those are well disturbed, those are sorrowful unto repentance, who through the collision of the chariots confess and make satisfaction because they were in that collision—not through malice but through ignorance. For one of them, for example Saul or another person formerly hostile but afterwards corrected and a faithful companion of the chariots, says: “I did not know; my soul disturbed me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6). [Col. 0558D]

“I did not know,” he says; “I acted in ignorance; in unbelief I opposed them ignorantly, when I suddenly saw the chariots of Aminadab. But now, having considered the dignity of his chariots, my soul has disturbed me. Heal its contritions, O Aminadab.”

How beautiful are the chariots! How splendid the charioteers! “Their appearance,” he says, “is like lamps, and like lightning flashing to and fro.” In Ezekiel likewise you have: “Their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of lamps. This vision moved to and fro in the midst of the living creatures: the brightness of fire, and lightning coming forth from the fire” (Ezek. 1).

Where the chariots have collided, there the faces or appearances of the Gospels or evangelists are like lamps and like lightning flashing to and fro. Lamps illuminate; lightning terrifies. Thus, as they have powers, or the working of powers, as it is written in the Psalm, “The Lord will give the word to those who bring good news with great power” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate numbering]), while they preach everywhere, with the Lord working with them and confirming the word by accompanying signs (Mark 16), they illuminate human minds with the knowledge of truth and, through miracles, more strongly rouse them to hear and believe. [Col. 0559A]

He rightly calls them “lightning flashing to and fro,” because the miracles of evangelical preaching were seen and heard not in one part of the world only but throughout the whole world.

It follows:

He will remember his mighty men. Who will remember his mighty men? Nineveh will remember; the world will remember; and, for example, Rome, which at that time [Col. 0559C] was the head of the world, when the first collision of such chariots—or the crash of their collision—was heard in the streets. Her mighty men had been many: for instance, the Torquati, Corvini, Cornelii, Scipios or Africani, Caesars or Augusti. He says that she will remember men mighty such as these; and so it happened. For, in disparagement of Christian peace and contempt of evangelical grace, whenever the many triumphs of their mighty men—celebrated over the whole world, over Europe, Africa, and Asia—were recalled, they did so with their gods, as they said, being favourable. By the gods’ assistance, since religion and worship flourished in the temples, the greatness of the Roman Empire had advanced and expanded.

“But now,” they said, lamenting and declaiming in the streets, “rain fails because of the Christians. The gods are angry; therefore the Britons rise up, or the Danes resist—indeed, the Germans attack; the Alans despise our commands.” The world, he says, will remember its mighty men in such a manner: namely, that they were mighty without possessing God, Christ, or the Christian name; and that, had those mighty men been mighty today, no one would dare bring that name to their ears. But hear what follows: “And they shall stumble in their paths.” The world will vainly remember its mighty men in that way; for whoever remember them thus will stumble in their nets, will stumble as liars overwhelmed by truth.

For, conversely, the Rider-up-to-heaven himself will remember his mighty men, and will remember them effectually, so that the remembrance of them greatly profits. After his mighty men have departed this present life, after apostles or martyrs—surely his mighty men—have been slain [Col. 0560A] and carried to the tomb, he will remember them in such a way as to make them cooperate with the living and to confirm their word by the signs which follow.

Such remembrance, to give the reader greater pleasure, will occur according to the mystical example of that exceedingly mighty Samson. When the Philistines came shouting against him, the Spirit of the Lord rushing upon him, he seized the jawbone—that is, the mandible—of an ass which he found lying there, and with it killed a thousand men. When he was very thirsty, the Lord opened the molar tooth in the jawbone of the ass, which he had thrown from his hand; waters came forth from it, and, having drunk them, he refreshed his spirit and recovered his strength (Judg. 15).

According to this likeness, this one remembered his mighty men, who according to [Col. 0560B] the flesh were weak and ignoble, but according to the Spirit were strong and noble—and so mighty in the hand of Christ, the Mightiest One, that with those few he crushed the strength of the age, just as Samson destroyed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. When he cast them away—or seemed to cast them away—because he permitted them to be killed, as though he neglected their care, then he himself, that is, the Church which is his body, thirsted greatly and feared falling into the hands of enemies, that is, unbelievers. Against these enemies the apostles and martyrs, while alive, had been a great support by word and deed.

Thus the Lord opened their tombs, so that frequent streams of miracles might issue forth, from which the Church refreshed her spirit and recovered her strength, so that she might confidently say that Christ her God is “God not of the dead but of the living” (Mark 12), and that all her mighty men live then—and live better—when they are dead to the world. Therefore, he says, those who remember their mighty men shall stumble in their paths, because this one too will remember his mighty men with a good and effective remembrance, in order to prove that their strength was vain and the strength of these men true—men with whom he himself will judge Nineveh, that is, the world, according to the truth of the aforesaid preparation which goes before.

Thus what follows will come about: “They shall swiftly climb her walls, and a shelter shall be prepared. The gates of the rivers are opened, and the temple is torn down to the ground; the soldier is led away captive; and the maidservants are led along, moaning like doves and murmuring in their hearts.”

The literal sense concerning the overthrow of that Nineveh is clear: [Col. 0560D] the Chaldeans swiftly climbed her walls; because of their exceedingly long siege they prepared shelters for themselves to ward off the heat; when the gates of Nineveh were opened—Nineveh having a multitude of citizens like rivers—the enemy entered and destroyed the temple as he would a marketplace or public buildings; the soldier was led captive into Babylon; and the maidservants—that is, metaphorically, the lesser cities, or certainly captive women—were led before the faces of the victors. Such terror prevailed that grief did not even burst into sobbing and wailing; rather, within themselves they groaned silently and swallowed their tears in a dim murmur, like cooing doves.

But in a war of men, such as that of the Babylonians against the Assyrians, once they had swiftly climbed the walls, why would a shelter be prepared for them? Those who besiege have need to provide themselves with shelter from the heat only so long as they cannot take the walls by climbing or by assault. Therefore the men of the army, the ascenders to heaven—the men who, as was said above, go in scarlet—are those who swiftly climbed Nineveh’s walls; and after them a shelter was prepared for us.

More plainly stated: these are the holy martyrs, the holy apostles. The holy martyrs, I say, sons of the holy apostles, are those who swiftly climbed Nineveh’s walls, while the gates of the rivers had not yet been opened. This happened afterward, as follows immediately: “The gates of the rivers are opened.” The gates of the rivers—the gates of the peoples—were shut: gates which the rulers, kings, tyrants, Caesars, and emperors [Col. 0561B] of this world had established and closed, so that the rivers, that is, the peoples, might not be allowed to come out to the roads along which the Gospel-chariots collided in the streets. Edicts hung publicly; laws and proscriptions were set forth on public tablets, decreeing that anyone who went out to evangelical faith and assumed the Christian name should undergo a capital sentence or any other sentence of death. This was the shutting up of the rivers, that is, of the peoples; these were the unopened gates and the iron bars of the gates.

The men of the Lord’s army, famous and illustrious men, did not wait for the gates of the rivers to open themselves, for the rulers of the peoples to grant permission to confess or proclaim Christ. They swiftly climbed Nineveh’s walls, steadfastly passed beyond the laws of the rulers of the age, and of their own accord brought in Christ’s name. They did not fail to know that this undertaking would be dangerous to their bodies; indeed, they preferred to gain souls at the cost of their bodies. As they climbed, they were seized, held, and brought before kings and judges; standing there, accused, they did not deny him; questioned, they confessed Christ; afflicted with diverse punishments and condemned to diverse deaths, some even, when roasted, gave thanks (2 Cor. 11).

There was great heat from the sun there; but “a shelter shall be prepared,” he says. For when those persecuting drivers mentioned above had been removed, the heat of persecution sometimes grew cool. For example, this occurred when Diocletian was expelled from power and Maximian died. “I announce to you,” said a distinguished martyr as he was dying, [Col. 0561D] “that peace has been restored to Christ’s Church: Diocletian has been expelled from power, and Maximian has died today.” This was the preparing of a shelter: he did not allow them to be tempted beyond what they were able to bear, nor for longer than they could bear it, but with the temptation also made a way out, that they might endure.

Why say more? The Holy Spirit commanded and said: “Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23). At last the gates of the rivers were opened, and the temple was torn down to the ground. The gates of the rivers, I say, were opened: the laws of the rulers were erased when the rulers who had written them against the Christian name died; and [Col. 0562A] the eternal gates were raised—the good gates, the just laws through which Christ, the King of glory, might enter: the laws of pious rulers, the enactments of Christian emperors.

Thus the temple was torn down to the ground: the worship of idolatry was destroyed. For when the gates were opened, the rivers burst forth. Harmful laws were removed and better laws given, which did not forbid but rather proclaimed that Christ should be worshipped. Peoples streamed eagerly together to the faith; adulterous Jupiter was abandoned with Juno, Venus, and all his shameful offspring; and the temples were destroyed or converted into churches of Christ.

Then the soldier was led away captive—with a good abduction, a blessed captivity—so that he who had been free from righteousness, had served this Nineveh, that is, this world, indeed even the devil, might become a slave of righteousness (Rom. 6) and serve God his Creator. And her maidservants were led along: that is, the humble or lowly people of the world were led before the chariot of Christ, the good captor mentioned above. Of such persons the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1).

This is not said because he chose the lowly in such a way that he did not wish to choose the noble. For both the soldier was led away captive and her maidservants were led along: that is, nobles and lowly persons alike, without respect of persons, were subjected to the service of Christ the victor. Rather, the Apostle says that at the beginning of the Gospel God did not first choose the noble, but the ignoble (ibid.). Why? “That no flesh may glory in his presence”: which would indeed have happened if the noble had first been called and the lowly then brought to Christ’s faith through them. [Col. 0562C]

What he immediately adds—“moaning like doves, murmuring in their hearts”—must be understood of both the soldier and the maidservants, that is, both nobles and lowly persons. But why moaning, and from what cause murmuring? Certainly not because they were led away captive or were led along before the chariot of this triumphal conqueror; rather, they moaned because they had been free from this Lord whom they had not known, and servants of Nineveh, that is, of this world. They murmured in their hearts—that is, reproached themselves in their consciences.

For “to murmur” is sometimes understood in a good sense, as there: “They shall roam about for food; if indeed they are not satisfied, they shall murmur” (Ps. 58). This [247] means: those who have been converted shall roam about for food, that is, to incorporate others into themselves by their preaching; and if they are not satisfied—that is, if their preaching does not bear fruit—they will complain and grieve. Therefore here also, when he says, “moaning like doves, murmuring in their hearts,” it is rightly understood as though he said: grieving and sorrowing over past sins, and, as has been said, reproaching themselves in their consciences.

For although by the grace of the victorious and triumphant one who leads them they know that they have been saved, they nevertheless do not forget what they were; and they do not cease grieving and lamenting this in their hearts. An example is the man who said—and still today confesses and says—“I am the least [Col. 0563A] of the apostles, not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15). Again: “Formerly I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1).

On such grounds they are rightly called moaning, not merely moaning in any fashion, but “moaning like doves.” For the dove has moaning in place of song; and for these persons it is very sweet thus to moan, so that when they sing something in praise of their captor—for example: “You ascended on high; you took captivity” (Ps. 67), or according to another translation, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4)—when, I say, they sing something of that kind, then at last they should know that they have sung rightly when the voices of those singing are frequently interrupted by the violent and intensely voluntary sobs of the soul, and tears are drawn from their eyes.

There are groanings like the groanings of the dove, which knows only how to sing by groaning or groan by singing. This is so sweet and pleasant that the Psalmist testifies: “My tears became my bread by day and night” (Ps. 41).

Where such captivity has been led away, what kind of Nineveh remains?
