He says: “And Nineveh—her waters are like a pool of waters; but they have fled. ‘Stand, stand!’ Yet there is none who turns back. ‘Plunder gold, plunder silver!’ Yet there is no end of wealth, above every desirable vessel.” These and the matters following, which are spoken against Nineveh, are such that you rightly understand what is said in the title of the prophecy: “The burden of Nineveh.” For Nineveh is a burden, that is, the condemnation of the universal multitude, the innumerable multitude, [Col. 0563C] in comparison with whose vast number those are few who have gone or are going out of Nineveh in the manner described above, who have left or are leaving the world condemned and to be condemned at the final judgment.

What kind of Nineveh is this; what kind does it remain; what kind is it to be found and judged? “Like a pool of waters,” he says. Although peoples are commonly understood by the name “waters,” nevertheless, since it follows, “there is no end of wealth,” abundance of possessions is more suitably understood. Nineveh is blamed; the world is blamed; and Nineveh is accused of covetousness when it is said, “like a pool of waters,” that is, an insatiable receptacle of riches, on account of which it despised God.

“Her waters,” he says. What are “her waters”? He seems to have made an ellipsis, that is, an omission of expression. Grammarians call an ellipsis a defect of expression in which necessary words are lacking, as in “to whom a quiver of gold”: “was” is missing. This is not unusual in the divine Scriptures, as in the Psalm: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains” (Ps. 74). For there is missing: “an escape-route is plainly open.” And in the Gospel: “If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before” (John 6).

Thus here too, when he says, “and her [waters],” necessary words are absent. What they should be is gathered from what follows: “but they have fled.” For this makes it understood that he means: the waters of Nineveh—that is, the riches of the ungodly and their glory or pleasures, everything that is in the world, the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes, all things under the sun—remain [Col. 0564A] here and do not follow them when they die, according to the saying: “When the rich man dies, he shall not take everything, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48). Here, I say, these things remain; “but they have fled.” What does “they have fled” mean? They have died quickly.

“Fool,” God says, “this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?” (Luke 12). The Holy Spirit of Scripture elegantly customarily calls the brevity of human life a flight, as there: “Man comes forth like a flower and is cut down, and flees like a shadow” (Job 14). Again: “My days were swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good” (Job 9).

Therefore the waters of Nineveh are very unfaithful, for they do not follow their lover. Conversely, concerning the good waters, which are not the waters of pools or cisterns but living waters of springs, it is surely clear that they are believers. They do not leave their possessor or lover when he dies, but go with him and follow him to the heights, and there as he passes onward. “This man,” says another prophet, “shall dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks shall be his height; bread is given to him; his waters are faithful” (Isa. 33).

Yet in a marvellous manner, because he had said, “but they have fled,” that is, they passed swiftly from this life naked and carrying nothing with them, he calls out to them, in a marvellous manner and with hostile mockery: “Stand, stand; plunder gold, plunder silver.” For how great and hostile a mockery it is to cry to those fleeing—whom the whirlwind of death carries away wholly against their will—“Stand, stand!” And how much more bitter it is to say, “Plunder gold, plunder silver,” than to say, “You plundered gold, you plundered silver,” although even this would be bitter enough to say in their flight.

“Stand, stand,” he says, and immediately adds: “Yet there is none who turns back.” “Plunder,” he says, “gold; plunder silver,” and immediately attaches: “There is no end of wealth, above every desirable vessel.” By these words their insatiable greed is proclaimed. This rebuke is exceedingly forceful and surpasses all the lofty diction of worldly rhetoricians: under the name of Nineveh the Holy Spirit, the holy Paraclete, rebukes the world for sin in this prophet of his name, adding further: “Devastated, torn apart, and mangled; a melting heart, weak knees, failure in every loins, and the faces of all like the blackness of a pot.”

It was too little to rebuke the sin of greed alone, unless he also rebuked the totality of evils of which greed is, indeed, the root. In seven resounding expressions—the number by which totality is customarily signified—he forcefully proclaims all the evils that follow greed and of which it is itself the root. First he calls it devastated; second, torn apart; third, mangled; fourth, with a melting heart; fifth, weak in the knees; sixth, failing in all the loins; seventh, with the faces of all like the blackness of a pot.

It is devastated by inconstant action; torn apart by the opposition of sects and hatreds alike; mangled by the continual recurrence of mutual robberies and killings; it has a melting heart through the sorrow of envy; weak knees through the weakness of distrust; failure in all its loins, so that there is no virtue of self-control. For as much as it swelled in pride, so much did it flow into lust. The last thing he placed—“the faces of all like the blackness of a pot”—is the same as saying that all have become like the devil.

For the Lord speaks to Jeremiah: “What do you see?” “I see,” he says, “a boiling pot, and its face from the face of the north.” And the Lord said [248] to me: “From the north evil shall be opened over all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1). A boiling pot retains from the fire itself an enduring blackness, very far unlike gold or silver, which comes out of the fire with a greater and more brilliant purity. Thus the devil and his entire city, this whole world lying in the evil one (1 John 5), become worse from their very evils, greatly unlike the City of God, which appears more beautiful when it is refined in the fire of tribulation, like gold or silver which, as has already been said, shines more brightly when tested by fire.

Who can enumerate the calamities of the wretched world, which he proclaimed in these few—namely, seven—expressions? There are histories; divine and secular books are read that recount these evils and the causes of evils: the four passions of the soul—pain or sorrow, fear, joy, and hope. From these four passions, as the secular writers too hold, arise the evils of this world. These passions are indicated here, as is fitting, by the descriptions when, after stating the preceding evils—“devastated, torn apart, and mangled”—he adds these four: “a melting heart, weak knees, failure in every loins, and the faces of all like the blackness of a pot.”

For what is a melting heart but sadness, pain, or envy? Weakness of the knees, moreover, is fear of this age; and whoever has that fear is undoubtedly weak in the knees for every work of virtue. The joy of the age is especially in the loins; accordingly, by “failure in every loins” we understand insatiable pleasures. The hope of the world was not in the world but in demons and in the demons’ *thecae*, that is, images (idols). Since it is written of these: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113), we rightly understand here also: “the faces of all like the blackness of a pot,” that is, they are like the one in whom they hope, in whom they trust—the blackened devil, [Col. 0565D] the prince of darkness.

Who, reading those histories—indeed, those grim and bloody tragedies—would not shudder and marvel that the world still stands? Yet there is an evil of this world which he has not yet mentioned: an evil worse than all evils, an evil which convicted this guilty world and removed all excuse concerning every evil. What is this evil? Surely that it does not receive the Saviour, the Son of God, who comes to it.

As the Holy Spirit is about to declare this evil, he marvellously changes his voice, because this evil is unlike the other evils; and therefore, changing his voice, as if in a judicial proceeding, he asks with judicial majesty by crying out, and cries out by asking: “Where is the dwelling-place of the lions, and the pasture of the lion-cubs? To where went the lion, that the lion-cub might enter there, and there was none to terrify him? The lion seized enough for his cubs, and killed for his lionesses, and filled his caves with prey and his lair with plunder.”

According to the letter, this is said concerning Nineveh: the palace of the nobles was the dwelling-place of kings, to which the lion, the king of Babylon—that is, Nebuchadnezzar—went, together with each of his lesser kings, the lion-cubs; and there was no one to resist them.

According to the anagogical sense, concerning the lion who came into this world, we state with reservation what we think. Since our elders understood this lion to be the devil, we prefer to understand as that lion, as that lion-cub, the one of whom the patriarch Jacob said: “Judah is a lion-cub; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you lay down as a lion and as a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49). For he alone is truly that lion whom no one can terrify; and he filled his caves with prey and his lair with plunder, because: “From the prey, my son, you have ascended”; and he himself says of himself: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12).

Therefore, since up to this point the world is rebuked for sin under the name of Nineveh, when it says, “And Nineveh is like a pool of waters,” and the rest, it seems fitting to us to understand that it is rebuked for righteousness when it says: “To where went the lion, that he might enter there”—where one must supply, “and he was not received by Nineveh,” that is, by this world. For herein is the righteousness of God: that, according to the truth of his promise made to the fathers, Christ came into this world. When this occurred, God the truthful one was justified in his words; and the world is rebuked for this righteousness because it did not receive it.

For let us follow the sequence of what is said. “Where,” he says, “is the dwelling-place of lions and the pasture of lion-cubs?” Though there are or were many dwelling-places of Nineveh—that is, many cities of this world—which deserved to be called dwelling-places or pastures of lions, lion-cubs, bears, leopards, and every kind of wild beast, nevertheless we gladly understand one dwelling-place of lions and one pasture of lion-cubs to be sought here by name, so that the dwelling-place itself is certainly named, and it is not unknown what the lions and lion-cubs did, or who they were, or when they lived.

For we judge that it was Jerusalem which was rightly called, or should be called, Nineveh for the same reason that it is called Sodom and Egypt, as we have in the Apocalypse: “Their bodies,” he says, “shall lie in the street of the great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified” (Rev. 11). For the same reason, I say, it is called Nineveh: for it was itself the world which rejoiced when the Lord was crucified, as he said to his disciples: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16).

When did the lion, or lion-cub, go to it, to enter there? Surely when he descended from heaven and the Word of God was made flesh from that people: the lion and lion-cub, that is, the mightiest God and the Son of the mightiest God. He went to enter there, but it did not wish this; hence he says to it: “How often I wished to gather [Col. 0567A] your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23).

The great strength of this lion or lion-cub is briefly proclaimed when it says, “and there was none to terrify him.” For he alone could say: “The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 12). How did this lion seize enough for his cubs and kill for his lionesses? How did he fill his caves with prey and his lair with plunder? “From the prey,” he says, “my son, you have ascended”: that is, you were lifted up on the cross, shattered and despoiled hell, and, invading as the stronger one the court of that armed strong man, you plundered all his weapons in which he trusted and distributed the spoils (Luke 11).

Therefore the lion seized enough for his cubs, that is, Christ himself did so for his apostles or preachers. By dying and giving them the Holy Spirit, he gave them power and opened a way for them to carry out throughout the whole world the ministry of that same seizure or despoiling. He seized enough, I say, because none of those called saints according to his purpose (Rom. 8) has been or will be lacking; none at all is lacking whom he who foreknew and predestined them to be conformed to himself (ibid.) calls, justifies, and glorifies.

But how did he “kill for his lionesses,” or for which lionesses? Surely there is one lioness and many lionesses belonging to him: his one lioness is the Church, and his many lionesses are the particular churches throughout the world. Whoever is incorporated into them is killed in the manner signified when the Spirit said to Peter: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 10). This is the prey with which he filled his caves, and this [249] is the plunder with which he filled his lair: his caves, I say, meaning the many dwelling-places in his Father’s house; and his lair, meaning the paradise of delights.

There he deposited his prey; there he placed his plunder: truly just prey, and plunder seized with judgment, because he did not prey upon or plunder what belonged to another, but rightly restored to himself what was his and had been unjustly taken away.

Who can adequately sense, as it deserves and as the matter itself stands, the sharpness of this interrogation, when he cries out for this reason: “Where is,” he says, “the dwelling-place of lions and the pasture of their lion-cubs?” With what intention do we think “where is” is said here? “Where is” is used in two ways. At one time, when someone is sought in order to be reproved, as when the Lord sought Adam and said: “Where are you?” (Gen. 3). At another time, when someone is sought in order to show that he no longer exists, as Job says: “Though the pride of the ungodly rises to heaven and his head touches the clouds, in the end he shall perish like dung, and those who saw him shall say: ‘Where is he?’ Like a flying dream they shall not be found” (Job 20).

Whichever of these two senses is intended here in “Where now is the dwelling-place of lions?”, it greatly pertains to the matter which we have set forth. Nevertheless, since we have already said that Nahum means “Comforter,” and that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, stands in this: to rebuke the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, it is more pleasing to understand that, in saying “where is,” that dwelling-place of lions and pasture of lion-cubs is sought because, when they saw the lion already mentioned coming to enter there—the lion from the tribe of Judah, Christ—as a lamb, they received him wickedly as lions and lion-cubs. “They received me,” he says, “like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion-cub dwelling in secret places” (Ps. 16).

Those lions were the chief priests, and the lion-cubs were the Pharisees. The dwelling-place of lions was the city of Jerusalem; the pasture of lions was the rich temple. There they made prey of the people; and for the same reason that place was the pasture of lion-cubs, just as it was rightly called—and was—that house “a den of thieves” (Luke 19).

And indeed, where the world is rebuked, the rebuke rightly begins from that such dwelling-place [Col. 0568B] of lions, because the lion who came into this world—the lion from the tribe of Judah, Christ, of whom we have spoken—offered that dwelling-place his bodily presence, so that he might first enter there and repentance and remission of sins then be preached in his name to all nations (Acts 13). Foolish lions and stupid lion-cubs, who supposed that by killing him they could turn aside his purpose! For by dying he seized enough for his cubs, as has already been said; and from the dwelling-place of lions itself he seized so sufficiently that none of all those whom he wished to have was lacking. “As many as had been ordained to eternal life believed,” Luke says (ibid.).

Therefore that dwelling-place of lions had first to be rebuked, as has been said, and made an example of the destruction of the world, or of the judgment by which the world is to be judged through fire. This is what he immediately did after seeking it out: with that dwelling-place of lions as if standing there accused, he pronounced this sentence: “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall burn your chariots to smoke; the sword shall devour your lion-cubs; I shall cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers shall no longer be heard.”

This sentence came long ago upon that dwelling-place, and the whole world heard its outcome. “Behold, I am against you,” says the Lord of hosts. Who is this Lord of hosts who says these things, except the lion who, as has been said, went to the city to which he speaks? For he himself is the Lord of hosts; and he fittingly now calls himself the Lord of hosts when he says: “Behold, I am against you”—supply, “I come with the army of the Romans.”

For not only armies of angels are mine, but also armies of men: armies of all nations serve me, even when they do not know it, and do my will when nation rises against nation and kingdom against kingdom. In a marvellous way, by my just judgments, they serve with an intention not just but utterly unjust. “Behold, I am against you,” I say: no longer as a lamb, as formerly in the abundance of mercy, but as a lion with his armies, with the Roman armies, in wrath and righteous fury. Thus “behold, I shall come against you, and burn your chariots to smoke, and the sword shall devour your lion-cubs.” This I shall do by the hands [Col. 0569A] of my armies, by the hands of the Romans.

“Your chariots”—that is, your pride, your cities, all the instruments of your pride, and the temple itself, the chief chariot of your exaltation—I shall burn to smoke. That is, not so that the fire is extinguished and something half-burned remains, as commonly happens when help comes running together and the blaze is quenched before it devours all; rather, after all is consumed and the fire is dying for lack of material, the remains will turn into ashes and smoke, according to the example of Sodom. Of Sodom it is written: “Abraham rose early in the morning, to the place where he had previously stood with the Lord; he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of that region, and saw ashes rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace” (Gen. 19).

Just as there was no one to extinguish Sodom, and no one for whose sake God should spare that region, after Lot went out with his people, so there will be no one to extinguish you when I set you ablaze—you to whom I went and from whom I departed. You shall burn to ashes and smoke; then the sword shall devour your lion-cubs, that is, the children who are in you shall fall by the edge of the sword, and those who remain shall be led captive among all nations (Luke 21).

“I shall cut off your prey from the earth.” What prey of yours, except your house—formerly my house—which, though it ought to have been called and to be a house of prayer, you made a den of thieves (Luke 21)? That prey of yours I shall cut off so entirely that it will not exist: “there shall not remain one stone [Col. 0570A] upon another which will not be destroyed” (Luke 21).

“And the voice of your messengers,” he says, “shall no longer be heard.” By messengers, whom in Greek we call *angeloi* (“angels”), we understand priests, according to that saying in Malachi: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). The voice of messengers or angels of this kind was once heard, because priests offered sacrifices for the people, prayed, and were heard. But hereafter, he says, their voice will not be heard, and neither prayers nor sacrifices from their hands will be received.

Hence he speaks in Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I shall not hear, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1). Accordingly, when he says “the voice of your messengers,” it must likewise be understood: “and no longer of my messengers.” For formerly the priests of that temple, like its prophets, were called and were messengers of the Lord. Concerning priests, the example has already been given: “the lips of the priest” (Mal. 2), etc. Concerning prophets, moreover, there is this example or testimony: “And Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, said among the messengers of the Lord” (Hag. 1), etc.

Formerly, I say, the priests and prophets of that temple were called angels or messengers of the Lord; but since that city or people denied Christ before Pilate’s face, they are no longer messengers of the Lord. Therefore he deliberately says, “the voice of your messengers,” and “not now mine” must be understood.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0569]

[Col. 0569C] 250 In the Gospel of Christ, in which, the Apostle says, “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of those men who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom. I)—of whom, under the name Nineveh, we understand in this prophet the whole body—it is a great and evident testimony to the truth that, as we have shown in what precedes, the Jews were the first to undergo the manifest judgment of that same wrath. Christ is true, and the Apostle of Christ truthful, in whom Christ had long since been speaking. “Upon those,” he says, “who are contentious and do not yield to the truth, but believe unrighteousness, [there shall be] wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that works evil” (Rom. II); and immediately adding, “of the Jew first, and also of the Greek” (ibid.).

As he had foretold, as he had set down beforehand—“of the Jew first”—so it came to pass. For since the Jew and the Greek, or the Jew and the Gentile, doing evil, are the world condemned and yet to be condemned, the Jew was the first already to undergo his share of condemnation; so that there is now no doubt, nor ought there to be any, that the Greek also is subject to it, since at the end of the age both alike will be judged. We judge this to be of very great importance for elucidating this prophecy: namely, that in the remaining matters which follow, unquestionably [Col. 0570C] proclaiming wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of man that works evil, we should always keep in mind that saying: “of the Jew first, and also of the Greek.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER III.

Woe to the city of blood, wholly full of the rending of falsehood; plunder will not depart from you. O city of blood, city of the devil, opposed to the city of God! “Upon every soul of a human being who does evil, upon the Jew first and also upon the Greek.” Woe to you for this very reason, that you are a city of blood: because you have shed blood and have been built in bloodshed. You first, O every soul of the Jew doing evil, are a city of blood more than every soul of the Greek, since by killing Christ you filled up the measure of your fathers, who killed the prophets and the righteous, [Col. 0570D] so that upon you might come all righteous blood which has been shed, from the blood of righteous Abel onward (Matt. 23).

Woe to you, because you are a city of blood—not only, as has already been said, in the manner of the soul of a Greek or a Gentile, but more abundantly; for the Greek or Gentile who shed the blood of martyrs did not have the Law and did not know the promises. You, possessing the Law, hearing the promises and the prophets, killed both the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself. And indeed every [Col. 0571A] city is full of the rending of falsehood; but you, the soul of the Jew, more abundantly than the soul of the Greek. For the Greek soul in many matters held down God’s truth in unrighteousness, or exchanged it for a lie; and, though it knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks. But you both saw and hated Truth itself, born from your own flesh; you surrounded it with lies and, on the pretext of a lie, handed it over to death.

I do not say, “a city full of falsehood,” but, what is more, “full of the rending of falsehood.” For not every Greek lies in one way, since falsehood itself is split and torn among him into many sects; nor does every Jew lie about the holy Scriptures in one way, but now invents one thing and now another, in order to escape whenever some vigorous soldier of truth—who is Christ—pursues him. [Col. 0571B]

Woe to you, because plunder will not depart from you; that is, the guilt of rapacity or avarice will be forgiven you. It has proved for you the root of all evils and the cause of murderers, for which things you will be called—and truly are—the city of blood.

“The sound of the whip, and the sound of the rushing wheel, and of the neighing horse, and of the jolting chariot, of the horseman mounting, and of the flashing sword, and of the glittering spear, and of a multitude slain, and of a heavy ruin; and there is no end of corpses.”

“According to the Hebrew,” says blessed Jerome, “the description of an army preparing itself for battle is so beautiful and like a picture that all my speech is inferior.” [Note: [Col. 0571D] *Commentary on Nahum*, chapter 3.] Whatever that Babylonian army may have been, however terrible—the army which overthrew Nineveh at that time—it can bear no comparison with the greatness of the power, wrath, indignation, anguish, and tribulation which will come upon the whole world on the day of the universal judgment. It is toward this that the spirit of prophecy tends, and the purpose of the present discourse strives to follow. [Col. 0571C]

“The sound,” he says, “of the whip; the sound of the rushing wheel.” Where did this man hear the sound which he mentions? Without doubt he heard it within: in the inner human being, where there are—or ought to be—ears for hearing the mysteries of God’s kingdom, such as the Lord required when he cried to the crowds: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13).

There are seven sounds on the victorious side: the sound of the whip; the sound of the rushing wheel; the sound of the neighing horse; the sound of the jolting chariot; the sound of the horseman [Col. 0571D] mounting; the sound of the flashing sword; and the sound of the glittering spear. For what follows—“a multitude slain,” “a heavy ruin,” and “there is no end of corpses”—belongs to the misery of the afflicted side.

By this sevenfold number of sounds we understand the totality of the upheavals which will precede the destruction of great Nineveh, that is, of this world, according to those words of truth which cannot pass away: “There will be signs in sun and moon and stars,” and so forth, down to: “for the powers of the heavens will be shaken” (Luke 21).

And since we have already said, following the Apostle, that wrath is coming “upon every soul doing evil, upon the Jew first and also upon the Greek” (Rom. 2), it now aptly returns to mind [Col. 0572A] that, as Josephus relates, the Jew heard voices so many times when he was about to receive the firstfruits of condemnation—that is, when the Romans were to come for the destruction of Jerusalem:

“Jesus,” he says, “son of Aman, a commoner and a rustic,” having come to the feast day four years before the war began, suddenly began to cry out: ‘A voice from the East, a voice from the West, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the Temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against all this people.’” The seventh voice, repeated most continuously, was: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem!”

By whatever spirit that man, struck with amazement, proclaimed those voices, we understand by the sevenfold number of both those voices and these voices that the totality of evils or [Col. 0572B] miseries is signified: there, first for the Jew; here, equally for Jew and Greek; miseries which will then come upon the whole world.

God will not, indeed, use horses and chariots and the other instruments of war proclaimed here in order to judge this world. But, as is just, since this proud and bloody world sinned through such things, those terrors by which it will be judged are proclaimed under the names of the same things. In this sense we also understand the saying: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 20). Likewise it is fitting to say: All who, abusing their power, have wielded the whip, the rushing wheel, the neighing horse, the jolting chariot, the mounting horseman, the flashing sword, and the glittering spear—or brandished and poised them—especially against those who belong to the Lord God, will perish beneath the inundating whip, the rushing wheel, the neighing horse, the jolting chariot, the mounting horseman, the flashing sword, and the glittering spear. They themselves will lie slain and crushed by a heavy ruin; [Col. 0572C] nor will there be an end of corpses, because they will be corpses for eternity, since, dead by eternal death, they will lack without end the true life, which is God.

It follows: “And they will fall among their bodies, because of the multitude of the prostitutions of the beautiful and pleasing harlot, who possesses sorceries, who sold nations through her prostitutions and families through her sorceries.”

“They will fall among their bodies,” he says: namely, before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge, at whose coming all human beings must rise with their bodies and fall into hell—all the ungodly with the very [Col. 0572D] bodies in which they sinned. For what reason? “Because of the multitude,” he says, “of the prostitutions of the beautiful and pleasing harlot, who possesses sorceries.” Who is that harlot? Covetousness. For what other harlot can be called or imagined, with whom this world, departing from its Creator, has committed fornication?

She is the one who, adorned with many beautiful instruments of created things, has deceived the unhappy world in many ways through the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes, so as to make it serve the creature rather than the Creator. For she appears beautiful and pleasing to the corrupted eyes and ambitious minds of those who refuse to consider or weigh [Col. 0573A] how much more beautiful God may be, the Creator and Lord of all things.

This harlot also has sorceries: namely, the snares of evil spirits mingled with her pleasure. For example, evil spirits so attach themselves to beautiful things of gold or silver that, hiding in images and giving answers, they have filled the world with the belief that works of human hands—images of gold or silver—are gods. Thus this harlot sold nations through her prostitutions and families through her sorceries; for through the drunkenness of covetousness it came about that human souls, so delighted by the beauty of gold and silver, prostituted themselves to images.

She sold not only nations but also families in such prostitutions or sorceries: that is, not only those who did not know God and had not heard his name through any Scripture, but even those who had received the Law and thus were in some fashion members of the household of God the Creator. She very often made them commit fornication with her, as almost all the divine books testify everywhere:

“Behold, I am against you,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will uncover your private parts before your face, and I will show the nations your nakedness and kingdoms your disgrace. [Col. 0573B] I will cast your abominations upon you, disgrace you with insults, and make you an example. Everyone who sees you will recoil from you and say: ‘Nineveh has been laid waste.’”

Above he had said: “Behold, I am against you,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will burn your chariots up into smoke”; and now the Lord says: “Behold, I am against you, and I will uncover your private parts before your face.” There he rebukes the pride; here, the luxury of this world—evils which are chief in the perversion of the whole human being, because pride exalts the spirit and luxury corrupts the flesh.

“I will uncover,” he says, “your private parts before your face.” The same is expressed in the Psalm: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49). For now, through the pride of your mind, you disdain to see or know what kind, or how great, is the stain of your shame. You are not ashamed to follow insatiable luxury and passive lust; and even if you see it, it does not shame you. Rather, “you rejoice when you have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2); and “you proclaim your sin like Sodom and do not hide it” (Isa. 3). [Col. 0573C]

Then, certainly, when the greatness of tribulation and anguish leaves you no leisure to be so proud, rejoice so, and exult so, the naked consciousness of shame will appear more clearly upon your face—in your eyes, in unceasing memory, as though in a book always open—so that you will always be compelled to read whatever you did, said, or considered in your mind. Nor will I uncover your private parts only to you, O every soul of a human being doing evil, whether Jew or Greek; no, not to you alone will I uncover them in the manner already described. Rather, “I will show the nations your nakedness and kingdoms your disgrace.”

To which nations and kingdoms, and for what purpose, will I show them your nakedness and disgrace? Certainly to every nation which I have made, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “They will come and worship before you, and glorify your name” (Ps. 86). I will show them for this purpose: that, seeing the cause of [Col. 0574A] your condemnation, they may also know the praise due to judgment, or to the justice of the Judge; and, knowing it, may say:

“Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages. Who will not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name? For you alone are holy; for all nations will come and worship before you, because your judgments have been made manifest” (Rev. 15).

Again: “Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just; because he has judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth by her great prostitution” (Rev. 19).

So that they may say this, or know how to say it, I will show them your nakedness; “I will cast your abominations upon you and disgrace you with insults”—understand, with your own insults—“and make you an example,” so that they may take from you material or instruction for divine praise, [Col. 0574B] and may always recognize in you the proof of God’s just severity, or severe justice.

But how will everyone who sees you recoil from you and, recoiling, say: “Nineveh has been laid waste”? Namely, because a great chasm will be fixed between you and everyone not held with you in your destruction; and he will be very glad that he can recoil from you and cannot cross to you even for an hour to offer any consolation. For when he has said, “Nineveh has been laid waste,” he will add nothing further, nor join himself to you by any word or taste of comfort.

For it follows: “Who will shake his head over you? From where shall I seek a comforter for you?” Shaking the head is sometimes understood as mockery and sometimes as consolation. As mockery, as there: “I became a reproach to my enemies; they saw me and shook their heads” (Ps. 109). Again: “They mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their head” (Ps. 22). These things were foretold of the passing-by people who blasphemed the crucified Lord, shaking their heads (Matt. 27). [Col. 0574C]

But as consolation, as in Job: “Then all his brothers and all his sisters came to him, and all who had known him before; they ate with him, shook their heads over him, and comforted him” (Job 42). The context distinguishes whether the shaking of the head is that of comforters or of mockers. When he had said here, “Who will shake his head over you?” he immediately added, “From where shall I seek a comforter for you?” Therefore, “Who will shake his head over you?” is the same as saying: Who will have compassion on you? Who will comfort you? And it must be understood: no one.

Again, when he says, “From where shall I seek a comforter for you?”, that response which Abraham gave to the burning rich man aptly returns to mind. What he said to one must be understood as said to all: From where shall I seek a way of access for you, so that I may send Lazarus to cool your tongue? (Luke 16). “In all things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can any cross from there to us.” Therefore, there is no place from which I can seek a comforter for you: all the time of your consolation has passed. You received good things; you received consolation in your life. [Col. 0574D]

It follows: “Are you better than populous Alexandria, who dwell among rivers, with water around her, whose wealth is the sea, whose waters are her walls? Ethiopia was her strength, and Egypt; Africa and Libya were her strength, and were helps to you. Yet she herself also will be carried away into exile, led into captivity. Her little ones have been dashed to pieces at the head of every street; lots will be cast for her illustrious men, and all her nobles will be bound with fetters.”

At the time when this prophecy was written, the city now called Alexandria was called No; much later it received its name from Alexander the Great of Macedon. Under its earlier name, No, it was the metropolis of Egypt and was always exceedingly populous. Indeed, those who committed the deeds of Alexandria to memory assert that it was the foremost city. Thus it is said to Nineveh: Are you more populous or more powerful than Alexandria? The situation of Alexandria is described: situated upon the Nile and the sea, it is surrounded on both sides by waters and rivers. [Col. 0575A] The very position of the provinces and city shows that Ethiopia, Egypt, and Africa were its defense.

This city also, says the prophet, will be taken by the king of Babylon and led into captivity (Jer. 38). Her little ones will be dashed to pieces at the head of every street, and her illustrious men or nobles will be allotted by the lot of the victors for fetters. Are you better than she? No: you also, therefore, will be made drunk and despised, and you will seek help from an enemy—understand, just as she did, by a just judgment.

By this comparison or parallel between Nineveh and Alexandria, the spirit of prophecy suggests a comparison between those manifestly opposed to God, such as the Assyrians then were, and those entangled in the business of the age, such as the Alexandrians especially were; yet they do not blaspheme God by the public profession of their faith, but even profess to know God. Appropriately, then, “Alexandria of peoples” may be understood as those who are neither so impious that they can be judged by the Church as already condemned before God, nor so attentive to the religion which they profess that they deserve to be called Judah or Jerusalem. [Col. 0575B]

Therefore, if Nineveh—that is, the condemned world—complains at the final judgment concerning the sentence of its condemnation, the question is asked: “Are you better than populous Alexandria?” The sense is: Would you, the whole company of the ungodly, justly escape unpunished, when even the multitude which did nothing against God with you—the multitude living a secular life, yet not attacking God’s truth by force—has borne, or will bear, a judgment deserved by its merits, because it gave excessive attention to the stormy business of the age?

This is according to the likeness of Alexandria, which is as busy as it is populous; it dwells among rivers and has waters round about it which serve as walls for its defense. From Ethiopia, Egypt, and Africa many riches are more conveniently carried to it, so that its wealth can be called a sea. Very many such persons are contained within the boundaries of that which is called Jerusalem; and although each, according to his own merits, is or has been there, some are punished temporarily and some even eternally, according to [Col. 0575C] the likeness of populous Alexandria, whose little ones, it says, are dashed to pieces at the head of every street, and whose illustrious men or nobles are afflicted with fetters.

This is the basis and meaning of what the Apostle Peter said when, after saying, “For it is time that judgment begin with the household of God” (1 Pet. 4), he immediately added: “But if it begins with us first, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?” (ibid.). Along with him, according to the present passage of this prophecy, let us say: If, by God’s judgment, the violence of persecution has very often fallen upon the house of the Lord because, when they ought to have been attentive to spiritual things, they pursued carnal things instead and became worldly—though on account of the name of faith they were in almost every respect like profit-seeking Alexandrians—what will be the end of those who do not believe at all and contradict God’s Gospel both in word and deed, being in every respect like the proud and ungodly Assyrians? [Col. 0576A]

And since we have already mentioned the rich man clothed in purple and the beggar Lazarus, who were set forth as two examples for the whole human race: if Lazarus, known to God by name, was not allowed to go unpunished but received evil things in his life, what must your end be, O rich man, who are both unknown to God by name and received good things in your life? Are you better or more righteous than Lazarus, so that Lazarus should now be comforted with one simple consolation, because while he lived he had no consolation in that life, while you should be comforted with a double consolation: both having been clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day, and now receiving cooling for your tongue from Lazarus’s finger dipped in water? (Luke 16). The order and justice of God’s judgment is not so arranged.

Therefore you too will be made drunk, O Nineveh, of which that rich man is an example: “You will be made drunk,” he says, “with wormwood and gall” (Jer. 23). “And you will be despised, and you will seek help from an enemy.” [Col. 0576B] Namely, just as that man sought help from Lazarus, whom he had made his enemy. Lazarus first sought help from an enemy, lying at the rich man’s gate and desiring to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table—certainly an enemy, because he was unwilling even to give crumbs. In return, afterward the rich man sought help from Lazarus, who was justly not his friend, and did not obtain it.

According to their example, O Nineveh, O world wholly given over to avarice and pride: many who must be carried into Abraham’s bosom often seek, and have sought, help from you in some necessity. Not only have they not obtained help, but they have even found punishment with you. It is perfectly clear that they sought help from an enemy: from you, who hate them and oppose God. Recompense will be rendered to you in return, so that you too will seek help from an enemy—that is, from everyone whom you unjustly made your enemy by persecuting him—and will not obtain it. Rather, it will be said to you: “Remember that you received good things in your life, and this man or that man likewise evil things. [Col. 0576C] Now therefore he is comforted here, but you are tormented” (Luke 16).

“All your fortifications are like fig trees with their first figs: if shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the eater.”

If you look to that Nineveh which Nebuchadnezzar overthrew, the expression is hyperbolic. For Nineveh’s fortifications—its walls, towers, or towns—did not yield so easily to the Babylonians that they could be compared, in their fall, to early figs which, when shaken by a light touch, fall into the mouth of the devourer. But concerning this whole world, it will happen just as it is said, or as the letter sounds. Most easily, just as the fruit of such fig trees is shaken down by a slight motion—and not onto the ground, so that the eaters might at least have some small effort, but immediately into the devourer’s mouth—so on the day of judgment, when “our God will come openly and will not keep silence,” when “fire will blaze before him and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49), the fortifications of the whole world will fall in a great earthquake: whatever and of whatever kind they are, whether spiritual or material; both those of which Cain was the first builder (Gen. 4), and those which every spirit of error has constructed against the truth. They will fall into the mouth of devouring hell, the swallowing abyss, the fire of Gehenna. [Col. 0577A]

It follows: “Behold, your people are women in your midst.” This too, as the literal text sounds, must truly be understood of the Assyrians. For though they had previously been strong and terrible men, in the end they became like women—especially the kings of the Assyrians, who ought above all to have been men. The last king among them, as Pompeius Trogus relates, was Sardanapalus, a man more corrupt than a woman.

When Arbactus, his prefect and commander over the Medes, obtained admission to see him—with great effort and ambition, since no one before him had been permitted it—he found him among a troop of prostitutes, carding purple wool. Clothed as a woman, he surpassed all women in bodily softness and wantonness of eyes, distributing skeins of yarn among maidens. This was at that time the first cause of the destruction of the Assyrian empire. “Behold, therefore,” he says, “your people are women in your midst.” And immediately he adds: “Your gates will be opened wide to your enemies; fire will devour your bars.” [Col. 0577B]

That this is spoken reproachfully of this world is clear from contrast with the praise above, by which he commended the men of the heavenly Rider: “The shield of his mighty men is fiery; the men of his army are in scarlet; the reins of his chariots are fiery” (Nahum 2). These are men. To these the gates of this Nineveh will be opened wide, when the Lord comes to judgment with the elders of his people; and the people of Nineveh, women in her midst, will be captured and carried away into eternal captivity. Then fire will devour your bars, O Nineveh, because the age will be judged by fire and will be unable to resist.

It follows: “Draw water for yourself for the siege; strengthen your fortifications; go into the mud and tread the clay; grasp the brick. There fire will consume you; you will perish by the sword; the locust-grub will devour you. Gather yourself like the locust-grub; multiply yourself like the locust. You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven.”

With respect to that Nineveh, this must be understood literally. The siege is near. Therefore draw water, and take care that the besieged city does not lack drink. Fortify the towers; make bricks, so that you may rebuild the breaches in the walls. And when you have done all these things, you will be devoured by the sword as the earth is by the locust-grub. But though you have multiplied like the locust-grub and, like the locust, gathered together, and amassed [Col. 0577C] your riches like the stars of heaven, you will be scattered and flee—as locusts, locust-grubs, and the small offspring of locusts called *atelebi*, when warmed by the sun, fly away and cannot be found.

For this is the nature of locusts: stiffened by cold, they fly about through warmth. The *atelebus* is a small locust, between a locust and a locust-grub. With small wings it crawls more than it flies and always remains in one place; for this reason, wherever it appears, it consumes everything down to the dust, because it cannot depart before its wings have grown. Thus far, then.

But when I consider the present chapter in my mind and look within, I first confess that I am terrified by the force of its sayings and can scarcely bear the meaning which meets me, because of its weight. Then I say that those are blessed who have not begotten children, remembering likewise the Lord himself saying: “For behold, days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed’” (Luke 23). The madness of the world rebuked in this passage is so great, and the gravity of the matter rebuked by the Holy Spirit is so great, that speech long hesitates, overcome by amazement and not knowing by what expression to break forth. [Col. 0578A]

Therefore I wish to recite the entire chapter again: “Draw water for yourself for the siege; strengthen your fortifications; go into the mud and tread the clay; grasp the brick. There fire will consume you; you will perish by the sword; the locust-grub will devour you. Gather yourself like the locust-grub; multiply yourself like the locust. You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven.”

Where will the discourse begin? From what point shall we seek an entrance into explanation? I wish first to begin with the statement: “You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven.” For once we have entered through this part, the rest will become clearer.

What, then, is the meaning of “You have made your trading more numerous, O Nineveh, O world—of which Nineveh was then, as it were, the head—than the stars of heaven,” except: You have made your generations more numerous than those ever appointed to be called saints according to God’s purpose, who are all stars of heaven? Truly, you have made your trading more numerous, trading in the commerce of the flesh through an unhappy commerce, so that you may be gathered like a locust-grub and multiplied like a locust; and the littleness of this locust-grub or locust is far indeed from the dignity of heaven’s stars. [Col. 0578B]

Only the number and order of the stars of heaven belong to the purpose of the Creator, who blessed the first male and female and said: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it” (Gen. 1). The gathering or multiplication by which you are gathered like a locust-grub and multiplied like a locust does not arise from the grace of that blessing, but from the wrath and unhappiness of sin: from the wrath of the same Creator, who said to the woman after sin had taken effect, because of the guilt of transgression: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3).

And what does “I will multiply” mean except “I will permit you to be multiplied by a just judgment”? For you, O Nineveh—you, I say, O world—do not desire to generate for me; you do not wish to make children for me, nor intend to fashion from your flesh stars of heaven for me. Instead, devoting yourself to your pleasures and ambitiously desiring only to multiply upon earth, you go—and will obstinately and intemperately go—into the mud; you tread—and will tread—while kneading; and you will grasp the brick. [Col. 0578C]

Do what you do: go into the mud, tread while kneading, grasp the brick. While you give yourself to intercourse, you truly go into the mud. While you are swiftly driven from above by the whirlwind of lust, powerless over yourself, you surely tread while kneading. While you embrace and are embraced, you undoubtedly grasp the brick. This is your portion: a filthy portion, a great unhappiness. Whom do you serve by acting thus? For whom do you generate when you act thus?

“There fire will consume you; you will perish by the sword; the locust-grub will devour you.” Fire will consume you—the fire that is not extinguished; you will perish by the sword by which the devil was long ago struck; and the locust-grub will devour you, that is, the worm that does not die. For the locust-grub is a worm: at times flying, indeed, but weighed down by its own weight, because its little wings do not sufficiently help it; it is dragged down and, wearied in flight, falls to the ground. [Col. 0578D]

These expressions, therefore—“Go into the mud, tread while kneading, grasp the brick”—are of the kind which grammarians or rhetoricians call *concessive*, a beautiful mode of expression so framed that in commanding they forbid, and in forbidding they command. Yet, lest they seem to be a persuasion not understood, certain words are intermingled which openly oppose the apparent command, lest hearers suppose that what is said is commanded or recommended. This is clearly the case here. For when he had said, “Go into the mud, tread while kneading, grasp the brick,” he immediately added: “There fire will consume you; you will perish by the sword; the locust-grub will devour you.” Where he said, “Gather yourself,” he immediately added, “like a locust-grub”; where he said, “Multiply yourself,” he at once added, “like a locust.” Immediately [Col. 0579A] he introduced a truly chilling observation, containing a great deal of reproach: “You have made your trading more numerous,” he says, “than the stars of heaven.”

Is not such concession in such a matter a great mockery from above? For there is a kind of mockery in heaven, as the Psalmist says: “He who dwells in heaven will mock them” (Ps. 2). And what sensible person has ever seen or heard a thing more deserving of heavenly mockery than this world’s pursuit of procreation? Take this one example or proof.

The mad nations, and even the Romans who seemed wise to themselves, decreed that there should be *proletarii* in their cities—called *proletarii* because, having no occupation, they were occupied solely in providing sufficient offspring. Unhappy and miserable men: sufficient offspring for what? Certainly for killing, so that the devil might not lack material for his almost daily sport of human blood, his daily spectacle. For legions destined to die were led out day after day into battle, where they were cut down like dry straw—not to say thousands of people, but rather myriads of legions. [Col. 0579B]

Who has not heard—or rather, who has been able to hear enough, if he had leisure to read or listen—of the continuous deaths of human beings from the foundation of the world, perishing by sword, famine, and pestilence? I pass over the common condition of death which heavenly justice—indeed, mercy—brought upon the whole human race, saying: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), lest a human being, dead in soul, should live forever in bodily life and be taken to judgment without death intervening, like the demons, for whom, though they do not die, the judgment of eternal death has been laid up.

The present discussion concerns the fact that human beings do not wait for natural death: whenever they gathered and assembled in so many battles, in such great multitudes, rushing upon the sword, I would be astonished if anyone who wished to count the hundreds of thousands dying from the histories could cease being astonished. For this purpose, among their other madnesses, they also established *proletarii* in cities, as has been said, so that others might not be lacking to replace those who had been killed, in order to be killed themselves. [Col. 0579C]

Did not the world, then, even for this folly, make itself worthy that he who dwells in heaven should mock it, saying: “Go into the mud, tread while kneading, grasp the brick,” and so forth, down to: “You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven”? That is, as we have said, you have generated more persons for death and hell than there are, or ought to be, among all the elect, for whose birth God made male and female and blessed them.

But the very stars of heaven—that is, God’s elect, the children of blessing—weep under this mockery and lament themselves, recalling the mud which was the beginning of their origin, and understanding the saying, “Go into the mud,” to refer to it; they confess themselves to be mud. And weeping they say: “And now, Lord, you are our Father; but we are mud, and you are our maker, and all of us are the works of your hands” (Isa. 64). Again, each of them says: “Remember, I pray, that you made me like mud, and that you will bring me back to dust. Did you not pour me out like milk?” (Job 10). [Col. 0579D]

In saying these things, they “come before”—or anticipate—“his face in confession” (Ps. 95). For as though God had forgotten from how fragile and worthless a material he made those from whom he demands heavenly strength, that they should be strong and desire to ascend bravely into heaven and possess stations of which the visible stars of heaven offer a certain likeness—the stars he mentioned in the present passage when he said to this world: “You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven”—they remind him, their Creator or Former, from what he made or formed them.

Does God, then, know how to say something such as “Go into the mud” to persons of this kind, rather than extending his right hand to the work of his hands so that they may not enter into the mud? And even if one enters by an ordered entrance—that is, according to the law which he himself established, who created male and female and blessed them—does that mockery of him who dwells in heaven apply to such a person? (Ps. 2.) Why? Because they do not have the same cause which the Scripture here set forth beforehand, saying: “for the siege.” [Col. 0580A]

What cause is indicated by the words “for the siege” except that for which the children of this age are rejected by God: because they want to have here a city that remains? For this cause, as though necessarily and reasonably, the nations rushed into lust, and each sex, as it were, poured out and drew up the immoderate pleasure of the flesh.

Each sex, then, must be reproached for its own part: the female, when it is said, “Draw water for yourself” [Col. 0581A]; the male, when it is said, “Enter into the clay.” For that drawing water means, for a woman, yielding herself immoderately to a man, is clear from the saying of the Wise Man: “Like a thirsty traveller she will open her mouth at the fountain, and she will drink from every water near at hand” (Ecclus. 26). Thus, to build fortifications in this manner—namely, with the woman drawing water and the man entering into the clay—means, for the cause mentioned above, to replenish by rivalry the legions destined to die.

I pass over that final extreme of shamefulness, which the Apostle, rightly abhorring it, strikes with terrible force: “Their women exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature; and likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned in their desires toward one another, men committing shamefulness with men” (Rom. 1). [Col. 0581B] For the present intention of Scripture, it suffices to reproach what seemed to have some rationale: namely, that they should produce many children because of siege, in order to reclaim the habitation of the land or of whatever city. I say that this mockery—“Enter into the clay,” and the rest—does not apply to them; nor does the following apply there: “Fire shall consume them,” or “They shall perish by the sword,” or “The locust shall devour them.” Yet in this time those are more blessed who remain according to the Apostle’s counsel: namely, that one released from a wife should not seek a wife, and those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Cor. 7); reckoning also among the other tribulations of the flesh the possibility that what they beget may come to the number of the stars of heaven, since it has here been said: “You have made your trading more numerous [Col. 0581C] than the stars of heaven.”

Finally, even the fathers and patriarchs—to whom God first said to Abraham, “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can” (Gen. 15), and then, “So shall your seed be” (ibid.)—even these fathers, I say, came to make their trading more numerous than the stars of heaven; that is, not all whom they begot belonged to the number of stars of this kind. “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother,” says the Lord, “and I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated?” (Mal. 1).

It follows: “The caterpillar has spread out and flown away. Your guards are like locusts, and your little ones like locusts of locusts, which trust in [255] hedges on a cold day. The sun has risen, and they have flown away, and their place, where they had been, is not known.” Because he had said, “Gather like the caterpillar,” “Multiply like [Col. 0581D] the locust,” intending us to understand the immoderate and superfluous abundance of unhappy generations and conceptions, which, like winged little worms, daily spring up by birth from the flesh of this world, he continues the metaphor and exposes the great absurdity of their vanity, beginning thus: “The caterpillar has spread out and flown away.”

How highly, indeed, does he value the exaltation or expansion of the children of this age, when he compares them with a caterpillar that has spread itself out and flown away? Praise be in all things to the Holy Spirit, because he has found for them a fitting likeness. For example: Alexander the Great, whose kingdom we understand under the caterpillar in the prophet Joel (Joel 1), when he had magnified himself almost to the ends of the earth, born, as is reported, from incest with [Col. 0582A] Olympias, the wife of Philip of Macedon—was he not an expanded caterpillar, a worm? But he, having spread out, flew away; that is, he quickly died, namely in the thirty-first year of his age and the twelfth of his reign.

And if someone else lasted longer, expanding himself for a few months or years, should anyone’s expansion be thought long-lasting, however many years it may have been? Certainly, one who lives for more years in this age and enlarges himself has expanded himself only briefly and quickly died. For him to have died is for the caterpillar to have flown away. And it is well said not, “It spread out and flew,” but, “It spread out and flew away”—that is, it departed never to return.

How slight is the moment of this life, concerning which even he who dwells in heaven says mockingly (Ps. 2): “Your guards are like locusts, and your little ones [Col. 0582B] like locusts of locusts.” Who are your guards, O Nineveh, but the rulers of the age, powerful not in God but in the world? These, then, seem to be giants; but behold, they are like locusts. Let young men leap in chariots, flutter on horses, and glory in their shins; meanwhile, Wisdom looking down on them from above laughs and says: “The almond tree shall blossom; the locust shall grow fat” (Eccles. 12). What does “the locust shall grow fat” mean except that those youthful legs which now leap will swell, and, if they reach swift old age, will be weighed down by their own swelling?

Unhappy flowering; wretched fattening: when grey hair blossoms through the dryness of old age, while, conversely, the leg or shin grows fat through useless moisture. And who are the little ones of whom he says, “Your little ones are like locusts of locusts,” except the lowly multitude—the common people or plebeians—who, in their estimation, while they flatter the more powerful, regard these powerful men as giants? [Col. 0582C] Certainly, however much they flatter, they cannot make the powerful like elephants and those under them like oxen or ox-herds; rather, they are like locusts of locusts—that is, the smallest creatures—bearing the dominion of small beings.

How aptly he adds: “Which trust in hedges on a cold day; the sun has risen, and they have flown away, and their place, where they had been, is not known”—in accordance, namely, with the nature of locusts, which is such that, benumbed by cold, they take flight in warmth. What do we understand by “a cold day” except a time of adversity, when circumstances require that some nation or kingdom should rightly be afflicted? Then the poured-out multitudes of armies settle like locusts in cities or around cities, and consume everything both in villages and in fields. For example, the Assyrians at that time went up against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and besieged Jerusalem. [Col. 0582D] It was a cold day: that is, they deserved affliction because of their sins. But the sun rose and the locusts flew away, because the Lord became propitious, and in one night the camp of the Assyrians—one hundred and eighty-five thousand men—was destroyed (4 Kings 18).

Did not locusts of this kind fly away quickly, and was their place, where they had been, not known? So every multiplicity or gathering, which he had called “gathering like the caterpillar” and “multiplying like the locust,” quickly passes and will pass away. [Col. 0583A] But the fixed stars of heaven will remain in the height of the firmament, of which he said: “You have made your trading more numerous than the stars of heaven”; for many are reprobate, few elect (Matt. 20).

It follows: “Your shepherds have slumbered, O king of Assyria; your princes shall be buried. Your people are scattered over the mountains; there is none to gather them. Your destruction is not obscure; your wound is most grievous. All who have heard your report have clasped their hands over you. For over whom has your wickedness not always passed?”

In these words we hear that judgment concerning which the Holy Spirit convicts the world: because “the prince of this world has been judged” (John 16). For the king of Assyria is himself the prince of this world. Until this point the discourse was against Nineveh, that is, against this world; and under the name Nineveh the world was convicted of sin and righteousness (ibid.), as we said at the beginning. [Col. 0583B] Now, under the name of the king of Assyria, that same prince of this world is shown to have been judged. Thus, from this passage it may be made plain that the Paraclete Spirit, who speaks in this prophet, rightly convicts the world concerning his judgment; in keeping with the prophet’s own name, for *Naum* is interpreted from Hebrew as “comforter.”

“Your shepherds have slumbered,” he says, “O king of Assyria.” The shepherds of the king of Assyria are those who, as was said above, by entering into clay, treading, subduing, and holding the brick—that is, by exercising the work of generation far too immoderately—have gathered like the caterpillar and multiplied like locusts. In what respect are, or were, these men shepherds of the king of Assyria? Namely, because they fed or feed the sheep of the king of Assyria: sheep for slaughter—that is, [Col. 0583C] the superfluous multitude of human beings, who, as we sing in the psalm, “are placed like sheep in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Isa. 48).

O unhappy shepherds, who begot those whom they fed, and fed those whom they begot, for the king of Assyria: those by whom hell might be filled and death, feeding upon them, be sated! Such shepherds, he says, have slumbered. What does “have slumbered” mean? They have died; and for this, praise be to God, because by so slumbering they have ceased to feed—or to be begotten—for the king of Assyria.

For what would there be, had they not so slumbered and ceased generating? When the caterpillar has been gathered in such abundance and the locust multiplied to such a degree in the life of these shepherds; when even today dying flesh has such pride and such luxury that the multitudes of those being born [Col. 0583D] have very often had to be cut down by pestilence, famine, beasts, and sword; when, besides, natural death daily harvests them everywhere, and still the world is full—what, do you think, could have happened if these shepherds had not slumbered or did not slumber? That is, if human beings did not die, from the time when, made transgressors, they began obeying the king of Assyria?

Therefore praise be to God for having said: “Now, therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also of the tree of life and live for ever” (Gen. 3). For if human beings were to live until the day of judgment as demons live, and were also to generate, which demons do not, how disastrous this would have been—let whoever can consider it. God mercifully imposed bodily death on a human being already dead by the death of the soul; nor did he make the human merely mortal in any fashion, but willed him to be of the briefest life. For “the days of our years are seventy years; but if in powers”—that is, in the stronger, who endure longer—“eighty years; and what is beyond them is toil and pain” (Ps. 89). [Col. 0584A]

It was not so before the flood: some lived nine hundred years, others eight hundred, or seven hundred. But because, on account of that slight prolongation of life [256], human beings were so proud and so luxurious—as Scripture indicates when it says, “Now giants were upon the earth in those days; and the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful” (Gen. 6), etc.—God rightly and fittingly willed that the experiment itself should make known that it was beneficial for a human being dead in soul to be mortal in flesh. He thus confirmed the sentence he had laid down: “Lest he take of the tree of life and live [Col. 0584B] for ever”; confirming it, I say, by declaring: “My Spirit shall not remain in man for ever” (ibid.).

Moreover, this slumber—that is, the dissolution of the flesh through death—has been imposed in common not only upon the shepherds of the king of Assyria, but also upon the aforesaid stars of heaven, that is, those saints called according to purpose. [Col. 0584B] But observe what follows: “Your princes shall be buried.” Where shall they be buried except in hell? “The rich man died,” says the Lord, “and was buried in hell” (Luke 16). And in Ezekiel he himself says: “There is Assyria and all its multitude, its graves around it, all slain, who fell by the sword, whose graves were given in the lowest parts of the pit” (Ezek. 32).

This is what your shepherds or princes have in addition, O king of Assyria: all human beings, both good and evil, slumber the sleep of bodily death; but the wicked alone shall be buried in hell, because they are your shepherds or princes. [Col. 0584C] And will they ever be recalled from there to here? “Your people,” he says, “are scattered over the mountains; there is none to gather them.” What he says, “Your people are scattered,” is what he had said above: “The caterpillar has spread out and flown away; the sun has risen, and the locusts of locusts have flown away.” And what he says, “There is none to gather,” is what he had said: “Their place, where they had been, is not known.”

The cause of so great a destruction and irrevocable judgment is pride; therefore, when he had said, “Your people are scattered,” he added, “over the mountains.” For by mountains must be understood that loftiness which is reproached in the same king of Assyria in Isaiah in these words: “And it shall come to pass, when the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that I will visit the fruit of the magnificent heart of the king of Assyria and the glory of the loftiness of his eyes” (Isa. 10). Therefore, your people are scattered over the mountains—that is, because of pride—because your people are children of pride, over whom you are king, O Assyria; as it was said to blessed Job concerning you: “He sees every high thing, and he is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).

Your people are not scattered, nor your shepherds or princes dispersed, as a people is scattered while fleeing; rather, they are so dispersed that they cannot flee, and may indeed see one another’s graves burning with sulphur and fire, but cannot help or assist one another. [Col. 0585A] Certainly, in the scattering of this people of the king of Assyria, the scattering of the Jewish people must not escape us. Nor should we forget or be ignorant that they themselves are the king’s people—indeed, that this people is above all the people of the king of Assyria; and Jews are especially indicated also by the interpretation of this name, for “Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who set straight.” Who are those who set straight except those who set themselves straight? And what people set themselves straight more than the Jews, who, “seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10)?

Therefore, among your shepherds and princes, O king of Assyria, in the midst of your people scattered over the mountains—that is, because of the height of pride—O prince of this world, these are especially to be considered. Their scattering God showed beforehand in accordance with his ancient counsel [Col. 0585B], because his ancient spirit was already long ago speaking: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget. Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 85).

It happened according to the counsel of that ancient disclosure. First, those shepherds or princes of yours, whom he marked out when he said, “For behold, they have seized upon my soul; the strong have rushed upon me” (ibid.), slumbered and were buried: surrounded by the Romans, they died and were buried in hell. Then the wretched surviving people was scattered, led captive among all nations, and there was none to gather them; because Christ, who alone gathers and restores what is gathered, was taken from them and went to the Gentiles, and made firm what had been shown to him [Col. 0585C]: “Do not kill them; scatter them in your power” (ibid.). That is: do not uproot them utterly from the land, but scatter them throughout all lands in your power, in your might. Why, even today? “Lest my people ever forget” (ibid.).

It should therefore be noted that the Jews’ dispersion took place so that they might confirm the faith of the Gentiles not in one place only, but throughout all the earth: while they asserted that he had been crucified by their ancestors, and did not deny possessing the Scriptures in which he was foretold to us, their continued life made the faith of the Gentiles more certain even through their testimony.

At last the Paraclete states against you, O king of Assyria, why, and concerning what judgment, he ought to convict the world: because you have been judged. “Your crushing,” he says, “is not obscure; your wound is most grievous.” The crushing by which you have been crushed is that by which the woman crushed your head, according to the decree of the Lord the Judge, which he pronounced against you at the beginning, saying to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; she shall crush your [Col. 0585D] head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3).

“You shall lie in wait for the heel” of the blessed woman, the blessed Virgin Mary—indeed, also for the heel of her seed, which is Christ. He himself, not unaware of this, said: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 13). Therefore, because you had nothing at all in him, and nevertheless came against him seeking, as though due, the debt of sin—that is, demanding the penalty of death—you were crushed by his heel; you were overcome by his end, that is, by his passion or death.

Who has not heard of this crushing of yours? [Col. 0586A] “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18): namely, the sound and words of the heavens which proclaimed or announced this glory of the Son of God, that by dying he had crushed your head. Your crushing, therefore, is not obscure, because it has plainly been related throughout all the earth and plainly announced to the ends of the world. Accordingly, the Paraclete rightly convicts the world concerning judgment, because it cannot excuse itself on the ground that it has not heard the judgment by which you were judged, or the crushing by which you were crushed.

Likewise, who has not heard that your wound is most grievous? For in the same Gospel in which your aforementioned crushing is narrated or announced, your most grievous wound is also narrated: the wound by which you were struck in heaven, so that you fell, while the Lord saw you, O Satan, “falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). [Col. 0586B] That wound is the wound of a sword, a most grievous wound—not most grievously, but indeed most fittingly inflicted. It is most grievous because it is incurable; but it was inflicted most fittingly because you were most justly condemned and struck.

Most justly, I say, because you sinned not merely in some ordinary way but proudly: a murderer from the beginning, who did not stand in the truth, in whom there is no truth, who, when you speak falsehood, speak from your own resources, because you are a liar and the father of falsehood (John 8). Thus you sinned maliciously; and for this reason you received the most grievous—that is, incurable—wound of the sword. Yet it is remarkable that, although your wound is so grievous, you still live. You do not truly live; rather, you falsely claim to live and defend yourself as though living.

Hence the wonder in the Apocalypse concerning the beast which has a wound of the sword and lived, or whose mortal wound was healed: “According to your lie, the wound of your death [257] [Col. 0586C] has been healed” (Apoc. 13), and you, having a sword-wound, live. But according to God’s truth, your wound is so grievous that it is insatiable for ever, and you are so dead that you can never in any way breathe again into life. On account of this judgment the world is convicted: the world allied with you and worshipping you in temples or images as a god and as though alive. Since your judgment was revealed in Christ’s Gospel, anyone not separated from you is convicted more justly.

[Col. 0586D] “All who have heard your report have clasped their hands over you.” To hear a report is more than merely to hear something, just as to have “ears to hear” (Matt. 11) is more than merely to have ears. For where such words or terms are doubled, a twofold hearing is required or understood: that of the body and that of the heart. Therefore, all who heard your report—that is, those who heard and believed in your crushing or in your most grievous wound—“clasped,” he says, “their hands over you”: that is, how devoutly they gave thanks to him who crushed you, who struck you with the most grievous wound.

For faithful and devout people, when they first hear good news of God’s works or benefits, are accustomed, in a swift movement of pious feeling, to raise eyes and clasped hands, and with these signs of faith to praise and glorify the Lord Most High, seated upon the throne. Thus, by the words “they clasped their hands over you,” a great abundance of rejoicing and gladness is signified, [Col. 0587A] in view of righteous judgment and just vengeance.

“For over whom has your wickedness not always passed?” By asking, “Over whom has your wickedness not always passed?” he affirms with greater force that his wickedness has always passed over all.
