For from the time when the malignant and malicious one lied through the serpent, saying, “You shall by no means die; eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3), his wickedness has always and unceasingly passed from one person and through one person into all human beings, as the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and death through sin; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5). Over whom, then, has his wickedness not passed? Who was not conceived in iniquities, and whom did not his mother conceive in sins? (Ps. 1.)

This, then, is the great reason why all who heard your report clasped their hands over you: because one man, who alone came forth without sin, condemned and crushed you, whose wickedness passed through one person over all; and he freed and justified them from wickedness. Hearing, they rejoiced; and rejoicing and believing, they clasped their hands over you.

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Habakkuk

[Col. 0587]

**258.** My mind had long been eager to enter upon Habakkuk, the eighth of the prophets, even while it was still wholly held in attentive concentration upon the preceding prophet, namely Nahum. For it still moved in almost continuous meditation around the ending of Nahum, and already, as though from some nearby place, there was heard this great cry of Habakkuk: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear?” (Hab. 1); “I shall cry out to you while suffering violence, and you will not save.” Again: “O Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. 3).

I confess that the inward ear of the human person heard the force of such a cry not without a certain divine awe. For it desired to enter there, mindful of that verse: “I shall rejoice over your words as one who finds abundant spoil” (Ps. 118). I felt something of the desire of the merchant seeking fine pearls, who does not vainly judge that he has at last found one precious pearl when he finds in the Law and the Prophets the faith or righteousness that is Christ, through whom the Holy Spirit undoubtedly spoke.

Christ himself—the pearl of great price, the treasure of the Father’s heart, the golden heart—knows that, as one searches the Scriptures and searches the prophets, one seeks him. The soul that searches in this way invokes the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets, that he may so show beforehand, already here through this mirror and in this riddle of prophetic discourse, the beauty of such a pearl, as to grant her always to possess that same pearl in the age to come and to see it as it is.

But the Apostle says: “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that we have conducted ourselves in the simplicity and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God” (2 Cor. 1). With this example there is added, for consolation, also that you, O ecclesiastical and religious men, kindly and spiritual friends whom I named beforehand in the preface to the exposition of Nahum, comfort my smallness with good hope of obtaining fruit, by these and similar words:

Therefore persist, good man, and “act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Prov. 30), so that you may finally enjoy in the kingdom of God, eating and drinking at his table with a full mouth, those delights which in this pilgrimage you now taste only in brief foretaste.

Therefore a faithful mind should not fear anyone’s detraction as though excessively burdened by it, so as to fall away from good study and grow slack with hands hanging down. Rather, let it remember the lizard, which, though it has no wings, uses its hands and dwells in the houses of kings; and the cock girded about the loins, and the ram—nor is there a king who can resist them.

## First Book of Commentaries on the Prophet Habakkuk

**259. Chapter 1**

[Col. 0587B]

The burden which Habakkuk the prophet saw. At what time Habakkuk lived we are taught by Daniel: he is read to have been sent with a meal to Daniel in the lions’ den (Dan. 14), says blessed Jerome, although that story is not read among the Hebrews. Whether one accepts that Scripture or does not accept it, he writes here as a prophet, knowing things to come. And as the prophet Nahum, whom he follows here, had a prophecy against Nineveh and the Assyrians who laid waste the ten tribes called Israel, so this man saw a burden—that is, a grave matter, full of weight and toil—against Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar, by whom Judah and Jerusalem, together with the Temple, were overthrown.

“How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry aloud to thee while suffering violence, and thou wilt not save? Why hast thou shown me iniquity and toil to behold, and plunder and injustice against me?” [Col. 0588B]

The prophet rightly received here the name Habakkuk, which is interpreted “embrace” or “wrestler,” because in some sense he enters into a contest and struggle, and, so to speak, into an embrace with God after the manner of a wrestler. He ventures to summon Him to a discussion of justice and to say to Him: Why is there such great iniquity in human affairs, and why does the unjust prevail over the just? “How long, O Lord,” he says, “shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry aloud to thee while suffering violence, and thou wilt not save? Why hast thou shown me iniquity and toil to behold, plunder and injustice against me? And judgment has come to pass, and contradiction is stronger. Therefore the law is torn apart, and judgment does not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment goes forth.”

He seems to speak of the condition of his own times: the wicked Nebuchadnezzar prevailed against righteous Judah. This, he seems to say, is why judgment did not reach its end—because it is unjust and perverse that the righteous king Josiah should be slain by an unrighteous king (2 Chron. 35), that Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael should serve as slaves (Dan. 1), while the Babylonian emperor rules, and Belshazzar drinks from God’s bowls among his harlots and concubines (Dan. 5).

But does it belong to prophetic perfection merely to have seen the evils of one’s own time, which any other person could not have failed to know? Why, then, did he thus preface the title: “The burden which Habakkuk the prophet saw”? We must also consider that the Apostle Paul understood—and indeed the Holy Spirit who had taken Paul up understood—that what immediately follows, “Look among the nations and see; marvel and be astonished; for a work has been done in your days which no one will believe when it is told,” refers to the times of evangelical grace [Col. 0589B].

For when the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13), we subsequently read that Paul and those with him came to Antioch in Pisidia. Entering the synagogue of the Jews on the sabbath days, they sat down. Then Paul arose (ibid.) and gave the people a discourse of exhortation, which he concluded thus: “See, therefore, lest that which was spoken in the prophets come upon you: See, you despisers, and look; marvel and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work which you will not believe if anyone tells it to you” (ibid.). The wording is slightly different, namely according to the Septuagint translators.

If it seems inconsistent with this that, following the Apostle, we should refer the passage to the times of evangelical grace because what immediately follows is, “For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation”—for this was not future but had long ago occurred in the Apostles’ time—we likewise say that, when Habakkuk wrote this, it had already occurred: the Lord had already raised up the Chaldeans, and they possessed the dwellings of the nations and had already led Judah into captivity.

Therefore, entering upon the text of the prophecy, let us, as far as we can, magnify the majesty of its mystical meanings; and, following the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets, let us not doubt that Christ Jesus crucified himself speaks in this prophet [Col. 0589D]. “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry aloud to thee while suffering violence, and thou wilt not save?”

Is this not equal or similar to what he long before said in the Psalmist: “My God, my God, look upon me; why hast thou forsaken me? My God, I shall cry by day, and thou wilt not hear” (Ps. 21)? If David truly spoke that not in his own person but in Christ’s, why should this prophet not likewise say these similar words in the person of that same Christ? Truly this is fitting, and it accords with the Holy Spirit, that words which He spoke through the prophets should be assigned to that person concerning whom He rightly has concern: the one who was truly righteous, because he did not commit sin, and who therefore, while suffering as though a sinner, while the unjust prevailed against him and he cried out yet was not heard for a time, could confidently seek judgment—as we plainly have in the present words.

For, being a strong wrestler, he summons God to judgment and says: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?” Yet he cried with a mighty cry and was heard, although here too in the Psalm he says, “I shall cry, and thou wilt not hear” (Ps. 21). Of this the Apostle says: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

He does not ask as one ignorant, in order to learn how long, or until when, he ought to cry and cry aloud, and how long his hearing or salvation should be delayed—although the Apostle immediately says in the same passage: “And indeed, though he was a Son, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered” (ibid.). For he knew; but he did not yet know by experience the toil of obedience. Nor was it hidden from his knowledge that he had to cry and cry aloud unto death, even death of the cross, and that before the completion of that obedience he ought not to be heard, and ought not to be saved [Col. 0590B].

It is very pleasing, as has been said, to understand this calamity as spoken in the prophet’s person. Yet we do not say this in such a way as to deny that the prophet himself shared in this crying or loud outcry. Rather, we truly say that whatever this man or any other cried or cried aloud that was worthy of God’s hearing was the cry and loud outcry of him whose Spirit, as he spoke in them, so also cried and cried aloud.

Hence, just as in one place he was commanded to be called “Hasten to strip away the spoils; make haste to plunder” (Isa. 8), because, before he knew how to call out, before he had a mother and an adoptive father in the world, he often delivered Jerusalem from enemies, so nothing prevents him from being called, “Hasten to cry; make haste to cry aloud.” For before he was born of a mother and laboured in the assumed humanity, he himself cried and cried aloud in the saints who had faith in the promise and in his coming; without faith in him, no one was worthy to be heard.

Indeed, many were heard because of him, but not in such a way that transgression should be completed, sin should receive its end, iniquity should be blotted out, and everlasting righteousness should be brought in. Christ was not to be heard in that way until he himself, in his own person, completed obedience unto death, even death of the cross (Phil. 2). This was to be the completion of the crying and loud outcry.

His words, “I shall cry aloud while suffering violence,” have a venerable meaning if you recall what he says elsewhere: “Then I paid for what I had not seized” (Ps. 68)—that is, I endured a death which I did not deserve. Accordingly, he immediately asks, as it were: “Why hast thou shown me iniquity and toil, to behold plunder and injustice against me?” His words, “Thou hast shown me,” have the sense of “Thou hast imposed upon me.” “Thou hast shown me,” he says, “iniquity”—understand, not my own; “thou hast shown me toil,” that is, thou hast imposed upon me the task of labouring on account of iniquity, not mine but another’s.

Isaiah also speaks of this: “And the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all; and the Lord willed to crush him in weakness; and because his soul laboured, he shall see and be satisfied” (Isa. 53) [Col. 0591A]. He also showed him plunder, as Isaiah immediately says in the same passage: “I shall give him many as his portion, and he shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because he delivered his soul unto death” (ibid.).

We must carefully observe that, when he had said “plunder,” he added, “and injustice against me.” For thou, O God, didst show him plunder—just plunder—so that he might justly despoil the strong man armed, that is, the devil, who had unjustly despoiled others. Yet those who above all ought to have received him, that they might fall to him as part of the spoil, rejected him most unjustly. This is rightly understood where, after saying, “Thou hast shown me plunder,” he adds, “and injustice against me.”

The fact that he showed him iniquity, toil, and plunder, as just stated, was not against him, because in all things he willingly undertook obedience. But the injustice by which they rejected him was against him, because it was not from God, although by God’s just judgment they had been blinded and made heavy so as to do this.

Nor does he say, as though ignorant, “Why hast thou shown me these things?” just as he says in the Psalm, “Why hast thou forsaken me?” (Ps. 21). Rather, he poses such a question in order to answer it thus: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (ibid.), that is, because the sins of my own people demand that thou shouldst be far from my salvation.

It follows: “Judgment has come to pass, and contradiction is stronger.” “Judgment has come to pass”—understand, perverse judgment. For it follows: “Therefore the law is torn apart, and judgment does not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment goes forth.” What is perverse judgment but the judgment of those who contradict? For after stating, “Judgment has come to pass,” he added, “and contradiction is stronger”; and what is contradiction but the tearing apart of the law? For he immediately added, “Therefore the law is torn apart,” and so forth [Col. 0591C].

Now, in order that a readier approach may be opened to the inner meaning, we must first note that he did not say: “Therefore the wicked prevails against the just because the law is torn apart and judgment does not reach its end; therefore the wicked prevails against the just because perverse judgment goes forth.” Rather, conversely, he says: “Therefore the law is torn apart and judgment does not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the just.”

For this concerns not that perverse judgment by which unjust judges often, for bribes, acquit the wicked and condemn the just, but that by which people presume to judge God himself as though unjust whenever they see the righteous wearied by adversities and the wicked prospering. The prophet Malachi speaks to such persons: “You have made the Lord weary with your words; and you said, ‘In what have we made him weary?’ When you said: ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such persons please him’; or, ‘Where is the God of judgment?’” (Mal. 2).

With this point noted, let us now return to the words of the prophecy already set before us. “Judgment,” he says, “has come to pass, and contradiction is stronger” [Col. 0592A]—where thou, O Lord, didst show me iniquity and toil, to behold plunder and injustice against me; where I cried and thou didst not hear, cried aloud to thee while suffering violence and thou didst not save. There, and in similar events—that is, because of similar events—judgment has come to pass, namely perverse judgment; and contradiction is stronger than the speech of those who say what is true, for example: “Thou art righteous, O Lord, and thy judgment is right” (Ps. 118).

It is stronger, I say, than the speech of those concerning whom it is likewise written: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72). The contradiction is that of those who say: “He who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such persons please him”; or, “Where is the God of judgment?” They strengthen their contradiction with arguments which appear to them obvious facts, because they see the peace of sinners, because there is no regard paid to their death, because they are not in the toil of men and are not scourged with men; indeed, they have acquired riches abounding in the world. On the other hand, the righteous have been scourged all day, and their correction comes in the mornings (ibid.).

“And I, who was or am the most righteous of all, was scourged and corrected before all others, was made their derision, was delivered to a most shameful death; and all who saw me mocked me, spoke with their lips, and shook their heads, while I cried, while I cried aloud: ‘My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?’” (Ps. 21; Matt. 27; Mark 15).

Because the wicked thus prevails against the just, contradiction is stronger, since it fortifies itself with present arguments, tears apart the law, blasphemes the God and Lord of the law, and resists more powerfully those who are upright in heart, opposing itself to them as they say, “How good is the God of Israel” (Ps. 72). In this way the law is torn apart, and judgment does not reach its end: that is, those who hold the true judgment—that God is good, God is just, and God cares for human affairs—are not granted victory. Rather, perverse judgment goes forth: namely, that everyone who does evil is good in the Lord’s sight and that such persons please him.

But does the wicked always prevail against the just? Does that wicked one, namely the Jewish people, who then prevailed against the Just One, crucified him, and tore him apart by shaking their heads and saying, “He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he desires him” (Ps. 21); or, “Ha! you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself” (Matt. 27), and words like these—does that wicked one, I say, remain always strong, and is that Just One always weak?

Certainly not. Rather, he immediately speaks with a changed voice: “Look among the nations, and see, and marvel, and be astonished; for a work has been done in your days which no one will believe when it is told. For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, walking over the breadth of the earth, to possess dwellings not their own. It is horrible and terrible; its judgment and its burden shall proceed from itself. Its horses are swifter than leopards and more rapid than evening wolves, and its horsemen shall spread abroad.”

What a change in voice, though not in person! How great is the difference between the one and the same person who previously spoke in weakness and who now speaks in power! We have already mentioned that Paul recalled this passage in the Acts of the Apostles, where, after entering the Jewish synagogue at Antioch and delivering a discourse of exhortation to the people, he concluded it thus: “See, therefore, lest that which was spoken in the prophets come upon you: See, you despisers, and marvel, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work which you will not believe if anyone tells it to you.”

He spoke dreadfully; he pronounced it terribly: “See, therefore, lest it come upon you.” For it is dreadful and terrible not to believe the work which, the Lord says, “I work in your days,” because of what immediately follows: “For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans,” and the rest. Unless we follow the apostolic meaning and attend to the days of which he understands this to have been said in the prophets, how will it stand, or be true, that “I work a work which you will not believe if anyone tells it to you: for behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans”?

Did the Jews not believe, or would they not have believed if it had been told them, that work in which he formerly raised up the Chaldeans and King Nebuchadnezzar to walk over the breadth of the earth? Indeed, what need was there to tell it to them, especially when they were captives in Babylon and both city and Temple had been burned with Chaldean fire? Who among them could have been ignorant of it? Add that, as was said above, in the Apostles’ time—and indeed in the time when Habakkuk prophesied—that which the letter seems to say in this passage, “Behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans,” was not future but already accomplished [Col. 0593C].

Therefore, “Look among the nations and see and marvel,” or, according to the Septuagint translators, “See, you despisers, and marvel, and perish,” and the other words are, as they truly are, the words not of one about to judge but of the Just One already judging—he against whom the wicked Jewish people had prevailed, so that he could say: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry aloud to thee while suffering violence, and thou wilt not save?” Or: “My God, why hast thou forsaken me?”

“Look,” he says; “see,” he says; “marvel, O you Jewish despisers, and be scattered among all nations.” For what cause? “Because a work has been done in your days which no one will believe when it is told.” What is that work? “For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation,” and the rest.

Truly the Jews did not believe this work when the Apostles proclaimed it; nor do they believe it now when the Christian successors of the Apostles proclaim it: namely, that I myself, who while dying on the cross cried as though forsaken; I who died and was buried—I myself, I say, now live, have now risen, and am still with thee, O God the Father; and, a few years after I died, I shall raise up Chaldeans, that is, a bitter and swift nation like the Chaldeans—like them, I say, that is, a nation that repeats a true and most exact likeness of what those men, called Chaldeans among the Gentiles, once did to you. Thus, in the same month—indeed, on the same day of the year—with the city set ablaze, they will also set your Temple ablaze, on which those Chaldeans formerly set it ablaze.

For Josephus too, considering this point not to be neglected but rather to be wondered at, wrote as follows (*Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 14) [Col. 0594A]:

> Titus withdrew into Antonia, having resolved that on the following morning he would attack with his whole army and besiege the Temple. Yet plainly the sentence of God had long since condemned it to fire; and, as the cycles of time rolled on, the fated day had arrived—the tenth day of the month of August—on which it had also formerly been burned by the king of Babylon.

Again, after narrating that same conflagration, he says:

> One may marvel at the exactness even of the recurring time. For it preserved, as has been said, both the month and the day on which the Temple had first been burned by the Babylonians.

Nor do we judge that this destruction was suitably called a raising up of Chaldeans solely because of such resemblance, but also because of the invisible assault of evil spirits, who were assuredly present at the same time. To them the Jews were undoubtedly delivered in soul and body, and they were signified by the Chaldeans both in name and in reality. In name, because “Chaldeans” is interpreted “fierce”; in reality, because they led the people of God captive from their own land, just as, through the working of evil spirits, all the elect, taken captive under sin in Adam, came into the exile of this world.

It was a great matter, a great evil, and so great that the Holy Spirit deemed it worthy to say through the mouth of the Apostle, “See, you despisers, lest it come upon you” (Acts 13). He warned them, but it did them no good, because they did not see, did not take heed for themselves lest it should come upon them. Therefore it had to happen thus; the truth of judgment had necessarily to be fulfilled; and so it came about.

He who had been raised from the dead raised up other Chaldeans, another Babylon—that is, Rome. “The church which is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you,” says the Apostle Peter (1 Pet. 5), referring figuratively to Rome; that is, he means Rome itself to be understood as Babylon in every respect through the similarity of things. Why, on the same principle, should we not understand the Chaldeans here as Romans?

“This is the work,” he says, “which no one will believe when it is told.” The Jews do indeed believe—indeed, they know well and know only too well—that the Romans came and did to them things like those done by the Chaldeans, even worse things than the Chaldeans did. But they do not believe those who tell or preach that he whom they crucified, who died and was buried, performed this work or could have performed it: that he rose again, ascended into heaven, and, possessing all power in heaven and on earth, could have done this to them [Col. 0594D].

“No one believes,” that is, those who believe are very few. For there were indeed some Jews who believed; but in comparison with those who did not believe, they were and are very few. Thus one may rightly say, “No one believes,” just as the same truth is stated in Isaiah: “The righteous man perishes, and no one considers”; or, “perceives with the heart”; “and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers” (Isa. 57).

Nevertheless, we understand “Chaldeans” here first of evil spirits and secondarily of Romans, differing only in this mystery as riders differ from horses, since it is said: “Its horses are swifter than leopards,” and the rest. Let us therefore now examine the words themselves more carefully.

“Behold,” he says, “I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, walking over the breadth of the earth, to possess dwellings not their own.” This is the burden that Habakkuk the prophet saw; this is the wrath and affliction which followed the Passion of Christ the Son of God, as he himself said: “For there shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath upon this people; and they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led captive into all nations” (Matt. 24; Luke 21) [Col. 0595A].

He raised up fierce Chaldeans, visible and invisible Chaldean enemies, when he brought in the Romans and at the same time delivered the wicked one, who had prevailed against the Just One, to evil spirits. Who does not know that nation to be bitter and swift? How bitter are evil spirits to the human race, and how swift in pursuing and overtaking every soul that flees in winter or on the Sabbath—that is, every soul caught in the cold of unbelief, which first remembers its salvation precisely when, as it is not a time for work, so neither is there permission to flee.

How swiftly that nation overtook the wicked one delivered to it by the Just One who speaks these words, because he had unjustly prevailed against him. What he then says—“walking over the breadth of the earth, to possess dwellings not their own,” and immediately thereafter, “its horses are swifter than leopards and more rapid than evening wolves”—requires admiration more than exposition, if you recall how Roman power walked over the breadth of the earth and what great deeds it accomplished.

Certainly it would not have poured out so much blood throughout the world, both its own and that of others, unless a bitter and swift nation had sat upon its back as upon a horse: the invisible nation of which we have already spoken. When he further says, “to possess dwellings not their own,” he reproves both horses and riders: the Romans, indeed, most greedily possessed what belonged to others; and the evil spirit, when in the Gospel he says, “All the kingdoms of the world have been delivered to me, and I give them to whom I will” (Matt. 4), plainly presumes to possess dwellings not his own.

But we are now chiefly concerned with those dwellings in which, Isaiah says, righteousness once dwelt, “but now murderers” (Isa. 1). The city of Zion, or Jerusalem, and the Temple were dwellings which that nation did not possess and which were not its own so long as righteousness dwelt in them: the righteousness of faith and hope, which had been placed there in the promise of Christ’s coming, in which Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 5 [probably 15]) [Col. 0595D].

It did not, I say, possess them, even though it laid them waste for a time, as the former Chaldeans had done when Nebuchadnezzar, after burning the city and Temple, led the inhabitants captive into Babylon. But from the time when the wicked husbandmen cast out and killed the son, the lord of the vineyard (Matt. 2 [probably 21]), that nation possesses those same dwellings, formerly not its own; for from then on no righteousness dwells, or can dwell, in the ceremonies of those dwellings.

What kind of nation is this? “It is horrible,” he says, “and terrible; its judgment and burden shall proceed from itself. Its horses are swifter than leopards and more rapid than evening wolves, and its horsemen shall spread abroad.” He declared two things concerning this nation: that it is horrible and terrible; and he distinguished it into two parts, namely horses and riders. Understand the horses as human beings and the riders as demons, the evil drivers of human beings: horses, then—that is, terrible men; riders—that is, horrible demons; both horses and riders, both human beings and demons, are surely Chaldeans, that is, fierce ones. Thus the nation is horrible and terrible.

But did God make it horrible and terrible? Certainly not, says the Lord himself; rather, “its judgment and burden shall proceed from itself.” What is judgment except condemnation? And what is burden except the hardening or heaviness of one’s own heart? In short: when someone sins knowingly, so that one can truly say of him that “he is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment,” then it is true to say of him that his judgment proceeds from himself.

And when someone takes up the sword, not as God’s minister, not in order to be an avenger in wrath upon one who does evil, but to indulge his own will or envy, or even to compel others to do evil—as Antiochus did, and all like him—it is true to say that his burden proceeds from himself [Col. 0596B].

Such is the whole nation of Chaldeans, the entire multitude of evil spirits and ungodly people: they are condemned by their own judgment, having exalted themselves against their Creator; and in every affliction which they, being fierce and proud, inflict, they serve their own envy or will. Thus God justifies and excuses himself—God the author of no evil, the good Creator who makes no creature evil—when he says of this nation: “Its judgment and burden shall proceed from itself.”

How, then, does he say that he will raise up such a nation? For he says: “Surely I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter nation,” and the rest. The ready answer is that it is one thing to make a bitter nation and another to raise up a bitter nation, or to give power to a bitter nation, which the order of justice sometimes requires. For example, God did not make Pharaoh evil; but, when Pharaoh was evil, he raised him to royal power, because this was expedient. Sometimes it is expedient for God’s people that one who is evil should also become powerful, becoming in God’s hand a rod of wrath and staff of indignation. From this come the benefits of which Solomon speaks in Proverbs: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser; but if thou rebuke the wise man, he will understand instruction” (Prov. 19).

Therefore, the burden of this bitter nation, this horrible and terrible nation, “shall proceed from itself,” he says: that is, its heart will be burdened by voluntary impiety, and all its striving will be toward evil. Hence God is not to be blamed as the author of its bitterness; rather, he is to be praised because he makes good use of its bitterness, so that, while pestilent people are scourged, some fool may advance to wisdom, frightened by their example; and those who are wise, as Daniel and his companions formerly were, when struck by the same scourge, may understand discipline more fully [Col. 0596D].

Who, further, are or were the leopards and evening wolves, to whom the horses of this nation are said to be swifter and more rapid? It is pleasing to understand the leopards as Greeks, because in Daniel the Greek kingdom is clearly signified by the leopard in the vision (Dan. 7). We judge the evening wolves to be Persians and Medes—namely Haman, the enemy of the Jews, and his accomplices—who are understood by the bear in the same vision.

For like evening wolves, hungry wolves, they wished to leave nothing for the morning but to devour everything, and they planned to destroy the entire Jewish race from which Christ would be born. Swifter and more rapid than those wolves and leopards already mentioned were the Chaldean horses, the Babylonian horses—whether you understand the former Babylon in which Nebuchadnezzar reigned, or the second Babylon, Rome, of which it was said above: “The church which is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you” (1 Pet. 5). For Peter calls Rome Babylon because of its outpouring of manifold idolatry.

For he wrote that epistle at Rome in the time of the Emperor Claudius, before sending Mark—whom he mentions there, saying, “And Mark, my son” (ibid.)—to Alexandria [Col. 0597B]. In what, then, were these horses swifter than those leopards and more rapid than those wolves? In this: that they reached the point to which they aimed and attained what they pursued. Both Babylonian powers burned the city and Temple and led the people into captivity. The earlier Babylonians kept the people captive among themselves because they wished it; the later ones sold them and scattered them as captives among all nations because they wished it.

But those leopards and wolves were not swift enough to attain what they desired. Queen Esther and Mordecai wisely outstripped the wolves, namely Haman and his accomplices (Esther 2); and Judas Maccabaeus and his companions courageously turned back the leopards—that is, the Greeks with Antiochus Epiphanes—from their undertaking (1 Macc. 4). No one outstripped the horses already mentioned; no one drove them back. Rather, as has been said, they reached the place toward which they aimed and completed what they wished: even to the fire, to the smoke, to the irrecoverable destruction of city and Temple.

Add what follows: “And its horsemen shall spread abroad.” We have already said that the riders are evil spirits and their horses human beings. It was too little for vengeance that human bodies fell by the edge of the sword, unless their souls also fell as prey to evil spirits. “Its horsemen shall spread abroad,” therefore, he says: that is, evil spirits shall fill everything, with no good spirits opposing them, since the latter had already departed, saying—as Josephus reports (*Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 17)—“Let us depart from these dwellings.”

> On the feast-day called Pentecost, at night the priests entered the inner Temple according to their custom to perform divine services. At first they perceived a certain movement and noise; then they heard a sudden voice saying, “Let us depart from here.”

Certainly the event that followed sufficiently establishes that all the protection of good spirits departed from there, and that a multitude of evil spirits spread into the place left desolate. These are what we here call the invisible riders of visible horses—that is, the harsh drivers of warlike human beings [Col. 0597D].

Hence it continues: “For its horsemen shall come from afar; they shall fly as an eagle hastening to eat. All shall come for prey; their faces are a burning wind.” Truly its riders came from afar, because by nature or condition evil spirits are far removed from every human being. Thus such a nation is called horrible above: they are far from humankind in nature and rush against humankind with savage hatred.

And because, being spirits, they are swift, it was too little to say, “They shall come”; he added, “They shall fly.” By the word “fly,” which belongs to birds, he fittingly expressed the natural swiftness of savage spirits. Nor will they fly in any manner whatever, but “as an eagle,” he says, “hastening to eat.” The eagle is king of birds; yet birds (*aves*) are so called either from their greed for eating (*aviditas*) or because they do not have fixed paths but range through pathless places (*avia*).

At the same time it should be known that the image of an eagle was the emblem on Roman standards. Thus, when he says “as an eagle hastening to eat,” with marvellous appropriateness of comparison he declares the swiftness, greed, power, and great violence of such riders—that is, evil spirits—hastening with those Chaldeans or Babylonians, namely their Roman human horses, as has been said, to devour the souls permitted to them [Col. 0598B].

“All,” he says, “shall come for prey; their faces are a burning wind.” When he says “all,” understand both horses and riders together—that is, human beings and demons alike. Of the riders, that is, the demons, it is superfluous to say how greedily they came as robbers to carry off souls. But as for the human beings, there are many examples in histories of how intent they were upon plunder and how hateful was their greed; here it has seemed good not to pass over one especially terrible example.

“Josephus says (*Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 27): ‘Among the Syrians, a certain deserter was caught gathering gold coins from the excrement of his belly. For deserters came after swallowing them, while the rebels searched all of them; and there had been a great quantity of gold in the city. When this trick was discovered, a rumour spread through the whole camp that the deserters came full of gold. A multitude of Arabs and Syrians were cutting open their bellies in search of the spoils; and, I think,’ he says, ‘no calamity more savage than this befell the Jews. In a single night the entrails of two thousand were laid open.’”

Therefore, truly, “all shall come for prey”; and he immediately adds, “Their faces are a burning wind” [Col. 0598D]. And truly it occurred thus, because what had been foretold to Moses was fulfilled: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deut. 32). Visible enemies kindled visibly burning fire, and that fire was kindled in the Lord’s wrath. But invisible enemies carried the prey of souls down to invisible fire, fire that burns unquenchably; and this burns and will burn “unto the lowest parts of hell”—that is, unto the end, or without end, because as the kingdom of God shall have no end, so there shall be no lowest limit of hell.

It follows: “And he shall gather captivity as the sand. He shall triumph over kings, and tyrants shall be a laughingstock to him. He shall laugh at every stronghold; he shall heap up earth and take it. Then his spirit shall change and pass over, and he shall fall. This is the strength of his god.” [Col. 0599A]

There should be no doubt concerning whom these words are spoken: it is the devil himself, king of the horses and riders, of
of whom he had previously spoken as the king of the Chaldeans, that is, the king of all the fierce sons of pride, both malignant spirits and impious human beings. When the discourse concerned his horses and horsemen, it suddenly passed to him who is their head. For, lest you doubt that the discourse is about him, it thus swallowed him up and identified him: “This is the strength of his god—his own.” He did not say, “This is the strength of his god”; for the devil neither has God nor wishes to have him. Rather, he said, “This is the strength of his god—his own,” because he himself is his own god, his own maker—something, indeed, which he dared to say. Thus in Ezekiel he is rebuked under the name of Pharaoh in these words: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh [Col. 0599B] of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say, ‘The river is mine, and I made myself’” (Ezek. 29). And elsewhere the Lord says against him: “You have said, ‘I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God’” (ibid., ch. 28).

Therefore there is no doubt that he of whom these things are said is the devil himself, and the passage thus concludes: “This is the strength of his god—his own.” Now let us follow the words themselves in order: “And he shall gather captivity as the sand, and he shall triumph over kings,” and so forth. I am not unaware that many of the things said here, or said previously, may be understood of Nebuchadnezzar; but because I have chosen once for all to follow apostolic authority—for, as stated above, the Apostle Paul refers to this prophecy when he says to the Jews, “See that there come not upon you that [Col. 0599C] which is spoken in the prophets” (Acts 13), and so forth—I confess that my mind does not willingly return to that fleshly Nebuchadnezzar. This is especially so since Habakkuk is read somewhere to have been a contemporary of Daniel, at whose time the events that we read concerning Nebuchadnezzar had already happened, rather than being future (Dan. 14).

Nevertheless, whether this prophecy was composed before or after that Nebuchadnezzar gathered Judah into captivity, no one ought to be ignorant that he bore the type of the devil, and that under his name the devil is condemned in the holy Scriptures, just as he is under the name of Pharaoh and under the name of Assyria, in their respective places and times.

Therefore, “he shall gather,” he says—that is, he shall not cease gathering—“captivity as the sand”: the devil, captor of the human race, for as long as [Col. 0599D] the human race endures in this world. He began to gather in Adam, and from him he does not cease, nor will cease until the end of the age, to gather captivity as the sand—that is, an innumerable captivity. For who could count the captivity of the human race which he has gathered and will gather, even though those whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son have now been set free into faith in Christ? (Rom. 8). And if there is less cause for concern about the rest of the multitude of humankind, still the prophet, because of human affection, had cause to grieve for his own people. For the Lord himself, seeing the city, wept over it (Luke 19), plainly considering the double death justly about to overtake it: the double captivity of souls and bodies. [Col. 0600A]

Likewise, if we rightly weigh what has already been said—that the Apostle Paul looked to the present passage against the contemptuous Jews, saying, “See, therefore, that there come not upon you what was spoken in the prophecy,” and so forth—the same must be understood concerning his laughter over every fortress, and concerning the words, “the tyrants shall be his objects of ridicule.” We gladly receive that Paul understood it thus, and that Christ, who spoke in him, wished it so, as though he said: “See that this does not come upon you: that the devil, through the hands of the Chaldeans, that is, the Romans—for at that time Rome was another Babylon—gather from you captivity as the sand; that it does not come upon you that, while he triumphs over kings, your own tyrants, your seditious and utterly wicked leaders, become his objects of ridicule; that it does not come upon you [Col. 0600B] that he should laugh with his deceitful smile and bitter jest over every one of your fortresses—over Antonia, Phasael, Mariamne, Hippicus, Machaerus, Masada, and all your other strongholds; over the Temple and over the city—and should heap up a mound and take it.” In all this he displayed, as one who had before his eyes the great and astonishing spectacle of death on which he feeds, as much or as great a spectacle as is nowhere recorded among any people or nation, if we survey all the histories and tragedies of the nations.

Let us read Josephus (*Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 46) as far as the destruction of the last fortress, called Masada; and it is evident that there the devil had something at which to laugh. For that was the final event: when the mound had been [Col. 0600C] heaped up and the fortress was being taken, the Sicarii within, nine hundred and sixty in number together with women and children, followed the counsel of their leader Eleazar. Believing that they would obtain the reward of eternal blessedness if they slaughtered themselves rather than permitted themselves to be taken alive, they acted as follows. Ten were chosen by lot from their number to strike down all the rest. The whole company lay prostrate, arranged together and embracing their wives and children with their hands, offering themselves with prepared mind to be slain, while those ten performed that most wretched service. Then, since the slayers themselves were ten, nine submitted themselves to be killed by the one. That final man, having surveyed the multitude of the dead lest someone perhaps remain alive amid so great a [Col. 0600D] slaughter and need his hand, and having learned that all had been killed, set fire to the royal buildings; then, driving his sword violently through his whole body by his own hand, he fell beside his own people. Only two women and five children hid in the underground passages; from them the Romans learned how the event had occurred and were amazed.

This was the final, but not the only, madness of Jewish death. How greatly, do you suppose, did the devil laugh at such things? And although he had things at which to laugh among other nations also, this was a unique spectacle, without comparison: there he himself, undoubtedly acting in the Romans, heaped up the mound, took that city Jerusalem, and carried away from it a captive multitude of souls. For, as Josephus also testifies, it came to pass that the city, having been advanced to the highest degree of prosperity, was cast down into the uttermost [Col. 0601A] disasters. In short, I do not doubt that, after all the adverse events of the ages, any calamities, if compared with those of the Jews, would be surpassed.

It follows: “Then the spirit shall be changed, and shall pass through and fall. This is the strength of his god—his own.” Lest you think that he of whom he spoke is a human being, he calls him “spirit,” undoubtedly wishing the devil to be understood. For he did not say, “Then his spirit shall be changed,” which might fittingly be said of some human being; rather, “Then,” he says, “the spirit shall be changed”—namely, that spirit of whom I speak, who is not flesh but spirit.

But what is it to say, “Then the spirit shall be changed,” except as though he said, “Then that spirit shall not be God”? For this is chiefly the difference between the false god and him who alone is the true God: the former is mutable and varies through many accidents; the true God is unchangeable [Col. 0601B] and subject to no accidents. Most beautifully, therefore, by this expression, “then he shall be changed,” that spirit is denied to be God. And why, or in what respect, is he denied to be God by the words “then,” that is, “at that time he shall be changed”? Clearly for a certain and great reason: because formerly that spirit was thought to be god by his own presumption. Hence here immediately, reproachfully, he is called “his own god,” in the words, “This is the strength of his god—his own”: that is, of him who is his own god, saying, “I made myself” (Ezek. 29), as we have already recalled above with the prophet’s testimony.

When this prophecy was composed, that spirit and his demons were worshipped as god, and were adored in images; and then he was truly a god to himself in his folly. Indeed, “he is exalted above all [Col. 0601C] that is called God or that is worshipped,” says the Apostle (2 Thess. 2). For it was to happen that immediately after the laughter with which he laughed over that Temple, over its city and fortifications, over Judea—in which alone God had until then been born—while he was regarded among the Gentiles as a god, immediately, I say, he would be convicted of vanity, and such a change would occur concerning him that he would be recognized not as God but as the devil, and would lose that greatest court of his, namely the Roman Empire. Conversely, God—or the Son of God, Christ—in place of the one Temple over which he was justly permitted to laugh, and in place of the one people, Judea, among whom he ought to have been known, would possess innumerable temples throughout the world and be worshipped by all nations, once that one had been expelled [Col. 0601D] both from the temples and from the hearts of those nations themselves.

“Then,” therefore, he says, “the spirit shall be changed”—that is, by a great change, so that the mutable devil, who was thought to be and wished to appear the unchangeable God, may be shown to be mutable. This change will befall him after the likeness of that Chaldean, or king of the Chaldeans, who, puffed up by the same spirit, said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built into the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” [265] Immediately he was changed into the madness of an ox: “You shall eat grass like an ox,” says the heavenly voice, “and seven times shall be changed over you” (Dan. 4). After that likeness, I say, “the spirit shall be changed,” so that he too will eat grass like an ox, as was said concerning him [Col. 0602A] to blessed Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he shall eat grass like an ox” (Job 40).

Nor will he be changed in this way only; rather, “he shall also pass through,” he says, “and fall.” Therefore this is not a good change, whose end is that he shall pass through and fall. It is a perverse change, because it was not made by him who alone is unchangeable. For apart from him everything that exists is mutable; but he made the change of some things and did not make that of others. He made the change of the good into good—for example, that of the heavens, that is, of the saints, of whom it is written in the Psalm: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; all shall grow old like a garment. And as a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101 [102]). [Col. 0602B]

This change of the heavens is good, and the unchangeable God brings it about—the same change which we hope for when the dead rise incorruptible. One of those heavens, the Apostle Paul, says: “And we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15), that is, we shall be made incapable of suffering. Hence the title of the forty-fourth Psalm: “For the end, for those who shall be changed”—understand, by the perfect change which shall be in the future, when they are converted from sorrow to joy, from imperfection to perfection, however contemptible and despised they may seem in this world. It is not reproached in them, nor is it reproachable; indeed, it is promised and proclaimed with joy that those whose Lord is God shall be changed. But it shall be reproached in him who is his own god because he shall be changed; and it is added: “[Col. 0602C] and shall pass through and fall.”

But if someone objects concerning the heavens already mentioned that they too shall pass through, because it was said, “They shall perish, but you remain,” he should know that their perishing is their temporary passing away according to the flesh. At the same time, let him observe the order of the statements: this spirit is first changed, and then shall pass through and fall. But those heavens first perish, and then, “You, Lord, shall change them, and they shall be changed.” The end of this one is to fall, because he was changed through his own fault; the end of theirs is to be changed, because their strength—that is, their hope—is laid up in heaven.

How far, then, shall he pass through, or what shall he pass through? He shall pass through his number; he shall pass through until he completes his number. For he has his number, [Col. 0602D] and this is wisdom, as it is said in the Apocalypse: “Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast” (Rev. 13). For it is the number of a human being, and his number is six hundred and sixty-six. The number of a human being is six, because the human being was made on the sixth day. But the number seven is in some manner the number of God, because he rested on the seventh day. The number of every human being who does not attain the Lord’s rest—“as I swore,” he says, “in my wrath, that they shall enter into my rest”—of all, I say, who abuse either God’s creation or themselves, and do not possess the love of the Creator, or who serve the creature rather than the Creator, is six. But in the devil himself this number is tripled—indeed, multiplied tenfold three times—because the number is six hundred and sixty-six. For what reason? [Col. 0603A] Clearly because his judgment is threefold: he has been judged a third time, so that the heavenly Majesty may fittingly say concerning him, “Three times I swore in my wrath, that he shall enter into my rest” (Isa. 14).

For of old he was cast out of heaven because of pride, because he exalted himself against God. Then he received the judgment of a curse in the serpent through whom he deceived humankind (Gen. 3). Thirdly, he is to be struck with an increase of judgment or condemnation in that man of sin, the son of perdition, whom he is about to enter (2 Thess. 2). He shall pass through as far as that, and then at last, when his number has been completed, “he shall fall,” he says—namely, as the Lord says concerning him to blessed Job, because he shall be cast down while all look on (Job 40).

“This,” he says, “is the strength of his god—his own”; and this is the expression of one reproaching him: “This is strength”—that is, such is his strength, certainly a deceitful [Col. 0603B] strength, a vain strength. For is it true strength to ride, to gather captivity as though of human beings, to triumph over kings and have tyrants as objects of ridicule, to laugh over every fortress, heaping up a mound and taking it, and then to be changed, to pass through, and to fall? This is not true strength, but blind arrogance; not lofty omnipotence, but swollen impotence.

Yet for the time being, before he falls or is cast down, as has already been said, into the eternal fire prepared for him and his angels (Matt. 25), he appears strong to himself because he is thought able to do something—strong, I say, and god, exalting himself above everything called god or worshipped as god, as was said above; his own god, and, as he himself says, made by himself (2 Thess. 2). [Col. 0603C] Therefore the Judge, the Word of God, branded him with ridicule in the final word. For when he had said, “This is the strength of his god,” he added, “his own”—that is, of one who made himself, as he presumptuously claimed for himself. But this has already been shown above from the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. 29).

Now, having considered these matters, let us hear what follows: “Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And we shall not die. O Lord, you have set him for judgment, and you have established him as strong in order to correct.” These words, and the rest down to: “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the fortress, and I shall look to see what may be said to me and what I may answer to him who rebukes me”—the prophet speaks in his own person. For immediately [Col. 0603D] he adds: “And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, that he who reads it may run. For the vision is still far off, and it shall appear at the end and shall not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it shall surely come and shall not be late.”

These words, therefore—“Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, and shall we not die? O Lord, you have set him for judgment, and established him as strong in order to correct”—he gave in reply to what he had heard inwardly, what he had heard in the Spirit. He had heard the person of Christ, Son of Man and Son of God, first speaking from the weakness in which God forsook him: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry and you will not hear?” and so forth, down to: “Then the spirit shall be changed, and shall pass through and fall. This is the strength of his god—his own.”

To those two utterances, [Col. 0604A] the former belonging to weakness, the faithful prophet returned these two answers. For when he says, “Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And we shall not die,” this is rightly understood here as the voice of faith and confession, the voice of devotion and of a compassionate mind, a mind bent and inclined toward the agony of the Son of the son of man agonizing in his passion—when an angel from heaven appeared to strengthen him, and, praying more at length, “his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.” He therefore speaks to him in such a manner as the Holy Spirit, who speaks through him, wishes each of us to speak whenever we recall that agony or passion and contemplate with mindful recollection him hanging on the cross for our sake.

For in these words there is confession of truth [Col. 0604B]—not just any confession, but confession with wonder, and wonder [266] with confession. “Are you not,” he says, “from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One?” Are you not the Word who was in the beginning with God, and God the Word, and the Word made flesh? And because you have died, will it come about for us that we shall not die? Truly, you are from the beginning. For another Scripture also says so, which the Apostle likewise recalls to the Hebrews as spoken in your person: “And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; all shall grow old as a garment; and as a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101 [102]; Heb. 1).

Take courage, therefore, O my Lord, my Holy [Col. 0604C] One, because it is not unto folly for you that God appears to have forsaken you; rather, it is unto great wisdom. For great shall be the fruit of your death, because we shall not die. For even if the heavens—that is, the saints—perish by bodily death, you, the first to resume the flesh, shall remain; and those growing old like a garment through the condition of mortality, you shall change like a cloak by the true resurrection of that same flesh, and they shall be changed, so that thereafter they may always, unto eternity, be incorruptible and incapable of suffering.

Moreover, this further point which he immediately adds—“Lord, you have appointed him for judgment, and established him strong for correction”—he worthily addresses to the same Lord Christ, who lives by the power of God, whose weakness, taken from us, has passed through [Col. 0604D]. For, “You have appointed him for judgment; you have established him strong for correction.” Whom do we suppose this to mean, if not that mocking devil, concerning whom he had just heard the same Lord say: “He shall triumph over kings, and tyrants shall be a laughing-stock to him; he shall laugh at every stronghold, heap up a rampart, and take it. Then his spirit shall change and pass away and fall—this is the strength of his god?” He says: “Lord, you have appointed him for judgment; you have established him strong in order to correct him,” plainly after the likeness of Pharaoh, to whom you said: “For this very reason I have set you up, that I may show my power in you and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. IX).

Therefore, not merely him, but especially him, Lord, you have appointed for judgment, that you might display your power upon him and that your name might be known [Col. 0605A], not only throughout all the earth, but also throughout every heaven and all the earth. Where did you appoint him, or in what did you establish him? For we must not suppose that your appointing is to do evil, or that your establishing is to will someone to be proud. You did not appoint him in that way, nor did you establish him strong in that way; nor did you do so to any of the wicked or powerful men. Certainly you did not make Pharaoh, Asshur or Nebuchadnezzar, the exceedingly proud Haman, Antiochus, or Herod evil, nor did you will them to be proud. Rather, when they were evil and proud, you placed them on high—and this for judgment; you established them strong—and this for correction.

For the person corrected for this purpose must be known, so that others may be corrected or instructed by his example. Where, then [Col. 0605B], did you appoint him for judgment, and where did you establish him strong in order to correct him? On the holy mountain of God, just as you yourself say in Ezekiel: “You were the outspread and protecting cherub; and I placed you upon God’s holy mountain. You walked in the midst of fiery stones; you were perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you” (Ezek. XXVIII).

You knew what he was like; and because you knew that you wished to correct him, you placed him there, so that he might first become known and only then be corrected. For unless he had been known, not so many would have been instructed by his example. The same may be said of Pharaoh: unless he had been raised to the kingdom, today we should not know so well either him or the correction by which he was corrected. There you appointed him to his own judgment; there you established him strong [Col. 0605C]—strong, I say, like a cedar, having the foundation of his own root firm.

Not only strong, but also beautiful and great. For likewise in Ezekiel you say concerning him: “Lord God, behold Asshur, like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches, thick with foliage, lofty in height, with its top raised among dense boughs. No tree in the paradise of God was comparable to it or to its beauty, for I made it splendid” (Ezek. XXXI). Therefore, it is not to be censured but is rather worthy of praise, because it is just, when you now say: “Then the spirit shall change and pass away and fall.”

Nor would I dare to censure this either [Col. 0606A]: that among the other works of his tyranny, by which he tyrannizes while acting in this world, “he shall laugh at every stronghold”—especially at my stronghold, over my people, over the Temple and the city Jerusalem—“he shall heap up a rampart and take it.” Nor, I say, in censuring this, but rather I say: “Your eyes are pure, so that you do not see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity.” By contrast, the eyes of perverse judges are impure; and therefore woe to them, because they see evil and look upon iniquity, while they call evil good and good evil (Isa. V).

This reason alone is sufficient, if I ask—or if anyone else asks—why you allowed him to laugh over that stronghold or city and take it, though it is your people and a place consecrated to you; and though [Col. 0606B] you are merciful by nature, especially since, seeing that city and perceiving the devil’s mocking laughter threatening it, you wept over it (Luke XIX). If anyone, I say, asks why this is so, this reason or answer is sufficient, whether for me or for any other person.

For example, to the Apostle Paul when he says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. IX), and so forth—such grief ought to accept this explanation, so that it may say: “Your eyes are pure, so that you do not see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity.” That is to say: you cannot favor those who do evil, those who commit iniquity [Col. 0606C], even though they are your kinsmen according to the flesh, just as our kinsmen are the kinsmen of the prophets and apostles, who have great sorrow and continual grief for them.

What we say here, “you cannot look upon iniquity,” you confirm in the Gospel when you say: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John V). For you had already stated that in your judgment there is no respect of persons, saying: “Those who have done good shall go forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V); and it must be understood: without distinction between Jew and Greek.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0605]

[Col. 0605D] 267 A person speaking to God and wishing that so great a Majesty should carry out his will must possess some true strength—that is, righteousness—so that he asks none of those things which it would not be fitting for the righteous God to do, nor wishes Him to remember mercy in such a way as to forget judgment. Thus Abraham could reason with God, though he confessed himself to be dust and ashes, because, when interceding for Sodom, he added nothing beyond what was just. For it would not have been just before God for them to be spared if at least ten righteous persons were not found among so great a multitude [Col. 0606D] (Gen. XVIII).

Thus Jacob could wrestle with God and be, or be called, strong against God, because in wrestling he wished to extract nothing unjust; indeed, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, he demanded the blessing by which he hoped to be justified (Gen. XXXII). Thus Moses could hold back God when He said, “Let me go,” because he did not demand of Him what would be unjust—that He should dismiss unpunished the authors of sin in the matter of the calf—but that He should judge or punish them in such a way that He nevertheless remained truthful and just in what He had promised Abraham and confirmed by an oath in renewing that promise [Col. 0607A] (Exod. XXXII).

So too this man, in accordance with the name Habakkuk, which is interpreted “wrestler,” can wrestle with God and speak as if in rebuke, because he does not defend the wicked or unrighteous men, over whom he saw that the devil had been permitted to make sport; rather, conceding that judgment upon them was just, as he said last: “Your eyes are pure, so that you do not see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity,” he advances in his argument with God only this: while the unrighteous are punished in this world—as the impious Jews were punished by the hand of the Romans—many righteous persons also suffer as though they were unrighteous, because powerful men of this world are driven by that same spirit of which the Lord Himself spoke above. He begins thus: “Why do you not look upon those who act wickedly, and remain silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself?”

We undertake to treat these matters and what follows [Col. 0607B] with before our eyes the desire of those saints—of whom this man is one—who desire Him that is to come, and the second coming of Him to whom he speaks. When He comes, it will no longer be permitted either for the unrighteous to act unrighteously or for the wicked to devour one more righteous than himself. For what else does this man say and cry than what the souls of those slain beneath the altar say and cry, “because of the word of God and because of the testimony which they hold,” crying with a loud voice and saying: “How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. VI).

Finally, is not what was said to them—that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow-servants and brothers should be fulfilled—similar to what was answered to this man: “It will appear at the end, and it will not lie; if it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late” [Col. 0607C] (Hab. II)? Therefore, since he is a prophet, there is no doubt that he speaks of kings to arise far in the future, looking toward the times of Christ who was to come. Thus it is fitting to understand this complaint, “Why do you not look upon those who act wickedly?” and the rest, as the groaning of one because of the persecutions or oppressions which saints and righteous people endured under that same beastly empire under which Christ Himself suffered, and under which, in vengeance for His blood, that famous destruction of Jerusalem occurred.

“Why,” he says, “do you not look upon those who act wickedly?”—that is, the leaders of the impious, who establish impious laws and decrees of iniquity throughout the whole world. “And why are you silent, O Lord, while the wicked devours [Col. 0607D] one more righteous than himself?” For any wicked ruler in this world, a satellite of the devil—as Nero was, and very many after him—those whom, I say, he could not strip of piety and make firm in his own service, he swallowed up bodily by inflicting death upon them. This was the wicked man’s devouring one more righteous than himself: You remained silent; You deferred vengeance, although their blood cries daily to You.

“And you make man like the fishes of the sea, and like a creeping thing which has no ruler.” Here one must understand: Why do You so make them? Why do You permit this to happen? And as though someone asked in what respect He made human beings like fishes of the sea and creeping things without a ruler, he immediately adds: “He lifted up all with his hook, drew him in his net, and gathered him into his dragnet.” And the sense is this: just as fish or creeping creatures of the sea have no ruler, so human beings seem to have no care from You, nor to be governed by Your providence; because, just as a hook lifts up everything, a dragnet draws, and a net surrounds or gathers everything—both what is good and what is bad among fishes—so that wicked man reduces to his own power everything good and everything bad in humankind. You are silent; You permit him to rage against righteous people, so that they are thought not to have God [Col. 0608A].

And this is strange, although they have and know You as God, and cry daily to You, saying: “Be merciful to our sins for Your name’s sake. Let not the nations perhaps say, ‘Where is their God?’ Let the vengeance for the blood of Your servants which has been shed enter into Your sight; let the groaning of those in chains come before You” (Ps. LXXVIII). Meanwhile You remain silent, and that wicked man is allowed to lift up everything with his hook, draw everything in his dragnet, gather everything into his net; though wicked, he obtains dominion over all, both righteous and unrighteous, and has power to devour or kill them.

“Therefore he will rejoice and exult, and for that reason he will sacrifice to his dragnet and offer sacrifice to his net, because through them his portion has been made fat and his food choice” [Col. 0608B]. There is no doubt, nor is it unknown, that a wicked man enjoying great dominion rejoiced greatly and, trusting in the abundance of his riches, exulted greatly—so much that, disdaining the human condition, he preferred and commanded that he be called a god. We may say this, for example, of Gaius, as Josephus also writes (*Antiquities*, book XXVIII, ch. 16):

> “As time went on, lifted up by the greatness of his rank, he lost human understanding and wished himself to seem like the Godhead, dishonouring the true divinity. For he ordered his own statue to be erected at Jerusalem in the temple of God; when the Jews resisted, he compelled them, unwilling though they were, after defeating them in battle.”

“Therefore,” he says, “he will rejoice and exult”: plainly, with foolish joy and deceitful exultation. Not every wicked person will rejoice in such a way or exult so greatly as to imagine himself God or wish to be regarded as God; but he will do what follows: “Therefore he will sacrifice to his dragnet and offer sacrifice to his net.” What is the wicked man’s dragnet, and what is his net? Although something else may also be understood, above all [Col. 0608D] his gold and silver are his dragnet and his net. For in nothing does the wicked person prevail more than when he has abundant gold or silver. Men gladly enclose themselves in such dragnets, and greedy people willingly gather themselves into such a net; they call blessed the wicked person whose these things are, readily follow him, and embrace his dominion with submissive hands.

Knowing this, a certain Antony, ill-famed because of Cleopatra, when he arrived at Actium, having prepared for himself a naval force, and found nearly a third part of the rowers consumed by hunger, was unmoved: “Only let the oars remain safe,” he said, “for rowers will not be lacking so long as Greece has men.” For he had begun upon Artabanes, king of Armenia, whom he had compelled, bound with a silver chain, to confess the royal treasures [Col. 0609A]. Once these had been taken away, furnished, of course, as if with a great dragnet and a great net, he hastened to enclose and draw to himself both East and West—in short, the entire Roman empire—while he himself was caught in the devil’s net, namely in love for the aforesaid Cleopatra, queen of Egypt.

Therefore, since the saying of the wise man is also true: “All things obey money” (Eccles. X), I would rightly say that the wicked man’s dragnet and net are his gold and silver. Moreover, did he not make gods for himself out of gold and silver? Did he not make images and sacrifice to them? Indeed, he invited peoples subject to himself to sacrifice, compelled them to worship, and killed the person unwilling to do this—the worshipper of the Creator alone. Thus, in accordance with this man’s complaint, the wicked devoured one more righteous than himself [Col. 0609B]. Therefore he truly sacrificed to his dragnet and offered sacrifice to his net. For what reason? “Because,” he says, “through it his portion has been made fat and his food choice.”

For he put all his hope in gold and silver, as has already been said; he did what he wished with people, acquired glory among them, gained power, attained honour, and fulfilled his pleasures. To abound in these things was surely for his portion to be made fat. He also ensnared many of those who seemed religious in his same dragnet or net, and made them like himself; in respect of these persons, or of such persons, it is now rightly said: “And his food is choice.”

“For this reason, then, he spreads out his dragnet, and never ceases to kill nations” [Col. 0609C]. He seems by repeating himself to have said, “he spreads out his dragnet,” what he had previously said, “he drew him in his dragnet.” Nevertheless, it is plainly evident that the wicked man had, or has, two dragnets: one by which he captured peoples and nations voluntarily—this is gold and silver, as has already been said; the other by which he also compelled unwilling persons—this is every decree of his wicked laws, which he spread throughout the world, commanding all to be killed who would not sacrifice to his dragnet and net, his silver and gold, his golden and silver images, as has already been said. Hence there immediately follows: “And he never ceases to kill nations.”

Finally, this is the sum of the complaint: that by shedding the blood of righteous people the wicked devours one more righteous than himself. Nebuchadnezzar is recorded as the first to do this [Col. 0609D]. For before him, although there were those who sacrificed to gold and silver, no one is recorded as having spread out his dragnet in such a manner as to issue a law for nations to be killed if they would not sacrifice. He spread it out thus: “It is commanded to you, peoples, tribes, and languages: at the hour when you hear the sound of trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and worship the golden statue which King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. But if anyone does not fall down and worship, let him at that same hour be cast into the furnace of burning fire” (Dan. III).

The Lord indeed seemed there to remain silent while the wicked devoured one more righteous than himself, but not altogether. He permitted the three boys to be cast into the fire, certainly men more righteous than that wicked man; but after the three had been thrown in, four walked unbound in the midst of the fire, and “the appearance of the fourth,” says the very man who saw it, “is like a Son of God” [Col. 0610A] (ibid.). Yet how great thereafter was to be, and was, the devouring of righteous persons and slaughter of nations for the same cause!

Accordingly, this man alone does not cry to God, saying, “Why do you not look?” and the rest which has been stated thus far; all saints and all righteous persons so devoured also cry and say with a loud voice: “How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. VI). Nor do their souls alone cry in that age; rather, with them and for them, the Church of the living in this present age cries to Him, desiring the coming of the Judge and Saviour, who will render righteous judgment concerning all things [Col. 0610B].

It follows, CHAPTER II: “I will stand upon my watch, and plant my step upon the fortification, and I will contemplate, to see what shall be said to me and what I shall answer to the one rebuking me.” Isaiah says something similar: “Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand, standing continually by day, and I stand upon my watch through all the nights” (Isa. XXI). And truly, one who speaks to God and asks an account of His judgments must stand above his watch and plant his step upon the fortification, lest perhaps he slip in speech concerning His Spirit, or say anything beyond what is proper.

“Do not speak rashly,” says Ecclesiastes, “and let not your heart be swift to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few” (Eccles. V).

“I will stand,” he says, “upon my watch, and plant my step upon the fortification.” But what is that watch, or what is that fortification? Surely, true humility of mind. That virtue is indeed a firm fortification and the faithful guard of all virtues. Nor could anyone easily find another place or another rock from which Moses was worthy at least to see God’s back, when He said to him: “Behold, there is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock. And when my glory passes by, I will put you in the cleft of the rock” [Col. 0610C] (Exod. XXXIII), and so forth.

Finally, you do not find that place named there, but the Spirit of the same God named it beautifully and magnificently in the Psalmist: namely, the exceeding humility of mind. For He says: “And He said that He would destroy them, had not Moses His chosen stood in the breach before Him” (Ps. CV). Now He Himself testifies that such a place—that is, the breach—is, as has been said, the exceeding humility of mind, when He says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).
