Knowing, therefore, that the firmness of such a place is safe, and that from it it is best to wrestle with God, this man says: “I will stand upon my watch [Col. 0610D] 269 and plant my step upon the fortification, and I will contemplate, to see what shall be said to me and what I shall answer to the one rebuking me.” Just as Moses, already mentioned, in the same place contemplated God’s back, that he might see what would be said to him and what he would answer to the one rebuking him and saying, “Go, descend; your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, has sinned” (Exod. XXXII), and so forth.

Finally, this man too contemplated with his step firmly planted, lest the foot of pride should come upon him, and saw what would be said to him and what he would answer to the one rebuking him—that is, pressing him with holy fear, good and necessary fear. For it follows: “And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, so that he who reads it may run; for the vision is still far off, and it will appear at the end and will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late.”

These things and what follows were said to him while he was attentive, saying: “And I will contemplate, to see what shall be said to me.” After this he shows that he found what he should answer to the one rebuking him: “O Lord,” he says, “I have heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. III), and so forth. Therefore, because he stood firmly and was strong in demanding, he saw what he contemplated in order to see [Col. 0611A].

For he says: “And the Lord answered me”—that is, He showed me, and with the prophetic eye I saw what end awaited those who act wickedly, and how He who now seems silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself would speak and judge. Then, so that others too might know to hope, He said to me: “Write the vision”—that is, write what you saw; write what I answered you. Write, I say, the vision, not obscurely or secretly, but “make it plain upon tablets,” that is, in plain and manifest speech, “so that he who reads it may run,” with nothing hindering his understanding, in this manner: “For the vision is still far off, and it will appear at the end and will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late” [Col. 0611B].

What here is not plain and open to understanding? “The vision,” he says, “is still far off”: that is, He will not immediately come, seen upon earth and conversing with human beings; He went far away, ascended into heaven, while the angels said: “Thus shall He come, as you saw Him ascending into heaven” (Acts I). He is still far away; He has gone far away because He was received into heaven. But He will appear at the end and will not lie—concerning all that He spoke while conversing with human beings. For example: “The powers of heaven,” He says, “will be shaken, and then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI); or: “You shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. XXVI), and similar sayings.

Whoever desires to see Him thus coming, and also despises the present life in which he cannot see Him, and says with the Apostle, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Col. 0611C] (Phil. I)—whoever he may be—should also hear this and know it was said to him: “If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come”; that is, it will most certainly come. And when it comes, it will not be present as something late, but all the past time will appear to have been—as true as it is—of exceedingly brief duration.

Meanwhile, until He appears at the end, the Gospel shall be preached to every creature. “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark, last chapter). This is what immediately follows: “Behold, the unbeliever: his soul shall not be right within himself; but the righteous shall live by his faith.” Behold, He will appear—that is, He will appear quickly—and one who does not believe His Gospel, even if he works greatly, his soul will not be right, that is, it will be condemned. The Apostle testifies to this by sound and manifest reasoning in this brief testimony: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it,” namely, the Gospel, “from faith unto faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous shall live by faith’” [Col. 0611D] (Rom. I). And elsewhere: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. II).

And who is the unbeliever except the proud? For pride is an efficient cause of unbelief. Hence he immediately adds: “And just as wine deceives one who drinks it, so shall the proud man be, and he shall not be adorned; he who has enlarged his soul like hell, and is himself like death and is not filled, and will gather to himself all nations and heap up to himself all peoples.” Therefore pride is a great drunkenness, and it so overturns the mind and weakens every power of sense and reason that it cannot distinguish what it hears.

The Lord Himself confirms this in the Gospel with words of this kind: “How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John V). By saying, “you receive glory from one another,” He meant, “you who are proud.” He most beautifully avoided harshness of expression without passing over the meaning. Therefore, if someone asked what it is to be proud, let him answer: “to receive glory from one another”; he has certainly used a true, beautiful, and irrefutable definition.

Moreover, the sense of this saying—what it is to receive glory—is expanded by the present words: “he who enlarged his soul like hell,” namely, always seeking greater things; “and is himself like death and is not filled,” namely with money; “and will gather to himself all nations and heap up to himself all peoples” [Col. 0612C], as Nebuchadnezzar did in his own time, Alexander the Great in his own time, and Rome in its own time—which, as was said above, was another Babylon.

Did not all greedy and ambitious people of those kingdoms receive glory from one another, and, for the reception of glory, rush against one another so that one might seize glory from another? Truly, just as wine deceives one who drinks it, so people of that kind were and are deceived by the spirit of pride; they are not adorned with the ornament of faith, but are naked, abhorring the humility of the cross as contrary to the spirit of pride by which they are intoxicated or deceived.

What will become of them when He appears at the end? Or rather, to follow the chapter set forth in the singular number: how will the proud man be judged, and how will he not be adorned? He says: “Will not all these take up a parable against him, and the speech of his riddles? And it shall be said: ‘Woe to him who multiplies what is not his—how long?—and loads dense mud upon himself. Will not those who bite you suddenly rise up, and those who tear you awake, and you will become plunder to them? Because you despoiled many nations, all who remain of the peoples will despoil you, because of the blood of a man and the iniquity of land, city, and all who dwell in it’” [Col. 0612D].

By asking, he more forcefully affirms when he says, “Will not all these”—that is, the peoples, or those remaining from all peoples—“take up a parable against him,” and so forth. Sacred Scripture is accustomed to call the righteous or elect “the remaining” or “the remnant,” as there: “And everyone left in Zion and remaining in Jerusalem shall be called holy, everyone who is written for life in Jerusalem” (Isa. XL). And elsewhere: “That which has escaped of the house of Judah and that which remains of Israel shall take root downward and bear fruit upward, because a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem, and salvation from Mount Zion” (Isa. XXXVII).

Therefore here too, those of whom he says, “Because you despoiled many nations, all who remain of the peoples will despoil you,” we rightly understand as saints or righteous persons who survived or survive—whom the aforesaid proud man, having enlarged his soul like hell and like death, could not devour, that is, draw into consent with his own soul or will [Col. 0613B], though he strove and laboured to do so by fire, sword, famine, beasts, and every kind of torment. This was what Nebuchadnezzar first began, as stated above, when he proclaimed punishment to the peoples, tribes, and languages which he had gathered and heaped up to himself: “If anyone does not fall down and worship the statue, he shall at that same hour be cast into the furnace of burning fire” (Dan. III).

How many similar things, indeed greater things, did the greater power of the other Babylon—that is, Rome—do? How did it gather all nations to itself and heap all peoples to itself, and with how many deaths proposed did it wish to eradicate from human memory this vision, of which it is now said: “It will appear at the end and will not lie”? Truly, the proud man—say Nero or Decius, or indeed the devil himself, who worked the ministry of iniquity through them—expanded like death and hell and devoured, so far as lay in him, absolutely all nations. Yet there are and shall be some who, marvelling at the felicity of their outcome and the blessedness of their escape, and looking at what they escaped from, cry out and all say: “If the Lord had not been in us, let Israel now say; if the Lord had not been in us when men rose against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” [Col. 0613C] (Ps. CXXIII), and so forth.

“Will not all these”—that is, against the proud man, indeed against the devil himself and against the whole multitude of the sons of pride whose head he is—“take up a parable and the speech of his riddles?” For “the saints shall judge nations and rule peoples” (Wisdom III); or, as it is written elsewhere, “They shall stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labours” (ibid. V).

How will these take up the parable and rule peoples? Or what is this parable and what is its riddle? The parable is the holy prophetic or legal Scripture, because almost all of it, or the greater part, is full of parabolic and enigmatic expressions. A parable is a comparison drawn from unlike things. For example, when the word of God or a judicial sentence is compared to a material sword, as in the psalm, where we sing concerning these remnant ones—that is, all saints—“The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords [Col. 0614A] are in their hands,” and so forth, as far as: “that they may execute on them the judgment written.”

Moreover, a riddle is an obscure proposition which is not easily understood unless it is explained, as is this: “Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. XIV). Expressions of this kind are found everywhere in the Scriptures, and they serve not only to conceal pearls from swine, but also so that good minds may be exercised by their difficulties. “For the wise man hearing will become wiser, and the intelligent will possess guidance. He will perceive a parable and its interpretation, the words of the wise and their riddles” (Prov. I).

Therefore, he says, they will take up against him a parable and the speech of his riddles: that is, they will fulfil Scripture and make manifest its obscurities, which are difficult and scarcely understood by few people until first the things signified in them occur, and thus what was obscure is opened by the event itself. As if you asked what kind of utterance that is which he calls a parable, he immediately adds: “And it shall be said: ‘Woe to him who multiplies what is not his—how long?—and loads dense mud upon himself.’” For it is parabolic that he calls multiplied riches “dense mud.”

Likewise, what follows—“Will not those who bite you suddenly rise up, and those who tear you awake, and you will become plunder to them?”—is parabolic or enigmatic, because these remnant persons now under discussion, namely all saints or righteous persons, do not customarily, as the letter sounds, bite or tear with their teeth or seize with their hands [Col. 0614C].

It should also be known that this will indeed then be said, but such a thing will not then begin to be said—when He appears at the end, when He who departed from here as one judged comes as judge. It has already begun to be said from the time when He departed, commanding that the Gospel be preached to every creature. “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his—how long?—and loads dense mud upon himself” began to be said from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, in which, the Apostle says, “the wrath of God from heaven is revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (Rom. I). At the end that same woe will be pronounced so that he goes into eternal fire.

Likewise, through the Gospel it has begun to happen that these remnant ones suddenly rise, bite the wicked man, awake and tear him, and that he becomes plunder to them, so that they separate many from him. This is to bite and eat, in accordance with what was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” [Col. 0614D] (Acts X). But at the end it will happen in such a way that a sword comes forth from their mouth, and that two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance upon him (Ps. CXLIX), or the judgment written.

For that converting many from ungodliness is here the biting and tearing of the wicked man’s body is also proved by the fact that the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will his friends cut him in pieces? Will merchants divide him? And will you fill nets with his skin, and fishers’ huts with his head?” (Job XL)—that is, as I will. This now happens for the good of those whom these teeth—such as are described in the Song when He says to the beloved, namely the Church, “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” [Col. 0615A] (Song IV)—these teeth, I say, namely the apostles or preachers, who are here called the remnant, draw, as if by eating, into their own body. But then what follows will happen for the harm of that same wicked man, who to his own harm rejected the desire of these teeth.

“Because you despoiled many nations, all who remain of the peoples will despoil you.” Though despoilings are inflicted in many ways, the worst of all is that by which a nation, people, or any human being is despoiled of the honour due to the one God, its Creator; then it is truly naked. Hence this passage in Exodus: “Moses therefore, seeing that the people had been made naked—for Aaron had despoiled them unto the shame of their filth and made them naked among their enemies” (Exod. XXXII). By “the shame of their filth” he means the guilt of the calf which they made; having made it, they were stripped of God’s help and grace.

How many nations and peoples did this wicked man, against whom these things are said, despoil in this manner? Therefore, because you despoiled many nations—that is, separated them from the Creator’s grace by such wicked persuasions—these remnant ones will despoil you from among them by judging, so that, just as you refused to be adorned by your Creator, you will likewise no longer be able to glory in that creature of God which you preferred [Col. 0615B].

And there is added further: “Because of the blood of a man, and the iniquity of land, city, and all who dwell in it.” The blood of a man is homicide, and this is indeed iniquity. But the “land” to which iniquity can be attributed is surely nothing other than a human being. Likewise, “city” means nothing other than those dwelling in it, since iniquity is not, nor can be, the iniquity of a city’s walls, buildings, or stones, but of the human beings dwelling in the city.

There thus appears to be here a trope which grammarians call in Greek *tautologia*, and in Latin *eloquium*: when one thing is signified by several words, so that the truth or greatness of the matter may be set forth more splendidly. Yet this also should be known: although every homicide is or has been an iniquity of this wicked man, the blood of the City is especially reckoned to him as an iniquity against God. I mean the City of God: formerly Jerusalem, where alone the temple of the Lord stood, and now the Catholic Church throughout the world, of which the Psalmist says, “The rush of the river makes glad the City of God” [Col. 0615C] (Ps. XLV).

The wicked Nebuchadnezzar, king of the first Babylon, shed the blood of that City. But the wicked Nero, emperor of the other Babylon, began to shed the blood of this City; of this Babylon Peter says in his epistle: “The Church which is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you” (I Pet. V). One city has been made out of both, according to faith and election; and the blood of this City of God is the iniquity of the Babylonian land, the city of the devil.

Among all bloodshed, the chief matter is the blood of the one man Jesus Christ, whom we rightly understand here when he says, “because of the blood of a man.” The Jews who shed it were and are a part of the body of the wicked man to whom it is said: “All who remain of the peoples will despoil you.” Finally, they too are especially despoiled and to be despoiled—especially, I say, and first—as the Apostle says: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of man that works evil” [Col. 0616A] (Rom. II): “of Jew first, and also of Greek.”

In what were these first already despoiled? Surely in this: they lost not only place and nation, but also “the adoption as sons” (ibid. VIII), glory, covenants, legislation, worship, and the promises which were theirs—and Christ Himself, who is from them according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen. All who remain of the peoples have now despoiled them of every good thing, according to the figure of Jacob, whom God loved, who despoiled the firstborn Esau of the very fine garments which Rebecca had at home and put them on himself (Gen. XXVII).

Thus they were justly despoiled, since they were and are, as has been said, part of the wicked man’s body which despoiled many nations, especially of worship or knowledge of the Creator. And they, so far as lay in them, despoiled far more wickedly, because they killed Christ, the expectation of the nations, so that His name might perish and neither they nor the nations might have Him.

Therefore, since the Apostle also says, “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” (Rom. III)—and he had introduced a testimony not from Moses but from the Psalms—let us not doubt that these things which the law, that is, sacred Scripture, speaks here are spoken by it to those who are under the law, and are proclaimed against every soul of man working evil: first the Jew, then the Greek or Gentile.

“Woe to him who gathers evil greed to his house, so that his nest may be on high and he thinks himself delivered from the hand of evil” [Col. 0616B]. Who is it that gathers, or has gathered, evil greed to his house more than the Jewish people, the Pharisaic assembly? “All,” says the Apostle, “have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. XIII). Taking this testimony from the psalm, he immediately adds what we said above: “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law.”

Therefore we should not doubt that this too was said first to him who is or was under the law: “Woe to him who gathers evil greed to his house, so that his nest may be on high.” For the Jew truly did this. Indeed every wicked person gathers greed, and for this reason woe is to him; but the Jew gathered not just any greed, but evil greed, and therefore woe is first to him.

For what, I ask, does he mean by “evil greed”? Who ever heard in the Scriptures of “good greed,” such that it was necessary here to state or add a distinction of this kind by saying “evil greed,” as though in opposition to it? What sort of greed then was or is the Jew’s, that it is rightly called evil and the addition is not superfluous? Surely such as the whole world has heard of: because he made the house of God, which was or ought to have been a house of prayer, into a den of thieves (Matt. XXI; John II), and for that very reason killed the Lord of the house because He argued against that same greed [Col. 0616D].

How evil was this greed, especially among those who were sons of strangers and had fathers poor in spirit. Greed is nowhere good, but there it was exceptionally and exceedingly evil. And for what person, or what house as it were, did he gather such evil greed? Surely for what had been the Lord’s house; because by gathering evil greed he made that house his own—indeed, his own den, a den of thieves—and the evil of his pride, which he immediately denoted by adding, “so that his nest may be on high.” For greed does not exist without pride. Hence Wisdom, after saying, “Nothing is more wicked than a greedy man,” immediately adds: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Eccles. X). He therefore rightly said, “so that his nest may be on high.”
of it, mocking the house that exalts itself as though it were a bird’s nest, and, he says, “he thinks that he will be delivered from the hand of evil”—understand: on account of the height of that lofty nest. Another prophet, foreseeing this, says: “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this’” (Jer. VII), etc. Likewise another, after saying: “Its rulers,” namely those of Zion or Jerusalem, [Col. 0617B] “gave judgment for bribes, and its priests taught for payment, and its prophets practised divination for money,” immediately added: “Yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils shall not come upon us’” (Mic. III). This is plainly the same as what he says here: “And he thinks that he will be delivered from the hand of evil.”

Then, turning toward the one of whom he was speaking, he attacks him thus: “You have devised shame for your house; you have cut off many peoples, and your soul has sinned, because the stone shall cry out from the wall, and the timber that is between the joints of the buildings shall answer.” Truly every covetous person has devised—that is, by devising covetousness, has acquired—shame for his own house. How great that shame is is made plainly intelligible in the passage from Wisdom mentioned above [Col. 0617C], where, after saying, “Nothing is more wicked than a covetous man,” it asks, “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” It then adds: “For when a man dies, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” (Ecclus. X).

Now the Jew who, as has already been said, amassed such evil covetousness, devised—that is, acquired—shame for his house in two ways. First, the shame which he could have heard from another prophet, namely Micah. For after saying what we mentioned before—“Yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils shall not come upon us?’”—he immediately added: “Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple [Col. 0617D] [shall become] the heights of forests” (Mic. III).

Certainly Caiaphas especially devised this sort of shame for that house, when he prophesied, saying: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for one man to die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI). For in saying this, he trembled with fear where there was no fear, and craftily increased the alarm—or rather the pretence of alarm—of his associates, who said: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” Thus, by devising, “you have cut off,” he says, “many peoples”; that is, you were the cause that many peoples were cut off. For, as Josephus reports (book VII, ch. 25), throughout the whole time of the slaughter, eleven hundred thousand were killed; and, he says, most of these were foreigners, not natives. For they had assembled [Col. 0618A] from every region for the feast-day of Unleavened Bread, and were suddenly surrounded by war, so that first a deadly pestilence arose among them from the confined space, and then famine more swiftly followed.

Therefore, he says, “you have cut off many peoples, and your soul has sinned”; that is, your wicked intention has sinned. For your sin [272] arose not from ignorance but from the malice of your design. “Woe to you, because the stone shall cry out from the wall, and the timber which is between the joints of the buildings shall answer.” For who is this stone, if not he who, through the parable of the vineyard, signified himself (Matt. XXI) as one to be cast out beyond the gate of the city and crucified? There, where he delivered the parable and heard from the Pharisees their judgment concerning the wicked husbandmen—who were themselves—he said: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected [Col. 0618B], this has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’?” (Ps. CVII).

And what is the timber between the joints of the buildings, if not the wood of the cross, through which the two structures were formerly joined, so long as there were enmities between human beings and God, and the Lord of angels, but through the cross were reconciled or joined? (Col. I). Thus the phrase “the timber that is between the joints of the buildings,” or of human beings, is rightly understood: the structure which is on earth or from the earth consists of two walls, namely the ancient synagogue before Christ’s coming and the new Church after his coming. Since he joins these walls together in himself, he is called, and is, the corner-stone. Hence elsewhere the same Apostle says: “For he himself is our peace, who made [Col. 0618C] both one” (Eph. II), etc.

“The stone from the wall,” therefore, he says, “shall cry out”—understand, against you—“and the timber which is between the joints of the buildings shall answer,” namely, against you. What will the stone cry, or what will the timber answer? Plainly what follows: “Woe to him who builds a city with blood, and prepares a town by iniquity.” So that there may be no doubt to whom that stone or that timber cries this woe, another prophet, namely Micah, says: “You who build Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity” (Mic. III).

Therefore the one to whom belongs the “Woe to him who builds a city with blood and prepares a town by iniquity” is the Jewish people, the Pharisaic assembly, which filled up the measure of its fathers: for its fathers indeed [Col. 0618D] killed the prophets, while it killed the Lord of the prophets, so that upon it might come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth. But did it really build the city in this way, or prepare the town in so great an iniquity? By no means; but in its utter foolishness it thought so. For it said: “Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXIII). Therefore it lost its place and nation, because it thought that shedding blood was the building of a city, and that perpetrating iniquity would be for it the means of preparing a city to possess forever.

In another sense, however, it truly built a city with blood and genuinely prepared a town by iniquity—not for itself, but for the living God; not that earthly town or city, Jerusalem, but the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God [Col. 0619A]. For as many prophets as it killed, as many wise men and scribes as it slew, crucified, scourged in its synagogues, and persecuted from city to city, so many living stones did it square—stones of whom you may rightly sing to the great Architect, the Holy Spirit:

> Polished by their cutting and their pressures,  
> They are fitted to their places,  
> Set in order by the craftsman’s hand,  
> To remain in the sacred buildings.

Having duly reflected upon this, when he saw, depicted by a painter’s art, a distinguished martyr undergoing blows from clubs and leaded scourges, he composed the following distich:

The stone of the eternal city is hammered, O Christ, and this gem of thine is polished more brilliantly by the punishment that serves thee.

In such a work—or building—the Jewish people are both foremost and most notorious. “The stone,” he says, “[Col. 0619B] shall cry out from the wall, and the timber that is among the joints of the building”—as has already been said—“shall answer: Woe to him who so builds a city, who so prepares a town.” For the result is good indeed, but the intention is wicked. When or where, according to the truth of this prophecy, did that stone, the cornerstone, cry this woe? Surely when and where he said: “Behold, I send to you prophets, and wise men, and scribes,” etc., down to: “Amen, I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation.” For immediately he added, most gravely: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who killest the prophets and stonest those who are sent to thee” (Matt. 23). What is to be understood there, unless “Woe to thee”? For he had previously uttered woe seven times, as, prudent reader, you will be able to enumerate in that same place—namely, in Matthew [Col. 0619C]: “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”; “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”; “Woe to you, blind guides”; “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”; “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”; “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”; “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees”—with reasons appended to each denunciation. The last and seventh is this: “You who build the tombs of the prophets,” down to, “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers; therefore behold, I send to you prophets, and wise men, and scribes,” etc.

Is not this ungodly man, this people condemned by a sevenfold woe, that Cain of whom it was said, in reference to the one man of this name, “Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain” (Gen. 4)? Since this number is insoluble, it signifies an unforgivable sin. More might be said on this point; but, avoiding weariness for the reader, let us pursue the rest.

[Col. 0619D] He says: “Are not these things from the Lord of hosts?” Suppose that he said: “Was not this made by the Lord, and is it wonderful in our eyes?” (Ps. 116). What is this, except that “the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,” and that this stone “shall cry from the wall,” while, as has already been said, the wood of his cross, which is among the joints of the building, shall answer? “Are not these things,” I say, “from the Lord of hosts? Was not this made by the Lord?” Assuredly these things are from the Lord of hosts; assuredly this was made by the Lord. The proof follows:

“For peoples shall labour in much fire, and nations unto emptiness, so that they fail.” In connection with this prophetic saying [Col. 0620A], let us recall that saying in the Acts of the Apostles: “And now,” says Gamaliel, “I say to you, men of Israel, depart from these men; leave them alone. For if this counsel or work is from men, it will be destroyed; but if it is from God, we shall not be able to destroy them, lest perhaps we be found even to be fighting against God” (Acts 5). He spoke this wisely. But here the Holy Spirit had foretold: “For peoples shall labour in much fire, and nations unto emptiness, so that they fail”; and so it happened. They laboured in much fire—understand, the fire of envy—that is, the Jews laboured, and the nations, that is, the Gentiles, laboured to destroy the counsel and work proclaimed concerning this cornerstone. But they laboured in vain and failed, because they could not destroy it. Indeed, as they came to this stone—to come to whom is the failure of futile labour for good—they themselves also were built up as living stones.

[Col. 0620B] Are not these things therefore from the Lord of hosts? Was not this made by the Lord? For if this counsel or work had not been from the Lord, it would certainly already have been destroyed, since so many nations and peoples laboured to destroy it. And what cause rendered their labours vain? He says: “For the earth shall be filled, so that it may know the glory of the Lord, as waters covering the sea.” What could be truer, firmer, or more perfect than this saying? For “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 8; Acts 4); and, as he filled it, the earth was filled so as to know the glory of the Lord: so that those who had been unlearned and without letters might become wise and eloquent; that those who had been earthly—indeed, who had been earth—might become heavenly, [Col. 0620C] might become heavens, knowing the glory of the Lord and declaring the glory of God. And this not in any ordinary manner, but “as waters covering the sea.”

What does this mean? How great would waters have to be to cover the sea by their multitude, or such that, in comparison with them, the sea should seem to be nothing! That would be a marvel; yet no less marvellous is the fact that the sea—that is, the wisdom of all—was surpassed by the abundance of heavenly wisdom given to the simple. This is the illumination of those who believe Christ’s Gospel, who say: “This was made by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes.” Conversely, the rest were blinded—namely, those who, as has been said, desired to destroy this counsel or work—of whom he here says: “For peoples shall labour in much fire, and nations unto emptiness, so that they fail.” For this reason [Col. 0620D] they were blinded. It follows:

“Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, sending forth his gall and making him drunk, that he may look upon his nakedness. Thou art filled with dishonour instead of glory. Drink thou also, and be made drowsy; the cup of the Lord’s right hand shall encompass thee, and the vomit of dishonour shall be upon thy glory.” This passage is made clearer by that from the Psalm: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 63). “Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back continually.”

Thus, in a remarkable way, after saying, “The earth shall be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord”—which is the illumination of the nations—he set in opposition the cause of the blindness [Col. 0621A] that befell Israel, saying: “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend.” Blindness itself is the woe; its cause is that he gave drink to his friend. For he is the friend who says in the Psalm: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” He is so truly a friend that he became a brother and a blood-relative of our nature; for, though he was God, he became man and was incarnate from that people.

To this friend he gave drink, sending forth his gall and making him drunk with bitterness, so that he might look upon his nakedness: that is, so that he might prove that he had been forsaken by God. For the ungodly said: “He professes to have knowledge of God; he called himself the Son of God. Let us see whether his words are true. For if he is the true Son of God, he will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries. Let us test [Col. 0621B] him with insult and torment, and prove his patience. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.”

The Psalm declares this most wicked curiosity of theirs, this, as it were, investigation of nakedness, in his own person: “Those who watched for my soul plotted together, saying: ‘God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to rescue him.’” The ungodly man investigated, found—or imagined that he saw—his nakedness; for he heard him say: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). Immediately, surely, lest anything of his gall should be lacking for making drunk the one whose whole cup of suffering was a draught of bitterness, he offered vinegar also to his mouth (John 19).

Therefore woe to him, because he so gave drink to his friend and blood-relative brother that he might look upon [Col. 0621C] his nakedness—his weakness—in order to make or obtain proof that he was not the Son of God; indeed, that he had been forsaken by God. He announces this abroad and blasphemes, like the accursed Ham, who proclaimed abroad his father’s nakedness; but how much greater is this matter than that resemblance! For Ham did not give drink to his father—did not, I say, give him a pleasant cup of wine in order to make him drunk and look upon his nakedness (Gen. 9). But this ungodly man gave his friend a drink of bitterness, sent forth his gall, and made him drunk, in order to look upon his nakedness. And, as the prophetic Spirit foretold through Moses: “Their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and their grapes are from the outskirts of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, [Col. 0621D] and their cluster most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32).

“He is filled,” he says, “with dishonour instead of glory” (ibid.). Who is filled with dishonour instead of glory? Is it he who gave drink to his friend, or the friend himself to whom the drink of gall was given? Surely it is the friend himself who is filled with dishonour: that is, he suffered disgrace, endured death—death, moreover, of the cross—which the ungodly man imposed upon him as the supreme dishonour, saying, “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2). Filled with so great a dishonour, he suffered it for glory, knowing that the result would be that from then on he would sit at the right hand of Power in the glory of God the Father. “For this reason,” says the Apostle, “God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things heavenly, [Col. 0622A] earthly, and infernal, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

But how—and how vehemently—he turns against the one who gave his drink, who sent forth his gall, who made his friend drunk and put him to sleep with the sleep of death, and thus looked upon his nakedness: that is, desired him to be naked and forsaken by God! “Drink thou also,” he says, “and be made drowsy.” And what will you drink? “The cup of the Lord’s right hand shall encompass thee, and the vomit of dishonour shall be upon thy glory.” The cup of the Lord’s right hand—that is, the wrath of the almighty Lord—shall so encompass you that, as it is written concerning him: “Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68). What is your table except your Law, the sacred Scripture entrusted to you, first set before you for eating and drinking?

[Col. 0622B] There is the cup of the Lord’s right hand: that same table of yours, that same Law or Scripture, shall encompass you as a snare customarily encompasses its prey. For it shall itself be a snare to you, who have the spirit of error, as you swallow or drain the retribution of your gall which you gave your friend to drink. Drink this, and be made drowsy: so that now your eyes may be darkened and you may not see, and afterward you may be made drowsy—not as that friend of yours who, after your gall had been exhausted, said, “I lay down and slept, and rose again” (Ps. 3)—but so that you may lie buried in eternal death, which truly is to be made drowsy.

How different, moreover, is what follows—“the vomit of dishonour shall be upon thy glory”—from what he had said before: “He is filled with dishonour instead of glory.” [Col. 0622C] The dishonour with which that friend of yours was filled for glory, and the dishonour by whose vomit you are defiled upon your glory, do not have the same character. For the dishonour with which he was filled came upon him from without: he was mistreated not for his own sins but for those of others, and he endured it for future glory. But the vomit of your dishonour comes from within; it proceeds from yourself, like the vomit of one who has disturbed himself. For you have dishonoured yourself by vomiting lies from your heart, and that vomit bursts forth upon your former glory.

There is also this great difference: he first endured dishonour, and glory then followed, as was fitting; but you first gloried, hastily receiving glory from one another [Col. 0622D] (John 5), as he reproached you in a certain place, and the vomit of dishonour then followed. This is the known order of the heavenly dispensation: the ungodly person is first gloriously exalted and then disgracefully humbled; but the godly person, precisely because he lives godly, is first humbled and suffers dishonour, and afterward his horn is exalted in glory.

It follows: “For the iniquity of Lebanon shall cover thee.” This is joined to what he set forth before: “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend,” etc. Woe to you, he says, because the iniquity of Lebanon shall cover you: that is, your hypocrisy shall condemn you. For *Libanus* (“Lebanon”) is interpreted “whitening” [*candidatio*] 274, and sometimes under this name the Temple is understood, as in Zechariah: “Open thy gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour thy cedars” (Zech. 12). Therefore the iniquity of Lebanon—that is, [Col. 0623A] the iniquity of the Temple—the very beauty of religion, all of whose whiteness is your hypocrisy, shall especially cover you: it shall condemn you most greatly.

For the Lord himself sufficiently bitterly indicates how great the hypocrisy of that religion was, repeatedly saying in one continuous course of speech: “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. 23), in the passage from Matthew mentioned above. There, after he had thundered woe upon them seven times, he called them hypocrites on every occasion, with only one exception, where he said: “Woe to you, blind guides.” Paul too, not ignorant of the iniquity of this whitewashing, when he stood in the midst of the council and Ananias the high priest ordered him to be struck on the mouth, said to him: “God shall strike thee, thou whitewashed wall” (Acts 23). And what else was this than to say, “The iniquity of Lebanon shall cover thee”? And indeed, what he said to one he said to all: he said it to that whole priesthood and people; and what he said came to pass, and the whole world heard that blow.

Immediately, I say, [Col. 0623B] having denounced that ungodly people, the prophetic speech turns to its hearers and speaks thus: “And the devastation of the beasts shall terrify them, because of the blood of man, and the iniquity of the land and city and of all who dwell in it.” As it was said, so it happened. For beasts came from the forest, of whom the Psalmist says: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste”—that is, thy vineyard—“and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. 79). This was surely because of the crime by which, when it should have produced grapes and brought wine to the aforementioned friend—its Lord or owner, indeed its planter—it sent forth its gall and made him drunk with the bitterness of death.

The boar came, namely Vespasian; and the solitary wild beast, namely Titus his son, came from the forest—that is, from the city of Rome, where there was a multitude of errors and where savage men lived like beasts in a forest. The devastation caused by these beasts terrified them because of the blood of man and the iniquity of the land, the city, and all who dwelt in it. From that time onward, they lost the audacity by which, first among all nations, they had dared to kill and crucify prophets, wise men, and Scribes sent to them, to scourge them in their synagogues, [Col. 0623C] and to persecute them from city to city (Matt. 23). Have they not been deterred since that time from such audacious cruelty, such cruel audacity? For they now dare to kill no one, or at least to scourge anyone in their synagogues—especially as captives everywhere in the world, and as the footstool of the Lord who sits at the right hand of the Lord and rules in the midst of his enemies, who are indeed they themselves. And though other nations have been permitted such acts, the very law of their captivity allows nothing of the sort to them at all.

It follows: “What profiteth the graven image, because its maker has graven it; the molten image and the false representation, because its maker trusted in his fabrication so as to make dumb idols? Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ ‘Arise!’ to the silent stone. Can it teach? Behold, it is covered with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it. But the Lord is in his holy Temple: let all the earth be silent before him.”

This woe is now the fifth, and, as we must understand the preceding woes also to be, it is that wrath which, as we have already recalled above, the Apostle says is revealed [Col. 0624A] from heaven in the Gospel of God against every soul of man who works evil, “of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (Rom. 25). That is, upon the soul of the Jew first, and then of the Greek or Gentile. This wrath, because of the requirements of the time, was expressed more obscurely in the prophets; but in the Gospel it is revealed so clearly that you may truly say: “As we have heard, so we have seen” (Ps. 47). For after woe had been pronounced four times against the soul of the Jewish man who works evil—and had thus concluded: “The devastation of the beasts shall terrify them because of the blood of man”—he then says in the fifth place: “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ ‘Arise!’ to the silent stone,” etc.

Is this not what we have seen as we heard it? For once the Jews had been deterred from daring to kill or persecute the preachers of the Gospel—which occurred through the devastation by beasts, that is, through the destruction wrought by the hands of the Gentile Romans—then the Gospel more freely denounced idolatry, and proclaimed woe throughout the whole world against every soul of Greek or Gentile man who bows down to wood and stone, or to gold and silver.

[Col. 0624B] Observe also the sequence of the present text. For it does not begin by saying, “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ ‘Arise!’ to the silent stone.” Rather, it first addresses the man gently, and by questioning arouses him to rational consideration. “What profiteth,” it says, “the graven image?” It means that the answer should be understood and supplied: “Nothing.” It then gives the reason why it can be of no profit. “Because,” it says, “its maker has graven it”—namely, one who cannot give breath or life to his own fabrication. He made a molten image and an image of whatever thing he wished: of corruptible man, or birds, or four-footed creatures, or serpents; a false image, certainly—that is, one deprived of every truth of the substance whose likeness it appears to bear. And for this reason its maker carved it, because he trusted in his fabrication: a rational man so deceived that he made dumb idols, “which have mouths and shall not speak, have eyes and shall not see, have ears and shall not hear, have nostrils and shall not smell” (Ps. 113); for there is no breath in their mouths.

Once this has been rationally set forth, whoever does not believe the Gospel proclaiming the true God is surely without excuse, because the argument is irrefutable. Therefore only now does he cry out in terrible denunciation: “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ ‘Arise!’ [Col. 0624D] to the silent stone.” Equivalently, it may be said: Woe to those who know God, or hear God’s Gospel, and do not glorify him as God, because of their own will they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man.

Can the one to whom he says, “Awake! Arise!” teach, when it is stone or wood? “Behold, it”—understand, its god—is covered with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it: no breath, I say, whether of man, bird, quadruped, or serpent—of whatever being an image may have been fashioned in wood or stone, gold or silver. Thus its maker carved a false image. But he whom we proclaim, God and Lord, is in his holy Temple: in the Temple [Col. 0625A] of his body, which, having been destroyed by the ungodly, he himself raised after three days. “Let all the earth be silent before him”: namely, by not daring to blaspheme or to name any god other than him, and by rendering him the reverence of this silence, in humbly asking from him grace—that is, the remission of sins.

For concerning this matter, does either reason or the Scripture of truth allow any silence? (Isa. 62). On the contrary, we are told [Col. 0626A]: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence.” It must briefly be defined: to be silent before the face of the Lord is to fear the Lord. Even if this has not yet occurred—for many contradict him—it shall certainly occur on the day of judgment, as the Psalmist strongly affirms, when he announces what shall without doubt happen as though it had already happened: “Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth trembled and was still” (Ps. 75).

## BOOK III

[Col. 0625]

[Col. 0625B] 275 Conscious, as it were, of rashness, I fear that almost everyone will rebuke me as rash, because I have dared to enter upon the broad expanse of the field full of blessing—the field, that is, of Holy Scripture—which the Lord has blessed, in which or from which comes every sweet fragrance and fruit of blessing: what shall I answer to those who rebuke me? Let them believe that, hastening in spirit, I am imitating with timid purpose Ruth the Moabitess, when she said to her mother-in-law: “I will go into the field and gather the ears of grain which have escaped the hands of the reapers, wherever I may find the favour of a master of the household gracious toward me” (Ruth 2).

As Boaz commanded his servants on her behalf that no one should trouble her, so may all who see these things think that Christ, born of that humility [Col. 0625C], commands them not to be indignant with me as though I acted presumptuously. And even if anyone should wish to be indignant, the poor little soul, nevertheless anxious for itself and taking precautions against the coming famine of which the Psalmist speaks—“For the undefiled, whose days the Lord knows, shall not be confounded in the evil time, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied” (Ps. 36)—will persist in the work begun, and there, before its own face, will labour to obtain the food that endures unto eternal life (John 6).

## PRAYER FOR IGNORANCES
This title is golden, and a word of great importance, of which the wise man truly says: “The words of the wise shall be weighed as in a balance” (Ecclesiasticus 21). For what is the prophet’s prayer “for ignorances,” or what does it mean that the prophet prays for ignorances? If he is a prophet—indeed, since he is a prophet—how does he profess himself to be among ignorances? If this title had preceded his prophesying, or before he had written anything prophetic, we might suppose that he wished to invoke the holy Spirit of prophecy and intended to deserve the designation or office of prophet. But now it is not so: he had already prophesied; he had already committed prophetic mysteries to writing. Is, then, prophesying and possessing prophetic knowledge the earlier or lesser thing, while praying for ignorances is later and more advanced? Certainly it is so.

Yet no one should suppose that these two things are alike: to have ignorance of God, and to pray for ignorances. For example, Paul, while he had ignorance of God, had been “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” [Col. 0626B] (1 Tim. 1), and persecuted the Church of God; but when praying for ignorances he was already the great Apostle, a chosen vessel, full of wisdom, crying aloud: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). Why delay over many instances? To pray for ignorances—or even to see this very thing, that one is among ignorances—belongs altogether to the perfect and to those with whom God speaks.

“I beseech thee, Lord,” says Moses, “I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before yesterday, since thou hast spoken to thy servant; I am slow and impeded of tongue” (Exod. 4). Isaiah too cries: “Woe is me, because I have kept silence; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips; and mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord [Col. 0626C] of hosts” (Isa. 6; the source’s “IX” is evidently an OCR error). But what need is there for individual examples? Finally, Wisdom says of all such persons: “The vision which the man spoke, with whom the Lord is, and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said: I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me. I have not learned wisdom, and I do not know the knowledge of the holy ones” (Prov. 30; the source’s “III” is evidently an OCR error).

Far is this man from one who seems wise to himself, or has appeared so, and concerning whom Ezekiel therefore says reproachfully: “An outstretched and protecting cherub” (Ezek. 28). The title itself, therefore, shows that this is the man with whom the Lord was, and who was strengthened by God dwelling with him. Accordingly, what this strengthened man and mighty wrestler, Habakkuk, saw and heard, the Church of Christ has long marvelled at; and may we, hearing his amazement, be able to understand it and worthily marvel with him, and ourselves pray for ignorances.

“Lord, I have heard thy report, and was afraid. Lord, revive thy work in the midst of the years. In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known; when thou art angry, thou shalt remember mercy.” What report of the Lord, and of what kind, did he hear and fear? Clearly that which he himself later declares: “God,” he says, “will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran; horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden,” and so forth. Truly, to hear such a report and to fear or tremble belongs to a faithful and wise mind. For how great a thing is this: that God and Lord, coming into this world—the majesty of all, most high, dreadful and adorable to all the powers of heaven—[Col. 0627A] having assumed flesh, hung with hands nailed to the horns of the cross; and that the fault of rebellious servants was the cause why so great a Lord should suffer this and be so ill-treated?

Whoever among those same servants hears this report—that is, perceives or understands it; for to hear the report is to receive in the ear of the heart what the bodily ear has heard—whoever, I say, has heard and considered this, how could he fail to fear, how could he fail to tremble? Suppose that, astonished, he said: “Alas! What will become of us evil servants, for whose crime so great and such a Lord had to be so ill-treated?”

I know someone, God being witness, who in a vision, raising his eyes upward, thought that he beheld the height of supreme and unbounded greatness, and, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, [Col. 0627B] felt the power of that divine virtue; and as though in the midst of that same height, greatness, and immensity, saw standing that Son of Man, exceedingly exalted and ineffably most high, who was crucified for us. While he was pressed by that vision with a weight great indeed, yet sweet beyond expression, the thought I mentioned came into his mind: “Alas! What will become of us evil servants, for whose crime so great and such a Lord had to be so ill-treated?” Immediately another thought, as if sent down from the Son of Man himself, answered this thought most sweetly: “Nor would I now be such a great Lord, had I not been so ill-treated for the servants’ sake; and what was the cause of my passion is also the cause of my glory and honour.”

Whatever these things may be, this at least I may rightly say: this work is so great and so incomprehensible that whoever has been worthy to hear its report rightly fears and prays for ignorances. For no one ought to be ignorant of this matter; yet in considering it there is no one who does not have ignorance, because no one can fully consider or assess it. Such fear, however, is not servile or penal fear, but holy fear, “enduring for ever and ever,” which love does not cast out but brings within; in it angels praise, dominations adore, and powers tremble before the majesty of the eternal God. This is sufficiently clear from the matter itself. For when he said, “I have heard thy report and was afraid,” [Col. 0627D] it is not permissible to understand: lest what I heard would happen should come to pass. For he immediately says: “Lord, revive thy work in the midst of the years.” He desired and prayed that the very thing which, hearing that it would occur, he feared, might happen more quickly. Therefore this is good fear, holy fear, of which the Psalmist says elsewhere: “I will worship toward thy holy temple in thy fear” (Ps. 5).

“Lord,” he says, “revive thy work in the midst of the years.” In a wonderful manner, this man is not timid but reverently fearful, and both prays and prophesies. For what is “in the midst of the years”? What are these years, in whose midst he prays that the thing which he feared on hearing would take place? We gladly understand these years as the years of human life, which the Psalmist reckons: “The days of our years are threescore years and ten” (Ps. 89). Some stronger and more long-lived persons have indeed exceeded this number; but “if in the strong, fourscore years, and beyond them labour and sorrow” (ibid.); therefore the years of a human life are seventy.

Now the Lord was to revive his work in the midst of this number of years: the work that had been put to death, the work which is the human race. Heaven indeed and earth and sea and all things in them are works of the Lord; but the human being is a particular work of the Lord, the work of the Lord’s hands. For God spoke concerning the other things, and they were made; but in making the human being, he took clay, formed it, and made a work of his hands. Thus Isaiah says: “And now, Lord, thou art our Father; we indeed are clay, and thou art our potter, and we all are the works of thy hands” (Isa. 64; the source’s “LIV” is evidently an OCR error). And holy Job: “Thy hands made me [Col. 0628B] and fashioned me wholly round about” (Job 10).

Therefore, even though the Lord made the other things, the human being is nevertheless a distinctive work of the Lord’s hands. The devil, through the serpent, put this work to death by the death of the soul, followed, by God’s just sentence, by the death of the body. He was to revive this work, thus mortified, in the midst of the seventy years of human life. And so it happened. For when the Lord himself had become man, at a little less than the midpoint of seventy years—namely, at the age of thirty-three—by dying and rising again he revived his work, the human race. By dying, he destroyed the death of our souls; by rising again, he restored the life of our bodies.

Thus, in a wonderful manner, he feared, who in that very fear prophetically prayed that the thing feared might happen sooner; and, praying, prophesied what should be accomplished sooner. Again he says: “In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known.” What wilt thou make known in the other middle of the years? For we said that in the midst of the years of human life thou didst revive thy work—that is, thou didst raise up thy temple, the temple of thy body not made by hands, destroyed by Jewish impiety—and with it didst restore the life of the human race. What wilt thou make known in the other half of the years except this very fact: that thou hast truly revived thy said work?

For when forty years have been completed from the time when thou didst build that work of thine, that temple of thine, from the body of the Virgin Mother, then what thou hast accomplished will have become known, when the Romans come—[the source's *manis* is uncertain]—and fulfill thy truth in the destruction of the temple made by hands—the temple concerning which thou didst endure slander from those who said: “This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days” (Matt. 26); and again: “Ha! thou who destroyest the temple of God and rebuildest it after three days” (Matt. 27). For “there shall not remain one stone upon another which shall not be destroyed.”

Wonderful and fearful is the swiftness of thy work, Lord: for in the midst of our years—forty years, which are the years of our life—thou wilt revive it, as has already been said; and in the other midst of the same years thou wilt so make known what thou hast done that rivalry with the Jewish temple, the temple made by hands, cannot conceal or obscure the glory of this same work of thine. For it shall be destroyed, in great wrath; then there shall be great distress for this people. But what then? “When thou art angry, thou shalt remember mercy.” We shall not be like Sodom, nor shall we become like Gomorrah; but a remnant from us shall be saved.

Thus Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we should have been like Sodom, and should have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). Its meaning is: unless the Lord had ordained that a remnant should be saved from us, and that all Israel should be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, our whole nation would have been consumed without any remnant, just as all the Sodomites were consumed by fire and sulphur, except Lot, who was not one of them (Rom. 11; Gen. 19).

What in the Septuagint is read, “You shall know in the midst of two living creatures,” I do not wish to pass over, especially because it is customary in the assembly or congregation of the Church. “The simple interpretation and opinion of the crowd,” says blessed Jerome, “understands it of the Saviour: that he was recognized when crucified between two thieves. Those, however, speak better who understand that the Saviour was perceived and believed in the first Church, which was gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, with two peoples enclosing him on either side. Some understand the two living creatures as the two Testaments, New and Old, which are truly living and life-giving, which breathe, and in whose midst the Lord is known.”

It follows: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.” Until this point he had exclaimed in wonder; now he begins to set forth more fully the matter itself, at whose greatness he had been astonished and for which he had prefaced an exclamation. “God,” he says, “will come, and the Holy One [Col. 0629C] will come.” From where will he come? From the south, from Mount Paran. What we know or believe concerning Christ the Son of God, and therefore speak, we gladly understand in these words of the prophet: that he came forth from God and came into this world, having become man, through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

For the Holy Spirit, as in many passages of Scripture, so here also, is rightly understood by “the south,” because it is a warm wind and a warm region, set opposite the north, by which the evil spirit, contrary to the Holy Spirit, is customarily signified. The person of God the Father himself is fittingly signified by Mount Paran—or, according to the Septuagint translators, by the shady and densely wooded mountain—because his judgments are incomprehensible, his ways unsearchable, and the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge immeasurable (Rom. 11). This is indicated, as we said above, by the title itself: “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorances.”

Moreover, “God” and “the Holy One” is Christ the Son of God himself: truly God and holy man, in no way conceived in iniquities, “who did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). “This one,” therefore, he says, “will come from the south”: that is, the Holy Spirit will bring it about that he comes. For he will come because of his great love; because of his great love God the Father will send him (1 Pet. 1:12; citation as printed). But what else is the love of the Father who sends and of the Son who is sent than the Holy Spirit? Therefore he will come from the Holy Spirit: that is, as [Col. 0630A] we have already said, the Holy Spirit will bring about his coming; and it will be the Holy Spirit’s operation that an incorrupt virgin shall conceive him as true God and give birth to him as true man.

According to these three persons of the one true and supreme Godhead, this prophetic canticle is subdivided by three divisions. The sign of these divisions is *semper* (“always”), which in Hebrew is *selah* and has been rendered by Greek translators as *diapsalma*. It should be known that it occurs only in the Psalter and in the present place. “And I think,” says blessed Jerome, “that it is the marking of a musical sound, or certainly that it indicates the perpetuity of what has been foretold; and wherever *selah*, that is, *diapsalma* or ‘always,’ is placed, there we should know that both what follows and what precedes pertains not only to the present time but to eternity.”

The first division begins with this verse: “His glory covered the heavens.” The second: “Dividing the rivers of the earth.” The third: “Thou hast cursed his sceptres.” The first division indeed concerns God the Son of God, of whom he had said: “God will come from the south”; for, he says, “horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden,” and so forth. In the second division it is clear that he speaks to another person: “Thou hast gone forth,” he says, “for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with Christ.” That person is rightly understood as the Holy Spirit, whom we take to be signified by the south, and who gave visible signs of his presence, going forth with his Christ for the salvation of his people; this will be explained more fully in its place. In the third division there is another person to whom he speaks: “Thou hast cursed his sceptres.” Later, saying, “But I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus,” we gratefully understand the person to whom he speaks and confesses this concerning his Lord Jesus to be the Father. Now let us follow the sequence of the words themselves.

“His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.” Thus he speaks. These words and those following are uttered as one filled with fear and astonished, by another hearing in the inward person, after he had prefaced: “Lord, I have heard thy report and was afraid.” He had said: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran,” or from the shady and densely wooded mountain. Now, as though you asked what kind or how great this God is, and how great the holiness of the Holy One is: “His glory,” he says, “covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.”

When he says, “His glory covered the heavens,” what else does he intend to indicate except that he is as shady and densely wooded as the mountain itself—that is, as the Father himself from whom that same God came? Finally, he testifies that he is exceedingly shady and dense, exceedingly incomprehensible, when he says, “His glory covered the heavens.” This is as though he said: “His divinity is incomprehensible even to the heavens,” that is, to all angelic spirits. So great and so glorious is this God. If you ask how holy he is: “The earth,” he says, “is full of his praise.” He finely distinguishes the glory of God from the praise of God. For he is glorious because he is God; he is praiseworthy because he is holy. And as the glory of his divinity covered the heavens, as has been said, so the earth is full of the praise of his holiness, the praise of his holy humanity. Neither can the heavens—that is, the angels—fully behold the glory of his divine brightness, nor can human beings on earth adequately praise, as is fitting, the holiness and humility of his humanity. The great and exalted God has no end; God made man, holy and good, admits of no full estimation.

What then, if his glory covered the heavens? How will he be known, if he is shady and dense? He says: “His brightness shall be as the light.” As though he said: He is not so shady and dense that he cannot be seen; he is not so incomprehensible that he cannot be known. For he will shine, and his brightness shall be as light: that is, it will sufficiently illuminate creation. He possesses inaccessible light, but knows how to emit a bearable brightness. Creation cannot enter or penetrate the depth of light itself; but light itself can proceed to creation in a tempered brightness.

His glory shone upon the very heavens which it covered, and it shone upon earth, where, having become man, he lay hidden among human beings. His brightness is the effect of his wondrous works: he performed wonders in heaven and on earth, and as often as he performed wonders, so often he emitted brightness. Such is his brightness, and shall be as light, because it sufficiently illuminates and shall illuminate his angelic and human creation for knowing himself.

What is more shady, what more densely obscure, than what follows: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden”? By “horns” he means standards and trophies of the cross, to whose arms his hands were nailed. For, “being in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross” [Col. 0631C] (Phil. 2). Therefore on the cross his strength was for a while hidden, when he said to the Father: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26); and: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid.); and on the cross itself: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23).

What could be so shady, so dense? “We,” says the Apostle, “preach Jesus Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). But how, or for what purpose, was his strength hidden there? Clearly, as a hook is hidden in flesh—that is, the barb of iron—in order that the fish may be caught. For this is what the Lord says to blessed Job concerning Behemoth or Leviathan: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with a hook?” [Col. 0631D] (Job 40). The words “as I can” are understood.

Accordingly, when he says, “Horns are in his hands,” he does not wish us to notice only that his hands were nailed to the horns or arms of the cross; otherwise he would more properly have said, “His hands are on the horns.” Just as we do not customarily say “the cross is in Christ,” but “Christ is nailed on the cross,” so still more he wishes us to consider that, because of the nailing by which he was nailed to the cross or raised up upon the cross, all power or all kingship, which is customarily signified by a horn, was given into his hands—or hand—as he himself foretold: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12); and as he afterwards said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

The prophet himself immediately declares what would result from the fact that [Col. 0632A] his strength was hidden there. For he says: “Death shall go before his face, and the devil shall go forth before his feet.” What is this except as though he said that Leviathan will be caught by that hook? For just as a fish caught by a hook comes forth before the feet of the one who catches and draws the hook from river or sea, so, he says, the devil shall go forth before his feet: that is, he will come into his power, and “the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12).

He said two things: “Death shall go before his face,” and “the devil shall go forth before his feet.” These are what we believe and proclaim, and what, believing, we hope: that death flees before his presence. For he rose again and granted us the glory of resurrection; and he caused the devil, author of sin and death, at the preaching of his Gospel, to go forth and to be trampled underfoot before his feet—that is, before his preachers.

It follows: “He stood and measured the earth. He looked and dissolved the nations, and the everlasting mountains were broken; the hills of the world were bowed down by his eternal paths.” He who died on the cross, where his strength was hidden, rose from the dead; his strength was now assuredly neither hidden nor to be hidden, but thereafter manifest. He stood—understand, at the right hand of the power of God—to overcome the remnants of sin and to wage war against the enemies of his Gospel. “Behold, I see the heavens opened,” says Stephen the first martyr, “and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7; the source’s “V” is evidently an OCR error). Isaiah too had long before declared: “The Lord stands to judge, and stands to judge the peoples” (Isa. 3).

The Lord therefore stood, strong and mighty, “the Lord mighty in battle” [Col. 0632C] (Ps. 23), having the conquered devil beneath his feet. “And he measured the earth.” How did he measure it except as judge of the living and the dead? Surely what had been written of David—that “he struck the Philistines and struck Moab, and measured with a line, making them equal with the earth; and he measured two, one to kill and one to keep alive” (2 Kings 8)—must reverently be understood concerning this one of the mighty hand: that he measured the earth, measuring two lines, one line of mercy and one line of judgment; the line of mercy to make alive, the line of judgment to kill.

Thus, in measuring the earth he looked upon the nations; he had mercy upon the nations; he measured over the nations the line of mercy to make alive. But over the Jews he measured the line of judgment to kill, so that, blinded, they might “fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21). The saying, “He looked and dissolved the nations,” and what follows, “the everlasting mountains were broken and the hills of the world were bowed down,” finely indicates the same thing that we say about the look of mercy with which he looked upon the nations. For what is “dissolved” except softened unto repentance? Conversely, the wicked person is said to have hardened his heart (John 12). And what are “the everlasting mountains were broken and the hills of the world were bowed down,” except that the princes of the world were grieved unto repentance: the greater ones, understood by mountains, and the lesser, signified by hills? “The earth was moved and trembled,” says the Psalmist, “and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and [Col. 0633A] moved, because he was angry with them” (Ps. 17). Good is the breaking which occurs through his eternal paths; for this is the broken and humbled heart which God does not despise (Ps. 50). All this was, or is, the measuring of the one line, the line of mercy to make alive.

But what immediately follows—“For iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”—is the measuring of the other line, the line of judgment to kill. For the discourse here concerns that Ethiopian who will not change his skin, and that Midian which always and stubbornly “turns aside judgment,” according to the very name *Madian* (Jer. 13). For *Madian* is interpreted “turning aside judgment” and signifies those who do not believe that judgment will come.

Therefore he who looked upon and dissolved the nations with the look of mercy, he also “saw for iniquity”—that is, judged iniquity—every unbeliever, every soul of an unbelieving human being who does evil, “of the Jew first, and also of the Greek” (Rom. 2). Indeed, the tabernacle of Ethiopia is every soul of a Jew doing evil, rather than the tabernacle of Lebanon—that is, the temple itself, in whose brightness or religious worship he used to glory and say: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this” (Jer. 7).

It may truly be said that, since darkness came about noon when the Saviour was crucified, and according to that foretokening “blindness happened to Israel” (Rom. 11), their eyes were darkened; and the temple itself, together with all the sacred things of the Jews, became tents of Ethiopia. For just as Ethiopians are blackened by the heat of the brilliant sun nearby, so the Jews were, in a wondrous manner, made worse by their envy at the Saviour’s presence, and their eyes were darkened by hatred of the light. Therefore “for iniquity he saw the tents of Ethiopia”: that is, he judged and condemned, as true and consummate iniquity, all the festivals and ceremonies of Jewish religion which had formerly been dwellings for himself.

Finally, he says, “The skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled.” This prophet and another, namely Isaiah, who, after saying, “Thou hast overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor” (Isa. 9), immediately added, “as in the day of Midian” (ibid.), direct us to that place in sacred history where Gideon, leader of Israel, wonderfully troubled the camp of Midian. [Col. 0633D] All Midian and Amalek and the peoples of the east had assembled together. Gideon had sought a sign in the fleece, desiring to know whether the Lord would save Israel through his hand, as he had said. He divided the three hundred men whom he had retained with him from all Israel into three groups, and gave them trumpets in their hands, empty jars, and lamps in the midst of the jars. When all, according to the leader’s command and example, sounded in three places around the camp and broke the jars, they held lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right, crying: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Then the whole camp was thrown into confusion, and, fleeing, they cut one another down by mutual slaughter (Judg. 7).

In likeness to that event, he says, “The skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”: that is, all the sacred things or mysteries of the Gentiles who turn aside judgment, who do not believe that judgment will come. That Gideon bore a type of Christ according to the interpretation of his name—for *Gedeon* is interpreted “encircling the womb”—that his three hundred men signified Christ’s martyrs, contending and dying for faith in the holy Trinity, that the breaking of the jars signified the deaths of frail bodies, and the flash of the lamps signified the grace of miracles which shone forth after the martyrdoms, through which all the fanatical practices of the Gentiles were overcome and confounded—these matters the holy Fathers have treated more fully. Since they are found in their proper places, we do not set them down here, avoiding the reader’s weariness.

Therefore, he says, “The skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”: that is, the vanities and false frenzies of those who will not believe, according to the preaching of the Gospel, that judgment will come, will be overcome and destroyed through the wondrous and unheard-of battles of martyrs who surrender their bodies to tortures and conquer by dying.

It follows: “Art thou angry with the rivers, Lord? Or is thy fury against the rivers, or thy indignation against the sea?” Other prophets too could sometimes ask, and did ask, questions of this sort; except that this man asks with greater wonder.
