For example, when Daniel saw in a vision that the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the Red Sea, and that four great beasts, different from one another, were ascending from the sea; and afterwards that thrones were set and the Ancient of Days sat [Col. 0634C] (Dan. 7), and that by his judgment that great beast was slain and the authority of the other beasts taken away—Daniel himself might have marvelled and asked in the same manner: “Art thou angry with lions, Lord? Or is thy fury against leopards or bears, and thy indignation against winds and sea? Is it such things that concern thee, so that thou sittest in judgment on their account?”

And, since reason itself gave the answer, it followed that those images signified other, greater matters. Desiring to know these, he says: “I approached one of those who stood by, and sought from him the truth about all these things” (ibid.). Similarly, Zechariah asks about many things and says: “What are these, my Lord?” (Zech. 1). But this man, more astonished and stirred by greater wonder—for he saw and heard with prophetic ear or eye that which gave him cause to fear, as he prefaced: “Lord, I have heard thy report and was afraid”—asks and says: “Art thou angry with the rivers, Lord? Or is thy fury against the rivers, or thy indignation against the sea?”

And doubtless he was answered. For inanimate elements had incurred some anger; and just as Daniel and Zechariah, when questioning, were told what the things they saw were or signified, so this man also was told. Yet no such mystery was ever so expounded to anyone that he was permitted to write it plainly for understanding; rather, the command was: “But thou, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time.” What he saw when he said, “Art thou angry with the rivers, Lord?” and so forth, becomes clearer from what follows, when he says: “The waters saw thee, O God, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by; the deep gave its voice,” and so forth.

Therefore, just as in the legal words, “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain” (Deut. 25), when we hear the Apostle say, “Is God concerned for oxen?” (1 Cor. 9), we know to answer: No; but the spiritual law said this concerning preachers. So in these prophetic visions, when he says, “Art thou angry with the rivers, Lord?” he who sees, or the prophet, and we who desire to possess the mind of the seer, should know to answer: No. Under the names of mountains and hills, horses and chariots, rivers or waters, shining arrows and flashing spear, and the other things for which God is no more concerned than for oxen, we should understand those matters for which God is without doubt concerned.

Let those rivers be understood by us spiritually: those whose voices were heard, or those waters and that sea and those rivers which could hear, concerning which it is written in the psalm: “The rivers lifted up, O Lord, the rivers lifted up their voice. The rivers lifted up their waves, from the voice of many waters. Wonderful are the risings of the sea; wonderful on high is the Lord” [Col. 0635B] (Ps. 93). For the rivers which lifted up their voice are the sacred doctrines of the Catholic faith, the Lord saying: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7).

But the other rivers, the contrary rivers, which lifted up their waves from the voices of many waters, are those of which the great dragon boasts, as the Lord speaks in Ezekiel: “Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who liest in the midst of thy rivers and sayest: The river is mine” (Ezek. 29). They are my peoples, restless and impetuous, who lifted up their waves—the waves of persecutions and seditions—against the voices of many waters, that is, because of the voices of Christ’s disciples possessing an abundance of heavenly graces.

That sea is the whole world, the world of the ungodly and unbelieving, whose risings, like those of a sea, were wonderful; but the Lord on high is wonderful, he who restrained those risings. Whatever the terms may be, both in these and in the other things which follow, we must understand those realities toward which it does not conflict with reason that the supremely wise and supremely just Lord should be angry or indignant.

It follows: “Thou who ascendest upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation. Arousing, thou shalt arouse thy bow: the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes.” Because he has once asked, “Art thou angry with the rivers, Lord?” and by asking has opened for us the way of question and answer, let us ask about these things also: “Didst thou, Lord, ascend, or wilt thou ascend, upon four-footed horses? Wilt thou ride in chariots, like kings or consuls? Wilt thou bend a bow, become an archer, pierce men’s shoulders, strike between lung and stomach, or will an arrow come out through their fleshy heart?” And we shall answer: No.

For thou wilt indeed ascend thy horses, but thy horses are human beings who willingly submit to the bridle of thy obedience. Thou wilt indeed ascend [Col. 0636A] thy chariots, but thy chariots are thy four Gospels, or the four mysteries of thy Gospel running through the whole world: namely, thy incarnation, thy passion, thy resurrection, and thy ascension. These are without doubt our salvation; without faith in them there is no salvation for us.

With these horses and chariots of thine, “arousing,” he says, “thou shalt arouse thy bow”: that is, by preaching thou shalt proclaim thy coming judgment, that thou wilt come to judge the living and the dead, as those witnesses of thy resurrection and ascension saw thee going into heaven. For to preach that judgment is in some manner like a man bending his bow: because, as a bow strikes from afar, so the day of judgment comes from afar, such that before it strikes it cannot be foreseen.

“Thou shalt arouse the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes.” What are those oaths? Thou didst speak oaths to two men, namely Abraham and David, saying to Abraham: “By myself I have sworn, because thou hast done this thing” (Gen. 22). And, as Scripture says, in swearing to David: “The Lord swore truth to David” [Col. 0636B] (Ps. 131). Nevertheless, all thy utterances may be called oaths because of their firm and indissoluble truth. For thou art that Angel of whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “And the Angel whom I saw standing above the sea lifted his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and the things in it, and”
and the earth, and the things in it, and the sea, and the things in it, because time shall be no more” (Rev. 10), etc. Whatever you have spoken is so firm and so true as though you were swearing, [Col. 0636C] truly by yourself, or by the blessed Trinity, living for ages of ages. “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). By mounting upon your horses and chariots, and by raising your bow, you will fulfil all that you have spoken as oaths, the end of which will be to give your tribes a land truly flowing with milk and honey. Always.

It has already been said above that, from the verse, “God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran,” or from the shadowy and dense mountain, by which we understand the holy Trinity, this canticle is divided by a threefold division; and the sign of each division is *semper* (“always”), for which *diapsalma* is written in Greek and *selah* in Hebrew. Wherever it is placed, we should know that either what follows or what precedes does not pertain only to the present time. What has already been said plainly pertains to the person of God and of the Holy One, who was to come from the south and from the shadowy and dense mountain—that is, from the Holy Spirit and God the Father. Now, after the interposed “Always,” what follows is said to the person of the Holy Spirit. This is especially clear from the verse: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.”

He says therefore: “You divide the rivers of the earth; the waters saw you, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by.” Lest we understand rivers, waters, or torrents of waters here in the ordinary sense, the preceding question forbids it: “Were you angry with the rivers, O Lord, or was your fury against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea?” [Col. 0637A] Therefore, by “the rivers of the earth”—that is, all the wise men, or all the eloquence of worldly philosophy—you, good South Wind, you Spirit of wisdom, will divide them; you who will cause the river of God, that is, evangelical teaching, to run without division, with accompanying signs.

Why will you divide those rivers? Assuredly so that, broken up and weakened by their divisions, they may have little or no power, and the shod may pass through them. For this is what is said in Isaiah: “The Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall raise his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and shall strike it into seven streams, so that the shod may pass through it” (Isa. 11). The tongue of the Egyptian sea is the talkativeness of the wise men of this age; the Holy Spirit has made it foolish. When it was divided and set against [Col. 0637B] itself, all those whose feet were, or are, shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace passed through it more easily (Eph. 6).

When this had been done, “the waters saw you,” he says, “and the mountains were in pain”: that is, the peoples recognized you and the rulers grieved—some with the grief of repentance, others with the grief of envy. Many peoples indeed will swell, as waters sometimes swell; but their swelling will end. This is what he now says: “the torrent of waters passed by.”

It follows: “The deep gave forth its voice; the height shall lift up its hands. The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place; they shall go in the light of your arrows, in the splendour of your flashing spear.” When the torrent of waters—that is, all the assault and persecution of those who then harassed your people—had passed, then the deep, that is, hell, [Col. 0637C] praised you; then also those above, that is, the angels, clapped their hands in applause and, as it were by the gesture and dance of raised hands, displayed the victor.

Your sun and moon, and every splendour that had formerly shone upon the people, but had afterwards all been covered by the weight of evils and the terror of darkness, received their light again and recovered their former brightness. Your arrows and your flashing spear—that is, your blows and your instruction—provided light for your people. Finally, in the light of your arrows and in the splendour of your spear, which rebuked them in order to correct them, your people walked, fearing you, loving you, and holding you in great wonder.

Immediately there follows: “In wrath you shall tread down [Col. 0637D] the earth; in fury you shall strike the nations with astonishment. You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ. You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare the foundation as far as the neck.”

The mind, wishing to proceed and hasten onward, is still recalled to the matters already stated. For it seems to itself to have said less than it wishes. It has, indeed, passed over altogether the tenses of the verbs, as though they had been varied in these prophetic words by chance and without any reason. The prophet had said in the future tense: “You shall divide the rivers of the earth”; and suddenly he began to recount an event in the past tense: “The waters saw you, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by.” Then immediately he returns again to the future tense: “They shall go,” he says, “in the light of your arrows; in wrath you shall tread down the earth; in fury you shall strike the nations with astonishment.” [Col. 0638A] Then at once he returns again to the past tense: “You went forth,” he says, “for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ,” etc.

Does the Holy Spirit customarily vary the tenses of his words in the prophets in this manner by chance and without regard to any reason? Certainly not without reason; and although that reason is not wholly clear to us, it is sweet and pleasant to perceive something of it. Careful attention suggests this: prophetic discourse speaks in the past tense especially of things which were to come to pass or be done at a definite time. But it declares in the future tense those things which would not cease to happen on every day until the end of the age.

For the Lord was not to lack preachers in the world, nor the preaching of the future judgment until the end of the age; [Col. 0638B] therefore he declared it in the future tense: “You shall mount upon your horses, raising, you shall raise your bow.” But that the power of his divinity should lie hidden in the weakness of his passion was something to occur at a definite and brief time; therefore he said in the past tense: “There his strength was hidden.” The same distinction appears more clearly there, where, speaking of his passion, he says in the past tense: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21), which had to happen only once. But in the future tense: “I shall declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you” (ibid.), which happens and will happen until the end of the age.

Accordingly, I should like to return to the words, “You shall divide the rivers of the earth”; yet first it is somewhat relevant to our present subject to consider that going forth of which he says: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.” “You went forth”: that is, invisible God, you gave visible signs of your presence or your coming among men. Thus you went forth with your Christ. Therefore the one to whom these words are addressed is a person other than Christ himself. Nor should the person of the Father be understood here, because no authority of Scripture reports that that person appeared to human beings in such a way as to furnish visible signs of his presence. The Son of God, invisible God, became visible man; and with him thus going forth, the Holy Spirit went forth for the salvation of his people, so as to give a visible sign of his coming. For he descended even upon Christ, his Christ, in bodily form like a dove (Matt. 3). [Col. 0638D] And he appeared over the disciples of his Christ as fire, and sat upon each of them (Acts 2).

Thus he went forth for the salvation of his people with his Christ—that is, to save his people with his Christ, our Saviour. In his first going forth he was seen at the waters of the Jordan, where his Christ was being baptized. Fittingly, then, the work of that salvation begins from the likeness of waters, in praise of him who went forth for the salvation of his people: “You shall divide the rivers of the earth,” he says; “the waters saw you,” etc.

The verb “to divide” (*scindere*) is more apt and more significant than if he had said “to send forth” or “to open.” For by this single word he signifies both the desolation of evil rivers and the outpouring of good rivers. An example concerning evil or contrary rivers has already been given above: “The Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, [Col. 0639A] and shall raise his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and shall strike it into seven streams, so that the shod may pass through it” (Isa. 11). Concerning good rivers it is said elsewhere that “waters were divided in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness; and what was dry land became a pool, and thirsty ground springs of water” (Isa. 35). Evil rivers are rivers of the earth; good rivers, however, are not of the same earth, but are divided—that is, they are given to the earth through distributed grace.

Both began to happen at the Jordan waters, from that very going forth in which the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, went forth to the Jordan waters with his Christ for the salvation of his people. From that point Jesus Christ began publicly to preach to them and to cast out demons by the finger of God. “The waters saw you thus going forth,” he says, “and [Col. 0639B] the mountains were in pain”: that is, the peoples recognized you and the rulers envied you. For the crowds marvelled, but the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. 9).

“The waters saw you,” I say, “and the mountains were in pain,” because crowds went out to meet your Christ with palm branches, crying a devout Hosanna; and the chief priests envied him, plotting his death (Matt. 21). “You see that we are accomplishing nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12). Of any such person it is said in the Psalm: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. 7). The mountains likewise saw you—that you were with your Christ, and that he performed many signs not in Beelzebub (Luke 11), but in you. Yet the waters saw [Col. 0639C] you and praised you, while the mountains saw you and envied you. Then, he says, “the torrent of waters passed by” (Ps. 113).

What was that torrent of waters there, if not the deep and seditious malice of the Jews? Just as we rightly understand by the name of waters those crowds that saw and praised, and by the name of mountains the chief priests and Pharisees, so by the name of the torrent of waters we rightly understand the council which they assembled and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Hence your same Christ had long before said through the Psalmist, praying: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. 68). There “the torrent of waters passed by” must be understood as “over your Christ.” It passed by, I say: it came indeed, but did not remain over him long. It entered even to [Col. 0639D] his soul—that is, until he died.

But what follows at once? “The deep,” he says, “gave forth its voice; the height lifted up its hands; the sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place.” After the torrent of waters had passed by, the deep at once gave forth its voice. For as soon as he said, “It is finished,” and gave up his spirit, immediately the lower regions trembled, and the people of the saints who were in that deep abyss gave forth their voice—a tearful voice which we understand so well by faith as though we had been present there. That voice was such as this: “You have come, Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, that you might this night lead the bound from their prison cells.”

After such a voice from the deep, the height also lifted up its hands. For he rose from the dead; and when all the multitude of heaven saw this, filled with blessed wonder, it applauded and rejoiced in dancing. [Col. 0640A] Without delay, then, the sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place. For this same Christ of yours ascended into heaven and stood, or sat, at the right hand of the power of God; and his Church, lifted from the lower regions, also stood at the right hand, as the Psalm foretold: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44).

From this point it began to happen, does happen, and will happen until the consummation of the age, what immediately follows: the tenses are changed—that is, there is a transition from past-tense language to future-tense language. “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the splendour of your flashing spear; in wrath you shall tread down the earth; in fury you shall strike the nations with astonishment.” For the apostles were enlightened and began, through preaching, to send forth bright words of truth. These words are arrows—your shining arrows—showing by their light the way of life and piercing the hearts of peoples to repentance by their sharpness. Thus in the Psalm: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you in the heart of the king’s enemies” (ibid.). [Col. 0640B] The sense is: the words of your preaching are sharp, reaching to the soul and killing not human beings but human vices. Peoples pierced by them in the heart of the king’s enemies—that is, in their own heart, since they were formerly hostile to God the King or to God’s kingdom—shall fall beneath you; that is, reduced beneath your authority, they shall worship you.

Nor will there be preaching words alone; terrible signs will follow. Therefore, after saying, “In the light of your arrows,” he fittingly added, “in the splendour of your flashing spear.” The flashing spear is the power of performing signs. In its splendour and in the light of those arrows, he says, shall go—understood of both preachers and hearers of the Gospel. Thus it has happened, does happen, and will happen until the end of the age.

The light of the arrows and the splendour of the flashing spear advanced so far that Christian faith gained supremacy over the world and exercises upon the nations, with the strength of good zeal, the severity of religious instruction. Therefore he says to the Lord, the Holy Spirit, concerning arrows of this kind and such a spear: “In wrath you shall tread down the earth; in fury you shall strike the nations with astonishment.” Where instruction is exercised over the earthly-minded habits of human beings, there the earth is trodden down in wrath; and where Gentile-living persons are punished according to the measure of their sin—for example, when they are “delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Cor. 5)—there the nations are struck with astonishment through just fury.

Now at last we must consider more carefully his words: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.” For this repetition, “for salvation with your Christ,” must not be supposed empty. There is indeed one Spirit and one salvation of his people; but in the Gospel two goings forth of the same Spirit are recorded, and the work of that same salvation is twofold. The first going forth was in the form of a dove at the waters of the Jordan (Matt. 3). The second going forth was in the upper room over the apostles, in fire and divided tongues (Acts 2). This has already been said above.

Further, regarding the twofold work of salvation, it should likewise be known that the first work is forgiveness of sins and the second distribution of gifts. He began to perform the forgiveness of sins—the first and most necessary work—from the passion of his Christ. For when Christ rose from the dead and stood in the midst of the disciples, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20); and we must understand: for the forgiveness of sins. For it follows: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” The distribution of gifts, the second work of salvation, had indeed been effected in part in certain persons before Christ’s passion, so that some had the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, faith, prophecy, the working of miracles, and discernment of spirits. After his passion, however, it was accomplished more abundantly on the day of Pentecost, when kinds of tongues were additionally given, so that from then on this same salvation might become known among all nations. [Col. 0641B]

This work is accomplished individually in each believer: first, when one is born again from water and the Holy Spirit (John 3); and then, through the laying on of hands (Acts 19), one is confirmed by the anointing of chrism. Thus, having gone forth for salvation, “you struck,” he says, “the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare the foundation as far as the neck.”

The wicked one is always the devil, and his house is the world, or everything in the world: namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2). What then do we understand as the head of this house, except either the devil himself, the prince of the world, or original sin, which was the head and beginning of his kingdom or house? You struck this head with the blow of the stone—that is, with Christ’s passion—and therefore it is rightly said that you went forth for the salvation of your people. Then you laid bare the foundation of the same house as far as the neck: that is, whatever errors or vices there were in the world, you left none unshaken, whether what was hidden, as the foundation of a house is hidden, or what lay open, as the neck of a body lies open. For, inwardly fervent and outwardly wise and eloquent through those fiery tongues which you showed outwardly, they did not cease until they made public how great a folly was the wisdom of this world and how great a sacrilege were the things called sacred in Gentile temples. [Col. 0641C]

This is the third “Always,” of which it has already been said once and twice what it signifies. It follows: “You cursed his sceptres, the head of his warriors, coming as a whirlwind to scatter me. Their exultation is like that of one who devours the poor in secret.”

Since this canticle is divided by a threefold division, the sign of which is *semper*, or *diapsalma*, now placed for the third time, and since the two persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit are plainly distinguished in the foregoing, it is pleasing to refer this third part of the canticle to the proper person of the Father, so that it may be a canticle or praise of the whole Trinity.

“You cursed his sceptres,” he says, etc. It is as if he said: The wicked one was not struck only on this occasion, nor was he first struck when Christ suffered; he had long before been condemned, and his condemnation is threefold. First, you cursed his sceptres; second, you cursed the head of his warriors; third, you cursed all his warriors, coming as a whirlwind to scatter me. You cursed his sceptres when in heaven you condemned his pride, when he wished to hold the sceptres of heaven and the divine rule and to make himself the Most High. For he said in his heart: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). But you cursed those sceptres—that is, because of that presumption you condemned him irrecoverably. [Col. 0642A]

You cursed the head of his warriors when you said to the serpent, through which he had deceived man—an act that was the beginning of his warfare against the human race, and on account of which that serpent is rightly called the head of his warriors—“Because you have done this, you shall be cursed among all animals and beasts of the earth” (Gen. 3), etc. In the serpent, he himself was cursed; and from it he received the designation by which he is called the ancient serpent.

You continue to curse all his warriors, coming like a whirlwind to scatter me and all like me who fear you. The first of them was Pharaoh, king of Egypt; the last will be Antichrist. For Pharaoh, after the word of promise, was the first to wish, like a whirlwind, to scatter me—that is, to take away from me the effect of the oath which you swore to Abraham in the promise of the blessed seed, that is, Christ. For, in order that no seed might come, he commanded all male children to be killed (Exod. 1). But who does not know what befell him and the rest?

“You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters.” When he had dared, in pursuit, to enter after them, he was drowned with his army in the sea; there you cast him down, and he perished with his chariots and horsemen. [Col. 0642C] They were the first of all who openly persecuted your name; all the rest, inasmuch as they are or were like them, have acquired and continue to acquire a like condemnation. Such warriors are justly cursed, because they rejoice in the very fact that they are free to kill and persecute—which is to become like the devil or Antichrist. This is what he says: “His exultation is like that of one who devours the poor in secret” (Ps. 9). For who is the one who devours the poor in secret, except the one who, while lying in wait to seize the poor and seizing as much as he can, says in his heart: “God will not require it”?

It was indeed great and glorious that the sea covered that fleshly Pharaoh and the chariots of his armies, while you made a way in the same sea for your horses—or human beings. But it is greater and far more glorious that the same water, through Christ’s sacrament, conveys those who believe in him to the eternal kingdom, covering all sins, which are the spiritual camp of the Egyptians; and that in the sea of this age, where there was the mud of many waters—that is, the excessively carnal and turbid conduct of the nations—you made a way for your horses, of which I spoke above: “You shall mount upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation.” [Col. 0642D]

“I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled.” This verse has the same meaning and renews the same thought which he set forth at the beginning: “O Lord,” he says, “I heard your report and feared.” He explained what he heard and feared; and then, as it were by that part of a well-ordered discourse which rhetoricians call the conclusion, returning to the first proposition, he says: “I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled.”

This disturbance or trembling is desirable, because it is lowly and possesses the great benefit of the divine regard. For he says: “But to whom shall I look, except to the poor man and one contrite in spirit, trembling at my words?” (Isa. 66). Therefore, with his belly troubled and his lips trembling at the voice which he had heard within, he desires that the same disturbance or trembling may be increased in him, and in desiring says: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, [Col. 0643B] and let it bubble up beneath me, so that I may rest in the day of tribulation and may go up to our girded people.”

“I rejoice,” he says, “that I have now been able to say, ‘My belly was troubled’—something that he cannot say who lacks tenderness of belly, or rather has hardness of heart like the hardness of stone, whose heart God has not softened. Pharaoh king of Egypt is widely known in the holy Scriptures to have been such a person. I rejoice, I say, that, considering your works, O Lord, I trembled through the spirit of humility. Yet I desire that you increase humility of heart in me, so that, speaking to you, my Lord, I may more and more acknowledge that I am dust and ashes and shall soon become rottenness and a worm.

“Let that rottenness—that is, the memory of that rottenness by which I shall later decay—enter into my bones and bubble up beneath me: that is, let it humble everything in me that is strength or good work, and let it grow more and more in the root of my heart, in the depth of my conscience. Thus it will come about that I may rest in the day of tribulation. Knowing this, your Christ, when he said, ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart,’ immediately added: ‘And you shall find rest for your souls’ (Matt. 11).”

And what is this day of tribulation? One need not look far: the present time in which we are and live is a day of tribulation. Whether you call it “day” in the singular or “days” in the plural, it is a day of tribulation; the days are evil because they are full of adversities and full of sins. “Blessed is the man,” says the Psalmist, “whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law, that you may give him relief from evil days” (Ps. 93). [Col. 0643D] Intending this relief, your aforementioned Christ began in the cited passage: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” For what else is “I will refresh you” than “I will give you relief from evil days”? And showing wherein: “Take,” he says, “my yoke upon you, and learn that I am gentle and humble in heart”; and finally he adds: “And you shall find rest for your souls.”

Therefore, to admit rottenness into one’s bones and to have it bubbling beneath oneself—that is, because one is conscious of the rottenness which one will soon become as a human being—to be gentle and humble in heart: this is already to rest, not only in the future but also in the present age.

But what does it mean that, after saying, “that I may rest in the day of tribulation,” he added, “and may go up to our girded people”? What else but that to be gentle and humble in heart is to be truly girded, and to go up to the girded people, the people from whom the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and is seized violently? By what other girding than the spirit of humility do you suppose Moses was girded (Num. 10), so that he held fast the God of all flesh, the mightiest of spirits, when he said, “Let me go” (Exod. 32), and bent him to his own will? It must be known without doubt that without this girding there is nowhere any strength of righteousness. [Col. 0644A]

Though a person may possess many works, without this defence of righteousness he is nothing. Nor is that people his girded people who, with loins girded, eats the flesh of the lamb and goes up through the sea, as he had now said: “You made a way in the sea for your horses.” In this the synagogue places its confidence above all, because it is impossible for those to be justified who, seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10).

This is what he immediately says most aptly through a metaphor: “For the fig tree shall not blossom, and there shall be no shoot in the vines. The yield of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall not bring forth food. The flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls.” Under this number of six he rejects all the works of the law, which permits work on six days. He rejects them because the Jewish worker of the law does not seek to observe the Sabbath of the Lord; he does not have faith and humility, which Christ commends when he says, “You shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

The fig tree, the vine, and likewise the olive in the present passage are the synagogue; and the fields not bearing food are Jewish ceremonies. [Col. 0644C] The flock and the herd are the lesser and greater Jews, or the people and the priests. All the works of those who do not possess Christ’s faith and humility are rejected. By saying, “For the fig tree shall not blossom,” etc., it is as though he said: “Therefore I so earnestly desire the grace of humility, because in the works of the law there is no fruit of righteousness, no shoot of righteousness, no work of righteousness, and no life-giving food at all for the soul.”

In what respect has the flock been cut off from the fold and the herd fled from the stalls? In that the Jew does not believe, is unwilling to submit to God’s righteousness, and does not hear the voice of the Lord, the good shepherd. Hence he says: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John 10). Again: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8).

“But I shall rejoice in the Lord and exult in God Jesus my God; God the Lord is my strength.” What he says is this: Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness because it was not from faith but as if from works. But I shall believe not as if from works, but from faith, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For in saying, “I shall rejoice in the Lord,” he confesses the Father; in saying, “I shall exult in the Lord Jesus my God,” he confesses the Son; in saying, “God the Lord is my strength,” he confesses the Holy Spirit.

“And he shall make my feet like those of deer, and shall lead me victoriously upon my high places, singing in psalms.” For just as deer’s feet are swift for leaping thickets and seeking high places, so through this faith I shall be swift, so that I may attain the law of righteousness and not stumble at the stone of stumbling (Rom. 9). This righteousness of faith shall lead me upon my high places—that is, above the righteousness of works. It shall lead me, I say, as victor: the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, [Col. 0646A] singing in psalms the victory of my course, ascribing it not to my works but to his grace, and for this giving eternal thanks.

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Zephaniah

[Col. 0645]

**284** Your promise is true, Jesus Christ, faithful witness; your promise is true and trustworthy, by which, promising the Paraclete Spirit, you said among other things: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16). Everything the prophets spoke, everything written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, is yours; and “all things whatsoever the Father has are yours” (ibid.). Therefore, in the Scriptures I seek nothing other than you—you know this—and in this respect I desire to be like “the man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation upon the rock” (Luke 6).

Where greater difficulty arises in finding you, there I have generally found you yourself more fully; and only then, in the individual books of the prophets, have I thought that I had reached the rock upon which to lay foundations, when, through diligent meditation, beneath the obscurity of the letter I found your desirable glory. For I do not fail to recognize the reason why the prophets necessarily had to cover the mysteries of your brightness with compacted words—a reason which, as far as I was able, I have explained more fully at the beginning of this work.

Now, therefore, ready to enter, while seeking you, upon Zephaniah—the ninth in the order of the twelve prophets—I invoke the Holy Spirit whom you gave, who, by opening the Scriptures that bear testimony concerning you, has until now glorified you and does not cease to glorify you: that he may receive also from this which is yours and declare to me, seeking your glory, that glory of yours—for I have hope of eternal life only through faith in and knowledge of you.

## Commentary on the Prophet Zephaniah

### Book One

[Col. 0645]

**285 Chapter 1**

[Col. 0645]

“The word of the Lord which came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.”

Apart from this prophet, Joel, who is second in the order of the prophets, and Zechariah, who is eleventh, none of them has his father’s name in the heading. “The Hebrews hand down,” says blessed Jerome, “that whenever a prophet’s father or grandfather is named in the heading, they too were prophets. If this is true,” he says, “the prophet Zephaniah was descended, so to speak, from a prophetic lineage and from the glorious stock of his ancestors. For he had Cushi as father, Gedaliah as grandfather, Amariah as great-grandfather, Hezekiah as great-great-grandfather; and he himself, as the last charioteer, completed such a four-horse team.”

But whatever the value of that tradition, this is more pleasing: in accordance with the character of the prophecy that follows, the names are fitting, and according to their interpretation the quality of the matters or meanings written by him or through him corresponds to them. Thus, in accordance with the name Cushi, interpreted as “humility” or “my Ethiopian,” the Lord will say in this book: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants” (Zeph. 3). In accordance with the name Gedaliah, interpreted as “greatness of the Lord,” and the name Hezekiah, which signifies “strength of the Lord,” he will declare magnificently and forcefully: “Near is the great day of the Lord, near and exceedingly swift; bitter is the cry of the day of the Lord; there the mighty man will be distressed.” And in accordance with the name Amariah, rendered “word of the Lord,” after the most vehement proclamation of greatness and strength, he will give a word of exhortation, beginning thus: “Gather yourselves [Vulgate: Assemble], gather together, nation not beloved, before the wrath of the Lord’s fury comes upon you” (Zeph. 2).

Moreover, in accordance with his own name, Zephaniah—rendered by some as “watchtower,” by others as “secret of the Lord”—he truly begins as a watchman of the great matter, namely the Lord’s judgment, which is indeed a great secret, because no one except God knows that day and hour: “Gathering, I will gather all things from the face of the earth, says the Lord: gathering man and beast, gathering the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea.”

Certainly the Lord who says these things is the Son of God, God himself and Lord. This is especially clear because much later he will say: “Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection, for the future” (Zeph. 3), etc. For not just any one, but a particular one of the three persons of the blessed Trinity was to have a day of resurrection; and that person is none other than the Son of God, God and Lord—then still to become man, to suffer, die, and rise again; but now already made man, having suffered, died, been buried, and raised from the dead, while still having in the future a day of universal resurrection, for which we wait as he himself commands.

Therefore, he who says here, “Gathering, I will gather all things from the face of the earth, gathering man and beast, gathering the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea,” is the same one who says in his Gospel: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). And concerning him the Psalmist says to God the Father: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea” (Ps. 8).

Does God care for oxen and sheep, birds and fish? (1 Cor. 9.) Or should these not rather be understood as referring to every people and nation, to the diversity of all tribes and tongues, to all human beings or nations, whose characters are so divided and pursuits so varied that some may rightly be called like oxen, others like sheep, others like birds, and others like fish? He drew all these things to himself. “You subjected all these things,” the Psalmist says, “beneath his feet.”

It remains future, as the Apostle says of him: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him,” since many oppose him (Heb. 9). Yet what was said has already happened: “You set him over the works of your hands.” For because of the suffering of death, he has already been crowned with glory and honor. “All authority in heaven and on earth,” he says, “has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

How, then, or in what way will those who obstinately are his enemies and oppose him be subjected to him? Surely in the manner—or in that event—which immediately follows: “And the ruins of the wicked shall come, and I will destroy men from the face of the earth, says the Lord.” The evangelists Matthew and John have made this clearer to us than light. For what is said here, “Gathering, I will gather all things from the face of the earth, and the ruins of the wicked shall come,” the Lord of all says thus in Matthew: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him,” etc., down to: “And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous,” etc. (Matt. 25). In John it is said in this way: “Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5).

Thus this prophetic utterance is neither doubtful nor obscure: “Gathering, I will gather all things from the face of the earth, says the Lord—gathering man and beast, gathering the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea; and the ruins of the wicked shall come, and I will destroy men from the face of the earth, says the Lord.” For both this and the subsequent words of the prophet—“Near is the great day of the Lord, near and exceedingly swift; bitter is the cry of the day of the Lord; there the mighty man will be distressed; that day is a day of wrath,” etc.—speak of that great and universal judgment which we have all heard will occur on the last day.

After this beginning, however, and before he says, “Near is the great day of the Lord,” two judgments are foretold, then future and to be carried out upon Judah and Jerusalem: one because of the blood of the prophets which their fathers shed; the other because of the blood of the Lord himself, by shedding which their sons were to fill up the measure of their fathers.

Here I wish to set down the text concerning each vengeance, or judgment, which, as has been said, was to come upon that city and has now come. It follows: “And I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will destroy from this place the remnant of Baal, and the names of the temple-servants together with the priests; and those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven; and those who worship and swear by the Lord, and swear by Melchom; and those who turn back from following the Lord, and who have not sought the Lord nor inquired after him.”

This was spoken, and was subsequently fulfilled through King Nebuchadnezzar and the army of the Chaldeans. The passage concerning what was to be done through the hands of the Romans follows: “Be silent before the face of the Lord God, for near is the day of the Lord; for he has prepared a sacrifice and sanctified those whom he has summoned,” etc., down to: “They shall build houses and shall not inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and shall not drink their wine.” Immediately after this comes the statement concerning the great day of universal judgment: “Near is the great day of the Lord, near and exceedingly swift,” etc., down to: “For he will bring a consummation, and that swiftly, upon all the inhabitants of the earth.”

Let us now treat the statements in their order.

“And I will stretch out,” he says, “my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” This is connected with the foregoing so that where he said, “And the ruins of the wicked shall come,” you should understand: first the Jews and then the Greeks (Rom. 2), according to the Apostle’s meaning. For the Jew, before the Gentile, received the evils which he deserved, even in his own times. Both histories record this and prophecies attest that it was ordered by divine providence.

“Take,” the Lord says to Jeremiah, “from my hand the cup of the wine of this wrath, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to whom I send you.” “And I took,” he says, “the cup from the hand of the Lord, and gave it to drink to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me: Jerusalem, and all the cities of Judah, its kings and its rulers” (Jer. 25); and then, he says, “to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to the kings of the land of the Philistines, the kings of Tyre, the kings of Sidon, the kings of the islands, the kings of Arabia, the kings of the West, the kings of Zimri, the kings of Elam, the kings of the Medes, all the kings of the north and all their rulers, and all the kingdoms of the earth which are upon its face. And you shall surely drink. For behold, in the city upon which my name is invoked, I begin to afflict; and shall you be acquitted as innocent?” (ibid.).

Therefore, he says, “The ruins of the wicked shall come”; and it must be understood: first the wicked Jews, and then the wicked Greeks or Gentiles. For even in these particular acts of vengeance, which occur temporally, when nation rises against nation and kingdom against kingdom, through my judgment, I will first stretch out my hand over Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem—namely because of the blood of the prophets which they shed, and especially because of Manasseh, upon whom these crimes more particularly rested.

The prophetic utterance immediately identifies him, saying: “And I will destroy from this place the remnant of Baal, and the names of the temple-servants together with the priests; and those who worship and swear by the Lord, and swear by Melchom; and those who turn back from following the Lord, and who have not sought the Lord nor inquired after him.” For they had finally come to such impiety that, in the temple of God—as Ezekiel writes and the Fourth Book of Kings indicates—they set up a statue of Baal, which the Lord calls the image of jealousy, and in the same sanctuary worshiped idols together with God (Ezek. 14).

Accordingly, he significantly called the priests of idols not “priests” but “temple-servants”; and he means both those temple-servants and the former priests of God, as long as Baal was there; also those who upon the roofs, according to the rite of the Gentiles, worship the host of heaven, namely the sun, moon, and remaining stars; and those who swear by the name of the Lord and at the same time by the name of Melchom, the idol of the Ammonites.

“I will destroy from this place,” he says, chiefly, as has already been stated, because of the sins of Manasseh, who provoked the Lord more than anyone else in such matters and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood “up to the mouth” (4 Kings 21). Indeed, after Scripture had narrated concerning King Josiah: “Nevertheless,” it says, “the Lord did not turn away from the wrath of his great fury, with which his fury was enraged against Judah because of the provocations by which Manasseh had provoked him” (4 Kings 23).

There are seven declarations, a number by which totality is commonly signified. The first is: “I will destroy from this place the remnant of Baal.” The seventh: “They have not inquired after the Lord.” If they are considered or counted in reverse order thus: they have not inquired after the Lord; they have not sought him; they turn back from following the Lord; they swear by the Lord and by Melchom; they worship upon the roofs the host of heaven; they bear the names of temple-servants; and they worship Baal—what follows is always worse than the preceding evil.

For not to inquire after the Lord is indeed evil; but not to seek him while he may be found is worse; to turn back from following the Lord—that is, to despise the Lord and refuse to understand his will—is certainly most evil in matters of religion. Further, against religion, to swear by the Lord and swear by Melchom—interpreted “their king,” a name which might not seem impious to the simple—was evil. But to worship upon the roofs the host of heaven, something which might itself be done in rustic simplicity, was worse. Yet to be temple-servants or priests in the temple of the Lord while Baal was there was certainly most evil. The supreme accumulation of all evils was Baal himself.

Thus, by seven declarations, the whole extent and variety of all evils, greater and lesser, is denounced, on account of which Judah and Jerusalem then deserved wrath, so that the Lord who says these things might stretch out his hand over its inhabitants.

But he who did not yet know how to call father or mother—because he had not yet been born—afterward did so by that birth in which he learned and knew how to call father or mother: father, certainly, his adoptive or foster father; mother, the Virgin. Therefore his name could rightly be called: “Hasten to stretch out your hand; make haste to destroy sinners from their place and send captives into Babylon.” So, through another prophet, he was commanded to be called: “Hasten to take away the spoil; make haste to plunder” (Isa. 8), because before the child knew how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria were to be taken away, with him acting.

It follows:

Be silent before the face of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is near; for he has prepared a sacrifice, he has sanctified those whom he has called. And it shall be, on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, that I will visit punishment upon the princes, upon the king’s sons, and upon all who are clothed in foreign apparel; and I will visit punishment upon every one who enters arrogantly over the threshold on that day, who fill the house of the Lord their God with wickedness and deceit.

What does he mean when he says—or with what persons in view does he say—“Be silent before the face of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is near”? It has already been said that he who begins thus, “Gathering, I will gather all things from the face of the earth,” is Christ the Son of God [Col. 0650B], who, lifted up from the earth, was to draw all things to himself and judge the living and the dead on the last day. Later he says of that day: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and exceedingly swift.” Before that final judgment he was to execute two judgments upon that earthly Jerusalem: one, already accomplished, through Nebuchadnezzar and the army of the Chaldeans, because of the blood of the prophets which they shed; the other through the hands of the Romans, because they killed the Lord of the prophets himself. Of the first judgment, to be wrought through the Chaldeans, he had said: “And I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem,” etc. Now, about to speak of that which was to be wrought through the Romans, he begins thus: “Be silent before the face of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is near” [Col. 0650C].

For what purpose, then, or with whom in view does he issue this proclamation? I can understand it here as referring most readily to those insolent madmen, glutted and drunk on that Passover night, who, when they heard this Lord, adjured by the high priest to say whether he was the Christ, the Son of God, reply, “You have said it; and from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven,” cried out: “He is deserving of death.” Then they spat in his face, veiled his face, struck him with blows of the fist, and slapped his face, saying: “Prophesy to us: who is it that struck you?” (Matt. 31 [probably 26]). And in many other ways they insulted his face.

What kind of proceeding was this in a judgment, while the Holy Spirit was speaking through the mouths of the prophets [Col. 0650D]? Therefore, O irreverent and undisciplined men, ill-born and ill-reared, what are you doing? “Be silent before the face of the Lord God”; restrain your mouth before the face of the Lord God, a man to be feared in his majesty even by all the powers of heaven. How you dishonoured him! Be silent, for the day of the Lord is near. And, as Moses said: “The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to be present” (Deut. 32). Woe to you on that day of this Lord—and you will be silent. You will be silent, I say, for that day of the Lord will be for you a day of destruction, because he has prepared a sacrifice and sanctified those whom he has called. He has prepared, I say, a sacrifice—that is, himself; and by preparing such a sacrifice he sanctified those whom he called, namely those whom he foreknew and predestined before the ages to become his own, and whom in their respective times [Col. 0651A] he called throughout all preceding ages, up to that day on which you spat upon, veiled, and slapped his face, and shook your heads against that same face, saying: “Ha!”

All that he endured was the preparation of the sacrifice; and in that sacrifice of his body and blood he sanctified those whom he called with the sanctification which is the remission of all sins (Rom. 7 [probably 3]). What remains now except that your house be left desolate to you? Surely there is no reason for which he should delay the judgment of your punishment, since the assumption has already taken place: since, in a wondrous manner, life has been assumed from among you who were dead. That day of the Lord, on which this will occur, is near.

The prophet cried this out in his own person: “Be silent,” he says, “before the face of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is near” [Col. 0651B]; and he did not say, “great, near, and exceedingly swift.” Therefore the explanation proceeds more readily, because nothing conflicts with our observance of the distinction of times made according to the text of this prophetic Scripture, or according to the order of the Lord’s judgments.

There follows the speech of the Lord, who had spoken previously: “And it shall be,” he says, “on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, that I will visit punishment upon the princes, upon the king’s sons, and upon all who are clothed in foreign apparel; and I will visit punishment upon every one who enters arrogantly over the threshold on that day, and who fill the house of their Lord God with wickedness and deceit.” The day of the Lord’s sacrifice is the time from the Lord’s Passion, at which time, forty years later, this visitation of which he now speaks took place, as the whole world heard. That visitation arose chiefly from the chief priests [Col. 0651C]. Hence he rightly says first: “I will visit punishment upon the princes.”

Who, moreover, were the king’s sons except these men themselves and the other Jews, glorying as though in the unique nobility of their race? For they boasted most insolently, saying in one place: “We are Abraham’s seed and have never served anyone” (John 8). Again: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (ibid.). Because of such pride he himself called them “sons of the kingdom,” when he spoke thus: “I tell you that they shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the sons of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness” (Matt. 8). Those whom he there calls sons of the kingdom, here we rightly understand as sons of the king—that is [Col. 0651D], proud men exalting themselves over the whole human race because of their singular nobility, as sons of King God; especially since, while plotting murder against the true and only Son of God, they said among other things: “We have one Father, God.”

What does the prophetic utterance signify in saying, “Upon all who are clothed in foreign apparel”? Do you suppose that hypocrisy is foreign apparel? Indeed, exceedingly foreign. What, among garments, is more foreign than sheep’s clothing upon ravening wolves? What, I say, is more foreign than for one who is inwardly full of wickedness to appear righteous to human beings outwardly? What is more foreign than the widening of phylacteries, the enlargement of fringes, and sitting upon Moses’ seat—especially in the case of those whose works are not to be followed? Such were the scribes and Pharisees. Certainly for this reason this visitor, who according to the truth of this prophecy was already to visit punishment upon them, cries “Woe!” against them seven times in a short discourse in Matthew (Matt. 23) [Col. 0652A].

Then he says: “And I will visit punishment upon every one who enters arrogantly over the threshold on that day, who fill the house of their Lord God with wickedness and deceit.” Of whom can this more truly be said—that he enters arrogantly over the threshold—than of one who does not wait for the gatekeeper to open to him, but violently enters the sheepfold (John 10)? There are many such people also in this age; and in that age Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, who, through an ill-fated bargain, tore apart the supreme priesthood which they had purchased, dividing the pontificate between themselves in alternating annual terms [Col. 0652B]. And who could doubt that this was said of those who filled the house of their God with wickedness and deceit, when the Lord God himself rebuked them with his own mouth: “You have made my Father’s house, which ought to be a house of prayer, a den of thieves” (Matt. 21)?

In saying this, did he not also signify by his action the visitation expressed in these prophetic words? For he made, as it were, a whip of cords and drove all of them out of the temple, thereby terribly indicating that they would immediately be cast out of the kingdom of God—or rather, that they possessed nothing in that temple or kingdom of which they boasted themselves to be sons.

“And it shall be in that day,” says the Lord, “a sound of crying from the Fish Gate, and a howling from the Second Quarter, and a great breaking from the hills.” They called the Fish Gate the gate nearest the sea among all the approaches to Jerusalem [Col. 0652C], concerning which Ezra also reports: “The sons of Asanaah built the Fish Gate; they roofed it, and set up its doors, bolts, and bars” (2 Esd. 3). When he says, “and a howling from the Second,” he means the gate in that same region of the second wall, concerning which it is written in the Book of Kings: “Therefore Hilkiah the priest, Maican, Achobor, Saphan, and Asaza went to Huldah the prophetess, wife of Sellum son of Tecua, son of Araas, keeper of the garments, who lived in the Second Quarter” (4 Kings 22).

By “a great breaking from the hills” he speaks of Mount Zion and the higher part of the city, because, when the heights and citadel of a city have been occupied, descent to the lower ground is easier. From these events, then—events wholly destined to happen—the prophet conceived the sense by which he divided the outcry threefold: into a sound of crying from the Fish Gate, a sound of howling from the Second Quarter, and a sound of great breaking from the hills [Col. 0652D].

It is marvellous to tell and dreadful to the senses—or to the understanding—how it is established that this happened according to that very division of sounds in the most famous destruction of wretched Jerusalem. For even before it was surrounded by the Roman army, and throughout the entire siege, it was within itself divided, mangled, and torn apart by a threefold sedition, most atrociously, most horribly, and beyond what can be spoken or believed. The three leaders of the factions were John, Eleazar, and Simon. Eleazar and his followers occupied the upper city and the temple; Simon the lower city; John held the middle (Josephus, *Jewish War*, book 6, ch. 1) [Col. 0653A].

Who has ever heard of things like those done within? Truly they were so great that they may rightly be judged worthy of prophetic exposition. Then there was indeed a sound of crying from the Fish Gate—that is, from the lower part of the city, where Simon tyrannized; a howling from the Second—that is, from the middle, where the beast John raged; and a great breaking from the hills—that is, from the temple and the city’s citadel, where Eleazar ruled in such a way that he stained the very altar of the temple with blood and made a pool, in the sacred courts, from the blood of varied corpses of his fellow citizens.

How much did you suffer, O most wretched city, from the Romans—compared with what you suffered from your own people and fellow citizens? Or rather, what city or nation ever endured from foreigners such things as you endured from your own people [Col. 0653B]? But let every pity cease, since you were condemned by your own judgment. For you said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Therefore the breaking that follows is as harsh as it is just.

“Howl, inhabitants of the mortar.” Here *pila* is not to be read with a short syllable, but with a long one, so that we understand a mortar to be meant, in which grain is pounded: a hollow vessel also suited to medical use, in which barley gruel (*ptisanae*) is properly made. It is aptly said, “you who dwell in the mortar,” because, just as grain is pounded by a pestle striking from above, so an army rushing down from the Fish Gate, the Second Quarter, and the hills would fall upon the people.

Whoever wishes to consider the calamities of that siege and the straits of the besieged city (Ezek. 16) will surely perceive how fittingly he employed the comparison in saying “inhabitants of the mortar” [Col. 0653C]. For as grain is gathered into a mortar so that, unable to leap away while the pestle strikes from above, it may be pounded, so the people flocking together from all the cities and regions of Judaea were confined by the sudden siege; and, more cruelly from within through the monstrous savagery of the aforesaid leaders of sedition than from enemies outside, they were unspeakably tortured by sword, famine, and pestilence. They were enclosed by the wondrous judgment of God, so that one wishing to flee to the enemy for relief could not do so.

There follows: “All the people of Canaan have fallen silent; all who are laden with silver have perished.” Who is this Canaan? Surely the Jewish people, to whom another prophet says: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite”; and Daniel says to the aged elder: “Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you” [Col. 0653D]. Why, however, does he here assume this name, preferring to say “the people of Canaan” rather than “the people of the Jews”? Surely because of the true character of their deeds or deserts, and because of terror. For another prophet also says: “Terror and a snare, an oracle and destruction, have come upon us” (Lam. 3). For prophet and priest are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord.

The deceitful people had to be deceived, so that, while they supposed something of this kind concerning others, they might allow some prophets to live and preserve Scripture, useful to future ages. Therefore all the people of Canaan—which is interpreted “their movement,” that is, the Jewish people, who shook their head against the Lord [Col. 0654A], their feet having already been moved because they did not stand in the truth—have fallen silent: understand, before the face of the Lord. For we must remember that, in beginning above, he said: “Be silent before the face of the Lord God, for the day is near.”

That people, that assembly of the ungodly, who then jeered, who then did not keep silence, who not only failed to show reverence but dishonoured the Lord’s face with mouth and hands—behold, they have fallen silent; behold, they have lost authority to speak. And as it was said of a conspicuous one among them, “Let another receive his bishopric,” so it is certain of that whole people that it no longer has teaching authority. And as its name has here been changed for the worse—for the prophet did not say, “All the people of Judah have kept silent,” but “all the people of Canaan”—so they have lost their honour and every voice, sold into the final slavery [Col. 0654B], captive not merely in some fashion, not as formerly in Babylon, but dispersed through that very captivity throughout the whole world.

The cause of every evil and of their total destruction was avarice, extending even to the price of blood. Therefore there follows: “All who are laden with silver have perished.” Judas the traitor was the example of this cause for the whole Canaanite people. For as he, entangled by desire for silver, sold the Lord’s blood to them for thirty pieces of silver and therefore perished miserably, so that whole people was especially intractable because it was entangled in the nets of silver; and especially for this reason they hated the Lord, because he argued against their avarice.

According to the number of silver pieces for which he sold the Lord’s blood and they purchased it, both seller [Col. 0654C] and buyers were entangled in thirty curses. In Psalm 108 the first is: “Set a sinner over him”; the last: “Let them be covered with their shame as with a double garment.” Indeed, the force of the wording is this: he did not say, “All who possess silver have perished,” but “All who are laden with silver have perished.” To possess silver is far different from being entangled in silver.

For Abraham, David, and many other saints and righteous persons possessed silver; they were rich in gold and silver and yet did not perish. Why? Because they possessed money as masters, not, as slaves of money, placing their hope in silver wealth. Those who hope or trust in silver are entangled in silver, and all such people perish. This distinction is necessary where the Lord says to his disciples: “How difficultly those who have riches shall enter into the kingdom of God” (Luke 18). For the disciples could have been—and, says the evangelist Mark, were—astonished at his words. But Jesus, answering again, said to them: “Little children, how difficult it is for those trusting in riches to enter into the kingdom of God”; and only then did he say: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark 10) [Col. 0654D].

Thus he excepted those rich persons who, although they possess money, do not trust in it. That sentence bears only upon those rich persons who, because they trust in riches, are both “laden with silver,” as this prophet says, and made so gross by that entanglement that it is exceedingly difficult for them to enter into the kingdom of God.

There follows: “And it shall be at that time: I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will visit punishment upon the men fixed in their dregs, who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil.’” With what spontaneous condescension the Holy Spirit provides against the prophet, or anyone else, being troubled by the concern which troubled the blessed old man Abraham when he heard the Lord speak of Sodom: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should become as the wicked. This is not like you, who judge the whole earth” (Gen. 18) [Col. 0655A].

The Lord granted him, and grants this prophet also, that it is not his way to kill the righteous with the wicked. Now anyone who had sinned against the Lord in ignorance, and who, once the truth had been heard or known, was going to repent—as three thousand of them did in one day at Peter’s preaching (Acts 2)—could in some sense be called righteous. Such a person, I say, could in some manner already be called righteous, as Abimelech said of himself: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant nation?” (Gen. 20). For he had taken Abraham’s wife in ignorance.

Thus the Lord frees this prophet, or any other person, from such concern when he says: “And it shall be at that time: I will search Jerusalem with lamps,” etc. It is as though he said: Before that day of visitation arrives—the day of crying, howling, and great breaking—I shall do what the wise woman does, who, having lost one drachma, lights a lamp [Col. 0655B], sweeps the house, and diligently seeks until she finds it (Luke 13 [probably 15]).

I shall light not merely one lamp, but many: that is, I shall clothe the apostles with the Holy Spirit and power from on high (Luke 24), so that they may be my witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth, beginning from Jerusalem and from all Judaea and Samaria (Acts 1). Certainly this will be to search Jerusalem with lamps, so that wherever the lost drachma may be, it will be unable to remain hidden: that is, whoever is of God and worthy of the heavenly city Jerusalem will not remain in the guilt of unbelief.

For as a lost drachma, a golden drachma, when sought with lamps, gleams out of darkness in the light of the lamps and is found, so all who are ignorant yet righteous—such as the aforesaid Abimelech testified himself to have been—when they hear the truth of the words spoken and see the brightness of the signs [Col. 0655C], will burst into a cry of confession, be pierced in heart, and say, “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). Having undertaken repentance and been baptized, they will be saved. Thus, by searching Jerusalem, until all who have been preordained to eternal life believe, I shall then visit punishment upon the men fixed in their dregs, who say: “The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil.”

For they will be condemned by their own judgment, hating my lamps and loving their dregs. And just as those who wallow in the dregs of lust, secretly commit fornication, defile and are defiled, do not wish to be sought with lamps—indeed, they hate and abhor lamps—so those wicked men, whose eye is envious toward the truth, hating both me and my Father [Col. 0655D], loving their sins and hating righteousness, loving this present age and hating the age to come, will not desire to hear the words of God spoken with the testimony of signs. Rather, of those whom I shall send to them—prophets, wise men, and scribes—they will kill and crucify, scourge, and persecute from city to city (Matt. 23); and they will say: “What these men say is false. The Lord will not do good to the good, nor evil to the evil”; that is, there will be no day of judgment, or certainly this one whom they call Lord, whom we crucified, is nobody: he was not, nor will he be, such as can do us good or evil.

Therefore I will visit punishment upon them, so that all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel, may come upon them. And I shall say to them: “Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you” [Col. 0656A]. This is what immediately follows: “And their strength shall become plunder, and their houses a desolation; they shall build houses and not inhabit them, and plant vineyards and not drink their wine.”

What could be more manifest in fulfilment than these things? Their strength, by which they were first wickedly strong against God and then against human beings, became plunder. How were they strong against the Lord? Surely as a madman is strong against a physician. Their strength, in seeking to establish their own righteousness, was not and is not true strength; it is altogether false and deceptive, like the strength of a madman when he strikes the physician.

Then it is marvellous, and brought about by God’s wondrous judgment, that they presumed so much on their strength against human beings as to undertake an implacable war against the Romans, conquerors of all nations [Col. 0656B]. No plundering among any nations has been heard of like the plundering of their strength. How did their house become a desolation? Surely in that the temple was abandoned by every protection of heavenly spirits, saying, “Let us depart from these dwellings”—a saying which Josephus testifies was plainly heard.

The building of that house, that is, of the temple, had been greatly enlarged in recent times and made most beautiful with towers and porticoes. The city itself was adorned with fine houses and filled with wealth; the surrounding country, wonderfully planted everywhere with vineyards and trees of diverse kinds, was exceedingly fruitful. But everything was cut down, everything destroyed and burned with fire; they were reduced to desolation, and those among them who survived the sword were led captive into all nations. Thus the truth appeared of him who said: “They shall build houses and not inhabit them, and plant vineyards and not drink their wine” [Col. 0656C].

Having set these matters forth, let us hear with astonished ears what this watchman, who does not permit us to sleep, immediately cries out, says, and announces from his lofty watchtower. He says: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and exceedingly swift. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be afflicted there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and alarm, against fortified cities and lofty battlements. And I will afflict men, and they shall walk [Col. 0657A] as blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord. Their blood shall be poured out as dust, and their bodies as dung. Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of his zeal the whole earth shall be devoured, for he shall make a speedy end of all the inhabitants of the earth.”

O what a great cry and exclamation—how forceful for every human being, unless he is deaf and has no ears to hear! What did he see, that he cried out so? What was the vision of his mind, whose voice has such sharpness? Blessed Pope Gregory, rightly astonished at the force of this cry, says: “Consider, dearest brothers, in the presence of so great a Judge, what terror there will be on that day, when there will no longer be a remedy for punishment; what confusion there will be for one whom his guilt requires to blush in the assembly of all human beings and angels; what dread, when he sees him wrathful whom the human mind cannot grasp even when tranquil! Beholding that day, the prophet says: ‘That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and alarm.’ Consider therefore, brothers, with what severity the prophet saw the day of final judgment become bitter to the hearts of the reprobate, since he cannot express it with so many designations” [Col. 0657B].

What could he have observed more aptly from the duty of a good speaker, in accordance with the nature of the matter, than that the hearer should be made attentive in the opening of the discourse—or rather, of the declamation? With what word, what utterance, could the watchman better arouse attention than by saying, “It is near” [Col. 0657C]? He contemplated carefully; with penetrating and clear sight he saw that what seems far off to bleary-eyed and half-blind people is near, though they say, “This will happen in distant times.”

Not content to say once, “The day of the Lord is near,” he repeated: “It is near and exceedingly swift.” And truly, according to the magnitude of the danger, it is near and exceedingly swift. Nor does this appear vain to one who has some perception of God, before whose eyes a thousand years are as yesterday that has passed—or, what is shorter, as a watch in the night, that is, one of the four watches of a single night. Indeed, their years will be counted among things held as nothing—that is, they will be reckoned among them (Ps. 89).

That day will be great: such a day as has not been since days began, nor ever will be again. What sound, then, does he immediately note when he says, “The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be afflicted there”? What else can we suppose it to be except this: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25) [Col. 0657D]? Truly it is a bitter sound. “There,” he says—that is, in that utterance—“the mighty man shall be afflicted.” And who is mighty except the proud one? The mighty devil, his mighty angels, and the mighty human beings who follow him will be afflicted there; in that utterance they will be afflicted.

Is he then truly mighty who will be afflicted by that utterance? Rather, he is falsely mighty, truly weak. He is called mighty not because he is so, but because he appears so. But then he will not appear so even to himself, nor will he be able to deny that he is weak, when by a single utterance that mighty king of the mighty shall be cast down before the sight of all (Job 40).

With what force, with what mighty breath, desiring to describe the greatness of that day, he says: “A day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and alarm” [Col. 0658A]. He proclaimed one and the same day six times with terrifying additions, and he did not add it a seventh time. Why? I suppose, surely, because there will be nothing there of the seventh day, nothing of the Lord’s Sabbath; but without rest, without any hope of repose, the mighty man shall be afflicted there.

For all that he proclaimed by so many names will be “against fortified cities and lofty battlements,” that is, against ungodly human beings and proud angels.
