When he says fortified cities, understand: fortified apart from the Lord; and when he says lofty angels, understand the height of princes who exalt themselves against the true and only exalted Lord. These are the fortified cities, and these the lofty angels, whom the Apostle expresses more plainly—as was necessary in the Gospel, in which this wrath, or day of God’s wrath, is revealed. For, after saying, “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven,” he continues: “against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those human beings who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Rom. 10 [probably 1]), etc. [Col. 0658B].

Does not that which the Lord the Judge himself says immediately after the prophet’s words fit such persons and stand reserved for them by righteous judgment? “And I will afflict,” he says, “men, and they shall walk as blind men.” And the prophet, immediately confirming the judgment, gives the reason: “Because they have sinned against the Lord.” For those who here voluntarily shut their eyes against the truth will rightly walk there as blind men, because, “when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was voluntarily darkened. Professing themselves wise,” and indeed, although many of them perceived the invisible things of God from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that were made, nevertheless—even more—they became foolish and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed creatures, and serpents [Col. 0658C].

Therefore there is indeed cause for the judgment, because they sinned against the Lord. Since for this very reason God also gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they might dishonour their bodies among themselves; and gave them over to shameful passions, so that both women and men might change natural use into that use which is contrary to nature; and gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things unfitting (ibid.), this sentence, entirely full of their rejection, is right and just: “Their blood shall be poured out as dust, and their bodies as dung.”

What he then adds—“Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath”—requires no proof even in the present time. Indeed, it is known and certain that neither gold nor silver will come there with those who possessed them; for it is written elsewhere: “When he dies, he shall take none of it away, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48) [Col. 0658D].

Further, what follows removes every aid of gold and silver: “In the fire,” he says, “of his zeal the whole earth shall be devoured, for he shall make a speedy end of all the inhabitants of the earth.” For if, in that fire by which the world will be judged, the whole earth will be devoured—as is true, since elsewhere he says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24)—where will gold and silver appear, since they too are earth? And even if they were pleasing, could they belong to those people? “They brought nothing into this world” (1 Tim. 6), and therefore sinners will then possess nothing but sins. Consequently that righteous fire of the Lord’s most righteous zeal will swiftly make an end of all those dwelling upon the earth, precisely because, despairing of heaven, they have dwelt upon earth with their whole mind.

## Chapter II
Gather yourselves, assemble, nation not beloved, [Col. 0659B] before the decree gives birth to a day passing away like dust, before the wrath of the Lord’s fury comes upon you.

This is the office and practice of a watchman of the faith, of a faithful envoy: not to be satisfied with crying out what he has seen or announcing the matter for which he has undertaken an embassy, but also to add of his own accord some exhortatory speech, by which, making the hearer well disposed, he may hasten to rouse him to the necessary precaution—a great part of good assistance. The Apostle finely shows this concerning himself when, having first said to the Corinthians, “God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and has placed in us the word of reconciliation; for Christ, for whom we discharge an embassy” (II Cor. V), he then adds: “And as helpers we exhort you not to receive the grace of God [Col. 0659C] in vain” (II Cor. VI).

So this prophet, when in the manner of a watchman he had cried out with prophetic mouth the evils which he had seen coming—first upon particular regions and then upon the world as a whole—then, as though moderating the vehemence of his denunciation a little, begins more gently and exhorts in these words: “Gather yourselves, assemble”—that is, in an assembly, a congregation, by which we can and ought to be joined to God the Creator. Whoever does not do this is “like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I).

Hence he says: “Before the decree gives birth to a day passing away like dust, before the wrath of the Lord’s fury comes upon you.” Dust is movable; when the wind blows, it scatters and casts it from the face of the earth, because it has not come together, [Col. 0659D] has not been gathered into one by receiving the dew through which it could adhere to itself. But when the wind has cast it away, where will it appear, or how and from where can it again come together or be assembled?

Thus, indeed, the decree of the Almighty will give birth, upon the impious and unbelieving, to a day that passes away and makes them pass away like dust, because they did not come together and were not assembled to God and Lord through the saving dew of his grace, through water and Spirit. By this, all who do not perish have become one body with that head. Peter, knowing this, spoke in the same sense when he said: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts II). For he knew that the decree would first give birth upon that generation to a day passing away like dust, so that they might be scattered as captives among [Col. 0660A] all nations; and afterward, together with the other impious nations, the wrath of the Lord’s fury would come upon them on the day of universal judgment.

The expression, “before the decree gives birth,” is entirely fitting for him who says through another prophet: “I have kept silence; I have always been silent; I have been patient; like a woman in labor I will speak” (Isa. XLII). For a long time he restrained and deferred that wrath of his fury; but at last he will reveal it all the more harshly in proportion as he has endured more patiently. Like a woman carrying something in the womb, who restrains her voice for a long time and can restrain it, but when the hour comes brings forth with crying and groaning what she has held within herself.

Likewise, the address, “nation not beloved,” has the same sense, though it sounds less severe, as John the Baptist’s saying: “Brood of vipers, who has shown you [Col. 0660B] how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Matt. III). The Lord himself also says: “A wicked and perverse generation seeks a sign” (Matt. XII); and Peter, as stated above, says: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts II). Neither here nor there was this said apart from the judgment of the Law. Moses first said: “Crooked and perverse generation, do you thus repay the Lord?” (Deut. XXXII); and, “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom,” etc. (ibid.).

It follows: “Seek the Lord our God, all you meek of the earth, who have practiced his judgment. Seek the righteous one; seek the meek one, if perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury; for Gaza shall be destroyed, Ashkelon shall become a desert, Ashdod they shall cast out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted.”

Just as, when the wrath of God from heaven began to be revealed through the Gospel against all human impiety [Col. 0660C] (Rom. I), it was first necessary to speak the word of God to the Jews and afterward to turn to the nations (Acts XIII), so here the prophetic Spirit, having foretold that the wrath—or day of the Lord’s wrath and fury—was near and very swift, first addressed the nation not beloved, the Jewish nation, with exhortation: “Gather yourselves and assemble.” Then he addresses all the nations, saying: “Seek the Lord our God, all you meek of the earth.” And he repeats this same word, “seek,” three times: “Seek the Lord our God; seek the righteous one; seek the meek one.” I judge this to mean nothing other than: Believe in the Father; believe in the Son; believe in the Holy Spirit.

Those who received or receive such exhortation [Col. 0660D] are rightly called meek and persons who have practiced God’s judgment. Conversely, the Jews who rejected the word and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life (I Cor. XI) are called a nation not beloved. Indeed, all the meek, precisely because they are meek and receptive to God’s word, have practiced and do practice the Lord’s judgment, judging themselves so that they may not be judged. The beginning of this judgment is to sentence themselves as sinners and liable to death to the Lord’s cross—that is, to be baptized into his death and buried with him through baptism into death. The perfection of this same judgment or righteousness is thereafter to walk in newness, just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father (Rom. VI).

It is striking that he says to such persons, “if perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury.” Will even [Col. 0661A] they scarcely be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury? Does not the apostle Peter say this also? For he says: “But if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe God’s Gospel? And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (I Pet. IV). Therefore, however meek a person may be, however much he may have practiced the Lord’s judgment, he should always distrust himself and not suppose that he has attained it, since no righteous person can be saved if judged without mercy.

Every impious person and sinner is rightly understood under the names of the Philistine cities—Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron—for, I think, a double reason. The first is that the Philistine nation is named first among all the nations that envied the Lord’s glory and the meek of the earth, namely Moses and the others coming up [Col. 0661B] from the land of Egypt. “The peoples,” it says, “went up and were angry; anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia; then the rulers of Edom were troubled,” and the rest (Exod. XV). The inhabitants of Philistia were named first because they were the first to grieve and the first prepared to attack Israel as it came up. For it is written: “When Pharaoh had sent the people away, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near, lest perhaps they should repent when they saw wars rising against them” (Exod. XIII).

The other reason is that the meanings of these names denote the perversity of all who, after the likeness of the Philistines, hate and persecute all the devout who flee to him and leave this wicked age behind. Gaza is interpreted “his strength” [Col. 0661C]; Ashkelon, “weighed” or “murderous fire”; Ashdod, “fire of generation”; Ekron, “uprooting” or “barrenness.”

And the sense is this: all who congratulate themselves on bodily strength and secular power, and say with the devil, “By the strength of my hand I have done this” (Isa. X), shall be despoiled and reduced to nothing on the day of the Lord’s fury. Likewise, one who has burned to shed blood and caused many souls to stumble shall receive the measure of his crime, be weighed down by the very weight with which he acted, and in him will be fulfilled: “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V), when he is burned with the devil in the fires of Gehenna.

Likewise, one who has burned with lust and raged in the fire of generation: “For all adulterers [are] like an oven, their hearts” (Hos. VII) [Col. 0661D]—such a person shall be cast out, not in darkness or in hidden judgment, but at noon; that is, when the saints receive full brightness, he shall be cast into darkness and have no fellowship with the saints. Again, one who has not merely borne no fruit, but by the perversity of his teaching has uprooted very many, shall himself also be uprooted.

Therefore, seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth; and do not be like Gaza—that is, like those who are wrongly strong [292] and not meek, who, seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X), for such Gaza shall be destroyed. Seek the Lord, all you meek; and do not be like Ashkelon—that is, those burning with the fire of murder, whose hands are full of blood—for such Ashkelon shall be deserted, as Truth said: “Behold, [Col. 0662A] your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Seek the Lord, all you meek, and do not be like Ashdod—that is, like those who, voluntarily intensifying natural pleasure, have turned it into frenzy and kindled for themselves a burning fire. For such Ashdod is cast out at noon—that is, it shall be condemned by manifest judgment. Such Ashdod, I say, shall bear the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah, according to another prophet who says: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. I).

Seek the Lord, and do not be like Ekron—that is, like the barren vineyard of the Lord of hosts, the house of Israel, which, when it ought to have produced grapes of judgment and righteousness, produced wild grapes (Isa. V) of iniquity and outcry. For such Ekron, such barrenness, shall be uprooted.

[Col. 0662B] The wrath of the Lord’s fury is indeed reserved for all unbelieving nations, but especially and above all for that nation which first resisted and stirred up persecution against Christ’s Gospel or the sacrament of baptism, after the likeness of the Philistines. As was said above, that nation first envied Israel and was ready to resist and make war upon it as it came up from the land of Egypt in the crossing of the Red Sea.

It follows, therefore: “Woe to you who inhabit the line of the sea, nation of the lost.” A nation inhabiting the line of the sea is a nation near Christ’s baptism, just as the Philistine nation was near the sea through which Israel passed. For how near it was to that sacrament of eternal salvation, among whom Christ, dying, instituted that sacrament; among whom he poured water and blood from his side; among whom [Col. 0662C], after giving the Holy Spirit, he shone by many signs and wonders, showing that the Lord himself was leader in mercy to the people whom he redeemed. At the crossing of the Red Sea there went before them three thousand people, because on that very day of Pentecost they were baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Acts II).

Woe to you, nation of the lost; woe to you who so inhabit the line of the sea. Though you could have drawn to yourselves such a line—the line of allotment by which the land of God’s kingdom is divided—you not only did not draw it, but envied those who came in and drew it. “The word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the Philistines; and I will destroy you, so that there shall be no inhabitant.”

No one doubts that the land of the Philistines is the land of Canaan; and it has already been said, and is commonly proved by many testimonies of Scripture, that in the present [Col. 0662D] passage Canaan means the Jew. Therefore, against you, O Canaan, and O land of the Philistines—against you, not Jews but Canaanites; not the land of the Jerusalemites but the land of the Philistines, that is, “of the drink of those who fall”—the word of the Lord is against you. What I say is not for good but for evil; not in grace but in wrath; not in mercy but in vengeance.

For it follows: “And I will destroy you, so that there shall be no inhabitant.” “The line of the sea shall become resting-places for shepherds and folds for sheep; and the line shall belong to those remaining of the house of Judah. There they shall feed in the houses of Ashkelon; in the evening they shall rest, because the Lord their God shall visit them and turn back their captivity.”

Whether it happened literally as the text says—whether the land of the Philistines [Col. 0663A] was left desolate and without any inhabitant—God knows. “I will destroy you,” he says, “so that no inhabitant may remain”; and you shall come to such desolation that all your most fortified cities will become sheepfolds for shepherds. Whatever happened to that land properly called the land of the Philistines, and to the land of Moab and the land of the sons of Ammon, concerning whom he will speak later, we who know that the book was sealed (Dan. XII) and the visions of the prophets closed, as we read that some of them were commanded, must not doubt that the mysteries of spiritual realities are concealed under the names of bodily realities, and that all things must be applied to Christ. As we read in the Apocalypse, he has the key: he opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens (Rev. III), because all things are unlocked in him.

Therefore [Col. 0663B], against you, O land of Canaan, land of the Philistines—that is, against you, O Jews—the word of the Lord is spoken. For you are now the seed of Canaan and not of Judah; you are the land of the Philistines, that is, of the drink of those who fall, since you gave God’s Son Christ gall for his food and, in his thirst, gave him vinegar to drink (Ps. LXVIII). Hence your table has become before you a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block (ibid.).

“I will destroy you,” he says, O land of this kind, “so that there shall be no inhabitant.” As the Psalmist likewise says: “Let their habitation become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in their tents” (ibid.). Thus it happened: none of you dwells in that land of yours or rules there.

What then shall become of the line of the sea, of which it was said a little earlier, “Woe to you who inhabit the line of the sea”? It shall become [Col. 0663C] resting-places for shepherds and folds for flocks. Who are the shepherds, and what are the flocks or sheep? Surely those shepherds whose chief is that good Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John X). And they are the sheep of whom he himself says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (ibid.).

The line of the sea which you Jews [Col. 0663D] inhabit—that is, everything you possessed, or appeared to be near, in the sacrament of Christ’s baptism which covered our enemies, the spiritual Pharaoh and his army: namely, the Law and the Prophets, all the oracles of God entrusted to you—shall be rest for these shepherds and folds for the flock, like the sheep whom the Lord brought in.

Is it not so, O Jews—indeed, O Canaanites or Philistines? These sheep and their shepherds, that is, Christians and their teachers, now rest in that line once yours, because they knowingly read your Law and Prophets. That line of yours, composed in the Hebrew language, then rendered into Greek and translated into Latin, has made broad spaces for all nations. Behold, we rest in its spaces, and they are folds for the flocks—that is, our readings and meditations.

It is remarkable that you yourselves continually strengthen these folds for us, Christ’s sheep, lest they grow old or be weakened and decay through age; and everywhere in the world you supply us ample material for their strengthening, while you carry your children captive among all nations—indeed, now ours [Col. 0664A]—so that, whatever is preached about Christ to Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, you may be present with your writings openly testifying that whatever the voice of Gospel preaching reports to their ears as new is neither new nor fabricated.

What is then added, “and the line shall belong to those remaining of the house of Judah,” when properly considered with the preceding saying, clearly indicates the union of other and other sheep into one fold. For who are those who remain from the house of Judah, or what does it mean to remain from the house of Judah? Surely, to remain from the house of Judah is to be saved from the same nation of the lost, the Jewish nation. Those who remained or will remain in this way were the first apostles, and those who believed after them or through them, [Col. 0664B] and they will be the remnant that shall be saved after the fullness of the nations has entered in (Rom. XI).

[293] It is therefore finely distinguished thus: “The line of the sea shall be resting-places for shepherds and folds for flocks,” which is rightly understood of the shepherds and flocks of the fullness of the nations. And finally: “The line shall belong to those remaining of the house of Judah,” which is likewise rightly understood of the remnant that remains and shall remain from Israel, upon which blindness has come (Rom. XI).

Of both alike—of the sheep and shepherds from each of the two groups—we must understand what is added: “There they shall feed in the houses of Ashkelon; in the evening they shall rest.” What does “there they shall feed” mean except that they shall possess in that line? For a line is a possession, according to: “The Lord’s portion is his people [Col. 0664C]; Jacob, the line of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXIII). Or at least, a line is the measured extent of a possession, according to: “He cast out the nations from before them and divided the land among them by lot, by the line of allotment” (Ps. LXXVII).

Whichever way one takes it, the sense of the whole is this: “There they shall feed in the houses of Ashkelon; in the evening they shall rest”—as though he said: They shall be counted in the Lord’s allotted portion; they shall be placed in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the heavenly dwellings which Ashkelon—that is, “murderous fire,” namely Jewish impiety—boasts as its own houses. But those children of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness, while these, coming from east and west, shall recline in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matt. VIII).

Why is this so? “Because,” he says, “the Lord their God shall visit them and turn back their captivity [Col. 0664D].” Who is this Lord who will visit them, except the one who said concerning them and himself: “There shall be one fold and one shepherd”? For he himself says of this visitation through another prophet: “Behold, I will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock” (John X), “on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep” (Ezek. XXXIV), etc., up to: “Behold, I judge between flock and flock, ram and goat, between the fat flock and the lean flock” (ibid.).

Two things are said there: “I will visit my sheep,” and “I will judge between flock and flock.” Likewise two are said here: “The Lord their God shall visit them,” and “he shall turn back their captivity.” He will visit them—understand, at his first coming—so that he himself may be Shepherd and may carry the lost sheep back to his flock upon his own [Col. 0665A] shoulder (Luke XV). He will turn back their captivity at his second coming, when he will indeed judge between flock and flock (Ezek. XXXIV) and separate sheep from goats. Then he will say to the sheep at his right: “Come, [Col. 0666A] blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you”; and to the goats at his left: “Depart from me, accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665A] 294 The whole body of adversaries, or those who oppose the truth, is divided threefold: one division is that of the Jews, another of the heretics, another of the pagans. The word of the Lord is directed against all these divisions, in the order in which we have now named them. For the word has already been uttered against the Jews, and they have been designated by the names of Canaan and the land of the Philistines, in the words: “The word of the Lord is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines.” The heretics are immediately distinguished under the names of Moab and the sons of Ammon, when He says: “I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, with which they reproached my people and exalted themselves against their borders.” Then the impiety of the pagans is condemned under the name of the Ethiopians, when He says: “You also, Ethiopians, shall be slain by my sword.” Immediately thereafter, he himself who is the head of all enemies—the devil, destroyed and yet to be destroyed—is designated under the name of Assyria, when He says: “He shall stretch out his hand over the north, and destroy Assyria.”

Finally, it is quite plausible that such meanings should be understood under these names, especially since we know that the prophets were commanded not to speak everything openly, but rather to shut up the discourse and seal the book, to bind up the testimony and seal the law among the disciples of the Lord, with the promise: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). Moreover, this too supports our position: neither present events nor the histories written concerning things done supplies any experiential proof or testimony for one who takes these names—Canaan or the Philistines, Moab and the sons of Ammon, and the Ethiopians—simply and according to their common sense.

For although they have not been exempt from the evils which have occurred or occur in the world, nowhere is anything read of such a kind or so great as the letter of the present prophecy seems to sound to those who hear it merely literally. For example, it immediately speaks thus: “As I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah: a dryness of thorns, heaps of salt, and a desert forever.” Likewise concerning the land of the Philistines. For when did what it says come to pass: “It shall be the resting-place of shepherds and folds for flocks”? When was there no inhabitant in it, and when did it come to such desolation—though it rejoiced at the overthrow of Judaea—that all its most strongly fortified cities became sheepfolds for shepherds, and it became so uncultivated and so covered with briars and nettles that shepherds from the remnant of the Jews rested in Ashkelon in the afternoon and caused their flocks to lie down in a city once noble?

[Col. 0666A] Therefore, let us proceed confidently along the path begun, and be content to have understood the words of the Holy Spirit spiritually.

“I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, with which they reproached my people and exalted themselves against their borders. [Col. 0666B] Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah: a dryness of thorns, heaps of salt, and a desert forever. The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them. This shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed and exalted themselves above the people of the Lord of hosts.”

We must explain, as far as we are able, why heretics are designated by these names, or in what resemblance they are called Moab and the sons of Ammon. It has already been said above why the Jews are rightly called Philistines: namely, because, just as when the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt through the Red Sea, the Philistines, who were neighbors of the sea, were the first to grieve and the first prepared to make war upon them, so, when the sacrament of baptism was established, the Jews, among whom it was established, were the first to see and envy, and the first to persecute the evangelical faith. They were intoxicated with an evil draught—that is, with the spirit of error—and raved in accordance with the name *Philistines*, which is interpreted “those falling through drink.”

We must now say of the heretics why they are rightly called Moab and the sons of Ammon: because, just as Moab and the sons of Ammon descended from Abraham’s kin, yet always hated Abraham’s race, so heretics say that they believe in Christ, yet have always tried to overthrow the catholic faith of Christians. And who does not know that Moab and the sons of Ammon were born from Abraham’s kin through incest? For the daughters of Lot, Abraham’s nephew, slept with their father; the elder daughter bore Moab, while the younger bore Ammon (Gen. 19). *Moab* is interpreted “from the father,” while *Ammon* means “a turbulent people.”

What people, however, is more turbulent than the assembly of heretics, who give others to drink of turbid and muddy teaching, as it were turbid water? Heretics also are from their father the devil, just as are the Jews, to whom the Lord himself said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8; no. 25). Therefore, as the Philistines, so Moab and the sons of Ammon—that is, as the Jews, so also the heretics—shall be a desert forever; for, having abandoned God and been abandoned by God, they shall undoubtedly perish forever.

“For,” He says, “I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon”: that is, of the heretics, who indeed reproached my people, [Col. 0667A] the Christian people, after the example of Moab, and exalted themselves against their borders after the example of the sons of Ammon.

What was the example of Moab? Surely this: that the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who, at Balaam’s suggestion, called them to their sacrifices; and they ate and worshipped their gods, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor. Great was that reproach of Moab; and, Phinehas says, the stain of this crime remains among us to the present day, and many of the people fell. After the example of that reproach or stain, there was and is the reproach of heretics or heresiarchs, such as Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, Arius, and very many others.

In what respect? Namely, in that they did not err through ignorance; but just as Moab acted knowingly and according to a preceding plan, so that it might render Jerusalem deprived of God’s aid, and brought it about that Israel was initiated into Baal-peor, so these men too knowingly revealed, each one, the shameful and disgraceful images of their doctrines, in order to strip the ecclesiastical people of every honor of truth and draw it into destruction.

[Col. 0667B] But what, or what kind of, was the example of the sons of Ammon? In what respect did they formerly exalt themselves against Israel’s borders? “Israel,” says the king of the sons of Ammon, “took my land when it came up from Egypt.” In reply Jephthah, leader of Israel, says: “Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the sons of Ammon; rather, the Lord God overthrew the Amorite, fighting against him for His people Israel; and do you now wish to possess his land? Are not those lands which Chemosh your god possessed rightfully due to you? But those which the Lord our God, the victor, acquired fall to our possession” (Judg. 11).

There was then a vehement dispute against the sons of Ammon, who in this manner signified that they exalted themselves against Israel’s borders. Before this, too, joined with the king of Moab, they had struck Israel and possessed the city of palms (Judg. 3). In accordance with the example of that dispute, heretics have maintained an unceasing and obstinate dispute against the catholic Church, and have exalted themselves against its boundaries: against the boundaries of faith which our fathers, the prophets and apostles, established—adding something to their establishment, or subtracting something from it.

[Col. 0667C] They did not fear what is written in the Apocalypse: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the tree of life and from the holy city” (Rev. 22). Is it not also written in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2)?

But they, though dwelling in regions of the earth—some in Asia, some in Europe, some in Africa—divided against one another and united against the catholic Church, each striving to establish its own party as the catholic Church, diminished the Church’s borders no little, so far as lay in them. They wished to confine within a part Christ’s possession, ordained to extend to the ends of the earth. [Col. 0668A] Thus they exalted themselves against the borders of the people of the Lord, and reproached and blasphemed.

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.” What does it mean that Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah? “A dryness of thorns, heaps of salt, and a desert forever.” What use is the dryness of thorns except that they may be thrown into the fire, or fire put beneath them so that they may burn? And what use is a heap of salt, especially salt that has become tasteless, except to be cast out and trampled underfoot? (Matt. 5).

Therefore what He says is this: because they are thorns from which figs are not gathered, and a bramble from which grapes are not harvested (Matt. 7), they shall be handed over to fire like Sodom and Gomorrah. Indeed, it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites on the day of judgment than for those who did not receive you, the Lord says, nor hear your words (Matt. 10). If this shall be so for those who neither receive nor hear, how much more for heretics, who receive deceitfully and hear deceitfully, so that, while professing one part, they may overthrow the whole?

Justly, therefore, He says, they “shall be a desert forever”; that is, their sin shall not be forgiven them, neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. 12). This truly is to be a desert, since outside the house of God, which is the Church of God, from which they themselves went out, there is nothing but desert. Does not the Law itself say this also? “The Ammonites and Moabites,” it says, “shall not enter the assembly of the Lord even after the tenth generation, forever” (Deut. 23).

[Col. 0668B] Yet if they ever spoke or wrote anything savory—for they too have been said to become heaps of salt—“the remnant of my people,” He says, “shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them” (Gen. 19). Nor is it surprising if among the memorials of dead and dying heretics something is found which catholic men may use well, as it were salt, since, as a type of them, Lot’s wife, who was the grandmother of these sons of Moab and Ammon, died in such a way that she was turned, dead, into a pillar of salt.

Salt by nature is necessary for every food: it gives flavor to dishes and stimulates appetite. Indeed, cattle, herds, and beasts of burden are especially prompted by salt to feed, becoming much more abundant in milk and producing cheese of much more agreeable quality. But she who was turned into a pillar of salt might perhaps benefit cattle, herds, or beasts of burden that licked her in this manner; yet did she herself taste it? Certainly not.

[Col. 0668C] Thus, whatever they wrote—whether useful histories, moral teachings, or allegorical expositions—will benefit them nothing. But the remnant of the Lord’s people shall plunder those books; the survivors, that is, the boys of the Lord’s people who have not perished, ecclesiastical men who read and hear as catholics, shall possess them. They shall read them as Jews read some great or small work—for example, Josephus, or any of the others.

“This,” He says, “shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed and exalted themselves above the people of the Lord of hosts.” Although sins are many, there is one definite sin because of which heretics became, as was said above, a desert forever. [Col. 0669A] It is this: to be proud, and not through ignorance but through pride or envy to utter words against the truth of God.

For the Lord says: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemy of the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12). The person charged with so great a sin is one who knows God’s truth yet strives against it with all the powers of his intellect; and he is proved to speak a word against the Holy Spirit precisely when, understanding—or rather, refusing to understand—the words of Scripture, which are certainly words of the Holy Spirit, he speaks what is contrary.

What else, then, does this prophetic discourse assert when it says, [Col. 0669B] “This shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed,” except what the incarnate Word himself confirms in His Gospel?

It follows: “The Lord shall be terrible against them, and He shall bring to nothing all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship Him, each from his own place—all the islands of the nations.” Truly miserable are those against whom the Lord is terrible. How can this be? Is not God by nature sweet and gentle, serene and desirable to behold? Indeed, angels desire to look into Him (1 Pet. 1:12), looking with wondrous and ineffable manner always, and always desiring to look. Excessively miserable, therefore, are those whose conscience makes them shrink from the face of loving-kindness, and thus perish from the face of God, as wax melts before fire (Ps. 67).

Already in this life such wretches feel that terror; and, as though to console their pain somehow, they deny that what they know to exist exists, as though their holding truth in falsehood could destroy, or be capable of destroying, the truth. “And He shall bring to nothing,” He says, “all the gods of the earth.” Here must be supplied or understood: those who made themselves gods.

[Col. 0669C] For just as the gods of the earth, against whom He is not terrible and whom the Lord will not bring to nothing, are those of whom the Psalmist, after saying, “The princes of the peoples have assembled with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46), added: “For the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” (ibid.). The sense is this: the preachers, who were at first earthly, became gods and sons of the Most High; made mighty through faith and good works, they were greatly exalted by miracles. Thus many were brought forth into the faith, and many also among the princes—that is, kings and other high officials—were assembled with the God of Abraham by believing.

Therefore here He is speaking only of those who made themselves gods, since pride had been mentioned beforehand: “they exalted themselves above the people of the Lord of hosts.” Here they are called gods in the same manner as, in the Song of Songs, the companions of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions” (Song 1).

[Col. 0669D] These gods, these companions of the Lord—who are they, if not the heretics of whom this discourse speaks under the names of Moab and the sons of Ammon? Certainly the Lord is terrible against them, and He has brought their magnificence to nothing. For although for a short time they exalted themselves above the people of the Lord of hosts, in the end they perished like a dung-heap; and whatever harvest each such person had, the hungry consumed, and the armed man carried it off.

Once they have been brought to nothing, “men,” He says, “shall worship the Lord, each from his own place—all the islands of the nations.” This was said, and is to be said, mockingly against gods of this sort, who no longer have their own place—or rather, whose place will no longer look upon them or know them—as is said through blessed Job: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who goes down to the underworld shall not come up; nor shall he return any more to his house, nor shall his place know him any more” (Job 7).

[Col. 0670A] These men who did not abandon their own place, all the islands of the nations—that is, all the Churches which stand in the midst of the nations like islands, although they are battered on every side by sea-waves—stand firm and do not abandon their place. They shall worship the Lord from their own place: Him who was crucified, Jesus Christ, God and man. Their place is with God himself, as He said to Moses: “Behold, there is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. 33), and so forth.

That place is humility, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “Had not Moses, His chosen one, stood in the breach” (Ps. 105)—that is, in profound humility of mind before Him. Heretics are charged with not having found this place; and to them shall happen what has thus far been said: “This,” He says, “shall happen to them because of their pride, because they blasphemed and exalted themselves above the people of the Lord of hosts.”

It follows: “You also, Ethiopians, shall be slain by my sword.” It has already been said above that the Church has three kinds of enemies: Jews, heretics, and pagans. The Jews are designated under the names of Canaan and the Philistines, the heretics under the names of Moab and the sons of Ammon, and the pagans here under the name of Ethiopians.

[Col. 0670B] Why pagans under the name of Ethiopians? Because, just as Ethiopian skin is blacker than that of other nations, so the impiety of pagans is more evident than that of Jews or heretics. For Jews and heretics have, in some fashion, covered themselves with a certain whiteness of the divine name; but pagans worshipped not one God but many demons in public error. Therefore not only Canaan and the Philistines, Moab and the sons of Ammon, but “you also,” He says, “Ethiopians, shall be slain by my sword”: that is, not only Jews and heretics who received the Law, but you pagans or Gentiles also, who do not have such a law, shall be condemned by my judgment.

For there is no distinction with God. “For all who sinned without the Law shall perish without the Law; and all who sinned in the Law shall be judged through the Law” (Rom. 2).

It further follows:

“[Col. 0670C] He shall stretch out His hand over the north, and destroy Assyria.” It is well known that in the holy prophetic Scriptures the devil is signified by the name of the north and by the name of Assyria. He himself, namely the devil, is the head of enemies; and just as the head is preeminent over the limbs, so he is preeminent over all enemies, against whom the sword of the Lord has been drawn. Of this sword it has just now been said: “You also, Ethiopians, shall be slain by my sword”; and immediately it is added: “He shall stretch out His hand over the north, and destroy Assyria.”

And in the Song of Deuteronomy, after the preceding words: “If I whet my sword like lightning and my hand takes hold of judgment, I shall repay vengeance to my enemies and render recompense to those who hate me. I shall make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32), it is finally added: “from the blood of the slain and from the hand of the enemy’s head” (ibid.). Thus here and there, though in different words, the certain and unavoidable condemnation of all the wicked and of the devil himself is announced with the same meaning.

There was indeed a fleshly Assyria, that race of Assyrians whose empire was dissolved around the time of this prophecy, and Nineveh, the capital of that empire, which the Chaldeans overthrew. Immediately He says of it: “He shall make the beautiful city a solitude and a trackless place like a wilderness. Herds shall lie down in its midst, all the beasts of the nations; the pelican and hedgehog shall dwell on its thresholds. The voice of a singer shall be in the window, a raven upon the lintel, because I shall bring its strength to nothing. [Col. 0671A] This is the glorious city, dwelling in confidence, which said in its heart: ‘I am, and besides me there is no other.’ How has it become a wilderness, a den for beasts! Everyone who passes by it shall hiss and shake his hand.”

There was, I say, that fleshly Assyria and the city Nineveh, here called beautiful; and its desolation by the Babylonians was so great as may be understood from these words: “the pelican and hedgehog shall dwell on its thresholds; the voice of a singer in the window, a raven on the lintel”—signs of desolation.

[Col. 0671B] Nevertheless, a thing accomplished in part does not destroy the understanding of what is to occur in the whole; rather, it confirms it all the more. Through the experience of great cities which have been destroyed, the hearer is compelled to believe the evangelical truth: “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7), and the Lord will also judge the whole world at the end in the likeness, namely, of Nineveh and Babylon.

Now, regarding the overthrow of Nineveh as an example of the whole world that will perish, this has been said elsewhere and abundantly proclaimed by holy teachers. Hurrying on to the remainder, we wish only to say what it means for this beautiful city to say in its heart, “I am, and besides me there is no other,” and how everyone who passes through it shall hiss and shake his hand.

Certainly, to say, “I am, and besides me there is no other,” is to be proud, to trust only in present things, and to believe or hope for no other life after this one. It belongs to the wicked to think thus, who, as Wisdom relates, said to themselves, thinking wrongly: “Short and wearisome is the time of our life, and there is no relief at the end of a human being; no one has been known to return from the underworld. For we were born out of nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been. Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and everywhere let us leave marks of gladness, for this is our portion and this our lot” (Wis. 2).

[Col. 0671C] When the entire company of the wicked says these and similar things in its heart, who speaks except this beautiful city, Assyria—the whole covetousness of this world: “I am, and besides me there is no other”?

But everyone who passes through it—who, with the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, confesses himself a stranger and sojourner upon the earth, and does not wish to have here an abiding city but seeks the city to come (Heb. 13)—when he sees that the pelican, hedgehog, and raven will possess this beautiful city, no longer beautiful as it now appears but desolate, when the form of this world has passed away (1 Cor. 7), shall hiss and shake his hand. That is, judging it worthy neither of conversation—much less of consolation—he shall despise and mock it with only a gesture of mouth and hand.

It follows:

### Chapter III

**Woe to the provoking and redeemed city.** The dove did not hear the voice and did not accept correction; [Col. 0672B] she did not trust in the Lord; she did not draw near to the Lord her God. Her princes in her midst are like roaring lions; her judges like wolves in the evening, leaving nothing for the morning. Her prophets are madmen, faithless men; her priests have defiled the Holy One and acted unjustly against the law.

Against this city the intention of judgment began with the words: “And I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Zeph. 1), and it is completed with the words: “Woe to the provoking and redeemed city.” For what other city is provoking toward God—the city which Holy Scripture everywhere and almost universally accuses of having provoked the Lord? She is both provoking and redeemed; and she is the more damnably provoking because she was redeemed by so many benefits.

Her provocations are related here with great astonishment, since first she herself is called a dove, and then she is declared either to have possessed, or to possess, the savagery of lions and the ferocity of wolves. “The dove,” he says, “did not hear the voice and did not accept correction”: that is to say, the city or people once gentle became rebellious and persists as incorrigible. For what was gentler than Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the other patriarchs, Moses and David, and the other saints, prophets, or righteous persons? If you consider them and the whole election of that people or city, the city is rightly called a dove. Conversely, if you attend to those who killed the prophets and righteous persons, who forsook the Lord, worshipped Baal and other monstrosities, and committed other sacrileges, [Col. 0672D] you will truly say that she did not hear the voice, did not accept correction, did not trust in the Lord, and did not draw near to the Lord her God.

Indeed, if you consider how that same city acted against the Lord himself—how the evil and adulterous generation, by killing him, filled up the measure of their fathers—you rightly observe the saying: “Her princes in her midst are like roaring lions; her judges, evening wolves, left nothing for the morning; her prophets are madmen, faithless men; her priests have defiled the Holy One and acted unjustly against the law.” Who would not wonder at such things in her who was, or ought to have been, a dove? How did a dove produce lions? How did she nourish wolves? How did she foster madmen? How did she rear faithless men? How did she bring forth from her own offspring such priests [Col. 0673A] as would defile the Holy One—who would, as though in accordance with the law, make the Holy of Holies accursed?

For they said: “Behold, the law says that everyone who hangs on a tree is accursed by God” (Deut. 21). But this man is said to be holy, to be himself blessed, of whom the Psalm says: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117 [118]). Let us therefore hang him on the gibbet: he will be not blessed but accursed; he will be not holy but defiled like a leper. In this manner they defiled the Holy One; and, in thus defiling the Holy One, they plainly acted unjustly against the law.

For the law spoke thus and first laid down this condition: “When a man has sinned, so that he is to be punished with death” (Deut. 21); then it added: “and, having been sentenced to death, he has been hanged on a gibbet” (ibid.). But that man had not sinned in a way deserving death; rather, he was holy and is holy. Therefore, in defiling the Holy One, in pronouncing accursed by their own judgment one whom they know to be blessed, they acted unjustly against the law, while wishing to make the law the patron of their impiety.

“The Lord is righteous in her midst; he will not do iniquity. Morning by morning he will bring his judgment to light, and it will not be hidden.” They acted most unjustly in that manner, defiling the Holy One and resolutely wishing him who is blessed to be accursed. But the righteous Lord in her midst will not do iniquity; for he is neither unjust nor able to be unjust, nor can he give or write an unjust law. Would it not be iniquity if he permitted a man to be accursed merely from the punishment of his gibbet, when the cause for the gibbet had not preceded it? He will not do this, [Col. 0673C] nor did he do it. He will not endorse such a judgment of the priests, nor did he give the priests such a decree of law.

He first stated the cause: “When a man has sinned, so that he is to be punished with death”; and then added, “and, having been sentenced to death, he has been hanged on a gibbet.” This does not depart from justice or equity. Then follows what belongs to mercy: “His corpse,” he says, “shall not remain upon the tree, but you shall bury it on that same day” (ibid.). For those who died have always wished to be buried, or at least not to lack burial. And he added a remarkable reason for this regulation: “For everyone who hangs on a tree is accursed by God; and you shall by no means defile your land, which the Lord your God has given you as a possession” (ibid.).

In a remarkable way, O priests, while you attempt to defile the Holy One, the law against which you acted unjustly caught you in its own cunning. Thus you could neither make him accursed nor, by leaving him unburied, defile the land with the body of the Holy One. Rather, without your knowing it, through you provision was made for the whole world: you buried the prince who was to rise again and the author of resurrection.

Therefore the righteous Lord will not commit iniquity; the law of the righteous Lord will not agree with you; he will not be like you, as you wickedly supposed. But what then? “Morning by morning he will bring his judgment to light, and it will not be hidden.” You gave your judgment concerning the Holy One at night, crying out that he was guilty of death (Matt. 26), because he did not deny that he was the Holy One of God, because, when you questioned him, he confessed that he was the Christ, [Col. 0674A] the Son of the blessed God. But the Lord will give his judgment in the morning; in the morning he will make manifest what his judgment concerning that Holy One is, and he will do so in the light, so that it will not be hidden.

For he will say to him: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 107 [108]); and he will answer: “I will awake at dawn” (ibid.). And so it will be. Thus he will give his judgment in the morning, give it in the light, and it will not be hidden. Rather, “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18 [19]): it will be heard how very differently and unlike you unjust persons the righteous Lord judges concerning his Holy One, in your midst, while you see and hear and pay the penalties for your unjust judgment.

“But the wicked man did not know shame.” This too is spoken with astonishment; and indeed it is astonishing impudence not to blush or be ashamed, when God’s judgment in the matter of that Holy One is manifest in such clear light, according to what the Psalmist sang: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42 [43]). In the same manner it is said here, “the wicked man did not know shame,” to whom the Lord says in Jeremiah: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3).

And now, as though you asked how or by what action God gave his judgment in the light, he immediately adds: “I destroyed nations, and their corners were scattered. I made their roads desolate, so that no one passes through them. Their cities are desolated, with no man remaining and no inhabitant.” This, he says, is my judgment on account of the Holy One whom they defiled; and it is so manifest that no one now asks about it, since all know and see [Col. 0674C] that I destroyed those who acted so unjustly. Nor were they few: they were so great a multitude that I rightly said “nations,” because I destroyed first all their cities and dependent villages, all their tribes, their various territories, and finally Jerusalem itself, the metropolis.

This is what he says: “I destroyed nations, and their corners were scattered”—that is, their princes; indeed, their lions and wolves, as was already said. Once, how crowded were that most celebrated city and temple, than which nothing in the whole world was more majestic! How its roads were packed with converging crowds of people! But now he has made them deserted, so that no one passes through them; and just as I said in true judgment, “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23), so in true judgment I did what is expressed in the words: “Their cities are desolated, with no man remaining and no inhabitant.”

Did I do this too hastily, then, and show no patience? On the contrary: “I was silent; I kept silence for a long time; I was patient” (Isa. 42). “I said: Yet you will fear me; you will accept correction, and her dwelling-place will not perish because of all the things for which I visited her. Yet, rising early, they corrupted all their thoughts.”

The sense is this: I sent my prophets, rising early and calling them to repentance, and I said: I have indeed done all these things to you, Jerusalem; but I did them so that you might fear me, accept correction, and your dwelling-place—that is, the temple—might not perish because of all the crimes you had committed. But conversely, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, while I called them to repentance, [Col. 0675A] rose early, as though deliberately and contentiously, so that with the very haste by which they ought to have returned to me they might carry out all their thoughts and show by deed what they had conceived in mind.

Accordingly, when he says, “I said: Yet you will fear me; you will accept correction,” because what he said did not occur, it must be understood as expressing doubt—as though he said: “I said: Perhaps you will fear me; perhaps you will accept correction.” I commanded my prophets, saying: “Speak my words to him; perhaps he will hear and fear, or cease, and his dwelling-place will not perish”—which will happen unless he fears me and accepts correction.

For God sometimes speaks as though expressing doubt, although nothing is doubtful to him. He himself says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, you shall say to the children of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they themselves will hear, or perhaps they will cease, since they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 2). Likewise: “You shall therefore speak my words to them; perhaps they will hear and fear, or cease, since they are rebels” (ibid.). His speaking in this fashion, as though uncertain, is accommodation to, or for the sake of, those who are uncertain or may be uncertain unless they experience the matter, and who do not revere God’s just judgments unless experience has taught them that those whom God rejected or judged were incorrigible.

It follows: “Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my future tribulation, because my judgment is to gather nations and assemble kingdoms. And I will pour out upon them my indignation and all the wrath of my fury. For in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be consumed, [Col. 0675C] because then I shall restore to the peoples a chosen lip, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder.”

After he had proclaimed the severity of righteous judgment against the impious and sinners, and against that Jerusalem which deserved to be called provoking, he now finally turns to her who has the ear of faith and intimately discloses to her the things of grace and mercy. He calls her the daughter of Zion, names her Israel, calls her the daughter of Jerusalem: “Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem,” and so forth to the end, where he concludes: “For I will make you a praise and a name among all peoples of the earth, when I restore your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord.”

“Therefore,” he says, “because, as I said at the beginning, ‘I will gather, gathering, all things from the face of the earth’—that is, I will draw all things to myself (John 12), namely on the day of my resurrection, after I have been lifted up from the earth (ibid.)—and because I shall do all these things which have been said to those who do not await me and do not believe in me: you, wait for me; you, believe and hope in me, on the day of my resurrection for the future—that is, from the day on which I rise from the dead until the last day. For then I shall carry out judgment, and this will be my judgment: to gather nations and assemble kingdoms.”

For then the Son of Man will sit upon the seat of his majesty; all the angels will come with him, and all nations will be assembled before him (Matt. 25). Wait for me on the day of my resurrection, having the eyes enlightened by clear and certain faith in my resurrection; whoever does not believe it is not in the day but in the night. Wait for me, remembering that saying of the angels who witnessed me: “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1).

When he says, “to gather nations and assemble kingdoms,” it is understood: at the left hand. For what follows is: “And I will pour out upon them my indignation and all the wrath of my fury,” namely when I say to them: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). “For in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be consumed”: that is, all the impious, who did not look to heaven but performed wholly earthly works, both those who sinned without the law and those who sinned under the law. For “as many as sinned without the law shall perish without the law; and as many as sinned under the law shall be judged by the law” (Rom. 2).

But you will be at the right hand when you hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). Then you will be that queen of whom it was said to me: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44 [45]). “Because then I shall restore to the peoples a chosen lip”: then I shall repay to the peoples the fruit of lips confessing my name. For to confess my name is to possess a chosen lip, a pure lip, worthy of eternal life and everlasting song.

In what shall I repay them? In this: “that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder.” Is this a small recompense? Or is it a small thing to call on the Lord’s name and serve the Lord there? Rather, the good of invocation and service there is great, splendid, and surpasses every desire. Knowing this, the Psalmist, after saying, “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel” (Ps. 121 [122]), added: “to confess the name of the Lord” (ibid.). Nor could he have spoken more magnificently.

And in the Apocalypse, one of the elders says to John: “These are they who came from great tribulation; they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple” (Rev. 7). Therefore, as the letter there sounds, the Christian or spiritual person ought not to suppose that kingdom, or the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to be paved with gold or strewn with gems and pearls; for the kingdom of God consists not in gold or precious stones, [Col. 0676D] but in confession of the Lord’s name and service to him.

There one serves with perfect service, which the prophet here indicates with remarkable brevity when he says, “with one shoulder.” What is “with one shoulder” except with an undivided heart? It is not so here in this exile, where we are set to serve the same Lord. For this world has many variations, and the minds of mortals, even of the righteous and perfect, are scarcely wholly at one with themselves for a single hour. Therefore what is promised there cannot be here.

But we should know—and state more plainly—the cause why it can be possible there to serve with one shoulder, with an undivided shoulder. What is it? It is that the king and Lord of that city and kingdom is one and only one: God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the one, undivided and inseparable King of dominion. He is himself one and the same; he remains of unchangeable substance and immutable will; and the will of the three persons of the one God is always one. Hence he possesses undivided rule, because he himself is undivided and unchangeable, according to his own saying: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3).

Accordingly, what he says here—“that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder”—I judge to be nothing other than what was said in the Psalm, although with the clauses only rearranged: “Its participation is in the same thing. For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121 [122]). For what else is it to call upon the Lord’s name than to confess the Lord’s name? And what else is it to serve this Lord with one shoulder than that its participation should be in the same thing?

It follows: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the children of my dispersed ones, will bring an offering to me.” If he had said thus, “Because then I shall restore to my people a chosen lip, that it may call upon the Lord’s name,” the Jew would think it possible to contend, as he usually does, that this is said only of himself, as though God were the God of the Jews alone and not also of the Gentiles. But now, when he says, “I shall restore to the peoples,” he cannot deny that God also cares for others, and that God had long before provided elsewhere for himself confessors of his name.

And so it is. “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia”—that is, to the ends of the world, it is understood—the sound of Gospel preaching will go forth (Ps. 18 [19]). And from there, O daughter to whom I speak, to whom I say “Wait for me,” and to whom I shall immediately say, “Praise, daughter of Zion; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem”—from the ends of the earth, I say, my suppliants, namely the apostles, will bring me an offering consisting of my dispersed ones: that is, they will gather my dispersed ones into one, which will surely be a great offering to me.

Knowing this, the Evangelist says that Caiaphas, being high priest that year, prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but in order that he might gather into one the children of God who were dispersed” (John 11). This has been said to you, O daughter, for great consolation. For though there went forth from you those who ought to have been yours—“criminal sons, an evil seed” (Isa. 1)—nevertheless you will be multiplied and will rejoice in children [Col. 0677D] who will surely come from afar. This is magnificently signified by the words, “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia,” not because they are to come from Ethiopia alone. For through another prophet I said: “Behold, these will come from afar; behold, those from the north and the sea; and these from the southern land” (Isa. 49). Rather, the whole body of the nations is rightly signified by the rushing rivers and Ethiopia’s blackness, on account of the darkness of ignorance in which they were and the persecution by princes or tyrants.

At the same time he gives very great praise to his suppliants because they are to cross the rivers of Ethiopia and then bring him the offering of his dispersed ones: that is, they are to overcome the savagery of all persecuting tyrants and bring him a Church from among the Gentiles, according to the type that preceded in the coming of the queen of Sheba from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10).

But, O daughter, will those Ethiopians, my suppliants, always remain black? Or will you always be an Ethiopian woman, so that you may always have something for which to blush? No: hear what follows. “On that day you shall not be ashamed of all your devices by which you transgressed against me, for now I shall remove from your midst the boastful men of your pride; and you shall no longer exalt yourself upon my holy mountain.”

A great promise, a great consolation. For the present, before that day comes—the day of my resurrection—you are ashamed, and not without cause, when you speak and confess with truthful confession something such as Isaiah’s words: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64). But on that day it will not be so, especially because what I now promise you in the prophets and Psalms will come to pass: “A fountain shall be open to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman” (Zech. 13). Therefore David, exulting in good hope through the Holy Spirit, says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]).

Indeed, although he also says elsewhere: “Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33 [34]), nevertheless in the present life, while you remain subject to mortal condition and that day of my resurrection is not yet complete in you, you are in a sense now ashamed, according to the words: “What fruit then did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). But this shame brings glory, and when glory fully succeeds it, it will pass away.

For when the fullness of that day comes, the fullness of my resurrection; when the members rise as the head has risen—will the recollection of former blackness bring any shame? Rather, the recollection of miseries itself will be most abundant material for song, according to the words: “I will sing the mercies of the Lord for ever” (Ps. 88 [89]). Will anyone else be able to reproach you because you were an Ethiopian woman, or reproach me because I took an Ethiopian woman as my wife?

Miriam has now been covered with white leprosy like snow and remains outside the camp seven days, because she murmured against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife (Num. 12). And, to speak more plainly, the impurity of her iniquity has now made the Synagogue known to the whole world: cast out not only in soul from the kingdom of God but also in body from the city and temple once belonging to God; she remains outside, scattered in mind and body, according to the words: “Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 58 [59]). Until the seven days pass—that is, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters in—she will not be recalled into this camp, because she reproaches you or your suppliants for having been Ethiopians and reproaches me for joining such persons to myself as the Church.

How much more, in the fullness of that day, in the universal resurrection, will every mouth be stopped! I foretell to you that then I shall remove from your midst the boastful men of your pride: namely, those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are in the synagogue of Satan—truly boastful and proud, especially because, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10). This pride is called your pride in the same way that they are called your sons or sons of Abraham, and say that they have God alone as their Father (John 8).

When this has occurred, you will no longer exalt yourself on my holy mountain; rather, you will stand in the great and eternal firmament of holy humility, knowing and perfectly understanding what you now know in part (1 Cor. 13), and truthfully confessing that by his own works no one ever has been or ever can be justified in God’s sight (Ps. 142 [143]). Rather, “all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. 3); and then this will require no proof, because the matter will be manifest.

The boastful will be removed; and who will remain there? He says: “And I shall leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and the remnant of Israel shall hope in the name of the Lord.” Those are rightly called, and truly are, boastful who trust in themselves as righteous and presume upon the works of the law. Those are rightly called, and truly are, poor and needy who know themselves to be sinners and perceive that they are justified only through faith in Jesus Christ.

Such a people, so poor and needy—poor in spirit, knowing that it needs, or has needed, God’s glory, which is to be justified freely through faith in Jesus Christ (ibid.)—“I shall leave,” he says, “in your midst,” so that those coming from east and west may recline in Abraham’s bosom, while those boastful children of the kingdom are cast into outer darkness (Matt. 8). Yet it will someday happen that the remnant of Israel shall hope in the Lord’s name, namely when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in (Rom. 11). What will it be for them to hope in the Lord’s name, except to lay aside the obstinacy by which they suppose themselves justified by their works, and to believe that all justification lies in the Lord’s name alone, in faith in Jesus Christ?

It follows: “They shall not do iniquity, nor speak falsehood; and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouth, for they shall feed and lie down, and none shall make them afraid.” Happy is that day of resurrection, in whose fullness no one will sin either in word or deed. Great and blessed is the recompense for every soul or person who now, even if he has committed iniquity and spoken falsehood, no longer wishes to commit iniquity or speak falsehood. Great and blessed, I say, because he will then receive this stability: he will no longer be able to commit iniquity or speak falsehood. For the blessed soul, inseparably joined or united to God its Creator through the spirit of eternal love, will no longer be able to have an evil will.

“Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem”—understand: because you possess this promise. Praise God the Father; shout for joy to God the Son; rejoice and exult in God the Holy Spirit. The holy Trinity is one God, from whom you have received your being daughter of Zion, Israel, and daughter of Jerusalem: daughter of Zion through faith, Israel through hope, daughter of Jerusalem through love.

“The Lord has removed your judgment; the King of Israel, the Lord, has turned away your enemies. [Col. 0680A] In your midst you shall not fear evil any longer.” Truly beautiful, though very hidden, preaching of the holy and indivisible Trinity. The Lord God the Father has removed your judgment; the King of Israel, God the Son, has turned away your enemies; the Lord the Holy Spirit is in your midst. Therefore you will not fear evil any longer, because him whom you now see through a mirror in an enigma you will then see face to face (1 Cor. 13). Death will be no more (Rev. 21), death which was your judgment pronounced upon all humankind when Adam sinned. “Neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain shall be any more, because the former things have passed away” (ibid.).

“On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem: Do not fear, Zion; let not your hands be weakened. The Lord your God in your midst is mighty; he himself will save. He will rejoice over you in gladness; he will be silent in your love; he will exult over you in praise.”

How gladly does the soul that loves the Trinity consider that here the Holy Spirit, speaking through the prophet’s mouth with unquestionable truth, as it were dances a ringing little melody of faith and triples his measures of delight, so that the awakened soul of the hearer, by meditating on these words, may already begin to taste and contemplate that her God is the holy Trinity. Since the world at that time could not bear its name—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we need not ask why the prophet did not distinguish it here as the Lord himself declared it in his Gospel: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Behold, in four modes he has sung of the work which the indivisible unity of the Trinity does, or will do, concerning us. First, it sounds as a voice of exultation—indeed, the sound of one feasting: “Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem.” Second: “The Lord has removed your judgment; the King of Israel has turned away your enemies; the Lord is in your midst.” Third: “On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem: Do not fear, Zion; let not your hands be weakened. The Lord God in your midst is mighty; he himself will save.” Fourth: “He will rejoice over you in gladness; he will be silent in your love; he will exult over you in praise.”

How beautifully, in these four forms, is the voice of one and the same praise varied, each form distinguished by three clauses. How beautifully, I say, if you consider that there are four things which the unity of the Trinity performed in the one Christ, as its greatest work for our sake—things which no soul worthy to be called Zion, Israel, and Jerusalem may fail to know. What are they? The incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension.

The incarnation is the work of the Trinity, because the Father sent the Son to be incarnate; the Son himself entered the Virgin’s womb; and the Holy Spirit formed for him a true body, true flesh from the Virgin’s flesh, and brought it about that he should assume our flesh as a true human being with a rational soul. The passion is the work of the Trinity, because the Son drank the cup which the Father gave, and, as the Apostle says, through the Holy Spirit offered himself as a sacrifice to cleanse our conscience from dead works (Heb. 9).

The resurrection is the work of the Trinity, because the Father said, “Awake, my glory”; [Col. 0681A] the Son answered, “I will awake at dawn” (Ps. 56 [57]); and on that same day the Holy Spirit proceeded from his mouth, as he breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). The ascension is the work of the Trinity, because the Father said, “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109 [110]); the Son ascended and sat down; and the Holy Spirit, coming from that session upon the disciples, distributed to them varieties of gifts (1 Cor. 12).

Therefore, because God became human: praise, Zion; shout for joy, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. For you are daughter of Zion because, as God promised the patriarchs, he sent his Son. You are Israel because your nature, assumed with the Son of God, the Word of God, into one person, is truly made straight with God according to the name Israel. You are daughter of Jerusalem because through the same union of divine and human natures you who were from the earth have been joined in peace with heavenly things.

And already, because he suffered for you, he has removed your judgment—the judgment of death—and turned away your enemies, namely evil spirits and the prince of this world himself, whom he cast out. Once he was cast out, the Lord is in your midst, and you will not fear the evil of ancient transgression, the paternal trespass. Yet while you live in the body, there is still something you fear: namely, death of the flesh and bodily suffering. But it is certain for you, and ought to be certain, that on the day of universal resurrection it will be said to you: “Do not fear,” namely because death will be no more (Rev. 21); “let not your hands be weakened,” because you will be made changed and impassible.

But the joy with which he will rejoice over you in gladness, the silence with which he will be silent in your love, and the exultation with which he will exult over you in praise (Isa. 61)—the praise of the holy Trinity—“eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2).

It follows: “I gather the trifles who had departed from the law, because they were from you, that you may no longer bear reproach on their account.” By “trifles” he means frivolous persons: those who slander the Lord himself, of whom this discourse speaks, as Wisdom testifies, saying: “His life is unlike that of others, and his ways are changed. We are regarded by him as trifles, and he abstains from our ways as from impurities” (Wis. 2).
