Such “trifles,” he says—those frivolous people who departed from the law, saying against the Lord and against his Christ, “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us” (Ps. 2)—[Col. 0681D] “I shall gather, because they were from you”: that is, I shall bind them in bundles to burn them (Matt. 13), and their hands will bear judgment precisely because they were from you, because they received the law, because they were Abraham’s seed, because they were Israelites, because they were ministers of Christ. Hence they were a reproach to you, and because of them my name was blasphemed.

I shall gather them so that you may no longer bear reproach on their account, so that Sodom or Gomorrah may no longer justify itself in comparison with you (Ezek. 16), nor may the sea say that Sidon should be ashamed (Isa. 23). This indeed is what manifest Gentile society says whenever it insults you on account of some who live among you in a Gentile manner.

“Behold, I shall slay all who afflicted you at that time.” Not only those who were from you and went out from you—indeed, they were not from you, as one of yours says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). I say, not they alone, but all who afflicted you, whether sinning under the law or without the law, I shall slay at that time: judging by the law those who sinned under the law (Rom. 2), and consigning to destruction without the law those who sinned without the law (ibid.).

“And I shall save her who limps, and gather her who was cast out; and I shall make them a praise and a name in every land of their shame, at that time when I bring you in, and at the time when I gather you.” Great is the condescension of the Most High Lord, which we all know, according to the Psalmist’s words: “For the Lord is high and regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137 [138]); and he has done, and does, this. For, he says, “See your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful; but God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1).

What other meaning is pleasing here when he says, “I shall save her who limps, and gather her who was cast out”? For by the lame and the cast out the prophetic discourse rightly denotes all weak or powerless things, all foolish, ignoble, and despised things. “I shall save,” he says, “and gather such people; and I shall make [Col. 0682C] them a praise and a name in every land of their shame”: that is, I shall make them praiseworthy and renowned there where they were nameless, and consequently appeared unworthy of praise, by shaming and destroying through them the wise, strong, and powerful persons in whose eyes they were held ignoble and seemed contemptible.

This, I say, I shall do “at that time when I bring you in, and at the time when I gather you”: that is, I shall make renowned and illustrious not only in the age to come but also in the present age those princes of yours called from lowliness. Thus, as he said to Moses, “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7), so these too may be called—and be—gods of the earth, according to David’s words: “The princes of the peoples have been gathered with the God of Abraham, because the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” (Ps. 46 [47]). “I will give”

For I will make you a name and a praise among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord.

By “all the peoples of the earth” here we understand those chosen from all the peoples of the earth, who say in the Apocalypse: “You have redeemed us for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Rev. V).

Whom does he promise to make a name and a praise, and for what merit, when he has restored their captivity before their eyes? Surely those whom we have already called “the princes of the peoples,” by whose labor and diligence, with God’s grace cooperating with them, this very work has been and is being done—namely, that their captivity is restored, and will be restored, before their eyes. [Col. 0683A] This restoration of captivity, now begun, will then be complete when the dead rise again and are set at the right hand, immediately to receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world (Matt. XXV).

Great will be the spectacle of restored captivity for those who were once captives, and great their wonder at their present happiness, as they recall the greatness of the former misery of their past captivity. Therefore, after saying, “when I restore your captivity,” he splendidly adds, “before your eyes.”

Then these princes, fathers, or apostles, and all who have been or are helpers in restoring this captivity, [Col. 0684A] will be a name and a praise—that is, renowned and praiseworthy—to those whose captivity they heard would be restored. In a wholly just order, they will rejoice to have them as princes or fathers—indeed, as saviors after God.

The Lord says all these things—understand, the One who does not lie and whose every word must necessarily be fulfilled. “Heaven and earth,” he says, “will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV).

## Rupert’s Prologue to the Prophet Haggai

[Col. 0683]

302 Haggai is tenth in the order of the twelve prophets. The Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, willed that he should be marked beforehand by his name, so that he should be called Haggai—namely, in accordance with the matter concerning which He was to speak through his mouth. For the name *Haggai* means “festive,” and his eye indeed foresaw a great festivity when he spoke the things now before us: when the Lord said through him, “This people says: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built” (Hag. 1); and when, at the Lord’s command, he questioned the priests, saying: “If a man carries consecrated flesh in the fold of his garment, and touches with its edge bread, or cooked food, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it be consecrated? And if one defiled in soul touches any of these things, shall it be defiled?” (Hag. 2).

Whoever understands why these and other similar sayings or questions were worthy to be written down surely perceives the great and fitting reason for this name also, Haggai—that is, “festive.” Nor does he doubt that this man received such a designation by the will of God, who “foreknew the holy ones, and predestined them, and called them, justified them, and glorified them” (Rom. 8).

For was there any other festivity in the prophetic heart than the joy which he had, or could have had together with the people, over the rebuilding of the handmade temple—again to be defiled, again to be burned beyond recovery? Certainly, the rebuilding of that temple, which he saw before his eyes, was material for great festivity; nevertheless, not in itself, but because of Christ, the festivity of all saints, angels, and human beings. For it was to come about that, once the temple had been rebuilt, the walls of the city would later also be rebuilt, the city would again be inhabited, and, once the city had been rebuilt, the people would again grow together in the land; from them Christ would be born, preserving the truth of the promise made to Abraham and David and confirmed by oath.

Therefore, with the Holy Spirit’s help, we receive everything Haggai says here in such a way that we do not doubt that he is directed wholly toward Christ. And then we too may in some fashion be called, or be, Haggais—that is, festive—by contemplating that very thing which this man, who was by divine foreknowledge called Haggai, was to contemplate.

## Commentary on the Prophet Haggai

### Book One

[Col. 0683]

303 **Chapter I**

[Col. 0683B]

“In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.’ And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: ‘Is it time for you to dwell in panelled houses while this house lies desolate?’”

First, this deserves notice: just as Nebuchadnezzar in the holy prophetic Scriptures is compared with, or shown to resemble, the devil, because he led God’s people captive from Jerusalem into Babylon, in likeness of the devil who in the first parents thus took the human race captive from paradise; so Zerubbabel and Jesus son of Jozadak, and the other children of the exile, who went up from Babylon and rebuilt the temple and city of God, signified those fathers—or patriarchs—and the people. Nor did they merely signify them: they were also a part of those who, making their way from this world toward God, merited that Christ, the temple not made by hands, should be born from their flesh.

For just as that temple was built by the children of captivity, so Christ was born from the fathers who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth (Heb. 11). Hence he himself called his body a temple: “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). “For,” says the Evangelist, “he was speaking of the temple of his body” (ibid.).

Therefore, when it says here: “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,’” and, having said this, adds nothing further except once more introducing, “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai,” then surely this very statement—“This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built’”—must be understood as something that could not have been known except through the word of the Lord, something Haggai could not have known unless he were a prophet, unless the word of the Lord had come to him or by his hand.

And what is this, unless that which we still hear and see today? For this conspicuous people, marked and known by its public captivity—the Jewish people—says that the Messiah has not yet come, that the time for building the house of God has not yet come.

But we say and believe—and therefore speak—that the time came long ago; this temple was built long ago, and “in it dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2). It was built from the flesh of the Virgin Mary. “No,” they say, “the one born of Mary was not, and is not, the Messiah. Another will come; we still await him.”

While this people says this, does it not commit sacrilege? For it makes its patriarch and father a liar when he says: “The sceptre shall not be removed from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49). If he spoke truly—indeed, because he spoke truly—then when the sceptre was removed from Judah, while Herod the foreigner reigned, born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother, the Messiah had already come. That was the time, as has already been said, for the Lord’s house to be built—the house of which it is also said in parables: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9).

When this is observed, it is surely clear that the words, “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet; thus says the Lord of hosts,” were not prefixed in vain or without the dignity of prophetic authority; only then was this brief statement appended: “This people says: The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.” For in few words the great evil of this people was signified: namely, that it would not receive Christ while he lived, but would await another. Thus he himself says: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me. If another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5).

Here is another passage: “And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: ‘Is it time for you to dwell in panelled houses while this house lies desolate?’” And surely what he says—“Is it time for you to dwell in panelled houses while this house lies desolate?”—

304—is so great, and must be understood so magnificently, that it is worthy of the word of the Lord and of a prophetic mouth, since it was uttered with such a prefatory declaration: “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet.”

Indeed, it is a great and exceedingly foolish falsehood that this people, while saying that the time for building the house of the Lord has not yet come, nevertheless maintains that it is time for itself to dwell in panelled houses. That is, while it denies that Christ has come, it nevertheless asserts that the dwellings of paradise or of the kingdom of God are already possessed by the fathers, and that it itself is altogether owed that inheritance.

For the truth is that access to the kingdom of heaven could not have been open to anyone except through Christ’s coming; and that “there is salvation in no one else,” nor is there “another name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4). Ask a Jew in whom, or from what source, he trusts that he will be saved or enter paradise if Christ has not come. He will answer that through Abraham or through his own righteousness he has been made fit for the kingdom of God. Therefore, says the prophet, “this house lies desolate”: that is, Christ’s coming has no grace, no usefulness. For why was Christ promised, or why should he have come, if a human being could be saved by his own righteousness without his coming?

Thus the people is rebuked by the prophet in these words: “My people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2). Here likewise it is rebuked enigmatically: “This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built’; and, ‘Is it time for you to dwell in panelled houses while this house lies desolate?’”

For one evil is to deny that Christ has come; another is to claim for itself or its fathers the houses, that is, the dwellings, of God’s kingdom, and to judge Christ’s coming unnecessary in order that the saints might be brought into those dwellings.

It should be known, however, that the rebuilding of that handmade house was necessary because of this house not made by hands—because of the future incarnation of the Word of God, the Son of God. For if that house and city had not been rebuilt and the nation restored, whence would Christ’s promise, coming, or purpose have been fulfilled? Especially since he had said through the other prophets: “For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

Thus, even if what we now understand in the prophet’s words was not understood at that time, nevertheless the literal sense itself contributed something: those who understood the words in that sense were stirred to build that house. Hence it is written in the Book of Ezra: “The work was not done until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the Persians. But Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews who were in Judaea and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak arose and began to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, helping them” (1 Ezra 5).

Nevertheless, that the people at that time said, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,” is not established by Ezra’s Scripture. Rather, it says: “All the people cried out with a great cry in praising the Lord, because the temple of the Lord had been founded” (1 Ezra 3). Yet this displeased some among them and caused them to weep, because it was smaller than it had been. For, as Josephus also relates (*Antiquities*, book 15, ch. 11), although it had been one hundred and twenty cubits high, it was rebuilt to a height of sixty cubits by Darius’s command; Herod finally restored it to its former size.

“Many,” says Ezra, “of the priests and Levites, and the heads of families and elders, who had seen the former temple before it was founded, wept with a loud voice when this temple stood before their eyes; while many raised their voices in joyful shouting. Nor could anyone distinguish the sound of the joyful cry from the sound of the people’s weeping” (1 Ezra 3).

How, then, will it be established that the words “This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built’” were spoken according to the letter? Therefore, whatever may have been the situation then, let us take care to understand it as we began to do: as the word of the Lord, as prophecy directed toward the times or mysteries of Christ, toward which all prophets direct their attention.

It follows: “And now thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways. You have sown much and brought in little. You have eaten and have not been satisfied. You have drunk and have not been filled with drink. You have clothed yourselves and have not been warmed. And he who gathered wages has put them into a bag with holes.”

Even as the letter sounds, these matters are not easily established from the histories. For the interruption of the work, which was not resumed until the second year of King Darius’s reign, was brought about by the enemies of Judah and Benjamin, because they hired counsellors against them to frustrate their plan throughout all the days of Cyrus king of Persia (1 Ezra 4). If the work was interrupted against God’s people’s will, how is that interruption reckoned to them as a crime and punished upon them by the barrenness of the earth, lack of drink and food, and lack of warmth or clothing?

Therefore, as has already been said, whatever the situation then may have been, let us take care, as we began, to understand spiritually the words of the Holy Spirit. O Jews, who sin in both respects: both when you say, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,” which is to say, “The time of Christ’s coming has not yet come” (John 4); and when you presume to dwell in panelled houses while this house lies desolate, which is to trust in the works of the law as though Christ’s grace were not necessary for your salvation.

“Set your hearts upon your ways”: consider carefully your works or actions. For this is what has happened to you: like one who sowed much and brought in little; like one who ate and was not satisfied; like one who drank and was not filled with drink; like one who clothed himself and was not warmed; like one who gathered wages and put them into a bag with holes.

For you have sown much salvation. “For salvation is from the Jews” (John 4); but you have brought in little, because whatever you could have had from the fathers is little—indeed, it contributes nothing—to those who do not receive Christ, the seed of blessing. You have eaten and have not been satisfied, because, pursuing the chaff of the killing letter, you have not reached the grain of the life-giving Spirit (2 Cor. 3). You have drunk and have not been filled with drink, because you read without understanding, unwilling to take part in the wedding of the Lord’s incarnation, where water is made wine. You have clothed yourselves and have not been warmed: adorned with the illustrious names of the fathers and with the priesthood of the law, clothed in outward religion, you have nevertheless remained as cold as the nations, not having the love of God in yourselves. And whoever among you gathered wages—that is, performed some deeds according to the commandments of the law—has lost them as one who puts wages into a bag with holes loses them, because without faith in Christ works are of no use.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways. Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house; and it will be acceptable to me, and I shall be glorified, says the Lord.”

Since this house, which we call the house or temple of the body, in which “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2), has already been built, how is it still said—or to be said—to this people by the command of the Lord of hosts: “Go up to the mountain, bring

305 wood, and build the house”? How, I ask, unless it is as though one said: Believe that Christ has come; believe in the Crucified One; believe that he rose and ascended into heaven.

Certainly, those first men built this house who received the promises and “from whom is Christ according to the flesh” (Rom. 9). Yet we too who came later, whenever we preach or recite the book of the genealogy of this same Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, and attest at the summit of that genealogy that Jesus, born of Mary, is the Christ—then surely we ascend the mountain which, according to Daniel’s vision, filled the whole earth (Dan. 2). And insofar as, either by believing ourselves or by preaching to others, we increase the number of believers, we bring wood and build the house; and “such building,” or “such a house,” “will be acceptable to me, and I shall be glorified, says the Lord.”

“You looked for much, and behold, it came to little; and you brought it into the house, and I blew it away.” O Jews, you do not do what I commanded you—to desire justification through faith in Jesus Christ—but you looked for more: that is, you wished to be justified by works, as though your work were greater than his faith. And behold, it came to little; this is sufficiently clear because, whatever works you brought into the house, I blew away, and they were scattered like a little dust scattered by someone blowing upon it. You too, with your works, were scattered among all nations by that same blowing.

“For what reason?” says the Lord of hosts. “Because my house lies desolate, while each of you hastens to his own house. Therefore the heavens above you were restrained from giving dew, and the earth was restrained from giving its produce. And I called for drought upon the land and upon the mountains, upon the grain, wine, and oil, upon whatever the ground produces, upon human beings, livestock, and every work of the hands.”

As we said above, it is difficult to establish from the histories that this happened according to the letter: namely, that the people said, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,” and that therefore the heavens were restrained from giving dew and the earth from giving its produce. For, as Ezra remembers and carefully recounts, they were carrying out the work with great eagerness, at the same time praising the Lord and chanting in hymns and thanksgiving: “For he is good, for his mercy is forever upon Israel” [Col. 0689A]—until the accusation of the enemies of Judah and Benjamin brought it about that the work was interrupted, as we recalled above (1 Ezra 3).

The evident reason, then, why barrenness of the earth or drought should justly have befallen them from the day on which the work was interrupted is not apparent, unless it is quite credible that, having been forbidden to build the house of the Lord, they yielded too readily to those who forbade them and became negligent and sluggish concerning the building of the Lord’s house. They rejoiced that this occasion left each person free to build his own house as a dwelling.

But however things were done then, we know that Haggai was one of the prophets through whom the Holy Spirit spoke. Therefore we do not doubt that, under words by which the people of that time were stirred up and strengthened, he indicated in prophetic fashion mysteries of things to come. Let us therefore continue in the manner begun.

“For what reason,” says the Lord of hosts, “when you looked for much, behold, it came to little; and when you brought that very thing into the house, I blew it away? For what reason have I hated and rejected your festivals?” (Isa. 1). Namely, “because my house lies desolate, while each of you hastens to his own house”: that is, because you do not seek to be justified through Christ, whose body alone is the house of righteousness and the temple of the whole Divinity; and, not subjecting yourselves to his righteousness, each of you hastens to establish his own righteousness (Col. 3; Rom. 10).

Therefore the heavens above you were restrained from giving dew: the apostles were restrained from delivering the word among you. And the earth—that is, the Church spread throughout the world—was restrained from giving its produce: it was restrained from bringing the Gospel to you, not because it is bound to desire your salvation, but because it cannot benefit you for salvation while you are unwilling. “And I called for drought.” Likewise, through another prophet, he says: “I commanded the clouds not to rain rain upon you—once my vineyard” (Isa. 5).

It follows: “And Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jesus son of Jozadak the high priest, and all the remnant of the people, heard the voice of the Lord their God and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him to them; and the people feared before the Lord. And Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, among the messengers of the Lord, spoke to the people, saying: ‘I am with you, says the Lord.’ And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Jesus son of Jozadak the high priest, and the spirit of the remnant of all the people; and they entered and performed the work in the house of the Lord of hosts their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.”

There is no need to linger over what is evident. Yet this must not be passed over: the two men, Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest, who rebuilt that handmade temple, furnished a kind of model for all who have received, receive, and will receive faith in the temple not made by hands, namely Christ’s body.

For one of them—Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was the son of Jeconiah—belonged to the royal tribe; but Jesus son of Jozadak, the priest, was of priestly stock. Are not all who strive for, or attain, the spiritual temple not made by hands, the body of Christ—both priest and king—priests and kings? “But you,” says Peter, “are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). And in the Apocalypse the voice of their thanksgiving is this: “For you have made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Rev. 5).

Moreover, the fact that they entered and performed work in the Lord’s house in the sixth month reminds us, because of the perfection of the number six, of what the angel said to Mary when the Word who is God, the wisdom of God, entered into the Virgin’s womb and was soon to build for himself a house from her flesh: “This is the sixth month for her who is called barren” (Luke 1).

Perhaps the sixth month of the second year of Darius, in which they entered and worked in the Lord’s house here, and there the sixth month from John’s conception, in which, as the Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, the temple of the Lord’s body was begun, delight the reader on account of the perfection, as already noted, of the number six, which consists of its own parts. For three is its half, two its third part, and one its sixth; these parts, when joined together, make six. Numbers of this kind, which are very rare, mathematicians call perfect.

Thus, reminded by the number itself, we gladly proclaim here also that among all the works of the world nothing is more perfect than the temple of Christ’s body, built in the liberation of the captivity of the human race, after the type of that handmade temple built when the captivity of God’s people returning from Babylon was released.

### Chapter II
It follows: “In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the Lord came through the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying: Who among you remains who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? [306] Is it not, in your eyes, as though it were nothing? But now be strengthened, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strengthened, Joshua son of Jehozadak, great priest; and be strengthened, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts. The word which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my Spirit shall be in your midst. Do not fear; for thus says the Lord [Col. 0690D] of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I shall shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and I shall move all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come; and I shall fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. Silver is mine, and gold is mine, says the Lord of hosts. The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts; and in this place I shall give peace, says the Lord of hosts.”

We have set out this entire chapter together, so that the mind which readily grasps its literal sense may, with eager delight, penetrate the whole mystery hidden within it. Clearly, when, as we have already said above, the temple of the Lord was founded, “many,” says Ezra, “even of the priests and Levites, and chiefs of fathers’ houses, and elders who had seen [Col. 0691A] the temple before it was founded, wept aloud when this one was before their eyes; while many raised their voices in joyful shouting; and no one could distinguish the sound of the joyful cry from the sound of the people’s weeping” (1 Esdras 3). This was the reason why the Lord said: “Who among you remains who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not as though it were nothing in your eyes?” For the temple being made was almost half as large as it had formerly been.

Looking to this, or having this in view, he says: “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts; and in this place I shall give peace”—that is, forgiveness of sins—“says the Lord of hosts.” Indeed, because that temple was smaller than the former one, Herod demolished it and restored it to its former size, adorning it with many great buildings; but the Lord of hosts was never pleased to count as glory what a ruinous man and impious king had accomplished, striving to equal or even surpass King Solomon, of great renown and supreme wisdom (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XV, final chapter).

That glory was true glory for that place or temple: there God became man and deigned to be offered there according to the custom of the Law, which says: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2); and there, in that city, before the gates of the city, being crucified for the whole world, he gave peace—that is, forgiveness of sins—to those who believed, both to the Jews who were near and to the Gentiles who were far off (Ephesians 2).

Now it is pleasing to say that those in whose eyes the house being founded was as though it were nothing, since they had seen it in its former glory, and who wept aloud while the younger people, who had not seen the former temple, shouted for joy, presented some likeness of those who, believing at the time of evangelical preaching and coming from the circumcision, stirred up a great disturbance and troubled those who believed from among the Gentiles, as we find in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13, 14). For the latter house was as though it were nothing in their eyes compared with that which they had formerly seen: that is, the faith of Christ and the rite of the new sacrifice, the true sacrifice, of which Christ himself is the author, “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). It seemed to them incapable [Col. 0691D] of bringing salvation unless they were circumcised and observed every custom delivered by Moses (Acts 15).

But what does the prophetic discourse say? “And now be strengthened, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strengthened, Joshua son of Jehozadak, great priest; and be strengthened, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts; and act, for I am with you, says the Lord of hosts.” As he said, so it came to pass: everyone in whom was the Lord of hosts, the Paraclete Spirit, was strengthened. For the disciples were filled with the joy and consolation of the Holy Spirit; and in the daily increase and multiplication of believers, there came about daily—and comes about, and shall come about until the end of the age—that which was said: “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.”

The climax of this same glory will be what he says: “Yet once more, in a little while, I shall shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land, and I shall move all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come.” Great shall that shaking be; glorious shall be the sight of that Desired One. Thus he himself says: “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars, and upon earth distress of nations in bewilderment at the roaring of the sea and its waves; people fainting with fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven shall be shaken. And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Luke 21). Then, without doubt, the glory of this latter house—Christ and the Church—shall be full and perfect.

Therefore, after he had said, “and the Desired One of all nations shall come,” he immediately added: “And I shall fill this house [Col. 0692B] with glory, says the Lord of hosts.” Meanwhile, glory is not yet perfect, because, as the Apostle says, we glory not yet in reality but “in hope of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 5). There will be the full fruit of faith, because we have spiritually gone out from the land of Egypt, believing in Christ and sealed with the Holy Spirit in baptism. He himself promises this: “The word which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my Spirit shall be in your midst.” “You shall see him as he is” (1 John 3); you shall see face to face, when that which is partial has been done away with (1 Corinthians 13).

That he so often repeats, “says the Lord of hosts,” ought not to produce weariness in the reader or hearer; rather, it should make the hearer attentive, receptive, and well disposed, so that he may perceive that the reward of which he hears is great and worthy of God who promises it.

“In the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests concerning the Law, saying: If a man carries consecrated flesh in the fold of his garment, and touches with its edge bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it become consecrated? And the priests answered and said: No. Then Haggai said: If one defiled by a dead person touches any of these things, shall it be defiled? And the priests answered and said: It shall be defiled. Haggai answered and said: So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord; and so is every work of their hands, and all that [Col. 0692D] they have offered to him shall be defiled.”

Behold, this is the third time that the word of the Lord came to Haggai. By his question he indicates a beautiful and delightful mystery of faith, which no one except a believer and a devoted student of evangelical grace can perceive. In the first answer, when the Lord—or the prophet—asks: “If a man carries consecrated flesh in the fold of his garment and touches with its edge bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it become consecrated?” and the priests answer, “No,” the Jews together with their priests are convicted and judged from their own mouths that they cannot be justified by the Law.

For who was the man who carried consecrated flesh, hidden and wrapped in the fold of his garment, except Moses, who concealed beneath the veil of the Law the sacraments of Christ’s most holy flesh and passion? [307] This is what is preached everywhere in the holy Church, what the Apostle teaches in every Church, together with the whole company of Christ’s disciples: whatever Moses handed down or wrote concerning the ceremonies of the sacrifice of the paschal lamb and the rest was a type of Christ’s saving passion. Thus, to give such a Law was without doubt to carry consecrated flesh in the fold of one’s garment; and the letter of that Law instructed the people concerning foods and drinks. This was to touch bread, stew, wine, oil, or any food with the edge of the garment.

But is anything of that kind consecrated when touched by the edge of the garment whose fold carries consecrated flesh? “No,” say the priests knowledgeable in the Law—and what they say is true. Therefore neither you, O Jews, nor your fathers have been consecrated by the Law. For what is the Law except a garment or cloth, in whose fold consecrated flesh—the flesh of Christ—is carried, that is, prefigured?

By the second answer, when, to the Lord’s question, “If one defiled by a dead person touches any of these things, shall it be defiled?” the priests answer, “It shall be defiled,” the Jews together with their priests are beyond doubt convicted and judged from their own mouths to be so unclean that every person who shares in their ceremonies is defiled. For who is “defiled by a dead person,” that is, by a human death, except the Jewish people, who killed Jesus Christ, “the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Timothy 2), and whom that people still does not cease to blaspheme?

Therefore: “So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord.” It is understood: it has not been consecrated by the Law which Moses gave. Just as bread or stew touched by the edge of the garment is not consecrated when a man carries consecrated flesh in its fold, so “every work of their hands, and everything which they offer there”—namely, in their synagogue or assembly, where they are polluted “by a dead person,” that is, by the death of Christ—shall be defiled. As I long ago said through Isaiah: “Do not continue to bring a vain sacrifice. Incense is an abomination to me. My soul hates your new moons and your solemnities” (Isaiah 1).

It follows: “And now set your hearts from this day onward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord: when you came to a heap of twenty measures and there were ten; when you entered the winepress to draw fifty jars and there were twenty. I struck all the works of your hands with scorching wind, blight, and hail; and there was none among you who returned to me, says the Lord.”

As the letter sounds, we cannot demonstrate from the histories that this happened because of the delay or interruption of the work on the house of the Lord, as he says: “I struck all the works of your hands with scorching wind, blight, and hail”; nor that at that time they were so hard and stubborn in evil that he should speak with such grave complaint: “and there was none among you who returned to me.” We should therefore rather look to that to which he directs us by saying beforehand: “And so every work [Col. 0694A] of their hands, and all that they offer there, shall be defiled.” To what does he direct us by saying “there,” except to these times, when the Jew has without doubt been polluted by a human death—as has already been said—by the death of Jesus Christ, whom in killing he became a murderer, and therefore all that he offers is defiled?

Let us not doubt that the Spirit of prophecy also speaks these things in that same place and persists in this declaration until the present day. “And now,” he says, “set your hearts from this day onward, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord.” The day before stone is laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord is the whole time which is now passing, before the Jews are willing to be built up, like living stones (1 Peter 2), in the house or temple which is Christ’s Church. This will happen when “the fullness [Col. 0694B] of the Gentiles has entered” (Romans 11), or has been built into it.

The fault of their unbelief, on account of which all that they offer is defiled, and shall be so long as they remain there—that is, in the pollution by which they are polluted through the death of him whom they killed—the fault, I say, of their unbelief, is beautifully and subtly indicated by these mystical words: “When you came to a heap of twenty measures and there were ten; when you entered the winepress to draw fifty jars and there were twenty.”

For when did the Jews come to the heap and enter the winepress, except when they heard Christ, the firstborn from among themselves, preaching, and saw him dying? He is the heap of twenty measures; this number is two tens, because he is of a double substance—not man alone, but God and man. His Church too is a heap, as he himself says to it in the Song of Songs: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” (Song 7). But he does not say that that heap is of twenty measures. This one alone is the heap of twenty measures, because, as we have already said, he is of a double substance: God and man.

But when you Jews came to such a heap, the heap of twenty measures became ten measures for you, and half was lost to you, because you regarded not God and man, but man alone. Likewise, his death or passion became a winepress. Thus another prophet, looking upon him, says: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one treading the winepress?” (Isaiah 63). And he himself answers: “I have trodden the winepress alone.” This winepress produces fifty jars, that is, forgiveness of sins. For this number, the fiftieth, signifies forgiveness according to the Law, which consecrated remission in the fiftieth year; hence it is called the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25), that is, the year “letting go.”

But when you Jews entered such a winepress, the winepress of fifty jars became for you twenty jars, a number far short of fifty, the number of forgiveness; more than half was lacking to you. For of the whole that ought to have been received, three parts are missing to you, and only two have been received. Five parts ought to have been received, which complete the whole as five decades rise to fifty and make the sacred jubilee.

What are the two parts which you received? You know that he was born of Mary and suffered or died, though you do so with a perverse heart. What are the three parts which you omitted? You do not believe that he rose again, ascended into heaven, and is to come to judge the living and the dead. Therefore do not be ignorant, nor pretend not to know, why the Lord said that every work of your hands and all that you offer are defiled, just as, according to the Law, everything touched by one defiled by a dead person is defiled. For this is the reason why you came to the heap of twenty measures and made ten: you had Christ, God and man, present before you; seeing the man, you refused to recognize God from his works. And you entered the winepress and made twenty out of fifty jars, leaving three parts of the whole and receiving only two: that is, you experienced him as truly man and truly dead, but you do not accept him as victor over death, ascender into heaven, and coming judge of the world.

What he next adds—“I struck all the works of your hands with scorching wind, blight, and hail, and there was none among you who returned to me”—is what [308] we see even now: after they suffered a pitiable destruction, fell by the edge of the sword, had city and temple burned, and those who survived were led captive among all nations, they know that he who foretold it is truthful; yet almost none is willing to return to him, being stiff-necked and hard of heart.

It follows: “Set your hearts from this day and henceforth, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid; lay it upon your heart.” Although he has said—and said truly—“there was none among you who returned to me,” nevertheless, because it will come to pass that a remnant of them will be converted, namely when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered (Romans 11), he still exhorts them and says: “Set your hearts,” and so forth.

In saying, “From this day and henceforth, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid, lay it upon your heart,” I should understand no day more readily than the day of the birth of him who is here in question, our Lord Jesus Christ—the temple, indeed, of the Lord, the temple not made with hands. For on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month—that is, December; for although it is the tenth month from March for the Romans, it is the ninth from April for the Jews, for whom, according to the Law (Exodus 12), April is the first month of the year—on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, I say, that is, December, Christ was born of the Virgin, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December].

He was born at midnight, and that night belonged to the preceding day, because at that time, unlike now after the resurrection of the same Lord, the day preceded the night rather than the night the day. Therefore I would most readily understand the day mentioned here as the day of his birth: among the Romans it is the twenty-fourth day of December every year; among the Jews, because they reckon months by the moon, it falls on the twenty-fourth day of the same month not every year, but only in the thirteenth year of the lunar cycle.

“From this day,” he says, “and henceforth”—the day on which, when Christ was born, the foundations of the temple, that is, of his most holy body, were laid. Thereafter, through succeeding days and years, it was built up as he advanced “in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings” (Luke 2). Set your hearts upon this; consider what and how great were the mighty works performed, how great the evils that came upon you through unbelief, and how great the blessings which came to believers.

If, as though ignorant, you ask what those blessings are, I shall say at once: “Is the seed yet in the sprouting? Have the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree not yet flowered? From this day I shall bless.” By asking, he more emphatically affirms what nobody doubts: namely, that in the ninth month, December—which, as has been said, is the ninth month for the Hebrews from April—the seed is not in sprout. The nature of the season does not permit it; neither vine nor fig nor pomegranate nor olive tree is flowering.

So, indeed, when Christ was born, almost nowhere was there a seedling of righteousness or a flower of holiness, such as might bear fruit in the vine, fig tree, pomegranate, and olive tree, by which we understand righteous persons. As at the season of the year in which Christ was born, whatever greenness is in the seedling, vine, fig tree, pomegranate, or olive tree lies hidden within, all things being bound by cold, so whatever righteousness existed in a few people was suppressed under the reign of the impious Herod (Matthew 2). Because of him especially, it was unsafe—even if Mary’s virginity, impregnated by the Holy Spirit, had already become known—for anyone openly to speak of Messiah, that is, Christ, or to say that the time of his coming had arrived; since, under the reign of a foreigner, “the sceptre had been removed from Judah and a ruler from between his thighs” (Genesis 49; printed citation: Genesis 29).

Therefore, placed by prophetic vision in contemplation of that day or time, he says: “Is the seed yet in the sprouting, or has the tree flowered?” The answer is understood: No. Immediately he adds: “From this day I shall bless. Set your hearts; I say again, set your heart, and see that it is so. For from that day, as I blessed, seed appeared in the sprouting; vine, fig tree, pomegranate, and olive tree flowered.” That is, the fruit and splendor of every righteousness began to grow and advance.

First, in the little innocents whom the ruinous Herod killed, how did godliness spring up? How did the olive tree flower? Throughout the world a certain spiritual paradise began to bloom with lilies of chastity and roses of martyrdom; and it has abounded in such fruit until now, and shall abound until the end of the age, that it was fitting for the Lord God to say to his own glory: “From this day I shall bless.”

It follows: “And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying: I shall shake heaven together with earth; and I shall overthrow the throne of kingdoms, and break the strength of the kingdom of nations; and I shall overthrow the chariot and its rider; and horses and their riders shall come down, each by the sword of his brother.”

Zerubbabel, ruler of the children of Judah, who rebuilt the temple in name and deed, and in his very rule bore a likeness of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as many of the righteous and prophets did, according to his own saying: “In the hand of my prophets I have been likened” (Hosea 12; printed citation: Hosea 21). In name, because Zerubbabel means “born in Babylon.” And who was born in Babylon more conspicuously than he who, “being in the form of God, emptied himself,” coming into this world, which truly is Babylon, “made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2)? He did so in order to release us from captivity and, as the Psalmist had sung, “ascending on high, to lead captivity captive” (Psalm 68; Vulgate numbering 67).

In deed, because by his hand they founded that temple made with hands, and his hand completed it. And who else but Jesus Christ himself founded the temple not made with hands, his own body (Mark 14), and has now completed the Church, which is his body (Ephesians 1), the fullness of it, with living and chosen stones? (1 Peter 2). In his rule, because he was prince and leader of the children of Judah (Hebrews 3). And what is Judah, which means “confession,” but the whole body of those confessing the Lord? And who does not know that Jesus is the prince of our confession?

When, therefore, we hear that the word of the Lord came to Haggai in order that he might speak to Zerubbabel, we rightly understand that the celebration and fulfillment of the whole of our salvation, and the entire truth of prophecy, beginning from Christ’s birth from the Virgin Mary, was undertaken and directed toward him.

But what is the meaning of these four sayings which he joins to the promise, “I shall shake heaven and earth”: “And I shall overthrow the throne of kingdoms; and I shall break the strength of the kingdom of nations; and I shall overthrow the chariot and its rider; horses and their riders shall come down”? He seems to have said the same thing repeatedly: “I shall overthrow the throne of kingdoms” is the same as “I shall break the strength of the kingdom of nations,” and likewise the rest.

But let us recall Daniel’s vision in which four great beasts came up from the sea: the first like a lioness; the second like a bear; the third like a leopard; the fourth terrible, wonderful, and exceedingly strong, with great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder beneath its feet. Then the Ancient of Days sat, thrones having been set; and one like a Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven and came as far as the Ancient of Days, who gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, after the beast was slain and the dominion of the other beasts also taken away (Daniel 7).

[309] What was prefigured for Daniel by such images is here promised in words. This Zerubbabel, born in Babylon for our sake, as has been said, to whom these four things are spoken, is that Son of Man, after the four beasts have been slain or removed, whose power, honor, and kingdom are established and shall not perish.

For there were four kingdoms which, from the time of these prophets, exalted themselves against God and through which the devil strove to destroy the place and people from whom Christ, the salvation of the world, had to be born, according to God’s oath to Abraham. Therefore four things are said here. “I shall overthrow the throne of kingdoms,” namely the throne of the Babylonians; “and I shall break the strength of the kingdom of nations,” namely of the Persians and Medes; “and I shall overthrow the chariot and its rider,” namely the Greek kingdom and the impious Antiochus who exalted himself against God in that kingdom, called Epiphanes, or “the Illustrious” (1 Maccabees 1).

And he rightly called that kingdom a chariot, because after the death of Alexander the Great it was divided into four kingdoms, as had been signified to Daniel: “the he-goat became exceedingly great; and when it had grown, the great horn was broken, and four horns sprang up beneath it toward the four winds of heaven” (Daniel 8). “And horses and their riders shall come down,” namely the Roman Empire, whose horses were many and whose riders were numerous.

Where shall they come down? Surely to the place which Daniel means us to understand when he says: “I saw that the beast was slain, its body destroyed and given to be burned with fire” (Daniel 7). And concerning this kingdom especially it should be observed that, after saying, “horses and their riders shall come down,” he added, “each by the sword of his brother,” because, as is almost universally known, the Roman Empire very often tore itself apart in civil wars.

These kingdoms have already, indeed, been overthrown and broken piecemeal and gradually; they shall be overthrown and come down. But then, when the Lord accomplishes what he had prefaced by saying, “I shall shake heaven together with earth”—that shaking of which all Scriptures speak, in which “the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Luke 21)—then all things shall be overthrown together and shall come down, namely into hell. For Isaiah says: “For this reason hell has enlarged its appetite, and its lofty ones and glorious ones shall come down to it” (Isaiah 5).

It follows: “On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I shall take you, Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and set you as a signet; because I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts.”

How shall I take you on that day? Namely, I shall show that I have taken you and that your kingdom is legitimate, while every throne of kingdoms and every kingdom of nations has been usurpation. For “they reigned, but not through me; they became princes, and I, the Ancient of Days, did not know them.” Wrong was done to me in my commonwealth, because they did not have regard for my grayness, that is, my antiquity, and dared, as far as lay in them, to violate my right.

For in my kingdom—in the world, which wholly is and ought to be mine by right, because I made the world—no one ought to reign except through me. Whatever human beings, new and recent creatures, have done, I, the Ancient of Days, shall do what belongs to me: I shall order my kingdom and appoint my king from myself, taking you, O Zerubbabel, my servant. For you are my servant for the same reason that you are Zerubbabel: because, “taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), you were born in Babylon, that is, in the world. You are son of Shealtiel, that is, son of God’s petition: the son whom the whole company of saints or righteous people requested from me, their God, with long and great desire, that I might send you.

“I shall take you,” giving you power, honor, and kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve you, and your power shall be an eternal power which shall not be taken away, and your kingdom shall not be destroyed. “I shall take you,” he says, “and set you as a signet.” This is the signet which, as he himself says of himself, the Father sealed and sanctified (John 6). The Apostle also says: “He is the image of the invisible God and the figure of his substance” (Colossians 1; Hebrews 1).

By saying “as a signet,” he does not diminish the reality of the signet, just as, in the Psalm, when it says, “We became as those comforted” (Psalm 126; Vulgate numbering 125), the reality of consolation is not diminished. We too commonly say, “You acted like a faithful person, like a friend”; and in saying this, we clearly pronounce someone truly faithful and truly a friend. Therefore, “as a signet” means truly a signet, by which, as wax placed beneath a king’s ring or image is sealed and adorned with its likeness, so the believing and faithful soul is sealed and adorned.

Where shall I set you? Surely in my sight, at my right hand, in my glory, in my omnipotence, so that you may have all power in heaven and on earth, because I have chosen you, O form of a servant, to be one person with the form of God.

That in so brief a verse “says the Lord of hosts” is repeated three times should not seem wearisome or superfluous to us, but delightful and meaningful. For truly the Lord Father says this utterance of sweetest promise to the form of a servant; the Lord Word says it; the Lord Holy Spirit says it. And it is the work of the whole Trinity that that form sits at the right hand of God, such that his bride rejoices and says: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song of Songs 5).

[310] **RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH**

[Col. 0699]

O attentive soul, you now enter Zechariah, whom you have long viewed from afar, the eleventh in the order of the twelve prophets. Who but the true and holy one “who has the key of David” shall open the door of understanding and put into your mouth speech that is right and well sounding? (Revelation 3).

What is it that you ponder in your mind, now standing and knocking at the door of this prophet—or rather, almost of a most beautiful evangelist? “I saw by night,” he says, “and behold, a man riding upon a red horse” (Zechariah 1; printed citation: Zechariah 8). In saying this, he makes me recall something which, I do not know how, some wise person may receive: “For I saw by night, and behold an immensity of light, and a homeland of a sweetly reddening threshold, shining with ruddy serenity beyond all speech; and in it a sweet song, the song of a multitude continually singing and resounding harmonious praise without interruption.”

As I approached that place, certain little children came out from it to meet me, rejoicing and applauding. “This,” they said, “is the one who speaks thus and thus about our Lord; he says these things and others like them.” Meanwhile, an ineffable sweetness of that homeland flooded the inmost recesses of my being, and the Spirit told the understanding soul that it ought to be joined to that harmony.

Are these not childish things? Yet you, O Lord our God, whose name is wonderful in all the earth: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8). Therefore, whoever hears these things, whether he wishes to take them as belonging to a child or to a man, must stretch the string of understanding and strike the lyre of the breast, breathing your faith, O Christ; and he must ask the Spirit of your love to compose the melodies of ready praise. For he long ago inspired this: that from the treasures of the prophets I should hope for and desire to gain nothing other than your testimonies—the faithful testimonies of your Gospel, which has been proclaimed to us. For these are the Scriptures which bear witness to you, as you said to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have life; and they are they which bear witness to me” (John 5).

Behold, standing at the entrance of this Scripture, I sing what is true and meditate upon it with diligent mind: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones; the righteous ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 19; Vulgate numbering 18). Let it be done to me according to what you have said, you our God and Lord: “Open wide your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Psalm 81; Vulgate numbering 80).

**THE FIRST BOOK OF COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH**

[Col. 0699]

[Col. 0699C] **311.** In the eighth month, in the second year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Barachiah, son of Addo, the prophet, saying: “The Lord was angry with anger against your fathers.”

This Haggai and Zechariah were contemporaries and prophesied together under Darius, in the second year of his reign, helping and strengthening the Jews, as is written in Ezra: “Then Zerubbabel son of Salathiel and Joshua son of Josedec arose and began to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, helping them” (1 Esdras 5). Haggai began to prophesy two months [Col. 0700C] before Zechariah: for the word of the Lord came to this man in the eighth month, but to that man in the sixth month of the same year, the second of King Darius. Thus, as he preceded him in time as a prophet, so he precedes him in the order of Scripture.

Moreover, Darius, in whose second year they prophesied, the son of Hystaspes, ruled the Medes and Persians as the fourth ruler after Cyrus. Cyrus was succeeded by his son Cambyses, Cambyses by the two Magian brothers, and, after they were killed, this Darius was made king. From the first year of King Cyrus, who ordered the Lord’s temple to be rebuilt in Jerusalem [Col. 0701A] and sent back nearly fifty thousand captives to Judaea, forty years are counted, during which only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid; for the neighboring nations, by the command of King Cambyses, prevented them from building either the temple or the city.

In accordance with the greatness of grace or merit by which he was worthy to be enrolled in the book of life, he also received a name among men: he was called Zechariah, which is interpreted “the remembrance of the Lord,” the son of Barachiah, that is, “son of the blessing of the Lord,” and son of Addo, that is, “son of the testimony of the Lord.” By these names he is proclaimed a son of great grace; and that grace is to be recognized from the very fact that the word of the Lord came to him—the work upon whose threshold we now stand—and begins thus:

“The Lord was angry with anger against your fathers. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall return to you, says the Lord of hosts.”

As at the end of Haggai, so at the beginning of this book the threefold repetition of the Lord’s name shines forth. Are we to suppose that this was said by chance or without rational purpose: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall return to you, says the Lord of hosts”? Certainly not by chance, nor without rational purpose; rather, because he was a prophet and, with prophetic eye, was wholly intent upon that acceptable time and day of salvation when it would be said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28); and when those sins, on account of which the Lord had been angrily wrathful against their fathers, should be washed away through Christ’s blood.

Against what fathers, then, and with what anger had he been angry? We make Holy Scripture far too narrow if we understand no anger other than the captivity of one generation, which in its own time was led away into that Babylon—a certain small part of this world—and no fathers other than the Jews who died in Babylon, fathers of the Jews who returned from there. Yet it was surely not a very great anger merely to pass from one nation to another and from one kingdom to another people. I say, not very great to one who considers the greater wrath, of which this was a kind of likeness and faint [Col. 0701D] shadow; through this as through an image, the childish understanding of human beings is gradually led to recognize the great wrath and true captivity into which it fell through Adam and from which it was delivered through Christ.

“The Lord,” he says, “was angry with anger against your fathers”—that is, with the anger which you too have borne, as another prophet says in confession: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we have borne their iniquities” (Lam. 5). That anger cannot be appeased, nor can that wall of enmity be dissolved, except through faith in Jesus Christ (Eph. 2), unless you hasten to be sealed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“You shall therefore say to them,” he says: “‘Thus says the Lord of hosts’—the Father; ‘Return to me, says the Lord of hosts’—the Son; ‘and I shall return to you, says the Lord of hosts’—the Holy Spirit. Return to me, **312** and I shall return to you”: that is, believe in me, and, when anger has been removed, I shall receive you into reconciliation.

“Do not be like your fathers, to whom the earlier prophets cried out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Return from your evil ways and your most wicked thoughts. But they did not hear or attend to me, says the Lord.” This resembles what the Holy Spirit says in David: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works” (Ps. 94 [95]), and so forth.

What this passage says, “Do not be like your fathers,” is there expressed as, “Do not harden your hearts as in that provocation, where your fathers tempted me.” And what this says, “They did not hear or attend to me,” is there: “But they did not know my ways.” Therefore, it is fitting to see that the day to which the Apostle leads us in the words, “Today, if you hear his voice” (Heb. 4), is the very day to which this passage looks when it says, “Do not be like your fathers.”

“For,” says the same Apostle, “since it remains for some to enter into that rest, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again fixes a certain day in David, saying after so long a time: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterwards have spoken of another day” (ibid.).

And indeed “today,” in this time of saving grace which has shone upon the world, from Christ’s passion and resurrection [Col. 0702C] onward, it is said not only to the Jews: “Do not be like your fathers, to whom the earlier prophets cried out, and who did not hear or attend; do not harden your hearts, like your fathers who tempted me and fell in the wilderness and did not enter into that rest.” It is said also to all of us human beings, from whatever people or nation we may be: “Do not be like your fathers Adam and Eve, who entered into that rest—that is, Paradise—and made themselves unworthy of the same rest.”

Yet this also must be known: whoever are murmurers or rebels in their Christian profession, whatever people or nation they belong to, may rightly call those men their fathers who, having crossed the Red Sea, though they seemed to have left Egypt, did not enter into the land of promise but fell in the wilderness (Num. 14); likewise, those who afterwards did not listen to the prophets sent to them. All murmurers and all rebels are their children—by imitation, evidently. Thus the Greek no less than the Jew, if he understands the saying, is addressed: “Do not be like your fathers,” and so forth.

It follows: “Where are your fathers and the prophets? Do they live forever? Yet did not my words and my ordinances, which I commanded to my servants the prophets, overtake your fathers?”

It is as though he said: At least let distress now give understanding to hearing (Isa. 28), since, when you lived in peace, you refused to believe the prophets whom I sent, paying attention rather to your own false prophets. Where now are those fathers of yours and those prophets? Truth mockingly asks after those false prophets, of whom Jeremiah says: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you, ‘You shall not serve the king of Babylon,’ for they speak a lie to you. I did not send them, says the Lord, and they prophesy falsely in my name” (Jer. 27).

“Do prophets of this kind,” he says, “live forever?” Indeed, they died sooner; for example, that Hananiah who had falsely prophesied against Jeremiah—or rather against the Lord. “The Lord has not sent you,” Jeremiah says, “and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore you shall die this year, says the Lord, for you have spoken against the Lord.” And he died in that year, in the seventh month (Jer. 28).

Do they therefore live forever? By no means. But “my words and my ordinances, which I commanded to my servants the prophets”—these live, and these overtook your fathers. “And they turned and said: As the Lord of hosts intended to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, so he has done to us.”

This does not seem a good conversion or a gracious saying; indeed, it is a murmuring reproach against divine severity, in that they say: “As the Lord of hosts intended to do to us, so he has done.” How much better and more graciously did Daniel and his companions speak: “O Lord God, great and terrible, we have sinned; we have acted wickedly. Everything which you brought upon us and everything which you did to us, you did in true judgment; righteousness belongs to you, but confusion of face to us,” and the rest of similar kind (Dan. 9).

The conversion of such persons is right and their speech pleasing, since they accuse themselves in such a way as to justify God. “Your fathers,” he says, “did not do so; rather, they turned and said: ‘As the Lord of hosts intended to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, so he has done to us.’” In saying this, they do not justify themselves, because they cannot; but neither do they proclaim God’s justice, because they refuse to do so.

You may see even today the Jews—undoubtedly the very worst sons of fathers of that sort, evil fathers—remaining so perverse that, if you ask why they are captives, they say nothing other than this: “As the Lord intended, as it pleased the Lord, he has done to us according to our ways”; and they never wish either to confess or to know the reason for which the Lord intended, or should have intended, thus to act. They say indeed, “He has done to us according to our ways,” but refuse to say what those ways were.

Nevertheless, the divine and prophetic discourse continues: “Do not be like your fathers”; while they protest by their deeds—or rather, “We shall be like our fathers.” Hence they are without excuse.

“On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Sebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Barachiah, son of Addo, the prophet, saying: I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse; and he stood among the myrtle trees which were in the deep, and behind him were red, mottled, and white horses. And I said: Who are these, my lord? And the angel of the Lord who spoke in me said to me: I will show you what these are. And the man who stood among the myrtle trees answered and said: These are those whom the Lord has sent to go through the earth. And they answered the angel of the Lord who stood among the myrtle trees and said: We have gone through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.”

This is a very great and wonderful vision, on a single day—namely, the twenty-fourth of the eleventh month in the second year of Darius—to Zechariah, to whom the word of the Lord had first come in the eighth month. I say, this vision is very great and far too clear for our dim-sighted eyes to bear, dazzled as they are by excessive brightness.

It begins with the man riding upon the red horse and standing among the myrtle trees which were in the deep; it ends where Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, is crowned with the crowns of Helira, Tobiah, Hidaiah, and Hen son of Sophaniah. With what voice, with what words, shall I express the beauty and majesty of so great a vision? May the very author and arranger of prophetic visions, the Spirit of the Lord, be present; for this prophetic history is a kind of prophetic picture of your expectation and coming, Christ Son of God; of your passion and glorious resurrection or glorification, Christ Son of Man; and of your second coming, when at the last you shall be crowned with God’s glory and honor, **313** and there will be no end to your crowns and no end to your kingdom.

The faithful mind rejoices to contemplate, however inadequately, such a lovely history of your praise, and a tongue devoted to your name desires to speak it. “I saw,” he says, “by night, and behold, a man riding [Col. 0704C] upon a red horse, and he stood among myrtle trees which were in the deep.”

He had prefaced the passage as follows: “The word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Barachiah, son of Addo, the prophet, saying”; and before he adds the Lord’s own welcome words—“I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy,” and so forth—he makes a digression. Luke likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, after prefacing, “Peter stood up in the midst of the brethren and said” (Acts 1), makes a digression, though a shorter one than this, adding: “Now the crowd of persons was about one hundred and twenty” (ibid.).

Thus the statement which he prefaced—“the word of the Lord came to me, saying”—must be understood by anticipation. For he will narrate more fully the order of what occurred, and at last begin the Lord’s gracious utterances themselves: “I saw,” he says, “by night.” Appropriately, by night, so that the very time of the vision might suit the sadness and grief in which he was, namely because of the long desolation of his people and place. For the same reason Daniel also saw at night: “I looked,” he says, “in a vision of the night” (Dan. 7).

The night was long and cold, and no less dark. For it was the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Sebat, which among us is called February. On the twenty-fourth day the moon is nearly at its waning. Thus the length of the night, the severity of the cold, and the lack of light—of the moon’s faint illumination—suited the grief in which the prophet needed the consolation of heavenly visitation and speech. This was such a visitation: “Behold, a man riding upon a red horse.”

Why was he riding upon a red horse, except in order to do what he afterwards says: “I shall return to Jerusalem in mercies”? That man is the Lord himself; and he seemed to mount upon a horse because the time had come for him to return to his city, because the time for showing mercy to it had arrived. What was that horse, except his human nature? He had not yet indeed become man, but this was being prepared, and what was to occur in reality was signified by the present vision.

For this reason he fittingly seemed to mount a horse, being about to return to Jerusalem in mercies: because Jerusalem had to be rebuilt for this reason, that there might be a place from which, according to the promises made to the fathers, he himself, having become man, might be born. He saw—or called—the horse red because of his own crimson blood.

John saw the same horse in the Apocalypse as white: “I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and the armies which are in heaven followed him” (Rev. 19). It is one and the same horse: there it was seen as white because of his innocence; here, red because of the blood of his passion. What does the Church mean when she says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5)?

“And he stood among the myrtle trees which were in the deep.” Myrtle is temperate in nature, and books of medicine declare this tree suitable for curing illnesses, especially many ailments of women. Myrtle is said to be named from the sea (*mare*), because it commonly grows on seashores. Hence Virgil says:

> “The most delightful shores, with myrtles . . . [lacuna]”

And:

> “[lacuna] myrtles, loving the shores.”

What then do the myrtle trees signify except the holy and truly health-giving Scriptures of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms? And was not this man of whom we speak already then standing among such myrtle trees? “Search,” he says, “the Scriptures, and they are those which bear witness of me” (John 5). Clearly, to have testimony from all the holy Scriptures is to stand among the myrtle trees.

“And,” he says, “the myrtle trees were in the deep.” Truly there is a great depth in Holy Scripture. Hence the Psalmist says: “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41 [42]); that is, if you are to penetrate the depth of one Scripture, the associated depth of another Scripture is of great help. There the man stood; there he may be found and known, if he is sought. But he is not found by one who does not wish to seek, like someone standing among myrtle trees: neither is he so exposed that he is quickly seen by those who pass carelessly by, nor so hidden that he cannot be found by diligent seekers.

From the time when Moses sacrificed the lamb in Egypt as a type of him and marked the doorposts of houses with its blood (Exod. 12)—indeed, from the time when the father Abraham, about to sacrifice his only son Isaac, placed him upon the altar (Gen. 22)—from that time onward the horse upon which this man rode began to be seen as red. For wherever you turn among such myrtle trees, the sacrament of this man’s passion, prefigured both in the mystical deeds and sayings of patriarchs and prophets, presents itself to your eyes.

“And behind him,” he says, “were red, mottled, and white horses.” Behind him, I say, and not before him; for he is before all, and the firstborn among many brethren. All his holy brethren, moreover, are the Lord’s horses: some red through martyrdom, some white through the radiance of virginity, some mottled through the gift of diverse charisms. They follow him, as was said above from the Apocalypse: “The armies which are in heaven followed him” (Rev. 19). All horses of this kind have one rider, God; and for that reason they make a harmonious army.

“And I said: Who are these, my lord?” To whom he spoke, or whom he questioned—whether the man himself who stood among the myrtle trees, or his angel, that is, the one assigned to him, who spoke in him—is not easily discerned. But it is plain who gives both replies. For first it is added: “The angel of the Lord who spoke in me said to me: I will show you what these are”; and then: “The man who stood among the myrtle trees answered and said: These are those whom the Lord has sent to go through the earth.”

Had the person so answered not been a prophet, the answer or demonstration—“These are those whom the Lord has sent to go through the earth”—would not have been sufficient. But because he was a prophet and already possessed spiritual understanding, he could understand; therefore he asked no further question. We, however, ask how the Lord sent those whom we have called his horses to go through the earth, and with what meaning they answer and say to him: “We have gone through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.”
