To find this first, the following must be added: “And the angel of the Lord answered and said: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy upon Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year.” Therefore the Lord’s horses—that is, holy men such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the rest—uttered a great complaint when they said: “We have gone through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.”

It is as though they said: “You, Lord, sent us to go through the earth. At your command we became unsettled and were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth; and, confessing this, we showed that we sought a homeland and awaited the city which has foundations, whose designer and builder you are, God (Heb. 11). For if we had remembered that homeland, we certainly had opportunity to return. But now we desired a better one, that is, a heavenly country.

“Yet the preparation for that heavenly country ought to have been this earthly Jerusalem; for we cannot find the heavenly city which we have desired unless the promise is fulfilled from here, and what is written comes to pass: **314** ‘And a man was born in her; the Most High himself founded her’ (Ps. 86 [87]). We have gone through the earth; we have passed from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people—some freely, leaving our own land at your command; some led away captive against their will—and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. But Jerusalem and the land of Judah are neither inhabited nor at rest: the land whose habitation and repose alone are necessary for our hope, expectation, and salvation, in order that what was promised to us may be done; that you, O God, may be justified in your words (Ps. 104 [105]); that you, O Christ, may be born from the seed of Abraham and from the seed of David (Gen. 12); that the law may go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 25 [uncertain citation]).

To this truly great and entirely fitting complaint of such horses of the Lord, the angel of the Lord answers and joins in: “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy upon Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year.”

This angel of the Lord who answers is rightly understood not to be the man who stood among the myrtle trees, to whom they also spoke when saying, “We have gone through the earth.” That man had indeed previously been called the angel of the Lord, and they also “answered the angel who stood among the myrtle trees”; but he is not the one who says, “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy?” and so forth. For it follows: “And the Lord answered the angel who spoke in me with good words, consoling words.” He who spoke in the prophet is only an angel; but the man—or angel—who stood among the myrtle trees is himself the Lord of hosts.

But someone will say: if that man, that angel who stood among the myrtle trees, is, as has been said, the Lord of hosts himself, how does he say—or how is it fitting for him to say—“These are those whom the Lord has sent”? This is surely a superfluous question, since not only is the Lord’s or God’s person manifold, but one of the two speaks of the other, as in: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48); and elsewhere: “The Lord is with me as a mighty warrior” (Jer. 20).

It follows: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy; and with great anger I am angry against the wealthy nations, because I was angry a little, but they added to the evil. Therefore thus says the Lord: I shall return to Jerusalem in mercies; my house shall be built in it, says the Lord of hosts, and a measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.”

The angel who spoke in the prophet now does what he promised a little earlier. For, when he was asked, “What are these, my lord?” he answered: “I will show you what these are.” “Cry out,” he says, “saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Jerusalem,” and so forth. It is as if he said: “You ask about the man standing among the myrtle trees, why he rides upon a horse. Behold, I tell you that he is a great sign of the Lord of hosts, who is exceedingly angry against the nations which afflicted Judah and Jerusalem. He mounts the horse and goes against them.”

For what reason? Because, he says, I, as a father, or as a husband loving his wife, “have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy”—a good jealousy—visiting their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges. The rod at that time was the power of the Babylonians; the scourges were captivity and the burning of the temple and city. But the nations to whom I handed over my children for this very purpose “added to,” or “helped in,” evil.

What did they add? They sought, of course, to accomplish that which, if it had been accomplished, would have caused them to undergo not merely a rod or scourges, but something more than a rod, more than scourges: namely, the addition of death. For they desired to do this and to compel them to this end—that they should abandon me, their God—and they inflicted dreadful torments and various deaths on those unwilling to agree.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: I shall return to Jerusalem in mercies.” What you have now seen—the man mounting the red horse, with red, mottled, and white horses behind him—and concerning which you asked, “Who are these, my lord?”—the red, mottled, and white horses are the Lord’s army. And this man is called, and is, the Lord of hosts, because so many horses, and many more than you saw, go after him. Therefore, when you see this, do not fear the wealthy nations, but rightly say what another said to his servant: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them” (4 Kings 4).

When he said and prayed this, the Lord opened the servant’s eyes, and he saw: behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire before Elisha. Behold, you too have seen the Lord’s horses and him mounting his own red horse, with these words: “I shall return to Jerusalem in mercies; my house shall be built in it, and a measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.” Cry this out and solemnly declare it to the children of the migration, that they may be strengthened, knowing that the Lord is returning to them in mercies; and say: “I saw him mounting.”

“Cry out again, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with good things; and the Lord shall again comfort Zion, and shall again choose Jerusalem.” Do not, he says, cry out only this: “My house shall be built, and a measuring line shall be stretched over Jerusalem.” But as he himself was petitioned by me when I said: “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you were formerly angry?” so receive my answer concerning Jerusalem and the other cities of Judah: “My cities,” he says, “shall again overflow with good things”—understood as temporal goods—and therefore the Lord shall again comfort Zion with everlasting consolation, and shall again choose Jerusalem with perfect election. Thus, as he says in another prophet, it may be called “the city of the righteous, mother of cities, the faithful city” (Isa. 1); and what he says in the same prophet may be fulfilled: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and from Jerusalem the word of the Lord” (Isa. 2).

“And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these? And he said to me: These are the horns which scattered Judah and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four craftsmen; and I said: What have these come to do? And he answered, saying: These are the horns which scattered Judah, each man apart, so that none of them lifted up his head; but these have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah in order to scatter it.”

Behold, by a certain likeness of armies advancing to wars in different ways, on this side the Lord of hosts appeared riding upon a red horse, with red, mottled, and white horses behind him; on that side appeared four horns—that is, armies or kings of armies, namely of the nations which, he says, scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.

For the four nations which, in their kings as horns of pride, assailed the divine name and crushed God’s people were the Babylonians, Medes and Persians, Macedonians, and Romans. The angel, questioned by the prophet, explains this here, and Daniel sets it forth most fully: in the vision of the statue with a golden head, silver breast, bronze belly beneath the navel, and legs and feet of iron and clay, he interpreted these four nations (Dan. 2). Again, in another vision, he showed the same nations under another figure: four beasts—a lioness, a bear, a leopard, and a fourth terrible beast, to which he gave no name (ibid. 2).

No one who has read both secular and sacred literature doubts that the Medes and Persians were one kingdom after Cyrus’s victory. What the Babylonians, Medes and Persians, and Greeks—that is, the Macedonians—did; how they scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem as with horns; how the horn of the Roman Empire crushed and scattered not only that Jerusalem which was no longer Jerusalem, but spiritually Sodom and Egypt (Rev. 11), where our Lord was crucified, but also Christ’s Church, the true Judah, the true Israel, and the true Jerusalem—by cruel edicts and public laws sent through the whole world or among every people—who does not know or who has not heard? (Rev. 2).

Such horns were indeed shown together in the prophetic vision, but they did not oppress God’s true people simultaneously. The Babylonians succeeded one another, then the Medes and Persians; the Macedonian kingdom succeeded the Persian kingdom; and the Roman Empire the Macedonian kingdom.

Similarly, regarding the craftsmen, it must be understood that they were shown to the prophet together, coming to terrify the horns of those kingdoms; but they did not destroy them at one and the same time, nor did all of them destroy everything. Rather, each, at definite times, terrified and broke particular horns. They were opposed to one another, and each resisted the other.

Who are or were these four craftsmen? It is certainly not unreasonable to understand them as the princes—that is, the angels—who presided over the several kingdoms, as is shown in Daniel in these words: “I,” says the angel, “came because of your words. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days.” And below: “Do you know,” he says, “why I have come to you? Now I shall return to fight against the prince of the Persians. When I went forth, behold, the prince of the Greeks came” (Dan. 10).

Just as we read of the prince of the Persians and the prince of the Greeks, so we do not doubt that there was some prince of the Babylonians and some prince of the Romans: angels, of course, presiding over the several kingdoms—evil angels, evil princes, belonging to the Evil One in whose power the world lay. The deeds of their dominion bear evident witness to this: cruel deeds and bloody acts, whose dreadful narratives fill both secular and sacred books.

The one people of God had a good angel as its good prince, namely Michael. Thus the angel who spoke to Daniel says in the same place: “Yet I shall tell you what is written in the Scripture of truth, and none is my helper in all these things except Michael, your prince” (ibid.).

The first of those whom the Lord showed the prophet—the first of such craftsmen, namely the angel who presided over the Babylonians—crushed the horns of the nations which had scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. This happened when, with the permission or ordering of God, the righteous judge, they overthrew Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian kingdom, and many surrounding nations, while no one could resist the prince of the Babylonians.

Yet neither he nor the other craftsmen—that is, the evil princes—acted as they did because they were angry that those kingdoms had afflicted God’s people. The second, the prince of Persia, crushed the horn of the Babylonian kingdom; the third, the prince of the Greek kingdom, mutilated the Persian horn with his own horn; the fourth, the prince of the Romans, very swiftly broke the Greek horn. These, I say, did not act thus for that reason. Rather, always greedy for human blood and finding delight in the sight of human slaughter, they willingly made use of God’s permission. That permission is just and good; they, however, always use it unjustly and wickedly, just as, conversely, God always makes good use of their evils.

It should therefore be noted that, when the prophet asked, “What have these craftsmen come to do?” the angel repeated what he had already said: “These are the horns which scattered Judah”; and added what he had not said: “each man apart, so that none of them lifted up his head.” Only then did he speak of the craftsmen: “These have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah in order to destroy it.”

The meaning is this: the horns which scattered Judah—that is, the kings or kingdoms which took Judaea captive or crushed it—were each exceedingly great and strong in their own times. Thus, while they scattered Judah, man by man, no one could or ought to lift up his head. But when one rises against another and smites, breaks, or wears down another’s strength as though with the hand of a craftsman and an iron hammer, then an opportunity is given to lift one’s head and resist the now-broken horns of the nations.

For example, the Greek kingdom was one great horn among the four horns; but it was divided against itself, because from one kingdom four kingdoms arose when, after Alexander’s death, his sons each took possession of the kingdom in his own place. Now consider: if that kingdom had remained whole and one, would Judas Maccabaeus have lifted up his head against it? (1 Macc. 1). Certainly this could have happened through God’s help; but God chose that it should happen in this order: that the divided kingdom should become weaker, and that, besides, that great craftsman, the principality of the Roman Empire, should come upon it and strike and terrify it with his own hammer.

The histories recounted bear witness to this: Antiochus Epiphanes, against whom Judas Maccabaeus rightly and justly lifted up his head, had long been worn down by the forces of that same growing and strengthening Roman Empire. When, by command of Roman envoys, he wished to add Egypt—indeed, to his own kingdom—he was shamefully turned back (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 12, ch. 6).

In these matters too, God’s providence is praiseworthy. Just as, when Israel first came up from Egypt, he divided the Red Sea into divisions for them to cross, so thereafter he divided against themselves the kingdoms of the nations, in whose midst every true Israelite who tends toward God lives as a pilgrim; so that their discord might become an occasion of salvation for the holy and elect.

## Chapter II
And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring line; and I said: “Where are you going?” And he said to me: “To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great its breadth is, and how great [Col. 0711B] its length.” And behold, the angel who was speaking in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him, and said to him: “Run and speak to this youth, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst; and I myself, says the Lord, shall be for her a wall of fire round about, and I shall be glory in her midst.”

Great is the joy of the angels, great in these words is the exultant rejoicing of heavenly spirits and earthly men over the event that has occurred. For the Lord of hosts prevailed; and, the horns of the kingdoms of the nations having been broken, God’s purpose came to its effect, so that Jerusalem might be built and in it a temple for the name of the Lord (2 Esdras 6). The angels rejoice, and men wish to share in their joy. Truly there is great [Col. 0711C] cause for rejoicing; but you should understand not only that handmade temple which Zerubbabel founded and completed, nor only that city whose walls Nehemiah built—when only one horn of the Babylonian kingdom had been broken by the craftsman of the Persian kingdom—but the temple not made by hands and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. This is now being built as a city after all those four horns have been broken, as the Psalmist says: “whose participation is in the same” (Psalm 121). Its temple was built long ago—indeed, it was also destroyed by Jewish impiety and raised up after three days. The city has no other temple, for John says: “I saw no temple in it; for the Lord Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Revelation 21).

Without doubt this prophetic vision tends toward this, and for this reason the angels rejoice: that they will always have such a temple with men, and always have such a city with men. But why, above all, was the vision of angelic congratulation to be displayed at that time concerning this matter, unless because that earthly city and handmade temple, which were then beginning to be rebuilt, were certain instruments or beginnings of that heavenly city? For, as has already been said, Christ had to be born from that place and city or people, according to God’s promises; and hence there was already joy at that time, because, when the temple and city had been rebuilt, the hope of the saints did not perish and the promise remained. Therefore see how eagerly they now rejoice.

“Behold,” he says, “a man, and in his hand a measuring line”; [Col. 0712A] and that line eagerly signified what was being done and stirred up the beholder to inquire further. Nor did he delay: “Where,” he says, “are you going?” “To measure,” he says, “Jerusalem, and to see how great its breadth is and how great its length.”

He briefly declared that the building was not uncertain, nor ought it to be delayed. But did that man, whose task it is to hold the line in his hand, not yet know how long Jerusalem was, or how broad it ought to be? If the question concerns that earthly or handmade city, it was no great matter for that man to know or see; nor did any of the prophets judge it worthy to commit to writing and transmit to our knowledge how great its breadth or length was. But concerning the heavenly city, of which that city was a kind of pattern, there is no doubt that the measurer of its [Col. 0712B] length and breadth is the man in whose hand is the line: he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, has equal authority over every distribution of gifts. He sees such dimensions in such a way as to make them seen, and does not permit anyone to be unaware how great its length should be—namely, faith even unto death—or how great its breadth—namely, love even unto death. For he says: “Be faithful unto death” (Revelation 2). And: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). Such, indeed, is the length and such the breadth to be possessed in this age, where a person may die for faith and lay down life for love.

But in that age which, once reached, will have neither death nor mourning nor crying nor pain any more (Revelation 21), what will length and breadth be but the recompense of this length and breadth? To see this was for him truly to display and promise perfection. In response to the man’s statement, “Behold,” he says, “the angel who was speaking in me went out,” perhaps to inspect those dimensions. But the prophet had to be taught not to take in a merely human sense what he had heard concerning breadth and length. Therefore, he says, another angel went out to meet him and said to him: “Run and speak to this youth, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall.”

Why, do you think, does the angel here call the prophet a youth, except because, as has already been said, he needed instruction? There is a kind of childishness of understanding which [Col. 0712D] was not yet blameworthy in this man, since he had not had much time for hearing or seeing such things. But it is reproved in those who, because of the time, ought to be—and are not—perfect, or teachers; as the Apostle says: “You have become weak, needing milk and not solid food” (Hebrews 5). For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a child. But solid food belongs to the perfect, to those who by practice have their senses trained.

This saying of the Apostle is also made clearer by the present example. Here, with uplifted eyes, he saw a man holding a measuring line, and he heard him say: “To measure Jerusalem and to see how great its breadth is and how great its length.” If in that vision he understood nothing else as yet [Col. 0713A] than the dimensions of that earthly city, he was certainly a youth: he had a childish understanding. Meanwhile, the vision which he saw, because he rejoiced only in an earthly building, was not solid food but a kind of nourishment of milk. He was therefore rightly called a youth; but by the present instruction of the heavenly spirits he was soon to advance into a man, as they said: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst; and I myself, says the Lord, shall be a wall of fire round about her, and I shall be glory in her midst.”

The meaning is this: Jerusalem, which is built through us and measured by this man through himself, is not enclosed by a handmade wall, but all her construction is spiritual. The Lord himself is her wall, a wall of fire round about, whereby [Col. 0713B] the firmness of that city is sufficiently indicated. For it is written: “As wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Psalm 67). Who there will fear an enemy? Who will be anxious about an adversary? Thus the present passage splendidly illuminates for one who has outgrown a child’s understanding what was said in the Psalm concerning this same Jerusalem: “Mountains are round about her, and the Lord is round about his people” (Psalm 124).

Further, when he had said, “I, the Lord, am a wall of fire round about,” he added, “and I shall be glory in her midst.” This likewise is far above a child’s understanding: namely, that he will be in the midst not as a local and earthly man among local and earthly men, but as God, the Creator of spirits, among angels and men in the temples [Col. 0713C] of their hearts, in the houses which are the bodies themselves of the saints and the inner recesses of their souls. What this is or will be, “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isaiah 64).

Certain children who never advance—children a hundred years old—think that what is said here, “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst,” will come to pass carnally: that Jerusalem will have such happiness that, because of the multitude of all men and cattle, she cannot have a wall, but the Lord’s protection will be her wall and she will enjoy the glory of him dwelling in her midst. To such a youth, a hundred-year-old youth who dies accursed, that is, the Jewish people, no angel runs or is sent to speak (Isaiah 65); for it does not wish to hear or understand according to the understanding of elders.

But we, with this youth who advances into manhood by hearing and understanding, understand the saying, “because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst, she shall be inhabited without a wall,” as we now plainly see with open eyes. What king or emperor could make a wall so great or so extensive that it enclosed the whole world? Yet unless it enclosed the whole world, it could not surround this Jerusalem, namely the Church, because it is spread throughout the whole world. In her, “men” are those who have spiritual understanding, while “cattle” are those who understand simply; and they assist those who, though spiritual, [Col. 0714A] sow their spiritual things among them and reap their carnal things (Romans 9). In the present age this Jerusalem, the pilgrim portion of the heavenly Jerusalem, is therefore inhabited without a wall, because it is not contained in one place or one nation, but, as has already been said, is spread through the world. In that age, however, to which she is transferred daily from here, much more is there neither a wall round about her, nor ought there to be, nor can there be, except the Lord, who will also be glory in her midst.

It follows: “Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north,” says the Lord, “for I have scattered you into the four winds of heaven,” says the Lord. “Ho, Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts: After glory he sent me to the nations that plundered you. For whoever touches you touches [Col. 0714B] the pupil of my eye. For behold, I lift up my hand over them, and they shall become spoil for those who were enslaved to them; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me.”

How aptly, how wisely, while the Holy Spirit speaks to elders and delights the mature mind of the hearer, he meanwhile indulges a child—the sort of people the entire population then returning from Babylonian captivity was. He wished to raise above that people’s understanding this man whom the angel called a youth, saying: “Run and speak to this youth” (Isaiah 65). But he by no means indulges the hundred-year-old youth of whom we have already spoken; rather, he tells him that he will die.

How, or to what end, does he indulge that youth—that is, the simple people? Clearly, by speaking in such a way that such a youth may feel himself summoned by divine invitation from Babylon to rebuild the city or temple, the rebuilding of which, as has already been said, was a preparation for human salvation. Whoever knew how to hope for nothing beyond restoration of the place and people, and who was delighted even by this small thing, was a youth. But whoever desired the restoration of that place not for the place itself but for him who was to come from it, namely Christ, was a man—indeed, an elder.

Doubling the vocative, he says: “Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north”; and likewise a third time: “Ho, Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.” “Flee from the land of the north” means the same as “Flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.” For the regions of the world, which the Greeks call *climata* (“climates” or zones), are understood in relation to the position of Jerusalem [Col. 0714D] and the temple; and Babylon, where God’s people were captive, lies to the north.

Therefore, “Ho, ho, flee; Ho, Zion, flee,” is understood with a childish, yet not useless, understanding: “See how the Lord repents of the evil he did to us; how he grieves over the famous city and noble temple, in the city alone of which he was glorified and in the sole temple of which his name was invoked.” Nor is this surprising: for his name was great there, and great honour was paid to it. Cyrus did not compel us to return there, but merely granted permission to return: “Who among you,” he says, “of all the people of the Lord God of heaven? May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judaea, and build the house of the Lord his God of Israel” (1 Esdras 1). How earnestly he invites us to be willing to depart promptly from this land, the unclean land of Babylon, when he says: “Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north; Ho, Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.” And how greatly he repents of what we have suffered: for whoever thereafter touches us touches the pupil of his eye, and those to whom we were enslaved will become spoil for us—that is, we shall lead captive those who led us captive.

This understanding, as has been said, is childish but useful, because, however it happened, it happened that the place and people from which Christ, the salvation of the world, had to be born were restored. The understanding in Christ’s disciples, however, is so much more useful as solid food is better than milk. First, the person speaking here must itself be recognized. From what will it be recognized? Certainly from his saying: [Col. 0715B] “The Lord of hosts sent me after glory to the nations which plundered you,” and again, “You shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me”; and, “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in your midst, says the Lord.”

Who is this Lord of hosts whom the Lord of hosts sent after glory? Who, I say, but the Lord, Son of the Lord Father? For God the Father and Lord sent into this world, after glory, the Son—whom we rightly believe and faithfully confess to be Lord and God. After what glory? Surely after the glory of divinity, lofty and infinite: after he was in the form of God, which is nothing other than being in the glory of God. Hence the Apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Col. 0715C] (Philippians 2), and so forth.

Therefore let this prophetic saying be pleasing and gracious to us, for it is a faithful testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ—not merely one testimony, but among many one most beautiful and most clear. Therefore, from this point let the mind direct itself to that point at which, after the horns of the nations had been broken, as already said, God, victorious in his purpose, fulfilled his promise and the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us this (Luke 1), by sending into this world the Son of his love because of the exceeding love with which God loved the world (Ephesians 2).

This is the most beautiful order of the prophecy: that after his return to Jerusalem in mercies, by which his house was built [Col. 0715D] in it, and after the breaking of the four kingdoms signified by the four horns—kingdoms which, succeeding one another, the dragon, the devil, used in persecuting that people in an effort to turn aside the fulfillment of the promise—we should consider that he who had been promised came; and that we should hear these words, “Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north,” and the rest, as the utterances of his present coming.

For what else is “Flee from the land of the north,” or “Flee, Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon,” than the beginning of his Gospel preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of God has drawn near” (Matthew 4)? Finally, to be unbelieving and of an unrepentant heart is to remain in the land of the north—the cold wind, by which the devil is customarily represented in Scripture. Conversely, to flee from the land of the north is to believe [Col. 0716A] and repent in hope of reaching the kingdom of God. Likewise, to dwell with the daughter of Babylon is to serve vices and desires; conversely, to flee Babylonian habitation is to cease from those same vices and desires.

The two reasons given here—“For I have scattered you into the four winds of heaven,” and “After glory he sent me to the nations that plundered you”—form one argument and contain the meaning of the one reason which the Evangelist wrote: that Jesus was to die “to gather into one the children of God who had been scattered” (John 2). This argument is divided in this passage in such a way that it aims, for everyone having ears to hear, to instill fear in its first part and then to suggest love. For when, after saying, “Flee from the land of the north,” that is, “Do not be of an unrepentant heart,” he adds, “For I have scattered you into the four winds of heaven,” the attentive hearer is shaken by fitting fear, if indeed he understands how or for what reason that scattering occurred, by which the elect are born scattered and intermingled with the wicked and reprobate in this world—those who ought to have existed together and been born only in paradise.

Likewise, after saying, “Ho, Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon,” he adds: “For after glory he sent me to the nations.” A great occasion for contemplating God’s love is offered to one who considers how truly it has been said: “How good God is to Israel.” For he so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John 3). And how good is that same only-begotten one who, though he was in the form of God [Col. 0716C] (Philippians 2), took the form of a servant for our sake and, after the glory of brightness which he had with God before the world was made, was filled with reproaches, giving his cheek to one who struck him (Lamentations 3), and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Philippians 2).

The present passage of the Scripture of truth testifies that both he who sent and he who was sent are the Lord of hosts. For lest someone perhaps should fail to hear, it was not enough for it once to say of him who was sent after glory that he is Lord: it repeated it a third time, saying “says the Lord,” with only a few words intervening; and it twice asserted that he who sent is the Lord of hosts. For this Lord who was sent has already said once: “You shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me”; and after a few words he will again say to the daughter of Zion: “And you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you.”

Meanwhile see how wisely, with what remarkable art of wisdom, he lays hold of the aforementioned youth—that is, the people of that time, who did not know how to hope for such a thing and could not feed upon the solid food of so great a promise, and therefore needed to be nourished with the milk of the letter. Thus, after he said, “After glory he sent me to the nations,” he added, “which plundered you,” and continued: “For whoever touches you touches the pupil of his eye—or of my eye; for behold, I lift up my hand over them, and they shall become spoil for those who were enslaved to them.” For the letter gives this sense: that such a reversal of affairs should occur that those returning from Babylonian captivity, multiplied and strengthened, with the Lord present among them, [Col. 0717A] would go against the Babylonians and the other nations by whom they had been plundered, plunder them in turn, and make prey of those whom they themselves had served, by the same kind or manner of plunder or slavery.

The error of the youth, or childish understanding, is good for us and will profit all ages: for, made more eager by such hope, they returned and built, and they received and preserved the Scripture—which indeed serves for us Gentiles, though it appears to act against us and promise things contrary to us—with greater favour, as Scripture truly possessing divine authority.

But God did as he had intended: he lifted his hand over the nations that plundered the Jews of the adornment of city and temple, and to whom the Jews served and still serve. Chief among these nations were the Romans; and behold, they themselves are spoil for the Jews, namely the apostles, who are indeed Jews. How are the nations, or Romans, spoil for the apostles? Certainly as little fish are spoil for fishermen. For when he called certain of them, he said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mark 4). These are they, and all like them, whom whoever touches touches the pupil of my eye—not so that I become blind, but so that those who touched them may be blind, and I may hide my face from them, just as someone avoids the blow of a plotting adversary by hiding and turning away the pupil of his eye.

It follows: “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion, for behold, I come and shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and they shall be a people to me; and I shall dwell [Col. 0717C] in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you. And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the sanctified land, and shall again choose Jerusalem. Let all flesh be silent before the Lord, for he has risen from his holy dwelling-place.”

As we have already touched upon, this person of the Lord of hosts who speaks here twice says, “The Lord of hosts sent me.” For, being about to say, “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion,” he had ended the foregoing passage thus: “And you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me”; and behold, after first saying, “And I shall dwell in your midst,” he adds once more: “And you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you.” This is beautiful and worthy of consideration: the Father, truly the Lord of hosts, unquestionably sent the Son, who is truly the Lord of hosts; and the Holy Spirit, truly the Lord of hosts, sent him. The two persons, Father and Holy Spirit, sent the one person of the Son. Thus in Isaiah he himself says: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48).

Certainly, when the Blessed Virgin Mary conceived, upon the angel’s announcement, the Son who is Lord of hosts, the Father, Lord of hosts, sent him, and the Holy Spirit, Lord of hosts, sent him into the womb of the same virgin. The Father did so, as he himself says: “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Psalm 44). The Holy Spirit did so, as the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1); and to Joseph: “For that which has been conceived in her is conceived of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1).

On this account, “Praise [Col. 0718A] and rejoice, daughter Zion,” says the Lord himself who was sent, God by generation from God the Father and man by the operation of the Holy Spirit, “for behold, I come and shall dwell in your midst.” What is “in your midst” except in communion with your nature, possessing the substance of true flesh? For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Therefore, “in your midst” means that, except for sin, he assumed everything belonging to your condition: first dwelling for nine months in the lodging of a woman’s womb; then wrapped in swaddling cloths in a cradle—indeed, in a manger; circumcised and brought to the temple with the legal offering; and for thirty years enduring all things belonging to human frailty. Except for sin, as has already been said, in every way he was found to be a man, and he also underwent the experience of death.

Such a coming and such dwelling together of the Lord is truly great matter for praise and joy. Thus he prefaced it: “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion.” Every soul which, by contemplating so great a good in faith, deserves to be called and to be Zion—John’s soul, truly a daughter of Zion—first rejoiced after that mother of joy, in whose midst, in whose womb, this Lord already dwelt. Therefore she praised in joy and rejoiced in praise, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit exults in God my Savior” (Luke 1). After her, John’s soul first praised and rejoiced. “For behold,” Elizabeth says, “as soon as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy” (John 3). When the time for speaking came, he expressed the cause of that joy with beautiful praise in these words: [Col. 0718C] “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of his voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled” (2 Corinthians 6).

What the Lord then says—“And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day and shall be a people to me”—is plain and clear. For from the time this day dawned, or the time arrived of which the Lord says in Isaiah, “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you,” while the Apostle responds, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6), from that time many nations are joined to the Lord and are his people. Before this day, however, “God was known only in Judaea; his name was great in Israel” (Psalm 25). And other nations are rightly joined to the Lord and become his people, even though Jews who claim that they alone are daughter Zion—and do not belong to daughter Zion—may envy and take offense. For what? Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Yes, of Gentiles also (John 3).

“And I shall dwell,” he says, “in your midst”: namely, at the second advent, not as at the first advent, when I come, as I have said, to dwell in your midst. At the first advent [Col. 0718D] I am passible, mortal, and to be judged; at the second I shall dwell in your midst as the impassible and immortal God, Lord of judgment. The fruit of the first dwelling in your midst is this: that many nations may be joined to the Lord. The effect of the subsequent dwelling will be what John says: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see [Col. 0719A] him as he is” (1 John 3). That seeing will be perfect knowing, concerning which he says here: “And you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you.”

What then is meant by the fact that, after saying, “Many nations shall be joined to the Lord and shall become a people to me,” he adds: “And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the sanctified land, and shall again choose Jerusalem”? Certainly, because he had to do what other prophets are commanded to do: namely, to close up the word (Daniel 12), to bind up the testimony. For this was expedient; men could not have borne it if God had plainly told them what he intended. See how he veils the saying, “Many nations shall be joined to the Lord,” by saying, “And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion.” Since *Judah* is interpreted “confession,” and all nations confessing Christ are signified by this name, the people of Judah hearing these things could suppose that, however many nations might be joined to the Lord, they themselves alone ought nevertheless to be the Lord’s portion. That opinion neither harmed nor harms God’s purpose; indeed, it benefits it, because while they were well disposed, Scripture was preserved for us.

The meaning is this: the Lord shall possess as his portion Judah—that is, those foreordained to life, the saints called according to his purpose, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Hebrews 12). All these are Judah: they believe and confess alike, and are the Lord’s portion. The Lord shall possess them in the sanctified land, in the land of the living, where everything that exists is wholly holy. He shall possess them so that none of their number is absent; and because those who ascend there from this earthly Jerusalem are not sufficient, he will still choose also from other nations, taking those who are to be Jerusalem.

Are not weak hands rightly strengthened and feeble knees made firm by these sayings? Are they not right to say to the faint-hearted: “Be strong, and do not fear” (Isaiah 35)? It follows, therefore: “Let all flesh be silent before the Lord, for he has risen from his holy dwelling-place.” It is as though he said: Let the four horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem be silent; let all who presumed to reign without the Lord’s knowledge and without the Lord’s approval be silent. For the Assyrians with the Babylonians, the Persians with the Medes, the Macedonians or Greeks, and the terrible Romans—iron-like, as they seemed—are flesh. “Let them be silent,” he says, “before the Lord, for he has risen from his holy dwelling-place,” because his thrones have been set in place, judgment has sat, and it has been decreed that the horned beasts be slain (Daniel 7), their authority removed, and authority, honour, and kingdom given to the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, so that the saints of God Most High, whom the reigning beasts mocked as aliens and captives, may receive the kingdom and possess it for ever and ever.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0719]

[Col. 0719C] “We have,” says the Apostle Peter, “the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day should dawn and the day-star arise in your hearts” (2 Peter 1). It is sweet to hear, and sweeter to experience, that the prophetic word is a burning and shining lamp, which the Holy Spirit prepared for his Christ. By it he may be seen in this night “through a mirror, in an enigma,” until that day dawns in which he is to be seen face to face in eternal vision (1 Corinthians 13).

Let this be our purpose: that in the light of this lamp we may desire to exult, not for an hour but in the eternal glory of that same Christ. The beginning of this exultation is that, while meditating upon prophetic testimonies, we may know in part and ourselves prophesy in part (ibid.), [Col. 0719D] until that which is perfect comes and that which is in part is done away. With this singleness of eye, having progressed thus far, let us now pursue the luminous order of this prophecy, a lamp truly shining. In its light every soul that loves Christ’s brightness with unfeigned love ought to exult in heart and mouth; and let this be our hope, which wisdom promises: “A man shall be satisfied with good from the fruit of his mouth” (Proverbs 13).

A considerable portion of the great and beautiful vision has been traversed: namely, from the saying, “I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse,” to the saying, “Let all flesh be silent before the Lord, for he has risen from his holy dwelling-place.” In this portion we must consider that the kingdoms of the world which fought against God were frustrated, and that, after they had been passed over, the kingdom of God came with Christ’s birth. What follows is:

## CHAPTER III
And he showed me Jesus the high priest, standing before the angel of the Lord; and Satan stood at his right hand, to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you. Is not this a brand snatched from the fire?” And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the angel. And he answered and said to those standing before him, saying: “Remove the filthy garments from him.” And he said to him: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you and clothed you with change of garments.” And he said: “Put a clean turban upon his head.” And they put a clean turban upon his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the Lord stood by, and the angel of the Lord solemnly charged Jesus, saying: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you also shall judge my house and guard my courts; and I will give you walkers among these who now stand here. Hear, Jesus, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men of portent. For behold, I am bringing my servant, the Rising One. For behold, the stone which I have set before Jesus: upon one stone are seven eyes. Behold, I will engrave its engraving, says the Lord of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day. On that day, says the Lord of hosts, each man shall call his friend beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.”

In the preceding words, “After glory he sent me to the nations,” and, “Behold, I come and will dwell in your midst,” and so forth, the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation is signified. In the present passage the sacrament of his temptations and passion shines forth; in what follows, however, comes the triumphant joy of his resurrection, where immediately after this the prophet will say: “I saw, and behold, a wholly golden lampstand” (Zech. IV), and so forth.

“And he showed me Jesus the high priest.” The Hebrews, says blessed Jerome, wish Jesus the high priest to be understood as the son of Josedek, who governed the people with Zerubbabel, and whose adversary stood at his right hand, not at his left; because the accusation was true, since he, together with the others, had taken a foreign wife—a matter written of most fully in Ezra and Malachi, who follows this prophet. But our people, he says, reason thus: that he is the great priest (I Ezra X; Mal. II) to whom it is said, “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX); and since he cannot be seen in himself, he is shown by the Lord to the prophet, standing before the angel of the Lord, whom they wish to be the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX). This is not because one is one person and the other another, so that we receive two persons in the Son; rather, because one and the same is shown as though defiled as a man and is said to appear as the angel, the mediator of God and men.

According to this interpretation, he says, this seems difficult: that the angel says to Jesus that, if he walks in the ways of the Lord and keeps his commandments, he too shall judge his house and guard his courts, and that the Lord will give him walkers from among those standing before him.

For our part, we do not without reason wonder if there was ever a scrupulous dispute among teachers concerning a matter of this kind, since it is a vision of the night; for it began thus: “I saw by night” (Zech. I), and so forth. For in visions, not the very person or substance of anyone, but the likeness or image of a person or substance, whether of a human being or of any other thing, ordinarily appears—except spiritual substances such as angels. Thus, just as in this same vision the four horns, and in Daniel’s vision the four beasts, were not the four kingdoms themselves but certain images of the four kingdoms (Dan. VII), so here Jesus was neither the substance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his humanity did not yet exist, nor that Jesus son of Josedek, high priest of that time, who, being a man and possessing a body, could not have appeared in a vision of the night. What was seen was an image of a man, merely a likeness sufficient for the prophetic office, to signify those things concerning our Lord Jesus Christ which already then time or reason required to be signified.

If anyone asks why it pleased God to signify him in that likeness rather than another, he should know that the Holy Spirit so honored almost all the holy and upright men of ancient times who contributed something by their own labor to the coming kingdom of God, with the mysteries of that same kingdom, that each of them set forth some likeness, of whatever sort, of the King of the kingdom of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence in those holy men so many deeds and sayings have been sought out and discovered by holy teachers as types of the same Lord. Among the principal examples were Isaac, Joseph, David, and Solomon, so long as he remained watchful in wisdom.

These two, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jesus son of Josedek, greatly benefited, or contributed to, the whole world in this respect: for at the return from Babylon they were leaders, and they founded and completed the temple, laboring for the recovery of the place or people from which salvation would come, since “salvation is from the Jews” (John IV). Therefore the Holy Spirit honored them, so that in their names or figures the mysteries of the coming Christ might be signified, because their labor and work served his advent or kingdom.

With these matters set forth, let us now follow in order the words and actions of the present vision.

“And you showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him.” What this signified is indicated in the same vision by these words: “Hear, Jesus, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men of portent. For behold, I am bringing my servant, the Rising One,” and so forth. Thus that Jesus, whose likeness or image, as it were, he saw standing before the angel of the Lord in the night, was a portent of the servant of God—of that servant, I say, who is called the Rising One; who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself for our sake, taking the form of a servant. Hence he is rightly called the servant of the Lord, because he served for our sake and was obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

In that form of a servant, the high priest was to stand before the angel of the Lord: “You made him a little lower than the angels,” he says (Ps. VIII). This expression, “standing before the angel of the Lord,” fittingly indicates that lowliness. Still more fittingly and reverently does the Gospel indicate it: when, having entered into agony, he prayed at greater length and sweated a bloody sweat, an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him (Luke XXII)—the greater strengthening the lesser, as one who would never die strengthening one about to die at once.

That Satan stood in that vision at Jesus’ right hand to oppose him is what this servant said of himself: “For the ruler of this world comes” (John XIV)—understand: seeking something of his own in me. He stood to oppose him, yet it was not said that he did oppose him or could oppose him; for it was to be so that the ruler of the world would indeed come to him, but, he says, “he has nothing in me” (ibid.). He stood not at the left but at the right, because in this one there was to be nothing left-handed, but everything right-handed: that is, nothing evil, but everything good. Therefore he stood at the right, because there was nothing on the left, intending, namely, to make left-handed what was right-handed: to pervert the good things he said and did, as the Gospel Scripture of his truth relates (Matt. XII, XXVII). For he was accused as an evildoer when he was a benefactor.

Thus formerly the same Satan stood at Job’s right hand to pervert his good deeds, when he said: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job I), and so forth.

“And the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you.’” Why did he not say, “Go away, Satan,” or, “Cease opposing, Satan”? Clearly because, in opposing thus, Satan would be of great benefit: not only in order that there might be for us an example of patience, to which we are instructed by the apostle James, who says, “You have heard of Job’s patience, and have seen the Lord’s end” (Jas. V), but also that the Savior’s patience and the Redeemer’s passion might redeem the world.

Therefore, the Lord says, “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan”: that is, let him indeed stand by, but not according to the full extent of your will. Certainly it was also a rebuke when he said concerning blessed Job: “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless, spare his life” (Job II). Similarly, concerning this one, let it be said by all power: Let the flesh be in the hand of the adversaries whom you inflame; nevertheless, do not hold his soul in hell, and let his flesh in the tomb not see corruption. The Lord said this: “May the Lord rebuke,” and “may the Lord rebuke.” Thus from one person two persons of the Lord are summoned to rebuke, because the Trinity—one God—wrought the victory of the Lord’s passion, which is a great rebuke of the devil. For the Father gave that cup to the Son, and the Son, the Apostle says, offered himself through the Holy Spirit (Heb. IX).

“Is not this a brand snatched from the fire? And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.” In accordance with the likeness in that vision, the Lord Jesus was a brand snatched from the fire: either because in this world, a great furnace and vast workshop of sin, he escaped sin—he did not commit sin, nor did he contract it by conception—or because, when he descended into hell, it was impossible for him to be held by it. He was indeed clothed in filthy garments, yet not his own but those of others. For “the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all”; and Isaiah, taking upon himself, I say, the estimation of the ungodly, says: “We accounted him as a leper, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. LIII).

That Jesus, the man of that period, was indeed defiled by his own sins, since he had taken a foreign wife, or, as Malachi says, had taken “the daughter of a foreign god” (Mal. II). But Christ Jesus, who was signified in that night by the image of that Jesus, was clothed in filthy garments not by his own sins but by those of others.

“And he stood before the angel, who answered and said to those standing before him: ‘Remove the filthy garments from him.’” The angel of the Lord said this by the authority or command of the Lord speaking within him, although he did not insert here what the same angel of the Lord later inserted: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you [plural] walk in my ways,” and so forth. Who, then, were those who stood before the angel’s face—indeed, before the face of the Lord speaking in the angel or through the angel? They were not persons of any ordinary kind; they are truly great, whose office it is to remove filthy garments, to remove iniquities and sins.

Later in this vision he says: “Two olive trees [stand] above the lampstand, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left; and I said, ‘What are these two olive trees?’” (Zech. IV). And again: “What are the two olive branches which are beside the two golden beaks?” (ibid.). When questioned a second time, the angel says: “These are the two sons of oil, who stand before the Lord of the whole earth” (ibid.). We understand these same two sons of oil to be standing here before the angel who speaks or acts in the person of the Lord. Who they are will more fittingly be discussed, to the best of our ability, in that passage. For the present I will say only this: the filthy garments, which were our iniquities, were taken away from the Lord Jesus in his passion through the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of sins and the distributor of diverse graces.

Thus he immediately said to him: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you and clothed you with change of garments.” When he says “your iniquity,” we should attend at once to what we shall later explain as the meaning of these words, when he says: “Behold, I will bring my servant, the Rising One,” and so forth. He concludes thus: “And I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.” Therefore, “I have taken away your iniquity from you”: that is, the iniquity of your land, the iniquity of your Church, the sins of all who believe in you. “And I clothed you,” that is, those who are yours, “with change of garments,” because, cleansed from iniquity for you, they shall be adorned with diverse gifts of grace; and, greatly to God’s glory, “where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V).

“And he said: ‘Put a clean turban upon his head’; and they put a clean turban upon his head and clothed him with garments.” This is what we now see: as the Apostle says, the Lord Jesus Christ, because of the suffering of death, “crowned with glory and honor” (Heb. II). The turban—that is, the high priest’s cap or mitre, upon which a plate was placed on the priest’s forehead bearing the Tetragrammaton, the ineffable name of the Lord—signifies the crown of glory and honor upon the head of our Lord Jesus Christ. He became obedient unto death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name above every name (Phil. II).

The garments, of which it says, “and they clothed him with garments,” are those gifts already mentioned, which are given to his Church, which is his body. Hence, just as we read in another translation, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV), so we no less truly sing, “You received gifts in men” (Ps. LXVII), because, by reason of the unity of person between head and body—between himself and the Church—he himself received in us whatever gifts we receive, since, being truly God, he himself gives them.

What has thus far been shown in the vision, and why it was shown, the angel himself will shortly explain in the words which follow, addressed beforehand to that Jesus: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you also shall judge my house and guard my courts; and I will give you walkers among these who now stand here.”

We rightly understand these words to have been spoken to that man Jesus without any hidden significance or mystery. This is especially clear because, after first saying, “If you walk in my ways,” he defines the person or cause of that man by adding, “You also shall judge my house and guard my courts.” For when he says “you also,” he sufficiently indicates that the preceding matters, and those which follow, are spoken or enacted concerning another, for the sake of another.

It is rightly promised to such a man, in a conditional mode of speech—“If you walk in my ways”—that he shall judge the house of the Lord [something appears to be missing here], since, as has already been said, he had taken a foreign woman contrary to the commandment of the law of the Lord. He was a priest (I Ezra X), whose lips ought to guard knowledge, from whose mouth they seek the law (Mal. II), because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. And when he says, “You also shall judge my house,” we must understand: otherwise and more happily, with a better end than Eli, who fell from his seat and in falling lost the dignity of judicial honor (I Sam. IV).

His temporal rule and transitory guardianship are designated by the words, “And I will give you walkers among these who now stand here.” But the one of whom, or for whose sake, the preceding words have been spoken and the following words will be spoken, possesses eternal rule and everlasting guardianship: rule and guardianship over things past, present, and future. This he indicates by adding: “Hear, Jesus, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men of portent. For behold, I will bring my servant, the Rising One.”

It is as though he said: When you receive the account of his vision from the prophet who narrates it, Jesus, high priest—you and your friends dwelling before you, whose images he sees in the night and who hear the words spoken concerning you—hear and know that they are men of portent. That is, the vision which he sees concerning you and your friends is a portent of things to come, things which will beyond doubt be great. “For behold, I will bring my servant, the Rising One,” and in this vision, where you are shown, you and your friends signify his coming.

Just as in this vision your friends are seen dwelling before you, so before that Rising One, my servant, whom I shall bring, many who have become friends from enemies shall dwell. To them he himself will say at the very moment when Satan stood at his right hand, as is foreshadowed here: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends; and no one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends” (John XV).

He is called the Rising One from this source because he is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I); and he is called servant because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II).

As he said these things, a stone was also seen before Jesus. “Upon one stone are seven eyes. Behold, I will make its engraving, says the Lord of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.” That the stone is the Lord Jesus Christ—the chief cornerstone, chosen and laid in the foundation—and that the seven eyes upon this one stone are the seven Spirits of God, who rested upon him, is known, or ought to be known, to almost everyone. For God did not give the Spirit to him by measure, and “in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Col. II). This stone was rejected by men, but chosen and honored by God (Mark XII).

How was he rejected by men? The chosen one was suspended outside the gate upon wood (Acts V), so that he might become the curse of the law; for the law says, “Cursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Gal. III). This was the rejection by the builders. “But behold,” he says, “I will engrave its engraving and remove the iniquity of that land in one day.” The sense is: I shall cause this stone to be wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier’s spear, and in his passion I shall remove the iniquity of the land in one day, of which it is written: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII).

## CHAPTER IV

“On that day each man shall call his friend beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.” For from the time of the Lord’s passion the Gospel began to be proclaimed, which is to be called beneath the vine; and the law began to be understood spiritually, which is to be called beneath the fig tree, when the Holy Spirit reveals that the law and the prophets bear witness to Christ’s Gospel.

“And the angel who spoke in me returned and awakened me, like a man awakened from his sleep. And he said to me: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘I saw, and behold, a wholly golden lampstand, and its lamp upon its head, and seven lamps upon it, and seven pouring-vessels for the lamps which were upon its head, and two olive trees above it, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left.’ And I answered and said to the angel who spoke in me: ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel who spoke in me answered and said to me: ‘Do you not know what these are?’ And I said: ‘No, my lord.’ And he answered and said to me: ‘This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: Not by an army nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts.’”

Just as in the preceding section we understand the lowliness of his passion, in which he “was made a little lower than the angels” (Heb. II), so in the present section we understand the glory of the resurrection of the same our Lord Jesus Christ. In that glory he was crowned with glory and honor, set over the works of the Father’s hands, and glorified with the glory which he had with God before the world existed (John XVII).

For what is the wholly golden lampstand, with its lamp upon its head, except Christ himself—the glory and light of all angels and human beings—illuminating by the lamp of his divinity, which became known to the world through the power of his resurrection, those who are or were in darkness?

It should therefore be observed and wondered at together that, after Jesus was seen clothed in filthy garments, and after they were removed—“Behold,” says the Lord, “I have taken away your iniquity from you”; and again concerning the same person, “I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day”—the angel is said to have returned and awakened the prophet like a man awakened from sleep (Zech. IV). For so it was to be, and so it happened: after the iniquity of the land of the Lord Jesus, which is his Church, was removed in one day—in the day of his espousal, in the day of the joy of his heart (Song III)—when blood and water came forth from his side opened by the soldier’s spear (John XIX), so that his filthy garments, the filth that was the iniquities of us all (Isa. LIII), as we have already said above, might no longer remain, he himself slept three days in the tomb and on the third day was awakened from his sleep.

Therefore the prophet significantly said, “He awakened me like a man awakened from his sleep,” thereby indicating that in himself was prefigured the awakening of that man, the Lord Jesus, from the sleep of his death. Moreover, the angel’s return, expressed in the words “the angel who spoke in me returned,” signifies that he had withdrawn for a time, as a sign of that withdrawal which that man proclaimed when he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI; Matt. XXVII).

Therefore, “I saw,” he says, “and behold, a wholly golden lampstand”; and we see the Lord Jesus glorified and the world illuminated by the glory of his resurrection. Even before his passion, the head of his beloved—that is, his divinity—was the finest gold; but his body, being capable of suffering and mortal, was not yet gold. Therefore the lampstand was not yet wholly gold, because the body, by reason of its mortal condition, was somewhat obscure and less glorious than it is now.

Its lamp is above its head, and its seven lamps rest upon it: the Holy Spirit is upon him, from the time when he rose again, more manifestly in him. For, because the Spirit is one, he is called one lamp; and because he is sevenfold, because his gifts are seven, he is called seven lamps. The lamps and the oil-pouring vessels—that is, the little vessels in which is the oil poured into the lamps—signify the same thing: the seven gifts of the Spirit, with this sole difference, that the effect differs from its cause. For as the individual [Col. 0727D] vessels feed the individual lamps, so the individual gifts of the Spirit produce particular works, through which those who have received the Holy Spirit become clear in their own measure, so that people may see them and, edified by their good example, glorify God.

What are the two olive trees, the olive trees above the lampstand, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left? Accordingly, the prophet inquired about this and the rest also: “And I answered,” he says, “and said to the angel who spoke within me: ‘What are these, my lord?’” When he had answered and said, “Do you not know what these are?” and the prophet had said, “No, my lord,” then, being prepared to hear, he would doubtless become more attentive to understand. At last he says: “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit,’ says the Lord [Col. 0728A] of hosts.”

By this answer he could indeed—although it was a good answer—he could, I say, understand, since he possessed prophetic grace for understanding, what the lampstand was; what its lamp above its head was; and what were the seven lamps and the seven vessels for the lamps which were above its head. Yet I did not yet understand what the two olive trees were, one on the right of the lamp and one on its left. And what is meant by the answer: “Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit,” says the Lord?

We have already said that the golden lampstand is the Lord Jesus, glorified by the glory of the resurrection because of his suffering of death; and that the seven lamps upon it, with as many vessels, are the holy sevenfold Spirit, given from that time onward—a Spirit who until then, namely for the remission of sins, had not been given (John 7). For whence comes that saying: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid.)?

But what is meant by its being said in this way to Zerubbabel: “Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit”? A brief saying suggests the understanding of a great matter. Its sense is this: before, according to the present vision, the Lord comes to dwell in your midst, O daughter of Zion—he by whose suffering the iniquity of that land is removed in one day, as was signified by the command to take the filthy garments away from Jesus; he who, glorified by the glory of resurrection and ascension, gives the holy sevenfold Spirit, as is signified by the golden lampstand with so many lamps—before that Lord comes, [Col. 0728C] all those who, having zeal for him, went up or are to go up with an army and with strength to stand against adversaries for his house, will have acted rightly and laudably: as the judges of Israel did, as faithful David did, and as the Maccabees will do.

But when that same Lord has come and has been glorified, when he has said to all what he was to say to one: “Put your sword back into its place” (Matt. 26), then “not by an army, nor by strength” means: you will no longer fight for me; for it will not be necessary, says the Lord. Before I came, action by army and strength was like defending a tree lest it be cut down, a tree from which the fruit of eternal life was hoped. For the devil was working through ungodly people in order that that nation might cease to exist, from which it had been promised to the fathers that I was to receive [something; object uncertain]. I was born; and therefore it is now no longer by army or strength, but by my Spirit, because the struggle is now necessary not against human beings but only against the devil. Since he is a spirit, he must be fought and overcome not by army or strength but by my Spirit.

Therefore under the name Zerubbabel we rightly understand the Lord himself, as has been said more fully concerning him in Haggai; for at that time they employed army and strength in building (Hag. 2). Thus Nehemiah says: “Half of the young men were doing the work, and half were ready for battle, with spears, shields, bows, and breastplates; and the leaders stood behind them throughout all the house of Judah, those building on the wall, carrying burdens, and labouring. With one hand each [Col. 0729A] did the work, and with the other held a sword. For every one of the builders had his sword girded to his loins, and they built; and the trumpet-player was beside me” (2 Esdras 4).

These words concern the city walls. That handmade temple too was not rebuilt without some human strength, since the following royal decree had been issued: “Any person who changes this command, let a beam be taken from his house; let him be raised up and fastened upon it, and let his house be confiscated” (1 Esdras 6). But that one thing was accomplished altogether without army and without strength, by the Spirit of the Lord: the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12). To him it is immediately said: “Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel? Into a plain!”

For the great mountain opposed to the mountain of the Lord—the impassable mountain, the shipwrecking mountain—is the devil, who ruled in this world, concerning whom the Lord himself says: “For the ruler of this world is coming” (John 14), namely, to oppose me, as was signified above where Satan stood at Jesus’ right hand to oppose him. This is what is now said: “Who are you before Zerubbabel?” By saying “Who are you?” he is utterly disregarded, because he is wholly reprobate. The words that sometimes follow, “into a plain,” may be understood as though “to cast down and bring low from your pride” were supplied; except that he never descended, nor will descend, into a plain in that manner.

Rather, he is rebuked because he stood as a great mountain against the plain—that is, against the humility of our Lord, whom, as already said, we understand through Zerubbabel—and did so in vain. For in this plain, that is, in this [Col. 0729C] meek and humble heart, is the Holy Spirit, whom the evil spirit cannot resist.

It follows: “And he will bring forth the chief stone and make grace equal to its grace.” Who but my Spirit, of whom I said: “I, the Lord, not by army nor by strength, but by my Spirit”? Who, I say, but my Spirit will bring forth the chief stone—that is, Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, indeed the corner-stone and honoured stone—and make grace equal to his grace? He will bring him forth, that is, cause him to grow, so that, according to the prophetic dream which Daniel interpreted to the king, he may become a great mountain and fill the whole world (Dan. 2).

He will also make grace equal to his grace, so that he may not be alone but may be “the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8). For this is the grace which the Lord Jesus received according to his humanity: that he is called, and is, the Son of God. For what does our nature have, even in the Only-begotten One, that it did not receive? (1 Cor. 6). Therefore, he says, the Holy Spirit will make grace equal to his grace—that is, he will make many brothers and co-heirs of his. Hence comes the saying: “See what manner of grace God has given us, that we should be called and should be children of God” (1 John 3).

Yet, although in this respect the grace which God has given us has been made equal to his grace, we nevertheless are not, nor shall we be, equal in every way; for he alone is Son by nature, while all of us are called and are sons of God by adoption. The difference is indeed great; but what does it matter, since we are now children and co-heirs of the only and only-begotten Son?

“And the word [Col. 0730A] of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this house, and the hands of Zerubbabel will complete it; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. For who has despised small days? They shall rejoice and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel—these seven, the eyes of the Lord, which range throughout all the earth.’”

The angel had not yet answered the questioner concerning the entire furnishing of the lampstand; indeed, afterward he questioned again, as follows after this: “What are these two olive trees at the right of the lampstand and at its left?” And again, a second time: “What are the two olive branches which are beside the two golden beaks?” Therefore this passage inserted here—“And the word of the Lord came”—also pertains to the meaning of the same lampstand, especially because they shall see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel; and immediately he adds: “These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which [Col. 0730B] range throughout all the earth.”

Accordingly, both these words and the preceding statement, “He will bring forth the chief stone and make grace equal to his grace,” prevent and rebuke us from taking the intervening words—“The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this house, and his hands will complete it”—only in the sense that comforts the children of that time, namely: “You began building this handmade house in fear and amid delay because adversaries hindered you; but you will shortly see it completed, so that from the very speed of the work you may know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you.”

You shall know this, I say, from the words: “For who has despised small days?” That is: to whom would it not seem wonderful that so great a work should at some time be accomplished within a few or small days? Now the few days are from the second year of King Darius, from the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of that same year—on which day, namely, I speak to you in the word of the Lord—until the third day of the month Adar in that year, namely, the sixth year of Darius. Certainly these are few days for so great a work: only four years are counted; and that the work was completed in so few days is attested by the book of Ezra. For after saying, “The elders of the Jews built and prospered according to the prophecy of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo,” it immediately adds: “And they completed this house of God by the third day of the month Adar, which was the sixth year of King Darius” (1 Esdras 6).

Rightly, therefore, after saying, “And you shall know that the Lord of hosts [Col. 0730D] has sent me to you,” he immediately adds a fitting argument in the form of an emphatic question: “For who has despised small days?” That is, who would not take the great speed of so great a work as testimony or proof that the Lord had sent me to you?

But how does it profit us to know that small number of days, except for a sense higher than the childish one, which ought to delight the mature: namely, that it is evident that no more than the small number of days required by the ordinary nature of a human being’s formation passed in the forming of the unmade temple of the Lord’s body? Thus that house was built in four years, while this proper temple of God was brought forth at birth into this light after nine months had elapsed from conception.
