Nor is this contradicted by what the Jews say against the Lord in the Gospel: “This temple was built in forty-six years” (John 2). For, raging with hatred born of envy because he had said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid.), they counted not only the time during which the temple was built, but also the years of obstacles and delay, during which the work was hindered and deferred from the decree of King Cyrus until the second year of Darius.

And, to embrace more fully what he said—“And you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you; for who has despised small days?”—we must know that no more than precisely nine generations were to pass between Zerubbabel, in whose time this prophet prophesied, and Joseph, husband of Mary. For Zerubbabel begot Abiud; Abiud begot Eliakim; Eliakim begot Azor; Azor begot Zadok; Zadok begot Achim; Achim begot Eliud; Eliud begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Matthan; Matthan begot Jacob (Matt. 1). After him that unmade house of the Lord was founded in the womb and came forth from the womb of the Virgin who had, but did not know, a husband, Joseph.

Who despised, or ought to have despised, days so few as to say, for example, “This will happen only after long ages”? Then those who would be faithful, who awaited the redemption of Israel, knowing by experience that the Lord of hosts had sent me and had truly spoken these things through me, “shall rejoice,” he says, “and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel”—that is, Christ born of the line of Zerubbabel.

But why does he call it a tin stone, rather than a golden stone, or a chrysolite, or, as he said above, a golden lampstand? Here we must know that the glory of Christ’s humanity until his suffering of death was far less than it began to be by the power of the resurrection. Even before the passion, indeed, “the whole fullness of divinity dwelt” in him (Col. 2), and the sevenfold Spirit remained and rested upon him (Isa. 11). Thus he said that he saw the seven eyes of the Lord upon the tin stone, just as he saw seven lamps upon the golden lampstand. But as gold is more precious than tin, and a golden lampstand than a tin stone, so the humanity of that same mediator between God and human beings is more glorious after the resurrection than it was before the passion.

It follows: “And I answered [Col. 0731D] and said to him: ‘What are these two olive trees at the right of the lampstand and at its left?’ And I answered a second time and said to him: ‘What are the two olive ears which are beside the two golden beaks, in which are golden pouring-vessels?’ And he said to me: ‘Do you not know what these are?’ And I said: ‘No, my lord.’ And he said: ‘These are the two sons of oil, who stand before the Ruler of all the earth.’”

A very attentive and earnest inquiry received scarcely a brief answer. Even if it was intelligible to the prophet, as one already possessing the gift of understanding, it nevertheless contained a meaning as closed to people of that time as though no answer at all had been given him. Even today the sense of this answer is doubtful and uncertain to many: some would have the two olive trees signify Moses and Elijah; others, the Law and the Gospel, with the Gospel at the right and the Law at the left.

But what shall we, the least, say if neither explanation suffices? Since the seven lamps upon the golden lampstand signify the Holy Spirit, whom God the Son, glorified with God the Father and crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, gave, and since the two olive trees are of such dignity that they stand beside the two golden beaks of the lampstand—one on the right and one on the left of the lampstand or lamp—we judge that nothing worthier or more fitting can be understood than two gifts of that same Holy Spirit.

For the Spirit was given twice: first, in the remission of sins through the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; second, in distributions [Col. 0732B] of graces through the glory of that same Jesus Christ, glorified in resurrection and ascension and seated at the right hand of Majesty on high. One olive tree is at the left and one at the right of the lampstand, because the first gift, which is for remission of sins, proceeds for believers in him from the humility of the passion; while the second, which is for the distribution of graces, proceeds from the glory of sitting with the Father.

These are the two golden beaks: namely, the humility of the passion, to be adored, and the glory of exaltation, to be preached. Beside them the two olive trees are seen standing, because where he suffered and died, there he granted to those who awaited him remission of sins, to dead and living alike. Hence, immediately after death, when he stood alive again in the midst of his disciples and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). And then, on the fiftieth day, from where he sits at the right hand of the Father, he gave the distributions of graces to the apostles, signified by the divided tongues that appeared to them as fire (Acts 2).

“These,” therefore, he says, “are the two sons of oil”: that is, the two gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the two effects of his almighty grace, who stand before the Ruler of all the earth. For it is always ready and prepared for the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to give remission of sins and, beyond that, whatever distributive grace he may wish, and to distribute it as he wills.

## Chapter V

“And I turned and lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, a flying scroll. And he said: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘Behold, I see a flying scroll. Its length is twenty cubits and its width ten [Col. 0732D] cubits.’ And he said to me: ‘This is the curse which will go forth over the face of the whole earth; for every thief, as it is written, shall be judged, and every one who swears shall likewise be judged by this. I will bring it forth, says the Lord of hosts, and it shall come to the house of the thief and to the house of the one who swears falsely in my name. It shall remain in the midst of his house and consume him, his timbers, and his stones.’”

It was to happen that, after the things signified thus far in this vision—namely, after the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord Jesus, and after the Spirit had been given while the apostles preached—the Jews would not believe; indeed, they would persecute and kill the preachers of the Gospel. Accordingly, all the curses of the Law, which Moses wrote in Deuteronomy, were to come upon them, such as: “Cursed shall you be in the city; cursed in the field; cursed your barn; cursed your remnant; cursed the fruit of your womb” (Deut. 28), and so forth.

Rightly, therefore, and in the order of the events, after the Lord said: “Behold, I come and will dwell in your midst” (Zech. 2); after Jesus, his filthy garments removed, was clothed in changes of raiment; after the golden lampstand stood with seven lamps and two olive trees, or olive branches, which are the two sons of oil—that is, the two gifts of blessing already discussed—the flying scroll is seen. “This,” he says, “is the curse; and I will bring it forth, and it shall come to the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely in my name.” For “he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Ps. 108).

The scroll’s flight signifies the swiftly approaching course of the curse. For, as the Psalmist said, “May his name be blotted out in one generation” (ibid.), so it was to be and so it came to pass: the curse, that is, vengeance upon the Jewish people, was not delayed beyond forty years. The scroll’s length, that is, the curse’s length, is the eternity of damnation; and its width is the temporality of tribulation. For unbelieving Jews have been condemned, in both the present and the future age, for vengeance upon the blood of the Lord Jesus and his prophets.

The width of the curse is indeed ten cubits, because the temporal tribulation by which they “fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations” (Luke 21) is a just vengeance for the Decalogue which they transgressed. But the length of the same curse is twenty cubits—that is, double—because eternal damnation will punish not the body only, as present tribulation does, but both body and soul with the fire of Gehenna.

“This,” therefore, he says, “is the curse which goes forth over the face of the whole earth”—and undoubtedly first over the land of Judea. For “wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, [shall come] upon every soul of a human being, of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (Rom. 2). Indeed, the order of the present prophecy requires us to understand “the face of the whole earth” here as the whole land of Judea which received the Law: not Jerusalem alone, but every city of Judea, because the curse flew over that entire land and was poured out upon that entire nation.

Hence it further says: “For every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged; and every one who swears shall likewise be judged by this.” How is it written there, namely in the scroll of the curse? After the words, “Cursed shall you be in the city,” there follows: “Cursed shall you be when you come in, and cursed when you go out” (Deut. 28). Whoever wishes to read or count them will readily find how many and how dreadful are the sentences of cursing which are uttered by name in an unbroken succession.

For there are thirty such sentences, most of them drawn from imprecatory pronouncement. The first is: “The Lord will send upon you famine and hunger” (ibid.); the thirtieth: “He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail” (ibid.). That these words or sentences are curses Moses himself confirms when he concludes: “And all these curses shall come upon you, and pursuing you shall overtake you until you perish” (ibid.). After this he likewise proclaims other matters belonging to the curse, though not in the manner of one commanding, but in the prophetic manner of one announcing and speaking.

I have said this because there is truly something worthy of consideration and wonder in the fact that so many sentences of cursing had been prescribed as the number of silver pieces they were to give as the price of the Lord’s blood. Likewise, if you count carefully, you will find the same number of curses in Psalm 108. The first is, “Appoint a sinner over him”; the last, “May they be clothed with their shame as with a double garment.” Does not the mind, all the more delighted by these things, rightly join and combine the number of the scroll’s length and the number of its width, so that the scroll is thirty cubits in size, just as there are thirty sentences of cursing and thirty silver pieces which that thief, the assembly of the Jews, gave as the price of the Lord’s blood?

For as length and width make one magnitude, so the ten cubits of width and the twenty cubits of length rightly come together and make thirty. And who does not know, who doubts that what he said came to pass: “Every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged; and every one who swears shall likewise be judged. I will bring it forth, and it shall come to the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely in my name; it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume him, his timbers, and his stones”? Who does not know, who does not hear, that it happened exactly so?

For that scroll of cursing came to the thief’s house: to that house which, though it ought to have been a house of prayer, became “a den of thieves” and “a house of trade” (Matt. 21). And that thief who had done this added perjury to his robberies in that house; indeed, he falsely and deceitfully adjured even the Son of God himself, one declaring: “I adjure you by the true God: tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God” (Matt. 26). Every such thief and swearer or adjurer—that is, both people and priest—was judged as it was written there, exactly as Moses wrote. The curse consumed him, his timbers, and his stones, so that the timbers were burned by flames and not one stone was left upon another of that entire house. Nor has that scroll, which is the curse, passed away from that people; rather, it still remains in their midst.

It follows: “And the angel who spoke within me went forth and said to me: ‘Lift up your eyes and see: what is this that is going forth?’ And I said: ‘What is it?’ And he said: ‘This is the ephah going forth.’ And he said: ‘This is their eye throughout all the earth.’ And behold, a talent of lead was being carried; and behold, one woman sat in the midst of the ephah. And he said: ‘This is impiety.’ And he cast her into the midst of the ephah and threw a mass of lead upon its mouth. And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, two women coming forth; and wind was in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a kite; and they lifted the ephah between earth and heaven.’ [Col. 0735A] And I said to the angel who spoke within me: ‘Where are these carrying the ephah?’ And he said to me: ‘That a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar; and it shall be established and set there upon its base.’”

The greater and chief part of the Jewish crime and of its ensuing punishment is indicated by the mystical marvel, the marvellous mystery, of the letter of this chapter. In the preceding passage he spoke of the thief; he spoke of the one who swore falsely. Yet from these two descriptions you do not yet have the measure or fullness of those crimes, which the Lord himself, knowing—or rather foreknowing—it long ago, said: “You too, fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. 23). That measure is rightly understood here to be foreshown by the ephah.

For when he had lifted up his eyes to see, and had been made attentive by the question, “What is this that is going forth?”, and himself asked what it was, he heard: “This is the ephah going forth, and this is their eye throughout all the earth.” According to the order maintained thus far in the present vision, this is rightly understood, as already said, as the measure of the fathers who killed the prophets. When the sons had filled it by killing the Lord of the prophets himself; by stoning or killing, scourging in their synagogues, and persecuting from city to city the evangelical prophets, wise men, and scribes sent to them, it was just that every righteous blood shed upon the earth should come upon them, from the blood of righteous Abel onward (ibid.), as he himself said; and so it happened.

And it should be observed that he also called the ephah an eye, saying: “This is their eye throughout all [Col. 0735C] the earth.” For it is certain, and known throughout all the earth, that in killing Christ not through ignorance but through envy, and in persecuting his apostles, they filled that measure or ephah and sinned knowingly, having an eye open and seeing in sinning. For he says: “If you were blind, you would not have sin” (John 9); and elsewhere: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15). Truly, then, he says, “This is their eye throughout all the earth,” because their sin was not produced by error or ignorance, but by an evil eye—evil, that is, envy—and this was heard throughout all the earth.

But this also should be observed: when he said, “This is the ephah,” he added “going forth,” because that ephah of iniquity had long been active within, in private gatherings and secret deliberations, concerning how they might ensnare Jesus in speech (Matt. 22), how they might seize and kill him by deceit (Mark 14). What they had so long discussed finally, after prolonged deliberation, went out into public. Hence the Psalmist’s saying, rightly understood both of the betrayer and of the whole assembly of enemies who said, “When will he die and his name perish?” (Ps. 40): “His heart gathered iniquity to itself; he went out and spoke the same thing. All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evils; they established an iniquitous word against me” (ibid.).

Certainly, while they acted thus, the ephah was active within; but it went forth [Col. 0736A] when, their plan decided, they came out as against a robber with swords, clubs, and seditious cries, and demanded and brought about his crucifixion (John 18).

“And behold,” he says, “a talent of lead was being carried; and behold, one woman sat in the midst of the ephah. And he said: ‘This is impiety.’” The talent of lead is the weight of judgment or condemnation, great indeed and heavy in proportion to the greatness and gravity of the unforgivable offense—that is, of the impenitent heart.

For such a sin is impiety; and its persistence, which we still see today, is fittingly signified by the woman’s sitting in the midst of the ephah. For the impious fathers sit even now in the chair of pestilence, blaspheming and teaching their sons to blaspheme Christ; and thus the woman sits in the midst of the ephah [Col. 0736B], that is, of the filled measure, since, even while they fall beneath the sword and are scattered into captivity among all nations, their impiety still pleases them.

What, then, follows? “And he cast her into the midst of the ephah, and threw the mass of lead upon its mouth.” This both happens and will happen after the present life. It has already happened, as was signified and said above, where the prophet saw the flying scroll: “This,” says the angel, “is the curse”; and, “I will bring it forth, says the Lord of hosts, to the house of the thief, and it shall consume him, his timber, and his stones.” This, I say, has already happened, because that Temple has been destroyed and the city that had been has been destroyed. But the greatness of the ephah, and of the impiety sitting in its midst, demands that the justice of God should not be satisfied with this single vengeance. Therefore, “he cast her into the midst of the ephah” [Col. 0736C], “and threw the mass of lead upon its mouth.” And immediately, he says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women came forth, and the Spirit was in their wings, and they lifted up the ephah between earth and heaven,” etc.

It is remarkable that both the woman, who is impiety, “was sitting in the midst of the ephah,” and that “he cast her into the midst of the ephah,” if the letter is taken as it sounds. How could she be cast into the midst of the ephah when she was sitting in the midst of the ephah? [p. 327] But surely this ephah, not made by human hands, which is the measure of sin brought to fullness, has another sense: namely, that no one is handed over to his sin unless he has voluntarily handed himself over, according to the saying: “He dismissed them according to the desires of their hearts” (Ps. LXXX); and, “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy.”

For to cast impiety—that is, [Col. 0736D] the impious soul—is to convert it; and this happens when it has reached the fourth crime, as the Lord says in Amos: “For three crimes of Judah, and for four,” or, “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back” (Amos II). The first crime is to have had an evil will; the second, to have committed an evil deed as well; the third, to have acquired the habit of evil action; the fourth, to resist the reproving law or justice of God and to utter words of blasphemy. What sort of—and how great—a punishment is due for this fourth crime is indicated by the words: “And he threw the mass of lead upon its mouth.” For the mass of lead, or talent of lead, signifies, as has already been said, the weight of God’s condemnation or judgment [Col. 0737A]; and the fact that the impiety of this ephah—that is, of the often-mentioned measure—is unforgivable is attested by the Lord himself: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit,” that is, whoever knowingly calls good evil, as the Jews or Pharisees then did and heresiarchs afterward did, “shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII).

Finally, what are the two women who, devoted to carrying so great a weight, as he says, “lifted the ephah between earth and heaven”? We know from the prophetic Scriptures two women, and their names: “The elder was Oholah, and her younger sister Oholibah,” says the Lord to Ezekiel. Again: “Their names were: Samaria, Oholah; and Jerusalem, Oholibah” (Ezek. XXIII). And afterward: “Son of man, will you not judge Oholah and Oholibah [Col. 0737A] [Col. 0737B], and declare to them their crimes, because they are adulteresses and blood is upon their hands?” These and similar statements were made figuratively. For just as a woman is called—and is—an adulteress when, abandoning her husband, she joins herself to another man, so Oholah and Oholibah, having abandoned the God of their fathers, worshipped foreign gods. Blood was upon their hands because they killed the prophets sent to them. And Oholibah, the younger, raged more than Oholah; that is, Jerusalem raged more than Samaria.

How? Undoubtedly because Jerusalem, having done the same things that Samaria did—killing prophets and pursuing idolatry—added the greater deed: killing the Lord and choosing Barabbas. This was to fill up, as has already been said, the measure of the fathers, which is understood through the ephah [Col. 0737C] (III Kings XVIII; Matt. XI, XIV). The following aptly accords with this sense: among Oholah, that is, Samaria, the woman Jezebel killed the earlier prophets; and among Oholibah, that is, Jerusalem, the woman Herodias killed the last of the prophets—and more than a prophet—John.

Therefore the two women are the fathers and the sons: the fathers, who filled almost half the measure of bloodshed, and the sons, who filled the measure completely, and thereby made one and the same ephah common to themselves to carry, along with the weight of impiety. These women had wings like those of a kite—namely, pride like the devil’s—because, as it is written in the Psalm: “Pride took possession of them; they were covered with their iniquity and impiety; and their iniquity came forth as if from fat” [Col. 0737D] (Ps. LXXII). The earlier woman said, “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (III Kings XII); while the later woman, when Pilate said, “Shall I crucify your king?” cried out, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

“And the Spirit,” he says, “was in their wings”: surely the spirit of blasphemy, one and the same in the pride of such women, so that the former mocked the father, patriarch, and David, while the latter mocked the Son of David. It is altogether helpful to remember this whenever there is mention of that measure now under discussion, on account of this kind of ephah: namely, that the denial of David and the schism which the fathers made, by separating themselves from the house of David and worshipping the calves which Jeroboam made, was the beginning of the impiety that the sons completed by denying Christ before Pilate [Col. 0738A].

Did not the fathers, in saying, “We have no share in David,” already become deniers of that same Christ whom the sons denied? For a promise had been made to David himself that Christ would be born from his seed; and therefore, just as the Lord said to Samuel, “They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them” (III Kings VIII), so one may say most truly of them that they denied not David but Christ, lest he should reign over them. They preferred Barabbas to the Son of David, just as those their fathers preferred Jeroboam to David himself.

“And they lifted,” he says, “the ephah between earth and heaven.” What is meant by such a statement, “They lifted it between earth and heaven”? We know, indeed, that what is to be carried or conveyed is, in being conveyed, lifted between earth and heaven. But what does this statement mean except to intimate that you should consider the reality of which this whole portent was a sign? What is that reality? Clearly it is the very vengeance for bloodshed, of which, as said above, the ephah and the impiety sitting in the ephah were the sign. What kind of vengeance is this for that bloodshed or iniquity? Behold: it is manifest, and we see the Jews, who filled that measure, as has often been said, lifted between earth and heaven [Col. 0738B].

How so? Because neither their own land receives them nor heaven admits them. Having been led captive among all nations, do they not remain without touching their own land? Much less can they touch heaven—that is, attain the kingdom of heaven—since they are unbelievers. This was not the only portent of the matter: that they lifted the ephah between earth and heaven. [Col. 0738C] There was also this: Judas, the standard-bearer of their crime, perished between earth and heaven. For, hanged, he burst asunder in the middle; and, as one writer says, “hated by heaven and earth, he perishes between the two,” and all his entrails were spilled out (Matt. XXVII; Acts I).

Thus that people, hated by heaven and earth, driven from the earthly Jerusalem and unworthy of the heavenly Jerusalem, perished between the two; and thus the remnant of the same people was scattered, just as the entrails of the aforementioned traitor, hanging between earth and heaven, were spilled out [Col. 0738C]. How much better, more beautiful, and sweeter is the sign or portent that the two men who had explored the land of promise, returning, carried a cluster of grapes with its branch upon a pole (Num. XIII). [Col. 0738D] Compare those two men with these two women, and their burden-bearing with these women’s burden—if, indeed, they can be compared, since they are altogether contrary.

For just as these two women signified evil fathers and the evil sons of evil fathers, who filled up their measure, so, by contrast, those two men mystically signified good fathers, among whom the patriarchs and prophets were the best, and good sons of good fathers, among whom the apostles are the best. And just as the ephah which the women lifted between earth and heaven was a portent of the measure of crimes brought to fullness, so, conversely, the cluster which the men carried on a pole was a sign of the piety and justice that hung upon the cross [Col. 0738C].

Let us now proceed through what follows. [Col. 0739A] “Where,” he says, “do these women carry the ephah?” “That a house may be built for it,” he says, “in the land of Shinar, and that it may be established there upon its own base.” The land of Shinar is called the land of Babylon, where proud men built the tower; their languages were confused, and they themselves were scattered into all lands (Gen. XI). Shinar is interpreted as “the shaking out,” or “the stench, of teeth”; and especially in this place it signifies that land which David calls “darkness” and “the land of forgetfulness,” and holy Job “a dark land, covered with the gloom of death.” The former says: “Will your wonders be known in darkness, or your judgments in the land of forgetfulness?” (Ps. LXXXVII); the latter cries: “Leave me, Lord, that I may lament my pain a little, before I go to a dark land, covered with the gloom of death [p. 328]” (Job X).

Into that land of Shinar, into that land of the stench of teeth [Col. 0739B], these women carry their ephah—women whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword (Ps. LVI)—so that a house may be built for it there, and there it may be established upon its base. What is that house? What is that base? The house is that of death; the base is that of perdition standing firm and enduring. For, as the Psalmist says, “Their tombs are their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII); and there is no hope or expectation there of passing to another house, of migrating to another place. O, then, what an evil establishment, which he proclaimed in a wondrous manner, uttering it thus: “That a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar, and that it may be established and set there upon its own base.”

## Chapter VI
It follows: “And I turned and lifted up my eyes, and I saw, and behold, four chariots coming forth [Col. 0739C] from between two mountains; and the mountains were of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses; in the second chariot, black horses; in the third chariot, white horses; and in the fourth chariot, dappled and strong horses. And I answered and said to the angel who spoke within me: ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel answered and said to me: ‘These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the Ruler of the whole earth. The black horses were going out toward the land of the north, and the white went out after them; and the dappled went out toward the land of the south. But those which were strongest went out and sought to go and range throughout the whole earth.’ And he said: ‘Go, and traverse the earth.’ And they traversed the earth. And he called me and spoke to me, [Col. 0739D] saying: ‘Behold, those which go out into the land of the north have made my Spirit rest in the land of the north.’”

It must be remembered that this is one vision, seen in one night: from the words, “I saw by night; and behold, a man riding upon a red horse,” down to what he will say afterward, “And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius” (Zech. 7). According to the order of events which then were to be done, but which now have almost all been accomplished, there remains only the second coming of that same Man, namely our Lord Jesus Christ.

We behold a most beautiful ordering of the vision; and the mind is greatly delighted as it seeks and loves the glory of such a man, because it finds here, in right order, the history of salvation, the history of grace and truth: how God, and the Word, or Son of God, mindful of his purpose, mindful of the promise spoken and sworn to Abraham and [Col. 0740A] David, returned to Jerusalem in mercies, and his house was built in her. And the four horns which scattered Judah and Jerusalem—that is, the four kingdoms through which the devil attempted to abolish that same promise—were worn away; and then the Lord came: “O daughter of Zion,” and dwelt in your midst. For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

And the same God, the son of Josedech—that is, Son of the Lord of righteousness—clothed in changing garments, that is, because of the passion of death, was crowned with glory and honour; and, ascending into heaven and becoming a great lampstand, a golden lampstand of seven lamps, he shone throughout the whole world, giving to his apostles, or preachers, the holy sevenfold Spirit. Those who wished to extinguish so great a light, having filled up the measure of their fathers’ crimes, received, as was said most recently, their own amphora and the impiety of blasphemy to be borne away into the land of Shinar, together with the leaden mass of condemnation.

What then happened after their destruction which ought to be understood through these four chariots coming forth from between two mountains—whose first has red horses, the second black, the third white, and the fourth strong dappled horses? Let us lift up our eyes with the prophet and extend our gaze throughout the whole world. And behold, the world is full; and ever since the blessed apostles were illuminated by that lampstand, it began to be filled with fiery chariots and running horses, concerning which Habakkuk also sings to the [Col. 0740C] Lord: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3).

The first chariot, in which were red horses, is that of the apostles and martyrs. The second chariot, in which were black horses, belongs to penitents, who, beginning from apostolic times, established among those who had shed Christ’s blood the cenobitic life for us. Hence, even to this day, throughout the world the order of monks remains black both in profession and in habit. The third chariot, in which were white horses, is the order of virgins, of both sexes, adorning with its whiteness the whole cavalry of Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts.

Accordingly, this must be noted: after saying, “The black horses went out toward the land of the north,” he says, “and the white went out after them” [Col. 0740D]. For the order of life necessary for criminal sinners, which those earlier persons undertook in order to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, is followed by very many who are guilty neither of murder nor adultery nor any other crime—indeed, by many whose bodies are uncorrupted and whole. Of these blessed Pope Gregory says: “What else should I call them but both righteous and penitents?” Clearly, this is precisely to enter the land of the north: to pursue a more austere life, differing from a more relaxed life enjoying many delights, though not unlawful or prohibited by the law, as much as the rigour of the north differs from the pleasantness of the south wind or the west wind, and winter’s cold from spring’s mildness.

Thus the wording must be observed, because it is said, “The black horses went out into the land of the north,” with this sense: [Col. 0741A] because they were conscious of their sins, they committed themselves to the purpose of a stricter life.

The fourth chariot, in which were strong dappled horses, is that of shepherds and teachers, and of all those in whom the divisions of graces are eminent, concerning which the Apostle says: “To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another, faith; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the grace of healings” (1 Cor. 12), and so forth. Is this a small matter, or was it unworthy among those great things which were to come—and concerning which much has already been said and remains to be said—that these orders of the Church of the Gentiles should be displayed in prophetic vision? Indeed, which prophet kept silence concerning such things and concerning the Gentiles who were to be saved? From what source did the Divinity take up these orders, if not proclaiming them in the joy of the Holy Spirit?

Moreover, what are those two mountains from between [Col. 0741B] which these chariots are seen to come forth, mountains said to be of bronze? These two mountains are the two Testaments, the Law and the Gospel. They are called mountains on account of the loftiness or dignity of the heavenly mysteries which they contain. That loftiness is also signified by the fact that the Law was given on a mountain (Exod. 20), and that the Lord began the evangelical discourse when seated upon a mountain and opening his mouth (Matt. 5).

These mountains are bronze mountains because of the resonance and permanence of both Law and Gospel; for neither the legal nor the evangelical Scripture can be broken (John 10). “One jot or one tittle,” says the Lord, “shall not pass from the Law until all things are accomplished” (Matt. 5); and “heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” [Col. 0741C] (Matt. 24).

The four chariots came forth from between these mountains because both Testaments receive the four aforementioned orders of the Church. And, as it is said in another likeness, “They shall give forth a voice from between the rocks” (Ps. 103), so here one may rightly say that these chariots run forth from between the two mountains, the bronze mountains: that is, from the shared meaning or agreement of Law and Gospel, they will preserve purity of life, knowledge, and teaching.

Finally, what is meant by the angel’s answer to the prophet’s question, “What are these, my lord?”—“These are the four winds of heaven which go forth to stand before the Ruler of the whole earth”? What else than what Wisdom says: “A multitude of wise men is the health of the world” (Wis. 6)? Therefore these four chariots are called the four winds of heaven, because just as winds, by blowing, scatter clouds and frost, and by stirring it make healthier the air which would become more corrupted in stillness, so these orders, each remaining in its own office and, when the time requires, running and hastening, stir people up to know God their Creator. Unless they were made attentive by frequent admonition, they would not even consider, corrupted in mind, that anything remains after the present age, or that at the end there is any difference between a human being and a beast.

Hence is what John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four [Col. 0742A] winds of heaven, that they should not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree” (Rev. 7). For the four angels were the four evil angelic princes—that is, the angelic powers—of the four chief kingdoms: Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman. Of one of these the good angel who spoke to Daniel says: “The prince of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days” (Dan. 10).

For those kingdoms, or the princes of those kingdoms, to hold the four winds of heaven meant to restrain these chariots from the worship or service of God; that is, to restrain those who worship God—the orders, as we have said—from serving the Creator. But another angel, who came up from the rising of the sun and had the seal of the living God, cried out and checked them (Rev. 7). This angel is none other than that Man who, [Col. 0742B] at the beginning of this vision, rode upon a red horse, and after whom were red, dappled, and white horses: namely, the saints of the former people of the Old Testament.

But this chariot, these four winds of heaven, which came forth from between the two mountains after those women had departed carrying their ephah-measure, are the saints of the later people. When the Synagogue denied Christ—as long before it had done when it said, “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (3 Kings 12)—the other woman, namely the divided body of the ten tribes, believed in him; and they stand before him even now, as before the true Ruler of the whole earth.

Among them this difference of horses must not be passed over: there were no black horses there, but only red, dappled, and white; here, however, there are red, black, [Col. 0742C] white, and dappled horses. What is to be inferred from this except that repentance—already said to be the blackness of the horses—was publicly preached by no one at that time? For this blackness began from the days of John, who first preached the baptism of repentance, immediately followed by the Gospel proclamation of the Lord himself: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3).

In the Law, moreover, I think that even the word “repentance” is found nowhere. Rather, “Whoever has done this or that shall surely die.” Except that, long after the Law, the prophets came and cried something about repentance to kings and people who had generally forsaken the Lord and worshipped the golden calves made by Jeroboam, Baal, Astarte, and the other monstrous gods, both in Jerusalem and in Samaria. From the days of John, as has been said, the kingdom of heaven began to suffer violence (Matt. 11): such violence that it was no longer said, “Criminals shall surely die; he who has done or shall do this or that shall surely die,” but rather, “Repent, and bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3); “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”; “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2). The first of these John preached; the second the Lord himself; the third the Lord’s apostles after his passion, by his command. From that time, the asylum of repentance lies open to all sinners of whatever people or nation who flee to it, however criminal or wicked; the kingdom of heaven lies open to their violence.

Accordingly, it should be observed that concerning the black horses, as has been said, which go out toward the land of the north—that is, sinners who in repentance surrender themselves to a stricter life—the Lord says: “Those who go out toward the land of the north have made my Spirit rest in the land of the north.” The meaning is this: those who have repented, or do repent, of their sins—which is to go out toward the land of the north, where voluntary labour afflicts the penitent’s body like icy severity—by that very act of going forth have made the spirit of my wrath rest, that is, cease, so that I no longer am angry with them, since they themselves have been angry with themselves. For just as the sinner, by sinning, has provoked the Lord, so the sinner, by acting in repentance, makes the Spirit of the Lord rest.

Without doubt, when he says, “They have made my Spirit rest,” the spirit of wrath must be understood. The Psalmist bears witness: after first speaking of sinners’ conversion—“The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken” (Ps. 9), and the rest—he adds: “At your rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the spirit of your wrath” [Col. 0743B] (Ps. 17).

But if the black horses, in going out into the land of the north, make the Spirit of the Lord rest, what do you think of those who go out after them as white horses? To state it more plainly: if wicked people, by doing repentance, bring joy to God and the angels of God, according to the parable of the hundred sheep and the one found which had been lost, or of the ten drachmas and the one found which had been lost (Luke 13), what do you think of those who, guilty or conscious of no crime, follow the purpose or rule established for criminal penitents? Surely these not only make the Spirit of the Lord rest, but also greatly delight him; and where the former receive pardon, these obtain an everlasting crown.

It has been said of the black and white horses that they went forth; and nothing has been said of the red horses, which were first. But it is expressly said of the dappled horses, which were fourth, that they went forth toward the land of the south. Then immediately follows: “But those which were strongest went forth and sought to go and range throughout the whole earth. And the Lord said to them: ‘Go, and traverse the earth.’” Hence one may also judge that those which had been mentioned first as red horses are now called, at the end, the strongest. For no more than four chariots have been numbered above; nothing has yet been said concerning the red horses; and it is in no way contrary to reason that the same horses should be called both red and strongest.

It remains, therefore, to speak of their going forth. “The dappled,” he says, “went forth toward the land of the south.” It has already been said above that the Lord’s dappled horses are, or are called, those to whom diverse charisms of the Holy Spirit have been given: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, the grace of healings, kinds of tongues, interpretation of words, prophecy, or discernment of spirits, and the like. Now the Holy Spirit is customarily designated by the name of the south wind. And what is the land of this south wind but the sacred Scripture—legal, prophetic, evangelical—which the Holy Spirit certainly composed in its entirety?

What then is it for dappled horses to go out toward the land of the south [Col. 0744A], except for men learned in the faith and possessing the aforesaid graces of distribution to withdraw themselves from every care of the world and devote themselves solely to the sacred Scriptures, studying them and expounding the words of the Holy Spirit? Such work belongs to such persons because they are not merely black or white but dappled: that is, not merely executors of a holy purpose or adorned with holiness of life, but holy and learned alike, possessing certain powers of speech, eminent ability, and other such qualities which many do not possess, though they may be of praiseworthy and stricter life than these. For the very south wind, whose land this is—the Holy Spirit, the Lord—has not given them such riches, “dividing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Finally, just as we read of a certain rather simple man who is reported to have asked in the assembly of the Fathers whether the prophets came before Christ or Christ before the prophets, so we cannot deny of many persons of holy life, like that man, that they greatly lack the grace by which the holy and true One, “who has the key of David, opens and no one shuts” (Rev. 3), opened the understanding of his apostles—already holy, but until then unlearned—after his resurrection, so that they understood the Scriptures (Luke 24).

“Those which were strongest”—namely, those whom he had previously called red—sought to go forth and range throughout the whole earth, because the strongest soldiers of Christ, by voluntary love, ran to sufferings for his faith; by voluntary devotion they surrendered [Col. 0744C] their bodies to punishments for God. This was expedient, and such strength was necessary for the Christian faith, since idolatry certainly had many defenders, whose folly could be confounded or overcome by nothing better than the death or blood of the martyrs.

And it must be noted that the strongest horses were not first told, “Go, and traverse the earth,” and then sought to go forth and range throughout the whole earth. Rather, they first sought to go forth, and only then were told: “Go, and traverse the earth.” For a Christian who is unwilling or fearful is not commanded either to thrust himself into suffering or to expose himself to persecutors; indeed, permission is given to flee, as the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” [Col. 0744D] (Matt. 10). Thus, to those willing and desiring the crown of martyrdom, its grant is shown to be given through great grace, when the strongest horses, wishing to go forth, are told: “Go, and traverse the earth.”

For example, one of such riders among the strongest horses sought to go forth, and it was said to him, “Traverse the earth,” when the blessed Lawrence said to Pope Sixtus, “Where are you going without your son, Father?” The Lord answered him through that man’s mouth that he would follow after three days.

A good caution, a necessary caution, is required for all the Lord’s horses, however strong they may be: however greatly they desire to go forth to martyrdom, they should not go unless they await, and seek through prayer, the gracious assent of heavenly grace. For this kind of battle is dangerous unless great consolation from the Holy Spirit is present; and many have fallen into the abyss of denial while trusting that they were acting bravely and voluntarily surrendering themselves.

How strong in this order was the Apostle Peter! Yet in him it pleased supreme Wisdom to establish an example warning against excessive self-confidence in such matters. When he had said, “Lord, I am ready to go with you into prison and into death; I lay down my life for you; and even if all are scandalized in you, I shall never be scandalized; and if I must die with you, I shall not deny you”—when, while still young, he had girded himself so boldly and walked where he wished—one serving-maid came up to him and said, “You too are one of them.” On hearing this, he feared death and denied life (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; [Col. 0745B] John 13).

He ought to have waited for another to gird and lead him. This indeed happened after he had grown old, after he had learned wisdom and true strength; for it belongs to an aged mind and grey understanding to know that this strength is not in man but in God. Therefore both present reason and ready example ought to have taught the strongest horses that, when they wished to go forth, they should await the nod of him who says, “Go, and traverse the whole earth”—that is, “Offer yourselves to endure death for my sake.”

Since one who is about to die says, or is read to have said, “I shall go the way of all the earth” (3 Kings 2), “to go out into the whole earth,” or “to traverse the earth,” is rightly understood here as not fearing death and hastening to a better life.

Finally, this also must not be passed over: appropriately, those whom in the ordering of the chariots he had called red horses, here—where he reports that those wishing to go forth are told, “Go, and traverse the earth”—he does not call red but strongest. For the Lord’s horses are red not before they shed their blood for the Lord, but after they have shed it. To put it more clearly: before their sufferings, confessors are white horses; in their sufferings and thereafter forever, they are martyrs and red horses.

After all these things which have thus far been said and done, in the same order in which they were prefigured in this vision, from the words, “I saw by night; and behold, a man riding upon a red horse,” what remains according to Christ’s Gospel except that the Son of Man himself should come, seated on the throne of his majesty and wearing the crown of the kingdom upon his head? For, having become man for us, having been born in this captivity, and having lived among men in this Babylon, he released our captivity through his passion, brought many sons into glory, and brought back into one those who had been scattered—after the likeness of those who, when captivity was then released, came up from Babylon and, after rebuilding the Lord’s temple, began again to dwell in Jerusalem.

It follows therefore: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Take from the exiles, from Holdai, from Tobiah, and from Idaiah; and on that day you shall come and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who have come from Babylon. And you shall take silver and gold, and make crowns, [Col. 0746A] and place them upon the head of Jesus son of Josedech, the high priest. And you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, a man—East is his name—and above him he shall rise, and he shall build a temple for the Lord. He himself shall bear glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne, and a counsel of peace shall be between them. And the crowns shall be a memorial in the temple of the Lord for Helen, Tobiah, Idaiah, and Hen, the son of Zephaniah. And those who are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall be, if in hearing you hear the voice of the Lord your God.’”

Here is the end of the splendid and most beautiful vision which began thus: “I saw by night; and behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees.” This is the end of that nocturnal vision, wonderfully presenting the prophetic history of our sacred salvation, which we who believe now see and rejoice to be fulfilled. For, as has often been said already and must always be known, according to the great mystery of godliness contained in it, that Man, the Lord of hosts, returned in mercies to the Jerusalem which the Babylonians had then destroyed, and his house was built in it. Although the four horns of the chief kingdoms mentioned above greatly scattered Judah and Jerusalem, nevertheless God accomplished what he had purposed, because it had been promised. Christ came from there; and, according to the Scriptures and in accordance with this vision, the things concerning him have now reached their end. [Col. 0746C] As has already been said, nothing remains except that he who, the victor and salvation of all, was perfected through suffering, rose again, and ascended into heaven, should return crowned with glory and honour (Heb. 2), visible to the whole world, to angels, and to human beings.

Because this is a vision, however, and the prophet saw all these things by night, we should not insist too strongly here upon the literal sense when it says, “Take from the exiles, from Oldai,” and so on. The Hebrews, being devoted to the letter, indeed hand down that Daniel and his three companions, returning from captivity, offered gold and silver in the house of the Lord; and that from this the Lord ordered crowns to be made, as the wording here has it. They also say that the persons are designated under changed names: Oldai, Tobiah, Idaiah, and Hen are Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, and Daniel [Col. 0746D] (Dan. 2).

Moreover, that “Helen” is placed in the second instance in place of Oldai was done because *Helen* means “dream,” and Daniel, with his companions, obtained from God the revelation of the mystery of the dream which the king had seen (ibid.).

Yet whether this was accomplished in fact or was only shown in vision, let us contemplate the great and admirable matter of which it is clearly a portent. For above, in this same vision, it was said: “Hear, Jesus, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, because they are men of portent” (Zech. 3). There not everything was said to him which he was commanded to hear, nor was everything there explained to his friends which they were commanded to hear. Their names were not written there, nor was it made explicit why or in what respect they were called portentous.

Behold, their names are expressly given once and again. First: “Take from the exiles, from Oldai, Tobiah, and Idaiah, silver and gold, and make crowns.” Then: “And the crowns shall be a memorial in the temple of the Lord for Helen, Tobiah, Idaiah, and Hen son of Zephaniah.” Certainly these men are portentous both through their names, their gold and silver, and the fact that crowns made from them are ordered to be placed upon the head of Jesus son of Josedech.

And rightly Jesus was there clothed in filthy garments, which were taken away from him, and it was said to him: “Hear, Jesus, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, because they are men of portent.” Rightly, I say, was this part of the portent deferred for them, because first [Col. 0747B] those things had to be done which, through the golden lampstand and the other written things up to the present place, we have said are signified as one whole. Only then was that which is signified in the present chapter to be future—and shall be future: the resurrection in glory of those four orders of the holy Church which we have said are to be understood in the four chariots, and the crowning of the Lord Jesus from them, or on account of their salvation.

These four men—Oldai, Tobias, Idaiah, and Hen—portend this. For *Oldaia* means “supplication of the Lord,” a name fitting the chariot in which are black horses: that is, the order in which, as was said above, sinners converted to repentance entreat the face of the Lord. *Tobias* means “good of the Lord,” and therefore suits the chariot in which are white horses: that is, the order in which there is no stain of crime, indeed in many a great brightness of virginal purpose. Such an order, or anyone of that order, is rightly called “good of the Lord,” so that one especially well known among them may even be called “beloved of the Lord.”

*Idaia* means “known to the Lord.” Thus it aptly suits the chariot in which are dappled horses: that is, the order of those to whom the Holy Spirit distributes diverse graces, so that in teaching, governing, and strengthening others they are more known to the Lord than the rest, and he may deign to say to any of them, “I know you by name” (Exod. 33). *Hen* means “glory.” Thus the name suits those strongest horses which went forth and sought to go and range throughout the whole earth: namely, the glorious order of martyrs, who bore abroad the banner of the divine name, went forth to battle against the devil and his visible and invisible wounds, and watered and adorned the holy Church throughout the whole earth with their rose-coloured blood. To have done this is their greatest glory.

Therefore, “You shall take,” he says, “from these men silver and gold, and make crowns, and place them upon the head of Jesus son of Josedech, the high priest,” because the Lord is crowned through each virtue of his elect. Indeed, when they all are crowned, the Saviour receives a crown in each of them; for every crown of all the saints is his grace, his work. Not gold alone nor silver alone, but both gold and silver are taken to crown Jesus, because we glorify him not only by the meaning of the Scriptures, which is understood through gold and silver.

The place where these crowns are made is the house of Josiah—that is, “saved”—son of Zephaniah—that is, “the visitations of the Lord.” By this name the Church is rightly understood, which the Lord saved in its entirety by his visitation, according to the type of Zacchaeus’s house which he himself visited. “Today salvation has come to this house” [Col. 0748A] (Luke 12), he says.

“And you shall speak to him, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, a man—East is his name—and beneath him he shall rise,’” and the rest. In placing crowns upon the head of Jesus son of Josedech, one is commanded to speak to him and tell him what thing he and his friends, the men of portent, signify—as though saying: “What is being done here signifies something else; it is a portent of another matter. For according to this signification, behold, there comes—behold, he is near—a great man, a strong and mighty man, to whom no other is equal. And if you wish to know what he is called, or by what name he is named: East is his name.”

No man besides him is rightly named by this name, because he alone is always in rising, and he never has a setting. When he is thought to be setting, he rises most of all: that is, when he is to die in the flesh to this world, then he rises among those in the underworld who fear God; and, immediately ascending above the setting, he rises alive, for heaven and earth, never to die. This lies wholly in his power; and therefore I say to you that this very name is his.

“East shall rise beneath him”: that is, through him the multitude of believers shall be enlarged; in the glory of those rising again it shall be glorified. Hence what follows immediately: “And he shall build a temple for the Lord, and he himself shall construct a temple for the Lord.” He did not repeat with superfluous repetition what he had once said—“And he shall build a temple for the Lord”—by adding, “and he himself shall construct a temple for the Lord.” Rather, because the one and same Church is built in the present age as the Gentiles are converted, and will be constructed in the future when we all rise again, he rightly was not content to say once, “He shall build a temple for the Lord,” but repeated, “and he himself shall construct a temple for the Lord.”

Then “he himself shall bear glory,” namely, the glory signified by these crowns, because great will be his glory in having brought so many sons into glory (Heb. 1). For if those who have believed through someone’s ministry are that person’s glory—as the Apostle says, “You are our glory, as we also are yours, in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0748D] (2 Cor. 1)—how much more is it, and shall it be, the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ that he himself is the salvation of all? As the same Apostle says, “It pleased God through him to reconcile all things in himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1).

Leaving unspoken what comes first: “In him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers; all things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (ibid.). If these grounds are joined to those already stated, how great, do you think, is the glory of the crowns of the one and same God and man, Jesus Christ?

Therefore, “he himself shall bear glory, and shall sit,” he says, “upon his throne, and shall be a priest upon his throne.” How just this is, someone can think better than express: that he should sit and rule over all things through whom all things were created, and should be priest forever through whose blood all things were made peaceful. Let him rule, I say, upon his own throne and be priest upon his own throne. This cannot rightly be said of any saint, because none of them has the right to call the throne of dominion or priesthood his own. It belongs only to this Lord and sole priest, whose majesty is one and the same as the majesty and throne of God, as he says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty” [Col. 0749B] (Matt. 25), and so forth.

What does this doubled expression mean—“he shall rule upon his throne, and he shall be priest upon his throne”—except that the one person of whom these things are said was to be, and now is, both king and priest? Thus, because he is king, “he shall rule,” he says, “upon his throne”; and “he shall be priest upon his throne.” It is sufficiently plain that the meaning is that kingship and priesthood shall meet in one person, and one and the same person shall possess the twofold throne of kingdom and priesthood.

Immediately it is added: “And a counsel of peace shall be between them.” One must understand: between the ruler and the priest—not because Christ is divided, but because the two offices which had until then been separate, one royal person and another priestly person, are united in Christ. Therefore, “between them” means between the offices once they have been joined inseparably in one person; “a counsel,” he says, “of peace shall be,” because through that union there is peace for us. As has already been recalled from the Apostle, through him it pleased God to reconcile all things in himself and to make peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.

“And the crowns,” he says, “shall be a memorial in the temple of the Lord for Helen, Tobiah, Idaiah, and Hen, son of Zephaniah.” This is what we await: for all the saints and friends of the Lord, whom we have said are signified by these persons, the crowns themselves, made for the Lord Jesus from their gold and silver, shall be an everlasting memorial in that heavenly temple of the Lord. They are made from their understanding and speech, through which the Holy Spirit glorified, and does not cease to glorify until the end of the age, that same Lord Jesus.

We see that what also follows has happened, is happening, and shall happen until the end of the age: “And those who are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord.” This will especially befall us who have come from the Gentiles, because we were far off. The Apostle wishes us to remember this when he speaks to the Ephesians: “Therefore remember that you, who were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in this world—now in Christ Jesus you who were far off have been made near through the blood of Christ” [Col. 0750B] (Eph. 2).

Now we come by believing; then, where the memorial of crowns shall be placed, we shall come by rising again, and we shall build—or rather, having been built as living stones, we shall remain in the temple of the Lord.

At the end of the discourse he turns familiarly to those of whom he was speaking: “And you shall know,” he says,
for the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall be, if you listen attentively to the voice of the Lord your God. And now indeed we know that the Lord has truly sent prophecy to us, and that the Holy Spirit has spoken truth through his prophets (Acts 28); yet we know only in part, because that which is perfect has not yet come (1 Cor. 13). For we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Cor. 5). But then we shall know by experience, when he appears with the crowns already mentioned, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). And this, he says, shall be if you listen attentively to the voice of the Lord your God—that is, if you keep his commandments; for faith alone, without works, is not sufficient to merit so great a glory.

## Book Three

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749D] 333 How sweetly the bride sings to her beloved in the Song: “I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother, into the chamber of her who bore me; there you will teach me” (Song 8). And how sweet it is to learn by experience the force of this melody! For what is it to take hold of the beloved, except to find the meaning of Christ in the Scriptures? And what is it to lead him, once taken hold of, into the house of the mother and the chamber of her who bore me, except to set him forth, in speech or writing, for the common benefit or instruction of the Church? Such was the soul of Paul, who, recently regenerated by the sacraments of the Church, came to know Christ well—Christ already known to that same Church—and made him more fully known from the Scriptures, both by speech and by letters. “There,” she says, [Col. 0750D] “you will teach me,” because in such an act there is a merit of reciprocity: the one who has taught the Church by precepts ought himself still to be taught further things, according to that saying: “To everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. 13).

Therefore, in this hope, soul, run through your course as you have hitherto run, seeking the glory of that same beloved; and enjoy that which is partial until that which is perfect comes.

It follows:

## Chapter VII

“And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius that the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev; and Sherezer and Regem-melech, and the men who were with him, sent to the house of God to entreat the face of the Lord, to speak to the priests [Col. 0751A] of the house of the Lord of hosts and to the prophets, saying: ‘Must I weep in the fifth month, or must I sanctify myself, as I have done now for many years?’ And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months through these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves? Are these not the words which the Lord spoke through the former prophets, when Jerusalem was still inhabited and prosperous, she herself and the cities around her, and when the south and the plain were inhabited?’”

Almost two years had passed between this vision and the preceding one. For in the second year of Darius, in the tenth [Col. 0751B] month, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, he says, “I saw by night” (Zech. 1); and here, in the fourth year of Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month, he says that the word of the Lord came to him, immediately adding the cause or occasion for which the word of the Lord came to him in that year or on that day. “Sherezer and Regem-melech,” he says, “and the men who were with him, sent to the house of God to entreat the face of the Lord,” and so forth.

Since these men asked and said, “Must I weep, as I have done for many years?” the prophet is commanded to speak to all the people and say, “Did you fast a fast for me?” and so forth. Hence it may be understood that nearly all the people shared the opinion of Sherezer and Regem-melech, who had sent to the house of God concerning such a question. The Hebrews, as blessed Jerome says, maintain that these were Persians and leaders of King Darius, fearing the Lord. In truth, their understanding, and that of the people, was imperfect: because they saw or heard that the Temple had been built, they thought that no reason remained for them to weep and fast. Their question itself plainly shows that, intent upon temporal and visible things, they had little or no concern for eternal and invisible goods.

They remembered that in the fifth month Jerusalem and the Temple had been overthrown and the people carried into captivity; and that in the seventh month Gedaliah was killed by Ishmael, and the remnant of the people scattered—and for this reason they fasted and mourned each year (4 Kings 25; Jer. 41). [Col. 0751C] But they did not sufficiently concern themselves with that universal captivity by which the human race has been so thoroughly enslaved in Adam; nor did they greatly long for the coming of the Deliverer, which had hitherto been deferred; nor did they suppose that those things gave them cause to weep and lament. If they had fasted and mourned with these causes before their eyes, the Lord would never have answered in this manner: “Speak,” he says, “to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: Did you fast a fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?”

Daniel, while fasting, received a very different answer, because he had set before himself very different reasons for fasting. “Daniel,” says the angel Gabriel, “I have now gone forth that I might teach you and that you might understand. From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth. But I have come to declare it to you, because you are a man of desires. Therefore attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened upon your people” [Col. 0752A] (Dan. 9), and so forth. Certainly he fasted a fast for the Lord, because, as a man of desires, he desired the things that are the Lord’s: namely, not merely that that city and handmade Temple should be rebuilt, but—what is far greater and incomparably better—that transgression should be brought to an end, sin should receive its completion, iniquity should be blotted out, everlasting righteousness should be brought in, vision and prophecy should be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies should be anointed (ibid.).

Therefore, since the one and same Lord speaks here through the prophet, saying, “Did you fast a fast for me?”—and the answer to be understood is, “No”—and, “When you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?”—and the answer to be understood is, “Yes”—while elsewhere he says through the Apostle, “He who eats, eats for the Lord; and he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord” (Rom. 14), we must clearly and diligently distinguish between the person who, when he does not eat, does not eat for the Lord—that is, when he fasts, fasts for the Lord—and the person who does not eat or fasts, not for the Lord but for himself; 334 and likewise between the person who, when he eats, eats for the Lord, and the person who, when he eats, eats not for the Lord but for himself.

Indeed, the person who fasts or does not eat in order that, through this labor of repentance, he may make satisfaction to almighty God for his sins and receive the fruit of eternal life—that person fasts a fast for the Lord; that person does not eat [Col. 0752C] for the Lord. But the person who fasts or does not eat in order either to escape a temporal punishment, as Ahab did (3 Kings 21), or to receive passing praise, as any hypocrite does (Matt. 6), does not refrain from eating for the Lord but for himself.

Likewise, the one who eats in order to be able to perform the work of the Lord—such as he wishes his apostles or evangelists to be, saying, “Eating and drinking; for the laborer is worthy of his reward” (Matt. 10)—eats for the Lord. Conversely, one who works, even though it be a holy work, even though it be God’s work, solely in order to eat, works not for the Lord but for himself, and eats for himself. Further, if he is unwilling to work and yet eats, he eats not for the Lord but for himself.

Let him therefore say, [Col. 0752D] “Did you fast a fast for me?”—and the answer understood is, “No,” because you did not fast for the kingdom of God; you did not fast in order that you might deserve to recover, at the coming of the seed promised to Abraham, namely Christ (Gen. 22), the heavenly city of Jerusalem which you lost in Adam. Let him say, I say, “Did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” And let the reply be, “Yes,” because you did not eat in order to work the work of God, so that, sustained by provisions for the journey, you might be able to reach the homeland or kingdom of God.

And who could adequately express how fittingly, with what timely denunciation, he immediately strikes them by saying: “Are these not the words which the Lord spoke through the former prophets, when Jerusalem was still inhabited and prosperous, she herself and the cities around her, [Col. 0753A] and when the south and the plain were inhabited?” For since they were children, little or not at all concerned about great and everlasting evils, lamenting temporal evils alone, and fasting and mourning for them, he rightly speaks, as it were in mockery: “Are these not the words which the Lord spoke,” and so forth.

But if they had said: “Through these seventy years we have fasted and mourned because Jerusalem was desolate and we were captives; but much more must we fast and mourn because his promise or coming has not yet come,” he would never have spoken in this way, nor would he by any means have mocked them concerning lesser evils.

It follows: “And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Judge my judgment, and show mercy and compassion, each one to his brother; do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the poor; and let no man devise evil in his heart against his brother. [Col. 0753B] But they refused to attend; they turned a withdrawing shoulder; they made their ears heavy lest they should hear; and they made their heart adamant lest they should hear the law and the words which the Lord of hosts sent in his Spirit through the hand of his former prophets. And great indignation came from the Lord of hosts. And it came to pass: as he spoke and they did not hear, so they shall cry and I shall not hear, says the Lord; and I scattered them among all kingdoms which they did not know; and the land was desolated by them, because there was no one passing through or returning; and they made the desirable land into a wilderness.”

By the former prophets, through whose hand the Lord of hosts sent these words in his Spirit—“Judge true judgment,” and so forth—[Col. 0753C] he means those who lived before the captivity. Among their chief figures was Isaiah, through whom God spoke thus: “Seek judgment, assist the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow. If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you” (Isa. 1). The Law too, when first given, was full of sayings of this kind.

But what he says—“they refused to attend; they turned a withdrawing shoulder; they made their ears heavy lest they should hear”—is less than what they actually did. For they not only did not listen; they even killed the prophets when they cried out. They were hard-hearted, untamable, and like adamant, a stone of the greatest strength and hardness, which breaks all metals but is itself broken by none; hence the Greeks call it *adamas*, “untamable.” There is this remarkable fact concerning it: though it possesses such hardness, when it is moistened only with the blood of a he-goat—an animal given to lust—it is immediately dissolved. Thus the comparison is very apt: “they made their heart adamant,” because, though they were of very hard neck and indomitable heart against God, they were most yielding to the flow of every lust. Thus Isaiah rightly appears to have said of them: [Col. 0753D] “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive in your ears the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (ibid.).

Why this recollection? Plainly, so that the Lord may be known to be just, while they are shown to be without excuse: for what happened to them did not happen through some hasty impatience on the Lord’s part, [Col. 0754A] but through their own persistent impenitence. For who would not agree that great indignation was justly brought about by the Lord of hosts because they added contempt against the Holy Spirit to their sins—the Spirit in whom the Lord of hosts sent them words through the hand of the prophets?

Accordingly, by this reciprocity, “it came to pass,” he says, “as he spoke”—that is, the Holy Spirit—“and they did not hear, so they shall cry and I shall not hear, says the Lord; and I scattered them among all kingdoms which they did not know; and the land was desolated by them, because there was no one passing through or returning; and they made the desirable land into a wilderness.”

But why, when this is a narration of past events and in all the rest every statement runs in verbs of the past tense, does he alone extend these words into the future: [Col. 0754B] “So they shall cry and I shall not hear,” when he might have said, “So they cried and I did not hear”? Why, unless that you may understand that he is unchangeable and steadfast in the truth of judgment: as he did then, so he ought to do again if they again sin? Finally, he was not ignorant that this too would come to pass: their descendants would do worse things than their fathers had done; and therefore, when they cried, he would not hear them, nor ought he to hear them—a fact now manifest to all nations.

How bitter, moreover, is this reproach of the unhappy: “The land was desolated by them, and they made the desirable land into a wilderness”! For it is truly most unhappy both to suffer the misery of desolation and, beyond that, to be charged with the crime that they themselves caused the very desolation; and that the land itself appears justly to weep and complain against them and say: “Not God, who judged that this should occur; not Nebuchadnezzar, who came up against me by God’s judgment; but you, most wicked settlers—you did it. From you comes the cause why I, the desirable land, have been desolated and made a wilderness.” [Col. 0754C]

And very fittingly in the present passage the Lord, to whom no land is desirable and nothing earthly is desirable, calls the land “desirable,” because when they said that they had fasted and mourned because of the desolation of the land, they confessed all too openly that the land had been desirable to them, but that they did not desire the heavenly promise. For they said, “Must we weep and fast?” believing it enough that they saw temporal captivity ended.

Therefore it is clear how 335 bitterly this was said—“they made the desirable land into a wilderness”—by him whom they themselves, though naturally sweet, had made bitter to themselves. [Col. 0754D] But what is this cause: “because there was no one passing through or returning”? He first said, “The land was desolated by them,” and only then added, “because there was no one passing through or returning.” Had he said, “The land was desolated, and there is no one passing through or returning,” we would think merely that the manner of desolation had been expressed: namely, that no one walked through the land in going and returning. But now he seems to have given not so much the manner as the cause of the desolation, in saying, “because there was no one passing through or returning.”

We must therefore inquire what it means that there was no one passing through and returning. At once there comes to mind the saying in the Psalm: “a spirit going and not returning” (Ps. 77), because that saying and this have a similar meaning, as they have almost the same literal sound. For what else is “going and returning” than “passing through and returning”? [Col. 0755A] There, however, “a spirit going and not returning” means falling into evil and not rising again from evil. Thus here also, “because there was no one passing through and returning” means: because among those passing into evil there was no one who returned to good, the land was desolated by them.
