For is not the impenitent heart, which he noted above when he said, “they made their heart adamant,” and “they turned a withdrawing shoulder,” a cause fully sufficient to vindicate the righteous anger of the Judge? Truly, then, they themselves made their land—the desirable land—into a wilderness, and it was desolated by them because there was no one passing through and returning: that is, because, though all were transgressors, none—or scarcely any—was a transgressor repenting of his transgression. [Col. 0755B]

## Chapter VIII
It follows: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and with great indignation have I been jealous for her. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have returned to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called the city of truth, and the mountain of the Lord of hosts, the holy mountain. Thus says the Lord of hosts: Old men and old women shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, each man with his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days.”

Up to this point he had spoken, as it were, with laughter and mockery, in accordance with what Wisdom says to such persons [Col. 0755C]: “I also will laugh at your destruction, and will mock when that which you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1). Now, laying laughter aside and removing mockery, he speaks glorious things concerning you, O Zion, city of God. No insignificant or small part of you was that earthly Jerusalem which was then being rebuilt: this was according to the election to be taken from that people, and especially in order to fulfil the promise concerning Christ, the eternal King, who was to be born and reign in you.

“I have been jealous,” he says, “for Zion with great jealousy.” The Lord’s jealousy is good: it is to love human beings and hate human vices. The devil’s jealousy, by contrast, is evil: it is to hate human beings and love their vices. Hence the same Lord, in order to restrain iniquities, had delivered the people into captivity; and the city of Zion, together with the temple, was consumed by fire [Col. 0755D]. This was indeed a great zeal: not to spare his own temple and city, not to spare the people among whom alone the knowledge of his name existed. “He has not,” says Jeremiah, “remembered the footstool of his feet in the day of his wrath” (Lam. 1).

“I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy.” Yet he might also have said this in earlier times: “I have been jealous for my people with my jealousy,” as often as, according to the Psalmist, “he was angry in his wrath against his people, and gave them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Ps. 105)—namely, the Mesopotamians and Moabites, Canaanites and Midianites, the children of Ammon and the Philistines. Then too, I say, he could have said, “I have been jealous with great jealousy,” because under those enemies likewise he afflicted them grievously [Col. 0756A].

But at the time of which the present discourse speaks, he had done more. They had not merely served the Babylonians while remaining in their own land; rather, when the desirable land had been desolated and turned into a wilderness, they were held captive in Babylon for seventy years. Rightly, therefore, not content with saying, “I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy,” he added, “and with great indignation have I been jealous for her.” The meaning is: I have not merely been jealous so that hostile nations subjected them to slavery, as often happened; but, adding great indignation to jealousy, I also took from them the land and the place sanctified in my name, and handed it over to Babylonian fire—something which had not previously occurred.

Why? Because they not only abandoned me, as of old, and worshipped foreign gods, but also killed the prophets and shed much innocent blood [Col. 0756B]. That great jealousy and great indignation came through just judgment.

But now the same Lord of hosts says these things—understand, things of mercy—mindful of what he swore in his holy place, speaking of David: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not scatter my mercy from him” (Ps. 88).

“I have returned to Zion,” namely in that the city itself is again being built and the temple has been rebuilt. Afterwards I shall come and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, having become man, so that Jerusalem itself, and everyone who hears without unbelief the law and word of the Lord which shall go forth from it, may say—and may truly be able to say—that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1) [Col. 0756C].

Likewise, he says, Jerusalem “shall be called the city of truth,” namely in respect of the elect, the prophets and apostles, and all righteous persons who were, are, or shall be from that nation. Having become man from their flesh, I shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; hence it too shall be called and shall be the city of truth—that is, the city or land from which Truth deigned to arise, as the Psalmist foretold: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84).

Rightly, therefore, it shall be called “the city of truth and the mountain of the Lord of hosts, the holy mountain,” concerning which mountain much has been said in the prophets, as in Isaiah or Micah: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. 2; Mic. 4), and so forth [Col. 0756D].

These promises are spiritual, suited to spiritual persons, and desirable to them. But those to whom the discourse was addressed were carnal and desired carnal things, as has already been shown by their question: “Must I weep, or must I sanctify myself, as I have done for many years now?” They thought they no longer had any cause for weeping or fasting, content solely with the temporal joy they saw in the ending of captivity and the rebuilding of the earthly city and temple.

Therefore the divine discourse condescends to the carnal; and like an aged father lisping, as it were, with children in order to soothe them: “Old men and old women,” he says, “shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, each man with his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days; and the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets” [Col. 0757A]. These words beautifully declare and proclaim that the restoration of the city shall be full and complete—the restoration they greatly desired, for the loss of which they had fasted and wept.

It follows: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: If it seems difficult in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, shall it also be difficult in my eyes?” It is clear that they were such persons as ought to be soothed with earthly and temporal goods, persons to whom spiritual or heavenly things should not yet be preached. For, as he himself says elsewhere: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3) [Col. 0757B].

Likewise here, since it seemed difficult in their eyes that what he had said should come to pass—“Old men and old women shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem,” and so forth—it is fitting for him, who nowhere says what is unsuitable, to say: If these earthly matters seem difficult to you, namely that old men and women should dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, men with staffs in their hands because of the multitude of their days, and the streets of the city be filled with boys and girls at play—all of which are earthly things—how much more difficult will it seem if I tell you of spiritual or heavenly things which shall come from that same city! Yet whatever it is that I have said or shall say to you, however difficult it may seem in your eyes, it will by no means be difficult in mine.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will save my people from the land [Col. 0757C] of the rising and from the land of the setting of the sun; and I will bring them, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, in truth and righteousness. Thus says the Lord of hosts: Let your hands be strengthened, you who hear in these days these words through the mouth of the prophets, on the day when the house of the Lord of hosts was founded, that the temple might be built. For before those days there was no wage for men, nor was there wage for beasts; neither was there peace for one going in or going out because of tribulation; and I dismissed every man against his neighbour. But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, says the Lord of hosts; rather, there shall be a seed of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, and the earth shall give its increase, and the heavens [Col. 0757D] shall give their dew; and I shall cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things. And it shall be: as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I shall save you, and you shall be a blessing. Do not fear; let your hands be strengthened. For thus says the Lord of hosts: As I purposed to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord, and I did not spare, so, having turned, I have purposed in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Do not fear. Therefore these are the things which you shall do: speak truth, each one with his neighbour; render truth and a judgment of peace in your gates; let none of you devise evil against his neighbour in your hearts; and do not love a false oath. For all these are the things which I hate, says the Lord.”

All these things, as they are said, are rightly understood simply; nor is it necessary, for the sake of mystical or allegorical senses, to depart from the condition of that time in which the prophet, at the Lord’s command, spoke to the people [Col. 0758A]. Above all and before everything else, it must be known that all this consolation and exhortation tends toward Christ and looks to Christ’s coming. Nor would the Holy Spirit, who undoubtedly spoke these things through the prophet’s mouth, have been concerned for the rebuilding and renewed inhabiting or filling of that land and city, except for the sake of Christ himself, so that there might be a place from which he could be born, in accordance with God’s faithful promise. For he had to be born from no other source than that nation, the seed of Abraham, the house and family of David.

It was fitting, therefore, that the people should be encouraged and made favourably disposed by consoling promises and inducements to dwell in that place and rebuild and restore the former condition of land and city, now that the temple had been rebuilt. To that temple the same Lord and Ruler was to come, according to another prophet [Col. 0758B].

Yet what is here said concerning the handmade temple, in part, in one nation—indeed, in the small remnant of one nation—may truly be said likewise concerning the unmade temple of the Lord’s body in its universality, throughout the whole human race (Mal. 3).

“Before those days,” he says, “before the house of the Lord was founded, there was no wage for men nor wage for beasts”—that is, all your labour was fruitless, and both people and beasts failed in agriculture, trade, and various works, their vain efforts frustrated. “Neither,” he says, “was there peace for one going in or going out because of tribulation, and I dismissed all men, each one against his neighbour.” That is to say: enemies were abroad, sedition at home, and sadness everywhere because of frequent wars and domestic plots, while neither brother keeps faith with brother and every kinship is hostile [Col. 0758C].

Is it not likewise true—indeed, more truly—that before the temple of the Lord’s body was founded, before God became man from the Virgin’s womb, there was no price for the human race? Truly there was no price either for men, that is, Jews, or for beasts, that is, Gentiles. “There was no peace,” he says, “for one going in or going out”—that is, for one being born or dying—because of the tribulation, understood as sin: for every person entered this world in birth with sin and departed in death with sin, since the dividing wall of enmity had not yet been broken down (Eph. 2) [Col. 0758D].

At what price, indeed, could even a man—that is, a Jew—be redeemed? At the price of the blood of goats or calves? (Heb. 9). Therefore there was no peace, no remission of sins; and “I dismissed,” he says, “men, each one against his neighbour,” as persons possessing the seed and spirit of concord.

“But now I will not deal as in the former days.” But how? “There shall be a seed of peace,” undoubtedly according to the Gospel: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). This peace must be understood as nothing other than the reconciliation of God and humanity, nothing other than the remission of sins, which he was then accomplishing through his blood while saying these things [Col. 0759A].

In view of this, who would regard as unimportant what he immediately says: “As you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I shall save you, and you shall be a blessing”? For the people that was then a curse, so that something like this was said—or could be said—to one whose destruction a person desired, “May it happen to you as it happened to that wretched people, whose land was reduced to a wilderness, whose city Jerusalem was burned with fire, and who were carried off captive,” that same people is now a blessing through Christ, the seed of peace, as has been said, because in him all nations shall be blessed.

The same point belongs also to what he immediately says: “As I purposed to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord of hosts, and I did not spare, so, having turned, I have purposed in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.” For truly our fathers Adam and Eve provoked the Lord to anger not only by transgressing the commandment, but also by defending their sin (Gen. 22) [Col. 0759B]. For this reason he purposed to afflict us, and in a certain sense did not spare, in order that in another and better manner he might show mercy. He expelled them from Paradise, burdened with sentences of death and punishments, yet merciful.

“But as I then purposed to afflict you, so,” he says, “having turned, I have purposed in these days to do good”—namely through, or for the sake of, my unmade temple; for just as that temple, dissolved by death, was raised after three days, so I shall make all of you rise again.

I do not know how it happened that, almost against my will, I have come to something different from what I said above. For I said of these prophetic words that all things, as they are said, are rightly understood simply, and that there is no need, for the sake of mystical or allegorical senses, to depart from the condition of the time in which these things were spoken [Col. 0759C]. I said that in order to avoid weariness; but the familiar sweetness of mysteries drew the unplanned course of discourse inwardly by its fragrance and held it for a little while.

Since, therefore, he has touched on the remaining matters, why should he omit the beginning of the present chapter, where the Lord had said: “Behold, I will save my people from the land of the rising and from the land of the setting of the sun, and I will bring them; and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God in truth and righteousness.”

Finally, even if at that time, when the temple was restored through Zerubbabel’s hands and the city wall through Nehemiah, the Lord saved his people, that salvation was not so great as to be worthy of such lofty declarations from the Lord’s mouth [Col. 0759D]. But when the temple already mentioned was established—the unmade temple of the Lord’s body—then the people of the Lord truly are saved from the land of the rising and from the land of the setting of the sun. For “many shall come from east and west and recline in Abraham’s bosom” (Matt. 8). This indeed is to be brought and to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. They are the Lord’s people, and he is and shall be their God in truth and righteousness—that is, in Christ, who is Truth itself, the way of righteousness, and eternal life (John 14).

But now let us hear at last what answer the Lord gave, after these things, when questioned about fasting. “And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become joy and gladness and splendid festivals for the house of Judah. Only love truth and peace, says the Lord of hosts” [Col. 0760A].

Sarasar and Ragomelech had previously asked through messengers whether they ought to fast in the fifth month, or, after the temple’s rebuilding, bring the fast to an end and lay aside mourning. Having set forth many intervening matters—what they should do and what they should hope—the Lord answered thus through the prophet. They asked about one fast, that of the fifth month; but in answering, the Lord also delivered his judgment concerning the other fasts: the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months.

The fast of the fourth month—called July among the Latins—was on the seventeenth day of that month, when Moses descended from Mount Sinai, cast down and broke the tablets of the law (Exod. 32), and when, according to Jeremiah, the city walls were first breached (Jer. 52) [Col. 0760B]. In the fifth month—called August among us—when a sedition arose among the people because of the scouts of the Holy Land, they were commanded not to go up the mountain but to wander far from the Holy Land for forty years, so that, except for the two, Caleb and Joshua, all should fall in the wilderness (Num. 14). In this month too the temple at Jerusalem was burned and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and the people were carried into captivity (4 Kings, final chapter).

In the seventh month, called October among us, Gedaliah was killed, and the tribe of Judah and the remnant of Jerusalem were scattered (Jer. 41) [Col. 0760C]. In the tenth month, called January among us, Ezekiel, who was in captivity, heard—as did all the captive people—that the temple had been overthrown in the fifth month, as we learn most fully in that same prophet (Ezek. 24).

They fasted these fasts rightly because of sorrowful and mournful causes, but they did not understand how to fast. They wished one of them—the fast of the fifth month—no longer to be observed, because they saw captivity ended and the temple rebuilt. The Lord, however, wished the fast to be observed not merely until the temple had been rebuilt, but until sin should be destroyed and transgression come to an end [Col. 0760D]. Thus, after saying, “The fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months shall become joy and gladness and splendid festivals for the house of Judah,” he immediately added:

“Until peoples shall come and dwell in many cities, and inhabitants shall go, one to another, saying: ‘Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord, and seek the Lord of hosts.’ ‘I too will go.’ And many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the face of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall seize, and shall take hold of, the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you’” [Col. 0761A].

What else is this than to say: until he who is to be sent comes, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations? For it was not before him, but when and since he came, that peoples came and come, and dwelt and dwell in many cities—that is, in many churches. From that time the inhabitants of such cities go one to another, saying, “Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord, and seek the Lord of hosts.” To say this is surely to proclaim Christ’s Gospel and to exhort and build up one another. Thus, while one says, “Let us go,” and another replies, “I too will go,” many peoples and strong nations come—and do not cease to come until the end of the age—to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the face of the Lord.

It is superfluous to establish or demonstrate that many peoples also go to that earthly Jerusalem, where the Lord of hosts was seen upon earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), and from which salvation went forth after Christ’s death and resurrection; as is written elsewhere, “For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2). To that earthly Jerusalem, I say, where his glorious tomb is, many peoples go to seek the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord [Col. 0761B].

Here I prefer to understand that Jerusalem which the Psalmist beautifully describes: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity. For thither the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121).

Until when shall this happen, until this comes about? “The fast,” he says, “of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months shall become joy and gladness and splendid festivals for the house of Judah.” How shall they become joy and gladness and splendid festivals? Evidently by fasting not with sadness, as sad hypocrites fast; not, I say, with sadness, but with gladness, according to the saying: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 6), and the rest [Col. 0761C]. For there is a splendid festival where there is the cheerful purpose of one who desires that, in his very fasting, he may please the Lord alone.

What then, you ask? When that time of which you speak comes—“until peoples shall come”—shall one not fast in those months? The Lord will certainly not require, but rather forbid, those fasts of old. Is this not precisely what the truth of the Gospel teaches? “Then,” it says, “the disciples of John came to him, saying: ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?’ Jesus said to them: ‘Can the children of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days shall come when he will be taken from them, and then they shall fast’” (Matt. 9) [Col. 0761D].

Thus the bridegroom’s absence is the cause of fasting. Until he came, until he was born and was present among them, fasting was necessary; while he was present, his disciples—the children of the bridegroom, or children of the wedding, as another Evangelist wrote (Mark 2)—ought not to have fasted. And again, after and since he was taken from them, they rightly fast until they are with him.

Someone may say: “Then was John not among the bridegroom’s children, since he fasted?” Certainly he was even the bridegroom’s intimate friend; but this was up to that time concerning which the Evangelist, describing his conduct, says: “John was clothed in camel’s hair and ate locusts and wild honey” (Mark 1). He had not seen that same bridegroom; he knew indeed that he had come, but did not know him by sight [Col. 0762A].

It is a wonderful mystery that here too, in the prophet, where he said fasting was to continue “until peoples should come,” he added: “In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall seize and take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’” And in the Gospel according to Matthew, where he said, as we have already recalled: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. 9), and so forth—while he was saying these things, behold, a ruler came and worshipped him, saying: “My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she shall live.” As he rose and followed him with his disciples, behold, a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years came up from behind, touched the fringe of his garment, and was made whole from that hour (ibid.) [Col. 0762B].

Who would not delight in the very similar appearance here, both in the prophet and in the Gospel: one and the same meaning containing the power of the mystery, while the literal surface is not very dissimilar? For the multitude of the Gentiles announced here in prophetic words—“Ten men from all the languages of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man”—is signified in mystical deeds by the woman who touched the fringe of his garment, namely, the garment of a man who was a Jew according to the flesh.

And what is it for the woman to approach from behind and touch the fringe of his garment, except for the multitude of the Gentiles to believe in him not before but after his ascension, to keep his commandments, and so to be freed from the flow of blood—from every uncleanness of sin? [Col. 0762C]

It is also pleasing to consider and compare what follows in that same Gospel passage with what is added in this prophet. By touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment, the woman was healed; afterwards the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, for whose sake the same Lord had risen and was going, was raised. The girl, as Mark makes clearer (Mark 5), was twelve years old; and the woman had been in a flow of blood for twelve years. Therefore, when the woman began to be ill, that girl was born; and when the woman was healed, that girl died.

Here a great spectacle of mystery lies open. In accordance with this likeness, when the Gentile world began to flow with the bloody worship of idolatry, then the Synagogue was born from the patriarchs Abraham and the others to whom the word of promise was given; and when the Gentile world was healed through Christ’s Gospel, then the Synagogue died through envy [Col. 0762D].

Now let us see how the following words of the prophecy correspond with these.

## Chapter IX
The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus its resting-place. Likewise, in the Gospel there immediately follows the account of the two blind men who, crying, “Have mercy on us [Col. 0763A], son of David” [Matt. 9], were enlightened; and here in the prophet is added: “For the Lord is the eye of man, and of all the tribes of Israel.” By the land of Hadrach and the land of Damascus, just as by the girl who died and the woman who was healed, and by man and all the tribes of Israel, of whom the Lord is the eye—just as by the two blind men who were enlightened—we understand two divisions of the nations, or of humankind, namely Jews and Gentiles, and whatever has been or will be done concerning those same divisions, both through judgment and through mercy.

Those things which have been done or are done through judgment in both groups are signified here in the prophet by Hadrach and Damascus, and in the Gospel by the girl’s death and the woman’s flux. For Hadrach is composed of two whole words [Col. 0763B]: *ad* means “sharp,” *rach* “soft and tender.” Thus this very name strongly denotes the Synagogue, having within itself two opposites: softness in the mouth and sharpness in the heart, as the Psalmist testifies: “His words,” he says, “were softer than oil, yet they are darts” [Ps. 54].

Therefore the girl died—that is, therefore the Synagogue was abandoned by God—because, whether an occasion arose from the fasting already mentioned or from any other matter, they spoke peace with their neighbor Jesus Christ, while evil was in their hearts. Damascus, moreover, signifies the Gentile world—the same thing signified by the woman suffering a flow of blood—both by its name and by the reality. By name, because Damascus is interpreted “drinking blood”; by reality, because that place is said to be where [Col. 0763C] righteous Abel was killed by his impious brother [Gen. 4].

Moreover, why he added, “its resting-place,” he immediately indicates: “For the Lord,” he says, “is the eye of man, and of all the tribes of Israel”—that is, the illumination no less of the Gentile than of the Israelite people. Both are signified by the two blind men, whose enlightenment the evangelist Matthew immediately records after the healing of the woman and the raising of the girl. Hence Damascus is the Lord’s resting-place; hence he rests through faith among the Gentiles, because he has become their eye, because he has enlightened them, so that he might be known by the Gentile person, whereas previously God was known only in Judah [Ps. 75], and his name was great only in Israel.

Forgiveness is asked for this uncultivated discourse, since it suffers difficulty from the greatness of its meanings. While it turns over and attempts to express a most manifest reality, a most delightful clarity [Col. 0763D], the faithful mind, intent upon its meanings, is deprived of the service of voice and tongue. For it is not at all easy to adorn in words a matter whose sight is dazzled by the mind’s own exertion.

Truly to be adored is the divinity of Christ, the Son of God, and to be proclaimed is the wisdom of truth. When he received the question about fasting from those who said, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” [Matt. 9], he looked back to this passage of prophetic truth, where the question concerning fasting had been posed and the Word of the Lord itself had given its answer.

For the lover or seeker of truth, who loves the truth that is Christ himself, nothing is sweeter—nothing, I say, more delightful—in this pilgrimage than, by the clear gaze [Col. 0764A] of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, to recognize faces looking mutually upon one another: “which,” he says, “bear witness concerning me” [John 5].

Now it is permissible briefly to retrace and more attentively construe the very course and path of the text. “In those days,” he says, “in which ten men from all the languages of the nations shall take hold, and shall seize the fringe of a Jewish man, saying, ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’” This utterance contains an ellipsis, and one must supply: fasting will no longer be observed by strong peoples and nations who come to seek the Lord of hosts. It will not, I say, be observed—or ought to be observed—for causes such as those for which you observe it: because the former tablets were broken by Moses in anger on account of the guilt of the calf made by Aaron [Exod. 32]; because, on account of the slander of the spies and the rebellion of the people [Col. 0764B], the Lord was angry and said, “They shall not see the land for which I swore to their fathers; and your children,” he says, “shall wander in the wilderness for forty years, until the bodies of their fathers are consumed in the wilderness” [Num. 14]; because the Babylonians burned the city and the Temple and led the people away captive; because Ishmael killed Gedaliah, and the remnant of the people was scattered [4 Kings 25; Jer. 41].

For these and similar causes, in those days those who come to seek the Lord will not observe fasting. Why? Because the Lord himself says: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for its fullness pulls away from the garment, and the tear becomes worse. Nor do they put new wine [Col. 0764C] into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish” [Matt. 9].

Indeed, to have hope of heavenly or eternal things and yet weep and fast over a past loss of earthly or temporal things is, in a certain way, to put a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, to put new wine into old wineskins. Rather, let new wine be put into new wineskins: that is, let the new hope of heavenly goods, on account of those heavenly goods themselves while they are delayed and not yet grasped, have weeping and fasting; and thus both are preserved [ibid.], because hope will not be put to shame, and the labor of fasting will be rewarded with more abundant satisfaction.

In the same way, let unshrunk cloth not be sewn into a new garment, lest, when inserted into the old, it make a worse tear—as Cerinthus did [Col. 0764D], who wished to mix the faith of the new Gospel with legal ceremonies, and thus could possess neither the old nor the new garment of righteousness.

Concerning the fringe of the Jewish man which, he says, ten men from all languages shall take hold of, enough has already been said above. But since many who believe from among the Gentiles are innumerable to us, why did he say “ten men,” when he could have said, “Many from all languages”? To this it must briefly be answered that God’s mercy would have been content with so many, and for so many—that is, for ten—he would have spared Sodom, had he found ten righteous persons there. For the Merciful One descended as far as this number: “I will spare the entire place,” he says, “for fifty; I will not destroy it if I find forty-five; I will not strike for forty; I will not do it if I find thirty [Col. 0765A] there; I will not kill for twenty; I will not destroy for ten” [Gen. 18]. He descended no further.

Therefore, in saying that ten men will take hold of the fringe of the Jewish man, he means as many as that same man, Jesus Christ—Jewish according to the flesh—came to call, justify, and glorify from all the languages of the nations: as many as God foreknew and predestined before the ages to be made conformable to the image of his Son [Rom. 8]. In accordance with this sense, elsewhere too every election, every tithe, and every elect or righteous person is rightly called a “tenth.” In Isaiah the Lord says: “That which had been left in the midst of the land shall be multiplied, and still there shall be a tenth in it” [Isa. 6]. And in the Second Book of Maccabees it is written thus: “But Judas Maccabaeus, who had been the tenth, withdrew into a desert place” [2 Macc. 3].

What, finally, or what kind of burden [Col. 0765B] is that which he immediately adds: “The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus its resting-place”? For it has already been said why the things signified here by Hadrach and Damascus are rightly the same as those signified in the Gospel by the dead girl and the woman suffering a flow of blood. Therefore, since the word of the Lord came here to the prophet because of the question about fasting, no burden other than the burden of fasting is to be sought, whether in the land of Hadrach or in the land of Damascus—that is, whether among the Jewish people or among the Gentile people—but in very different ways.

For among the Jewish people fasting is a famine of hearing the word of the Lord, because the girl already mentioned fasts with hunger and has died—that is, the Synagogue—until he commands [Col. 0765C] that food be given to her, namely when the remnant of that same people is converted, as Gospel truth mystically signified. For when he had raised the girl, he commanded that food be given to her [Mark 5]. But among the people that believed from among the Gentiles, fasting is, and ought to be, hunger and thirst for righteousness. Hence, in the Gospel passage mentioned above, when the woman came to touch the fringe of his garment, he himself said: “But days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they shall fast” [Matt. 9], and so forth.

Concerning what he immediately says, “For the Lord is the eye of man, and of all the tribes of Israel,” enough has already been said above. It follows:

[Col. 0765D]

“Hamath also shall be within his borders; and Tyre and Sidon, for they have taken up wisdom. And Tyre built herself a stronghold, and heaped up silver like earth and gold like the mud of the streets. Behold, the Lord shall possess her, and strike her strength in the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire. Ashkelon shall see and fear; Gaza also shall grieve exceedingly, and Ekron, because her hope has been confounded. A king shall perish from Gaza, and Ekron shall not be inhabited; and a divider shall sit in Ashdod, and I shall destroy the pride of the Philistines. And I shall take his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth; and he too shall be left for our God, and shall be like a leader in Judah, and Ekron like a Jebusite. And I shall encamp around my house against those who serve me, going and returning; and no oppressor shall pass over them any longer, because now I have seen with my eyes.”

Here he sets forth seven names of nations or Gentile cities: Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza [Col. 0766A], Ekron, and Ashdod. He declares them to be within the Lord’s borders, because he had said, “For the Lord is the eye of man, and of all the tribes of Israel”; and likewise a little earlier: “Ten men from all the languages of the nations,” he says, “shall take hold of the fringe of the Jewish man.” Now the number seven customarily signifies universality. Therefore it is the same as if he had said that all nations are within the Lord’s borders, plainly in the same spirit and with the same intention as the apostle Paul, when Jews and Gentiles dispute, speaks against the Jew: “Where then is your boasting? It is excluded. Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also” [Rom. 3].

But why, when the prophet had the same intention, did he name these nations or cities rather than others—Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod? Surely because they are nearer in location or geographical position to the land of Judaea than the rest. That Hamath is near the Israelite land is evident even from the fact that it is written in the Book of Kings: “So Solomon at that time kept a solemn feast, and all Israel with him, a great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath as far as the brook of Egypt” [3 Kings 8]. There is no doubt concerning Tyre and Sidon; likewise it is certain that Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron [Col. 0766B], and Ashdod—the cities of the Philistines—are sufficiently near that land.

If, then, he wished to put certain nations in place of all nations, and to signify their universality by the number seven, as has been said, why put more distant rather than closer nations or cities—indeed, why not rather neighboring than remote ones? Therefore [Col. 0766C], lest any tribe of Israel boast against the Gentile person: “Hamath also,” he says, “is within his borders, and Tyre and Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod”; that is, the one and same God is God of Gentiles no less than of Jews.

For they had once taken up for themselves a vain wisdom, but now a true one. Once, indeed, Tyre—that is, any nation—built its stronghold, deceived as it was, and thereafter through empty philosophy; but behold, it has taken up true wisdom when, or from the time when, it seized, as already stated, the fringe of the Jewish man. Once, I say, it heaped up silver like earth and gold like the mud of the streets; but behold, it has now demonstrated that the gold of its wisdom was mud and the silver of its eloquence earth.

“The Lord shall possess her, and strike her strength [Col. 0766D] in the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire”:" that is, whatever previously lived in her shall be killed and destroyed by the baptism of water and Spirit. For by the sea the water of baptism and by fire the Spirit are rightly understood; through these the strength of a person or nation is struck and devoured when, laying aside the pride of the old person, it is baptized in the humility of the new person, Jesus Christ—that is, in his death. “For all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” [Rom. 6].

“Ashkelon shall see,” that is, any nation, “and shall fear,” and by fearing shall begin to become wise. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Ps. 10]. “Gaza shall see,” that is, any nation, “and shall grieve exceedingly,” namely over its sins and errors; it shall grieve, I say, with the sorrow of repentance, which sorrow is the preparation [Col. 0767A] for everlasting joy. “And Ekron”—supply, “shall see and grieve exceedingly”—“because her hope has been confounded,” namely with that confusion of which the Apostle speaks: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” [Rom. 6].

“And a king shall perish from Gaza”—supply, the one who previously reigned there—“and Ekron,” that is, any nation, “shall not be inhabited,” namely by that king by whom it was previously inhabited, who was the prince of this world. “And a divider shall sit in Ashdod,” that is, in any nation: namely, that divider who will eat butter or honey so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good [Isa. 7]. Thus he shall sit as on his threshing-floor, commanding it to be winnowed and the wheat separated from the chaff [Matt. 3].

“And I shall destroy the pride of the Philistines”—supply [Col. 0767B], by the means already stated—because Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod are cities of the Philistines. Their pride is then fittingly scattered when those who were proud become humble.

Although almost all these things signify grace, in their literal wording they appear to sound like wrath; and this the prophetic Spirit arranged with great wisdom. For it is well known that the Jews always hate the salvation of the Gentiles. Therefore it was useful that the promises of Gentile salvation be wrapped in obscure and ambiguous words, lest Scripture itself become hateful to the Jews on account of the Gentiles, among whom it had to be kept for the benefit of future ages—as we now see, since, kept by them, it has reached us.

“And I shall take his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between [Col. 0767C] his teeth; and he too shall be left for our God.” From whose mouth shall I take his blood, and from between whose teeth shall I take his abominations? Surely from the mouth and teeth of each believer who sees and grieves exceedingly, doing repentance for his sins. From the mouth and teeth of every such person I shall take his blood and abominations, so that you may no longer remember either that he ate sacrifices offered to demons or that he even shed the blood of martyrs.

Hence comes that saying: “I shall not gather their assemblies from blood, nor shall I remember their names upon my lips” [Ps. 15]. For this is the meaning: I shall not gather those who have repented in order to judge them or take vengeance on them for their former sins; and I shall not remember the names of those who acted impiously [Col. 0767D], for which they were called robbers, murderers, and adulterers, nor punish them for these things.

Consider that all these seven names—Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod—are very bitter and such that it is a great benefit for the Lord not to remember them. For Hamath is interpreted “indignation,” Tyre “narrowness,” Sidon “hunting,” Ashkelon “base fire,” Gaza “strong,” Ekron “barren,” Ashdod “fire of generation.” Are not all these evil: indignation and narrowness; hunting—understood as diabolical hunting; base fire, or murderous fire, that is, homicidal anger; strength, without doubt, that resists God; barrenness—understood as barrenness of soul; and fire of generation [Col. 0768A], that is, lust?

“But I shall not be mindful,” he says, “of names such as these”: that is, I shall not punish the converted or repentant person for things whose names have meanings of this kind. “And he too,” he says, “shall be left for our God.” How good it is to be left for our God: namely, that when evil names have been abolished, the person may be left for God and therefore live; that the remaining human being may live for God; that the good human substance which he himself created may remain, and no evil accidents at all survive.

Nor is it without significance that he says, “he too”: namely, no less the Gentile than the Jew—the Hamathite, Tyrian, Sidonian, Ashkelonite, Gazan, Ekronite, and Ashdodite—no less than the Jerusalemite or Ephrathite, or one named from any other tribe or city of Israel, “shall be a leader in Judah,” namely [Col. 0768B] the same person shall be, as it were, a bishop or apostolic man in the holy Church of Christ’s confession. And he who was Ekron—that is, barren—shall be a Jebusite, that is, a Jerusalemite. For this city is called by three names: Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem. This agrees with the Apostle’s saying: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek” [Rom. 3].

“And I shall encamp around my house,” that is, the Church, “from among those who serve as soldiers for me, going and returning.” He did not say, “I shall encamp around my house from among Jews,” or “I shall gather from Greeks”; but without distinction or respect of persons, “I shall encamp,” he says, “from among those who serve me, going”—that is, working obediently—“and returning”—that is, attributing not to themselves but to me what they have done, seeking to establish not their own righteousness but God’s righteousness, submitting themselves [Col. 0768C] in every respect to the righteousness of God [Rom. 10].

“For in truth I have found,” Peter says, “that God is not one who shows partiality; but in every nation the person who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” [Acts 10].

“And no oppressor shall pass over them any longer”: namely, the devil, the evil creditor and impious exactor, who by persuading humanity to sin exposes it to debt, and exacts the debt from every person who does not have Christ the Son of God as Redeemer, God the Father as patron, and the Holy Spirit as advocate. That exactor, I say, shall no longer pass over them, nor trample upon them or choke them, because “now I have seen with my eyes”: that is, I have visited them in the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, whose eyes are my seven eyes—the eye of wisdom, the eye of understanding, the eye of counsel [Col. 0768D], the eye of fortitude, the eye of knowledge, the eye of piety, and the eye of the fear of the Lord [Isa. 11].

In these my eyes I have now seen both the violence of the exactor and the misery of those from whom he exacts. He said, “Now I have seen,” in the sense of “Now I have had compassion.” For God’s seeing is his coming to aid; God’s sight is the greatness of a benefit. For example, when Abraham perceived the greatness of the benefit in the saying, “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him,” he called the name of that place, “The Lord sees.” Hence it is said even to this day: “On the mountain the Lord will see” [Gen. 22].

## Book Four

[Col. 0769]

[Col. 0769A] **341** From what has hitherto been said, beginning with the words, “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh [months] through these seventy years, did you fast a fast unto me?” and continuing to “The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be his resting-place” (Zech. VII–VIII), it has been sufficiently shown that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, alone and uniquely is the remedy both for mourning and for fasting: on account of his delay, until he should come, fasting was rightly to be practised; and on account of his presence—since the bridegroom has been taken away from his children—fasting is nevertheless rightly to be practised.

Rightly, I say; for he is the laughter of the saints, whence comes the joy of angels. As a type of him, Abraham’s only son, born to his father, was commanded to be called Isaac (Gen. XXI), which is interpreted “laughter”; and his mother said, “The Lord has made laughter for me.” And the [Col. 0769B] father made a great feast on the day of his weaning. What follows will now become clearer if the mind retains this heading concerning eternal laughter and everlasting joy.

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a Saviour; he is poor, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass. And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem; the bow of war shall be scattered. And he shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.”

Concerning this, after the Evangelist had said, “When he had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives” (Matt. II), and so forth, “All this,” he says, “was done that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Say to the daughter [Col. 0769C] of Zion, Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, seated upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of a beast under yoke’” (ibid.).

Therefore, what he says—“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a Saviour, poor, and riding upon an ass, upon a colt, the foal of an ass”—is clearer than light and requires no exposition. For the moment, we are concerned only with his saying, “Rejoice,” and, not content with having said “Rejoice,” adding “greatly.” The reason for the word “rejoice” is plain: above he had said that the solemnities of the fasts were to be observed until peoples should come and dwell in many cities, and nations should seize the fringe of a Jewish man. Since, by his prophetic eye, he sees that Jewish man coming and, as it were, present, he fittingly places himself in contemplation of his presence and says, [Col. 0769D] “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem.” Surely, as he here speaks, “the children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. IX).

But by adding “greatly,” he means that the rejoicing should not be of just any sort; for the rejoicing of the children of the bridegroom, already mentioned, is far different from the rejoicing of the children of this age. They were children of this age to whom, while speaking, he said among other things: “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. He was a burning and shining lamp; but you were willing for an hour to rejoice in his light” (John V). I mention these persons because “to rejoice for an hour” and “to rejoice greatly” are contrary things; and, in opposition to that rejoicing in which they wished to rejoice for an hour, it was said to the daughter of Zion, “Rejoice greatly.”

For what was it to wish to rejoice for an hour in John’s light, except to seek or hope for temporal glory in John’s preaching? Thinking him to be the Christ, whom they had heard would come as a great king, they already wished to see, under so great a king, the kingdom of the Jews become great and dreadful to all peoples: such as the Roman kingdom then was, the Greek kingdom had been in its time, the Persian and Median kingdom in its time, and the [Col. 0770A] Babylonian or Assyrian kingdom in its time. Indeed, they wished or hoped that the Jewish kingdom would become greater than any one of those kingdoms had been; nevertheless, it was to be temporal and earthly, because they did not possess—and did not wish to possess—knowledge of Christ’s kingdom, the kingdom of God, which is heavenly and everlasting.

Therefore they wished to rejoice for an hour; but to rejoice in that way is not to rejoice greatly. Such rejoicing does not suffice for true blessedness. You therefore, daughter of Zion, rejecting the slight rejoicing of this age, rejoice greatly: that is, rejoice with that rejoicing which the condition of your king proclaims to you—your king who comes to you, the righteous king, your saving king.

What is his condition? “Poor, and riding upon an ass, upon a colt, the foal of an ass.” Truly poor—that is, gentle and humble—as he himself says: “Learn from me, for I am [Col. 0770B] gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). Truly poor, because in this world he possessed no foot-breadth of any land, nor wished to possess one (Acts VII). “And riding,” he says, “upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (John XII; Matt. XXI).

Consider at what time this poor man did these things. He did so when, as he came to Jerusalem, crowds who had come for the feast-day were to meet him with palm branches, crying: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord” (Mark XI); “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David”; “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” At that time he chose to sit upon a little ass, thereby plainly declaring what he later made known in words: “My kingdom is not of this world; my kingdom is not from here” (John XVIII). Thus by sitting so, he gave an answer to his plotters, who slandered him regarding the title of king and wished to say that he made himself king in defiance of the majesty of the Roman Empire.

Indeed, they might have been satisfied, had they not been enemies pursuing him with great hatred, because they saw **342** that he sat not on a great horse but on a small ass, and that around him were not the splendours of weapons but the fragrance and sweetness of olive branches. These things sufficiently excused him from wishing to take an earthly kingdom away from any human being.

According to the letter, indeed, he did not sit upon both—that is, upon the ass and the colt—but according to the spiritual sense this could occur and does occur. For he sits and reigns over people of the Jewish nation as over the ass, and over the humble of the Gentile peoples as over the colt: king of both, Saviour of both. Therefore rejoice greatly: that is, glory not in the honour or power of the rulers of this age, but in the humility of your king, to whom everlasting glory succeeds.

“And I will destroy,” he says, “the chariot of Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be scattered.” Whether the Father or the Holy Spirit has spoken of the Son to Zion or Jerusalem—“Behold your king,” to whom it is fitting to say, “And I will destroy the chariot and Ephraim,” etc.—he then speaks again concerning the Son: “And he shall speak peace to the nations.”

Jerusalem signifies the elect from among the Jews, and Ephraim the elect from among the Gentiles; while the chariot and the horse, which “I will destroy,” signify the pride and vanity of this age. Hence, having come down in humility and been converted to this king, Christ, they say to others who persist in the same pride: “These [trust] in chariots, and these in horses; but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. XIX).

At the same time, according to the letter, he strikes Ephraim and Jerusalem, since at that period the kings of Samaria, who were from the tribe of Ephraim, and the kings of Judah, whose metropolis was Jerusalem, had multiplied chariots and horses for themselves, and had frequently waged war against one another.

“And the bow of war,” he says, “shall be scattered”—namely, in those who, not content with the command of the peaceful king, namely, “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and let each be content with his wages” (Luke III), also follow the counsel that, like the apostle Peter, they should altogether turn their sword away or put it back in its place (Matt. XXXVI). Of such persons Isaiah also speaks: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isa. II), and so forth.

What immediately follows—“And he shall speak peace to the nations”—is what the Apostle says: “Coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near” (Phil. II). This peace, namely, is the reconciliation of God and human beings, the remission of sins. And just as here, after saying, “And he shall speak peace to the nations,” he immediately adds, “And his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth,” so also in the Psalm the same Spirit, after saying, “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Ps. XVII), immediately adds: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (ibid.).

He shall rule from the Indian Sea to the British Sea, or from the eastern sea to the western sea; and his power shall extend thus. Yet that dominion or power shall begin from the river and reach to the ends of the earth: that is, from the time of baptism it shall spread throughout all lands; or “from the river” means, understood, the Jordan—that is, from the Jews—and it shall spread to all nations. For Isaiah says: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples” (Isa. II).

[Col. 0772A] He now turns in apostrophe to him of whom he was speaking and says: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

By saying, “You also,” he evokes our wonder, because it is truly a matter of marvellous condescension that neither envoy nor angel came, but you yourself, God made man, descended to hell—and this in your blood, which is a great and wonderful work of love, since “no one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

We call that blood the blood of your covenant, because your covenant—the covenant of eternal inheritance (Heb. IX), which you wrote for your heirs—you confirmed by your blood, by your death. In that blood of yours, which ran with water from your side when it was opened by a soldier’s lance (John XIX), you sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water: your prisoners, I say, who, gathered from the origin of the world through all ages or generations until the hour of your Passion, awaited you in the pit of hell, where there is no water—understood, water that might wash anyone from sins. Therefore water had to flow from here to there, water with your blood had to pour forth from here even to there, because there it was not and could not be obtained.

And it was surely this: that water and blood came forth from a human body here, in this region of the living, and effected cleansing there. For that power, the divine power or efficacy that caused both blood and water to come forth from a body already lifeless, could itself cause the dead immediately to lack every stain of sin and the contagion of the first transgression, as though flooded by a great sea.

“You sent them forth”—understood, by saying to them: “Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope.” That is, return to paradise as prisoners, not as despairing persons. For he made accessible to you the stronghold of the blood of the covenant, when the flaming sword was extinguished—the sword which the avenging sentence had placed before paradise and by which it had fortified paradise against transgressors (Gen. III).

It follows: “Today also, declaring, I will repay you double, because I have bent Judah for myself as a bow; I have filled Ephraim; and I will raise up your sons, Zion, over your sons, Greece.”

Although it may be understood otherwise, yet I would by no means understand it more gladly than as being also the voice of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit, to that same Son to whom he had said, “You also, in the blood of your covenant,” and so forth. “Today also”—that is, at this very time, or on the third day of your Passion or death—declaring and saying, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. CVII), “I will repay you double.” Namely, because you were obedient unto death, even death of the cross (Phil. III), you shall possess all power in heaven and on earth, in both the divine and the human nature—whereas previously you possessed it only in the divine nature.

Moreover, in this too I will repay you double: both those of yours who had died from the origin of the world and descended to hell shall be restored to you; and others shall be born to you, not only from Abraham’s flesh but also from all nations, as I signified when I said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II). And this shall occur because “I have bent Judah for myself as a bow; I have filled Ephraim”: that is, because I have prepared an apostle from the Jews and apostolic men from the Gentiles. The multitude of those nations is signified by the name Ephraim, which is interpreted “fruitful.”

For as an archer bends his bow for himself and fills his quiver with arrows to be brought forth at the appropriate time, so I have bent for myself and filled such men with the word of preaching. Their words shall be like arrows reaching the heart, burning as they pierce and fighting as they burn, so that sinners may first be pierced by fear and then burn with love, as the Psalmist says: “Sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals” (Ps. CIX).

That is to say: the subtle judgments of him who is absolutely mighty, namely the Lord, penetrate human hearts like arrows, together with the authority of the holy Fathers. These examples, burning in a pierced heart, lay waste the vices of the penitent; and therefore they are called desolating coals.

In this matter the apostles from the Jews are first, and the Greeks second. Therefore he says: “And I will raise up your sons, Zion, over your sons, Greece.” He puts Zion for the Jew and Greece for the Gentile. The Apostle likewise wishes this to be understood when he says: “Wrath and indignation upon every soul that does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; glory and honour and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. II).

Therefore, “I will raise up your sons, Zion, over your sons, Greece”: that is, I will strengthen the apostles from Judaea so that they may not fear to go to the nations and preach to the nations. He could indeed have said, “I will raise up your sons, Zion, over the sons of Greece”; but he preferred to speak in this manner, in which there is greater familiarity and a stronger sense of mutual rejoicing, in proportion to the greatness of the grace or benefit which he himself who speaks has bestowed upon both.

“And I will make you like the sword of the mighty; and the Lord God shall appear over them, and his missile shall go forth like lightning. And the Lord shall sound the trumpet, and shall go in the whirlwind of the south; the Lord of hosts shall protect them, and they shall devour and subdue with sling-stones; and, drinking, they shall be drunken as with wine, and shall be filled like bowls and like the horns of the altar. And the Lord their God shall save them in that day, as the flock of his people, because holy stones are lifted up over his land. For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine causing virgins to flourish?”

How beautiful is the surface of the letter; how great a beauty of evangelical grace does it contain within! Is this not precisely what we believe, what we know has occurred down to our own time, since you, Christ Son of God, “in the blood of your covenant sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water”—that is, since by dying you despoiled hell and ascended from there victorious with all your own?

For from that time God the Father raised up the sons of Zion, that is, your apostles; the Holy Spirit raised them up over the sons of Greece, as you said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). And from that time God the Father made you, the Holy Spirit made you, like the sword of the mighty: namely, so that through you there might occur that which is strongest, which you yourself signified by saying: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a person’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X).

This came about through the ministry of the sons of Zion, through the preaching of your apostles. Whence came such force and effect to their preaching? “And the Lord God,” he says, “shall appear over them, and his missile shall go forth like lightning.” That is to say: as they go forth and preach everywhere, “the Lord will work with them and confirm the word by the signs that follow” (Mark XVI). For his missile going forth like lightning means his Gospel flashing forth with miracles.

“And the Lord shall sound the trumpet and shall go in the whirlwind of the south.” What does it mean to sound the trumpet except to proclaim the coming judgment for the hearing of the whole world? For example, when the Apostle says, “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings” (Rom. I), and so forth, does not the Lord sound the trumpet and go in the whirlwind of the south—that is, in the force of the Holy Spirit? For, in the likeness of a sounding trumpet and a great tempest, he frightened the nations with pronouncements of this kind: “The Gospel of Christ is not to be ashamed of, because it is the power of God; because in it the righteousness of God is revealed.”

And truly the Lord of hosts says, “He shall protect them”: namely, so that they may neither fear nor be ashamed, and so that each of them may say, “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God” (ibid.), and so forth.

“And they shall devour,” he says, “and subdue with sling-stones.” A good devouring, by which persons are transferred into the body of the Church; and good sling-stones, namely the mysteries of Holy Scripture revealed to them. When these were heard or understood, Greece submitted itself; the Gentile world fell silent as if struck by stones, and, conquered, acquiesced.

Whence did they have this power: to be so strong for devouring, so mighty for casting and subduing with sling-stones? “And, drinking,” he says, “they shall be drunken as with wine, and shall be filled like bowls and like the horns of the altar.” Did this not happen? Did not the apostles drink and become drunk? Did not those who saw them say so? For when they had received the Holy Spirit and spoke in various languages as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance, people were amazed and wondered, saying, “What can this mean?” But others, mocking, said, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II).

And truly these are full of new wine; truly they are full of new wine, but not of the sort of new wine those people supposed. Did Peter, because he said, “These are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day,” altogether deny that they were drunk? Certainly he did not altogether deny it, but removed a particular kind of drunkenness by saying, “Not as you suppose” (ibid.). It was as if he said: They are indeed drunk, but not as you thought.

Therefore, “drinking, they shall be drunken as with wine”: that is, receiving the Holy Spirit, they shall be in such a state that they are said to be full of new wine. “And they shall be filled like bowls”: that is, they shall possess a full capacity not only for knowledge but also for eloquence. For a bowl has a wide-open mouth; and therefore, by this likeness, the totality of languages is rightly suggested—the languages given to them so that they might receive or know, and utter to all nations, the mighty works of God.

[Col. 0775A] And because abundance of speech or languages does not suffice unless the holy strength of good zeal is also present, after saying, “They shall be filled like bowls,” he added, “And like the horns of the altar.” The Lord commanded that four horns of the altar be made, saying to Moses: “You shall make also an altar of shittim wood, five cubits in length and as many in breadth” (Exod. XXI)—that is, square—and three cubits in height. “Its horns, moreover, shall rise from it at the four corners.”

How were those horns of the altar filled? “You shall make,” he says, “two poles for the altar of shittim wood, which you shall cover with bronze plates; and you shall attach rings, and they shall be on either side for carrying it” (ibid.). In accordance with this likeness, the apostles were filled with the knowledge of both Testaments, as though with two poles of shittim wood and rings of charity, for carrying the altar, which is Christ. The apostles were and are certain horns of that altar, namely by bearing before kings and nations the strongest testimony to him.

Therefore, “They shall be filled,” he says, “like bowls and like the horns of the altar”: that is, by one and the same Spirit they shall become both most learned and most courageous in carrying—that is, in proclaiming to all nations—Christ, according to the mystery of that man-made altar, whose horns were commanded to be furnished with rings and poles in order that it might be carried.

“And the Lord their God shall save them in that day, as the flock of his people, because holy stones are lifted up over his land.” The meaning is this: As a shepherd [Col. 0775C] saves his flock, so he shall save the multitude of believers. This will arise from the fact that, just as round stones can readily be rolled and are more swiftly moved according to the will of the one who wishes to lead them somewhere, so they follow the Saviour’s command. Through the weakness of the flesh they are tender, like a flock of sheep; through the strength of patience they are hard like stones; and through the willing disposition of obedience they are always rolling onward and hurrying to carry out commands.

“For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine causing virgins to flourish?” This may be connected with what precedes as follows. I said, “They shall be filled like bowls and like **344** horns of the altar”; and one must understand: with the exceedingly beautiful gifts of the Lord, namely grain and wine. Whoever understands grain and wine spiritually perceives that they are truly the Lord’s good things. For the Lord’s grain is the Lord’s word, and the Lord’s wine is the Lord’s Spirit.

As bodily hunger is expelled by visible grain, and wine not only quenches thirst but also invigorates natural heat, so the soul lives by the word of God, and the mind is stirred by the sweetness of the Holy Spirit to love God. From the time of evangelical preaching this began to happen so abundantly that, just as at harvest-time the fullness of a grain-field is usually seen, and just as, in the abundance of early and latter dew or rain, the growth of a well-cultivated garden delights the eye, with roses flowering and lilies gleaming white, so throughout the whole world one may everywhere behold both elect men and virgins of the female sex.

What else could delight the blessed Trinity in this world more than this sight? Let him therefore say: “For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine causing virgins to flourish?”

It follows:

## CHAPTER X.

Ask the LORD for rain in the season of the latter rain, and the LORD will make snow; he will give them rain in showers, to each one grass in the field, because the idols have spoken what is useless, the diviners have seen a lie, and dreamers have spoken in vain; they offered empty comfort.

It must be very well understood—for to know this belongs to the wise—that this good and beautiful thing of which he had said, “What is his goodness, and what is his beauty, but the grain of the elect and wine causing virgins to grow?”—this good and beautiful thing, I say, is the gift of God alone, and for that reason must be sought from him. For whoever has been earnest concerning the shoot of virginity [Col. 0776B], concerning the grain of God’s word, has not failed to learn, but has learned by experience, that it cannot rise from the soil of our flesh, even if someone plants or waters, unless God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3). He therefore who has shown this good or beautiful thing rightly also suggests the counsel of seeking it from the source from which it can be obtained. “Ask,” he says, “from the LORD rain in the latter season, and the LORD will make snow, rain in showers.”

It is as though he said: Wherever the Lord’s grain and the wine of virginal growth are desired, wherever there is a resolve of chastity or a purpose of virginity, there the burning of the flesh, lusting against the spirit, is felt more keenly. But do not fail; do not despair. Ask from the Lord, and the Lord will give snow and rain in showers: snow by which he may cool and temper the heat of the flesh; rain in showers, by which the soil of the heart [Col. 0776C], drenched with rain, may bring forth the grass of grain, by which humanity lives, which strengthens the human heart. For snow sometimes signifies evil, as in blessed Job: “Those who fear frost—snow shall fall upon them” (Job 6). At other times it signifies good, as in Solomon’s Proverbs: “Like the coolness of snow on the day of harvest is a faithful messenger; he gives rest to the soul of the one who sent him” (Prov. 25).

“Ask,” he says, “from the LORD in the latter season.” Great and forceful is this exhortation, and by this saying it touches each person’s conscience. Who can boast that he sought such snow or rain and obtained it at a very late time? Almost all flesh delights first in its own burning before it asks the Lord for coolness. Therefore, as though not daring to say [Col. 0776D], “Ask in the morning season,” he says, “Ask in the latter season.” If not in the morning, ask at least in the evening; ask, I say, and pay no heed to idols, diviners, or dreamers, “because the idols have spoken what is useless, the diviners have seen a lie, and dreamers have spoken in vain; they offered empty comfort.”

For what have they said? “O human being, you who say that wine causing virgins to grow is God’s beautiful thing: why then did God in the beginning create male and female? Why did he form bodily members fitted for the uses of intercourse? Take care, then, lest, in believing or preaching that virgins are God’s good and beautiful thing, you set yourself against God’s institution or decree.”

There are, however, many who do not dare to speak against it so directly, since a more abundant answer can be given them. They speak otherwise and flatter themselves with excessive indulgence. “That man [Col. 0777A] or that woman could do it: that holy apostle, or that holy woman whom God received, was able to produce and preserve God’s shoot, the shoot of virginity, because the time was favorable, or because a constitution of colder nature prevailed. The time is now more fragile; we, O sister—or O brother—are of a weaker nature. It is better to do this than to burn. She could do it; you will not be able to preserve virginity or to be continent.” Nor were there lacking those who said that, in that age, marriage would not count as impiety for virgins.

When you hear these or similar things, know that they are idols, and speak what is useless; they are diviners, and see a lie; they are dreamers, and, speaking in vain, offer empty comfort.

Therefore they were led away; they shall be afflicted like a flock, because they have no shepherd. My wrath is angry against the shepherds, and I will visit punishment upon the he-goats [Col. 0777B], because the LORD of hosts has visited his flock, the house of Judah, and has made them like the horse of his glory in battle.

“Therefore,” he says, because they are dreamers and speak in vain; because they are diviners and have seen a lie; because they are idols—that is, deceivers—and have spoken what is useless in order to overthrow the good thing of God, which is the grain of the elect, and to destroy the beautiful thing of God, which is wine causing virgins to grow—therefore both they and those who agreed with them, while they offered empty consolation, “were led away into the diverse paths of lusts, and shall be afflicted like a flock,” namely, a flock of he-goats, an animal exceedingly lustful. For he immediately says, “And I will visit punishment upon the he-goats.” Thus, like a flock of he-goats—that is, stupid and senseless as he-goats—they shall be afflicted, namely, by many and diverse sufferings of disgrace [Col. 0777C].

For because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie—which is the act of such diviners and dreamers—the Apostle says: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, unto uncleanness” (Rom. 1); therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions; therefore God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are unfitting (ibid.).

In accordance with this meaning, when he says here, “because they have no shepherd,” it must equally be understood: neither do they belong to the shepherd—namely, the one who says, “I am the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10), “I am the way and the truth” (John 14). This is not because they have not heard such a shepherd or have not known this way and truth, but because, though they knew the shepherd, they did not obey him as shepherd; or, as the Apostle says: “Though they knew [Col. 0777D] God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1), but rather exchanged truth for a lie.

“Therefore my wrath is angry against the shepherds, and I will visit punishment upon the he-goats”: that is, I shall judge alike the teachers of lusts, because they are rotten shepherds, and their hearers or imitators, because they are lustful he-goats. For the shepherds are already condemned by their own judgment in showing the he-goats the paths of lust; the he-goats, in gladly assenting to the shepherds. Indeed, from this point they are without excuse, because “the LORD of hosts has visited the house of Judah and has made them like the horse of his glory in battle.”

By the name “house of Judah,” which means “confession,” he indicates all those opposed to them; for they, as has already been said, though they knew [Col. 0778A] God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, and therefore were given over to passions; and therefore they are not delivered, because they take pleasure in the passions themselves. These, on the contrary, knowing God, glorified him as God and gave thanks; accordingly they are called the house of Judah—that is, the house of [p. 345] confession and praise. The LORD of hosts visited such a flock as his own flock: a flock not of he-goats but of sheep.

How did he visit it? “He made them,” he says, “like the horse of his glory in battle”: that is, as a glorious horse in battle exults boldly, advances armed to meet the enemy, despises fear, and does not fall beneath the sword, so these are strong and steadfast within and without—within against every assault of lust, without against the persecutor’s sword. Hence those others, as has already [Col. 0778B] been said, are without excuse, because they too, like these, are human beings and flesh; and, had they wished, they likewise would have had God as their helper.

Therefore there immediately follows: “From him comes the cornerstone; from him the peg; from him the bow of battle; from him every exactor goes forth together. And they shall be like strong men, trampling the mud of the roads in battle. And they shall fight, because the LORD is with them. And the riders of horses shall be confounded; and I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph.”

The house of Judah rightly speaks and confesses in accordance with its name; it rightly worships and understands the horse of the Lord’s glory. To say this, indeed, is to glorify God almighty and give thanks: “From him,” it says, “comes the cornerstone; from him the peg; from him the bow of battle; from him every exactor goes forth together.” What [Col. 0778C] does this mean? Every good proceeds from him.
