The cornerstone—that is, faith; the peg—that is, hope; the bow of battle—that is, charity, apart from which there is no knowledge and no strength for fighting—comes from him; it is his gift.

Likewise, every exactor—that is, every worker who, from the consciousness of a good work, justly dares to demand a reward, like the one who said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4). Every such exactor, I say, goes forth from him; from him he receives that very thing which he has performed, for which he deserves to demand reward or crown.

We have called the cornerstone faith, because just as two walls approaching from opposite [Col. 0778D] directions are joined by a corner, so by one and the same faith the election of the Gentiles is joined to the election which is from the Jews. We have called the peg hope, because one who has slipped upon a slope, if he takes hold of a firmly fixed peg, stands safely and both holds and is held, lest he fall utterly into the depths of a precipice; so one who could be endangered by various temptations and descend into the abyss of despair is lifted by hope and springs back to the height of divine mercy. We have called the bow of battle charity, because surely nothing is so strong against the devil, nothing in the whole armor of virtues so powerful and effective against the combats of lusts, as charity, through which faith works, through which hope is strengthened, and through which every struggle of the soul is already rewarded in the present with a kind of recompense, while the mind, conscious of good, is daily [Col. 0779A] nourished by the sweetness of this true good.

We have called the exactor the faithful worker, standing in faith, laboring in hope, running in charity, and therefore demanding reward or crown from God, the faithful debtor. All these things are from him. The elect mentioned above ought to know this; and especially that beautiful shoot of God, namely virgins, ought, I say, to know these things and answer against idols speaking what is useless, diviners seeing a lie, and dreamers speaking in vain and offering empty comfort, as has already been said above.

“And they shall be,” he says, “like strong men, like those trampling the mud of the roads in battle; and they shall fight, because the LORD is with them.” “Like strong men,” he says, “like those trampling”: that is, truly strong, truly trampling, as in the saying, “We became like those comforted” (Ps. 125), that is, truly comforted.

Against [Col. 0779B] what are they strong? What do they trample? They are strong against the mud of the roads, trampling the mud of the roads, or dung in the midst of the streets. “The adulterous woman,” Wisdom says, “shall be trampled like dung in the midst of the streets” (Sir. 9). He says two things: “like strong men,” “like those trampling.” Not first trampling and then strong, but first strong and then trampling. For before they conquer lusts, they must fight as strong men; afterward they can trample them as victors, so that, even if they feel a movement of vice, they may be indignant against what they had formerly fought with labor.

And it should be noted that he first supplied three things because he had said, “From him comes the cornerstone, from him the peg, and from him the bow of battle”; and now he says, “They shall be like strong men; they shall be like those trampling; and they shall fight, because the LORD is with them.” Therefore they are strong in the cornerstone [Col. 0779C] of faith, trampling with the peg of hope, fighting with the bow of battle in the strength of charity.

But what need will there be to fight after they have been allowed to trample? This must be understood: after someone has conquered within himself and trampled the mud of the roads, that is, the dung of lusts, it remains for him to fight also for others with the bow of battle, in the strength of charity, with the fervor of good zeal—rebuking, exhorting, reproving—especially those entrusted to him. For, as is customary, it is fitting and expedient that the governance of souls be entrusted not to just anyone, but to a proven and experienced conqueror of lusts.

“And the riders of horses shall be confounded, and I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph.” It is evident both from Scripture and from everyday [Col. 0779D] examples that, by God’s just judgment, confusion of lust follows pride of mind. Further, by what name could the proud be marked more aptly and suitably than by this saying, “riders of horses”? It is as though he said: that glory shall follow the humble, that they may trample the mud of the roads; that confusion shall follow the proud, that they may be befouled by the same mud of the roads.

What, then, does he mean when he immediately says, “And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph”? Concerning the house of Judah it has already been said above that these are those who confess and glorify God almighty as God and give thanks; and for this very reason the Lord made them like the horse of his glory in battle. This is repeated here in a brief statement: “And I will strengthen the house of Judah.” But why, in the present discussion [Col. 0780A], does he mention Joseph, saying, “And I will save the house of Joseph”?

In reply, it must be understood that Joseph is among the best known and noblest conquerors of lust, because he refused to consent to his mistress when she said, “Sleep with me”; though a captive, and because of his fidelity to chastity, he was ensnared by a false accusation and consigned to prison (Gen. 39). Therefore the house of Joseph unquestionably signifies all those who labor for chastity, so that those who hear and remember these things—Joseph’s labors and how the Lord saved him from those very labors—may be stirred to imitate Joseph, and may know by experience that for all who contend for faith and chastity a great reward is prepared and great honor is laid up with God.

“And I will restore them, because I will have mercy on them, and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them [Col. 0780B] off. For I am the LORD their God, and I will hear them; and they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as with wine; and their children shall see and rejoice, and their heart shall exult in the LORD.”

This needs no assertion from us: as he now says, “I will restore them because I will have mercy on them,” there is no other cause of our conversion, because we have been converted, than gratuitous mercy, or merciful and compassionate grace. What he then adds—“and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them off”—in what sense can it be understood better than as if he had said: “They shall be as I held them in predestination”? For before he cast us off in Adam and Eve, whom he expelled from paradise—indeed, before heaven and earth were made—[p. 346] we all were with him, each according to the measure in which he was to grow in merit, and according to the number by which the whole company of the elect was to be completed. And because this will come about not from themselves but from the grace of the Deliverer alone, he rightly continues: “For I am their God, and I will hear them.”

Then, in saying, “And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim,” he has sent us to the sacred and mystical history in which Ephraim, though younger by birth, became first through the blessing of his father crossing his hands. “I know, my son, I know that this Manasseh is the firstborn; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall grow into nations”; and he set Ephraim before Manasseh (Gen. 48). “They shall therefore be like the mighty men of Ephraim”: that is, believers from the Gentiles shall be preferred and shall be more numerous and stronger than the Jews, just as Ephraim, who was younger by birth, was preferred to the elder [Col. 0780D] and became greater than Manasseh, who was first by birth.

“And their heart,” he says, “shall rejoice as with wine”: that is, they shall have joy, not outwardly but inwardly. For they shall suffer persecution from the world, but inwardly they shall be filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit. What he next says—“And their children shall see and rejoice, and their heart shall exult in the LORD”—the reality itself proves today to have been spoken truly. For we, children of the saints and children of the martyrs, to whom they gave birth into the certainty of Christian faith by their blood, see their glory and rejoice; seeing and rejoicing, we venerate them, and our heart exults in the Lord because we have such fathers and patrons with Christ.

“I will whistle for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them; and I will multiply them as they were multiplied before; and I will sow [Col. 0781A] them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me, and they shall live with their children.”

Again and again he impresses and repeats that all the glorious things said or capable of being said of them are not from their merit but from his grace. For what is “I will whistle for them” except, “I will draw them by secret inspiration,” which is like the whisper of a gentle breeze? (3 Kings 19). Therefore, “I will whistle for them”: that is, whatever good they have or can have will be from my Spirit. “And I will gather them,” namely by that same Spirit of mine into the unity of faith, “because I have redeemed them”; because for this purpose I died—because, as the Evangelist says, it was necessary for me to die in order that I might gather into one the children of God who had been scattered (John 2). “And I will multiply them as they were multiplied before”: that is, no others, nor fewer, will believe and be converted than were foreknown and predestined before [Col. 0781B] all ages.

How, or by what increase, Lord, will you multiply them? “And I will sow them,” he says, “among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me.” Here there comes to mind what he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12). For principally he himself was the grain to be put to death and made alive: put to death by the unbelief of the Jews, made alive by the faith of the peoples. But secondarily every one of the saints or martyrs was and is a grain of wheat. Hence it was said above that the grain of the elect is God’s good and beautiful thing (Zech. 9).

When, therefore, the saints are sown after the manner of grain [Col. 0781C], so that through the word of one teacher many are instructed and through the passion of one martyr very often many receive an occasion for believing—those who were far removed from God—does it not become quite clear how truly he said here in prophetic proclamation: “I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me; they shall live with their children,” namely, those who through their labor have been acquired for God and born to eternal salvation?

“And they shall return, and I will bring them back from the land of Egypt; I will gather them from the Assyrians, and bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and no place shall be found for them.”

It is well known that in Scripture Egypt signifies this world, Assyria the devil, and the Assyrians demons. Hence in Isaiah the Lord says: “My people went down at first into Egypt to dwell there as a sojourner, and Assyria [Col. 0781D] oppressed him without any cause” (Isa. 52). The meaning is this: Just as the sons of Jacob went down into that physical Egypt, multiplied there, groaned under bondage as though in a prison (Exod. 1), and afterward the bodily Assyrian, Sennacherib and his multitude (4 Kings 19), and likewise Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, slandered and carried him captive without cause, because he had done nothing against him (4 Kings 17), so in the beginning, when there were only two in paradise, male and female, Adam and Eve, in those two persons all the people of the elect and predestined to life descended into the darkness of this age, where God, the true light, is not seen, and the devil reduced them to the tribute of death, envying and hating them without any cause, since humanity had not caused the devil to fall [Col. 0782A] from heaven.

Further, the land of Gilead and Lebanon is the land of promise. Gilead means “heap of testimony”; Lebanon, “whiteness.” By these names martyrs—that is, witnesses—and all saints of shining confession are plainly signified. Therefore, he says, “They shall return, and I will bring them back from the land of Egypt; I will gather them from the Assyrians, and bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and no place shall be found for them.” That is, they shall turn to me, as it is written: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD” (Ps. 21); and I shall gather into one those rescued from the present evil age and delivered from the power of wicked spirits, as the Evangelist says, “that he might gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11). And I shall bring them to the land [Col. 0782B] of the living, which is the land of Gilead and Lebanon—that is, of the martyrs and all the saints—and their multitude shall be so great that human estimation cannot discover what place, or how large a place, could suffice for them to dwell in.

“And he shall pass through the strait of the sea and strike the waves in the sea; all the depths of the river shall be confounded, the pride of Assyria shall be humbled, and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart. I will strengthen them in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name, says the LORD.”

He still holds us in contemplation of the mystery to which he sent us by saying, “And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt.” That spiritual understanding is not obscure, but very well known even to the little children of the Church: just as Israel went up from Egypt through the Red Sea [Col. 0782C], Pharaoh having been drowned with his chariots and horsemen, in order to possess the land which the Lord had decreed to give them—and did give them—so the whole company of the elect, ascending from the present age, reaches that land of the living only through the sacrament of baptism, the devil being drowned—that is, renounced—together with all his pomps, by the power of that sacrament.

Therefore, when he says, “And he shall pass through the strait of the sea,” the Lord is understood, “and strike the waves in the sea; all the depths of the river shall be confounded; the pride of Assyria shall be humbled; and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart.” He fittingly concludes, as it were, the prophetic narrative—the narrative of works of mercy and compassion—which he had begun in this way: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9). [Col. 0782D]

For “he shall pass through the strait of the sea and strike the waves in the sea” means nothing else than that he will accomplish what was signified in the division of the Red Sea, when Moses, by the Lord’s command, lifted his rod over the waves of the sea (Exod. 14), and the sceptre of Egypt departed—namely, having been struck by Moses’ rod—and could not pursue the children of Israel. More could be said on this subject, but, as has already been said, [p. 347] the mystery of that event is known to almost everyone; and one who dwells too long on familiar matters brings weariness to the reader. Let us therefore pursue the rest.

## Chapter XI
Open, Lebanon, your gates, and let fire devour your cedars. Wail, fir tree, because the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have been laid waste. Wail, oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down. The sound of the wailing of the shepherds, because their magnificence has been laid waste. The sound of the roaring of lions, because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste.

“All the ways of the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Again: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100). According to these two, this passage of prophecy is divided. For from that which was said much earlier, “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth” (Zech. 8), and so forth, up to what is now said, “Open, Lebanon, your gates,” nearly all the promises were promises of mercy, now fulfilled in deed. But from what is said, “Open, Lebanon, your gates,” down to that which is said much later, “His arm shall be dried up with drought, and his right eye, darkening, shall be darkened,” all these things are dreadful pronouncements of truth and tokens of righteous judgment.

How much sweetness, how much pleasantness and delight, is there there in this saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem” (Zech. 9). And, conversely, how much bitterness, severity, and calamity are here for those to whom he says: “Open, Lebanon, your gates, and let fire devour your cedars; wail, fir tree; wail, oaks of Bashan.” Therefore, as hitherto we have considered mercy in those who believed or believe, so from what follows let us consider righteous judgment upon those who did not believe.

“Open,” he says, “Lebanon, your gates.” Lebanon, than whose mountain that land had—or has—nothing more lofty, here signifies the Temple, than which that people had nothing more august. “Open,” that is, you will be unable to close or bar yourself against the Romans or enemies; but let them enter your inner places, “and let fire devour your cedars,” that is, your cedar planks, your gilded panels.

I think Lebanon itself—that is, the Temple—experienced the command of the prophetic voice; for, as Josephus also testifies (*The Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 17), when destruction was imminent, its gates opened without human hands.

“The eastern gate of the inner Temple,” he says, “was bronze and exceedingly heavy. After midday it could scarcely be shut by twenty men, and was secured with iron bars; it had high bolts let down into a stone threshold made from one continuous block. Yet it was seen to open of its own accord at the sixth hour of the night. When this was speedily reported by the Temple guards to their commander, he went up and could scarcely close it.”

Nor is this surprising. For this divine, prophetic voice commanded it: “Open, Lebanon, your gates”; and by such an opening it signified that its gates would immediately be opened to enemies.

The fir tree that is told to wail, and the cedar that has fallen, were those rulers, those proud persons, whom he expresses more openly by saying: “Because the mighty have been laid waste.” And fittingly, as by the name Lebanon he signifies the Temple, so by the names fir tree and cedar he designates the leading Jews and the chief priests, who, as fir and cedar trees on Lebanon, so exalted and magnified themselves in that Temple.

And because, owing to the magnitude of the evils, it is not enough to have said it once, he repeats it in slightly different words: “Wail,” he says, “oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down.” Still more and more he presses the point: “The sound,” he says, “of the wailing of shepherds, because their magnificence has been laid waste; the sound of the roaring of lions, because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste.”

Those whom he had called fir trees, cedars, and oaks, he now calls shepherds and lions; shepherds in name because of their priestly office; lions in deed because they made prey of the people. By the name “fortified forest,” which he says has been cut down, and by the name Jordan, whose pride he says has been laid waste, he signifies the multitude and confidence of the Jewish people, among whom the aforesaid chief priests were as fierce as lions, as stiff and proud or exalted as oaks, cedars, and fir trees.

Who has not heard of the fall of such cedars and fir trees? To whose ears has that wailing not come? “Even to the present day,” says blessed Jerome, “the faithless tenants, after the killing of the servants and, finally, of the Son of God, are forbidden, except for mourning, to enter Jerusalem; and, in order to be permitted to weep for the ruin of their city, they buy the privilege at a price. Thus those who once bought the blood of Christ buy their own tears, and not even their weeping is free. On the day on which Jerusalem was captured and destroyed by the Romans, you may see a mournful people come: feeble old women and old men, worn out by rags and years, gathering together, displaying in their bodies and clothing the wrath of the Lord.”

Surely the same Lord who had said above to those who had fasted and mourned for seventy years because of the destruction wrought by the Babylonians, “Did you fast a fast for me?” (Zech. 7), despises the wailing of these people still more, and far more severely.

Thus says the Lord my God: “Feed the sheep for slaughter, whose possessors killed them and did not grieve, and sold them, saying: ‘Blessed be the Lord, because we have become rich.’ And their shepherds did not spare them. And I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land,” says the Lord.

It must be remembered what we have already said: just as the things previously spoken proclaim the mercy of the King of Zion and Savior of Jerusalem, so these proclaim the judgment of that same King and Judge of all. The prophet says, “Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the sheep for slaughter”; and after a few intervening words the Lord says, “I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land”—which is the same as if he said, “I will not feed.”

Understanding is required here as to how the Lord says, “Feed,” and the Lord says, “I will not feed.” For, if it seems too slight a matter, and if “I will not spare” does not appear to mean the same as “I will not feed,” later he says more plainly: “I will not feed you. What is dying, let it die; and what is being cut off, let it be cut off.”

Accordingly, it seems fitting here to write out the entire portion of the text required by the sense. When the Lord God had said, “Feed the sheep for slaughter, whose possessors killed them and did not grieve, and sold them, saying, ‘Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich’; and their shepherds did not spare them”—when, I say, the Lord had said these things, immediately in reply the Lord said: “And I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land. Behold, I hand over each person into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king; and I will not deliver them from their hand. And I will feed the sheep for slaughter because of this, O poor of the flock. And I took for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I fed the flock. And I cut off three shepherds in one month, and my soul was grieved by them. For their soul was changeable toward me, and I said: ‘I will not feed you. What is dying, let it die; and what is being cut off, let it be cut off; and let those that remain devour, each one, the flesh of his neighbor.’”

Understanding, as we have said, is needed here, because it is the Lord God who says, “Feed the sheep for slaughter,” and the Lord God who says, “I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land.” Likewise, it is the Lord who says, “And I will feed the sheep for slaughter because of this, O poor of the flock”; and it is the Lord who immediately afterwards says, “I will not feed you. What is dying, let it die; and what is being cut off, let it be cut off.”

Therefore, that the door of understanding may be opened more fully, this must first be said: when the Lord saw the city Jerusalem, he wept over it, saying, “If only you too had known” (Luke 19), and the rest. Now that city, that people, was sheep for slaughter: that is, a people destined for everlasting death and eternal perdition.

What then was fitting for the man Jesus Christ—whom indeed the prophet signifies in saying, “Thus says the Lord my God”—to say concerning a city or people of this kind, except, “Feed the sheep for slaughter”? For since in the one and same Jesus Christ we know there to be, as there are two natures, so also two wills, there is no doubt that according to the will of his human nature, by which he could also weep over them, he wished that they might be preserved.

But what would it be to preserve them except to feed sheep for slaughter? For the more worms sprang from the luxuriant flesh of that multitude, the more victims would arise for death or slaughter. Therefore the same Lord Son—or the Lord Father, or the Lord Holy Spirit—says: “I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land.”

But what then? “Behold,” he says, “I hand over each person into the hand of his neighbor,” so that they may clearly be killed and torn apart by one another in internal dissensions, in accordance with their choice of Barabbas, the robber and insurgent, whom, after condemning Jesus Christ the Prince of Peace, they preferred for themselves; “and into the hand of his king,” namely Caesar, who was their king and ought to have been their king, according to their own confession: “We have no king but Caesar” (Matt. 27).

Josephus can satisfy those wishing to know how truly, in that siege, he delivered them each into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king; how truly he said, “They shall lay waste the land”; and how truthfully he further added, “I will not deliver them from their hand.”

Nevertheless, lest the tears of the human will, of which we have already spoken—when, seeing the city, he wept over it (Luke 19)—should arise wholly in vain, he says, “And I will feed the sheep for slaughter,” namely for forty-two years, so that those among them who wished to repent might have time for repentance. For so many years passed from the Passion of the Lord to that wretched destruction.

He shows in a remarkable manner that the cause of that slaughter fell back upon the priests or high priests, when, after saying, “Feed the sheep for slaughter,” he adds: “Whose possessors killed them and did not grieve, and sold them, saying: ‘Blessed be the Lord, because we have become rich.’” And lest there be doubt whom he touches, he immediately adds: “And their shepherds did not spare them.”

Therefore their possessors were most avaricious priests and most rapacious high priests. Such shepherds killed souls and did not grieve; indeed, they rejoiced because from the killing of those souls they gained some monetary advantage. In this way they sold the unhappy people as their own possession, preferring to secure some small profit from those perishing rather than incur, as they feared, loss to their purses through those who lived and followed Christ.

O how unjustly, how impiously, they thought God like themselves when, selling those sheep in this way, they said: “Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich.” Let such blessing of theirs be cursed, for the Lord himself says in another prophet: “I will curse your blessings, and I will curse them, because you have not laid it to heart” (Mal. 2).

“Because of this, O poor of the flock”—you who, because you are poor, that is, humble, have escaped the slaughter, and who perhaps grieve over those sheep for slaughter, as one of you who grieves says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart” (Rom. 9). O poor persons of this kind, he means: attend still to what, or how, I have done with that flock, that you may better recognize how just is the judgment of their slaughter.

“And I took for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I fed the flock. And I cut off three shepherds in one month,” and so forth, as above.

“I took for myself two staffs,” that is, twice I made a covenant with human beings to be their God: first with Noah and with all human beings or nations; second with Abraham and his seed. For to Noah I said: “Behold, I establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you” (Gen. 9). But to Abraham: “I am, and my covenant is with you” (Gen. 15). Again: “I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you, throughout your generations, as an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you” (ibid.).

Therefore I took for myself two staffs: first, the governance of all nations, because I am the Creator of all; then, the governance of Abraham’s seed, because the nations went in their own ways. I called one staff Beauty, and the other I called Cord, because the remaining nations were a certain beauty of mine, the beauty and adornment of the world; but Abraham’s seed was to be the proper cord-measure of my inheritance, as it was said by me to him: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

With that staff which I called Cord I fed the flock: that is, I gave them the Law, whom I led out from Egypt like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. “And I cut off three shepherds in one month”: that is, by my sentence, in one month—the first month—Miriam, Moses, and Aaron died. “And my soul was grieved by them”: that is, I was angry with them, so that I condemned them by a sentence of death.

For what reason? “For their soul was changeable toward me”: that is, they did not glorify me with perfect or continuous love, namely at the waters of contradiction. And he said to them: “Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land which I shall give them” (Num. 20).

It must be known, as we have said above, that all these things, from “Open, Lebanon, your gates,” to what was said above, “The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel,” belong to the grounds of the Lord’s judgment or truth, all whose ways are mercy and truth (Ps. 24). Therefore it was relevant that he should not omit to say that, by a severe judgment, he cut off even shepherds of this kind whom he greatly loved.

Now, if you ask what he did with the other staff, which he called Beauty—he who with the other, called Cord, fed the flock, that is, governed the Israelite or Jewish people—he immediately says: “And I said: ‘I will not feed you. What is dying, let it die; and what is being cut off, let it be cut off; and let those that remain devour, each one, the flesh of his neighbor.’” And in saying these things: “I took,” he says, “my staff called Beauty and cut it off, that I might make void my covenant which I made with all peoples; and it was made void on that day.”

“I fed one flock,” he says—that is, I undertook the governance of one people. But to the remaining nations, in saying, “I will not feed you,” I cut off the staff; or, by cutting off the staff, I said, “I will not feed you.” For what benefit is there in feeding bodies where souls are known to be dead? What dies or is cut off in the soul, let it die and be cut off also in the body.

When I said these things, death did not rest, the sword did not cease; nations were everywhere slaughtering and being slaughtered by one another. Yet, remarkably, those who died and were cut off were born in rivalry and in such madness that even proletarians were settled in cities. What good did this do except to fill hell?

It follows: “And the poor of the flock, who keep watch for me, knew that it was the word of the Lord. And I said to them: ‘If it is good in your eyes, bring my wages; and if not, refrain.’”

“The poor of the flock”—that flock of which I said above, “I fed the flock,” that is, I undertook the governance of the Israelite people and gave them the Law. Who were, or are, the poor of that flock? Holy and humble persons; some of them, even if rich in possessions, were poor in disposition or spirit, as David himself the king. These poor persons knew that it was the word of the Lord: that is, that the judgment upon the nations is righteous.

But when or how did this one who fed the flock say to them, “Bring my wages”? Surely when he gave them the regions of the nations and they possessed the labors of peoples (Ps. 104). Then he said to them, “Bring my wages,” which the Psalmist immediately explains: “That they may keep,” he says, “his ordinances and seek his law” (ibid.). For this is the whole wage of this shepherd; and in this he rejoices that he has been well rewarded, if the flock he feeds seeks and keeps his law and ordinances.

And because a rational flock has free choice, and this shepherd desires a wage not compelled but voluntary, he fittingly says: “If it is good in your eyes, bring it; and if not, refrain.”

But what did they do? What wage did they bring to so great a shepherd? He says: “And they weighed out my wage as thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Throw it to the potter—the splendid price at which I was valued by them.’”

The Jews, or the chief priests and Pharisees, gave thirty pieces of silver to Judas the betrayer in order that he might hand him over to them. He calls those pieces of silver his wage and a splendid price. Who can worthily express in words the measure of the deed, or the character of so great a matter?

That shepherd who had possessed two staffs and, content with one, cut off the other—that is, who, caring for the one flock of the Israelite people, had dismissed from his care the immensely great flock of all nations—that shepherd, such and so great, namely God and Lord of all made man, who had fed this single flock with so much care and in such marvelous ways as we read in the Scriptures, required his wage for himself; and they weighed out such a wage for him: namely, they gave thirty pieces of silver to the betrayer as the price of his blood.

And he calls this a splendid price, surely with the gravest irony, because it was not splendid. Who, then, can adequately weigh or worthily articulate such a thing? Truly no one except God alone, the Potter or Maker (*plastes*). Therefore, he says, “I threw it to the Potter,” and “I threw them into the house of God to the Potter”: namely, that he who alone knows may pronounce the judgment worthy of this matter.

“I threw them”: that is, I caused them to be thrown, namely when Judas, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood”; and, having thrown down the pieces of silver, he went away and hanged himself with a noose (Matt. 27). Who caused this except the one who speaks here: “And I threw them into the house of God”?

Meanwhile, in this text, since it is the Lord who says, “They weighed out my wage,” and the same one says, “The Lord said to me: Throw it to the Potter,” and since this Potter or Maker is plainly God, it is most beautiful here to observe the dialogue of the whole Trinity. For this is a great matter, whose magnitude is also indicated by the fact that, against it, the common Godhead sets forth a judgment not in one but in three persons of its substance.

And what is the sentence of judgment? It follows: “And I cut off my second staff, which was called Cord, that I might dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.”

The sense is this: just as I had cut off the first staff, so I cut off my second staff; that is, just as formerly I said to the whole flock of nations, dissolving into idolatry, “I will not feed you,” so I said much more bitterly to the flock of the Jewish nation, “I will not feed you.” Thus it came about that I dissolved the brotherhood between Judah and Israel: that is, that the evil might be fulfilled of which that former dissolution was a foreshadowing, when the brotherhood between Judah and Israel was dissolved.

At that time the ten tribes separated themselves from the tribe of Judah and from the house of David; they made for themselves king Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim; they separated themselves from the holy and lawful Temple of God; and instead of God they worshiped golden calves (3 Kings 12).

According to that beginning of evils, by which the brotherhood between Judah and Israel was dissolved, I cut off this second staff: so that, just as at that time no one could again unite the ten tribes called Israel with Judah, over whom the house of David reigned—for no king of Israel ever departed from the sins of Jeroboam, that is, the worship of the calves which he made, although many great wonders were done through the prophets, especially Elijah and Elisha, and Israel could not return to the kingdom of the house of David (3 Kings 18)—so no one may be able to unite the Jews with the confessors of Christ or convert them so that they may be willing to submit to the kingdom of the Son of David, the kingdom of Jesus Christ, from whom they severed themselves by denying him before Pilate and crucifying him whom, as has been said, they valued at thirty pieces of silver.

It follows: “And the Lord said to me: ‘Take for yourself again the implements of a foolish shepherd, because behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit what is abandoned, nor save what is broken, nor nourish what stands; but he will eat the flesh of the fat ones and break off their hoofs.’”

“Because,” he says, “I took two staffs, and because, as has been said, this is how it happened—they whom I fed the flock gave me such an evil wage—there is yet one thing that I shall do, as the order of justice and the logic of judgment require. Take for yourself the implements of a foolish shepherd: namely, a bag, staff, pipe, and whistle. For what purpose? ‘Because behold,’ he says, ‘I will raise up a shepherd,’ and so forth.

Just as Isaiah, to show the captivity of the people, walked naked (Isa. 20); and Jeremiah went to the potter’s house, in order by the breaking of the vessel which ran upon the wheel and was formed in the hand of the craftsman to show both Israel’s destruction and God’s power (Jer. 18); and Ezekiel, in order to show not only by speech but also by dress the overthrow of Jerusalem, the flight of Zedekiah, and the burdens of the captives, broke through the wall and was carried upon shoulders (Ezek. 12)—so you too, assume the dress of a shepherd, that you may announce the foolish shepherd who is to come.

Now the foolish and unskilled shepherd is undoubtedly Antichrist, who is said to be coming at the consummation of the world; and what he will be like is indicated. This shepherd will rise against them because the good shepherd who had fed them was rewarded with so wicked a wage and valued by them at so shameful a price.

Hence he says also in the Gospel: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me. If another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5): namely, the foolish shepherd—knowingly opposed to me, not erring through ignorance but resisting through malice.

For it is also written in the Psalm: “The unwise and the fool alike shall perish” (Ps. 48). It must be understood that fool and unwise person differ in this: the unwise person is one who does not know; but the fool is one who knows, yet nevertheless acts contrary to the principle of justice which he knows.

That shepherd will not do what I, the good shepherd, have done. I visited the abandoned; he will not visit the abandoned. I sought the scattered; he will not seek the scattered. I healed the broken—that is, I converted the sinner; he will not heal the broken. I nourish that which stands, while I lead what is good to something better; he will not nourish that which stands—indeed, he will do the opposite. “He will eat the flesh of the fat ones and break off their hoofs”: that is, he will deceive many who appeared wise and will take away the faculty of discernment, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error (Matt. 24).

“O shepherd and idol, abandoning the flock: a sword upon his arm and upon his right eye. His arm shall be dried up with drought, and his right eye, darkening, shall be darkened.”

How fitting is this hostile appellation, “O shepherd and idol,” as addressed to one who is the particular adversary of him who calls him so. For he who calls him is Christ, and that one is so particularly Christ’s adversary that he is called Antichrist, that is, contrary to Christ.

“O shepherd and idol,” he says: falsely a shepherd and truly an idol. Falsely a shepherd, I say, because he abandons the flock; and truly an idol, because he is falsehood. For just as the Son of God is called and is Truth, so you, son of the devil, are rightly called and are falsehood.

You will display yourself as though you were God. Yet you are not merely, I say, a worshiper of idols; rather, you are an idol and not God. You wish to be regarded as the one of whom it is written: “With him are strength and wisdom” (Job 12); but this is not so. Rather, over your arm—that is, over the strength that you boast of—and over your right eye—that is, over the wisdom that you arrogate to yourself—the sword of one stronger and wiser, indeed of the one who alone is strong and alone is wise, has been drawn.

That is the sword by which long ago in heaven your father the devil, and you with him, were struck. And it is astonishing that, though struck, you still live—that is, that you presume to call yourself the living God—when your wound is a mortal wound.

The wonder of this matter is expressed in the Apocalypse in these words: “And one of its heads was, as it were, slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed” (Rev. 13). Again: “Saying to those who dwell on the earth that they should make an image of the beast, which has the wound of the sword and lived.”

Your mortal wound has not truly been healed, nor do you truly live. But you, mad shepherd and dead idol, are healthy and alive only in your display. Such an arm of yours—not true strength but rebellion against the Most High—“shall be dried up with drought”; and such a right eye of yours, wholly left in God’s sight—not true wisdom but truly malice—“darkening, shall be darkened,” so that you may be cast maimed and blind into the depths of hell.

## 351. BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791A] “Willing,” he says, “to show wrath and make known his power, God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might make known the riches of his glory, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9).

The present text of the prophecy reminds us of this truly apostolic saying. For truly the Holy Spirit, with the magnificent grace of the prophetic mouth, sang in the preceding material what riches of his glory God would show in vessels of mercy, especially from the words, “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion” (above, ch. 9), down to “Open, Lebanon, your gates.” And he indicated, from that place down to the cry concerning the arm and right eye of the foolish shepherd, that is, Antichrist, how great vessels of wrath the unbelieving Jews would be.

Accordingly, it was fitting for that same holy prophetic Spirit to declare that the exultation of the daughter of Zion, or the jubilation of the daughter of Jerusalem, which he spoke of or intended, would not be secure in this age, but would be pressed by many human tribulations, according to certain titles of the Psalms inscribed “For the winepresses” (Pss. 8, 80, 83), that is, “For tribulations,” by which the holy Church is pressed in this world, according to the saying: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

It follows, therefore:

## CHAPTER XII

“The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel,” says the Lord, “who stretches out heaven and founds the earth and forms the spirit of man within him. I will make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness to all the peoples round about; and Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem. And it shall be in that day: I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone to all peoples. All who lift it shall be torn by cutting, and all the nations of the earth shall gather against it.”

What is “a threshold of drunkenness” except a house of fullness? Clearly, this cannot in any way be said or understood truly of that earthly Jerusalem. For after it weighed out the aforesaid wage of its shepherd, thirty pieces of silver, it became miserably a house of famine—not only of famine in hearing the word of God, but also of bodily famine, which compelled even mothers to eat the flesh of their children, in accordance with the curse of the Law of Moses:

“You shall be besieged within your gates, and you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters whom the Lord your God has given you, in the distress and desolation with which your enemy shall oppress you” (Deut. 28).

Therefore Jerusalem here, as in many places of Scripture, signifies the Church journeying in this world. While it journeys, although not yet in reality, it is already in hope the heavenly Jerusalem. This is the one which the Lord has made “a threshold of drunkenness,” according to the saying: “In a place of pasture he has set me; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. 22).

For drunkenness is not always spoken of in an evil sense, since the Psalmist says: “The Lord awoke as one asleep, like a mighty man drunk with wine” (Ps. 77). Why, however, is “threshold” here understood as standing for the whole house, and “threshold of drunkenness” as meaning a house of fullness? Plainly because where the refreshment or fullness of the Church was first prefigured, the sign of the feast was commanded to be placed on the threshold and on both doorposts, so that, seeing the blood, the Lord might pass over the door and not allow the destroyer to enter the houses of Israel and harm them. Certainly that lamb which was eaten within signified this (Exod. II). Hence Jerusalem—that is, the house or Church of Christ—deserves in this passage to be called “a threshold of drunkenness.”

This is perceived by all the surrounding peoples. For the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place, among those who are saved and among those who perish; to some indeed a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2). Those for whom this fullness became a fragrance of death unto death are the very ones who besieged Jerusalem.

But what is this which he immediately says: “And Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem”? Surely it is the very thing which the Apostle, after saying, “Perils from my own people, perils from the Gentiles” (2 Cor. 11), and so forth, added as well: “Perils among false brothers.”

Such confessors as bear the Christian name and profess to know God but deny him by their deeds are rightly understood in this place by “Judah,” which is interpreted “confession,” because they are said to be in the siege against Jerusalem.

But that Jerusalem is not such as can easily be moved and carried about by every wind (Titus 1). This is what he says: “I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone to all peoples; all who lift it shall be torn by cutting.” He took this comparison from a custom of the nations, of this kind: in villages, towns, and fortified places, round stones of very great weight were set up, on which young men customarily exercised themselves and lifted them according to their differing strength—some up to the knees, others to the navel, others to the shoulders and head, and some above the crown, displaying the magnitude of their strength with arms raised and hands joined.

“On the citadel of Athens, beside the statue of Minerva,” says blessed Jerome, “I saw a bronze sphere of very great weight, which, because of the weakness of my small body, I could scarcely move. When I asked what it was for, the inhabitants of the city answered that the strength of athletes was tested upon that mass, and that no one went down into a contest before his ability was known through lifting the weight.”

The sense, then, is this: I will make Jerusalem—that is, the Church—like a burdensome stone, against whose weight the forces of all peoples, or all nations of the earth that gather against it, cannot be matched, so that by shaking it they may be able to drive it from the faith of Christ and carry it where they will. Rather, those who try to shake it will themselves be cut down, torn, broken, and tortured with panting breath.

“In that day,” says the Lord, “I will strike every horse with stupor and its rider with madness; and over the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike every horse of the peoples with blindness. And the leaders of Judah shall say in their hearts: ‘May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God.’”

In this passage the house of Judah is not understood in the same sense as above. For there it was said: “And Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem.” But here it is said: “And the leaders of Judah shall say in their hearts, ‘May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened in the Lord.’” Likewise: “Over the house of Judah I will open my eyes”—which opening of the eyes is a remembrance of mercy, an outpouring of grace.

The leaders of this Judah, of whom each will say in his heart, “May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened in the Lord,” were the apostles and are apostolic men. It was and is their great desire that the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, the children of the Church—should not fail in the tribulations inflicted upon them by every horse and its rider, that is, by every human power and by everyone who is exalted in the height of power.

Whom, therefore, “I will strike,” says the Lord, “with stupor, madness, and blindness”—and, as the Apostle says, first the Jew and then the Greek, that is, the Gentile (Rom. 2). For the Jews were first struck with madness and blindness, according to the prophecy which says: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes” (Isa. 6), and so forth.

Conversely: “Over the house of Judah I will open my eyes,” that is, I will illuminate my leaders—my apostles—with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. These leaders became fiery on the day of Pentecost when they received the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire, as it is written: “And divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them, and rested upon each of them” (Acts 2).

It follows, therefore:

In that day I will make the leaders of Judah like a fiery brazier among wood, and like a flame among hay; and they shall devour to the left and to the right all the peoples round about. Hay signifies lighter sins; wood, graver sins. [Col. 0793D] The apostles consumed such hay and such wood in those converted to faith in Christ, by the power received from him who said to them: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). How did they consume them, or how do they consume them? As a fiery brazier consumes wood, as the face of fire consumes hay (Deut. 4). For our God, the Holy Spirit whom they received, is a consuming fire; hence he also gave a fitting sign by appearing as fire. Accordingly, the remission of sins—which comes not from human beings but from the Holy Spirit—is rightly signified here by the fiery brazier and face of fire, consuming wood and hay: devouring the peoples, that is, the sins of the peoples, on the right and on the left and round about. On the right was the Jew; on the left [Col. 0794A] the Greek, or Gentile. They had to go about on either side, preaching the remission of sins through faith in Christ; hence some called Paul a circuit-rider of the world. In short, what immediately follows came to pass:

And Jerusalem shall again be inhabited in its own place, in Jerusalem; and the Lord shall save the tents of Judah as at the beginning, so that the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not boast magnificently against Judah. Although the whole body of the elect is one Jerusalem, one Judah, and one house of David, nevertheless in this place Scripture compels us to seek, find, or demonstrate a distinction between Judah and Jerusalem, or the house of David: when, where, and how [Col. 0794B] the house of David and the glory of Jerusalem’s inhabitants boasted greatly against Judah. Thus we understand by the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem those Jews who believed in Christ; by Judah, those converted from the Gentiles. Surely in the Acts of the Apostles we have when and how Jewish believers boasted greatly against those who believed from among the Gentiles. “Why,” they ask, “did you go in to uncircumcised men and eat with them?” (Acts 11). For he had entered Cornelius’s house and, because the Holy Spirit had fallen upon those with him, commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Again, certain men coming down from Judaea taught the brethren at Antioch that unless they were circumcised [Col. 0794C] according to the custom of Moses, they could not be saved; and no small dissension arose between them and Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15). Was this not the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem boasting greatly against Judah—that is, believers from the circumcision against believers from the uncircumcision?

The Apostle Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans (Rom. 2), devotes himself wholly to excluding this kind of Jewish boasting, not by the law of works but by the law of faith. And behold: in this conflict righteousness grants victory not to the house of David but to Judah—not to the believing Jew but to the faithful Greek. Therefore he says: “The Lord shall save the tents of Judah as at the beginning,” that is, he shall save the Church of those who confess him, not by the law of works—namely circumcision and ceremonies—but by the law [Col. 0794D] of faith, by which Abraham too was saved in the beginning. For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 18; Rom. 4). How was faith reckoned to him as righteousness? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision; for he had not yet been circumcised.

In this manner what was said before will happen: “Jerusalem shall again be inhabited in its own place, in Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, he says, shall be inhabited in Jerusalem: that is, the whole company of the elect shall have peace with God, namely remission of sins; and this peace is signified by the name Jerusalem. The word “again” also has some bearing on the matter, because it had formerly begun to dwell in that place, the Paradise of delights, namely in Adam; and just as all sinned in him, so all [Col. 0795A] who were set there in him were cast out from there in him. Hence Isaiah says to this same Jerusalem: “Your children have been cast out; they have slept at the head of all the streets, like a trapped beast, full of the Lord’s indignation and the rebuke of your God” (Isa. 5).

In that day the Lord shall protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and whoever stumbles among them in that day shall be like David; and the house of David shall be like the house of God, like the Angel of the Lord before them. The day so often foretold here is the whole time from Christ’s resurrection until the Day of Judgment, which will be the day of the universal resurrection. Indeed, in one and the same place the Lord calls all this time both “day” and “time” in Isaiah, saying: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49). The Apostle briefly explains this: “Behold,” he says, [Col. 0795B] “now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). In this time, in this day, the Lord protects the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, the whole multitude of those believing in him—so that, as the Apostle says, there is no distinction between Jew and Greek (Rom. 3).

For this is what he says: “Whoever stumbles among them in that day shall be like David.” This may suitably be understood as follows: the Gentile who stumbles in worshipping idols shall be like the Jew, who worshipped only one God and therefore trusts in himself and exalts himself above the Gentile—so much so that, to settle the dispute, it was necessary for the Apostle to argue most forcefully in writing the Epistle to the Romans. Nor should we pass over the fact that this expression subtly suggests the Apostle’s meaning when, having recounted the sins of the Gentiles, he turns to the Jew and says: “In judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things which you judge” (Rom. 2). That is, [Col. 0795C] “whoever stumbles among them in that day shall be like David.” For David too stumbled.

Therefore, as was already said—“so that the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not boast greatly against Judah”—so it must now be said that neither can be preferred to the other, namely the Jew to the Gentile, since “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3). Thus the sins of the Jew, like those of the Gentile, shall be forgiven through faith in Jesus Christ (ibid.); and this is for the one who has stumbled to be like David, and David like the one who has stumbled. [Col. 0795D] And lest you perhaps say: “What great thing is it for one who has stumbled—that is, a Gentile—to be made equal in grace through Jesus Christ to a Jew?” he immediately says: “And the house of David shall be like the house of God, like the Angel of the Lord before them.” Therefore the one who stumbles ought to rejoice that he is like David, that is, like a Jew of the same faith as David; because consequently he too, equally with that Jew, is like the house of God, like the Angel of the Lord. Thus the one and uniform fellowship of angels and human beings, Gentiles as well as Jews, is one house, one heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God; and this is “before them,” that is, in the vision in which all alike shall see God.

“And it shall be in that day that I shall seek to turn away all the nations that come against Jerusalem.” This needs no explanation or interpretation of gentleness or mildness. For although this verb can sometimes signify mercy, nevertheless no one doubts or is ignorant that, on that Day of Judgment, the Lord must turn away all the nations that come against Jerusalem, those which shed the blood of so many martyrs and did not repent. But first the remnant from the Jews must be converted. Therefore he says:

And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers. They are not yet the house of David or inhabitants of Jerusalem while they remain unbelieving; but by pouring out upon their remnant the spirit of grace and prayers—that is, the spirit of remission of sins, which is the first and great gift of grace—it shall come about that they become the house [Col. 0796B] of David and inhabitants of Jerusalem. After this shall come that Day of Judgment of which he said: “In that day I shall seek to turn away all the nations that come against Jerusalem.” Hence there immediately follows:

And they shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with lamentation, as for an only-begotten son; and they shall grieve for him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn. In that day the lamentation of Hadadrimmon in the plain of Megiddo shall be great; and the families of the land shall mourn, family by family. The family of the house of David by itself, and their women by themselves; the family of the house of Nathan by itself, and their women by themselves; the family of the house of Levi by itself, and their women by themselves; the family of Shimei by itself, and their women by themselves. And all the remaining families, family by family, and their women by themselves.

Hadadrimmon is a city [Col. 0796C] near Jezreel, once called by this name and now called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Megiddo. There the righteous King Josiah was wounded by Pharaoh, surnamed Necho; over him Jeremiah wrote lamentations, which are read in the Church, and the book of Chronicles testifies that he wrote them (2 Chron. 35). But when what is spoken here shall occur—“they shall look upon me whom they pierced, and shall mourn with lamentation as for an only-begotten son”—will there not, I ask, be a greater mourning than there was for the death of righteous King Josiah?

That lament was indeed great and wisely ordered: the family of the house of David, the royal family; the family of the house of Nathan, who was a prophet; the family of the house of Levi, from whom the priesthood sprang; [Col. 0796D] the family of the house of Shimei, from whom companies of teachers arose; and the remaining families, all of whom he includes without names because they had no privilege of rank—all mourned him, men separately and women separately. Yet however great that mourning was, it is nothing compared with the magnitude of the future lamentation, when he whom they pierced shall appear to be seen. He mentions that mourning here only on account of a certain slight resemblance, as very great matters are sometimes more clearly understood through comparison with smaller matters.

It was a small thing that men mourning for a man arranged the manner and order of their lamentation thus: each family separately, and within each family the men separately and the women separately [Col. 0797A] mourning apart. But it will be a great thing that, in that lamentation, all tribes of the earth—and especially those who pierced him, indeed all sinners and impious persons who did not repent—will mourn separately. Although all will be gathered for one judgment and all descend to one prison, that is, hell, each soul will be apart from every other soul, much occupied with itself and looking neither upon friend nor companion.

Again, it is a small thing that in this world a mother mourns for an only son or grieves at the death of a firstborn. But it will be a great thing that then they shall mourn and grieve for the true Firstborn, the true Only-begotten. For what is this, O Synagogue, unhappy mother? The only-begotten Son of God, born from your flesh, is dead to you. He is dead to you, I say, not only because you killed him, but also because you do not believe that he has risen, do not wish to know that he is alive, and cannot bear to hear it. [Col. 0797B] And yet, however grievous it may be, it is a tolerable evil when, in this world, a mother loses in death a son whom she had as her only one, even though she hopes that no other will be born to her. But it cannot be told or adequately conceived how utterly miserable it is to have lost the one and only Saviour, so that now it is permitted neither to recover him nor to have another. There follows:

## Chapter XIII

In that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman. And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts: I will destroy the names of idols from [Col. 0797C] the land, and they shall no longer be remembered. The discourse returns again to the earlier times; this return is called recapitulation and is frequent in the prophetic Scriptures. From the words, “You also, by the blood of your covenant, sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9), through the lamentation just mentioned, the discourse proceeded in the same order as the events were to occur: from the Passion of the same Lord to the end of the age and the Day of universal Judgment. Now it returns to the time of the Lord’s Passion itself, and to the point from which it had spoken in saying, “You also, by the blood of your covenant, sent forth your prisoners from the pit.” It now speaks again from that point: “In that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David.” For what is this fountain of the house of David except the sacrament of baptism, which flowed from the side of the Son of David when it was opened by the soldier’s spear? [Col. 0797D] “For blood and water came forth” (John 19): blood, that we might be redeemed; water, that we might be reborn. From then until the consummation of the age, throughout this acceptable time, throughout this day of salvation, that fountain stands open to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, to the Christian religion and to all who dwell through faith within the holy Church.

354 For what purpose is the fountain open to them? “For the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman”: that is, for the remission of sins in the believer from the circumcision and in the believer from the Gentiles, who flowed with the blood of idolatry. The fountain is open for the washing of all; it must be closed to none. And it should be noted that the fountain is said to be open, and is open, only to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. For those who are opposed to the house of David and outside Jerusalem, because they do not have faith, it is a garden enclosed, [Col. 0798A] a fountain sealed (Song 4). And it fittingly follows at once:

“In that day,” says the Lord of hosts, “I will destroy the names of idols from the land, because they shall no longer be remembered.” For the flow of idolatry, which is the blood of the menstruous woman, is washed away by the fountain of baptism, so that all names of idols are erased and are no longer remembered in the person upon whom they had been written, once he has been faithfully washed in that fountain. Hence the same Lord says in Ezekiel: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and I will cleanse you from all your idols” (Ezek. 36).

And I will remove the prophets and the unclean spirit from the land. And it shall come to pass, if anyone shall prophesy further, that his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: “You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.” And his father and mother, his parents, shall pierce him when he prophesies. And it shall be in that day that the prophets shall each be ashamed of his own vision when they prophesy; nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie. But he shall say: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who cultivates the soil, for Adam has been my example from my youth.” And it shall be said to him: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” And he shall say: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me. Sword, rise against my shepherd and against the man joined to me,” says the Lord of hosts. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.”

The soul intent upon Christ desires to treat the most beautiful and splendid letter of this present chapter in such a way that deeds of no lesser splendour may be built upon it as upon a foundation. He had said: “In that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman”; and Christ unquestionably poured out that fountain from his side in his Passion. Therefore, since the passage also ends, “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered”—which, on the authority of Christ himself, is certainly spoken likewise concerning his Passion—let us not stray far away, but linger in expounding these things concerning the mystery of that same Passion.

Whom then does he touch when he says, “the prophets and the unclean spirit,” joining the two together? Who were, at that time, the evil prophets who possessed an unclean spirit? Surely those who prophesied this evil prophecy for themselves from their own heart: [Col. 0798D] “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11). Indeed, except for what they first said—“If we let him go on thus”—all that they said was reckoned to them as prophecy: that all would believe in him; and, because they themselves did not believe, that the Romans would come and take away both their place and nation.

Among them was one Caiaphas, the greatest of such prophets. Since he was high priest that year, he possessed authority to pronounce: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.” The Evangelist says: “He did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied [Col. 0799A] that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11). Such prophets and the unclean spirit, which, ignorant of the mysteries of God, inspired such prophecy in them—“I will remove,” he says, “from the land,” because it is just that the Romans should come and that what they imagined in fear should happen to them.

“And it shall be, if anyone shall prophesy further,” and so forth. The great Prophet prophesied further concerning himself, because they—and Caiaphas especially—prophesied that it was expedient for him to die; but he himself prophesied that it was necessary also for him to rise from the dead. This was “further,” that is, beyond their prophecy, the prophecy of death, because he prophesied the prophecy of resurrection. For he said: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will raise it up.” But he spoke of the temple of his body (John 2).

Therefore, when someone shall prophesy further—someone whom I do not wish to name, because it is not expedient—his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: “You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.” His father was the Jewish people and his mother the Synagogue, who begot him according to the flesh; and this is what they said to him. For when they had nothing else with which to accuse him, finally, having brought forward two false witnesses, they alleged: “This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 26). And when, in answer to the chief priest’s demand, “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God,” he replied, “You have said it; and henceforth you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven,” they cried out: “He is guilty of death” (ibid.). Was this not to say: “You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord”?

“And his father and mother who begot him shall pierce him when he prophesies.” As it was said, so it was done. When he had prophesied—that is, not before, but after he had completed the appointed time of his preaching—then at last, because before this they could not, they crucified him. This, I say, came to pass because they crucified him, not because he had spoken a lie, but because they said: “You have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord, and therefore you shall not live.”

“And it shall be: in that day the prophets shall each be ashamed of his own vision when they have prophesied.” This too came to pass. [Col. 0799D] Those prophets just mentioned, who said, “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” (John 11), one of whom said, “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people,” were put to shame by their own vision, by their own deep counsel. For in a wonderful way, although what they thought did not occur, what they said did occur: all did believe in him, and through his death he gathered into one the scattered children of God. The Romans came and took away their place and nation, not because they let him go on thus, but because they did not let him go on thus. Hence came great shame to them, but honour to us who believe.

“They shall not,” he says, “cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie”—understand, as they were then covered, because, as has been said, they prophesied in such a manner, lying in prophesying and prophesying in lying. How were they then covered with a sackcloth mantle? Surely like sad hypocrites (Matt. 6)—indeed, more than hypocrites and more than sad, because they were murderers and cruel. The fear which they feigned before the people, saying, “The Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11), and that dreadful necessity of committing so great a murder which they assumed in order to embitter and incite the people so that they should not let him go, was the sackcloth mantle in which those deceptive and cunning men had already clothed themselves, so that they might appear very reluctant, very compelled, and consequently grieved to kill him.

But he shall say: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who cultivates the soil, 355 for Adam has been my example from my youth.” And it shall be said to him: “What are these wounds [Col. 0800B] in the midst of your hands?” And he shall say: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.” We must carefully observe the change of persons, because the discourse now concerns several prophets, now one prophet. At first it was said concerning several: “I will remove the prophets and the unclean spirit from the land”; and at once concerning one it was added: “And it shall be, if anyone shall prophesy further.” Again, concerning several it was said: “And it shall be in that day that the prophets shall be ashamed; nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie”; and at once concerning one it was added: “But he shall say, ‘I am not a prophet,’” and so forth.

This must also be understood: Scripture itself convicts those many men of wickedness and an unclean spirit. But it does not convict this one man of falsehood; rather, it recounts that his father and mother said, “You have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.” Now let us attentively hear what this man says and what is said to him. “But he shall say: ‘I am not a prophet’; and it shall be said to him: ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he shall say: ‘With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.’”

It is very remarkable, but not unknown, that he whom father and mother pierced and to whom they said, “You shall not live,” is the one who will speak; that he who was dead will speak; that, while speaking, he will have wounds in the midst of his hands and say: “With these I was wounded.” What is lacking here in the prophetic letter except that he plainly said: “He who was pierced and died shall rise again and, standing in the midst of his disciples, shall say: ‘See my hands and my feet,’ or, ‘Put your finger here,’ or, ‘Put your hand here, and recognize the places of the nails’?” (John 20).

Surely something, however slight, had to be lacking in the letter; for who at that time could have borne it? If even the apostles could not bear it before Jesus was glorified, when he said to them, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16), how much less could these and similar matters have been borne at the time when they were written, unless they had been closed and sealed? Hence the wisdom of the Holy Spirit is to be admired and praised: through the mouths of the prophets, he spoke in such a manner about what would one day need to be known that his words were not understood when they ought not to have been understood.

Therefore, he says, those prophets “shall not cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie”; but with their heads uncovered—as the holy law commands the head of an adulterous woman to be uncovered (Num. 5)—with their heads uncovered, that is, with the city and temple, or place, removed, which had been their adornment and for the sake of which they covered themselves by feigning fear, he who was pierced shall say. After he has been pierced, he will be able to speak, because he shall rise from the dead: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who cultivates the soil.”

He can say this in mocking fashion, since he is Wisdom, who speaks in parables: “I too will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1). Thus this is said with the gravest irony: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who cultivates the soil, for Adam has been my example from my youth”—understand, “in your estimation”—because this is how you wished and how you falsely said: “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee” [Col. 0801B] (John 7). Again: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” (ibid.). And: “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 13). Therefore let him say: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who cultivates the soil,” or, in the same sense, “I am a carpenter,” because “Adam has been my example,” that is, “I am a sinful man like Adam, from my youth”—that is, from the point at which human nature has discernment of good and evil. And I am such, likewise, in your judgment, because you said on another occasion: “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner” (John 9).

Nevertheless, whatever you may say, it is now clear whether a prophet could arise from Galilee, at least from what I said concerning you: “They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations” (Luke 21), and so it happened. It is now clear, I say, whether I, as a cultivator or carpenter, ought not to have known letters, when on the contrary I have made and sent to you so many prophets and so many wise men. And it is now clear whether I was a sinner after Adam’s example, when you received so great and such a punishment because of this blood of mine.

Here is the gravest irony, that is, a statement which in its expression bears the contrary meaning; or even sarcasm, that is, hostile mockery, in accordance with the passage from Wisdom already cited: “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1), and that in the Psalm: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them” (Ps. 2).

But the words may also rightly be understood otherwise, truly and simply, as the letter sounds. For if John, questioned by those who said, “Are you a prophet?” could answer truthfully, “No” (John 1), because he was more than a prophet—for a prophet announces things to come but does not also show them—how much more may this one do so, who is not merely in some way more than a prophet but is also Lord of the prophets, and who not only announced or showed future things, but himself brought about those things which he announced or foretold. He himself is also a cultivator of the soil. Surely he is such and so great a cultivator that his field is the world: “He who sows the good seed,” he says, “is the Son of Man; and the field is the world. The good seed are the children of the kingdom” (Matt. 13).

Therefore: “I am not only a prophet, but I am a man who cultivates the soil”—that is, I am greater than the prophets and all the children of the kingdom by as much as the cultivator is greater than, and better than, the seed he has sown. And truly, “Adam has been my example.” For when the Apostle had said, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” he immediately added, “who is a figure of the one to come”; and, explaining what he had said, he continued: “For if many died through one man’s offence,” and so on, up to: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. 5).
