Therefore, he says: “I am not a prophet, but I am the man who was God and am man; and, having become man, I have sown, as a cultivator in the field of this world, the prophets and every good seed—that is, all the children of the kingdom—and I do not cease sowing until the consummation of the age, because Adam has been my example.” That is, just as, because of Adam’s sin, the soil of the flesh produced for him not children of the kingdom but thorns and thistles, so because of my righteousness the soil of the Holy Spirit—of which it is written, “Your good Spirit shall lead me into the right land” (Ps. 142)—may produce for me not thorns and thistles but children of the kingdom. In this Adam has been my example from my youth, that is, from the human nature from which, or in which, I was made visible and became a visibly labouring cultivator whose entire cultivation is spiritual.

He says these things when he has been pierced, has died, and risen; and it shall be said to him: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” For how long, and in what manner, and by whom or by what persons, do you think this will be said to him? Surely it will be said to him without ceasing for ages of ages; it will be said in ineffable wonder by God the Father, to whom he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2); it will be said by the holy angels, who long to look into him; and it will be said by the human beings whom he redeemed by his death (1 Pet. 1). It will be said to him: [Col. 0802C] 356 “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” O great miracle, wonderful spectacle, especially in the Lord who rules all, to have wounds in the midst of his hands! And he shall say: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.” O great sacrilege, sacrilegious murder: that such wounds were inflicted in the house of those who loved him! He shall not say, “With these I was wounded by those who loved me,” but “in the house of those who loved me.” For those who inflicted the wounds did not love me. Yet theirs were the houses of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and others such as these, who loved me and awaited me, who had been promised to them.

Yet to say this is not to answer the question, “What are these wounds?” For it is one thing to ask, “What are these wounds?” and another to ask, “Where were these wounds made?” The question is: what are these wounds? Therefore he will say additionally: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me,” and then at last he will say what the wounds are. He will say: “It is the cup which the Father gave me to drink” (Matt. 26). For what immediately follows has equivalent force, because the voice which follows is the voice of the Father giving the cup:

“Sword, rise against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me,” says the Lord of hosts. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.” As though he said: “You ask what these wounds are, and I tell you that they are testimonies of obedience, signs of the Father’s will and command. The Lord of hosts, God the Father, did not spare me, his own Son (Rom. 8), but delivered me up for you all. And he said: ‘Sword, rise against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me.’”

That is to say: “O death, prevail against my Son, my good shepherd, against the man who cleaves to me”—that is, joined in unity of person to the Word, who is consubstantial with me. At this saying, as though the sword were asking, “How, or to what extent, shall I rise against this shepherd of yours?” he immediately declares: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.” Hence, while the shepherd himself was being struck, he spoke thus: “All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night. For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered’” (Matt. 26).

Therefore, to those who say, “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” the voice of the Father is fittingly added: “Sword, rise against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me; strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.” The sense is: They are memorials of paternal love and signs of my obedience, because he did not spare me, his own Son (Rom. 8), and I became obedient to him for you all unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2). There follows:

“And I will turn my hand upon the little ones; and in all the land there shall be two parts, and they shall perish and fail, but a third part shall be left in it; and I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as gold is burned, and test them as silver is tested.”

After the shepherd has been struck, and the sheep have been scattered—while the shepherd himself wills it and says, “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way” (John 18)—“I will turn,” he says, “my hand upon the little ones”; that is, I will reveal to the little ones the mystery of the striking by which the shepherd was struck.

Throughout the whole land there will indeed be, besides the little ones, two parts: one part of the wise and one part of the prudent [Col. 0803D]; that is, one part of Jews and one part of Gentiles, trusting in their own wisdom and pleasing themselves in their own prudence. Hence the shepherd who was struck—or the striking of the shepherd—will be a stumbling-block to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles. There will be, I say, two such parts: one of the wise and one of the prudent. But I will hide these things both from the wise and from the prudent, and reveal them to the little ones (Matt. 11), that is, to the humble.

What shall I reveal to them? Surely, that the struck shepherd—that is, Christ Jesus crucified—is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The prudent Jews will be scattered among all nations, body and soul; the wise Greeks will fail as captives, worn out by opposition or persecution. But the third part will remain in him: the Christian part, the part of the little ones, to whom, as I have already said [Col. 0804A], I will turn my hand.

This is the source of that confession by the same shepherd: “I confess to thee, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). Certainly, the wise and prudent already mentioned will afflict the little ones; from among them they will scourge, crucify, and persecute them from city to city, and will even burn some of them with fires. Yet all these things will work together for good to the little ones. For through these sufferings which they endure I will burn them as gold is burned, and I will test them as silver is tested.

According to this comparison of silver and gold, which is tested by fire, all these things will work together for their good. Hence, in blessed Job, the Church of the little ones—or some individual little one of this kind—rejoices and says: “But he himself knows my way, and he will test me like gold that passes through fire. My foot has followed his steps; I have kept his way and have not departed from his commandments” (Job 23) [Col. 0804B].

“He will call my name, and I will hear him. I will say, ‘You are my people,’ and he will say, ‘The Lord is my God.’ And behold, the days of my Lord will come, and spoils shall be divided in your midst.”

Who is it that will call my name, if not a little one, or the people of the little ones? He will call my name—namely, God and Father of his Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1). For this is my name; and in this name I will hear him and console him in all his tribulation.

Is it not a great thing that I should say, “You are my people,” and that he should say, “The Lord [Col. 0804C] is my God”? For blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen for his own inheritance. Let him therefore say, “You are my people”; let me say, “Behold, the days of the Lord will come, and I will divide spoils in your midst”—namely, the distributions of the gifts of the Holy Spirit and revelations of the mysteries of the kingdom of God, which are indeed precious spoils.

Thus the Psalmist says: “I will rejoice over thy words as one who finds abundant spoil” (Ps. 118). Likewise: “The king of powers is of the beloved, of the beloved; and the beauty of the house is to divide spoils” (Ps. 67).

What follows:

## Chapter XIV
And I will gather all nations against Jerusalem for battle; the city will be taken, the houses plundered, the women violated, half the city will go out into captivity, and the remainder of the people will not be removed from the city. Then the Lord will go forth and fight against those nations, as he fought on the day of battle. [Col. 0804D]

Where he said, “I will turn my hand against the little ones, and in all the land two parts shall be cut off, and a third part shall be left,” he also spoke of the two parts: “they shall be destroyed and perish.” Now he states as plainly how they are destroyed and perish as we see with our own eyes that it has happened. For all nations gathered in battle against that earthly Jerusalem—namely, the Romans, rulers drawn from all nations; the city was taken, houses plundered, and women undoubtedly violated, as victors commonly do at their pleasure; and half the city, namely that part which survived the sword, went out into captivity.

It should be noted that he did not say “half the multitude,” but “half the city” [Col. 0805A], which was far fewer. For those who fell by the sword, and those enclosed within who died of hunger, were far more numerous than those led away captive; yet not all of them were the people of the city. People had gathered from all 357 regions, as Josephus reports, for the feast day of Unleavened Bread, and were suddenly surrounded by war (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VII, ch. 25). The total number of captives taken during the whole war was ninety-seven thousand, while the number killed throughout the siege was one million one hundred thousand.

The multitude that had come from so many regions for the feast, shut up within and having no provisions—neither having made provision nor foreseen the siege—more quickly ended its wretched life within through the torture of famine. But the people of the city, though enduring for a longer time in great scarcity [Col. 0805B], did not all perish inside from hunger: half came into the victor’s hands and went out into captivity. What of the remaining part of the city, or of the people? “It shall not,” he says, “be removed from the city.” Why shall it not be removed? Because the victor will have no need of it. For it will be dead by sword, famine, and fire, along with the rest of the incoming multitude.

In this manner the Jews, who were one of the parts mentioned above, will be destroyed. How will the other part—namely, the pagans—perish? “The Lord,” he says, “will go forth and fight against those nations”—understand: with the sword of his mouth, by the power of his Spirit—“as he fought on the day of battle,” that is, according to the mystical likeness of the battle in which he drowned the Egyptians in the sea. He will go forth in that very going forth which Isaiah foresaw [Col. 0805C], when “the law shall go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

And it came to pass that, just as Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen was drowned in the sea, so those nations and their rulers—the kings, Caesars, consuls, governors, priests of temples, and high priests—together with their idols and their entire fanatical cult, passed away and were reduced to nothing. And behold, the third part remains: the Christian part has been left.

“And his feet shall stand in that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives shall be split in its midst eastward and westward by a very great cleft valley. And half the mountain shall be separated to the north, and half of it to the east; and you shall flee to the valley of their mountains [Col. 0805D], because the valley of the mountains joins onto the adjoining place; and you shall flee as you fled before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. And the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with him.”

The Lord’s feet are the beautiful feet—the apostles. These feet, he says, shall stand upon the Mount of Olives, that is, upon the faith of the patriarchs and prophets; they shall dwell in the Scriptures and speak according to the authority of the Scriptures which proceed from him. He fittingly says of that mountain that it is “opposite Jerusalem on the east,” because the holy Scripture of the patriarchs and prophets is altogether opposed to that earthly Jerusalem and altogether directs its attention to that East of which this same prophet said much earlier: “Behold, says the Lord, I will bring my servant, the East” (Zech. 3).

It is so opposed to that Jerusalem that it sometimes even calls her Sodom or Gomorrah, as in this passage: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). [Col. 0806A] It is so directed to the East—that is, so intent upon Christ—that he himself cannot be known, nor can its meaning be discovered, except by one who, in reading or hearing, looks toward Christ.

“And the Mount of Olives,” he says, “shall be split in its midst eastward and westward by a very great cleft valley.” The Mount of Olives was split in its midst because the heart of the fathers withdrew from their children, and the heart of the children from their fathers. One part of the mountain is toward the east and one toward the west, because the heart of the fathers looks toward Christ and the light of faith, whereas the heart of the children, looking toward Antichrist, suffers the blindness of the setting sun.

Again he says: “And half shall be separated to the north, and half of it to the east.” What is separated to the north is the same as what he had called being split to the west; but he repeats it in order to introduce the remnant that will be converted when “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered” (Rom. 11): “and half of it to the east.” Between the fathers, who long ago were split from their children toward the east, as has been said, and those children who will at last be separated eastward through faith, there is a very great cleft, a great interval [Col. 0806B], indeed large enough to receive the great multitude of Gentiles entering in.

The apostolic truth agrees with this interpretation when it says: “Some of the branches were broken off; but you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted among them and became a sharer in the richness of the olive tree” (ibid.). “And you shall flee,” he says, “to the valley of their mountains, because the valley of the mountains shall join onto the adjoining place.” Today we see that the Jews flee the height of the mountains, where the light of truth is; they thrust themselves back into the valley beneath the mountains, loving their darkness and unable to endure the sight of the sun’s face, which lies open upon the mountains.

“You shall flee,” he says, “because the valley of the mountains shall join onto the adjoining place”; that is, because the Gentiles, passing beyond you, will fill your place, and the cleft will not remain empty. Thus the former mountain of the fathers and the latter portion of the children, with the Gentiles grafted between them, will become one Mount of Olives, one people of saints. Meanwhile, how will you flee? “As you fled,” he says, “before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah.” The same thing was signified by that earthquake [Col. 0806D] which occurred in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, when he attempted to claim for himself an unlawful priesthood and was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chron. 26).

Therefore you, O Jews, are leprous, because, in accordance with this comparison, conscious of a leprous forehead, you flee to the valley. Your priesthood will no longer exist. You will dwell in a separate house, after the likeness, as has been said, of King Uzziah; and theirs is and shall be the priesthood—of all those whose foreheads, from which you flee, are renowned and radiant—according to that saying: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

“And the Lord my God shall come,” he says, “and all the saints with him. And in that day there shall not be light, but cold and frost; and there shall be one day, known to the Lord God, neither day nor night.” This is the end of all things. Thus, he says [Col. 0807A], “the Lord my God shall come,” just as they saw him going into heaven (Acts 1). Though the wicked flee, they cannot escape; all the saints will come with him, not ashamed, not having leprosy on their foreheads, and therefore, with unveiled foreheads and glad hearts, will meet him, stand by him, and sit around him.

And in that day, O fugitives, what I say will happen to you: “There shall not be light, but cold and frost.” How, then, will you escape then, you who flee now, if there is no light but cold and frost? What is it to flee in frost and cold, and without light? Therefore it shall happen to you as the Spirit, in the Psalm, grants by righteous judgment: “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them” (Ps. 34).

By contrast, for the saints there will be eternal light, an unfailing day. This is what he immediately says: “And there shall be one day, known to the Lord God.” For who else knows that day but the Lord God? “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” what kind of day he has prepared for his saints (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). And why do I call it a day? “It shall be neither day nor night,” he says. That is to say: when I say “day,” someone judges this term in its ordinary sense; but according to its proper meaning, it will be neither day nor night—that is, there will be neither sunrise nor sunset. But what then? “At evening time there shall be light”: after all ages of ages [Col. 0807B], however many can be counted or imagined, there shall be light, and unfailing light will be awaited.

“And in that day living waters shall go out from Jerusalem: half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the last sea. They shall be in summer and in winter; and the Lord shall be king over all the earth.” “We believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4): this day is the day of resurrection, which he announces and repeats when he says, “And in that day.” This day extends from the morning watch of the Lord’s resurrection to the universal resurrection, and beyond.

“Living waters,” he says, “shall go out from Jerusalem.” From what Jerusalem? Surely from the heavenly Jerusalem, Jerusalem the city of the living God, where there is the vision of the Blessed Trinity. From there, he says, living waters shall go forth—waters, I say, of the resurrection of the dead. That resurrection of the dead is twofold: there is the resurrection of souls, the first resurrection, which is the remission of sins; and there is the resurrection of bodies [Col. 0807C], the second resurrection, by which “all who are in the tombs shall come forth at the voice of the Son of God” (John 5).

He therefore rightly divided the living waters: “half of them toward the eastern sea,” which has already occurred—namely baptism for the remission of sins; and this is the resurrection of souls. “And half of them toward the last sea”: this indeed has already occurred in the Head, that is, in Christ, but in the body, that is, in us, it will occur on the last day. This is the regeneration of all things, according to the saying: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit” (Matt. 19), etc. And this is the resurrection of bodies, the recompense both of souls and bodies.

“These living waters,” he says, “shall be in summer and in winter.” In summer, which is now, when it is permitted to work and to flee, they will be for the resurrection of souls. [Col. 0808A] But in winter—namely, at the final judgment, when it will be permitted neither to work nor to flee—they will be for the resurrection of bodies, for the recompense of the saints, both of souls and bodies. And then the Lord will be—that is, then it will appear that he is Lord, and no other, king over all the earth—when what the Lord the Father said to him is fulfilled: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109).

“In that day the Lord shall be one, and his name one. And all the land shall return as far as the desert, from the hill of Rimmon southward of Jerusalem; and she shall be raised up and dwell in her own place, from the gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate, to the gate of the corners, and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses. And they shall dwell in her, and there shall be no more anathema [ban, curse]; but Jerusalem shall sit secure.”

“In that day,” he says, “the Lord shall be one,” as though he said: At present there are many who are called gods and many who are called lords. But as it is written in the Psalm, “Their memory has perished with a noise, but the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 9), so I say here: on that day the Lord will be one; once the names of gods and lords have been driven out, his name alone shall be and remain.

“And all the land shall return as far as the desert.” This literal sense, almost to the end of the book, is undoubtedly deliberately framed by the Holy Spirit so that it may attract a child to favor it—the Jewish people, with its childish understanding, which gladly hears such things [Col. 0808C] and understands them thus: that when the Messiah sits to reign in a golden and jewel-adorned Jerusalem, he will remove every idol; worship of divinity will no longer vary; the Lord will be one; and all the land will return as far as the desert—that is, to its ancient state—and Jerusalem must be built, according to these place-names, from the hill of Rimmon southward, and so forth.

For, knowing what and how many pearls he had gathered in this book, he judged it useful to close the case and seal the purse, lest wicked swine not only trample them underfoot (Matt. 7), but turn and tear the prophet himself to pieces. This would undoubtedly have happened, so that even the Scriptures themselves would not have reached us. We can say nothing more useful than that this intention must be understood in these words and in those that follow, which are of this sort: “And all who are left from all the nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up year by year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles,” etc. [Col. 0803D]

Nevertheless, this deception does not mislead, but contains a meaning of truth which a man ought to understand, one who has put away the things of a child (1 Cor. 13). For all the land—that is, the whole Church, the whole ecclesiastical order, which is now divided among diverse places and discordant languages—all of it, I say, as far as the desert, that is, as far as those who are more contemptible in the Church and seem to possess fewer spiritual gifts, shall return from the hill of Rimmon, which means “most high,” to the south of Jerusalem. That is, from the height of faith, and through faith itself [Col. 0809A], it shall come to the full brightness of the heavenly vision, so that there may be one city of all and, as has already been said, one Lord of all.

“And she shall be raised up and dwell in her own place”: that is, in the kingdom prepared for her from the foundation of the world. “From the gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate”—which appears to mean the same as saying, from the end of the world to its beginning. For the gate of Benjamin, which means “son of the right hand,” is rightly understood as that summons by which it will be said to those at the right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). The former gate is that very foundation of the world: namely, the blessing by which, to the first human beings after their creation, he said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1). For from then until the aforementioned summons by which those placed at the right hand will be called [Col. 0809B], the people of whose restoration the discourse here speaks are gathered.

“She shall also be raised up as far as the gate of the corners”: that is, as far as the fulfillment of the promise and hope of the patriarchs, to whom, after the curse that entered through sin, the word of promise concerning the seed of blessing was made. That blessing will be revealed at the gate of Benjamin when he says, “Come, blessed ones.”

“She shall also be raised up and dwell from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses.” Hananel means “most pleasing to God.” And who is most pleasing to God, if not the Son beloved by God the Father? And who is the king if not that same one who is most pleasing to God? Moreover, the mighty tower, the tower built with battlements, from which hang a thousand shields, all the armor of the strong, is Holy Scripture (Song 4). The king’s winepresses, however, are his sufferings.

“Jerusalem shall be raised up and dwell from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses”: that is, it shall glory both in those who, instructed and armed by the power of the holy Scriptures, were able to destroy every argument exalting itself against the knowledge of God (2 Cor. 10) [Col. 0809C], and in those who, advancing to that love than which no one has greater—namely, that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends (John 15)—did not shrink from giving up their bodies for Christ’s faith.

“And they shall dwell in her,” he says, “and there shall be no more anathema, but Jerusalem shall sit secure.” This is what we read also in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the dwelling-place of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them; they shall be his people, and the Lord himself shall be their God. And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying [Col. 0809D], nor pain shall be any more” (Rev. 21); the former things have passed away. Here he comprehends all these things under the word *anathema*, saying, “There shall be no more anathema.”

“And this shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all the nations that fought against Jerusalem: the flesh of every one standing upon his feet shall waste away; his eyes shall waste away in their sockets; and their tongue shall waste away in their mouth.” Will this be the whole plague? Have not some persecutors who afflicted the Church of the Lord received such punishments even in the present age? Let us read ecclesiastical histories concerning what Valerian, Decius, Diocletian [Col. 0810A], Maximian, the most savage Maximinus, and Julian the Apostate suffered; then the facts will prove that even according to the letter the truth of the prophecy has been fulfilled: their flesh rotted, their eyes wasted away, and their tongue dissolved into stench and pus.

Has he forgotten what is known to everyone: that they “shall be tormented with fire and sulphur in the presence of the holy angels and before the Lamb, and the smoke of their torments shall ascend for ages of ages”? Or, as the Lord himself says with his own mouth: “They shall go away into eternal punishment; they shall go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 27 [citation as printed]). Therefore he has spoken here according to the trope called *tapeinosis*, that is, the understatement of a great thing, when speech does not attain what it intends [Col. 0810B]. He does not so much weaken the condition of the great reality by feeble words as indicate that no one can reach its magnitude in words.

“In that day there shall be a great tumult of the Lord among them, and each man shall seize his neighbor’s hand, and his hand shall be joined upon his neighbor’s hand. Judah also shall fight against Jerusalem, and the wealth of all the nations round about shall be gathered together—gold, silver, and very many garments. And the plague of the horse, mule, camel, donkey, and all the beasts that were in those camps shall be like this plague. And all who remain of all the nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up year by year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles. And whoever does not go up [Col. 0810C], from the children of the earth, to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, shall have no rain upon them. And if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come, neither shall it have rain. But there shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of tabernacles. This shall be the sin of Egypt, and the sin of all nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of tabernacles. In that day, what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be ‘Holy to the Lord’; and the pots in the house of the Lord shall be like bowls before the altar. Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the Lord of hosts; all who sacrifice shall come, take from them, and cook in them; and there shall no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts in that day.”

The direction of this brief final recapitulation has already been stated. It tends toward closing and binding up the mystery of the whole prophecy, so that it might not be understood before the appointed time, as Daniel was commanded: “But you, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time; many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12); and as Isaiah was told: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8). [Col. 0810D]

The whole prophecy is indeed closed, and is revealed only in Christ himself; but this chapter is also the bond that closes it. Yet the envious child—that is, the Jewish people—could not suspect that in the prophets any good was being decreed for the Gentiles, or that an end would at some time be imposed upon carnal ceremonies. Once a carnal and childish understanding was permitted them; but now, annulled in Christ, error is inexcusable, so that one may truly say of it: “The child of a hundred years shall be cursed,” or “shall die” (Isa. 65).

For what he says—“In that day there shall be a great tumult of the Lord; each man shall seize his neighbor’s hand, and his hand shall be joined upon his neighbor’s hand; Judah also shall fight against Jerusalem; and the wealth of all nations round about shall be gathered, gold, silver, and very many garments”—has already occurred, not as they hoped and still hope, expecting insatiable avarice and awaiting on earth a golden, jewel-adorned Jerusalem [Col. 0811A], but as befitted the working of the Holy Spirit, whose whole city is not earthly but heavenly, and whose whole warfare is not against human beings but against human vices.

That great tumult of the Lord, therefore, is the one of which the Psalmist says: “You have shaken the earth, O Lord, and troubled it” (Ps. 2 [citation as printed]), namely through your preachers, shaking us earthly people toward repentance. “Each man seized his neighbor’s hand, and his hand was joined upon his neighbor’s hand,” in such a way that both Gentiles and Jews—indeed, more Gentiles than Jews—might say, healthfully broken: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). And they might be answered: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The tumult was not only this, in which it was good to be disturbed, troubled into repentance, and, as with hands joined, to seek and give counsel for salvation. It was also this: Judah—that is, the Jew or Jewish people—did indeed fight against Jerusalem, not alone but first [Col. 0811B]: against the evangelical faith and the Church that desires to live in heaven and come to the vision of peace. The Jew did not fight alone, I say, but first; afterward the pagan also fought. But what resulted? “The wealth of all was gathered around: gold, silver, and very many garments.”

The Jew had gold, silver, and very many garments—namely, adoption as sons, glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, worship, and promises (Rom. 9). Likewise the pagan had gold of talent, silver of polished eloquence, and many garments in the useful arts and studies. All these riches were gathered to Jerusalem, that is, to Christ’s Church. Moreover, the material gold, material silver, and manufactured garments of all nations were rightly gathered to this Jerusalem, because when impious kings or rulers died, pious kings or rulers succeeded them. Since this Jerusalem had sown among them spiritual things, it not unworthily reaped their material things (2 Cor. 9). [Col. 0811C]

Where are those who fought against her? “Their memory has perished with a noise” (Ps. 9). What concern is there for them? “So,” he says, “shall be the plague of horse, mule, camel, donkey, and all the beasts which were in those camps, like this plague.” It is as though he said: God cares no more about their destruction than he does about the destruction of the horses and mules on which they sat and rode while fighting against Jerusalem, or about the destruction of the camels, donkeys, and every beast of burden that carried their provisions after them.

And rightly so. “In their lifetime they were compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). How has this also already occurred, or how is it occurring, which he says: “All who remain from all the nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up year by year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles”? Let us lift our eyes over the whole world and count, if we can [Col. 0812A], the tabernacles of the Lord of hosts—that is, churches or basilicas of martyrs and of all the saints. When we commemorate their consecrations, do we not year by year celebrate the feast of tabernacles, giving thanks to the Lord for our departure from the Egypt of this world?

When Israel once departed from Egypt through the vast, terrible, broad wilderness, in which there was no house, country estate, town, or cave, it made booths and tents for itself (Lev. 23), which are now called *papiliones* (“butterflies,” i.e. tents) from their resemblance to a little butterfly. It was commanded that the solemnity of Tabernacles be held in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month (Deut. 16), so that they might remember God’s benefits at all times after they had begun to live in cities.

We do not fail to know when and how we went out, from what Egypt and what darkness we departed. We celebrate year by year, in the consecrations of churches, that departure signified by mystical sacraments, going up to Jerusalem—that is, contemplating in mind [Col. 0812B] that blessed homeland and heavenly city, of which in these tabernacles we possess a small indeed, yet holy and consoling, image.

“And whoever does not go up from the children of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, shall have no rain upon them.” The rain is heavenly teaching, the knowledge of God. Hence the saying: “May my teaching grow like rain, may my speech flow like dew, like rain upon grass and like drops upon the herbage.” It is therefore a great punishment and a great loss for those who do not go up to this feast of Tabernacles: no rain is upon them because they do not hear the Word of the Lord.

Not content with having expressed this punishment once, he repeats the same point a second and third time: “And if the family of Egypt also does not go up and does not come, neither shall it have [rain]” (Deut. 32 [citation as printed]); understand, rain. “But there shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.” This second repetition contains more than the first statement. There he merely said: “No rain shall be upon them.” But here, after saying, “Neither shall it have [rain],” he immediately added: “But there shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all nations.” [Col. 0812D]

The meaning is this: among pagans alien to the Word of God will be reckoned the heretics who refuse to go up to Jerusalem—that is, to the Catholic Church—to hear the Word of God according to the rule of faith. We understand them here under the designation “the family of Egypt.” For what reason? Because a temple was once built in Egypt, in imitation of the temple at Jerusalem, by the high priest Onias (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XIII, ch. 4), who thought that he was fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19).

In the time of the Maccabees Onias made that temple, and with him innumerable multitudes of Jews settled in Egypt. The Scripture of the Second Book of Maccabees is addressed to them: “The Jewish brothers in Jerusalem and the region of Judea send greetings and good peace to the Jewish brothers in Egypt” (2 Macc. 1). Its chief purpose is to maintain that the temple at Jerusalem alone was legitimate, and that the one they possessed in Egypt was contrary to the law. So long as the temple at Jerusalem stood, or ought to have stood, those who withdrew from it [Col. 0813A] and kept another temple in Egypt were rightly called “the family of Egypt.” Likewise, by analogy with them, heretics who separate themselves from the Catholic Church are rightly called “the family of Egypt” and are reckoned among the nations, in the words: “No rain shall be upon them, but the plague with which the Lord will strike all nations.”

In the third repetition he adds still more, saying: “This shall be the sin of Egypt, and the sin of all nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.” That is to say: because they have ignorance of God, owing to the fact that rain is not upon them, they will be without excuse. Why will rain not be upon them? Surely because they will not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles; that is, they will not possess the knowledge of God because they will not submit to the Church, where God’s Word is preached. Therefore they will be without excuse because of this sin of theirs—not because they did not understand, but because they refused to understand.

They will be convicted of having refused to understand by this: they refused to go up there; they refused to celebrate the holy feast. This feast is gladly reading or hearing the holy Scriptures and, for love of them, at times withdrawing from the servile works of the world. Therefore, whoever has no rain upon him will not be excused; “but whoever is ignorant shall be unknown.” [Col. 0813C]

“In that day, what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord.” Where such a feast of Tabernacles is to be celebrated, its celebrants and festive attendants, or caretakers of the tabernacles, must have food and clothing. From where will they obtain them? They neither sow nor reap, but are always occupied with the feast, devoted to instruction in and meditation upon the holy Scriptures. They shall have enough for these things. “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33).

How will this be? “What is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord.” That is to say: the faithful rich person will offer to the Lord what is superabundant for himself. The horse’s bridle signifies every necessity. For among all a horse’s equipment—that is, its trappings—what is more necessary, or as necessary, as the bridle? Therefore, “what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord”: what exceeds his necessity, the faithful rich person will offer to the Lord. Not the bridle [Col. 0814A], but what is upon the horse’s bridle; that is, he will be taught to offer the Lord not what a faithful person cannot do without, but what is superabundant for him.

Hence the Apostle: “If readiness of will is present, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have” (2 Cor. 8). “For it is not that there should be relief for others and hardship for you, but that by equality, at the present time your abundance may supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, and equality may result.” Thus, since he cannot give his horse’s bridle without hardship to himself, the Lord will be satisfied with that small amount which is above the bridle, that it may be consecrated to him. That is, because it is difficult for a person to strip himself of necessary goods, he requires only that superfluities be offered to him [Col. 0814B]; and these will benefit those who celebrate the aforesaid feast of Tabernacles—that is, those who lead a religious and spiritual life.

“And the pots in the house of the Lord shall be like bowls before the altar.” Whatever is above the horse’s bridle, as has already been said—that is, every superfluity consecrated or offered to the Lord by the rich of this world—is rightly signified by the name “pot,” because meat is cooked in a pot, and whatever persons of this sort offer to the Lord is carnal. Bowls, however, in which meat is not cooked but wine is poured, signify spiritual things.

“The pots in the house of the Lord,” therefore, “shall be like bowls before the altar”: whatever carnal things are offered to the Lord for the use of those who serve him shall be as sacred as altar vessels, or as any object belonging to spiritual ministry. Thus it is equally sacrilege to steal from or corrupt anything belonging to the Church, whether from its carnal or its spiritual goods. [Col. 0814C]

He confirms this more and more by saying: “Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the Lord of hosts.” That is to say: everything carnal offered to the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and Judah—that is, among those who lead a spiritual life—shall be so consecrated that no one will call anything his own, but all things will be held in common. Hence he adds: “All who sacrifice shall come, take from them, and cook in them.” That is to say: all who renounce the world and offer themselves to the Lord shall come; they shall take from the things offered to the Lord by the rich, which, as has been said, were superabundant for them; and they shall use them for food and clothing, and they shall be distributed to each according as there is need (Acts 4).

“And there shall no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts in that day.” Whoever in the house of the Lord—that is, in a spiritual vocation—presumes to possess something as his own and delights in that most wicked vice should know that the Holy Spirit severely denounces him under the name “merchant.” “There shall no longer be” means that such a merchant ought no longer to exist in the house of the Lord of hosts, lest perhaps he suffer in his soul the punishment which Ananias and Sapphira suffered in their bodies (Acts 5). [Col. 0814D]

**362. RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE PROPHET MALACHI.**

[Col. 0815]

Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets, the Hebrews consider to be Ezra the priest, because this prophet likewise recounts everything contained in Ezra’s book; and for that reason they say that he has no title, because this book itself serves as its title. Thus Malachi—that is, Ezra—is to be believed to have come after Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied under Darius. Hence, concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, he says: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place a clean offering is consecrated” (Mal. 1).

Therefore, since Ezra was a prophet—since he is the same person as Malachi—it is not surprising that we read thus in his book, namely Ezra: “The leaders came to me, saying: ‘The priests and Levites have taken wives from the daughters of the peoples of the land, and for their sons; and they have mingled the holy seed with the peoples of the lands.’ And when I heard this report,” he says, “I tore my cloak and tunic, plucked out the hair of my head and beard, and sat grieving,” etc. (1 Ezra 1).

Surely, since, as has already been said, he was a prophet, there can be no doubt that by the prophetic Spirit he understood of what, or how great, an evil that transgression was a portent: namely, that after the captivity had ended and the Temple had been rebuilt, such a violation should be found in Judah or Israel. We shall speak more fully of this where, in this book of his prophecy, he says: “Judah has transgressed, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and Jerusalem; for Judah has defiled the holiness of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god” (Mal. 2).

Be present, O Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouths of the prophets, so that, having completed this little work on the twelve prophets, we too—though by no means insignificant among the sons of Levi, whom the sovereign Lord, when he comes to his holy Temple, will refine like gold and silver—may offer you sacrifices of praise; and may our sacrifice please you as their sacrifice did, as in the days of old and as in ancient years, of which we shall speak in its proper place.

# COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET MALACHI

## BOOK ONE

**363. CHAPTER 1**

[Col. 0815A]

“The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel by the hand of Malachi.”

“Burden,” that is, the weight of a most grievous judgment. This superstition maintains that, according to this prophecy, the unhappy Jewish people, like Cain who killed his brother Abel, being liable to a sevenfold guilt, were to be punished sevenfold; that is, by remaining incorrigible, they would incur the unending wrath of God. For the number seven, which is called masculine—that is, strong—both by ecclesiastical writers and by pagan philosophers, is considered indivisible; and by it universality is commonly signified. By this number seven, I say, this prophecy indicates the sin of their rebellion and their hardness of neck.

It is pleasing now to sketch these instances. First he addresses them thus: “I have loved you, says the Lord.” But they insolently reply: “In what have you loved us?” Then, secondly: “You despise my name.” Immediately they answer: “In what have we despised your name?” Then, thirdly: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar.” But they say: “In what have we polluted you?” Then, fourthly: “You have wearied the Lord with your words.” To this they answer: “In what have we wearied him?” (Mal. 2). Then, fifthly: “Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord.” Immediately they say: “In what shall we return?”—as though they had not heard him say, “You have departed from my ordinances and have not kept them” (Mal. 3). Then, sixthly: “Can a man afflict God? For you have pierced me.” But they say: “In what do we pierce [you]?” (ibid.). Then, seventhly: “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord.” But they say: “What have we spoken against you?” (ibid.).

Thus, accused seven times and rebuked on seven counts of their guilt, seven times they shook off the yoke of a stiff neck, giving no utterance of confession, but in everything breathing the horror of perpetual rebellion. As was said above, their punishment is thereby signified as endless, because their guilt is sevenfold—that is, incorrigible—and therefore, as has been said, indissoluble, after the example of Cain. For one may discern in Cain’s sin a sevenfold increase of unpardonable sin, because, continually advancing toward worse things, he nowhere performed repentance.

First, he did not divide rightly, when Scripture says: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, is it not evil?” (Gen. 4, according to the LXX). He offered rightly indeed, because he offered to God, to whom he owed the offering; but he did not divide rightly, because, while offering his possession, he kept himself for himself and did not present his heart to God.

Second, he envied his brother, who offered rightly and divided rightly. Third, he acted deceitfully, saying: “Let us go out into the field.” Fourth, he killed him. Fifth, he insolently denied it, saying: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Sixth, he despaired, saying: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4). Seventh, even when condemned, he did not repent, but kept an unrepentant heart to the end.

Lamech, who killed him, aptly distinguishes himself from Cain when, confessing his guilt and saying, “I have killed a man to my wound, and a young man to my bruise,” he calls that same Cain both “a man” because of his age and “a young man” because of his folly. He immediately says: “Vengeance shall be taken on Cain sevenfold, but on Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (ibid.). That is to say: as Cain’s sin was perpetual and incorrigible, so his punishment shall be endless, according to the meaning of the number seven, which is indivisible and, apart from units, cannot be divided into other equal parts. But Lamech’s sin, being terminable or remissible—since he confesses, in killing, his wound and acknowledges his bruise—shall likewise have a dissoluble punishment, according to the meaning of the number seventy-seven, which is divisible, because apart from units it may also be divided into other equal parts. For it contains seven times eleven and eleven times seven.

Now the Lord had said: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Lest this seem contrary to what was said, “But on Lamech seventy-sevenfold,” it must be understood that both here, where the Lord says, “He shall be punished sevenfold,” and elsewhere, wherever he says, “Whoever does this or that shall surely die,” one must supply: “unless he repents.” But this cannot be supplied here, where Lamech said, “Vengeance shall be taken on Cain sevenfold,” because when he said this Cain was already dead and had lost the time for repentance.

Therefore, “the burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel by the hand of Malachi” means that the most grievous judgment of the word of the Lord against its Jewish despisers is contained in this work, in this writing of Malachi, whose name means “my angel.” For he is an angel, that is, a messenger of the Lord. It should be known that after Israel—that is, the ten tribes—was carried off into captivity, the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin too were indiscriminately called by the former name, Israel.

“I have loved you, says the Lord. And you said: ‘In what have you loved us?’ Was not Esau Jacob’s brother, says the Lord, and I loved Jacob, but hated Esau?”

To those who know the truth, or refuse to know it, it is evident that the Lord truly loved Jacob and his race. For this love of which he says, “I loved Jacob, but hated Esau,” is known by its fruit. Why recount many things? The Lord’s love caused Christ to be born from Jacob’s race. Although Esau was the firstborn, God desired not for him but for the younger brother this blessing: “Let peoples serve you, and tribes worship you. Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed; and whoever blesses you, let him be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27).

This blessing is fulfilled in Christ. Who does not know that prophets and countless saints or righteous persons sprang from that race, and that the fruit of the love with which he loved Jacob appears in this? He himself says through another prophet: “I am he who made you come up from the land of Egypt and led you in the wilderness for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite; and I raised up prophets from among your sons and Nazarenes from among your young men” (Amos 2). Is not this an abundant fruit of love: a multitude of prophets, an army of Nazarenes—that is, saints—and Christ himself, the Holy of holies?

The Apostle does not wish us to be ignorant of this, saying: “The adoption as sons belongs to them, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9).

If you compare with these those born from Esau and the inheritance which he powerfully inherited in this world, is not his inheritance truly a solitude or desert, and are not his offspring desert-dragons?

[Col. 0818A]

Therefore he fittingly says at once: “I have made his mountains, Seir, a desolation, and his inheritance a dwelling for desert-dragons.” We do not know from the Scriptures that this happened according to the letter—namely, that Idumea was so destroyed that its mountains were reduced to everlasting desolation and its inheritance to desert-dragons. Therefore he continues:

“If Idumea should say, ‘We have been destroyed, but we shall return and rebuild what is desolate,’ thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘They shall build, but I will destroy; and they shall be called the borders of wickedness, the people against whom the Lord is angry for ever. Your eyes shall see, and you shall say: “May the Lord be magnified beyond the border of Israel.”’”

As has already been said, this cannot be proved from Scripture to have happened according to the literal sense. But according to the Spirit it is true; according to spiritual grace it is plain: the Lord has been magnified beyond the border of Israel; and in comparison with his magnificence, of which we have spoken above, both Idumea and every earthly thing, opposed to the heavenly grace in which Jacob was loved, have been and shall be destroyed.

“And they,” says the Lord, “shall build, but I will destroy; and they shall be called the borders of wickedness, and the people against whom the Lord is angry for ever.” Yet all these spiritual goods of Jacob, and those granted to his race, of which we have spoken, are held as nothing by the carnal Jews against whom this prophecy is composed, and they insolently say: “In what have you loved us?” Surely, as the Psalmist says: “Speaking deceitful things in the anger of the earth, they devised deceits” (Ps. 34). They were angry and are angry because of the land which they lost and from which they were led captive among all nations. They do not reckon that this befell them because of their sin, so as to confess their fault and, with pardon, receive heavenly grace; rather, in anger they say: “In what have you loved us?” That is: “It is false; you have not loved us.”

Then the Lord says: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If therefore I am a Father, where is my honor? And if I am a Lord, where is my fear?”

A very fitting reminder against those who, when the Father said, “I have loved you,” replied as though insolently: “In what have you loved us?” The meaning therefore is this: a son honors a father who chastises him by receiving his discipline. I have chastised you with the chastisement with which a father customarily chastises his children, as Wisdom says: “He chastises every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3; Heb. 12). This chastisement is temporal: in this world you are chastised by the Romans, having suffered destruction and captivity throughout the earth. You reject this discipline and do not honor me by confessing your guilt and repenting. Therefore you are not sons; therefore you are bastards and not sons, because you are outside discipline, with a rebellious mind and cruel hatred.

Again, a servant honors his master by fearing his threats. Therefore, since you are not sons, since you reject discipline—that is, since you do not come to your senses through temporal affliction—I threaten you, as servants, with eternal punishment, the fire of Gehenna, so that at least, fearing this, you may repent.

[Col. 0819A]

Therefore you are not even servants. You are not sons but bastards; you are not servants but enemies, says the Lord of hosts, to you, O priests who despise my name. And you said: “In what have we despised your name?” “You offer polluted bread upon my altar.”

The Lord of hosts, whose name the Jewish priests despise today, and who therefore says, “You despise my name,” is God the almighty Father, whose name is, as we invoke him, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. They despise him. When they insolently ask, “In what have we despised your name, Lord?” he says: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar.”

Truly, from the time when you killed Christ at the feast of Unleavened Bread, from that time, O Jews, you offer polluted bread. Henceforth every bread which you offer is polluted; everything which you offer is not sacrifice but sacrilege; everything, I say, which you offer is polluted and unclean.

“And you say: ‘In what have we polluted you?’ In that you say: ‘The table of the Lord is despised.’” What is the Lord’s table today but the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, the sacrifice of bread and wine? Surely such a table of the Lord is despised by you, O Jews, because there are no bulls’ flesh and calves’ blood there, nor other such things. Therefore that table, which is truly called and is the Lord’s table, is despised by you, because no bulls are there: no goat or calf is there, no sheep or dove or turtledove is sacrificed there.

But I say: “If you offer a blind animal for sacrifice, is it not evil? And if you offer a lame and sickly animal, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor; will it please him, or will he receive your person? says the Lord of hosts.”

Without doubt, if I ask you whether it is evil to offer for sacrifice a blind, lame, or sickly animal, you answer: “It is evil,” not only because reason is immediately available, but also because the Law prohibits it (Lev. 22). Yet every brute animal is blind, lame, and sickly in comparison with a human being, who is rational; how much more in comparison with Christ, who is both man and God, the power of God and the wisdom of God? (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore you speak wrongly when you say: “The table of the Lord is despised,” despising that table upon which the sacrifice is Christ’s body and blood. Rather, your sacrifice is contemptible, because, as has been said, it is blind, lame, and sickly.

[Col. 0819D]

But the sacrifice which you despise on the Lord’s table because of its apparent smallness—bread and wine—sees, walks well, and is sound. “Offer it,” he says: offer to your governor that which is blind, lame, and sickly, and find out whether it will please him or whether he will receive your person, says the Lord of hosts. Surely it will not please him, nor will he receive it; indeed, he will reckon an injury done to him. Why? Certainly because, when you had readily at hand and could have offered that which sees, walks well, and is sound, you offered what is blind, lame, and sickly.

So too, certainly, when there is readily at hand what you may offer as a sacrifice able to remit sins—namely, the true body and blood of Christ—you insult me by offering a brute beast, says the Lord of hosts.

“And now entreat the face of God, that he may have mercy on you; for this has been done by your hand. Will he perhaps receive your persons? says the Lord of hosts.”

This is also what Peter said to them in the Acts of the Apostles: “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved among you,” and so forth, as far as, “Repent, and save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts 2). “For this has been done by your hand,” he says: namely, you offered not merely what was blind, lame, or sickly, but even a seditious robber and murderer, because, in honor of the feast day, you granted Barabbas life, while you killed Jesus, the author of life (Matt. 27). “Entreat the face of God, that he may have mercy on you.”

“Who among you will shut the doors or kindle my altar for nothing? I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord of hosts; and in every place sacrifice is made and a clean offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord of hosts. But you have polluted it by saying: ‘The table of the Lord is defiled, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire which consumes it.’ And you have said: ‘Behold, what labor!’ and you have blown contempt upon it, says the Lord of hosts.”

This is a most manifest prophecy concerning the rejection of the Jewish priesthood, together with a rebuke for avarice, when it says: “Who among you will shut the doors or kindle my altar for nothing?” Everything, he says, you do for profit; and not even such a small thing as shutting the doors, kindling the altar’s fire, or blowing upon it do you do without payment, always gaping after temporal wages and empty of the love of God.

“I have no pleasure in you,” he says; indeed, as I said through another prophet: “I have never required these things from your hands. I have not desired the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1). Again, through another prophet I said: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers or command them, on the day when I led them from the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But I commanded them this word, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and walk in every way which I have commanded you’” (Jer. 7).

How much less shall I now accept an offering from your hand, when your hands are full of blood?

Certainly I shall not accept it; rather, I shall turn my eyes away from you. “Your incense is an abomination to me; I will not endure the new moon, Sabbath, or other festivals: your assemblies are wicked. My soul has hated your new moons and solemnities. They have become burdensome to me. I have labored in enduring [you]”—understand, for forty-two years. I could scarcely endure for so long and defer what had to happen: namely, that the Romans should come and take away both your place and your nation.

I shall not accept your offering; but the rejection of your offering brings no loss to my name. “For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name.” For Jerusalem is not the sole place in which I must be worshipped; rather, in every place true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4). And they offer to my name a clean offering: an offering of bread and wine, the sacrament of the body and blood of their Redeemer. This offering is so clean that outwardly it has none of the horror of bloodshed, while inwardly, or invisibly, it cleanses the bloody pollution of every sin.

Thus, among the Gentiles who offer such an offering, my name is great. But you, once my peculiar people, have polluted it; and that saying is fulfilled: “A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have stumbled from their paths” (Ps. 17).

[Col. 0821B]

You have polluted my name in this: although it is a clean offering and cleanses every transgression, you say, “The table of the Lord is defiled, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire which consumes it.” That is, because it is made in commemoration of the passion and death of the Lord whom you killed, with the sign of the cross on which you hung him. Hence you curse that very sign and are tortured by a cruel conscience. In your hearts you say that this table, which we call the Lord’s table, is defiled; and you say that what is placed upon it is contemptible, surely because it is not flesh of the kind which you used to offer and eat—adding, as was said through another prophet, “your burnt offerings to your sacrifices” (Jer. 7).

At the same time, when it is said to you that the fire of this table of the Lord is an invisible fire, the fire of the Holy Spirit, this is contemptible to you because it does not appear visibly, nor does a bodily fire consume the sacrifice.

“And you said: ‘Behold, what labor!’” You said this, I say, and you say it in your hearts, because the entire ministry of the Lord’s table celebrated among the Gentiles, being, as has been said, a commemoration of the Lord’s passion, is a great labor, a great torment of your conscience.

Therefore “you have blown contempt upon it”; that is, you blaspheme it with the most wicked breath of great envy and great anger. I do not know how it can be understood from the book of Ezra that, according to this literal sense, the people returned from Babylon considered the worship of religion less worthy because the Temple’s ornament was lacking, and considered what was placed upon it polluted because the altar alone had been built of rough, unpolished stones, without a Temple, without the buildings of the city, without the construction of walls; and that, murmuring because of poverty and making offerings unwillingly, they said: “Behold, what labor!”

For there it is written that they willingly offered for the house of the Lord in order to build it in its place, that they gave according to their ability, that the people gathered as one man, and that they built the altar of the God of Israel in order to offer burnt offerings upon it, as written in the Law of Moses the man of God (1 Ezra 3); and that they sang together in hymns and confession to the Lord, “for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever,” and that all the people shouted with a great cry, praising the Lord.

[Col. 0822A]

Were the Jews of that time, then, worthy of such rebuke? But you, O Jews—you, O priests and high priests of the worst age, of whom, according to another prophet, “Woe, because you have set yourselves apart for an evil day and have drawn near to the throne of iniquity” (Amos 6)—you, I say, are struck by this utterance, because it is a prophetic utterance; and it foretold future things when this angel, this messenger of the Lord, spoke these words.

Therefore let us hear what he says further:

“And you have brought in, from plunder, what is lame and sickly; and you have brought in an offering. Shall I receive it from your hand? says the Lord of hosts. Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock and, making a vow, sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord; for I am a great king, says the Lord of hosts, and my name is terrible among the Gentiles.”

## CHAPTER 2

“And now this commandment is for you, O priests. If you will not hear, and if you will not lay it upon your heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send want among you, and I will curse your blessings; indeed, I will curse them, because you have not laid it upon your heart. Behold, I will cast your arm away from you, and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities, and it shall take you away with itself.”

“To you,” he says, “is this commandment, O priests, who have made my Father’s house—which ought to have been a house of prayer—a den of robbers. From this, that is, from your robbery, from the plunder which you seize from the people, you sell oxen, sheep, doves, and the other things offered, to those who had come from afar and had nothing to offer. To you, I say, is this commandment.”

For by acting thus you indeed “brought in, from plunder, what was lame and sickly”; that is, you brought in an offering worthy of every contempt. “Shall I receive it from your hand? says the Lord.” Rather, I shall say: “Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock and sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord after making a vow.”

Who has a male in his flock and offers it defective, who sacrifices a defective thing to the Lord, if not you, O priests of Jewish unbelief? You have Christ incarnate already from your own race, yet you persist in offering a brute beast to the Lord. You are accursed, O deceitful ones, who, knowing that he has come, pretend that you do not know he has already come. And you offered not merely some blind or sickly thing, not merely some defective thing—which every brute beast is, because it cannot cleanse sins—but even Barabbas the robber, murderer, and rebel, to the Lord: you released him in honor, as it were, of the Lord, according to the custom of the feast day (Matt. 27).

And thereafter you never wished to offer that male of the chosen flock, the Lord; rather, you put forward brute animals, as though they pleased him, as though he wished to eat bulls’ flesh and drink goats’ blood (Ps. 49).

It is fitting that he himself, the great King, the Lord of hosts, makes his name terrible among the Gentiles (Isa. 5), because you would not hear, because you would not lay truth upon your heart, but set the veil of unbelief against its brightness and gave neither glory nor honor to his name. He sent want among you, commanding his clouds not to rain upon you, as is now evident: you possess neither prophetic grace nor any other heavenly grace. He cursed your blessings and cursed them again—that is, as another prophet says, he crushed you with a double crushing—so that not only did the Romans take away both your place and your nation, but evil spirits also carried off your souls (Jer. 7), according to the Psalmist’s true saying: “They shall be given into the hand of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62).

[Col. 0823B]

He rightly and justly cursed your blessings, because you wished to curse his blessings and cursed them as far as you could. For the Holy Spirit, who is itself the Lord’s blessing, had said in the Psalm: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117). But you took as though it were the Law’s defense its saying: “He who hangs on a tree is cursed by God” (Deut. 21), and by the condemnation of the gibbet you wished to make accursed him who came blessed in the name of the Lord.

He very rightly cast away your arm and scattered upon your faces the dung of your solemnities; and, he says, that dung “shall take you away with itself.” For because you wished to possess only the arm—that is, the right foreleg—of a brute beast, which was allotted to you by the Law according to its ceremonies, while you rejected and held in contempt the strongest arm of the Lord, Christ the Son of God, he rightly threw an arm of that sort to you as to dogs: so that it might not be handed to you even within Jerusalem, but, cast outside, you might scarcely reach it and gnaw it as captives and scattered persons; carrying about not my solemnities but the dung of your solemnities. This dung has also taken you with it, so that you are the possession or portion of dung, possessing no portion in the land of the Lord’s solemnity.

“And you shall know that I have sent you this commandment, that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me; he stood in awe before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. In peace and equity he walked with me, and he turned many away from iniquity. The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the Law. You have made void the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts.”

Why this so favorable recollection of Levi? Surely, in order to show that the priests had wholly degenerated from ancestral faith or righteousness through their own fault; that the reproach of sons does not belong to their fathers; and that wicked sons, certainly, do not share in the praise of their father’s righteousness.

It is as though he said: Because you shut my doors and kindle my altar, receiving tithes from the people, you suppose yourselves to be to me like Levi—as Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, and the other men or priests of those times, your forefathers from Levi’s tribe, were—because according to the flesh you are Levi’s sons by hereditary right; as though they had pleased me for no other reason than because you perform the ministry of bloody sacrifice. It is not so.

“You shall know,” and learn by experience, “that I have sent this commandment to you, that my covenant might be with Levi.” What kind of covenant? Certainly not a covenant of shutting doors and kindling an altar, slaughtering beasts and eating flesh, but a covenant of life and peace; and this was my covenant with him.

How was it so? “I gave him fear, and he feared me; he stood in awe before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. In peace and equity he walked with me, and he turned many away from iniquity.” All these are priestly qualities, which you do not possess. Therefore you are not priests.

“The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” But your lips do not preserve knowledge; the Law is not in your mouth—whose proclamation is the fulfillment of angelic office. Rather, you have departed from the way, which is the knowledge of God, and have caused many to stumble in the Law. For, as was said through another prophet: “All of you are a snare for the young” (Isa. 42). Therefore you are not priests.

“You have made void the covenant of Levi”—made it void, I say, not for Levi himself but for yourselves, so that it profits you nothing to be sons of Levi according to the flesh.

We must know when that happened which he now says: “My covenant was with Levi”—namely, when, after departing from Egypt and coming to Mount Sinai, Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, who were of Levi’s tribe, and seventy of Israel’s elders went up and saw the God of Israel. And the Lord said to Moses: “Come up to me on the mountain and remain there, and I shall give you tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written, so that you may teach the children of Israel” (Exod. 24). This was the covenant of life and peace.

But the things which he commanded after the guilt concerning the calf do not belong to the covenant of life and peace. Hence Ezekiel distinguishes these and other matters in this way: “Therefore I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which a man shall do and live by them” (Ezek. 20). Then it follows: “And the house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness”—namely, by making and worshipping the calf. “They did not walk in my commandments,” he says, “and they rejected my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live by them. Therefore I also gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they shall not live.”

These things must be carefully considered: what kind of commandments those were which he gave before, and what kind he gave after the guilt concerning the calf. Then it will be more certainly clear how far apart are the matter for which Levi is praised in the words, “My covenant was with him, of life and peace,” and that in which ungodly priests gloried, supposing themselves to be before God as Levi was. It follows.

Therefore [Col. 0825A] I too have made you despised and abased before all peoples, because you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the law. Is not one the father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why then does each of us despise his neighbor, violating the covenant of our fathers? Therefore, he says, because you have made the covenant of Levi void, I too have made you despised and abased before all peoples, as I testified above when I said: “Behold, I will cast dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals.” And it should be noted that, among all the things they did by failing to keep the Lord’s ways, this passage charges them with this as a grave offense: “and you have shown partiality in the law.” For the Lord of all, who for our sake became poor, experienced this injustice and iniquity against himself and said to them: “And on the Sabbath you circumcise a man. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath? Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7 [Col. 0825B]). That is, do not grant greater authority, because Moses was a leader and God appointed him judge over you, to Moses in a lesser deed than to me in a greater deed, since I judge no one; indeed, I say, “Who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12). For this was to show partiality in the law: because of the lowliness of his appearance to despise his deeds, though most glorious, and because of the brightness of another’s countenance—namely Moses’—to magnify his lesser deeds by immoderate flattery and say: “We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9).

In ordinary matters too, it is unjust to show partiality. Thus James says: “If you say to the rich man, ‘Sit here in a good place,’ but say to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit at my footstool,’ do you not judge among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?” (James 2 [Col. 0825C]). Against such injustice he rightly inveighs, saying: “Is not one the father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why does each despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?” (Hebrews 11)—that is, of those who pleased God through humility, who became God’s friends not by outward appearance but by faith, who, journeying in poverty of spirit, acquired for us the land to be possessed. See how unfitting it is for the children of humble pilgrims to be proud in showing partiality.

It follows: “Judah has transgressed, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and Jerusalem; for Judah has defiled the sanctification of the Lord which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god. May the Lord cut off from the tents of Jacob the man who does this, master and disciple alike, and one offering a gift to the Lord.”

It is insufficient to refer in this denunciation only to the fact that those who returned from Babylon transgressed by this: priests and Levites took wives from the daughters of the Canaanites and other nations, and joined themselves and their sons to the peoples of the lands (1 Esdras 6, 10). It is insufficient, I say, to refer only to this, since these are words of prophetic authority, words of the Holy Spirit, always directed toward spiritual and heavenly things. Therefore, as befits the majesty of one speaking of spiritual things, let the whole discourse now begun be directed to spiritual matters.

How did Judah take the daughter of a foreign god? What is this daughter of a foreign god? Certainly, the law of ceremonies without the law of faith is the daughter of a foreign god. Where Judah despised the law of faith, by which Abraham first pleased God, and retained the ceremonial law in foods and drinks and bodily ordinances, there he transgressed; and from the time he killed Christ he has possessed the daughter of a foreign god. For whatever he seems from that time onward to observe in such ceremonies is not the religion of the true God, but the religion of a foreign god: an abomination and a defilement of the Lord’s sanctification, which he loved with perverse love, preferring to kill Christ rather than lose the sanctity of place or nation, according to the fear which he pretended when he said: “If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11 [Col. 0826A]).
