“May the Lord cut off,” he says, “the man who does this”; and so it happened. For both master and disciple, and the one offering a gift to the Lord—that is, elders and people alike, Pharisee and high priest alike—were scattered, both from the earthly and from the heavenly tents of Jacob.

But let us hear further growth of wickedness, an intensification of the crime. He says: “And this again you have done: you have covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning, so that I will no longer look upon the sacrifice or accept any propitiatory offering from your hand. And you say, ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised; yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.”

O how great is the anger, how great the jealous wrath of the Lord! “This,” he says, “you have done again” [Col. 0826C]. You have dared to weep before my eyes; you have dared to groan in my ears; you have dared to cover the Lord’s altar with tears. How great is this wrath: the most merciful Lord says, “You have done this; by weeping and groaning you have provoked me to greater anger, and so provoked me that I will no longer look upon sacrifice or accept any propitiatory offering from your hand, even on this day.” What a marvel! What tears are these? What kind of weeping, what kind of groaning, belongs to wretches who offend the Lord of mercy so grievously?

But we should not wonder: their weeping is wicked and criminal, because it proceeds from love of the present age and despises the age to come. Such was Esau’s weeping and lamentation: he wept and lamented until his father Jacob said to him, “Your blessing shall be in the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above” (Genesis 27 [Col. 0826D]). Hence comes God’s anger, a just anger, whose reason he immediately and subtly indicates. For when they say, “Why, offended by our tears, will you not look upon sacrifice or accept any propitiatory offering from our hand?”, he answers: “Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised; yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.”

The meaning is this: you have despised the wife of your youth, the wife whom you first knew, because you have abandoned the faith by which your father Abraham pleased God, by which God chose and received our fathers. Did not God bear witness between you and such a wife? For the promise to Abraham and his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law but through the righteousness of faith. Indeed, when Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Romans 4 [Col. 0827A]), and, as is written in the same place, “On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying, ‘To your seed I will give this land’” (Genesis 5 [sic]), the law had not yet been given, nor had Abraham himself yet been circumcised. Therefore I rightly say that faith was the wife of your youth, your companion, and the wife of your covenant, between whom and you the Lord bore witness—that is, made a testament. But you have despised her; and though through faith you are justified in Abraham, you strive to be justified through the law, having despised faith. This is to desire to establish your own righteousness and refuse submission to the righteousness of God (Romans 10). How then do you dare to cover the Lord’s altar with tears, to weep before the Lord’s eyes and groan in the Lord’s ears—you adulterer of the law, despiser of faith?

“Did not one make [it], and the remnant of his Spirit? And what does the one seek, except the seed of God?” This means: Is not one and the same God he who both bore witness with that already mentioned wife of your youth and made the testament, and whose Spirit made the remnant—that is, the New Testament? And what does this one God and his Spirit seek, except the seed of God: that you should believe in the Son of God? This is what God the Father seeks, who made the first testament; this is what the Holy Spirit seeks, who made the remnant, that is, the second testament: that you should believe in the Son of God and be a worshipper and lover of the one undivided Trinity.

“Therefore guard your spirit, and do not despise the wife of your youth. When you hate her, dismiss her,” says the Lord God of Israel. “But iniquity shall cover his garment,” says the Lord of hosts. “Guard your spirit, and do not despise.”

“Your spirit,” he says, means the faith of your fathers, which you must preserve, if you wish to live, as much superior to the law of ceremonies, or the letter of the law, as spirit is superior to flesh; for “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3; Galatians 5). And do not despise such a wife, the wife of your youth, who, working through love, bears children of life. You despise her when, wishing to establish your own righteousness, you regard as nothing God’s righteousness—which is the righteousness of faith—and refuse to submit to it. Yet she is the wife of your youth, because through her you grew to maturity, acceptable in the fathers, for four hundred and thirty years before the law was made [Col. 0827D]. For so many years elapsed before the giving of the law, from the word of promise believed by Abraham. Therefore do not despise her; rather, guard her—that is, love her.

But if you hate her, dismiss her. For just as, because of your hardness, you were permitted to dismiss your fleshly wife if you hated her (Matthew 19; Deuteronomy 24), lest perhaps you kill her if compelled to keep her, so concerning this wife of your spirit I say to you: dismiss her when you hate her, so that, if you do not wish to believe in Christ, you may at least not persecute those who believe. It is also more tolerable not to believe in Christ than to receive his faith in such a way as to wish to subject it to bondage and impose circumcision and the other ceremonies of the law upon it. According to the Acts of the Apostles, certain believers—though few—attempted, after no small dissension had arisen with the apostles, to bring persecution upon the apostles (Acts 15 [Col. 0828A]).

In granting permission, he said, “When you hate her, dismiss her.” But lest that concession seem to excuse one who hates her, he turns to the hearers: “But iniquity,” he says, “shall cover his garment”; that is, the iniquity of one who hates such a wife shall become manifest to all and shall be marked out through all ages. Then, turning again to them, he repeats and reinforces what he had said: “Guard,” he says, “your spirit, and do not despise.” Rather despise the killing letter; follow and preserve the life-giving Spirit.

It follows:

“You have made the Lord weary with your words” [Col. 0828B], “and you have said, ‘How have we made him weary?’ In saying, ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him’; or else, ‘Where is the God of judgment?’”

That there were many among the Jewish people, even before the final impiety by which they killed Christ and, persecuting his apostles, rejected his word, who said, “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him,” is indicated by this statement from the book of Maccabees: “In those days lawless children came forth from Israel and persuaded many, saying, ‘Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us, because since we separated from them many evils have found us.’ And they went to the king, and he gave them authority to practice the ordinances of the nations.” According to these people, or in the person of such people, Psalm 72 says: “For I was envious of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.” Again: “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” and so forth.

To speak and think in this way, and to say, “Where is the God of judgment?”, belongs to those wholly alien from faith. “There is no providence,” they say, “in human affairs. Everything is carried along by uncertain chance, nor is it governed by God’s judgment; indeed, evil people please him and good people displease him.” How greatly a statement or thought of this sort offends God he strongly suggests when he says: “You have made the Lord weary with your words.” While God the Father and God the Holy Spirit spoke these and similar words through the prophets to the priests and rejected their sacrificial flesh, the only-begotten Son was already, and meanwhile, speaking as he prepared himself for the work of our salvation, and said in the Psalm: “You did not require burnt offering or sin offering; then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Psalm 39 [Col. 0828D]). To this saying the Father’s following response is most fitting:

## Chapter III

“Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare your way before your face.” That this angel is John, the Lord himself testifies when he says: “What did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you’” (Matthew 11).

Therefore, the old priesthood having been rejected and a better priesthood introduced, a man who was a priest by birth is sent beforehand to prepare the way for the true priesthood, for the great priest, of whom he immediately says: “And at once the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the testament whom you desire.” Note that he says “at once.” For there was no long interval: at once, namely, this one was conceived in the sixth month—that is, the sixth month from John’s conception—and this one was born in the sixth month from John’s birth.

Both are angels, because both are priests, both keeping knowledge, as was said above: “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Both, I say, are angels, but not in the same manner. The former is only a man and priest; this one is both Lord and priest—that is, Lord and God, and man and priest. Thus the wording rightly distinguishes their respective status: of the former it says only, “Behold, I send my angel”; but of this one, “And at once the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the testament whom you desire” [Col. 0829B].

But to whom does he speak in saying, “whom you seek,” except to the true sons of Levi, whom he later mentions affectionately: those who awaited Israel’s redemption and consolation, such as the righteous Simeon at that time (Luke 2)? Further, what does “he shall come to his holy temple” mean except “he shall come to his priesthood”? For he is the firstborn. Priesthood belonged to firstborn sons both before Moses and before Abraham. Thus Melchizedek, who was priest of the Most High, is said to have been Shem himself, Noah’s firstborn. According to this custom, Esau ought to have been priest because he was the firstborn; but his younger brother deprived him of this birthright. And those garments of which it is written, “Rebekah clothed him in the very good garments of Esau, which she had at home” (Genesis 27), are believed to have been priestly garments.

But when the law came, the firstborn were commanded to be exempt from priesthood and redeemed by a price, because they could contribute nothing to the world by priestly service. The tribe of Levi entered into priesthood and every ministry of divine worship because it had contributed something: Moses and Aaron, who belonged to Levi’s tribe, had led the people, freed from Egyptian bondage, out to sacrifice to the Lord; and through their appointment the people began doing this in the wilderness [Col. 0829D]. They had indeed contributed little by leading out that people, and they contributed little by sacrificing the flesh or blood of goats and animals; but at that time no other sacrifice existed that could suffice for sin.

When the efficacious sacrifice came, the sacrifice of flesh and blood had again to be removed. Since the priests did not seek the sacrifice of faith, the one Firstborn had to receive the honor of the firstborn—that is, priesthood: he who is one and the same, firstborn of all, priest, and sacrifice. Knowing this, the divine evangelist, after saying of her whom he had related conceived as a virgin, “And it happened, when they were there, that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth,” immediately added: “And she bore her firstborn son” (Luke 2 [Col. 0830A]). Therefore he is firstborn before every creature, firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8; Colossians 1), and for that reason a worthy priest coming to his temple, to his priesthood.

“Behold, he comes,” says the Lord of hosts. “And who can think of the day of his coming?” Truly no one, except one to whom the Holy Spirit reveals it, either through an angel or through himself: through an angel to Joseph, son of David (Matthew 1), and through himself to righteous Simeon (Luke 2). For he will come hidden; he will come meek and humble in heart, with no pomp preceding or following, no trumpet of clamour or contention sounding. “And who shall stand to see him? For he is like a refining fire, or like fullers’ herb. And he shall sit refining and cleansing silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi. And he shall strain them like gold and like silver, and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness. And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord, as in the days of old and as in former years.”

“Who,” he says, “shall stand to see him?” Truly neither the priesthood, nor the city, nor the temple of those who will have no eyes to see him, who will by no means have a sound eye and therefore will have their whole body dark (Matthew 6). For he is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb: sending fire upon the earth (Luke 12), namely the Holy Spirit, who will consume unbelievers like refining fire, but cleanse believers like fullers’ herb through the grace of forgiveness of sins; and, like refining fire through holy zeal, he will make them burn with love for heavenly goods. Hence it next says: “And he shall sit refining and cleansing silver.” It repeats this by saying: “And he shall purify the sons of Levi” [Col. 0830C].

For as silver is in the hand of a goldsmith or silversmith, so are the sons of Levi—that is, all the Lord’s ministers—in the hand of this sovereign Lord. How or in what will he purify them? “He shall strain them,” it says, “like gold and like silver.” What is strained is naturally strained so that all sediment may be separated from the good liquid. And what was the former priesthood but a sediment-laden liquid? Let us speak of the best priests. Aaron, Phinehas, many others, and lastly Zechariah, John’s father, were excellent priests; their ministry was like gold and silver, but gold not freed from dross and silver full of sediment. There was the gold of faith, the silver of knowledge or good teaching; but the dregs of fleshly ceremonies were mixed in.

Therefore he shall strain his gold and his silver: rejecting the ceremonies of the flesh and the “not good” ordinances (Ezekiel 20), mentioned above, in which there was no life, he shall preserve for his priesthood only the gold of faith and the silver of good commandments. Nor will he strain from the hearts of his priests merely the sediment of such ceremonies, but that of every sin; and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness—not their own, but God’s righteousness—in the body and blood of Jesus Christ, who is their righteousness (Romans 4 [Col. 0831A]).

“And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord, as in the days of old and as in former years.” That is, the priests of the New Testament, who shall deserve to be called Judah and Jerusalem, shall be justified and glorified not by the law of works but by the law of faith. Through this law of faith, before the law of fleshly ceremonies entered in, the days of old and former years pleased God: that is, holy people, radiant fathers, and splendid patriarchs—not only from Moses back to Abraham, but from Abraham back to Noah, and to Abel. How great their number was or has been—the number, that is, of those days or years, namely saints and most holy persons—God knows. But we must know this: as they pleased God, so we too must please him through the law of faith.

Conversely, what shall befall you, O priests of flesh, enemies of the Spirit, enemies of faith? Certainly what follows:

“And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who defraud the hired worker of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and have not feared me, says the Lord.”

O how harshly the words sound: “I will draw near to you in judgment”! “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Psalm 142), says one who prays in spirit and truth. Another, too, who has praise from God and the testimony of righteousness, blessed Job, says: “Even if I have anything just, I shall not answer, but shall entreat my judge” (Job 9). Again: “If a man wishes to contend with him, he cannot answer him one thing in a thousand” (ibid.). If holy people, the days of old and former years, say this—and say it truly—what will sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who defraud hired workers of their wages, oppress widows and orphans, and do not fear me, says the Lord, do when I shall be not merely a judge but a swift witness against crimes such as these?

And truly a witness, because I saw and heard; because, as I once said, “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18). So now—indeed, even more now—I descended; I ate butter and honey, that I might know to reject evil and choose good (Isaiah 7). And by eating such things—that is, by living among human beings—I have now learned, I have now experienced in myself, that the outcry I heard concerning the blood of the righteous and prophets whom you killed is true. Therefore I shall be a swift witness, because I saw and heard, because I too received my portion from your hands [Col. 0831D].

“For I am the Lord and do not change, and you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.” This is a true and just judgment: I, the Lord, cannot change from good to evil; conversely, you have not changed from evil to good. As I seek the righteousness of faith now, so I have always sought it; and conversely, as you have now departed, so you have always resisted the Holy Spirit with stiff neck and uncircumcised ears. Therefore I say that you are not consumed—that is, you are not changed. “From the days of your fathers you have departed from my ordinances and have not kept them” [Col. 0832A].

Stephen the first martyr says the same more clearly and, given the occasion and subject, more bitterly: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so also do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers—you who received the law by the disposition of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7).

It follows: “Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord.” What is it like to say this to the righteous, to those who trust in themselves as righteous? Certainly it appears an injury to them to be told, “Return,” since because of Abraham’s flesh they seem to themselves to be God’s special and proper people. Displaying their little offspring, vermin springing from lustful flesh, they are accustomed to laugh and say to themselves and to us: “These are the infant sons of God.” Therefore follows: “In what shall we return?” They mean to imply, “We have turned aside nowhere; we are near to God; we are Abraham’s children; we have one Father, God” (John 8 [Col. 0832B]). How, or in what, can we draw nearer to God?

On the contrary, the Lord says: “Will a man nail God fast, that you nail me?” This means: Rather, you are exceedingly turned away and perverse, turned away beyond example and turned against me. For no human being ever, except a Jew, and no nation ever, except the Jewish nation, nailed its Lord fast or suspended its God on wood. You afflicted me; you nailed me to wood. And you say: “In what have we nailed you?” “In tithes and first-fruits; and in want you are cursed, and you nail me fast, the whole nation.”

The meaning is this: because I reproved you for tithing mint, rue, dill, and cumin, while leaving aside the weightier matters of the law, judgment and the love of God (Matthew 23; Luke 11), therefore you nailed fast me, your God, because of the want that you feared, or pretended to fear, saying: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11 [Col. 0832C]). Accordingly you are cursed, so that scarcely anyone is ignorant that you are Cain, to whom it was said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth. Therefore now you shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you cultivate the earth, it shall not yield its fruits to you. You shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Genesis 4).

It is remarkable that, though you are thus wanderers and fugitives upon the earth, O accursed ones, you still nail me fast—the whole nation, a nation as though sworn to the devil and filled with one spirit of blasphemy. For when, against me whom your fathers nailed fast, you wicked sons breathe the same and no lesser hatred and blaspheme wherever you dare, certainly you nail me fast; and you are guilty of no less a crime than your fathers, who nailed me when present and visible. O desperate ones, insane through despair, like that Cain already mentioned, who said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for.”

But I, on the contrary, open for you the gate of forgiveness and the door of mercy, saying: “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, and let there be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord” [Col. 0833A], “whether I shall not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out for you blessing unto abundance. And I will rebuke the devourer for you, and he shall not destroy the fruit of your land, nor shall your vine be barren in the field, says the Lord of hosts; and all nations shall call you blessed. For you shall be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts.”

I said this, and I say it: do not do as you have done until now, tithing mint, dill, and cumin while leaving aside the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith. “These things you ought to have done, without omitting the others” (Luke 11; Matthew 23). Therefore bring the whole tithe, the whole, I say, into the storehouse, and let there be food in my house: not merely bodily food from bodily goods owed by you, but also—and this is better and prior—spiritual food from spiritual goods owed by you to God: judgment, mercy, faith, and the rest of that kind. Then test me in this; indeed, as I said through another prophet: “Come and reason with me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1 [Col. 0833B]), whether I shall not open to you the floodgates of heaven, whether I shall not do the other things which I said, unless I spoke truthfully elsewhere: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matthew 6). But you do not seek God’s kingdom; and moreover you impiously murmur over temporal goods.

It follows: “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord, and you have said, ‘What have we spoken against you?’ You have said: ‘Vain is the one who serves God, and what profit is there because we have kept his commandments and walked sorrowfully before God? Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed; for those who do wickedness are built up, they have tempted the Lord and have been saved.’”

It is known and evident that the Jews have always hated the salvation of the nations, and that they were indignant because of the salvation of the nations—because God granted us repentance unto life—and refused to receive God’s grace. This is sufficiently demonstrated even by the parable of a man who had two sons. The younger departed into a far country with his portion of property; after squandering it in dissolute living, he returned. His father received him and held a great feast for his return. The elder brother, indignant, would not enter; and when his father pleaded with him, he answered: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command; yet you never gave me even a young goat to feast with my friends. But after this son of yours, who devoured his property with prostitutes, came, you killed for him the fattened calf” (Luke 15 [Col. 0833D]).

Are not these words similar to these: “Vain is the one who serves God, and what profit is there because we have kept his commandments and walked sorrowfully before God? Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed; for those who do wickedness are built up, they have tempted the Lord and have been saved”? For this is to say: “Behold, we are Abraham’s children; we have one Father, God” (John 8). “We have served God our Father for so many years and have never transgressed his command, and there is no profit in it for us. But the nations that have not served him—behold, they are blessed; though they have committed wickedness, behold, they are built up. Wherever we go, wherever we turn, we hear music and dancing; we see a great feast of God being celebrated with them. The best robe, ring, and shoes—everything priestly, everything royal—has been given to an alien people” [Col. 0834A].

“These words of yours,” he says, “the words of your envy which you have spoken against me, have prevailed against me; and they have so prevailed against me that I can do nothing with you except convert very few of you.” Thus the Evangelist Mark, surely by divine inspiration, said somewhere concerning me: “And he could do no mighty work there, except that he healed a few sick persons by laying his hands upon them; and he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark 6).

“Then those who feared God spoke each with his neighbor; and the Lord gave heed and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear God and think upon his name.” What did those who feared God say? Certainly they glorified God, saying: “Therefore God has granted repentance unto life even to the nations” (Acts 11); and they praised the mercy and the irreproachable judgment of the Father who says: “Let us eat and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15 [Col. 0834B]).

Moreover, they rightly rebuke you, the elder brother, indignant and murmuring at the younger’s return and reception, and saying that you have never transgressed my command [printed: *praeteriens*; read perhaps *praeterient*], with words such as these: “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every man who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, because you do the same things that you judge” (Romans 2 [Col. 0834C]). This is certainly most true. For what sins or vices have ever been heard of among the nations which have not also been heard of or known among the Jews, or the people of Israel, on the authority of the holy Scriptures?

Therefore those who feared God spoke well and truly, each with his neighbor: that all have sinned and need God’s grace (Romans 3), and that God is not the God of Jews only but also of nations. The Lord gave heed and heard how and what they spoke; and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear God and think upon his name, so that all things may be rehearsed in judgment and they may be justified from their words, just as, conversely, those who spoke wickedly will be condemned from their words. Hence too the saying in Isaiah: “But I come to gather their works and their thoughts with all nations and tongues” (Isaiah 66).

In that book of remembrance, in that gathering of thoughts, there will certainly not be lacking the confession of the penitent people from the nations which conceded the Father’s mercy: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15 [Col. 0834D]).

“And they shall be mine,” says the Lord, “on the day which I make, as my special possession; and I will spare them, as a man spares his son who serves him. And you shall return and see what is between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve.”

Then, he says, those whom you envy, against whom you are tormented by spite, whom you disdain while trusting in yourselves as righteous, “shall be mine as a special possession on the day which I make,” the day which I have determined to make; and I shall spare them. Though once sinners, I shall spare them, I say, when they repent and serve me in the service of devout confession, as a man spares his son who serves him in whatever ways. “And you shall return and see” what you do not now see, nor wish to see—wholly turned away and looking downward, away from the face of truth. You shall see, I say, what is between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve; and by certain experience you shall then know that one who serves God is not vain.

## Chapter IV
“Behold, the day shall come, burning like a furnace; and all the proud, and all who practice wickedness, shall be stubble; and the coming day shall set them ablaze, says the Lord, leaving them neither root nor shoot. [Col. 0835B] But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings. You shall go forth and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall tread down the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet, on the day which I make,” says the Lord of hosts.

This will be the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not: the difference between stubble, which the furnace certainly consumes quickly, and human beings whom the serene sun has gladdened by its rising. The one and same day of the Lord, the one and same sun of righteousness, when it appears manifest to all in judgment, will be so terrible to the proud and to all who practice wickedness that they cannot stand before its face—just as stubble cannot stand in the flame of a burning furnace, or as wax melts before fire (Ps. 67). It shall burn them to destruction, [Col. 0835C] just as, when stubble is burned, neither root nor shoot remains. But for those who fear my name it shall be as the sun at the beginning of spring—not merely any sun, but the sun of righteousness, with healing in its wings.

In these words the twofold blessedness of those who fear God is beautifully expressed. For in saying “the sun of righteousness,” he signifies the justification of souls, by which those who fear the Lord will be blessed on that day; and in saying, “healing in its wings,” he denotes the immortality and incorruptibility of bodies, by which the blessed—that is, those who fear the Lord—will be blessed on that same day and from that same day.

Likewise, this will be the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not: the difference between a calf released from its tether and ashes, which the calf, as it [Col. 0835D] leaps forth, tramples, tosses up, and scatters to every wind. For he says: “You shall go forth and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall tread down the wicked on the day which I make,” says the Lord God of hosts. These words beautifully signify both the eternal youth of the saints, to be renewed by the resurrection of the dead, and the irrecoverable old age of the wicked, who, because of pride—the source of every sin—have been consumed by fire and made ashes.

It follows: “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded at Horeb for all Israel: statutes and judgments.” [Col. 0836A] What is this to say, in such a matter, except as though he said: The Lord, already mentioned, and the angel of the covenant, is he of whom Moses, in whom you hope, will accuse you. “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5).

Therefore, he says, remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded at Horeb for all Israel, statutes and judgments—namely, where they said to Moses: “Speak to us yourself, and we shall listen; but let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. 20). “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever will not listen to his words, which he shall speak in my name, I myself shall exact vengeance” (Deut. 18).

At that time there were given [Col. 0836B] the good precepts of the Decalogue and judgments in which there is life, not the ceremonial observances belonging to the flesh. “Remember,” he says, because, if you remember the law of that time and place, you will also remember me; for then and there Moses wrote concerning me: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with anathema.”

I would not dare to settle anything concerning Elijah’s coming. For some teachers, with whom nearly all of us agree, believe that he will literally come, restore all things, and pay the debt of death. Others do not believe this at all; the distinguished man, blessed Jerome, seems to agree with them, saying: “Although many [Col. 0836C] among us believe that he will literally come, restore all things, and pay the debt of death.” Yet, when the Lord was questioned 372 by the apostles concerning Elijah’s coming, he answered: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished” (Matt. 17), wishing John to be understood under the name of Elijah. Hence he subsequently added: “If you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah, who is to come” (Matt. 11).

Nevertheless, whether it is the very person of Elijah, or, as others hold, rather his prophecy, that is promised in these words, “Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet,” one thing is certain: a remnant from Israel will be converted (Rom. 11). And when the aforesaid father says, “But it was fitting to feast and rejoice, because your brother [Col. 0836D] was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15), the elder son—who is now angry and refuses to enter—will acquiesce. Thus the heart of the fathers will be turned to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, so that the children may believe that this Jesus Christ, who suffered under Pontius Pilate, is he whom the fathers awaited as coming, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes: the day of judgment, in which he shall strike the earth with anathema—that is, those who do earthly works—when he comes manifestly, he who once came hidden.

*The Commentaries on the Twelve Minor Prophets are finished.*

[Col. 0837]

# COMMENTARIES OF THE REVEREND LORD DOM RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE SONG OF SONGS, CONCERNING THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD

## PROLOGUE

373 He who wrestles with a man like himself, or contends in a contest, needs bodily strength, so that, emerging as a victorious athlete, he may deserve to be crowned with a fitting laurel. But he who presumes to wrestle with God and to lay violent claim to the kingdom of heaven needs another and better strength: namely, strength of mind. For what use is bodily strength there? God is spirit; and just as one who worships him “must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4), so likewise one who wrestles with him must wrestle in spirit and truth.

We have an example of this praiseworthy strength in our father Jacob, as Scripture says: “When Jacob rose early, after bringing across all that belonged to him, he remained alone; and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he said to him: ‘Let me go, for dawn is now rising.’ He answered: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ And, blessing him, he said: ‘If you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men’” (Gen. 32).

Following that example, this man still permits himself to be overcome by the one wrestling with him whenever a diligent and faithful mind occupies itself so long with the word of God that it extracts from it the blessing of the Holy Spirit, which is the true and profitable understanding of the mystery or of the Scripture that God has rationally sealed, so that it may not be easily grasped: “because pearls were not to be cast before swine” (Matt. 7). Nor is such a mind overcome by any difficulty so as to desist until it has grasped what it seeks, although in some fashion the word of God flees and commands that it be released.

Therefore, O Lady Mary, Mother of God, and incorrupt mother of the eternal Word of God and man, Jesus Christ: armed not with my merits but with yours, I desire to wrestle with this man—that is, with the Word of God—so that from the Song of Songs I may wrest forth a work worthy to be called *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, for the praise and glory of that same Lord and for the praise and honor of your blessedness.

This desire has not newly come upon me. Some years ago, when I was younger, I had wished to gird myself and undertake a work bearing this title, namely, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, on the following occasion. I speak before the Queen of Heaven; I ought not to be mocked by any fellow-servant saying, “Behold, the dreamer” (Gen. 37). I sat as though alone in a vision of the night, and behold, something like “the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19), passing through both ears, deposited within me more swiftly than one can speak these verses:

> A woman conceived God in her mind, Christ in her body;  
> Being intact, she brought him forth, with no man acting.

When I had returned to myself and reflected in my mind upon the verses thus received, and privately recounted to some people, not without wonder, whence or in what manner I had received them, the verses became known to many, though they did not know whence I had received them. From the many and varied things I heard, an occasion presented itself for me to desire to write something concerning the Incarnation of the Lord, though I would be turning a great burden upon weak shoulders.

At about the same time this other thing also happened. A brother of innocent life and of pure, simple youth told me that he had seen your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, sitting upon his altar, with a company of saints around him; and that I was sitting quietly beside him and holding the Song of Songs.

Meanwhile these things seemed to have passed away, and my memory of them had grown old, when behold, one of the lovers of the Word of God incarnate from you, O Blessed Virgin—Father Cuno of the monastery of Siegburg—began, by some means I do not know, opportunely and importunately to urge me to write something of this kind, such as I have now proposed. He often roused me when I was almost willing to sleep, and made me keep watch much.

Then at last I remembered what I have just related, and also a certain promise of yours: for in a vision you seemed to say to me, “You shall celebrate Easter with the blessed Trinity.” For I was speaking with you and had a sweet conversation about the blessed Trinity, not knowing that it was you. But after I received that answer from you, when I wished to know who so holy a woman might be and demanded this in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, you graciously revealed yourself, with star-like eyes, to be the Mother of Mercy.

I follow the divine foretokening, in the hope that I may someday deserve to behold your face and to hold the Song of Songs before Christ, according to what we sing in the psalm: “They shall indeed come with exultation, bearing their sheaves” (Ps. 25).

First it must be said concerning this third book of Solomon, upon which, as a foundation, I desire to build the edifice bearing this title, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, why it is called the *Song of Songs*; and then why it is not called *Song* in the singular, but *Songs of Songs* in the plural.

Everything called a song in the Scriptures is so called because of some benefit of God to be sung, and because, by thanksgiving, it approves its author as neither forgetful nor ungrateful for the benefit and grace received. In the Scripture of the Old Testament there are six songs well known or distinguished in number; this, however, is the seventh and also the last.

The first is the song of Moses, servant of God, for the benefit by which God liberated his people, the children of Israel, after Pharaoh had been drowned in the Red Sea with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. 15). The second is another song of the same Moses, the song of Deuteronomy, which he wrote to be sung both for that benefit and for the other benefits of the same event (Deut. 23). The third is the song of the prophetess Hannah, [Col. 0839] who had been barren, which she sang for Samuel’s birth (1 Sam. 2). The fourth is the song of Isaiah, which he both wrote and prophesied to be sung: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me” (Isa. 12), for the 374 benefit by which Judah was to be delivered from the Assyrians. The fifth is the song of King Hezekiah, which he sang or wrote for God’s benefit in recovering from his illness (Ezek. 38). The sixth is the song of Habakkuk, which he prophetically sang concerning the future overthrow of the devil, according to the type of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (Hab. 3).

The seventh, as I have already said, and likewise the last, is this song of God’s greatest and singular benefit: the song of love, by which God descended into the Blessed Virgin, so as to beget from her a son, Christ Jesus, true man and “God over all, blessed” (Rom. 9). This benefit surpasses all the other benefits of God bestowed upon the human race. It is therefore rightly called the *Song of Songs*, because the benefit sung in it is the benefit of all God’s benefits.

But why is it not *Song* in the singular, but *Songs of Songs* in the plural? The way of answering this question is prepared by considering the subdivision into four *periochae*, that is, recapitulations. Their sign is this refrain repeated three times: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the field, that you do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wills it” (Song 2).

The same mystery is contained throughout all the *periochae*. The first celebration of one and the same love extends from, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1), to “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The second extends from, “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains” (Song 2), again to, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The third, longer one, begins: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness?” (Song 3), and continues to the third adjuration: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The fourth begins, “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” (Song 8), and continues to the end.

I do not fail to realize how great and what sort of a task I have undertaken: namely, to set down some foundation of history or of an event accomplished, and upon it to build the great mystery contained beneath these utterances. For a mystical exposition stands more firmly and is not permitted to drift if it is reasonably constructed upon the history of a definite time or of a demonstrable event.

The labor is great and difficult; yet from this very fact there is consolation for hope, because the word of God is such that, after the likeness of the aforementioned man who wrestled with Jacob, it can be overcome, if its wrestler—that is, its investigator—knows how to wrestle lawfully. What is it to wrestle lawfully? Surely, to employ the strength of true and holy humility in prayers and tears. Thus Jacob overcame (Gen. 32), as another Scripture testifies, in which the Holy Spirit says of him through Hosea: “In his strength he contended with the angel, and prevailed over the angel; he wept and entreated him” (Hos. 12).

May therefore the Lord of hosts grant such strength; and sweet victory will follow the welcome contest.

# BOOK ONE OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, CONCERNING THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0839]

[Col. 0839A] “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” What is this exclamation, so great, so sudden? O blessed Mary, a flood of joy, the force of love, a torrent of delight, covered you wholly, possessed you wholly, and utterly intoxicated you; and you felt what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man (Isa. IV), and you said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” For you said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I). What was that word? What had he spoken with you? “You have found grace,” he says, “with the Lord: behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid.). And afterwards: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.).

[Col. 0839B] Was not this word of the angel both the word and the promise of the Lord’s kiss of the mouth, now imminent? Therefore let the prudent assessor weigh both sayings in the balance of reason: both “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” spoken by a rejoicing soul or heart; and “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word,” spoken by an exulting mouth. Are they not of the same weight? Is not the sense the same beneath different words or utterances? “As you heard and believed,” as you said in prayer for yourself, “let it be done to me,” so it was done to you. God the Father kissed you “with the kiss of his mouth.” What eye saw this? What ear heard it? Into whose human heart did it ascend? But to you, O Mary, he revealed himself: both the one kissing, the kiss, and the mouth of the one who kisses.

Any soul of far lesser grace, when it conceives some good gift or perfect gift, descending from above from that same Father of lights (James I), is so inspired and inwardly feels within itself such a touch from the one kissing, that it does not hesitate to say: “God has revealed [it] to us by his Spirit” (I Cor. II). How much more did you, O blessed one, in receiving the unique gift, when the Holy Spirit came upon you and the power of the Most High overshadowed you, receive such a revelation. Indeed, your soul melted (Cant. V) when the Beloved spoke—that is, God the Father spoke with a wondrous, ineffable utterance—when he entirely implanted into your mind and your womb the substance of his Word together with that love of his, the Holy Spirit. In this you were seen to have neither an equal before you nor one to follow you.

[Col. 0840B] It was enough for you to say to the angel, “Let it be done to me according to your word,” O angel of God, in order that he might “kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; but, turning toward the beloved God himself, your soul did not cease to speak and rejoice amid its experience of unutterable sweetness. The sum of this rejoicing is: “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments. Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you.”

In Isaiah that same God says: “Hear me, house of Jacob and remnant of Israel, you who are borne from my womb, who are carried from my belly. Even to old age I am he, and even to grey hairs I will carry you.” Therefore he is rightly said to have breasts; and the Psalmist, not unaware of this, said: “If I have exalted my soul, as a weaned child upon his mother, so is recompense in my soul” (Ps. 130). What, then, do we rightly understand by his breasts but his sweetness? And what is his sweetness but the Holy Spirit?

Such sweetness is fittingly distinguished into two breasts, because there are two gifts of the same Holy Spirit. One gift is given for the remission of sins; no one among the saints of old was nourished at the breast of this gift before this Blessed Virgin. The other gift consists in the various divisions or distributions of graces; at this breast the ancient saints were nourished, and they prophesied and performed many miracles.

[Col. 0841B] Rejoicing in the unutterable sweetness of both these breasts, when you conceived, O blessed Virgin, when there was done to you according to this word of the angel, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”—by which two clauses the two aforementioned gifts of that same Holy Spirit were signified—what else could you say but: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments”?

You had not experienced the vice of this age, the wine of carnal pleasure, without whose intoxication no woman except you ever could, or could ever, conceive; yet you knew how to judge how much better and stronger, sweeter and more powerful, was the pleasure or love of God in whom you conceived, undoubtedly having drunk from that torrent of his delight (Ps. 35).

And you indeed could have said truthfully: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50). For since you were from the mass corrupted in Adam, you were not free from the inherited stain of original sin. But before the face of this love, no sin—neither that sin nor any other—could stand; before the face of this fire every straw perished, so that the whole dwelling might become holy, in which God would dwell for the full nine months: wholly pure matter, from which the holy wisdom of God might build for itself an eternal house (Prov. IX).

[Col. 0841D] And because, together with such sweetness of love, the precious charisms of fullness of grace were infused—charisms distributed by the same Spirit among the other saints and elect—you could rightly call those “breasts” “fragrant with the finest ointments.” For these charisms are the finest ointments: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, the grace of healings, workings of powers, prophecy, discernment of spirits (II Cor. XII), and so forth. Those who possess them are of good savour and emit a pleasant fragrance, like the finest ointment. Hence the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who always triumphs through us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge; because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II).

Among the other fragrances of the ointments with which you were anointed, prophecy gave forth its fragrance even long before you were born. For he had perceived this with prophetic nostrils who said: “And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. VIII). Was he alone who approached you, O faithful prophetess? Rather, all the prophets approached you, because the prophecies of all and all the Scriptures converged upon your meaning when the Holy Spirit came upon you (Luke I). For where the Word of the Father wholly implanted himself, how could the Scriptures be absent, which went forth from that Word, their fountain?

Such and so good are these breasts. What follows? “Your name is oil poured out.” Whose breasts they are, his is the name: that is, whose love or Spirit brings about conception, his is the Word or Son who is conceived. For the Son is the Father’s name, especially such a Son, such a Word, through whom God is exceedingly named and exceedingly renowned in heaven and on earth. For through the Word all things were made which God made. And who can estimate his power?

[Col. 0842B] Yet behold, this name, so powerful and so great, is oil poured out. A wondrous thing! What is stronger than the Word, and what is sweeter than oil? Has the Word, then, been changed from its nature? No. But the qualities of creatures with whom it has dealings are diverse—indeed opposite—from virtue on one side and vice on the other. For example: the devil in heaven was proud through vice; you, Virgin, appeared humble on earth through virtue. Because of qualities so diverse and so contrary, the same Word showed himself to him as a river and to you as oil, according to the saying: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV).

But how, or in what respect, is this oil poured out? Certainly in this: that he proceeded from God and came from his invisible realities to our visible ones, as he himself said to the Jews: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me. For I proceeded from God and came” (John VIII). The oil, therefore—that is, your name—was poured out because the Word of your power, with the sweetness of compassion, proceeded from the secret place of your substance.

And therefore “the young maidens loved you.” Nothing is truer. Unless the oil had been poured out in this manner, unless your Word had proceeded in this manner, the young maidens—that is, imperfect souls—would not have dared to love you; indeed, they would not even have dared to hear you. For example: “They stood afar off, saying to Moses: Speak to us, and we will hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. XX).

[Col. 0842D] And elsewhere Moses says: “And you came near to me and said: Behold, the Lord our God has shown us his majesty and greatness. We have heard his voice from the midst of the fire, and today we have proved that, when God speaks with man, man lives” (Deut. V), and so forth. So greatly did the young maidens then fear, for the oil had not yet been poured out. But now, when you pour it out—as you then promised, saying to Moses, “They have spoken all things well; I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brethren, like you” (Deut. XVIII), and the rest—when, I say, you pour it out in this manner, “behold, the young maidens loved [you]”: that is, they will most certainly love you with perfect charity (I John IV), which casts fear outside. For consideration of so great a benefit will give confidence and stir the minds of believers to reciprocal love.

“Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Up to this point our discourse, in wonderment, was attempting to imitate your exclamation, O beloved of the Lord, as though its manner of speech were more elevated; henceforth let our discourse be gentler in exposition.

She says, “Draw me after you.” When the angel departed, “Mary arose,” says the Evangelist, “and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.” For the angel had said to her: “And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has herself conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word shall be impossible with God” (Luke I).

[Col. 0843B] All saints who truly possess the holy Spirit of charity have this as their particular characteristic: they rejoice over benefits bestowed upon others just as they rejoice over those granted to themselves by God. Then they hasten to offer one another their presence, to exchange sweet conversation, and, vying with one another, to render the services of devoted charity, whether convenient or inconvenient. What is this but being drawn and running in the fragrance of the Lord’s ointments?

The ointment was precious, the benefit great, which the Lord had given the barren woman: the conception of so great a man, who was to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, and than whom none greater had arisen among those born of women (Luke I; Matt. XI). She had perceived the fragrance of so great and such an ointment; she had received from the angel himself the report or message of so great and such a benefit. And, taught by the Holy Spirit, the great prophetess was not unaware what end or fulfillment would result from this, as from the other things.

Therefore the woman of desires was drawn after the Lord; she was drawn and ran in the fragrance of such ointments. And this very running—that is, going with haste into the hill country—was to say, “Draw me after you.” For one who truly loves is both drawn and desires to be drawn.

When, therefore, she was being drawn—or when she had been drawn and ran—what did she say? “The king brought me into his cellars.” How, or to whom, did she say this? Certainly she spoke this to her kinswoman Elizabeth and to the child who had already been six months in that woman’s womb, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit overflowing in her mind and already at work in her womb. For she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.

[Col. 0843D] “And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, that the child leaped for joy in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, and cried out with a loud voice and said: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke I), and the rest. Therefore she truly said it, and wonderfully said it, she who by greeting her kinswoman suddenly made her a prophetess, so that Elizabeth immediately knew all those things whose sum is: “The king brought me into his cellars.”

Truly this is a most beautiful and excellent mode of exposition, when God himself, the Holy Spirit himself, the prophetic Spirit, speaks for the modest maiden. “He who has not been tried,” says the wise man, “what does he know?” (Ezech. XXXIV.) “A man experienced in many things will think many thoughts, and he who has learned many things will relate understanding.”

[Col. 0844A] I mention these things because in truth only one who has been tried in what he has received and in what God has revealed to him can fittingly consider the Virgin’s reverent silence, or her keeping of her mouth concerning God’s secret. For who, from the boy Joseph, son of Jacob (Gen. XXXVII), who first saw and recounted dreams—the vision of which was indeed a visitation sent from the Most High—down to the present day, has so known or been able to observe a time for silence and for speech as never at some point to need rebuke, instruction, or caution against the scandal of those who envy him, as his father rebuked him?

Therefore, the more anyone has been tried in such matters and has experienced what an evil envy is, the more he knows and can expound the understanding of this matter: that you, Blessed Virgin, were truly faithful and truly of great faith—not only because you believed the angel announcing the good news, but also because you kept this secret and never hastened to make your blessedness a wonder to anyone by declaring what God had done for you, except to one to whom God himself or the Holy Spirit had first revealed it.

The Evangelist wishes us to ponder this carefully when he says once and again: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke II). Let us now continue the words under discussion: “The king brought me into his cellars.” She herself indeed said this in other words, namely in the words of her Canticle, by which her soul magnified the Lord; but, as has already been said, the Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, first revealed it to Elizabeth.

[Col. 0844C] And what are the cellars of God the King? Certainly, the sacred mysteries contained in the holy Scriptures. For these are cellars better than chambers of spices, silver, gold, perfumes, the finest ointment, and every storehouse of royal equipment and all treasures such as the kings of the earth—and especially Solomon, that temporal king—could possess. “Into his cellars,” she says, the king—not any kind of king, but the King of heaven and earth—“brought me.” For he hid nothing from me, but intoxicated me with all his sweetness. For how could he fail to give me all things with himself, when he wholly infused into me his Word, which was and is in his heart?

This should not be understood as just any introduction, but as an introduction with the right of possession, as it is the right for a lawful bride, with the marriage documents, to be brought into her dowry. What did Elizabeth say to this when she perceived it inwardly with the ear of her heart? “We shall exult and rejoice in you.” She truly said this, and said it with a great cry. For she said with a loud voice: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke I).

[Col. 0845A] Was this not to say, “We shall exult and rejoice in you”? Already we—I and the child in my womb—begin to leap for joy at the sound of your greeting. From this, both we and those who shall come after us “shall exult and rejoice in you,” and we shall sing, saying that Eve made us weep, but Mary made us exult. For what she sorrowfully took away, you restore in life-giving offspring. Therefore “we shall exult and rejoice in you.”

How “in you”? I shall state it somewhat more plainly. “Mindful of your breasts beyond wine, the upright love you.” This is, and will be, the matter or cause of our exultation and joy in you: the remembrance of your breasts, because you will be proclaimed to have nursed at your virginal breasts him who created you. For we shall say: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, O Christ, and blessed the breasts which you sucked” (Luke XI).

And if something else mystical can rightly be understood by the breasts, nevertheless this cause will be beloved by all: because he who feeds the angels with the sweetness of his vision sucked your breasts, O blessed Virgin. Mindful of this fact “beyond wine”—that is, beyond everything that seems sweet or pleasant in this world—“the upright love,” that is, they will most certainly love you.

[Col. 0845B] The first among those upright, and the first to be so, is this child, who at the sound of your greeting, by which you greeted me, has already leaped for joy in my womb and rejoices in you. He has already begun to exult and rejoice in you, and he will not cease to exult, mindful of your breasts beyond wine—that is, rejecting the whole world and the commerce of carnal pleasure, dedicating his virginal manhood to God—because of the sweetest milk of your breasts, breasts which, full with virginal milk from heaven, gave suck to God.

O how many of both sexes will love you for this reason and do likewise. Is this memorial of you a small matter? Rather, among all the memorable things which God has done, this is pre-eminent and worthy of the expectation of every creature: that he who is the food of angels, having become man from you for humankind, deigned to be nursed at your breasts. Therefore the upright, precisely because they are upright, because they are not envious but rather well-disposed, mindful of your breasts, will love you.

What is the fruit of this love? What recompense or reward? Abundance. For the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you” (Ps. 121). Of what is there abundance for those who love you, O holy Jerusalem, except of that which is loved in you? Your good—that is, the good given by God—is of such a kind that whoever loves it can make it, and does make it, his own.

[Col. 0845D] Therefore, by loving in you the fact that you are the Mother of the Lord, the faithful soul itself becomes a mother: “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven,” he says, “is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII). And if we seek the sum of that paternal will, it is to believe, hope, and love. Thus we are upright not for a small reward by possessing faith; we are mindful by possessing hope; we love you by possessing charity.

It follows: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon. Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.”

The matter itself requires us to ask how long, or for what duration, the Blessed Virgin Mary remained with her kinswoman Elizabeth. Certainly for three months, nearly until the time of Elizabeth’s childbirth was completed. For Elizabeth, who was called barren, was in her sixth month when Mary, filled with the good news, arose and went with haste to the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. “But Mary remained,” says the Evangelist, “with her about three months, and returned to her own house” (Luke I). And immediately he adds: “But Elizabeth’s time for giving birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son” (ibid.).

[Col. 0846A] Therefore Mary was no longer there when Elizabeth bore her son. Why, I ask, was she not present? Why did she not wait for the festivity of such great joy and exultation? Why did she not defer her departure until she saw the child whom it was a joy to see? She was not unaware that the angel had said to Zechariah: “And there shall be joy and exultation for you, and many shall rejoice at his birth” (ibid.). Likewise: “And behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words” (ibid.).

Why did she not wait to see this miracle: the man who had been mute, his mouth and tongue opened, speaking at the naming of John and blessing God? Was it not more fitting for her than for any other person to offer congratulations and to hear from the mouth of the prophet the words of the Canticle: “And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (ibid.)?

Why then did she who might seem to have had reason not to come previously, at least come on that day with her kinswoman’s neighbours and other relatives and offer congratulations? On the contrary, having already come long beforehand, she departed precisely in order not to be present among those rejoicing and congratulating.

[Col. 0846C] We would not know the reason, nor notice the fact itself—namely, her departure—unless this utterance, spoken by the Holy Spirit in her person, had awakened our understanding: “I am black, but beautiful.”

What, then, was this? What do we suppose the neighbours and kinsfolk who had gathered in such numbers would have done or said, if they had found her among them with child? “Joseph her husband, to whom she was betrothed, because he found her with child, being a just man, was unwilling to expose her, but wished to dismiss her secretly” (Matt. 1). Therefore she was black in his eyes, and she still is in the eyes—or in the estimation—of those who, though they are the sons of their mother, of whom we must speak later [Col. 0846D], fight against her by contradicting us who believe and confess that she was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Yet she could say, and truly does say, “I am black, but beautiful”—“black,” I say, that is, I was found pregnant; “but beautiful,” that is, made pregnant by the Holy Spirit while virginity remained intact.

It was well done, excellently provided for, that, when the multitude later came to rejoice at John’s birth, she should return to her own house, lest they should discover her to be with child before the blessed Joseph himself, who was worthy to be corrected by the angel saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). Nor would this alone have sufficed [Col. 0847A], unless, before the days were fulfilled for Mary to give birth, she had also changed her location. For it could have given neighbours and acquaintances occasion to speak, because she gave birth so soon, scarcely six months after, at the angel’s warning, blessed Joseph had taken his wife.

Thus this too was well provided for: “There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled” (Luke 2), so that through this occasion both the Scripture might be fulfilled which had foretold that Christ would be born in Bethlehem, and the Virgin might be freed from every question of her neighbours as to how she had given birth after so brief an interval since she had been taken in marriage. Let her therefore say: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Black according to the opinion of those who see wrongly; beautiful according to the faith of those who believe rightly.

[Col. 0847B] How black, and how beautiful? “Black like the tents of Kedar; beautiful like the skin of Solomon.” For just as Ishmael, to whom Kedar belongs, was black—that is, a wild man—and was rightly cast out with his mother, Sarah saying: “Cast out the bondwoman and her son; for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. 21), and pitched his tents in the wilderness opposite all his brothers; so I too seemed rightly liable to be cast out, so that my husband Joseph was unwilling to expose me, but wished to dismiss me secretly. There was great compassion in his wish to dismiss me secretly, since the Law decrees much more harshly concerning such a maiden (Deut. 32), such as I could be thought to be while pregnant.

Therefore I am “black like the tents of Kedar,” because, just as he was to be cast out with his mother, so I, with that which I had conceived, seemed liable to be cast out [Col. 0847C], unworthy of my husband’s house and inheritance. Kedar, as has already been said, belongs to Ishmael. But why did it please him here to say “the tents of Kedar” rather than “the tents of Ishmael”? Plainly because Kedar means “darkness,” while Ishmael is interpreted “the hearing of God”; and the name of darkness rather than that of God’s hearing better suits my supposed blackness.

Conversely, just as Solomon’s skin—that is, the outward splendour and all the dignity of that most wise king—shone incomparably, so that none of the kings could ever be compared with him, so the brightness of my virginity is wonderful above all saints and sons of God’s kingdom. No saint, nor even Isaac himself—though so far preferred and to be preferred to that Kedar—ever could or ever will be compared with him who was born from me.

[Col. 0847D] But why did he not say, “like Solomon,” but “like the skin of Solomon”? Surely because Solomon’s skin was beautiful, but Solomon himself was not exceedingly beautiful. For within he had a certain deformity, even while the beauty of his skin shone. “For the Lord said to him: Because you have had this within yourself, and have not kept my covenant and my commandments which I commanded you, I will tear your kingdom away by rending it” (3 Kings 12), and so forth. What does “you have had this within yourself” mean, unless it is as though he said: Such as you have now shown yourself, by following foreign gods, such you were even when outwardly you honoured me with every act of worship and with the construction of a beautiful temple.

Therefore it was better to say “like the skin of Solomon” than “like Solomon.” Thus “I am beautiful” [Col. 0848A], because not as he had it within himself, but as he outwardly built a handmade temple, and as it is said, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9), so from me God built for himself a temple not made with hands, and Wisdom built herself a house not made with hands.

“Do not, daughters of Jerusalem, look upon me because I am dark,” that is, corrupted, because I have a swelling womb, because I was found with child. It was not a man who did this, for I know no man; rather, the sun has thus darkened me. The true Sun, God far more beautiful than the sun, filled me with himself and made my womb swell from himself. Is this to be darkened? Not in your sight, daughters of Jerusalem, who have the single eye; but it is so in the thoughts of the proud, whose eye is evil.

Joseph’s eye was not evil [Col. 0848B], but had a certain excusable cloud of ignorance; it was swiftly cleansed when the angel of the Lord told him that I had been darkened with sound skin, not by a flame of fire from below but by the Sun from above: that, while virginity remained intact, I was pregnant; and that not an earthly man but the heavenly Father, through the Holy Spirit, had made me pregnant. Not all the rest, however, follow the truth once it is known.

But what of this: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep”? “The sons of my mother” are the Jews, sons of the synagogue [variant: “synagogue”]; indeed, those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. These “fought,” that is, most certainly did fight against me, considering, and wishing to maintain, that I am dark: that the sun did not truly darken me [Col. 0848C], but that I am black with utter blackness, “like the tents of Kedar.” From them I have suffered, or shall suffer, battles of words and battles of blaspheming tongues. It was preached to them that I am not black but, as I have already said, “beautiful like the skin of Solomon”; but, filled with zeal, they fought back and contradicted my defenders with blasphemy.

Therefore we said: “It was necessary for the word of God to be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord commanded us: I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49). In this way “they made me a keeper in the vineyards”: that is, among the Gentiles, who indeed were not vineyards, but through my guardianship were made into vineyards of the Lord. They made me so, I say—that is, through their unbelief they brought it about that I was made so. For I did not reject them first; rather, they rejected me first and judged themselves unworthy of my guardianship.

[Col. 0848D] Thus, by a just judgment, I left such sons of my mother, and did not keep my vineyard: I did not help or defend my people against the Romans’ coming and taking away their place and nation. They thought that, if they rejected me, I must wander in the wilderness like Kedar or like Hagar (Gen. 16). But it is not so. In place of the one vineyard which ought to have been mine—my own nation, my own blood and flesh—I acquired many vineyards; I enlarged many churches among the Gentiles. All of them possess, and desire to possess, my guardianship, trusting in my merits and relying upon my intercessions [Col. 0849A], and continually crying to me for such guardianship.

Having spoken these things to the daughters of Jerusalem—such as she avoided, as was said above, lest they should look upon her and find her with child amid that crowd coming to Elizabeth to congratulate her—she immediately turns to her Beloved and says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions.”

To one seeking the meaning of these words, and not doubting that they truly suit so great and blessed a Virgin, there presents and reveals itself a great and wondrous mystery of that Gospel reading: “When Jesus had become twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast-day, and when all things were completed [Col. 0849B], as they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it,” and so on, down to, “And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you” (Luke 2).

What then? Did it happen by chance that the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, that his parents supposed him to be in the company, that they sought him among kinsfolk and acquaintances and did not find him, and that, returning to Jerusalem and seeking him, after three days they found him—not somehow or anywhere, but sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them? Would the Evangelist write this so carefully unless he knew the matter to be full of mystery? John says: “There are also many other things which Jesus did; if they were written down one by one [Col. 0849C], I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” (John 21). If you consider the event alone, what importance has this among so many other things, that the Evangelist should not have omitted it while omitting those others?

Therefore, in these words, “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon,” and in that event in which this same loving and beloved woman said, “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you,” it is profitable to behold one and the same mystery. For what is the company of those returning from the feast-day except the multitude or system of Jewish ceremonies, carnal ceremonies? These did not precede the commandments of life, but accompanied them. And, if you consider the order of the Law rightly, after the good commandments were given, by doing which a person would live in them [Col. 0849D], these ceremonies and non-good commandments, in which they would not live, took their beginning from the guilt of the calf (Lev. 18; Ezek. 20; Exod. 23). This was the most burdensome yoke which “neither we,” says the apostle Peter, “nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15).

Concerning these matters a great dispute was to arise, and did arise, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Certain men who came down from Judaea taught the brethren that, unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved, and that it is necessary to command them to keep the law of Moses” (ibid.). This was what Jesus’ parents did when they supposed Jesus to be in the company. But Jesus was not there. Rather, he was—and had to be—in the midst of the teachers, hearing and questioning the words of life.

[Col. 0850A] This had been foretold through the prophet Jeremiah: “I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but I commanded them this word, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way which I command you” (Jer. 7)—understood: on Mount Horeb before the guilt of the calf, where I gave the ordinances and commandments of life, written on tablets by the finger of God (Exod. 20).

You, Blessed Mary, certainly ought to have been the teacher for discerning these things, and the teacher of teachers—that is, of the apostles—according to the words: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing in abundance from Lebanon” (Song 4). Because the Holy Spirit taught them, did they therefore have no need of the teaching of your voice? On the contrary: your voice was to them the voice of the Holy Spirit. Whatever further help or testimony those mortals needed, to confirm the respective understandings which they had received from that same Spirit, who distributes to each severally as he wills (1 Cor. 12), they received from your devout mouth [Col. 0850B], trained for speaking and well ordered for silence, as the fitting time required.
