And because Scripture makes no mention of you in the above-mentioned place in the Acts of the Apostles, where, after a disturbance had arisen over Jewish ceremonies, the apostles and elders assembled to consider this matter, should it therefore be thought that that assembly omitted you and did not consult the Holy Spirit from your breast and mouth? (Acts 15.) Rather, both there and in other affairs you, as leader, resolved every question—yet in such a way that you did not cry out, nor contend, nor was your voice heard abroad (Isa. 42). For, as was said before us, you alone are the Virgin who destroyed every heretical perversity.

Say, therefore: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions.” You asked to be told, so that you might know how to tell others. But I ask: Did you not know? Did you not know what the prophets knew? Surely you would not know unless it had been revealed to you from above. And your God, your Son, foreknew that he would rise from the dead, yet the Psalmist says in his person: “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, and raise me up, and I will repay them” [Col. 0850D] (Ps. 40).

Someone may say: What then does it mean that, in the aforesaid Gospel passage, while these things were being signified, she said: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, I and your father, sorrowing, were seeking you,” and so forth, down to: “And they understood none of these things”? To this I say: And what is that which the Evangelist immediately adds: “His mother kept all these words, pondering them in her heart”? Here, then, are two things apparently opposed. For if she did not lack knowledge, how could she seek in sorrow and, sorrowing, seek? But if she lacked knowledge, how and about what did she ponder in her heart?

Therefore the statement inclines neither to the right nor to the left: for this truly great prophetess did not fail to know what was taking place, since she was full of grace; yet she sought in sorrow because, serving the divine dispensation by her silence, although she sought with those who sought, she observed the time for silence and shared the sorrow of the sorrowing [Col. 0851A].

But how is there an answer, in the person of the Beloved, to her words, “Tell me”? Both the question and the reason for the question can better be explained together with the answer. “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, return and go after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.” O most beautiful of women, O blessed among women, whose beauty is blessedness, whose beauty is the very blessed fruit of your womb: your condition is such and so great that, if you do not fail to know yourself, you immediately know what you ask when you say, “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at noon,” [Col. 0851B] and you need not fear “lest I begin to wander among the flocks of my companions”—that is, among the conventicles gathered around the seats or teachings of the scribes and Pharisees, who make themselves my companions or equals; who wish to be justified in their ceremonies; and who, “seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God,” which is Christ (Rom. 10).

For how did you obtain this beauty, by which you are the most beautiful of women? By faith and humility, or by works of the Law? Surely by faith and humility. For that prophetess, your kinswoman Elizabeth, full of joy and exulting in the Holy Spirit with the child in her womb, says: “Blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled” [Col. 0851C] (Luke 1). She did not say, “Blessed is she who has been found in works of the Law.” Behold, blessedness comes from faith.

You too immediately sang: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.” And behold, blessedness comes from humility. Therefore your whole beauty is from faith and humility—indeed, faith and humility are your entire beauty—and this is my place of rest: the place in which your Beloved delights, pasturing and lying down at noon; that is, in this time of full grace, when the figure has now passed away, reality has shone forth, the shadow has been driven off, and the Sun of truth has risen.

“If you do not know this,” then what I said follows: “Go out and follow the tracks of the flocks,” namely, of those who wish to be justified in the Law or in the flesh. “And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds” [Col. 0851D]; that is, have carnal pupils, after the example of the aforesaid companions of mine, whose every flock consists not of sheep but of kids, since they are not justified from their sin but, rather, are destined to die in their sin. To whom, henceforth, will it be permitted to glory in the flesh? (John VIII.) Behold, she who bore from her own flesh the Word made flesh: if she does not know herself—that is, whence she pleased the Most High—she is told, “Go out and depart.” And in the Gospel, when a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked,” what answer was given her? “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke XI). For this is the chief efficient cause of blessedness; without it, she could not have been blessed [Col. 0852A] or called blessed. Nevertheless, steadfastly and incontrovertibly we say: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked”; and rightly we say it, knowing that she fortified and richly adorned, fulfilled and guarded the lodging of her womb which she offered to her Creator, and the nourishment of her milk which she supplied to his mouth, with precious faith and gracious humility—never at any time lacking knowledge of herself.

It follows: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” This is what I do not wish you to be ignorant of; and, if you rightly weigh it, O my beloved, you do not fail to know yourself. What was that cavalry of mine “among Pharaoh’s chariots,” or in what sense was it among Pharaoh’s chariots? A great and wondrous spectacle for one who beholds it: there Pharaoh’s chariots; here my cavalry. [Col. 0852B] Pharaoh’s chariots were indeed very numerous, armed with iron; many were also adorned with gold or silver. But my cavalry was a single rod—the rod of Moses and Aaron (Exod. VII). That rod rode against Pharaoh’s lofty chariots in this way; in this manner it made war. First, changed into a serpent, it devoured the rods of the magicians; then, striking the river’s waters, it turned them into blood; then, stretched out over streams, rivulets, and marshes, it brought frogs over the land of Egypt; then it struck the dust of the earth, and gnats came to be upon human beings and beasts; next it filled the houses of the Egyptians with flies of various kinds; then it caused all the living creatures of Egypt to die; then there came sores of swelling blisters; then, stretched toward heaven, it caused thunder and hail [Col. 0852C] mingled with fire, and lightning flashing across the land of Egypt; then, stretched over the earth, it caused the locust to rise up, and it devoured every herb that the hail had left; then, stretched toward heaven, it caused dreadful darkness throughout all the land of Egypt; finally, raised over the sea, it turned it into dry land and divided the waters, and the children of Israel passed through the midst of the sea; and when it was again brought back over the sea, it covered with waters the chariots and horsemen of all Pharaoh’s army (Exod. XIV).

Rightly, then, is such a rod called the Lord’s cavalry: alone it sufficed against so many chariots and horsemen of Pharaoh, and won the victory. How, or in what respect, “have I compared you, my beloved, to such cavalry of mine”? Namely, in that the rod, when placed before the Lord in the tabernacle of testimony, was found on the following [Col. 0852D] day to have sprouted; swollen buds had burst forth into flowers, and, their leaves spreading wide, these had formed into almonds. For there were certain persons like those companions of mine, contending for the priesthood and drawing their assemblies against Moses and Aaron, just as these companions of mine claim the priesthood for themselves through the flesh of bulls and the blood of goats, against my priesthood—the eternal priesthood, established by an oath according to the order of Melchizedek (Heb. IX; Ps. CIX). Therefore I said: “Return Aaron’s rod to the tabernacle of testimony, that it may be kept there as a sign against the rebellious children of Israel, and that their complaints against me may cease, lest they die” (Num. XVII). To that sign, to that “cavalry of mine,” I compared [Col. 0853A] you, my beloved.

For as that rod devoured the rods of sorcerers and enchanters, crushed all Egyptian pride, and then sprouted, put forth leaves, flowered, and bore fruit—not planted, not quickened by the earth’s sap, but raised above nature’s usual course by heavenly power—so you, most beautiful among women, my beloved, destroyed every heretical perversity and cast down the pride of the devil: flowering in conception, fruitful in childbirth; a virgin in conception, incorrupt in childbirth; a virgin before childbirth, incorrupt after childbirth. Are you not, then, most beautiful among women? Truly, most beautiful.

“Your cheeks are lovely like those of the turtledove; your neck like necklaces.” Your beauty is chastity, which appears abundantly and shines conspicuously in your cheeks, because your eyes do not wander abroad; rather, like the solitary and most chaste bird, the turtledove, you delighted in solitude, and the angel found and greeted you alone. The cheeks of the woman whom Wisdom describes are not so lovely: “Adorned,” it says, “in harlot’s attire, prepared to ensnare souls; talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, unable to keep her feet at home.” But, to pass over such women: compared with your cheeks and your eyes, the modesty or chastity, religious devotion or reserve, of all chaste virgins, widows, and continent women is no reserve, no modesty; it either is not chastity or scarcely deserves the name. Add to this that “your neck” is “like necklaces.” For just as necklaces protect the chaste breasts of matrons—and are called *monilia* because they fortify (*muniunt*) the breast, lest any stranger, [Col. 0853C] that is, any unchaste person, should lay a hand upon it—so your neck safeguards your words: not only lest anything idle, harmful, or disordered break forth in speech, but also lest your very good, your secret, the divine mystery entrusted to you, lightly find a path or utterance, so that a foreign ear, or some daughter—even one who seems to be a daughter of Jerusalem—who perhaps would not know how to guard such pearls as they ought to be guarded because of swine, and especially because of Herod and his accomplices, may understand them (Matt. VII). Truly, therefore, you are most beautiful among women: most beautiful in your cheeks, most beautiful in your neck—that is, in the most fitting restraint both of your eyes and of your words.

What do your friends or intimates say to this—such as the apostles were at first? “We will make you golden necklaces, inlaid with silver.” A *murenula* is a certain ornament for the neck, so called in common speech because a chain of winding order is woven from gold drawn out into pliant little rods, in the likeness of the serpent called a *murena* [eel]. It is also sometimes woven from rods of gold and silver. Hence it is said here: “We will make you golden necklaces, inlaid with silver.” Gold and silver here mean the same as in the Psalm which says: “The wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII). The gold on the dove’s back, or hind parts, is the inward meaning of Sacred Scripture; the silver is its outward expression, whose brilliance the graces and ornaments of worldly eloquence, however refined or carefully wrought, can in no way equal [Col. 0854A]. Therefore, by golden necklaces inlaid with silver we rightly understand the discourses of the saints: golden in meaning, silver-bright and eloquent in expression.

The sense, therefore, is this: O Virgin of virgins, how has this come about—that you have neither been seen to have a predecessor like yourself nor will have a successor? Open the way for speech; from time to time uncover your neck, guarded by silence; and entrust the secret briefly, in speech, to the safe ears of faithful friends, so that you may tell us how, or through what, you pleased the Most High; what he was to you, first in your heart or womb, then in your household intercourse or conversation, while you nursed him at your breasts and bore him in your trembling arms. For we are faithful craftsmen, trustworthy workers in silver; and, in praise of him who did these great things for you, we shall make necklaces of truth—ornaments of blessing and thanksgiving—blessing and giving thanks because he so acted toward you, so that there is no place where the voice of this praise is not heard: a resonant voice, lofty praise, which, celebrating your name together, continually surrounds you and in some manner hangs from your neck.

“While the king was at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” This I tell you, O friends, and this gold is genuine. If you have silver, make me, as you said, necklaces—indeed, not for me, but for the Lord—remembering that saying of the Wise Man: “Glorifying the Lord as much as ever you can, he will still surpass it; his magnificence is wonderful. Blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, for he is greater than all praise. In exalting him, be filled with strength; do not weary yourselves, for you will not attain” (Ecclus. XLIII).

For while he was in the bosom or heart of the Father, from those highest regions of his he looked upon my humility. This is what I say: “While the king was at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” What is, or was, the king’s repose except the heart or bosom of the Father? Those aforesaid shepherds, or his companions, who make themselves his equals and draw after themselves flocks not of sheep but of kids, said that this king did not exist before me, that he took his beginning from me, that he was merely human and that there was in him nothing above humanity. Yet before I was—indeed, “before Abraham came to be”—he is and was (John VIII), and he was in that repose of his. For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I). While he was thus, “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” and, delighted by that fragrance, he descended into my womb. Long ago, offended in Eve by the foul smell of the evil of pride, and for that reason turned away from the human race, he was now delighted by the good fragrance, the nard of my humility, and thus turned back to humankind.

Therefore I call my humility my nard, because, just as nard is an aromatic plant which, though a small shrub or a little spike, does not raise itself high, but is leafy and exceedingly fragrant, with a flower of excellent scent and a sweet little root, and is proved useful for many purposes, so my humility, by its own estimate or judgment, is indeed a small and exceedingly lowly thing; but in the king’s judgment it is more precious than all the works of the Law, in which people seem righteous and great to themselves. It uniquely delights the king himself, his Father God, and also the Holy Spirit, like a sweet fragrance, such as never breathed, nor could breathe, from any sacrifice whatsoever until then [Col. 0855A]. O friends, this I have experienced. From that repose of his, he perceived and regarded my humility; he was greatly delighted, and it pleased him that in this sex he had found such humility—in this sex, I say, from which pride, entering the human race at its beginning, corrupted the whole mass.

Previously he had found trustworthy humility in the male rather than in this sex; and among others, two men were especially renowned for this grace, Abraham and David. One may discern from their words how humble they were in their own eyes. Though Abraham was so great that God spoke with him and he was held to be God’s friend, he did not forget himself: “I will speak,” he says, “to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). David likewise, though anointed king and pursued by Saul, says: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog and a single flea” (I Kings XXIV). Therefore God is not merely unashamed, but the Most High God did not disdain to swear to these two that he would accomplish, O friends, this mystery which you behold in me [Col. 0855B].

At last, in this sex he found the same grace, and perhaps a more abundant one. Do not press me to explain how great a humility “the meek and humble of heart” found in me (Matt. XI). I cannot utter it; I cannot reach it with words: this matter is ineffable. What or how great this good is, no one knows except the one who receives it; and when one has received it, one can declare it to no one except God, who understands it as he sees it. This only shall I say: it is rest of mind, and whoever has found it has, without doubt, found rest for the soul. “I sought this rest in all things” (Ecclus. XXIV); and the king, looking down, saw where he detected from me the fragrance of this nard. He saw, I say, that he could rest here in the sweetness of a quiet—that is, humble—soul [Col. 0855C]; and he descended from that repose of his and rested in my tabernacle. Here he rested; here he dwelt for the full nine months; and he who was Lord became the son of that same handmaid of his.

Do you wish to hear, friends, what this beloved of mine was thereafter to me, and I to him? Behold, I tell you: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.” Compare this with the saying of one of you, one of the friends, righteous Simeon: “Behold,” he says, “this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be contradicted; and a sword shall pierce your own soul” (Luke II). I say further: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” If you know these things, if you rightly weigh them, you will surely find in me both cause to be pierced with compunction together with me and cause to be sweetly consoled with me [Col. 0856A].

Do not attend only to that hour or day when I saw such a beloved seized and cruelly treated by the wicked: mocked, crowned with thorns, scourged, crucified, given gall and vinegar to drink, pierced with a lance, dying, and buried. For then indeed the sword pierced my soul; but before it pierced it in this way, it made a long passage through me. For I was a prophetess; and from the time I became his mother, I knew that he would suffer these things. When, therefore, I cherished in my bosom, bore in my arms, and nursed at my breasts one so begotten from my flesh, such a son, while always holding before my eyes such a future death of his and foreseeing it with a prophetic—indeed, more than prophetic—mind, what kind, how great, how prolonged a suffering of maternal sorrow do you think I endured? This is what I say: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.” O dwelling, sweet indeed, but full of unutterable groanings! Outwardly he was pressed to the breasts and nourished at those same breasts; yet inwardly, between the breasts, in my heart foreknowing what was to come, there was always present the manner of death by which he would die [Col. 0856B]. Nevertheless, I also knew that he would rise again. Foreknowledge of this was sweet. Thus “my beloved was to me a bundle of myrrh,” because he was to die, and “a cluster of Cyprus,” because he was to rise again and die no more.

“A cluster,” I say, “of Cyprus”—that is, of the land or island producing translucent clusters and excellent wine—because the wine of the resurrection is not merely any wine, but the finest; and this is “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” that is, “the fountain of the kid,” for this is what Engaddi means. Why, then, have I said this? Surely because this beloved of mine came not to call the righteous but sinners (Luke V), so that those who had been dead through sin may rise in the first resurrection (Apoc. XX); and this is at the fountain of the kid, the font of baptism, the laver of regeneration, by which those who were kids are regenerated as sheep, and those bound by sins become saints. Coming to such a fountain, they are not yet vineyards, but they become vineyards—transplanted from one place and planted in another. Hence each one of them says: “For if we have been made one with the likeness of his death, we shall be so also with his resurrection” (Rom. VI). In these plantings, in these vineyards, this cluster of Cyprus appears [Col. 0856C]; the sweetness of the resurrection of this beloved of mine is tasted.

Do you wish to know what he was like to me meanwhile in conversation? Such, certainly, as should be understood from these words: “And you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.” What else was it for him to say these and other such things to me, and for me to answer him thus and thus, except for him and me to treat most familiarly of the Scriptures concerning me and him? For is not this very saying, “Behold, you are beautiful,” from those Scriptures? “Behold,” Isaiah says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. XI). Again: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. VIII).

Therefore this is what he said: Behold, O my beloved, what that prophet foretold has been fulfilled in you. For when you were born from the house of David, then the rod came forth from the root of Jesse—when, I say, you were born, you who are as much humbler than the people of this age as any little rod is smaller and more slender than great cedars and mighty oaks. Of these the same prophet, before saying, “A rod shall come forth,” had said: “And those lofty in stature shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled; the dense thickets of the forest shall be overthrown by iron, and Lebanon with its lofty trees shall fall.” But when I was born from you, then the flower rose from the rod, upon whom the sevenfold Spirit of the Lord shall rest. Therefore, “Behold, you are beautiful”; and again I say, “Behold, you are beautiful”—beautiful in virginal loveliness, beautiful through your only-begotten Son. Beauty thus doubled has never belonged, nor ever will belong, to anyone else [Col. 0857A].

I add this further most beautiful thing: “Your eyes are those of doves.” What are “the eyes of doves” except the gifts of the seven graces—that is, the seven spirits resting upon me? For the seven eyes which, according to the prophet Zechariah, are in one stone, are the seven spirits of God which, according to the already mentioned prophet Isaiah, rest upon the flower. These eyes of mine are your eyes, “the eyes of doves,” eyes of every grace. For you were made a participant in every grace or spirit from the time when you received me in your chaste womb—me upon whom it rests, in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II).

When he said this to me, what did I say to him? “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely; our little bed is flowering; the timbers of our houses are cedar, and our ceilings cypress.” This I said to him. Consider carefully, O friends, what is the order of this Scripture, this song-like Scripture, in which you desire to contemplate our secret, the secret of beloved and beloved. Here and in the passages which follow, it is not I to the beloved and he to me, but “my beloved to me,” and I to him—except that once you heard, “I to my beloved, and his turning toward me.” In almost everything the beloved precedes the beloved woman in honor, as a son does his mother. He says to me: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful”; and I say to him: “Behold, you are beautiful and comely, my beloved.” He says to me: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters”; and I say to him: “As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among sons” [Col. 0857D].

What do you think of this? Ought he not, being God and man, to have been preceded in every way in honor by a human being? Yet in this discipline he possessed all primacy. Hence, after the Apostle had said to the Philippians: “Do nothing through contention or vainglory, but in humility each judging others superior to oneself, not each considering what is one’s own, but what belongs to others,” he immediately says: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God” (Phil. II), and so forth. For, just as in other matters, so also in considering me, he humbled himself; in some manner not considering that he himself was God, but considering that I was mother and he was son, he judged me superior to himself—as the Evangelist also means us to understand when he says: “And he went down with them and was subject to them” (Luke II).

Thus, when my beloved says to me: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves,” and I say to him: “Behold, you are beautiful and comely, my beloved,” know, friends, that these words do not come merely from the lips, but these utterances have a foundation in reason and truth. For he truly venerates in me that I am his mother and a virgin. In him I adore that he is God and man. Therefore I say: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved,” and “comely.” You say to me: “Behold, you are beautiful,” and I say to you: “Behold, you are beautiful.” From the time that I was made beautiful, you, who were always beautiful, became more beautiful [Col. 0858A]. For you truly increased your beauty in this: though you were God, you deigned to become human. Hence you are beautiful and comely: so beautiful that you are the very substance of beauty, so comely that you are the very glory of the human race.

Therefore you rightly say to me: “Behold, you are beautiful,” and I say to you: “Behold, you are beautiful,” because you are my beauty. Thus, whatever beauty I possess must wholly be attributed to you. For it is not the rod that is the beauty of the flower, but the flower that is the beauty of the rod. Therefore it is only in the opinion of the false and deceitful that I am “black like the tents of Kedar.” On the contrary, I am beautiful, and you are beautiful, and “our little bed is flowering.” The bed, I say, is my womb, in which you rested for the full nine months and from which you emerged as the most beautiful flower, with the seal of my virginity preserved. Nor shall we now be cast out into the wilderness “like the tents of Kedar”; rather, in our city we shall have houses, and shall have many splendid riches: namely, churches. For the timbers of such houses of ours are cedar, and their ceilings are cypress [Col. 0858C].

For just as cedar is incorruptible and fragrant wood, and cypress, a wood nearly akin to cedar, possesses exceptional strength and is suitable for the beams of temples, never yielding beneath a burden because of its impenetrable solidity but enduring with the same firmness it had at the beginning, so our household—the apostles and apostolic men, teachers and rulers of the churches—will be unfailing in enduring virtue and steadfastness. And our houses, made by hands, shall stand as long as the age endures, bearing the inscription: “A terrible place, the palace of God, the gate of heaven.” This fruit, and one still richer, shall follow you, the falling flower. What does the beloved say to this?

## Chapter II
“**I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.**” Since you say, O my friend, that I am fair and comely, for I am “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”: that is, the glory of the human race and the honour of humble parents—fathers poor in spirit, namely Abraham, Isaac, 383 and Jacob, David also, and the rest. Though they were mountains in merits, they were valleys in mind; though rich in possessions, they were poor in spirit.

I am therefore their glory or beauty, truly a flower, truly a lily, because I am “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44). [Col. 0859A] No one among the children of men possesses such a form as I do. For the lily is a plant with a milky-white flower: though its whiteness is in its leaves, the appearance of gold shines forth within. Thus I am “the flower of the field” or “the lily”: a milky-white flower, that is, a most pure child. I am the flower, I say, and the lily of chastity: though my flesh or humanity is sufficiently pure outwardly, within is the incomparable appearance of Divinity.

What else should the Beloved say? When I say, “You are fair, my beloved, and comely,” should he turn away and be so humble and meek of heart as to try to reject the truth about himself? This is impossible. Indeed, if we deny him, as one of you—namely, his friends—says, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. And there, before he became man, he said: “See that I alone am, and [Col. 0859B] there is no other God besides me” (Deut. 32); and here, having become man, he says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” Wherever, whether to his Jewish enemies or to you, O friends—his apostles or disciples—he said anything in this sense, it is surely devout to consider this: he remains faithful and cannot deny himself, especially when so great a cause required it—the cause of human salvation. For their sake he had come; they had to believe in him; therefore he had to say who he was and whence he had come.

Moreover, he is a faithful witness not only to himself but also to others, so as to bear witness and declare concerning each what merit or name belongs to them. Thus he says to me—whom above he proclaimed once and again to be fair—“As a lily [Col. 0859C] among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” This remained to be said, since he had said to me, “Behold, you are fair, my friend; behold, you are fair,” and I to him, “Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and comely.” This, I say, remained to be said: that he himself is truly fair, and that I am fair in likeness to him.

When, then, he had said, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” he immediately also bears faithful witness concerning me: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” Where and when was this lily, “the lily of the valleys,” among thorns? Surely in Judaea, when he endured so many and such great blasphemies from the impious; when he bore insults, blows, and scourges, and was moreover crowned with a crown of thorns.

So once Abraham the father, lifting up his eyes, saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among brambles [Col. 0859D]; taking it, he offered it as a burnt offering for his son (Gen. 22). That ram, an innocent animal, prefigured this lily of innocent whiteness; those brambles prefigured the blasphemies and curses of the Jews. They were behind Abraham because this “flower of the field,” or “lily of the valleys,” had not yet come, but was to come in his own time.

Therefore there, among Jewish slanders or accusations, was the “lily among thorns”; and so also, he says, is my friend among the daughters. By “daughters” he means not daughters of Jerusalem, but daughters without qualification—that is, empty and wandering heresies. For when “daughters” are named without qualification, they almost nowhere have a good meaning; as there: “The daughters ran upon the wall, but they embittered him, contended with him, and those who had darts envied him” (Gen. 49). And elsewhere: “Many daughters [Col. 0860A] have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov., final chapter).

Thus both the thorns and the daughters are, respectively, the blasphemies of the Jews and the sects of the heretics. Whatever thorns of this kind tore me also tore my friend; whatever daughters of this kind envied you and slandered me. Where I was pricked by thorns—indeed, nailed fast by nails—you suffered in my presence, wounded in mind; and where daughters disparage your virginity, I too am slandered with envy. But just as I endured thorns and yet overcame them, so it shall truthfully be proclaimed of you also: you have destroyed all heresies.

To this I say: “**As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.**” The apple tree is a fruit-bearing tree; the trees of the forest are without fruit. So my beloved [Col. 0860B] produces the fruit of good work, while the sons are idle and useless (Matt. 23). For they say and do not do. In this alone do they importunately glory: that they are sons. “We are Abraham’s seed,” they say; “Abraham is our father; we have one Father, God” (John 8). These are sons and, as it were, companions of my beloved.

Thus by their own judgment they are sons of God, sons of Abraham; but in truth they are “trees of the forest”—indeed, they are from their father the devil. And, like “trees of the forest,” because they not only fail to produce good fruit but also produce evil fruit, and are dens of lions, dwellings of dragons, and hiding-places of every beast—that is, of evil spirits—they will assuredly be cut down and cast into the fire.

But what fruit, how good a fruit, did my beloved produce among them? Surely [Col. 0860C] the fruit of eternal life, because he is not merely a good tree but the tree of life. I have experienced this. How? “**Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.**” From the time the angel spoke to me, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1), I sat beneath his shadow. I did not stand for an hour beneath that shadow, so as sometimes to suffer the heat of the flesh and sometimes to receive refreshment; rather, I sat continually, because I always had peace and rested continually “under his shadow. And his fruit was sweet to my throat,” that is, to my heart.

Which of you does not know that his fruit is sweet? For he drove the bitterness of death away from us and bestowed the sweetness of eternal life. [Col. 0860D] An evil fruit—or rather, an evil bite—by which Adam, through Eve, lost life and found death; a good fruit, by which the human race, through Mary, lost death and found life. This is his fruit. For why did he come, why did he grow up among the trees of the forest, except to produce such fruit, by which he might cancel the guilt of the first transgression—the bite of the forbidden tree?

When the time came to eat this fruit, “taking bread and wine and blessing them, he said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body. Take and drink; this is my blood’” (Matt. 26). You did not see there the appearance of flesh and blood; indeed, neither did Eve see the likeness of God promised her by the serpent. You saw only bread and wine; indeed, Eve saw only a fruit beautiful in sight or appearance. [Col. 0861A] Yet she believed what she did not see—she believed, I say, the serpent saying, “You shall by no means die, but you shall be like gods,” rather than God saying, “You shall die on whatever day you eat from it.” She believed the serpent more than God.

By a just law, therefore, in order that the guilt of that evil credulity may be expiated, faith is required: that you should believe what you do not see. Believe, I say, God who says, “This is the body, and this is the blood,” rather than the serpent, who says through heretics, “It is not flesh; it is not blood; and you shall be like sons of God.”

When he had done and said these things, leaving a table prepared in the sight of the living and suited to them, he immediately departed to the dead or sleeping. Himself falling asleep and dying, he descended—his soul to souls and [Col. 0861B] his body to bodies—into the same womb of the earth into which they had been received; and thus he fed and gave them drink from himself (Ps. 80). Henceforth they sit forever beneath his shadow, “and his fruit is sweet to their throat.”

To me especially his shadow was sweet. Drawn toward him by the love of the spirit and the nature of the flesh, while he was in this present life, I not only sat beneath his shadow in the manner described above, but also always desired to see his face and to have him always present with me. But what happened? “**The king brought me into the wine-cellar and set love in order within me.**”

We came to the wedding, where he also turned water into wine. When he was immediately about to perform this first of his signs, he said to me: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2). [Col. 0861C] For I had said to him, “They have no wine.” And this was indeed true: they had no wine, not merely because, as the letter sounds, the wine had failed, but because in all the weddings of this age the true wine had failed through the sin of the first man—namely, the incorruption of souls and the immortality of bodies.

His concern was greater for wine of this kind; but, he said, “My hour has not yet come”: the hour, namely, of pouring out this wine, of restoring through my death and resurrection the incorruption of souls and the immortality of bodies. With so great a matter before me, “what is there between me and you, woman?” The work of God must be set before your affections. Not your will—indeed, not mine—but the will of my Father must be done.

By these and other words of this kind, “he brought me into the wine-cellar [Col. 0861D] and set love in order within me”; that is, he made me understand that he had come in order to transform the watery weakness of the human race into his wine, that is, into the strength of his immortality; and that I ought to place the divine will above my affections. For this is to have love set in order: to desire, indeed, that such a beloved should not die, but to desire still more the salvation of the entire human race.

[Col. 0862A] Peter’s love was disordered and still needed ordering, when he took him aside and said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you!” (Matt. 16). For he had said that he would be handed over into the hands of men and killed. Long before, he had taught me the order of love: that I should indeed bear grief, and the sword of just grief, in my mind or soul, but should not wish to turn aside God’s purpose, which would result in glory and honour for him and everlasting salvation for the human race.

What then? “**Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I am sick with love. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. Behold, he has gone; behold, he has withdrawn.**” Seized by the impious and killed, he went into the tomb, descended into hell, rose again, and, after being seen for a little while, withdrew into heaven.

[Col. 0862B] But you who are his friends, whoever love him, know this: each of you says, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). How much more do I, who bore him, desire to be with him? Truly I do not merely desire it in some ordinary way, but “I am sick with love.” Therefore, “Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples.” Let this be my consolation.

Sick with love because of my beloved’s absence, by what can I be consoled except by this: that you, O all peoples, may believe, and through believing may have life in his name? By believing, “strengthen me with flowers”; by doing good works and receiving the fruit of eternal life, “surround me with apples.” Thus it will come about that I do not grow weary from the fatigue of delay.

In this is “his left hand under my head”: while I am delayed, I am strengthened by your flowers and surrounded by your apples, because your progress [Col. 0862C] and your salvation are my joy. Nevertheless, I am “sick with love,” but in this I am consoled. This is “his left hand under my head”: to see fulfilled what has been written concerning him and what he himself promised concerning himself; to see this gift which he poured forth, namely the Holy Spirit, whom he sent on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2); to see the Gospel preached everywhere with accompanying signs; believers multiplied in his name; the world blooming anew with his churches and bearing fruit in every virtue; every knee, “of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth,” bent in his name; and every tongue “confessing that he, the Lord Jesus Christ, is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

This “left hand,” I say, “is under my head”: that is, a great consolation indeed, but less than my expectation or desire. What is that expectation? What is that desire? “And his right hand will embrace me”: that is, the glory of the Father, in which he is, will surround and fill me wholly when he has led me out of this present age and taken me to himself. The Psalmist briefly indicates [alternative reading: suggests] what that right hand is like [alternative reading: may be], saying: “And delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15).

## Second Book

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861D] 385 “Your ordinances, O Lord,” says the Psalmist, “were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118 [119]). What is the place of our pilgrimage [Col. 0862D] but the present low estate of our mortality and susceptibility to suffering, which elsewhere he also calls the valley of tears, where we must endure much—namely hunger, [Col. 0863A] thirst, and other miseries, and finally death itself? If, then, in such a place, in such a pilgrimage, your ordinances are already songs, how much more so in your city, O Lord? Yet what ordinances of yours are greater than those which we have or understand in these utterances called the Song of Songs? Therefore, with all our strength, with every string of the rational lyre—namely, body and soul—stretched tight, let us sing these ordinances of yours in the melody we have begun, with your help, Holy Spirit; for this heavenly Song must be learned here, so that knowledge or understanding of it may rightly remain with us in that age.

The beginning of the second section, that is, recapitulation, is this: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the stags of the field, that you do not [Col. 0863B] awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wishes.” Why, I ask, was it necessary for the beloved to sleep? For her sleep was by no means of little necessity, since the Beloved’s adjuration on her behalf is so solemn. Why, then, was it necessary for her to sleep, or rather, what was sleep for her? Once this is understood, how necessary her sleep was will become clearer.

What, then, was sleep for her? Surely that which the Evangelist wishes to indicate when he says: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2). And, repeating himself elsewhere, he says: “And his mother kept all these words in her heart.” This was sleeping: to keep guard over her mouth and not disclose the secret entrusted to her, because the time was evil, lest [Col. 0863C] Herod discover where the King of the Jews who had been born was. Thus it was altogether necessary that the beloved should sleep and should not wish to keep watch among the talkative daughters of Jerusalem.

For there were not lacking daughters of Jerusalem of this sort, who, although well disposed, nevertheless did not know how to maintain silence in every circumstance as was fitting. Therefore it was not expedient for this beloved to be awakened from the sleep of holy contemplation, to make herself common to them, and to rouse herself to answer them—even if others were saying something, for example the shepherds, who certainly said certain things (same chapter, at the end). For the Evangelist says: “And all who heard wondered at the things which had been spoken to them by the shepherds” (Luke 2). And if, I say, either then or afterwards, because of the many wonders that occurred, others [Col. 0863D] were speaking, it befitted her to remain silent and not be disturbed, lest the matter become too widely known and she herself endure a greater burden of persecution than that flight in which it had been necessary to flee into Egypt.

Therefore, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wishes”: that is, I firmly strengthen the mind of the beloved, lest before the time for speaking she tell you what happened to her, or how it happened, even though you press your inquiries insistently. By what do I adjure you? By the roes and stags of the field. Truly, this is a great adjuration. For I too swore to stags and roes, namely to your fathers, kings and patriarchs—especially Abraham and David—to accomplish this word which I have now accomplished, [Col. 0864A] by which word, indeed, the beloved sleeps in the slumber of fitting silence.

If now, while you question her and she answers everyone, the report should spread too widely, and Herod should find and kill the child before the Gospel had been established, how would my oath remain valid—the oath which I swore to Abraham your father, that in this seed of his all nations would be blessed? Therefore I adjure you by those fathers of yours, whom you revere.

Why were those fathers roes or stags? Surely because, just as roes, like birds, occupy steep and lofty places, dwell on high, and remain among the highest rocks, so they did not seek a permanent city but desired a better one, that is, a heavenly city (Heb. 11:13); dwelling in tents and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners [Col. 0864B] on the earth. And just as stags, when they have eaten something of the serpent kind, desire with the greatest swiftness to come to springs of water, so they, knowing that through the serpent they had contracted original sin from their first parents, longed that the fountain promised in the aforesaid blessing, in which there is remission of sins, might be born for them. Hence: “As the stag longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41 [42]).

—“The voice of my beloved: behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. My beloved is like a roe and a fawn of stags.”

When the beloved wishes, do not awaken or compel her to wake; but when she wishes, and where she wishes, and to whom she wishes, she opens and speaks the mysteries of the Scriptures. [Col. 0864C] And she says: “The voice of my beloved”—understand: it is such as I am about to declare; and this is the sense of his voice, that is, of Scripture, since it concerns him and me, which I shall expound.

I would now state the voice itself, the beloved’s very words which she speaks to me; but perhaps you first wish to hear something else: why this matter was delayed so long, and why, before he came together with me, so many generations passed—namely, “from Abraham to David fourteen generations, and from David to the Babylonian captivity fourteen generations, and from the Babylonian captivity” to him “fourteen generations,” as the Evangelist carefully distinguishes (Matt. 2). Why did he delay his coming so long? Is he slow or sluggish? On the contrary, according to the testimony of the Scriptures, he is most swift in his work. [Col. 0864D] The sum of that testimony is: “Behold, he will come, leaping 386 upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. My beloved is like a roe and a fawn of stags.”

For the prophetic Scriptures, testifying to his speed, say: “Call his name, Hasten to take away the spoils; hurry to plunder” (Isa. 8). Again: “And behold, he shall come swiftly and speedily; there is none fainting or weary among them” (Isa. 5), and many similar things. Whence, then, the delay? I shall say: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.”

Pay close attention, so that you may understand the matter. For the “wall of ours” of which I speak is not a small thing, and because of it he came so tardily—he who, even before he came, was called hasty and swift, and who, when he had come, accomplished so quickly and speedily that for which he came. What was it? How long a time did he spend accomplishing that which is written of him: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its height” (Ps. 18 [19])? During a space of more than thirty-two years he ran that great course in exultation, “leaping” and “skipping,” like a roe or a fawn of stags: from heaven into my womb, from my womb to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb again to heaven.

For what “wall of ours,” then, did he wait so long, he who is so swift in his work? Surely because of the wall of hostilities, built up not only from one original sin but also from many [Col. 0865B] actual sins. The first of those actual sins was that the sons of Jacob, the sons of Isaac, the sons of Abraham—to whom the promise had first been made—sold their brother Joseph into slavery out of envy, and he served for fourteen years (Gen. 37). For when he was sixteen years old, he was sold; and when he was brought out of prison and stood before King Pharaoh, he was thirty years old (Gen. 41).

Therefore, just as in one place the righteous Judge, that is, the Lord, says: “According to the number of days during which you surveyed the land, a year shall be reckoned for a day, and for forty years you shall bear your iniquities” (Num. 14), so in that case also let us judge it just that he should say: According to the number of fourteen years during which Joseph served after being sold, a generation shall be reckoned for a year, and for fourteen generations the seed which I promised to your fathers—that is, Christ—shall be delayed. Therefore, he says, from Abraham [Col. 0865C] to David were fourteen generations—understand: and Christ did not come; and until then the angry Lord delayed him (Ps. 88 [89]), over which Moses also lamented in the passage cited above.

Moreover, David, in whom the fourteen generations ended, although he too had already received the same promise together with the Lord’s oath, sinned no less than those before him. He struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, took his wife, and killed him with the sword of the sons of Ammon (2 Kings 11). Therefore the Lord ought to be angry on this account no less than he had formerly been angry. Hence, he says, from David to the Babylonian captivity were fourteen generations—understand: and Christ did not come.

Furthermore, in the Babylonian captivity, which was a punishment for those who were carried away, there was a sin or crime no less grave: the kings of Judah, and especially Manasseh, had shed very much innocent blood, until they had filled Jerusalem to the brim, besides their sins by which they made Judah sin, so that they did evil before the Lord (4 Kings 21). Thus from the Babylonian captivity to Christ were fourteen generations—understand: and only after so many generations did the same Christ come.

After such a “wall of ours, behold, he stands”: that is, because of these and other sins of our race, to whom he had been promised, [Col. 0866A] he made a just delay. “He stands,” I say, “looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices”: that is, visiting us through the prophets and remembering us because of our fathers. For the windows in this wall were Moses and the prophets, each of whom in his own time shone out amid the multitude of sinners, amid the very heap of sins, not permitting the wall to be so unbroken that the Beloved had no entrance through which to look inward here and give an audible voice, making intelligible speech.

The lattices, however—that is, the front part of the building—were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the first fathers of our race. Through them he looked ahead in that he had mercy on us for their sake, remembering what he had promised and what he had sworn to them. This is what I myself sang: “He has received Israel his servant, remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever” (Luke 1).

“And my beloved speaks to me: Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed, flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land, the fig tree has put forth its early figs, the flowering vines have given their fragrance.”

These words are surely the words of one who longs. But what is the Beloved’s longing, or what is his love, except charity, except the Holy Spirit? To long with such longing is rightly called loving with love; it is also called rejoicing, as in: “The Lord shall rejoice in his works” (Ps. 103 [104]). Indeed, he is even said to ask, surely with the same [Col. 0866C] longing, according to that passage in Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel,” says Moses, “what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and love him?” (Deut. 10).

Moreover, he speaks not merely with the mind of one asking, but of one earnestly desiring, when he says likewise in Deuteronomy: “They have spoken all things well. Who will grant that they have such a mind as to fear me and keep all my commandments at all times, that it may be well with them and with their children for ever?” (Deut. 5). And in Isaiah he says: “Would that you had attended to my commandments; then your peace would have become like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea” (Isa. 48).

These things, and many similar things, are written, testifying to the tranquil longing of the Beloved: the charity of the impassible one, not passion but the delight by which he always willed, always desired, what was beneficial to his creature, the human race. If he is ever rightly said to have wished or desired anything, how much more this thing, in which the sum of salvation consists: that fullness of time in which he would be made of a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, that they might receive adoption as sons (Gal. 4).

Therefore receive these words of the Beloved, speaking to me—“Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come,” and so forth—as the words of one longing, as of one hastening and wishing that the material of so great a salvation might now be present: namely, myself, whose flesh would be the material of the flesh he was to assume. He spoke to me as though present and commanded me to arise and make haste—that is, to be born and quickly prepare the lodging of my womb for him.

And truly, before I was born, I was present to him; before I was made, I was well known to him. For if you say, and say truly, that “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and immaculate before him in charity” (Eph. 1), do you not also rightly think and, thinking rightly, say of me that he chose me before the foundation of the world, that I should be holy and immaculate before him in charity? And if Wisdom, as she herself testifies, even before she was made, “was playing before him upon the circle of the earth, and her delights were with the children of men” (Prov. 8), how much more was Wisdom playing and taking delight with this handmaid of the Lord, the wonder of all the sons or daughters [Col. 0867B] of men?

“Arise,” he says, “make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one”—and in all these things you are opposed to Eve. For Eve was, as it were, an enemy; Eve, as it were, a viper; Eve, as it were, deformed and dishonoured. 387 An enemy to me, a viper to her husband, disgraceful confusion to herself: an enemy through the pride by which she swelled within; a viper through the malice which, conceiving from the serpent, she easily yielded when tempted from without; dishonourable through the itching of lust which immediately began to gush forth, so that, recognizing herself naked, she covered her private parts with a leaf (Gen. 3).

But you are “my friend” through humility, “my dove” through charity, “my beautiful one” through chastity. You did not fear God; rather, with a humble mind you pleased the Most High, and behold, you are a friend. You did not lend your ear to the serpent; rather, I set enmity [Col. 0867C] between you and the serpent, and behold, you are a dove. You did not incur the nakedness of lust; rather, the Holy Spirit shall overshadow you, and behold, you are beautiful.

Come therefore, Mary, come; for Eve fled into hiding. Come and believe the angel bringing good news; for Eve believed the whispering serpent. Come and crush the serpent’s head; for Eve, enticed by its head, delighted by its belly, is bound by the serpent’s tail. Come and say, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1); for Eve, both hiding and defending herself, said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

This is the voice of my Beloved, and this is what he says to me: “Arise, make haste, and come.” Arise through faith, make haste through hope, come through charity. “For now winter has passed, rain has gone and departed, flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land, the fig tree has put forth its early figs, the flowering vines have given their fragrance.”

For behold, the spring equinox has now passed, and the Paschal feast is at hand while I speak these words to you, while outside the angel announces and within I follow the voice of the announcer. At that time, undoubtedly, according to the course of the sun and the nature of the air, “winter has now passed, rain has gone and departed.” Therefore, from the very character of the season, take an omen of great blessedness: because through what is said to you, through what is done with you, the winter of sin has passed—that is, will most certainly pass—and the rain of heavenly wrath has gone and departed—that is, will most certainly go and depart.

That winter came because Eve, of whom I have spoken, fled and hid herself from the face of God; and that rain struck the earth, that is, the whole human race, because she sinned. This is the rain; this is heavenly wrath: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions,” and so forth, down to: “For you are dust, and into dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). Such rain has gone and departed—that is, it will most certainly go and depart—through me, the fruit of your womb.

Then many flowers will appear—that is, they will most certainly appear—holy and diverse flowers: some red or purple through martyrdom; others white through confession or, in imitation of us, through the incorruption of virginity. Then too “the time of pruning has come,” and it will soon come to pass that the superfluities of the law are cut away, and it is said to our flowers or flowering fields and trees: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden beyond these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication” (Acts 15), and that you do not do to others what you do not wish done to yourselves. “By keeping yourselves from these things, you shall do well” (ibid.).

Then too “the voice of the turtledove has been heard,” that is, will most certainly be heard “in our land.” The “voice,” I say, “of the turtledove”—of that little indeed but most chaste bird—namely, the preaching of the Gospel, whose beginning is the beauty of our chastity and your virginal conception, “has been heard,” that is, will be heard, “in our land”: in our Church, throughout the whole earth.

Then, at the voice of such a turtledove, “the fig tree has put forth”—that is, will most certainly put forth—“its early figs”; and “the flowering vines have given”—that is, will most certainly give—“their fragrance.” The fig tree, I say, that is, the synagogue, will put forth and boast of its works or righteousnesses; but when figs of this kind fall, it will remain barren, and I, coming to it and seeking fruit, shall not find any (Matt. 21).

But “the flowering vines,” that is, the Gentiles beginning to believe, “will give fragrance,” that is, a good report, so that friends may rejoice and say: “First we give thanks to our God through Jesus Christ for you all, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world. Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.”

Again, “the voice of my Beloved”; again he speaks to me and invites me to arise, calling me by the same names: “Arise,” he says, “my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove.” And immediately, as though I were asking where I should arise, where, or in what I should be a mourning dove: “In the clefts,” he says, “of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.”

For he knows the disposition and state of my mind: that his nails, which before they were made I foresaw with prophetic mind and read of in the prophet saying, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21 [22]); and the spear-thrust in his side, which likewise I foresaw and read in the prophet: “They shall look,” says Zechariah, “upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12)—that his nails, I say, and spear would already be wounds in my soul, and that in them I should groan like a dove.

He was therefore saying: “My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall,” that is, a soul groaning because of the piercing of the nails—I who am the rock—because of the wound in my side—I who am the wall. For I am one and the same, at one time a rock and at another a wall. That is: where I was still mortal and capable of suffering, there I was a wall; but where I had already risen from the dead, there, from that time onward, I was the most solid rock. Yet the hollows or clefts made in the wall while it was still capable of suffering did not disappear in the rock which is now impassible; indeed, they will appear on the day of judgment.

Continue what you are doing; contemplate what you are contemplating; and in this manner always show me your face. By showing it, correct what Eve sinned in hiding her face from me. Where did she hide it? In the midst of the tree of paradise—namely, in that very place in which she sinned. For, “Of the tree which is in the midst of paradise,” she said, “the Lord commanded us not to eat and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.” She ate, and when she heard the voice of the Lord God, Scripture says, “she hid herself from the face of the Lord God in the midst of the tree of paradise” (Gen. 3).

Thus she hid herself in the very thing in which she sinned, because she took pleasure in her sin and defended it. She did not show me her face when I said, “Where are you?” Her voice did not sound in my ears—the voice of confession, which should have sounded at least when I said, “Why have you done this?” Just as when I blessed her and her husband, saying, “Increase and multiply,” no voice sounded in my ears: for she sang no song of thanksgiving for so great a benefit, by which I established her as mother of so great a race, destined to possess so great an inheritance of the kingdom of God.

But you, “show me,” as you do show, “your face; let your voice sound in my ears,” that I may hear, and that the friends may hear also. One of them, or the first, heard it while he was still enclosed in his mother’s womb, and leaped for joy at your voice, which thus sounded in my ears: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1). There, at my voice and at your voice, he began to hear and rejoice. Hence he also said elsewhere: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3). Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.

Since, then, the friends also listen, and I delight in hearing the countenance of faith and hearing the voice of confession and thanksgiving, 388 “show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.”

In what sense is your voice sweet? Namely, in that you are my dove, intent upon the clefts already mentioned, and, like a dove, have groaning instead of song. Singing, you groan; groaning, you sing. And the very exultation by which your spirit rejoiced in God your Savior is full of groans, full of tears. In what sense is your face beautiful? Namely, in that your faith is great and your humility great. This is the beauty desired by the King, as the Psalmist says: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44 [45]).

“Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards; for our vineyard has blossomed.”

Herod is the fox; the little foxes, or foxes, are all those of that time who sought the child’s life. Hence, concerning one of his descendants of the same name, when it had been reported to him and the Pharisees said, “Go out and depart from here, because Herod wishes to kill you” (Matt. 2), he said: “Go, tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13).

Herod, then, was a fox, especially because he was not only cruel but also deceitful: he said, “Go and inquire diligently concerning the child; and when you find him, report to me, so that I also may come and worship him” (Matt. 2). That there were then already others with him of the same deceitfulness is clear also from the angel’s words to Joseph: “Arise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the child’s life are dead” (ibid.).

Therefore, “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards”: that is, let those who seek the child’s life be killed swiftly, die, and perish. Do you not see how these little foxes “destroy the vineyards”? For Herod does not cease to kill almost all who were of royal stock; he does not cease to search, in order utterly to destroy the house of David, from which he had heard that Christ the King would be born. Do you not see, finally, that this beast bit the tender shoots, that the cruel beast killed the infants in Bethlehem of Judah, the city of David?

Catch them, catch them, “for our vineyard has blossomed.” That vineyard which is ours—the vineyard or vine on whose account they destroy the other vineyards—was hidden among them as a single slender rod is commonly hidden in a great forest because of its smallness. This vineyard of ours, I say, has blossomed. Its fruit is still a flower, not a cluster; it has not yet ripened. Therefore it is exceedingly harmful to cut down or destroy such a vineyard or its flower.

Let it first grow, and let fruit come from the flower; let the Gospel be established, and let it be known by signs and powers that the Holy of Holies has come. This will be for the flower to become fruit and the cluster to ripen. Then, if such a cluster is cut, let it be preserved and borne upon the pole of the cross, so that by the proof of its resurrection and sweetness it may be known what its land and what its kingdom are like—a kingdom to which these little foxes, “which destroy the vineyards,” do not belong.

Thus long ago the two men among the scouts whom Moses sent to explore the land of promise carried away on a pole a branch with its grape, together with the other fruits of the land, saying: “We came into the land to which you sent us, which truly flows with milk and honey, as may be known from these fruits” (Num. 13). Let the mystery of that deed be observed, and let our vineyard be defended from foxes until its flower becomes an early-ripening cluster, recognizable by its own taste and destined to give the world proof of the land of the living.

“My beloved is mine, and I am his, he who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

This is why “all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1): because “my beloved is mine, and I am his.” For how is he mine and I his except as was said through the prophet: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7)? Thus he is mine and I am his. It need not be stated in words, for it can be perceived better by the mind; indeed, it can neither be expressed in words nor comprehended or estimated in the mind, what or how great this is.

Let us also recall here the old history, from which may be gathered both how terrible is that which is contained beneath these so pleasing words, “he who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline,” and how seriously it is said of Emmanuel: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good.”

What is that old history? “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah,” the Lord says to Abraham, “has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18). “And two angels came to Sodom, while Lot was sitting in the gateway of the city. He strongly urged them to turn aside to him. When they had entered his house, he made a feast, baked unleavened bread, and they ate. But before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded his house, all the people together from youth to old age. And they called Lot and said to him: ‘Where are the men who entered your house tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them’” (ibid., 19).

Two angels indeed had come; but it must be carefully observed that it is subsequently written thus: “Lot also said to them: ‘I beg you, my lord, because your servant has found grace before you, and you have magnified your mercy which you have shown me, in saving my life,’” and so forth. Therefore, both in the three angels who came to Abraham at midday and in the two who came to Sodom in the evening, one and the same God is to be recognized, who both worked through them and spoke in them: “I will go down,” he says, “and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Thus you may rightly say even of that time already past: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good,” since he had a feast both with Abraham and with Lot in order to gain experience of that great evil, and he fed with them until the day breathed and the shadows inclined, that is, until morning. For thus it is written: “And when morning came, the angels urged him, saying: ‘Arise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you also perish together in the wickedness of the city.’”

O how terrible to the impious, and how venerable to the devout, is that which is understood, according to the likeness of that deed, in these words: “He feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” What are the lilies but Joseph, the friend of the Beloved, and I, the beloved, to whom he says: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters”? Truly, both are lilies, namely because of their virginal marriage and most chaste cohabitation.

The Beloved feeds among such lilies “until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” Emmanuel “eats butter and honey,” that is, whatever food is necessary for the body, “that he may know to reject evil and choose good.” For he once said: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come to me; I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled it in deed, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” And now he says, because the outcry of the blood of the holy prophets, which the Jews shed, “has come to me: I will go down to see whether they are such, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

For I am about to make the universal judgment, of which the sulphurous burning of Sodom was an example, according to the saying: “Reducing the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, he condemned them to destruction, making them an example to those who would act impiously” (2 Pet. 2). If I did not carry out judgment in Sodom until I first knew by experience whether it was so or not, how much more, before I make that universal judgment, must I experience it, so that I may know to reject evil and choose good, beginning thus: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4).

When I have received this experience in myself, when they have filled up the measure of their fathers by killing me, the Lord of the prophets, as their fathers killed the prophets (Matt. 23), then judgment will begin from their blindness, according to the likeness of the Sodomites. For thus it was said and thus it was done: “And behold, the men put forth their hand and brought Lot inside to themselves, and shut the door; and they struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Gen. 19).

Thus blindness will happen in Israel among those who are not so much Israelites as Sodomites, according to Isaiah: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 41 [probably Isa. 1]). And when the day has breathed—understand, the day of my resurrection—and the shadows of sins and ignorance have inclined in those, namely, who have repented, then I shall overthrow them as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah on that morning; not that no remnant will remain, according to the prophetic saying: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire” (Amos 4). Again: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1).

This is what the Beloved says to me. And what do I say to him? “Return; be like a roe or a fawn of stags, my beloved, upon the mountains of Bethel.” What was this but a prayer for the salvation of the remnant of my people? Would I have less compassion or charity for my people than the friends, namely the prophets and apostles?

For example, Isaiah says: “Why, O Lord, have you caused us to stray from your ways and hardened our heart so that we should not fear you? Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your inheritance” (Isa. 63). And the Apostle says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that great sorrow and continual grief are in my heart” (Rom. 6 [probably Rom. 9]), and so forth.

Therefore do not doubt that I too pleaded for the salvation of the remnant of my people. The substance of that plea is this: “Return; be like a roe or a fawn of stags, my beloved, upon the mountains of Bethel”—that is, for the fathers of the house of God, for this is what Bethel means. Blindness will indeed happen in Israel, so that they cannot find you who say, “I am the door” (John 10), according to the aforesaid likeness of the Sodomites, whom you struck with blindness so that they could not find the door. But return upon the mountains of Bethel: that is, as Isaiah says, “Return for the sake of your servants” (Isa. 63); remember your mercy, as you spoke to our fathers (Luke 1), so that at least, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11).

Alternatively: “Return; be like a roe or a fawn of stags, my beloved, upon the mountains of Bethel.” You who feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline; you who eat butter and honey in order to know to reject evil and choose good—and do so among the lilies of chastity, who are the best: the father and I, the virgin mother—when the day has breathed and the shadows have inclined, return: that is, rise at dawn, “very early in the morning, when the sun had already risen” (Mark 16), in full light, when the shadows of our mortality have inclined and been destroyed in our restoration.

Return swiftly; do not delay, for my soul longs for you. I know indeed that you will return swiftly, according to the prophetic saying: “He will restore us to life…”

“…us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence” (Hos. 6); and according to what you yourself said: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. 12). The period of three days is indeed short; but for your beloved and dove, longing and groaning with a wounded heart, you have not hastened sufficiently, my beloved. Shorten this very three-day period, and in returning be like “a gazelle or a young stag”: that is, be exceedingly swift in completing your course. Do not spend the entire three-day period in the heart of the earth—that is, in your tomb.

It is enough, [Col. 0873D] for fulfilling the truth of the Scriptures, if you spend only a small part of the first day—that is, its final three hours—and some part of the third day, namely six hours, which is half a night, together with the second day, that is, with the Sabbath, lying in the tomb. For three complete days contain seventy-two hours. That would be too long. Thirty-three hours suffice: a number composed of two threes, a ten and a unit. The blessed Trinity, against whom the first human being sinned, must be appeased in you, through you, and from your very self, my beloved—my flesh and my blood, my God and my Lord. But let this occur with the greatest speed and haste, just as a gazelle or a young stag is swiftest upon the mountains, [Col. 0874A] in accordance with your name, by which you were commanded through the prophet to be called: “Hasten to take away the spoil; make haste to seize the plunder” (Isa. 8).

Therefore, when scarcely thirty-three hours have passed, return over the mountains of Bethel: that is, rise again and appear to the rulers of the house of God, namely to your apostles and to me. For you are the great object of my longing above all—as also of theirs, indeed much more than of theirs—according to the saying of the patriarch Jacob to his handsome son Joseph: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills should come” (Gen. 49). How truly he called you “the desire,” I have experienced especially within my own womb; and this must be made known to your friends.

## CHAPTER III

“In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves. [Col. 0874B] I sought him and did not find him. I will rise and go about the city, through the lanes and squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him. The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loved? A little while after I had passed beyond them, I found him whom my soul loved. I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.”
