You perceive this within yourselves, friends, all who have the holy Spirit of love, all who love the Lord God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your soul. You perceive this, I say, friends and daughters of Jerusalem: great longing belongs to this love. The nearer this beloved one is possessed, [Col. 0874C] the more ardently he is desired. Those who possess desire to possess; those who see desire to see. For angels see, and yet, as Scripture testifies, they desire to look into him.

But I did not merely possess or see him: I carried him in my womb, bore him, offered him a mother’s milk, and contemplated him attentively. What do you suppose—how many nights did I spend wakefully watching and hearing him? The day did not suffice for so great a longing; throughout whole nights, in my bed, in my chamber, I kept vigil, cherished, and adored him as a little child; I heard and adored him when already grown, when in sweet converse he poured upon me through his eyes—the eyes of his body—the sight of his divinity, yet tempering it so that I could endure [390] him whom angels and the powers of heaven tremble before, [Col. 0874D] according to what you hear him say in this very book of Canticles: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee away” (Cant. VI).

Thus I had him in my bed; but afterward it happened that I did not find him there. For he said, “What is there between me and you, woman?” (John II). From the time when he was baptized by John, it began to be the case that I did not find him in my bed or chamber, in that secret place of my dwelling. For immediately “he was led into the wilderness by the Spirit” (Matt. X, XIX), and afterward, having returned, he preferred the Gospel to these affections, so that he said, “What is there between me and you, woman?” He also taught others to do likewise: namely, to leave father and mother for the sake of the Gospel (Luke IX).

Therefore I sought him in longing and did not find him, that I might possess the solitary one in solitude. So I said: “I will rise and go about the city through the lanes and squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves.” And I said it and did so. For when he went about cities and villages preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, I followed and sought him. “I sought him and did not find him.” For he was so intent upon that work that he in some manner seemed to disown recognition of me, his mother.

Indeed, one day, when “he was speaking to the crowds, someone said to him: Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside seeking you. He answered the one speaking to him and said: Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father [Col. 0875B] who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII; John XIX; Luke VIII; Mark III). In this way he seemed to disown recognition of me, his mother. This is what I mean when I say, “I sought him and did not find him.”

Afterward I stood beside his cross. But did that mean that I had found my beloved? Rather, I found the sword that pierced my soul. He was buried; the tomb was closed and sealed. And with what disposition did I seek him? With what longing did I long for him, knowing that he would rise from the dead? There “I did not find him. The watchmen who guard the city found me.”

Who were these watchmen, or what city did they guard? His disciples, because they were appointed to guard—or rather, to build—the true city [Col. 0875C] of Jerusalem, concerning which, or unto which, that beloved himself said through Isaiah: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not cease to praise the name of the Lord” (Isa. XXVI). These watchmen were already then awake, because mourning and weeping, they could not sleep.

These watchmen found me; and the women who, keeping watch all night, came to the tomb—who had also bought spices in order to anoint him when they came (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI)—found me, bringing me eagerly the good news that he had risen and that they had seen him. And I said: “Have you seen him whom my soul loved?” “We have seen,” they said, “we have seen the Lord. ‘He has truly risen and appeared to Simon’” (Luke XXIV). He was also seen by [Col. 0875D] two men going to Emmaus; then he stood in our midst and said, “Peace be with you,” and showed us his hands and side (John XX). We offered him a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb; he ate before us and said: “These are the words which I spoke to [Col. 0876A] you while I was still with you” (Luke XXIV), and so forth.

In these and other ways we saw him on that very third day on which he rose. These things those watchmen told me. But I desired to find him in such a way that no one thereafter would despise me when I said, “I found him; I saw him.” And so it came to pass. For a little while after I had passed beyond them, I found “him whom my soul loves”—and not in any ordinary way, but I saw him ascending into heaven, and I saw his apostles, after the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, preaching the glory of the Lord (Acts I).

This was my finding of him whom my soul loves; and from that finding I held him, so that I might bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me—that is, the Synagogue. This has already happened in part, because many Jews believed in him; others, however, [Col. 0876B] with their hearts closed, rejected both me and him (Acts II, III). But I shall not let him go until I bring him there. “For,” Scripture says, “though the people of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall return” (Isa. X).

The beloved one, most beloved among beloved women, is an example to other souls, that they likewise, according to their measure, may seek their beloved and desire to find him. We seek the beloved in the bed when, amid some small repose of this present life, we sigh in longing for our Redeemer. We seek by night because, although the mind now keeps watch in him, the eye is still darkened. But whoever does not find the beloved must rise and go about the city—that is, traverse the holy Church of the elect in mind and inquiry—and seek through the lanes and squares; that is, by passing through narrow and broad ways, and considering whether one may find any traces of him among them. For there are some even in secular life who possess something in their conduct worthy of imitation.

As we seek, the watchmen who guard the city find us: the holy Fathers, who safeguard the estate of the Church, meet our good endeavors so as to instruct us by their words or writings. When we pass a little beyond them, we find how we love: for although our Redeemer was a man among men in humility, in divinity he was above men. Therefore, when the watchmen are passed beyond, the beloved is found; for when we perceive the prophets and apostles to be below him, we recognize that he who is God by nature is above humankind [Col. 0876D]. Thus he is first sought in order to be found, and, once found, held more tightly. As we have said, all holy desires grow through delay; but if they fail through delay, they were not desires.

## BOOK III

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875D] 391 The third recapitulation of the songs begins with a most powerful opening: an exclamation so great in its wonder that it can awaken and make attentive even a drowsing hearer. For, after the preceding adjuration—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and stags of the field, that you do not stir up or awaken [Col. 0876D] the beloved until she herself wills it”—which has been treated above, the divine voice immediately exclaims:

“Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?”

What, I ask, is the object of this wonder? Without doubt it is the wonder of this singular beloved one, this most holy Virgin. And what do we wonder at? Or what does the Holy Spirit indicate to us as worthy of wonder through words such as these: “She comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer”?

O happy disposition of mind, which has so great a proclamation of praise. It is your humility, O handmaid of the Lord, blessed Mary, that the Holy Spirit commends with such wonder. Your fragrance—the eminent fragrance of your humility—ascended to him as truly the sacrifice of a contrite spirit. For what are smoke and dust but a tearful spirit and a deeply humble conscience?

In its own estimation, true humility is harmless smoke, as it were from a burnt ember or charred brand, and dust of dry, thirsty earth, according to the saying: [Col. 0877B] “For my days have failed like smoke, and my bones have dried up like an ember” (Ps. CI); and as Abraham said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). But this is not how God judges you. He distinguishes you otherwise, and better.

You say: “I am dust of the earth, such as the wind scatters and the breeze carries away.” He says: “No; you are perfumer’s powder, or the powder of a perfumer; powder of myrrh and frankincense, such as the Holy Spirit, the perfumer, prepares from the finest frankincense, which is sweetness of mind, and the choicest myrrh, which is the mortification or incorruption of the flesh.”

You say: “I am foul smoke before divine eyes, like smoke that rises failing from an oven or smoke-hole, and fails as it rises.” He says: “No; you are smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense, such as is fitting [Col. 0877C] to rise from the golden censer before the golden altar, even to the eyes and nostrils of the Lord” (Apoc. VIII).

Such smoke—or rather, such a “column of smoke”—you, blessed Mary, breathed forth as a sweet fragrance to the Most High, instructed and made lean by heavenly disciplines. Such were you coming up through the wilderness: that is, possessing a soul deeply solitary. For if the true humility of any soul can be solitary even among crowds—so that it places hope in nothing except God—as Esther, though she was queen, then truly said: “My Lord, who alone are our king, help me, solitary as I am, who have no helper other than you” (Esth. XIV), how much more truly were you solitary, and as though in a wilderness: you who did not know a man, nor desire to know one; and who were almost left by him to whom you had been betrothed—not because the holy angel, who found you solitary, greeted you as solitary, commends you; and because your son was to be born into this world as though fatherless (Matt. I).

Therefore the exclamation is worthy, and the wonder worthy: “Who is this who thus comes up through the wilderness,” or “from the wilderness”? Truly she is marvelous, and greatly unlike her who went down through paradise and fell from paradise: not slender through humility, but exceedingly gross and rigid through the swelling of her mind.

Therefore, do you wish to know how great the Most High’s care was for this woman—he who does not care for the proud? “Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, chosen from the mightiest of Israel; each has his sword upon his thigh [Col. 0878A] because of the terrors of the night.”

For what is the bed of Solomon, the true and truly peaceable king, who made peace between us and the Lord, except that in which the divine nature joined human nature to itself? And what is that, except your womb, beloved of the beloved, the virginal womb? There the divinity of the Word of God—the Word who is God—enclosed himself, and inseparably joined to himself, in unity of person, the human nature formed from your flesh. And behold, the bridegroom—that is, God possessing our flesh with a rational soul—the bridegroom, I say, Christ, God and man, as we sing in the psalm: “He himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII).

How do sixty mighty men surround such a bed of so great a Solomon? Or who are those sixty mighty men? It is a great and marvelous mystery, worthy of hearing and knowing; but first something must be asked. Why did the holy Fathers possess swords, or why did they lawfully use swords?

Today, or in this age, since the Gospel has shone forth, since that bridegroom came forth from his chamber, the use of the sword is not permitted to saints striving toward perfection. “Put your sword back into its place” (Matt. XXVI), says that same bridegroom to Peter, who zealously and faithfully contended for him. What he said to one he said to all, so that we may know that after the time of war, this is now the time of peace (Mark XIII).

Why is this? For what reason was there then a time of war, and is there now a time of peace? Clearly because the devil wished to cut down and uproot, by the barbarous swords of the nations or of impious kings, the root or good tree—that is, the race of Abraham, to whom the promise of the blessed seed was first made (Gen. XII, XXII). The sacred histories are full of this. Therefore it was then a time of war; therefore material swords were then necessary, so that Abraham’s race might be defended, so that the root [392] of Jesse might be defended—so that the race and root of David might be defended and protected until you, blessed Virgin, should be born, the bed, as has been said, of the true Solomon.

O then, true and good counsel, by which sixty mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel surrounded Solomon’s bed. And who are, or were, those mighty or mightiest men? Let us count all those who laudably used swords to defend Abraham’s hope or expectation, along with the prophets whose books survive and who, against the material swords of impious kings, drew the spiritual sword, the sword of the Word of God, not only in speaking but also in writing. They are sixty mighty men (Eph. VI).

The first is the most mighty Abraham, girded with a sword, as was proved in the case of those from whom he recovered the spoil and rescued Lot, his brother’s son, from the four kings (Gen. XIV). The second is Isaac, consecrated by his father’s sword and afterward renowned for a greatness more than royal, so that King Abimelech said to him: “Depart from us, for you have become far more powerful than we” (Gen. XXVI). The third is Jacob, likewise mighty with the sword, as Joseph himself testifies when speaking to his son: “I give you a portion beyond your brothers, which I acquired by my sword and my bow.” The fourth is the same Joseph, powerful by the power [Col. 0879A] of a king, as though a king or a king’s father (Gen. XLI).

The fifth is Moses; the sixth, Aaron; the seventh, Phinehas; the eighth, Joshua; the ninth, Caleb son of Jephunneh; then the twelve judges who judged and delivered Israel, making twenty-one (Judg. III). The twenty-second is Samuel (1 Kings VII); the twenty-third, David (1 Chron. XXIII); the twenty-fourth, Elijah; the twenty-fifth, Elisha; the twenty-sixth, Jehoiada, most illustrious priest and blessed of the Lord; the twenty-seventh, Zechariah his son. They abolished from Judah and Jerusalem the worship of Baal, which Elijah and Elisha had exterminated from Samaria through Jehu, after Jezebel had been killed, once Athaliah, her most impious daughter, was slain. The twenty-eighth is King Hezekiah; the twenty-ninth, King Josiah; the thirtieth, the most noble prophet Isaiah.

After these come the twelve prophets whose books survive, who are also called the “Minor” Prophets, making forty-two. The forty-third is Jeremiah; the forty-fourth, Ezekiel; the forty-fifth, Daniel, together with his three companions Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, making forty-eight (Dan. III). The forty-ninth is Ezra; the fiftieth, Nehemiah; the fifty-first, Zerubbabel; the fifty-second, Jesus, the high priest son of Jozadak, at the return from captivity and the rebuilding of the city or temple.

The fifty-third is Mordecai with Queen Esther; both are rightly counted as one, because Esther’s royal dignity or eminence was Mordecai’s sword. The fifty-fourth is Mattathias; the fifty-fifth, Judas Maccabaeus. After him Jonathan and Simon succeeded one another as leaders; then Judas and John, also called Hyrcanus, the sons of Simon, the last to fight against the leopard—that is, the king of the Greeks—making fifty-nine. Add to these Solomon himself, the king through whom the Holy Spirit spoke these things (2 Chron. XXIII), and they make sixty.

For King Jehoshaphat was indeed among the mighty, but not among the mightiest of Israel, because he gave aid to an impious man and was joined in friendship with those who hate the Lord, through Athaliah, daughter of Jezebel, wife of the son of Jehoram. She introduced Baal-worship into Jerusalem and every impiety for which the swords of the mightiest Israelites became necessary (3 Kings XXII).

“All holding swords, [Col. 0879D] and most skilled in war.” Truly they held swords, and held them rightly: priests as much as kings, patriarchs as much as commanders, prophets as much as judges, if you properly consider the reason of the time already described. For the “bridegroom had not yet come forth from his chamber,” and the devil still labored through his agents and fellow-servants: the Egyptian kings; the Israelite kings divided from David’s house; Assyrian or Babylonian kings; Persian or Median kings; Greek or Macedonian kings. The ancient serpent, the devil, labored—indeed, had labored and strove—seeking to oppose God’s purpose, lest the promise be fulfilled, lest this bed or bridal chamber be established, lest there be a source from which this blessed and beloved Virgin might be born, [Col. 0880A] from whose womb the beloved had to come forth like a bridegroom from his chamber.

These were the terrors of the night meant in the words, “each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.” Hence they were indeed most skilled for war, because they kept before their eyes such a cause for warfare. And truly, considering this cause, it helps and delights one to hear Elijah, or any other prophet or priest, say while striking and killing the impious: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood,” because such a man was without zeal for justice.

It is a remarkable spectacle: when Solomon, that royal or temporal king, said these things, he himself had sixty mighty men surrounding his own bed—that is, his most peaceable and tranquil kingdom. For from his father David he had received thirty-seven mighty men, the first of whom was Eleazar, son of David’s uncle Ahoi, while the last recorded is Uriah the Hittite.

And indeed the mystical sense stands thus: Eleazar was among the three mighty men; and Abishai, brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief among the three; and Benaiah son of Jehoiada performed these deeds and was himself named among the three strong men, who were among the thirty more noble men. This is as though the text had regard to the mystery of those who were to contend for faith in the Trinity, in distinct orders according to thirty and three, each number being ternary—the one simple, the other denary—yet in total making thirty-seven.

To these add the eleven princes whom King Solomon had while reigning over all Israel, and the twelve officers who provided [Col. 0880C] provisions for the king and his household. Scripture records all of them by name, both princes and officers, and they make sixty—except that Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a most valiant man and a man of great deeds, is by this arrangement counted twice.

Those sixty mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel, both through strength of mind and bodily courage, then surrounded the bed—that is, guarded the most tranquil temporal kingdom—of Solomon. And, as in the other praiseworthy and memorable things accomplished by Solomon, so also in this number of mighty men the wisest king foresaw a great and most beautiful sacramental mystery, concerning which enough has already been said as far as possible.

Then, indeed, swords were necessary, as has been said; now only the testimonies of the Scriptures are necessary. Those Scriptures were themselves divinely provided among those same swords, so that they might then be composed and now read in their own time, and that by reading and believing them we might have life in them (John V).

Therefore it immediately follows: “King Solomon made for himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. Its columns he made of silver, its backrest of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

The litter of King Solomon is all the Scriptures of truth: one table of the Lord who governs all things and provides for all, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has placed me” (Ps. XXII). For what does “in a place of pasture he has placed me” mean except that he has made me study the Scriptures? There he governs me—that is, lest I understand anything perversely—and I shall lack nothing necessary for my understanding.

Such a litter is exceedingly high and has an ascent. What kind of [393] ascent? A purple one. What is the purple ascent? Christ, God and man, who suffered for humankind’s salvation and was made purple by his blood. To believe this is to ascend. Whoever thus ascends is admitted by it to the refreshment of life which is in the divine Scriptures. Whoever does not thus ascend, whoever does not believe, never understands the Scriptures.

For this reason the Jews do not understand and are blind: they do not ascend through this “purple ascent.” They do not believe that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, and that he whom their fathers crucified is God and Lord, the true King Solomon, the eternal king. For example: “Give your judgment, O God, to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI), and so forth. How can anyone understand these words and similar ones who accepts another Solomon, another king or son of a king, other than the man who reigned in his own time and died like other men? This king’s litter is much too lofty for him; he cannot reach any of the life-giving foods that wisdom has prepared there.

From what did King Solomon make this litter? From the woods of Lebanon: that is, from holy people, people incorruptible in faith, to whom the woods of Lebanon—that is, cedars—bear a certain resemblance because of their incorruptible nature. How did he make it? In the manner in which the Word of the Lord came to them. For King Solomon himself was the Word of the Lord; through the Holy Spirit he filled their hearts and made their tongues eloquent, so that those not taught by men or through men might know how to speak of heavenly things. Thus they spoke and wrote the pastures of life by which a human being lives, as he himself says: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII; Matt. IV).

There is silver there; there is gold there. For “he made its columns of silver and its backrest of gold.” What is that silver, and what is that gold? The silver is the exceedingly bright outward expression; the gold is the inward majesty of meanings. Gold, I say—or rather, what lies hidden within is “more desirable than gold and much precious stone” [Col. 0881D] (Ps. XVIII), while what outwardly appears is brighter than silver.

“The words of the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “are pure words, silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. II). When he calls them pure and silver, he speaks by analogy: as a chaste woman is free from the stain of corruption, and as well-refined silver is rendered free from all impurities, so no falsehood and no superfluity can be mingled with the Lord’s words or sayings.

This litter of King Solomon—that is, the whole body of canonical Scriptures—surpasses all human wisdom and all the eloquence of this world’s rhetoricians. Here souls begin to live [Col. 0882A] and live forever.

“He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.” How did he pave it? Let King Solomon himself say. We have heard him say: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII). For when the Pharisees asked him which was the great commandment in the Law, he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” And he immediately added: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (ibid.).

He spoke truly, and he spoke an ancient truth. For what else has the Lord required from of old? “And now, Israel,” says Moses, “what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear and love him with all your heart and with all your soul?” (Deut. X). Therefore King Solomon “paved the midst of the litter with love”; that is, he placed the primacy of love in the middle of the Scriptures, because that upon which all other things depend is rightly called, and is, central and principal.

For what purpose did he thus “pave its midst with love”? For the daughters of Jerusalem. What daughters of Jerusalem? Those faithful souls who love Jerusalem as their mother, yet who do not possess manly—that is, perfect—strength in works of righteousness: namely, strength to abandon everything for King Solomon and to be able to shed their own blood for him, or in a virginal vocation continually to celebrate the sacred and blessed feast of bridegroom and bride, beloved and beloved woman, of whom this discourse speaks [Col. 0882C].

How, or in what respect, does it benefit such daughters that King Solomon “paved the midst of the litter with love”? Clearly in this: they can make their own—and do make their own—what belongs to others, what belongs to men or the strong. For example, they are not bodily virgins, but by loving the good of virginity in you, blessed Mary, they make it their own. No woman other than you bore King Solomon, a king so great and so magnificent; but they, by loving in you this so great a privilege, become mothers of the same king.

Likewise, they are not martyrs, nor are they sufficient to fight among the strong and shed their own blood for love of King Solomon; but they love the martyrs, and by loving them make their glory their own. I will say more: they are not gods, but by loving God they are gods, or sons of God, as it is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI).

Accordingly, what follows? “Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal and on the day of his heart’s joy.”

Therefore, daughters of Zion, or daughters of Jerusalem: because King Solomon made such a litter for himself and because “he paved its midst with love” for your sake, come to the wedding. Come and behold: “go forth and see this king,” this peaceable “Solomon,” the prince of peace, “in the diadem,” his royal and nuptial love—what he is like, how great, and how glorious. Do not consider only what he is like in my flesh, how he was born in a lodging-place, how he was laid [Col. 0883A] in a manger. Go forth from these narrow limits and see him in his diadem, “with which his mother crowned him”: namely, the ancient Church of patriarchs and prophets, to whose faith he was promised and from whose flesh he was descended.

Before he was born, his mother made for him that precious diadem by which he was to be crowned and through which he was to be recognized as a great and glorious king. What is this diadem? Clearly, the most illustrious authority of prophetic truth. As many as are its proclamations, so many are the gems and precious stones of this Solomon’s diadem. It was prepared on the day of his espousal, when he came forth from my womb “like a bridegroom from his chamber,” and on the day of his heart’s joy, when, crowned with a crown of thorns, he completed his labor and was afterward gladdened by the triumph of resurrection.

[Col. 0883B] On that day of his joy, on that “day of his espousal,” and in that diadem he is to be seen; from that diadem his greatness is to be known. For example: “A little child has been born to us; a son has been given to us” (Isa. IX), and the rest, unto now and unto eternity. And elsewhere: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you have lain down as a lion and as a lioness. Who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins” (Gen. XLIX), and so forth.

From such prophetic sentences and sayings, from such gold and stones—so many and so precious—was the diadem of the true King Solomon made or assembled. Therefore do not consider him only in the manger; but go forth in mind from the lodging in which he was born [Col. 0883C] and from [394] Pilate’s praetorium or tribunal in which he was judged. See him in the manger and at the same time in the diadem; on the cross and at the same time in that glory and honor with which God the Father crowned him.

And what is the fruit of seeing him? Surely that promised by the prophet: “His eyes shall see the king in his beauty.” Whoever here, where we walk by faith and not yet by sight, sees—or desires to see, through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. II)—King Solomon in such a diadem, shall see that same king in his beauty; shall see him face to face when that which is perfect has come and that which is in part has been done away. It follows:

## CHAPTER IV

“How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are. Your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which is hidden within. Your hair is like flocks of goats [Col. 0883D] which have come up from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing. All bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet thread; your speech is sweet. Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from that which is hidden within. Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle feeding among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”

O wondrous beauty, which the most beautiful author of beauty itself so marvels at and praises in seven proclamations. He considered the eyes, [Col. 0884A] hair, teeth, lips, cheeks, neck, and breasts; and for each one the beloved sang a distinct theme of worthy praise.

Let young people hear these things and conduct themselves in relation to such singing like the joyful and glad children of a wedding, far unlike those to whom he says elsewhere: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matt. XI)—that is, we showed you the things in which God delights, and you neglected to make yourselves suitable to them.

What is sung in these seven measures? What is praised in you, most beloved among beloved women, Virgin of virgins, by the praiseworthy beloved whom the whole choir of angels praises? Simplicity, purity, innocence, teaching, modesty, humility, and integrity of mind and body, or incorrupt virginity, are praised. In the eyes, simplicity; in [Col. 0884B] your hair, purity of thought; in the teeth, innocence; in the lips, teaching; in the cheeks, modesty; in the neck, humility; and in your breasts, virginity with fruitfulness is wondrous and splendid.

Your simplicity is your prudence; your purity is longing for heavenly things; your innocence is devotion; your humility is true strength against the devil; your virginity is the glory of mothers or matrons. These are the sweet measures of heavenly music, which we gladly hear and understand in these words now to be examined more carefully. This is the first description of your beauty.

“Oculi tui columbarum, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet.” — “Your eyes are those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within.”

The eyes of doves and the eyes of stags differ in this: the former possess the sweetness of those who love simply, whereas the latter possess the manifold bitterness of the envious. The simplicity of doves has seven marks of natural virtues. For this little bird is, first, without gall; then it eats nothing living; it feeds the young of others; it always gathers the whiter grains; it nests in rocks; it has groaning instead of song; it willingly remains beside streams, so that, when it recognizes from its shadow the hawk that is coming, it may swiftly escape.

You above all, O Mother of mercy, are without gall: for you never had any envy, any hatred—the familiar property of rapacious ravens. The dove eats nothing living; and you are far removed from those of whom it is written: “They devour my people as food for bread” (Ps. XIII [XIV], LII [LIII]). The dove feeds other birds’ young, and we who were strangers according to the flesh to your race—behold, we live by your merits. The dove gathers the whiter grains, and you, pondering in your heart the testimonies from the Scriptures, kept the secret of God entrusted to you (Luke II). The dove nests in rocks; and you, remaining in the solitude of faith, escaped the poisons of the ancient serpent. The dove groans instead of singing; and groaning was sweet to you, because before all mortals you were wounded in spirit. The dove remains beside streams; but how close to you, or to your breast, is every stream of the Scriptures! The coming of the spiritual hawk could never take you unawares, overtake you, or even approach you.

Therefore your eyes are those of doves; and this is true beauty, apart from what lies hidden within—which God alone sees in you, but which is, because it is unexperienced by us, ineffable, indeed inconceivable. For if someone said—and, with God as witness or knower, said without lying—that he had been caught up into paradise, or into the third heaven, so that he did not know whether he had been caught up in the body or apart from the body, and that he had heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (2 Cor. XII), how much more often were you, Queen of Heaven, present among heavenly things! For angels stood around you in the manner of midwives, singing glory to God; and amid these things did you learn or attain something which is hidden and ought to remain hidden from us?

“Your hair is like flocks of goats which have come up from Mount Gilead.” When did “flocks of goats,” or what “flocks of goats,” appear “from Mount Gilead”? Certainly rational flocks: flocks of rational “goats” then appeared when people began to be such as those of whom the Apostle says: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins,” and so forth down to “in caves of the earth” (Heb. XI [the printed text has II]). When did such people begin to exist, or whence did people of this manner of life appear? Surely when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, they appeared “from Mount Gilead,” that is, from the city of the same name, Gilead. For thus it is written:

“Elijah the Tishbite, of the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: ‘As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whose presence I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except according to the word of my mouth.’ And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Depart from here, go eastward, and hide yourself’” (3 Kings [1 Kings] XVII), etc.

These things were said and done by that first founder and institutor of those called the sons of the prophets, whom the authority of the venerable Fathers agrees were monks in the Old Testament. And he is rightly said to have appeared, because Elijah, their aforementioned founder, is introduced there so suddenly that Scripture nowhere before mentions who he was or from whom he was born.

What are “your hairs,” or whence are your hairs, like those flocks? Surely your most subtle thoughts were directed toward fleeing into the desert of the Gentiles, because of the blood which the Synagogue had abundantly shed, just as they fled into wildernesses because of the blood which Jezebel first shed—according to her name, which is interpreted “flow of blood”—when she killed the prophets of the Lord. In this your “hairs” are “like” those flocks: that is, like them—indeed, more than them—all your thoughts, all your meditation, sought solitude and rest in all things, far from Jewish storms; for, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God—the sinful Synagogue, in every respect like Jezebel, whom Elijah, whose name is interpreted “the Lord God,” and thereafter the sons of the prophets, not without reason fled, according to the saying:

“And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest? Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude, and I waited for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and the storm” (Ps. LIV [LV]).

And you are a dove like them; and which of them is like you, the dove? This likeness lies in the hair, not only because of the things already said, but also because you too long endured martyrdom in your thoughts, foreknowing the future Passion of your Son, just as they, long needy, distressed, and afflicted, were all found approved through the testimony of faith (Heb. XI).

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing; all bearing twin young, and none among them is barren.” What a beautiful order! First the eyes, then after the eyes the hair, and after the hair the harmless teeth are washed. Look, friends, to the left; consider Eve, the hateful woman set opposite this beloved one, whose eyes, hair, teeth, lips, cheeks, neck, and breasts were ill-starred. Her eyes were not like doves’ eyes, but like the eyes of rapacious ravens. For it is written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Gen. III). Such ambition had the promise: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (ibid.).

Therefore her hair—that is, her ambition—was not like the flocks of goats mentioned above, whose characteristic is heavenly desire, but like that prince over all the children of pride, who said in his heart: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Job XLI [Isa. XIV]). And what were her teeth like? Surely like the teeth of lions, which bit and, by biting what was forbidden, killed the souls of her future offspring. For if it has been truly said or written of her children: “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows” (Ps. LVI [LVII]); and, “God will break their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will shatter the grinders of lions” (Ps. LVII [LVIII]), how much more rightly could someone say of her, who bit by such counsel and whose bite produced so evil an outcome, that her teeth were iron weapons, her teeth were grinding-stones or molars?

But “your teeth,” O my beloved, are “like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up”—that is, they shall most certainly come up—“from the washing.” For when I shall have set forth from myself, from my side, the washing of regeneration—when I shall have poured out the washing of blood and water (John XIX) and bestowed the invocation of the Holy Spirit—then the sheep for whom I lay down my life will be washed and cleansed in the same washing. Nor content with simple cleansing, they will lay aside their fleeces: the fleeces of possessions, the fleeces of their resources, so that they may possess nothing as their own, but all things may be held in common among them.

All such shorn sheep bear twin young, and none among them is barren. In what sense do they bear twins? Namely, in that they have both fulfilled or kept the commandment and added the counsel to it. What is the commandment, and what the counsel? Certainly the commandment is not to seize what belongs to another; the counsel is to leave even one’s own things (Matt. V). They have joined this counsel to the commandment; and this is the twofold good, this is the fruitfulness of twin offspring.

Thus, O my beloved, are your teeth: that is, you set before yourself the innocence of such persons, since you are the teacher of that very innocence—far more excellent than any such sheep or rams, whose teeth, of course, are not used wickedly, namely to bite one another, slander one another, and consume one another. And indeed, whatever flock is such knows you as its teacher; but you, humbler than all, think more highly concerning almost all, and you seem to yourself to imitate my goats and sheep, though you surpass them far beyond measure.

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” In what respect are your lips like a scarlet ribbon? Surely because your speech does not disagree with truth, but strongly agrees with truth. This is the beginning of truth: that one should not defend oneself against God; rather, let some son or daughter of Eve accuse himself before God—Eve who dissolved friendship between herself and God by insolent self-defense. If she had had such a ribbon, if she had bound herself to her Creator with the bond of perfection, which is love, the wall of enmity would not have arisen in the midst (Eph. II).

Upon your lips are “confession and beauty”; upon your lips are “holiness and magnificence” (Ps. XCV [XCVI]). She was mute before God, but you magnified the Lord with most ardent mind and sweetest voice; and this is the scarlet ribbon, because charity is fiery. Bound well to him by it, you clung to God so that you are one spirit with him (1 Cor. VI). Hence “your speech is sweet,” because the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, and the speech which overflows outward tastes the sweetness which abounds within.

Behold, Rahab the prostitute tied the scarlet ribbon, or scarlet cord, in her window as the sign of her faith: that she had received and saved the messengers of Joshua, or Jesus (Josh. II). So the Church, once sinful and filthy with the prostitution of idolatry, continually utters your sweet speech—by which your soul magnified the Lord (Luke I)—as the pledge of her salvation, and always preaches with unbroken faith all evangelical teaching, in which your lips undoubtedly confirmed the Apostles themselves (1 Cor. I). And of every soul which, by its preaching, binds those who think differently into unity, so that all may say the same thing, and does this “in charity and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I), it is true to say: “Her lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” But in this grace you are incomparable with all others after me, your Beloved, to whom the Spirit says especially in the Psalm: “Grace is poured out upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV [XLV]).

“Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within.” A pomegranate is called *malum Punicum* because its kind was brought from the Punic region. It is also called *malum granatum*, because within the roundness of its rind it contains a multitude of seeds. Physicians deny that bodies are nourished by eating this fruit, but think it should be used in such a way as to appear medicinal rather than nourishing.

“Thus,” he says, “your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate”: that is, you are modest, as befits a virgin, very unlike those daughters to each of whom it had to be said: “The forehead of a harlot has been made yours, and you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. III). A fragment of pomegranate is both red and more fragrant than an intact pomegranate. Thus you are uniquely modest, and through your good reputation you will profit many by a good example.

But what does it mean to say, “apart from what lies hidden within,” except as if he said: “And that which lies hidden inwardly in the conscience is still more praiseworthy”? O truly praiseworthy modesty, where the conscience within is pure and the face outwardly modest! For where there is something of which the mind ought to be ashamed, it is not so praiseworthy if shame suffuses the face when it is seen. Therefore what is your modesty but supreme religious devotion? And without doubt this virtue ought to be compared to the pomegranate, because it is pleasing to the eyes of those who behold it, and sometimes by its silence edifies no less than a sermon of preaching.

Hence, on the lower edge of the high priest’s tunic, down to its feet, the Lord says to Moses:

“You shall make, all around it, pomegranates of violet-blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, with bells mingled between them, so that there shall be a golden bell and a pomegranate, and again a golden bell and another pomegranate. Aaron shall wear it when performing the office of ministry, so that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the Sanctuary in the presence of the Lord, and he shall not die” (Exod. XXVIII).

The pomegranate amid the bells is the devout and diligent silence—especially of the female sex—within the fellowship of faith or teaching of preachers. Such above all were you, Virgin of virgins, in assisting, or even directing, the preaching Apostles. Although your words are not read or heard where they preached, your works and merits are not unknown: they are no less, indeed greater, than the ringing of the preachers.

That artificial pomegranate was also red, since it was made not from violet-blue alone—whose airy color signifies heavenly life—but also from purple and twice-dyed scarlet. And thus are “your cheeks,” O beloved modest one and teacher of fitting modesty, or of necessary religious devotion: your modesty is so much the more praiseworthy as your conscience is more glorious, safer, and more secure.

“Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements.” What was David’s tower? Do you suppose it was that man-made tower of which we read, “David captured Zion; this is the city of David”? No: David’s tower was not man-made, to which your neck, O beloved, ought to be compared; it is David’s humility. And this meaning is more pleasing.

“The daughters of Zion,” says the Lord God in Isaiah, “were lifted up and walked with neck outstretched; they went with beckoning eyes and clapped” (Isa. III). This was their pride. Therefore they could be conquered. But your neck was in no way stretched out; it is like David’s tower—that is, like David’s humility—by which he stood strong before God and unconquerable against men. For he, like the tenderest little worm of wood, though an anointed king, said to Saul when Saul pursued him: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a single flea” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] XXIV).

This tower was built with battlements, and a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty. That is: other virtues followed upon his great humility, especially courage and wisdom, as it is written: David, sitting in his seat, is most wise, like the tenderest little worm of wood, who killed eight hundred in one assault. O what a tower, what battlements! From it hang a thousand shields, all the armor of the mighty: because through humility he received the ability to sing and write so many words of strength, of wisdom, and of truth that a thousandfold number is intended—words so powerful that no falsehood can withstand all the mighty who are armed from them.

Thus is your neck—indeed, beyond that tower—your neck, that is, your humility, which is seated or manifest in your unextended neck, built with battlements; and from it hang a thousand shields, all the armor of the mighty. For nothing is lacking there of all that is contained in the Scriptures of truth; and neither the invisible devil nor the visible heretical human being ever could, or ever will, prevail against it. Add this greatest point: the humility of your father David received the mysteries of the Word, in order that he might sing; but your humility, O daughter of David, conceived the same Word in his substance and gave him birth incarnate.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, feeding among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” O breasts truly most welcome and beautiful, two breasts formed by the hand of the Most High! These are virginity and fruitfulness, whose beauty is to be especially seen in your breasts, beloved one: chaste, female breasts which gave me milk. Look, friends, upon these breasts; indeed, behold in these breasts these two things, virginity and fruitfulness. Are they not like two twin fawns of a roe? Nothing like it has ever been seen in our mountains or hills, nor shall it be seen in ages to come: that a single roe should bear two such twin fawns, that it should happen to a single woman both to nurse a son at the same breasts and to remain a virgin.

Look upon this and marvel; see and rejoice together, because this roe bore such twin fawns: because this woman, while she leaps across mountains like a roe, while she directs her mind toward heavenly and higher things, happily received these twin gifts of full grace, so that she might be both mother and virgin. What shall we do with these twins? They feed and are fed among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline: that is, they are to be guarded in secret, held in silence, and not publicly preached as twins until I rise from the dead—which is the day’s breathing and the declining of the shadows of mortality.

These things are altogether secret among the lilies: that is, in, or with, those who have both the brightness and the sweet fragrance of chastity. The first of these was she in whose womb the infant leaped at our fragrance, far unlike those daughters who have, as it were, seven demons—the opposites of these seven descriptions of your beauty which I have now set forth: loftiness of eyes, arrangement of hair, greediness of teeth, incontinence of lips, irreverence of cheeks, excessive raising of the neck, and frequent abuse through subjection and breaking.

The time will come when these things of yours, now secret, must be proclaimed to God’s glory. First this will happen: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense.” How shall I go? I shall go up to Jerusalem, and all things written concerning me shall be fulfilled: “For I shall be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked and scourged; and after they have scourged me, they will crucify and kill me” (Matt. XVI, 20 [cf. Matt. XX]). This will be going to the mountain of myrrh—namely, being put to death or killed, as the prophets were put to death by the fathers of these people. On the third day I shall rise from the dead; afterward I shall ascend into heaven and sit at the right hand of the Father, according to the saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX [CX]). This will be going to the hill of incense. For from that point it will be known and preached that I am God, according to the saying: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God” (Isa. IX). This will be preached and confirmed by the signs which follow; and thus incense will be offered to me as to the true God, when the idols of the Gentiles and the altars of demons have at once been destroyed, to which incense and sacrifice have hitherto been offered by the ignorant and erring.

What next? “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come. You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” When I have passed through the mountain of myrrh and arrived at the hill of incense—that is, when I have risen from the dead, and, crowned with the glory and honor of resurrection and immortality and seated at the Father’s right hand, begin to be worshipped and honored with incense, that is, with every divine religious service, as God, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit—then finally you also “shall be crowned”; then finally I shall say to you: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”

How shall I say this to you? Surely through the great and manifest preaching of the Gospel. Even now you are beautiful; but it has not yet appeared that you are wholly beautiful and that there is no blemish in you—namely, that you conceived or bore as a virgin and nursed me from virgin breasts. It will be preached to the Gentiles that in you there is no blemish before God. Then at last I shall say to you: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come; you shall be crowned.”

Whence shall you be crowned? From the summit of Amana, which is interpreted “night bird”; from the peak of Sanir, which is interpreted “tooth of vigils”; and Hermon, which is interpreted “anathema,” or “accursed thing.” You shall come from Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening”: that is, you shall depart from this body, a whitened body, a virginal body; and you shall be crowned from all these—that is, from the body or members of him who is fittingly denoted by these names, from the kingdoms of this world.

For the kingdoms of this world are rightly called certain heads or peaks of the night bird, the tooth of vigils, and the truly accursed devil, separated from God; because he is the prince of darkness and, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. V), he is rightly called both a night bird and a tooth of vigils. I also call those same kingdoms dens of lions and mountains of leopards, since the kings of kingdoms—the kings of the Babylonians, Persians, and Medes, and the kings and consuls or emperors of the Romans—are they not lions and leopards, who have torn the world to pieces through so many wars and so many massacres?

From the dens of such lions and the mountains of such leopards you, my beloved, shall be crowned. How? Namely, they will believe in me, the fruit of your womb, and the salvation of those who believe will be your crown. Thus you shall be crowned: both Queen of the saints in heaven and Queen of kingdoms on earth. For wherever that saying concerning the Beloved is preached, “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII), it will also be preached concerning you that you, O beloved, are the mother of this crowned one and consequently Queen of Heaven, rightly possessing the whole kingdom of your Son. With this in view, kings and emperors will crown you with their crowns; they will consecrate their palaces to my name and dedicate them to your honor, so that they may cease to be what they were: mountains of leopards and dens of lions.

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride. You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” For who ever had, as you have, my sister and bride, one of the eyes? Scripture tells of a certain holy and truthful woman that, since she was barren and therefore prayed to the Lord with a bitter spirit, weeping abundantly and multiplying her prayers before the Lord, it afterward adds: “And the woman went to her house, and her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] I).

What was that uniformity of countenance, no longer changing in different directions? Surely it was identity of thoughts and the intensely focused perseverance of the same prayers—thoughts which, certainly, you discern, O friends, who say: “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. IV).

This is one of the eyes: this uniformity of countenance, of the face of the spiritual, inward eyes—by tireless charity to direct a righteous prayer perseveringly to the Lord as it was begun, and always to think the same thing. And who is such in this regard as you, O singular beloved, whom, alone among all lovers, the love of the Beloved has wholly occupied and wholly possesses? In this one thing, my sister, my bride—my sister through faith, my bride through the Holy Spirit, through true love—you have wounded my heart. Through this one of your eyes you have wounded my heart, and therefore my inward parts could not restrain themselves toward you.

Nor only “in this one of your eyes have you wounded my heart,” but also “with one lock of your neck”: that is, with the exceeding humility of your heart. I have always seen that lock as one; I have observed that humility to be always uniform and unfailing. What is more slender than one hair, and what subtler than humility? What is more flexible than hair, and what more yielding than humility? A single hair scarcely appears; your humility scarcely allows that you can be counted among human beings.

This is the lock of the neck: the humble thought of a woman without a head—without, I say, a head, that is, a husband—who neither has nor wishes to have one. For “the head of the woman is the man” (Eph. V [cf. 1 Cor. XI]). You judged yourself unworthy of this head; you considered yourself unworthy of a husband and of every worldly age. Knowing this, the friends say—and say truly—that you first made to God an excellent vow, the vow of virginity. Nevertheless, you accepted the name of bride; you did not refuse to be betrothed to a man; and amid these things you fixed ever more firmly upon me that one of your eyes and that aforementioned lock of your neck: strong in faith, steadfast in hope, immovable in charity.

For if Abraham and Sarah could faithfully hope (Gen. XII) that I would not neglect their marriage but preserve it undefiled in Pharaoh’s house—and therefore neither did Abraham refuse that Sarah should be taken into that house, nor did Sarah herself flee it—how much more did you, most faithful one, hope that I would be faithful, able and unwilling to neglect preserving your virginity inviolate in the bridegroom’s house, especially that of one faithful and just; and therefore you did not flee the solemnity of betrothal?

Thus, always and everywhere having one, or unity, of the eyes—that is, a countenance not changed in different directions—you “have wounded my heart.” You cast into me that one lock of yours, namely a humble and contrite spirit, as a most sharp arrow, and “have wounded my heart.” Others, strong and mighty, once held me and did not release me when I said, “Let me go” (Gen. XXIV [cf. Gen. XXXII]); and in wrestling they were strong against God. But you also “have wounded my heart.” They, by wrestling and conquering, obtained for themselves an eternal blessing and the necessary pardon for their sinful people. But you—what did you find, what did you receive, by wounding my heart?

“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.” The friends hear this and understand that I say and marvel at this: that you are mother and virgin; and that this is the fruit of your one eye and one lock of your neck—that, when you considered yourself unworthy of a husband, you were made worthy of God; when you judged yourself unworthy to make offspring in Israel, you were made worthy to bring salvation about in Israel; when you considered yourself unworthy to nurse a human son, you were judged worthy, with beautiful breasts, most beautiful breasts, virginal breasts, untouched breasts, to nurse the Son who is God and human.

Hearing these things, they do not grow weary of the many utterances of the rejoicing Beloved concerning your breasts and bosom, and the other instruments of your beauty—your eyes, hair, teeth, and lips—because they are friends; indeed, “they rejoice with joy because of the voice of the bridegroom” who rejoices (John II [cf. John III]), according to the saying: “The Lord shall rejoice in his works” (Ps. CIII [CIV]). These voices are voices of our joy: of the Father’s, Son’s, and Holy Spirit’s joy in these works of ours, in your breasts or bosom.

Once it was said, “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe”; now again: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!” And a third time: the works of the Trinity are more beautiful—these works more welcome and much more beautiful than those first works when he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I), forming Adam from earth and fashioning Eve from his rib. For is it not far more beautiful, as now, to make a man from a woman’s womb without a man, than then to have made a woman from a man’s rib? There a woman was made from a man, who would bring ruin; here a man was made from a woman, who would save those ruined, and for that purpose he was made.

The beauty of that delightful work is more joyfully seen in your breasts or bosom, when the form of such great beauty has already been accomplished, when he who is nursed has already been born and is nursing at your breasts—female breasts, virginal bosom. What, then, is this comparison: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine”? Or what great thing is it to say: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine”? For in wine is luxury. One of the friends, writing to our young women, says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is luxury” (Eph. V). What great thing, then, is it to say that your breasts are more beautiful than what is not beautiful?

For wine, or that present thing signified by wine, is not beautiful, since it is luxury, or pleasure of the flesh; or that drunkenness, going before, by which no breasts except your breasts ever nursed a son. Therefore this is what, in the schools of human beings, is called *tapinosis*, that is, abasement: diminishing the standing of a great thing by feeble words. For the virginity or integrity of the breasts which nursed me, the Son, is a great thing; and this very beautiful thing is not sufficiently praised when it is declared more beautiful than the marital or conjugal matter—namely, the nursing of children whose beginning is wine, that is, the luxury found in wine.

Likewise, according to the trope which people call metonymy, he shows by that which contains what is contained. I could say thus: your breasts alone, which nursed me, are beautiful. All the breasts of other women, from the time they received the capacity to nurse their children, even if they previously had some beauty, ceased to be beautiful; so that, in fact, every one of those being nursed may truthfully say: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L [LI])—namely, in Adam’s iniquities, in Eve’s sins. For from those iniquities, from those sins, together with other evils, came also this wine: namely, the excess of luxury, through which women’s conceptions are multiplied by God beyond number, so that the elect may be considered few in comparison with the reprobate.

But what are your ointments? For I say: “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” What then are your ointments, my sister, my bride? Your alms, which you expended upon me. Friends hear, and will hear, of a certain woman pouring oil upon the head and feet of your Beloved as he reclined, and say that “the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John XII). They understand that woman to be our Church, which as often as it bestows alms upon our poor, so often pours its ointments upon my feet and distributes spices. For these are true spices and precious ointments: to give food to any hungry one among my enemies, drink to the thirsty, to receive the stranger or traveler, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, and, if he is in prison, to come to him (Matt. XXV).

“Above all these spices is the fragrance of your ointments”: that is, the sweetness of your alms, because you were most bountiful toward me not as others are toward my members, but toward me myself. And indeed, by maternal right and natural affection, you owed me all things; nevertheless, as I regarded your faith, humility, and charity, more than maternal, all things were to me the best ointments, the sweetest alms. Thus no fragrant alms, of whatever kind, which are bestowed upon me in my least ones can in any degree be compared with those ointments.

“Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” It was too little that I said above, “Your speech is sweet,” for it is far too little that sweetness should be in speech unless the heart too is sweet. You are sweet in mouth and sweet in heart. This is what I now say: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb,” adding, “Honey and milk are under your tongue”—that is, in your soul. There your soul tastes sweetly for itself the honeycomb of your speech, the honeycomb dripping from your gracious lips.

I am your honeycomb; I am your honey and your milk, because I am your God and your Son. Your soul perceives this; your lips utter this. You cannot speak other than what you have in your breast: your lips speak “from the abundance of the heart” (Luke VI). And although you were silent before others at times, you could not be silent toward me. From the time you saw me born, you have been consecrated with me by the honeycomb of sweet speech, and likewise by the kiss of my mouth, the kiss of your mouth; and thus satisfaction was rendered to your faith, hope, and love—to faith speaking through love: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I).

What shall I say of the swaddling cloths in which you wrapped me and laid me in the manger? Surely what is true: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” Of all your garments—namely, all your good works which you performed toward me with maternal and more than maternal charity—those cloths were the firstfruits. And because all that you then did to me, or then did on my account, came from the great and powerful fire of charity joined with the sweetness of humility, I rightly say, and the friends rightly agree, that “the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” For in all things you served me, faithful mother and virgin, as God, to whom alone the fragrance of incense is due in his sacrifice, although I was your little one, a little human being.

399. BOOK FOUR.

[Col. 0893]

[Col. 0893D] What are we doing, “O my soul, why are you sad, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 41). Behold, we are in the midst of the wedding-feast [Col. 0894D] of a man, a king, which he made for his son, whom he willed to be incarnate of a virgin. And you tell [Col. 0895A] me that terrible, greatly fearsome thing: “The king came in to see those reclining, and saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment; and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?’ But he was silent. Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness’” (Matt. 22). Where are you tending? Why do you press these things upon me? Do you fear that you do not have a wedding garment? And indeed, if the matter concerns charity, since charity itself is the wedding garment, you did not enter these nuptials, to sing the praises of these nuptials, without charity. Let the mother of the nuptials herself, conscious and witness to the fact, testify that you did not approach without such a garment. Once, when she seemed to be conversing with you, while you were discoursing with her concerning [Col. 0895B] sacred mysteries and the glory of the holy and indivisible Trinity, and she said, “How do you dare to speak of such things?”—her inquiry, however, being made with a serene face and cheerful expression—you answered thus: “I love the blessed Trinity, and from this I know most certainly that, when speaking of it, I shall never stray outside the truth.” Therefore do not be sad, my soul, nor trouble me; “but hope in God, for I shall yet confess him” (Ps. 41)—without straying, which would be almost to be cast into the outer darkness—and hear with joy the following utterance of the Bridegroom: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, are you”—O Mother of God—“a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard: henna with nard, nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon, with every [Col. 0895C] tree of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes, with all perfumes; a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow mightily from Lebanon.”

Behold a new paradise, new plantings, planted by one and the same planter of the ancient paradise, the Lord God. “The Lord God,” Scripture says, “had planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, in which he placed the man whom he had formed. And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to behold and sweet for food; also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads” (Gen. 2). That is the ancient paradise, the earthly paradise; this is the new paradise, the heavenly paradise. The planter of both [Col. 0895D] is one and the same Lord God. In that one “he placed the man whom he had formed”; in this one he formed the man who was with him in the beginning. “From” this “ground he brought forth every tree beautiful to behold and sweet for food, also the tree of life in the midst of paradise.” This ground, this his earth, he blessed; and from it he brought forth the shoots of every grace and the patterns of every virtue: likewise the very tree of life, Christ—God and man—the Lord of the heavenly paradise. “From” that “place of delight a river went out to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads.” From this paradise came forth that river or stream of which the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad [Col. 0896A] the city of God” (Ps. 45); it is divided from there into the four Gospels. That paradise could not keep man, nor did man wish to keep that paradise. Therefore, since that admission into such a paradise, an earthly paradise, did not profit those first parents or us in them, because they did not observe the command they received, another paradise is planted anew, so that, entering it, we may eat of the tree of eternal life and not die. These are the streams of the Beloved, over which the Beloved rejoices in the present passage and speaks thus: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, are you”—O Mother of God—“a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard.”

About to say, “Your streams are a paradise,” he first said, “A garden [Col. 0896B] enclosed, my sister, my bride”; then again, “a garden enclosed,” and afterward, “a fountain sealed.” Now the beginning of the streams of this garden was that, as the angel announced to her, she conceived and bore a son (Luke 1). What, then, do these words proclaim except both the virginity of the one conceiving and the integrity of the one giving birth? Therefore let us too happily say with the Beloved; let us all say with believing hearts and harmonious voices: “You are a garden enclosed, O Mother of God, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” Why “garden”? For a garden is so named because something is always springing up there: while the earth produces something once a year, a garden is never without fruit. In what sense, then, are you a garden, O beloved of the Beloved, except because something was born before you that never ceases, and your fruit never withers or fails?

[Col. 0896C] But it is especially wonderful—indeed true and delightful—that the garden is said to be enclosed. For how can it be a garden if it is enclosed? Nothing like this has ever been heard of among the multitude of all our gardens; nor could a garden be called, or be, a garden that had no entrance through which at least one gardener might enter or leave. This garden alone, or this unique garden, is shut and enclosed; this womb alone is fruitful and incorrupt. Therefore, O my sister and bride, how the friends rejoice because you are such a garden, such a fountain! In body, “a garden enclosed”; in mind or soul, “a fountain sealed.” And why are you twice called “a garden enclosed”? Clearly because of conception and because of childbirth [400]: for in both there is a miracle, wonderful and beloved to the minds of the faithful, since you were neither corrupted in conception nor violated in childbirth. In both, the friends and all our young maidens rejoice and gladly confess it.

And why “a fountain sealed”? And with what kind of seal, or for what reason, sealed? Surely because the Holy Spirit came upon you and the power of the Most High overshadowed you (Luke 1). The Holy Spirit himself is the seal of this fountain of ours, the seal of your breast. And this is a twofold defense for our protection, a twofold joy of our friends: because your womb was accessible to no man, to no fleshly intercourse, and your mind was never penetrable by any vice or any spiritual wickedness. Wonderful it is that, though you are thus “a garden enclosed,” thus “a fountain sealed,” nevertheless—or rather, all [Col. 0897A] the more—you send forth every good thing by which the world is filled; and “your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard,” a paradise of the Scriptures or of doctrine together with good and holy works.

“Your streams,” or your paradise: “henna with nard, nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes with all the choicest perfumes.” This number of aromatic herbs, namely the number seven, is well known to our friends as signifying universality, and especially as consecrated by the Holy Spirit, the sevenfold Spirit who accomplishes this very thing by resting upon me, the first flower of this garden. He accomplishes, I say, this very thing: that you are a garden enclosed; that your streams are a paradise so great [Col. 0897B] and so beautiful, as may be observed from these seven kinds of spices. Among them nard is chief, and therefore deserves to be proclaimed or counted twice, when I say, “henna with nard, nard and saffron.” For it is your humility, which greatly delighted the Most High and delighted me, your royal Beloved, as you yourself say: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1).

Whatever graces, whatever virtues, whatever heavenly workings the world has received are your streams, so that where formerly there were thorn and briar, briar and thistle, burdock and thornbush, nettle and buckthorn—the whole multitude of wickedness—there may be “henna with nard, nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon, myrrh and [Col. 0897C] aloes,” the whole fullness of graces, according to the mystery of this number, the number seven, “with every tree of Lebanon, with all the choicest perfumes.” What are all the trees of Lebanon there? And what are the choicest perfumes, or what do they do there? Surely, the trees of Lebanon are certain of our friends—those friends who are sons, or household members, of our wedding-feast. Yet they are also the great and lofty powers of the world, endowed with ample means, so that our little ones, little ones of the spiritual calling, are supported by their alms, just as tiny sparrows nest in the branches of the trees of Lebanon. Hence the passage inscribed in the Psalm: “The trees of the field shall be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted; there the sparrows will build their nests” (Ps. 103).

Such nests for our sparrows, and all the alms which the powerful and rich friends, or sons of our wedding-feast, make or will make, are the choicest perfumes—perfumes of marvelous fragrance—as is indicated concerning me, your Beloved, where the sinful woman bought precious ointment and poured it over my head or feet as I reclined, “and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 2). Most beautiful is the variety, or diversity, of these your streams, of this paradise of ours: there both the height of the trees of Lebanon and the lowliness of every aromatic shoot—whatever may properly be understood by the shrubs already mentioned—offer a common spectacle of the number seven, while in their midst breathe the choicest perfumes, that is, every work of piety, especially alms. By these may be supplied whatever such household members of our wedding-feast, as has been said, may lack of the spiritual life, though entangled in worldly cares, yet our friends through faith.

[Col. 0898A] Thus formerly in the tabernacle of the Lord, goats’-hair coverings sheltered fine linen and purple by a friendly extension (Exod. 26); thus those who abound less in spiritual things always share their carnal goods with spiritual persons, in order that they may rightly become participants in the spiritual goods of those persons. These are “your streams, my sister, my bride”: streams of the garden enclosed, streams of the fountain sealed, the paradise of God the Father; my inheritance, of your Beloved, Son of God and your son; the work of the Holy Spirit—the one Church, from among your many streams, spread throughout the whole earth. It will always look to you and cry to us concerning ourselves, as the faithful woman from the crowd raised her voice and said [Col. 0898B] to me: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11).

You are “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters”: a fountain of gardens, that is, mother of the Churches; a well of living waters, that is, the treasury of all the holy Scriptures. These living waters—namely, all the holy Scriptures which alone are called, and are, canonical—flow mightily from Lebanon; that is, they flowed from the ancient people, the Jewish people. For the nobility of that people is customarily signified mystically by Lebanon. From that people, O my sister and bride, you and I are descended according to the flesh; and one boundary of its land is the mountain bearing this name. All living waters flow from this Lebanon: all the utterances of God came together upon this people of ours, not in any ordinary way, but with [Col. 0898C] force.

For such waters had to flow with force; the utterances of the Lord had to run strongly, because very many were attempting to resist them, and very many still oppose them and dare to contradict them. Therefore our friends, through whom the utterances of God were administered, had to be endowed not only with divine authority but also with very great worldly power. He who was almost the first to sing in manifest words the mysteries of our kingdom and the powers of the age to come had to become a king: King David, mighty and, in accordance with his name, a warrior strong in hand. Thus he might break by the authority of royal power the childish or immature minds of the people—who did not know how of their own accord to care for things future and invisible, but were excessively eager for these present visible things—tempering terror with persuasion, namely with the sweetness of musical song.

Likewise almost all the rest of our friends through whom God’s utterances flowed were armed with strength and terror, and all used swords. By material swords, I say, these living waters, necessarily armed in this manner, truly ran through them with force. Moses, the first, or the gentlest, of them, when he began, receiving from our fullness, to pour forth living waters—that is, to write the holy and mystical law—took up a sword and ordered it to be taken up; and in one day he slew twenty-three thousand men, makers of falsehood (Exod. 32), by the first onset of the living water, that is, of the law received.
