[Col. 0899A] And they indeed, after ministering in temporal matters, each in his own time died; but the rush of the living waters endures also in the mouth and hands of those who did not write. The most renowned of these was Elijah, who in one day slew four hundred men with great force (3 Kings 18). Therefore you, my sister and bride, are “a well of living waters,” that is, a sanctuary of the holy Scriptures; and this is why I say, “Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard.”

For as in the beginning a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole 401 surface of the earth, just as, I say, “a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads” (Gen. 2), so from you, O friend, O blessed earth, that fountain rose which was with God and was the true light, as it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 55). That fountain, I say, rose from you—not as having its origin or beginning from you, but as coming into you from the Father’s heart by hidden ways, together with all the living waters, that is, with all the Scriptures of truth; and as making in you the eternal fountain or well of wisdom, it thus rose from you.

For what purpose did it rise? Certainly to water the surface of the earth: to instruct or cultivate the Church throughout the whole world. For this purpose the river goes out from the place of delight, namely “to water paradise”; for this, I say, from you, O delight or place of God’s delight, the holy Gospel will take its beginning, so as to water the spiritual paradise throughout [Col. 0899C] the world; and it will be divided “into four heads,” that is, into the four mysteries necessary to salvation: my incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. For these must necessarily be preached and known, because without confession of them our paradise does not come into being, and without faith in them the world is not saved.

The living waters, I say, will be divided into these four heads, that is, principal mysteries, because all the Scriptures subtly direct their attention to these four, calling them the face of a man, the face of a calf, the face of a lion, and the face of a flying eagle. Then the friends will understand what the Scripture of the Law intended even before the Scriptures, when it said: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. 49); what it intended in prescribing such a rite for sacrificing a calf (Lev. 4); what it intended in saying to Moses, “I shall raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like you” (Deut. 18); and what it intended when it sang: “Like an eagle stirring her young to fly and hovering over them, he spread his wings, took them up, and bore them upon his shoulders” (Deut. 32).

[Col. 0899D] Concerning two of the faces—the face of the man and the face of the calf—all agree about me: namely, that I was made man and, being mortal, underwent death. But concerning the face of the lion and the face of the flying eagle, not all agree likewise: namely, that I both rose again and ascended into heaven.

Thus, too, concerning two heads of the river that goes out from the place of delight and is divided into four heads—namely, the river Gihon, called Nile among the Egyptians, and the river Pishon, also called the Ganges—it cannot be denied that they issue from that earthly paradise. But regarding the other two, worldly writers attempt to refute our Scripture, saying that it is not as Scripture says, because they—namely the Tigris and Euphrates—seem to rise in Armenia from a single source. They neither understand nor observe that Scripture did not say that the river of paradise begins within paradise to divide into four heads; rather, it says, “A river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads”: that is, into all rivers and sweet, drinkable waters, of which those chief rivers are the heads.

[Col. 0900A] For the waters were naturally false and bitter; but, ascending through that, as it were, breast of the earth, namely the paradisal earth, they were changed into sweetness, so that they might water the entire surface of the earth. Sweet and drinkable themselves, they made the earth outside paradise habitable for the human race, which was to be captive—namely, fertile in herbs, trees, and seeds. And among the other waters which received sweetness from that breast, those rivers, Gihon and Pishon, Tigris and Euphrates, are preeminent.

Likewise, the waters of the Scriptures are sweetened from you, my sister and bride: from your womb, or through your womb, they have been made living. Otherwise they are very bitter—indeed dead and death-dealing. “For the letter kills,” says one of our friends (2 Cor. 3). What else, indeed, is all that Moses says, all that is read from the prophets among the sons of our mother who fight against you, but letter without spirit, a body without a soul? Therefore those who drink dead waters die; those who read and follow the letter alone, which kills, are killed.

[Col. 0900C] How, then, will this come about? How will such a paradise of your streams be planted or enlarged? “Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; breathe through my garden, and its spices shall flow.” This will happen when the north wind rises and the south wind blows. Who is that north wind? Surely he who said: “I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14); he of whom it was said through the prophet: “From the north evil shall be opened upon all the earth” (Jer. 1). He is “the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Rev. 12).

Whence will such a north wind rise? How will he rise from the hidden ambushes where he lay long ago and crawled as a slippery serpent, when he deceived the first woman, as she said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. 3)? He did not rise there to attack, but hissed while crawling in order to deceive. For he had no power before the woman, whom God had made innocent, voluntarily gave him her consent. Between you and him, my sister and bride, God placed enmities; and therefore he has utterly despaired of you—or rather, he has no hope whatever that by his fraud, deceit, or arts against you he can deceive you.

Therefore I say to him: “Arise, north wind” (Rev. 12). Why do you lie upon the earth? Why do you lie in wait [Col. 0901A] for our heel? You accomplish nothing by lying in wait. Rather, arise, employ your strength, and rage with the whole force of your malice. You acted formerly as a serpent; now act as a great dragon, a red dragon having seven heads. I do not say this as one commanding; I speak with the mind of one permitting. For you began to rise long ago; nor is it other than if I said: Do what you do; rise, you who are rising; rage, you who are raging.

For when did you begin to rise? Surely before this second woman came into being, against whom you will be unable to do anything by deception. When you heard the word of promise now fulfilled, spoken to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), you immediately rose, because you perceived that the enmities foretold between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed, were at hand. You rose; you raised your head—the first head—in the kingdom of Egypt. For you said, speaking in Pharaoh: “Kill and cast into the river every male child that is born; preserve every female” (Exod. 1), and other things of the same kind, until, pursuing those who were departing, you said: “I shall draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” (Exod. 15).

Thus, you who had been a deceiving serpent became a persecuting dragon: a great dragon, a red dragon, that is, bloody. After that first head, you raised your second head by slaying, through the hands of Jezebel and her house, the heralds of this mystery and forerunners of this sacrament, the prophets of the Lord (3 Kings 18). Then you raised a third head in Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (4 Kings 25); then a fourth in the kingdom of the Persians [Col. 0901C] and Medes through Haman, who wished to destroy our race, so that there might be no one from whom I could be born (Esther 3). Then in the kingdom of the Greeks you raised your fifth head through Antiochus Epiphanes; and thus, O north wind, you have now risen five times (1 Macc. 1). The sixth head is now the Roman Empire. The seventh has not yet come, namely the kingdom of Antichrist.

“Arise,” therefore, “O north wind”; that is, do what you do. For I do not command you to do evil which you have never done; but I permit you to rise, because you wish it. Shake forth this sixth head of yours; bring it about that this seed of the woman is handed over into the hands of the Romans. 402 Thus, “arise, north wind; and come, south wind”: come, Holy Spirit, to whom the Devil, the north wind, is opposed; “breathe through my garden, and its spices [Col. 0901D] shall flow.” Then what I said before shall come about: “Your streams are a paradise,” which has never happened in this way. For never, O south wind, have you so come against the north wind that, by breathing through my garden, you made a new paradise flow forth—that is, caused a new Church to be propagated from the multitude of the nations.

## Chapter V
“Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his orchards.” As my beloved speaks to me, so it is. I am “a garden,” I am “a fountain of gardens,” I am “a sealed fountain,” I am his grace, “a well of living waters,” and my “streams [are] a paradise of pomegranates.” Let him therefore come into his own garden, that he may eat the fruit of his orchards. I do not invite my beloved as Eve invited her husband. She invited [Col. 0902A] her husband to eat a fruit not his own, a fruit belonging to another, a forbidden fruit; I invite my beloved into his own garden, to eat the fruit of his orchards—not of others’ orchards, but the fruit of his own orchards—as he says: “My food is to do the will of the Father” (John 4): the salvation and life of the human race which he himself fashioned, blessed, and restored when it was lost.

And among all the fruits of his orchards, what is more properly his own than I, who am the first of the firstfruits of the orchards—indeed, even the fountain of gardens? Let him therefore come into this garden of his, and, by carrying me over into that third heaven, into that third paradise to which he went and to which, while I watched, he ascended (2 Cor. 12), let him eat the fruit of his orchards: let him complete and bring to its end [Col. 0902B] the grace of those works of his which were enacted in me. Since you went into heaven, you often return to that place which you call the paradise of my streams, and you eat of the pomegranates, which are best among the firstfruits of those same streams of mine. For you now eat as many fragments of pomegranates as there are blessed souls of your martyrs and confessors whom you assume from here and convey into that hidden place of everlasting life.

When will you thus come into this garden of yours, to this fountain of gardens which you name? When will you thus come to me, so that where you are, there I too may be with you?

“Come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk [Col. 0902C] my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink, and be intoxicated, beloved ones.”

All things necessary for the salvation or restoration of humankind I accomplished while you were silent. My sister, my bride, now that I rest, some share of that same work is due to you. Why do you hasten so greatly toward your rest? By being born, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, I worked salvation for the world. Now you must remain with my friends and witnesses, and offer fitting testimony to all that has taken place, together with the necessary working of signs and miracles.

Let my friends listen attentively and recount to all the children of our wedding these four things that have occurred: that “I came into my garden,” that “I gathered my myrrh with my spices,” [Col. 0902D] that “I ate my honeycomb with my honey,” and that “I drank my wine with my milk.” For by descending into your womb and taking flesh, so that I, who was true God, might be born as true man, I came “into my garden.” By dying and descending into hell, intending to return with all my saints and elect who had awaited me from the beginning of the world, “I gathered my myrrh with my spices.” By rising again, “I ate my honeycomb with my honey.” By ascending into heaven, “I drank my wine with my milk.”

By descending, I say, into your womb and becoming man, I “came into my garden.” For what is not mine? I indeed—I myself—am the Word “through” whom “all things were made, and without” whom “nothing was made” (John 1). And that paradise of which Scripture [Col. 0903A] says, “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning” (Gen. 21 [probably Gen. 2]), was planted through me. And you, another garden, “an enclosed garden,” were made through me; and the whole paradise of your streams was, or is to be, planted through me. Therefore I called it “my garden.”

But not so could that first man of whom it is written: “The Lord therefore took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to cultivate and guard it” (ibid.)—not so, I say, could he say: “Come into my garden.” For he had neither made nor planted the paradise; nor had he himself been formed in paradise. I both made the garden and was born in the garden; or, to use other words, I both founded the city and was born in the city, as it is written: “A man was born in [Col. 0903B] her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86).

That paradise was not his own, and all the more it befitted him to cultivate and guard what had been entrusted to him. Since he did not do this, it was necessary that I should come into my garden and, by labouring and serving beyond what was owed, should correct the sin of him who did not even perform what was owed. How did I correct it? “I gathered my myrrh with my spices”: that is, I stretched out my hands upon the cross, with this result, that all my own might be saved whom he, by harvesting the death of his soul, had destroyed.

For it had been said to him: “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). He did not obey; rather, in disobedience he stretched uncontrolled hands toward what was forbidden. This was his harvesting: for he had sown an impious [Col. 0903C] thought, swelling inwardly and thinking himself to be like God. This, I say, was his harvesting—not myrrh, but Gehenna; not the death of the body, which is at times precious, as the psalm says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 13 [probably Ps. 115:15]), but the death of the soul, which is an evil death, as the Psalmist likewise says: “The death of sinners is most grievous” (Ps. 33 [probably Ps. 34:21]). He harvested that death; by that death he immediately died when he plucked and bit the fruit from the tree, according to the truth of the saying: “For on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2).

“But I gathered my myrrh,” namely, the death of the body alone—a precious death. Earlier I had sown righteousness; I had sown humility and voluntary obedience, since I was not, [Col. 0903D] as he was, merely man, but both God and man. I considered that whereby I was less than the Father, namely the nature of the flesh, as it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8); and according to that nature I so maintained the order of righteousness that I was subject to all and obedient to the Father, as one lesser to one greater, as man to God, as creature to Creator, according to the Law of Moses.

For example: “Three times in the year,” he says, “all your males shall appear before the Lord your God” (Exod. 34): namely, at the feast of Unleavened Bread, at the feast of the firstfruits of the month, and at the feast at the year’s end, which is the feast of Tabernacles. This part of righteousness or obedience was especially a sowing-ground of myrrh for me, because from it [Col. 0904A] came to my enemies the opportunity to kill me: although I knew that they were plotting my death, nevertheless, because of the commandment of the Law, I went up to Jerusalem. Thus it came about that I gathered “my myrrh with my spices”: that is, through obedience I came “even unto death, indeed the death of the cross” (Phil. 2), with and through which I drew all things to myself (John 12) and acquired all my elect from the foundation of the world (Eph. 1).

What then? “I ate my honeycomb with my honey”: that is, I rose from the dead and received back my flesh, never again to die and ever to live, united to the Word—the Word God—which I am and was. 403 A wonderful contrast, a marvellous correction! That first man, when questioned or rebuked concerning his sin, because [Col. 0904B] he defended himself, not only did not escape the death of the soul which he had incurred, but also acquired in addition the death of the body, God saying: “Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). But I, because I delivered up myself for sin—not mine but another’s—obedient to the Father, not only did not lose the life of my soul, as though because of the curse of the Law, which says: “For he who hangs upon a tree is cursed by God” (Deut. 21), but I also quickly recovered the life of the flesh. And behold, I am a human being alive in both respects, namely in body and soul, contrary to that man, who was dead in both.

Accordingly, both my honey with my honeycomb and “my honeycomb with my honey I ate,” because my honey recognized its honeycomb, and my honeycomb breathed again by means of my honey, so that no [Col. 0904C] myrrh can ever again intervene. That is, life and the Word—which I am, everlasting sweetness—again adorned my flesh, and the flesh passed into the glory of divinity, so that it can now neither die nor can death any longer have dominion over it.

Our friends did not yet know this mystery when, appearing to them alive again, I said: “Have you here anything to eat?” (Luke 24). Then they offered me a portion of roasted fish and a honeycomb. Before them I ate not first the honeycomb and then the portion of roasted fish, but first the portion of roasted fish and then the honeycomb; and, taking the remains, I gave them to them. By this sign I taught that they too, following my example, must first be dried by sufferings and afflictions, and afterward be satisfied with the honeycomb by rising with me.

Likewise my enemies did not know the mystery [Col. 0904D] of this saying which I spoke and now speak: “I gathered my myrrh with my spices”; and nevertheless they gave me myrrhed wine to drink (Mark 15), wine mixed with gall (Matt. 27). After that honeycomb of resurrection comes this consummation of glory and honour: “I drank my wine with my milk,” that is, I was gladdened by the joy of the ascension, Scripture being fulfilled which says: “You will make him glad with joy in your presence” (Ps. 20). For I am that king of whom he said: “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and he shall exult exceedingly in your salvation” (ibid.). That joy, that vehement exultation, is what I now say: “I drank my wine with my milk.”

For I ascended with jubilation (Ps. 46), [Col. 0905A] and from this not only the heart rejoices but the flesh also exults; therefore I said: “I drank my wine with my milk.” This wine of mine caused me to forget former labours, according to that saying: “Give strong drink to those who mourn, O Lemuel, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit. Let them drink and forget their want, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. 31). I drank, and I gave to drink wine with my milk to those who had been bitter in spirit together with me. They drank and forgot their want and sorrow: the want by which they had previously been needy, being “unlettered and ordinary men” (Acts 4); and the sorrow by which they had grieved because of my passion, as I had foretold to them when the hour of my passion was already approaching: “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John 16). Again: “And you therefore now indeed have sorrow; but I shall see you again, [Col. 0905B] and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (ibid.).

Those who saw and heard them, not knowing this mystery—that I had drunk and had offered them to taste my wine with my milk—said, not knowing what they spoke: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2). Finally, I had given them the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete Spirit, who is one and the same as both my wine and my milk: my wine, because he is joy in present goods; my milk, because he is consolation concerning past evils; my wine, because he is love of God; my milk, because he is love of neighbour. And I said to them: “Eat, friends; drink, and be intoxicated, beloved ones.”

What will you eat, and what will you drink? Surely the remains which, after taking them, I gave you: the remains of my honeycomb and my honey, the remains of my wine and my milk—not without remains also of my myrrh or of my roasted fish. I do not invite you to eat and drink as the serpent invited the woman Eve, and the woman her husband; indeed, against what they ate I set before you an antidote of necessary eating and drinking. The serpent gave them nothing of his own but urged them to seize what belonged to another. I give you from what is mine: from my honeycomb and my honey, from my wine and my milk; indeed, also from my body, my blood, and my Spirit.

This Spirit speaks truth to you, contrary to the lie which the serpent spoke to them. For what did he [Col. 0905D] say to them? “For God knows that on whatever day you eat of that tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods; and for that reason he forbade you to eat” (Gen. 3). In saying this, that spirit of blasphemy alleged that God bore great envy toward humankind. But what does this Spirit of truth say to you? The Son of God knows that “if you remain in him, and he in you” (John 15), you will be like sons of God, you will be gods, you will be “all sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81), because your eyes will be opened; your understandings will be opened, so that you may understand the Scriptures. And for that reason he said to you: “Take and eat: this is my body. Take and drink: this is my blood” (Matt. 26). In saying this, this Spirit of grace reveals God’s great goodwill toward us.

“Eat,” [Col. 0906A] therefore, “friends; drink, and be intoxicated, beloved ones.” I speak to you of one likeness among those concerning the serpent. For not without reason did I say: “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3). I say, not without reason, because behold, I speak to you of one likeness concerning the serpent. What is this one likeness? “Eat,” he says, “and you will be like gods.” “Eat and drink,” I say, “and by grace you will be what I am by nature,” namely sons of God.

Neither those first human beings saw in the fruit of the forbidden tree what they heard—namely, the effect of divinity—nor do you see with bodily eyes, in bread and wine, that they are as I say, my body [Col. 0906B] and blood. They saw only the fruit of the tree; you see only bread and wine. That serpent demanded that he be believed more than appeared visible, and he was believed. I too require you to believe me concerning more than you can see with bodily eyes; and I must be believed, so that death may be driven out by the same order by which it entered, and life, wickedly lost by credulity, may be restored to those who rightly believe.

For by what order was life lost and death brought in? Plainly by the order in which the death of the soul came first and the death of the flesh followed. For on the day when the first human beings ate what was forbidden, on that same day they died by the death of the soul, the death of sin; and afterward, by the death of the flesh, they returned to dust on their own day or at their appointed time. There too, friends, you became dead in respect of the soul and mortal in respect of [Col. 0906C] the flesh. For “in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15), and each of you knowingly confesses this.

But what does the Spirit now say? “Awake, awake; arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath, and have drunk to the dregs the cup of stupor, and drained it even to its lees. Two things have met you: desolation and destruction, famine and sword. Your children have been cast down; they slept at the head of every street, like a beast caught in a snare, full of the Lord’s indignation and the rebuke of your God” (Isa. 51). What he calls the Lord’s indignation is the death of the soul; what he calls the rebuke of your God is the death of the body. This is the cup which, he says, you drank [Col. 0906D] from the Lord’s hand—understand: from the hand of him rebuking you and saying, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

For you drank the cup of the soul’s death not from the hand of the Lord your God, but from the hand of the serpent, your ancient enemy. You drank the cup of bodily death from the Lord’s hand because, once the life of the soul had been removed, the life of the body, if it had been perpetual, would have been exceedingly useless. “These two things,” he says, “met you.” And then he adds: “Therefore hear this, poor woman, drunk but not with wine. Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the dregs of the cup of my indignation. You shall not add to drink it any longer” (Isa. 41 [probably Isa. 51]).

This is now being done, beloved ones, while I say to you: “Eat, friends; drink, and [Col. 0907A] be intoxicated. Friends,” I say, “and beloved ones. For I no longer call you servants, but my friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). Therefore I do not say, ‘dear ones,’ but ‘most beloved ones,’ because my love toward you is the greatest possible. “For no one has a greater love than this, that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (ibid.). This I do.

For behold, while I die, while I am delivered over to death, and now, having been sold, struggle in death, I also set before you my body to be eaten and my blood to be drunk, so that, as I have already said, death may be driven out of your souls and bodies by the same order by which it entered. For first the death of the soul is driven out when you eat and drink the sacrament [Col. 0907B] of my death or passion, because, as I said elsewhere, “He who eats me shall himself live because of me” (John 6). After this the death of the body will be driven out, namely when you all rise again—which you faithfully believe because I first rose again—as I likewise said concerning him “who, eating me, lives because of me: and I will raise him on the last day” (ibid.).

Someone may say: How then will your holy fathers live, who did not eat or drink this sacrament of life except only in a figure and on one occasion, when “they ate manna in the wilderness” (Exod. 16; 1 Cor. 10) and drank water from the rock which followed them? To this I say: as divine wisdom provided the same table for you while living, in the manner suitable to you, so it provided it for them when dead, in the manner suitable to them. For they have been dispersed: their souls indeed are in the underworld in the rest of hope, but their bodies rest in graves. I too will be dispersed—“I, the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6): my soul indeed to their souls, but my body descends to their bodies, namely into the womb of that earth in which they were received.

Immediately their souls live again in the full and perfect life which they had in some measure lived in hope; but on the last day they will rise with you in the resurrection of the body. Thus will be fulfilled what one of you says, and what the faith of all of you firmly holds: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15).

I did not establish for you this sacrament of so great a salvation from the beginning; until now I did not offer you this food and drink of eternal life while you went about with me preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God. For it was neither the time nor did the order demand that you be given food or drink of new salvation before you were cleansed, before your stain was erased: the stain of ancient guilt which they contracted by eating what was forbidden, and which the said human beings, your first parents, transmitted to all of you who would be born. But neither you nor our ancient friends—the holy ones from the beginning of the world—could be cleansed otherwise than by the shedding of my blood, “the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3), namely of the blood and water flowing from my side.

Therefore I ought not earlier to have done or said to you: “Take and eat, [Col. 0908A] friends; take and drink, beloved ones.” Not earlier, I say, but at the very moment of my passion or death, by which you were cleansed. Hence I say to you that “you too are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15). For because you believed and remained with me in my trials, from the time when I began to struggle you began to be cleansed. Accordingly, since you were already clean, cleansed from original sin which the first man contracted through food, I caused this food and drink to be set before you—and, after you, before our other friends and children yet to be born—in such an order that they must first be washed by the water of baptism. That water, after the sanctification of the Word with the seal of the cross, or exorcism, of my passion or death, will be no other water, but the same water which, together with [Col. 0908B] my blood, I shall pour forth from my side when dead and pierced by the soldier’s spear. Only then may each become a participant in this food and drink in the manner in which I delivered it to you.

“Be intoxicated,” therefore, “beloved ones”; be intoxicated, I say, so that you forget your want and remember sorrow no more. For “the body indeed is dead,” that is, most certainly destined to die, “because of sin; but the spirit lives because of justification” (Rom. 8). Forget, beloved ones, in the intoxication of your wine, in the abundance of the Holy Spirit, and in the sweetness of our wedding, every death and every mode or form of death and punishment; whatever sorrow and whatever joy, whatever fear and whatever hope the world can have, bring, or has brought. These are [Col. 0908C] the present wedding festivities at which you have deserved to be present, and your blessed eyes were the first granted to see their celebration.

For you are the chief guests of the wedding, who were the first of all to deserve to taste water made wine. Indeed, the very fact that you do not possess worldly sadness or pain, that you despise worldly joy, that you do not fear human fear, and that you do not place hope in a human being—these four passions, plainly, are certain chief streams of dead water, indeed of dead waters—but that you grieve only according to God (2 Cor. 7), rejoice only in the Holy Spirit, fear God alone, and hope in God alone: this very thing, I say, is already a foretaste of wine made from water and the beginning of intoxication. But fullness will come; the intoxication will be completed afterward, according to that saying in the psalm: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35).

Behold, my sister, my bride, these are the things which I did and said to my friends and beloved ones, coming “into my garden,” gathering, as I have said, “my myrrh with my spices,” eating “my honeycomb with my honey,” and drinking “my wine with my milk.” But what you desire and say after all these things—“Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his orchards”—this desire, that I should immediately take you, whom I called an enclosed garden, whose streams are, or are beginning to be, through the whole world a paradise of pomegranates; that I should take you, I say, [Col. 0909A] an enclosed garden and fountain of gardens, to myself, “that where I am, there you too may be with me” (John 14)—reason requires that this be deferred. First, so that this world may not be left free to say that it has never seen the woman concerning whom it hears this new thing from the preaching of our Gospel: “that God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4).

It is most beautiful and orderly that, while our adversaries carry about with them books which say, or contain in writing, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7), and our friends preach that in this fullness of time this has been fulfilled, with “signs following” to confirm the words spoken (Mark 16), you too should be present [Col. 0909B] between the preceding books and the following preachers and signs. You, I say, a worker of miracles and teacher of all holy religion—such a woman as no eye has ever seen, such as from the beginning, when Eve was made, neither has been, nor is, nor will be in her thoughts, words, deeds, in every fragrance of sweetness, and in every flower and fruit of honour and honesty (Ecclus. 24).

Behold, persons of a contrary spirit will come—spirits divided against themselves and opposed to the enclosure of my garden, to the virginity of my womb [variant: your womb], and to your paradisal streams—who will say many diverse, indeed contrary, things: namely the Carpocratians, Valentinians, Apollinarians, Paulianists, Jovinianists, and others deceived, or destined to deceive, by the spirit of error. [Col. 0910A] Through them the ancient serpent will hiss, so that some may say that I was merely a man, begotten by two sexes; others, that I assumed no bodily substance from you but passed through you as through a pipe; others, that I was not a true human being, but appeared as a phantasmal human in mere appearance; others, that I did not always exist, but took my beginning from you; others, that after I was born you bore children by Joseph.

Therefore you must be delayed and kept in this pilgrimage until you destroy these and every other heresy, faithfully recounting what must be truly preached and written: recounting, I say, as time and occasion require, that you conceived me not by a man but by the Holy Spirit coming upon you; that I did not pass through you as through a pipe, but assumed from the very [Col. 0910B] substance of your flesh the true substance of flesh; that I received not a phantasmal but a true and truly human body, and raised it into heaven; that I did not take my beginning from you, but before you—indeed, in the beginning before all ages—I existed as God’s Word, God from God; and that after I was born you remained ever a virgin, according to what was said to the prophet Ezekiel: “This gate shall always be shut” (Ezek. 44).

Those gates and all such streams of yours—it will be your time [the syntax is uncertain] for me to do with your soul what, desiring it most ardently, you say: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his orchards.”

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909C] O blessed Mary, not only the friends, but also very many young women, have long since heard the voice of the bridegroom praising your beauty and saying that “you are wholly beautiful,” and adding further [otherwise, saying], “apart from that which lies hidden within.” What is that which “lies hidden within,” if not the most excellent treasure of intention or conscience? For this almost all of us overlook as we read: that you, a teacher of religion and faith, lived among the blessed apostles, among human beings, and were commonly seen amid crowds. Why did you not rather remain in seclusion? Why did you not establish for yourself the secret place of contemplation? Was any mortal ever seen more than you to have taken wings like a dove, that she might fly and rest, flee afar off, and [Col. 0909D] remain in solitude? (Ps. LIV.) For many did this—not Elijah or Elisha alone (III Kings XVIII), but also very many sons of the prophets. What then? For what reason did not you likewise, or even more so, conceal from human beings the precious pearl of your beauty in that manner? We ask this, and it is worthy of knowing; and behold, we have now found and see it—not indeed wholly as it is, but as through a mirror (I Cor. XIII). For in place of a mirror, for considering this matter, we have especially this passage of Scripture, these most beautiful words of the Song of Songs, which begin thus:

“I sleep, and my heart keeps watch. The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my immaculate one, because my head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the night. I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch. I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped the finest myrrh, and my fingers were full of the most precious myrrh. I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved. But he had turned aside and passed on. My soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought [Col. 0910D] him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me. The watchmen who patrol the city found me: they struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.”

Behold here, O most blessed Mary—behold here your life shines dimly for us “as through a mirror in a riddle” (I Cor. XIII): your illustrious life, which, as we have now grown accustomed to say or sing, illumines all the Churches. Nearly the whole meaning of this chapter concerns that which is hidden within you; and it is above us, just as the beloved said above: “Your eyes are doves, apart from that which lies hidden within; like a fragment of pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from that which lies hidden within” (Song IV). Let us therefore bring this mirror near and contemplate from it diligently with the eyes of the heart, that we may at least in some measure know your most holy manner of life.

“I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” What else is this than that very saying elsewhere uttered by the Wisdom of God dwelling in your breast: “In all things I sought rest” (Ecclus. XXIV)? And what are these sayings—“I sleep,” and so forth, “In all things I sought rest”—except: “I have chosen the better part” (Luke X), leaving behind all [Col. 0911B] anxieties and cares of the world? Indeed, many daughters, or many souls, have thus slept, or have wished to sleep; but you possess the whole mastery of this sleep and hold the entire primacy of the heart’s wakefulness.

What else does the beloved himself say to us in the Psalm: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV)? For this is the same as though he said: Sleep, you, and let your heart keep watch. Thus we understand what you say: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch”—namely, because you indicate to us that your life, which we are to follow, is such as was signified in shadow in your father Jacob. When he too slept, then his heart kept watch, as it is written: “When he had come to a certain place and wished to rest there, he took some of the stones lying there, placed them beneath his head, and slept in that same place. And he saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, its summit touching heaven; the angels of God also ascending and descending by it, and the Lord resting upon the ladder” (Gen. XXVIII), and so forth.

Likewise, as has already been said, it has been and is the lot of many souls not only to sleep according to that likeness in holy leisure—that is, to be free from earthly cares and to keep watch in heart upon heavenly things through contemplation—but also, in the same way in which Jacob then slept, to sleep bodily and through dreams to behold heavenly things with the soul, according to the saying: “Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” [Col. 0911D] (Joel II).

But, O you heaven of God, sole dwelling-place of the Lord, in both modes of wakefulness you proved far more eminent than all mortals or earthly human beings, far more diligent in contemplating him “into whom angels desire to look,” and more capable. Why then did you have dealings with human beings, even holy ones? Why did you speak or associate with mortals, even apostles? Why did you not rather, like the most chaste turtle-dove, the solitary wandering turtle-dove, seek solitude more remote than John the Baptist’s, more secluded than Elijah’s, so that holy angels might know you habitually and minister to you—not for an hour, as the angel fed Elijah once and again (III Kings XIX), nor for a time, as ravens, his servants, fed that same prophet, but continually, until, your days completed, not merely one fiery chariot, but the entire host of angels should come and meet you with their king, your Son, to bear you into the ethereal heaven?

In answer to us as we ask such questions, you say: “The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my immaculate one, because my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” This is to say: My beloved is outside, as though under the open sky; he has no roof, no house. “Foxes,” he says, “have dens, and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII). For what is this? Does he have even a house of his own? Rather, he says, “I have left my house; I have divided my inheritance; my dwelling has become to me like a hyena’s cave” [Col. 0912B] (Jer. XII).

Therefore, having no house of his own any longer and not yet having gained another—that is, rejected by the Jews and not yet known by the Gentiles—he stands, as it were, outside and knocks, asking to be received within; and this is the voice of my beloved knocking: “Open to me, my sister, my dove, my friend, my immaculate one.” “My sister,” through faith; “my friend,” through hope; “my dove,” through charity; “immaculate,” through complete incorruption of mind and body—which is highly praiseworthy in the mother who conceived and gave birth. “Open to me,” that is, your mouth; “speak,” insofar as concerns the strengthening of the Gospel; and accept in this an interruption of your desired rest, so that for my sake you may break the silence pleasing to your singular modesty.

For what reason? Namely, “because my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” “For I have become a stranger to my brothers, and an alien to the sons of my mother” (Ps. LXVIII); and just as the head of one who is outside and has no roof “is full of dew, and his locks,” or uppermost hairs, are full “of the drops of the night,” so “the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” (ibid.). The holy Scriptures themselves, which all cling to me, the Word of God, as locks cling to the head, are corrupted by the perverse interpretations of those very persons. As they cast me out beyond their gates in order to crucify me, so they have cast me far from their hearts, hating both me and my Father; and as on that night they spat upon my face, so they obstinately hurl blasphemies against my head [Col. 0912D] and defile my locks. They are like the falling dew, or the falling drops of night, because they have fallen from God’s grace when, blaspheming, they deny that I am God, the Son of God, and distort in a contrary sense the Scriptures that bear witness to me.

Open, therefore, your mouth together with my other witnesses, and make it so that, in all whomsoever, I may have a place where I may lay my head.

Where and when was this voice of the beloved knocking? Within, in the inner person, where the same beloved is accustomed to speak also to you his friends, as Scripture says of one of you: “The Spirit said to Philip: Draw near and join yourself to this chariot” (Acts VIII). For if the beloved dwells in you and speaks inwardly to you, you need not be taught what I myself meant when I said, “the voice of my beloved knocking.”

If it is asked when: certainly after he ascended into heaven, while this sex too was moving toward him, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “All these were persevering with one accord with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts I). Just as men, so women also were now beginning to live in common, not only Jews but Greeks also, when, after the gift of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel was preached. Hence the saying: “In those days, when the number of disciples was increasing, a complaint of the Greeks arose against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministry” (Acts VI). Especially because of such matters there came “the voice of the beloved knocking” and saying: “Open to me, my sister,” namely, lest saving [Col. 0913B] doctrine, ministry, a rule of life, and moral discipline should be lacking even to the weaker sex.

But I say: “I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” For long ago, my beloved, I desired a perfectly solitary life, in which one lives as though naked of a tunic or every garment, resting in the secrecy of one’s bed with one’s feet washed and free from all dust. How shall I again become entangled in the cares which are not absent from superiors in communal life, even though the life of those living in common and possessing nothing of their own is or may be religious? For such a life cannot be conducted without daily food or ministry, and it has some dust—indeed, it is very often exceedingly dusty, and especially full of murmuring—as you have already heard at the beginning, O friends: “A complaint of the Greeks arose against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministry.”

Nor is it surprising that, when this sex—the frail sex—takes refuge with us from the mud of the world, there should be some dust of this kind; since even in your sex, namely the male sex, there are certain blameworthy things and many traces of the former manner of life remain. But I speak to my beloved as he knocks, and I repeat what is known to him: I, more singularly than all others, have put off my tunic; in mind and deed [Col. 0913C] or outward habit I have left all things, and I have so washed my feet—my conscience or intention being cleansed by the Holy Spirit—that no remnant whatever of the dust mentioned remains.

How now shall I “put on my tunic,” so that, although I have left all my own things, I should care for the affairs of others, becoming anxious for others and a mistress of the household for the widows who come daily, or for virgins who are yet to come? How shall I “defile my feet, which I have washed”—that is, turn my eyes or any other senses toward earthly things, though I have dedicated them all, my senses and thoughts, to you alone, my beloved? For though your guardianship is always with me, true humility is always anxious; and my soul especially, which is singularly full of your love, regards as dust and accounts as filth whatever, through some necessity, it ever says or thinks apart from you, though it be lawful, though not idle, indeed though it may seem somewhat useful.

What happened to me as I spoke these or similar things, while wakeful and wishing to sleep in heart? “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.” How, O beloved one, did your beloved put his hand through the opening? What is that hand? What is that opening? What is that touch? What is that trembling? How did “my belly tremble,” or what is your belly? We wonder and ask these things because we have no experience of such matters.

One of the ancient friends says: “The Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth, and said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have set you over nations and kingdoms” (Jer. I). Likewise another says: “I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me, and there the hand of the Lord God fell upon me. And the likeness of a hand, being sent forth, seized me by the lock [Col. 0914B] of my head” (Ezek. X).

In our own age one of the young women recounted to her intimates, to whom she did not hesitate to entrust her secrets because of their proven affection, that on a certain night the likeness of a hand had been thrust from the head of the bed upon her breast while she was almost awake—indeed, not asleep at all, though experiencing something slight of ecstasy. The touch was most sweet, as if it were of a right hand. Taking it in both her own hands, she caressed it with the sign of the cross, passing over it inside and outside, with which caresses that hand seemed greatly delighted. And when, after those delights of the holy sign with which she was caressing the hand, she attempted also to touch the arm and to reach the very person whose hand she held, that hand swiftly, as if rebuking her, moved and shook itself free—sweeter than oil, swifter than a bird’s feather; and by its movement it made known that he whose hand it was did not wish to be grasped.

The same young woman—that is, the soul given to these nuptials and intent upon nuptial songs—also related that the beloved, visible in a vision of the night, thrust his hand in a wonderful manner into her breast, as though through an opening, and seized her heart within. Holding it for some time in a most sweet embrace, he caused that heart, leaping and dancing within that hand, to rejoice with ineffable joy.

Furthermore, concerning that trembling, holy and divine trembling, she faithfully recounted that the following experience had happened to her. In a vision she beheld, in a certain church, an image of the Savior crucified in an elevated place—namely, where it customarily stood, displayed before the people who prayed or adored. As she fixed her attention upon it, the image appeared alive, with a countenance as though kingly, radiant eyes, and an altogether venerable aspect; and that beloved one deigned, with magnificent expression, to bring his right hand down from the crossbeam and make the sign of the cross over her who beheld him. For this was no vain vision: it immediately imparted to the beholder an awareness of great power. Finally, just as a leaf of a tree trembles when a violent wind shakes it, so, when she suddenly woke from this vision, she trembled for some time in bed with a sweet trembling—yet a gentle and exceedingly pleasant trembling. Before she awoke, while still in the vision, the power of the aforesaid sign snatched the beholder upward more swiftly and easily than can be told, her hands stretched out toward those hands nailed to the cross, so that her mouth too seemed joined to his mouth and her whole body brought close to his body. When she awoke from sleep, she remained for a while, as already said, wakefully trembling with that divine trembling in great delight.

Let these few words suffice as an experiential account of the divine hand, touch, and trembling. But when your person is at issue, O beloved of the unique Beloved, how great and of what sort are these things, so that what the hand of the Lord must be believed to have done in your case might be gathered at least somewhat from the likeness of these examples? These things are great and far exceed our thoughts. Let us rather hear you recounting the rest—things so holy and so mystical, possessing in their meaning the spirit of life so far beyond the letter.

“I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped the finest myrrh, and my fingers were full of the most precious myrrh . . .” I rose, I say. For how could I sleep any longer, or fall asleep again? How could putting on the tunic be burdensome to me, or enduring dust upon my feet seem irksome, once, after the voice of my beloved knocking, his hand also came and by its touch instilled that ineffable fear into my belly?

“I therefore rose to open to my beloved”: I exerted myself so that, with Christ’s apostles, I might assist the Gospel as it ran forward through the words and deeds of my beloved. For this is what I say: “My hands dripped the finest myrrh, and my fingers were full of the most precious myrrh.” It was necessary especially that I should provide, for widows who had left all things and imitated the apostolic life, a manifest example of mortifying vices and a public norm for those soon to come, and that I should establish a new and hitherto unheard-of example of holy virginity for those who would undertake it. This is indeed “the most precious myrrh,” that is, the most costly.

But to mortify the flesh not for God, nor for the edification of beholders, but to gain one’s own glory from the mouths of those who praise—this is indeed for the hands to drip myrrh, but not approved myrrh. Indeed, in such a case there are not even fingers that may be called full of myrrh, because in such a work there is no power of discernment, which is usually understood through the distinction of the fingers.

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.” “The bolt,” I say, “of my door,” that is, the closure of my mouth. For what is signified by the bolt except the fastening of silence? The bolt of the door is therefore opened to the beloved when the silence imposed upon the mouth is loosed for Christ’s sake, that those who hear may be edified. And how beautiful, reasonable, and disciplined is this order of speaking! First myrrh drips from the hands and the fingers are shown full of the most precious myrrh; then the bolt of the door is opened to the beloved—that is, first a praiseworthy life is prepared as an example, and then teaching that seeks the faith of its hearers is publicly uttered. Hence it is written of the beloved himself that he began “to do and to teach” (Acts I). It was not said first to teach and then to do, but first to do and then to teach.

“And he [Col. 0916A] had turned aside and passed on.” “I,” she says, “opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, and he had turned aside and passed on”—that is, I opened my mouth in teaching so as to make the beloved known to those who heard, but he was no longer with us; having been received into heaven, he was not to return again to remain among mortals.

Then, O beloved one, did you not know this? Before you opened the bolt of your door in the manner now described, had you not seen that he had ascended into heaven, and did you not know that he would not return to dwell again among mortals? “I knew,” she says, “and knew well. But what then? ‘My soul melted when my beloved spoke.’” When or where did he speak? Certainly when and where I “opened the bolt of my door to my beloved,” speaking, that is, for the benefit of hearers those things which belong to the beloved: then and there the beloved spoke. For it was not I who spoke, but he spoke in me (Matt. XI). For if any one of you friends says—and says truly—“Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII), then without doubt the same beloved has spoken in me whenever I opened the bolt of my door to him, whenever I moved my tongue and lent my voice to the Word of God, which he himself is.

Therefore, when the beloved spoke, “my soul melted.” I wept; and because of violently bursting sobs, I could utter only broken words and interrupted sounds. Could I indeed speak of him without tears? Yet that very weeping was consolation to me, a kind of delight, just as each of you finds his own tears sweet when they flow in remembrance of the same beloved, according to the saying: “My tears became my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI). How much more was this so for me, when it was daily said to me, “Where is your God?” (ibid.), your Son? Or when I said: My God, my Son—who was thus incarnate or born from me, who thus struggled and endured such things for my sake and before my eyes—has left me in this exile.

What was it like for me to recall or recount his words: the words of the dying beloved, or of one immediately to die, especially as he commended the precept of charity, the commandment of love, from that most holy supper when he was betrayed to those last words: “Woman, behold your son”; and to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John XIX)? There was fire, there was a sword: the fire of love, the sword of sorrow; and my soul was the victim of a holocaust. For fire burned it and a sword passed through it. Thus, as the fat of a sacrifice melts from fire and as blood flows from a sword wound, so “my soul melted”—not only once, there where he himself was dying, but as often as, when I opened the bolt of my door, he spoke in me. For as often I felt in my heart’s depth and wounded mind what I now say: that he had turned aside and passed on. The very remembrance of these things renewed the feeling in me, so that I felt more and more that he was no longer here, no longer visibly present.

“I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer [Col. 0917A] me.” I sought him, namely, by constant meditation; I called by continual prayer. But though seeking in this way, I did not find him, and though calling, he did not answer me. Sweet is the light, and it is delightful to the eyes to see the sun; but I felt it sweet to see my flesh living in him, and I counted it delightful to see face to face him whom I had borne, shining above all things at the Father’s right hand. I did not find him at once, not as soon as I wished. In response to this he said to me: “The watchmen who patrol the city found me. They struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak.”

Who were or are those sentinels, those keepers of the walls who patrol the city? Certainly the friends and the first among our friends, who say in their book, the book of the Acts of the Apostles: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, select from among yourselves seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this task. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts VI). These were the sentinels; and this was for them to keep watch, patrol the city, and guard the walls: namely, to devote themselves continually to prayer and the ministry of the word, according to that prophetic saying: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have stationed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not cease to praise the name of the Lord. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no rest until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth” (Isa. LXXII)—that Jerusalem, certainly, of which the Psalm also says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXVIII).

Those watchmen did this so that every day in the temple and about the houses they did not cease teaching and preaching Jesus Christ. They found me, for they were seeking me. How did they seek me, and how did they find me? They all sought me with pious concern, especially he to whom I had been entrusted by the beloved, who said, “Behold your mother” (John XIX), and who received me into his own home. They sought me with great hope that something worthy of their inquiry might be in me, since they knew what had happened in me or through me—what kind of mother had borne what kind of Son. They thought that something of the treasures of the Most High remained in me, treasures which the Holy Spirit coming upon me had stored up at the conception of so great a Son.

And this was indeed true: for though my Son came forth from my womb in his bodily birth “like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII), nevertheless the whole fullness of grace which I had received persisted, and will persist, in my heart and thoughts from then and unto eternity. Therefore they sought and found me full of unutterable groanings (Rom. VIII). How did they come to find me so? Certainly through some likeness to themselves. For I groaned, and they likewise groaned; and we had the same cause in our groanings, truly foretold by the beloved himself: “Little children, I am with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I told you: Where I go, you cannot come; so now I tell you” (John XIII).

This was the common cause of our groanings and tears: that we could not go where he had gone. Not that he had left us orphans, since he had left us with his promise and the hope of his promise, according to these words: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and will receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV). Yet meanwhile, while our departure was delayed, it was with us as he said elsewhere: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. IX). If the sons of the bridegroom had to fast, how much more did I, the mother of that same bridegroom, have to fast and weep?

In this they found me; for what I carried in my mind could not be hidden from them. What next? “They struck me and wounded me.” How, or with what weapons, did they strike me? By conferring and conversing, and by casting into the midst their all-too-spontaneous, indeed all-too-violent groanings. They “struck me”—those groanings and tears which they could not retain even had they wished to do so; and therefore, with the reins released, they let their tears run as freely as the tears themselves wished.

Then each brought his own portion into the midst, remembering the words of their Father, my Son, the aforesaid bridegroom, our beloved: remembering the final words of such a Father, which he uttered as he was dying and, as it were, drawing his last breath; remembering what testament he had written for those same children, what inheritance he had left them, how piously concerned that testator had been in dying for the peace and concord of his heirs, and how, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII). These were their darts; with these they struck and wounded me—while they themselves in turn were struck and wounded by me with sharp arrows, the arrows of the beloved speaking in me, as the Psalmist says: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX). Thus, by mutual blows and mutual wounds, we struck one another and were struck; we wounded and were wounded with most sweet blows and most delightful wounds—such wounds that whoever has not experienced them assuredly has no health of heart.

Meanwhile those keepers of the walls took my cloak from me: that is, I made known to them, so far as was necessary, all that had been secret in me. For until then I had kept all the words concerning that beloved, pondering them in my heart (Luke II), and had thus covered them as though beneath a cloak; but then I brought them forth openly, preaching and even writing those things concerning the beloved which were necessary and greatly profitable for the Gospel.

Wearied by these and other means, and wholly dead beforehand to this world, I turn to our daughters and sisters—the widows of our Gospel, or whatever persons of our sex had been entrusted to me—and say to them: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.” O daughters of Jerusalem, who are true daughters of Abraham, seed of Judah, and daughters also of David according to faith, because you believe in him who, though Son of God according to divinity and king of the heavenly Jerusalem, became my Son, or Son of Man, “of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I)—“I adjure you,” namely by that very fact through which you are “daughters of Jerusalem,” if you find my beloved. If before me—as often happens, disciples before their teacher—you depart from the body and come before the presence of my beloved, “tell him that I languish with love”: that because of love for him, because of my great desire to see his face, I endure weariness of this life and bear with sighing mind and tearful eyes the lingering delays of my present exile.

What was, or what did, such an adjuration accomplish? Did that beloved not know the love of one who languished, or the languor of one who loved, unless it were told him? “Lord,” Peter says, “you know all things; you know that I love you” (John XXI). How much more, O beloved one, so wise and faithful, could you yourself, without intermediaries, say to the beloved—and without doubt often did say—My beloved, no heart is hidden from you, no love concealed from you; you know that I languish with love. To what end, then, does this adjuration tend, or what does it accomplish? Certainly this: that the mother, herself struck, may strike her daughters; herself wounded, may wound them; and may bring about in them an experience of some of her salutary wounds—if not immediately in all, at least already in some.

Thus, hearing daughters, or daughters perceiving in their mother so great a desire for the future life which is not seen, may themselves feel in mind that the beloved is such that any man or woman rightly despises this present age because of him, and amid the delays of present life desires more and more to know him, at least through a mirror, at least in a riddle (I Cor. XIII). Therefore they immediately say: “What is your beloved above a beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved above a beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

This inquiry was exceedingly timely, if we look to those times of which we are now speaking, when you, O beloved one, were present in the flesh for the sake of the beloved’s Gospel and were kept in the body—a necessary teacher, a most suitable witness. For already then there began to be heard not only Jews blaspheming openly, but also many and diverse heretics who, under the Christian name, labored to corrupt Christian truth. From the same spirit of wickedness there were to spring up, though with diverse and mutually opposing errors, very many broods of vipers, like the heads of the ancient Hydra which, as the story goes, grew back in greater number when the former ones had been cut off.

Therefore the door of truth had to be knocked upon and the oracle of the Holy Spirit consulted—namely, the sanctuary of your breast—so that by your living voice you might set forth the whole rule of faith that must necessarily be held, with the testimony of the Scriptures, which you, a great prophetess capable of containing all prophets and prophecies, held in memory.

“They say: What is [Col. 0920A] your beloved above a beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved above a beloved?” What is that same Son of yours, God from God the Father, O Virgin of virgins, O holiest of holy women? “What is your beloved above a beloved, that you have so adjured us?” For we who are already daughters of Jerusalem have no doubt that he is beloved above beloved—that is, God from God. Yet provision must be made not only for us who now live in your time, but also for all other daughters of Jerusalem who will come after us, so that, certainly taught by you and confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, they may know to despise heretics and burn only with holy desire for the beloved.

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands. His head is finest gold; his locks are like raised palm branches, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside brimming waters. His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh. His hands are golden and well-turned, full of hyacinths. His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires. His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as cedars. His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

Such is your song for us, divine prophetess,

Such as sleep is for the weary upon the grass, such as, in heat,  
Sweet water is for quenching thirst from a leaping stream.

This song of yours is truly most beautiful, and, as it is called, [Col. 0920C] it is the Song of Songs. Nothing could friends hear more gladly, nothing could young maidens receive more delightfully—any who have ears to hear and a ready understanding, by which they may discern a lawful song. You have said what manner of beloved he is, and you have set forth his wondrous qualities, briefly indeed, but delightfully, as the truth of the matter itself is, as all the Scriptures of truth harmoniously proclaim.

“My beloved is white and ruddy.” Whence white, and whence ruddy? White, surely, in holiness; ruddy in suffering. Someone may say: If then he is white, why is he ruddy? If holy, why did he suffer? For the Holy Spirit, marvelling at this in David, after saying: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat [Col. 0920D] of pestilence” (Ps. I), and so forth—thereby of course indicating in words that he would be white, that is, free from every blackness of him “in whom all sinned” (Rom. V), for they were in his loins when “he went in the counsel of the ungodly, and stood in the way of sinners, and sat in the seat of pestilence,” by thinking evil, transgressing the commandment, and defending or transmitting to his descendants his hereditary sin—then added and said: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II). The meaning is: Since he was thus white and altogether spotless, why did they thus assemble [Col. 0921A] and make him ruddy with his own blood?

And in Isaiah: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one treading in the winepress?” (Isa. LXIII). For he had first said: “I who speak righteousness and am a defender mighty to save” (ibid.); this is truly to be white, truly spotless. And immediately there is added there what is said here: “chosen 410 from thousands”: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (ibid.).

Therefore we too ask—whether we, or the young maidens, who have not yet learned this mystery in full but are still learning—if he is white, why is he ruddy? If holy, why did he suffer? And the friends, old and new, answer us: “Because he was wounded for our iniquities, he was crushed for our crimes” (Isa. LIII); [Col. 0921B] “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII); and the beloved of the Beloved himself says: “For the sins of my people, I struck him” (Isa. LIII).

But from what thousands was he chosen, except from all the saints? And in what was he chosen, except in doing alone that which none of them was fit to do? Thus in Isaiah, after it had been said of the whole company of saints—the one city which fell in Adam—“Awake, awake; arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath, and have drunk to the dregs the cup of stupor” (Isa. LI), the greatness of the weakness of all those thousands is immediately shown by the following words: “There is none to sustain her among all the sons whom she bore, [Col. 0921C] and none to take her by the hand among all the sons whom she nourished.” Furthermore, turning to her herself, he says: “Your sons have been cast out; they have slept at the head of every road, like an ensnared beast, full of the indignation of the Lord and the rebuke of your God” (ibid.).

Truly great was the weakness of all those thousands. Not only could they not sustain Jerusalem or take her by the hand; they themselves also “were cast out and slept at the head of every road like an ensnared beast”—ensnared, plainly, by sin, by original sin; and therefore “full of the indignation of the Lord, full of the rebuke of God,” that is, made dead in respect of the soul and mortal in respect of the body. Yet in this Chosen One a single hope remained for all of them, [Col. 0921D] as the words that follow immediately promised: “Thus says your Ruler, the Lord and your God, who fought for his people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the dregs of the cup of my indignation. You shall no longer drink it; and I shall put it into the hand of those who humbled you’” (ibid.).

This is the work of the Chosen One: that he could do, and did, what no other did or could do—namely, take from the hand of the human race, that is, of all those predestined to life, who all are called and are one Jerusalem, the cup of wrath and the dregs of the cup, that is, the sentence of the twofold death, of soul and body. Whence had he this, that he should be such and so great a Chosen One? In what is he distinguished? How does he differ from all others?

“His head is finest gold.” This is [Col. 0922A] his own distinctive property, and from this comes what is truly said of him: “More beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV), because his head is finest gold; that is, his principal nature is true divinity. For he is God, the Word of God, which “was in the beginning with God. And the Word was God” (John I). He subsists as one and the same person in two natures, divine and human; and therefore his divine nature is rightly called his head, because it is the beginning, as he says in one place: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII).

What is of such weight as this gold? What is as beautiful as this golden head? What as precious as this Word? I, the beloved, felt in myself beyond expression the weight of this gold when it descended from heaven into my womb. Yet it possesses a wonderful and inestimable efficacy of itself, by which it knew and could so sweetly strengthen the womb of mortal condition and this frail sex that not only was the smallness of my womb not broken, but it was even delighted by his weight. For he is the one whom the angels tremble before, whom the whole world cannot contain, “beneath whom,” Scripture says, “those who bear the world are bowed down” (Job IX). [Col. 0922B] This efficacy is his grace, without which no creature can subsist beneath him. This he possesses beyond all the thousands: such a head and one of such weight; and hence he is beloved from among thousands.

“His locks are like the raised branches of palms, black as a raven.” The locks of his head are all the Scriptures of truth. For as locks proceed from the head and are in some sense its adornment, so all divinely inspired Scriptures are received from the fullness of this Word, or Chosen One, and all bear testimony to this Chosen One.

These locks are “like the raised branches of palms,” that is, like palm leaves, which are called raised because they rise upward rather than hanging down as those of other trees do. The palm is a tree, an emblem of victory, its branches spread out in the manner of a human palm; it has a tall and graceful stem, is clothed with long-lasting foliage, and retains its leaves without any succession of renewal. Truly then “his locks”—those of the Chosen One, or of the beloved golden head—are “like the raised branches of palms,” because the Scriptures of truth, of which that head, God the Word, is indeed the beginning, do not look earthward [Col. 0922C] as human writings do, but reach upward and seek the things above (Col. III). For you follow not the letter that kills, but the Spirit that gives life (II Cor. III); and they are very long-lasting—indeed, more lasting than the raised branches or leaves of palms. For “heaven and earth,” he says, “shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke XXI); and: “One iota or one stroke shall not pass away from the law until all things are fulfilled” (Matt. V).

They are black as a raven because, as was said elsewhere, “dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII), that is, hidden knowledge is in the prophetic and legal Scriptures. Thus you may truly say that there is great blackness in the locks of the beloved’s head, so that the sense or understanding is the same. But see what follows: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting by full-flowing waters.”

His eyes are his seven spirits, the seven gifts or seven graces of one and the same Spirit. Compare these opposites: “his locks black as a raven, and his eyes like doves washed with milk,” and see what follows. Holy Scripture, certainly, is black as a raven to those who do not possess the holy and life-giving Spirit, because it appears obscure and harsh to them; but to those possessing spiritual grace, which is understood by the eyes, it is white—indeed, bright—like the eyes of a gentle dove, a milk-white dove.

For example, it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a bondwoman and one by a free woman (Gen. XXI). And [Col. 0923B] the law says: “Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Deut. XIX), and so forth. But in the prophets: “Go,” says the Lord, “take for yourself a wife of fornication, and beget children of fornications” (Hos. I), and so forth. In these and similar passages the aforesaid locks are black, not merely in some fashion, but like a raven, because they are not only obscure but even seem harmful according to the literal sense. But when the aforesaid eyes, the spiritual eyes, are applied, it becomes apparent that they are bright, dovelike, honorable, and holy according to the mystical sense. And as great as the distance between the blackness of ravens and the brightness of milk-white doves, so great—indeed greater—is the distance between the letter that kills and the Spirit that gives life (II Cor. III).

Therefore “his eyes,” that is, the graces of the Holy Spirit abiding in him, are “like doves washed with milk,” very white doves, “which sit beside streams of water and by full-flowing waters”; that is, they give themselves wholly to the Scriptures of the prophets and examine all the holy Scriptures, which are most full of heavenly mysteries, 411 according to the Psalmist’s words: “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. I). For what did he do or teach without the authority of the Scriptures?

First, when he came out from the desert after his fast and temptation, he unrolled the book of Isaiah the prophet delivered to him and found the passage in which it was written of him: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because [Col. 0923D] he has anointed me” (Isa. LXI), and so forth. “Today,” he said, “this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke IV). Thus beginning, he undoubtedly both spoke and acted in all things under the authority of the Scriptures, always attending to the Scriptures.

And, to mention one thing by way of example: at the very beginning of his preaching, did he ascend the mountain, as the Gospel recounts—“because, seeing great crowds, he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth, he taught them”—without examining the Scriptures or meditating upon the law of the Lord, especially that he “had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt.
