VI)? Certainly not. Rather, he examined and meditated on both, namely, what he had done long ago and what he was later to do: for long ago he had given that same law on a mountain (Exod. XX), and later he was to ascend the mountain, that is, the very height of heaven, and, opening his mouth and likewise opening the understanding of his disciples that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV), was to teach them all truth (John XVI). [Col. 0924A]

Rightly, then, “his eyes,” those of the beloved, are like doves—not just any doves, but doves “sitting beside streams of water and by full-flowing waters”—because his thoughts or understandings never at any time turned themselves away from the contemplation of the holy Scriptures.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers.” The cheeks are the lower parts of the eyes, where beards begin. For beard in Greek is called *geneion* (γένειον). What, then, is understood by the beloved’s cheeks except his outward appearance? For a person’s cheeks declare what he is; hence the same place is called the countenance, because by it the inclination of the mind is shown. Therefore, “his cheeks,” it says, “are like beds of spices,” because they are signs of the hidden graces and virtues that are in him; to those who behold them with a single and benevolent eye, they are pleasing, [Col. 0924B] “like beds of spices planted by perfumers”—that is, not planted haphazardly, but carefully arranged—and they delight both the sight and the smell of their beholders.

“His lips are lilies, distilling the finest myrrh.” The preaching of the Gospel is pure, and every teaching of the beloved is holy and true, as even his adversaries acknowledged, though not simply, when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII). The beginning of his preaching was repentance, John preceding him in this very matter, as the Gospel Scripture itself plainly shows: “In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. III). Likewise: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee, and from that time he began to preach and say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. IV).

And elsewhere, whenever the occasion presented itself, he showed that this was the reason for his coming: to call sinners to [Col. 0924C] repentance (Luke V). This is also the teaching of his friends concerning all people: that they should “put to death their members which are on earth” (Col. III). Thus truly “his lips are lilies distilling the finest myrrh,” because he teaches purity and calls to repentance. Not just any myrrh, but “the finest myrrh,” that is, true and best, in no way corrupted by the desire for empty glory. “When you fast,” he says, “do not become sad like hypocrites. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that you may not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father, who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

---

“His hands are turned and golden, full of hyacinths.” In what sense are “his hands turned and golden”? Surely in working miracles, so that he could confidently say: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works” (John X)—the works, namely, which I have done among you, of a kind and in a manner that no one else has done.

For no one else had hands so turned and so golden in performing signs or wonders; that is, no one among all who have wrought wonders in this world was so swift and powerful in such deeds. He who works with a lathe works more easily, more quickly, and more perfectly. Thus this beloved worked the wonders he wished far more easily, much more quickly, and far more perfectly than any among all workers of miracles who have existed from the beginning of the world. They, indeed, by much toil, by many outlays of prayer and fasting, by much [Col. 0925B] crying of heart and voice, deserved to obtain or achieve from another—from God—the effect of whatever power they did not have in themselves or from themselves. But he, by a nod alone, by will alone, by command alone, and sometimes in silence, worked what he wished.

For example, when he said at the wedding: “Fill the jars with water” (John II), not only did he not cry out or pray, but he did not even command or say by voice or movement of his lips, “Let the waters be changed,” or “Be changed into wine.” Instead, utterly silent on this matter, he said: “Draw now, and carry it to the steward” (ibid.), knowing and being certain that nature had sufficiently perceived the silent nod of its Creator. Nor is this surprising. He was and is the ancient turner, who shaped heaven and earth, and the spherical bodies of sun, moon, and all the stars, with his lathe—that is, with his most swift command.

Whence are his hands so turned? Surely because they are golden. And what does “golden” mean but divine? For the substance of the incarnate Word is true gold, true divinity. And whence is it that his hands move so swiftly? Because although they were veiled by the weakness of flesh, they nevertheless remained as turned as they were and were made in no respect weaker or slower.

Add also this praise of wisdom to such great commendation of strength and swiftness: they are “full of hyacinths,” that is, precious stones. Who are those hyacinths? Surely the heavenly reasons for the very wonders which he performed—the things toward which he directed himself, which he held before the inward eyes: inward understandings, [Col. 0925D] most beautiful understandings. When you join them to the outward work, understand them clearly, and set them forth at the proper time, you display most beautiful hyacinths added to finest gold.

For example, in order to give sight to the man blind from birth, “he spat upon the ground, made clay from the spittle, anointed his eyes, and said to him: ‘Go and wash in the pool of Siloam’” (John IX), and so forth. Here his turned and golden hands shone forth, because he acted swiftly and, as God, performed a divine work by his own power. Now add the reasons why he acted thus, when he could have said, as he said to another: “Look; your faith has made you well” (Luke XVIII), and behold, the same hands are “full of hyacinths.” What are those reasons? They are surely those which the holy Church diligently observes to this day in her catechumens: first anointing their eyes with faith in, or teaching concerning, the Incarnation of the same beloved Son of God—in which Incarnation, as though the spittle of God’s mouth, he joined himself to the dust of earth, and one and the same person, God and man, came forth from the womb of a virgin to enlighten the human race 412—and then sending them to the font of baptism, in which by the Holy Spirit the whole person is enlightened and lives.

“His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.” What a belly, how beautiful and how graceful! Yet his head is more beautiful and his hands more beautiful. For “his head is finest gold, and his hands are golden, but his belly is ivory.” Ivory is indeed beautiful and precious, but gold is far more beautiful and far more precious. Thus the human nature or substance of this beloved, once passible and tender, is beautiful and precious indeed; but his divine nature, in the one and same person of the beloved, is far more beautiful and far more precious, never passible and ever immortal, as it was before all ages.

Truly beautiful and graceful is the ivory belly, because, as ivory is the entire beauty and value of the great body, namely of the elephant, so this belly—that is, the humanity or flesh which he assumed from the human race, and especially from the race of Abraham, from whose seed he willed to be born—is the glory and adornment of the whole world. Ivory is more beautiful and more precious than the flesh or remaining body from which it is taken; nevertheless, the flesh of this beloved is more beautiful, purer, and incomparably holier than the entire mass from whose seed [Col. 0926C] it was taken.

For such is the condition of humankind that there is no one who cannot truthfully say: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. L), except this one and only, unique and solitary one, whom I his mother conceived without any iniquity and without any sins: now incorrupt, a mother untouched in conception, unharmed and whole in childbirth and after childbirth. Thus “his belly is ivory,” that is, he himself as man is most chaste, cold to every vice, very firm against all things of flesh and blood, impassible and pure, “holy, innocent, undefiled, and altogether separated from sinners” (Heb. VII).

Such is this belly; and although it is not gold or golden, as the head is gold and the hands are golden, it is nevertheless adorned with sapphires. That is, although his humanity is not identical with his divinity, it shone with divine things and was glorified with every privilege of divinity from the very beginning: when he wailed in the cradle, with heaven ministering and the star giving sign, he was worshipped by the Magi; unto the consummation (Matt. II), that is, “unto death, even death of the cross” (Phil. II). When this belly was pierced by the nails and the soldier’s lance (John XIX), heaven was darkened and darkness came to be (Luke XXIII);

---

“and the veil of the temple was torn, the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened” (Matt. XXVII), and afterward the other things happened. Considering these, you rightly say: “Under his feet was, as it were, a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. XXIV).

---

“His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases.”

“His legs” are his ways: mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth, as the Psalmist says: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). For truth itself is true judgment. These “legs,” these ways, are “marble columns,” that is, most straight and most firm; and there is none who can weaken or justly reprove them. “For the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. XVIII).

For example, at the place and time mentioned above, when this beloved hung crucified between two thieves, he mercifully received the one who repented and took him with himself into paradise, while by just judgment he rejected the other who blasphemed (Luke XXIII). Likewise, when he receives the people who once were not his people—the Gentile people who believe and confess—and abandons the people once his own, the Jewish people, who do not believe, indeed who contradict and blaspheme, who can justly reprove or alter this? No one, surely, because all these ways of his are straight. Therefore “his legs are marble columns.”

What also could be truer than what is said: “which are founded upon golden bases”? Golden bases are the counsels of divine wisdom. Indeed, those wondrous columns are so founded upon such bases that in judging or showing mercy this beloved [Col. 0927C] can do nothing from himself. He could weep over the city of Jerusalem (Luke XIX), foreseeing the overthrow and condemnation of his people, and yet he could not incline his mind so as to turn away the wrath impending over them. For his legs stood inflexible, like “marble columns upon golden bases”; that is, he regarded not what the will of his humanity might be, but the grounds of divine justice.

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as cedars.”

“His appearance,” his beauty, is like that of Lebanon. Which Lebanon? Surely that to which the Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, spoke through the prophet Zechariah: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. I). This Lebanon was the temple of the Lord, the temple which Solomon built for the Lord, whose beams and paneling he made almost entirely from the woods of Lebanon, from cedar timbers, and overlaid with gold.

In what respect is the beloved’s appearance like the appearance of such Lebanon? First, in that, as that Lebanon, that temple, was the head and glory and Holy of Holies to that earthly city of Jerusalem, so this beloved is head, glory, and Holy of Holies to the heavenly city of the Jerusalem above, the city of the living God. According to the mysteries of this temple not made with hands, all the structures of that temple made with hands were constructed, as was also the tabernacle which Moses completed in the wilderness at the Lord’s command.

For as the Lord said to Moses concerning the making of the tabernacle, “See and make according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV), so, without doubt, a heavenly pattern of the heavenly building was shown to David, who possessed the Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, in order that he might prescribe how it should be made. As the Scripture of the book of Chronicles says: “David gave Solomon his son the plan of the porch, the temple, the storehouses, the upper room, the chambers, the inner sanctuaries, the house of propitiation, and also all that he had conceived concerning the courts” (I Chron. XXVIII), and so forth, down to the words: “All these things,” says David, “came to me in writing from the hand of the Lord, that I might understand all the works of the pattern” (ibid.).

Since David was a prophet, who also said, “I have understood beyond the elders and beyond all who teach me” (Ps. CXVIII), there is no doubt that he too saw, with the same eyes by which Moses had seen the pattern for making the tabernacle, the pattern according to which he gave his son Solomon the plans [Col. 0928B] for making the temple. The “pattern,” I say, was heavenly: the great mystery of the temple not made with hands, to be constructed by the Holy Spirit from the womb of a virgin—that is, of the holy body—as the beloved himself testifies when he says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But the evangelist says: “He spoke of the temple of his body” (John II).

Therefore “his appearance is like Lebanon”; that is, he is himself the glory of his eternal city and the Holy of Holies in the heavenly Jerusalem, as was prefigured in that temple made with hands, in that earthly Jerusalem built of incorruptible wood and covered with gold.

But not only in this respect is “his appearance [Col. 0928C] like Lebanon,” and he “chosen as cedars.” For as Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia which on one side forms a boundary of the land of Judaea, abounds in cedars rooted in itself and raised high, so this “mountain of God, a fertile mountain” (Ps. LXVII), truly white and pure according to the very name Lebanon, brought forth great and most renowned fathers, themselves rooted in him according to faith and proceeding from him. Thus he says of David, the father of his flesh: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches. I am the root and offspring of David” (Rev. XXII).

Thus in this respect too “his appearance is like Lebanon” and he is “chosen as cedars,” that is, he is likened to the holy ones or ancient fathers, as he says in the prophet Hosea: “I have spoken through the prophets, I have multiplied visions, and I have been likened in the hand of the prophets” (Hos. XII). For example, just as Isaac, when led away to be sacrificed, did not resist, yet survived his own holocaust alive (Gen. XXII); just as Joseph, after overcoming his brothers’ envy, passed from prison to the chariot of dominion and saved Egypt from the peril of famine (Gen. XLI); and just as David, though the least among his envious brothers, was taken from their midst, anointed king, struck down proud Goliath, and after Saul’s many persecutions at last sat upon the royal throne (I Sam. XVI)—so this beloved shone gloriously amid adversities and, overcoming every envy and death itself, ascended into heaven and sits at God’s right hand, according to the words: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” [Col. 0929A] (Ps. CIX).

Likewise, it is easy to draw abundant illustrations from many others, so that you may know intelligently that it is as the beloved says: “chosen as cedars.”

Here ends the description: “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.” The beloved’s throat is the experience of his divine sweetness, which has not yet appeared but is reserved for the future as a reward for present faith and love, as the Beloved himself says: “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father; and I shall love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV).

“He says: ‘His throat is most sweet,’” and does not say how sweet it is or what it is like. For each of the other things he gave or added a certain comparison: finest gold for the head; raised palm branches for the locks; doves beside streams of water for the eyes; beds of spices for the cheeks; lilies for the lips; a lathe and gold with hyacinths for the hands; ivory adorned with sapphires for the belly (Isa. LIV); marble columns with golden bases for the legs. But the throat, as has already been said, he calls like nothing at all, but only “most sweet,” so that from this you may reflect that the inward sweetness of divinity is ineffable and inestimable. Thus it was rightly said that what God has prepared for those who love him is such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II). Nor indeed are the comparisons already given for the other things sufficient.

By saying, “and he is altogether desirable,” the tone [Col. 0929C] of the speech strives to make up for the deficiency of a single expression. Truly he is altogether desirable, “and ever desirable,” because when he is possessed, then he is desired all the more; his vision is in desire and desire is in vision, as it is written: “into which angels desire to look” (I Pet. I).

---

“Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” As far as speech could [variant: “thus”], she described a lovable, beloved, desirable man. This picture is not like that which she beheld who was not our mother—that earthly Jerusalem, or rather not Jerusalem but Oholibah, sister of Oholah, as she was called—of whom it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “When she saw men portrayed on the wall, images painted in colors, their loins girded with belts and dyed tiaras on their heads, all having the appearance [Col. 0929D] of rulers, the likeness of the sons of Babylon and of the land of the Chaldeans where they were born, she was inflamed with desire for them at the sight of her eyes and sent messengers to them in Chaldea” (Ezek. XXIII).

This picture, I say, is not like that; yet emulate that sight and that desire toward a better end. “I speak in human terms,” says one of the friends, “because of the weakness of your flesh. For as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI).

And I say to you: as she—not Jerusalem, but Oholibah—presented her eyes to look upon men portrayed on the wall, to look upon images of Chaldeans painted in colors, to look upon their belts, [Col. 0930A] their tiaras, and their appearance, so now present your eyes, your inner eyes, to behold this beloved: to behold his golden head, his shining eyes, his venerable cheeks, his white and glorious lips, his turned and golden hands, his ivory belly adorned with sapphires, his most straight legs; and touch his most sweet throat, according to the words: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII).

Judge righteous judgment concerning all things, namely, that this one is far better than Moses. For he himself required this when he said to the Jews: “If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses is not broken, are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath? Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment” (John VII).

For God indeed spoke to Moses, and through his converse with God his face shone (Exod. XXXIV); yet he did not have a golden head, nor hands that were turned and golden—that is, he was not God and man, but merely a man. And even that his face became radiant and that he performed anything with hands of whatever kind, he received from this one’s fullness, as did all others.

“Such,” I say, “is my beloved, and he is my friend,” and he was my friend before he was my beloved. For he first loved me and looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid with friendly eyes; and for this reason I loved him, because he did great things for me (Luke XI; John I)—great things, I say, which are truly those of a friend.

And this is now being done, that he too may become your beloved, and that you may know, or come to know already in part, how truly worthy of love and altogether desirable he is. For you said: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us? Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned aside? And we shall seek him with you.”

## CHAPTER VI
“My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.” Therefore, O beloved, most beloved among the beloved, you did not say to the daughters of Jerusalem, “I adjure you, if you find my beloved,” as though you did not know where your beloved had gone. Rather, they considered that they ought to learn from you, and you teach them where they should find him. But why did you not say, “My beloved has ascended into heaven,” but instead, “My beloved has gone down into his garden” [Col. 0930D]? Clearly because you are speaking not yet to unbelievers, but already to believers—namely, to the daughters of Jerusalem. For they could not truly be called daughters of Jerusalem unless they possessed faith, unless they believed that the beloved had risen and had already ascended into heaven.

Yet this they needed to know for the perfection of faith: although he had ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless remained here through the presence of his majesty, through the invisible presence, grace, or operation of his divinity, as he says: “Behold, I am with you always, unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Therefore, “my beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies”; that is, he remains here [Col. 0931A] with us, where he once descended in order to do the will of his Father—which is to pasture in the gardens—as he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV); and in order to gather his elect to himself—which is to gather lilies—as one of the chief friends says concerning this very Beloved: “He was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John XI).

Since these things are so, daughters of Jerusalem, do not suppose that it was said to you, “I adjure you, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love,” as though he had departed from here and could in no way be found here. For he is God and Lord, who is everywhere and fills all things, as his wise knower says: “Should it then be thought that God dwells upon the earth? For if heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built!” (III Kings VIII). Although he is not here according to visible presence, although he raised his human form into heaven and a cloud received it from our sight (Acts I), still he is within you here; you are his bed of spices, he pastures in you, and you are the lilies that he gathers.

## Book Six

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931B] Before your “shoots became a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard” (Song IV), you were praiseworthy and the fairest among women, and you were praised by the voice of your beloved, saying: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within” (ibid.), and so forth. How much more, after you rose at the sound of his knocking and because of his hand touching you, in order to open to him; after you opened the bolt of your door; and after he became the paradise of your shoots, planted by your words and examples—how much more you ought to have been praised with a fuller praise of beauty, because you were beautiful not for yourself alone, but very many became sharers in your beauty.

The Beloved again repeats the song of praise, and multiplies the measures of most beautiful song [Col. 0931C] in remembrance of you, you having first uttered such words:

“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who pastures among the lilies. You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away. Your hair is like a flock of goats which appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep which have come up from the washing. All have twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden parts. There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number. My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her. Who is this [Col. 0931D] who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps?”

“I am,” you say, “my beloved’s”—understand: “I opened the bolt of my door; I gave obedience to my voice,” so that the daughters of Jerusalem might hear and not fail to know what he is like. “I am,” I say, “my beloved’s, who pastures among lilies”—that is, who loves pure hearts and chaste bodies—“and my beloved”—understand: “in return he gives me praise and beatification, with a sweet song and the perfection of song, as it were with eight strings.”

For he is both the psaltery and the harp of God [Col. 0932B] the Father, to whom the Father says in the Psalm: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. LVI, CVII). In ancient times harps were made with eight strings, on this principle: the eighth was identical with the first, a consonance musicians call the greatest *diapason*. Consider, therefore, this song: how it proceeds through eight well-sounding measures, so that the eighth sound is identical with the first—“terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps.”

For the first measure is: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps.” The second: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.” The third: “Your hair is like a flock of goats which appeared from Gilead.” The fourth: “Your teeth are like a flock of sheep which have come up from the washing.” [Col. 0932C] The fifth: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden parts.” The sixth: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number; my dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her.” The seventh: “The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.” The eighth: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps?”

Therefore this perfect song and greatest consonance of love, and the eighth measure, sound the same as the first because, not content with my own happiness, I laboured to teach and order the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem, so that one and the same assembly and choir might be [Col. 0932D] a battle-line of camps: a choir praising the Beloved, a battle-line fighting against the devil for the Beloved’s sake. Now each of these melodic phrases must be studied more carefully.

“You are beautiful,” he says, “my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps.” This is the perfection of beauty: that you are not sweet only, nor terrible only, but both sweet and terrible—“sweet as Jerusalem, terrible as the battle-line of camps” which is well ordered. In what respect are you “sweet and lovely as Jerusalem”? Clearly in this: your soul always beholds the peace above, and from your visitation many souls learn to lead a heavenly way of life. Thus they are called, or are, daughters of Jerusalem, because they choose the best part, according to the saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV).

But what is meant by “an ordered battle-line of camps” [Col. 0933A]? This comparison is not devoid of profound meaning and must therefore be carefully considered. We know and recognize that an army’s battle-line appears terrible to enemies when it has been pressed and packed together so that nowhere seems broken. For if it is arranged in such a way that an empty place is left through which an enemy may enter, it is plainly no longer terrible to its enemies. So, when we draw up the battle-line of spiritual warfare against wicked spirits, it is supremely necessary that we always be found united and held closely together by charity, and never broken by discord. However many good things may exist in us, if charity is lacking, through the evil of discord an opening is made in the battle-line through which the enemy may enter to strike us.

You possess the whole inheritance of this best part, and in it you are a leader: of that best part, I say, whose sweetness is already to see or contemplate the peace above, according to the name Jerusalem, and whose likeness to camps is to be in readiness against wicked spirits. Yet, O beloved, O true Jerusalem, do what I say: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.” Even when you possessed me present in bodily presence, you kept your eyes—both the eyes of mind and those of body—always fixed upon me; and now, when I am absent from you in body, you continually contemplate me with spiritual eyes.

“Turn your eyes away” [Col. 0933C]—turn them away, I say, so that your contemplation may be prudent and discerning, knowing that I, your Beloved, am incomprehensible because I am God. The more subtly anyone contemplates his substance or nature, the more insufficient he finds himself to comprehend it; so that you may rightly say of this also: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII).

Is it therefore good and pleasing to the Beloved, for this reason, to turn one’s eyes away? It is certainly in some manner good: namely, when you turn them away from me in such a fashion that you turn your eyes toward yourself—that is, when you contemplate the most high divinity in such a way that you recall the weakness of your frail condition, and know most clearly that this very fact, that you see God, is not due to your own power but to divine grace.

“Your hair is like a flock of goats which appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep which have come up from the washing. All have twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your eyes.” Why does the Beloved repeat these melodic phrases of praise, when above he sang the same things in the same way among the rest, unless because it deserves a double honour that you kept wholly intact, amid that throng [Col. 0934A] in which the usefulness of the Gospel required you to take part, the same purity of thoughts, the same innocence of life, and the same modesty of chastity which you had previously possessed in the solitude of silence? This was according to the will of the Beloved knocking and saying: “Open to me, my sister, for my head is full of dew and my locks with drops of the night” (Song V).

These matters—namely the hair, teeth, and cheeks—have already been discussed there. Yet something must still be said about the cheeks, which friends may gladly hear, by which young women may be built up, and by which the daughters of Jerusalem may delight. Nature so formed us in the womb that the knees are opposite the cheeks. Hence knees are called *genua* from cheeks, *genae*. For there they are joined to one another, and are akin to the eyes, the signs of tears and mercy. Indeed, they say that a human being is born folded up and is formed so that the knees are upward, by which the eyes are shaped to be hollow and recessed. Hence, when people prostrate themselves upon their knees, they immediately weep. Mother Nature wished us to remember the womb, where we sat in darkness before coming to the light.

Certainly, whoever carefully considers this reason knowingly and reasonably praises and approves the practice, familiar to holy and learned thoughts, of bending the knees more frequently before the Most High God and pressing tearful cheeks to bent knees, so that the Creator who dwells on high may look upon and recall how he formed us in the womb. Thus holy Job also reminds him in these words: “Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay, and will bring me back to dust” (Job X), and so forth, as far as: “Although you hide these things in your heart, yet I know that you remember all things” (ibid.) [Col. 0934C].

He has discovered no small insight who has attained this, so as knowingly to offer himself to the Creator in the manner found by the prophet Micah when he said: “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend my knee to God Most High?” (Mic. VI). Nor is such a posture or disposition pleasing in appearance and lovable only to God, but also to human beings. Each person is held in greater reverence in proportion as, more frequently and more earnestly bending the knees, he lowers his cheeks, eyes, or whole head. Conversely, excessive lifting-up of head, eyes, and cheeks is very hateful to God and people; and the rebuke of such persons, especially from the mouth of God, conveys great censure. For example, when he says: “Because the daughters of Zion have been lifted up, and walked with stretched-out neck and went with signals of their eyes [Col. 0934D] and clapped” (Isa. III), and so forth. Again: “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high” (Prov. XXX).

But you, O beloved, adorned nature: you were the first to resolve never to raise your cheeks for the gaze of any man, but wisely to bow yourself, humble in mind and body, only before the Creator, with the Holy Spirit as guide and teacher. In him your faithful father David says: “Come, let us adore and fall down, and weep before the Lord who made us” (Ps. XL). Very many of both sexes follow you, greatly pleased by what they hear: “As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from your hidden parts.”

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and young women without number. My dove, [Col. 0935A] my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her.”

What does this mean except that, although many women are faithful and praiseworthy because of the faith which works in them through love (Gal. V), nevertheless none of them is like you? For, as we truthfully proclaim, you have been seen to have neither a like predecessor nor a like successor. Queens are rightly called those souls which possess perfect charity: following your same Beloved, they seek nothing earthly but him alone; they flee sin not from fear of Gehenna but from love of your eternal life; and by loving virtue they hate wickedness.

The concubines, however, are those who serve under fear, and who do not possess the perfection to wish to add counsel beyond the commandment: namely, to leave all things and follow this Beloved alone (Matt. XIX). They indeed have Christ as their foundation, but nevertheless love some things belonging to this world.

What, then, do these numbers—sixty and eighty—intend? Does any significance attach to this title of Scripture, that is, “Song of Songs”? Certainly: for they produce the first consonance which musicians call the *diatessaron*. For between them there is the relation called *epitriton*, that is, sesquitertian: the greater number, eighty, contains in itself the whole lesser number, sixty, and in addition its third part, that is, twenty. This numerical proportion in music produces the *diatessaron*, which is translated “through four,” and this consonance is so called because it consists of four [Col. 0935C] strings or voices, containing two tones and a semitone. Therefore “sixty queens and eighty concubines” means souls devoted to the word of God and made such partakers of God’s word that they can bear the fruit of teaching. They differ in merits, as was said above, but by unity of confession they sweetly sound the consonance of faith in the Beloved’s ears.

How, then, do the numbers eight and six, which here have multiplied ten, differ from one another, so that he wished rightly to signify queens by six and concubines by eight? They differ in this: six is a perfect number, whereas eight is imperfect and deficient and divisible down to its ultimate units. Six is perfect, indeed the first of perfect numbers, because it is constructed out of its own parts. It has a half, namely three; a third, namely two; and a sixth, namely one; and these parts, added together, restore the sum of six. Eight, on the other hand, is less than itself in its parts. It has a half, namely four; a fourth, namely two; and an eighth, namely one; and these parts added together make seven, a sum smaller than eight itself, of which they are parts [Col. 0935D]. Thus this too makes clear why six suits queens and eight concubines, rather than eight queens and six concubines.

“There is no number of young women”; that is, in the Gospel more abound than belong to the heavenly bridal chambers, according to the saying: “I have declared and spoken; they have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). Young women are rightly called those who have not yet advanced even to the fear of God, and who therefore need the safeguarding or instruction of human beings, since they do not yet possess within themselves the instruction of divine fear or love. Many such persons—something greatly to be feared—are found outside the number, because they never come from youth to perfect age: the age of the inner human being, which one of the friends indicates when he says, “Let us meet in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Jesus Christ” (Eph. IV).

“My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her.” “She is one,” I say, and has no equal [Col. 0936B]: among the queens indeed none is like her. To what “mother” is she one, and for what “mother who bore her” is she chosen? Clearly, she is one to her mother Jerusalem—to that Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all—and she is chosen for her mother who bore her, namely, the ancient Church: the Church of patriarchs, prophets, and righteous kings, from whose flesh she was born and to whom, according to faith in the promised blessing, she is the gateway or material basis. To that mother and this mother who bore her, she is one and chosen, because neither among angels nor among human beings has she had, or will have, an equal or predecessor or successor. Truly a dove, because full of grace; truly chosen, because she would not merely herself be saved, but would bear salvation itself.

“The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.” Foreseeing and foreknowing this herself, when she had said, “Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke I), she added: “For behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (ibid.). Is it not the case, according to the present letter of the text, that the generation of queens, the generation of concubines, and the generation of young women—all these generations, I say—will call her blessed? Truly, though unequal in merits, yet alike in faith, behold they see her; behold they contemplate her, the one, the chosen one; and with inexpressible wonder they continually raise their voices from all their places, nevertheless praising her and calling her most blessed—not only [Col. 0936D] here in this exile of mortality, but also, and much more, in that first realm of life and immortality, where they see her reigning and, by reigning, possessing the kingdom of the Beloved by the right fitting for a mother to possess her son’s kingdom.

And what did they say in praising and proclaiming her most blessed? “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps?” How beautiful is the order in this praise, in this proclamation of your beauty, O most blessed one: first, “rising like the dawn”; then, “beautiful as the moon”; then, “chosen as the sun.”

When you were born, O blessed Virgin, then the true dawn rose for us: the dawn announcing the everlasting day. For as the daily dawn is the end of the past night and the beginning [Col. 0937A] of the coming day, so your birth—from Abraham’s seed, illustrious from David’s stock, to whom the promise of blessing was made with God’s oath—was the end of sorrows and the beginning of consolation; it was the end of sadness and became for us the beginning of joy.

But when the Holy Spirit came upon you, and as a virgin you conceived the Son and as a virgin gave birth, then and from then on you were beautiful with divine beauty: beautiful, I say, not merely in any fashion, but “as the moon.” For as the moon shines and gives light with light not its own but received from the sun, so you, O most blessed one, do not possess from yourself the very fact that you are so radiant, but from divine grace—full of grace.

But when you were assumed from this world and transferred to the heavenly bridal chamber, then and from then on you were “chosen as the sun”: “chosen,” I say, for us, because just as we adore and worship as true God the Son of God born from you, the true and eternal sun, so also we honour and venerate you as Mother of the true God, knowing that every honour bestowed upon the mother undoubtedly redounds to the glory of the Son. By nature, indeed, you are not the same as that sun; nevertheless you are so great that the sun himself honours you with the honour due to children toward their parents. For he who said, “Honour your father and mother” (Exod. XX), undoubtedly himself honours his mother and wishes her to be honoured by all his friends. The end of the song sounds the same as its beginning: “terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps,” as has already been said above.

Then, immediately, what you had said, O beloved, to the daughters of Jerusalem when they asked where your beloved had gone—“My beloved has gone down to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens”—he confirms as gratefully received in these words: “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley and to inspect whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.” Thus, my sister, as you said last, I “went down,” namely from heaven into my garden, “a garden of nuts.” For I was made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. IV), and that law is indeed to me like a garden of nuts. For just as a nut, beneath its bitter husk and within its hard shell, contains a sweet kernel pleasant to eat, so beneath the bitter utterance, or killing letter, and the exceedingly hard yoke of ceremonies, it contains a sweet and life-giving spirit [Col. 0937D] (II Cor. III).

Why did I come down here? “To see the fruits of the valley, and to inspect whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.” But what happened instead is not fit for song and does not belong to the Song of Songs, if you consider the conduct of those who were so ungrateful for my descent. Our friends and our young daughters of Jerusalem have long known well the event, according to the parable which I spoke, of this kind: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge and dug a winepress in it” (Matt. XXI), and the rest down to: “Lastly he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.’ And they seized him, cast him out of the vineyard, and killed him” (ibid.) [Col. 0938A].

According to that parable, I went down into the garden of nuts—that is, I was made under the law—in order to see the fruits of the valley, that is, to console those who awaited me in a spirit of humility, according to the saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me. He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal those broken in heart, and to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those confined,” and so forth (Isa. LXI; Luke IV). And not only this: I went down to inspect whether the vine had flowered—the vineyard, namely, of which prophetic Scripture says: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil,” and the rest down to: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V).

But those husbandmen cast me out and killed me. Nevertheless, although they did these things to me, some part of them at last repented and spoke this song: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.” Where was this said? When our friends said to them: “Therefore let all the house of Israel know most certainly that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ.” Hearing this, they were pierced in heart and said to them: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts II). And one especially well known among such persons says: “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (I Tim. I). In these and other ways the repentant Synagogue, or some part of the Synagogue, said: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.”

But why did it say, “My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab,” and not, “The chariots of Aminadab troubled me”? Consider first, friends, the chariots of Aminadab themselves, and you will see that it matters greatly that it says, “My soul troubled me,” rather than, “The chariots troubled me.” The chariots of Aminadab are the four Gospel mysteries of the Beloved: namely, his incarnation or divinity, his passion, his resurrection, and his ascension. “Because of such chariots,” it says, “my soul troubled me”: that is, the Pharisaic assembly stirred me up into seditions so that I could not discern the course [Col. 0938D] of such chariots, being prevented from a sound estimation of those chariots by the counsels and wicked deliberations of that such soul of mine.

For the Pharisaic assembly was, or ought to have been, my soul: that is, it ought to give life to or govern the people as the soul gives life and animation to the body and all its limbs. They were teachers or wise persons, knowing the Law and the Prophets—indeed, even taking away the whole key of knowledge. Such a soul troubled me, so that I could not enter into knowledge and understand the chariots of Aminadab, to which the Law and Prophets bore witness (Luke XI).

In what respect, or why, is the Beloved called Aminadab? What was the point of calling him Aminadab in such a matter? Clearly this: the one and same Beloved is King and great Priest, and in himself united both persons, that of priest and that of king, according to the type or likeness of that man Aminadab, who, though he was of the royal tribe, namely Judah, gave his daughter in marriage to Aaron, a priestly man of the tribe of Levi, as is written in Exodus: “Aaron took as wife Elisabeth, daughter of Aminadab, sister of Naason, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (Exod. VI).

That Aminadab, indeed, did not bring back, nor ought to have brought back, to himself his daughter once given to Aaron. But this Aminadab, this Beloved and Firstborn, reclaimed and brought back to himself his priesthood, which had always belonged to the firstborn before Moses and Aaron, though for a time and by reason of a certain dispensation—of which much might be said—it had been entrusted to the tribe of Levi. He reclaimed, I say, his priesthood with exultation and by running his course in the aforesaid chariots, voluntary in all things: voluntarily incarnate and born, voluntarily suffering; and in his own passion voluntarily made both Priest and Victim. This accords with the very name Aminadab, for it is interpreted “the willing one of my people.”

Moreover, he not only reclaimed and brought back his priesthood in this way, but restored it to its ancient appearance and original form, as David had foretold in the Spirit: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Therefore, “my soul troubled me,” it says, “because of the chariots of Aminadab” [Col. 0939C]: troubled and confused by evil zeal through envy, lamenting its own case as though it deserved pity, because it had heard the runners or charioteers of these chariots saying: “This Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the traditions which Moses handed down to us” (Acts VI), and many similar things, whether before or after this Aminadab completed his course.

But the utterances of this same Aminadab, running in his chariots, were as follows: “Return, return, O Shunammite; return, that we may behold you.” You, O Shunammite—that is, captive or despised—you, O faith, dignity of the true priesthood, almost consigned to oblivion because of carnal ceremonies, so that the Synagogue neither knows nor recalls that its father Abraham was justified not through the law but through you, that is, through faith, as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV; Gen. XV)—return; and again I say, return; and a third time I say, return; and a fourth time I say, return: namely, according to these my chariots.

For I was born for this and suffered for this, that you might return; and, rising and ascending into heaven, I did not cease to call out for your return. And when you return, you are to me the Shunammite, who will warm either me or my Father, the Ancient of Days, according to this likeness: “King David had grown old and was advanced in days. Though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed. Therefore his servants said to him: ‘Let a young virgin be sought for our lord the king, that she may stand before the king and cherish him, sleep [Col. 0940A] in his bosom, and warm our lord the king.’ Therefore they sought a beautiful young woman throughout all the borders of Israel, found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king,” and so forth (III Kings I).

For this, as also other things, was spoken allegorically and should be regarded among all things that happened in figure (Gal. IV). The garments with which the aged king David was covered but not warmed are the carnal ceremonies which God, the Ancient of Days, did not delight to receive when they were offered to him; indeed, he said: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (I Cor. XIX; Ps. XLIX), and much else like this.

But the Shunammite, the beautiful maiden, alone is worthy to stand before God the King, sleep in his bosom, and warm him: that is, to obtain the glory of his charity, burning well—namely, the remission of sins [Col. 0940B]. “Therefore, O Shunammite, return, that we may behold you”:  that is, all who wish to be, or truly to be called, children of Abraham should hope to be justified by that by which Abraham was justified, namely not from the law but from faith. And we shall behold you; we shall rejoice over you. This ought to be known to friends—indeed, to the multitude of young women—and therefore I say to them:

## Chapter VII
“What will you see in the Shulammite but the dances of camps?” What else, I ask? The blood of victims? The mark of circumcision? Nothing at all but the dances of camps: that is, the praises or songs of those who fight [Col. 0940C] or sing—something most sweet, something truly most beautiful. “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise,” says the Psalmist himself, “and render your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX [50]). By praising, the choirs fight; by fighting, the camps praise; and it is altogether right to submit oneself to God’s righteousness rather than seek to establish one’s own righteousness (Rom. X [10]). You will see nothing else, nor desire to see anything else. And if anyone, O friends, should wish to show your hearers otherwise, you, together with the Holy Spirit, by the spirit of counsel, will answer in opposition: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication, and that you do not do to others what you do not wish done to yourselves. If you keep yourselves from these things, you shall do well” (Acts XV [15]).

Therefore this alone must be seen and attended to in the Gospel, according to the faith of the Fathers: that there may be dances of camps—dances in the one faith, speaking the same thing (I Cor. I [1]); camps, by resisting sin even unto blood. “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince.” I speak to you, O Shulammite, to whom I said, “Return,” and who now are returning. I call you the daughter of the prince, and say this to you because “your feet are beautiful in sandals.” Do you ask, maidens, why I call the Shulammite, already mentioned, the daughter of a prince, or whose daughter of a prince I say she is? Learn this from the friends, and especially from him in whose soul that return shone forth most brightly—the return to which, bending toward her, I said: “Return, return, O Shulammite.”

For the soul of that man returned notably from the law of works to the law of faith. [Col. 0941A] He teaches us to recognize the daughter of the prince in these words: “It is written,” he says, “that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But he who was of the slave woman was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was of the free woman was born through promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants” (Gal. IV [4]), and so forth down to: “Therefore, brethren, we are no longer children of the slave woman, but of the free woman—the freedom by which Christ has made us free. Stand firm, and do not again be held under the yoke of slavery” (ibid.).

That free woman of whom he speaks according to Scripture was called Sarah. Now Sarah means “princess”; and by this very name, and by the manner of her begetting, she allegorically signifies the Jerusalem above, the free woman, who is mother of all according to faith. For she does not bear according to the flesh, but according to faith. Conversely, the slave woman Hagar, both according to her name—which means “foreign woman”—and according to the manner either of her bearing or of her condition, signifies that Jerusalem which now is and is in bondage with her children.

Therefore the daughter of the prince, the beautiful and lovely Shulammite, is faith itself, or the offspring of faith, to whom I now say: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince.” Does not the slave woman, or the daughter of the slave woman, walk with bare feet? Certainly with bare feet; and for this very reason she is charged with a servile condition, since nakedness of the feet is an indication of slavery—unless it is done for God’s sake, according to the saying: “Loose the sandal from your feet, for the place upon which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III [3]).

But here the matter is not bodily sandals [Col. 0941C] but those of the spirit, in which to be unshod, whether man or woman, is the height of ignobility and an impoverishment worse than slavery. Therefore the serpent bit the heel of the slave woman; but you, O daughter of the prince, well shod, have crushed the serpent’s head. You especially, O princess and lady, uniquely beloved, and, as I have already said, “my one dove, the one of her mother”—that is, of the free generation, the generation not of flesh but of faith—you who conceived and bore me, a man, not from a man’s flesh but from the Spirit of God, the father or prince of children not of flesh but of faith or promise.

“Your hip-joints are like ornaments fashioned by the hand of an artisan.” This praise—great praise—is set against, indeed against the most bitter reproach of the aforesaid slave woman, spoken through the prophet Ezekiel [Col. 0941D] from the Lord’s mouth: “You spread apart your feet for every passerby, and multiplied your prostitutions” (Ezek. XVI [16]). The spreading or parting of the feet is itself the disjoining of the thighs, wholly blameworthy, surely because of what is understood: namely, the multitude of prostitutions. Conversely, the joining of the thighs is itself the fitting together or continuity of the feet, praiseworthy likewise because of what is understood: namely, the beauty of chastity and the safe, well-guarded seal of purity.

This is especially so in you, O singular, unique, and most noble Shulammite; in you, O beloved and most beloved of beloved women, who first, without precedent, resolved so to preserve the joining of your thighs [Col. 0942A] that, a virgin unknown and never to be known by any man, you might be worthy to be joined to God, the author of your integrity. How great is this honor! How great this dignity! Thus “your hip-joints are like ornaments”: that is, your virginal integrity and perpetual custody of chastity, fortified by heavenly protection. Whose work is this? Whose power? Surely that of God Most High. “And this itself,” says a certain wise man, “is wisdom: to know that continence is God’s gift” (Wis. VIII [8]). I say therefore, not ornaments of any ordinary kind, but “ornaments fashioned by the hand of an artisan”—that is, ornaments which God alone can make and give, or could make and give.

“Your navel is like a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” This praise also, O free Shulammite, stands against the reproach of the slave woman which we have in the prophet already mentioned [Col. 0942B] in these words: “When you were born, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed with water for cleansing” (Ezek. VIII [sic; XVI]). By these words he surely censures the excess of lust; for lust is in men in the loins, but in women in the navel, as the Lord testifies when He speaks of the devil to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL [40]).

Therefore, “your navel [is] a rounded bowl”: what does this mean unless it is as though he said, “The virtue of chastity is perfect in you, and you have been freed from every fleshly appetite for pleasure”? For it would have been too little in praise of true virtue merely to say, “Your hip-joints are like ornaments fashioned by the hand of an artisan,” unless this also were added: “Your navel is like a rounded bowl, never lacking [Col. 0942C] cups.” For by the preceding verse the deed or inclination of fleshly intercourse alone is denied; by this following one, even the appetite of thought. If this were present, the “navel” could never truly be said to have been so cut off—indeed circumcised—as “a rounded bowl”; nor would there further be added, “never lacking cups.”

What is it for the navel not to need cups, except not to burn or thirst with the desire of lust? Thus a certain wise man says of a wicked woman: “Like a thirsty traveler, she will open her mouth at springs and drink from every nearby water” (Ecclus. XXVI [26]). Therefore you, O Shulammite, O daughter of the prince, are chaste in heart and body, whole and incorrupt in mind and flesh, clean in thought and deed. But for this praise to be complete, it must be said [Col. 0942D] that you are also useful and modest in speech. This is what I, your beloved, now say: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.”

“Your belly”—the belly of the inner person, as I said elsewhere: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII [7])—is “like a heap of wheat”: that is, it never lacks the bread of God’s word, but rather abounds in every grain that others have sown. There has been brought into it all that the faith of the prophets labored to produce. By way of example: Isaiah, who said, “I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. VIII [8]). For you, O beloved, are that prophetess [Col. 0943A] whom every holy and faithful prophet approached, toward whom he directed his course, and in whom every holy and faithful prophecy was fulfilled.

Hence, “your belly [is] like a heap of wheat,” because you wisely gathered this wheat by meditating upon the Scriptures, as it is said somewhere: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke II [2]).

Such a heap is well “surrounded by lilies,” because the beauty of chastity, just as it produces clarity of understanding for comprehending the Scriptures, also gives every person authority to be worthy to speak openly what he has stored up or pondered within: the words of God, the Lord’s wheat.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle. Your neck is like a tower of ivory.” [Col. 0943B] This praise of the free woman also stands against the reproach of the slave woman—indeed, of the slave women who from one became two. “Son of man,” says the Lord to the prophet Ezekiel, “there were two women, daughters of one mother; and they committed fornication in Egypt; in their youth they committed fornication there; there their breasts were pressed down, and the breasts of their virginity were bruised” (Ezek. XXIII [23]).

How great is the injury of slavery in such a pressing down of the breasts and such a bruising of the bosom! And how great is the glory of freedom here, according to these images—namely, twin fawns of a gazelle and a tower of ivory! Therefore you, O free Shulammite—especially you, whose two breasts are twin things unheard of in all ages, virginity and fruitfulness—you, I say, O singular beloved, are free from every yoke [Col. 0943C] of sin according to these likenesses of the gazelle’s fawns and the ivory tower.

What is your neck, and what kind of neck is it? Certainly not stretched out; rather, graciously bowed down. This humility of yours is great strength, most beautiful strength, truly “like a tower of ivory,” which is lovely in appearance and strong in height. Strong for whom, lovely for whom? Strong for God, lovely for God; but terrible and inaccessible to the devil. In what way is it strong even for God? Surely as is shown by these examples: “Because you have been strong against God,” He says to your faithful father Jacob, “how much more shall you prevail against men?” (Gen. XXXII [32]). And to Moses: “I see,” He says, “that this people is stiff-necked. Let me alone, that my wrath may blaze against them and I may destroy them, and make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII [32]).

Yet Moses did not let Him alone; indeed, he wrestled so long that God, seeing that He could not overcome him, said to him: “I have forgiven according to your word.” By what strength did this man or that man wrestle? Surely by humility, as the Psalmist says of the former: “Had Moses, his chosen one, not stood in the breach” (Ps. CV [106])—that is, in exceeding humility of mind before Him. Of the latter, the prophet Hosea, after saying, “In his strength he contended with the angel, and prevailed over the angel, and was strengthened” (Hos. XII [12]), immediately expressed the manner of his strength by adding: “He wept and entreated him” (ibid.).

Therefore, O beloved, “your neck,” which is [Col. 0944A] your humility, is “a tower of ivory”: that is, most strong and most beautiful. Beholding it, the Most High gave you these sweet twin fawns, these two breasts—virginity and fruitfulness. And behold, you possess these three distinctions; for your humility is the third.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.” In what sense are “your eyes like pools”? Surely because their waters do not fail; and you especially, beyond all mortals, can always say with contrite heart: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI [42]). Therefore I said “like pools,” not just any pools, but “pools in Heshbon,” that is, in the greatest contrition. For Heshbon is interpreted “girdle of sorrow”; hence this name suitably signifies the greatness of contrition.

“Which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude”: that is, in the first portion of the land of promise. Heshbon was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon; and that city was given to the children of Reuben as a possession beyond the Jordan. “The children of Reuben and Gad,” Scripture says, “came to Moses and Eleazar the priest and requested that land; and Moses commanded Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families, saying: If the children of Gad and the children of Reuben cross the Jordan with you, all armed for battle, give them the land of Gilead as a possession” (Num. XXXII [32]). It is therefore rightly said, “which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude,” because it was the first possession of the people which had multiplied in Egypt and was entering the land of promise.

[Col. 0944C] This bears very closely upon the mystery: namely, that the pools should thus signify those which are “at the gate of the multitude.” For they are the first experiences of the sweetness above, of the blessed possession, so that they may already truly be called the land of promise, according to the great mystery of Scripture, which says: “When Othniel son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb, had captured it”—that is, Kiriath-sepher, which means “city of letters”—“Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as wife.” As she was going on the way, her husband prompted her to ask her father for a field. When she sighed while seated on the donkey, Caleb said to her: ‘What is it that you want?’ She answered: ‘Give me a blessing. Since you have given me dry land, give me also water-fed land.’ Therefore Caleb gave her the upper water-fed land and the lower water-fed land” (Josh. XV [15]; Judg. I [1]).

According to the likeness of this event, the soul receives the upper water-fed land when it afflicts itself with tears out of longing for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower water-fed land when, weeping, it fears the punishments of hell. Therefore, in the words, “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude,” this is the mystical sense, as though it were said: Your eyes, from love and longing for the beloved—by which you languish and are pierced with compunction—flow with tears; and these tears are pools in Heshbon, that is, waters flowing from the girdle of sorrow. This compunction is water-fed land, a kind of beginning of heavenly sweetness and eternal inheritance, just as Heshbon and the land beyond the Jordan were the first possession of the land [Col. 0945A] of promise for that daughter of the multitude, namely the Israelite people. And those ascending or having ascended to receive the promise of eternal inheritance are no fewer in number than that multitude.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” Truly noble, truly free Shulammite, having a distinguished nose! But that ignoble slave woman has her nose cut off; her ears too are cut off, as was said through the prophet mentioned above: “Therefore, O Oholibah, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will stir up all your lovers against you” (Ezek. XXIII [23]), and so forth down to: “They shall cut off your nose and ears, and those who remain shall fall by the sword” (ibid.). As it was spoken, so it was done.

Does such a slave woman have a nose or ears? If she had a nose, she would perceive something from afar; she would think of or desire something from the age to come. If she had ears, she would not attend to the letter alone, but would hear the life-giving Spirit in the letter. But now she delights only in present things, and does not hear Him who so often invites people to hear, saying: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XIII [13]). Therefore she has neither ears nor nose.

But you, O free woman, have an intact nose, a distinguished nose, as has already been said: you who, by sound perception and drawing desire, seek “not the things which are seen, but the things which are not seen” (II Cor. IV [4]), according to this: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI [11]). How is your nose of such a kind? “Like the tower of Lebanon, which looks [Col. 0945C] toward Damascus”: that is, toward the bloody son of the aforesaid slave woman. For Damascus means “drinking blood,” and signifies him of whom the Apostle speaks, saying: “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. IV [4]).

A most strong nose of hope and discernment was needed against every such false brother, persecuting in play and playing in persecution (Gen. XXI [21]), lest he wholly mock you and, if he injures the body, at least deceive the soul. This nose of discernment is certainly strong, “like the tower of Lebanon,” when, rightly despising visible things and hoping for invisible things, it resists strongly and is not broken by visible adversities, according to the saying: “You have led me, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX [61]).

How does this tower look toward Damascus? Surely by having a perception contrary to his perception, according to the saying: “Those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit” (Rom. VIII [8]). This looking also contains a manifest reproach of Damascus, the same son of the slave woman. For just as that Damascus, in the inner person, has lost every nose of discernment and spiritual understanding, so outwardly too he has lost a kind of nose of his own, a great nose: namely, the city Jerusalem, the noble Temple, and the other distinctions that have been destroyed. With these removed, circumcision [Col. 0946A] of the flesh has become as shameful as the face of any person is made ugly when the nose is cut off.

Thus she who looks toward him also despises such a Damascus and says: You proud slave woman, with your son Damascus, what would you do if either you had a nose, or he were your nose, when you think yourself beautiful though you do not even possess a nose outwardly? What, I ask, would you do if your Temple and your city had remained? Rightly, then, O free Shulammite, “your nose looks toward Damascus,” standing firm “like the tower of Lebanon.”

“Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like royal purple joined to channels.” Carmel means “knowledge of circumcision.” The head is the ruling part of the body, and is taken for the heart, which is the ruling part of the inner person, according to the saying: “When these things begin to happen, lift up your heads”—that is, make your hearts glad—“because your redemption is drawing near.” [Col. 0946B] Therefore, “your head is like Carmel”: that is, your heart possesses the knowledge of circumcision, so that whoever wishes to be justified according to God and according to the faith which is in you may be circumcised lawfully and as is necessary.

Did not Moses also prescribe this circumcision, the circumcision of the heart? “Circumcise,” he says in Deuteronomy, “the foreskin of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer.” What is this circumcision but perfect love of God? For elsewhere, having said, “The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed” (Deut. XXX [30]), he immediately adds: “That you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (ibid.).

Moreover, you possess the true knowledge of circumcision of the flesh in this: that you do not doubt that it ought to have ceased once the seed came and was revealed, in faith of whose coming Abraham received “the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith” (Gen. XVII [17]; Rom. IV [4]). I have spoken of the knowledge of circumcision; what shall I say of the knowledge of the law? Surely this: that you understand the whole law—that is, the law of ceremonies—spiritually. This is what I say: “And the locks of your head are like royal purple, joined to channels.”

“The locks of your head” are the perceptions of your heart while meditating or reflecting upon the mysteries of God’s law. For example: what mystery is contained in the unblemished calf commanded to be offered for the sin of the priest who had sinned and caused the people to transgress? (Lev. IV; Lev. V.) [Col. 0946D] What mystery in the he-goat from the goats, in the she-goat, in the sheep, in the turtledove, and in the young pigeon? What mystery in the whole rite of sacrifice? While you meditate upon these and other matters of that sort, “the locks of your head”—that is, the perceptions of your heart—are “like royal purple,” since you refer all things to the mystery of the Passion of your beloved, who because of what He suffered was made king and crowned with glory and honor, and “sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. I [1]).

And the king’s Passion is rightly called “royal purple,” not only because of the purple color of the blood which He shed in His Passion, but also because of the mock purple garment which they put around Him, when He was immediately to undergo the three sufferings of the Passion: to be scourged, crucified, and struck with a lance. For they, mocking Him, clothed Him in purple as though He were a king; but He in earnest accepted both the purple and the reed as a scepter in His right hand (Matt. XXVII [27]), because through these very things it was most certainly brought about that in heaven and on earth He should receive both the purple of kingship and the scepter of dominion.

Therefore that purple is rightly said to be “joined to channels,” because just as purple is more deeply dyed and becomes more precious the nearer and longer it is joined to the channels of dye, so the Passion of the beloved is more glorious because, above all other sacrifices, it proceeded according to the counsel of divinity. The hidden things of that counsel are, as it were, channels through which ran this most precious purple dye, by which this beloved—who was white in virginity [Col. 0947B]—was made red by His death or Passion, and remains forever red: God truly glorious and man exceedingly beautiful, and in both substances one King, always and everywhere victorious.

“How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights! Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.” What is it to be beautiful and lovely “in delights,” except to have, amid an abundance of grace, gentleness and the deepest humility of heart? For the gifts of graces and understanding of the Scriptures or heavenly mysteries are truly delights; and humility of heart is true beauty, a lovely thing and a virtue pleasing to God. These are united in you, O dearest one: such delights and such beauty.

For what did He say? “Your stature is likened to a palm tree [Col. 0947C] and your breasts to clusters.” And, so that there may be no doubt which palm tree I mean, He says further: “I said, I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruit; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, your fragrance like apples, and your throat like the best wine.” Great, then, is the humility which this beauty expresses: “Your stature is likened to a palm tree,” because it is as though I said: You are likened to me in every disposition of your mind; you are likened to me, I say, in that I ascended the cross, meek and humble in heart.

I foretold this ascent of mine, and none of the friends will doubt that I spoke it to you. For if I told the friends themselves: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified” (Matt. XX [20]), with many other things bearing upon this meaning; indeed, if I even told enemies: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII [12]), how much more, O dearest one, did I say—or ought I to have said—“I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruit; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, your fragrance like apples, and your throat like the best wine”?

This was to say: I shall be lifted upon the victorious cross, and by dying a fruitful death shall swiftly accomplish the salvation of all believers. Then your doctrine—the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel—shall openly be preached at the fitting time, as sweet clusters are eaten in autumn; the good fragrance of your good works shall spread everywhere; and your speech shall be most sweet and pleasing to me, like the best wine. You [Col. 0948A] reply: “Worthy of my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew.” And truly, as you say, so it is. For as the best wine is worthy for kings to drink, “for their lips and teeth to chew,” so your speech is worthy for me to hear and for all my friends and witnesses to proclaim.

What shall we do, or where shall we go, with such great delights of the beloved? For our people, who were first invited to these delights, “would not come, but went away carelessly, one to his field, another to his business; while the rest seized our friends and, having insulted them, killed them” (Matt. XXII [22]). What then shall we do? “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me. Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages. Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bring forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have bloomed. There I will give you my breasts. The mandrakes have given fragrance at our gates. All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved.”

I have spoken this, “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me,” meaning that He did not reject it, but had this purpose: that we should go out. For He had long before said to His fellow citizens: “Amen, I say to you that no prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke IV [4]); and, having said this and spoken a few further words, “He Himself, passing through their midst, went His way” (ibid.), plainly signifying that He would pass away from His own citizens, go out into the field, and lodge in the villages.

Therefore, in agreement with God’s purpose, “Come, my beloved,” I say, “let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages,” so that those who were rustic may become members of the household, and those who were villagers may become citizens of God; and so that, according to the prophetic oracle, “The wilderness and trackless place may rejoice, the solitude exult and blossom like a lily; budding, let it bud, and exult with joy and praise, and let the glory of Lebanon be given to it” (Isa. XXXV [35]). This glory is that they may see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God—a vision of which this Lebanon, that is, the Jewish people, makes itself unworthy by rejecting the Word of God.
