Let us go out there; let us lodge there; and, while lodging there, let us rise early for the vineyards, undoubtedly now multiplying them by our dwelling there. “Let us see whether [Col. 0948D] the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bring forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have bloomed.” For then “the vine has flowered” if, in such villages, some have now been born from the flesh of the rustic Gentiles who are predestined for eternal life and who will without doubt soon believe. Then “the flowers bring forth fruit” if they are found teachable in doing good works. Then, too, “the pomegranates have bloomed” if some are found among them whose faith is sufficient to endure even unto martyrdom—which will undoubtedly come to pass.

“There I will give you my breasts,” namely by nourishing the multitude of children whom fruitful grace will bear for you into a new infancy. How is it so certain that a multitude of children ought to be born there where sterility has hitherto existed? Surely from the testimonies of Scripture, which testify that this must occur, and also from present experiences, because “the mandrakes have given fragrance at our gates.”

Mandrakes bear sweet-smelling fruit and are also called ἀνθρωπόμορφος, “human-shaped,” because they have a root resembling the form of a human being. Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink to those whose body must be cut because of a medical treatment, so that, being put to sleep, they may feel no pain; it is also said to cure sterile women so that they conceive. “Therefore the mandrakes have given fragrance at our gates”: that is, there is ready evidence that what the prophetic Spirit promises to the Gentile world, hitherto sterile, must now happen: “Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear; sing praise and cry out, you who did not give birth; for the children of the desolate woman are many more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV [54]), and so forth.

“At our gates,” I say: that is, while we were still within our own borders, the Jewish borders, we perceived the fragrance of this kind. For the Ethiopian eunuch had already come to Jerusalem to perceive the fragrance, and was returning seated in his chariot and reading Isaiah the prophet, when, behold, the Holy Spirit, perceiving his fragrance, said to Philip: “Go near and join yourself to this chariot” (Acts VIII [8]). And we were still at our gates [Col. 0950A] when the alms of Cornelius the centurion gave fragrance in the Lord’s presence (Acts X [10]).

To this fragrance also belongs what was later shown in a vision by night to one of the friends: “A certain Macedonian man stood and begged him, saying: ‘Cross over into Macedonia; help us’” (Acts XVI [16]). In these and other ways “the mandrakes gave fragrance at our gates,” signifying fruitfulness arising from a place of sterility.

But shall I give you my breasts only there? Indeed, “I have kept for you all fruits, new and old, my beloved.” So long as those who are to be born children of the living God in the place where it was said, “You are not my people” (Hos. I [1]), are little children; so long, I say, as they are too weak to hear profound discourse and “need milk, not solid food” (Heb. V [5]), so long “I will give you my breasts.” But when they have become perfect and “by practice have their faculties trained to distinguish good and evil” (ibid.), then in them I shall give you solid food. For I have kept for you all things new and old, all mysteries of the Old and New Testaments, pondering them in my heart (Luke I [1]), to bring them forth in their proper and fitting time.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949C] 422 It has happened, O most beloved of the beloved, as you said: “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages.” Blessed was the day; blessed for us were the times of this your departure to us from those who rejected you, when the friends, conscious of your counsel, said to them:

“To you indeed it was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII [13]). Had they not only heard that prophetic saying which they went on to cite: “For thus the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth’” (Isa. XLIX [49])? Indeed, they had heard and understood many other oracles of this grace, including that most secret saying which you here uttered, O full of grace: “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages.”

O what joy, what exultation of that barren and deserted woman, who had no husband, when she heard from the prophetic Scriptures the testimony, certain and assured, of your coming out to her and of her salvation! “And when the Gentiles heard this,” Scripture says, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord; and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Acts XIII [13]). In accordance with that joy, she herself speaks in this passage, exulting, rejoicing, and praising.

## CHAPTER VIII
“Who will grant me that you be my brother, suckling at the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me? I will take hold of you [Col. 0950C] and lead you into my mother’s house and into my mother’s chamber; there you will teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the new wine of my pomegranates.”

This wondering question, “Who will grant me that you be [my brother],” resembles that other: “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). And this exultation, “I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me,” resembles your answer to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). For she who says these things is like you, as it is fitting that a daughter should resemble her mother. Are you not her mother, who bore life and salvation? Is she not your daughter, namely by imitation of faith? If Abraham is rightly called, and is, the father of nations, and Sarah the mother of nations (Gen. 17), namely [Col. 0950D] on account of faith, how much more are you, O most faithful of the faithful, mother of us all?

Therefore she says, utterly astonished by the aforesaid report and by a great abundance of joy: “Who will grant me that you be my brother, suckling at the breasts of my mother?” She calls her beloved her “brother,” and describes him in a sweet description: “suckling,” she says, “at the breasts of my mother.” Whose “mother,” unless the Virgin Mary’s? Therefore she said nothing of a father, because in this brother—so that he might be conceived or born and become a son of our nature or flesh—no man accomplished anything. All that makes him our brother comes from his mother. He sucked his mother’s breasts, but did not flow forth from his father’s stock. This mother is a mother, because this flesh is our flesh; and this faith is your faith, O Mary—our faith.

The greatness of joy cannot be contained within [Col. 0951A] the believing heart as it marvels at its blessedness: that God, the Son of God, has become its brother—its brother, O mother, from you, whose breasts he sucked. It bursts forth and cries: “Who will grant me that you be my brother, suckling at the breasts of my mother?” It adds: “So that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me?”

For she was despised, being barren and deserted, without a husband—that is, without God in this world. She was despised, I say, and was called “the uncircumcision,” as the Apostle says, by that which is called “the circumcision made in the flesh by hands”; and she was alienated from the commonwealth of Israel (Eph. 2). “Therefore I shall find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me,” namely, when I can say that most true saying: “Many are the children of the desolate woman, more than [Col. 0951B] of her who has a husband.”

O brother of the vineyard, O you who suck at the breasts of my mother, what is it to find you outside? What is it to kiss you? To find you outside is to go forth to you outside the camp; for as you suffered outside the gate, so you “became a stranger to your brothers and an alien to the children of your mother” (Ps. 68). To kiss you is to venerate your reproach and intimately to know the mysteries of your godliness. For insofar as we know and love them, we who love you kiss you as lovable.

What fruit, what benefit comes from this finding and this kissing? “I will take hold of you,” she says, “and lead you into my mother’s house and into my mother’s chamber; there you will teach me.” How will this happen? When I have obtained your kisses, when you have revealed your mysteries to me [Col. 0951C], then I, hitherto barren, shall have from you children of renewed youth. By your working, I shall appoint them for myself as male and female readers, male and female singers, priests or bishops, approaching the grace of prophecy and apostleship; and from them I shall establish schools of readers and choirs of singers. I shall employ the trumpets of preachers and the tongues of interpreters, so that they may explain to me the Scriptures which concern you and which until now have lain hidden within one language.

And so, with the battle-line of my camp marshalled, I shall break into “my mother’s house, into my mother’s chamber,” where until now “beasts rest, and dragons or ostriches dwell, and shaggy creatures dance, and screech-owls answer one another” (Isa. 13), while adulterous Jupiter is worshipped [Col. 0951D] and the hosts of the land’s other beings—not gods, but demons. Having driven them all out, I shall bring you in there, so that both in my mother’s house and in my mother’s chamber—that is, both in royal palaces and in temples once belonging to demons—your name may be invoked.

“There you will teach me,” openly and with freedom of speech, according to your custom, as you said: “I have spoken openly to the world, and I have said nothing in secret” (John 18).

---

“And I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the new wine of my pomegranates.” What else, or what greater thing, can I give? This is what he too found to give, who said: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate numbering]). The sense is: first the Lord repaid me good for evil, and then good for [Col. 0952A] good. “What shall I repay him?” Deliberating thus, I came to this, since I cannot do anything greater: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.”

This is what I now say: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine”; that is, I shall offer a sacrifice consecrated and truly holy by the invisible mystery of your Passion. Nor shall I do only this; I shall also give you the new wine “of my pomegranates,” that is, the death—precious in your sight—of your holy martyrs, who in great numbers will arise from me as imitators of your death. This will be your cup; it will not be the blood of brute animals. For concerning this, either you or your Father, God of gods and Lord, has said: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? [Col. 0952B] Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and render…” (Ps. 49), and so forth.

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” O sons or daughters, it is indeed a great and arduous undertaking to bring my brother in this way into my mother’s house and into my mother’s chamber, and consequently we must endure many afflictions; but do not be greatly afraid. He, present everywhere, will console me with a twofold consolation. For “his left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” His left hand—that is, temporal prosperity at times—will support me, lest I fail amid my labours; nor will it allow me to be tempted beyond what I can endure. And his right hand, namely the certain hope of eternal recompense, will gladden and delight me more strongly and more abundantly.

This consolation will already come to me in this age [Col. 0952C]: kings and princes themselves will be given to me for service. But in that right hand, where immortality reigns, I shall behold in eternal vision, in his beauty, the one himself (1 Cor. 10)—my brother, my beloved, King of kings and Lord of lords. And already I desire, by the pursuit of contemplation, to taste beforehand so great a good.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it.” My brother himself knows this: that I meditate, or desire to meditate, only upon the embrace of his right hand. “Do not,” he says, “rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it.” Do not rouse her, I say, in the manner in which Martha wished to rouse her sister Mary. For Mary, sitting at [Col. 0952D] the feet of the beloved, heard the words of his mouth. This was rest. But Martha, who busied herself about much serving (Luke 10), wishing to rouse her, said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her therefore to help me.”

No one should doubt that this saying, “Do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it,” was addressed to all daughters of that kind, who do not know how to discern bodily service, or the active life, from the dignity of contemplation. For she who “has chosen the better part,” whoever applies herself to the Word of God, is the beloved. The others, who “are anxious and troubled about many things,” like that Martha, are daughters.

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” From this verse [Col. 0953A] to the end, the most illustrious song concerns that woman chosen and beloved from among the gentiles. Her election is the grace of the brother; it is the fruit or effect of evangelical preaching, from the time when that began to happen, O most beloved woman of the beloved, which you said: “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages.”

The election from among the Jews—which came through the Gospel in small number—marvels at this fruit alone of your going forth, and says: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” From the wilderness—that is, from the field and the villages—to which you, O beloved and beloved woman, desired to go forth and to remain according to the aforesaid counsel.

“Who is this?” Where was she? Where was she hidden? A wondrous thing. For us she did not exist; she was nowhere. Yet she existed for him; she was in him, of whom it has been truly said [Col. 0953B]: “What was made, in him was life” (John 17 [citation as printed]), and of whom another of his friends says: “He calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4).

What is she like, then; how does she come up? “Abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved.” Rightly should we marvel at how many and what kinds of delights she abounds in: the delights of graces, “which are manifested for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12), namely the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healings, workings of miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of utterances.

But how, or for what purpose, is she leaning upon her beloved? Assuredly, so that she may not fear human fear, and so that she may not fail in the tribulations which have found her or will find her: the tribulations and persecutions of visible and invisible enemies [Col. 0953C]—pagans, Jews, heretics, and evil spirits. For how could she endure among all these things unless she leaned upon her beloved? Should she lean upon herself or upon anyone else? Then certainly she would fall; she could not stand. But now she says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation: whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid? Though camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear. Though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope” (Ps. 26). To say and do this is assuredly to lean upon the beloved.

How did this happen? How did she come up in such a manner and in this condition? “Under the apple tree I roused you; there [Col. 0953D] your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated.” Do you, the election from among the Jews, marvel as though you did not know? Do you not know the reason why this woman had to come up in such a condition and manner? I tell you the reason: your mother, she who bore you, forsook me; she denied me, her husband and her king. Therefore I took another wife, having given her a bill of divorce; and she is the one who comes up in this way.

Where did this happen? Under the apple tree, where I roused you; beneath the wood of the cross, where I redeemed you. I therefore said “under the apple tree,” that is, beneath the tree bringing forth its fruits, because the wood of the cross was not a barren tree but brought forth the fruits of life and salvation. There I roused you; but there your mother, the Synagogue—she who bore you, the Jewish people—was corrupted, saying, “We have no king but Caesar”; there she was violated, crying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (John 19; Matt. 27).

Therefore [Col. 0954A], she having been repudiated, this woman came up in such a manner; and, as one among you says: “Blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the gentiles enters in, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11).

Now hear what this woman, at whom you marvel, says—this strong woman, of whom it is truly said: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoils” (Prov. 31). “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, because love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it. If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing [Col. 0954B].”

What, I ask, does this strong woman, as has now been said, request except that the heart of her husband may trust in her? For what does it mean to say, “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,” except: “Let your heart trust in me; let your arm be strengthened by my assistance”? And, O beloved, what in this passage are your heart [p. 424] and your arm, except the Scriptures of truth, which were written according to your heart, and the remembrance of your wonders, from which it is known how great and how mighty your arm is? Set me as a seal upon that heart of yours; set me as a seal upon that arm of yours.

For what reason? Surely because of the threefold madness that barks against me: Jewish, pagan, and heretical madness. I am ready, prepared [Col. 0954C], and devoted, in return, strongly to defend that heart of yours and protect that arm of yours, as an imperial seal, as a trustworthy testimony, with wondrous strength and a wondrous hardness which no one can break. I call my strength love; I call my hardness jealousy. Why so? Because “love is strong as death; jealousy hard as hell.” What does this mean except, as if it were said: Love has great zeal; jealousy has intolerable wrath.

Attend, friends, to what is said; observe carefully what is being done and what has been done up to this point, ever since this strong woman came up from the wilderness, abounding in delights and leaning upon her beloved—the woman who asks this: that the heart of her husband may trust in her.

[Col. 0954D] Who has ever been able to endure the zeal of love which she has for the heart of her beloved, the wrath of jealousy which she has toward the arm of her beloved? Like death, like hell, she spares no one and is merciless to all who think wrongly concerning the Scriptures of truth, which are written according to the heart of her husband, her beloved; or who preach wrongly concerning the arm of strength by which the omnipotence of her husband, her beloved, wrought the salvation of humankind. Although she is most compassionate in remitting sins, does she not nevertheless put to death only those who speak outside or against the Word of truth, and consign their souls to hell? Can she tolerate anything contrary to the heart of her beloved—that is, to the Scripture of truth? She cannot tolerate it. Those who do this she casts out and slays with the sword of anathema.

[Col. 0935A] We do not speak without experience. No soul possessing the spirit of love is more offended by anything, or more grievously provoked by any evil, than when it hears something concerning the Scriptures contrary to the meaning of this friend’s heart, contrary to the honour of this beloved arm. However gentle its nature may be, it immediately becomes unyielding in this matter; and to adversaries its impulse appears like the movement of death, its anger like the wrath of hell. This is evident from Moses, who, though he was the meekest of all people dwelling on earth, when the cause demanded it became harsh like death, severe like hell, so that he said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join himself to me” (Num. XII; Exod. XXXII); and by his most stern command each slew brother, friend, and neighbour, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day.

[Col. 0955B] He indeed proved this with a material sword, as did many others after him, such as Elijah and mighty David: for truly love is strong as death, and jealousy is truly hard as hell. But this most beloved woman rages with the spiritual sword on behalf of the heart and arm of her beloved, standing firm like an inviolable seal. For she has neither command nor consent from her beloved for the material sword, since she heard him saying, “Put your sword back into its place; it is enough; let them go thus far” (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII).

“Her lamps,” he says, “are lamps of fire and flames.” Whose lamps? Those of love or jealousy. The lamps of love are lamps of fire; the lamps of jealousy are lamps of flames. As fire, once stirred, produces flame, so love, [Col. 0955C] when it perceives something not according to the heart of this husband, not according to the meaning of this beloved, brings forth jealousy—at once shining and burning, illuminating friends and burning enemies.

What if the enemies are strong? What if they have crowds of peoples, and even the swords of kings and emperors, as they once had? Nevertheless, let the heart of her husband trust in her. For love will nevertheless be strong as death and jealousy hard as hell; indeed, then these lamps will burn and shine all the more—lamps of fire and flames. Hence he says: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it.” We have heard and seen many waters, that is, overflowing persecutions by the populace, [Col. 0955D] and rivers, namely persecutions by powerful rulers. Although they poured in violently, they could not extinguish or overwhelm love, nor restrain her jealousy enough to make her keep silence concerning even one word of the most faithful doctrine—for example, that which is called ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance.”

Every loss, and death itself, which heretics could inflict, was counted as nothing by this beloved woman. This is what he says: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, she would despise it as though it were nothing.” Her love for the Word is so great that, compared with such a pearl as she has retained within, she despises as nothing whatever could be taken away outwardly. “Behold, you have seen and heard a strong woman.”

She does not trust that such strength resides in herself, but in him who alone is the true strength of the strong; as you saw her ascending, leaning upon me, her beloved. This strength, I say, is not from herself but from our providence, according to the merciful purpose of our care which we had for her, as the following words show: “Our little sister has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken with? If she is a wall, let us build upon her battlements of silver; if she is a door, let us fasten it with boards of cedar.”

[Col. 0956A] The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit held such counsel concerning her in a great matter, a great undertaking (Matt. X), because the time or condition of her affairs was and is such that, scarcely born and scarcely standing on her own feet, she was already to be addressed and led before kings and governors, to give an account of our faith and of the profoundest mysteries of our works, against Jews who gloried in the Law, against philosophers swollen with their wisdom and eloquence, amid the swords of judges and a thousand kinds of death. This is surely marvellous to those who know how to marvel at the matter as it deserves.

Therefore, after taking counsel, we said: “Our little sister has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken with?” For indeed, on the day when she first had to be addressed—when, under Nero and the other persecutors, a legal charge was first brought against her concerning the faith which she embraced—she was small in number and little in understanding, that is, simple; she did not possess breasts, namely the Law and the Prophets. Therefore we said: “If she is a wall, [Col. 0956B] let us build upon her battlements of silver; if she is a door, let us fasten it with boards of cedar.”

In cities or houses, a wall is one thing and a door another. Similarly, in this beloved woman, in this body which is the Church, one person is, as it were, a wall, another, as it were, a door. This may be more clearly distinguished from the condition of that time when this beloved woman first had to be addressed, as has already been said. One person was strong enough to endure torments or reproaches; he was indeed a wall, in accordance with the saying: “I, the Lord, have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall; they shall fight against you, and shall not prevail, because I am with you.” Another was weaker in this respect [Col. 0956C] and perhaps, fleeing persecution, wished to hide; yet he possessed some grace—for example, the grace of priestly office and the knowledge of instructing the unlearned and baptizing believers. He was surely a door, because just as one enters a city or house through a door, so believers are incorporated into the Church through such ministry.

Therefore, “if she is a wall,” he says, “let us build upon her battlements of silver”: that is, if she can worthily stand or persevere for the faith in the struggle of contest, let us supply her with every necessary testimony of truth, so that she may know how to answer no less than if she had read the Law or the Prophets, according to the saying: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not premeditate how you are to answer; for I shall give you a mouth and wisdom [Col. 0957A] which none of your adversaries shall be able to answer or contradict” (Matt. X). Again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

And was it not so done? If you carefully consider the confessions and answers of the martyrs—at least in those records faithfully and simply written without the embellishment of human ingenuity, where their answers were recorded exactly as they were spoken—are not their answers to us battlements, and not merely ordinary battlements, but battlements of silver? For they are chaste and purified, and possess much brilliance and splendour, according to the saying: “The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. XII).

“If she is a door, let us fasten it with boards of cedar”: that is, let us make him who has not such great strength or endurance as to be able to bear the torments of suffering, but whose office or devotion it is faithfully to make a way or entrance for those wishing to enter the kingdom of God by baptizing or catechizing them with the Word of God, [Col. 0957B] a memory incorruptible and sweet, after the likeness of cedar, fragrant and decay-resistant wood; according to that Davidic saying: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. XCI). For there are many gifts of grace which may avail and suffice for those who, even if they desire it, do not attain the palm of martyrdom.

What does she say to these things? “I am a wall, and my breasts are a tower, since I became in his sight as one finding peace.” The meaning is: At first, when I was already to be addressed and was beginning to answer concerning our faith according to your love, I was little, as you say, my beloved, and had no breasts. But now I am a wall, and I have breasts—not ordinary ones, but like a tower. For as time advanced, my writers came, my interpreters were strengthened, and they translated the Law and Prophets, and the whole Old and New Testament together, from the single treasury of the Hebrew language into various languages, especially Greek and Latin. And behold, I have been strongly furnished with spirit and letter, possessing also among my own children born to me eloquent teachers and interpreters of both Testaments.

[Col. 0957C] Therefore I said: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” Yet this is not from myself, but from the grace of my beloved. Therefore I added this also: “Since I became in his sight as one finding peace,” that is, since I received through faith the remission of sins. For from the time when I believed, I found peace for his sake and was reconciled to God through the death of my beloved, his Son. And, advancing and growing from that point, I have also received this grace, that nothing is lacking to me from the Scriptures of either Testament. “Behold, my breasts are like a tower,” because pagans, Jews, and heretics can do nothing against them.

“There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One in her who has peoples. He entrusted it to keepers. A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” This beloved woman says this concerning herself to grace and glory; and the beloved immediately replies: “My vineyard is before me. Your thousand, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who keep its fruits.”

[Col. 0957D] With regard to the case of this beloved woman who says this, it is highly relevant to recall and explain in what the vineyard of her beloved was planted—namely, whether in faith or in works. Concerning this vineyard, both the Law and the Prophets speak much in his Gospel. Therefore she now says: “There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One in her who has peoples.” Who is this “she who has peoples”? Faith or the Law? Certainly not the Law, but faith. The Lord’s vineyard was planted in faith, not in the Law, as the Apostle says: “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed—that he should be heir of the world—was not through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV). And shortly afterward: “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all Abraham’s seed—not only for the one who is of the Law, but also for the one who is of the faith [Col. 0958A] of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have made you the father of many nations before God, whom you believed’” (ibid.). Again, concerning the same man: “Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: ‘So shall your seed be as the stars of heaven’; and he did not become weak in faith” (ibid.), and so forth.

Therefore faith is she who has peoples, because through faith Abraham became father of peoples, father of many nations. What then, O my jealous rival, O Synagogue or carnal circumcision, do you boast against me, as if you alone were the Lord’s vineyard by works of the Law? Before the Law the Lord’s vineyard was planted in faith, and you have turned aside into perversity; but that planting remains. “I,” says the planter himself, “planted you as a chosen vine, wholly true seed. How then have you turned into a degenerate, foreign vine?” (Jer. II).

“What then is the Law?” says the Apostle. “It was added because of transgressions” (Gal. III). Hence another prophet also says: “A vineyard was made for the Beloved on a horn, the son of oil, and he fenced it in” (Isa. V), and so forth. “Made upon a horn”—that is, it was planted in faith, because the firmness of faith is signified by the horn; concerning which the Apostle says: “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all Abraham’s seed” (Rom. IV). “He fenced it in”: what else is this but the fact that the Law was added because of transgressions? (Gal. III.)

[Col. 0958C] Thus no doubt remains that the vineyard was made or planted for the Peaceful One—that is, for the beloved, “for he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II)—not in the Law, but in faith. Consequently, this beloved woman, namely the Church from the nations, is not defended by some novel argument when she is justified by faith apart from works of the Law.

“He entrusted it to keepers,” that is, to patriarchs, leaders, judges, priests, prophets, and kings. And, as Isaiah says, “He also built a tower and a winepress”—that is, the temple and altar—“in its midst; and he expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isa. V). Thus “the foreign vine turned aside into perversity” (ibid.).

The subsequent words—“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit; my vineyard is before me; your thousand, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who keep its fruits”—are better understood in contrast to that vineyard “which turned aside into perversity.” “I purchased her for myself,” says the Lord in Hosea, [Col. 0959A] “for fifteen silver pieces, and a cor of barley, and half a cor of barley; and I said to her: ‘For many days you shall wait for me; you shall not commit fornication, nor belong to a man; and I too shall wait for you’” (Hos. III), and so forth.

A most beautiful mystery is hidden in these numbers: here in the twelve hundred silver pieces; there in fifteen silver pieces, a cor of barley, and half a cor of barley. The sum of this mystery is that this woman is both a virgin and joined to a husband, whereas that other woman is neither a virgin nor joined to a husband. For the thousandfold unity signifies her virginity, while the two hundred signifies her union or marriage. Mathematicians or abacists know better what is meant and why unity is called virgin: in their treatises they have the principle that, multiplied by itself, it creates nothing, because once one is one—a property belonging to no other number. For other numbers, multiplied by themselves, produce others: twice two makes four, and three times three, nine.

[Col. 0959B] Further, the number two hundred signifies this woman’s marriage, and this is most blessed because this beloved woman, who is from faith, is always joined to her husband and always remains a virgin. Conversely, the fact that the other woman’s price remained neither in unity nor reached duality mystically signifies both her widowhood and her defilement, when it is said: “I purchased her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, and a cor of barley and half a cor of barley” (ibid.). If you consider the silver pieces, they are neither ten, which would be decimal unity, nor twenty, which would be decimal duality, but fifteen—a number greater than unity and less than duality. Likewise, there is neither merely one cor of barley nor two cors, but a cor and a half of barley: greater than the monad, less than duality.

[Col. 0959C] Thus for her also this is most unhappy: she is neither a virgin nor has a husband. Now let us briefly return to the sequence of this text: “There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One in her who has peoples,” that is, every planting that the truly Peaceful Beloved planted—he through whom “we were reconciled to God” (Rom. V)—was planted in Abraham’s faith, through which he inherited all peoples. “He entrusted it to keepers”: he committed it to governors. “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit”: that is, every faithful and virtuous worker, skilled in the Scriptures and eloquent in speech, expends all the resources of faithful discourse in preaching, that he may receive in due time something of its fruit.

All his silver pieces are a thousand—that is, all his words accord in one faith, since, as was said above, this number is a thousandfold unity, as mathematicians know well. To this the Beloved replies: “My vineyard is before me.” The sense is: I have not changed; where I planted, there I seek; and I have my vineyard—not in the Law, but in faith. For if “those who are of the Law” (Rom. IV) are heirs, faith is emptied and the promise abolished; and this would involve changeableness, which cannot belong to God.

[Col. 0959D] Whoever you are who spend in this vineyard the thousand silver pieces already mentioned, “your thousand, O Peaceful One,” are for you those who make or obtain peace—that is, remission of sins—“and two hundred [Col. 0960A] for those who keep its fruits,” namely, so that in virginal marriage, in the heavenly nuptials signified by the two hundred, they may eternally enjoy the Beloved and his beloved together.

“You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen: make me hear your voice.” Who says this is evident. The Beloved says to the beloved woman, “You who dwell in the gardens.” In what gardens does the beloved woman dwell except in the loveliness of the Scriptures, in the delight of virtues beautifully flowering, sweet-smelling, and ever green? “Make me hear your voice,” he says. How? Certainly as it is written: “You shall tell your son on that day, saying: ‘This is what the Lord did for me. For with a strong hand he led me out of Egypt. And it shall be as a sign on your hand and as a memorial before my [your] eyes, and that the Law of the Lord may always be in your mouth’” (Exod. XIII; Deut. VI).

For I truly led you out of Egypt, from the darkness of this world, from the slavery of sin, into that land flowing with milk and honey, so that you might dwell in these gardens, in all the mysteries of the Scriptures, where there are truly springs and streams of milk and honey flowing from the Spirit of God and from Jesus Christ, your beloved, who is man. Therefore, as I said, “make me hear your voice,” so that the Law of the Lord may “always be in your mouth”: now in preaching, now in prayer, now in psalmody. For in these ways I gladly hear your voice. And so that you may do this still more wisely and diligently, behold, I tell you: “Friends listen”—even those whom you do not see with bodily eyes, namely the holy angels, according to the saying: “In the sight of angels I shall sing psalms to you” [Col. 0960B] (Ps. CXXXVII).

What, finally, do you say, O beloved woman? “Flee, my beloved; make yourself like a gazelle or a young stag upon mountains of spices.” O voice worthy to be heard by the Beloved, a voice from a faithful heart and humble mind! For this is what every faithful and wise soul is accustomed to say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII); I am not worthy that you should show in me some frequent miracle of your presence or visitation.

“Flee, my beloved,” I say. I do not seek glory in the present life, but desire grace; I do not seek the splendour of miracles, but long for the remission of sins. “Flee, my beloved,” I say, and perform such leaps, like the leaps of a gazelle or a young stag, [Col. 0960C] not upon me but “upon the mountains of spices,” upon the exalted merits of saints and the perfect. Those who are holy and perfect, and have a present cause making miracles necessary, have reason to speak otherwise. For example, the prophet Elisha, conscious of his merits and having a present cause for which miracles were necessary, said to Elijah: “I ask that your spirit may become twofold in me” (IV Kings II). And so it happened: he performed twice as many miracles as Elijah, in order to recall some of the people from the impiety of Jezebel and from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin.

But in this too, “Flee, my beloved,” so that you may always remain incomprehensible. For this must be granted to your majesty: that you cannot be comprehended and are ever desired and desirable, while we remain ignorant, as long as we are in this body, “how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX). Flee, cautious and provident toward us, lest while we live we should ever suppose that we have comprehended you; yet we follow, that we may comprehend.

Mountains—mountains of spices—behold, upon you the Beloved is “made like a gazelle or a young stag.” But let one of the friends, a very wise man, say to someone—if he also knew how to console one afflicted or lawfully struck: “Call, then, if there is one who will answer you, and turn to one of the saints.” O holy mountains, we recognize the cause of each and all of us in that one man to whom this was said; and therefore we receive with discernment, and desire to follow, the counsel given to him without discrimination.

[Col. 0961B] For Job—whose name means “suffering”—both in that Satan sought him in order to test him (Job I), and in that, when tested, he was found faithful, prefigured in himself the sufferings and groanings, and the consolations that followed, of all “who desire to live piously in Christ and suffer persecution” (II Tim. III). He is recognized in his answers by all and only those who, for the cause of piety, are afflicted either outwardly and visibly or inwardly and invisibly by invisible enemies.

To which one of you, then, shall we turn? In which of you all shall we more swiftly overtake and apprehend the fleeing Beloved? O Blessed Mary, mountain of mountains, virgin of virgins, holy one of holy ones: indeed, we turn to all the mountains of spices and call upon them to answer us; and this is what each of us says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me” (Ps. CXX). But especially we turn to you; above all others we lift our eyes to you; above all we sigh for your help. By the mystery of your womb, [Col. 0962B] and by the sword which “pierced through your soul” (Luke XX), obtain for us that we may see the very illumination of the eternal mountains: namely, the Beloved and the Beloved from the Beloved, and together the love of both—that is, God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one living and true God, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0961] End of the seventh and final book on the Song of Songs.

[Col. 0961]

COMMENTARY OF RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON SAINT JOB.

PROLOGUE.

427 Some wrongly suppose that blessed Job was of the race of Esau, as Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0961] Jerome, *On Hebrew Traditions in Genesis*], because it is written at the beginning of the book: “There was a man in the land of Uz.” For Uz was the firstborn of Nahor, as it is written in Genesis: “It was reported to Abraham that Milcah also had borne sons to Nahor: Uz the firstborn, and Buz his brother.” Philo also writes [Note: [Col. 0961] *On Antiquities*] that he was the husband of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter.

Moreover, from the line of Buz, the second son of Nahor, as was stated, came that diviner Balaam, according to Hebrew tradition. In this book he is called Elihu the Buzite (in the Vulgate, *Eliu*), at first a holy man and prophet of God, but afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, while wishing to curse Israel, called by the title “diviner.” Nor is it remarkable that he lived until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, namely one hundred and forty years after Joseph’s death, since Job himself may have lived at the same time. For when Job was struck, he and his friends were older men, as the same Elihu testifies when he says: “I am young in years, but you are more ancient,” and so forth.

For let us suppose that he was struck precisely at the time when Joseph died, in Joseph’s one hundred and tenth year. Certainly, when Job was struck, he was one hundred and thirty-six years old; for after his affliction he lived one hundred and forty years, and this Scripture itself reports that he finally died at the age of two hundred and seventy-six. Nothing, therefore, inconsistent or contradictory follows from the view that blessed Job was, according to Philo, Dinah’s husband and that Elihu, who speaks against him, was Balaam himself. At the same time, it should be known that Job himself may have written this book; yet this Scripture should not be thought older than the Mosaic Law. For, although Job lived more than twice as many years as Moses—Moses lived one hundred and twenty years, while Job, as stated, lived two hundred and seventy-six—he could plainly have been earlier in age but later in death than Moses.

Among the Hebrews, this book is almost entirely—namely, from the passage, “Let the day perish on which I was born,” to the words, “And I repent in ashes and dust”—composed in hexameter verses, with dactyl and spondee in movement. Yet because of the character of the language it frequently admits other feet also: not feet of the same syllables, but of the same temporal quantities. At times the rhythm itself proceeds sweetly and melodiously in numbers free from metrical law, a fact understood more by metrists than by the ordinary reader.

It is chiefly subject to Ethics, that is, moral doctrine, although it also often treats physics and contains much concerning theory, which in sacred literature is taken as Logic; these are the three parts of philosophy. Its purpose, moreover, is this. The holy man, having experienced in himself that many righteous people in this world suffer as though they had committed wicked deeds, just as, conversely, many unjust people fare as though they had performed good deeds—and desiring, indeed God desiring, he who permitted him to be tested, to restrain the excessively rash judgments of people, who are accustomed to assess a person’s merits from prosperity or adversity—issued this Scripture, most useful for all citizens of heaven exiled in this world. By it they might be instructed never to judge a person’s sin from the magnitude of the scourge, since this is unjust, as even one of the pagans says [Note: [Col. 0963] Ovid, *Epistle of Phyllis to Demophoon*]:

> I pray that whoever thinks deeds must be approved by their outcome  
> may be denied success.

Led by this rashness, Job’s friends did not speak rightly before the Lord. Therefore, intending to recount the evils that he suffered, while first setting forth the merits of his goodness, praised also by the Lord’s testimony, he begins thus: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.”

COMMENTARY ON JOB.

[Col. 0963]

428 CHAPTER I.

[Col. 0963A]

VERSE 1.—“There was a man in the land of Uz.” The dwelling-place of the holy man is specified, namely the land of Uz, which is a land of Gentiles, so that this may contribute to his praise: in accordance with the Bridegroom’s proclamation, “A lily among thorns” (Song II), he was good among evil people. Since he was uniquely to contend with the devil, as if before the spectacle of an arena, the sacred text of the History describes the components of this strong athlete—namely, the four principal virtues of the mind—saying: “That man was simple,” and the rest. For in being called “simple,” prudence also must be understood, since the simplicity of the saints is not without prudence, according to Truth’s command: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X).

Thus, as has been said, prudence is signified when he is called simple; courage when he is called upright; justice when he is called fearing God; and temperance when he is called turning away from evil. After these interior goods, exterior ones are appropriately added.

VERSE 2.—“And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.” It is as though he said: And, what is great, he possessed the virtues mentioned above amid the fruitfulness of offspring. For the fruitfulness of children often draws a parent’s heart toward avarice. Further, what follows also increases this praise.

VERSE 3.—“And his possession was seven thousand sheep.” It enhances his praise that you should consider how great the holiness was of a man whom neither affection for so many heirs inclined toward avarice, and who, though so occupied, found leisure for such constant service of God. It is evident that he possessed all these things without attachment, because he lost them without grief. And that man—so righteous—was great, that is, rich, among all the people of the East. Who does not know that they are exceedingly wealthy? It is as though it were plainly said: He was richer than the rich. And this man—that is, such a great man—was present to his sons in concern even when absent in body.

VERSE 4.—“His sons”—remarkably harmonious amid great wealth—“went and made,” that is, were accustomed to go and make, [Col. 0964A] “a feast,” which can scarcely be held without fault, “in their houses,” namely in all their own houses, omitting none through equal affection. Each one, I say, “made a feast” for his other brothers “on his own day,” that is, on the day of the week assigned to him in the order of age. “And sending”—that is, extending honour to the inferior sex—“they called their three sisters,” that is, in undivided love, “so that they might eat and drink with them.” All this is praise of their father’s instruction.

VERS. 5.—“And when the days of the feast had passed in a circle,” that is, had run their course, “Job sent,” taking care for their salvation, “and sanctified them,” namely through the purification of sacrifices. This is what follows: “Rising early in the morning [Col. 0964B], he offered burnt offerings for each one,” namely seven burnt offerings, since there were seven sons. Note that he who is said to offer sacrifices on the eighth day is declared to have served the Lord, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, in hope of the resurrection that will be celebrated in the eighth age of the world. “He offered,” I say, “burnt offerings. For he said: Lest perhaps”—that is, not affirming, but doubting out of concern—“lest perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed,” that is, by antiphrasis, cursed, “God in their hearts.” For we must not rashly judge the hearts of others. Note this: he had taught that they were perfect in deed and word, yet he feared for them concerning thought alone, saying, “in their hearts.” “Thus,” that is, so holily and so carefully, “Job did all [Col. 0964C] the days,” that is, perseveringly.

Allegorically. “A man named Job,” which is interpreted “sorrowing,” namely our Lord, who “himself bore our sorrows” (Isa. LIII), “was”—indeed, is—that is, dwells through faith “in the land of Hus,” that is, in the heart of a people ruled by Counsel. For Hus is interpreted “counsellor.” And the Wisdom of God, namely Christ, says: “I dwell in counsel, and am present among learned thoughts” (Prov. VIII).

“And that man was simple and upright,” that is, meek and just, “and fearing God,” as it is written: “And the Spirit [Col. 0965A] of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI); “and departing from evil,” namely because “he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth” (I Pet. II).

“And there were born to him seven sons,” that is, apostles to be filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit; “and three daughters,” that is, weaker peoples, yet established in faith in the Trinity. “And his possession was seven thousand sheep,” that is, the innocence of the perfect, coming from the pastures of the Law to the grace of perfection. “And three thousand camels,” that is, the faith of Gentiles believing in the Trinity, who, twisted in their habits and burdened with crimes, came away from the worship of idols; or the peoples of the Samaritans, who, like camels, as it were chew the cud but do not divide the hoof, because they receive the Law in part and despise it in part, [Col. 0965B] since they do not know the faith of the resurrection. “Also five hundred yokes of oxen and five hundred she-asses.” This number is completed by multiplying fifty tenfold. Fifty signifies the rest of the Jubilee, while ten expresses the sum of perfection. By oxen, moreover, Judaism is here represented; by she-asses, the folly of the Gentiles. Thus the same thing that was signified above by the sheep and camels is also signified by the oxen and she-asses: namely, that Judaism and the Gentiles are gathered to Christ for possession in eternal and perfect rest, as five hundred yokes of oxen and five hundred she-asses. And because through the faith of the oxen those first foolish in the world, and later even the cunning, were gathered, it is fitting that, after the multitude of animals has first been described, there is added at the end, “and a very great household.”

And that [Col. 0965C] man—of whom it was said, “Behold, the man whose name is the East” (Zech. VI)—was great among all the Easterners, that is, among all saints established in faith in that same East. For adoption makes the other saints Easterners, whereas the nature of his divinity exalts him as the true East. “And his sons,” that is, his holy apostles, his preachers, “went through the houses,” that is, through different regions, “and made a feast,” that is, ministered to their hearers the banquets of virtues, “each on his own day,” that is, according to his own understanding. “And when the days of the feast had passed in a circle,” that is, when the ministry of preaching had been completed, sending the Holy Spirit, “he sanctified them,” because our Redeemer prayed to the Father for the apostles who were to preach. For he said: “Lest perhaps my sons,” that is, my preachers, “have sinned and blessed,” that is, cursed, “God in their hearts.” For to curse God is to claim for oneself glory from his gift. “Thus Job did all days,” because without interruption the Redeemer offers a burnt offering for us, when he displays to the Father his Incarnation on our behalf.

Morally: “A man,” namely each of the elect acting manfully, “named Job,” that is, sorrowing, namely over present things and hastening toward eternal things, “was”—indeed, is—“in the land of Hus,” that is, he inhabits a mind that gives counsel and does all things with counsel. “And that man was simple,” etc. This does not change from the way in which it was explained above [Col. 0966A] in the historical sense. “And there were born to him,” namely through the conception of good thought, “seven sons,” that is, the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit: “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isa. XI), and so forth. For although these graces rested in their fullness in Christ alone, nevertheless every elect person participates in them according to his measure. “And three daughters,” namely faith, hope, and love; whatever he does manfully is inwardly adorned by their beauty. The sum of perfection is fulfilled, as it were, in the number ten through the seven sons and these three daughters.

“And his possession was,” namely in the pastures of truth, “seven thousand sheep,” that is, his thoughts, harmless in perfect purity of heart. For in “seven thousand” perfection is signified; in the name “sheep,” purity or innocence. “And three thousand camels,” that is, likewise thoughts which, under knowledge of the Trinity, willingly bend themselves in the desire for humility. For the camel voluntarily offers its back for carrying burdens. Or they are understood from the example of the Lord, of whom it was said: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. XXIII). Or certainly they are those who possess something of the world and something of God: they do not indeed wholly divide themselves from every earthly work, but nevertheless chew the cud by administering temporal things well. “Also five hundred yokes of oxen,” that is, concordant virtues under Christ’s yoke, ploughing up the hardness of the mind; “and five hundred she-asses,” namely wanton impulses restrained by governing reason. “Five hundred,” I say, that is, desiring, as was said above, the perfect rest of eternal peace. “And a very great [Col. 0966C] household,” that is, innumerable thoughts which, like little maidservants, chatter noisily when their mistress Reason is absent, neglect their work, but fall silent when she returns and resume their proper work.

“And that man was”—indeed, is—“great,” that is, a companion in contemplation, “among all the Easterners,” that is, surpassing minds among the heavenly spirits, cleaving to the Eastern, that is, divine, light, and saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). “And his sons,” namely those mentioned above, go through the houses “and make a feast,” that is, each virtue according to its own manner feeds the mind, “each on his own day,” that is, each virtue in its own illumination. “And, sending, they invite their three sisters,” that is, faith, hope, and love, “that they may eat [Col. 0966D] and drink with them,” that is, that they may rejoice in every good work of each virtue.

And because good works themselves sometimes defile us with a slight measure of pride, it is fittingly added: “And when the days of the feast had passed in a circle,” that is, when the meaning or effect of each virtue has been completed, “Job sent and sanctified them,” because the wise person endeavours to cleanse, by strict reconsideration, everything that has been done. “Rising early in the morning,” that is, abandoning the night of humanity—“early,” I say, that is, in the light of compunction—“he offers a burnt offering for each son,” that is, for each virtue he sacrifices the victim of devout prayer. For he says: “Lest perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts,” that is, lest perhaps my virtues, while outwardly doing good, have secretly devised evil, and, arrogating to themselves what they are, have cursed God.

Jeremiah aptly and subtly suggests this through the men who came to offer gifts to God and were slain in the midst of the city by Ishmael (Jer. XLI). For minds devoted to divine works, unless they guard themselves with great vigilance, lose the life of their treasure, when the enemy steals upon them as they carry the offering of devotion along the very path. Ten men redeemed themselves so that they should not be killed; this is hope, hidden in the field of repentance, which perfectly cleanses every virtue through the sacrifices mentioned above. “Thus Job did,” that is, thus does this sorrowing man, “all days,” because he runs swiftly in a good work to no purpose if, before reaching the goal—[Col. 0967A] that is, the prize of life—he falls away from his purpose.

Behold, as though a mirror of our mind were set before our eyes when the temptation of such a man is described. In it the devil presents this contest, having not Job himself but God as the object of his attack, in the following order.

VERS. 6.—“Now on a certain day.” First it should be noted that the temptation of the righteous man, by which he is led to victory, is said to have begun by day. By contrast, the soul of the rich man in the Gospel is required at night (Luke XII), and Solomon received wisdom at night, though he was not to persevere (III Kings III). “Therefore on a certain day, when the sons of God came,” namely the elect angels, whom Paul calls ministering spirits (Heb. II), when, I say, these “sons of God,” who are sent to us, “came,” namely by a movement of spirit, “and stood before the Lord,” from whom they depart by no turning away of mind, “Satan also was present among them.” He was present, I say, so as to be seen, not to see; among them, that is, unable to conceal himself from him who sees all things, just as a blind man does not see the sun, yet is flooded by the sun’s rays.

VERS. 7.—“To whom,” namely not to the elect angels but to Satan, whom he does not know—that is, whom he rejects—“the Lord said: Whence do you come?” For it is fitting that he should, as though not knowing, inquire into the paths of one whom he condemns in judgment. God’s saying, “Whence do you come?” is his rebuking the paths of Satan’s malice. “Satan answered”—whose answer, of course, is that he cannot conceal anything from almighty majesty—“I have gone around the earth and walked [Col. 0967D] through it.” Aptly: because he despised to stand at rest on heaven’s summit, he therefore does not fly over the earth but walks it, burdened by the weight of sin, labouring and anxious, and circles in the orbit of toil, according to the saying: “The wicked walk round about” (Ps. XI).

VERS. 8.—“And the Lord said: Have you considered my servant Job?” Understand, what kind of man he is, and have you observed “that there is none like him upon earth?” God’s saying this is his making his elect such persons by justifying them that the apostate angel may envy them. “A simple man,” etc. This has already been said above.

VERS. 9–10.—“Does Job,” who has received so many good things upon earth, “fear God for nothing,” that is, gratuitously? Does he behave innocently? This is the devil’s speech: out of envy he seeks cracks through which to condemn, and, as it were, sets a worm at the root of a flourishing tree.

VERS. 11.—“But stretch out”—understand, toward me—“your hand,” that is, your power, namely leave to strike; “and touch,” that is, permit me to touch, “all that he possesses.” It is as though he said: Withdraw everything you have given; “unless he blesses you to your face,” that is, unless, by cursing, he despises your grace and favour. This is the devil’s speech: to pant with the heat of malice for the affliction of the good.

VERS. 12.—“Behold”—understand, I release you to the course of your malice—“all that he has,” that is, all his substance and his children, “are in your hand,” that is, in your power; “only”—understand, this I forbid—“do not stretch out your hand against him,” that is, against his body. It is as though he said: I do not release you as an enemy in such a way that I strike my citizen from every side. “And Satan went out,” that is, was released, “from the face of the Lord,” that is, from the bonds of discipline, because the will that had long been restrained proceeded to action.

VERS. 13.—“Now when”—understand, while he sought a time suitable for temptation—“on a certain day his sons and daughters were eating and drinking in the house of their first-born brother,” this occurred through God’s ordering and disclosing it to us, because the joy of satiety foretells tribulation.

VERS. 14–19.—“A messenger came to Job and said: The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses,” etc. These and the other words of the messengers require no explanation for the present in the historical [Col. 0968C] sense, except that, through the cunning impulse of the tempter, the losses are reported as both numerous and sudden: while this or that messenger was still speaking, another arrived. And when one says, “the oxen were ploughing,” the recollection of the fruit of their work makes the cause of grief increase. Another says, “The fire of God fell from heaven”—the “fire,” I say, “of God”—as though to say: You endure the punishment of him whom you sought to appease by so many sacrifices.

VERS. 20.—“Then,” that is, at last, when his children had been lost, “Job arose and tore his garments,” which was a sign of great grief; “and, having shaved his head,” because he had kept his hair for adornment during a time of tranquillity, “he fell upon [Col. 0968D] the ground and worshipped,” thus keeping the two commandments of love. He fell, expressing in his grief love for his neighbours; and he worshipped, not abandoning love for God. He carefully considered what kind of man he had come here as—that is, in what condition he had been born.

VERS. 21.—“Naked,” he says, that is, possessing nothing, “I came forth from my mother’s womb,” calling the earth, which bore us all, his mother. For he continues: “Naked shall I return there,” namely, when I am buried dead. Yet, seeking consolation more from the justice of the Creator, he says: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away.” “The Lord,” I say, not the devil, “has taken away.” Thus, in taking away, he who gave received what was his; he did not take away what was mine. And directing the inclination of his will toward God, to whom nothing but what is just is pleasing, he says: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done.” And he concludes all that he thinks right with blessing, sounding forth a hymn of glory: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

VERS. 22.—“In all these things Job did not sin with his lips,” that is, with his inward lips, “nor did he speak any foolish thing outwardly with his mouth against God.” Allegorically. All the days on which, as stated above, our Redeemer unceasingly offers for us the burnt offering of his body and blood are one day: the day of revealed wisdom, the day of salvation, of which the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). And the Psalmist says: “Today, if you hear his voice” (Ps. XCIV). Of this day it is now said: “Now on a certain day, when the sons of God,” namely those who had been scattered, “came into remembrance to stand before the Lord,” that is, “to be gathered into one,” as the Evangelist says (John XI), “Satan also was present among them”: the sons of God serving to aid the elect, and Satan serving to test them.

“To whom the Lord said.” What God’s speaking is, and what Satan’s answering is, has already been explained. “Whence do you come?” It is a rebuke, because he who formerly was endured as though unseen is rebuked by the incarnate Lord. “I have gone around the earth,” namely, I have drawn all nations after me from Adam onward, “and walked through it,” that is, I left no one free from guilt. “Have you considered my servant Job,” that is, Christ in the form of a servant, “have you discerned him?”—because you say: “What have I to do with you? I know that you are the Son of God” (Mark I). “Have you considered,” I say, “that there is none like him on earth,” that is, among human beings who are only human, because he is God and man. “A simple man,” etc. This has been explained above.

And Satan, because what he had suspected concerning Christ’s divinity became doubtful to him through pride, says: “Does he fear God for nothing?” Is it not rather for the present glory of miracles by which he is rewarded that he “fears God,” withdrawing so fully from evil that, though he is a man, he is thought to be God? Does he not walk free of sin because “you have hedged him about,” that is, his soul, lest he be tempted like other human beings, “and his house,” that is, his body, “and all his substance [Col. 0969D] round about,” that is, his elect, so that I dare not attack them? “You have blessed the works,” namely his miracles, “of his hands,” that is, his healings, so that they may be many; “and his possession has increased in the land,” that is, those believing in him have multiplied. Satan’s saying these things to God is his thinking such things enviously.

“But stretch out,” and the rest through “Now when on a certain day,” are to be understood as above, except for the phrase, “they are in your hand.” Here this must be understood as the power not to destroy, but to tempt and sift like wheat (Luke XXII). “Now when on a certain day his sons and daughters,” that is, the apostles and inferior disciples, “were in the house of their first-born brother,” that is, within the bounds of the Jewish people, who is called first-born because he came to the worship of God before the Gentiles, “eating and drinking wine,” that is, preaching the Gospel, “a messenger,” namely prophetic speech, “came,” that is, was fulfilled, saying: “Therefore my people has gone into captivity, because they have had no knowledge” (Isa. V).

It was fulfilled in this way: “The oxen were ploughing,” that is, good workers were zealously and harmoniously occupied with the word; “and the she-asses,” that is, simple people, “were feeding,” that is, being taught, “beside them,” that is, agreeing with their teaching; “and the Sabeans rushed in,” that is, the enslaving evil spirits; “and took everything,” namely into the captivity of unbelief; “and struck down the servants,” that is, those not yet strong in faith, “with the sword,” namely of despair; “and I alone escaped”—understand, prophetic speech—“alone,” because prophetic speech survives every persecution and announces Christ.

“While he was still speaking, another came,” that is, another utterance of prophetic speech was fulfilled, namely this: “The zeal of fire has seized an untaught people.” This was fulfilled as follows: “The fire of God,” that is, the flame of envy, by God’s permission, “fell,” that is, blazed forth, “from heaven,” that is, from the hearts of leaders, who are called heaven, according to the saying: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak” (Deut. XXXII); and it “consumed the sheep and servants whom it had touched,” that is, it overturned from the faith those simple people whom it had touched to its own consent.

VERS. 17.—“Another came,” that is, another utterance of prophetic speech was fulfilled, for example this: “Those who hold the Law did not know me” (Jer. II). It was fulfilled [Col. 0970C] as follows: “The Chaldeans,” that is, the fierce ones, namely the authors of persecution, “formed three bands,” that is, the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees divided themselves, “and attacked the camels,” that is, the minds of the weak—for example, the Samaritans—“and took them,” that is, they attempted to turn them away from faith and hope in the resurrection; and the rest as above.

VERS. 18–19.—“And behold, another came in,” that is, another utterance of prophetic speech was fulfilled, namely this: “My neighbours stood far off” (Ps. XXXVII); or this: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (Zech. XIII). This, I say, was fulfilled in this way. “While your sons and daughters were eating,” as explained above, “suddenly a violent wind,” that is, a strong temptation, “rushed in from the region of the desert,” that is, from Jews abandoned by God, or from unclean spirits, “and shook,” that is, stirred to persecution, “the four corners of the house,” that is, the four orders of the Synagogue: priests, scribes, elders, and Pharisees. “And it fell,” namely into the cruelty of persecution, “and crushed your children,” that is, overwhelmed the apostles with despair.

VERS. 28.—“Then Job arose,” namely among the dead, or rose up for vengeance, “and tore his garments,” that is, he rejected from himself the Synagogue which had clung to him; “and, having shaved his head,” that is, after the dignity of the priesthood had been stripped from its rulers, “he fell to the ground,” that is, he came to the knowledge of the Gentiles. For in this place earth means sinful Gentile life, since the sinful human being was told: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). “And he worshipped,” that is, he made others worship, according to the saying: “Therefore I will confess”—that is, I shall gain confessors—“to you among the Gentiles, and I will sing to your name” (Ps. XVII), that is, I shall cause it to be sung.

VERS. 21.—“Naked,” he says, that is, regarded as a mere man and without the adornment of divinity, “I came forth,” that is, withdrew, “from the womb,” that is, from the carnal understanding, “of my mother,” namely the Synagogue. As a type of this, when the Egyptian woman wished to hold Joseph in incestuous embraces, he left his cloak in her hand and fled from her naked (Gen. XXXIX). Thus our Lord, leaving in the Synagogue’s hand the letter of the Law, by which his mysteries are covered, fled to the Gentiles, saying: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb,” as was said above. Naked in divinity, conspicuous, I shall return there, namely at the end of the world, when the multitude of the Gentiles shall have entered in (Rom. XI). The Lord—from whom, insofar as I am human, I received all things—gave, namely the Synagogue awaiting my Incarnation; the Lord took away, namely that same Synagogue when it despised my presence. In all these things Job did not sin: “For he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII; I Pet. II).

Morally. Since each person is such as his thought is, then the sons of God come “to stand before the Lord” when we turn heavenly things over in the palace of the mind through the breadth of contemplation; and Satan is among them when he inserts himself to disturb good thoughts. The rest, through “Satan went out from the face of the Lord,” is to be understood almost as above. Therefore, after Satan has gone out—that is, after one who must be instructed by temptations has been permitted to be tempted—it follows: “Now when on a certain day his sons and daughters,” that is, the virtues mentioned above, “were eating and drinking,” that is, receiving the banquets of life, “in the house of their first-born brother,” that is, in the sacraments of faith—for faith is the first-born of all virtues, since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI)—“a messenger came,” that is, discernment returns to conscience, and often alone survives when other virtues perish.

“The oxen,” he says, “were ploughing,” that is, weighty meditations were exercising themselves in good pursuits, for example in Holy Scripture; “and the she-asses,” that is, the simple movements of the heart, “were feeding beside them,” that is, they were governed according to the meaning of that same Scripture; “and the Sabeans rushed in,” that is, evil spirits, “and took everything,” enslaving them in evil desires, in accordance with their name; and “struck the servants,” that is, the guards of the heart, its watchfulness, “with the sword,” that is, they overthrew them by their attack.

“Another came.” The same discernment is called another messenger when it reports another thing, and it said: “The fire of God,” that is, envy by God’s permission, “fell from heaven,” namely the aerial heaven, that is, from unclean spirits who wander in the air. “And it consumed the sheep it had touched,” that is, innocence, “and the servants,” that is, purity of heart, by touching them with the burning of a wicked suggestion. It also said: “The Chaldeans,” that is, the fierce ones, namely the same evil spirits, “formed three bands,” that is, they attacked the mind through unlawful action, superfluous speech, and disordered thought; and struck [percusserunt: “they struck”] “the camels,” that is, good administrations of temporal things, “and the servants,” that is, the faculties presiding over these, with the sword of imprudence.

It also said: “While your sons and daughters,” and the rest as above, “were eating, suddenly a violent wind,” that is, a strong temptation, “rushed in from the region of the desert,” that is, from unclean spirits abandoned by God, “and shook the four corners of the house,” that is, the four virtues of steadfastness: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. “And it fell and crushed your children,” that is, it extinguished all the virtues.

[Col. 0972B] “Then Job arose,” that is, after these things, the person tempted, upon whom the Lord has looked, rises up to contend; “and tore his garments,” that is, he reconsiders all his works; “and, having shaved his head,” that is, after rejecting vain thoughts, “he fell to the ground,” that is, he confesses his weakness, and “worshipped,” confessing his sins. “Naked,” he says, “I came forth,” that is, I was reborn by no merits of my own, “from my mother’s womb,” namely from the first grace. “Naked,” that is, placing hope in mercy alone, “I shall return there,” that is, to the same grace. The Lord mercifully gave; the Lord justly took away. “As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done”: namely, since he has the power to take away as well as the generosity to give, it is fitting to have recourse to his judgment. “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” that is, in all his judgments I shall bless the Lord.

And speaking in this way, “in all these things Job did not sin,” because the sorrowing mind must carefully guard against the fire which burns it like gold turning, through excessive unlawful speech, into the ashes of straw. There is no obstacle to understanding the same thing said concerning virtues also of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For to some are given prophecies, to others kinds of tongues, and to others powers of healing (I Cor. XII). But because these gifts are not always present in the mind in the same manner, it is clearly shown that, lest the mind be lifted up in presumption, they are sometimes beneficially withdrawn. When this happens, it is right to say: “The Lord gave; the Lord took away,” etc.

[Col. 0972D] Because Satan sees that he has been defeated in the first contest, yet foolishly hoping for evils against the holy man—for the wicked cannot believe good things, even when they have experienced them—he renews himself for other wars of temptation in the following order.

CHAPTER II

VERS. 1, 2, 3.—“And it came to pass on a certain day,” through “But you moved me.” These matters have been discussed above and are not altered here. Yet the phrase “Whence do you come?” must not now be understood as before. For since he has been defeated, the weakness of his pride is now rebuked, as though it were openly said: Behold, you are conquered by one human being placed in weak flesh, though you attempt to raise yourself against me, the maker of all things. “But you,” he says, “moved me against him”—understand, by maligning him. He says “moved me” in our human manner, since we strike only when moved. “That I might afflict him”—understand, by permitting you—“for nothing,” that is, for no fault needing to be cut off. Thus, in the Lord’s speech truth is maintained, and in the deed righteousness: he is not struck for nothing, because his merit is increased; and yet he is struck for nothing, because no sin committed by him is punished.

VERS. 4.—“Satan answered: Skin for skin.” He still maligns him, asserting that Job therefore bears the scourges patiently because he guards against being struck himself, just as, when we see a blow coming toward our face, we put our hand before our eyelids to protect our eyes from the blow. This is what he says: “A man will give skin for skin.” Explaining what he has said, he adds: “All that a man has he will give,” that is, permit to be taken away, “for his soul,” that is, for his life, lest, if he becomes angry and curses, he himself also be struck.

VERS. 5.—“But,” that is, if you do not grant that this is so, “stretch out,” that is, permit me to exercise, “your hand,” that is, your power, “and touch,” that is, let me touch without restraint, “his bone and his flesh; and then you will see,” that is, thus you will discover, “that he blesses,” that is, curses in impatience, “you to your face.”

VERS. 6.—“Behold,” says the Lord—understand, I stretch it out—“he is in your hand,” that is, in your power to strike as and as much as you wish; “yet preserve his life,” that is, do not kill him utterly.

VERS. 7.—“Therefore Satan went out from the face of the Lord,” [Col. 0973C] in the way already explained above, “and struck Job with a most grievous ulcer.” By saying “most grievous,” the text expresses the quality of the ulcer; by saying “from the sole of his foot to his crown,” its extent.
