VERS. 8.—“And he”—understand, rightly considering what he was, namely that his body was a shattered earthen vessel—“scraped his discharge with a potsherd,” that is, with a fragment of an earthen vessel; indeed, potsherd against potsherd, mud against mud, not granting to the stricken flesh his fingers or the softness of clothing. “Sitting on a dunghill,” he placed his body there so that, considering his own frailty, he might increase from his surroundings the force of his self-contempt; so that his mind might weigh what the substance of flesh was, and learn from the stench of the place that the body would swiftly return to stench.

But when he had fixed his mind on high, the enemy sought a lower ladder—that is, his wife’s heart—by which he might climb to Job’s heart, renewing the snares of his ancient art. For, knowing how Adam is accustomed to be deceived, he returns to Eve.

VERS. 9–10.—“Then his wife said to him: Do you still remain in your simplicity?” She repeats the words of Eve. For what is it to say, “Abandon simplicity,” except to despise obedience? And what is it to say, “Bless God and die,” except, by transgressing the commandment, to live beyond the condition in which you were created? But our strong Adam lay on the dunghill, whereas formerly Adam had stood weak in Paradise. “You have spoken,” he says, “as [Col. 0974A] one of the foolish women.” He does not say, “as one of the women,” but “as one of the senseless women,” because it is not sex but will that is blameworthy in women; and their perverse thinking belongs to the folly that has come upon them, not to created nature. “If we have received good things,” namely gifts, whether temporal or eternal, “from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”—namely present scourges. “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips,” etc.; that is, he neither spoke proudly against the one who struck him nor kept silent concerning what was right against the one who counselled him otherwise.

VERS. 11.—“Therefore, when Job’s three friends heard,” etc. That they were zealous for good is clear not only from their coming to console the afflicted man, but also from the fact that they were friends of so great a man.

[Col. 0974B] VERS. 12, 13.—“And when they had lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him,” namely because the wound of the stricken man had altered his appearance. The rest is sufficiently clear in itself. But whether “they sat with the afflicted man for seven continuous days and seven nights,” or whether they devoted themselves with equal constancy to visiting him by day and night, we do not know.

ALLEGORICALLY. The beginning of the allegory should now be placed where, after words often repeated, something new is added. “You have moved me against him,” he says—that is, against innocent Christ—at the time, namely, when I was moved against the first man, on whose account this second man came to suffer blows. “You have moved me,” I say, “in vain,” namely because he committed no sin (Isa. 53). “Skin for skin,” and as above. “Nevertheless preserve his life” [Col. 0974C], that is, do not suppose that he can be held in hell. “Satan went forth,” etc. “From the sole of his foot to his crown,” that is, beginning with the pure human beings, Abel and the rest, he advanced in raging cruelty as far as the very head of the Church. He “scraped off the discharge with a potsherd,” namely with his flesh, made firm through the Resurrection: that is, he wiped away the sins of our flesh; “sitting on a dungheap,” that is, resting among the Gentiles whom he had previously rejected, and rejoicing over the sinner doing penance. “And his wife said to him”: that is, all those who are carnal within the Church say this to the body of Christ, which is the true Church when it is set amid affliction. “Do you still remain in your simplicity?”—that is, despising transitory things and desiring eternal things alone? [Col. 0974D] “Bless God and die”: that is, despise eternal things and, by dying, escape present evils. “You have spoken,” says each of the elect, “like one of the foolish women,” namely as one of those who, by pursuing fleeting things, are deservedly called women. “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord,” that is, if we are striving toward eternal goods, “why should we not endure” temporal “evils?”—“In all these things he did not sin,” etc., as above.

“Then the three friends of Job, having heard.” The friends of blessed Job represent heretics, because even if they approach with a good intention, they nevertheless lapse into fault by speaking without discernment. The perversity of these heretics is also gathered from the interpretation of their names. Eliphaz means “contempt of God,” Bildad “oldness alone,” Zophar “scattering mirror.” The heretic, I say, scatters by attacking the “mirror,” that is, the mysteries of faith which are contemplated. The names of the places from which they come—Teman, that is, “the South”; Shuh, that is, “speaking”; Naamah, that is, “beauty”—point to the same thing: namely, that heretics are hot like the South, burning for dispute; that they are lofty in speech; and that they are fine in appearance, namely through the superfluous polish of their eloquence. “For they had agreed” with one another, namely because they think in accord against the Church, though they disagree among themselves, “that, coming together,” that is, agreeing together in falsehood, “they might visit him and console him”: namely because, while they desire to teach the holy Church, they approach it as though to console it. “And when they had lifted up their eyes from afar,” namely because those who savor earthly things are below, [Col. 0975A] “they did not recognize him”: that is, they do not recognize the Church laid low by wounds because of hope for future things, since they themselves desire present things as something great.

“And having torn their garments,” that is, splitting their followers into many parties, “they scattered dust,” that is, earthly understanding, “upon their heads,” that is, upon their hearts, “toward heaven,” that is, against the command of heavenly utterance. [Col. 0975B] “And they sat with him upon the ground,” because they pretend to accommodate themselves to the holy Church as though it were weak; “for seven days,” that is, in all matters in which they understand the true light—for seven denotes universality, and day understanding—“and seven nights,” that is, in all matters in which they suffer the darkness of ignorance.

Or, to sit on the ground with Job is to believe, along with the holy [Col. 0975C] Church, in the true flesh of the Redeemer. Hence the Lord says: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20), that is, you shall hope in the Incarnation of the Mediator. “And no one spoke a word to him,” namely while he was silent, because heretics are our friends when we are mute; when we speak, they oppose us. Hence the reason is added: “for they saw that his grief was very great,” namely because the adversary fears to speak when we are pierced by very great grief through the love of God.

MORALLY. Satan’s striking blessed Job “from the sole of his foot to his crown” signifies morally that, when he receives permission, he pierces the entire body of the mind with the temptations he brings. His “scraping off the discharge with a potsherd” signifies that the force of strict discipline cleanses, by judgment, every pollution of thought. His “sitting on a dungheap” indicates that the humbled mind, in doing penance, sets its sins before itself. His wife’s saying, “Do you still remain in your simplicity?” etc., signifies that carnal suggestion wears out the mind with an assault of despair. The “friends” who gather as if to console are vices which cover themselves under the appearance of virtues; for example, immoderate anger wishes to appear justice, and lax indulgence mercy. That “no one spoke a word to him because they saw his grief was great” signifies that, as soon as vices attack, they recoil rejected from a sorrowful heart. For if the heart truly grieves, vices have no speech against us.

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1, 2.—“After this Job opened his mouth” [Col. 0976A], now indeed a victor, since “in all these things he did not sin with his lips,” nor “spoke any foolish thing against God” (Job 1). “After this,” I say, now at rest and not stirred; tranquil now, after overcoming all that might have disturbed him, “he opened his mouth.” This wording indicates that what follows must be awaited reverently, because what was contained in him as in a closed vessel was precious, and is now brought forth through his opened mouth.

“And he cursed his day.” What he says must not be received simply as the letter sounds. For why would so great a man curse something which he knew could not cease to exist? Surely that would be an idle word, for which, without doubt, an account must be rendered on the Day of Judgment (Matt. 12). He therefore curses the devil, not with the envy of revenge but by the judgment of justice, like a victor pronouncing deserved sentences upon the conquered, as follows:

VERS. 3.—“Let the day perish on which I was born.” That is, let the apostate angel perish, who, pretending to be day for Adam in Paradise, shone out by promising divinity and saying, “Your eyes shall be opened” (Gen. 3); but, showing himself to be night, he obscured for that man the light of immortality. For he does not say, “Let the day perish on which I was created”; for man was created on the day of righteousness. Rather, he says, “on which I was born,” because every human being is born in the time of sin.

“Let it perish,” I say, not so that it shall not exist, but so that it shall be in misery. For shortly afterward follows: “And let it be wrapped in bitterness.” What is entirely lost and utterly nonexistent cannot be wrapped in bitterness. “Let the day perish,” I say: namely, the devil. “And the night”: that is, this same one, who feigns himself to be day but is truly night; “in which,” that is, according to whose malice, “it was said,” namely by God, “A man has been conceived,” that is, deceived. This was when he said ironically: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3).

VERS. 4.—“May that day,” namely the one that deceives by counterfeit light, “be turned into darkness”: that is, may it be shown to be what it is, namely dark, so that it may not deceive by false prosperities, as by daylight, and draw men through real darkness into the darkness of sin. “May God not seek it from above.” As though he said: Let him indeed seek—that is, redeem—the human being who fell into sin from weakness through another’s malice; but let him not seek—that is, not redeem—the one who, bearing no weakness from flesh, fell through pride by his own malice [Col. 0976D]; “and may it not be illumined by light,” that is, may it never receive the light of its former condition.

VERS. 5.—“Let darkness,” that is, the blindness of its own error, “obscure it; and the shadow of death,” that is, forgetfulness—for just as death extinguishes life, so forgetfulness extinguishes memory—so that it may never again rise to the light of repentance through remembrance of the divine regard. “Let gloom seize it,” namely now, before the final punishment—that is, the confusion of its own error; “and let it be wrapped,” namely in the future, “in bitterness,” that is, let it be tortured eternally and, as though in a covering, bound in the punishment of Gehenna.

[Col. 0977A] VERS. 6.—“Let a dark whirlwind possess that night,” namely the night which, as has been said, pretends to be day, at the time when “our God shall come manifestly, and a mighty tempest shall be round about him” (Ps. 49). “Let it not be counted among the days of the year”: that is, among the elect human beings or angels, who are like the days of that year, namely of the full and perfect time—indeed, of the infinite age—of which Isaiah says in Christ’s person: “That I might proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. 61). “Nor numbered among the months”: that is, among the multiplied Churches or among the orders of angels. For just as a month is completed from multiplied days, so individual Churches are completed from many human beings, and individual orders of angels from many angels.

[Col. 0977B] VERS. 7.—“Let that night be barren,” that is, let it be separated from the multitude of the heavenly country; “and not worthy of praise,” namely of the praise of divinity, through desire for which it fell and which it dared to usurp for itself in idols.

VERS. 8.—“Let those curse it”—supply, the night—all the elect spirits who condemn its darkness, “who curse the day,” that is, who oppose its counterfeit brightness, unwilling to follow its pride; those who are “ready to rouse Leviathan.” Leviathan means “their addition,” because he promised to add divinity to the first human beings, who had been well created. Leviathan, I say, now shut in the pit of the abyss, they are ready “to rouse,” that is, to call forth again for more open contests at the end of the world.

[Col. 0977C] VERS. 9.—“Let the stars,” that is, hypocrites, “be darkened,” for the present, “by its gloom,” that is, by its malice, so that such persons may appear outwardly as they lurk inwardly within themselves. “Let it await the light.” This must be referred to its body, that is, to the same hypocrites, or to all who destroy in their works the faith which they hold merely in name. Let its body, I say, await “the light,” that is, Christ, according to: “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord”; and let it not see “the rising,” supply, “of the dawn arising,” that is, the beginning of the Church made bright in judgment. For in judgment it will be like dawn, but in the kingdom like full day. This has nevertheless already been fulfilled in Judaea, which belongs to this same body and is called the Synagogue of Satan: it awaited the light, that is, Christ who was to come, and was unwilling to see him present.

[Col. 0977D] VERS. 10.—“Because it did not shut.” He returns to the head itself and gives the causes of such great curses: “Because it did not shut,” he says, that is, did not permit to be shut, “the doors of the womb which bore me,” namely the womb of Paradise, which conceived the human race in the formation of Adam and Eve. It did not shut them; rather, so that they might be opened for casting man out, it broke apart the heavenly commands in the heart of that human being. “Nor did it take evils from my eyes,” that is, it inflicted them. For it would be said, as it were, to take them away if it ceased, and to shut if it ceased from assault. Thus we speak of robbers as sparing the lives of those whom they seize if they do not take them away.

[Col. 0978A] MORALLY. When blessed Job saw the fall of mortality varying through prosperity and adversity, and saw it as contemptible, he made it known by cursing, saying: “Let the day perish,” that is, the prosperity or pleasure of sin, “on which I was born,” that is, led into the work of sin; “and the night,” that is, adversity or blindness of mind, “in which,” that is, on whose occasion, “it was said, A man has been conceived,” that is, a weak person has been brought to consent to sin. For “man” is sometimes used for weakness, as it is written: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. 7).

“May that day,” that is, the same pleasure, “be turned into darkness”: that is, may it be known at the very beginning of its course [434] to what end of destruction it carries one; and when sin begins to flatter, may the watchful mind foresee its end also, namely the punishment which follows. “May God not seek it from above,” that is, may he not pardon it, when he comes in judgment; “and may it not be illumined by light,” that is, may it not then be made public in the sight of all. “Let darkness obscure it,” namely the day: that is, let the inscrutable judgments of God mercifully overtake it; “darkness,” I say, “and the shadow of death,” that is, the death of Christ’s flesh. It is called the shadow of death because, in comparison with true death, which is that of the soul—the death by which we were dead—it is only a shadow, that is, a certain likeness of death. For he mercifully accepted one simple death only, namely that of the flesh, and overcame our twofold death, namely of flesh and soul. He also wished to signify this when he lay in the tomb for one day only, but for two nights. Therefore it is rightly said, “and the shadow of death.”

“Let gloom seize it,” that is, let the affliction of repentance disturb it with worthy sorrow; “and let it be wrapped in bitterness,” that is, in the suffering or weeping of that same repentance. “Let a dark whirlwind possess or crush that night,” namely the aforesaid night: that is, let the spirit stirred by sorrow possess or crush it, according to what is written: “With a violent spirit you shall break the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47), that is, with the spirit of repentance you shall confound the examination of joy. For this is what Tarshish means.

“Let it not be counted”: that is, let it happen in this way, so that it “is not counted among the days of the year,” namely when the time of the present life, signified by the year, has been completed, when the days of this year—that is, the virtues of the present life—will be counted. Let that night of sin not be counted among the days of the year, that is, among the virtues which it would darken if it were counted among them; “nor numbered among the months,” that is, among the manifold acts of virtue, which acts are produced from virtues as months are completed from multiplied days. As though he plainly said: When you count good deeds, O God, in order to reward them, do not then also seek out the evils committed in opposition.

“Let that night,” supply, sin, “be barren,” that is, without a doubled defense, as Adam doubled his defense when he said: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion, she gave me, and I ate” (Gen. 3). “Let it be barren,” I say, “and not worthy of praise,” that is, cherished by no flattery, as happens “when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 10). But the person who truly pursues his own fault is indicated when it follows: “Let those curse it,” that is, let those who despise and trample worldly things—the light, namely, of prosperity—strike that fault by repentance; for such are true penitents. They are “ready to rouse Leviathan,” that is, through their true conversion they inflame against themselves the malice of the envious devil, so that, as though roused, he desires by hurling the darts of temptations to pierce the heart that resists him, a heart which he had long possessed by undisputed right.

Because the merit of this very fault demands that, as long as one lives here, no one, however holy, can fully contemplate the light of divinity, the permission of justice adds: “Let the stars be darkened by its gloom” [Col. 0979B], that is, let those who already shine with great virtues nevertheless endure the unseen darkness of the remaining traces of that same night. Let this same night, that is, the consciousness of the same fault, “await,” that is, desire, the eternal light; and, as long as one lives here, let it not see it as it is, nor “the rising of the dawn arising,” that is, the new birth of the future resurrection. “Because it did not shut,” that is, opened, as was said above, “the doors of the womb which bore me,” that is, the desires of carnal concupiscence which perverted me; “and did not take evils,” namely the evils of corruption, “from my eyes,” that is, inflicted them and made me experience them.

Thus far he has inveighed against the night itself, that is, the devil, author of sin; now he inveighs against himself in the person of the human race, because a true penitent ought not so to accuse the deceiver, the devil, as to excuse himself, since it is written: “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18).

VERS. 11.—“Why,” he says, “did I not die in the womb?” etc. Since sin is committed in the heart in four ways—suggestion, pleasure, consent, and defense—and is likewise consummated in action in four ways, because first the hidden fault is committed, afterward openly disclosed without shame, then brought into habit, and finally nourished by the obstinacy of despair—the perfect man pursues those same modes in this complaint: “Why did I not die in the womb,” that is, in the serpent’s first suggestion: I recognized what death would follow me. “Why, when I came forth from the womb,” that is, when I passed from inward suggestion to outward pleasure, “did I not immediately perish,” that is, did I not understand that I was perishing inwardly?

VERS. 12.—“Why was I received upon the knees?” That is, why was consent given support to pleasure? “Why was I suckled at breasts?” That is, why did I flatter myself with excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion, she gave me, and I ate” (Gen. 3)?

VERS. 13, 14.—“Why,” I say, “did I do this and this?” “For now”—that is, if I had not done so—“now, sleeping,” that is, suffering no conflict of the flesh and having no struggle of agitated weakness, “I would be silent and at rest in my sleep,” that is, in profound peace and security, being led at last without bodily death into the rest of the eternal homeland. “At rest,” I say, “with kings,” that is, with the highest dignitaries of angelic power. They are rightly called kings, according to: “The prince of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. 10); “and with the consuls of the earth,” namely with these same spirits. They are aptly called consuls because, through them announcing the will of the Creator, we find counsel for relief from the distress of our tribulation.

Or thus: “With kings,” that is, with the future rulers of Christ’s Church. For where redeemed humanity now ascends after Christ’s Passion, there surely humanity would have arrived even without redemption had it not sinned. Preachers are rightly called kings and consuls of the earth: kings because they rule themselves; consuls because, after sins have been put to death, they provide a remedy of life for sinners.

VERS. 15.—“Who build for themselves,” namely by fleeing the crowd of worldly cares, “solitude,” that is, a tranquil life; “who in this way possess gold,” that is, live wisely. He calls wisdom gold, concerning which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure and oil rest in the dwelling of the righteous, in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21).

VERS. 16.—“And fill their houses,” that is, adorn their consciences, “with silver,” that is, divine utterances. For “the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11). With such persons, I say, I would rest. “Or like a hidden miscarriage,” that is, like the elect who arose before the time of redemption—indeed before the Law was given—yet sought to mortify themselves under the natural law. Therefore they are called a miscarriage; and because, apart from the few about whom Moses wrote, “Their multitude is hidden from us,” he added “hidden” after saying “miscarriage.” “Like a miscarriage,” I say, “or like those who were conceived,” namely through the admonition of the Law received, “but did not see the light,” that is, did not attain Christ’s Incarnation. Of them he himself says: “Many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke 10).

VERS. 17.—“There,” that is, in this light which is the dwelling of all the elect, “the wicked,” namely the Gentile peoples, “ceased from turmoil,” that is, they found rest for their souls when they were converted at his coming, whom the fathers established under the Law had long awaited. “And there they rested” [435], namely because they took his sweet yoke upon themselves, “weary in strength,” that is, failing in that useless strength by which they had been strong in earthly things.

VERS. 18.—“Weary,” I say, through a health-giving failure, “and formerly bound,” that is, those who, before they reached that light, had been bound by the burden of their corruption, rested together “without distress,” namely without the corruption that weighs down the soul. Why? Because of what follows: “They did not hear the voice of the taskmaster.” Tempted in the present life, they indeed heard the voice of the taskmaster, that is, of the devil. He is called a taskmaster because in Paradise he lent money—that is, sins—to humanity, and as iniquity increases he demands it daily with interest. They heard him, I say, but did not heed him, because they disdained to consent.

VERS. 19.—“The small and the great are there,” that is, in that light there is a difference of merits, according to: “In my Father’s house there are many dwellings” (John 14). “The small,” I say, “and the great,” because there one surpasses another in recompense according to merits; “and the servant,” that is, one who had been a servant of sin, “is free there from his master,” namely free from that same sin, free, I say, because he will suffer absolutely no shame from past sin.

VERS. 20.—“Why is light given to the miserable?” Above he had said, “Why did I not die in the womb?” and then, contemplating the heavenly rest that humanity lost by sinning, he finally said this also: “The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” Now he considers that the prosperity or honor of the present world is an increase of misery rather than consolation for humanity. For it flatters secretly and deceives one, so that one may not feel oneself to be an exile or recall what one has lost. Considering this, I say, he says: “Why is light given to the miserable?” That is, why do those who know themselves to be miserable in this exile receive the brightness of transitory prosperity? And why is “life” given—that is, why does temporal glory smile upon—“those who are in bitterness of soul,” because they have been cast far away here from the face of their Creator?

VERS. 21.—“Who await death,” that is, desire that the complete mortification of all life of temporal glory may be accomplished in them; “and it does not come,” namely because often, by God’s hidden judgments, they are compelled either to preside in government or to be occupied with offices laid upon them. They await death, I say, “as those digging for treasure”: that is, as those who dig for a treasure labor more eagerly at digging when they think that they are drawing near to the hidden treasure, so these too, the nearer they come to their end, show themselves more fervent in work.

VERS. 22.—“And they rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave,” that is, the secret place of divine contemplation, in which the soul is hidden from earthly tumults as the body is hidden in a grave.

VERS. 23.—Why is light given “to the man whose way is hidden,” that is, who, thinking anxiously, does not know to what end his life, whatever its character, will come, or whether it pleases God, even if it seems good? “And God surrounded him with darkness,” that is, ignorance, because, by taking from us the light of his vision, “he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17).

VERS. 24.—“Before I eat, I sigh.” Surrounded by darkness, as has been said, “before I eat”—that is, before I am fed by contemplations of the heavenly light—“I sigh,” that is, I am afflicted by groaning; and so, when I have gained it through groaning, I am scarcely at last refreshed by contemplation. For unless I sigh, I do not eat, according to: “My tears were my bread” (Ps. 41). “I sigh,” I say, “and my roaring is like flooding waters,” that is, swelling with many streams, while I tremble before God’s hidden judgment: trusting that I shall reach God, yet fearing that I shall not; weeping for the past and dreading the future.

VERS. 25.—“For the fear that I feared,” namely lest I be abandoned, “has come upon me; and what I dreaded,” namely lest I incur the power of your wrath, “has happened.” For what reason did this happen?

VERS. 26.—“Did I not dissemble?” That is, though I saw myself surpassing others in power, did I not think of myself so humbly in my heart, as though I did not know these things? “Did I not keep silent?”—supply, with my mouth. “Did I not rest?”—supply, in action. For through these three—heart, mouth, and action—the mind is kept in check when it is lifted up by the prosperity of this world. “And indignation came upon me,” although I acted so well. From this let each person consider what punishments await sinners, if even the righteous are chastened here by such powerful scourges.

The friends of blessed Job, as was said above, represent heretics in this: they understand certain things very correctly, but amid these they lapse into perversities, which must now be weighed more subtly. Where you hear two parties—the accusers and the defense—contending before the tribunal of the whole Church of Christ, the friends accusing on one side and blessed Job defending himself from their accusations on the other, the passage now admonishes us to distinguish more clearly the intentions of each party.

What, then, do the accusers intend? Setting forth his case under a conjectural issue, they offer many things as arguments, all of which amount to this, as though they proposed it in this way: We plainly show that God struck Job by an equitable judgment; and then they add the reason: according to the severity of the scourge by which he is struck more harshly than other human beings, so also is the magnitude of the sin in him by which he offended God more grievously than other human beings.

In striving to repel or weaken this intention, blessed Job, his own defender, sets forth many arguments in reply, all of which have this principal intention, as though he proposed it in this way: Let the whole Church of God, which from the beginning to the end of the age is a pilgrim in this world, understand that God has not afflicted me by an equitable judgment according to your understanding; and then he adds the reason: the magnitude of the sin in me, by which I have offended God more grievously than other human beings, is not proportionate to the severity of the scourge by which I am struck more harshly than other human beings. He confirms this argument where, among other things, he says: “For my heart has not reproached me throughout all my life.” But now that the intention has been set out, the argument itself begins with this force:

## CHAPTER IV

VERS. 1, 2.—“Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it ill.” This too belongs to heretics: they begin to speak gently and, after proposing soft words, introduce harsh ones. “If we begin to speak,” he says—that is, to show you the causes of your affliction—“perhaps you will take it ill,” that is, impatiently. But, though it be so, “who can hold back the conceived word [or: will be able to hold back it]?”—supply, no one. He infers this from his own experience, because he despairs of everyone. But it is faulty reasoning to make a vice common to all from the vice of some.

VERS. 3.—“Behold,” he says, “you have taught many,” etc. As though he said: Behold, it is clear what manner of life you had, you who taught others. “You have taught many,” supply, while speaking but not acting; “and you have strengthened weak hands,” that is, hands failing in good work, while you yourself did nothing. “Your words,” that is, your admonitions, “have strengthened the wavering,” those who did not hold firmly to their resolve; “and you have strengthened trembling knees,” supply, to undertake the arduous path.

VERS. 5.—“But now a scourge has come upon you and you have failed.” That is, now it is plain how weak you yourself were, though you strengthened others, in that “when the scourge came upon you, you failed,” in that “it touched you and you were immediately troubled.”

VERS. 6.—“Where is your fear, your strength [436], your patience, and the perfection of your ways?” That is, where is that by which you seemed to be reverent, strong, patient, and perfect? He properly distinguished his life by listing four stages. For on God’s way, unlike the way of the world, not boldness but fear gives rise to strength; therefore he rightly placed strength after fear. And because strength is shown only in adversity, patience is immediately placed after strength, and after patience the perfection of one’s ways, since perfection is born of patience. But he accuses him of having possessed those virtues hypocritically when he adds:

VERS. 7.—“Remember, I pray, who ever perished innocent, or when were the upright destroyed?” He offers a faulty argument. For if no innocent person ever perished, the prophet would not say: “The righteous perishes, and there is no one who considers it” (Isa. 57).

VERS. 8, 9.—“Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity, who sow sorrows,” namely by acting perversely, “and reap them,” namely by thereby increasing in temporal prosperity, “perish at God’s breath.” By “breath” he intended to express God’s punitive visitation, in likeness to ourselves, who when angry are inflamed by the breath of wrath. For he follows by explaining what he had said: “And they were consumed by the spirit of his anger.” But this too is faulty. For such people are often permitted to endure for a long time and to be happy, and “are not in the labor of men, nor are they scourged with men” (Ps. 72).

After he had admonished him as if gently, he now adds open rebuke:

VERS. 10.—“The roar of the lion,” that is, your severity; “and the voice of the lioness,” that is, the talkativeness of your wife; “and the teeth of the lion’s cubs have been broken,” that is, your devouring sons, feasting together, have been destroyed. Stern Eliphaz declares all these things as justly condemned, and repeats his exultation in domination:

VERS. 11.—“The tiger has perished,” that is, the variety of your pretense has been extinguished. For the tiger, an animal sprinkled with spots, here signifies blessed Job’s mark of variety. “The tiger,” I say, “has perished because it had no prey,” that is, your hypocrisy fails because flattering praise has been taken away. In the Septuagint, however, not “tiger” but “myrmecoleon” is written, which in Latin is called “lion of ants,” or indeed “ant and lion.” And rightly so: for winged creatures it is an ant, but for the ants themselves a lion. As though he plainly said: You were not struck unjustly, because you were timid toward your superiors and bold toward your inferiors.

Typically, however, the lion signifies the devil; the lioness, the devil’s city, Babylon; and the lion’s cubs, any reprobate followers of malignant spirits. As though heretics plainly say: We are therefore crushed by no scourges, because by overcoming through the merits of our lives we trample the devil, earthly glory, and all the reprobate. The tiger or myrmecoleon—that is, the ancient adversary—also has no prey in us, because he lies conquered by our efforts. These words are spoken in mockery. Then, demanding reverence for what he is about to say, as heretics customarily do:

VERS. 12.—“But,” that is, in a far different way, “a hidden word was spoken to me,” that is, a holy and profound word, not from the common knowledge of others; “and my ear,” that is, my understanding, “received, as it were furtively,” that is, not through the door of common understanding, “the veins,” that is, the innermost sense, “of its whisper,” that is, of its concealed speech. And while seeking to say deeper things, he himself bears witness that what he puts forth is not true, adding:

VERS. 13, 14.—“In the terror of a night vision.” For vision is uncertain when sleep usually takes possession of people; but such visions are far inferior to us who keep watch for heavenly things. And lest you despise it as something cheap, fear—namely of mind—held me, and trembling—namely of body.

VERS. 15.—“And when the Spirit,” namely the divine Spirit, “passed before me,” that is, while my understanding perceived it—“passed,” I say, rather than stood still, lest you think what was seen could readily have been comprehended—“the hairs of my flesh stood on end,” that is, the vision was so true that even the body trembled with divine horror. And he adds whence the horror arose.

VERS. 16.—“Someone stood,” he says, namely one of the invisible beings, “whose face I did not recognize,” since he was not of the company of mortals. “An image stood,” I say—an image of a man rather than a man—“before my eyes”; and, lest you suppose that he was some mortal person, “I heard a voice,” not of a gross body, but “as of a gentle breeze.” Such indeed is the arrogance of heretics: they boast that such things, or things like them, happen to them. But because these things truly happen in holy men, the same words must be discussed more carefully.

The hidden word is said to be spoken to the minds of the elect when the power of the only-begotten Son of God—who is the Word, hidden in the beginning with God (John 1)—is revealed to believers in their hearts through the utterance of the Holy Spirit. “And as if furtively,” he says—that is, swiftly and secretly—“my ear,” that is, my understanding, “received,” not merely the whisper, that is, his utterance, namely the utterance of the Spirit, but “the veins of the whisper,” that is, the sources and causes of that utterance: fear, love, and such things.

Yet it may also be understood otherwise. So long as “we know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13), the very inspiration by which we are instructed in the mind is not yet speech, but is rightly called, as it were, a whisper, or the veins of a whisper. And because the mind, considering his power, is held back in fear, it is fittingly added: “In the terror of a nocturnal vision,” that is, in fear of hidden contemplation, and therefore nocturnal, because we do not see steadily what is to come, but doubtfully and in part. But because the mind is not caught up to the heights of contemplation unless it has first been lulled from earthly desires, it is rightly added: “When sleep is accustomed to seize men.” For then the soul deserves to perceive heavenly things when it truly says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5).

“Fear,” he says, “held me, and trembling”—that is, every firmness of human strength shook—“and all my bones,” that is, my strong deeds, “were terrified,” that is, were reckoned of no value by me. And precisely where I had believed myself especially strong, there I staggered before the Judge’s presence. “And when, while I was present,” that is, while I was perceiving invisible things, “the Spirit,” namely the Spirit of God, “passed by”—that is, permitted himself to be seen not steadily but swiftly—“the hairs of my flesh stood on end” [Col. 0985C], that is, superfluous thoughts fled away.

Yet, that I might adhere a little more broadly to contemplation, “someone stood,” namely the same Spirit-God who was passing by. For he is the one who passes by, because when known he cannot be held; and he is the one who stands, because, insofar as he is known, he appears unchangeable. “Whose face I did not recognize”: that is, the mind, habituated to visible things and thereby made dull, could scarcely raise the gaze of its understanding even a little toward the invisible God. “Someone stood,” I say, namely “an image before my eyes,” that is, the Son of God. For the Son is the image of the Father and, as the Apostle says, “the imprint of his substance” (Heb. 1).

“And I heard a voice as of a gentle breeze,” that is, inward knowledge of the Holy Spirit. “Of a gentle breeze,” I say, because the Holy Spirit, while we are in this life, shows his brightness only faintly to the bleary eyes of our mind. Of this gentle breeze it is said to Elijah: “After the commotion, fire”—that is, after the divine terror of repentance, the fire of love burns the heart of the converted sinner ashamed of his sins, as is signified by Elijah’s having “covered his face with his cloak; and after the fire, a sound of a thin breeze” (3 Kings 19). This is here called the voice of a gentle breeze: a brief and sudden apprehension of the incomprehensible substance of eternity.

Now let him who has heard the voice of the gentle breeze say what he learned from it:

VERS. 17.—“Will a human being be justified in comparison with God?” Supply: no. For human righteousness, compared with the righteousness of God [Col. 0986A], is so annulled as a lamp is darkened when placed in the beam of the sun. “Or will a man be purer than his Maker?” Supply: as you seem to yourself to be, you who, preparing a complaint against the scourge, accuse the justice of him who strikes? Supply: no.

VERS. 18.—“Behold, those who serve him”—an argument drawn from greater beings—“are not stable,” that is, unchangeable; and he proves this from its result when he adds, “and in his angels,” that is, in apostate spirits, “he found perversity.” The Godhead alone is unchangeable in nature and always is what it is. The holy angels, who, when the apostates fell, fixed the movement of their own mutability by the zeal of good will, received as their reward that, bound by bonds of love to him who is always the same, they can no longer change [Col. 0986B]. “They,” I say, “were not stable.”

VERS. 19.—“How much more those,” namely human spirits, “who inhabit houses of clay,” that is, bodies made from clay, “who have an earthly foundation,” that is, the earthly material of which they were made, “will be consumed,” namely by vices, “as by a moth”—supply: as a garment is consumed? As if he said: Just as a moth is born from a garment and consumes it silently, so sins committed by you have consumed you while you do not know it and while you seem righteous.

Otherwise: perversity is found in angels because the priests themselves, who, as Malachi says, “are angels of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2), are not without sin. “How much more those who inhabit houses of clay,” that is, those who follow carnal pleasures, “who have an earthly foundation,” that is, “who lead an earthly life” [Col. 0986C]: undoubtedly these are much more in sins. This is what follows:

VERS. 20.—“From morning until evening,” that is, from the beginning of life to its end, “they are cut down [or: will be cut down],” that is, wounded by the blows of iniquity.

VERS. 21.—“But those who are left,” that is, despised—those whom the present age leaves behind and rejects as insignificant and unworthy—“will be taken away,” that is, raised up, “from among them,” as Paul testifies when he says, “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful” (1 Cor. 1), and so forth. This is aptly signified in the Book of Kings by the Egyptian boy, who, exhausted on the way, was left behind by the Amalekites; David found and refreshed him, and he led David to the Amalekites as they feasted (1 Kings 30).

“They will be cut down,” I say—the persons mentioned above—in this way: “They will die, and not in wisdom,” that is, they will lose life and wisdom together; and, without understanding, “they will perish,” namely, “for ever.” Thinking Blessed Job like such people, Eliphaz adds mockingly:

CHAPTER V

VERS. 1.—“Call, then, if there is anyone who will answer you.” As if he plainly said: Since you are such a person, however much you cry in affliction, you do not have God answering—that is, helping—you. After this mockery he introduces a statement true in itself, but unjustly uttered against so great a man.

VERS. 2.—“Anger kills a foolish man [or: Truly, anger kills].” As if it were openly said: Anger through zeal disturbs a wise person; but you, who foolishly murmur against God, it slays through vice. “And envy kills the little one.” We cannot envy except those whom we consider in some respect better than ourselves. Therefore one killed by envy is little, namely in comparison with the person whom he bites with envy. But this is falsely said against Blessed Job, because, made miserable, he did not envy the prosperous.

The friends of Blessed Job learned many mystical things from familiarity with him. Hence Paul also uses their words and, adopting them to support his own assertion, testifies that they were spoken from truth. Therefore Eliphaz’s words, with which he speaks to Blessed Job, may be weighed mystically:

VERS. 3.—“I saw a fool,” etc. “I saw,” namely with astonishment, “a fool,” that is, the Jewish people, who despised Wisdom himself incarnate, “with a firm root,” that is, steadfast in extinguishing the life of the elect; “and I cursed his beauty,” that is, his prosperity, “at once,” that is, without any hesitation. “I cursed,” I say, that is, I assented to the judgment of his destruction, saying:

VERS. 4.—“May his children be far,” that is, all who were begotten by his preaching, “from salvation”—supply: eternal salvation. This will indeed be so: “They will be far away and will be crushed in the gate,” that is, in Christ, who says, “I am the door” (John 10), “and there will be no one to deliver [or: rescue] them.” This will be so because “there is salvation in no other” (Acts 4).

VERS. 5.—“Whose,” supply: the fool’s, “harvest,” that is, the literal knowledge of the Law, “the hungry man will eat,” that is, the Gentile people, once fasting from knowledge of God, will understand spiritually; and “the armed man will seize him,” namely the Jewish people, unwilling to eat—that is, to understand. This armed man is the devil, called in the Gospel the strong armed man. Finding no rest among the converted Gentiles, he says of this fool, that is, of the Jews: “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Luke 11).

“And the thirsty,” that is, the same Gentiles, “will drink,” that is, sweetly receive, “his riches,” namely his divine utterances [Col. 0987D], which are aptly called riches; elsewhere too they are called “silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11). Eating and drinking differ here because certain obscure things, which we understand only when interpreted, we as it were eat; but those things that are easy we as it were drink without chewing, receiving them just as we find them.

Morally, concerning the same fool: “I saw a fool.” This is the difference between a fool and an unwise person: an unwise person is one who does not know; a fool is one who does not guard against an evil which he knows. “I saw,” he says, “a fool with a firm root,” that is, supported by temporal prosperity; “and I cursed,” that is, I declared the future condemnation, “his beauty,” that is, his glory [Col. 0988A], “at once.” Notice that he added “at once”: that is, I did not hesitate as some weak people do, whose voice is: “But my feet were almost moved, because I envied the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72). Sometimes they act like those who first say, when they see glorious people dying, “See how insignificant man is.” But “at once”—that is, in the very course of his prosperity—“I cursed.”

“May his children,” that is, his imitators, “be far from salvation.” This will be so, because “they will be crushed in the gate,” that is, on the day of judgment, which will be the exit from the present age and the entrance into the future one. “And there will be no one to deliver,” because redemption will no longer be possible. “Whose,” supply: the fool’s, “harvest”: for the fool has a harvest, that is, the capacity for preaching [Col. 0988B] and sometimes even its office. “The hungry man eats his harvest,” namely whoever lacks knowledge but pants toward God with holy desires; in accordance with the Lord’s command, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23) [Note: [Col. 0987] “Observe and do everything whatsoever they tell you; but do not act according to their works”], he learns what he hears from whomever he hears it and performs the good which he has learned.

“And the armed man will seize him,” that is, the devil, cloaked in that man's foolishness and in his own deceit. “And the thirsty will drink,” that is, will hear usefully, “his riches,” that is, his utterances: dull indeed, but loving. By saying these things he reproves Blessed Job for foolishness, to whom he had also said above, “Behold, you have taught many” (Job 4), etc.

And as though you asked why the gift of understanding is given to the negligent and often not given to the diligent, he immediately adds: “Nothing happens on earth without cause” [Col. 0988C], because the fool too receives the gift in order that he may be more justly crushed, while the diligent person obtains it more slowly in order that he may receive a greater reward for the labor of seeking. “And sorrow will not arise from the ground”—supply: but from divine dispensation—whether it be your present sorrow or that of some fool when he is punished.

VERS. 7.—“Man,” that is, the carnal man, one like you, “is born for labor,” because he labors in everything. If he gains, he is tormented by cares; if he loses—supply: as you have now lost—he is wearied by grief. “And the bird [is born] for flight,” that is, for joy, because, as Solomon says, “Whatever happens to the righteous will not make him sorrowful” (Prov. 12).

VERS. 8.—“Therefore I too will entreat,” that is, I will not murmur as you do, but “will entreat the Lord, and to God,” that is, to God’s good pleasure, “will I set my speech.”

VERS. 9.—“Who does great things,” supply: by changing prosperity into adversity, “and unsearchable things,” namely to human reason, “and wonders without number,” in heaven as well as on earth. And in this he strikes at Blessed Job as though Job had earlier raised questions against God about his adversities, saying, “Why is light given to the wretched?” (Job 3), and the rest. He also touches mystically upon some of the wonders, saying:

VERS. 10.—“Who gives rain,” that is, the grace of heavenly preaching, “upon the face of the earth,” that is, into human hearts, “and waters all things with waters,” that is, with gifts of the Holy Spirit—not Judea alone, but every human being without respect of persons.

VERS. 11.—“Who places the humble,” that is, those humbly using the same gifts, “on high,” namely so that they may be judges with Christ; “and raises the mourners,” that is, those who flee prosperity and endure adversity for his sake, “into safety,” making them joyful through certainty of eternal salvation.

VERS. 12.—“Who frustrates the thoughts of the wicked,” namely of those rising against the good, “so that their hands cannot accomplish what they began” [Col. 0989B], that is, so that they do not prevail in doing as much harm as they wish.

VERS. 13.—“Who catches [or: seizes] the wise in their own craftiness,” by turning to good what they maliciously do: for example, Joseph’s sale (Gen. 45), and Saul’s intention when he demanded from David a hundred Philistine foreskins (1 Kings 18). “And he frustrates the counsels of the perverse,” so that nothing comes about according to their intention; for example, Caiaphas’s counsel concerning the killing of the Lord (John 11). Now, because he has mentioned persecutors, he adds these words concerning their blindness, inflicted by God’s just judgment:

VERS. 14.—“In daytime they will encounter darkness,” that is, in the very presence of truth their perfidy will blind them; “and as in the night,” that is, as in the darkness of their former error, “so they will grope,” going along by stumbling, “at noon,” that is, while the Sun of righteousness is present. This suits the Jews who said: “How long do you take away our life? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10).

VERS. 15.—“But he will save.” As if he said: They, in their blindness, will persecute; but he—namely God—will save “the poor man,” that is, Christ, “from the sword of their mouth,” as they cried and said, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19), “and from the hand of the violent man,” that is, of the Gentile power which crucified him by its hands, namely by raising him again.

VERS. 16.—“And,” when he has been raised, “there will be hope for the needy,” that is, for the humble people of believers: hope, that is, confidence in eternal life or resurrection. And because, when he who was judged comes to judge, the unbelieving will be mute, it is aptly added: “But iniquity will draw together,” that is, restrain or close, “its mouth,” hitherto opened wide in insult against the Creator.

MORALLY. We must now investigate morally how these things are generally done by the wicked. Because the reprobate are tortured by the extended sting of their envy at the good deeds of the righteous, it is rightly said: “In daytime they will encounter darkness,” that is, in the light of good works, with the eyes of their heart shut, they will seek, as if groping, something which they can accuse in the elect. Hence it is added: “And as in the night,” that is, in dark envy, “so they will grope at noon,” that is, in the full light of good work.

This is aptly signified by the fact that, while angels protected Lot, the Sodomites were struck with blindness and could not find the door of his house (Gen. 19). When the light of the good shines before men (Matt. 5), the wicked are blinded by the dart of envy; they cannot recognize good in their neighbors, nor, though going about, can they find an entrance for accusation [Col. 0990A]. “Thus,” I say, “they will grope. But he will save”—supply: God—“the poor man from the sword of their mouth,” that is, from their slander or the persuasion of their tongue; “and from the hand of the violent man,” that is, from the adversity of exalted power: the poor man, namely one of those whom the Lord blesses when he says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5).

“He will save the poor man,” I say, that is, the humble man. This will occur in such a way that “there will be hope for the needy,” and when he reaches the fruit of this hope, what is then added will happen: “But iniquity will draw together its mouth,” that is, every proud person who now disparages will be silent. Eliphaz nevertheless speaks against Blessed Job because he suspects Job to have been such a person and to have been struck for that reason. Hence he adds:

VERS. 17.—“Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects.” For he thought that Job was not being tested, but corrected. And so that this too may advance you toward blessedness, “therefore,” he says, “do not reject the Lord’s rebuke.” For he supposed that the things Blessed Job had said above had been said in murmuring. “Do not reject it,” I say.

VERS. 18.—“For he wounds,” namely the flesh, “and heals,” namely the mind; “he strikes,” namely you now, “and his hands will heal,” namely so that you may not perish eternally. This is what follows:

VERS. 19.—“In six tribulations,” that is, in all the tribulations of the world, which was completed in six days (Gen. 2) and runs through six ages, “he has delivered you,” namely, from your sins in the mind by afflicting the flesh; “and in the seventh,” namely, where souls rest when their bodies have been laid aside. For God rested on the seventh day (Gen. 2), and therefore the seventh age of the world, in which souls now rest, is signified by this seventh day. “In the seventh tribulation,” I say, “evil will not touch you”—supply: the evil which now touches the souls of the reprobate before the resurrection. In all these ways he will deliver you, if you do not reject his rebuke.

VERS. 20.—“In famine,” namely of the word, “he will rescue you from death,” that is, “he will feed you with the bread of life and understanding” (Ecclus. 15); “and in war,” that is, in temptation, “from the hand of the sword,” that is, from the deed of sin, he will rescue you.

VERS. 21.—“You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue,” that is, from the reproach of inflicted insult, so that, seeking no praise, you may not even feel the insults of detraction. “And you will not fear calamity,” namely of the manifold adversary, “when it comes,” that is, when it attacks you, because you will be prepared and enclosed by his protection.

VERS. 22.—“At devastation,” namely of the reprobate, “and famine,” namely of those who will be removed so that they may not eat bread in the kingdom of God—“at their devastation and famine, I say, you will laugh,” that is, in the eternal banquet you will rejoice in your own security and their destruction. You will laugh, I say, because then the impious and lost will not be objects of compassion or pity. “And you will not fear the beasts of the earth,” namely the devil, who envied in beastly fashion man made from earth and who will then rage, because now you are not seduced by him even when he flatters.

VERS. 23.—“You will not fear,” I say, “but your covenant,” that is, your dwelling together, “will be with the stones of the regions,” that is, with the saints and elect of the Churches, which are many only because of diversity of places. “And the beasts of the earth,” that is, the evil spirit, “will be at peace with you,” that is, you will find that they have made peace with you in this: that, by attacking you, they drive you unwillingly toward the love of God. “At peace,” I say, not pacified, because they possess no peace whatever; but by their attacks they drive you unwillingly, as was said, toward desiring peace.

Or thus: “The beasts of the earth,” that is, movements of the flesh, “will be at peace with you,” because, while provoking you by temptation, they compel you to tend toward love of inward rest. In either sense the same result follows:

VERS. 24.—“And you will know,” namely through its present beginning, “that your tent,” that is, your body, which the mind inhabits, “will have peace”—the full and perfect peace of the future. For peace from vices begins here; it will then be complete when the flesh has been changed through resurrection. And because there is no chastity which love does not commend, it is added: “And in visiting your likeness,” that is, in loving your neighbor [Col. 0991C], “you will not sin,” because you will not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself (Tob. 4:16; Matt. 7:10; Luke 6:31). Our neighbor is rightly called our likeness because in him we see what we are, what we were, or what we can become. Moreover, according to secular philosophers, one person and many persons are one person in species.

VERS. 25.—“And you will know also,” namely by doing what has been said, “that your seed will be abundant,” that is, the word of your preaching will be multiplied beyond counting for you; “and your offspring,” that is, your imitators, will arise like the grass of the earth: either innumerable, or despising the verdure of all earthly things. “Your seed,” I say, “will be so abundant” that

VERS. 26.—“You will enter the grave in abundance,” that is, into the secret place of contemplation. The grave here signifies the repose of the contemplative life, to which no one should aspire except after being trained by the labor of the active life. Otherwise, one enters the grave not in abundance but in want; and one must fear what is said in Exodus: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. 19). That is, if a mind subject to irrational desires is raised to the heights of contemplation, it is killed by stones, that is, by blows of heavenly weight [Col. 0992A].

Therefore, just as Jacob first took Leah, bleary-eyed indeed but more patient, before beautiful yet barren Rachel (Gen. 29), so, if you first practice the active life, which is more laborious, you will properly and orderly enter the contemplative life. Or thus: “You will enter the grave in abundance,” that is, after accumulating good works in the present life, you will be hidden in the secret repose of the heavenly homeland, “as a heap of wheat is brought in”—supply: into the granary—“in its season,” namely after rains and winds, after the heat of the sun, after threshing and the separation of chaff.

So, I say, after the utterances of truth, by which every faithful person is now made rich as by rains; after the shaking of winds, that is, temptations; after illumination by the sun, that is, the heavenly light; withdrawing from the fellowship of the carnal as from the entanglement of chaff, one is brought into the granary of heavenly peace. He himself indicates that he did not say these things literally when, after everything, he adds:

VERS. 27.—“Behold, this which [or: as] we have investigated is so.” For what is investigated plainly does not lie before the eyes. Hence it is clear that in these words a more subtle meaning surpasses the surface of the letter. But after all this he comes to the foolishness of boasting, saying: “What you have heard, ponder in your mind,” because he shows his serious ignorance in wishing to teach one better than himself.

CHAPTER VI

Certain things mixed into the words of Blessed Job seem, before human tribunals, to exceed the limit of patience [Col. 0992C]. But the inward Judge, before the trial, preferred him, saying, “There is none like him on earth” (Job 1); and after the trial rebuked his friends, saying, “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42). Therefore Job’s words are right: he neither exceeds patience nor murmurs at his affliction. Rather, speaking in the voice of the human race, he desires death—which entered the world through sin (Rom. 5)—in this way:

VERS. 2.—“Would that they were weighed,” etc. He does not vainly or superfluously wish for something that will never happen; rather, he prophesies what will truly happen and awaits it with desire, saying in the voice of humankind: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath,” that is, death, “and the calamity which I suffer,” that is, eternal death itself—for he does not say, ‘the calamity which you see,’ but “which I suffer,” that is, for which “I sigh all the days in which I now serve” (Job 14)—“would that the sins, I say, and the calamity which I suffer for my sins, were weighed in a balance,” that is, in the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2).

He calls him a balance because in him “mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. 24); placing our sins in the pan of truth, or judgment, and, opposite them, our calamity which we suffer for them in the pan of mercy. Mercy, unable to bear the weight of our calamity, immediately inclined the balance itself—that is, Christ, God and man—even unto death; and it raised the pan of judgment with such force that it shook off our sins and, according to the prophet, cast them “into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7). And this is what he says:

VERS. 3.—“As the sand of the sea,” which is very heavy, “this calamity would appear heavier. Therefore,” because this has not yet happened, “my words are full of grief,” namely:

VERS. 4.—“Because the arrows of the Lord are threats against me,” that is, the sentence of condemnation which he imposed upon humanity because of sin. “Their indignation drinks up,” drawing inward one intent on outward things, “my spirit,” namely my carnal and proud spirit; “and the terrors of the Lord,” that is, the threats of the future judgment, “make war against me,” that is, they restrain me from foolish joy. He now shows conversely why his words are rightly full of grief.

VERS. 5.—“Will the wild ass roar,” that is, will the Gentile people—like a wild ass, that is, an untamed ass, bound by no bonds of God’s commandments and confined by no stalls of discipline—“will it roar,” that is, will it groan, fasting as now from the word of God, “when it has grass,” that is, when it has received the aforementioned present grace of the Redeemer? “Or will the ox low,” that is, the Jewish people, accustomed to draw the yoke of the Law: will it low, that is, will it say, ‘Do you think I shall see it? Do you think I shall endure? Do you think that nativity will find me here?’ Will it, I say, low thus “when it stands before a full manger,” that is, when Christ has given his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk in the full manger (Augustine, *On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin*), that is, at the holy altar?

Or if you ask why, before that time of grace, the Gentiles did not wish to turn to God through the instruction of the Old Testament:

VERS. 6.—“Will,” he says, “the unsalted be able to be eaten?” That is, can the Gentiles willingly receive the tasteless literal commandment of the Jewish Law—for example, circumcision of the flesh, and such things—“which is not seasoned with salt,” that is, tempered by the life-giving Spirit? “Or can anyone,” supply: any Gentile, “taste,” that is, observe, “what when tasted brings death,” that is, that through which sin, gaining strength, as the apostle says (Jas. 1), produces death [“When it has been completed, it gives birth to death”]? “For,” he says, “I would not have known covetousness unless the Law said: You shall not covet” (Rom. 7).

The wild ass, I say, will not then roar, but will say:

VERS. 7.—“Things which my soul formerly refused to touch,” namely the sacraments of the Old Scripture, “now, because of distress,” that is, because of the force of love, “are my food.” And will the ox then low? No; but it will say the same: “Things which my soul formerly refused to touch,” that is, the Gentiles whom I formerly despised as brute and unclean, and that race of people “which, when tasted,” that is, when joined to me in covenant, “brought death”—for God had prohibited me from making a covenant with foreigners—“now, because of distress,” that is, because of the scarcity of the children of Israel, who refuse to be converted, “are my food,” that is, they have been made one body with me through faith [Col. 0994A]. We have in Acts of the Apostles when the ox, that is, the Synagogue, said this: the apostles themselves said, “Because you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

MORALLY. These things may morally be taken thus, so that the faithful soul, chastened by fear of punishments, says: “Because the arrows of the Lord are threats,” and so forth. This does not differ from the meaning given above. But because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4), so that it may wish to see him whom it formerly feared servilely, it aptly adds: “Will the wild ass roar?” and so forth. Here the wild ass signifies those who are placed in the field of faith and bound by the reins of that office; the ox signifies those upon whom the yoke of an office or order undertaken presses. These now roar and low, as it were, when they are excluded from the vision of God whom they desire [Col. 0994B].

But “will the wild ass roar,” that is, some private faithful person, “when it has grass,” that is, the ever-green glory of the same vision of God? “Or will the ox low,” that is, someone pressed beneath the yoke of holy order, “when it stands before a full manger,” that is, when he has been admitted fully to see God? Or, if you ask why before that time he cannot cease from lowing or be satisfied, what will he eat in the meantime? “Can the unsalted be eaten?” That is, can tales “which the wicked have told” (Ps. 118), or anything of that kind, which is not seasoned with salt—that is, divine wisdom—delight him?

Or if you ask: Why does he not hasten to escape from here through martyrdom? Can anyone by his own strength “taste,” that is, say or do, for truth, something “which, when tasted,” that is, when said or done, “brings death,” namely martyrdom? Rather, progressing more and more, he subsequently says what follows: “Things which my soul formerly refused to touch,” that is, the bitterness of persecutions which I formerly feared, “now, because of distress,” that is, because of weariness with my pilgrimage, “are my food,” that is, are delightful to me—so much so that, desiring them, I say:

VERS. 8.—“Who will grant that my request may come?” Namely, because I ask that my soul may be filled with them. “And may God grant me what I await?” Namely, that state in which the patience of the saints will be rewarded. May he himself grant this desire.

VERS. 9.—“And may he who began,” supply: to crush me, as you see, “himself crush me,” namely even unto perfect purification, lest something hard remain in me on account of which he might abandon me to the adversary to be crushed.

VERS. 10.—He, I say, “may loose,” that is, may keep “his hand” bound by no withdrawal or turning away, nor say, “My zeal has departed from you” (Ezek. 16); “and may he cut me down,” namely from the state of my pride—that is, humble me. “And may this be my consolation,” that is, may it make me know in this that I am not worthy of his hatred: “that, afflicting me with sorrow, he does not spare me,” namely in the present life. “For whom the Lord loves he corrects [or: chastises]” (Heb. 12). “Nor will I contradict the words of the Holy One,” that is, I will not murmur against the reasons set forth against me. I say “the Holy One,” lest you suppose that I speak these things with a swollen or reproachful mind. This is my request because of the distress mentioned above.

VERS. 11.—“For what is my strength?” That is, how great do you think the hardness of my heart is? Is it so great “that I should endure,” that is, bear my pilgrimage without grief? “Or what is my end?” Supply: is it not God, toward whom I run with the whole course of this life? “What,” I say, that is, what kind of end is this end of mine? Is it so insignificant that “I should act patiently,” that is, that I should not grieve because I have not yet attained it, or bear the delay patiently? No. “That strength,” that is, hardness, “belongs to stones” [Col. 0995B], that is, to insensible people, who often receive even heavenly blows yet are softened by no stroke of discipline.

But:

VERS. 12.—“Neither is the strength of stones,” namely of such persons, “my strength, nor is my flesh bronze.” That is, my flesh is not like bronze, which gives back sound without feeling it—for it sounds but does not feel. No, my flesh which has been struck does not utter the voice of confession without devotion of heart. Lest, however, you suppose that I claim this tenderness of heart for myself:

VERS. 13.—“Behold,” supply: I say, “there is no help for me in myself.” Nor is there help in the exhortation of any person who might build me up. This is sufficiently clear because “even those close to me have departed from me.” He proves that they never clung to him in prosperity through love by adding this universal statement:

VERS. 14.—“He who takes mercy away from his friend,” that is, who is not with his friend in adversity and does not sympathize with him, “forsakes the fear of the Lord,” that is, proves that he does not possess it. For the parts of that fear of the Lord are love of God and love of neighbor. Therefore they did not love me, their neighbor or friend, in prosperity, whom they abandoned without mercy in adversity. It follows that they loved what was mine: they clung to me not for my sake but for the sake of my possessions. This is what he shows by a comparison:

VERS. 15.—“My brothers have passed me by like a torrent which swiftly passes through valleys.” That is, as a torrent swells with waters running down from mountains and dries up when those waters fail, so my friends flowed toward me while prosperity endured, and have now flowed away when it failed. He now gives a judicial sentence also concerning such people:

VERS. 16.—“Upon those who fear frost,” that is, who shrink from temporal misery—for frost freezes below and therefore signifies the cold of earthly adversity—upon those, I say, who shrink from the frost of the temporal misery which they see in me, “snow will rush down,” that is, a graver judgment from above. For snow falls from above and therefore signifies the wrath of God coming down from on high.

VERS. 17.—“At the time when they are scattered, they shall perish.” [Col. 0996A] He remains within the metaphor. “Snow,” he says, “will rush upon them”; and just as snow shines for a time, then, as soon as it grows warm, melts and perishes, so they too, though bright for a time, “at the time when they are scattered”—that is, through the separation of soul and body—“shall perish.” And when they have grown warm [when it has grown warm], that is, when they have been distressed by the divine judgment, “they shall be dissolved,” like the snow mentioned above, “from their place”: that is, from the delight of their flesh to which they had clung.

VERS. 18.—“The paths of their steps are entangled”: that is, because they are excessively hindered by love of earthly things, even if they wish to escape sins, they fall back upon themselves and, avoiding one thing, are turned back, like blind persons, into another. Since they think only of what passes away and take no care for what remains with them, “they shall walk,” he says, “into emptiness,” carrying with them nothing but their sins, “and shall perish.” Restricting his hearers from imitating them, he turns to them and says:

VERS. 19.—“Consider the paths of Teman,” that is, of the South Wind. For *Teman* means “South Wind,” and here signifies a lax and undisciplined manner of life, because it is a warm wind. “Consider,” namely, “the roads of Sheba.” *Sheba* means “net.” It is as though he said: Consider to what end the life of those comes who live loosely and carelessly; and therefore the steps of such persons are caught in the nets of sins, as was said above. “And wait a little”: that is, defer this world’s temporal delights, so that you may find eternal ones.

VERS. 20.—“They are confounded because I hoped.” “Wait,” [Col. 0996C] I say, “a little,” and you will see how those who already are confounded and ashamed (Wisdom 5) will be troubled, groaning in dreadful fear, “because I hoped”: that is, because they cannot wrest from me the hope which I have placed in God. “They also came as far as me”: that is, they saw not only the wounds of my body, but now, by observing the steadfastness of my mind amid adversities—and on the day of judgment, by beholding my glory together with the holy Church—they “came,” and will come, “as far as me, and are covered with shame.” Now, because, as was said above, “I hoped”; but then they will be covered with shame when they are driven away from the glory which they will see. He has spoken these things, in the person of the Church, about those who depart from her in time of temptation [Col. 0996D] (Luke 8); now he reproves his friends as belonging to their number, saying:

VERS. 21.—“Then [Now],” that is, a little while ago, “you came,” namely, to comfort me; and now [at once], that is, so quickly, “seeing my wound, you fear”: that is, you recoil, and in horror of me you now for the first time tremble at the dreadful judgment of God. As though he said: Why have I so quickly become burdensome to you? Have I been troublesome to you in any respect? This is what he adds:

VERS. 22.—“Did I say, Bring to me, 441 and from your substance give [or: donate] to me,” because I have become poor? I did not say this, which perhaps would have been burdensome to you. Or did I say:

VERS. 23.—“Deliver me from the hand of the enemy,” that is, from the strength or assault of Satan? “And rescue me from the hand [Col. 0997A] of the strong,” that is, from the powers of evil spirits? Nor did I say this, which would certainly have been impossible for you. Now, by concession, he speaks ironically:

VERS. 24.—“Teach me, and I shall be silent”: namely, because this is what you want—that, while you teach, that is, reprove, me, “I may be silent,” namely, about the truth of my conscience. “And if I have been ignorant of anything,” that is, have sinned unknowingly, “instruct,” that is, correct, “me.” That he uttered this irony without any swelling pride he plainly indicates by what he adds a little below: “You rush upon an orphan.” As though he said: This is not teaching or instructing, but rushing upon me as an orphan. I am an orphan in that the whole world has abandoned me.

[Col. 0997B] Now he both reproves them humbly and instructs them wisely.

VERS. 25.—“Why have you disparaged,” namely, in the preceding speech, which Eliphaz thus ended: “What I have heard, I have pondered in my mind” (Job 5)—“why, I say, have you disparaged words of truth,” namely, those which I thus ended: “And indignation came upon me” (Job 3)—“when there is none among you,” namely, so single-eyed toward me, “who can rightly accuse me.” For no one ought to accuse unless he speaks irreproachably and from charity. But you:

VERS. 26, 27.—“You compose speeches only for reproving,” not also for improvement, “and you utter words into the wind,” that is, without the weight [Col. 0997C] of discernment; “and you strive to overthrow,” namely, from his hope, “your friend,” that is, one who loves you even now, when you withhold the due benevolence. Thus the holy Church loves even the salvation of her slanderous heretics.

VERS. 28.—“Nevertheless,” that is, although I love you when you do not love me, “fulfil what you have thought [or: begun],” namely, if you do not cease, out of love for truth alone. “Fulfil it,” I say, lest you think that I evade a rational hearing. “Give ear,” that is, the good will of your heart; and, with that good will purifying the eye of understanding, “see whether I lie”; and, having seen this—that is, having discerned it:

[Col. 0997D] VERS. 29.—“Answer, I beseech you”: that is, speak things consonant with your own judgments, “without contention”; since the heat or desire of disputing causes heretics and all perverse persons, when they perceive the truth, to speak falsehood—which is to speak a word against the Holy Spirit. “Answer,” I say, “and, speaking what is just, judge”: that is, distinguish it from what is unjust.

VERS. 30.—“And” when you have thus applied yourselves, “you will not find”—that is, you will not invent—iniquity to be in my tongue, “nor will folly resound in my throat,” even by your own judgment. From this point, beginning and continuing his speech while his friends interrupt, he explains more fully the meaning which he rightly perceives.

## CHAPTER VII

VERS. 1.—“The life of man [Col. 0998A] upon earth is warfare.” As though he said: Why do you think that I said, “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3), and the rest? Do you think that I spoke of the particular day of my birth, rather than of the entire time of human mortality, which is set in an evil day—or, more truly, in night, that is, in the prince of darkness? I spoke of that day because in it, that is, on account of it, “the life of man,” which ought to have been the vision of eternal peace, “is warfare upon earth.”

“And as the days of a hired laborer,” namely, waiting in toil and heat for the end of his work, so are “his days,” that is, his life—namely, the life of the man who was created not to be a hired laborer but a son, a citizen; not a stranger, not a beggar, but a lord. Therefore I now grieve, because:

[Col. 0998B] VERS. 2.—“As a servant longs for shade,” so, serving in the heat of affliction in this present exile, I long for shade, that is, for the refreshment of that rest whose fullness the first man lost; “and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work,” being without his wage before it is completed:

VERS. 3.—“So I too have had,” that is, have passed through, “months,” that is, cycles of changing life. For the moon, by going round and changing itself, completes a month. “Months,” I say, “empty,” that is, cycles not yet rewarded and still ignorant of their end; for, though I serve faithfully, “I do not consider that I have attained” (Philippians 3). “And I have numbered for myself laborious nights,” that is, adversities filled not only with deprivation but also with torments, [Col. 0998C] reckoning in hope a reward for myself for each one.
