It is quite clear how these words apply universally to the Church. What follows is plainly evident in her own person; but we understand these things less plainly—that is, only by exposition—in the holy Church.

VERS. 4.—“If I sleep, I shall say, ‘When shall I rise?’ And again I shall awaken [or: And again I shall wait for evening].” For in the night one longs for day, and then for evening, because pain plainly does not allow present things to please; “and I shall be filled with pains until darkness.” This is clear in Job’s own person, since the mind of one afflicted is always directed by expectation toward other things. Yet the cause of this same pain is made known in what he says:

[Col. 0998D] VERS. 5.—“My flesh is clothed with rottenness,” and the rest. Namely, because “from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him” (Isaiah 1). But these things must also be expounded in the person of the Church, whom her own mutability wearies in this pilgrimage.

“If I sleep,” that is, if I have been caught up in contemplation, I am so mutable that “I say, ‘When shall I rise?’”: that is, when shall I be released again to outward things? For even a strong mind sometimes says to itself, feeling its way: “The bow is not always kept drawn.” “And again,” namely, when I have been released into outward things, “I shall await evening,” that is, I shall long for the silence of contemplation; “and I shall be filled with pains until darkness,” that is, until the present life comes to an end.

Or thus: “If I sleep,” that is, if I am in the torpor of idleness, longing for exertion, I say: “When shall I rise?” “And again I shall await evening”: that is, in rest I seek the exertion of action, and in exertion I seek the leisure of rest. And this cause chiefly brings this mutability upon me, namely, upon the Church: that “my flesh”—that is, the carnal persons who are my members—“is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust”: that is, they are indeed clean through faith, but unclean through their works. And this is the reason why “my skin”—that is, those who attend only to outward things, as skin stretches outwardly over the body—“has dried up,” namely, from the moisture of heavenly things, “and is drawn tight,” namely, by loving present things and not stretching forth toward eternal things.

VERS. 6.—“My days,” namely, the days [Col. 0999B] of present mortality, “have passed more swiftly than a web is cut off by the weaver.” This is a very fitting comparison. For, as a web, fastened below and above, is attached to two pieces of wood, so the present life is enclosed by birth and the setting of death. And as, the more the woven web is rolled up below, the more what remains to be woven above is unrolled and becomes less, so the more days of our life have passed, the fewer remain to come.

“But my days,” he says, “have passed more swiftly,” because in weaving there is often delay, and the hand of the worker rests in idleness; but there is no delay in the unfolding of days. “And they have been consumed without any hope”: that is, in passing they leave behind nothing for which I ought to hope in them. Now, raising his eyes to God from the miseries mentioned above, he says:

[Col. 0999C] VERS. 7.—“Remember me, O God”: namely, because unless you remember, “my life is wind,” that is, empty and lost; “and my eye shall not return,” namely, to the former vision of you—my eye darkened by the serpent’s persuasion when he said, “Your eyes shall be opened” (Genesis 3). “It shall not,” 442 I say, “return to see good things.”

VERS. 8.—“The sight of man shall not behold me,” unless, namely, you remember me: that is, the mercy of the Redeemer shall not look upon me. “It shall not behold me,” I say, that is, the incarnation of your Word shall not visit me. For the visitation of the Son of God assuming human form is fittingly denoted here by “the sight of man.”

Or thus: Remember me while I live, because the sight of man—that is, the grace of the Redeemer—does not look upon a soul once stripped of flesh for repentance. “Your eyes are upon me,” that is, the strictness of your judgment, if you do not first remember—that is, look upon—me; it will stand against me, “and I shall not stand,” that is, I shall not rise to endure your judgment. I shall not stand, I say, but:

[Col. 0999D] VERS. 9.—“As a cloud is consumed and passes away,” being driven on and scattered by the heat of the sun so as to vanish, “so he who descends to hell,” drawn away by an evil spirit and melted by the heat of the sun—that is, by the regard of the heavenly judgment—“shall not ascend”: that is, he shall not return to the exercise of action.

VERS. 10.—“Nor shall he return again to his house,” that is, to the present life, or to the dwelling of his body, or to the contemplation of his Creator; “nor shall his place know him any more,” that is, his place—God the Creator—shall no longer seek him. God the Creator, his “place,” who, pursuing the fugitive, so to speak, found the man whom he had lost in order to retain him.

VERS. 11.—“Therefore I too,” while I live and while I have a place for repentance, “will not spare my mouth”: that is, I shall open my mouth against myself and deal harshly in the words of my own confession. “I shall speak,” that is, I shall declare my iniquity, “in the tribulation of my spirit,” that is, in weeping and tears; “I shall confer,” that is, I shall take counsel, “with the bitterness of my soul,” concerning how I may hide myself or flee from the eternal blow of so great a Judge.

To confer with the bitterness of one’s soul is to oppose reason to thoughts of despair which bitterness of soul suggests amid grievous adversity, in this way:

[Col. 1000B] VERS. 12.—“Am I the sea, or a sea-monster?” That is, am I the dwelling-place of the devil, or the devil himself, “that you have surrounded me with a prison,” O bitterness of my soul? That is, because you force me to despair and do not allow me to expand myself in spiritual joy; you constrain me greatly.

VERS. 13.—“If I say, ‘My little bed will comfort me’” in my affliction—that is, the secret place of my conscience—“and I shall be relieved,” namely, from this weight of sorrowful cares, “speaking with myself,” that is, reflecting on some good things of which I am conscious, “upon my couch,” that is, in the secret place of my heart:

[Col. 1000C] VERS. 14.—“You will terrify me through dreams,” that is, through imaginations which bring back to me the adversities I have suffered or the things still to be feared in the future judgment, “and through visions,” that is, thoughts, “you will shake me with horror,” namely, at my evils.

VERS. 15, 16.—“Wherefore my soul chose hanging, and my bones death. I despaired; I shall by no means live any longer.” These words cannot stand in the literal sense, especially because immediately afterward follows: “Spare me, O Lord,” which does not accord with despair. Unless what he says—“I shall confer with the bitterness of my soul”—is understood so that the things above, “Am I the sea, or a sea-monster?” and the rest, are words of reason, while these words, “My soul chose hanging; I despaired [perhaps: *desperata*, ‘despairing’],” are words of bitterness wickedly suggesting despair.

But they may properly be understood mystically thus: “Hanging,” that is, lifting the heart upward toward God, “my soul chose,” that is, my intention; “and death,” that is, mortification, “my bones chose,” that is, the harmful strength of the flesh, according to the saying: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Colossians 3). In this way the following sense is connected: “I despaired,” that is, I despised the good things of this present life; “I shall by no means live any longer,” namely, in them, because I chose to die to the world. Thus what follows is not inconsistent: “Spare me, O Lord,” which clearly shows that the statement was not one of despair. “Spare me,” I say; for it is fitting that you should spare me: [Col. 1001A] “for my days are nothing” if you do not spare me—that is, the days of my present life. And he confirms this by adding:

VERS. 17.—“What is man,” since he has become mortal through sin? Nothing, namely. I marvel at this: “because you magnify him,” enriching him with the bounty of reason and the honor of bestowed virtue; “or because you set [or: why do you set] your heart upon him?” That is, why do you bring one so weak to the scrutiny of your judgment?

VERS. 18.—“You visit him,” that is, you enlighten him by the light of your knowledge, “in the morning,” that is, after the darkness of his error has been driven away; “and suddenly,” that is, after this visitation, “you test him” by sudden temptation.

VERS. 19.—“How long” shall that continue by which “you do not spare me,” as was said above, “nor let me go,” namely, from this weariness of mortality, so “that I may swallow,” that is, receive into the belly of my soul, which is the mind itself, “my saliva [or: swallow my saliva]”: that is, the sweetness of your divinity? Saliva, which comes down from the head, signifies the sweetness of divinity. For God is the head of Christ; it is held, as it were, in the mouth like saliva, but is not swallowed because of weakness. The sweetness of divinity can indeed now be tasted by the perfect; but because mortal weakness cannot contain its fullness, it is as saliva that cannot be swallowed. Confessing the cause of this weakness, he adds:

[Col. 1001C] VERS. 20.—“I have sinned.” And, desiring to make satisfaction, he adds: “What shall I do to you, O guardian,” that is, inspector, “of men?” I do not know, namely. For whatever I can do, I would owe to you even if I had not sinned. He continues in complaint: “Why have you made me contrary,” that is, hostile, “to you?” Hence the Apostle says: “When we were enemies, Christ died for us” (Romans 5). “You have made me,” I say, “contrary to you, and” therefore “I have become burdensome to myself”: that is, I weigh down my soul with a corruptible body. If it is because I have sinned—indeed, it is because I have sinned that “I have become burdensome to myself.”

VERS. 21.—“Why do you not take away my sin?” namely, original sin; “and why do you not remove my iniquity?” namely, actual sin. “Why,” I say, “do you not take it away,” either through the coming of the Redeemer, who takes away [Col. 1001D] the sins of the world (John 1), or through imitation of the resurrection? “Behold,” because I have sinned, “now,” that is, in the death of the flesh, “I shall sleep in the dust; and if in the morning,” that is, on the day of judgment, “you seek me,” that is, diligently examine me with mercy set aside, “I shall not stand,” that is, I shall not escape condemnation.

## CHAPTER VIII

VERS. 1, 2.—“But Baldad [Bildad] the Suhite, answering,” that is, no longer enduring words of instruction, “said: How long will you speak such things?” For the words of the just are always burdensome to the unjust. Hence he who here says “How long?” shows that words of edification can no longer be endured. “How long,” he says, “will you speak, and how long shall the abundant spirit”—that is, the overflowing spirit—not, I say, “of wisdom in your heart,” but “of speech from your mouth”—remain unchecked? In saying this he charges Job with having much eloquence but little wisdom.

[Col. 1002A] VERS. 3.—“Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty overthrow what is just?” From what blessed Job had said—“Would that my sins and the calamity which I suffer were weighed in a balance; this would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” (Job 6)—he drew a perverse understanding and constructs against him this accusation: that Job had called God a perverter of judgment. He makes a show of defending the rectitude of the heavenly judgment, lest Job should seem to wish only his own sins, rather than those of others also, to be weighed in the balance.

VERS. 4.—“Even if your sons,” he says, “sinned, and he abandoned them into the hand of their iniquity,” and the rest. As though he said: Your sons were justly destroyed not only for your sins but also for their own. But although this is so:

[Col. 1002B] VERS. 5.—“Yet you,” whose negligence caused them to perish because you ought to have corrected them, 443 “if early in the morning”—that is, with the night of your sins wiped away by repentance—“you rise up to God,” from whom you have withdrawn while you lie in sin, “and entreat the Almighty”; and because prayer is not heard unless it is offered from a clean heart:

VERS. 6.—“If you walk pure,” namely, in thought, “and upright,” namely, in deed, “before him,” that is, where he sees in your inner self, “he will immediately awaken for you,” he who now appears to sleep from not helping one who goes astray, “and will restore in peace”—that which now lies ruined—“the dwelling-place of righteousness,” [Col. 1002C] that is, the state of this present life, in the manner I have described, if you make yourself righteous. “He will restore it,” he says, “in peace.”

VERS. 7.—“So that, if your former things were small, your latter things may be multiplied exceedingly.” Thus heretics promise afflicted Catholics peace—namely, from their own contention—and an increase of temporal goods, if they turn to their sect, which they consider pure like the dawn. And since they also cite the sayings of the ancient Fathers as an argument for their error, he fittingly adds:

VERS. 8, 9.—“Ask the former generation, and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers. For we are of yesterday,” that is, unlearned, “and know nothing,” except what we learn from the fathers. “Investigate,” [Col. 1002D] I say, and from things past you will find this: “because our days upon earth are like a shadow,” since, just as those things which are past have fled away, so these things now present also flee away.

VERS. 10.—“They,” namely, the fathers, “will teach you” what you do not wish to learn from us, “and from their heart,” not, as it were, from a superfluous mouth, “will utter words.”

VERS. 11.—“Can a reed flourish without moisture?” By this comparison Baldad intends to show that blessed Job, like a hypocrite, had formerly flourished in praise or worship of God because of his temporal gifts; and that now, with these gifts withdrawn, he had withered exceedingly by murmuring against God’s justice. What he says is indeed very forceful; but because he says it against a wise man, he ought rather to have said it to fools, as though he were pouring water into rivers for thirsty gardens—after the manner of heretics, whose tongue is often so moved by truth as to strike at their own life.

“Can it flourish,” he says—that is, can it possess the greenness or appearance of any virtue—“the reed,” that is, the hypocrite, “without moisture,” that is, without some gift of heavenly grace or without the stimulus of human praise? A reed is a grass without knots, with which crops are covered. It signifies the hypocrite, who displays himself as free from fault and strives, by the reputation of holiness, to surpass truly righteous persons. “Or,” namely, can “the sedge grow without water?” That is, can a hypocrite be conspicuous without some power of knowledge or signs given him from above? Sedge is a very sharp and hard grass, like esparto, signifying the hypocrite in what follows, namely, because:

[Col. 1003B] VERS. 12.—“While it is still in flower,” that is, in praise, “and is not plucked by the hand”: for whoever dares to reprove a hypocrite is immediately cut by the harshness of that hypocrite’s life; “before all other grasses it withers.” That is, before the term of life, when all flesh withers, of which it is said, “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40)—before life’s end, I say—the life of hypocrites dries up, that is, it withers away from the greenness of assumed uprightness.

In this he denounces blessed Job with excessive bitterness: as though Job, like a reed, had quickly withered in the heat of tribulation because he was a hypocrite; and as though, like sedge, he had cut the hand of one plucking it, because he had opposed Eliphaz’s preceding statements as though they were thorny sayings.

[Col. 1003C] VERS. 13.—“Such,” he says, “is the life [or: way] of all who forget the Lord”: it fails in virtue before life’s end. “And the hope of the hypocrite,” that is, human praise, which he seeks by great labors, “shall perish,” that is, shall diminish, driven by the passing moments of time.

VERS. 14.—“His folly, which now pleases him, shall not please him”: for he is exceedingly foolish who seeks the coin of a passing word from that by which he could have merited the kingdom of heaven. “And as a spider’s web,” woven with great labor, is scattered by a light wind, so “his confidence”—that is, the good work in which he trusts—is taken away by the light breeze of human favor.

[Col. 1003D] VERS. 15.—“He shall lean,” namely, at the examination of the inward Judge, “upon his house,” that is, upon the life praised by flatterers; “and it shall not stand,” but shall fall, as is plainly apparent to all in the parable of the ten virgins (Matthew 25). “He shall support it,” namely, by recounting his works, “and it shall not rise,” when the Judge says: “Do I know you? Depart from me” (ibid.). Thus he will be rejected in judgment.

VERS. 16.—“The reed,” that is, the hypocrite, “appears moist,” watered by charity, “before the sun comes,” namely, Christ coming to judge; “and in its rising its shoot comes forth.” That is, just as the reed springs up together with its flower, which other grasses do not do, so the hypocrite, as soon as he begins to do something good, seeks what holy men do not seek: to be honored by all.

[Col. 1004A] VERS. 17.—“Over a heap of stones,” that is, because of a crowd of admiring people, “his roots become thick,” that is, his thoughts multiply toward the display of a good work; “and among the stones,” that is, among those who look upon him, “he will dwell,” that is, he will strive to remain in the good work.

VERS. 18.—“If the inward Judge swallows him up from his place,” that is, from the favors of present life, in which he has placed his whole mind, “he will deny him and say: ‘I do not know you,’” that is, I do not approve you, as he says to the foolish virgins in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25). And deservedly.

[Col. 1004B] VERS. 19.—“For this is the joy of his way,” that is, of his present life: “that others may again spring up from the earth,” that is, from imitation of him—so that many hypocrites may be propagated.

VERS. 20.—“God will not cast away the simple.” As though he said: Do not imitate that man, but be simple, because God “will not cast away the simple,” whose simplicity is now despised, “nor will he stretch out [or: does not stretch out] his hand to the wicked”: that is, he will not raise from lowliness those mentioned above, who seek earthly glory.

VERS. 21.—“Until your mouth be filled with laughter,” that is, until your mouth is made glad by the abundance of everlasting joy, “and your lips with jubilation,” that is, with the ineffable song of heavenly praise. But “until” is not said because, after the jubilation of the elect, God will stretch out his hand to the wicked; rather, as it is said: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Psalm 109 [110]), after which the Son will not cease to sit at the Father’s right hand. So here it is said, “Until your mouth be filled with laughter,” after which God will not cease to strike the wicked—that is, to punish them in hell.

[Col. 1004C] VERS. 22.—“Those who hate you,” if you are simple, “shall be clothed with confusion,” namely, in the final judgment, when their shame will be full: because the inward Judge will see outwardly, and guilt will be present inwardly before their eyes. “And the tent of the ungodly,” that is, the construction of their earthly happiness, “shall not stand,” because it has no foundation of truth; it will fall into an irreparable ruin, cast down forever into hell.

## CHAPTER IX

VERS. 1, 2.—“And Job answered and said: Truly I know that it is so.” Blessed Job, sitting as a most equitable judge to discern the opinions of those who contradicted him—as is the practice of all good people—endeavors so to uproot what wounds as to preserve what restores. That is, he judges the perverse in such a way as to adopt what is rightly said, declaring: “Truly I know that it is so”: namely, that, as you say, God does not pervert judgment and that the confidence of hypocrites shall not stand (Job 8). 444

Then he continues the very speech which Baldad had interrupted, returning to Eliphaz’s words and, by means of an intervening distinction, connecting it thus: “Truly I know that it is so,” as Baldad says, “and that man, being set in opposition to God, is not justified,” as Eliphaz had said above. For he had said: “Can a man be justified, set in opposition to God?” (Job 25). The answer implied is: No. For a person subjected to God receives righteousness; one set in opposition loses it. This is what he says:

[Col. 1005A] VERS. 3.—“If he wishes to contend with him,” that is, if he wishes to arrogate the glory of his virtue to himself and not to God, “he cannot answer him one thing in a thousand”: that is, he cannot show in himself even the beginning of good living while he presumes upon perfection of life. Here one is taken for the beginning of good living, and a thousand for perfection of life. For as the number ten, multiplied by itself, tends toward a thousand (for “ten times ten are a thousand” [the numerical wording appears corrupt]), so unity, by multiplication, is brought to ten, in this way: “once ten, once ten are” [the printed text is incomplete or corrupt]. Here, therefore, the beginning of good living is signified by one, and perfection by a thousand. It is as though he plainly said: If he claims perfection for himself, he does not even possess the beginning of good living.

And lest anyone easily suppose that it is possible to enter into contention with God:

VERS. 4.—“He is wise in heart,” because he subtly knows our hidden things, “and strong in might,” because he powerfully strikes what he knows. He proves this from effects: “Who,” he says, “has resisted him and had peace?” Certainly neither the angelic spirit, who, falling by resistance, became unpeaceful and restless in himself; nor the first parent of the human race, who, as soon as he resisted the commandment, first felt within himself the shameful conflict of the flesh.

[Col. 1005C] VERS. 5.—“He who removes mountains.” This refers to what Eliphaz had earlier said against Job: “Behold, those who serve him are not stable” (Job 4), and so forth. Yet Eliphaz did not say this against Job concerning proud angels. God’s wonderful grace works with the blessed man so that, with his patience rewarded by the power of the prophetic Spirit, he foresees another similar future event concerning human pride—namely, concerning the Israelite people. For the proud unbelief which God found in that people is similar to the perversity which, as Eliphaz says, he found in his angels. Hence he says:

[Col. 1005D] “He who removes mountains,” that is, the apostles, from the Jews to the Gentiles; “and they did not know,” namely, the Jews, whom “he overthrew in his wrath”: that is, they did not know how much inward light they would lose, or that by expelling the apostles they themselves would be overthrown from the grace of God.

VERS. 6.—“He who shakes,” namely, through Titus and Vespasian, “the earth,” namely, Judaea, “from its place,” with city and Temple overthrown; “and its pillars,” that is, the priests, rulers, teachers of the law, and Pharisees, “shall be shaken [or: are shaken]”: that is, they shall not be permitted to dwell in that land.

[Col. 1006A] VERS. 7.—“He who commands the sun,” that is, the shining life of preachers, “and it does not rise,” namely, for the Jews, from whom God turns away the minds of preachers. “And he shuts up the stars,” that is, the same preachers who illumine the night of present life with the brightness of doctrine; he removes them from those people “as under a seal,” that is, so that they may at some time be sent to them again, just as we seal something away in order to bring it out when the fitting time comes.

VERS. 8.—“He who alone stretches out the heavens,” that is, spreads abroad, for the knowledge of all nations, the apostles expelled from the Jews, concerning whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18 [19]); “and walks,” namely, through those same apostles in the working of miracles, “upon the waves of the sea,” that is, upon the surges of persecution which the world raised. He himself, wonderfully strengthening the virtue of the preachers, laid those waves low.

[Col. 1006B] VERS. 9.—“He who,” in this manner and order, “makes Arcturus,” that is, the holy Church, which, like Arcturus, turns throughout the entire night with seven stars and does not set—indeed, by turning it rises. Thus the Church, ordered in a certain way by the sevenfold Spirit, does not fail when wearied by all tribulations, but is rather strengthened and renewed by adversities. “And Orion,” that is, the holy martyrs. Orion arises in the very severity of the wintry season, and by its rising stirs up storms. Likewise, martyrs who were to endure the troubles of persecution came before the face of heaven, as it were in winter; and, as they bore witness to the faith, the cold mind was stirred into a storm of persecution against the faithful. [Note: [Col. 1005D] Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book IX, chapter 11.]

[Col. 1006C] “And the Hyades,” that is, the holy doctors. When, after the martyrs had been taken away and Christ’s faith shone more clearly, they came into the world’s knowledge, they appeared before the face of heaven like the Hyades appearing after Orion at the proper season. And, in accordance with the name *Hyades*—for they are called *Hyades* from the Greek ὑητός (*hyetos*), “rain,” in Latin, because when they rise they undoubtedly bring rains—they poured down the rain of holy preaching upon the parched earth of the human heart. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Ibid.]

“And the inner regions of the south,” that is, the hidden ranks of angels, in whom there is, as it were, the warmth of the south wind—that is, the full love of the Holy Spirit. He placed the angelic ranks, signified by “the inner regions of the south,” after Orion and the Hyades because God prepared the fellowship of angels for the martyrs and doctors mentioned above.

[Col. 1006D] VERS. 10.—“He,” namely God, besides these things which have been said, “does great and unsearchable things, whose number is without number.” They are “great” in power, unsearchable in their reason, innumerable in their multiplicity. Such and so great is he—alas!

VERS. 11.—“If he comes to me,” namely, by the bestowal of some gift, “I shall not see him”: that is, I shall not know the judgment of the giver, whether it is reward or advancement toward better things—whether he rewards merit here, or nourishes one on the way in order to bring him to his homeland. “And if he departs,” that is, if he permits me to be tested, [Col. 1007A] “I shall not understand,” namely, whether this happens for testing or for condemnation. “I shall not understand,” I say, because after I once willingly lost the eyes of my mind, I now seem to recognize neither the rising nor the setting of the sun.

VERS. 12.—“If suddenly he interrogates,” by summoning the unprepared to his judgment, or striking them with harsh blows, “who shall answer him,” trusting in his own merits? Or “who can say to him, ‘Why do you do thus?’” No one, certainly. For the Apostle says: “O man, who are you to answer God? Shall the thing formed say [or: does the thing formed say] to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Romans 9.)

VERS. 13.—“God,” that is, He who is so wise in heart and so mighty in strength, is one “whose wrath no one can resist” [Col. 1007B], unless he receives the power from God Himself—as Moses did, to whom God said: “Let me alone, that my fury may be kindled against them” (Exod. XXXII). By saying this, He who certainly could not have been held back had He not wished it, was rather granting Moses boldness to plead. But, to take His wrath literally, when He wishes to reject that same Jewish people, “no one can resist Him, beneath whom they are bowed down,” that is, conversely, while the Jews are rejected, those “who bear the world” are inclined to faith in Him—namely, also the kings of the nations. For those who govern the world bear it. Hence they are called in Greek *basileis*, that is, “bases of the people.” For βασιλεύς (*basileus*, “king”) is said to be composed of the Latin *basis* and the Greek λαός (*laos*), which in Latin means “people.”

Or thus: “those who bear the world” are angelic spirits, who, since they are all ministering spirits [Col. 1007C] (Heb. II), are rightly said to bear the world; they are bowed beneath Him, that is, trembling, they bend before His strength.

VERS. 14.—“How great then am I,” namely, I who am constrained by the burden of corruption, “that I should answer Him,” whom even angelic creation, as has been said, trembles before or is unable fully to contemplate, “and speak with my words,” 445 words exceedingly childish in comparison with His wisdom, with Him—disputing, that is, about His judgments?

VERS. 15.—“Even if I have something just, I will not answer Him,” if He should choose to judge strictly; “but I will entreat my Judge,” because human righteousness is imperfect and fearful, and therefore needs prayer.

[Col. 1007D] VERS. 16.—“And when He has heard me calling upon Him”—as is sometimes recognized in this: that, by the infusion of His love, He reveals His grace to one praying more attentively—“I do not believe,” that is, I do not confidently trust, “that He has heard my voice,” when a sudden temptation strikes the soul that had been raised toward God, according to the Psalmist: “They mount up to the heavens, and descend to the depths” (Ps. CVI [107]:26).

VERS. 17.—“For in the whirlwind,” that is, in the disturbance of the elements, namely when He comes manifestly, “He will crush me,” unless I now anxiously fear being crushed; “and He has multiplied [another reading: will multiply] my wounds, even without cause.” As though he said: [Col. 1008A] From this too it is gathered how terrible He is: that He has multiplied my wounds, that is, the condemnation of the human race, “without cause.” This is especially remarkable in infants, though not unjust: “without cause,” namely without actual sin, they are cast down into hell for original sin alone. Yet this may be understood especially of blessed Job, in the sense in which the Lord Himself had said of him: “But thou hast moved me against him, that I should afflict him in vain” (Job II).

VERS. 18.—“He does not allow my spirit to rest,” troubled, namely, by evil report, because people believe that I have been struck for my crimes. “And He fills me with bitterness,” in this way: outward torments tear me, while inward temptations disturb me.

[Col. 1008B] VERS. 19.—“If strength is sought,” namely, for escaping these evils, He is “most mighty,” that is, omnipotent; and therefore it is sought in vain. “If the justice [another reading: equity] of judgment” is sought—namely, so that He may not multiply my wounds without cause—this also is sought in vain. For, whereas a matter in court is customarily handled through witnesses, “no one dares give testimony for me.” But neither do I dare justify my own cause, because:

VERS. 20.—“If I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me”: by its very presumption it will show me to be worthy of condemnation. “If I show myself innocent, it will prove me perverse,” because, as was said above, “He is wise in heart” (v. [Col. 1008C] 4).

VERS. 21.—“Even if I am simple,” that is, innocent, yet, for the reasons stated above, “my soul has not known [another reading: will not know] this,” that is, has not arrogated it to itself. Or certainly, “because no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccles. IX:1). What follows fits this sense well: “I shall be weary of my life,” because of this uncertainty.

VERS. 22.—“It is one thing that I have spoken,” that is, this is the sum of what I have said: “He Himself will consume the innocent and the wicked.” For one who is innocent, compared with His righteousness, is shown not to be innocent; and thus He consumes the innocent, while He consumes the wicked by eternal punishment. Or certainly, He is said to consume the innocent [Col. 1008D] and the just because, though they are divided in the life of the mind, nevertheless by the desert of the first sin they are equally drawn to bodily death: “the learned man dies likewise as the unlearned” (Eccles. II). What remedy he longs for he indicates by adding:

VERS. 23.—“If He scourges,” that is, since our life is crushed for sin by the avenging scourge, “let Him kill once,” that is, let Him come who may die once for us without sin, and by His single death—that is, the death of His flesh alone—remove our double death, that of body and soul. “And let Him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent,” that is, at the long desires of the righteous. For every deferred desire is a punishment; hence [Col. 1009A] Solomon says: “Hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. XIII). Let Him not laugh, that is, let Him not make light of the long desires of those awaiting the Savior, who would die once for sin. For God’s laughter is His refusal to pity human affliction. Having expressed this desire, he immediately adds the very sequence of Christ’s Passion:

VERS. 24.—“The earth,” that is, Christ’s flesh, which He took from earthly material, “was given,” namely, to be crucified, “into the hand of the wicked,” that is, into the hands of the devil’s ministers and satellites. “He covers the face of its judges”: the devil veiled, with the cloud of malice, the minds of the priests and rulers, of Pilate and the mocking soldiers, so that they should not know their Author. “But if it is not he”—the devil, that is, or the Jewish people, who [Col. 1009B] did this—“who is wicked, then who is?” Hence, sighing because he was not worthy to reach that time, he adds:

VERS. 25.—“My days were swifter than a runner.” A runner’s task is to wait just a little, until he sees what he is to announce. Therefore, when all the elect foresee that their days will end before the awaited time of redemption, they rightly grieve that they are taken away more swiftly than a runner. Thus it is plainly added: “They fled,” that is, they passed away before Christ’s coming, “and did not see the good,” that is, Christ Himself, who, being God, is the highest good.

VERS. 26.—“They passed by,” possessing hope alone, “like ships bearing apples,” that is, like those who carry fruit to others and themselves enjoy only its fragrance. So, I say, my days possessed only the hope of the coming Redeemer. Or certainly, just as apples carried in ships are mixed with straw so that they may reach land unharmed, so the days of the elect preceding Christ’s coming set forth spiritual fruit in their Scriptures through the scattered straw of history. “They passed by, I say, like an eagle flying to its food”: with mind uplifted, contemplating the Creator’s light in the manner of an eagle gazing upon the sun’s rays with unblinking sight, foreseeing Him who was to be incarnate, and awaiting with longing hope the accomplishment of this, they were like that eagle greedily flying down from the heights to its food.

VERS. 27.—“When I shall say”—I, the ancient [Col. 1009D] people of God; for these things are spoken in the person of those ancients who preceded Christ’s advent—“when I shall say: I will by no means speak thus,” that is, when I deny the Christ whom I await as future, “I change my face,” that is, I so confound and distort the countenance of the inward person that I am no longer recognized by my Creator, “and am tormented with pain,” that is, I am consigned to eternal damnation.

Morally, the same words must be expounded thus: “My days,” that is, the days of the human being who was created to stand for the vision of light, “were swifter than a runner,” that is, they hasten toward their end each day more swiftly than a runner, because they unfold without any interruption, whereas a runner does not run entirely without taking breath. [Col. 1010A] “They fled,” namely, from their proper state, “and did not see the good,” because by tasting what was forbidden, man lost the eyes by which he could see the highest good. “They passed by like ships bearing apples,” carrying the fruits of the earth through waves: so man now perilously carries, amid the waves of the world, the natural goods of the soul which he received when created in Paradise. And as apples have fragrance without weight, so memory breathes to us the good we have lost, but without the power of enjoying it. “They passed by, I say, like an eagle flying to its food”: just as the eagle, flying, casts itself down again to food through the appetite of its belly, so the mind, which ought to contemplate God alone, now delights in bodily [Col. 1010B] pleasures because it touched food contrary to the command.

“When I shall say, I will by no means speak thus,” that is, I will by no means attempt to investigate why God, who is supremely good, made man, whose days, as stated, He knew would pass away thus; “I change my face,” that is, through consideration of heavenly reverence I restrain my mind, “and am tormented with pain,” grieving that I am compelled to understand matters that concern myself. Nor is it only now, because I am under the scourge, that I impose silence upon my mouth; throughout my whole life I have feared to add my own sins to the common condemnation of the human race.

VERS. 28.—“I feared all my works,” [Col. 1010C] that is, I feared even the good deeds done by me, lest perhaps some deceit of human ambition or negligence should intervene—things which must always be diligently feared in good works. I feared, I say, “knowing that Thou dost not spare [another reading: wouldst not spare] the offender,” because Thou cuttest away our sins either through our repentance or by Thyself, even when Thou forgivest them. Thus, when David said, “I have sinned,” the prophet answered: “The Lord also has taken away thy sin” (II Kings XII), namely, transferring it from eternal condemnation to the scourge of temporal distress. Hence I too, trembling beneath hidden judgment, say:

VERS. 29.—“But if even so I am wicked,” and my works displease Thee, though they now seem to people to have been done hypocritically, [Col. 1010D] “why have I labored in vain,” without the weight of reward? He proves this from the greater by adding:

VERS. 30.—“If I have been washed as with snow-water,” etc. As though he openly said: Truly, if I am thus wicked, then I have labored in vain. For even “if I have been washed as with snow-water,” that is, with tears shining before Thee in the brightness of true humility, or poured out in a desire not earthly but heavenly—just as snow does not spring from the earth like a fountain, but descends from the air—if, I say, I have thus been washed, “and my hands have shone,” before Thee, “as though most clean”: not truly most clean, for that is impossible while I remain in this mortal body, but [Col. 1011A] “as though most clean hands,” that is, having, to the extent possible, some imitation of perfect purity:

VERS. 31.—“Yet Thou wilt dip me in filth,” that is, Thou wilt show me to be immersed in filth, “and my garments will abhor me,” that is, will make me abominable—my corruptible members. Hence follows:

VERS. 32.—“For I shall not answer a man who is like me,” that is: Thou, to whom I must answer, art not such as a man like myself, who benevolently praises what he sees to be praiseworthy, but does not know what is lacking to perfection. “Nor art Thou like a man who can be heard with me equally in judgment,” because all that I do is open to Thee, while I myself do not know in how many ways I am reproved. Here take “equal” in the sense of “peer,” as in hearing and being heard, seeing and being seen, which are not unequal when one human being is judged with another. Of this equality he further says:

VERS. 33.—“There is no one able to reprove both.” As though he said: I cannot myself be heard on equal terms, and the Mediator has not yet come, “who can reprove both,” that is, God presiding in judgment on the one side, and man standing under judgment on the other, “and lay his hand upon both,” by correcting human guilt through the inspiration of righteousness, and tempering God’s wrath by dying.

VERS. 34.—“Let Him take His rod away from me,” [Col. 1011C] that is, let Him come and remove from me the severity of the Law which says, “Whoever has done this or that shall surely die”; and let “His terror,” namely servile fear, “not frighten me,” as the Spirit of adoption as sons consoles me.

VERS. 35.—“I will speak,” with this confidence, “and will not fear Him,” because “perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV). “For while fearing,” that is, while having “the spirit of bondage in fear” (Rom. VIII), “I cannot answer,” that is, repay His deeds with works worthy of them.

CHAPTER X.

VERS. 1.—“My soul is weary of my life,” that is, when I have advanced as stated, then love of this present life is turned into weariness through desire for the life to come. And whereas before I defended myself, then [Col. 1011D] “I will abandon my speech against myself,” that is, I will begin to accuse myself of having erred; and not like many who speak joyfully of things that should be mourned, but “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul,” that is, I will confess my sins in the sorrow of repentance.

VERS. 2.—“I will say to God: Do not condemn me.” This is certainly not defending one’s sin, but imploring pardon by confession. “Show me,” Thou who judgest me, “why Thou judgest me thus,” that is, show that by scourges Thou makest me secure for the judgment to come, and dost not, as in the case of the wicked, begin through present evils to inflict the torments that follow. Or, if the words are referred specifically to Job himself, he asks this because he does not know for what fault he, who had lived blamelessly, is struck. For he grieves under the blow and cannot discover the cause of the blows. It follows:

VERS. 3.—“Does it seem good to Thee,” Thou who art supremely good, “if Thou slanderest me,” that is, entraps me by fabricated accusations, “and oppressest me, the work of Thy hands,” that is, dost violence to Thy creature, remembering that Thou madest it freely; “and helpest the counsel of the wicked,” that is, the purpose of evil spirits, by willingly receiving their accusations?

VERS. 4.—“Hast Thou eyes of flesh,” unable to see inwardly the human spirit, such that Thou dost not know me unless I am exposed by others’ accusations? “Or as man sees”—namely, by testing and investigating—“so wilt Thou see?” Thou, who knewest me perfectly even before time?

VERS. 5.—“Are Thy days as the days of man,” temporal and fleeting, “and Thy years,” failing and passing, “as human times,” which never remain in the same state (Job XIV)?

VERS. 6–7.—“That Thou shouldst seek out my iniquity and search into my sin? And knowest that I have done nothing wicked,” that is, Thou wouldst not know whether I had done evil unless it were told Thee, “when there is no one who can deliver from Thy hand,” that is, bear witness to Thee concerning a human being, because Thou knowest what is in man (John [Col. 1012C] II). He drew material for so devout a confession from what Eliphaz had said against him: “How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation, are consumed as by a moth!” (Job IV). Hence he adds:

VERS. 8.—“Thy hands made me and fashioned me.” As though he said: The house of the body is indeed clay, but made by God; its foundation is indeed earthly, but fashioned by God. These words also destroy the perverse doctrine of the Manichee, who tries to maintain that the spirit was created by God but the flesh by Satan. He also sets the dignity of his creation before the mercy of his Judge. “For He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. CXLVIII). But when He decrees to make man, He first says—something to be weighed reverently—“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). He sets this, therefore, before the compassion of the Maker. As though he said: Why dost Thou despise with such low estimation one whom Thou didst make with such dignity? “Thy hands,” that is, Thy care and counsel, “made me,” not as the other creatures, by the voice of command alone, but with the dignity of workmanship; “and fashioned me wholly round about,” more elegantly, that is, than the other animals. And when Thou hast made me thus, “dost Thou suddenly cast me down,” as Thou didst the angel, who had no occasion of sin arising from weakness and therefore had to be cast down without remission?

VERS. 9.—“Remember, I beseech Thee,” that is, consider [Col. 1013A] my weakness: that “as clay”—as earth becomes clay when water is mixed with it—so Thou “hast made me” when the soul moistens the flesh; “and wilt bring me back into dust,” namely, into the material of my origin through death. And Thou who hast fashioned me in the manner stated, in what order hast Thou propagated me in weakness?

VERS. 10.—“Hast Thou not milked me like milk,” namely in the seed, “and curdled me like cheese,” namely in the flesh?

VERS. 11.—“With skin and flesh”—that is, through the stages of coagulation—“Thou hast clothed me; with bones and sinews,” strengthened little by little, “Thou hast knit me together.” And lest these benefits of condescension should seem scant:

VERS. 12.—“Thou hast bestowed life and mercy upon [Col. 1013B] me,” by the wondrous breathing in not only of the life which I share with beasts, but also of bestowed reason. And again, because Thy gifts need guarding, “Thy visitation has preserved my spirit.” Yet these same things which were said of the formation of the outward person may be understood again in the reformation of the inward person.

“Remember, I beseech Thee, that Thou hast made me as clay,” by pouring the grace of the Holy Spirit into the earthly mind, as water is poured into dust to make clay; “and wilt bring me back into dust,” by withdrawing that same grace to some degree, leaving the mind desolate in the hour of temptation. Shaken by that temptation, and now pondering Thy gifts more subtly, I say: “Hast Thou not milked me like milk,” through the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, that is, drawn me away from the practice of my former way of life; “and curdled me like cheese,” so that I should no longer flow away through desires of the flesh? And lest the flesh should never murmur—for temptation is sometimes useful—“Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh,” that is, surrounded me with the siege of carnal impulses; but lest, shaken by these, I should fail, “Thou hast knit me together with bones and sinews,” that is, strengthened me with virtues and the bonds of commandments. And in such a way or order Thou hast bestowed on me “life,” by which I might rise from the death of sin, and “mercy,” helping thereafter in good work, because without Thee I could do nothing; and “Thy visitation,” that is, either the stroke of the scourge [Col. 1013D] or the compunction of Thy love, “has preserved my spirit,” the human spirit, lest, unguarded, it lose its received gift.

VERS. 13.—“Although Thou hidest these things,” Thy works or benefits, “in Thy heart,” so that “man does not know his end” (Eccles. IX), and, knowing what he is today, does not know what he will be tomorrow—yet why should I tremble concerning myself, when “I know that Thou rememberest all,” that is, that Thou gatherest together all nations? Knowing this, why should I despair?

VERS. 14.—“If I have sinned,” that is, if I have willingly committed sin, “and Thou hast spared me for an hour,” that is, immediately, in that Thou hast washed away my sin through tears of repentance permitted to me, “why dost Thou not allow me to be clean from my iniquity,” so that, even unwillingly, I should endure the memory of that same sin with delight? If pardon has removed the sin, why has it not also wiped it from memory?

VERS. 15.—“And if I am wicked,” that is, if I return to sin and forsake Thee, “woe,” that is, eternal condemnation, “is to me. And if I am righteous,” that is, taking care not to persist in sin, “I will not lift up my head,” while I resist sin, afflicted by the labor of struggle. This is what follows: “Filled with affliction and misery,” because in fighting the enemy I grieve for wounds past and fear those to come.

VERS. 16.—“And because of pride,” that is, lest the mind, conscious of virtue, raise itself in pride, “Thou wilt seize me like a lioness”: as a lioness seeking food for her cubs falls into a pit through appetite for the bait placed there, is received into a trap, and is raised up enclosed by bars, so Thou wilt raise by the helps of mercy to the heights from which he fell the human being cast into this pit of mortality because of forbidden food. Yet daily also, because of pride, someone is “seized like a lioness”: through the vice of self-exaltation he is permitted by divine dispensation to fall into the pit of desire; once he has known his weakness, he is at length restored to pardon by heavenly mercy. Hence it is aptly added: “And returning, Thou dost wondrously afflict me,” that is, Thou who by leaving me had rendered me insensible, “returning,” namely by touching my heart and showing how pitiable I am, “dost wondrously” afflict me through tears and groans. [Col. 1014C] “Wondrously,” I say, not punitively, because the mind, rejoicing in the punishments of its own compunction, marvels amid its tears. And lest, relaxed through idleness, the mind torment itself—or rather, lest it blush at its own blackness within itself.

VERS. 17.—“Thou renewest,” that is, multipliest, “Thy witnesses,” that is, the elect who suffered for truth, “against me,” so that I may be provoked by their examples to act manfully. “Against me,” I say, because everything they do or have done stands opposed to our perversity, as does Thy word itself, of which Thou sayest to me: “Agree with thine adversary” (Matt. V). “And Thou multipliest”—through those whom Thou lovest and yet so wondrously afflictest—“Thou multipliest,” I say, that is, Thou showest to be manifold, “Thy wrath,” while we infer that Thou dost, by manifold strictness [Col. 1014D] or judgment, strike the hardness of the wicked, since Thou so punishest the slight offense of those elect, or exercisest their constancy. “And punishments,” that is, penitential afflictions, “fight within me,” stirred by consideration of them.

Having at length supplied the reason why or in what sense he had said above, “Why did I not die in the womb?” (Job III), he now repeats this very point, as by a concluding summary:

VERS. 18.—“Why didst Thou bring me forth from the womb,” in which I was conceived—that is, from Paradise in which I was formed? “Since,” namely, I was justly to be brought forth, “would that I had been consumed,” that is, hidden in humility, “so that no eye might see me,” namely the devil’s eye; that is, that he might not perceive that through the exaltation of my mind I could be led into headlong transgression. If I had thus “been consumed,”

VERS. 19.—“I would have been as though I had not been,” because I would not have been found by the devil, “transferred from the womb,” that is, from Paradise, without bodily death, “to the tomb,” that is, to the peaceful fellowship of angels.

VERS. 20.—“Is it not,” from this, that “the small number of my days will shortly come to an end?”—though I was created so that I could have possessed unending life. “Leave me therefore,” that is, do not take away the awareness of pain; or help me by setting my sins before my eyes, “that I may bewail my pain a little,” because unless Thou mercifully release me from the guilt of sin in this manner, I cannot go forth to repentance, bound by habit in the tomb of conscience. That I may bewail, I say,

VERS. 21.—“Before I go,” to that place where mourning bears no fruit, “and return no more,” because mercy that spares does not thereafter set free one whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned to places of punishment. “Before I go,” I say—where? “To a dark land,” that is, to hell, which is not inappropriately called a land, because whoever is captured by it is held fast. “Dark,” I say, “and covered by the gloom of death,” that is, separating the condemned from the true light of everlasting life.

VERS. 22.—“A land of misery,” that is, of pain, “and of darkness,” that is, of eternal blindness, “where is the shadow of death,” that is, the obscurity of separation from God, without whom the soul does not live; “and no order,” not because each condemned person is not followed by retribution according to the measure of his crime, but because there the flame does not give light as it does here, nor is fear absent when pain is present; rather, fear is in pain and pain with fear. Hence it is added: “And [another reading: But] everlasting horror dwells there,” because those delivered to the fires both feel pain in their torments and are always struck in their pain by dreadful fear.

CHAPTER XI.

VERS. 1.—When blessed Job came forth as a strong athlete into the spectacle of human beings and angels, Eliphaz first opposed him, Bildad second, both with untiring strength; finally Zophar the Naamathite sets himself against him, [Col. 1015D] whose reply begins with insults, when he says:

VERS. 2.—“Will not he who speaks much also hear?” It is the custom of the insolent always to answer rightly spoken words with their opposite. “Will not he,” he says, “who speaks much,” that is, who is excessively talkative—such as you are; for wisdom, flowing from the mouths of the righteous, sounds like superfluous chatter in the ears of fools—“also hear,” namely, an answer according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself? (Prov. XXVI). “Or will a man full of words be justified?” Certainly not; rather, silence is the practice of righteousness. But the poison spoils the arrow of a true statement—indeed, it rebounds blunted—because the one whom it strikes is strong [another reading: sees], when it attacks the uprightness of a good man. And, like all wicked persons who cannot patiently hear good things, he prepares to reply.

VERS. 3.—“For thy sake alone,” he says, that is, because of you alone, “will men be silent”—namely we, who are both many and wise? “And when thou hast mocked others,” that is, worn them out by excessive talkativeness, “wilt thou be confuted by no one,” that is, will you be shown to be far less wise than you imagine? Certainly this will not be so, because you must be confuted.

VERS. 4.—“For thou hast said: My speech is pure, and I am clean in His sight.” It is characteristic of the malice of wicked persons that they do not consider themselves criminal if they invent crimes against the innocence of good people. Thus this is falsely attributed to the words of blessed Job, though he is nowhere recorded above as having said it. Zophar also represents such persons in this respect: with an ironic concession, wishing verbally for what is good, he says:

VERS. 5.—“But would that God would speak with thee,” that is, would that you yourself did not speak, puffed up with the understanding of your flesh, but that God might speak in you; “and open His lips to thee,” that is, make His judgments known to thee, in whose effect God’s will is made known, just as the human mind is expressed when lips are opened in speech.

VERS. 6.—“And show thee His secrets,” namely, those of which he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments and unsearchable His ways!” (Rom. XI). Displaying that he surpasses his friend in knowledge of these secrets, he at once adds: “And that His law is manifold” [Col. 1016C]. For God’s law is truly manifold—that is, charity, which “is the fulfillment of the law” (Rom. XIII). It is rightly called manifold because, through diligent care, it extends itself to all acts of virtue, as one root spreads into many branches. Would that He “showed this to thee, and thou understoodest,” namely in this way: “that much less is exacted of thee by God,” that is, that you are beaten less “than thy iniquity deserves.” This accusation is not free from a charge of great wickedness: he rebukes a just man even with an accusation of iniquity. Like a confused cutter of wood, while he carelessly swings his axe, the iron slipping from the handle strikes his friend sharply. And still ironically he adds:

[Col. 1016D] VERS. 7.—“Perhaps thou wilt comprehend the footsteps of God,” that is, whence, where, or by what means the gifts of His Spirit come; thou wilt know whenever thou hast heard His voice; “and thou wilt find the Almighty unto perfection,” though neither angelic nor human mind, however greatly enlarged, suffices to comprehend Him.

VERS. 8.—“He is higher than heaven.” In this too there is great injustice: he refutes by a multitude of objections the foregoing ironic proposition, as if blessed Job granted it—namely, as if he trusted himself able truly to find the Almighty and comprehend His footsteps unto perfection—saying: “He is higher than heaven,” etc. His arguments are gathered as follows. Through the narrowness of your understanding, being a human being, you cannot measure or attain the height of heaven, or the courses and locations of the stars. But He “is higher than heaven,” not only than the structure of heaven, which, as supreme wisdom established it, so He transcends by the immeasurability of His Spirit; He is also higher than the elect spirits who are in heaven, because they do not perfectly penetrate the vision of such exaltation. Therefore, “what wilt thou do,” so as to comprehend Him? Again, you do not see through the depth of hell. But He is “deeper than hell,” not only than that dark and penal place, which He surpasses and upholds, but also than all the evil spirits in hell, whose wiles He judges and condemns far more subtly than they themselves had supposed. Therefore, “whence wilt thou know,” such a profound mind of the Lord? Again, you do not know the length of the earth—unless perhaps you presume upon geometrical conjectures—and cannot measure the breadth of the sea. But He

VERS. 9.—“Is longer than the earth and broader than the sea,” not only because He encompasses these elements by confining them within the presence of His power, but because He investigates both the long-suffering of all the righteous who are on earth and the deeds of sinners, who may be signified by the sea, and according to their merits condemns or rewards them. Therefore, “what wilt thou do?”

Or morally thus: “He is higher than heaven,” that is, than any righteous person whose “citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III), whom He surpasses by His greatness. He is “deeper than hell,” that is, deeper than the sinful person disturbed by the darkness of his desires; He searches and judges that person more fully than the person himself can search himself. He is “longer than the earth,” that is, than the person fixed and fruit-bearing in the fertility of hope; for our hope itself cannot now comprehend the fruits He will repay. He is “broader than the sea,” that is, than the person who still fluctuates and is driven by the wind of his mutability; He consoles and instructs that person with a breadth of charity greater than the person himself supposes. Say now, you who murmur about your own overthrow alone, and, thinking that you have comprehended such majesty, dare to prescribe what it ought and ought not to owe you. Say, I say:

VERS. 10.—“If He overturns all things, or gathers them together into one,” so that heaven falls and earth opens, and likewise heaven and the remaining elements are compressed into the one ancient chaos; or so that one who was heaven through a heavenly manner of life suddenly becomes hell, possessed by the darkness of temptation—“if,” I say, “He thus overturns all things or gathers them together into one, who,” being stronger, “will contradict Him?” Or who, being wiser, can say to Him, “Why dost Thou do thus?” Certainly, no one.

VERS. 11.—“For He alone knows the vanities of human beings,” that is, He detects and anticipates their vain thoughts; and therefore no one can resist Him. “And seeing iniquity”—which is worse, since a mind deceived by vanity slips into iniquity—“does He not consider it,” that is, judge it justly and at the fitting time? Indeed He does: namely, when

VERS. 12.—“A vain man,” who has fallen from vanity into iniquity, is further “lifted up in pride” from iniquity itself, “and thinks himself born free like the foal of a wild ass,” that is, like any wild animal held in no one’s possession—free, that is, from the law or command of the Creator. This is already a diabolical sin and does not merit pardon. He stated this universally on Job’s account; it must doubtless be granted, because it is true. He now applies it to Job in particular, not only falsely but most offensively:

VERS. 13.—“But thou hast made firm,” that is, hardened, “thy heart, and stretched forth,” that is, lifted up in pride, “thy hands toward God,” that is, thy works, because thou hast arrogated God’s gifts to thyself.

VERS. 14.—“If iniquity,” etc. As though he were plainly concluding, he says: Therefore, O human being, you will escape the judgment you suffer only if you do this: “If thou put away from thee the iniquity that is in thy hand,” that is, the sin open in outward action, “and injustice does not remain,” that is, does not persist, “in thy tabernacle,” that is, pride in thy mind.

VERS. 15.—“Then thou shalt be able,” through diligence in prayer, “to lift up thy face without stain,” that is, thy mind, with conscience not accusing it; “and thou shalt be steadfast,” no longer doing what would bring plagues again, “and shalt not fear,” because the consciousness of steadfastness will banish fear.

VERS. 16.—“Thou shalt also forget misery,” that is, all the evils of the present life, [Col. 1018C] through the sweetness of God which thou shalt taste beforehand; “and thou shalt not remember it as waters that pass by [another reading: that have passed by]”—for the calamity of the present life passes away—because no concession will overwhelm thee.

VERS. 17.—“And like the brightness of noon,” that is, shining with ardour, “there shall arise for thee,” that is, a bright and fervent renewal of virtue, “at evening,” that is, after temptation. Or “at evening,” that is, at the end of the present life, “like the brightness of noon,” that is, outward brightness shall arise for thee, according to the saying: “It shall be well with him that feareth God in his latter end” (Ecclus. I). “And when thou shalt think thyself consumed,” that is, when previously thou hast almost been bowed down to despair, “thou shalt arise as the morning star,” namely, that which precedes the sun [Col. 1018D] and heralds the coming day; that is, thou who shortly before didst fear that thou wouldst fall into the night of guilt, shalt now announce to others the brightness of the life to come and show forth the day of righteousness. Or thus: “And when thou shalt think thyself consumed,” namely by outward pressures, “thou shalt arise as the morning star”; that is, though falling outwardly, thou shalt be renewed inwardly.

VERS. 18.—“And thou shalt have confidence,” namely, that thou shalt reap in joy, “because hope is set before thee,” namely that hope for which one sows in tears. “And, though dug about,” that is, outwardly disturbed, “thou shalt sleep secure,” that is, thou shalt attain everlasting security. Or thus: “Though dug about,” that is, penetrating into thy inward parts and digging out harmful thoughts, “thou shalt sleep secure,” [Col. 1019A] according to the saying: “I sleep, but my heart waketh” (Cant. V).

VERS. 19.—“Thou shalt rest,” namely, in the sweetness of a good conscience, “and there shall be none to make thee afraid,” that is, none to separate thee from the charity of God. “And many shall entreat thy face,” namely, that thou mayest stand as an intercessor with God on their behalf. Thus heretics, or any perverse persons, when they speak holy things, suddenly reveal in their own promises what they love: namely, that they live, as it were, innocently because they wish to appear to men as intercessors. But immediately returning to words of rectitude:

VERS. 20.—“But the eyes,” he says, “of the wicked,” that is, their intentions—for the eye signifies intention, according to the saying: “If thine eye be single” [Col. 1019B] (Matt. VI), etc.—“the eyes, I say, of the wicked,” that is, the intentions of carnal desires, “shall fail,” that is, when their life comes to an end; “and escape shall perish from them,” that is, they shall find no means by which they may hide themselves from the wrath of the Judge. “And their hope,” that is, the thing which they themselves desired, “shall be an abomination of the soul”; that is, every spiritual person shall abhor their desires and count them as dung (Phil. III).

## Chapter XII

VERS. 1.—Blessed Job, who is indeed a member of the holy Church—which recalls even the proud from the height of their self-estimation and, by the hand of discernment, restores them to the harmony of equality—seeing that the minds of his friends had become swollen through the words of learning which they had brought forth, “answered and said”:

[Col. 1019C] VERS. 2.—“Then are you the only men?” That is: since now all of you have in turn advanced against me, though with differing mockery yet with the same intention, while one compared me to a roaring and crushed lion, another to a perishing tiger because it has no prey, another to a rush that withers when the sun appears, a third to the colt of a wild ass which thinks itself born free—“then are you the only men,” that is, and not I, “and shall wisdom arise [variant: die] with you,” so great, indeed, that in comparison with you I am a beast? You ought not to judge so. For:

VERS. 3.—“I also have a heart,” that is, a rational one, “as well as you; nor am I inferior to you,” that is, I am no less capable than you of reason and instruction [Col. 1019D].

VERS. 4–5.—“He who is mocked by his friend, as I am,” namely undeservedly, who, though speaking reasonably, am compared with beasts, “shall call upon God”; namely, because he has no outward place in which to rest, he shall return more confidently inwardly to God—so that, though he is now “a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich,” that is, true shining knowledge, yet despised in the hearts of the proud because of a lowly person or temporal misery, he may have testimony from God; “prepared,” namely in the sight of all, not for the present, but “for the appointed time,” namely when “we must all stand before His judgment-seat, that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to what he hath done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V). But now [Col. 1020A] it is their time, in whose thoughts he is despised: theirs, I say, is the time to be rich. But what concern have I, sitting upon the dunghill, with riches of this kind? Since they were false, I too have lost them.

VERS. 6.—“The tents of robbers abound in such things.” And they themselves, abounding in the world, from the very riches which they have obtained (Ps. LXXII), “boldly provoke God,” namely by proud thoughts and by hoping in the uncertainty of riches, “when He has given,” that is, permitted, “all things into their hands”; namely because what they seize sometimes benefits those from whom they rob for their cleansing, but brings greater condemnation upon themselves. This may also be understood of those who, receiving gifts of teaching, become puffed up through those same gifts [Col. 1020B] (I Tim. VI), and, wishing to seem greater than others, provoke God by such pride. They are truly robbers, because, while speaking what they do not do, they take up for the use of their own speech the words of the righteous. These things are said jointly to the three friends. Now the discourse turns to Sophar, who had spoken last, saying: “It is higher than heaven, deeper than hell; and how shalt thou know it?” (Job XI).

VERS. 7–9.—“Certainly,” he says, “ask the beasts,” etc. As if he said: Why do you set before me the height of heaven and the depth of hell when I seek knowledge of God? “Ask,” that is, consider, “the beasts,” because from works—which are also abundantly available to us—we know the Maker. Or thus: “Ask the beasts,” that is, persons more sensuous, [Col. 1020C] “and they shall teach thee. The birds of heaven,” that is, lofty-wise persons, “and they shall tell thee. Speak to the earth,” that is, to those wise in earthly things, “and they shall answer thee; and the fishes of the sea,” that is, the curious men of this age, “shall relate to thee.” These various sorts of people shall teach thee, shall tell thee, answer thee, and relate to thee some praise or confession concerning the majesty of the Creator, because “every one aboundeth in his own sense” (Rom. XIV), although they have not ascended the height of heaven nor penetrated the depth of hell which thou dost set before me. “Who knoweth not that the hand of the Lord hath made all these things?”—and therefore that He ought to be known from them? These words may profitably be understood both literally and morally, because every creature which is looked upon gives, as it were, the voice of its own testimony through the very form which it possesses. From these, I say, He ought to be known:

VERS. 10.—“In whose hand,” that is, power, “is the soul of every living thing,” whether for giving or taking away, “and the spirit of all human flesh,” that is, the spiritual understanding by which He can give life to souls dwelling in the flesh among all the nations [Col. 1020D].

VERS. 11.—“Doth not the ear judge words, and the palate of him that eateth taste?” As if he said: What wonder if not all receive understanding equally? Do not the five bodily senses proceed from one brain and yet differ from one another? Does not the ear judge words merely by receiving sound, while the palate of one eating judges taste also by acting—that is, by mixing saliva with food? Thus, not in everyone, but only

VERS. 12.—“With the aged is wisdom, and in length of time prudence”; that is, those already practised in the exercise of good works not only hear God’s words, but also taste and savour them through understanding. The sluggish hearer differs from the prudence of their understanding as much as the ear differs from the palate which judges taste. In this he also rebukes the inexperience of his friends, who through arrogance do not savour the very words of teaching which they utter. And he turns Sophar’s words, which he had spoken unskilfully, to the use of rectitude when he adds:

[Col. 1021B] VERS. 13.—“With Him are wisdom and strength.” As if he said: You have said much concerning God’s strength, but you have kept silence concerning His wisdom, which reveals itself to little ones (Matt. XI). Yet with Him there is not strength alone, but wisdom also. And first wisdom, then strength: because Wisdom, that is, the Word of God, first comes through the Incarnation and reveals itself to little ones; afterward strength displays itself against the proud through judgment. “He hath counsel,” namely in ordering His own things, “and understanding,” in knowing ours. You have said much, I say, about the Lord’s strength, and what you said is true: “If He overthrow all things, or compress them into one, who shall gainsay Him?” (Job XI). I too say this; I too think it.

VERS. 14.—“If He destroy,” that is, abandon a person, [Col. 1021C] “there is none to build,” that is, to replenish, according to the saying: “Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Ps. CXXVI). “If He shut up,” that is, if He refuses to open to one who has entangled himself in a miserable habit, “there is none to open,” namely so that he may find escape through repentance. Thus, I say, I agree concerning the strength of which you spoke; but concerning wisdom, of which you kept silence, I add:

VERS. 15–16.—“If He withhold the waters,” namely of His wisdom, “all things shall be dried up,” because no one, unless He grants it, shall drink the water of saving wisdom (Ecclus. XV). “If He send them forth,” namely through the sevenfold outpourings of the Holy Spirit, “they shall overturn the earth,” that is, the earthliness of the human mind; and, what is wondrous, where earth had been, they shall cause heavens to appear, which “declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII), so that there may be a means of knowing Him concerning whom you said, “How shalt thou know?” (Job XI). Now, as though by a recapitulation, he repeats what he had proposed: “With Him are strength and wisdom.” Here the order is reversed, for above he had said, “With Him are wisdom and strength,” but now he says, “strength and wisdom.” Above, he indicated that He would afterward exact in the strength of judgment those things which He had first taught. Here he shows that He will first destroy the reprobate in the strength of judgment and afterward perfect the fulness of wisdom for the elect in the light of His vision. He now treats more fully of each, that is, of strength and wisdom. “He knoweth,” that is, detects, “the deceiver,” and yet justly permits him to deceive, so that he may always fall headlong from evil into worse evil, according to the saying: “He that hurteth, let him hurt still” (Apoc. XXII:11). “And him that is deceived,” He knows, and yet permits him likewise justly to be deceived, so that, because they often commit evils which they know, they may also fall into evils which they do not know. Intending to speak of strength together with wisdom, he began by setting forth wisdom, the cause for the exercise of strength; strength is exercised in this manner together with that same wisdom.

VERS. 17.—“He bringeth counsellors,” that is, those preachers who preach counsels of life in order to gain temporal profit, “to a foolish end,” that is, to the end at which fools shall arrive; “and judges,” namely those who judge wrongly or before the time, “into stupor,” that is, confusion of mind. [Col. 1022B] In this he strikes at his friends also, who devise counsels through the arrogance of teaching and rashly judge one who has been smitten.

VERS. 18.—“He looseth the belt of kings,” that is, the chastity of those who knew how to rule themselves, namely because of pride, which lifted up their spirit; “and girdeth their loins with a cord,” that is, with the delight of carnal sin, so that lust may rule in their loins.

VERS. 19.—“He leadeth priests,” namely those unworthy of the priesthood, “without glory,” according to the saying: “They that despise me shall be ignoble” (I Sam. II); namely, that they may have no glory before God from the salvation of subjects which they did not seek. “And He overthroweth the mighty,” namely so that, instead of eternal [Col. 1022C] glory, they may take pleasure for a time in temporal rule.

VERS. 20.—“Changing the speech of the truthful,” namely so that they dare not speak the truth which they do not practise; “and taking away the teaching of the elders.” This may more plainly be understood of the Jews, whose speech was changed because they denied Him present whose coming they had foretold; and their teaching, as of elders, was taken away and delivered to the young Church from among the Gentiles. She too says: “I have understood more than the aged” (Ps. CXVIII). And in this way:

VERS. 21.—“He shall pour contempt upon princes,” that is, He shall make contemptible the Jews who seemed to rule; and “lifting up those,” namely the Gentiles, “who had been oppressed,” that is, had lain in unbelief, [Col. 1022D] into the true freedom of faith.

VERS. 22.—“Who revealeth,” namely to those same Gentiles, “deep things,” namely mysteries, “out of darkness,” that is, from the hidden words of the prophets, “and bringeth into light,” namely through the allegorical sense, “the shadow of death,” that is, the Law, which ordained that sinners should be punished by bodily death. But in every nation or rank He daily “pours contempt upon princes,” that is, He makes the proud contemptible and humbles those who presume upon their own strength; and He lifts up those who had been oppressed, namely by vices, into virtues, when they have been humbled by their sins. In this manner He “revealeth deep things out of darkness,” that is, He makes known a veiled meaning from His hidden counsels, and brings into light the shadow of death, that is, wicked [Col. 1023A] action performed in imitation of the ancient enemy, of whom it is written: “His name was Death” (Apoc. VI). This shadow of death, I say, He brings into light: He makes it visible to the sinner who previously did not see it, so that he may escape. There follows concerning the same strength and wisdom:

VERS. 23.—“Who multiplieth nations,” namely as they are daily born, “and destroyeth them,” namely as they daily die; and “restoreth those overthrown,” namely by death, “to wholeness,” because the dead shall rise again. Or thus: “He destroyeth them,” namely because He now leaves them in unbelief, “and shall restore them,” that is, at some time He shall bring them back to the state of faith.

VERS. 24.—“Who changeth the heart of the princes of the people of the earth,” that is, of the scribes and Pharisees—the hearts, that is, of the chief priests of the Jewish nation—“and deceiveth,” that is, justly permits them to be deceived, “so that they walk vainly through trackless places”; that is, so that they vainly attempt to extinguish Christ’s name, toward which no path lies open. Therefore he says, “through trackless places.”

VERS. 25.—“They shall grope as in darkness, and not in light,” that is, they shall test Christ and err as though they were in the darkness of ignorance and not in the light of the prophetic Scripture and His present miracles, through which they could have believed; “and He shall make them wander,” namely because they do not marvel at Him raising the dead, while they now despise Him whom they saw to be mortal.

## Chapter XIII

VERS. 1.—“Behold, all these things,” namely concerning His wisdom and strength, “my eye hath seen,” namely inwardly by the prophetic spirit; “and mine ear hath heard,” namely inwardly from the divine voice; “and I have understood each one,” namely in what order or toward what end they should always be done. But he who does not understand what he sees, as Pharaoh did not understand the dream (Gen. XL), or as Belshazzar did not understand the writing of the hand (Dan. V), is not a prophet. Thus far, from the place where he said, “Certainly, ask the beasts” (Job XII), he has answered Sophar’s words. Then, because he had heard all three friends alike, he answers them thus:

VERS. 2.—“According to your knowledge,” namely that which you have displayed in turn, “I also know, nor am I inferior to you.” Had he not humbled himself, he could have said, “I am superior to you,” since he surpassed them by the spirit of prophecy. “I also know,” I say, namely that with Him are strength and wisdom.

VERS. 3.—“Yet I will speak to the Almighty,” namely because charity casts out the fear of that great strength.
