Supported by such aid, “I desire to dispute with God,” because He Himself gives confidence, who says through the prophet: “Come, and let us reason together” (Isa. I). He will do this later, when he says, “Answer me, how many iniquities I have,” etc. But first, before I dispute with God, “argue against me.”

VERS. 4–5.—“You,” showing that you are “forgers of lies and cultivators of perverse doctrines,” because, contradicting one who speaks truth, you willingly and deliberately invent perversities. By these words he openly shows that they oppose his judgments under the appearance of heretics. “Would that you kept silence, that you might be thought wise.” For Solomon says: “Even a fool, if he hold his peace, shall be counted wise” (Prov. XVII).

VERS. 6.—“Hear my reproofs,” namely those already uttered, “and attend to the judgment of my lips,” namely to what I am about to say: that is, listen attentively.

VERS. 7.—“Doth God,” with whom strength and wisdom are self-sufficient, “need your lie,” that is, your flattery, “that you should speak deceits for Him,” namely by falsely accusing me?

VERS. 8.—“Do you accept His person,” that is, His authority, as though you were as blameless as He; “and do you strive to judge for God,” that is, as God, who is free from sin, without regard for the common frailty of mankind?

VERS. 9.—“Or shall such presumption please Him,” from whom nothing can be hidden—whether in what mind a person judges, or by what fault He may reprove the judge himself? “Or shall He be deceived as a man,” so as to agree with you and order His judgment concerning me according to your opinion? Shall He, I say, be deceived by your frauds as a man is deceived by his flatterers? Not so; rather:

VERS. 10.—“He Himself shall rebuke you,” saying: “You have not spoken rightly before Me” (Job XLII), because “in secret,” that is, in duplicity, “you accept His person”: you arrogate to yourselves His authority to judge on His behalf, thinking one thing and speaking another. This is to judge secretly or with doubleness.

VERS. 11.—“As soon as He shall stir Himself,” that is, as soon as He who now keeps silence shall have declared His judgment concerning me and you, “He shall trouble you,” namely by saying against you such a thing as this: “Thou thoughtest wickedly that I would be like unto thee” (Ps. XLIX); “and His terror shall fall upon you,” that is, it shall awaken you from the sleep of torpor in which you have closed your eyes against the truth.

VERS. 12.—“Your remembrance,” namely that which you establish for yourselves in the world through an earthly mind, “shall be compared to ashes,” namely to ashes “which the wind driveth from the face of the earth” (Ps. XII), unless you repent. [Col. 1024D] These things are to be understood as spoken in their persons to all heretics. “Your remembrance,” I say, which is now agitated by knowledge that puffeth up, “shall be compared to ashes, and your necks,” that is, all the gestures and affections of your pride, “shall be reduced to mire,” that is, shall lie despised in corruption.

VERS. 13.—“Keep silence a little,” that is, do not behave contentiously, “that I may speak whatever my mind shall suggest to me”: not, as you do, from the sense of the flesh, but from the sense of the mind, that is, from intellectual power.

VERS. 14.—“Why do I tear my flesh,” that is, why, I say, or with what hope—surely not from a desire for human praise—“do I tear my flesh,” that is, strictly restrain carnal thoughts? “I tear it, I say, with my teeth,” that is, with the inward senses of the mind, in the manner of one who, angry with some enemy, shows the indignation of his soul by clenched teeth. “Why, I say, do I tear,” that is, count as vile, “my flesh, and carry my soul,” namely the more precious part, “in my hands,” that is, preserve it, lest through care for the flesh it sin in all that it suffers?

VERS. 15.—“Even though He should slay me,” namely He who delivered me to the smiter, “I will hope in Him,” that is, I will love Him, while speaking no folly against Him. “Nevertheless I will rebuke my ways before His face,” that is, I shall not derive this confidence of my hope from my own merits.

VERS. 16.—“And He Himself shall be my Saviour,” namely [Col. 1025B] when I have not trusted in my own merits. He proves this by excluding the contrary: “For no hypocrite shall come into His presence,” because he does not rebuke his ways before Him, but justifies himself before men.

VERS. 17.—“Hear my speech,” that is, my plain utterance, “and receive in your ears my riddles,” that is, words of mystery containing inward power: hear them with the ears of the inward man.

VERS. 18.—“If I shall be judged,” namely I, such a man as this, who do not defend myself as a hypocrite but, as I have said, rebuke my ways before Him, “I know that I shall be found righteous”: not, as you assert, a hypocrite; righteous, I say, because my iniquity has been cleansed through the present judgment. But the whole disputation that follows [Col. 1025C] compels a deeper consideration of this. For here begins the disputation of which he said a little earlier: “I desire to dispute with God.” We must therefore inquire what case he means to present, in which he affirms that he shall be found righteous. He does not intend to propose for discussion or conclusion that he is without sin; for he said shortly before, “I will rebuke my ways before His face,” and shortly afterward he will say, “Who can make clean one conceived of unclean seed?” (Job XIV); and almost everywhere he continues in the same vein as when he said above: “My garments shall abhor me” (Job IX). What case, then, does he now wish to lay before God with such vigour? Certainly this: whether it be fitting for God to bring man with Himself [Col. 1025D] into judgment. In advancing this case, secure through the wonderful virtue of humility that he will attain victory, he says of His judgment:

VERS. 19.—“Who is he that will be judged with me?” That is, let one come who shall answer for God against me. “Why am I consumed in silence?” I will not be silent; I demand a hearing. Thou wilt confess Thyself defeated, O God, when Thou shalt choose to adopt man rather than bring him into judgment with Thyself.

VERS. 20.—“Only do not two things unto me,” namely those which I shall immediately specify, “and then I will not hide myself from Thy face,” that is, having entered into debate with Thee, I shall not flee. As though he said: Since in this disputation Thou, who art also my adversary, dost preside as my Judge, show favour through these two things only which I request.

[Col. 1026A] VERS. 21.—“Remove Thy hand,” that is, Thy strength—namely the Law striking in strength—“far from me,” so that Thou mayest not now employ great strength or the weight of Thy majesty, but reason alone; and let not Thy terror make me afraid, but rather let love give me confidence to speak.

VERS. 22–23.—“Call me, and I will answer Thee,” etc. As if, having already won goodwill, he said: Whether I am a sinner is not now in question; there is no controversy between Thee and me on that point. “Call me,” that is, question me, “and I will answer Thee” how many iniquities I have. “Or at least let me speak,” that is, ask questions, “and do Thou answer me how many iniquities I have,” because I think the same as Thou dost concerning my iniquities. Prudently making this division in the manner of a most skilled rhetorician, he immediately states [Col. 1026B] wherein he and God agree, before saying wherein the controversy lies. First it should be observed that he says “iniquities and sins,” which in ordinary speech differ in that *iniquity* conveys more than *sin*. Every person freely confesses himself a sinner, but sometimes is ashamed to call himself unjust. Likewise he says: “Show me my crimes and offences,” or I will show Thee. Crimes and offences differ in that a crime exceeds an offence in the gravity of sin. Sometimes a crime is found in an act, whereas an offence is more often in thought alone. Concerning these things, I say, I think as Thou dost. I shall now say what it is concerning which I desire to dispute.

VERS. 24.—“Why dost Thou hide Thy face?” That is, why hast Thou deprived me of the light of Thy vision, and dost Thou, so great a Being, regard [Col. 1026C] me, so little a one, as “Thine enemy”? Even if I have sinned, is what Thou dost fitting to Thy strength, fitting to Thy wisdom?

VERS. 25.—“Against a leaf driven by the wind dost Thou display Thy power?” That is, against man, who fell in Paradise from the forbidden tree—that is, who possessed matter for falling or transgression—and therefore is rightly called a leaf. Hence Isaiah also says: “We all have fallen as a leaf” (Isa. LXIV). Against man, I say, who is carried by temptations as a leaf is carried by the wind, dost Thou “display Thy power,” that is, dost Thou deign to exercise Thy strength? And dost Thou “pursue dry stubble,” that is, the same man, born of the earth, once flourishing in Thy grace and abundant in the grain of blessedness, [Col. 1026D] now dry in sin, bereft of the blessedness of immortality as of his grain, and lying like dry stubble, so as to deliver him to eternal fires? He proves this most vehement proposition by the reason which follows, and completes the entire argument in five parts. It is worth distinguishing them, and not without purpose, since he himself declares in this place that he means to engage in a disputation, saying: “I desire to dispute with God.” He therefore proves the proposition by the reason which follows:

VERS. 26.—“For Thou writest,” that is, carefully recordest, “bitternesses against me,” that is, causes of bitterness—sins—as a persecutor. This is what follows: “And Thou wilt consume me with the sins of my youth.” [Col. 1027A] Here it should be considered how grave are the sins of young and old, if even the righteous so fear what they committed in their weak age. He reinforces this reason by confirmation.

VERS. 27.—“Thou hast put my foot in the stocks,” that is, by a strong sentence Thou hast bound my faculty of judgment because of original sin, so that even willing, I cannot escape this exile; “and Thou hast watched all my paths,” that is, my actual sins also; “and Thou hast considered the footprints of my feet,” that is, the examples of my actions. With such attention dost Thou pursue one such as I.

VERS. 28.—I, “who am to be consumed like rottenness,” that is, worn away by the corruption of the flesh, “and like a garment eaten by the moth,” that is, one who is often [Col. 1027B] pierced in mind by sins even unknowingly, as a garment is eaten silently by the moth.

## Chapter XIV

VERS. 1.—“Man born of a woman,” etc. From this point he introduces an embellishment, which is the fourth part of the argument. In this embellishment almost the entire pillar of his strength consists: namely, the exceeding humility by which he presses upon God. Through it Moses was able to hold Him who said: “Let me alone, that my fury may be angry” (Exod. XXXII), standing before Him in the breaking of the heart (Ps. CV). “Man,” he says, namely the man whom Thou pursuest, [Col. 1027C] “born of a woman,” that is, out of weakness, or through her by whom the beginning of guilt commenced, “living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” This is especially unhappy: he is narrowed by time and enlarged by miseries, namely:

VERS. 2.—“Who cometh forth like a flower,” that is, is born shining in the flesh and exposed, tender and frail, to the varieties of this world as to many injuries of the winds; “and is crushed,” that is, reduced through bodily death to corruption. And not after a long delay, but swiftly, “he fleeth as a shadow,” that is, cold from the warmth of divine love, he passes unsteadily away; and until he is utterly crushed, he never “continueth in the same state,” passing from infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, and thus through each age, finally into death.

VERS. 3.—“And dost Thou deem it worthy to open Thine eyes upon such a one,” that is, to exert Thy wrath? This is what follows: “And to bring him into judgment with Thee,” [Col. 1027D] namely concerning that which is impossible for him?

VERS. 4.—For “who can make clean one conceived of unclean seed, except Thou alone?”—namely, Thou who art clean through Thyself? He adds further concerning the shortness of man’s life:

VERS. 5.—“The days of man are short”; Thou art eternal. “The number of his months,” how great it is, “is with Thee,” that is, in Thy power. Hence follows: “Thou hast appointed his bounds,” both for living and for making progress, “which cannot be passed.” For Thou hast appointed how long he shall live temporally, and he cannot live longer, although sacred history reports that fifteen years were added to Hezekiah’s life (IV Kings XX; Isa. XXXVIII). [Col. 1028A] He deserved by pardon to pass beyond the time at which he deserved to die; yet he could not, by all the power of his kingdom, pass beyond the limit which Thou hadst appointed him. Having completed the embellishment, true wisdom, mistress of all eloquence, now adds the conclusion:

VERS. 6.—“Depart,” therefore, he says, that is, remove Thy wrath “from him,” not indeed altogether now, but “a little,” so that they may suffer the punishment of mortality in the body, but that the soul may “rest” from the disturbance of vices. For no one can rest from these while Thou art angry; rather, he to whom Thou hast been angry because of his pride is delivered [Col. 1028B] over to disgraceful passions. Let him “rest,” I say, meanwhile, “until his desired day come, as that of a hired labourer,” that is, when he shall receive eternal rest as recompense for his labour.

VERS. 7.—“A tree hath hope.” Now, at the end of the speech by which he intends to bend judgment, he instructs mercy in the conclusion, showing by an analogy the remedy which he hopes for or desires amid the miseries already described. “The tree,” he says, that is, Christ, the strength of all good things in whom all righteousness is rooted, “hath hope,” namely my hope stored up in Himself, sure and great, for which He will suffer Himself to be cut down. For “if it be cut down,” namely through the Passion of death, “it shall grow green again,” namely through the glory of the Resurrection, “and its branches shall spring forth,” that is, His faithful shall be multiplied.

VERS. 8.—“Though its root grow old in the earth,” that is, though His preaching become despised and rejected among the Jewish people, [Col. 1028C] “and its trunk die in the dust,” that is, though His flesh be extinguished and buried:

VERS. 9.—“At the scent of water it shall bud,” that is, by God’s power it shall rise from the dead, “and make a crown of foliage,” namely a gathering of apostles and all the faithful, “as when it was first planted”; that is, it shall be acknowledged or believed to be such as it was before God became man, and glorified with the Father in the glory which it had before the world existed (John XVII).

VERS. 10.—“But man,” that is, whatever sinner refuses to graft himself by faith into this tree, “when he shall be dead,” namely in guilt, “and stripped,” namely of righteousness, “and consumed,” namely in punishment [Col. 1028D]—“where, I ask, is he?”

VERS. 11.—“As waters withdraw from the sea,” so “in that day all his thoughts shall perish” (Ps. CXLV); and how? “As a river, emptied, dries up,” to which the empty body after the soul has been withdrawn is rightly compared.

VERS. 12.—“So man,” namely such a man, “when he sleepeth,” namely in death, “shall not rise again,” namely for this world, so as again to be inundated either with adversities, signified by the sea, or with worldly prosperities, understood by the river because its water is sweeter and drinkable. For he shall rise for another world, not for this one which he loved. This is what follows: [Col. 1029A] “Until heaven be worn away,” that is, until the end of this world.

What is here lacking may be seen in Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, book XII, chapter 5 after its beginning, through chapter 17 of the same book; *Patrologia*, vol. LXXV.

## Chapter XV

VERS. 15.—“Behold, among the saints,” which is the greater thing, “none is innocent [variant: immutable], and the heavens,” that is, those who, though by nature earthly men, became heavens by pursuing heavenly things, “are not clean in His sight,” namely in their own judgment. One of them says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I).

VERS. 16.—“How much more abominable and useless is man,” namely such as thou art, “who drinks [Col. 1029B] iniquity like water,” that is, who commits it without any reconsideration?

VERS. 17.—“I will show thee,” namely what I think concerning thee. “Hear me: what I have seen,” that is, not mere reports, but “what I have seen,” what I have understood, what I have experienced, “I will declare.” And I ought to declare it.

VERS. 18.—“For wise men,” namely those whom I ought to imitate, “declare and do not conceal the sayings of their fathers,” that is, the judgments of their fathers.

VERS. 19.—“To whom alone,” namely not also to fools, “the earth was given,” that is, the stable and fruitful Church of the elect. This too is characteristic boasting of heretics. “And no stranger,” he says, “shall pass through them,” that is, the devil shall not prevail [Col. 1029C] against them—against you, however, he is proved to have prevailed. The devil is called a stranger according to the saying: “For strangers,” that is, evil spirits, “are risen up against me” (Ps. LIII).

VERS. 20.—“All the days of the wicked man are spent in pride.” This is what he had proposed to recount; and with excessive presumption, beyond judgment, Eliphaz—who in his first speech had reproved him for hypocrisy—now, in this second encounter, establishes that he is wicked. For he begins to speak of the wicked man as though he had experienced in blessed Job what he above professed to have learned universally concerning every wicked man, when he said, “What I have seen I will recount to you.” Yet he still retains some little regard for his friend, in that he does not expressly call him wicked by name, but speaks generally of the wicked man on his account, saying: “All his days the wicked man is proud.” As though he said: What is manifest in you—you who were proud in prosperity and now despair in adversity, which itself is great pride. For in what follows he speaks against him, or on his account, as though he were wicked or despairing. He is “proud,” I say; and this is remarkable. For “the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain”; that is, it is remarkable that he exalts himself as though certain of his future, whose life is held under the penalty of uncertainty.

VERS. 21.—“The sound of terrors,” that is, the expectation of condemnation, “is always in his ears,” that is, in the conscience by which he is accused; “and when there is peace,” that is, when forgiveness of sins has been promised to the penitent, “he,” namely the despairing man, “suspects snares,” that is, deceit. This is what follows:

VERS. 22.—“He did not believe,” that is, he does not hope, “that he can return” through repentance “from darkness,” namely from his condemnation, “looking on every side at the sword,” that is, taking the judgment of that same condemnation as certain.

VERS. 23.—“When he moves himself to seek bread,” that is, the sustenance of this present life, “he knows,” conscience accusing him, “that the day of darkness is ready at his hand,” that is, in his work: he fears what he does, but does not avoid what he fears.

[Col. 1030B] VERS. 24.—“Tribulation will terrify him,” namely that same prepared day of darkness; “and distress will surround him,” namely, as he is always anxiously considering what objection he may raise against truth, “like a king prepared for battle,” that is, despising to ask for the terms of peace even when an embassy has been sent (Ps. CXXI).

VERS. 25.—“For he has stretched out his hand against God”—something which Antichrist, the head of all the wicked, will especially do—“and has strengthened himself against the Almighty,” namely, he prospers for a short time.

VERS. 26.—“He ran,” that is, he acted without hindrance, “against Him with uplifted neck,” that is, with boldness, “and armed with a fat neck,” that is, with pride, supported as it were by much flesh through an abundance of possessions.

[Col. 1030C] VERS. 27.—“Fatness covered his face,” that is, his mind: namely, the desired abundance of earthly things; “and fat hangs from his sides,” that is, from those joined and attached to him. For whoever clings to a powerful and wicked person likewise swells from his power or from the fatness of possessions.

VERS. 28.—“He will dwell in desolate cities,” that is, he will take pleasure in the bands of perverse men forsaken by God, “and in deserted houses,” that is, in the praises of people abandoned by God, “which are reduced to tombs,” that is, which have fallen away from the building of life.

[Col. 1030D] VERS. 29.—“He shall not become rich,” understand, inwardly; “nor shall his substance endure,” namely because he swells outwardly. Nor shall he “send his root into the earth” [or: “his own root”]: namely, because his life is quickly uprooted at the movement of the hidden decree, and because his thought is never planted in desire for eternal life.

VERS. 30.—“He shall not depart from darkness,” that is, he never seeks by repentance the light of righteousness. “Flame shall dry up his branches,” that is, his dependents who cling to him: carnal desires will inflame them. “He shall be taken away,” that is, condemned, “by the spirit of his mouth,” that is, because of the unbridledness of his mouth, which he set against heaven and did not restrain from speaking against God.

[Col. 1031A] VERS. 31.—Let no one who is such “believe, deceived in vain by error,” that, if he believes, “he is to be redeemed at some price,” that is, by almsgiving obtained from plunder, since he does not restrain himself from vices.

VERS. 32.—“Before his days are fulfilled,” namely those which he imagines to be long, “he perishes” [or: “will perish”], that is, he is snatched away from the present life; “and his hand withers” [or: “may wither”], that is, it is found dry from every good work.

VERS. 33.—“Like a vine in its first blossom his cluster shall be harmed,” that is, just as a vine—or an olive tree—when it puts forth blossom is harmed by a light breeze: his cluster is his work, which seemed perfected through hypocrisy. This is what follows:

[Col. 1031B] VERS. 34.—“The congregation of the hypocrite is barren.” Here, as in the other matters mentioned above, he still strikes at blessed Job indirectly: as though he, who seemed in prosperity to have borne fruit for God, has now, shaken by the scourge, been harmed so quickly that he is carried into rebellion against God. Concerning his supposed deserts he pronounces a universal sentence of condemnation, saying: “And the fire,” namely of Gehenna, “shall devour the tabernacles,” that is, their bodies, in which their souls dwell, “of those who gladly receive gifts”: whether a gift from the hand, that is, money; or a gift from the mouth, that is, praise, which hypocrites love.

VERS. 35.—“He conceived pain.” At last, at the end of his speech, he turns to his hearers and, striking the wicked man mentioned above—whom he undoubtedly wishes blessed Job to be understood as—with what is, as it were, a final blow, says: “He conceived pain,” which is to ponder evil in the mind, “and gave birth to iniquity,” which is to perpetrate evil in deed; “and his womb,” that is, the disposition of his heart, “prepares deceits,” which is to seek excuses in sins.

CHAPTER XVI

VERS. 1, 2.—“But Job answered and said: I have often heard such things.” In this reply blessed Job intends to show in himself what holy Church also loses in the time of affliction: freedom of speech. For in the minds of the reprobate there is no authority which temporal prosperity does not commend. He also treats of the patience of that same Church, which is accustomed patiently to endure as though charged against herself the evils of others falsely imputed to her, and thus strives to restrain her friends from such injury. “I have often heard such things,” understand, such as you say; “I have often heard,” that is, I have become accustomed to bear them patiently. “You are all burdensome comforters,” because, since the office of a comforter is to lessen sorrow, he ought not in a time of mourning to bring words of rebuke. For even if there are matters that ought rightly to be reproved, they should be deferred in affliction, lest by rebuking he increase the sorrow of the afflicted person which he had intended to relieve.

VERS. 3.—“Will windy words have an end?” that is, certainty or any usefulness—words serving inflation rather than uprightness? “Or is anything troublesome to you if you speak?” Understand, no. As though he plainly said: You speak all the more because you hear nothing troublesome about yourself from me. Hence it is added:

[Col. 1032A] VERS. 4.—“I too could speak words like yours,” unless, by preserving justice, I declined to speak such things. “And would that,” or rather, “if only your soul were in place of my soul.” This saying is shown to be a prayer rather than a curse: namely, that friends who did not know how to sympathize through charity with his sorrow might learn by experience how they ought to pity another’s affliction.

VERS. 5.—“I too would comfort you with words,” that is, unlike you with me, I would not burden you with importunate rebukes. “And I would move my head,” that is, I would stir the feeling of my mind, “over you”—you who, over me, moved your heads without affection of mind, indeed with exultation.

[Col. 1032B] VERS. 6.—“I would strengthen you,” so that you would not despair in tribulation, “with my mouth,” that is, with speech harmonizing with affection or with a compassionate mind; “and I would move my lips,” that is, temper my words, “as though sparing you”—you who in no way spare me. “As though sparing,” I say: not indeed sparing, but as though sparing; namely, if there were matters in you deserving reproof, I would not spare you utterly, because I would not remain altogether silent; yet I would seem to spare you, because I would await a time suitable for rebuke.

[Col. 1032C] VERS. 7.—“But what shall I do?” This statement refers to what he had said: “I too could speak words like yours.” “But what shall I do? If I speak, my sorrow does not rest; and if I am silent, it does not depart from me.” Thus certainly holy Church, when she does not see the perverse corrected by her speech, does not have her sorrow relieved; and when she is silent, she grieves all the more, precisely because she is silent, over their lack of correction.

VERS. 8.—“But now sorrow has oppressed me.” This other statement refers to what he had said: “Would that your soul were in place of my soul; I too would comfort you with words.” As though he said: But now the authority of my speech is broken by the fact that my life is judged to have deserved the sorrow which I suffer. No one is ignorant how almost all these things which follow suit blessed Job. But they are applied to the condition of holy Church in this way. Holy Church is pricked by her sorrow when she sees the perverse growing in their wickedness; “and all her limbs are reduced to nothing” when all the weak, by imitation of the wicked, are made worse in their weakness.

[Col. 1032D] VERS. 9.—“And my wrinkles,” he says—that is, the double-minded persons in my body who do not amend the wickedness of their duplicity—pursue me and reproach me in the time of adversity. “And the false-speaker is stirred up,” that is, strengthened: namely, all who distrust the promise of eternity, “against my face,” that is, openly, “contradicting me.” In prosperity, when they did not dare openly to contradict me, I endured them, as it were, behind my back.

[Col. 1033A] VERS. 10.—“He has gathered his wrath against me.” The malicious spirit rules in their minds; he has gathered “his wrath”—which until then had been dispersed through hidden temptations—“against me,” that is, in my affliction he heaps it all together and concentrates it in purpose. And with his “threatening teeth,” that is, raging in his persecutors and executioners, “my enemy,” namely the devil, “looked upon me with terrible eyes”: that is, by the counsels of the wicked, rightly called his eyes on account of their cunning or worldly learning, he devised cruel punishments against me.

[Col. 1033B] VERS. 11.—“They opened their mouths over me,” that is, they do not fear to preach the evils of their error against me, “reproaching,” that is, mocking the doctrines of the right faith. “They struck my cheek,” that is, they especially persecute those whom they see set openly before others and usefully placed over them, and who crush the lives of carnal persons by the word of correction, as with certain teeth, in order to incorporate them into me. In the literal sense also he expresses his humiliation very sorrowfully, because whoever is struck on the cheek is reckoned unworthy of every honor or reverence. And by doing this “they were sated with my punishments,” because then the reprobate think that they have done some great thing when they kill the lives of preachers.

[Col. 1033C] VERS. 12.—“God has shut me up,” in all these ways, “with the wicked man,” that is, with the ancient enemy, permitting my flesh to his power; “and into the hands of the ungodly,” namely malicious spirits or cruel men, “he delivered me”—to the destruction of the flesh, not of the soul.

VERS. 13.—“I, once wealthy, have suddenly been crushed.” This too is very evident in blessed Job himself. But holy Church is suddenly crushed in this respect: evils become so much heavier to the unprepared minds of the weak as they are endured more unexpectedly. “He seized my neck,” that is, he restrained my freedom. For the neck, as it signifies pride in the wicked, so in the good it signifies the upright bearing of freedom. This answers what Eliphaz, speaking above of the wicked man in order to taunt blessed Job, had said: “He ran against God with uplifted neck, armed with a fat neck” (Job XV). As though he said: Therefore I seem now to have run against God with uplifted neck and armed with a fat neck, because now the enemy “has seized my neck,” that is, has crushed my freedom; “he broke me,” first in the loss of outward goods, then also by the grievous ulcer of my body; “and he set me up for himself as a target,” that is, with none resisting, he loaded me with many blows, just as a target is freely set up to be struck by the shooting of arrows. This is sufficiently plain both literally and typologically, because blessed Job was covered with wounds on every side, and holy Church was set up as a target for her persecutors, as the Apostle says: “For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this” (I Thess. III), that is, that we have come for this purpose: to be struck.

[Col. 1034A] VERS. 14.—“He surrounded me with his spears; he wounded my loins; he did not spare.” These things suit both Job himself and holy Church universally. But what follows, “and he poured out my entrails upon the ground,” cannot stand literally at all, unless by entrails poured out upon the earth you understand the affection for his children, who were crushed and destroyed. Perhaps it may suitably be understood in that way. But holy Church, while she is surrounded by spears from her enemy, that is, attacked by darts of temptations in her members, has her entrails—that is, those who seem to serve the inner sacraments—poured out upon the earth, that is, often drawn away to secular business.

[Col. 1034B] VERS. 15.—“He has cut me down with wound upon wound.” This too is clear literally in blessed Job, because while one messenger reported his losses, another came while he was still speaking, and at last Job himself was struck in his own person (Job I). But Church is cut down with wound upon wound in her weak members when sin is added to sin, so that guilt may be more vehemently increased. And because the ancient enemy is strengthened by such a sequence, it is rightly added: “He rushed upon me like a giant,” because the malignant adversary, when he cannot be resisted, fights as a giant does. Yet in this, and in all the things said above, blessed Job plainly suggests to those who understand devoutly according to the letter that he was not so wicked that the things which Eliphaz shortly before had said concerning the wicked could deservedly be said of him. For, in describing the devil’s blazing envy against himself by such an image, he indicates more clearly than light to attentive readers that the same devil had risen hostile against him in treason, and had deprived him only of bodily goods through hatred of that soul which he could not turn away from God. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1034C] VERS. 16.—“I sewed sackcloth upon my skin,” that is, I continued visible affliction upon my outer man; “and I covered my flesh with ashes,” that is, the sackcloth—the harshness of the blow inflicted upon me—had this effect: it made me recognize that I am ashes. If one wishes to refer this to the universal Church, her flesh or skin is likewise covered with sackcloth and ashes when, because of the sin of the flesh, penitence is imposed upon any of her members. Hence it is well added:

[Col. 1034D] VERS. 17.—“My face has swollen with weeping.” In Job this saying plainly expresses the greatness of his sorrow; but in the Church it likewise signifies the great sorrow of the prelates, who, being set openly as the face, mourn with motherly affection the inward death of their subjects. “And my eyelids,” he says, “have grown dim.” This too is plain literally, since from excessive weeping the eyes of those who mourn are sometimes darkened. Typologically, the eyelids of holy Church are those who keep watch through the night of this present life over the paths which must be foreseen for the people subject to them. When they do not understand God’s hidden judgments, the eyelids of holy Church are indeed dimmed.

[Col. 1035A] VERS. 18.—“I have suffered these things”—namely all the things stated above—“without iniquity in my hand,” that is, not on account of any definite or named sin which I know myself to have committed, “when I had pure prayers to God,” that is, when, without the leaven of hypocrisy of which you accuse me, I offered God acceptable sacrifices. Yet this is more truly and consistently fitting for holy Church to say concerning her Head, of whom it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II). Yet he suffered, while he had pure prayers to God, that is, while he even prayed for his persecutors (Luke XXIII). Blessed Job himself likewise had pure prayers to God in that he remained kindly disposed even toward his abusive friends and offered sacrifices acceptable to God for them.

[Col. 1035B] VERS. 19.—“Earth, do not cover my blood.” With remarkable purpose, through prophetic grace, he adjures that earth which does not cover Christ’s blood but confesses it, and marks both doorposts—that is, of soul and body—with the manifest and public confession of his Passion: the earth, I say, that is, holy Church. He adjures it not to cover, that is, not to allow to remain covered, his blood flowing down in gore; earnestly desiring that it may be found in everlasting remembrance among those who, from the beginning of the world, have shared in the testimony of Christ’s blood. “And may my cry,” that is, my desire which inwardly cries aloud to God, “find no place,” that is, no opportunity, “of hiding in you,” that is, of passing away without remembrance.

[Col. 1035C] VERS. 20.—“For behold, my witness is in heaven”—in heaven, I say, alone; for even my friends on earth detest me. “And my confidant,” namely he who alone knows my heart, “is in the heights,” understand, where he cannot be approached by mortal man. If this is understood as a type of the Savior himself, whose blood, as stated above, the earth—that is, the Church—does not cover in silence, but both celebrates in the sacrament and confesses in public faith, his “witness” and “confidant” are he himself and the Father, of whom he says: “And the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John VIII). Likewise in the Psalm: “Lord, you have examined me and known me” (Ps. CXXXVIII), etc.

[Col. 1035D] VERS. 21.—“My friends are wordy,” understand, you are: because, leaving matters themselves aside, you compose only words, speaking things irrelevant to the matter. Therefore “my eye drops toward God,” that is, my intention flows in tearful compunction as I say: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my confidant.”

VERS. 22.—“And would that he were judged thus”: that is, if—and would that it happened—“a man were judged with God as a son of man is judged with his companion”; namely, so that, just as he knows what he himself says, he might also acknowledge whatever is said against him. Here one must understand: We would certainly hear from him some cause of my suffering other than the one you suppose. “To God,” I say, “my eye drops.” Nor without reason.

[Col. 1036A] VERS. 23.—“For behold, a few years pass,” that is, a short time remains until I find that witness; “and I walk the path by which I shall not return”—the path, of course, of death, which is the way of all flesh, narrow and difficult, by which I shall not return to endure again these evils which I now suffer.

CHAPTER XVII

VERS. 1.—At the remembrance of that path—indeed, through fear of the divine judgment—“my spirit shall be made thin,” that is, it will not grow fat with pride like the spirit of the wicked, but “shall be made thin,” that is, humbled. “My days shall be shortened,” that is, I shall reckon them to be short, as they truly are; “and the grave alone remains for me,” because, disregarding all present things, it remains only to consider what I shall be in the grave.

[Col. 1036B] VERS. 2.—“I have not sinned,” namely so greatly that, as you suppose, I am wicked or hypocritical; “and my eye shall dwell amid bitterness,” that is, amid present scourges: not, as you think, despairing, but it shall “dwell” and persevere—my eye, that is, my intention.

VERS. 3.—“Deliver me, Lord.” Understand: I say this not in despair. “Deliver me, I say, Lord”: send the Christ, my Deliverer, whom you are going to send; “and set me,” that is, cause my substance to be established in that your Only-begotten Son, “beside you; and let the hand of anyone”—whether Jew, pagan, or heretic—“fight against me,” that is, against the faith of the Church, which is my faith.

[Col. 1036C] VERS. 4.—“You have made their heart”—namely, of those in whose type my friends fight against me—“far from discipline,” that is, by your just judgment you have allowed it to be far. “Their heart,” I say: for even if the body is under discipline, when perhaps it is sometimes scourged—as, for example, Jews are killed by the Romans and led captive among all nations—yet the heart is not under discipline when, through so many evils, it is not brought back to humility and repentance. “Therefore they shall not be exalted,” understand, with you; for they are exalted in their own estimation—or rather, therefore they shall be cast down, as it is written: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. LXXII).

[Col. 1036D] VERS. 5.—“He promises prey to his companions.” Having spoken of the multitude of the wicked, he suddenly returns to the head, as frequently happens in Scripture. “He promises prey,” namely the ancient enemy, “to his companions,” that is, the evil spirits: namely, the souls of those whose heart, as has been said, is far from discipline. “The eyes of his children,” that is, the wicked intentions of his followers, “shall fail,” because they love what they cannot hold for long. This is especially apparent in Job himself, whom, as he said above, his enemy “surrounded with his spears” (Job XVI), intending thereby to carry off his soul as prey, conquered by this temptation. Of him he adds:

[Col. 1037A] VERS. 6.—“He has made me a proverb of the people.” He explains this consequence by saying: “And I am an example before them,” because whenever anyone wishes to curse another, he takes his curse from my likeness and wishes upon his adversary the punishment which he sees has happened to me. This has also happened in many ways to holy Church, whose type he here bears, in her martyrs.

VERS. 7.—“My eye has grown dim from indignation,” that is, the understanding of one who possesses within himself some light of truth is troubled in amazement at the divine judgment when he sees himself despised and scorned by the wicked; “and my limbs”—my limbs, I say, alone, not my soul—“are reduced almost to nothing,” because they flow with gore.

[Col. 1037B] VERS. 8.—“The just shall be astonished at this,” namely, that evils commonly happen to the good and goods to the wicked. This is what he said above: “My eye has grown dim from indignation.” “And the innocent man,” namely one not yet perfect—for one may be called innocent who has done neither good nor evil—the “innocent man,” I say, that is, the imperfect man, “shall be stirred up against the hypocrite”: he will envy him his temporal glory, saying something like: “But as for me, my feet had almost slipped; my steps had almost been poured out, because I was envious of the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII). In this way the innocent man is stirred up against the hypocrite if he is imperfect; but if he is perfect, he is stirred up in a better manner, because he will despise the hypocrite flourishing together with his flower.

[Col. 1037C] VERS. 9.—“And the just man shall hold to his way,” that is, he shall not abandon his purpose, saying: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII); “and he of clean hands,” that is, of holy works, “shall add strength,” advancing good beginnings toward perfection.

VERS. 10.—“Therefore,” that is, since these things are so, O hearers, “turn and come,” that is, be humble and show goodwill; “and I shall not find among you,” understand, if you turn, “any wise man,” that is, one who thinks himself wise and does not rather wish to retract what has been said by you against me, who am innocent. This is what holy and apostolic Church says to her hearers: “If anyone among you thinks himself wise, let him become foolish, that he may become wise” (I Cor. III).

[Col. 1037D] VERS. 11.—“My days have passed,” that is, my prosperity has failed—those things, understand, which commonly impede the true wisdom to which I invite you; “my thoughts have been scattered,” that is, earthly cares, which are not absent in prosperity and which tormented my heart, have been laid aside from my heart.

[Col. 1038A] VERS. 12.—“Night,” that is, the very adversity of my affliction, my thoughts, in being scattered, “have turned into day,” that is, into great rejoicing; because it sometimes pleases the just more to suffer evils through adversity than to be wearied by earthly cares through prosperity. “And again after darkness,” namely of the present life, “I hope for light,” that is, the vision of divine brightness which I lost in the first parent. Or, because adversity and prosperity here never cease to succeed one another in turn, it happens that in light night is apprehended, while in night light is anticipated. Thus the saying, “again after darkness I hope for light,” may be understood as though he said: After the present adversity of sorrow, I expect the prosperity of divine consolation.

[Col. 1038B] VERS. 13.—“If I wait,” that is, even if I bear present evils patiently, “hell is my house,” because whoever departed—that is, died—from this world before Christ’s coming, however holy he might have been, could not yet be delivered from the regions of hell. Yet because they were held there without torment, he immediately adds: “And in darkness I have spread my bed,” that is, by striving in good works I prepared for myself rest in that place of darkness. And because this came from the punishment of infirmity:

VERS. 14.—“I said to corruption: You are my father.” As though he said: Therefore “hell is my house,” because the first man became corruption by sinning. “I said,” I say, “to corruption”—that is, inwardly I judged humbly of you, O corruption—“that you are my father,” because I was born from you with sin, which is the cause of corruption; and “to the worms,” that is, to that same corruption, I said: “You are my mother and my sister.” “My mother,” because I was born from you, O corruption; “my sister,” because I came with you into this world.

[Col. 1038C] VERS. 15.—“Where then now is my expectation?” That is, what expectation can the just now have except God alone, the just and justifier—except him who, when he comes, will by the power of his righteousness free the captives of sin and death? “And who shall consider my patience?” Understand: I do not fail to know. But what is short to the one who disposes it is long to the one who desires it. For while he delays:

VERS. 16.—“All that is mine shall descend into the deepest part of hell,” not indeed bodily, but with the soul alone descending there. For I reckon myself wholly to be where I can perceive what I shall receive, because there I shall find, from all that I have done, the recompense of rest. He calls the upper regions of hell “the deepest hell,” because, in relation to the height of heaven, even this expanse of air may not improperly be called hell. Hence, when the apostate angels are plunged into this dark air, the Apostle Peter says: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, casting down those who fell, delivered them, dragged down into Tartarus, to be kept for punishment at the judgment” (II Pet. II). “Do you suppose that at least there will be rest for me?” For I both desire it and yet still doubt whether I shall receive rest, because, however just a person may be, while he lives each doubts concerning himself and does not think before his end that he has attained it.

[Col. 1039A] CHAPTER XVIII

VERS. 1, 2.—“Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you cast about words?” In this reply Bildad intends the same thing which Eliphaz had intended in the preceding reply above: namely, to establish that blessed Job, in God’s eyes, has been convicted as wicked by the witness of his present scourge. Therefore one must distinguish carefully in their words both what they rightly think concerning the reprobate and what they foolishly say against blessed Job. First, Bildad reproves him for boasting, saying, “How long will you cast about words?” At the same time he denies that his words have any final cause—that is, usefulness—when he says, “To what end?” so that you understand, “to none.” Then he reproaches him with ignorance, adding: “Understand first, and then let us speak.” Thus heretics also think the constancy of holy Church is pride; they suspect that she does not understand what is said; and they complain indignantly that they themselves are despised, with proud resentment, saying what follows:

[Col. 1039B] VERS. 3.—“Why are we reckoned as cattle,” understand, beings without understanding, “and have become filthy,” that is, contemptible, “before you?”

VERS. 4.—“You who destroy your soul in your fury,” just as your body has now been destroyed by a most grievous ulcer. For both these men and all heretics consider to be fury what the elect do or say through the fervor of a mind zealously concerned for good. “Will the earth be forsaken,” understand, by God, “for your sake”—for the sake of this fury of yours—unless the whole world agrees with you alone and thinks with you? “And will rocks be moved from their place,” that is, will men firm and eminent in wisdom be moved from their own judgment so as to depart from it for your judgment?

[Col. 1039C] VERS. 5.—“Surely”—whether you wish it or not—“the light of the wicked man shall be extinguished,” that is, the prosperity of his fleeting life shall be ended sooner because of the impiety with which he abuses it, as is proved in you; “nor shall the flame of his fire shine,” namely, the flame he kindled in his heart from the fervor of carnal desires. Understand: it shall not shine, but shall be drawn into darkness. Without doubt, so it shall be.

[Col. 1039D] VERS. 6.—“Light shall be darkened,” that is, the joy of temporal things shall wholly fail, “in his tabernacle,” that is, in his conscience; “and his lamp,” that is, carnal joy. “For a lamp is light in a vessel; but light in a vessel is joy in the flesh.” [Note: [Col. 1039D] Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XIV, chapter 8.] “Therefore the lamp that is above him,” that is, carnal joy, which is not under his control—so that he uses it well—but is over him, possessing him wholly and making him a slave of sins, “shall be extinguished,” as has been said, that is, drawn into darkness.

[Col. 1040A] VERS. 7.—“The steps of his strength shall be straitened,” that is, the advances which are now made wide by his vigorous wickedness shall be constrained by punishment; and “his own counsel shall cast him down,” that is, shall plunge him into the darkness of eternal punishment: namely, the counsel which he now has, which now pleases him—to desire present things and despise eternal ones. It shall cast him down, I say, and he shall justly be permitted to come to the precipice.

VERS. 8.—“For he has set his foot in a net,” that is, he voluntarily admitted the sin by which he is held against his will; “and he walks in its meshes,” that is, when he strives to free himself, then he truly sees by how hard bonds he is held. This is what follows:

[Col. 1040B] VERS. 9.—“A snare shall seize his sole,” because his end is bound in sin, according to the saying: “Sin, when it is completed, brings forth death” (James I). The completion of sin is expressed by the sole, which is the end of the body. Thus the sole is held by a snare when completed sin is not easily escaped, because the sinner is held by vicious habit when he tries to flee. Hence it follows: “And thirst shall rage against him,” namely through that very bondage—the devil, who thirsts to drink the death of the sinner. Or thus: “Thirst shall rage against him,” that is, through the habit of sin the sinner’s desire is kindled more and more, because he thirsts for the pleasure, although he fears the death placed beside the entrance of pleasure.

[Col. 1040C] VERS. 10.—“His trap is hidden in the earth,” that is, the snare of his sin is entangled in earthly gain, because the plotting enemy shows the gain which he may desire, but hides the snare of sin by which he may bind his soul. “And a decoy,” namely one so placed that, while bait is shown, the decoy itself is not seen at all by the passer-by—“a decoy,” I say, “for him,” that is, the danger of deception—lies “upon the path,” that is, where the enemy sees the course of his advancing thought.

[Col. 1040D] VERS. 11.—“Terrors shall frighten him on every side,” that is, he suspects all others to be against him such as he himself endeavors to be against everyone; “and his feet shall entangle him,” that is, those aforementioned terrors shall not permit him to proceed to right action. For it often happens that someone fears to be good, lest he suffer from the wicked what he remembers having done to the good.

VERS. 12.—“Let his strength be weakened by hunger,” that is, the strength of his rational soul, by which man is strong in one respect, although in another respect—that is, through corruptible flesh—he is weak. His “strength,” I say, that is, his soul, is weakened by hunger, understand, by hunger for the Word of God; “and want shall invade his ribs,” that is, that same prolonged hunger shall consume the perceptions of his mind, by which hidden thoughts are protected as entrails are protected by ribs. It shall invade, I say, so that the entrails of thoughts, which might have remained sound in concealment, may be poured forth outwardly in pursuit of the appearance of external glory.

VERS. 13.—“Let the beauty of his skin be devoured,” that is, his temporal glory, which is wholly in the skin, that is, outwardly; in contrast to which it is said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV). “And let the firstborn of death consume his arms,” that is, his works—the firstborn sin, namely pride. For since sin is the death, namely, of the soul, and pride is the first sin, pride is rightly called the firstborn of death.

VERS. 14.—“His confidence is torn away from his tent,” that is, from the earth in which we serve as soldiers for a time—namely, the confidence which he had possessed in an abundance of temporal things. “And destruction shall tread upon him like a king” [Col. 1041B], that is, sin or the devil himself; for while alive he is oppressed here, and at the time of his death, because he is carried off to punishment through this, he is subjected to demonic power.

VERS. 15.—“Let his companions, who are not, dwell in his tent,” that is, let apostate angels, his companions, abide in his mind through wicked thoughts—angels who “are no longer,” namely, who withdrew from the highest Being and tend, as it were, toward non-being, because they once fell away from him who truly is. “Let sulphur be scattered in his tent,” that is, let the sin of the flesh rule in his mind, which, filling the mind with certain foul smells, prepares eternal fires; and therefore it is aptly signified [Col. 1041C] by sulphur, which is fuel for fire.

VERS. 16.—“Let his roots be dried up below,” that is, let his thoughts, clinging below to the lowest things, be scorched by utterly wicked temptations. “But above,” that is, by the judgment from on high, “let his harvest be crushed,” that is, after this life let his works be brought to no means of life; indeed, let them be cast away from the reward of the righteous.

VERS. 17.—“Let his memory perish from the earth.” The words are covertly turned toward the head of all the wicked, namely Antichrist. “His memory,” he says, that is, the praise of his earthly power, “shall perish from the earth,” namely, where he strives to extend it; “and his name shall not be celebrated,” that is, shall not, as he intends, [Col. 1041D] be glorified “in the streets,” that is, in the breadth of the world. For streets, indeed, were named from breadth by a Greek designation.

VERS. 18.—“He,” namely God, “will drive him from light into darkness,” that is, from present honour to eternal punishments; “and will remove him from the world,” that is, from this world, namely to the depth of hell.

VERS. 19.—“He shall have neither offspring,” that is, his teaching shall not endure, “nor descendants among his people”: namely, all who are born into evil deeds from his wicked persuasion; “nor any remnant in his lands,” because all his iniquities are brought to an end with the end of the world.

VERS. 20.—“Those who come after shall be astonished at his day” [Col. 1042A], that is, he will then display such great signs and commit deeds so cruel that those whom he finds at the end of the world will be amazed; “and horror shall seize the first,” namely Enoch and Elijah, because he will pierce them with the pain of bodily death. Though they will have constancy from virtue, they will have fear from the flesh.

VERS. 21.—“These, then, are the tents of the wicked,” that is, not those which he now proudly builds with many fittings, and in which he now spreads the name of his glory, but those previously mentioned (above, v. 15), in which sulphur is scattered and the companions of him who is not dwell. “These,” I say, “are the tents of the wicked,” namely in eternal punishments; “and this,” that is, such is “the place of him who does not know God,” that is, who does not approve of retaining God in knowledge, but is lifted up [Col. 1042B] against him.

## CHAPTER XIX

VERS. 1, 2.—“Then Job answered and said: How long do you afflict my soul?” The aims of both parties, stated above, must be kept firmly in mind: namely, that the whole argument of blessed Job’s friends aims at establishing, from the magnitude of his scourging, the magnitude of impiety in him; while his own defence aims at clearing not only himself but also all the righteous who are scourged in this world from such a judgment—namely, lest, when they suffer adversities, they be immediately believed to suffer them for their sins. Unless these aims are clearly distinguished, it is difficult to understand especially what he will shortly say: “At least now understand that God has afflicted [Col. 1042C] me not according to equal judgment,” etc. (below, v. 6). “How long,” he says, “do you afflict my soul,” namely, a soul grieved and anxious because you wish to pronounce it guilty before every Church of God which is to hear these things in the present age; “and crush me with words,” namely, by the mere multitude of your assertions, and not by the truth of the case which you maintain? “How long,” I say?

VERS. 3.—“Behold, ten times you have confounded me,” namely, because you have spoken five times and it was necessary for me to answer five times, grieving that I have argued in vain against your accusations by the reasoning of truth. “And you are not ashamed,” that is, not even reverence for a friend restrains you, “in oppressing me,” that is, in doing violence [Col. 1042D] to my case, and in being angry because it is evident that you cannot harm me.

VERS. 4.—“Indeed, even if I have erred,” namely, as you have often slanderously alleged, “my error shall remain with me,” that is, it will harm me, not you.

VERS. 5.—“But you exalt yourselves against me,” that is, you are not content that it should not harm you, but you insult me deliberately; “and reproach me with my disgrace,” namely, judging from my affliction that I am impious.

VERS. 6.—“At least now,” that is, after you have confounded me ten times, finally blush to oppress me; “understand,” that is, infer from my former life, “that God has afflicted me not by equal judgment,” that is, not by making his scourges equal to my deeds. For I did not say, “by unjust judgment,” but “not by equal judgment,” that is, by repaying like with like, as you suppose; “and has surrounded me with his scourges,” 458 that is, has struck me on every side, so that no earthly or friendly consolation remains by which my spirit may breathe [Col. 1043A].

VERS. 7.—“Behold, I shall cry out,” namely, under these same scourges, “suffering violence,” namely from your judgment, “and no one,” namely among you, “will hear,” that is, will sympathize; “I shall cry aloud,” that is, I shall speak as vehement and piercing pain demands, “and there is no one,” namely among you, “who judges,” namely my case as it truly is. What shall I cry, what shall I cry aloud? Namely this, that:

VERS. 8.—“He has fenced in my path,” that is, my reasoning—namely, in that he has surrounded me with his scourges—“and I cannot pass,” that is, answer you with authority, because my evils, which you allege as evidence of my impiety, are too manifest on every side. I cannot “pass,” I say, through these things, because it is exceedingly difficult, and nearly impossible, for me to make you concede that I can suffer such great evils from God and yet not be impious. For you think that no one can be so struck by a just God unless he is impious. “He has fenced in my path,” I say, “and has placed darkness in my way,” that is, in my understanding—namely, ignorance of his hidden judgment, because I have been unable to penetrate why I am thus scourged [Col. 1043B].

VERS. 9.—“He has stripped me of my glory.” As if he said: Therefore, when I cry and cry aloud, none of you hears, because “he has stripped me of my glory,” namely, that glory which you once revered in me; “and has taken the crown from my head,” namely, that crown in which, when I shone, you, seeing me, ceased to speak and put your finger upon your mouth (Job XXIX).

VERS. 10.—“He has destroyed me on every side,” namely, in every resource which used to command honour for a rich man, “and I perish,” that is, I live in poverty and want; “and, as from an uprooted tree,” namely, one whose hope of greenness is taken away when it is uprooted, “so he has taken away my hope,” namely through the sudden death of my children, who, had they survived, would have made me less contemptible in your eyes [Col. 1043D]. After this:

VERS. 11.—“His wrath has been angry against me,” that is, against my very body; “and he has treated me thus,” that is, he has cast me outside the wall of his protection, “as his enemy,” that is, as unworthy to dwell with his citizens.

VERS. 12.—“At the same time,” that is, as soon as they saw me deprived of his protection, “his robbers came,” that is, the evil spirits sent by him, “and made a way through me,” that is, they boldly broke forth to trample me; “and besieged my tent round about,” that is, they struck my body from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head (Isa. I), a body which is the tent of the soul dwelling in this pilgrimage.

VERS. 13, 14.—“He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me as strangers. My kinsmen have abandoned me, and those who knew me have forgotten me.” This is plain, because all his relatives abandoned him when he was struck down; indeed, they even recoiled from him. For friends depart when the thin dregs of a dried-up cask are gone—which is a lesser matter; how much more when, his possessions lost, the master of the house sits alone on a dunghill and runs with discharge? Yet it must not be omitted that the brothers of our Lord, whose type he bore here, as has often been said—because he could die—namely the Jews, his brothers and kinsmen according to the flesh, also acquainted with and knowing him through the Law and the Prophets, despising him, abandoned him. For “he came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John I) [Col. 1044A].

VERS. 15.—“The lodgers of my house and my maidservants regarded me as a stranger.” This too is plain in the literal sense: for just as swallows are present in summer but depart in winter, so the lodgers, maidservants, servants, and all the household throng, which in the calm summer of prosperity stood ready around the rich man’s tables, saw such a winter of adversity and all flew away. But in the person of the Lord these words are understood thus: “The lodgers of my house and my maidservants,” that is, the priests of my temple and the Levites, “regarded me as a stranger,” that is, they were unwilling to receive or venerate me incarnate; “and I was as a traveller in their eyes,” because, turning aside to them briefly, as a traveller for lodging, I soon passed on to reign over the election [Col. 1044B] of the Gentiles.

VERS. 16.—“I called my servant,” namely, the Jewish people, that is, I bestowed many benefits of miracles upon it, “and he did not answer [respond],” that is, he did not render worthy works. “With my own mouth I entreated him,” that is, through my incarnate presence I humbly taught him in person. “He did not answer,” I say. Indeed:

VERS. 17.—“My wife abhorred my breath,” that is, the Synagogue, once joined to me, disdained to believe in my divinity. In the literal sense he adequately expresses his contempt and misery: a servant did not answer when he called—indeed, when he entreated with his own mouth—and his very wife abhorred his breath [Col. 1044D]. “And I entreated,” he says, “the sons of my womb,” that is, those closest to me by blood; and:

VERS. 18.—“Fools also despised me,” namely, though they had once been accustomed to fear me as wise. “And when I withdrew from them, they spoke against me. Those who had once advised me abhorred me,” namely, now openly showing that they had been friends of my table when they clung to me in prosperity. Or thus, in the person of Christ: “I entreated the sons of my womb,” that is, I humbly taught those whom I powerfully created through invisible divinity, or whom I conceived before the ages through hidden predestination, to be brought forth in the ages when created. “Fools also,” that is, not only the Pharisees and doctors of the Law, but also the crowds, the unlearned people who followed them, “despised me; and when I withdrew from them,” that is, when I did not show signs before them—when, I say, “I withdrew,” that is, when I did not give a sign to those tempting me—“they spoke against me,” namely saying, “He has a demon” (Matt. XI), and, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. XIII), and such things [Col. 1045A]. And:

VERS. 19.—“Those who had once advised me abhorred me,” that is, the teachers of the Law, who advised me, divided many from me by their counsels. “And he whom I loved most,” that is, that same order of Pharisees and teachers of the Law, whom I had most highly honoured among the people by taking them into my own lot, “became hostile to me [turned away from me],” namely by drawing the crowds of the people to agree with them, so that I might be nailed to the cross. And finally:

VERS. 20.—“My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed,” that is, my steadfast courage in my passion found only a few women remaining near it, my disciples having fled. Holy women are signified by the skin because the skin remains outwardly upon the flesh of the body, and the holy women were stretched, as it were, over the body of the Church then being born, serving the Lord in outward ministries by preparing bodily provisions. The disciples are signified by the flesh because, while they preached to the peoples, they clung as flesh to his bone; but at the time of the Passion, when in weakness they trembled, that same flesh was, as it were, consumed. “And only lips were left around [Col. 1045B] my teeth,” that is, after the strength of faith was shaken, words alone remained among my teeth, namely the apostles; that is, those who should have bitten into the life of carnal persons by rebuking it retained among themselves only words of conversation about me. In the literal sense, however, what he says is more plainly evident: “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed,” because the greatness of his pain had consumed it; “to my skin,” I say, because the flesh flowed away in discharge. “My bone clung,” and “only lips were left around my teeth,” that is, though the whole body was now useless, his understanding remained sound; right words were still present, and reason furnished him with the means of speaking what was true [Col. 1045C].

VERS. 21.—“Have pity on me, have pity on me.” As if he said: Since God has fenced in my path in all these ways, 459 therefore I shall cry out, and no one will hear, as was said above. But “at least you, my friends,” that is, at least because you were my friends, out of reverence for our former affection, “have pity, have pity on me,” that is, sympathize with me, “for the hand of the Lord has touched me,” a hand whose purpose concerning ourselves you cannot foresee. Remember that you too are under the same hand, and consider from me the mutability or impotence of your nature.

VERS. 22.—“Why do you persecute me like God,” that is, as though you yourselves had, after God’s manner, no infirmity; “and are you satisfied with my flesh,” that is, do you, delighted by my punishments, speak against me?

VERS. 23, 24.—“Who will grant me”—namely, since now, when I cry out, as I said above, no one hears me—who will grant me “that my words may be written,” because there will be many able to be built up by my patience? “Who will give that they may be inscribed in a book,” that is, in human hearts, “with an iron stylus,” that is, by the strong decree of God, “and upon a plate of lead,” that is, among the Jewish people; “or indeed [otherwise, ‘with a chisel’] that they may be carved in flint,” that is, among the Gentiles, who worship stones and are hard of heart? For Judah is signified by lead, which is softer than iron, because it readily received the Law, saying to Moses, “All that the Lord has commanded we will do”; yet that same Law could more quickly be erased from its heart, because shortly afterward it worshipped a molten calf (Exod. XXXII), and did many similar things at different times. The Gentiles, however, are understood by flint because Christ’s faith could indeed be written in them with greater difficulty, but, once written, could not be erased by any violence of persecutions [Col. 1046A]. Or thus, without distinguishing Gentile and Jew: “that they may be inscribed,” he says, “upon a plate of lead,” that is, in the hearts of those in whom greed formerly reigned. For in the prophet Zechariah too, greed is signified by a talent of lead; this is said to be cast into the midst of the ephah, because the heart of the greedy man is always enlarged in ambition, and the woman sits in it, of whom it is also said: “This is wickedness” (Zech. V), because wickedness is always held in greed. “Or indeed,” he says, “that they may be carved in flint,” that is, in any heavy and hard heart. When asked why he so greatly desires his words to be written, he gives the reason:

VERS. 25.—“For I know,” he says, “that my Redeemer lives.” As if he openly said: For I, who now cry and cry aloud without being heard [Col. 1046B], know that I shall one day be seen and heard, because my Redeemer lives—the Redeemer, namely, who fell into the hands of the ungodly. He does not say “my Creator,” but “my Redeemer,” foreseeing that through his Passion the human race was to be delivered from perpetual death; “and on the last day I shall rise from the earth,” because he will beyond doubt one day effect in us the resurrection which he displayed in himself.

VERS. 26, 27.—“And again,” that is, after I have been stripped, “I shall be clothed with skin”—not another’s, but “my own”; “and in my flesh,” namely not another’s but my own, different indeed in glory but not different in substance, “I shall see my God, whom I myself shall see, and not another.” Not, he says, in such a way that I die and another rises, but I myself shall rise and see God, “and my eyes shall behold him.” A truer or more complete expression of the real and perfect resurrection could not have been given. “This hope is laid up,” that is, is certain, “in my bosom”; for we believe nothing to be more certain to us than what we hold in our bosom [Col. 1046D].

VERS. 28.—“Why then”—namely, since even in such great affliction faith in me is so pure—why, I say, “do you now say, ‘Let us persecute him,’” that is, let us prove by arguments that he is impious; “and let us find the root of the word against him,” that is, let us take an origin for speaking from which we may spread branches of accusation against him—namely, because such a sin will be sought in him on that day of resurrection and judgment [Col. 1047A].

VERS. 29.—“Therefore flee from the face of the sword,” that is, repentantly cease from speaking or doing perversely through fear of that judgment; “for the sword is the avenger of iniquities,” namely, the sword of divine punishment; “and know,” that is, perceive in fear, “that there is judgment,” that is, that an account of good and evil will be required.

## CHAPTER XX

VERS. 1, 2.—“Zophar answered: Therefore,” he says, namely because I see in you the punishment of evils and hear from you that the hope of the righteous is laid up in your bosom, “my various thoughts succeed one another,” doubting to which I should more readily yield: to the scourge which convicts you, or to you who presume upon your righteousness; “and my mind is drawn in different directions,” because what I see in you is different—indeed opposed—to what I hear from you [Col. 1047B].

VERS. 3.—“I will hear the instruction with which you reprove me,” because above you reproached me by saying that you would show us to be fabricators of falsehood, and such things; “and the spirit of my understanding,” by which I can discern whether those things were rightly said, “will answer you [otherwise, ‘me’],” namely according to what you deserve to hear.

VERS. 4, 5.—“This I know,” namely, to have been proved by the facts themselves, “from the beginning, since man was placed upon the earth.” I know this from then until now, and I also have its proof in you: “that the praise [Col. 1047C] of the wicked is brief,” just as your own praise has now vanished; “and the joy of the hypocrite,” namely, such as you too were, “is like a point,” that is, brief. This, I say, has been proved in you, and it will always be so.

VERS. 6, 7.—“If his pride rises to [otherwise, ‘even unto’] heaven,” as yours once rose, “and his head touches the clouds,” as you, towering above others, seemed to yourself to touch heaven: if, I say, his pride rises to heaven, that is, seems to live a heavenly life, and his head—that is, the exaltation of his mind—touches the clouds, that is, makes itself equal to the merits of the saints, “he shall perish at the end like dung,” as you [Col. 1047D], who now sit alone on a dunghill, wretched and ruined. He shall perish “like dung,” I say, that is, either like you or in any other way, condemned for the stench of his vices. “And those who had seen him,” namely exalted and lifted up, “shall say, ‘Where is he?’”—not by asking, but by marvelling at the brevity of his praise and joy.

VERS. 8.—“Like a flying dream he shall not be found,” because while his joy seems to be held, it is lost; like a dream in which some poor persons often marvel joyfully that they have become rich, that honours are brought to them, and that masses of wealth and the like are theirs; but when they suddenly awake, they find how false was that in which they rejoiced. Thus, I say, the hypocrite’s joy flies away and is not found [Col. 1048A]—neither here, where he was lifted up, nor in the eternal rest in which he imagined himself to be. “It passes [otherwise, ‘will pass’],” namely his praise or joy, “like a vision of the night,” because when he awakens in bodily death, he undoubtedly realizes that, while asleep, he had seen human favour around him.

VERS. 9.—“The eye which saw him,” that is, his admirers who gazed at him in admiration, “shall not see him,” when he is taken away in death; “nor shall his place look upon him any more,” that is, the tongue of flatterers, in whose favour he rested, shall admire him no longer.

VERS. 10.—“His sons,” namely those born from imitation of him, “shall be worn down by want,” because they will not deserve to be filled with the bread of wisdom; “and his hands,” that is, his works, “shall repay him his sorrow” [Col. 1048B]. They shall repay him, I say, that is, they shall discharge to him eternal punishment as a kind of debt. Why? Because while he lives, he will behave in this manner.

VERS. 11.—“His bones,” that is, the sense and reason by which a human being is governed, “shall be filled,” that is, habitually corrupted, “with the vices of his youth,” namely those by which he began to corrupt himself in his youth; “and they shall sleep with him in the dust,” that is, they will persist in him until the end of life, when dust returns to dust, 460 and therefore they will not deserve pardon, because such sin as impenitence is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

VERS. 12.—“For when evil is sweet in his mouth,” that is, when he delights in his heart to commit sin, “he hides it beneath his tongue,” that is, he covers his malice with bland speech, according to the saying: “A dissembler deceives his friend with his mouth” (Prov. XI). This is rightly said of the hypocrite, of whom it continues:

VERS. 13.—“He spares it,” namely the evil which he hides beneath his tongue. He spares it, I say, because he loves it and does not wish to pursue it by repentance; “and he will not abandon it,” until, as has been said, he sleeps with it in the dust; “and he conceals it in his throat,” that is, in the hidden place of thought, unwilling to disclose it by humble confession. For he wishes to appear righteous, not to be so [Col. 1048C].

VERS. 14.—“His bread in his belly,” that is, the satisfaction of his temporal pleasure in his mind, because he delights persistently in evils, “shall be changed inwardly into the gall of asps,” that is, in recompense it will embitter his soul through fellowship with evil spirits. Or thus: “His bread,” that is, his knowledge, “in his belly,” that is, in his mind, “shall be changed into the gall of asps,” that is, into the poison of error and deception; because he wrongly understands the word of teaching which he seeks badly, and expounds it still more wickedly in order to corrupt his hearers [Col. 1048D].

VERS. 15.—“The riches which he has swallowed he shall vomit out,” that is, the divine utterances which he has read he shall, blinded by God’s just judgment, hand over to forgetfulness; “and God shall draw them out of his belly,” that is, out of his mind, because God, by just judgment, tears from his memory what he refused to preserve. And as it is said in Zechariah of the flying scroll, “Every thief shall be judged as it is written there” (Zech. V), so it is fulfilled in the hypocrite: he is judged a thief of Holy Scripture, because by saying righteous things he steals for himself the praise due to the life of the righteous [Col. 1049A].

VERS. 16.—“The head of asps rises [otherwise, ‘he sucks’].” As if he said: Therefore he will be punished thus, because the head of asps, that is, the beginning and chief of all vices, namely pride, rises—that is, is great—and lifts itself up against God in his mind. “And the tongue of the viper kills him,” that is, his own tongue, by which he infects others while corrupting good morals with evil speech.

VERS. 17.—“Let him not see”—because he is such, let him not see—“the streams of the river, the torrents,” that is, the sweetness of the Holy Spirit moving with force, according to the saying: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). This river is “of honey and butter”: namely, together with the sweetness of the Divinity, signified by honey—for it is made from the dew of heaven—it also inspires into the human mind the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, rightly signified by butter, because butter is drawn from the flesh of an animal. Let him not see it, I say, either here through the prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit or in the future through the full vision of God; but rather:

VERS. 18.—“He shall pay for all that he has done” [Col. 1049B], namely amid the torments of hell, “yet shall not be consumed,” because, handed over to avenging flames, he always dies and is always preserved in death, so that he whose life here was dead in guilt may there have a death living in punishment. “According to the multitude of his inventions, so shall he suffer,” that is, as he devised many iniquities from his desires, so he shall receive punishments heavier than others.

VERS. 19.—“Because, breaking in by power, he stripped the house of the poor,” namely through greed. As if he said: For he did not sin, as many do, from weakness or ignorance, but fulfilled greed by his violent pride. He broke into and stripped the poor man’s house; he seized it, “and did not build it,” that is, though it would have sufficed for condemnation not to build it, or not to give what was his. For the coming Judge will say to the reprobate: “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat” (Matt. XXV). And he not only did not build the poor man’s house, but even plundered it, which adds to the fullness of condemnation [Col. 1049D].
