VERS. 20.—“His belly is not satisfied,” because greed is not extinguished by the things desired, but grows, after the manner of fire: when it receives wood to consume, it increases; and from that by which the flame seems to be compressed for a moment, it is soon afterward seen to spread. “And when he has what he desired,” that is, when he has gathered all riches through iniquity, “he shall not be able to possess it,” because he will soon be carried away to a place where those riches cannot follow him [Col. 1050A].

VERS. 21.—“Nothing remained of his food,” that is, he gave nothing to the poor, not even of the crumbs falling from his table; “and therefore nothing of his goods shall remain,” namely in the lower regions—not even enough for him to deserve a drop of water.

VERS. 22.—“When he is full, he shall be straitened,” that is, when he has become rich, he shall be distressed; for while living he will be choked by cares, and when dead he will be buried in hell. “He shall burn,” first with the punishments of desire and afterward with the care of keeping his money; “and every sorrow shall rush upon him,” because in the present he is wearied by desires and in the future tormented by punishments. And since perverse desire is punished by such great torments:

VERS. 23.—“Would that his belly might be filled!” For the things by which it is filled in the manner described above are so destructive that they are wished for him to his harm. For that filling of the belly, that is, of the covetous mind, may come upon him to bring about what follows: “That he,” namely God, “may send upon him the wrath of his fury,” that is, the condemnation of eternal judgment; “and rain upon him his war,” that is, abundantly send forth the dense arrows of his judgments [Col. 1050B].

VERS. 24.—“He shall flee weapons of iron.” As if someone were to raise this excuse: he violently acquires so much because he provides against the necessities of the present life. Be it so. “He shall flee weapons of iron,” that is, present necessities, which are indeed hard but transitory, just as iron is hard but is nevertheless consumed by rust; “and he shall run into [otherwise, ‘rush into’] a bronze bow,” that is, God’s judgment, which is both hard and eternal, just as bronze is hard and is more difficult to consume by rust. And as a bow strikes from ambush, so that judgment comes upon the wicked while they do not attend to it. “He shall run into,” I say, “a bronze bow” [Col. 1050C].

VERS. 25.—“Drawn out and coming forth from his sheath,” that is, proceeding from the hidden contrivance of perverse thought to manifest works. Drawn out, I say, by the devil who leads him, and coming forth through his own will to plunder his neighbours; “and flashing,” that is, shining briefly like lightning and striking what lies before it. For precisely where the wicked man is shown splendid, there action is taken so that many may be struck. “Flashing,” I say, “in his bitterness,” because after brief splendour he will be carried away to bitter torments. “Horrors shall go and come upon him,” namely evil spirits, who will say to his soul, “Bend down, that we may pass.” They shall go and come, I say, because while he is thus drawn out and comes forth, every vice ravages his mind; and if some evils leave, others in turn occupy it. This is what follows:

VERS. 26.—“All darkness is hidden in his secret places,” that is, all malice lies concealed in his treacherous thoughts. “A fire not kindled” [Col. 1051A] shall devour him because of these evils—that is, the fire of Gehenna, which the justice that foreknows future things created, in a marvellous manner, from the very origin of the world, so that it might once begin to exist for the punishment of the reprobate, but might never end its burning even without wood. “He who is left in his tent shall be afflicted” by that same unkindled fire, that is, although he wishes to die, he is retained in his flesh, in which he previously dwelt willingly while feeding himself with delights. Thus he shall come to that fire. 461

VERS. 27.—“The heavens shall reveal,” that is, the saints shall judge, “his iniquity,” namely that which he has worked against them; “and the earth,” that is, sinners also, because he injured them too—or the less perfect multitude of the elect, which, in comparison with the heavens, that is, the apostles, is indeed earth, but fruitful earth—“shall rise up against him” [Col. 1051B].

VERS. 28.—“The offspring of his house shall be laid bare,” namely in accusation, the aforesaid heavens revealing it: that is, every sin now hidden in his conscience. “It shall be carried away in the day of God’s wrath,” that is, on the day of judgment. It shall be carried away, I say, from the face of the inward Judge, before whom it now seems to stand through hypocrisy by doing what is right; for now is the day of God’s patience, but in the time of vengeance the day of his wrath will come upon the wicked.

VERS. 29.—“This,” namely this condemnation, “is the portion of the ungodly man from God,” namely, a man separated from God, because he chose not to have God himself as his portion, but to divide for himself a portion apart from God—which is certainly not good. “This is the portion,” I say, “and the inheritance of his words,” namely of all that he has spoken proudly or idly, “from the Lord,” to be repaid to him. Zophar offered these things in such a manner as to conclude the life of blessed Job by what he had said against the hypocrite, as though Job’s iniquities, in Zophar’s judgment, had been revealed even according to the letter by the heavens, and the earth had risen against him: fire fell from heaven and consumed his servants and sheep; the Chaldeans and Sabeans took his oxen, she-asses, and camels and struck his servants with the sword; and now he was afflicted, “left in his tent,” that is, in the body struck [Col. 1051C] with a most grievous ulcer. But he, not abandoning the path of his humility, adds:

## CHAPTER XXI

VERS. 2.—“Hear, I pray, my words,” etc. In this answer he shows the preceding argument to be weak, with which Zophar had begun thus: “This I know from the beginning, since man was placed upon the earth, that the praise of the wicked is brief” (Job XX). For according to Zophar’s intention it follows that no wicked person prospers in his way until the end of his life, which is undoubtedly false. Hence Job himself will shortly oppose this: “Why then do the wicked live, are lifted up, and strengthened with riches?” (v. 7), etc. By this saying he greatly weakens the argument which Zophar seemed recently to have confirmed for himself. For just as not all the wicked are cast down from their prosperity before death in the present age, so surely, by the same judgment of God, not all the righteous are rewarded in the present life with the good fruit of their merits [Col. 1052A]. First, after his custom, he seeks a favourable hearing, saying: “Hear, I pray, my words, and repent,” namely because you think excessively wrongly about me and argue your case from a weak conjecture. Hear, I say, so that it may benefit you. But if it cannot benefit you:

VERS. 3.—“Bear with me.” Bear with me, I say, at least, “and I will speak,” because this is within me: even if I cannot benefit you, yet I will speak for the sake of others; “and after my words, if it seems good to you, laugh.” As if he said: If you listen, you will repent; if you bear with me unwillingly, after my words you will laugh, because the teaching of humility is a heavy burden to proud minds [Col. 1052B]. Someone might say: “Since ‘the righteous man is his own accuser’ (Prov. XVIII), why do you strive so greatly to repel what is charged against you?” To this he answers:

### Verse 4

“Is my dispute indeed against a man, so that I ought not rightly to be distressed?” That is: do you accuse me of having sinned against a man—a thing which ought indeed humbly to be admitted—and not rather against God, which is devilish and undeserving of pardon? For if a man sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him? Is my dispute, then—that is, the charge brought against me by you, on account of which I argue—against a man? You say, namely, that I am ungodly, that my spirit swells against God, and the like [Col. 1052C]. Is this such a matter that I ought not rightly to be distressed?

### Verse 5

“Attend to me,” namely, so that I may be distressed and speak; “and be astonished,” considering what I have done and what I suffer; “and lay your finger upon your mouth,” that is, restrain yourselves from so great a prejudgment. Or, because fingers signify discernment, “lay your finger upon your mouth” means: speak with discernment.

### Verse 6

“And I,” that is, I also, “whenever I remember, am terrified,” that is, I shudder—namely, on hearing what you say. How much more would I not wish to be such as you assert that I am? “And trembling shakes my flesh” [Col. 1052D] through horror at so great a crime as you charge against me.

### Verse 7

“Why then do the wicked live?” As though he said: If, as you suppose, I suffer these things because I am wicked, “why then do the wicked live, are raised up,” namely, in honours, “and strengthened by riches,” since they are allowed to stand, as it were, long and firmly in this life? He now enumerates their prosperity point by point.

### Verse 8

“Their offspring remains before them”: that is, as an increase to their great prosperity, they are given a great patrimony and heirs; a short phrase is materially uncertain in the supplied reading; nor are their heirs themselves barren. For there is “a crowd of relatives and grandchildren before their eyes.” Nor does domestic quarrelling sadden their joys.

### Verse 9

[Col. 1053A] “For their houses are secure and at peace”: secure in vices, at peace from adversities; “and the rod of God is not upon them”—that is, because they are outside discipline, they must consequently be understood not to be sons (Heb. 12). Thus they prosper within; nor does less prosperity smile upon them in their fields.

### Verse 10

“For their ox”—that is, their cow; for the language of Scripture calls an animal of common gender an ox—“their ox, I say, conceived and did not miscarry.” This is the first prosperity of a lord’s herds: that the herd, not being barren, conceives. The second is that conception comes to birth; hence it follows, “the cow gave birth.” The third is that it is brought through nourishment to maturity; hence it also follows [Col. 1053B], “and was not deprived of her offspring.” After the fruitfulness of the herds, the fruitfulness of the household is added.

### Verse 11

“Their little ones go forth like flocks”: namely, so that, just as many things have been granted to them for possession, so many children may spring up to guard them. “And their children rejoice amid lights,” namely, in these things:

### Verse 12

“They take up tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the instrument.” As though he said: While the masters swell with honours and possessions, those subject to them rejoice in amusements.

### Verse 13

“They spend,” in this manner, “their days in prosperity.” But what then? “And in a moment,” he says—that is, swiftly, not after a long distribution of possessions or honours, but ending their life together with their prosperity—[Col. 1053C] “they descend to hell”: that is, they are suddenly transferred from brief and sudden joys to eternal pains. And this happens to them deservedly.

### Verse 14

“They said to the Lord God”—by their conduct, even if not in words—“Depart from us.” This is to sin not through ignorance but deliberately, and, by defending a vicious will, to shut the mind against the Almighty. “We do not desire knowledge of your ways”: that is, we do not approve it. For they refuse to know what they disdain to do.

### Verse 15

“Who,” they say, “is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” The implied answer is: no one. “The fool has said in his heart, There is no God” (Pss. 13, 52) [Col. 1053D]. For they do not believe him to exist whom they do not behold bodily. “And what profit,” they say, “is it to us if we pray to him?”—since he does not give what we worship him for? Such people speak thus because God himself becomes wearisome to those who love the world, since he will not give what they love; and when God is not sought in prayer, the mind more quickly grows weary in prayer.

### Verse 16

“Nevertheless”: that is, although they spend their days in prosperity and their prosperity ends only with the end of life—prosperity, 462, which has been taken from me while I live—yet “their goods are not in their hand,” that is, under the dominion of their mind. Rather, they themselves are servants of their riches and are bound by them; “in a moment, as has been said, they descend to hell” [Col. 1054A]. “Let their counsel be far from me”: that is, far be it from me to be like them in ungodliness, as you suppose. I would rather groan under the present scourge than, rejoicing with them now, afterward endure eternal punishments.

Someone might say: How have you just said, “their goods are not in their hand,” when above you said, “they spend their days in prosperity” (v. 13), and so forth? To this he replies in sorrow or astonishment:

### Verse 17

“How often is the lamp of the wicked extinguished?” That is, how often is their joy, while it seems complete, darkened—whether by the untimely death of a child, by some other loss of household property, by the envy of superiors, or by harsh conflict with equals—“and a flood of pain comes upon them”: that is [Col. 1054B], unexpectedly, the surge of some adversity comes, while amid the changes of present life they think themselves borne along on a prosperous voyage. “And he apportions the pains of his wrath?” God, that is, sends or alternates his wrath against them in portions—against those whom he strikes both here and in the life to come. Now, I say, the lamp of those who are thought happy in comparison with me is extinguished; but in the future:

### Verse 18

“They shall be as chaff before the face of the wind”: that is, by the sentence of the Judge they shall be carried away into eternal fire, just as light chaff is swept away by a great wind; “and as ash which the whirlwind scatters.” Thus the dry souls of those who appeared green for a moment [Col. 1054C] shall be assigned to eternal destruction in the whirlwind of the manifest coming of our God.

### Verse 19

“God will reserve for his children the father’s pain”: namely, he who repays, as it is written, the sins of fathers upon children and grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation (Exod. 20), will repay it, I say, to children who follow their fathers. For concerning those who do not follow them it is likewise written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18). “And when he has repaid, then he will know”: that is, then for the first time he will understand—he who previously “did not wish to understand, that he might do good” (Ps. 35).

### Verse 20

“His eyes shall see his own destruction,” because he would not see his own fault; “and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty,” because [Col. 1054D], while pardon is offered him, he remains unrepentant. And deservedly he “shall drink.”

### Verse 21

“For what does he care about his household after him?”—whether it perishes through neglect or even through his bad example? Blessed Job recalls this not without reason, in keeping with what he had said shortly before (v. 16): “Let their counsel be far from me.” For he had been so concerned for his household that, rising early, he offered burnt offerings for each of his children, saying: “Perhaps my children have sinned against the Lord” (Job 1), and so forth. “He cares nothing for his household”: that is, he does not care whether it perishes by his example, as stated, or is struck for its own sin; “even if the number of his months is cut in half”: that is, even if his life is to be shortened because of his sins [Col. 1055A], yet, with pride urging him, he is not restrained from sin. But if you ask why God has permitted them to be thus blinded:

### Verses 22–26

“Will anyone teach knowledge to God,” he says, “who judges the lofty ones?” As though he openly said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9). “Who judges the lofty ones,” that is, the angels: establishing some in eternal light, casting down others who fell voluntarily into the vengeance of eternal condemnation.

His incomprehensible judgments arrange this: “One dies strong and healthy, rich and happy; his inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are watered with marrow. But another,” like myself, “dies in bitterness of soul without any possessions. Yet together,” that is [Col. 1055B], alike, “they sleep in the dust [another reading: and worms cover them].” As though he said: Since they alike return to the earth, riches ought not to exalt the mind, nor poverty disturb it.

### Verse 27

“Certainly I know your thoughts”: namely, because from my present scourge you infer that I am ungodly; “and your unjust judgments against me,” that is, judgments not corresponding to my deeds. I know, because you compose against me what you say universally about the ungodly. “I know,” I say.

### Verse 28

“For you say,” tauntingly: “Where is the house of the prince?”—of one once swelling with pride in authority—and, putting me forward as a spectacle and example to others, “where,” you say [Col. 1055C], “are the tents of the wicked?” That is: all such men, like this one, perish together with their tents.

What has been said may also be taken allegorically of the unrighteous rich man. “His inward parts are full of fat” (v. 24): that is, his mind is full of the swelling of pride, which is stretched by abundance of possessions as fat arises from food. “And his bones are watered with marrow” (ibid.): that is, dignities, by which he is supported as by bones, are enriched by riches; or his hardened habits are fattened by evil desires. “Another dies in bitterness of soul” (v. 25), desiring to possess riches and unable to do so. “Yet together they all sleep in the dust”: that is, they close the eyes of their minds in earthly desires. “And worms,” that is, carnal cares, “cover them” (v. 26)—both him who has and him who, desiring, does not have [Col. 1055D]. “Certainly I know your thoughts,” namely, as displayed in words or deeds. For it follows: “and your unjust judgments against me,” and the rest as was said above.

### Verses 29–30

“Ask,” concerning what I have said, any one of the travellers—that is, those who use this world not as their homeland but as a road—and “you shall find that he understands these same things”: namely, that “the wicked man is reserved for the day of destruction,” he who prospers here on his journey, “and is brought to the day of wrath,” while he is permitted to flourish here. Nevertheless:

### Verse 31

“Who will rebuke his ways before him?” Although this cannot seem applicable to every ungodly person—since many ungodly persons are rebuked in many ways—it is rightly understood as spoken concerning Antichrist, the head of all iniquity [Col. 1056A]. His deeds cannot be rebuked by a human being except in his absence; hence “before him” is properly added. “Who,” I say, “will rebuke him, and who will repay him for what he has done,” except God?

### Verses 32–33

“He shall be brought to the tombs”: that is, he shall be received into the foul hearts of the reprobate, because only those receive him in whom souls dead to God are found. “And he shall watch over the heap of the dead”: that is, in the assembly of sinners he confidently displays the snares of his cunning.

And do not wonder that, by God’s judgment, Antichrist will be brought to such people or permitted to deceive them; for “he was sweet”—even before he came. “Sweet,” I say [Col. 1056B], “he was to the gravel of Cocytus”: that is, to those same reprobate persons, the same spirit of error was accepted in heart and mouth rather than the Spirit of truth. They are always devoted to fleeting pleasures; hence they are rightly compared to gravel, the little stones of rivers, and they tend toward lamentation, signified by Cocytus—the river which the sages of the world believed to flow in the underworld. Cocytus, moreover, means “lamentation” in Greek, though it commonly denotes the lamentation of women or of any weak persons. Thus Antichrist was, or will be, sweet to the gravel of Cocytus: that is, to reprobate persons who live in a dissipated manner, whose lamentation is truly the lamentation of the weak.

And when he comes, “he shall draw every human being after him”: that is, everyone wise merely in a human way [Col. 1056C], for all the reprobate shall flock after him. “And before him,” that is, before he comes, he shall draw not all—for many are converted from the devil to God—but “innumerable persons.” Therefore he first says, “he shall draw every human being after him,” which is less, and adds, “before him, 463 innumerable persons,” which is more. Although “every human being” seems greater than “innumerable human beings,” the innumerable people whom he draws before himself during five years are far more numerous than all whom he finds present in his own time, namely, three years. Therefore he rightly first says, “he shall draw every human being after him,” which is less, and “before him,” which, as stated, is more.

### Verse 34

“How then do you console me?” That is, how do you accuse me in vain? For he says “console” by antiphrasis: you infer from this adversity that I am an ungodly hypocrite, although many wicked people appear happy, and especially he will prosper who is undoubtedly the head of all ungodliness. “Since your answer has been shown to contradict truth.”

## Chapter 22

### Verses 1–2

“Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: Can a man be compared to God?” Behold, Eliphaz now attacks blessed Job for the third time openly, with no reverence for a friend. For he no longer seeks, while speaking generally against the ungodly, to strike indirectly, as he had done once and twice; rather, he attacks Job personally, charges him with false crimes, and elaborates them in detail [Col. 1057A].

He begins with praise of God, as one who thinks that he is rendering service to him. “Can a man,” he says, “be compared to God, even if his knowledge were perfect?” The implied answer is: No. For in comparison with God, our knowledge is ignorance.

### Verse 3

“What profit is it to God if you are righteous?” The implied answer is: none. For in everything that we do rightly, we help ourselves, not the Lord himself. “Or what do you give him, if your way is blameless?” The implied answer is: none. “For,” says the Psalmist, “you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15).

### Verse 4

“Will he rebuke you because he fears”—your strength, namely—“and come with you into judgment?” like earthly kings, who pre-empt by contrived occasions the suspected power of those subject to them, lest it increase, in order to diminish or utterly remove it [Col. 1057B]. “Does he rebuke you,” he says, “and enter into judgment with you out of this fear?” This is utterly idle, the speech of those wholly unable to measure their words. But he immediately breaks from idle speech into insulting speech, saying:

### Verse 5

“Is it not because of your great wickedness and your infinite iniquities” that he rebukes you? “For you took a pledge” from a widow, and the rest—things which, because they are very clear according to the historical sense, need not be expounded literally; but it must be shown how they accord with the falsehood of heretics.

### Verse 6

The heretics say to holy Church: “You took the pledge of your brothers”: that is, from those who came from us to you, you uselessly required a confession of error; through this they lost the pledge, that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit which they had received from us. “And you stripped the naked,” that is, the simple and unwary, “of their garments”: you deprived them of the adornments of diverse graces [Col. 1057C].

### Verse 7

“You gave no water to the weary”: that is, to one thirsting for the cup of truth, but gave him error to drink. “And you withheld bread from the hungry”: that is, sound doctrine, which we had given, by other teachings.

### Verse 8

“By the strength of your arm”: that is, through the forcefulness of your preaching, you possessed the whole earth; “and, being mighty,” not by the power of truth but by the force of power, “you held it” [Col. 1057D].

### Verse 9

“You sent widows away empty”: that is, peoples separated from us, their lawful pastors, without sound preaching. “And you broke the arms of orphans”: that is, you crushed the well-begun works of our disciples.

### Verse 10

“Therefore you are surrounded by snares,” namely, of your faithlessness; that is, fitting adversity has found you. “And sudden fear troubles you”: that is, the distress which you neglected to consider while prosperity burned within you.

### Verse 11

“And did you think that you would not see darkness”: that is, the disturbance of your joy, in which you presumed that you shone? And did you think that “the rush of flooding waters,” that is, the force of coming tribulations [Col. 1058A], would not overwhelm you? He compares tribulations to swelling waters because they rush in one upon another, like surging waters. “Did you think,” he says—this is taunt and mockery—and he adds:

### Verse 12

“Do you not consider”—now, that is, as you did then when you performed these evils—“do you not consider, I say, that God is higher than heaven and exalted above the summit of the stars,” and therefore does not see what is done on earth? Do you not think this?

### Verse 13

“And you say: What does God know,” intent as he is upon higher things, “and does he judge, as it were, through darkness,” if he sees anything?

### Verse 14

“Clouds are his hiding-place” [Col. 1058B]. Do you say this because the airy regions lie between us and the heavenly seat, and “he does not consider our affairs,” because, caring for things above, he gives less attention to the lowest things, and “walks around the poles of heaven,” so that he cannot see the inward things?

In thinking this, you are deceived. For he is so present to each individual that he never fails all together; he attends to all in such a way as to be present to each; he surrounds outward things so as to fill inward things; he rules the highest things so as not to forsake the lowest; he is present to the lowest so as not to depart from the highest. But you, thinking otherwise as stated:

### Verse 15

“Do you wish to keep the path of the ages?” That is, do you wish to persist in pride? For the path of the ages is pride, just as, on the contrary, the path of our Redeemer is humility. Hence it is added concerning that same path of pride [Col. 1058C]: “which wicked men have trodden,” that is, have habitually walked—namely, all who pass through this life in self-exaltation.

### Verse 16

“They were taken away,” namely, from the present life, “before their time”: that is, sooner than they supposed, while promising themselves longer spans of this life. For since they turn the time granted them not to the fruit of repentance but to the use of iniquity, they lose the span of life which they might have received from divine mercy. “They were taken away,” I say, “and the river,” that is, the course of mortality, “overthrew their foundation”—the foundation which they had fixed in earthly things, because they had not taken care to pass to eternal things [Col. 1058D]. They belonged, as it were, to the earthly generation of Ham, who is described as the first to have built a city on earth. In him it is clearly shown that he laid his foundation on earth who was alien from the solidity of the eternal homeland. “The river,” therefore, “overthrew their foundation.”

### Verse 17

“They said to God: Depart from us.” This was also said by blessed Job and expounded above. “And they thought the Almighty as though he could do nothing.” This also was said by blessed Job in the same sense but in other words: “Who is the Almighty that we should serve him?” (Job 21). Thus, I say, “they thought him as though he could do nothing.”

### Verse 18

“Although he filled their houses with good things,” namely temporal things; for he does not withhold his gifts even from the ungrateful, so that harsher punishments may then punish those whose wickedness gifts here did not overcome [Col. 1059A]. “Let their judgment be far from me.” This also was said by blessed Job. For he says: “Let their counsel be far from me” (Job 21).

### Verse 19

“The righteous shall see” their destruction “and rejoice”: then, namely, when, cleaving to the strict Judge with the perfect security of rejoicing, they will have nothing in themselves to fear. “And the innocent”—he who now grieves as he sees them dying in wickedness—will then “mock them”: that is, he will not be moved by any pity for them, agreeing with supreme justice in the eternal punishment of sinners.

### Verse 20

“Is not their exaltation cut down?” That is, their pride, when they are dragged either from the present life to destruction or from the presence of the eternal Judge to the fires of eternal Gehenna [Col. 1059B]. “And fire shall devour their remnant”: that is, also the flesh which they leave here and receive again in the resurrection, so that 464 they may burn in the flesh in which they sinned.

### Verse 21

“Submit therefore to him”: that is, agree with our judgment concerning him; “and have peace,” not resisting heavenly judgments; “and through these things you shall have the best fruits,” that is, you will perform works pleasing to God. Thus heretics too promise peace and the best fruits only to those who submit to them, because they cease to quarrel with those who think as they do, and believe that only those who agree with them can perform good works.

### Verse 22

[Col. 1059C] “Receive,” he says, “from his mouth”—the law which we teach as proceeding from it—“and place his words in your heart,” words which until now, through hypocrisy, you possessed not in your heart but only on your lips.

### Verse 23

“If you return to the Almighty.” So that the statement proceeds in the person of heretics—for, as said, its literal meaning is sufficiently clear—“If,” he says, “you return to the Almighty,” from whom you departed through error, “you shall be built up,” that is, you shall recover prosperity; “and you shall put iniquity far from your tent,” that is, from both your heart and body, since you will be cleansed both in thought and in deed.

### Verse 24

“He will give flint in place of earth”: that is [Col. 1059D], in place of all those things in which your actions are weak, he will restore solid strength; “and golden torrents in place of flint”: that is, in place of strong action, the brightness of doctrine. For golden torrents flow, as it were, from strength when the brightness of sacred teaching streams from the mouths of those who live well.

### Verse 25

“And the Almighty will be against your enemies”: that is, he will take a stand against evil spirits; and, as he drives them away by his power, “silver shall be heaped up for you”: that is, the bright talent of divine speech shall abound within you. Thus you will say with the Psalmist: “Depart from me, you wicked, and I will search the commandments of my God” (Ps. 118). Certainly he could not search them while he endured the snares of evil spirits in his mind [Col. 1060A].

This is also signified in the action of Isaac under the malice of the Philistines, who filled the wells which Isaac had dug with heaps of earth (Gen. 26). For when unclean spirits inject earthly thoughts into those studying Holy Scripture, they remove, as it were, the discovered water of divine knowledge.

### Verse 26

“Then,” namely, when this silver has been heaped up for you, “you shall abound in delights upon the Almighty”: that is, you shall be satisfied at the feasts of Holy Scripture in love of him; and, according to the words, “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” (Song 8), while you are fed with mystical understandings, you shall daily be raised up to contemplate heavenly things. “And you shall lift up,” in this way, “your face to God” [Col. 1060B]: that is, your mind, through the inward image known and visible to God. When anyone is weighed down by the guilt of sin, his conscience, struck back, fears to lift that image to God.

### Verse 27

“You shall pray to him, and he shall hear you”—he who until now was unwilling to hear you while you despised his commands. “And you shall fulfil your vows”: that is, you will be able to maintain a good resolution, once guilt, or the punishment of guilt that now hinders you, has been removed. For often through guilt the power to do good is taken away from one who wills it.

### Verse 28

“You shall decree a matter, and it shall come to you”: you who now, while unjust, cannot obtain what you seek. “And your light shall shine in your ways”: that is, your righteousness in your deeds will be an example to others [Col. 1060C]. You will have these best fruits if, as I said above, you receive the law from his mouth.

### Verse 29

“For he who has been humbled,” that is, who has humbly received his law, “shall be in glory,” according to the saying: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23; Luke 14, 18). “And he who has lowered his eyes”—who has looked upon no one with contempt, but has judged himself less and inferior to all whom he sees—“shall be saved”: that is, he shall ascend to the height of truth, because he has abandoned the false summit of pride.

### Verse 30

“The innocent shall be saved,” namely, in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom. “But he shall be saved by the cleanness of his hands” [Col. 1060D], because, in the final examination, the justice of the inward Judge saves the person whom God’s mercy here frees from unclean deeds, so that he does not presume upon his own strength.

Although Eliphaz uttered all these things correctly, he did not know to whom he spoke; for he ought not to have dared to teach one better than himself. Yet, as Solomon says, “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1): for good spirits are winged, and, while they fly toward higher things through the hope of truth, they avoid the snares of deception set by wicked men.

## Chapter 23

### Verse 1

“But Job, answering,” begins to state his conduct in plainer words, but completes his speech with the pursuit of lofty mysteries. How unwillingly and under constraint he enumerates his good deeds—because he endured false accusations and was thus, according to the Apostle, compelled to become foolish (2 Cor. 2), though he ought rather to have been commended by his friends—how unwillingly, I say, he does this, he himself shows when he begins his answer in this way:

### Verse 2

“Even now”: that is, while you, who ought to have consoled me, instead compel me by opposing me to console myself by recalling the good things I have done, “my speech is in bitterness” [Col. 1061A]. That is, I speak not with vain boasting but with a bitter mind. “And the hand of my wound is made heavier upon my groaning,” because the purpose of disordered consolation has multiplied the blow which it ought to have diminished.

Or, to refer this more subtly to the figure of holy Church: “The hand,” he says, “of my wound is made heavier,” because the elect consider their first wound, that they were separated from the vision of their Creator; but when further adversities still come upon them in this life, the hand—that is, the force—of their wound is made heavier upon their groaning.

Desiring now to have God as witness that he is about to speak truth concerning himself:

### Verse 3

“Who will grant me,” he says, “that I may know and find him,” so that he may bear testimony for me, “and that I may come even to his throne,” so that my case may be tried between me and you while he presides? He does not desire this vainly, for it will shortly happen when God rebukes his friends and bears testimony to Job, saying: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42) [Col. 1061C].

### Verse 4

“I will set judgment before him”: that is, I call him as witness of my conscience. “And I will fill my mouth with rebukes”—with my rebukes, I say, not praises; because the good deeds which I am about to mention are not so much praises as rebukes, since I utter them not in boasting but in the bitter grief of sorrow.

### Verse 5

“So that I may know the words which he will answer me”: this is what a bitter and humble conscience deserves. “And that I may understand what he will say to me”: that is, what testimony he will bear by the equity of his judgment. And directing himself toward this:

### Verse 6

“I do not wish that he should contend with me in great strength, nor press me by the weight of his greatness” [Col. 1061D]. For the mind of any righteous person is crushed if it is judged strictly by the Almighty. Who, indeed, can be found righteous before him if he examines human life according to the majesty of his strength? I do not desire that. But what do I desire?

### Verse 7

“Let him set equity against me,” rather than strength: that is, weighing human measure, let him conform and adapt himself so that human weakness may be able to endure him.

By these words he seems wonderfully to implore the coming of Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and men, who descended from the strength of his divinity and took on our weakness, so that weak man might at last be able to find access to him through grace. “Let him set equity against me,” I say, as stated [Col. 1062A], “and let my judgment attain victory”: that is, then, victorious through the judgment of my acquittal, 465 I shall exclude the adversary who lies in wait. But what shall I do? How shall I come to his throne?

### Verses 8–9

“If I go to the East, he does not appear,” and so forth. The desire of one seeking the face of the Lord in truth could not have been expressed more ardently. This is sufficiently clear in the literal sense: the Creator of all is not in any one place, because he is everywhere; invisible and uncircumscribed, he contains all things within himself and sees all things. Hence it follows:

### Verse 10

“But he himself knows my way.” As though he said: I cannot see him who sees me; I cannot behold him who scrutinizes me minutely. Yet these words can be understood differently: “If I go to the East,” that is, if I raise my mind in contemplating his majesty, “he does not appear,” because mortal thought cannot prevail to see what he is. “If to the West,” that is, if I lower the eyes of my mind to consider human mortality, “I shall not understand him” [Col. 1062B]; rather, I shall recognize myself to be unworthy of his vision. “And if I go to the left,” that is, if I consent to the pleasures of sinners, “what shall I do?” What progress shall I make? For he cannot be known in the delight of sin. “If I turn to the right,” that is, if I exalt myself because of my virtues, “I shall not see him”; rather, I shall be more severely tried through pride.

“But he himself knows my way.” As though he said: Although I do not see him, I nevertheless trust that before him I may speak the good things I am about to say concerning myself, because “he himself knows my way”: that is, both what I have done and with what intention or humility I now recall these things. He knows. “And he tested me like gold which passes through fire”: that is, the flame of desire in which my soul melts while, as said above, “it seeks him and does not find him,” together with the scourge by which I am tormented, will make me purer for himself [Col. 1062C].

Now, since, though we do not see him, we stand before his throne, who is everywhere present, hear how, as I said, “he himself knows my way.”

### Verse 11

“My foot has followed his footsteps.” As though he said: I have by no means walked in wickedness as you said; rather, “my foot,” that is, every movement or progress of my purpose, “has followed his footsteps,” that is, the examples of his mercy. “I have kept his way,” that is, his law—namely, that law which all naturally know even without Scripture, whose summary is: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4)—“and have not turned aside from it” [Col. 1062D].

### Verse 12

“From the commands of his lips”—those, namely, which he spoke to the holy Fathers beyond the natural law—“I have not departed.” Nor have I observed these merely on the surface; “but in my bosom,” that is, in the secret of my heart and in the root of pure intention, “I have hidden,” that is, committed to memory, “the words of his mouth,” words spoken to me by his authority.

And if you ask why I have acted with such carefulness and such intentness, I give you the fearful reason, saying:

### Verse 13

“For he alone is”: that is, he has no equal; therefore one must not walk carelessly before him. “He is alone,” I say, because his being is not such as the being of angels, men, heaven, earth, sea, or air. Therefore he must be feared carefully, because “no one can turn away his thoughts”: that is, his judgments, once fixed, can never be changed by anyone. And because “it is fearful to fall into his hands” (Heb. 10), “his soul”—that is, his all-penetrating and all-ordering power—“has done whatever he willed” [Col. 1063A]. For both in apostate angels and in perverse human beings he fulfils his will even from that by which they seem to resist his will. Therefore, I say, he must be feared, because:

### Verse 14

“When he has fulfilled his will in me,” that is, when he has afflicted me with present scourges as much as he wills, “many other like things are ready with him”: that is, if he plans to strike, he still finds means to increase the blow, whether temporal or eternal.

### Verse 15

“And therefore I am troubled at his face”: that is, throughout my life I have feared him. “And considering him,” namely in the inner chamber of my heart through contemplation, and thus standing before his majesty, “I am troubled by fear”: that is, I always regard his sentence upon me as uncertain. And I have this spirit of the fear of the Lord not from myself but from his house [Col. 1063C]. This is what follows:

### Verse 16

“God has softened my heart,” so that I might fear him—whom the hardened do not fear, whose hearts are of stone—“and the Almighty has troubled me,” with useful dread, lest I should be hard of mind and consequently fall into evil.

VERSE 17.—“For I have not perished because of the darkness that threatened.” As though he said: Let not the present scourge make this fear of the Lord in me seem incredible to you, nor say: If you were so fearful, why then are you perishing? Do not, I say, speak thus: “For I have not perished,” namely in the present life, “because of the darkness that threatened,” that is, in order that, warned by such a blow, I might by repentance escape the future darkness owed, as you suppose, to my impiety; “nor has gloom covered my face,” that is, my mind [Col. 1063D], namely, God’s forgetfulness, so that I need to be roused by such a scourge. This is hidden from you, but not from God. This is what follows:

CHAPTER XXIV

VERSE 1.—“Times are not hidden from the Almighty,” namely neither past nor future; how much less, then, my present circumstances? “But those who know him,” that is, who seem to themselves to know him—those who think lofty thoughts (Rom. 12) and are wise in their own eyes (Rom. 11), namely people like yourselves, who presume above me and pronounce his judgment by your own understanding—“do not know his days,” that is, the ancient and mature ordering of his eternity, by which the things concerning me and similar matters are arranged.

VERSE 2.—“Some have moved boundary-stones,” that is, [Col. 1064A] the wicked, who do those things which you say that I, as wicked, have done, are altogether different persons—far removed from me—and indeed proceed in the opposite direction from me. This and the following words are such as though holy Church were speaking of the treachery of heretics: “Some,” that is, strangers to me, who went out from me because they were not mine, “have moved boundary-stones”—the ancient boundaries of the Scriptures which the holy Fathers established. “They have plundered flocks,” that is, untaught peoples, “and have fed them,” nourishing them with deadly doctrines in order to destroy them.

VERSE 3.—“They have driven away the ass of the fatherless,” that is, they have turned from the way of truth into [Col. 1064B] their own error anyone who is unlearned and labours in earthly affairs, yet is useful to the little ones—that is, God’s tender elect—and supplies them with assistance. “And they have taken the widow’s ox as a pledge,” that is, sometimes even a preacher of the Catholic faith, so that others may follow him. For this is what he means by “as a pledge.” When a pledge is taken away, something is indeed held, but something else is still sought. Therefore an ox is taken “as a pledge” when the preacher himself is seized for the purpose of making others follow. Of these he adds:

VERSE 4.—“They have overturned the way of the poor,” that is, the lives of those who do not possess the silver and gold of divine speech and can therefore be more easily overthrown; “and together they have oppressed the meek of the earth,” namely those whose meekness lacks discernment and is devoted to earthly things.

[Col. 1064C] VERSE 5.—“Others,” I say—not I, whom you compared to a wild ass, thinking himself born free—but others, wholly unlike me: “like wild asses in the desert,” that is, released from the fear of the Lord, “they go out,” namely from the common society of human beings, so as to appear more reverent by taking what seems a solitary path. “They go out, I say, like wild asses to their work”: not God’s work, but their own, as it is written: “The wild ass accustomed to solitude, in the desire of its soul, draws in the wind of its love” (Jer. 2); that is, the empty man [466], alien to the bonds of faith and reason, in the ambition of his own heart draws to himself that knowledge which knows not how to build up but only to inflate. “They go out, I say, like wild asses. And watching for prey,” that is, intent [Col. 1064D] upon corrupting sacred Scripture and twisting it to serve their own understanding, “they prepare bread for their children,” that is, false teaching for their followers.

VERSE 6.—“They reap a field not their own,” that is, in the hearts of hearers who received the good seed of God’s word from faithful men, they sow tares over it, which they reap to their own harm; “and they gather the vintage of his vineyard, which they have violently oppressed,” that is, they destroy the religious labour of one whom they can overcome by disputes.

VERSE 7.—“They leave men naked,” that is, stripped of good works: teaching them to live in such a way that their shamefulness is displayed; those “who have no [Col. 1065A] covering in the cold,” that is, no good work amid unbelief.

VERSE 8.—“Whom the rains of the mountains soak,” that is, whom the sacred words of teachers had only now begun to instruct; and, “having no covering,” with which their sins might be covered, “they embrace stones,” that is, they seek out holy martyrs, that they may deserve to have intercessors. Against such people, I say,

VERSE 9.—“They have used violence,” because they cannot persuade by gentler words, and so rage with violence in words and deeds; “plundering the fatherless,” namely those whom the merciful Father placed in the bosom of holy Church to be tenderly nourished; “and they have despoiled the poor multitude,” that is, they have taken from an untaught people the garment of faith.

[Col. 1065B] VERSE 10.—“The naked,” that is, those adorned with no good work, “and those walking without clothing,” that is—what is worse—doing evil and shameful deeds; and “the hungry,” that is, those sometimes desiring to return to repentance—“they have taken away the ears of grain,” that is, by pernicious persuasions they have destroyed in their minds the sayings of the Fathers stored there. These are fittingly signified by ears of grain, because, when the Fathers often utter them in figurative expressions, the covering of the letter, as it were the chaff of the awns, is removed, so that one may reach the marrow of the Spirit.

VERSE 11.—“They have taken their midday rest among their heaps,” that is, having no power of persecution in themselves, they delighted [Col. 1065C] in joining themselves to the multitude of those “who have trodden the winepresses,” that is, who were blood-stained by cruel deeds. Hence also David the prophet, beholding the affliction of holy Church, wrote a psalm “for the winepresses” (Ps. 8). “Having trodden the winepresses,” I say, that is, spattered with the blood of the saints and sated with slaughter, “they thirst,” that is, they still persist in doing crueller things. And in doing this,

VERSE 12.—“From the cities,” that is, from the many places or congregations of churches, “they have made men,” that is, the strong and perfect, “groan.” Thus Paul groaned because of his concern for all the churches, saying: “Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11); and, “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Gal. 3); and many similar things. “And the soul of the wounded,” that is, of the righteous who waste away over another’s fall [Col. 1065D], “cried out,” namely to God; “and God does not permit it to go unavenged,” although he permits it to happen, since he permits no injustice except in a just order.

VERSE 13.—“They themselves were rebels against the light”: they sinned not through ignorance but through pride, rebelling in word and deed against the light of knowledge which they possessed; this is to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit. “They were rebels,” I say: they set the shield of their pride against the darts of truth, lest they should be salutarily wounded in their hearts. And because they were first “rebels” knowingly, they were afterward blinded so that they might not know. This is what follows: “They did not know his ways,” that is, they were given over to a reprobate mind, and their foolish heart was darkened, because, knowing God [Col. 1066A], they did not glorify him as God (Rom. 1); “they did not know,” I say, “nor did they return by his paths,” that is, they were not converted to God by the narrow way of repentance, because by a just judgment their heart was both darkened and hardened. Still under the names of two most wicked crimes, namely murder and adultery, he denounces the wickedness of the heretic.

VERSE 14.—“At the first dawn,” he says, that is, in the joy of his prosperity. For murders are not, as the letter might suggest, committed more by day than by night; rather, in prosperity, as has been said, “at first dawn the murderer rises,” that is, he is lifted up in the glory of this present life; “he will kill the needy and poor,” that is, one conscious of weakness and humble. “But at night” [Col. 1066B], that is, in adversity, when through God’s ordering he has suddenly lost the glory of the power he received, “he will be like a thief,” because, although he changes his place, he does not change his mind; he secretly approves evil plans because he cannot harm by force.

VERSE 15.—“The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness.” Nothing prevents this from being understood literally as well: one who desires to commit adultery seeks darkness. But because the statement is directed against heretics, “the eye of the adulterer,” he says, “watches for darkness”; that is, as an adulterer in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure through darkness, so the heretic adulterates God’s word in hypocrisy, because he desires not to beget spiritual children of God but to display his own knowledge by preaching; and he takes, as it were, another’s wife [Col. 1066C] when he entices a faithful soul into his error. “The eye,” he says—that is, his intention—“watches for darkness,” namely so that people may not notice, “saying, ‘No eye will see me,’” namely no human eye; for he does not fear God’s eyes. A human eye, I say, because what, as was said above, is done in the mind can penetrate human sight only with the greatest difficulty. “And he will cover his face,” that is, by what he does it will happen that in him the likeness of God, which is the face of the human heart, will be so confounded that Christ will say to him on the day of judgment, “I do not know you.” Thus, by covering his face, what does he do?

VERSE 16.—“In darkness he breaks into houses,” that is, [Col. 1066D] he tries to wound the consciences of the righteous, especially in darkness, that is, in a time of adversity, when, while they were prospering, he did not dare to speak perversely. “He breaks in,” I say, “as in the day,” that is, in their prosperity “they had made an agreement among themselves,” because, while they did not dare to speak, they were occupied only with malicious plans against them.

VERSE 17.—“If the dawn suddenly appears,” that is, if after adversity some righteous person is exalted by a high authority, “they regard it as the shadow of death,” because those who remember that they have acted perversely fear to be reproved. And this is because “in darkness,” that is, in sins, “they walk as in light,” namely the light of righteousness: they are as secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous, and are so glad in their present blindness [Col. 1067A] as though they already enjoyed the light of their eternal homeland.

VERSE 18.—“He is light,” namely any such person, “upon the surface of the water,” that is, lighter than the surface of water, since if any breeze of temptation touches him, it carries him off without any delay of reconsideration. “Let his portion be cursed in the earth,” because though for a time he is blessed—that is, prospers—he is nevertheless held under the guilt of everlasting curse; “nor let him walk by the way of the vineyards,” that is, by the uprightness of the churches, which way is right faith or the rectitude of justice.

VERSE 19.—“Let him pass to excessive heat,” that is, to impatience, ever acting quarrelsomely and burning for disputes, “from snowy waters,” that is, [Col. 1067B] from the reading of the Scriptures, chilled by unbelief or wrongly understood. As though he said plainly: Since he does not humbly bind himself under the yoke of discipline, from the cold of his unbelief he slips through immoderate wisdom into error. For of such persons it is written: “As a cistern has made its water cold, so it has made its wickedness cold” (Jer. 6). “And let his sin be brought even to hell,” because before the end of this present life it is not corrected by amendment and repentance.

VERSE 20.—“Let mercy forget him,” that is, may he be unable afterward to find mercy from the Almighty whom he now does not fear as just; for forgiveness for a sin not corrected here is vainly sought there. “The worm is his sweetness” [Col. 1067C]—that is, while he lives, his flesh, which is truly decay and worm; its desire is wholly directed to prospering in this world, surpassing others, and swelling with possessions and honours. But graves bear witness what flesh is—or rather, that the substance of flesh is truly a worm. Which person would wish to touch the grave of parents or friends, however much he had loved them while alive? Therefore, while flesh is desired, consider what it is when lifeless, and then one understands what is loved. The holy man, speaking thus through his wounds and words so as also to signify our condition, still adds concerning the punishment of that same wicked man: “Let him not be remembered,” namely by God, because it is not worthy of such majesty that before the sight of his remembrance there should stand this—not [Col. 1067D], I say, a human being, but a crawling thing of such vileness, whose “sweetness,” as has been said, “is a worm.” “Let him not,” I say, “be remembered, but let him be crushed like an unfruitful tree,” that is, not only cut down through the death of the flesh, but also crushed through eternal condemnation—“like an unfruitful tree,” and therefore rightly to be cut down and cast into the fire. And truly unfruitful:

VERSE 21.—For “he fed the barren woman,” that is, he indulged with pleasures the flesh, which produces no good thought; “the barren woman,” I say, “who does not bear,” that is, who never ceases to be barren but persists in her desires. “And he did no good to the widow,” that is, he was unwilling to have mercy upon his own soul. Because it had been widowed from God, Christ [Col. 1068A] came to join it to himself, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18). To do good to that widow is to labour at consoling her as she is worn down by love for her dead Husband. But this man did her no good, because he laboured in nothing for her. Or, to continue the interpretation concerning the heretic: “He fed,” namely the heretic, “the barren woman,” that is, by feeding with the preaching of his error he made the people barren and erring. “And he did no good to the widow,” that is, he scorned to serve and labour with holy Church, whose husband Christ is now absent.

VERSE 22.—“He drew away the strong,” that is, he dragged proud and powerful people of the world into his error. “In his strength,” that is, in eloquence that is brilliant and contentious, “and when he stands,” that is, so long as he lives, “he does not believe in his life” [Col. 1068B], that is, he despises holding true opinions about God. Yet even one who seems within the body of the Church to hold the right faith, if he lives perversely, does not believe in his life, because he professes to know God but denies him by his deeds (Tit. 1). Someone might say: Why then does he live? The answer follows.

VERSE 23.—“God gave him a place for repentance,” that is, he endures him in wickedness so that, by waiting patiently, he may restrain him from wickedness and lead him to repentance. But he abuses that place of repentance for pride—that is, according to his hardness he stores up wrath for himself (Rom. 2)—and even if he is waited for a hundred years, he does not come to his senses. Hence he is more justly condemned, as it is written: “The sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. 65). Here the number one hundred [Col. 1068C] is put for the infinite, because no length of time restrains him from committing sin. “For his eyes,” that is, the intentions of his heart, “are in his ways”: knowingly wandering, and knowing a better way, he does not withdraw from present things but continually fixes himself upon vices alone, in order thereby to satisfy his mind.

VERSE 24.—“They are raised up for a little while,” namely the wicked, “and they shall not endure,” as elsewhere it is written: “I saw the wicked exceedingly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. 36). Thus smoke, once it has risen on high, is scattered; mist condensed in the morning is wiped away by the sun’s rays; grass rejoicing in the morning dew [Col. 1068D] is suddenly dried by heat; and so the foaming bubbles of water emerge in rivalry and, bursting in rivalry, perish. “And they shall be brought low like all things,” namely the things upon which they themselves rely. For all earthly things are, as it were, brought low, since even the elements pass away and are changed. As though he said plainly: They cannot stand at all, because even the things upon which they rely flee away. “They shall be brought low,” I say, “and taken away, like all things,” because they do not cling to him who is above all things. “And like the tops of ears of grain,” that is, the awns, which emerge joined together but, as they gradually grow, become bristling and stiff and are separated a little from one another: so these people, who are joined by the communion of nature, divide against one another as they grow in turn, [Col. 1069A] and, striving in different vices, each seeks to surpass the other. Thus, I say, “they shall be crushed,” so that once they are crushed, the grains—that is, the righteous—may appear, having been hidden while the awns, that is, these same unjust persons, stood; and so that when the latter fall into eternal punishments, the righteousness of the saints may be shown to shine in how great a truth. This will occur when the threshing-floor of holy Church is thoroughly cleansed by the winnowing fan which, according to John, is in the Judge’s hand (Matt. 3), and when the chaff has been winnowed out for burning, the wheat is stored in the barns of heaven (Luke 3).

VERSE 25.—“But if it is not so,” he says, “who can convict me of having lied?” As though he said plainly: All things are as I have set them forth. Yet if they were not so, you could not rebuke me [Col. 1069B], because while you are still subject to your own faults, you cannot reprove another’s falsehood. “And set my words before God,” namely at the tribunal of truth, because by sinning you yourselves hide his face from yourselves. Having said these things against those who are proud in fleeting power and puffed up by empty honours, blessed Job was about to continue what he had begun concerning his character; but Bildad,

CHAPTER XXV

VERSE 1.—Unable to endure silence, and stirred by the statement he had just made—“If it is not so, who can convict me of having lied and set my words before God?”—interrupts his speech, saying:

VERSE 2.—“Power and terror are with him,” etc. As though he said: You have said, “Who can convict me of having lied?” [Col. 1069C] But I say: “With him who makes peace in his high places,” that is, who, by casting down the spirits that rose proudly against him, established peace and the concord of humility in heaven—with him, I say, “is power,” namely even to convict you, “and terror,” namely the present scourge by which he has already terribly convicted you, so that others who see you are frightened. This was said far too harshly against the holy man. For Bildad wishes it to be understood that blessed Job was struck by the same justice, or for the same fault, for which the devil was cast from heaven and abandoned the concord which he had disturbed in the high places—that is, in the heavenly realms. “Power,” I say, is with him, and:

[Col. 1069D] VERSE 3.—“Is there any number to his armies?” For you said, “And who can set my words before God?” (Job 24), as though he had no one to report your words before him. “Is there,” I say, “a number?” That is, are there not innumerable spirits able to report daily, by day and night, the words and deeds of human beings before the Creator? They are all certainly harmonious, as was said above (v. 2), although Daniel says: “The angel, prince of the Persians,” that is, the angel who presides over the Persians, “resisted me” (Dan. 10). Angels do not oppose one another through discord, but through agreement in justice, because they set forth in turn the merits of the nations subject to them. “And upon whom,” he says, “does his light not shine [variant: rise]?” [Col. 1070A] That is, besides the fact that all things [468] are reported to him by angels, whom do his eyes not see? And in the presence of those eyes, which behold both good and evil, can anyone be justified by his words or deeds?

VERSE 4.—“Can a man be justified when compared with God?” That is, you are that man, comparing yourself with God when you say, “I desire to dispute with God” (Job 13), and many similar things; and most recently, “Who can convict me?”—as though you were equal to God, whom alone no one can convict. “Can he, I say, be justified, or can one born of woman appear clean?” That is, even if you had no stain apart from this—that you were born of a woman—since the persuasion of guilt was imposed upon man.

VERSE 5.—“Behold, even the moon,” that is, the heavenly [Col. 1070B] Church, which the present sun of divinity illuminates, “does not shine,” except insofar as it has the light of that same sun; “and the stars,” that is, all the holy angels, “are not clean in his sight,” that is, in comparison with him. Indeed, those among them who compared themselves with him became darkness.

VERSE 6.—“How much more is man decay,” that is, not merely any kind of man who will someday become decay, but a man who is already decay—one sitting on a dung-heap and scraping the discharge from his side?

CHAPTER XXVI

VERSES 1–2.—When the friends’ words ended with this final insult, blessed Job, relying on a loftier keenness of mind, continues what he had begun; and his final sayings are as forceful as they are conclusive. For even legal advocates [Col. 1070C] are accustomed to reserve for the conclusion the argument by which they foresee that they will surpass their opponents. “Whose helper are you?” he says. This is the great and worthy indignation of a powerful soul, unable to bear that Bildad should seek to appear God’s helper. For although there are some helpers of God, he never deigns to have such helpers as this man was, who thought that he was helping God in condemning his innocent neighbour; in doing this he was not so much a helper as a flatterer, not so much a praiser as a mocker. Whose helper, I say, are you? “Is it of the weak man,” that is, of him whose staff I have broken? “And do you support the arm of him who is not strong,” lest the Lord’s arm, tender and delicate, should grow weary [Col. 1070D] in holding me while I resist? Just as those hired to mourn at a funeral say and do almost more than those who grieve sincerely, so you, a mocker, are moved more than a true praiser. “And you support,” I say, “the arm of him who is not strong,” that is, you thrust yourself forward to help as though he had not struck me forcefully enough, whereas, contrariwise, in order that he may strike more steadfastly, he himself wishes to be held, as it is said to him through a certain person: “There is none to rise up and hold you” (Isa. 64).

VERSE 3.—“To whom have you given counsel?” He maintains what he said much earlier: “With him are strength and wisdom” (Job 12). For after speaking of strength—“Whose helper are you?” etc.—he now adds concerning wisdom: “To whom have you given counsel?” “Counsel,” I say, to whom have you, like a legal advocate [Col. 1071A], “given,” by composing many accusations against me, so that he who struck me might enumerate them against me and not appear to strike unjustly when I cry out, “I desire to dispute with God” (Job 13)? “Perhaps,” namely, you have given counsel “to him who has no wisdom?” It would indeed be an act of charity to give counsel to one who lacks wisdom, because he needs counsel; but to give it to God, who is Wisdom itself, is a most perverse and importunate flattery. “And you have shown your abundant prudence,” namely by desiring to be wise beyond what is fitting, and by inventing, as if in God’s favour, evils against your neighbour which plainly do not exist.

VERSE 4.—“Whom did you wish to teach?” namely who ought to speak against me. “Was it not him who made the [Col. 1071B] breath?” and who therefore knows better by himself what is in that breath.

VERSE 5.—[Col. 1071B] “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.” He now rebukes the swelling of empty wisdom through teaching concerning that same strength and wisdom of God, and utters words full of mysteries. “The giants,” he says, are apostate angels or proud people; “they groan beneath the waters,” that is, beneath the abyss of God’s judgments, not knowing the things of God because God has not revealed them to them through his Spirit; and “those who dwell with them,” that is, those who join themselves in delight to their glory, likewise groan. This is undoubtedly an act of divine strength: bound in fitting bonds and drawn down by the cords of hell, they are reserved [Col. 1071C] for the day of judgment, when they will receive from him the completed sentence against whom they swelled in pride. But the following is an act of his wisdom:

VERSE 6.—“Hell is naked,” that is, the devil cannot conceal his malice “before him; and there is no covering for perdition,” that is, for all who share in his condemnation, because there is nowhere for them to hide; “for all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4).

VERSE 7.—“He stretches out the north over the void.” “With him are strength and wisdom” (Job 12): he stretches out “the north,” that is, the devil cast out from the hearts of the elect and stripped of his vessels and weapons, “over the void,” so that he is content to cover the hearts of those empty of God’s grace; “and he hangs the earth,” that is, holy Church, firm in faith and fruitful as soil in good works, “upon nothing,” that is, upon Gentile peoples, owing to no merit of theirs, as it is written in the psalm: “You shall save them for nothing” (Ps. 55). He next unfolds with wondrous reasoning the order in which this occurred.

VERSE 8.—“He binds the waters in the clouds,” which is undoubtedly a work of his wisdom. “He binds the waters,” I say: he distributes the gifts of his teaching with discernment “in the clouds,” that is, in the apostles and other holy preachers, “so that they do not burst forth together downward”; that is, so that the measure of teaching is not dispensed equally to all, but is apportioned according to their capacity [Col. 1072A], lest untrained hearers, who must still be cherished as little children, be overwhelmed by the immensity of mysteries. To such people the apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 2). And it is written in the Law: “If anyone digs a cistern and does not cover it,” that is, if someone penetrates the hidden things of Scripture with strong understanding and does not cover them in silence before those who cannot comprehend, “and an ox or ass falls into it,” that is, if some simple person is scandalized, whether his life be clean or unclean, “the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals” (Exod. 21), that is, he will be held guilty and obliged to do penance for them.

VERSE 9.—“He holds,” I say, “the face of his throne” [Col. 1072B], that is, in the manner described above he conceals the glory of his kingdom, so that while we remain in this mortal flesh we may not see how great are the ministries of the angels or the other secrets of God. Or, because he speaks these things against his friends, who thought that they comprehended the reasons for his affliction, it is rightly said in this way: “He holds the face of his throne,” that is, he does not show you, or people like you, the reason for his judgment; “and he spreads his cloud over it,” because, remaining invisible, he exercises his hidden judgments over us.

VERSE 10.—“He has set a boundary around the waters,” that is, he has fixed a limit to the knowledge of humankind: perfect knowledge of his eternity is granted to no one [Col. 1072C], “until light and darkness are brought to an end,” that is, until the course of the righteous and unrighteous is completed. Their contrary difference is rightly signified by light and darkness, between which, as the apostle says, there is no fellowship at all (2 Cor. 6).

VERSE 11.—“The pillars of heaven tremble,” that is, holy angels or supreme preachers are shaken with trembling because of [469] this judgment of divine ordering; “and they fear at his nod,” not with penal fear, but with reverent wonder as they contemplate the omnipotence of the Creator. More clearly still, he adds concerning that same strength and wisdom.

VERSE 12.—“By his strength,” he says, that is, through his incarnate Word, “the seas were suddenly gathered together,” [Col. 1072D] that is, hearts of worldly people, formerly discordant, were gathered into the concord of one faith; “and by his prudence he struck the proud one,” that is, the patience and humility of his death, by which he made provision for us, conquered the devil.

VERSE 13.—“His Spirit,” sent from heaven after this victory, “adorned the heavens,” that is, enriched the holy apostles by making the weak strong, the fearful fervent with good zeal, and the unlearned learned. The Holy Spirit is rightly said to have done this, since unless the apostles received his promised gifts, they would have shone with no adornment of strength or other virtues. This is an act of God’s wisdom; what follows is praise of his strength. “And by his midwifing hand,” he says—that is, by his right hand [Col. 1073A] guarding little ones, or receiving Adam’s children in order to regenerate them—“the twisting serpent came forth [variant: was brought forth],” that is, the armed strong man, the devil, was cast out from his own court. He is called the twisting serpent because through a serpent he deceived the human race, and was permitted to enter for this reason: that through that very vessel he might be known for what he is—twisting and slippery. Twisting, because he did not stand in the truth; slippery, because, unless his first suggestion is resisted, he suddenly slips, unnoticed, wholly into the innermost parts of the mind.

VERSE 14.—“Behold, these things are said in part of his ways,” that is, of his strength and wisdom; “and when we have scarcely heard a small drop of his words,” namely these few things which we announce by the prophetic [Col. 1073B] Spirit concerning his first coming, “who can behold the thunder of his greatness?” that is, who can endure his sonorous and terrible second coming? For he calls the knowledge of his first coming “a small drop of his words,” because whatever is lofty and terrible that we know from contemplating him through his first coming is, in comparison with the immensity of heavenly secrets to be revealed through the second coming, like a small drop compared with great thunder.

CHAPTER XXVII

VERSE 1.—“Job also added,” namely after he had fittingly answered what Bildad had said to insult him. For Bildad had spoken of God’s strength, by which he cast the prince of discord, the devil, from the heights of heaven [Col. 1073C]—he who makes concord in his high places—and of the rest; and blessed Job had answered prophetically concerning that same strength and wisdom by which God was to cast the same devil also from the hearts of those human beings whom he chose. To these things, I say, the most valiant athlete added, having overcome in a threefold contest, as though against three gladiators, standing victorious in the middle of the arena and displaying to the spectators the golden arms of the virtues by which he had prevailed. Therefore he added, taking up his parable—not some musical instrument called a parable, for music is an untimely telling in mourning—but his parable, that is, his likeness: words in which he speaks divine [Col. 1073D] mysteries parabolically, more fully describing in his own person the state of the Church. Yet, according to his custom, he begins with plain speech:

VERSES 2–3.—“The Lord lives,” namely he of whom the fool said, “There is no God,” or, if there is, he must not be believed to care for human affairs, since evil often happens to the good and good things to the wicked. “The Lord lives,” I say—that is, I call as witness the living One who is Lord—“who has taken away my judgment,” namely from the mouths of people, so that contrary to my merit they now think me wicked. He has taken it away, I say—he who does not disdain to care for human affairs, as fools suppose, who, seeing the peace of sinners, became envious “and said: ‘How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?’” (Ps. 72). Yet according to the counsel which he himself [Col. 1074A] knows, “he has taken away my judgment; and the Almighty has brought my soul to bitterness,” namely by giving my striker a just power, though he had an unjust will. I call the living One as witness; I call the Almighty as witness, “because while breath remains,” that is, the discernment of good and evil, “in me”—for it follows—“and the Spirit of God is in my nostrils,” that is, God’s inspiration in the gift of discernment; for in sacred Scripture discernment is commonly signified by the nose: while, I say, the power remains in me to distinguish good from evil.

VERSE 4.—“My lips shall not speak iniquity”; and, that you may understand more clearly what iniquity, “nor,” he says, “shall my tongue devise falsehood.” See that this is to utter blasphemy against the Holy [Col. 1074B] Spirit: to possess through the gift of the Holy Spirit discernment of good and evil, and, once the truth is known, knowingly to contrive falsehood to the contrary—as heretics do.

VERSE 5.—“Far be it from me,” namely this sin, “that I should judge you righteous,” with respect to the matter now at hand, since you think that the merits of good or evil persons must be assessed from the outcome of temporal advantages or disadvantages. For if I judged you righteous in this opinion, I should sin by lying, not only against my conscience but also against all the saints, who, although they justify their hearts and wash their hands among the innocent, are nevertheless scourged all day long, and their chastening comes in the mornings (Ps. 72), that is, in the present time, “when judgment begins with the house of God” (1 Pet. [Col. 1074C] 4). Far be it, I say: “Until I fail,” that is, while I have the lamp of truth burning within me, “I shall not depart from my innocence,” that is, with a deceitful tongue I shall say nothing against that same truth.

VERS. 6. — “My righteousness, which I began to hold fast,” that is, from my earliest age—namely, by never opposing the truth once known to me—“I will not abandon,” that is, overcome by your contention. I began, I say, to hold it fast. “For indeed my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life.” I do not say, indeed, that I have never sinned, since above I said: “I have sinned; what shall I do to thee, O watcher of men?” (Job 7); and again: “Though I should wash myself as with snow-water, yet thou shalt plunge me in filth, and my garments shall abhor me” (Job 9). But this I say: that I have never knowingly spoken falsehoods contrary to truths, nor by doing evil pretended to do good, nor been, as you now suppose, a hypocrite. In such matters, I say, my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life. Indeed:

VERS. 7. — “Let my enemy be as the ungodly man, and my adversary as the unrighteous.” As though he said: So far am I from being a hypocrite or ungodly, as you assert, that whoever is my enemy or adversary cannot be pious or righteous, but rather must be what is opposed to piety—that is, ungodly or unrighteous. He could have said: “You rather, who oppose me, are ungodly or unrighteous.” But he expressed himself more humbly, as also [Col. 1075A] our Lord did when he could have said to the blaspheming Pharisees: “You are against me; you scatter.” He moderated the same rebuke, because these were their first attacks, and said: “He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth” (Luke 11). So here too, because his friends had once been such but now opposed him, he moderated the rebuke, as has already been said.
