And because, while speaking perversely, they claimed the cause of justice as though acting for God, he does not say absolutely, “ungodly” or “unrighteous,” but “as the ungodly,” “as the unrighteous.” As though he said: I do not prejudge the intention of the heart, which perhaps is deceived through ignorance; this I know: that in speech you resemble the ungodly and the unrighteous, in that by opposing me you fabricate lies. I am not, [Col. 1075B] I say, a hypocrite.

VERS. 8. — “For what is the hope of the hypocrite?” That is: if I were a hypocrite, what hope—what reward to be hoped for—would remain to me? The answer is: none. For no hope remains to the hypocrite “if he greedily seizes,” that is, if through the intemperance of ambition he anticipates praise in the present life, and God does not deliver his soul—that is, in the future—because he has now received his reward. This is what follows:

VERS. 9. — “Will God hear his cry?” namely, when he says: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25)—“when distress comes upon him,” namely, when, as is written elsewhere, “sudden calamity rushes upon him, and destruction comes like a storm” (Prov. 1).

VERS. 10. — “Or can he delight in the Almighty?” That is, can he obtain praise from God who sought and received praise from men? And can he “call upon God at all times”—that is, will he effectively call upon him in time of distress whom he despised in the time of earthly prosperity?

VERS. 11. — “I will teach you by the hand of God.” After removing from himself the mark of hypocrisy, which greatly tends to weaken the authority of a teacher; after, I say, overthrowing the arrogance of his friends by a many-sided answer, he now declares that he will teach, so that it may plainly appear that in what follows he plants what is right, while in what preceded he uprooted what was perverse. “I will teach you,” he says, “by the hand of God,” that is, by an authority not mine but God’s; or “by the hand of God,” that is, by wisdom, which is the Son of God, because you presume upon your own wisdom. “I will teach,” he says, “what the Almighty has,” namely, in us his servants; for we have nothing from ourselves, but whatever we have is God’s gift and his work. “Nor will I conceal it,” namely, so that God may be glorified, who wills that our light should shine before men for his glory.

VERS. 12. — “Behold, you all know,” namely, even without my teaching, what wisdom or good works God has in me. “And why do you speak vain things without cause?” That is, without ignorance, which is wont to be an excusable cause of speaking vainly. By asking this, he says in some fashion what the Apostle said: “I have become foolish; you have compelled me; for I ought to have been commended by you” (2 Cor. 12). Then he teaches what he is not, intending at last to say what he is or has been.

VERS. 13. — “This,” he says, “is the portion of the ungodly man with God, and the inheritance of violent men, which they shall receive from the Almighty”: violent men, I say, that is, those who do violence to the Word of God and violently bend his commandments toward a perverse interpretation. I shall immediately state what that portion or inheritance is:

VERS. 14. — “If his children are multiplied,” that is, his followers—of the ungodly man, or of every heretic—“they shall be for the sword,” that is, they shall be struck by the sentence of the coming judgment; “and his grandchildren,” that is, those born from the preaching of the children who err, “shall not be satisfied with bread,” that is, they shall not be refreshed by the knowledge of truth.

VERS. 15. — “Those who remain of him,” that is, those who, after some of his people have been converted, remain in unbelief, “shall be buried in destruction,” that is, they shall be tormented in the fires of hell; “and his widows shall not weep,” that is, the peoples subject to him, happily deserted by that corrupter, shall rightly rejoice. Or certainly, the widows do not weep because, remaining in their error and deeming their preacher holy, they comfort themselves with false hope lest they mourn.

VERS. 16. — “Though he heap up silver like earth,” that is, though he expend God’s utterance upon earthly praise, “and prepare garments as mud,” [Col. 1076C] that is, though he collect testimonies of Sacred Scripture loosely and corruptibly in order to defend himself:

VERS. 17. — “He has indeed prepared them,” that is, he has indeed spoken many things learnedly; “but the just man shall put them on,” that is, he will use the heretic’s statements, collected as they are, for the service of truth; “and the innocent shall divide the silver,” that is, he will distinguish rightly spoken things from perversely spoken things and arrange them carefully and discerningly, fitting to each person what is suitably appropriate. Doing this, he will rejoice, according to the Psalmist, “over God’s utterances, as one who finds great spoil” (Ps. 18).

VERS. 18. — “He has built his house like a moth.” That is, by corrupting the minds of his hearers, he will make in them a place for his unbelief, as a moth, by destroying garments, builds itself a house in them. But why do I call it a house, since such a dwelling does not endure? This is what he adds by way of correction: “And like a watchman he made himself a booth.” That is, he does not truly build himself a house having a foundation, but a booth; for every repose which, like a watchman or hired servant, he promises to himself or his own is destroyed with time, and after this life is not found at all, just as a watchman’s booth is not established on any foundation.

VERS. 19. — “The rich man, when he shall sleep.” The discourse passes from the particular destruction of heretics, or of all who misuse received knowledge, to the general definition concerning all the elect. The rich man, he says—that is, one who hopes in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6), or the proud man, whatever the source of his pride—“when [Col. 1077A] he shall sleep,” that is, when he dies, “shall take nothing with him,” because “his glory shall not descend with him” (Ps. 48). “He shall open his eyes”: when he dies in the flesh, then his soul is compelled to see. “He shall open,” I say, “his eyes, and shall find nothing,” according to the Psalmist: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75); like that rich man who, tormented among the dead, found not even a drop of water in his hands with which to cool his tongue (Luke 16).

VERS. 20. — “Want shall seize him like water,” namely, want of every refreshment. This want is rightly compared to water, because hell swallows those it receives in its depths, which are also commonly designated by the name of lakes. “A storm shall oppress him by night,” that is, suddenly, while he is unguarded, the whirlwind of judgment shall scatter him.

VERS. 21. — “A burning wind shall take him away,” namely, as he dies: that is, the devil, who by his breath kindles every living person to vices. Of him Jeremiah says: “I see a seething pot, and its face from the face of the north” (Jer. 1). Whoever is protected from its burning says the words from the Song of Songs: “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat” (Song 2). The devil, the burning wind, who kindles the living to vices, carries the dying away to eternal torments. “And like a whirlwind he shall snatch him away,” namely, terrified and stupefied on the last day; “he shall snatch him,” I say, “from his place,” which place for him is [Col. 1077C] carnal pleasure and every delight of temporal life.

VERS. 22. — “And he shall cast upon him,” namely, God shall cast his scourge upon him now, “and shall not spare,” namely, in the future: that is, he strikes in the present and does not spare in the future. For the saying that God does not judge twice for the same thing must not be understood so that whoever is struck here for his crime is believed consequently to be freed from punishment in the future. Otherwise Herod and Antiochus, who were struck in the present life, would be thought saved. Yet, if one accepts the view that any fault cannot be punished twice, this must be understood of those struck for sin and dying in their sin, because their punishment, begun here, ends there. Therefore it is one scourge also in those who are corrected: it begins temporally but is completed in eternal punishments, according to the saying: “A fire is kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest hell” (Deut. 32). Therefore he casts upon him and does not spare. “Fleeing from his hand,” namely, from the hand of him who strikes, “he shall flee”: that is, every penitent person shall escape, according to the words: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands”—that is, he shall cleanse his works through repentance—“in the blood,” that is, in the punishment, [Col. 1077D] “of the sinner” (Ps. 57) which he beholds.

VERS. 23. — “He shall clasp his hands over him,” that is, seeing the sinner’s fate, he corrects and strengthens his own works, fearing lest he too should perish in the same way; “and he shall whistle,” [Col. 1078A] that is, he shall gaze intently in wonder “over him,” namely, seeing his destruction. Or, turning to spiritual words, he shall draw together a mouth previously loosened, as in a whistle, so that he now believes and preaches what he did not formerly believe, when he saw the wicked prosper. “He shall whistle,” I say, “while looking upon his place,” that is, his destruction, in which he shall be fixed for eternity.

CHAPTER XXVIII

VERS. 1. — “Silver has the sources of its veins.” As though he said: And you indeed whistle over me, looking at my place—that is, marveling at this dung-heap on which I sit. You have whistled, I say, that is, you have said many subtle things; but “silver has the sources of its veins,” that is, the divine utterance has definite origins of the intentions for which it was spoken or written by holy men, origins which you have not discerned. Therefore you have not rightly heaped up against me, or wholly in contempt of my poverty—whereby you think yourselves rich—the silver of sacred utterance. “Silver has the sources of its veins,” as has been said, “and there is a place where gold is melted.” By “gold,” I say, is meant true wisdom: right faith is as it were its proper place, in which alone it is found; without faith there is no wisdom, though it may appear to exist. Nor can anyone, even if he gives his body to be burned, shine or be true gold before God unless he suffers within the Catholic faith. Yet he said this concerning himself, who also said above: “The Lord has tested me as gold” (Job 23), judging himself to be purified in the furnace of tribulation. “And there is,” he says, “a place where gold is melted,” as though he said plainly: My soul does not shine with the splendor of eternal beauty unless it has first burned here in the workshop of tribulation or in the fire of charity. Nor is gold melted only in such a place, but also, toward this same place of melting:

VERS. 2. — “Iron is taken from the earth,” that is, a strong man, soon to become a defender of truth, is brought forth separated from earthly conduct; “and stone,” that is, he likewise who had been hard-hearted and insensitive, “melted by heat,” that is, pierced by the fire of divine love, “is turned into bronze”: he is established in a good purpose, so that in preaching the truth he may be heard afar off like sounding bronze. Men do not yet know what is done in this furnace, but “the Lord will come and bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. 4). This is what follows:

VERS. 3. — “He has set a time for darkness,” namely, the time when he will illuminate it and make manifest the counsels of hearts. “And he himself considers the end of all things,” that is, he knows both what each person is now in the furnace of tribulation and what he will come forth as; likewise, what each person is now in his conscience and what that same person will be hereafter. “The stone also of darkness,” that is, the stony heart of the ungodly which charity does not soften; “the stone,” I say, “of darkness,” that is, the hard mind darkened in the subtlety of divine judgments; “and the shadow of death,” [Col. 1079A] that is, every imitator of the devil, who imitates the devil as a shadow imitates a body.

VERS. 4. — “The torrent separates from the pilgrim people.” That is, the heat of the aforesaid melting causes men to think wrongly and judge wrongly with divided minds concerning holy men, who are pilgrims in this world but citizens of heaven. For this is why those who lack the inward affections of piety now detest the saints as ungodly: they see them cast into the furnace of tribulation. Thus you now judge me ungodly because you see me overwhelmed by the torrent of miseries. These men, I say, bearing hearts of stone, the torrent of affliction now separates—that is, causes them to think wrongly—as has already been said. But in the future the torrent of dreadful judgment shall separate them, of which it is written in Daniel: “A swift fiery river went forth from before him” (Dan. 7), namely, from the Ancient of Days sitting to render judgment. This river, this torrent, shall then separate from the saints those who are now separated from them by hatred. “Those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten,” that is, those whom the preacher of truth does not traverse. For the preacher of truth is the “foot,” that is, the bearer, of Christ, “who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8). “Whom he has forgotten,” I say, “and the walls [variant: pathless places],” that is, those unwilling for the Word of God to open a way—for example, as the Jews refused to do, to whom those beautiful feet bringing peace said: “Since you have rejected the word of God and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Concerning this people he then adds:

[Col. 1079C] VERS. 5. — “The earth from which bread sprang,” that is, Judaea, which first possessed the bread of God’s word, namely knowledge of the Law, “has been overthrown by fire in its place”: that is, in its pride, or within itself, it was consumed as it burned with the fire of envy against Christ and his nascent Church.

VERS. 6. — “Its stones were the place of sapphire.” That is, the holy men—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—were the dwelling-place of heavenly grace, which is beautifully expressed by sapphire because it has an ethereal color: living and elect stones of the kind concerning which the Lord also promises through the prophet to the Church that is to come, saying: “Behold, I will lay thy stones in order” (Isa. 54), that is, I will distinguish within you holy souls by the diversity of their merits. “And its clods,” he says, “were gold”: that is, those same holy men, who knew themselves to be dust and were moistened by the dew of heavenly grace. For clods are compacted from dust and moisture. When, I say, they knew themselves to be dust—as did he who said, “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18)—because they shone through the excellence of life, they lay in that land as golden clods.

VERS. 7. — “The bird did not know the path,” that is, it did not believe in the Savior’s ascension, by which, ascending, he raised the fleshly body to the heights of heaven; “nor did the vulture’s eye behold it,” that is, the purpose of the death of that same Redeemer was not made clear to it—the Redeemer who lowered himself from heaven to the depths, to the corpse of our mortality. He is therefore rightly compared to a vulture, which is often caught in death when it descends in flight from on high to a dead animal. For he too, when he sought a dead animal—that is, condemned humanity—found death among us, though he was immortal in himself.

VERS. 8. — “The sons of merchants,” or traders, “did not tread it.” A merchant is so called from *insisting* or persistently applying himself to work. By the name of merchants are designated the holy prophets, who sought by prophecy to train the conduct of the Synagogue toward faith. Their sons are called the holy apostles. “The sons of merchants,” he says, “did not tread it”: that is, the apostles did not press down its life, as it were with the foot of virtue, by preaching, because they were driven from its borders. “Nor did the lioness pass through it,” that is, the holy Church did not utterly destroy its people’s unbelief. The Church is rightly called a lioness because she is the wife of the lion from the tribe of Judah. Concerning her Jacob, after saying of Christ, “Resting, thou hast lain down as a lion” (Gen. 49), immediately added, “and as a lioness” (ibid.). Christ himself plundered hell powerfully, “as a lion”; but after him the Church, coming forth from Judaea, attacked the whole world, acting powerfully against ancient idolatry, “as a lioness.” “The lioness,” I say, “did not pass through it.” But what then?

VERS. 9. — “He stretched out his hand to the flint,” that is, he raised the arm of preaching toward the hardness of the Gentiles. “He overthrew the mountains from their roots,” that is, he humbled from the depths of their thoughts the powerful of this world.

VERS. 10. — “He cut out streams in the rocks,” that is, in hard hearts struck by his fear he opened the flowing waters of Sacred Scripture. “And his eye saw every precious thing,” that is, every humble person, small in his own eyes; for before God that person is precious who is worthless and despised in his own estimation. “Every precious thing,” I say, “his eye saw”: that is, the regard of his grace enlightened every humble person.

VERS. 11. — “He searched out also the depths of the rivers, and brought hidden things into light.” That is, by pouring into them the Spirit of understanding, he opened through them the ancient obscurities of the prophets, which burst forth like “the depths of rivers” from the breasts of the ancient fathers, namely Moses and the rest. “And hidden things,” namely, things hidden from the Jews—for “a veil has been placed over their heart” (2 Cor. 3)—“he brought into light,” so that the holy Church may now recognize through the Holy Spirit what the Synagogue formerly refused altogether to understand through the letter. And all these things were accomplished solely by his grace. For unless he himself had freely come to us, when or where would we have sought this wisdom of God, or at what price would we have purchased it? This is what follows.

VERS. 12. — “But where is wisdom found?” Namely, the wisdom that found us. “And what is the place of understanding?” It is surely nothing other than the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which this same wisdom of God is understood. Where, I say, is “Christ, the wisdom of God,” found, and where is his Holy Spirit, “who breathes where he wills” (John 3), sought? And moreover, unless he gives himself freely, at what price can he be purchased? The implied answer is: at none. Hence it follows:

VERS. 13. — “Man does not know its price,” namely, because there is none. “Nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly,” that is, in the earthly soul of the rich, enslaved to carnal pleasures. Having proposed these two points—“where is it found?” and “man does not know its price”—he answers them by what follows.

VERS. 14. — “The abyss says: It is not in me,” [Col. 1081B] that is, the hearts of people made fluid by the Fall and dark by duplicity. While they desire to be wise carnally, they show themselves foolish in spiritual matters. “And the sea says: It is not with me,” that is, the bitter malice of worldly minds bears witness by its very deeds that they are separated from true wisdom, since no one rightly apprehends it unless he strives to withdraw himself from every fluctuation of carnal actions, according to the saying: “Write wisdom in a time of leisure, and he who is lessened in activity shall apprehend her” (Ecclus. 38). And the Psalmist says: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45). This is what he means: “The abyss says: It is not in me; and the sea says: It is not with me.” He returns to what he had proposed: “Where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?” But to the other point he had proposed—“Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly”—he returns in what follows:

VERS. 15. — “Fine gold shall not be given for it, nor shall silver be weighed in exchange [variant: comparison] for it.” “Fine gold,” he says, means the brightness of the angels, who, persevering in the innocence in which they were created, shine with the brightness of righteousness and are stained by no impurities of sin, even the least. It shall not be given for wisdom because, for the redemption of humankind, no angel was to be sent for this Wisdom, who is Christ; rather, it was necessary and fitting that the creature be set free by the Creator himself. “Nor shall silver,” he says, “be weighed in comparison with it”: that is, the life of righteous preachers is not equal to the purity of his righteousness. For divine utterances are often signified by silver. Therefore the life of holy writers or preachers, however much it shines with the light of holiness, does not exchange for you the coming of heavenly Wisdom by his own presence; for however holy they may have been, in comparison with the only-begotten Son they are reckoned to have had no merit.

VERS. 16. — “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India,” that is, with worldly wise men, painted over and laying ornaments of eloquence upon their foulness. For by India, which produces a black people, this world is understood, in which human life is born dark through sin. The dyed colors of India are those worldly wise men who, lacking the excellence of things, falsely represent themselves as other than they are through compositions of words, as though with colors laid over them. Therefore true wisdom “shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India,” because, though it lacks painted ornaments of eloquence, it pleases like a garment without dye. “Nor with the most precious sardonyx,” that is, with any earthly human being. Sardonyx has the appearance of red earth, and therefore all people may be signified by sardonyx, because they are from earth: their first parent Adam was formed from earth, and in the Latin tongue earth is also called *red*. “Neither with sardonyx, therefore, nor sapphire”: that is, neither with an earthly person nor with any angel. Sapphire has an airy appearance, and therefore fittingly signifies holy angels. Or thus: “Nor with the most precious sardonyx,” that is, with the fathers of the Old Testament; “nor sapphire,” that is, with the teachers of the New Testament. For through sardonyx, which, as stated, resembles red earth, the first earthly man (1 Cor. 15) and those born according to him may rightly be signified; but through sapphire, which, as stated, has an airy appearance, the new man Christ, who is also called heavenly (ibid.), and those regenerated from him are aptly figured. It should be known that sardonyx and sapphire, which are certainly not precious, are described as precious so that, when we recognize that they are not precious, we may seek another meaning in their interpretation.

VERS. 17–18. — “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it.” What wise person could suppose this to mean literally: after it has been said that gold is not equal to this wisdom, it is then added as though intensifying the claim that not even glass, which is far cheaper than gold, can equal it? By gold and glass, therefore, is signified that heavenly country, that society of all the blessed, whose hearts both shine with brightness and are transparent through purity. John mentions this in the Apocalypse, saying: “The city itself was pure gold, like clear glass” (Rev. 21). But “it shall not be equal to it,” he says—namely, to Wisdom, who is the only Son of God—because although it is written, “When he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3), nevertheless it is again written: “Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 80). For all the saints are precious as gold and transparent to one another, as is signified by glass. They shall be like this Wisdom in image, but they shall not be like him in equality. “Nor shall vessels of high and eminent gold be exchanged for it”: such vessels of gold and precious vessels through the grace of God poured in were Elijah, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist. Whoever thought Christ, God’s Wisdom, to be one of these—as when, to the question, “Whom do men say that I am?” the disciples answered, “Some Elijah, others Jeremiah, others John, or one of the prophets”—whoever, I say, thought this, exchanged a high and eminent vessel of gold for Wisdom. But “vessels of high and eminent gold shall not be exchanged for it,” because the elect venerate the life of every saint for its sublimity, but do not accept them unto error; knowing them to be mere human beings, they do not compare them at all with God made man. “They shall not be exchanged for it,” he says, “nor shall they even be mentioned in comparison with it,” because the “high and eminent vessels of gold,” venerable to us through participation in Wisdom, are not even to be mentioned in comparison with Wisdom. For through participation in that Wisdom all the elect are something; through themselves they are almost nothing. [Col. 1083B] This that man understood wisely who said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). “But wisdom is drawn from hidden places.” That is, it does not subsist as made from nothing, like all the things mentioned above; rather, “it is drawn from hidden places,” that is, from the secret heart of the Father. Being invisible, it is found only invisibly. It is rightly said also to be drawn, because as we draw breath so that the body may live, so the spirit is drawn from the innermost depths of Wisdom “that the soul may subsist unto life.” Hence the Psalmist says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118).

VERS. 19. — “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” That is, no saint, however full of virtues—signified by topazion—can equal him. This stone is precious and is called *topazion*, as though *topandium*, because it shines with every light; for *pan* in Greek means “all.” No one gathered from this world’s blackness, signified by Ethiopia, can be equal to him of whom it was said: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). A certain topaz of Ethiopia wished to equal himself to him when a certain heresiarch said: “I do not envy Christ for having become God; if I wish, I too can become so.” To refute their pride, it is fittingly added: “Nor shall the purest dyes be compared with him [variant: the purest dye shall be compared with him].” That is, not even those who are not proud like the aforementioned heretics, but are truly humble and truly holy, shall be equal to him, because they know that they possess the beauty of virtues not from themselves but from the gift of grace bestowed upon them. They would not be dyed if they possessed holiness by nature. It should be noted that above, when he said, “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India,” he did not add “purest.” Here, in order to distinguish the dye of true virtues from that artificial display of the philosophers, in calling them dyes he added “purest.”

VERS. 20. — “Whence, then, does wisdom come?” Namely, the wisdom already said to differ so greatly from all others: from angels, signified by “fine gold”; from all expositions of sacred utterance, signified by “silver”; from worldly philosophers, denoted by “the dyed colors of India”; from all fathers of the Old and New Testaments, signified by the stones “sardonyx and sapphire”; from those who have already reached that heavenly country, signified by “gold and glass”; also from the prophets, who were high and eminent vessels of gold; and from the proud splendor of heretics, who seem to themselves to be “topaz,” having forgotten through pride that they came “from Ethiopia,” that is, from the blackness of Gentile life. “Whence,” I say, “does it come?” Can it be approached and brought here from there? The implied answer is: no. For it comes from where it arose: it is begotten from the invisible Father, and its way is hidden. For “who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 3). But you say: it is apprehended through the Spirit of understanding. Well: “And what is the place of understanding?” As though he said: From him from whom this Wisdom arises proceeds this Understanding. “Whence, then, does that Wisdom come,” or “what is its place?”

VERS. 21. — “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things,” because “no one has ever seen God” (John 1), from whose invisible heart this invisible Wisdom is invisibly born and Understanding proceeds.

After it has been said concerning the eternal Wisdom of God, “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things,” it is rightly added: “It is hidden also from the birds of heaven.” This Wisdom is hidden, certainly, not merely from the birds that “ate the seed by the way” (Matt. 13); for it would be no great thing to say that it is hidden from evil spirits, but also from those birds that rest in the branches of the great tree (ibid.): the tree, I say, which grew from the planted mustard seed. That tree is Christ, who was a mustard seed when he died in the humility of the flesh, and a tree when he rose through the power of majesty. This Wisdom is hidden even from those birds, I say, who rest in its branches—that is, spiritual men who find relief from the weariness of this world in the sayings of his apostles—because, established in this corruptible flesh, even those who already fly by the merit of holy contemplation do not penetrate by sight the omnipotence of his nature.

VERS. 22. — “Destruction and death”—namely, the devil, inventor of death and destruction, and all the spirits subject to his pride—“have said” concerning this Wisdom which is God: “With our ears we have heard its report,” namely, but have not also seen it. For to see God is to possess him. The wicked spirits do not see this Wisdom because through pride they do not possess it. “We have heard its report,” therefore, they say, but, rebelling against its light, have by no means seen it. They say this insofar as they openly make known to all, by their own perversity, that they did not stand in the truth. Who then knows it? What follows answers:

VERS. 23. — “God understands its way.” This is undoubtedly the saying in which Wisdom itself speaks concerning itself: “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11). “God,” he says, “understands its ways, and he himself knows its place.” For this Wisdom has a way and also a place; but it has its way in one manner and its place in another. It has a way through the passage of humanity; it has a place through the abiding state of divinity. Its way also is precisely this: that it comes to our heart and inwardly pours itself into us; its place, however, becomes the heart in which it abides when it comes. Therefore, concerning this Wisdom, which is the Son of God, and this Understanding, which is the Holy Spirit—by whose coming to us we are enabled to know that Wisdom—a human being indeed hears a voice, but “does not know whence it comes or whither it goes” (John 8). “But God understands its way,” that is, the wound of his love through which he pours it into the human soul, as seed naturally implanted in himself; “and he himself knows its place,” namely, that same soul, or even an angelic creature, into whose inmost parts, through the embrace of spiritual marriage—as into the womb of a loving bride—he pours the seed, that is, that Word or Wisdom. “He himself knows its place,” I say: not only what it is now, but also what it will be. This is what follows:

VERS. 24. — “For he beholds the ends of the earth,” that is, he has immediately before his sight the end to which each of all those who are in the world will come. “And he looks upon all things which are under heaven,” namely, choosing from among all those in whom by his grace he may place this same Wisdom.

VERS. 25.—“Who gave weight to the winds,” that is, [Col. 1085C] he gave gravity and stability to souls once light; for, when the aforesaid Wisdom fills souls that had formerly been light, she makes them mature and weighty. Or certainly, to “give weight to the winds” is to temper, with a mingling of weakness, the glory granted here to the elect through virtues. Hence it is added: “And he weighed the waters by measure,” that is, he gives to his saints the gifts of that same Wisdom, or of his Spirit, in measure—so that they may by no means be able to advance as far as they wish, lest they be lifted up into pride. For example, Elijah, though he had risen high through so many virtues, was held in a certain measure, afterwards fleeing Jezebel—though a queen, yet nevertheless a mere woman (3 Kings 19). Likewise Paul, who, having recovered the bodily light which he had lost for a time together with the abiding light of the heart, escaped from that same city by being lowered in a basket through the wall (2 Cor. 11)—the city which he had entered after the vision of Jesus. Indeed, he who had been caught up even to the third heaven still wept under the goad of the flesh, as a child struck with blows (2 Cor. 12). Thus he weighs out to his elect the waters of his gifts in measure (Rom. 12), so that they may be displayed by miracles and preserved by weaknesses. “God, I say, understands her ways, and he himself knows her place.” And I shall tell you when he knew her.

VERS. 26.—“When he set a law for the rains,” that is, when he sent her for the Incarnation, then he saw her—that is, he caused his incarnate Wisdom to be seen. “When,” he says, “he set a law for the rains,” [Col. 1086A] that is, when he gave the preachers a command of watchfulness: namely, this command, this law, that they should fulfill in their lives what they hastened to urge by their speech. “He set a law, I say, for the rains, and a way for the sounding storms,” that is, he made for those same preachers an entrance into human hearts smitten with fear of the future judgment. For first a law is set for the rains—that is, a command for the preachers’ manner of life—so that afterwards a way may be opened by their preaching; for that voice penetrates the hearer’s heart which preserves in deed what it has sounded forth. When he did this,

VERS. 27.—“Then he saw her,” that is, as has already been said, he caused his incarnate Wisdom to be seen, “and declared her, and prepared her, and searched her out”; that is, he caused her to be declared and prepared by [Col. 1086B] preachers, and searched out by hearers. For whoever, by living well, makes her propitious prepares her for himself. And it should be noted that four things are said of her: “He saw, declared, prepared, searched out.” For he “saw” her because she is substance or form; he “declared” her because she is the Word; he “prepared” her because she is remedy; he “searched” her out because she is hidden.

VERS. 28.—“And he said to man”: because she could not be penetrated by the human mind—for who can understand a Word without time, or a form without circumscription?—because, I say, she cannot be comprehended by man, “he said to man,” that is, he gave man this sign by which the same Wisdom may be known: “Behold, [Col. 1086C] the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil, understanding.” It is as though he plainly said: Return to yourself, man, and search the secrets of your heart. If you find that you fear God, it is certainly evident that you have something of this Wisdom. “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). And if you depart from evil—that is, if you refrain from doing evil not through slavish fear, but hate evil through the chaste fear of the Lord and turn your entire will away from evil—then know that you possess understanding, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which, beginning with the fear of the Lord, you will persevere and attain that same Wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXIX

VERS. 1.—“Job also continued, taking up his parable.” This break is fittingly placed, because up to this point he has expounded to his friends the wisdom [Col. 1086D] God had given him, though they despised him as foolish; henceforth he will humbly relate his good works, though he seemed to have done evil works and was condemned as a hypocrite or ungodly man. It is clear, moreover, that he speaks mysteries under the forms of outward words, since he is said to have taken up a parable in order to speak. “His parable,” I say. For when he recounts his own affairs, he announces what is to come upon holy Church; and the very order of the matter requires that, through his words, the final days of holy Church at the end should be signified. Then that dragon who now, as John says, is held shut up in the abyss, will be brought out of the pit of the abyss (Apoc. 20): that is, what is now concealed through fear will then publicly open against the Church, out of the hearts of the wicked, all its serpentine [Col. 1087A] venom. And all the elect will remember us who have lived through peaceful times of faith, because they will be troubled and assailed by the sayings and deeds of the wicked. Thus blessed Job, beholding those times, as has been said, recounts his own past and foretells what is to come to others, saying:

VERS. 2.—“Who will grant me that I may be as in the former months?” First, according to his own moral sense, this should be understood thus: “Who will grant me”—supply, *whom you suppose, through hypocrisy, to have been righteous—“who, I say, will grant me that I may be as in the former months,” that is, that according to the intention of my former life I may find consolation and mercy, “according to the days,” that is, according to the works of the days, “in which God guarded me,” namely from every hypocrisy or ungodliness with which you charge me?

VERS. 3.—“When his lamp shone,” that is, the simple and bright intention of his love, “over my head,” that is, over my mind, in every good work which I began to do; “and by his light I walked in darkness,” that is, by the witness of his eyes I entrusted to him all the hidden things of my heart. That I might be, I say,

VERS. 4.—“As I was in the days of my youth,” that is, that I might appear in God’s testimony as I remember myself to have been in his sight, when I embraced the purpose of righteousness and began to grow young in good—that is, to make progress—“when God was secretly in [Col. 1087C] my tabernacle,” that is, when amid the cares and activities of the world I embraced God in my heart, though this was hidden from all people.

VERS. 5.—“When the Almighty was with me”—supply, as the sweet consolation in my conscience of a loving soul, and the devout and singular joy of inward familiarity—“and around me,” that is, outwardly, “my children”—supply, not neglected because of my inward occupation. For God’s indwelling does not constrict the mind; rather, it enlarges it and brightens the countenance for the care to be bestowed upon the advantage or salvation of neighbors.

VERS. 6.—“When I washed my feet with butter,” that is, when I delighted gladly and abundantly [Col. 1087D] in the Lord. And this is expressed by an elegant comparison: there was such sweetness in the house of his heart, loving God and neighbor, as there is an abundance of milk where, if feet are washed with butter, the household’s sustenance suffers no loss. “And the rock,” he says, “poured forth for me streams of oil.” That is, the firmness of divine help enriched me both with peace in outward circumstances and with gladness of mind.

By allegory, these same words are to be understood in the person of the Church as follows. “Who will grant me,” says holy Church, scattered by the final persecution, “who, I say, will grant me that I may be as in the former months,” that is, adorned with holy pursuits and ordered in religious assemblies as formerly, when congregations of saints flourished through villages and cities, standing in their orders in a fixed number of those living communally, just as the individual months proceed in the order of the year according to the number of days; “that I may be, I say, according to the days in which God guarded me,” namely from such great pressures as now hem me in on every side, when the ancient dragon has been released, who now devours many of my children by deception whom I cannot guard. “When,” she says, “his lamp shone over my head,” that is, when his Holy Scripture adorned my assembly and my heart. For Holy Scripture is a lamp: “to which,” says the apostle Peter, “you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place,” etc. (2 Pet. 1). “It shone,” she says, “over my head,” that is, it illumined the darkness of my mind through men publicly preaching and holy men studying it—men whom persecution now [Col. 1088B] partly kills and partly drives away. “And by his light I walked in darkness,” that is, through its instruction I comforted the dark ignorance of the present life, 475 in which, as in the night, the true sun is not seen (1 Cor. 13), whose face we are promised we shall see in the future (Apoc. 22). That I might be, I say, “as I was in the days of my youth,” that is, when, now grown to maturity, I was married to Christ, God incarnate, and made fruitful by the conception of children through the ministry of preaching. “When God was secretly in my tabernacle,” that is, inwardly, in the hidden place of the heart, arranging that glory of mine which appeared outwardly as it were in golden fringes through the grace of teaching and miracles. “When the Almighty was with me,” namely cooperating and confirming the word with signs following (Mark 16). “And around me were my children,” namely, very many who served the heavenly commands, of whom the charity of many has now grown cold because iniquity abounds (Matt. 24). “When I washed my feet with butter,” that is, when I poured upon, and cleansed away, by the richness of good work the dust gathered from the glory of preaching. For preaching is scarcely carried on without some fault being incurred. Or certainly feet are washed with butter when hearers give the due support to holy preachers; Paul was anointed with this butter when he said: “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain” (2 Tim. 1). But also, when rulers call their hearers back to their hearts [Col. 1088D] so that they may lament the evils they have perhaps committed, they wash their feet with butter, because they supply the ointments of repentance for their wounds, which they have suffered by attending to outward things. “And the rock,” she says, “poured forth streams of oil for me,” that is, Christ—of whom Paul says, “the rock, however, was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)—poured forth for my use streams of Holy Scripture: for example, the book of Matthew, the book of Mark, the book of Luke, the book of John. These now seem almost to cease flowing, because the violence of persecutors blocks their channels, that is, holy preachers. Or the streams of oil are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10). Since Christ, ascending on high, gave these to men (Eph. 4), the rock surely poured forth streams of oil—streams which in that final persecution flow neither through public preaching nor through consoling miracles.

VERS. 7.—“When I went out to the gate of the city.” To retain first the simple historical course of the exposition: as the truth, compelled to come forth little by little from the conscience of the blessed man together with its companion, piety, defends itself with modest testimonies, it shows that there is in him neither ungodliness nor hypocrisy according to the accusation of his friends. “I went out,” he says, “to the gate of the city,” namely that I might be present as a voice and example of teaching or discipline; “and in the square they prepared a seat for me,” that is, I possessed an authority of severity or teaching free from every pretense and publicly approved.

VERS. 8.—“Young men saw me,” that is, the wanton, [Col. 1089B] “and hid themselves,” fearing the uncorrupted equity of the judge and the severity of the reprover; “and the elders, rising, stood,” namely mature and weighty men, revering wisdom pleasing to them.

VERS. 9.—“The princes ceased to speak”—supply, lest the lowest of men should dare to chatter foolish tales. “They ceased,” I say, “to speak and laid their finger upon their mouth,” that is, even if they spoke, they took care to maintain the modesty of discernment.

VERS. 10.—“The leaders restrained their voice”—supply, before I arrived they had begun to say what deserved rebuke—“and their tongue adhered to their throat,” that is, while I spoke, there was the deepest silence in listening.

VERS. 11.—“The ear that heard”—supply, my judgments [Col. 1089C] pronounced—“called me blessed”; thus no one then, as you do now, accused or branded me with ungodliness,

VERS. 12.—“Because I had delivered the poor man crying out, and the orphan who had no helper.” This, indeed, strongly contradicts the ungodliness with which you charge me.

VERS. 13.—“The blessing of him who was perishing,” that is, of the one who would have perished unless I had helped him, “came upon me,” because I justly rescued from a slanderer one who was unjustly endangered; and I comforted the heart of the widow, which was certainly not merely not ungodly but most godly. But after these words, regarded in the veneration of sacred history, the mysteries of allegory must now be investigated. [Col. 1089D] “I went out,” says holy Church, “to the gate of the city,” that is, after the manner of the ancients, who were accustomed to stand at the gate and judge the cases of those entering (Deut. 15; 2 Chron. 18; 2 Kings 15; Ruth 4), I exercised myself in holy actions through which, as through gates, an entrance into the kingdom of heaven is obtained. Of these the Psalmist says: “That I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9). “And in the square they prepared a seat for me,” that is, in the breadth of great authority freedom of teaching was granted to me. “Young men saw me and hid themselves,” that is, the immature, supported by no gravity of counsel, feared to be detected in their secret actions; “and the elders,” that is, all who are perfect and mature in the ripeness of their morals, whose senses were gray and whose old age was an unstained life among the aged (Wis. 4), [Col. 1090A] “rose and stood,” that is, by their humility they showed how far they had advanced in good actions. “The princes,” that is, the authors of heretical perversity, “ceased to speak,” that is, to devise perverse doctrines against the Catholic faith; “and laid their finger upon their mouth,” that is, they falsely complained that they were being repressed, not by force of argument, but by the violent hand of ecclesiastical power. They “laid their finger upon their mouth,” I say, that is, in indignation and murmuring they indicated that they were forced into silence by violence. “The leaders restrained their voice”—their voice only, not their mind as well—namely those same authors of heresy; “and their tongue adhered to their throat,” that is, they did not dare to speak perversely, [Col. 1090B] but, concealing everything within themselves, nevertheless perished in their silence. It must be supplied as though she said: But now, that is, in the final storm, according to what Jeremiah, seeing long beforehand, said: “Even the *lamiae* have bared the breast and nursed their young” (Lam. 4). Now, I say, heretics, like *lamiae*, freely preaching their bare breast—that is, their error—nurse their young, that is, strengthen their followers in ungodliness. “The ear that heard,” that is, the hearer obedient to faith or discipline, “called me blessed,” that is, advancing through sound teaching, he gladdened me by his good actions; “and the eye that saw,” that is, enlightened by God to understand truth, “bore witness to me,” that is, joined itself to me in defending that same truth, “because [Col. 1090C] I had delivered the poor man crying out,” etc. These words are not altered; but as they were expounded above in the person of blessed Job, so they must also be understood in the person of the Church, which is called blessed by its hearers for a double reason: because it both feeds its children by speaking and protects them by defending them, like a fruitful tree which refreshes those beneath it with food and shelters them from heat by its shade. And holy Church provides this not only bodily, as has been said, but spiritually as well. For it delivers the poor man crying out when it forgives guilt to the penitent sinner. It also delivers the orphan when, after the death of his former father, the devil, it regenerates each person to God; and the blessing of him who was perishing comes upon it, because when it causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, [Col. 1090D] it saves his soul from death (Jas. 5). It also comforts the heart of the widow when it recalls to the faithful soul, as it were, the good memory of her husband and recounts the Lord’s eternal rewards. It follows:

VERS. 14.—“I was clothed,” he says, “with righteousness”—and not in such a way as to leave any part of myself naked to sin, but “it clothed me”—supply, this same righteousness—“as with a garment.” For as, “with a garment,” 476 when I am clothed I am surrounded on every side, so I observed righteousness in such a way that I did not shut the doors against sin on one side while opening an entrance on another. “I was clothed, I say, with righteousness as with a garment, and with judgment as with a diadem”—supply, I adorned or crowned myself—namely, by diligently examining each day what I owed to God and what to my neighbor, as it is written: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12). These judgments are rightly compared to a diadem, because through the glory of a great work they lead to the crown of eternal reward.

VERS. 15.—“I was an eye to the blind.” He appropriately begins to enumerate, through works of piety, the parts of righteousness with which he said he was clothed, because then an offering of uprightness is true before God when the branches of righteousness proceed from the root of piety. “I was an eye,” he says, “to the blind, and a foot to the lame,” that is, I offered the blind man my hand personally, and myself bore up and sustained the lame man. And from this it is inferred how greatly the bowels of his mercy poured themselves out over the needy and poor. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1091B] VERS. 16.—“I was a father of the poor”: namely, the force of his mercy had imitated nature itself, since he showed himself a father to the poor by giving, not from fear of condemnation but from love of God and neighbor. According to allegory, holy Church says, “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame,” when it enlightens by preaching the one who does not see where he should go; and when it sustains by aid the one who, through weakness of mind, cannot go where he sees—that is, cannot do what he understands. Likewise, it is both father and mother of the poor. For some members in the body of the Church serve the light to be contemplated in the Scriptures; others, like a foot not at all separated from earthly action, support the whole body in the affairs of the present life; others, like a hand, protect the poor by extending alms. “I was a father,” I say, “of the poor, and I investigated with the utmost care the cause which I did not know,” that is, I was never hasty in pronouncing sentence, nor did I rashly judge what had not been examined. We rightly fear to commit this, if we weigh carefully the examples of our Creator, who, though all things are naked and open before his eyes, nevertheless did not choose to judge Sodom’s evils merely on report, but said: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied; I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18). This was said and written so that we, who are human and can be deceived, might be restrained from hastily pronouncing judgment. Once the cause had been investigated:

[Col. 1091D] VERS. 17.—“I broke,” he says, “the jaws of the wicked,” that is, against the person who, in the case under investigation, failed on the side of justice, I brought forceful and strict accusation and crushed the hidden snares which he clenched like molar teeth in order to harm his neighbor; “and from his teeth I took away the prey,” that is, by the equity of judgment I freed the one whom he already thought he held. The Church likewise does not cease to do this spiritually: it has taken prey from the teeth of the wicked as often as it has rescued a soul from the bite of error by preaching. What prey it took from the mouth and teeth of the wicked one, namely the devil, when by converting it seized the ravager Saul (Acts 9)! And whereas by persecuting the faithful he had gathered a people for the devil, it brought about that, by knowing the faith, he himself was gathered to [Col. 1092A] Christ. These and the things I have already mentioned I did.

VERS. 18.—“And I said: I shall die in my little nest,” that is, I shall take nothing from anyone or inflict evil, but rather I shall cherish those who need my breath and protection until I die, “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matt. 23). And by doing this to the extent of my power, “like a palm tree I shall multiply my days”: that is, just as the palm is constricted below by the wrappings of its bark but expands above in the breadth of beautiful greenery, so I, even if I am constricted in the present and bound to the rule of equity, shall in the future be enlarged before God and multiplied by the length of eternal days. But the Church, building for itself a nest—that is, [Col. 1092B] a most peaceful repose of faith—in which it cherishes its growing children in the bosom of charity until they fly to heaven, likewise says: “In my little nest,” that is, in the holy and peaceful rest of this faith, I shall persevere until death, “and like a palm tree I shall multiply my days.” This is not altered.

VERS. 19.—“My root is open beside the waters,” that is, all my thought is open to receive the streams of truth. Or, to apply this to the voice of the Church: “My root,” she says, that is, the Incarnation of my Redeemer, “is open beside the waters,” that is, according to his human nature he has been visibly shown to human beings. For the Incarnation of the Redeemer is the root of holy Church, because the whole Church flourishes as one tree, as it were, in faith in him; “and dew shall remain [Col. 1092C] in my harvest”—supply, I said—that is, the grace of God coming upon me will bring this about: it will carry my purpose through to the maturity of good works.

VERS. 20.—“My glory shall always be renewed,” that is, in order that I may be glorious, the fault of the old life will continually be erased in me through newness of spirit. For as our life is washed with tears and exercised in good works, as it is trained by holy meditations, it is restored without ceasing to its newness. “And my bow,” that is, Holy Scripture; for the bow signifies Scripture. Hence the Psalmist says: “He bent his bow and prepared it” (Ps. 7), because by Holy Scripture he set forth threats to all sinners. “My bow,” I say, “shall be renewed in my hand,” that is, Holy Scripture shall be fulfilled in my action. For the bow is renewed in the hand when whatever is learned through study in sacred speech is completed in life. These and these things I taught; then, says holy Church—supply, but now my hope was indeed true concerning many, yet very many of those in whom I had greater confidence have now become more bitter enemies of the faith.

Without changing the order of speech, while blessed Job sets forth his own personal affairs in words, he gives voice in meaning, as has often been said, to the affairs of holy Church. For he says:

VERS. 21.—“Those who heard me awaited my judgment,” etc. One must unquestionably believe that such was the reverence of his subjects toward him; yet his words are such that, while speaking of his own case, he proclaims ours, in this way: “Those who heard me awaited my judgment and, attentive, were silent for my counsel”—supply, not like these insolent and swollen persons, who, refusing to receive the words of truth, run through the judgments of preaching as though teaching them, and dare to assail me as I give right counsel.

VERS. 22.—“They dared add nothing to my words”—not as now heretics, unbridled in their worst freedom, presume to “add to my words” when they endeavor to correct the rectitude of my preaching. They were silent, I say, “and dared add nothing. And upon them there distilled,” that is, according to the hearers’ capacity, it was bestowed in measure, “my speech.” [Col. 1093B] In saying, “They dared add nothing to my words,” the reverence of the hearers is praised; in adding, “and upon them my speech distilled,” the teachers’ dispensation is indicated. This is also mystically signified by the fact that, at the Lord’s command, not only bowls but also cups were prepared for the table of the tabernacle (Exod. 25): for in the teaching of sacred discourse, not only great and hidden matters, which intoxicate, must be offered, but also small and subtle matters, which provide knowledge as it were through a taste. Therefore, where he states that his speech distilled, he fittingly adds:

VERS. 23.—“They awaited me as rain,” that is, with true humility, recognizing the dryness of their hearts, they thirsted for the drink of holy preaching, saying to God in their hearts: “My soul is to you like land without water” (Ps. 142); “and they opened their mouth,” that is, their heart, to my teaching, “as for the latter rain,” that is, rain long desired, because the latter rain (Luke 26) is Christ’s Gospel.

For, according to what is written, “I will give you the early and the latter rain” (Deut. 11), the Lord gave the “early” rain abundantly when, in the former time, he granted understanding of the Law; but the “latter” rain when, in the last days, he caused the mystery of his Incarnation to be preached. After expressing the hearers’ reverence and attention, he adds concerning his own severity:

VERS. 24.—“If ever I smiled at them, they did not believe it.” This must be believed both according to the history, and understood morally: that the holy man was such, and that holy Church should strive to be such in its prelates, that even while smiling he could be feared. In him it is highly praiseworthy that, amid such gentleness and mildness of piety—by which he was a father of the poor—he possessed at the same time such severity that he could be feared even while smiling. In the administration of ecclesiastical government likewise, matters should be moderated so that a prelate may be feared when smiling and loved when angry: lest excessive cheerfulness make him contemptible, or immoderate severity hateful. “And the light of my countenance,” he says, that is, the eyes of my heart, of which it is written: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccles. 2), whereas “the eyes [Col. 1094A] of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Prov. 17). “The light,” I say, “of my countenance did not fall to the ground,” because the eyes of my heart did not look upon earthly things through desire—supply, but were in my head, that is, were directed toward God, who is the Maker of all. This may suitably be understood according to the history; and in the mystical sense it is also evident that the “light,” that is, the inward eyes of the Church, contemplates its head, that is, Christ. For Christ and his body, which is the Church, are one person. And when he, namely Christ, as it were smiles upon us, we do not believe it: though his many gifts already attest it and we receive the grace of his favor, we nevertheless still waver under his judgment because of our weakness. And his light [Col. 1094B] does not fall to the ground, because the brightness of his vision does not appear to sinners, who, insofar as they are sinners, are earth. For it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). Upon such a person the light of the Lord’s countenance does not fall, as it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord.” But since what follows is clear according to the history as well, it must be pursued, as begun, from the same head of holy Church.

VERS. 25.—“If I wished,” he says, “to go to them”—“I wished,” I say, because my coming to a person is not according to that person’s merit, but according to the counsel of my will. “If therefore I wished,” he says, “to go to them,” that is, to enlighten their heart by the visitation [Col. 1094C] of the Holy Spirit, “I sat first,” namely so that they might “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6), because the desire for me in their thought is not equal to other desires. “And when I sat”—supply, in their hearts—“as a king,” governing the surrounding movements of their souls, “with an army standing around,” that is, a multitude of virtues against the seditions of vices, “yet I was a comforter of those who mourn,” by that consolation in which I say: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). And again: “But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice,” etc. (John 16). But there is no obstacle to understanding of the body, which is the Church, what has been said of the head. For in it the order of teachers presides like a king, surrounded by the multitude of its faithful, where piety is joined with authority, and authority is not absent from piety. “When I sat as a king with an army standing around”: behold the authority of rule. “Yet I was a comforter of those who mourn”: behold the ministry of piety. For discipline or mercy is greatly lacking if either is maintained without the other. Hence the Samaritan pours upon the wounds of the half-dead man not wine alone or oil alone, but both (Luke 10), because, as the Psalmist says, “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22). We are struck by the rod of discipline, but supported by the staff of piety. Moses offers an example of both: out of piety and love for his subjects, he restrained God saying, “Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them” (Exod. 32). But immediately, coming to the same people for whom he had obtained pardon, he said: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate, and let each man kill his neighbor.” And on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXX

VERS. 1.—“But now,” he says, “those younger than I mock me,” that is, they despise my words: namely, heretics, who, compared with the universal Church, may rightly without doubt all be called younger in time, because they came forth from her, not she from them. “Younger, I say, whose fathers”—that is, the inventors of their error, for example Arius, Albionus, [Col. 1095B] Macedonius, and the rest—“I would not have deemed worthy to set with the dogs of my flock,” that is, with the holy preachers of my faithful people. For, intent upon their Lord by vigils night and day, they uttered, so to speak, the great barks of preaching. Of these the Psalmist says: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies” (Ps. 67), that is, the voice of your preachers has gone forth from the nations once hostile but now converted. With these “dogs,” I say, I would not have deemed worthy to place their “fathers,” that is, their heresiarchs.

VERS. 2.—“The strength of whose hands,” that is, the magnitude of works which seemed to perform great things beyond others, “was as nothing to me,” because they did not work through charity and therefore those works [Col. 1095C] profited them nothing. “They were considered unworthy even of life,” that is, I judged them not to deserve the reward of life, since under Christ’s name they fought against Christ’s name through ostentation in their works.

VERS. 3.—“Barren through want and hunger,” because, striving to investigate God’s secrets beyond their capacity, they produce no good shoots of life; rather, they grow increasingly dry through want of grace raining from above and hunger for the Word of God. “Who gnawed,” namely because, unable to penetrate the inward marrow of God’s Word, they plucked at its outward husk. “They gnawed,” I say, “in solitude,” separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, “squalid through calamity and misery,” that is, despised because of the ruin of their morals [Col. 1095D] and perversity of thought.

VERS. 4.—“And they ate herbs and the bark of trees,” that is, in Holy Scripture they scarcely knew a few tender and outward matters. For by herbs plain sayings are signified, and by the bark of trees the outward utterances of the Fathers. Or certainly, to eat herbs is to observe the least precepts from Holy Scripture while despising the greater ones, for example: “You tithe mint and dill and cumin, and,” says the Lord, “have left aside the weightier matters of the Law” (Matt. 23). “And the root of junipers,” that is, avarice; for the juniper has pricks instead of leaves, since what it produces is bristly and like thorns. The “root,” I say, “of the juniper,” is avarice, “which is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6), from which the thorns of all [Col. 1096A] sins are produced; “it was their food,” because with all the powers of their mind they thought upon it and fed on it as if on nourishment.

VERS. 5.—“Who, from the valleys”—supply, the aforesaid things, “herbs and the bark of trees”—“snatching from the valleys,” I say, that is, gathering from the humble sayings of the Fathers in a proud spirit, “when they found individual things,” namely, glorying that these agreed with their own party, “ran to them with a cry,” that is, they hastened to spread abroad to the ears of men everything they thought, with a desire for praise.

VERS. 6.—“They dwelt in the deserted places of torrents,” that is, they trusted in the preaching of those whose utterances have already been dried up by the response of Catholics. For the inventors of perverse doctrines are rightly called torrents because, cold from the warmth of charity, they swell as it were in the torpor of wintertime; nor do they flow with perpetual fullness, but are dried up like torrents by the heat of the sun—that is, by Catholic arguments. The deserted places of “torrents,” therefore, are those who, craving the conveniences of temporal life, forsake heavenly gains. “In the deserted places,” I say, “of torrents; and in caves of the earth,” that is, in the hidden and clandestine conventicles of an earthly sect, in accordance with the woman who, in Solomon, as a type of heresy, urges: “Stolen waters are sweeter,” etc. (Prov. 9). “Or upon gravel,” that is, among the minds of those people who are established by no stability of gravity and are like gravel—that is, very small stones carried along by river water—because they are neither fixed nor founded upon the rock of faith (Luke 8).

VERS. 7. — “Who rejoiced among things of this sort”: that is, because perverse minds take delight in the iniquities which they ought to mourn; “and counted it a pleasure to be under thorns”: that is, though caught among the thorns of sins, they believed themselves to be amassing an abundance of virtues.

VERS. 8. — “Sons,” that is, imitators, “of fools and of the ignoble”: namely, of those who were teachers of errors. They are called “fools” because they strayed from true wisdom; “ignoble” because they do not belong to that noble one of whom it is said: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31). That is, Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, is noble at the end of the age, when he sits with the apostles to judge the earth—that is, the living and the dead. “Sons,” I say, “of fools and of the ignoble, and utterly not children in the land”: that is, having no portion in the holy Church, which in that world is indeed “the land of the living” (Ps. 26), and which will receive none but the wise and those made noble by divine regeneration.

Yet there is no obstacle to understanding, of the perverse and carnal who are nevertheless situated within the right faith, what was said under the figure of heretics; for the Church rightly counts them no less as adversaries than those who stand outside the faith. He therefore says: “Those who gnawed,” that is, who violently seized what belonged to others—as, conversely, it is written of those who take another’s goods by flattery: “And his enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. 71). “Those who gnawed,” I say, that is, who by force, as though gnawing with their teeth, seized another’s goods, “in desolation”: that is, in deprivation of every good. For they would not seize others’ possessions unless they had first remained inwardly solitary and empty, deprived of the cultivation of virtues.

“Wasted by calamity and misery”: that is, not by “calamity” alone, or the infirmity of nature—which, though created good in the first man, fell into weakness through the fault of its own will—but also by “misery,” namely that of actual sins. When these are added to the necessities of weak nature, they become miserable and foul in their hideous skin, as though calamity had burst forth outwardly. “And they ate herbs” [Col. 1097B]: that is, by mockery they consumed the good beginnings of the weak, according to the saying: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). “And they ate the bark of trees”: that is, by detraction they cut down the strength of certain persons which rose high. “And the root of junipers was their food”: that is, while devoted to avarice, as was said above, and reaching after temporal possessions, they do not perceive how great is that very avarice which, like the juniper mentioned before, has prickles instead of leaves—that is, thorns of cares instead of pleasures. It delights now in its root, but later, as it were from its branches, it pierces in punishment.

“Who from the valleys”—namely, those which they do not care to surpass by the ascent of virtue—“from the valleys,” I say, of the present life, which in comparison with the things above is a low valley and the deep place of exile, in which the holy man weeps while ordering ascents; “when they found these things, snatching them one by one”: that is, whenever opportunities arose, they were able to seize them; “they ran to them with a cry”: that is, they even quarreled over a small pittance. At times too, having daily broken the peace, they strove to seize the places and offices of the holy Fathers, whose merits they did not seek to attain.

“They dwelt in the deserted places of the torrents”: that is, in this life they desired to acquire those things which our torrents—that is, the holy preachers—have left behind. These, like torrents, overflow as it were in winter with a multitude of waters, while in the present life, which is dark and cold in comparison with the future, they flow toward us with divine words. But when the summer sun comes, they withdraw themselves, because when the light of the eternal homeland has shone forth, they cease preaching. “They dwelt,” I say, “in the deserted places of these torrents”: that is, they eagerly set themselves upon those things which the righteous leave and despise; “and in the caverns of the earth”: that is, in evil thoughts, where they hide themselves from human eyes as in caverns. “Or upon gravel”—supply, “they dwelt”—that is, relying on the flux of the present life and seeking to set their foot where, as upon gravel, when the foot is placed on the surface, it slips by the very rolling instability of the ground and falls down to the depths.

“Who rejoiced among things of this sort,” because, as Solomon says, “such rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2): attending to the temporal things which they receive and neglecting the eternal goods which they lose. “They rejoiced,” I say, “among such things, and counted it a pleasure to be under thorns”: that is, under the grave vexations of cares. For, pressed by sinful pleasures and by affection for the present life, they fail to perceive how harsh are the things they endure. Thus, according to Jeremiah’s lament, they are “made drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3). For just as one made drunk with wormwood finds what he has taken bitter, yet does not understand the same bitterness with which he is filled—for every drunken person does not know what he suffers—so the things an avaricious person endures for love of this life are bitter, yet, blinded by desire, he does not recognize that bitterness.

He is also denounced by the prophet, who says: “Ephraim, a heifer taught to love threshing” (Hos. 10): that is, all covetous persons, even when they might be free from work, nevertheless hurry to submit themselves to earthly toils; just as a heifer accustomed to the labors of threshing, when released, often returns of its own accord to the same work. Why is this? Because, as follows, they are “sons of fools”: that is, imitators of the wicked who went before them, from whose perversity they learned this. “Of fools,” I say, “and of the ignoble”: not of those nobly foolish, according to the Apostle’s saying, “If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3); but of those who “are slaves of sin” (Rom. 6), which is beyond doubt a great ignobility. And they are “utterly not children in the land,” that is, in the holy Church, being unknown before the divine eyes because of the rejection of their deeds; to whom it will one day be said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25). For whatever they formerly seemed verbally to venerate while placed within the holy Church, they afterwards, to the contrary, mock and attack. Hence it is plainly added:

479 VERS. 9. — “Now I have become their song, and I have been made their proverb,” because, as the wicked increase, faith and truth will be held in reproach and charged as crimes; and each person will be the more detestable the more praiseworthy he is.

VERS. 10. — “They abhor me”—supply, all the wicked—“and flee far from me,” not by the steps of their feet [Col. 1098D], but by the quality of their morals; “and they are not ashamed to spit in my face”: that is, they not only slander me in my absence, but even in my presence, insulting me, they cast forth loose words like flowing saliva. And because he knows that he suffers these evils by the Lord’s permission, he adds:

VERS. 11. — “He has opened his quiver”—supply, the Lord—that is, from his hidden counsel he has sent forth an open sentence, like an arrow from a quiver; “and he has afflicted me”: namely, with the arrow of his wisdom which, in the time of my prosperity, he held as it were in a closed quiver.

“And he has put a bridle in my mouth,” namely, that I may be silent [Col. 1099A], because there are none to hear my preaching; and, being silent, I may say: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136). And likewise I may do what the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted” (Tit. 3). He has therefore “put a bridle in my mouth”: that is, because I saw no progress from preaching in certain persons, I restrained my impulse toward them.

And because the holy Church suffers evils from those in whom it had formerly trusted with genuine love, since they appeared to serve under Christ’s name:

VERS. 12. — “At the right hand,” he says, “of the East”: that is, from those whom I counted, as it were, my right hand—that is, as of great importance—and who appeared to belong to him whose name is East, by the light of whose righteousness the night of our injustice is illuminated. From these, I say, as it were “at the right hand of the East, my calamities immediately arose”: that is, at once, in the time of adversity, my tribulations increased.

But if those who are truly faithful are called the right hand, calamities arise at the right hand of the East because, when the occasion of persecution bursts forth, the righteous suffer the cruel assaults of the wicked. “They overthrew my feet”: that is, they drew into the error of their doctrine those who, like the extremities of a body, are in me—that is, those who serve earthly works and therefore can more readily be deceived by adversaries. “And they overwhelmed my paths as with waves”: that is, by their sects [Col. 1099C], which they devised, they overwhelmed, as it were by a storm, the ships of hearts.

VERS. 13. — “They have scattered my paths.” Let blessed Job say this of evil spirits, his hidden enemies; let the whole Church say it of her persecutors. “They have scattered my paths”: that is, they disturbed the ways of the weak by crafty persuasion. “They laid snares for me”: that is, those of mine whom they could not openly drag toward evils, they perverted by pretending good things. “And they prevailed”: that is, by laying snares they brought their will to effect. “And there was no one to bring help,” because almighty God sometimes abandons for a time those whom he loves eternally. Thus it is written: “For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isa. 54), and many similar passages.

VERS. 14. — “As though a wall had been breached”: that is, as though the defense of faith in Christ had been destroyed. For our Redeemer is called a wall, as it is written: “A Savior shall be set in it as a wall and a rampart” (Isa. 26). As though, I say, the wall of faith or the fortification of discipline had been breached, “and the gate opened”: that is, permission of power granted to them, “they rushed upon me, and cast themselves down upon my miseries”: that is, they raged irrationally against a wretched one. [Something is missing.]

VERS. 15. — “And like a cloud”—one which rises high, but which a gust drives onward in its course—“my salvation passed away”: that is, all earthly prosperity, which is lofty to the perverse but has no stability. I too once flourished in it, and for that reason was held in reverence even by the wicked.

VERS. 16. — “But now my soul withers within me”—supply, so that it may grow green with eternal exultation—“and days of affliction possess me,” as it is written: “You humbled us in the place of affliction” (Ps. 43). For the place of affliction is the present life; days of joy will follow afterwards.
