VERS. 17. — “By night my bone is pierced with pains.” He enumerates the parts of this same affliction; and, as has often been said, he so describes his own experiences that what he tells may also apply to those falling away from the Church. “By night,” says the holy Church, “my bone”—that is, in this night-like time of tribulation, those who are strong in my body and bear the morals of the weak steadfastly, just as bones bear flesh. “My bone,” I say, “is pierced with pains”: that is, even the strong, overcome by torments, fall away into unbelief. “And those who consume me do not sleep”: that is, evil spirits who consume carnal persons know no rest from their temptations, just as the multitude of worms, issuing through the hollows of ulcers, tore the holy man’s body and, without sleeping, did not even allow him to sleep.

VERS. 18. — “My garment is consumed in their multitude”: that is, according to the history, my body. But allegorically, the garment of the holy Church is the religious life of believers, especially those living in common; it is then, as it were, consumed by the multitude of worms when, through the assault of evil spirits or cruel persons and the scattering of believers, religious life is destroyed. Nor do they merely try to extinguish the life of faith in me; “they have also girded me as with the collar of a tunic”: that is, they strive to take away from me every word of preaching. For just as, when the collar of a tunic is drawn around the wearer’s neck, if the neck is constricted, both the use of the voice and vital breath are choked off, so they seek to make me wholly unable to dare speak of faith or of Christ’s name. Thus:

VERS. 19. — “I have been compared to mud”: that is, I am contemptuously trampled like mud; “and made like ashes and dust”: namely, in the judgment of the reprobate, who, supposing that no fire of any good remains within me, judge me inwardly to be such as they see me outwardly. Why is this? Because of what follows:

VERS. 20. — “I cry,” he says, “to you, O God, and you do not hear me. I stand, and you do not regard me.” It is as though he said: Therefore I am more securely trampled as mud and despised as ashes and dust, because you do not hear me crying in my pains; you do not regard me standing—that is, persevering in supplication—meaning that you do not heal me; indeed, you do not cease to afflict me.

VERS. 21. — “You have changed toward me into one who is cruel.” Just as God is said to be jealous without jealousy, angry without anger, and repentant without sorrow or repentance, so the holy man, using the language of our mutability, now says: “You have changed toward me into one who is cruel”: that is, you do not spare me in striking severely. Thus here “cruel” may be understood as striking severely and not sparing guilt that must be punished. So also: “Behold, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel and full of indignation,” etc. (Isa. 13). “You have changed toward me,” I say, “into one who is cruel”—though you have no cruelty in yourself—“and in the hardness of your hand,” that is, in the stroke of your strength, which is hard, that is, contrary to my will, “you oppose me,” just as a physician’s instrument cutting a wound hurts the sick person.

VERS. 22. — “You lifted me up,” namely, by the glory of the present life, which appears lofty but is supported by no stability. This is what follows:

“And, setting me as it were upon the wind, you dashed me down violently” [Col. 1101B], because the breeze of fleeting prosperity lifts anyone only so that it may suddenly cast him down more grievously into low places; and, falling suddenly, he learns that, when lifted up, he had been sitting upon the wind. These things fit his own person in particular, not according to what he was, but according to what he seemed to be. For, formerly supported by outward possessions, by the very means through which he was judged to have risen, he now appeared to have fallen, dashed down. “You dashed me down,” I say, and at last:

VERS. 23. — “I know that you will hand me over to death, where the house appointed for every living person is.” This plainly fits him according to the history, because before the grace of the Redeemer even the righteous descended to the bars of hell. Allegorically, however, it fits the holy Church speaking in the person of the weak, who, while living carnally, come to the house of death. There are indeed some who, after falling into the pit of their pleasures, quickly draw their foot back from the depths by repentance. Hence it is plainly added:

VERS. 24. — “Nevertheless, you do not stretch out your hand for their destruction,” because by striking you save them from sins; “and if they fall, you yourself will save them”: that is, if they sin, you wound them for bodily health, so that, cast down outwardly, they may rise inwardly.

VERS. 25. — “Formerly I wept for one who was afflicted.” It is as though he said: The impiety or hypocrisy which you have charged against me has always been as far from me as may be gathered from this: I not only gave to the poor, which a hypocrite can do for vain glory, but I also wept for one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor—something which neither a hypocrite can do nor an impious person knows how to do. This also accords with the voice of the holy Church: whenever she sees afflicted persons in the lamentations of repentance, she joins her own continual tears to theirs in prayer; and as often as she aids one stripped of virtues with the prayers of her intercession, so often she has compassion on the needy. And in doing this:

VERS. 26. — “I expected,” he says, “good things”—supply, things to come through the grace of renewal—“and evils came to me,” namely present evils. “I looked for light,” that is, the joy of recompense, “and darkness broke forth” [Col. 1102A]: that is, the evils of present sorrow, which I have already mentioned and shall yet speak of.

VERS. 27. — “My inward parts boiled without any rest.” Although this is sufficiently clear according to the history—for his “inward parts” so “boiled” that, as he said above, “even his wife abhorred his breath” (Job 19)—allegorically it must be said that the inward parts of the holy Church boil: that is, she endures, amid the fierceness of persecution, even those whom she had previously carried in herself as inward parts through the love of faith. Since they formerly knew her secrets, the more they know where she suffers most, the more grievously they do not cease to afflict her. Of these it is plainly added: “Days of affliction came before me”—supply, before this final persecution—“came before me,” I say, because even in times of peace I endured their evil customs with affliction of soul.

VERS. 28. — “I went about mourning.” According to the letter, it is remarkable that the holy man, having said above, “You lifted me up” (v. 22), adds below: “I went about mourning.” For at one and the same time, in the conduct of good persons, there is commonly outward honor at the summit and inward sorrow of afflicted humility. “I rose without anger; I cried out in the crowd.” This too is praiseworthy in the same holy man. Impatience is always a companion to the punishment of power. Hence it is all the more praiseworthy in holy persons that, while enduring the clamor of those subject to them, they rebuke through love those whom they bear with gentleness; thus, against the tumult of insolent persons, they have a cry but not anger. And lest you think it a small thing that he conducted himself with such tranquility:

VERS. 29. — “I was a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches.” “Of dragons,” I say, that is, of malicious persons, of whom the prophet also says: “They drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. 14): that is, they were puffed up with malicious pride. “I was a brother of dragons,” I say: that is, I lived among malicious persons; “and a companion of ostriches”: that is, I was a companion of hypocrites. For the ostrich, which has feathers but does not fly, signifies hypocrites, who have the appearance of holiness but do not have its power. This fittingly applies both particularly to blessed Job, who was good among evil persons at the height of great strength, and generally to the elect people of the holy Church, which in its time of peace endures malicious persons and hypocrites within itself. For he refuses to be Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test. Hence the angel of Pergamum is told: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is,” etc. (Rev. 2).

VERS. 30. — “My skin has been blackened upon me.” According to the history, the force of the statement is clear from the punishment of suffering. Allegorically, however, this fittingly accords with the voice of the holy Church. “My skin,” she says, “has been blackened”: that is, the weak, who in me serve outward usefulness, through fear of persecution have lost the bright color of righteousness and have come to the blackness of iniquity [Col. 1103A]. Jeremiah laments this under the figure of the chief metal, saying: “How the gold has grown dim; the finest color has changed!” (Lam. 4). “And my bones dried up from the heat”: that is, strong men, in whom the whole framework of my body is held together, are tormented by the fire of their zeal, because “my skin”—that is, the life of the weak—“has been blackened,” grieving and saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11), and similar things.

VERS. 31. — “My harp,” he says, “has been turned into mourning.” It is as though he says openly: In the time of my peace, by some I preached small things like a harp-player; by others, great and resounding things like an organ-player [Col. 1103B]. But now “my harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep,” because, when I see myself despised, I mourn those who do not hear the song of preaching; for I weep, indeed, for those whom I cannot draw by exhortation.

## CHAPTER 31

From this point he begins to narrate more carefully the good deeds that he performed. These, for the most part, must be retained according to the text of the historical sense alone, lest, if they are investigated more than necessary, blood answer from the breasts of his words instead of milk, according to Solomon’s saying: “He who presses the breasts too hard brings forth blood” (Prov. 30). Thus, in the course of sacred Scripture, the literal sense alone must in part be retained as reason requires, while in part the brightness of allegory must be sought.

Thus it is mystically represented in Jacob’s action, when, setting rods before the eyes of the sheep so that they might conceive while looking at them, “he partially stripped them of their bark; and when the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the places that had been stripped, while the parts that remained intact stayed green; and in this way a variegated color resulted” (Gen. 30). So, I say, in the sayings of this and the other preceding Fathers, when we often avoid the literal sense, we as it were remove the bark; and when we often follow the literal sense, we as it were retain the bark.

Accordingly, in enumerating the virtues by which he reasonably repels from himself the charges of hypocrisy and impiety brought against him by his friends, he first indicates with what strength he fortified himself, saying:

[Col. 1103D] VERS. 1. — “I made a covenant with my eyes”: namely, that I might keep the thoughts of my heart chaste, lest I first look carelessly upon what I would afterwards love unwillingly. Thus the prophet David (Ps. 50), who, his mind raised up, was often present to inward mysteries, because he carelessly looked upon another man’s wife (2 Sam. 11), later, darkened in mind, unlawfully joined her to himself. “I made,” I say, “a covenant with my eyes”: that is, I compelled my eyes to be harmonious with and obedient to my mind, “that I should not even think of a virgin,” already possessing the spirit of him who, restraining not only the lust of the flesh but also that of the heart, would say: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5).

He then adds the reason or intention for which he pursued purity, which no hypocrite cares for, since he seeks to please people.

VERS. 2. — “For what portion,” he says, “would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from on high?” Supply: none. For if my mind wastes away in weak desires before his sight, the maker of heavenly things, who is the author of purity, refuses to possess me as his own. By this saying he by no means intends it to be understood that sin never touched his mind in thought, but that it never overcame him through consent. And because the considered end of evils is a swift consolation for the good, he immediately adds:

VERS. 3. — “Is there not destruction for the wicked?” Supply: certainly there is—namely this: that God has no portion in him from above. “And alienation”—which among the Hebrews is called *anathema*—“alienation,” I say, from the inheritance of God, “for those who work iniquity”: supply, is there not?

VERS. 4. — “Does not he”—supply, he who watches others—“does not he himself consider my ways,” that is, my actions, “and count all my steps,” that is, the movements of my mind, supply, in order to bring them back for judgment? And indeed he maintained a life of perfection among the ancients; yet, because his intention, through the prophetic spirit, reaches forth to the coming of the Redeemer—who so considers each person’s ways and so “counts steps” that not even the smallest thoughts and slightest words, which have grown cheap among us through use, remain unexamined in his judgment—turning toward him, he weighs how much he still lacks of perfection. Hence he adds:

VERS. 5. — “If I have walked in vanity, and my foot has hastened in deceit”: that is, if I ever did anything lightly, or anything destructively.

VERS. 6. — “Let him weigh me in a balance”: that is, let him come in the mediator between God and human beings; “and let God know my simplicity”: that is, through his more subtle precepts, let him make me know how far I still differ from true simplicity. Why he calls the Lord Christ a balance has been said elsewhere, where he says: “Would that my sins and the calamity that I suffer were weighed in a balance” (Job 6). But now he has added “just.” For the just balance is he in whom all our merits are weighed in an even scale, and in whose precepts we recognize how much our life lacks. For as often as we are summoned to the examples of his life, so often are we weighed in this balance.

VERS. 7. — “If,” he says, “my step has turned aside from the way”: that is, if my thought has left the path of righteousness by consenting to error; “and if my heart has followed my eyes”: that is, if in looking I have ever followed what I perhaps desired when stirred by a harmful delight; “and if a stain has clung to my hands”: that is, if the uncleanness of thought at once passed into action.

VERS. 8. — “Let me sow, and let another eat.” Above he had said: “I made a covenant with my eyes,” and so forth, knowing that an evil thought often comes through the eyes to the mind. Now he says: “If my heart has followed my eyes,” considering that sometimes it first arises in the mind, and, once arisen, the eyes perversely serve it. It is as though he openly said: Nor did I wish indiscriminately to see what I might desire. If, he says, I have done these or those things, “let me sow, and let another eat”: that is, may whatever I say not profit me, but may another be filled by good work; and may my offspring be uprooted—that is, may my followers not enter the land of the living, in which all the elect are planted as it were, because they are to remain firm forever. For a teacher’s offspring is uprooted when one who is born by his word is killed by his example. This is beautifully represented in Solomon, when the woman, while asleep, killed the son whom she had been accustomed to nurse while awake. Yet the sword of the wise one found the true mother of the living child (1 Kgs. 3), because the wrath of the strict Judge shows in the final examination whose fruit lives and whose dies. “Let my offspring be uprooted,” I say, if I have done the things mentioned above or those which are to follow.

VERS. 9. — “If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman, and if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend.” By saying, “If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman,” he shows that he did not even entertain the thought of the stain of fornication; by adding, “and if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend,” he clearly makes known that he was innocent of the guilt of adultery. If he had ever done this, he asks that the same fault be turned against him as punishment, saying:

[Col. 1105C] VERS. 10. — “Let my wife be another man’s prostitute, and let others bend over her.” Showing by his expression how grievous it is to suffer this, he says:

VERS. 11. — “For this,” he says, “is wickedness and a very great iniquity.” Supply: Therefore, since I avoided this because it is “wickedness” and “iniquity,” I am not wicked; I am not, as you my friends have charged, impious. It is “a very great iniquity.” Defining this same iniquity of lust, he says:

VERS. 12. — “It is a fire devouring even to destruction”: that is, not merely staining unto defilement, but also “uprooting all the offspring” of virtues. For however great other efforts at good works may be, if the crime of lust is not washed away, they are overwhelmed by the magnitude of this sin. Having spoken of the virtue of chastity, he immediately shows how humble he also was.

VERS. 13. — “If,” he says, “I have despised to submit to judgment with my male servant or my female servant when they disputed against me”—supply: “let my shoulder fall from its joint.” For he will later pronounce this curse. It is surely a great thing that his heart should possess such humility that female servants and male servants were permitted to come to judgment with him as equals, though his authority in governing was so great that, in his presence, leaders restrained their voices and princes ceased speaking, as was said above (Job 29).

VERS. 14. — “For what shall I do,” he says—supply, if I had despised to submit to judgment with them—“what,” I say, “shall I do when God rises up for judgment,” namely, he with whom I share no common nature? And when “he asks”—supply—why I despised communion of nature in male or female servants, “what shall I answer him?” For there is nothing in which I am temporarily above others, when I am to render an account to him who without end rules over all persons in every place. “What shall I answer?” I say.

VERS. 15. — “Did not he who made me in the womb make him also, and did not one form us in the womb?” It is as though he says: The swelling of pride must be pressed down by the hand of most humble consideration. For nature made all human beings equal, but the hidden dispensation, varying the order of merits, sets some above others. Thus, when the Lord said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” he did not say, “Let your terror and dread be over” the human beings who were to come, but “over every animal of the earth” (Gen. 11). Therefore, when holy persons exact fear from those who live perversely, they rule not over human beings as such but over brute animals, because insofar as such persons are beastly, they ought also in that respect to lie subjected to fear.

VERS. 16. — “If,” he says, “I denied to the poor what they wanted.” His friends accused him of impiety. In response, after his deeds of chastity and humility, he fittingly adduces, point by point, the marks of compassion and adds works of liberality: “If,” he says, “I denied to the poor what they wanted”—to those poor, I say, whom the Lord calls blessed, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5). For those who are not truly poor, that is, humble, often want things that are certainly not expedient for them, and which therefore must be denied. “If,” I say, “I denied to the poor,” that is, the humble, “and if I made the eyes of the widow wait”: that is, I did not darken the light of mercy by delaying my gift, according to the saying: “Do not say, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I shall give to you,’ when you can give at once” (Prov. 3). And in order to show that he had not merely furnished many things to outsiders, but had also received needy persons into his own household fellowship:

VERS. 17. — “If,” he says, “I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it” [Col. 1106D]: namely, because I would have judged it an injury to compassion if I ate alone what the Lord of all created for common use. And he indicates that he possessed these bowels of compassion not from himself, but through the Creator’s grace, when he says:

VERS. 18. — “For compassion grew with me from my infancy, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” Although compassion depended upon his own choice in growing along with him, it is nevertheless clear that it did not depend upon his own choice to come forth with him from the womb.

VERS. 19. — “If,” he says, “I despised one passing by because he had no clothing, or a poor person without a covering.”

VERS. 20. — “If his sides have not blessed me, and if he was not warmed by the fleece of my sheep” [Col. 1107A]. It is as though he said: In love of neighbor, suppressing in one and the same order both the vice of pride and that of impiety, I looked humbly upon anyone passing by and warmed him compassionately. He indicates that he had mercy upon a neighbor unknown to him, whom he calls a passer-by, because for a compassionate mind nature counts for more than acquaintance.

VERS. 21. — “If I lifted my hand against the orphan”: that is, nor did I then wish to carry out my affairs, by force, against an orphan, “when I saw myself superior in the gate”: that is, when I saw that even in judgment I was superior by right. For “in the gate” means in judgment, because among the ancients the elders customarily sat in the gate to decide the disputes of litigants by judicial examination, so that those at discord might not enter the city in which they ought to live in harmony. At last he adds the sentence of a curse, should he have failed to fulfill in deed any of the things he had said:

VERS. 22. — “Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be broken with its bones.” It is as though he openly says: If I refused to do the things I have said, may I lose the bodily member given to me for action itself. Or, if this sentence of the curse is to be referred to spiritual understanding, it is plainly clear that the arm is joined to the body through the shoulder. And as the arm signifies the good works of those who act, so the shoulder signifies the bond of social life. The prophet, seeing this, says: “They shall serve him with one shoulder” (Zeph. 3). Therefore, he says, “Let my shoulder fall from its joint”: by impatience let the mind abandon brotherly concord and be cut off from the whole fellowship of all good persons. “And let my arm,” that is, all my activity, “be crushed with its bones,” that is, with its virtues. But with what consideration he did good things and abstained from evil things he adds, saying:

VERS. 23. — “For I always feared God as waves swelling over me,” namely, lest, while navigating amid the care of temporal affairs, I should incur the eternal death which he threatens; “and I could not bear his weight,” because in consideration of the terror by which heaven and earth will be shaken, the mind trembles with fear and, turning away the eyes of its attention, refuses to look upon what it foresees.

After enumerating the virtues mentioned above, what remains except that he should make known with what disposition he possessed even his riches? For he says:

### Verse 24

“If I have regarded gold as my strength,” that is, if I had despaired of the Creator by placing my hope in a creature. “If,” he says, “I have regarded gold as my strength, and have said to refined gold (*obrizum*; variant *obrizo*), ‘You are my confidence,’” that is, to an unworked mass of gold. For by *obrizum* we mean an unworked mass of gold. He did not place his confidence in it, because, fixing his hope and love in the grace of the Creator alone, he sinned neither through the quantity nor through the beauty of gold, fearing to hear the words: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things which you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12). [Col. 1108A]

### Verse 25

“If I have rejoiced,” he says, “over my great riches, and because my hand found very much”: for holy men, amid the misery of this pilgrimage, count all the abundance of the present life as poverty. For the love of the heavenly inheritance, they either scatter it by giving or abandon it by despising it.

### Verse 26

“If I saw the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in brightness”: these luminaries are seen in one way for use, in another for worship. “If,” therefore, he says, “I saw them”—understand, in the manner in which they are customarily worshipped by their devotees.

### Verse 27

“And my heart rejoiced secretly, and I kissed my hand,” namely, in worship of them. “Secretly,” I say—understand: because you say that I was a hypocrite; for you know that I did not do this evil openly. [Col. 1108B]

### Verse 28

“This too is a very great iniquity”: namely, to serve the creature rather than the Creator—“iniquity,” I say, “and denial against God Most High.”

But why does he now mention as remarkable that he did not worship the sun and moon? This is to be understood more subtly. After testifying that he had not placed confidence in gold nor rejoiced in great riches, he adds: “If I saw the sun,” and so forth. It is as though, after despising earthly abundance, he plainly intimated: Why should I say that I did not rejoice in gold, when I did not even delight in bodily light itself? Comparable is what the prophet, fleeing the desire for outward life, said: “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” (Jer. 17). [Col. 1108C]

But if it is pleasing to investigate allegorically as well the things that have been said according to the historical sense, then in the words, “If I regarded gold as my strength, and said to refined gold, ‘You are my confidence,’” what do we understand by gold except the brilliance of noble understanding? And what by refined gold except the mind? For the brilliant intellects or minds of the saints are humbly subjected to divine gifts and receive distinct gifts of grace bestowed upon them, just as gold is placed in an ornament so that an arrangement of gems may be set above it. Of this gold it is written: “Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure—what profit is there in either?” (Ecclesiasticus 20:32 [OCR/printed citation: XLI].) [Col. 1108D]

“If, therefore,” he says, “I regarded gold as my strength,” for however greatly I might shine in intellect, I did not judge myself to be anything by my own powers. “If I rejoiced over my great riches,” that is, over the many gifts which I received from God as money lent to me, according to the words: “To whom much is given, much will be required” (Luke 12), and so forth. These gifts are sometimes taken from the proud mind and restored when it has been humbled.

This is mystically represented in the event when the sons of the prophets were cutting wood in the Jordan, and one of them lost an axe-head which slipped from its handle into the depths; then Elisha came, sent the handle downward, and the iron floated upon the surface and returned to the handle (4 Kings 6). The iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart. To cut wood by this means is to rebuke those who act wrongly. When this is done through vain glory, the iron is lost in the water—that is, the gift is lost in disordered activity. But our Redeemer, who is figured by Elisha, sends down, as it were, a piece of wood and restores the iron when he humbles the sinner’s heart and renews lost understanding. [Col. 1109A]

“If, therefore, I rejoiced,” he says, “over great riches, and because my hand found very much”: that is, I was not proud because I received many gifts of understanding from heaven. “If I saw the sun when it shone”: that is, I did not rejoice in the brightness of my good work when it shone before men, so as to regard the favor of presumption because I gave others the light of example. “And the moon moving in brightness”: that is, I did not rejoice that my reputation was upon many lips. For reputation is somewhat like the moon, which receives illumination from the sun: it receives its power from a good work and scatters the favor of approval like brightness of light. Yet many who gaze at the moon do not see themselves, because they begin not to know themselves when they fix the eyes of their mind upon passing favor. [Col. 1109B]

“And if my heart rejoiced secretly”: that is, I was in no way arrogant—not only in words, but not even in silent thought. “And if I kissed my hand”: that is, neither did I praise with my own mouth what I had done. A person kisses his own hand with his mouth when he praises what he has done and attributes the merit of the work to himself by the testimony of his own speech—“which,” I say, “is a very great iniquity,” namely because it is pride. For whoever attributes to himself what he accomplishes is proved to be proud against the grace of his Maker. “And denial against God Most High.” For it is clear that one denies God whose grace he despises while arrogating to himself the powers of good work. [Col. 1109C]

### Verse 29

“If I rejoiced,” he says, “at the downfall of one who hated me”: this is alien to charity, which alone proves who are the disciples of almighty God, as Truth itself says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

For although the Psalmist says, “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57:11), the righteous person does not take this as said concerning the downfall of his own enemy, but concerning the downfall of God’s enemy. Nor do the words, “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance,” contradict the words, “Love your enemies” (Luke 6). For he does not say, “Love God’s enemies,” but “your enemies”: that is, we ought to forgive injuries done to ourselves, but to seek vengeance for injuries done to God. Therefore, he says, “I did not rejoice at the downfall of one who hated me,” nor “exult that evil had befallen him,” so that, loving even an enemy and grieving for my adversary when he fell into misfortune, I myself might grow in goodness. [Col. 1109D]

### Verse 30

“For I did not give my throat to sin, that I should seek his life by cursing.” It is greatly remarkable where this man had read, “Love your enemies,” or where he had read, “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12). He had not given “his throat to sin,” as follows: “that I should seek his life by cursing”—that is, that I should curse him and say to God: Kill the man I hate. [Col. 1110A]

### Verse 31

“If the men of my tent did not say”—namely, with impunity, since I did not seek vengeance—“Who will give us of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?” That is: who will grant that we may see his death, or the punishments inflicted upon him, which we greatly desire?

This can nevertheless be understood mysteriously in the person of the Redeemer, because “the men of his tent,” namely Jews and Gentiles, desired to be satisfied with his flesh: the former plotting to destroy him by consuming him; the latter desiring to satisfy their hungry minds with his flesh through the daily sacrifice of offering. But now, following the force of the historical sense alone, it is fitting to consider with what great strength his mind, attentive to all things, was divided between outward and inward concerns. [Col. 1110B]

### Verse 32

“The stranger did not remain outside; my door stood open to the traveler.” It is as though he said: Since a gift offered with a heart bound by malice is not accepted by almighty God—as is shown by the words, “God looked upon Abel and his offerings” (Gen. 4)—when the men of my tent said, as was mentioned above, “Who will give us of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?” I dismissed this from my heart. Then, through this inward purity of heart, I offered outward gifts, namely: that “the stranger did not remain outside and my door stood open to the traveler”; and also that I might deserve, by confessing my sins, to have them washed away, although the heavenly Father would forgive them. This is what follows. [Col. 1110C]

### Verse 33

“If I concealed my sin as a man does, and hid my iniquity in my bosom.”

By this saying both his humility and his strength are commended. For a person’s acknowledging his iniquity and, once it is known, disclosing it by the voice of confession, is an act not only of humility but also of strength. Indeed, because of the shame belonging to weakness, it is often a more difficult struggle to disclose sins that have been committed than to avoid sins not yet committed. And because true humility always gives rise to secure authority.

### Verse 34

“If I was afraid,” he says—that is, I was not “afraid of the great multitude”: namely, while others were outwardly disturbed against me, I myself remained inwardly undisturbed. “Of the great multitude,” I say—understand: of those who despised me. For he continues: “And if contempt from my neighbors terrified me, and I did not rather remain silent”—namely, in that I did not strive to commend myself. Why? Because there is great security of heart in possessing no worldly desire. Since I possessed none, I did not fear to be wholly despised, nor did I desire to be judged praiseworthy or thought wise. [Col. 1110D]

“If,” I say, “I did not rather remain silent and did not go out of my door”—that is, out of my mouth—which I would have done if I had disclosed by words the secrets of my heart, and had gone outward through my tongue as I remained inwardly in conscience. Our Lord commends an example of this in himself: so that he might die openly as man, he remained hidden as God, and “did not go out of the door” when, questioned by Pilate, he kept silence. Amid the hands of his persecutors he offered to suffering the body which he had assumed for the elect, and he did not wish to show to those resisting him what he was. But the holy man, knowing that he could not attain the highest things by so many virtues, seeks a helper. [Col. 1111A]

### Verse 35

“Who,” he says, “will give me a helper [or: a hearer]?” Namely, the only-begotten Son of God, who, by assuming human nature laboring in this mortality, may help it, “so that the Almighty may hear my desire”: namely, on that day when he, “offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry in the flesh, was alone worthy to be heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

He makes clear by the words added that he seeks this helper, saying: “And let him who judges write a book.” “He,” I say, “who judges,” as he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5)—before he comes to judge, let him come to “write a book,” that is, to establish the New Testament. He is also signified in Ezekiel by “a man clothed in linen and having a writer’s inkhorn at his loins” (Ezek. 9): namely, because he deigned to have parents from the priestly tribe, he is, as it were, clothed in linen; or certainly because linen grows from the earth but not, as wool does, from corruptible flesh, he is described as clothed in linen, because he took the garment of his body not from the corruption of sexual union but from the Virgin Mother. [Col. 1111B–C]

“And having a writer’s inkhorn at his loins”: these are, of course, the posterior part of the body, because after he had completed all things and returned to heaven, he wrote the New Testament through those who came after him, that is, through the apostles. “Let him,” I say, “write a book.”

### Verse 36

“So that I may carry it on my shoulder”: that is, that I may observe in my actions what he hands down through the aforesaid New Testament; “and crown myself with it like a diadem”: that is, that in recompense for that observance I may receive the crown of victory. For to carry the book on one’s shoulder is to fulfill Holy Scripture by acting upon it; and to be crowned with it as with a diadem is to receive eternal recompense. And because no one suddenly becomes perfect in observing God’s commandments:

### Verse 37

“By each of my steps,” he says, “I will declare it”: that is, as I go from virtue to virtue, I shall teach others what I myself do. Concerning these steps—that is, stages of progress—the Lord says in the Gospel: “The earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4). Likewise Daniel, speaking of these advances, says: “A hand touched me and raised me upon my knees” (Dan. 10); then he adds, “and I stood,” but adds, “trembling.” Immediately he continues: “And he said to me: Do not fear” (ibid.). [Col. 1111D–1112A]

Certainly, by these three expressions which he distinguishes thus—“He raised me; I stood trembling; and he said, ‘Do not fear’”—he makes known in himself to us the entire order of our progress. For, as has been said, no one who leaves the lowest things becomes perfect at once. Rather, first he makes progress as it were upon his knees, because, bent over upon the joints of his hands, he is already in great part lifted from the earth. Then he stands, as it were trembling, before the Lord’s voice, when, raised above earthly desires, he fears God’s words all the more as he knows them more fully. Finally, because “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4), the divine voice says to him, as it were: “Do not fear” (Dan. 10).

“By each of my steps,” therefore, he says, “I will declare it”: that is, I shall provide an example for others so that they too may go from virtue to virtue. But if I do not do this, at the final recompense—when the workers of righteousness are rewarded with eternal joys—I shall reap eternal pains. This is what follows.

### Verse 38

“If my land cries out against me”: that is, if subjects reasonably grieve against the injustice of their ruler. For when either a private household justly murmurs against its master or the holy Church against any one of its prelates, “if,” I say, “my land cries out against me”—that is, if those already cultivated by the plough of doctrine see any innocent person oppressed by me, they rightly lament this in merciful compassion; and:

### Verse 39

“If I have eaten its fruits”—that is, the fruits of my land—“without payment”: if, while reaping my subjects’ material things, I did not sow spiritual things for them; “and if I afflicted the life of its cultivators”—that is, of the land—if I envied those laboring in God’s work. [Col. 1112B–C]

### Verse 40

“Let thistles grow for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley”: that is, instead of goods which refresh eternally, let evils which prick be returned to me in judgment.

It should be noted that, just as wheat is better than barley, so a thorn is harsher than a thistle. It is as though he said: If this is not so, then in return for the great goods signified by wheat let the least evils, understood by the thistle, answer to me; and in return for the least goods, understood by barley, let greater evils, signified by the thorn, answer to me.

## Chapter 32

Now there remain the words of Elihu, which must be weighed with so much the greater circumspection as they are uttered with a more fervent spirit through the boldness of youth. These are not easily understood unless they are assessed in light of the Lord’s subsequent correction. For the Lord says of him: “Who is this that envelops counsels in unlearned words?” (Job 38).

When he says “counsels” but does not immediately add what kind, he undoubtedly wishes them to be understood as good. For we always understand “counsels” in a good sense when they are set down without an added reproach, as it is written: “The sluggard seems wiser to himself than seven men speaking counsels” (Prov. 26). But just as good is often not spoken well, and therefore, though the good itself is approved, the manner of the speaker is rightly reproved, so this man, because he “envelops counsels in unlearned words,” is rightly reproved by the Lord as unknown and alien, who says: “Who is this?” This is said only of one who is not known. But he is not known—that is, he is rejected—because he is arrogant. [Col. 1112D–1113A]

Here, in Elihu’s person, is represented the type of certain teachers who are faithful yet arrogant; and the whole swelling pride of such people is quite fittingly expressed in this man’s words. His intention differs from that of the friends who spoke above. For, as has already been said, they intended, from the severity of the scourge by which blessed Job was struck more grievously than other men, to make him be believed more impious than other men. Elihu, however, intends to display his own knowledge, as one pursuing vain glory and striving to set himself above all men. He rebukes the friends for foolish judgments, but Job himself for unworthy merits.

In this arrogance he approaches more closely to likeness with the devil, who, despising the good of fellowship with the angels, proudly sought the likeness of the Most High and attempted, as it were, to rise to a certain summit of singularity. Therefore the discourse now comes to the arrogant words of Elihu, when, after blessed Job’s speeches have ended, it is said:

### Verse 1

“Then these three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed righteous in his own eyes.”

The statement made about him, “because he seemed righteous in his own eyes,” the historian of this sacred narrative reports as the judgment of the friends. For, ceasing to answer, they appear to have said such things as: “Do not pour out speech where there is no hearing” (Ecclesiasticus 32). This man seems righteous to himself, and therefore the rebuking speech does no good, because, in defending his works, he resists the justice of the God who scourges him. [Col. 1113B–C]

### Verse 2

“And Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was angered and indignant.”

So far as the present matter is concerned, this description of the person contains neither more nor less than that the very names—his own, his parent’s, his place, and his family—express the mark of arrogance in those situated within the holy Church. For *Elihu* means “This is my God,” or “The Lord is God”; *Barachel*, “Blessing of the Lord”; *Buzite*, “Contemptible”; *Ram*, “Lofty,” namely, the people of God.

By these names, as has been said, every arrogant person is described: one for whom “the Lord is God” by right faith, and who says “my God”—as Elihu’s own name signifies; one in whom there is the “blessing” of the heavenly gift, as the father’s name signifies; one who preaches eloquently and is not separated from communion with the Christian people, as the family of Ram signifies. But precisely because he is arrogant, he is “contemptible,” as the name of the place, Buzite, signifies.

“He was angered and indignant,” it says. He was angered against Job because Job said that he was righteous before God: that is, because he had recalled works of righteousness concerning himself, as though he had concluded in this manner: Therefore I am righteous—which Job had not done. [Col. 1113C–D]

### Verse 3

“Moreover, he was indignant against his friends”: that is, he swelled above them from the magnitude of his supposedly correct judgment, “because they had found no reasonable answer”: that is, though they had found many things and said much in disputation, they had found or said nothing worthy, nothing corresponding to the profession of wisdom which they held, by which to conclude against him; “but had merely condemned Job”—understand: nor had they confirmed their proposed condemnation by adequate reasoning.

This is indeed the custom of the arrogant. They judge some to know nothing and others not to live well; situated within the Church, they press adversaries by the force of their speech, while attacking the Church itself through the fault of pride. [Col. 1114A]

### Verse 4

“Therefore Elihu waited while Job spoke, because those who spoke were older.”

It is as though it were openly said: Why, then, did he remain silent so long? And, though arrogant, how was he able to endure silence, especially since he judged the things said against Job to be inferior to his own understanding? Namely, “because those who spoke were older”: so that, when he should say loftier things after the speeches of the elders, he might gain the palm of speaking. Like an athlete awaited as necessary, he would overthrow, after delaying the contest, the strong gladiator who had conquered others.

According to the typological interpretation also, Elihu, by whom the arrogant are signified, is rightly described as younger than those by whom heretics are figured. For after the conflicts of heretics arose—conflicts because of which subtler arrows of understanding were sought within the Church—after these conflicts, I say, arrogant men, inflated by the pride of knowledge, began to exist within the same holy Church. Their intellects burn fiercely, and when they find fitting material, they swell arrogantly. [Col. 1114B–C]

### Verse 5

“When he saw that the three could not answer”: that is, that Zophar the Naamathite had failed in the final reply. For after a threefold contest, when in the third encounter he ought, according to the order of speaking maintained so far, to have answered, he was silent. When, I say, Elihu saw this, “he was exceedingly angry,” so that by the very movement and freedom of his anger he might openly show that he was conscious of possessing great wisdom, and that he, though younger, could easily supply what the elders had failed to provide. [Col. 1114C–D]

### Verse 6

“And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: ‘I am younger in years,’” and so forth.

Wise men are accustomed, at the beginnings of their discourses, to win their hearers’ goodwill. This man, though arrogant, strives to do this at the beginning of his discourse, but immediately departs from the attempt, because humility is a difficult thing for proud minds. “I am younger in years,” he says. Though it would have been sufficient to say this, he adds the superfluous phrase, “but you are older,” because every arrogant person is superfluous even in speech.

“Therefore, with bowed head, I was afraid to declare my opinion to you.” By this statement he arrogates to himself also the virtue of humility and reverence, which he does not in fact possess, as the following words sufficiently testify: “I was afraid,” he says. [Col. 1114D–1115A]

### Verse 7

“For I hoped”—understand, something which did not occur—“that greater age” than mine “would speak”: that is, would possess speech and would not, like children, stammer and mutilate wisdom; “and that the multitude of years” in you “would teach wisdom,” both through experience and through instruction.

### Verse 8

“But, as I see”: that is, as I now experience in you, “there is a spirit in men,” the producer of wisdom without a multitude of years, “and the inspiration of the Almighty,” not the quantity of age, “gives understanding.”

He would say this rightly if he did not claim that same understanding for himself above others. But there are four kinds of arrogance: when someone thinks that he possesses good from himself; or, if he believes it given to him from above, thinks that he has received it for his own merits; or boasts that he has what he does not have; or, despising others, desires to be seen as singularly possessing what he has. Although this man confesses that wisdom is given by the Lord, he falls into the kind of arrogance by which he rejoices to be wiser than others and vainly exalts himself as though because of a singular good. This he indicates in the words that follow. [Col. 1115A–B]

### Verses 9–10

“The aged are not wise, nor do the elders understand judgment. Therefore I say”—understand: I, though younger, am wise—“listen to me,” because you cannot speak; “I too will show you my wisdom,” because you have shown yours, which is nothing. And it is right that you should listen to me.

### Verse 11

“For I waited”: that is, I did not interrupt “your words; I listened to your prudence”—that is, to your imprudence. For he said “your prudence” ironically. “I listened,” he says, “and waited until you debated with words.”

### Verse 12

“And while”—that is, as long as—“I thought that you were saying something” worthy of hearing or of waiting for, “I paid attention.”

By this saying he openly declares that he was silent at the elders’ words from the zeal of a judge rather than from the desire to learn; and by speaking he shows how proudly he had been silent. Those who are situated within the holy Church commonly weigh in its adversaries not the years of time but the intention of their words. “I thought,” he says, “that you were saying something,” and therefore “I waited.” [Col. 1115C–D]

“But, as I see”—understand: in present experience—“there is no one who can refute,” that is, convict, “Job and answer from among you to his words,” by which he strives to dispute with God and justify himself. I say this, and therefore I shall speak:

### Verse 13

“Lest perhaps you say, ‘We have found wisdom’”—in him—because, though it is wholly contradictory, “God has cast him down, and not man”: God, who casts down no wise person, rather than man, who, erring in judgment, often casts down what ought not to be cast down.

Or thus, according to the typological interpretation: “God has cast him down, and not man.” It is as though arrogant but faithful persons say to heretics: Because you see the holy Church flourishing for a time in human esteem, do not believe that it has been rejected by God. For it does not follow, because man has not cast it down—that is, because you see it honored by all people—that God has cast it down. Rather, earthly glory is granted to it as an aid, so that through this it may be carried all the more abundantly to heavenly things. “Do not say,” I say, “that we have found wisdom in him,” because:

### Verse 14

“He has spoken nothing to me”: that is, I count for nothing whatever he has said. “And I will not answer him according to your words”: that is, I shall rise higher, discover deeper things, and say firmer things. Yet the arrogant do not answer the holy Church in the same way as heretics do: they do not contradict it by preaching perversely, but by living perversely. [Col. 1116A–B]

### Verse 15

“They were afraid and did not answer further”: namely, Job’s friends who had spoken. “They were afraid,” I say, astonished and waiting to hear what worthy thing this man would bring forth after so vast a gap of promises.

Or, since Elihu continues, “Since therefore I waited and they did not speak,” this too may be understood as spoken by him, a loud reproach of indignation. It is as though Elihu openly says: Because Job proclaimed whatever he wished, these men who have hitherto professed wisdom “were afraid and did not answer further; they took words away from themselves”—that is, they became mute and speechless from fear. [Col. 1116B–C]

### Verse 16

“Since therefore I waited”: that is, I yielded for a long time, I gave silence for a long time, “and they did not speak” things worthy of speech; “they stood”: that is, they ceased as though they did not possess speech; “nor did they answer further,” after Job had proclaimed his works.

### Verse 17

“I too will answer my part”: that is, knowledge proper to myself and unlike theirs; “and I will show my knowledge,” which can be useful like a treasure and therefore ought not to remain hidden.

This is the intolerable vice of arrogance: every arrogant person praises his own wisdom with his own mouth, as this man says, “I will show my wisdom.” For arrogant persons do not all speak in order to restrain those teaching perversely; rather, they desire to display themselves, and consider it their part not so much to possess knowledge as to show it.

Against this it is said through Moses: “A vessel which has no covering or binding above it shall be unclean” (Num. 19). That is, a person who does not possess the restraint of disciplined silence is rejected as unclean and defiled, and is cast out from God’s house. Is not the man here a vessel without a cover who inopportunely displays whatever wisdom he thinks he has, as though removing his cover? “See,” he says. [Col. 1116C–D]

### Verse 18

“I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me”: namely, through the multitude of words—“the spirit of my belly,” that is, the knowledge conceived in the depths of my heart. And lest you think my knowledge some ordinary knowledge, or one comparable to the stagnant waters which are the knowledge of others—lest, I say, you think my wisdom watery:

### Verse 19

“Behold, my belly,” that is, my mind, “is like new wine”: it boils, that is, it contains within itself the vigor of true and living wisdom and suffers from silence. This is what he adds: “Without a vent, it”—that is, the new wine—“bursts new wineskins.” “New,” I say, lest I say old, which is customary.

Lest anything similar happen to me—that is, lest my belly burst with the boiling new wine of wisdom:

### Verse 20

“I will speak and breathe a little”: that is, I shall be relieved by speaking, as though I opened a vent in the wineskin. This is what follows: “I will open my lips and answer.”

What this man arrogates to himself through vain glory, holy men often suffer through true wisdom. For their “belly,” that is, their mind, kindled by the Holy Spirit, suffers like a vessel full of boiling new wine when it is “without a vent”—that is, when, seeing things that ought to be rebuked, it is restrained by silence. [Col. 1117A–B]

Jeremiah testifies to this. When, because his hearers were uncorrected, he had said, “I will no longer speak in the name of the Lord” (Jer. 20), he immediately added: “And it became in my heart like a burning fire” (ibid.). That is, while I outwardly kept silent because I was weary of speaking, inwardly the fire of the zeal of charity grew.

Likewise David, when he said, “I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Ps. 38), namely when my speech does no good, immediately added: “And my pain was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall burn” (ibid.).

And he aptly says of this new wine “that it bursts new wineskins,” because the fervor of the Holy Spirit can be contained not only by the old life, but scarcely even by the new. “I will answer,” he says, so that I may neither praise you nor approve Job in the things he has said. This is what follows. [Col. 1117B–C]

### Verse 21

“I will not accept the person of a man”: that is, I will not praise your knowledge or favor you because you are older or distinguished persons. “And I will not make God equal to man”: namely, to this man who disputes with God as with his equal. “I will not make [him] equal,” I say: that is, I will not tolerate his appearing equal. And I ought to do this quickly and without delay.

### Verse 22

“For I do not know how long I shall remain”: namely, in this life, where there is opportunity to exercise wisdom or perform righteousness; “and whether after a little while my Maker may take me away,” I do not know.

He rightly says “after a little while,” because however long the time of this present life may be, it is short precisely because it does not endure. It should be noted, moreover, that here he falsely claims for himself the four principal virtues of which the true wise person is composed: fortitude, in that he is violently angry; prudence, that is, the knowledge which he declares he wishes to show; justice, in that he says: “I will not accept the person of a man, and I will not make God equal to man.” [Col. 1117D–1118A]

But in temperance he contradicts himself. He now claims it for himself, as though mindful of winning goodwill: “With bowed head,” he says, “I was afraid to declare my opinion to you, and I waited until you debated.” But he himself testifies that he wholly lacks it when, demanding attentive hearers, he says: “My belly is like new wine without a vent; I will speak and breathe.” For by these words he testifies that he is intemperate in keeping silence.

Finally, after this defective preface addressed to the friends, he turns to Job himself.

## Chapter 33

### Verse 1

“Therefore hear, Job, my words, and listen to all my speeches.”

Behold another beginning, no less defective. For, like a president of wisdom, he seems to himself to sit upon a certain summit of greatness. He does not ask the attention of the person to whom he speaks, as those who desire to help do; rather, with the raised staff of a proud tongue, sternly and forcefully, he demands and commands—this being characteristic of the teaching of the arrogant. “Hear,” he says, “my words,” because I shall now speak eloquently; “and listen to all my speeches,” because they are such that not one of them ought to fall to the ground. [Col. 1118A–B]

### Verse 2

“Behold, I have opened my mouth”: therefore do not expect a cheap treasure of wisdom. “Let my tongue speak”: that is, let no one make noise against me or interrupt the common audience of silence. “Let it speak,” I say, “in my jaws”: that is, let it be permitted me to speak quietly, and let there be no need for me to shout aloud. [Col. 1118B–C]

### Verse 3

“My words are to be poured forth from my simple heart; and my lips will utter a pure judgment” (*pura*, “pure,” variant *puram*, “a pure [judgment]”): that is, speech not lacking the weight of great understanding and free from every pretense.

By this statement he believes that he wins goodwill; but he pollutes it by manifest pride, since he arrogates to himself simplicity of speech, a thing of great virtue and great praise.

### Verse 4

“The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.”

In a good order he asserts that he was first made and then enlivened. Yet he is unclean like a man who suffers a flow of seed, as was said through Moses (Lev. 15), because, by moving his tongue through vain and unnecessary words, he pollutes by its flowing what ought rightly to be understood and mentioned in its proper place, since he does not know to whom or about what he speaks. [Col. 1118C–D]

### Verse 5

“If you can, answer me”: that is, although you have been cast down even to the dunghill, when I have spoken I give you room to answer. “Stand against my face”: that is, oppose my words, if you can, by any reasoning; I shall not despise you. Why? Namely:

### Verse 6

“Behold, God made me just as he made you”: that is, although I have not been cast down by him as you have, “I too have been formed from the same clay”—but the differing merits of our lives have produced a differing condition. [Col. 1119A]

VERS. 7.—“Nevertheless,” that is, although you are so much my inferior, “let not my wonder terrify you.” What he has said he explains by adding: “And let not my eloquence be burdensome to you”; that is, although my eloquence is admirable—indeed, a kind of marvel—“let not my eloquence terrify you or be burdensome to you.” It should be noted that, whereas Paul says, “I beseech you, brethren, to bear with the word of consolation; for I have written to you in few words” (Heb. XIII), and likewise thinks humbly of great matters in his other sayings—as is the manner of all the saints—this man vainly exalts himself over trifles. Thus very distinct are the flavors of fruits which proceed from different roots of thought. “Let it not,” I say, “be burdensome to you”; and however [Col. 1119B] burdensome it may be to you, or however it may terrify you, the present occasion requires that my eloquence should answer you.

VERS. 8.—“For you said in my hearing,” that is, in the presence of me, an intelligent man, “and I heard the sound of your words,” that is, you cannot deny that you said:

VERS. 9, 10, 11.—“I am clean and without fault; I am spotless, and there is no iniquity in me. Because He has found complaints against me, He has therefore deemed me His enemy. He has put my feet in the stocks; He has watched all my paths.” He perversely derived these words from what he had heard blessed Job say. For Job had said: “I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hand, when I offered pure prayers to God” (Job XVI). He twists this so as to say, [Col. 1119C] “For you said, I am clean and without fault,” and the rest. Blessed Job had also said: “For you write bitter things against me, and deem me your enemy. You have put my feet in the stocks” (Job XIII), and the rest. This too he twists thus: “Because He has found complaints against me, He has therefore deemed me His enemy,” and the rest as above. But how Job said these things has been explained in its proper place.

VERS. 12.—“This, then,” that is, to pass over the rest, “this, I say, is that in which you are not justified”; that is, even if you had said or done nothing else worthy of blame, this point alone sufficiently proves that you are not righteous as you suppose yourself to be. Here, inflamed after the manner of a horse rushing into its course of display, he prepares for himself a field in his attacks upon blessed Job [Col. 1119D] out of an iniquity falsely attributed to him. “I will answer you,” he says, that is, on this one point. For the sum of all that I shall say is this: “God is greater than man.” You ask what this has to do with the matter? I shall say.

VERS. 13.—“You contend against Him because He has not answered you in all things.”—“You contend,” I say, namely where you said: “I desire to dispute with God” (Job XIII), and shortly afterward added: “Answer me how many iniquities and sins I have” (ibid.), etc. “I will answer you,” I say, in this manner:

VERS. 14.—“God speaks once.” It is as though he said: Why do you contend against Him, demanding that He answer you in each particular? This is not His manner. “He speaks once [Col. 1120A] and does not repeat the same thing a second time”; that is, He does not alter a judgment once fixed, for He is not changeable. But He has already spoken once to you, and answered how many sins you have—that is, that you have many and great iniquities. He has answered you, I say, in that by striking you He has repaid you with what your deeds deserved. Do you contend, then, that He should answer you again and again? He speaks once, and in the manner in which He has spoken to you—namely, suddenly—to others like you.

VERS. 15.—“Through a dream, in a vision of the night,” that is, when they sin securely and say, “Peace, peace” (Jer. VI); “through a dream,” I say, “in a vision of the night,” that is, amid their prosperity, which, like a vision of the night, swiftly passes away: “when sleep falls [Col. 1120B] upon men,” that is, when “they sleep by night, and are drunken by night” (I Thess. V), “and sleep in their beds,” that is, cherish this same security amid pleasures and idleness.

VERS. 16.—“Then He opens the ears of men,” namely those which they have closed to His commands, “and, instructing them, teaches them by discipline,” because, as it is written, “Affliction alone gives understanding to hearing” (Isa. XXVIII). This is the meaning with regard to those whom Elihu believed blessed Job to resemble. But because he said universally and without qualification, “God speaks once,” and God speaks both to the good and to the wicked, the same statement must also be interpreted in a favorable sense.

“God speaks once,” he says; that is, God once composed through the Holy Spirit the sacred Scripture by which He makes His will known to us. “Once,” I say, because it is not changed. This is what he adds: “and He does not repeat it a second time,” because He does not answer in private utterances within the hearts of individuals, but constructs such a discourse as satisfies the questions of all.

Or thus: “God speaks once,” that is, He has no Word other than His only-begotten Son; “and He does not repeat it a second time,” because He begot this very Word—that is, the Son—as the one and only Son. And when does God “speak” this Scripture which endures—that is, inspire it into worthy minds—or His own unique Word, on whom “all Scripture inspired by God” (II Tim. III) depends? “Through a dream [Col. 1120D] in a vision of the night,” that is, when the faithful soul can truly say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V), namely when, with a tranquil mind, it rests from the activity of this world. So Moses too, fleeing in the wilderness as though from the restless tumults of earthly desires, fell asleep and thereby deserved to receive the divine voice (Exod. III).

“In a vision,” I say, “of the night,” because whatever we know of God in this life is, compared with the future light in which “we shall see Him as He is” (I John III), like a vision of the night. “When sleep falls upon men,” he says, because to cease from outward activity is to sleep; “and they sleep in their beds,” that is, they rest sweetly in the testimony of a good conscience. “Then He opens [Col. 1121A] the ears of men,” so that, freed from the tumults of worldly affairs, they may, as was said, hear the causes examined in the inward judgment and may be men—that is, act manfully. “And instructing them,” that is, affecting them with tears, “He builds them up by discipline,” that is, He wounds the mind through repentance and compunction; for the lamentations of compunction are like certain wounds of a blow.

And just as an outward blow cleanses wounds, as Solomon says, “The bruise of a wound wipes away evils” (Prov. XX), so compunction, through the vengeance of repentance, pierces the mind when it has become lax; as the same Solomon immediately adds: “And wounds in the innermost parts of the belly” (ibid.), that is, the force of compunction in the hidden recess of the mind. The soul is intensely affected by four kinds of this compunction, when [Col. 1121B] it either considers where it has been and humbles itself, like him who says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV); or asks and considers within itself where it will be, fears, and says: “Lest perhaps I should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX); or sorrowfully considers where it is and says: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (II Cor. V); or mournfully sees where it is not and says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII).

“Therefore,” he says, “He instructs them”—God, as has been said—either by striking them with the bruise of a wound so that they may return to their senses, as He has now struck you, O Job; or by wounding them with the blows of compunction in the innermost parts of the belly, that is, of the mind, so that, if they are good, they may advance to better things.

[Col. 1121C] VERS. 17.—“That He may turn a man away from the things he has done,” that is, from past sins; “and deliver him from pride,” lest he transgress His commands through pride.

VERS. 18.—“Rescuing his soul from corruption,” namely from present vices; “and his life,” rescuing it in the future, “that it may not pass into the sword,” that is, eternal damnation. Note that He first frees from “corruption” and afterward from the sword, because He surely rescues there from the vengeance of punishment the life of the one whose mind He here withdraws from the delight of sin.

VERS. 19.—“He also rebukes through pain upon the bed,” that is, amid temporal rest, namely, according to the Psalmist, “his whole bed” (Ps. XL), [Col. 1121D] that is, He turns all the rest of the present life in sickness, that is, He disturbs it by present affliction. “He rebukes,” I say, not only in the mode described above, but also as follows: “And He causes all his bones to waste away,” that is, He permits all his virtues, in which he might have been puffed up and exalted had they not been assailed by any temptation, to be so diminished by the reminder of weakness that they seem to him to be nothing. Then nothing pleasant is seen; everything encountered is sad.

VERS. 20.—“Bread becomes abominable to him in his life,” because, through the weariness of an infirm conscience, he finds that whatever formerly satisfied him pleasantly and willingly is turned into bitterness. For although bread [Col. 1122A] has many meanings in sacred Scripture, it also signifies the pleasantness of human delight. Thus Jeremiah says of the Synagogue: “All the people groan and seek bread” (Lam. I), that is, transitory delight. For it follows: “They gave all their precious things for food,” that is, they bent all the virtues of the mind toward the desire for transitory delight.

VERS. 21.—“His flesh will waste away,” that is, every outward pleasure; for by flesh is understood fleshly delight. This pleasure, I say, is worn down by the pain mentioned above. And what comes about through this? “The bones that had been covered will be laid bare,” that is, those strong things of the virtues which had long lain hidden, as it were, beneath the flesh will be revealed. For no one knows how much he has advanced except amid adversities, [Col. 1122B] according to the saying: “God tested them as gold in a furnace” (Wis. III), etc. But while the flesh wastes away, what follows comes to pass:

VERS. 22.—“His soul has drawn near to corruption,” that is, he has recognized how weak he is in himself, so that he attributes to the Lord, not to himself, that which is far from destruction; for he knows that by his own strength he is near destruction. “And his life to deadly things,” namely, has drawn near, because from the infirmity of the flesh he sees himself near sins that bring death, and in terror says: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII). Yet this is useful to him: in seeing through adversities that by his own strength he is near death, he acts strongly in all things and lives more steadfastly by fleeing to divine protection.

After Elihu showed in what temptation the human race is placed—for he has so set forth the temptations of certain individuals in particular that they may be understood universally of all—he immediately applies the remedy of healing to this general pestilence.

VERS. 23.—“If there shall be an angel for him,” namely one sent from heaven, that One who is called by the prophet “the Angel [Counsellor] of great counsel” (Isa. IX).—“If,” I say, there shall be sent “one speaking out of thousands,” that is, having nothing in common with sinful men except the truth of human nature alone, being born when and how He willed, dying when and how He willed, [Col. 1122D] and unlike them in all other respects; “speaking,” I say, that is, showing Himself to the Father as man in order to intercede for men (Heb. VII), “that He may declare the righteousness of man,” namely in that He presents Himself as a righteous man.

VERS. 24.—“He will have mercy upon him and say, ‘Deliver him.’”—“He will say,” I say, by doing what has been said. For thus to speak for him, or to declare his righteousness, is surely to exercise great mercy and to pray to the Father for his deliverance, “that he may not descend into corruption,” lest, as the prophet says to the soul exalting itself, “Who are you more beautiful than? Descend and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. XXXII), he should descend into eternal destruction [Col. 1123A] and perish with the unbelieving and ungodly. “I have found whereby I may be propitious to him”: this too He will say—“I have found,” I say—because when no intercessor for men appeared before God, I made myself God and man in order to make propitiation for men, according to the saying: “You did not require holocaust and sacrifice for sin; then I said, Behold, I come” (Ps. XXXIX).

VERS. 25.—“His flesh has been consumed by sufferings,” that is, in the flesh itself in which he sinned he has received punishments. For innumerable punishments of bodily life oppress the human race. “Let him return to the days of his youth,” that is, let him be renewed in the integrity of his former life, and, redeemed, return to that for the attainment of which he had been created. And because having such an advocate for him makes us more confidently eager for a state of prayer, the passage fittingly adds concerning this redeemed man:

VERS. 26.—“He will pray to God,” having a sacrifice to offer in prayer, which he did not previously have, “and God will be favorable to him.” “And he will see His face in jubilation,” that is, after the immense bitterness of sins, the light of truth will break forth for his mind in hidden and ineffable joy. For jubilation is said to occur when an ineffable joy is conceived in the mind which can neither be concealed nor unfolded in words. Hence David says: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII). He does not say, “which speaks it,” but “which knows it,” because jubilation can indeed be known by the understanding, but cannot be expressed in speech. “He will see,” I say, “His face,” namely through contemplation, which, though it is not a solid or lasting vision but a certain likeness of vision, is nevertheless rightly called the face of God. For since we recognize anyone by the face, we not improperly call God’s face the contemplation by which we recognize Him. “He will be favorable to him,” he says, “and will restore to man his righteousness,” namely that righteousness for which he was created: that he may delight in cleaving to God and no longer believe the flattering promises of the crafty serpent. “His righteousness,” he says, that is, righteousness given to him; as we say, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI). Behold, we call it “ours,” yet pray that it may be given to us. Once this righteousness has been received, what will he do?

[Col. 1123D] VERS. 27.—“He will look upon men,” that is, attend to the holy or righteous, whom he rightly calls men, that is, those living rationally. In contrast, concerning those who live irrationally it is written: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). But concerning the righteous who live rationally, as stated: “But you,” says the Lord, “are the flock of my pasture, you are men,” because fleshly delight does not affect you after the manner of beasts (Ezek. XXXIV).—“Men,” I say, that is, saints, “he will look upon.”—“And he will say, ‘I have sinned,’” that is, by comparison with them he will recognize how far below men he has fallen through sin. For as soon as he considers the deeds of those who act well, he reproves himself, while inward shame inflicts punishment upon him.

Thus it is well said through Ezekiel: “Son [Col. 1124A] of man, show the house of Israel the temple” (Ezek. XLIII), that is, the soul of every righteous person, which God inhabits by inspiring it, “that they may be confounded by their iniquities, and may measure the structure, and blush at all that they have done”; that is, that they may see in the other the good which they neglect, and blush in themselves at the evil which they do. In the same prophet, the flying creatures striking their wings one against another (Ezek. III) signify that the minds of saints, as they despise earthly things and are lifted upward in flight to heavenly things, are stirred in their desire for heavenly things by considering one another’s corresponding virtues.

“He will look,” therefore, he says, “upon men and say, ‘I have sinned,’” like the one who said: “For I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV), and the rest. “I have sinned,” I say, “and truly have done wrong”; that is, I do not say “I have sinned” in the way that one often says it who believes that he has not sinned, wishing to seem humble and righteous because he knows it is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII). Rather, from the depths of my heart I say: “I have sinned and truly have done wrong; and I have not received as I deserved,” that is, I have not been struck as severely as I deserve. Therefore, because he agrees with his deliverer by coming to know himself:

VERS. 28.—“He has delivered his soul from going into destruction, and while living he shall see the light,” namely the light of truth, which one dead in heart cannot see, although the dead—that is, the ungodly—will also see the light which is Christ. But they will see only the form of His humanity; the living, that is, the righteous, will see Him with the unclouded eyes of the heart in the form of divinity.

VERS. 29.—“Behold, all these things,” namely those said above concerning the man tried and scourged: that bread becomes abominable to him in his life; that his soul draws near to corruption and his life to deadly things; and what follows, “He will pray to God and God will be favorable to him; he will see His face in jubilation; and He has delivered his soul from going into destruction, so that while living he may see the light”—“all these things,” I say, “God works three times in each individual” man. This must be considered carefully.

“Three times,” he says: that is, in conversion, temptation, and death. “God works these things in each individual,” namely that, according to the sequence set out above, sorrow first afflicts and great joy afterward raises up. In the first occurrence, namely conversion, when someone thinks of renouncing all things and following Christ, familiar fleshly delight confronts him, and the habit of his old perversity assails him; this afflicts him with sorrow and anxiety of heart. Thus bread becomes abominable to him in his life, his soul approaches corruption, and his life deadly things. For in this conflict, while the Bridegroom calls on one side and the flesh calls him back on the other, he is made wholly bitter within himself. But because divine grace quickly comes to his aid and brings him, thus constrained, more broadly into the freedom of new [Col. 1125A] conversion for consolation, immense joy comes to his heart, as follows: “He will pray to God and God will be favorable to him,” etc., as stated above.

Likewise, in the second occurrence, namely temptation, the matters set forth above happen to him no less, when, after the sweetness of consolation with which he is commonly received at the beginning of conversion, he afterward experiences the hard labor of trial. So also the children of Israel: after God had more gently nursed and nourished them as they came out of Egypt, they afterward endured varied struggles of temptation. Then, I say, “bread becomes abominable to him in his life,” and the rest, as stated above. But because the merciful God permits us to be tested by temptations, not rejected, the work of His consolation intervenes, and again what [Col. 1125B] follows comes to pass: “He will pray to God and God will be favorable to him,” etc., as stated above.

In the third occurrence, namely in death, he becomes bitter far more than in the two occurrences mentioned above, while he fears the heavenly judgments even over every movement of his thoughts. And fear becomes sharper in proportion as eternal recompense is nearer. For when James says, “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. III), and John, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I), what should be thought concerning the rest? What will the planks do if the pillars tremble?
