Or how will shrubs stand unmoved if even cedars are shaken by the whirlwind of this fear? Yet the souls of the righteous, often purified by the very terror of death, rejoice even before they are stripped of the flesh.

Thus three [Col. 1125C] times—in conversion, temptation, and death—“God works all these things in each individual”: namely, that first “bread becomes abominable to a man in his life, his soul draws near to corruption, and his life to deadly things”; then “he will pray to God and God will be favorable to him, he sees His face in jubilation, and He delivers his soul lest it go into destruction, so that while living it may see the light.” And why does He do these things?

VERS. 30.—“That He may recall their souls from corruption,” namely from vices, having strengthened them through this threefold exercise, “and illuminate them with the light of the living,” that is, with that light which He Himself is, in whom all live. For this light seen by bodily eyes is the light of the dying.

[Col. 1125D] After these true and mystical statements, Elihu, swollen with the pride of knowledge, exalts himself. What wise men commonly do—namely, at intervals amid their speech to restore or renew their hearers’ attention or goodwill—he tries to imitate; but, according to his puffed-up understanding, he descends into empty words.

VERS. 31.—“Attend, Job,” he says, “and hear me”; that is, be an attentive listener and look to me; “and be silent while I speak.” I, that is, I who possess authority to speak by reason of wisdom. Thus he spoils his imitation of the effort to win attention, and soon also distorts the semblance of goodwill by adding:

VERS. 32.—“But if you have anything to say, answer me,” that is, though you have nothing. Therefore he confidently [Col. 1126A] grants with irony, saying: “Speak, for I desire you to appear righteous,” that is, I desire that, if possible, you should prove by reason that you are what you assert yourself to be, namely righteous. Since he did not make this concession sincerely, he does not wait for the answer he had requested but immediately adds:

VERS. 33.—“But if you have not,” that is—indeed, because you have nothing to say—“hear me,” because I have something to say. “Be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.” In this he thinks he is observing the third thing customarily joined with those mentioned above: making the hearer teachable.

CHAPTER XXXIV

VERS. 1.—“Elihu then made a pronouncement.” By the term “pronouncement,” what is indicated but the swelling of self-exaltation? “He also spoke these things,” namely after turning from blessed Job to the hearers.

VERS. 2.—“Hear,” he says, “you wise men, my words; and you learned men, listen to me.” It is as though he said: You wise and learned men, who alone are able to understand what I shall say, hear what I say.

VERS. 3.—“For the ear tests words, and the throat judges foods by taste.” It is as though he said: Just as the ear does not know foods, nor the throat words, so no foolish person understands the judgment of the wise. By these words he also demands their attention; and by what he immediately adds he seems to renew and restore their goodwill.

VERS. 4.—“Let us choose judgment for ourselves,” [Col. 1126C] that is, for I condescend to you in the concord of equality; “and among ourselves let us see what is better,” namely, so that by agreeing judgments this man may be condemned.

VERS. 5.—“Because Job said: ‘I am righteous, and God has overthrown my judgment.’”

VERS. 6.—“For in judging me there is falsehood; my arrow is violent without any sin.” The continuous sequence of Job’s actual words testifies that blessed Job did not say this. But he who had sought a judgment from a fault he invented immediately pronounced the sentence.

VERS. 7.—“What man,” he says, “is like Job?”—that is, none—“who drinks derision like water,” that is, who ridicules God without the restraint of fear. For water, when drunk, is taken so freely that no thickness of its own delays its swallowing. So this man, he says, in the pride of his tongue, is opposed by no trembling of heart. This is commonly characteristic of arrogant superiors: they desire to rebuke their afflicted hearers more harshly than to comfort them gently. For, as it is written, “In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. XIV): they know how to strike rigidly but do not know how to sympathize humbly. Yet they suppose that the saying belongs to them: “The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails deeply fixed” (Eccl. XII). But the words of the truly wise so prod that, when they correct severely, they do not lose the grace of inward sweetness. “He drinks,” I say, “derision,” that is, he ridicules God.

[Col. 1127A] VERS. 8.—“Who walks with workers of iniquity and goes with ungodly men?”

VERS. 9.—“For he said: ‘A man will not please God, even if he runs with Him.’” To an injurious assertion he attached a false reason. Whoever reads Job’s words recognizes that he did not say this.

VERS. 10.—“Therefore, men of understanding, hear me,” that is, because you have understanding, you alone are worthy to hear what I say. “Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.” Though he says it vainly, he says it truly and soundly. For God’s being ungodly, or the Almighty’s being unjust, are altogether contrary and incompatible things, and can never coexist. “Far be it,” I say. He proves this from the effect that follows.

VERS. 11.—“For He will render to a man his work,” namely to the good man, which is an act of mercy and opposed to impiety: namely, to give grace for grace; “and according to the ways of each,” namely the wicked, “He will repay them,” which surely belongs to equity and is contrary to injustice. Yet this does not always happen in this life. As Solomon says: “There are righteous men to whom many things happen as though they had done the works of the wicked; and there are wicked men who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous” (Eccl. VIII). But he still confirms his unqualified, and therefore defective, reasoning by adding:

VERS. 12.—“For truly God will not condemn in vain, nor does the Almighty overthrow judgment,” namely, as Job charges that it has happened in his own case. But if someone should say that not God indeed “overthrows judgment,” but someone else whom He has set over human affairs does so, this too is false. For:

VERS. 13.—“Whom has He appointed over the earth,” that is, over men, “or whom has He placed over the world which He made?” [Col. 1127C] That is, over heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them—no one; rather, He does not neglect to govern by Himself what He created. And what He created, and created well, He surely governs well. Anyone may experience this in the following manner.

VERS. 14.—“If he directs his heart toward Him”—the heart which is crooked and twisted while it desires low things, but is directed when it is raised to things above. [Col. 1127D] “If,” he says, “a man directs his heart toward Him, He will draw to Himself his spirit and breath”; that is, He will convert to the desire for Himself both inward thoughts, signified by “spirit,” and outward actions, denoted by “breath.” Through this desire what follows will occur:

VERS. 15.—“All flesh will fail together,” that is, it will no longer serve any motions, because with a certain sword of His severity He kills all that lived evilly in it. Jeremiah had killed himself with this sword when he said: “And after You showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jer. XXXI); that is, after I saw spiritual things, I extinguished everything in me that lived carnally. For fleshly pleasure is understood by the thigh. “Flesh will fail,” I say, as stated; [Col. 1128A] “and man will return to ashes,” that is, he will remember that he is ashes, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “You will take away their spirit,” that is, their pride, “and they will fail and return to their dust” (Ps. CIII); that is, they will recognize themselves to be nothing and be humbled by their frail condition.

Here too, sensing that he has spoken acutely, Elihu immediately bursts forth in swelling pride:

VERS. 16.—“If, therefore, you have understanding,” he says, “hear what is said, and listen to the sound of my discourse.” See how, little by little, his arrogance advances through the escalation of his words. Above he had said: “If you have anything to say, answer.” Now he considers whether Job can at least hear what is said. Then, rebuking him more sharply:

[Col. 1128B] VERS. 17.—“Can one who does not love judgment be healed?” That is, can one who does not love correction—namely you, who murmur against God’s scourge—be delivered from the fault for which he is struck? He implies this and immediately applies it to Job because he had proposed it with reference to him. “And how do you condemn so greatly Him who is righteous,” namely God, “so greatly,” that you say what I mentioned above: “In judging me there is falsehood,” and the rest? Why, I say, do you accuse God “so greatly”?

VERS. 18.—“Who says to a king, ‘Apostate,’” that is, who subtly weighs and rebukes even the swelling hearts of rulers. For to rebuke someone for pride is to say, “Apostate.”—“Who says,” I say, “to a king, ‘Apostate,’” namely: Why do you rule with authority and power? “Who calls leaders ungodly,” that is, who justly rebukes those who, while presiding through domination, draw their subjects by the example of their pride into ungodliness. For an ungodly leader is one who shows, through examples of arrogance, the way of error. He uttered a good statement, but it should not have been uttered against blessed Job. For God was not scourging him because he was ungodly or apostate.

Those who shut their eyes to invisible things and feed upon visible things often honor a man not for what he himself is, but for what surrounds him. But almighty God examines human life solely according to the quality of merits. Therefore, after the statements above, this is fittingly said:

VERS. 19.—“Who does not accept the persons of princes,” that is, of the proud—because He often punishes them more severely, according to His own saying: “To whom much has been given, much is required” (Luke XII)—“nor recognized the tyrant,” that is, the proud man, “when he disputed against the poor,” that is, against the humble. “He has not recognized,” I say, because He says to the proud: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke XIII). And it is just that He accepts no person: “For all are the work of His hands,” namely both the poor and tyrants. And that God does not accept persons is sufficiently clear from what follows:

VERS. 20.—“They shall die suddenly,” that is, unexpectedly. However late the wicked may be taken from this life, [Col. 1129A] they are taken suddenly because they do not know how to foresee their end by reflection. “Suddenly,” I say, “they shall die in the midst of the night,” that is, in the blindness of their ignorance; “the peoples shall be troubled,” that is, however ungodly people who now neglect to be troubled by humility of heart will then be troubled by the Judge’s sentence. “And they shall pass away,” namely, as they pass day by day through the moments of life, so they will pass away in dying. “And they shall remove”—the heavenly judgments, namely—“the violent man without hand,” that is, invisibly, so that he may be snatched away by an invisible force under the pressure of a sudden end—namely, you, who, being violent, have been taken away by invisible power.

VERS. 21.—“For His eyes,” he says, “are upon the ways of men, and He considers all their steps,” namely He who was in no way believed to consider them [Col. 1129B] when this violent man perpetrated unpunished every evil he could. And because not even the smallest thoughts of man are hidden from Him who says through the prophet, “Remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. I), he fittingly adds:

VERS. 22.—“There are no darknesses, nor is there a shadow of death,” that is, there is no ignorance and no forgetfulness with God. He sought to signify forgetfulness by the shadow of death because death, coming between, causes what was in memory no longer to be; or the shadow of death may be understood as change, because every change is, as it were, a kind of alteration through death. For what changes, in a sense, kills what it was. Such change is not in God, as it is written: “With whom there is no change, [Col. 1129C] nor shadow of turning” (Jas. I). Therefore, “there are no darknesses, nor is there a shadow of death, in which,” that is, through which, “those who work iniquity may hide,” because it belongs to the divine nature alone to penetrate the shadows of ignorance and the darkness of changeability.

VERS. 23.—“For it is no longer in a man’s power,” namely in the violent man’s power, whom, as stated above, divine judgments remove, “to come to God in judgment.” This is as though he said: Therefore you say in vain, “I desire to dispute with God” (Job XIII), and presume that your judgment will attain victory. But although Elihu does not know to whom he speaks, he knows what he says. For whoever God [Col. 1129D] punishes by eternal recompense, “it is no longer in his power to come to God in judgment,” namely that judgment of which the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we should not indeed be judged” (I Cor. XI); and of which it is elsewhere written: “Judge with God, and wait for Him” (Job XXXV); and again: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. XII).

In these judgments no instrument is lacking that should fully punish its guilty persons. For conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and sorrow tortures. In contrast, concerning the negligent man under the figure of Ephraim it is said: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. VII), that is, malignant spirits have devoured his virtues and he did not grieve in repentance; “and gray hairs are scattered upon him, and he did not know it” (ibid.), that is, [Col. 1130A] he grew old in his vices and did not take care to be renewed in the spirit of his mind.

Therefore every reprobate person, once condemned, will no longer come to that judgment in which man now profitably judges himself, in which, according to the precept of the Law, “a fire which always burns upon the altar” may be kindled—that is, the flame of charity in the heart, consuming sins—“which the priest shall nourish,” that is, every faithful person who is a member of Christ the great Priest, “placing wood upon it in the morning” (Lev. VI), that is, with the darkness of the mind driven away, gathering together the testimonies of the saints in order to stir himself up.

491 After he has said much concerning the punishment of the wicked, he suddenly introduces the hidden judgment.

VERS. 24. — “He will crush many and innumerable persons,” namely those who seemed to stand, “so that their foot may slip” (Deut. 32) from the state of righteousness, “and he will make others stand in their place,” so that others may obtain the place of life when they fall. This happens daily; but because the end of neither party is yet seen, it is feared less. “He will crush many and innumerable persons,” as Judas was crushed after the ministry of the apostleship; “and he will make others stand in their place,” as that thief found the cause of life even at the very moment of death. The boundary of this hidden judgment is indicated when the angel of the Church of Philadelphia is told: “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Rev. 3). This is the hidden judgment beneath which one must always fear, “that he who thinks he stands should take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10), especially since elsewhere it is written: “They have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39). This judgment, I say, the Lord secretly, yet justly, orders.

VERS. 25. — “For he knows their works, and therefore he will bring on night, and they shall be crushed.” Because of their preceding sins, God will cause them again to be enveloped in the darkness that follows sinning. “He will bring on night,” that is, he will not free them from night; for to have blinded them in night itself is to have refused to free them from the darkness of blindness.

VERS. 26. — “He struck them as ungodly men in the place of those who see,” that is, in the Church, which is the place of those who see, in which alone God is to be seen. Of it the Lord also says to Moses: “There is a place with me, and [Col. 1130D] you shall stand upon the rock and see my back” (Exod. 33). “In the place, I say, of those who see,” that is, in the Church, where, though they know the truth of faith, they deny it by works, “he struck them as ungodly,” that is, as truly ungodly persons. For *quasi* [“as”] is not always used for resemblance, as in “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6), but also for truth, as in: “And we saw his glory, as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1). What he says, “in the place of those who see,” he expresses more plainly:

VERS. 27. — “Who, as though deliberately, withdrew from him,” that is, those who sinned not through ignorance or weakness, but, what is worst, deliberately. Such were those of whom the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken [Col. 1131A] to them, they would not have had sin” (John 15), and so forth. “And they were unwilling,” he says, “to understand all his ways.” He does not say that they could not understand or had not heard. “For Wisdom cries aloud in the streets,” as Solomon says (Prov. 1), “and Prudence gives her voice, standing in the midst of the paths.” Yet they “were unwilling to understand his ways”: the ways of incarnate Wisdom, which are the modes of living; ways, I say, despised by sight but to be revered by understanding. This applies especially to the Jews, who, while they pride themselves on the glory of the present life, did not perceive the loftiness of the Lord’s humility.

VERS. 28. — “So that they caused the cry of the needy to come to him.” For it happened through their fall that, when they fell, the needy—that is, the humble [Col. 1131B] people of the Gentiles—were put in their place; and that God “might hear,” that is, heed the misery or longing of those same humble Gentiles. As their type, the cry of wounded Lazarus reached God, when, according to his name, he was helped—for Lazarus means “helped”—and “was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man,” by whom the Jewish people are signified, abusing in pride the abundance of the Law, “was buried in hell” (Luke 16). Let no one dare to investigate or censure the deep judgments of God.

VERS. 29. — “For when he grants peace,” that is, reconciles the Gentile people to himself, “who is there that shall condemn” those same Gentiles for the stains of their former sins? “When he has hidden his face,” namely from the Jews, who previously were, as it were, seeing; “when, I say, he has hidden his face,” that is, his grace or knowledge, “a veil having been placed upon their heart” (2 Cor. 3), “who is there that shall behold him?” “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10). Who would dare to investigate or censure this judgment? And if the lord of the vineyard wishes to give a denarius to the last laborers, who worked one hour, to whom does he do injury? (Matt. 20). “And over the nations,” he says, “and over all men”: this judgment is exercised by an invisible examination, so that he secretly rejects some and chooses another, yet unjustly rejects none.

[Col. 1131D] VERS. 30. — “Who makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people”: that is, he who permitted you, O hypocrite Job, once to be powerful, because of the sins of those over whom you were powerful. Allegorically, however, it is thus: because the aforesaid Judaea would not have the true king over it (Luke 19), it will receive a hypocrite. “God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie” (2 Thess. 2), as the Lord himself says: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5). Universally also—that is, concerning every nation or rank—it must be understood that, when they deserve it, God gives them a king in his wrath (Hos. 13), because the hearts of rulers are arranged according to the merit of peoples. It is also certain that the life of peoples is often made worse through the fault of pastors. But even if their life is rightly censured, subjects ought to revere them even when they displease.

Thus the good sons, coming backward, covered the shameful parts of Noah when he was drunk (Gen. 9). For those cover, as though turned away, the shameful parts of their father who, while rightly judging the deed of their prelates, revere their office. For the benefit of subjects, rulers serve temporal concerns; and from that whereby subjects are made comely without disturbance, prelates are, as it were, defiled in dust. Thus, in order that fine linen might shine and scarlet gleam in the interior of the tabernacle, skins and hair-cloth above bore the rain, wind, and dust (Exod. 35).

[Col. 1132B] Now Elihu, after introducing many inward and sublime matters, again addresses blessed Job, verbally assuming the form of humility under a certain appearance of discipleship, saying:

VERS. 31. — “Therefore, since I have spoken to God,” that is, according to God, “I will not prevent you also,” namely, from speaking. And because he remembers having said strong things, he is confident that he has not erred:

VERS. 32. — “If I have erred,” he says, “teach me.” For he would not say this if he believed himself to have erred. But this is the characteristic deceit of arrogant persons: they inquire about error precisely when they know that they have not erred. Yet unable long to remain in the appearance of humility which he assumed only outwardly—for humility is a steep height to proud minds—when he sought to ascend its form, with the steps of his soul exhausted, he slips down, as it were, from steep and rugged paths.

VERS. 33. — “Does God require it of you,” he says, namely the “iniquity, if I have spoken,” which displeased you? As though he said: Why is my iniquity now censured by you, when it would not be required by you in judgment? I shall render an account before God. But it is not iniquity that I rebuke you. For you began to speak, and not I; and therefore you are blameworthy, since those who begin to speak in a dispute are usually more blameworthy than those who answer. But if you know anything better, speak. Behold, he again cloaks himself under the covering of an inquiry; but soon, impatient even of simulated humility, he bursts forth again in pride:

[Col. 1132D] VERS. 34. — “Men of understanding,” he says, “let them speak to me.”

VERS. 35. — “But Job has spoken foolishly.” Therefore let him not speak to me. “And his words do not sound of instruction,” because he condemns God, who judges him, of falsehood or injustice, and contentious­ly justifies himself both against God and against men. Then, with the harshness of pride extending even to the hardness of a curse:

VERS. 36. — “My father,” he says, “let Job be tested unto the end”; that is, O God the Father, let Job still be struck, because under the hand that strikes he still sins and accuses you, the just avenger, of injustice. As though he said what Ezekiel says: “Dig through the wall, and you will find greater abominations” (Ezek. 8); that is, if you strike Job further, it will become ever more plainly manifest to all, from his rebellion, how abominable he is. “Let him be tested,” I say, “unto the end; do not cease from the man of iniquity,” namely, from striking him, until his mouth is stopped.

VERS. 37. — “Who adds blasphemy to his sins”: namely, when scourged, he blasphemes, whereas he ought to repent of the sins for which he suffers scourges. After this curse, still speaking as if in God’s defense, he says: “Let him meanwhile be bound among us,” namely, while God has not yet fully answered him who summons him to judgment; “and then,” when, bound by us, he has perceived his weakness, “let him summon God to judgment [Col. 1133B] by his words,” if he wishes.

CHAPTER XXXV

VERS. 1. — Therefore Elihu spoke these things again. Being excessive, he strives to begin again, so as to recall his hearers’ attention as though they were about to hear something new.

VERS. 2. — “Do you think your thought just,” he says, “when you said, ‘I am more righteous than God’?” He perversely twisted this from what blessed Job said: “Let him set equity against me, and let my judgment attain victory” (Job 23). With what intention Job said this has been explained in its proper place. But this corrupter of piety further adds falsely:

VERS. 3. — “For you said,” he declares, “What is right does not please you; or what profit will it be to you if I sin?” [Col. 1133C] Thus, in order that he may seem able justly to rebuke what has been said, he invents by lying what was not said.

VERS. 4. — “Therefore I shall answer your words,” he says, “and your friends with you.” In the following words he discusses with keen force what he deceitfully invented for himself as matter for speaking.

VERS. 5. — “Look up to heaven,” that is, to the heavenly spirits, or to the bodily substance of heaven itself; “look up, I say, and behold; contemplate the skies,” that is, all heavenly things, so that at least through them you may infer what follows: “that God is higher than you.” For, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom, through the greatness or beauty of the creature the Creator can be intelligibly seen (Wis. 13). And since you cannot comprehend the things that he made, you understand likewise that he who made these things “is” far more “higher than you.” Since, then, he “is so much higher than you”:

VERS. 6. — “If you sin, what harm will you do him?”—when you cannot even throw a stone so high. “And if your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do to him?” That is, will you be able, with those same iniquities as with many weapons, to break into so lofty a firmament?

VERS. 7. — “But if you act justly, what will you give him?”—to him who possesses the heavens and has power over all things whatsoever? “Or what will he receive from your hand?”—he from whom, unless he gives it, you have nothing?

[Col. 1134A] VERS. 8. — “Your ungodliness will harm a man like yourself,” namely, either by tormenting him through persecution or defiling him through perversion; “and your righteousness will help a son of man,” in the manner in which it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6). And again: “A brother helping a brother shall be exalted like a fortified and strong city” (Prov. 18).

Yet, on the contrary, it often happens that human ungodliness, while thinking that it harms the good, benefits them more. Like a threshing-floor, it presses and cleanses the life of the elect, separating it like grain from chaff. Thus Pharaoh’s pride benefited the children of Israel, because, compelled by labors, they cried to the Lord; and it came about that, heard by him, they were led out to the promised land and glorified by heavenly gifts and miracles. “Your ungodliness,” I say, “will harm a man like yourself.” Yet even this will not go unpunished. For:

VERS. 9. — “Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out,” namely, to God. We may rightly call all wicked persons oppressors: not only those who seize external goods, but also those who strive by evil morals or examples to dissipate what is inward in us. “They will cry out, I say, because of the multitude of oppressors,” that is, because oppressors are many. “And they will howl because of the force of the arm of tyrants,” because they are not only many but also strong, and oppress mightily.

VERS. 10. — “And no one said,” namely, one of those crying to God; “no one said, I say, [Col. 1134C] ‘Where is God, who made me?’” For he will avenge so openly that no one will need to doubt whether God has seen the violence of the “tyrants” or the “multitude of oppressors.” As though he said: He will avenge justly and severely upon all, as upon you also. For now, of all those whom you have oppressed, no one needs, in seeking vengeance, to say: “Where is God who made me, who gives songs in the night?” That is, who is accustomed to give joy in tribulation?

For, according to the book which Ezekiel testifies that he received, “lamentations, and a song, and woe were written” (Ezek. 2). Just as sacred Scripture teaches or promises us, in the present life, the lamentations of repentance and the woe of pressures or tribulations—the Lord saying: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16), and “Repent, for the kingdom of God has drawn near” (Matt. 3)—so too we are commanded to have a song, that is, the joy of hope, so that, “rejoicing in hope, we may be patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12). “Who teaches songs, I say, in the night,”

VERS. 11. — and “who teaches us,” namely, the mysteries of heavenly life, “above the beasts of the earth,” that is, above those who desire low things through the practice of carnal life, “and instructs us above the birds of heaven,” that is, makes us frustrate the pride or cunning of evil spirits, so that they cannot take away the seed of God’s word cast into our hearts. Moreover, Paul knew that he had been instructed above the birds of heaven when he said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” [Col. 1135A] (1 Cor. 6). No one, I say, of those who, pressed by the multitude of oppressors and the arm of tyrants, cried to the Lord, said this.

VERS. 12. — “There,” namely in tribulation, “they will cry,” as was said above, “and he will not hear because of the pride of the wicked.” That is, he will indeed hear at times; but, “because of the pride of the wicked,” which is to be wickedly increased, according to: “Let him who does harm do harm still” (Rev. 22), “he will not hear,” that is, he will defer the hearing, so that while the life of the former is worn away in purification, the wickedness of the latter may be completed. This is done by just judgment, as it is written also of their very head: “He shall act and prosper” (Dan. 8), and again: “And deceit shall prosper in his hand” (ibid.).

VERS. 13. — “Therefore God will not hear in vain,” that is, he will hear only as is fitting and as is useful for those crying out; “God will hear,” according to: “A helper in due times” (Ps. 9). “And the Almighty beholds the causes of individuals,” that is, what is expedient for each person. For as a wise physician he cuts away the poison of corruption with the blade of tribulation; and precisely by seeming not to hear the sick man’s cries, he brings about the end of the sickness. Therefore, O whoever you are, who are broken by that very delay of help:

VERS. 14. — “Even when you say, ‘He does not consider,’” that is, when, troubled by the storm of despair, you think that God does not care for human affairs, “judge before him”: by recalling his benefits to mind, quickly place your shaken mind in the harbor of hope, “and wait for him,” for his help will come and will not delay, though it may seem slow to you. “Wait,” I say, and “do not be envious when you see the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72).

VERS. 15. — “For now he does not bring his wrath,” namely upon the ungodly, for whom the scourge of eternal condemnation is reserved in the future; “nor does he greatly avenge wickedness,” namely now, in those whom he condemns forever. This is fittingly signified by the fact that when Ham sins, his son Canaan is cursed, the father saying: “Cursed be Canaan the servant; he shall be servant to his brothers” (Gen. 9). For what does it mean that, when Ham sins, his son receives the sentence of vengeance, except that the wickedness of the reprobate is struck, as it were, not in themselves but in their posterity? Here they indeed accomplish their deeds without punishment, but afterward they are struck. “Therefore,” he says, “Job has opened his mouth in vain,” namely when he says: “Why then do the wicked live, are exalted, and strengthened with riches?” (Job 21), and similar things; “and he multiplies words without knowledge,” that is, not knowing what he says. As though he said: He knows nothing, yet says much.

CHAPTER XXXVI

VERS. 1. — “Elihu also added and spoke these things”: as though he had said nothing yet, he begins again and loquaciously puts forward what he thinks, while accusing blessed Job of the fault of loquacity.

VERS. 2. — “Bear with me a little,” he says. As though he said: Although “my eloquence is burdensome to you, and my wonder terrifies you” (ch. 33), bear the wisdom which is laborious for you to hear, and I shall show it to you; for I still have something to say for God, to whom I render service while refuting you.

VERS. 3. — “I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning,” because I speak with one to whom a single statement is not enough, because he does not understand. “And I will prove my Maker just.” In this way, while speaking as if for God’s justice, he thinks that whatever flows arrogantly from him may be excused in human judgments.

VERS. 4. — “For truly,” he says, “my words are without falsehood.” He bursts out ever more openly into impudence, having none of that glory in which the soul of a holy teacher glories, as it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” [Col. 1136B] (Ps. 44). Hence he adds: “And perfect knowledge will be proved to you.” He plainly thinks that he will say great things, but the heart which thought this of itself could not teach him. After breathing out the swollen thoughts of his mind in words of self-exaltation, he added a weighty statement, saying:

VERS. 5. — “God does not cast away the powerful, though he himself is powerful.” That is, temporal power, or even the union of marriage, although they sometimes harm, harm not of themselves but through the things surrounding them: the evils which grow around them from the care of this world. Power in its proper order is good, but it needs the cautious life of one governing it. “Therefore,” he says, “God does not cast away the powerful,” merely because they are powerful, since he himself is powerful; for this would undoubtedly be contradictory. To be powerful and to cast away the powerful because they are powerful is plainly self-contradictory. But whenever he casts them away—as he once cast you away when you were powerful—he does this because of their ungodliness. This is what follows:

VERS. 6. — “But he does not save the ungodly.” As though he said: He condemns not the rightful power of the powerful, but their perverse action. “He does not save the ungodly,” I say, “and he grants judgment to the poor”: that is, by judgment he makes the humble free; or certainly, he grants judgment to the poor because those who are now wickedly oppressed he will then make judges over their oppressors, so that the more they were despised in this world in great humility, the more they may then rise to a higher summit of power, having received their seats.

VERS. 7. — “He will not take his eyes from the just,” namely when the just person here is torn by the cruelties of the unjust without vengeance, so that God seems to have taken his eyes from him. “He will not take his eyes,” I say, but prudently delays vengeance. “And he places kings upon the throne forever”: that is, those who, by not consenting to the movements of their temptations, know how not to succumb but to rule over them, he transfers from this power of governance to the power of recompense; “and they are exalted,” so that those who were temporarily wearied in ruling themselves may be placed forever upon the throne of inward exaltation, according to: “To him who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne” [Col. 1137A] (Rev. 3), and so forth.

VERS. 8. — “And if they are in chains,” that is, still in the restraint of this pilgrimage, or even in the punishment of temporal affliction, “and bound with the cords of poverty,” that is, if they grieve because they lack the true riches reserved for the future,

VERS. 9. — “he will show them their works,” that is, he will bring to their remembrance that they themselves deserved this pilgrimage or affliction, “and their crimes, because they acted violently.” He will show them, for example, as he revealed his crimes to Paul when Paul said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man” (1 Tim. 1), and so forth.

VERS. 10. — “He will also open their ear,” [Col. 1137B] that is, he will cause them to perceive the desire for eternal goods, “that he may correct,” that is, make them recognize the evils they committed; “and he will speak, that they may return from iniquity,” that is, he permits adversities to happen to them so that their strength may be made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12), according to: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle” (Ps. 31).

VERS. 11. — “If they hear and keep,” that is, if they rationally understand such speech, “they will complete their days,” namely their present days, “in good,” that is, in right action, “and their years in glory,” that is, in heavenly recompense.

VERS. 12. — “But if they do not hear,” that is, if they are unwilling to be corrected by scourges, “they shall pass by the sword and be consumed in folly,” because even here they already feel the punishments of the blow, and in the future do not escape just recompense. To show that this is just, he immediately adds:

VERS. 13. — “Dissemblers and crafty persons provoke the wrath of God.” As though he said: They do not hear—that is, they do not acknowledge their crimes; indeed, they are transferred from present scourges to eternal punishments because they are “dissemblers and crafty,” that is, because they cunningly wished to appear holy, and in this provoke God’s wrath. When he called them dissemblers, he aptly added “crafty,” because unless they are ingenious, they cannot suitably feign what they desire to seem. “They provoke God’s wrath,” I say. In what? Namely in what follows: “Nor will they cry out when they have been bound,” that is, they will not confess their sins when caught in the scourges of punishment. For a person who acts wickedly and begins to form human judgments about himself under an appearance of holiness, even when struck by a scourge, refuses to reveal himself as wicked, because he has become accustomed to appear holy. Therefore what follows will happen to them:

VERS. 14. — “Their soul will die in the tempest,” namely the soul that rejoiced in the worst tranquility of human praise. For they seemed to live tranquilly when they took care to rejoice in the praise of holiness. “Their soul will die in the tempest,” I say, so that a danger which could not have been foreseen in such tranquility cannot be avoided; “and their life,” namely of those thought to live manfully, “will die among the effeminate,” [Col. 1138A] that is, among the luxurious, whose mind is corrupted by delight in transitory things.

But as another translation reads: “Their life is wounded by angels,” that is, by messengers of truth. Angels wound the life of the effeminate when messengers of truth attack it with the darts of holy preaching; indeed, at judgment they condemn it with God. Because he has spoken of the condemnation of the reprobate, he adds concerning the deliverance of the humble.

VERS. 15. — “He will rescue the poor man from his distress,” namely when he frees each humble person from this affliction of his pilgrimage. “And in tribulation he will open his ear,” that is, with blows he will open the hearing of the heart, which the prosperity of this world often closes.

[Col. 1138B] VERS. 16. — “Therefore he will save you very broadly from the narrow mouth.” As though he said: Therefore you also, O Job, if you are not a dissembler and crafty person, and if, when bound—that is, struck—you confess your sins, he “will save you from the narrow mouth,” that is, from the gulf of sins, into which whoever falls plunges himself, as it were, into a well or pit. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let not the tempest of waters engulf me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor let the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. 68). For he whose mind is disturbed by iniquity is swept away as by a tempest of water; and he who has committed iniquity in deed has already fallen into a pit. If long habit has weighed him down, the pit has already narrowed its mouth over him. “But he will save you,” he says, “very broadly from the narrow mouth,” namely [Col. 1138C] of the gulf—“very broadly,” I say—“and having no foundation beneath it.”

For the gulf of hell is rightly believed to have no bottom, because whoever is seized by it is devoured without limit. Wishing to express its boundlessness, the prophet says: “Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit” (Isa. 5 [printed “IV”]). “But the rest of your table,” he says, that is, the refreshment of inward satiety, “will be full of fatness,” that is, it will be prepared in the delight of eternal blessedness. The Prophet, hungering for the feasts of this table, says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is manifested” (Ps. 16).

VERS. 17. — “Your cause has been set forth as that of an ungodly person; you shall receive cause and judgment.” As though he said: If you too, O Job, are such a person, your cause will indeed by lot be judged as that of an ungodly person, because you are judged through the fatherly scourge on account of sins—whether you, or any son whom God the Father loves or receives. But afterward “you shall receive cause and judgment”: that is, you shall then judge all things all the more because all things are now more searchingly judged in you.

VERS. 18. — “Therefore let not anger overcome you, so that you oppress anyone”: that is, do not murmur against God or grow proud against any human being. “Nor let the multitude of gifts”—that is, neither the abundance of wisdom nor the esteem of judgment, which are God’s gifts—“incline you” away from true virtue. It should be noted that he does not say, “Let the multitude of gifts exalt you,” but, “Let not the multitude of gifts incline you,” that is, abase you wrongly. For everyone who is temporally exalted is thereby inclined downward: while raising himself outwardly, he falls inwardly.

In some manuscripts it is written, “Nor let the multitude of places incline you,” as though the arrogant were saying to the holy Church: Since you are now everywhere honored with the reverence of faith, beware lest you be lifted up by the pride of that same reverence.

VERS. 19. — “Lay aside your greatness without tribulation”: that is, even while you are not in tribulation and possess peace or prosperity, do not at all trust that you have greatness. “And all the strong ones by strength,” namely lay them aside, lest you trust that you possess them. Do not glory that it was said to you: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44): that is, former fathers, strong and great, are summoned by death to their reward; but weak persons are strengthened for conflicts in their place.

VERS. 20. — “Do not prolong the night,” he says: that is, do not be foolish or plunge yourself into such darkness of ignorance “that peoples may rise in their place,” namely in the place of the strong; that is, so that you substitute the multitude of common people—that is, weak persons—for the strong. Arrogant men say this because they do not believe that those whom they once knew as weak can become strong; and they disdain to honor as changed or as prelates those whom they remember as contemptible or private persons.

Or, morally understood: “Lay aside your greatness without tribulation,” that is, because in adversity itself you now recognize that you previously thought great things of yourself in vain, learn to think humbly even when [Col. 1139C] you are not in tribulation. “And all the strong ones by strength”: that is, lay aside, as has been said, without tribulation, all movements of the heart that presume too greatly upon their own strength. For presumptuous movements of the heart are strong ones; and we lay them aside when, under the pressure of trouble, we are compelled to consider what we are. “Do not prolong the night,” that is, do not entertain sorrow that persists unto despair, “lest peoples rise in their place,” that is, lest multiple and unworthy thoughts spring up in place of the aforementioned strong or proud movements of your heart.

Trusting to subdue these peoples—that is, foolish thoughts—through divine help, the Prophet says: “My protector, in him I have hoped, who subdues peoples beneath me” [Col. 1139D] (Ps. 143), so that they may not carry the mind away through the precipices of fantasies, but thoughts, subjected to reason, may humbly rest.

VERS. 21. — “Take heed,” he says, “lest you turn aside to iniquity,” that is, lest you be lifted up in pride; “for you have begun to follow this after misery.” As though he said: I therefore now advise you to beware of pride because, from the time you began to suffer evils, you have inflamed yourself with the fiery brands of impatience in an ardent heart. Elihu said these things of blessed Job because he did not know that all Job’s words proceeded not from the iniquity of impatience but from the virtue of truth; Job did not err from the judgment of the inward Judge even while justifying himself.

Elihu, learned and arrogant, sometimes says what soothes and sometimes what stings. He now leaves the low ground of morality and ascends to the heights of prophecy. Nor should it be wondered that an arrogant man could be filled with the prophetic spirit, since Saul, the son of Kish, was among the prophets (1 Sam. 10), and, what is greater, even the she-ass received rational words from a vision of an angel (Num. 22). But just as that same she-ass uttered words of reason without thereby attaining a change into rational nature, so now Elihu, or any unworthy person, sometimes receives holy prophetic words, yet does not attain the glory of holiness. Thus one must receive from his teaching what corrects, while carefully guarding against the pride that wounds.

VERS. 22. — “Behold,” he says, “God is exalted,” namely the Redeemer of the human race, who, though he is seen humble in weakness, remains exalted—exalted, I say, “in his strength.” For although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God (2 Cor. 13); indeed, he himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1). And none is like him among lawgivers, such as Moses, Joshua, or even the prophets (Matt. 16), one of whom people said the same Son of Man to be—some saying John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah (Luke 9). “None,” I say, “is like him among” such “lawgivers,” because all these, freely called from sins, return to innocence, whereas this man is without sin, a Son without adoption. Those indeed lead others back by preaching what they have experienced in themselves; but he never committed what he rebukes.

VERS. 23. — “Who,” he says, “can search out his ways?” Namely, no one. Hence the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways” (Rom. 11 [printed “II”]), namely both in the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles, and in other such matters. “Or who can say to him, ‘You have worked iniquity’?” As though he said: If his action cannot be searched out, how can you rebuke him? For no one judges well what he does not know.

VERS. 24. — “Remember,” he says, “that you do not know his work,” that is, his judgments, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Your judgments are a great abyss” [Col. 1140D] (Ps. 35). Again: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17). And elsewhere: “The abyss is the garment of his clothing” (Ps. 103). You do not know his work, I say, “of which men have sung,” that is, whose power either the heavenly spirits or any perfect teachers make known to us. As though he said: The works of him of whom all the strong have spoken exceed the measure of your knowledge precisely because you are bounded by humanity. Yet, although no subtlety of human understanding penetrates his greatness,

VERS. 25. — “All men see him,” because they behold him by reason. For the Apostle says: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” [Col. 1141A] (Rom. 1). And “each beholds him from afar”: that is, they do not see him by direct vision, but still reflect upon him only through admiration of his works. Even the elect behold him from afar here, because they do not yet apprehend his brightness by the keenness of inward vision. And lest, when you ask where they see him or where they behold him from afar, you should suppose him local:

VERS. 26. — “Behold,” he says, “God is great,” that is, he is both here and everywhere: “God is great” and unbounded, “surpassing our knowledge,” that is, greater than our knowledge can comprehend. Whatever we now know of the splendor of his greatness is beneath him; and then we know something, as it were, in part, when we recognize that we cannot know him worthily. “God,” I say, is great, and not only great but eternal. This is what follows: “The number of his years is unsearchable,” because his eternity neither arises from a beginning nor is bounded by an end. And although some creatures too are eternal, all such eternity is unlike the supreme eternity, because whatever besides him is eternal began to be eternal; but God, as has been said, is both without end and without beginning.

After recounting His greatness and eternity, it remains also for us to hear what He does.

**VERSE 27.**—“He who draws up,” he says, “the stars [*stillas*, ‘drops’] of rain”: that is, those saints who shine by the merits of their lives so that they also rain by the speech of preaching—such as Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other [Col. 1141C] prophets were. “He draws up,” I say, when He removes their souls from this corruptible flesh; “and He pours out showers like torrents”: that is, through the apostles who came after them He gives a more abundant teaching. For after He had taken those men, at their death, into His hidden places, a fuller power of preaching flowed forth through these. Or thus: “He draws up,” namely from the Jews, the “stars of rain,” that is, the holy apostles, so that they may not rain upon them the teaching of His grace; “and He pours out showers like torrents”: that is, the teaching of that same grace more abundantly waters the whole world. Or both events may fittingly be understood as occurring in the Church: when He received the apostles’ souls, released from their bodies, into His hidden places, He concealed, as it were, the stars of rain from the face of heaven [Col. 1141D]; but afterward He gave rains in the manner of torrents, because through the tongues of subsequent expositors He disclosed streams of divine knowledge in a more copious outpouring. For what the apostles spoke briefly, these men greatly expanded in exposition.

**VERSE 28.**—“Which,” understand, “the torrents,” that is, the teachers, “flow,” he says, “from the clouds”: that is, they received the source of profound preaching from those same holy apostles. For unless the power of understanding had begun from the holy apostles, it would by no means have flowed more abundantly through the mouths of teachers. “They flow from the clouds,” I say, “which cover all things from above”: namely, when our understanding strives to pass to divine things, it must first be formed through the examples of the saints who went before. Thus, when clouds cover the air, if we lift our eyes toward [Col. 1142A] heaven, we do not see heaven but the clouds themselves; and our sight is first nourished by the intervening air, so that afterward it may contemplate the rays of the sun. For example, if we are kindled in the pursuit of devotion and charity toward the Lord, we are formed by contemplating Peter and John as clouds. For what was more devout than Peter, who, hastening to the Lord, did not fear to tread the yielding surface of the sea? (Matt. 14.) What was more loving than John, who through love rested upon the very breast of our Creator? (John 21.) Likewise, since the prophets too are clouds, as was said above, if we desire to obey heavenly commands, we lift our eyes to the obedience of Abraham, who, commanded to sacrifice his only son, did not refuse (Gen. 22). And if we devote ourselves to patience, what do we behold more patient than Isaac, who carries the wood [Col. 1142B], asks about the burnt offering, is shortly afterward bound and says nothing, is placed upon the altar and does not resist? (Gen. 6 [probably Gen. 22].) So too, taking examples of virtues from the rest, we behold, as it were, clouds, so that afterward we may be able to see the true Sun in Himself. “The clouds,” he says, “cover all things from above”; and this occurs only through the divine will or grace. This is what follows.

**VERSES 29–30.**—“If He should choose to spread out the clouds like His tent”: that is, to diffuse throughout the breadth of the world the saints or His ministers, in whom He dwells—manifest in work, yet hidden in heart. For clouds, that is, holy preachers, are rightly called His tent, because God, coming to us through grace, is veiled within the minds of His [Col. 1142C] preachers. “If He should choose,” I say, “to spread out the clouds,” as has been said, “and to flash forth with His light from above”: that is, to perform His miracles through those same preachers, by which He may illuminate human darkness, “He will also cover the ends of the sea”: that is, He will bring even the ends of the world to faith and unite, in one faith, the boundary of East and West.

**VERSE 31.**—“For by these,” he says, “He judges peoples”: that is, by the drops of these clouds, which are the words of preachers; by these flashes of miracles He calls to repentance the terrified hearts of peoples. For when they hear heavenly things and behold wonderful works, fearing eternal torments they judge themselves, lest they be judged by God. “And He gives food [Col. 1142D] to many mortals”: namely, by these same means, so that holy preachers may terrify sinners with eternal punishments and feed penitents with the joys of the heavenly kingdom. It should be noted that he does not say “to all,” but “He gives food to many mortals,” because it is written: “Faith is not for all” (2 Thess. 3). And he rightly and in due order says that through these “clouds” He first “judges peoples” and afterward “gives food,” because the word of preaching first shakes the sinner with fear and afterward nourishes him through the hope of consolation. But when He “gives food to many mortals,” as was said—that is, to the humble alone—He does toward the proud what follows.

**VERSE 32.**—“In mighty men [*in manibus*, ‘in hands’] He hides [Col. 1143A] the light.” Mighty men are those who exalt themselves with proud thoughts and are wise in their own eyes and prudent before themselves (Rom. 11). From them “God hides the light,” that is, knowledge of the truth. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “And reveals it to little ones” (Matt. 11; Luke 10), that is, to the humble. Yet sometimes the light of heavenly grace also looks upon such mighty men. Hence it is added: “And He commands it,” understand, the light, “to come again,” because the light of truth, which is hidden from proud minds, is revealed to those same persons when afflicted and humbled. This may be understood particularly of the Jews, from whom the light of truth is now hidden because of pride, but will come again at the Lord’s command. For “though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be [Col. 1143B] saved” (Rom. 9), that is, at the end of the world they will be received into faith.

**VERSE 33.**—“He announces concerning it,” understand, concerning the light, concerning that heavenly country over which He Himself presides, which He fills and refreshes by His vision, and whose true inheritance is light; “He announces,” I say, “to His friend”: that is, to the guardian of His mind, who keeps His will or command. For a friend is said to be, as it were, a guardian of one’s mind.

What does He announce to him concerning this light? “That it is his possession”: namely, because He Himself, in utmost compassion, took up our low estate and joined the lowly to the highest. Therefore it was announced to redeemed humanity concerning that light “that it is its possession, and that it may ascend to it.” This would indeed have been impossible unless He Himself, as has been said, “made a little lower than the [Col. 1143C] angels” (Ps. 8), had descended to us.

## CHAPTER 37

**VERSE 1.**—“At this,” he says, “my heart was terrified”: that is, it was carried away in an excess of wonder; “and was moved from its place”: that is, it was torn away from delight in the present life and transferred to love of eternity. “At this,” I say—understand, at the announcement that a human being can ascend to this light—“my heart was terrified,” as has been said. Whose heart would not leap in wonder at this compassion? Whose dullness would not be struck with awe at the sublimity of so great a contemplation? He adds how what has been foretold is announced, how someone is touched in inward thought and made receptive to spiritual things:

[Col. 1143D] **VERSE 2.**—“He shall hear a hearing in the terror of His voice.”—“He shall hear [*audite*, ‘hear ye’],” namely inwardly: that is, he will suddenly be touched by the inspiration of divine grace, and this not in joy but “in terror.” Being still a sinner, and carrying a heart oppressed by lowly thoughts, he is first made to understand that all he does is punished by the strict judgment of the eternal Judge. Note that when sacred Scripture indicates that something is heard by hearing, it calls it “a hearing heard,” as Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard Thy hearing, and was afraid” (Hab. 3). Hence here also: “He shall hear,” he says, “a hearing in the terror of His voice.” But because the hearing that first occurs in the terror of God’s voice is afterward changed into sweetness, it follows: “And the sound proceeding from His mouth”: that is, the Spirit of love [Col. 1144A] proceeding from the Father according to the Son’s promise. For by “mouth” the only-begotten Son is rightly signified, as in: “Let Him kiss me with the kiss of His mouth” (Song 1), that is, let Him touch me with the sweetness of my Redeemer’s presence. He is called by the name of “mouth” as though the Word were openly named; just as we too are accustomed to call the tongue “speech.” By “sound” likewise the Holy Spirit is rightly understood, concerning whose sign it is written: “There came suddenly from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind” (Acts 2). But what is this that has been said above, “He announces to His friend” (Job 36)?

**VERSE 3.**—“He looks beneath all the heavens, and His light is over the ends of the earth”: that is, He reaches toward the highest things and does not abandon even the lowest [Col. 1144B]; thus He is present to heavenly spirits without being absent from human beings. To these, as already said, He announces by inward speech the vision of His light for which they should hope (ibid.). But if one prefers to understand by “the heavens” those of whom it is written, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18), that is, the holy apostles, who especially heard the above-mentioned sound—the Holy Spirit proceeding from the mouth of God—then “beneath all the heavens,” he says, that is, beneath the inward brightness of the holy apostles or of all preachers, “He looks”: that is, He knows how greatly each one shines inwardly in grace and truth. “And His light,” that is, His knowledge, “is over the ends of the earth”: that is, it looks upon even the extremities of sinners, because after the exalted life of saints, He also encompasses the morals and deeds of [Col. 1144C] preachers by the illumination of His grace. Or it may be understood thus: “His light is over the ends of the earth,” that is, the preaching of heavenly grace gathers within itself to faith the boundaries of the world. When He announces in the aforesaid manner, what follows will occur:

**VERSE 4.**—“After Him a roaring sound will roar”: that is, the roar of repentance will follow His aforesaid voice heard in terror. For when God enters the mind, it is unquestionably the case that, the more able it now is to see what is just, the more ardently it desires to punish itself, which it mourns to be unjust, with groanings. But because the more abundantly fault is wept for, the higher the knowledge of truth is attained, it is rightly added of that same terror of God [Col. 1144D] announcing: “He will thunder with the voice of His greatness,” namely, so that the regard of grace may strike with sudden fear the mind benumbed by carelessness and neglect. For God then “thunders with the voice of His greatness,” when He makes known how great He is to a mind already well prepared through lamentation. “And it shall not be investigated,” he says, “when His voice has been heard,” because even the mind enlightened by the voice of the Spirit coming upon it does not investigate it, according to the saying: “The Spirit breathes where He wills, and you hear His voice, but do not know whence He comes or where He goes” (John 3). For example, who can investigate how, through one event occurring outwardly, the hearts of those who behold it are penetrated in opposite ways? Thus, when Lazarus was raised, many believed (John 12), while many were thereby stirred to zeal for persecution. [Col. 1145A] “It shall not be investigated,” I say. Therefore it is well added:

**VERSE 5.**—“God will thunder wondrously with His voice.” For it is a wondrous thunder that God incomprehensibly penetrates the human mind by hidden power, oppressing it with fear through hidden impulses and forming it in love. It is as though the soul, marveling at what it hears and saying in some fashion what was said through Moses when manna came down—“*Manhu?*,” which is interpreted, “What is this?” (Exod. 16)—were astonished. For when the soul receives heavenly manna, it is amazed at the new character of its refreshment, namely, at the voice of God thundering. “Who,” he says, “will do great and unsearchable things”: because He displays outwardly the perfection of the work, but the very quality of the operation remains hidden [Col. 1145B] within. And though some plant or water outwardly, He alone gives the growth inwardly (1 Cor. 3). But because he to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit thunders magnificently and wonderfully, as has been said, afterward abounds in the waters of heavenly teaching, it is rightly added in praise of that same One who thunders and announces the light to be possessed:

**VERSE 6.**—“Who commands the snow” [Col. 1145C]: that is, the bright justice of the saints, “to descend,” namely for fraternal charity, “to the earth”: that is, to the humble words of preaching. For as snow formed in the air returns to the earth from which it had been raised as water, so the righteous, condescending to sinners, never cease to remember what they themselves were. When Paul did this, he said: “The charity of Christ constrains us” (2 Cor. 5). “Therefore He commands the snow to descend,” as has been said, “and the rains of winter”: that is, to the preaching of saints, which suits this life as rain suits winter, and which will cease, as it were, in summer, when in the future life we shall no longer need to be watered by the preaching of saints. It is rightly added: “And to the rain of His strength.” The rain of God’s strength is the preaching of divinity; for example: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). And he rightly asserts first that He commands “the rains of winter,” and afterward “the rain of His strength,” because whoever is filled by God thundering progresses gradually in His knowledge; accustomed to lesser things, he at last searches even the deep things of God [Col. 1145D] in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 2), as did he who in old age deserved to write, “In the beginning was the Word.” That Gospel is beyond doubt a certain rain of divine strength. And because God requires good works both from the hearer and from the preacher, he rightly adds after the rain of preaching:

**VERSE 7.**—“Who seals in the hand,” that is, in the work, “of all human beings,” both teachers and hearers, “that each may know his works”: namely, “that each one may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5). “He seals,” I say, “in the hand,” which is rightly said of the rational creature, since by the natural law it is not permitted to be ignorant whether what it does is evil or right. Perhaps the Psalmist had this in view [Col. 1146A] when he said: “Deep calls to deep in the voice of Thy cataracts” (Ps. 41), that is, in the preaching of saints. For one deep calling to another deep in the voice of cataracts is for persons convicted by preachers’ sayings concerning the present judgment of conscience to come to the future judgment of condemnation. After a sentence has been uttered concerning each person’s perversity, the discourse turns to the very author of perversity, since it immediately adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“The beast will enter into his hiding-place”: that is, at the end of the world the devil will enter into the condemned man Antichrist. The beast is the devil, who by deceiving the first human being tore apart the life of the human race. When, after the thunder of the aforesaid clouds—that is, after the voices of preachers [Col. 1146B]—he has invaded that man, what else will occur than that “the beast will enter into his hiding-place”? Nor will he merely “enter” for a time; rather, as follows, “he will remain in his den”: that is, not as he may enter the minds even of good people, in whom, however, he cannot remain; but he will so hold that hiding-place or den by entering that he will possess it by holding it forever. Yet even now, before he openly appears, he possesses the hearts of all the reprobate as though they were his own den—for example, the Jews, in whose counsels he lay hidden for a long time, but suddenly broke forth in their cries against our Redeemer: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23). They also handed over to the Gentiles, that is, to Roman authority, for execution Him whom they themselves could not lawfully [Col. 1146C] kill. Hence it is openly added:

**VERSE 9.**—“From the inner regions comes the tempest, and from Arcturus the cold”: that is, from the Jews will arise persecuting malice, and from the Gentiles the killing power. For by “the inner regions,” namely those of the south: when sacred Scripture sets the inner regions against Arcturus, it denotes the region of the south, distinct from the parts of the north. By the inner regions of the south, which the hotter sun possesses, the Jewish people are signified, since they knew the one God as though they had the noonday sun. But by Arcturus, upon which the sun has no course whatever, the Gentile people are represented: having no knowledge of God, it remained cold beneath the north as though without a sun. “From the inner regions [Col. 1146D],” I say, “came the tempest, and from Arcturus the cold,” when what Jewish envy demanded, the Gentile judge carried out under Roman authority. Against this envy it adds:

**VERSE 10.**—“When God blows, ice thickens”: that is, when the Holy Spirit breathes upon believers, the numbness of still heavier envy grew in the minds of unbelievers. For example, when the envious said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after Him” (John 12), and similar things. But because God could melt so great an ice of unbelief and liquefy unbelieving hearts to love Him: “And again,” he says, “the waters are spread abroad very widely.” That is, hearts frozen through unbelief melt again through tears of repentance, according to the psalm: “Turn, O Lord, our captivity [Col. 1147A] as a torrent in the south” (Ps. 125). For example, Paul was liquefied, as it were, from ice into water, when the numbness of his inward cold was changed into the irrigation of preaching. Hence it adds:

**VERSE 11.**—“The grain desires clouds”: that is, all the elect, who are surely God’s grain, to be stored in heavenly barns, need preachers. These rain words as clouds and, as workers in the Lord’s harvest, never cease to do what they speak. “And the clouds,” he says—that is, the same preachers—“scatter their light”: that is, by speaking and acting, as has been said, they provide an example of life.

**VERSE 12.**—“They go around in a circuit,” namely to illuminate the souls of those who are in darkness, “wherever the will of their governor [Col. 1147B] leads them”: that is, not where they themselves wish, but where the grace of God calls. “For everything,” he says, “that He commands them upon the face of the whole earth.” For they find the way of preaching more open to the degree that they are led to it, not by their own impulses, but by the directions of their Master.

**VERSE 13.**—“Whether in one tribe,” that is, in Judah alone; “or in His own land,” that is, throughout all Judea; “or in whatever place of His mercy,” that is, among the Gentiles—“He commands them,” understand, the clouds, “to be found.” One tribe is certainly Judah, a tribe conspicuous above the others and numerous; His land is all Israel; but the place of mercy is the Gentile world, which received reconciliation from mercy alone and has now, according to Hosea, obtained mercy. Hence Paul says [Col. 1147C]: “The Gentiles,” he says, “glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15). At one time God bestowed His clouds, that is, His teachers—the prophets—upon the tribe of Judah alone; at another He recalled the Israelite people to ancient grace after correction and captivity; at another He displayed miracles of power to all nations. But the arrogant man, because he perceived future things through the prophetic spirit, immediately adds in boastfulness:

**VERSE 14.**—“Listen to these things, Job”: understand, you who until now have not had ears to hear. “Stand”: understand, you who lie fallen through vice. “And consider the miracles of God.” It is as though he said: Do not, after the manner of rebels, fall with eyes open by resisting the truth which you understand. Still examining him about future things and humbling him as though for [Col. 1147D] ignorance, he says:

**VERSE 15.**—“Do you know,” he says, “when God commanded the rains to show forth the light of His clouds?” That is, do you already discern preachers who are to be sent into the world, so that the rains—that is, teachings—may make manifest the brightness of doctrine or the grace of those same preachers? It is as though he said: No one knows when the rains will display the light of the clouds, because no one comprehends when God gives the power of preaching, by what means He makes Himself known, or how the glory of preachers shines forth.

**VERSE 16.**—“Do you know the paths of the clouds”: that is, the narrow and strict life of those same preachers; “their great and perfect knowledges”? For their knowledge is great and perfect precisely in this: through knowledge they raise themselves to high things, while through humility they bend themselves to recognizing their own ignorance, confessing that they do not possess from themselves the knowledge which they now possess [Col. 1148A] in part. He adds, judging by an analogy that this is done by the gift of the Holy Spirit alone:

**VERSE 17.**—“Are not your garments warm when the earth is breathed upon by the south wind?” It is as though he said: As “your garments” grow warm when the south wind blows, so all who are joined to the Church by the unity of faith—of whom the prophet also says to that same Church: “As I live, you shall put them all on like an ornament” (Isa. 49)—so, I say, all the elect possess true knowledge and perfect [Col. 1148B] humility, not from themselves but from the Holy Spirit, who is customarily signified by the south wind. These things are indeed said generally of the holy Church, yet they are also to be understood particularly of her individual members. For just as garments attached to a living body grow warm when, covering its exhaling pores, they retain the heat issuing from within, and, once warmed, give back to the body the heat they received by retaining it; so hearers are kindled by the word of teachers, and the life of teachers likewise advances through the progress of hearers. It is as though he said openly: You wrongly credit yourself if you observe that some have advanced through you, because unless the fervor of the Holy Spirit touched them, they would remain cold—those whom you suppose to have grown warm through you. But after saying this forcefully, stirred by slight arrogance, he adds mockingly:

[Col. 1148C] **VERSE 18.**—“Perhaps you made the heavens with Him”: that is, angelic spirits or holy human beings, “who are solid as cast bronze”: that is, they persist in the divine structure; and just as bronze is not easily consumed by rust, so they are not corrupted by the vice of pride and remain firm in temptation, as the Lord Himself says: “You are they who have remained with Me in My temptations” (Luke 22). Although he intermingles strong statements while seeking to mock, he always returns to superfluous words.

**VERSE 19.**—“Show us,” he says, “what we should say to Him”: understand, you who enjoy so great a light of understanding, “for we are wrapped in darkness,” understand, of ignorance. Immediately leaping back from mockery, he adds contemptuously:

[Col. 1148D] **VERSE 20.**—“Who will tell Him what I say?” That is, who can recount before God—or even after hearing them—the things which I utter, unheard by others, because I keenly perceive the praises of God? “Even if a human being,” he says, “has spoken to God”: that is, one who, while he is silent about God, seems to be something by reason of the rational nature in which he was created. But if he begins to speak about God and rises above himself by intellectual sight, he will be shown to be nothing, because the things contemplated in God are so great that he is “swallowed up,” that is, confesses himself to be nothing, by the immensity of His greatness. But because so great a divine greatness had not yet been revealed through His works, he adds:

**VERSE 21.**—“But now they do not see the [Col. 1149A] light”: namely because, according to the prophet, “The people sat in darkness, and light had not yet risen upon them in the same darkness” (Isa. 9). He immediately adds how this light is to be seen by all: “Therefore the air will suddenly be gathered into clouds”: that is, peoples or nations which, like air, are not made firm by any solidity. For their minds are fluidly scattered here and there in the manner of air. “The air,” I say—that is, worldly minds—“will be gathered into clouds”: that is, through the grace of the heavenly regard they will be strengthened and bound to apostolic faith. These apostles are indeed firmer than the prophets, as clouds are heavier than empty air. Or, so that the entire statement may be understood of the apostles: “The air will suddenly be gathered into clouds,” when the apostles themselves, formerly scattered in earthly desires like air, followed the Lord at a single command—or rather were transformed [Col. 1149B] by the sudden sound of the Holy Spirit’s coming—so that they thought firm things through faith and, after the manner of clouds, received the waters of knowledge. “The air,” I say, “will suddenly be gathered into clouds; and the passing wind will drive them away”: that is, the course of temporal life will remove the apostles themselves from the flesh. And when they have been removed, what will happen?

**VERSE 22.**—“From the north,” he says, “comes gold”: that is, from the Gentile world, once bound by the cold of sin, precious faith will arise through their deaths; “and from God,” that is, from the inspiration of God’s grace, “fearful praise.” “Fearful,” I say, in such a way that Judea will fear to forbid it. Hence it is written: “When they heard these things, they kept silence and glorified God, saying: Then God has granted repentance unto life even to the Gentiles” (Acts 11). Finally Elihu, perceiving the incomprehensible greatness of God, says:

**VERSE 23.**—“We cannot find Him worthily.” “Worthily,” I say, because though we can find Him, we cannot find Him worthily. For whatever we perceive of Him is by faith, not yet by sight. And why not worthily? “Great,” he says, “in strength, judgment, and justice,” understand, He is. “In strength,” namely because He conquers the strong adversary. “And in judgment,” because although He humbles His elect here, He will at some time exalt them. “And in justice,” because although He now bears long with the reprobate, He will at some time condemn them.

**VERSE 24.**—“Therefore men will fear Him”: that is, those strong in understanding; “and all who seem wise to themselves will not dare to contemplate Him.” He does not say, “the wise,” but “those who seem [Col. 1149D] wise to themselves”: that is, skilled indeed, but arrogant. They “will not dare” to “contemplate” Him; rather, they will condemn themselves by their own words. Thus Elihu, while he perceives many things strongly, touches upon himself at the conclusion of his speech. For arrogant men—learned, indeed, but not living rightly—when they act perversely become heralds of their own condemnation: “turned,” namely, “into a crooked bow” (Ps. 77), that is, condemning themselves by their own words, just as a crooked bow strikes the one who draws it.

## CHAPTER 38

**VERSE 1.**—“But the Lord, answering Job out of the whirlwind.” In this divine answer one must consider that the purpose is to examine blessed Job lest his very victory cast him down by the sword of pride; and for this reason the Lord sternly reproves his righteousness in order to preserve him for life. For he was not raised in the praise of God, like a ductile trumpet produced by hammering, as greatly as he was struck by the greater chastisement. [Col. 1150A] Yet he had to be humbled, though prostrated by ulcers, just as he stood firm in virtues. “Answering,” therefore—that is, answering the estimate which perhaps could arise within him; for what more often kills the soul than virtue of which it is conscious?—“answering,” I say, “out of the whirlwind”: that is, out of terrifying and fearful power, beneath which Job, scourged as he was, was surely in a great whirlwind, “He said”: that is, He spoke inwardly through Himself, sounding the force of His judgment upon Job’s heart without words. This manner of divine speech is more effective than all the ways in which He customarily speaks, whether through an angel, another creature, or a vision, because inwardly a word is uttered without noise, a word which opens [Col. 1150B] hearing but knows no sound.

**VERSE 2.**—“Who is this who wraps up judgments in unskilled words?” That is, one who indeed speaks good judgments, but does not observe time, place, or person, and confuses everything through the lightness of arrogance. When He says, “Who is this?” He plainly indicates that He disapproves of him. For we say, “Who is this?” only of someone whom we do not know. But for God, to know is to approve; not to know is to disapprove. Therefore, turning words toward Job in order to instruct him after rejecting that man, He says:
