**VERSE 3.**—“Gird up your loins like a man”: that is, restrain luxury, “like a man”: that is, a strong person. But since blessed Job was endowed with such chastity, what is commanded him except to restrain the luxury of the heart—that is, to repress the self-glorification [Col. 1150C] which sometimes steals in from awareness of virtue? It is as though He said: You who had first conquered the luxury of corruption, now restrain the luxury of pride, lest you glory proudly in patience or chastity. This is to circumcise, as the Law commands, the foreskins of the heart (Jer. 4). “I will question you,” He says: that is, by examining with My words what you do not know, I will show you; “and you answer Me”: that is, understand and humbly acknowledge how much you lack of the perfection of knowledge.

**VERSE 4.**—“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” That is, when I foreknew and predestined the preachers and rulers of the holy Church, concerning whom it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86). For they bear the Church in [Col. 1150D] their faith or doctrine just as material foundations support a building. “Tell Me, if you have understanding.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Who set its measures,” understand, the Church’s, “if you know? Or who stretched the line over it?” This was done when the Lord, distinguishing the boundaries of the Church by the subtlety of His hidden judgment, called holy preachers to other regions of the world, according to what was said to Paul in a vision: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16), while He restrained others, as when the apostles attempted to go into Bithynia and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. If you have understanding, I say—an understanding which many do not possess when they arrogantly assume a measure that they may not have, without humble fear, not considering that all depends upon the power of the [Col. 1151A] Measurer—

**VERSE 6.**—“Upon what,” he says, “were its bases,” understand, the Church’s, “made firm?” That is, upon whom did the holy teachers lean, so that they might sustain the entire weight of the Church by the fixed gravity of their conduct, just as bases sustain columns? Columns, however, bear the weight of the whole structure. These bases were overlaid with silver in Moses, the Lord saying: “You shall make four columns, and their bases overlaid with silver” (Exod. 26), because the preachers of the Church, adorned with the divine word, bear in speech and deed the sayings of the four Evangelists. Or the bases are also the prophets, who, because they were the first openly to speak of the Lord’s Incarnation, likewise bear the structure of ecclesiastical [Col. 1151B] faith placed upon them. Whether, then, they signify prophets or teachers, “upon what,” he says, “were its bases made firm?” Understand: unless upon Me, who wonderfully hold all things and inwardly, as the primary source, furnish the origin of external goods. “Or who laid its cornerstone?” All the foregoing might seem woven together as a historical account of the origin of the world, unless this were suddenly added—something not done at the world’s origin—which shows that what was said above was not about the origin of the world. “Who,” he says, “laid the cornerstone”: that is, who sent Christ for the salvation of this Church? In coming, He joined the nations of the Gentiles to the Israelite people, indeed human beings to blessed angels in heaven, just as a cornerstone in a material building joins different [Col. 1151C] walls. For of this stone the Prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 112).  

**MORAL SENSE:** “Where were you,” He says, “when I laid the foundations of the earth?” That is, faith in the sinner’s heart. For by “earth” a sinner may be understood, since it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). A foundation is laid for that earth when, as the sinner is converted, the first virtue—faith—is granted in his heart by God’s inspiration. “Where were you?” I say. It is as though He said: Recall where I found you when I made you firm by My fear, and do not exalt yourself against Me because of My gift. “Tell Me, if you have understanding: who set its measures?” Understand: unless I did, when I gave to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, and so forth (1 Cor. 12). “Tell Me,” I say: that is, recognize from whom [Col. 1151D] you have received, “if you have,” that is, humility or discernment. By this the man who said, “I have not walked in great things or in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130), restrained himself beneath the hand of the Measurer. He therefore set the measures of the human heart—that is, of the earth—so that our lesser works may be accomplished and our greater works moderated; and He showed the line to be stretched over it—that is, the examples of the Fathers who went before—as the rule to be followed in life. “Upon what were those bases made firm?” Understand: unless upon Me? Those “bases,” I say, are its intentions, from which virtues are borne as columns from bases. These are truly, as it were, bases upon a foundation only when they are strengthened [Col. 1152A] in Christ. Otherwise, unless they rest on this foundation, they build upon themselves losses of ruin that are the heavier the higher the buildings they bear outside the foundation. Or, “Who laid its cornerstone?” That is, who gave the twofold understanding of sacred Scripture, receiving and joining together letter and spirit? “Who,” I say, “laid,” that is, gave it, unless I Myself, who, assuming human nature, join two peoples in Myself and open the literal sense of the Law to spiritual understanding? And, as though asking when He did these things, then, he says,
VERS. 7.—“When the morning stars praised me together,” that is, in harmony, “and all the sons of God rejoiced?” That is, the angels, the rational spiritual nature created first in time, as it were in the morning; and the elect human beings. Thus, when the morning stars—that is, the angels, created in the morning, that is, in the beginning, as has already been said—were singing, “Glory to God in the highest,” and the elect people were rejoicing (Luke 2), that is, experiencing such joy at Christ’s Incarnation as could not be expressed through the narrow confines of speech. Since the Lord knew these things would certainly come to pass, he sets them forth not so much as things to be done as relates them as accomplished. But while the good thus rejoice, envy on the other hand inflames the wicked; yet the Lord restrains it for our protection:

VERS. 8.—“Who,” he says—supply, if not I—“shut up the sea with doors,” that is, the bitter world by the opposition of holy persons, so that, through their miracles and the reverence accorded them, the waves of persecutors’ wrath might be broken as the waves of the sea; “when it burst forth as though issuing from a womb,” that is, when it raged in action, bringing to completion the wicked conception of carnal thought?

VERS. 9.—“When,” he says, “I made the cloud its garment,” that is, when I darkened the face of its heart with the veil of its own folly, “and wrapped it in darkness”—supply, the darkness of ignorance—“as in swaddling-clothes?” Namely, so that it might not be able to persecute as much as it wished, just as an infant’s feet and arms are bound in swaddling-clothes lest they be tossed this way and that in unrestrained freedom. Who, I say, did these things, if not I?

VERS. 10, 11.—“I surrounded it with my boundaries,” that is, I broke the waves of its anger, as it were, upon the level shore of hidden providence. “And I set a bar,” that is, the strong faith of my Incarnation, “and doors,” that is, holy preachers strengthened by that same Incarnation of mine, just as doors are strengthened by a bar. They are rightly called doors for this reason also: they are open to those who follow and closed to those who resist. For example, Peter both received Cornelius, who was seeking the mysteries of faith (Acts 10), and repelled Simon, who sought miracles for money (Acts 8). “I set,” I say, “a bar and doors. And I said: Thus far you shall come,” that is, at some time, through faith, you shall reach these preachers of my Incarnation, “and here you shall break your swelling waves,” that is, you shall be ashamed to have acted wickedly against the faith.

[Col. 1153A] Since in this shutting-in of the sea doors are mentioned a second time, the Lord set doors against this sea a second time: first, by giving the commandments of the Law, he restrained the human race from the worship of idols; afterwards, by giving the Testament of new grace, he corrected it from a carnal understanding of the Law. For example, through the Law he had said, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20); but through the Gospel he says: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). “Who, therefore,” he says, “shut up the sea with doors,” that is, restrained the human race by the precepts of the ancient Law, “when it burst forth as though issuing from a womb,” that is, when, growing into the advance of carnal life, it ran forth to its own desires? “When,” he says, “I made the cloud its garment,” namely, so that they might abandon their former deeds of perversity and yet not see future goods with certainty. “And I wrapped it in darkness as in swaddling-clothes,” that is, before the preaching of the Spirit had been openly revealed, I instructed it by figurative speech and restrained it by the precepts of the letter suited to its understanding. And because he enclosed his people by the boundary of commandments against the immoderate wanderings of the soul, he says: “I surrounded it with my boundaries.” But because, when the Mediator too had been sent, he restrained the motions of the human race: “I set,” he says, “a bar and doors,” that is, I sent the Redeemer and gave the teachings of new life. For just as doors are strengthened by a bar, so the new commandments are strengthened by the authority of the Redeemer who gave them.

Morally:

But because these things are said to blessed Job in order that the glory arising from so many virtues of his heart might be repressed, let us also discuss this same matter morally. “Who,” he says—supply, if not I—“shut up the sea with doors,” that is, constrained by my fear your heart, or the heart of any human being, after the hidden fluctuations of temptations had at last subsided from its own motions; “when it burst forth as though issuing from a womb,” that is, when it was unrestrained, beginning from youth to think perversely. For youth is the womb of perverse thought. For the Lord says through Moses: “The sense and thought of the human heart is inclined to evil from its youth.” “When,” he says, “I made the cloud its garment,” namely, so long as a human being is mortal, so that the glory of immortality might not yet be open to his gaze; “and wrapped it in darkness as in swaddling-clothes,” namely, so that, still weak in understanding, it might be bound by its own infirmity from contemplating sublime things. Wrapped in these swaddling-clothes, Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13), etc. “I surrounded it with my boundaries,” that is, I humbled it under the measure of contemplation, so that though it desires more, it may not rise beyond what is granted it. “And I set a bar and doors,” that is, charity and the other virtues. This raging sea would scatter those virtues unless charity, set over against it from the hidden interior of the mind, bound them together; as the Apostle says, it “is the bond of perfection” (Col. 3). “I set,” I say, “and I said: Thus far you shall come and go no farther,” that is, you shall be tempted only by this or that vice, and yet you shall not carry out the evils suggested to you. “And here you shall break your swelling waves,” that is, after so great or such a temptation, the regard of my fear shall restrain your proud motions through the locked barriers of virtues. These questions are put to him as though it were plainly said: In vain do you weigh yourself outwardly by good works if you do not consider me, who inwardly restrain the waves of temptation.

VERS. 12.—“Have you, after your rising, commanded the dawn, and shown the morning its place?” Supply: as I have. Clearly, the rising of his divinity has neither before nor after. Therefore this is better understood of the rising of his humanity, which began and ended, and began to have before and after in time. “Have you,” therefore, he says, “after your rising commanded the dawn”—supply, as I have, who after the darkness of error gave commands to the new Church, which is whitening, as it were, like dawn after night. In the present life it falls short of the brightness of the future life by as much as dawn falls short of the splendor of the noonday sun. “And have you shown the morning,” that is, the same Church, “its place”—namely, the place to which it is to pass from the present world—as I say to it: “Wherever the body may be, there also the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24). And again: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17). He rightly declares that he did this after his rising, because when he assumed the weakness of human birth, he expanded into the love of an innumerable multitude the knowledge of future glory previously understood by only a few.

These things have been said concerning the illumination of the elect; what follows concerns the condemnation of the reprobate.

VERS. 13.—“Have you,” he says, “taken hold of the ends of the earth and shaken the ungodly out of it?” Supply: as I have, who, coming to the Synagogue at the end of the ages, chose from it a few who were cast down and humble, and who are therefore called the ends of the earth. “I took hold,” I say, “while shaking,” that is, I stirred even the hearts of the reprobate with immense fear, as they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12), and similar things. “And I shook the ungodly out of it,” namely, the chief priests and Pharisees, whom, because they rejected the spiritual teachings of faith, I drove even from the glory of carnal sacrifice. When they have been shaken out, what follows will occur:

[Col. 1154D] VERS. 14.—“The seal shall be restored as clay,” that is, the same Israelite people, whom, filled with the prophetic knowledge of me, I had made a seal of the mystery to be preserved, shall return, as it were, to the bricks which it had left in Egypt. For when I come, it loves the earth more than me; and, returning through unbelief to the spiritual Pharaoh, it serves in mud and brick by setting its mind on earthly things. “It shall be restored,” I say, “as clay. And it shall stand like a garment,” that is, it shall not cling to me through the understanding of charity. And it shall stand in the way that coarse and unpolished garments are said to stand when they do not fit the limbs of the wearer well. But because its standing is from pride:

VERS. 15.—“Its light shall be taken away from the ungodly,” he says, that is, from the Jews, that knowledge of the Law in which they take pride; “and the uplifted arm shall be broken,” that is, the proud performance of the Law shall be rejected. Paul says that “by works of the Law no flesh shall be justified” (Rom. 3).

Morally: “Have you,” he says, “taken hold, while shaking, of the ends of the earth?” That is, have you, as I do, permitted the final times of the Church to be shaken with darkness under the persecution of Antichrist—that is, to be most violently disturbed—and will you shake “the ungodly out of it,” that is, permit some to fall away from the Church into unbelief, those “who profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. 1), so that, when the breeze of temptation stirs, they may pass into a heap of chaff? And so what follows comes to pass: “The seal shall be restored as clay,” that is, those who now seem, within the bosom of the Church, to be a seal through faith shall then be restored as clay before the eyes of all, because they will be revealed as wicked. For sacred Scripture is accustomed to call faith a seal and wickedness clay. “And it shall stand like a garment,” that is, broken and cast down, it shall lie. Just as a garment, when put on, is stretched over the body, but when taken off is folded and crumpled. Or thus: “It shall stand like a garment,” that is, it shall endure only briefly in this life which it loves. For a garment endures only briefly. Hence it is written: “All shall grow old like a garment, and like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed” (Ps. 101).

Now, in plainer words, he adds concerning the same persons: “Its light shall be taken away from the ungodly,” that is, their very understanding, which they misuse; as the Lord says: “From him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away” (Matt. 25). This will happen especially when, under the onset of that final persecution, all the wicked lose what they seemed to believe rightly. Then, consoling those terrified by the same persecution of Antichrist: “And the uplifted arm,” he says, “shall be broken,” that is, the proud height of Antichrist, by which he will raise himself so far as to claim falsely that he is God above human beings, exalting himself above everything called God or worshipped (2 Thess. 2), shall be destroyed by the brightness of the Lord’s coming.

Yet all these things can still be understood otherwise. For the more we break down the words of God in exposition, the more abundantly we profit. Just as a pigment, the more it is ground, the more its potency increases in the cup. “Have you,” he says, “taken hold,” that is, drawn to yourself, “while shaking,” namely with salutary fear, “the ends of the earth,” that is, the sinful human being, who is customarily signified by earth? “Have you,” I say, “taken hold? And shaken the ungodly out of it?” Supply: as I do, who often shake sinners by frightening them at their extremities, hold them by converting them, and tear the ungodly movements of thoughts out of their hearts. It is as though he said plainly: Look upon the power of my mercy, and restrain the pride of your justice.

And because even one who has been converted is followed through the death of the flesh by the punishment of ancient guilt: “The seal,” he says, “shall be restored as clay,” that is, the human being whom God, creating him in his own likeness (Gen. 1), made as a certain seal of his power, shall return to the earth from which he was taken (Gen. 3); “and it shall stand like a garment,” that is, until the time of resurrection the empty and stripped body shall endure, a garment, as it were, in which the spirit is clothed while it lives. But this punishment is common to the proud and the humble. The special punishment of those who are proud is this: “Its light shall be taken away from the ungodly,” that is, the glory of the present life. It shall be taken away, I say, through the death of the flesh, which restores the elect to their light, namely the eternal light, and takes from the reprobate their own light, namely the present one. “And the uplifted arm shall be broken,” that is, the loftiness of heart violently seized contrary to the order of nature shall be scattered beneath the weight of divine justice.

And because no human being could know what followed after death unless the Creator of life came as far as death, he immediately adds:

VERS. 16.—“Have you entered into the depths of the sea?” Supply: as I have, who penetrated not only the sea of this world but also the depth of this sea, that is, the confines of hell; and, as the prophet says, “made the depth of the sea a way, that the redeemed might pass through” (Isa. 51), namely all the elect. “And have you walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss?” That is, existing free among the dead (Ps. 87), have you moreover released others from the bonds of sin? The more wondrously he considers this descent of his, the more frequently he pours it into redeemed humanity. For, repeating it further, he adds:

VERS. 17.—“Have the gates of death been opened to you?” That is, are the hostile powers conquerable—supply, as they are to me, who overcame their strength by dying? “And have you seen the dark doors?” That is, by looking upon them, have you crushed the deceitful malice of those same hostile powers, or have you condemned by dying the rulers of death? We too see those dark doors, that is, malignant spirits, who, while unseen in ambush, open the way of death, when, illuminated by the rays of heavenly light, we say: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. 117). But because after his death and resurrection the Church was spread throughout all nations:

VERS. 18.—“Have you,” he says, “considered the breadth of the earth?” Supply: as I have, who, when I sought the narrow confines of death, spread my faith throughout all nations, so that according to the prophet the Church might enlarge the place of its tent and stretch out the skins of its tabernacle (Isa. 54), and that which had formerly been confined in the one nation of Israel might be enlarged, extending to the right and the left.

Morally: We must consider how this common good takes place in each of us. “Have you,” he says, “entered the depth of the sea?” That is, the hidden recess of the human mind, which, like a sea fluctuating in its various thoughts, is itself thrown into confusion by its swift movements. “Have you,” I say, “entered? And have you walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss,” that is, of that same mind—supply, as I have, to whom alone the mind or spirit of a human being is penetrable? I enter its depth when, troubling and shaking it by my knowledge, I move it to repentance; and I walk, as it were, in the uttermost parts of the abyss when, penetrating the dark heart, I tread down the invisible waves of vices. “Have the gates of death been opened to you?” That is, are the perverse thoughts of the heart known to you? They are called gates of death because through them one enters into death. “And have you seen the dark doors?” That is, the same hidden evil thoughts of the human heart? Have you seen them, I say—supply, as I have, whose eyes alone see what is in the human heart? (2 Chron. 6.) “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?” That is, the good thoughts or virtues of that same human mind. For as every vice narrows, so every virtue enlarges the soul. Blessed Job is asked whether he has considered the breadth of the earth so that he may be humbled by the example of another’s breadth. It is as though he said plainly: Consider those whom the innumerable evils of the present life cannot constrain, and cease to glory in the condition of your heart amid blows.

Then the Lord tests him by a grave question: “Tell me,” he says, “if you know all things,” that is, if you think that you possess complete knowledge.

VERS. 19.—“In what way,” that is, in whose heart, “does light dwell,” that is, illuminating justice; “and what is the place of darkness,” that is, in whom does the blindness of wickedness endure?

VERS. 20.—“So that you may lead each thing to its boundaries,” that is, judge whether one who is now seen to be wicked will end life in wickedness, or whether one who appears righteous will conclude life in the perfection of righteousness. “And may understand the paths of its house,” that is, who will receive a dwelling in the eternal kingdom and who eternal condemnation in punishment. It is as though he said: Since you do not know who will turn from evil to good or return from good to evil, neither do you understand what will be done with you according to what your merits require. And lest he complain that he does not know his end, he is reminded that he does not even understand his beginning.

VERS. 21.—“Did you then know,” he says—supply, before you existed—“that you would be born? Or did you know the number of your days?” Namely, the days during which you were to live on the earth—supply, as I did, who knew that I would be born, and who, living always substantially in divinity before the beginning of my humanity, foreknew concerning myself what I would assume through a beginning in the Virgin’s womb.

VERS. 22.—“Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or seen the treasuries of hail?” Supply: as I have, who comprehend the cold and hard hearts of the wicked, signified by “the treasuries of snow and hail,” and make them serve the benefit of the elect: while they rage, they torment them, yet unknowingly purify them.

VERS. 23.—“Which,” he says, “I have prepared for the time of the enemy,” namely this present time, when “the adversary the devil prowls about like a roaring lion” (1 Pet. 5), “for the day of battle and war,” that is, of temptation both hidden and open.

Yet this entering into “the treasuries of snow” can be understood in a good sense, because God sometimes enters cold hearts of the wicked in order graciously to make from them workers of righteousness and defenders of the right faith. For example, how great a hailstone did he take into his hand when, through Saul—who certainly had been snow or hail through his cold insensibility—he struck down so many hearts resisting him? He prepared this snow or hail “for the time of the enemy,” that is, of the devil or of all worldly wisdom opposing the wisdom of God, “for the day of battle and war,” so that it might fight against every disorder both by the brightness of righteousness and by the rebuke of stern speech. Since this is accomplished through the coming of the Mediator, there follows rightly:

[Col. 1158B] VERS. 24.—“By what way”—supply, unless by me, who “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14)—“is light scattered?” That is, by what way does the power of preaching, flashing forth in the voices of the apostles, shine broadly? Light is scattered, I say. “And is heat divided over the earth?” That is, the distribution through the Church of graces by which all its members, necessarily joined to one another, are kindled.

But because after the scattering of light the division of heat is added, heat may be understood to signify persecution. For when light was scattered—that is, when the life of believers shone brightly—heat was divided over the earth, that is, the cruelty of unbelievers was inflamed and divided: persecution raged now at Jerusalem, now at Damascus, now in other distant regions.

Otherwise: “By what way is light scattered?” That is, the Spirit, who “breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3). Light is scattered, I say, because all its gifts are not bestowed upon any one person. From this scattered light heat is divided over the earth, that is, over the soul, because the cunning enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees shine with the light of righteousness. Heat is said to be divided because individuals are not harassed by all vices, but by certain neighboring and adjacent ones. For, first having observed each person’s particular endowment, the adversary sets snares of temptation before one person through joyful circumstances, before another through sorrowful ones. And it should be noted that heat is said to be divided by the same way through which light is scattered, because the same grace of the Holy Spirit which illuminates our minds with its light also, by its ordering, moderates the temptations of the adversary, lest many come at once and happen to assail the soul beyond what it can bear. And because, as has been said, with light scattered and heat divided, the outward words of preaching too are bestowed, it rightly follows:

VERS. 25.—“Who,” he says, “gave a course to the most violent rain,” that is, to preaching going forth with force, namely so that even amid the straits of persecution the word of God might run, not only like a violent but like a most violent rain? To persuade people to believe eternal or invisible things is indeed a violent rain of preaching, but not a most violent one. But to persuade them, for the hope of future things, to despise present things, or not to fear various kinds of death, is not merely a violent but a most violent rain. “Who, therefore,” he says, “gave a course to the most violent rain,” namely so that so many elect persons would not merely abandon possessions but would also give up their bodies to torments; “and a way to the sounding thunder,” that is, efficacy to the preaching of heavenly terror? When this proceeded from the converging prophecy of the ancient Fathers, it sounded forth terribly like thunder from the shaking of clouds. “Who,” I say, “gave this way?” Supply: if not I. “For,” Paul says, “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3). And if you ask for what purpose he gave it:

[Col. 1159B] VERS. 26.—“That it might rain upon a land without human beings,” that is, upon the Gentile world living without reason, “in a desert,” namely one displaying no appearance of good work, “where no mortal dwells,” that is, no human being; because, while no one in it sought God rationally, it was, as it were, occupied by wild beasts alone.

VERS. 27.—“That it might fill the pathless and desolate land,” that is, the same Gentile world, to which the way of the word of God had not been opened and which had been deprived of the fruit of rational counsel and good work; “and might bring forth green plants,” that is, the knowledge of doctrine and fitting actions. For when the Gentile world received the rain of holy preaching, it put forth both works of life and words of doctrine. Thus, according to the prophet, in the dens where dragons had previously dwelt—that is, among peoples possessed by evil spirits—there sprang up the green growth of reed and rush (Isa. 35): great writers, signified by the reed, and lesser hearers, understood by the rush. The same things said universally concerning the Gentile world occur individually within the bosom of holy Church whenever a mind formerly dry is watered by grace when it comes and, after its former aridity, is clothed with the greenness of knowledge, as though plants had been brought forth. Our Creator, commending this grace still more deeply, says:

VERS. 28.—“Who is the father of the rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?” Supply: if not I, who as Father brought forth the doctrine of heavenly rain and measured preaching like drops of dew—that is, poured it out by paternal grace upon dry human beings? After speaking of the gift by which the Gentile world is called, he adds concerning the severity by which Judea is rejected.

VERS. 29.—“From whose womb,” he says, “did the ice come forth?” That is, from whose hidden bosom was Judea, made cold through unbelief, cast out? “And who begot the frost from heaven?” That is, who permitted these same Jews, frozen by wickedness, to be born from heaven, that is, from the holy Fathers? For when Caiaphas and the entire impious people of the Jews proceeded from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose life was lofty and heavenly, what else but frost was begotten from heaven? Concerning their hard obstinacy he adds:

VERS. 30.—“The waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone.” That is, just as Gentiles, because they worship stones, are rightly called stones themselves, so the hearts of the Jews, once soft and penetrable to faith, are turned into insensibility. And while the hearts of the Gentiles are softened toward faith, the hearts of the Jews are hardened through unbelief. “And the surface,” he says, “of the abyss is bound fast,” that is, in the matters that have been said, the incomprehensibility of divine judgment—of which it is written, “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35)—cannot at all be penetrated by the eye of the human mind.

Otherwise: “From whose womb did the ice come forth?” That is, from whose heavenly secret was Satan, the cold teacher of wickedness, cast out? “And who begot the frost from heaven?” That is, who permitted that same Satan, well created in heaven, should bind the minds of his followers in the cold of guilt, falling like frost from heaven? When he came to earth, “the waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone,” that is, human beings, signified by waters, are hardened in imitation of that same devil, certainly a hard and dark stone. For waters are peoples. “And the surface of the abyss is bound fast,” that is, his deceitful counsels cannot be discovered by the deceived human beings; and while the appearance of his persuasion is displayed above as something good and solid, his hidden malice in the depths is not seen.

Otherwise: “From whose womb did the ice come forth?” That is, by whose hidden judgment has it happened that one who within the bosom of holy Church was powerful in signs, knowledge, or prophecy is later rejected, so that I may say to such persons: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13). They become ice and come forth as from a womb when, seeking praise from human beings for the virtues they have received, they are separated from the inward parts of heavenly mercy. This is said to blessed Job in order that he may be humbled regarding his virtues, lest he grow cold through pride in that in which he had grown warm by living well. Therefore he adds: “And who,” he says, “begot frost from heaven?” That is, who permits heretical unbelief to arise from sacred utterance, which is indeed heaven because it opens for us the day of understanding? The Lord declares that he himself begets this frost in the same way as he says: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 4). For to harden is mercifully not to will to soften; and to beget is justly or usefully to permit something to be begotten. “For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest” (1 Cor. 11).

When this has occurred, “the waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone,” that is, although such people are changeable and soft, they claim to be strong and stable; and though they abandon virtue of purpose, they display themselves through hypocrisy as strong in good works. “And the surface of the abyss is bound fast,” that is, their changeable and unstable conscience is hidden from human beings by a superimposed appearance of holiness.

Or, if anyone wishes to take these matters in a good sense: the Lord, who first presents himself as the Father of rain, subsequently declares that ice comes forth from his womb and that he begets frost from heaven, in order to show that delay is sometimes useful for the growth of virtues. For just as seed that has been sown, if frost presses upon it after rain, takes root more fruitfully the more quickly it is held back from appearing outside, and is compelled to multiply by that very thing by which it is prevented from advancing, so likewise, after the seeds of the word have been moistened by the rains of hidden grace, if at times the rigor of discipline binds them, they eventually abound more strongly; and a good work is perfected through chastening which, if displayed before the proper time, is drained of the grain of perfection. “From whose womb,” therefore, he says—that is, from the secret of inward providence—“did ice come forth?” Namely, so that weakness may restrain the wills of the elect even in good desires. “And who begot frost from heaven?” That is, who confirmed the checking of virtue, so that willing is indeed present to a human being, but he does not find the ability to accomplish it (Rom. 7). And because through the practice of self-stirring the elect compose themselves in a certain rigor of life, “the waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone,” that is, weak minds are strengthened in the solidity of virtues; “and the surface of the abyss is bound fast,” that is, the motions of the fluctuating soul are checked by the superimposed rigor of holy resolution.

But the Lord also begets, as it were, ice from his womb or frost from heaven when he permits his elect to encounter adversity in the present life; by severely pressing them, he certainly makes them stronger. Then “the waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone,” because minds which had flowed softly amid prosperity are hardened when constrained by adversities; “and the surface of the abyss is bound fast,” that is, the deep mind is usefully restrained when those same adversities come upon it, lest, through joy—as commonly happens—it reveal the secrets of the mind and lose them by revealing them. Fearing this, the prophet says: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine” (Isa. 24).

VERS. 31.—The Lord says: “Will you be able to join the glittering stars of the Pleiades?” They are joined by their mutual nearness though separated from one another; they are situated together, yet cast forth the rays of their light in varying ways. That is, will you be able to join all the saints who appear to preach in different times and are separated by the visible form of their persons yet united by the intention of their minds? For example, Abel, Isaiah, and John were divided in time but not in preaching. “Will you,” I say, “be able to join Pleiades of this kind,” that is, saints—supply, as I can? No. For it belongs to divine power alone to unite in the brightness of intention those sent at separate times and endowed with dissimilar virtues. For the intention is one in John’s saying, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1), and Isaiah’s saying, “Like a lamb before one who shears it, he shall be silent” (Isa. 53), and Abel’s, who spoke of this same Lamb by offering him (Gen. 4).

“Or will you be able to scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” Arcturus illuminates the nocturnal spaces in its circuit without setting; it revolves with seven stars in such a way that now it raises three to the heights and inclines four toward the depths, and now raises four above and presses three below. “Will you,” I say, “be able to scatter an Arcturus of this kind,” that is, holy Church, which, enduring the circuit of labors through the whole night of this world, never sets or fails? It continually turns so that now it lifts up the Trinity as though three stars, while inclining the works founded upon the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—as though four stars. For example, when it says through Paul that “Abraham was not justified by works, but believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4); but then, lowering faith and raising works, it inclines three stars and raises four when it says through James: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2).

At some time the Lord scatters the circuit of Arcturus, because he changes the labors of the Church into rest; and he joins the Pleiades because he unites all the saints to himself through the sight of the vision. Yet Arcturus, which rises from the region of cold, may signify the rigid and harsh Law, while the Pleiades, which rise in the East, signify the grace of the New Testament. But our Creator, since he possessed in himself simultaneously, wholly, and enduringly the operations of the sevenfold Spirit, joined, as it were, the Pleiades of the New Testament and scattered the Arcturus of the ancient Law; that is, by opening spiritual understanding, he dissolved the labor of the letter of the Law. “Will you,” therefore, he says, “be able to join?” etc., as has been said.

But because in the very mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation the light of truth is shown to some, while the hearts of others are darkened through scandal:

VERS. 32.—“Will you,” he says, “bring forth Lucifer at its time?” Supply: as I do, who send my Christ in the fullness of time, who, like Lucifer rising at dawn from the dead, overcomes the darkness of human mortality by the splendor of his light, “the bright and morning star,” as John says (Rev. 22). “And do you cause the evening to rise over the children of earth?” That is, do you permit Antichrist to rule in the hearts of unbelieving Jews, as their deserving requires? For that evening would in no way rise over these children of earth if they had wished to be children of heaven. And lest a human being dare investigate this hidden judgment of God:

VERS. 33.—“Do you,” he says, “know the order of heaven?” That is, do you comprehend the hidden predestinations of heavenly dispositions? “And will you establish its reason upon the earth?” That is, will you examine it by consideration, or make it manifest before human hearts?

Yet blessed Job is now questioned concerning the investigation of incomprehensible judgments for a particular reason, as though it were plainly said: You ought to endure all that you suffer with greater patience in proportion as, being ignorant of heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer these things. Since Job was not unaware that this is wonderfully done by the Lord, he is questioned repeatedly by the divine voice, and is further told:

VERS. 34.—“Will you lift up your voice into the cloud?” that is, will you direct the tongue of your preachers toward the darkened hearts of unbelievers, “and will the rush of waters cover you?” that is, will the crowd of resisting peoples persecute you?—as it did me, whom wicked and unworthy hearers, namely the Jews, surrounded while I preached to them [Col. 1163A]. Their blindness too was signified by the cloud in the Book of Kings which filled the house of the Lord (III Kings VIII). “How long,” they say, “do you keep our soul in suspense?” (John X). And thereafter all the wicked cover me as a rush of waters, because they neither understand me speaking through holy preachers nor behold me enduring through those who die. He recounts these things which God suffers from human beings in order to lessen the grief of afflicted humanity. It is as though he plainly says: Weigh my sufferings carefully, and bear yours with equanimity. Immediately, because wicked people despise preaching, he adds also the miracles which they may revere.

VERS. 35.—“Will you,” he says, “send forth lightning flashes” [Col. 1163B], that is, preachers shining with miracles, “and will they go,” that is, pierce the hearts of their hearers with heavenly reverence, “and, returning, say to you: Here we are?” They say this to me when they attribute what they accomplish not to their own powers but to me. For lightning goes forth when a preacher performs a miracle; it returns when he attributes what he has done not to himself but to its Author. Hence elsewhere it is written: “Let the rivers return to the place from which they go forth, that they may flow again” (Eccles. I): that is, holy preachers look back to their Author, lest through presumption concerning themselves they lose the grace which they have received. Concerning these same preachers he asks next:

VERS. 36.—“Who has placed knowledge in the inward parts,” that is, in the human heart—knowledge divinely inspired [Col. 1163C], given not merely in speech but also in understanding? He fittingly commends this wisdom by adding a comparison: “Or who has given understanding to the cock?” That is: just as the cock first distinguishes the hours of the night and only then gives forth its awakening cry, so the holy preacher should first consider the quality of life in his hearers and only then shape a fitting voice of preaching for their instruction. Like a cock crowing, he should shake off with his voice the sleep of sluggishness, announcing the coming light; for example, when he says: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII).

And, that he may preach with authority, he must restrain sensual indulgence, as it is written (Prov. XXX): “There are three things [Col. 1163D] which go well: … the lion, strongest of beasts, which fears no encounter;” plainly because Christ is the Lion from the tribe of Judah: “The prince of this world comes,” he says, “and he has nothing in me” (John XIV). The lion, I say, is strongest; and there is “the cock, girded about the loins,” that is, the preacher resplendent in chastity; “and the ram, and there is no king who can resist him,” that is, every prelate who leads a people following him like a flock of sheep: no persecutor who meets him can hinder his purpose.

Therefore the preacher, like a cock girded about the loins, sings beforehand of the light. And just as the cock in the deeper hours of the night is accustomed to form stronger and more prolonged cries, but, as morning approaches, gentler and shorter ones, so he too, while preaching to minds still wicked, announces in lofty and great utterances the terror of the eternal Judge to those sleeping as though in deep night—first rousing himself by good deeds as by certain wings. But when the light of truth is already present in his hearers, he turns the greatness of his cry into the gentleness of sweetness. “Who,” I say, “gave the cock this understanding?”—unless it was I.

VERS. 37.—“Who will recount the ordering of the heavens,” that is, the force of heavenly secrets, “and who will make the harmony of heaven sleep,” that is, silence the concordant speech of preachers?—unless it be I. For when our Creator begins to disclose the ordering of the heavens, he makes the harmony of heaven sleep: when he is shown to us already in direct vision, the words of preachers are withdrawn. “No longer,” says the prophet, [Col. 1164B] “shall a man teach his neighbor, saying: Know the Lord; for all shall know me, says the Lord” (Jer. XXXI). Who, I say, has done these things?

VERS. 38.—“When dust was poured upon the earth,” that is, at the resurrection, when the dust of the dead is restored into solid limbs; “and the clods were compacted,” that is, when firm limbs are gathered from dust. Divine speech describes future things as though past. Or it may be understood so as to continue the foregoing discussion of the cock’s understanding: “Who,” he says—unless it be I—“will recount the ordering of the heavens,” that is, will enlighten the minds of the elect with knowledge of heavenly secrets, “and who will make the harmony of heaven sleep,” that is, will by a just judgment conceal from the hearts of the reprobate the harmonious hymns of angels and the joys of the heavenly powers?—unless it be I, who began to do this then, “when dust was poured upon the earth,” that is, when, through my appearing in the mystery of the Incarnation, sinners—whom every blast of temptations swept away—were established in the Church by the reason of faith; “and the clods were compacted,” that is, from that same dust, namely, the same sinners were united by the gathering of charity, just as dust is coagulated into clods by moisture. It is as though he said: Then first I opened spiritual secrets, and not without mercy, to some; and not without justice I closed them to others, when, rejecting some, I adorned others within the Church through the concord of charity. Of this Church, which seizes many nations, he adds:

[Col. 1164D] VERS. 39.—“Will you catch prey for the lioness?”—that lioness of whom Job had also spoken above against proud Judaea: “No lioness,” he says, “has passed through it” (Job XXVIII). “Prey,” I say: will you catch multitudes from the Gentiles for this lioness?—as I do. “Or will you fill the desire of her cubs,” that is, will you satisfy through the gain of souls the hungry wishes of the apostles or of other preachers? For the apostles are called cubs—that is, tender ones, or weak through fear—since, after the Lord’s Passion, they sat behind closed doors for fear of the Jews (John XX). Hence it follows:

VERS. 40.—“When they lie in their dens and lie in wait in caves” [Col. 1165A], that is, fearing the assault of the world, they await a fitting occasion for teaching; just as lion cubs “lie in dens” until, when the time comes, they are strengthened openly to seize prey. And because the Gentile world itself, taken through the mouth of the apostles, hungers to take others in turn:

VERS. 41.—“Who,” he says, “prepares its food for the raven?” that is, knowledge of God for the Gentile world black with sins, “when its young cry to God,” that is, when its preachers pray, “wandering because they have no food,” that is, burning with desire as they seek to receive all peoples into the bosom of the Church?

Or thus: “Who prepares its food for the raven?” that is, who grants understanding of the divine Word to any learned preacher who is black as a raven in his own estimation—that is, humble—“when its young,” that is, his disciples, “cry to God, wandering because they have no food of their own,” that is, ranging about because they need the nourishment of teaching suited to them? For the raven allows its young to suffer hunger before they grow black through feathers, until its own likeness is visible in them through the blackness of their plumage. So too a teacher does not bestow upon disciples born to him in faith the nourishment of lofty doctrine before he knows that they have mourned their former sins; for perhaps they do not yet know how to consider their own weakness and therefore do not display, against the glory of this world, the blackness of humility. “Who, then,” he says, “prepares food for the raven when its young cry out?”—unless it is I. For when the aforesaid discernment is cautiously preserved by preachers, a more abundant supply of preaching is divinely given to them.

CHAPTER XXXIX

VERS. 1.—“Do you know,” he says, “the time when the wild goats give birth on the rocks,” that is, at what time preachers, who are called rocks because of the firmness of their faith, ought to be sent to bring forth spiritual children for God? “Or have you observed the hinds in labor?” that is, have you weighed the affections of those same holy Fathers? For example, one of them says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV).

For such fathers possess certain resemblances to wild goats, which give birth on rocks and, if ever they fall from the high summits of cliffs, receive themselves unharmed upon their horns; and also to hinds, which are accustomed to tear apart discovered serpents with their bites and, when they cross rivers, lay their heads upon the backs of those going before them, so that by succeeding one another they do not feel the labor. Thus they too give birth, as it were, on rocks, when in the teaching of the Fathers—who, as has been said, are called rocks because of their firmness—they bring forth souls to conversion. Whatever temporal downfall may come upon them, they are saved by receiving it upon the testaments of Holy Scripture as upon certain horns. They likewise “long, as the hart, for fountains of waters” (Ps. XLI); and while cautiously passing through the fleeting moments of this present life as through rivers, they observe what is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfil [Col. 1166A] the law of Christ” (Gal. VI).

By hinds, however, teachers may be understood; by wild goats, because they are small animals, hearers, who give birth as it were on rocks because they are made fruitful for the performance of holy works through the examples of the Fathers who have gone before. To observe with careful consideration the times—that is, the progress—of these hearers, and also the labors of the teachers as of hinds in labor, belongs to God alone. Hence he adds:

VERS. 2.—“Have you counted the months of their conception?” that is, the length or multiplicity of the anxiety or desire with which holy Fathers are affected concerning the progress of their spiritual children, whom they have as it were conceived and for whose salvation they are anxious. “Have you counted,” I say, “the months of conception, and have you known [Col. 1166B] the time of their birth?”—that is, when they may be able to accomplish what they desire—unless it be I, who also consider in them what follows:

VERS. 3.—“They bend themselves for their offspring,” that is, they descend from that immensity of contemplation which they attain to the weakness of their hearers; for example, as he who says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal” (I Cor. III), and similar words. “They bend themselves,” I say, “and give birth,” that is, in this way they more effectively advance their hearers; “and they send forth cries,” that is, they are tortured by sorrow over little ones in danger. For the hind in labor sends forth a cry when Paul says: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Gal. III), and the rest.

But because those born through the preaching of the Fathers sometimes go before their own teachers into the kingdom, and while the teachers remain in this life are brought to completion through martyrdom, it follows:

VERS. 4.—“Their children are separated.” Immediately expressing this separation, he says: “They go forth to pasture,” that is, to that pasture [of] eternal verdure where nothing will be lacking. “They go forth and do not return to them,” because, having escaped the distresses of the present life, they no longer require to receive from their teachers the preaching of life.

After much has been said, under the figurative bending of the hinds, concerning the virtue of teachers, he proceeds to those who seek the secrets of a withdrawn manner of life.

VERS. 5.—“Who,” he says, “has sent the wild ass free [Col. 1166D] into the wilderness?” that is, who has granted the life of those who live withdrawn from the crowds of people? “Who,” he says, “has sent him free?” That is: who, unless I, has given such grace that, earthly desires being trodden underfoot, the mind, secure, is freed from the appetite for temporal things? “And who has loosed his bonds?” that is, who has broken the restraints of carnal pleasures, so that with an enlarged heart he may run in the narrow course of his purpose?

VERS. 6.—“To whom I have given a home in solitude”—in solitude, I say, not only of the body but also of the heart. For bodily solitude is of no use without solitude of heart. “I have given a home in solitude,” that is, silence in a solitary life; “and his dwelling places in the land of salt,” that is, his manner of life in the kindling of thirst. For saltiness is accustomed to kindle thirst, and holy men in the dwelling places of this life are kindled so that they thirst, and thirst so that they may be satisfied, as it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V).

VERS. 7.—“He despises the multitude of the city,” that is, he avoids the corrupt pursuits of human society. “He does not hear the cry of the taskmaster,” that is, he does not heed the violent temptations of the devil, because he does not consent to them. For this taskmaster’s speech is an evil suggestion, but his cry is violent temptation. The devil is called a taskmaster because once in paradise he supplied the human being with the coin of evil persuasion and daily exacts the guilt of this debt.

This taskmaster may also be understood as the belly, whose words, as though it were crying out, abstinent men despise when they repress the violent [Col. 1167B] desires of life. Although there are many contests of virtues against countless vices, the belly alone is aptly called the taskmaster here because it alone cries out. For one does not rise to the conflict of the spiritual contest unless the appetite of gluttony is first subdued; when it is not restrained, all the virtues are overwhelmed at once through the lust of the flesh. Thus the chief of the horses destroys the walls of Jerusalem (IV Kings XXV): that is, the belly, to which cooks render most careful service, destroys the virtues of the soul when it is not restrained. The speech of this taskmaster is the necessary demand of nature; its cry is the appetite of gluttony exceeding the measure of necessity. Despising this, the wild ass, as has been said:

VERS. 8.—“Surveys the mountains of his pasture” [Col. 1167C], that is, he sets in order in his heart the ascents of virtues through lofty contemplation of eternal refreshment (Ps. LXXXIII), by which he strives to take his place among the higher powers of angels. “And he seeks out every green thing,” that is, he desires eternal goods which are not withered by any temporality.

All these things said about the wild ass may also be understood otherwise. To show through whom the aforesaid virtue of preaching is given, a recollection of the Lord’s Incarnation is at once appended: “Who has sent the wild ass free into the wilderness?” Nor is it unfitting that the Lord should be figured by this animal, since he also says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI), and through the prophet, according to the Septuagint translators, it is said: “The beetle cried out from the wood.” “Who,” therefore, he says, “has sent the wild ass free?”—unless it be I; that is, who has sent Christ like an animal of the field, destined to benefit the Gentile world once uncultivated, “free,” I say, “into the wilderness,” that is, free from every sin and therefore free among the dead (Ps. LXXXVII), into the Gentile world that was once deserted? “And who has loosed his bonds?” that is, who transformed the weaknesses of his Passion into the glory of the Resurrection, raising him up when the pains of hell had been loosed (Acts II)?

“To whom I have given a home in solitude,” he says: namely, human hearts in the Gentile world to possess. For the Gentile world was a wilderness in which there was no patriarch, no prophet, no one using reason to understand God. “A home in solitude,” I say, [Col. 1168A] “and his dwelling places,” that is, the various Churches which in this life are pitched temporarily like tents, “in the land of salt,” that is, in that same Gentile world, which, producing no verdure of good understanding, had a perverse taste.

“He despises the multitude of the city,” that is, he disdains to imitate the life of those to whom he came, namely the Jews: when they wished to make him king, he fled (John VI); and when they sought to kill him, he came willingly to the cross (John XVIII). And because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II), “he does not hear,” he says, “the cry of the taskmaster,” that is, he despises the snares of the ancient enemy. As said above, he is rightly called a taskmaster because, by persuading, he inflicted guilt, and by raging, exacts punishment. His speech is crafty persuasion before a person’s death; his cry is violent plunder after death. He does not hear this cry of the taskmaster—that is, he does not fear it—when he says: “For the prince of this world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

Indeed, according to the prophet, he overcame this taskmaster’s sceptre, as in the day of Midian (Isa. IX): that is, by delivering the Gentile world, he destroyed the devil’s kingdom, as was prefigured in the likeness of the day of Midian, when Gideon fought with three hundred men against Midian by a new kind of warfare. Holding trumpets in their right hands and burning lamps within jars in their left, they broke the jars amid the sound of the trumpets; the enemies, terrified by the flash of the lamps, were put to flight (Judg. VII).

Thus at his coming our Redeemer, signified [Col. 1168C] by Gideon—whose name means “encircling the womb”—also entered the Virgin’s womb by wondrous power. The Redeemer, I say, with three hundred men, that is, with all worshippers of the Trinity, gave them trumpets, that is, the terrifying words of heavenly teaching, and lamps within jars, that is, the bright gifts of the Holy Spirit within fragile bodies. Thus they bore the trumpets of the word in their right hands and the jars in their left—that is, they held the words of God in greater care and their own bodies as less precious. With such men he invaded the kingdom of this taskmaster; when battle was joined, the trumpets sounded—that is, the sound of preaching went forth—and, when the jars of bodies were broken through many kinds of sufferings, the brightness of miracles shone like light. This taskmaster, the devil, fled [Col. 1168D]. Midian also designates him by its very name, for it means “declining judgment.” He fled, I say, from human hearts, defeated in judgment and unable to resist Christ the victor.

Therefore he does not hear the cry of this taskmaster; rather, conquering and casting him out, he “surveys the mountains of his pasture,” that is, he raises up high and exalted persons, from whose conversion and humility he is fed. Hence it is written: “He beholds the heights of the mountains” (Ps. XXXIV), that is, he converts the pride of the proud from wickedness to better things. “And he seeks out every green thing,” that is, he loves those whose flesh, through his preaching, blossoms anew in virtues. They are truly green in proportion as they fix the root of their thought in the lot of an unfading inheritance.

[Col. 1169A] Having overcome the taskmaster, as has been said, because gradually the strong things were confounded by the weak things of the world (I Cor. I), and because, as the life of the humble rose in honor, the pride of the proud fell, he next speaks of these same proud persons, or powerful people of the age, at last taking upon themselves the light yoke of Christ:

VERS. 9.—“Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?”—as it serves me, to whom the powerful people of the world, once trusting in their pride, are at last made subject. The rhinoceros is wholly of untamed nature; if captured, it dies from impatience. It has only one horn on its nose, whence it is called *rhinoceros*: for *rhinoceros* in Latin means “horn in the nose.” The rhinoceros, I say, through its ferocity and horned nose, signifies the pride or exalted folly of the powerful. Since it can be tamed or subjected not by human strength but by divine miracles, he says: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?”—as it serves me through those whom I send. “Or will it remain at your manger?” that is, will it seek or await from you the food of the Scriptures? For this rhinoceros remains, as it were, at the Lord’s manger when it patiently endures to stand confined at the food of the Word, in order that by feeding and remaining it may grow fat. And because, thus fed, it subsequently works also by preaching:

VERS. 10.—“Will you,” he says, “bind the rhinoceros with your strap for plowing?” that is, will you make it preach at your command? For the straps of the Church are the precepts of discipline [Col. 1169C], by which this rhinoceros is not merely bound, but also yoked for plowing—that is, for breaking up with the plowshare of the tongue the soil of the human breast. “Or will it,” he says, “break the clods of the valleys after you?” that is, those who through their hardness neither receive the seeds of the Word themselves nor permit others to bear fruit from seed received, just as clods lying upon cultivated soil press down the sown seeds and choke what is springing up. It will break such “clods of the valleys,” that is, oppressors of the humble, “after you”—as after me, who, after entering the mind of any exalted power, also train it to crush the enemies of faith.

VERS. 11.—“Will you place confidence in its great strength?”—as I do, who bend to the worship of my veneration the powers which I temporarily bestow upon an earthly ruler. “And will you leave your labors to it?” This I do when, after an earthly ruler has been converted, I entrust to him the Church which I purchased with my blood.

VERS. 12.—“Will you trust it,” that is, will you be certain of the secrets of its heart, “that it will return your seed,” that is, faithfully preserve it uncorrupted, “and gather it to your threshing floor?”—as I trust and know that it will govern my Church rightly, though formerly it scattered and winnowed it with a proud horn.

Blessed Job hears what the rulers of the Gentile world do, so that he may not in himself be lifted up over the glory of so great a virtue. But even when Holy Church has no open enemies outside, she endures false brothers within. Therefore, after the Lord said that this rhinoceros was bound with straps, he immediately added the hypocrisy of the wicked.

VERS. 13.—“The feather,” he says, “of the ostrich,” that is, the outward appearance of the hypocrite, “is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk,” that is, the true religion of spiritual persons. The hypocrite, who imitates the life of the good but does not possess the reality of holiness, is signified by the ostrich, which has feathers like those of the heron or hawk but does not possess the swiftness of their flight. Just as hawks and herons have small bodies supported by denser feathers, and therefore fly swiftly across, while the ostrich is clothed in sparse feathers and weighed down by its enormous body, so the elect have little in them which weighs them down and much which raises them to heaven; but the hypocrite, even if he does a few things which raise him, commits many which weigh him down. Therefore, he says: “The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk.”

VERS. 14.—“When it leaves its eggs upon the earth,” that is, because the hypocrite neglects to nourish his hearers through good examples. For when the hypocrite speaks rightly to his hearers, the ostrich as it were lays eggs; but when he does not lift them from earthly actions through good examples, the ostrich as it were leaves those eggs upon the earth. “Will you perhaps warm them in the dust?” he says. It is as if he said: as I do, who warm the ostrich’s eggs when I kindle with the fire of my love the souls of little ones even in the midst of sinners, who are rightly called dust [Col. 1170C].

VERS. 15.—“It forgets,” he says, “that a foot may trample them,” that is, it does not care if the course of evil action perverts the souls of its hearers, “or that a beast of the field may crush them,” that is, that the devil, the plunderer of the world, may seize or corrupt them. It forgets, I say, and, living without compassion:

VERS. 16.—“It is hardened toward its young as though they were not its own,” that is, it regards its neighbor as a stranger even if it itself has begotten that neighbor for God—very unlike him who, bearing tender affections toward his children, says: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (I Thess. III). Thus the negligent hypocrite is sluggish toward heavenly things but burns anxiously for earthly matters: “In vain,” he says, “it labored, with no fear compelling it” [Col. 1170D]; that is, in foolish labor, while caring for earthly things, “there it trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII).

It must be known, however, that some people retain the habit of holiness and yet cannot carry out the merit of perfection. Such persons should by no means be thought to run among the number of hypocrites, because it is one thing to sin through weakness and another through malice. But why the hypocrite, abandoning heavenly things, applies himself to earthly ones, is next explained under the name of the ostrich:

VERS. 17.—“For God,” he says, “has deprived her of wisdom,” that is, he has not given her wisdom. For it follows: “Nor has he given her understanding.” Although to deprive and not to give are different things, here what he said, “has deprived,” he repeats by adding, “has not given.” “Has deprived,” I say, means “has not given,” just as God is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exod. XX), because, as Pharaoh’s merits demanded, he did not soften it [Col. 1171A].

VERS. 18.—“When the time comes,” that is, if some temptation against faith breaks out, “it raises its wings on high,” that is, at that time it reveals in pride its thoughts, formerly pressed down and as it were folded. “It derides the horseman,” that is, it despises the holy soul which rightly governs its body and presides over it as over a bridled horse. “It derides,” I say, “the horseman and his rider,” that is, it proceeds even to insult the Creator, who, when he possesses the soul of any elect person rightly governing its body, as has been said, certainly mounts the horse. Thus, as its defects increase, the hypocrite arrives at graver evils: first it presents itself as good when it is not; afterward it openly despises the good; finally, leaping even to insult of the Creator, it advances into worse things.

Again, in another sense, with mortality set aside, the fierce and proud power of this rhinoceros and the hard, forgetful folly of this ostrich are explained. This rhinoceros, which in Greek copies is also called *monoceros* (“one-horned”), is said to possess such great and untamed strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. But a virgin girl is set before it; when she opens her bosom, it wonderfully lays aside all ferocity, rests its head upon her, and thus the deceived beast is suddenly found as though unarmed and is captured. It is also described as boxwood-colored. When it engages in combat with elephants, it wounds the bellies of its opponents by striking them with the single horn which it bears on its nose, so that it easily brings down an assailant [Col. 1171C].

Therefore, by this rhinoceros may be understood that people of singular pride concerning whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Deliver me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. XXI). Accordingly Blessed Job, who bears the type of Holy Church, is told: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?”—as it serves me, who see it lifting itself in a single horn even against me and yet subject it to myself when I will.

But for this to become clearer, let Paul, from this people, be brought forward: first in pride, afterward preeminent in humility. He bore a horn on his nose when he trusted that he pleased God by his cruelty. Every hunter feared this rhinoceros, because every preacher was afraid of his savagery [Col. 1171D]. But, in order to capture him, the Virgin opened her bosom: that is, when he was going to Damascus, the incarnate Wisdom of God manifested herself to him (Acts IX).

“Will the rhinoceros, then, be willing to serve you?”—as it serves me. “Or will it remain at your manger?”—as this man, through Ananias, was bound by me to the sacrament of baptism. “Will you bind him to plow with your strap?” that is, will you constrain him by your command to preach, so that he may say: “Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel” (I Cor. IX). “Or will he break the clods of the valleys,” that is, the impediments of the humble, “after you”—as after me; for example, when he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V). For when, by rebuking the hardness of the Law in the humble mind of believers, he crushed it, what else did he do but break clods in the valley after me?

“Will you place confidence in his great strength?”—as I do, who send him far away to the Gentiles “to bear my name before kings and Gentiles” (Acts IX). “And will you leave your labors to him?”—as I do, who do this so that he may say: “I fill up in my flesh those things which are lacking of the sufferings of Christ” (Col. I). “Will you trust him that he will return seed,” that is, fruitful preaching, “to you, and gather your threshing floor,” that is, enlarge the breadth of the Church into one faith? You will not trust him. For Ananias also said: “Lord, I have heard from many concerning this man how much evil he has done to your saints,” and so forth (Acts IX). He did not believe that the man who had hitherto winnowed the Lord’s threshing floor with the horn of pride would gather it.

What was done in Paul ought also to be believed to have occurred in others. For many from the pride of that people were converted to the grace of humility. Yet for the most part the Synagogue remained in unbelief, and of it he next says: “The feather of the ostrich,” that is, the voice of the Synagogue, which creeps among low things and never raises itself from the earth, “is like the feathers of the heron and hawk,” that is, like the ancient fathers, who were able not only to look forward in understanding to the things which they could comprehend but also to fly over them in life. “Like,” I say; for “the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII).

“It leaves its eggs on the earth,” that is, it drives away to the Gentiles the apostles born from its own flesh. “Will you perhaps warm them in the dust?” that is, will you raise up their offspring among the despised Gentiles, so that the hope that could exist in them as in an egg may advance to the life of many? “It forgets,” that is, it does not care, “that a foot may trample them or a beast of the field crush them,” that is, it not only did not give life to its children but afterward also envied those whom a foot tramples and a beast of the field crushes when, through decrees of persecution, the bestial cruelty of any tyrant rises against them. Indeed it itself tramples and crushes them: “It is hardened toward its children as though they were not its own,” namely, because it finds them living otherwise than itself.

And in doing this it labored in vain, because, in persecuting them, it did not render service to God as it supposed (John XVI). It labored, I say, “with no fear compelling it,” but through cruelty alone. For it did not persecute them, as it pretended, because it feared that divine religion would perish, but because the jealousy of envy tortured it. “For God,” he says, “has deprived her of wisdom,” that is, by a just judgment he placed a veil upon her heart. This is what follows: “Nor has he given her understanding,” namely, by which she might understand the letter of the Law spiritually.

VERS. 18.—“When the time comes,” that is, when Antichrist comes, “it raises its wings on high,” that is, it openly carries out persecution with pride. “It derides the horseman and his rider,” that is, it blasphemes not only the Lord’s humanity, which is assuredly the horse of divinity, but divinity itself, which then mounted the horse when it united to itself the animate flesh which it formed from the Virgin’s womb [Col. 1173A].

Certainly, by the name “horse” the slippery life of the wicked is sometimes signified, as it is written: “Do not become like horse and mule” (Ps. XXXI); sometimes temporal dignity, as Solomon says: “I saw servants upon horses” (Eccles. X); sometimes this present age itself, as Jacob says concerning Dan the serpent, that is, concerning Antichrist: “Biting the horse’s hoofs,” that is, narrowing the end of the age, “so that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. XLIX), that is, so that whoever has been exalted in this age may fall into eternal torments which he does not know. Sometimes every holy preacher is understood by the name “horse,” according to the words: “You sent your horses into the sea, troubling many waters”: that is, you sent your preachers into this world to stir up many peoples wickedly asleep beneath the tempest of vices. In this sense it is now said:

VERS. 19.—“Will you give strength to the horse?” that is, will you give the holy preacher constancy to endure adversities? “Or will you surround his neck with neighing?” that is, with the enticement of preaching by which he calls people to heavenly things? “Will you surround his neck,” I say, so that action may not exceed speech, and life may not contradict voice?

VERS. 20.—“Will you rouse him like locusts?” that is, will you make this holy preacher soar to heavenly things in the heat of persecution, as locusts scarcely raise themselves from the ground in the morning hours—that is, in a time of mildness—but, once the heat has flared up, fly all the higher as they fly more eagerly? For then, roused by the sun’s heat, locusts plant their legs firmly and spread their wings. So the saints establish themselves by right action in persecution and leap up to behold lofty things. Thus, when I have roused the horse, “the glory,” he says, “of his nostrils is terror,” that is, by glorious hope he awaits, as though scenting from afar, the vision of the strict Judge; and whereas the wicked fear his coming, the righteous vehemently desire it. And while he glories in his nostrils—that is, in his hope—this expectation is nevertheless terror to sinners:

VERSE 21.—“He paws the ground with his hoof,” that is, from the hearts of his hearers he drives out earthly thoughts; and he first empties himself of worldly cares, so that he may be an example to them [Col. 1173D], saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. III), and the like. Hence Isaac is rightly described as digging wells among a foreign people; yet the Philistines, lying in wait, fill up those wells (Gen. XXVI). For when unclean spirits observe us diligently digging the heart, they pour into it heaped-up thoughts of temptations, lest we be hidden there from the wrath of God, according to the prophet who says: “Hide in the pit of the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. II); that is, once earthly thoughts have been cast out, rest in humility of mind. “He digs the ground,” I say; and in doing this, “he exults boldly,” that is, he rejoices steadfastly amid adversities, according to that saying: “They went from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” [Col. 1174A] (Acts V).—“He exults,” I say. “For whatever shall happen to the righteous man shall not make him sad” (Prov. XII). Nor does he merely exult: he also “goes forth to meet the armed,” that is, when the perverse break forth and rage against the defense of righteousness, he exposes himself to them. For example, Paul: when at Ephesus the flame of zeal was carrying him toward the rushing crowds in the theater, had not the reins of charity restrained him, while his friends begged him not to enter the theater (Acts XIX).

VERSE 22.—“He despises fear.”—“For who shall separate us from the charity of God?” (Rom. VIII).—“He despises,” I say, “nor yields to the sword,” that is, no kind of death terrifies him from carrying out the command of his rider.

VERSE 23.—“The quiver shall rattle over him,” that is, against him an insidious contrivance of the wicked shall be prepared, as is said through the Prophet: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver” [Col. 1174B] (Ps. X). This quiver rattled over Paul when forty men who had conspired for his death deceitfully sought to have him brought out of prison (Acts XXIII). But because the holy preacher is in no way terrified by such things, “the spear and shield shall be brandished,” that is, the cruelty of persecutors is openly displayed for tortures. The spear is brandished so that the holy man may be struck; but the shield is put before him so that he may not be heard—that is, while his body is tortured, the mouth of the speaker is silenced by hostile replies. For those who rage in persecution grieve not so much because they do not soften the preacher’s heart, as because through his words they lose others also. But is the holy preacher—for example, the frequently mentioned Paul—restrained from his fervor by these things? [Col. 1174C]

VERSE 24.—“Boiling and raging,” he says, that is, inflamed and eloquent through the Holy Spirit, “he swallows the ground,” that is, even amid his punishments he draws the sinner to himself. “Nor does he regard the trumpet’s blast as sounding,” that is, he neither hears nor cares for the voice of worldly authorities: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). He may be cast down; he cannot be overcome. Indeed, he exults still more in adversities. Hence it follows:
