VERSE 25.—“When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Aha!’” That is, when he perceives that suffering is certainly drawing near to him, he exults in the exercise of virtue. For he has “a desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Col. 1174D] (Phil. I). And although as a man he trembles somewhat through weakness, nevertheless, through the certainty of hope, he hastens joyfully toward the reward of recompense. “He says,” I say, “‘Aha!’”—which a brute animal certainly cannot say. Therefore the discourse concerns a rational horse. And for this reason this horse overcomes every conflict: for “he scents battle from afar,” that is, before the contest he prepares his mind for the contest. Paul admonished his disciples of this when he said: “Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves” (II Cor. XIII).—“He scents battle,” I say, “the exhortation of commanders and the howling of the army”—understand, “from afar he scents” them—that is, long beforehand he considers what the authors of errors may be able to command against the elect, [Col. 1175A] and how unanimously the multitude subject to them may rage. He says that the commanders exhort, but that the army howls, because those who preside over unbelievers almost rationally persuade the evil things they command, whereas the multitude subject to them follows their voices with a bestial, clamorous madness. Scenting this howling, Paul says: “After my departure grievous wolves shall enter among you” (Acts XX). And concerning the exhortation of the commanders: “In covetousness,” he says, “they shall make merchandise of you with feigned words” (II Pet. II).

“Will you give the horse strength?” Understand: as I do, who before all things give to every soul over which I preside the strength of faith. “Or will you clothe his neck with neighing?” That is, with the confession of that same faith: namely, that what he believes unto righteousness he may confess with his mouth unto salvation [Col. 1175B] (Rom. X). “Will you rouse him like locusts?” Namely, so that, although he still retains the old life by habit, he may nevertheless perform new things by intention, after the manner of a locust which clings to the ground indeed with bent knees, yet suspends itself from the ground with wings spread out in some measure. But when he has thus begun to live well: “The glory of his nostrils,” he says, “is terror”; that is, he indeed glories in hope—for hope is expressed by the nostrils—but when he beholds in his mind the future judgment, he fears the very thing in which he glories. What then does he do? “He paws the ground with his hoof,” that is, by strict abstinence he subdues the vices of the flesh. When this is done, “he exults boldly,” that is, he who previously feared now, with his vices subdued, awaits the coming of the Judge [Col. 1175C]. And thus exulting, “he goes forth,” he says, “to meet the armed,” that is, he foresees from afar the snares which malignant spirits lay; and he “goes forth to meet” them when he wonderfully discovers their deceits. “He despises fear,” having no dread of any temptation, “nor yields to the sword,” that is, he is not so terrified as to be silent or to abandon the care of his neighbors, whom he restrains from that same sword—that is, from sin—by saying: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI), and the like.

But the ancient enemy seeks sharper darts of temptations against so hardy a soldier in proportion as he sees himself more vigorously despised. This is what follows: “The quiver shall rattle over him,” that is, a hidden temptation shall be prepared against him. “The spear [Col. 1175D] and shield shall be brandished,” that is, a manifest temptation too is set before one who knows it. For the arrow attacks God’s horse by ambush when the crafty enemy conceals vice under virtue—for example, when he suggests self-exaltation because chastity has been preserved. The spear wounds him at close quarters when he tempts even one who knows it with manifest wickedness, for example lust or anger. But what does God’s horse do against these things? “Boiling,” he says, “and raging,” that is, examining himself with excessive ardor, “he swallows the ground,” that is, by making progress in heavenly things he consumes his earthliness. “And he does not regard the blast of the trumpet as sounding,” that is, he refuses, as it were, to see his virtues, concerning which empty glory is suggested. “When he hears the sound of the trumpet,” that is, when temptation has begun to strike him, “he says, ‘Aha!’”—that is, he rejoices and exults, because, considering the usefulness of the heavenly dispensation, he gains greater confidence from the very severity of temptation [Col. 1176A]. For a worse security has overthrown many.

And because the tempter sometimes attempts to be present unexpectedly, “he scents battle from afar,” that is, from every matter he perceives long beforehand what conflict of vice is growing. “The exhortations of the commanders”—understand, he perceives them beforehand—that is, the pretenses of the principal vices; “and the howling of the army,” that is, the irrational multitude of the vices which are born from them. For example, pride is the first commander of vices; for pride is the root of all wickedness. It usually exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “You ought to seek greater things, so that, in proportion as you are able to surpass others in power, you may also be able to benefit them.” But God’s horse, with his nose—that is, with the virtue of discernment—“scents,” that is, judges, that if this exhortation of the commander is admitted, a howling army immediately follows: namely the other vices born from pride—vain glory, envy, anger, sorrow, avarice, gluttony, and lust [Col. 1176B]. These are the seven principal vices, against which our Redeemer came filled with the sevenfold Spirit. Each has against us its own army, that is, a multitude of vices. When God’s horse discovers their howling—that is, their confusion—by the virtue of discernment, as has been said, he is rightly said to scent battle from afar.

Now that through the horse we have learned the strength of the holy preacher, let us also learn through the bird his contemplation.

VERSE 26.—“Will the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, and spread its wings toward the south wind?” That is, have you bestowed understanding upon anyone so that, while the Holy Spirit blows, he may spread the wings of his thoughts, cast off the weights of his old manner of life, and assume the feathers of virtues for the use of a new flight? For wild hawks are accustomed, when the south wind blows—or, if there is no wind, against the ray of the sun—to spread their wings; and so, when their pores are opened, either old feathers fall out or new ones grow [Col. 1176C]. Thus, each year the hawk casts off its old feather when a new one grows. Domestic hawks, however, require protected and warm places if they are to grow feathers better.

Yet by this hawk the renewed Gentile world may be signified. He says therefore: “Will the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom?” It is as though blessed Job were plainly told: Look upon the future feathers of virtues among the Gentiles, and cast off the old feathers of pride. It follows:

VERSE 27.—“Will the eagle be lifted up at your command?” That is, will the life of believers, obedient to your commands as to mine, be suspended in heavenly things? “And will it place its nest in high places?” That is, will it set the dwelling of its mind there and say: “But our conversation is in heaven” (Phil. III)? This it does at my command alone.

VERSE 28.—“It dwells on rocks,” that is, it establishes the station of its mind in the sayings of the ancient and mighty Fathers, who are called living stones (I Pet. II); or in contemplation of the heavenly powers, which already are fixed in secure solidity through the strength of their eternity [Col. 1177A]. “It dwells on rocks,” I say, “and makes its abode on steep flints,” that is, it contemplates those same most mighty choirs of angels. They are steep because one part of them fell and one part remained. The intact ones indeed stand in respect of the quality of their merit, but are precipitous in respect of their numerical quantity. “On steep,” I say, “flints and inaccessible rocks.” Surely the steep flints themselves are the inaccessible rocks. For the brightness of angels is exceedingly inaccessible to the heart of sinful human beings.

VERSE 29.—“From there,” he says, “it beholds its food,” that is, from those angelic choirs it directs the eye of the mind toward contemplating the glory of the heavenly majesty; and, since it has not yet seen that glory, it still hungers. And because, weighed down by the interposition of corruptible flesh, it cannot see God as he is: “Its eyes,” he says, “look afar off,” that is, it does not yet see God face to face, but through an enigma and a mirror [Col. 1177B] (I Cor. XIII). These words and those of Isaiah are wonderfully proved to be of one spirit: “This man shall dwell in the heights; the strongholds of rocks shall be his high place; bread is given to him, his waters are sure. His eyes shall see the King in his beauty; they shall behold the land afar off” (Isa. XXXIII). For what Isaiah says, “he shall dwell in the heights; the strongholds of rocks shall be his high place,” is said here: “it dwells on rocks, and makes its abode on steep flints and inaccessible rocks.” What is said there, “bread is given to him, his waters are sure; his eyes shall see the King in his beauty,” is said here: “from there it beholds its food.” And what is said there, “they shall behold the land afar off,” is said here: “its eyes look afar off.”

But the holy preacher, contemplating heavenly things as has been said, when he sees that his hearers cannot grasp them, descends to the words concerning the Lord’s Incarnation alone. Hence it is immediately added:

VERSE 30.—“Its young lick blood.” It is as though he plainly said: He himself is fed by contemplation of the Divinity; but because his hearers cannot apprehend the secrets of the Godhead, they are satisfied by the blood of the crucified Lord. To them he also says: “For I judged not myself to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” [Col. 1177C] (I Cor. II). And “wherever the corpse shall be,” he says, “there it is immediately present”; namely, as is said elsewhere: “Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Matt. XXIV; Luke XVII). That is, where Christ sits, who suffered and died, there it dwells with mind suspended in contemplation.

Or thus: “Wherever the corpse shall be,” that is, wherever it discovers a sinner, “there it is immediately present”—namely, so that, being now spiritually alive, it may benefit others lying in the death of sin. Such was the frequently mentioned Paul, who was now making for Judaea, now Corinth, now Rome, now Ephesus, now Spain, in order to announce the grace of eternal life to those lying in the death of sin. Having heard of so many virtues of the saints, blessed Job is understood to have been astonished and, under the dread of amazement, to have fallen silent. For it follows:

[Col. 1178A] VERSES 31–32.—“And the Lord added and spoke to Job: Shall he who contends with God so easily be silent? Surely he who rebukes God ought to answer him.” Here one must understand: But you have easily fallen silent and do not answer me. And it must immediately be inferred: Therefore you did not dispute contentiously with God, as your friends accused you of doing, nor did you run against me with neck uplifted; for whatever you uttered as though reproving God you derived not from the swelling of pride but from the quality of your life, knowing that there was no vice in you which ought to be cut away by so great a scourge. For one who is contentious does not yield to one wiser than himself.

VERSE 33.—Blessed Job, surpassing the human race in virtues, overcame his friends in speaking; but, more sublimely instructed by God speaking, he was silent in coming to know himself. For at the words of the inward speech he rightly recognized himself as guilty. Thus he says:

VERSE 34.—“I who have spoken lightly, what can I answer?” It is as though he said: My disputing inquiry why you have surrounded me with your scourges, though I have lived rightly, is as frivolous as if a thing fashioned should say to its maker: “You have now formed me sufficiently; why do you still press such harsh fingers upon me?” Or as if a seal should say to its engraver: “I now please those who see me and am praised by all; why do you still attack me with your graving-tool?” Therefore, “I who have spoken so lightly”—and have recognized this lightness of mine from your words, namely, from your showing by many comparisons that it belongs to you, not to me, to perfect the saints or to see what is lacking in each—“what can I answer?” Understand: nothing [Col. 1178C]. Therefore “I will put my hand upon my mouth,” that is, I will be silent, and, confessing that I have been defeated in the case, I will restrain my mouth. “I will put my hand upon my mouth,” I say: that is, with the power of good work, signified customarily by the hand, I shall wipe away the faults of careless speech. This is what follows:

VERSE 35.—“I have spoken one thing which I wish I had not said, and another,” that is: before the scourges I believed myself righteous among men—this is the one thing; after the scourges I found myself hard—this is the other. “To which,” he says, “I shall add no more,” because now, the more subtly I understand you speaking, the more humbly I examine myself. Yet universally, by “one” and “another” he plainly shows that every sinner in repentance ought to have a twofold groaning: namely, because he did not do the good he ought to have done, and did the evil he ought not to have done [Col. 1178D].

CHAPTER XL

VERSES 1–2.—“But the Lord, answering Job out of the whirlwind, said: Gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and declare to me.” It has already been discussed at length in the first discourse why the Lord now repeats this: namely, to renew the hearer’s attention. For he who in the preceding discourse set forth much concerning the works of his mercy or grace is, in this other discourse, about to speak great and wonderful things concerning his terrible judgment, so that to a worthy and proved man he may reveal all his ways, which are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV) [Col. 1179A].

VERSE 3.—“Will you make my judgment void, and condemn me, that you may be justified?” It is as though he plainly said: While you consider your good deeds but do not know my hidden judgments, in disputing from your merits against my scourges, what are you doing but hastening to condemn me in order to justify yourself?

VERSE 4.—“And if you have an arm,” that is, if you beget the Son who works all things, “like God; and if you thunder with a voice like his?” Understand: like my voice, by which I terribly manifest to the whole world my Son, consubstantial with me.

VERSE 5.—“Clothe yourself with splendor”—understand, as I do, of whom alone it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendor” [Col. 1179B] (Ps. XCII).—“And raise yourself on high”—understand, as I do, who show myself in my own nature to be impenetrable to human minds. “And be glorious”—understand, as I am, who, enjoying myself, have no need of praise added from without. “And clothe yourself in beautiful garments”—understand, as I do, who have taken the choirs of holy angels into the service of my splendor, and present to myself the Church as a kind of glorious garment, having neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. V). In saying these things to blessed Job, the Lord by a wonderful dispensation of mercy exalts him while reproving him; for in surpassing him by comparison with himself, he shows him superior to all others.

VERSE 6.—“Scatter,” he says, “the proud in your wrath”—understand, as I do, who endure them when, even in a time of tranquility, they are united against me, but when I come in judgment scatter them in my wrath. “In wrath,” I say, not because any inequality of anger arises in me, but because, remaining unchangeable in myself, I shall appear tranquil to the righteous and angry to the unrighteous [Col. 1179C]. “Scatter,” I say, “the proud. And, looking upon every arrogant person, humble him”—understand, as I do; for the arrogant whom I now rightly regard so that they may be converted, I shall one day regard so that they may be punished.

VERSE 7.—“Look upon all the proud and confound them”—understand, as I do—“and crush the ungodly in their place,” that is, in their sin. For the place of the ungodly is pride itself, which is the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. X).

[Col. 1179D] VERSE 8.—“Hide them together in the dust,” that is, permit them to be blinded by a just judgment, so that they may be oppressed by earthly affairs and may be, according to the prophet, “a cake baked under ashes which has not been turned” (Hos. VII). That is, let them conceal beneath lower cares the intention by which they ought to seek God, just as the ash-baked cake presses its cleaner part underneath. They would also be turned if they drove away the ashes of carnal desires. “Hide them in the dust,” I say. “And plunge their faces into the pit,” namely, so that they may fall into the depths while by pride they seek a higher place. Do these things—these things which I have said:

VERSE 9.—“And I too will confess that your right hand can save you.” It is as though he plainly said: If you can do these terrible things which I myself have set forth, I shall ascribe to you, and not to myself, all the good things you have done.

At last the Lord shows his good servant the wickedness of the ancient enemy, so that, knowing his cunning, he may learn how much he ought to fear him, according to the prophet who says: “The lion shall roar: who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?” (Amos III). For he reveals all that enemy’s machinations: all that he seizes by oppression, all that he surrounds by ambush, all that he terrifies by threats, all that he flatters by persuasion, all that he breaks by despair. Therefore he begins all the contests of his evasiveness by saying:

VERSE 10.—“Behold Behemoth,” which means “animal,” namely the devil, “whom I made with you,” that is, rational as you are. For no animal in the whole creation of things is rational except angel and human being. “Whom,” I say, “I made with you”: for whatever cannot use reason was not made with man. “He shall eat hay like an ox,” that is, as an ox feeds only upon hay, so he will count it great prey only to seize those who seem to lead a clean—that is, spiritual—life. As the prophet says: “His food is choice” [Col. 1180B] (Hab. I): that is, those who seem chosen in human judgments but, before God’s subtle examination, are hay, become incorporated into him. To any such person it is also said through a certain wise man: “Pass on, guest, and adorn the table” (Ecclus. XXIX), that is, spread abroad the praise of God’s altar so that your reputation may profit others, while you yourself pass on as a guest; for you do not wish to remain in the degree of holiness and at sacred things. “He shall eat hay,” I say. And how or whence shall he prevail?

VERSE 11.—“His strength,” he says, “is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly,” that is, both sexes—male and female alike—are laid beneath him through the weakness of lust. For lust is in the loins in men, but in the navel of the belly in women. And those properly become his body who, deceived by the blandishments of shameful suggestions, yield to him in the flux of lust. “His strength therefore,” he says, “is in his loins,” that is, in the men adhering to him; “and his power is in the navel of his belly,” that is, in the women who are joined to his body through their softness, like his navel. Thus, acting powerfully throughout the whole time of this declining age, he will grow stronger especially at the end of the world [Col. 1180D]. This is what follows:

VERSE 12.—“He tightens his tail like a cedar,” that is, his end, when he enters into his own vessel—namely, that lost man who is especially called Antichrist. By turns raised up through worldly honors, through signs and wonders of counterfeit holiness, and through the swelling of power, he will rightly be compared with a cedar. For as the cedar, by growing upward, leaves the other shrubs beneath it, so Antichrist will then possess the glory of the world temporally beyond the measure of human beings. These things have been said of the head of the wicked. What follows concerns his members. “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined,” that is, the assertions of the preachers of his wickedness corrupt innocent souls while hiding beneath twofold arguments, of words and of deeds. For this Behemoth has as many witnesses as he possesses preachers of his wickedness. If anyone refutes them, they immediately hide themselves under a kind of covering of defense; for “the sinews are intertwined,” and, badly entangled, cannot be loosened by correction [Col. 1181A].

VERSE 13.—“His bones,” he says—that is, those stronger persons in his body, by whose hardness the multitudes adhering to the devil are supported as flesh is supported by bones—“his bones are like pipes of bronze,” that is, they are effective in pernicious persuasions, since, like senseless metal, they possess the sound of good speech but not the understanding of good life. Yet they possess the authority of speech because, supported by possessions and wealth, they are made firm, as it were, with brazen strength. “His cartilage,” that is, those who are not so strong but through ambition strive to seem what they are not, like cartilage which has the appearance of bone but not bone’s hardness—“his cartilage,” I say, that is, those weaker in him, is “like plates of iron,” that is, as iron is harder than other metals, so they are more wicked in the commission of evils.

But now, according to these words of the Creator, let us examine what the ancient enemy does in human beings even now, before he assumes that condemned man. “He tightens his tail like a cedar,” that is, he strengthens the end or completion of vice so that sin can scarcely be overcome by the captive human being [Col. 1181C]. For the head of this Behemoth—that is, the first suggestion—is, as it were, soft and tender and easily crushed; but the tail, that is, wickedness completed or made habitual in a person, is like a cedar, because evil habit is bound almost inextricably. He also tightens his tail when he generally inflicts more grievous sins upon those whom he has captured at the time when he knows they are approaching the end of their present life.

His subtler arguments are disclosed when it is added: “The sinews of his testicles,” that is, the destructive arguments of his machinations, “are intertwined.” For his witnesses are his evil suggestions, by which he grows ardent in the corruption of the mind and begets the offspring of a wicked deed in the violated soul. Such witnesses are “intertwined,” I say, because they make many sin in such a way that, if perhaps they desire to flee the sin, they cannot escape it without another snare of sin [Col. 1181D]. Yet the entanglement of these sinews is loosened when one passes through lesser offenses to the greatest virtues.

“His bones are like pipes of bronze,” that is, while his counsels sound sweetly like pipes, they incline the mind toward harmful things. For this is the difference between suggestions and counsels: by suggestions he openly introduces harmful things; but by counsels, strengthened by the subtlety of his natural intelligence, he draws a person to guilt while seeming to advise for good. For example, he says to the avaricious person: “What you have at present is indeed sufficient; but what will you do when it fails? What exists may fail sooner if you do not prudently prepare what is lacking” [Col. 1182A]. Likewise, when he fits his own counsel to every vice, “his bones are like pipes of bronze,” because his destructive counsels flatter their hearer with the sweetness of an advising voice.

But this Behemoth also then arouses harder temptations when he conceals snares of wickedness before the eyes of the tempted under the appearance of virtue. Hence it is added: “His cartilage,” that is, vices which put forth the appearance of uprightness but do not possess uprightness itself, just as cartilage displays the appearance of bone but does not have the firmness of bone. “His cartilage,” I say, that is, the vice believed to be a virtue, is “like plates of iron”: the more deceitfully it displays its cunning under the pretext of good, the more harshly it holds the mind in guilt.

But now we have heard what kind of nature this being has who presents himself in such evasive ambushes in order to deceive. Let us hear what his condition is.

VERSE 14.—“He,” he says, “is the beginning of the ways,” that is, of the works or creatures of God. The beginning, I say, because when God was creating all things, he first created this one and made him more eminent than the other angels. It is as though he plainly said: He is able so powerfully to accomplish so many things because, in creating him in the order of things, the Creator made him first in substance. Hence the prophet says: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his height” [Col. 1182C] (Ezek. XXXI), and so forth. That is, those hosts of heavenly powers, though created in lofty exaltation, were nevertheless neither set above nor made equal to him.

Having heard of so many powers of the ancient enemy and the greatness of his created condition, lest anyone collapse under immeasurable fear or the shock of despair, God revives our weakness by revealing the grace of his dispensation. “He who made him,” he says, “will apply his sword,” that is, will restrain his malice, so that he may not be permitted to strike human minds as much as he desires. For example, how his sword was folded back even in your case is shown by my saying: “Behold, he is in your hand; but preserve his life” (Job II). How much the sword of his malice is folded back is shown in the Gospel, when, unless supreme power had granted permission, he would not have been allowed even to rage among the swine (Mark V).

The more familiarly the proud serve the ancient enemy, the more highly they swell within themselves through the successes of this life. Hence it follows:

VERSE 15.—“The mountains bring him herbs,” that is, the proud offer him their fleeting and slippery pleasures. These pleasures indeed are the herbs of mountains, because they grow from the hearts of the proud; when he finds them, this Behemoth extends the belly of his malice, refreshed. “All beasts,” that is, all unclean spirits—“beasts,” I say, “of the field,” that is, devastators of this age—“play there,” that is, upon those mountains. For unclean spirits play when they subject the human soul to diverse vices, saying with the prophet: “Bow down, that we may pass over” [Col. 1182D] (Isa. LI). And where does he rest through evil desires?

VERSE 16.—“He sleeps under the shadow,” he says, that is, he securely lies down and rests in the torpor of a cold mind, in which charity has grown cold because iniquity abounds (Matt. XXIV). For he is disturbed by no pricks of punishment arising from deeds or thoughts; he is wearied by no heat of heavenly desire. “Under the shadow,” I say, “and in the covert of the reed,” that is, in the hidden and covered thoughts of those people. They have a certain likeness to a reed, because through foolishness they are empty, yet outwardly beautiful in appearance and display. And in a wonderful way he himself sleeps quietly precisely where he does not permit those whom he possesses to rest, like a light wind shaking a reed. “In moist places,” he says, that is, in the minds of earthly people flowing with carnal desire, because they are not dried from the moisture of vices by any strength of discipline [Col. 1183A]. When they are sometimes rebuked by teachers of virtue, they protect one another by opposing the rebukes of the righteous. This is what follows:

VERSE 17.—“Shadows protect his shadow,” that is, the deeds of the most wicked protect those still more wicked by perverse patronage. For when someone more wicked defends one who acts wickedly, he darkens that shadow so that it may not be illumined by the light of truth. “The willows,” he says, “will surround him,” that is, unfruitful people will serve him familiarly. Of their barren life it is said against Babylon: “On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. CXXXVI): that is, because the hearers yield no fruit, our preaching ceases. “The willows,” I say, “of the torrent,” that is, lovers of this passing age, unfruitful toward God as has been said [Col. 1183C].

We have heard what is bestowed upon him by his clients; now let us hear also what he himself does in them.

VERSE 18.—“Behold, he will swallow up the river and not wonder,” he says: that is, from the beginning of the world he draws the human race into the belly of his malice, while scarcely a few elect escape, and does not regard this as anything great. Rather, he counts great what follows: “And he is confident that Jordan may flow into his mouth,” that is, he is confident that he can swallow up even some of those marked with the sacraments of baptism. For by the name Jordan, in which our Lord was baptized, all the baptized are rightly signified. And as often as any Christian falls into wickedness, so often does Jordan flow into his mouth.

The name Jordan, according to its interpretation, bears upon this meaning; for it means “descent.” This Behemoth is confident that he can swallow up that descent when he seeks by ambush to seize those whom he knows cast themselves down from the glory of the present life for love of the heavenly homeland [Col. 1183D]. He accomplishes this also as often as persons of that sort, struck by vain glory, fall more grievously from on high. What then? Will there be no aid of consolation? There certainly will be; for it follows:

VERSE 19.—“He will take him with a hook in his eyes”—understand, he who made him, as was said above. He will take him with a hook. Suddenly the coming of the Lord’s Incarnation is announced. For who does not know that in a hook bait is displayed and the barb concealed? The bait invites in order that the barb may pierce. There, that is, in the Lord’s Incarnation, was humanity, to draw the devourer to itself; there was divinity, to pierce him. Therefore he was captured as by a hook in his eyes, that is, in him whom he saw set before him: while he desired in him the bait of flesh, he was transfixed by the barb of divinity [Col. 1184A].

Our Head did this in himself. It is immediately added what he does through his members. “And with stakes,” he says, “he will pierce his nostrils,” that is, by penetrating his crafty ambushes with the sharp counsels of the saints, he will render them powerless. For by stakes, which are sharpened in order to be fixed, the counsels of the saints are signified; by them they take care not to be circumvented by Satan. But by nostrils, through which things even at a distance are perceived by smelling, his craftinesses are expressed. We pierce those nostrils with stakes when we carefully look around lest he turn what the mind begins well toward an end of wickedness [Col. 1184B]. But if he who is both God and man does not capture him, will he who is merely man capture him? No. Hence it follows:

VERS. 20. — “Can you draw out Leviathan,” that is, the same devil, “with a hook?” *Leviathan* is interpreted as “their addition”—that is, of human beings—by way of mockery; for when he claimed to add divinity to man, he took away immortality. Or it is so called because he daily extends and adds to the fault of transgression which he introduced, by his most evil suggestions [Col. 1184C], even unto death. This Leviathan, I say, who thirsts for the death of all—“can you,” [512] he says, “draw him out with a hook?” That is: as I can, by the aforesaid mystery of the Incarnation? The line of this hook is that lineage of the ancient Fathers recorded in the Gospel: “Abraham begot Isaac” (Matt. 1), and so forth. “Can you draw him out, I say, and bind his tongue with a cord?” That is: as I can? For then I shall bind his tongue with that cord of which it is written, “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4)—that is, with the indissoluble faith of the Trinity—so that, once the truth is known, false teachings may fall silent; for example, the error of the Academics and the superstitions of the astrologers.

[Col. 1184D] VERS. 21. — “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?” That is, will you encircle or encompass his snares with the omnipotence of your power—as I do? For just as snares are denoted by nostrils, so the omnipotence of divine power is denoted by the ring. When, by the assistance of its hidden judgment, Behemoth is restrained from his cunning cruelty, a ring, as it were, is placed in his nostrils. “Or will you pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” That is: as I do—namely, so that he may lose even those whom he has already taken, and they may, as it were, fall from his mouth when, after sins committed, they return to innocence? Certainly a bracelet does not differ in meaning from a ring: wherever it is placed, it constricts by encircling, and likewise signifies the more attentive protection of hidden judgment around us. This Behemoth held Peter in his mouth when Peter denied him; he held David when David fell at once into adultery and murder [Col. 1185A]. But when each returned to life through repentance, this Leviathan lost them, as it were, through an opening in his jaw.

VERS. 22. — “Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak soft words to you?” That is: as to me, to whom he says, “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Matt. 8); indeed, whose body will say on the day of judgment, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25).

VERS. 23–24. — “Will he make a covenant with you?” That is: as with me, from whose judgment he does not depart even by opposing it, and by resisting he advances my purposes no less than if he had sworn that he wished to cooperate in my interests. “And you will take him,” he says, “as an everlasting servant.” That is: as I do, who use him according to my will [Col. 1185B], for example as a craftsman uses his hammer? An everlasting servant, I say: not only in this life, while he purifies the elect by persecuting them, but also in the age to come, while the righteous, beholding the torments from which they have escaped, grow in my praise. In this, surely, his great folly is mocked: he always benefits the very one whom he always strives to harm. Hence it follows: “Will you make sport of him as of a bird?”

It should be noted that he who was first called Behemoth, meaning a beast, and afterwards Leviathan, by which a dragon is understood, is now called a bird. By reason of his brutish understanding, through which he abandoned heavenly things, he is a beast; by reason of the malice by which he deceived man, he is a dragon; by reason of the subtlety of his nature, of which he is proud, he is a bird. Among those also whom he defiles through lust he is a beast [Col. 1185C]; among those whom he makes malicious he is a dragon; among those whom he raises up through pride he is a bird. “Will you make sport of him as of a bird?” That is: as I do, who in the Passion of my only-begotten Son show him bait but conceal the snare? “Or will you bind him for your maidservants?” That is: as I do, who, when I defeat him not through the strong things but through the weak things of the world, bind him, as it were, not through my servants but through my maidservants?

These are the maidservants whom, according to Solomon (Prov. 9), Wisdom sent to summon people to the citadel—that is, to the house which Wisdom herself built for herself from the flesh of the Virgin—because the incarnate Wisdom of God chose to have weak and despised preachers. What, then, will become of him, thus mocked and thus bound?

[Col. 1185D] VERS. 25. — “His friends,” he says, “will cut him in pieces,” that is, the holy preachers. They will cut him in pieces, I say, with the sword of the word of God; “the merchants will divide him,” that is, the same friends. For those who are friends through faith are merchants through action. They will cut and divide him, because by preaching they will separate his members from him.

VERS. 26. — “Will you fill nets with his skin, and fish-traps with his head?” That is: as I do, who, calling fishermen and making them fishers of men (Matt. 4), first fill with his skin the net of which it is written, “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13)—that is, I gather the outermost and lowest persons [Col. 1186A]—and afterwards, by subduing prudent adversaries to myself, I fill, as it were, the fish-trap with his head.

VERS. 27. — “Will you lay your hand upon him?” That is, your power? As though he said plainly: Can you restrain him by your own strength, as I can? Why he asks this he makes clear by what follows: “Remember the battle, and add no more to speak.” That is: remember how strong is he against whom you must fight, and that you cannot lay your hand upon him unless you are sustained by my help.

You are then especially helped when you are girded with the scourge; for when you are encircled by outward sufferings, you are freed from inward passion. Remember this, I say, “and add no more to speak,” because it is better for you to be subjected to harsh bodily scourges [Col. 1186B] than to be deceived by the blandishment of hidden temptation. But because this Leviathan’s guilt is beyond remission, and because, from the height which he arrogates to himself, he falls cast down to the lowest depths beneath all things:

VERS. 28. — “Behold,” he says, “his hope will deceive him”—the hope by which, presumptuously exalting himself, he said, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Rather, “he will be cast down in the sight of all,” when the eternal Judge appears in terror, the legions of angels stand by, the entire ministry of the heavenly powers is present, and all the elect are brought to this spectacle. Then, I say, this cruel and mighty beast, led captive into the midst, will be cast down to be burned in the eternal fires of Gehenna; and the Judge will say to his entire body: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” [Col. 1186C] (Matt. 25).

You might now ask why he raises so powerful an enemy against the contest of our weakness.

## CHAPTER XLI

VERS. 1. — “No,” he says, “I will raise him up not as a cruel one,” but as a just one, because I permit him to rage not against those subject to me but against those who resist me. Therefore fear, and add no more to speak, as was said above: “For who,” he says, “can resist my countenance” with impunity?

VERS. 2. — “Or who has first given to me, that I should repay him?” That is: who can glory before me on the basis of his own merits? No one has first bestowed anything upon me; nor does anyone perform anything good unless my mercy has first gone before him [Col. 1186D]. “Who,” I say, “has given to me, that I should repay him? All things that are under heaven are mine.” Under heaven—that is, all things which man alone can touch or see. Therefore, when he offers me from these some service or gift, he does not himself give first to me, since he has received it from me, whose all things are. All things under heaven are mine. Therefore Leviathan himself, who fell beneath heaven, is mine also: though he lost my blessedness, he did not escape my dominion.

VERS. 3. — “I will not spare him,” he says, “nor his mighty words.” This must be referred to his body, that is, to all the wicked, because the devil will not seek pardon for his sins. Yet that man of sin, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth [Col. 1187A] (2 Thess. 2), perhaps, terrified, will incline to prayer. But “I will not spare him,” he says, “despite mighty words and words artfully composed for entreaty”: that is, mighty words, whether his own or those of his entire body, composed to beg mercy, will not avail to prevent his being cast down in the sight of all, as was said above. And because the more subtly the Lord sees his snares concealed from us, the more mercifully he reveals them:

VERS. 4. — “Who,” he says—that is, except I—“will uncover the face [513] of his garment?” That is, the deceit of his pretence, which is so great that he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11). He himself uncovers this garment of pretence when he inspires his servants to beware of the malice which the devil hides under the habit of holiness. Hence he further adds: “And who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” That is, who will examine his words, detect and expose their falsity, except I?

VERS. 5. — “The gates of his face,” he says—that is, the wicked teachers through whom each person enters after being deceived, so that this Leviathan may seem to reign in the principate of his power—“who will open the gates,” except I, who make the teachers of error, hidden under the appearance of holiness, manifest to my elect by clear knowledge? Why no one but he can open these gates he explains by adding: “Around his teeth is terror” [Col. 1187B]. That is, around the teachers of his error, and as though forming their guard, stands the protection of secular powers.

For by “teeth” he means those whom he had above called “gates”: they are gates because they open an entrance to perdition, and teeth because they crush from the firmness of truth those whom they seize in terror. Terror surrounds them because around them are those who afflict the minds of the weak; and what is said by the former in flattering words is commanded by the latter with striking swords.

VERS. 6. — “His body”—that is, all the wicked, of whom he is the head—“is like molten shields.” That is, they are hard through obstinacy, but frail in life, just as cast shields are sturdy in receiving the blow of arrows but fragile when they fall. Thus they receive words of correction impenetrably with the shield of proud self-defence, but are dissolved by their own fall [Col. 1187D] and broken by their own disasters. They are well compared to shields, because they are shielded—that is, they defend themselves in every sin which they commit. Thus the prophet says concerning the Jews, justly hardened: “Lord, you will give them a shield of heart: your toil” (Lam. 3). That is, they repel from themselves the words of preachers because they despise your sufferings.

“His body,” I say, is “like molten shields, compacted with scales pressing one upon another”: that is, when corrected, it defends and excuses itself by whatever evasions it can, as the dragon’s body is covered with scales so that it may not quickly be penetrated by a missile. Sometimes also the wicked person, when caught in his excesses, is supported by those like himself. Hence it follows:

VERS. 7. — “One is joined to another”—that is, scale to scale—because those united by a like guilt are also tightly bound together by a concordant perversity of obstinate self-defence. “And not even breath passes through them”: that is, they by no means permit the breaths of holy exhortation to enter them.

VERS. 8. — “One adheres to another”—that is, like to like—as Solomon says: “The assembly of sinners is a bundle of tow” (Ecclus. 21). “And those holding together will by no means be separated”: that is, by defending one another they will be strengthened by one another.

Having described the body, the discourse returns to the head and declares how the ancient enemy exerts himself.

VERS. 9. — “His sneezing,” he says, “is the brilliance of fire.” That is, the final agitation by which he enters into the damned man will shine with many prodigies, as with a certain brightness of fire [Col. 1188B]. And just as, in a sneeze, an inflation rising from the chest, unable to find opened pores through which to escape, reaches the brain and, immediately emerging through the nostrils, shakes the whole head, so that man of sin, swollen with the dignity of the present age, strives to prevail against the righteous as much as he desires. Thus, at the end of the world, he strikes more violently, as it were, Satan’s brain—that is, his exalted understanding; and, when the head is disturbed—that is, the author of all wickedness dwelling in him—he comes forth, as it were, through the nostrils, when his entire pride is displayed through the open blasts of malice, together with the brightness of miracles, as with the brilliance of fire.

“And his eyes,” he says—that is, his counsellors or overseers, namely those of Antichrist—“his eyes,” I say, that is, the powers of the world who will adhere to him [Col. 1188C], are “like the eyelids of dawn”: they feign themselves messengers of true light, since they present the faith which they find in Christ as the night of error and promise that veneration of Antichrist is the true morning.

VERS. 10. — “From his mouth”—that is, from these same counsellors, who are called eyes because they foresee and mouth because they preach—“lamps proceed,” because they kindle the minds of their hearers to love faithlessness. “Lamps,” I say, “like burning firebrands”: that is, claiming for themselves the appearance of holiness, yet performing works of wickedness. When a firebrand is kindled, it indeed has a sweet smell, but gives a dim light. They smell sweet through a simulated righteousness [Col. 1188D], but burn dimly through penetrating wickedness.

VERS. 11. — “From his nostrils”—that is, from the snares of his miracles—“smoke goes forth”: that is, dark uncertainty is produced, so great that, if possible, even the elect might be led into error. “Smoke,” I say, “like that of a heated and boiling pot”: that is, he makes souls burn with the violent movement of their thoughts, as with foaming waves, just as a heated pot contains waters boiling within it. For the conscience, stirred by his temptations, rises with as many boilings as the thoughts within it swell. Hence he adds further:

VERS. 12. — “His breath”—that is, his secret suggestion—“makes coals burn”: that is, it draws the minds of the reprobate, kindled by inward desires [Col. 1189A], toward unlawful pleasures. Unless they had within themselves a spark of fire—that is, of desire—they would not become burning coals through the breath, that is, the suggestion, of the devil. “A flame,” he says, “goes forth from his mouth”: that is, the prompting of hidden speech is instilled into the mind, for the mind burns with desires when it is stirred by his suggestions.

The ancient enemy, as has often already been said, attacks more fiercely at the end of the world in order to tempt, because he becomes more ardent in cruelty the nearer he feels himself to punishment. Then he raises the neck of his pride higher, and through that condemned man whom he bears he wickedly displays everything in which he temporarily prevails. Hence it is now said:

[Col. 1189B] VERS. 13. — “Strength will abide in his neck”: that is, in the pride by which he is raised up against God. Thus it was said through the prophet: “Deceit will prosper in his hand” (Dan. 8), because whatever he wickedly wishes, he can also carry out powerfully for a time. And because everyone who becomes known as a friend of his through corrupt conduct first loses the true riches of the mind: “Want,” he says, “will go before his face”—that is, before knowledge of him—because no one adheres to him unless he is one to whom, as to the angel of Laodicea, John says: “You are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3). And because no members of his body disagree among themselves:

VERS. 14. — “The members of his flesh cohere with one another.” That is, he exercises his cruelty all the more strongly because all carnal persons, who are indeed his members—as Paul says to the spiritual, “You are the body of Christ and members of a member” (1 Cor. 12)—“the members of his flesh,” I say, all who are subject to carnal vices, oppose themselves more harshly to the life of the good in a destructive unity [Col. 1189C].

The Lord raises our weakness, trembling at these things, when he immediately adds what he will do to so great a beast: “He will send lightnings against him.” “He will send,” I say—the coming Judge—“lightnings,” that is, the sentences of terrible judgment. “Against him,” I say, “and they are not transferred to another place,” because, once the wheat has been received into the barns, the chaff alone will be cast into the fire: that is, while the righteous rejoice, the reprobate alone [514] will then be struck [Col. 1189D]. But because punishment does not correct this Leviathan:

VERS. 15. — “His heart will be hardened like a stone,” because it will never be softened by any conversion of repentance. “And it will be compressed like a smith’s anvil”: that is, it will be fitted only for the blows of eternal condemnation, just as a smith shaping an anvil fashions it only by hammer-blows. An anvil is set up for this purpose: that it may be struck by repeated blows.

VERS. 16. — “When he is lifted up”—that is, when, at the coming of the strict Judge, he is hurled down into final damnation—“when he is lifted up, angels will fear.” That is, the messengers of the heavenly country will fear. For when he is swept away in the whirlwind of judgment, those who may then be found in bodies—the holy preachers—although strong and perfect, will tremble, shaken by immense terror, and, terrified, will be purified [Col. 1190A].

Yet there is no obstacle to understanding this of the holy angels—that is, the heavenly spirits—provided that past events are described under the form of the future. When he was lifted up by falling from the citadel of blessedness, the angels feared and were purified by terror, since when he fell, the punishment of the sin of one who had grown proud became the occasion for humble angels to discover and establish an increase of merit. Therefore, when he is cast down, as has already been said, there will be in them—whether in the holy preachers, who are themselves called angels because they are messengers of life—a joyful trembling and a secure fear.

But since we have learned of this Leviathan’s end, let us meanwhile hear of him before he perishes:

VERS. 17. — “When the sword,” he says, “shall seize him”—that is, when that man of his, whom he has sharpened by the malice of deceit and who pierces the hearts of the weak, receives him into himself; or when his own wrath, rightly signified by the name of sword, seizes him so completely that, while desiring to rule all, he cannot rule his own wrath—“when the sword seizes him, neither spear nor breastplate will be able to stand” [Col. 1190B]. That is, neither the missile of preaching nor the steadfastness of the patient. For the spear with which we inflict wounds rightly signifies preaching, and the breastplate with which we are protected signifies patience. “They will not be able to stand,” that is, if heavenly help is lacking.

[Col. 1190C] VERS. 18. — “For he will regard iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.” That is, he will consume the strength of preachers as straw in the fire of his wickedness; and the steadfastness of the patient, signified by bronze, which is not easily dissolved by rust, he will reduce “like rotten wood” to dust—unless divine help strengthens his elect. And he so possesses the minds of the reprobate, designated by straw and rotten wood, that, pierced by no missile of truth, he does not leave them. Hence it follows:

VERS. 19. — “The archer will not put him to flight.” That is, he does not depart from the hearts of those whom he possesses at the rebukes of any preacher. Whoever is seized by him despises “the sharp arrows of the mighty” (Ps. 119), that is, the words of the preachers. “The stones of the sling,” he says, “are turned to stubble for him”: that is, all the strong men of the Church are contemptible to him as weak persons.

For the sling, which is cast in a circle and from which stones fly out to strike the breasts of adversaries, signifies the holy Church. While it is carried through the cycle of tribulations by the revolving course of times, strong men come forth from it, by whom the words of the wicked are struck as with stone blows. Thus the prophet says: “They shall devour and subdue with the stones of the sling” (Zech. 9), that is, they shall break the hearts of the proud through the strong men of the Church [Col. 1190D]. But what wonder if stones are turned to stubble for him?

VERS. 20. — “He will esteem the hammer as stubble”: that is, he will contemptuously regard as nothing the judgment of divine retribution coming down from above and striking him [Col. 1191A]. “And he will mock the brandished spear”: that is, God himself, preparing the strict sentence at his destruction. And since he is such:

VERS. 21. — “The rays of the sun will be beneath him”: that is, even certain learned men, who seemed to scatter light through the keenness of wisdom as through rays, will serve him. As it is written in the Apocalypse: “The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to him to afflict men with heat and fire; and men were scorched with great heat” (Rev. 16). For when wise men are led away into error, the weak are more deeply affected by temporal desires through their example.

Of these it is further said: “He will spread gold beneath himself as mud”: that is, he will trample the purity of life of certain persons through unlawful desires, so that even those who formerly shone against him with the splendour of virtues may serve his accustomed footprints [Col. 1191B]. For in this place gold signifies the brightness of holiness, while mud signifies either the greed of earthly things or the carnal filth of pleasures. Yet it must be understood that gold which could be spread beneath him like mud was never gold in the sight of God. But what will he do with those wholly tossed about by earthly desires?

VERS. 22. — “He will make the depth of the sea boil like a pot”: that is, he will strive to stir up the life of worldly people against the life of the elect through the flame of cruelty. The deep sea boils like a pot when he violently inflames the hearts of lovers of the world. “And he will make it,” he says, “as when ointments boil”: that is, he will make them think that they render service to God (John 16), and, just as boiling ointments emit a pleasant fragrance, they will seem to themselves to exhale a good reputation. And, that they may be deceived by him still more:

VERS. 23. — “The path will shine after him”: that is, miracles will shine, wrought by his words or wickedness, in order to drag the deceived toward present pleasures. “He will reckon the abyss as growing old”: that is, he will cause hell to be considered as something that will someday end. Even now there are those who neglect to put an end to their sins because they suppose that the judgments from above will sometime have an end, though Truth says: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” [Col. 1191D] (Matt. 25). And while they strive to declare God merciful, they do not fear to preach him false.

The Lord now briefly indicates the immensity of his power:

VERS. 24. — “There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him,” because although he fell below human beings through the deserving of his actions, he nevertheless surpasses the whole human race by the condition of angelic nature; he did not lose the greatness of his nature when he lost his dignity. “He was made,” he says—that is, by his own perversity—such “that he should fear no one”: that is, so that he might disdain to be subject even to him by whom he was created, whom he ought to have feared with chaste fear. His pride is further described as he adds:

VERS. 25. — “He sees everything lofty”: that is, he looks down as from on high upon all persons as placed beneath him, because, while he strives against his Creator in intention, he disdains to think anyone like himself. The ancient enemy, who is signified by a bodily animal, is openly described as seeing all things from on high, because pride, issuing even into the body, more openly holds dominion over the eyes [Col. 1192A]. Now, at the end of the Lord’s speech, one point is expressed more plainly, by which his members are briefly shown to us: “He himself is king over all the children of pride.”

Like a tyrant, he seizes a city under siege when he bursts into the mind through the vice of pride. Therefore, because our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble and this Leviathan is called king of the proud, we plainly recognize that pride is the most evident mark of the reprobate, while humility is the mark of the elect. Thus, when the mark possessed by each person is known, it is discovered under which king he serves.

## CHAPTER XLII

VERS. 1–2. — After the Lord had shown his faithful servant how strong and cunning Leviathan, his enemy, was, blessed Job answered both points: [515] against his immense strength, “I know,” he says, “that you can do all things”; against his hidden machinations, “and no thought is hidden from you.” Hence he immediately reproaches Leviathan himself, saying:

VERS. 3. — “Who is this, who conceals counsel without knowledge?” That is, he conceals his frauds against our weakness, yet does not know how to conceal them from our Protector [Col. 1192C]. I know, I say, that nothing is hidden from you; “therefore I have spoken foolishly.” That is, in comparison with your wisdom, everything which I seemed to know is foolish. In this way Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, after he heard the Lord speaking, found himself to be of impeded and slow speech (Exod. 4). And Isaiah, after he saw the Lord, knew himself to be a man of unclean lips (Isa. 4). Thus all holy men, the more they advance in contemplation, the more they despise what they are.

“I have spoken foolishly,” therefore, he says, “and of matters surpassing my knowledge beyond measure,” because in your words I have recognized more of the secrets of your wisdom than I had supposed, and from this I have discovered that I had exceeded my measure. What then?

[Col. 1192D] VERS. 4. — “Hear, and I will speak”: that is, receive my desire, and I will eagerly long for you with ready desires. “I will question you, and answer me”: that is, I will profitably recognize my folly, and you teach me.

VERS. 5. — “By the hearing of the ear I had heard of you, but now my eye sees you.” That is, as sight is superior to hearing, so what I have gained after the scourges differs from what I formerly was.

VERS. 6. — “Therefore I myself reprove myself”: namely, the more I see myself, the more I displease myself. “And I do penance,” because recognition of self-reproof is nothing unless the tears of repentance follow. “I do penance,” I say, “in dust and ashes”: that is, I acknowledge that I am dust and ashes [Col. 1193A].

VERS. 7. — “And after the Lord had spoken,” and so forth. Behold: with the parties present and awaiting the verdict, the Lord pronounces, from the invisible rule of his discernment, the judgment, showing who in this dispute had spoken more rightly. “You have not,” he says, “spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.” Behold, by God’s judgment blessed Job, who was thought to have sinned in speaking, is praised as victor; and by the same judgment those are condemned who believed themselves to surpass his merits by speaking for God. “As my servant Job,” he says: by identifying him, as it were, by the particular title of servitude, he demonstrates that everything Job had said in his own defence was said not in contumacious pride but in humility [Col. 1193B].

Then, sternly rebuking Job’s friends through justice and graciously converting them through mercy:

VERS. 8. — “Take for yourselves seven bulls,” and so forth. It should be noted that they are commanded to offer the sacrifice of their conversion to the Lord not by themselves but through Job, because heretics—whom, as has often been said, they represent—when they return from error cannot appease God or obtain their salvation except through the prayers of the Catholic Church, signified by blessed Job, whose faith they had assailed with perverse assertions. “Take seven bulls and seven rams,” he says: that is, you who were of bull-like pride, and rams—that is, wandering leaders of diverse flocks—humble yourselves to the sevenfold Spirit [Col. 1193C]. “But Job my servant will pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be imputed to you.”

It is as though he said openly to heretics: I will not accept your sacrifices, I will not hear the words of your petitions, unless through the intercession of the Church, whose profession concerning me I recognize as truthful. For it alone is that through which God willingly accepts sacrifice; it alone intercedes confidently for those in error; it alone, I say, is the house in which the true sacrificial victim, the Redeemer, is offered. Thus it is said through Moses concerning the sacrifice of the lamb: “It shall be eaten in one house; and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside” (Exod. 12). “He will pray for you,” he says. For “you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.” What he had once stated by declaration, he confirms by repetition, because whatever is repeated in divine speech is more strongly affirmed.

VERS. 9. — “So Eliphaz the Temanite went,” and so forth. The interpretation of these names was discussed at the beginning. “And the Lord accepted the face”—that is, the intention of charity—“of Job.” And because whoever strives to intercede for others gains support for himself all the more through this charity, he rightly adds:

VERS. 10. — “The Lord also turned to the repentance of Job when he prayed for his friends.” That is, even while penitent for himself, he deserved to be heard all the more quickly because he devoutly interceded for others. How much he obtained for himself is immediately shown when it adds: “And the Lord added double all that Job had possessed” [Col. 1194A], so that the consolations supplied might overcome the losses of temptation.

VERS. 11. — “Then all his brothers came to him,” and so forth. “And they ate bread with him in his house, and shook their heads over him.” In eating bread charity is signified; in the shaking of the head, amazement. “And they comforted him concerning all the evil which the Lord had brought upon him”: that is, they rejoiced over him. To comfort the sorrow of one who has been struck is to rejoice with him after the blow on account of pardon. “And each gave him one sheep and one golden earring.”

Although all these things are truly said according to the historical account, the very gifts which were offered compel us toward the mystery of allegory. “The Lord added double all that Job had possessed”: that is, the holy Church, which is one person with her head, and now possesses the Gentiles alone, will in the end have all Judea that is found agree with her; or rather, for the holy Church to receive double at its end is for each of us to rejoice both in the blessedness of the soul and in the incorruption of the flesh. Hence it is written: “They shall possess double in their land” (Isa. 61), because at the end of the world they will possess two robes: together with blessedness of mind, they will possess also the glory of the flesh.

But what follows testifies more particularly to the conversion of the Jewish people at the end of this age. “Then all his brothers came to him”: that is, they will come to him by believing—all who shall be found from the Jewish people—his brothers [Col. 1194C], I say, “and all his sisters”: that is, those who will be strong as brothers and those who will be weak as sisters; “and all who had known him before,” namely through knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, though at the time of his Passion they did not know him because they despised him.

“And they will eat bread with him in his house”: that is, in the holy Church, which is his house. They will be nourished by the fruit of sacred Scripture. “And they will shake their heads over him”: that is, their ruling faculty, which is the mind, will suffer a movement from its insensibility through fear of the truth. “And they will comfort him concerning all the evil which the Lord had brought upon him.” They will comfort him, I say, with that consolation which, not finding in his Passion, he said: “I sought one to comfort me, and I found none.” For the subsequent progress of the hearer is a great consolation to the preacher.

“And each will give him one sheep”: that is, they will offer him an innocent life; “and one golden earring”: that is, the precious virtue of obedience. Of this Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15). It should be noted that with the earring a sheep, and with the sheep an earring, is offered, because the ornament of obedience is always joined to innocent minds, according to the saying: “My sheep hear my voice” [Col. 1194D] (John 10).

VERS. 12. — “And he had fourteen thousand sheep,” and so forth. When it is said, “The Lord added double all that Job had possessed” (v. 10), it is plain that the animals [516] were doubled. That he added the children twofold is clear in this way: he afterward restored ten in the flesh, and preserved in the hidden life of souls the ten who had been lost [Col. 1195A]. In the allegorical sense, the animals must be understood in the same way as was explained in the first part of the book; for the Psalmist says to the Father: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8).

The holy Church, however, which in its beginnings was oppressed by innumerable temptations and lost both the Israelite people and many from the Gentiles—namely, those whom it could not win—receives double at the end, because the number of faithful people from every nation increases more abundantly within it.

VERS. 13. — “And he had seven sons and three daughters,” and so forth. He also receives seven sons and three daughters because, to the minds of those whom he begets through seven virtues, he joins faith, hope, and charity unto the summit of perfection, so that his offspring may rejoice the more truly because they judge that none of the virtues is lacking to his faithful. By the names of the daughters, moreover, he signifies the entire human race which is chosen through the kindness of the Creator and the mercy of the Redeemer. These names follow:

VERSE 14.—“And,” he says, “he called the name of the first Day, and the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third *Cornustibii* [Horn-and-Pipe].” For since the human race, when created, shone with the light of innocence, and, when redeemed, has diffused the fragrance of sweetness through the exercise of good works, the first daughter is rightly called Day, and the second not inappropriately Cassia. And because, in the third order, the human race, renewed also by the resurrection of the flesh, is received into that harmony of eternal praise, the third daughter is called *Cornustibii* [Horn-and-Pipe]. For we who were created light, or day, and who are now redeemed Cassia, shall at some time be *Cornustibii*, received into the exultation of eternal praise. Since these names are taken from virtues, the translator fittingly took care not to set them down as they were found in the Arabic language, but to make their meaning clearer by translating them into Latin. He formed *Cornustibii* from *cornu* (“horn”) and *tibia* (“pipe”), and legitimately coined it in whatever gender he chose.

[Col. 1196A] VERSE 15.—“But no women were found so beautiful as Job’s daughters in all the earth,” because, before the bride reaches the marriage chamber, she casts off from herself every ugliness of life and, preparing herself for the bridegroom’s love, adorns herself with the forms of virtues. Of this beauty of the soul it is said in the Psalm concerning the holy Church: “The king has desired your beauty” (Ps. XLIV). And a little later: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (ibid.).—“And their father gave them,” namely, the daughters, “an inheritance among their brothers.” The custom of the old life did not permit women to receive an inheritance among males. But now that our merciful Redeemer has come—of whom Job is here a type—let no one conscious of his own weakness despair of receiving the inheritance of the heavenly patrimony, because “In my Father’s house,” he says, “there are many dwelling-places” (John XIV), so that sisters may be admitted with brothers—that is, the weak with the strong. There no one suffers loss through inequality, because what each receives is sufficient for that person.

[Col. 1196B] VERSE 16.—“And Job lived one hundred and forty years”; that is, the Church lives after the resurrection in the perfection of eternity, rightly signified by this number. For if we multiply fourteen by ten, we arrive at the number one hundred and forty. Fourteen, composed of ten and four, signifies the perfection of the Law’s Decalogue and of the Gospel. Therefore the Church, extended to the summit of perfection according both to the Decalogue of the Law and to the four books of the Gospel, lives forever. “And he saw his sons,” namely, those whom he had gained for God, “and his sons’ sons,” namely, those whom the successors of the apostles had begotten; “he saw,” I say, “unto the fourth generation,” that is, unto the resurrection. For the first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace, and the fourth in the future resurrection. And as it were in the fourth generation the Church dies—that is, she is wholly removed from the present world—“full of days,” that is, fully rewarded with the recompense of good works.

This book of Job ends happily. Amen.

[Col. 1195]

COMMENTARY OF THE REVEREND LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTES.

THE EPISTLE TO GREGORY WHICH PRECEDES THE FOLLOWING WORK BEGINS.

517 To Lord Gregory, a man of most illustrious memory, S., humble and the Lord’s sweepings, greetings. “Blessed,” says the Psalmist, “are those who search the testimonies of the Lord, that they may seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). This blessedness, I think, most beloved one, you have found; and therefore I judged it most fitting that you who have found it should “find life and draw salvation from the Lord” (Prov. VIII). For I received the writings of your charity, in which you earnestly urged me to publish something for you on Ecclesiastes, according to our translation—that is, the Hebrew truth—because the work of blessed Jerome according to the tradition of the Seventy Interpreters seemed, as it were, mutilated and misshapen, and very far removed from the Hebrew.

I read it and read it again, and without doubt perceived it to be as you indicated. Love surely has no price. A friendship that can cease was never true. Let whoever pleases shine with gold; let gleaming metals shine from heaps of sumptuous dishes: charity cannot be compared with them. I therefore beg you not to lose from your mind together with your eyes a friend who is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve. Believe me—believe me, brother—not with such longing does a sailor tossed by storm look out for harbor; not so do thirsty fields desire rain; not so does an anxious mother, sitting upon the curving shore, await her son, as I have always desired you. Now I greatly fear that the carbuncle of this affection is about to be extinguished.

For how do you wish to hand over to me the teacher’s chair, when I was never a pupil beneath the rod? You measure me by your own virtues; being great, you exalt the small; and you take the lowest place at the banquet, so that you may be promoted by the judgment of the master of the house. Yet it is not proclaimed without reason that human minds shine in a clear day and grow pale beneath a gathered cloud; I believe my mind will confirm the saying by its example. For when I write to you, the sense of the words will furnish an expression which I otherwise lack. Moreover, obedience rightly claims primacy among all virtues, for it makes many attempt what they cannot do. Therefore those who, considering their own ability, comply with commands are to be held worthy of praise for devotion. Relying, then, solely upon charity, than which nothing is more commanding, I shall satisfy your wish. While I undertake this boldly, I know myself guilty of presumption. Yet I could not repeatedly refuse you when you asked—on this condition only: that the reading be for you alone, and that no second eye observe it.

COMMENTARY.

[Col. 1197]

518 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 1197A]

CHAPTER I.

VERSE 1.—“The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king in Jerusalem.” Ecclesiastes was the son of King David; he was also called Solomon and Jedidiah. In these three names the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity is declared: for just as one man has three names, so three persons are designated in one substance of the Godhead. Solomon means “peaceful”; Jedidiah means “beloved of the Lord.” Further, in Greek *Ecclesiastes* is the one who gathers together an assembly—that is, a church. We may call him a preacher, because he speaks to the people and his discourse is directed not specially to one person but generally to all. He performs the role of all; one man speaks to many; one man teaches all.

Now, as though by majesty, by the motion of his hand and the regulation of his countenance, he calms various disturbances, even great and arrogant tumults. At one time he assumes the person of the weak, at another that of the wise. He sits as a poor man, indulges himself, and undertakes every great enterprise as a rich man. He pretends to be avaricious in order to destroy avarice. He desires the things of the flesh, and he desires the things of the Spirit. For as many as are human beings, so many are human pursuits. Ecclesiastes writes his book under the appearance of persons so diverse, in order that, becoming all things to all with the Apostle, he may gain all (I Cor. IX).

Will not each one of us be a son of David and king of Jerusalem, if he keeps with devout and diligent mind the things written in this book? Whoever rules himself energetically and wisely will be king of Jerusalem. For it is greater to rule oneself well than to possess the kingdoms of many. This book is like the basin which Moses made from the mirrors of women (Exod. XXXVIII). In such mirrors he taught men to observe not merely faces, but also human minds. Ecclesiastes likewise made this book from bronze and women’s mirrors, for the inspection of human minds. It is clearer than a mirror, more resonant than sounding bronze. It resounds in words; human life is represented in women’s mirrors.

Therefore Ecclesiastes sees in this mirror whatever human beings do in the world. He considers the distinct arts, whatever is done by people; and scarcely any art is exempt from this book. Here the learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIII) has material from which to bring forth things new and old. Plato, Pythagoras, Socrates, Aristotle, and all who treat logic and ethics seasoned their books with the spices and fullness of this book. For what physicist or philosopher could investigate more deeply the hidden recesses of nature, or see its inner things more keenly? For he himself, as is read, discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop. The Hebrews indeed say that this book is Solomon’s repentance: because, trusting in wisdom and riches, he offended the Lord through women (III Kings IV).

VERSE 2.—“Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” We ought not to read in passing, or lightly esteem, what he says: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes.” For who could see vain things more than Ecclesiastes? Rightly, he who governs the commonwealth alone can know and understand what vanity is, what vanity of vanities is, and that all is vanity. For he has uttered these three things most plainly.

Whoever lives so vainly that he does not understand himself to be vanity unless he is strengthened by the Word of God—such a person cannot understand what vanity of vanities is. Therefore such a person, being senseless, is vanity of vanities; and the fable rightly tells him what the ox said to the gnat, which thanked him for having wintered in his ear during the cold season: “I noticed neither your coming nor your going.” Therefore Ecclesiastes says of such persons: “Vanity of vanities.”

But from what, we may suppose, has the heart of Ecclesiastes now emerged? It seems indeed to have suffered shipwreck. He had seen small animals with great ones; he had ascended the height of heaven; he had penetrated the depth of the abyss; he had seen the great whale raging without mercy in this great and spacious sea. Natural philosophers report that when someone is swallowed by the waters, he sinks three times and is lifted up from the waves three times; but at the third occasion he is either freed or killed. So, in the shipwreck of the world, as the bilge-water of danger rises, Ecclesiastes, seeing so much and fearing so much, is submerged and recalled; and he cries out, “Vanity of vanities!” Again he is submerged and recalled, with a loud cry: “Vanity of vanities!” A third time submerged and freed, now standing in harbor like a shipwrecked man, he cries on: “All is vanity!”

But why do we count man among the number of vanities, when he was made in the image of God, presides over all things under the sun, and through him God is worshiped and served? Surely because David, the father of Ecclesiastes, also says: “Yet every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII). What vanishes more than smoke? What is more vain than a shadow? As a shadow changes its course, so man changes hour by hour. “He fails like smoke” (Ps. LXVII): thus the foolish man wastes his time. Therefore man is vanity of vanities if he wishes to think only earthly things and not heavenly ones; if he thinks the things of the flesh, not those of the Spirit. If, then, a living man is vanity, what will he be when dead? He is vanity of vanities, of whom scarcely even an image now remains. To be and not to be, to die and not to be able to die—is that not vanity of vanities? If death cannot bring death to an end, what could ever be more vain? Therefore “the whole creation groans and travails until now,” until it is freed in the hope of the grace of the children of God (Rom. VIII).

But since it is written, “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I), why is his work called not only vanity but even vanity of vanities? In Exodus we read that Moses’ face was glorified to such an extent that the children of Israel could not look upon it (Exod. XXXIV). The Apostle Paul says that this glory, in comparison with evangelical glory, is not glory: “For even that which was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (II Cor. III). We too may therefore say in this manner that heaven and earth, sea and all things in them, are indeed good in themselves, but compared with God are reckoned as nothing.
