It is as if, seeing the tiny flame of a lamp, I were content with its light, and afterward, when the sun had risen, could no longer see what had shone. I would see also the light of the stars hidden by the sun’s splendor. So, seeing the elements and the manifold variety of things, I indeed marvel at the greatness of the works; but when I reflect that all things pass away, that the world grows old toward its end, and that God alone always is what he has been, I am compelled to say: “Vanity of vanities,” and so forth.

VERSE 3.—“What profit has a man from all his labor which he labors under the sun?” Why does he whose heart was like the sand of the sea (III Kings IV), and like the stars of heaven, ask, as though ignorant and uncertain, what a man has from all his labor? He leaves the statement suspended so that its ambiguity may provoke our zeal for inquiry. He asks as one uncertain, so that we may not be uncertain; he wishes to learn as a disciple, so that we may know; he asks in order to tell us that our labor is not altogether vain.

For although he labors vainly and without fruit who has cast his seed upon rock, beside the road, or among thorns, yet what is sown in good ground will spring up with a hundredfold yield. Those who have borne good fruit will receive from the Lord the eternal rewards of labor; but those who have produced evil fruits will be burned with eternal fire (Matt. XIII; Mark IV; Luke VIII). Thus Adam, the first man, receiving the first punishment for the greatness of his crime, handed down to Ecclesiastes the first mark of vanity, making us together with himself children of vanities. Therefore it is written: “Man is born for labor, as a bird for flight” (Job V). Through Adam, love of labor has been implanted in all people, exercising us as heirs unto labor and vanity. One gathers wealth, educates children, seeks honors, constructs buildings; and, suddenly taken away by death in the midst of his work, he hears: “Fool, this night your soul shall be taken from you; and whose shall those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke XII). Especially since he carries away nothing from all his labor, but returns naked to the earth from which he was taken.

Therefore let whoever labors see to it that he is not deprived of the fruit of his labor. Although Ecclesiastes left the fruit of labor unexpressed, it was nevertheless revealed by the Lord in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). For when Ecclesiastes wrote these things, this precious ointment had not yet been poured out; the severity of the Law had not yet been tempered by the antidote.

VERSE 4.—“A generation passes away, and a generation comes; but the earth stands forever.” The first generation of the world was from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to the coming of the Lord; the sixth, from the Lord’s coming to the end of the age. The generation of the Jews—that is, the Synagogue—also went before; the generation of the Gentiles—that is, the Church—followed. Thus, as some die, others are born; and after no longer seeing those whom you had seen, you begin to see those who did not exist.

What vanity is more vain than that the earth, made for the sake of human beings, should remain forever, while man himself, lord of the earth, is suddenly dissolved into dust? Although the Lord says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. XXIV), he says this not with reference to their substance, but to their renewal. For at the time of judgment they will be renewed by fire poured down from above; and thus, according to Ecclesiastes’ statement, the earth stands forever. What the philosophers of the Gentiles have maintained concerning the earth’s immobility and spherical rotation, Ecclesiastes seems to approve.

VERSE 5, 6.—“The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, being born again, it turns through the south and bends toward the north.” In few words he comprehends much, setting before us both the history and the allegory of things. Let us first taste how sweet is the kernel of allegory. For while he compares us with things, and things with us, in all that he says he marks the causes of vanity. And, as those who treat natural philosophy say, whatever the world—called in Greek *kosmos*—suffers, man also suffers, who is called in Greek *mikrokosmos*, that is, a little world. What the world possesses generally in itself, man is said to possess particularly.

Therefore, as the sun now rises, now sets, and again returns to its rising, so man rises when he is born, sets when he dies, and returns to his mother earth, from which he was taken. What is this but vanity of vanities? Further, we rise as the sun whenever we receive the fire of faith. Again, we set as the sun when we lose the fire of faith. For this is signified by the regions of the north, where perpetual cold exists. Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness, freed us from the mist of this vanity: driving away the darkness of sins, and rising in our breasts, he warms us by his breathing and shines through us by his working. Therefore, when we set by departing into the night of sin, the true Sun, Jesus Christ, also sets and withdraws from us. When, because of sin, we bend toward the north, the author of mercy also bends with us, that he may free us from darkness into the kingdom of his brightness. He turns through the south toward the south wind when he causes us to grow warm by the fire of his love. He is born again with us whenever, leaving sin behind, we are numbered among his children.

But now, to return to the historical sense: the sun itself, given to mortals for light, indicates the world’s destruction by its rising and setting. After it plunges its burning wheel into Ocean, it returns by paths unknown to us to the place from which it came; and, when the circuit of night is completed, it again hastens forth from its chamber. It does this in order to teach, by the changes of times and by the rising and setting of stars, that human life slips away and perishes without recognizing it.

[Col. 1201C] “The spirit, traversing all things in a circuit, goes on; and it returns to its circuits.” Who is this spirit? For this name is homonymous and has many meanings. There are those who say that this spirit is the sun, thinking it to be a living creature that breathes, is active, and completes yearly circles in its course, as the poet says:

> Meanwhile the great sun rolls around the year.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* III.284)

And elsewhere:

> And the year rolls back into itself along its own tracks.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* II.402)

520 Or because, as the same poet says:

> The spirit within sustains the shining globe of the moon  
> and the Titanian stars; a mind, implanted through its limbs,  
> moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.424–26)

Others think that this spirit is the wind which surveys and circles all things. For this reason painters customarily depict winds with wings and feathers; they are fashioned as though they blow through bodily pipes, with reeds issuing from an open mouth. The wise men of this world—that is, philosophers—understanding through the things made, as the Apostle says (Rom. I), God, the Creator of all things, called this spirit mind, intellect, or soul, as though it filled and vivified everything. They say that it gives life to all things, causes all things to grow, and nourishes all creatures by pouring itself inwardly through the limbs of the world’s mass. Plato called this the soul of the world. Confirming it by fixed numbers and cubic perfection, he represented the art of nature in the art of geometrical figure.

Although these men could not see the truth fully, they nevertheless refer beginning and end to one reality, believing that the course of all things returns into itself, just as a cycle turns back upon itself by revolving. Our spirit is also called the soul; through it we breathe, live, and move. It governs the human body and gives life to all things; in contemplating it surveys everything, traverses the height of heaven and the depth of the abyss. It feels, remembers, and understands. It is swift, subtle, keen, and mobile, so that it does not rest even when the body sleeps. In dreams it sees things to come; it understands good and evil; it foreknows many things; it sees absent things as present; it recalls what it knows; it fashions in imagination things it does not know. It is wholly smooth and round in itself (Wis. VII). Having all these things not from itself but from God, it gives thanks to him and sings with the Psalmist: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. CXIII).

Let that holy David now raise for us a ladder, so that we may climb higher and, with Isaiah, behold with far-reaching vision (Isa. XXI): “By the word of the Lord,” he says, “the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth” (Ps. XXXII). This Spirit is God, who, like a circle, in power and divinity penetrates and encompasses everything that he has made. Certainly, if any figure may be compared to the Godhead, none is more fitting than a circle, in which neither beginning nor end is seen. A circle begins from itself and ends in itself. The Godhead possesses, as it were, one being and nature with this circle: it encompasses heaven, earth, and sea, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII).

VERSE 7.—“All rivers enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers issue, they return, that they may flow again.” Under the metaphorical names of waters and rivers, human beings are signified, because they return to the earth from which they were taken, yet the earth is not filled by the multitude of the dead.

Those who dispute concerning natural things ask many questions about why the sea does not overflow when all rivers and all waters fall and rush into it. Some say that the sun nourishes its heat with moisture and thus, through the excess of its heat, diminishes the sea’s superabundance. They prove the greater from the lesser: if some garment is sprinkled with a few drops of water, it is commonly dried by the sun’s heat. Others say that when winds disturb the sea, they carry away a multitude of waters with them, scatter them through the clouds, and cause them again to fall upon the earth as rain. They likewise prove the greater from the lesser. For they say that roads and crossroads are often softened by rains, and then, when winds blow upon them, dry and become hard again.

Others say that the arch of heaven encircles the sea and vomits back from heaven the waters it has drunk. This, they say, is proved by the fact that rains fall after the appearance of a rainbow. Others reason more subtly. They say that the earth stands in the middle of Ocean, which surrounds it completely. Therefore, just as our flesh commonly sweats through tiny pores, so the earth has its own pores, through which it receives into itself the salty moisture of the sea flowing back, and leads it into its veins until the sea’s saltiness, well and purely filtered, entirely disappears and, transformed, takes on a sweet taste.

The sea’s waves flow out upon the lands, and the rivers of the lands pour themselves back into the great and winding belly of the sea. But while the salty sea drinks in the sweet waters of the lands, resenting, as it were, an unfamiliar sweetness, it vomits the sweet waters from itself and casts them into the hidden veins of the earth. Nature supports this opinion also, because sweetness and bitterness are contrary to one another and cannot exist together in one subject. Against these many diverse opinions of the wise men of this world, our Ecclesiastes, himself the Creator of the waters, says that the waters return through hidden veins to the heads of the springs, and from the womb of the abyss continually bubble up at their sources.

[Col. 1203B] VERSE 8.—“All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” This concerns not only physical matters but also ethical ones: knowledge is difficult; speech cannot explain the causes and natures of things; the eye cannot contemplate them as their dignity requires; nor can the ear, even under a teacher’s instruction, attain the summit of knowledge. Yet not everything difficult is wholly impossible. Persistent labor often conquers what initially appears impossible and difficult. At times speech unfolds and opens what the order of nature has entangled. Some things are difficult and are not explained by speech; other difficult things philosophers and wise persons resolve.

But who can satisfy the ear by speaking? It always itches; it always longs to hear new things. So many causes of things cannot satisfy ears; so many forms of things cannot fill the eyes. Although, according to the witness of Ecclesiastes, all things are difficult, let us use some example by which we may overcome difficulties. It is said fabulously, and not without reason, that sleep has two gates, one of ivory and the other of horn. But horn, though hard and rough, is so shaped and thinned by hot water that one may see through it; and what was impossible by nature you have made possible by art. But who can polish and bend ivory, although it is more precious than horn, so that it becomes penetrable to our sight? This is altogether impossible.

Horn is translucent to us when we are capable in mind and action, and what is difficult to us by nature is rendered very easy by our art and labor. Ivory does not permit us to see through it; therefore it signifies things wholly difficult and hidden, from which it turns away both our eyes and our ears.

VERSE 9, 10, 11.—“What is that which has been? The same is that which shall be. What is that which has been done? The same is that which shall be done. There is nothing new under the sun; nor can anyone say: ‘Behold, this is new’; for it has already gone before in the ages which were before us. There is no remembrance of former things; nor indeed will there be remembrance among those who shall be in the last time of the things which shall afterward come to pass.”

In few words he comprehends much, and, with Aristotle, distinguishes substance and accident. For every thing is either substance or accident, so that neither can accident exist without substance, nor substance without accident. Accident cannot exist without some underlying foundation of substance; but substance itself can in no way be seen without an accident laid upon it. Thus color, which is an accident, exists in a body, which is substance. But when you see a body—that is, substance—you observe it marked by an accident—that is, by some color. Thus it comes about that neither does substance exist apart from accident, nor is accident separated from substance. Where substance has existed, accident immediately follows.

Thus Ecclesiastes, when he says “has been,” “is,” and “will be,” plainly indicates substance; but when he says “what has been done” and “what shall be done,” he shows the various events of things together with their accidents. He seems, therefore, to speak of the matters listed above—generation after generation, the mass of the earth, the rising and setting of the sun, and everything that we learn by thought, sight, or hearing—not in a general way, as though there were nothing in the nature of things that had not already existed before. For from the beginning of the world human beings have been born and died; the earth has stood poised above the waters; and the sun has risen and set. And, not to say more: God the Creator granted birds to fly, fish to swim, land animals to walk, and serpents to crawl.

The Comic poet says something similar: “Nothing is said that has not been said before.” If nothing new can be said in speech, how much less in the governance of the world, which was so complete from the beginning that God rested from his works on the seventh day (Gen. II). Therefore let the heresy of the Epicureans perish, who falsely assert that there are, or have been, many worlds, saying that the souls of the dead always pass back into other bodies and live again. Thus Pythagoras, as they themselves invent, transferred himself into a peacock; the soul of Pythagoras rested in Ennius and, in its sixth lot, in Virgil. Ecclesiastes destroys all these notions when he says: “There is no remembrance of former things; nor indeed will there be remembrance among those who shall be in the last time of the things which shall come to pass.”

See: he whom I had suddenly been astonished and amazed to hear cry out, “Vanity of vanities!”—why does he delay, why does he linger to render the reason for his saying and cry? Why has he made such a long digression? He wishes to keep us in suspense and, as it were, deceive us by not giving the reason for himself. But, Ecclesiastes says, far be it from me: I shall quickly render the reason through myself. Surely, having said, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” I may seem guilty of impiety and to have sinned against God if I counted his creatures among vanities. But “my heart has not so turned back” (Ps. XLIII) that I should not “think of the Lord in goodness” (Wis. I). For he who made all things good made no evil at all. He who made no evil—how did he make all things vain?

Look at the threefold creation: heaven, earth, sea. Nothing in them is vain; nothing in them is uncertain. The earth stands forever; as some human beings die, others are daily born. When will you see the host of heaven—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—wander from its appointed course? The sea and springs are restrained by fixed bounds; chance has no power in the nature of things. Therefore, if you, human being, strain beyond measure to comprehend such difficult things, your eyes and ears are overcome. No example is lacking; rather, the continual order of things strengthens faith: throughout the whole course of time, what has been, what has been done, and what still remains to be done.

This was the reason that persuaded us to set forth so many and such great matters beforehand: it does not permit the work of the Creator to be counted among vanities. For I praise the creature; yet I praise more highly the Creator of the creature. Therefore, lest I become vain, lest I receive vanity, I confront myself first, accuse myself, and set myself before my own face (Ps. XLIX); and, so that you may see yourself in me, I first begin with myself.

VERSE 12, 13, 14, 15.—“I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and I set my mind to seek and to investigate wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun. God gave this most grievous occupation to the children of men, that they might be occupied with it. I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit. The perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite.”

Behold, our advocate openly shows everyone whence he was able to have such a grace of knowledge. “I set my mind,” he says; “I applied my heart to study; instruction favored the student, and the keenness of a lively intellect was added. I did not spend my life, as certain idle people do, in leisure, but with my whole breast I panted to investigate the work of my Creator. I sought, found, and turned over everything by pondering in my mind. I marked lofty and astonishing things which I know occur, but why they occur thus I do not know. God gave us this occupation: that we should labor, find, and yet not see why the things found occur as they do.

Why was Esau rejected before he was born? By what merit was Jacob loved before he was born? (Rom. IX). For what sins are infants tormented by a demon? For what crime are little children who die without baptism held in infernal fire? The just and unjust alike fall without any distinction; they labor together; they are destroyed by an equal plague. The unjust man reigns; he harshly oppresses the just man unjustly, as it seems to me. Evils attend the good, and abundant goods attend the evil. These things appear and are read of as so great and so numerous that I could sooner count the stars of heaven, the drops of rain, and the sands of the sea. Yet in all these things the Lord is just; and, as the Psalmist says, “The judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV). Paul likewise says to the Romans concerning such matters: “O man, who are you that you should answer back to God?” (Rom. IX).

Therefore to dispute against the justice of the Lord is vanity of vanities and affliction of spirit. For the perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite. Those are called perverse who have been corrupted from the straight path. This is against heretics, who introduce certain natures that cannot receive healing. Truly, God, who made all things and created everything good, made angels and us rational and in his own image, and set us over all creatures (Gen. I): the angels over us, and us over the other creatures. But their prince, the devil, fell from heaven like lightning (Luke X); and, envying human beings the blessedness which he himself lost, he became perverse and makes countless others perverse with him, so that the Lord’s true saying may stand: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX).

### Verses 16, 17, 18

I spoke in my heart, saying: “Behold, I have become great, and I have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; my mind has contemplated many things wisely, and I have learned. I gave my heart to know prudence and learning, errors and folly; and I recognized that in these too there was toil and affliction of spirit: because in much wisdom there is much indignation, and whoever increases knowledge also increases toil.”

Here Ecclesiastes assumes the person and treats the case of lovers of criticism and of those who truly philosophize. He whom divine grace has filled so that he can say with the Psalmist, “My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times” [Col. 1206B] (Ps. 118), is truly wise. And this is the beginning of wisdom: that he should recognize his own dignity—that he has been created and re-created in the image of God. Therefore, according to his exalted glory and by the merits of good works, he becomes a temple of God. Such persons preside not only over the other irrational creatures, but also over those who live, like irrational beasts, according to the manner of cattle.

Certainly, whoever is truly a Christian surpasses those who were in Jerusalem before it was built into the heavenly city, before it was renewed with the jewels of virtues and the gold of faith. For this is the city of which John speaks in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared by God” (Apoc. 21).

If anyone thus wisely contemplates divine things [Col. 1206C] and considers what wisdom intends concerning divine matters, what prudence intends concerning matters that are moderately useful, trampling down errors and follies, that person, walking by the way of learning, sees very much and contemplates many things. In learning, avoiding, and retaining such things there is much toil and affliction of spirit.

The wise Ecclesiastes had seen these things; nevertheless, he does not count knowing good and evil among vain things. For to know evil and avoid it is virtue, just as always to do good is the perfection of good people. “I considered all things that happen in the world, and I discovered nothing but vanity and evils—that is, miseries of spirit, by which the soul is distressed with diverse thoughts.”

Yet it greatly profits one to learn what the Pythagorean letter is: broad and spacious on the left [Col. 1206D], but narrow and constricted on the right. The narrow way burdens us; the broad way pleases us. Yet in each there is toil, in both affliction of spirit: how one may turn aside from the broad way, and how one may pass through the narrow one. For who can love virtues unless he fights “against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places”? (Eph. 6). There is toil in fighting and toil in loving. Virtues must be pursued as they stand in the midst of vices. But who resists vices without a struggle? If you are sober, a dog barks on this side and a ravening wolf presses on that. On one side hypocrisy pricks the humble person; on the other, pride. Thus one virtue is surrounded by two vices, and “no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). For virtue lies not in beginning but in completing.

Moreover, those whom heavenly wisdom divinely illuminates have toil and affliction [Col. 1207A] of spirit. For those devoted to wisdom are in a sense indignant that wisdom is closed by many seals, and that its treasures cannot be opened without great toil and contrition of their spirit; and the more they labour, the less they believe themselves to know. They also add toil in order that they may know more. And because they cannot know everything, toil is added to them. Thus much knowledge causes us much indignation.

One person is wise in one way, another in another; and the more a person has attained wisdom, the more he is indignant that he remains subject to vices and far from the virtues that he has abandoned. For he sees another law in his members, opposing the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin and death (Rom. 7). Sighing for the heavenly joys he has lost, he desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ [Col. 1207B] (Phil. 1). But this sighing and grieving is great knowledge; not knowing this is great madness. For it is a great thing to know what one does not know.

It should, moreover, be noted concerning Solomon that he was not wiser than Abraham, Moses, and the other saints, but only than those who had been before him in Jerusalem.

## Chapter II

### Verses 1, 2

I said in my heart: “I will go and abound in delights, and enjoy good things.” And I saw that this too was vanity. I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: “Why are you vainly deceived?”

Ecclesiastes now assumes the form of one who does not know the nature of the good, who considers the luxury of flesh and delights to be the highest good and places all his hope there. Giving little attention to what is fitting and what is not, whither virtue leads and whither error carries one, he lives his life for the moment [Col. 1207C].

Such a person speaks through the mouth of Ecclesiastes: “If much indignation burdens the wise person, and he who adds knowledge adds toil, why should I torment myself day and night with the love and pursuit of learning? Much meditation shakes the bones, consumes the body, and often makes people mad and witless. I am wise enough for myself. Why should I toil to know the arts called liberal? Why should I read Plato, Socrates, and Aristotle? My poverty urges me to provide for myself, to undertake a long hope, to acquire riches, to live with them, and, abounding in so many goods, not to lose the joys of the flesh. Let my flesh delight itself, free from the rule of the mind.”

Ecclesiastes confronts such words, saying: “It is not good to delight oneself in this way [Col. 1207D], living not for the spirit but for the flesh alone: to be swollen with food, to have the heart weighed down by drunkenness, and to be bound by the cares of the flesh as by the fetter of death. I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: ‘Why are you vainly deceived?’”

Therefore, as anger belongs to a human being, but not carrying anger into effect belongs to the wise, so all flesh indeed desires the things of flesh and by certain enticements draws the soul toward deadly pleasures. But it belongs to the good to extinguish the burning of pleasure by a greater love of God, and to subdue the wanton beast by the reins of fasting, so that it seeks not lust but food, desires its rider, and carries its God with measured and composed gait.

Still, I approve honourable laughter; I approve serious joys of the mind. At times it is good to laugh, if the cause is good and there is moderation. Let laughter not be unrestrained [Col. 1208A] or too prone to vice, lest it turn to evil use. As a drunkard wanders and does not know where he is going, so one who lets his laughter burst forth without restraint wanders from the way.

Further, joy is good if its cause is good and moderation is present—if someone rejoices in the Lord. Yet so long as one lives in this mortal body, one ought not rejoice too fully. Since he sees another law in his members opposing the law of his mind, he will account as vanity that which he now sees “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). But one who delights himself more than is necessary is foolish, loving the empty shadow of joy, and will never be able to grasp true gladness. This is the snare and empty shadow by which one is deceived who never deserves to rejoice.

Hence the Lord says: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down in dissipation” [Col. 1208B] (Luke 21); and elsewhere: “Woe to you who now rejoice and laugh, for you shall weep and mourn” (Luke 6).

Certainly Crassus judged laughter to be error; he is said to have laughed only once in his entire life. But this was either above or below human nature. For laughter is proper to human beings, and it is very remarkable that he could abstain from what was proper to him. It was below human nature if, through a defect of mind, he was always sad in avoiding laughter; it was above human nature if, in avoiding laughter through virtue, he fulfilled the precept of Ecclesiastes.

### Verse 3

I considered in my heart withdrawing my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my mind to wisdom and avoid folly, until I should see what is useful for the children of men—the work that they must do under the sun during the number of the days of their life.

Here no one other than the speaker above is speaking; but, assuming the persons of many, he seems to stir up wars or single combats. He now indicates what the spirit desires and what the flesh wishes. The person who above, armed with carnal weapons, reigned amid delight and wandering in the citadel of pleasure, was imposing rule upon the spirit against the dignity of nature. Now the spirit attacks and conquers him with other weapons, with strength recovered. It takes away the weapons in which he trusted and effaces his laws with its own laws.

“Let presumptuous pride,” it says, “yield to the subdued flesh. It ruled unjustly; now let it serve justly under a just ruler. For, as someone has said, we make greater use of the rule of the mind and the service of the body. Let it therefore learn to bear the yoke; let it suffer the bit in its mouth [Col. 1208D]. It will easily be conquered if the seed of vice is removed. Let it abstain from wine, because it becomes wanton when drunk with wine.”

A person stupefied by wine does not know himself; and from what vices will one abstain who does not know himself? One who indulges in wine is not content with simple food; and one swollen with many foods is weighed down in body and soul. One vigorous in understanding, who nourishes himself on a simple diet, can investigate the goods that are from God, which wisdom will reveal to him; he will also investigate the evils that he ought to avoid. Such a person will see what is useful to us, not once or often, but throughout the whole time of life. “He who perseveres to the end, this one shall be saved” (Matt. 10).

Since God created many good things for human use, why does this man forbid his flesh wine alone? We know that wine was created by the Lord for gladness [Col. 1209A] (Ecclus. 31), because it is written: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). The power of wine is apparent even in flowering vineyards, because no serpent or venomous animal can endure for long the scent of a flowering vine. While must is still warm and fresh, it bursts sound vessels if they do not have vents. So wine, drunk immoderately and taken excessively, often bursts and corrupts us.

As fire tests iron, so wine tests the human heart. If the iron is good, fire prepares it for various uses; if bad, it breaks it wholly into fragments for the fire. What fire is more grievous to us than wine? The salamander alone among living serpents cannot die in fire. Since it is the most harmful of all serpents—for by touch alone it infects the fruit of trees—it has from nature the power to live in fire. Certainly [Col. 1209B] I wonder all the more whether the mind can ever live well beneath the fire of wine.

We have many examples of how great evils have often happened through wine. Noah, who first among us discovered the use of the vine, lay drunk and uncovered in his tent, and struck Canaan with the sentence of a curse (Gen. 9). Lot escaped sulphur and fire as he fled, but, more grievously wounded by the fire of wine, could not avoid the embraces of his daughters (Gen. 19). Priests were kept from wine at the time of sacrifice (Lev. 10), lest through wine’s sweetness they lose the reason of their mind.

I believe wine also to be one of the four matters which King Darius proposed for decision (3 Ezra 3). For these four were wine, the king, woman, and truth. Thus the wise rightly abstain from excessive wine, because unless the brain is sound [Col. 1209C], every member will be diseased. Cicero also says: “The chief point of an art is to teach what one should do.”

For there are some who do not know their own measure and are so foolish and senseless that, in movement, gait, dress, and ordinary speech, they give laughter to those who wait for it. As though they understood what adornment is, they deck themselves in clothes and bodily finery and prepare banquets of a more sumptuous table. Yet learning is expected from priests (Mal. 2); such are the precepts of the old Law, and the Apostle writes more fully to Titus (Titus 1). For an innocent and speechless manner of life harms by silence as much as it benefits by example. The madness of wolves must be deterred by the barking of dogs and the staff of the shepherd.

### Verses 4–11

I magnified my works: I built houses for myself and planted vineyards; I made gardens and orchards and planted them with trees of every kind; I built pools of water for myself, to irrigate a forest of growing trees; I possessed male and female slaves and had a large household; I also had herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep, more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. I amassed for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces. I acquired male and female singers, and the delights of the daughters of men: cups and pitchers for service in pouring wine. And I surpassed in riches all who were before me in Jerusalem; wisdom also remained with me. I denied my eyes none of the things they desired, nor did I forbid my heart to enjoy every pleasure [Col. 1210A] and to delight in what I had prepared. I judged this to be my portion, if I made use of my labour. But when I turned to all the works my hands had made and to the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun.

Now that the person has changed, the argument also changes. Ecclesiastes has spoken many superfluous things in describing his magnificence. But if we follow the bare letter, would not Heraclitus and Democritus, the wise men of the world, who in differing moods condemn all things as vain—Democritus by laughing, Heraclitus by weeping—if they had seen or heard of these things, have condemned this king, magnificent and exceedingly wise, for pursuing and approving such vanities?

If he indicated nothing beyond what the letter sounds, Ecclesiastes would not have been better than Sardanapalus, who wrote upon his tomb, declaring what kind of man he was: “How much I possessed, how much I ate, how much I left behind.” Surely the same could have been written upon the grave of an ox or an ass. But although the letter is such in the husk, it is sweeter in the kernel. Whoever wishes to eat the kernel must crack the nut. David says: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” [Col. 1210B] (Ps. 118). If so great a prophet confesses the darkness of ignorance, how much should we think ourselves, little children and almost nursing infants, surrounded by the night of ignorance?

The joy of the world, then, is unpunished wickedness: people may indulge in luxury and fornicate, trifle at spectacles, gorge themselves with drunkenness, and defile themselves with shameful conduct; and famine, fear of war, illness, or any adversity does not punish these evils. Rather, all things are available in abundance, in the security of an evil mind: this is the world’s joy.

But God’s thought is one thing, man’s another. It is great mercy that God does not leave wickedness unpunished and, lest he be compelled to condemn in Gehenna, chastises now with the scourge. “Because of the greatness,” he says, “of his anger, he does not exact [punishment], because he is greatly angry.” Severity is, as it were, fierce truth.

Let us return, then, to the wonderful works of our Ecclesiastes. “I magnified my works; I built houses for myself.” God magnifies the forms of his works which he makes in the world, he who makes all things wisely. He builds many houses for his own, because “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). The diversity of merits rightly distinguishes these dwelling places for us. Christ the Lord comes to people filled with such virtues [Col. 1210D] and makes dwelling places with them. Hence the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3).

“I planted vineyards.” From the plants of our faith has grown the vineyard of God the Father. He digs, prunes, propagates, trains, digs twice, enriches with manure, and surrounds it with hedges and a wall, employing its cultivators at appointed hours; one denarius is given to all, first and last alike (Matt. 20).

“I made gardens and orchards.” Ecclesiastes properly arranges the beds of his garden; but our Ecclesiastes cultivates and arranges our minds—the minds of which the Apostle says, “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 12)—in beds of virtues, so that they may bear fruit in continual greenness. Certainly [Col. 1211A], there are as many beds there as spiritual gifts, as it is written: “To one is given the word of wisdom” (1 Cor. 3), and so forth. “One plants, another waters, but God gives the increase” (ibid.).

“And I planted them with trees of every kind.” The orchard planted with trees of every kind is the Church of Christ, built of holy people, differing from one another in the merits of virtues. These trees bear spiritual fruits; for from them arise love, patience, mercy, gentleness, peace, and the other goods. Although the trees are properly fruit-bearing, there are also woods outstanding in height which, if they do not bear fruit, nevertheless support those that do bear it. For “he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward” [Col. 1211B] (Matt. 10).

“And I built pools of water for myself, to irrigate a forest of growing trees.” What is signified by pools through which water is conveyed, except art and skill, by which use supplies what nature lacks? When many, invited to believe neither by preaching nor signs and wonders, had not obeyed, at last through God’s regard and inspiration they were converted by the help of art and skill, and the good soil bore fruit a hundredfold (Matt. 13).

“I possessed male and female slaves.” The Church nourishes male and female slaves: she trains male servants, trusting in strength, and female servants, fervent in modesty, for the service of their ruler. The male servants are more useful in merits and strength, yet servile fear does not restrain them; rather, spiritual adoption grants that they be called no longer servants but friends of the Lord [Col. 1211C] (John 15). These, counted among the sons, have now learned to cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8; Gal. 4). The female servants, however, are inferior in merits and virtues: perfect love has not yet strengthened them, nor has love yet cast fear out of their hearts (1 John 4).

“And I had a large household.” The Apostle describes the Church’s large household, saying: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4), and so forth. As many members as there are in the body, so many ministers there are in the house of the Church; and as many vessels as there are in the house, so many officers he wishes the household to have. Condition subjects the former; devotion subjects the latter. The rod strikes the former; ready willingness instructs the latter [Col. 1211D]. And we are each members, one of another (Rom. 12), until we come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness (Eph. 4), where there will be neither slave nor free, Jew nor Gentile, barbarian nor Scythian, but God will be all in all (Col. 3).

“Also herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep, more than all who were before me in Jerusalem.” When he says “more than all who were before me in Jerusalem,” this does not concern Solomon’s great glory in having been richer than his father, the one king before him, since Jerusalem was ruled only under Saul. Therefore one must consider more deeply what Jerusalem is, and how Ecclesiastes was richer than all those who had preceded him in Jerusalem.

The Church too has herds of cattle and great flocks [Col. 1212A] of sheep. Oxen and sheep in the Church are those who live simply yet are outstandingly useful. For the sheep nourishes us in four ways, inwardly and outwardly: it feeds the strong with flesh, gives milk to the little ones, covers naked limbs with its fleece, and wards off cold with its skin. So the holy Fathers nourish with the milk of the word those whom they beget by the word of preaching, and fatten them with the flesh of Jesus Christ. Those naked of good works and sluggish from the coldness of the mind, they warm with the heat of inward devotion, being covered by virtue. What clings more closely to flesh than skin? Thus they will be closer to such children in their assistance.

Observe carefully that no multitude is added in the case of male servants, female servants, and household-born slaves; but in the case of oxen and sheep it says, “herds and great flocks of sheep.” For in the Church there are more herds than people, more sheep than male servants, female servants, and household-born slaves. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints” [Col. 1212B] (Rom. 8). Those are sufficiently delicate who wish both to rejoice here with the world and later to reign with Christ. That day will come, will come, when this corruptible and mortal thing puts on incorruption and immortality; then the earth and its peoples will fear the sound of the trumpet (1 Cor. 15).

“I amassed for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces.” If we count the great treasures of silver and gold and the abundant possessions of kings and regions, the Church is richer—not merely than Ecclesiastes, but than all kings anywhere on earth who are called rich. Eloquent speech is represented by silver, and the pure life of the righteous by gold. Hence David says: “The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11).

Worldly learning contributes gold to the Church; the wisdom of philosophers contributes silver also. When the scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13), is brilliant like silver and proved in life like gold, he ensnares the worldly wise in the nets which worldly wisdom itself lays, and the cunning of the divine word captures the cunning men. Truly, prudence of the flesh is caught by its own arts.

How many who come from east and west, and how many kings who rule themselves well, fill the treasures of Christ’s Church with bright and noble wealth—namely, with the silver of faith and the gold of goodness [Col. 1212D]. Offering to the Lord with most devoted and ready mind whatever beauty or honour they possessed, they reserved nothing for themselves out of all things. Their will was that the true Ecclesiastes should be enriched by their wealth and works, and that through him they should therefore be delivered from every evil.

For when the Lord comes to judge, the world will bellow mournfully, and tribe will strike breast against tribe; kings once most powerful will tremble with naked side. Then Jupiter, truly blazing, will be displayed with his offspring; foolish Plato will be led forth with his disciples; Aristotle’s arguments will be of no avail. Then all the righteous will exult and rejoice, saying: “Behold our crucified God; behold the judge who, wrapped in swaddling cloths, cried in a manger. See, Jew, the hands you fastened; see, Roman, the side you pierced.”

[Col. 1213A] “I acquired male and female singers, and the delights of the daughters of men.” The male and female singers in whom Ecclesiastes delighted were scarcely a faint shadow of the singers of the true Ecclesiastes, who continually rejoice in the house of the Church, singing sometimes with their own voice, sometimes with the striking of hands, sometimes with breath of mouth.

Among the male singers are Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name (Ps. 98); for Samuel was not a priest, but a Levite. Among the female singers is Moses’ sister Mary, amid maidens playing tambourines (Ps. 67). The male singers include David, Jeduthun, Ethan, Heman, Asaph, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, and Zechariah; the female singers, Deborah and Mary, the mother of the Lord.

Male singers, modulating heavenly examples in a sweet high voice [Col. 1213B], draw us after themselves, so that we may “run after the fragrance of their ointments” (Song 1). Female singers sing earthly songs in low tones, so that they may console those who are still with them in every affliction (2 Cor. 1). Male singers both understand and sing the mysteries of things; female singers are still learning so that they may be able to sing the mysteries of things.

Male singers, strong against every adversity and full of hope for heavenly desires, sing beforehand in high tones, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3); and David: “I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High” (Ps. 9). “Most High,” he says, means with the highest devotion of heart.

Female singers, subdued while the war of the flesh rages, grieve for their sins and sing in low tones throughout the octave, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” [Col. 1213C] (Rom. 7). And David: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119). And we read in Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). For this purpose we labour and face danger in the warfare of this age: that we may be crowned in the age to come.

Nor is it strange to believe this concerning human beings, since the Lord himself was tempted (Matt. 4), and Scripture testifies concerning Abraham that the Lord tested him (Gen. 22). The companies of angels sing as male singers, rejoicing that they have been so established by God that they can neither sin further nor wish to do so. The angelic choirs sing as female singers, rejoicing with the woman that she has found the tenth drachma which was lost (Luke 15).

An angel, as a male singer, sings aloud at the Lord’s cradle: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good will” (Luke 2). An angel, as a female singer, comforts the agony of the Lord Jesus, seeing bloody drops fall from his body [Col. 1213D] (Luke 22).

“Cups and pitchers for service in pouring wine.” The Church is not without little pitchers and cups. The Son of God himself drank the cup which the Father gave him (John 18). She has smaller pitchers and weightier cups; she has cups of mercy and pitchers of wrath. Mercy gives life; the pitcher of wrath gives death.

When he was eating the last Passover with his disciples, he drank the pitcher of the Law, which was to be removed; he gave the second cup, namely the first fruits of the Gospel, the sacraments of his body and blood. That blood redeems all people and consecrates those redeemed. The Lord drank the pitcher when he drank from the brook on the way, passing to life and paying what Adam owed. Rising from the dead, he received the great cup when he drank the new fruit in his Father’s kingdom.

This also sometimes happens in the Church. Confession gives us the pitcher of faith when, with our members mortified [Col. 1214A], we are tortured in the secrecy of the mind as though in martyrdom. Christ gives his own a greater cup to drink when they give their bodies over to punishment for him, for “no one has greater love than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). What is more pleasing than these things, what more delightful than these delights? Compared with them, the delights of the children of men are nothing.

If we count these delights of the Church, or of Ecclesiastes, we find seventeen: houses, vines, pools, orchards, gardens, male servants, female servants, boys, herds, flocks, gold, silver, the wealth of kings, male singers, female singers, little pitchers, and cups. This number seventeen always consecrates the mysteries of sacred things, whether through the ten commandments of the Law or the seven charisms of the Holy Spirit. For there are ten commandments of the Law and seven charisms of the Gospel.

What a multitude of kinds this number of kinds produces! For if you count together seventeen, sixteen, fifteen, fourteen, thirteen, twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven, six [Col. 1214C], five, four, three, two, and one—as though born under one witnessing mother—you will find one hundred and fifty fish, which Peter’s net of faith drew from the great sea of this world to the shore of the Gospel. As many fish as Peter had, so many riches does Ecclesiastes possess, multiplied in themselves; and what Peter’s fish signify, the kinds of Ecclesiastes signify. Therefore, as Ecclesiastes excelled all who were before him in Jerusalem, so the kingdom of the Church excels and shall excel for ever above all peoples of the earth.

“Wisdom also remained with me.” Democritus is praised by philosophers because he devoted himself so attentively to philosophy that he did not care that other people’s cattle before his eyes were eating and devouring his cultivated field. But Ecclesiastes was worth more than Democritus even in this respect, because, though established amid such great riches as he described, he says, “Wisdom remained with me.” For it is a great thing not to lose virtue of soul amid so much wealth and glory.

But when he says, “Wisdom remained with me,” this is understood not of fullness but of a part. For our Lord Jesus Christ alone was wise without diminution of wisdom; because, as the Apostle says, “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” [Col. 1214D] (Col. 2). Nothing can grow in one who is perfect; nothing is lacking in one who is full. Although it is written of him, “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2), this advance is said not with respect to himself but to those to whom he appeared to advance. For day by day he showed in portions the wisdom with which he was fully endowed without increase.

“And I denied my eyes none of the things they desired, nor did I forbid my heart to enjoy every pleasure.” The eyes of the soul and the vision of the mind desire spiritual contemplation; but the sinner, ignorant of this, keeps his heart from true delight. For this is our portion and everlasting reward, if here we labour for virtues. Whoever is wise and abounds in such great goods as our Ecclesiastes possesses should not defraud either his eyes or his heart of delight in enjoying the goods prepared by living wisely.

“But when I turned to all the works my hands had made and to the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I saw vanity and affliction [Col. 1215B] of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun.” There is indeed vanity and affliction of spirit when one prepares with much labour of mind and body things which it is unlawful to use. And when he says at the end of the sentence that nothing remains under the sun, he marks and rebukes those whom worldly glory and excessively favourable circumstances have delighted. It is foolish to desire things that are vain and cannot endure.

### Verses 12–14

I turned to contemplate wisdom, errors, and folly. “For what man is there,” I ask, “who can follow the king, his maker?” And I saw that wisdom surpasses folly as much as light differs from darkness. The eyes of the wise are in his head; the fool walks in darkness.

A remarkable matter. He who had just been planting, sowing, and building; who had just been seeking whatever the desire and craving of his soul commanded, seeing nothing in human affairs but vanity [Col. 1215C], changes his disposition, alters the use of desire, and turns to contemplate wisdom. If wisdom were easy to find, Ecclesiastes would not seek it so often, sigh for it so often, or return to it so often, as though driven back and summoned forward by hope of victory. If he could easily retain it once found, he would not seek errors and folly at the same time.

But one who wishes to investigate and know good things ought to seek and know their opposites also. For one who wishes to pluck a rose must beware of being pricked by the thorn. What will a person do wisely if he does not know the distinction between good and evil, if he does not see the contraries or opposites of wisdom and folly? Errors and folly very often, through the pursuit and fault of pretence, usurp for themselves the role of wisdom.

If the first virtue is not to do evil, supreme wisdom is to be without folly. But the person who, having known God, then comes to know himself will be without folly. Whoever knows God ought to live according to his example. For the one who imitates the Lord follows him.

Why, then, does Ecclesiastes speak in doubt, saying, “Who is the man who can follow his Creator?” when the Lord himself exhorts people to follow him, saying: “Be holy, for I am holy” [Col. 1215D] (Lev. 19). “You shall be holy and perfect by following me.” Grace therefore gives us the perfection and holiness which he himself possesses substantially; and by following him, we are by grace what he is by nature.

When, then, he says doubtfully, “Who is the man who can follow his Creator?”, he exposes the heart of one who believes wrongly and thinks it easier to stretch out one’s hands against a torrent than to follow the man who is one’s Creator. Then, speaking from his own heart, he receives and supports this person as he falls through despair, as though with shoulders placed beneath him, and says: “Run, my son, run. Take up the shield of faith. Toil and faith conquer the hardest things. God helps the bold and supplies strength. Run; follow God your Creator. He draws after him those who follow him.”

When the first wheel of a cart is drawn, it pulls the following wheel after itself; the latter indeed follows, but does not overtake the former. As the first makes the second run after it, so God helps you as you run and draws you to himself.

“And I saw—and you also see—that wisdom surpasses folly as much as light differs from darkness.” The true light is the Son of God [Col. 1216B] (John 1); he is the true wisdom of the Father. That we are called wise and sons of light comes from grace, not from nature. Light is in the one who clings to the Lord; by comparison with that light, we are called darkness. Yet the person who sees this light with the eyes of the heart, even from afar, is called wise and is wise.

Therefore he fittingly says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head.” For one who has come to a perfect man and has merited that Christ should be his head will always keep his eyes fixed on Christ; raising them upward, he will never think of lower things. For he follows the king who is his maker.

“The fool walks in darkness.” Lacking the reason of light, he does not raise mouth, eyes, or heart on high; he neither follows nor imitates the king who is his maker. He is not among those of whom Christ says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” [Col. 1216C] (John 8).

VERS. 15–17.—And I learned that the end of both is one. And I said in my heart: If the same end shall befall both the fool and myself, what profit is it to me that I have devoted greater effort to wisdom? And speaking with my mind, I perceived that this too was vanity. For there shall not be an everlasting remembrance of the wise man any more than of the fool, and the times to come shall alike cover all things with oblivion: the learned man dies just as the unlearned. Therefore I grew weary of my life, seeing that all things under the sun are evil, and that all is vanity and affliction of spirit.

Ecclesiastes had said that the wise differ from fools as much as light differs from darkness; and he had expounded this in a rational order [Col. 1216D], confirming it with true citations of authoritative sayings. Whom, then, would these words not kindle and inflame to seize the standard of wisdom? Yet once more we are pierced by the two-pronged hook of doubt. For someone who doubts what such a difference can be between wise and foolish persons, since all are of one condition, speaks against Ecclesiastes as though reproaching him: “Why,” he says, “do you distinguish those whom God and nature unite? God does not thus distinguish those whom from the beginning he created from one material of earth, to whom he granted a soul of one nature—for God daily creates new souls in them. Thus God and nature created the unlearned and the learned alike. Although we differ in accidents, our kind unites us in one species. You equate the fool with night, the learned with day. Your promises inspire faith; but hope deferred afflicts the soul” [Col. 1217A] (Prov. 13). “Therefore, lest I become night, so that I may be light and a child of light, I wish to expend all my strength; and, as though prepared to fly heavenward, I am ready to soar like the eagle that delights in the brightness of the sun. But a fact frightens me which frightens even the fool: namely, that one end has been appointed for all; that in dying the wise man differs in nothing from the fool; and that many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’ (Ps. 4). The learned dies like the unlearned; and when he is dead, what remembrance of light will remain to him? What profit is it to him that he bestowed greater effort upon wisdom?”

Ecclesiastes meets these objections and refutes himself, saying: “You complain in vain that you gave greater effort to wisdom: you said these things with your heart, but not while speaking with your mind. You have a fleshly heart; your heart savours what is fleshly and scarcely perceives spiritual things. But the mind, which [Col. 1217B] is the higher part of the soul, perceives more rightly and overcomes vanity and falsehood. The mind surpasses heart and flesh; it meditates on heavenly things and contemplates mysteries. Therefore, speaking with my mind, not with my heart, I know—and know well—that one and the same end does not await all, but that, as they differ in life, so they differ in death. For what everlasting remembrance will there be of the fool? As cattle wholly perish with their bodies, so the fool wholly perishes along with his name, his gold and silver, and his wealth acquired everywhere. His soul, since it is immortal, indeed lives, but amid eternal punishments; it would be better for him if it could die in its substance. But the man who is wise and lives wisely, as soon as he dies, is freed from this body of death and flies freely to heavenly things, changing his life for the better.

“It is better [Col. 1217C] to fight for a short time, bear the rampart-burden, take up arms, grow weary beneath the breastplate, and afterwards rejoice as a victor, than through the impatience of one hour to serve for ever. To those who love, nothing is hard; no labour is difficult to one who desires. Consider how much Jacob endured for Rachel, the wife promised to him. ‘Jacob served for Rachel seven years,’ Scripture says, ‘and they seemed in his eyes like a few days’; whence he himself later recalls: ‘By day I was scorched with heat, and by night with frost’ (Gen. 29, 31). Let us likewise love Christ and continually seek his embrace; then every difficulty will seem easy, and all things that are long we shall consider brief. ‘The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it’ (Matt. 11): unless you knock and do violence to the kingdom [Col. 1217D] of heaven, you will not possess it.

VERS. 18–21.—Again I detested all my labour, in which I had worked most diligently under the sun, because I must leave it to an heir after me, though I do not know whether he will be wise or foolish; and he will rule over my labours, for which I sweated and was anxious. Is anything so vain? Therefore I ceased, and my heart renounced further labour under the sun. For when one man labours in wisdom, learning, and care, he leaves what he has acquired to an idle man; and this too is vanity and a great evil.

Let us apply the words of Ecclesiastes to the Church of Christ. The holy Fathers, outstanding teachers, watchful over the holy Scriptures, laid up treasure for their children. But if we, an age worse than our forefathers, degenerate so badly that we do not turn the writings of the Fathers to [Col. 1218A] the use of life, is this not vanity and a great evil? For we ought to be good heirs of good parents, and meditate upon their writings day and night, so that we may be ready against those who corrupt the holy Scriptures. For although holy unletteredness is good, holy learning is nevertheless better. Holy unletteredness benefits only itself; and, insofar as it builds up the Church of Christ by the merit of its life, so far does it harm if it does not resist those who destroy her.

At the end of his most sacred vision Daniel says: “The righteous shall shine like the stars, and those who understand”—that is, the learned—“like the firmament” (Dan. 12). It is clear how greatly righteous unletteredness and learned righteousness differ from one another. Why is the Apostle Paul a vessel of election? (Acts 9). Surely because he is a vessel of the Law and a treasury of the holy Scriptures. Whenever [Col. 1218B] I read him, I seem to hear not words but thunder. Let us read his Epistles, especially those to the Romans, Galatians, and Ephesians, in which he is wholly engaged in combat; and we shall see, in the testimonies which he takes from the Old Testament, how skilful, how prudent, how dissembling in what he does he is. His words appear simple, as though those of an innocent and rustic man, one who knows neither how to lay snares nor to evade them; but wherever you look, there are thunderbolts. He clings to the issue; he tears apart everything he touches; he turns his back in order to overcome; he feigns flight in order to kill.

Let us now return to what went before. Ecclesiastes seems indeed to be speaking again about riches and possessions: that, when we are suddenly taken away by death according to the Gospel (Luke 12), we do not know what sort of heir we shall leave behind—whether foolish [Col. 1218C] or wise—who will enjoy the fruit of our labour. This also happened to Solomon. For he did not have a son like himself in Rehoboam, who diminished David’s kingdom by ten tribes (3 Kings 12; Ecclus. 47). From this we understand that not even a son is worthy of his father’s inheritance if he is foolish.

VERS. 22–25.—For what profit will a man have from all his labour and affliction of spirit, in which he has been tormented under the sun? All his days are full of pain and miseries, and even by night his mind does not rest: is not this also vanity? Is it not better to eat and drink and show his soul good things from his labours? And this too is from the hand of God. Who will so devour and abound in delights as I?

How varied are the impulses of our nature within us is apparent from the words of Ecclesiastes, who now speaks against the lavish man and now in the voice of the frugal man. “What profit,” he says, “is it that a man always labours under the sun without any return? Labour without fruit is vain. There is someone harsh, excessively devoted to the pursuit of work beyond what is necessary, and patient of toil: neither night nor day does he rest. Who would not pity a man whose whole life is tortured by miseries and hard labours? He never has peace, nor rest; he has no honourable pleasure. When the night ought to afford him timely rest, the continual care of his wakeful heart consumes him. Is not this vanity?” This is from the standpoint of the lavish man.

Another speaks from the standpoint of the frugal man: “By no means,” he says, “should you prevent a man from applying himself to labour, lest the body and heart of an idle person grow numb in heavy lethargy. But [Col. 1219A] I ask: is it not more reputable and more beneficial for the limbs that a person should live in a manner suited to human nature—eating, drinking, enjoying his work, and showing his soul the worthy gains of his labours? He will not be ungrateful to the giver of life and of things, from whose hand these sufficiencies have been bestowed. Certainly, if there is moderation on both sides, then there will be a clean and fitting nourishment for nature.”

Behold, the impulses which Ecclesiastes observed and set forth: impulses that at one time vary among many persons, at another in one person. Setting himself forward as an example, he says: “Who will so devour and abound in delights as I?” As though he said: “I abound in enjoyment, but I do not overflow into extravagance: there is moderation in frugality, moderation in enjoyment.”

This, for the present, according to the letter, lest we seem wholly to pass over the simple sense and, while pursuing spiritual [Col. 1219B] delights, to despise the poverty of the historical sense. For what has wisdom, knowledge, and virtue—in which he testified that he had laboured—to do with earthly wealth, when it belongs to wisdom, knowledge, and virtue to tread earthly things beneath the feet? What good is there, or what gift of God, in yearning after one’s possessions and pursuing pleasure as though it were fleeing; in converting another’s labour into one’s own delights; and in thinking it a gift of God if we delight in the miseries and labours of others?

It is good, therefore, to take the true food and true drink which we find in the divine books in the flesh and blood of the Lamb. For who can both eat and, when necessary, refrain, except the one who commands that what is holy not be cast to dogs (Matt. 7), and teaches how food is to be given to fellow-servants in due season [Col. 1219C] (Prov. 31), and, according to another sense, to eat only as much honey as is sufficient when it has been found?

VERS. 26.—To the man who is good in his sight God has given wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he has given affliction and superfluous care, that he may add and gather and hand it over to one who has pleased God. But this too is vanity and a futile solicitude of mind.

The beginning of wisdom is the source of right living. The good man receives it as the reward of his merits; and, when knowledge of lesser things has also been bestowed, joy is increased for the wise and knowing man. Hence our Lord, exhorting us to wisdom, says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6). No one understands more wisely than he who seeks heavenly things. To him who seeks heaven and possesses earth through knowledge, joy is added as a crown of merit, and he rejoices for ever.

Conversely, an evil man receives, in requital of his merits, that he may be continually weighed down, while pursuing vain cares, by the futile solicitude of his mind. Behold, the sinner, a sinful son of Adam, still hears what Adam heard when he sinned: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; cursed is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). Great, therefore, is the vanity and futile solicitude of mind for the sinner: always to long after labour in acquiring and multiplying possessions, and not to be able to use what he has acquired, because the fruit of his labours is handed over to one who has pleased God.

Therefore we read in the Gospel: “To everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. 25). Thus God transferred Esau’s birthright to Jacob, who was dear to him and consecrated by his father’s blessing [Col. 1220A] (Gen. 27). Likewise Reuben, the firstborn, because he defiled his father’s bed, lost the double portion of the firstborn—namely, kingship and priesthood (Gen. 49). Joseph, the son who increased, was reckoned as firstborn (ibid.); Judah earned the honour of the royal name (ibid.); Levi was adorned with the mitre of the priests (Deut. 33).

Nature, therefore, has great force, but grace works more powerfully. It is said that a monkey bears twin offspring: it loves one and hates the other. When it hears hunters and dogs, it tries to flee, clasping the beloved one to its breast and in its hands; but the hated one, seeing itself abandoned, leaps upon its mother’s back and clings the more importunately. The mother, burdened by the weight of both young, while fleeing in fear of danger throws down the beloved one and transfers her love to the one whom she had previously hated. Thus good hope is worth far more than an evil misfortune.

## CHAPTER II

Although I had previously learned from the ministry of the sacred books that God grants more than is asked of him, and often bestows things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2), yet I have now proved it in my own case, dearest Gregory. But love has no measure, patience knows no limit, and desire cannot endure delay. Therefore, forgetting my own strength and thinking not of what I can do but only of what I wish, I, a disciple, desire to teach a master and, as the common [Col. 1220C] proverb says, a sow [to teach] the discoverer of the arts. You who supplied the first spark to my tinder, who urged me to this study both by word and example, and who, like a hen, gathered her chicks under her wings (Matt. 23), receive, though the style be unpolished, what remains of our Ecclesiastes.

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1–8.—All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted periods. A time to be born, and a time to die. A time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted. A time to kill, and a time to heal. A time to destroy, and a time to build. A time to weep, and a time to laugh. A time to mourn, and a time to dance. A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather them. A time [Col. 1220D] to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces. A time to acquire, and a time to lose. A time to keep, and a time to cast away. A time to tear, and a time to sew. A time to be silent, and a time to speak. A time for love, and a time for hatred. A time for war, and a time for peace.

Why did we wonder that there should be so great a difference between good and evil, learned and unlearned? Behold, wisdom, expanding the mind and heart of Ecclesiastes, led him through the whole world and taught him that the world is diversified by continual alternation in condition and action, and that nothing occurs except through contraries. Therefore, marking with the clearest eye of the mind individual things, times, and causes—setting times against times and things against things—he reduces innumerable contraries to the number of things: not to [Col. 1221A] a number he happened to discover, but to that which natural reason assigned to the matter.

For twenty-eight numbers were created by nature our mother: seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one; if you join them naturally, they make twenty-eight, four times seven. This number also, as is known to arithmeticians, is perfect after the first six; it consists of its own parts. For it has its half, that is, fourteen; its fourteenth, that is, two; its seventh, that is, four; its fourth, that is, seven; and its twenty-eighth, that is, one. Thus fourteen, two, seven, four, and one added together make the perfect sum of twenty-eight.

Therefore, just as through six, in the first order, he who created all things by the Word made all perfect things perfect (Gen. 1–2), so equally through this number, whose proper parts are equal, nature—or rather the God of nature speaking through Ecclesiastes—shows how all things that run through time proceed, and how the things beneath heaven and the sun vary. In this world wisdom always agrees well with nature, and nature never says one thing while wisdom says another.

It is also known that whatever people do, they perform with the fingers of their hands, and the form of the fingers figures what they do. Certainly, as many joints and articulations as there are in the hands—namely, fourteen in the right hand and fourteen in the left, making twenty-eight together—so many are the variations of all things here. As the right hand is opposed and set against the left, so all opposed things are contrary to one another. It is difficult for the human soul not to love something; and it is necessary that, toward whatever affections our mind is drawn, love of the flesh be overcome by love of the spirit, desire be quenched by desire, and whatever is diminished on one side grow on the other. Rather, let it continually repeat: “On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Cant. 3). “Mortify,” says the Apostle, “your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3). Hence he himself later said confidently: “I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Thus it is of no benefit to keep the belly empty after two [p. 528] or three days if it is at the same time overwhelmed.

### A time to be born, and a time to die

Taking occasion from the mouth of Ecclesiastes, according to the diversity of times and things, here the Church and there the Synagogue, as though disputing, declare what seems proper to each.

**SYNAGOGUE.** It was my time to be born when my father Abraham, fleeing the fire of the Chaldeans, almost alone worshipped the one God (Gen. 11), who created all things from nothing.

**CHURCH.** My time to be born was likewise beneficial, when Eve was made from the side of the sleeping man (Gen. 2). I was born with Christ, grew to maturity with Christ, and in the figure of Eve was sanctified from the blood and water of his side (John 19). All who believe in Christ are sanctified with me. But a time to die comes whenever anyone departs from good works, loses life, and finds death. In this order we are born; in this order we die.

### A time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted

**SYNAGOGUE.** It was my time to plant when God planted me (Ps. 79), like a fruitful olive tree (Ps. 51). in the Lord. Moses, Aaron, and the prophets transplanted me, in order to take away from me the sour juices of the natural law and cultivate me, rooted in the second law, so that I might bear sweet and delightful fruits. But the time to uproot will come when, after the branches have been broken through unbelief (Rom. 11), the Jews shall be turned into foul dregs. Mine was a time to plant and a time to uproot.

**CHURCH.** Mine too was a time to plant, when the Lord planted me so that I might be a vineyard of Soreth (Isa. 5; Jer. 2). I am the vineyard; Christ is the vine; Christians are the branches (John 15); spread throughout the whole world, we die. The time to die will come later, when the children of Israel depart from the worship of the most high God. In this order we are born; in this order we die. [Col. 1222B] The believing Apostles and disciples are clusters; the grapes of the clusters are the fruits of those who do good works. But it is a time to uproot, because the Lord says: “If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out as a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns” (ibid.). Mine was a time to plant and a time to uproot.

### A time to kill, and a time to heal

**SYNAGOGUE.** Mine was a time to kill when Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon, Amalek, the foreigners, and the inhabitants of Tyre were slaying me; when at different times the Philistines, Chaldeans, and Assyrians afflicted and killed me. It was a time to heal when, through Moses and Aaron, Joshua, Samson, David, and the Maccabees, vengeance came, though tardy, through these mighty men. It was a time to kill and a time to heal.

**CHURCH.** I ask you, my sister Synagogue: who can heal one who has been slain? What advantage is your vengeance? Vengeance does not heal, but adds deaths to deaths. Your law does not heal: your law punishes the guilty with death. “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin, came, as Simeon testifies, “for the fall and rising again of many in Israel” (Luke 2). He first killed and then healed: he killed sins; he made virtues live. Therefore he says: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32). It was a time to kill and a time to heal.

### A time to destroy, and a time to build

**SYNAGOGUE.** It was a time to destroy the Temple under Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. 52), which grieved me exceedingly; and a time to build under Darius (1 Ezra 6), which rejoiced me altogether. Thus I was destroyed, thus I was built.

**CHURCH.** Spiritual destruction and building make my face glad. If sin dwells in our mortal body, let the strong man arise and put on the arms of virtue. Let him assault the enemy, destroy the city of sin, and restore to Christ the city destroyed by the devil. Let him sweep, cleanse, and adorn the city of his breast, so that the Lord, who has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8), may dwell there when he comes. Therefore we cannot build good things unless we first destroy evil things, just as the word given by God to Jeremiah commanded him first to root up, dig down, and destroy, and afterwards to build and plant (Jer. 1). Thus I was destroyed; thus I was built.

### A time to weep, and a time to laugh

**SYNAGOGUE.** A time to weep hangs over me, when I remember and see the holy city Jerusalem, revered by all nations, so desolated, so bereft of her sweetest children, and subjected to reproach and a monstrous spectacle. Alas for the remnant of my race, taken captive and reduced to servitude—chosen by the Lord himself from among all nations and marked by circumcision, to whom God entrusted his mysteries!
