Behold, the Law inscribed by the finger of God upon the second tables is silent; the ark of God, the throne, and the propitiatory are lost—a portent, for which I am now unhappily no longer to be propitiated. Yet a time to laugh is promised me: the rebuilding of the Temple, and Jerusalem once more to be enclosed with new walls. The restored Law and freedom returned to the nation released from bondage will make things almost equal to the former condition under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. I take the former for weeping, the latter for laughter.

**CHURCH.** In a time of weeping I can scarcely restrain myself from tears, which compunction of heart gives. At first I am pierced by fear, afterwards by love. For, recalling within myself what, how great, and how many things I have done against the law of nature and holy religion, I am compelled to cry: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin; for I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me” (Ps. 50). At last, receiving confidence and trusting in pardon, I am pierced by love. No longer fearing evils, but hoping for the rewards of eternal life, I wholly fail and melt away through longing for the eternal fatherland, as wax melts before fire and snow from the mountains before the sun. But the grace of Christ promises a time to laugh: then the final day will console us all, when the greatest reward shall be given—eternal glory for ever and ever to those who here laugh well. I take the former for weeping, the latter for laughter.

### A time to mourn, and a time to dance

**SYNAGOGUE.** Mine is a time to mourn, because the Hebrew people, stiff-necked and rebellious against their God, perished far from their land, uprooted together with the root of their name. Why should I mention the ten tribes, whom the king of Assyria conquered and transported far beyond the mountains of the Medes, placing them, as it were, beneath another hemisphere? There is no hope of return, no hope of mercy. The two tribes called Judaea were devoured by the fourth beast, terrible and great, which Daniel saw—namely, the Roman Empire—through Titus and Vespasian. Shall I not mourn these things? Shall I not beat my breast? Yet I await a time to dance, when Messiah shall come (John 4) and restore all things to us (Matt. 17). Thus I judge that I must mourn; thus I judge that I shall dance.

**CHURCH.** That there is for you, O Synagogue, and for me a time to mourn and a time to dance, our Lord teaches well in the Gospel. Marveling at the unbelief and hardness of the Jews, he says: “To what shall this generation be likened? It is like children crying to their companions, saying: ‘We mourned to you and you did not mourn; we sang to you and you did not dance’” (Matt. 11). These children are holy teachers, called children because of their simplicity. The Jews, children in understanding and contemporaries of the law of nature, when they heard the words of salvation from those singing and preaching to them, refused to believe in him in whom belief is life (John 6, 11, 17). The children pressed their companions, giving warnings of salvation and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4); but they did not mourn at these words and did not grieve for their sins.

Thus neither time was beneficial to you, O Synagogue. But for me, throughout the five ages of the world, there was a time to mourn [p. 529], because the worship of my Beloved had perished—he who had sent me bridal pledges through the patriarchs and prophets, his confidential messengers. Yet I held firmly the certain, though long-deferred, hope of dancing, knowing that he would come, though late, at the appointed time. While I was thus drawn in alternation—pain on one side, love on the other—at last came the desire of the eternal hills (Gen. 49), leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills (Cant. 2).

And what leaps were ever made by any of all the saints like his? His first leap was from heaven into the womb of the Virgin; the second, from the womb into the manger; the third, from the manger to the cross; the fourth, from the cross into hell; the fifth, from hell to his body, raising it up; the sixth, from earth to heaven. Two leaps still remain: the seventh, when he comes to judge the living and the dead; the eighth, when from judgment he shall leap with his faithful into his glory. Burning with his love and fragrant with his scent, we shall run; and not only shall we run, but we shall also leap, since we wish to run in such a way that we may attain, so that the movement of the body may show the affection of the heart. Thus I judge that I must mourn; thus I judge that I shall dance.

### A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather them

**SYNAGOGUE.** We understand simply a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them as occurring when someone, not rightly guided by the nail of reason, destroys, builds, and changes squares into circles. There was also a time to scatter stones when the splendid Temple of Solomon, that beautiful work which David built in the citadel of Zion, was overthrown by hostile force; and when the second work, which the care of the prophets built after the likeness of the first, so utterly perished and was so completely destroyed that not one stone was left upon another. But a time to gather and rebuild shall come when the golden age arrives and all things are restored to their former state. And we shall marvel that not Jerusalem alone, but even the ashes of Gomorrah and Sodom are restored into great cities. This is to scatter, and this to gather, stones.

**CHURCH.** It is otherwise. For you, O Jews—you, I believe, are figured here—you are stones by hardness of heart, though not by your natural condition, fit for no work of virtue; everywhere you are scattered as worthless things through streets and crossroads. Yet there shall be a time to gather you, because God is able to raise children to Abraham from stones (Matt. 3), once they have first been fashioned by the morals of Abraham. For though their number should be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved (Rom. 9).

Moreover, the Law written on tablets of stone makes you stones, or stony persons, and compels you to scatter stones. Is not this commandment of the Law a hard stone: “Whoever does this or that shall surely die”? (Exod. 18 and elsewhere). Is not this a hard stone: “You shall restore eye for eye, tooth for tooth”? (Exod. 21). It is time to gather and put away these stones, because the Gospel cries out, full of the bowels of mercy and compassion: “I do not will the death of the sinner,” it says, “but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18). Did you not, wishing to test Jesus, desire to stone the woman taken in adultery? But the Lord, justly merciful and mercifully just, confounded you by reason; and, gathering the stones, he acquitted the guilty woman and did not dissolve the commandments of the Law (John 8). This is to scatter, and this to gather, stones.

### A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces

**SYNAGOGUE.** The Lord showed a time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces through Jeremiah, who was commanded to loosen the girdle from his loins. He loosened it and hid it in the great Euphrates (Jer. 13); after a long time, at the Lord’s command, he recovered it wholly rotten and fit for no use. Giving the explanation of that of which he had previously given the figure, he said: “As a girdle closely surrounds the loins, so I embraced the children of Israel with a more abundant love, that they might be my people and I their God. But after they rotted through vices and sins and departed from me, removing them from the embraces of my loins and heart, I myself depart farther from them.” Behold, a time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces.

**CHURCH.** We too, if we do good things, shall doubtless be a girdle. If we love him, he will love us. But if we are foul and rotten, we neither love him nor are loved by him. There was likewise for you, O Synagogue, a time to embrace, when that saying was in force: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1). Now a time to withdraw from embracing has followed, as the Apostle says: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7).

But if we wish to ascend to higher things, we shall see wisdom embracing those who love her: “Honour her,” he says, “and she shall embrace you” (Prov. 4), and holding them more tightly within her arms and bosom. Further, because the human mind cannot always tend upward, think upon divine and higher things, or remain continually in contemplation of heavenly realities, but must sometimes yield to bodily necessities, there is therefore a time to embrace wisdom and hold her tightly, and a time to relax the mind from the sight and embrace of wisdom, in order that we may attend to the care of the body and to those things which our life requires without sin. Behold, a time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces.

### A time to acquire, and a time to lose

**SYNAGOGUE.** It was a time for the Jews to acquire, when a sure hope and sure faith flourished in them, and when, aided by the merits of the holy Fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—they conquered and expelled the Canaanites and acquired for themselves the land of their possessions. Afterwards came a time to lose, when, abandoning their God who had led them out of Egypt, they were struck down and expelled by their enemies. This was a time to acquire and to lose.

**CHURCH.** O wonderful and miserable time—wonderful indeed for us, miserable for you! In this single instant of time our salvation and your destruction coincide: when you lose, I acquire; when you groan, I exult; when you fall, I rise. You die through unbelief; I live by faith and belief.

There is also another way of acquiring and losing. I acquire earthly things and, devoted to cares, give more earnest attention to the active life; but when I am touched by love of the contemplative life, I rejoice to lose all that I have acquired for Christ, for whose love I sigh, saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Cant. 1). There is also another way of losing, which is written in the Gospel: “He who loves his soul shall lose it, and he who hates his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life” (John 12). A great and wondrous saying: how love for one’s own soul may cause it to perish, and hatred prevent it from perishing. If you love wrongly, then you hate; if you hate rightly, then you love. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving. This was a time to acquire and to lose.

### A time to keep, and a time to cast away

**SYNAGOGUE.** How pleasing and how glorious was the time for me when he who neither sleeps nor slumbers kept me (Ps. 120)! One who has him as guardian can do nothing harmful; one who has such a guardian cannot go astray. But because a time has come to cast away (Ps. 101), he has cast me away because of my iniquities. He has now removed the guardianship of the holy angels whom he had set over us, lest we should be oppressed by evil angels. Therefore, forsaken on every side by my guardian, I am oppressed, despised, and cast away, thrown aside as more worthless than seaweed. Thus there is a time to preserve; thus a time to cast away.

**CHURCH.** For me likewise there is a pleasing and most glorious time in which the grace of Christ always keeps those who believe in him. It keeps them in their going in and their going out: their going in to him when we believe, and their going out when we are released from this body. There is a time for you to cast away and to be cast away. You cast away those who believe in Christ by persecuting them; you are cast away by Christ and from the kingdom of heaven—a kingdom from which your deeds cry aloud that you have long since fallen [p. 530]. Thus there is a time to preserve and a time to cast away.

Time to tear, and time to sew. SYNAGOGUE. The time for tearing was when Jeroboam, by tearing me from one body, made unequal portions: when the kingdom was divided, as an ounce divides an as; he granted ten parts to the king of Samaria, while Jerusalem could scarcely retain a sixth; Samaria boasts of being set over ten tribes, Jerusalem over two tribes (III Kings 11). Thus the people once renowned and glorious throughout the whole world were cut off, not only from their kingdom, but even wholly from the name and worship and knowledge of God. [Col. 1226D] Yet the patriarchs and prophets promise us a time of sewing together, since they foretold that we would be gathered from the four winds and reign in Jerusalem. But this hope, prolonged so long, nearly makes me hopeless. For hope deferred afflicts the soul. This is a time for tearing and a time for sewing.

CHURCH. Let it be as you say, O Synagogue; but that rupture destroyed you more completely and crushed you more severely when, as our Lord Jesus Christ was dying for the life of the world, the veil of the Temple was torn (Matt. 27), and all the Temple’s mysteries, which the Law had concealed beneath Moses’ veiling covering, were laid bare. The splitting of the rocks also showed that your heart was of stone, and that you had been torn away from God and cast out from his members. [Col. 1227A] For us, however, there is a time for tearing and a time for sewing, when the grace of Christ, tearing the veil of Moses which the veiled Law concealed, reveals it in plain speech. He himself tears and sews what no one else can tear: for, by tearing the Law, he sews for me a garment of the Gospel, using examples taken from the torn Law. The Law is an old garment, to which a patch of new cloth must not be applied, lest the tear become worse (Matt. 9). For the repair of new cloth spoils the old garment. Old wineskins also, which your Law has sewn, are torn if they receive new wine that must be preserved. The new Law which Christ gave made new wineskins, in which the new and bright wine of the Gospel is to be kept. This time for tearing and sewing was signified by what the Lord said in the Gospel:

> I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd. (John 10)

This is a time for tearing and a time for sewing.

Time to be silent, and time to speak. SYNAGOGUE. It is a time of silence for me, because all things are silent: the Law itself is silent; the author of the Law and giver of the Law is silent; and, angered by my sins, he makes everyone silent. There is no leader, no king, no prophet, no patriarch through whom God’s words used to be signified to me. No one now foresees my future; no one recalls the past to me. What leader sings songs of victory? All the things are silent which, through allegory, prefigured for me the rule of right living. There is neither robe nor oil, no incense, no burnt offering; no trumpet sounds [Col. 1227C] for war, no horn for jubilee; no lyre gladdens its hearers with a sweet song in remembrance of me. I have long been mute; but there will be a time of speaking, when the Messiah, my supreme delight, comes. Then, released by joy from the law of nature, every creature shall declare the praises of its Creator. Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear. Mountains and hills shall sing praise before him, and all the trees of the forests shall clap their hands (Isa. 35, 55). Such was my time of silence, and such shall be my time of speech.

CHURCH. I think, indeed, that the Pythagoreans, whose discipline requires silence for five years and speech thereafter for those who have been taught, derived the origin of this rule from here. Let us therefore also first learn to be silent, so that afterward we may open our mouths to speak. Let us be silent [Col. 1227D] for a fixed time and attend closely to our teacher’s utterances. Let nothing seem right to us except what we learn, so that, after much silence, we may become masters from being disciples. Such was for me the time of silence and of speech.

Time to love, and time to hate. SYNAGOGUE. Alas, through how many changing courses of time I am tossed! How happily I rejoiced when I passed through the time of love! My father Abraham joined me to the Lord to be loved, and God, Esau having already then been rejected, began to love me not by merit but freely, in Jacob. Through that gracious love of my ruler, I counted myself worthy to be preferred above all; I alone pleased myself, as beloved by God above all nations, marvellous to the world through a new Law and new sacred rites. With what love of heart he held me beloved, [Col. 1228A] who said:

> Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye! (Zech. 2)

> … But what should we lovers not fear?

> … What can anyone believe everlasting in the order of things?

So great a love has perished; so great a fire has grown cold. Amid sleeping ashes scarcely a little spark remains, from which a slight fire revives itself. I am full of evils, delivered over to hatreds, burdened with dangers. Thus mine was a time of love; thus there was a time of hatred.

CHURCH. Nature—or rather God, the author of nature—commands us to love one another, as he himself loved us (John 13). Let the bride love her husband, and the husband his bride; brothers one another; fathers their children, and children their parents. He commands that through the affection of love we all be joined into one. Let my neighbour be another self to me; let friend belong to friend. By a new command God thus [Col. 1228B] joins us to one another. How a time of hatred follows this, the Lord declares when he says:

> If anyone comes to me and does not hate father or mother, wife or children, or lands for my name’s sake, he cannot be my disciple. (Luke 14)

This is the new Law: to pursue with hatred what you love, and to love what you hate. If you have a father or mother, a sister or brother, who is opposed to virtue and salvation, let that person be hateful to you and be cherished by no love. What is more dear than foot, hand, or eye? If it causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you (Matt. 5). Or certainly, there is a time for loving the Law and the things commanded by the Law—circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbath, new moons—and a time for hating it, when the grace of the Gospel succeeds it. Thus mine was a time for love; thus there was a time for hatred.

[Col. 1228C] Time for war, and time for peace. SYNAGOGUE. Alas for me! Who does not know the time of war?

> Whoever wishes to know the causes of wars,  
> the sequence of evils through wars,  
> will regret having seen me, because nothing remains of my former prosperity.

I am sustained only by hope, but am distressed by its excessive delay. When the Messiah comes, when the times shall be golden, there shall be so great a peace as to surpass almost all belief. Then, besides many other benefits of a blessed life, there shall occur what the noble prophet Isaiah says:

> The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; calf and lion and sheep shall live together, and a little child shall lead them. Calf and bear shall feed together, their young shall rest together, and the lion shall eat straw like an ox. The infant at the breast shall delight over the hole [Col. 1228D] of the asp, and the child who has been weaned shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk. (Isa. 11, 65)

CHURCH. It is indeed very wonderful and venerable to us that our Lord Jesus, our peace and our joy, places times of war before times of peace, saying:

> I came not to send peace, but a sword. (Matt. 10)

This drawn and hard sword separates all the affections of heart and body that stir up wars against themselves and against their own salvation. Therefore he says, “For I came to divide” (ibid.), etc. The Apostle Paul, in this battle-array of war and peace, forewarns us to arm ourselves with the shield of faith, breastplate of hope, and helmet of salvation, so that we may resist spiritual wickednesses (Eph. 6). How many troops and how many cohorts the sevenfold army leads in this battle-array is well [Col. 1229A] known to those who resist the seven capital vices. While we now wrestle with such enemies, we have a time of war; but the time of peace will grant us victory, when, the vices which the practice of the flesh gathers having been subdued, there shall be peace in our land, where there shall be supreme freedom and supreme delight. Therefore we shall sing joyfully:

> The love of God has been poured out in our hearts. (Rom. 5)

Whence? Ask the Lord’s granary: through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. If, therefore, you receive some rich man as a guest, you suffer cramped conditions: where is he to stay, you do not see; where is a bed to be made ready for him, where for his wife, where for his children, where for his household? “What am I to do?” you ask. “Where shall I go? Where shall I move?” Receive the rich Spirit of God: you will be enlarged, not cramped. You will say to your guest: “You have enlarged my steps” (Ps. 17). When you were not here, [Col. 1229B] I suffered straits; you have filled my little room, yet you have not shut me out, but my narrowness. Receive this guest, and let him not be a guest like passers-by. For he ought not to depart after giving; when he comes, let him dwell in you, and he will give. Belong to him; let him not leave you or move away from there. Hold him completely, and say to him: “Lord our God, possess us.”

VERS. 9, 11.—What profit has a person from his labour? I saw the affliction which God gave to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. He made all things good in their time, and gave the world over to their inquiry, so that man might not discover the work which God has done from beginning to end. Who saw better or more sharply than Ecclesiastes how great an affliction of mind was given to human beings, who are stretched by a righteous desire when they wish to know things [Col. 1229C] above themselves? He whose mind ranged through all creation, whose heart was like the sand of the sea, though exalted in every respect, though exercised by much reflection, could not stretch and extend so broad a mind far enough to know all that Wisdom does and orders sweetly (Wis. 8). Because he could accomplish but a little of this, and did not think that we could know it, he discourages those worn out by searching from discovery.

He who made whatever good things exist made all things good in their proper time, not all things good at every time. Some things are good, yet are not good unless done at their proper time. Some things are good, yet are not good unless done well. Therefore the comic poet says:

> He has won every vote who has mingled the useful with the—

> He will win every vote who considers the demands of the time,  
> and knows how to give to each person what is fitting.

[Note: [Col. 1229D] Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 343. The latter two verses perhaps belong to Rupert himself. EDITION OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.]

[Col. 1229D] Whoever wishes to know and examine everything—what things are good in themselves, what use causal agency, why they are good, when they are good, and in what manner they are good—is burdened by anxiety of heart and affliction of the flesh. What person, guided by reason, can discover the natures of all things, the causes of their natures, and the principles which God has worked from the beginning: this mass of the world, the vault of heaven, the weight of the earth—whether hanging or poised in rest—the risings, settings, courses and returns of the stars, the seven wandering bodies against the fixed sphere, lightning, blasts of wind, the crash of thunder; finally, all things made by God’s wisdom: how they subsist, why and how they come to be? God, not allowing us to lie numb in the lethargic torpor of idleness, gave these things to our eyes and minds to behold, so that one who claims the art of disputing and debating might set down a premise from one side, add another from the other, and draw a conclusion; yet no one from sunrise to its setting can, by meditation, by the eye of the heart, or by speech of the mouth, encompass everything which the Almighty made and which remains from age to age.

There are many arts, and each art has its value in its own practice. Grammar comes first: it instructs us in letters and cases. Music knows the value of the art of singing, arithmetic of counting. Astronomy measures the stars, geometry the lands. Rhetoric extends the right hand; dialectic closes it. Wisdom therefore hedges her house with thorns. If I wish to crawl through them—for who will open the gates to me?—I pay the price in being stretched and torn; if I pass through, I am pricked by thorns. They who investigate so many arts with so many anxieties, examining causes in order that they may seek in words the reasons for what God does, are thus afflicted. Why do you suppose Ecclesiastes said this? So that a person, conquered by contemplating his Maker, whose work he cannot penetrate, may know that he must be worshipped and may embrace the perfect honour of the Maker’s workmanship.

VERS. 12, 13.—And I knew that nothing was better than to rejoice and to do good during one’s life. For every person who eats and drinks and sees good from his labour: this is God’s gift. Those who receive carnally what this letter signifies think that Ecclesiastes speaks in the words of those who believe the highest good to consist in enjoying bodily pleasures, “whose god is the belly” (Phil. 3). The Epicureans allude to no other words when they say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. [Col. 1230C] 15). Since we shall live only a short time, let us now drink in luxury. A long hope of the future is not pleasing for a short life. But Ecclesiastes does not invite us to such feasts; rather, Solomon says elsewhere:

> But write them down for yourself threefold, in counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer words of truth to those who put questions to you. (Prov. 22)

There is in our heart a threefold inscription and rule for the Scriptures: first, that I understand according to history; second, according to tropology; third, according to spiritual understanding. In history, the order of the things written is preserved. In tropology, we rise from the letter to greater things; and whatever was done carnally in the former people we interpret according to its moral sense and turn to the benefit of our own soul. In spiritual contemplation we pass to higher things, leave earthly matters [Col. 1230D] behind, and speak of the blessedness to come and heavenly things, so that meditation upon the present life may be a shadow of future blessedness.

Thus, although Ecclesiastes has displayed the inclination of belly-worshippers, he nevertheless teaches that nothing is better than rejoicing in one’s life, practising good works, and, in accordance with the Apostle, being content when we have food and clothing (1 Tim. 6); and that whatever we can have beyond these things we should spend in feeding the poor and relieving the needy through generosity. Moreover, because the Lord’s flesh is true food and his blood true drink (John 6), according to the anagogical sense the sole good we possess in this age is to feed on his flesh and drink his blood, not only in the mystery, [Col. 1231A] but also in the reading of the Scriptures. For the true food and drink received from the Word of God is knowledge of the Scriptures. Therefore, whenever Christ’s blood is poured out, it is poured out for the remission of sins; you ought to receive it so that your sins may always be forgiven. Whoever sins continually must continually have the remedy. To preach what you have received, moreover, is not pride but devotion. If the bread is daily, why do you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily that which benefits you daily. So live that you may deserve to receive daily. As our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is true Son—not as human beings are sons through grace, but as Son from the Father’s substance—so the flesh which we receive is true flesh, as he himself said, and [Col. 1231B] the drink is true drink.

VERS. 14, 15.—I learned that all the works which God made endure forever; we cannot add anything to them or take anything away. God made them that he might be feared. What has been made remains; things which will be have already been; and God restores what has passed away. Many have disputed much about these matters, and different people have thought very differently. Some, seeing that the causes of events do not correspond to the causes of merits—that evil often comes to the good and good to the evil, and that all alike, with no distinction of merit, rejoice in an equal lot or are burdened by equal disaster—were overcome by the counsel of the Maker. Understanding everything only by appearances, they doubted uncertainly, or rather denied, that God exists and that the world is governed by providence rather than chance. Others, whom sounder reason [Col. 1231C] instructed, grasped the truth from the causes of things. They recognized that God has therefore ordered all things by a fixed principle and commanded the elements to serve human sight, so that, seeing these things, people may understand that there is providence and may fear him, as they understand the Creator from the equality, movement, order, and constancy of things. “For the invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity” (Rom. 1).

Agreeing with these teachers, Ecclesiastes philosophized thus: “With the greatest diligence I learned, and did not idly invent, that all works which God made endure forever with such completeness that we can add nothing to them or take anything from them.” Why did he who rules and made the world make all these things? Surely, that he might be feared, that God might be believed to be true. Why should he be feared? Because he is God; and in Greek he is called **Theos** (Θεός), that is, “fear.” Since God is said to mean fear, he who is God is rightly feared. God alone, therefore, is perfect; his work endures forever, yet is not coeternal with its Creator, because God is eternal, reigning without time, whereas the work is perpetual, remaining within time.

“What has been made remains.” Things which will be have already been, and God restores what has passed away; or rather, the past, present, and future—all that we see—have been, are, and will be. The sun that rises for us existed in the world before we existed, and will rise after we have died. We have named the sun so that from this we may understand that the other things also are the same [Col. 1232A] as they were. If they appear to perish under the condition of death, they do not perish, because they grow again in renewed life; nothing utterly dies, but is reborn and, as it were, returns to life with a certain interest added. And if this is said of all things in the world, there is no doubt concerning humanity: the dead person is reborn.

VERS. 16, 17.—I saw under the sun wickedness in the place of judgment, and injustice in the place of righteousness. And I said in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and then will be the time for every matter. This vanity and vice under the sun is as widespread as the sun’s light is known to extend through the world. Nations and peoples, provinces, kingdoms, cities—the whole world complains of this: a wicked and unjust king sits upon the throne of judgment. What is worse than an unjust king? “The king’s honour loves judgment” (Ps. 98); but, conversely, one corrupted by the arguments of the depraved judges wickedness. This is the wickedness which Zechariah describes in this way:

> This is the ephah going forth. And he said: This is their eye in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead was carried; and behold, one woman sitting in the midst of the ephah. And he said: This is wickedness. And he cast her into the midst of the ephah and put the mass of lead upon its mouth. (Zech. 5), etc.

The ephah, which he called by another name “the eye,” is that intention of which the Lord speaks: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6). Thus the evil eye is an evil intention which bad rulers have when they oppress the righteous because he is poor and exalt the unjust because he is rich. It should be noted and wisely considered that, after saying “this is the ephah,” he added, “going forth.” For that ephah of iniquity is first occupied inwardly, when rulers oppress their subjects in private and wear them down in little assemblies and secret counsels. When, having acquired confidence to condemn and received money, they condemn publicly, the ephah goes forth. Let all who are set over others hear this example. Let them fear first to be an ephah hidden in secret, lest afterwards they become an ephah going forth publicly. For it is written: “If the serpent bites in silence, no less is he who secretly slanders” (Eccl. 10). And the Psalmist says: “He went forth outside, and spoke the same thing” (Ps. 40).

The talent of lead is the weight of judgment or condemnation, surely great and heavy [Col. 1232D] according to the greatness and gravity of the unforgivable offence—that is, of the impenitent heart. For such an offence is wickedness, and the woman’s sitting in the middle of the ephah fittingly signifies its persistence, which we still see today in many people. Bad princes and kings continue to sit in the chair of pestilence because of gifts which blind even the minds of the wise, condemning the righteous and justifying the wicked. It is very remarkable that the woman, who is wickedness, sat in the midst of the ephah, and yet “he cast her into the midst of the ephah.” As the letter reads, how could she be cast into the middle of the ephah when she was sitting in its middle? But the case is otherwise in this ephah, which is persistence in sins: no one is handed over to his or her sin unless that person has willingly handed himself or herself over, according to the saying: “And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. 80); and, “Let the one who harms continue to harm” (Rev. 22). For to cast wickedness—that is, a wicked soul—into it means not to convert it. This occurs when it has reached the fourth crime, as the Lord says in Amos: “For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not overthrow him” (Amos 2).

The first crime is to have had an evil will; the second, to have committed an evil deed; the third, to possess the habit of evil action; the fourth, to resist the law when reproved, or God’s righteousness, and to utter blasphemous words. What punishment is due to this fourth crime, and how great, is indicated by what was said: “And he put the mass of lead upon its mouth.” For the mass or talent of lead, as has already been said, signifies the weight [Col. 1233B] of God’s condemnation or judgment, namely, that the wickedness of this ephah is unforgivable. The Lord himself testifies:

> Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit—that is, whoever knowingly calls good evil and, in despair, does not repent—shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. (Matt. 12)

Finally, what are the two women who lifted the ephah between heaven and earth? We know two women in Proverbs, where it is written: “The leech has two daughters, saying, ‘Bring, bring’” (Prov. 30). The bloodsucker is the devil, who has two daughters, lust and avarice, continually saying, “Bring, bring,” because both are insatiable and never satisfied. They had wings like those of a kite: that is, pride like the devil’s; for, as is written in the Psalm: “Pride possessed them; they are clothed in their iniquity and wickedness” (Ps. 72).

Therefore, when I see evil people rule and lament that good people remain subject to them, I could rightly despair; I could think evil thoughts about the Lord. But Ecclesiastes meets this response and says what the wise person ought to say in such circumstances. Whoever kicks against justice shall not go unpunished, and whoever labours for righteousness shall receive a just reward. The utterly just Judge of the world, examining all things in the general judgment, will give reward to the righteous and requital to the unjust. Then will be the time for every matter, and with a just balance he will separate the good and the evil.

VERS. 18–22.—I said in my heart concerning the children of men that God might test them and show them to be like [Col. 1233D] beasts. Therefore there is one end for human beings and beasts, and the condition of both is equal: as a human being dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and a human being has nothing more than a beast. All are subject to vanity, and all go to one place: they were made from earth, to return together to earth. Who knows whether the spirit of Adam’s children rises upward, and whether the spirit of beasts descends downward? And I discovered that nothing is better than for a person to rejoice 533 in his work, and that this is his portion. For who will bring him to know what shall be after him?

He who wished to be God by knowing good and evil (Gen. 3), and would not have died if he had tasted from the tree of life, by corrupting the nature of the first condition lost all his posterity as heirs of his sin. Ecclesiastes now laments their lot: “I said,” he says, “in my heart concerning the children of men, whom those first human beings Adam and Eve begot, that they left us, their children, nothing of that eternal and blessed life; but God willed that we should be heirs of guilt and heirs of punishment, in order to test us and show, by ruling over us, what we are—whose father, Adam, after transgressing God’s command, wished to be God.” Therefore this complaint surpasses all our complaints:

> If our fathers ate sour grapes, why are our teeth benumbed by another’s food?  
> Given over to cruel death, I always yield to toil: what then am I but a beast? What more can I do than it?  
> Rising and setting, the course of life, one breath—these are equal for us and brute animals; therefore we are rightly placed under an equal condition.

For the sixth day saw human beings and beasts created together; and that first earth from which four-footed creatures were created first made me. Therefore we and the cattle are deservedly recalled to one place. Made from earth, we shall return together to earth. But whence does the spirit come, or where does it go? Who has been able to see and judge an invisible nature? Yet those who boast that they know the causes and hidden principles of things say that the spirit of Adam’s children rises upward, to live there forever; they also say that the spirit of beasts is dissolved with the flesh, or descends into the earth to perish. But who has come from there to teach me of things unseen what remains for me after death?

As I ponder these and similar things uncertainly and waveringly, I finally discovered that nothing is better than:

> Than by gathering the fruit of one’s works and one’s share of labour,  
> to draw from anxious life a pleasant forgetfulness,  
> while it is allowed, and death delays itself on slow wings.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] The middle verse is wholly Horace’s (*Satires*, book II, satire 6, v. 52); the other two are partly Horace’s (ibid., vv. 93, 97) and partly our author’s.]

For who will bring him to this: that he may foreknow what is to happen to him and what will be after death? Ecclesiastes speaks these words in the voice of one who is compassionate and weak; in this way he rebukes carnal understandings. But if you wish to seek the spiritual meaning, you will find something pleasant in having sought it. For, with respect to spiritual understanding, since “the Lord will save human beings and beasts” (Ps. 35), and elsewhere, “I am a beast before you” (Ps. 72), and in all the prophets human beings and cattle are said to be saved in Jerusalem, and the land of promise to be filled with cattle and herds: who knows whether the saint, who is worthy of the name “human being,” ascends to heaven, and whether the sinner, who is called a beast, descends into earth? For, owing to the uncertainty and slipperiness of this life, it can happen that a righteous person falls and a sinner rises. And sometimes one more rational and learned in the Scriptures—that is, a human being—does not live circumspectly, as is worthy of his knowledge, and is led down to hell; while some simpler and more rustic person, called a beast in comparison with a human being, lives better, is crowned with martyrdom, and becomes an inhabitant of Paradise. [Col. 1235A]

The Gentiles also know in part what Ecclesiastes knew. For among the Romans it was customary, at the celebration of a triumph, amid the victorious eagles and laurel crowns, amid many emblems of vain pomp, to carry before the triumphant man’s eyes the tail of an animal fixed upon a spear as a standard; and behind the triumphant man sat a lictor, striking the victor’s side and saying in his ear: “Remember that you are an animal and a mortal human being.” In these practices those who performed them signified that we have a certain comparison with beasts.

But what does it mean that “all are subject to vanity”? If earth is vanity, are heaven also, angels, thrones, dominions, powers, and the other virtues? Yet things which are good in themselves, as created by the good Creator, are called vanity in comparison with greater things. For example: a lamp is as nothing compared with a torch; a torch gives no light compared with a star; compare a star with the moon, and it is cheese; join the moon to the sun, and it does not shine; compare the sun with Christ, and it is darkness. “I am who I am,” he says (Exod. 3). Therefore, if you compare every creature with God, it has no abiding existence. “Do not give your sceptre,” Esther says, “to those who are not” (Esth. 14)—that is, to idols or demons.

CHAPTER IV

VERS. 1, 3.—I turned to other things and saw the oppressions committed under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, with no one to comfort them; nor could they resist their oppressors’ violence, being deprived of everyone’s assistance. And I praised the dead more than the living, and judged happier than both the one not yet born, who has not seen the evils [Col. 1235C] done under the sun.

He who lamented the frail condition of our nature and grieved that we are equal to beasts now laments that we are not of equal condition, that we are not content with the compact of an equal life. “I saw,” he says, “the oppressions committed under heaven, and that the tears of the innocent arise especially from this: that no one deserves to be their comforter, and that the innocent person’s good life cannot resist the sinner, but the whole consolation of those left alone consists in tears. And I praised the dead more than the living, and judged happier than both the one not yet born.”

In comparison with the miseries which oppress mortals in this age, I judged the dead happier than the living, in accordance with Job, speaking of the underworld:

> There those weary in strength rest; all who had been bound are now secure, not hearing the voice of the taskmaster. (Job 3)

But happier than both—the living, that is, and the dead—is the one not yet born. One still suffers evils; the other has escaped the shipwreck, as it were naked. But the one not yet born is happier in that he has not yet experienced the world’s evils. He says this not because the one not yet born exists before birth and is happier in not yet being burdened by a body, but because it is altogether better not to exist and not to have consciousness of being than to exist or live unhappily. So also the Lord speaks concerning Judas, signifying his future torments: “It were better for that man not to have been born” (Mark 14), meaning that it would have been better for him to be nothing at all than to suffer eternal punishments.

Others understand this passage more deeply, saying that those who have died are better off than those who live, even if they were sinners before; for the living are still in battle and, as though enclosed in the prison-house of the body, are held captive, whereas those who have undergone death are already secure and have ceased to sin. Thus John, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women (Matt. 11), is less than the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven and, freed from the body’s burden, does not know how to say with the Apostle: “Wretched human being that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7).

But they say that happier than both is the one not yet born, who has not seen the evils by which people are oppressed in the world; and that our souls, before descending into these bodies, dwell among the heavenly beings and remain blessed so long as they are held in the angelic choir of the heavenly Jerusalem. [Col. 1236B]

VERS. 4.—Again I considered all human labours, and I observed that their enterprises are exposed to a neighbour’s envy; and this too is vanity and superfluous care. What vanity rules in the world more extensively than envy? Envy, which was the first path to death, scarcely deigning to accept an equal and never deigning to accept a superior, cast Satan from heaven and Adam from Paradise; it set the first brothers, Cain and Abel, against one another; it first sold Joseph, and afterward Christ. It stirred Dathan and Abiram against Moses and Aaron, and they went down alive into hell. Nothing is more grievous, more wicked, or more just than envy. What is more grievous, since often the envious person first suffers an evil of which the other knows nothing? What is more wicked than laughing at others’ evils and grieving at others’ good fortune? If you grieve, the envious person laughs; conversely, if you laugh, that person grieves. Who has ever been fortunate enough to escape envy’s tooth? And what is more just than it? It does nothing unpunished: it avenges upon itself whatever it sins against in me. The envious person is gnawed and gnaws whenever he wickedly hates. This too is vanity and superfluous care: that one person envies another because the other acquires good things.

VERS. 5, 6.—The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh, saying: “A handful with rest is better than both hands full with labour and affliction of spirit.” Now you may see one person sink into one vanity and another into another. Above, he had complained that one full of riches was subject to the envy of neighbours; now [Col. 1236D] he presents the words and posture of the slothful fool, who, foolishly avoiding one vice, runs into its opposite. Poverty, the cause and nourisher of hunger, meets the person fleeing envy; nor is base negligence absent. This person deserves to be pelted with cow dung: hyperbolically, he eats his own flesh and does not perform the good which bodily need requires, nor does he devote himself to the good things required by the needs of the soul. He consoles himself in his heart, saying: “Let the rich man, burdened with vices and riches, lie exposed to envy and suffer many dangers because of his labour. I think otherwise; I provide for myself rather better. A handful with rest is better than both hands full with labour. Content with my poverty, I shall live without care, so that I may lead a long and secure life. Far from me be labour; far from me be contrition of heart.”

[Col. 1237A]

> The empty traveller will sing in the robber’s presence.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 10.22.)

VERS. 7. — Considering, I found yet another vanity under the sun: there is one man, and he has no second—not son, not brother—yet he never ceases to labor, nor are his eyes satisfied with riches; nor does he reflect, saying: “For whom do I labor and deprive my soul of good things?” This too is vanity and a most grievous affliction. Natural affection seems to excuse the person who cares and provides for those nourished by his household concern—his brothers, wife, children, and servants. Yet it does not absolve him from vanity, since all things are vanity, because he prefers earthly things to heavenly. But the man from whom nature, and the God of nature, has cut off all the ties of natural affection—so that he has neither brothers, children, spouse, nor dear relatives [Col. 1237B] for whom and on whose behalf he might labor earnestly—if he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it (Ps. 38), what can be judged more vain or more foolish?

He is alone: he is not worthy to have God as his companion. He has no brother—than whom none is dearer to him—a brother who is helped by a brother and is impregnable (Prov. 18); for one who has no brother, who has helped him as a brother? Nor has he a son: by whom has he himself stood in a father’s place? By the example of his life he has begotten no one for Christ; by the support of his goods he has begotten no son for himself. This man defrauds his own soul of good things; or rather, for whom does he labor? For himself: while he feeds his eyes only with riches, his soul is satisfied by none of his riches, because he shall not see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps. 26).

VERS. 9–12. — Therefore it is better for two to be together [Col. 1237C] than for one, for they have profit from their partnership: if one falls, he is supported by the other. Woe to him who is alone, because when he falls, he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they warm one another; how shall one alone be warmed? And if someone prevails against one, two resist him. A threefold cord is not easily broken.

Having rejected the solitary man and marked and reproved his labor, Ecclesiastes passes to those who are harmoniously united and love one another mutually. What better thing, what sweeter thing, can a man possess than one with whom he may speak all his secrets as though with his own heart? Love conquers all; no bitterness conquers it. Ever higher than earthly things, it soars on two wings. It now tears apart, now sews together, now joins all the affections which the use of nature seems to produce. “Love is strong as death” (Song 8), [Col. 1237D] a love scarcely found in full measure during the five ages of the world among the friends whom it does not concern me to enumerate.

For what is it to us that, maddened by the Furies, Orestes killed his friend Pylades; that the three-headed dog would have devoured Pirithous, had Theseus not rescued him from the three-formed mouth; that Tydeus loved Polynices, Patroclus Achilles, or Damon Pythias so loved one another that Dionysius wished to be one of them—he who was no one’s friend and had no one dear to him? In them he marvelled that love was stronger than death:

> He marvels at this man as a pledge in death,  
> and at that man as faithful under death.

But let the Gentiles sing their own songs; let fable chatter to itself that Pollux redeemed his brother by an alternating death, signifying that the twin stars named after them rise alternately [Col. 1238A] and set alternately. Let us turn over divine matters; let us return to what is ours.

“Woe to him who is alone.” For by whom shall the solitary man be comforted? An unjust brother struck and killed Abel when he was alone (Gen. 4). Lot alone was taken captive with the Sodomites; Abraham, his uncle, having struck down the enemies, freed him (Gen. 12–14). Aaron helped his brother Moses; conversely, Aaron would have perished through his lapse in making the calf, had he not risen again aided by the prayer of Moses his brother (Deut. 2). Jonathan loved David, and David Jonathan, with a singular love (1 Sam. 18). Why say more? Above all is set forth the one and only Lord Jesus Christ, who, having loved his own, loved them unto the end (John 13). He himself also said: “If two of you agree concerning any matter whatsoever that they ask, [Col. 1238B] it shall be done for them by my Father” (Matt. 18). And again he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18).

What mediator is better than he? If he is with you, if you two are one, you will have the benefits of a blessed companion: for he supports you when you waver, he raises you when you fall. If a strong armed man prevails against you alone, resist him more strongly, with Christ fighting beside you. Love is not alone, nor will he be less than two. Though one person is seldom strengthened, many are made firm by love; if two are one, the bond of love is firm. If two are one in Christ, nothing is firmer than this knot, nothing harder than this strength. And if you believe in one God under a threefold name, you may far more readily break a threefold cord than dissolve the knot of such a union.

[Col. 1238C] But alas, how many—grievous sorrow!—though made threefold by the bond of faith, are, however difficult it may be, torn away from the piety of Mother Church. Such a cord was also present in Judas the apostle; but because after the morsel Satan entered into him (John 13), that cord was broken. He says therefore: “A threefold cord is not easily broken.”

Ecclesiastes, wise and prudent in his words, when he said this, did he perhaps make the cord threefold? He did not say “threefold” nor “cord” without cause. Nor did he use the word *rope* (*funis*), but *little cord* (*funiculus*), its diminutive. In the little cord, therefore, is shown the long succession of ages, extending and coiling the chain of causes and the revolutions of affairs, which we pursue from sunrise to sunset. If you wished to compare all this unstable time with perpetual eternity, one day in the courts of the Lord would be longer than thousands (Ps. 83); eternity exceeds time more than a long rope exceeds a shorter cord.

[Col. 1238D] Since profound mysteries are marked by definite numbers, is there any number more rightly sacred than three? Without three, no thing, art, or cause is denoted. Wherever I turn, wherever I resort in reading, I see almost everything bound by a threefold cord. For all things are tripled: beginning, middle, and end. Without the connection of three, no body whatever is made solid: for it is long, broad, and deep. There are three ages of the world, and in them three laws: the natural law, the Law of Moses, and the law of the Gospel. The threefold cord which dialectic binds by proposing, [Col. 1239A] assuming, and concluding is very difficult to untie.

God made all things according to the pattern of numbers and set his final hand upon all things by means of three. For one, two, and three, if joined together, make six; and behold, through its three parts he shows that God himself delights in the odd number three. By three things—measure, number, and weight—God made created things; and he distributed them into three: heaven, sea, and earth, tripling time into present, past, and future. Should faith, hope, and charity be absent from these? Yet all is surpassed by the fact that for three days and three nights the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth, as Jonah was in the belly of the whale (Matt. 12; Jonah 2); and that on the third day the Lord Jesus rose from the dead; indeed, above all, by the fact that the very wisdom of God, unknown to all men, is distinguished in three persons [Col. 1239B] and revealed to the faithful according to his will. Such a cord, then, does Ecclesiastes make threefold for you: not one twisted from the bark of the linden, or from flax or hemp, but one joined to itself by the threefold bond of realities.

VERS. 13, 16. — Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who does not know how to look ahead. For one may sometimes come forth from prison and chains to a kingdom, while another, born in a kingdom, is consumed by poverty. I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second youth, who will rise in his place. The number of all the people who were before him is infinite; and those who are to come afterward will not rejoice in him. But this too is vanity and affliction of spirit.

Ecclesiastes, most careful to know the vicissitudes of all things, teaches what kind of wheel drives a reigning man and rolls him beneath its circuit: [Col. 1239C] now raising him up, now casting him down to heights or depths; lifting one from prison to a kingdom, and shutting in prison one cast down from a kingdom. Thus the order of all things is always rolled about. Those who delight in the simple sense of the words are content with this; one more eager and wise will seek more deeply who the king is, who the youth is, who the young man is, and who the second is.

Behold, O man, you may learn what you are; you may learn, I say, who you are. You will be youth, old man, king, or former king; foolish or wise; poor or rich. Certainly you yourself will be both the first youth and the second. You alone will be all things; in all things you are all and one; and, changing the role of person, you are always other and the same. Man, however, is not simple but double in one body: there is the carnal man and [Col. 1239D] the spiritual man. The carnal man serves the flesh; the spiritual man, the spirit.

> Each is drawn by his own pleasure.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* II.65

Without, the carnal man thrives; within, the spiritual man thrives. One is outward in years; the other outweighs him in merits. Whatever you possess outwardly, you retain inwardly as well. And as the carnal man advances outwardly through age, so human virtue gives perfection to the inner man. Thus here you are a child and there an old man; here a youth, or the second; now a king, now wise; likewise you are foolish and poor.

The outward king, a child, lives without wisdom; and because sinful infancy lacks law, he rules as an impure child, unworthy of the name of child. He neither governs nor is governed, and is unworthy of the name of king. Hence the saying: “The child a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. 65). But the inward king, a child, is not without the law of God: he is a child, [Col. 1240A] he is pure, worthy of the name of child; he governs and is governed, and is worthy to be called king.

After the general proposition, plain to all, that a poor and wise youth is better than an old and foolish king, and that it frequently happens that the former, through his wisdom, even coming out of the king’s prison, rules in place of a perverse ruler, while the foolish king loses the dominion which he held, we may interpret this passage concerning Christ and the devil. We may understand Christ as the poor and wise child: a child, according to the saying, “It is a great thing for you to be called my child”; poor, because “though he was rich, he became poor” (2 Cor. 8); and wise, because “he advanced in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2).

He was born in the kingdom of the old man, and therefore says: “If my kingdom were of [Col. 1240B] this world, my servants would certainly fight for me, that I should not be delivered to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not of this world” (John 18). In the kingdom of that foolish old man, who showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory (Matt. 4), the best child was born. From the house of prisoners, concerning whom Jeremiah speaks in the Lamentations, saying, “To humble under his feet all the prisoners of the earth” (Lam. 3), he proceeded to a kingdom; and he goes into a far country against those who would not have him reign over them, and after a little time the king returned (Luke 19).

Therefore Ecclesiastes, in a prophetic spirit, saw all the living who can share in the youth who says, “I am life” (John 14), abandon the old foolish king and follow Christ. At the same time, the two peoples of Israel are signified: the former, which existed before the Lord’s coming, and the latter, which will receive Antichrist in place of Christ. The former has not been utterly rejected, for the first Church was gathered from Jews and apostles; and at the end the Jews, because they will receive Antichrist in place of Christ, will not rejoice in Christ.

VERS. 17. — Guard your foot when entering the house of God, and draw near in order to listen. For obedience is far better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what evil they do.

Ecclesiastes commands only that one’s foot be guarded when one enters the house of God, as though no watch over the other members were enjoined. But by the name “foot” the intention of the mind is signified: by it we are directed aright; by it the cause of all things [Col. 1240D] is discerned. He is directed aright who walks with a straight foot. “If your eye is single, your whole body shall be full of light” (Matt. 6). Know, therefore, that it is good if you properly frequent the temple of God; believe it is good if you reverently attend holy things. You enter the house of God worthily if you ask the Lord for that which you ought rightly to be heard asking. You guard your foot if you gladly advance to good works. If you ask for unworthy things, you do not walk well with an uncertain foot.

But one who stands far from the Lord and is remote from him does not hear him, because he is not ready to obey him. He stands beside God and hears the Lord near at hand who performs the commands established by law and grace. Enter God’s house in such a way: for you make a useful vow when you send prayers from a pure heart to the Lord’s ears—not if you sacrifice a thousand [Col. 1241A] oxen with a numerous herd; no more acceptable victim will approach which can cleanse sin.

For the sacrifices of the foolish Jews were destroyed and condemned along with their masters, as it is written in Zechariah: “And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold a flying scroll. And he said: What do you see? And I said: Behold, I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits and its breadth ten cubits. And he said to me: This is the curse that goes forth over the face of all the earth” (Zech. 5), and so forth. This was to happen because the Jews would not believe in Christ and would persecute and kill the preachers of the Gospel; therefore all the curses of the Law which Moses wrote in Deuteronomy would come upon them, such as: “Cursed shall you be in the city; cursed in the field; cursed shall be your storehouse” [Col. 1241B] (Deut. 28), and so forth.

The flight of the scroll, therefore, signifies the swiftness of the coming curse, because, as the Psalmist had said, “Let his name be blotted out in one generation” (Ps. 108), it was to be so—and it was so done—that the curse and vengeance upon the Jewish people were not delayed beyond forty years. The length of the scroll, that is, of the curse, is the eternity of condemnation; its breadth is the temporality of tribulation. For unbelieving Jews, in vengeance for the blood of the Lord Jesus and his prophets, are condemned both in the present age and in the age to come. The breadth of the curse is indeed ten cubits because the temporal tribulation by which they fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations is a just vengeance for their transgression of the law of the Decalogue. [Col. 1241C] But the length of the same curse is twenty cubits, that is, double, because eternal condemnation will punish not only the body, as present tribulation does, but both soul and body in the fire of Gehenna.

“This,” he says, “is the curse that goes forth over the face of all the earth”—and certainly first over the land of Judaea. For “wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress” come “upon every soul of man who works evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Greek” (Rom. 2). And indeed the sequence of the present prophecy demands that “the face of all the earth” here be understood as the entirety of the land of Judaea which received the Law: not Jerusalem alone, but all the cities of Judaea, because the curse flew over that whole land [Col. 1241D] and was poured out over that entire nation.

Hence it is further said: “For every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged; and every one who swears shall similarly be judged” (Zech. 5)—as it is written there, namely in the scroll of the curse (Deut. 28). From “Cursed shall you be in the city” down to “Cursed shall you be when you enter, and cursed when you go out,” it is easy for anyone wishing to read and count them to see how many and how dreadful sentences of curse are expressed by name in uninterrupted succession. There are thirty such sentences; most are taken from imprecatory declaration. The first is: “The Lord shall send upon you famine and hunger”; the thirtieth: “He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail.” For Moses himself confirms that they are words or sentences of curse, concluding thus: “And all these curses shall come upon you, and pursuing you shall overtake you, until you perish” [Col. 1242A] (Deut. 28).

After this he declares other matters likewise belonging to the curse, though not in the manner of one uttering imprecations, but in that of one announcing and speaking prophetically. I have said these things because it truly contains something worthy of consideration and wonder that precisely as many sentences of curse were prescribed as silver pieces were given for the price of the Lord’s blood. In Psalm 108 also, if you count carefully, you will find the same number of curses: the first is, “Set a sinner over him”; the last, “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double garment.” Is not the mind, delighted especially by these points, right to join and combine the number of the scroll’s length with the number of its breadth, so that its total measure is thirty cubits, just as there are thirty sentences of curse? Thus there were thirty silver coins which the thief—that is, the assembly of the Jews—gave as the price of the Lord’s blood.

Finally, as length and breadth make one magnitude, so the ten cubits of breadth and twenty cubits of length rightly come together and make thirty. And who does not know, who doubts, that what he says came to pass: “Every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged; and every one who swears shall be judged accordingly”? “I will bring it forth, and it shall come to the house of the thief [Col. 1242B] and to the house of him who swears falsely by my name; and it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume it, with its timber and its stones” (Zech. 5).

Who does not know, who has not heard, that this happened altogether in this manner? For that scroll of curse came to the house of the thief, to that house which, though it ought to have been a house of prayer, had become a den of robbers and a house of commerce (Matt. 21). And the thief who had done this had added perjury to his robberies in that house; indeed, he had deceitfully and fraudulently put the very Son of God under oath, one of them saying: “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 26).

Every such thief and every such one who swears or adjures—that is, both people and priest—was judged, as it was written there, altogether as Moses wrote; and the curse consumed him, his timbers, and his stones, so that the timbers were burned in flame and not one stone of that whole house remained upon another [Col. 1242C] (2 Chron. 36; Matt. 24).

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 1242D]

“We have,” says the Apostle Peter, “the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the morning star rise in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1). It is sweet to hear, sweeter to experience, that the prophetic word is a lamp burning and shining (Ps. 131), by which, certainly, the Holy Spirit ministered to his Christ; and by this lamp he may be seen in this night through a mirror in an enigma, until that day dawns when he is to be seen face to face (1 Cor. 13), in eternal vision.

Let this be our purpose: that in the light of this lamp we may not desire to rejoice, not for an hour, but for the eternal glory of that same Christ (John 5). The beginning of this rejoicing is that, meditating on prophetic testimonies, we may know in part and ourselves also prophesy in part, until that which is perfect comes and that which is in part is abolished (1 Cor. 13). With this singleness of eye, let us, having proceeded thus far, pursue the bright order of our Ecclesiastes—the lamp that truly shines. In its light it is fitting for every soul that loves Christ’s brightness with unfeigned charity to rejoice in heart and mouth; and this is our hope which wisdom promises: that a man shall be satisfied with good things from the fruit of his mouth. A considerable and most beautiful part of Ecclesiastes has therefore been traversed; now, dearest brother Gregory, let us pursue the remainder.

## CHAPTER V

VERS. 1–2. — Do not speak rashly, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word [Col. 1243B] before God. For God is in heaven and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few. Many cares are followed by dreams, and in many words folly is found.

Ecclesiastes, wishing to draw man back from every vanity, carefully warns him neither to utter anything with his mouth nor to whisper anything in his heart before God, who sees the heart and governs the mouth. Yield, O man; yield to your God. Lay yourself beneath him, because he is far higher than you. For he dwells in heaven, the highest and most exalted One, seeing lowly things from on high. If you can touch heaven from earth with your hands, then you may also attain by human words to what the nature of God is, what his supreme substance is. Hence, if you say anything or turn anything over in your heart, say nothing rashly; turn nothing over rashly in your heart. Be brief in speech; be faithful and teachable in heart.

As many dreams follow many cares, so very many vain things follow many words. Talkative people have rarely been without the mark of folly. Who can believe that he who is above all things can be comprehended by human minds? Yet it is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). You, therefore, should read the writings of the saints, and wisely believe what you cannot understand concerning God. For it is useful not to know what is dangerous to seek. But many, speaking rashly and more hastily than is right before God, because they refuse to hold the two reins of heart and tongue, fixing their eye upon the rays of divinity, are led astray by the reflected light of a corrupted mind, [Col. 1243C] and, stripped of humanity, become like beasts—gross in savagery and loquacious in chattering.

VERS. 3–4. — If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it, [Col. 1243D] for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him; but whatever you vow, pay. It is much better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfil what was promised.

The divine and human law, old and new, commands that if you vow anything to God, you must fulfil it, lest you become guilty concerning your vow. When has the violation of vows ever gone unpunished? Jephthah’s only daughter was made of little account because of his vow, in whose killing he fulfilled his vow (Judg. 11). Yet evil vows are not to be fulfilled. The people of Israel on Mount Sinai, in the darkness of the cloud, having heard the words of the Lord giving them the law, said: “All that the Lord has commanded we shall do” (Exod. 24); yet frequent vengeance pressed upon them as persons guilty both of their vow and of sin.

The Lord, authorizing this principle, said: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). He also added an example of not looking back: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17). Fleeing Sodom but returning to it in her mind and looking back, with her face turned back along with her mind, she was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19), giving a useful example to every age that a vow must not be treated rashly. She stands as she stood; as she looked then, so she looks now, displaying the fault that transformed her form. You may see her individual members: legs, feet, calves, belly, groin, breast, arms, mouth, nostrils, eyes, forehead, and even hairs. From this marble body of salt a certain moisture flows, which herds and flocks lick without any harm; and the more they lick, the more there is for them to lick. [Col. 1244B] By this sweet and savory example God seasons us and, as it were, makes us peppered. The example lives, although in the image nothing lives.

VERS. 5–6. — Do not give your mouth so as to make your flesh sin, nor say before the angel: “There is no providence,” lest God perhaps be angered by your words and destroy all the works of your hands. Where there are many dreams, there are very many vanities and innumerable words; but you, fear God.

Spirit and flesh struggle against one another in us with great conflict, and each has its own will. “The Spirit is what gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6); “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26). Therefore, that you may be a more prudent, ready, and wise person, Ecclesiastes warns you not to loosen the reins of the untamed flesh that wanders, nor the reins of the untamed tongue that speaks. [Col. 1244C] “Do not,” he says, “give your mouth over to the contagions of the flesh.” He does not forbid you to open it when you wish or close it when you wish. Open it for good things; keep it locked against evils.

But he indulges the flesh too much and governs his mouth badly who, opening his mouth to vanity, dishonors himself with such words as these: “I am flesh; I am subject to a fragile condition; a short life remains. What profit is there in losing this little life? Since I am flesh, and flesh is subject to death, I shall nevertheless live in a manner suitable to fleshly nature. Who will threaten me with a future judgment, when I shall receive whatever my life deserves? Ignorance or forgetfulness will conceal what I do. Chance governs the world: what ordering of things is there? None at all.”

Whoever opens his mouth to say such things has been given over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are unfitting (Rom. 1). But why did he say “flesh,” when he might more reasonably have said “mind”? For who makes the flesh sin except through the mind? Those who are flesh sin; those who are not flesh do not sin—those who are begotten of God the Father more by mind than by flesh.

Therefore those are mistaken who say that there is no ordering of affairs in the world and that fortune rolls all things about. Nothing is undistinguished; nothing is ungoverned. God holds heaven; angels the ether; we inhabit the earth. The angelic order is distinguished into nine ranks; each is marked by its proper name, indicating the rank that befits it. Some preside over others or stand in harmonious order; some praise the Lord; others are sent in service for our salvation, visiting peoples and governing kingdoms. To each of us an angel is given [Col. 1245A] to guide us to good, remove evils, and lead us to what is right.

Thus the Lord Jesus, showing us childlike humility in a child, said: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 14). Therefore let your angel be your safe guardian. If, in his presence, you open your mouth to speak evil, he will not be your guardian but your most severe avenger. Whatever you do, whatever you say, he who accounts no filth of sin as negligible penetrates the secrets of the heart. He who relies on innumerable words broods over the dreams of an old sick man. You who know who and what God is, who governs all things: fear him by loving him, who rules the world.

VERS. 7–8. — If you see the oppression of the poor, violent judgments, and justice overthrown in a province, [Col. 1245B] do not be astonished at this matter; for one higher than the high watches, and there are others still higher above them; moreover, the king of the whole earth rules over one who serves.

Ecclesiastes anticipates the mind and will of one who refuses to believe that the world is governed by law because the impiety of injustice holds dominion. Do not wonder, he says, that a wicked person harasses the poor, or because supreme law is often supreme evil to you. Whoever is wicked will not depart unpunished, nor will one punished unjustly go unavenged. The due penalty will come to evil, though with a limping foot. “He who is filthy, let him be filthy still; and let him who is righteous be justified still” (Rev. 12).

If you consider the condition of our nature, those who share the same lot receive the same law. But freedom of choice, which has now corrupted everything, has taken away equality in the condition of life. One rules; another is subject. You abound in resources; I lack even scant provision. One governs; another is governed. One serves; another rules. One punishes; another is punished. We deserve this through freedom. Virtue, vice, force, sloth, deceit, skill, and law make unlike those whom the Creator made alike. Fault made them such; grace did not make them such. Who, then, will attribute these things to God? Who will reproach him because we suffer evils which we earn the right to endure?

Not human beings alone are marked by this lot of inequality, nor does inflicted oppression harass only the poor. Fish, beasts, birds, and black serpents, which mother nature created, are unequal in their lot. Whence comes trickery among fish, or fraud among brute animals? By skill, beast deceives beast, fish deceives fish in the water. There is a wolf on land; there is a wolf in the sea: both are glutted with nearly the same madness of appetite. [Col. 1245D] One predator devours another predator, and yet another devours him. The locust that devours many things is devoured by the *seleuce* [an uncertain zoological term]. Who gave the eagle dominion among birds? Who gave the lion dominion over every kind of beast? He terrifies all by his roar; no one terrifies him.

But lest I be astonished at myself, nature thus instructs me, knowing how to distinguish law and right by a sure boundary: it holds me under its right and restrains me by its law. Nature maintains the law God set before it. It has also received laws as bridles laid upon it, lest it roam more freely than is right. We were all created equal, yet the prescribed law prevents us from being equal, because the use of nature admits more and less. We are unequal in strength, abilities, and practical skill, receiving more or less. The honors of the world are also unequal, and earthly dominion is distinguished by its ranks.

[Col. 1246A] Why, then, should I wonder if I am restrained by right or law? This man surpasses me; one greater rises above him. There are others who rise higher still above them and govern, just as a king surpasses those whom the mechanism of the world serves. Ecclesiastes said nothing other than what Peter or Paul, and God himself, would say. For Paul says: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13). Again: “Let every soul be subject to the authorities” (ibid.). And the Lord says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22).

He who presides over many recognizes the world as subject and marvels at the reciprocal order: that one and the same creature both serves and rules—the lion serves small creatures, the fly rules larger ones.
