He whom many fear also fears many; and he whom small creatures fear, though great, fears small creatures. Why does the elephant fear the mouse? Why does the lion fear the white cock? The scorpion kills the very strong lion by stinging it, and the dragon brings down the enormous elephant by guile. Understand “kings” either as those who surpass princes, whom the true King exercises here in the shadow of kingship; or, more truly, understand the rulers of heaven—not as governing individual or public kingdoms. Recognize that even these are equal not in merit or rank, but in name and function. For no power is equal to another. In God alone is there equal and supreme power.

VERS. 9–11. — The covetous man will not be filled with money, and he who loves riches will gain no fruit from them; this also, therefore, is vanity. Where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them. And what profit is there to the possessor, except that he sees his wealth with his eyes? Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, [Col. 1246C] whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not permit him to sleep.

The saying is true: the covetous man is always needy, for not even God himself fills his heart. The people hiss at him; the covetous man alone praises himself. The great Saint Paul, vessel of election, compares him to an idolater (Eph. 5). Though all detest the covetous man, God himself condemns him all the more by his own word, saying: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6). Mammon is the god of the covetous, the god of the greedy. He who worships it does not worship me, but departs far from me. And if a humped camel could pass through the narrow eye of a needle, then the rich covetous man would enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19). But both are impossible: neither does a camel enter a needle, nor will the covetous man enter heaven.

You who store up for yourself and feed your soul as though on an empty picture, hear what is said to the rich man in the Gospel: “This night your soul shall be taken from you; and whose shall those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12). One who sleeps thus, one who dies thus—full of riches, full of vices—does not have sweet sleep in the prison of death. But those who have done good, whether rich or poor, shall be given sweet sleep and everlasting rest.

VERS. 12–16. — There is another most grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches kept to their owner’s hurt. For they perish in a most grievous affliction; he has begotten a son who will be in utter poverty. As he came naked from his mother’s womb, so shall he return, and he shall take nothing with him from his labor. A thoroughly miserable evil: [Col. 1247A] as he came, so he shall return. What profit, then, has he from laboring for the wind? All the days of his life he eats in darkness, amid many cares, misery, and sorrow.

He gathers such riches as will bring very many evils upon their owner who troubles the Church by schism, who stores up wrath and indignation for himself (Rom. 2). The son whom he begets, because he becomes more wicked than his father, will be burdened in mind by poverty and extreme want. Unworthy to be clothed in the first robe of faith, naked, poor, and wretched, he returns to the earth, consigned to punishments without end. Such riches are sought by those who are not wise even while seeming wise; and such will be the fruit of riches received by those whom wisdom does not build up but puffs up.

Let the simple mind, therefore, learn what the simple letter says. Ecclesiastes frightens the greedy and covetous, lest anyone love the riches of the world more than is right, showing how weak, vain, and miserable it is to persist in such great cares in pursuit of wealth, which fortune, rolling beneath her feet, now transfers to this man, now carries away to that one. Whoever keeps accumulated riches cannot retain them as his own, but renders them back as though received on loan. And he who had sought them—with the ant as his teacher in gain-making—after losing all through some robbery, fraud, theft, or fire, oppressed on every side by gloomy cares and miseries, hides while eating in darkness; and, like a hoarse cicada, laments his poverty and consoles his pain with tears.

VERS. 17–19.—This therefore seemed good to me: that a person should eat and drink and enjoy gladness from his labour, at which he has laboured under the sun, during the number of the days of his life [Col. 1247C] which God has given him; and this is his portion. And to every person to whom God has given riches and substance, and has granted power to eat from them, enjoy his portion, and rejoice in his labour—this is God’s gift. For he will not greatly remember the days of his life, because God occupies his heart with delights.

Having first set forth the evils which we must avoid, he now adds the good things which we must do. He had said that it is evil and a most grievous vanity to seek and love excessively fleeting riches. Reflecting upon this statement—that the appearance of things and the succession of days flow on, wearing us down in their flowing and themselves destined to perish—he observes that it is good for each person to gather the fruits of his labours, passing the time in a pleasant life and by no means defrauding himself of the share of goods [Col. 1247D] given him. If you have the means from riches to live gladly and enjoy possessions, why should you remember your former life—how you spent your past years? Forgetting the things behind and exerting yourself toward those before you (Phil. III), you will continue for yourself the joys of a happy course, because God, increasing your advantages by a free gift, occupies your heart with the nectar of delights.

“Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV), and it is fitting that we should feed upon these delights. He enjoys good things, he is rightly made glad, who, casting off the burden of worldly things, receives from them only such a portion as his life requires—according to the Apostle, content with food and clothing (I Tim. VI)—and, not recalling the days his life has chosen, runs toward the prize [Col. 1248A] of life (Phil. III), desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I). This man will receive what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the heart of man (I Cor. II).

Therefore he enjoys good things and his heart is gladdened who meditates diligently upon the words of Holy Scripture: from them he eats, from them he drinks; he is given drink and food; and so, enjoying the portion given him, he labours beneath the sun—now seeing in part and prophesying in part, hoping that he will see the whole when the partial is abolished (I Cor. XIII). Thus rejoicing in God’s gift, he delights in Him who already fills his heart with such great delights. He too enjoys good things and delights in enjoying them whom the bread of the Lord’s body satisfies and that cup of sacred blood intoxicates; whoever is worthy of it will feel himself blessed. With such delights God glorifies all the elect.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 1248B]

VERS. 1, 2.—There is another evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is indeed frequent among men: a man to whom God has given riches, substance, and honour, and whose soul lacks nothing of all that it desires—yet God does not grant him power to eat thereof, but a stranger consumes it. This is vanity and a great misery.

If we turn these things to allegory, the man to whom God gave riches without delights and honour without power of use is the people of the Jews. God gave it the riches of the sacred Law, which it lost at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the people of the Gentiles, when that people did not believe, was called and deserved to receive the glory and riches promised to them. Hence it is written in a certain prophet: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots coming forth from between [Col. 1248C] two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses” (Zech. VI), etc.

Let us raise our eyes with the prophet, since he himself did not see these chariots and horses except with uplifted eyes. Let us raise, I say, the eyes of the mind and extend our view over the whole world. Behold, the world is full; and since the blessed apostles were enlightened from that lampstand which the prophet saw, it has begun to be filled with burning chariots and running horses, of which Habakkuk also sings to the Lord: “You will ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. III).

The first chariot, I say, was red horses: it is that of the apostles and martyrs. The second chariot, I say, was black horses: it is that of penitents, who, beginning from the times of the apostles, established among those who had shed Christ’s blood the cenobitic life; hence even to this day throughout the world the black order of monks persists, both in profession and in habit. The third chariot, I say, was white horses: it is the order of virgins of both sexes, adorning with its whiteness the whole cavalry of Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts.

For this should be noted: when he had said, “In it were black horses; they went out toward the land of the North,” he says, “and the white ones went out after them.” Very many follow that order of life necessary for the wicked, which those earlier penitents undertook in order to bear fruits worthy of repentance (Luke III)—not guilty of murder, adultery, or any other crime, but indeed for the most part bodily incorrupt [Col. 1249A] and whole. Of such persons blessed Pope Gregory says: “What else should I call them but righteous and penitents?”

Clearly this is what it means to go out toward the land of the North: to pursue a more austere life, differing from a more relaxed life, which enjoys many delights—though not unlawful or forbidden by the Law—as greatly as the severity of the North differs from the mildness of the South or the West Wind, and as winter cold differs from spring’s gentleness. Hence the wording should be noted: “Those in which were black horses went out into the land of the North,” so that the sense may be: because they were conscious of their sins, they committed themselves to the purpose of a stricter life.

The fourth chariot, in which were dappled, strong horses, is that of pastors and teachers, and of all in whom those distributions of graces are eminent, of which the Apostle says: “To one is given through the [Col. 1249B] Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another kinds of tongues, to another the gift of healings” (I Cor. XII), etc.

Is this a small matter, or was it unworthy to have these orders of the Church of the Gentiles displayed in prophetic vision among those great ancient things of which something has already been said and more remains to be said? Indeed, which of the prophets kept silence concerning such matters, or did not joyfully proclaim in the Holy Spirit the Gentiles who were to be saved, from whom the Divinity took these orders?

Moreover, who are those two mountains from between which these chariots are seen to emerge—mountains, namely, called mountains of bronze? These two mountains are the two Testaments, Law and Gospel. They are called mountains because of the height or dignity of the heavenly mysteries they contain; for height is also signified by the fact that the Law was given upon a mountain (Exod. XIX), and that the Lord began the Gospel discourse sitting on a mountain and opening his mouth (Matt. V). These mountains are mountains of bronze because of the resonance and permanence of both Law and Gospel, which cannot be annulled.

VERS. 18.—The Scripture, both legal and evangelical: for, “Not one iota or one stroke,” says the Lord, “will pass from the Law until all things are accomplished”; and “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. V, XXIV). From between these mountains the four chariots came forth, because both Testaments receive the four aforesaid orders of the Church. And just as it is said in another figure, “From between the rocks they shall give forth voices” (Ps. CIII), so here [Col. 1249D] you may rightly say that these chariots run forth from between the two mountains, the mountains of bronze. From the common sense—or concord—of Law and Gospel, they will preserve the order of life and purity of knowledge and doctrine.

What, then, does it mean that, when the prophet asked, “What are these, my lord?”, the angel answered: “These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the ruler of all the earth”? What else but what Wisdom says: “A multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wis. VI)? Therefore these four chariots are called the four winds of heaven, because, as winds by blowing disperse clouds and frost and, by stirring it, make healthier the air which would become more corrupt through stillness, so these orders of which we have spoken, [Col. 1250A] each standing in its own offices—or, when time requires, moving about and hastening—rouse people to know God their Creator. Unless they were made watchful by repeated admonition, they would not even think, their minds corrupted, that anything remains after the present age, or that at the end there is any difference between a human being and a beast.

Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of heaven, so that they might not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree” (Rev. VII). The four angels of the four corners were evil princes—that is, angelic powers—of the four chief kingdoms: Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman. Of one of these the good angel who spoke to Daniel says: “The prince of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days” (Dan. X).

For those kingdoms, or their princely rulers, to hold the four winds of heaven meant to restrain these chariots—that is, those worshippers of God of whom we have spoken, serving the Creator—from the worship or service of God. But another angel, who ascended from the rising of the sun and had the seal of the living God, cried aloud and restrained them. He is none other than the man who rides upon the red horse, and after whom are red, dappled, and white horses: the saints of the former people, of the Old Testament.

But these chariots, these four winds of heaven, which, after those women departed with their jar, came forth from between the two mountains to stand before the Ruler of all the earth, are the saints of the later people. When the Synagogue denied Christ—as it had long before denied David—the other woman, namely the division of the ten tribes, believed in Him and stands before Him even now as truly the Ruler of the earth.

VERS. 3–6.—If anyone should beget a hundred children, live many years, have many days of age, and his soul should not enjoy the goods of his substance, and he should lack burial, I pronounce that the stillborn child is better than he. For it comes in vain and goes away into darkness, and its name will be erased in oblivion. It has not seen the sun nor known the distinction between good and evil, even if he should live two thousand years and not have enjoyed good things.

He who had a hundred children is the people of the Jews, which begot in figure the holy patriarchs, kings, and prophets. For the number one hundred is square, and is the third vanity. And just as the angelic number and heavenly order are signified by ten drachmas and ten sheep multiplied tenfold, so now those who are perfect, full of virtues, and square in faith are fittingly signified by a hundred: they do the good which they preach.

Thus the Hebrew nation—although it is hyperbolically said, since no one has lived so long—came itself to two thousand years, which we find from the time of Abraham’s calling to the Passion of the Lord and Saviour, who was born from his stock. Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” was a Hebrew from Heber, in whose house and family the original language had remained; from that time it was called Hebrew after him. He was born [Col. 1251A] in the 191st year from the birth of Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided; 502 years after the Flood; and was the tenth generation from Shem, son of Noah. For Shem begot Arphaxad; Arphaxad begot Shelah; Shelah begot Heber; Heber begot Peleg; Peleg begot Reu; Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; Terah begot Abram.

Cainan, indeed, who is placed by Luke the Evangelist between Arphaxad and Shelah (Luke III), is not found in the Hebrew. Further, the Hebrews hand down, and distinguished ecclesiastical men maintain as true, the following reason why his own land—that is, the land of the Chaldeans—was unworthy of such a man: Abram was thrown into the fire because he refused to worship the fire worshipped by the Chaldeans; delivered by God’s help, he fled from the fire of idolatry. And this is said to be the meaning of: “Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. XI): namely, that, because he refused to worship fire, he was consumed by fire. For Abram, they say, though surrounded by the same fire, was delivered by God’s help. Hence the Lord later says to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. XV).

Otherwise, they say, there will be an insoluble difficulty in the later statement: “Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran” (Gen. XII). For if Terah, Abram’s father, begot Abraham when he was seventy years old and still in the region of the Chaldeans, and afterward died in Haran in the 205th year of his age, how is Abraham, departing from Haran after his father’s death, said to have been seventy-five years old, when from Abram’s birth [Col. 1251C] to his father’s death there are shown to have been 135 years? Therefore that Hebrew tradition is true: Terah departed with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans; Abram was delivered by God’s help; and from that time the days of his life and the time of his age are reckoned for him.

From that day, then, to Christ’s Passion two thousand years are counted, which that wicked nation completed in its death, having failed to deserve a burial—that is, the hidden place of holy contemplation.

“Do not all things go to one place?” “All things,” he says, not “all persons.” He marks not human beings alone, but whatever is subject to death, in order to show himself using the words of those who say that the soul has no life after the death of the flesh, that the whole human being perishes in dying, [Col. 1251D] and that we and cattle alike hasten, dying with our flesh, to one place of destruction. Hence Ecclesiastes, seeming contrary in his own words, says what one who does not know how to speak truth is accustomed to say.

“What difference,” he says, “whether one be stillborn or old, chaste or incestuous, happy or unhappy, if all of us are to come by dying to one place?” Asking this, yet not affirming it, he speaks so that you may understand him to say: Although mortals have one birth and one setting, their differing conduct in life will not assign them one place; for Abraham’s bosom is prepared for some, hell for others.

VERS. 7–9.—All human labour is for his mouth, but his soul will not be filled. What advantage has the wise person over the fool? And what has the poor person, except that he goes to the place where life is? It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know; but this too is vanity and affliction [presumption] of spirit.

Ecclesiastes does not depart from the causes of nature when he suggests to us the common practice of living, the evils we should avoid, and the good things we should do. Labour has been added to humankind to serve the mouth; the mouth serves the belly. The organs of our body are rationally arranged so that the supports of food may suitably sustain the stomach. But when is it enough for a person to indulge such labour? He eats and is hungry; while hungry, he seeks what he should eat. So that he may not thirst, he drinks; he drinks more than is necessary, so that he may thirst again.

Paul, who thought little of the greatest things of the world, knew what delights, riches, and foods were (I Cor. VI), reckoning all things in the world as dung (Phil. III). O labour! O empty fruit of life, to be reckoned as dung! No one receives the lot of life without grievous labour. One labours amid envy and toil in order to please Christ; another labours more grievously in order to please the world. One labours wisely at what is sufficient; the other labours less wisely.

And what advantage does the wise person have over the fool? What does one who labours foolishly have less than the learned? We mortals have one natural mode of existence. This one has more than that one if, directed by the straight keenness of his mind, he goes on to the life where no one labours; the other has less, because he does not walk where life is. The poor person for Christ and in Christ possesses many goods, always hoping for good things.

He who labours by learning and teaching, but not by doing good, has labour in his mouth, but his soul is not filled. For the Lord says: “Whoever does and teaches shall be called great [Col. 1252C] in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Thus whoever labours greatly through the desire of learning, yet cannot reap much fruit from his labours, has labour lodged in his mouth which does not penetrate to the heart; for, touching the mouth only, it gives no savour and does not illuminate the heart.

VERS. 10, 11.—He who is to come has already had his name called, and it is known that he is human and cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself. Words are many, and have much vanity in disputation.

Ecclesiastes declares most plainly concerning the Lord Jesus Christ that He was to come to us and, having assumed flesh, was to become human. “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV). It is too little to say that everything possessing the use of rational mind foretold His coming. The cherubim and seraphim daily proclaimed Him as Lord Sabaoth (Isa. VI). Adam already saw that He would become true man while His divinity remained intact, when He formed Eve from His side (Gen. II). The prophets called Him Christ (Lam. IV; Ps. LXXXVIII); Gabriel called Him Jesus the Saviour (Luke I; Matt. I).

The prophetic Sibyl wrote His name in the initial letters of her Greek verses as follows: “ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΟΣ ΥΙΟΣ ΣΩΤΗΡ”—“Jesus Christ, God, Son, Saviour.” She rightly calls Him Christ, that is, “Anointed,” because He was anointed above His companions (Heb. I); Jesus, that is, “Saviour” (Isa. XIX, XXVI, XLVI, LXIV; Zech. IX; Luke II), because He saves all things; ΥΙΟΣ, that is, “Son,” because He is the Son of God (Rom. I); ΘΕΟΣ, that is, “God,” because He made all things (Heb. I); and ΣΩΤΗΡ, that is, “Saviour” or “salutary one,” because He came to save that which [Col. 1253A] had perished (Matt. XVIII).

Even the Gentiles, seeing from afar and at a distance this name of the Lord who was to come in flesh, wrote thus in certain shrines of their temples: “ΚΥΡΙΟΣ, ΚΥΡΙΟΣ”—“Lord, Lord.” And though they were uncertain and did not sufficiently understand the Lord’s name, they nevertheless altogether revered it as a divinity to come. Paul too found written: “To an Unknown God” (Acts XVII).

God was not worshipped and known only in Jerusalem, nor only in Bethlehem under the guidance of the star (Matt. II); Rome itself also, head and glory of all kingdoms, knew Him when God came forth from the Virgin’s womb “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII). For through so many ages it had already known the event through a sign set before it. When the Romans had fortified their city with walls and ramparts so that it was impregnable, they also built a tower higher than the others. On its summit they wrote this inscription: “This tower will fall when a Virgin bears a son without a man.” After many ages had passed, when no knowledge of these things remained except through the inscription, on the most holy night when the Virgin bore her Son, the foretold tower suddenly fell, showing all people that the Saviour of the world had come.

Egypt too knew much concerning Christ (Isa. XIX), and in its temples read this inscription: “Life is to come.” Hermopolis, a city of Egypt, where the Lord fled from Herod’s face, saw much concerning the Lord, because when He came all its images fell together.

Words are many and possess much vanity in disputation. For in how many words, how vain, how diseased, did the foolish wisdom of the world argue concerning this—she who, while chattering in many words, is entangled in many empty errors!

## Chapter VII

VERS. 1.—What need is there for a person to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what is expedient for him in his life during the number of the days of his pilgrimage, and during the time that passes like a shadow? Or who can tell him what will be after him under the sun?

Because in many words there are many vanities, and amid many vanities there is no certain hope of salvation, someone who fears this—and, in fearing, does not confidently trust himself—hesitates, asks, and says what Ecclesiastes says: “What need is there for a person to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what is expedient for him in his life?” He is a pilgrim here, because he is born in order to die. He flees like a shadow (Job XIV) with the hours of time. Who can tell him what will be after him? A short life, the road of pilgrimage, time’s shadow, and uncertain hope, ignorant of the future, prove that there is no need to seek things greater than oneself.

What Solomon seeks is shown to you by one greater than Solomon (Luke XI): “The righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). The righteous person will be one who rightly seeks things greater than himself; one who wrongly seeks things greater than himself will be condemned. Here life is short; there life remains everlasting. Here time is shadowy; there is time without time. Here you live as a pilgrim and stranger in the world (Heb. XI); there you are a citizen of heaven. Know that these eternal and delightful things profit your life. Yet who can possess them unless he seeks things greater than himself?

Therefore you must seek what is beneficial [Col. 1254A]. What cannot not be is undoubtedly necessary; and what it is impossible not to be, that must be. Whoever therefore knows what helps and what harms knows what is necessary. Thus, if it profits to seek, if it is necessary to have found, speak affirmatively, persuasively, admonishingly: Why do you delay, O human being? Why are you idle? Why do you linger? It is necessary for you, even through struggle and labour, to seek things greater than yourself.

For a hunchbacked one, laden with so many burdens of sins, to pass through the eye of a needle is beyond one’s strength; yet it is nevertheless necessary to pass through. That foreigners and violent persons should seize for themselves the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XI) is beyond one’s strength; yet it is necessary to dare even this. Those who conquered the world by faith (Heb. XI) and were crowned by martyrdom would not have gained the palm of righteousness unless they had sought things greater than themselves. Yet struggle gives the crown by merits.

But if what you seek harms you and need not be sought, speak by questioning, dissuading, and forbidding: O human being, what need have you to seek things greater than yourself? What need had those to seek things greater than themselves who, daring in many vain words to contend, scattered pestilential heresies throughout the world by teaching perversely? They cherished with their fomentation the eggs of the asp; once these were broken, they caused a basilisk to burst forth, dealing the doom of death by the breath of its mouth alone.

That it is not necessary to seek things greater than oneself was learned by the first man, Adam. Deceived through Eve (Gen. III), he became less than himself because he desired things greater than himself. Through the tower of Babel, those who wished to go to heaven in order to make a name for themselves against the Lord (Gen. XI) had no need to seek things greater than themselves; nor did it profit them to build a most lofty tower, since their pride was conquered by the confusion of tongues.

VERS. 2, 3.—A good name is better than precious ointments, and the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for there the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what is to come.

One who conquers himself in order, through virtue, to lengthen the brevity of life does much and seeks things greater than himself, so that by making for himself an everlasting name he may live. For a good name gives fragrance like precious ointment—indeed, it is more precious than costly ointments. When Mary Magdalene anointed the head and feet of the Lord Jesus, she merited a name better [Col. 1254D] than precious ointment. Then the whole house was filled with the scent of the ointment, and it still fills the whole world with the fragrance of this name (Matt. XXVI). The thief Judas valued this ointment at three hundred denarii (John XII); God Himself valued the woman’s good name, saying: “She has done a good work toward me” (Matt. XXVI). Blessed ointment, so illustrious and so precious; blessed she who merited to have a good name better than precious ointments.

For those whose name is better than precious ointments are marked by the allurements and indulgent concerns by which they are not attracted, as though by splendid ointments. Thus many through war, many through philosophy, by strength, talent, and the goods of both the inner and outer person, sought a name that might be fragrant everywhere like ointment. Whoever seeks a great name by doing the good produced by goodness and nourished by holy delight possesses a name more fragrant than sweet ointment. But whoever seeks a great name by doing evil—a name born of ambition and nourished by wicked desire—has a name that stinks shamefully rather than gives fragrance.

Why, then, do we think Ecclesiastes said that the day of death is better than the day of birth? Clearly because the wise person philosophizes wisely on these matters. When the philosopher Plato was asked what philosophy was, he said: “Meditation on death.” Thus the appearance of being born is the appearance of nature; a human being is the appearance of life. When the infant falls prone upon the earth, he is so born: for he is always received upon the earth, not upon gold, silver, or silk, plainly showing that, made from earth, he will again become earth. Born for hardships and many sighs, he anticipates them by weeping.

Learn the first vowel from the first sound of the newborn child, whose mouth scarcely opened gives forth the first letter, repeating it: “Ha, ha; alas, alas.” For in being born he foretells the evils he will see in living. Nature, supplying all things, shows through the swan that the day of death is better than the day of birth: when it knows that it is about to die, it customarily celebrates funeral games for itself and sings its funeral laments in sweet melodies. Some barbarian peoples, taught by reason and believing that in dying they return to life, used to sing dirges and celebrate funeral obsequies with rejoicing, offering odes instead of tears.

He who fears death: what are the good things of life? He escapes death by death, but after life life returns. Death draws one to rest; birth causes one to bear pain. The person born is met by the most uncertain lot of life; nothing is more certain than the lot of death. If you submit to the laws of death, fragrant with the precious ointment of a good name, you will pass into eternal life. But when a sinner dies, he finally feels a limit imposed upon sin, so that the sum of evils may not increase. King Midas released a philosopher named Silenus, whom he had captured, at this price: that he might learn from him that not to be born is good, and that, having been born, to die quickly is better.

VERS. 4, 5.—Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of countenance the mind of the offender is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, and the heart of fools where there is gladness.

“The one who is angry,” says the Lord, “with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V). And David: “Be angry and do not sin” [Col. 1255D] (Ps. IV). The latter exhorts anger; the Lord forbids anger. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI). Job also says: “God fills the mouth of the truthful with laughter” (Job VIII). Thus Job praises laughter, while the Lord Himself condemns laughter; yet Solomon says that anger is better than laughter. Do you suppose, then, that such diverse voices disagree with one another? But it is not so. As a harmonious sound accords with itself through varied strings, so this concordant judgment accords here through varied words.

The people of Israel was guilty in the calf made by Aaron, when it sat playing, eating, and indulging itself. Far better than such laughter was the anger of Moses, whose sorrow of countenance and anger of heart, through rebuke, bent the heart of the offending people, so that, weeping for its sin, it was delivered from the Lord’s anger and wrath (Exod. XXXII). The gentlest man of all who dwelt on earth (Num. XII) was greatly angered when he broke the tablets written by God’s finger and when, by killing his dearest friends and relatives, he consecrated his heart and hands through the deaths of sinners.

By his anger holy Phinehas removed the Lord’s anger at Baal-peor (Num. XXV). Such also was David’s anger against Joab, when Solomon was commanded to kill him (III Kings II). Similar was Elijah’s anger (III Kings XVIII), and similar the anger of Mattathias, who zealously acted for the Lord with swords and anger (I Macc. II). Such was Peter’s anger (Acts II), and such was Paul’s anger (I Cor. IV): Peter by a word and Paul by striking with a rod caused those who sinned to be made sorrowful. Eli refused to be angry with his sinning sons (I Kings III), and the sons and father perished together in ruin.

If you laugh while sinning, be angry with yourself in sorrow. If your brother sins, be angry with your sinning brother. If he is properly saddened, repents, and stands in awe, approach him with the manner of compassion. If you are so saddened that by making your brother sorrowful you gain him, you will receive, as due reward, the name of one who endures patiently. Here he considers the heart of the wise to be one that ought to grieve, so that it may have the most certain hope of future gladness. Conversely, he considers the heart of fools to be one that ought to rejoice—those who cry daily in the streets: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (I Cor. XV). Whatever such fools hope for, they desire to happen carnally.

VERS. 6, 7.—It is better to be rebuked by a wise person than to be deceived by the flattery of fools, because as the crackling of burning thorns beneath a pot, so is the laughter of a fool; but this too is vanity.

What Solomon says, Solomon’s father says in the Psalm: “The righteous shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but may the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. CXL). The sinner’s oil denotes sinners’ praises. Praise therefore anoints the head; praise fattens the heart by deceiving it; but what has been fattened does not discern subtle matters. Thus the one who praises sinners’ evils sins unto death.

Accordingly, by almost as many modes as we die through sinning, we are given life. Each death has its own justification. Death will be mortal for the one lacking good hope. Thus he dies secretly who conceives wickedness in his heart; God raises such a one in Jairus’s twelve-year-old daughter (Mark V; Luke VIII). The dead person carried out is one who has committed stronger and greater sins; the Lord restores him also to life at the gate, in the raised young man (Luke VII). “Four days dead he stinks” (John XI): whoever is foul in an old crime. The four days signify four deaths, since people die through Adam, through the law of nature, through the Law of Moses, and through the law of the Gospel. Thus God raises us in Lazarus, dead four days.

When “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. X), he is deceived by the flattery of fools, dies in his sin, and will never deserve to be raised by the Lord. A disciple who desired to go to his father’s burial is forbidden by the Saviour’s command (Matt. VIII). How many monks, while pitying their father and mother, have lost their souls! We are not permitted to be defiled over father or mother (Lev. XXI); how much less over mother, sisters, cousins, household, or servants? We are a royal and priestly race (I Pet. II). Let us attend to that Father who never dies, or who dies for us, and who therefore, living, was dead, in order to give life to us who were dead.

If we have anything from Egypt which the prince of this world can recognize as his own, let us leave it with the Egyptian woman who holds the cloak (Gen. XXXIX). Let us render to parents what belongs to parents, provided that they live and glory that their children are preferred to them for the Lord’s sake. We shall also render an account for every idle word (Matt. XII), and everything that does not edify hearers becomes a danger to those speaking.

What is ever more wicked than a serpent as a cause of death? So nothing is more wicked than the tongue of a flatterer. As a variegated serpent moves its three-forked tongue in its mouth, so the flatterer has a three-forked tongue. If I detest good things, he too detests them; if I praise evils, he likewise praises them. If I should retract what I said, he too rudely retracts it. The leopard does not have colours so varied; the chameleon does not assume so many forms and colours—it changes into whatever appearances it sees, except the appearance of white and red. Thus the flatterer smiles upon everyone; and if he shares grief, he laughs then also. The foolish and wicked flatterer who laughs in this fashion makes a sound like burning thorns. This vice of flattery has so taken root and grown everywhere in our time that anyone who does not know how, or does not wish, to flatter is judged by everyone to be envious or malicious.

VERS. 8.—Calumny troubles the wise person and destroys the strength of his heart.

Who is this wise person whom calumny troubles—not lightly, but strikes with such a tempest that he loses the strength of his heart and wholly collapses? The philosophers’ statement is true: those four passions which generally envelop almost everyone do not in the least disturb the wise person, as is read:

> Mortals fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI

Those four disturb everyone except the wise. We might attach little value to the clever sophisms of the world, unless the Lord Himself seemed to approve them when He said: “Whoever believes in me and keeps my commandments is like a person who builds his house upon a rock. The floods came, the winds blew, and struck that house; and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon firm rock” (Matt. VII; Luke VI).

The righteous person, wisely steadfast in his resolve, had felt himself strong in spirit when he said: “If heaven should cling to earth, Isidore does not fear.” But one who is not wise, though he appears to be wise, has built himself a house upon unstable sand. If wind and rain assail it even slightly, it will immediately give way with a crash and a great sound in falling. Such is the wise person whom Ecclesiastes describes: having cast away his weapons, he lost the strength of his spirit and yielded ground whenever calumny pressed him.

VERS. 9.—The end of a discourse is better than its beginning. Many are wise at the beginning, but become foolish at the end, depart from what is good; and many who are foolish at the beginning, yet at the end take on the habit of right wisdom and, redeeming the delays of their beginning by the hours of their end, make good by honorable zeal what they had lost through sloth. Those who, despising trifles, take on the habit of the wise are of far greater and better zeal than those who seem wise at the beginning and later become foolish.

Plato, greatest of men and a great glory in his own time, showed that the end of one’s discourse is better. Formerly an athlete, formerly spending his strength in contests, formerly conquering all by bodily force, when he turned his heart to the study of philosophy, by wisdom he conquered all those whom he had conquered by his body. As he had formerly been victorious in wrestling, so afterwards he was victorious in philosophy.

Moreover our Plato, better and greater than Plato—Paul, formerly a blasphemer and an insolent man (1 Tim. 1), an athlete of the Law and a stern enemy of the Gospel—taught that the end is better than the beginning when he received the promised crown of glory (2 Tim. 4). The thief on the cross preferred the end to the beginning: his beginning gave him death, but his end gave him Paradise. The rich Zacchaeus and Matthew the tax collector made their end better for themselves than their beginning (Luke 19; Matt. 9). All who, wandering, are recalled to the sheepfold and to themselves know that the end is better than the beginning.

Far worse and far lower are those who, after beginnings worthy of praise, later became foolish and turned back, going after Satan (John 6). Such was Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord; such was Nicholas the heresiarch. Such were those disciples who forsook him because they refused, with blessed Peter and the other apostles, to understand the words of eternal life. Such was Balaam, sinning while wise and falling while seeing (Num. 24). At first he was worthy of the words of the Lord; an evil end made him worthy of the words of an ass (Num. 22): the words of an ass terrify the man whom the Lord himself does not terrify.

But why seek examples so far away? Behold, Ecclesiastes himself is at hand, held securely in our hands and fit for the purpose, saying that the end is better than the beginning. For who was so distinguished by an honorable beginning? To whom did God reveal such treasures of wisdom? (3 Kings [1 Kings] 3.) Yet he had an end worse than his beginning: becoming foolish at the end of his old age, he worshipped the idols of the nations (Ecclus. 47; 3 Kings [1 Kings] 11).

Better is the patient man than the arrogant.

Whatever goodness or virtue we possess, we have from him who is God by nature; but whatever vices we have from without, we have from him who is the author of sin, who ruined his own nature by sinning and infected ours when he caused us to sin. He is a liar and the father of lies (John 8); who, then, is more deceitful than he? Who claims more for himself? He claims that he is prince of this world.

Certainly God, who is patient, is better than him: God endures his unjust reign in this world and delays inflicting upon him the punishments of Tartarus, so that at the time of judgment he may be tormented in the fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25). Patient is he who, mercifully overlooking our condition, endures the evils which we deserve by sinning. How much he himself endured when made man and dying for us; and he exhorts us to endure as much, saying: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” [or: “gain your lives”] (Luke 21:19).

How much the saints endured in hope of eternal life! And who would not marvel that philosophers could endure so much merely in hope of empty praise? Many of them judged that no one should be admitted as their disciple unless he patiently submitted himself to every insult. I shall tell you something astonishing. If no one wished to give them blows or stripes, or torture them with insults, they paid considerable fees to hired men to give them punches, slaps, and harsh blows, so that, after being tested in this way for a long time, they might be worthy to pursue philosophy. Thus one man, having suffered every sort of blow and grievous insult, said boastfully to his examiner: “Am I now worthy of the name of philosopher?” “Yes,” the other replied, “if you had kept silent.” Thus anyone who vainly claims skill for himself rightly loses his praise.

Therefore all who have given precepts for right living condemn the person who arrogates too much to his own strength and exalt those whom the breastplate of patience disciplines. For Jacob, Moses, and David endured much by being patient. Job, the mirror of moral patience, was far better than Elihu, despite Elihu’s great threats. Job lived better because he conquered patiently every evil inflicted on him. Elihu—who, it is said, was first called Elihu and afterwards Balaam—while arrogating too much to himself, boasting so greatly against Job and plotting such evils against Israel, was killed by the sword with the Midianites.

VERS. 10.—Do not be quick to anger, for anger rests in the bosom of a fool.

Ecclesiastes, seeing before and behind, so joins the middle first to the middle last that what he has said before may stand and what he now says may not be separated from it. For he had said that anger is better than laughter; lest anyone think that he had loosened the reins of anger, he commands that anger be wisely restrained. And, lest anyone be quick to anger, he adds the reason: anger rests in a man’s heart.

Hence James says, “Let every man be slow to anger” (Jas. 1); and Paul, the Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4). For just as one breath of the mouth fills many pipes so that a flute may sound harmonious notes, so spiritual grace breathes upon many, that many may speak one and the same thing. Therefore do not quickly or rashly submit your mind to anger. Whoever postpones anger diminishes the flame in his breast.

Do other sins, then, delight us? What cheerfulness does anger possess? What pleasure does it promise? It disorders the body and vexes the inward parts of the mind. Anger subdues the great and mighty; anger subdues the small. It is deeply shameful even in the holy and great that anger should have prevailed. And what is sweeter than honey? What is more bitter than anger? Anger destroys the bee, nor does the bee wash anger away with honey. Anger is one of the seven vices, and pride—the queen of death—begets it.

VERS. 11.—Do not say: “What do you suppose is the reason that earlier times were better than the present?” For such a question is foolish.

What Solomon says here is also said by our Lord, who is greater than Solomon, when he told his disciples, asking about times: “It is not yours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7). That earlier times are not better than later ones, but that all things proceed in an equal course, is shown by him who compares for himself three ages of the world: nature, the old Law, and new grace. He says of the last age of the world that it will be like the time in the days of Noah and in the days of Lot, when people lived for themselves, ate and drank, married, planted and built, sold and freely bought what belonged to others, until they were suddenly swallowed up by the flood (Luke 17); such will be the time when the world perishes by heavenly fire.

Since, therefore, you are forbidden to prefer one time to another, if you wish to compare things with times, and times with definite things, you will see no reason to say that one time is better than another. He who is supremely good made all times good, distributing to each its proper use according to the changing condition of things. But if the settled use of things is overturned by events fluctuating in uncertain turns, the time itself thereby becomes neither better nor worse. If death, wars, famine, storms, or wasting pestilence from corrupted air sometimes come upon us, the time is not at fault. For an evil use of time brings about an evil event.

When, by sinning, we overturn the good use of life, the world fights against us senseless people on behalf of its Maker, overturning the temperateness and established use of time. For it resents being subjected to our use when it sees us abusing the Creator’s gifts.

VERS. 12, 13.—Wisdom is more useful with riches, and is more profitable to those who see the sun. For as wisdom gives protection, so money gives protection; but learning and wisdom have this advantage: they give life to their possessor.

Ecclesiastes varies his words greatly after the manner of an orator; and, speaking to many, he imitates the voices of many. Speaking previously in his own voice, he had said that wisdom was more precious than all wealth. Now, speaking in the words of one not rightly wise, he compares wisdom with wealth and seems in some manner to prefer riches. “Wisdom,” he says, “is more useful with riches; as wisdom protects, so money protects.” It is as though he said: wisdom protects and benefits; money protects and benefits. A thing is not complete in itself, nor does it possess the whole matter in itself, when it receives a supplement from an abundance of riches.

Having said this in the words of one not perfectly wise, to whom wisdom is worthless without wealth, he now states what true wisdom is: “Learning and wisdom have this advantage: they give life to their possessor.” This riches can neither confer nor possess.

Here the voice of the Gospel harmonizes well with Ecclesiastes. When the rich young man, who could not become perfect through the works of the Law, heard from the Lord: “One thing is lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19), let us consider how wisely Wisdom spoke. “Sell what you have,” he says: do not sell part of your possessions, but all. And when you have sold them, what follows? “Give to the poor”—not to the rich, not to relatives, not for luxury, but for need. Whether the recipient is a priest, a kinsman, or a relative by marriage, consider nothing in him except poverty. Let the bellies of the hungry praise you, not the lavish banquets of those who belch.

Therefore what Ecclesiastes says—“Learning and wisdom have this advantage: they give life to their possessor”—is the same as what the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come, follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven.” The followers of Christ, who became rich through spiritual poverty (Jas. 2), testify what benefit wisdom brings with riches. The naked gymnosophists of the world also testify to this, showing what naked wisdom can accomplish.

Such was Socrates, who, from desire for wisdom, sold all that he had and threw its price into the sea, saying: “I shall drown you, lest I be drowned by you.” Why should I speak of you who, for the sake of the pursuit of wisdom, foolishly imagining yourself wise, gouged out your eyes lest you see anything that you might desire? Thus wisdom without riches is worthless to very many, who do not know the end for which wisdom ought to be possessed, nor how greatly wisdom differs from its shadow.

[Col. 1261B] VERS. 14.—Consider the works of God: no one can correct the person whom he has rejected.

If we run through the whole of Ecclesiastes, we shall see that this alone is being impressed upon us: among the many things that God has made and will make, this is greatest of all—that no one can correct the person whom he has rejected. When Cain sinned and killed his brother, the Lord graciously called him back; but he, despairing of the physician’s remedy and of God’s mercy, said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4).

The Lord repeatedly summoned Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to mercy by signs and wonders; but because his heart was hard, he could by no means be softened (Exod. 9). The holy Daniel warned Nebuchadnezzar to redeem his sins by alms (Dan. 4); but since wholesome rebuke did not bend the proud man, God so despised and rejected him that for seven years, cast out from human society, he ate grass like an ox.

Coming into the world, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, rebuked everyone, yet did not correct everyone. Like the rising sun upon good and evil alike, he hardened the hearts of the wicked as soft clay, for no admonition drew them to belief; while he softened the hearts of the good as wax, whom sound correction drew to belief. Why no one can correct those whom he has rejected is considered by John, God’s intimate companion, writing what he learned when he reclined upon Jesus’ breast (John 21). “Therefore,” he says, “they could not believe, though they saw the Lord’s miracles, because Isaiah the prophet said: ‘Harden the heart of this people and make their ears heavy, lest perhaps they see and understand, and I heal them’” (Isa. 6).

The almighty Lord, who wills all people to be saved (1 Tim. 1, 2; Luke 19, 9; Matt. 18; John 3), does not make heavy a person’s heart, eyes, or ears. But because human beings have been given freedom of choice, God is such toward people as they make themselves toward God. Hence the Psalmist says: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17 [18]). This does not mean that he ceases from the nature of his goodness, but that he denies the gifts of his goodness to you, wicked and perverse as you are.

VERS. 15.—On a good day enjoy good things, and beware of an evil day; for God has made this as well as that, so that man may find no just complaint against him.

No day is good or evil in itself; rather, a good or evil event, a good or evil ordering of causes or things, makes any given day good or evil. This quality comes to a day from outside; for the day is attached to its cause and is called by it, since a day is a subject which receives whatever happens to it externally. A day is good when a wealthy abundance of things befalls it and the whole use of time is harmonious; conversely, a day is evil when abundance of things is lacking and the whole use of time is discordant.

When a pleasant day makes all things prosper for you, use what you have acquired rationally, and thus you will wisely guard against every evil. The person who enjoys acquired goods well is one who fears to sin and fears lest the evil day of judgment overtake him. For he who gave us time to act well will make a bad time for the punishment of sins. Thus he will say to the good: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25); and, conversely, to the wicked: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

And why should we wish to cast just complaints against our Creator, claiming that he made us of too fragile a condition, so that we can sin, die, and be led into eternal torments? We complain in vain. There is nothing of which we can justly complain concerning our Lord, who created us such that we can protect ourselves and rule ourselves, if by living well and wisely we destroy evils through caution.

Through good and evil things, which are opposed to one another, the world is subject to you by contraries. In it they indeed fight, yet they do not contend without peace: cold with heat, moist with dry, evil with good, light with darkness, soft with hard. Such is the power of the mind that it joins these contraries by discerning what their measure, order, or cause may be. If good things prevail, moderation gives you a shield, so that you may act prudently and not be overcome by boasting. But if evil things prevail against you, patience gives you a shield, so that you may act steadfastly and not collapse in despair.

As a soldier in camp, so a human being living in the body: in order that you may guard against evils, never live secure in yourself amid good things. Imitate the industry of the swallow. Nature has given it concern for itself: if its house, inadequately secure, shakes as though threatening collapse, it flies away and nests there no longer. When does the swallow ever trust itself sufficiently? It never eats standing still, but takes its meal while flying through the air; for it continually fears for itself, and, guarding against evils, scarcely trusts itself. To be sure, it does not know whom or why it fears: no bird-catcher attacks it, nor does any fierce bird assail it; nevertheless, safe on every side, it fears and takes precautions, so that you too may fear and take precautions.

Who teaches you more effectively to beware of evils while enjoying the lot of good things: Solomon by his words, or the swallow by the actions it has received from nature? Our guest, the swallow, teaches us by another example as well. It has learned to treat its young, which are born blind, with the juice of celandine (*chelidonia*); by a remedy it supplies the sight which nature denies. So learn, O human being, to treat the eyes of your mind, that you may guard against evils, as Ecclesiastes teaches.

VERS. 16.—I have seen this also in the days of my vanity: a righteous man perishes in his righteousness, and a wicked man lives a long time in his wickedness.

Here I think this vanity is especially marked: the person who dies in righteousness is thought to have perished, while the one who perishes by living is thought to have lived long. For the righteous person dies early, lest wickedness change his understanding (Wis. 4); but the wicked person, in order to perish eternally, grows old in the dregs of sin.

The first Adam, who began to live a vain life, saw a righteous man perish in his righteousness when Cain killed his righteous brother Abel; and wicked Cain seemed to have lived long in his evil because he died only in the seventh generation (Gen. 4). Josiah seems to have perished in his righteousness, because, after a short life and an even shorter reign, he quickly perished, killed by wicked Necho (4 Kings [2 Kings] 23). What weariness did the life of long-lived Manasseh cause: having completed more than fifty years in the kingdom, he filled Jerusalem to the brim with the blood of the saints whom he killed (4 Kings [2 Kings] 21). Isaiah was sawn asunder by him because of righteousness.

Yet he did not perish so as to cease to exist; he perished so as to be better off. Ezekiel by the sword, Amos beheaded with a bar, Jeremiah after imprisonment—and, they say, stoned—perished in the righteousness of the Lord, yet they did not perish. How many under the old Law, how many in the time of new grace, perished in the righteousness of the Lord and did not perish; and how many, grown old in their evil, lived for a long time!

Therefore the righteous person who sins perishes in righteousness itself, yet does not perish by sinning, because the Lord disciplines him, saying: “Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline” (Rev. 3); and again: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24). Thus, lest he should perhaps perish, the righteous man perishes by being drawn back from sin; and, like a tender calf, he stands at the altar, made a victim. But the wicked person, living in evil, will perish by living: left to himself like a wild ass, wickedly free, never rebuked, never drawn back from sin, he earns endless destruction by living long.

VERS. 17.—Do not be excessively righteous, and do not be wiser than is necessary, lest you become stupefied.

As a plumb line measures the work to be done, so the virtue of justice is the plumb line of the remaining virtues and the straight line of character. The line of justice knows neither deficiency nor excess. The line of justice directs those virtues which stand in the middle, withdrawn from vices on either side, so that nothing is lacking to them and nothing is excessive. If you wish to be prudent, courageous, or moderate, you cannot be prudent, courageous, or moderate without justice. Everything excessive turns into a vice.

Therefore the law of the world, natural law, and the law of religion, having laid the firm foundation of right in justice, forbid you to be more righteous than necessary or excessively wise. Excessively righteous is the person who is an immoderate avenger of fault. Excessively righteous is the person unwilling to forgive sins. Excessive justice takes from you the rewards of justice: condemning your brothers’ warts while not condemning your own tumors. Thus he forbids excessive righteousness who says, “Be merciful” (Luke 6), that you may receive the same yourselves: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (ibid.).

Ecclesiastes warns you not to be wiser than is necessary, and the Apostle Paul confirms this, saying: “Do not think lofty thoughts, but think unto sobriety” (Rom. 12). Socrates also says: “What is above us is nothing to us.” Three say one thing, but God inspires the one through the three.

Paul practised what he taught and avoided what he forbade. He was not excessively righteous, becoming all things to all people that he might gain all (1 Cor. 9). Nor, lest he become wiser than necessary, did he tell anyone the secret words which he heard (2 Cor. 12). Saul, excessively righteous beyond what was necessary, spared Agag the Amalekite against the command and became stupefied, because he was handed over to an unclean spirit and grievously tormented (1 Sam. 15). The man to whom ten thousand talents are forgiven, but who refuses to forgive his fellow servant a small sum, became excessively stupefied when the Lord handed him over to wicked torturers (Matt. 18).

Novatian was excessively righteous and excessively wise, attempting to take away pardon from penitents. The Pelagian was excessively righteous, saying that a human being does not need God’s help in order to do good works. Even Ecclesiastes lacks no Gentile examples of the great harm of being excessively righteous and excessively wise. Worldly wisdom made very many philosophers greatly stupefied, drunk and soaked with its dregs. Democritus, Chrysippus, Zeno, and Cleanthes, more righteous than was right and wishing to know more than they did, laid hands on themselves, carrying their stupefaction to death. Empedocles became excessively stupefied, excessively righteous in his own eyes: wishing to be a god, he threw himself into the fires of Etna.

VERS. 18.—Do not act very wickedly, and do not be foolish, lest you die before your time.

He who above restrained the righteous man within a fixed boundary, so that he might not be excessively righteous or wiser than necessary, now wishes to set a measure even to our wickedness. Since we have free choice to sin; since it is human to sin but diabolical to persist in sin, a measure will often lighten our evils. A person is wicked, but not very wicked, when he blushes after sinning and hastens to repentance. He is very wicked who always wishes to sin without the remedy of repentance.

The weasel knows how to overcome serpent venom by treating itself with fennel; the stag, by running water. The roe deer draws iron out of itself by tasting dittany; bears are healed by eating ants, and lions by eating fine flour. Roe-deer blood heals the leopard. If some wild beast falls ill, it will be cured by drinking a dog’s blood. O how foolish, how stupid is the person who does not know what a beast does not fail to know!

This is the reason why you are forbidden to be foolish and very wicked: lest you die before your time. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram died before their time because of excessive wickedness, for they went down alive into hell (Num. 16). Job therefore seems contrary to Ecclesiastes when he says: “You have established his bounds, which cannot be passed” (Job 14). How does the person who dies before his time on account of his iniquity not pass the bounds established for him?

But nature has a time that cannot be passed; the fool, however, believes that he has his own time, which neither nature gives nor grace grants, but which the presumption of vain hope alone imagines. Thus Job is true, and Ecclesiastes is true. Job affirms the time of nature, which cannot be passed; Ecclesiastes attributes no time of his own to the fool, and denies that it is his time when he dies, because, living wickedly and foolishly, he wastes the times for living.

Those whom Paul the Apostle calls back to good works had wasted their own time by acting wickedly, when he says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” Behold, it is clear from the words of the Apostle and Ecclesiastes that one who is defiled by excessive sins loses his own time. For the person whom God created to live by wise conduct, if through folly he dies before his own time, will neither live nor die in his own time. For the one who dies while living undergoes death again when dying, although he ought to live well so that he might not die as a fool.

VERS. 19.—It is good for you to uphold the righteous man; yet do not withdraw your hand from him, because the one who fears God neglects nothing.

See what glimmers in the words of Ecclesiastes, briefly marking both laws. The law of the Gospel casts the shadow of the Law from itself. The old Law is: “Love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5). Let the person who acts wickedly fear evils, but let the good person hope for good things. Yet because the Law brings nothing to perfection (Heb. 7), the evangelical law, unwilling to be confined within this limit, surpasses the command of the Law by loving enemies and doing good to those who hate it (Matt. 5).

You see, then, that Ecclesiastes briefly notes both. When he says that it is good to uphold the righteous person, he agrees with the Law, because it is good, giving good things to the righteous. The Law which hates its enemy does not know how to spare the sinner. This is also what Paul the Apostle confirms to Timothy, saying that the Law is good if one uses it lawfully (1 Tim. 3). The Law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the wicked. Therefore the righteous person willingly and spontaneously does what his law compels the wicked person to do.

But what follows—“Do not withdraw your hand from the righteous man”—is the perfection of evangelical grace. The law of the Gospel forgives the sinner a thousand times and a hundred thousand times; and, just as the use of salt, air, fire, water, earth, and rain is given alike to good and bad, so it extends the hand of mercy to all. If the righteous person should stray for a time by sinning, do not withdraw from him the hand of mercy: “The Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord loves the righteous” (Ps. 145 [146]). Therefore, that you may call back the righteous person who has gone astray, imitate the elephant: if it happens to see a human being wandering, it has compassion and, going ahead, leads the follower back to the road.

VERS. 20, 21.—Wisdom has strengthened the wise man more than ten rulers of a city. For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.

Above he had said that both those near to us and strangers should be treated well. Someone could therefore answer: “If I wish to do good to all, I have nothing from which to do it; nor can a righteous person possess such great riches, which usually abound more among sinners.” Therefore he now says: Help with counsel those whom you cannot help with material things; cherish them with consolation. For wisdom can provide more for one in distress than any very great powers can provide. Do even this with prudence. For it is a great scale of justice to determine to whom, how much, for how long, and of what kind one should give, whether in material assistance or in counsel.

The ten rulers are suitably understood as governing the city, that is, the Church, because ten ranks in the Church strengthen the wise person. There are the doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, priest, bishop, archbishop, and apostolic pope. Although these live justly and hold their office rightly, they nevertheless cannot strengthen the wise person unto perfection. For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin. But if Wisdom breathes into the heart of the wise person, so that he does the good things which he has learned, it will strengthen him more than the ten aforesaid rulers of the Church.

Otherwise: the ten rulers who have power and stand in the city are angels, who have attained the perfect number ten and assist humankind. But if anyone considers every aid, greater is the aid of Wisdom—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ. After the angels said, “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed; let us leave her, and let each one go to his own land” (Jer. 51), then the master of physicians himself came down and healed us—sprinkled with blood and drenched with the gore of sins, we who had spent all our substance on physicians—by the touch of his fringe (Luke 8).

He healed in the city, that is, in this world, and strengthened the wise person. “To everyone who has, more will be given and added to him” (Luke 19). But because the human being, placed in sins and fixed in the mud of the deep (Ps. 68 [69]), needed greater help, Wisdom itself therefore came. But why should we investigate these things concerning heaven? Let us descend to earth and return to ourselves. What does a person seek in heaven which he contains within himself?

For natural philosophers also understand the rulers of the city and the city in this way. A human being, a lesser world consisting of four elements, is a city and will provide ten rulers for that city from himself. Ten members lift our body upward: namely, the two joints, foot, leg, thigh, genitals, belly, breast, throat, and head, which rises above the citadel of the city. God gives these as rulers to each person’s own city. The ten toes and the equal number of fingers—what an ornament, and how great a defense and usefulness they provide! And when the rulers of the city are tripled by nature, the human being will go more safely and, like mighty David, will have thirty warriors against every enemy of the soul (2 Sam. 23).

Above these rulers, above these bodily nobles, wisdom alone strengthens the wise person, lest he despair because there is no person on earth righteous enough to do good without sinning. But one strengthened through wisdom will govern the senses and bodily limbs—called rulers by Ecclesiastes here—in such a way that wisdom may reign in the city of the heart. If these powerful rulers in the city of the body wish to become too powerful against the mind, wisdom strengthens the wise person against them, that he may restrain the members that seek to rule with force and compel them, once subdued, to serve the Holy Spirit.

VERS. 22, 23.—Moreover, do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you; for your conscience knows that you too have often cursed others.

The air is struck more by empty words than by winds; and the earth does not feel as many stormy disturbances from the great whirlwind of winds that shakes the air as a person suffers motions when tossed upon the high sea of shipwreck in the heart, while the ear itches for everything. Therefore, lest through the itching of your old heart and ears you bend the ears of heart and body toward every breeze of rumor: if a light breeze of favor blows from the south, let false goodwill not bend you from justice. If the harsh north wind rushes in, threatening storms, let not even then a violent whirlwind drive you from the straight path.

There is another vanity: what is more vain than fame? Fame lends its ears to every word. Fame hears your servant cursing you. What is more vain than one who trusts fame too much? If perhaps fame tells you the truth, that your servant may have cursed you, let your own conscience be your judge so that you may not be an avenger. When you condemn your servant, judge yourself, lest he too condemn you, since you have cursed another.

CAPUT IV.—CHAPTER IV

Jacob saw a ladder from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it and the Lord resting above it (Gen. 28), so that he might extend his hand to the weary and, by his example, urge those ascending onward to their labor. Hence that place is called Bethel, that is, “the house of God,” in which there is daily ascent and descent. For the saints fall if they are negligent, and sinners recover their former rank if they are converted and wash their defilements with tears. I say this not to discourage those descending, but to urge on those ascending. An example is never rightly taken from the wicked; even in worldly matters, incentives to virtue always arise from the better side.

Forgetting my purpose and the brevity proper to a letter, I wished to say more to you, dearest brother Gregory. For in relation to the dignity of the subject and to the worthiness of your person, all that is said is too little. But let us now return to our Ecclesiastes.

[Col. 1267C] VERS. 24, 25.—I have tested all things by wisdom. I said, “I shall become wise,” but wisdom itself withdrew farther from me. Far more than it was, and a profound depth: who shall investigate [find] it?

How well does a person test whatever he tests in wisdom! Wisdom is like light to a person and a guide on the way. “He who walks in the light,” the Lord says, “does not stumble” (John 11). The one who tests everything in wisdom—what more does he desire than to become wise, so that he may test everything wisely? Here is the labor. Therefore the lover of wisdom prayed: “Give me, Lord, Wisdom, the attendant of your throne” (Wis. 9), that she may be with me and labor with me.

Thus no human being can be wise without labor. If I say, “I shall become wise,” Wisdom withdraws farther from me, holding our powers beneath herself. For the person who knows much seems to himself to know less; and whoever knows that he does not know regards himself as a mere smatterer. Hence Ecclesiastes, wishing to become wise, stunned and overcome by the heavy labor of acquiring wisdom, says: “The deep is profound: who shall investigate it?” Paul the Apostle too, desiring to pursue the way of wisdom, following in his mind Wisdom retreating from him and unable to grasp her, cried in a most exalted voice: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

In how many places does Scripture mark this height and depth in which the wisdom of God lies hidden, withdrawing far from us! The well from which the Samaritan woman drank was deep (John 4), but Jesus, coming, showed her the living fountain. Deep was the well concerning which Moses sang in the wilderness: “Let the well rise up,” they sang together (Num. 21), and the rest. All who desire to become wise dig out this deep and profound well of God’s wisdom; and, astonished at such height and depth, they cry: “Who shall investigate such a height of the wisdom and knowledge of God?”

The three wells of Abraham are three wells of wisdom. The three wells are the three arts possessed by wisdom: moral, natural, and rational. This height and depth frightened even the philosophers and held them back everywhere. For Socrates, deterred from philosophy because wisdom lay hidden under so deep a covering, and as though throwing down his arms without glory, said that he knew nothing except that he knew that he did not know.

[Col. 1268B] **VERS. 26, 27.**—“I surveyed everything in my mind, that I might know, consider, and seek wisdom and reason, and that I might recognize the impiety of the fool^547 and the error of the imprudent; and I found woman more bitter than death: she is the snare of hunters, her heart a net, and her hands are fetters. He who pleases God will escape her; but the sinner will be taken by her.”

With the chariot of his understanding and the feet of his mind, Ecclesiastes surveys and investigates everything that happens. By reflection, skill, or labor, he knows, considers, and seeks what wisdom is—the source from which all things made from the beginning flow—and what is human reason, flowing from the fountain of wisdom. He also knows how great is the impiety of a person who becomes foolish and senseless, allowing the natural power of intellect within to grow sluggish; and how great is the error of those unwisely wise, if, by living foolishly, they extinguish within themselves the spark of wisdom that flashes from the fire.

[Col. 1268C] See how many evils beset human life. The life of one who is impious or errs imprudently is thought bitterer than death. In all things there is nothing more grievous than death; yet the bitterness of woman is more grievous than death. Hence hunters weave snares and nets—I mean those hunters of our souls, who surround us, encircle us with their hunting-net, capture us in snares, and hold us fast in bonds. Such was Nimrod, the mighty hunter before the Lord, who first built Babylon (Gen. 10). There is no bond or glue more tenacious than a woman’s love, and no bitterness greater than this.

[Col. 1268D] Who has not tasted woman’s bitterness? The devil deceived Eve in Paradise, and through her the first-created man was expelled (Gen. 3); through her death entered the world (Wis. 2). What wise man, what strong man, what saint escaped woman’s snares? Solomon was wise, Samson exceedingly strong; yet neither escaped woman’s nets. David also, who was according to God’s heart, was caught in a woman’s snare. But, having been delivered, he sings: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123).

Samson, whom Delilah bound with snare and fetters, learned too late that woman is more bitter than death (Judg. 16). Solomon himself, caught in the snare of women and worshipping foreign gods, showed that an evil woman is more bitter than death (3 Kings [1 Kings] 11).

Yet no one should suppose that Ecclesiastes rejects the nature of woman.

[Col. 1269A] The apostle Paul does not reject it when he says: “The head of woman is man; the head of man is God” (1 Cor. 11). Paul commends nature; Ecclesiastes, while not condemning nature, appears to condemn the vices which arise in corrupted nature. He accuses the evil person and praises the goods of nature. When a woman, having conquered the weakness of her sex, becomes manly in virtue—such a woman as Peter commends for the adornment and cultivation of virtues, and for the pure garment of modesty—who would believe her to be found more bitter than death? (1 Pet. 3). But who does not know that a woman who abuses the softness of the female sex to weave for us snares, nets, and bonds is more bitter than death?

An evil woman is more bitter than Sardinian herbs. One who eats the Sardinian herb dies laughing; but who dies laughing except one who loves or is loved? The Sardinian herb kills only the body of the eater; the bitter woman poisons both the body and soul of her lover.

[Col. 1269B] But if we turn the meaning of “woman” toward allegory, she signifies as many things as woman herself does. The devil himself is denoted in the woman, because the power of our Lord renders his strength effeminate. The name “woman” also denotes the sin of the flesh: just as woman is soft, so the flesh is softened into sin.
