Those whom heresies denote are likewise denoted by the name “woman.” As the foolish woman draws foolish people to herself so that they may be filled with stolen bread and furtive water, so heretics summon the senseless to themselves, that a stolen baptismal water may wash them and that they may feed them with stolen bread, not wine. The name “woman” also applies to idolaters: just as menstrual blood weighs down the whole female sex,

[Col. 1269C] so blood sacrificed at altars weighs down idolaters.

**VERS. 28–30.**—“Behold, Ecclesiastes said, I have found this, adding one thing to another, that I might find the reason which my soul still seeks and has not found: one man among a thousand I found; but among all women I found none. Only this I found: God made man upright, but he himself has entangled himself in countless questions. Who is like the wise man, and who knows the solution of a word?”

“This,” he says, “I found, after examining all things carefully: by sinning little by little and adding one offense to another, we have made for ourselves a great number of sins. My soul sought whether an upright woman might be found; and although I found scarcely a few good men—so that one might be found among a thousand—I could find no good woman at all. For all led me not to virtue but to lust.” Since the human heart is diligently inclined toward evil from infancy, and since almost all have offended God, woman, amid this ruin of the human race, is more easily led into a fall. Of her the pagan poet says: “Woman is ever changeful and fickle.” And the Apostle says: “Always learning, and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3).

And lest he should seem to condemn the common nature of humankind and make God the author of evil, as Creator of those unable to avoid evil, he shrewdly guarded against this and said that God created us good, but that, because we have been left to free choice, we fall through our own fault into worse things, while seeking what is greater and devising many things beyond our powers.

[Col. 1270A] Otherwise: while daily considering with myself the reason of each thing, I could find no thought that was not outwardly disturbed by a perverse thought. But among a thousand men I found the true human being, created according to the image of the Creator; and this not among just any thousand, but among a thousand men whom no woman can complete in number—among a thousand who did not approach a woman and therefore remained most pure.

All this, however, must be understood tropologically. Among many diligent students sweating in daily meditation, a thought that is pure and worthy of the name “man” is scarcely found. We may also take “men” as thoughts and “women” as works, and say that it is difficult for anyone’s thought to be found pure; works, because they are carried out through the body, are [Col. 1270B] always mingled with some error.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERS. 1.**—“The wisdom of a man shines in his face, and the most mighty will change his countenance.”

Above, he had taught that it is difficult to find a good man, and he had answered the objection that presented itself: human beings were created good by God but voluntarily fell into sins. Now, almost exultingly, he lists what good God gave to man: namely wisdom and reason, providence, knowledge of God’s hidden mysteries, and entrance by the understanding of the heart into his secrets. Indirectly, moreover, he speaks of himself: that no one was as wise as he, no one knew so well the solutions of problems, and his wisdom was praised by all the people—not hidden within, but shining forth on the outward body and mirror of the countenance; beyond all other people, it had portrayed the prudence of his mind upon his face.

[Col. 1270C] And indeed, although many promise wisdom, it is difficult to find anyone able to distinguish a wise man from those who merely seem wise. And although very many claim to be able to solve the hidden things of the Scriptures, rare is the person who finds the true solution.

The words that follow, “The wisdom of a man shines in his face,” may be explained through Paul’s words: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3); and through the Psalmist’s song: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).^548 Here he calls human wisdom nothing other than the wisdom of God; though it is God’s wisdom, in proportion to the capacity of a human being it begins [Col. 1270D] to belong to the person deemed worthy to possess it.

Every heretic and defender of false doctrine has an impudent countenance. Thus Marcion and Valentinus say that they are of a better nature than the Creator. This might in some measure be possible if they maintained that they had hope of such a thing, rather than already possessing that nature.

Nor has worldly wisdom been silent concerning the saying that a person’s wisdom shines in the face, since philosophers discerned this in the very shape of the countenance. For Plato, speaking through the mouth of Timaeus concerning the soul of the world fashioned by wisdom, shows that the rounded and spherical shape of the head was made by God in the citadel of the body after the model of the world: the body is subject to the head as a slave; the front parts of the head are preferred to the rear; and it is adorned with eyes and senses, the handmaids of the mind. This he called the visage and face.

[Col. 1271A] These words of Plato are, I think, very near the truth. For the mind sits upon the throne of the head and rules, as it were, from a citadel, governing the five senses and assigning to each its due service. But why does Plato say that the form of the head is rounded and spherical? Surely what Moses said, “God formed man in his own image” (Gen. 1), Ecclesiastes says here: “The wisdom of a man shines in his face.” Therefore, what Moses understood, what Ecclesiastes understood, Plato too may perhaps have understood, when in philosophizing he depicted the form of the head as rounded and spherical.

The philosophers, who thought the body divine, said that it was rounded and spherical. Just as round things have neither beginning nor end, so God has neither beginning nor end, as he himself says: “I am A and Ω, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1). What is called spherical is solid within. Such a head is God: rounded and circular in himself, encompassing all things, spherical by solid power.

[Col. 1271B] The human head too has a rounded and spherical form because it is the image of God, but it slopes from the sphere into a cone. What is a cone? A cone is called a rounded line bent out lengthwise, stretching from one point. What the rounded form of the head, bent back into a cone, signifies, I believe the ancient fathers wished to transmit to us not so much by letters as by signs. For painting gives form to the human figure: we see how a picture surrounds the head, its rounded form sloping into a cone and curving down to the chin.

[Col. 1271C] Pictures are the books of the simple. What writing shows the learned, painting shows the unlearned: that the rounded form is fitting for God, but the bent form for man. The figure that slopes from the round into a cone signifies that reason flows down to us from the rounded mind of God and makes us like God, though not equal to him. Wisdom flowing thence shines in the human face, so that a person may know that he was made in God’s image. But if wisdom does not shine in his face so that he stands just and upright, his face will be changed—not by an alteration in the natural visage, but in honor. For when the face is changed, what is man but an empty name?

**VERS. 2–4.**—“I observe the king’s command, and the precepts of God’s oath. Do not hasten to depart from his presence, nor remain in an evil work; for he will do whatever he wills, and his word is full of power, nor can anyone say to him: ‘Why do you do thus?’”

This indeed seems to command obedience to kings and authorities, in accordance with the Apostle (Rom. 13). But I think it is now said of that King of whom David says: “Give your judgment, O God, to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71); and elsewhere: “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength” (Ps. 20). For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5), who is King, the Son of God the Father-King.

[Col. 1271D] His precepts, therefore, must be kept; his will must be performed. This is what is written in the book of Tobit: “It is good to conceal the mystery of a king” (Tob. 12). Above all, he warns us not to debate why God commanded each particular thing, but that the devout human mind should hasten to fulfill whatever it sees commanded. Thus “his delight shall be in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1).

[Col. 1272A] Wisdom, then, keeps God’s precepts as oaths. Since God is true by nature, truthful, and truth itself—saying nothing but what is true and doing nothing but what is fixed—what is it to swear except to speak truth? That God’s oath is truth-speaking is affirmed by the Lord Jesus when he says in John: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 8). *Amen*, that is, “truly,” confirms the word of the Gospel. Whoever swears confirms a matter by the name of one greater. But by whom greater than himself could the great and supreme One swear? Therefore God swears by himself, swearing through “Amen, amen.” The wisdom of God preserves this very oath: that what it says may remain true and fixed in the order of things.

**VERS. 5–7.**—“He who keeps the commandment shall experience nothing evil. The heart of the wise understands time and answer. For every business there is a time and an opportunity; and great is human affliction, because he does not know the past and can learn the future from no messenger.”

[Col. 1272B] The natural law, the old law, and the new law contain very many commands, to which practice binds us. Of these, what command had Ecclesiastes considered when he said that whoever keeps it will experience nothing evil? God’s commands are many, but all are one. All commands arise from one command, as many branches grow from one tree. This is the command of which our lawgiver, the supreme Lawgiver, said to his disciples: “This is my commandment: that you love one another” (John 15). “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

[Col. 1272C] The apostle John, even to extreme old age, always had this old and new commandment on his lips: “Beloved brethren, love one another.” When the brethren asked why he repeated this so frequently, he answered: because if this one commandment is fulfilled, all the rest will be fulfilled. The law of nature also rests upon this command: that no one should do to another what he does not wish done to himself (Tob. 6; Luke 6; Matt. 7).

Ecclesiastes considered the force of this command and, gathering everything under one command, gave a general precept: “He who keeps the commandment,” he says, “shall experience nothing evil.” Those who kept the Lord’s command suffered many evils, armed by love of virtue with the weapons of faith. Ecclesiastes saw this and considered it carefully, and therefore said with the greatest caution: “He shall experience nothing evil.” He did not say, “He shall suffer nothing,” but “He shall experience nothing evil.” Whoever suffered evils for keeping the commandment experienced sufficiently and well that they had suffered no evils, when they deserved to receive the crown of eternal life.

[Col. 1272D] Hence Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, boasts: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in the saints” (Rom. 8).

Those not adorned by true faith and God’s wisdom are disturbed by ignorance of times and events. Uncertain about the past and future, they desire only present things; they complain about times and the order of things, as though times were evil and the order of events uncertain. But those adorned by true faith and God’s wisdom do not complain about times or the order of events; they know the moments of things and the changes of times. For the heart of the wise understands how one may answer someone doubtful about the causes of things. It knows that, as God’s mind governs the affairs of the world,

[Col. 1273A] nothing happens in the world except at a fitting time. From the smallest things the wise heart has learned to reason that all worldly affairs are conducted in order and according to reason.^549 It knows that the human mind, ignorant of its future and past lot, is always open to anxiety concerning present things.

**VERS. 8.**—“It is not in man’s power to restrain the spirit; nor has he power over the day of death; nor is he allowed rest when war presses on; nor will impiety save the impious.”

Every word that is equivocal in Aristotle signifies many things under one name. But if a true definition is made, each thing will be distinguished from another either by species or by a proper characteristic. Since, then, “spirit” signifies many things under an equivocal name, by what proper meaning does he here distinguish the equivocal things from one another? Surely it is the human spirit which governs the breathing limbs. [Col. 1273B] When the day of death comes, who can prevent it from being loosed from the weight of the fleshly mass? Only he could prevent it by his own authority who said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John 10).

What use is presumed power to a person when the day of death is imminent? What can one who is dying accomplish? The mighty, who exceeded the limits of human strength, have learned in dying what man is and what he can do. What rest allows a dying person to cease? War presses upon one living, and indeed upon one dying. While alive, one must fight against vices; while dying, one must suffer the evils of death because of the vices of the flesh. If the impious person persists in impiety, the freedom of impiety will not save him from the snare of death. How great is death’s victory!

[Col. 1273C] Allegory too wishes to set forth its meaning here. The Spirit is God; the Spirit is the Lord. As it is written in the Gospel: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3). Who can restrain him who breathes where he wills? The Spirit lives in us whenever, and so long as, we live well for him. If we die to him, he himself does not die; but we die, because by not living in him we deserve that he who can do all things should be unable to give us life. Therefore he is thought to have no power on the day of our death. Hence Paul says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5). When we are extinguished by vices, we extinguish the Holy Spirit within us.

**VERS. 9.**—“I considered all these things, and gave my heart to all the works that are done under the sun. Sometimes one man rules another to his harm.”

With what great zeal is one carried toward great wisdom who, by considering whatever God and man do, understands that in all vanities nothing is more vain than that a human being, ruling another human being, becomes the cause of evils to him. Wisdom itself teaches how the presumption of ruling is the cause of evil. “You rulers,” it says, “who hold kingdoms and cities, I shall try with fearful and harsh judgment; I shall torment you mightily, you who rule mightily; and a harder torment awaits you who are strong” (Wis. 6).

[Col. 1273D] There are two modes that corrupt the right of dominion. A ruler’s discipline that is more lax than justice demands is a cause of evil, and a ruler’s discipline that is harsher than justice demands is a cause of evil. Eli made himself contemptible by ruling too leniently (1 Sam. 2). [Col. 1274A] King Adonibezek ruled more harshly than justice: “As I have done,” he says, “I have received in return from the Lord” (Judg. 1). “After cutting off the extremities of the fingers of their hands and feet, I fed seventy kings beneath my table—alas, now the extremities of my own fingers and feet are cut off.”

**VERS. 10.**—“I saw the impious buried, who even while still living were in a holy place and were praised in the city as though for righteous works; but this too is vanity.”

There is no need to illustrate in another’s words what the Lord explains with his own mouth. Solomon saw those living wickedly and buried in ostentatious splendor; he who is greater than Solomon saw them better than Solomon did. Solomon saw outwardly; the Lord Jesus sees within. Speaking with a human mouth to the Scribes and Pharisees, he considers the inward parts of the heart as God: “Woe to you,” he says, “Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, full of dead men’s bones.” Men praise them, marveling at the workmanship, for they do not see the bones rotting in the beautiful marble. “So you appear outwardly righteous, but inwardly you rot—though living in flesh, already buried by sinning.”

[Col. 1274B] Ecclesiastes rebukes those who are in a holy place; the Lord too rebukes them even in a holy place, saying: “The Scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat.” By teaching good things, they approve them; by not doing them, they condemn them. They are thought to hold the key of doctrine, but their works are not good, since they neither open the gate of heaven to themselves nor permit those wishing to enter to do so (ibid.). To be in a holy place is a great virtue—but only if you stand with a right and unstained foot. To stand even in a holy place is rash and vain if you walk with a crooked and defiled foot.

As Solomon saw the impious praised in the city, so the Lord saw the impious praised in the city: “Woe to you, Pharisees,” he says, “who tithe rue, mint, and dill, yet are not righteous, because you suppose the sum of righteousness to consist in this and wish to be praised in the city” (ibid. and Luke 11). What the Lord says, the wise people of the world also say: “Whoever wishes to be praised will be blessed by no virtue.” When someone asked Socrates what the way of virtue was, he replied: “I shall show you a short but perfect way: live in such a way, and be such a person, as you yourself wish to appear.”

Many have seen, together with Solomon, and marveled that men of virtue often lack even the honor of a tomb, while infamous persons are buried with fame and praise. That pagan too saw this, not without grief, who inscribed the following verse on the tomb of the unjust Carbo:

> Carbo lies covered by a marble tomb, Cato by none;  
> Pompey by a small one. Do we believe that gods exist?

**VERS. 11, 12, 13.**—“But this too is vanity. For because sentence against evildoers is not quickly pronounced, the children of men commit evils without any fear. Yet because the sinner does evil a hundred times and is sustained by patience, I have known that it will be well with those who fear God, who reverence his face. Let it not be well with the impious; let his days not be prolonged, but let those who do not fear the face of the Lord pass away like a shadow.”

[Col. 1274D] Mercy is naturally inherent in God, and power is inherent in him as well. Mercy nourishes us; power rules and disciplines us. Sometimes grace overcomes the power of mercy, and so, while the sword of power hangs long suspended, the delay of death offers hope and pardon to the guilty. This is the two-edged sword proceeding from the mouth of the Lord, as is read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 1), because it strikes from this side so that you may die.

[Col. 1275A] Ecclesiastes now explains how this occurs. Since the Lord’s sentence does not quickly punish the wicked, they abuse God’s mercy and sin more freely. No fear restrains them; they do not believe God cares for our mortal affairs enough even to see evils—or, if he sees them, they think he has overlooked them because he does not immediately punish the wicked. Unpunished license has been granted to the wicked. But when has unpunished license made anything go unpunished? What does the Lord say through his prophet Isaiah? “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury; that staff in their hand is my indignation” (Isa. 10). Thus a place for doing harm is given according to degrees of merit.

[Col. 1275B] Brooms that sweep floors are worn away by their very sweeping. Thus unpunished impiety is the greatest of evils. Mercy granted to the evil becomes a cause of evils; mercy granted to the good becomes a cause of good things.

Ecclesiastes, distinguishing things from their causes, reasons about this mercy of the Lord, whose sentence remains suspended so long. If the evil of the sinner who repeats it a hundred times is voluntarily deferred, so that hope of pardon may be given him, from this I have learned that one who fears the Lord and reverences his face deserves hope of pardon—whether by not sinning or by redeeming sin. Let there be good hope for the good; hope is offered also to the evil. God sustains the righteous and the unrighteous alike by forbearing patiently.

[Col. 1275C] Yet there is someone more boastful and as though strong, who, bearing nothing by suffering but snarling with hostile mouth at what God endures by a hidden judgment, reviles the one whom God endures without himself enduring anything from him. Speaking now in this man’s voice, Ecclesiastes changes his words: “Most impious man, let no good thing be yours, you who have always loved evils. Let your life be short, since many are weary of your living; let all who do not reverence their Creator pass away like a shadow.”

**VERS. 14.**—“There is another vanity that occurs upon earth: there are righteous persons to whom many things happen as though they had done the works of the impious; and there are impious persons who are as secure as though they had performed the deeds of the righteous. This too I judge most vain.”

[Col. 1275D] Ecclesiastes varies his words greatly, but unites them in meaning. Above, having noted persons and the causes relating to persons, he expressed the one feeling of many: he complained that vengeance upon evils came slowly; he had learned by hope that good things ought to be hoped for by those who fear God; and he had assailed the impious with curses. See, he observes another vanity arising on earth from the seed of this vanity, and in astonishment speaks thus to himself: “Will the good truly think that I have learned that good things are to be hoped for by those who fear God, when they see many holy and righteous persons unjustly suffering evils so great that only the perverse ought justly to have endured them? For although man may impatiently curse the impious, the impious person lives securely for a long time, sustained by God and harmed by no curse. How great a vanity is it that evils come to the righteous and good things to the unjust?”

How many things people judge vain which God denies are vain. That it is not vanity but a definite dispensation that very many good things happen to the wicked and very many evils to the righteous is confirmed in the Gospel by Father Abraham. While comforting Lazarus’s soul in his bosom, he could not release from hell the rich man who had been buried. And he said why: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke 16).

[Col. 1276A] That it is not vanity but dispensation when evils sometimes happen to the righteous is further shown by the Lord Jesus, in whose mouth no falsehood was found. When he heard that Pilate had mingled the blood of certain sacrificers in the Temple, he said to the crowds: “Do you suppose that the Galileans who were cruelly slain, or the eighteen whom the tower of Siloam fell upon and killed, had sinned more than all others? I do not say this. But unless I see you repent, you too will perish as they perished” (Luke 13). How well he distinguishes, he alone who knows hearts, that both righteous and evil persons may be tested by judgment.

[Col. 1276B] **VERS. 15.**—“Therefore I praised gladness, because there is nothing good for man under the sun except to eat, drink, and rejoice; and this alone he shall take with him from his labor during the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.”

What, I ask, can I say? Shall I believe that Ecclesiastes, with a vain heart, so often praised vain gladness? Did he think that we could be made blessed by this good alone: that we should merely delight in bodily food? But the Lord Jesus, truer than Ecclesiastes, proclaims that those will reign and be blessed whom spiritual poverty has enriched here—those who weep, hunger, and suffer very many evils (Matt. 5). Certainly what Truth said must be true. Therefore those who mourn, are poor in spirit, thirst, and hunger will rejoice and be truly blessed.

[Col. 1276C] The true conclusion, which proves the true premise, denies that those who delight merely in bodily sights will rejoice or be blessed. Solomon is therefore not contrary to one greater than Solomon; rather, often changing his language in accordance with the person whose role he adopts, he does not say this in his own voice but in the words of the Epicureans, for whom seductive pleasure is held to be the highest good. Or, if he said it in his own voice, he praises those feasts which wisdom prepares and seasons with its own salt.

**VERS. 16, 17.**—“And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to understand the distraction that goes on upon earth: there is a man who by day and by night takes no sleep with his eyes. And I understood that man can find no explanation of all God’s works which are done under the sun; and the more he labors to seek, the less he finds; even if the wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it.”

A most grievous distraction of mind torments very many people; Ecclesiastes applies his heart to know it. For when something appears difficult, it is necessary and useful to apply the heart to investigate it. This distraction is said to be active “upon earth”; it does not torment the ground that we tread. “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth” (John 3): by the name “earth” are denoted those who think earthly things (Phil. 3). Ecclesiastes applies his attention to the philosophers of the world, who are continually distracted in speaking of earthly things.

[Col. 1276D] What philosophers develop in so many and such books Solomon explains in almost three words. [Col. 1277A] We know there are two schools of philosophers, warring against one another from opposed sides. The ancient philosophers, who bore the name of wisdom, devoted themselves daily to examining the causes of nature. Wishing to discover all God’s works to the last detail, they always sought and always set down what was to be sought; and what they sought they found in some measure, while what they could not find they knew that they did not know. Such persons were distracted by zeal for wisdom.

Socrates too, distracted by zeal for wisdom, said: “My end of living will also be my end of teaching.” Another was greatly distracted by zeal for wisdom, of whom it is reported that, when nearly a hundred years old and dying, he wept and said: “Alas for me, because I am dying now, just when I was beginning to become wise!” Ecclesiastes denotes such a man as one who watches night and day, so intent upon examining the causes of nature that all marvel at him, and Ecclesiastes more than the rest.

[Col. 1277B] See, with new and stronger assaults the newer philosophers press the older philosophers and overturn philosophy by a new doctrine: whatever the older thinkers said about the causes of nature and the course of things, they retract and refute, declaring that nothing can be known and nothing discovered, because knowledge of truth eludes them. Ecclesiastes, directing his attention to these vanities, notes their claim that there is no knowledge of things, that nothing can be known and nothing found.

Let us suppose that these philosophers, shaken by the weight of things, are like foxes so terrified at the thunder of heaven and crash of the world that, fleeing, they seek a hiding-place beneath the earth. Ecclesiastes, older and wiser than they, censures both these and those; he teaches these and teaches those. He censures the ancients who confess that everything can be known, and the moderns who think nothing can be known. He shows what they think, so that, if they think rightly, they may seek rightly. He wishes the ancients to think that things can be known, but not all things.

[Col. 1277C] That God acts and alone governs all things, we know with complete certainty. But how and why God wills to vary these things—why a good person is sick, an evil person strong, one rules, another serves, why he enriches this person and impoverishes that one, and why many other things happen—cannot in any way be known by us, because knowledge of these belongs to God alone.

But those who think that nothing can be known and nothing can be discovered—what do they think they know, when they take knowledge away from themselves? Who among men would ever say that nothing can be known unless he knew many things? Certainly, one who knows why he does not know this or that knows much. One who takes away his own knowledge while knowing knows very much. Nature has given each animal its own kind of knowledge. One who thinks that he knows nothing has subjected himself to cattle. Cattle have intelligence, but it is not equal to ours; by reason we are set above every beast.

[Col. 1277D] “Even if the wise man says that he knows,” Ecclesiastes says in reply, “he will not be able to discover it.” Who can deny that this is true? Worldly wisdom does not know very many of God’s secrets. This wise man whom Ecclesiastes discriminatingly notes was perhaps Socrates, who thought himself wise when he first said that nothing can be known and nothing discovered; or he was Arcesilaus, who, following Socrates’ knowledge, made a philosophy for himself out of knowing nothing.

## CHAPTER IX
### Verses 1–4

“I considered all these things in my heart, so that I might carefully understand: the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; yet a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred. But all things are kept uncertain for the future, because all alike happen equally to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to one offering victims and to one despising sacrifice; as with the good man, so with the sinner; as with the perjurer, so with him who swears truthfully. This is worst among all things done under heaven: that the same things happen to all. Hence the hearts of the children of men are filled with malice and contempt during their life, and after this they are brought down to the underworld. There is no one who lives forever and who has confidence concerning this matter.”

As wave comes upon wave in the great and troubled sea, so care upon care torments the heart of Ecclesiastes as he recounts vanity. What form of vanity is more grievous? What care for knowledge can be more vain? Behold, speaking in the person of someone devoted to vanity, he discusses the question: who is worthy of the Lord’s love, and who unworthy? Since no one can discover this, what profit is there in seeking it? And what human being can understand the mind of the Lord?

There are righteous and wise persons, and their works are in the hand of God, who governs both willing and ability, lest they wish to know more than is necessary. Yet what human being cannot understand that those who live justly and act wisely are worthy of God’s love? This grave confusion of affairs confounds the truth: the same things come to the righteous and the unrighteous, and the world honors good people neither with love nor with esteem. Just as good reputation commends good people, so it also praises the wicked. Distracted by such things, a person, since he knows nothing to be certain, does not know whether God deems them worthy of his love.

Therefore those things which are in themselves neither good nor evil, but which the wise of this age call “intermediate,” because they happen equally to righteous and unrighteous persons, disturb simple people: why do they happen thus? Consequently they think there is no judgment, since the distinction of all things lies in the future, while here all things are confused.

But we think quite otherwise. We believe that all these things occur not by chance but by God’s providential ordering. For just as the threshing-floor threshes grain together with chaff, so now the threshing-floor of the world threshes the righteous together with the unrighteous. As grain cannot grow without chaff, so the evil must grow together with the good. As chaff is a covering for grain, so evil people are a trial for good people. God tests both and distinguishes both.

When he gives good things to the wicked, he tests them by granting good things here, so that they may have no hope of good things eternally. When he gives evils to the good, he tests them by granting evils here, so that they may have no fear of punishments forever. The abundance of things given here draws the wicked man toward worse things: ungrateful, abusing things freely received, and despising God, he thinks God ought not to be worshipped because he does not always give good things to the just and evil things to the depraved. Thus, although the life of the wicked man has been tested, he does not know that he is being warned not to hope for pardon, because he does not cease from sinning.

But the abundance of things given here draws the good man toward better things, furnishing with gracious gifts one who lives well. Thus, although the life of the good man has been tested, he believes that he is being warned to hope for pardon, because he now ceases from sinning and so placates him whom he had despised by sinning.

Nevertheless, all these things are kept uncertain until the future judgment, until God, the Judge of the world, separates his own grain from the chaff with the winnowing-fan. “There is no one who lives forever.” Who lives forever except God, who made all things?

### Verses 5–6

“A living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they shall die, but the dead know nothing further, nor will they have any further reward, because their memory has been given over to oblivion. Their love also, their hatred, and their envy perish together; nor do they have a share in this age or in the work done under the sun.”

What does the comparison of the nature of dog and lion mean? They are united in genus, indeed, but dog and lion differ in species. Let the literal sense first suggest to us the nature of dog and lion; afterwards the Spirit will give allegory, he who gives us life through spiritual understanding, lest perhaps the letter kill us through carnal understanding.

The lion lives after the fashion of a tyrant, fitting with no one; preserving himself by natural freedom, he deems no one worthy of regard, as though by right he ruled over all beasts. What king terrifies human beings as the lion terrifies beasts? Beasts are often struck lifeless by the lion’s roar. Although he seeks prey, although he lives on blood, nevertheless he has moderation in eating and moderation in drinking: he eats and drinks on alternate days; wherever he goes, he erases his tracks with his tail and removes the hunter’s signs of pursuit. The lion sleeps with open eyes; he knows how to spare a stranger and a fallen person. Such is the life of the lion.

The dog’s life is contrary to the lion’s. The dog delights that a human rules over him, and obeys so readily as to deserve favor. He serves for love of his belly, without love of freedom; for he has no moderation in eating. He is accustomed to gorge himself until vomiting; he is accustomed to relieve gluttony by vomiting; and again he is accustomed to relieve hunger with his own vomit. Thus the nature of dog and lion is distinguished.

Yet there is a point at which lion and dog agree. When a captured lion is tamed, he always wishes to keep with him a little dog, by whose caresses he softens the force of his ferocity. Thus, in order that the lion, terrible by the ferocity of his nature, may be afraid, the innocent puppy is beaten; frightened by this, the lion is terrified, forgets that he is a lion, bears chains on his neck, and fears to be subject to his master.

Behold: you can recognize what Ecclesiastes saw, and what either the life of the lion or the life of the dog signifies. But let us press toward higher things. Let us say that the Canaanite woman, to whom it was said, “Your faith has saved you” (Matt. XV), is the dog according to the Gospel; but that the dead lion is the people of the circumcision, as the prophet Balaam says: “Behold, the people shall rise up like a lion’s whelp, and rejoice like a lion” (Num. XXIII–XXIV).

We from the nations are the living dog; but the lion that is dead is the Jewish people, abandoned by the Lord. And this living dog is better before God than that dead lion. For we who live know the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but they who are dead know nothing and await neither promise nor reward, but their memory is ended. They neither remember what they ought to have known, nor does the Lord now remember them.

The love by which they once loved God has also perished; and likewise their hatred, concerning which David spoke boldly: “Did I not hate those who hated you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies?” (Ps. CXXXVI); and also their zeal, according to which Phinehas was zealous (Num. XXV) and the knees of Mattathias trembled (1 Macc. II). It is clear that they have no share in the age, for they cannot say: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. LXXII).

Moreover, you may find by another figure an explanation of who is dog or lion, who lives or dies. The dog signifies the ungodly, but the lion the righteous. He who lives well is confident as a living lion and is frightened neither by anyone’s encounter nor by anyone’s disturbance. Joined to Christ, he does not join himself to the world. By the freedom through which he serves the Lord, preserving himself, he deems no one worthy of regard, but serves God alone with his whole mind. The righteous terrify those who are savage and brutish in heart. As frightened beasts are scattered when a lion roars, so, when God’s herald cries out, brutish and bestial people fall away from the habit of their customary savagery.

As the lion preys, so the righteous man preys: the lion upon beasts, the righteous upon people. The latter nourishes; the former kills. The righteous man has no excess in eating; sobriety is for him a delightful pleasure. As the lion sleeps with open eyes, so the righteous man watches as though sleeping, as is read in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, and my heart watches” (Cant. V). The righteous spares the fallen and the stranger.

As the lion is frightened by the patient beating of a cub, so people are often withdrawn from sin by the punishments of others. Thus it is said in Proverbs: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man will become wiser” (Prov. XIX, XXI). For he fears to sin when warned by the blows inflicted on another.

Whenever the lion lives in this manner, he lives better than a living dog. The righteous man, while he lives as a lion, lives better than a living dog. But if the lion’s virtue perishes, dead in the righteous person who sins, the righteous man will be worse than a living dog. The dog, formerly unclean and gluttonous, becomes better when he heals wounds by licking them with his tongue, than the righteous man who, by dying, degenerates from lion-like virtue and the blessed life.

The Lord also seems to suggest this when he says: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing repentance, rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV).

### Verses 7–8

“Go therefore, eat your bread with gladness, and drink your wine with joy, because your works please God. Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head.”

Because he had said above that, once people die, their memory is handed over to oblivion, according to the poet’s words:

> No conflict remains with the conquered, nor with those deprived of heaven,

and because thereafter under the sun there is nothing further, he now introduces, as a human error and custom, the way people mutually exhort one another to enjoy the good things of this age. In the manner of poets and rhetoricians he says:

“O human being, since after death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing, hear my counsel. While you live in this brief life, enjoy pleasure; use feasts; crush your cares with wine. Understand that these things have been given to you by God for use. Walk adorned in white garments; let your head breathe fragrances of ointments. Whichever woman pleases you, rejoice in her embrace. Run through this vain and brief life with vain and brief pleasure. For beyond these things you will have nothing further to enjoy. Seize quickly whatever can delight you, lest it perish. Nor should you fear foolish fictions—that in the underworld an account must be rendered for every work, whether good or evil. For there is no wisdom in death, no feeling after the dissolution of this life.”

And, he says, let Epicurus, Aristippus, the Cyrenaics, and the other beasts of the philosophers speak thus. But I, carefully reconsidering matters within myself, find not that, as some wrongly suppose, all things are done by chance and varying fortune plays with human affairs, but that all things occur by God’s judgment.

For neither should one swift of foot suppose that he possesses his course merely because he runs, nor should the strong man trust in his own strength, nor should the wise man think riches and resources are gathered by prudence, nor should an eloquent and learned man suppose that by eloquence and learning he can find favor among the people. Rather, all things are done by God’s ordering. Unless he governs all things by his decision and builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless he guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain (Ps. CXXVI).

Therefore there is not, as they think, a single event and an uncertain condition of this life; for when they do not expect it, snatched away by sudden death, they will come to judgment. And just as fish are caught by hook and net, and birds flying freely through the air are ensnared when they do not know it, so human beings will be led, according to their merit, to eternal punishments when death suddenly comes and judgment falls upon those who think that all things are carried along in an uncertain state.

This is according to that interpretation in which we wished briefly to embrace the whole. Now each point must be interpreted as though he speaks not in another’s person, but in his own.

“Go and eat your bread with gladness, and drink your wine with joy.” Since you have learned that all things are ended by death, and that in the underworld there is no repentance and no return to virtues, hurry while you are in this age; yield, perform repentance while you have time; labor. For God gladly receives repentance.

A simpler interpretation is also profitable, according to: “Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do all things in the name of the Lord” (1 Cor. X); and elsewhere: “Drink wine with counsel” (1 Tim. V). For he who abuses created things beyond measure does not possess true gladness and a good heart.

But it is better to understand it thus. He whose works have pleased God cannot lack the true bread and the wine pressed from the vine of Soreth. Therefore, since the command has been given to us which says, “You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you,” let us keep the commandments, and we shall be able to find bread, wine, and spiritual nourishment.

But to him who does not keep the commandments and glories in an abundance of bread and wine, it is said through Isaiah: “Do not say, ‘Behold, I know it’; for you have neither known nor understood, nor from the beginning have I opened your ears to you. For I know that you are utterly contemptuous” (Isa. XLVIII).

The words, “Go and eat your bread with gladness,” are the voice of that Ecclesiastes who speaks in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII); and in Proverbs: “Come, eat my bread and drink my wine” (Prov. IX).

“Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head.” Keep, he says, your body clean and be merciful; or thus: let there be no time when you do not have white garments; take care lest you ever be clothed in polluted garments. The sinful people are indeed described in dark garments of luxury. But you, put on light, and do not put on the curse written concerning Judah: “Let him put on cursing as a garment” (Ps. CVIII). Put on “the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience” (Col. III). And, when you have stripped off the old person with his deeds, put on the new, who is renewed day by day (Eph. IV; Col. III).

As for the words, “let oil not fail from your head,” one must know that oil has this nature: it both nourishes light and relieves the weariness of the exhausted. There is spiritual oil, the oil of exultation, of which it is written: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your companions” (Ps. XLIV; Heb. I). With this oil our face must be made cheerful; with it the head of the fasting person must be anointed. Sinners cannot possess it, to whom it is said: “There is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isa. I). For they have the contrary oil, which the righteous man detests, saying: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. CXL). Heretics possess this oil, and with it they desire to pour over the heads of those whom they deceive.

### Verses 9–10

“Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, throughout all the days of your unstable life which are given you under the sun during all the time of your vanity; for this is your portion in life and in your labor with which you labor under the sun. Whatever your hand can do, do earnestly; for there will be neither work, nor calculation, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, whither you are hastening.”

A person often transgresses the law of nature—the law established by nature, love, and grace—when bridegroom troubles bride or bride troubles bridegroom. Therefore, lest we wish to violate right and justice, and lest any bitterness separate those whom love joins, Ecclesiastes directs us to habits of peace and fidelity.

“Let the bridegroom,” he says, “enjoy life with his beloved bride; and likewise let the bride enjoy life with her beloved bridegroom, throughout all the days which this unstable life gives here.” He enjoys life who lives without complaint. Who ever enjoys life well when his bride is angry? What bride enjoys life well for herself when her bridegroom is angry?

How is unstable life given to you in these days? First you are an infant, then a child; next an adolescent, afterwards a young man, then an old man, and finally decrepit. You can never become stable, because you change every hour, variable both in the affections of the heart and in the movements of the flesh.

You who grieve, accusing unstable life, O human being, are given this share of profitable labor under the sun: that you may do diligently whatever your hand can do. Now, because you excel by reason, knowledge of things is added to you, and wisdom will strengthen your heart. Do work here, from which eternal reward may be given you in the future. For when death compels you to hasten to the underworld, there you will not do work from which you may hope for even a little good.

David, terrified by the shadow of death, says: “In death there is no one who remembers you; but in the underworld, who will confess you?” (Ps. VI). The Savior likewise commands: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX).

As for his words, “in the underworld, whither you hasten,” note this so that you may also believe that Samuel truly was in the underworld before Christ’s coming, although all the saints were held under the law of the underworld. But that saints are not held in the underworld after the Lord’s resurrection is attested by the Apostle: “It is better to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). But he who is with Christ is certainly not held in the underworld.

Whoever wishes to make unstable days stable through work ought to work with his beloved wife. Allegory will certainly give him a beloved bride. What bride, I ask, is more closely joined and friendlier than wisdom, which is also sweeter than life? Let whoever wishes to live well love her and betroth her to himself. For wisdom brings every gain of good with her; without it, no mind can possess even the appearance of love. You will be like a dry tree unless you grow green through wise wisdom.

Nature moreover offers a remarkable example: the viper is overcome by love for the sea-eel, *muraena*, and, hastening to mate with her, vomits up all its venom. Therefore the unchaste lover, with the hiss of a flattering voice, calls his unchaste beloved to the shore of the sea; nor does the eel shrink from the poison by which the viper is darkened.

The image of the serpent teaches you, O human being, what you should avoid and what you should do. Let the bridegroom avoid adultery, lest he become a viper; in order to please his bride, let him vomit out all venom. Let the bride patiently bear the venomous anger of her husband, if he vomits it out; and let her wisely endure the poison. Thus their unstable life is made stable by their manner of living.

### Verse 11

“I turned to another matter, and I saw under the sun: the race is not for the swift, nor battle for the strong, nor bread for the wise, nor riches for the learned, nor favor for the skillful; but time and chance are in all things.”

He who is bound in iron fetters and weighed down by heavy bonds of lead—for “wickedness sits upon a talent of lead,” and the Psalm says, “They are weighed down upon me as a heavy burden” (Ps. XXXVII)—is not suited for that race of which it is said: “I have finished the race; I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. IV). But even he who is light and whose soul is not weighed down cannot reach the finish without God’s help.

Likewise, when battle is against contrary powers, concerning which it is written, “Sanctify war” (Jer. VI), even though he is strong, he will not be able to conquer by his own strength. Even one perfect among the children of men and wise cannot possess the living and heavenly bread except through wisdom’s invitation: “Come, eat my breads” (Prov. IX).

And because there are riches of which the Apostle says, “Be rich in good works” (1 Tim. VI), and elsewhere, “You have become rich in every word and in every knowledge” (1 Cor. I), according to the wise man, one cannot gather these riches unless he has received them from God, whose riches they are. Favor also, unless it accompanies knowledge and is granted by God, cannot be found even by a learned man.

Knowing this, Paul says: “I labored more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV). And again: “His grace in me was not empty” (ibid.). Finally, a human being does not know when the time will come in which a changing event and the end of all things will follow.

This is according to the anagogical sense. But, to speak more simply, the Epistle to the Romans accords with this passage: it belongs not to one who wills nor to one who runs, but to God who has mercy (Rom. IX).

What does he mean by, “nor bread for the wise”? Daily experience proves it in many who, though exceedingly wise, lack necessities. “Nor favor for the skillful”: for you may see the most unlearned people flourish in the Church, and because they have cultivated boldness of countenance and acquired fluency of tongue, while giving no thought to what they say, they suppose themselves prudent and learned—especially if they have the favor of the crowd, which is more moved by lighter sayings. Conversely, one may see a learned man remaining obscure, suffering persecutions, enjoying no favor among the people, and wasting away in want and poverty. All these things happen because all things are carried along in an uncertain state, and recompense for merits is not in the present but in the future.

### Verse 12

“A human being does not know his end; but as fish are caught by a hook, and as birds are caught in a snare, so human beings are caught in an evil time, when it suddenly comes upon them.”

We have already said above that, while human beings do not know it, either distress or destruction comes upon them.

But according to allegory one must know that “the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea” (Matt. XIII); and conversely, that heretics have a net by which fish are caught for destruction. Their net is pleasant speech, flattering language, pretended or forced fasts, humble clothing, and imitation of virtues. If they begin to dispute concerning higher matters, lift their mouths on high, and seek the depths of God, they set a snare in high places.

Therefore, as fish and birds are caught by such a net and such a snare, so, when iniquity has multiplied, the love of many has grown cold, and signs and wonders have occurred—so that, if possible, even the elect are deceived (Matt. XXIV)—we must know that churchmen also, who are called “sons of man” and are of little faith, can quickly fall.

It should also be noted that throughout the whole book, wherever “children of men” is said, the Hebrew has “sons of man,” that is, sons of Adam. Nearly all Scripture is full of this idiom, calling the whole human race sons of Adam.

### Verses 13–16

“I also saw this great wisdom under the sun: a little city, and few men in it; a great king came against it, surrounded it, built fortifications round about it, and the siege was completed. But a poor and wise man was found in it, and he delivered the city by his wisdom; and afterwards no one remembered that poor man. And I said: Wisdom is better than strength. How then was the poor man’s wisdom despised and his words not heard?”

While others hold all things uncertain and suppose that the righteous have nothing more than the unrighteous, I found wisdom greatest in this: it often happens that a city is small and its inhabitants few, yet it is surrounded by an army of innumerable enemies, and the people inside are destroyed by siege and famine. Suddenly, contrary to everyone’s expectation, a humble and poor man is found who, because he has wisdom, while all the rich, great, powerful, and proud are in danger and terrified by the siege, thinks, investigates, and discovers how to rescue the city from evils.

O complete forgetfulness of human beings! After they have been liberated, captivity dissolved, and freedom restored to their country, no one remembers that wise poor man; no one gives thanks for salvation. Rather, all honor the rich, who were unable to offer any help in the danger.

Otherwise: the little city is the human being, who is also called by philosophers the lesser world; and the few men in it are the members of which the human being himself is composed. When the great king, the devil, comes against it and seeks an entrance through which he may break in, there is found within it the humble, wise, and pious thought of the inner human being, and it saves the city surrounded by enemies.

When a person has been rescued from danger—whether persecution, distress, any adverse circumstance, or sin—the outer human being, who is the enemy of that poor wise human being, does not remember the inner human being and does not submit himself to his counsels, but again enjoys his own freedom.

Otherwise: the little city, with few men in it, is the Church in comparison with the whole world. Against it the great king, the devil, often rises—not because he is great, but because he boasts that he is great—and surrounds it with a siege, whether persecution or some other kind of distress. There is found in it a poor and wise man, our Lord Jesus Christ, who became poor for our sake and who is himself Wisdom. That poor man delivers the city in his wisdom.

How often have we seen the lion sitting in ambush with the rich—that is, with the senators and rulers of this age—and plotting against the Church, only for him to fall before the wisdom of this poor man. When this poor man has conquered and peace has been restored to the city, scarcely anyone remembers him, scarcely anyone considers his commands. Instead, surrendering themselves wholly to luxury and pleasure, they seek riches which do not deliver in time of necessity.

### Verse 17

“The words of the wise are heard in silence more than the cry of a ruler among fools.”

One human being differs from another in character. Often a difference of character does not make people one merely in outward appearance. The distinctive species of the human being is rational; it differs from every species that lacks reason. But not all individuals have the same grace, so that every rational being enjoys reason. For whoever wisely uses reason is wise; therefore scarcely anyone among rational beings is counted as wise.

Distinguishing their characters, Ecclesiastes says: “The words of the wise are heard in silence more than the cry of a ruler among fools.” For the wise man does not shout, but wisely and fittingly discerns what he should say, to whom, why, how, and when. This color, this beauty, befits the wise man. The wise man discerns all things, so that he may be equal to all things. The weightiness of matters gives weight to the words of the wise.

Amos says: “The lion will roar; who will not fear?” (Amos III). Whose words are heard in silence? God is wise, and he roars like a lion. He terrifies us so that we may fear, threatening Gehenna to sinners. Whoever fears hears the words of the wise in silence. And whoever hears in silence and in fear of God gladly obeys the words of the wise.

In the wise God are his wise servants. Hence the same Amos says: “The Lord has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (ibid.). Whoever prophesies by God’s inspiration speaks words which you can hear in silence. Those act wisely who first perform the good things which they say. Therefore their words live in silence.

But he who trusts in himself and thinks himself a ruler, if he wishes while speaking and shouting to use reason badly, does not know how to restrain shouting by reason, but only confounds reason by shouting. Although such a self-confident man may be a ruler, he is not well heard when he speaks by shouting with words confused rather than articulated.

Such a person is often seen teaching in the Church: through shouting and verbal ornament, he twists his whole body into the gestures of an orator. His hearers are fools; he himself is more foolish, selling himself and buying them with applause. Such a person does not roar; he brays.

### Verse 18

“Wisdom is better than weapons of war; and one who sins in one thing will destroy many good things.”

Truly wisdom is better than strength, for from it all good things receive both beginning and end. Who will love God with his whole soul, whole strength, and all his powers unless he knows wisely what God is? This is the end of the commandment (1 Tim. I), the fountain of believing, as the Apostle Paul says; and according to the variation of things, it wishes now to be called love, now wisdom.

Therefore we should understand that through one sin many former acts of righteousness perish; that virtues mutually follow one another; that whoever possesses one possesses all; and that whoever sins in one thing is subject to all vices (Jas. II). The saying of the philosophers also agrees with this. If anyone wishes to possess all virtues together, one will give all, or one will take all away. Certainly the prudent person will be just, steadfast, and moderate. The just person will be prudent, steadfast, and moderate. Whoever is prudent and steadfast will be just and moderate. Therefore one who sins in one virtue lacks every virtue. If the fourth is absent from three, the three disdain to be present.

## Chapter V

Divine Scripture says: “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” (Ecclus. XXII). Therefore, dearest brother Gregory, despising the charm of rhetorical art and the beauty of childish, applause-seeking eloquence, we flee to the gravity of the holy Scriptures. There is the true medicine for wounds; there are sure remedies for griefs; there the mother receives her only son upon a bier (Luke VII); there it is said to the surrounding crowd, “The girl is not dead, but lives” (Luke VIII); there the man dead four days comes out bound at the voice of the crying Lord (John XI).

We also have the obstacle of mutual love. Let us love in spirit, be bound in affection, and imitate the strength of mind found in holy men, whom Christ the Lord received into his glory. Let our little page sing of them; let all writings resound with them. Let us hold in remembrance those whom we cannot have bodily. And let us never cease to speak of those with whom we cannot speak.

Let us return, then, to our Ecclesiastes.

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

“Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment. Wisdom and glory are more precious than a little folly for a time.”

Observe, O human being, how very small Ecclesiastes judges those whom he wished to compare with dying flies, which spoil the sweet fragrance of fragrant ointment. What this ointment is, David the noble lyre-player sings, saying: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity: like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII), and the rest.

This head is Christ; the beard is the human being manly in heart; the Church is the garment; we are the borders of this garment. This ointment descends upon the head, beard, and border of Christ’s garment when God anointed him above his companions (Ps. XLIV). We, however, are his sharers, as the border of the garment is anointed by a drop of ointment flowing from him.

Zion signifies the Church; Mount Hermon signifies the Synagogue. Or understand Zion as the good and Hermon as sinners. Thus the ointment descends upon Zion as dew upon Hermon. What, then, is the sweet ointment except spiritual grace? This ointment descends from heaven upon our head when the Holy Spirit anoints us in baptism; it descends upon our beard when it makes our works, while we live, manly; it descends from heaven upon the borders of the garment when, at the end of life, we are consecrated with sacred anointing.

There is also an ointment supplied by wisdom, compounded from the manifold fragrance of virtue. How often do dying flies, mixed into the ointment itself among its blended spices, spoil the ointment! As you see flies mixed with ointment, so you see good and evil people mixed in the Church. A fly often intrudes upon wisdom when evil words spoil the good character of the wise man; when the cunning of a fool wishes to be called wisdom and conceals itself under wisdom’s name, carefully doing evil when the deceitful person pretends to be prudent.

Why should I repeat every kind of virtue? Our evil will perverts the genus of virtues. Virtue is the genus of individual virtues, which, harmoniously joined, smell sweet like precious ointment. Whoever loses his genus, what retains he among its species? “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment.” At times they spoil the ointment in themselves, at times in their brothers: when they sin, they spoil it in themselves; in their brothers, by drawing them away from the straight path.

That dying flies signify sinners will be proved both by Holy Scripture and by the nature of flies. For the flies which, according to Isaiah, rule over the part of the river of Egypt (Isa. VII) spoil the sweetness of oil in each believer, leaving the odor and traces of their impurity. From these flies the prince of demons is also called Beelzebub, which is interpreted either “idol of flies,” “man of flies,” or “having flies.”

What Scripture shows, the nature of flies also shows. If a spider bites anyone with its venomous mouth, those who write on natural history say that the person can be healed by a crushed fly applied above it. Thus you, O human being, overcome the venom of malice and wickedness by the virtue of humility. The spider sucks flies caught in its nets; so vain wisdom sucks the sinner dry.

Vain wisdom sucked dry a certain man like a fly when, disdaining flies and dying like a fly, he denied that God had made every living creature. If flies are killed in water, after some hours they revive. Let us believe that nothing is done in vain and nothing said in vain. A killed fly does not always revive altogether, but rather often does.

When we are baptized, all of us are buried in the washing. Whoever lives well, rising from the font, has revived. But whoever has lived wickedly has not revived from the righteous font. Whoever sins against the Lord, wandering like a fly and roaming importunately while foolishly thinking himself wise, if afterwards, having become wise, he is made foolish for Christ, his folly is more precious than someone’s glory bestowed upon him by vain wisdom.

David’s folly for a time protected him from an enemy whom strength, wisdom, and glory in war could not have protected (1 Sam. XXI). That foolish madness of his was more precious than strength and military glory. For someone also says: “To feign folly in the right place is supreme wisdom.” As a strong man commonly disarms an enemy with the enemy’s own weapons, so God stripped the strong devil of his own weapons. God made fitting use of that devil’s folly for a time; as David killed Goliath with his own sword (1 Sam. XVII), so he destroyed the devil, king of the flies, with the devil’s own sword.

The Apostle Paul likewise says: “But we preach Christ crucified: to Jews a stumbling-block, and to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. I).

VERS. 2, 3.—The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left. But even when a fool walks along the road, [Col. 1288D] since he himself is senseless, he regards everyone as fools. Ecclesiastes, always in agreement with nature, now seems to place the wise man’s heart on the right and the fool’s on the left contrary to nature. For natural philosophers teach that men’s hearts are on the left side and women’s on the right. If this is so, how can what he says be true: “The heart of the wise is on the right, the heart of the fool on the left”? The learned and the unlearned, the good and the evil, the just and the unjust, however much and however greatly they differ in suffering and acting, nevertheless do not differ in nature or in the placement of their limbs. Therefore the wise man’s heart is not elsewhere, nor the fool’s elsewhere.

Philosophers, inventing, and poets, philosophizing, have discussed right and left at great length. Does not Pythagoras’ letter, the pattern of human life, show the right-hand path to the good and the left-hand path to the evil? [Col. 1289A] Virgil, equal to philosophers and greater than poets, understood the same thing where he writes:

> The right-hand path, which more directly leads beneath the walls of Dis,  
> by this way lies our road to Elysium; but the left  
> exacts the punishments of the wicked and leads to impious Tartarus.

And in the Gospel it is commanded: “Let not the left hand know what the right hand of the wise man does” (Matt. 6). And when we are struck on the right cheek, we are not commanded to offer the left cheek to the striker, but “the other” (Matt. 5). For the righteous person has no left side: everything in him is right-handed. And when the Savior comes to judge, the sheep will stand at the right, and the goats at the left (Matt. 25). And in Proverbs it is written: “The Lord knows the right-hand ways, but those which are crooked are on the left” (Prov. 4).

Therefore, whoever is wise [Col. 1289B] always thinks of the world to come, which leads to life—that is, to the right. Yet we must not suppose that the saying, “Do not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (Deut. 5), contradicts this brief statement. Here the right side is understood as good; there, not so much the right as the turning aside to the right is condemned, lest we be wise beyond what it is necessary for us to be wise. For virtues lie in the mean, and every excess is a vice.

The meaning of the following little verses, “And when a fool walks on the road, since he himself is senseless, he regards everyone as fools,” is this: as the fool himself sins, so he hopes that all sin similarly, and judges everyone from his own disposition.

VERS. 4.—If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place; for healing [Col. 1289C] causes the greatest sins to cease. Who this mighty one is, and who this spirit of the mighty one is—would that we did not know; would that we could at least forget! Very often either this mighty one or his spirit presses hard upon us and compels us to leave our place. True faith is our place, because in it we stand.

This mighty one is he of whom the Lord speaks: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). This mighty one rules over as many wicked spirits as the deceived human being succumbs to vices. This mighty spirit, speaking through the serpent to the woman, after he had deceived her, rose also against Adam as a conqueror, cast him down from his place, and expelled him from Paradise (Gen. 2). This spirit also rose against David and transfixed him with the darts of love and ambition [Col. 1289D] (2 Sam. 11; 1 Chron. 21). Through the maid at the door he shook Peter, so that Peter denied the Lord of majesty (John 18). Nor shall I pass over Mary Magdalene, over whom this spirit, rising powerfully with seven demons, reigned (Mark 16). Who can number those over whom this spirit has risen and compelled them to abandon the place of their faith?

Although this mighty spirit, this strong prince, comes against us with ten thousand, our prince will meet him with a doubled army, namely twenty thousand (Luke 14). What, then, does the single army mean, and what the doubled one? 556 This spirit fights with a single army: he can kill us but cannot make us alive. Our king fights with a soldier twice as strong as his, because he can both kill and make alive. He has two cords and two legions, of life and death, like the most valiant David. This king makes alive those whom that spirit slaughters; he raises those whom the other casts down. He lifts to heaven those expelled from Paradise; with his bracelet he pierces Leviathan’s jaw [Col. 1290A] (Job 40), in order to draw sinners back from the mouth of the mighty one.

Foreknowing the wars of this mighty one, Solomon warns us to arm ourselves beforehand with the weapons of freedom, lest perhaps, by fleeing, we be compelled to yield our place. Whoever protects himself with these weapons of freedom, that spirit of the mighty one does not rise against him. But if anyone perhaps has yielded the place of faith by fleeing, let him recover freedom and the weapons of virtue: that mighty spirit will descend from him and depart. Freedom is of such great price, which the praise of virtue adorns.

[Col. 1290B] VERS. 5–7.—There is an evil which I saw under the sun, as though proceeding by error from the face of a ruler: a fool placed in high dignity, and rich men sitting below. I saw slaves on horses and princes walking on the ground like slaves. He recalls, therefore, that he has observed this injustice in the world: that he sees God’s judgment as unjust, and that, whether through ignorance or apart from his will, it happens that either in worldly authorities or in the government of the Church, those who are rich in speech and wisdom, and likewise rich in good works, sit in lowly station, while some imprudent person holds primacy in the Church.

This happens through the influence of him who has power in the world, while he oppresses powerful and learned men [Col. 1290C] and does not permit them to appear among the people; but those whom he knows to be imprudent he makes greater in the churches, where the blind are led by the blind into the pit (Matt. 15). What follows also supports this sense: “I saw slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.” Those who are slaves of vices and sin—or are so lowly that all regard them as slaves—being suddenly puffed up by dignity bestowed by the devil, travel empty roads; while every noble or prudent man, crushed by poverty, walks in the path and service of slaves.

Others explain the mighty one and ruler, from whose presence ignorance seems to proceed, as God, thinking that in this inequality of affairs people suppose that he judges neither justly nor according to what is equitable. Some, moreover, think that this should be joined to what precedes, [Col. 1290D] so that he is himself the mighty one concerning whom it was said before these verses: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place” (v. 4).

Let us therefore not be sad if we seem lowly in this world, knowing that before the devil fools are exalted and the rich cast down, slaves bear the insignia of masters, and princes walk in the lowliness of slaves. It should be noted, however, that here too the horse is understood in a good sense, as in: “Your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8). Thus nature makes even slaves ride on horses. Pythagoras, celebrated everywhere for philosophy, was a slave because he had received this condition from nature; yet, seizing from the spark of natural reason a flame as though from tinder, he kindled a bright fire. Hence he shone through philosophy, philosophy concealing his servile condition. [Col. 1291A] And who, I ask, runs on horseback as he ran in philosophy?

Ill fortune took from Plato, captured by pirates, the freedom which nature had given him; but what fortune took away, nature, as the saying goes, received back. What he lost by chance, he redeemed by wisdom. How many such slaves does nature cause to ride on horses? How many masters, rich in possessions and powerful in honor, does it allow to go upon the earth and sit below, because, slothfully sitting still, they do not seek the heights of the earth? Thus worldly wisdom agrees with Ecclesiastes.

VERS. 8.—He who digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent. The interpretation is partly plain and partly mystical. For elsewhere Solomon himself says: “He who sets a snare will be caught in it” (Sir. 27); and in the Psalm: “He opened and dug a pit, and fell into the hole which he made” (Ps. 7).

The tearing down of a hedge or wall means ecclesiastical doctrines and the institution founded by apostles and prophets. Whoever destroys these and wishes to pass beyond them is struck, in the very thing he neglects, by the serpent. [Col. 1291B] Of this serpent it is also written in Amos: “If they descend into hell, I shall command the serpent, and it will bite them” (Amos 9). Holy Moses shows what the serpent’s nature is: “The serpent,” he says, “was more cunning than all the animals” (Gen. 3). The serpent is more cunning, but the human being is wiser. Cunning corrupts; wisdom wisely avoids corruption.

Come then, human being: do wisely what the serpent does through cunning. When it comes to drink, it vomits out all its venom, lest the power of venom mixed with water perhaps cause it death. So too, Christian, when you go to the washing of faith and the harbor of life, first vomit all the venom of sin from your heart, lest the power of venom, mixed with life, bring you death. It fears a naked human being and pursues one who is clothed. Perhaps it feared Adam and Eve when naked; and, so that it might not fear them so much, it deceived those whom it feared. It still pursues us, clothed in sins, trusting that those whom it conquered it can still conquer.

The serpent knows how to preserve its head if it is ever struck, showing that the head is the seat of life. So let the human being preserve his head, Christ, if he is struck. He whose head is Christ has his life placed in Christ. When the serpent feels itself growing old, it fasts for forty days until it sheds old age with the skin which it casts off. For whom is it more fitting to live forty days in fasting [Col. 1291C] than for us, who have grown old in sins, if we wish to become young again by laying aside old age for Christ?

[Col. 1291D] VERS. 9, 10.—He who moves stones will be distressed by them; and he who splits wood will be wounded by it. If iron is blunted, and not as before, but has become dull, let it be sharpened with much labor, and wisdom will follow after diligence.

In Isaiah also holy stones are rolled upon the earth. They do not stand fixed in one position there, but pass onward; and, always striving toward higher things, they hasten to depart from here. From these living stones the Savior’s city is built in the Apocalypse (Rev. 21), and the Apostle does not fail to say that the Church is built from them. Therefore, if anyone, perverted by heretical art, removes these stones from the Church’s building, he will later suffer torments.

But because Scripture says without qualification, “He who moves stones,” and does not add “good” or “evil,” the reverse must also be understood: namely, that an ecclesiastical man—a bishop or presbyter—if, according to the command of Leviticus concerning a leprous house, he removes a stone [Col. 1292A] to be crushed into dust and ashes (Lev. 14), will grieve in the very act of attempting to take a stone from Christ’s Church, saying with the Apostle: “Weep with those who weep; mourn with those who mourn” (Rom. 12); and: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11).

“And he who splits wood will be wounded by it.” Heretics are unfruitful woods, groves without useful fruit. [Col. 1292B] Therefore planting them is forbidden in the temple of God (Deut. 16), and the empty shades of foliage—that is, of merely resounding words—are despised. Although, therefore, the man who cuts down these woods with the sword of his speech is prudent and learned, he will be endangered by them unless he pays careful attention, especially if what follows happens to him: “If the iron is blunted and he has marred its face”—that is, if his disputation is found weaker and does not have the sharpness by which to cut through every opposing argument, but the chief part of his heart grows dull—he will pass over to the adverse side, and perverse strength will strengthen him. He will then begin to have strength, 557 and to have wisdom which is superfluous and does not help its possessor.
