“If the iron is blunted and is no longer as before, it will be confused; it will be strengthened by virtues, and the remainder of strength is [Col. 1292C] wisdom.” If, he says, someone sees that through negligence he has lost knowledge of the Scriptures, that the sharpness of his intellect has been dulled, and that, disturbed, he no longer remains what he had already begun to be—this sometimes happens when someone who possesses a little knowledge, puffed up into pride, ceases to learn and read; then, little by little, because nothing is added to him, what he has is taken away, his breast remains empty of instruction, and the iron which had been sharp becomes dull. For idleness and sloth are a kind of rust of wisdom.

If anyone has suffered this, therefore, let him not despair of a remedy for health, but let him go to a teacher and be instructed again by him. After labor, diligence, and abundant sweat, he will be able to recover the wisdom he had lost. And this is what is said: “He will be strengthened by powers,” [Col. 1292D] that is, through labor, sweat, diligence, and daily reading he will attain wisdom; and his strength will have this end: that he receive wisdom.

VERS. 11.—If a serpent bites in silence, the secret slanderer has nothing more than it. The plain meaning is this: serpent and slanderer are alike. For as the serpent, biting secretly, inserts venom, so this man, secretly slandering, pours out the poison of his breast against his brother, and has nothing more than a serpent. Since the human tongue was created for blessing and for the edification of one’s neighbor, he makes it equal to a serpent when he perversely abuses its powers.

Otherwise: if the serpent, the devil, secretly bites someone [Col. 1293A] and infects him with the venom of sin while no one knows it, then, if the one struck remains silent and does not do penance, nor wishes to confess his wound to a brother and teacher, the teacher and brother, who have a tongue for healing, will not easily be able to help him. For if the sick person is ashamed to confess to the physician a wound of which the physician is ignorant, medicine does not cure it.

Look [consider], therefore, human being, at the nature of the serpent and the tongue of the slanderer, and you will see why a slanderer is like a serpent. A serpent dies if struck once; it returns to life if struck a second time. Whatever crawls along the ground by creeping is called a serpent. Therefore the sinner is understood through the serpent, because he seeks earthly things, not heavenly.

[Col. 1293B] As the serpent dies if struck once, so a human being dies through sin if struck by the first blow. The first temptation of the flesh gives the sinner the first blow. For when the flesh sins, it kills us with the sword of the law. If the mind inspired by God grants the sinner a second blow, the destruction of sin makes us, like the serpent, live again. He properly dies who is struck while the heart is silent. But if, crying aloud, he implores God to help and, confessing his sins to God, shows the grievous wound, a good teacher will remove with his mouth whatever the sinner has contracted through love of the earth. And, as though sucking out the serpent’s own venom, he will make the struck man live well again, though he had died through sinning.

VERS. 12, 13.—The words of a wise man’s mouth are grace, but the lips of a fool will cast him down; the beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his mouth is the worst error. [Col. 1293C] Ecclesiastes teaches how greatly the wise differ from the foolish by distinguishing their causes and consequences. “The words,” he says, “of a wise man’s mouth are grace, but the lips of a fool will cast him down.” When a wise man speaks, not only are his words judged pleasing, but grace itself seems to speak to you. Grace makes welcome whatever wisdom says.

If the fool’s simplicity could confine folly within a fixed limit, there would be nothing in all the matters which wisdom and grace wisely order well that could offend us. But folly attacks, with a great host of fools, whatever wisdom says and whatever grace says. Such people, as Solomon says, “their lips will cast down.” There is weight in these very few words of Ecclesiastes. He does not say, “The fool’s words will cast him down,” but, “His [Col. 1293D] lips will cast the fool down.” When a fool speaks to a fool, he does not seem to put forth words, but rather to make sounds with confused heart or mouth.

As a stork, thrown back upon its back, flings its lips about and beats the air with a clashing beak, so the clashing lips of fools sound through emptiness and cannot render the sweet voice of words. This may also be understood of heretics, who do not comprehend the sayings of prudent men; rather, preparing themselves for contrary disputations, they wrap both the beginning and the end of their speaking in clamorous vanity and shameless error, and, knowing nothing, speak more than they know.

VERS. 14, 15.—The fool multiplies words. A human being does not know what was before him, and who can tell him what will be after him? The labor of fools will afflict [Col. 1294A] those who do not know how to go to the city. He speaks either generally about all fools who do not know God, or specifically about heretics.

Read Plato; turn over Aristotle’s subtleties; examine Zeno and Carneades more carefully, and you will prove true what is said: “The labor of fools will afflict them.” They indeed sought truth with every effort; but because they had no guide and forerunner on the way, and thought that by human perceptions they could grasp wisdom, they did not arrive at the city of which it is said in the Psalm: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Ps. 72). For the Lord will scatter in his city all the shadows, diverse images, and personae which they put on for themselves in various doctrines.

Of that city it is also written elsewhere: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45); and in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5); and in Isaiah: “I am a strong city, a city which is besieged.” For all the wise of the world and heretics seek to attack this city of truth and wisdom, though it is firm and strong. And what we have said of philosophers must also be understood of heretics: they labor and are afflicted in vain in the study of the Scriptures, since they walk in a wilderness and cannot find the city. Of their error the Psalmist also speaks, saying: “They wandered in the wilderness; they did not find the way to a city of habitation” (Ps. 106). [Col. 1294B]

VERS. 16, 17.—Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning. Blessed is the land whose [Col. 1294C] king is noble, and whose princes eat at their proper time, for refreshment and not for luxury. He seems indeed to condemn the rule of the young and to condemn luxurious judges: in some, wisdom is weak because of age; in others, even mature age is enervated by pleasures. Conversely, he seems to approve a ruler of good character and liberal education, and to praise those judges who do not at all prefer pleasure to the business of citizens, but, after much labor and administration of the commonwealth, are compelled to take food as a necessity.

But to me something more sacred seems hidden in the letter: namely, that in the Scriptures those are called young who depart from ancient authority and despise the gray precepts of their parents; who, neglecting God’s commandment, desire to establish the traditions of human beings. [Col. 1294D] Of them the Lord also threatens Israel in Isaiah, because it would not accept the water of Shiloah, which goes quietly (Isa. 8), and had overthrown the ancient pool, choosing for itself the rivers of Samaria and the torrents of Damascus: “I will give,” he says, “young men as their rulers, and mockers shall rule over them” (Isa. 3).

Read Daniel, and you will find God as the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7). Read the Apocalypse of John, and you will find the Savior’s head white as snow and like white wool (Rev. 1). Jeremiah also, because he was wise and his gray hairs were reckoned to him as wisdom, 558 is forbidden to call himself young.

Woe, therefore, to the land whose king is the devil, who is always eager for novelties and, like Absalom, even rebels against his father (2 Sam. 15); which [Col. 1295A] has as judges and princes those who love the pleasures of this age, who, before the day of death arrives, say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22; 1 Cor. 15).

By contrast, blessed is the land of the Church, whose king is Christ, the son of freeborn persons, descended from the stock of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the prophets, and all the saints—persons over whom sin did not exercise dominion and who therefore were free. From them was born the freer branch, Saint Mary, having no shrub or shoot at its side, but whose whole fruit burst forth into the flower that speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am a flower of the field and a lily of the valleys” (Song 2).

Its princes also are the apostles and all the saints, who have as king the son of freeborn persons, the son of the free woman, begotten not from the slave-girl Hagar but [Col. 1295B] from Sarah’s freedom (Gal. 4). Nor do they eat in the morning or hastily: they do not seek pleasure in the present age, but will eat at their proper time, when the time of recompense arrives. And they will eat for refreshment, not for luxury. Every good thing of the present age is luxury; that of the age to come is perpetual refreshment.

VERS. 18, 19.—Through sloth the roof-beam will be brought low, and through weakness of hands the house will leak. They make bread for laughter, and wine so that the drinkers [the living] may feast, and all things obey money. Our house, which was erected with the human being’s upright posture, and the dwelling which we have in heaven—if we are slothful and too slow for good works—will be brought low; and every roof-beam which ought to bear aloft the lofty summit will fall to the ground [Col. 1295C] and crush its inhabitant. When the assistance of hands and virtues grows numb, every storm from above and every whirlwind of clouds will break upon us.

What we have interpreted in one person can better be understood of the Church: through the negligence of its rulers all its height falls, and the enticements of vices are found where the governance of virtues was thought to be. “They make bread and wine for laughter, so that the drinkers may feast.” We explained above that through the sloth and negligence of teachers the Church is brought low, its summit falls, and its timbers are rained upon. Now therefore he speaks of the same teachers. Since he seemed to accuse them because they kept silent and did not exercise the office of teachers, and because bishops and presbyters established in the Church did not labor in word and doctrine—as Titus is also urged to do, and Timothy is commanded not to neglect the grace which he had received through the laying on of hands—but reckoned themselves presbyters and bishops only in order to receive wages, and as mute teachers sought the double honor due to those who labor in doctrine and word, [Col. 1295D] he now, conversely, accuses those who speak in the Church and teach the people, but teach what the people delight to hear: they flatter the sinner in vice and stir up the noise of their hearers.

When speech in the Church becomes wanton and promises blessedness and the kingdom of heaven to the crowd, does it not seem to you that they make bread for laughter and mix wine for drinkers? Or perhaps those who teach seek riches, food, and wealth through pleasing promises [Col. 1296A]; or perhaps the Church’s bread—which is for mourners and not for laughers, for “blessed are those who mourn, because they shall laugh” (Matt. 5)—is prepared amid mirth and joy.

What follows, “and all things obey money,” must be understood in two ways: either that the teachers themselves, after growing rich through flattery, exercise rule among the people; or surely, because silver always stands for speech—“the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11)—this confirms that the ignoble mob readily yields to eloquence and an oration composed of the foliage of words.

Those who have the bridegroom with them and are therefore forbidden to mourn and fast (Matt. 9) make bread in laughter—laughter from which Isaac received his name (Gen. 21)—and prepare wine for the joy of drinkers. Therefore every holy man who, as Christ commands, is a teacher of the Church, makes bread in laughter and joy and ministers cups of wine in gladness. The silver to which all things obey is also the five, two, and one talents of the householder in the Gospel, and the ten minas entrusted to servants for trading (Matt. 25; Luke 19). [Col. 1296B]

VERS. 20.—Do not slander the king in your thought, and do not curse the rich man in the secrecy of your chamber; for the birds of heaven will carry your voice, and that which has wings will report your utterance. The plain commandment also edifies hearers: we are not, overcome by anger and fury, to break out into cursing and slander against kings and rulers, because contrary to expectation it sometimes happens that [Col. 1296C] what we have said against them is reported to them, and we incur danger through the lack of restraint of our tongue.

When he says, “A bird will carry your voice, and that which has wings will report your utterance,” it must be understood hyperbolically, as when we customarily say that even the walls, before which such things are spoken, will not conceal what they have heard. But it is better to understand the commandment thus: we should know that we are commanded not merely to say anything rashly against Christ, but also, in the secret places of the heart, though we are constrained by varied tribulations, to think nothing blasphemous and nothing impious.

And because we owe to our neighbor the love which we show to Christ—“You shall love the Lord your God, and your neighbor as yourself” (James 11)—this too is commanded: that we should not [Col. 1296D] slander the saints behind their backs, nor gnaw with a biting tongue at those whom we see enriched with knowledge, wisdom, and virtues. For the angels who go about the earth and are ministering spirits, and who say in Zechariah, “We have gone through the earth, and behold, all the earth is at rest” (Zech. 1), carry our words and thoughts to heaven after the manner of birds, while we secretly think that God’s knowledge escapes us.

CAP. XI

VERS. 1.—Cast your bread upon the passing waters, for after many days you will find it. He exhorts us to almsgiving, because one ought to give to everyone who asks and do good without discrimination. For just as one who sows upon irrigated ground expects the fruit of the seed, so one who gives to the needy sows not a grain of seed but bread itself, expecting, as it were, its multiplication at interest; and when the day of judgment comes, he will find much more than he gave. [Col. 1297A]

Otherwise: whenever you see in any person that water of which it is said, “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7), do not be reluctant to offer him the bread of wisdom, rational bread, the bread of discourse. For if you do this frequently, you will find that you have not cast the seed of teaching in vain.

I think that something similar is said in Isaiah: “Blessed is he who sows upon water, where ox and ass tread” (Isa. 32): that teacher is accounted worthy of blessedness who sows upon the irrigated breast of his hearers, among a people gathered both from Jews and from Gentiles.

Ecclesiastes was not far from natural philosophy when he judged that bread should be cast upon waters. For water is one of the four elements, in which our image is reflected as in a mirror. Often, when your face stands opposite, you see in water what you are like, what you do, where or how you turn yourself. Solomon wishes the human being to cast bread upon these waters, so that he may observe in them the good things which are done. Whoever sees himself in a mirror sees in himself what beauty he lacks and what ugliness is present. Whoever, looking at himself in the waters, rightly corrects his deeds will find the bread of life flowing back through the waters. [Col. 1297B]

559 VERS. 2.—Give seven portions, and also eight, because you do not know what evil will be upon the earth. In Ezekiel also seven and eight steps are read for the ascent to the temple (Ezek. 40), and after the ethical Psalm there are fifteen Psalms of Ascents, through which [Col. 1297C] we are instructed first in the Law (Ps. 118), and, the number seven having been completed, afterward ascend through the octave to the Gospel. We are therefore commanded to believe with equal reverence in each Testament, both Old and New.

The Jews gave seven portions, believing in the Sabbath, but did not give eight, neglecting the resurrection on the Lord’s Day. Conversely, the heretics Marcion and Manichaeus, and all who tear apart the old Law with a hasty mouth, give eight portions, accepting the Gospel, but do not assign to it the number seven, rejecting the Instrument of the ancients. Let us therefore believe in both Instruments. For we cannot now comprehend in our minds the worthy torments and worthy punishment reserved for those who live on earth—Jews and heretics—who deny one of the two. [Col. 1297D]

VERS. 3.—If clouds are full, they will pour rain upon the earth. If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will be. Keep the commandments prescribed to you above, so that the clouds may pour out their rain upon you. For wherever you prepare a place and a future dwelling for yourself, whether toward the south or the north, there you will remain when you have died.

Otherwise: this is why we said above (v. 7), “Cast your bread upon the surface of the water, and give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6): for clouds too, when full, distribute their riches to mortals. You, like a tree, however long-lived you may be, will not exist forever; but suddenly submerged by a storm of death, as by winds, wherever you fall, there you will remain forever—whether the final time finds you harsh and cruel, or gentle and merciful. [Col. 1298A]

Otherwise: it is said to God in the Psalms, “Your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 35); and in Isaiah God threatens the sinful vineyard: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5). The clouds, therefore, are the prophets and every holy man. When one has gathered many disciplines in his heart, he will then be able to rain down the commandments of teaching and say: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let it pour out rain upon the earth” (Deut. 32), to which it is said: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (ibid.).

But concerning what follows, “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will be,” let us take [Col. 1298B] the example from Habakkuk, where it is written: “God will come from the south” (Hab. 3). And, as far as I judge, the south is always understood favorably and the north unfavorably, as in: “Arise, north wind”—that is, depart and go away—“and come, south wind” (Song 4). Therefore the tree which falls in this life, and is cut down by the condition of mortality, and which sinned while it stood, is afterward placed in the region of the north; or, if it bore fruits worthy of the south, it will lie in the southern quarter. There is no tree which is not either in the north or in the south.

This also signifies what is written: “I will say to the north, ‘Give,’ and to the south, ‘Do not forbid’” (Isa. 43). For the south wind and east wind are never commanded to bring people, because those who are afterward led to the east and south must be in the other regions. Thus the north brings its inhabitants to the south, and the southwest wind to the east. For they cannot make progress if they remain in their former dwellings. [Col. 1298C]

VERS. 4, 5.—He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap. Just as you do not know what the path of the spirit is, or by what process bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all. He who considers to whom he should do good, and does not give to everyone who asks him, often passes over the person who deserves to receive.

Otherwise: the person who preaches God’s word only when the people listen gladly and a favorable breeze blows toward their conduct is a negligent sower and an idle farmer. For in the midst of prosperity, while we do not know, adversities arise. [Col. 1298D] God’s word must be preached in season and out of season, and in the time of faith we must not consider the storm of adverse clouds. Of this it is said in Proverbs: “Like a violent and useless rain are those who have forsaken wisdom and praise impiety” (Prov. 28).

Without considering the clouds or fearing the winds, one must sow amid storms. Nor should one call one time favorable and another useless, since we do not know what the way and will of the spirit which governs all things may be. Just as one does not know the way of the spirit and soul entering into the little child, and you do not know the varieties of bones and veins, nor how, in the womb of the pregnant woman, a human body is formed from a base element into diverse shapes and limbs—how from the same seed one thing softens into flesh, another hardens into bones, another pulsates in veins, another is bound in sinews—so you cannot know the works of God, who is the maker of all. [Col. 1299A]

From this he teaches that adversities are not to be feared and that we must not rashly judge about the winds and clouds mentioned above, since the sower ought to continue in the course and order proper to him and reserve the outcome for the Lord’s judgment. “For it is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

VERS. 6.—In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease; for you do not know which will spring up more, this or that, and whether both together will be better. The one whom Solomon sends out to sow his seed morning and evening, the Lord Jesus himself sends in the morning to prune the vineyard. What Solomon says, “Let not [Col. 1299B] your hand cease,” the Lord says to those standing idle at the eleventh hour: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matt. 20).

Whoever serves God from the first morning of life dreams in the morning and in the morning tends the vineyard by pruning. He sows late and tends the vineyard late by digging who does nothing in the morning time of life, but at the last stage of life returns to himself and to his heart, seeking good fruit for himself however late and tardily, redeeming the time until he reaches life’s final hour. “Those who bore the burden and heat of the day from morning,” says the Lord; “the first will be last, and the last first” (ibid.). Thus Solomon now also says: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease.”

### Verses 7–8

Sweet is the light, and pleasant to the eyes is the sight of the sun. If a man lives many years and rejoices in all of them [Col. 1299C], he ought to remember the time of darkness and the many days; when these come, the things that have passed will be convicted of vanity.

What man's lot is is clear from the words of Ecclesiastes. So long as we live and are well, love of the light always lives within us, though it is the last thing to leave the mind. For what delights us so much as to see the bright sun? But lest this sweetness prove harmful to your life, and lest you rejoice more than is necessary in looking upon the sun, observe how Ecclesiastes examines the matter. “If,” he says, “a man lives many years and rejoices in all of them, he ought to remember the time of darkness and the many days.” Eternal death or everlasting life shows these days not to be short, but rather long and enduring. The sweetness of your life will become bitter to you when, in exchange for the light of this brief life, you suffer darkness [Col. 1299D], and reckon all things vain and transitory.

When Ecclesiastes sets these facts and causes before us, he warns us to enjoy the sweetness of the true light, since the sweetness of the present light—the sweetness of this life—is not eternal. Rather, he exhorts us to behold the true sun with a pure heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). It is not always good to see the present sun, which by its reflected light commonly oppresses those who look upon it. By its excessive brightness the sun sometimes scorches us. God is the true light, and in Him there are no darknesses at all (1 John 1). As God is like light, yet light is not what God Himself is, so God is as it were the sun, yet the sun is not what God Himself is. Since it is called the sun because it alone shines in the world, all the stars being dimmed by its light [Col. 1300A], therefore God is the true sun, because He alone shines everywhere, proceeding from the Father’s mouth as heat proceeds from the sun. The fourth day did not see this sun begin to shine; rather, it shone before time had its ages, for of itself it shines above all ages.

### Verse 9

Therefore rejoice, young man, in your youth; let your heart be glad in the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart and according to the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.

He had said that the light of this world is most sweet, and that a man ought to rejoice in the days of his life and seize pleasure with every effort; for the eternal night of death is impending, when one may no longer enjoy what has been gathered, and all that we possessed passes away as though a shadow [Col. 1300B]. Now, therefore, he exhorts the young man and says: “O youth, before old age and death come upon you, rejoice in your youth; take whatever seems good to you in your heart and pleasant to your sight; enjoy the things of the world as you please.”

Again, lest he be thought to be urging men to luxury by saying this, and to be falling into Epicurus’ doctrine, he removes this suspicion by adding: “And know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.” Thus, he says, use the things of the world, knowing that at the end you will be judged.

### Verse 10

Remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and pleasure are vain.

By “anger” he includes every disturbance of the mind; by “evil of the flesh” he means all bodily pleasures [Col. 1300C]. Therefore, he says, enjoy the good things of this age without sinning either through desire or through the flesh. Leave behind the old vices to which you were enslaved in your youth through the folly of vanity, because youth is joined to foolishness.

## Chapter 12

### Verse 1

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years draw near of which you will say: “They do not please me.”

Remember your Creator often, and so pass through the life of youth that you keep the final death in mind, before the time comes upon you when every sorrowful thing follows.

### Verse 2

Before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain.

If we understand this of the general consummation of the world, this chapter accords with the Lord’s words, in which He says: “There shall be tribulation and distress such as has not been from the beginning of creation, nor shall be. For the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Matt. 24). These are the guardians of the house, so that the house is understood here as the world, while the strong men are the opposing powers deceived by error and destined to be scattered.

But if the particular consummation of each individual is referred to the end of this life, then sun, moon, stars, clouds, and rains will cease to exist for the one who has died.

Otherwise: Rejoice, young man—O Christian people—and enjoy the good things which God has granted you; yet know that in all these things you will be judged by the Lord. Do not suppose that because the former branches have been broken off [Col. 1301A] and you have been grafted into the root of the good olive tree, you are therefore secure. Rather, remove anger from your heart and pleasures from your body; and, leaving all other vices, remember your Creator before the day of evil comes upon you—the incurable day in which punishments are prepared for sinners—lest, when you have sinned, the sun of righteousness set for you at noon, the light of knowledge perish, the radiance of the moon—that is, of the Church—be withdrawn, and the stars set, of which it is elsewhere written: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15).

Before the clouds return after the rain: lest the prophets, who have watered believers’ hearts with the rains of their speech, after seeing that you are unworthy of their shower, return to their own dwelling—to Him, namely, by whom they were sent.

### Verse 3

When the guardians of the house are shaken, and the strongest men tremble.

The guardians of the house are understood either as the sun and moon and the remaining host of stars, or as the angels who preside over this world [Col. 1301B]. The strongest men are understood as demons, who have themselves received the designation “strong” from the strong devil; when the Lord overcomes and binds him, He plunders his house according to the parable of the Gospel (Luke 11).

Otherwise: Those who refer everything written here to the human body think the guardians of the house signify the ribs, because the internal organs are enclosed by them and all the softness of the belly is protected. They take the strongest men to be the legs; they adapt the sun, moon, and stars to the eyes, nostrils, and ears of the whole body. They do this because necessity compels them below to understand what follows not of angels and demons [Col. 1301C], sun, moon, and stars, but of the parts of man.

“And the grinders will be idle because they are few, and those looking through the openings will grow dark.” At the end of the world, when the charity of many has grown cold (Matt. 24), and the souls of teachers who are able to offer heavenly food to believers have diminished and been transferred to heavenly things, then those who saw in part in this world the light of knowledge will begin to be enveloped in darkness. For if Moses is told, “I will place you in the cleft of the rock, and thus you shall see my back parts” (Exod. 33), how much more does every soul behold truth through an opening and certain dark caverns?

Otherwise: They think that “the grinders cease because they are diminished” is said of the teeth, because when extreme old age arrives, the teeth too are worn down or fall out; foods ground by them are sent into the belly [Col. 1301D]. And they take “those looking through the openings growing dark” to mean the eyes, whose sight grows dim and whose vision is obscured when they are weakened by age.

### Verse 4

And the doors in the street will be shut, when the sound of the grinding is low, and they will rise at the voice of the bird.

When the voice of the grinder has grown weak and the teaching of the masters has ceased, everything will consequently cease; among these, the doors in the street will be shut, so that, in accordance with the foolish virgins of the Gospel, each person has the doors of his own street shut, and they cannot buy oil. Or certainly, while the foolish virgins wander through the street, those who entered with him shut the bridegroom’s chamber [Col. 1302A] (Matt. 25). For if narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, while broad and spacious is that which leads to death (Matt. 7), then when the charity of many grows cold, the door of teachings is rightly shut in the streets.

In the following verse, where he says, “They will rise at the voice of a bird,” or “of a sparrow,” we shall make use of this interpretation whenever we see a sinner rise through repentance at the voice of a bishop or priest. This may also, though unusually and without following the sequence of the chapter, be understood of the bodily resurrection, when the dead rise at the voice of the archangel (1 Thess. 4). Nor is it surprising if we compare an angel’s trumpet to a sparrow, since every voice is faint in comparison with Christ. And, so far as I can remember, I do not recall ever having read of a sparrow in an unfavorable sense. The righteous man says in the tenth Psalm: “I trust in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10); and elsewhere: “I have kept watch and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 101); and in another place: “For the sparrow has found herself a house” (Ps. 83).

Otherwise: They take the doors shut in the streets to mean an old man’s feeble steps, because he always sits and cannot walk. They interpret the low sound of the grinder as the jaws, because they cannot grind food and, with breath scarcely drawn, his thin voice can barely be heard [Col. 1302B]. Further, his rising at the voice of the bird indicates that, as his blood grows cold and the moisture by which sleep is nourished dries up, he wakes at a slight sound and rises hastily in the middle of the night when the cock crows [Col. 1302C], no longer able often to turn his limbs in bed. They also take the deafening of the daughters of song to mean the ears, because old men’s hearing becomes more impaired, and they can distinguish no differences among voices or take pleasure in songs. Barzillai indeed says this to David when he refuses to cross the Jordan (2 Sam. 19).

### Verse 5

They will also fear heights, and terrors will be in the way.

That is, they will be unable to walk over steep places; with weary knees and trembling steps, wavering even on a level road, they will fear stumbling in their walk.

The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper berry will be scattered; for man will go to the house of his eternity, and mourners will go about in the street.

By metaphor, Ecclesiastes’ discourse is still about the parts of man [Col. 1302D]: when old age has come, the hair has turned gray, the feet have swollen, desire has grown cold, and man has been dissolved by death, then he returns to his earth and to the house of his eternity—the tomb—and, when the funeral rites have duly been celebrated, a crowd of mourners proceeds before the funeral.

Some interpret the blossom of the almond tree as the sacred spine: as the flesh of the buttocks diminishes, the spine grows prominent and blossoms. By the caper berry, therefore, is signified that the desire of old men grows cold and the organs of intercourse are dissipated.

### Verses 6–8

Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is shattered over the fountain, and the wheel is broken over the cistern, and the dust returns to its earth whence it was, and the spirit [Col. 1303A] returns to God who gave it. “Vanity of vanities,” said Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity.”

He returns to what went before, and after the great hyperbaton which he had inserted from the place where he said, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the sun and moon grow dark,” and so forth, he now concludes the sentence he began with a similar ending, saying: “Before the silver cord is broken,” and this and that take place. The silver cord signifies this bright life and the breath granted to us from heaven. The return of the golden band likewise signifies the soul returning to the place from which it descended.

The two remaining expressions—the shattering of the pitcher over the fountain and the breaking of the wheel over the pool—are figurative riddles of death. For just as a shattered pitcher ceases to draw water [Col. 1303B], and if the wheel by which waters are raised from pools and wells is broken, the use of the water is cut off, so, when the silver cord has been severed and the soul’s stream has returned to its fountain, man perishes; and, as follows more plainly, the dust returns to its earth whence it was taken, and the spirit turns back to God who gave it.

Accordingly, those who think that souls are sown together with bodies, and are generated not by God but by the parent of the body, are quite laughable. For since the flesh returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it, it is manifest that God, not men, is the parent of souls.

After describing human destruction, he fittingly repeats the beginning of his book: “Vanity of vanities,” said Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity.” For since all mortal labor, of which the whole [Col. 1303C] volume has disputed, reaches this point—that dust returns to its earth and the soul returns to the place from which it was taken—it is great vanity to labor in this age and to acquire nothing for the future.

### Verses 9–10

And because Ecclesiastes was most wise, he taught the people and set forth what he had done; and, searching diligently, he composed many parables. He sought useful words and wrote most upright sayings, full of truth.

The wisdom by which Solomon surpassed the whole human race he also professes here at the end of his little work: he was not content with the instruction of an ancient king, but voluntarily immersed himself in profound questions, and composed proverbs and parables to teach the people—promising one thing on the surface but containing another in their marrow. For we are taught even in the Gospels that proverbs [Col. 1303D] do not sound merely as the written words say, since the Lord spoke to the people in parables and proverbs, but explained them privately to the apostles (Mark 4). From this it is clear that the book of Proverbs too does not contain plain precepts, as simple people suppose; rather, as gold is sought in the earth, a kernel in a nut, and fruit within the hairy coverings of chestnuts, so the divine meaning in them must be searched out more deeply.

He adds to this that he wished to know the causes and natures of things, and God’s ordering and wisdom: why each thing was made and how it was made. Thus what David hopes that, after the dissolution of body and soul, he will see when he returns to heaven, saying, “I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” [Col. 1304A] (Ps. 8), Solomon now seemed to find in the present life: that the human mind, enclosed within the barrier of a body, might comprehend the truth known to God alone.

### Verse 11

The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply in, given by the counsel of teachers from one shepherd.

Lest he seem, after the law of the Lord, rashly to emerge as a sudden teacher and claim a doctrine which Moses received not so much of his own accord as first through God’s anger and then through divine inspiration, he says that his words are the words of the wise. These correct sinners after the likeness of goads, move the sluggish steps of mortals by the piercing sting, and are firm as nails driven deeply and securely in; they are uttered not by the authority of one man [Col. 1304B] but by the counsel and agreement of all teachers.

And lest human wisdom be despised, he says that it was bestowed by the human shepherd; that is, though very many teach, the Lord is nevertheless the one author of doctrine. This passage is against those who suppose the God of the Old Law to be one and the God of the Gospel another: for the one shepherd formed the counsel of the wise, and the wise are both prophets and apostles.

At the same time, it should be noted that the words of the wise are said to sting, not to caress, nor to touch licentiousness with a soft hand; rather, they inflict pain and a wound upon those who err and, as we said above, upon those slow to repent. Therefore, if anyone’s utterance is that of a wise man—for “the words of the wise are like goads”—when it calls a sinner to conversion, is firm, is given by the counsel [Col. 1304C] of the saints, granted by the one shepherd, and founded upon a solid root, then it is such a word. I think that Saul, not yet Paul, heard himself pierced by this goad on the road of error: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9).

### Verse 12

Beyond these things, my son, do not seek further. There is no end to making many books; frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh.

Apart from these words given by the one shepherd and approved by the counsel and agreement of the wise, do nothing and claim nothing for yourself. Follow the footsteps of your elders, and do not depart from their authority. Otherwise, an infinite number of books will meet the one who seeks many things; they will draw him into error and make him labor in vain as he reads.

Or else, this teaches that one should pursue brevity and follow meanings [Col. 1304D] rather than words, against the philosophers and teachers of this age, who attempt to establish the falsehoods of their doctrines through variety and multiplication of speech. In contrast, divine Scripture is compressed into a brief compass; as much as it is expanded in meaning, so much is it restrained in expression. For “the Lord has made a finished and shortened word upon the earth” (Rom. 9), and His word is near in our mouth and in our heart (Deut. 30).

Otherwise: Frequent reading and daily meditation are usually a labor more of the soul than of the flesh. For just as whatever is done with hand and body is accomplished by the labor of hand and body, so what pertains to reading is more a labor of the mind. Hence it seems to me that the preceding words about the multitude of books [Col. 1305A] should be understood otherwise than most people think.

It is the custom of Scripture, although there are many books, to call them one volume if they do not disagree among themselves and write concerning the same matter. Thus the Gospel and “the law of the Lord, spotless, converting souls” are each called in the singular (Ps. 18), though there are several Gospels and many commandments of the law. Likewise, the sealed volume in Isaiah’s discourse (Isa. 29) is all divine Scripture, and Ezekiel and John feed upon one scroll or chapter (Ezek. 2; Rev. 10). The Savior also, prophesied by the voices of all the saints of old, says: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. 29).

According to this meaning, then, I think the present command prohibits the making of many books. For whatever you say, if it is referred to Him who “in the beginning was with God, the Word, God” [Col. 1305B] (John 1), is one volume; and innumerable books are called one law, one Gospel. But if you argue things diverse and discordant, and in excessive curiosity draw your mind here and there, even in one book there are many books. Hence it is said: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10). Such books, therefore, have no end. Every good thing and all truth are bounded by a definite end; but evil and falsehood are without end. And the more they are sought, the greater grows their succession.

Study and meditation upon this matter are a labor of the flesh—of the flesh, I say, not of the spirit. For the spirit also has its own labor, according to what the Apostle says: “Yet I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15). And the Savior [Col. 1305C] says: “I have labored crying out” (Ps. 68).

### Verse 13

Let us all hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man; and God will bring into judgment all things that are done, for every error, whether it be good or evil.

The Hebrews say that, when Solomon’s other writings had become obsolete and had not endured in remembrance, this book too appeared fit to be erased, because it asserted God’s creatures to be vain, regarded the whole as nothing, and preferred food, drink, and pleasures to everything that passes away. Yet it deserved authority from this single chapter, so as to be placed among the number of divine volumes, because he compressed all his discussion and his entire catalogue into this, and said that the conclusion of his sayings was very easy to hear [Col. 1305D] and contained nothing difficult: namely, that we should fear God and perform His commandments. For man was born for this: that, understanding his Creator, he should worship Him through fear, honor, and the work of God’s commandments.

For when the time of judgment arrives, whatever has been done by us will stand before the Judge, await for a long time an uncertain sentence, and each person [Col. 1306A] will receive according to his work, whether he has done evil or good (2 Cor. 5). For we shall render an account on the day of judgment even for every idle word uttered not deliberately but in ignorance (Matt. 12).

Otherwise: Since fear belongs to servants, and perfect love casts fear out (1 John 4), and divine Scripture speaks of a twofold fear, both of the foolish and of the perfect, I think that the fear here meant is the fear perfected in virtues, according to the saying: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear Him” (Ps. 33). Or certainly, because he is still man and has not yet received the name of God, this is the rationale of his nature: that, placed in the body, he should fear God, because God brings every deed—that is, all human beings—into judgment for everything in which they have thought otherwise than He ordained and declared, whether in this direction or that [Col. 1306B]. For “woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5).

The spirit of one who loves is tender and keenly sensitive to every feeling of pain, most beloved brother Gregory. If you handle it too carelessly, it quickly withers like a rose; if you hold it too harshly, it melts like lilies. I remember having read that affection is often wounded by one’s countenance. Therefore, although I am summoned by love, lest I be deficient toward you in the duty owed, I now undertake the task of writing more willingly than on many previous occasions.

First, because the request of our Lord William ought not to lack some provision for the journey; then because I thought that my little book, which at your command I completed on Ecclesiastes, would have somewhat greater recommendation if it were sent to you through one whom you love sincerely and without pretense. For it often happens that a cheerful bearer embellishes even trifling things [Col. 1306C]. In him the vein of brotherly feeling is strong.

But I fear to prolong my testimony, lest he judge that I have served his praise more than modesty. For those whose mind is honorable have a delicate brow. We must flee the flatterers’ fawning and the harmful blandishments of deceit as certain plagues of the soul. Nothing so easily corrupts human minds; nothing strikes the mind with so sweet and soft a wound. Hence the Wise Man also says: “The words of flatterers are soft, but they strike the inner parts of the mind” (Prov. 18). This vice reigns especially in the present age; and, what is more serious, it is regarded as humility and goodwill. Thus it comes about that one who does not know how to flatter is considered either envious or proud.

Therefore, dearest one, I congratulate you and pray that the Lord may deign to increase the friendship now being born. I, ashes and the most worthless part of clay, soon to become ashes, have enough if the weakness of my eyes can endure the splendor of your character. You are pure and whitened as snow; I, defiled by every filth of sins, wait day and night in trembling to pay the last farthing [Col. 1306D].

[Col. 1307]

## Of Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, on the Work *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, upon Matthew

### Prologue

You urge me, O Christ-loving Cuno, formerly venerable abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, but now bishop of the Church of Regensburg, to compose a new work, *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man, Set over the Works of the Father’s Hands*, or seated at the right hand of Majesty on high, that all things may be subjected to Him (Heb. 1); and to construct the edifice of this work upon the Gospel foundation, the Gospel according to Matthew.

How desirable this is to me—and, as you say, to you—that, since lately, with you as adviser and almost commander, I published my latest work, *On the Victory of the Word of God*, I may now be worthy to write concerning the glory and honor, as already stated, of the Son of Man, because of the hope laid up in the truth of that same God and man, who says: “By your words you shall be justified” (Matt. 12).

You yourself know how impatiently until now I have heard you urging this upon me, and how harsh and almost intractable I have been in response. Why was this? Evidently for many reasons. In many ways the care of the house of the Lord entrusted to me constrains me no less than it constrains you. Moreover, it is not easy for a sinful man to open his mouth and draw in breath (Ps. 118), since this belongs only to those who desire the Lord’s commandments. Add—as you yourself know, having heard and seen it—that many read my writings only in order to lie in wait for me. Thus there happens to them what this same Son of Man, who is to be glorified and honored, said: “But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6).

Already here, at the beginning of my discourse, I could answer as he deserves that man whom you know well: because he did not read with a single eye, he walked in darkness and stumbled, thereby showing himself not only envious but also quite unlearned. The insults which he stirred up against me might receive in writing a fitting—not unjust—rejoinder; but “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32; Rom. 12). When Shimei, son of Gera, son of Benjamin, cursed David with a most evil curse, throwing stones at him and scattering dust, David said: “Let him alone; let him curse, perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me with good for this curse of today” (2 Sam. 16).

I have stated the causes that trouble a mind well disposed toward the sacred Scriptures. Thus the crowds going before and following hindered Zacchaeus, small in stature, when he wished to see who Jesus was and ran to see Him (Luke 19). Thus the Pharisees murmured because Jesus had turned aside to this same apostle and evangelist Matthew (Matt. 9), that is, “the gifted one.” But he, persevering, made Him a great feast in his house.

Likewise, whoever is gifted with spiritual grace from above must, with perseverance amid crowds of cares and amid the slanders of the envious, run to see Jesus, to contemplate his Savior, so that he may receive Him into the house of his breast and make for Him, if he can do no more, at least a feast of good and faithful speech; for “a good word is above the best gift” (Prov. 15). Therefore may He Himself be present—the One who saw this publican and, by seeing him, made him an apostle and evangelist. Then at last I shall endeavor to accomplish what you require and what I have found desirable for myself, with the hope of heavenly consolation set before me.

## Book One

[Col. 1307]

[Col. 1307A] 564 “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1): this book is a heavenly book; whereas the book of the generation of Adam is an earthly book, of which it is thus written: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created man, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them, and he blessed them, and called their name [Col. 1308A] Adam, on the day when they were created” (Gen. 5). “As that first man was of the earth, earthly, but this last one is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15), so that book of Adam’s generation is an earthly book, while this book of the generation of Jesus Christ is a heavenly book.

In that earthly book all the reprobate are written, according to the saying: “Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded; [Col. 1309A] those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17). In this writing all the elect are written, to whom the Lord himself says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Indeed, all alike—both elect and reprobate—were enrolled in the earth, or in the earthly book, through the sin of that first man, in whom all sinned. But through the righteousness of this last man all the elect have been transferred into the book of life, the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, through whom they were justified (Rom. 5).

How were they transferred into such a book? Plainly, by believing in this Jesus Christ, just as it is written concerning Abraham, the first father in this genealogy: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15; Rom. 5). For in what did he believe God in order to be justified, [Col. 1309B] except in the promise of the seed, which is this same Jesus Christ? For God had said to him: “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be” (Gen. 15). And on this promise he had departed from his land and from his kindred: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (ibid.), which seed is Christ.

Therefore, when you hear, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac” (Matt. 1), and so forth, do not make this book seem small to you. Do not attend only to the fact that Abraham according to the flesh begot Isaac, and Isaac according to the flesh begot Jacob, and likewise the rest; attend rather to this: Abraham according to the promise begot Isaac, and Isaac according to the promise begot Jacob. Once this has been noticed, the book appears more extensive [Col. 1309C] and its page grand through almost every generation, because the word of promise, laid up in the memory, makes one reconsider what God said, and in what manner, to those holy Fathers.

Here we must now consider this very book of the generation, in that it ends as follows: “Jacob begot Joseph” (ibid.). Could he not have followed that line by which he would have arrived at the man who begot Mary according to the flesh, unless he judged that generation to be more excellent which is of faith or promise—which is the hearing or keeping of the Word of God? For the Lord himself testifies to this and wishes us to recognize it. When a certain woman, raising her voice from the crowd, said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked,” he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep [Col. 1309D] it” (Luke 11). And elsewhere: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12).

Blessed, therefore, are those whose flesh does not attain to being fathers or to the generation of Jesus Christ, but whose soul, by hearing and keeping the word of God, has become the mother of that same Jesus Christ. Most blessed, however, are those who are fathers or parents of so great a son in both ways. Foremost among them are those two great patriarchs, whose names are so conspicuously proclaimed at the beginning of this book: son of David, son of Abraham. As for the truth of the fleshly descent—that the blessed Virgin Mary was, or is, their daughter according to it—it needs no support from our assertion. But it is not superfluous to recall how she was their daughter according to that descent by which any soul is the mother of the same Jesus Christ through faith or through keeping the Word of God. Namely, through possessing faith and humility, she became a daughter of Abraham, a daughter of David.

For she possessed faith: when the angel announced to her what had been unheard in all ages—or rather, when God, in whom Abraham had believed, spoke to her through the angel—she swiftly believed (Luke 1). She possessed humility: hearing and believing that she was made the Lord’s mother, she professed herself a handmaid, saying, “Behold [Col. 1310A] the handmaid of the Lord” (ibid.), after the likeness of her aforementioned fathers, Abraham and David. How great their humility was is openly known from their own words. Thus her father Abraham, while God conversed with him and he with God, and while he was counted a friend, [Col. 1310B] said among other things: “Since I have begun, I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18).

565 Moreover David, though he had been anointed king by the Lord’s choice and Saul pursued him, said: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a single flea” (1 Sam. 24). Thus the invisible God, who was to be born from them as visible man, meek and humble, had already taught them inwardly, as he himself would say: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). And he had prepared for himself a mother like himself, who might truthfully say: “Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke 1).

Consider now how many and what sorts of titles adorn this beginning, or heading, of the Gospel: “The book of the generation [Col. 1310C] of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” Four most eminent marks of the glory and honor of this Son of Man are well known: he is God and man, king and priest. If you consider rightly, none of these is left unspoken here. For by the very name Jesus, that is, Savior—the reason for this name or title being that he saves from sins, as the angel said to Joseph: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1)—by that name, I say, Jesus, and by the very cause of the name, namely saving from sins, which belongs to God alone, he is asserted and recognized to be God, true God.

Moreover, by the following name, Christ, which means “anointed,” he is proclaimed the anointed King and anointed Priest: King and Priest who rightfully succeeded his fathers, the father who was king and the father who was priest—David the king, Abraham the priest—as this radiant title proclaims in saying, “Son of [Col. 1310D] David, son of Abraham.” For David was king, and Abraham was priest, since in obedience and faith he offered his son to God as a burnt offering (Gen. 22). Abraham was the firstborn of his father Terah and, according to the custom by which firstborn sons are said to have been priests down to that time, he was himself priest; and after him Isaac was priest. But Esau lost this birthright through gluttony (Gen. 25).

This son is the son of those fathers or patriarchs, who were surely men; and he himself is man, or Son of Man, because he assumed true flesh from their flesh. Therefore, as has been said, four marks are to be seen in the present title: that he is [Col. 1311A] God and man, King and Priest. “This man was born in Sion, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 46, 86). This Priest offered himself and was sacrificed like a calf. This King, like a lion or lion’s cub, went up to the prey (Gen. 49); sleeping with his eyes opened in his death, and, after despoiling hell, he rose from the dead. This God, like a flying eagle, ascended above all the heavens.

According to these four names of his nature or office, he set before us four mysteries of piety which we must believe: namely, his incarnation or birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. No Christian ever was permitted, or will be permitted, to be ignorant of any of them. From these we know what Jesus Christ is like: truly good and truly strong. For, as good, he willed [Col. 1311B] for our sake to become man and to undergo the passion; and, as truly strong, having conquered death, he rose and ascended into heaven.

Since he is thereby known to be such, behold we discern the four faces of one living creature, where the prophet Ezekiel says: “The likeness of the faces of the living creatures: the face of a man, and the face of a lion; the face of a calf and the face of an eagle above” (Ezek. 1). Although he speaks of four living creatures, he nevertheless intends at first one living creature, as much further on, when he says: “The first face was the face of a cherub; the second face the face of a man; the third, the face of a lion; and the fourth, the face of an eagle. This,” he says, “was the living creature which I saw by the river Chebar” (Ezek. 10).

The one living creature is the one Jesus Christ; the four faces, or four living creatures, are the four aforementioned mysteries of one and the same Jesus Christ. [Col. 1311C] These faces shine upon the righteous because Jesus Christ sees them, as it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33). In seeing them, he makes them conformed to himself, or to any one of these his faces, much more effectively than a mirror, penetrating them and forming his own image in them.

He saw the righteous and blessed Matthew, as Matthew himself says of himself: “As Jesus passed by, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew” (Matt. 9). This true sun saw him, I say, and formed in the mirror of his breast the face of a man. He saw another and formed in him his own face, the face of a lion; he saw another and impressed in him the face of a flying eagle. These are the four [Col. 1311D] Evangelists, who are secondarily called the four living creatures. For the first four, of which we have spoken, are the four mysteries; the one living creature is Jesus Christ.

David sang with prophetic mouth, together with the ten-stringed psalter, and wrote with his pen of this man and the mysteries of the man: the mysteries, I say, of man and priest, king and God. He also expressed together the four titles—God, man, king, priest. For example: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 46, 86): there he declares him to be man. “God ascended amid jubilation” (Ps. 46): there he calls this same person God, for he who descended is the same who ascended (John 3). “But I have been established by him as king upon Sion, [Col. 1312A] his holy mountain” (Ps. 2). Again: “Lord, save the king” (Ps. 19); “Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice” (Ps. 20); and elsewhere: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23): there he proclaims him king. “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109): there he declares him priest.

Likewise, the mysteries or sacraments of the man, or seed of Abraham; of God, or the flying eagle; of the priest, or calf; of the king, or lion—the mysteries, I say, of the incarnation or birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension of this same Jesus Christ, his Son—the soul of blessed David conceived in prophetic heart, brought forth in prophetic speech, as has been said, and committed to writing [Col. 1312B] for all ages that would come after him to read or sing.

Abraham did not do this, though he was a prophet, since he possessed no letters. For Moses, long after him, was the first to receive letters, written by the finger of God (Exod. 24, 32). Rightly, therefore, although Abraham was earlier than David, the Evangelist did not say “Jesus Christ, son of Abraham, son of David,” but reversing the order said, “son of David, son of Abraham.”

Furthermore, this also must be known: although these two are the fathers to whom the promise concerning this same Jesus Christ was made, the word of the same promise was greatly enlarged in relation to David. For to Abraham it was said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22); but to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon my throne” (Ps. 131). [Col. 1312C] It is greater to be the king of Abraham’s seed than to be Abraham’s seed. Hence I rightly say that the word of promise was greatly enlarged in David. I would add also that it is greater to be a patriarch, king, prophet, and psalmist—as David was or is—than to be only a patriarch and prophet, as Abraham was or is. Thus in every respect the divine Evangelist wisely preferred to say “son of David, son of Abraham,” rather than “son of Abraham, son of David.”

Having set these matters more fully before us in the title, we must now proceed to the book of the generation itself. “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob.” In both cases, when it says “begot,” it is most fitting to understand: “whom he received in the promise and consecrated to God as priest.” This feature of beauty, 566 or worthy lineage, [Col. 1312D] is especially fitting for the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, because, as the Apostle says: “It is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of promise are counted as the seed” (Rom. 9).

How are Isaac, whom Abraham begot, and Jacob, whom Isaac begot, not children of the flesh but children of promise? Namely, because they received not merely the inheritance of their father’s faith, but even their being begotten resulted not so much from the operation of nature as from the gift of grace. Abraham had a barren wife, Sarah, and Isaac had a barren wife, Rebecca. “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife,” Scripture says, “because she was barren; and the Lord heard him and gave Rebecca conception” (Gen. 25).

[Col. 1313A] Isaac consecrated his son Jacob as priest by his word, when Jacob was clothed in Esau’s exceedingly fine garments, which Rebecca kept at home. Esau, as the firstborn, ought by the custom mentioned above to have exercised the priesthood in them. But Isaac himself had no need to be consecrated or blessed by his father’s word; for, since he had been offered to the Lord as a burnt offering as a type of this coming Son, Jesus Christ, from that time he was more than a priest—that is, not priest only, but victim as well.

Concerning what I have just said, that Abraham received Isaac, and Isaac Jacob, in promise, the Apostle writes thus: “For this is the word of promise: At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son. And not only she, but Rebecca also,” and the rest down to: [Col. 1313B] “Not by works, but by him who calls, it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger’; as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. 9).

“Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” With the generation of Judah and his brothers, that ancient custom ceased whereby, as already said, firstborn sons had until then exercised the priesthood. Reuben, who was the firstborn, sinned, and therefore did not merit the priestly blessing; indeed, he incurred diminution: “You poured yourself out like water,” his father says, “do not increase; because you ascended your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. 49).

The former custom of priesthood did not, however, cease in such a way that at least one of the younger brothers should exercise the priesthood, as the younger Jacob had done when Esau was set aside. Rather, the priesthood itself [Col. 1313C] altogether ceased while they were in Egypt, where they had sold their brother Joseph, until, when they cried out to the Lord and said, “Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord” (Exod. 5), Aaron, Moses’ brother, arose as priest from the tribe of Levi.

The Lord took that tribe in place of all the firstborn sons of Israel, and the sons of Levi were meanwhile priests and ministering keepers of the archives (*scriniarii*) in place of all the firstborn, until this firstborn Son of Man should come, the priest of glory and honor, and, setting aside his deputies, assume his own priesthood. Indicating this, the divine Evangelist, after speaking of Mary, whom he had of course narrated to have conceived as a Virgin, said: “And she bore her son,” and immediately, not idly, added, “the firstborn” (Matt. 1; Luke [Col. 1313D] 2), so that the discerning hearer may understand that he is therefore a worthy priest—the one of whom it was said: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

What, moreover, was the order of Melchizedek, except to offer the sacrifice of bread and wine by the right of the firstborn? For Noah was the firstborn, as the most learned affirm, and he is the same person who was called by another name, Shem. What, then, were the birthrights given to Joseph? For it is written in Chronicles: “Reuben was indeed the firstborn of Israel; but when he had violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, son of Israel, and he was not accounted the firstborn” (1 Chron. 5).

What, I ask, were the birthrights given to Joseph’s sons? [Col. 1314A] Surely not the priesthood itself, which, as was said, none of them is recorded to have exercised in Egypt, but that one portion of which Jacob said to his son Joseph, blessing his sons and setting Ephraim before Manasseh: “Behold, I am dying, and God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48).

The Evangelist mentions that portion when he says: “Jesus came to a city of Samaria which is called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to Joseph his son” (John 4). Thus up to that time a twofold inheritance came to the firstborn: the honor of priesthood and one portion of property beyond his brothers.

[Col. 1314B] Jacob indeed blessed Joseph with most sweet blessings, concluding thus: “May they be upon the head of Joseph and upon the brow of the Nazirite among his brothers” (Gen. 49). But because nothing of Joseph is written such as Scripture plainly affirms that the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did—namely, building an altar to the Lord and calling upon the Lord’s name (Gen. 12)—or such as Jacob plainly first vowed to the Lord—offering tithes and victims (Gen. 28)—it is clear that the priesthood of the firstborn ceased in Jacob. Meanwhile the sons of Levi were deputies for the firstborn, until this Firstborn and Only-Begotten of the Virgin should come, the Firstborn and Only-Begotten of God.

Since the purpose of the present work, according to its plan, tends toward the glory and honor of the Son of Man, and the four faces mentioned above are the highest emblems of that glory [Col. 1314C] and honor, I do not wish to pass over the fact that here, in the blessings of Judah, the first face of that living creature presents itself: the face of the lion. For, as John says in the Apocalypse, “The first living creature was like a lion” (Rev. 4).

Ezekiel indeed mentions the lion’s face first, but he nowhere says that it is, or is not, the first face, where he says: “The likeness of their faces: the face of a man and the face of a lion, the face of an ox and the face of an eagle” (Ezek. 1). Elsewhere he mentions first neither the face of a man nor that of a lion, but that of a calf: “The first face, the face of a cherub” (Ezek. 10), that is, of an ox or calf; “the second face, the face of a man; and the third, the face of a lion” (ibid.), and so on.

Since John alone calls the first face the lion’s face, it is evident that he expresses them in this manner not according to the order in which the mysteries of the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ were accomplished, but according to the order of the Scripture of Moses: “The first living creature was like a lion; the second living creature was like a calf; the third living creature had the face of a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (Rev. 4).

For behold, in the first place is the lion’s face: “Judah, a lion’s cub, you have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you have lain down like a lion, and like a lioness” (Gen. 49). Then behold “the second face, the face of a calf,” as he says: “The second living creature was like a calf.” “If a priest sins, causing the people to sin, or if the whole congregation of Israel acts in ignorance and through lack of knowledge does what is against the Lord’s commandment, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished calf for sin” [Col. 1315A] (Lev. 4), and the rest—things which in a wonderful manner and truly sacred and mystical order represent the mystery of the passion of Jesus Christ, whose blood, according to the meaning of that rite, “cleansed our conscience,” as the Apostle says, “from dead works” (Heb. 9).

Moreover, “the third face, the face of a man,” is sufficiently expressed in these words of Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from among your brothers, like me” (Deut. 18), and so forth. When he says “like me,” he testifies that nothing is lacking to him from 567 the truth of human nature. We plainly have the fourth face, the face of the flying eagle, in these words of the Song of Deuteronomy: “As an eagle inciting her young to fly, and hovering over them, [Col. 1315B] spread her wings and took them up and carried them upon her shoulders” (Deut. 32).

It clearly pertains to the glory and honor of Jesus Christ, the Son of Man, that not only the prophets and Psalms, of which we have spoken above, but Moses himself first recorded these four mysteries of piety. Without faith in them no human being lives; from knowledge of them we know the goodness and strength of such a man, so great a God, such a king, so great a high priest. Knowing this, he himself said: “It is necessary that all things written of me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

“Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar.” The story is well known: Tamar was Judah’s daughter-in-law, and he begot Perez and Zerah by her, not knowing that she was his daughter-in-law. When she had conceived [Col. 1315C] these twins, it was reported to Judah: “Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has committed fornication, and behold, her womb is swelling.” And he said: “Bring her out, that she may be burned” (Gen. 38). Without delay, when he learned the matter, he said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to Shelah my son” (ibid.).

Who does not know that Jews were born from that fornication—indeed, nearly all the nobility of the Jewish people and the whole royal line? Why then did the Jews, troublesome to all people as they were troublesome to God and to our Lord, boast by saying, “We are Abraham’s seed” (John 8), “we were not born of fornication”? He indeed said: “I know that you are Abraham’s children” (ibid.); yet he did not say, “I know that you were not born of fornication.” [Col. 1315D] For Tamar really did commit fornication, she who conceived them. By recalling this, he could have refuted the proud; except that he himself first had to do what he teaches through his Apostle, who says: “Giving no offense to anyone” (2 Cor. 6).

Moreover, the cloud of that fornication not only darkens the splendor of the glory and honor of the Son of Man, but also illuminates the condescension of his goodness: for, as he deigned to become man for sinners, so he deigned to be born from sinners. The Evangelist, not making light of this grace and wishing us to recognize it, includes in this genealogy of the Savior only women of this kind whom Scripture reproves: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba.

“For Salmon,” he says, “begot Boaz by Rahab,” who is known to have been a prostitute and to have been saved from the ruins of Jericho by faith [Col. 1316A] (Josh. 2). “Boaz begot Obed by Ruth,” who is known to have been a Moabite woman. In her case there occurred the remarkable fact that, while two sentences of the divine law were in conflict with one another, she herself emerged to salvation.

For the Law says: “Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth generation, shall not enter the assembly of the Lord forever, because they would not meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia of Syria, to curse you” (Deut. 23). Again the Law says: “If a man dies without children, his brother or kinsman shall take the dead man’s wife and raise up seed for his brother” (ibid., 25).

Thus the very Law which condemned her because she was a Moabite woman supported [Col. 1316B] Boaz in taking her because she had been the wife of his kinsman. In this way she not only entered the assembly of the Lord, but even holds a principal memorial in the assembly of the Lord, so that the seed raised up from her begot David, leader and king of the assembly of the Lord, in the second generation. For Obed, who was begotten from her, begot Jesse; “and Jesse begot David the king.”

Boaz therefore was not merely excused but justified in taking a Moabite wife, since, as has been said, the Law justified him. But the man who had previously taken her was justified not by the Law but excused by necessity: namely, the famine which had occurred, on account of which, as Scripture relates, “A man departed from Bethlehem of Judah to live as a foreigner in the country of Moab with his wife [Col. 1316C] and two children. His name was Elimelech, the name of his wife Naomi, and of the two sons one was called Mahlon and the other Chilion. They took Moabite wives, one of whom was called Orpah and the other Ruth; and they remained there ten years, and both died” (Ruth 1).

But unless necessity had excused them, they should not themselves have taken Moabite wives, nor would Boaz, or any other person, have been bound by law to take her by the right of kinship. Conversely, just as the Law of God received sinful women and foreigners because of faith, and this Evangelist judged them worthy to be named, so it removed and rejected certain members of the household of the seed because of impiety.

For he says, “Joram begot Uzziah.” He cuts three out of the middle: namely, Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah. [Col. 1316D] For what reason? Plainly because of their most impious mother Athaliah, whose murders they imitated by killing the prophets of the Lord, just as she and her mother Jezebel did in Samaria (2 Chron. 22). Manasseh too shed much innocent blood (2 Kings 21; 2 Chron. 33); nevertheless, he was retained because he repented.

This truly pertains greatly to the Evangelist’s intention, mentioned above. Unless he judged that generation more excellent which is of faith or promise, which is hearing or keeping the word of God, than that which is of the flesh, he could have composed the genealogy so as to arrive at the father who begot the blessed Mary according to the flesh. What place, indeed, should those men have among the Lord’s fleshly ancestors, under whom the prophets of the word of the Lord were not even permitted to speak?

Thus Joash killed the prophet and priest Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada, because he dared to speak in the name of the Lord; he did not remember the mercy which Jehoiada, Zechariah’s father, had shown him, but killed his son [Col. 1317A] (2 Chron. 25). After him Amaziah, when the prophet said to him from the Lord, “Why have you worshiped gods who did not deliver their own people from your hand?” (2 Chron. 25), answered: “Are you the king’s counselor? Be silent, lest I kill you” (ibid.).

All the others, moreover, except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, sinned; nevertheless, under them the prophets were permitted to prophesy, which mattered for such a genealogy. One of these prophets says: “Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the Spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26).
