[Col. 1317B] Therefore these alone are expelled from the present record, from the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, who would not allow the word to be heard or the heralds of God’s word to live.

“Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” Behold that ladder which appeared to Jacob in sleep when, obedient to his parents, he went into Syria to take a wife from his own kindred. “Behold,” I say, “a ladder standing upon the earth, its summit reaching heaven, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, who said to him: ‘I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac’” (Gen. 28), and so forth.

Although another useful sense of that ladder may be given according to a moral interpretation, [Col. 1317C] nevertheless that ladder is this generation of Jesus Christ. The two sides of the ladder are the chief fathers or princes of this generation, Abraham and David, to whom the promise was made, with the oath of him who promised. The highest rung of the ladder, upon which the Lord leaned, is blessed Joseph, Mary’s husband, from whom Jesus, who is called 568 Christ, was born.

How did this God and Lord lean upon him? Surely as an orphan upon a guardian, since he was born into this world without a father. He leaned upon blessed Joseph so that this man might be the best of fathers to the little child, and that, through his fatherly support, the boy might be sustained together with the Virgin who had borne the child.

“Therefore all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon are fourteen generations; [Col. 1317D] and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ are fourteen generations.” What is the meaning of this careful enumeration of generations, this division made with such care, as it were by a summative or concluding calculation? Did the divine Evangelist arrange or encompass the generations in this way uselessly or without weight of reason—the Evangelist in whom, or through whom, the Holy Spirit undoubtedly spoke? Though he had been a tax collector and an unlettered man, he was taught to write not by man nor through man, but by the Holy Spirit.

Without doubt, whatever he says has weight; and what he now says contains a force of meaning which I do not wish to pass over. [Col. 1318A] For we suppose—indeed, we have learned from experience—that many wonder why God’s goodness delayed so long in fulfilling his promise, namely, in setting before the world the incarnation of his Son, his Word.

Whoever is prepared or wishes to give an account to every questioner concerning the righteousness of the faithful God who promised can carefully observe through these τεσσαρεσκαίδεκάδας (*tessareskaidekadas*, “sets of fourteen”)—that what is more to be wondered at, to the glory and praise of the righteous and, as has been said, faithful God, is that he remained unchangeable and steadfast in his promise or purpose, although he had been offended in many ways and very grievously by those to whom he had made the promise. This threefold number of fourteen generations subtly indicates those offenses.

Let someone then ask: Why did God delay his Christ so long? Why did he not [Col. 1318B] immediately give him to the first fathers to whom he had promised him? Why was not the blessed Virgin immediately, or soon afterward, born from one of them, to conceive and bear Christ? This was what the man desired who, when he was being sent to Pharaoh, said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4). And immediately it follows: “The Lord, angry with Moses, said: ‘Aaron your brother the Levite—I know that he is eloquent’” (ibid.), and the rest.

It is as though he said: When I said, “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send,” the Lord was angry; and therefore, regarding what he asked, he did not even give any answer, but spoke of other things. Why was the Lord angry? Plainly because of the sin of the house of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom he had made the promise: Jacob’s sons, out of envy, had sold their brother Joseph as a slave, and he had served for fourteen years.

[Col. 1318C] For he was sold when he was sixteen years old; and when, having been brought out of prison, he stood before King Pharaoh, he was thirty years old (Gen. 37). Therefore, just as in one place the righteous judge, that is, the Lord, says: “According to the number of forty days in which you explored the land, a year shall be reckoned for a day, and for forty years you shall bear your iniquities” (Num. 14), so let us judge that there also the judgment was just when he said: “According to the number of fourteen years during which Joseph, having been sold, served, a generation shall be reckoned for a year; and for fourteen generations the seed promised to your fathers, which is Christ, shall be delayed.”

“Therefore,” he says, “from Abraham to David are [Col. 1318D] fourteen generations”: it is understood that Christ did not come, and that the angry Lord delayed him until then—whence Moses also groaned in the passage mentioned above.

David, in whom the fourteen generations ended, had himself already received the same promise with the Lord’s oath; yet he sinned no less than those before him: he struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, took his wife, and killed him by the sword of the sons of Ammon (2 Sam. 11). Therefore the Lord ought to have been no less angry on this account than he had formerly been, and hence: “From David to the deportation to Babylon are fourteen generations”—and Christ did not come.

Moreover, the deportation to Babylon, which was a punishment for those deported, was occasioned by no lesser sin or crime: the kings of Judah, and especially Manasseh [Col. 1319A] (2 Kings 2 [materially uncertain citation]), had shed much innocent blood (Matt. 2 [materially uncertain citation]), until they filled Jerusalem even to its bounds with innocent blood, besides their sins by which they caused Judah to sin, doing evil before the Lord.

“Therefore, from the deportation to Babylon,” he says, “to Christ are fourteen generations”: it is understood that only after so many generations did that same Christ come. At that time, indeed, the murderous Herod was staining the earth with much blood; but his impiety ought not to have been imputed to Abraham’s race or David’s seed, so that Christ would be delayed because of him. For he was not a Jew but a foreigner, being born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother.

“Jacob begot Joseph, husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” [Col. 1319B] In calling him Mary’s husband, he ascribes to blessed Joseph a great and true title; for if he is Mary’s husband, he is also the Lord’s father. Does not the Law itself decree that she who is betrothed is already a wife? “If,” it says, “a man has betrothed a virgin girl, and someone finds her in a city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and”

“They shall be stoned to death” (Deut. 22). The girl, because she did not cry out when she was in the city; the man, because he violated his neighbor’s wife. Therefore Joseph was Mary’s husband, and she herself was his wife. Accordingly, neither was this writer mistaken in saying, “Joseph, the husband of Mary,” nor did another Evangelist lie in calling him the father of Christ, who was born of her: “And his father and mother,” he says, “were wondering at the things said concerning him” (Luke 2).

Moreover, not only did the Evangelist call Joseph the husband of Mary [Col. 1319C], but the angel earlier also declared Mary to be Joseph’s wife—which amounts to the same thing: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife.” O true and holy marriage, a heavenly marriage, not an earthly one! For how, or in what respect, were they married? Assuredly, in that they had one spirit and one faith; there alone the corruption of the flesh ceased. Therefore the Apostle spoke most truly: “Because the first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven” (1 Cor. 15)—not because this Jesus Christ, who was born of Mary, came from heaven with flesh and passed through Mary as through a pipe, as certain heretics have said; but because the life or union of the spouses was wholly [Col. 1319D] heavenly, and the Holy Spirit was the conjugal love of both. Their manner of life was indeed in heaven; presiding in both, he entrusted this man’s wife to the faithfulness of her husband and, forming a human being from the flesh of the Virgin, thoroughly poured into this paternal husband love for the child who was being born.

“All the generations, then, from Abraham to David, are fourteen generations,” and so forth, as above.

How the angels of God ascended and descended by the ladder of the man. For we have already said above (Gen. 28) that the ladder which Jacob saw in a dream, standing upon the earth, and so forth, its top touching heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, was a mystery of the incarnation of this Jesus Christ; and that Joseph, whose paternal care the Lord born of Mary [Col. 1320A] required, was that step of the ladder—step 569—upon which he seemed to lean.

What, then, did it signify that the angels of God too were ascending and descending upon it? Assuredly, that you may understand what is beyond doubt: that the one and same person who was born of Mary, at one and the same time when he was born, was both greater than the angels and less than the angels. He saw angels ascending—that is, having God above themselves, upon whom they desire to look (1 Pet. 1); and this truly is to ascend. He saw the same angels descending—that is, considering as less than themselves the one and same man, as the Psalm says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8).

Was it not a descent, as to one less or lower, that of which the Gospel relates: when he had entered into agony and prayed more earnestly, “there appeared to him an angel from heaven strengthening him” (Luke 22)? Yet in that manner they no longer descend, no longer look upon one less than themselves, since, when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, what had likewise been written came to pass: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8).

Here it is also pleasing not to pass over what the Lord says concerning the devil in blessed Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook? And will you bind his tongue with a cord?” Likewise: “In his eyes you shall take him as with a hook” (Job 40). For this genealogy of Jesus Christ, from Abraham to Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus, called Christ, was born, is like a long fisherman’s line. To that line an iron hook is fastened, covered over by flesh [Col. 1320C], so that the fish, enticed by the food visible outside, strangles itself upon the iron hidden within.

The divinity of Jesus Christ was like iron to the devil; and, by assuming from Mary the true nature of flesh, it hid its strength there, knowing without doubt that he who was a murderer from the beginning would seek to attack his flesh with death, and would thus be caught by the iron concealed within and drawn out and cast outside—as we believe has happened, and therefore speak of it.

This genealogy of Jesus Christ according to Matthew is indeed a line of this sort; but that according to Luke, ascending upward in the longer weaving of the genealogy, truly became as it were a circle. Thus nothing could be understood more aptly than the course of that same [Col. 1320D] generation in the words likewise spoken by the Lord to blessed Job: “Will you put a ring in his nostrils, and pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” (ibid.).

For what? When it begins thus, “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli,” and ends thus, “who was of Adam, who was of God” (Luke 3), does it not, I ask, join beginning and end and make a circle? For when a line is bent in one continuous stroke so that its beginning and end are joined, does not a circle take shape—for example, such as a bracelet is?

Behold Jesus Christ, of whom it began thus: “And Jesus himself, beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph,” is God and man. It began with man and made the end of its course in God [Col. 1321A]. Did it not therefore begin, as it were, a long, slender line—or a slender, extended rod—of gold or iron from Jesus Christ, and bring it back to Jesus Christ, when it says, “who was of Adam, who was of God,” since the one and same Jesus Christ is God and man, and Adam was not the work of any god other than this God?

Truly, therefore, O devil, this is the ring which God placed in your nostrils; this is the bracelet by which he pierced your jaw. He joined the beginning to the end—that is, God to man—and so these, namely beginning and end, met one another in the Virgin’s womb, so that the inflexible ring might hold your pierced nostrils fast and such a bracelet might pierce your devouring jaw: a bracelet of glory and honor. By it you are even now drawn along in folly; and what you had greedily bitten, being unable to retain it, you discharge through the opening of your jaw.

Where or when this joining of beginning and end occurred, Luke writes more fully and this writer expresses more briefly when he says: “Now the generation of Christ was thus: When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1321B].

Here this book of generation shines more brightly, and in this lies the entire value of the book: that everyone who reads or hears may believe that Christ’s generation was thus, because the Virgin Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit before they came together. How unlike this generation is to the other generations—even to the generations of righteous persons, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or David!

There was indeed some resemblance of generation, because all those fathers had barren wives; hence those who were born from them bore in many of their deeds a type of this Jesus Christ, who was truly born from a barren womb. For what is as barren as virginity? Holy Scripture records that seven mothers were barren: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel (Gen. 18, 25, 30), the woman who bore Samson (Judg. 13), Hannah the mother of Samuel (1 Sam. 1), Bathsheba, mother of Solomon and wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Sam. 11), and Elizabeth, who bore the forerunner of the Lord (Luke 1).

Those born from these women were great, and in many of their deeds, as has already been said, they displayed certain wonderful resemblances to the Lord, who was to be born of virginity, which is naturally barren [Col. 1321D] and does not bear: namely Isaac and Jacob, Joseph and Samson, Samuel and Solomon. Of John, who was the seventh, it is said that “among those born of women none greater has arisen” (Matt. 11); and he signified the Lord himself not so much by his deeds, as the others did, as by pointing to him with his finger.

The eighth barren woman—that is, virginity—received the nearest testimony from her barren kinswoman Elizabeth: “For with God,” says the angel, “nothing shall be impossible” (John 1; Luke 1). Therefore there was, as said, some resemblance in those cases; yet this Evangelist reasonably says here, “Now the generation of Christ was thus.” That is to say: the generation of every one of the others was such that none of them was generated otherwise than through the coming together of man and woman, as is the course of nature; but Christ’s generation was such that, before man and woman came together, the woman was found to be with child.

This is the wonderful and unheard-of thing which Jeremiah foresaw: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 13).

Having considered thus far this book of the generation of Jesus Christ, a great and evident door has been opened for contemplating in order the four faces of the one living creature which, Ezekiel says, he saw beside the river Chebar (Ezek. 1), so that this contemplation may be the chief aim of our undertaking, as the title prefixed to this work indicates: *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*.

For when Ezekiel had said, “And the glory of the God of Israel was over it”—namely, over the eastern gate of the house of the Lord—he immediately indicated what glory of the Lord he meant: “It is,” he says, “the living creature which I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, with four faces to one [living creature]” (ibid.), and so forth. From this chapter one ought already to observe what the face of man is like, how beautiful and how glorious, when the Evangelist says: “When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1322B].

And from this chapter onward, as far as the sequence of his Passion—which, as has been said above, is the face of the calf—it is pleasing to contemplate the beauty of this face, the face of man, so far as he himself deigns to show it; and to him we cry with heart and mouth: “Show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79).

How great is the beauty of this man’s face: that his mother was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1322C]. Great is this honor of the human race: that a man of our nature, of our condition, subject to suffering and death, was incarnate or conceived by the Holy Spirit—that is, not from male seed, but from the power and operation of the Holy Spirit.

Rightly, then, this face, conscious of such beauty, says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2); that is, the honor of the human race and the glory of humble parents.

Such beauty, such a pearl of splendor, ought not at that time to have been made public to envious eyes. For there was one who would say: “Do not cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them underfoot and, turning, tear you to pieces” (Matt. 7). For, to pass over others for the moment, what a swine was Herod then! What swine all his disastrous attendants were! Would it not therefore have been to cast this exceedingly splendid pearl before swine for the pregnant or childbearing Virgin to proclaim of herself that what she had in her womb was from the Holy Spirit?

For inquiry would have been made into how or by whom she had conceived, if she had borne a child while having no husband. Therefore it should be reckoned to the praise of him from whom she had conceived—that is, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel—that his mother was betrothed. For truly, in accordance with this very name or designation by which he is called and is the Spirit of counsel, he made himself worthy and provided worthily that she should be betrothed and, through this circumstance, freed from every inquiry.

The bridegroom [Col. 1323A], or the name of a bridegroom, kept the heavenly marriage secret; it guarded the closed doors of the bridal chamber, so that the light of splendor within was not openly visible to passersby, except insofar as it was fitting to indicate it through subtle rays from chinks or slanting windows.

Therefore she was betrothed; therefore it pleased the Holy Spirit that she should have a bridegroom, so that, just as Saul was deceived when David was anointed king, Herod—or the devil dwelling in Herod—might likewise be deceived in this sacrament of the King and Lord, the Son of God, the Son of David, incarnate or born from a Virgin’s womb.

How was Saul deceived when David was anointed? When Samuel said: “How shall I go? For Saul will hear and kill me.” The Lord said: “Take a calf from the herd in your hand, and say: ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord’” (1 Sam. 16).

Assuredly, in accordance with this analogy the Spirit of the Lord, the Spirit of counsel, had so arranged matters as if saying in his secret counsels: “Let this Virgin take a man from the people and be betrothed to him, so that when she has conceived and borne a child, she may say: ‘I have taken a husband; I have celebrated a marriage.’ Thus, just as the sacrifice of a calf then delivered Samuel, as though he had come to Bethlehem for no other reason, so the supposition of bodily intercourse may free this Virgin from every inquiry, as though nothing had been born in her other than what is accustomed to be born in marriage or from marriage.”

Yet Joseph did not know this beforehand, but afterward learned it when an angel announced it to him in a dream: “Joseph,” he says, “son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for what is born in her [Col. 1323C] is from the Holy Spirit.”

For he was afraid to take her; he did not wish to expose her publicly, but wished to send her away secretly. “He thought these things because he was righteous,” says the Evangelist. And truly this was the conduct of a righteous man—not only righteous, indeed, but also merciful: on the one hand, he feared to consent to another’s sins; on the other, he shrank from using the permission or severity of the Law, which says: “If virginity is not found in the girl, they shall cast her out before the doors of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death; and she shall die, because she has committed an abomination in Israel by fornicating in her father’s house; and you shall remove evil from your midst” (Deut. 22).

He wished to do neither of these things: neither to expose her nor to bring her to judgment. He chose this one course above all and preferred it: namely, to send her away secretly. This belongs to perfect righteousness.

Here it is fitting to ask: Why did God permit such fear to come upon him? Why did he not prevent it? Why did he not send beforehand the very angel whom he was eventually to send—namely, when he sent him to the Virgin to whom Joseph was betrothed? Clearly, that he might be tested and that it might become evident, both to the holy angels and to us human beings, that he was righteous and such a man as deserved fittingly to be called Joseph, son of David.

For his father David likewise preferred exile to availing himself of the permission of the Law which says: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Lev. 19; Matt. 5). The Lord had delivered Saul, who hated and persecuted him, into his hand. “Now,” said Abishai, “I will pin him to the ground with the spear in one stroke; no second will be necessary.” David said: “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his day comes for him to die, or he goes down into battle and perishes, may God be merciful to me if I stretch out my hand against the anointed of the Lord.” “After this David arose and went to Achish, king of Gath, and dwelt with Achish in Gath” (1 Sam. 26–27).

How did this righteous Joseph intend secretly to send away her to whom he was betrothed, unless he meant to depart for some region, as David did, and as many others did because of adverse circumstances? Moreover, he deserved to be called son of David so notably, in such a matter and at such a time, when the angel said, “Joseph, son of David” (Matt. 1), because he had the same faith as his faithful father David. For he believed something previously unheard of: namely, that she who had conceived was a Virgin, according to these words of the same angel: “For what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (ibid.), and so forth.

For this saying of the angel, received in a dream, is the fulfillment of the promise or covenant in which Abraham the father was justified by believing and called the friend of God (Jas. 2). Joseph at once obeyed God, believing, kindly disposed toward the girl, a righteous man up to that point and thereafter most righteous.

The Holy Spirit is especially named from this act: because, as the angel says, “what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” Before this, he was called the Spirit of God or the Spirit of the Lord; and you will not easily find throughout the whole course of the Old Testament this distinguished name, namely “the Holy Spirit,” except where David says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50) [Col. 1324C].

Nor did David himself say “Holy Spirit” in an absolute sense, but added “your,” just as nowhere in the other legal or prophetic Scriptures is “Holy Spirit” written absolutely; rather, it is written relatively, as has been said: “Spirit of God” or “Spirit of the Lord.”

From this place, almost for the first time, this reverent and distinguished title, proper and absolute—“the Holy Spirit”—rang in our ears: when the angel said both to Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1), and to Joseph, “What is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

For what reason? Unless because—something to be considered with great reverence—the Spirit of the Lord appeared especially from this work which he performed in Mary to be truly holy [Col. 1324D].

Someone may ask: since the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, why is this title, “Holy Spirit,” assigned as proper to this person, and why ought this person alone to be called thus?

To this I say: assuredly because the whole operation of this person is nothing other than sanctification. This distinction of operations must be carefully observed: God made everything that was made through the Son, and sanctified everything that is holy through his Spirit. For what is his Spirit but his love? And how could any rational creature ever be, or be able to be, sanctified otherwise than by loving the Creator?

Therefore, although, as has been said, the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, still this person alone ought rightly to be called the Holy Spirit, because his proper operation is the sanctification of the creature. Without him neither angel nor human being is holy. An angel who does not possess him is a devil; a human being who does not possess him is Antichrist or a member of the devil.

No one is unaware that the supreme instance of this sanctification is what was born in blessed Mary; indeed, that conception is the beginning of the same operation, namely sanctification. Finally, she is the first person upon whom this Spirit came with that gift on account of which he is called the Holy Spirit—namely, the gift which is remission of sins.

This same Spirit of the Lord had indeed come upon many before her [Col. 1325B], but with another gift, namely the division of graces. For there are two gifts of this Spirit: one is remission of sins; the other, already mentioned, is the distribution of diverse graces, concerning which the Apostle says: “To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith; to another gifts of healing; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of words” (1 Cor. 12).

Many received such graces before blessed Mary, and some of those who received them were not holy—for example Saul and Balaam. But the Spirit of the Lord deferred the other gift, which is remission of sins, until Christ’s coming. Concerning it the saying was made: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

Blessed Mary was the first of all mortals to receive this gift at the very hour of conception, when the angel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

And truly, in order that what was born of her might be wholly holy, she herself had to be sanctified—that is, cleansed from every sin, both actual sin and, what was greater, original sin. Nor did she then receive only this gift of the Spirit, remission of sins, but also the other gift, the division of graces: so that she possessed every operation of miracles and, especially, faith and prophecy, or every prophetic grace [Col. 1325D].

For she is that prophetess of whom Isaiah said: “And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. 8). He had first said: “And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a great book and write in it with a man’s stylus: ‘Swiftly take away the spoils; hasten to plunder.’ And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Barachiah” (ibid.).

What was that great book which, he declares, he was commanded to take and to write in with a human stylus, and after obtaining witnesses, “I approached,” he says, “the prophetess, and she conceived and bore” (ibid.)? What, I ask, was that great book except the whole of Holy Scripture, as much as had been written up to that time by Moses and the prophets?

For him to take this book and write in it with a man’s stylus was to receive prophetic grace and to write his own portion concerning the coming of Christ, the Son of God, in such a way that it could be read and understood by a human being. And what was it for him, after doing this, to approach the prophetess who conceived and bore, except for him to be known by this blessed Virgin, and for the book of Isaiah to be comprehended in her mind as were the other Scriptures, as the sudden illumination of the Holy Spirit coming upon her taught her?

Therefore he rejoices that he had thus approached this prophetess and that he has as witnesses of this matter Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Barachiah—that is, all believers from both peoples, Gentile and Jewish. For Uriah, whose name means “God is my light,” is the earlier people, namely the Jewish people, to whom alone God was once known; hence it could say, “God is my light.” Zechariah, however, whose name means “one mindful of the Lord,” is the later people, namely the Gentile people, now mindful of the Lord, because what the former people expected would happen, this people knows and remembers has already happened: namely, that this prophetess conceived and bore a Son.

Both peoples today bear witness to him that he wrote truth in that great book. Thus this blessed Virgin Mary, prophetess of prophets, received both gifts of the Spirit together; and this is “full of grace,” according to the angel’s greeting: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1), because when she received or conceived the Word of God, the Word of the Lord, she simultaneously received both gifts of the Spirit of God.

In second place, John, the friend of the bridegroom and the Lord’s forerunner, deserved to share from his mother’s womb in both gifts of the same Spirit, as the same angel who spoke to blessed Mary had foretold: “He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (ibid.). His mother perceived this at that moment when, crying out with a loud voice and herself filled with the Holy Spirit, she said: “For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy” (ibid.).

Therefore, just as the angel truly said to this blessed Virgin, “full of grace,” so the Lord said most truly concerning John: “Among those born of women none greater has arisen” (Matt. 11). He was the first to receive from the fullness of grace of which it was said, “Hail, full of grace”; and by the same Spirit this mother of the Lord and this friend of the Lord were sanctified [Col. 1326D].

From then on, he who had previously been called the Spirit of God or the Spirit of the Lord began to be proclaimed more exaltedly as the Holy Spirit—first from the angel’s mouth, and then throughout the whole Gospel of Christ. I do not doubt that this title sounds more venerable to everyone who has ears to hear, although the name Spirit of God, Spirit of the Lord, is also very greatly venerable.

The reason for the name Holy Spirit which we have stated, namely remission of sins, the angel immediately explains clearly when he says: “She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself shall save his people from their sins.” As new as the name Holy Spirit is, so new is this rationale of the name: “For he himself shall save his people from their sins.”

Nowhere in the Law or the Prophets is remission of sins—the chief gift of the Holy Spirit—expressed in words so plain [Col. 1327A]. What other or better new thing should we seek in the words of the Holy and True One who says: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall never again go out; and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name” (Rev. 3)? Or in those promises of the Lord in Ezekiel: “And I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezek. 36)?

Whatever or however great the things said concerning holy newness, the sum of all is remission of sins, which has its beginning here, where the angel said: “For he himself shall save his people from their sins.”

Likewise, this name “Son of God,” or “Son of the Most High,” is new. For, just as has already been said regarding the name Holy Spirit, so it is not pointless to consider or recall regarding this name that one will not easily find it in the ancient legal or prophetic Scriptures. 572 For just as he who in the Law or Prophets was called the Spirit of God or Spirit of the Lord is now proclaimed from the Gospel as the Holy Spirit, so he who in those Scriptures was called the Word of God or the Word of the Lord is now called the Son of God, since the angel thus announced: “Therefore that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” And again: “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High.”

This Son, this God, certainly existed in the beginning; he was born from the Father’s heart. But he was a hidden Son, a hidden God; and from time to time he spoke something such as this concerning the future: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; ask of me’” (Ps. 2), and so forth. Yet he was not commonly heard, did not speak openly, and was not known. Therefore confession of his name was not required from human beings by the same right by which it is now required.

From the time when he who was begotten of God became the son of our nature, confession is rightly required from us both of this Son and of the Holy Spirit by whom he was conceived, just as it is of the Father, whose Son this one is and whose Holy Spirit that one is. We must not say merely, as formerly, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” but, more clearly, “God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, in whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17) [Col. 1327D].

It is customary also to consider here, when he says, “She shall bear a Son,” that blessed Mary is that heaven of which it had been written: “He opened the gates of heaven and rained down manna upon them to eat” (Ps. 77). For if the soul of any righteous person is heaven, how much more is this singular dwelling or seat of God?

How many, then, or what are the gates of this heaven which the Lord opened? There are two: one of the mind, the other of the womb. God opened the gate of her mind because this blessed woman believed the things that had been said to her. He opened the gate of her womb because the Virgin conceived without a man, the Virgin bore, and after childbirth remained a Virgin. For who but God could so open the gate of the womb that she would both bear a child and remain a Virgin?

Hence the passage in the prophet Ezekiel: “And he brought me back by the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faced east; and it was shut. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall enter through it; and it shall be shut for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate and go out by its way’” (Ezek. 44).

It is well known in ecclesiastical faith, common in praises of Christ and in the writings of the holy Fathers, that this shut gate is the incorrupt mother, shut for the prince—that is, for the honor of Prince Jesus Christ. The prince sat in her, since from the day of conception he dwelt nine months in the lodging of her sacred womb [Col. 1328B]. Entering by the way of the vestibule—that is, through the hearing of faith—he went out by her way as God and man, one and the same Lord God of Israel, so that no man passed through her: neither inserting himself in conception nor opening a way for the one about to be born.

But let us return to the passage of the former prophecy: “He opened the gates of heaven and rained down manna upon them to eat, and gave them bread from heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77).

The Jews thought that the Psalmist had said this of that transitory manna which their fathers ate in the wilderness (Exod. 16). For when, acting inquisitively and wishing to live idly, they said: “What sign, then, do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness,” they immediately added: “As it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (John 6).

But in thinking or holding this, they were greatly mistaken, if they thought that angels also lived upon such food; for it immediately follows: “Man ate the bread of angels.” “Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven’” (ibid.).

And the sense is this: the bread concerning which it is written—the text you raise against me—“He gave them bread from heaven to eat,” was not given in past time, nor did Moses give it, but “my Father gives you” in the present time. For “I am the living and true bread [Col. 1328D] which came down from heaven” (ibid.). And the Spirit said in David concerning this time, “Man ate the bread of angels,” although he used a verb in the past tense, saying “ate,” as prophets frequently do when announcing future things in words of the past tense.

Therefore, when what the angel said came to pass—“She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus”—then “the Lord opened the gates of heaven and rained down for us manna to eat, bread of heaven, bread of angels.”

According to the likeness of the event thus written: “In the morning also dew lay around the camp, and when it had covered the surface of the ground, there appeared in the wilderness something small” (Exod. 16), and, Scripture says, the house of Israel called its name *man* [manna]—according, I say, to the likeness of that sign, this came to pass here.

The Holy Spirit came upon the blessed Virgin, and in the Holy Scriptures he is customarily signified by dew. This, indeed, was dew lying in the wilderness: being poured into the womb of the solitary Virgin, accessible to no man. He moistened the Virgin’s womb from heaven, not from his own substance, but from the natural moisture of her incorrupt flesh.

In this there is a wonderful and great difference from every conception of all flesh: the generative power of the sacred body was stirred up not by a man approaching from without, but by the Holy Spirit working within. Then, for the small thing to appear in the same wilderness was for the most subtle and most powerful Word to be present in the same hidden place; it mingled with that moisture as rennet. Thus, as the Israelites said to one another, “*Man-hu?*” [“What is it?”] (ibid.), so let us—and much more so—say, “What is this?” (ibid.).

Let us also say because of this: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1), because every woman who conceives conceives through love for a man, but you alone conceived through love for God—that is, through the Holy Spirit.

This we, the house of Israel, call *man* [manna], and its taste is to us like fine flour with honey, on which we feast daily both by hearing heavenly teaching and by receiving the sacred Eucharist.

Now all this was done in order that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, a virgin shall be with child and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7), which is interpreted, “God with us.”

Who has not heard this prophetic saying? Who has not understood it? Wherever the Gospel of this book of the generation of Jesus Christ has been preached, this distinguished proclamation also has been preached; this fitting testimony to truth has been recited; and it has been made known and become familiar even to the little children of the Catholic Church [Col. 1329C].

But do not, O reader or hearer of the present Gospel, regard as a small thing what this pen has set down from a great prophet, a great and noble seer: “Behold, a virgin shall be with child, or conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” even though it has written only this small portion of him. Consider not the quantity written but the writer’s intention, and know that, in writing this little, it sends you to read what follows.

It has beautifully opened, as it were, the door of a house and, by bringing in a lamp, has familiarly indicated what is within. What is within? What do you see? You see a threefold calling, or giving of names, to this Son of whom the angel here said: “She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.”

First, there it was said: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7). Second, in the same place it was said: “Call his name, ‘Hasten to take away the spoil; hurry to plunder’” (Isa. 8). Third, likewise it was said: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9).

Therefore, truly divine and by the Spirit—
…illuminated by the holy evangelist, [it] cast light inwardly upon the prophetic truth in a brief saying [Col. 1330A], yet illumined the broad and long house of that same prophetic truth. Although much has been written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning this child—as he himself knew when he said, “For it is necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24)—it should be known that in no prophet, in no psalm, nowhere in the whole Law, is he designated by name as he is here in Isaiah. It should therefore be observed that the holy evangelist did not idly choose to employ, in the present matter, this prophetic testimony in preference to the others.

Concerning the name Emmanuel—since it means “God with us,” an interpretation which he took care to add not without purpose—we hold the same view as concerning that saying of the other evangelist [Col. 1330B], “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). This word and its meaning admirably disclose to us what mystery is contained in that passage where, as we noted above, “the house of Israel called the name” of the food or bread which the Lord gave, “Man” (manna), which was like white coriander seed; and it is then added: “its taste was like fine flour with honey” (Exod. 16).

For what, according to the mystery stated above, is fine flour with honey but the flesh of this Emmanuel together with divinity? What is the taste where such an Emmanuel is seen? For the vision of him is the life-giving food and the immortal, unfailing delight of holy angels and of all blessed spirits or human beings. Though we believe this and in some manner know it, it is nevertheless impossible [Col. 1330C] to know it as it is until, by seeing, we eat, and thus by eating experience that he truly is fine flour with honey: that is, true and pure humanity with sweet and gracious divinity.

And see how beautiful and rational is the order of this name and of the others, which I remember having noted briefly long ago in another work.

First: Emmanuel, that is, “God with us,” for the reason that comes first in order: because God, made man, dwelt among us (John 1).

Second: “Hasten to take away the spoils; hurry to plunder,” for this reason: because by dying he overcame the strong, armed devil and distributed the spoils (Luke 11).

Third: “Wonderful,” because he rose from the dead and, ascending into heaven, [Col. 1330D] crowned with glory and honour, sits at the right hand of God (Ps. 108 [109]; Matt. 28; Acts 1–2).

Fourth: “Counsellor,” because, in giving the holy Paraclete to his apostles, he took counsel with that same Spirit of counsel concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles (Mark 13; Acts 2, 13).

Fifth: “God,” because thereafter he is truly worshipped as God by the whole world.

Sixth: “Mighty,” because he will appear truly mighty in the awaited judgment.

Seventh: “Father of the age to come,” because, once the judgment has been completed, he will reign no longer as the lord of servants, but as the father of sons.

Eighth: “Prince of peace,” because he will indeed be praised forever and receive thanksgiving as the author of that peace through which we, who had been enemies, are reconciled to God by his death (Rom. 5; Eph. 2).

“And Joseph, rising from [Col. 1331A] sleep, did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; and he took his wife, and did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son, and he will call his name Jesus.””

“Upon sinners he will rain snares,” says the Holy Spirit in the Psalm, and immediately adds, “Fire, sulphur, and a storm-wind are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10 [11]). The meaning is this: the Lord, whose eyelids examine—that is, test—the children of men (ibid.), so composed his Scripture that sinners might be ensnared by it: those who, loving iniquity, hate their own soul. Their curiosity is like fire; their exposition, by which they perversely interpret the Scriptures, is like sulphur; their wordiness in disputation is like a storm-wind. All these are at present the portion [Col. 1331B] of their cup; another portion is reserved for them in the future.

Among these was the impure Helvidius, against whose blasphemies the distinguished man, blessed Jerome, defended the virginity of the blessed Mary in a notable letter. Since he was a sinner and loved iniquity, this saying of the evangelist—“and he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son”—ensnared him so that he said: “The adverb *donec* [‘until’], or *usque* [‘up to’], indicates a fixed time; once that time is completed, what had not been done up to the prescribed point in time comes about—as in the present case: ‘and he did not know her until she had borne a son.’ Therefore,” he says, “it is evident that she was known after giving birth, since only the begetting of the son delayed that knowing.”

He then endeavoured to prove that one cannot be called “firstborn” [Col. 1331C] unless he also has brothers, just as one is called “only-begotten” when he is the sole son of his parents. And with shameless and heretical speech he maintained that those called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel (Matt. 12) were born of the Lord’s mother and Joseph after the birth of Jesus Christ.

The whole world abominates that monster, Helvidius, just as the aforementioned catholic and orthodox man abominated and sufficiently refuted him, saying among other things: “You say that Mary did not remain a virgin? I claim still more for myself: that Joseph himself, through Mary, was a virgin, so that from a virginal marriage a virgin son might be born. For if fornication does not befall a holy man, and it is not written that he had another wife, while he was rather the guardian than the husband of Mary, whom he was thought to have had [as wife], [Col. 1331D] it follows that he remained a virgin with Mary—the man who deserved to be called the Lord’s father.”

Therefore Christ was born, and in his birth God himself, who promised, was proved faithful and true. We all rejoice, saying with the Psalmist: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144 [145]). Again: “For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are done in faithfulness” (Ps. 32 [33]).

“For,” says the Apostle, “however many promises of God there are, in him is the ‘Yes.’ Therefore through him we also say, ‘Amen,’ to God for your glory” (2 Cor. 1). Truly, for your glory God was in some manner overcome, though stronger; and our mighty wrestler, the father Jacob, conquered through faith one who willingly allowed himself to be conquered. What we say is written thus:

[Col. 1332A] “And when Jacob had risen early and had brought all across, he remained alone; and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. And he said to him: ‘Let me go, for dawn is now rising.’ He answered: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ And he said: ‘If you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?’ And he blessed him in that same place. And Jacob said: ‘I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved’” (Gen. 32).

In accordance with that great and wonderful presage, this was to happen and did happen when Jesus Christ was born: man, or the race of Jacob, was found victorious, demanding from God what had been promised; and God, debtor for his own promise, was as it were justly overcome. Was this wrestling wrong or unknown? [Col. 1332B] Can it not at least be recognized from what he said to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked; let me alone, that my wrath may burn against them and I may destroy them” (Exod. 23 [perhaps 32])? There Moses was strong and prevailed in the same manner as his father Jacob, 574 in the place or at the time already mentioned. Of him it is written thus also in Hosea: “In his strength he strove with the angel, and he prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us” (Hos. 12).

From this it is clear what that struggle was like: for he wept and entreated him. According to that presage, it was to happen—and did happen—that God, angered because he had often been offended and angered by many of their devices, would threaten to depart, indeed even to scatter and destroy [Col. 1332C] Jacob’s race. Yet there were never lacking among that people, though few, men in whom was the strength—that is, the faith—of Jacob, wrestling and prevailing against the strength of God, and saying in some manner, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

Each such person wept and entreated him; and this was to prevail and to be strong against God. This was that Moses, whose example has just been given, who wrestled strongly, standing “in the breach,” that is, in profound humiliation of mind before him. When God said, “Let me alone,” Moses himself prayed to the Lord his God, saying: “Why, Lord, does your wrath burn against your people? Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself” (Exod. 32), and so forth.

Thus Moses many times wept and entreated him; thus David wept and entreated him; and thus many others wept and entreated him, whose weeping and entreaty it would take far too long to recount in order. What more need be said? Jacob was strong against God and did not let him go unless he blessed him; and he blessed him in that same place. Likewise, against God—that is, against the wrath of God—the offspring of that same Jacob was strong and did not let him go unless he gave them his Christ, who is the blessing of all nations.

Then he touched Jacob’s thigh-sinew at the place where he blessed him, and it immediately withered. What does this mean except that it was fitting that, once the promise had been fulfilled, once this Jesus Christ had been born, from that time onward all the old careful reckoning of genealogies [Col. 1333A] before God should be regarded as nothing—indeed, as folly or fables?

For it must be understood that every distinction so carefully made in the Law among tribes, families or generations, households and kindreds—for example, what is said concerning the sons of Judah according to their generations, families, households, and kindreds, that they numbered so many thousands (Num. 36), and especially the command that each should take a wife from his own tribe and family—was directed wholly and solely to Christ. It was for the truthfulness of God, to confirm the promises to the fathers, so that when he came and was born it might be known without uncertainty, and proclaimed to the glory and praise of the just and faithful God, that as he promised and swore, so he acted: by sending, for the blessing by which all nations shall be blessed, from the seed of Abraham [Col. 1333B], from the tribe of Judah, from the stock, house, and family of David.

Once, therefore, he came—once he was born—what concern remains with that thigh, with that division or calculation of tribes, generations, families, houses, and kindreds? Indeed, all of it must be considered utter folly. “Avoid,” says the Apostle, “foolish questions, genealogies, [Col. 1334A] quarrels, and disputes about the Law, for they are unprofitable and vain” (Tit. 3).

Therefore let the end of all genealogies be what the same Apostle says: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1).

And if from David’s seed, then also from Judah’s tribe, so that the truthfulness of God may be confirmed, who says through the mouth of the patriarch Jacob: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49). And if from Judah’s tribe, then from Abraham’s seed, to whom it was first said: “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. [Col. 1334B] 22).

From this point onward Jacob’s thigh becomes withered, as indeed it truly is. For it has in fact withered, so that neither king, leader, prophet, nor priest can now be hoped for from it; and all vigour or verdure of that kind has so failed in it that whoever places hope in the flesh of that people is faithless—indeed, worse than a faithless person—and will receive Antichrist under Christ’s name.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1333]

[Col. 1333C] Certain heavens were to declare the glory of God—the glory which we intend to proclaim—and to recount the honor of the Son of Man, in accordance with that prophetic saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Psalm 18).

The beginning of that glory and honor is the matter discussed thus far: namely, that “he placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself [came forth] like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber” (ibid.). This no longer requires exposition, since even little children have heard—and infants have spoken—how he proceeded like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber: those who were born, or rather reborn, from that bridegroom’s virginal marriage, and received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God (Rom. 8).

Nevertheless, nearly everyone also knows that those heavens which were to recount this glory were the apostles: vocal heavens, speaking heavens. For “there are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

To what end is this said? Clearly, for the praise and admiration of the divine counsel and its most beautiful ordering: because, when Christ was born amid the events which the divine Evangelist immediately relates, he at once prefigured the subsequent declaration of such heavens and the announcement and hearing of such a firmament, whether on account of the hearing of the Gentiles, who were to believe through the voices of those same heavens, as follows:

### Chapter II
“Now when Jesus,” he says, “had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: Where [Col. 1334C] is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.”

Did not the heavens already then declare this glory? Certainly they declared it, and signified that the other heavens, of which we have already spoken, would declare it. And just as the magi then—namely, wise Gentiles—recognizing and following the brightness or illumination of that inanimate heaven, that is, the star, came saying, “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” so it was to come about that the Gentiles, understanding the illumination of the rational heavens—that is, of the apostles—namely, the gift of the Holy Spirit which they had received, would come and ask that repentance unto life be granted them.

Again, just as then “Herod,” because of the magi or their inquiry, “was troubled, and [Col. 1334D] all Jerusalem with him, and he sought the child to destroy him,” so it was to come about that, when the Gentiles received the Gospel of Jesus Christ, that same city of Jerusalem and the whole Jewish kingdom, disturbed by uprisings, would attempt utterly to destroy the preaching of the apostles and, as it were, to kill Christ himself—by killing, crucifying, scourging, and persecuting from city to city (Matt. 23) many of the prophets, wise men, and scribes whom he sent.

Nevertheless, just as Joseph was then told, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt,” and Joseph did so, withdrawing into Egypt with the child and his mother, so it was to come about that Christ, speaking in his apostles, would say: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves [Col. 1335A] unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

Likewise, just as, “after Herod’s death, he again rose, took the child and his mother, being warned by an angel, and came into the land of Israel,” so it will be, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11).

But, to return to our undertaking: what did such a sign contribute to this glory of God? “We saw,” they say, “his star in the East.” This, I say, is what it contributed. Such a sign mattered greatly, if you remember rightly that when the Lord made a covenant with Abraham—from whom the book of the generation of Jesus Christ begins, and to whom the promise of the blessed seed was made—he also led him outside and said: “Look toward heaven and count [Col. 1335B] the stars, if you can” (Gen. 15). And afterward: “So shall your seed be.” “On that day,” Scripture says, “the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your seed I shall give this land” (ibid.), and so forth.

Hence the Apostle says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though of many, but as of one: ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. 3). This is the one “for whom are all things and through whom are all things,” who came to bring many sons into that glory (Heb. 2), so that, just as the stars in heaven are innumerable, they might be made radiant and unchangeable through him, and what the faithful and true One promised might be fulfilled: “So shall your seed be.”

Rightly, therefore, they gave not just any sign but a new star of heaven [Col. 1335C] because of such a promise, as though saying to us: Praise and rejoice together, because the covenant which God made with Abraham he has not made void (Gen. 17); he has fulfilled what he promised: “Look at the stars: so shall your seed be” (Gen. 15).

Knowing this, the angels were the first to glorify him on that same night. Their host was great, and the multitude praising and saying was large: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). Rejoicing with us, they also added: “And on earth peace to men of good will” (ibid.).

This too was relevant: after the evangelist had said, “Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea,” he immediately stated both the place and the time of the birth, saying, “in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of Herod.” To what end [Col. 1335D] was this relevant? Surely to the truthfulness of that same God, who spoke beforehand through the patriarch Jacob in this manner: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49); and who, just as he promised and swore to Abraham, also promised David of Bethlehem that this Jesus Christ would be born from his seed.

The sceptre and ruler were not to be taken from Judah before this one came; otherwise God, who spoke in the patriarchs and prophets, would not appear faithful and true. In the patriarch just mentioned he approximately fixed the time, and in the prophet Micah he designated the place beforehand: “And you,” he says, “Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a ruler who shall govern my people Israel” (Mic. 5).

Had not the sceptre been taken [Col. 1336A] from Judah, and had the ruler from his loins not failed, when Herod reigned, born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother? Therefore, by saying, “in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod,” he knowingly supplied proofs of the truth, declaring briefly and sufficiently that it had to happen thus: that Christ had to be born at the time when he says he was born, and that this had to be the place of his birth, because of God’s truthfulness and for confirmation of the prophets’ words. Yet he had been conceived in a city of Galilee named Nazareth.

For whatever reason Joseph and Mary may then have been or lived in that Galilean city, although they were of David’s house, God nevertheless made wondrous provision for Jesus to be born in Bethlehem of Judaea: Roman imperial power served prophetic truth. For Caesar Augustus served it in this way: both by removing the sceptre and ruler from Judah, giving the kingdom of Judaea to Herod, a foreigner, with Antony’s support—hence he is called “in the days of King Herod”—and by issuing an edict “that the whole world should be enrolled” (Luke 2). This led “Joseph, with Mary his betrothed wife, who was pregnant, to go up to Bethlehem, the city of David, because he was of the family and house of David” (ibid.).

Thus, in a wondrous way, both Roman power, though unaware, and the inanimate heaven, though perceptive, served the birth of Jesus Christ and prophetic truth: the Roman empire by issuing such an edict, and heaven by producing such a sign—that is, a new star. Hence that prophetic utterance was fulfilled: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24).

Although divinely inspired, the magi did not know the place itself. For they came first not to Bethlehem but to Jerusalem, asking: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” They thought that the King of the Jews might be born and should be sought more in a lofty than in a humble place, more in a royal city than in an ordinary village, more amid a crowd of rich people than in the quiet of the poor. Thus they came to Jerusalem; but this was like ignoring a small shoot and looking upward to the lofty trees of the forest.

Yet the Holy Spirit had said through the prophet: “The high in stature shall be cut down, and the lofty shall be humbled; the dense thickets of his forest shall be overthrown by iron, [Col. 1336D] and Lebanon with its lofty ones shall fall. And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 10), and so forth. The meaning is: among the proud there will be conflicts; they will fight one another and fall. This especially happened then, when Herod, a murderer—indeed, a parricide—raged at every trace of David’s line and gnashed his teeth against every royal family. He spared neither his wife nor his father-in-law, who were of royal stock; he also cruelly condemned his own sons to death.

The devil raged vainly; he was mad to no purpose in that axe with which he was cutting. For the flower was to rise not from lofty cedars or sturdy oaks, but from a slender rod hidden among shrubs: that is, Christ was to be born not from proud, purple-clad rich people, but from a humble virgin, such as could scarcely have been recognized among ordinary people.

The magi did not know this. God could indeed at once have done what he afterward did: namely, arrange that the star which they had seen would immediately go before them as they came from the East, until it came and stood above where the child was.” But this delay was useful, so that those who had received a sign from heaven might meanwhile hear from Scripture the firm support of testimony—a support which equally benefits us now, for whose sake it was written, as it benefited those for whose sake it was then read aloud.

What, finally, is to be said about the gifts they offered? Their joy has been heard of and made famous throughout the whole world. For when they saw the star going before them, which they had seen in the East, and standing “above the house where the child was, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; [Col. 1337B] and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshipped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

Truly they were inspired from heaven, truly taught by a heavenly ministry, and possessed a true and heavenly ground for rejoicing. What, I say, can be said here except that they themselves were prophets and that their gifts were prophetic? They bore witness to truth, gentleness, glory, and honor: the truth of assumed flesh; gentleness, that is, the humility of the Passion; the glory of kingship; and the honor of divinity—of one and the same Jesus Christ.

“The four faces,” says the prophet, “were one: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of a flying eagle” (Ezek. 10). It is agreed that these four faces are four mysteries which no one professing Christianity may fail to know: the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of the same Jesus Christ. The whole purpose of this present little work is occupied with examining these faces.

They found one of these faces present, namely the face of a man, and falling down they worshipped it; the others they wondrously prefigured by mystical gifts. Myrrh signifies the face of the calf, that is, the mystery of the Passion, in which he was to be sacrificed and in burial his body was to be embalmed with a mixture of myrrh and aloes. Gold signifies the face of the lion, that is, the glory of the Resurrection, through which the flesh he had assumed from us as mortal was made as much better as gold is more beautiful and precious than the dust or clay of earth. Frankincense signifies the face of the flying eagle, that is, the loftiness of the Ascension and the confession that he is at the Father’s right hand. From there, after the Holy Spirit had been given to human beings, it was recognized that the same Son of God is God, to whom a lawful sacrifice of incense ought rightly to be offered, equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The whole holy Church offers him such myrrh by believing and confessing that he truly suffered, died, and was buried, and by mortifying in itself the evils of vices for his sake. Most especially, however, the army of martyrs offers it, for they shared his Passion through the bitter taste of death.

Likewise, the whole Church offers him such frankincense by believing and confessing that he is truly God and that “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him” (Col. 2). Most especially, however, the holy order of priests offers it: living celibately for his sake, they are continually present at the altar, to offer him worthy incense and unceasingly perform every holy ministry of his sacred altar.

Likewise, the whole Church offers him such gold by believing and confessing that he who was mortal and died has risen and reigns immortally. Most especially, however, the power of kings and princes and the wealth of faithful rich people offer it, when they faithfully offer him gold and silver for building churches in his name, and enrich with lavish gifts the house of him “who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8), in accordance with that prophetic saying, most true both according to the letter and according to the spirit: “He shall live,” that is, he shall rise, “and to him shall be given of the gold of Arabia. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. 7 [citation as printed; likely Ps. 72]).

The evangelist therefore rightly magnified these gifts in sacred speech, and announced them so magnificently that, before saying, “They offered him gifts,” he prefaced it with, “and opening their treasures.” For they were truly treasures and deserve to be called treasures—not so much the purses or whatever sort of cases in which such substances could be carried enclosed, as the very hearts of those offering them. From their abundance, grounds so holy could be invisibly offered to the invisible God—grounds which the holy Church reverently understands through those visible substances.

He also magnified their joy in this way: not content with saying, “They rejoiced with great joy,” he added “exceedingly,” because they truly rejoiced; “they rejoiced with great joy.” Their joy was in the Holy Spirit, who stored up judgment and exultation over them. They lacked nothing of the fullness of knowledge or faith required of us, who are instructed by the continual reading of Holy Scripture. This is shown by their gifts when properly considered.

And see how great is the difference between modes of learning—how greatly the instruction of one who deserves to be taught through an angel or a human being differs from that of one who deserves to be taught through the revelation of the Holy Spirit alone. The Jewish “shepherds,” who “were in the same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock” (Luke 2), learned that Christ the Lord, the Savior, had been born to them not through a human being but, what is greater, through an angel. Yet they were not so taught or instructed that they fell down in worship or offered gifts; they only came, “learned concerning the word spoken to them about this child, and returned glorifying and praising God” (ibid.).

These men, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, taught neither by a human being nor by an angel, but by the Holy Spirit in the manner already stated, perfected praise. Three men deserved to become an example of faith, confession, and worship for the three parts of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa.

Meanwhile, it is fitting reverently to consider how truthfully Holy Scripture said concerning this such Son of Man: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). For, as he was made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4), so he was also made subject to the laws of nature and the laws of infancy: visibly doing nothing for himself and speaking nothing to human beings by himself. He deigned to have angels as guardians, who would act for the child and speak for the little infant, and that only in dreams, which are not the higher mode of vision.

Before and after this abasement of such a Son, we read that angels were visibly seen by men and women servants of this Lord. But while he was lower, they appeared not openly but in dreams. When he had descended into the virgin’s womb, “an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.” Again, in a dream, the same blessed Joseph was told: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.”

“In a dream,” likewise: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.” Again, “in a dream,” when he feared to go into Judaea because “Archelaus reigned in place of Herod his father, he was warned and withdrew to the region of Galilee.” These magi too received an answer “in a dream” “not to return to Herod, and they returned to their own country by another way.”

Thus the holy angels speak in dreams to the servants of their Lord as though they disdained to speak openly—not because they disdain the servants of their Lord, but because, according to the will of that same Lord, they honor the Scripture of truth. They know and acknowledge themselves to be greater not only than the servants of their Lord but even than their Lord himself. The final judgment or testimony of this superiority occurred there where, as the same Lord agonized in his Passion, “an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22).

We do indeed read that angels ministered to him while he was still lower than the angels, as it is written: “The tempter left him, and angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4). But this does not greatly oppose the present sense, since an angel ministered to Elijah once and again in this manner: “Elijah threw himself down and slept under the shade of a juniper tree; and behold, an angel of the Lord touched him and said: Rise and eat. He looked, and behold, at his head was bread baked under ashes and a vessel of water. Therefore he ate and drank, and slept again. And the angel of the Lord returned a second time and did likewise” (3 Kings 19).

Since an angel ministered to Elijah so that he afterward fasted forty days and forty nights, what wonder is it if angels ministered in the same way to this Son of Man when he had fasted forty days and forty nights? These things have been said because they should avail us for knowledge of heavenly discipline and for veneration of this teacher who says, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). As by nature or the human condition, so by the very exercise of nature he deigned to be lower than his angels, as he himself testified: “For the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20).

What then of his mother herself? Did not even she speak, or could she speak? Indeed, that which another evangelist mentions once and again especially became her: “But Mary kept all these words in her heart” (Luke 4 [citation as printed]). “A time to keep silence,” says Solomon, “and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3). The wise and prudent virgin did not fail to understand such discernment.

Therefore, praising her, the bridegroom—who was God to her and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose child she conceived and bore—says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4). Certainly Christ, the Son of God, fittingly says this to his bride, the Church; yet the person of God the Father may no less fittingly say the very same words to his beloved blessed Mary, immediately adding: “Your outflowings are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of the orchard” (ibid.). He had also said before this: “Your lips, O bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” (ibid.).

For about as long as the Son of Man had to remain made a little lower than the angels, so long it was a time of silence for the Blessed Virgin, and so long she was silent, so long she remained in silence, like “a garden enclosed.” “A garden,” I say, “enclosed, a fountain sealed,” to which no one deserves to approach or to hear its secret except one who is known; no one to whom such a garden and fountain would not judge unworthy that the enclosure or seal of its mouth should be opened.

But when the Son of Man was crowned with glory and honor by rising and ascending into heaven, where he sits at the Father’s right hand, then it became a time of speaking for that Blessed Virgin—and of speaking such things to friends, that is, to the holy apostles, as they could not formerly have borne. Knowing this, the Son of Man had said in one place: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16).

When the Spirit of truth came, he himself, first and foremost, taught them all truth; but the Blessed Virgin too added the testimony of her voice, speaking to faithful ears in such a manner that her beloved God rightly says: “Your lips drip honeycomb, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue. Your outflowings are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of the orchard: cypress with nard, nard and crocus, reed and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloe with every finest ointment; a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing with force from Lebanon” (Song 4).

Therefore the Son of God, made man or Son of Man and thus made a little lower than the angels (Heb. 2), while the magi and blessed Joseph, his foster-father, received dreams, but angels kept watch in his protection, escaped the malice of murderous Herod: “he fled into Egypt and remained there until Herod’s death.” Why was this? “That,” says the evangelist, “what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Hos. 11).

Understand him to have said this so that he might be made like his brothers in every respect, as the Apostle says: “For nowhere does he take hold of angels.” Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. “For because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted” (Heb. 2).

For what son, what one of all his brothers, has God not called out of Egypt? The faith of the saints knows, and it is most frequently spoken in the mouth of the faithful Church, that for all the sons of God this world is Egypt—this world in which, “while we are in the body,” says the Apostle, “we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5). And in that region of the world commonly called Egypt was figuratively represented how God calls every son out of the Egypt of this world, that is, “out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2): through that by which, as sacred history relates, God called that people who served a fleshly Pharaoh in Egypt out from there, by such a wondrous order, into the land of promise (Exod. 5).

Beyond this universal exile, in which we all are exiles in the Egypt of this age because of Adam’s transgression, “in whom all sinned,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 5), those people had this further circumstance: they lived as exiles in that Egypt and served the fleshly Pharaoh in mud and brick because of their own sin, since they had sold their brother Joseph there as a slave (Gen. 37).

Therefore, because this only-begotten Son had to be made like his brothers in every respect, except only in sharing sin, he had to flee and live as an exile in that Egypt. Thus, beginning in this way, he was to run the entire course of this present life in his temptations so as to present in himself a true likeness both of the exile and of the calling or return of his brothers, who are all the elect: both that by which the children of Israel lived as exiles in Egypt and were called out of it, and this by which we all live as exiles in the Egypt of this age and, because we are children, are called from it daily.
