Therefore, “that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Hos. 11)—that is, so that he might be made like his brothers in every respect and “be tempted in every respect according to their likeness, yet without sin” (Heb. 4)—because they have been or are to be called to the true land of promise, he had to flee into Egypt and live there as an exile. He had neither original sin, for which he ought to have been an exile in this world as all we are, nor actual sin, for which he ought to have lived as an exile in that Egypt, as that people did because of their domestic sin already mentioned—the people from whom he himself was born according to the flesh.

There served in exile the one who, after the promise made to Abraham, first endured persecution: Joseph. Then Jacob and all his house entered there. In that place of exile, this one took the beginning of his sufferings or temptations.

That people Israel, called out of that Egypt, crossed the sea and afterward was tested in the wilderness for forty years, because it put the Lord to the test. This child Israel, as the prophet says—“Because Israel is a child, and I loved him”—after he was called from Egypt, crossed the sea in the manner fitting for him (Hos. 11): that is, he was baptized in John’s baptism and immediately led by the Spirit into the wilderness. He did not test God for forty years, but was tested [Col. 1342A] for forty days.

Likewise, that people Israel did not enter the land of promise until after it had been exercised by temptations. This child Israel did not proclaim, “The kingdom of God is at hand” (Matt. 4), until after he had overcome temptations; and he says, “Behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17).

Thus he had been made like those brothers, namely the elect of the former people; but the likeness was not yet complete or brought to its end. We come to another Egypt, of which the land of Egypt was a figure. What is that Egypt but hell? There the captive people of his brothers—that is, the people of the saints—were held. All of them he immediately led across the Red Sea, that is, through the sacrament of the blood and water flowing from his side. That sea covered their enemies—that is, their sins—and still covers our enemies, we who have been baptized by the same sacrament.

Was he not then made like his brothers in every respect, as he had to be, in order to make like himself those whom he descended through many temptations even to hell to make co-heirs and co-participants with himself? The beginning of all that he endured was his flight into Egypt. Therefore the evangelist fittingly recalled that testimony and applied it to him: “That what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’”

Above all, it was not where he recounts the angel’s saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into [Col. 1342C] the land of Israel,” which Joseph does; but where he recounts that, “rising, he took the child and his mother by night and withdrew into Egypt,” that he introduced this prophetic testimony: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

What if he intended Judaea itself, or Jerusalem itself, to be called Egypt on account of Egyptian persecutions? For it is written in the Apocalypse: “Their bodies shall lie in the street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified” (Rev. 11). And the Lord speaks through the prophet to Jerusalem itself: “And now what have you to do in the way of Egypt, that you may drink troubled water?” (Jer. 2).

There are more examples of this kind than can all be written in the present place; through them it can be shown that earthly Jerusalem was called both Sodom and Egypt, and that the Jewish people were rightly called Egypt and Canaanite—or rather Hittite—than Israel.

Why, however, should it be preferable in the present passage to call that Judaea or Jerusalem Egypt rather than Sodom or Canaan? Clearly because of the likeness of the present sin: “Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him,” because he had heard that the King of the Jews had been born in Bethlehem. “And sending, he killed all the boys who were in it and in all its borders.” Is this not like what Pharaoh commanded the midwives of Egypt, saying: “When you act as midwives for Hebrew women and the time of birth has come, if it is a male, kill him; if a female, preserve her” (Exod. 1)? And likewise to his people: “Every male child that is born, cast into the river; every female, preserve” (Exod. 1).

Certainly, in Herod here and in Pharaoh there, there was one devil; in each the one and same spirit of malice raged. There Pharaoh wished all males to be killed so that there might be no seed from which Christ would be born according to the promise spoken to Abraham. Here Herod hastened to kill all the children in Bethlehem and throughout its borders so that, while all were being killed, the one whom alone he feared might not escape.

Therefore it is neither absurd but rather reasonable and true to say that this Son was then called out of Egypt when Joseph fled carrying the child to that place which the authority of Scripture spiritually calls both Sodom and Egypt. Hence the evangelist rightly says that this prophetic saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son,” was fulfilled not when he returned to the land of Israel, but when he withdrew into Egypt. The sense is: I rescued him from Herod’s hand and from the hand of all those who sought his life, who were truly Egyptians.

It is difficult and excessively lengthy to examine and discuss what follows the saying, “And out of Egypt I called my son,” so that it may plainly be established that it concerns the time and event for which it has been taken as a testimony to Gospel truth. Therefore, setting these matters aside, we must consider also what he next adds.

“Then,” he says, “was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: [Col. 1343C] ‘A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and wailing, Rachel weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted, because they are not.’” In Jeremiah it is written thus: “Thus says the Lord: A voice of lamentation, weeping, and mourning was heard on high—Rachel weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted because they are not” (Jer. 31).

After inserting a few words concerning the consolation of the lamenting or weeping woman, he makes sufficiently plain the reason why the fatal Herod killed the children according to the truth of the Gospel: “For the Lord shall create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (ibid.). That is, she shall not receive seed from outside, but within she shall conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son.

But were only those infants killed in Bethlehem and throughout its borders because of this man whom the woman encompassed—because of this King of the Jews born from the Virgin? No indeed: countless thousands of martyrs throughout the world were killed. But those infants were the firstfruits, and Rachel—that is, Mother Church—still mourns them all and refuses consolation because they are not, until they rise and live immortally with him who is, as he says: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3).

Why, however, should such a mother—the Church—be named Rachel in the present place? Clearly because Rachel was the mother of the one who first, from the time of the promise, suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake. “For Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104). Rachel, I say, was called his mother.

Therefore Mother Church, or any soul whatever which sympathizes with a Christian suffering persecution for righteousness’ sake, is rightly called Rachel in this prophet. And everyone who suffers persecution for righteousness’ sake is likewise rightly called Joseph in another prophet, namely Amos: “Like David,” he says, “they imagined themselves to possess instruments of song, drinking wine in bowls and anointing themselves with the finest ointment, and they suffered nothing over Joseph’s crushing” (Amos 6).

He did not say, “they suffered nothing over their brother’s crushing,” but “Joseph” is placed for “brother,” so that any brother or son of Mother Church might be signified by the proper name of the one among the brothers whose fame is distinguished, whether in the evils he suffered or the good things he repaid. He said this with wonderful propriety, because, as was stated above, this man was the first from the time of the promise to suffer crushing—that is, persecution [Col. 1344B] for righteousness’ sake (Matt. 5)—so that “iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104).

Moreover, how this mother both weeps and refuses to be comforted can be felt better through experience than by hearing reading alone. For one who has experienced how sweet this weeping is—whoever he may be—says: “My tears became my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 41).

But someone may say: If it is good for this mother to weep for her children, if it is best to refuse consolation or reject it, how does the Lord in the same place through the same prophet address words of consolation to her as she weeps and restrain her from weeping? For where he said, “A voice of lamentation, weeping, and mourning was heard on high—Rachel weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted concerning them, because they are not” (Jer. 31), he immediately continues: “Thus says the Lord: Let your voice rest from weeping and your eyes from tears, because there is a reward for your work, says the Lord; and they shall return from the land of your enemy, and there is hope for your latter end, says the Lord, and your children shall return to their own borders” (ibid.).

How does the Lord console her and yet she refuse consolation? If, as was said, her weeping is good, how is it said to her, “Let your voice rest from weeping”? To this I say: the weeping whose voice was heard on high is not one and the same as the weeping whose voice God does not wish to hear when he says, “Let your voice rest from weeping.”

For one kind of weeping comes from the Spirit of God, another from the spirit of this age. Hence the Apostle: “For godly sorrow works steadfast repentance unto salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death” (2 Cor. 7). Not many words are needed. For the kind of weeping the Lord forbids when he says, “Let your voice rest from weeping and your eyes from tears,” he himself defines through the Apostle when he says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4).

Finally, what he here adds in consolation—“because there is hope for your latter end, and your children shall return to their own borders” [Col. 1345A]—is the same as what the Apostle there adds: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thess. 4), and so forth.
up to: “Therefore comfort one another with these words” (ibid.). The other weeping—the weeping or mourning of sorrow that is according to God—not only does the same Lord not forbid, but he even pronounces it blessed: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). Therefore Rachel both weeps praiseworthily and praiseworthily refuses consolation; and she has a reasonable cause for doing so, namely, “because they are not,” that is, because her children have not yet attained that immutability of which it is said in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is into the same thing” [in idipsum] (Ps. CXXI). [Col. 1345B] Although the souls of the saints are in heaven, they do not yet possess “the same thing,” since their bodies still sleep in the dust (Job XXI), part of them still lives as pilgrims in this world, and those who will belong to their number are still to be born. But when, as the Lord says through the prophet, “the children for whom Rachel weeps shall return to their own borders”—that is, when God, as he himself says through the Apostle, “will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (I Thess. IV)—then there will be “the same thing”; then the mother will be comforted over her children, because they are, because “then they shall see as he is” (I John I), him who says: “I am who I am” (Exod. II).

“But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared [Col. 1345C] in a dream to Joseph,” and so forth, up to: “and, warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And coming, he dwelt in a city called Nazareth, that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘For he shall be called a Nazarene.’” Since the rest is sufficiently clear in itself, this alone requires inquiry: why, after saying, “and he dwelt in a city called Nazareth,” does he add this reason: “that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘For he shall be called a Nazarene’”? What then? Unless he had dwelt or been brought up in the city called Nazareth, would he not have been a Nazarene—that is, consecrated to God?

To this I reply: he would indeed, certainly, have been a Nazarene—that is, consecrated, or *Nazaraeus*, that is, holy—but he would not have been called so. Yet it was necessary that he be called so, because the Holy Spirit had thus foretold through the prophets that he is holy—indeed, the Holy of holies himself. For example: “Woe,” says Isaiah, “to the sinful nation, the people burdened with iniquity, the evil seed, the wicked children. They have forsaken the Lord; they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned away backward” (Isa. II). Again: “But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the Spirit of his holiness” (Isa. LXIII). And the angel speaks to Daniel: “That transgression may be brought to an end, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be abolished, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX).

We also understand the very Hebrew word *Nazaraeus*, which the Evangelist here uses, as retained from the prophets [Col. 1346A] or prophecies: “‘The blessings of your father have been strengthened,’ says the prophet and patriarch Jacob, ‘by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills comes’” (Gen. XLIX). This, without doubt, is Christ, the desire of the angels (I Pet. I) and of all the saints who desire to look into him; Joseph bore his type in that he was “sold as a slave” (Ps. CIV) and, after the confinement of prison, was made lord or prince of the land of Egypt. And immediately he adds: “Let them be upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazarene among his brothers” (Gen. XLI, XLIX).

We may also say that, according to the Hebrew truth, it is written in Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise from his root” (Isa. I). Moses likewise, when he writes the law of the Nazarene, says among other things: “Then the Nazarene shall shave, before the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, the hair of his consecration” (Num. VI); and shortly thereafter: “After this the Nazarene may drink wine” (ibid.). And to what do all these things tend, if not to Christ? Otherwise, unless everything said there is to be carried, according to the life-giving Spirit, over to the spiritual mysteries of this one who is truly consecrated and truly holy, what benefit is there in such a letter?

It was necessary, I say, as has already been stated, that he be called thus, because the Holy Spirit had so foretold through the prophets. And why did he foretell this? Namely, because it is necessary for eternal salvation that every believer know and confess that this one alone is holy; that he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth [Col. 1346C] (Isa. LIII); and that he is so holy, so without sin (I Pet. II), that he also takes away and is able to take away the sins of the world. Therefore, in order that material might be supplied for so great a name, so that he who was this might be called this—namely, *Nazaraeus* or *Nazarenus*, that is, consecrated or holy—it was fittingly brought about that “Joseph, warned in a dream, withdrew into the regions of Galilee and dwelt in a city called Nazareth.”

For from this occasion—indeed, through the working of God’s Spirit, who knows how to use even evil men well—Pilate wrote above his cross that famous and splendid title in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews” (John XIX). The Holy Spirit took no small care, or showed no small providence, that this title should not be corrupted by the Jewish chief priests, [Col. 1346D] who said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said: I am King of the Jews’” (ibid.). For who but the Spirit of God caused the soul of that wicked man to stand firm, so that he answered them: “What I have written, I have written” (ibid.)? There the evil servant served well the prophetic titles of certain Psalms—namely Psalms fifty-five, fifty-six, fifty-seven, fifty-eight, and fifty-nine—titles which are, almost word for word, “To the end: Do not destroy; for David himself, in the inscription of the title.”

Although the other Evangelists passed over the name “Nazarene” in that title, John, seeing keenly with an eagle’s eye that it greatly concerned the name of the crucified one that he should be known as truly Savior—which is “Jesus”—and truly King, as was charged against him as a crime, [Col. 1347A] and likewise as truly Holy, which is “Nazarene,” did not pass it over. He wrote out for us the whole title: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews” (ibid.).

Above all, this should be firmly remembered: when the Evangelist said, “he dwelt in the city Nazareth,” he did not add the reason by saying, “that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘For he shall be a Nazarene,’” but, “For he shall be called a Nazarene.” For he was not, nor is, holy because he “dwelt in Nazareth”; rather, because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. But dwelling in that city brought it about that he who is fittingly called *Nazaraeus*, or *Nazarenus*, in accordance with his holiness, should be called so. Thus every language—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—calls him; and not only the languages of human beings, but also those of evil and good angels alike, and of godly and ungodly people alike.

And, more wonderfully still, evil angels or malignant spirits, tormented by his presence, are recorded as the first to have called him by this name: “What have we to do with you, Jesus the Nazarene? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Mark I). Moreover, the good angels, rejoicing at his resurrection, solemnly proclaimed precisely this: “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here” (Mark XVI). Ungodly people—not Pilate alone, when he wrote the aforementioned title, but also those who arrested him—exalted him by their confession and immediately experienced the force of the same word. For, when he asked them, “Whom do you seek?” they answered him once and again: “Jesus the Nazarene” (John XVIII). And when he said, “I am,” they drew back and fell to the ground (ibid.).

This glorious and honour-worthy Son of Man proceeded in this order until the thirtieth year of his age, as the Psalmist had foretold: “Attend, proceed prosperously, and reign” (Ps. XLIV). The Pharisees, not considering this order—indeed, unwilling either to consider or investigate it, and therefore deliberately erring, since their own malice had blinded them—said on one occasion to Nicodemus, who had come to him by night: “Are you also a Galilean?” (John VII). “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.” For he had said: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him [Col. 1347D] and knows what he does?”

Likewise, when, because of his words, some among the crowd said, “This is truly the prophet,” others, “The Christ,” certain persons said: “Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Christ comes from the seed of David and from Bethlehem, the town where David was?” (ibid.). As though it could not happen, or had never happened, that a person born in one place might be brought up in another. Indeed, even if he had been born in Galilee, where he had been conceived, Christ would nevertheless truly have come from the town of Bethlehem; for his mother was a Bethlehemite of the house and family of David.

Otherwise Scripture lies when it says that Elkanah, Samuel’s father, was an Ephrathite—that is, a Bethlehemite (I Sam. I); and the leader of the people at the return from Babylonian captivity, [Col. 1348A] called Zerubbabel because he was born in Babylon, would not be of Judea, nor would any others who were born there during the seventy years of captivity. This is against the perversity of those who, while seeming to build, rejected this stone. Hence they are without excuse for their sin: if they had wished, they could quickly have known what we younger men know and preach, namely, that although he was brought up in Nazareth, he nonetheless came from Bethlehem, the town where David was; and he did not merely come from it in some manner, but was born there.

We gladly linger over prophetic testimonies, because they are especially effective for the glorification of the Son of Man, whose glory and honour the present work undertakes to proclaim (Joel II). Since he himself knew this, when he had said, “I still have [Col. 1348B] many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI), he immediately added: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you. All things whatsoever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (ibid.).

Matthew, once a tax collector, was one of those to whom these words applied; and consequently they were not yet able to bear all those things which he had to tell them from the Scriptures, “because they were unlettered and ordinary men” (Acts IV). What he promised came to pass: after his resurrection and ascension the Spirit of truth came and taught them all truth, as appears both from these five prophetic testimonies which Matthew has now set down here and from others which both he [Col. 1348C] and the other Evangelists use most fittingly at appropriate occasions and places.

This was what he meant when he said, “He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you”: namely, that the whole mystery of the Scriptures is his; “the things are his,” they belong to this Son of Man, and all “that the Father has”—understood as what lies in the treasures of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—tends toward him. Whenever we rightly understand any of these things, which indeed occurs through the Spirit of truth, then what he promised takes place: “He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” Thus he himself is glorified in our hearts, while through the testimonies of the Scriptures, which cannot be annulled, he is known to be what he is: truly the Son of God and likewise truly the Son of Man.

But how could it fittingly or appropriately have happened that he alone, while he was among human beings, lowly and humble—he alone, I say, as though the first—should bear witness to himself of such great majesty? [Col. 1348D] If he had gone out among the crowds, if he had entered the assembly of the Pharisees and Scribes—whose pride was as towering as their torment of envy was great—and said to them: “Behold, I am he of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the prophets” (John I); behold, I am the Messiah; “you believe in God; believe also in me” (John XIV)—how could he consistently then say to us: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI)?

Certainly it did not befit him, who is Wisdom itself, to proceed in this way; nor does it befit any of Wisdom’s children to be the first to proclaim whatever grace may have been bestowed upon himself. It befitted him, whose saying is: “Blessed is he who is not offended in me” (Luke VII), to take care that every occasion of stumbling might be removed—at least for those who did not willingly or slowly take offense, as the Scribes and Pharisees especially wished to do. Therefore it happened, and indeed had to happen, that the Evangelist immediately adds to the matters related thus far:

## Chapter III.

> “In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, saying: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’ John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt [Col. 1349B] about his loins. His food was locusts and wild honey. Then Jerusalem and all Judaea, and all the country about the Jordan, went out to him, 581 and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.”

Therefore this John, a great man, by reason of his very greatness owed much to the humility of the Son of Man: namely, because of the need of that same one who, having become poor and needy for our sake, needed for our sake a great testimony. Thus one so great and such as he came, that, bearing testimony, he might be worthy to be heard—indeed, might be incapable of being despised. For what sort of prophet, or how great, is this prophet, whose greatness other great and holy prophets prophesied, as testified by him who sent the prophets themselves? “For this,” he says, [Col. 1349C] “is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee.” For it is written in the prophet Malachi (Mal. III), and he himself, greatly confirming this, thus pronounced concerning the same man: “Amen I say to you, there has not arisen among those born of women one greater than John the Baptist.”

And John himself, not overly forward—indeed, thoroughly examined and very importunately pressed by his questioners (Matt. III; Luke III)—said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said” (ch. XL), whom this evangelist also mentions in the present passage, as do the other evangelists. When this angel came, this voice crying out came so gloriously that, conceived in an aged and barren womb, with Gabriel the archangel announcing it beforehand, [Col. 1349D] he was filled with the Spirit while still in his mother’s womb. So many signs accompanied his birth that all the neighbors were afraid, these events were spread abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: “What thinkest thou this child shall be? For the hand of the Lord was with him” (Luke I).

But perhaps we know these proofs of his greatness because we read them. Those, however, who were then present did not know—or had forgotten—things long past, because it was now his thirtieth year. Yet it must be understood that for this reason he was no less worthy of reverence in their eyes; indeed, this above all increased their reverence for him: he came unknown, because his manner of life had not been among men. Hence he was thought to be Elijah; and, [Col. 1350A] what is greater still, the people supposed and all pondered in their hearts concerning him whether perhaps he himself was the Christ.

Of all these things which indicate his greatness, this evangelist first set down the following: “For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying: A voice of one crying in the wilderness,” etc. Great is this proclamation concerning John: that he is a voice. He is not called vocal, or one possessing a voice, but “voice,” as he himself confessed, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John I). And a voice is, assuredly, the voice of another. Whose voice, then, is John? Certainly, of one crying out. And who is the one crying out, except he whose whole life, the whole time during which he dwelt here in the flesh, was a cry or loud outcry?

For this reason the Apostle says: “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications [Col. 1350B] to him who could save him from death with a loud cry and tears, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. V). John was the first voice of this one who cried out thus. For humility had no voice, but dwelt by itself in the town of Nazareth, and his thirtieth year of age was already beginning.

This is what he intends to say: just as the word of any one of us needs a clear or resonant voice in order to be heard better, so the Word of God made flesh needed John’s testimony, so that people might stumble less at him—and this indeed came about. For not only among the simple, but even among the envious and those willingly suffering scandal, John’s authority very often defended his cause. Thus, when [Col. 1350C] they said to him, “By what authority doest thou these things?” he answered and said to them: “I too will ask you one question; if you tell me, I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. Whence was the baptism of John—from heaven or from men?” But they reasoned among themselves, saying: “If we say, From heaven, he will say to us: Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From men, we fear the crowd; for all held John to be a prophet.” And answering Jesus, they said: “We do not know.” And he said to them: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. XXI).

Nor should anyone attend only to those times, or to the people of that age or nation, but to all peoples and nations until the end of the world. For wherever and as long as Christ’s advent is preached, this same witness John is present, and, testifying with his finger, confirms that Christ was not, is not, and will not be anyone other than he who was thought to be Joseph’s son. Such was the power of the greatness and authority of that friend and witness, that then at least a few received the Son—at least twelve—beginning from that voice by which he said: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). And even if no more had received him—though some others did receive him—these spiritual sons, as many as the sons whom his father, the first Israel, had according to the flesh, could have sufficed for that holy Israelite to propagate the spiritual race.

Luke the evangelist, a discerning author of most beautiful discourse, announces this advent of John in the following manner: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of [Col. 1351A] Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the Word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness. And he came into all the region of the Jordan” (Luke III), etc.

How beautifully does this narrative accord with that prophetic vision of Daniel: “I was watching in the vision of the night, and behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet” (Dan. VII). And shortly thereafter: “I was watching, therefore, in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming, and he came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, [Col. 1351B] and he gave him power and honor and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed” (ibid.).

For what was it to see that beast, such as it was, not only devouring but also crushing, except what Luke here finely recalls: that the Roman Empire not only subjected the kingdom of the Jews, like other nations, to its dominion, but also crushed it into tetrarchies? For in order to crush the power of the Jewish kingdom, because of the excessive arrogance of that nation, it scattered it into tetrarchies—that is, among four rulers: Pontius Pilate, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias. Nor did it crush only the kingdom, but also the supremacy of the priesthood, dividing it between two men, Annas and Caiaphas. It was yet to trample the rest beneath its feet; this it then did when it took away the nation and the place, and scattered into captivity those who survived the war.

Now, therefore, let us lift up the eyes of our mind and the prospect of faith. For what the prophet there saw in the vision of the night—one like a Son of Man coming in the clouds, after that terrible, wonderful, and exceedingly strong beast had devoured and crushed—this is what the evangelists here recount: that this true Son of Man came and was made manifest in Israel, 582 and that he made the beginning of his coming with John’s baptism, after the great power of the Roman Empire had subjected to itself the kingdom of the Jewish nation and crushed it into tetrarchies, as has already been said.

“For,” says the Apostle Peter, “beginning [Col. 1351D] after the baptism which John preached, Jesus of Nazareth—how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power” (Acts X [printed XV]), etc., as far as: “For he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead; to him all the prophets bear testimony, that all who believe in him receive remission of sins through his name” (ibid.). Therefore, beginning his work with John’s baptism, he who until then had lain hidden, dwelling with his parents at Nazareth and subject to them—how far did he proceed? “He came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him, and he gave him power and honor and a kingdom” (Dan. VII), etc. “He is,” says Peter, as has just been quoted, [Col. 1352A] “the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead”; and, as David says: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor, and hast set him over the works of thy hands; thou hast subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII).

This is what I have undertaken to discuss in the present work: the glory and honor of the Son of Man, concerning whom “a good word is above the best gift” (Ecclus. XVIII; Jas. I). He himself, desiring this, says to the beloved soul: “Thou who dwellest in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear thy voice” (Cant. VIII).—“The Word of the Lord came,” says the already mentioned evangelist Luke, “upon John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness” (Luke III). And this same John, in another evangelist, declares what had been said to him, or for what purpose the Word of the Lord had come upon him, in this manner: [Col. 1352B] “And I did not know him; but in order that he might be made manifest in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water” (John I). Again: “And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (ibid.).

From the preceding things narrated by evangelical Scripture, it is sufficiently clear that John did not know him—in the sense in which the faces of people are mutually known, or can be known, by those who either live together or have at some time looked upon one another. For Jesus, still a small child, not yet two years old, fled into Egypt; and John, a boy of unknown age but nevertheless still in tender years, withdrew into the wilderness. Therefore, he did not know him by his face, although in spirit he could have known that he had already come; through whose action he leaped for joy, enclosed in his mother’s womb (Luke I).

But “that he might be made manifest,” he says, “in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water”—and preaching is understood. Matthew first expresses this here: “John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, and saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” This preaching of his prepared the way for this Son of Man to be manifested in Israel and to appear in the clouds of heaven, proceeding, as was mentioned above, “even to the Ancient of Days”; that is, he would choose for himself apostles, of whom it was said through the prophet: “Who are these that fly like [Col. 1352D] clouds?” (Isa. LX). He would have these men as witnesses, would ascend into heaven in their sight (Acts I), and would be preached through the whole world with their testimonies.

And it should be noted that this first forerunner of the Lord, explicitly naming it, preaches the kingdom of heaven. It must be understood that the kingdom of heaven alone is the sole and legitimate kingdom, whereas all kingdoms of the earth were robbery, except the throne of David alone, which was preparatory to this kingdom of heaven. By kingdoms of earth we mean those which existed without God and passed away without hope of the kingdom of heaven. Their chief heads were the lioness and the bear, the leopard, and that unnamed fourth beast, which beasts Daniel saw in the above-mentioned vision (Dan. VII [printed VIV]). By them we understand four principal kingdoms: [Col. 1353A] the first, the Babylonian kingdom, carried the people of God captive; the second, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, under the action of most arrogant Haman, wished utterly to destroy that same people; the third, the kingdom of the Greeks, inflicted upon that people the evils narrated in the books of Maccabees; the fourth, the Roman kingdom, handed over the Son of Man himself to Pontius Pilate through the Jews and cruelly killed his martyrs until the times of Constantine.

What Daniel saw there after those beasts as given, or to be given, to the kingdom of the Son of Man, and what was said to him—“But the saints of the most high God shall receive the kingdom, and shall possess the kingdom for ever and ever and ever” (ibid.)—is the kingdom which John, preaching, announces beforehand: “Repent,” and then at last adds the reason: “For the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”

Here, too, we must not pass over the fact that this is the distinctive proclamation of prophetic grace: wherever you read or hear that the word of the Lord was made to someone, and that holy men are prophets or called prophets because the word of the Lord was made to them. John is the last of them all; the evangelist writes that the word of the Lord came upon him (Luke III), in order that he might come preaching and baptizing, and thus the Son of Man might be manifested in Israel. But the first of them all was Father Abraham, concerning whom it is written: “The word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, saying: Fear not, Abraham; I am thy protector” (Gen. XV); and shortly afterward: “And immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: This man shall not be thy heir, but he that shall come forth from thy womb shall be thy heir,” etc. (ibid.). By these words, assuredly, the advent of this same Son of Man was promised.

Therefore, when he says here, “In those days John the Baptist came,” it must be understood: he came as a witness. Thus another Evangelist declared it sublimely, first saying: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” (John I), and immediately adding: “He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him” (ibid.). He came as a witness not only from the wilderness into all the region of the Jordan, but also from his mother’s womb into the light of this present life. For this reason he was given to righteous old people; for this reason he was conceived in a barren womb; [Col. 1353D] for this reason he was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb; for this reason he was born amid the joy of many and the wonder of very many; for this reason, led by the Holy Spirit, he fled from the world into the wilderness and led an angelic life; and he conducted every part of his life blamelessly, venerable in food and clothing and remarkable in every holiness, so that he might be a fitting witness. In all these ways he came as a witness.

He was a priest and by right ought to have succeeded his priestly father. But rejecting the former insignia of the old priesthood, and knowing well that the law of ceremonies was to be ended in his days, he chose only to preach and to consecrate penitence in himself—a penitence which is the best part of the priestly office. For he knew, like that blessed and righteous Simeon—he knew, I say—and “had received an answer from” the same “Holy Spirit” which had prepared such a man as a beautiful vessel of its grace, [Col. 1354A] that he would “not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ” (Luke II); and that he must seek the king of the kingdom of heaven, not by display or promise of courtly purple, but through the preaching of stern penitence. For “that he might be manifested,” he says, “in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water, and preaching a baptism of repentance” (John I).

Someone may say: Could it not have happened in another way that he should be manifested in Israel, without preaching repentance? To this I say: it indeed could have happened, but of all the ways in which this could be done, this way was the best, more suitable to the matter, and more necessary. For what? Was not the Son of Man come for this? Was not the Lamb of God born for this: that he might undertake penitence for the sins of the entire human race, and, beginning penitence with a fast of forty days, persevere in performing it through very many labors, “unto death, even death on a cross?” (Phil. II).

Was it not through that death that “this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Ps. CXVII), namely: when that stone was rejected, when that Son of Man was cast outside the city and hung upon the cross, and had already yielded up the spirit, his side was opened by a soldier’s lance, “and immediately blood and water came forth” (John XIX)? This was, and is, his baptism, concerning which he himself, long after being baptized with John’s baptism, said: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how am I constrained until it be accomplished?” (Luke XII). With that baptism we were to be baptized, and have been baptized. Hence the Apostle says: “For all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI).

Therefore this mode of manifestation was best and most fitting: “that humility should precede glory” (Prov. XV), and glory follow humility; and that there should be shown beforehand there with what fruit he would consummate the penitence he had undertaken. For it was humility that the Lord came to the baptism of a servant and, among sinners undertaking penitence, he who committed no sin undertook a baptism of repentance. What glory, and of what kind, immediately followed this humility? “Behold,” he says, “the heavens were opened to him, [Col. 1354D] and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” This was both a glorious miracle and a sign of greater glory.

Likewise, the glory of the resurrection was to follow the humility of death, which, as has been said, was the consummation of the penitence undertaken for our sake. When that glory shone forth, the heavens were certainly opened to him; he himself ascended into heaven; and the grace of the Holy Spirit descended not then upon him but upon those baptized in his name who believed in him. Yet in another sense it truly descended upon him, because he is the head and they are his body, upon whom the Holy Spirit descends. Nor does it descend upon them for any other reason than because Christ himself is in them, as [Col. 1355A] the Apostle says: “Christ dwells through faith in our hearts” (Eph. III).

But how did John come to know him so quickly, so as to say to him when he came, in those memorable words from a humble heart: “I ought to be baptized by thee, and dost thou come to me?” For according to John, as was mentioned above, he said—indeed, he said once and again—“And I did not know him” (John I). How, then, did he know him so quickly? The brief answer is that he knew him by the power of the prophetic Spirit, certainly because he wished to be known, since the time had now come for him to be known.

The Apostle speaks of that power of the prophetic Spirit: “If all prophesy, and an unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; even the hidden things of his heart are made manifest, [Col. 1355B] and thus, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you” (I Cor. XIV). He says this in praise of prophetic grace: that “the hidden things of another’s heart are manifest” to it. John was a prophet, and had already received prophetic grace from his mother’s womb; he had been filled with the prophetic Spirit.

But, to add this also: what other Word of the Lord had come upon John, son of Zacharias, in the wilderness, as Luke recalls, except that Word itself which had been made flesh from the womb of the Virgin Mary? Was the Word that had come upon John so that he might come and make manifest in Israel the man assumed, or the flesh which it had assumed, not to show him quickly the one whom he sought and for whose manifestation he had come in obedience to the Word?

Therefore, since the power of the prophetic Spirit is, as has been said, “to make manifest the hidden things of the heart” (ibid.), even of one unwilling, how much more ought the hidden things of the heart of the Lord Jesus to have been made manifest to John, especially when he wished it? Thus John knew, not his mind by his face, but—what is more wonderful—his face by his mind. And the Apostle says that whoever he may be “whose hidden things of heart are thus made manifest, falling upon his face, shall worship God, declaring that God is truly among you” (ibid.). But the Lord Jesus, whose role is not to worship but to be worshipped—how did he honor that grace, the prophetic grace, to which the hidden things of his heart had been made manifest, so that John could say, “I ought to be baptized by thee,” or, according to [Col. 1355D] John, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I)?

And how did he honor that grace? Namely, by declaring that God, the Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, and a more-than-prophetic Spirit were truly in John’s mind. For, where it was fitting, he said: “But what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee. Amen I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI), etc., as far as: “And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (ibid.).

But where was fulfilled for this same John what he said: “I ought to be baptized by thee”? [Col. 1356A] For it must truly be weighed in the balance of reason that a prophet of truth, a man of such merit, an angel of such great proclamation, said this to such and so great a Son of Man, at such a time and for such a reason. Where, then, was it fulfilled for him? Where he was baptized by the Son of Man who came to his baptism. Assuredly, there where the same Lamb of God, whom he pointed out with his finger, bore the sins of the world.

Where was this? Certainly where the Lamb himself was sacrificed, sanctified our doorposts with his blood, and so scourged Pharaoh with his Egyptians (Exod. XII) that he conquered him whom the great plagues of the ten legal commandments had not conquered: Pharaoh not carnal but spiritual, that is, the devil, prince of darkness. Where he led him forth openly, confidently nailing him to the cross (Col. II), and, when struck by the lance, poured out the great sea, the Red Sea—that is, blood and water—from his side. There what John hoped for was fulfilled, and what he knew in saying, “I ought to be baptized by thee”; nor was it fulfilled for John alone, but also for all the saints and elect who had awaited him from the beginning of the world.

And indeed, John could know that he was holy from his mother’s womb, since he had been filled with the Holy Spirit while still in that womb. But because the Lord was near him, as it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. XXXIII); because, I say, the Lord was near him, John knew at close hand, in contrition of heart and humility of spirit, that the Lord alone, born of a virgin, was without sin. He himself, though consecrated by a great gift, had nevertheless been begotten from the union of male and female. He chose, as it were, not to know that holiness and judged it insufficient for himself unless the blood of that Lamb whom he saw and to whom he spoke should be shed for him—the Lamb alone holy, alone undefiled.

And truly, unless that sea had covered our enemies, unless that blood had been shed and that water had flooded forth—the blood of redemption and the water of cleansing—neither John nor he to whom before John it was said, “Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee; and before thou camest forth from the belly, I sanctified thee” (Jer. I), [Col. 1356C] nor any of the saints, would any holiness have sufficed, whoever were called holy; as Aaron, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “And they provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron the holy one of the Lord” (Ps. CV).

For there are many ways in which anything is customarily called holy, lest, when you hear “holy,” you should immediately think it perfect and free from every sin. “For it is written in the law of Moses that every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke II). “Sanctify to me,” says the Lord, “every firstborn which opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of men and of beasts; for all are mine” (Exod. XIII). And in the law concerning the Nazirite it is written: “He shall be holy while the hair of his head grows; all the days of his separation he shall be holy to the Lord” (Num. VI).

John, indeed, was holy in these ways also: as a firstborn, before whom his barren mother had borne none; and likewise as a Nazirite, as the angel says: “He shall drink neither wine [Col. 1357A] nor strong drink” (Luke I). But will every such holy person, holy because he is a firstborn, be thought free from sin? Or will a Nazirite—because he does not drink strong drink or wine and no razor comes upon his head, whether Samson or another such person—therefore possess perfected holiness?

Nevertheless, according to that mode of holiness which the infusion of the Holy Spirit effects, “among those born of women none has arisen holier than John” (Matt. XI). But he nonetheless needed the baptism of Jesus Christ, the Holy of Holies—that is, the shedding of his blood or his death—and therefore said in true humility: “I ought to be baptized by thee.”

Now see how fitting it was for this holy man, this firstborn, this Nazirite, to be clothed as the evangelist reports, saying: “John himself had a garment of camel’s hair”; and to be praised by the Lord saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments?” (ibid.), where “no” is understood, and it follows: “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (ibid.).

Truly, such a dress was fitting for him: a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt about his loins, as for Elijah, concerning whom likewise it is written: “A hairy man, girded with a leather belt about his loins” (IV Kings I). For the character of each was such, and their zeal stern, and their life such as did not indulge itself by becoming lax and luxuriating in flowing pleasures.

The present Scripture at once testifies this concerning John: he did not flatter sinners gently. For, “seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said: ‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not wish to say within yourselves: We have Abraham as our father. For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham. For now the axe has been laid to the root of the tree. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire.’”

Behold, truly a man not clothed in soft garments, since his speech is far harsher than the camel’s hair with which he was clothed. Thus he could not be in kings’ houses; rather, in the house of King Herod and Queen Herodias he was beheaded because of such words—words [Col. 1357D] of truth—by which, himself not soft, he offended too severely the soft ears of sinners, eager for flattery, in rebuking them.

In Luke, the sense and almost the very words are the same, except that here he makes clearer on whose account he chiefly began in this manner, “brood” or “offspring of vipers”: namely, on account of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who were heretics among the Jews. For Pharisees, translated from Hebrew into Latin, means “separated,” because they put forward the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they called *deuteroses* [secondary traditions]; hence they were called separated from the people, as though by righteousness. Sadducees means “the righteous.” For they claimed for themselves what they were not. They denied the resurrection of the body and taught that the soul perishes with the body. These received only the five books of the Law, rejecting the prophecies of the prophets.

Therefore, when Luke says: “He said then to the crowds who came out to be baptized by him: ‘Offspring of vipers’” (Luke III), while Matthew, after first saying, “Then Jerusalem and all Judaea and all the region about the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins,” only then begins: “But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: ‘Brood of vipers,’” it is clear that he rebukes the entire nation, indeed, for its raging wickedness, but not the whole nation equally: namely, because the Jews, envying and biting one another, were to be consumed by one another. Yet the Pharisees and Sadducees above all would be the authors or cause of so great an evil for themselves and of the coming wrath, [Col. 1358B] so that everyone who knew how, or was able, to escape it ought to be rare enough to be a marvel.

Nor was he alone or first in thus denouncing them. Moses before him, among other things, said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. XXXII). Is it less to say “the gall of dragons” or “the venom of asps” than “brood” or “offspring of vipers”?

We might suppose that the Pharisees to whom he said these and other things had come to him wishing to receive baptism, since the evangelist says: “But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism.” Yet this is contradicted by what another evangelist more clearly suggests: that they had come to lay traps. “The Jews,” he says, “sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him: ‘Who art thou?’ And when at length he answered the questioners: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said’” (John I; Isa. XL), [Col. 1358C] after this answer of his he immediately adds: “And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees” (ibid.). After this statement, it follows: “And they questioned him and said to him: Why then dost thou baptize, if thou art neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” (ibid.).

From this, Matthew’s statement is better understood: “Seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism”—that is, they had come not to be baptized themselves, but to slander the one baptizing. This is especially so since another evangelist also says: “And all the people hearing, and the publicans, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism. But the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God’s counsel within themselves, not having been baptized by him” (Luke VII).

What was that counsel of God, and what sort of counsel, which the Pharisees rejected? Certainly, to repent and to produce fruits worthy of repentance. But those Pharisees trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others, as the truth of the Gospel testifies in appropriate passages. Hence in Luke it must be carefully observed that “the crowds asked, saying: ‘What then shall we do?’ The publicans coming to be baptized asked and said: ‘Teacher, what shall we do?’ The soldiers also asked, saying: ‘And what shall we do?’” (Luke III).

The crowds asked; the publicans asked; the soldiers also asked, saying, “What shall we do?” But nowhere do we read that the Pharisees asked and said, “What shall we do?” It is thus clear what and what sort of counsel of God it was, and how the Pharisees rejected God’s counsel by not being baptized with John’s baptism: 585 namely, because they were proud, trusting in themselves as righteous (Luke III), “wishing to establish their own righteousness and not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X). Hence, with great hauteur, they are recorded as rebuking Christ, the teacher of piety and the Son of the Father of mercies, saying to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners?” (Matt. IX).

But he whom “thou, O Lord, hast instructed and taught out of thy law” (Ps. XCIII) desires this: to know how to repent; he desires to be able to produce fruits worthy of repentance. He knows, he confesses, that there is no righteousness, that every righteousness from works is vain unless it has testimony from faith in this Son of Man, Jesus Christ. Unless his blood, flowing with water from his side, as was said above, had cleansed all the righteous, all righteousnesses would be unclean and filthy, according to that truthful confession of Isaiah, the righteous and to-be-justified prophet: “We have all become as unclean persons, and all our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV).

But they, falsely righteous and truly sinners, had as the shield of their heart, lest they should know this righteousness, the father of their flesh, Abraham—as though Abraham’s flesh, because they had sprung from it, could suffice for their righteousness. Therefore, after he had said, “Therefore produce fruit [Col. 1359C] worthy of repentance,” he added and said: “And do not wish to say within yourselves: We have Abraham as our father. For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham. For now the axe has been laid to the roots of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire.”

As he says this, we fittingly recall that prophetic saying from the mouth of Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord. For he shall be like a tamarisk in the wilderness, and shall not see when good comes; but he shall dwell in dryness in the wilderness, in a salt land and uninhabitable. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be [Col. 1359D] his confidence; and he shall be like a tree transplanted beside waters, which sends out its roots toward moisture, and shall not fear when heat comes. And its leaf shall be green, and in the time of drought it shall not”
nor will it be anxious, nor will it ever cease to bear fruit” (Ps. 1). What else, I ask, is it to wish to say within themselves, “We have Abraham as our father,” or “Abraham is our father,” and to say this against the Lord, than to trust in a human being and make flesh their arm, so that their heart departs from the Lord? For precisely in order to depart from the Lord in their hearts—or rather, in order to ensnare the Lord in his speech—they are sometimes recorded as saying: “Abraham is our father” (John 8); “We were not born of fornication” (ibid.); likewise, “We are Abraham’s seed” (ibid.); [Col. 1360A] and, “But we are Moses’ disciples” (John 9). Is this not trusting in a human being and making flesh one’s arm? To rely on Moses and on Abraham’s flesh, to despise God’s counsel, and to boast against the Son of God—who alone is the glory of Abraham and of Moses; without him Moses is without glory, and Abraham is nothing but dust and ashes.

“Therefore,” he says, “do not wish to say this within yourselves.” For everyone who boasts in flesh against God’s counsel, so as not to produce fruits worthy of repentance, is accursed. Such a man is accursed like Canaan, concerning whom his father pronounced this curse: “He shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9). Indeed, such a person is like that same Canaan: he is a Canaanite and not a Jew. For the Lord says to Jerusalem through Ezekiel:

[Col. 1360B] “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16).

Such a person, I say, is not like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps. 51), but like a tamarisk in the desert, in a salty and uninhabitable land. This tree is, of course, named from bitterness, for its taste is exceedingly bitter; and it grows in solitude and stony ground. “Already,” he says, “the axe has been laid to the root” of trees of this kind, so that every tree “which does not bear good fruit” may be cut down and cast “into the fire,” whether it is an olive tree or a tamarisk. For even if it has grown from the root of the good olive, whether it be a wild olive or a tamarisk, it has been cut off because of barrenness, because of unbelief. Hence the Apostle says:

> “For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you. [Col. 1360C] See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off” (Rom. 11).

This he said concerning the invisible cutting off by which the unbeliever is cast out of God’s kingdom, cut down by the axe of divine judgment. Yet there was also another cutting off of those to whom, or on account of whom, he said, “Do not wish to say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’” and so forth: namely, that by which they were also to be cut off bodily and uprooted from their land by a visible axe—that is, by the Roman hand. Of this the Psalmist had foretold:

> “As in a forest of trees, with axes they cut down its gates together; with axe and adze they cast it down; they burned your sanctuary with fire,” etc. (Ps. 73).

[Col. 1360D] Moreover, what does he mean when he says, “For I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones”? What stones, or what sort of stones, did he see or point out with his finger? For he did not merely say, “from stones,” but significantly said, “from these stones”—a pronoun which we commonly use when we point with a finger, or can point, to the very things about which we are speaking.

The true sense, indeed, is that by the stones the Gentiles are rightly understood, who worshipped stone images, and from whom we too have been—or are being—raised up as children of Abraham through faith in Jesus Christ. Yet no such stones, no such people, are recorded as having been present or as having come to John at the Jordan. What stones, then, did he see or point out at the Jordan? Do you suppose they were those which Joshua took from the Jordan,

[Col. 1361A] and those which, at the Lord’s command, he placed in the channel of the Jordan?

> “Choose,” says the Lord, “twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the Jordan’s channel, where the feet of the priests stood, twelve very hard stones. You shall place them in the place of encampment where you pitch your tents this night.” Now the children of Israel did as Joshua commanded them, carrying twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan’s channel, as the Lord had commanded him, according to the number of the children of Israel, as far as the place where they encamped; and there they placed them. Joshua also placed another twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan’s channel where the priests bearing the ark of the covenant stood; and they are there to this present day (Josh. 4).

Concerning this and the other matters, [Col. 1361B] the Apostle’s authority establishes that “all these things happened to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10). Since this is so, are not those stones spiritually for us the prophets and apostles—living stones, great stones—who bear our faith as a foundation and continually awaken in us the necessary remembrance, through deeds and words, of the Lord’s works?

For why was this commanded by the Lord concerning those stones, and why was it done?

> “When,” he says, “your children ask you tomorrow, saying, ‘What do these stones mean?’ you shall answer them: ‘The waters of the Jordan failed before the ark of the covenant of the Lord our God as it crossed through it. Therefore these stones were set as a memorial for the children of Israel forever’” (Josh. 4).

Nothing is truer than that these stones—namely, the prophets and apostles, signified by those stones—

[Col. 1361C] were set as a memorial for us forever. If Christ’s Apostle truly said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), when he was speaking of the inanimate rock from which the people drank, how can Christ’s forerunner fail truly to say that these stones, which Joshua placed as a memorial at the Lord’s command, are the prophets and apostles? Some of them—the prophets—he placed long ago; others—the apostles—he was without doubt about to place immediately thereafter (Eph. 4).

The prophets, indeed, because they contain more profound or obscure mysteries, lie hidden as though beneath waters in the middle of the Jordan’s channel. But the apostles, because they testify with unveiled and open face to the works of the Savior, stand, as it were, at Gilgal—which is interpreted “revelation”—always exposed beneath the open sky to the sight of all.

[Col. 1361D] Therefore he says, “Do not begin to say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones.” That is: do not argue that you have no need of repentance or fruits of repentance, or that the kingdom of heaven belongs to you by inheritance because you are Abraham’s children according to the flesh. For Abraham’s flesh alone has no greater power to attain the kingdom of heaven than these stones. Indeed, many born of Abraham’s flesh are children of the devil; but through the word of those whom these stones figuratively represent, many will be born who are truly Abraham’s children, truly God’s children.

For faith alone makes children of Abraham; flesh alone profits nothing (John 6). And every person of this sort is blessed, according to the prophet [Col. 1362A] mentioned above, because he trusts not in a human being but in the Lord—the Lord in whom Abraham himself trusted, though Abraham was not God but a human being. Such a person does not make Abraham’s flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord; rather, the Lord is his confidence. Therefore he will not be like a tamarisk in the desert, nor dwell in dryness in a salty and uninhabitable land; but he will be like a tree transplanted beside waters, sending out its roots toward moisture, so that it may never cease to produce fruits worthy of repentance.

Meanwhile, while he was speaking these and similar things to the crowds—things which the other Evangelists also do not pass over—this most loving forerunner of the Lord, possessing prophetic knowledge, did not fail to know that it was not assigned to his time or office to preach to all nations that the one whom he preceded, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2), had himself been born from the Virgin beyond the ordinary nature of humanity.

[Col. 1362B] As one truly instructed in the spirit of humility, he humbly confesses this and attributes it to his own unworthiness. After saying beforehand, “I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance; but he who is coming after me is stronger than I,” he immediately adds, “I am not worthy to carry his sandals; he himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”

By the sandals, since they are made from the skins of dead animals, is signified the humanity of the same Son of Man, Jesus Christ, in which he was mortal and capable of suffering. Hence the saying: “I shall extend my sandal into Idumea” (Ps. 107), that is, “I shall make known to the Gentiles the mystery of my incarnation.” This was to be done through the apostles.

[Col. 1362C] John himself was not to live until the time when the apostles bore the Lord’s sandals in this manner—that is, when they began publicly to preach, with accompanying signs, that Jesus Christ, God and man, was born of the Virgin: because “the Word was God in the beginning with God, and the Word was made flesh” (John 1); and, as the angel said to Joseph, “That which is born in the blessed Virgin is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

Therefore, when he says, “But he who is coming after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry,” it is easy to see how gladly he would have undertaken a human being’s office, and with what love he would have gone on to announce and declare this glory of the Son of God, the Son of Man, with those heavens (Ps. 18).

[Col. 1362D] By thinking thus of himself and judging himself so unworthy, he observed the rule of true humility. For he did not consider that he alone was the Lord’s forerunner, indeed also the Lord’s angel, as the prophetic Spirit had foretold of him in Malachi (Mal. 3). Rather, he considered that there would be heavens who, as has already been said, by bearing Jesus Christ’s sandals would declare his glory as God.

This is the rule which the Apostle briefly prescribes to the Philippians in these words:

> “Do nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility esteem one another as superior. Let each person consider not what is his own, but what belongs to others” (Phil. 2).

He, I say, judging thus, considering not what was his own but what belonged to others, and regarding the apostles as to be his superiors,

[Col. 1363A] observed the rule of holy and true humility, lowering himself as though he were less than them all. But did the Lord of judgment judge him so? By no means. Rather: “Amen, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11). Therefore none of all those who bore the Lord’s sandals—who in their own time preached by public proclamation, with accompanying signs, the Lord’s Incarnation from the Virgin—is greater than you, O John the Baptist.

Moreover, the strength intended in his saying, “He who is coming after me is stronger than I,” he does not actually express—marvelously, because it cannot be expressed and is ineffable—but indicates it briefly when he says:

[Col. 1363B] “His winnowing fan is in his own hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his own threshing floor, and gather his own wheat into the barn; but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

How great, I ask, is this strength: to have his winnowing fan in his own hand! For he did not even say, “whose winnowing fan is in the hand of God.” Similar is what we read in Isaiah: “His dominion is upon his shoulder,” or, “The rule has come to be upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9). Neither does this man say, “whose winnowing fan is in God’s hand,” nor did that one say, “his dominion,” or “his rule,” “has come to be upon God’s shoulder.” Rather, so that you may observe that he is sufficient unto himself in his own strength, this one says, “whose winnowing fan is in his own hand,” and that one asserts that “his rule has come to be upon his own shoulder.”

[Col. 1363C] Nor does this speaker say, “He will thoroughly cleanse the Lord’s threshing floor and gather the Lord’s—or God’s—wheat into the barn.” Rather, he says, “He will thoroughly cleanse his own threshing floor, and gather his own wheat.” Therefore he is Lord of the threshing floor and owner of all the wheat; he is himself the most mighty God, whose winnowing fan it is and whose own hand suffices for winnowing, just as his own shoulder is sufficient for bearing dominion or rule, and is fully strong without the resources of another.

Therefore he is God—God, I say—and he himself is the almighty Lord, who requires no one’s help. What shall we say to the strong? What shall we say to the proud? Surely that they themselves are chaff, while the humble and those who fear the Lord are wheat. [Col. 1363D] But the Lord’s Word—the incarnate Word, the Word abiding fully and dwelling in the breast, breathing from the mouth of this Son of Man—will be and is to them, by comparison, like a violent wind, which will exterminate all the reprobate and proud far more easily than a violent breeze or wind can remove any chaff, however strong, from someone’s threshing floor.

[Col. 1364A] “The wind,” the Lord himself says through the prophet, “will carry them all away; the breeze will take them up” (Isa. 57). Which persons, if not all those strong with deceptive strength, concerning whom he had already said: “When you cry out, let your gathered company deliver you” (ibid.)? He had also said beforehand to them, “You poured out a drink offering; you offered sacrifice” (Isa. 40). Therefore the wind, he says, will carry them all away—understood to mean those wickedly strong, visible or invisible—and the breeze will take them up. In saying this, he indicates the great strength of the Godhead and its great strength over against the weakness of every creature.

There are many sayings in Scripture [587] concerning a human being, according to the image of one who blows: “The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40), because the Spirit of God has blown [Col. 1364B] upon it. And in Job: “I have seen,” says Eliphaz the Temanite, “those who work iniquity, sow sufferings, and reap them, perish by the blast of God and be consumed by the breath of his wrath” (Job 4). These and similar passages are intended by the holy Spirit of sacred Scripture to make us recognize the ease of divine omnipotence: it is exceedingly easy for God quickly to cast down whatever seemed strongly to stand against his power.

[Col. 1364C] In the same place in Isaiah, where he had said what has already been quoted—“The wind carries them all away; the breeze takes them up” (Isa. 57)—he later added: “For my spirit shall go forth from before my face, and I shall make breath” (ibid.). The reading is frequent, but the experience is very rare in this present life: that someone whom the Godhead deigns to admit to such experience, by touching his breast or lips in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, should be affected in this way by a sensible touch. Blessed Pope Gregory understands this touch in the passage where the Lord, speaking to Elijah, says:

> “After the wind, an earthquake: the Lord was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake, fire: the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19)—and there the Lord is.

Indeed, the subtlety of the Godhead surpasses every sense not only of the body but also of the soul; yet when he wills, he affects not only the soul but even the body sensibly by his touch. This touch, when he wills, is sweet; and when he wills, it is exceedingly terrible. Thus whoever has felt it has scarcely any need thereafter to be taught in words [Col. 1364D] what a truly most mighty God, the God of spirits, he is; nor does such a person wholly fail to know—though it cannot at all be spoken—what that trembling is like by which even the holy angels are said to tremble before the Lord’s majesty.

## Book Three

[Col. 1363]

[Col. 1363D] “All who thirst,” says the Holy Spirit, “come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat” (Isa. 55). In the present passage the waters are the Scriptures, in which the mysteries of spiritual graces are contained, [Col. 1364D] as also there: “Drink water from your own cistern, and streams from your own well. Let your springs flow forth abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5). These waters are the Lord’s waters, and whoever buys [Col. 1365A] them, they become his without ceasing to be the Lord’s. What, I ask, is the reason why, when He has invited all who thirst to the Lord’s waters, He especially invites to buy those who have no silver? For He says: “And you who have no silver, hasten, buy.” Certainly, in every earthly transaction those who have, or seem to have, silver are more usually invited to buy. But this transaction is altogether heavenly, altogether spiritual. What, then, is it not to have silver, except not to put confidence in secular philosophy or in the cleverness of speech? For in the case of those who do not possess such silver, humble self-awareness itself is a great price of purchase. Such was Moses when he said to God: “I beseech thee, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before, and since thou hast spoken to thy servant [Col. 1365B] I am more impeded and slow of tongue” (Exod. 4). And the Wise Man speaks in the Proverbs: “I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me; I have not learned wisdom, and I do not know the knowledge of the holy ones” (Prov. 30).

Why then, O rival, do you mock? Why, detractor, do you tear me to pieces? I confess that I have heard your teachers (*catygetas* [*cathegetas*]), all of them wise and skilful in mystical discourse; and I possess no riches of such silver whatsoever. And if I have learned anything from secular philosophers, it does not count for me as riches or as silver coins. But was I therefore to despair of these waters? On the contrary, I was rather to hope, since among all who know, I hear that those who have no silver are especially invited to buy. Mock as much as you please, though you wish to read my writings only in order to lie in wait for them; and, if you please, say even this: “How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?” (John 7). For if we share the reproach of Him against whom this was said, we shall also share His glory and honour.

Therefore the present bitterness of the belly, resulting from eating the book, must be disregarded; for he who devoured it says: “It was in my mouth like sweet honey, and when I had devoured it my belly became bitter” (Rev. 10). We must proceed, once the journey has been begun, in God’s work and in the purpose signified by the title prefixed to the work concerning the glory and honour of the Son of Man.

“I indeed,” says John, “baptize thee in water” (John 1). What reason, or what sort of reason, is there for being baptized or baptizing in water? It was God’s counsel that baptism should be in [Col. 1365D] water, as another Evangelist indicates: “But the Pharisees,” he says, “and the lawyers rejected God’s counsel against themselves, not having been baptized with John’s baptism” (Luke 7). What, therefore, is the rationale of such a counsel of God, a knowledge of which may profit us?
