His “judgments,” indeed, “are incomprehensible and His ways unsearchable,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 11); yet these things and others like them do not forbid us to be His praisers or to desire knowledge of God’s ways. They merely forbid us to be excessive searchers into majesty (Prov. 25). We ask, therefore, what reason such a counsel of God has—not by searching too deeply, but by desiring to praise God’s majesty; and as “we know in part and prophesy in part” concerning other things (1 Cor. 13), so concerning this also let us rejoice that, although we do not know it perfectly, something gleams forth in part by which we may be delighted.

What is that? Surely, God wisely ordered by such a counsel that the human creature should be restored to its proper order. For man had exalted himself too highly above himself, because he wished to be like God, according to that false whisper of the serpent: “Eat, and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). Many men descended from the first man, imitating that swelling pride, wished to be called gods. Some of them, indeed, after their death were regarded as gods through the foolish error of men; but Caesar Augustus, in whose time this Son, Jesus Christ, was born, was not afraid to be regarded as a god even while living. Hence Flaccus, flattering him, says:

[Col. 1366B]

> To thee, present among us, we render ripe honours,  
> And set up altars by which men must swear in thy name.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book II, epistle 1.)

This was the first height of our heart: that human beings wished to be like gods. And this is Adam’s sin, “in whom,” says the Apostle, “all sinned” (Rom. 5). Now the human condition, or the beginning of the human condition, is lower not only than God the Creator but even than a creature of God—indeed, to state it more plainly, lower not only than God but even than the element of water. For God formed man from the mud of the earth; and that element was and is lower than the element of water, and lay hidden beneath it, until God said: “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, [Col. 1366C] and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1).

Greatly, therefore, had the earth swelled and departed from its order when earthly man desired to be like the Most High. He had to be restored to order and taught to know what sort of creature he was, and, as a testimony to that confession, to be submerged beneath the element of water—an element than which the earth is heavier and more sluggish, from which man took his beginning and which, as has already been said, lay altogether concealed beneath the waters at the beginning. It is of great importance in the logic of justice to remember this condition, to renounce diabolical pride, to press the body down beneath the water, and thereafter to remember that, because of pride, God said to man: “For you are dust, and unto dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

Accordingly, one must carefully observe that “when [Col. 1366D] Jesus came from Galilee to John at the Jordan to be baptized by him, John forbade Him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by Thee, and dost Thou come to me?’ But He answered and said to him: ‘Permit it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.’” For He who was truly meek and lowly in heart considered that, although He was the Holy of holies and had absolutely no sin, He nevertheless possessed a body taken from the earth; and that it belonged to righteousness for Him to show in Himself the remedy of humility which He had come to teach, by submitting to water the flesh He had assumed from us—a flesh which, in Adam, had aspired to exalt itself into likeness with the Creator of all. “And thus,” He says, “it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.”

John considered that He had been conceived of the Holy Spirit, and not without reason judged that this was sufficient for His complete righteousness. But He did not contradict John when he said, “I ought to be baptized by Thee”; nevertheless, so that humility might receive its full satisfaction, He wished also to signify in His own bodily condition how far man is beneath God. He did so by subjecting to water His body, which has its foundation in earthly matter and above which water is and was superior at the beginning. Whoever do not imitate Him in willingly descending shall receive the penalty of descending unwillingly. For it is written: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 62). They rejected God’s counsel, but it will not be without consequence for them to reject God’s judgment.

This was already one testimony of water that He was truly meek and [Col. 1367B] lowly in heart. Another witness to the same gentleness was added: namely, the form of a dove. “For he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon Him. And I,” says John, “saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1). A splendid glory, and the glorious honour of the Son of God, the Son of Man: while He submits Himself to the waters, the heavens are opened to Him, and the Holy Spirit descends upon Him in visible form, while at the same time a voice is heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 12).

Yet in all these things glory was not already consummated; rather, this was the beginning of glory. Its end would later be like this beginning: when, baptized with that baptism of which He said, “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I constrained until it be accomplished” (ibid.), He should immediately rise from the tomb in the ascent of resurrection; the heavens should be opened to Him so that He might enter into His glory; and from there He should send the Holy Spirit to His disciples, the Father saying to Him: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109).

He therefore truly says, “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness,” because, in likeness to the things that were being done there, it was afterwards to come about that He would die “for our offences and rise again for our justification” (Rom. 4). Although this same mystery could have been celebrated in any other waters—for example, “at Aenon near Salim” (John 3), where John is afterwards said to have baptized because there were many waters there—nevertheless it is more pleasing, and gives greater delight, that this occurred in the Jordan waters. For what reason? Clearly, because a sign or figure of these things had long ago shone forth in those same waters.

For that river, the Jordan, began to be memorable when Moses had died and Joshua had succeeded him: its waters were divided, and it afforded the children of Israel passage through its bed, while the priests carrying the ark of the Lord’s covenant stood on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan. “And the children of Israel,” Scripture says, “carried from the bed of the Jordan twelve stones, as the Lord had commanded, according to the number of the children of Israel, to the place where they encamped; and there they set them. Joshua also set another twelve stones in the bed of the Jordan, where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there unto this [Col. 1368A] present day” (Josh. 4).

We understand those twice-twelve stones to be the prophets and apostles. “All the prophets,” says the Lord, “and the law prophesied until John” (Matt. 11). The twelve stones, therefore, were rightly placed in the bed of the Jordan: placed, I say, not carried across; nor did they cross the Jordan, because the prophets prophesied—or ought to have prophesied—Christ as one who was to come only as far as John’s baptism. But beginning with John’s baptism, He chose twelve apostles and lost none of them. “And He commanded us,” says Peter, “after He rose from the dead, to preach to the people and testify that He was the one appointed by God as judge of living and dead; to Him all the prophets bear witness” (Acts 10). Thus “they rightly carried twelve other stones from the midst of the Jordan to the place where they encamped, and set them there.”

Joshua, whose name is interpreted “Saviour,” who succeeded Moses and brought the children of Israel into the land of promise—something Moses did not do—is this Son of Man Himself. He caused the Gospel to succeed the Mosaic law, and through it opened the kingdom of heaven to those believing in Him. The priests who stood in the midst of the Jordan, so that all things might be fulfilled and until the hastening people had crossed over, are understood more fittingly as none other than this same Son of Man, the first priest of the new priesthood, and John, the last priest of the old priesthood, or the end of the law and prophets.

Therefore, although, as has been said, the Lord, baptized with John’s baptism in any other waters, might have signified the sacrament of His own baptism, it is rightly more pleasing, and more pertains to the honour of the Scriptures, that He was baptized and manifested by that baptism in the Jordan waters. Here there fittingly occurs what the Apostle says when, after saying, “No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5), he adds: “So also Christ did not glorify Himself to become high priest, but He who spoke to Him: ‘Thou art my Son’” (ibid.), and so forth.

Finally, by that preaching of repentance and John’s baptism, the Son of Man Jesus Christ was called and glorified by God to become high priest, as Aaron was—that is, according to what had been prefigured in Aaron. For Aaron was commanded to perform the priesthood only after he had first been washed with water; and he received the priestly garments: linen drawers, a linen tunic, a girdle and robe, an ephod and breastpiece, also a turban and on his forehead a plate of sacred veneration bearing the Tetragrammaton (Exod. 29; Lev. 8), the ineffable name of God. This eighth adornment of the high priest especially signifies that Church and that honour of which we speak, belonging to the Son of Man, of whom the Apostle says: “Wherefore God also exalted Him and gave Him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2), and so forth.

To set down what glory and honour each of the other garments mystically signifies is not the business of the present undertaking, except only this: that what happened to Aaron in figure, when at the beginning of his consecration he was first commanded to be washed with water, happened to this supreme and true priest, who at the beginning of His ministry or priesthood was to be baptized with John’s baptism. The remaining ministries of that old priesthood were figures or shadows of the mysteries of this heavenly and true priesthood; but in great measure the likeness fails. For Aaron and the other priests, because death prevented them from continuing, “had daily need, as the priests first, to offer sacrifices for their own sins, then for those of the people” (Heb. 7). But this One had no such need; rather, He did this once, offering Himself not for His own offences, but for those of the people.

The beginning of the sacrifice or offering by which He offered Himself was the fast which He immediately undertook: “And when He had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards He was hungry” (Matt. 4). Thus, beginning to perform repentance not for His own sins, as has been said, but for the people’s offences, He did not cease to labour, working the work of salvation, in all things “obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

Therefore God, faithful and true, fulfilled what He had spoken. Long ago the people feared to hear the voice of the Lord God: “I will hear,” they said, “the voice of the Lord my God no more, and I will see this great fire no more, lest I die.” And the Lord said to Moses: “They have spoken well in all that they have said. I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren like thee, and I will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (Deut. 18). It is certain that this prophet is this Son of Man.

How did that people ask for Him, or know how to ask? For when Moses had said, “The Lord thy God will raise up for thee a prophet from thy nation and from thy brethren, like me; him thou shalt hear,” he added: “As thou didst ask of the Lord thy God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered” (ibid.). We do not find that the people asked otherwise than as Scripture reports: “But all the people saw the voices and the lamps, and the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking; and terrified and shaken with fear, they stood afar off, saying to Moses: ‘Speak thou to us and we shall hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die’” (Exod. 20).

If, therefore, God accepted these words of the people as a petition for this Lord of the Prophets [the text appears to read *Prophetarum Domini*], as though the people had thus asked, as Moses himself had asked: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send” (Exod. 4), what ought we to understand except the abundance of the grace of Him who answers prayer? Where He is asked even humbly, He is accustomed to give superabundantly. Thus the Apostle says: “Now to Him who is able to do all things superabundantly beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—to Him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, through all generations, for ever and ever. Amen” (Eph. 3).

God, I say, faithful and true, fulfilled here what He had spoken there. And the dove bears witness to this—indeed, the Spirit of God, whom John saw descending like a dove and coming upon Him; and John, as another Evangelist testifies, says: “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1).

How unlike are the forms here and there! Here, the form of a dove; there, voices and lamps—or a very great fire—a smoking mountain, and the sound of a trumpet. Therefore one should not lightly overlook that, in another Evangelist, John the Baptist, after saying, “I baptize in water” (ibid.), added, “But one has stood in the midst of you whom you do not know” (ibid.), and so forth. Suppose that he had in view the already mentioned promise to Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren like thee” (Deut. 18), and that he therefore said, “But one has stood in the midst of you whom you do not know,” so that you may understand it as if he had said:

He whose strength the people could not endure, signified to them under the form of fire, to whom they said: “I will hear the voice of the Lord my God no more, and I will see this great fire no more, lest I die. Speak thou to us and we shall hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (ibid.)—He, I say, having become like Moses in the hidden strength of fiery zeal, that is, a true man as Moses was, stands in your midst as one bearable and approachable, meek and lowly as a dove, not as fire. And He is now raised up from among you for you, such that the Lord may speak to you and you may not die any more than if Moses spoke to you—if you are willing to hear Him. But if you are unwilling to hear, there it was said: “I will be an avenger” (ibid.); and here I say to you that “His winnowing fan is in His hand, and He will thoroughly cleanse His threshing-floor, and gather His wheat into the barn, but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3).

Nowhere does the sacred canonical Scripture report that the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord, gave such a sign of His presence over any of the saints or in any of their works. Who other than this Spirit of the Lord worked through Moses in the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt? Indeed, it was not only the magicians who confessed this, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8); Isaiah also proclaims it thus: “Where is He who brought us up from the sea with the shepherds of His flock? Where is He who put in their midst the Spirit of His Holy One? Who led Moses at the right hand by the arm of His majesty; who divided the waters before them to make for Himself an everlasting name; who led them through the depths, like a horse not stumbling in the desert, like an animal descending into the plain? The Spirit of the Lord was his guide” (Isa. 63).

Thus this Spirit worked through Moses in Israel’s departure from Egypt; and when, on the fiftieth day, He wished to give a sign of His presence or operation, not the form of a dove but the form of fire appeared, so that the people said what was stated above: “I will see this great fire no more, lest I die.” Likewise, when, on the fiftieth day after the resurrection of this Son of Man, He came upon His disciples and wished to give a sign of His presence, not the form of a dove appeared, but “there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire” (Acts 2).

Likewise, He who used to carry Elijah away was undoubtedly this Spirit of the Lord; hence Obadiah says: “And when I have departed from thee, the Spirit of the Lord will carry thee to a place that I do not know” (3 Kings 18). And when He wished to give a sign of the grace He had bestowed upon Elijah, not the form of a dove but the form of fire appeared. “For as they went on and conversed—namely, Elijah and Elisha—behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses divided the two of them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” (4 Kings 2).

Neither here nor there was the substance of the Holy Spirit Himself seen by mortals, nor could it have been seen; but where and how He willed, He gave a fitting sign of His operation or presence. Thus He was nowhere seen over the Lord Himself in the form of fire, and never over any saint in the form of a dove. Why? Clearly because the divine nature, whose fullness dwells bodily in this Son of Man Jesus Christ (Col. 2), is sufficiently ardent in itself, according to the saying: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). Therefore it was expedient for us that His power should be tempered by mercy; and this was fittingly signified by the form of a dove.

But our nature—that is, human nature—is lukewarm in itself, indeed excessively cold, according to the saying: “And because iniquity has abounded” (Rom. 5), “the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24). Therefore it was expedient that human beings should be warmed by God’s good zeal, which zeal was fittingly signified by the form of fire. In no way would I more willingly understand what John also says in Luke: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3), and Isaiah: “When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and washed her blood from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4), than by considering that the two gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by these two expressions: “in the Holy Spirit and fire,” or “in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.”

For this one and same Lord is both Holy Spirit and fire; He is one and the same both a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. He is a spirit “of judgment,” that is, of discernment, because, distinguishing the faithful from the unbelieving, He grants remission of sins through faith: this is the first gift. He is a spirit “of burning” because He afterwards kindles with the fire of good zeal the person cleansed from sins: this is the second gift. By both gifts Christ’s baptism is completed and consummated, together with the water which came forth from His side. Therefore John, after saying of himself, “I baptize you in water,” immediately, in order to declare how much better Christ’s baptism would be than his own, said: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (ibid.).

Before His passion, the Lord Himself used to confirm to His apostles this promise of John—indeed, His own or His Father’s promise. After His resurrection Luke describes Him recalling it in this manner: “And while eating with them, He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, He said, you have heard through my mouth: for John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1).

They had already received a part of that promise, namely the first gift of the Holy Spirit, which is remission of sins. For, standing in their midst on the day He rose, He breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them” (John 20). Nevertheless, while eating with them He commanded them to await the Father’s promise, because the second gift of the same Holy Spirit remained, concerning which He afterwards said: “But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts 1), and so forth.

As He alone was conceived of the Holy Spirit, so He alone baptizes here in the Holy Spirit. For John was indeed filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, but he was not conceived of the Holy Spirit; and therefore he could not baptize in the Holy Spirit. Rather, with the other saints, he received the grace of the Holy Spirit from this One’s fullness, as he himself testifies elsewhere: “And of His fullness we have all received” (John 1).

Finally, what does it mean, or why did a voice come from heaven saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”? (Matt. 17). What, I say, but the same thing as “the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon Him,” and the same thing as “the word,” as Luke recalls, “coming upon John, son of Zachariah” (Luke 3)? For this purpose the word of the Lord came upon John; for this purpose the Holy Spirit descended; for this purpose the Father’s voice was heard from heaven: that a sufficient and lawful testimony might be completed concerning this man—that He was the Christ, that He, and no other, was the Son of God: this poor man, this Jesus of Nazareth, He who was thought to be Joseph’s son.

All this was done as a testimony to this truth, so that the testimony might be established according to divine law; for it is written in the law: “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 19). Hence John the Evangelist says: “And there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5). The person of the Father was heard in the voice which came from heaven; the person of the Holy Spirit descended like a dove when the heavens were opened; the person of the Word was present indeed in the flesh, but was silent, nor did He at that moment speak His own testimony, although elsewhere He says: “I am He who bears testimony of myself” (John 8).

But He bore testimony in John, because, as has been said, “the word of the Lord had come upon John” for the purpose of rendering that testimony. Considering the testimony of these three, He Himself said to His adversaries: “If I bear testimony of myself” (John 5)—where the meaning must be understood as, *if I bear testimony of myself as men commonly bear testimony concerning themselves and commend themselves through empty glory*—“my testimony is not true. There is another who bears testimony of me, and I know that the testimony which He bears of me is true. You sent to John, and he bore testimony to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from man; I have a testimony greater than John” (ibid.).

These and other things He said against their malicious envy. Refusing to accept and pretending not to know the testimony of God—who cannot be deceived in testifying, and whose testimony could be known from manifest works—they sent to John, a man whom they hoped could be deceived. But he was not deceived; rather, he bore testimony to the truth.

They sent to him, hoping that he could be deceived and acting with the desire that he might be deceived, when a question arose between John’s disciples and those Jews concerning purification: “And they came to John and said to him: ‘Rabbi, He who was with thee beyond the Jordan, to whom thou didst bear testimony—behold, He baptizes, and all are coming to Him’” (John 3). They began in this manner so that the flame of envy or jealousy might burn John’s soul, and so that, becoming like them—that is, envious with the envious—he might say something contrary to the truth. But he bore testimony to the truth, saying: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (ibid.), and so forth, down to: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (ibid.).

The greatness of the testimony must reverently be acknowledged both from the form of the dove and from the fact that, when the Father said, “Thou art my beloved Son,” He added, “in whom I am well pleased.” For the form of the dove—that is, the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon Him in the form of a dove—testifies to this: that “in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily,” just as a dove is a whole thing, lacking no part of its body.

And this statement, “in whom I am well pleased,” testifies to this: that this Son is the sole and unique glory of God the Father, and that in this One alone God, the wondrous worker of all marvellous and good things, truly glories. For He made nothing such as this Son: uncreated according to divinity, created and made according to humanity. Before man had been made, He was, as He is now, “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; and in Him,” says the Apostle, “all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all things, and all things subsist in Him” (Col. 1).

Once He was made man, from that time “He is,” says the same Apostle, “the head of the body, the Church; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that He may hold first place in all things, because in Him it pleased all the fullness of divinity to dwell bodily, and through Him to reconcile all things in Him, making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (ibid.). The glorious Father, therefore, rightly says here too, “in whom I am well pleased,” and in the psalm calls Him His glory, saying to Him: “Arise, my glory” (Ps. 107).

Thus far, concerning His manifestation, as far as ability permitted. But once manifested, in what order or manner did He begin to proceed?

## Chapter IV

“Then,” says the Evangelist, “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; and when He had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards He was hungry.” Behold what a wise and beautiful counsel of healing divinity: that He should lead this second man into the wilderness to fast and endure temptations, rather than again into paradise to eat, where He had placed the first man.

Some have doubts about this because what follows says: “The devil took Him into the holy city.” And again: “He took Him onto a high mountain.” But it is truly and without any question rightly understood that He was led into the wilderness by the Holy Spirit: that His own Spirit might lead Him there where the evil spirit would find Him to tempt Him; and that the second man might conquer by the same means by which that evil spirit boasted that he had conquered the first man. For against the first man, our parent, he advanced in three temptations, since he tempted him by gluttony, vainglory, and avarice; and in tempting him, overcame him. But, as has been said, he fell before the second man when tempted in the same ways.

Thus the Lord God Himself, who took the man whom He had formed and placed him in the paradise of delight to cultivate and guard it, and commanded him, saying: “Of every tree of paradise eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 2), and allowed him to be tempted, so that what was in his heart might become manifest to angels and to all succeeding ages—He Himself took this second man, whom He had formed from a virgin womb, or, as another Evangelist wrote, “drove Him out into the wilderness” (Mark 1): “drove Him out,” I say, as one guilty and bearing the guilt of that first man, because “He laid on Him the iniquities of us all” (Isa. 53), so that by fasting He might begin to endure punishment for whatever they sinned in that one man who ate.

It is exceedingly beautiful to compare the first man and the second in this respect: the former was placed in a place of pleasantness and abundance; with the exception of one tree, all the delights of paradise were set before him; yet, amid such and so great an abundance, tempted by gluttony in one matter, he succumbed so easily. But this One was driven out into a place of horror and vast solitude, and a fast of forty days was imposed upon Him. When it was completed, He was hungry; nevertheless, when tempted in that hunger by necessary bread, He did not succumb to temptation. Thus He usefully showed the tempter through His miracles that He was the Son of God—a matter to be discussed more fully later.

This comparison between the second and first man is, I say, exceedingly beautiful. Yet because God “laid on Him the iniquities of us all,” not only that original sin but also actual sins, and because He is that child of whom the prophet foretold: “For Israel is a child, and I loved him” (Hos. 11), “and out of Egypt I called my Son”—a prophetic proclamation which the present Evangelist mentioned above—it is pleasing to explain more fully the mystery of the temptations which this child endured for us. And since there were three temptations, we shall set forth in order from the sacred Scriptures the causes or reasons for each.

Therefore Israel the child, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus, called out of Egypt, after He had dwelt at Nazareth, where He was also brought up, after He had crossed the waters of baptism, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; and “when He had fasted forty days and forty nights,” He too was tempted and was found faithful in three temptations, in order to empty out and abolish the same number and same temptations of His fathers, the children of Israel. They, after being brought out of Egypt and crossing the waters of the Red Sea, were led about through the wilderness for forty years and were tempted, because they tempted and were found unbelieving. That their temptations were the same in number and kind as those endured by this aforementioned child—“Israel the child whom I loved,” says the Lord in the Prophet—must be shown in order through Scripture.

The first temptation concerned bread, as it is written: “The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. And the children of Israel said to them: Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to the full. Why have you brought us out into this wilderness, to kill this whole multitude with hunger? Then the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you” (Exod. 16), etc. This was the temptation not of believers but of unbelievers: not because they asked for bread, but because they asked wrongly and without faith. Hence, with a more sacred understanding preserved, comes the saying: “They tempted God in their hearts, to ask food for their souls; and they spoke wickedly of God. They said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Can he give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” (Ps. 77). Because they tempted him thus, they were therefore tested in the very matter in which they had tested him.

For when the Lord had said, “Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you; let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day,” he added: “that I may test him, whether he will walk in my law or not. But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they used to gather each day.” When they had done this, it was proved in two ways that they did not walk in God’s law. For when it had been said to them, “Let no one leave any of it until morning,” they did not listen; but some of them left it until morning, and it began to swarm with worms and rot. Likewise, when it had been said to them, “It is the Sabbath of the Lord; therefore it will not be found,” nevertheless they went out to gather it, and did not find it. “And the Lord said: How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law?”

Thus that foolish people sinned through this vice, namely through the intemperance of gluttony. And, if you consider rightly, this plague—the vice of gluttony—is an exceedingly great affliction of humankind. From it arise many savage and deadly vices of the flesh; and this iniquity [592] arose from the root of the sin by which the first man, of whom it was said above, bit the forbidden tree.

How did this our child Israel [Col. 1376A] punish and correct this vice in himself? First, “he fasted forty days and forty nights”; then, when he was hungry, he refused to eat at the tempter’s suggestion. “He fasted, I say, forty days and forty nights”; and to afflict him by fasting further or longer would have been excessive severity. For the sacred law, to which God made man deigned to obey in all things, says: “But if the judges see that the one who sinned is deserving of blows, they shall cast him down and have him beaten before themselves. According to the measure of the sin shall be the measure of the blows—yet only so that it does not exceed the number of forty, lest your brother be shamefully torn apart before your eyes” (Deut. 25).

This one and same child, so often mentioned—Christ—was both Judge and, as it were, defendant. Before the judging divinity inherent in him, his true humanity lay prostrate and was beaten by the blows of fasting: not because he had sinned, but because he had taken upon himself the sins of our gluttony. The fast ought not to have been extended further, because, as has already been said, the sacred law commanded that the measure of lashes should not exceed forty. Therefore the glory of one already scourged ought to follow his humiliation—not empty glory, but true glory, the glory of God.

It would have been empty glory had he acted according to the tempter’s suggestion, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (John 2). Perhaps you suppose that he would have manifested his glory if, at the tempter’s word, stones had become bread, just as he later manifested his glory when, at his command, water was changed into wine. But it was not so. “There he made the beginning of signs, and thus manifested his glory” (ibid.); that glory was not empty, but glory with a fruit—which fruit the Evangelist at once presents, saying: “And his disciples believed in him” (ibid.).

Would the treacherous tempter, the ancient adversary, have believed in him if he had changed stones into bread? Someone says: It would have benefited us for faith or for recognizing God’s glory, had we read that this had happened. On the contrary, what we do read benefits us more toward God’s glory: the Son of God deemed it beneath him to share with the devil the testimony of his divinity, and instead answered, “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” And, when the devil had been removed from participation in—or presence at—the refreshment, “angels came and ministered to him.”

For it is written thus in the book of Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God led you forty years through the wilderness, that he might afflict and test you, and that what was turning in your mind might become known: because man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that shall go forth from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8).

The second temptation was the affliction of thirst and lack of water, concerning which it is written: “Therefore the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin, by their stages, according to the word of the Lord, and camped at Rephidim. There was no water there for the people to drink. And they quarreled with Moses, saying: Give us water to drink” (Exod. 17), etc., down to: “And he called the name of that place ‘Temptation,’ because of the quarrel of the children of Israel and because they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?” (ibid.).

Thus, in a remarkable way, the people both tempted and were tested; and, because they tempted, they were justly tested. For Moses testifies in the passage cited above that the Lord tested the people: “The Lord your God,” he says, “that he might afflict and test you, and that what was turning in your mind might become known” (Deut. 8). That there also the people tempted the Lord is sufficiently indicated by this saying: “And he called the name of that place ‘Temptation,’ because they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?”

Over this matter—that is, the lack of water—the people not merely once but on another occasion also tempted and were tested; and Moses and Aaron too fell into that temptation, so that they said: “Hear, rebels and unbelievers: can we bring water for you out of this rock? And the Lord said to them: Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I shall give them.” This was the vice of inquisitiveness: “because they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?” (Num. 20).

How was this child Israel, so often mentioned, tested concerning this vice? “The devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: He commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone. Jesus said to him: It is written [Col. 1377C]: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” This too, like the first answer, is written in the book of Deuteronomy: “You shall not tempt,” Moses says, “the Lord your God” (Deut. 6); and immediately adds, “as you tempted him in the place of temptation” (ibid.). That place is certainly to be understood as no other than the one already mentioned, of which he says: “And he called the name of that place ‘Temptation,’ because they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?” (Exod. 17).

Certainly, when he says here, “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God”; and afterward, “It is written,” he says, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone,” this must not be understood as though he wished to correct the devil and teach him, as if he said: “O devil, do not tempt me, the Lord your God, because Scripture contradicts you and intends to restrain you from this; you say to me, ‘All these things I shall give you, if, falling down, you worship me’; but rather you ought to worship me, the Lord your God, because Scripture says to you, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone.’” Even to suppose this is utterly absurd.

For would God, or the Son of God, deign to be called the devil’s God or Lord? Far be it! It is indeed a great grace for the Lord God, Creator of all, to be willing to be called anyone’s God. Hence, when the Apostle had spoken splendidly at length concerning the faith of the fathers—“By faith,” he says, “Abraham, who is called, obeyed in going out to the place which he would receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Heb. 11), etc.—he then added: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (ibid.). If he is not ashamed to be called even the devil’s God or Lord, what grace or blessedness is expressed in this statement concerning the fathers: “therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God”?

Accordingly, when he says to the devil, “It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone”—when, I say, he says, “It is written”—this is to be understood as addressed to a human being; for indeed whatever the Law says or commands is written not for the devil but for humanity. The sense, therefore, is: Neither I as man, nor any other human being, ought to give ear to you, so as to tempt the Lord his God or, falling down, O devil, worship you; rather, he ought to hear the voice of Scripture saying, “You shall not tempt,” and, “You shall worship the Lord your God alone” [Col. 1378B].

The third temptation was that of the people who, because they had tempted, were rightly to be tested. Aaron too fell into this temptation, so as to act contrary to this word of the Law: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone.” For just as a child is sometimes left to his own will, that, when his master or tutor has been removed, he may reveal through the opportunity of freedom what sort of zeal he possesses, so that same people were left to themselves when Moses went up the mountain. There he remained forty days and forty nights, and no date had been fixed for his return.

Then occurred what Scripture reports: “When the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered against Aaron and said: Arise, make us gods to go before us. For we do not know what has happened to this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 32). Then the people truly fell, and in the form of a calf worshiped the devil. And who has not heard, or who, reading it, has not been able to marvel at how stubborn and how prone to such a fall that people always were?

But this other Israel came, who alone fulfilled the Law, who performed all the commandments of righteousness commanded by the Law. It should therefore be noted that he takes all the testimonies by which he repels the tempter solely from Deuteronomy. For Deuteronomy means “second law”; and he too is called—and is—the other or second Israel, according to that prophetic testimony (which this Evangelist also mentions, and which we have treated in its proper places): “For Israel is a child, and I loved him; and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos. 11).

Therefore this is the other or second Israel, after that Israel, father of the twelve tribes, who first went down into Egypt, and after the Israelite multitude which came up from there; and this second law was especially established for him. For the law of carnal ceremonies was imposed upon that transgressing people Israel, and the other books of Moses are occupied with their ritual. In this book of Deuteronomy, that is, of the second law, almost nothing is treated concerning ceremonies; rather, all is commandments of righteousness, commandments of charity. Almost all these things are spoken familiarly in the singular, containing spiritual mysteries of life and salvation; and Israel is thus addressed as though one man, because here there was truly to be one man [Col. 1379A] who would faithfully and perfectly fulfill everything that a human being owed to God. This is the true Israel, truly upright with God.

For example: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances, which I command you today, that it may be well with you?” (Deut. 10). This one heard and fulfilled well these and similar sayings, which are spoken so familiarly, as if to one person. And, undergoing the same temptations in which that former Israel—the people of Israel—was found unfaithful in the persons of the reprobate and scarcely, only to a small degree, faithful even in the persons of the elect, this one was found faithful (Ecclus. 44), as the present Gospel passage testifies. Thus was fulfilled for him the faithfulness of the covenant which, after saying, “that you may keep what I command you today” (Deut. 28), it immediately indicates by adding, “that it may be well with you” (ibid.).

But what sort of showing by the devil do you suppose that was? How could the devil show a human being all the kingdoms of the world and their glory at once and, as Luke says, “in a moment of time” (Luke 4)? The nature neither of things nor of eyes allows that from any mountain, however high, a human being can see at once and in a moment all the kingdoms of the earth and the glory of all kingdoms. Sacred Scripture remembers nothing of the kind anywhere, except what blessed Pope Gregory reports concerning a man of venerable life, Benedict by name and grace (Dialogues, book 2, chapter 35): while the brothers rested, Benedict diligently kept watch and anticipated the hours of night prayer; standing at a window and praying to the almighty Lord, he suddenly saw a light poured down from above put all the darkness of night to flight and shine with such splendor that this light, radiating amid darkness, surpassed day.

A very wonderful thing followed in this vision: as he later related, even the whole world was brought before his eyes, as though gathered under a single ray of the sun. Yet that event possesses another ground for wonder: as has already been said, to the soul that sees the Creator every creature is narrow; and what is said to have been gathered before that holy man’s eyes was effected by almighty God with the man. Heaven and earth were not contracted, but the mind of the beholder was enlarged; caught up in God, he was able without difficulty to see all that is beneath God.

When Gregory says this, adding also: “Therefore, in that light which shone to the outward eyes, there was an inward light in the mind, which, because it bore the beholder’s mind upward, showed him how narrow all lower things were”—when, I say, he says these things, he plainly maintains that this was a sight of the mind rather than of the eyes. We marvel at and venerate what almighty God did with a human being; but what shall we say of what the devil, the tempter, did with God made man, the Son of God? If any Scripture narrated that he had similarly acted upon any human being, showing that person the entire world in a moment of time, we would not hesitate to call it a showing of spiritual wickedness and a phantom vision. Did the devil dare to attack with his phantasms this man whom he was examining to see whether he was the Son of God? A faithful mind shudders even to think it.

But do not recoil from it, because the greater the tempter’s injury, the more glorious the victor’s patience. Compare such phantasms with the phantasms we endure whenever we are tempted by “everything that is in the world: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). How few of us are there who are not, in some temptation, soothed by the enticement of desire, perhaps even unwillingly? Nor is this surprising: we suffer phantasms inwardly. Yet phantasms of this kind which come from outside or occur outside sometimes not only fail to delight, but are even burdensome to the bodily senses. And if they were brought by the tempter to this Son of Man, they undoubtedly came and went without his sin, so that you may say with the Apostle: “Tempted in all things according to our likeness, yet without sin” (Heb. 4).

“But when Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee; and, leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen’” (Isa. 9). “From that time Jesus began to preach and say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

As long as John preached, Jesus did not undertake the office of public preaching. But after, in John’s imprisonment, the mouth of the prophets and of the Law was closed—for all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John—then at last that which had been prophesied succeeded: the Gospel of Christ shone forth. He had indeed done certain things, already had disciples, and taught them, as the Evangelist John recounts more fully. He had also performed many signs in the presence of his disciples, the beginning of which was the changing of water into wine (John 2). And the same Evangelist says of these that, “when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name” [Col. 1380D], among them Nicodemus: “For no one,” he says, “can do these signs which you do, unless God is with him.” “And John had not yet been put into prison” (John 3). Yet, as has been said, he had not undertaken the public office of preaching, nor had he called the disciples who had begun to come and hear him to leave everything and follow him.

The present Evangelist begins his narrative from Jesus’ withdrawal into Galilee, passing over the words, “when he had heard that John had been handed over.” Beyond the meaning stated above, this too must be considered in this designation of time: by his example he taught what he was to say through his Apostle, that “no offense should be given to anyone” (2 Cor. 6). For those who wished to take offense did take it—especially the Pharisees, who rejected the counsel of God by not being baptized with John’s baptism (Luke 7). They wished it to be thought that something occurred between Jesus and John, and between their disciples, through rivalry and empty glory.

Hence the passage in the Evangelist John: “There arose therefore a question from John’s disciples with the Jews concerning purification. And they came to John and said to him: Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and all are going to him” (John 3). Again, shortly afterward: “When Jesus therefore knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did” (John 4).

Both matters, therefore, were reasonably observed in his beginning to preach only after John had been handed over: namely, that the Gospel might succeed in due order to the Law and Prophets, of which John was the end; and that, so far as depended on him, he might “give no offense to anyone.” But Luke narrates more clearly why, withdrawing into Galilee, he so soon left the city of Nazareth and came to dwell in Capernaum. For they said: “Is not this Joseph’s son?” “And all in the synagogue,” he says, “were filled with anger; and they rose up, drove him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain upon which their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong. But he, passing through the midst of them, went away; and he came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught there” (Luke 4).

“This happened,” he says, “that what had been said through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali,’” etc. The prophet had spoken thus: “In the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, and in the last time the way of the sea beyond the Jordan was made heavy” (Isa. 9). Why did he not write the citation in full? He omitted two principal parts: “in the first time it was lightened, and in the last time it was made heavy.” Why, I say, did he omit these parts? Clearly because it was not the intention or will of the preacher and evangelist that that land, lightened at the first, should be made heavy at the last: that is, that Judaea, illuminated by the preaching and miracles of the Lord present among them, should finally reject the Gospel of him taken up into heaven and judge itself unworthy of eternal life.

It was indeed to happen; and Isaiah, by revelation of the prophetic Spirit, foretold that it would happen thus. Nevertheless, the Lord did not begin to preach with the intention that at the last time—that is, after all the mysteries of our salvation had been completed—Judaea should make its heart heavy and reject the word of faith. Those tears are witnesses; that lamentation is witness, when he saw the city and wept over it, for it was not his will that it should so harden its heart as not to recognize the time of its visitation (Luke 19). This alone was the intention of his preaching: “to give light,” as Zechariah also sang, “to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1).

Rightly, therefore, the discerning Evangelist signified that this alone was his intention, saying, “that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled,” etc. The prophetic Spirit aptly proclaimed, in so great a matter, “the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan,” because it contributed in some measure to the blessedness of so good a message to name the place from which was first heard that which all the saints awaited with such attentiveness. The marvelous eloquence of holy wisdom strives to suggest this in the same prophet, saying: “Lift up a sign to the peoples; behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 62).

Imagine even John himself, who had then been handed over and soon afterward, as was to happen, beheaded, hastening to the underworld and lifting up a sign to all the saints who, from the beginning of the world, had awaited this one in darkness and in the shadow of death, and saying: “Behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard from the land of Zebulun and from the land of Naphtali and from the way of the sea beyond the Jordan—Galilee, that is, beside the Sea of Galilee.”

As has already been said elsewhere, the diligent reader or attentive hearer ought not to look only at that small portion which the Evangelist cites from prophetic testimonies, but also at the chapters connected with the passages he takes up—those preceding and those following. It is as though you ought, by bringing in a lamp, to see what a house is like inside and what its disposition is at its center and around it, if perhaps by design it had been made somewhat dark without windows. And indeed, since brevity was necessary, the Evangelists did not have leisure to write out the full extent of the testimonies. So too, because the work might perhaps become tedious, we have no leisure to pursue everything which he illuminated by brief indication; nevertheless, it is pleasing to pause for a little while over some part of them.

After prefacing, “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9), the same prophet soon says among other things: “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian. For a little child has been born to us; a son has been given to us” (ibid.). The burden, or “yoke of his burden,” of the people who walked or sat in darkness, was sin; “the rod of his shoulder” was sin; “his oppressor” was the devil; “the sceptre of that oppressor” was the right or dominion of death.

How, Lord, did you overcome these things? Surely by a new kind of battle, “as in the day of Midian”—that is, according to the mystical likeness of the battle in which, as we have in the book of Judges, the leader Gideon defeated Midian with three hundred men. For on that day the battle was not fought as other leaders, judges, and kings of Israel fought before or afterward. Rather, dividing the three hundred men into three groups, he gave them trumpets in their hands, empty jars, and lamps within the jars. When they sounded all around the camp in three places and broke the jars, they held the lamps in their left hands and the sounding trumpets in their right, and cried: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Thus all the camp was thrown into confusion; the Lord sent a sword throughout the whole camp, and they cut one another down. Gideon had said to them beforehand: “What you see me do, do likewise” (Judg. 7).

The prophet foretold that, from the time of Gospel preaching, battle should be waged according to the likeness of that battle and the kingdom of the devil, the oppressor, should be overcome. For what reason? “For,” he says, “a little child has been born to us; a son has been given to us.” Before this child was born to us, before this son was given to us, it was not merely permitted but even praiseworthy for kings, priests, prophets, and patriarchs to contend with the sword and to make war with blood, as David did and as the renowned Maccabees did against the nations which, moved by the devil’s spirit, sought to exterminate the Israelite people—so that the word of promise might be emptied and there might be no one from whom this child could be born to us, as the faithful God promised to the fathers and to Abraham, the first believer.

But now [595], because “a child has already been born to us, because a son has been given to us”—a child or son, Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace—what need is there for material weapons? What danger is there if the tree is uprooted, since all its fruit has been taken and safely stored away? Let the manner of battle be changed, and let there be fighting as was done in the days of Midian. Let there be lamps in fragile jars, in earthen vessels: that is, gifts of heavenly graces in the corruptible members of mortal bodies. Let there also be trumpets of the word of God, whose sound terrifies visible and invisible enemies. Let the jars be held in the left hands, the trumpets in the right: that is, let the body be held in the lesser place, and the word of God to be preached in the greater, with care or diligence.

What if the fragile jars of the bodies are broken? Then certainly they will shine all the more brightly with the clearest light of miracles [the printed *flammabit* should read *flammabunt*]; and martyrs, crowned with precious death, will thereafter fight more strongly. That first Gideon did this according to the letter, and said: “What you see me do, do likewise” (Judg. 7). This first Son of Man did it according to the Spirit, and said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

Since battle was thus to be waged, since the material sword was no longer necessary, let us see what soldiers or leaders of the host he chose for himself. “Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. And he said to them: Come after me, and I shall make you become fishers of men. But immediately, leaving their nets, they followed him. And proceeding from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in a boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately, leaving their nets and their father, followed him.”

Just as the sun, by its own sight, not only sees mirrors but also forms its image in them, so that its image shines back from them, so in a certain manner this true sun saw Peter and Andrew, James and John: simple men, having no share at all in darkness. Therefore the light was grasped by them; through faith the image of this true light was formed in their hearts. But that power of darkness was not able to grasp it; bearing dull hearts, they rejected it. For example, they said: “Where did this man get all these things? What is this wisdom given to him, and these works of power which are performed through his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon?” (Matt. 13). “And there,” the Evangelist Mark says, “he could do no work of power, except that he healed a few sick persons by laying his hands upon them; and he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark 6).

And what sort did he find or see these men to be, whose purity of heart and bright faith he penetrated? “He saw them casting a net into the sea,” or “mending their nets; for they were fishermen.” But why did God choose the poor rather than the rich? Indeed, why did he will that those “whom he chose before the foundation of the world, whom he foreknew and predestined to be made conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8), whom he purposed to call, justify, and glorify, should be born or become poor in this world?

Surely it was for their instruction. Awareness of poverty is a great instrument and powerful lesson by which the creature holds fast to, or recognizes, that which before the Creator is most beautiful and entirely just: namely, its proper order. What, or what kind of, proper order? Certainly that order which the Apostle strives to make known to us with a great cry and mighty exclamation, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who first gave to him, and shall be repaid by him? For from him, through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen” (Rom. 11).

This is the lawful order, the necessary order: that the creature be subject to the Creator, knowing and confessing that from him, through him, and in him are all the good things possessed by a blessed human being or a holy angel. And for the recognition or remembrance of this holy truth, as has been said, the retained memory—the furnace (*caminus*)—of former poverty is of great value: the poverty from which the children of Israel were called, and in which Peter and the other apostles were found—unlettered and ordinary men, and moreover poor in worldly resources.

What more need be said? The more gifts of God the saints were to receive, the more they needed awareness of poverty, so that they might bear those same gifts steadily and firmly, founded in the spirit of humility. For “the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord” (1 Sam. 2); but, as blessed Jerome says, the Hebrew has “the afflicted of the earth,” “and he set the world upon them” (ibid.). This affliction is humility, which makes them constant and strong to bear the world.

Finally, what causes one bodily object or material thing to move more slowly and another more quickly when wind blows or a hand moves it, the virtue of humility causes in minds: when spiritual prosperity follows, the mind is not puffed up, because it remains conscious of its former poverty or any former misfortune. The world which the Lord set upon such afflicted persons is his Church, whose governance he entrusted to them. Hence the saying addressed to this Simon Peter: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16). Upon the rock of faith confessed by Peter he built his Church, and entrusted its governance to Peter, to the other apostles, and to those like them.

What, finally, are we to say about the change of name which, as has already been said above, another Evangelist recorded more explicitly, while this one did not pass it over altogether, saying, “Simon, who is called Peter”? What cause or [Col. 1385B] rationale was there for this change? Surely Jesus Christ, the Wisdom of God, would not change a man’s name idly—that is, without cause or reason.

While we inquire about one man, let us also recall another. He who said to this man, “You are Simon son of Joanna; you shall be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter” (John 1), had formerly said to another: “What is your name?” When he answered, “Jacob,” he said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel” (Gen. 32). Apart from these two—one of whom is very well known in the Old Testament, the other in the New—we do not find others in the holy Scriptures whose names God changed, although he assigned names to some, as to Isaac, and enlarged or diminished the names of others, as Abram and Sarai, calling the former Abraham and the latter [Col. 1385C] Sarah.

What, then, was the cause or rationale of these changes of name? One may suppose that, in both cases, the cause of the altered names was an impending alteration of circumstances. In the former case, to whom it was said, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel,” the intended change of affairs was this: “Because if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?” (ibid.). For what else is it to prevail against men than to kill men? From that time, the race of Jacob, or Israel, had not merely permission but even a command to kill sinners—first of all the Canaanites, whom the land rightly ought to vomit forth.

For example: “Go,” the Lord says to Saul, “and strike Amalek, [Col. 1385D] and utterly destroy all that belongs to him. Do not spare him, but kill from man 596 even to woman, and child and nursing infant” (1 Sam. 15). This was not merely permitted, but was commanded so emphatically that, when Saul had spared them, the Lord said to Samuel: “I repent that I have made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words in deed” (ibid.). But in the beginning it was not so: “Whoever kills Cain,” says the same Lord, “shall be punished sevenfold” (Gen. 4).

The answer which the Lord gave to those who said to him, “Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given, and that a wife be dismissed?” (Matt. 19), ought to be given in much the same way if you ask why the Lord commanded men to be killed, saying, “How much more will you prevail against men?” He answered [Col. 1386A] and said: “Moses permitted you to put away your wives because of the hardness of your heart. But from the beginning it was not so. And I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (ibid.).

In the latter case, the intended change of affairs is this: “Put your sword back into its place.” For he had drawn his sword and, striking the servant of the chief priest, had cut off his ear (Matt. 26). If, therefore, as has been said, you ask why the Lord commanded sinners to be killed, and why he said, “How much more will you prevail against men,” the answer should be given in much the same way as concerning “the bill of divorce”: namely, that the Lord commanded this to be done because of hardness of heart, but that from the beginning it was not so.

Whose hardness of [Col. 1386B] heart? Certainly that of such people as the Amalekites or Canaanites, and the rest whose hearts the devil had hardened, so that they not only served the creature rather than the Creator, but also tried by every means either to make the people of Israel—the Creator’s sole worshipper—conform to themselves, or utterly to extirpate the root of that nation, so that there might be no source from which the blessing God promised to Abraham could be fulfilled. Jacob himself demanded that blessing, saying: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32); and he heard: “You will prevail against men.”

Because of such hardness of heart the Lord commanded sinners to be killed; and those who did this—the judges of Israel, the patriarch David, and the renowned Maccabees—are praised. “But from the beginning it was not so: ‘Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,’ says the Lord” (Gen. 4).

And now he says the same to this man whose name he had changed, signifying, as has been said, a change of circumstances: “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword”—that is to say, unless they repent. And in another Evangelist, when the apostles say, “Lord, behold, here are two swords,” he says to them: “It is enough” (Luke 22). Likewise: “Allow it thus far” (ibid.).

The prudent hearer ought to understand this as though he said: Material swords have now done enough, and warfare with them was necessary up to this point, for the protection of the flesh from which I, Jesus Christ, had to be born. Now lay aside swords of that kind [Col. 1386D] and fight with a new manner of warfare, as they fought on the day of Midian—that is, as was signified there when Gideon overcame Midian (Judg. 7).

Of that warfare it was said above: “Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every infirmity among the people. And his report went through all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, afflicted with diverse sicknesses and torments, and those who had demons, and lunatics and paralytics; and he healed them. And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis and Jerusalem and Judaea and from beyond the Jordan.”

Such works—works of mercy, of which these were the beginnings—were foreshadowed by the sign—[paud, an uncertain reading]—or manifestation [Col. 1387A] of the Holy Spirit’s presence which appeared over him: namely, the form of a dove. This bird is naturally gentle and has seven marks of mercy which natural philosophers commonly enumerate: it is without gall; it has a groan instead of a song; it commonly nests in the holes of a rock or the hollow of a wall; it eats nothing living; it chooses the whiter grains; it nourishes other birds’ young; and, sitting beside full-flowing streams, it foresees and escapes the treacherous hawk.

The beginnings of all works of mercy, signified by these seven natural excellences of the dove, are those related here, expressed in seven phrases: healing every sickness and every [Col. 1388A] infirmity; all who were ill; those afflicted with diverse sicknesses and torments; those who had demons; lunatics; and paralytics. Likewise, the fact that great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judaea, and beyond the Jordan was the beginning of the many peoples or nations who were to run to him, according to Isaiah: “And nations that did not know you shall run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you” (Isa. 55). In this beginning the incarnate Wisdom of God contemplated the end or fulfilment of his purpose, about which more will still have to be said.

## Book Four

[Col. 1387]

[Col. 1387B] 597 The Church, proclaiming in the Song of Songs the beauty of her beloved, says among other things: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting beside full-flowing streams” (Song 5). What is this saying except that his studies, so long as “he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3), were always directed toward the sacred Scriptures, as had been foretold in the first Psalm: “But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. 1).

It was fitting that the Holy Spirit should signify studies of this kind by descending upon him in the form of a dove, because all spiritual graces rested in him, and his soul, with the eyes of all graces opened, sat beside full-flowing streams: that is, it contemplated all things [Col. 1387C] in order to fulfil the Scriptures of truth, whatever “had been written concerning him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” (Luke 24). And—something which we ought to consider with great reverence—according to the ordering of the things which he contemplated, he arranged his outward bearing and actions.

Hence, immediately after the matters stated above, the following comes next:

## Chapter V
“Seeing the crowds, he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.’”

For it was to come about—and this did not escape him, and without doubt he meditated upon it; indeed, “as he said in a certain place, he was constrained until it should be accomplished” (Luke 12)—that he should ascend into heaven and there “sit at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. 1), according to the words, “Ascending into heaven, he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4), or, “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). Appropriately, since he was to ascend to the height of heaven, he himself ascended a mountain—that is, an elevated place on earth—which must be understood as either Tabor or some other high mountain in Galilee. For, after he had finished his discourses, it immediately follows: “And when he had entered Capernaum, seeing the crowds, he went up such a mountain,” because it was to come about that, having seen the crowds, he would ascend, as has already been said, to the height of heaven.

For what did he do here throughout his entire life except see the crowds? He truly saw them: he saw the crowds of humankind, and he did not see them in just any fashion, but so as to undergo experience of our miseries, according to the words, “For he himself knew our frame” (Ps. 102), that is, he himself assumed and experienced in himself that our mortal body is frail. He saw them so as to pity them; and he pitied them so as to console our miseries—that is, to work for us the blessedness of eternal salvation through his passion and death.

When this had been done, and he had taken his seat at the Father’s right hand, his disciples were to approach him—namely, by an approach of mind and progress in faith, persevering in hope of the promise which he had promised them and “waiting for the promise of the Father, which, he says, you heard through my mouth” (Acts 1), and so forth. Therefore it was fittingly done and fittingly said: “And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.”

Likewise, it was to come about that, while seated there at the Father’s right hand, he would more and more “open their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24), namely, by “teaching them all truth” (John 16) through the Holy Spirit whom he gave them, as he had promised. A fitting sign of this matter is found in what the evangelist says here: “And opening his mouth, he taught them,” and so forth.

Let us now enter upon the course of this text or discourse. “‘Opening,’ he says, ‘his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.’” In secular literature, such an expression or phrase, “opening his mouth,” is regarded as a fault and called a pleonasm—that is, the superfluous addition of one word—as in the phrase, “Thus she spoke with her mouth.” For no one speaks except with the mouth, nor can anyone speak otherwise than by opening his mouth.

But in the sacred writings, and especially here, it is by no means a superfluous addition; rather, it bears greatly upon the matter, if you consider that mouth of the Lord to which the divine evangelist ought to have attended. What is that mouth of the Lord except the Scriptures through which the Spirit of the Lord speaks to us? These had been closed—closed, I say, and sealed according to the circumstances of the time—and those who wrote them had the Lord’s command to close them. For example: “But thou, Daniel, close the words; seal the book until the appointed time” (Dan. 12). And to Isaiah: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8).

How, or for whom, were the Scriptures that foretold Christ closed? Certainly by proclaiming spiritual things in such a way that they appeared to convey carnal things, especially to those whose mind was subject to the flesh and devoted to earthly desires. For example: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and gold shall be given to him from Arabia” (Ps. 17). Reading these and similar words, and hoping that under the reign of the Messiah they would possess an earthly Jerusalem of gold and jewels, the Jews judged rich persons—and those prospering in other goods or ways in which the world vainly rejoices—to be blessed.

Thus the mouth of the Lord was closed—that is, Scripture, which is the Lord’s mouth—and no such mouth could be opened except by his own teaching. What did he say first when opening it? “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

This was the first song of blessedness sounded by the glorious lyre, the resonant and sweet lyre, in which all the music of the Father, the whole wisdom of God, was and is implanted. Long before, in the Prophet, he had said to it: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56). Of old, lyres were made with eight strings; and the same note that sounded on the first sounded on the eighth, according to the natural principle of music, because there are only seven distinctions of notes, and the eighth note is the same as the first. This is not unknown to skilled singers—that is, musicians. And what is by no means least delightful in this song of the Beatitudes is that the first and eighth propositions are identical: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

This exposition of the eight Beatitudes has been most frequently sung by nearly all teachers, and there is no need to add anything to their treatment except this alone: to show that, as in other matters, so also here our Lord spoke according to the certain authority of the Scriptures.

For that the poor in spirit are truly blessed, and that theirs is the kingdom of heaven, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob provide example or testimony. They were poor in spirit, as the text of sacred history relates and the Apostle recalls: “Confessing,” he says, “that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth. For those who say these things show that they seek a homeland; and if indeed they had remembered that homeland from which they had gone out, they had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly homeland” (Heb. 11). Is this not poverty of spirit: not to seek one’s homeland on earth, but humbly to await the one laid up in heaven in the hand of God? “Therefore,” he says, “he is not ashamed to be called their God; for he has prepared a city for them” (ibid.). What else is that city but the kingdom of heaven?

That the meek are truly blessed, and that they shall possess the earth, Moses provides example or testimony. Of him the truthful Scripture says: “Moses was a man most meek above all men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12). So do Joshua and Caleb, who, being meek, did not disparage the land which they had surveyed for forty days, as the other, unmeek men did, who provoked the Lord. Accordingly, those others did not possess it; but Joshua and Caleb, being full of another spirit, praised it and accordingly possessed it (Num. 13).

Moses himself did not possess the land which Israel was entering to possess—the land beyond the Jordan, the land of Canaan (Num. 14)—but he possessed and possesses the land of the living, for which alone the Psalmist sighed in spirit: “I believe,” he says, “that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). In this very matter, in not possessing that land of Canaan, he was meek; that is, he did not defend himself, which is the trait of a meek mind. For when the Lord told him that he would not enter that land, because of what had occurred at the waters of contradiction, he immediately answered: “May the Lord God of the spirits of all flesh appoint a man over this multitude, lest the people of the Lord be like sheep without a shepherd” (Num. 27).
