In his own cause, indeed, he was meek; but what he was like in God’s cause is attested by the zeal with which he was zealous “over the guilt of the calf” (Exod. 32), and by the chasm in the earth which swallowed Dathan and Abiram when he said to the Lord: “Do not regard their sacrifices” (Num. 16).

That those who mourn are truly blessed and shall be comforted is attested by the deeds of the judges who came after Moses and Joshua down to Samuel. Their mourning and crying out to the Lord—by which they confessed that because of their sins they had been delivered, and repeatedly were being delivered, into the hands of the nations—were followed by glorious consolations. The first mourning of those times even gave its name to a place, as it is written: “And the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of the weeping. ‘Why,’ he said, ‘have you done this?’ And when the angel of the Lord spoke to all the children of Israel, they lifted up their voice and wept; and the name of that place was called the place of the weeping, or of tears” (Judg. 2).

The final mourning was Samuel’s mourning for Saul, as it is written: “I repent,” says the Lord, “that I have made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words in deed. And Samuel was grieved, and cried unto the Lord all night” (1 Sam. 15). And shortly afterward: “Nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, because the Lord repented that he had made him king” (ibid.). And the Lord said to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul?” (ibid.), and so forth.

The consolations by which those mourners were comforted were so glorious that those through whose hands the Lord consoled Israel when it cried to him were even called saviours, since they bore in some measure the role and type of the coming Saviour, by saving Israel with temporal salvation (Judg. 3). Samuel, the last of them, obtained through mourning such a consolation that he was sent by the Lord to anoint David king (1 Sam. 16): David, leader of temporal salvation and source or origin of eternal salvation—that is, father according to the flesh of Christ the Saviour, named after Abraham.

That those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed and shall be filled is exemplified or testified by the prophets, the sons of the prophets, and all who feared the Lord. Under the kings of Israel—Ahab and Jezebel and the rest, who killed the prophets of the Lord and undermined the altars—they fled and hid in desert places, afflicted by want and hunger. Elijah is the best known of these. Fleeing from Jezebel’s threats, “he walked in the strength of one meal forty days and forty nights” (3 Kgs. 19). Of such persons the Apostle speaks with groaning: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, distressed; of whom the world was not worthy; wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of the earth” (Heb. 11).

They are truly blessed, of whom it is so truthfully proclaimed that the world was not worthy. They hungered and thirsted with bodily hunger and bodily thirst; they hungered and thirsted for righteousness, and with spiritual hunger and spiritual thirst they longed for righteousness itself—that is, for Christ, whom they awaited. For what would one who was hungry and thirsty do to a person who took away his only bread or necessary drink? Surely, if able, he would kill him.

Elijah, the foremost or best-known among those who hungered and thirsted for righteousness—that is, for Christ—regarded the priests and prophets of Baal as persons of this kind. Accordingly, in one day he killed four hundred and fifty of them, because, so far as lay in them, they made the people of Israel unworthy to receive or be given Christ, everlasting righteousness, according to the promise made to the fathers (3 Kgs. 18). This man, one or chief among them, after hungering and thirsting in mind for righteousness, was taken up in a fiery chariot and transferred to a place where he neither hungers nor thirsts (4 Kgs. 2). This alone is sufficient evidence for believing true what Truth says: that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, because they shall be filled.

That the merciful are truly blessed, because they shall obtain mercy, let that Obadiah be an example, who was merciful and showed mercy to those who, as said above, hungered and thirsted for righteousness while fleeing the persecution of King Ahab and the most impious Jezebel. “Have you not,” he himself says to Elijah, “been told, my lord, what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the Lord: that I hid one hundred men of the prophets of the Lord, fifty by fifty in caves, and fed them with bread and water?” (3 Kgs. 18).

He is said to have been that third captain of fifty whom Elijah spared, when he said: “Man of God, do not despise my life and the lives of your servants who are with me. Behold, fire came down from heaven and devoured the first two captains of fifty, and the fifties who were with them. But now I beseech you, have mercy upon my life” (4 Kgs. 1). He obtained mercy because he had been merciful; and not mercy merely, or in any ordinary degree, but also great grace, namely prophetic grace. Thus was fulfilled in him what Solomon said: “He who is inclined to mercy shall be blessed, for he has given of his breads to the poor” (Prov. 22).

Later, having left the service of King Ahaziah, he became Elijah’s disciple and prophesied; and he is reported to be the one who stands fourth in the order of the twelve prophets. Therefore, from his example too, it is certainly true that the merciful are blessed because they shall obtain mercy; likewise true is what was said elsewhere: “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. 10).

That the pure in heart are truly blessed, because they shall see God, Daniel and his companions provide a further example. We learn his zeal to be pure in heart from what is written: “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not be defiled by the king’s table or by the wine of his drinking; and he asked the chief of the eunuchs that he might not be defiled, and said: ‘Test, I beseech you, your servants for ten days’” (Dan. 1), and so forth. “To these youths God gave knowledge and instruction in every word and wisdom; but to Daniel understanding of all visions and dreams” (ibid.).

Among the other things which this pure-hearted man saw, greatest and most beautiful is that he saw God, insofar as God could be seen by a mortal human being: “I beheld,” he says, “until thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat; his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool. I beheld, and behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven, and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, and he gave him power and honour and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him” (Dan. 7).

If, while still alive and mortal, he saw God thus through purity of heart, in what manner, or with what blessedness, does he see him after this life? Thus present experience testifies in Daniel that the pure in heart are blessed because they shall see God.

That peacemakers are blessed, and are called and truly are children of God, was experienced in themselves by those who saw this opening of the Lord’s mouth and heard this teaching from him while present. For they were the first peacemakers and ministers of perfect peace—certainly peace among themselves and with all people. How among themselves and with all people? In this manner: just as they had left all other things in following the Prince of Peace, so that same Prince of Peace shook material weapons, every instrument of war, out of their hands, saying to one, or the first, of them, Peter: “Return your sword to its place” (Matt. 29 [sic]). From that point onward they never handled weapons of war at all, save that sword, the spiritual sword, which “is the word of God, living and effectual, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4).

Those previously named as blessed—the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst—sometimes used military arms, and nevertheless were or are blessed, because in their own time they were zealous for the Lord, and by killing the impious opened the way of the life to come, which is Christ. That is, they defended the tree of their lineage lest, by the devil’s will, it should be wholly uprooted from among the nations—the tree from which the fruit was to be born—as we have said more fully elsewhere.

“Ecclesiastes says, ‘A time of war and a time of peace; a time to kill and a time to heal’” (Eccl. 3). In short, the time of war and the time to kill was then, and it was more fitting to kill than to be killed, when the devil tried through impious human beings to destroy the root from which the seed was expected to come, which is Christ. He began with Pharaoh, who commanded all his people: “Whatever male is born, cast into the river; whatever is female, preserve” (Exod. 1). Finally there was another Pharaoh, indeed another in person but the same in malice, pursuing the departing Israel: “I will draw my sword,” he says; “my hand shall kill them” (Exod. 15).

Moses indeed, as has already been said above, “was most meek above all the people dwelling on the earth” (Num. 12); nevertheless he willingly stretched out his severe hand over the sea, that the waters might return upon the Egyptians, their chariots, and their horsemen. For this act he sang a glorious song to the Lord (Exod. 14); he himself fought and conquered the Amorite, and avenged the children of Israel upon the Midianites (Num. 21). To pursue the rest would take too long.

Yet this had to be shown: then and thereafter, until the promise was fulfilled in Christ’s birth, there was a time of war and a time to kill. Those who fought and killed are deservedly praised in the Church of God, especially David and the renowned Maccabees. But after Christ was born, the time began to be one of peace and a time to heal. This ministry the first apostles undertook; and behold, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God,” he says, and certainly my brothers: “Go,” he says, “to my brothers and tell them: I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John 20).

How were they ministers of peace between God and human beings? They were sent by Christ risen from the dead, who said—what he had never before said, once, twice, and three times according to John—“Peace be unto you” (ibid.). “God,” they say, “reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their offences to them, and placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God exhorted through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5), and many similar things.

Notice also that in the order of the Beatitudes the Sabbath-rest of peace stands in the seventh place. The eighth Beatitude, which says, “Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” embraces them all: the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers. For all have suffered and suffer persecution, whoever wishes to imitate them. “For all,” says the Apostle, “who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

Likewise, the promise, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”—which is both the first and the eighth promise—embraces all the intermediate promises. For the kingdom of heaven is also the land which he promises to the meek, “for they shall possess the earth”; and the consolation which he promises to those who mourn, saying, “for they shall be comforted”; and the fullness which he promises to those hungering and thirsting for righteousness, saying, “for they shall be filled”; and the mercy which he pledges to the merciful, “for they shall obtain mercy”; the vision of God, which he promises to the pure in heart, “for they shall see God”; and the glory of the children of God, which he promises to peacemakers, saying, “for they shall be called children of God.”

In these Beatitudes, although he did not pass over his disciples who were present, but touched upon them also, especially in saying “Blessed are the peacemakers,” he did not yet speak in such a way as to declare to them what grace, or degree of grace, they had been predestined and called to receive. For he did not address them in the second person; but immediately afterward he begins to do so.

“Blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you, and say every evil thing against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 23 [sic]). “For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.” Having shifted from the third person to the second, he addresses his disciples who were present, and likens or equates them with the prophets—whose memory was surely great and glorious among the living children whose fathers had cursed and persecuted them, and had even killed most of them.

“There is magnificence of the highest rank and greatest honour in this saying: ‘For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.’” Yet, given the greatness of the matter, it was little merely to have said: “So they did to the prophets.” Add what he immediately says: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer, except to be cast out and trodden under foot by men. You are the light of the world.”

Why did he, seated on the mountain, immediately after opening his mouth and at the beginning of so great a discourse, mention salt and light in this manner, saying: “You are salt; you are light”? To what did he look back, or to what treasures of wisdom and knowledge did he wish to lead forward his hearers? Certainly to that mountain—indeed, to the holy, just, and good law—which he himself had formerly given on Mount Sinai, where a certain light appeared, as is written: “The third day had now come, and morning had grown bright; and behold, thunders began to be heard and lightnings to flash” (Exod. 19). Again: “And all the people saw the voices and the lamps” (Exod. 20), and so forth.

Among the mystical sacraments of that law which was then given, he commends salt with the utmost care: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, season it with salt; you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2). In one and the same passage of Scripture he repeated the commendation of salt three times, lest perhaps you should not understand the first or second occurrence, or suppose that the mystery of salt is not of great concern to God.

Therefore, when seated on the mountain and about to say, “I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil it,” he first says, “You are salt; you are light.” He surely wishes his disciples to understand—as afterward, when they received the Holy Spirit and were illuminated by him, they undoubtedly did understand—that the things seen or done on Mount Sinai were related to these matters and belonged to the rationale of what he was beginning to do: sitting upon a mountain and teaching his disciples, and what he would accomplish when seated on high at the right hand of Majesty and sending them the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. Thus it came about that they were the light of the world.

To discuss for the moment the meaning of salt: certainly, by saying, “You are the light of the world,” he makes this understood—that this light of the world had been signified by those flashes and lamps which shone there amid smoke or the densest cloud. Thus it was plainly said there: “For lightnings began to flash, and a very dense cloud covered the mountain” (Exod. 19); and again, “All the people saw the voices and lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain” (Exod. 20).

The flashes and lamps amid smoke and the densest cloud were the apostles, shining by teaching and flashing with miracles amid the Jews, whom the smoke of envy had blinded and the densest cloud of unbelief had covered.

But now, following the text in order, let us enter upon this discourse under the guidance of him who spoke it. After he had said, “For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you,” it is as though those blessed persons—whom he decreed ought to rejoice and exult amid curses and persecutions “because,” he says, “your reward is great in heaven”—asked: What are we, and what end shall befall those who persecuted the prophets before us and will persecute us? He said to them: “You are the salt of the earth.”

He spoke briefly; but in the brevity of the saying there is a great meaning and great force of argument. He did not merely say, “You are salt,” by which phrase the benefit for those who use it well could alone have been indicated. But he said, “salt of the earth”; and what does this phrase portend but the devastation of a hostile land? For we read that certain cities were sown with salt in the victors’ wrath, so that no growth might arise in them.

It should therefore be understood as though he had said: “All the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (Matt. 23), joining with your blood—whom they will persecute as they persecuted the prophets before you—shall become for this generation like a sowing of salt, so that it shall be barren and bear no seed of any good, just as a city sown with salt in the anger of its conquerors is barren and uninhabitable.

This is against those who preferred to sow salt in their land rather than take it into food—that is, who preferred to persecute, and so far as they could, annihilate rather than reverence and receive apostolic teaching. They thereby judged themselves unworthy of eternal life and became transgressors of the holy law which says: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, season it with salt; nor shall you remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2).

The Jews were destined to transgress this commandment—which, lest you think it small or to be lightly esteemed, Scripture tripled and exalted so highly as to call it “the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God”—by despising, indeed by persecuting, the evangelical teaching whose administration was beginning through or with these men.

As salt dries up superfluous or harmful humours of flesh and cleanses it from decay, so apostolic teaching was to cleanse the necessary precepts of the Decalogue and all the ordinances of legal righteousness by drying up carnal ceremonies; and throughout all lands it was to salt the bodies of believers with the counsel of chastity, so that they might not decay or be corrupted utterly by foul lust. O how many companies even of boys and girls it salted, so that their flesh was wholly dried up, and they persevered and endured, incorrupt and undecayed, in continence and sound virginal chastity down to feeble old age, down to the end of life!

Second in rank of merit or grace after the apostles, apostolic men, orthodox Fathers, and catholic doctors are called and are salt and light of the world. For, handling and reconsidering the sacred Scripture of the law and prophets wisely and faithfully, they season with pure discourse whatever in it seems to sound carnal, so that it may have a spiritual savour; what was closed may be opened, and what seemed obscure and dark may become clear and luminous.

Great, therefore, is the dignity and great the glory in this saying: “You are salt.” But hear what follows: “But if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer, except to be cast out and trodden under foot by men.”

“Therefore do not think highly, but fear” (Rom. 11), O every one of you who trusts that he has attained the order of those to whom it was said, “You are salt,” being conscious of a word of wisdom or knowledge that perhaps abounds in you beyond others. For it sometimes happens that salt loses its savour; it sometimes happens that one who possesses knowledge abuses it in pride. Through elevation of mind, he speaks things contrary to his knowledge or conscience: knowing the truth, yet envying another and begrudging place to one who perhaps spoke first, or to one younger to whom something better was revealed, he regards it as his own loss and is afflicted as though under torture because he is proud and exalted.

To strive in this way is to hold the truth in unrighteousness; it is “to change the truth of God into a lie” (Rom. 1); it is “to speak a word against the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 12). This was the sin of the Pharisees when they said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (ibid.). They spoke thus through envy, although they knew that he cast out demons by the finger of God—that is, by the Spirit of God.

This was Arius’s sin, and the sin of all heresiarchs whom the Holy Spirit judged unworthy of the remedy of repentance, because, knowing God, they did not glorify him as God nor give him thanks. So too the Apostle speaks, under the name of ancient sinners, pagan sinners, who “changed,” he says, “the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 11 [sic]).

Wherever this happens, where a teacher or master becomes foolish according to such examples, say that the salt has lost its savour. And where it has thus lost its savour, with what shall it be salted? By what other teacher shall it be corrected? Truly, by none; and you will pour out discourse in vain, because there is no hearing there. “Avoid,” says the Apostle, “a heretical man after the first and second admonition, knowing that one of this kind is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3).

“The Lord says, ‘It is good for nothing any longer, except to be cast out and trodden under foot by men.’” Therefore he cast out the Pharisees, fathers and predecessors of such people, not only from the kingdom of God but also from their earthly kingdom and their handmade temple. For there was no means by which salt that had lost its savour could be salted, since they spoke, and did not allow others to speak, a word against the Holy Spirit; that is, they denied not through ignorance but blasphemed through envy him who had come, Jesus Christ. “For now,” he says, “they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15).

Likewise, those who possess the knowledge of God and shine in such a way, and are so illuminated, that they can shine upon and illuminate others, should not doubt that “You are the light of the world” is spoken to them, second in rank of grace or merit.

There is one light that is not illuminated but illuminates, a light shining naturally and not receiving from an accidental gift the means by which it shines; and for that reason, or consequently, it is the true light, as we have in another evangelist: “There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). By enlightening, it brought about the fact that it could truthfully say to these persons: “You are the light of the world.”

Between that true light, which illumines, and this light which is illumined, there is no comparison, though there is some likeness. But the relation of those who have been illumined so as to be able to illuminate others by the word of teaching, to those who have indeed been illumined but do not have the capacity to illuminate and instruct others, is like the relation of the brightness of the firmament to the stars. Thus it was said of these to Daniel: “Those who have been learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12).

What, then, is meant by the fact that, after first saying, “You are the light of the world” [Col. 1398A], he immediately adds: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”? What does this concern except the humility—and what corresponds to the humility—of those worthy to be called and to be the light of the world?

For every one of such persons is small in his own eyes and wishes to remain hidden, because he does not judge himself worthy of human regard, or even worthy to be regarded as a human being; and he scarcely dares to notice that the Most High, though seeing all things, deigns to know or behold him. Yet how great, how spacious, is that city in which “God dwells, whom heaven and the heaven of heavens [Col. 1398B] cannot contain” (3 Kings 8)! And upon what mountain is such a city set, except upon the height of heaven, according to the saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 2)?

It cannot be hidden. The order or rationale of divine judgment and counsel does not permit it to be hidden or unknown, since “it was built for this purpose, and for this purpose a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song 4): so that all who are endangered among adversaries, who strive for the faith among Jews, pagans, and heretics, may know to flee to this city and be strengthened in it; armed by judgments drawn from it, so that they may have the means of being armed for the cause in which they are engaged.

Here is another comparison: “They do not light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, [Col. 1398C] that it may give light to all who are in the house.” According to this comparison, you to whom I said, “You are the light of the world,” have not been enlightened, nor have you received the brightness of God’s wisdom and knowledge—which begins then, but will be perfected when you receive the gift of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, with tongues of fire appearing (Acts 2)—in order that you might be covered or concealed in silence, content with perpetual hiding-places; nor have you, nor any of those who possessed before you or will possess after you such grace, received it otherwise than so that, through their ministry, God might become known to the world.

Even if any one of them wished to hide in caves and caverns of the earth, and did hide for a time, nevertheless, when the cause required it, [Col. 1398D] he came forth outside and appeared in public at God’s command or appointment, so that, diligently carrying out the office for which he had been predestined and to which he had been called, he might impart to very many the benefit of the light in which he shared.

For example, John, the burning and shining lamp, wished to remain hidden in the wilderness; and there, unknown to men from his tender years almost until his thirtieth year, he wore out his life. Did not the lamp meanwhile lie hidden, as it were, beneath a bushel? Yet assuredly “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1)—from whom John had what he had as a lamp, as he himself confesses when he says, “And from his fullness we have all received” (ibid.)—had not enlightened him for this purpose, nor had filled him “with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” [Col. 1399A] (Luke 1), so that there alone, if he were to live, he might alone and silently employ for himself beneath the bushel of an eremitical life the light of a good conscience.

When the heavenly messenger announced his birth to his father, he also set forth, in due order, his name and the course of life he was to live. He announced nothing of that sort, but reverently declared what was God’s purpose: “He,” he says, “shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people”—that is, with zeal for justice, reproving and correcting sinners, to preach repentance. He voluntarily underwent that wilderness hiding-place; he obediently undertook this office of public preaching from him through whom he says: “But he who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one [Col. 1399B] who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1), and so forth.

Therefore, by the words and examples of divine authority, we are taught that God gives the bright grace of his wisdom or knowledge to anyone precisely so that such a lamp may be placed upon some lampstand, in order that it may shine upon all who are in the house and gain many. I said “some lampstand,” because according to John’s Apocalypse there are seven golden lampstands, in the midst of which the Son of Man walks; and “the seven lampstands,” he says, “are the seven churches” (Rev. 1).

Moreover, by the number seven, by which universality is customarily signified, we understand all the churches Christ has throughout the world; and this is assuredly what he desires: that one who, by his gift, excels in apostolic faith and knowledge, [Col. 1399C] with a life not at variance with it, should neither be neglected or despised by another’s judgment, nor flee from his own judgment, but should be placed upon a lampstand and shine in God’s house by word and example, remembering in every respect this saying: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

For by this saying vain glory is excluded, and the benefit of many is sought, since the intention of one doing good before people is commanded to be not that he himself “who seems to act,” but God who works through him (1 Cor. 12), may be praised and glorified: “God, the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift, and every perfect gift descends” (James 1).

After these preliminaries, at the beginning [Col. 1399D] of the discourse—by which they could have been prepared to listen attentively, receptively, and favorably—the teacher of heaven enters upon the broad expanses of his profound sermon and says: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill.”

After he had declared to others what dignity was theirs and had so honored his lesser disciples as to say to them, “You are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world,” he wished also to indicate, though humbly, what ought to be hoped concerning himself; and he judged that it was fitting that this should not be known in vain. For what he says of himself, “I have come to fulfill the Law,” is great; but lest his speech seem to smell of boasting because of the greatness of the matter, his manner of teaching admirably moderated it, when at the very outset he took care to preface an excuse and in a sense request a just estimation of himself, saying: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law and [Col. 1400A] the Prophets.”

Certainly, if he had mentioned the Law alone, saying, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law,” and had then said, “I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill,” this would have been great, as has already been said—far more than any human being could ever truly say of himself. But when he adds “and the Prophets,” and says of both, namely the Law and the Prophets, that he has come to fulfill them, I ask: how great is this? Is it not equivalent to saying: All the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets will be fulfilled in me, for indeed all things written are about me?

But, as already said, the greatness of the matter is made sweeter to the hearers by the manner of speaking; likewise in what he immediately adds: “Amen, indeed, I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law, until all things are fulfilled.” How much sweeter and more reverent it sounds to say, “until all things are fulfilled,” than if he had said, “until I fulfill all things”! What things? Namely, whatever the Law and the Prophets declare. “Not one iota or one stroke,” he says, “will pass away until all things are fulfilled.”

And until when, or for how long, will they be fulfilled? “Until heaven and earth pass away”—that is, until the consummation of the age, until the day of judgment (1 Cor. 7), when the present form of this world has passed away or is passing away, and there will be a new earth and new heavens (2 Pet. 3).

What, then, does the Apostle mean when he says, “There is indeed a setting aside of the former [Col. 1400C] commandment because of its weakness and uselessness” (Heb. 7), whereas the Lord himself here says, “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things are fulfilled”? In response, it must be known that there is a certain difference between the things signified by the name “Law.” Not to draw out an overly long thread in answering: it is one thing for God to have given the Law according to his good pleasure, which he did before the guilt of the calf; another for him to have imposed a law, not without punishment or severe judgment, after—or in the very course of—the guilt concerning the calf.

Here we must recall the words of the same Lord to the prophet Ezekiel: “I brought them out,” he says, “from the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness; and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which a human being shall do and live [Col. 1400D] by them. And the house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness,” and so forth, down to: “Their eyes were after the idols of their fathers.” Immediately it follows: “Therefore I too gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live, and I defiled them in their gifts” (Ezek. 20).

He says that he gave or showed them commandments and judgments which a human being should do and live by: namely, the commandments, “You shall have no strange gods before me; you shall not make for yourself a carved image” (Exod. 20), and the other words of the Decalogue; and the judgments, “If you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve you six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment” (ibid., 21), and the rest, all of which Moses recounted and wrote for the people, concluding thus: “This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.”

But after [Col. 1401A] they made the calf, and—as we have already said from the prophet—their eyes were after the idols of their fathers, where the sin of the calf is to be understood, which they committed according to Egyptian custom, just as their fathers had done: the commandments that were not good, and the judgments by which they would not live, which he says that he gave them, are those of which almost the whole book of Leviticus consists. For example, concerning clean and unclean animals, whether to be eaten or not eaten; concerning the defilement of leprosy and the cleansing of the leper (Lev. 11, 13, 32 [perhaps 14]); and other such matters, in which life certainly does not consist—just as it does not consist in sacrifices of flesh or the blood of bulls, goats, rams, or lambs. Of these God himself also says in Jeremiah: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the flesh, for I did not speak to your fathers or command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but I commanded them this word, saying: Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people” (Jer. 7).

Therefore, when the Lord here says, “Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law,” while the Apostle there says, “There is a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness” (Heb. 7), it is worthwhile to know this distinction within the Law: so that here you understand the good commandments and the judgments which a human being should do and live by; but there, the commandments that were not good and the judgments by which they would not live, concerning which the Apostle says in the same place: “For the Law brought [Col. 1401C] nothing to perfection” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “For the Law, having a shadow of the good things to come and not the very image of the realities, can never, by the same sacrifices continually offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near” (Heb. 10). And much else to this effect.

Yet even if such a law or commandment was weak and useless according to the letter, for which reason it was set aside, nevertheless, to those who understand according to the Spirit, it is known and clear what shadow it possessed of future good things: that nothing of such a law has passed or will pass away, since almost all things have already been fulfilled in Christ or through Christ; and whatever remains is now being fulfilled and must be fulfilled until the end of the age.

Nevertheless, when he says in the preceding passage, “Not one iota [Col. 1401D] or one stroke will pass from the Law,” the Law of those commandments and judgments must especially be understood which, as said above, he first gave or showed them—as he says in Ezekiel—so that they might not provoke him (Ezek. 20), that is, before the guilt concerning the calf. For he treats of this kind of Law in what follows, beginning thus: “Therefore whoever shall abolish one of these least commandments and shall teach people accordingly shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

First, I should like to divide the whole sermon into four divisions, namely according to the four principal virtues, which the pagans could indeed name but were not granted to know according to their heavenly or spiritual dignity: justice, temperance, fortitude, and prudence.

The first division or part begins here, where he says: “For I say to you that unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” It ends where it is said: “Therefore be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” The whole sequence of this part tends toward the perfection of justice, in accordance with the purpose of the saying already discussed: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.”

The second begins with what he immediately says: “Take heed not to do your justice before people in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6), and ends where he says: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow; sufficient for the day is its own evil” (ibid.). This entire part tends toward the virtue of temperance, especially restraint from the desire for vain glory, and then from anxiety about the belly or body, and at the same time from slavery to Mammon.

The third extends from: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7), to: “Enter through the narrow gate; for narrow is the gate and constricted the way which leads to life” (ibid.). Without doubt, it shows that the movement toward the kingdom of heaven requires persevering fortitude, strong perseverance.

The fourth extends from: “Beware of false prophets” (ibid.), to the end of the sermon, and undoubtedly leads the hearer to prudence and instructs the Christian to be prudent and provident.

In each of these parts, he most sharply censures the Scribes and Pharisees, as devoid of every virtue, by opposing them to the virtues and designating them by four different names. For in the first part of the sermon he calls them openly Scribes and Pharisees, saying: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees.” In the second, he calls them hypocrites once, twice, and a third time, and additionally calls them pagans, saying: “Do not sound a trumpet before yourselves, as hypocrites do; and when you pray, you shall not be like hypocrites; and when you pray, do not use many words like the pagans; and when you fast, do not become sad like hypocrites” (Matt. 6).

There were [Col. 1402D] and are hypocrites among the Gentiles as well, whom the present discourse also condemns for intemperance, because they are so hasty for their reward that they prefer to lose the eternal reward, which is deferred, rather than lack the temporal reward—that is, human praise—which is available now. But the greatest of all hypocrites, and the teachers of every kind of hypocrisy, were the Scribes and Pharisees; and the Savior directs this present discourse especially against them.

Likewise, in the third part of this division, when he says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine,” he designates by this appellation all, from whatever people they may be, whose fortitude is foul: namely, to bite like dogs and rush in like swine in order to trample and tear apart. But the Scribes and Pharisees were especially such people [Col. 1403A] as well.

No less, among those whom he designates when saying, “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves,” the Scribes and Pharisees were the greatest of those false prophets. Thus they are shown to be entirely devoid of the virtues which we have perceived shining forth in the several divisions of this sermon: justice, temperance, fortitude, and prudence. By the names by which they are designated in each of these parts: for the Scribes and Pharisees have no true justice; hypocrites, such as they were, have no temperance in receiving their reward; swine trampling pearls and tearing people apart, such as they themselves were, have no true fortitude; false prophets—indeed wolves hidden beneath sheep’s skin—have no prudence, for what is thought to be their prudence is wickedness.

Having tasted these things beforehand, we must now, as it were, enter inward through the great and manifest door of this most beautiful sermon, opened by him who opened it.

“Therefore whoever shall abolish one of these least commandments and teach people accordingly shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” Therefore, since, he says, I have come not only not “to abolish the Law,” but also “to fulfill” it, it is mine to pass judgment and pronounce sentence upon those who not only do not fulfill it, but even abolish it. Who are or were they then? Certainly the Scribes and Pharisees, whom he vigorously strikes immediately throughout the whole fabric of this sermon and elsewhere in the Gospel.

And what are these least commandments, which, as though pointing with his finger, he calls “one of these least commandments”? Certainly those set forth below: “You have heard that it was said: You shall not commit adultery,” and so forth. Are these, then, least? Certainly they are least. Otherwise, what need was there for him to fulfill them, as he says, “I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill,” if they were great and sufficient? In what respect, or to what extent, they are least will be more fittingly said below.

But what is it for such a teacher to be called least in the kingdom of heaven? Surely, not to enter the kingdom of heaven. For it follows: “For I say to you that unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, [Col. 1403D] you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” How truly least is one who falls from on high and loses his episcopate! “Let his days,” says the Psalmist, “be few, and let another take his episcopate” (Ps. 108). Judas the traitor first suffered this, whose apostleship another received (Acts 1); and after him, the Scribes and Pharisees. As Judas was the leader in seizing Jesus, so he was their example in losing the episcopate and hanging—or strangling—himself.

For just as he went away and hanged himself with a noose, and another received his apostleship or episcopate, as has been said, so the Pharisaic assembly and the whole Jewish people, persuaded both by them and by the chief priests, condemned themselves by their own sentence, crying, “His blood be upon us [Col. 1404A] and upon our children” (Matt. 27). And another people—the Christian people—received their high-priesthood or priesthood.

And just as Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver, the price of blood, so to every such person who is not reconciled with his adversary it is said shortly afterward here: “You shall not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing.” Therefore, when he says, “He shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” “least” must be understood as the greatest reproach, so that “least” means “contemptible,” according to that saying in the vision of Obadiah, where, after saying to Edom, “Behold, I have made you little among the nations” (Obad. 1), he immediately adds: “You are exceedingly contemptible” (ibid.).

“But whoever shall do and teach shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” What does “shall do and teach” mean? Does it mean “one of these least commandments”? Certainly not, certainly not. For one who “keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2): how much more one who does or observes perhaps one thing, but stumbles in all the others? Therefore, in saying, “But whoever shall do and teach,” [Col. 1404B] he expressly says neither one of these least commandments nor one of the great commandments; but, content to have said, “whoever shall do and teach,” as though withdrawing into himself the hand or finger of one meek and humble in heart, he says: “This one shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

For he professes this and similar things concerning himself, not boastfully, but, as the Apostle says, “He remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2). And indeed very many did and taught, among whom the best were those blessed hearers to whom he said: “You are the light of the world; let your light shine before men,” and so forth. Yet they did not do so fully, nor were they so steadfast, constant, or unchangeable in doing, that they ought in every respect to be magnified for what they had done, if they were called to judgment without mercy. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).

This one alone is he who wholly did and wholly taught through himself; but through them, insofar as it pleased his grace. Therefore they too are, or shall be, called great in the kingdom of heaven, but their greatness does not attain to his greatness, [Col. 1404C] which he signifies in this sermon by so often saying: “It was said to the ancients; but I say to you.”

Between this great one “who did and taught” and that least one “who abolished and taught” are those in the middle: one who did but did not teach, because he did not have knowledge or the capacity for teaching; and one who neither did nor taught, perhaps because he had no opportunity to act. This one will judge all these great ones, so that that least one who abolished and taught will not enter the kingdom of heaven, though he seemed to himself to be a son of the kingdom; whereas one who neither did nor taught, because he could not and did not know how, may by grace have some place in the kingdom of heaven. Considering such a person, the Apostle says: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as justice” [Col. 1405A] (Rom. 4), etc.

One who did but did not teach—namely every person in the people who was a hearer and could not be a teacher—will have his place or rank in that same kingdom of heaven, somewhat different from those who did and taught, among whom the first were the apostles. And this great one, as has been said, will far surpass even them.

From the authority of his greatness he immediately says: “For I say to you that unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Therefore the Scribes and Pharisees will not enter the kingdom of heaven; and, he says, I tell you this as one great, as arbiter of the kingdom of heaven, as he whose word is in power and whose power in his word is supreme.

And why will the Scribes and Pharisees not enter the kingdom of heaven? Because their justice does not abound; rather, it is deficient and nonexistent. For what if they do not kill me with their own hands? “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.” They pretend not to transgress this saying or commandment, since they do not kill me with their own hands. “But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.” Do you ask why? Because anger is the will to kill. And because he wills to kill, he is rightly already judged a murderer, according to the saying: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

We must not understand here every sort of anger—for example, a sudden rising motion of a heated mind, which nevertheless subsides gently—but anger [Col. 1405C] of the kind Cain is written to have had: “Cain was very angry,” Scripture says, “and his face fell. And the Lord said to him: Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” (Gen. 4). For he was angry in such a way that he thought of killing.

Whoever is similarly angry, whoever he may be, “shall be liable to judgment”—that is, undoubtedly, to divine judgment. For he cannot yet be held liable to human judgment as a murderer, because the hatred that is in the heart is hidden from people, Scripture saying: “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Kings 16). But if the hatred which was previously hidden is disclosed by some sign, then he will be liable not only to divine judgment but to human judgment as well.

Therefore he says: “Whoever says to his brother, *raca*, shall be liable to the council.” For a council is an assembly of people for passing judgment, of those who have received the ecclesiastical ministry of dealing with or judging sins. Some have said that *raca* is a word signifying nothing, but expressing a movement of an indignant mind. Grammarians call such interjections parts of speech that signify an effect of the stirred emotions, as when one in pain says “alas!” or one angered says “hem!” Others have said that the word is properly Hebrew. *Raca* means “empty” or “vacant,” a person whom we may call, in common insult, “brainless.”

Therefore, “whoever says to his brother, *raca*”—that is, whoever discloses to people by such a vocal or oral sign as *raca* the hatred conceived within his heart, so that it is beyond doubt and can be proved by reliable witnesses—[Col. 1406A] whoever hates his brother “shall be liable to the council.” A lawful judgment will be made against him by people, so that he may rightly even be removed from the Lord’s altar until he both makes satisfaction to God and is reconciled to his brother.

“But whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” Those who insult others’ misfortunes commonly say, “Fool.” For example, after Julian was killed among the Persians, when news of his death was announced in the city of Antioch, all who thought that they had cause for celebration rejoiced—not only in churches and at the tombs of martyrs, but also in theatres—and, proclaiming Christ’s victory, they all cried together: “Utter fool, where are the prophecies? God and his Christ have conquered.”

Yet they rightly insulted and rightly spoke in this way, since they spoke not to a brother but, on the contrary, to the most bitter enemy and adversary of our brother, our best brother Jesus Christ, from whose faith proceeds “every useful brotherhood or fatherhood named in heaven and on earth” (Eph. 3). But to insult a brother in this way, to say to him, “Fool,” is an exceedingly great sin, as evidence of a hardened heart possessing insatiable hatred. Thus the sentence, “He shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna,” is just; and it must be understood: unless he repents.

That curse of Shimei belonged to this degree of sin, when he cursed King David as he fled from the face of his son Absalom, weeping, with covered head and walking barefoot, saying: “Get out, man of blood and man of Belial! Behold, evils press upon you because you are a man of blood.” And he went on cursing and throwing [Col. 1406C] stones at him and scattering dust (2 Kings 16).

The Scribes and Pharisees, more malicious than all people and, as the prophet foretells, “set apart for an evil day” (Amos 6), were thus angry with their brother; thus they said *raca* to their brother; thus they said, “Fool”: sons of Gehenna, liable to Gehenna’s fire, even while they trusted in themselves as righteous. They did not kill their brother with their own hands, but were angry with their brother, who says in the psalm: “They hated me without cause” (Ps. 34, 68). They were intensely angry with him in implacable hatred, for no other reason than that which Wisdom testifies they said: “Because he is contrary to our works” (Wis. 2).

The whole school of the Church reads and sings, and long usage has worn smooth, that Cain, who “was very angry and his face fell” (Gen. 4), since he had no cause other than that his own works were evil while those of his brother were just, was a type of this hatred by which the Scribes and Pharisees hated this brother according to the flesh, Jesus Christ—again for no other reason than that his works were good and theirs evil, and he rebuked their avarice in his teaching.

Were they not already liable to judgment because of such hatred? But they added to this sin: not only did they hate him in their heart, but they also said *raca* to this same brother—that is, every evil word which hostile indignation could suggest. For example: “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. [Col. 1407A] 13). And elsewhere: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John 10), and many similar things.

And if they had done or said nothing more, would they not already have been liable not only to divine judgment but also to the council of the Church? For the whole council of patriarchs and prophets would therefore have a sentence against them, saying: “Woe to those who call good evil” (Isa. 5). But they added still more: they insulted him in his passion and mocked him in his very death, which was, as shown above, to say, “Fool” (Matt. 27).

For when that brother was dying—the one who says in the psalm, “As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I pleased” (Ps. 34)—those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Aha! You who destroy [Col. 1407B] God’s temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself” (Matt. 27). Earlier, too, when they had seized him, they mocked him as if he were foolish and derided him as a fool, striking him with fists and saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (ibid., 26).

In all this they seemed to themselves—or wished to appear—righteous and not transgressors of the Law which says, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 10 [probably 20]); when they said, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” and did not kill him with their own hands—thus righteous, thus unimpeachable keepers of the Law—so that “they would not even enter the praetorium of a Gentile, lest they be defiled,” says the Evangelist, “but might eat the Passover” (John 18).

Therefore he rightly and truly said: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven”—that is, unless you not only restrain your hands from killing, but also free your mind from anger or hatred; and, what is more, your mouth from every sound of indignation; and, what is more abundant still, your tongue from insulting any brother in whatever evil may have befallen him.

What, finally, is the difference between the judgment which was said to the ancients—“Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment”—and this judgment which we hear here: “But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment”? There must indeed be some difference in the judgment where there is so great a difference in the guilt to be judged: as great as is understood here between homicide perpetrated [Col. 1407D] by hands and homicide which is entertained in mind or thought so that it may be done.

A human judge, established by law, judges homicide perpetrated in act; God alone judges homicide not carried out in deed but considered in the mind in order that it may be done—at least through the natural law written in hearts, which is this: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” This judgment was first established in Cain, when, after he had become very angry, the Lord said to him: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” (Gen. 4), and so forth.

But where the deed of homicide is manifest, a human judge judges according to the nature of the case, as the Law says: “Whoever strikes a person intending to kill him shall surely die. But whoever did not lie in wait, and God delivered him into his hands” (Exod. 21), and the rest, which would take too long to pursue.

What counsel, then, remains? We have heard the judgment: that one whose anger has advanced so far that he says “Fool” to his brother shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna—Gehenna, which is no longer merely a judgment, but the final sentence of judgment. Is the Gospel ever forgetful of mercy during this time in which judgment is preached in the Gospel? Certainly not. Rather, always and everywhere, before judgment is concluded, it extends the hand of mercy and offers counsel for seeking pardon.

Hence what immediately follows: “Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has anything against [Col. 1408B] you, leave your gift there before the altar, and first go to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.”

As with the other matters, so every sinner or person guilty of murderous hatred, from whatever people or nation, should think this too addressed to him; yet he should know that the first intention of this discourse concerns the Jewish body, or the assembly of Scribes and Pharisees, since almost this whole sermon was delivered to them—indeed against them—as is readily evident from its very sequence.

Therefore, O evil college, council of wicked Scribes and Pharisees, chief priests and elders: if you wish, you can remember that your brother has something against you—the brother whom you hated without cause, to whom you said many things reproachfully in indignation, “Raca,” and whom you addressed with much cruel mockery, “Fool.” Why do you strive to offer your gift at the altar? Do you not know? Have you not heard? For God says in the prophet: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Mal. 1); and elsewhere: “Do not continue to bring a vain sacrifice. Your new moons and your solemnities my soul has hated. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayers, I will not hear” (Isa. 1).

For what reason? “For your hands are full of blood” (ibid.). This is what he now says: that your brother has something against you. Therefore, if you remember this and earnestly desire to offer your gift—
If you wish to offer your gift, leave your gift there before the [Col. 1408D] altar, and go first to be reconciled with this brother of yours—namely, according also to the counsel of the apostle Peter, who says: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins” (Acts 2). For this is to be reconciled with this brother. Once this has been done, then, on coming, you will offer your gift: a holy gift, a true sacrifice—not the flesh of bulls, the blood of goats, or of calves, but the life-giving body and true blood, the holy and spotless sacrifice, of that same brother to whom you have been reconciled.

How many from that council or proud, hatred-filled order of Scribes and Pharisees would receive this counsel of humility, this gracious and salutary good pleasure? Yet some, though few, were to receive it [Col. 1409A]: having heard the words of Peter and the other apostles, they are reconciled to this brother, being baptized in his name. But among them how great was the division, how great the disagreement, as the Book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies—especially concerning the abandonment or alteration of the offering or rite by which the gift had previously been offered (Acts 15, 21).

It follows, therefore: “Be quickly at agreement with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen, I say to you: you shall not go out from there until you have paid the last farthing.” In agreement with this saying, the Apostle says:

> “Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Heb. 3; Ps. 94),

and the rest. Having prefaced these words, he enters upon a long and excellent discussion concerning the abandonment, as has already been said, of the ancient offering and the offering of a better one. Among other things he says: “For there is indeed a setting aside of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness” (Heb. 7).

Finally, [Col. 1409B] the adversary of those who were of this sort was the word of the Gospel and every preacher of evangelical truth, having power to hand over to the judge one who did not agree with him—and not only to the judge, but even to an evil officer, under the presence or judgment of the judge. Thus one of those apostles just mentioned says to the Corinthians:

> “Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, him who has so acted: when you and my spirit are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus [Col. 1409C] Christ, with the power of the Lord Jesus, to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Cor. 5).

And he writes to Timothy: “Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1).

And what wonder if the word of God, or any minister of God’s word in the Gospel, is called the adversary of a sinner—and especially of the Jew, or of the rebellious and unbelieving Scribe and Pharisee—when God himself, or the Spirit of God, has by prophetic authority been called their enemy? Isaiah says: “But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the Spirit of his holiness” (Isa. 63); “and he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.” And Jeremiah speaks in lamentation [Col. 1409D]:

> “The Lord has become as an enemy; he has cast down Israel, he has cast down all her walls.”

And again he says: “He has bent his bow as an enemy; he has strengthened his right hand as an adversary” (Lam. 2).

Therefore, O Scribe of the killing letter; O Pharisee of great arrogance, deserter of the life-giving Spirit; O Jew, loud proclaimer of manifest circumcision, together with your fleshly and bloodthirsty priests and high priests: do not harden your heart. Rather, be at agreement with this adversary—with this word of grace and truth, and with his tongue and mouth—in which the apostolic tongue, the mouth of evangelical preaching, began to oppose you. Otherwise, perhaps, shaking the dust of their feet against you, he may hand you over to that Judge who said through Moses: “But whoever will not hear his words which he shall speak [Col. 1410A] in my name, I myself will exact vengeance” (Deut. 18).

That Judge and Avenger has an officer—an officer, I say, and a servant—of whom he speaks to Job: “Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” (Job 40). That servant, that officer, if you are handed over to him, will cast you into prison, into the lower hell. How long will you be there? “Amen, I say to you: you shall not go out from there until you have paid the last farthing” (Matt. 16). You weighed out thirty pieces of silver, the price of his blood (Zech. 11); and until you repay them to the last farthing, you shall not go out from there.

But when will you be able to repay the whole? Will you have with you in that prison those pieces of silver which you gave to the traitor and which the traitor returned to you, so that you may pay them back? Will there be leisure there to weigh out farthings, thirds, ounces, or even whole [Col. 1410B] pounds from the treasures that you stored up here for yourself? Certainly not. It is not your treasure, but only your sin and the punishment of sin, that will follow you there.

> “Do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied; for when he dies, he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48).

Therefore, you shall not go out from there until you have paid to the last farthing—that is, you shall never go out from there. A farthing has two *minuta* (“mites”). Yet in calculations of weights, which reckoners (*abacistae*) use and have also written down, a farthing has three ounces; an ounce is the twelfth part of an *as*. Now an *as* is some whole quantity—whether a pound or something else—which is to be divided into twelve equal parts [Col. 1410C]. Accordingly, it should be noted that he did not say, “until you pay as far as a farthing,” but “as far as the last farthing,” so that by “the last farthing” you may understand one of the smallest coins, such as what is called among them a *chalcus* or a *sicilicus*, into which the final fractions of ounces are divided. For in another evangelist it is written thus: “I tell you, you shall not go out from there until you have paid even the last mite” (Luke 12).

But do not suppose, O unhappy and unreconciled trader, that only the aforesaid silver coins—the price of a brother’s blood—will be exacted from you in that prison. The entire plunder which you amassed in such madness, with such greed for gain, will also be exacted: so that you made the very house of God, which ought to have been called [Col. 1410D] and to have been a house of prayer, into a den of robbers (Matt. 21; John 2). Therefore, because this brother disputed against your avarice, you conceived in your mind an implacable hatred against him.

From the beginning, when your fathers sold their brother Joseph for twenty pieces of silver (Gen. 37), you have continued sick with the disease of avarice; and you have advanced so far that you killed this brother while he was disputing, as has already been said, so that you gave and received thirty pieces of silver as the price of blood. You could have escaped the exacting punishment for so many evils by a brief and ready reconciliation, and by the friendly voice of confession gained forgiveness for your entire offence.

In the second place, every person who worships with you one and the same God is your brother: every person who blesses “the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the [Col. 1411A] Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1). If you are angry with such a brother, if you have said “Raca,” if you have said “fool,” you are likewise liable, on his account, to the hell of fire, as a murderer. For the apostle John testifies that “everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

If, therefore, you offer your gift at the altar—whether prayer or any offering whatsoever—hasten, according to the present counsel, to remove such leaven; for it is also, according to the holy and mystical law, leavened with malice and wickedness [the text apparently reads *quia [lege, est]*, “for [read: it is]”]. Perhaps the very brother whom you hate, or someone else, knowing alone that you sin by being angry with or hating a brother, reproves you privately, between yourself and him alone. Because he reproves you, he is in a manner your adversary; and he does not cease to oppose you—bringing another with him if you refuse to hear him alone, and even telling the [Col. 1411B] Church if you refuse to hear the two. From that point, you must beware lest the adversary hand you over to the judge—that is, lest you become to him as a Gentile and a publican, should you refuse to hear even the Church (Matt. 18).

For this is undoubtedly to hand one over to the judge: to reckon one among those outside, concerning whom the Lord will judge. “For what have I to do,” says the Apostle, “with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are within? But God will judge those who are outside” (1 Cor. 5).

Moreover, whatever brother it may be with whom you are angry, whom you hate, and whom through hatred you have injured by an evil or insulting word, will not be difficult toward one asking reconciliation, because of him [Col. 1411C] who said: “If your brother sins against you and, turning, repents, or says, ‘I repent,’ forgive him” (Luke 17). And there are many similar sayings.

Nevertheless, David is not found unjust [Col. 1412A] in this action: Shimei, who had cursed him, came to him and, prostrating himself, said: “Let not my lord impute iniquity to me; do not remember the injury of your servant; for I, your servant, acknowledge my sin” (2 Sam. 19), and so forth. “Then indeed he said, ‘You shall not die,’ and swore to him” (ibid.). But afterwards, when the days approached for him to die, he said among other things to his son Solomon: “You also have with you Shimei, who cursed me with a most grievous curse when I was going to the camp; but you are a wise man, and you will know what you should do to him, and you shall bring down his grey hair with blood to hell” (1 Kings 2).

David, I say, is not found unjust in this action, because Shimei did not seek reconciliation with a true heart. He did not repent out of a desire for justice, but fell down servilely [Col. 1412B] through fear of punishment. For he hated in his heart the king whom he had cursed when he was fleeing, and whom he saw seated again in his kingdom after receiving his greeting. He changed his voice, not his mind.

Scripture also indicates this when it says: “He also, namely Benaiah son of Jehoiada, killed an Egyptian man, a man of worthy appearance, having a spear in his hand” (2 Sam. 23). It calls that Shimei an Egyptian by his manners, not by his birth; and “having a spear in his hand” means having in the power of his own mind a sentence given to him. Solomon gave it in this manner: “On whatever day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know that you shall be put to death.” And Shimei said: “The saying is good” (1 Kings 2).

Thus David acted as the avenger not of himself, but of God and of the law, which says: “You shall not curse the ruler of your [Col. 1412C] people” (Exod. 22). Thus he ordered Shimei to be punished, while nevertheless being able safely to say: “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 8).

## BOOK V

[Col. 1411]

[Col. 1411D] Although many things were said to the ancients, and all are included under the single name of the Law—which the Lord himself says that he came “not to abolish, but to fulfil”—one may reasonably ask why, out of so many, he set forth only a few, namely only six sayings, as examples, so that the ways in which the fulfilment of which he spoke was to be carried out might appear; and why he selected these rather than others here, and arranged them in such an order.

The first is: “You shall not kill”; the second: “You shall not commit adultery”; the third: “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce”; the fourth: “You shall not swear falsely”; the fifth: “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth”; the sixth: “You shall love your neighbour, and hate your enemy.” As I have already said, one may reasonably ask why he arranged these rather than others in such an order, adding to each in turn: “But I say to you.” To this it must briefly be answered that the matters contained under these sayings or commandments are so necessary for the Christian advancing toward the perfection of righteousness that without them he cannot be perfect in that same perfection which, after carefully commending these sayings, he finally declares: “Be perfect yourselves, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

For this is the first work of righteousness: to be of one mind in faith and brotherly love. What else did he take care to impress upon us when, after prefacing, “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill,’” he added, “But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother,” and so on until, “Be reconciled with your adversary”? After this beginning of righteousness, what is so beautiful, so worthy of God, as to labour for the attainment of chastity? This indeed he proclaims with vehement earnestness when, after prefacing, “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’” he added, “But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth, until, “than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna.”

Moreover, the pursuit of chastity was to be exercised with such discernment that it should create no stumbling block for nature itself—that is, lest the preaching of chastity become an occasion of adultery. Guarding against this, the Apostle also says: “To those bound in marriage I give command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife is not to depart from her husband” (1 Cor. 7). Upon this matter he immediately instructs us, when, after saying, “It was said, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce,’” he adds: “But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, causes her to commit adultery.”

When, however, the Christian has advanced this far, so as to be girded with the virtue of chastity, then that further attainment of righteousness may at once delight him: namely, to free himself, so far as he can, from all worldly affairs. Intending this, after he had said, “It was said to the ancients: [Col. 1413B] ‘You shall not swear falsely,’” he added, “But I say to you: Do not swear at all,” and so forth. For without oaths, how can worldly affairs be conducted? Therefore, when he says, “Do not swear at all,” he wishes a person to be free from every worldly business.

Certainly, one who has undertaken this part of the counsel will consequently undertake this also: that he should desire not merely to inflict no injury, but even to endure injury for God’s sake. Thus, after prefacing, “It was said: ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth,’” he immediately added, “But I say to you: Do not resist evil,” and so forth. After these things there remains one further necessary seal of righteousness, which he immediately places upon them: “It was said,” he says, “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy; but I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,” and so forth. [Col. 1413C] He concludes these words thus: “Be perfect yourselves, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

Now the sequence of all these matters must be followed more carefully, in accordance with his purpose or beginning.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” As above the intention of murder, so here the intention of adultery is condemned, even when no act follows. For to look upon a woman in order to desire her is what else than to gaze upon a woman while having the will to commit adultery with her? Rightly therefore, just as “the one who is angry with his brother,” or “the one who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3), and is therefore liable [Col. 1413D] to judgment, so also the one who looks upon a woman in order to desire her “has already,” he says, “committed adultery with her in his heart,” and is likewise liable to judgment.

Yet it is still too little to restrain such a look, if you wish to make true in yourself him who uttered these words when he said: “I came not to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it.” Therefore hear what follows: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you. For it is expedient for you that one of your members perish, rather than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna.” For here the sense is [the text adds *est*, “is”]: In order that you may be perfect in chastity, you must not only pluck out your left eye, but also cast away your right eye, if it causes you to stumble; that is, you must flee not only the desire for adulterous intercourse, but [Col. 1414A] also dissolve and cast away even lawful love and the lawful union of marriage, if the woman nevertheless does not consent to live with you, or if, because of her cohabitation, you must incur danger to your life or to eternal salvation.

For in this manner your right eye truly causes you to stumble, if either a wife does not permit you, her husband, or a husband does not permit you, his wife, to remain in the faith of Christ. The Apostle, faithfully standing upon this foundation, says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart. For a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such a case” (1 Cor. 7). For example, suppose that a Jewish or Gentile man or woman wishes to be converted to Christ, or has already believed in Christ, and suffers scandal because of the marital union, so that either the marriage must be dissolved or loss of faith must be endured. Would you not say to such a one, without hesitation and most certainly: “It is expedient for you that one of your members perish, rather than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna”?

If in this matter we ought not to recognize the claims of affection even for brothers, children, relations by marriage, and kinsfolk—indeed, if it is expedient for a person to cut off portions of himself lest, while wishing to gain others, we ourselves perish eternally—then this is why it is also said of the high priest, whose soul is dedicated to the worship of God: “He shall not be defiled for father, mother, or children” (Lev. 21); that is, he shall recognize the claim of affection of no one except him to whose worship he has been dedicated.

“It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.’ But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, causes her to commit adultery. And whoever marries [Col. 1414C] a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

Therefore do not be too hasty, O hearer of evangelical peace, in plucking out your right eye; do not hasten too much, as though for the Gospel’s sake, to break the bond of marriage, which we have said above is fittingly signified by the right eye. Above he told you: “Pluck out your right eye if it causes you to stumble”; he did not say, “Pluck out your right eye lest perhaps it may cause you to stumble.” To make my meaning clearer: the Gospel does not tell you, “Dismiss your wife,” whom the Christian faith found living with you, lest perhaps she seduce you; rather it tells you: “Dismiss her,” if on account of the faith she hates you and does not consent to live with you.

The Apostle assists your understanding toward the necessary caution when he says: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband” (1 Cor. 7); and immediately afterward: “For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” (ibid.).
