For it could happen, and has sometimes happened, and the Apostle could know that it would sometimes happen, that through a woman a man might be saved, and through a man a woman might be saved. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was almost lost through the fault of idolatry: for when departing with her husband, she had stolen the idols of her father Laban. Yet she was saved through her husband, who said, shortly before she died while endangered in childbirth: “Cast away the foreign gods, and be cleansed; [Col. 1415A] and change your garments. Rise, and let us go up to Bethel, that I may make there an altar to God, who heard me in the day of my distress and was my companion on my journey. Therefore they gave him all the foreign gods that they possessed; and he buried them beneath the terebinth” (Gen. 35).

Therefore, O you who are married, whichever married woman or man you are who have found your spouse or partner in the marriage bed and preceded that partner in coming to faith in Christ, while Christ’s Gospel shines forth, wait and do not despair that one who is slow may yet be able to follow. For you have not only reason, but examples also, why you should not despair of your spouse’s salvation. “For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified in the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband” (1 Cor. 7), as was Rachel, of whom I have spoken. But this has sometimes happened and may still happen.

There is only one cause for which it is permitted to dismiss even one unwilling to leave and consenting to live with you: namely, fornication. For that cause alone frees you, so that you are not judged to have caused her to commit adultery when another marries her, because she had committed adultery before you dismissed her. The Law also, when it told the ancients to give a bill of divorce, did not altogether keep silence about this judgment: namely, that both the one who dismissed and the one who married the dismissed woman were guilty of adultery.

What, then, has he said here beyond what was said to the ancients? Namely, that under the Gospel this cause is not to be admitted: that someone should dismiss his wife because of hatred; nor is this at all lawful for any other reason than the cause he mentioned, fornication. When that cause alone has intervened, the one who dismisses is not entangled in the guilt of adultery. In the latter part of this Gospel the Saviour explains more fully that Moses commanded a bill of divorce to be given because of the hardness of husbands’ hearts, not by granting discord, but by removing murder (Deut. 24). For it is far better that discord, though sorrowful, should arise than that blood should be shed through hatred.

Again: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely. But you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you: Do not swear at all—neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair [Col. 1415D] white or black. But let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no. What is beyond these is from evil.”

First, it should be understood here that this saying of the Lord, “Do not swear at all,” differs somewhat in its reasoning from the other sayings of the same Lord. For neither letter nor spirit of the Law anywhere contradicts the commands not to be angry with your brother, not to look upon a woman “in order to desire her,” not to dismiss your wife “except on account of fornication,” not to resist evil, but rather to “offer the other cheek to one striking the right cheek,” or to “do good to those who hate you and pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

But the Law does not seem to have left it to your own choice not to swear at all. For it says: “If the thief remains hidden, the master of the house from whom some thing entrusted to his keeping was stolen shall be brought before the gods, that is, the priests, and shall swear that he has not stretched out his hand against his neighbour’s property in order to commit fraud” (Exod. 22). Again: If anyone entrusts to his neighbour any animal whatever for safekeeping, and it dies, is injured, or is captured by enemies, and no one has seen it, an oath shall be taken between them that he has not stretched out his [Col. 1416A] hand against his neighbour’s property; and the Lord shall accept the oath, and he shall not be compelled to make restitution (ibid.).

How, then, does he tell us not to swear at all, unless in this sense only: that he wishes us to possess in this world as our own nothing that provides an occasion, or even a necessity, for swearing? And truly this is the ordered progress toward the perfection of righteousness: after you have plucked away from yourself your right eye in the manner explained above, then follow completely the counsel given to the person: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matt. 22). Once you have done this, it will lie within your own choice not to swear at all.

What he next says—“Neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by the city Jerusalem, nor by your head shall you swear”—is now not merely counsel but command: for to swear by the elements of the world is altogether a sin. The Jews always practised this most evil custom of swearing by the elements, as prophetic utterance frequently reproves them for doing: they honoured creatures and bodily things with the worship and service due to God. For one who swears certainly either venerates or loves that by which he swears.

Yet here he seems to increase the reverence to be accorded these things when he says of heaven, “because it is God’s throne”; of earth, “because it is his footstool”; and of Jerusalem, “because it is the city of the great King”; and therefore, he says, do not swear by these things. Does he magnify these things in the sense that their majesty must not be profaned by the audacity of swearing by them? On the contrary, he judges them unworthy of the words of an oath. God alone is the sole Creator, and it is by him that one ought to swear if necessity compels an oath. For the Law says: “You shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth” (Exod. 23). Again: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him; you shall cling to him, and swear by his name” (Deut. 6).

This had been granted by the Law, as it were, to children: just as they offered sacrifices to God and not to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because they did this rightly, but because it was better to render this to God than to demons. Therefore, when he says, “Neither shall you swear by heaven,” and adds this reason, “because it is God’s throne,” and likewise of earth, “because it is his footstool,” it is as though he said: Heaven is so much inferior to him by whom alone swearing has been permitted as a seat is inferior to the one sitting upon it; and earth is so much inferior to him as a footstool is inferior to the one beneath whose feet it lies.

Likewise Jerusalem is, to say the most that can be said, the city of a great king—perhaps David, who captured it, or Solomon, who enlarged it, or even God, because the temple of God was founded in it. Why then do you swear by these things, when heaven is not God but, in your understanding, the footstool of God’s feet, because of what he says in the Prophet: “Heaven is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66); when Jerusalem is not God but the city of the great King? And what shall I say of your head? Why do you swear by your head, that is, by yourself, when you did not make yourself? For only he was fittingly able to swear by himself whom no other made, “because,” as the Apostle says, “he had no one greater by whom to swear” (Heb. 6).

He said these things especially with reference to that time, against the Jews, who by swearing by angels, the city Jerusalem, the temple, and the elements, honoured creatures [Col. 1417B] and bodily things with the worship and service due to God. Observe, then, that here the Saviour did not forbid swearing by God, but by heaven and earth, by Jerusalem, and by your head.

But evangelical truth does not admit an oath, since every trustworthy statement should stand in place of an oath. For he says: “But I say to you, do not swear at all. Let your speech be yes, yes; no, no. What is beyond these is from evil”—understood as from the evil of the one by whose weakness or hardness he is compelled to swear.

For example, Abraham was the first man who is recorded as having sworn. The fact that he swore was due to the evil of the man who said: “Swear therefore by the Lord that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my offspring, but that according to the mercy which I have shown you, you will show mercy to me and to the land in which you have lived as a stranger” (Gen. 21). That man was a king, and if Abraham had not sworn when asked by him, Abraham could have appeared more suspect to him.

Similarly, the fact that the Apostle swore to the Corinthians—if what he says falls short in no respect of an oath—“God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie” (2 Cor. 11); and likewise, “I die daily through your glory, brothers”—was due to their evil. Rebuking them, he says: “I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you” (2 Cor. 12).

Once the Christian has begun to follow this counsel not to swear at all—which, as has already been said, he will finally be able to keep only if he frees himself [Col. 1417D] from every worldly affair—what follows, in accordance with his aim of advancing to the perfection of righteousness, except that he should wish to render evil to no one for evil, and should not even resist one who does injury? It follows therefore: “You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you: Do not resist evil.”

Just as the saying to the ancients, “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce” (Deut. 24), so too the saying, “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21), was not a command but a concession or permission, on account of hardness of heart. Such a heart is by no means satisfied by equal retaliation and does not rest unless it has been sated with the punishment of cruelty. Thus here too is the fulfilment of the Law: a person is taught not only not to demand retaliatory punishment, but the ecclesiastical man is trained for endurance of every injury.

“If anyone,” he says, “strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to one who wishes to contend with you at law and take your tunic, surrender to him your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two. Give to the one who asks of you; and do not turn away from one wishing to borrow from you.”

Truly because of this teaching the Saviour says in one place: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). For do not those who do the opposite labour and bear burdens—those who strike back, so far as they can, one who strikes them on the cheek; those who contend with stubborn dispute lest they be overcome by someone wishing to take their tunic or cloak? Conversely, do not those who follow the present counsel find rest even in this present age?

Then what he says, “Give to the one who asks of you,” will be done gladly; indeed, it will be done joyfully, because, as the Apostle testifies, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). How great the gladness there! How great the festivity! Yet it should be noted that he did not say, “Give to the one who asks of you whatever he asks.” For who could always do this? Perhaps he asks for gold, but you have no gold or silver. Therefore say what the Apostle Peter said when the lame beggar looked intently at him, expecting to receive something from him: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you” [Col. 1418C] (Acts 3). For “if readiness of will is present,” the Apostle says to the Corinthians, “it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Cor. 8). And if there is nothing else, offer a good word in reply, because it is written: “A good word is above the best gift” (Prov. 15).

It should be understood that our Lord, who teaches these things, first and especially did what he taught. He gave to the one asking; indeed, he did not wait to be asked, but of his own accord gave more than anyone could know how to ask. As the same Apostle says: “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for our sakes he became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (1 Cor. 8).

To one striking him on the cheek he offered not merely the other cheek but his whole body, that it might be filled with reproaches, as had been said through the prophet Jeremiah (Lam. 3). To one wishing to contend with him in judgment—namely Pilate or the Jewish people—he answered not a word; and to those taking “his seamless tunic, woven from the top throughout” (John 19), he surrendered all his clothing, so that what was written might be fulfilled: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21).

Moreover, when he further says, “Whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two,” it is understood to mean another two thousand paces. He himself had done this, much more gloriously than the letter sounds, shortly before (Acts 1). Here it must first be understood that the sacred Law permits one thousand paces for one observing the Sabbath. But what is, or ought to be, the Sabbath of a spiritual person except a hidden and tranquil meditation upon spiritual things?

Without doubt he kept such a Sabbath in the wilderness when the tempter approached him. Truly this was to be compelled to go a thousand paces: to dispute with the tempter during such a Sabbath (Matt. 15; Luke 4). But he not only endured being compelled once—that is, he not only endured being tempted once—but went with him another two, because besides the first temptation he endured two more: being taken by him into the holy city and led onto a very high mountain. Then he said to him: “Depart, Satan.”

Perhaps you too, O soul of the great Apostle, or of whatever apostolic man, wish to keep Sabbath. You have taken off your tunic, washed your feet, and wish to keep Sabbath in the chamber of hidden contemplation. [Col. 1419B] But “behold, the voice of your beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one’” (Song 5). In saying this, he wishes to compel you to go a thousand paces, which is a Sabbath-day’s journey, as has already been said. He wishes, I say, to compel you, so that, laying aside the repose of solitary contemplation which you had chosen, you may rise, open to him, and go to proclaim his Gospel.

Do this in one part of the world, in Asia, where Jerusalem or Judaea is situated, where his Gospel ought first to be spoken. Go with him another two thousand paces: that is, do not be content to preach in Asia alone, but labour in preaching in Africa and Europe also; preach through labouring, labour through preaching the Gospel. In this way you are beautifully compelled, going with him not merely one thousand paces, but another two, and so they make three thousand paces, because there are three parts of the world.

In such a compulsory service, have you suffered more injury for him than he suffered for you? The devil the tempter compelled him, God and man; but God the Saviour compelled you, a mere human being. Meanwhile, we ought to justify God, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Son himself who speaks here to us; and when we do not receive what we ask from him, nevertheless say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144).

For what then? Did he say only: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 26 [perhaps an erroneous citation]); “Ask and you shall receive; ask and it shall be given you” (Luke [Col. 1419D] 11)? Did he not also say: “Give, and it shall be given you,” and, as we have in the present passage, “Do not turn away from one who asks of you” (Luke 6)? We wish to hear, “Ask and it shall be given you,” and we disregard, “Give and it shall be given you.”

Certainly, just as in Isaiah, where after saying first, “Seek judgment; aid the oppressed,” and so forth, he then finally adds, “Come and reason with me” (Isa. 1), so here you must be learned in the Law: when you have done what he says—“Give to the one who asks of you, and do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow from you”—then at last come and reason with him because you have not received, according to this promise: “Ask and you shall receive.”

One saying remains, O Christian, to be spoken to you; and there were six sayings of the Lord, so that when, as through six days of sayings, you have worked well and fulfilled the Law, then at last, a man who has completed his service, you may rightly enter into the rest of the Lord and be worthy to keep the Sabbath-rest of the children of God.

What is it? “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust.”

You could offer the other cheek to one striking your right cheek even while angry, and say—not, as the Apostle did, declaratively, “The Lord will strike you,” but as an imprecation: “MAY the Lord strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23). You could surrender your cloak as well to one taking your tunic, even while angry, and say—not, as the same Apostle did, threatening or foretelling, “The Lord will repay him,” but cursing or imprecating: “MAY the Lord repay him according to his works” (2 Tim. 4). Thus you would not yet be acting against the least commandment of the Law, “You shall love your friend,” nor against this permission of the Law, “And hate your enemy.”

But for you who are striving toward the highest degree, so that you may be a child of your Father in heaven, it is not fitting to use the permission to hate your enemy. Rather, it is expedient that you love him while he is still an enemy and pray for him. Why then did the Law say, “And hate your enemy”? Is it not the voice of the same one whose voice is also the Gospel? Why then did he delay so long this most kindly saying, “Love your enemy”?

Namely, because this was impossible for the Law, which was weak in this respect through the flesh, as the Apostle says: “In that it was weak through the flesh” (Rom. 8)—that is, through the flesh of those who were under the Law, because they were carnal. Just as, because of the hardness of their hearts, he permitted them to give bills of divorce to their wives, so likewise because of their hardness of heart and the weakness of their flesh he permitted many other things, one of the best known being this: “And hate your enemy”; or, in this form: “The kinsman of the slain man, as soon as he catches the murderer, shall kill him” (Num. 35).

You say to me, then: Is there not today among people the same hardness of heart and weakness of flesh? There is indeed, but an example has been added which the ancients lacked. Teaching ought to have greater force where the teacher commends it by his own works. A commandment ought to be heard when the teacher’s example has strengthened it. Behold, the Son of God, teacher and master, came from heaven: what he commands, he did; what he teaches, he showed by deed.

He loved his enemies: “For,” says the Apostle, “when we were enemies, he reconciled us to God” (Rom. 5). At the very moment of death he prayed for those persecuting and slandering him: “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23); and he pardoned the guilt of his death to all who wished to believe.

This example assists his teaching. Because it was lacking when the Law was given, the Law itself was weak; and since it could not give the spirit of love, it was impossible for it to effect such a thing or compel people to perfection. But this one gave both an example of perfection [Col. 1421A] and the spirit of love; therefore from that time onward he truly demands imitation from us, setting before us a great hope, which, when it comes, certainly exceeds every merit: that we may be children of God, brothers and co-heirs of the only Son of God (Rom. 8).

And in this saying, when he declares, “That you may be children of your Father who is in heaven,” there is implied a great difference between the many children and the only Son of God himself. For he loved his enemies not in order that he might become the Son of God, but because he was the Son of God, according to the nature of his goodness. All the others, however, should love their enemies not because they are children of God, but in order that they may become children of God, through imitation of that goodness “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust.”

If you understand this in a twofold sense, it is of greater force. For it is indeed a great proof of his goodness or kindness that he makes this visible sun rise upon good and evil alike, and rains the rain necessary to the earth upon just and unjust alike. But far greater is this: that he makes known the Sun of righteousness, the true Sun, Christ his Son, to good and evil persons alike, both those who are from the Jews and those who are from the Gentiles; and, watering all with the voluntary rain of evangelical preaching, exhorts them to produce the good fruit of faith or repentance.

“For if you love only those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do? Do not even the Gentiles do this? Be perfect therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

Where the work is more laborious, where the labour is more strenuous, there or from there the reward is greater and a more glorious crown is obtained. Yet many people, measuring God’s commandments by their own weakness rather than by the strength of holy persons, think that what has been commanded is impossible. They say that for virtue it is enough not to hate enemies, but that to love them is more than human nature can bear.

These things are not impossible, but all may be observed, since there are several examples among righteous people who observed them. Stephen the Protomartyr prayed for the enemies stoning him (Acts 7), and Paul desired to be anathema for his persecutors (Rom. 9). Even before the example of this Son of God, of whom it is said—and who himself did this thing, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23)—David, though not commanded, mourned Saul and grieved for Absalom, both persecuting him, both seeking his life (2 Sam. 1).

I said that David acted uncommanded because the Law had not commanded that an enemy be spared or that one should grieve over an enemy. But the Gospel, as in the other matters mentioned above, so in this one supplies the Law’s deficiency.

How great is the grace of this saying—“Be perfect therefore yourselves, as your heavenly Father is perfect”—appears more clearly by contrast: namely, from what the serpent said to our first parents in persuading them to transgress the commandment: “Eat, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). That one, hissing, whispered an evil way as though toward perfection; this one, demonstrating it, proclaimed the good way to true perfection.

“Be perfect,” he says: be perfect not, I say, “like gods,” but like children of God. Be perfect, I say, according to that measure of perfection by which your heavenly Father is perfect: that is, not by hating God’s friend, as the serpent urged should happen, but by loving even enemies, of which thing the heavenly Father himself offers you an example.

That wicked teaching led humanity away to complete dissimilarity from God. This righteous teaching will conform you to the likeness of that same God, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you children of the Most High’” (Ps. 81).

“By this,” says the apostle John, “the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest” (1 John 3). For the children of the devil are those who do not even love friends, imitating in this the devil, who did not love—indeed, hated—his Creator, although the Creator had made him freely great, beautiful, and wise, as is attested in Ezekiel (Ezek. 28; 31), and had placed him upon God’s holy mountain, that is, in heaven. He persuaded humanity (Gen. 3) to have neither faith nor love toward that same Creator, and, following his example, to despise him through a perverse desire for likeness to him—that is, for his divinity.

By contrast, the children of God are those who love even enemies, wishing that they might become friends. They imitate God himself, who, when we were enemies, freely offered us the grace of reconciliation with such abundance of love that he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. 5, 8).

Inviting his hearers to this imitation, when the Son of God had said, “Be perfect yourselves,” he immediately set forth not the quantity but the quality of perfection, adding: “As your heavenly Father is perfect.” This is to say: As he loved you when you were enemies, in order to make friends out of enemies, so you too love your enemies, taking pains, as far as you are able, that they may be converted and become friends.

Having explained these matters, he immediately says:

## CHAPTER VI.

> “Take heed not to do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.”

After those matters hitherto treated—the sayings concerning righteousness, the sayings concerning the fulfilment of the Law, in accordance with his declaration, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfil it”—he now begins to speak against intemperance, exhorting and forming his followers [Col. 1422D] in the virtue of temperance. He begins in this manner, wishing us to be attentive, when he says: “Take heed not to do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.”

Therefore, the venerable and truly heavenly virtue of temperance begins here to be preached—a virtue which the pagans, that is, the Gentiles, empty philosophers, did not know, any more than the other virtues. They declaimed their names indeed in connection with trivial matters, but were ignorant of their nature and dignity, and had no foundation upon which to build them. “I,” he says, “previously told you: ‘Let your light shine before people’; but I did not say, ‘in order to be seen by them.’” That would be to wish to keep sabbath or to glory without God. Rather, I said: “So that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven”; that is, to seek [Col. 1423A] God’s glory and to tend toward his sabbath-rest, where he too rests from his works. Otherwise, if you hasten to receive your reward here—a momentary reward, in the estimation of people, in the praise or favor of the populace, how slight and how meager it is—“you will not have,” he says, “a reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

> “Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, in order to be honored by people. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.”

Therefore, he says, because one who does righteousness before people for the purpose of being seen by them will have no reward, “when you give alms,” and so forth. Among good works proceeding from the root of love, almsgiving is first or chief; prayer follows [Col. 1423B], and then fasting. A little earlier, wishing the root of love to be planted or fixed within the heart, he said: “You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, love your enemies,” and so forth.

If, therefore, the root of love is fixed in the heart, almsgiving is good, prayer is good, and fasting is good and useful. Here the planter of that same love treats of them, because they are life-giving fruits and obtain the reward of eternal life. Yet these same things may be forced outward without the root of love; but with such a yield, all the beauty of these fruits is hypocrisy. For *hypocrisis* means “gilding” (*deauratio*). We understand this Latin term to mean that any object shining on its surface with a golden color is perceived [Col. 1423C] to be inwardly without gold.

Thus, to put it more closely, the hypocrite is one who gives alms, prays, and fasts, yet, lacking inwardly the gold of love, walks doubly: his inner chambers are foul, while his surface is golden. But almsgiving not of that sort—almsgiving that is not hypocrisy, that is, gilding, but is wholly golden, wholly itself gold, whose vein or source of veins is love, whence the true gold of mercy is customarily mined by the hand—this is precious; this ascends to heaven and there delightfully feeds the King of kings and Lord of lords. It is a pleasing drink to him and covers him as a garment, as he himself will testify with his own mouth on the Day of Judgment: “For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” and the rest, down to, “When you did it [Col. 1423D] to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV).

And it should be noted that there are six works of this grace, having a certain likeness to the six days in which God completed the world and everything in it, in that it too earns its own sabbath, so that whoever performs these things may also “rest from his works,” as the Apostle says, “as God did from his” (Heb. IV). The first is: “I was hungry and you gave me to eat”; the second: “I was thirsty and you gave me to drink”; the third: “I was a stranger and you took me in”; the fourth: “I was naked and you covered me”; the fifth: “I was sick and you visited me”; the sixth: “I was in prison and you came to me.”

For those who have performed these things will enter into the sabbath, that is, into the rest [Col. 1424A] of the Lord, when he who rested in himself after six days calls and says: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” The intemperate hypocrite has defrauded his soul of the good of that sabbath-rest, so great and so excellent, because, when giving alms, he sounded a trumpet before himself; he wished to be seen in the synagogues, wished to be heard in the streets, desired to be honored by people, and vainly sought, emptily received, and fruitlessly carried away this reward.

> “But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

For what need is there to employ the left hand where the right alone is sufficient? What need is there for the whole body to be moved or disturbed by running about, shouting, and sounding a trumpet, when the right hand alone, by the slight motion of extending itself, [Col. 1424B] can pour out more than the poor person dared request, and give more than your ability or willingness permits? Would that, while the left hand remained still, you would be willing to give as much as the outstretched right hand can offer before it grows weary or fails.

Therefore do this “so that your almsgiving may be in secret.” Long ago Wisdom also said in Proverbs: “A hidden gift extinguishes anger, and a present in the bosom the greatest indignation” (Prov. XXI). This is that repayment of God which he immediately promises in familiar terms: “And your Father,” he says, “who sees in secret will repay you.” In what sense is he your Father? Surely because you are not content to observe what was said to the ancients, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy”; rather, in fulfilment of that saying: “If your enemy [Col. 1424C] was hungry, you fed him; if he was thirsty, you gave him drink, so that you might overcome evil with good” (Rom. XII)—which is the praiseworthy perfection of all almsgiving. Hence he is your Father, and you are the child of so great a Father, in accordance with the declaration: “Do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.”

The same reasoning and judgment apply to prayer and to fasting: namely, that the wickedness of hypocrisy is to be avoided in them. By it all the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees was leavened—namely, almsgiving, prayer, and fasting—for just as, in giving alms, they sound a trumpet before themselves, so too “they love,” he says, “to pray standing in synagogues and at the street corners, in order to be seen by people. And when they fast, they become sad, in order to appear to people to be fasting.” In each case the righteous Judge delivers one and the same sentence: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.”

Now we must consider what the shaper and teacher of worthy prayer says: “When praying,” he says, “do not speak much like the Gentiles. For they think that they will be heard because of their wordiness; therefore do not be like them. For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” The Gentiles devoted no little effort to verbal expression and the arrangement of words. Among poets Virgil is the greatest or most famous such figure; among historians, Sallust; among orators, Marcus Tullius [Cicero]. If you compare the writings of such men with the holy and divine Scriptures, their chief difference is this: among them [Col. 1425A], trifling and ignoble matters, being earthly and containing nothing heavenly or spiritual, are adorned with words; but in the holy Scriptures, matters do not adorn words—rather, words are reverently adorned by matters. There, carefully sought words, scarcely following the subject-matter [OCR uncertain: *jusque lege vixque*], are forced to lend a kind of majesty to perishable things. Here, however, great and divine matters are followed spontaneously by words; and although the words are beautiful, they are so covered over by the majesty of the things that, unless one pays close attention, eloquence, though present, scarcely appears, gladly accompanying its mistress, wisdom.

“Therefore do not be like them,” he says. Do not think, as they do, that you will be heard through wordiness, and that you can bend or overcome God the Judge by long and elegant speech rather than by the truth of things; [Col. 1425B] nor think that it is necessary to make God teachable or to teach him. “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”

At this point a certain heresy arises, likewise a perverse dogma of the philosophers, who say: “If God knows what we pray, and knows before we ask what we need, we speak pointlessly to one who knows.” To them a brief answer must be given: we are not informants but petitioners. It is one thing to report to one who does not know; it is another to ask one who knows. In the former there is judgment; here there is submission. There we faithfully report; here we pitiably entreat.

More must be said and understood reverently: this beautiful interchange between God and human beings—prayer—must not exist merely for receiving [Col. 1425C], but also for meeting him; that is, when God’s benefits are arriving and the free gifts of the Most High are flowing abundantly, holy prayer should make a solemn and religious response, according to the Psalmist: “And in the morning my prayer shall come before you” (Ps. LXXXVII).

For example, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord,” says Mary; “let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I). At last, it was already happening: she had already heard the word from the angel’s mouth and was conceiving; nevertheless, praying, she said and cried out for herself with an inexpressible cry of the heart: “Let it be done to me according to your word.” This is much like a choir receiving a worthy person, or a solemn gathering proceeding to meet someone—not so that he may come, but because he has come.

Hence we receive daily both spiritual and bodily food with prayer. Though we already have before our eyes or nearly hold in our hands the Lord’s bread of eternal life, and the sustaining bread necessary for this temporal life, nonetheless we pray and say: “Give us this day our daily bread,” because the benevolent will of God, who gives all things, desires the inner countenance of the recipient to be made like itself: what is given by the benefit of divine love should be received with desire, prayer should testify to that desire itself, and thanksgiving should follow prayer in fellowship. Therefore, when he says, “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him,” he does not wish us to think the practice of prayer idle or superfluous, but to avoid wordiness, knowing that long ago he also said of Behemoth to blessed Job: “I will not spare [Col. 1426A] his powerful words, composed for entreaty” (Job XLI).

But what if prayer is prolonged from the affection of divine inspiration? Will it be counted as wordiness and contrary to the instruction: “When praying, do not speak much like the Gentiles”? By no means. Otherwise, what will become of the psalmic prayers—that is, the many psalms proceeding in a rhetorical or supplicatory manner, neither so brief nor lacking elegant composition? I say nothing of the many ecclesiastical prayers which devout assemblies commonly meditate privately and chant publicly, most of them lengthy and composed in brilliant language by learned persons. At present I speak only of the psalms, which we do not doubt were composed by the authoring Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit. [Col. 1426B] Must they then be despised because of the pronouncement, “Do not speak much”?

Accordingly, it must be observed carefully that he did not merely say, “Do not speak much,” but added, “like the Gentiles.” It should therefore be understood as though he had said: Do not speak much, unless perhaps words of prayer flow abundantly from the affection of divine inspiration.

Here is another example. “Knowledge puffs up,” says the Apostle, adding, “but love builds up” (1 Cor. VIII). Does he condemn knowledge in saying this? Certainly not; rather, he commends love and desires it to be present in us together with knowledge. For knowledge without love, it is indeed true, puffs up; it is worldly knowledge. But knowledge with love builds up greatly [Col. 1426C], for it is God’s gift, since the spirit of knowledge is one of the seven spirits of the Lord, fifth in order, which the Prophet enumerated thus: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. II).

Thus, just as the Apostle criticizes knowledge not for its own sake, but for a certain barrenness when it lacks love, saying, “Knowledge puffs up,” so the Lord rejects long and eloquent prayer not for its own sake or for its very length, but for a similar baseness, when someone who lacks holy desire multiplies words in the manner of the Gentiles. For if both are present, it not only benefits the person praying but also builds up the hearer; and so that it may build up more abundantly, much of the Church’s prayer is seasoned with the pleasant sweetness of music. [Col. 1426D]

For hearing musical sweetness in psalmody and prayer has power to invite or awaken in our breast the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to the example of the prophet Elisha, of whom it is written thus in the Book of Kings: “‘As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand,’ he himself said to Joram king of Israel, ‘if I did not respect the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would neither attend to you nor look at you. But now bring me a minstrel.’ And when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Make trenches and trenches in this torrent-bed’” (4 Kings III), and so forth.

I do not doubt that many have attained some small experience of this matter and have sometimes felt, according to that example, in hearing or chanting praise, or prayer sounding well and slowly with musical modulation, that an impulse of the Holy Spirit shook their inmost parts: an overflowing affection of divine inspiration, a great power of holy compunction. Finally, by some power of nature unknown to me, I am affected far more when I hear the Church choir singing sublimely with a multitude of sounds—for example, that prayer of Moses, “I beseech you, Lord, forgive the sins of your people” (Exod. XXXII), and likewise what the same Moses prayed to the same Lord and said: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself openly, that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII)—than if I read or hear the plain wording of that same prayer as it is written in the historical book [Col. 1427B].

What, then, is the value for us of this instruction in brevity, by which he wishes to form us when he says: “Thus, therefore, you shall pray”? Surely this: an infirm mind can better escape by concision or brevity the vice of boastfulness or self-exaltation, which commonly steals in through wordiness. Moreover, this manner of prayer, which cultivates brevity, is easier than other forms and more suitable both for all little ones and for the greater.

For there are three modes of prayer in which the Lord is pleased, and a fourth which wholly displeases him. The first mode is when prayer is prolonged through the affection of divine inspiration, as was just said. So it was with Hannah, who multiplied prayers to such an extent that Eli judged her drunk. “And it came to pass,” says Scripture, “when [Col. 1427C] she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth. But Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard at all. Therefore Eli thought her drunk and said to her: ‘How long will you be drunk? Digest for a while the wine with which you are soaked’” (1 Kings I).

Like her, the Church from the Gentiles, formerly barren for God but now having borne many, fittingly multiplies prayers before the Lord. And from the time she began so to speak, Eli—that is, the empty wisdom of the old priesthood—judged her drunk. For they said: “These people are full of new wine” (Acts II), not knowing and mocking the grace which afterwards caused this barren woman to bear children.

The second manner of prayer, which the Lord commends in the present passage, is this: the person praying should know that the Lord hears not in a loud voice or in wordiness, but in contrition of heart; and that prayer ought to be brief and pure, as this: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth.

The third manner is when someone prays inwardly with a concealed prayer, not only without a loud voice but even without movement of the lips. Moses prayed in this way when Pharaoh was pursuing him and the Lord said to him: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV). For he then said nothing with his mouth to the Lord, but his great cry was great desire. Hence the Psalmist: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparations of their heart” (Ps. IX).

The fourth manner of prayer, as has already been said, wholly displeases the Lord: namely, where there is wordiness without the affection of divine inspiration. This alone is possessed, or can be possessed, by hypocrites, who speak much like the Gentiles, standing in synagogues and at street corners, or praying while standing and desiring to be seen. Of the three modes of prayer already mentioned, he prescribes as more convenient and suitable for little ones and great alike the easier manner—namely, the shorter one, content with few words—saying: “Thus therefore you shall pray: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,’” and so forth.

This prayer perhaps appeared inadequate to the Lord’s disciples, still untrained, because of its brevity. For, as Luke relates, when he was praying in a certain place, after he had ceased, one of his disciples said to him: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples [Col. 1428B]” (Luke II). What sort of thing was this: that the disciples of the Lord should ask him to teach them to pray just as the man John had taught—for John was a man? Yet no one but God alone can teach us to pray as we ought. Hence the Apostle: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII).

Therefore, since they wished to be taught as a human being can teach another human being, as John, a man, could have taught his disciples (Luke XI), what or how did he answer them? “When you pray,” he says, “say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name; may your kingdom come; give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us [Col. 1428C] our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us; and do not lead us into temptation.’”

If the form of prayer which he himself voluntarily taught on the mountain according to this evangelist Matthew seemed insufficiently composed or inadequate to them, and they therefore asked elsewhere to be taught, as John taught prayer, he fittingly not only did not increase the composition or length of their prayer, but even shortened it. For he omitted two of the seven petitions, the third and the last: “May your will be done as in heaven and on earth,” and “but deliver us from evil”; and he omitted the very brief praise which here in Matthew he prefaced—as it is customary to begin prayer with praise—after the first address: “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

Without delay, so that it might become more and more clear to one who speaks with God that one need not weary oneself with long or elaborate speech: “Which of you will have a friend, and will go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey and I have nothing to set before him’” (Luke XI)? Surely one who comes thus to a friend’s door brings no long, premeditated, carefully composed or polished speech; rather, even if he must stand and plead the whole night, his speech is one and the same, brief, repeated a hundred times and resounding a thousand: “Friend, lend me three loaves.”

According to this example, “Ask,” he says, “and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you.” What do we ask? What do we seek? The good Spirit, he says: “For if you, though you are evil, [Col. 1429A] know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those asking him”—understood: the Spirit who will teach you to pray. For you said: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples,” not knowing that teaching of this kind belongs not to John or any human being, but to the good Spirit alone, the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, if you seek a short path to acquire the knowledge of prayer, you will not have such need either of this brief prayer according to Matthew or of that briefer one according to Luke. Only persist in asking the Father, petitioning the Friend: “Give me the good Spirit; give me the Holy Spirit.” When he has given him to you, you will truly possess the knowledge of prayer; and, in a marvelous way, you will be so intensely occupied in prayer that you will scarcely be able to utter a word [Col. 1429B], because continuous groaning, wholly occupying the office of the voice, will leave no leisure.

Hence this saying: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII). But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God.

We rightly receive, then, this Lord’s Prayer and its parts—the seven petitions, the first of which is “Hallowed be your name,” and the last, “But deliver us from evil”—as the first rudiments of that knowledge or teaching by which we are formed for prayer. For these were delivered, as it were, to children, who had not yet received the Paraclete Spirit and sometimes said: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.”

Even if we have become so perfect that, as was said above, that Spirit prays or intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings, this prayer nevertheless—the Lord’s Prayer, the first of all prayers—must not fall from our mouths, lest we appear great in our own eyes and as though we had no need of this prayer, which has been proposed as if to children, that is, beginners, so that they may have some beginning of dissimilarity from the wickedness of hypocrites, whose whole prayer is wordiness (Eph. II).

Indeed, it is brief and suited to the small; yet it can also delight and exercise the great. Above all, there is this address: “Our Father.” Who is he to whom we say, “Our Father”? We, once children of wrath, children of Gehenna, children of death, children of the devil, say “Our Father” to the Father of mercies, the Father of the heavenly homeland, the Father of everlasting life, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, God equal and coeternal with himself (Rom. VI; Gal. III). Through the grace of this only-begotten Son we speak thus to this Father, by whom we have been born again, because we had been badly born; and by a marvelous shortening our evil lot has thus been changed, since we became children of God by believing in him who, though he alone was the Son of God, became a participant in our nature (1 Pet. I).

All creation marvels at this grace; the holy Church proclaims it throughout the world; angels venerate it; archangels revere it; thrones magnify it; dominions glorify it; principalities praise it; powers adore it; virtues bless it; cherubim and seraphim desire to look into it. This brief praise, “who art in heaven,” indicates that we too should marvel at so great a grace [Col. 1430A]. For what teachable child in prayer, what child ready to invoke a father, would not marvel that this Father, while he is in heaven—that is, may be seen only in invisible things, which are invisible to us—has begotten us here in this visible world, where no human being sees him? Thus the apostle James says: “Of his own will,” he says, “he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some firstfruits of his creation” (Jas. I).

Although by the name “heavens” the invisible homeland is signified, where the holy angels dwell and to which Christ ascended on the fortieth day after his resurrection, in the sight of the apostles, nevertheless the aforementioned nine orders of angels are also called, and are, heavens. In heavens of this kind our Father is. This is their blessedness: that God is in them—that is, that he remains and does not change—as he says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III). They always possess in themselves his unchangeable essence; they always, without any end, are and will be blessed and immortal; and they will immortally feed on that highest good with which they are full and will remain full.

Hence all Christians—great and small, rich and poor, noble and common, masters and servants, kings and beggars, rulers together with the lowly populace, absolutely all without any distinction of nation or condition, sex, age, rank, or office—say “Our Father” to him; none of us says, “My Father.” There is one firstborn and only-begotten Son, a Son not of grace, as we are, but of nature alone. To him it belongs to say, “My Father”; and when he was delivered up, he said: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). Nowhere is he read to have said, “Our Father” [Col. 1430C]. Why is this? Clearly because God is Father differently to him and to us: he begot him; he adopted us.

After this address has been prefaced, the first petition is: “Hallowed be your name.” The Lord’s name always was and is holy; yet there is a manner of its sanctification useful to us, which he promised through the Prophet in this way: “I will sanctify my great name, says the Lord, so that all nations may know that I am the Lord when I have been sanctified in you before them.” Then, as though someone asked, “How will you sanctify your name?”, he says: “For I will take you from the nations, [Col. 1430D] gather you from all lands, bring you into your land, pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in your midst” (Ezek. XXXVI), and the rest. By these words, plainly, the grace of Christ’s baptism is foreshadowed.

Therefore, for believers in Christ to be taken from the nations, gathered from every land, and baptized for the remission of sins—this is the sanctifying of your name, O God, Father of all, because in this way those upon whom your name is invoked become holy. Indeed, this sanctification is truly the sanctification of your name, because it is given not so much to them as to your name, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Not to us, Lord, not to us; but give glory to your name” (Ps. CXIII).

So that this sanctification might extend to more people, Christ himself was first sanctified by the same baptism by which he was baptized in dying, as he foretold: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke II). And at the very point of his Passion, after praying to the Father, “Sanctify them in the truth,” he immediately added: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (John XVII). For what is it for the Holy of holies himself to be sanctified, except that he be sanctified for the sins of all and that the iniquities of us all, which God had laid upon him, be taken away? (Isa. LIII.) In that act of sanctification, O God the Father, your name was sanctified, because through the outpouring of blood and water from his side those upon whom your name had been invoked were sanctified [Col. 1431B] and received remission.

Thus, when we say, “Hallowed be your name,” we say: Let the nations be converted and receive remission of sins through your name. This is the sum of all the prayers which we offer, whether for our catechumens, for heretics and schismatics, or even for the faithless Jews and for pagans still unbelieving: that they may be converted to the true and living God and to his only Son Jesus Christ, our God and Lord—“Hallowed be your name.”

The second petition is: “May your kingdom come.” When he instructed his disciples by this prayer, the sacrament of baptism, which is for us the sanctification of the Lord’s name, had not yet been instituted; likewise [Col. 1431C] the kingdom of God had not yet come (Matt. IV), but was drawing near, according to the beginning of the Gospel proclamation: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Luke XVII). For from the moment when the prince of this world was cast out, the kingdom of God came and is within us. Foretelling that this would happen shortly through his Passion and resurrection, he said: “For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (John XII).

Until then death reigned. Although the Law had entered in, sin nevertheless tyrannized, as the Apostle says, after declaring, “But death reigned from Adam to Moses,” and so forth: “But the Law entered in so that transgression might abound” (Rom. V). Why, then, do we still pray: “May your kingdom come”? Clearly, so that all things may be subjected to the King of his kingdom, and that the whole of what the Psalmist said may be fulfilled. After saying, “You crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the works of your hands,” he added: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. VIII).

Hence the Apostle says: “But now, we do not yet see all things subjected to him; but we see the Lord Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor” (Heb. II). And elsewhere he says: “Then comes the end, when Christ hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule, power, strength, and dominion. For he must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet. But the last enemy to be destroyed [Col. 1432A] will be death” (1 Cor. XV).

Therefore, although the kingdom of God has already come and is already within us, ever since Christ was crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, we nevertheless still pray, “May your kingdom come”: that is, let it be brought to completion by the final destruction of death; let nothing remain unsubdued to him, and let no stumbling block remain, according to his saying elsewhere: “And they shall gather out of his kingdom all stumbling blocks” (Matt. XIII).

The third petition: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” According to the sense just stated, this is almost superfluous; thus Luke, in his concern for brevity, omitted it, as was said above. For who reigns without his will being done? (Luke XIX.) Nevertheless, there is a certain difference: he reigns over good and evil alike, even over those who said, “We do not want this man to reign over us”; as he says in the Prophet: “And I will reign over you in my wrath” (Ezek. XX). But his will is present only in the good and holy. Hence he says to Jerusalem: “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate; but you shall be called My-Will-Is-in-Her” (Isa. LXII). Conversely, he says to the reprobate: “I have no will in you” (Mal. I).

Therefore, when we say, “May your kingdom come,” since he will reign even over his adversaries, we rightly pray that he himself may cause our submission to be voluntary, by saying: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For in heaven—that is, in the blessed spirits—his will has been and is done, and nothing resists him, since the adversary was cast down with his satellites. He fell because he resisted through the rebellion of an evil will; hence he was also called the Devil and Satan (Rev. XII).

And if his wills are many, because his commands are many—as he says in the Psalm: “For the saints who are in his land, I have made all my wills wonderful in them” (Ps. XV)—this is his chief will: that we may live and be saved. Hence the Son himself says: “This is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose none of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day.” And again: “This is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John VI).

The fourth petition: “Give us this day our supersubstantial bread” [Col. 1432D]. Here indeed we read “supersubstantial,” but in Luke, “daily bread.” We may understand supersubstantial bread to be that which is above all substances and surpasses all creatures, he who says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (ibid.). Others simply think, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Having food and clothing, we are content with these” (1 Tim. VI), that the saints are concerned only with present food; hence also the later command: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. VI). Jacob, setting out as a wanderer, is first recorded as having asked or hoped for such bread from God: “If,” he says, “the Lord is with me and keeps me in the way in which I walk and gives me bread to eat” (Gen. XXVIII), and so forth.

Another bread is the word of God, concerning which it is said: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII; Matt. IV). God threatens its lack through the Prophet to a sinful people: “I will send you a famine,” he says, “of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII). A third bread is the flesh of Christ, which he gives us from the holy altar, as he said: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world” (John VI).

Whichever of these three you consider, it is God’s gift, and no one besides him can give it. If you inquire concerning sustaining bread, who else makes the earth produce it? If concerning spiritual bread, which is the word of God, how is it given except through God’s inspiration? “How,” says the Apostle, “shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. XX.) If concerning sacramental bread, who but [Col. 1433B] God can make it be given to you for life and received by you for the remission of sins? Therefore: “Give us this day our daily bread,”

Thus even a wise man, even a king, may speak so as truthfully to confess—and not be ashamed to confess—saying: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. 39).

The fifth petition: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” How we, whose debts are many, should forgive our debtors, the very author of this prayer taught by his own example—he who owed nothing to anyone. For when he was being crucified, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 22). For he knew that among them were some who did not know what they were doing, and who would say [616; Col. 1433C] to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). Very many of them were going to believe, and his blood was forgiven them, in accordance with the petition of him who said: “Father, forgive them.” Likewise, we ought to wish this for all our debtors and not seek vengeance from them; then, with unrestrained mouth and secure mind, we shall be able to say: “Forgive us as we forgive.”

But what if they do not fail to know what they are doing, but persecute us and kill us out of envy, especially on account of Christ? Are we required to forgive them if we wish our own debts to be forgiven? Indeed, not only without blame but even justly we cry out what is very well known and customary: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your saints which has been shed, and repay our neighbors [Col. 1433D] sevenfold into their bosom” (Ps. 78). Does not the very person of Christ utter similar words in the Prophet—indeed, words nearly more severe? “Let,” he says, “their wives be childless and widows, and let their husbands be slain by death,” and the rest, which he concludes thus: “Do not be merciful to their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before your face. Let them fall before you; in the time of your wrath deal with them” (Jer. 18).

This agreement does not compel us to forgive our debtors monetary debts or debts of any other things lawfully owed to us—unless perhaps out of mercy, when the debtor, reduced by poverty, is unable to repay. For even the Lord himself by no means remits what is lawfully due to him, or what someone has once vowed to him, whether it be good or evil [Col. 1434A]; nor does he permit one thing to be exchanged for another. Rather, he says: “If anyone changes it, both what is changed and that for which it is changed shall be consecrated to the Lord and shall not be redeemed” (Lev. 27).

The sixth petition: “And lead us not into temptation.” Does God, then, customarily lead people into temptation, so that we say to him, “And lead us not into temptation”? Certainly not into the temptation of evil, the temptation of desire, or of sin. “Let no one,” says the apostle James, “when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God. For God is not a tempter of evils. He himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1).

There is another temptation, namely tribulation, which this world brings upon many in various ways; and God is accustomed to test his saints by such temptation. Hence the saying [Col. 1434B] through Wisdom: “God tested them and proved them as gold in the furnace” (Wis. 3). Rightly and wisely, fearing to be so tested—that is, afflicted—and being fearful, we say to God and ask the Father: “And lead us not into temptation.” But someone says: Is it not glorious and desirable to be crowned after being tested and proved in tribulation? Did not holy martyrs become glorious through temptations of this kind? Should we not therefore rather desire temptation?

If it pleases one to understand here also the temptation of sin, “And lead us not into temptation” must be understood only as though it said: “And do not permit us to be led into temptation.”

The seventh petition: “But deliver us from evil. Amen.” As has already been said above, according to Luke he omitted this, as also that third [Col. 1434C] petition, “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth,” for the sake of brevity, while wishing more fully to impress upon those who had not yet understood from this first instruction that those who pray ought not to speak much. And indeed, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” seem to signify one and the same thing, since not being led into temptation is plainly to be delivered from evil. Nevertheless, evil is the more universal name for those things which harm and are opposed to human nature or salvation. For, not to mention other things, death itself is an evil, hell is an evil, and the devil is evil—from whom may the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, deliver us. Amen: this seal of the Lord’s Prayer is interpreted “truly” [Col. 1434D] or “faithfully.”

Behold, this is the Lord’s Prayer, divided into seven parts—that is, petitions—and it is itself the model of all prayers, so that whatever we wish to ask from God our Father, we may test here whether what we ask is pleasing to God or suitable for our salvation. For if the intention of the petitioner departs from any one of these petitions, he does not ask at all in the name of the Savior; and therefore he should not claim for himself the promise of him who says: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16).

And indeed, in all the petitions the Father’s goodness shines forth; but in the fifth—“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—both goodness and severity shine forth together, which he immediately confirms thus: “For if you forgive people their sins [Col. 1435A], your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offences; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.” How well the goodness and severity of the loving Father and righteous Judge has, through this condition, provided reconciliation for all who seek it, just as he himself had earlier prescribed, saying: “Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar; first go and be reconciled to your brother, and then, when you return, offer your gift” (Matt. 5).

We read that this same Lord, when he set forth his commandments and judgments to his people through Moses, spoke thus: “Whoever strikes a man intending to kill him shall surely be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hand, I will appoint for you a place to which he must flee [Col. 1436A]” (Exod. 21)—it is understood: lest the relative of the slain man kill him; this he lays down more fully elsewhere (Num. 35).

What stronger or more securely fortified city could there be for offenders to flee to than this union of justice or charity: “If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you”? For who, wishing to be a son of this Father, would dare to break the bars and bolts of this city and take vengeance upon one who has fled into it, desiring reconciliation?

Therefore, since he had said above, “First go and be reconciled” (Matt. 5), and since a person might plead the difficulty of reconciliation—suppose that the Lord had said, “I will appoint for you a place to which you must flee” (Exod. 21), that is, I will establish a condition concerning the forgiveness of sins, into which your brother, fearing to fall, may accept your satisfaction.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 1435]

[Col. 1435B] 617 “Mercy and truth,” says the Psalmist, “God loves; the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83). In accordance with this truthful song, the Son of God speaks the things which we have now considered and are considering: “But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” And: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” There is mercy there; there is the truth which God loves. And what will he repay you with, if not grace and glory? Conversely, imitators and crafty persons provoke God’s wrath—such, indeed, as were those supreme hypocrites, the Scribes [Col. 1435C] and Pharisees, against whom he says: “Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do.” And: “When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites.” In these three works he declares that he loves truth. For this is the third: “But when you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

Moses is recorded as the first of all to have fasted. For from the time when the first man transgressed the law of self-restraint, [Col. 1435D] not obeying the command to refrain from one tree, no one is recorded as having considered how he might in any way win the favor of the Lord’s face by fasting—a face which that man, by disobediently eating forbidden food, had offended. Moses, already mentioned, is not recorded as having been commanded to fast; rather, he fasted voluntarily, that he might be found worthy to receive and write down the word proceeding from the mouth of God, by which man lives (Deut. 8). Again he fasted, that he might obtain forgiveness [Col. 1436B] of sin for the people, as Moses himself says: “And I fell down before the Lord as before, forty days and forty nights, neither eating bread nor drinking water, because of all your sins which you committed against the Lord and by which you provoked him to anger. And taking your sin which you had made—the calf—I burned it with fire” (Deut. 9).

Fasting, therefore, is a thing of divine authority: not because God commanded it or his finger wrote it on the tablets, but because no mortal man could fast for forty days and forty nights, once and again, without the power of God. By fasting Moses came very near to God, from whom the first man, by eating, had withdrawn exceedingly far. Moses, Elijah, and Daniel, having a good cause and intention for fasting, worthy of God, made fasting glorious and praiseworthy: namely, they intended and awaited this, that God would send the seed promised to Abraham—that is, Christ. When he came, there was no longer a need to fast until he should be taken away from them, as he himself said to the Pharisees when they asked why his disciples did not fast: “Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9).

The gloomy hypocrites neither had nor have this cause for fasting; yet they fasted and frequently fast, without desiring Christ. And with a remarkable hardness of empty heart they sometimes labor more in fasting than those who desire Christ and eternal life. The word “they disfigure” (*exterminant*) signifies something quite different from what is commonly understood. An exile is “dis-territorialized” (*exterminatur*) when he is sent beyond the boundaries. Thus, for this expression we should always understand “they demolish” or “disfigure.” The hypocrite demolishes his face so as to feign sadness; perhaps while his mind is glad, he bears mourning [Col. 1437A] in his countenance.

What follows—“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face”—is spoken according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people commonly anoint their heads on feast days. He therefore commands that, when we fast, we should show ourselves cheerful and festive. But what are we to do, whose custom neither is nor has been to anoint the head on feast days? How shall we do what he says: “But when you fast, anoint your head, that you may not appear to people to be fasting”? Therefore it is not superfluous here to admit an anagogical sense: to anoint our head is to gladden the heart, which is our governing part. For, as concerning almsgiving, so also concerning fasting, it is rightly understood to have been said: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). Finally, to rejoice in the Holy Spirit [Col. 1437B] is to be anointed with oil, because the Holy Spirit is called oil, as in the passage: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44).

We can rejoice in this joy while fasting if our conscience bears witness that, during the fasting itself, it is nourished by holy longing for the Bridegroom who has been taken from us. The hypocrites do not seek this joy and are therefore here called gloomy. Those others did not know it, of whom the prophet Zechariah speaks thus: “Sarasar and Rogomelech, and the men who were with him, sent to the house of God to entreat the face of the Lord, so that he might say to the priests and prophets of the Lord: ‘Must I weep in the fifth month, or must I sanctify myself, as I have done for many [Col. 1437C] years now?’” (Zech. 7). Since the Babylonian captivity had been ended and the handmade temple was being rebuilt, they thought that no reason remained for them to weep or fast. As though that captivity alone had to be mourned, rather than the universal captivity of the human race which occurred in Adam; and as though the rebuilding of that handmade temple were the end of all evils, rather than the future temple—the temple of the Lord’s body—which in due course had to be built, then destroyed, and raised after three days.

Therefore they ought to have been answered thus, and thus they were answered: 618 “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months throughout these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (ibid.). That is to say: Do you not, in this manner, seek not God’s glory but your own, while you mourn and fast over temporal matters because they are lacking, or so that they may abound, and do not care that the kingdom of God is delayed and has not yet come? It shall not be so; rather, “the fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah for joy and gladness and splendid festivals, until peoples come and dwell in many cities, and ten men from all the languages of the nations take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man” (Zech. 8), and so forth. What the Gospel here says—that one fasting should anoint the head and wash the face—the prophet had there said: that fasting ought to become joy, gladness, and splendid festivals.

There is, therefore, a threefold distinction among those who fast. Some fast for the kingdom of God because, by the hidden counsel and just judgment of divinity, it is delayed and has not yet come to them. Others fast because of the unhappy remembrance of adverse events that happened in temporal affairs. Others fast from a desire for human praise, that they may be glorified by people as righteous, because they are filled with wretched ambition. In accordance with these distinctions, he continues by exhorting his own and says:

“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not dig through or steal.” For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

Is storing up treasure only the gathering of money? Indeed, to perform works of whatever sort, whether good or evil, is to store up treasure. For just as one who does good stores up eternal glory—therefore it is written of one who fears the Lord, “He has stored up delight and exultation for him” (Sir. 15)—so also one who does evil is rightly said to store up wrath. Hence the Apostle says: “But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. 9). Here we must understand this chiefly of good works, namely almsgiving, prayers, and fasts, because the discussion has so far concerned these.

Thus, those who fasted without anointing their heads or washing their faces are those whose treasures, stored on earth, have been destroyed by moth or rust. For a head is very moth-eaten and a face rusty where the entire fruit of fasting consists in being seen and glorified by people, while, because of their sadness and the emaciation of their gloomy countenance, wicked hypocrites are thought holy. Conversely, those who have anointed their heads with the oil mentioned above and washed their faces, in accordance with “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9)—whose cheerfulness is the hope laid up in heaven—are those whose treasures, stored in heaven, are destroyed neither by moth nor rust. For the dryness of moth never touches the head that delights in the Holy Spirit.

Almost midway between these are those whose reason for fasting has an earthly foundation, though not altogether and not like the reason of hypocrites, but simply and almost childishly—like those mentioned above, who, when the Babylonian captivity had ended and the temple was being rebuilt, said: “Must I weep in the fifth day [month], or sanctify myself, as I have done for many years now?” (Zech. 7). For persons of this kind do not indeed possess the knowledge of fasting rightly; yet we do not therefore attribute to them the wickedness of hypocrites. For it is one thing truly to grieve for losses of temporal possessions and to mourn without pretense; it is another, without any contrition of mind or spirit, to twist an anointed head round like a hoop and spread out sackcloth and ashes, in order to acquire a reputation for holiness.

For cruel murderers too could fast in this way, while meditating upon cruelty or murder itself. For example, Jezebel says: “Proclaim a fast, and have Naboth sit among the foremost of the people; and send two men, sons of Belial, against him, and let them bear false witness, saying: ‘Naboth has cursed God and the king.’ Then bring him out, stone him, and let him die” (3 Kgs. 21). This was one thing; quite another was the case when “Ahab heard the words of Elijah, tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with head bowed down, so that evil might not come in his days” (ibid.). In that case Ahab, by fasting, was not a hypocrite, storing something up for himself so that the Lord might say: “Because he has humbled himself on my account, I will not bring evil in his days” (ibid.).
