Nevertheless, he stored up this very thing on earth, “where thieves dig through and steal.” [Col. 1439B] Such indeed was Jehu: although by the Lord’s command he destroyed Ahab’s house, he nevertheless pursued not the Lord’s glory but his own desire; for when he reigned, he did not do the Lord’s will by abandoning the calves made by Jeroboam (4 Kgs. 9).

What, then, is it to store up treasure in heaven? Or indeed, what is this heaven in which we are to store up treasure? Certainly not the aerial heaven, nor that which was made on the second day, as it is written: “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,’ and God called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1); but the third heaven, which was made in the beginning, as it is likewise written: “In the beginning God created heaven [Col. 1439C] and earth.” It is the invisible heaven, the invisible homeland of blessed spirits, and is called “the heaven of heaven” (Ps. 113), because in comparison with it the earth, this heaven, and whatever can be seen by earthly eyes are earth.

How ought we to store up treasures in that heaven? Surely by fasting, giving alms, and mourning in every other way, because the Bridegroom, who has been taken away from us his children, went there and has not yet returned. This cause is heavenly; and therefore one who has it is rightly said to store up treasure in heaven—in a safe place, since thieves do not dig through or steal there, nor do rust and moth destroy. Once there were thieves there: namely, the devil and his angels, who, as if digging through, desired to steal the honor of divinity. But they were unable to do so. Rather, all the honor and beauty bestowed upon them by the Creator was destroyed by the rust and moth of most wicked hypocrisy. For, as it is reproached to him through the prophet, “He walked perfect in his ways amid fiery stones” (Ezek. 28). That perfection was hypocrisy: appearing to be what he was not, like the Most High. Rusted by that hypocrisy, he is now no splendid angel but a foul devil, displaying a moth-eaten head.

Such thieves were there, but they are there no longer, nor will they be; and that heaven, purified by their fall, did not afterward admit, nor will ever admit, moth or rust. Store up treasure there, he says; and then, addressing the conscience of each person familiarly: “For where your treasure is,” he says, “there your heart [Col. 1440A] will be also.” What sort of saying this is may be understood to some extent by comparison with oneself: a person, driven or reminded by the need of a vow, a promise, or any debt, often turns his heart toward the place where he knows that he has deposited something by which he can free himself. Who could lawfully repel him from receiving his treasure whenever he wished or whenever the time came? Now is any injustice ever done in heaven, so that, when the time comes, his heart—that is, he himself, being admitted—may not go there to enjoy the treasures he stored there? Meanwhile, while he lives, his heart is always there, where he has entrusted to the Lord’s hands and sent ahead whatever good works may enable him to be redeemed on the day of judgment.

“The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be!” Its meaning is this: I did not say universally to all of you who give alms, “Let your alms be in secret”; nor, “But when you pray, enter into the chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father”; nor, “But when you fast, anoint your heads.” Rather, I spoke in the singular: “But when you give alms,” and so forth, because I do not say this to everyone, nor ought it to be said to everyone, but to you individually, to one or another—likewise to each person whose eye may be weak, whose intention is not yet sufficiently [Col. 1440C] firm.

“For the lamp of your body is your eye”; and you must understand that, according to this comparison, the lamp of your work is your intention. “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light”; and you must understand that, by the same comparison, if your intention is without hypocrisy and without the cloud of any wretched vanity, then your whole work will be full of light. “But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark”; and likewise you should know that, if your intention is hypocritical, your whole work will be dark, whether it is fasting, prayer, or almsgiving. “Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be!” That is: if good works which you perform before people are rejected because of hypocrisy, what judgment do the evil works done in secret deserve?

Therefore, have a single eye—that is, a good intention—in your heart, and act as you wish. For if such an eye is single, then what you do is certainly acceptable to God: whether you sprinkle your head with ashes or thoroughly anoint it with oil while fasting; whether you make a long or short prayer; whether you give alms to the poor before many witnesses or with no one knowing. This single eye, this good intention, is to desire that people, seeing your works, may glorify the Father who is in heaven. Conversely, the evil eye, the bad intention, is to seek to be glorified by people. This makes everything you do dark, whether ashes or oil are on your head, whether your prayer is long or short, whether your alms are public or secret. Meanwhile, while the eye has not yet been purified, while your intention can be injured by a slight wind or breath of wretched vanity, take care, as I said, that you are not seen by people to be fasting, giving alms, or praying.

“No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon. Therefore I tell you: do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear.” So far there had to be restraint from the malignant excess of the hypocrites, whose very restraint in food contains a great vice of intemperance. He now adds something still better and more perfect: that those suited to spiritual pursuits should desire to be released and free from every occupation of worldly cares, from every anxiety concerning marketable things also, in accordance with: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10).

He begins thus: “No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other.” He first sets forth this general proposition concerning masters, whose truth reason itself readily grants, in order then appropriately to introduce the particular proposition, resting upon the same firmness of truth: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” For it should be known that “two masters” is not the same as if he had said “two men,” or “two kings or powers.” One person may serve two men, two kings, or two powers, because two kings or two rulers can be in harmony with one another, as Solomon and Hiram, king of Tyre, were mutually allied (3 Kgs. 5). The craftsman Hiram could serve them both in the building of the Lord’s house: King Hiram sent him as a prudent and highly skilled man, who knew “how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, marble, wood, purple, [Col. 1441D] violet, fine linen, and scarlet,” and prudently to devise whatever was needed in the work (2 Chron. 2).

But that no one can serve two masters is truly said because lordship is the arrogance of pride, and a duality of lordship can never exist without the rupture of opposition. For there is one Lord, one God (Eph. 4); the others called gods or lords are called so only by supposition and are not such. Nevertheless, custom has prevailed that each person is called and is lord within his own right; thus, for example, King David was called lord and king in his own kingdom. Two masters began to exist there when the unity of lordship was split into duality, when his son Absalom seized lordship against that same father (2 Sam. 16). Certainly no one could serve those two. Either he hated one and loved the other—as, for example, Hushai, who, because he was a good servant, loved the good master and hated the evil one, dwelling with Absalom and, by marvelous and admirable cunning, providing for and serving David’s safety. Or he endured one and despised the other—as Ahithophel, who certainly did not love Absalom, but endured him in order to despise David, his lawful master. For did one who gave him the counsels we read of love him, or know how to love? Indeed, the same judgment must be made of nearly all Israel: namely, that it loved neither Absalom nor Sheba son of Bichri nor Jeroboam nor the other kings whom it had. For it killed and changed them so often; yet it endured their lordship in order that it might despise the lawful lordship of David’s house, repeatedly saying, as Scripture recalls: “What portion have we in David?” (2 Sam. 20); or, “What inheritance have we in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kgs. 12).

Therefore, he says, you cannot serve God and Mammon. These are two masters utterly opposed to one another, like truth and falsehood, like justice and injustice. God, indeed, is the true Lord and alone rules by right. But Mammon—that is, the prince of this world—is a false master, rules unjustly, and lies utterly about all the glory of the world when he says: “Because all these things have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Matt. 4). For not he, but the Most High alone “rules in the kingdom of men,” as was declared from heaven to Nebuchadnezzar, “and gives it to whomever he wills” (Dan. 4).

No one can serve these two masters; no one can love both or hate and despise both. If one loves the true Lord, one hates pride, as David, mentioned above, says in the psalm: “I have hated iniquity, but I have loved your law” (Ps. 118). But if one loves the false master, one hates the true Lord, as of the Jews the Savior says: “But now,” he says, “they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15); and they say, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “We have made a covenant with death, and made a pact with hell” (Isa. 28). This is horrifying and excessively harsh even to hear: that someone should hate God and make a pact with the devil and hell. It belongs wholly to the ungodly and the desperate.

But to endure one and despise the other—and not only to endure God while despising the devil—sometimes happens even to the elect; for example, to David already mentioned. At one time he endured the devil, whom he never loved, and despised God: namely, when he was tempted and sinned against Uriah. “Why then,” says the Lord, “have you despised the word of the Lord, so as to do evil in my sight? Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house for ever, because you have despised [Col. 1443A] me” (2 Sam. 12), and so forth. He despised the good Lord, enduring the evil master for the advantage of perverse pleasure. That master is also called there “the stranger,” because he is far from the city of God. For Nathan’s statement that the rich man, sparing to take from his own sheep and cattle to provide a meal for the stranger who had come to him, took the poor man’s ewe, is a parabolic expression signifying how David endured the evil master and despised the good one.

Again, the same David, despising the evil master as he was accustomed to despise him in all things except that affair of Uriah the Hittite, endured the good Lord—understand, the Lord correcting him because he had numbered the people—and said: “I am in great distress; but it is better that I should fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, than into the hands of men” (2 Sam. 24).

Since, therefore, you cannot serve these two masters, I tell you—and advise you—to withdraw so far from the evil master, namely Mammon, that you should not even “be anxious for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear.” For this anxiety has scandalized many, causing them to endure the evil master and despise the good Lord—not merely for an hour, as temptation scandalized holy David, but to the end, as it did Saul, who preceded him. For Saul, being excessively anxious about worldly honor and the present life, not only endured the evil master unwillingly during life, through contempt for the Lord; at the end of his life he willingly submitted to him, consulting the spirit of Python and eating the calf served by the woman who practiced divination (1 Sam. 28).

One person is scandalized more, another less, by the cares of this age and anxieties of this life. It is indeed lawful and permitted by the law to possess means, to provide what is necessary for one’s household or estate, to care among children and grandchildren, servants and dependents, for what befits a lord or father. But this way is dangerous, lest, beginning as if from necessity, you reach the point of serving Mammon—that is, riches—from love; and lest not you alone rule them [read *illis*], but they rule you, and, while you think that you are going strongly against the current of the river, overcome by desires and enslaved, you are swept down to lower things.

Perhaps you say: If I follow this counsel of perfection—if, selling all that I possess and distributing it among the poor (Matt. 19), I follow you, Christ—where will food come from? Where clothing? To this I say: “Is not the life more than food, and the body more than clothing?” He who bestowed the greater things will surely also bestow the lesser. “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?”

If, therefore, birds are sustained by God’s providence without care and toil—birds which exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose souls are mortal, and which, when they cease to be, will never be again—how much more are human beings, to whom eternity is promised, governed by God’s will? Do you not sing in the psalm: “The trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted shall be filled; there the sparrows will make their nests. The heron’s house is their leader” (Ps. 103). Do not be afraid. Under those names and words there is prophecy concerning you: that your Father cares for you when, poor and having left everything, with no anxiety over what you shall eat or wear, you have become like sparrows, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.

For your one teacher is Christ; and he, like the heron, a great bird, strong enough even to defeat the eagle, the king of birds, though it has flown into heaven, nevertheless remains with you all days until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28). The house of this heron is the apostolic life which Christ himself, your teacher, constructed. If you wish to be sparrows, if, leaving everything, you wish to follow this Teacher, his house will go before your flight, crying out to the trees of the field, speaking to the cedars of Lebanon, and commanding the powerful and rich of this age: Spread out your branches and receive these sparrows; pour out your treasures and feed these voluntary poor. Let these sparrows nest among you; build monasteries, found churches in which these poor may live, so that morning, noon, and evening they may be free to recount and proclaim (Ps. 54), and God will hear their voice as they cry out and pray, both for you and for themselves.

Why, then, are you anxious about your food, and why, because of anxiety over this matter, do you fear to leave everything and follow? “Are you not worth much more than they?”—that is, the sparrows, by whose comparison I invited you to the wisdom of faith. One human being, made in God’s image, is of more worth and greater value before God than many great buffaloes or oxen, not to mention small sparrows.

“But which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” Perhaps you say: Sparrows are small, they have little bodies, and therefore can be fed with little; but we are large and thus need more and greater food. But I say: “Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” For I know you: when one is ashamed to appear shorter than another, whoever it may be, man or woman, stretches himself; but however much one stretches, one cannot add one cubit to one’s stature, and it is much if by stretching one can add a single handbreadth.

Therefore, when he says, “Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” and you answer, “No one”—since indeed no one can do this by thinking, though one does it by adding years and growing according to nature from infancy into completed youth, not by thought but by the law of nature established by God—you are again reproved. For he who made you large and caused you to grow beyond the size or measure of a sparrow can also increase your food beyond what is necessary.

“And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” Those who, because of voluntary poverty and heavenly conduct, are called sparrows, are likewise called lilies and other beautiful flowers in Scripture because of the beauty of chastity and the fair variety of the other virtues. Here the Wise Man says: “Hear me, divine fruits, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water. Have a sweet fragrance like Lebanon. Bloom as flowers like a lily, and give fragrance” (Sir. 39). 621 And in the Song of Songs Christ says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2). And there are many similar passages.

Accordingly, while he forbids anxiety over food and clothing, he fittingly directs his elect to consider sparrows and lilies, to which divine authority had assigned a likeness in the ancient Scriptures: “Consider,” he says, “the lilies of the field, how”—and the rest, which he concludes thus: “For if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace, how much more you, of little faith?” (Matt. 6). Certainly much more—but it must be understood, in the kingdom of God. For to wish to be clothed thus in this present age is counted folly, “because not even Solomon,” he says, “in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (ibid.).

What then does he mean by his sharp declaration, “How much more you, of little faith”? Or what is it to be of little faith? It must not be lightly or negligently observed that he says here, “you of little faith,” while elsewhere he praises greatness of faith, as in: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you have asked” (Matt. 15). Let us therefore desire to know fixed boundaries: when faith has reached them, it is great; when it has not yet reached them, it is small or very small.

So that we may not make a long detour in inquiry, a ready seal or indication of great faith is at hand in the place where those blessed three young men said to King Nebuchadnezzar, at the very hour when they were to be cast into the blazing furnace: “For behold, the God whom we worship is able to deliver us from the blazing furnace and free us from your hands, O king. But if he does not will it, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor do we adore the golden statue which you have set up” (Dan. 3).

For in this is recognized the greatness of faith, the strength of faith, the strength of a faithful mind: after saying, “God is able to deliver us,” they added: “But if he does not will it, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship or adore your gods.” Following their example, whoever says: God whom we worship is able to feed us, because he also feeds the sparrows; God is able to clothe us, because he so clothes the grass which is today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace—and yet adds: But if he does not will to feed or clothe us, nevertheless we shall by no means serve you, O Mammon; rather, having left everything, we shall follow him, not anxious about what we shall eat or with what we shall be clothed—such people are of great faith, because their faith extends itself wholly into the age to come.

On the contrary, those are of little faith who take offense unless they are protected by everyone or defended against adversaries, and unless they enjoy every prosperity; nor do they think that God has care for them or that there is any providence of God. “And they said,” says the Psalmist, “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these sinners, abounding in the world, have obtained riches. Therefore in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent; and I have been scourged all day, and my chastisement is in the mornings” (Ps. 72). Such persons, since they are excessively anxious about food or clothing and murmur unless they are filled, are rightly called of little faith even in the profession of the perfect, who leave all things and follow Christ. To them applies what he himself said to certain persons coming to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of my loaves and were filled” (John 6).

We therefore think that we have found definite boundaries between great faith and little faith. For the former says and thinks something like that saying of blessed Job: “Even if he should kill me, I shall hope in him” (Job 13). The latter, however, says something like this: “I am afraid and cannot leave Egypt, lest I suffer a lack of water and thirst in the wilderness” (Exod. 17). Great and useful is the matter which he seeks to impress upon us; and therefore, not content to say it once, he repeats the same thing a second and a third time:

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or with what shall we be clothed? For the nations seek after all these things. For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek therefore first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Its own evil is sufficient for the day” (Matt. 6).

Because this one thing is exceedingly useful and necessary—namely, to keep sabbath, or rest, in the study or contemplation of the Word of God, which is the better part that, as the Lord himself says, Mary chose (Luke 10)—therefore, as has already been said, he repeated a second and third time the sentence concerning the casting away of the heavy burden of anxiety imposed by the belly, an occasion of miserable servitude for many, so that, serving Mammon, they cannot serve God.

Where he says a second time, “Do not be anxious,” he immediately adds two reasons: “For the nations seek after all these things—your Father knows that you need all these things.” One restrains by fear; the other is full of consolation. For what is it to say, “The nations seek after all these things,” unless it is as though he said: “You will be like the nations, whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3), if you put God behind this anxiety which I forbid? For when he says, “The nations seek after all these things,” one must also understand: and beyond this age they seek nothing further.

“Their storehouses are full,” says the Psalmist, “overflowing from this one into that; there is no breach in their wall, no passage through, nor cry in their streets; and they called blessed the people to whom these things belong” (Ps. 143). For they seek these things as though they were the highest blessedness. Thus this saying strikes us like a rebuke. Then, because we need food and clothing, wishing us to cast all our anxiety upon him because he has care for us, he says: “For your Father knows that you need all these things.” He knows, I say, and knows well. For what does he not know? He also knows the cause for which it has come about that you need all these things.

Our fathers were in Paradise, well clothed in innocence alone; and they did not need the bread which you now eat in the sweat of your face, being sufficiently satisfied with the fruits of Paradise alone. They transgressed with their eyes by desiring, and with their mouth by eating, the fruit of the forbidden tree (Gen. 3); and from that time you need all these things: food to repel hunger, clothing to drive away cold and cover shame. Does he merely know that you need them, and does he not also will—as he is your Father—to provide what you need? Does he lack the will, unless you murmur and by murmuring compel him to will?

This paternal providence has testimony from many other passages of Scripture: it is always present with the righteous and men of perfect faith, never abandons them, and exercises its power most especially, and with unwonted power, where human resourcefulness can in no way provide for itself. For example: in one place the Lord fed Elijah through an angel; elsewhere through ravens, birds of prey; elsewhere through a widow’s little jar of flour (1 Kings 17, 19). Elisha, having few loaves, said to the servant: “Give to the people that they may eat”; and they ate, and there remained over according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 4).

“Seek therefore,” he says, “first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.” What is the kingdom of God but the Word of God? For by that through which all things were made (John 1), all things are governed; and to serve in this is surely to reign. Whenever, therefore, we gather to hear or expound the Word of God; whenever we read holy readings or gladly hear them, and strive to fulfil them in deed, as often do we seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Here indeed, while we live, we seek and are able to seek; but we cannot find it fully except after this life.

This kingdom of God is a treasure hidden in a field (Matt. 13): a treasure carefully shut up and sealed in the field of the legal and prophetic letter, a letter for the most part parabolic or enigmatic. To find this treasure is to understand the sacred Scriptures; and, for joy of the treasure, to sell all and buy the field—that is, for delight in the heavenly goods or kingdom of heaven promised in the holy Scriptures, to cast away every anxiety according to this present evangelical counsel, and to embrace the study of those same Scriptures alone, so that a person may always be unencumbered for expounding or hearing the Word of God. “Do this first,” he says, “and all these things shall be added to you” [Col. 1448A].

Oh, how many this kind of study has quickly advanced not only to sufficiency in these things, namely food and clothing, but even to the greatest honors! “Above health and all beauty,” says one, “I loved wisdom, and I resolved to possess her instead of light. But all good things came to me together with her” (Wis. 7). “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Its own evil is sufficient for the day.”

He had already said once and twice, “Do not be anxious.” Why does he repeat it yet a third time, unless because the matter he intends is great, and it is difficult and exceedingly laborious to uproot from the depths of our heart this root of bitterness, the root of covetousness? Notice how terribly he forbids anxiety in this third repetition. For when he had said, “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow,” he immediately adds: “For tomorrow will be anxious for itself.”

Let that rich man hear this, and whoever is like him, whose field, when it had brought forth abundant crops, led him to think within himself: “What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my fruits? And he said: This I shall do: I shall pull down my barns and build greater ones, and there I shall gather all that has grown for me and my goods; and I shall say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12). He was very anxious about tomorrow, who so delightfully extended his anxiety over many years.

But “tomorrow”—I do not mean a future time, short or long, for which one is accustomed to say “tomorrow,” as there: “Tomorrow my righteousness shall answer for me” (Gen. 30)—rather, the tomorrow-day, as people commonly call the day following the next night, according to the setting and rising of the sun, the daily day, “will be anxious for itself.” For it follows: “But God said to him: Fool, this night they shall require your soul from you; and the things which you have prepared, whose shall they be?” (Luke 12). Imagine that he had said: Fool, why are you anxious, not merely for many years, but even for tomorrow? For tomorrow will be anxious for itself.

This seems to mean the same as if he said to him: Tomorrow will be full of another anxiety, not for you but for itself; nor will the condition of tomorrow, an evil day, allow you to have any exercise of reason—much less anxiety—for, as Ecclesiastes says, “There shall be neither reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell, whither you are hastening” (Eccles. 9), your soul having been required from you this night. A dreadful occupation, which so entangles the whole person that he can neither seek nor admit the consolation of reason, knowledge, or wisdom.

Otherwise: “Tomorrow,” that is, the one who comes on the morrow, will be anxious, or can be anxious, either to hear Moses and the prophets, having them (Luke 16), or to plan greater barns for himself, as you planned. If he plans it, it will be said and done to him as it was said and done to the one who went before—whether to you or another: “Fool, this night they shall require your soul from you; and the things which you have prepared, whose shall they be?” For how rare is the servant of Mammon who, even on the day before his soul is required of him, and almost at the very point of death, does not persist wickedly in being anxious for many years.

Although many similar things can be said—and have been said by our predecessors—about tomorrow, the anagogical sense is more pleasing and proceeds more readily. For according to anagogy, tomorrow is an evil and accursed day, opposed to the present day, the day blessed by the Lord, concerning which the Holy Spirit speaks in David: “Today, if you hear his voice” (Ps. 94). The Apostle recalls it in these words:

“Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. Take heed, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God; but exhort one another every day, while it is called Today, as it is said: Today, if you hear his voice” (Heb. 3).

And afterward: “And indeed, concerning the works made from the foundation of the world, he said somewhere of the seventh day thus: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works”; and again in this place: “They shall enter into my rest. Since therefore those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again appoints a certain day, saying in David, Today” (Heb. 4), and so forth.

Opposed to this blessed present day, in which God rests, is that tomorrow-day, namely the devil or Mammon, against whom he said above: “No one can serve two masters; you cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6). For what other day do you suppose is that day which holy Job curses?

“For Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, and he spoke: Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived. Let that day be turned into darkness; let God not seek it from above, and let it not be remembered, nor enlightened with light” (Job 3), and so forth.

For every person is born on that day: he is born in sin, lives in sin, and dies in sin, unless he is visited by this day, this holy and blessed Today; and, visited or enlightened by it, changes his origin and renews his birth, so that, born in Adam, he may be reborn in Christ, and, dead to sin, may live to God.

That day is called tomorrow because, with the night of iniquity intervening, it is wholly separated from this Today. Moreover, it is not truly a day, though it is called and wishes to seem a day; in reality it is night. Therefore the holy man, cursing it, said both things: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived.”

We must now say how no one is to be anxious for that tomorrow-day, how that day is anxious for itself, and how its evil is sufficient for it. For the Lord said these three things: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow; for tomorrow will be anxious for itself; for its own evil is sufficient for the day.” To be anxious for that tomorrow-day is to serve Mammon, to serve lusts, to love the world and the things in the world. This is rightly forbidden because, just as surely no one can see both the present day and tomorrow simultaneously, so no one can love the world and God simultaneously, or serve God and Mammon simultaneously.

For what reason? “For,” he says, “tomorrow will be anxious for itself.” What does this mean: tomorrow will be anxious for itself? Surely the devil, Mammon, or prince of this world, will communicate nothing of his anxiety to God and will have nothing in common with God. Indeed, if he had said, “He is anxious for himself,” this would seem to mean merely that he is so; but the future tense, “he will be anxious,” conveys something more, because it intimates the eternity of the division or separation: as he is now, so he will always and eternally be divided and separated from God, and without any end will separately seek what is his own, not what is God’s (Phil. 2), never desiring by any regard to be reunited with God.

Why does this happen to him? Whence comes such persistence in separation? He says: “Its own evil is sufficient for the day.” How, or in what respect, is its evil sufficient for such a day? Namely, in that it says: “I need no one; I am God, and I have sat in the throne of God, and I shall be like the Most High” (Ezek. 28; Isa. 14), and the like. Therefore, “the day’s evil is sufficient for it”: that is, it appears to be pride that is sufficient to itself. Humility, however, says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

## Chapter VII

“Do not judge, that you may not be judged. For with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with what measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you.”

This is not a new commandment, but the old commandment which we heard from the beginning. For through Moses the Lord had said the same: “Do not hate your brother in your heart, but rebuke him openly, lest you bear sin on his account” (Lev. 19). Finally, that here the Lord spoke of the hatred involved in judging—“Do not judge, that you may not be judged,” and the rest already quoted—he immediately makes clear when he says by such a comparison:

“But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, and do not see the beam that is in your own eye? Or how do you say to your brother: Allow me to cast the speck from your eye; and behold, there is a beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first cast the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck from your brother’s eye.”

Therefore, when he says, “Do not judge, that you may not be judged,” he means: Do not, in judging, harbor hatred in your hearts. For that we should not judge at all, or reprove or correct, is opposed both by evangelical and legal authority: legal authority, because in the same chapter, immediately after saying, “Do not hate your brother in your heart,” it adds, “but rebuke him openly”—understood with the intention that you should wish to gain him, which belongs not to hatred but to love; evangelical authority, as there: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother; but if he does not hear you, take with you yet one or two, that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses.” If he does not hear them either, tell it to the Church (Matt. 18).

At the same time evangelical authority supplied what was less apparent in the legal text: the latter said only, “rebuke openly”; the former set out in what order you ought to proceed so as to rebuke publicly, or tell the Church a sin not publicly committed but known to you alone. We must therefore beware of judgment which proceeds from the root of hatred, if not for love of justice, then at least for fear of the just requital immediately added: “For with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged.”

For if you judge from hatred, not of the case but of the person, you too shall be judged—not with the judgment of love, but of God’s hatred, who hates every person judging hatefully; indeed, “You hate,” says the Psalmist, “all workers of iniquity” (Ps. 5). Yet these words, and almost all the rest, are spoken especially against the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees, so that those who wish to be disciples of truth and bear the Christian name may withdraw as far as possible from their likeness.

For they at that time judged badly and measured with an unjust measure, condemning sinners and publicans, and reproving the Lord himself because he welcomed and associated with them. They said: “Because this man receives sinners and eats with them” (Matt. 9), and the like. Surely they themselves were rather to be judged, because their sin was so much greater than the sin of publicans and prostitutes, as the size of a beam exceeds the smallness of a speck. Thus he says most fittingly to each of them: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not see the beam in your own eye?”

This is like saying: Why do you detest the ignorance of the publican, saying, for example, “But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed” (John 7), while failing to consider the hatred in your heart, because “you have seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15)? To hate not only me or my Father, but any brother whatsoever, is to have a beam in one’s eye. How, then, do you say to your brother, “Allow me to cast the speck from your eye,” when behold, there is a beam in your own eye? Perhaps what you see—or think you see—in your brother’s eye is not a speck but the shadow of a speck; but you see and distinguish badly because you do not see the beam in your own eye.

But let it be granted that there really is a speck in any brother’s eye: a speck of sudden anger or of suddenly rushing desire, such as was in David’s eye when, angered by Nabal’s insults, he wished to avenge himself (1 Sam. 25), and when, looking from the roof upon Uriah the Hittite’s wife washing herself, he saw and desired her (2 Sam. 11). Since you are like Shimei, how can you judge or give counsel concerning such specks? Or how would it suit you, with so great a beam of hatred in your own eye, that, cursing, throwing stones, and scattering earth, you should say something such as this: “Depart, man of blood and man of Belial! The Lord has repaid you for all the blood which you have shed” (2 Sam. 16).

Indeed, even if you speak more mildly, with your beam of inveterate hatred, so as to say something like this—“Therefore do not reject the Lord’s correction, for he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal” (Job 5)—or this: “Therefore let not anger overcome you so that you oppress anyone, nor let the multitude of places [or: gifts] incline you” (Job 36)—it is said to you: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck from your brother’s eye.”

Now because wise Abigail, wife of foolish and senseless Nabal, did not have such a beam in her own eye, she perceived—and was able to perceive—how to cast the speck from the eye of David, suddenly angered; and she did so by reasoning of this kind: “Let this iniquity be upon me, my lord,” and so on until: “When therefore the Lord has done for you, my lord, all the good things he has spoken concerning you, this shall not be to you, my lord, for groaning and a scruple of heart: that you have shed innocent blood, or avenged yourself” (1 Sam. 25).

David, his eye at once cleansed—that is, the rush of anger calmed—said to Abigail: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me; and blessed be your speech, and blessed are you, who prevented me today from going to bloodshed and avenging myself with my own hand” (ibid.). Hence that Abigail, according to her name, which means “the joy of my father,” ought to be a memorable example to every faithful soul: it should strive for peace and reconcile, or calm, any angry person it can before the effect or act of sin which anger suggests. This endeavor is truly that of the highest Father.

Likewise, because the prophet Nathan did not have that beam in his eye, he perceived—and was able to perceive—how to draw from David’s eye the speck of the sin which he had committed through desire concerning Uriah the Hittite’s wife, beginning as though he were speaking of another and gently leading him from this, until David said in repentance: “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. 12). But the aforementioned Shimei, because he had a great beam of hatred in his eye, not only did not draw out the speck which then was in David’s eye, but even cast in the enduring or long-lasting fire of righteous zeal, so that, being about to sleep with his fathers, David said to Solomon his son:

“Because he came down to meet me when I crossed the Jordan, and I swore to him by the Lord, saying: I will not kill you with the sword, you shall not allow him to be innocent. But you are a wise man and know what you shall do to him; and you shall bring down his gray hairs with blood to hell” (1 Kings 2).

## Book Seven

[Col. 1453A] I have learned by experience; yet fearing this very thing I confess it, and confessing I fear it: I have learned and experienced something, however small, concerning a certain manner of speech by which the Beloved is accustomed to speak to holy and beloved souls. We heard this in the Song of Songs, when any one of them says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows; and my beloved speaks to me: Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2). Repeating the same thing, “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one,” he continues thus: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face beautiful” (ibid.).

What necessity compels me to confess that I have learned something of this kind by experience? I think it is because someone almost takes offense at me, the very one who writes and treats the mysteries of Scripture, imputing it to presumption and vain glory, and mockingly asking what need there is for me to write these things, when so many holy Fathers before us have written so much and so sufficiently.

What then? Shall I write also of that experience of the Beloved—how he says, “Arise, hasten,” how he says, “Let your voice sound in my ears”? Truly I would not dare; but I have not been afraid, nor shall I be afraid if you wish to hear it again, to tell this in your ear, O friend, who yourself often urge me to write. To the rest I say: let it suffice that I have said this. Even if I should wish to be silent or cease from the labor of writing, I cannot; I know and clearly feel that this is not granted to me, and I rejoice in it.

I have learned that Job’s friend spoke truth when he said, “Who can hold in a conceived word?” (Job 4), if he had possessed the virtue of discernment. Certainly he could not hold in a superfluous or evil conceived word: this is vicious and foolish, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “An arrow fixed in the fleshy thigh, so is a word in the heart of a fool” (Ecclus. 19). But, conversely, not to be able to contain a conceived word that is good and necessary is glorious, as Jeremiah could not contain it. Having said, “The word of the Lord became to me reproach and derision all day; and I said: I will not remember him, nor speak in his name” (Jer. 20), he added:

“And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I was worn out, unable to bear it” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, however those now present may judge us, those to come will judge more gently. “For while we live,” says the illustrious Jerome, “and are contained in a fragile vessel, the efforts of friends seem to help and the reproaches of rivals to harm. But after earth has returned to its earth, and pale death has taken away both us who write and those who judge us, and another generation has come, and, when the first leaves have fallen, the green forest has grown up, then talents alone are judged, without distinction of names. The reader does not consider whose or what sort of thing that is which he is to read: whether the author be bishop or layman, emperor and lord, whether he lie clad in silk or in the meanest cloth, soldier and servant, or in purple; he shall be judged not by diversity of rank, but by the merit of his works.” Let us now continue what we began.

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.”

In his teaching, a servant of the Lord who possesses knowledge of the Scriptures, and is therefore called “a scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 13), must exercise great moderation. Above all, he must attend to place, time, and person. For if an intemperate teacher, an immoderate preacher, pours out his discourse without consideration of these things, it often happens that he gives what is holy to dogs and casts his pearls before swine.

Have not dogs and swine—that is, unclean and insolent people—also insultingly examined and searched out many of those who carefully hid, according to time and place, the pearls of which we speak? Having trampled the pearls, they tore apart those persons themselves. For they killed many and persecuted very many more, not that they might possess the pearls themselves, but that the pearls themselves might nowhere appear.

The first one who speaks these words gave a great example of this caution in his own action: namely, he composed his Scripture in such a way that it could not be understood by everyone or just anyone. It did not seem sufficient to him that, at the building of the Babylonian tower, he confused the language which was one for all and the speech which the whole earth had in common (Gen. 6), and thus removed all nations from reading the Scriptures which he was to hand over to one nation alone, namely the Hebrew nation.

For even in that one people of God which received the Law, which was believed to possess the oracles of God, there were and would be no lack of such swine and dogs, unworthy of the pearls of heavenly mysteries and persons to whom not every holy thing ought to be given. This would have occurred, or would occur, if the Law and Prophets had been expressed in plain speech without figures and enigmas. Therefore he composed such a Scripture that it could not easily be understood toward what it aimed or what mystery of the kingdom of God it contained. And as he did then, so he teaches when he says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine.”

Why? “Lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.” There are two reasons: lest injury be done to the pearls, and lest our indiscretion become danger to our life or an occasion of death. “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it shall be opened.”

Therefore it neither harms nor will harm the holy flock of the humble that the pearls are hidden from swine and dogs, and that because of dogs all that is holy is stored within. For he “who has the key—indeed, who himself is the key of David—who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3), is always at hand. As he knows to whom and to what kind of persons he must shut, so he knows perfectly to whom he must open and give. By asking, seeking, and knocking, those who are worthy make themselves known.

Here strength is needed. What strength? Surely that, or one like it, by which Jacob, the father of the strong, wrestled with the angel and, becoming victor, said when told, “Let me go”: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32). And he blessed him in the same place. What sort of strength, then, was that? What did he himself perceive who said: “Because if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?” (ibid.).

Certainly that strength was unutterable groaning, the tears of a troubled spirit, and the prayer of a contrite and humbled heart, by which Moses too was able to hold the same God when he said, “Let me go” (Exod. 32). Finally, Hosea also testifies to this—indeed God himself speaking in Hosea. Having said of him: “In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was directed with the angel, and he prevailed over the angel and was strengthened” (Hos. 12), he adds: “He wept and entreated him” (ibid.).

Therefore humble strength, strong humility, is needed here, where holy things are hidden and the pearls of heavenly meanings are held shut within an obscured and sealed letter. As Jacob wrestled with that angel, in whom God undoubtedly was, who also confessed himself conquered, so the lover of God’s Word must wrestle with discourse or Scripture which is from God, and not let go until he conquers the one who wills to be conquered and comprehends the useful meaning hidden in the letter. For it is a most beautiful contest to persevere in asking until one finds, in knocking until it is opened to oneself.

How much he delights in such a contest, and how truly he desires to be conquered—the one who seems to resist by not opening more quickly—he wishes us to observe when he immediately says:

“Which of you is the man whose son asks him for bread, and will he give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he offer him a serpent? If therefore you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more shall your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?”

This argument has its own intention, and there is no doubt that it is this: that we should not become children of distrust because our Father delays to give to those who ask him or to open to those who knock. The Father does not will this; rather, he wills that where something is more closed, there you should exercise yourself more, and strengthen your hope in exercise through the reflection that he is Father. When he delays to give or open, he delays so that you may learn that you have nothing which you have not received, and may not glory in yourself as though you were sufficient to yourself (1 Cor. 4)—which glorying was or is that of the Evil One—but may think and speak according to the Apostle’s example:

“Yet we have confidence, not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3).

“If therefore you,” he says, “though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more your Father?” And what kind of Father? Certainly good, and the only good one (Matt. 10), in comparison with whom you are all evil and have no good except from his incidental gift. Adam, surely an evil father, who consigned both himself and all his posterity to death, nevertheless would not give a stone to his son asking for bread, nor offer a serpent to his son asking for fish.

Herod indeed, under whom this very Lord who speaks these things was born, provided his own sons with something worse than a stone, namely a deadly sword; but he did not do this to those asking for bread or fish, but rather—as it seemed to him—to persons plotting death against their father. “How much more,” he says, “will your Father” give you, when you ask, in order to understand Scripture—which is truly bread—for an opening of the heart? He will by no means do the opposite and give you a dull, stony heart.

Likewise, if you ask for a fish—that is, if in reading you wish to know Christ, whose mystery lies hidden in the legal and prophetic Scripture in something like the way a fish is hidden in water—he will by no means offer you a serpent, leading you into error and into a meaning remote from Christ, whom you seek in the Scriptures with devout desire. It is not his way to give a spirit of error to those asking for the Spirit of truth.

In another Evangelist it is further written: “Or if you ask for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” (Luke 11). It is pleasant to speak of this, because all the ancient saints, just as they asked and sought the bread of the Word of God and the fish, that is, Christ, so they most earnestly requested an egg from the Father of mercies; and prophetic oracles undoubtedly affirmed that it would be given.

What egg, or what sort of egg? Surely that one upon which the Holy Spirit would deign to overshadow, coming upon it in the manner of a bird sitting upon her egg, until the chick should be formed within it. For so it was to be, and so it was done. O blessed Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit came upon you and the power of the Most High overshadowed you (Luke 1), and thus you conceived and bore the Son, a bird: that is, not earthly but heavenly, not carnal but spiritual, though possessing true flesh and an earthly body.

The former children undoubtedly asked for such an egg, especially those who possessed not only faith but also prophecy of so great a mystery. For example, he “who,” as was said above, “wrestled with a man until morning” and said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32), undoubtedly sought in that blessing: May that egg come from my stock, so that, the Holy Spirit overshadowing, “a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31).

We too, when we diligently and eagerly seek testimony from the Scriptures in order that we may know certainly that this has now been done, assuredly ask the Father for an egg. Nor will the Father offer us a scorpion, so that we might suppose concerning the blessed Virgin anything contrary to truth or belonging to heretical depravity.

“Therefore, whatever you want people to do for you [Col. 1457A], do also for them. For this is the Law and the Prophets. Enter through the narrow gate, because broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it. How narrow is the gate and confined the way that leads to life! And few are those who find it.”

Therefore, he says, since your Father is ready to give good things to those who ask, ask reasonably, seek wisely, knock prudently. For what? Namely, that “whatever you want people to do for you [626], you also do for them.” For if you have not given, by what right will something be given to you? If you have not forgiven, with what justice will you be forgiven? Therefore do as I have said. “For this is the Law and the Prophets.” This is their whole sum: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22). Hence the Apostle says: “[Col. 1457B] For the one who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law: for, You shall not commit adultery; You shall not kill; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13).

How laborious this is for flesh and blood! For this rule—“Whatever you want people to do for you, do also for them,” or, “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others”—extends even to an enemy. Do you not wish that your enemy, if he finds you, should spare you, as David spared Saul? Thus this rule extends even to an enemy, especially because Wisdom says, and the Apostle recalls: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him [Col. 1457C] water to drink” (Prov. 21; Rom. 12). And the Lord says: “Do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6). How laborious this is, I say! Therefore he says: “Enter through the narrow gate.” He who says, “Enter through the narrow,” and so forth, does not deny that these things are laborious. But for whom is this gate narrow and this way confined? Certainly for the proud and swollen, who were and are many. Such people have gone by the broad and spacious way into destruction. But is this gate equally narrow and this way confined for the gentle and humble? Certainly not. Rather, as he says to them, “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11), so he truly says to the same people: My gate, my life; and although at the beginning it appears narrow and confined, it is afterwards [Col. 1457D] found to be such that you say what the Psalmist said from experience: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118 [119]).

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.” Here prudence is needed: the prudence of the Spirit, which is one of the divisions of gifts; for it is the discernment of spirits (1 Cor. 12). Without this grace false prophets cannot be recognized, because they are double: ugly within, beautiful in their fair skin; inwardly ravening wolves, outwardly like simple sheep, falsely displaying every humility and gentleness. Such people came of old, and were to come, in order to overthrow, if possible, the New Testament as well [Col. 1458A].

Whence is discernment, or certainty in this discernment, to be obtained? “From their fruits,” he says, “you shall know them.” Their fruits are their works. They can also be recognized and judged from their words. Here, as has already been said, prudence is needed—prudence armed with the word of God and furnished with the eyes of scriptural knowledge, such as are praised in the Song of Songs for being like doves resting “by the streams of waters, beside the fullest channels” (Cant. 5). Whatever anyone says must be compared with the Scriptures, which holy men received—not from a human being nor through a human being, but from the Holy Spirit through the revelation of Jesus Christ—in order that they might speak and write. “Even if we,” says the Apostle, “or an angel from heaven should preach to you something besides that which you have received, let him be accursed; and again, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1) [Col. 1458B].

This saying, this judgement, likewise belongs to all those who received not from a human being nor through a human being, but through the Holy Spirit; hence all their writings alone are called, and are, canonical. “If anyone,” says John at the end of his Apocalypse—and it would have been fitting for any other prophet or apostle to say the same—“if anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life” (Rev. 22).

But let us now follow the Lord’s own words. “From their fruits,” he says, “you shall know them. Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? So every good tree produces good fruits; but a bad tree produces bad fruits [Col. 1458C]. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire. Therefore, from their fruits you shall know them.”

In all this we have an obvious meaning; but we seek the principal intention. It is the duty of a good hearer to observe not only what the heavenly speaker says, but especially what he chiefly intends. Thus this is the meaning, or this intention, of these words: just as you know how to distinguish the tree from which you gather a fig or a grape, knowing that it is not a thorn, thistle, or bad tree, so also distinguish me, from whose mouth you receive both truth and the work of truth. For example, when I say to one centurion, “Go, and let it be done for you as you have believed” (Matt. 8), and likewise to another, “Go, for your son lives” (John 4); when I say to a leper, “I will; be cleansed” (Luke 5), and it happens immediately; and when I perform many other things far greater than these—by these things, I say, distinguish me from false prophets. For the two cannot both be true: that, while fabricating from my own heart and speaking falsely in the name of the Lord, I should be a bad tree, yet should produce fruits so good that you yourselves perceive that I work many good works among you [Col. 1458D].

Behold, I speak “in the name of the Lord” (Deut. 18), that is, professing either that the Lord is my name, or that the name of the Lord is not always myself but is in me. My Father, the Lord God, bears witness to this when he says of me in one place: “Observe him and listen to his voice; do not think him to be despised, for he will not pardon you when you sin, and my name is in him” (Exod. 23) [Col. 1459A]. Thus, I say, I speak “in the name of the Lord,” professing that the Lord is my name and that, among the prophets, I am to be proclaimed as the great Prophet who rules. For I say:

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven shall enter the kingdom of heaven. For many shall say to me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I shall declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’”

Therefore I am both Lord and judge of those who invoke me as Lord—so secure and fully possessed of my own lordship that those who invoke me as Lord must beware lest, by the very invocation of this name of mine, they be judged unworthy by me whom they invoke [Col. 1459B]. A remarkable rebuff to flattery, in which “the kings of the Gentiles, and those who rule over them” (John 18) are commonly especially delighted, above all at the beginnings of their reigns. For how many people then already knew to say to him, “Lord, Lord,” except perhaps those who needed healing and were beginning to feel his power? Yet he took no concern for such people, because he was born for this and came into the world for this: to bear witness to the truth (ibid.), that is, to himself. “For I,” he says, “am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8). Thus he spoke, as was fitting for him: already with great power and majesty.

Hence later the Evangelist says: “The crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 7) [Col. 1459C]. Not, I say, as the scribes and Pharisees, because he was plainly not pleased by this assent or flattery, by being called Rabbi by people. What authority, or what kind of authority, do they and all others like them possess [627] in teaching? They are servants of popular applause, desirous of glory; they care wholly about the reputation of their speech and not at all about the advancement of their hearers. Truly powerless, truly possessing no authority: if windy praise blows upon them, they become disconsolate and diminished. But he, who seeks the gain of souls alone and does not receive glory from human beings—the teacher and example of all who seek not their own glory but God’s (John 5)—first does himself what he teaches, rejecting flattery both from those then present and from those to come, and saying: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven shall enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1459D].

His Father is the one Person who says in the Psalm concerning this his Son, his Word: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44 [45]); but for us, children of adoption, one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is Father. Thus it should be observed that almost everywhere he says “Father” or “of the Father” without the determination of this possessive pronoun *my* or *of my*, the things he says are lesser than the majesty of his divinity; as there: “And as the Father gave me commandment, so I do, because the Father is greater than I” (John 14) [Col. 1460A]. But where he specifies “my Father” or “of my Father,” he does not speak without an indication of divine majesty, as here: “but whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven,” with the thought supplied from his saying to me, “Lord, Lord, he shall enter the kingdom of heaven.” He adds further: “Many shall say to me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?’” and the rest as above. “Wherefore shall I declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’?”

Surely because what they prophesied they prophesied for themselves: that is, in prophesying they sought not God’s glory but their own glory and temporal advantage, like Balaam, who, though he prophesied good and true things, gave evil counsel. For at his suggestion the women of Midian deceived the children of Israel at Baal-peor (Num. 24) [Col. 1460B]. Similarly, many who cast out demons in his name—whether by exorcizing and baptizing people, or by dedicating to the true God altars and temples in which a multitude of demons had dwelt and been worshipped—and who performed many mighty works for people, works which appeared to be mighty indeed but were not truly mighty works, but rather imitations of mighty works, sought a reward other than the Lord’s and received their reward. Therefore, “I shall declare to them, ‘I did not know you.’” I shall declare, I say: that is, I shall say what I previously concealed, allowing them to appear righteous in their own eyes, according to the saying: “I was silent; I always kept silence; I was patient; like a woman in labour, I shall speak” (Isa. 3) [Col. 1460C].

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a man who built his house upon a rock. And the rain came down, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house; and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon a rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them is like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. And the rain came down, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house; and it fell, and its fall was great.”

This is a fearful declaration, which on that day will thus reveal the foundations of the consciences of false prophets and of all who work iniquity, just as a storm of rain, a flood of rivers, and blasts of rushing winds reveal the foundations of a house founded not upon a rock but upon loose and shifting sand [Col. 1460D]. For they shall fall and collapse in a great ruin at the blast of this voice: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25)—not because you heard my words, but because you did not do them. But the house of those who, by hearing and doing, have placed their foundations upon the rock will stand firm. Those who are at the right hand will not fall by going with those at the left into punishment; rather, they will ascend into eternal life to receive the everlasting kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds marvelled at his teaching. For he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” [Col. 1461A]. He states what a powerful reason there was for their amazement, “by which the crowds marvelled at his teaching. For,” he says, “he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.” What, I ask, is it to have authority in teaching? Or rather, what is it not to have authority in teaching? For from this opposite we better learn what it is to have authority in teaching.

Therefore, not to have authority in teaching is to speak good things while being evil scribes and Pharisees, wishing to please people and flattering the wealthy so as to obtain some advantage from them. Against such people the prophetic word in Ezekiel vehemently inveighs in this way: “Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and make pillows beneath the head of every age, to ensnare souls! When they ensnared the souls of my people, they gave life to their souls and profaned me among my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, in order to kill souls that do not die and to give life to souls that do not live, lying to my people who believe lies” (Ezek. 13) [Col. 1461B].

For what is it to give life to souls that do not live and kill souls that do not die, except to justify the wicked and condemn the godly for gifts? For this is the equivalent of sewing cushions beneath every elbow of the hand and making a pillow beneath the head of every age—and this for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, that is, for temporal gain or advantage, altogether trifling and meagre in comparison with the loss of justice which such a flatterer of another’s sin knowingly brings upon himself [Col. 1461C]. Do such people then possess authority in teaching? Rather, they are servants of servants, powerless and venal dependants. This one Teacher, the true Teacher, taught the way of God in truth; and among the other things he argued against their greed, he flattered no one ever, so much so that in Jerusalem, a great and wealthy city, he did not even have lodging for a single night at any time.

## Chapter VIII

“And when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.’ And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed’” (Matt. 4 [probably 8]).

Both before and after the sermon delivered on the mountain, the Evangelist relates that the Lord Jesus healed very many sick people, without stating separately how or from what illnesses they were delivered. For before this he said: “And he went about all Galilee, teaching in the synagogues and preaching the Gospel of the word; and they brought to him all who were ill, afflicted by various diseases and torments, and he healed them” (Matt. 4). But after the sermon, having narrated three cases separately—namely, that of this leper, the centurion’s servant, and Peter’s mother-in-law—he again says: “And when evening had come, they brought to him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits by a word, and healed all who were ill” [Col. 1461D]. Thus few things have been written out of many, but they are sufficient for the undertaking adopted by the writing Evangelist.

Therefore this glorious Son of God, honourable Son of Man, descended from the mountain of heaven into the plain of this world [628] in order to heal the infirmities—that is, the sins—of every person: first the Jew, and then the Gentile [Col. 1462A]. He contemplated the healing of the Jew in the cleansing of the leper, who was himself a Jew; and for this reason he said to him, as a pupil of the Law: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” But he contemplated the healing of the Gentile in the healing of the centurion’s servant, who was himself a Gentile. For this reason he judged himself unworthy that the Lord should enter, and, as Luke recalls (Luke 7), the elders of the Jews almost acted as advocates for him, saying: “For he is worthy that you should grant this to him, because he loves our nation and himself built our synagogue for us.”

Rightly, therefore, to the leper he said not only “I will,” nor only “be cleansed,” but also stretched out his hand and touched him; whereas he did not touch the centurion’s servant, nor even enter to him. That is, he healed the Jew in such a way as to assume flesh from him and dwell in his midst—which indeed was to touch him—whereas to the Gentiles he did not come in person, but after he had completed the whole work of salvation and ascended to heaven, he sent them his preachers [Col. 1462B].

When we say or read that the Jew—that is, the Jewish people—was first healed by the presence of the Saviour, we do not consider only those few who were then found in the body and believed before or after his Passion, but the whole election of that people: all who had already departed from the world, from the time of the promise made to Abraham until that time. For then they were saved and brought out from the lower regions by him whose future coming they had believed.

Accordingly, the diversity of the illnesses themselves must not be considered carelessly. For the one from the Jews was only leprous, whereas the centurion’s servant was both paralytic and grievously tormented. In correspondence with those two persons, this means that the Gentile people had more evil than the Jewish people, because it was possessed by the devil, worshipping demons as God; for God was not known to it. But the Jew, as one not deprived of reason, knew God even in his leprosy and was subject to the Law [Col. 1462C]. For upon whom did the Law rule more heavily than upon a leper? The hands of Moses are written to have been heavy (Exod. 17); and truly, upon no one was the hand of the literal Law heavier than upon a leper.

“Whoever,” it says, “is stained with leprosy and set apart at the decision of the priest shall have torn garments and an uncovered head; his mouth covered with a garment, he shall cry out that he is contaminated and unclean. For all the time that he is leprous and unclean, he shall live alone outside the camp” (Lev. 2 [probably 13]) [Col. 1462D]. There is also the judgement of the Law concerning other uncleannesses—namely, concerning the discharge of semen and menstruation (Lev. 15)—and also concerning other bodily blemishes: namely, if someone is blind, lame, has a small, large, or crooked nose, a broken foot or hand, is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a white spot in his eye, a continual scab, an eruption on his body, or is ruptured: “he shall not,” it says, “approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord, nor the breads to his God” (Lev. 21) [Col. 1463A].

But concerning one who is grievously tormented—that is, one who is possessed by a demon, as was this centurion’s servant—the Law decreed no judgement anywhere. Thus in every respect, as has already been said, the Jewish people, a pupil of the Law, was signified by the leper; and the Gentile people, by the servant of a Gentile man. Both were to be healed of their sins through the grace of this Son of Man, who in his outward works undoubtedly meditated day and night upon the salvation of souls, the salvation for which he had come: the salvation both of those who were under the Law, such as the leper, and of those who were without the Law (Rom. 2), such as this servant, captive to his own understanding.

But what if either the Jew, after being cleansed from Pharisaic leprosy, or the Gentile, after being delivered from a demon—that is, from the worship of demons—having been saved through faith in Jesus Christ by the washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit, sins again? Can he afterwards be saved, or recalled to salvation? Certainly he can, if he produces fruits worthy of repentance. “My little children,” says the apostle John, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins—not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2) [Col. 1463B].

The divine Evangelist immediately sets forth a mystical example of this matter. For he says: “And when Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying down and feverish; and he touched her hand, and the fever left her. And she rose and ministered to them.” What indeed is the house of Peter—a faithful man, and one fervent in faith—except the Church of the living God? Therefore Peter’s feverish mother-in-law is a soul that has Christian faith indeed, but is dangerously afflicted by the passion of some sin or vice. Luke the Evangelist also recalls this: “They asked him concerning her” (Luke 4). Thus Peter’s mother-in-law, into whose house the Lord Jesus had come, is, as we have said, a Christian soul or one belonging to the household of faith. When it begins to burn with vices and sins and nearly loses the breath of life, the faithful pray for it, and love is strengthened in it by the prayers of all [Col. 1463C].

Moreover Luke also recalls that “standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her” (ibid.); Matthew says that “he touched her hand, and the fever left her.” Luke, as already stated, says: “Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her.” Both express the action of one rising, because “she rose immediately and ministered to them,” namely to the Lord and his disciples. Hence it must briefly be said that to stand over one who is feverish is to shake such a soul terribly by the regard of his fear, and to disturb it by the remembrance of the future judgement, so that it says: “All my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. 6).

For before the knowledge of truth, the soul is nourished by the sweet breasts of grace, so that it may know its Creator. But, I say, after the recognition of truth and the reception of faith, when it has committed some grave sin, Jesus does not again so easily bestow upon it indulgence that is readily inclined; rather, it is terrified as though by the visitation of a judge standing over it [Col. 1464A], as, for example, when he says: “Whoever sins against me, I shall blot him out of my book which I have written” (Exod. 31 [probably 32]).

But to touch the hand of one lying down is to strengthen and help one who wishes to resist the violence of sin. By what other means could anyone be delivered from this body of death? (Rom. 7). Finally, when he wishes, a person can lie down and have a fever, or bring any sort of affliction upon his body; but that he should rise from bed and be free of that affliction is not in his own will, but rather rests in the physician’s healing. Likewise, when he wishes, he can live without law—that is, lie in sins with an evil security, without fear of God—but that he should rise and receive health of soul does not rest in his own strength, but in the grace alone of the Deliverer [Col. 1464B]. Even if willing is present, he does not find how to accomplish the good after willingly handing himself over to evil.

Hence comes that saying of the Apostle, sighing in the person of such people: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. But I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Therefore, in the mystical sense, the fact that, as Luke writes, “he stood over her” is an act of severity; but the fact that, as Matthew says here, “he touched her hand” is an act of helping or liberating grace [Col. 1464C].

Moreover, in both the one account and the other—as in the remaining cases—there is clear and certain attestation of truth in this event.
