For he is to be believed in his sayings, because the Lord, possessing authority over life and death, or life and health, merely stood and commanded; he stood and touched; and the fever fled.

Meanwhile, this also must be said to you, whoever you are who are, or desire to be, a prudent hearer of the Gospel: do not seek the order of events in everything written by the Evangelists. For they do not intend to set out the order of deeds or the times at which events occurred; rather, each follows the divinely provided heavenly mystery, like spiritual living creatures, full of eyes before and behind (Ezek. 10) [Col. 1464D]. Would the order of deeds in this author and in Luke be so different, as you can observe, unless a mystical cause underlay it?

Indeed, just as skilled craftsmen and excellent goldsmiths, when each wishes to make some precious vessel or a beautiful crown for a royal head, do not concern themselves with the particular time or price at which each gem was acquired; rather, they attend only to how the gems, arranged upon the gold, may better please the eyes of beholders by their variety. So these most faithful makers of evangelical truth were obliged to attend not so much to the times or chronological order in which miracles were performed as to the qualities of the miracles themselves, selected from innumerable events and arranged in fitting places, so that they might suffice for the splendour of truth and offer testimony to the glory and honour of this Son of Man: that, as he is true man, so also he is true God [Col. 1465A].

Hence comes that saying in the Psalm: “For you have gone before him with blessings of sweetness; you have placed on his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. 20 [21]). For what is the crown of precious stone upon his head except this Scripture, the maker of testimony concerning him, illumined by divine miracles at the beginning of evangelical preaching? Therefore do not greatly seek chronological order in the deeds where there shines an order of mysteries far more beautiful, concerning which something has already been said and more remains to be said.

For it has been said that it was to come about that first a small part of the Jewish people would be healed of its leprosy, then the Gentile people of its frenzied error; and afterwards, that every person now faithful and Christian who was again oppressed by actual sins would be freed by the grace of the merciful God. This would happen in accordance with the figures of the cleansed leper, the centurion’s servant delivered from a demon, and Simon’s mother-in-law, whom the same Lord healed from fever by a mighty command [Col. 1465B]. Was this not also to happen in the case of heretics, as it did? As the apostle John said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John 2 [probably 1 John 2]).

It follows, therefore: “And when evening had come, they brought to him many who had demons; he cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were ill.” Luke writes this same event: “Demons came out from many, crying and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (Luke 4) [Col. 1465C]. In this present event there was a great, manifest, and evident proof of his divinity or divine power, because, like the other things, he did this by his own authority. And this belongs to the testimony of truth, so that he could truly say: “The works which the Father has given me to complete, these works themselves bear witness concerning me” (John 5).

But according to the mystery already set forth, the spirits or demons which he cast out by a word, and which “came out from many, crying and saying, ‘You are the Son of God,’ while he, rebuking them, did not permit them to speak,” are or were heretics: feigned, pretentious, and crafty people, of whom Simon in the Acts of the Apostles was the first (Acts 8). He too believed, but his faith or confession, and that of others like him who cry, “You are the Son of God,” is like the confession of demons, whom the Son of God did not allow to speak; for faith or confession on the lips is not beautiful if love is not in the heart [Col. 1465D].

But what is the point of this: after the Evangelist had said, “and he healed all who were ill,” he immediately added, “that it might be fulfilled what was said through Isaiah the prophet, who says: ‘He took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses’” (Isa. 53)? For where this is said through Isaiah the prophet, the prophetic discourse concerns his Passion, as these following words clearly show: “And we thought him like a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities, crushed for our crimes. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed” (ibid.) [Col. 1466A], and the rest.

And truly this was his taking our infirmities and bearing our sicknesses: being wounded for our iniquities and crushed for our crimes; being beaten with scourges even to the bruising of his most holy body; being led like a sheep or lamb to slaughter; and, in that very slaughter, being reckoned among criminals. All these things are written in that prophetic passage from which the Evangelist took this chapter. What, then, is the present citation of such a passage except a devout and prudent consideration of so great a physician and of his purpose? For because his purpose was to bear our sins, which are truly infirmities and truly sicknesses of our souls, it was very devout and beautiful for this Evangelist to consider in his heart and indicate in his writing that he began to perform his work—the bearing or healing, as stated, of the sicknesses of souls—by bodily sicknesses, so that first, by visibly healing them, the true physician might become known, and only then might he come to heal the sicknesses of souls [Col. 1466B].

For he did indeed perform the beginning of signs in the presence of his disciples by changing water into wine (John 2), but this was his public office of preaching, when John had not yet completed his course. After John was handed over, then, from that time onward, he began both to preach the kingdom of God and to perform miracles—namely, to heal bodily infirmities—so that, as has already been said, people might thereby come to the healing of souls. And both the things already said and those still to be said are great and mystical proofs or testimonies concerning the authority of this Son of Man, the divine authority of this God and man.

But what does this inserted passage mean, which the Evangelist has inserted among these deeds? “Now when Jesus saw many crowds about him, he ordered them to go across the water. And one scribe approached and said to him: ‘Teacher, I shall follow you wherever you go.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’ Another of the disciples said to him: ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.’ But Jesus said to him: ‘Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead’” [Col. 1466C–D].

What, I ask, does it mean that he inserted these sayings of the Son of Man, so different and addressed to two people, amid his deeds—that is, his miracles? For up to this point he had clearly shown his authority: how with authority he said to the leper, “I will; be cleansed”; how he said to the centurion, “Go, and let it be done to you as you have believed”; how fever fled from his touch or command; how he cast out spirits by a word and healed all who were ill. Among them, as Luke recalls, demons came out, and he rebuked them and did not permit them to speak. He will immediately relate how, rising up, he commanded the winds and the sea, so that there was a calm, and they obeyed him.

What then shall we say? Clearly, if in the deeds done the divine Evangelist has attended to the course of things to be done in the Church, such as we have begun to expound, you have at hand the reason why he wished to pass over—or to insert in such a place—these very different sayings addressed to two people [Col. 1467A]. For it was to happen that, after the leprosy of souls among the Jews had been healed and the demonic vexation of frenzied error among the Gentiles had been calmed; while in Peter’s house, which is the Church, the fever of vices was again being healed, and heretics having an evil spirit were removed from the Church and for that reason were unworthy to speak about the Son of God—it was also to happen, I say, that many would seize upon, or appear to undertake, the purpose of perfection: some through rash presumption, others through fearful devotion.

Surely the example of those who were to approach in presumption is the one who said: “Teacher, I shall follow you wherever you go.” But the example of those who approach when called or admonished with fear is the one who says: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father” [Col. 1467B]. How many, do you suppose, have there been or are there in the Church who, following the very different examples of these two, have had or have different outcomes in their profession? The Evangelist therefore rightly judged that this too should not be passed over, so that, foreseeing the disturbances thereafter to come in the Church, whether from false brethren or from manifest adversaries who persecute, he might add: “And when he went up into the boat, his disciples followed him; and behold, a great commotion arose on the sea,” and so forth.

“Now let us consider these same words: ‘Seeing,’ he says, ‘many crowds around him, he gave orders to go across the water’ [Col. 1467C]. As at that time he saw many crowds around him, so too with the eyes of his divinity—to which all things are present—he foresaw the multitudes of Gentiles who would believe in him. Again, this deserves reverent consideration: just as he was to say to many who believed in him, through the Holy Spirit poured into their hearts, by the inspiration of holy desire—in which there is weariness of present things and longing for heavenly or future things—just as, I say, he was to say and by his ineffable utterance to bring about their crossing over or leaving the world and escaping the tumult of worldly cares (as those now do who choose the communal or solitary life), so then he gave orders to go across the water. It was not said that he gave orders to the many crowds that were around him [Col. 1467D], nor was it said that he gave orders to his disciples, who were then very few; rather, the Evangelist said indefinitely: ‘He gave orders to go across the water.’ Why? Unless because this command, according to this mystical sense, is not so much a precept as a counsel. For just as, on one occasion, when his disciples said, ‘If the case of a man with his wife is so, it is not expedient to marry,’ he answered, ‘Not all receive this saying,’ and then: ‘He who is able to receive it, let him receive it’ (Matt. 19); so concerning every water-crossing of worldly cares, in which believers may indeed lawfully become entangled, but with which they cannot be perfect, it must be understood wisely and discerningly that he commanded, or commands, certain persons to go across the water, yet does not impose upon all [Col. 1468A] the necessity of altogether abandoning marriage and the care of all domestic concerns. To cross the water in this manner is to follow Christ.

“But observe carefully what, and how, that bold Scribe said: ‘Master, I will follow you wherever you go.’ First, the very form of address is unpleasant, when he says ‘Master’ and does not say ‘Lord’: unpleasant, I say, and without love. For, if you rightly recall, those who addressed him with love addressed him thus: ‘Lord.’ For example, Peter’s address when he said, ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you’ (Matt. 14). The address ‘Master,’ or ‘Rabbi,’ belonged to the Pharisees, for whom it was pleasing to be greeted, to receive greetings, to call others Rabbi, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23). The impious Judas could address him in this way: while the others each said, ‘Is it I, Lord?’ he, being bitter and treacherous in heart, said, ‘Is it I, Rabbi?’ (Matt. 26). Indeed, it is good and pleasing to say both together, ‘Master and Lord’; hence he himself says, ‘You call me Master and Lord, and you say well, for so I am’ (John 13). But to say only ‘Master,’ or ‘Rabbi,’ and not ‘Lord,’ belongs to a distant heart—that is, one removed from the intimacy of love.

“Further, how great a presumption it is to say, or to have said, to this Master and Lord: ‘I will follow you wherever you go!’ For who has ever followed him wherever he went, or to whom did he himself say with his own mouth, ‘Follow me wherever I go’? Yet this is no wonder: for he was a Scribe [Col. 1468C], an order of men exceedingly presumptuous and boastful concerning their own righteousness; hence they were often sharply censured by the Lord himself. For example, he says: ‘The Scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses; but they do all their works in order to be seen by men’ (Matt. 23), and similar things.

“How, then, did he answer him? Certainly as he ought: ‘Foxes,’ he says, ‘have dens, and birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’ How unlike this answer is that which he later gave to Peter, still very bold and more confident than was fitting. For Peter had said, ‘Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death,’ and likewise, ‘Why can I not follow you now? I lay down my life for you.’ He answered him: ‘Do you lay down your life for me? Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock shall not crow until you have denied me three times’ (Matt. 26; John 13) [Col. 1468D]. Truly the answer is unlike, because that one was a rebuke, whereas this is altogether a rejection. And rightly ought it to be unlike, because Peter’s confidence sprang from the root of love, but this man’s presumption proceeded from the root of pride and wickedness.

“He could fittingly have said: Just as foxes lie hidden in dens, and birds of the air settle pleasantly in little nests, so malignant spirits—rightly called little foxes because of malice, and birds of the air because of exaltation—have occupied every lodging-place of your heart; and therefore you speak falsely in saying, ‘I will follow you wherever you go.’ In this utterance there are both deceit [Col. 1469A] and pride together: you wish both to deceive me and, through excessive ambition, to seem holy. But the venerable Master of holy discernment and moderation kept silent about the name of the malignant spirits, while sufficiently declaring the same thing.

“How many even today—indeed, it was necessary to recall them—are there in whose hearts malignant spirits lie, while with their mouths they profess a holy manner of life, as foxes in dens and birds in nests, so that there is no place in them where the Son of Man may lay his head? This Master and Lord does not repel the simple in this way; rather, he draws them to himself as though by force. For it follows: ‘Another of the disciples said to him: Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father. But Jesus said to him: Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead’ [Col. 1469B].

“In Deuteronomy Moses says, blessing Levi: ‘He who said to his father and his mother, “I do not know you”; and to his brothers, “I do not recognize you”; and they did not acknowledge their sons: these have kept your word and preserved your covenant; they shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel’ (Deut. 33). He said this concerning perfection. For he had first said: ‘Your perfection and your doctrine are for your holy man, whom you tested in perfection and judged at the waters of contradiction’ (ibid.). Therefore this man who said, ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father,’ fell somewhat short of perfection: he had not said to his father, ‘I do not know you’—especially to such a father that the Lord, in the authority of his love, would say to him: ‘Leave the dead [Col. 1469C] to bury their own dead.’ Certainly this man’s father was not like Zebedee, the father of James and John; otherwise he would not have been called dead, one to be buried by the dead. Yet James and John, when the Lord called them to follow him (Matt. 4), did not say: ‘Lord, permit us first to go and bury our father.’ Thus this man was not yet, in his very calling, of the same perfection as they were—the perfection which Moses, as has already been said, praises in Deuteronomy.

“What then? Clearly he was an example of such persons as some whom we have experienced even today: though they desire to follow Christ the Lord in a perfect way of life, they are held back by fleshly affection, by affection for father and mother [Col. 1469D], or for any relative whose love Holy Scripture or the love of God then contradicts, if those relatives are dead to God—that is, if they oppose the way of the Lord. It is therefore assisting grace when the incarnate Word says to one who is weak: ‘Follow me,’ and ‘Leave the dead to bury their own dead.’ Accordingly, following this example, you may rightly say to one whose desire for conversion you know to be delayed by fleshly affection—for example, by affection for a father living according to the flesh and therefore dead—‘Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God.’ But if he leaves even an innocent father, such as Zebedee, already mentioned, for others to bury, in order to follow Christ, then he acts much more with the apostles, namely James and John [Col. 1470A], who left their father Zebedee.

“‘When he entered the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. But he was sleeping. And they approached him and woke him, saying: Lord, save us; we are perishing. And he says to them: Why are you fearful, you of little faith? Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.’ Like the rest, the Son of Man did this also by his own power; therefore they immediately marveled and said: ‘What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?’

“Moses shone in this kind of miracle, namely in employing the service of the elements against Pharaoh in the land of Egypt. It has already been said above that the signs he performed were not such as those most especially worked by this Son of Man, who, as Isaiah had foretold and this Evangelist recalls, ‘took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses’; he bestowed the benefits of his powers chiefly upon the substance of man [Col. 1470B], beginning with the healing of bodies in order thereafter to reach the healing of souls. Yet is not this man greater, in this aspect of power—namely, commanding the elements—than Moses and all workers of miracles? Truly, he is incomparably greater, because none of them did anything by commanding; nor did Moses himself act by command, but received from the fullness of another, namely God or his Word—from the fullness, I say, of him alone of whom it was said, and had to be said, that ‘he commanded.’ Moses did not command; rather, it was commanded to him by this one, who said: ‘Stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, and let them be turned into blood; stretch out your hand over the rivers, and bring up frogs upon the land of Egypt’ (Exod. 7–8). And after many similar commands, he finally says: ‘Lift up your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the children of Israel may go out through the midst of the sea on dry land’; and again: ‘Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may return upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and horsemen’ (Exod. 14) [Col. 1470C]. Moses did all these things by another’s command, namely God’s, but by his own command nothing: for he was a man and not God. This one alone commanded the winds and sea by his own authority, for he was God, and they obeyed him.

“Moreover, to continue the course concerning mysteries which we have begun: the divine Evangelist beautifully set down this miracle in such order, because after those things which have been said so far, this too was to happen in the Church: the violence of open persecution by great rulers among the Gentiles, like a storm raised by great movements of winds on the sea, would be indicated, and the little boat of the Church, as though Jesus slept, would be fiercely troubled almost to the danger of life and salvation. What is Jesus’ sleeping in the boat except the withdrawal from the Church of the assistance of aiding grace? And when this happens, it happens in order ‘that those who are approved may become manifest’ (1 Cor. 11); that those who could be deceived by prosperity may be taught by adversity; that those who were in sins may be purified; and [Col. 1471A] that many martyrs may be crowned.

“Thus, as often as the Lord Jesus, as it were, sleeps or has slept in the boat, and a great disturbance arises in the sea so that the boat is covered by waves—as often, that is, as, through the most orderly providence, he delays and for a time withdraws necessary defenses—the restless devil, agitator of the winds of this age (such a wind was Nero, or deadly Decius, or Diocletian or Maximinus), raises persecutions and stirs the sea—that is, the multitudes of the Gentiles—by their laws and edicts to the deaths or oppression of the saints. Alas, how often, when such a disturbance arose, was the boat covered by waves! How often, while most cruel pagans persecuted and killed, was the holy Church crushed under countless calamities!

“Then the disciples approached [Col. 1471B] and awakened Jesus as he slept, invoking the same Savior. For example, by saying those words of David: ‘Arise, why do you sleep, Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever’ (Ps. 43); and again: ‘Arise, Lord, help us and deliver us for your name’s sake’ (ibid.); and elsewhere: ‘Help us, lest perhaps the Gentiles say: Where is their God?’ (Ps. 78). But this awakening both was and must always be sweet and gentle, not troublesome: that is, with faith and without despair, with perseverance and without impatience. Otherwise, to those who awaken him he himself says: ‘Why are you fearful, you of little faith?’ As though he plainly said: Is it not written that ‘the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity’ (Ps. 124)? And what does ‘will not leave’ mean except that he will not permit it to endure long?

“Remember the earlier and later Egyptians, Assyrians or Babylonians, Medes and Persians, and the other barbarian nations and ungodly kings of men: whoever stretched out and raised their rod—that is, their power or dominion—over the lot of the righteous, to afflict or destroy those who were perhaps—that is, by the gratuitous election of mercy—predestined to eternal life. Did they endure long? Did not even their apparent temporary predominance work together for good for the righteous and for those who love God? Why then are you fearful? [Col. 1471D] Is it because Nero crucifies Peter and cuts down Paul with the sword? Do not fear; do not be fearful. Rather, ‘in your patience possess your souls’ (Luke 21), because this rod will not endure so long that the righteous, as though deprived of help, must stretch out their hands to iniquity; rather, it will quickly be broken and cast into the fire to burn.

“‘Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.’ The Lord Jesus’ rising and commanding the winds and sea is his exercising or stirring up his power—namely, in order to help the elect and take vengeance upon the reprobate. This has often happened particularly; but it will happen universally and once for all when, in the last judgment, he rises, as it is said in the Psalm: ‘The earth trembled and was still when God arose in judgment’ (Ps. 45). For he used the past tense for the future, as is customary in prophetic speech, saying: ‘From heaven you made judgment heard; the earth trembled and was still,’ when he meant to say, You will come from heaven and make judgment heard—understood in his saying, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom’ (Matt. 25), and the rest. Then the earth will tremble and be still: that is, the ungodly will fear and cease persecuting the saints [Col. 1472A].

“Then indeed he will rise against all; but now he sometimes rises against particular parties and stands in terror, to avenge the killings of saints upon adversaries and murderers. Thus, for example, he had then risen and stood—clearly threatening the Jews and about to bring destruction upon nation and place—when Stephen, the first martyr, while standing before the council and gazing into heaven, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand, and said: ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’ (Acts 7) [Col. 1472B]. Thus too, when the Lord rises at times in other cases, or against others, after great disturbances there is calm, and peace is restored to the churches.

“‘When they had come across the water into the country of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass by that way. And behold, they cried out, saying: What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us? Now there was, not far from them, a herd of many swine feeding. And the demons begged him, saying: If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine. And he said to them: Go. And they went out and entered into the swine. And behold, the whole herd rushed headlong into the sea, and they died in the waters.’

“With what kind and how great a power this glorious Son of Man had hitherto cast out demons, as the Evangelist said shortly before, that ‘he cast out spirits by a word,’ is especially clear from this example. The literal sense is evident: it plainly indicates that this Son of Man is the true God, at whose presence legions of demons tremble and confess that they cannot endure him; and, tortured and compelled to leave by his nod alone, so many malignant spirits beg that, since they are forced to leave, they may at least be allowed to enter the swine [Col. 1472C].

“Yet one question is not idly raised: how did it please this one so mild and gentle, who would allow no one to be unjustly harmed by himself, according to the words, ‘He will not strive nor cry out, nor shall his voice be heard abroad in the streets’ (Isa. 42)—how, I say, did it please him to give or send another person’s swine to malignant spirits, so that they might rush headlong into the sea and die in the waters? Whoever asks this must know that the people of that region were such that they deserved to suffer not only the loss of their swine, but every kind of punishment. For, if you weigh the matter rightly, just as he said: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles which were done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes’; and immediately added: ‘Nevertheless, I say to you that it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you’ (Matt. 11), so he could truly have said to these Gerasenes [Col. 1473A] as well. For they not only did not believe after seeing such great miracles, but even begged him to depart from their borders. He departed, and what happened to them was what happened to the other foolish regions—according to the likeness of the swine themselves, which, driven by demons, rushed headlong into the sea and died.

“The exposition of this mystery must now begin from the very opening of the present reading. Therefore, when the Lord came into the country of the Gerasenes, two demon-possessed men came out from the tombs to meet him, exceedingly fierce; because, when he came to dwell in this life to defeat the devil, the prince of this world [Col. 1473B], the two deaths of the human race, under the leadership of that very prince of sin and death, ran against him. What are those two deaths? One is the death of bodies, and one the death of souls; against both he had to contend. Thus they are well said to be two, exceedingly fierce, and to have come out of, or dwelt in, tombs: for the death of souls is exceedingly fierce, and through the death of bodies we come to dwell in tombs.

“The death of souls, indeed, which met him, prevailed against him in nothing, as he himself says: ‘The prince of this world is coming, and has nothing in me’ (John 14). But the death of bodies was permitted to prevail against him for a time, so that, by taking or admitting our single death, he might abolish the double death. What is truer than the statement: ‘Exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass by that way’? For who from the whole human race escaped untouched by the fierceness of death? ‘All sinned in Adam,’ says the Apostle, ‘and all die in Adam’ (Rom. 5). When Adam sinned, he himself immediately died by the death of the soul; and we died in him. And when it was said to him, ‘You are dust, and to dust you shall return’ (Gen. 3), he was consigned to the death of the body, and we with him [Col. 1473C]. Thus truly no one could pass by that way: there was no one who would not see death and who would rescue his soul from the hand of hell.

“But this one came, over whom no death had any claim. And because, through one death—namely that of the body—an injustice was done to him, both deaths justly fell beneath him, not without great torment to the prince of both deaths and his attendants, whom he expelled with him. For just as his descent into hell was desirable to the company of saints, so it was grievous and intolerable to the legions of demons. Therefore they said: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?’ That time, in which they know they are to be tormented, will be the final judgment, when their prince with them, and they with their prince, will be cast before all into eternal fire, as it is written in Job (Job 14) [Col. 1473D].

“How, finally, was fulfilled in the mystery what was signified by the miracle—namely, that the whole herd of swine rushed headlong with violence into the sea and died in the waters? Certainly in the manner foretold knowingly by the Son of Man himself: ‘When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man,’ and so forth, down to: ‘Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself; and entering in, they dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first’ (Matt. 12). By such a single man he intends the unbelieving and blasphemous Jews, who should be regarded not so much as Jews as Canaanites, not so much as calves as swine. For they became worse through the Savior’s good work, and died through envy precisely because he conquered one death in himself and both deaths in his faithful people. They were handed over to malignant spirits and, through their frenzy, rushed headlong into the sea [Col. 1474A].

“Indeed, by stirring up implacable seditions, as many writers—and Josephus above all—relate, they attacked the Roman Empire; in astonishing madness and remarkable obstinacy, they provoked the conquerors of all nations to kill them and to destroy their place and nation. What was such madness except swine driven by malignant spirits rushing headlong and violently into the sea? Therefore, if you consider or look back at what they were in Egypt before receiving the Law, and what they did or received after the Redeemer’s coming, you may rightly say that their latter condition was worse than their former. Thus they were hurled, both in soul and body, into every abyss of miseries, like those swine, beneath which, because of the demons’ frenzies, not even their own sense—brutish though it was—could remain.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1474C]

“‘Entering the boat, he crossed over and came into his own city. And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you. And behold, some of the Scribes said within themselves: This man blasphemes. And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: Why do you think evil in your hearts? Which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? But that you may know that the Son of Man has power to forgive sins’—then he says to the paralytic—‘Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house. And he rose and went to his house. But the crowds, seeing this, feared and glorified God, who gave such power to men.’

“The Son of Man himself here declared, by his own mouth, the power which we intend to consider and know for his honor and glory, in a matter in which it was especially expedient for us that this Lord should be powerful: namely, the forgiveness of sins. Until this point he had not said that he had power to forgive sins, wisely using the providence of discernment so as not to say it before proving it by deeds. And the spirits whom he cast out by a word, tortured, confessed him to be the one of whom the prophet had foretold: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you shall come a leader who shall rule my people Israel’ (Mic. 5) [Col. 1474D]. The sum of the words that follow there in the same prophet is: ‘to save his people from their sins’ (ibid.). Therefore, after the preceding deeds had established that he was, and ought to be believed to be, that leader of Israel, the messianic leader—that is, Christ—then at last, when about to heal the paralytic, he said: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’ Thus, as present miracles and ancient prophetic oracles confirm the present utterance, those slow to believe—and indeed impatient even to hear—might be less offended, who cannot be taught without offense.

“For they were liable to be offended in this matter, and were offended by a voluntary offense, especially the Scribes and Pharisees, who did not seek truth but envied it. For immediately when he said, ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’—‘behold,’ says the Evangelist, ‘some of the Scribes said within themselves: This man blasphemes. Who can forgive sins except God alone?’ He saw their thoughts and said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’ Perhaps they said this also within themselves; but he answered them concerning that by their own conscience, and concerning this by the manifest power of the deed, since the command, ‘Rise and walk,’ was followed by its effect. In both ways he convicted the unbelievers, so that they had no excuse for their sin [Col. 1475B].

“But what answer was proper to the question, ‘Which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or “Rise and walk”?’ Other than that it is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven’? For to the Son of Man himself one was as easy as the other; but for men it is far easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ than to prove the forgiveness of sins itself by the testimony of power, such as immediately followed.

“According to this example, this happens almost daily in the city of the Lord, namely in the Church, which is indeed the city of the Lord, the city of the great King. He crossed over and came to it after, as was said above, he had both calmed the fierceness of the death of our bodies and dissolved the cruel dominion of the death of our souls. For as often as we do what the apostle James says: ‘Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him’ (James 5)—as often, I say, as we do this, we offer to the Lord a paralytic or one infirm from any cause. And, just as seeing their faith he said, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ so now ‘the prayer of faith will heal the sick person; and if he is in sins [Col. 1476B], they are forgiven him.’

“Moreover, according to a deeper sense, the paralytic is then healed by the Lord when one who formerly did nothing now begins to work, as the Apostle says: ‘He who stole, let him steal no longer; but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need’ (Eph. 4). For did not the one who did no work and stole what belonged to others have a true paralysis in his hands? Likewise, did not one who was mute with regard to beneficial and good speech have a true paralysis in his tongue? Thus, when the Lord works in such matters, either by himself alone or with his ministers cooperating, so that the one who was thus paralytic now labors well, working with his hands, and so that ‘no evil speech proceeds from his mouth,’ as the same Apostle immediately says (ibid.), ‘but whatever is good for the edification of faith, that it may give grace to those who hear,’ then the crowds rightly glorify the Lord, who gave such power to men [Col. 1476C].

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 1475]

[Col. 1475C] 634 O Wisdom of God, who opened the mouth of the dumb and made the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis. 10): I, once dumb and an infant, but now with opened mouth and a tongue almost eloquent, magnifying you and having begun to make for you, from your gold and your gems, a kind of royal crown [Col. 1475D] of glory and honor, greatly indeed at all times, but now especially, desire to be helped by your ordering and assistance. For now I am not, as hitherto, intent upon only one work, nor debtor to only one debt; rather, beset as though by two great and avaricious moneylenders, I cannot refrain from satisfying both, desiring to be faithful.

“One of them is an angel—that is, the bishop of the Church of Cologne—to whom, I believe, you committed me through your most merciful providence, in a time of persecution, as an adopted son to a father. The other is the master of the household of your house, namely of the monastery of Siegburg, to whom I cannot say how greatly I am indebted. The latter first urged me to undertake this work entitled *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*. But the other, the greater friend, exceedingly pleased by a favorable report of, or experience of, my studies, commanded and requested—and in both ways, by commanding and requesting, compelled me—to turn my whole heart, with your grace, Lord, to the Books of Kings [Col. 1476C], and, with your help, to begin as great a work as I could, and, as it seemed to him, a useful one; and never to despair of your help in bringing it to completion.

“What was I to do, with my mind almost divided between these men? Was I stubbornly to resist my father and bishop? Yet he not only commanded in this way but even entreated me, while I refused for some time; so that, if I had not obeyed, I would have seemed rebellious against piety itself. Was I to abandon this work which I had already begun at the request, as has been said, of the lesser friend? But he was distressed about it with so burning a holy desire that, seeing my necessity—that I could not refuse one who was greater and more worthy—and looking upon this work, so far as it had then been written, he said only: ‘I grieve for you, I grieve for you,’ gazing at the manuscript, which he could scarcely bear to leave incomplete [Col. 1477A].

“Therefore, compelled by necessity, I gave one half of my heart to one and one half to the other; but, O Wisdom, I desired to give all of it to you, who say: ‘My son, give me your heart’ (Prov. 23). Believing and knowing that all things are possible to one who believes (Mark 9), behold, I have devoted myself so to charity that, at one and the same time, two secretaries sitting around me dip their pens in my mind. Hence, if anything has been well said, let all be ascribed to you; but if anything sounds less good, let it rightly be pardoned on account of necessity.

> “As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and said to him: [Col. 1477B] ‘Follow me.’ And rising, he followed him.”

This must be proclaimed and heard to the glory and honor of the Son of Man: that he saw this man, and saw him so effectually that it may truly be said of him: “You are the God who saw me” (John 1). For how, or with what eyes, did he see him? If the question concerns the eyes of his human head, with which he had sight as a man, did he see this man alone? Certainly not: with such eyes he also saw those who shortly before (Matt. 8) begged him to depart from their borders, and those who crucified him. Different are the eyes by which he saw this man: the eyes of graces, which, according to Zechariah, are in one stone (Zech. 3), and according to the Apocalypse of John, are the seven eyes in the head of one Lamb (Rev. 1). These eyes ought not to be unknown to anyone by their names; [Col. 1477C] namely, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). With these eyes he saw this man; and while seeing him with his outward eyes, through these inward eyes he recognized that he was one of those whom he had foreknown and predestined before the ages.

Thus, seeing him, he said: “Follow me.” And rising, he followed him. Matthew himself was like a brightly shining mirror, yet not placed before the sun’s gaze, but hidden in darkness and beneath the roof of excessively worldly cares. For he was a tax collector, exacting public duty or tribute from commercial ships amid shouting or the bustle of the marketplace. [Col. 1477D] But when Jesus saw him—when salvation and the true sun saw him—he shone forth from that gaze; and because such a Son of Man saw him, he restored his image, and the face of a man was formed in him.

He also saw another, and by his gaze the face of an ox was formed in him; he saw another, and as he looked, the face of a lion was formed in him; he saw another, and by seeing him he formed in him the face of a flying eagle (Ezek. 1, 10; Rev. 4). This wondrous gaze is that grace of which Paul, the vessel of election, speaks in admiration: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8). Before eternal times he foreknew and predestined; [Col. 1478A] but in time he called each person in his own time, as he now called this man and said, “Follow me.”

How cheerfully he presented himself to the caller, how eagerly and lovingly he opened the doors of his heart to the one knocking, the outward event sufficiently indicates: “he made a great feast for him in his house.” Therefore, in this man especially, the truth of that saying of the Lord is most clearly demonstrated: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3). He entered Matthew’s house and first dined bodily with him; afterwards Matthew dined with him at a spiritual supper. Indeed, the present Scripture—the Gospel Scripture—proves this, because he truly dined with the Lord who [Col. 1478B] 535 belched forth for us this first writing of the New Testament as one truly satisfied.

The Pharisees, neither knowing nor wishing to know this mystery, when the Lord reclined with him in his house, and when many tax collectors and sinners also reclined with the Lord Jesus and his disciples, said: “Why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners?” But he wisely and most fearfully stopped their mouths: wisely, indeed, in saying, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” But fearfully in adding: “For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” By this saying or word he struck fearfully those who [Col. 1478C] trusted in themselves as righteous. Whom does he call righteous here except the proud? And whom does he call sinners except the humble?

Woe to such righteous persons, who are righteous in their own judgment but not in God’s; who wish to seem righteous when they are not. Conversely, happy are the sinners who recognize their own unrighteousness and hunger and thirst for God’s righteousness. For he came to call them alone; for their sake he descended from heaven and “humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

Then the disciples of John came to him and said: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?” And Jesus said to them: “Can the children of the Bridegroom fast while the Bridegroom is with them? But days will come [Col. 1478D] when the Bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast.”

How weighty and wise this response is may better be understood by comparison with the prophetic Scripture. In Zechariah the Lord says: “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months through those seventy years”—that is, because Nebuchadnezzar had burned the city and temple with fire and carried the people into captivity, and because Ishmael son of Nethaniah killed Gedaliah and with him the remnant of the people (4 Kings 25; Jer. 41)—“did you fast a fast for me?” and so forth, down to: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities, until peoples come and dwell in [Col. 1479A] many cities” (Zech. 7–8). This was to occur through the coming of this Bridegroom, concerning whom it is immediately said there: “In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall seize the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you’” (ibid.).

For concerning the fringe of the Jewish man, you have immediately here in the Gospel that “a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years came up from behind and touched the fringe of his garment” (Matt. 9). The sum of that prophetic discourse is this: those in whom the hope and expectation of the promise was deposited—or ought to have been—should fast, not so much because of the temporal misfortunes that had occurred, and because of the Babylonian captivity that had lasted seventy [Col. 1479B] years, as because of their sins and because of that universal captivity of the human race which occurred in Adam.

But since the Babylonian captivity had been ended and the temple was being rebuilt, each of them said: “Must I mourn in the fifth month, or consecrate myself, as I have done now for many years?” That is, because the temple was being rebuilt, they believed that no cause remained for fasting. They were therefore rightly rebuked by the one who said: “Did you fast a fast for me?” (Zech. 7). For those who mourn and fast because temporal goods are lacking do not fast for the Lord. But those who fast because they do not have the Bridegroom present—as they did not yet have him, whereas we did have him but no longer have him—these fast a fast for the Lord.

[Col. 1479C] Therefore, since the desire and expectation of the Savior ought to have been the reason for fasting for all, as it was for Moses, Elijah, and Daniel, while he himself was now present but was later to depart, it was sweet and pleasant, as an act of holy love, that fasting should be interrupted at least briefly because of his presence; for that time, the time of his presence, was like a time of marriage. Therefore he says: “Can the children of the Bridegroom mourn while the Bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the Bridegroom is taken from them, and then they will fast.”

It is as though he said: You who are not, and do not wish to be, children of the Bridegroom, nor even deserve to be children of those who fasted from longing for the Bridegroom’s coming—indeed, you are among those to whom God truly says, [Col. 1479D] “Did you fast a fast for me?”—for you too fast as they did, because at some time some adversity has occurred in transitory matters: you, I say, fast as much as you please; but these cannot fast for joy at the Bridegroom’s presence. “But days will come when the Bridegroom is taken from them, and then they were fasting.”

> “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. For it takes away its fullness from the garment, and the tear becomes worse.”

Certainly they will fast in those days soon to come, when the Bridegroom has been taken from them: when he has suffered, died, and been buried; has risen; and has ascended to heaven, no longer bodily dwelling among them in this world. But will they [Col. 1480A] fast as you fast? Certainly not; for that would be like putting a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. Your fasts, indeed, are the fasts of the old man; but these men, being children of heavenly marriage, are new men.

If, therefore, they fasted for causes such as those for which you fast—namely, because Moses cast from his hands the first tablets written by the finger of God and broke them at the foot of the mountain (Exod. 31); or because the scouts whom Moses had sent to spy out the land returned and disparaged it, whereupon the whole multitude fell into revolt and God in anger swore that they would not enter that land until that generation had been consumed over forty years, according to the number of forty days during which they had surveyed the land (Num. [Col. 1480B] 14); or because Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, or Nebuzaradan his captain, captured the city, burned the house of the Lord, and transported the people to Babylon; or because afterward Ishmael son of Nethaniah came and struck Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land, together with the Jews who were with him, and the whole remaining people rose up and fled into Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (4 Kings 25; 2 Chron. 36; Jer. 41)—if, I say, they fasted for such causes, that would be for new men to lament the dirges of the old man. This is wholly unfitting for those to whom “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Mark 4; Luke 8).

For as a patch of unshrunk cloth, when put into an old garment, takes away its fullness and makes the tear worse, [Col. 1480C] so anyone made a participant in this holy newness, if he incorporates himself into traditions of this Pharisaic kind, becomes worse than any old man. Thus he is neither old nor new, possesses neither condition, because he has wished to mingle both together in himself.

But why did he not state openly what he intended—what he wished to be understood from these words, “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for it takes away its fullness from the garment, and the tear becomes worse”? Why did he conceal, close, and seal so good and true an understanding from them? Surely because this was advantageous for them, but it was not advantageous for the mysteries of God’s kingdom themselves to be made public or entrusted to them.

“For,” he says, “neither do they put new wine into [Col. 1480D] 636 old wineskins. Otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.” According to this comparison, it would have been harmful to teach them plainly why his disciples did not then fast but would fast later. For the Pharisees were among those who had asked. And just as old wineskins burst when new wine is poured into them, and the wine perishes with the skins, so they would have burst still further through envy if he had openly said something of this sort in their hearing; and the discourse would have been uselessly poured out, especially since Wisdom says: “Do not pour out speech where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32; John 2).

For this reason another Evangelist says: “Jesus himself did not entrust [Col. 1481A] himself to them, because he knew all men and because he had no need for anyone to bear witness concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man” (Zech. 7).

Therefore, although he could have said, “Fasting was required until I came, and when I depart fasting will be required after me,” according to the truth of the prophetic Scripture already mentioned above, he preferred to temper his discourse in such a way that, while the matter became known to future generations, it might remain preserved with him, and those then present might not burst through envy.

What, then, of what he immediately added: “But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved”? Were not even the children of the Bridegroom—concerning whose failure to fast this question had arisen—already new wineskins? They were not yet wholly [Col. 1481B] new, but they were capable of holy newness. Therefore, in one place he said to them also: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). When were they made wholly new? When, after his resurrection, they received the Holy Spirit, by whose grace he makes people new (John 20; Acts 2). Then new wine was put into new wineskins, and both were preserved: that is, all the mysteries of the Scriptures were revealed to them; they tasted the love of the Bridegroom and the sweetness of heavenly marriage; made drunk by this wine, they were saved; and they faithfully poured out again the well-preserved wine to those whom they were commanded to serve.

> “While he was speaking these things, behold, a certain ruler came and worshiped him, saying: ‘My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.’ And Jesus rose and followed him, and his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years came from behind and touched the fringe of his garment. For she said within herself: ‘If I touch only his garment, I shall be saved.’”

[Col. 1481C] I cannot sufficiently admire the beauty of glory and honor in the face of this Son of Man, in his wondrous deeds, according to the arrangement made here by this divine Evangelist. For what is the point of the fact that, while answering the question about fasting and excusing the Bridegroom’s children for not fasting, this event immediately follows concerning a woman who, for such a reason and with so great faith, touched the fringe of his garment? What, I say, is its point, except to intimate by deeds that, as has already been said, it was not yet expedient for him openly to declare in words that he was the man of whom Zechariah, in the passage above mentioned—when likewise questioned about fasting by those asking, “Must I mourn in the fifth month, or consecrate myself, as I have now done for many years?” (Zech. 7)—so ended his reply as to say: “Until peoples come and ten men from all the languages of the nations seize the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: ‘We will go with you’” (Zech. 8).

[Col. 1481D] This arrangement, therefore, is very venerable and worthy of devout consideration. For what else did the prophet foretell after his answer concerning fasting—“In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall seize the fringe of a Jewish man”—than what he wished here to signify [Col. 1482A] through the woman who touched the fringe of his garment and was healed of her flow of blood?

For this woman was a figure of all nations, which indeed, by believing in him whose face they had not previously seen, in some sense approach from behind; and by following his footsteps—that is, by keeping his commandments—they truly touch the fringe of his garment. And what, in this sense, was the flow of blood except the pollution of sins, and above all the exceedingly foul worship of idolatry? The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, for whom he had been asked and to whom he was going, represented the Synagogue.

It must therefore be carefully noted that, as Mark writes more clearly, the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was not dead but already at the point of death (Mark 5). But when the woman was healed by touching the fringe, messengers came to the ruler of the synagogue and said: [Col. 1482B] “Your daughter is dead; why trouble the master any further?” Likewise this must be diligently observed: the girl who died was twelve years old, and the woman who was healed had been subject to the flow of blood for twelve years. Thus, when the girl was born, that woman began to bleed; and when the woman was healed, the girl died.

What mystery is more beautiful, true, and splendid than this? For when the Synagogue was born in the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the flow of idolatry began to issue forth among the nations. But when the multitude of the nations, believing in Christ, was healed and saved from such a flow by faith, then the Synagogue, which up to that point had been very sick through many tribulations, [Col. 1482C] died altogether through envy and became without God. Again, “when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11). Therefore the fitting completion of beauty in this mystery is that, after the woman was healed of the flow of blood, he then entered, took the hand of the dead girl, “and the girl arose.”

> “As Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out: ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David.’ When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him; and Jesus said to them: ‘Do you believe that I can do this for you?’ They said to him: ‘Certainly, Lord.’ Then he touched their eyes, saying: ‘According to your faith be it done to you’; and their eyes were opened.”

We remember our purpose, [Col. 1482D] as we ought: namely, that the purpose of this work is to consider the four faces of the one living creature—the face of a man, the face of an ox, the face of a lion, and the face of a flying eagle. These are the four mysteries of the one Christ, Son of God and son of man, which cannot be unknown to Christian faith: his incarnation, his passion, his resurrection, and his ascension.

We are attending to the face of the man, and suppose that we see this face in part and contemplate it through a mirror if we pause to discern what intention may have been present in his deeds and sayings. Looking, then, upon the face of this Son of Man, we ask what he intended in so earnestly requiring the merit of faith that he said to these blind men: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” And immediately: “According to [Col. 1483A] your faith,” he says, “be it done to you.” A little earlier he said to the woman: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.” Throughout all the Scriptures, both Old and New Testament, he seeks faith, approves faith, and praises faith.

The reason or purpose of his condescension is of no small importance: to cure, by a fitting antidote, the old folly of excessive credulity whereby the devil was believed when he spoke through the serpent and said: “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). The woman believed the devil rather than God, imagining that she would thus be enlightened. Let us, on the contrary, believe the truth if we truly 637 wish to be enlightened.

This consideration is very beautiful both wherever else the Lord seeks or finds faith and especially in these blind men, when, before enlightening them, he asks: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” Our own cause was signified in them, as may especially be known or perceived from the fact that, once their eyes had been opened, he charged them, saying: [Col. 1483B] “See that no one knows.” We quite profitably recall this as an example for ourselves, whenever we seem to have received some privilege of enlightenment through which the human race has been enlightened by faith. For why are we to see that no one knows, except so that the enlightened eye of the heart may escape the evil onset of boasting or pride?

Yet they did what is immediately added: “But when they had [Col. 1483C] gone out, they spread his fame throughout that whole region.” We too do fittingly if it is not our own enlightenment that our tongue proclaims, but the glory of the Enlightener that our works proclaim. Therefore, in the two blind men let us understand every person, whether Jew or Greek, who then truly asks from that true light, confidently and effectually, for the grace of illumination—provided that he has a genuine and tested coin to offer, not a counterfeit faith.

> “When they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke; and the crowds marveled, saying: ‘Never has anything like this appeared in Israel.’”

This is one of the things we marvel at while attending to the face of this Son of Man: that never thus appeared in Israel; never upon [Col. 1483D] earth was such a face seen among all the faces of patriarchs and prophets, and of all people who have done memorable deeds upon the earth. This must be distinguished by faithful discernment: never was there such a human face as this.

“But the Pharisees said: ‘He casts out demons by the prince of demons.’” The Pharisees, divided from God, breathed forth what great straits and poverty of their bitter hearts! Since they could not say, “He does not cast out demons,” they turned instead to say: “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” But since they said this not only once and blasphemed similarly in other places as the following passages will indicate, let us now hasten to other matters. We have lingered beyond our purpose too long in contemplating [Col. 1484A] the face of the man, while we must also contemplate the other faces, and fear that the work will become excessively long and tedious.

> “Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity. But when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were troubled and lying down like sheep without a shepherd.”

In this place especially, the face of the man which we behold is admirable, because it is a face of piety, mercy, and compassion. The people then looked upon by that kindly face were troubled and lying down like sheep without a shepherd, since under the name of shepherds they had wolves—Annas and Caiaphas—of whom the prophet rightly said [Col. 1484B]: “Her princes in her midst are like wolves seizing prey, to shed blood, destroy souls, and greedily pursue gain” (Ezek. 22).

How were sheep troubled and lying down under such men—not shepherds but wolves? Surely as the same prophet says elsewhere among other things: “What was weak you did not strengthen; what was sick you did not heal; what was broken you did not bind up; what was cast away you did not bring back; what was lost you did not seek; but you ruled over them harshly and with force” (Ezek. 34). In what way, then, or in what did he have compassion on them, except by now setting about to do what he there had forcefully foretold that he would do? “Behold,” he says, “I myself shall demand my flock from the hand of the shepherds, and I shall make them cease from feeding my flock; the shepherds shall no longer feed themselves; and I shall deliver my flock from their mouth” (ibid.).

But did he see only the crowds and have compassion only upon those whom he then beheld with bodily eyes? Certainly not: with inward eyes he also saw all the crowds of every nation that would believe in him. Having compassion on all, he immediately introduced another comparison and said to his disciples:

[Col. 1484D] > “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”

To this day every householder of the Lord’s harvest laments this: the harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. To put it briefly, there are indeed many crowds of believers in Christ, many communities living under a sacred profession in monasteries or hospices; but among this multitude, few are laboring—that is, few have attained such progress that care or oversight of the weaker may safely be entrusted to them.

What, then, should one do to whom the stewardship or management of such a harvest has been committed? He should certainly ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into the harvest: that is, he should with every urgency ask God to multiply spiritual grace among more of his subjects. Let him first imitate the Holy Spirit, the foremost of such stewards, and faithful Moses. “Why,” Moses said to the Lord, “have you afflicted your servant? Why do I not find grace in your sight? Why have you placed the burden of all this people [Col. 1485A] upon me? Did I conceive this multitude or bear it, that you should say to me: ‘Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse usually carries a little child, and bring them into the land for which I swore to their fathers’?” (Num. 11).

Finally, what Moses intended in these words, what he sought by this great and vehement lament, God—the hearer of his heart—makes clear in his response. He says: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; lead them to the entrance of the tent of the covenant and make them stand there with you, so that I may come down and speak with you, and take from your spirit and give it to them, that they may bear with you the burden of the people and you may not be weighed down alone” (ibid.).

Therefore, whoever is the steward of the Lord’s harvest should, following this example of faithful Moses, [Col. 1485B] ask for assistance; and it will be given him, provided that he is free from every sinister jealousy, likewise following Moses’ example. For when a young man ran and reported to Moses, saying: “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp” (ibid.), and Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ minister and one chosen from many, immediately said: “My lord Moses, forbid them” (ibid.), Moses replied: “Are you jealous on my account? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit!” (ibid.).

Meanwhile, it should be noted that, whereas in another Evangelist he says, “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers” (Luke 10), here this Evangelist says more forcefully, “that he may cast out laborers into the harvest.” What does it mean to say “cast out,” [Col. 1485C] except that very many of those entrusted with the talent of labor are gladly idle, and sometimes wish, under the apparent pretext of holiness and perfection, to live more secretly for themselves alone, although they could benefit others also? May the Lord cast out such people—namely, by confronting their consciences and rebuking those who harmfully conceal the talent entrusted to them. May he cast them out, I say, to labor, because truly it is a casting out to leave one’s desired rest through fear of the Lord.

## Chapter 10

[Col. 1485D]

> “Having summoned his twelve 638 disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity. Now these are the names of the twelve apostles: first Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean; and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.”

In Luke, after the twelve apostles have already been summoned and named, the Lord, when about to send others also to preach, says the words which you read here that he said before summoning these twelve: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke 10), and so forth. This fact could rightly trouble the mind with a question if it were first established that the Lord, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, could never or nowhere say the same discourse except once and in one place. [Col. 1486A] But who demands this of a preacher: that what he said in one place or at one time he not repeat or say in other places or at other times, especially since not all can be present in one place, nor can all equally retain in memory what they have heard once?

Now in this work also, attentively consider the face of the Lord. “Having summoned his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and infirmity.” If shortly before, when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke, the crowds rightly marveled and truly said, “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel,” how much more should all marvel at this, that he gave such authority to his disciples, and say: “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel”? Was Moses such a one? Did he by his own authority produce frogs and flies, [Col. 1486B] or give anyone this power to produce them? Therefore this is our God, and no other shall be esteemed beside him: he himself cast out, by his own authority, not ordinary frogs or flies but the princes of flies—that is, demons of filth—which neither Moses nor anyone else did; and he gave to people, whom he wished, the authority to cast them out.

“First,” he says, “of the Apostles, Simon, who is called Peter.” This very name Peter was given him by the Lord himself, when he was called Simon. For another Evangelist, Mark, after saying, “and he gave them authority to heal and cast out demons,” immediately sets down these same names of the twelve apostles [Col. 1486C]: “And,” he says, “he gave Simon the name Peter” (Mark 3).

He who changed the name of this one person in the New Testament, so that he who was called Simon should be called Peter, is the same one who likewise changed the name of one person in the Old Testament, so that he who was called Jacob should be called Israel (Gen. 32). For he himself is the writer of names, such as he has deigned to know; and he has a book written with the most splendid names. Knowing this, Moses said: “Either forgive the people this sin, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.” The Lord answered him: “Whoever sins against me, I shall blot out of my book”—with the implication, “and not you” (Exod. 32). For afterwards he says: “You have found grace in my sight, and I know you yourself by name” (Exod. 33).

Nor is it without significance that he changed the name of that man in the Old Testament [Col. 1486D] and this man in the New. If an intelligent observer is present, the mystery of this change is most beautiful: it was being done so that what had been said through the prophet might occur: “I shall call my servants by another name, in which he who is blessed shall be blessed upon the earth” (Isa. 65). Of those many servants of God, the former is father according to the flesh, whereas our Lord Jesus Christ himself is Father according to the Spirit.

Thus this also is a most beautiful spectacle in mystery: that father according to the flesh, the origin of a multitude, begot twelve sons; while this Father according to the Spirit, the beginning of Christianity, [Col. 1487A] begot twelve apostles. And as the former father according to the flesh changed the original name, so this spiritual Father changed it—not for himself, indeed, but for his chief vicar.

Simon is interpreted “obedient”; Peter is named from the rock. By his very name he foreshadowed the firmness of the Church or of the catholic faith, which he himself outstandingly confessed thus: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). Saul also had his name changed so that he was called Paul; but this change differs, because the Lord himself is not recorded as having changed it to him orally.

Andrew: “handsome” or “shining.” John: “in whom is grace,” or “the Lord’s grace”; and his brother James—both called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder,” evidently because of the steadfastness or greatness of their faith. Philip: “mouth of a lamp.” Bartholomew: “son of him who suspends the waters.” Thomas: “abyss” or “twin”; hence he is also called in Greek δίδυμος (*didymos*, “twin”). Matthew: “given,” who was also Levi, namely [Col. 1487B] from the tribe from which he arose. James of Alphaeus: surnamed to distinguish him from the earlier James, who is called son of Zebedee, as this one is son of Alphaeus. Simon the Cananaean: distinguished from Simon Peter, from the Galilean village of Cana, where the Lord changed water into wine. Thaddaeus, who is also Judas of James—understand, his brother—elsewhere called Lebbaeus, having a figurative name from the heart, which we might render diminutively as “little heart.” Judas Iscariot took his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, by a certain foretokening of his future condemnation. For Issachar is interpreted “reward,” signifying the price of betrayal for which he sold the Lord.

But why, you ask, did the Lord admit such a man not only to discipleship [Col. 1487C] but even to apostleship? Did he not know? The brief answer is that he did this for our consolation: for the consolation of the future Church, and especially of those who preside over churches, so that when someone among them is lost, they may answer detractors and say to those who mock them: “Do not be surprised: it happened even to Christ.”

“Jesus sent out these twelve, commanding them and saying: ‘Do not go on the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. As you go, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received; freely give.’”

It was not, as most suppose, that the Lord then [Col. 1487D] ordained the twelve apostles when he summoned them in this manner and gave them such power; rather, he merely chose them and fixed their number at twelve. To be chosen is not the same as to be ordained or consecrated. When, then, did he ordain or consecrate them? Surely when the great high priest himself, having performed his office, entered the holy places through his own blood (Heb. IX): then he consecrated them; and then, when he rose from the dead, he gave them full and perfect authority in these words: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX); and likewise: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

For this is the sum of apostolic authority and power: to forgive sins by the grace of the Holy Spirit in those baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This authority or power you will not find that he gave them either at the present place or anywhere in the whole Gospel before his Passion. For here you read that he told them to preach, heal the sick, cast out demons, raise the dead, and cleanse lepers; but not also to baptize and forgive sins. They did indeed baptize at one time—namely, when the year 639 was completing its course, while John had not yet been handed over—but they did not baptize at the Lord’s command. Rather, they did so only following the example or baptism of John, whose disciples most of them had been.

But why, when sending and instructing the twelve, did he say at the very beginning of their instruction: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans”? Surely because the time had not yet come, nor did the order of divine providence or evangelical preaching require that this should already happen. For what could then be preached to the Gentiles? That they should be circumcised, or that they should be baptized? Circumcision, certainly, was already coming to its end in Christ, whereas the sacrament of baptism had not yet been instituted. For this sacrament was instituted in Christ’s Passion or death. Hence the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death,” and so forth (Rom. VI).

Rightly, therefore, he says: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans.” But what then? “Rather,” he says, “go to [Col. 1488C] the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Accordingly, for the business then urgently requiring to be done in his bodily presence, he allowed them to go only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel: sheep without a shepherd, troubled and cast down human beings. For they had neither leader, prince, king, nor high priest, but had wolves under the name of shepherds—fierce wolves, ravening wolves—and were therefore perishing. And what are we to do for those sheep?

“As you go,” he says, “preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” For it belongs to the condition of sheep that the kingdom of heaven should draw near—that is, that the great Shepherd of the sheep has now come to visit his sheep, as he foretold through the prophet Ezekiel: “Behold,” he says, “I myself will require my flock from their hand” (Ezek. XXXIV). Again: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep” (ibid.).

And because not all the sheep themselves were to recognize their visitation or their shepherd—indeed, many of them, with goatish horns, were to strike the best sheep, killing, crucifying, scourging, and persecuting them from city to city—he says later: “Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, between ram and goat” (ibid.). And again: “Behold, he judges between fat and lean cattle, because you pushed with side and shoulder and butted with your horns [Col. 1489A] all the weak cattle, until they were scattered abroad” (ibid.).

The consummation of this judgment will be when “the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him. Then he will sit upon the throne of majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him; and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left” (Matt. XXV). This will be the kingdom of heaven: the goats being sent into eternal fire and the sheep passing into eternal life. “And I shall bring them,” he says, “into their own land; I shall feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the streams, and in every inhabited place of the land. I shall feed them in the richest pastures, and their pastures shall be on the high mountains of Israel, and there they shall rest” (Ezek. XXXIV).

This, I say, is the kingdom of heaven; and because this Shepherd has now come, I therefore tell you to go to the sheep to whom this was promised through prophetic Scripture and preach, “saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” And because it is difficult for them to believe that I am the Lord God himself visiting his sheep, “as a shepherd visits his flock,” do what I tell you: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.” Do these things as a testimony, so that the sheep may rejoice at their visitation, while the goats may be without excuse.

In all these things, moreover, let the intention of greed be absent from the working of power. For you have “freely received,” and therefore “freely give.” “For who among you first gave to me [Col. 1489C] and shall be repaid?” (Rom. XI). This power which I have given you is not repayment for anything you have given, but wholly spontaneous and gratuitous giving. Nor have you alone received freely: before you also, prophets, patriarchs, and all others who say—and say truthfully—“From his fullness we all have received” (John I), received freely whatever working of miracles and whatever grace they received. Therefore you too, “freely give.”
