For whoever does not give freely will not be like those grateful and gracious persons—for example, Elisha, who, when Naaman the Syrian, whom he had cleansed of his leprosy, said to him, “I beg you, receive a blessing from your servant,” replied: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, I will not receive it”; and though Naaman pressed him, he absolutely refused. Rather, such a person will be like Gehazi, who said: “My master has spared this Syrian, not accepting from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I shall run after him and receive something from him.” He ran and received it; and when he returned, Naaman’s leprosy clung to him (IV Kings V).

“Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor a staff. For the laborer is worthy of his food. Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart.”

This is that ordinance of the Lord which the Apostle recalls when writing to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what belongs to the sanctuary? Those who serve at the altar share in the altar. So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (I Cor. IX). For why should preachers of the Gospel have neither gold, silver, nor money in their belts, nor a bag, unless because these are neither necessary nor expedient? For, sowing spiritual things, they ought by right to reap material things from those among whom they sow, according to this judgment pronounced by the most just Lord: “For the laborer is worthy of his food.”

Yet there is something to be considered here. For whereas, in this Evangelist above—

> [Note: Col. 1489D (13). A defective phrase, whose complete sense is obtained by supplying what is missing as follows: “Whereas in this Evangelist [the possession of a staff is altogether forbidden, in another it is] thus,” etc. Editor of the *Patrologia*.]

—thus it is written: “And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff only” (Mark VI). Indeed, if we knew of only one staff, this question would be more difficult to resolve. But there are two staffs: one is that of the kings of the Gentiles, the other that of the disciples of Christ. The staff of the kings of the Gentiles is the staff of domination; the staff of Christ’s disciples is the staff of love, the staff of pastoral office, diligently watchful over the care of souls.

That staff which is one of domination was not granted to the ministers of the Gospel of peace, and it is forbidden here in the words, “nor a staff”; and more fully there: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors; but you are not to be so” (Luke XXII). But the staff of discipline, the staff of pastoral concern and vigilance, he not only never forbade, but commanded from the beginning—from the beginning, I mean, from the time when he first began to send shepherds of souls.

For Moses and Aaron were the first of such shepherds. When he sent them, the Lord certainly did not command them to take anything on the way except a staff only. He himself says to Moses: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered: “A staff.” He said: “Throw it upon the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent,” and so forth (Exod. IV). And immediately thereafter: “Take this staff also in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs” (ibid.). What else did he command Moses or his brother Aaron to take on the way except that staff alone?

Thus, surely, he commanded all evangelists and all preachers of the Gospel to take nothing else upon their way except the vigor of pastoral care, the law of life and discipline, [Col. 1490D] and, as a sign of this, sometimes also to carry a material staff in the hand. But the staff of domination, as has already been said, he forbids in this Evangelist. Knowing this, the apostle Peter says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (I Pet. V); and Paul says to the Corinthians: “I did not come again to Corinth, sparing you—not because we lord it over your faith, but because we are helpers of your joy. For by faith you stand” (II Cor. I). What if you did not stand? Certainly then “I would come to you with a staff; but now in a spirit of gentleness” (I Cor. IV).

What, then, were evangelists to do, or what were they to do, if they were not permitted to possess gold or silver, nor money in their belts? He says: “For the laborer is worthy of his food.” And immediately he adds: “Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart, eating and drinking what they have,” as Luke records more plainly (Luke X). With this confidence, ministers of the word of the Lord do not admit—and ought not admit—gold, silver, or belts fertile in money into their company. For every hearer of the same word of the Lord is indebted to them, to fill with bodily food that mouth from which he has received the word of life, which is spiritual food, so that he may confidently say: “If we have sown our spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX).

Has this hope ever disappointed any servant of the word of the Almighty? On the contrary, even if almost the whole world should at some time hunger and need bread, you will not see abandoned the righteous person in whose heart the word of God is at home and in whose mouth it is familiar (Ps. XXXVI). And Scripture speaks truly: “The Lord will not destroy the soul of the righteous by hunger” (Prov. X).

For example, when kings and princes were hungry in Israel, and Elijah, the most steadfast minister of the word of God, remained alive but had no one to feed him, the Lord said: “Withdraw from here and hide yourself by the brook; there you shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you” (II Kings XVII). Again, when after some days the brook had dried up—for rain had not fallen upon the earth—he said: “Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and you shall remain there; for I have commanded a widowed woman there [Col. 1491C] to feed you” (ibid.).

Thus every occasion for greed or miserable anxiety has been removed, so that the mind of evangelists may be free: that gold may not rule them, but they may rule gold and all the things human beings possess; and that from all things they may deign to receive nothing but food and clothing. How, then, could anyone dare to withhold or begrudge them these things—namely, food and clothing? Truly, in no way, unless he wishes to judge himself unworthy of eternal life. For this is the judgment of him who sends forth his ministers of the Word for his own work.

“Into whatever city or house you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart. And when you enter the house, greet it, saying: Peace to this house. If the house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you. And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you leave that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Amen I say to you: it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city.”

This is what the grateful ought to rejoice in and the ungrateful ought to fear. For the grateful are distinguished from the ungrateful, those who receive from those who do not receive, by a wonderful and terrible judgment. Peace rests upon the former; upon the latter heavenly wrath rushes, according to the example of Sodom and Gomorrah. Let us recall what happened in Sodom, and by its likeness we shall be able to perceive more clearly the truth of the present matter.

“Two angels sent to Sodom came in the evening, while Lot sat at the gate of the city” (Gen. XIX). He—Lot, that is—did not wait for them to request lodging or to inquire who in his house was worthy of such guests. Rather, going to meet them and bowing down, he begged them and by his entreaty prevailed upon them to turn aside to him. And because, once they had entered his house, he made a feast, baked unleavened bread, and they ate, their peace came upon that house, so that they said to him: “Arise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you too perish along with the wickedness of the city. Save your life; do not look back behind you” (ibid.), and so forth.

While saying these things, “they took hold of his hand, and of the hand of his wife, [Col. 1492B] and of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him; and they led him out and set him outside the city” (ibid.). Thus a certain peace rested upon him, but wrath came upon Sodom and Gomorrah: namely, fire and a rain of sulphur, which overthrew them.

According to this likeness, the Lord says to his evangelists: “If the house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, as you depart, shake the dust from your feet; and it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city.” As it was said, so it came to pass. For upon the Church of the Gentiles, which received the apostles of Christ and readily responded, as was worthy, to those saying, “Peace to this house,” apostolic peace came and rested—peace which is Christ himself, as they say: “He himself is our peace” (Eph. III).

But what has already happened to that earthly city Jerusalem—or rather to Sodom and Gomorrah—which did not receive this peace, and not only did not receive it but even crucified it, the entire world has heard. And on the day of judgment there is no doubt that its sin will be judged more intolerable than the sin of the Sodomites, as Jeremiah says in the *Lamentations*: “The iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and hands did not seize in her” (Lam. IV).

For what is meant of that Sodom by the words, “and hands did not seize in her,” except that the Sodomites indeed wished to assault the men who had entered Lot’s house, but in it—that is, in Sodom—there was no one whose hands seized them (Gen. XIX)? They surrounded the house, certainly, but their hands did not seize those men. Yet that city which the prophet calls the daughter of his people surrounded the Lord himself with weapons, seized and apprehended him with hands, mocked him, spat upon him, scourged him, crucified him, and killed him. Most rightly, therefore, it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city and every nation which, following its example, did not receive the ministers of salvation sent to it. Observe also the force of this separation and dreadful anathema in the words: “As you leave that house or city, shake even the dust from your feet”—which Luke very plainly records that they did in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIII).

[Col. 1493A] “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves; but beware of men. For they will hand you over in councils, and scourge you in their synagogues; and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.”

Therefore he said above, “and whoever does not receive you,” because he knew that they would not be received by all; indeed, by very many they would be cast out and handed over to death. He himself too was first to be cast out and handed over to death. How was he to be cast out? How handed over? “Like a sheep,” says Isaiah, “he shall be led to slaughter; and like a lamb before the one shearing him, he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). They had also heard John the Baptist say: “Behold the Lamb [Col. 1493B] of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

In many places of the Gospels he uses such names—shepherd, sheep, and lambs—calling himself shepherd, not king, and his disciples sheep, not soldiers. Although this must everywhere be carefully observed, it is particularly pleasing in the place where a trap was being set for him through the royal title by those saying: “How long do you take away our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John X). For *Christ* is a royal title, and they said this so that, if they caught him under that title, they might accuse him before Caesar or even safely attack him, as though on account of their loyalty to Caesar.

Thus the wise in heart escaped; thus the meek and humble in heart mocked the proud and envious: “I speak to you,” he says, “and the works which I do in the name of my Father bear witness concerning me; but you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life,” and so on, down to: “I and the Father are one” (ibid.). This is certainly no less than if he had openly said to them, “I am the Christ.”

Thus here too, when he says, “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves,” and wherever he professes himself shepherd and calls his followers sheep, he brings a twofold benefit: he trains them in gentleness, that they may learn from him that he is meek and humble in heart; and he seeks to have peace with all people, so that they may have no occasion for a just complaint against him.

The outcome proved how truthfully he had foretold this: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” For wherever they carried out the duty of their mission, they were attacked and torn in diverse places by impious men, like sheep by wolves; and although badly treated, they did not open their mouths, being among all people and before all people as prudent as serpents and as simple as doves.

In what respect were they prudent as serpents? Surely in this: when they were scourged, killed, stoned, and driven from city to city, they acted and suffered most cautiously and vigilantly. They surrendered their bodies to ravening wolves, but kept their hearts for God their Creator, according to the likeness of the serpent, which, when struck, presents its whole body to the striker, being especially anxious for its head. Since it cannot avoid wounds, it at least protects, as best it can, the head wherein its life resides.

Is not Christ, the Lamb of God, the head of sheep such as these? While they surrender their bodies to punishments and endure the loss of this present life in order to gain Christ, they are indeed found prudent as serpents. But in what respect are they simple as doves? Namely, because they do none of those things which ravens usually do—ravens, I mean, that is, wicked, rapacious, greedy people, who quarrel for the world or for the things of the world, bite one another, and tear one another apart.

Thus, since they seize nothing, desire no one’s property, and look upon all things innocently with simple eyes, the eyes of doves, they not only do not seize, but even relinquish, giving for the use of the poor. Like sheep, they do not resist those who take their milk and wool, and moreover expose their bodies to those who strike them, guarding only their head, Christ. Thus, I say, wolves, lions, and bears are given no occasion for tearing them, scourging them, killing them, or persecuting them from city to city.

“But beware of men. For they will hand you over in councils, scourge you in their synagogues, and lead you before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.” This is the effect of the likeness of serpents, when he said, “Therefore be prudent as serpents”: namely, “beware of men,” so that you may understand, or infer, “lest human beings strike the head; cover it wholly, and expose the body to be struck,” according to the likeness of the serpent described above.

For this is to beware of men: to be attentive and very careful that what human beings plot may not happen—that they may not either shake you by terrors or seduce you by flatteries, so that through fear of death you neglect Christ, who is your head. It is very terrible, if you weigh it rightly, that after saying, “They will scourge you in their synagogues, and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake,” he added, “as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.” Testimony of what thing, and at what time is this testimony to be revealed?

Surely on the day of judgment, when it will be brought about that, as he said above, it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans than for the city which, he says, did not receive you. For what will it be like on that day to see such testimony against themselves, so that they cannot excuse themselves and say: “Lord, when did you send to us your messengers to foretell this judgment, and we did not receive them?” For the King, seated upon the throne of his majesty, will say to them: “Amen I say to you: behold these are those whom I sent among you as sheep in the midst of wolves; and behold the scars of the scourges with which you scourged them in your synagogues. Indeed, behold the marks of the nails in my hands and feet, by which you fastened me.” Hence I now know to reject evil and choose good, having sure testimony against you, both from myself and from these persons whom you killed and persecuted as you did me and for my sake; and thus the judgment is beyond reproach.

“But when they hand you over, do not think about how or what you are to say. For in that hour what you are to say will be given to you. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

As being wary of human beings, as he said above, belongs to serpentine prudence, so what he now says, “Do not think about how or what you are to say,” belongs to the simplicity of doves. Simplicity of this kind is the companion of truth, which does not seek a corner. When it is challenged from without by questions, it immediately looks within and knows, and wishes, to speak nothing but what it finds written in the book of its conscience by the Spirit of God writing—that is, suggesting. The Spirit himself also appeared over our Lord in the form of a dove, to signify the simplicity of his own truth (Matt. III).

Something similar ought to be done by us, as though this same best instructor said to us: When you come to expound the word of God, do not premeditate with what ornaments of language you may adorn the sense of Holy Scripture. For words will be given to you, coming spontaneously from the Spirit of your Father; and the more spontaneously they come, the less weariness they will bring you and the more delight they will bring to hearers or readers. O how sweet and excellent it is that the things we speak or write should be such [Col. 1495C] that an intelligent hearer or kindly reader refuses to credit them to us, and says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you!”

“But brother will hand brother over to death, and father son. Children will rise against parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

As we have heard this foretold, so we have seen it done, so that we may confidently say: “As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts” (Ps. XLVII). For what is said beforehand there, “There were pains as of a woman in labor,” refers especially to holy martyrs, whose pains were not small, above all when brother handed brother and father son over to death, and children rose against parents and put them to death because of Christ’s name. Truly there were great pains there, yet not pains of just any kind, but “as of a woman in labor.”

For, he says, whoever perseveres to the end will be saved; and salvation will cause such a person to forget all pains, just as a son born causes the woman who has given birth to forget. “For when she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John XVI). Great, therefore, even in these pains, is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise; great are the glory and honor of this Son of Man. For just as the Holy Spirit had foretold concerning him: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. CIX), so he himself foretells to his future soldiers that they too will drink in like manner, offered drink by kindred, friends, and parents, and that therefore they ought to lift up their head unto salvation.

What if some of the more tender cannot endure pains of this kind? He says:

“But if they persecute you in this city, flee into another. Amen I say to you: you will not finish the cities of Israel before the kingdom of God comes.”

Therefore, whoever you are—whether a prudent and simple preacher or hearer of the Gospel, prudent as a serpent and simple as a dove—do not presume so much upon the Spirit of fortitude that you forget this counsel. For how do you know whether you truly possess the Spirit of fortitude? Indeed, how do you know whether you are worthy of love or hatred? (Eccl. IX). Do not therefore too hastily cast yourself into the furnace of temptation. Rather, fearing that perhaps you are not worthy of martyrdom, when they persecute you in one city flee into another, because “it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX), and necessity more justly than choice produces the crown.

Nevertheless, if you have truly experienced what gift or grace of heavenly fortitude you possess, and the Holy Spirit has in some way revealed this to you, it is beautiful and praiseworthy to take up the banner of the cross voluntarily, run against the enemy in the battle-line of faith, strengthen the weak, and offer them an example of the strength to be hoped for from God. Otherwise, it is safer to flee in the spirit of humility, in the spirit of the fear of the Lord, because even Peter, chief of the apostles, when he seemed strong to himself, was frightened by a maidservant at the door (Matt. XXVI).

Perhaps you say: “Where shall I flee? What city shall I approach? Will many cities open to us as we flee?” To this he replies: “Amen I say to you: you will not finish the cities of Israel before the kingdom of God comes.” As if he said: Until now there have been few cities of Israel—so few that Jezebel, who reigned in Samaria with her most impious daughter Athaliah, who reigned in Jerusalem, once held them all. At that time there were so few cities in Israel that once Jezebel alone, who reigned in Samaria, together with her most impious daughter Athaliah, who reigned in Jerusalem, held them all; and when prophets were killed in one city, they had no other city to which they could flee, but wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and afflicted (Heb. XI), except that Obadiah, according to his name the servant of the Lord, fed one hundred of them, fifty by fifty, in caves (III Kings XVIII).

But now there will be so many cities of Israel, so many cities or churches throughout the world dedicated to my name—I who am the true Israel—hospitable cities, churches of the poor, receiving the faithful, that no one can finish them before the kingdom of God comes. For no one lives or will live so long in this pilgrimage that, by fleeing, he can pass through all the cities which will believe in me, gladly receiving, comforting, and honoring such fugitives, and not vainly considering that in them they receive me.

“The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord. It is enough for the disciple to be like his master, and the servant like his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household? Therefore do not fear them.”

The purpose or intention with which he said, “The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord; it is enough for the disciple to be like his master, and the servant like his lord,” he makes clear by adding: “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” This sufficiency most sweetly consoles all disciples of truth and all servants of the Most High when they are handed over in councils, scourged in synagogues, led before kings and governors, hated by all, and put to death for the Lord’s name.

They ought not seek anything further, lest the disciple become contrary to the master or the servant unlike his lord in an opposite way. For nothing is more contrary than for a disciple to desire to be above his master or a servant greater than his lord. This is to wish to be glorified by human beings and called a benefactor, when that Lord so great was rejected by human beings and called Beelzebub; it is to wish to reach the kingdom of God through pleasures, when he, the master of humility, reached his kingdom through death—even death on a cross. Let the perfect disciple and faithful servant judge it enough for himself to be like his master and lord: master in that he is human, lord in that he is God. According to this judgment, let him answer the adversary if the latter taunts him in tribulation, saying: “Where is your God?” or, “Surely your God does not care for you.”

“Therefore do not fear them. For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known. What [Col. 1497C] I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.”

Do not fear them, he says; do not fear their judgment when they judge you wrongly, hate you because of my name, and cast out your name as evil. What would it be to fear them or their judgment except to despair of God’s providence, as though he would not care or deign to answer for his humble servants and bear true testimony to their good conscience? Do not at all fear them with such fear. For nothing is covered that will not be known. “The Lord will come,” says the Apostle, “who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then praise will come to each from God” (I Cor. IV).

Certainly, some of the evil deeds of the elect will be covered and some will remain hidden, since it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI); and Wisdom says to God: “Overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance” (Wis. XI). By this saying it sufficiently indicates that the merciful God wishes somehow that something of our sins should remain hidden even from himself. But concerning each person’s good deeds, or the consciences of good people—of which ignorant people often judge wrongly, making undiscriminating judgments against them—concerning good things, I say, there is absolutely “nothing covered that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known.”

How much God has also revealed and made known in this present life concerning his elect, even against their own wishes, while they hide themselves for the preservation of humility and take care that their works not be seen by human beings. He himself knows whom, how, and for whose benefit it is fitting to reveal or make known even now, before that universal illumination or manifestation which, as was said, the Apostle declared must be awaited: “Do not judge before the time,” he says, “until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV).

He wished blessed Job to be revealed and known as one who was simple, upright, feared God, and departed from evil (Job I). And he made countless saints known, who in humility had wished to remain hidden within themselves—not only through good works, but also sometimes by beneficially revealing through their own words the secrets of their hearts—so that they might do what is immediately added here:

“What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim from the housetops.” What does he himself say in darkness, and what does the Word of God—God himself, Jesus Christ—speak in the ear, if not the revelations of God which, in secrecy as though in darkness, where people do not see, he imparts through the Holy Spirit when and as he wills? It is good indeed to conceal this humbly and to keep hidden when and how anyone received the grace by which he was enlightened; but it is best to disclose it for God’s glory and honor when usefulness demands it or just necessity requires it.

For example, no one usefully suppresses in silence the manner in which he received God’s secret gift more effectively than Paul, the vessel of election, usefully proclaimed it when he wrote to the Corinthians, among other things concerning himself, that he had been caught up to the third heaven, or into Paradise, and had heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12). Did he not, in writing such things, speak in the light what had been said to him in darkness, and proclaim from the housetops what he had heard in the ear? Certainly, even if he did not tell or write everything that he heard in that third heaven, in that Paradise—“for,” he says, “I heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter”—nevertheless you rightly observe that this very fact, that he was caught up to that place, was said in darkness and heard in the ear. For none of mortals saw that he had been carried there or heard the secret words, nor could anyone have heard them, unless he who saw and heard had himself related it concerning himself. Behold, therefore: he spoke in the light what had been said to him in darkness, and proclaimed from the housetops what he had heard in the ear. All who proclaim the grace granted them, when the cause of just necessity requires it and the wind of wretched vanity is far absent, imitate him.

“And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” Here one may rightly say: “Grant, Lord, what you command, and command what you will.” Behold, you command us not to fear those who kill the body, and reason agrees that he should rather be feared who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. But what flesh does not fear being killed? Peter, first of the apostles, feared; and, fearing death, he denied Life. Why was this, except that you had not yet granted him not to fear? Who, unless you grant it, does not fear? After you had granted it to him, he was able to do what you commanded. Therefore be our strength, and accomplish in us what you will us to do.

Yet faith must first know that by teaching you command and by commanding you teach; then hope must pray, and charity obtain, that you yourself give what you command. But as one must have true faith, so also one must have firm hope, lest anyone, however insignificant, suppose that he will not be required by the Most High because he appears small and abject to himself. For it is written: “For he who avenges their blood has remembered them; he has not forgotten the cry of the poor” [Col. 1499B] (Ps. 9). Again: “For the poor shall not be forgotten unto the end; the patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end” (ibid.). It follows, therefore:

“Are not two sparrows sold for an as? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows.” See how forcefully the majesty of truth comes to meet this humility. “Are not,” he says, “two sparrows sold for an as?” This is a true proposition, since it is truly known to all that two sparrows are given for a paltry price; and they are far inferior in body and soul to a single rational human being, who consists—or subsists—of these two. “And not one of them,” he says, “will fall to the ground without your Father.” Accept this also, whoever you are, or desire to be, a disciple [Col. 1499C] of so great a teacher.

But perhaps you hesitate and say: How does one sparrow not fall to the ground without our Father, when God has no concern even for an ox, which is certainly larger than a sparrow? For when the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians, “For it is written in the law of Moses [Deut. 26]: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain,’” he immediately added: “Is God concerned for oxen? Or does he say this for our sake? Certainly it was written for our sake, because the one who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving the fruit” (1 Cor. 9), and so forth. How then does not one of the sparrows fall to the ground without your Father, if God has no concern even for oxen, so much larger than sparrows?

To this I say: the Apostle was speaking about the written law, and its sense is that God had no concern that a law should be written concerning irrational oxen. But here the Son of God speaks about God’s providence: he himself provides how and whence he may give food to all flesh (Ps. 135), so that he not only brings bread forth from the earth for humankind (Ps. 103), but also provides fitting food for the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, according to David’s saying: “Who gives their food to the cattle, and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 146).

Therefore accept this too: “Not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father”; and likewise what follows: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered.” Christian faith requires you not to doubt the future resurrection, not only with all the members of the body, [Col. 1500A] but also with eyelids or eyebrows, and with all one’s hairs. When, as a Christian, you have accepted this, you are immediately and sweetly constrained by a most powerful syllogism, drawing the conclusion: “Therefore do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows.” You are worth more, that is, you are of greater value. For the human being is a rational creature, and his life is far more enduring than this present age: the human being does not die, but only the body; and that body itself shall rise again and shall live forever with the soul without end.

“Therefore everyone who confesses me before people, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before people, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven.” Therefore, he says, since one human being is worth more than many [Col. 1500B] sparrows, do not doubt that God has care for you; and, as has already been said, do not fear those who kill the body, but confess me before your killers. For the judgment upon this shall be such that whoever confesses me, I shall confess; and whoever denies me, I too shall deny before my Father.

Surely it will be glory for the one whom such a person confesses on that day; but shame for the one whom he denies—or who “will be ashamed,” as we read in another Evangelist—that is, will blush to confess that he belongs to him. The Apostle magnificently remembers this when he says to the Hebrews concerning the holy Fathers: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God,” namely because they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth, having no abiding city here and seeking a better one, that is, [Col. 1500C] a heavenly city (Heb. 11). Surely, when God is said not to be ashamed of them, the opposite is simultaneously affirmed concerning the unbelieving: God will be ashamed to be called their God. And woe to those whose God he cannot, without prejudice to his honor, be—the very persons whom he cannot confess and save!

“Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies are those of his own household.” When he says, “Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace,” one must understand: peace as the world gives it, the sort of peace the world brings and seeks. For elsewhere, after saying, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you,” he immediately adds: “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” There is therefore a peace of the world which this Lord and Prince of Peace did not come to bring. It is contrary to the peace of God, of which the Apostle says to the Galatians: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace” (Gal. 5). Again: “And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds” (Phil. 4).

He himself is the Prince of this peace (Isa. 9), and he came to bring it: first reconciling through his blood all things in heaven and on earth (Col. 1), and then, as the Apostle says, “preaching peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2). This peace is the remission of sins. But the world, lying in evil, does not seek this peace, but [Col. 1501A] the peace which the Valley of Vision—namely Jerusalem—then had, to which this true peaceful one said: “Indeed, in this your day, the things that belong to your peace” (Luke 19). This peace was, as Isaiah says in the burden concerning that same Valley of Vision, “this joy and this gladness: killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’” (Isa. 22).

“I have not,” he says, “come to bring peace of this kind, but a sword”: that is, the separation of the children of God’s peace from the children not of peace but of iniquity, as is immediately added in the same passage: “If this iniquity shall be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord of hosts” (ibid.). Who does not know, who has not heard, that what he foretold here that he would do has very often happened, or is happening: “For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law”? Notice also how beautifully and aptly he sends his disciples to prophetic authority, that they may recognize how ancient is the steadfastness of this truth, saying: “And a man’s enemies are those of his own household.” For so it had been foretold in Micah: “Do not trust a friend, and do not put confidence in a leader. From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth; for son dishonors father, daughter rises against her mother, daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7).

By recalling this final sentence of the prophecy, “And a man’s enemies are those of his own household,” he plainly indicates that the prophecy itself bears witness to his words, and that the Scriptures cannot otherwise be fulfilled unless he does as he says: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword.” There are other family connections too which the sword of the Gospel divides; but among many, these two suffice: one, namely that of a man and his father, belongs to the more important relationships; the other, that of a mother-in-law and her daughter-in-law, to the lesser relationships—so much so that harmony between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law is rare. Hence, in a certain comic poet, a mother-in-law, perceiving that she was suspected by her daughter-in-law of this vice and wishing to excuse herself, says:

> . . . . It is not easy to clear oneself [or: to be cleared].  
> (Terence, *Hecyra*, act 2, scene 3.)

[Col. 1501D] Thus they have persuaded themselves that all mothers-in-law are wicked. Therefore, when he says, “For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,” it is as though he said: I have come to divide absolutely all relationships, both greater and lesser, demonstrating that evil peace must be broken and discord of the flesh endured for the sake of concord with God.

“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” Behold the sword that separates; behold the severing of kinship. Behold the division which divides one and the same person against himself: “He is not worthy of me,” he says, [Col. 1502A] “who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than me; he is not worthy of me who does not take up his cross in order to follow me.” This is the word of one judging; it is the sword of one separating. For who that has a heart of flesh, who does not have a heart of stone, can patiently hear: “He is not worthy of me”? “Let father or mother rather perish, let son or daughter rather perish, let the flesh itself or this present life rather perish,” says every sensible hearer of this word, “than that I, O Christ, should not be worthy of you.” Thus he leaves every kinsman and every friend and despises himself when he perceives that he cannot retain any of these while preserving the dignity of Christ’s discipleship.

Is this command new? Is it not an ancient command, which we have heard from the beginning? For Moses says in the blessing of Levi: “He who said to his father and to his mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to his brothers, ‘I am ignorant of you’; and they did not recognize their sons—these have kept your word and preserved your covenant; they shall keep your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel. They shall place incense in your wrath, and a whole burnt offering upon your altar” (Deut. 33). What follows—“Bless, O Lord, his strength, and receive the works of his hands” (ibid.)—you rightly understand concerning the strength required here when he says: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.”

For to take up one’s cross and follow Christ—whether in persecution by surrendering one’s body to punishments for God’s sake, or in peace by breaking the desires of the flesh, whether from fear of Gehenna or longing for eternal life—is great strength and a great work: strength worthy of blessing, a work worthy of the Lord’s acceptance. Whoever does not do this not only loses glory but also incurs punishment. For it follows: “Whoever finds his soul will lose it.” Who is the one who finds his soul, if not the one who does not wish to take up his cross so that he may pass through this present life pleasantly? Concerning one who in persecution so finds his soul that, by denying Christ, he gains this advantage—keeping in the body the soul which the persecutor’s sword could have driven out—it is more than sufficiently established that he loses it in eternal destruction.

Conversely: “Whoever,” he says, “loses his soul for my sake will find it.” Christian faith does not need the demonstration that this saying is true, because it is altogether certain that the pious martyr, losing his soul, will find it preserved in the bundle of the living. What, then, remains for these fatherless and orphaned persons when they have lost father or mother for the Gospel’s sake, or for these bereaved persons when they have left son or daughter for Christ’s sake? What, I say, except that Christ himself should be concerned for them? For none such is mistaken when he says in the Psalm: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is concerned for me” (Ps. 39). Do not the words of that concern immediately follow here? For it continues:

“Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name [Col. 1503A] of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward. And whoever gives even one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you—shall not lose his reward.” How many, do you suppose, did he know would desire to receive him and would wish to receive the reward of prophets and righteous persons? Therefore the Lord carefully prepared many hosts by these words for those whom he saw would lose father or mother for his sake, so that each of them might say even this: “For my father and mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 26).

As it was said, so we see it accomplished: there are more hosts of such persons—namely, prophets and righteous persons whom fathers and mothers have forsaken—than can be overcome by their number. For, not to mention other modes of receiving them, so many monasteries and so many hostels have been prepared for their reception that, when righteous persons of this sort have failed—persons in whom Christ declares that he himself is received—in very many places the property or estates offered to God for such persons have in large part reverted to the use of worldly fathers and mothers, sons and daughters, who do not follow Christ.

Now consider the very words: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” In another Evangelist he states this same point thus: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever receives one whom I send receives me; but whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (John 13). Therefore true worshippers do not act superfluously when they welcome arriving guests by bowing down to the ground in worship. For Christ is worshipped in them, and he is also received.

I shall say more: God the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit are worshipped in them, and they are also received. For when he had said, “Whoever receives you receives me,” lest someone’s thought at that time perhaps strike him and say, “What great thing is it to receive this mortal human being, who can suffer injuries and be crucified?” he immediately added: “And whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” And who sent him, except God the Father and the Holy Spirit? Though this scarcely requires proof among us, he himself speaks thus in Isaiah: “Come near to me and hear this. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time before they came to be, I was there” (Isa. 48). This is as if he said: In the beginning I was God; and in speaking to humankind I testified not in secret, but with great signs and wonders, that I was to come. And I who was speaking—indeed, I was there, namely with God—behold, I am present, made human, sent by the Lord [Col. 1504A] my Father, and sent and cooperatively brought forth through the Virgin’s womb by the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, in those who are sent, God himself, who sends them, is rightly worshipped. Do we do this without ancient example or authority? Or, in doing so, are we blamed as worshipping a creature? When Abraham stood by the oaks of Mamre, “three men appeared to him, standing near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the door of his tent, and worshipped and said, ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes’” (Gen. 18), and so forth. Again Scripture says: “The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting in the gates of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them, and worshipped, bowing to the ground” (Gen. 19). Is not angelic substance, just as much as human substance, a creature? Yet God was worshipped in them and received in them.

For this reason Abraham, worshipping before three, addressed one: “Lord,” he said, “if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant” (Gen. 18); and Lot, worshipping before two, said: “I pray, my lord, since your servant has found favor before you” (Gen. 19), and so forth. What then will be the reward for this reception? He says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward.” Therefore the reward of God [perhaps: “his”] who is received and of the one who receives him will be one and the same. For he did not say, “a reward from the prophet,” or “a reward from the righteous person,” but “he shall receive a prophet’s reward, a righteous person’s reward.” Great recompense, generous repayment.

[Col. 1504C] What is the reward of the prophet or the righteous person who, in order to prophesy or proclaim God’s kingdom, and in order to keep God’s righteousness, loved neither father nor mother, neither son nor daughter, more than all these [reading uncertain; Latin: *plusquam illos omnes amavit*], and who took up his cross and followed Christ, not fearing to lose his soul for righteousness’ sake? What, I say, is the reward of such persons, except openly to see Christ himself? For this he promised as the highest reward to those who love him: “Whoever loves me,” he says, “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14).

Therefore, O receiver of a prophet, recipient of a righteous person, in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous person—that is, because you have recognized him as a prophet or righteous person—since so great a reward is proposed to you, gladly do what you do; with good will offer what you offer; give what you have, whether little or much. For you shall not lose your reward, even if you are able to give no more than a cup of cold water. And if at the time you cannot give even that, at least let willingness not be absent, because “peace on earth [is] to people of good will” (Luke 2).

## BOOK NINE

## CHAPTER XI

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished giving commands to his twelve disciples, that he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. But John, when he had heard in prison of the works of Christ, sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” John was a prophet [Col. 1505A] and more than a prophet, as the Lord himself testified of him in this very reading: “What,” he said, “did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

Which of the prophets did not know, or did not declare, that Christ would suffer? All knew it; all foretold it; and today it is evident to readers that their Scriptures throughout almost their entire course signify the saving mystery of his most holy Passion. Hence Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled it” (Acts 3). To be ignorant of this belonged to those who either had not read the prophets or had not understood them. How, then, could John even be called, or be, a prophet—let alone more than a prophet?

Since this reasoning rightly leads us to conclude that John, like the other mysteries of Christ, knew this matter too, it remains to ask what he was inquiring when he said, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” and why it was necessary for him to ask this by sending two disciples. Surely he was asking whether Jesus himself was the Messiah—that is, the Christ—who was expected to come. Thus we also read that the Samaritan woman said: “I know that Messiah, who is called Christ, is coming. When he comes, he will announce all things to us” (John 4). Nor is it strange that here, concerning one and the same matter and one and the same person, he used both present and future tense, saying, “Are you the one who is to come?” For the crowds whom he fed with five [Col. 1505C] loaves and two fish likewise said: “This truly is the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6). Here and there, “is to come” means the one concerning whom the Scriptures or prophets testified that he would come.

Thus, as has been said, he asked whether Jesus himself was the Christ, or whether another was to be expected under this name. But why did he ask one whom he had proclaimed, by prophesying, baptizing, and pointing out, to be that very person? Certainly for an important reason which the Evangelist did not omit, introducing the words, “When John had heard in prison of the works of Christ.” What does the statement mean that John heard, in prison, of the works of Christ, and therefore, having sent two disciples, asked him such a question? Did not John himself, before he was sent to prison, hear of Christ’s works—among which that most beautiful work was that, invited to a wedding, he turned water into wine? (John 2.) Did he not also hear the voice of the Father from heaven saying concerning him: “You are my Son, in whom I am well pleased”? (Matt. 3.) If a question was needed, why did he not inquire when prompted by those earlier signs?

The reason, therefore, which, as has been said, the Evangelist indicated by introducing, “When John had heard in prison of the works of Christ,” must be considered more carefully. Clearly this is meant: although his works were truly works of Christ—that is, works such as no one else could have performed unless he alone were Christ, the Son of God—nevertheless, among these works he did not openly say that he was the Christ; indeed, he even forbade his disciples to say so.

For example, after questioning his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16), and then, “But who do you say that I am?” (ibid.), Peter answered: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” Christ pronounced him blessed for his knowledge and confession of the truth (ibid.), yet forbade them to say publicly that he was the Christ, as the Evangelist reports elsewhere: “Then,” he says, “he commanded his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ” (Luke 9). The reason for this command is easily known from what immediately follows: “From that time,” the Evangelist says, “Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, and be killed, and rise on the third day” (ibid.).

For it was to happen that, on the pretext or accusation of a royal title—namely, “Christ”—he would be handed over to the Gentiles by the Jews, who would say: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). For this reason especially he gave that command. Do we then say that he wished to avoid death and therefore kept silent about the occasion of death, namely the royal title, and commanded his disciples to keep silent about it? By no means. Rather, just as his death ought not to be greatly delayed, so it was certainly expedient that it should not be too greatly hastened. First the Gospel had to be established, and such great things had to be done as were done, some portion of which, when written, could prove the mystery of Christian faith by sufficient testimonies.

When the time came, after he had taught and performed sufficient signs, then—this deserves close attention—not only did he forbid no one, but he also admitted a great crowd and many children to make a public acclamation of the royal title, saying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the kingdom of our father David which is coming! Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (Matt. 21; Mark 11; Luke 19). It has been shown that before the time of his Passion our Lord, although he had declared and proved by works that he was the Son of God, nevertheless kept silent about the royal title, which is “Christ,” because it would be too offensive not only to the Jews but also to the Roman power; and he commanded his disciples to keep silent about it.

We have demonstrated this in order that the nature of John’s concern may consequently become clear: John, “when he had heard in prison of the works of Christ, sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” What, then, was his concern? About what was he concerned? We have heard with our own ears, and learned by hearing, that even now Jews hostile to this name say: “You say it, his disciples said it, but he himself did not say that he is Christ, that he is the Messiah whom we expect.” Do you suppose that John’s own disciples, who, zealous for their teacher, sometimes spoke such words as: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you gave testimony—behold, he is baptizing, and all are going to him” (John 3)—do you suppose, I say, that they sometimes also said: “Rabbi, you said that he is Christ, but he does not say that he is Christ”?

Therefore, wishing them to hear from Christ’s own mouth that he himself was Christ, and knowing that he remains faithful to them and cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2), John “sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’ And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, [Col. 1507B] and the poor receive the Gospel. And blessed is whoever is not scandalized in me.’ As they were departing, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in royal houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Behold, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.”’”

Consider carefully, reader or hearer, what kind of answer this was, and how suited it was to the matter and the time. For in Malachi, where is written what he declared—“Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mal. 3)—there immediately follows: “And immediately the Ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple. Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts” (ibid.).

Perhaps you, whoever you are, a disciple of John and a disciple of the Lord’s grace, though not yet perfected in knowing the certainty of that which you have so often sung in the Psalm—“The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 1 [probably Ps. 12])—would have wished, I say, that to this question, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” he had answered: “I am; no other is to be expected.” Such an answer would indeed have been a pure word, true silver. Yet among people it would not have appeared a pure word; it would not have been valued as silver tried by fire—for their judgment is so unjust that he himself, knowing and foreseeing it, said especially concerning his own person: “Amen, I say to you: no prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke 4).

Therefore, wise and Wisdom itself, he brought forth the pure word of his answer from the place where nothing is said or written that is not silver tried by fire, and where no one but an impious person dares say that it is not irrefragably true. Now, therefore, because we too are disciples of the Lord’s grace and the Lord Jesus speaks to the crowds concerning John, let us complete an agreeable syllogism.

Christ himself gives the premise: “For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before [Col. 1508A] your face.’” Let us supply the minor premise: But immediately thereafter in the same prophet follows: “And immediately the Ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple.” Let all the crowds of Christians conclude: Therefore another is no longer to be expected; for most certainly he who was expected to come has already come: the Ruler whom you sought, O servants of the Lord; the Angel of the covenant whom you desired, O you to whom both the covenant and the promise were entrusted (Rom. 4, 9). This Angel of Great Counsel confirmed its hope in that very covenant.

Now, I say, he has come. For according to the truth of Scripture he had to come immediately where this angel was sent, appointed for this purpose: to prepare the way before his face. But if you doubt the identity of this Ruler [Col. 1508B] and ask, “Where is he?” or “Who is he who has already come?”—if the pointing finger that says, “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1) does not suffice you—receive another testimony, which Scripture set before this testimony: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the good news.”

This is the testimony of works—works that are indeed Christ’s works, which John heard of while in prison, and which no one but Christ could perform. This testimony, I say, compared with that testimony of Scripture to which he directed us when he said of John, “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face,” does not permit one to remain ignorant—unless one wishes it—that this Jesus of [Col. 1508C] Nazareth, “who was thought to be the son of Joseph” (Luke 3), is that Ruler and Angel of the Covenant whom you sought and whom you desired.

John once did not know this: namely, which man it was, with what face or appearance he walked among people, among whom or in whose midst the one who was to be called, or to be, Christ the King had been brought up—the one by whom the whole world, and John himself, had to be baptized. As a prophet he knew that he had already come; but he did not know who he was, or where he was, until the Holy Spirit pointed him out by descending like a dove and remaining upon him. Thus he himself said: “And I did not know him; but that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water” (John 1). Again: “And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in [Col. 1508D] water said to me: He upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (ibid.).

He said this testimony about himself, certainly, out of the integrity of his witness, wishing his hearers to know that he did not bear witness to Christ through human favour. He thus showed himself to be a suitable witness: in giving testimony he did not regard the person, but the case. Although he knew the case, he did not yet know the person. This, I say, he did not know; and, without detracting from the greatness of prophetic grace, he could fail to know which man, with what face or appearance, was the Messiah—that is, the Christ—whose coming was certain.

So Samuel knew indeed, since the Lord had spoken to him, that among Jesse’s sons a king had already been chosen: “For I have provided for myself a king among his sons.” But he did not know which of [Col. 1509A] those sons was God’s chosen one, so much so that, when he saw Eliab, he said: “Surely his anointed is now before the Lord?” (1 Samuel 16). Likewise, with the other sons he so fulfilled his office and awaited the Lord’s judgment that, when he finally anointed David, he could truly say: “And I did not know him.”

Behold what John sought when he asked: “Are you he who is to come?” For this faithful friend sought and intended this: that the Son of God, not content with John’s testimony, might reveal himself by a testimony greater than John’s—648—the testimony of God his Father—as he himself says to the Jews in another evangelist: “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from a human being” (John 5). Again: “But I have a testimony greater than [that of] John. For the works which the Father has given me to accomplish—the very works which I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me,” and so on, as far as: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they are those which bear witness concerning me” (ibid.).

What are the works that the Father gave to this his Son Jesus Christ as testimony, except those which he now mentions: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the good news”? And what or what kind of Scriptures are those which, commanding us to search them, he says “bear witness concerning me,” except such as one may taste here in this chapter: “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel [Col. 1509C] before your face, who shall prepare your way before you”—if, at least, you read what follows.

Therefore, what John desired he heard from Christ’s own mouth: a testimony greater than John—or rather, testimonies—of which the Psalmist rightly said: “Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out” (Psalm 119). For there are two testimonies here: one in marvellous works, the other in the exposition of the Scriptures. These testimonies are truly wonderful, and therefore our soul ought to search them.

The first must be searched in such a way that we do not look only to those blind persons who then saw after bodily illumination, those lame persons who then walked bodily, those lepers who then were bodily cleansed, or those dead persons who then rose in body. For there was not the completion but [Col. 1509D] the beginning of the works “which the Father gave me,” he says, “to accomplish” (John 5). Their completion was certainly in his death and resurrection, when by dying he conquered our death and by rising restored life, so that now he dies no more and death has no further dominion over him (Romans 6)—and this we too hope for, not uncertainly.

And now, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, he completes these works. For truly the blind see and the lame walk: we ourselves were blind, lame, leprous, deaf, dead, and poor; and this ought to count greatly for us as testimony from him who answers concerning himself. For through faith in him we see, walk, have been cleansed, and hear; countless persons have risen from the death of sin after Mary’s example (Luke 17); and thus [Col. 1510A] we have received the good news, so that we who were poor have become rich in word and knowledge (1 Corinthians 1).

So far as a faithful mind was able, it has sought to refine and polish the gold of this present passage, so that you, reader or hearer, might more brightly perceive from the words themselves both the intention of John’s question and the majesty of Christ answering what was asked. Yet I do not wish to pass over this: in beautifully returning testimony to John, his witness, this “Faithful Witness” (Revelation 1) began with words eminently fitting to the matter itself.

“What,” he says, “did you go out into the wilderness to see?” It must be understood that, when he said this, John was then not in the wilderness but in prison; nor was Christ himself in the wilderness, but was speaking to the crowds about John in one of their cities. For it had previously been stated that, “having given instructions to his twelve apostles, he departed to teach and preach in their cities.” Therefore he looked back to that going out of the crowds, and wished the crowds to remember that departure, of which Mark, writing the heading, “The beginning of the holy Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1), immediately adds:

“As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way. A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. And the whole region of Judaea and all the people of Jerusalem went out to him, and were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins” (Mark [Col. 1510C] 1).

John’s own words made those departures of the crowds memorable to us. Among them the greatest was this: when the people were expecting and all were reasoning in their hearts about him, whether perhaps he himself might be the Christ, “he confessed: I am not the Christ” (John 1).

Therefore this faithful witness, who will render testimony to all on the day of judgment and to each person according to his merit, says: “Did you go out to see a reed shaken by the wind?” Certainly not: for he was not bent; he did not yield to empty glory; and he counted the popular breeze or wind of such high estimation as nothing. It was another matter when, caring nothing for pleasing people, he rebuked Herod himself: “It is not lawful,” he said, “for you to have your brother’s wife” (Matthew 14; Mark 6).

[Col. 1510D] Therefore he continued: “But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments?” Certainly not, “for behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses.” John, however, is not in the king’s house but in the king’s prison. Men dressed in soft garments—that is, flatterers, who flatter the sins of their kings, pliant and agreeable to rulers as though they were beneficent when they are wicked—such as Herod, perpetrator of adultery, behold, dine and drink in banquet-halls around the royal couches. But John is thorny, armed in rough clothing, so that he cannot be stroked, in accordance with the saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Ecclesiastes 12). Such a man is shut outside the banquet, in prison; nor is he admitted into those royal houses otherwise than by having his head brought in [Col. 1511A] on a dish: the dancer’s reward, the price of her dancing.

These two questions, to each of which “No” is undoubtedly added, made the hearer attentive to the third question, to which the questioner himself adds in this way: “But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” And he immediately proves, with a reason added, that this is so. “For this is he,” he says, “of whom it is written” (Malachi 3): “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.”

Here attentive ears were needed, so that, on hearing this scriptural text, not only the crowds then present but also all peoples and nations who would hear it might open their eyes, look around, and, by reading what follows in this chapter—of which we have already spoken above—know what, and how great, an answer was given to the intention of this question: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?”

And what, or how great, is this? Certainly it is as though he said: John performs before my face the office of an angel. How the office of an angel differs from the office of a prophet, a learned scribe must seek out and bring forth from the holy Scriptures. Having sought these things, he will be able to hear and say: It is the office of angels not only to announce things to come or already imminent, but also to be sent to particular persons through whom these matters must be administered, and to prepare their hearts by the preparation of their discourse, so that they may be worthy of the working of Divinity, to which it is necessary that faith—[Col. 1511C] by which the righteous lives—should attain familiarly. The first in this office, after the word of promise, were those three angels who appeared to Abraham in the figure of the Holy Trinity and were received into his hospitality (Genesis 15), while the Lord spoke in them and said: “Returning, I shall come to you at this time, with life accompanying, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.” 649 The last of the angels administering that same promise was Gabriel, sent to the Virgin Mary to prepare her receptive mind by this announcement: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1).

But the office of prophets was to proclaim the same promise, or his advent, without being sent to particular persons. For example: “Hear therefore,” says Isaiah, “O house of David: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7). Neither this prophet nor any other prophet was sent to a particular person in order to announce such a thing, except John, this more-than-prophet, who was sent for this purpose: by pointing out the Christ who was present to humanity, he might prepare the way before his face by that very pointing-out. Because of this excellence John is more than a prophet and is an angel.

Accordingly, this faithful witness, Jesus Christ, declares in a most brilliant testimony:

> “Amen I say to you: among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist. Yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

This well-known and supremely clear saying, celebrated throughout the world, requires only that the purpose of so great a testimony [Col. 1512A] also be known: that is, that one should know what cause led the Lord to utter such a magnificent testimony about his forerunner at that particular place and time. What cause, then, should we suppose it to have been, except the great humility of most blessed John?

For this more-than-prophet, knowing that he was not to be preserved until the time when the mystery of the most holy Incarnation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, ought openly to be preached, ascribed this very fact to his own unworthiness. Thus, before he had been sent into prison, he said: “He who is to come after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (John 3). Did he not say the same thing inwardly when he was held in bonds to be killed and thus would not live to see that time?

Certainly, the faithful friend of the Bridegroom considered blessed and worthy of every honour those to whom it should fall to carry those sandals—that is, at the fitting time to preach openly to the whole world the mystery of that Incarnation. No one, indeed, has been or can be able fully to unfold the sacrament of so great a matter as it is. Yet John considered himself far unequal, far inferior, to those blessed persons, precisely because death was to come first, so that he could not be the companion or fellow traveller of those who carried those sandals and preached this Gospel.

Accordingly, consider him comforted by the consolation of this magnificent declaration. For if no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen among those born of women—not even among the apostles or evangelists, who certainly were born of women—who then is this one least in the kingdom [Col. 1512C] of heaven who is greater than he? Do you suppose it is an angel of lesser merit, though all angels, however diverse in merit or order, are greater than John because he is of the least merit? But we do not know who such an angel would be; for Scripture has announced nothing to us about anyone of that sort.

Or does the kingdom of heaven consist only of angels and not also of human beings? The kingdom of heaven is also customarily understood as the present Church, as in the saying: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matthew 13). For there will be no scandals in that heavenly Church which could be taken away. Therefore, will whoever is least, or of the least merit, in this kingdom of heaven be greater than John? Certainly, on that interpretation the opposite saying would follow: “Among those born of women none has arisen less than John the Baptist.”

Therefore we must ask who this least one in the kingdom of heaven is; and he is quickly found, because in truth he is the one who speaks these words: Christ Jesus, the Son of God—least, or most insignificant, of us all; lesser than all little children; humbler than all the humble; serving in a marvellous manner as the least, reigning as the greatest. As he says: “He who is greater among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20). Again: “For who is greater, the one reclining or the one who serves? Is it not the one reclining? But I am among you as one who serves. And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom” (Luke 22): by that appointment, namely, that there each person is greater insofar as he is lesser in his own estimation—that is, humbler.

Someone might ask: [Col. 1513A] “Where is that kingdom? Or when will that kingdom of heaven come?” He therefore says:

> “But from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

In another evangelist, when the same Lord was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he said to them: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor will they say, ‘Behold, here,’ or ‘there.’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). Here he said something more, yet he refers to the same thing.

For when he preached, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4), those who did not understand the mystery of God’s kingdom doubtless often asked, and more often discussed among themselves, where that kingdom of God was or when it would come. Therefore, wishing them to know that the kingdom of God was the presence of the coming of Christ himself the King, and that entering that kingdom meant repenting according to the preaching or testimony of John the Baptist, he said when questioned by the Pharisees: “Behold, the kingdom of God is within you”; and here, answering the thoughts of the crowds: “But from the days,” he says, “of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

It is as if he said: The kingdom of God, or kingdom of heaven, is not now, as in former times, awaited as something that will come from far away; it has already come, it is already within you, so that it can be grasped. For it is grasped, seized by hand, suffering violence from the violent—that is, sinners who repent—and this has been so from the days of John the Baptist; for before him it was not so. Before his days it was foretold, but had not yet come.

This is what immediately follows: “For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” They prophesied—that is, they foretold that Christ would come. But John, coming after all of them, does not prophesy or foretell as they did, but points with his finger. As soon as he came, the kingdom of God was known to have come, according to the prophetic truth mentioned above, where, after the words, “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before your face” (Malachi 3), there immediately follows: “And at once the Ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” [Col. 1513D] (ibid.).

Therefore, as has now been said, all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John—understand, concerning the first advent of Christ or the kingdom of God. But from his days until now, that is, as long as “now” is spoken of—or, as the Apostle says, while it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice” (Hebrews 4)—namely, from those days of John to the consummation of the age, the kingdom of God is no longer prophesied or foretold, but is present. And the violent, namely sinners who because of their sins would have had no claim in the kingdom of God, having become strong through that spirit of humility by which Moses, a mortal man, could restrain God when he wished to be angry (Exodus 32), piously seize the kingdom of God by violence. The kingdom of God itself suffers violence, and not merely in some fashion: it willingly suffers violence of this kind. 650 [Col. 1514A] And this continues until now, that is, until the consummation of the age. Such is the state of affairs from the days of John.

“And if you are willing,” he says, “to receive it”—if you are willing spiritually to understand the spiritual Scripture or prophecy which says: “Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And he shall turn the heart of fathers to sons, and the heart of sons to their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with anathema” (Malachi 4)—“if, I say, you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come”: that is, the one of whom you read that he is to come. He is Elijah, certainly, not in identity of person but in spirit and power: a great sacrament, a great mystery. Therefore he says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
