Here perhaps someone who has heard will ask: even if John had Elijah’s spirit and power in other respects, did he not come very unlike Elijah at least in the greatness of zeal? For Elijah said: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts” (1 Kings 19). He had slain with the sword four hundred and fifty men, the prophets of Baal; and thus he not only rebuked by word but also persecuted with steel the impiety of King Ahab and his wife Jezebel (1 Kings 18). John did nothing of the sort.

For indeed, as it was said of Elijah, so it is fitting to say of John: “He arose like fire, and his word burned like a torch” (Ecclesiasticus 48). For example, he said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance; [Col. 1514C] for already the axe has been laid to the root of the trees” (Matthew 3), and similar things. Yet he struck no one either with an axe or with a material sword; rather, he himself lost his head by the sword in the prison of Herod and Herodias (Mark 6). Elijah, on the other hand, escaped Ahab’s fury and Jezebel’s threats, carried up in a fiery chariot (2 Kings 2). Is there not, then, even in this respect a great dissimilarity between Elijah and John?

To answer briefly: first it must be said that, just as our Lord here declares, “For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John”—with Christ’s advent understood—yet now there is no longer a need to prophesy, because he has come whom they prophesied would come, so one may truly say that not Elijah alone, but all the holy and righteous persons until John, rightly and necessarily girded themselves with swords, struck with the sword, and, as was said to us previously, beat tyrants and slew sacrilegious persons. But from the days of John, neither John himself nor any man of spiritual purpose is permitted to draw the sword.

“But put your sword back into its place,” says the Lord (Matthew 26); and what he said to Peter alone, he says to all: “Enough; let them go this far” (Luke 22). The meaning is: Until this point it was necessary for all who awaited God’s kingdom, because it had not yet come, to use material swords to defend their race, from whose flesh, according to the promises, the kingdom of God had to come. If that race had been uprooted by the nations, as the devil wished, there would have been no source from which the promises could be fulfilled—just as, when a tree has been cut down, there is no source from which to hope for fruit.

Therefore, “until this point,” he says—understand: swords were necessary; “now let them be; it is enough.” Accordingly, we do not seek in John that part of Elijah’s spirit which consists in striking with the sword from good zeal. Rather, we rejoice that it was absent from him, because John marked the beginning of another time. Looking back at the earlier time, one may rightly say, for the reason I have given: “A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time for war, and a time for peace” (Ecclesiastes 3).

Thus far, answering according to the intention of John’s question, supreme Wisdom has brought his discourse to an end. His answer has shed light along this path which we are following, so that we may see and not fail to understand what John wished his disciples to know when he sent them to ask: [Col. 1515B] “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?”

Finally, it is worthwhile to know the conclusion of this discourse, which is as follows:

> “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who cry out to their companions, saying: We played for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn. For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. And Wisdom has been justified by her children.”

The meaning is this: I have told you about John that he is an angel and that he is Elijah: an angel, not by community of nature but by the dignity of his office; Elijah, not by identity [Col. 1515C] of person but by spirit and power. And if you have ears to hear, you should consequently have heard and understood that I am the Ruler whom you seek and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, and that I now come for the salvation of the human race, before my day comes—the great and terrible day of judgment.

But you are neither prepared nor willing to be prepared to receive either his forerunning or my advent. Divided against yourselves, you are unprepared; and the end of each will prove how unprepared you are: my end and John’s end. “To what, therefore, shall I compare this generation?”—in whose time John preceded like an angel and I, the Ruler, immediately came, having remained among you thirty years and a little more, the span of a generation. “It is like children sitting in the marketplace,” and so forth.

How good are the children who say, “We played; we lamented.” How evil and foolish are the children to whom they say, “You did not dance; you did not mourn”! The first and best teacher of the children who play was our Lord Jesus Christ himself, of whom God the Father speaks in Isaiah: “Behold, my servant shall be exalted and lifted up and shall be exceedingly high” (Isaiah 52). Elsewhere the same servant says: “Behold, I and the children whom God gave me” (Isaiah 8).

The playing of such children was that which this first child began in this way: he ate with tax collectors and sinners, in order that by this most kindly condescension they might become well disposed to hear the good news, namely, that forgiveness of sins had been prepared for them. At such playing the Jews did not dance; they did not rejoice or stir themselves up to good works. Rather, they envied this player and his children, namely the apostles, and especially blasphemed him. Therefore he says: “The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold, a gluttonous [read: glutton] man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”

The first or greatest among the children who lament was John, exceedingly severe in rebuking sins: “Brood of vipers,” he said, “who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 3). “Now he was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his loins, and he ate locusts and wild honey” (Matthew 3). All this was lamentation. At such lamentation they did not mourn, because they did not repent; indeed, [Col. 1516B] they even detested him as though he were mad. Therefore he says: “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a demon.”

Is not this generation therefore inexcusable? Certainly it is inexcusable, like foolish children. Yet God, or the Wisdom of God, is not liable to accusation, so that he can steadfastly say: “What more should I have done for you which I did not do?” (Isaiah 5). Therefore he says: “And Wisdom has been justified by the children of men.” It has truly been justified by that justification which the Psalmist desired when he said: “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 51).

A truly great and glorious justification, of which the Apostle speaks thus: 651 “For what if some of them did not believe? Shall their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Rather, God is true, and every human being a liar, as it is written” (Psalm 116), “that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Romans 3).

God could therefore have said, “And God was justified in his words,” by faithfully fulfilling what he promised to the fathers and, by assuming flesh, becoming near to this ungrateful and lying generation. But because he had introduced a comparison of children, he preferred to say, “And Wisdom has been justified by her children,” because the children who say, “We played; we lamented,” are the children of Wisdom, and their playing or lamenting is the justification, praise, and glorification of God’s Wisdom, whose supreme work is the Incarnation or advent of the Son of God.

[Col. 1516D] “Then Jesus began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented. Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you perhaps be exalted up to heaven? You shall descend to hell. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps they would have remained until this day. Nevertheless I say to you that it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites on the day of judgment than for you.”

In a remarkable way, after the declaration, “And Wisdom has been justified by her children,” this follows: “Then Jesus began to reproach those cities.” For this chapter is truly great and has been treated with scrupulous care by the holy Fathers, who certainly strove to justify that same Wisdom in all things. For here is an apparent objection: “If the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. If the mighty works done in you, O Capernaum, had been done in Sodom, perhaps they would have remained until this day.” Why, then, did he not send preachers there or there? Why did he not arrange for mighty works to be performed among them?

It consequently appeared that he had not wished them to be saved; and, failing a reason, some wished us to be content with this alone: that all God’s judgments are just, and that no one can penetrate the entire depth of those judgments of God [Col. 1517B] (Romans 11). But, stirred by the importunity of certain modern writers, who are unable to think otherwise than contrary to that saying of the Apostle, “Who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2), we observe that it does not follow that God did not wish those Tyrians, Sidonians, and Sodomites to be saved because he did not arrange for mighty works to be performed among them [addition: “while such works were being done among them”], works by which they would have been stirred to repent.

Rather, it must consequently be understood that he did not concern himself with their repentance. For must every kind of repentance be of concern to God Most High? Certainly not; rather, that repentance which is according to God, such as he himself then began to preach, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4).

But there is another repentance, according to the world, such as impious Ahab could perform when he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head because of Elijah’s words: “If Ahab dies in the city, dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, birds of heaven shall eat him” (1 Kings 21). Did this man repent for the sake of the kingdom of heaven? Certainly not, but for the sake of the earthly kingdom, for his present life, and lest he be cast out unburied, contrary to royal honour.

Likewise, did the Ninevites repent for the sake of the kingdom of heaven? Certainly not, but solely so that Nineveh might not be overthrown (Jonah 3). But is repentance undertaken for such a cause—that is, being saved, or being safe? For that repentance brings salvation which is according to God: which is performed in hope of the age to come, in fear of Gehenna, and in love of eternal life.

Therefore it must be carefully noted that he did not say: “If the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, or in Sodom, they would have been saved.” Rather, he says: “They would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes,” and “perhaps they would have remained until this day”—neither of which is the same as saying that they would have been saved.

Thus, therefore, that Wisdom may in this also be justified not only faithfully but knowingly by her children, the intention of the present chapter had to be sought more diligently; and, God granting it, it soon became clear. For our Lord, in saying these things, intends to show [Col. 1518A] that the Jews are worse than all nations, even unbelieving ones. For He proclaimed two things to them and performed miracles so that they might believe: namely, both the temporal destruction of their place or nation, which was to come and did come through the Romans; and the eternal punishment of the fire of Gehenna, prepared on the day of judgment for the devil and his angels, and for impious human beings. Although He preached both to the Jews, they did not repent. Had a single word been preached to the Sodomites, Tyrians, and Sidonians, accompanied by the testimony of so many miracles—namely, the temporal destruction which they were going to suffer—they would have repented, as the Lord was accustomed to say through the prophets. For example: “And if I sent you to them, they themselves would hear you. But the house of Israel are unwilling to hear you, because they are unwilling to hear me” [Col. 1518B] (Ezek. 3). This was also proved in the Ninevites (Jonah 3). But had the other matter—the kingdom of God—then been preached to them, they would neither have believed nor repented. Therefore they would not have been saved, and for that reason He did not take care to send preachers to them.

Having said this concerning a difficult question, let us now examine the very words of the present chapter. “Woe to you,” He says, “Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” Since *Chorazin* is interpreted “this mystery of mine,” we are rightly admonished by this very name to pursue the mystical sense in these words, beginning with the interpretation of the names. Chorazin, therefore, upon which woe is pronounced, means, as has already been said, “this mystery of mine”; it signifies the pride or vain wisdom of that generation against which He speaks most especially. Since these things are hidden from it—as He will say later [Col. 1518C]—it is as though this were said to it in some manner: “This mystery of mine is hidden from you; it is to be revealed not to you, but to little ones.”

Bethsaida, upon which woe is likewise pronounced, means “house of fruits,” or “house of hunters,” and signifies the avarice of those whom, when He cast them out, He addressed: “It is written,” He says, “My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21). Capernaum, whose exaltation He strikes down when He says, “You shall descend even to hell,” means “village of consolation” and denotes all those who receive consolation from this world. For example, that rich man who said to his soul: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” [Col. 1518D] (Luke 12); and, having said these things, as though exalted to heaven, on that same night he descended even to hell.

Those characterized by these three names were the best-known children of that generation, because they refused to dance not through ignorance but through pride and envy; and because of avarice they refused to mourn at the song or lament of Gospel preaching. By contrast, the nations, which were ignorant and wandered astray, and which would believe upon hearing the Gospel and seeing miracles, are mystically designated by the names Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom. Tyre indeed means “straitness,” Sidon “hunting,” and Sodom [652] “a dumb or silent beast.” Such was paganism. For it was in straits: like Tyre surrounded by the sea, so it was surrounded by the deep sea of ignorance. It was hunting: that is, ensnared in the nets of evil [Col. 1519A] spirits, regarded as gods, as it supposed. It was dumb, or like a silent beast, because, knowing only the things of the flesh, it did not know how to think or speak of the things of the Spirit.

Before Christ’s coming, some such persons—the Ninevites, namely—repented solely through fear of temporal destruction. But after the coming of that same Christ, how many nations did so merely upon hearing of judgment or of the age to come, while the Jews persisted in unbelief, although both matters, as has already been said above, had been preached to them. In these and other judgments of this sort, Wisdom is justified by her children; and they possess this not from themselves, but by the revelation of heavenly grace: that they know how to justify her.

Therefore the Evangelist immediately adds: “At that time Jesus answered and said: I confess to thee, Father, [Col. 1519B] Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was well-pleasing before thee.” He looked back to things which He knew were said of Himself in the Scriptures, one of which is that already set forth above: “Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee” (Mal. 3), so that He might say: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.” Therefore it was most beautifully and most holily said: “At that time Jesus answered.”

With regard especially to those Scriptural utterances which are spoken from the person of the Father to the Son, or concerning the Son, this must be understood: they contain mysteries so great and so glorious that the Son Himself rightly ought to answer them [Col. 1519C] by confession—that is, by praise. For example: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). To this saying from the person of the Father, the Son answers: “I will arise,” He says, “at dawn” (ibid.); and immediately follows: “I will confess to thee among the peoples, O Lord, and sing psalms to thee among the nations” (ibid.). And in another psalm He says: “Therefore I will confess to thee among the nations, O Lord, and sing a psalm to thy name” (Ps. 107).

He had previously spoken concerning the little ones to whom these things were to be revealed: “A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17); but concerning the wise and prudent, from whom these things were hidden and were to be hidden: “Foreign children have lied to me; foreign children have grown old, and have limped from their paths” [Col. 1519D] (ibid.). Therefore, speaking and confessing—that is, praising—according to the Scriptures of truth, after saying against the proud: “We played for you and you did not dance; we lamented and you did not mourn,” He is, as it were, consoled by the consolation that He foretold through the prophet in this manner: “Alas, I will be comforted over my enemies and avenge myself on my foes, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Isa. 1). And repeating the reverent address because of the greatness of the matter: “Yes,” He says, “Father, because thus it was well-pleasing before thee.”

Certainly, in saying and confessing this, He Himself, the first and chief, does what He had said—“Wisdom has been justified by her children”—for the assumed man justifies Wisdom in His judgments [Col. 1520A]. And it should be noted that He calls God, the Creator of all, His Father and the Lord of heaven and earth. For by His nature alone God is Father; but He is Lord of heaven and earth, that is, of all visible and invisible things. It follows:

“All things have been delivered to me by my Father. And no one knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” To what end does this supreme declaration tend? Clearly, so that those hearing might perceive that He was not, “as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3), but rather the Son of Almighty God, who has all things in His power. He could indeed have said, “I am not the son of Joseph, but I am the Son of God”; but this form of speech would have aroused greater envy. He therefore preferred to say: “All things [Col. 1520B] have been delivered to me by my Father.” In this statement the sound is gentler, while the meaning is the same. For none but God alone can deliver all things to His Son.

Moreover, He says this with the authority of Scripture. For example: “I was looking,” Daniel says, “in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven, and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, and he gave him power and honor and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” (Dan. 7). Furthermore, by what follows He shows that He is far above being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph. “And no one,” He says, “knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” Did they not suppose that they knew the man who spoke these things [Col. 1520C]? Indeed, they thought that they knew Him exceedingly well, especially the people of His own country. Hence it is later written: “And coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues, so that they wondered and said: Whence has this man this wisdom and these miracles? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not his sisters with us? Whence, then, has he all these things? And they were offended in him” (Matt. 13). To such a degree did they think they knew Him altogether—and they thought wrongly.

Appropriately, therefore, He who, as the Apostle says, “if we deny him, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2), appropriately, I say, and most necessarily for the whole world, confesses [Col. 1520D] that He is the Son of God. For truly, those who had the ears required for what He was about to say—when He said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear”—would understand this. This confession is a great confession. For just as the Evangelist relates of John that, when he was asked, “Who are you?” “he confessed and did not deny; and he confessed: I am not the Christ” (John 1), so also, in accordance with this confession, when here He was asked, “Are you he who is to come, or do we await another?”—“I confess to thee, Father,” He says, and so forth—the discerning hearer may rightly say that He confessed and did not deny, and confessed: “I am Christ, the Son of God.”

Nor does this meaning destroy the former one, by which, when we say that confession is taken as praise, we are accustomed to use the testimony of the present word, by which He said: “I confess to thee, Father.” [Col. 1521A] For confession of the truth is truly praise of Him: the truth which He began to confess at that time, confessing Himself to be the Son of God in these words, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father,” and, “No one knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” And He persevered in this confession even unto death, when before Pilate He said: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: that I should bear witness to the truth” (John 18). And before the chief priest, who said, “I adjure you by the living God that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 26), He answered: “You have said it” (ibid.).

For this name He was martyred, Himself the faithful witness, when the Jews cried to Pilate: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, [Col. 1521B] because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19). And lest anyone doubt that that testimony is rightly called confession, the Apostle Paul says to Timothy: “I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment” (1 Tim. 6). Truly it is a good confession, by which incarnate Truth affirms both: namely, that Jesus Christ Himself is the Son of God, and that the two natures, divine and human alike, are not two persons but one person. For He does not say, “All things have been delivered to [653] the Word implanted in me,” but, “by my Father”; although it is of course certain that Christ’s divine nature, the Word who is God, has never lacked anything, whereas what it had not previously possessed—namely, all power in heaven and on earth—was delivered only to the human nature [Col. 1521C].

Meanwhile, it must be understood that just as, when He said, “Neither does anyone know the Father except the Son,” He added, “and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him,” so when He first said, “No one knows the Son except the Father,” it must be understood: “and he to whom the Father wills to reveal him.” For concerning the revelation by which the Son reveals the Father, we have this testimony: “Father, I have manifested thy name to the men whom thou hast given me” (John 17), and other such passages. So also, concerning the revelation by which the Father reveals the Son, we have that testimony: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

[Col. 1521D] The operation of that revelation is the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through whom the Son is known, the Father is known, and He Himself is known—the Spirit who is one Spirit of both. How great are the riches and consolation in this revelation, He wishes to make understood from the words which follow: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.” How true these words are, he knows who has deserved to experience them: one who, after laboring and being burdened, heard this inviting voice and was refreshed.

For example, the Apostle Paul, who said, “It is written: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, [Col. 1522A] what God has prepared for those who love him,” and immediately added, “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2), experienced it himself. For he had labored in this matter, especially in that, “still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts 9), he persecuted them even unto death, binding and delivering men and women to prisons. And he had been burdened not only with the burden of sins, but also with the burden of carnal ceremonies which he strove to bear, a burden which neither our fathers, nor the Apostle Peter, nor we were able to bear. He heard this blessed invitation, came, and was refreshed. Yet even then he was not filled with the full banquet, but refreshed for the present by a small taste, until that which is perfect should come.

What, do you suppose, is that perfection, or how much sweetness does it contain? [Col. 1522B] How greatly does it refresh? This small taste, I truly confess—and I believe without uncertainty—cannot be expressed in any language. It can be felt; it cannot be spoken. How much more, then, that perfection? And how few there are who can worthily weigh even what follows: “Take,” He says, “my yoke upon you, and learn from me that I am meek and humble of heart.” O you who labor, O you who are burdened—who, together with the yoke of sin and the burden of mortality common to humankind, have also borne the harsh dominions of kings or rulers, men who deserve to be called beasts rather than humans, as Daniel long ago prefigured through the four faces of beasts: the lioness, the bear, the leopard, and that terrible and wondrous unnamed beast, having great iron teeth [Col. 1522C] (Dan. 12)—you, I say, worn out and ground down beneath the yoke of such masters: “Come,” He says, “to me, and I will refresh you. Behold, my face is the face of a man; behold, I am that Son of Man who came after those beasts in the clouds of heaven, and came even to the Ancient of Days, the Ancient of Days who is my Father, to whom I now confidently say: ‘Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.’ I am not like those beasts, but I am a man meek and humble of heart.”

Under the yoke of those who are not men but beasts, you labored and were burdened; under my yoke “you shall find rest for your souls,” because “my yoke is sweet and my burden light,” so that you may knowingly say that to know me, to live, and to serve me [Col. 1522D] is to reign.

## Chapter XII

“At that time, Jesus went on the Sabbath through the cornfields; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat. But the Pharisees, seeing this, said to him: Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths. But he said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of presentation, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for priests alone? (1 Sam. 21.) Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt? (Exod. 29.) But I say to you that one greater than the temple is here. And if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Hos. 6), [Col. 1523A] you would never have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

O you little ones, to whom the Father has revealed these things: what worthy matter of revelation shines forth for you through this event? For the Lord Jesus did “many other things” which were not written; and if they were written “one by one, I suppose,” says the Evangelist John, “that the world itself could not contain the books to be written” (John 21). Why, then, among the many things not written, was this deemed worthy of being written among the few: that the Lord Jesus “went on the Sabbath through the cornfields,” and that “his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat; and the Pharisees, seeing this, said to him: Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths”? Why, I say, unless because the answer He gave them [Col. 1523B] bears greatly upon that venerable confession in which, as has already been said, He confessed Himself to be the Son of God, beginning thus: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

For He said: “But I say to you that one greater than the temple is here.” Again, He said: “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” It was expedient for us to know these things; for this reason they were written, and such proclamations of His majesty ought to have been written. For how great is this which He says: “I say to you that one greater than the temple is here”? Because of the honor of the divine name, the temple is a great thing, so that anyone who desires to be subject to God and to render reverence to Him [Col. 1523C] ought to render reverence to the temple. Certainly, when He says, “One greater than the temple is here,” He does not exclude even the altar, than which undoubtedly nothing is greater except God, whose altar it is. For because of the name of the Lord, to whom the altar is specially dedicated, the altar itself must be revered by every creature. Therefore, in this saying He confesses Himself to be the Son of God, who is truly greater than temple or altar because He is God. Likewise, when He says, “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath,” He solemnly asserts Himself to be Lord and God of all. For no one is Lord of the Sabbath except God Himself, who established the Sabbath.

Having said this concerning the glory of that confession, we must consider these two arguments for the innocence by which He defends His disciples, saying: “And if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ [Col. 1523D] you would never have condemned the innocent.” The first is that He said: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of presentation, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for priests alone?” David is then read to have done two things, in one of which mercy justifies the priest who gave the loaves of presentation to the hungry man, while necessity excuses him who ate them. But in the other David himself rightly accuses himself, saying to the survivor, namely [654] Abiathar: “I knew on that day that, since Doeg the Edomite was there, he would without doubt report it to Saul: I am guilty for all the lives of your father’s house” (1 Sam. 22). For he had deceived him by saying: “The king commanded me a matter and said: Let no one know the thing for which you have been sent by me” [Col. 1524A] (ibid. 21), and so forth.

I have said this lest it appear that He introduced an insufficiently fitting narrative as an argument for the innocence of the disciples who plucked and ate ears of grain on the Sabbath. For what the Lord defended, in His judgment, in that historical event, He sufficiently indicates by saying: “And if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent.” This sentence, taken from the prophet Hosea (Hos. 6), just as it justifies the priest on the ground of mercy—because he judged it better to give the loaves of presentation to a hungry layman than to observe the ritual of that sacrifice—so conversely condemns the Pharisees for cruelty, because they would rather that Christ’s disciples perish from hunger than permit ears of grain to be plucked on the Sabbath [Col. 1524B].

The second, or other, argument for the innocence of His disciples is this: “Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” They violate it, He says, according to the presumption of your prejudgment. But in truth they do not violate it, entering always into the first tabernacle and carrying out the offices of the sacrifices. “On every day,” the Law says, “continually two lambs of the first year: one lamb in the morning, and the other in the evening; a tenth part of fine flour mixed with beaten oil, having the measure of a fourth part of a hin, and wine for its libation in the same measure for one lamb. But you shall offer the other lamb in the evening, according to the rite of the morning [Col. 1524C] offering” (Exod. 29).

Doing this on the Sabbath just as on the first or second day after the Sabbath, they certainly violate the Sabbath if every work, without any exception, is a violation of the Sabbath. For what is more laborious: plucking ears of grain, or slaughtering two lambs of the first year, stripping their skins, and offering them with their libations morning and evening? But the Sabbath is violated only when someone performs servile work. The true definition of servile work is contempt for the commandment. For example: “When the children of Israel were in the wilderness and found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day, they brought him to Moses and Aaron and the whole multitude. They confined him in prison, not knowing what ought to be done with him. And the Lord said to Moses: Let this man surely die; let the whole multitude stone him outside the camp. And when they had brought him outside, they stoned him and he died, as the Lord had commanded” (Num. 15).

That man’s action did not arise from ignorance or weakness, but from pride, and his sin was contempt. He therefore rightly had to die as a violator of the Sabbath, according to this sentence prescribed in the same place: “But the soul that shall commit anything through pride, whether he is a citizen or a stranger, because he has rebelled against the Lord, shall perish from among his people. For he has despised the word of the Lord and made his commandment void; therefore he shall be destroyed and shall bear his iniquity” [Col. 1524D] (ibid.). One of them might say: “The priests who do these things on the Sabbath are without guilt because they do so in the temple of the Lord, at the command of Him who is Lord even of the Sabbath.” To this He answers: “But I say to you that one greater than the temple is here,” and, “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

If you do not believe these words, whoever you are, believe the works. For it follows: “And when he had passed from there, he came into their synagogue; and behold, there was a man with a withered hand. And they questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbaths?—that they might accuse him. But he said to them: What man among you, having one sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much better is a man than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbaths. Then he said to the man: Stretch forth your hand. And he stretched it forth; and it was restored whole like the other” [Col. 1525A].

If, I say, you do not believe the words, whoever you are, wise or prudent, who have not yet learned to be [Col. 1525B] little ones—those of whom this Son of God, this One greater than the temple and Lord even of the Sabbath, spoke above in His confession—believe the works. For would He work thus and thus if He had lied in this confession: “I confess to thee, Father,” and “All things have been delivered to me by my Father,” and “One greater than the temple is here,” and “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath”? He who falsely magnified himself—the one reproached through Ezekiel as having lifted up his heart and said, “I am God and I sit in the seat of God” (Ezek. 28), and, “I made myself”—because he lied, was therefore judged as proud and never did anything divine or useful.

I come to people whose self-exaltation is known from the Scriptures. Miriam the prophetess, sister of Moses [Col. 1525C] and Aaron, because she spoke against Moses, saying, “Has the Lord spoken through Moses alone? Has he not likewise spoken through us?” (Num. 12), did not escape unpunished; but, as one who had spoken proudly, she received a shameful punishment, for a white leprosy like snow covered her. Moreover, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, raised up in pride and claiming the priesthood for themselves, received a terrible punishment: some were consumed by fire from heaven, others swallowed alive by the earth (Num. 16). Saul also, once the chosen king of God, was cast away because of pride and delivered to an evil spirit (1 Sam. 16).

This man, confessing greater things concerning Himself than any of those sinful people, performed works greater and with greater authority than any righteous human being: such as that which immediately followed His saying, “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” Passing on and entering the synagogue on that very Sabbath, He did not pour out prayer, as any holy man might, but commanded as God, saying to the man with the withered hand: “Stretch forth your hand”; and he stretched it forth [Col. 1525D]. Therefore from this and the other works which He did after that great confession—works such as no one else ever did—it ought to have been clear and certain to you, O wise and prudent ones, that in confessing Himself the Son of God and Lord even of the Sabbath, He did not lie. But what follows?

“But the Pharisees, going out, took counsel against him, how they might destroy him.” Therefore their envy was the cause of the hiding of which He had said above: “Because thou hast hidden [Col. 1526A] these things from the wise and prudent.” For conquered both by the truth of His speech and the power of His miracle, and therefore without excuse for ignorance, “they took counsel how they might destroy him.” Nor did such wise and prudent persons cease, increasingly overcome by true Wisdom and provoked by good works, until they “destroyed him,” as it seemed to them. Therefore with just judgment, He says: “Thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent.”

He immediately indicated this hiding in mystical words: Wisdom is justified and is to be justified by her children. For it follows: “But Jesus, knowing it, withdrew from there; and many followed him, and he healed them all, and commanded them not to make him known.” Unless you understand the mystery in the words “he commanded them not to make him known,” this will seem contrary to what follows: “Then there was brought to him one having a demon, blind and mute; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. And all the crowds were amazed and said: Is not this the Son of David? But the Pharisees, hearing it, said: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons.”

Therefore there is a mystery in such a command. Certainly, the outward man, in the form of a servant, acting by the counsel or [655] judgment [Col. 1526B] of the Divinity dwelling within Him, so spoke and so commanded. This was His counsel; this was His judgment: to withdraw from the envious and blaspheming Jews, and to command His apostles or preachers not to teach or preach among them, according to that which was said through Isaiah: “And I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon my vineyard” (Isa. 5). The Evangelist adds the prophetic testimony relevant to this: “That it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying: Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him; he shall announce judgment to the nations. He shall not contend nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench, until he brings judgment forth unto victory; and in his name the nations shall hope” (Isa. 42).

For if, in His command not to make Him known, you attend only to what the letter seems to say, how was fulfilled through this what is here said, among other things, in the prophetic testimony: “He shall announce judgment to the nations . . . and in his name the nations shall hope”? But there is indeed a mystery in the command whereby, as has already been said, He is said to command the clouds not to rain upon His vineyard—that is, His apostles not to offer them Gospel preaching, but, shaking the dust of their feet against them [Col. 1526C] (Matt. 10), to turn to the nations. This also happened (Acts 13); and in doing so, He undoubtedly “announced judgment to the nations,” and “in his name the nations shall hope.”

For what reason had He to command in this manner that they not preach or teach among the Jews? That what was said concerning this servant of the Lord, this chosen and beloved one who served well in the form of a servant, might be fulfilled: “He shall not contend nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets.”

[Col. 1527A] Clearly, He wishes us to understand this: wherever Christ is preached to Jews, the preaching is full of contention and full of shouting. For they are unwilling to hear, but return words contrary to words and cry out without understanding, so that by shouting they may appear to have prevailed, or to have some reason why they ought not yield to the Gospel. Therefore, “He shall not contend,” He says, “nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets”; that is, He will command that He not be preached to them, because they are generally contentious and clamorous, according to the saying: “Do not pour out a word where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32). Hence the Apostle’s saying to Titus: “But avoid foolish questions and genealogies and contentions and disputes [Col. 1527B] about the Law, for they are useless and vain” (Titus 3). Likewise to Timothy: “But avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels. But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all” (2 Tim. 2).

What follows—“A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench”—may rightly be understood with reference to the Jews themselves, as may the saying: “When thou art angry, thou wilt remember mercy” (Hab. 3). For behold, when the Romans came and took away the nation and the place, and the city and temple were given to burning by fire, then indeed the reed was bruised; and from that time the flax smokes, openly displaying to all the memorials of its calamity through the long dispersion of captivity [Col. 1527C]. Yet He will neither break that bruised reed nor quench that smoking flax, “because blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations” should enter, and then the remnant will be saved (Rom. 11).

This is what He immediately says: “Until he brings judgment forth unto victory, and in his name the nations shall hope.” For that judgment, of which He said elsewhere: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9), leaving the Jews behind while the nations hope in His name, He brings forth—that is, causes it powerfully to attain both victory and, in this very respect, great success: because He has not altogether broken the reed, that is, the gentleness of the Jewish people, bruised in the manner described above; and has not altogether quenched the smoking flax, that is, the old [Col. 1527D] priesthood of that same people, burned by fire as has been said, but allows it, half-burned, even now to smoke in the dispersion of captivity.

This, I say, contributes greatly to that victory, in accordance with the sense of the verse spoken from the person of this servant through the Psalmist: “God has shown me [something] concerning my enemies; do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget. Scatter them in thy power and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58).—“Then there was brought to him one having a demon, blind and mute; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw; and all the crowds were amazed and said: Is not this the Son of David? But the Pharisees, hearing, said: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons.”

A truly mystical and divine order [Col. 1528A]: when the Lord Jesus, knowing their thoughts, “withdrew from there, and commanded those who followed him not to make him known, then there was brought to him one having a demon, blind and mute; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw.” For so it was going to be, and so it came to pass: when, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit and the authority of Scripture, they turned to the nations, leaving the blaspheming Jews behind, then the nations would hear with joy and offer themselves voluntarily. Their whole multitude, because it was possessed by the devil, prince of this world, worshipping idols and not knowing how even to name its Creator, and not knowing whither it was being led, was rightly designated by the man who had a demon, blind and mute.

[Col. 1528B] Yet this too was to come about: that because of that same conversion of the Gentiles, the Jews would blaspheme more and more, in a strange madness envying the Gentiles and hating their salvation, so that they could not even endure to hear that God cared for the Gentiles themselves. For example, when Paul, giving an account to the people, had narrated as far as this point: “And he said to me: Go, for I will send you far away to the nations,” they listened to him, Scripture says, up to this word; then they raised their voices, saying: “Take such a man away from the earth, for it is not fitting that he should live.” And as they shouted, threw off their garments, and cast dust into the air, the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks and beaten and tortured with whips, that he might learn for what reason they cried out against him in this way [Col. 1528C] (Acts 22).

In these and other ways, they were to contradict, blaspheming, the things said by the apostles. The beginning and at the same time the portent of so great a blasphemy was this which the Pharisees said when they heard it: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” And because, on account of blasphemies of this sort and their persistent impiety, they were to be divided against themselves in a certain likeness to the demons—of whose partnership in their division those sacrilegious men dared to accuse the Son of God—the most beautiful order of the venerable mystery continues thus:

“But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste; and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, [Col. 1528D] he is divided against himself. How, then, will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.”

“Knowing their thoughts,” he says: namely, that they did not err through ignorance, but blasphemed out of envy. Although he could have said something else, he chose first to say this: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand”—a true pronouncement indeed, whose truth they were to experience in themselves.

[Col. 1529A] For, as has already been said, this was to come about—and did come about—that their kingdom and their illustrious, exceedingly rich city of Jerusalem, surrounded externally by the Roman army, was internally divided against itself by a threefold division. John, Eleazar, and Simon were the leaders of the factions, holding the upper, middle, and lower parts of the city; and in astonishing madness they raged against one another so savagely that even their enemies, the Romans, pitied the harsh fate of the unbelievers, who were being destroyed amid those robbers’ frenzies, with no peace intervening.

Clearly, the Divinity to whom all things are present already saw this future event as present—indeed, by a most just judgment, decreed that it should occur—because they said and wished people to believe concerning the very Son of God that, having made an agreement with Beelzebub, prince of demons—a thing even to hear is impious—he cast out demons through him in a concerted operation. And, that you may understand the utter justice of the judgment, he asks them: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” It is as though he said: If you speak such a word against me, what will you do or say when, after I have been glorified, you see your sons—that is, the apostles—casting out demons through the manifest working of the Holy Spirit, not only from possessed bodies, but also from the temples or shrines in which they are worshipped as gods? What then will you say? You will surely say that they do these things by Beelzebub. For if you have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household members?

After first putting the question to them, he immediately adds: “Therefore they shall be your judges” [Col. 1529C]. For truly, if they had ceased blaspheming at least when they cried, “He is guilty of death,” and had not merely spoken such a word against the Son of Man, but had also “spat in his face and struck him with blows” (Matt. 25), and finally, as they passed by the crucified man, blasphemed him—if, I say, they had at least then ceased their blasphemy, and had not likewise blasphemed, even after his resurrection and ascension, the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, speaking in the apostles and proclaiming repentance and forgiveness of sins, they would not have been judged, nor would the apostles, their sons, have judged them. For example, the apostles would not have said, while shaking out their garments: “Your blood be upon your own heads; we are clean. From now on we shall go to the Gentiles” [Col. 1529D] (Acts 18).

Yet that division of their kingdom or city was not the whole judgment, but the beginning of judgment. Their complete and full judgment will be then, when those judges of whom he said, “Therefore they shall be your judges,” will sit upon twelve thrones, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19), so that the land of the Sodomites ought to fare more tolerably than they, namely on the Day of Judgment.

Now it is worthwhile to consider what the highest Wisdom intended to discover or prove by this syllogism—that is, this argument consisting of three parts: proposition, assumption, and conclusion. For after prefacing, “knowing their thoughts,” the Evangelist relates that he set it out thus: [Col. 1530A] “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.” Whether willing or unwilling, those who heard had to assent to this proposition. The assumption follows, which likewise, whether willing or unwilling, they would concede to be true: namely, that Satan was divided against himself, since this was their own assertion: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” Accordingly, making the assumption, he says: “And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself.” He immediately concludes: “How then will his kingdom stand?”

What does an argument of this kind mean? Does it not plainly indicate that he knew their thoughts to be such that they intended, within Satan’s kingdom, to stand against the Holy Spirit? This appeared unbelievable to one whose mind does not admit or believe that any human being ever entered into a covenant with the devil. Yet Isaiah prophesied concerning these men: “Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men who rule over my people in Jerusalem. For you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and we have made a pact with hell,” and so forth, down to: “And your covenant with death shall be abolished, and your pact with hell shall not stand” [Col. 1530B] (Isa. 28). It was of these men, I say, that Isaiah prophesied this.

For concerning what he says later, “And the Lord said: Because this people draws near with its mouth and glorifies me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and they have feared me by human commandment and teachings” (ibid., ch. 29), the Lord himself, in this same Evangelist, referred to them in this manner: “Hypocrites, Isaiah prophesied well concerning you when he said: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Matt. 15).

Thus, in a remarkable way, he surrounded their assumed blasphemy with the judgments of righteous wrath. He proposed: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.” By this pronouncement he intended, as has already been said, that during the Roman siege they would be divided against themselves and would thus fall and be laid waste. And thus, in concluding, “How then will his kingdom stand?” he strikes the same men more terribly with the judgment that they will fall with the devil on the Day of Judgment.

For what is it to ask, [Col. 1530D] “How will his kingdom stand?” except as though he said: How will that pact or covenant which you have made with death or hell—that is, with the devil—stand? For death or hell, the overflowing scourge—that is, the devil—will not be able to keep covenant with, or spare, those allied to it, such as you are. You said in vain: “When the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and are protected by falsehood” (Isa. 28).

Since, according to prophetic truth, you thus hope in the protection of falsehood as though in the protection of an enduring kingdom, you say this against me; out of hatred for me, you say that, through my action, “Satan casts out Satan”—which contradicts that very hope of yours. Fools and blind men: if Satan casts out Satan, how will Satan spare you [Col. 1531A] human beings allied to him? It will not be so. Rather, “When the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trampled by it. Whenever it passes through, it shall take you away; for morning by morning it shall pass through, by day and by night; and mere terror alone shall give understanding to what is heard” (ibid.).

Isaiah “prophesied well” and truly “concerning you”: “The overflowing scourge”—that is, surely the devil, death overflowing upon sinners—“when it passes through, you shall be trampled; when it passes through, it shall take you away.” Two things have been said: “When it passes through,” it will trample; “when it passes through,” it will take away. Behold, it shall pass through in the present judgment, of which I now say: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12), and then it will trample you. For when I rise [Col. 1532A] from the dead—which is for him to be cast out or to pass through—then it will trample you by the trampling of the Roman army.

But when I come in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead, and he “shall be hurled down before the eyes of all” (Job 40), which will be his passing through, then it “shall take you away,” so that neither he nor you may any longer exist or cause stumbling-blocks in the kingdom of God. In that manifest judgment he shall pass through for eternity; and therefore it is said thus: “Morning by morning, by day and by night, it shall pass through. For it shall cease for all eternity, and mere terror alone shall give understanding to what is heard” (Isa. 28), because before that casting down neither he nor those allied to him will understand how foolish they are or have been.

## Book Ten

[Col. 1531]

[Col. 1531B] I seem to have exceeded the measure of my purpose, my reverend lord Cuno, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, in the work *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, which you very earnestly required me to write, by the great authority of affection which you have been accustomed to exercise toward me.

For in this book, “The generation of Jesus Christ, Son of David, Son of Abraham,” or in this Gospel of Matthew, I had proposed to contemplate the four faces of one and the same living creature: the face of a man, the face of a calf, the face of a lion, and the face of a flying eagle. That is, I proposed to contemplate these four sacred matters, which a Christian may not be ignorant of: the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of the one and same Jesus Christ.

I had proposed this, I say, because this consideration pertains to the purpose of the work and accords with the title prefixed to it: *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*. Nor was it my intention to traverse the entire depth of this sea, or to treat the whole text of this Gospel in continuous exposition. But behold: although I had made such a plan, I have extended the volume and covered a great part of the Gospel narrative; and so, as though driven by a mighty wind, though I had planned to sail not far from port, I have allowed my sails to be driven almost to the middle of the sea.

I shall therefore recall the course of my discourse and endeavor to keep within bounds. Omitting treatment of the matters which follow in the Gospel, after what I have said thus far, as I was able with the Lord’s help, in contemplation of the face of the man, I shall proceed to contemplate the face of the calf. I wish to say something worthy of the promise or title of which you, a lover of the glory and honor of the Son of Man, were the author for me [Col. 1531D].

“Truly the Lord is faithful in his words” (Ps. 144 [145]); he spoke truthfully when he said: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Sam. 2). We now rejoice that the truth of this saying is shown also in you. For because you sought his glory with desire—and from the source of that desire also came your saying to me: [Col. 1532B] “Write for me a work on the glory and honor of the Son of Man”—he has himself made for you a holy garment, a priestly garment, for glory and beauty. May the end of this grace be that you find yourself there in the order of priests where, as the Apostle says, “each shall rise in his own order: Christ the firstfruits” (1 Cor. 15).

That the face of the calf is the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, we learn from the fact that, as we recalled at the beginning of this work, the sacred and mystical Law commanded a calf to be offered for sin as a figure of him. “If,” it says, “a priest sins, causing the people to transgress, or if the whole assembly sins in ignorance and through inexperience does what is contrary to the Lord’s commandment, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished calf for sin” (Lev. 4), and the other things which, in a wondrous manner and in an order truly sacred and mystical, figure the sacrament of the passion of Jesus Christ, “whose blood,” as the Apostle says, in accordance with the meaning of that rite, “cleansed our conscience from dead works” [Col. 1532C] (Heb. 9).

Likewise, at the beginning, when Moses was about to ascend the mountain and receive the stone tablets, the Lord saying, “Ascend the mountain and remain there; and I will give you two stone tablets, the law and commandments which I have written, that you may teach the children of Israel” (Exod. 24), he offered a sacrifice for the people, namely twelve calves. Other animals too were commanded to be offered: namely a male goat from the goats or a female goat, a lamb or a ram. All these breathed forth mystically the sacrament of that same most holy passion, and especially the lamb that was slain in the evening on the fourteenth day of the first month (Exod. 12). But the calf was the greatest of all those animals whose blood was poured out for this mystery; and therefore, rightly, the one face of the calf is here set in mystery for them all.

Our view of this face begins with what the Lord Jesus said to his disciples:

## Chapter XIII

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

[Col. 1533A] Surely no one is ignorant that that Passover was the slaying of a lamb in the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, and that the Jews were commanded to celebrate it every year according to their rite, in accordance with these words of the Lord: “You shall have this day as a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, by an everlasting observance” (Exod. 12). Likewise: “All the children of Israel must observe this throughout their generations” (ibid.).

Yet there was this difference: the Law had said, “On the fourteenth day of the first month, in the evening, is the Passover of the Lord; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s unleavened bread” (Lev. 23). At times this was not done, nor was it done in that year. For among the many traditions which the elders of the Jews had imposed in addition to God’s ordinances, they had also instituted this: if the fifteenth day of the month happened to fall on the day before the Sabbath, which we call Friday, the solemnity was not celebrated but postponed to the following Sabbath day. They said that it was difficult and inconvenient, for many reasons, to continue two Sabbaths—that is, to abstain from all work for two days. One chief reason was that the bodies of their dead, sometimes left unburied until the fourth day, would cause the nuisance of a stench.

Once this tradition is known, it resolves an important question for one who might ask: Since the Jews, having celebrated the Passover and eaten the lamb on the evening of the fourteenth day, ought on the following day, because it was the fifteenth, to have celebrated the solemnity and rested according to the Law, how were they permitted to conduct judicial proceedings, upon which they spent the whole day in condemning the Lord and those crucified with him? Knowledge of the tradition just mentioned quickly resolves this question. For they had been taught to defer the solemnity when the fifteenth day of the month fell before the legal Sabbath, and, instead of two Sabbaths, to celebrate one great Sabbath with a double solemnity.

Thus, after the Evangelist had said, “Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation, that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath” (John 19), he added this reason: “For that Sabbath was a great day” (ibid.). So much having been said about the tradition of the elders, which the slaves of sin observed, and by which they then regarded themselves as permitted to work on the fifteenth day of the month—and worked wickedly—let us now return to the matter.

“You know,” he says, “that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.” They indeed knew that the Passover would take place, but they did not know that on that Passover evening he would be handed over and on the following day crucified. He, however, not only knew it but had from the beginning predestined that it should happen in this way: so that, when the old Passover came to its end—that is, the slaying of the legal lamb—the true Lamb himself and the new Passover might immediately be sacrificed; and so that what had until then been signified as in a shadow might now occur in reality, and enduring truth might succeed the passing figure.

But should we think that even this is devoid of mystery: that he foretold this would occur after two days? He could have foretold it still earlier, saying “after three days,” or “after four days.” Therefore we do not permit even this detail to be empty: that he then foretold it, from which point he was to be crucified after three days, that is, on the third day. Hence we must know that, just as his burial lasted three days, so also his passion lasted three days; and by this passion the holy Trinity had necessarily to be appeased for human beings of all three periods of time awaiting this salvation: those before the Law, those who were under the Law, and ourselves who now live under grace.

This three-day passion of his is distinguished as follows. On the day when he said to his disciples, “You know that after two days the Passover will take place,” he was sold: Judas the betrayer spoke with the chief priests and magistrates, who agreed to give him money, and he promised them in turn to hand him over. When the following day had passed, and evening had fully come—that is, when the fifteenth day and the moon were shining—the Passover was celebrated according to custom. Then, while it was night, after Judas had gone out to betray him, Jesus agonized and prayed at greater length, sweating a bloody sweat (Luke 22); he was handed over, seized, bound, brought to the chief priests, and crucified on the following day.

Let us now enter upon the sequence of events:

“Then the chief priests and elders of the people were assembled in the court of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas; and they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.”

This was the counsel which the patriarch Jacob foresaw when he said: “Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of iniquity in warfare. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor let my glory be in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it is obstinate; and their indignation, because it is harsh” [Col. 1534C] (Gen. 49).

For if he had been attending only to what they had done at Shechem on account of the violation of their sister Dinah, what reason would there be to wish concerning the past, and to say, “Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor let my glory be in their assembly”? At the same time it must be noted that, when about to say these things and the rest to his sons, he prefaced them: “Gather together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel, your father. Gather together, that I may declare to you what shall happen to you in the last days” [Col. 1534D] (ibid.). Therefore this was a prophetic announcement of that future counsel which the chief priests—certainly of the tribe of Levi—then assembled to make, as has already been said. Nor did they cease in their obstinate fury until they killed the man by the death of the cross and pierced the wall with a lance: the wall of the temple not made with hands, of which the man himself said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

Because of such an assembly—because they assembled for such a counsel—he says: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. 49). For, on account of that crime, and their obstinacy and harsh indignation—that is, the envy by which they persist in cruelty—behold, they have been divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel: that is, among the peoples of Christians, who supplanted them and who, because of the uprightness of faith, are called and are the true Israel [Col. 1535A].

We understand the haste of that counsel and its deceitful purpose from the Evangelist’s addition: “For they said: Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.” The feast day, as said above, was to be that great Sabbath day. They did not wait for it, but crucified him on the preceding day, after he had been seized during the night before it. Therefore their plan was to anticipate the feast day and seize him amid the darkness of the night. They feared the crowds who had come up from other cities and regions for the feast day and followed him, for these were the very crowds who had glorified him as he entered the city of Jerusalem, preceding and following him with praises and palm branches [Col. 1535B].

“But when Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him carrying an alabaster vessel of precious ointment, and poured it upon his head as he reclined. But when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying: Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor. But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work upon me. For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me. For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it to prepare me for burial. Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be spoken of in remembrance of her” [Col. 1535C].

Since we are now entering, as has been said, upon contemplation of the face of the calf, we must not forget that the four faces in Ezekiel are said to be four living creatures in such a manner that they are nevertheless said to be, and are, one living creature. For after these four faces or living creatures have been described and repeated, it is written later: “This is the living creature which I saw beside the river Chebar” (Ezek. 10). Again, after first saying, “And when the cherubim lifted up their wings, they were raised from the ground before me, and the glory of the Lord God of Israel was over them,” he says: “This is the living creature which I saw beneath the God of Israel, beside the river Chebar” (ibid.). And after a few intervening words: “And the likeness,” he says, “of their faces was the same faces which I had seen beside the river Chebar, and their appearance and the movement of each went straight forward” [Col. 1535D] (ibid.).

To what end is this said? Namely, because here it is now pleasing to perceive that it was truly said concerning creatures of this kind that “they were full of eyes before and behind” (Rev. 4). For behold, in this face of the calf, in this sacrament of the Lord’s passion, although other things can be said and have been said concerning its eyes, this especially delights us: that two eyes are most clearly apparent, namely the outlook of mercy and the intention of judgment, before and behind—that is, both at the beginning and at the end of the same passion.

For here, before, at the beginning, there are two persons: in one is the outlook of mercy; in the other, the outlook of judgment—namely, the woman who had once been a sinner, and Judas, who stirred up the disciples’ indignation as they said, “Why this waste of ointment?” And behind—that is, at the end of the passion, when he was now about to expire—there are likewise two persons: in one is the outlook of mercy, and in the other the gaze of judgment—namely, on this side the thief who confessed, and on that side the thief who persisted in blasphemy.

Thus this face, the face of the calf, plainly appears full of eyes before and behind, so that you may rightly say of both its earlier and later gaze that “his work is before him” (Isa. 40): a twofold work, of mercy and judgment—mercy here toward the woman who had once been a sinner, and there toward the confessing thief; judgment here upon Judas, who was indignant and went away to the Pharisees, and there upon the blaspheming thief who died in his sin [Col. 1536A].

It would indeed be pleasant for us now to set down concerning the other faces or living creatures that they too, by a similar reasoning, are full of eyes before and behind; but perhaps it would weary readers. Therefore, at their proper places, we shall speak more appropriately of each one. Now, following the sequence of the text, it is worth considering the gentleness in the most holy passion of this face, the face of the calf.

“But when Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper,” and so forth, as above. John more clearly explains on which day before the feast of Unleavened Bread these things occurred, and in what manner, in these words: “But six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus, who had died and whom Jesus raised, was. They made him a supper there, and Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. Mary therefore took a pound of precious pure nard ointment, and anointed the head of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. Then one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: Why was this ointment not sold [variant: *venditur*, ‘is sold’] for three hundred denarii and given to the needy?” [Col. 1536C] (John 12).

In the literal wording John differs here from Matthew and Mark, in that Matthew and Mark wrote in this passage that the woman poured the ointment “upon his head,” whereas John says that she poured it “upon his feet.” As for the earlier pouring-out of the ointment, when she came to the Lord while still a sinner and about to be justified, in accordance with the merciful saying, “Many sins are forgiven her because she loved much” [Col. 1536D] (Luke 7)—which Luke narrates more fully, and John too plainly mentions before this passage, in the account of Lazarus’s death and resurrection, saying: “Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick” (John 11)—it is established that in that first pouring-out of the ointment it was done only upon the Lord’s feet. For a sinner could not immediately think herself worthy of his head.

But now, since John relates that the ointment was poured upon his feet and the other Evangelists upon his head, there is no doubt that she anointed both his head and his feet. And she now anointed his head because she was no longer a sinner, but had long since been justified, her many sins having been forgiven.

It is remarkable with what intention or understanding this devout woman rendered such service to the Lord. For she could not then know or foresee what the Lord himself, foreknowing it, said: “In pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it to prepare me for burial”; or, as another Evangelist wrote: “She has anticipated anointing my body for burial” [Col. 1537A] (Mark 14).

He, the calf of the Lord’s sacrifice, beheld the altar and tabernacle of such a calf, whose immolation was at hand: at whose door he himself was to be sacrificed, into whose inner parts his blood was to be carried, and at whose entrance the remainder of his blood was, according to the mystery of the sacred Law, to be poured out. But she knew none of these things, just as the Lord’s disciples themselves did not yet know the Scriptures, that he had to suffer and rise from the dead (John 20).

With what understanding, then, or pursuing what purpose, did she render such service to one about to die? Surely with the same understanding and the same purpose with which, when she first came to him, she watered his feet with tears, wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed them, and anointed his feet with ointment. In doing that she certainly brought forth the first fruit of repentance and made a fitting beginning of amendment. For it is clear that the woman, formerly devoted to unlawful acts, had used ointment upon herself for the scent of her flesh. Therefore what she had applied to herself shamefully, she now offered to God praiseworthily.

Accordingly, it is written of Hannah, Samuel’s mother: “Her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1), that is, she persevered in the same intention and prayer. This woman showed the same thing about herself by an outward act [Col. 1537C], making the end of her service like its beginning—or rather, because the end of a prayer, as of an action, is better, or ought to be better, than its beginning, she brought a good work, well begun, to a better completion.

For, as has already been said, at first she anointed only the Lord’s feet with ointment. Here, however, when the things concerning him were already drawing near their end, she both anointed his feet and poured ointment upon his head. What she rendered well, the Lord himself accepted better, and for a much more reasonable purpose: certainly because of a mystery to be discussed later.

The disciples viewed it otherwise. “When they saw it, they were indignant, saying: Why this waste?” Most of all was Judas the betrayer indignant—not simply, like the others, on account of the apparent waste of ointment alone, but, what was most wicked, because he grieved that a thing so profitable had not been entrusted to him, who was accustomed and eager to steal, so that he might steal it. “For,” says the Evangelist, “he said this not because he cared for the needy, but because he was a thief, and, having the money-box, he carried what was put into it” [Col. 1537D] (John 12).

But how was it said, or how should it have been said, “In pouring this ointment, she did it to prepare me for burial,” or, “She has anticipated anointing my body for burial,” when, as has already been said, she did not know in doing this that he was to be buried or to die? There is no need to linger over this question. According to ordinary usage of speech, she is rightly said to have done for burial what was known by him to whom all good action is subject to lead on to his burial—the one ordering whatever good either she did or all of us do.

So Jacob says to his sons: “You have caused this misery to me, in that you told Pharaoh that you had another brother” (Gen. 43). They had not done it with this intention, but he saw that it had resulted in the misery which he was then suffering in his soul. Therefore we must know that the woman did not pour out all the ointment which she had in the alabaster vessel.
