Finally, when the traitor Judas said, “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”, the Lord Jesus answered him thus: “Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial.” Therefore she did not pour it all out, but had kept some of it in reserve to pour out on the day of his burial, when that should come to pass. [Col. 1538B] And it came to pass that Joseph of Arimathea buried his body with linen cloths and spices, while Nicodemus also brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds; and this woman too was present, as the Evangelists testify (Matt. 27; John 19). Moreover, Judas both slanderously alleged that what had been poured out was wasted, and hastened to sell what had not been poured out, so that he might steal from the price. He spoke falsely; he slandered in vain. For he who received the ointment had no delight in extravagance, but rather a meditation upon his approaching death—a fact which he wished to make known when he said: “She has done it for my burial.”

What immediately follows—“Amen, I say to you, wherever [p. 660] this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that which she has done shall also be spoken of in memory of her”—stirs us more and more [Col. 1538C] to contemplate this face of the calf. For what does he indicate to us, or toward what does this face direct our gaze, by saying, “this Gospel,” if not toward the very sacrament of his passion, in which he stood, and of which he had spoken a little earlier, beginning thus: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified”? Certainly he truly and faithfully called “Gospel”—which means “good news”—the preaching of his own passion, burial, and resurrection, which was then to be heard throughout the whole world and is now heard. We have heard; we have believed; “therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4), because it is truly good news. And wherever this good news is preached, that which she has done shall also be spoken of in memory of her. And it is very profitably said from evangelical Scripture that we too should do likewise: we, that is, the whole Church gathered from all nations, sinful and justified by his grace.

For when the wealthy bestow the service of charity upon any of his least ones, because they are his faithful people—giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, receiving strangers, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and coming to those in prison (Matt. 25)—they certainly pour sweet and fragrant ointment upon his feet; and by doing this they pour it also upon his head, when, because they minister thus from temporal goods, seeking no vain glory or human praise whatsoever, they place their whole hope in heavenly things. [Col. 1539A] And, lest I say nothing also of spiritual services: when we have, or compose, a faithful and useful discourse concerning him, confessing or preaching him as God and man, we certainly pour good ointment both upon his head and upon his feet; and from the fragrance of such ointment the house is filled, the whole Christian assembly is made glad. O how often some have been indignant at such things—even some whom you could not deny to be disciples of the Lord—and have raged against the faithful soul so acting, compounding the finest ointment and pouring it upon the Lord’s head and feet; that is, writing faithful writings in accordance with the truth of the holy Scriptures, everywhere breathing forth or exhaling faith and confession of the true divinity and true humanity [Col. 1539B] of God and man: of God and of the man Jesus Christ. We read of such indignation in many persons, and we ourselves have experienced something of it in our own days on account of our little works.

But just as there the other disciples were simply indignant, while Judas, who was the fuel of their indignation, was indignant maliciously and out of desire for gain, so then and even until now Jews and heretics are indeed maliciously indignant; while some Catholics have simply been indignant and are indignant against us as we write and study in the Scriptures. They consider what we write almost a wasting of ointment, supposing that we do this from presumption and for vain glory. But at length the Lord speaks, the faithful witness and knower of every person’s intention, and says: “Why do you trouble this woman? [Col. 1539C] She has worked a good work upon me.” Finally, besides the common testimony which he will bear for all, and by which he will defend all on the day of judgment, even now he defends some such persons by whatever defence is needed, so that amid indignations themselves they may persevere and may be able to complete the good work which they have begun.

“Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you? But they agreed with him on thirty silver pieces. And from then on he sought an opportunity to deliver him up.” This work is set opposite to, or contrary to, the woman’s work, as evil to good. Clearly, just as he said of her, “She has worked a good work upon me,” so conversely the Lord might say of him: “He has worked an evil work upon me.” For she anointed me for burial with precious ointment; he sold me for crucifixion at a cheap price.

No Scripture reports that any of the saints or prophets—though many had been killed, so that at one time Elijah said, “I alone am left, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19)—was sold or bought as this Holy of Holies was sold or bought: that is, bought in such a way that his purchasers might kill him. Holy Joseph indeed was sold as a type of this one, but his purchasers did not buy him in order to kill him (Gen. 37). And the utterly impious Haman wished to buy the entire Jewish people in order to kill them, among whom there were certainly some righteous persons, saying to King Ahasuerus: “If it pleases you, [Col. 1540A] decree that it perish, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents to the treasurers of your treasury” (Esther 3). But neither did the king sell the people after receiving the silver, nor was Haman able to kill them by a favour granted him without payment.

This one Holy of Holies was bought in order that he might be killed, bought at a cheap price, namely thirty silver pieces—the price scarcely of a single brute calf, though this calf of the Lord was far better. How much better? “His head,” says the beloved in the Song, “is finest gold; his hands are golden, full of hyacinths. His belly is ivory, set with sapphires. His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases” (Song 5). This one so great was bought for thirty silver pieces, by a seller all too willing, who placed the price at the purchasers’ discretion and said: “What will you give me, [Col. 1540B] and I will deliver him to you?” Hence it was said through the prophet Amos: “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he has sold the righteous man for silver and the poor man for sandals” (Amos 2).

Finally, although that Israel did this very often, we nevertheless attend only to those things which we know from the Scriptures. First they sold the righteous man for silver, and the poor man for sandals, when the ten sons of Jacob sold their brother Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty silver pieces (Gen. 37). Since no more than two silver pieces from this price came to each of them, they could scarcely have bought themselves sandals from it. In that crime these men so filled up the measure of their fathers (Matt. 23), that Judas sold for thirty silver pieces, while the chief priests bought a poor righteous man so great and such as he was; namely, the two chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, who walked about solicitously and pompously, could scarcely have shod themselves sufficiently splendidly from that same price when the traitor returned it to them. [Col. 1540C]

In doing this, unhappy Judas truly went away, and it was truly said: “Then one of the twelve went away.” For he went away, and wholly departed from them; he abandoned his apostleship and left his episcopate to another (Ps. 108; Acts 1). He went away, I say: he walked in the counsel of the ungodly, stood in the way of sinners, and sat in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1). He departed from God, stood with the devil, and, having received thirty silver pieces, was nevertheless cursed thirty times in the prophet’s voice, in Psalm 108, before he was born.

The first curse is: “Set a sinner over him.” The second: “And let the devil stand at his right hand.” The third: “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned.” The fourth: “And let his prayer become sin.” The fifth: “Let his days be few.” The sixth: “And let another take his episcopate.” The seventh: “Let his children become orphans.” The eighth: “And his wife a widow.” The ninth: “Let his children wander and beg.” The tenth: “Let them be cast out from their dwellings.” The eleventh: “Let the moneylender search out all his [p. 661] substance.” [Col. 1540D] The twelfth: “And let strangers plunder his labours.” The thirteenth: “Let there be none to help him.” The fourteenth: “Nor any to have pity on his orphans.” The fifteenth: “Let his offspring be for destruction.” “The sixteenth: in one generation let his name be blotted out.” The seventeenth: “Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord.” [Col. 1541A] The eighteenth: “And let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.” The nineteenth: “Let them be always before the Lord.” The twentieth: “And let his memory perish from the earth.” The twenty-first: “And he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him.” The twenty-second: “And he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.” The twenty-third: “And he clothed himself with cursing as with a garment.” The twenty-fourth: “And it entered like water into his inward parts.” The twenty-fifth: “And like oil into his bones.” The twenty-sixth: “Let it be to him as a garment with which he is covered.” The twenty-seventh: “And as a belt with which he is always girded.” The twenty-eighth: “Let those who rise up against me be confounded.” The twenty-ninth: “Let those who speak evil of me be clothed with shame.” The thirtieth: “And let them be covered [Col. 1541B] with their own confusion as with a double garment.”

By what an evil and ruinous tithe, then, did wretched—yet not pitiable—Judas recover that which he had called a wasting of ointment! For he had said: “Why this wasting? Why was this ointment not sold [variant: is sold] for three hundred silver pieces and given to the poor?” Now a tithe of three hundred denarii is thirty denarii: the number for which, or by which, he sold the Blessed One and inherited thirty curses.

“Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? And Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: The Master says, My time is near; with you I keep the Passover with my disciples. And the disciples did as Jesus instructed them, and prepared the Passover.” The first day of Unleavened Bread was the fourteenth day of the first month, at whose evening the Passover took place—that is, the sacrifice of the lamb. The Lord said to Moses: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year,” and the rest down to: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread” (Exod. 12). “On the first day there shall not be leaven in your houses.” Likewise: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening” (Deut. 16).

To be sure, the first month is called Nisan among the Hebrews, and April among us. In accordance with the law, we observe it for the reckoning of Passover in such a way that the lunation whose fourteenth day falls upon [Col. 1541C] the equinox or after the equinox is reckoned as the first month. On the evening of that day, when the moon is fullest, the Lamb was sacrificed in a mystical rite and eaten with unleavened bread and wild lettuces. On that day, when in all houses the lamb, kept from the tenth day in order to be sacrificed at evening, was to be slaughtered, Judas sought an opportunity to deliver up the Lamb of God; and the opportunity was sought in this manner: “Go,” said the Lord Jesus, “into the city to a certain man, and say to him: The Master says, My time is near,” etc.

For he came into the city—that is, Jerusalem—from Bethany; and by coming there and remaining there longer, he gave the traitor an opportunity. For it must be known that on other days, after teaching in the Temple, he went out at evening [Col. 1542A] to Bethany and stayed there at night; so far was he from ever flattering anyone that, in so great and spacious a city, he never had lodging even for a single night. On the night when he was to be delivered up, he chose to remain longer, as has already been said, although, as the evangelist John writes, he knew all things that were to come upon him (John 18). For it would not have befitted the Prince of Strength, though encompassed by the weakness of our mortality, though at the approach of death he was afraid and weary (Mark 14), to flee his hour or his time by returning earlier than usual to Bethany.

For should he, would it have been just or lawful, to complete that ancient Passover anywhere other than Jerusalem, or to offer anywhere else the sacrifice of his body and blood which he offered on that night? [Col. 1542B] “Take heed,” says the law, “that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place which you see; but in the place which the Lord shall choose, in one of your tribes, you shall offer sacrifices, and shall do whatever I command you” (Deut. 12). Having been made under the law, he owed obedience to the law, so that he should offer the sacrifice not in Bethany or in any other place whatsoever, but in the place chosen by the Lord, namely Jerusalem.

When, do you suppose, did the Lord choose that place? Do you suppose it was when Solomon built the Temple in that city (3 Kings 8)? Rather, it was when Father Abraham offered his son Isaac there, when the Lord tested him and said: “Take your only-begotten son whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which [Col. 1542C] I shall show you” (Gen. 22). Already then the Lord had chosen that place for this sacrifice, of which he had commanded that Isaac be offered there by his father to him as a type. For where we read “into the land of vision,” the Hebrew has *Moria*, and it is the mountain upon which the Temple was later built, on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Thus it is written in Paralipomenon: “And Solomon began the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, in the place which David had prepared on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (1 Par. 3).

I have said this so that I may not overlook the reason why this calf, or lamb, which was to be sacrificed, had to approach the place of sacrifice: namely, because, having been made under the law, he had to obey the law (Gal. 4). Likewise, the same must be thought and said about his entry into that city, which he entered on the tenth [Col. 1542D] day. For it was not, as some think and say, because he entered the city then with such glory in order to provoke them to kill him; rather, it was in obedience to the law which says: “Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God”; they went up three times each year, namely at the feast of Unleavened Bread, at the feast of the month of firstfruits, and at the feast of Tabernacles (Exod. 23; Matt. 21; John 11). But the crowds of people who had assembled for the festival came out to meet him with such glory because they had heard that he had recently performed that miracle: namely, that he had called Lazarus, who had been dead four days, out from the tomb.

“Now when evening had come, he reclined with his twelve [Col. 1543A] disciples. And while they were eating, he said: Amen, I say to you that one of you will betray me. And greatly saddened, they began, each one, to say: Is it I, Lord? But he answered and said: He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me. The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed! It would have been good for him if that man had not been born. But Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: Is it I, Rabbi? He said to him: You have said it. And while they were dining, Jesus took bread, and blessed it and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat; this is my body. And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood [Col. 1543B] of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many for the forgiveness of sins. But I say to you: I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.”

The same narrative order is found in Mark (Mark 14): namely, that, [p. 662] between eating and drinking, while they ate the old Passover—that is, the roast lamb with unleavened bread and wild lettuces—the traitor was identified, when he said: “Amen, I say to you that one of you will betray me,” and so on, until he said to him, “You have said it.” And only then did the Lord deliver to his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, at which point no further mention is made of that traitor. In Luke, however, the text or order of the letter is otherwise. First [Col. 1543C] he describes both Passovers, the old and the new, in an unbroken narrative, and only then adds these words of the Lord: “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke 22), etc.

This diversity in the order of the narrative has produced differing opinions among great and catholic Fathers concerning Judas the betrayer: some saying that he was present; others maintaining that he had already gone out and was not present when the Lord delivered to his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood already mentioned. The pre-eminent Father Augustine, attending to the Evangelist Luke’s narrative or sequence of wording, held and wrote in many places that Judas was present and received this sacrament together with the other apostles. For example:

In the Gospel according to John, where it is said, “And after the morsel Satan then entered into him” (John 18), it is not said—as some careless readers suppose—that Judas then received Christ’s body. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to them all, Judas himself being among them, as Saint Luke narrates most clearly. Then they came to that point where, according to John’s narrative, the Lord most plainly identifies his betrayer by the dipped and offered morsel, perhaps signifying by the dipping of the bread that man’s hypocrisy. [Col. 1544A]

But blessed Hilary, following this narrative of Matthew, says in this very Gospel: “After Judas the traitor has been identified, the Passover is celebrated without him, the cup having been taken and the bread broken; for he had not been worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments. For it is understood that he departed immediately here, as he is shown returning with the crowds. Nor indeed could he then drink with [or: from] God, who was not going to drink in the kingdom, when he promised that all who drank this would afterwards drink with him from the fruit of this vine.”  
[Note: [Col. 1543D] St Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*, ch. 30, §2, *Patrologia*, vol. IX, Migne edition.]

If, therefore, a reason should require the question whether Judas was still with the disciples at that hour, or had gone out before it, which of these ought more to be heard or followed? Certainly the one whom the argument drawn from the text of the Gospel narrative supports more strongly. For only the prophets and apostles are such that it is impious to doubt them in anything concerning the Scriptures. Although this may be confirmed by the opinions of many who have treated the Scriptures, one statement of blessed Jerome on the verse of Psalm 86 is sufficient: “The Lord shall recount in the writings of peoples and of these princes who were in her.” “See,” he says, “what he says: ‘who were,’ not ‘who are,’ so that, with the apostles excepted, whatever else is said afterward may be cut off and have no authority. Though someone after the apostles be holy, though eloquent, he has no authority, because the Lord recounts in the writings of peoples and of these princes who were in her.”  
[Note: [Col. 1543D] St Jerome, *On Psalm 86*, *Patrologia*, vol. [Col. 1544D] XXVI, Migne edition.]

If, then, it is necessary or desirable to know whose argument is stronger, we must first see [Col. 1544C] how Luke does not differ from the other Evangelists, Matthew and Mark, in this narrative. For blessed Augustine did not here seek their agreement when he appeared to follow Luke’s narration. The answer already presents itself to those asking this question: when Luke had said, “And having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me; likewise also the cup,” he defined the matter thus, adding: “after he had supped” (Luke 22). Certainly, if it was after he had supped, it was also after these words: “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table.” For, as has already been said, according to the other Evangelists he spoke these words not after he had supped but while he was supping; and from that supper itself he offered Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas, as John reports, immediately went out (John 13).

The question now arises why this Evangelist needed to use such a manner of narration. This is the manner called recapitulation. “Accordingly, a certain Ticonius, as blessed Augustine says, argued most forcefully against the Donatists and set down a sixth rule in the book which he called *The Book of Rules*, because in it he expounded seven rules, by which, as by keys, the hidden things of the divine Scriptures are opened.”  
[Note: [Col. 1544D] St Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III, ch. 30, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, Migne edition.]

“The sixth rule he called recapitulation, a rule discovered with sufficient attentiveness amid the obscurity of the Scriptures. For some things are spoken as though they followed in temporal order, or were narrated in continuous sequence of events, when the narrative is secretly brought back to earlier matters which had been omitted. Unless this rule is understood, one goes astray. For example, it is written in Genesis: ‘But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed’ (Gen. 2). And immediately it follows: ‘And the Lord God brought forth every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food, also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil’ (ibid.). This therefore seems to be said as though it happened after God had placed the man in paradise; whereas, after briefly mentioning both that the Lord God had planted paradise and that he had placed in it the man whom he had formed, he returns by recapitulation and says what he had omitted, namely how paradise had been planted.”  
[Note: [Col. 1545D] St Augustine, *ibid.*, ch. 36.]

Many things of this sort are found in the Scriptures, and this rule, namely recapitulation, is very useful for elucidating their obscurity. Therefore, as was said, the question is why the Evangelist Luke, in writing of that supper of the Lord, chose to use this manner of narration. To those asking this, the first thing to establish is that Luke alone set down these words of the Lord, spoken at that earlier supper of the typical Passover, or paschal lamb, which he ate [Col. 1545C] with his disciples according to the custom of the ancient commandment:

“With desire,” he says, “I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that from now on I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: Take it and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (Luke 22).

Luke alone, as has been said, took care to write that the Lord said he had greatly desired to eat with his disciples the Passover of that year—the thirty-third year of his assumed humanity—and added this reason for his desire: that, having eaten that Passover and drunk the cup of the same typical Passover, he would not eat or drink it again until it should be fulfilled in the kingdom of God. It was therefore fitting [Col. 1545D] that he should immediately record the manner of its fulfilment, and for this reason postpone the things said at the same supper: “And taking bread,” he says, “he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: [p. 663] This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you” (ibid.). Thus, in the kingdom of God, is fulfilled that which was figured by that earlier Passover and earlier cup. For from that time the kingdom of God came, whose beginning was his passion, to which he was delivered on that night, to rise again on the third day. We therefore judge that we have stated [Col. 1546A] a sufficient reason why Luke alone wished to continue the narrative of both Passovers, old and new, and finally, by recapitulation, returned to the words which the other Evangelists testify were spoken before the sacrament of the new Passover.

I do not fail to know that many, indeed almost all, follow and more readily embrace the view of blessed Augustine rather than the opinion of blessed Hilary, though until now very few have known that Hilary thought or wrote otherwise. For they say that many people even today unworthily receive the same sacrament—and this is true—and that by receiving it they eat and drink judgment upon themselves. They say also—and this too is true—that this sacrament ought to be denied to no one except one who has confessed to, or been convicted of, a crime. And although this is established by another reason, indeed by many reasons, they rely especially on this argument: that the Lord did not deny communion in the same sacrament to Judas the traitor, any more than to the other apostles, since he had not yet confessed or been convicted.

But let us see whether Judas, according to the foregoing consideration, had confessed or been convicted, or not, when the Lord delivered this sacrament. For the Lord himself taught beforehand how, and in what order, one ought to arrive at the conclusion that someone is confessed or convicted in hidden crimes: “If,” he says, “your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses. And if he does not hear them, tell the Church. But if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. 18).

We must therefore see whether, just as we learn concerning the rest that Jesus began both to do and to teach (Acts 1), he also did in this matter what he taught. Judas, the false brother, was certainly sinning against him, because he was hastening to betray him; none of the brethren, that is, disciples, knew it except him who knew all things and from whom Judas could not conceal himself. Yet, suppressing the traitor’s name, he said: “One of you will betray me.” In saying this he certainly rebuked him between himself and him alone, because, apart from Judas himself, whom his own conscience could not conceal from him, no one knew of whom he spoke. Judas did not heed the rebuke; for, persisting in his intention, [Col. 1546D] he even dipped his hand with the Lord in the dish, cunning as he thought himself.

“Then,” as John narrates more fully, “while the disciples looked at one another and were uncertain of whom he spoke, one of Jesus’ disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at his breast. Simon Peter therefore signalled to him and said: Who is it of whom he speaks? Then that disciple, reclining upon Jesus’ breast, said to him: Lord, who is it? Jesus answered: It is he to whom I shall offer the dipped bread. And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas Iscariot” (John 13). By doing this he plainly brought in one other with him, namely John, to whom he had spoken, Judas himself hearing, because he was seated nearer, [Col. 1547A] so that what he had said might be fulfilled: “Every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses.” Judas did not heed them; indeed, he became worse, as the Evangelist indicates by these words: “And after the morsel Satan then entered into him; and with indignation he said: Is it I, Rabbi? And Jesus said to him: You have said it” (ibid.). This indeed was to tell the Church, since the assembly of disciples could hear it. Immediately he went out, not intending to hear the Church, but rather to do more quickly what he was doing—already a heathen and publican, the worst of heathens and publicans.

I have said this so that, if we follow the above-written opinion of blessed Hilary, we may nevertheless know that it remains established that holy communion is to be denied to no one unless he has confessed to, or been convicted of, a crime. Now, to return to the subject, one must consider in this chapter how great is the gentleness of the aforesaid face—the face of the calf—how great its reasonableness, and how great the beauty of truth and justice.

He did not previously deliver or institute this sacrament of his body and blood; rather, he first did so when he was already agonizing in his passion, on the very night on which he was betrayed, when the pile of wood was already being arranged upon which, according to the spiritual rite of the sacred and mystical law, the dismembered limbs of such a calf were to be set in order, with the fire of great charity, or of the Holy Spirit, burning beneath upon the altar—the fire through which he desired to be offered. Then he offered his own fat for sin: namely, all the benefit of his passion necessary for us, under these species of bread and wine, saying: “This bread is my body; this cup is the New Testament in [Col. 1547C] my blood, which shall be shed for you.” And rightly and reasonably so. For this sacrament, by which his death is proclaimed—as the Apostle says, “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor. 11)—when ought it to have been instituted or given, if not at the very point of his passion?

Finally, this was required by reason and by the order of our salvation: that this food of life, set against that food of death which the first man ate with evil intent, desiring to be like God—in which all of us sinned (Gen. 3), in which all of us were infected by the poison of pride—should be given only when we had already been cleansed from that old stain of original sin by his passion.

[Col. 1547D] But someone says: “That blood had not yet been shed; it was shed on the following day, when the apostles themselves, to whom he first gave this food and drink on that night, also had to be cleansed.” To this I say: This Lamb of God had already been sold; this calf of the true sacrifice was already being delivered up; and therefore they were already rightly regarded as clean and were already truly called friends, so that he could say to them: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you”; and immediately afterward: “You are my friends” (John 15). And note that he did not say, “Already you are clean because of my passion or death; already you are friends”; rather, he said: “Because of the word which I have spoken to you.” For his passion or death would not otherwise have benefited them unless the word which he had spoken to them had been believed, or had been mingled with faith. [Col. 1548A]

What he said to these, he also said, or could have said, to all the saints who awaited him from the beginning of the world: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.” For truly, because of the word of the law and the prophets which he spoke to them; because of that word of promise concerning Abraham’s seed—which is Christ himself—which he first spoke to Abraham (Gen. 15, 17, 22; Gal. 3): because of that word, I say, since they believed, they are already clean through it. And his passion, then being enacted, cleansed them: his blood, whose shedding was being prepared that night.

Therefore, although human reason cannot grasp how the sacrament already mentioned of his body and blood can be so—that bread becomes his body, and wine his blood—nor how he had formerly said, speaking of this mystery: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life [p. 664] of the world” (John 6), you may nevertheless reasonably say this: that this bread is rightly called, and truly is, Christ’s flesh, because for us who remain, who had not yet been born—for us who live or who come after the apostles—this eaten bread does the same thing that Christ’s crucified, dying, and buried flesh did in its own form for those earlier saints.

Christ’s dead flesh bestowed forgiveness of sins upon those earlier persons, received into the same womb of the earth in which their bodies, once buried, were contained. And that blood—which, while he was living, he shed in sweat on that night, and, when he was already dead, poured with water from his side for the forgiveness of sins—also works for us through the sacrament of that same flesh [Col. 1548C] and blood under these species of bread and wine.

Therefore, as I began to say, this sacrament had to be made or given not before the passion but at the very point of passion or death, so that all alike, both dead and living believers, might be washed from the stain of the old food, and all alike might feast upon this sacrament of the New Testament: the dead in a manner fitting to them, and the living in a manner fitting to them. Finally, the dead, because in their lifetime they had been more significantly initiated into the sacrifices signifying this sacrament—although few understood that Christ, then to come and die, was announced by those signs—rightly attained that perfection of refreshment of which we have spoken. Thus Christ’s dead soul or spirit descended to their souls, [Col. 1548D] through which it came about that they immediately saw and knew how sweet the Lord God is, who is the food of angels and feeds them immortally. And his body came down into the womb of that same earth in which their bodies had been placed, through which resurrection unto life was given to them, as is confirmed by the many who rose with him even then (Matt. 27).

For the living, that is, for us, to whom it is truly said and who faithfully believe that “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI), figures are no longer set before us to be fulfilled by Christ’s death, but the very truth of the thing itself: the true sacrifice, in which Christ’s death itself is proclaimed in explicit words together with the sign of his cross, wherein in a wondrous manner we both live and are dead. “For,” says the Apostle, “all we who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (ibid.). Unless, indeed, we had been made dead by that baptism, we could not proclaim his death in this food and drink.

Here it is pleasing to employ an illustrative comparison. In the book of Numbers it is written: “Moses sent scouts to inspect the land,” and: “Be strong,” he says, “and bring us some of the fruit of the land. And when they had gone up, they explored the land, proceeding as far as the valley of the cluster; they cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole” (Num. XIII). In accordance with the likeness of that historical event, both those who preceded Christ’s coming and we who follow it carry, as it were, that cluster with its branch: the great, sweet proof of the promise—namely, the wonderful sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. They carried it in the shadowy and signifying holy and mystical rites of sacrifices; we carry it in this one sacrifice of bread and wine.

Accordingly, it must here be observed that, of the two men carrying that cluster, the one who went before did not see what he carried, while the one who followed saw before him what he carried. In this, indeed, we and they are by no means indistinguishable: we, performing the true sacrifice, as has already been said, with explicit words and the sign of the life-giving cross, proclaim the Lord’s death, follow the Lord’s death, and bear the cross. For the cluster on the pole is Christ upon the cross, and this we contemplate with unveiled face. They, however, did carry it, but did not see; they read, but did not understand; and even those who were best, worthy to understand, who saw with prophetic eyes, were told not to disclose it. For example: “But you, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time. Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII). And to Isaiah: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. VIII).

Although our elders have said much sufficiently concerning this sacrament, and the reader’s weariness should be avoided, yet I wish to say one further thing suggested by my mind. Perhaps someone has already noticed that there is here a very great testing. And truly, whoever notices this is not mistaken [Col. 1549D]: for here is God’s testing, a testing that seeks faith; opposed to it is the devil’s testing, a testing that seeks faithlessness.

To bring forward testimony from a similar matter concerning this testing by God, behold, in Exodus the Lord says to Moses: “Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you. Let the people go out and gather enough for each day, that I may test them whether they will walk in my law or not” (Exod. XVI). I said “from a similar matter” because, certainly, when the Lord then rained manna from heaven, it happened to them as a figure of this sacrament (I Cor. X). Likewise, to produce an example of the devil’s testing from the opposite cause: the serpent—or rather, the devil in the serpent—said to the woman: “You shall by no means die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it [Col. 1550A], your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil. The woman ate and gave to her husband, and he ate” (Gen. III).

Thus, tested by the devil, they tested God; and the eyes of both were opened, not so that they might know good and evil, but so that they might fall from good into evil; not so that they might know themselves to be gods, but so that they might recognize themselves as naked. Yet we must not suppose that they first tested God only when, by eating what was forbidden, they dared to determine which would prove truer: God, who had said, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die” (ibid.); or the serpent, who said, “You shall by no means die, but you shall be like gods.” They had already begun to test God; before they heard outwardly the serpent’s evil counsel, they were inwardly testing God in their heart, turning over the desire for divinity. Unless they had first swelled inwardly, as has been said before us, they would not so easily have fallen when outwardly tested.

Otherwise, how would it have been just for God to test them by imposing a command which he did not fail to know they would transgress? For God is not a tempter of evils (Jas. I). To put it more plainly: God does not test anyone with a testing in which he is found a transgressor unless he has himself first been wickedly tested by that person.

For example, in the testing mentioned above, by which he tested the people, saying: “Let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day, that I may test them whether they will walk in my law or not; but on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather, because on the seventh day it shall not be found [Col. 1550C]” (Exod. XVI)—there were transgressors to be found. For the seventh day came, and some of the people went out to gather, but found nothing. Then the Lord said to Moses: “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law?” (ibid.). Did God, though untested, test by that testing those whom he knew would transgress? Certainly not: for the entire congregation of the children of Israel murmured, testing him by murmuring and murmuring by testing him, as we have in the Psalm: “They tested God in their hearts, that they might demand food for their souls; and they spoke wickedly against God. They said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” [Col. 1550D] (Ps. LXXVII).

But if God tests anyone by whom he has not himself been wickedly tested, every testing surely works toward that person’s glory. Thus not Abraham alone, whom God tested in the offering of his son, but almost all the saints are examples; concerning such persons Wisdom says: “Even if they suffered torments before men, God tested them and found them worthy of himself” (Wis. III). To all these Moses says what he says to Israel in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God led you through the wilderness in order to afflict you and test you, so that the things being turned over in your mind might become known—whether you would keep his commandments or not” (Deut. VIII). And afterward: “He brought streams out of the hardest rock; he fed you with manna in the wilderness, which your fathers did not know. [Col. 1551A] And after he had afflicted and tested you, at the end he had mercy on you” (ibid.).

Therefore, to return to my subject: in this sacrament there is a great testing by God, a testing that seeks faith, in order to nullify the faithlessness which the devil’s testing found in the first human beings, whom he persuaded to eat what was forbidden. “Now faith,” says the Apostle, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI). The thing, therefore, had to be unseen, in order that this substance might have a place. The thing, I say—that is, the flesh and blood—had to be unseen, not only lest the natural sensibilities of those eating and drinking should be offended, since to eat or chew with one’s teeth human flesh and to drink human blood is neither pious nor congenial to nature; but also in order that this substance of things hoped for, this evidence of things not seen, might have a place: namely, faith, in which, as the same Apostle says, “the elders obtained testimony” (ibid.).

Indeed, if you consider all the elders—that is, the ancient fathers—to whom Holy Scripture bears witness that they were faithful, and whom the Apostle there enumerates, adding this true statement, “But without faith it is impossible to please God” (ibid.), you find the faith of them all proved in relation to things not seen, which they could not yet see but only hope for. Some of these things were not only unseen, but also above nature. Therefore, in this sacrament, though it is a work of great and ineffable mercy, we are nevertheless tested by a wondrous truth through a wondrous judgment, so that those whose faith is genuine may be made manifest; and to them, without impairment of the rightness of judgment, mercy ought to pardon those bites of the forbidden tree, which the woman took and gave to her husband, through an evil suspicion of God and a perverse, excessive credulity toward the serpent.

Was not that which did not appear, which was not seen, believed there? Did they see with their eyes, in the fruit of that tree, the power able to effect so great a thing which the serpent promised in saying, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III)? And indeed, neither did that death appear or could be seen by the eyes, which God had threatened when he said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die” (Gen. II). Rather, they ought to have believed God the Creator, faithful in all that he has said; but they believed not the Creator but the serpent, not God but the devil.

That entire sacrilege is corrected through this sacrament in those who believe and, believing, receive it: humble in faith, faithful in humility; and consequently utterly unlike those parents. For those heard this promise as the price of transgression: “You shall be like gods,” being proud and wickedly credulous—and wickedly credulous precisely because proud. But these hear the voice of humility in the mystery or proclamation of his death: “You are my friends; remain in me, and I in you” (John XV). For how much sweeter is this voice: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him by love [perhaps: ‘by attraction’]” (John VI), than that which the serpent whispered: “Eat, and you shall be like gods.” The serpent certainly gave nothing of his own but urged them to commit theft; this one, however, gives not merely something of his own, but his own flesh and his own blood.

In those who do not believe and yet receive the sacrament with their mouths while unbelieving, this food and drink produces judgment, because they are found reprobate when tested, precisely because they lack faith and wickedly test God.

Concerning heretical persons, in that Psalm of parables which begins, “Give heed, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth; I shall open my mouth in parables” (Ps. LXXVII), it is said: “Their food was still in their mouth, and the wrath of God rose against them, and slew their fat ones, and hindered the chosen of Israel.” For their sin consists in saying: Let us test God, “because he struck the rock and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed; can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people?” (ibid.).

For this is the sense: Because God was able, when the side of the crucified Jesus Christ was opened—which was the striking of the rock—to cause water to flow with blood, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, made intelligible, and sufficient for our minds to drink, like overflowing torrents: because, I say, he was able to do that, can he also convert bread made by human hands into his body, and wine from these branches into his blood? Otherwise, unless you attend to the mystery, the literal sense does not hold together: “Because he struck the rock and waters flowed, can he also give bread?” For this bread, that is, manna, was, according to the history, given before water flowed from the struck rock. So far has the love of this sacrament detained us at greater length; now let us proceed to the rest.

“And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them: ‘All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night. For it is written [Zech. XIII]: I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. But after I have risen, I shall go before you into Galilee.’ Peter answered and said to him: ‘Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Amen I say to you that this very night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ Peter said to him: ‘Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you.’ And all the disciples said likewise.”

This going out to the Mount of Olives is that departure which we find in John in those dreadful and venerable words: “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV). What did it mean to say, “Rise, let us go from here,” and thus to go out to the Mount of Olives at the very hour of his betrayal, when Judas was speaking with the elders and was about to come immediately with a cohort and attendants, except to leave that city, as he had foretold through the prophet Jeremiah: “I have forsaken my house,” he says, “I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it has lifted up its voice against me; therefore I have hated it” (Jer. XII).

Thus, signifying that both this prophecy and what he himself had said two days earlier—“Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII)—were now being fulfilled, he says, “Rise, let us go from here.” “And they went out to the Mount of Olives.” For it is characteristic of the Wisdom of God to speak by deeds no less than by words.

Josephus too testifies that a similar voice was heard: “At night,” he says, “the priests entered the inner sanctuary in their accustomed manner to perform the sacred rites. First they perceived a certain movement and noise; afterward they heard a sudden voice saying: ‘Let us depart from here.’” [Note: [Col. 1553D] Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 12.] Thus, with the dreadful significance of these voices, the whole protection of salvation showed itself to be departing from that city, in accordance also with what the Lord had earlier signified when he himself went out from the Temple, as the Evangelist says: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple” [Col. 1553B] (John VIII).

The evils that followed proved that Jesus truly left both that Temple and that city, and that the whole protection of the angels departed from both. And fittingly, he went out not just anywhere, but then also, according to custom, to the Mount of Olives. For from there he was to ascend into heaven; after this had occurred, “they returned,” says Luke, “to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a sabbath day’s journey away” (Acts I). Nor is this contradicted by what the same Luke wrote: “He led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, blessed them; and it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven” (Luke XXIV). For Bethany is situated on the side of the Mount of Olives.

Therefore, he rightly went out to the place where his glory was to be consummated by the ascension, there to anticipate that same glory by prayer and to begin the struggle of his passion. Luke recounts this more plainly: “Having bent his knees, he prayed; being in agony, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke XXII). He briefly indicates the cause of this departure, on account of which he rightly said, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII), when he says: “All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night. For it is written: I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.”

We all know that scandal, and there is no need to show how they were scandalized, how all fled after leaving him, or how Peter, forgetful of the strength he believed his own [Col. 1553D], was so offended by the scandal of that night that he denied him three times, saying: “I do not know what you are saying; I do not know the man”; and only then, when the cock crowed, “remembered Jesus’ word, saying: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’; and, when the Lord looked upon him, went out and wept bitterly.” I say, there is no need for demonstration; but we are held to our purpose, and we delight in contemplating, in this sacrifice, not this face, the face of the calf. If anyone has leisure, let him sit with us and contemplate together, in the brightness of this face, the beauty of his eyes. And that this may be done more richly, the earlier event must be recalled to mind, for its mystery is effective in this consideration.

[Col. 1554A] On one occasion this our Lord commanded his disciples to get into a boat and go before him across the sea, until he dismissed the crowds. When he had dismissed the crowd, he went up alone onto the mountain; and when evening had come, he was there alone, praying. “The boat in the middle of the sea was tossed by waves, for the wind was contrary. But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea.” And when he said to them, in their distress: “Take courage; it is I; do not fear,” Peter said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” Coming down from the boat, he walked upon the waters. But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out: “Lord, save me.” Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, seized him, and said to him: [Col. 1554B] “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV).

That event, therefore, was wonderfully both an event and a kind of parable of the event to come, if it is agreeable to call a parable not only something spoken but also something enacted. For the Apostle too, after enumerating the arrangements of the first and second tabernacles, says: “which is a parable for the present time” (Heb. IX). Therefore Jesus, after dismissing the crowd, went up alone to the mountain to pray, because this was to happen and did happen: leaving the city, no longer to teach the crowd, he went out, as has been said, to the Mount of Olives alone to pray. The disciples indeed went out with him, but not as far as the place of prayer. For he said, “Wait here,” or “Sit here, until I go there and pray” (Matt. XXVI). And he took Peter, James, and John with him, but to them also he again said: “Wait here and keep watch” (ibid.). “And having gone a little farther,” or “having withdrawn from them as far as a stone’s throw,” he fell upon his face in prayer (Luke XXII). Thus, leaving them, he went away again a second and a third time and prayed. He was therefore alone, praying on that night, or in the deep evening.

But the boat was tossed by waves in the middle of the sea: that is, the disciples’ faith was exceedingly distressed, so that their eyes were weighed down with sorrow. Yet the Lord Jesus came walking upon the waters, because he was trampling underfoot with a ready spirit those storms that had arisen and were arising on his account, although the flesh was weak. For, indeed, while the flesh was weak, he said in prayer: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” [Col. 1554D]; but the spirit was ready: “Nevertheless,” he said, “not as I will, but as you will.”

There Peter’s confidence thought itself ready also: “Lord,” he said, “command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. XIV). For he had said: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.” “I shall lay down my life before you; I am ready to go with you both into prison and into death” (John XIII; Luke XXII). With this confidence, as though already strong and well equipped, he too walked upon the waters in order to come to Jesus. For when all the disciples fled after abandoning the Lord, “he followed at a distance as far as the courtyard; and, having entered, he sat with the attendants to see the end.” But behold, he saw the strong wind [Col. 1555A] and was afraid, and began to sink.

“For as he sat in the courtyard with the attendants, as has already been said, one maidservant, the doorkeeper, came to him and said: ‘You too were with Jesus the Galilean.’ But he denied it before all, saying: ‘I do not know what you are saying.’” Again, similarly buffeted by another maidservant, he said: “I do not know the man.” A third time, driven by a great wind from those who stood there, “he began to curse and swear that he had not known the man.” When he had thus begun to sink, he cried out: “Lord, save me” (Matt. XIV). For when the cock crowed, remembering Jesus’ word that he had said, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” he went out and wept bitterly. Thus, to weep in this way was to cry out and seek salvation. The Savior’s look made him cry out thus; Luke reverently expresses it when he says: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” [Col. 1555B] (Luke XXII).

After he rose, “as he also here foretold: ‘But after I have risen, I shall go before you into Galilee,’” he appeared to him, as it is written in the Gospel of the same Luke, because two of the disciples “returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon’” (Luke XXIV). The angel speaking to the women also wished to comfort him by naming him, saying: “But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee” (Mark XVI). Truly, therefore, Jesus stretched out his hand and seized him: for he preserved his rank for him, and preserved and established him as prince of the apostles.

It is now pleasing to examine that prophetic passage which this spark from his mouth ought to illuminate for us, when he says: “For it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered’” (Zech. XIII). A few words from what precedes and follows, carefully examined, will shed a beautiful light of understanding.

The preceding words are these: “And it shall be on that day, says the Lord God of hosts, that I shall destroy the names of idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered; and I shall remove prophets and the unclean spirit from the land. And it shall be, when anyone shall prophesy further, that his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord’; and his father and mother, his parents, shall pierce him when he prophesies. And it shall be, on that day [Col. 1555D], that the prophets shall each be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies, nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle [Col. 1556A] in order to lie; but he shall say: ‘I am not a prophet; I am a man who tills the soil, because Adam has been my example from my youth.’ And it shall be said to him: ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he shall say: ‘With these I was wounded in the midst [Vulgate: house] of those who loved me’” (ibid.).

After these words comes: “Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me, says the Lord of hosts: strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (ibid.). Then follows: “And I shall turn my hand toward the little ones. And it shall be in all the land, says the Lord: two parts shall be scattered and shall perish, and the third part shall be left in it. And I shall lead the third part through fire, and I shall burn them as silver is burned, and I shall test them as gold is tested. He shall call upon my name, and I shall hear him. I shall say: ‘You are my people’; and he shall say: ‘The Lord is my God.’ Behold, days of the Lord are coming, and spoils shall be divided in your midst” (Zech. XIII–XIV), etc.

That whole chapter of prophecy is illuminated for us, as has been said, by this brief, sparkling saying from the breast and mouth of the Lord himself, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II), when, after first saying, “All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night,” he adds: “For it is written: Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.”

Therefore, to use fittingly the Gospel comparison of the women grinding: the Lord himself says, “Two women shall be grinding together; one shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. XXIV). This prophetic passage must be placed like the lower millstone, and the already-begun Gospel narrative of the Lord’s passion must be laid over it like the upper millstone, so that, as the Lord’s hand moves it in swift rotation, we may grind the fruitful grain of wheat beneficially for ourselves, and make from its finest inner substance a bread of whitest flour for the use of eternal life. Christ is such a grain of wheat, who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). It is such a grain, I say, that it is never scattered by grinding; and while it remains whole, its inner substance shall never cease to flow out or burst forth.

For the present, let this be the end of this little book, and, when strength has been restored after weariness, let us begin the next with the already-mentioned chapter of prophecy.

## Book Eleven

[Col. 1555]

[Col. 1555D] To seek and find your glory in the Holy Scriptures, O Son of Man—your honor in prophetic and evangelical proclamations—is for us, amid the wearinesses of the present life, like a weary traveler laying down heavy burdens for a while, sitting beneath the shade of a fragrant tree beside a stream of ever-springing water, and in welcome leisure pursuing a fleeting dove, catching it, and touching it with gentle contact and harmless hands.

And indeed it is so. For Holy Scripture is itself that dove of which its author, the Holy Spirit, says in the Psalm: “The feathers of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of her back are in the pale gleam of gold” (Ps. LXVII). Let no one, therefore, wonder and say, “What is this man writing, or to what end?” when the holy Fathers have written sufficiently, and none of us is able to read all that they wrote. For if it benefits no one else, it at least benefits me who write what I write. This sweet study has, even now in the present life, some reward and some profit from its own exercise.

How pleasant it is, as I have said, for a traveler, having sometimes set down his burdens, to have before his eyes and handle the silvered little feathers of the dove and the golden hind parts of her back; so pleasant and delightful is it amid the cares of life to handle Holy Scripture, whose outward discourse, chaste and free from all superfluity, shines like silver, while its inward sense glows like gold.

> Each is drawn by his own delight.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* II.65

And I have this testimony of conscience, that I have said to this delight: “Draw me after you” (Song I). Behold the silver; behold the gold: namely, the chapter of prophecy undertaken at the end of the preceding book, which I proposed to treat together with the Gospel narrative of the Lord’s passion: “And it shall be on that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I shall destroy the names of idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered; and I shall remove prophets and the unclean spirit from the land” (Zech. XIII).

But he had first said: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman” (ibid.). Therefore, the day to which the spirit of prophecy here directs attention must be understood as the day of the Lord’s Passion, since the soldier’s lance, in opening the Savior’s side, opened a fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: a fountain of blood and water for those who believe in Christ. For this very reason they are called, and are, the house of David and inhabitants of Jerusalem: because they believe in Christ, the Son of David; and that Jerusalem in which David reigned was a kind of image of Christ’s eternal city.

“And that fountain,” he says, “shall be for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman”: of “the sinner,” I say, that is, of the Gentile people, who sinned without the Law; and of “the menstruating woman,” who sinned through the Law. Lest she presume upon the righteousness of her deeds, one of her best sons confessed and said: “We have all become as unclean persons, and all our righteousnesses are like a menstrual cloth” (Isa. LXIV).

[Col. 1557D] We must therefore inquire who or what sort of prophets were present on that day, since he said: “I shall remove prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.” Here the narrative of the Evangelist John immediately comes to mind. For he says: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said: ‘What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation.’ One of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them: ‘You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and not the whole nation perish.’ But he did not say this of himself; rather, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also [Col. 1558A] to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John XI).

“I shall remove such prophets,” he says, “from the land.” For, lest you suppose they were good prophets, he joined the unclean spirit to them. He says: “I shall remove prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.” Therefore, evil prophets, prophets filled with an unclean spirit, were to be removed from the land on that day—not only from the land of the living, but also from the land itself and the city which those mortal and dead-to-God persons then inhabited, who prophesied this evil prophecy for themselves from their own heart: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs,” and so forth.

Certainly, apart from their prefatory statement, “If we let him go,” everything they said was counted to them as prophecy: that all would believe in him; but that, because they themselves did not believe, the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation. Among them was Caiaphas, the greatest of prophets of this kind, who said: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people and not the whole nation perish.” “But this,” says the Evangelist, “he did not say of himself; rather, as high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.”

The prophet himself immediately and discreetly, as was fitting, added the reason why they were to be removed from the land. For he says: “And it shall be, when anyone shall prophesy further, that his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie [Col. 1558C] in the name of the Lord.’ And his father and mother, his parents, shall pierce him when he prophesies” (Zech. XIII).

The great Prophet prophesied further concerning himself: because they—and Caiaphas especially—prophesied that it was expedient for him to die, whereas he prophesied that it was necessary for him to rise from the dead. This was “further,” namely, beyond their prophecy, the prophecy of death: he prophesied the prophecy of resurrection. For he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (John II). But he said this of the temple of his body.

Therefore, when “someone shall prophesy further”—whom I do not wish to name, because it is not expedient—“his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.’” His father was the Jewish people and his mother the Synagogue, who begot him according to the flesh; they said this to him. For when they had no other charge to bring against him, at last, having suborned two false witnesses, they produced this: “This man said: ‘I am able to destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’” And when, in answer to the high priest’s saying, “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God,” he replied, “You have said it,” and “From now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming upon the clouds of heaven,” they cried: “He is deserving of death.” Was this not to say, “You shall not live, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the Lord”?

[Col. 1559A] How were those prophets put to shame by that vision of theirs? For he says: “And it shall come to pass on that day that the prophets shall be ashamed, each one of his vision when he has prophesied. Or how did those prophets, while prophesying, cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie? For this too follows: ‘Nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie’” (Zech. 13). Unless they had at some time covered themselves, he would vainly say, “nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle.” What, then, was it to cover themselves “with a sackcloth mantle,” in order to lie, but by most wicked hypocrisy to feign grief and pretend fear, so that the people might be frightened?

This was done by that prophet, Caiaphas, the most impious of impious prophets. Indeed, in order to lie—to magnify and confirm the lie of his vision, which they had alike declared in their council, that the Romans would come [Col. 1559B] and take away both place and nation unless they killed Jesus—he tore his garments. He had adjured the Lord Jesus, saying: “I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God.” And why he added “blessed,” you would not know unless because, in such a cause, he most foolishly presumed to flatter God Himself—with cruel flattery. When He who remains faithful, who cannot deny Himself, replied, “You have said it,” adding, “Nevertheless I say to you, from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming upon the clouds of heaven,” then, as has already been said, “he tore his garments and said, ‘He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?’”

And thus he drew over himself [Col. 1559C] the sackcloth mantle of simulated grief, in order to lie, to strengthen the lie, and to reinforce the falsehood, so that the credulous people, seeing it, might be more greatly frightened where there was no fear, as it is said in the Psalm: “There they trembled where there was no fear” (Ps. 32 [33]). In this manner their fathers used to cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle while shedding the blood of prophets and righteous persons—a measure which these men filled up.

For example: Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name, sealed them with his ring, and sent them to the elders and nobles who were in his city and lived with Naboth. The wording of the letters was this: “Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth among the foremost of the people. Set two men, sons of Belial, against him, and let them bear false testimony [Col. 1559D] against him, saying, ‘He has cursed God and the king’; then lead him out and stone him, so that he may die.” Therefore the citizens, elders, and nobles who were with him in the city did as Jezebel commanded and as was written in the letters she had sent them. They proclaimed a fast, set Naboth among the foremost of the people, and, having brought in two men, sons of the devil, made them sit opposite him (3 Kings 21), etc.

That fast, then, and everything subsequently done by imitators of those men, down to these hypocrites who, in order to lie and establish for themselves an evil word (Ps. 63 [64]), tore their garments—the Holy Spirit rightly and beautifully called, in a brief expression, a “sackcloth mantle,” with which, he says further, they shall no longer cover themselves in order to lie. For the authority to lie itself shall be taken from them; and in a remarkable way they shall be put to shame by their vision, by the lying vision which they prophesied when they said: “The Romans will come if you let him go thus.”

On the contrary, it came about that the Romans came precisely because they did not let Him go thus. And behold: not only, in accordance with their vision and its false sense, did the Romans take away place and nation, but also—what is more, and what they neither foresaw nor knew to fear—they took away their choicest possessions: namely, adoption as sons, glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the promises, and the entire inheritance of the fathers, from whom Christ came according to the flesh, [p. 669] “who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” [Col. 1560A] (Rom. 9).

All these things they took from them, and the Romans now possess them along with the other nations—Romans far different from those Romans who only took their place and nation from them, remained, and continued as pagans, because they neither cared, nor knew how to care, for those rich spoils, being content merely to have taken their place and nation under the leaders Vespasian and Titus.

Therefore they indeed served this Lord and King, Jesus Christ, in avenging His blood against the city Ariel, which is interpreted “Lion of God,” according to what He Himself said: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest” (Jer. 12); against the city of Jerusalem, which this true son of David—son according to the flesh of that David—conquered through them, according to this prophecy: “Woe to Ariel, the city [Col. 1560B] which David conquered. Year is added to year; the solemn feasts have run their course. And I will surround Ariel, and she shall be sorrowful and mourning, and she shall be to me as Ariel. And I will surround you like a sphere in a circle, and I will cast up a mound against you, and set fortifications against your siege. You shall be humbled; from the earth you shall speak, and your utterance shall be heard from the dust. Your voice shall be like that of a spirit-medium from the earth, and your speech shall whisper from the dust” (Isa. 29).

They served Christ the Lord and King in this matter, as I have said, and this was “woe to Ariel”; yet nevertheless, woe also to them, just as there was woe to Assyria. For it continues: “The multitude of those who winnow you shall be like fine dust, and the multitude of those who prevailed against you like a passing spark. And suddenly, in an instant, she shall be visited by the Lord of hosts [Col. 1560C] with thunder, earthquake, and a great noise, with whirlwind, tempest, and flame of devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that fought against Ariel—and all who served, besieged, and prevailed against her—shall be like a dream of a night-vision: as when a hungry man dreams that he eats, but on waking his soul is empty; or as when a thirsty man dreams that he drinks, but on waking he is still weary and thirsty and his soul is empty. So shall be the multitude of all nations that fought against Mount Zion” (ibid.).

Thus, in a remarkable way, the Romans came to punish—and themselves came under punishment. They fought against Ariel with material weapons, and behold, they were confounded. Nor is it now permitted them [Col. 1560D] to cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie; indeed, they are captives among all nations and have no place in which to assemble for similar lying.

But, on the contrary, someone says to them mockingly—He who, as already stated, “prophesied beyond,” that is, beyond what He had been asked by the high priest who adjured Him: “I am not a prophet; I am a man who tills the soil, for Adam has been my example from my youth” (Zech. 13). This is great mockery and most weighty irony: by denying He affirms more sharply, and by affirming He denies more forcefully.

“I am not a prophet,” He says—according to your judgment; for thus you said: “No prophet shall arise from Galilee; this man is not from God” (John 7; 9), and the like. “I am a man who tills the soil”—again, according to your judgment, you who say: “How does this man know letters, since he has not learned? Is this not the carpenter’s son?” [Col. 1561A] (Matt. 13). Yet what I foretold is true, and you are captives; nor is it now permitted you to cover yourselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to lie and kill one of your number.

You said, “For Adam has been my example from my youth,” maligning me as one who sought my own glory and saying, “Whom do you make yourself?” (John 8). And elsewhere: “Though you are a man, you make yourself God” (John 10). This was your reproach; but it is otherwise. I am far unlike Adam, and he was not my example—he who sought his own glory. Rather, I said, and what I said is true: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John 8). His judgment on my behalf against you is manifest.

For behold: He whom you pierced, who died, behold, speaks and answers those speaking to Him. This is what follows:

“And it shall be said to Him: What are these wounds in the midst of your hands? And He shall say: With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me” (Zech. 13). It is plain to the diligent and hidden from the negligent that He who here answers those asking is the one and only Son of Man, Jesus Christ. For who else, after dying and receiving wounds in the midst of his hands, was questioned or replied—or could be questioned and reply—except this one alone, who rose after death so that He might speak? The beginning of that speech was precisely this: to show [Col. 1561B] His wounds by saying, “See my hands and my feet” (Luke 24).

These glorious words, therefore, like the other proclamations of the prophets, were spoken of You, O Son of Man. And true is what You said, promising concerning the holy Paraclete at the very moment of Your passion: “He will glorify me, because he will receive of mine and declare it to you” (John 16). Whatever the holy prophets spoke is Yours, and truly Yours. For they wrote concerning You; they received from You what they were to write concerning You; and Your Paraclete Spirit, receiving as much as pleases Him and declaring it to us—that is, making us understand—glorifies You to us, so that even now we may see or know in part the brightness of such great glory and honor as Yours.

The sum of this glory and honor is that, although You died from the wounds which You received in the middle of Your hands, You still speak; and, in answering those who ask about them, You answer continually concerning those very wounds with a marvelous answer. For how long, how, and by whom—or by whom all—will You be asked, or told: “What are these wounds?” Surely forever and ever, without ceasing and with inexpressible wonder, this will be said to You: both by God the Father, to whom You became obedient unto death, even death on a cross [Col. 1561C] (Phil. 2); by the holy angels, who desire to look into You (1 Pet. 1); and by the people whom You redeemed by Your death. You will be asked continually what these wounds are, and You will say to them in words that shall never end: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.”

And, O great sacrilege—sacrilegious murder—that such wounds should be inflicted upon You in the house of those who loved You! You will not say, “With these I was wounded by those who loved me,” but “in the house of those who loved me.” For those who inflicted the wounds did not love You; yet according to the flesh they belonged to the house of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and others of that kind who loved You and awaited You, who had been promised to them.

Yet to say this is not to answer the question, “What are these wounds?” For it is one thing to ask, “What are these wounds?” and another to say where the wounds were made. The question is what these wounds are. Therefore, beyond what is required, He will say, “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.” And then at last He will say what the wounds are: “The cup is that which the Father gave me to drink” [Col. 1561D] (John 18).
