For what immediately follows is equivalent; it is the voice of the Father who gave the cup, and this saying sounds in our ears in His person:

“Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who cleaves to me. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Zech. 13).

It must be remembered why the discourse came to this place of prophecy: namely, because this face which we now contemplate—the face of the ox, before and behind full of eyes—when it was immediately about to be led to sacrifice, looked here, saying: “All of you will be offended because of me this night; for it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep [p. 670] of the flock shall be scattered.’” Therefore we too looked here, and saw this faithful passage or chapter of prophecy illuminated by the regard of this sparkling face. We saw, I say, the meaning of the prophecy made clear by this saying: “For it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.’”

For although the letter does not stand exactly so, the sense under that letter unquestionably contains this. What the letter says—“Awake, O sword, against my shepherd; strike the shepherd”—is spoken by the Father, who brings forth the sword or rouses it by His command; whereas what He says here, “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered,” is the sword’s answer, the answer of death. For what is this sword but death? I do not mean the death of sin, the death of the soul, which separates the sinning soul from the living God; [Col. 1562A] this sword is the death of the body, by which all of us are struck when the soul of each of us is separated from the body.

God roused this sword against the whole human race and struck us all when He said to the first man: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). We are indeed rightly all struck by such a sword, for we who were dead in soul through the death of sin would live bodily forever uselessly—indeed, most ruinously. But this Shepherd of God the Father, and the man who cleaves to Him—for He is one and the same person with the divinity of the Word—what did He do, that this sword might be roused against Him, so that He might say: “Father, strike the shepherd”? He did nothing; He had no sin in Himself. But to say this was to place in Him the iniquities of us all.

And what shall we say also about this: that in the prophecy, when it had said, “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered,” it immediately adds, “And I will turn my hand toward the little ones” (Zech. 13)? Has not He Himself illuminated this also for us? For when He said, “For it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd,’” etc., He immediately added: “But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.” Was this not the Lord turning His hand toward the little ones after His resurrection: appearing in Galilee to His disciples and saying there, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28)?

For He called such humble hearers His “little ones” not only there in the prophecy but also here in the Gospel, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

These three groups—the wise, namely Greeks or Gentiles; the prudent, namely unbelieving Jews, from whom these mysteries are hidden; and the little ones, that is, humble persons to whom they are revealed when they believe—are those three parts concerning which, after first saying, “And I will turn my hand toward the little ones,” He immediately added: “And it shall come to pass in all the land, says the Lord, that two parts shall be cut off and perish, and the third part shall be left in it. And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned and test them as gold is tested” (Zech. 13).

We see this, for the greater part, already accomplished. For the two aforesaid groups, the wise and prudent, concerning whom the Apostle says, “But we preach Jesus Christ: indeed, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1), have been cut off and have failed. But the Lord reserved the third part, the part of the little ones—that is, the humble—and led them through the fire of many tribulations, in order to test them as silver is tested and prove them as gold is proved.

Above, it has already been said concerning blessed Peter that, while he was walking upon the waters in order to come to the Lord Jesus, when he saw the violent wind he was afraid and began to sink (Matt. 14) [Col. 1564A]—that is, when he had thought himself strong enough to say, “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you. I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (John 13; Luke 22), he feared death at the voice of one maidservant and denied life. This was to begin to sink.

Yet he was not wholly submerged. And so that he might not sink, so that he might escape that storm, the Lord’s look accomplished it: “The Lord turned,” says the Evangelist, “and looked at Peter; and Peter, remembering the word of the Lord, went out and wept bitterly”—with tears of repentance (Luke 22). That was a venerable look, a look of mercy and propitiation, which produced repentance: good repentance, and stable salvation for him.

But behold another repentance, very different from it.

[Col. 1564B] “Then,” says the Evangelist, “Judas, who betrayed Him, seeing that He had been condemned, was led by repentance and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.’ But they said: ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself.’ And having thrown the silver pieces into the Temple, he departed; and going away, he hanged himself.”

Truly this repentance was far different and wholly contrary to the repentance of the Apostle Peter just mentioned: this repentance produced death, whereas that produced salvation. Here, as has often been said, we intend to venerate and honor the face of this ox, which was then being led to sacrifice when it looked upon Peter. And in declaring the splendor of its eyes, we say this: the same face that looked upon Peter also looked upon Judas, but with a different look. It looked upon Peter with a look of mercy, and upon Judas with a look of judgment.

For lest anyone suppose that the Lord’s gaze is always for the good of the person upon whom He looks, behold Scripture plainly says: “And now the morning watch had come, and behold, the Lord, looking upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, destroyed their army and overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were borne into the deep” (Exod. 14). And of both kinds of gaze together—of the gaze of grace or mercy and of the gaze of wrath or judgment—the Psalm speaks in consecutive sentences: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers; but the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy the memory of them from the earth” [Col. 1564D] (Ps. 33 [34]).

Therefore the very face which looked upon Peter in order to pierce him with saving repentance also looked upon Judas in order to trouble him into fatal repentance. We are now drawn to contemplate the justice of such a gaze, but first we should say something about the kinds of repentance, since it is said of this son of perdition that “led by repentance, he returned the thirty silver pieces, and went and hanged himself.”

One kind of repentance is that which the righteous and merciful God deigns to heal: namely, where the cause for doing repentance is faith in the world to come, fear of Gehenna, and desire for the kingdom of God. God took care to preach repentance of this kind not only through His messengers but especially through Himself when He came down from heaven, beginning His Gospel thus: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4).

Another kind of repentance is that whose cause is love of the present world. For this cause the impious Ahab repented concerning the blood of Naboth the Israelite, tearing his garment, fasting, sleeping in sackcloth, and walking with bowed head (3 Kings 21). For this cause also the Sodomites, Tyrians, and Sidonians would have repented, as the Lord says: “If the mighty works done among you had been done in Sodom, O Chorazin and Bethsaida, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11).

Of this sort of repentance [p. 671], because it does not produce salvation [Col. 1565B] (2 Cor. 7), God is never recorded as having taken care to preach it, either Himself or through His messengers—except that He sent the prophet Jonah to the great city Nineveh, although there he neither preached repentance nor was commanded to preach it, but only this: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. 3).

Since, then, there are these two causes of repentance, for which of them was this son of perdition led to repentance? Was it because of the world to come? Certainly not, since he was a devil, as the Lord Himself had long before said: “Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6). No, I say: he did not care for that world or possess any hope of it. Was it then because of the present world? Certainly not; for he abandoned that too wickedly when he went and hanged himself.

What cause, then, could there have been that led him to repentance? We do not inquire into this idly. It is obscure and uncertain to us, indeed, but by another similar case we may perhaps discover something. It is written concerning Ahithophel, who had been David’s counselor and, after going over to Absalom, had given futile counsel against David: “Seeing that his counsel had not been followed, he saddled his ass, rose, went to his house and city, set his house in order, and perished by hanging” (2 Kings 17).

For what reason did he hang himself? He saw that his counsel had not been carried out. That says too little, unless you understand at the same time that, as a malicious interpreter of signs, he inferred that Absalom would be deceived and David would return to his kingdom—something he judged an intolerable evil for himself, since among his other evils he had already advised Absalom to defile his father.

I should rightly call that case similar to this. For who does not know that David bore a likeness or type of this Jesus Christ, Son of God, and also his own son according to the flesh? To say something also in relation to the present mystery of the four faces: he was akin to the face of a man chiefly because Christ was according to the flesh from his seed (Ps. 131 [132]); and to the face of a lion because he was most strong—“he played with lions,” as Wisdom recalls, “as with lambs, and did the same with bears. Did he not slay the giant and remove reproach from Israel? He crushed enemies on every side and broke their horn, even forever, in all his work” (Ecclus. 47).

He likewise had much likeness to the face of an ox, because he was trained by many labors and foreshadowed Christ’s sufferings through many tribulations. Hence, as Wisdom likewise testifies, “Christ cleansed his sins and exalted his horn forever” (ibid.). No less does that pertain to the face of the flying eagle: with the eyes of prophetic grace he wondrously saw and sang the heavenly mysteries of the same Christ who would sit at the Father’s right hand. He saw, I say, and heard, so as among other things to report to us: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” [Col. 1566B] (Ps. 109 [110]).

His very name also approaches this likeness, for David is interpreted “strong of hand” or “desirable.” Ahithophel, on the other hand, bore, both in name and in deed, the likeness of this Judas, the son of perdition, of whom we are now speaking. Ahithophel is interpreted “my brother falling” or “rushing upon.” And just as he wished and intended that David should be cast out of his kingdom and utterly destroyed—that is, should die, and so his name perish—for he said to Absalom: “Let me choose twelve thousand men; I will arise and pursue David this night, for he is weary and weak-handed, and I will strike him” (2 Kings 17), so too this man wished our Lord not merely to die in any manner but to die so that His name might perish.

The Psalm attests this in the person of that same Christ. After saying, “My enemies have spoken evil against me: ‘When shall he die and his name perish?’” (Ps. 40 [41]), it immediately adds concerning this greatest plotter and worst of plotters: “And he entered in to see; his heart spoke vain things; he gathered iniquity to himself. He went outside and spoke the same thing” (ibid.). And, repeating the same point, after speaking of all of them—“All my enemies whispered against me; they devised evil against me” (ibid.), etc.—it describes this man more plainly: “For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has magnified treachery against me” (ibid.).

From this it is clear that not he alone, but especially he, wished the Lord Christ to die so that His name might perish: that is, so that neither report nor memory, and no teaching of His, might survive. Likewise Ahithophel intended that David, as has already been said, once expelled from the kingdom, should never again be able to reign, being forestalled by death.

For the same or a similar reason, therefore, each was led to repentance and each hanged himself: namely, because both this man and that perceived that events would not proceed according to his counsel. And from this comes the most beautiful completion of the likeness. How did Ahithophel perceive, or from what did he learn, that David would not be utterly destroyed according to his intention? Surely from the fact that Hushai, David’s friend, had come to Absalom as though he had abandoned David—although Ahithophel knew well that he had by no means departed from David in mind or was with Absalom in heart.

Could not Judas similarly have said concerning the Lord Christ that, though He had been condemned and would die, His name would nevertheless not perish because His disciples remained alive and would proclaim His name and resurrection? Indeed, he had wished that His disciples also should be arrested with Him. John the Evangelist states this more plainly: “Judas, who betrayed Him, stood with them. Therefore, when He said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground,” etc., down to: “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way,” so that the word might be fulfilled which He spoke (Isa. 8): “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18).

Hushai bore, both in name and in fact, the likeness of those disciples to whom He had already said, “I no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15). For Hushai is interpreted “silence.” Now *Chusai* is another name, unrelated to this, and “is interpreted Ethiopian,” says blessed Jerome, “[and] is written with different letters.” [Note: [Col. 1567D] St. Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*, book 1, ch. 10, v. 6, *Patrologia*, vol. 22, ed. Migne.]

Thus, in the name Hushai—which, as has been said, is interpreted “silence”—the silence of the fearful disciples was beautifully foreshadowed: they all fled after leaving Him and not only kept silent about Him from fear of the Jews, but Peter, the greatest among them, even denied Him. What sort of denial was this? Was it not only of the tongue, and not also of the heart?

For just as Hushai denied his friend David not in heart or mind but only in speech, when Absalom said, “Why did you not go with your friend?” and he replied, “By no means: I shall belong to him whom the Lord and all this people and all Israel have chosen, and I shall remain with him” [Col. 1567C] (2 Kings 16), so too the Apostle Peter denied Christ not in heart but in speech alone, when someone said, “You too are one of His disciples,” and he answered, “I am not.”

And just as Hushai’s departure from David in this fashion took place by David’s own will, David saying: “If you come with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘I am your servant, O king; as I was your father’s servant, so I will be your servant,’ you will overthrow Ahithophel’s counsel” (2 Kings 15), so too the fact that all the disciples fled after leaving the Lord and preserved themselves among the Jews by the silence mentioned above [p. 672] took place by the Lord’s own will. He said: “Where I go, you cannot come” (John 13); “Where I go, you cannot follow me now”; and “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way” (John 18).

Thus Judas’s counsel was overthrown, and they were preserved so that, after His death, His name might not perish for us, to whom they proclaimed: “He has risen.” From this notable likeness, I have wished to take evidence demonstrating that Judas’s repentance was grief born of cruel envy, and that his confession, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood,” may have differed little or not at all from the confession of the demons, who sometimes confessed Him not only to be righteous but even to be the Son of God.

[Col. 1568A] And because it is delightful to employ such likenesses in the holy Scriptures, let us not be weary of pursuing this begun comparison still further. Just as the hanging of that deserter Ahithophel, by which he died, was a dreadful omen to prodigal Absalom and to the people of Israel who went out to battle against David’s men, so the hanging of this traitor Judas—“who, having hanged himself, burst open in the middle and all his entrails spilled out,” as the Apostle Peter relates in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1)—was a horrible portent to the Jewish people, who did not cease to pursue the disciples of Christ, the son of David.

Indeed, there, after Ahithophel’s hanging, Absalom also hung suspended, as Scripture says: “When the mule on which he sat entered beneath a thick and great oak, his head caught in the oak; and, hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule on which he sat passed on, Absalom himself was pierced with spears. And the people of Israel were struck down by David’s men; and far more of the people were consumed by the forest than were devoured by the sword that day” (2 Kings 18).

And here, after Judas was hanged, the Jewish people received the whole inheritance of his condemnation, hanging between heaven and earth: having no hope in heaven because it judged itself unworthy of eternal life, nor possessing its own land. For the Romans came and took away place and nation; and in that siege, forty years later, the forest of the Roman army, under Vespasian and Titus, consumed far more of that people than the sword had ever slain on any day, according to what had been foretold by the Psalmist: “The boar out of the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has grazed upon it” [Col. 1568C] (Ps. 79 [80]).

Is this not to hang between heaven and earth, to have burst open, and to have all the entrails of the hanging one spilled out: namely, to have neither hope nor any share in heaven, nor any proper place on the earth which we tread; and, after the enormous crash of civil discord narrated by the historian Josephus, to have the surviving remnant of the besieged multitude, those who remained after the sword, carried captive into every nation?

Ahithophel, indeed, hastening to destruction, set his house in order, as the letter records: “And having set his house in order, he perished by hanging” (2 Kings 17). But the house of Judas—that is, the Jewish people just mentioned, rightly called his house because he himself was leader of those who seized the Lord Jesus—had long before been set in order by the prophetic Spirit in Psalm 108 [109] under thirty curses, which we too counted in the preceding passage. The first is, “Set a sinner over him”; the thirtieth, “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double garment,” according to the number of the thirty silver pieces which this seller of righteous blood received from those purchasers.

By the ordering of that prophetic Spirit, it was likewise ordained that Judas should return the same thirty silver pieces to the chief priests and elders, and throw them in the Temple, and that they, having received the silver pieces, should say: “It is not lawful to put them into the Corban, because it is the price of blood”; and, after taking counsel, should buy with them the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers. Who could suppose this happened by chance?

“Then,” says the Evangelist, “was fulfilled what had been spoken through the prophet, saying: ‘And they received thirty silver pieces, the price of the one valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel; and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.’” The prophet through whom this was said was Zechariah; but through the carelessness of copyists it became customary for Jeremiah to be named here in place of Zechariah.

The prophecy itself, which the Evangelist here abbreviated, is a great complaint of the Good Shepherd, in accord with what He says elsewhere: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34 [35]). For the Good Shepherd recounts that He fed the flock, from the words, “Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the sheep for slaughter, which those who possessed them killed and did not grieve,” down to, “And the Lord said to me: Take again for yourself the implements of a foolish shepherd” (Zech. 11). To transcribe and explain all these matters here would be excessively long.

The testimony which the Evangelist gave more briefly stands thus among the other words of that chapter: “And I said to them: If it is good in your sight, bring my wages; but if not, refrain. And they weighed out my wages, thirty silver pieces. And the Lord said to me: Throw it to the statuary, the handsome price that [variant: *quo*, ‘at which’] I was valued by them. And I took the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the house of God to the statuary” [Col. 1569C] (ibid.).

Finally, it must be understood that I tended the flock—that is, the children of Israel—under a condition and, as it were, an agreement; concerning them the Psalmist says: “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Ps. 76). And under a condition I gave them the Law on Mount Sinai and the land of Canaan. The Psalmist briefly expresses the substance of this condition or agreement in these words: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they took possession of the labours of the peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 104). What, then, does it mean here to say, “If it seems good to you, bring me my wages; and if not, refrain,” except to place before their own choice what they preferred [Col. 1569D], and to seek voluntary observance of the worship owed and of the Law received? For it is plain that God sought voluntary service from them. For example, he himself says through Moses: “I call heaven and earth as witnesses that I have set before you life and good, blessing and curse. Choose therefore life, that both you and your seed may live” (Deut. 30). And Joshua said to them: “But if it seems evil to you to serve the Lord, the choice is given to you: choose today what pleases you, whom you ought chiefly to serve” (Josh. 24).

Therefore, when he says, “If it seems good to you, bring me my wages; and if not, refrain,” it is as though he said: That son of the householder and lord of the vineyard, sent to the tenants at the season of fruits to receive the fruits of the vineyard—behold, after my Father [Col. 1570A] had sent his servants, some of whom you beat and others you stoned, he sent me to you last, saying, “They will respect my son” (Matt. 21). If, therefore, it seems good to you, give the fruits of the vineyard; and if not, at least refrain, so that you do not kill me, saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (ibid.). But they not only failed to give the fruits of the vineyard; they did not even refrain from this evil, but cast me out of the vineyard and killed me.

And that they might do this, they weighed out thirty pieces of silver, which I ironically call my wages, because they were not wages belonging to me or owed to me, but the price of my blood. The miracle of so evil a recompense was to be seen by the eyes of the Father, who had sent me to demand the fruits of the vineyard from [Col. 1570B] them. Therefore the Lord said to me: “Cast it to the statuary—a handsome price.” “Indeed, the price at which I was thus valued 673 by them” (Zech. 11). With most weighty irony he said “handsome.” That statuary—that is, potter or former of man—is God my Father. For I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the house of God to the statuary (ibid.), so that, seeing so unjust a recompense, he might render judgment and judge them from their own mouths, which said: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men and lease his vineyard to other tenants, who will render him fruit in its seasons” (Matt. 21).

To this meaning belongs what immediately follows: “And I broke my second staff, which was called a cord, that I might dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel” (Zech. 11). In this chapter of prophecy, which it would be tiresome to transcribe here in full [Col. 1570C], he had prefaced it thus: “And I took for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I fed the flock.” And afterwards: “And I took my staff, which was called Beauty, and broke it, that I might annul my covenant which I had made with all peoples.” The meaning is this: I had undertaken to govern all nations and had made a covenant with them, saying to Noah and his sons: “Behold, I establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you” (Gen. 9); and, he says, I called the staff of that government “Beauty.” For beauty or comeliness is no small distinction among all humankind. Then, separately, I had undertaken to govern the one flock of the Israelite nation. And I called the other staff [Col. 1570D] of this government “Cord,” according to the words: “The Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance” (Deut. 32).

But how did I break that former staff, which I had called Beauty? By allowing all the nations to go where they wished, just as Paul also says in the Acts of the Apostles: “We announce to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them; who in former generations permitted all nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14). But, he says, I broke the second staff, which I had called Cord, in order to dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel—by doing, that is, what those themselves judged, to whom and on whose account he had spoken the parable: “He will miserably [Col. 1571A] destroy those wicked men and lease his vineyard to other tenants.” As had been foretold, so it was done.

He broke his fruitful staff, which was called Cord; and this not in every sense, not so as to reject his people. “Has God,” says the Apostle, “rejected his people? By no means; for I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11). Rather, he did so as to dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. The meaning is this: Just as of old the brotherhood between Judah and Israel was dissolved, when the ten tribes were severed from the house of David, made Jeroboam king over themselves, and worshipped the calves which he made, while the tribe of Judah remained with the house of David, possessing the city of Jerusalem and the one temple of the Lord’s name (3 Kings [Col. 1571B] 12), so it is now.

For just as then, in that dissolution of brotherhood, the tribe of Judah—from which Christ had to be born—adhered to its king David, from whose house that birth was expected, because the Lord had sworn to him (Pss. 88, 131); and just as in Israel itself, that is, among the ten tribes, there were some remnants, the Lord saying, “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (3 Kings 19), so also “at this time,” says the same Apostle, “a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11). And among these there is as great a dissolution of brotherhood as could be signified by the image of a sword, when the Lord says: “Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon earth. I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to separate a man from his father, [Col. 1571C] and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10). “There are pains there as of a woman in labour” (Ps. 47), because of so great a dissolution of brotherhood.

For example, the Apostle Paul says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be accursed from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9). At last it is worth observing that, according to the character of the words, there is some difference between prophecy and the event accomplished. For in the event, the Evangelist says, “Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests [Col. 1571D] and elders,” and cast them into the temple (Matt. 27); but in the prophecy the Lord himself, who sought his wages and had fed the flock, says: “And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the house of God” (Zech. 11).

Likewise, although it was to happen, and did happen, that those buyers of blood would say: “It is not lawful to put them into the corban, because it is the price of blood,” and, saying this, would buy “with them the potter’s field as a burial-place for strangers,” it had thus been prophesied: “And the Lord said to me: Cast those silver pieces, or that price, to the statuary” (ibid.), that is, the potter. Therefore, what Judas did in returning the silver and what the chief priests and elders did in buying the potter’s field with it, he whose blood those pieces of silver were the price of says, in the words of the prophecy, that he himself did [Col. 1572A].

Observe carefully: it was not that those rich men, traders in the temple, who used to say—as was stated earlier in this same chapter—“Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich” (ibid.), weighed out such wages; it was not, I say, that they resolved to give the traitor thirty pieces of silver for the betrayal of the Lord—that the Lord did. Rather, it was that the traitor returned the same silver and that they, “having taken counsel, bought with it the potter’s field as a burial-place for strangers”: this the Son of God did, and this, he says, “the Lord appointed for me.”

And who would not delight to know the reason of justice—why the Lord did this, why the Son of God so greatly wished to do it that, before doing it, as though it had already been done, he sent forth in advance a prophetic trumpet sounding by the breath of his Spirit? Accordingly, stirred up by this, we ought to judge those silver pieces to have been most weighty and of the greatest importance, marked with the inscription of a great mystery, which he knew who made all things in wisdom. Let us weigh them more correctly in the scales of reason, because those who gave them as the price of the blood of the just man weighed them badly.

First it must be known that that silver belonged to the Lord, as likewise did all the rest and everything possessed by those enriched sons of poor men, whose fathers had possessed nothing. For the Lord brought them, having nothing, out of Egyptian slavery, in which they had long served because of the sale of their brother Joseph (Gen. 37; Ps. 104); unless it was that he gave them the lands of the nations and they possessed the labours of the peoples, under this condition, as has already been said above [Col. 1572C], that they should keep his ordinances and seek his law. “The land,” he says, “is mine; but you are my tenants” (Lev. 25).

Then he gave them, and thereafter multiplied for them, gold and silver—namely, from the labours of peoples now subject to them, from the regions of the Canaanites brought under their authority—because by a just judgment he had taken these things from those peoples on account of their crimes. Therefore these people had no right in those goods except this: that, serving the Lord, they might use the Lord’s goods as hired servants. Yet, using the Lord’s goods, they very often defrauded the Lord of his service, to such a degree that they consecrated these very goods, which they had received as wages for serving the Lord, to foreign gods and fashioned idols for demons. This is what the same Lord complains of through the prophet [Col. 1572D] Hosea, in these words under the likeness of an adulterous woman: “She did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver and gold for her, which they made into Baal. Therefore I will return and take my grain in its season and my wine in its season; and I will deliver my wool and my flax, which covered her shame” (Hos. 2).

It was a small matter that they made the Lord’s silver and gold into Baal. These sons filled up the measure of their fathers especially in this: that they made the silver of the same Lord the price of his blood. Therefore the time had now plainly come to do what had been prescribed in that prophecy: the time for the Lord to deliver his wool and flax, which covered the shame [Col. 1573A] of that adulterous woman; to deliver his grain and wine, his gold and silver. What beginning of this deliverance could have been more fitting, more just, or more venerable than that he should reclaim and snatch from the traitor’s hand, and cast in the temple to the aforementioned statuary—that is, to God his Father—those thirty pieces of silver, the price of his blood?

For truly the return of the silver itself was the beginning of the aforementioned deliverance of all the goods with which those men had dealt most sacrilegiously and cruelly. Its end or completion came when the Romans arrived and carried away all the gold and silver, both in the temple and outside the temple, together with the wool and flax which survived the fire. Thus was fulfilled what the Lord had threatened in the same prophet: “Lest perhaps,” he says, “I strip her naked and set her as on the day of her birth, make her like a wilderness, make her like a pathless land, and kill her with thirst” (ibid.).

But since the Lord also did this, as has already been said: “It is not lawful to put them into the corban, because it is the price of blood”; they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial-place for strangers. Who can doubt that a mystery worthy of knowing lies beneath this deed also? For we were strangers: to us the Apostle says, “You who were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise and without God in this world. And now,” says the same Apostle, “you are no longer strangers [Col. 1573C] and sojourners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2). Nevertheless, though our estrangement has changed, we are strangers, professing with him that “we do not have here an enduring city, but seek the city to come” (Heb. 13), and doing what he likewise says: “Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (ibid.).

Therefore, in buying “the potter’s field as a burial-place for strangers, as the Lord appointed for me,” they worked a mystery for us by the Lord God’s Son; and although ignorant, they served God’s justice. Namely, just as those silver pieces did not remain with the traitor, who had sold what was not his, so neither did they allow that price to remain with themselves, who had purchased the good labourer and Lord of the vineyard to kill him—not from their own goods, but from the goods of that same Lord, from the wages of that same [Col. 1573D] labourer.

Now corbona was the treasury; *corbona* is interpreted “offering,” and for that reason it was so called, because it was filled with offerings, offerings which in fact came to them. Therefore, lest those silver pieces should return to those from whom both the treasury itself and all other things were justly to be taken away, the Lord provided this; the Lord “appointed” this: that with them they should buy the aforementioned field, to be called the Field of Blood, an evil omen for them and a good one for us. For the Field of Blood is, for them, the whole Church of Christ, which faithfully drinks that blood to this day, crying to God against those accursed men, after the likeness of the blood of righteous Abel, concerning which the Lord speaks to Cain: [Col. 1574A] “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground. Therefore now you shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand” (Gen. 4).

But how are we strangers buried, or have been buried, in such a field? Who does not know? “All who have been baptized,” says the Apostle, “into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death,” etc. (Rom. 6). Meanwhile, the ox’s face—of which we speak in its honour—draws the yoke of obedience, even when adverse things come upon it, according to what was said in the prophet: “The face of the ox or calf was on the left; and the face of the lion on the right” (Ezek. 1); this will be discussed below. These are the things on the left: that he is mocked, scourged, and crucified.

[Col. 1574B] For he was first mocked by the Jews themselves and the chief priests, or the chief priests’ servants: they spat in his face, veiled his face, struck him with fists, and slapped his face, saying with cruel laughter: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” Then he was mocked by the Gentiles, to whom they delivered him—the soldiers of the governor [read: *praesidis*]. For when the whole cohort had assembled around him, “they stripped him, put a scarlet cloak about him, plaited a crown of thorns and put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand; and, bending the knee before him, mocked him, saying: Hail, King of the Jews. And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head with it”; then, after scourging him, they finally crucified him.

There was therefore a twofold mockery, one of dogs and another of calves: dogs, that is, Gentiles; frolicking calves, that is, Jews. As he himself cried in the Psalm, and still says as he cries: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me; they opened their mouth against me as a ravening and roaring lion,” etc. (Ps. 21). And afterwards: “For many dogs surrounded me; the council of evildoers besieged me; they pierced my hands and feet” (ibid.). In a remarkable way this prophecy maintained the order of the history, or event to be performed: just as it was to happen, and did happen, that he was first mocked and maltreated by Jews and then by Gentiles, so it first uttered its complaint concerning the Jews and the Jewish chief priests under the names of calves and fat bulls [Col. 1574D], which were, as it were, clean animals, because they thought or said that they knew God; and then concerning the Gentiles under the name of dogs, because, living without God and not even knowing his name, they were openly unclean.

All these things were on the left; hence this face is rightly said, as has been stated, to be on the left. The face was glorious and despised, as the mourning prophet says: “He rose up like a shoot before him, like a root out of thirsty ground. He has neither form nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we considered him despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, and as though his face were hidden,” etc. (Isa. 53). These, I say, were things of the left—that is, adversities—but through these left-hand things all things on the right came to us; through these adversities all prosperity came to us.

To those calves or bulls, indeed, these things of the left were disgraceful, and to those dogs contemptible. Hence the Apostle says: “To Jews, indeed, a stumbling-block; and to Gentiles, foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). But to us—that is, according to our understanding—that “foolishness of God is wiser than men” [than the Jews], and that “weakness [Col. 1575A] of God is stronger than men” [than the Gentiles], whom, under the authority of the passage quoted above, we dare to call calves and dogs rather than human beings. “Blessed,” he himself says, “is he who has not been scandalized in me” (Matt. 11). Knowing this, we are not scandalized but glory, and preach this face as especially glorious in this seeming foolishness and weakness 675, for we understand that even his insults are full of sacraments and of the majesty of judgment.

First, how much judgment does that fact still exercise upon them, that, in mocking him, they also veiled his face—a detail which the narratives of Mark and Luke did not omit (Mark 14; Luke 22)? For because they thus veiled his face, a veil was placed over their heart, according to that portent in which Moses placed a veil over his own face (Exod. 34): “To this day,” says the Apostle, “when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Cor. 3). And because, with his face thus veiled, they bent him down to strike him with fists, the prophetic Spirit says in the Psalm, by a fitting imprecation or just permission: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bend their back always” (Ps. 68).

Thus they hid his face from themselves, though he is said to have hidden it from them, Isaiah saying: “I will wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will await him” (Isa. 8)—that is, until he shows them his face, as the Apostle continues in the passage mentioned: “But when Israel turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed” (2 Cor. 3). Meanwhile he is hidden from them on account of the guilt of their veiling and of that rejection by which they rejected him, the chief stone, the cornerstone—not in any ordinary manner, but so insolently that, in rejecting him, they even spat in his face. For in what way do we reject something more than by spitting upon it? By what we spit upon, we signify that its smell is foul to us. Therefore those builders rejected this stone exceedingly, but in vain: for it has become the head of the corner (Ps. 117). And it is the beginning of strength, of which more will be said in the contemplation of the lion’s face.

Moreover, God heard with no unjust indignation their mocking laughter, when, striking him with fists and slaps while his face was veiled, as though he could not see, they said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” Foolish and blind men, we prophesy to you for him—that is, we answer according to true prophecy: the daughter of the robber struck him. She who struck him—your whole Synagogue—is called and is the daughter of the robber. For this is what the prophecy says, which he, whose face you veil, sees for us and shows to us: [Col. 1576A] “Now you shall be devastated, daughter of the robber” (Mic. 5). For what reason? “They have laid siege against us,” it says, “striking the judge of Israel on the cheek with a rod” (ibid.).

If you ask who that judge of Israel is, behold, we say that it is he who was born in Bethlehem of the Virgin Mary, but from the beginning—or from eternity—was God. For the passage immediately continues and says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you shall go forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (ibid.). Therefore you are the daughter of the robber, O synagogue of Satan, who struck the cheek of so great a judge; and he prophesies this to you, speaking through the prophets and speaking also through us.

Whose daughter of the robber are you? Are you not Barabbas’s? For Barabbas was a robber and had been cast into prison for sedition and homicide (Matt. 27; Luke 23). You asked that he, the author of sedition, be granted to you; but you killed this one, the prince of peace. Truly, then, you are the daughter of a robber and of such a father; you have justly inherited seditions and robberies. And for this reason you have been devastated: because you laid siege, forbidding them to speak, persecuting and killing those who foretold the coming of the Just One, namely, the judge already mentioned; and, when he was present, you struck his cheek.

The Gentiles also, to whom you delivered him, mocked him no less—indeed, mocked him even more. For in addition to spitting on him and striking him with slaps, as you likewise did, they also put a scarlet cloak about him in mockery of the royal title [Col. 1576C] concerning which you had accused him.

And plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and, bending the knee and saluting him as king, they struck his head with the reed. But in all these matters, you, daughter of the robber, have the greater sin, because you had received the Law and the prophets promising you the Messiah. Therefore you have no excuse for your sin, since knowingly and out of envy you mocked your Lord and King and handed him over to be mocked, scourged, and crucified. But those others, having or knowing nothing of that kind, did all these things, being far more excusable in comparison with you. For some of your own people, persuaded by you, acted through ignorance; but they knew nothing at all.

Let us at last go out to him, or with him, to the place called Golgotha, which is the place of Calvary, where, crucifying him, they divided his garments among themselves; and let us behold, in the humility or punishment of the one judged, the glorious and terrible mystery of the Judge. For there he, in the middle of two robbers, received the one on the right who repented: “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23); while the other, on the left, persevering in wickedness, he left in condemnation.

There too stood John, the dearest of friends, together with Mary his mother, beside his cross (John 19); the rest of his disciples had gone away—not by choice but through fear—and Barabbas the robber, released by the Jews, had gone away somewhere, I know not where. In these four persons, so different from one another, how great a mystery of this Judge shines forth—he who, as has been said, hung judged between the two robbers. You will then duly weigh it, if you consider at the same time that, when he sits to judge all nations upon the throne of his majesty, then the whole human race will be divided into four parts.

There will be those on the right who are judged and condemned, and there will be those who are not judged but judge. These are surely persons of apostolic perfection: “The saints shall judge nations” (Wis. 3), together with those princes to whom it was specifically said: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). The fourth part will consist of those who are not judged because they have already been judged, according to the saying of the Apostle: “For all who have sinned without the Law will perish without the Law” (Rom. 2).

Thus the very cross of Christ judged will be a kind of tribunal of that same dreadful Judge, because around him one robber was judged—that is, punished and saved; another, judged, passed from that judgment or punishment into eternal punishment, unrepentant and blasphemous to his end; and beloved John was neither then nor afterwards crucified or put to death by any other violence. The fourth, Barabbas, had indeed been condemned by God but was not judged by men; rather, as has been said, he was released.

The holy and mystical Law will make this mystery more resplendent for us, in a chapter of this kind:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: After the death of Aaron’s two sons, when they were killed for offering strange fire, he commanded him, saying: Speak to Aaron your brother, that he should not at all times enter the sanctuary, which is within the veil, before the mercy-seat by which the ark is covered, lest he die—for I shall appear in a cloud over the oracle—unless he first does these things. He shall offer a calf for sin, and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall be clothed in a linen tunic; with linen drawers he shall cover his private parts; he shall be girded with a linen belt and shall place a linen mitre upon his head. For these are holy garments; having washed, he shall put them all on. And he shall receive from the whole multitude of the children of Israel two goats for sin and one ram for a burnt offering.

“And when he has offered the calf and prayed for himself and his household, he shall make the two goats stand before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, casting lots over each: one lot for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat. The one upon which the lot for the Lord falls he shall offer for sin. But the one for the scapegoat he shall set alive before the Lord, in order to pour out prayers over it and send it away into the wilderness. When these things have been duly performed, he shall offer the calf and, praying for himself and his household, shall immolate it. Taking the censer, which he has filled with coals from the altar, and taking in his hand compounded incense for burning, he shall enter beyond the veil into the holy place; so that, when he has placed the spices upon the fire, their cloud, like vapour, may cover the oracle which is over the testimony, lest he die.

“He shall also take of the calf’s blood and sprinkle it seven times with his finger toward the mercy-seat on the east. And when he has slain the goat for the sin of the people, he shall bring its blood within the veil, as was commanded concerning the blood of the calf, so as to sprinkle it opposite the oracle and make atonement for the sanctuary from the uncleannesses, transgressions, and all sins of the children of Israel. By this rite he shall act for the tabernacle of testimony, which stands among them in the midst of the filth of their dwelling. No human being shall be in the tabernacle when the high priest enters the sanctuary to pray for himself, his household, and the whole assembly of Israel, until he comes out.

“But when he has come out to the altar which is before the Lord, he shall pray for himself and, taking the blood of the calf and goat, pour it upon its horns all around; sprinkling it seven times with his finger, he shall cleanse and sanctify it from the uncleannesses of the children [Col. 1578B] of Israel. After he has cleansed the sanctuary, tabernacle, and altar, he shall then offer the living goat. Placing both hands upon its head, he shall confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their offences and sins; laying them by imprecation upon its head, he shall send it into the wilderness by a man prepared for the task. When the goat has carried all their iniquities into a solitary land and has been released in the wilderness, Aaron shall return to the tabernacle of testimony.

“Putting aside there the garments with which he had formerly been clothed when entering the sanctuary, he shall wash his flesh in the holy place and put on his own garments. Then, after he has come out and offered his own burnt offering and that of the people, he shall pray both for himself and for the people, and burn upon the altar the fat offered for sins. But he who released the scapegoat shall wash his garments and body with water, and thus enter the camp. The calf and goat which were immolated for sin, and whose blood was brought in to complete the atonement in the sanctuary, they shall carry outside the camp and burn with fire—their skins, flesh, and dung. Whoever burns them shall wash his garments and flesh with water, and thus enter the camp. And this shall be an everlasting ordinance for you” (Lev. 16).

Our assertion is not needed, nor is our demonstration necessary, to establish that these and the other legal institutions were figures of heavenly things. Of certain prescribed observances the Apostle says: “It is therefore necessary that the figures of heavenly things be cleansed with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these” (Heb. 9). Indeed, when these arrangements were being made, God said also to Moses: “Look and make according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). Therefore, the immolation of the calf for sin, the offering of the ram as a burnt offering, the reception from the entire multitude of the children of Israel of two goats for sin with the ram already mentioned for a burnt offering, and the other prescribed things, were figures of heavenly things.

But the heavenly things themselves are those already mentioned: the immolation of Christ crucified, and the divided lots of the robbers crucified with him, while Barabbas was released at the request of the Jews. Let us therefore speak.

“He shall not,” it says, “at all times [Col. 1579A] enter the sanctuary which is within the veil, before the mercy-seat by which the ark is covered,” etc. Christ himself is both priest and sacrifice; he is calf, ram, and goat, though in different respects. He is priest because, as the Apostle says, “being present as the high priest of good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hand—that is, not of this creation—nor through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9), offering the sacrifice of bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109), in the sacrament of his body and blood.

He is the calf because it was necessary for him to suffer not only for us, but also for those who, until his coming, bore the yoke of the Law, lived justly, and were cleansed by the righteousness of faith. He is the ram—namely, sacrificed also for the rams, that is, for his apostles, of whom the Psalm says: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28). For they are rightly called rams for two reasons: either because they are leaders of the whole Church, as rams are leaders of the whole flock; or because, as rams fight with two horns, so they fight against their assailants with the two Testaments. In this they differ from calves—that is, the earlier saints—that they do not bear the yoke of the Law, “which,” as the Apostle Peter says, “neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15).

He is the goat, of course, for those whose graver sins he bore: whether those who were under the Law before his coming, or those whom, at his coming, he who is the end of the Law received or receives through repentance. Of this kind was the latter robber whom, as we said above, he received when he repented on the cross.

Therefore, with the calf, ram, and two goats, the priest then approached before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony when our Redeemer came to his passion, “obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). For the entrance of the holy and true tabernacle is the passion of that same Redeemer. Most especially, that wound of his passion by which one of the soldiers, striking his side with a lance, opened it, is the opening of that entrance through which we enter; nor is there another entrance apart from it through which we can enter into the glory of that heavenly sanctuary. But from that time onward we have become “a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2).

“From the whole multitude of the children of Israel,” he says, “he shall take two goats for sin, and one ram for a burnt offering. And when he has offered the bull-calf,” etc. There is one bull-calf and one ram because, plainly, among righteous and holy persons—on account of whose imperfect righteousness or holiness Christ had to suffer or be sacrificed as a bull-calf and as a ram—there is no duality and no division, but all are one. For even though they were not implicated in personal or actual crimes, they were nevertheless liable to original sin.

But there are two goats, to be separated by lot, because sinners or ungodly persons are divided in such a way that some, converted through repentance, receive forgiveness of sins in Christ’s blood, while others die impenitent in their sins. Christ’s blood does them no good; indeed, it comes upon them for judgment, as some of them invoked it upon themselves, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

He therefore says: “When the priest has offered the bull-calf and prayed for himself and for his house, he shall cause the two goats to stand before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, casting lots upon each: one for the Lord, and the other for the scapegoat.” This was fulfilled in this manner. Obedient to the Father’s will, the priest—the true Lord Jesus Christ—offered himself as a bull-calf and prayed for himself and for his house, which is the Church, [Col. 1580B] when, falling upon his face, he said: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt”; and, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground (Luke XXII).

Then, when he was seized and handed over to the governor Pilate, Pilate said: “Whom do you wish me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?” This plainly amounted to casting the lot over the two goats. For he himself is the goat who, in a different respect, is the ram and the bull-calf, as we mentioned above. “He whose lot comes forth for the Lord,” he says, “shall be offered for sin. But he whose lot is for the scapegoat shall be set alive before the Lord, that prayers may be poured out over him, and he may be sent into the wilderness.” And this too was fulfilled thus. The one whom they asked to have released to them was released, namely Barabbas the robber; but Pilate handed Jesus over, after scourging him, to be crucified. This was the offering of the goat allotted to the Lord for sin.

But what was the solitude or wilderness into which that robber Barabbas went when released? For this is what was said of the scapegoat: “He shall set him alive before the Lord, that prayers may be poured out over him, and send him into the wilderness.” The words, “that prayers may be poured out over him,” must be understood as imprecations. For elsewhere it is said thus: “Then he shall offer the living goat, and, placing both hands upon its head, confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions and sins; invoking them upon its head, he shall send it into the wilderness by a man prepared for this purpose” [Col. 1580D].

What, therefore, was the wilderness, or what was the solitude, into which Barabbas—that rejected goat—was sent, his head covered with evil prayers and dreadful imprecations? Without doubt, that solitude is the wilderness which must be understood in those words foretold by that priest: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII), preceded by such imprecations as these: “That there may come upon you all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you slew between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things shall come upon this generation” (ibid.).

Truly desolate is the house which salvation abandoned, which God abandoned, and which the Lord Jesus Christ abandoned when he was led outside and crucified beyond the city. Such prayers, or rather imprecations, “he shall invoke,” it says, “upon his head, placing both hands upon his head.” For he punished them not with one hand, nor by a single and simple judgment, but by a double judgment: namely, in this age and in the age to come, having condemned themselves by their own words: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Therefore both hands of the one invoking the curse were placed upon his head: first upon the head of Barabbas, and with him upon the people at whose request such a goat was released, bearing the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their transgressions and sins—bearing them, that is, as testimony against them that they should possess seditions by hereditary right, because they asked that the author of sedition be released to them.

[Col. 1581B] What, then, ought—or could—the man who released such a scapegoat do? And who was that man, or how was he prepared, since it is said: “He shall send it into the wilderness by a man prepared for this purpose”? “The chief priests,” says the Evangelist, “and the elders persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus.” That persuasion was the preparation; and that one man is fittingly understood as the one people, prepared by that persuasion.

What, then, ought the unclean man to do, defiled by such preparation and by contact with such a goat? “He shall wash,” it says, “his garments and his body with water, and thus enter the camp.” With what water shall he wash? Surely with the water of baptism, water mingled with blood, from Christ’s side—the one whose lot came forth for the Lord, that he might be sacrificed or offered for sins. Whoever repents because, having been persuaded, he released the scapegoat and asked that this one be slain, shall be washed with such water that he may be saved.

This too was fulfilled. “Repent,” says Peter, “and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts II). Again: “But you,” he says, “denied the Holy and Just One and asked that a murderer be granted to you, while you killed the Author of life. Repent therefore and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III). Hearing this, they were pierced in heart; first three thousand, and then five thousand, were baptized. Thus the one who, by releasing the scapegoat—that is, Barabbas—had killed the Author of life, washed the garments of his conscience and his body with water, and so entered the camp; he was added to the number of those who, believing from the beginning of the world until that hour, had been cleansed by the blood flowing from Christ’s side.

Not all acted thus; but whoever so willed was washed and entered clean into the camp of the saints. And concerning this rejected goat, sent away evilly, enough has, I think, been said for the present subject and occasion. Something must still be said about the others, which is highly delightful: namely, that only these three kinds of animals—the bull-calf, the ram, and the goat—pass beneath the shepherd’s rod. Such a shepherd was Moses himself, through whom these patterns of heavenly things were ordained. For he was feeding the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro when God called him from the bush [Col. 1582A] (Exod. III).

Look in this direction and you will find not more, but precisely the same number, of ranks among rational animals which pass beneath the rod of this good shepherd of whom we speak: for he laid down his life for his sheep and deigned to die for his flock. One rank consists of those who are gathered together and serve in lawful secular occupations; among and on account of these occupations, they may even use weapons, striking one another in opposition, like bull-calves with curved horns, yet shaking down no one, making no false accusation, and being content with their wages or just earnings (Luke III). Such persons say: “We are useless servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke XVII), because they have done precisely, and no more than, what was commanded. In their own rank they are, as bull-calves, beloved by their good shepherd.

For example, there is the young man in the Gospel who, when questioned about the commandments, replied: “Master, I have kept all these things from my youth.” “And Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “looking upon him, loved him” (Mark X). Another rank consists of those who bear no yoke of the age, nor desire the things that are of the world; indeed, they distribute to those who possess them the things that might have been their own. Like shorn rams, having laid aside their fleeces, they follow the same shepherd. They have horns indeed, but recurved ones, with which they do not pierce anyone: for if they are sometimes stirred by zeal, they direct the force of their strength not against human beings, but against human vices. Such were the Apostles; and all who strive, or have striven, to hold the way of apostolic perfection attain this rank.

The chief difference between them is this: the former merely keep the commandments; the latter have added, beyond the commandment, the observance of the counsel which says: “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all that thou hast, and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX).

The third rank consists of those who not only did not follow the counsel but did not even fulfil the commandment: like goats, who neither clothe their shepherd with their wool nor undertake his yoke in any work. Yet at length, after whatever crimes they have committed, being converted to repentance, they too receive forgiveness—provided, however, that they do not attain ecclesiastical honours or ranks, as the sacred canons reasonably determine [Col. 1582D].

Therefore, as many species of brute animals pass under the rod of a human shepherd such as Moses was, so many ranks of the elect pass beneath the hand of the supreme Shepherd, God and man. They possess certain resemblances of the kind already described; likewise the shepherds themselves, whether Jacob or the aforesaid Moses, performed certain acts in figure of Christ the good Shepherd, a fact which is scarcely unknown to some [variant: “to none,” or “to no one”].

Yet the chief difference in these matters is this: the condition of brute animals did not require their shepherd to die for them. But for these rational bull-calves, rams, and goats—that is, for all human beings—it was truly necessary that this good Shepherd should lay down his life for them and deign to die for them. They, moreover, were to die together with him when he died, in that manner by which we have already died and already risen again, as the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

This is a great difference: there, the shepherds or priests—Moses and Aaron and the rest of their lineage—did not die in the sacrifice, though the cattle were killed; but here both the Shepherd died, and all who belong to his flock necessarily died with him, as has already been said. It is exceedingly delightful to behold in this figure of the Law the sacrament both of the Shepherd dying for his flock and of the flock dying together with its Shepherd: there, only the blood of bull-calves and goats is carried into the holy places, while their bodies are burned outside the camp; but the ram alone, whole and entire, is commanded to be offered on the altar as a burnt offering [Col. 1583B].

Finally, the Lord Jesus Christ, the good Shepherd of rational animals, suffered outside the camp, that is, outside the city; and with his blood he cleansed all the earlier righteous or elect persons, and the firstfruits of penitent sinners—namely the robber who was crucified with him—as bull-calves and goats. But within, with the rams, that is, with the Apostles, on the preceding night, he himself, the true ram, after the typical supper of the Paschal lamb, offered the sacrament of his body and blood as a whole burnt offering. This is very well known to Christian, or Catholic, faith.

For this flock, dying together with its Shepherd, the law is the same and ought to be the same, as the Apostle says: “For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who walk in them” (Heb. XIII). And thereafter: “Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (ibid.). When he says these things and the rest, no one can now be ignorant or doubtful that he wishes both the Hebrews to whom he wrote and us, who have become one sheepfold with them, to go outside the camp of fleshly righteousness—the righteousness of those who serve only in foods and drinks and various baptisms, “which,” he says, “cannot make perfect the worshipper” in them (Heb. IX).

This is to be burned outside the camp, according to the likeness or imitation of this supreme bull-calf or goat who suffered outside the camp: to despise Jewish righteousnesses and submit to God’s righteousness. This is to communicate in his blood with the blood carried into the holy places: to crucify one’s flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V). Once these things have been accomplished, there also remains the offering, as it were, of the ram as a whole burnt offering: that is, not merely abstaining from unlawful things or desires, and keeping those commandments written upon the tablets by God’s finger, but also abstaining from lawful or permitted things. This was especially begun by the first holy Apostles, so that, in accordance with the very name “whole burnt offering,” their entire purpose might be a sacrifice; for *holocaustum* means “wholly burned.”

[Col. 1584A] There are still many mysteries in the chapter set forth above which pertain to the interpretation of this face, the face of the bull-calf. But because we fear becoming excessive—and weariness must be avoided even in precious matters—although omitting much, we cannot permit this point to pass untouched. It says meanwhile: “The priest shall also take of the blood of the bull-calf and sprinkle it seven times with his finger toward the propitiatory.” Elsewhere it likewise says: “When the bull-calf has been slain before the Lord, the anointed priest shall carry some of its blood into the tabernacle of testimony and, dipping his finger, sprinkle it toward the veil” (Lev. IV).

Finally, this bears greatly upon the honour of the Son of Man—to whom we have dedicated this little work—which the life-giving spirit of this sacred writing suggests to attentive observers. For why was this bull-calf slain? Why was Christ’s blood shed, except that we might receive, for the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit who rests upon him in sevenfold fullness? Therefore the blood of that significant bull-calf had to be sprinkled seven times toward the propitiatory, or toward the veil, by the priest’s finger, because the holy sevenfold Spirit could or ought to be given to us for the remission of sins only through the passion and blood of this Son of Man.

We do not say this as though patriarchs, prophets, and very many righteous persons had not received the Holy Spirit before his coming; but they did not receive this gift which is called, and is, the remission of sins. For there are two gifts of the Spirit: one is in distributions of graces, by which alone those earlier persons were enlightened; the other is in the remission of sins, and it had not been given before this gift, as the Evangelist testifies: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

Knowing this—that this gift would not be given except through his death and blood—he said on the very night on which he was betrayed: “I go to him who sent me; but because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. Yet I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John XVI). It is clearly established that he said this about his passion or death, rather than about his future ascension forty days after his resurrection; for on account of that departure, the disciples ought not to have been sorrowful but joyful, as Saint Luke records: “And they, worshipping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke XXIV).

It is altogether more correct to understand him as speaking about his passion or death: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away,” etc. This is especially so because the Evangelist had introduced the matter thus: “Before the feast day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII). Therefore that priest necessarily dipped his finger in the bull-calf’s blood and sprinkled it repeatedly toward the propitiatory or toward the veil, because it is true—and was truly said by Christ himself—that unless his blood had first been shed, [Col. 1585A] neither would the sacrament of baptism have been instituted nor would the Holy Spirit have been given in that capacity in which he is Paraclete, that is, Comforter—namely, in the capacity in which he is the forgiver or forgiveness of sins. This forgiveness is the one or supreme consolation of the saints and of all the elect [Col. 1586A], both those who preceded and those who followed, because all alike, both the former and the latter, were cleansed by his blood. Nor could the middle wall of enmity—which was signified by the veil before the propitiatory—otherwise be dissolved for them.

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 1585]

[Col. 1585A] It is delightful to hear, for thy glory and honour, O Son of Man; it is sweet to hear and understand, O glorious animal, while contemplating thy four faces, what Saint Ezekiel said when, by prophetic eyes, he saw thee beside the river Chebar: “When I looked at the living creatures, behold, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures, having four faces” (Ezek. I), etc.

This wheel is, surely, Holy Scripture, itself also having four faces. And just as the one living creature is four living creatures, so the four wheels are one wheel, because, as the sequence of prophecy itself has it, the faces of the wheels are the same as, or identical with, the faces of the living creatures. Therefore the saying is true and faithful: “When I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared,” etc. For when you, whoever you are, look upon these living creatures, then—and not before—this wheel appears to you. When, I say, you look upon or consider these often-mentioned four mysteries of the Son of Man—his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—then, and from that point onward, the meaning and aim of the Holy Scripture of the Old Covenant become visible and clear to you: it is round, revolving, perfect, and divided into four faces according to these four parts.

Of these parts, on this interpretation, the first is the book of Genesis; the second, the law of ceremonies or sacrifices; the third, the books of Kings; and the fourth, the books of the Prophets. For truly, if you carefully consider in the book of Genesis what God’s intention is directed toward, there is in this wheel the face of a man. For example, when God takes such care concerning the marriages of the fathers or patriarchs, as when Abraham says to the senior servant of his household: “Put thy hand under my thigh, that I may adjure thee by the Lord, God of heaven and earth, that thou shalt not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell” (Gen. XXIV), etc.—if in this and other similar passages you attend only to what was done and not also to the purpose of God who acted, the wheel does not appear to you; indeed, such Scripture is altogether obscure. But if you see that God was directing his purpose toward humanity—for he was directing it toward the incarnation of his Word, which he had ordained before the ages—the wheel appears: Scripture is bright, and in the wheel is the face of a man.

Likewise, in the legal ceremonies—in the sacrifice of the bull-calf, ram, and goat, and in every rite of sacrifice which God ordained through Moses—if you attend only to what was performed and not also to the intention of him who commanded these things to be done, the wheel does not appear to you; indeed, the entire letter of Scripture is cheap and contemptible. But if you see that God intended in them a figure of the passion of his incarnate Son, since it was necessary for the elect of that time to be initiated through these things, then the wheel appears to you. And in it you recognize the face of the bull-calf, which is the greatest of the animals that were sacrificed; and it is devout and honourable to recognize this face there.

Likewise, in historical deeds, in the military affairs of kings—of whom David was the first, concerning whom Wisdom says that “he played with lions as with lambs, and treated bears likewise as lambs of sheep” (Ecclus. XLVII)—and from him down to Judas Maccabaeus, of whom it is written: “He is like a lion in his deeds, and like a lion’s whelp roaring in the chase” (I Macc. III), does not this wheel have the face of a lion? For it recounts the great strength of faithful kings and leaders: as much as could or ought to suffice, as much as was required by the time and necessity, against the lions, bears, leopards, and other beasts of the devil. First, this was against the surrounding nations, of which the first and most enduring was the nation of the Philistines; then against the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Medes, Macedonians, or Greeks, through whom the devil laboured to uproot the tree fruitful in eternal fruit and to destroy the people from whom Christ was to be born, according to God’s promise, confirmed by an oath to Abraham (Gen. XV, XXII) and by an oath to David (Ps. LXXXVIII, CXXXI).

[Col. 1586C] Thus this third face of the wheel, that is, of Holy Scripture, is rightly called and is the face of a lion. In the Prophets, assuredly, you most rightly receive the fourth face of the wheel: the face of the flying eagle. That portion of Holy Scripture flies on high and fixes the open eyes of its entire intention upon the true sun, not only signifying him by deeds but also, what is greater, declaring in words the majesty of his divinity.

Therefore: “When I looked,” he says, “at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures, [having] four faces of a man” (Ezek. I): that is, when I believed and firmly held that God the Son of God truly became man, truly suffered or died, truly rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, then the Holy Scripture of the Old Covenant became intelligible to me, containing these things and wholly tending toward these four mysteries. Otherwise it would have remained closed and hidden from me, as it remains even now to all those who do not look upon these living creatures, especially the Jews, who do not receive and refuse to recognize these mysteries of our salvation. Hence the Apostle says: “Even unto this day the same veil of the Old Testament remains unrevealed, because in Christ it is abolished” (II Cor. III).
