We have learned by experience and, with thanksgiving, testify as persons who have experienced it that what he says next is true: “When the living creatures walked, the wheels beside them likewise walked; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together. And wherever the spirit went, there, as the spirit went, the wheels were likewise lifted up, following it; for the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. I). This, I say, is as it is said to be: we not only believe it, but see it ourselves with our own eyes.

Formerly, before the living creatures walked and were lifted up, the wheels neither walked nor were lifted up from the earth; rather, they were enclosed within Judaea alone. For the Scriptures had not been published in more than one language, namely Hebrew; and there, because they were not understood, they lay, as it were, upon the earth. Finally, except for a very few who possessed the grace of the prophetic Spirit, the Hebrews themselves did not know that the spirit of life was in the wheels, that beneath the literal structure there lay the power of heavenly ministry.

But now we ourselves see that these wheels walked and continue to walk from the time when the living creatures began to walk. We see that the Holy Scripture of the Old Covenant emerged from the narrow bounds of the land of Judaea, from the recesses of the Hebrew language, and walked even into the midst of the nations. Wherever the Gospel of the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ is preached or has been preached, there it is present beside it, so that whatever the Gospel says concerning these matters, ready testimony at once responds that it was necessary for these things to happen thus; and that the Messiah whom the Jews themselves awaited could not otherwise come, walk, or proceed than this Son of Man from Nazareth—this Jesus, son of Mary, “who was thought to be the son of Joseph” (Luke III)—came, walked, and proceeded.

In this there is something very remarkable and wonderfully provided by God: those who are enemies of these living creatures themselves turn these wheels beside them throughout the world. The Jews, who oppose and wish to oppose the often-mentioned four mysteries, carry in captivity among all nations the Scriptures written in their own, that is Hebrew, language as a testimony to the truth; and thus, even unwillingly, they affirm that it was so written and that it was necessary for it to happen thus.

Let us therefore proceed upon the journey begun, amid the ebbings and flowings of the running wheels which follow these living creatures, amid the voices of the creatures’ wings passing toward one another; from them we heard a great sound of commotion: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place” (Ezek. III). For this glory and this honour—the glory by which and the honour with which the Son of Man has been glorified and honoured—are the object of our devout attention in the present work.

[Col. 1587D] But what are you doing, my soul? As I perceive it, you are weary, and in proceeding you are beginning, as it were, to fall asleep. Say therefore to these living creatures, or to this one living creature having four faces; say to the spirit of life which is in the wheels: “My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me in thy words” (Ps. CXVIII).

You, Cuno—often spoken of and often to be spoken of by me, venerable bishop of the Church of Regensburg—have provided the cause of this weariness, and from you has arisen the occasion of the difficulty in which my mind now wavers and almost fluctuates in its course. Nearly three years ago, when you marvelled and wished to know, I had told you by what circumstance it came about that, after so many holy Catholic and most famous Fathers, whose writings had sufficiently filled the libraries of Christ’s churches, I, the *peripsēma* [“offscouring”] of all, should set my mind to writing so copiously and, as you were accustomed to say, so effectively or usefully that you could not doubt that this was God’s gift (I Cor. IV), and that this ability too is from above and has come down “from the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift and every perfect present” (Jas. I).

The ease of my manner of life increased your astonishment: namely, because you saw in me almost none of those preparations of the holy Fathers by which those intending to labour in studies of this kind successfully prepared themselves—as ministers of God, in the words of the blessed Apostle, in watchings, fastings (II Cor. VI), and other good practices. By employing these, the human understanding is accustomed to be made clear, so that one may deserve to proceed with right perception through the holy and venerable Scriptures of truth.

I had therefore told you the reasons, more talkative than a child, more timid than a hare, although I knew and was certain that there was nothing to fear from you. For you are utterly unlike those persons to whom what is fragrant often smells most offensive; the boy Joseph first experienced the excessively hostile and terrible eyes of such persons when he told them all his matters (Gen. XXXVII). Having heard the reasons, you, a man of simple eye and wholly luminous body, said: “Write these things for me.” When I utterly refused, you repeated and demanded again and again that I write them. And when you obtained nothing by bare entreaty, you cast around my neck an exceedingly great and strong bond by which to draw me: namely, an adjuration by the holy and dreadful Name: “By the Father,” you said, “and the Son and the Holy Spirit, I command you to write these things for me.”

I do not fail to understand, my father and lord, from what root or fountain of love such great and vehement insistence proceeded, by which you are ever eager to commend our little works to all whom you can: you are a man who has forgotten envy and who can say with blessed Job, “For compassion grew up with me from my infancy, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb” (Job XXXI). You judge that knowledge or remembrance of those matters which you so urgently compel me to write contributes somewhat to the commendation of my writings; and for their sake, when I refused, as I have said, you were so very urgent an exactor that you even employed an adjuration.

At last, therefore, because obedience is required by reverence for the Lord’s name, I shall recall my groans and divine consolation. I shall have as my model one of the orthodox Fathers, blessed Jerome, who, though he had already many detractors or was to have them, did not fear to write how great the concern of the heavenly Majesty had been for him: it drove him, beaten with stripes, from the study of secular books and compelled him to the study of the Holy Scriptures, to the benefit, as is now apparent, of all Christ’s churches throughout the world.

First I shall state this truth: the ability which you thus embrace and for which you congratulate me is a consolation from the merciful God, according to the good pleasure of his wisdom. After saying, “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments and alter the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. XXXI), it immediately adds: “Give strong drink to those who are sorrowful, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their pain no more” (ibid.).

For I was sorrowful and walked with a bitter spirit as a boy or young man. To state briefly the cause of this sorrow and bitterness, I say that I sat beside the river Chebar (Ezek. I). For this passage was then in my hands as I treated the four living creatures, or the four faces of the one living creature. That glorious living creature itself knows, and the spirit of life which is or was in the wheels knows, that when, at the beginning of this eleventh book, *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, this passage presented itself, I did not then intend on this occasion to turn aside here and obey you in a matter which I feared might be suspected of presumption and vain glory.

But when I had reached the aforesaid passage and, after contemplating the face of the bull-calf, wished to proceed to contemplate the third face, namely that of the lion, remembrance of you came upon me more insistently and vehemently than I had ever felt it occur before. It held me, as it were, by the hand and in some manner said to me: “Turn aside here; for unless you first accomplish the matter concerning which you were so adjured, you will nowhere be able to use your customary ability so as to proceed suitably.”

Why say more? As though the spirit which guided—or seemed to guide—me had stopped, I was compelled to turn aside here from the intended course; nevertheless, I was very changeable and for a long time uncertain, at one moment approving and at another disapproving this digression. At last it scarcely settled in my mind, and it seemed not too far removed from the will of Wisdom if I wrote how, and for what purpose, he gave me, in my sorrow and lamentation over such poverty, his strong drink and his wine: namely, present consolation from the Holy Scriptures, by which I might for a little while forget my pain.

Therefore I sat, as I have said, beside the river of great Babylon, beside the river Chebar, which is interpreted “heaviness” or “weight.” For I speak of that Babylon, whose king or prince—the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar, namely the devil—exercised tyranny within it and imposed his heavy yoke even upon the children of the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Having enclosed them all in Adam, he carried them captive into this his Babylon, into this evil age: subject to original sin and guilty of death.

This, O Lemuel, was the cause of my great sorrow and bitter spirit. For with intellectual hearing I heard the voices of exiles or captives lamenting and saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. CXXXVI). Taking up mourning in the hidden places of the inner person, I too wept everywhere and knowingly lamented; and in lamenting I praised, as Ecclesiastes teaches, the dead more than the living (Eccles. IV).

For those dead who have died in the Lord have attained the security of their own state, having returned to that blessed Zion from which all fell through Adam’s sin and whose remembrance made them weep while they were captives. But how can the living, so long as they are in the body and are absent from the Lord (II Cor. V), be secure? For there is no safe sitting or firm standing beside the river Chebar, or beside Babylon’s other rivers, especially since the Apostle too says: “Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X). The riverbanks themselves are muddy, marshy, and so slippery that you must always fear lest, when your foot is moved or slips, you fall into the river beneath.

Therefore, as I have already said, I praised the dead more than the living—not with any ordinary praise, but with groaning and mournful praise—as though I already feared that what is said in the Gospel had happened to me: “Two shall be in a bed; one shall be taken, and the other left” (Matt. 24). Or, to speak with this comparison according to our own number: three are born from one womb; two shall be taken and one left. “I alone am left,” he said, “and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19); and with words such as these I often repeated a mournful song.

What had happened to me already—by what words may I dare to express it? “When I was in the midst of the captives”—this is the seer of the heavenly living creatures, whom I had just recalled—when I was in the midst of the captives, “by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God,” and so forth, as far as “the likeness of a man was among them” (Ezek. 1). But what here resembles that event? Yet, having recognized—and already in part touched upon—the likeness between this great Babylon in which we are all born together, and that Babylon in which he was then captive with the captives, I am pleased, though with fear, to use language close to his: for my eyes were opened, and I saw the Son of God; awake, I saw the Son of Man himself living upon the cross.

I did not see with bodily sight. Rather, so that I might see, the eyes of my body suddenly disappeared and better eyes—that is, inner eyes—were opened, while I held and embraced in my bosom a wooden cross and upon it the image of the same Savior. I was sitting concealed behind the holy altar in a certain oratory of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, at clear dawn. I chose that image with many kisses, went around it, kissed it, and adored it—as I was accustomed to do—with frequent bows of my head. I was accustomed to do this, but at that dawn I did it with greater contrition, that is, humility of mind.

What was the sight of his countenance? Human speech cannot comprehend it in words. I will say only this: there I briefly perceived how truly he himself says, “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11), and how truly the Apostle says of him, “He was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5). In a wondrous and ineffable manner his countenance lowered itself, showing how reverently it received the kisses of the worshipper and the worship of the one kissing him.

There was no delay: I returned to ordinary sight and replaced the cross upon the altar in its proper place. Yet for some time that day an ineffable taste—the taste of his sweetness—remained in the mouth of my soul. Gradually it receded and at last failed, but it still makes me remember this verse: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33).

And what wonder is it if Truth spoke truly: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5), and if the Paraclete—that is, the consoling Spirit—deigns already in this world to give the first fruits of consolation to his little children? For little children, that is, the weak and feeble who mourn on account of their very weakness, have the greatest need of consolation. Hence the Lord himself, when he commanded that the joy and festival-day of his holy city Jerusalem be celebrated, said among other things in Isaiah: “Their children shall be carried upon shoulders and comforted upon knees. As a mother comforts her children, so will I comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted” (Isa. 66). It is well known that, although a mother loves all her children, she nevertheless gives herself more readily and eagerly to consoling her crying little child: she carries him upon her shoulder or in her arms, and comforts him upon her knees.

I shall therefore tell, giving thanks, what consolation he afterward granted me while I persevered in that above-mentioned—and shared by no one—lament of the captives saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136). What if someone who reads this despises it? Today no one despises the *Confessions* of blessed Augustine—that is, the books in which he confesses the Lord’s mercies. Perhaps while he himself was living, some reader did not think highly of them. Let us therefore take courage, since you, my Father, bishop beloved by Christ, promised that you would keep these matters more privately [Col. 1591C].

Indeed, if someone should seize upon and read these things, and think that I am to be despised as boastful, let him hear me say concerning these small matters what the Apostle said concerning his truly great ones: “For if I should wish,” he says, “to boast, I should not be foolish; for I shall speak the truth” (2 Cor. 12). [The supplied text cites 1 Corinthians 2; the quoted passage is 2 Corinthians 12:6.] In such a consciousness of truth there is, finally, no small consolation.

About the same time, with good hope, I fled to invoke the name of the Lord—the name invoked over us and in which we are sealed—and I invoked and adored the holy Trinity, with a supplicating invocation and faithful adoration. “The name of the Lord,” says Wisdom, “is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted. The wealth of the rich man is the city of his strength, and as a strong wall surrounding him” (Prov. 18). For I felt invisible enemies pursuing me; and therefore at morning prayer I ran to that name, that, like a most strong tower, it might raise me up; like a city of strength, fortify me; and like a strong wall, surround me. And this it began to do; I hope that it will complete it.

At the same time I saw a memorable vision, full of venerable sweetness, on the following occasion. I was sorrowful, and at the usual hour of that prayer or adoration which I have described, I gave myself to sleep. The cause of my sorrow was that peace had not come to me as quickly, nor as fully, as I wished, against the malicious beings rising up against me—as though, while we live, we could ever be safe or secure, when rather “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7), in which, if we contend lawfully, we surely strike and are sometimes struck.

Thus, sorrowful like a child whose will is not immediately done, I gave myself to sleep at the usual hour of prayer. And behold, half awake upon my bed, I saw a great light, like the sun, resting over me, and I heard the signal sounding in church, as happens when we are summoned at the appointed time to prayer. I seemed to rise and run to prayer. Let it be done to me according to the voices or words which I heard: one assembly of many people whom I did not know sang in one part of the church the fiftieth Psalm, “Have mercy upon me, O God,” while another assembly in another part of the church sang the twenty-sixth Psalm, “The Lord is my light.” A malicious adversary stood against me in a corner at the entrance to the oratory. When I saw him, I reproached him, as we usually reproach some phantom-like apparition with a gesture of the whole face rather than with words. Because of this, he rushed angrily upon me, and I awoke from that light sleep.

I could understand that these things occurred for my consolation. Yet I spent the entire day also in sorrow; and at the dawn—or hour before dawn—of the next day, omitting the prayer I was accustomed to make, I returned myself to sleep in sadness. Then behold: while lightly sleeping, it seemed likewise, as on the day before, that the signal was sounded for prayer. I rose and ran to the church. And behold, as though for a solemn feast of the Lord, a great crowd of various orders filled the church, especially monks, while a bishop of venerable white hair celebrated the solemnities of the Mass.

A great procession of venerable persons of both sexes came forward to make the offering, as though after the Gospel, when the holy sacrifice is usually offered. I too ran forward, as though to ask alms from those offerings. And behold, near the right side of the altar stood three persons, of an appearance most reverend and a dignity which no tongue can attain in words. Two persons were very old—that is, their heads were very white-haired. The third stood as a beautiful youth, of royal dignity, as could be recognized from his clothing.

One of the persons, as I said, of venerable white hair, with very gracious condescension and a serene countenance, took my hand, kissed me, and spoke a few words. I did not retain them in memory, but I know that they concerned the office or ministry of writing. That royal person, that beautiful youth, said nothing; yet he looked upon me as a brother—with what genuine affection, with what reverence and majesty—with a quiet and modest countenance, and penetrated my inmost heart with his gaze.

Not immediately, but afterward, I recognized that the holy Trinity was present in these three persons and that the youth was the Son of God, in this manner. Certain evil spirits, standing around me on either side before the altar, began to harass me—who was taller than those little beings—and to dig at my sides with troublesome little fingers. While they afflicted me thus, and I begged help from those whom I saw, the Lord Jesus, who had withdrawn a little way, though so that I could still see him, made himself known to me by name. The other persons said: “Wait a little; Jesus will come at once and help you” [Col. 1593A].

Hearing this, I invoked the Lord Jesus himself by name. Without delay he ascended again by the steps down which he had descended, as though with authority and reverend majesty. Powerfully driving away those spirits and swiftly tearing their hands from my sides, he freed me. Then those same three persons, equal in great and equal stature, stood around me, opened a very large book, and lifted me, placed upon that book, aloft. When this was done, he who had kissed me at the beginning spoke, graciously and familiarly strengthening me: “Do not fear.” Pointing to certain gold-worked shrines or reliquaries of saints upon the holy altar, which we commonly call *feretra*, he said: “You shall still be better than these are.”

This vision was so manifest that I can truly say, “Whether in the body or out of the body I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12). Yet this matter bears no comparison with the greatness of him who says that “he was caught up even to the third heaven, that he was caught up into paradise, and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to speak” (ibid.). For when I was being led to see these things, I know that I leapt from my bed and ran into the church by the straight and usual path, in the ordinary manner of one awake. When the vision was complete, I wished to follow the departing persons, but was not permitted. I saw that I was naked and without any clothing; hastening back from there to where I had come from, as soon as I touched the bed, I immediately awoke.

There is no need, beloved, for me to interpret for you the opening of the book or the statement of that person when he showed the golden memorials or reliquaries of the saints. Many have often heard and followed your judgment concerning me: that God truly opened his book to me—that is, Holy Scripture—and that I have said things somewhat better than many sayings of the holy Fathers, whose memory is deservedly celebrated in the holy Church and shines like gold. What shall I say next?

“If he scourges,” says blessed Job, “let him kill once for all, and let him not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent” (Job 9). I recall this saying now because, at the same time, he in some manner laughed at my punishment—that is, my expectation, which to my impatient mind seemed excessively long. I do not charge this against him. For I had long since forgiven him, namely with that most just forgiveness which blessed Job himself expresses in these words: “Let him loose his hand and cut me off; and let this be my consolation: that, while afflicting me with pain, he does not spare me, and that I do not contradict the words of the Holy One” (Job 6).

He certainly required from me such forgiveness—which is not to contradict the words of the Holy One, not to blame the judgments of the Holy One and Just One—when I grieved more than usual and wept more abundantly for the same reason, namely weariness of the present life, and for almost three days my countenance did not change. For I saw him sitting behind the holy altar, in such form or appearance that he ought truly to be called the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7). When I came nearer, he bore an enormous cross, the sign of great sorrow, and, stretching out his right hand, said, as the most merciful Father, friend of our nature, meek and humble: “Friend, forgive me what I have done to you.”

Immediately, with my hand, as a pledge of forgiveness, I struck his hand—how vehemently, how gladly! He grasped it firmly and drew my whole self, as it were, to embraces and kisses. But there was no delay: a great force of some holy and divine delight shook me from sleep.

Do these things seem childish? On the contrary, it is a very serious matter to forgive him whatever grievous thing he has brought upon us—all things whose beginning or sum was this: “Because thou hast heard the voice of thy wife and hast eaten of the tree of which I commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat, cursed is the earth in thy work,” and so forth, as far as, “Because thou art dust, and unto dust thou shalt return” (Gen. 3). Whatever evils he has brought upon us because of sin must surely be forgiven him, by heart and mouth saying something such as Daniel or the other fellow-captives said: “All that thou hast done to us, O Lord, thou hast done in true judgment, because we have sinned against thee” (Dan. 3).

Above all, it belongs to love and faith not to die patiently, but to live patiently in this world full of sins, and to follow the will of the Creator who disposes all things well, when one desiring to be dissolved is not quickly heard, longing to depart from this vale of tears to the joy of the vision of God.

I did forgive, therefore. Yet among the other things concerning which you adjured me, my Father, I shall tell how he laughed at my punishment and finally consoled me. A man of venerable appearance seemed to stand before me, looking at me familiarly. “You shall live,” he said, “for another eight years.” When I seemed to think that he had said this in jest, he repeated the same words: “I speak the truth: you shall live for another eight years.”

That night was the solemn feast of blessed Matthew the Apostle, upon whose Gospel foundation you required me to construct the present work, the work *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*. When I wished to kiss his holy hands, he did not permit it; repulsed in this way, I awoke. What do you think—how I counted for myself the following days, months, and years? For I understood it thus, and wanted him to have said it thus, as though he had entirely determined it and said: “You shall live eight years, and no more.”

Because of the excessive haste of my desiring mind, I did not consider—and did not wish to consider—that there might be something in which I erred, while the truth of the vision remained intact. Nor did I reflect upon Cassius, bishop of Narnia, to whom, as blessed Pope Gregory relates, the Lord gave this command through his priest: “Do what you are doing; work at what you are working; let not your foot cease, let not your hand cease. On the feast-day of the Apostles you shall come to me, and I will repay your reward.” [Note: [Col. 1593D] St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. IV, ch. 56, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVII, Migne ed.]

While he was still alive, the feast-day of the Apostles was approaching. He was therefore anxious then; likewise in the second or third year, he hung in expectation of death; and similarly in the fourth, fifth, and sixth. Who could despair of the truth of the revelation, when behold, in the seventh year, on the vigils of the awaited feast-day, a mild fever touched him, and “on the feast-day itself, after he had completed the solemnities of the Mass and received the mysteries of the sacred communion, he departed from the body”? [Note: [Col. 1595D] St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. IV, ch. 56, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVII, Migne ed.]

If it is permitted to compare small things with great, I too, like him, was swifter in feeling or understanding than the saying of the vision itself warranted. For just as he had not been told in full: “On the feast-day of the Apostles of the present year you shall come to me,” so neither had it been said to me that, immediately upon the completion of eight years, I was to end this life.

Thus seven years passed for me, and the eighth year had begun to run its course. With great expectation and almost continual meditation upon death, being almost wholly turned inward and more wakeful than usual, I began to wonder what was happening to me and how I ought to conduct myself in expectation of so great a matter. At that time I held in my hands the book of blessed Augustine, *The City of God*. This was the passage I was reading: “But since, under the daily accidents of this life, innumerable deaths in some sense threaten every mortal, so long as it is uncertain which of them will come, I ask whether it is better to suffer one by dying, or to fear them all by living.” [Note: [Col. 1596D] St. Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. I, ch. 11, *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, Migne ed.] And so forth.

On the occasion of this reading, I then examined my heart more intently, praising with Ecclesiastes the dead more than the living (Eccles. 4), as I have said above. Sighing, I formed this resolve: that I would seek from God, through attentive prayers, the truth or certainty of so great a matter, so that if the aforementioned vision had come from him, his graciousness might deign to confirm it for me through a repeated oracle.

For this task, it entered my mind to invoke the Holy Spirit. Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one substance, one divinity, and inseparable operation, nevertheless, just as the creation of man is the Father’s proper work, and redemption the Son’s proper work, so the illumination of this same man, the grace of revelations, and the distribution of all graces are the proper work of the Holy Spirit. Therefore I turned to him with my whole heart, and in so great a matter dared to address him. Yet there came before me and struck back the face of my mind that word in Isaiah, where the Lord, after saying, “Do not cease crying; raise thy voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their wickedness and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58), immediately adds: “For they seek me day by day and desire to know my ways, as though they were a nation that had done righteousness and had not forsaken the judgment of their God” (ibid.).

For it does not belong to all to seek the answers of the Lord, which were then dispensed through prophets, but only to those who exercise judgment and practice righteousness. Yet confidence in this was afforded me not only by common faith, but also by a certain personal conscience—or remembrance of the graciousness of the same Holy Spirit—because in those days I sometimes felt his visitation or regard in whatever ways. Concerning these matters restraint is appropriate, especially since the great Apostle also says: “But I refrain, lest anyone should think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears something from me” (2 Cor. 12).

Yet since up to this point I have spoken particularly on account of that common vision of the three persons—of the person who appeared to be the Father, and of the person of the Son, and how they comforted my sorrow—it seems fitting that I should also relate a vision, no less delightful, concerning the third person, the Holy Spirit. Whatever judgment anyone may make of this narrative, perhaps the kindness of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit receives it as thanksgiving, since God is accustomed to require thanksgiving from a human being for his benefits. For example, the Lord says: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found who returned to give glory to God except this foreigner?” (Luke 17).

I shall therefore tell it. Once I was lying in bed, not deeply asleep—indeed half awake—and behold, as it seemed, I had descended the steps of the brothers’ dormitory. Camps of many horrible spirits, cruel in face, stood arrayed against me. Since I had often been accustomed, even in sleep when some terror came upon me, to utter the name of the Holy Spirit, I deigned to say nothing else against them, but cast this name alone before their hideous faces: “Holy Spirit.” I call him himself to witness: driven backward as by a great whirlwind, they nearly fell on their backs, unable to endure the power of the name.

When I mocked them for this and, pausing a little in the utterance of the holy name, reproached them by a gesture of my whole face, they seemed to recover their strength from anger and rushed upon me as powerful men. I turned to flee into the meadow enclosed among the columns. There I found an ancient old man carrying a rod in his hand, and I recognized the Holy Spirit, calling out, “Little son, little son”—the name by which we are accustomed to call the little ones whom we have received from the sacred font—and strengthening me by that address with the gesture alike of one powerful and one helping, so that though a camp should stand against me, my heart would not fear; though battle should rise against me, in this I would hope (Ps. 26).

[Col. 1596D] Strengthened, therefore, I ran back from where I had come against those most hideous phalanxes. Having engaged them in the same way and order as before, and as the conflict grew heavier, I again fled to my patron. I called upon him for aid, repeating the cry of address just as someone calls upon the person who received him from the font. And behold, he was found in the same place—not as before, an ancient old man, but a very serene fire. Around him were great calm and security, so that, forgetting the whole adversity as though it had never existed, I attended only to that fire with lowered gaze and wished to behold it with the eyes of my inner self fixed intently upon it.

But he made for himself, as it were, a little shelter from himself, raising two veils on either side in the form of wings. As they gradually came together, they returned me, as though weaned, to ordinary consciousness from that contemplation. I was not ignorant of the interpretation: what the appearance of fire meant, and what the appearance of an old man comforting his godchild meant. For he is the author for us of holy regeneration in baptism; and he is the fire which our Lord Jesus Christ sent upon the earth and vehemently desired to be kindled (Luke 12).

I therefore joyfully confessed both things in the prayer or hymn which I then composed about him, in these words:

> As he was willing to die, so he teaches us also to die with him,  
> while, still living, he buries us in water,  
> O wondrous craftsman.  
>
> In place of a three-day burial,  
> a threefold immersion takes place:  
> that one may be buried as dead,  
> and emerge as rising again.  
>
> O God, with our ears we have heard;  
> our fathers have told us the work which you performed  
> (Ps. 43), when you proceeded in fiery tongues  
> from the throne of God,  
> that earth might become heaven,  
> that human beings might become gods (Acts 2).

But now let us return to the matter for which I included this account as well. The remembrance of the gift of that same Holy Spirit, by which he had sometimes gladdened my conscience, gave me confidence in those days through such visitations, as I said: that he might deign to confirm the vision for me through a repeated oracle, if it had come from him—the vision in which I had been told, “You shall live another eight years”—because seven years had passed and one remained.

For I was wearied, as Wisdom says in the Proverbs: “Hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13). Therefore, that what follows might happen to me—“Desire, when it comes, is a tree of life” (ibid.), and again, “Desire, if it is fulfilled, delights the soul” (ibid.)—I turned, as I said, to entreat the Holy Spirit concerning this matter. I dare to say that I did this like a stag, according to the faithful soul’s saying in the Psalm: “As the stag longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41).

For then my tears were my bread day and night (ibid.); for three days my countenance did not change (1 Sam. 1); and with wonderful intentness, thinking nothing or little about merits—which were none—I wrestled with your name, O Holy Spirit, resting upon faith. And I made a vow to you that I would render you everlasting thanksgiving for the benefit of obtaining so great an answer. And was this frivolous? For what else shall we do there? All who pass there pass “to the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 50). Elsewhere, after the Psalmist had said, “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel” (Ps. 121), as though you were asking why they go up there, he says: “To confess the name of the Lord” (ibid.).

Therefore I rejoice, O Lord, Holy Spirit, because I struggled thus—namely, by prayer and tears. For this was Jacob’s struggle (Gen. 32): to weep and to ask, according to the truth of prophetic Scripture. After the prophet Hosea had said, “And in his strength he was directed with the angel, and prevailed over the angel and was strengthened,” he immediately expressed the manner of his strength, adding: “He wept and entreated him” (Hos. 12).

I rejoice, I say, because I did not let you go unless you blessed me, and you blessed me in this manner. It was the night before the day which Christian religion calls the beginning of the fast, when heads are solemnly sprinkled with ashes, in a wholesome correction of that sin of the first parent by which he sought to be like God, though he was earth and ashes. While I slept lightly, I seemed to be talking with a friend. He asked what I ought to do, and why I so urgently persisted in seeking or finding such a thing. I replied that it was—as indeed it is—a great matter. Though I desired it, because of the many dangers of sins which occur here, I nevertheless knew that greater efforts were needed in order to prepare myself in some measure to depart.

When I had said such things, suddenly, having moved a little away from the one with whom I was speaking, I saw what seemed like heaven opening slightly above. From it there was swiftly lowered, faster than speech, as though a shining talent of ineffable, living substance. It fell into my breast, and by its magnitude or weight immediately shook me from sleep—heavier than gold, sweeter than honey.

When it had entered [read *illapsum*, not *elapsum*], at first it rested for a short while and held itself free from every motion, while I too lay still, perhaps on my back, awaiting the outcome of the event. Then it began to move about the womb of the inner man, the womb of the soul, whose capacity and extent I had not previously known. In a wonderful way, therefore, the living thing—true life—moved in circuits; and every following circuit was greater and much broader than the preceding one. Though many such circuits occurred, I did not think to count them.

In a wondrous and ineffable manner the inundations moved in circuits, one after another, and poured themselves in, until at last the final infusion, like a great overflowing river, made me understand and feel that the entire receptacle of the soul or heart was full and could contain no more. When this was done, it rested again for a little while: neither flowing in, as it had done, nor flowing out, as it afterward did. Meanwhile the inner man wished, as it were, to see more clearly the face of that living substance; but it somehow hid itself, so that its face could not be seen, though it was borne with very great weight and felt with great sweetness.

After it began to turn back and, making its circuits in another direction like a river, flowed out through the left side, the eyes of the inner man saw that, as the final circuit flowed forth, it paused a little. And behold, I saw that this most beautiful substance was like liquid gold.

When this had occurred and the sensation of that event had passed, not knowing what would happen next, I grieved only because he had said nothing according to my intention. For I would have received it as the greatest benefit of grace if he had said: “This year, as you expected, you are to depart from the body!” [Col. 1599A]

Behold, in this I obeyed the name of the Lord, by which you adjured me, venerable bishop, lover of the glory of the Lord’s name: namely, that I should write to you what I had immediately related orally—gladly and more privately, to your ears willing to hear the works of the Lord—how I received this capacity in Holy Scripture, concerning which you never wished to doubt that it came from the grace or Spirit of God.

And truly I dare to know and confess that it is a gift of the Most High for the consolation of my sorrow, of which I have spoken. Having received it, my soul no longer found in itself an impulse to entreat him concerning such a matter, or to hurry as before to seize the evening of this day, the end of this life. For it admitted the consideration that something must first be worked before a reward is demanded, since material for such works has been given even to us little ones.

Thus I was consoled, and the hope which he gave me in his word “comforted me in my humiliation” (Ps. 118), so that I do not doubt that what Christ, the Son of God and giver of that same hope, said happened to me: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7).

That Scripture, after saying: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well. Let your fountains be carried abroad, and divide your waters in the streets. Have them for yourself alone, and let no strangers share them” (Prov. 5)—by which saying it teaches us both to learn and to teach in the unity of faith, and to hold no understanding of Holy Scripture together with heretics—adds: “Let your vein be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth” (ibid.).

For this is what it means to me to rejoice with the wife of my youth: to have consolation in every study or exercise of Holy Scripture. This is that woman, Wisdom, to whom the Wise Man said: “You are my sister” (Prov. 7), and Prudence, whom he called his friend (ibid.). This is that woman whom you saw in a dream—if you remember—that I had taken as my wife, while you embraced the children born to me from her. And this indeed you do whenever you gladly read my writings and never wish to be without my books.

Now hear with what words Wisdom immediately afterward delights and rejoices with those who rejoice with such a wife, such a youth: “A most dear hind,” she says, “and a most pleasing fawn. Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, and delight continually in her love” (Prov. 5).

I shall not pass over what beginning I made and what first voice I uttered after that inundation of the river which I have described, when I wrote a little book of hymns in praise of the Holy Spirit. Listen attentively, as is your custom:

> For the great river which I poured out for the thirsty,  
> a forsaken, crucified rock—  
> thanks to Christ, because he made the city  
> glad:
>
> Here the poor man, who had neither silver  
> nor gold, drinks wine and an abundance  
> of milk. Hasten, all of you:  
> grace pours it out freely.
>
> Gladly let the pious voice of joy offer him  
> a sacrifice of praise. What better thing could I desire  
> than to take the cup of salvation  
> and fulfill my vows?
>
> Only govern my mind, O Holy Spirit;  
> fill heart and open mouth from what is yours—  
> you who command us to strike the festive timbrel  
> or to take up the psalm.
>
> Holiest of the holy, Divinity of divinities,  
> joy, light, medicine, life:  
> to you be praise with the Father and with the Son,  
> gracious Spirit. Amen.

[Textual note on the opening stanza: the transmitted wording is grammatically uncertain. It prints *fudi*, “I poured out,” and *petra deserta crucifixa*, “a forsaken, crucified rock”; these are retained rather than silently changing the verb to “he poured out” or treating *deserta* as an unexpressed “in the desert.”]

Thus beginning, I was turning over within myself a great body of matter, unable to issue abundantly through a narrow opening, while, binding words in metrical feet as I had been accustomed to do in the schools, I bestowed a long labor upon few utterances. For that saying of Wisdom which I mentioned above had not yet fully come to pass for me: [Col. 1600B] “May your spring be blessed” (Prov. 5); that is, I had not yet received the order of priesthood, though I might have received it. Yet it is written: “The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. 2). Therefore, as I suppose—and as I afterward learned by experience—I was meanwhile deferred for this purpose: that I might first stand in this rank, and only then receive the lawful opening of my mouth for expounding the sacred Scriptures according to the usage of the Church.

For so long a time discord had vexed the Church of Christ because of the schism of the Apostolic See; after the authors of it had died, it had nevertheless subsided a little. Because of that schism, and for other reasons also, many men—even those who seemed especially devout and who loved ecclesiastical purity—avoided their bishops when receiving orders. [Col. 1600C] They did so, indeed, with a single eye; but discernment is necessary in all things. For as long as the branch remains in the vine, it can bear fruit; but once it has been cut off and cast outside, it can no longer bear fruit (John 15). So likewise any minister of Christ’s sacraments in the Church: as long as he remains in the assembly of the whole body, whatever he administers is valid; but once he has been declared by lawful judgment to be cut off or condemned, whatever he may afterward seem to perform can indeed have the appearance of godliness, but cannot possess its power.

I too, with a simple intention, avoided those ordainers who were under ill repute. And therefore, as I have said, although certain younger men had already been ordained before me, I had not yet received priestly orders; [Col. 1600D] and perhaps, for the reason I have mentioned, this also was within me [read: *inerat*, “was present”]: I did not consider myself worthy.

But the Lord and Father of the wedding-feast came—and I shall not pass over how he came—he who called us to the wedding and said to me what he says to one reclining in the lowest place: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14). I was full, and went full, to my bed with long meditations, such as sometimes delighted me—indeed, often exercised me—and in which my spirit failed while pondering the days of old and keeping in mind the eternal years (Ps. 76), namely, that he who created and redeemed us would at last judge us in a fearful judgment. My fearful soul longed, if some opportunity might be granted, to anticipate that coming of the Judge; and I meditated in my heart how I might go before him and speak with him more privately. [Col. 1601A] The sum of those thoughts, as I remember, is expressed in these words of blessed Job:

> “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my wound is heavier than my groaning. Who will grant me that I may know and find him, and come even to his throne? I will set judgment before him and fill my mouth with reproaches, that I may know the words which he will answer me and understand what he says to me.”  
> (Job 23)

When, as I have said, I went to bed with thoughts of this kind, my sleep, as I slept, proved sweet to me in the following manner. I saw myself standing before the altar; upon it, in the middle, stood the Lord’s cross, [Col. 1601B] and upon it the image of the Lord and Savior. Looking more closely at him, I recognized the Lord Jesus himself there, crucified and living, with his eyes open upon me. When I perceived this, I immediately bowed my face and said to him: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23).

With what humility, with what reverent inclination of his head, he received this greeting I cannot at all express, except only this: the inward person who beholds it might in some measure perceive how truly he says of himself, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). Nor was this enough for me unless I might take him in my hands and kiss him in an embrace. But what was I to do? The altar itself was too high for me to reach him.

[Col. 1601C] Yet he himself willed what I thought or desired. For I perceived that he willed it; and at the nod of his will the altar itself opened in the middle and received me as I ran within. When I had hastened inside, I took hold of him whom my soul loves; I held him, embraced him, and kissed him long. I sensed how gravely he received this gesture of love, when, while I kissed him, he himself opened his mouth so that I might kiss more deeply. Clearly this was being done, this was being prepared by that signification, so that what the beloved in the Song of Songs desires might come to pass:

> “Who will give you to me as a brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I might find you outside and kiss you, and now no one will despise me? I will take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me; [Col. 1601D] there you will teach me, and I shall give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine from my pomegranates.”  
> (Song of Songs 8)

Thereafter something came to me in accordance with the sense of words such as these. When I had returned to myself and, during the watches of the night, most sweetly reconsidered such a vision, interpreting the opening of the altar and of the very mouth of the Lord Jesus to mean that I ought henceforth to understand more clearly the depths of his sacraments, love for the priestly office gradually poured itself into my mind. It grew so greatly that, when day came, I said to my spiritual father that I no longer wished to resist, but wished to go as soon as he commanded and receive the Lord’s yoke—[Col. 1602A] while keeping silent the reason for this which had happened, as I have said.

He rejoiced; and when the time for ordination first arrived, I received this sacred order, though unworthy. Nor did the mercy of my God, which had gone before me, follow me in this office with a lesser sign. For not more than thirty days had passed when, as I lay in bed near the close of day, and had scarcely closed my eyes in sleep, there came down from above something like the likeness of a man bent forward and extended evenly, concealing as completely as possible only his face. Descending into me, it filled the whole substance of my soul, impressing itself upon me in a way which I cannot at all express in words—far more swiftly and profoundly than even the softest wax can receive a strongly impressed seal.

Immediately I was shaken out of the sleep that had scarcely crept upon me; awake, I felt a sweet weight; awake, I was delighted. And what shall I say? “My soul melted” (Song 5); [Col. 1602B] my soul, Lord, almost failed, almost flowed out from my body. Oh, how true is the saying of our Preacher: “For youth and pleasure are vain” (Eccl. 11). But there was not vanity there, but truth; there was true and living delight, where there is fulfilled to the end what is written: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). Hence we sing in the psalm: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35).

[Col. 1602C] To have tasted such delight, even while living in the body, is sweet; it is a treasure of gladness and exaltation. Yet it may truly be said that, unless that sudden cleansing of holy delight had quickly restrained itself, it might swiftly have drawn my soul from its body like a torrent and carried it away with itself. Hence I now understand better how we should take what God said to the human being: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). But, as I have said, that overflowing force of love quickly stopped and gradually departed. From that time I opened my mouth, and when I wrote I could by no means cease; and even now, though I wished it, I cannot be silent.

May this be for me the fulfillment of what I mentioned above from the Song of Songs: namely, to find the beloved outside and kiss him, so that no one may now despise me; to take hold of him and bring him into my mother’s house [Col. 1602D] and into the chamber of her who bore me (Song 3), so that one of her children may profit from this, and that I may be taught by the Spirit of truth and give him “a cup of spiced wine” (Song 8)—that is, a good, right, and well-sounding discourse from the Holy Spirit—and “new wine from my pomegranates” (ibid.), namely, the delight of knowledge together with the fruit of good works.

If I have spoken the truth, if I have invented none of these things from my own heart, may the name of the Lord, by which you adjured me, my father and lord, be a most strong tower for me. May it be done to me according to what the Son of God, who is also the Son of Man, said: “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I shall love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14). [Col. 1603A] May the sun of righteousness shine upon me; may the Lord be my illumination and my God my mercy; and may he raise me from corruption and want, as in the prophet: “And I will lift you above the height of the earth and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father” (Isa. 58).

May he pardon me whatever befell me from the fear that I feared, whatever happened of those things which I dreaded, throughout the whole time of this prolonged pilgrimage or sojourning. May the number of my days be completed by the first and eighth beatitude, which is to possess the kingdom of heaven. And may there come to me what we say to him in the psalm: “For the poor is left to you; you will be a helper to the orphan” (Ps. 9). May that also apply to me which is said in Isaiah: “This man shall dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks shall be his height; bread is given him, his waters are sure” (Isa. 33). [Col. 1603B] May I enter the altar of God, the altar of the heavenly sanctuary, and there may my soul receive what true love says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). And may the immortal Bridegroom contain me in that body of his bride, the Church, to which he shall be joined in eternal love and everlasting marriage. For not without cause was I thus made a beginner, nor did you without cause earnestly adjure me to write such matters concerning myself.

[Col. 1603C] I should like here to say something briefly concerning the reason. Certain persons, thinking that they were rightly doing what is said in Job, “The wise confess and do not hide their fathers, to whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them” (Job 15), once—as I may speak in the words of the same blessed Job—afflicted my soul, wore me down with words, and pierced me no less than ten times, and were not ashamed to oppress me (Job 19). I contradicted certain opinions which they advanced, differing from the true and right sense, but which they seemed to have received from their great and very celebrated fathers—that is, their teachers—whose authority they thought it glorious to confess and not conceal.

Since I did not believe the authority of those fathers, being human beings although wise, and dared to speak better and more soundly according to the authority of the Scriptures—oh, what indignation, what reproach, was directed at me in this manner! “Understand first, and then let us speak: Why does your spirit swell against God, that you utter such words from your mouth? The wise confess and do not hide their fathers” (Job 15). [Col. 1603D] “Where are your fathers? What teachers, or what sort of teachers, instructed you?”

With such and similar words they pierced me not once, nor for a few days, but many times and for several years; until, supported by the strength of perseverance and the authority of the Scriptures, I won the palm of victory. You too assisted greatly and bore witness that it had happened to me not from a spirit of fear or from the presumption of my own heart, but by the gift of the Lord’s grace, through the condescension of the Holy Spirit: that I had such confidence for handling the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures, and that I could in no way have attained this ability except through the good Spirit, from whom, or by whom, all good things proceed.

[Col. 1604A] Therefore let those wise men confess as much as they wish and not hide their fathers, to whom alone, as they say, the earth was given—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures and of the liberal arts. [Col. 1604B] I, although I too have had certain fathers among my schoolmasters and have studied diligently in books of the liberal arts, profess this: a visitation from the Most High is better to me than ten fathers of that kind. Often struck upon the lips by his rod, and sometimes even shaken throughout my whole body—as I have on several occasions made known to your faithful ears—I speak in writing whatever that instructor suggests, holding this hope which Wisdom declares: “A man’s belly shall be filled from the fruit of his mouth, and the offspring of his lips shall satisfy him” (Prov. 18).

687 Now my freer discourse is directed to you, disciple of truth, seeker of holiness, lover of the Son of God and of the same Son of Man, bishop beloved for every good quality. For a long time I have rejoiced in this and rightly congratulate you for it: in you too the experience of the truth shines brightly, which says in the Gospel according to Mark: “Amen I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the Gospel, who shall not receive a hundredfold now in this time—houses, and brothers, and sisters, and father, and mother, and children, and fields, with persecutions—and in the age to come eternal life” [Col. 1604C] (Mark 10).

Before I praise the experience of this true saying which has been realized in you, I should like to say something for the sake of those who may hesitate here, or wonder and ask: Did all who left whatever, however great or however small, for Christ receive a hundredfold in this time or age? To say nothing of others, did hermits or anchorites receive in this age a hundredfold of what they had left for Christ?

For the sake of those in whom thoughts of this kind may arise, it should be noted that he did not say merely, “who has left for my sake,” but added, “and for the Gospel.” If “for the Gospel” were exactly the same and no more than “for Christ,” it would be superfluous, after saying “for my sake,” [Col. 1604D] to add “and for the Gospel.” We must therefore ask or know what he added in meaning by adding the words “and for the Gospel.” By this saying he added this meaning: you should understand that he declared perfection, worthy even of a present reward, to consist in this—that one, not content with one’s own salvation, leaves all things, follows Christ, travels about, hastens, awakens a friend, that is, preaches the Gospel, so that children who hear may follow Christ. This ministry belongs especially to the apostles, who were being instructed when he said these things to them; Peter, the first among them, had said to him: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you. What therefore shall we have?” (Matt. 19).

[Col. 1605A] Concerning persons of this kind, let someone name one “who has not received or does not receive in his own time houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, and fields, with persecutions”—that is, even amid persecutions, which are not lacking to those who wish to live devoutly in Christ (2 Tim. 3)—a hundredfold more than he left, and who is therefore free to preach the Gospel; only then let him doubt whether this promise is true or not.

For example: Peter was a fisherman, was not rich, and obtained his food by hand and craft. Once, after the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, he began to preach the Gospel, did he not receive a hundredfold what he had left when, called from his little boat, he followed Christ? Not to mention that he presided first in Antioch and afterward as great pontiff in the city of Rome, and had houses—[Col. 1605B] indeed, built churches—and possessed far more spiritual brothers, sisters, fathers, mothers, and children than anyone could possess according to the flesh. To leave all that aside: the single shared right of possessions or common resources at the beginning of the Gospel, where “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, nor did any of them say that anything which they possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 2, 4), was worth more to him than a hundred nets and a hundred little boats like the one he had left.

[Col. 1605C] Once this is observed, it is likewise clear that the phrase written thus in Matthew, “And everyone who has left these things for my name” (Matt. 19), means more than if he had said “for me”: namely, “for my name” should be understood as “in order to make me known,” which is done by preaching the Gospel.

Therefore, as I had begun to say, we congratulate you, venerable bishop, because in you shines a great proof of this truth. You left in one city a single house, I know not how modest, and certain relatives who, as I have learned, were not poor and possessed some fields. And behold, in this present age you have become lord of that same city. Is this not a hundredfold? Besides this, the hope is laid up in your bosom that in the future age you shall have eternal life.

This must be ascribed in praise of him who, before worldly times, foreknew and predestined all the saints, and in his own time called, justified, [Col. 1605D] and glorified each one of them (Rom. 8). He called you not at just any time, but at the very entrance of ardent youth, with a swift calling, so that you withdrew the foot which you had set, as it were, upon the threshold of the world; and, leaving all things behind, leaving even the country or province of your birth far behind your back, you fled as a stranger to monastic life, to the mountain prophetic of spiritual victory by its own name—for it is called Sigeberch.

For who accomplished this except the inspiration of calling grace? From its fruits it can be known that the planting of your conversion was a planting of the heavenly Father, which can never be uprooted (Matt. 15). Were you then a boy or youth when you saw a contest being waged over you between God and the Ancient One, as though it were uncertain which of them—God the Creator or Satan the corrupter—should possess you? Were you so inexperienced that you thought such a contest was being waged only over yourself, between parties so opposed? Rather, this contest has existed from the beginning over the entire human race: [Col. 1606A] whether God, who created us, or the devil, who deceived the first human being, ought to possess us.

At your urgent request I recently wrote for you a small work in twelve books, entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God*. I confess that I heard, to my own joy, that it is admired even by many wise persons and read most willingly by them. This conflict is ancient; it has been fought on behalf of all, is still fought for each individual, and in all—or on behalf of all—his elect God conquers. “For no one,” says the Son of God, “can snatch [Col. 1606B] out of my Father’s hand” (John 10); or, “No one,” he says, “shall snatch my sheep from your hand” (ibid.).

That singular vision concerning yourself was shown to you so that you might be more watchful; and, terrified, you fled, not having seen or been shown which side would conquer and which would be conquered—lest perhaps you should think that you had already attained. At that time you knowingly left all things for Christ, but you did not yet know that you had left them for the Gospel: that is, so that you might proclaim Christ to many others. But he who had called you to the work predestined for you knew this.

[Col. 1606C] You also did not know that a certain beginning of this future ministry lay in the fact that, having received from above a best gift—the talent of good natural ability or clear understanding—you, as a young man under obedience to your spiritual father, devoted it not only to younger men but also to your equals, being no more a teacher of learning than an example of monastic discipline. Therefore that talent or received gift deservedly increased in you, according to the saying: “To him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. 13).

Why say more? Then the little lamp of God was placed upon a most brilliant lampstand of no contemptible height, when you, whom the true light illumined and the true fire kindled, undertook the governance of the Church of Sigeberg. Oh, how many then began to rejoice in the light! Every single eye of those dwelling far and wide, especially in the great house that is the Church of Agrippina, or Cologne, gladly beheld the flame [Col. 1606D] of your light. And if there was any evil eye opposed to you, it did not dare confess even that you were burdensome to it to behold. Such was the authority of your light that it could immediately have regarded as spoken against itself the prophetic saying: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. 5).

[Col. 1607A] Meanwhile, while the household of the Lord, over which you had been appointed a faithful and prudent servant, and to which with flaming heart and luminous mouth you preached eternal life, deservedly increased and multiplied in merit and number, you nevertheless were small and almost nothing in your own eyes. This was especially perceived by those familiar with you, and by those who held more intimate conversation with you concerning the salvation of the soul. Perceiving this myself, I observed that the prophetic saying applied to you not a little, indeed very much:

> “Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed from my God’? Do you not know, or have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord, who created the ends of the earth, does not fail or grow weary; and there is no searching out of his wisdom. He gives strength to the weary, and multiplies might and power to those who have none.”  
> (Isa. 40)

And likewise:

> “I am your God, taking hold of your hand and saying to you: ‘Do not fear; I have helped you. Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead in Israel. I am your helper.’”  
> (Isa. 41)

[Col. 1607B] If you have not hitherto noticed that answers of this kind suit your humility, then at least notice it now, admonished by the increase of grace or greatness of the benefit: the Most High has some care for you. First, this designation, “Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead,” I shall explain as fitting you and those like you—indeed, all the humble in heart who have learned from the good Teacher, saying, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble” (Matt. 11).

[Col. 1607C] Every humble father of spiritual children is both a worm and Jacob: a worm in his own judgment, but Jacob in God’s judgment. Jacob was indeed a great man and had many male children; yet on account of one woman, whom he had begotten as his only daughter, he was afflicted and grieved (Gen. 34). So, likewise, men great in God’s sight—among all the living, you are the best known to me—though they have many virtues and many spiritual children, as you also had, have something like a daughter: that is, a hidden weakness. When anyone humbles himself before the Lord because of it, he is both a worm and Jacob: a worm, as I have said, in his own judgment; Jacob, however, in God’s judgment; and he is dead to himself—that is, he fears that he may die from that weakness—but lives to God.

Therefore, do not fear to have it said to you, “I am your helper.” And he proves it by the effects, because your way was not and is not hidden from me, nor shall your judgment pass away from me. Rather say this: “You, God, who saw me and my judgment—what you judged, namely that one who humbles himself shall be exalted—has not passed from you.”

I too, with God himself asking, ask you in his own words; when we had at times held secret conversation concerning the human being, I wished you to be comforted: “Do you not know, or have you not heard?” [Col. 1607D] (Isa. 40). Namely, what follows: “The everlasting God, the Lord, who created the ends of the earth, does not fail or grow weary” (ibid.), whenever or however often he wishes to heal the weak or honor the poor. For all things are possible and easy to him. “And there is no searching out of his wisdom,” he says (ibid.). In what respect? Surely, to speak according to the present matter, in that “he gives strength to the weary and multiplies might and power to those who have none” (ibid.): that is, he first allows his elect one to grow weary and recognize his weariness, so that he seems altogether not to exist, or to be nothing, and only then gives strength, only then multiplies might and power.

[Col. 1608A] It is not so with the strong; thus he does not deal with those who are healthy—that is, those who seem righteous to themselves and trust in their own strength. But what follows? Immediately he adds: “Boys shall fail and grow weary, and young men shall fall in weakness” (ibid.). Boys are rightly those who are inexperienced and have not fought in temptations; young men are those who consider themselves strong and, as it were, are proud of their own virtues.

We now do not doubt that you have clear judgment or experience that your way was not hidden from the Lord and that your judgment did not pass from your God. For when you did not know, when you were not present—indeed, when you were far away—the Church of Regensburg, bereft of its pastor, chose you as its pastor, that is, its bishop. This was a great grace and gift of the great High Priest, “who has passed through the heavens” (Heb. 4), as the Apostle says: “And he himself gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers” [Col. 1608B] (1 Cor. 12).

When clergy and people were divided into factions over choosing a pastor for themselves, and their party strife grew dangerous, with some shouting for this man and others for that man, and when, with the sedition gaining force, they were almost about to resort to arms, one man wiser than the rest, whose heart God had touched, suddenly put forward your name and advised that you be elected. Immediately that whole movement of parties subsided, and the unity of the Church, which had been divided, yielded to you alone. [Col. 1608C] By whose nod, by whose regard, should we believe this was done, except his of whom the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2)?

Rejoice, therefore, because, as I have already said, your way was not so hidden from the Lord that he did not see you, though little among the many whom he has to govern or order. “Then,” someone may say, “ought one to rejoice at such a thing? Ought one not rather to resist, following the example of Moses when he was sent to such a ministry, to become leader of the people of Israel and prince of their liberation, to lead them out of the land of Egypt?” (Exod. 3).

[Col. 1608D] To this I reply: Ought we not also follow the example of him who, when he heard the Lord’s voice saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isa. 6), said, “Behold, I am here; send me” (ibid.)? Moses’ humility is indeed praiseworthy and should be adopted as an example according to time and circumstance; but beyond humility he had another reason, understood from the words he spoke after refusing once, twice, and three times: “I beseech you, Lord, send him whom you are going to send” (Exod. 4). Who was that, except he of whom the patriarch Jacob foretold: “Until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49)? Thus he wanted Christ to be sent very quickly for the salvation of his people, and for that reason refused. As though he said: “I pray that not I, a deputy, but he himself may now come.”

Apart from this man, who intended such a reason, show me anyone who, when commanded to undertake such an office or ministry, commendably refused—unless perhaps you think Jeremiah refused when he said: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” [Col. 1609A] (Jer. 1). But he could say this not in refusing the ministry, but rather in desiring that the gift be increased in him; and this was immediately done, because “the Lord,” he says, “sent his hand and touched my mouth” (ibid.), and so forth.

Those, therefore, are especially praiseworthy who, by the impulse of love, offer themselves for their neighbors’ salvation, as Elisha too offered himself: “I pray,” he said to Elijah, “that your spirit may become double in me” (4 Kings 2)—namely, the spirit of working miracles, that I may be able to perform signs double those which you performed, through which the people may be moved and not forget to say what, through your action, it said: “The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God” (3 Kings 18), against whom impious Jezebel strives.

With a congratulatory spirit I say all this to your holy fatherhood, [Col. 1609B] and among these things I shall not omit what greatly pleases our eyes: that you possess something of the imitation of blessed Martin. Once he had taken up the episcopate, says the writer of his Life, it is not within our power to unfold what and how great he showed himself. For he persevered most steadfastly as he had been before: the same humility was in his heart, the same plainness in his clothing. Thus, full of authority and grace, he fulfilled the dignity of bishop without abandoning his monastic purpose and virtue.

[Col. 1609C] We saw you, bishop of a splendid city, proceeding in a fur garment covered or fastened over with a dark cape; behind you went conspicuous men of both clerical and lay rank, distinguished men, colored or variegated according to their custom or dignity with the pelts of foreign mice. They were wise in rejoicing that they had, or followed, as bishop one who despised such things: rich in resources, poor in affection and outward habit, humble in heart, plain in dress, sharing a common table with himself, and not abandoning, together with the dignity of bishop, his monastic purpose and virtue. This is what I said concerning the imitation of blessed Martin.

It is therefore evident that the vision of that holy woman which you heard was not vain. She reported that she had been told in a vision that blessed Martin was to be met on his own day, during the imminent Rogation days, which by custom are celebrated before the Ascension of the Lord. [Col. 1609D] She wondered at such news, knowing—and even retaining in memory while dreaming—that the feast of blessed Martin was not celebrated on those days, but at a very different time of year, on the eleventh day of November. Therefore, giving little attention to the vision, she kept silent about it as though it were idle, until you, whose coming she had not known before that vision, arrived as bishop-elect on the Rogation days.

With what great joy of clergy and people, with what rejoicing not only of the city but of the whole country, with what praises of Christ did you enter the city! Whose praise, whose honor was that? Was it yours, or owed to you? Therefore I wish to repay you in fitting words. For since you used to say, either to me or to others concerning me, that you attributed what I wrote no more to me than to an ass, I likewise say that I ascribe to you the glory of that reception scarcely more than I would ascribe the glory, honor, and praises of the crowds meeting the Lord with palm branches [Col. 1610A] to the one who was seated upon the little ass. For the little ass was worthy to travel a road strewn with people’s garments and surrounded by such flowers and palm branches, not for its own sake but for that of its rider (Matt. 21). So you too were worthy to be received in this manner not for yourself, but for Jesus Christ dwelling in your heart through faith (Eph. 3).

When that holy woman saw this, she recognized that the vision she had seen pertained to you, and afterward recounted it to all in whom she had confidence. I shall return to speaking of the marks of your humility, hoping—and earnestly desiring that my hope may be most firm—that you will persevere in it, and by persevering lay up glory for yourself in the future. For it is not glory that precedes humility, but, as Wisdom says, “humility precedes glory” (Prov. 15).

[Col. 1610B] You have rightly persuaded this to yourself, or to your heart, because of the humility of the Son of Man, whose glory and honor you love with blessed love. For he himself said: “It shall not be so among you, as among the rulers of the nations who lord it over them. But whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant; just as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20; Luke 22).

[Col. 1610C] Does not this Son of Man daily minister to us at the holy altar the ministry of that same redemption, namely, the sacrament of his body and blood? Why, then, are we not ashamed to be served when such a minister serves us, yet dare to lord it over anyone except vices alone? Hear one further thing which I shall tell you of matters like those I narrated above, because you so wished. When I was still more recent, and consequently more attentive, in the rank of this ministry—that is, in the office of priesthood—I saw, in a vision full of delight, this Son of Man ministering to us. What shall I say, or in what words shall I describe the dress and bearing of the one who ministered?

Finally, as though many were seated in a great house at a handsome and spacious table, he himself, venerable and lovable in appearance, having unfastened and laid aside the cloak with which he had been wrapped over his tunic, ministered on this side and that, dispensing bread and wine, with hands most fitting and a gait most splendid. There were, moreover, little hollow cakes of the whitest bread, receiving within themselves wine that had been poured in; and he served such a dish to all. I can say no more, except that he ministered—saving the majesty that cannot be expressed—and that it greatly befitted him so to minister, with such great affection, as though he were speaking those words from the Song: “Eat, friends, and drink; and be inebriated, most dear ones” (Song 5).

And indeed the saying is true—and was true for me then—that dreams arise from many cares; nevertheless, it is also true that good and true dreams often follow good cares (Eccles. 5). This was not one of those dreams which have caused many to go astray [Col. 1611A] (Sirach 34); rather, it leads toward truth, in that it sweetly and often recalls to me—and I desire that it may recall to you—that saying of the Son of Man: “But I am in your midst as one who ministers” (Luke 22). And, aided by this remembrance, may the fellow-servant of holiness not cease from the degree of humility which you have begun.

Why say more? “At all times,” says Wisdom, “let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. 9). I speak to one who understands: your garment is indeed black to men, but white to God and to those wise in the things of God; and the oil upon your head is charity in your heart—may it never fail.

I could indeed have feared loss because of your absence, according to the foretoken which I saw before [Col. 1611B] you set out. I saw myself maimed, my right hand torn away from its arm at the elbow; and this surely foreshadowed what has happened concerning you.
