Yet both aspects were good, because I had not altogether lost that right hand, though torn away, but carried it with the other, that is, the left hand; and at the same time it was as though a miracle occurred: in another place upon it, a tender right hand grew.

Accordingly, in truth, I have not altogether lost you, my right hand; but you will still be able to bring me some help by the left hand—that is, in the concern of this present life. Yet we have, and ought to have, greater assurance in the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter: namely, him who says through the Psalmist, “The Lord watches over you; the Lord is your protection, at your right hand” [Col. 1611C] (Psalm 120). Therefore, though I lack your presence, which I had as a faithful guard and as my right hand, I am not as one forsaken; rather, may he himself guard one who hopes in him—he who can guard and protect beyond every right hand.

Among other things, may the recollection of the miracle somewhat strengthen this hope—a miracle which I mentioned in the work I wrote on the Song of Songs, where the beloved speaks: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” (Song 5). I confess that I made that account concerning myself also; but because I feared my own folly, lest I should seem to boast vainly, I did not disclose it except under the necessity—not of a man—which I now have, since, as I have often said, you [Col. 1611D] adjured me. Therefore I transformed the account itself in such a way that I might tell the event truthfully, while the person could not be recognized.

690 At last, in the final chapter of this little book, let whoever reads these things know that he is entreated not to mock as though at a fool, but to attend sympathetically to the cause of a sorrowful little child: namely, that cause which I stated at the beginning of these matters, according to the words of Wisdom, saying: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the sons of the poor. Give strong drink to those who are dying, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit: [Col. 1612A] let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their pain no more” (Prov. 31).

Since I have cited the words themselves, I should like to explain them briefly. Lemuel, which is interpreted “in whom is God,” is Christ himself, of whom the Apostle says: “God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). Let us say that he finds this counsel of the Spirit of Wisdom pleasing and fulfils it gladly: “Do not, Lemuel, give wine to kings,” and so forth.

He says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little children” (Matt. 11). Thus here the kings, and there the prudent and wise, are the same: namely, the proud, “puffed up by the understanding of their flesh” (Col. 2). To these he says: “Do not give wine,” that is, do not open [Col. 1612B]—rather, close—the profound mysteries of divine things. For what reason? Clearly because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns: that is, no restraint of the mouth where knowledge puffs up (1 Cor. 8).

That secret is not there which the same Wisdom, desiring it elsewhere, after saying, “Let your fountains flow abroad, and divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5), added: “Keep them for yourself alone, and let no strangers share them” (ibid.). Since, therefore, there is no secret there, they make themselves common to strangers—that is, heretics. “Do not,” he says, “give them wine, lest perhaps”—as has often happened—“they drink in such a way that they forget judgments and alter the cause of the sons of the poor” (Prov. 31): that is, lest they judge wrongly concerning the Scriptures and interpret them otherwise than is expedient for the salvation of their hearers, whom you, poor one—you who are yourself [Col. 1612C] meek and humble of heart—have regenerated as your children from water and the Holy Spirit.

Those already mentioned as sorrowful, bitter in spirit, needy, and grieving are the little children—that is, the humble—such as those whose groan is: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 119); who refuse to be comforted in this world, and therefore mourn because the bridegroom has been taken from them (Matt. 9). Give strong drink to these; give wine to these: that is, let understanding be opened to them, that they may understand the Scriptures as they read the Law and the Gospel, and thus, by drinking, may meanwhile receive partial consolation until that which is perfect comes (1 Cor. 13).

I confess that I was one of these: formerly a little child both in the age of youth and in my own estimation, and now knowingly mourning and saying with blessed Job: “Let the day perish on which I was born, [Col. 1612D] and the night on which it was said: A man has been conceived. Let a dark tempest possess that night; let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months. Let that night be solitary and unworthy of praise” (Job 3). But I drank strong drink, I drank wine, in the manner and order which I have faithfully recounted. Since, as I think, I have thereby satisfied you, now, knowing the end of these matters, I shall append—or resume—the interrupted conclusion, in order to complete what remains of the work *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, hoping that I shall see you soon.

## BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 1613]

[Col. 1613A] “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place” (Ezek. 3), says that voice of great commotion which the prophet heard—as I had already begun to recall far above—and the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and again a sound of great commotion (ibid.).

From that commotion, O glorious living creature whom we now see through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13), beside the often-mentioned river Chebar—living creature of four faces, which are your four mysteries, namely incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—we now desire, in accordance with our purpose, to praise that face of yours which is rightly called the lion’s face: namely, the most mighty and unconquered power of your resurrection.

A true beginning and foretoken at once of that same [Col. 1613B] great commotion was what occurred when you cried with a loud voice and gave up the spirit: “Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose” (Matt. 27). They did not rise before you rose, but when you, the firstborn from the dead, rose (Col. 1), they rose.

The lion’s face had held itself back, while performing or suffering what belonged to the calf’s face, until it said, “It is finished,” bowed its head, and gave up the spirit; and when its side had been opened by the soldier’s spear, blood and water came forth (John 19), the price of redemption for souls and bodies alike. Immediately and from that time onward, to speak in the words of Wisdom: “As [Col. 1613C] the roaring of a lion, so is the wrath of a king; and as dew upon grass, so is his cheerfulness” (Prov. 19).

Against whom, I ask, was the king’s wrath immediately directed, like the roaring of a lion? Was it not against hell, everlasting death, the devil, prince of darkness, the ancient sinner, the proposer of death? And toward whom or what persons was his cheerfulness like dew upon the grass? Was it not toward all the saints or elect who had awaited him from the foundation of the world?

How did those spirits feel the roar of so great a lion, when even the earth, insensible and inanimate, felt it? For it was shaken, and by its shaking and the splitting of the rocks cried out that it could not bear that roar. Conversely, how did Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints experience the gladness of his countenance, when even the confessing thief experienced it like dew? For a little before he had heard him say: “Amen, 691 I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

Thus it was beautifully said and truly fulfilled: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall adore you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49).

According to these and similar things—which are both the sound of the wings of the living creatures [Col. 1614A] striking one against another and the sound of the loudly resounding wheels following the living creatures (Ezek. 3), that is, of the ancient Scriptures harmonizing with evangelical mysteries—this lion’s face is rightly said to be on the right. For the calf’s face is on the left, by which left is signified the adversity of the passion; while the lion’s face, as has been said, is on the right, by which is denoted the prosperity or glory of the resurrection.

I call it the left on account of the weakness of assumed humanity, while preserving the truth that, just as his resurrection of the flesh is the right hand for our bodies, so his passion is the right hand for our souls. For through his passion we have the first resurrection, that of souls; and through his resurrection we await the second resurrection, that of bodies, unto eternal life.

Therefore the calf’s face—that is, his passion—was on the left only for himself, insofar as his soul was sorrowful, distressed, and afraid (Mark 14). Meanwhile, for a most necessary reason, the Father held his right hand: that is, he wished his strength to be deferred, so that he might use it not then but at the fitting time, according to what he appropriately says in the Psalm: “You have held my right hand, and by your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” [Col. 1614B] (Psalm 72).

For even if this utterance can belong to any saint or righteous person, it is nevertheless fitting—and much more fitting—to understand it as spoken in this person’s voice. For truly, just as he himself said while praying, “Yet not my will but yours be done” (Matt. 26), God the Father held his right hand; by his own will God the Father restrained for a time that obedient lion’s roar.

A little earlier, that is, on the day before he was to suffer, he entered the city and, lightly brandishing the small whip that he had made of cords, drove so great a multitude of sellers and buyers from the temple, and overturned their wares or profits along with their seats (Mark 11). Then, when he was being betrayed, by saying, “Whom do you seek? I am he” (John 18), he cast to the ground the entire cohort of the governor and the servants of the high priests, together with the betrayer. The Father held that right hand so completely that he did not even come down from the cross when the Jews said: “If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27).

Therefore, after he held his right hand and led him according to his will, he also did what immediately follows: “and with glory you received me,” that is, you raised me gloriously from the dead.

Now let the discourse attend more closely to the chapter of prophecy written above, and let us say something, according to its very words, concerning that which pertains to the lion’s roar already mentioned. “And I heard,” he says, “behind me a sound of great commotion: ‘Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place,’” and the rest, as above.

Just as in this prophecy we have the sound of great commotion heard once and again, so we have already said that, in that roar of the lion—namely, in the descent into hell and in the resurrection of Jesus Christ—an earthquake occurred which was at once the beginning and the foretoken of a great commotion. It was its beginning, because immediately with that earthquake all heavenly protection was taken away from them, as the guardian powers of the temple cried out, Josephus also attesting: “Let us depart from these seats.” [Note: [Col. 1615D] Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 7, chapter 12.]

It was a foretoken because, in the veil of the temple being torn, there was indeed for us a revelation of heavenly mysteries; but for them, the tearing of the veil, together with the splitting of the rocks, was a foretoken of the irreconcilable factions by which from that time they were torn apart among themselves, also stirring up against themselves the earthquake of the Roman Empire.

Finally, I should like to mention this aspect of the lion’s roar as well, [Col. 1615B] because another prophet, Amos, begins in this manner: “The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give forth his voice; and the fair places of the shepherds have mourned, and the summit of Carmel has dried up” (Amos 1).

What were those fair places of the shepherds but the profits of the high priests or priests from the most beautiful temple? And what was the summit of Carmel, which is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision,” but the pride of the Jewish people, circumcised indeed in flesh but uncircumcised in heart and ears? “Therefore,” he says, “the fair places of the shepherds have mourned, and the summit of Carmel has dried up”: that is, the city and temple over which those shepherds gloried, saying, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is here” (Jer. 7), were laid waste; and all the verdure of spiritual grace was taken away from the Jews (Isa. [Col. 1615C] 15). For the clouds were commanded not to rain upon that summit of pride; the apostles were commanded, after shaking off the dust of their feet against them, to pass over to the Gentiles (Matt. 10).

These are the four parts of that great commotion, whose sound, as was stated before, holy Ezekiel heard behind him. For “the Lord will roar from Zion” is rightly understood thus: the Lord, as a lion or lion’s cub, will break hell, and before his face death will flee, according to what I recalled above: “Judah, a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have ascended.” “And from Jerusalem he will give forth his voice”: that is, beginning from Jerusalem, he will cause repentance to be preached in his name to all nations.

Is not such a voice of the Lord—that is, the preaching of the Gospel—also a lion’s roar? “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it,” says the Apostle; “for the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1). Yet in the present passage the Lord’s roar and the voice which he gave differ. Roaring by itself produces fear; but a voice, expressing speech, contains, together with terror, the rationale of instruction. And the Lord indeed roared only over hell, and by his roar terrified and put death to flight; but to the world—that is, to all nations—he gave his voice, expressed the rationale of teaching: his voice, I say, speaking by the Gospel through [Col. 1616A] the great commotion. “The nations were troubled,” says the Psalmist, “and kingdoms were shaken; he gave his voice, the earth was moved” (Psalm 45).

Nor was that commotion a simple one. For some were moved to persecute; others to repentance, believing in the judgment to come, according to the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another and according to the sound of the wheels following the living creatures. For one wing strikes against the other because there are two comings of this lion, and one is confirmed by the other: the second, in which he will judge, by the first, in which he was judged.

Such a striking of wings is great and powerful, and the sound of the striking is most terrifying. For example, when he says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. [Col. 1616B] 24). And the angels say: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). This, certainly, is attested by the sound of the wheels, the voice of the Law, Prophets, and Psalms. Then there will be another great commotion, when he comes thus to judge. “For the powers of heaven also shall be shaken” (Matt. 24). Hence he did not repeat idly what he had already said once: “and a sound of great commotion.”

Let these things be said concerning that earthquake, since both the earthquake that occurred at his death and that which occurred at his resurrection were a sign of the great commotion, concerning which no tongue can speak adequately because of the greatness of the events.

But what, finally, is that glory of the Lord, 692 which every voice both of the living creatures and of the following wheels proclaims and blesses, saying: “Blessed [Col. 1616C] be the glory of the Lord from his holy place”? What, I say, is that glory to which our purpose is chiefly directed in the present work, *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*? By what other name, that it may be recognized more clearly, should the glory of the Lord be called?

Surely, under this name, what is the truth of the Lord? And that truth of the Lord itself, what is it but the Word of the Lord? Yet the matter requires—and we shall state the reason—why in this passage we choose to call the Word of the Lord itself, in which the Lord glories, the truth of the Lord.

When the incarnate Word of the Lord stood under judgment before the governor, and had answered the one asking and saying, “Then are you a king?” (John 18), “You say that I am a king” (ibid.), he immediately declared his cause, the cause of his coming or incarnation, in this way: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: that I might bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice” (ibid.).

This is a very great heading, a most weighty meaning in brief speech. If you have grasped it, then you may truly say: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord.” Therefore, that it may become clear how great the glory of the Lord is in that truth, and how glorious a work of this Son of Man it is to bear—or to have borne—witness to the truth by dying and rising, we must first consider what the face of truth itself is like.

For the name “truth” must not here be understood in the ordinary sense only—the sense in which it may be used in our common speech, according to which even that pagan or comic poet could name truth, saying:

> Compliance makes friends; truth begets hatred.  
> —Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1, line 41

Whence, or by what, can you be better helped toward knowing the face of truth than from that which is opposed to it—namely, from the instability of vanity? Of what vanity, I ask? For the name or meaning of vanity is so broad that not only the phantasms of the devil—such as the magicians of Egypt produced before Pharaoh against the truth of God (Exod. 7–8)—but also all things done under the sun are called, and are, vain: “Vanity of vanities,” said Ecclesiastes, “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. [Col. 1617B] 1). And after enumerating many things done under the sun, he says: “I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing remains under the sun” (ibid.).

Certainly, he judged all things that do not remain to be vain precisely because they do not remain. Nevertheless, that these things should be judged vain, or accused of vanity, is due not so much to their temporal condition as to human desire: for people are vain and false when they presume to establish their blessedness in the use or abundance of such things.

For building houses, planting vineyards, making gardens and orchards, possessing male and female servants and a great household, herds as well, great flocks of sheep, gold, silver, and the wealth of kings and provinces, and other such things (Eccles. 2)—the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, and David could also possess these things, and yet did not walk in vanity by possessing them.

Above all, “God saw,” says Scripture, “all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). And the Apostle says of foods that “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4). Therefore, it is not their nature but the disposition of those who use them badly that makes them vain, when they are loved excessively or superfluously—namely, through the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Calling us back from these, the apostle John says: “For all that is in the world is the lust [Col. 1617D] of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2); this is not from the Father, but is from the world, “and the world passes away, and its lust” (ibid.).

Therefore, setting aside the multitude of intermediate vanities, I should like to investigate the supreme vanity, that which is rightly called vanity of vanities, so that, by discerning that defeated side, this victorious side—the truth of God, which has gained the praise of victory through the testimony of this Son of Man—may become better known, as he said, as I recalled above: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: that I might bear witness to the truth.”

The depth of Satan also has been investigated, “as they say,” says the apostle John (Rev. 2)—meaning those who knew him, or foolishly admired him. It has been investigated, I say, especially by the holy prophets. For in Ezekiel God reproaches him under the name of Pharaoh king of Egypt: “Behold,” he says, “I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers, and say: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself,’” and the rest, down to: “because you have said: ‘The river is mine, and I made it’” (Ezek. 29).

What, I ask, is this great dragon saying, “The river is mine, and I made it,” except saying: “The human race is mine, and I made it”? And whence, do you suppose, does Satan’s pride arise, that he dares say this? Consider that he glories thus and claims so much for himself because, as a most wicked hunter hissing through the serpent’s mouth, he corrupted the root of our origin in the first parents, so that a human offspring, manifold beyond number, might increase beyond number—beyond, I say, the number of those “whom God foreknew and predestined to become sharers in his kingdom” (Rom. 8), and whom he commanded to be born in blessing; for in blessing he said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 3).

For indeed, if transgression, authored by that malignant serpent, had not intervened, God would not have said to the woman: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions” (ibid.); there would not have flowed from the fluid of the flesh so great a river, abounding—indeed superabounding—with such surplus of the human race. Thus that vain and lying malignant rogue dared to call himself maker of the human race because he is the corrupter of human origin.

But what sort of intention his has been, and how evil it is—his intention in the activity of so great an adversary, “in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every seduction of iniquity” (2 Thess. 2)—we learn from Scripture concerning its first instance: entering the serpent and speaking through its mouth, he produced in the woman foolish wonder and seduced her. Its last instance will be when he enters the man of sin, namely Antichrist, and seduces those who rightly perish because they did not receive the love of truth, believing a lie; all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity will be judged.

What his intention is or has been, I say, is worth briefly declaring here and pertains to the present subject, so that, as proposed, through this opposite we may more clearly recognize God’s good and beneficial intention. This, then, was Satan’s intention, now frustrated through Jesus Christ: that the creature might not be able to know its Creator. For what reason? Clearly, because to know him is eternal life, which he—dead to God and author of death—envies to all.

Conversely, God’s intention in every work of his goodness, in every power and sign, and in true wonders, in all the Scriptures of truth which he created, has been and is that the creature might know its Creator in truth. For the same reason: certainly because to know him is eternal life, which he desires for us because he is good. For the Son says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” [Col. 1619A] (John 17).

This cause is truly great and worthy of God, for which he willed to be known 693 and glorified, to become an object of wonder, and to undertake a great contest against that intention of the devil, so that by conquering him he might be better known, because the fruit of knowing him is eternal life for the creature. “As Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these resist the truth: men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further; for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3).

Therefore, that you may more briefly perceive in a part this immense and prolonged contest, extended throughout the whole, let that fleshly Pharaoh represent the spiritual Pharaoh, the devil; let that local Egypt represent the whole world; let the Israelites dwelling as strangers in that Egypt represent all God’s elect, living captive in this age; let all the Egyptians of that time represent all the reprobate and alienated from God; let those two magicians represent all Satan’s ministers who have resisted truth, armed especially with sorceries or certain secret arts and incantations; and let Moses and Aaron represent all saints, prophets, or righteous persons who, having received the doctrine or ministry of truth, have been sent and have stood for this purpose and in this cause: to bear witness to truth.

What was Pharaoh seeking when he summoned the wise men and sorcerers so that they might likewise perform through Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts what Moses and Aaron did—each casting down his rod, which was changed into a dragon; changing waters into blood; and bringing frogs up over the land of Egypt, like Moses and Aaron, although they could proceed no further? (Exod. 7–8). What was he aiming at, except that the Lord God of the Hebrews might not be able to say what he did say: “That you may know that there is none like me in all the earth” (Exod. 9)?

But he and his magicians did resist the truth; yet they proceeded no further, and their folly became manifest when, through the sacrifice of the lamb, it was finally brought about that Israel could sing: “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, and working wonders?” [Col. 1619D] (Exod. 15).

According to the pattern seen in that part, it must also be viewed in the whole. For what was the spiritual Pharaoh, the devil, aiming at when throughout the entire world he employed and subjected to himself temples and possessed or frenzied priests, magicians and soothsayers, and poets who proclaimed shameful deities—as he supposed, similarly to God, indeed more extensively than God, who had prophets and priests only among one people? What was he seeking except that the world, darkened by his mist, might not know that which it is eternal life to know: namely, that there is no God but one?

It is not our purpose to show, nor is it permitted us to know, by what methods or arts he brought men corrupted in mind under his authority. For unless they had been corrupted of their own accord, lovers of pleasures and haters of truth, they would not so easily, so inquisitively, have admitted so great an adulteration of God’s creature—not unaware that it was wicked and impious to have a pact with him, but knowing it plainly and yet obeying, because of the temporal prosperity of this world which they loved too much.

For example: “Numa Pompilius, third [read: second] king after Romulus, founder of the Roman rites, had written down the explanations of those rites. He himself kept them as long as he lived, but wished neither the people nor the senate, nor even the priests themselves, to know them.” It is certain that by unlawful curiosity he had reached those secrets of demons which he wished himself to write down and retain, in order to have something by whose reading he might be stirred. Yet, although he was a king and feared no one, he wished that no one should know them, lest he teach men impious things; but he feared to destroy them, lest he have the demons angry with him.

Therefore he buried them where he considered them safe, namely in his own tomb, which he did not believe a plow could reach. Yet this happened. For the plowman of a certain Terentius, while driving a plow near the tomb of that same Numa, dug those books from the earth and brought them to the praetor in the City. When the latter had examined their beginnings, he referred so important a matter to the senate. There, after the leading men had read certain explanations why each institution had been established in the sacred rites, they decreed, like religious fathers, that the same books should be burned by the praetor. [Note: [Col. 1619D] St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book 7, chapter 24, *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, Migne edition.]

But let us return to the matter.

How vainly puffed up was that Satan, applauding himself because he had brought it about that not only the other works of God—of which, as Ecclesiastes says, nothing remains under the sun (Eccles. 2)—but even man himself, made in God’s image, could be convicted of vanity; so that Scripture also says: “Man has been made like unto vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. 143). Again: “Yet every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). And another Scripture says: “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and [Col. 1620D] is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14). For he had effected two such deaths: one of the soul, the other of the body, according to that mystical likeness in Egypt—or, as was said above, when the Magicians stood before Pharaoh and, being two, each threw down his rod, which was changed into a serpent, not knowing that the rod of God, Aaron’s rod turned into a serpent, would devour their rods. God, providing well for man, inflicted only the one death, that of the flesh, saying: “Lest perhaps he take of the tree of life and live forever,” and sending him out of Paradise, and saying to him: “Because you are earth, and to earth you shall go” [Col. 1621A] (Gen. 3). Yet even this death of the flesh, no less than the death of the soul, must be ascribed to the devil as its author, because through the sin of which he was the author both deaths entered into this world (Rom. 5).

Thus he vainly gloried in evil that he had, as a victor, subjected God’s most excellent creature, namely man, to vanity and death—unaware that, as has already been said, the rod of God changed into a serpent would devour the opposing rods; that is, that the death of the flesh, divinely provided, would abolish both deaths of the human race. By contrast, with how just a grief the chosen portion of all angelic and human creation mourned, rightly jealous for the honour of their Creator, because His work had not yet been brought to such completion in truth that the mouth of that impostor might be stopped—he who boasted [Col. 1621B] as though victorious, as though he had wholly and irrecoverably frustrated God’s purpose by drawing away a part of the angels and corrupting all human creation.

Hence John in the Apocalypse, after saying, “And no one was able in heaven, nor on earth, nor beneath the earth, to open the book or look upon it; and I,” he says, “wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it” (Rev. 5). In the person of weeping John, therefore, we understand the whole company: those who were in heaven, that is, the holy angels; those who were on earth, namely righteous people living in every generation; and those beneath the earth, namely the faithful dead, because in the underworld they had a long desire to behold [Col. 1621C] the glory of God. All therefore grieved with grief as great as John’s weeping ought to signify, because no one was found worthy to open the book and loose its seals—that is, to fulfil the mysteries of our salvation, or the promises enclosed in the Scriptures of truth.

Let us take an argument from some comparison. When that Philistine Goliath stood and cried out against the ranks of Israel, saying, “Why have you come prepared for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Saul’s servants? Choose a man from among yourselves, and let him come down to single combat” (1 Sam. 17); and after this and other such things boasted, saying, “Today I have reproached the armies of Israel” (ibid.), surely all the Israelite men grieved because no one could be found [Col. 1621D] to remove this reproach from Israel, while that Philistine came forward morning and evening and stood there forty days. All fled from his face, greatly fearing him, and said one to another: “He has come up to reproach Israel, to reproach the ranks of the living God” (ibid.). But what was the reproach or insult of one man in such a cause compared with so great a matter, so great an adversary, saying: “I am God, and I sat upon the throne of God; the river is mine, and I made it”—namely, the human race? (Ezek. 28, 29.) If, therefore, all the Israelites rightly grieved because of one such Philistine and that reproach of Israel, since they had no man to descend to single combat, how much more rightly did all the saints, both people [Col. 1622A] and angels, grieve for God’s glory because they had none to fight against such a mighty adversary as the devil, according to the comparison already given of John weeping greatly because no one was found worthy, either in heaven or beneath the earth, to open the book or look upon it.

Therefore the Lord, Father of the eternal Word and God of all consolation, who did not immediately but only after the forty days of that reproach—when all the Israelites had thoroughly learned that they ought not trust in their own strength—sent them the young David, whom He had provided for Himself as king among the sons of Jesse, in whom He might demonstrate the power of His name. David said: “You come to me with sword and spear and shield; but I come to you in the name of the Lord, that all the earth may know [Col. 1622B] that the Lord does not save by sword or spear” (1 Sam. 17). So He too, not immediately after the word of promise but after forty generations, the first reckoned in Abraham and the fortieth in Joseph, “sent His Son, Christ,” as the Apostle says, “in the fullness of time” (Gal. 4), to save not by sword or spear, but by His humility and patience.

Who could have believed that it would be so: that this little one, taken from his father’s house where he tended sheep, would provide such proof of the Lord’s power or name? For nothing like it had ever happened in Israel. Nor had anyone among all Israel’s many enemies hitherto come forth in such a manner as to challenge them to single combat and propose such a condition: “If he is able to fight [Col. 1622C] with me and strikes me down, we shall be your servants; but if I prevail and strike him down, you shall be servants and serve us” (1 Sam. 17). The cause, therefore, was venerable in the boy: for its sake he exposed himself to danger, having the firmest hope in the Lord’s name that he would remove the reproach from Israel, so that henceforth the Philistines might neither rule over them nor prevail against them. Venerable, I say, was the cause he declared: “that all the earth may know that the Lord is the God of Israel,” and that the whole Church might know this: that the Lord does not save by sword or spear; for the battle is His.

Likewise, who, unless God had revealed it by His Spirit, could have thought or hoped that a mortal man, assumed into God in every respect of our nature at the very moment of his conception, would be born for this and come into the world for this: to bear such testimony to the truth? As He said—and as I recalled above—“For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth.” What testimony, then, and of what sort or concerning what did He bear to the truth—that is, to the Word of God, to the Word who is God and who assumed Him? Surely He bore faithful testimony: that is, He demonstrated in Himself that truth, which is none other than the very Word of God, is no less unconquerable, untiring, and unchangeable in the humility or weakness of mortal nature than in the majesty or strength of His divinity; and no less so in the depths of hell than in the heights of heaven. He bore this testimony [Col. 1623A] to the truth by dying, descending into hell, rising from the dead, and ascending into heaven whence He had come, so that every angelic and human creature might know through this demonstration that “the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40); and, knowing this, that creation itself might live forever. For “this,” He says, “is eternal life: that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (John 17).

Whose eye ever saw this? Whose ear heard it? Into whose human heart did it arise that it should happen in this way, unless it was that of the few prophets to whom God revealed it through His Spirit? And, to say nothing of men, did even all the holy angels know this whole mystery?

For the Apostle says: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace has been given: to preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose which He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Eph. 3). He did not say that it might be made known to the Church through the principalities and powers in heaven—which would seem less wonderful—but “that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God which He accomplished in Christ Jesus might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places.” Thus, seeing the glorified Head of that same Church, they marvel and say: “Who is [Col. 1623C] this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah—this one beautiful in His robe, advancing in the greatness of His strength?” (Isa. 63). And elsewhere: “Who is this King of glory? Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23).

That we may not entirely fail to understand why their amazement is truly fitting, let us consider, as far as we can, the matter of so great a mystery, hidden from the ages and made known to them, according to the very words of the blessed Apostle: “Grace has been given to me,” he says, “to preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ,” and so forth, as above. What other riches does he mean by the most beautiful and most precious riches of Christ, which God the rich Father, creator of all things, stored up for His Son, except those contained in God’s treasury—the treasury of the Gospel of this same Jesus Christ? What other unsearchable riches did the Apostle who says these things preach among the nations? Therefore, Christ’s riches—the unsearchable riches—are all the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit: “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Him” (Col. 2), the fullness of grace and truth. For John the Evangelist says, “We saw His glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full”—understand, “we saw Him”—“of grace and truth” (John 1).

Before we speak of some of these riches, we think we should first speak of the dispensation of the mystery hidden; indeed, before that, of the mystery itself hidden from eternal ages in God, who created all things. I ask: of what hidden mystery does he say this? For once the mystery—or the hiddenness of the mystery—is known, the way opens without difficulty [Col. 1624A] to understanding the dispensation of the mystery of which he said, “and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the hidden mystery.” What then does he intend by “the mystery hidden from the ages,” adding, “in God, who created all things”? Perhaps the secret cause itself for which God created all things? For it is not without purpose or idly that he makes this reference here, saying, “in God, who created all things.” And what cause was there for which God created all things, unless it was this Son of Man? It must be said devoutly and heard reverently that God created all things for the sake of this Son of Man, who was to be crowned with glory and honour.

For when the Apostle in Hebrews had first said, “We see the Lord Jesus crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2), so that by God’s grace He might taste death for all, he immediately added: “For it was fitting for Him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” (ibid.). It should be carefully observed that he says two things: “for whom are all things” and “through whom are all things.” If he had said only “through whom are all things,” it would not be so remarkable or unfamiliar; for we all know that “through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1). But now he says these two things: first, “for whom are all things”; then, “through whom are all things.” Therefore He Himself is the cause for which God created all things. How beautifully and venerably he calls this the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.

For when God said, “Let this or that be”; “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters; let there be lights, and let them illuminate the earth” (Gen. 1), and so it was done, the angels knew concerning these and the other things that they were made through the Word; for it is said of all: “He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32, 148). But the reason why He made all these things was hidden in God. Therefore that cause is rightly called a mystery, because this was hidden in God—that is, known to God alone: why He created the angels and established the fabric of this world.

But now it has been made known, both to the angels in heaven and to people on earth, that all things were made not only through Him, but also for His sake. To make this [Col. 1624D] clearer, we must now speak of the dispensation of this same mystery. “And to enlighten all,” he says, “as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.” Among the matters especially included in the dispensation of the mystery—that is, of the secret cause for which God created all things, namely the Word of God and the same Son of Man, for whom all things were made, as has been said—the first work is the Incarnation, the second the Passion, the third the Resurrection, the fourth the Ascension. Of these four mysteries, necessary for eternal salvation—for without faith in them no one can be saved—our present discourse on *The Glory and Honour of the Son of Man* must be written.

Thus we understand one mystery in that hiddenness and four mysteries appearing in this dispensation, just as in the prophetic vision, often discussed already in this work, we understand one living creature and four faces, or four living creatures (Ezek. 1). Now consider how the holy angels were present in wonder at this fourfold dispensation of the mystery, since the Apostle said of this mystery: “that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places.”

When He was born of the Virgin Mary, an angel spoke to the shepherds that very night in great glory; and immediately after he announced the great joy, saying, “For today there has been born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David,” there suddenly appeared with him a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good will” [Col. 1625B] (Luke 2). Surely they rightly praised, rightly marvelled, and rightly glorified Him, because a great mystery had been made known to them: they saw in their same God and Lord upon earth a humility or mercy no less great than the majesty or power they had seen in heaven.

Again, when He suffered and agonized in His Passion, undoubtedly angels were present at so wondrous a spectacle of His patience and humility. Do you suppose that, because the Evangelist tells only of one—“there appeared to Him an angel from heaven strengthening Him” (Luke 22)—there were not more present? Indeed, He had them present; and, had He wished, He could visibly have produced those of whom He said to Peter: “Do you think that I cannot ask My Father, and He will now supply Me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26).

Again, when He rose from the dead, it is more than sufficiently established that all the holy angels received Him joyfully; and, as it is written elsewhere, “the morning stars praised Him, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38). Astonished by joy at so great a mystery made known to them, they said: “Who is this King of glory? Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 21). And they answered their own amazement: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle—He is the King of glory; the Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (ibid.). Two of them sufficed, as a judgment or testimony to the great festival of all, sitting visibly in white at His tomb [Col. 1625D] (Luke 24). When He ascended into heaven and the Apostles watched Him going into heaven, two of the blessed spirits who stood beside them in white garments sufficiently indicated the great festival of them all (Acts 1).

These things have been said so that we may in some degree perceive how great and joyous was the amazement of the holy angels concerning that mystery, according to these words of the blessed Apostle:

“And to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

As we are still to say something of this true glory of the Lord—or glorious truth—which thus conquers the devil’s truth and falsehood, we are led by great love for this same truth not to pass untouched over that suspicion of foolishness which the Apostle rebuked among the Gentiles: “But we,” he says, “preach Christ Jesus crucified: a stumbling block indeed to Jews, but foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1). For it appeared foolish to the wise among the Gentiles that God, though He is truly proclaimed almighty, permitted circumstances to occur that made it necessary for Him to become man and be crucified, according to the Gospel’s preaching, which seemed foolish to them.

Why, they ask, did the almighty God not rather ensure that neither man nor angel should fall, so that all things might stand unharmed without His labour? For, say the wise of this age, whose wisdom God made foolish, it was foolish to prefer—as you preach—to die for the dead rather than prevent the evil or cause which made it necessary for God, having become man, to die even for men; to prefer labouring to repair ruins rather than firmly establish the angelic and human creatures at the very beginning of creation, so that they could not fall. According to this worldly wisdom, it has seemed consequent even to some ecclesiastics that God willed the evil itself to occur for which, as already said, the Son of God made man had to die—lest, if they said otherwise, they should seem consequently bound to confess that almighty God is not almighty. Thus there is great difficulty for human understanding on either side, and on either side it furnishes presumptuous people with an occasion for blasphemy.

For these say: If God did not will evil to occur, yet the evil occurred for which He Himself had to labour even to death, then God is not almighty. Those others, on the contrary, say: If God is almighty and could have prevented evil from occurring, but evil nevertheless occurred by His permission, for which He was to labour even to death, then God is not wise [Col. 1626C].

To press us further with an example, the wise of this age—whose wisdom, as has been said, God made foolish—may say if they wish: If mighty Samson could have killed all his enemies, the princes of the Philistines, and with them so many men and women, without dying himself, would it not have been foolish to seek vengeance on them in such a way, and kill them in such a way, that he too should die? (Judg. 16.)

Augustine, the eminent Father, holding the royal middle way between these sides, said: “For who would dare to believe or say that it was not in God’s power to prevent either angel or man from falling? But He preferred not to take this power away from them, and so to show both how much evil their pride could accomplish and how much good His grace could accomplish.” Yet when he says this, he does not sufficiently remove the suspicion of those for whom, granted God’s omnipotence, it seems to follow that God willed evil to occur, since it occurred with His knowledge or foreknowledge.

What, then, shall we say to these things, except that there is something which almighty God can do, or cannot do? This is not first to be said by us; indeed, it was said long before us that God cannot be unjust. Mark too did not hesitate to use this word of negation in the Gospel. For when the Lord Jesus had gone to His own country, and they said, “Whence has this man all these things? Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?” “He could not,” Mark says, “do any mighty work there” (Mark 6)—namely, a work of faith, a work of hope, a work of charity. He intended such virtues, as he showed by adding: “Except that He healed a few sick persons by laying His hands upon them; and He marvelled at their unbelief” (ibid.). If, therefore, he says that the Lord of virtues, the true God, the almighty Son of almighty God, could not perform that work of virtue among His neighbours because they erred not through ignorance but blasphemed through envy, how much more rightly may you say of those evil and malicious spirits, proud and envious of the Creator’s glory, that He could perform no work of virtue in them?

Or do you suppose that both the angel fell from heaven and man was cast out of Paradise by falling from virtue into vice, rather than, indeed, by falling from vice into vice? The angel did not fall in such a way that one who was holy, or placed on some height of holiness, became wicked and lapsed into that which is contrary to holiness. Rather, the angel in heaven and man in Paradise had been placed there in order that he might become holy; that, by knowing and loving God, he might become holy and progress toward holiness. He therefore did not fall from holiness, which he had not attained, into wickedness, but from place to place: that angel fell or was cast out from heaven into this dark air, from the dwelling-places which in the Father’s house were from the beginning prepared in abundance for both angels and human beings. In falling he became the devil, because he became proud and pleased himself as though self-sufficient. This was not a fall from virtue into vice, but remaining in that in which he had been made—namely, in vanity, which is something intermediate between the true and undefiled being of God and that out of which He created all things, namely nothing.

The other kinds of things that come into being indeed return to that from which they were made, namely to nothing; and therefore, while they subsist, they are rightly called and are vain. But angelic and human creation, though not returning into nothing in such a way as to cease altogether to be, nevertheless remains in itself and scorns to enjoy God, who truly is; and so it is no less vain—indeed, is vanity itself.

[Col. 1627D] “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1); and man himself is vanity, or has been made like unto vanity. And the devil himself is not only vain, but also the prince of all vanity, because he scorned to enjoy God and did not will to remain in himself, as has already been said. Whether it was in God’s power that neither this one should fall from heaven nor man, imitating him, fall or be cast out of Paradise, let the Son of God Himself say—almighty from the Almighty, God from God: “I cannot,” He says, “do anything of Myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 15). Hence it must be understood that an unjust judge is one who acts from himself—that is, who judges otherwise than he hears or understands. It is impossible for God to do this, for He cannot at all be unjust. Therefore, as He heard, so He had to judge that He would not communicate or impart Himself to that creature which had dared to will itself sufficient for itself.

Thus, while God’s omnipotence and goodwill remain intact, with the devil falling and man deceived, evil occurred; and because of it the wise God had laudably to become man and die for all. Nor could man otherwise be saved. In this sense the faithful mind becomes not more sluggish but rather more eager to hasten forward and give thanks for God’s love, because He humbled Himself so greatly for us by necessity.

Now it is pleasing to return to the Apostle’s passage mentioned much earlier, where he says: “For it was fitting for Him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” [Col. 1628B] (Heb. 2). Here we first wish to ask whether this Son of God, of whom this discourse speaks, would have become man even if the sin because of which we all die had not intervened, or not. That He would not have become a mortal man, would not have assumed a mortal body, unless sin had occurred—because of which we too have all become mortal—is doubted by no one and unknown to no one except an unbeliever. We ask whether it was to be, and in some manner necessary for humankind, that God should become man, the head and king of all, as He now is; and what answer shall be made on this point?

Surely it is certain concerning all the saints and elect that all of them would have been born, though alone, if that sin of the first transgression had not occurred. Hence Father Augustine, in Book Fourteen of *The City of God*, says:

> “But whoever says that the first human beings would not have had intercourse or begotten children unless they had sinned, what does he say except that human sin was necessary for the number of the saints? For if, by not sinning, they would have remained alone—because, as such persons suppose, they could not have begotten children had they not sinned—then sin was necessary in order that not merely two righteous human beings, but many, might exist. But if this is absurd to believe, we should rather believe that the number of saints sufficient to fill that most blessed city would have existed, even had no one sinned, in the same number as is now gathered by God’s grace from the multitude [Col. 1628D] of sinners, so long as the children of this world beget and are begotten.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1627D] St Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, Book XIV, chap. 23, *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, Migne edition.]

Since, then, there is no doubt concerning all the saints and elect that they would all have been born up to the predetermined number according to God’s purpose—by which, before sin, He blessed them and said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1)—and since it is absurd to suppose that sin was necessary in order for them to be born, what should be thought concerning this Head and King of all the elect angels and human beings except that sin too was by no means a necessary cause for Him to become man among men, having the delights of His love with the children of men (Prov. 8)?

[Col. 1629A] For He is the Wisdom of God, which says concerning this its purpose: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His ways” (Prov. 8), etc., and concludes thus: “When He set the foundations of the earth in order, I was with Him, ordering all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before Him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth; and my delights were to be with the children of men” (ibid.). The purpose of so great a love, by which God had purposed that the Word of God should delight with the children of men, having a circumscribed form from human nature in the midst of angels and human beings, is wonderful and worthy of adoration, because the sin that came against it did not frustrate it. Rather, already then occurred what is said elsewhere: “But where transgression abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5).

For where did the transgression of so great a transgression abound so greatly? There, over and above the death of the soul—by which we died in those our parents through that original sin—there was added the other death, namely the death of the body, by the providence of God saying to man: “Because you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). There was added, by a gracious command, to the love of the obedient Son, that the Son Himself should become without sin such as we had become because of sin: that is, not only that He should not recoil [the text reads *resurgeret*, perhaps *refugeret*], offended, from assuming the nature which He had purposed to take, but that He should even descend for us to our death. This is precisely what the Apostle says, as we have already recalled: “For it was fitting for Him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” [Col. 1629C] (Heb. 2).

In this perfection, therefore—in that the author of our salvation was perfected through suffering—there is the weight of the Father’s command and the splendour of the Son’s obedience to the Father’s love. Of this same Son the Apostle says: “He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). And elsewhere: “He who did not spare even His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all” (Rom. 8). And the Son Himself, on the very night on which He was handed over, said to His disciples: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave Me commandment, so I do” (John 14). And because the Father gave this command through love, and the Son obeyed through love unto death on a cross, while this love itself is the Holy Spirit of the same Father and Son, the same Apostle rightly and venerably says to the Hebrews: “The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered Himself without blemish to God, has cleansed our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9).

A great glory immediately followed this glory of His humility and obedience. For “therefore God exalted Him and gave Him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). At this point it is most delightful to hear how graciously and venerably that same Apostle, the vessel of election, proclaims: “Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” [Col. 1630A] (1 Cor. 8).

He wishes us to be confident; he exhorts us to have confidence. This confidence is surely venerable and praiseworthy, because faith works it when faith has knowledge together with love. What then? Perhaps, with mind held in suspense, you look upon the heights of heaven; and there, seeing with the eye of contemplation this most high Son of God standing or sitting at God’s right hand, at the right hand of Majesty on high, trembling and struck in your heart with great fear, you say: “Alas! What will become of us wicked and criminal servants, for whose crimes such and so great a Lord endured so many and such great insults, even unto death—indeed, death upon a cross?”

When you have said this or something similar, it should not seem vain to you that He—as He is meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11)—might truthfully answer: “Nor would I now be such and so great, except because of you, except because of the sins of humankind.” And truly it is so; we ought to be as certain of it as if He were to give, or had given, such an answer in His own voice. For why was this man, or Son of Man, assumed into God? Why did He suffer or die? Was it not for the ungodly? Was it not for enemies? “But we see,” says the same Apostle, “the Lord Jesus,” Christ, “crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering” [Col. 1630C] (Heb. 2). Thus the ungodly and criminal were the cause of His being crowned and sitting at God’s right hand, crowned with the glory of kingship and the honour of priesthood.

Therefore He owes much to the ungodly who are converted to godliness through faith in Him; He owes much to enemies reconciled to God through Him. Hence we rightly have confidence, and our confidence pleases Him because it is just and reasonable. “Therefore,” he says, “let us approach with confidence.” Whither shall we approach? “To the throne of grace.” It is magnificently said and reverently to be heard. For what is the throne of grace? Surely the phrase “to the throne of grace” has a sweeter and more pleasing sound than if he had said, “to the throne of judgment” or “of justice.” Christ the Son of God’s throne is indeed a throne of judgment or justice; yet in this time it is more advantageous for us that it should first be a throne of grace. For whom, or what sort of people? Surely for sinners, of whom the same Apostle says, “I am the first” (1 Tim. 1), and “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

Finally, concerning the obtaining of which, after he had first said, as was just quoted, “Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with confidence,” he immediately added, “that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help”: he knew from his own great experience that, although he had been a sinner and a blasphemer, he had obtained from that throne of grace these two things, mercy and grace—mercy, namely, the remission of sins; and grace, moreover, the apostolic office. For the present, this is the work [Col. 1631A] or office not so much of a judge seated on the throne of judgment or justice as of the high priest seated on the throne of grace. But it will come to pass that a judge will sit on the throne of judgment, and a king upon the throne of justice, when these four living creatures return—or the four faces of the one living creature, of which we have spoken thus far.

For they will in one sense return, and in another they will not return. Both statements are written in the prophet: “They did not turn as they went, but each went straight forward” (Ezek. 1). And immediately afterward: “The living creatures went and returned like flashes of lightning” (ibid.). In what sense, then, will they not return? Surely in this sense: that Christ, who suffered once, will not suffer again. But in what sense will they return? [Col. 1631B] It must be carefully remembered that the four faces of the one living creature are the four mysteries of the one Christ which a Christian may not be ignorant of: the incarnation, the passion, the resurrection, and the ascension. They will return in this sense, certainly: that on the last day the Son of Man will sit upon the seat of his majesty, with the marks of his passion—that is, with the scars of the wounds which he received in his hands, feet, and side—and will show all that he rose in the truth of flesh. And with all his elect, who will be on the right, he will do what is said in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Like an eagle stirring her young to fly, and hovering over them, she spread her wings and took him up, and carried him upon her shoulders” (Deut. 32).

Of both matters—namely, [Col. 1631C] of not returning and of returning—the same Apostle says: “Nor yet that he should often offer himself, as the high priest enters into the holy places every year with the blood of another. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world. But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared to destroy sin through his sacrifice. And as it is appointed for human beings once to die, and after this judgment, so Christ also, having been offered once to take away the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, for salvation to those who await him” (Heb. 9).

When he says this, someone may reasonably ask: What has happened up to now, or is now happening, with all the saints who have awaited him since the beginning of the world, [Col. 1631D] if he is then to appear? For we say that he will appear of him whom we do not see. What, then, has happened to them? Do they not yet see the glory of the Lord—the glory and honor of this Son of Man seated at the right hand of God? Why, then, do they so earnestly desire to be away from the body (2 Cor. 5), unless that they may be present with God? Why do they desire to be dissolved, unless that they may be with Christ? (Phil. 1.) How, then, does he now say, “He will appear a second time for salvation to those who await him”?

Perhaps he says it on account of those who were then present in the body, in accordance with what he said to the Thessalonians: “Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). This is indeed rightly understood. Nevertheless, of all the saints who, absent from the body, are present with God, you may no less rightly say that they await him; rightly, I say, because they both see him and await him. For they do not yet see him wholly; they do not yet see God in their flesh. This is what they await: to see God in the flesh. “For I know,” says blessed Job, “that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior” (Job 19).

For such expectation, one rightly understands the saying, “He will appear a second time for salvation to those who await him.” And what, I ask, will his appearing then be like? With what a voice of the glory of the Lord, with what a great upheaval, [Col. 1632B] will he appear? “For,” says the same Apostle, “at a command, and at the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, he will descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (1 Thess. 4).

Great will be the roar of the lion holding and embracing his prey: namely, all the saints and elect set at the right hand, by whose whole multitude he has stripped the devil. He will roar over those at the left with such a roar as to say, “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” after he has said to those at the right, “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. 7 [probably 25]). Then, as was said to blessed Job (Job 40), before the eyes of all that Behemoth will be cast down—Behemoth meaning “beast,” namely the devil, a contrary lion, called a lion because of his ferocity. [Col. 1632C] But he who will roar over him and cast him down by his roar is called a lion because of his strength.

When this has happened, then at last every roar of this great lion will cease, since he will no longer have a reason to roar: all scandals having been taken away from his kingdom (Matt. 13). Then the eagle’s face will soar more loftily, while all its young fly together and follow wherever it goes—well-grown and well-proved, shown not to be degenerate, able and worthy with open eyes to behold the supreme brightness of the eternal Sun, to see face to face the glory of the supreme Godhead, the glory of the blessed Trinity, of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

What more can I say concerning this face, namely the eagle’s face? It rises too far above us for our sight to attain, as long as we travel in this mortal body. I wish to say only this: the vision of this face, the vision of the brightness of the Son of God, which those blessed ones will behold according to his own prayer—“Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am, that they may see my brightness which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17)—that vision, I say, will be fire to those who behold it; and not merely some ordinary fire, but even a furnace, according to Isaiah: “The Lord has said, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31).

Finally, in Zion—that is, in the present Church—the fire, however small it may be, is to know in part and to see through a mirror and in an enigma [Col. 1633A] (1 Cor. 13). But in that heavenly Jerusalem, to see face to face is a furnace: an inestimably great blaze of eternal love. These are the four incombustible fuel-supplies of the human being: “For whom are all things, and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, the author of their salvation was made perfect through suffering” (Heb. 2).

Does not the consideration, or frequent meditation, upon these things produce a certain fire of love in this Zion? First, concerning that which is first stated, “for whom are all things,” I ask: while you consider this, is not a bright flame of delightful love kindled in you from the underlying spark of faith? For what is this? The best Father, while he had his only Son in the secret place of his bosom, wished to store up for him treasures [Col. 1633B] of gold and silver, precious stones, and every good furnishing; to build a royal palace; and to provide all the appointments of a royal court: an abundant army, a numerous household, commanders, prefects, tribunes and centurions, male and female servants, retainers, and attendants, distinguished in beautiful variety, who might stand before him seated in their midst and serve him in their respective ranks.

For this reason he made all these things: heaven and earth—filling invisible heaven with the hosts of angels, and the earth with so many and such great generations of human creatures, among whom we too are found. Who would not answer to these things that even this cause alone demands great love and makes us debtors to him of great love and devotion? Add what is said secondly: “through whom [Col. 1633C] are all things.” For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). If all things indeed are through [Col. 1634A] him, then he is among all things. Add what is said thirdly: “who had brought many sons into glory.” For he alone was the one Son of God, but he did not wish to remain alone; rather, he wished to have many brothers, whom before all ages he had predestined to make conformed to himself—that is, to bring them into the glory of the sons of God (Rom. 8; Titus 1). Add that it was supremely fitting for him that, since so many sons of God, his brothers, had perished in Adam, he, the author of their salvation, should be made perfect through suffering.

How worthy of love are these things! Surely not to love him for these reasons is excessive ingratitude; it is utter wickedness. They are like logs laid, and ever to be laid, upon the altar to feed the fire of this holy affection, or righteous love, as it is written in the holy and mystical law: “The fire upon the altar shall always burn; the priest shall feed it, laying wood upon it every morning, day by day, and, having placed the holocaust upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings” (Lev. 6). This is the everlasting fire which will never fail on the altar.

And now indeed in Zion—that is, in the present Church—this affection or love is fire, as has already been said; but it is not yet so great that it can rightly be called a furnace. There it will be a furnace, where, because of the greatness of love and the torrent of delight of that blessed Jerusalem, [Col. 1634B] namely, of the entire assembly of all saints and elect, they will have leisure for nothing but thinking of God and looking upon him. The holocausts offered upon this fire and the fat of the peace offerings will be praises and thanksgivings, from which they will never be able to cease. For “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). Amen.

[Col. 1633]

## HYMN OR PRAYER OF RUPERT TO THE HOLY SPIRIT

Mentioned by him in the twelfth book; it may be sung, as may that hymn, “Come, Creator Spirit,” etc.

[Col. 1633D]

My God and my Lord,  
you are, O Holy Spirit,  
my weapons and my shield;  
come to my aid.

You are the Father’s gracious mercy,  
you are Christ’s true love.  
From you came the counsel  
for humankind’s salvation.

You drew God down from heaven  
into a woman’s womb.  
You are the love by which  
our flesh was joined to God.

You made the bodily dwelling  
in the Mother for the Son of God,  
raised upon seven columns  
through sevenfold grace.

The rod of Jesse brought forth a flower  
[Col. 1634D] upon whom you might rest.  
With your seven eyes  
the one stone appeared,

Fortifying the Lamb of God  
with so many horns, so many eyes.  
You set him in battle  
against bear, lion, and serpent.

And as he willed to die,  
so you teach us also to die with him,  
when you bury the living in water,  
O wondrous craftsman.

For the three days of burial  
there is a threefold immersion,  
that one is buried as dead  
and comes forth as risen.

O God, with our ears  
we have heard; our fathers  
[Col. 1635A] have declared to us  
the work that you performed.

When you proceeded in fiery  
tongues from God’s throne,  
that earth might become heaven  
and human beings might be gods,

The new heavens therefore thunder with miracles  
and rain down words.  
The earth, drinking the rain,  
conceived new grace;

From it, throughout the world, were born  
sons of adoption.  
In you, O Holy Spirit,  
we cry to God: “Abba, Father.”

Great, Lord, are these  
[Col. 1635B] your mercies,  
which restore my hope  
so that I may call upon your name.

O seal of faith,  
advocate of the faithful,  
light of fire and fount of light,  
hear the caller and come.

You see the force of my coldness;  
you know the ice of my heart.  
But breathe upon me, Paraclete:  
if you blow, waters will flow;

O finest honey, good wine,  
fill this lowly little vessel,  
[Col. 1636A] and it will become a vessel in glory,  
although it is an earthen jar.

The fire of God, by which the angel—  
who is both human being and God—  
standing beside the altar,  
filled the golden censer:

Purify my prayers;  
burn up my incense,  
that the smoking scent of spices  
may rise before God.

Give me eyes to see  
in Leviathan’s jaw  
the opening of God’s bracelet,  
Mary, through whom he came forth.

Good leader, grant strong  
[Col. 1636B] joy of compunction,  
by which the camps of penitents  
take the kingdom of God by force.

With you as guide, the face  
of the Father and the Son is to be seen;  
and you, flowing from them,  
are the fountain of life, the river of peace.

And now to you, gracious God,  
and to the gracious Lord be praise  
and thanksgiving,  
with the Father and the Son.

Amen.

[Col. 1635]

Even had Adam not sinned, the Son of God would have become human, 696. The Jews had the hardness of adamant, 334. A young girl denotes a soul which has not attained fear, 416, 376.
